## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library—complete, uniform, convenient, economical—of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, very carefully corrected by comparison with the most accurate editions and with certain manuscript codices; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions issued during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following either individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly set within the text itself, and also with titles at the upper margins of individual pages distinguishing and indicating their subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two comprehensive general indexes: one an index of subjects, through which, at a glance, may be seen whatever each of the Fathers has written on any theme; the other an index of Holy Scripture, through which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on each text of each book of Scripture, and in what places in their works. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of its correction, both the variety and the number of works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently uniform throughout the course of the whole work, the modest price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, now for the first time brought together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, containing the Latin Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.** Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the *Universal Clergy Library*, or Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been published in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin.—The two hundred and sixty volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,300 francs; the 1,300 volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for 1,800 francs.—The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are provided in it in Latin translation only.

# Life of Richard, Canon and Prior of Saint-Victor in Paris

[Col. IX]

From Book V, chapter 55, of the *Antiquities* of the same Church (edition of the works, Rouen, 1650, folio).

Richard, a Scot by nationality, canon of the Abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, was received by Gilduin, its first abbot, and made his profession under him. As a disciple of Master Hugh, called Hugh of Saint-Victor, he devoted himself to study under his teaching and made such progress that in time he became a man most thoroughly instructed in philosophical and theological learning.

When he had advanced in age and wisdom, he was called to the office of subprior about the year 1159. I find him subscribing in that rank, together with Abbot Achard and Prior Nanterus, to an agreement made between the canons of Saint-Victor and Frederick, lord of Palaiseau in the region of Paris, concerning tithes belonging to our church within that lordship. There are also extant manuscript letters addressed to him as subprior by a certain Lawrence, who had wholly entrusted himself to Richard’s direction. In them Lawrence asks our Richard, the subprior, to defend him from the quibbles of another religious, who was withdrawing from promises made to him in Richard’s presence.

In 1162, when Nanterus, a most holy man and prior, died on the day before the Ides of June [12 June], our Richard succeeded him—a man equal in virtues but surpassing him in learning. For almost eleven years he worthily discharged the office of prior amid the prosperous and difficult affairs of our church. They were prosperous, I say, when, in March and April 1164, he received Pope Alexander III, then residing in Paris, into our house and chapter with Abbot Ervisius and the entire community. On that occasion, he took pains to cause the pope himself to state orally what appeared desirable for the splendor of the Victorine house. This is shown by a manuscript letter later written by the same supreme pontiff to William, Archbishop of Sens:

> “Therefore,” says the supreme pontiff, “although we frequently admonished Abbot Ervisius both by letter and, when we were in Paris, orally—even in the chapter of the same house of Saint-Victor—to give attention to the observance of the rule, after we withdrew from those regions he not only failed to amend himself, but, like another Caesar, orders and disposes everything according to his own will, contrary to all the statutes of the order.”

These are among the many things said by the supreme pontiff. From them I infer Prior Richard’s tireless vigilance in fulfilling his office and preserving the discipline of the order against a wavering abbot. Yet he did not on that account relax anything of his studies or his constant writing. Since these things were known even among religious persons outside the house, some wrote to him, asking that he give them spiritual direction or provide copies of his treatises.

Two letters are read in the manuscripts of our library. The first is from William, prior of Ourscamp of the Cistercian order, to our Richard, in these words:

> To his beloved lord Richard, Prior of Saint-Victor, Brother William, called Prior of Ourscamp, greeting in the Lord.
>
> I myself brought back during Lent the little book of yours which you had instructed us to return to you. But because you were then not at Saint-Victor, I entrusted it to your hospitaller, Brother Hugh, telling him to return it to you as well. We ask, however, that you send us some little work of yours which we do not yet possess—namely, either that on Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, or *Make thy face to shine upon thy servant* [Psalm 31:16 / 30:17]. For we had begun to copy this also, but found it incomplete in your exemplar. Farewell.

The other is from John, subprior of Clairvaux, to our Richard, as follows:

> To his lord and father Richard, Prior of Saint-Victor, John, called Subprior of Clairvaux: the little that he is.
>
> I beg you, my lord, in the Holy Spirit, for the Holy Spirit, to write for me a devout prayer concerning the Holy Spirit. Write, my lord, according to the understanding and knowledge which the Holy Spirit has bestowed upon you. Write, my father, and send it to me; do not refuse me in this. Write, my lord, neither with excessive brevity nor excessive length, but so that I may be able to retain it by heart and offer it to the Holy Spirit at least once, whether by day or by night, dearest father, so that he may at least hear us. Farewell.

In 1170, in a charter of sale of woods and lands for the use of the Victorine Church at Bellum Robur, Beaurose, in Brige or Brie, under the seal of Maurice, Bishop of Paris, the following witnesses are recorded from among our brethren: Abbot Ervisius and Richard, Prior of Saint-Victor. I likewise read that they subscribed together in the same year to another charter of the same bishop concerning the sale of a tithe from Barra near Caprosia. In a third charter of that bishop, drawn up in the same year for the purchase of Alnetum near the meadow of Saint-Paul, an obedience of the house of Saint-Victor, Richard, Prior of Saint-Victor, is recorded as subscribing with Brothers Hugh of Sercelles, Robert, Prior of Saint-Paul, and Theobald of Taverny, canons of Saint-Victor.

In August 1171, when Saint Thomas, Archbishop of Canterbury, arrived at Paris in order to render thanks, as best he could, to Louis VII, king of the Franks, for the most humane hospitality shown him in the king’s territories, he came early in September to our house of Saint-Victor. There he was honorably and kindly received. On the octave of our holy Father Augustine—which that year fell on Friday, 4 September—he was admitted to our chapter and preached a sermon on the verse of Psalm LXXV, “In peace his place came to be.” This is recorded in a manuscript of our library. Yet would that the entire sermon had been copied, and that the holy conversations of so great a bishop with our Prior Richard had been committed to writing. From them we should learn many things necessary for inward and outward peace with God, with other people, and with ourselves; and thus we might be carried from the lesser Benjamin to the greater ecstasy of the mind, insofar as the remnants of our Richard’s *Benjamin Major* and *Benjamin Minor* are available to us.

It is now fitting to display his steadfast spirit amid adversity. Prior Richard did not live without distress of heart and deep sorrow of soul [Col. XI] while Ervisius, Abbot of Saint-Victor, governed all things according to his own will and relaxed the ancient discipline of regular observance, alleging either the disobedience of his subjects or the overly lax counsel of the senior brethren attending him. Accordingly, the supreme pontiff wrote an exhortatory letter to Prior Richard and the entire Victorine community, dated at Veroli, 13 May 1170. See it among the letters of Alexander III. [Note: [Col. XI] *Patrology*, vol. CC.]

Prior Richard did not cease to exhort and assist Ervisius in governing the Victorine household, in spiritual as well as temporal matters. But the abbot neglected to heed the counsels of so great a prior. Therefore, after two years, such a public outcry against him reached the supreme pontiff that he delegated as judges in the matter William, Archbishop of Sens, and Stephen of Bourges. When this came to the attention of Maurice, Bishop of Paris, he informed William, metropolitan of Sens, concerning the state of the Victorine house as follows:

> Your prudence knows more fully into what great and harmful confusion Brother Ervisius, Abbot of Saint-Victor, has led the Church and all the brethren, who are known to excel others both in religious life and learning, through his disorderly actions. Although he has attacked to the utmost of his strength the holy persons who were with him and persecuted holiness itself, yet, being unable to overthrow inward or outward discipline, he now seeks by diverse and countless kinds of external temptations to disturb their peace, etc.

He concluded by asking that he be removed from office by them.

When the aforesaid bishops, in accordance with the authority entrusted to them, visited the Victorine house, Abbot Ervisius voluntarily resigned his office before them about Easter 1172. In his place, chosen from among and by our brethren while Prior Richard presided, was appointed Guarinus, a man advanced in years and distinguished by gravity of character and learning. In the first year of his installation, namely 1172, the canons of Saint-Victor reached an agreement with the canons of Saint-Cosmas of Luzarches concerning the tithes of Laciacum-Plessiacum and Campiplatrosus. These were relinquished to the latter in return for four measures—two of wheat and two of oats—to be paid to us each year on the feast of Saint Remigius. The subscribers were Abbot Guarinus, Richard, Prior of Saint-Victor, Odo, former Abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, and Walter, Subprior of Saint-Victor.

Since I find that Walter was appointed to the office of prior after two years, I truly infer that our Richard died, according to the highest destiny, on the sixth day before the Ides of March [10 March] in the year of Christ 1173. On that day he is entered in our obituary register in these words:

> On the same day, the anniversary of Richard, prior of this Church, who by the example of his holy manner of life and by the elegance of his writings left us, in dying, a memory worthy of his name.

He was the fifth prior of our Victorine Church. Gilduin is named as its first prior in the bulls of Pope Paschal II in the year 1114, and afterwards its first abbot. The second was the venerable Thomas, slain for justice’s sake, 12 days before the Kalends of September [21 August] 1130. The third was the reverend Father Odo, appointed first abbot of Sainte-Geneviève in Paris on 24 August 1148. The fourth was the venerable Nanterus, taken from the living on the day before the Ides of June [12 June] 1162. The following couplet is read concerning him:

> Nanterus, prior, a man worthy to be glorified,  
> Deserved, as a virgin, to be raised from the cloister into heaven.

To him our Richard was given as fifth successor, until 10 March 1173. Therefore, whatever learned men may have written otherwise concerning the period of his life or government should be corrected according to our more exact and truthful observations.

His body was humbly buried in the cloister near the almonry door. But almost two centuries later, William of Saint-Land, doctor of theology and the twenty-second of our abbots, issued in 1348 the following verses in his praise, in a rather rough style:

> Rich in speech, the prior lies buried in this tomb;  
> Rebuking vices, the righteous man is joined to the righteous.  
> A canon of Saint-Victor, having conquered the devil,  
> He increased hope of pardon through theological teaching.  
> An imitator in religion of the heavenly King,  
> He flourished in learning, deeds, and understanding.  
> Following the Victor in the renowned gravity of his conduct,  
> He is secure among the host of the King, the Holy of Holies.  
> A Scot, devout, he lived through a great span of time,  
> A canon, a man friendly to religious life.  
> He was a teacher of sweet doctrine; and manifestly,  
> With you, Augustine, as witness in the dew-flowing Code of the triune Monad,  
> Conforming himself in doctrine and life,  
> He diligently cultivated in his heart the merits of your Victor.  
> Distinguished in title, learning, and character,  
> this man committed his body to this tomb, a priest devoted to you, Christ.

In 1531, when John Bordier, the thirty-fourth Victorine abbot, was renovating and raising the principal cloister of our house, the memory of our Richard was commended to posterity in the following poem engraved upon a bronze plate:

> Distinguished in character, talent, learning, and skill,  
> Learned Richard, you lie covered here in a dusty resting-place.  
> Scotland gave you birth in a happy delivery;  
> The French land cherishes you in its own bosom.  
> Cruel Fate did you no harm when, with harsh hand,  
> She broke the threads drawn out over too brief a time.  
> For numerous memorials of your labor survive,  
> Which will bring you everlasting glory.  
> As death approaches wicked houses more slowly with dragging step,  
> So it goes all too swiftly beneath the dwellings of the devout.

Richard of Saint-Victor is mentioned by Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel in the Appendix to Sigebert; Vincent of Beauvais, Book XXVIII of the *Historical Mirror*, chapter 58; Saint Antoninus, in volume III of the historical part, title 18, chapter 3; William of Saint-Land, our twenty-second abbot, in the *Eulogies of the Four Victorine Fathers* [Col. XIII]—namely Prior Thomas, Hugh, Adam, and our Richard; Benevenutus of Imola in the *Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World*, sixth age; Platina in the *Lives of the Popes*; Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; John Pits, an Englishman, in his book *On the Illustrious Writers of England*; Gilbert Genebrard and James Gualter of the Society of Jesus in their chronologies; and countless others throughout their writings. Nor should I omit the most eminent cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, Baronius in the *Annals* and Bellarmine in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

In that work Bellarmine calls into question whether the four books of *Excerpts* belong to our Richard, because in Book I, chapter 4, Richard writes among the inventors of theology John Scotus, who survived our Richard by more than a hundred years. But since Vincent of Beauvais, in the passage cited above, lists the books of *Excerpts* among the works of our Richard, and Vincent himself preceded John Scotus by approximately sixty years, I do not see how our Richard could include John Scotus among the inventors of theology in his own time—unless he is someone other than John Duns, the Franciscan, a Scot by nationality, renowned throughout the world, around the year 1308.

Therefore I am persuaded, not without evidence, that an error has slipped into chapter 4 of Book I of the *Excerpts*, whether through a copyist’s defect, a printer’s carelessness, or the substitution of one name for another—for example, Peter Lombard for John Scotus. Or perhaps it must be said that in Richard’s time there flourished in Scotland a certain John, extremely learned in theology, who taught theology there by some method, though his writings have not survived, and that his memory was thus lost under the name of the Franciscan John Duns. Otherwise I do not see how Vincent of Beauvais could have ascribed the books of *Excerpts* to our Richard, especially as they do not depart from Richard’s style.

Four manuscript books of *Excerpts* were formerly kept among the works of our Richard in our library; the grasping hand of a rogue stole them long ago. Therefore it has not been possible for us to determine whether John Scotus or someone else was named in chapter 4 of Book I, or whether, from the antiquity of the codex, he was a person other than John Duns Scotus of the Order of Saint Francis. For concerning John Eriugena, the opinion of the most eminent Cardinal Bellarmine prevails.

The complete works of Richard of Saint-Victor first appeared in print at Paris through the efforts of the canons of Saint-Victor in 1528; then at Lyons in 1534; and a third time in our own age, at Cologne in Germany in 1621. No one doubted that all were genuine works of Richard until the criticism of the most eminent Cardinal Bellarmine concerning the four books of *Excerpts*. That criticism may be moderated and refuted by our preceding observation, since those books, by Bellarmine’s own testimony, do not depart from the style of our Richard.

(These materials were drawn from archival documents and manuscript codices by Brother John of Toulouse, canon of Saint-Victor in Paris.)

[Col. XIII]

# Notice concerning Richard of Saint-Victor, by Abbé Hugonin

Licentiate in Letters of the Faculty of Paris; former pupil of the ecclesiastical school of the Carmelites.

[Col. XIIIa]

Richard was born in Scotland. His biographers do not say in what year, to what parents, or what his earliest education was. Like Hugh, his master, he left his homeland at an early age. He came to Paris, perhaps attracted by the reputation of the teachers who taught in that capital; perhaps led by the sole desire to consecrate himself to God in a community as renowned for learning and piety as that of the canons of Saint-Victor. In that house he took the habit of a canon and made his profession at Gilduin’s hands.

At that time it was not unusual to see young men from overseas seeking in France either learning in its public schools or a peaceful refuge in the many monasteries flourishing everywhere. [Col. XIIIb] At almost the same period we find Achard, a distinguished philosopher and profound theologian, who became Abbot of Saint-Victor and later Bishop of Avranches; Adam of the Petit-Pont, a disciple of Abelard, who himself taught grammar, rhetoric, and philosophy with distinction; John of Salisbury, Robert of Melun, and so many others that there is no need to mention them here.

[Col. XIVa]

We know few details of Richard’s life at Saint-Victor. The annals of that abbey, written by Simon Gourdan, praise his piety and zeal for maintaining discipline. He was first subprior; in that capacity, in 1157, he subscribed an agreement between the Abbey of Saint-Victor and Frederick, lord of Palaiseau. He subsequently became prior, and conducted himself with unusual prudence in the most delicate circumstances.

Abbot Ervisius, English by birth, was neither an edifying monk nor a capable administrator. The community of Saint-Victor had flourished before his time under the wise direction of Gilduin, Achard, and Walter. Ervisius squandered its property and almost ruined its discipline. Alexander III witnessed his disorders and sharply rebuked him during his visit to Paris. Ervisius paid little heed to these warnings and continued his scandals. We learn this from a letter of the same pope, in which he calls the Abbot of Saint-Victor another Caesar, disposing of everything according to his whims, despising the statutes of his order, and, far from profiting from the pontifical remonstrances caused by his negligence, showing himself ever more incorrigible.

[Col. XV]

Matters reached such a point that the supreme pontiff, moved by the wretched condition of this house that had formerly flourished so greatly, appointed three commissioners: William, Archbishop of Sens; Stephen, Bishop of Meaux; and Nicholas, Abbot of Val-Secret. They were to visit and reform the Abbey of Saint-Victor, with authority to depose the abbot if necessary and exile corrupt canons. The pope nevertheless wished the commissioners to act in agreement with the Bishop of Paris, the immediate superior of that house.

At the same time he wrote to King Louis VII, exhorting him to contribute his authority to the restoration of good order in the monastery. These two letters are included under the year 1169 in the manuscript annals of Saint-Victor. We do not know by what devices the abbot escaped, on this occasion, the punishment that he deserved; but it is certain that he did not profit from the indulgence shown him. Thus Alexander III was compelled, some time later, to write again to the king and the Archbishop of Sens, urging them no longer to defer the reform entrusted to them.

[Col. XVb]

He also notified the abbot and regular canons of that abbey by letter that the Archbishop of Sens, the Bishop of Meaux, and the Abbot of Val-Secret were to visit their monastery; and he commanded them to receive the visitors honorably and submit to their ordinances. The three commissioners went to Saint-Victor and recognized the evil reported to them. They resolved upon the abbot’s dismissal. But before carrying out that decision, they communicated it to Cardinals Theodinus and Albert—whom others call Alexis—legates of the Holy See, who were then at Paris.

About the Easter festivities of 1172, according to the author of the annals of Saint-Victor, Ervisius was induced to make an abdication described as voluntary. The resigning abbot withdrew to the priory of Saint-Paul des Aulnois, dependent on Saint-Victor and situated near Chevreuse. There he continued to live in dissipation and good cheer, and from there more than once disturbed again the peaceful retreat of the canons of Saint-Victor.

[Col. XVc]

It is not rash to believe that Richard was not a stranger to this reform, and that more than anyone else he suffered from his abbot’s whims and outbursts. But God provided him some consolations amid the pains and persecutions brought upon him by his zeal. During these trials he received at Saint-Victor, together with Ervisius, Alexander III, a pontiff so attentive to rewarding merit and so zealous for the maintenance of discipline.

Soon afterwards, a guest as renowned for apostolic steadfastness as for his sufferings must have gladdened his heart and strengthened his courage: Thomas of Canterbury. This bishop visited the canons of Saint-Victor, where several Englishmen had come to seek refuge. He was introduced into the chapter, where he delivered a discourse upon the words of Psalm LXXV, *in pace factus est locus ejus*—“in peace his place came to be”—of which a fragment was long preserved in the monastery.

[Col. XVIa]

Why should we not believe, with Baronius, Manrique, and the editor of Richard’s works, that the prior had dealings with Saint Bernard which were not without use to him in the delicate circumstances in which he stood? We know the interest which the Abbot of Clairvaux took in the canons of Saint-Victor and the veneration which the canons had for him. They honored as a precious relic a cup which the holy abbot had left at Saint-Victor during a visit he paid them. They owed certain temporal advantages to his protection; and it was at his request that they affectionately received Peter Lombard and supplied the assistance he needed. Finally, we have seen that the holy Abbot of Clairvaux had particular relations with Hugh of Saint-Victor.

[Col. XVIb]

Calm succeeded the storm in the Abbey of Saint-Victor, and Richard was able to spend the last years of his life in peace. Guarinus, or Guaerinus, Ervisius’s successor, was a pious and learned man. Alexander III, who knew his worth, wrote to the canons to congratulate them on so good a choice. The beginning of his administration was not without bitterness: Ervisius’s stay at Saint-Victor had necessarily left its marks. Nevertheless, the good governance of the new abbot and the support he found in the prior restored order and returned the abbey to its original splendor.

Richard could therefore continue peacefully to edify his brethren by his piety and enlighten them by his teaching and writings. His reputation was so great that foreign religious eagerly requested copies of his works. William, Prior of Ourscamp, of the Cistercian order, wrote to tell him that he was returning some works and to request another, namely the work treating Nebuchadnezzar’s dream. Garin, Prior of Saint-Alban, wished to have a complete list of Richard’s works. John, Subprior of Clairvaux, begged him to compose a prayer to the Holy Spirit.

[Col. XVIc]

“Write it,” he said to him, “according to the knowledge and discernment with which the Holy Spirit has endowed you. Let it be neither too short nor too long, so that I may learn it by heart and address it to the Holy Spirit at least once by night or by day.”

Several other letters addressed to Richard have been published in this edition. Though very brief and of little importance in themselves, they help show that Richard enjoyed the esteem of his contemporaries.

In 1172 an agreement was made between the canons of Saint-Cosmas of Luzarches and those of Saint-Victor, and Prior Richard signed it. Richard was therefore still alive in that year. But in the first month of 1174, Walter was performing the functions of prior at Saint-Victor. It may be concluded that Richard died in 1173, doubtless on 10 March, the day on which his anniversary is entered in the abbey’s necrology.

[Col. XVIIa]

This necrology praises Richard as a worthy prior who, by his good examples, the holiness of his character, and the beauty of his writings, left the most honorable memories. He was buried in the cloister beside the Door of the Almonry. [Note: [Col. XVIId] See *Histoire littéraire de France*, vol. XIII, pp. 472–488; *Vita Richardi*, at the head of the edition of 1650; Pagi, under the years 1134, no. 41, and 1140, no. 8; Henry of Ghent, *Description of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 26; Pits, p. 311; Alberic, *Chronicle*, under the year 1156; *Centuries of Magdeburg*, XII, ch. 10; Du Boulay, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. II, pp. 160, 260, and passim; Duchesne, *Writers of French Affairs*, vol. IV, pp. 757, 747, 745, and passim; Dubois, *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, Book III; Corrozet, *Antiquities of Paris*, Book IX, fol. 57.]

# Works of Richard of Saint-Victor

[Col. XVII]

## Different Editions of Richard’s Works

[Col. XVIIa]

Seven editions of the collected works of Richard are known.

The first was published at Venice in 1506, octavo. It is very incomplete. The second, folio, appeared at Paris in 1518; the third, folio, at Lyons in 1534; the fourth, folio, at Paris in 1550; the fifth, folio, at Venice in 1592; the sixth, quarto, at Cologne in 1621.

The last appeared at Rouen, published by Jean Berthelin, in 1650, folio. Until now it has been almost the only edition in use, although it is inaccurate and lacks every kind of elucidation. Yet the earlier editions, [Col. XVIIb] though no richer in such aids, are more faulty. The edition of 1650 presents itself as revised and corrected by the regular canons of Saint-Victor in Paris. It is in fact due only to the efforts of one of those religious, John of Toulouse, who placed at the beginning of the first volume a life of the author drawn, he says, from the manuscripts and charters of the abbey.

The edition published by Abbé Migne is more accurate and more complete. It contains letters absent from the preceding editions. Above all, Richard’s writings will be arranged in a more regular order.

They have been divided into three classes: exegetical writings, in which Richard explains certain passages of Holy Scripture; theological works; and Miscellanies, which include letters and several detached writings. This is, with little variation, the order indicated by the Benedictines in the *Literary History of France*.

We shall briefly give an account of these works in order to facilitate their reading.

I.

The first part comprises fourteen treatises. The first, entitled *Benjamin Minor*, is a treatise on mystical morality occasioned by the words of Psalm LXVII: *Benjamin in mentis excessu*—“Benjamin in the ecstasy of the mind.” Benjamin is the last and dearest of Rachel’s children; he is the work of contemplation. Rachel and Leah represent, the former reason, the latter love; the one truth possessed, the other virtue attained; from the one arise good intentions, from the other good desires. Just as Jacob must receive Leah before Rachel, so good actions lead to true knowledge; so reason is united to imagination, and sensibility to love.

What follows is only a development of these ideas. The children of Leah and Rachel are the faculties relating respectively to intellect or to love. Richard studies them psychologically; he teaches how to regulate them and lead them together to the same end, namely contemplation, or the soul’s repose in the possession and love of truth. It is not difficult to recognize Hugh’s doctrines concerning the profound distinction between sensibility and the knowledge of the physical world and of the spiritual world, and concerning the relations of the one to the other. Yet in this work these principles are indicated rather than clearly expressed.

In one passage Richard inveighs against the writers of his own time. He reproaches them for being excessively scrupulous in avoiding solecisms and negligences. “They are,” he says, “far more ashamed of a barbarism that escapes them than of a lie which they have contrived, and they fear offending the rules of Priscian far more than those of the Gospel.” He considers the highest glory to which a mortal can aspire to be that of converting others and transforming them from children of the devil into children of God. Such a ministry appears to him the most sublime gift; he prefers it to the power of working miracles and raising the dead.

The *Benjamin Minor* is the first of Richard’s works to have been printed. A separate edition appeared at Paris in 1489, quarto; it was reprinted separately in the same city in 1521, duodecimo. The same work has since been repeatedly published under the title *On the Twelve Patriarchs*.

The *Benjamin Major* differs little in method from the preceding treatise. The ark is called by the Psalmist the ark of sanctification: *Surge, Domine, in requiem tuam, tu et arca sanctificationis tuae* (Ps. CXXXI)—“Arise, O Lord, into thy rest, thou and the ark of thy sanctification.” Now wisdom conquers evil and brings about sanctification; and the perfection of wisdom is contemplation. This is the point to which Richard always returns. He first studies contemplation in itself and distinguishes six degrees of it. The first consists in considering and admiring bodily objects which strike our senses; the second is still merely the study of the productions of nature and art; the third raises us to the moral order, to meditation upon divine and human laws; the fourth, to knowledge of incorporeal and invisible substances—that is, our souls and angelic spirits; at the fifth degree reason rises above itself, and at the sixth it attains ecstasy. This treatise is almost wholly devoted to examining these different degrees that lead to contemplation. Richard seeks their figures in the various parts of the ark. He indicates the means that should raise the soul from one degree to another: grace, the cooperation of our own activity, and external teaching.

It must be admitted that his applications are sometimes forced and his reasonings somewhat subtle. He confesses that he had much leisure to compose this book and that much leisure is needed to read it. It has as an appendix a kind of recapitulation entitled “Allegory of the Tabernacle of the Covenant.” We shall quote a few passages which convey an idea of this kind of composition, difficult to submit to analysis.

“By the tabernacle of the covenant understand the state of perfection. Where the soul’s perfection is, there is God’s dwelling. The nearer one approaches perfection, the more closely one is united with God. But the tabernacle must have the court surrounding it. By the court understand the discipline of the body, and by the tabernacle the discipline of the soul. Where outward discipline is absent, inward discipline cannot be maintained. But the discipline of the body is useless without the discipline of the soul. The court is uncovered and in the open air: the discipline of the body is visible to all. The things which were in the tabernacle did not appear outside. Likewise, no one knows what belongs to the inner part of a person except the human spirit which is within that person. Reason is figured by the outer tabernacle, and understanding by the inner tabernacle. We call rational sense that by which we discern what belongs to ourselves, and intellectual sense that by which we rise to contemplation of divine things. By works, a person goes out from the tabernacle into the court. A person enters the first tabernacle when he recollects himself within himself; he enters the second when he rises above himself. In rising above himself, he certainly rises to God.”

A separate edition of this treatise appeared in 1494, quarto; and another, octavo, without date or place of publication, but before the end of the fifteenth century.

The opusculum entitled *On the End of the World*, or *On Meditating upon the Plagues Which Shall Occur near the End of the World*, is a sermon whose text is these words of Ecclesiastes: *Memento Creatoris tui in diebus juventutis tuae, antequam veniat tempus afflictionis, et appropinquent anni de quibus dicas: Non mihi placent* (ch. XII)—“Remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth, before the time of affliction comes and the years draw near of which thou shalt say: They do not please me.” The style of this discourse is natural, even elegant; moreover, it contains nothing requiring special explanation.

Richard composed his treatise *On the Tabernacle* at the request of his friends, as he himself tells us in the prologue. This work is divided into three parts. In the first he treats of the construction of the tabernacle, describes all its parts, and derives from it a tropological meaning. This composition is in the manner of the first two works which we have examined.

The second part is a straightforward literal explanation, or commentary, upon the description of Solomon’s Temple found in the Book of Kings. “The description of Solomon’s Temple,” he says at the outset, “is generally fairly clear. Several passages, however, are obscure and confused. Some persons, whom I willingly serve, press me to state my opinion on the passages requiring explanation.” The third part deals with the chronology of the kings of Judah and Israel. This last book is addressed, if not by the author, at least by the editor, to Saint Bernard. In it Richard reconciles, with scrupulous care and not without some acuteness, dates which appear contradictory. He shows that these difficulties arise sometimes from the negligence of copyists, sometimes from counting one and the same year both as the last of one reign and the first of the reign following; sometimes also from the coronation of certain kings before their fathers’ deaths, and consequently from the coexistence of two monarchs upon the same throne for several years. The author appended to this treatise two chronological tables, one in four columns and the other in five.

This work was printed at Paris in 1511 and 1540, and at Venice in 1590.

The *Mystical Annotations on the Psalms* are more extensive than those attributed to Hugh. They are a devout commentary upon certain passages of these divine songs. Psalm 28 alone is explained in its entirety. The Benedictines seem to us to exaggerate when they say that these remarks are purely mystical. Richard’s developments of the sacred text resemble those which a preacher might give; they form little sermons or homilies.

The explanation of the *Song of Songs* comprises forty-two chapters or sermons, inferior without doubt to those of Saint Bernard, yet not without merit. Here Richard is more sparing than elsewhere in allegorical interpretations, and gives his hearers useful moral instruction, often borrowed from Saint Gregory the Great.

The opusculum entitled *How Christ Is Set as a Sign of the Peoples* is an explanation of Isaiah’s words: *Radix Jesse stat in signum populorum*—“The root of Jesse stands as a sign of the peoples.” Richard explains that the prophet announces Jesus Christ raised upon the cross, calling and gathering together the two peoples—that is, the Jews and the Gentiles. This short treatise resembles sermons of that period both in form and in the instruction it contains.

The treatise on Ezekiel is a literal explanation of the living creatures, wheels, and buildings described in the prophet’s vision. Here Richard makes little use of his talent for allegory. He adheres to the letter and the immediate sense, which he says is the necessary foundation of every mystical interpretation. This book presupposes some knowledge of geometry and architecture. The author even appended plans that make his explanation clearer.

Richard himself tells us, in a short prologue, on what occasion he composed the work entitled *On Emmanuel*, and the aim he set before himself. “I came upon,” he says, “a treatise written and published by Master Andrew, and found in it several passages that were imprudent and insufficiently Catholic. In several places, indeed, he presents the opinions of the Jews concerning Holy Scripture less as Jewish opinions than as the true interpretation. Thus, concerning Isaiah’s passage, ‘Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son,’ he puts forward the Jews’ objections and explanations, and does not refute them, so that he seems to yield them the victory by neglecting to resolve their difficulties.” This imprudent doctor had made disciples, so that several understood the text not of Mary but of a prophetess. To remove this scandal Richard undertook the work. He first reports the Jews’ objections as they appeared in Doctor Andrew’s treatise; he then resolves them according to Saint Jerome’s interpretation, further supporting it with arguments of his own.

*Explanation of Certain Passages of the Apostle Saint Paul.* We would not wish to assert that Richard always clarifies the difficulties presented by the texts he interprets. But his theology is sound, and that is a merit not easily preserved when treating such matters.

There are two separate editions of this work: one at Venice in 1592 and the other at Rouen in 1606, both folio.

The commentary on the Apocalypse is addressed to a religious whose name Richard does not give. It is divided into seven books, each explaining a vision. We shall not attempt an analysis of this mystical paraphrase of the most impenetrable of our sacred books. One will find in it nourishment for piety, useful moral instruction, and, more than once, fine interpretations of the inspired text.

II. Theological Works.

[Col. XXIIA]

Richard of Saint-Victor’s principal dogmatic work is his treatise *On the Trinity*, which comprises six books. Following the example of the Fathers and of all ancient orthodox writers, he sets faith down as the starting point and necessary foundation of all theological knowledge; he repeats and comments, in the sense given by the ancients, on the prophet Isaiah’s celebrated text: *Nisi credideritis non intelligetis*—“Unless you believe, you shall not understand.” Faith is the entrance-gate of the sanctuary; through it alone does one enter. But once the gate is open, one must not remain on the threshold of this temple so rich in wonders of every kind; one must continually advance, striving to understand ever more fully the truths received by faith. “If,” says the illustrious Victorine again, “the beginning of every good resides in faith, its completion and perfection are found in knowledge. Let us therefore labor to attain that perfection; let everything serve us as a step by which to go from faith to knowledge; let us employ all our efforts to understand what we believe. . . . It is little for us to have sound and true sentiments concerning God; as I have just told you, we must strive to understand what we believe. We must labor without ceasing, so far as it is permitted and possible, to grasp by reason what we hold by faith. But what wonder if our soul is troubled and darkened in the presence of the mysteries of the Godhead, when it is defiled almost every moment by the dust of earthly thoughts? ‘Come forth from the dust, O virgin daughter of Zion!’ If we are true sons of Zion, let us raise this sublime ladder of contemplation; and, taking flight like eagles, let us escape the earth in order to soar in the heights of heaven.”

These words, seemingly dictated by the ardor of the purest enthusiasm, sufficiently show the importance Richard attached to theological speculation. Accordingly, he is not content to lay down principles concerning theology’s office, or to invite Christian scholars to a deeper study of revealed mysteries; he himself wishes to lead by example, by attempting to explain through reason the august mystery of the Holy Trinity. In this treatise the illustrious Victorine proposes to illuminate and confirm by reason the otherwise innumerable teachings of faith. He begins with a profound thought deserving the attention of Christian theologians and philosophers; it seems to us singularly fruitful in important applications. “Our purpose in this work,” he says, “is to bring forward in support of our faith arguments not only probable but necessary. For we are fully persuaded that, for all necessary things, there are arguments not merely probable but necessary, although it happens that our mind does not always perceive them. . . . Indeed, it is altogether impossible that what is necessary should not be, and should not have a necessary reason for being; but it is not granted to everyone to draw these reasons from the mysterious depths of nature and then place them within the reach of ordinary minds.”

Richard’s thought seems to us rigorously exact. Everything that is has a reason for being, either in itself or in another; what exists necessarily, what cannot fail to be, has a necessary reason for being: nothing is more certain. Our intellect may fail to see or distinguish this reason, but it must exist; its reality cannot be the object of serious doubt. Now the Trinity of persons in the unity of the divine nature is a truth necessary in itself, and faith teaches us that God subsists in three distinct persons. But if the Trinity is necessary, it must also have a necessary reason for being—a reason it bears within itself, in its own ground, in its own nature, and which is not distinct from itself. There is in God a reason for existing as three in persons; and when the thick veil which, in this world of sense, hides from us the sight of the divine essence is torn away, we shall see clearly that the Trinity of persons cannot fail to exist in the unity of that ineffable essence. There can therefore be no doubt that arguments whose logic is absolutely necessary exist in favor of the dogma of the Trinity. Although during the course of this life, half dark and half enlightened, our eye cannot penetrate to the ultimate root of these arguments, does it follow that, aided by the light of Christian revelation, it is incapable of apprehending them in their derivation and in that kind of luminous projection which the divine nature continually sends us? Richard does not believe so; far from admitting such incapacity, he is instead profoundly convinced that a Christian intellect can find in support of this august mystery arguments of unanswerable rigor.

Full of confidence in the truth of this principle, the illustrious theologian, after discussing in the first two books everything relating to the unity of the divine nature, resolutely enters upon speculations concerning the Trinity of persons. God’s absolute goodness and the supreme happiness he enjoys are the two general sources from which the author derives nearly all his arguments. Since God is the fullness of goodness, he must be the seat of perfect love; now love cannot exist without a plurality of persons. The name of love cannot be given to the affection by which a person loves himself; pure and true love necessarily requires several persons. Therefore in God, who is the type and law of perfect love, there must be more than one person.

Richard sets out at length the properties of love and carefully identifies the character proper to love as it must be in God. With equal attention he defines the essential elements of the supreme happiness which God necessarily enjoys, and endeavors to prove that this happiness cannot be conceived unless one admits three persons really distinct from one another in the divine nature. We shall not follow the author through his speculations; we confine ourselves to indicating their source and general tendency.

After establishing the Trinity of divine persons, our Victorine seeks to show how plurality of persons is reconciled with unity of nature; finally, in the last two books he examines and discusses the respective properties of each person.

We shall say with M. Laforêt, from whom we have borrowed this analysis and this very judicious and profound assessment of the treatise [Note: [Col. XXIIID] *A Survey of the History of Dogmatic Theology*, by M. Laforêt, Doctor of Theology, Professor in the Faculty of Philosophy and Letters, and President of the Pope’s College at the Catholic University of Louvain. Louvain, 1851.], that, taken as a whole, it is a work of great merit; perhaps, indeed, from the standpoint of theological speculation, it should be regarded as the most important work bequeathed to us by the Middle Ages. Yet we acknowledge with the same writer that the work has weak parts; that certain deductions to which the author appears to attach the greatest importance are far from rigorous; that some arguments do not prove their conclusion; that one sometimes encounters ideas that are not exact. But most of his speculations are very sound and even very profound. It is a treatise containing treasures of infinite value, unfortunately too little known by many theologians otherwise worthy of esteem.

The six books *On the Trinity* have as an appendix an opusculum treating of the attributes of each person and addressed to a certain Bernard, who had consulted Richard on these matters. Was this Bernard the famous abbot of Clairvaux? Baronius, Manrique, Dupin, and Thoulouse think so; the Benedictines doubt it, because they find in the works of the abbot of Clairvaux no trace of his relations with the prior of Saint-Victor. But we have seen in Richard’s notice that it was not only improbable, but almost impossible, that Saint Bernard—who knew the community of Saint-Victor, visited it, rendered it and requested from it services, and treated Hugh as his friend—should have had no relations with Richard, whose reputation was so great.

It was doubtless by counting the opusculum just mentioned that Vincent of Beauvais [Note: [Col. XXVD] *Speculum Historiale*, bk. XXVIII, ch. 58.] says that Richard composed a treatise on the Trinity in seven books. He adds that this is our Victorine’s principal work.

Henri Estienne issued a separate quarto edition in 1510; another exists from Nuremberg, 1518, octavo.

The book *On the Incarnate Word* is likewise dedicated to Bernard and answers a fresh inquiry addressed to the author by the same person. “You are not ashamed,” Richard says to him, “to weary my incapacity.”

This treatise on the Incarnation of the Word is at the same time an explanation of verses 11 and 12 of Isaiah chapter XXI: “One cries to me from Zion: Watchman, what have you seen this night?” “It is a very short book,” says M. Laforêt (p. 66), “but substantial, full of ingenious and often profound ideas concerning the necessity of the Incarnation.” This is the book’s principal subject.

We shall not dwell upon the small treatise entitled *How the Holy Spirit Is the Love of the Father and the Son*, nor upon that entitled *On the Most Excellent Baptism of Jesus Christ*. The latter was written at the request of one of Richard’s relatives. It is a work of piety rather than a theological treatise.

It will likewise suffice to mention a sermon on the mission of the Holy Spirit and a small opusculum in which he compares Jesus Christ to a flower and Mary to a stem.

There follows another sermon in which Richard explains to the religious of Saint-Victor how David’s sacrifice differs from Abraham’s. This sacrifice of Abraham, of which our Victorine speaks, is not that in which Isaac was to be the victim, but that which God prescribes to the father of believers in Genesis chapter XV in these terms: “Take a three-year-old heifer, a she-goat and a ram of the same age, a turtledove and a dove.” It is a kind of moral and allegorical commentary upon verse 14 of Psalm 65: *Holocausta medullata offeram tibi cum incenso arietum*—“I shall offer you fat burnt offerings, with incense of rams.”

In a discourse of the same kind, he explains the differences between Abraham’s sacrifice and that of Mary when she offered two turtledoves and two newly hatched doves.

Under the common title *On the Twofold Passover*, two further sermons have been placed: one for Palm Sunday, in which he speaks of the Passover of flowers and the Passover of fruits; the other for Easter Day, a paraphrase of Saint Paul’s words: *Pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus* (I Cor. VII)—“Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed.”

The three treatises *On the Destruction of Evil and the Advancement of Good* are, like several we have surveyed thus far, treatises of mystical morality in which Richard shows that, in order to acquire and preserve virtue, one must conquer oneself and submit to suffering.

Richard also wrote the treatise *On the State of the Interior Man* at a friend’s request. In the prologue he indicates that he composed it at several intervals and amid many obstacles, which might lead one to think this was during Ervisius’s final years. Perhaps this accounts for the many digressions scattered throughout the book, which he himself does not disavow. “He has done,” he says, “like a traveler who deliberately lengthens his route in order to visit and admire pleasant surrounding places.” The subject of this work is an explanation of Isaiah’s words: *A planta pedum usque ad verticem non est in eo sanitas*—“From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him.” Impotence, ignorance, and concupiscence: these are the three wounds of humankind, its threefold vice. From them result three kinds of sin: weaknesses, errors, and wickednesses. Three kinds of remedies must be set against them: God’s commandments, his promises, and his threats. Such is the substance of the work, which is divided into three parts. In the first he treats of the threefold vice; in the second, of the threefold sin; and in the third, of the threefold remedy. At almost every step the author compares the evils of the body with those of the soul, as well as the means of curing each. Here and there one might gather some information concerning twelfth-century medicine. We see, for example, that physicians distinguished three spirits in the human body: the animal spirit, which they placed in the head; the natural spirit, in the liver; and the vital spirit, in the heart. Yet beyond doubt the three parts of this treatise are more edifying than instructive, and one cannot too much admire the prodigious number of devout or mystical thoughts suggested to Richard by every word, and almost every syllable, of verses 5 and 6 of Isaiah chapter I.

Difficulties had been raised concerning the sense of these words of our Lord: *Quodcunque ligaveris super terram erit ligatum et in coelis; et quodcunque solveris super terram erit solutum et in coelis* (Matt. XVI)—“Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven”; and concerning these others: *Quorum remiseritis peccata remittuntur eis; et quorum retinueritis retenta sunt* (ibid.)—“Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain are retained.” Did the apostles and their successors really receive by these words the power to forgive sins? Two sinners come to a priest: one is hardened and thereby bound; the other is truly righteous and thereby loosed. Can the priest loose the one who is bound and bind the one who is loosed? Likewise, two criminals come to a priest: one penitent, the other impenitent. Can the priest forgive the sins of the impenitent one and retain those of the penitent one? Such were the questions discussed by certain theologians, and on which Richard’s opinion was sought. It was in answer to these inquiries that he wrote his treatise *On the Power of Binding and Loosing*. Yet this work is more moral than dogmatic. In it one finds edifying instruction rather than exact, clear, and precise solutions to the difficulties proposed.

The opusculum *On the Final and General Judgment* aims to show how, on the last day, the apostles will judge all people in an instant and with the greatest ease; how they will discover the secrets of every conscience; and how they will determine the precise measure of reward or punishment deserved by each person. This is again a kind of sermon, whose text is our Lord’s words: *In regeneratione, cum sederit Filius hominis in sede majestatis suae, sedebitis et vos super sedes duodecim, judicantes duodecim tribus Israel* (Matt. XIX)—“In the renewal, when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.”

“Is the spirit of blasphemy anything other than blasphemy against the Holy Spirit?” Such was the question proposed to the prior of Saint-Victor and examined by him in a short treatise. He does not resolve it, but inclines to believe with Hugh, his master, and Saint Augustine that, since God’s mercy is infinite, no sin is irremediable.

There follow two passages concerning the difference between mortal and venial sin. A person dies guilty of two sins, one mortal and the other venial. It is agreed that he will be eternally damned for the first. But the question is whether he will suffer, for the other, some additional punishment. Instead of expressing a definite opinion on this matter, Richard comments upon these words of Ecclesiasticus (ch. III): *Eleemosyna patris non erit in oblivionem, et pro peccato matris restituetur*—“The father’s almsgiving shall not be forgotten, and it shall be repaid for the mother’s sin.”

Separate editions of this treatise and of that entitled *On the Power of Binding and Loosing* were published at Paris in 1526, duodecimo; 1528, octavo; 1534, duodecimo; and 1543, sextodecimo.

Of the two treatises *On the Degrees of Charity*, the first, consisting of only four chapters, is addressed to a religious named Severinus, Richard’s friend, who had requested it. The author explains, after Saint Paul, the characteristics of charity.

In the second, he sets charity beside cupidity. Like profane love, charity has four degrees: it wounds, binds, makes one languish, and consumes. These two books are among those drawn upon by a compiler of the thirteenth or fourteenth century in composing a treatise on charity attributed to Saint Bernard.

III. Miscellanies.

At the beginning of the third part of Richard of Saint-Victor’s works, several letters have been placed which are not found in previous editions.

The first is addressed by Abbot Ervisius and his prior Richard to Robert, bishop of Hereford in England. This Robert is none other than the famous Robert of Melun, author of perhaps the first theological summa ever published. He was English by birth. He first taught at Paris, then at Melun, from which place he acquired his surname. John of Salisbury and Thomas Becket were among his pupils. The latter, in order to show gratitude to his former master, helped secure his elevation to the episcopal see of Hereford; as primate, he even consecrated him bishop. But Robert proved little worthy of such an exalted rank; he even joined those courtly prelates who took the king’s side against the holy archbishop of Canterbury. Ervisius and Richard write to reproach him for his conduct and to inform him that it was universally condemned by the scholars who had formerly applauded his successes.

The second letter, only indicated here, is addressed to Pope Alexander III. The prior of Saint-Victor strongly commends to him the cause of Thomas of Canterbury. It is signed by Richard and a former abbot of Saint-Augustine.

The third is that of William of Canterbury, whose name is indicated only by the initial N, prior of Ourscamp, mentioned in Richard’s notice.

The two following letters are anonymous and unimportant.

The others are letters addressed by the prior of Saint-Alban, or by his brother, to the prior of Saint-Victor. They offer several interesting particulars regarding the relations between these two abbeys.

The treatise *On the Education of the Interior Man*, which comes next, is divided into three sections, in which the author successively explains chapters 2, 4, and 7 of the prophet Daniel. It is a series of tropological interpretations of Nebuchadnezzar’s dream and history. The author concerns himself little with the literal sense, which is generally known. According to him, the author’s chief purpose is to show how good people gradually abandon virtue, how they depart from the perfection of the contemplative or active life, by what degree they fall into the abyss, and by what efficacious helps divine grace raises them again. Allusions and applications abound in this long treatise. Richard observes, for example, that as soon as scholars obtain a considerable office and attain some eminent dignity, they abandon study and often lose forever their taste for solitary labors.

For extracts, we refer to what we have said concerning it in the critique of the Works of Hugh of Saint-Victor.

IV. Manuscript Works.

[Col. XXIXA]

Trithemius [Note: [Col. XXIXD] *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, ch. 375.], in a long list of Richard’s writings, cites several which are not found, at least under the same titles, in the edition of 1650 or in the preceding editions.

*On the Study of Wisdom*; *On the Progress of Monks*; *On Mental Prayer*; *On the Offices of the Church*; *On the Four Winds*; *On the Acts of the Apostles*; *On Newness of Life*; *An Epitome of the Whole Bible*.

One observes that most of these titles would be [Col. XXIXB] applicable to certain pieces or fragments of Richard’s printed works. It is highly probable that Trithemius supplied these indications from manuscripts containing only simple extracts from the treatises of the prior of Saint-Victor; and this conjecture may be extended to other manuscripts, whether in the Ambrosian Library or in Belgium, listed by Montfaucon and Sanderus. Montfaucon [Note: [Col. XXIXD] *Bibl. Bibl.*, vol. I, p. 523.] finds in the Ambrosian Library two treatises by Richard of Saint-Victor, entitled:

*On the Praises of the Blessed Mary*; *The Fire of Divine Love*.

Perhaps this latter item is merely Saint Bonaventure’s *Stimulus divini amoris* (*Spur of Divine Love*). It might [Col. XXIXC] also not be distinct from the little work *On the Two Degrees of Charity*. See above. Montfaucon further finds among the manuscripts of Queen Christina:

*The Penitential Book of Richard the Second, canon of Saint-Victor*—a work which should be compared with the little works *On the Power of Loosing . . .* and *On the Difference between Mortal and Venial Sin*. But the word *second* gives occasion to observe that two Richards of Saint-Victor have sometimes been distinguished: namely, the one discussed here, and another who lived about the year 1242, whom Possevino [Note: [Col. XXIXD] *Appar. S.*, vol. II, pp. 322, 327.] identifies as the author of several writings otherwise attributed to the former by Possevino himself. This distinction [Col. XXIXD] between two Richards is in all likelihood an error occasioned by Henry of Ghent [Note: [Col. XXIXD] *De script. eccl.*, c. 26.] and Sixtus of Siena [Note: [Col. XXIXD] *Bibl. S.*, I, p. 275.], who omitted, in their article on Richard of Saint-Victor, his designation as a Scotsman.

Sanderus [Note: [Col. XXXD] *Bibl. mss. Belg.*, part I, pp. 32, 67, 112, 117, 223, 245, 254, 325.] cites the following manuscripts as so many works by Richard of Saint-Victor:

*On the Canon*; *Summa on the Virtues*; *On the Study of Wisdom*; *On the Seven Kinds of Temptation*; [Col. XXXA] *Treatise for Novices*; *Treatise on the Spiritual House of Our Body*; *Eighteen Sermons on Certain Sayings of Sacred Scripture*; *Six Sermons or Treatises on Psalms and Other Places in Scripture*; *Sermons on the Gospels*; *Two Sermons on the Words of Matthew: “Take the Child and His Mother”*; *Sunday Sermons*; *Sunday Sermons for the Whole Year*; *Several Sermons*; *On the Passion of the Lord*.

Finally, in the catalogue of English manuscripts [Note: [Col. XXXD] *Cat. mss. Angl.*, part III, nos. 727, 4077, 6160.] there are three items bearing the name of Richard of Saint-Victor:

[Col. XXXB] *Sermons*; *Treatise on Faith*; *Interlinear Gloss on Matthew and Mark*.

We have no means of verifying the authenticity of these works.

“Richard is very subtle,” says Dupin [Note: [Col. XXXD] Twelfth Century, p. 727.]. “He reasons correctly and methodically, like a good dialectician. His critical treatises are sufficiently accurate for his age. He is not very elevated in his expressions; and this is why his books of spirituality, although full of good sentiments, lack all the grandeur and force that might be desired.” The Benedictines find in Richard’s works neither so much dialectic [Col. XXXC] nor so little elevation. “His thoughts,” they say, “more ingenious than sound, his allegories more spiritual than rational, almost always communicate their own character to his style. Richard lacks neither ideas nor imagination nor even sensibility; and if his works are in fact no longer read, it is because they are written without method, criticism, logic, or taste. Moreover, his diction is far from being as familiar as Dupin supposes. One might rather say that it is not familiar enough. Often metaphorical, more often antithetical, it presupposes and displays much labour. The assonances with which it abounds are by no means [Col. XXXD] negligences, but supposed ornaments which required continual care and even effort; for the author seems to have set himself the constant rule of dividing almost all his sentences into two kinds of rhymed hemistichs. This may be recognized in the following lines, found at the opening of volume [I], pp. 274–275, with which we shall conclude this article:

> “When something is rashly undertaken against the divine command, a legal action of the contumacious is brought against majesty.
>
> [Col. XXXIA] But when we wish to appease injured majesty, we have recourse to its mercy.
>
> We have recourse to its goodness—indeed, also to its truth.
>
> For pardon has been promised to penitents by him who cannot lie at all.
>
> So night will pass only to return again; so day will return only to depart again.
>
> Morning, lest those who labour should fail; night, lest the unwary should become so.
>
> The one everywhere for healing; the other, on the contrary, for caution.”

This last observation is too general. If in some passages we find the fault pointed out by the Benedictines, it seems exaggerated [Col. XXXIB] to say that it is our Victorine’s habitual manner of writing. His style is often simple, clear, and precise, without affectation or elaboration, especially in his more serious works. We shall simply admit that, in the critique which the learned Benedictines made of Richard’s works in the thirteenth volume of the *Literary History of France*, we believe we have noticed a little ill [Col. XXXIIA] humour. They were put off by the tropological interpretations that occur there so often. It is well known that these were little appreciated in the seventeenth century. This critique is far inferior to that of the writings of Hugh of Saint-Victor. It is difficult to believe that both were made by the same hand.

We shall conclude by saying that, if Richard is Hugh’s disciple and continuator, if the doctrine of these two Victorines is the same, and if their method resembles one another, Richard seems to have been endowed with a less capacious mind and to have possessed learning less extensive and less varied. Even more than Hugh, he is above all a mystical and contemplative theologian; all his works disclose this tendency, and the greater part are devoted exclusively [Col. XXXIIB] to mystical theology. Yet it must be carefully noted that Richard’s mysticism, no more than that of his illustrious master, excludes either philosophy or speculation. It is a speculative mysticism, often abounding in profound thoughts; but knowledge always appears in it as secondary, and the mind passes through it only in order to attain love, which is the full life of the soul.

# THE FIRST, EXEGETICAL PART OF THE WORKS OF RICHARD OF SAINT-VICTOR

[Col. 0001]

# THE BOOK ON THE PREPARATION OF THE SOUL FOR CONTEMPLATION, CALLED *BENJAMIN MINOR*

## CHAPTER I. On the study of wisdom and its commendation. “Benjamin, a youth, in an ecstasy of mind” (Psalm LXVII).

[Col. 0001A]

Let young people hear a discourse about the youth; let them awaken at the Prophet’s voice: “Benjamin, a youth, in an ecstasy of mind.” Who this Benjamin is, many know: some by knowledge, others by experience. Let those who know by instruction listen patiently; let those who have learned by experience listen gladly. For whoever has once been able to know him through the teaching of experience—I speak confidently—no discourse about him, however lengthy, can satisfy that person. But who can suffice to speak worthily of him? For he is fairer in form than all the sons of Jacob, such as Rachel ought to have borne. Leah indeed, although [Col. 0001B] she bore more children, could not have more beautiful ones. For, as you read, Jacob is known to have had two wives. One was called Leah, the other Rachel: Leah the more fruitful, Rachel the more beautiful. Leah fruitful but bleary-eyed; Rachel almost barren, but of singular beauty.

But now let us see who these two wives of Jacob are, so that we may understand more easily who their children are. Rachel is the teaching of truth; Leah, the discipline of virtue. Rachel is the pursuit of wisdom; Leah, the desire for righteousness. Yet we know that Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and that these nevertheless seemed to him but a few days because of the greatness of his love. Why are you surprised? The greatness of his affection corresponded to the greatness of her beauty. Certainly, if I should attempt to say anything in praise of wisdom, whatever I said [Col. 0001C] would be too little. For what is loved more ardently than wisdom, or possessed more sweetly? Her beauty surpasses every beauty; her sweetness exceeds every delight. For she is, as someone says, “more beautiful than the sun, and above every ordering of the stars; compared with light, she is found before it” (Wisdom VII). For night succeeds light, but [Col. 0002A] wickedness does not overcome wisdom: “She reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things sweetly.” “I loved her,” he says, “and sought her from my youth; I desired to take her as my bride, and became a lover of her beauty” (Wisdom VIII). What wonder, then, if Jacob burned with love for such a bride, if he could not moderate such a fire, such flames of affection? Oh, how deeply he loved; oh, how he burned in her love, who said: “I loved wisdom above health and every beauty!” (Wisdom VII). For, as we have said, nothing is loved more ardently than this wisdom, nothing possessed more sweetly. Hence all wish to be wise, though very few can in fact be wise.

## CHAPTER II. On the desire for righteousness and its character.

[Col. 0002B]

Do we say the same of righteousness? Do we all equally wish to be righteous, though perhaps we cannot be righteous? Indeed, all could certainly have been righteous if they had perfectly wished to be righteous. For to love righteousness perfectly is already to be righteous. You may love wisdom greatly and yet lack it. Without qualification and without doubt, the more you love righteousness, the more righteous you will be.

But let us now see what the precepts of true righteousness are, and we shall discover why people so greatly detest Leah’s marriage. For we must ask why almost everyone so vehemently shrinks from Leah’s union while longing so intensely for Rachel’s embraces. Perfect righteousness commands us to love enemies [Col. 0002C], to leave parents, to leave behind everything that is one’s own, to bear patiently the evils inflicted upon us, and everywhere to decline glory when it is offered. But what is judged more foolish or more laborious by lovers of this world? Hence Leah is thought by them to be bleary-eyed and is called laborious. For Leah is interpreted “laborious.” To them it seems a great labour—and no smaller error—[Col. 0003A] to rejoice in tribulation and to flee the world’s prosperity as though from a plague. But because she does not reject the world’s abundance for necessity, yet does not admit it for pleasure, they call Leah bleary-eyed, not blind: they think she errs in her judgment of things. Therefore, if Leah signifies the desire for righteousness and Rachel the pursuit of wisdom, the reason is plain why Leah is almost universally despised, while Rachel alone is so greatly loved.

## CHAPTER III. On the twofold source of all good: reason and affection.

Yet I would gladly inquire more carefully into these two wives of Jacob and explain more fully whatever the mind suggests concerning them. To every rational spirit [Col. 0003B] there has been given a certain twofold power by that Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect present. One is reason, the other affection: reason, by which we discern; affection, by which we love; reason tending to truth, affection to virtue. These are the two sisters betrothed by the Lord: Oholah and Oholibah, Jerusalem and Samaria. These are the two wives of the rational spirit, from whom springs a noble offspring, heirs of the heavenly kingdom. From reason arise right counsels; from affection, holy desires. From the former arise spiritual perceptions; from the latter, ordered affections. From the latter, finally, comes every virtue; from the former, all truth.

It must therefore be understood that affection truly begins to be Leah when it strives to conform itself to the rule of righteousness. Reason is unquestionably affirmed to be Rachel [Col. 0003C] when it is enlightened by the light of that supreme and true wisdom. But who does not know how laborious the former is, and how pleasant the latter? Not without great labour is the soul’s affection restrained from unlawful things and directed to lawful ones; and rightly such a wife is called Leah—that is, “laborious.” But what can be sweeter or more delightful than to raise the eye of the mind to contemplate supreme wisdom? Therefore, when reason is enlarged to contemplate this, it is deservedly honoured with Rachel’s name. Rachel is interpreted “seeing the beginning” or “a sheep.” Therefore, that she may be worthy of such a name, let her fulfil what she finds written: “Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wisdom I). Certainly, whoever thinks of the Lord [Col. 0003D] in goodness already sees him, who is the beginning of all things, with the eye of faith. And she truly is a sheep if she seeks in simplicity. Do you see how it is not just any wisdom, but supreme wisdom sought in simplicity, that makes one Rachel? By now, I think, you do not wonder that Rachel is so greatly loved, when even her handmaid—I mean worldly wisdom, which in comparison with her mistress is reckoned folly—is sought with such love, as we see, by the philosophers of the world.

## CHAPTER IV. How, through the pursuit of wisdom, the soul is often secretly led into the exercises of righteousness.

[Col. 0004A]

How Leah is substituted while Rachel is hoped for is readily recognized by those who have learned how often this happens, not so much by hearing as by experience. It often happens that a soul insufficiently cleansed of the filth of its former way of life, and not yet fit for contemplating heavenly things, while placing itself in Rachel’s chamber, while making itself wholly ready for her embraces, while thinking that it already possesses her, suddenly and unexpectedly discovers itself in Leah’s embraces. For what do we call Sacred Scripture but Rachel’s chamber, in which we do not doubt that divine wisdom lies hidden beneath the fitting veil of allegories? Rachel is sought in such a chamber whenever spiritual understanding is investigated in sacred reading. But as long as we are still altogether unable to penetrate sublime things, we do not yet find Rachel, long desired and carefully sought. We begin, then, to groan and sigh, not merely to lament our blindness [Col. 0004B] but also to blush for it.

Thus, while we grieve and inquire how we have deserved this blindness, the evils which we have done confront us. Indeed, divine reading itself, when we are unwilling and are attempting something else in it, frequently impresses our foulness upon us and pierces our hearts in the consideration of it. Whenever, therefore, in divine reading we find compunction in place of contemplation, let us not doubt that in Rachel’s chamber we have found not Rachel herself but Leah. For as it belongs to Rachel to meditate, contemplate, discern, and understand, so it surely belongs to Leah to weep, groan, grieve, and sigh. Leah, as has been said, is affection inflamed by divine inspiration; Rachel is reason enlightened by divine revelation. Leah is affection conforming itself to the rule of righteousness; [Col. 0004C] Rachel is reason lifting itself to contemplate heavenly wisdom. But enough of these; now let us consider their handmaids.

## CHAPTER V. How imagination serves reason and sensuality serves affection.

Each of them, then, received her handmaid: affection, sensuality; reason, imagination. Sensuality obeys affection; imagination serves reason. Each handmaid is known to be so necessary to her mistress that, without them, the whole world would seem able to contribute nothing to them. For without imagination reason would know nothing; without sensuality affection would taste nothing.

For why is Leah so vehemently affected by love of passing [Col. 0004D] things, unless she takes multifarious delight in them through the service of her handmaid—that is, sensuality? Likewise, since it is written, “The invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made, from the creation of the world” (Romans I), it is plainly inferred that reason would never rise to the knowledge of invisible things unless her handmaid, imagination, presented to her the forms of visible things. For through the appearance of visible things, reason rises to knowledge of invisible things whenever it draws from the former a certain likeness to the latter. But it is clear that without imagination it would know no bodily things, and without knowledge of these it would not ascend to the contemplation of heavenly things.

The bodily sense alone beholds visible things, but the eye [Col. 0005A] of the heart alone sees invisible things. Thus the bodily sense is wholly outward, while the sense of the heart is wholly inward. Reason cannot go out, and bodily sense cannot enter into it. For it was not fitting that the delicate, tender, and singularly beautiful daughter should run about outside through the streets; nor was it proper for a servant irreverently to burst into his mistress’s secret inner chambers. Imagination, then, as a handmaid, runs between mistress and servant, between reason and sense; and whatever it receives outside through bodily sense, it represents within for the service of reason.

Thus imagination always attends reason and does not withdraw itself from its service even for a moment. For even when sense fails, it does not cease to minister. Placed in darkness, I see nothing, but I can imagine whatever I wish there. [Col. 0005B] Thus imagination is always and everywhere at hand, and reason can use its service everywhere. Sensuality likewise busies itself and is solicitous about frequent service, itself indeed always and everywhere ready to obey its mistress Leah. It is this that commonly seasons and sets before her the foods of carnal delight, inviting her to enjoy them before the time and urging her beyond measure. For what else is sensuality but that which inflames the soul’s affection with desire for carnal pleasures and intoxicates it with their delight? This is what goes before that laborious mistress as she goes out and leads her about here and there. For because Leah is bleary-eyed and sees little, she is not ashamed to follow its guidance. Hence Leah [Col. 0005C]—that is, the soul’s affection—now loves what should be despised, now despises what should be loved, because, while her eye is clouded in judging things, she is not ashamed to follow the appetite of the flesh. These are the two handmaids of Jacob’s two wives, whom Scripture names Zilpah and Bilhah: Bilhah belongs to Rachel and Zilpah to Leah.

## CHAPTER VI. On the fault of imagination and sensuality.

We have seen their service; but I think we should not be silent about their fault. Bilhah is talkative; Zilpah is turbulent. For not even her mistress Rachel can check Bilhah’s loquacity; nor can any abundance whatever entirely quench Zilpah’s thirst in her mistress. The wine for which Zilpah [Col. 0005D] thirsts is the joy of pleasure. The more she drinks of it, the more she thirsts; for the whole world does not suffice to satisfy sensual appetite.
