Therefore, since however much she drinks she always gapes for more drink, she is rightly called Zilpah, that is, “gaping mouth,” whose thirst is never quenched.

Imagination, moreover, clamours with such importunity in the ears of the heart that Rachel herself, as we have said, can scarcely—or not at all—restrain its outcry. Hence it often happens that, while we chant psalms or pray, we wish to remove from the eye of the heart the phantasms of thoughts or any images of things, yet cannot do so. Since, therefore, we daily endure against our will such clamouring thoughts, daily experience teaches us what Bilhah’s loquacity is and how great it is. [Col. 0006A] Whatever things have been seen or heard, or sometimes whatever we ourselves have done or said, it recalls to memory; and what it has once unfolded by narrating, it does not cease to repeat again and again. Often, even though no intention of the heart gives it assent as listener, it nevertheless unfolds its story, as though no one were listening. Thus decrepit old men or aged old women are accustomed to recount anything at all without any hearer and, as if some persons were present, to converse with them. Hence Bilhah, that is, “aged,” is not improperly so called, because she imitates the manner of the aged. But who does not know Bilhah’s chattering and Zilpah’s drunkenness, unless perhaps one does not know oneself?

## CHAPTER VII. What the principal affections are, and in what order or manner they are made into virtues.

[Col. 0006B]

We must now speak of their children, and first of Leah’s sons, since she too is read to have given birth first. Jacob’s sons by Leah, as we have said, are nothing other than ordered affections. If they are disordered, they cannot be called her sons. Leah’s sevenfold offspring, therefore, are the seven virtues. For virtue is nothing other than an affection of the soul that is ordered and moderated: ordered, indeed, when it concerns what it ought to concern; moderated when it is as great as it ought to be.

There are, then, seven principal affections which arise in turn from the one affection of the soul: namely hope and fear, joy and sorrow, hatred, love, and shame. All these may be ordered [Col. 0006C] or disordered; but when they have been ordered, only then are they to be reckoned among Jacob’s sons. If fear were not disordered, the divine word would never have said: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Psalm XIII). Likewise, if fear were not ordered, it would not be written: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Psalm XVIII). Likewise, if love were not sometimes ordered and sometimes disordered, Sacred Scripture would neither command the one nor forbid the other: “You shall love,” it says, “your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your strength, and your neighbour as yourself” (Deuteronomy VI). And elsewhere: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John II).

We must understand the other affections in the same way: sometimes [Col. 0006D] ordered and therefore good, sometimes disordered and therefore evil. But let us now see in what order the good ones, which we have also called Jacob’s sons, are begotten.

## CHAPTER VIII. How, or from what, ordered fear arises.

It is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm CX). This, then, is the first offspring of the virtues, without which you cannot possess the rest. Whoever desires to have such a son should attend not merely often, but carefully, to the evils he has committed: from these, to the greatness of his crime; from that, to the power of the Judge. From such consideration fear is born: that son rightly called Reuben, that is, “son of vision.” For in a certain way one is blind and does not see [Col. 0007A] if one does not fear to sin, does not foresee future evils, does not blush for one’s depravity, does not dread divine power. But if one begins to see these things, one likewise begins to fear; and the more perfectly one knows them, the more vehemently one fears.

You see, I think, how justly he is called Reuben, who is begotten from such vision. Rightly, when he is born, his mother cries out: “God has seen my humiliation” (Genesis XXIX), because then one truly begins to see and to be seen: to know God and to be known by God; to see God by the gaze of fear, and to be seen by God through the regard of compassion.

## CHAPTER IX. How sorrow arises or is ordered.

[Col. 0007B]

When the first son has been born and gradually grows, the second is born; for great fear must necessarily be followed by sorrow. The more vehemently anyone fears the punishment he has deserved, the more bitterly he laments the fault he has committed. But it must be known that, at whatever hour the sinner is converted and groans, he will be saved, according to the saying: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm L). What do you think? Is not such a son rightly called Simeon, that is, “being heard”?  Whoever truly repents and genuinely grieves will undoubtedly and without delay receive forgiveness. Prayer uttered from a contrite and humbled heart is heard more swiftly: humbled by fear, contrite by sorrow. Through Reuben it is humbled; through Simeon it is crushed and pierced in weeping: [Col. 0007C] “But blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew V).

## CHAPTER X. How hope arises or is ordered.

But what consolation, I ask, can there be for those truly penitent and bitterly mourning except the one hope of pardon? This is the third of Jacob’s sons, who is accordingly called Levi, that is, “added” or “addition,” because, after the former two have first been given, he is added to them. The divine word calls this son not “given” but “added,” lest anyone presume upon hope of pardon before fear and sorrow worthy of repentance. For one who, after committing crimes, flatters oneself with impunity without satisfaction is not so much raised by hope [Col. 0007D] as crushed by presumption.

By this name, therefore, divine Scripture intended to make us certain that we can neither have this son before the two former ones nor lack this third after the preceding ones. For truly and without doubt, the more frequently and vehemently a person is inwardly afflicted with sorrow over guilt, the more certain and secure he becomes through the pardon of forgiveness: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Psalm XCIII). Hence the Holy Spirit is called Paraclete—that is, Comforter—because he consoles, as often as gladly, the soul afflicted by tears of repentance. He visits it often, strengthens it gladly, and wholly restores it [Col. 0008A] to confidence in pardon when he sees it condemn its crimes by weeping and weep over them by condemning them.

## CHAPTER XI. When love arises or is ordered.

From that point, a certain familiarity begins to arise between God and the soul, and a friendship to be formed, because the soul perceives itself to be visited by him often and, at his coming, now not merely comforted but sometimes filled with an ineffable joy. Leah, unless I am mistaken, had a presentiment of this forming of friendship when, after Levi’s birth, she cried out with great exultation: “Now my husband will be joined to me” (Genesis XXIX).

God is the true bridegroom of the soul; we are truly joined to him when we cling to him through true love. Indeed, he then binds us to himself [Col. 0008B] when, through certain inward exchanges, he kindles us toward his love and binds us more closely. What heart is so hard and iron-like that divine compassion does not soften it by its presence and draw it by its sweetness? Thus it comes about that the one whom the soul formerly used greatly to fear, it begins afterwards ardently to love.

You now see, I think, that just as sorrow necessarily arose after fear daily increased, so love arises after hope has been born and advances through daily growth. This is the son of Jacob who is born fourth, and is called Judah in Scripture—that is, “confessing.” If we seek the reason for this name, we shall find it readily. For we know that everyone loves what one approves, and the more one [Col. 0008C] loves it, the more one approves it. And what is approving but praising? That, indeed, is true praise; that is pure confession: what rises from chaste love and proceeds from admiration of praise. Do you wish to know more clearly what is the voice of exultation and confession which Judah alone knows, or knows more excellently than all the rest?

## CHAPTER XII. What is proper to love.

Consider now a soul loving exceedingly and glowing with excessive love. Consider what it feels and what it says to itself concerning the one it loves greatly and admires deeply. What, then, does it say? What does it silently say to itself? “Oh,” it says, “how good, how [Col. 0008D] kind; oh, how pleasant, how sweet; oh, how lovable, how worthy to be embraced; how wholly admirable, how wholly desirable! Blessed is the one whom he loves! Happy is the one whom he judges worthy of his love! Happy am I if I may enjoy him; blessed am I if I am granted to possess him!” This, unless I am mistaken, is that voice of exultation and confession which always resounds from Judah’s mouth in the ears of divine compassion.

What do you say, Leah? What do you proclaim for Judah? What do you render to the Lord? What do you give in return for such a child? “Now,” she says, “I will confess to the Lord: I will confess exceedingly to the Lord with my mouth” (Psalm CVIII). Truly, certainly, and without doubt, you confess to the Lord not only often but without ceasing, if you love perfectly: “I will bless the Lord,” he says, “at all [Col. 0009A] times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm XXXIII). You always praise if you always love and always desire. For you would not love unless you approved. And what, as has been said, is approving but praising? This very praise is confession.

Do not think that it is enough for Judah to confess only with the heart, unless he also confesses with the mouth. For Judah desires both to commend to others and to kindle them in the love of him whom he judges worthy of everyone’s love and desires to be loved by all.

All this has been said concerning the confession of praise. But what shall we say of confession of sin? Does Judah perhaps not know this, although he knows the former so excellently? I do not think so, because I know that both kinds contribute greatly to God’s honour. And I know that whoever truly loves [Col. 0009B] gladly does whatever he recognizes to serve God’s honour. God’s goodness is greatly commended not only by his own generosity but also by our iniquity. For if it is great to bestow many things freely on those who deserve nothing, what and how great will it be to grant good things to those who deserve evil? Oh, what compassion, which none of our impiety can surpass! Some things he mercifully forgives; other things he abundantly bestows. He forgives our evils; he grants his own goods. Always ready to forgive, always prepared to give generously. Compassionate here, generous there; kind in both respects, good everywhere.

Let us therefore confess our evils to him; let us confess our goods to him. Let us confess that our evils are from ourselves, that he may mercifully forgive; let us confess that our goods are from him, that he may preserve [Col. 0009C] and increase them. Judah does this without ceasing, lest he appear ungrateful either for pardon granted or grace bestowed. Rightly, then, I think, this son is called Judah, that is, “confessing,” because true love always confesses.

Finally, since it is written, “God is truth” (1 John V), whoever blushes to confess the truth is proved not to love God: “The righteous,” Scripture says, “is the first accuser of himself” (Proverbs XVIII). Thus one who believes, or desires, oneself to be a lover of God has something to do—unless one thinks loving God to be something other than loving the righteousness of God. We now have the four sons of Leah: the first is fear of punishment; the second, sorrow of repentance; the third, hope of pardon; the fourth, love of righteousness. After this she ceases bearing children, for she considers herself able to be content [Col. 0009D] when she sees herself truly loving true goods.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, through love of invisible things, the mind is stirred to investigate invisible things.

But what do you think is happening in Rachel’s heart? By what fires of desire do you think she is driven when she sees her sister Leah rejoicing as the mother of children while she herself remains barren? Let us hear what she says and understand what she suffers. What, then, does she say to Jacob her husband? “Give me children,” she says, “or else I shall die” (Genesis XXIX). Without doubt, if the pursuit of wisdom does not advance, it soon declines.

But let us carefully inquire what it can be that makes Rachel, after Judah is born, burn more than usual with desire for offspring. We said [Col. 0010A] above that just as it belongs to Leah—that is, the soul’s affection—to love, so it belongs to Rachel—that is, reason—to know. From the former arises every ordered affection; from the latter, pure perception or understanding. But what else do we understand by Judah except ordered love: love of heavenly things, love of God, love of the highest good? Therefore, when Judah is born—that is, when desire for invisible goods arises and burns—Rachel begins to glow with desire for offspring because she begins to wish to know. Where love is, there is the eye. We gladly look upon the one whom we love greatly. No one doubts that one who has been able to love invisible things will immediately wish to know them and see them through understanding; and the more Judah—that is, the affection of loving—grows, the more intensely there burns in Rachel the desire [Col. 0010B] to bear children, that is, the pursuit of knowing.

## CHAPTER XIV. What is the first path for everyone entering upon the contemplation of invisible things: namely, through imagination.

But who does not know how difficult—indeed, how nearly impossible—it is for a carnal mind, still untrained in spiritual studies, to rise to an understanding of invisible things and to fix upon them the eye of contemplation? For it knows nothing yet except bodily things; nothing else presents itself to its thought except the visible things it is accustomed to think of. It seeks to see invisible things, and nothing occurs to it except forms of visible objects; it desires to behold incorporeal things, and dreams of nothing except images of bodily things. What, then, is it to do? [Col. 0010C] How is it to act? Is it not better to think of those things in whatever way it can than to consign them to forgetfulness or negligence? Indeed, if the mind loves well, it does not easily forget them; yet it is raised with much greater difficulty to their contemplation. Nevertheless, it does what it can and beholds them as it can. It thinks by imagination, because it is not yet able to see by the purity of understanding. This, I think, is why Rachel first has children by her handmaid before she bears from herself: because it is pleasant to her, at least by imagining, to retain the memory of those things whose understanding she cannot yet grasp by reasoning. For as Rachel signifies reason, so by her handmaid we understand imagination. Reason therefore advises that it is more advantageous to think of true goods in whatever fashion one can, and at least by a certain imaginary [Col. 0010D] beauty to kindle the mind toward desiring them, than to fix one’s thought upon false and deceptive goods. This is why Rachel wished to give her handmaid to her husband. No one is ignorant that this is the first path for everyone entering upon the contemplation of invisible things—unless perhaps one whom experience has not yet instructed in this knowledge.

## CHAPTER XV. How the divine Scriptures accommodate themselves to the contemplation of the weak

Nor should we pass over how the divine Scriptures accommodate themselves to this contemplation and condescend to human weakness. They describe invisible things through forms of visible things, and impress their memory upon our minds through the beauty of certain desirable [Col. 0011A] appearances. Hence at one time they promise a land flowing with milk and honey; at another they name flowers, at another fragrances; now through human songs, now through the harmonies of birds, they indicate the harmony of heavenly joys. Read the Apocalypse of John, and you will find the adornment of the heavenly Jerusalem described in many ways through gold and silver, pearls, and every kind of precious stone. Yet we know that none of these things is there, where nevertheless nothing whatever can be lacking. For none of such things is there in its literal appearance, where nevertheless all is there by likeness. In all these matters Bilhah has the means to serve her mistress usefully, since she presents their memory to her, wherever and whenever she wishes, according to her desire. [Col. 0011B] For we can imagine these things as soon as we wish. Imagination can never be more useful to reason than when it serves it in such a ministry.

## CHAPTER XVI. That one imagination is bestial, another rational

But, to continue what must be said concerning Bilhah’s sons, one must know that imagination is of one kind bestial, of another rational. The bestial kind should not be numbered among Jacob’s sons; nor will Rachel ever wish to make it her adopted son. Bestial imagination, then, is when, through things which we have just seen or done, we run to and fro with a wandering mind, without any usefulness and without all deliberation. [Col. 0011C] This is certainly bestial, for even a beast can do this. Rational imagination, however, is when from things that we know through bodily sense we imaginatively construct something. For example: we have seen gold; we have seen a house; but we have never seen a golden house. Yet we can imagine a golden house if we wish. A beast certainly cannot do this; it is possible only to a rational creature.

We often use imagination of this kind when we investigate more carefully what may be the goods or evils of the future life. Here there are nowhere only goods, nowhere only evils; rather, both goods and evils are mingled together. And although there are many in each class, they are never found alone. There, goods may be found without any admixture of evils, and evils likewise without any admixture of goods. [Col. 0011D] Again, just as here we find neither unmixed things, so neither do we find supreme things. There, we do not doubt that there are both supreme and unmixed goods, and evils likewise. Therefore, whenever from the many goods or evils that bodily sense experiences in this life one infers what sort of thing, or how great a thing, that supreme good or evil of the future life may be, and from imagining these things a certain image of future things is fashioned, such imagination is readily shown to be rational and seems to belong both to Bilhah and to Rachel. It belongs to Bilhah insofar as it is imagination; but to Rachel insofar as it is rational. Such offspring, then, belongs to imagination by birth and to reason by adoption. One bears such offspring, but the other rears it. It is born from Bilhah, but governed by Rachel.

## CHAPTER XVII. That when we speak of imagination, reason, and will, we take these terms in different senses

[Col. 0012A]

Let no one be troubled because I call both mother and offspring “imagination.” But I mean the relation between mother and son to be that between instrument and act; or the relation between mother and her offspring to be that between genus and species. For a genus, when a difference is added to it, produces from itself a species, just as union with a man makes a woman fruitful for offspring. We often call an instrument and its action by one name: for what we see, and that by which we see, we call “sight.” Thus, when reason, will, or understanding is named, sometimes the instrument, sometimes its action, is meant. And we know [Col. 0012B] that the instrument is always prior to its action and can exist without it. Action therefore has its being from the instrument, not the instrument from the action. Hence it is not unfitting to understand the mother through the instrument, and her son through the action.

Imagination, then, when it signifies an instrument, is that power of the soul by which it is able, whenever it wishes, to imagine anything whatever. When the mind uses this instrument to imagine something, there is undoubtedly produced a certain action, likewise called imagination. I wished briefly to mention this; but there is no need to linger over it longer. Let us now return to the order of our exposition.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the twofold contemplation that arises from imagination

[Col. 0012C]

We have said that rational imagination alone seems to belong to Rachel, and that what is not rational is judged altogether unworthy of her adoption. But rational imagination is of one kind ordered through reason, and of another mingled with understanding. We use the former when, following the known appearance of visible things, we arrange in the mind some other visible object, yet do not think from it of anything invisible. We use the latter when we strive to rise through the appearance of visible things to knowledge of invisible things. In the former there is imagination not without reason; in the latter, understanding not without imagination. These are Bilhah’s two sons: the firstborn is called Dan, and the younger is named Naphtali.

To Dan especially belongs the consideration [Col. 0012D] of future evils; to Naphtali, the contemplation of future goods. Dan knows nothing except bodily things, yet investigates things far removed from bodily sense. We do not doubt that the torments of hell are far removed from bodily sense, since we cannot see where or what they are; yet whenever we wish, through Dan’s ministry we hold them before the eyes of the heart. No believer, when reading in the holy Scriptures of hell, the fire of Gehenna, and outer darkness, believes that these are said figuratively; rather, he does not doubt that they truly and bodily exist somewhere. It follows, therefore, that although someone sets these things before the eyes of the heart through imagination, he does not immediately seek their [Col. 0013A] signification through spiritual understanding, because he does not doubt that they are stated not so much figuratively as historically. Thus we rightly said that consideration belongs especially to Dan, where we need imagination alone, although in such a matter we employ it not without rational ordering.

But when one reads of a land flowing with milk and honey, the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem made of precious stones, its gates of pearls, and its streets of gold, what person of sound sense would wish to take these literally? One therefore immediately has recourse to spiritual understanding and investigates what mystery is contained there. Do you see how such a description of future things seems to belong only to Naphtali, where it is fully recognized that imagination alone, without understanding, cannot suffice? [Col. 0013B] It was therefore rightly said that consideration of future evils belongs especially to Dan, but contemplation of future goods chiefly to Naphtali. Yet many things written concerning the torments of the wicked must be understood mystically, and likewise many things concerning the goods of the future life—although bodily things are described—must be understood simply.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the first contemplation and its characteristic

But this must be known—indeed, it cannot be unknown—that the consideration which consists in imagination alone comes more easily to one who meditates. For that which is mingled with understanding, the subtler it is, the more difficult it is to discover. This is why [Col. 0013C] Dan is born first and Naphtali afterward. In this twofold consideration, however, there is something very noteworthy: Dan, through a true imagining of present things, represents a fictive imagining of future things. Naphtali, by contrast, often rises through a fictive imagining of a described object to true understanding.

For it is not permissible to invent anything false by spiritual understanding concerning future and invisible goods, although it is without fault to see in imagination the torments of the wicked as very different from what they are. Who can fully contemplate them in this life as they truly are? Rather, each person depicts them figuratively at the judgment of his own mind, not as they are, but as he knows how to imagine them. Perhaps this is why such a son is here called Dan—that is, “judgment”—because in such representation [Col. 0013D] he follows not the instruction of experience but the decision of his own discernment. For since Dan forms in each person’s mind a representation of future things from that person’s own judgment, one rightly, I think, calls the maker of such things “Dan,” or judgment.

## CHAPTER XX. On the office of the first contemplation

There is, however, another explanation of this name, which perhaps is the subtler and therefore also the more useful. Whenever holy men feel themselves assaulted by shameful thoughts and provoked to unlawful delight, they are accustomed, even at the very entrance of temptation, to set future torments before the eyes of the mind; and by such consideration to extinguish, before base delight arises, whatever unlawful thing the mind suggests. [Col. 0014A] Thus they immediately punish themselves through consideration of punishment, and condemn the enticements of sin. Since through Dan’s office we detect, accuse, condemn, and chastise seductive thoughts, he is rightly called Dan—that is, judgment.

But why do we speak only of shameful thoughts, when perfect men strongly abhor even vain and useless ones, on account of what is written: “Woe to you who think useless things!” (Mic. 1); and again: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1). What then, I ask, will become of those thoughts which we perceive are not without some unlawful affection, when the Holy Spirit withdraws even from those that are without understanding? It often happens [Col. 0014B] that, while engaged in prayer, we endure in our heart certain phantasms of thought that intrude with great importunity. But should we neglect them without rebuking them? Ought we not rather sharply to accuse them and, as has been said, through the representation of punishment repress the incitement of sin and chastise our thoughts? Thus it is written: “Dan shall judge his people as one of the other tribes in Israel” (Gen. 49).

For discipline of actions belongs to Zilpah’s sons; ordering of wills, to Leah’s sons; judgment of assertions, to Rachel’s sons; and governance of thoughts, to Bilhah’s sons. Every thought, therefore, is judged as though within its own tribe when every error is corrected by its like: when will is amended by will, action chastised by action, [Col. 0014C] and assertion corrected by assertion. Whenever, then, we think something false, will something unjust, or do something disordered, we fully know that we are blameworthy. But do all judge themselves equally worthy of rebuke when they think something useless or disordered? Many rebuke themselves for a perverse deed or a wicked will; few judge themselves for a disordered thought. But because perfect men do this, and those who wish to be perfect ought to do it, Jacob therefore foretells or commands it, saying: “Dan shall judge his people as one of the other tribes in Israel.”

## CHAPTER XXI. On the usefulness of the first contemplation

[Col. 0014D]

For if Dan strictly guards his people and diligently exercises his judgment, it will come about that in the other tribes there will seldom be found anything that ought rightly to be condemned. For the mind which cuts off a seductive thought at the first suggestion is not easily carried away into wicked delight, just as a fault checked before wicked consent never passes into action. Dan must therefore be more vigilant and strict in judgment than all the rest, so that the other tribes may for the most part live without dispute or contention. Dan will always find in his own tribe something that he ought to examine and rightly rebuke, although among the others it may sometimes happen that some one of them can be found without fault. For the fault of the others is in the will; but this one’s [Col. 0015A] disorder often lies in necessity. I never approve evil, consent to evil, or carry out evil unless I myself will it; but evil can present itself to thought even against my will.

Yet it belongs to Dan to bring the rising evil immediately, when it knocks through thought, into judgment; to examine it carefully; to condemn it when detected; to strike the deceptive thought by another consideration; and to extinguish tempting evils through remembrance of torments. You now see, I think, how rightly this son is called Dan—that is, judgment. Of him alone there is doubt whether he ought to judge his people, since he alone, if it were possible, ought so to judge not only constantly but strictly that the others may have nothing to judge.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the second contemplation and its characteristic

[Col. 0015B]

But just as it belongs to Dan’s office to repress rising vices by representing punishment, so it belongs to Naphtali to inflame good desires by contemplating rewards. For Naphtali wonderfully kindles our mind toward the desire for them whenever he brings the image of eternal goods before the mind’s eyes; yet he customarily does this in two ways. At times he uses transference, at times comparison.

He uses comparison when, from the multitude or greatness of present goods, he infers how many or how great the joys of the future life may be. For example, often contemplating the brightness of the sun—that is, bodily light—he considers [Col. 0015C] how great that future spiritual light will be, if this bodily light is so great and so wonderful. For how great, do you suppose, will be that light which we shall share with angels, if this is so great which we share with beasts? What will be the future light of the blessed, if such is this present light of the wretched? Likewise, he infers the abundance of invisible goods from the multitude of visible goods. How many, then, do we suppose these are? But who could count them? How many delights are there for the eyes, how many for the ears and the other senses? How many colors, how many scents, how many tastes? If, then, there are so many delights of bodies, how many will spiritual beings possess? If we possess so much in time, how great are the things we await [Col. 0015D] in eternity?

In this manner, therefore, he uses comparison. He also uses, as has been said, transference when he transfers a description of visible things to signify invisible things. For example, he hears light named in the Scriptures, as it is written of God: “He dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6). He asks what this incorporeal light is which the invisible and incorporeal nature of God inhabits, and discovers that this light is God’s own wisdom, that it is the true light. For as this outward light illuminates the eyes of bodies, so that light undoubtedly customarily illuminates the eyes of hearts. See how Naphtali rises through the quality of visible things to knowledge of invisible things.

It is clear, then, how rightly [Col. 0016A] Naphtali is so called according to each interpretation. For *Nephtalim* is interpreted as “comparison” or “conversion.” He customarily converts any known nature of visible things into spiritual understanding. Therefore, because he converts almost whatever he finds written into spiritual understanding, he rightly received the name of conversion. And again, because, as has been said, he uses comparison constantly, he is likewise rightly named Naphtali—that is, comparison.

## CHAPTER XXIII. What is characteristic and distinctive of the second contemplation

It should be known, however, that the kind of contemplation which operates in pure understanding is known to be so much the more excellent than this kind of contemplation, designated by Naphtali, as it is more subtle. Yet contemplation of this kind has something singular and especially noteworthy about it. For minds that are still untrained and less exercised, it is easier to understand and more delightful to hear than other kinds. It comes more readily to one meditating and affects the hearer more sweetly. [Col. 0016B] It is plainly readier in meditation and more graceful in speech. Thus Jacob says of Naphtali: “Naphtali, a deer let loose, giving words of beauty” (Gen. 49).

He is called a deer because of ease in running, and “let loose” because of eagerness for running. A deer is a very swift animal that can run greatly and wishes to run greatly when it has been let loose. Therefore, unless I am mistaken, Naphtali is rightly called a deer let loose, because through the grace of contemplation he is able to range over many things, and because of the sweetness of contemplation he delights in ranging far. In such swiftness this Naphtali of ours lifts the contemplative mind—yet one somewhat exercised in such a task—now to the heights, now casts it down to the depths, now bears it through innumerable things, so that the mind itself which undergoes this often marvels at itself, having been taught by happy instruction how fittingly our Naphtali is called a deer let loose.

It should be noted how rightly he is compared not to a bird flying, but to a deer running. For a bird in flight is suspended far above the earth; a deer, however, rests upon the earth in order to leap, nor even in its leaps is it separated far from the earth. Thus indeed, [Col. 0016D] while Naphtali seeks the nature of invisible things through the form of visible things, he is accustomed to make certain leaps, but is unable to attain full flight, because in raising himself to the heights he draws along with him the shadow of bodily things and does not wholly leave the depths behind.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How great is the delight of the second contemplation

See how he is a deer let loose. But how he gives words of beauty, perhaps we shall show more clearly and establish more fully through examples. Do you wish to hear words of beauty, words of sweetness, full of loveliness and full of delight—such as Naphtali is accustomed, or ought, to fashion?

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1). [Col. 0017A] “Strengthen me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2). “Your lips drip honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” (Song 4). What, I ask, is sweeter than utterances of this sort? What more delightful can be found? What is heard more willingly or eagerly than such utterances? These words appear to sound of something carnal, and yet what they describe through themselves is spiritual.

Naphtali knows how to mingle carnal things with spiritual and to describe incorporeal things through bodily things, so that each nature of the human being, composed of bodily and incorporeal nature, may find in his sayings what wonderfully refreshes it. Perhaps this is why they taste so sweet to a human being: because, as has been said, they somehow refresh both natures. But there is in his sayings [Col. 0017B] something very wonderful and worthy of admiration: they almost always charm more delightfully when, according to the literal sense, they seem to say nothing of the sort. Such are these words: “Your hair is like flocks of goats which have climbed Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep, which have come up from the washing” (Song 4). “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus; your head is like Carmel” (Song 7).

When these and similar things are heard or read, they seem very pleasing; yet, if we follow the literal sense alone, we find in them nothing worthy of admiration. But perhaps what we so gladly embrace in sayings of this kind is that, through a certain pleasing foolishness of the letter, if I may put it so, we are compelled to flee to spiritual understanding. If, then, we consider [Col. 0017C] how swift our Naphtali is in meditation and how delightful in speech, we may readily perceive how rightly Scripture declares of him: “Naphtali, a deer let loose, giving words of beauty.”

## CHAPTER XXV. On the twofold offspring of virtues born from subdued sensuality

For the present, let what has been said concerning Bilhah’s sons suffice. It remains now to say something concerning Zilpah’s sons. Leah, then, seeing her sister Rachel already rejoicing in adopted offspring, was herself moved to give her handmaid to her husband, so that she too might exult with her sister in the adoption of sons. If, therefore, as was said [Col. 0017D] above, we should understand sensuality by Zilpah, what other offspring of virtue, I ask, can she bear except that one may learn both to live temperately amid prosperity and to have patience amid adversity? These are Gad and Asher, Zilpah’s two sons: namely, the rigor of abstinence and the strength of patience. Gad is born first and Asher afterward, because it is first necessary that we be temperate regarding our own goods, and afterward strong in enduring evils imposed by others.

This is the twofold offspring of virtues which Zilpah indeed bears in pain, yet to the great blessedness of her mistress. For through abstinence or patience the flesh is afflicted, but the mind is thereby disposed toward great peace and tranquillity. Thus, when Gad was born, Leah exclaimed, “Happily!” [Col. 0018A] and again, at Asher’s birth she declared, “This is for my blessedness” (Gen. 30). “For mine,” she says, not for his. For where sensuality is outwardly worn down through the flesh, there the affection of the heart is restored to the integrity of purity.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the rigor of abstinence, the strength of patience, and their character

For how great, do you suppose, is the peace or tranquillity of heart that desires none of this world’s delights and fears none of its adversities? [Col. 0018B] The first is acquired through Gad; the second through Asher. For what can one desire of this world’s pleasures who, out of love for abstinence, refuses offered delights? Or what can one fear of this world’s adversities who, strengthened by the virtue of patience, triumphs even over evils inflicted upon him? As it is written of the apostles: “The apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5); and as Paul commands: “Rejoicing in tribulation” (Rom. 12).

What, then, can diminish the joy of one who exults even in dishonor inflicted upon him or in any oppression? Whatever the flesh endures harshly for love of God belongs, therefore, to the blessedness of the soul. Where the body is worn down, the conscience is made glad. And the more unhappy one appears outwardly, the more blessed one is found inwardly. For blessed joy consists of two things: lacking what one does not wish, and possessing what one wishes. We call happy the person who suffers nothing he does not wish; and we [Col. 0018C] judge blessed the person to whom what he desires is available. Whoever, then, out of desire for heavenly things hates worldly pleasure can surely avoid his enemy everywhere through abstinence. Thus the rigor of abstinence is rightly called Gad—that is, “happiness”—because everywhere he tramples the world’s enticements which he detests.

Likewise, whoever loves bodily affliction for the love of God—where, I ask, would such a person fail to find something by which he might be afflicted? If, then, one is rightly believed blessed who everywhere finds what he loves, the strength of patience is rightly called Asher—that is, “blessed”—since what he desires meets him from every side. Behold two lovers: one loves God, the other the world. The former, for God’s sake, loves temporal affliction; the latter desires temporal fullness of goods. The former [Col. 0018D] can everywhere find what he loves for God’s sake; the latter can nowhere attain the fullness of goods for which he thirsts. Which is more blessed?

Again, behold two others: one hates this world’s adversity; the other detests worldly pleasure. But where, I ask, can the former avoid his enemy, or where can the latter fail to trample his foe? Which, I ask, is happier? Scripture says: “Blessed is the man who has not gone after gold and has not hoped in treasures of money” (Ecclus. 31). And again: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life” (Jas. 1). These are Gad and Asher: the former tramples worldly glory, while the latter willingly suffers the world’s oppression for God’s sake.

It must therefore be carefully noted and deeply retained that [Col. 0019A] sacred Scripture wished to call the labor of abstinence not calamity but happiness, and decreed to call the rigor of patience not wretched but blessed. We wish briefly to note here that by Gad we should not understand only abstinence in food and drink. Rather, by Gad and Asher we understand abstinence from every superfluous pleasure and patience in every bodily affliction, in all things that delight or torment the flesh through the five senses.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That sensual appetite is not moderated unless the wandering of imagination is restrained

But when, I ask, would Leah give her handmaid to her husband, or adopt such sons, unless she had been moved by her sister’s example? [Col. 0019B] For Bilhah, Rachel’s handmaid, must always first be brought under the husband’s power before Zilpah, Leah’s handmaid. Unless the wandering of imagination, which takes place through useless thoughts, is first repressed, the immoderate appetite of sensuality is undoubtedly not moderated. Whoever, then, wishes to moderate the desires for bodily pleasures should first accustom himself never—or at least rarely—to think of carnal delights. For certainly, the less often you think of such things, the less often, and undoubtedly the more faintly, you will desire them. This, unless I am mistaken, is the reason why Bilhah is first bowed under male dominion rather than Zilpah.

It is likewise clear that Leah would never make abstinence and patience—Gad and Asher—adopted sons unless she constantly saw the adopted offspring of her sister [Col. 0019C] Rachel. For who could ever persuade the heart’s affection to despise this world’s prosperity and fear its adversities unless, at the prompting of Dan and Naphtali, it were compelled not merely often but almost unceasingly to behold the torments of the future life or eternal rewards? Through continual consideration of future evils it is now easily persuaded to despise present goods. And again, through unceasing contemplation of eternal blessedness it is inflamed to voluntary endurance of temporal oppression. This, I think, is why Dan and Naphtali are born first and Gad and Asher afterward.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How through abstinence and patience the mind is strengthened for every obedience

[Col. 0019D]

Once Gad and Asher have been born, the time is now at hand for Reuben to find mandrakes, provided that he is not reluctant to go out. But why should we doubt that he wishes to go out, when we know that he is now fit to go out or to come in? For after so many children of his mother, and so many sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, he must be believed to be already grown and able and willing to go out and come in at his father’s command. But if, as was said above, we understand Reuben as fear of God, what should we understand by his coming in or going out? What is it for him to be within or to go outside?

Reuben is within when, in the secrecy of the heart, we tremble before God’s sight concerning our conscience. Reuben goes outside when, for God’s sake, [Col. 0020A] we also incline ourselves toward every obedience to human beings. Thus, to fear God for his own sake, but human beings for God’s sake, is for Reuben now to remain within, now to be found outside. Reuben therefore goes out at the wheat harvest when, under obedience’s command, he exercises himself in works of righteousness.

But when, do you suppose, does Reuben become strong for perfect obedience, unless Gad and Asher—that is, love of abstinence and patience—have encouraged him to despise pleasure and endure tribulation? For two things usually obstruct the perfection of obedience: that we may be forced either to abandon things we love or to endure harsh things. But if the mind has once been perfectly warmed by love of abstinence or patience, Reuben immediately submits himself to every obedience without any resistance. [Col. 0020B] For if I resolve within myself both to suffer adversities and not to delight in prosperity, what difficulty can afterward diminish my obedience? If I seek even hard and harsh things for God’s love on my own initiative, why should I not all the more endure them when obedience is added, for the glory of greater merit? Thus Reuben is rightly said to go out after Gad and Asher have been born, because fear of the Lord is strengthened through voluntary abstinence and patience for every obedience.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How human praise arises from abstinence, and how cautiously its desire must be moderated

But what a great and notable fragrance of good repute one spreads all around oneself who is hindered from the pursuit of obedience by neither moderation [Col. 0020C] nor poverty! These are the mandrakes that Reuben finds and that his mother Leah receives from him. For what ought we to understand by mandrakes, which customarily diffuse their fragrance widely, except the renown of good reputation? Leah receives them when offered praise touches the affection, when the mind is moved by the celebrations of its own praise and perversely delights in the breeze of popular favor.

Rachel asks for part of them; Leah grants it, in order that she may receive her husband, since she burns with desire for offspring. For the Holy Spirit does not make fruitful for the offspring of virtue the mind which, despite reason’s counsel, does not moderate its appetite for vain praise. There is one Spirit who enriches both sisters with the fruitfulness of offspring, because the same Spirit both illumines reason for knowledge of truth [Col. 0020D] and kindles affection for love of virtue. Reason therefore advises affection to moderate, under one governance, the appetite for human favor, if it desires to rejoice in union with the divine Spirit for multiplying the offspring of virtues. Possession of the mandrakes is thus brought under Rachel’s authority when the appetite for praise is moderated under reason’s dominion.

It should be noted how temperately Rachel asks not for the mandrakes but for a portion of the mandrakes. For reason is not unaware that it is very difficult for the mind, however resistant, not to be gladdened by praise when it is offered. Love of human praise must therefore first be moderated; afterward, if it can be done, it should be cut off altogether. This is why Rachel is read to have asked for part of the mandrakes; but Leah, speaking afterward to Jacob [Col. 0021A], does not boast merely of a part: “You shall come in to me,” she says, “for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes” (Gen. 30). “With mandrakes,” she says, not “with a part of my son’s mandrakes.”

While her husband is still absent, Leah scarcely grants a portion; but when he comes, more richly inflamed with desire for him, she wishes nothing of them to be retained for herself any longer. Thus indeed, when the human mind is touched by spiritual sweetness, it gladly forgets whatever it had previously desired from human praise. In this manner mandrakes are usefully transferred from Leah’s possession and brought under Rachel’s authority. For Rachel knows how to use mandrakes better than Leah: whatever the heart’s affection appropriates for self-praise, reason more rightly turns toward the glory of God. But what, we ask, is the reason that, among Leah’s [Col. 0021B] other sons, Reuben could find the mandrakes of good repute?

## CHAPTER XXX. From what human praise most commonly arises, and that true praise concerns a right will.

But we know that the works of virtues which nourish the other virtues almost always extinguish humility. For the works accomplished through Gad and Asher—namely, abstinence and patience—are apt to make the doer not timid but swollen with pride, not so much humble as self-willed. What, then, is more admirable? What is more worthy of universal praise than that, when, by the very thing through which reverence for the fear of God is often extinguished in others, it is not diminished but increased? Therefore, since we are accustomed to exalt with singular praise [Col. 0021C] one whom we see, even after works of virtue, tremble greatly not only at offending God but even at slight offense against human beings, Reuben is rightly said to have found the mandrakes after Gad and Asher were born: for we marvel that someone should advance through outstanding works not toward pride but toward fear.

It should certainly be noted that these mandrakes of which we have spoken are read to have been found neither after so many sons of Leah nor after the twin children of Bilhah, but immediately after the birth of Zilpah’s sons. For wills belong to Leah’s sons, thoughts to Bilhah’s sons, and actions to Zilpah’s sons. How can we marvel at, or when shall we praise, wills or thoughts, however upright and useful, which [Col. 0021D] we do not see at all? Although true praise concerns a right will, yet we do not praise it unless it appears in action. For through a good work a good will becomes known, so that it may rightly discover the praise of good repute, like mandrakes spreading their fragrance far and wide. Thus, as it were after Zilpah’s birth, Leah’s offspring is believed to find mandrakes when a good will, made manifest through a good work, is everywhere honored with wonderful proclamations of praise.

## Chapter XXXI. How both the discipline of the heart and that of the body are fortified by the virtues mentioned above

This point concerning the sons of these two handmaids must not be passed over carelessly, but retained in continual memory: by their unceasing watchfulness and vigilant guarding, the city of our conscience is wonderfully protected and greatly advanced. Bilhah’s firstborn orders it inwardly; Zilpah’s firstborn fortifies it outwardly. Through Dan, evils rising within are restrained; through Gad, evils attacking from without are driven back. For we all know that every temptation arises either externally or internally: internally through thought, externally through sensation. At one time it knocks within through thought; at another it prepares to break in from external things through the senses. The enemy is accustomed now to supply counsels of error from within, now to bring incentives of pleasure from without. But because the discipline of thoughts belongs to Dan, while the discipline of the senses pertains to Gad, Dan must surely keep watch for the judgment of discernment, and Gad [Col. 0022B] must fight bravely through the exercise of abstinence. It is the role of one to still civil discord; that of the other to repel hostile battle. The former watches against the treachery of citizens; the latter against the assault of enemies. The one against perfidy, the other against violence. For when Dan is negligent, the mind is easily deceived; when Gad acts too sluggishly, it is suddenly carried off into shameful pleasure. But what difference does it make whether the city of our heart perishes through force or fraud, whether civil discord or an enemy hand overthrows it?

## Chapter XXXII. That the discipline of thoughts cannot be preserved without discipline of the senses

We must know that bodily discipline [Col. 0022C] without discipline of the heart is undoubtedly useless; but the discipline of thoughts cannot at all be maintained without discipline of the senses. Hence it is quite clear that without the help of Gad, who ought to keep watch against outward things, Dan labors fruitlessly within to establish peace among the citizens. For what good is it, while Dan judges his people, continually to cut off the cause of discord, unless Gad endeavors to prevent the incitements of vices from entering through the gates of the senses—as though a hostile army? Even though Dan sits continually on the throne of judgment, even though he endlessly reconciles the quarrels of disputing thoughts, he surely toils in vain to settle discord among the citizens unless Gad, with equal diligence, fortifies our city through the discipline of the senses and strikes fiercely at the hostile ranks of vices with the battle of abstinence. Hence it is also written: “Gad, girded, shall fight before him” (Gen. XLIX). Then Dan usefully watches inwardly against the perfidy of traitors, when Gad externally excludes and assaults the enemies who come against him. Therefore Gad first girds himself, so that afterwards he may fight bravely. Gad undoubtedly girds himself when he restrains the dissipation of the senses by discipline. Gad fights in a strong battle when he slays fleshly desires by mortifying the flesh. For a great slaughter of enemies is made, and that hateful army of vices is more swiftly turned to flight, when the bodily senses are restrained from wandering by discipline and the appetite of the flesh is held back from pleasure by abstinence. In this way, as [Col. 0023A] we all can experience, Dan orders our city inwardly and Gad fortifies it outwardly.

## Chapter XXXIII. How the aforesaid virtues cooperate with one another in guarding the heart

Their brothers also stand by them, not sluggish in providing aid: Naphtali inwardly with Dan in establishing peace among the citizens; Asher outwardly with Gad in defeating the violence of enemies. Thus Gad and Asher keep watch against enemies; Dan and Naphtali are concerned with citizens. On this side Dan threatens; on that side Naphtali comforts. Dan terrifies with threats; Naphtali cherishes with promises. The former punishes the wicked; the latter rewards the good. One frightens hearts with the terror of hell; the other soothes minds with the hope of eternal blessedness. How greatly, then, do you think [Col. 0023B] this Naphtali, “giving words of beauty,” assists his brother in such a task, when by the sweetness of his speech he bends the minds of his hearers almost without delay wherever he wishes? Likewise, Asher assists his brother externally, and both fortify the city against the enemies’ attack. One protects one side; the other defends the other. Gad fights on the right; Asher battles on the left. Gad is assailed by the prosperity of this world; Asher by worldly adversity. But Asher easily makes sport of his enemy when he sees the part he protects fortified by the lofty rock of patience; and therefore, from the secure place of his station, he laughs at and despises his enemies as they struggle vainly from below. Consequently, his enemies do not so much trouble him by their attack as continually furnish him material for triumph. [Col. 0023C] Thus, disregarding his own assailants—that is, worldly adversities—he turns wholly against the persecutors of his brother, namely fleshly pleasures, and pursues them with severe judgment. But such terror suddenly overwhelms Gad’s assailants when Asher joins him in the contest of his battle that all immediately take flight; for they do not dare resist even for an hour when the brothers render each other aid in turn. The true enemies of the soul are fleshly pleasures. But, I ask, what place remains for corrupt pleasure amid torments which this our Asher is proved, for God’s sake, not merely to endure patiently but even to seek ardently? How rightly Asher—that is, “blessed”—is called so, according to that saying of the Lord: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. V).

## Chapter XXXIV. That perfect patience is always accompanied by mercy

Who could fulfill so magnificently that command of the Lord, “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke VI)? Who was able so easily and so wholeheartedly to pardon injuries inflicted upon him as one who has learned to rejoice in the torments of his own body rather than to grieve over them? Why should he not love his enemies, or why should he not gladly pardon them, when they inflict upon him what he desires? Therefore he has more compassion upon his persecutors than upon his own body, so that he may again and again be [Col. 0024A] blessed: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). O glorious man, O thrice and four times blessed man! Blessed because of his hunger for righteousness; blessed because of voluntary suffering; blessed because of meekness; blessed because of merciful compassion. For as those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are blessed, and as those who suffer persecution for righteousness itself are blessed, so likewise are the meek blessed, and the merciful blessed. And this our Asher, that he may be truly and multiply blessed, thirsts ardently for righteousness, gladly suffers for it, does not know how to be angry, and readily shows compassion. For although he hungers greatly for the bread of righteousness, he nevertheless disdains to eat it unless it is mixed with the oil of mercy. For from the abundant overflow of riches [Col. 0024B] that exceed his need, from the spoils of enemies gained through frequent victory, he has become very sumptuous; nor does any bread, however fine, now taste good to him unless it is sprinkled with oil—to such an extent that Scripture openly declares of him, saying: “Asher, his bread is rich” (Gen. XLIX). Who, do you think, so abounds in delights as he does, that he can truly sing: “I have delighted in the way of your testimonies, as in all riches” (Ps. CXVIII)?

## Chapter XXXV. Commendation of perfect patience

How greatly, do you think, does this Asher abound in the riches of spiritual consolations, and overflow with the delights of spiritual joys—he whose riches every adversity is accustomed not so much to diminish as to increase, [Col. 0024C] and whose delights no torment whatsoever can even interrupt? For the more harshly he is oppressed outwardly, the more delightfully he glories inwardly. These are those delights which not only the poor and obscure, but even kings and princes themselves thirst for and receive with such gratitude. I am lying if Scripture itself does not say this very thing of him: “Asher, his bread is rich, and he shall provide delights for kings.” For by what we think they are sweetly fed, by what we believe they are wonderfully delighted, not just any kings are meant, but truly those kings to whom the King of kings and Lord of lords has restored dominion over their own body and to whom He distributes the kingdom of His Father. To such kings, I say, how sweet it must be, how deeply it tastes to them, when they see a person not fearing torments through love of righteousness and not losing peace of heart and tranquility of soul even amid persecutions. For if there is joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance (Luke XV), how great then will be the celebration over any righteous person willingly dying for righteousness? Truly, “Asher, his bread is rich, and he shall provide delights for kings.” O what bread is his bread! O what delights are his delights, which taste so sweet to kings—such kings! Certainly these kings have already entered the marriage feast of the Lamb, have already sat down at that eternal banquet, have already fed upon the bread of angels and eternal delights, and are already made drunk with the torrent of pleasure; and yet they hunger insatiably for the delights of this Asher, and to this day, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, [Col. 0025A] amid such abundance of heavenly joys, they cannot satisfy this hunger or thirst of theirs. “Asher, his bread is rich, and he shall provide delights for kings.” How lavish, do you think, can he be toward the needs of the poor, when he has more than enough to prepare delights for kings? How greatly, do you think, do those still living in the valley of tears, whose own weakness weighs them down, marvel at and rejoice in his steadfastness, if even those whom that eternal blessedness has already absorbed delight so much in his works? “Asher, his bread is rich, and he shall provide delights for kings.” And whence has he such abundance of riches, such plenty of delights, except, as has been said, from the spoils of enemies in such frequent victory? For it is clear that the more the enemies of righteousness are crushed, the more abundantly the joys of conscience are heaped up: “Glory and riches are in his house,” says the Psalmist (Ps. CXI). And the Apostle, as though explaining this kind of glory and riches, says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). This is that house, or city—our conscience—in which the riches of spiritual goods abound when the sons of the aforesaid handmaids guard it with vigilant care: Dan and Naphtali striving to establish peace among the citizens, Gad and Asher acting manfully in defeating enemies. By the prudence of the former the citizens are pacified; by the constancy of the latter the enemies are defeated.

## Chapter XXXVI. How, and in what order, true joy arises

[Col. 0025C] When enemies, therefore, have been put to flight and citizens pacified, nothing now prevents, I think, our city from experiencing what that peace of God is which surpasses all understanding (Phil. IV), or how great is the abundance of sweetness which God has hidden for those who love Him (Ps. XXX). “He has hidden,” it says. What wonder, then, if any lover of the world does not know what God has hidden for those who love Him? For those who fix their hope on false and deceptive goods cannot discover what true goods are; hence they say: “Who will show us good things?” (Ps. IV). For there is hidden manna, wholly unknown except to those who taste it. Such sweetness belongs to the heart, not to the flesh; thus no carnal person can know it: [Col. 0025D] “You have given joy,” it says, “in my heart” (ibid.). Bodily delights, like the body itself, can be seen by the bodily eye; but the eyes of the flesh cannot see the delights of the heart, any more than they can see the heart itself. By what means, therefore, can one know spiritual delights, unless one does not shrink from entering into one’s own heart and dwelling within? Thus one is told: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV). This inward joy, which is felt within, belongs only to spiritual persons; it is Leah’s son, born to her in fifth place. For joy, as we have already said above, is one of the principal affections. When it is ordered, it can rightly be numbered among the sons of Jacob and Leah. We truly possess ordered and genuine joy when we rejoice in true and inward goods. The Apostle wished to encourage us toward the desire for such offspring when he said: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV). And the Prophet: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous, and glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. XXXI). For the sake of such offspring Leah gladly despised mandrakes, that she might be able to have such a son. For a mind that delights in human praise does not deserve to experience inward joy. Leah rightly bore such a son after the birth of Gad and Asher, because without abstinence and patience the human mind does not attain true joy. Therefore one who wishes to rejoice in truth must exclude not only false pleasure but also vain disturbance. Whoever still delights in low things is unworthy of inward gladness; and whoever is disturbed by vain fear cannot enjoy spiritual sweetness. Truth condemned false joy when it said: “Woe to you who now laugh” (Luke VI). It uprooted vain disturbance when it warned its hearers, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X). We overcome one of these by abstaining; we trample down the other by suffering. Thus false pleasure is uprooted through Gad, while vain disturbance is removed through Asher. These are Gad and Asher, who exclude false joy and introduce true joy. Now, I think, there will no longer be any question why such a son is called Issachar, since Issachar is interpreted “reward.” For what else do we seek through so many and such great labors? What else, I say, [Col. 0026C] do we await with such persevering long-suffering except true joy? We receive, as it were, firstfruits of this reward again and again, and a kind of pledge, whenever we enter into that inward joy of our Lord and taste it in some measure.

## Chapter XXXVII. Comparison of inward and outward sweetness

Sacred Scripture now calls this tasting of inward sweetness “taste,” now “intoxication,” in order to show how small and how great it is: small in comparison with future fullness, but great in comparison with any worldly pleasure. For the present delight of spiritual persons, however much it may increase, is found small when compared with the joys of the life to come; yet in comparison with it every sweetness of outward delights is nothing. O wondrous sweetness—sweetness so great, sweetness so small! How is it not great, when it surpasses every worldly thing? How is it not small, when it scarcely draws a tiny drop from that fullness? You instill but a little from so great a sea of blessedness into minds, yet you wholly intoxicate the mind into which you pour it. Rightly, such a little of so great a thing is called a taste; and rightly also, that which estranges the mind from itself is called intoxication. It may therefore rightly be called both taste and intoxication: “Taste,” says the Prophet, “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). And the Apostle Peter: “If indeed [Col. 0027A] you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (I Pet. II). And concerning intoxication, the same Prophet says: “You visited the earth and made it drunk” (Ps. LXIV). Hear a man soaked with this intoxication and wholly unaware of what was happening around him: “Whether in the body,” he says, “or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (II Cor. XII). How intoxicated, do you think, was he? How the world had been forgotten by him, who did not know himself!

## Chapter XXXVIII. What commonly hinders that inward joy

Certainly those who are still tossed by the waves of fleshly desires do not deserve to be intoxicated with this sweetness: “You visited the earth,” it says, “and made it drunk” (Ps. LXIV). Why, do you think, is the Lord said to have intoxicated the earth alone, and not also [Col. 0027B] the sea? But we know that a mind which fluctuates through varied desires, which is still agitated by the storm of worldly cares, is not admitted to that inward joy and does not drink from that torrent of pleasure—much less is it intoxicated by it. We know that the sea is always in motion, but the earth stands forever. So too the other elements are always in motion; while the earth alone stands, the others do not know how to stand. What, then, should we understand by the earth but the fixed stability of the heart? Therefore whoever desires or believes that he will be intoxicated by that cup of true sobriety must restrain the heart’s fluctuation and gather the movements of thoughts and affections toward the desire of the one true joy. This is that truly blessed earth: the tranquil stability of the mind, when the mind is wholly gathered into itself [Col. 0027C] and fixed immovably in the desire of eternity alone. This is the earth which Truth promised when it said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V). This is the earth of which the Psalmist, promising, warned, and warning, promised: “Dwell,” he says, “in the earth, and you shall be fed on its riches” (Ps. XXXVI). This is the earth which this Issachar, a strong ass, saw and desired, and for whose desire he marvelously burned: “Issachar,” it says, “is a strong ass dwelling between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good, and that the land was excellent; and he placed his shoulder beneath the burden, and became a servant under tribute” (Gen. XLIX). Therefore we must pass from land to land, from a foreign land to our own land, from exile to homeland, from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people, from the land of the dying to the land of the living, if we wish to know true and inward joy by experience. Let us too desire that land which this Issachar saw and desired. For if he had not seen it, he would not have known it; and if he had not known it, he would not have desired it.

## Chapter XXXIX. How inward sweetness is accustomed both to strengthen the mind for hard things and incline it to lowliness

For the sake of this land he became an ass and was made strong; he gladly placed his shoulder beneath the burden and became a servant under tribute. He had suddenly become very low in his own estimation, since he regarded himself as an ass—an animal almost [Col. 0028A] more contemptible than any other. He greatly desired the land he saw, for whose sake he endured every labor with strength. He had indeed seen that all our righteous deeds were like the cloth of a menstruating woman in comparison with the beauty of that land (Isa. LXIV). He had likewise seen that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII). Thus made low in one respect and strong in the other—humbled by the one and strengthened by the other—he gladly bent the shoulder of his strength beneath every labor; and in gaining divine glory, not his own, he paid worthy tribute to the true King. Do you wish to hear of another who, for a like reason, both became low in his own estimation and nevertheless grew strong for every labor? “I have become,” he says, “like a beast before you” (Ps. LXXII). And elsewhere: “For your sake,” he says, “we are put to death all day long” (Ps. XLIII). See how lowly, see how strong: lowly like a beast, strong to mortify himself. “Issachar, a strong ass dwelling between the boundaries, saw that rest was good, and that the land was excellent.” Therefore he had almost, but not completely, left this land of the dying; almost, but not completely, grasped that land of the living, since he dwelt between the boundaries. Because he was content with the most contemptible and fewest goods of this life, he held the outermost edge of this wretched land. Because through frequent transports of the mind he tasted beforehand the goods of everlasting life, he touched the beginnings of that blessed land. Issachar, a strong ass dwelling between the boundaries: because he did not reject the necessities of this life’s goods, he did not altogether leave this land; because he could grasp only certain last [Col. 0028C] things of the life to come, he did not fully attain that land. He endured this one out of necessity; he desired that one for delight; and thus he dwelt between the boundaries. He strove entirely to leave this one but could not; he sought to enter wholly into that one but was unable. Therefore he did what he could: he dwelt between the boundaries. Every day he strove toward that land; every day he fell back into this one; and in this way he remained between the boundaries. “Issachar, a strong ass dwelling between the boundaries, saw that rest was good, and that the land was excellent.” What wonder, then, that he saw it when he lived on its border? What wonder, I say, that he saw it, knew what he saw, and desired what he knew? [Col. 0028D] Therefore he placed his shoulder beneath the burden and became a servant under tribute. “He saw,” it says, “that rest was good.” Therefore there is rest there, and good rest. For if it were not there, he could not have seen it there. And if it were not good, he would not have placed his shoulder beneath the burden for its sake: “But the meek,” says the Prophet, “shall inherit the earth and delight in the abundance of peace” (Ps. XXXVI). See what kind of earth it is. Peace is there; rest is there. Peace complete, rest good; peace tranquil, repose peaceful. “He saw that rest was good, and that the land was excellent.” There is no labor in that land, but one cannot arrive at it without labor. One labors for its sake, but one does not labor within it. Outside this land true rest is not found; in this land no labor at all is found. There are two things: land and rest. Two set against two. Two goods against two evils. The two great evils are misery and desire—that is, punishment and fault. The two great goods are tranquility and stability. Against misery is tranquility of mind; against desire, stability of heart. To feel no affliction is to rest well. To be shaken by no waves of desire is undoubtedly already to dwell in the land. In such a land is such rest. The mind which is not yet wholly gathered toward inward joy does not experience what true rest is. Woe to me, wretched man, who to this day live as a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth: a wanderer, following desire; a fugitive, avoiding misery. What I desire is always lacking; everywhere I find what I must flee. Desire makes me a wanderer; misery [Col. 0029B] makes me a fugitive. Surely it is an evil land, a land of misery, such a land in which I live in this manner: “a land of misery and darkness, where there is the shadow of death and no order.” Such land is assuredly not stability of heart but hardness and insensibility of mind. But, “Your good Spirit, Lord, shall lead me into a right land” (Ps. CXLII). This is the land which Issachar saw and desired, because there was good rest there and the land itself was excellent. O happy one who could, if only for an hour, forget every evil and possess that inward peace or rest, even if only briefly! Likewise happy is one to whom it has been granted to gather the dispersions of the heart into one and fix desire in that fountain of true blessedness. The former is good, but this is best—according as Issachar saw [Col. 0029C] that rest was good and the land excellent. For it is good indeed to be far from every evil, yet it is much better—indeed best—to cleave to the highest good. Issachar knew this, and therefore did not wish to depart far from such a land, but lived between the boundaries in its neighborhood, desiring and seeking, through at least rare transports, to touch it quickly and as it were secretly, and also to eat more often from the fruits of that land. For, as you can know, the fruit of that lofty land is sublime, wondrous, and unique. A human mind, often satisfied and in some degree enriched by the fruits of this land, suddenly receives a marvelous strength against every danger; it immediately becomes so strong in hatred of every vice that it is no longer enough for it merely to admit none within itself by consent, unless it also endeavors manfully to pursue them in others and strike them with firm correction.

## Chapter XL. How, and in what order, hatred of vices arises in us

Let him then immediately be as strong against every danger as he is fierce an enemy of all vices. Hence, after Issachar, Zebulun is born, whose name is interpreted “dwelling of strength.” For what do we understand by Zebulun except hatred of vices: good hatred, ordered hatred, hatred of vices? The Prophet undoubtedly desired to order this affection in us when he said: “Be angry, and do not sin” (Ps. IV). [Col. 0030A] For what is it to be angry without sinning, and to be angry while not sinning, except usefully to be indignant at people’s vices without loving people merely for appearance’s sake? The same Prophet indicated that he had this son when elsewhere he said: “With perfect hatred I hated them” (Ps. CXXXVIII). And elsewhere: “I have hated every way of iniquity” (Ps. CXVIII). This is that outstanding soldier of God, who does not cease to fight the Lord’s battles, and whom Sacred Scripture in its customary language calls the zeal of the Lord or zeal for uprightness: “Zeal for your house, Lord, has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me” (Ps. LXVIII). And again: “My zeal has made me waste away, because my enemies have forgotten your words” (Ps. CXVIII). And Elijah says: “I have been zealous for the Lord” (III Kings XIX). And Phinehas fought with the zeal of the Lord and received [Col. 0030B] an eternal priesthood (Num. XXV). But whence, do you think, came such strength and such remarkable constancy to these men? Elijah alone rose up against one hundred and fifty prophets of Baal; Phinehas alone, rushing against the camp of the Midianites, ran adulterers through with the sword. See how much strength they receive; see how strong those become who eat from the fruits of that aforesaid land, who are refreshed by inward sweetness. Thus Zebulun—that is, the dwelling of strength—is rightly born after Issachar, whose name means reward, because after the sweetness of eternal recompense has been tasted, the mind is wonderfully strengthened against the enticements of temptations: suddenly scorning its own dangers, it vigorously avenges the injuries done to the Lord. Hence Moses, the meekest of all who lived upon the earth, after a forty-day fast, refreshed by a marvelous fullness of spiritual delights, suddenly burned with such zeal against the makers and worshippers of the idol that, immediately gathering to himself those who belonged to the Lord, he passed through the middle of the camp from gate to gate, striking, and cast three thousand transgressors to death (Exod. XXXII). So, indeed, Zebulun is born after Issachar: through the tasting of inward sweetness, hatred of vices is generated and the strength of true awe is acquired. This is Zebulun, who is accustomed to appease God’s wrath by being angry; who, when he piously acts severely by striking human vices, spares people better, as it were, by not sparing them. Without doubt, nothing so pleases God, nothing so appeases God, as zeal for souls.

## Chapter XLI. How rare it is to possess zeal for uprightness from a genuine hatred of vices

[Col. 0030D]

O how many have conceived and brought forth in their minds, by God’s grace, many offspring of the other virtues, yet have been unable to have this son! How many today do we see poor in spirit, rejoicing in hope, fervent in charity, greatly abstinent, exceedingly patient, yet far too lukewarm and sluggish concerning zeal for souls! Some, as if to preserve humility, do not presume to rebuke offenders; others fear to correct sinners lest they seem to disturb brotherly charity. Thus some in one way, others in other ways still, pretend—or believe—that their refusal to be zealous for the Lord [Col. 0031A] is a virtue or belongs among the virtues. On the other hand, many people who undoubtedly act in a spirit of fury think that they act with zeal for uprightness; and what they truly carry out from hatred of people, they think—or pretend—to perform from hatred of vices.
