But I ask those who are such, who believe that they have now begotten Zebulun, to question themselves: do they truly love those whom, as though at Zebulun’s urging, they chastise so harshly? Perhaps they have not yet been able to know by experience what those spiritual delights are to which they wish to appear to invite, by their lashes or even their rebukes, those whom they correct or scourge. For those must be believed to pursue offenders out of compassion rather than cruelty who have known by experience those inward joys to which they invite them through so many [Col. 0031B] pains. We read that Leah bore Judah and Issachar before Zebulun; and we have already said that charity is signified through Judah and experience of spiritual joys through Issachar. Judah and Issachar must be born first, because a mind still devoid of charity and inward sweetness cannot preserve the rule of uprightness in its zeal. For charity teaches how those whom Zebulun chastises ought to be treated. Knowledge of spiritual things teaches what that sweetness is to which those are invited or even compelled, to whom outward delight—namely fleshly pleasure—is forbidden and for whom, under Zebulun’s pressure, they are often reproved more harshly. Judah, therefore, ought to teach the manner, and Issachar [Col. 0031C] the reason for correction, so that, with Judah moderating, it may be done in a spirit of gentleness, and with Issachar suggesting it, it may nevertheless be done for the sake of benefit. Let Zebulun seek their benefit, not his own, so that his striking of offenders may serve usefulness, not vengeance.

## Chapter XLII. What the office of a true zealot is

Zebulun ought not only to correct offenders, but also to defend them against persecutors in time of tribulation. Otherwise it is not true zeal, nor can he truly be called Zebulun if he is readier to strike than to protect. For it is not without reason that this sixth and final son of Leah is called “dwelling of strength”; for Zebulun, as was said above, is interpreted “dwelling of strength.” See how a house protects and surrounds all who inhabit it, yet unless it is strong and firmly fortified, it will not be a dwelling of strength. So likewise perfect zeal, if it is rightly—and indeed truly—to be called Zebulun, must protect the weaker against the powers of the air by teaching and prayer, fortify them on every side against worldly dangers, and persevere in both not merely untiringly but invincibly. One must therefore keep watch on the one hand against the snares of the devil, on the other against the pressures of the world. Whoever you are, if you are strong in both, you are a dwelling of strength and deserve to be called Zebulun. Zebulun ought to be more ready—indeed always readier—to endure evils than to inflict evils. And [Col. 0032A] because he must sometimes become angry with those subject to him on account of fault, he surely grieves more when he is compelled to strike them for their fault than when he is compelled to punish in their defense. Therefore he gladly exposes himself to approaching dangers and voluntarily sets himself against the storms of raging tempests. Otherwise he dwells on the seashore in vain and establishes his dwelling in the harbor of ships in vain, if he trembles at the sea-like dangers of worldly oppression, unless he gently receives and kindly cherishes those long wearied by storms and at last cast ashore.

## Chapter XLIII. That it is the part of a true zealot to keep watch not only against violence but also against fraud
Zebulun, he says, shall dwell by the shore of the sea, and at the haven of ships, reaching as far as Sidon (Gen. XLIX). What reason, then, do you suppose there is for his dwelling on the shore, except that he may fortify the extremities of the land and, as a dwelling-place of strength, protect the weaker members of the Church? He therefore places himself in the path of the dangers of those whom he sees worn down by the continual storms of persecutions. For, that he may always be ready to bring help to the shipwrecked, he remains, as it is written of him, at the haven of ships. Those oppressed by prolonged temptations, who have suffered, as it were, certain shipwrecks and are now almost broken, he knows how to cherish with gentle consolation, to raise to a state of safety, and to call back to a kind of harbor of calm.

In this manner, therefore, Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea, at the haven of ships, reaching as far as Sidon. Extending himself more widely along the seashores and running hither and thither, while everywhere he watches over the protection of his own, while everywhere he prepares himself against the enemy’s assault, he reaches even as far as Sidon. Sidon is interpreted “hunting,” by which the fraudulence of deceptions is quite rightly understood. This Zebulun therefore strives not only to strengthen every weak person against the fury of persecutors, but also to snatch even the simple-minded from the snare of hunters. He reaches as far as Sidon, then, whenever he uncovers the snares of the crafty enemy, whenever he discovers the deceitful designs of false brethren—men whose speech, as the Apostle testifies, spreads like cancer (II Tim. II).

For this is the snare of hunters and, as it were, a net of malignant spirits hunting simple souls: namely, the tongue of flatterers, the tongue of slanderers, of those who sow discord among brethren and stir up anger and quarrels. Zebulun reaches as far as Sidon, therefore, whenever he forestalls the treacherous contrivance of one lying in wait, whether of malicious spirits or of faithless people. For we know that such hunting of souls occurs sometimes through the hidden suggestion of demons, sometimes through the open persuasion of people. Yet Zebulun knows how to detect each kind cautiously, and, having detected it, to expose it. Therefore he fixes the dwelling of his strength opposite the sea, on Sidon’s boundary: on this side to keep watch against the savagery of persecutors, on that against the fraudulence of those who lie in wait; and thus is fulfilled what is written of him: Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea, at the haven of ships, reaching as far as Sidon.

## CHAPTER XLIV. What perfect zeal for souls is, and how great it is.

Let him who can consider what manner of son this is, how great his strength: by whose office a person not only fortifies himself against vices but also strives to rescue others from the snares of sin; and, where he cannot turn their wickedness to the better, endeavors at least to restrain it by resistance. I do not know whether a human being can receive from God anything greater in this life; I do not know whether, for the present, God can bestow upon a person any grace greater than this: that through that person’s ministry perverse people may be changed for the better, and that from sons of the devil they may become sons of God.

Or will it perhaps seem greater to someone to raise the dead? Will it then be greater to raise flesh which will die again than a soul which will live forever? Will it be greater to recall flesh to the joys of the world than to restore to a soul the joys of heaven? Will it be greater to restore to flesh transient goods that will perish again than to give back to the soul eternal goods that will remain forever? O what a dowry, what great dignity, to receive such a grace from God! The bride of God ought not to have received another dowry from her Bridegroom; nor was it fitting that the heavenly Bridegroom should give His bride another dowry than this: that by the grace of adoption she might be able to bear many children to God and enroll, from among the sons of wrath and the sons of Gehenna, heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

Rightly, therefore, at Zebulun’s birth his mother Leah cries: “God has enriched me with a good dowry” (Gen. XXX). Do you see what it is, and how great it is, truly to possess zeal for righteousness, to bear hatred of vices in one’s heart, and to exercise it in truth? He who has begotten such a son sings confidently with the Prophet: “I have hated every way of iniquity” (Ps. CXVIII).

## CHAPTER XLV. How, and from what, ordered shame arises.

But after these six offspring of the virtues, will it at least be granted to anyone to live without sin, so that, after hatred of vices, one may at least be without vice? Who would presume this? Who would dare even to hope for it in this life, when the Apostle says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I)? Who is there—to say nothing of other matters—who can in this life wholly abandon and perfectly avoid even sins of ignorance?

Do even those who rebuke the faults of others utterly strip themselves of every contagion of sin? On the contrary, God often permits those through whom He plans to correct the errors of others to fall grievously, by an ordering of great mercy, so that from their own fault they may learn how merciful they ought to be in rebuking others. But how greatly, think you, are they ashamed? With what humility do they abase themselves when they see that they have fallen into that for which they rebuke others, or perhaps into something more serious—though they ought to have set others a model of uprightness?

Who, think you, can adequately weigh how great a confusion pierces their hearts when they see in their own lives what may rightly be reproved even by those whom, on account of their fault, they remember having often rebuked more bitterly and chastised more harshly? Hence Dina is born after Zebulun, because shame often follows excessive zeal when fault intervenes. For by Dina we understand nothing else than shame, but ordered shame: to be ashamed of sin alone is to have good, ordered shame. But one who has not yet deserved to beget Zebulun vainly believes that he can beget Dina.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Who or what ordered shame is.

Learn first to hate sin, and then you will begin truly to be ashamed of it. If you truly hate it, you are the more quickly ashamed of it. That shame is known to be genuine which hatred of vices precedes and accompanies. Otherwise, if you are caught in sin and, being caught, are confounded by shame, I do not believe that you are ashamed of the fault, but of the disgrace. Such shame arises not so much from sin itself as from injury to one’s reputation. You therefore have no reason to glory as though you had begotten Dina.

Perverse people too certainly have shame—but would that it were good, would that it were ordered! For if they had good shame, perhaps they would not be perverse. If indeed they were perfectly ashamed of sin, they would not commit it so readily. What kind of shame, think you, is it to be ashamed of poverty, ashamed of humility? They are not ashamed to be ashamed of that which the heavenly Teacher was not ashamed to descend from heaven to teach: “Learn of me,” He says, “for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI).

But these people, on the contrary, hating humility rather than pursuing it, are far more ashamed to have filthy clothing than a filthy mind. How many today would be more ashamed to commit a barbarism in prayer against Priscian’s rule than to utter a lie in speech against Christ’s rule. But why do we speak of these people, who often boast even of their crimes, when even those who appear spiritual do not easily overcome this shame? Often, while they serve their neighbors’ benefit in the office of preaching, while perhaps they argue against pride, it happens that they become proud because it is evident that they speak so subtly against pride. And if, perhaps while speaking—as often happens—they were to lengthen a short accent, they would perhaps be more ashamed of the fault in their speech than of the fault of self-exaltation. Believe me: one must not believe that this is the shame which we ought to understand through Dina.

## CHAPTER XLVII. How rare it is to possess true shame.

Do you wish to know still better how rare it is perfectly to tread underfoot human shame and to possess this true and ordered shame—that is, to have begotten Dina? Behold, I leave aside the carnal persons, since for the moment I speak only with spiritual persons. Behold, whoever you are who believe that you have now begotten Dina: if you were compelled to pass naked in body before a crowd, could you avoid being ashamed? Consider, then, whether you are equally confounded when you are defiled in mind by an unclean thought.

Why do you boast any longer that you have begotten Dina and possess ordered shame, if you are less ashamed of the shameful parts of your heart than of those of your body? If you fear the faces of people more than the gaze of angels? Is that which God made well truly more shameful than that which you made badly? Certainly God made even those parts of the body which we call shameful parts; but the shameful parts of the heart were made by no one but you.

Therefore, for one who considers attentively and judges rightly how rare, and how limited to few, it is fully to conquer human shame and to possess only that shame which is ordered, there will be no further reason, I think, to wonder that Leah should conceive or bear such offspring so late.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. What is proper to shame.

But, lest we seem silently to have passed over the meaning of the name, Dina is interpreted “this judgment.” This, therefore, is that judgment by which each person is summoned, convicted, and condemned by his own conscience, and is punished with the fitting penalty of confusion. For if one were not conscious to oneself, there would surely be no reason why one ought to be ashamed. And if confusion involved no punishment, there would be no reason why anyone ought so greatly to detest it or avoid it.

Thus, in a wonderful manner, the mind of each person, convicted by its own conscience and cast down by fitting confusion, at one and the same time pronounces sentence against itself and exacts vengeance upon itself. This, therefore, is that judgment in which one and the same person is both the one who judges and the one judged; the same person who condemns and who is condemned; one and the same person who is punished and who punishes.

It was not without reason, therefore, that Sacred Scripture chose to name this kind of judgment with a demonstrative expression. For *istud* always signifies demonstration; and what else does this addition do but stir the hearer’s mind to wonder? Truly, it is a marvelous judgment, worthy of wonder and worthy to be pronounced demonstratively: in this judgment, the more ardently someone loves himself, the more harshly he rages against himself; and the more vehemently he desires to spare himself, the less he spares himself. For the more anyone fears his own confusion, the more bitterly his confusion torments him.

But perhaps someone may think it surprising that, if this is rightly numbered among the virtues, it is expressed through the female rather than the male sex. Yet we all know that, although women possess a greater beauty of form than men, they nevertheless possess less firmness of strength for virtuous deeds. Who does not know how much shame, however honorable, softens the strength of the heart and how often it hinders strong deeds, while a person’s mind avoids being confounded beyond measure? Dina, therefore, is not a man but a woman; not a son but a daughter.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the usefulness and beauty of shame.

And perhaps it was not without reason that, after Zebulun’s birth, God decreed to give Leah not a son but a daughter, who might gently mitigate her brother’s boldness and soothe with her gentleness the impulses of one raging. For Zebulun, as is clear from what has been said, has vast impulses and bears a great spirit. But women, as we all know, know better than men how gently to address swelling spirits and sweetly to soothe the angry.

It therefore seems very fitting that Dina is born after Zebulun, so that her brother’s fierceness may be tempered by his sister’s gentleness. For in every way a person’s zealot-like impulse is greatly moderated when one finds in oneself something of which to be ashamed. This is surely the reason, unless I am mistaken, why Dina is born after Zebulun: that her modesty may govern her brother’s impulses.

But because Dina undertakes nothing useful, nothing great, she does not deserve to constitute a tribe among the people of Israel. Indeed, as has been said, while she fears excessive confusion, she not only fails to grow strong for strenuous and manly deeds but is accustomed even to impede them. Yet although she is found timid—as a woman is—in deeds of strength, she is prudent and watchful in guarding decency; and although she does not know how to please through strength, she nevertheless knows how to please through the beauty of her form.

For Dina is of admirable beauty and singular appearance; she easily draws the eyes of beholders into admiration of herself and quickly attracts the hearts of admirers to love her. For who does not know how the modesty of shame makes people commendable and lovable to all? Why indeed do we almost always embrace modest people more affectionately than others, except because, while we admire in them the restraint of shame and the grace of modesty, we are in some manner drawn by Dina’s beauty and captivated into love of her by the greatness of her beauty?

O how singular is this Dina’s beauty! How renowned is her love—she whose beauty almost everyone admires, and in whose love almost everyone delights! Let that son of Hamor, Shechem, bear witness to this: he clung to her with such burning love that he preferred all his males to be circumcised without delay rather than not have her.

## CHAPTER L. How a shamefaced mind oversteps the bounds of modesty when it is corrupted by pride and vainglory.

O how many there are even today who do not delay to accomplish, for love of Dina, what they had wished to do for God; and who, when an occasion of shame arises, do not delay to cut off the superfluities of their shameful parts—things which they ought to have cut off for God—in order to avoid injury to their sense of shame. They prefer to undergo the pain of circumcision in cutting away the superfluities of their lives rather than seem shameless and be without shame.

But who is Shechem, or who is his father? Or what do such names as Shechem, interpreted “shoulder” or “labor,” and Hamor, meaning “ass,” signify? Yet if we examine their deed, we more quickly discover who they are. For who are those accustomed to circumcise their shameful parts not so much for God as for Dina, not so much for conscience as for shame? Who else, I say, will they be than love of one’s own excellence and love of vainglory? Such a son from such a father: from love of one’s own excellence comes love of vainglory.

Now observe how foolish this Hamor is, and you will find why he is rightly called an ass. Let us see, then, from what he exalts himself and in what he glories. If it is in what he does not possess but believes that he possesses, what folly, I ask, can be devised more foolish than this? But if he possesses it, let him hear what the Apostle says to him: “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV). The glory rightly belongs not to the receiver but to the giver. For what does a human being possess as his own except sin? And what sort of thing is it to glory in one’s own evil or another’s good?

Such a boaster, therefore, is as truly foolish as he is rightly called an ass. Moreover, the fact that Shechem is called “shoulder” or “labor” seems to point to the same thing. For we bear burdens on our shoulders, and in doing so certainly labor. Shechem therefore puts his shoulder beneath the burden and gladly sweats, but solely in order to make a name for himself.

Let us recall now what we read concerning Issachar: “Issachar,” he says, “a strong ass, saw that rest was good and the land excellent, and put his shoulder beneath the burden” (Gen. XLIX). There Issachar regards himself as an ass and bends his shoulder to bear a burden. Here Hamor is called an ass, and Shechem is shown to have a laboring shoulder. You see that everything done for true joy is also practiced for vain joy. Issachar labors for the rest he has seen; Shechem for the vainglory that he desires. Yet he is rightly called not “laborious” but “labor,” because through his labor he is not brought to true rest. That he is rightly called labor is testified by the labor of hypocrites, who labor only to obtain the empty favor of people.

## CHAPTER LI. How a shamefaced mind is cast down from the rectitude of its intention.

This, then, is the Shechem who meets Dina as she goes out and corrupts her after overpowering her. Thus she loses, once she has gone out, the integrity that perhaps she could have preserved within. For because the beauty of shame is commended, praised, and loved by almost everyone, human praises immediately receive Dina as she goes out and abandons her inward place, quickly forgetting the memory of her weakness which had been accustomed to humble her; and while they caress her with favor, they corrupt her.

For while she delights in offered praise, what else happens but that she is corrupted through Shechem—that is, through love of vainglory? Yet Dina then suffers the losses of her corruption more by a kind of violence than by will, when she resists, as far as she can, the flattering perverse delight. For Shechem overpowers her as though unwilling as often as he draws, even against her will, into shameful delight a mind ashamed of the confusion of its corruption and therefore vigorously resisting.

But what cause, do you suppose, happened to compel her to abandon her own inward place and wander outward, except that, when we are excessively ashamed of our weaknesses, we begin to wonder whether others perhaps feel these same weaknesses in themselves; and it seems to us that we have found a kind of consolation if we discover that, even in our abasement, we have companions? Hence we begin to inquire more curiously into the pursuits of others, frequently to look about at their faces, gestures, and the bearing of their whole bodies, and gladly to learn their hidden matters from others’ reports.

Thus, while Dina tries to discern in others the state of their souls from outward signs, what else does she do but, abandoning what is her own, go out to see women and wander abroad? While Dina therefore curiously surveys women’s appearances, she finds some much and others less beautiful. And while she often silently compares them with herself, observing how many she far surpasses in the greatness of her beauty, what wonder if the appetite for vainglory assaults her more violently? Since she is not sufficient to repel its attack by resistance, what else occurs but that, conquered by Shechem’s strength, she yields?

## CHAPTER LII. How, at one and the same time, by what one is corrupted other virtues are sometimes nourished.

It should certainly be noted that at one and the same time Dina is corrupted and her brothers are occupied in feeding their flocks. For the mind that abounds in charity and the other virtues is accustomed, just as it grieves over its own evils, so also to rejoice over its neighbors’ goods. Therefore, while it surveys the lives of its neighbors, considers their goods, and compares its own goods with theirs, it cannot fail often to favor its own good qualities, nor can it fail to rejoice with others over their goods.

A devout mind, as it more diligently observes one person’s progress, another’s failure, this person’s weakness, and that person’s perfection, is touched by various affections, now by some and now by others in turn. It begins to fear for some, to grieve for others, to hope good things for these and better things for those. In some it sees what it loves, and finds cause to rejoice for them; in others it sees what it rightly abhors, and for which it ought rightly to grieve.

Thus, while good affections play around simple thoughts which arise here and there from the observed and pleasing discipline of neighbors, what else do Dina’s brothers, Leah’s sons, do but feed their flocks? Do you see how, at one and the same time, true love of neighbor does one thing and vain self-love another? True love of neighbor provides pasture for the brothers’ flocks; vain self-love supplies an occasion for Dina’s corruption.

That the matter does not escape the father even before word reaches the brothers suggests nothing else to us than that awareness of corruption strikes the mind first through thought rather than through affection. But when the matter lingers longer in the heart and is more often repeated in thought, it sometimes penetrates into the inmost part of the heart and pierces the heart’s affection. Therefore, when the mind is affected by anxiety over the matter and touched in turn by various affections, there is no doubt that word has now reached Leah’s sons, Dina’s brothers.

## CHAPTER LIII. With what urgency and caution a depraved intention must be corrected.

But how wildly, do you suppose, do they rage when they can no longer remain ignorant of, or at least pass over, their sister’s corruption? For what does Scripture say of them except that they were deeply angered, and again that they were enraged because of their sister’s violation? (Gen. XXXIV). This anger—or rather frenzy—of the brothers teaches us how much each person ought to be angry with himself, how to be indignant, how to accuse himself, and how sharply to rebuke himself, when he recognizes that he has defiled his conscience with empty glorying.

Therefore whoever he may be, in order to heal the swelling of his mind, ought to set his weaknesses before his eyes and recall to memory his faults—without which no one passes through this life. He should carefully observe how often he is shameful in deed, unworthy in speech, and unclean in thought, so that he may thereby plainly conclude how many things in his conduct he can find which ought rightly to be cut away, if he truly wishes to glory and not to glory shamelessly.

When reflection upon such a condition is turned over in the mind, what else happens than that a covenant of circumcision is established with Hamor’s son? For what else is it to say, “Cut away the shameful parts of your conduct,” than, “Circumcise the foreskins of your males”? And what else is it to say, “Otherwise you will be unable not to glory shamelessly,” than, “Otherwise you will be unable to be joined to Dina”? For if Shechem is glorying, and Dina worthy shame, what else will shameless glorying—glorying without shame—be than Shechem without Dina?

Inveterate habits, which are hard to conquer, are rightly signified by the male sex. These are the males whom Dina’s brothers wished to circumcise; yet Scripture testifies that they proposed this condition of circumcision deceitfully. It is evident, so that we may readily perceive it, that they had no intention whatsoever of giving their sister to such a husband; and, although he might have been able to fulfill the stipulated condition, they nevertheless judged him entirely unworthy of such a marriage.

Indeed, even if we could entirely cut away from our lives all that is shameful and be wholly cleansed from everything, we should nevertheless glory not in our own merits but only in the Lord. Thus perhaps Dina’s brothers proposed harsh terms to him so that he might altogether despair of union with their sister. But Shechem is more prepared to endure any hardship, however severe, than to bear separation from his beloved Dina. And it often happens, as we said above, that what we could not draw forth from our mind when we intended to do it for God, we ourselves find easy to accomplish when we fear that otherwise we shall incur loss of shame.

## CHAPTER LIV. How, and how cautiously, one ought to change one’s intention without abandoning honorable conduct.

What shall we say to these things? Shall we perhaps do better to groan silently than to answer anything, since we cannot deny them? I shall certainly say this: that which rightly displeased the brothers could not rightly appease them—the circumcision performed not so much for God as for Dina, not so much for divine ordinance as for human shame.

Yet it was evil in them to exceed the measure of just severity and utterly fail to preserve the measure of equity in avenging the injury. Jacob therefore rightly rebukes their rash boldness and justly condemns such undiscerning severity. O how much better it would have been to lead gradually to the true worship of God men circumcised, though not so much for God as for Dina, than to strike them down by an unforeseen and sudden death!

Let everyone therefore gather and carefully observe from this how one ought to spare those whom one has circumcised, though one remembers that one did not circumcise them for God. Who are circumcised in this manner except dispositions corrected without a good intention? Yet in such cases we ought not to destroy the honorable features of conduct, but to change the intention. Therefore they err—certainly they err—who reject good works even though they may perhaps have been begun with an evil intention. What else, then, do such avengers of their own errors do but violently rush upon the circumcised with Simeon and Levi and kill them?

## CHAPTER LV. By what consideration especially we ought to chastise the depravity of intention.

It is worthwhile also to consider carefully how so few could inflict so great a slaughter. But clearly they were aided by a choice opportunity of time, when the bitterness of pain had overcome those who had been circumcised and were to be killed by them. For this purpose the third day of circumcision was chosen, on which, Scripture testifies, pain is usually most severe.

But what are these days, and why are they said to be only three? If night rightly signifies ignorance, day signifies knowledge. The first day, therefore, is knowledge of those things which are outside us; the second, knowledge of those things which are within us; the third, knowledge of those things which are above us. Outside us are bodily things; within us, spiritual things; above us, divine things.

Therefore, for those who circumcise themselves yet do not do this for God, the first consideration ought to be—or rather usually is—when they carefully observe what hardship they have endured outwardly. The second consideration ought to be what they have acquired inwardly through so many sufferings of the body—or rather how much they have truly lost inwardly through the blemish of a perverse intention. The third consideration will be what recompense they ought to expect from God, whom they do not doubt that they have provoked rather than pleased by the service of feigned servitude.

On the first day of the first consideration, the forsaken license of a beloved habit returns to memory, and pain undoubtedly results—indeed, severe pain—because what was possessed with love is not left without pain. On the second day of the second consideration, the mind finds that, through losses of the body, it has come to losses of the mind; and the pain is surely the more just and perhaps the more grievous. On the third day of the third consideration, it discovers that it has endured grievous things by its own judgment but ought to expect graver things from divine judgment. This is that third day on which, Scripture testifies, pain is usually most severe.

For how great a pain pierces the mind when it carefully considers the evil it has endured, the evil it has committed, and the evil it has deserved: the evil it has endured outwardly in bodily torment; the evil it has contracted inwardly in the guilt of sin; the evil it has deserved from God before the Creator’s sight. Certainly, whoever among those uselessly circumcised can reach this day has grieved not merely grievously but most grievously.

## CHAPTER LVI. That in all its corruption the mind ought both to grieve patiently and not despair of its correction.

Yet a mind conscious of its own sin and confounded by its weakness ought both to grieve patiently and not despair of its correction. It must indeed grieve over its corruption and nevertheless hope for correction, so that, afflicted by measured grief and raised by confidence in hope, it may both make satisfaction for the past and provide for the future.

We have already said above how we are to understand grief and hope through Simeon and Levi. These are Dina’s two brothers, Simeon and Levi, fierce avengers of her wrongs—but would that they were as discerning as they are strong! It belongs to Simeon to make satisfaction for what was done wrongly; it belongs to Levi to raise the mind toward what must be provided for in the future. If, therefore, you grieve over corruption but despair of correction, you have Simeon, but alone. If you neglect satisfaction for the past but hope for caution in the future, Levi is there, but alone. For so great a matter, therefore, it is necessary that both come together and that each bring help to the other.

## CHAPTER LVII. How, and with what caution, a corrupted mind should be scourged through reproach for sin or the exaction of a debt.

But we must again consider that, in what they do forcefully, they often exceed the measure of just balance; this we easily demonstrate from the deed presently in our hands. Having seized their swords, they violently kill those bound to them by a covenant of alliance, and for the violated chastity of one woman they cause the sudden slaughter of so many men.

Simeon’s sword is reproach; Levi’s sword is exaction. Simeon is accustomed vehemently to reproach a corrupted mind for the evil it has done; Levi, however, is accustomed vehemently to exact the good that ought to have been done. What else, then, is it for them to fight with these swords than to scourge the mind with the goads of reproach and exaction?

Inflamed fiercely by these goads, the minds of some often lament inconsolably even things which they cannot possibly avoid. Driven by these goads, they often presume even to begin things which they are altogether unable to complete. Hence the immoderate sadness of some; hence also indiscreet abstinence, which drains not only the body’s strength but even the mind’s vigor.

For we have seen some, while Simeon raged, so swallowed up by irrational sadness that they could be raised at all by no consolation. We have known others to fall so grievously through immoderate abstinence that afterward no abundance of delicacies, no diligence of cooks, could restore them. Behold how these warriors—I mean Simeon and Levi—fight and take vengeance. For what else is it for them, with swords seized, to kill Dina’s lovers than, through reproach for unavoidable things or exaction of impossible things, so to weaken not only bodily strength but mental vigor that the mind cannot restrain itself from its excesses even out of human shame?

Hence Jacob rightly says to them: “Simeon and Levi are brothers, vessels of iniquity making war. Let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor my glory be in their assembly” (Gen. XLIX). O what warriors, who, wishing to seem to have acted bravely, kill the companions of their peace as cruelly as violently! “Vessels of iniquity making war”—but let not my soul enter into their counsel. O ill-advised men, who, while they presume here to do what they cannot accomplish, lose even what they could have accomplished! Therefore let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor my glory be in their assembly.

It is not good glorying to walk in things great and wonderful above oneself, so that one may seem to glory in one’s own strength. Such glorying, I say, is not good. Therefore, “Let not my glory be in their assembly; for,” he says, “in their fury they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER LVIII. How, through excessive affliction, the mind is sometimes unbridled even into shamelessness.

What is understood by “a man” except the vigor of the mind? What by “a wall” except the discipline of the body? That man, Dina’s lover, is therefore truly killed when, through excessive affliction, the mind’s vigor is exhausted and the soul is unbridled even into open shamelessness. Dina’s lover undoubtedly perishes by the sword when, through excessive affliction, the mind’s vigor fails so completely that, as was said, it cannot restrain itself from its excesses even out of human shame.

The wall is destroyed when, through immoderate abstinence, the rigor of previous discipline is wholly dissipated. But in warriors of this kind, what is most remarkable—indeed, most detestable above all—is that they yield to the counsel of no prudent person whatsoever; indeed, they do not even yield to their own experience, not even when they have already begun to fail in body and waste away in heart.

Their obstinacy is struck by the dart of a curse when Jacob says to them: “Cursed be their fury, because it is obstinate; and their indignation, because it is harsh” (Gen. XLIX). A marvelous obstinacy, but no less madness: they can be restrained from the impetus of their course, from the deviation of their error, only by the curb of impossibility. Behold how these vessels of iniquity making war know how to fight; behold what great things they do, and what great things are done, for Dina. For Dina males are circumcised; for Dina the circumcised are slain. All this is done for Dina, all for human shame.

## CHAPTER LIX. That not even ordered shame is good unless it is also moderate.

But perhaps you wonder: since above we reproved human shame, why do we now teach that it belongs to Dinah, when by Dinah alone we ought to understand ordered shame? But it is one thing for people to be ashamed because of God, and another for them to be ashamed because of themselves. “So let your light shine,” says Scripture, “that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5). It is good, therefore, to be ashamed of disgrace, not so much for our own sake as for the glory of God. And perhaps this is Dinah’s going out: being ashamed, for God’s sake, of human disgrace. For undoubtedly Dinah is found within when even our conscience is ashamed before God of its hidden things. Thus, to be ashamed before men for God’s sake is to possess good shame, of the kind which we do not doubt belongs to Dinah. Such shame, therefore, is ordered and may in one respect rightly be called human. Yet this kind is truly good only if it is not excessive. Certainly, if Dinah had still been a little girl, or had kept herself within the privacy of her chamber, she would not have incurred the stain of violation and would not have become the cause of such great evils.

## CHAPTER LX. A brief recapitulation concerning the number of the principal affections and the manner of ordering them

This is Dinah, who is born after Issachar and Zebulun: because, after one has tasted the joy of inward sweetness and acquired a true hatred of vices, one is ashamed of one’s own weakness more truly—and, the more truly, more vehemently. For by Issachar we understand joy of conscience; by Zebulun, hatred of wickedness; by Dinah, the beauty of shame. These indeed are the last three children of Leah. If we count them together with the preceding four, we find without doubt that there are seven. For we have already said far above that the principal affections are seven; when we order them within ourselves, we reduce them to the number of virtues. First fear is ordered, then sorrow; after these, hope and love. After these four, joy and anger are ordered; and last of all, shame. Thus Jacob’s begetting children of this kind by Leah means nothing other than that the mind, by ordering the movements of its affections, has produced from itself a worthy offspring of virtues. By Reuben, therefore, Jacob’s firstborn, we understand ordered fear; by Simeon, ordered sorrow; by Levi and Judah, ordered hope and ordered love. By Issachar is understood ordered joy; by [Col. 0044A] Zebulun, ordered anger; by Dinah, ordered shame.

## CHAPTER LXI. That ordered affections are truly good if they are also moderated

It must be known, however, that these affections are believed to be truly good when they are not only ordered but also moderated. For often, when they exceed the restraint of discernment, they lose the name of virtue. But perhaps we shall show this better by an example, if we take our examples from the firstborn of the brothers himself. Certainly, if immoderate fear were not dangerous, Jacob would never have said in speaking to Reuben: “You are poured out like water; do not increase, because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch” (Gen. 49). If by Reuben we ought to understand ordered fear, why, I ask, does Jacob command him not to increase, unless because it is evil for any ordered fear to exceed the measure of equity?

## CHAPTER LXII. The ways in which fear oversteps the measure of equity

This son often exceeds the measure of equity in two ways: either because he extends himself too little toward a single matter, or because he spreads himself indiscriminately toward countless, even useless, matters. Who would deny that Judas, after the crime of betrayal, ought rightly to have been afraid? But who does not see that the most detestable thing in him was this: while he would not, or did not know how to, keep measure in his fear, by despairing he heaped upon the evil that he might have corrected an end more detestable than its beginning?

But that excess of fear which pours itself out indiscriminately upon many things deceives more easily; for it sometimes steals even into perfected men. For which prelate, however perfect, while providing the necessities of life for those subject to him, so tempers the cares of his concern that he never fears beyond what is right because of adverse contingencies? Yet such fear belongs to Reuben only when it arises, not from love of the world, but from love of one’s neighbor. But who could enumerate all the doubtful eventualities of disadvantages arising on every side, over which he is compelled to tremble by the weakness, if not his own, at least of those subject to him? And who does not see how difficult—indeed, nearly impossible—it is never to exceed the bounds of just fear?

Hence it often happens that the more prudent a person is, the more anxious he is found to be; and the more penetratingly he knows how to foresee the uncertain occurrences of surrounding dangers, the more he is compelled to loosen repeatedly the reins of his fearful concern. This is also fittingly understood of what Jacob says to Reuben: “You are poured out like water; do not increase” (Gen. 49). For water sometimes signifies prudence of the flesh, just as wine often signifies special understanding. This water is changed into wine for someone when, through God’s inspiration, he is raised by the ladder of outward knowledge to an understanding of invisible things—when “the invisible things of God are clearly perceived, being understood by the things that are made from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1). Such water abounds in a person in proportion as his mind expands more copiously in knowledge of outward things. And the more abundantly this water grows, while it cautiously surveys everything, the more surely it produces and spreads a denser forest of fearful anxiety. Hence it is rightly said here: “You are poured out like water; do not increase.” Therefore, when the water of worldly knowledge abounds, one must take the greatest care that the fear of manifold anxiety not grow beyond measure.

## CHAPTER LXIII. To what shameless wandering excessive fear prostitutes the mind

Certainly, while Reuben was still a little child and lived his boyish years, he did not presume to violate his father’s bed, either because he could not or because he did not dare. Yet when grown, he burst forth into such audacity, as is read of him, that he violated his father’s concubine—namely Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant. But if Bilhah signifies imagination, how do we suppose that such a maidservant is violated? What is Bilhah’s violation except the disordered and shameless wandering of thought or imagination?

For excessive fear sometimes not merely corrupts imagination, I say, but prostitutes it, so that even during prayer it can scarcely, or not at all, restrain itself from its fornications. For when, through excessive anxiety, the mind often receives by imagination phantasms of worldly affairs even while praying, what else does Bilhah do but open her bosom to Reuben’s fornications? Consider, therefore, how unfitting it is that at the very time when you ought to beseech the Lord to remove eternal evils, you begin to keep only temporal dangers before your eyes and turn them over in your heart alone: to forget those things for which you came, and to remember only those things which you ought to have forgotten.

Hence it happens that a mind which formerly used imagination to set before itself alone, at every hour, the future good things or evils, later, subdued by excessive fear, cannot exclude from the inner chamber of the heart even briefly the attacks of worldly cares. Therefore, since imagination is often led by excessive fear to such an imprudent wandering of thoughts, the father rightly speaks to Reuben, reproaching him for Bilhah’s violation: “You are poured out like water; do not increase, because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch.”

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the force or efficacy of fear, without which we neither abandon evils nor begin good things

But to speak more openly of this affection: it seems to possess greater efficacy than the others, whether for good or for evil. For by it the mind is often cast down from its state of rectitude; yet, when cast down in any way, it is never restored without it. For who is freed from any sin, however small, without fear? Without fear we never abandon our evils; without fear we do not even begin to do good things.

Do not Jacob’s words plainly speak of this, if they are rightly understood, where it is said: “Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength, the beginning of my sorrow, first in gifts, greater in dominion” (Gen. 49)? There follows also that of which we have already said something: “You are poured out like water; do not increase.” How Reuben is the firstborn, and how he is the beginning of sorrow, is, I think, sufficiently clear from what has already been said above. But how he is Jacob’s strength, and the other things said of him, can easily be shown. “You,” he says, “are my strength.” For who has ever proved victorious in that battle in which spirit desires against flesh and flesh against spirit? Who, I ask, has defeated so numerous an army of his own desires if he fought without fear? Reuben is rightly called firstborn, therefore, because every good thing begins from the fear of the Lord; rightly called strength, because through the fear of the Lord the heart is strengthened against its desires; rightly called the beginning of his sorrow, because useful sorrow accompanies the fear of the Lord. For a person’s sorrow of mind to be truly his own and useful to him, the fear of the Lord must precede it.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the primacy of fear, and which affections rule over which others

“First in gifts, greater in dominion.” Among all God’s gifts which seem to pertain to human salvation, good will is recognized as the first and principal gift, through which the image of divine likeness is restored in us. Whatever a person does cannot be good unless it proceeds from a good will. Whatever is done from a good will cannot be evil. Without good will you cannot be saved at all; with good will you cannot perish at all. O wonderful gift! O singular gift! This is that first or principal gift attributed to the firstborn Reuben, because without doubt an evil will is changed into a good one through fear of the Lord. Why then should he not be first in gifts who receives the first and principal gift? First, because every good begins from good will; principal, because nothing more useful than good will is given to human beings.

“First in gifts, greater in dominion.” Who would deny that this Reuben is greater in dominion than the other brothers, since he often even rules over them all? Levi gives way before his presence, because when fear comes upon one, hope falls; Judah often withdraws at his command. Zebulun approaches, because when fear constrains, charity often grows cold and hatred rises. At his nod Issachar goes out and Simeon enters, because when fear enters, joy is often excluded and sorrow admitted.

We have seen how Reuben sometimes rules even over his brothers; let us see how he extends his dominion more broadly than the others. Certainly, there are things that we love and things that we hate; but we are accustomed to fear for both, since we often fear losing the former and encountering the latter. Judah and Zebulun divide the kingdom between them, but Reuben stretches himself over the whole; for true love extends only to good things, true hatred only to evil things, but fear pours itself out upon both the one and the other.

Zebulun admits his brother Simeon into a portion of his territory. For we grieve over adversities, but not over all of them, because we do not endure everything. Levi is less in dominion than Judah, yet much greater in dominion than Issachar. For there are more things that we ought to love than things that we dare to hope for. Yet it is evident that the material for hope is more abundant than that for joy, because the things we possess and rejoice in are few compared with those we hope to possess.

Judah and Zebulun therefore surpass the other brothers in the greatness of their dominion; nevertheless, they cannot extend themselves to Reuben’s measure. Thus Reuben precedes them all, leaving the others far behind him. For everything that people are known to love, hope for, hate, grieve over, or rejoice in can generate from itself causes of manifold fear. Often, concerning one thing that we love, we discover several causes for fear. For in as many ways as it can be lost, so many occasions of fear can it give.

This Reuben, therefore, greatly enlarges his kingdom; but strength is supplied to him not only by the multiplicity of hidden things, but also by the mutability of things apparent. Of what can I be secure, when I possess nothing that I cannot lose? When do I attain certainty of knowledge here, where I know immeasurably more things that I do not know than that I do know? Therefore, because fear spreads more broadly than the other affections, Reuben is rightly said, in comparison with his brothers, to be greater in dominion. Yet he is forbidden by his father to increase—namely, at the time when he had been poured out like water, when he had already gone up to his father’s bed and defiled his couch: “Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength, the beginning of my sorrow, first in gifts, greater in dominion. You are poured out like water; you shall not increase, because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch.”

See how great an evil Reuben presumed, because he grew beyond measure. Great danger is quickly incurred if our fear is not moderated by discernment.

## CHAPTER LXVI. How virtues are turned into vices unless they are moderated by discernment

So also we ought to believe concerning the other affections: they are dangerous unless we restrain them within the bounds of equity. Certainly, from the aforesaid deed of Simeon and Levi we can readily perceive how evil it is for sorrow and hope to exceed measure. Of them Jacob says: “Cursed be their fury, because it was obstinate, and their indignation, because it was harsh” (Gen. 49). Therefore, one must carefully guard against this in regard to all the affections: they must be not only ordered, but moderated.

For excessive fear often falls into despair; excessive sorrow into bitterness; immoderate hope into presumption; superfluous love into flattery; excessive joy into dissipation; unrestrained anger into rage. In this manner virtues are turned into vices if they are not moderated by discernment. Do you see how all the other virtues require the virtue of discernment, lest they lose the name of virtue?

## CHAPTER LXVII. How, and how late, discernment arises, although it is reason’s first offspring

This is Joseph, who indeed is born late but is loved by his father more than the others. For who does not know that the true goods of the mind can neither be acquired nor preserved without discernment? This virtue is therefore rightly loved in a special manner, since without it none is acquired, none perfected, none preserved. But we scarcely deserve to receive such a son except late, because we are instructed in the perfection of discernment only through great practice and through great experience.

Must we not first be exercised in the individual virtues, and discover what we can experience in each, before we can acquire full knowledge of all of them and judge each sufficiently? We learn much about discernment by reading, much by hearing, much from the judgment of reason implanted in us; nevertheless, we are never fully instructed concerning it without the teaching of experience. The one who must judge concerning all things ought to come after all of them.

First, then, we must strive to apply frequent diligence to the individual virtues. While we do so, we must necessarily fall often; and so we must rise often, learning through frequent falls with what watchfulness and caution we ought to acquire or preserve the goods of virtues. Thus, thus, while the discipline of virtues is learned through long practice, the mind, exercised for a long time, is at last brought to full discernment of moral conduct and rightly rejoices as though Joseph had been born.

Before his birth, while his brothers still do everything without discernment, the more they presume many things beyond their strength, the more often they fall more grievously and shamefully. Hence, as we have already said, Dinah is born after them, because the shame of embarrassment frequently accompanies a disgraceful fall. But after Dinah has been born, and as it were through the disgrace of their shame, the brothers discover and learn by experience that nothing is better than to be governed by counsel: “For a prudent man is better than a strong man” (Prov. 16). “A prudent man speaks victories, and he who does all things with counsel will never repent” (Prov. 21).

When, therefore, the necessary usefulness of counsel is known through experience, sought more attentively through diligence, and found, Joseph is in some manner born, by whom the virtue of discernment is understood. The reason is also clear why none of the maidservants, nor even Leah herself, but Rachel alone, could bear such a son. For to discern, as also to understand, belongs not to sensation, not to imagination, nor finally to affection itself, but to reason alone. If, then, by Rachel we understand reason, we readily find why Joseph can be born only of Rachel: because we do not doubt that discernment arises from reason alone. Such offspring from such a mother: Joseph from Rachel, discernment from reason.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the usefulness and property of discernment

This is that Joseph who alone among his brothers is clothed in a long tunic, because only that action which is moderated by the prudence of discernment is brought to the heel of perfection and the boundary of its due end. This is that Joseph who is loved by his father above all his brothers, because the guardian-virtue of all virtues is rightly preferred to the others. This is that Joseph, dreamer and interpreter of dreams: because true discernment, at the very point of temptation and amid the phantasms of suggestions themselves, detects future dangers from their character; it discloses to others the snares of impending evils through confession of their thoughts, and makes them cautious concerning future dangers.

This is Joseph, whom his own people envy and strangers revere; whom the Hebrews sell and the Egyptians buy. For people more quickly yield to counsel, and more readily submit to another’s prudence when they recognize the darkness of their own error than when they presume upon their own righteousness or prudence.

This is Joseph, spouse of the virgin, lover but not violator of chastity: because discernment is accustomed to be the guardian, not the corrupter, of inward purity. This is the boy and messenger who alone could remain with blessed Job through all his persecution, and who hastened at once to report to him the losses inflicted; because without discernment the mind neither recognizes nor corrects the losses of virtues. That boy does not know how to perish with those who perish; discernment does not know how to fail amid the losses of possessions or the increase of temptations, but how to advance. For the more sharply we are pressed by temptations and the more frequently we are exercised by dangers, the more perfectly we are instructed in discernment; and the losses of other virtues are often gains for discernment.

Thus Joseph knows not only how to grow with those who grow, not only to advance with those who advance, but also to move toward progress from the failure of his brothers and to acquire gains of prudence from the losses of others. Such a son is rightly called Joseph, for Joseph means “increase.” Hence his father rightly says of him: “Joseph is a growing son, a growing son and beautiful in appearance” (Gen. 49). He is rightly called increase, rightly called a growing son, who is always increasing and whose growth does not end until the end.

## CHAPTER LXIX. How useful, and likewise how difficult, it is perfectly to obey discernment

The greatness of this virtue is attested by Joseph’s dreams themselves and by his father’s words, where it is read: “Shall I, your mother, and your brothers indeed bow down to you upon the earth?” (Gen. 37). Father, mother, and brothers bow before this Joseph, because they sometimes obey discernment either by voluntary choice or compelled necessity.

For through discernment the sun of that intellectual world—the inward eye of the heart, namely the attention of the mind—is directed. Through discernment the subtlety of reason from which it arises is sharpened. Through discernment the entire brotherly kinship of virtues is moderated; and any virtue that does not acquiesce in its counsel, that does not submit itself to discernment, soon loses the name of virtue.

He is the one who does not neglect the negligences of his brothers; he is the one who rebukes their excesses. In his presence they may not presume anything beyond their powers; in his presence they may omit nothing through negligence. In his presence they may not turn aside to the right or to the left, do anything sluggishly or rashly, presume anything before its time, or delay anything beyond the fitting opportunity.

Hence comes that serious and almost irreconcilable discord between him and his brothers, of which Scripture does not remain silent when it plainly declares that his brothers hated him and could not speak peacefully to him. For Joseph’s admonitions seem to them very burdensome, his rules harsh, his counsels unbearable. What indeed is harder or more difficult than to neglect nothing that ought to be done, and in every action never to disturb measure, confuse order, or exceed the limit? Believe me: the mind exacts nothing more difficultly from itself than to keep measure in every one of its affections.

For Joseph’s brothers, when they undertake some great thing and hear applause on every side—“Well done! Well done!”—are accustomed to extend the hands of their effort not only toward useless things but even toward impossible ones. Frequently the affections of the mind are unbridled by such acclamation of flatterers into the audacity of immoderate presumption; indeed, when the intention of the mind is corrupted, they are often led and cast down into the crime of hypocrisy.

This is that worst crime, more abominable than the rest because especially hateful to God, for which Joseph accuses his brothers before his father, as Scripture itself plainly declares when it says: “Joseph accused his brothers before his father of a most grievous crime” (ibid.). No vice is more rightly understood as the one God especially detests than hypocrisy. For, as Augustine testifies, simulated righteousness is not righteousness but double iniquity. This vice is uncovered by Joseph when the evil that lies in ambush is detected and rebuked through discernment. This vice then corrupts the sons, and this vice then corrects the father, when it strikes the affection more harshly, occupies it for longer, yet does not bend the mind as far as consent.

## CHAPTER LXX. On the manifold office of true discernment

It belongs to Joseph, therefore, not only to look carefully around for this vice but for every lurking evil still hidden, to foresee it cautiously, detect it skillfully, uncover it promptly, and rebuke it more sharply. The care and guardianship of all his brothers belongs to Joseph; the discipline of each belongs to him; the ordering of what must be done belongs to him; the provision for things to come belongs to him.

His office is diligently to observe and frequently to examine how much the mind advances each day, or perhaps how much it declines; by what thoughts it is more strongly assailed and by what affections it is more frequently touched. This Joseph must know perfectly not only the vices of the heart but also the weaknesses of the body, and seek out and apply remedies for health according to what each requires.

He ought to know not only his own vices but also the gifts of grace and the merits of virtues; he must distinguish these carefully and weigh subtly which are goods of nature and which gifts of grace. He must have readily at hand the engines of temptation by which the evil spirit attacks him; the greatness of the consolations in spiritual joys in which he abounds; how often the divine Spirit visits him; and how, although the Spirit is one, he is not always touched by Him uniformly and in the same manner, but is now filled with the spirit of wisdom, now with the spirit of understanding, now with the spirit of counsel, or with other affections of that Spirit.

And, to conclude everything briefly, this Joseph of ours ought, as far as possible, fully to know the entire state and condition of the inner and outer person, and to inquire subtly and investigate diligently not only what that person is like but also what he ought to be like.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On reason’s twofold offspring: namely, the grace of discernment and the grace of contemplation

Through this Joseph the mind is continually instructed and is at length led to full knowledge of itself; through his brother of the same womb, Benjamin, it is at length raised to contemplation of God. For just as through Joseph we understand the grace of discernment, so through Benjamin we understand the grace of contemplation. Both are born of the same mother, because knowledge both of God and of oneself is received through reason.

Benjamin is born long after Joseph, because a mind that has not long been exercised and fully instructed in self-knowledge is not raised to knowledge of God. In vain does one lift the eye of the heart to see God who is not yet fit to see oneself. A person must first learn to know his own invisible things before presuming that he can grasp the invisible things of God. You must first know the invisible things of your own spirit before you can be fit to know the invisible things of God. Otherwise, if you cannot know yourself, with what face do you presume to grasp things that are above you?

## CHAPTER LXXII. How, through full knowledge of oneself, the mind is raised to contemplation of God

The rational mind undoubtedly finds itself to be the chief and principal mirror for seeing God. For if “the invisible things of God are clearly perceived, being understood by the things that are made” (Rom. 1), where, I ask, are the traces of knowledge more expressly impressed than in His image? We read and believe that the human being, according to the soul, was made in God’s likeness (Gen. 1). Therefore, so long as we walk by faith and not by sight (2 Cor. 5), so long as we still see through a mirror and in an enigma (1 Cor. 13), we cannot find a mirror more suited to a vision, so to speak, of His image than the rational spirit.

Let whoever thirsts to see God cleanse his mirror, cleanse his spirit. The true Joseph, therefore, does not cease to hold this mirror, wipe it, and gaze into it unceasingly: to hold it, lest by falling downward it cling to the earth through love; to wipe it, lest it be soiled in the dust of vain thoughts; to gaze into it, lest it turn the eye of its attention toward vain pursuits.

When the mirror has been wiped and carefully examined for a long time, a certain brightness of divine light begins to shine through it, and an immense ray of an unfamiliar vision appears to the eyes. This light had irradiated the eyes of him who said: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given joy into my heart” (Ps. 4). From the vision of this light, which the mind marvels at within itself, it is wonderfully kindled and encouraged to see the light that is above itself. From this vision, I say, it conceives the flame of desire to see God and takes confidence.

Thus the mind which already burns with desire for this vision, if it now hopes for what it desires, may know that it has conceived Benjamin. For it conceives by hoping and gives birth by desiring; and the more desire grows, the nearer it comes to birth.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. How arduous and difficult it is to obtain the grace of contemplation

Yet we know nonetheless—for we have learned this too from Scripture’s teaching—that “hope deferred afflicts the soul” (Prov. 13). Nothing so affects the mind as impatient desire. What, then, is sought more healthfully than the sweetness of this vision? What is felt more sweetly? What does the mind experience more delightfully? Rachel knows this, for reason cannot be ignorant of it: in comparison with this sweetness, every sweetness is bitter.

Hence she can neither relax her diligence nor moderate her desire. Hence comes that great anxiety of the woman in labor and that immensity of pain. From where, do you suppose, comes so great a magnitude of sorrow, except from unceasing diligence and impatient desire? Daily both labor from desire and sorrow from labor increase. Desire from diligence and diligence from desire are continually increased.

Rachel nevertheless knows that this undertaking exceeds her strength, yet she cannot moderate either her diligence or her desire. For the mind never attains such great grace by its own industry. It is God’s gift, not human merit. Yet no one receives such and so great a grace without immense diligence and ardent desire. Rachel knows this, and therefore multiplies her diligence and kindles her desire more sharply with daily increases.

For amid such anxiety of daily striving, amid such immensity of pain, Benjamin is born and Rachel dies: because, when the human mind is rapt above itself, it transcends all the narrow limits of human reasoning. For before what it beholds, lifted above itself and rapt in ecstasy, from the light of divinity, all human reason succumbs. What is Rachel’s death except the failure of reason?

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On that kind of contemplation which is above reason

Therefore, as Benjamin is born, Rachel dies, because the mind rapt into contemplation experiences how great is the failure of human reason. Was Rachel not dead then, and did not every faculty of human reasoning fail in the Apostle, when he said: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Cor. 12)?

Let no one, then, suppose that he can penetrate to the brightness of that divine light by argument, or believe that he can comprehend it by human reasoning. For if that divine light could be reached by any argument, it would surely not be inaccessible. Finally, the Apostle boasts not that he went there, but undoubtedly that he was rapt there: “I know,” he says, “a man—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—rapt up to the third heaven” (ibid.).

But this third heaven is the heaven that is between earth and heaven—that is, between body and spirit [the wording is difficult]. Yet the dignity of the human spirit is one thing, that of the angelic spirit another, and the excellence of the divine Spirit far different. For the excellence of angelic nature, free from both, far surpasses the dignity of the human spirit, which is subject to punishment and fault; but incomparably beyond both goes that Spirit who made both.

The mind of any person is truly raised to each of these heavens when, leaving the depths of earthly thoughts, it is fixed in their contemplation. Knowledge of oneself pertains to the first heaven; contemplation of God to the third. Who, then, do you think ascends to this third heaven, except the Son of Man who descended and is in heaven? Therefore, even if there are those who “go up to the heavens and go down to the depths,” they do not ascend except perhaps to the first and second, for they cannot reach the third. Human beings can indeed be rapt to this heaven; they cannot ascend to it at all by themselves.

Nevertheless, we can distinguish the knowledge of God that can be possessed in this life by three grades, and divide it into three heavens according to this threefold difference of grades. God is seen in one way through faith, known in another through reason, and perceived in another through contemplation. The first vision belongs to the first heaven, the second to the second, and the third to the third. The first is below reason; the third is above reason. Human beings can indeed ascend to the first and second heavens of contemplation, but they never attain that which is above reason unless, through an ecstasy of mind, they are rapt above themselves. That we ought to understand by Benjamin that kind of contemplation which is above reason may fittingly be inferred sufficiently from his mother’s death.

## CHAPTER LXXV. On the surpassing excellence of spiritual contemplations
For the height of such contemplation, every knowledge of created things is narrow and lies low, like the earth in comparison with heaven, scarcely occupying the place of a point. For in comparison with the knowledge of the Creator, however great one’s knowledge of creatures may be, what is it but what earth is to heaven, what the centre is to the circumference of the whole circle? Yet this earth—this lowest science of lower things—has its mountains and hills, plains and valleys. As creatures differ, so too will sciences differ.

To begin from the lowest point: there is a great difference between one body and another. For there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. Yet the difference between any body and a spirit is greater than that between any bodies whatsoever, however unlike. And among spirits themselves, some are irrational and others rational. Those, then, seem to have their eyes fixed, as it were, upon the depths, who still admire bodily things alone. But those already seem to be climbing upward who turn themselves to the investigation of spiritual things. Let the first and chief concern of a mind striving to ascend to the height of knowledge be to know itself. It is a great height of knowledge to have known oneself perfectly. Full knowledge of the rational spirit is a great and lofty mountain. This mountain transcends the summits of all worldly learning; from on high it looks down upon all philosophy, all the knowledge of the world. What like this did Aristotle discover? What did Plato discover like this? What could so great a throng of philosophers discover that was like it? Truly and without doubt, if they could have ascended this mountain by the keenness of their intellects, if their studies had sufficed to enable them to find themselves, if they had known themselves fully, they would never have worshipped idols, never have bowed their necks to a creature, never have raised their necks against the Creator. Here those who searched with searching failed. Here, I say, they failed, and could by no means ascend this mountain. “Let man ascend to the lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. LXIII). Learn, O man, to think; learn to think of yourself, and you have ascended to the lofty heart. As much as you daily advance in knowledge of yourself, so much you rise toward higher things. Whoever attains perfect self-knowledge has already reached the mountain’s summit.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. How rare, or how delightful, it is to put spiritual contemplations into practice and make them a source of delight.

O how few there are who ascend thus far, whether because they will not or because they cannot. It is very rare to climb this mountain; but much rarer to stand upon its summit and remain there; rarest of all to dwell there and rest in mind. “Who,” he says, “shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Ps. XXIII). First comes ascending, afterward standing. There is indeed labour in standing, but greater labour in ascending. Many failed in the very ascent because of the excessive toil of climbing; many descended quickly from its steep summit because of the labour of standing. Perhaps this seemed intolerable to them, since not only can one ascend this mountain only through great labour, but one is not granted to remain there without great difficulty.

But perhaps you have already ascended and have already learned to stand there; let not even this suffice you. Learn to dwell there and make your habitation there; whenever drawn away by any wandering of mind, learn to return there again. Without doubt, through much practice it will at length become a delight to you—so much so that you may remain there continually without any difficulty of labour; indeed, it will be a punishment to you rather to remain anywhere else than there. It is a marvellous delight to be able to remain on this mountain without labour. Peter bears witness, drawn by such great and unusual sweetness that he cries: “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. XVII). O happy one who has been able to ascend this mountain and rest in mind! O how great a thing! O how rare! “Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle? Or who shall rest in thy holy mountain?” (Ps. XIV). It is indeed a great thing to be able to ascend and stand; yet greater to be able to dwell and rest. To ascend and stand belongs to virtue; to dwell and rest belongs to blessedness. Both are certainly great; both worthy of admiration. The Prophet marvels at both: at the former because of the greatness of its difficulty, at the latter because of the greatness of its delight. Admiration at the difficulty is expressed in that cry: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Ps. XXIII). Admiration at the delight is expressed in that cry: “Lord, who shall dwell in thy tabernacle, or who shall rest in thy holy mountain?” (Ps. XIV). To ascend and stand—what great and what extraordinary strength! To dwell and rest—what great and what extraordinary blessedness! Who is fit for such a work? Who worthy of this gift? Lord, who shall ascend? Lord, who shall stand upon thy holy mountain? “Send forth thy light and thy truth: they have led me and brought me to thy holy mountain and into thy tabernacles” (Ps. XLII).

## CHAPTER LXXVII. That we strive in vain for the highest things without prevenient grace.

Do you see that only truth leads and brings one to this mountain? It leads; it is that which brings one through. I gladly follow truth: I have no suspicion of such a guide. Truth knows how to lead; truth does not know how to mislead. But what is truth? What do you say, good Teacher, Teacher Christ—what is truth? “I,” he says, “am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). Let him therefore follow truth who wishes to ascend the mountain. Follow Christ, whoever desires to climb this mountain. Have we learned from the Evangelist? “Jesus took his disciples, namely Peter, James, and John, and led them apart up a high mountain” (Matt. XVII). Thus the disciples of Jesus are led upward and apart, so that they may reach this lofty mountain. The path which leads to this mountain’s heights is steep, secret, and unknown to many. Those alone, I think, run without error; those alone arrive without hindrance, who follow Christ, who are led by truth. Whoever hurries toward the heights may go securely if truth goes before him; for without it he labours in vain. Truth is as unwilling to deceive as it is incapable of being deceived. Therefore follow Christ if you do not wish to go astray.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. How much full self-knowledge avails.

But lest the labour of the journey and the difficulty of the ascent alarm or turn you back, hear and consider what is the fruit of arrival. On this mountain’s summit Jesus is transfigured; there Moses is seen with Elijah, and each is recognized without an identifier; there the voice of the Father is heard speaking to the Son. What among these is not wonderful? What is not desirable? Do you wish to see Christ transfigured? Ascend this mountain; learn to know yourself. Do you wish to see and recognize Moses and Elijah without any guide? Do you wish, without teacher or interpreter, to understand the Law and the Prophets? Ascend this mountain; learn to know yourself. Do you desire the hidden mystery of the Father? Ascend this mountain; learn to know yourself. For from heaven came that saying: **γνῶθι σεαυτόν**—that is, “Know yourself.” Do you see, then, how much the ascent of this mountain avails, how useful full self-knowledge is?

## CHAPTER LXXIX. By what means we attain the height of knowledge.

But what are we to say of this: that he did not wish to ascend this mountain without three disciples, nor did Christ seek to take more than three with him? Perhaps we are taught by this work that one is not led to the height of this knowledge without a threefold endeavour. By diligence in work, diligence in meditation, and diligence in prayer, we gradually advance and are sometimes brought to perfection of knowledge. For we learn much by acting, discover much by investigating, and wrest much from God by praying. Indeed, countless things which we cannot discover either through practical experience or through rational investigation we are counted worthy to learn, through the persistence of prayer, by revelation of divine inspiration.

When these three companions are joined to it, truth advances within us and lifts itself on high; through daily increase it raises itself until it touches the summit of the mountain mentioned above. O how many today we see diligent in reading, idle in work, lukewarm in prayer, and yet presuming that they can reach this mountain’s peak. But when, I ask, will those attain it who do not have Christ as guide? For Christ does not wish to ascend except with the three disciples. Let him, then, who seeks to have Christ as the guide of his journey and leader of his ascent join diligence in work and prayer to diligence in reading.
