Without doubt, the mind is not raised to the perfect height of knowledge without great exercise, frequent application, and ardent desire—if it does not perfectly follow Christ’s footsteps and does not rightly enter upon the way of truth.

## CHAPTER LXXX. How divine revelation meets our highest endeavours.

Nor should this be left unsaid: many think that they have already grasped the highest reaches of this mountain, when it is clear that they have scarcely touched its outermost limits. Let this be a sure sign to you that you have by no means reached the mountain’s summit: you have not yet deserved to see Christ glorified. As soon as Christ your guide has placed you on the summit, he appears to you in another form and before your eyes is clothed with light as with a garment. As the Evangelist testifies, his garments immediately become white as snow, such as no fuller on earth can make, because that splendour of divine wisdom, seen from the lofty summit of contemplation, cannot at all be defined by the discernment of human understanding.

Observe, then, that Christ has one garment in the valley and another on the mountain. In the valley he indeed has an unbroken garment; but on the mountain he has a glorious garment. Simple truth knows nothing at all of the rents of schisms; therefore, whether in the valley or on the mountain, Christ wears only whole garments. Yet there is a great difference between a whole garment and a glorious one. Do you wish to know the difference between his garments and receive a clear distinction between garment and garment? “If I have told you earthly things,” he says, “and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John III). Distinguish, then, between teaching and teaching, and you will find the difference of the garments. O how great is the difference between the teaching by which earthly things are taught and that by which heavenly things are taught—and indeed neither is known without Christ, for without truth neither the one nor the other is known! For what truth is known where truth itself does not speak? Christ, then, teaches both, but earthly matters in the valley and heavenly matters on the mountain. Therefore, so long as you remain in the valley, so long as you do not ascend to the heights, Christ teaches you only about earthly and lowly things.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. How suspect every revelation ought to be which is not accompanied by the testimony of the Scriptures.

But if you now think that you have ascended to the lofty heart and reached that high and great mountain; if you believe that you now see Christ transfigured, do not readily believe whatever you see in him or hear from him unless Moses and Elijah come to meet him. We know that every testimony stands by the mouth of two or three. Every truth not confirmed by the authority of the Scriptures is suspect to me; nor do I receive Christ in his glorification if Moses and Elijah do not stand beside him. In the valley and in the mountain’s ascent, I often receive Christ without a witness; but never on the mountain’s summit or in his glorification.

If Christ teaches me concerning external things or my own inner things, I readily receive it, since in these matters I can test it by my own experience. But when the mind is led to the heights, when heavenly things are under discussion, when profound matters are treated, upon the summit of such sublimity I do not receive Christ without a witness. No revelation, however plausible, can be held certain without the testimony of Moses and Elijah, without the authority of the Scriptures. Therefore let Christ employ for himself two witnesses in his transfiguration, if he wishes that great and unusual light of his brightness not to be suspect to me. Thus, in accordance with the instruction of this matter, let him establish his testimony by the mouth of two or three: for proving the truth of his revelation, let him produce the authority not only of figurative but also of explicit Scripture.

It is a beautiful and exceedingly pleasant spectacle when, in a revelation of truth, clear reason proceeds from one side, while from the other a discourse both as clear as it is figurative comes forward to confirm the revelation. Otherwise, I shall fear the height of day, lest perhaps I be deceived by the noonday demon. For whence come so many heresies, whence so many errors, unless because the spirit of error transforms itself into an angel of light? Certainly you see that both are transfigured—Christ, namely, and the devil—but Christ confirms the truth of his light by two witnesses. Moses and Elijah therefore appear with the Lord on this mountain; they appear in majesty, not in the obscurity of the letter but in the brightness of spiritual understanding.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. How incomprehensible are the things which the mind sees in ecstasy through divine revelation.

See how great are the things that occur on this mountain; but greater still are those which follow. The disciples behold all this while standing; they have not yet fallen upon their faces. The Father’s voice has not yet been heard; the hearer has not yet been prostrated. Rachel has not yet died; Benjamin has not yet been born. For as soon as the Father’s voice thundered, it cast down the disciples. At the thunder of the divine voice, therefore, the hearer falls, because human understanding’s capacity succumbs before that which is divinely inspired. Unless it abandons the narrow limits of human reasoning, it does not expand the bosom of its understanding to receive the mystery of divine inspiration. Thus the hearer falls where human reason fails. There Rachel dies, so that Benjamin may arise.

Unless I am mistaken, the same thing is signified by Rachel’s death and the disciples’ fall, except that in the three disciples the failure of three faculties is shown: sense, memory, and reason. For bodily sense, memory of external things, and human reason are cut off where the mind, caught up above itself, is lifted into the things above. Let us consider how comprehensible is that which the Father’s voice uttered, and we shall understand how rightly the hearer succumbs: “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I pleased myself” (Matt. XI). It is one thing to say *complacui* (“I pleased myself”) and another to say *complacuit* (“it pleased me”); yet one Evangelist used the former and another the latter. It follows that, if *complacui* was truly said there, the sense expressed by the other Evangelist can also truly be understood; but the inference cannot be reversed. Truly and without contradiction, it pleased me in him in whom I pleased myself; but it does not immediately follow that, in anyone in whom it pleased me, I pleased myself. Therefore, unless *complacui* had been said there, the Evangelist would in no way have dared to say: “This is my Son, in whom I pleased myself.”

Certainly, if the Son were something other than the Father, the Son could please the Father, but the Father could not please himself in the Son. What is it to say *complacui*, except: as I pleased myself in myself, so I pleased myself in the Son? Or perhaps, in saying “I pleased myself,” he shows that he has a companion in this good pleasure: for just as the Father is pleasing in the Son, so in the Son he is also pleasing to the Holy Spirit. Or perhaps *complacui* is said so that it may be understood from this that, as the Father pleases himself in the Son, so he likewise pleases himself in the Holy Spirit. Which of these is more correctly said? Or rather, is the whole to be understood rather than any one of these separately?

These words could still be distinguished in other and other ways, if these did not suffice to indicate the depth of this ministry. It is certain, however, that whichever of these is chosen, if rightly understood it establishes unity of substance in distinct persons. For the words, “This is my Son,” show the distinction of persons: one and the same person could not be both Father and Son to himself. But what understanding can grasp how one is other than another in person and yet the same in essence? If you seek an example, you find none among creatures that can satisfy you; if you consult reason, all human reason protests. This assertion is so far above every human estimate and beyond every human reason that reason would never assent to it unless faith raised it to certainty concerning this matter. Rightly, then, at the revelation of this mystery the hearer falls, sense fails, and human reason succumbs.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. That the mind which is accustomed to remain in its innermost depths perceives divine revelations.

Rightly, such a revelation was made only on a mountain; for the depth of this mystery, so profound in its sublimity and so sublime in its profundity, ought not to have been revealed in a valley. Those who in conduct or thought are still in low places show themselves unworthy of the gracious bestowal of this gift. Let man therefore ascend to the lofty heart; let him ascend this mountain if he wishes to grasp and know those things which are above human understanding. Let him ascend through himself above himself: through knowledge of himself to knowledge of God. Let man first learn, in the image of God and in his likeness, what he ought to think concerning God. The ascent of the mountain, as has been said, belongs to self-knowledge; the things done above the mountain advance one to knowledge of God. The former undoubtedly belongs to Joseph, the latter to Benjamin. Joseph must necessarily be born before Benjamin. How can a mind which does not raise itself to consideration of itself fly with the wing of contemplation to things above itself?

The Lord descended upon this mountain; Moses ascended it. On this mountain the Lord taught concerning the construction of the tabernacle, and Moses learned. What is understood by the tabernacle of the covenant except the state of perfection? Therefore, when one ascends the mountain, attends diligently, searches long, and at last discovers what one is like, it remains for one to know by divine revelation what one ought to be like: what edifice of mind one ought to prepare for God and by what services one ought to please God. When, then, do you suppose that a mind still scattered among various desires, drawn hither and thither by diverse thoughts, will deserve to receive this grace? When can it ascend in contemplation to things above itself if it cannot yet gather itself into one, if it does not yet know how to enter into itself?

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. How the mind that longs for contemplation of heavenly things ought to gather itself inwardly.

Let it therefore learn to gather Israel’s dispersions, strive to restrain the mind’s wanderings, accustom itself to remain in its own depths, and forget all external things—whoever longs for contemplation of heavenly things, whoever yearns for knowledge of divine things. Let one form an assembly [*ecclesia*] not only of desires but also of cognitions, so as to learn to love the one true good and to think of it alone without ceasing: “In the assemblies,” he says, “bless God” (Ps. LXVII). For in this twofold assembly, namely of thoughts and desires, in this twofold unanimity of endeavours and wills, Benjamin is caught up on high, and the mind, divinely inspired, is lifted into the things above: “There,” he says, “is young Benjamin in ecstasy of mind” (*ibid.*). Where, do you think, except in the assemblies? “In the assemblies bless God, the Lord from the fountains of Israel. There is young Benjamin in ecstasy of mind.”

Yet each person must first make of one’s thoughts and desires a Synagogue rather than an Ecclesia. You know well enough that *synagogue* means “gathering together,” while *ecclesia* is interpreted “calling together.” It is one thing to gather certain things into one without their will or against their will, and another for them to come of themselves voluntarily at the command of the one calling. Insensible and brute things may be gathered, but they cannot be called together. The coming together even of rational beings is by voluntary inclination, so that it may rightly be called a convocation. You see, then, how great is the difference between calling together and gathering, and between Ecclesia and Synagogue.

If, therefore, you perceive that your desires are attached to outward pleasures and that your thoughts are continually occupied with them, compel them with great diligence to enter in, so that you may at least for the time being make a Synagogue of them. For whenever we gather the mind’s wanderings into one and fix all the movements of the heart in the one desire for eternity, what else do we do but make a Synagogue of that inner household? But when that throng of our desires and thoughts, attracted by the tasting of that inward sweetness, has learned to come voluntarily at reason’s command and to remain fixed in the depths, it may then rightly be considered worthy of the name Ecclesia. Let us therefore learn to love inward goods alone; let us learn more frequently to think of them alone; and, insofar as we know how to love Benjamin, we undoubtedly make ecclesiae.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. How pleasant and sweet it is to have the grace of contemplation as a familiar companion.

In assemblies of this kind Benjamin gladly remains, is marvellously delighted, and, when through joy he can no longer contain himself, is led above himself and lifted to the highest things in ecstasy of mind. For unless our Benjamin rested delightfully in contemplation of inward things, it would without doubt not have been written of him through Moses: “Benjamin, the most beloved of the Lord, shall dwell in him securely; all day long he shall abide as though in a bridal chamber, and shall rest between his shoulders” (Deut. XXXIII).

What do you think is the reason why this Benjamin remains in the bridal chamber all day, rests there continually, and is so unwilling to go out even for an hour? We know that bridegroom and bride are accustomed to remain together in bridal chambers, to be occupied with offices of love toward one another, and to cherish one another with mutual embraces and reciprocal affection. Therefore, whatever that beloved of our Benjamin may be, she possesses, unless I am mistaken, an admirable beauty and a singular excellence of form—she whose companionship he can never grow weary of and from whose embraces he would not wish to be absent even for an hour.

But if we now know what this Benjamin’s voice is, we have no doubt about how great is the beauty of his beloved: “I said to wisdom, ‘You are my sister,’ and I have called prudence my friend” (Prov. VII). Do you wish to hear that he cannot grow weary of the beauty of this beloved whom he calls sister and friend because of his chaste and most ardent love? “When I enter into my house,” he says, “I shall rest with her. For her conversation has no bitterness, nor her companionship any weariness, but gladness and joy, and good delight in her friendship” (Wis. VIII). Let each say what one thinks; I find no other cause that holds him bound within so that he cannot go out even for a short while.

But I know one thing: whoever burns with longing for such a friend loves her the more intimately the more familiarly he knows her; and the more often he enjoys her embraces, the more vehemently he burns with desire for her. Her frequent companionship ordinarily does not diminish desire, but increases it and more keenly kindles the fire of love. It is no wonder, then, why this Benjamin abides all day as though in a bridal chamber, since he enjoys the sweetness of such a bride and, resting between her shoulders, is continually delighted by her love. How frequent, do you think, are the ecstasies of mind he undergoes? How often, caught up in ecstasy, is he led above himself, while astonished by the greatness of her beauty he is suspended in admiration of her? And without doubt there is fulfilled in him what we read: “Young Benjamin in ecstasy of mind.”

It should certainly be observed how the testimonies of Scripture correspond with one another. What the prophet signifies by Rachel’s death, what the Evangelist signifies by the disciples’ fall, the Psalmist expresses in Benjamin through ecstasy of mind.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. On two kinds of contemplation.

Yet by Rachel’s death and Benjamin’s ecstasy we may fittingly understand distinct kinds of contemplation. It is clear that there are two kinds of contemplation above reason, and that both belong to Benjamin. The first is above reason but not beyond reason; the second is both above reason and beyond reason. Those things are above reason but not beyond reason which, although reason allows them to be, cannot be investigated or established by any reasoning. But we call those things both above and beyond reason to which all human reason seems to be opposed. Such are the things we believe concerning the unity of the Trinity, and many things which we hold by the unquestioned authority of faith concerning Christ’s body. For no human reason permits that there should be a threefold person in one simple nature, or that one and the same body should be in different places at the same time; and all reasoning seems without doubt to protest against assertions of this kind.

These, then, are the two kinds of contemplation, one of which belongs to Rachel’s death and the other to Benjamin’s ecstasy. In the first, Benjamin kills his mother, where he surpasses all reason; but in the second he even exceeds himself, where, in what is known through divine revelation, he transcends the measure of human understanding. This must be observed not only in Benjamin but also in all the brothers; indeed, it must be diligently noted in innumerable places in Scripture how divine Scripture, concerning one and the same matter, now extends, now restricts, and sometimes changes its signification. It usually determines these modes of changing signification in many ways, revealing its meaning now through place, now through action, or through any other circumstances. It is determined by place, as in the passage where Benjamin is said to have gone down into Egypt; by action, as in the passage where Joseph and Benjamin rush into one another’s embraces and join in reciprocal kisses.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. How contemplation descends into meditation, and how meditation rises into contemplation.

What is Benjamin’s descent into Egypt except the recalling of the mind’s gaze from contemplation of eternal things to the contemplation of temporal things; the lowering of the rays of understanding from the light of eternity, as it were from heaven’s summit, down to the shadows of mutability; and, amid so great a confusion of changing things, the weighing and in great measure penetrating of the rationale of divine judgments? And what is meant by Joseph and Benjamin meeting and joining kisses, except that meditation and contemplation often meet one another with reason’s attestation? For in general consideration, as Benjamin may signify the grace of contemplation, so Joseph may signify the grace of meditation.

More properly and expressly, however, Benjamin signifies pure understanding, while Joseph signifies true prudence. Benjamin signifies, that is, the kind of contemplation concerned with invisible things; Joseph, the kind of meditation concerned with morals. The apprehension of invisible things belongs to pure understanding, while discernment in moral conduct belongs to true prudence. By pure understanding we mean that which is without admixture of imagination; by true prudence, we distinguish it from what is called prudence of the flesh. True prudence concerns acquiring, increasing, and preserving true goods; prudence of the flesh concerns transitory goods, according to which “the children of this age are called more prudent than the children of light” (Luke XVI).

Thus Joseph falls upon Benjamin’s neck as often as meditation passes into contemplation. Benjamin receives his brother falling upon him when the mind rises from the exercise of meditation into contemplation. Benjamin and Joseph join kisses when divine revelation and human reasoning agree in one testimony to truth. Do you see how divine Scripture varies the mode of signification concerning one and the same matter, yet everywhere adds something by which it does not allow its meaning to lie wholly concealed? In Rachel’s death contemplation rises above reason; in Benjamin’s entry into Egypt contemplation descends as far as imagination; in the kissing of Benjamin and Joseph, human reason applauds divine revelation.

[Col. 0063]

# FIVE BOOKS ON THE GRACE OF CONTEMPLATION, OCCASIONED BY MOSES’ ARK; AND FOR THIS REASON, HITHERTO ENTITLED *BENJAMIN MAJOR*.

## BOOK ONE.

### CHAPTER ONE. On contemplation and its commendation.

[Col. 0063B]

Gladly would I, if it be permitted, by the gift of inspiration from Him who has the key of knowledge, unlock something of the mystical ark of Moses through the exposition of our little night-work; and if anything still lies hidden in this treasury of divine mysteries and repository of knowledge which may be drawn forth by our smallness for the benefit of some, we shall not shrink from setting it forth publicly and proposing it for common use. Much has indeed already been usefully said on this subject. Much still remains that may usefully be said about it. What this ark mystically signifies according to the allegorical sense, or how it signifies Christ, has already been said before our time by teachers and examined by more penetrating minds. [Col. 0063C] Yet we do not therefore suppose that we incur the reproach of rashness if we still speak morally upon the same subject.

Nevertheless, that our earnest treatment of this subject may become sweeter to us, and may draw our desire more vehemently into admiration of it, let us consider what that outstanding prophet thinks of it—the one who calls it the ark of sanctification: “Arise, O Lord, into thy rest, thou and the ark of thy sanctification” (Ps. 131). Does this thing called the ark of sanctification, we ask, have its name from the reality? It must be carefully observed and deeply retained that this, whatever it may be, is called the ark of sanctification for you, to whom our Teacher gives the command: “Be holy, as I also am holy” [Lev. 11]. [Col. 0063D] Therefore you who are being sanctified today and tomorrow for the third day, do not carelessly overlook the meaning of its being called the ark of sanctification.

But if Moses is rightly believed, we know that whoever touches it will be sanctified (Exod. 19). If this is altogether so, the whole people rightly seeks to touch it, if the power of sanctification proceeds from it. Oh, if only there might be found among you one man [Col. 0064B] like that man of Ramathaim, clothed in garments of glory as befits the high priest, worthy to enter the Holy of Holies, so that he might not only see but also touch this thing called the ark of sanctification, and be cleansed from his impurities. But what shall I say of that man, if perhaps the key of knowledge has been given to someone by Him who opens and no one shuts, so that he may see what this ark of sanctification contains within? For I think that something precious has been stored in this ark. I should greatly wish to know what this ark is which can sanctify those who approach it, so that it is rightly called the ark of sanctification.

As for wisdom, I do not doubt that it is that which conquers wickedness (Wis. 7). I know likewise that all who have been healed from the beginning were healed through wisdom (Wis. 9). And this too [Col. 0064C] is well established: no one can please God unless wisdom is with him. Who doubts that it pertains to sanctification for a person to be cleansed from every impurity, and for anyone’s mind to be purified from all malice and wickedness? For these are what defile a person. But one is purified through wisdom when the stronger one comes upon him and conquers wickedness—as one reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly (Wis. 8). And to be purified in this way is, I think, to be sanctified.

When the Lord was about to command Moses concerning the construction of the tabernacle, he first of all instructed him concerning the making of the ark, thereby indicating that all the rest was to be made for its sake. I think that the ark was the chief and principal sanctuary [Col. 0064D] among all those things which the tabernacle of the covenant contained. Thus, for one asking what grace that shrine may signify—the shrine more worthy than all the others—the answer readily occurs, unless someone perhaps doubts that Mary chose the better part. But what is that better part which Mary chose (Luke 10), except to be at leisure and see how sweet the Lord is? (Ps. 33). For, as Scripture says, [Col. 0065A] while Martha was occupied with care, Mary sat at the Lord’s feet and heard his word. Thus she understood by hearing the supreme wisdom of God hidden in flesh, which she could not see with the eyes of the flesh; and by understanding she saw; and thus, by sitting and hearing, she devoted herself to the contemplation of supreme truth.

This is the part which is never taken away from the elect and perfect. This is indeed an occupation bounded by no end. For contemplation of truth begins in this life, but in the life to come it is practiced in unbroken perpetuity. Through contemplation of truth a person is both instructed unto righteousness and perfected unto glory. You see, therefore, how rightly the grace of contemplation is understood in that shrine which, by a certain dignity of its own, is set before all other things in God’s tabernacle. O singular [Col. 0065B] grace! O grace to be preferred above all others, through which we are sanctified in the present and made blessed in the future! If, then, the grace of contemplation is rightly understood through the ark of sanctification, this grace is rightly sought, through receiving which one is not only cleansed but also sanctified. Without doubt nothing so cleanses the heart of every worldly love, nothing so kindles the soul to love of heavenly things. It is indeed this which cleanses; it is this which sanctifies: so that, through continual contemplation of truth, one may become pure through contempt of the world and holy through love of God.

## CHAPTER II. That this grace is useful and delightful to those who make progress in it

But that same thing which David calls the ark of sanctification is called by Moses the ark of the covenant. But [Col. 0065C] why an ark? Why the ark of the covenant—and not of just any covenant, but of the Lord’s? We know that precious things—gold, silver, and precious stones—are usually stored in an ark. Therefore, if we think of the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, we shall more readily discover what repository is suited to such treasures. What ark can be fit for this purpose except human understanding? This ark is fashioned and overlaid with gold by divine instruction when human understanding is advanced, through divine inspiration and revelation, to the grace of contemplation.

But when we advance toward this grace in this life, what else do we receive except certain earnest-money payments of that future fullness, where we shall cling perpetually to everlasting contemplation? We therefore receive this grace as an earnest [Col. 0065D] of the divine promise, as a pledge of divine love, as a kind of bond of covenant and memorial of mutual charity. Do you see how rightly it is called the ark of the Lord’s covenant, in which and through which such grace is figured? Anyone who desires, or believes himself able, to receive such a pledge of so great a love ought gladly to gird himself for every labor.

I do not doubt that any Hebrew servant among you will gladly serve six years for grace of this kind, in order that in the seventh year he may go out free without payment, and thereafter may freely devote himself to contemplation of truth. But if there is found among you someone who is Jacob, or who can worthily be designated by such a name—because he is a strong man and mighty in battle, a vigorous wrestler and overthrower of vices, overcoming some by strength and supplanting others by discernment—such a one [Col. 0066A] will surely gladly serve seven years, and seven more, for such grace, so that the days may seem few to him because of the greatness of his love, provided only that he may at last attain Rachel’s embrace.

For whoever wishes to attain her embrace must serve seven years and seven for her, in order to learn to rest not only from evil deeds but also from superfluous thoughts. Many people indeed, even if they know how to be at leisure bodily, are nevertheless wholly unable to be at leisure in heart. They do not know how to make “Sabbath after Sabbath,” and consequently cannot fulfill what is read in the Psalm: “Be at leisure, and see that I am God” (Ps. 45). For those who are at leisure in body but wander everywhere in heart do not deserve to see how sweet the Lord is, how good the God of Israel is to those [Col. 0066B] who are upright in heart (Ps. 72). And this is why their enemies mock their Sabbaths (Lam. 1).

But the true Jacob does not cease from labor until he reaches the end of his desire, serving with the true Laban, the truly “made white”—that is, glorified—whom the Father glorified with himself by the glory which he had before the foundation of the world (John 12); whom it was necessary to suffer and thus enter into his glory (Luke 24), so that glory’s brightness might be brought upon the form of a servant, and he might be truly whitened, made whiter than snow (Ps. 50), crowned with glory and honor, and made beautiful not only beyond the sons of men but even beyond angelic spirits: one into whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1). Do you see how great is this grace, for which one labors so patiently and so willingly, which is acquired with so much labor and possessed with so much delight? Moses indeed treats of this grace in several places in his writings under figurative language; but here he distinguishes it more fully by mystical description, where he divides it by kinds.

## CHAPTER III. On the nature of contemplation, or how it differs from meditation and thought

In order that we may more conveniently grasp, and more rightly judge, the matters to be said about contemplation, we must first seek to determine or define what it is, and how it differs from thought or meditation. We must know, then, that we view one and the same subject in one way through thought, investigate it in another through meditation, and admire it in another through contemplation. These three differ greatly from one another in their manner, although they sometimes agree in their subject matter. With regard to one and the same subject, thought acts in one way, meditation in another, and contemplation in a far different way.

Thought wanders by slow step through every byway, straying here and there without regard for reaching an end. Meditation strives, often by steep and rough paths, toward the end intended, with great effort of soul. Contemplation, in free flight, is borne with marvelous swiftness wherever its impulse carries it. Thought crawls; meditation walks, and often runs. But contemplation flies around all things and, whenever it wills, poises itself in the heights. Thought is without labor and without fruit. In meditation there is labor with fruit. Contemplation abides without [Col. 0067A] labor, with fruit. In thought there is wandering; in meditation, investigation; in contemplation, admiration. Thought arises from imagination, meditation from reason, contemplation from understanding.

Behold these three: imagination, reason, understanding. Understanding occupies the highest place, imagination the lowest, and reason the middle. Whatever is subject to a lower sense must also be subject to a higher sense. Hence it is clear that all things comprehended by imagination, and many others which lie above it, are comprehended by reason. Similarly, what imagination or reason comprehend falls under understanding, as do also things which they cannot comprehend. See, then, how widely the ray of contemplation extends, since it surveys all things.

And although one person may be occupied with thought, another with meditation, and another with contemplation regarding the same object, [Col. 0067B] they are carried along by the same path, yet by different motions. Thought always passes in wandering motion from one thing to another; meditation applies itself persistently to some one thing; contemplation expands under a single ray of vision toward innumerable things. Through understanding, indeed, the recess of the mind is expanded immeasurably, and the keenness of the contemplative soul is sharpened, so that it may be capable of comprehending many things and penetrating subtle ones. For contemplation can never exist without a certain liveliness of understanding. Just as it is through understanding that the mind’s eye is fixed upon bodily things, so it is manifestly through its power that, beneath one gaze, it is expanded in bodily things to comprehend so many infinite matters. [Col. 0067C] Finally, whenever the contemplative mind is expanded toward lowly things, whenever it is raised toward lofty things, whenever it is sharpened toward inscrutable things, whenever with marvelous agility it is carried almost without delay through innumerable things, do not doubt that this occurs by a certain power of understanding.

These things have been said for the sake of those who deem it unworthy that these lower things should fall under the gaze of understanding or pertain in any way to contemplation. Yet contemplation is called specially and properly that which concerns sublime things, where the mind uses pure understanding. But contemplation always concerns things either manifest by their own nature, familiarly known through study, or made clear through divine revelation.

## CHAPTER IV. Definitions of contemplation, meditation, and thought

[Col. 0067D]

It seems, then, possible to define them thus. Contemplation is the free and penetrating insight of the mind, held in suspense with admiration before the spectacles of wisdom; or, certainly, as that foremost theologian of our time was pleased to define it in these words: “Contemplation is the penetrating and free gaze of the soul, spread abroad everywhere upon things to be perceived.” Meditation, however, is the studious application of the mind, persistently occupied in carefully investigating something; or thus: meditation is the provident gaze of the soul, intensely occupied in the search for truth. Thought, however, is the unprovident regard of the soul, prone to wandering.

It seems therefore that all three have in common, and as it were substantially, a certain gaze of the soul. [Col. 0068A] For where nothing is perceived by the mind, none of these is rightly said or affirmed to exist. Contemplation and meditation have this in common: that they are occupied with useful matters and are chiefly—indeed, continually—engaged in the pursuits of wisdom or knowledge. But in this they especially differ from thought, which customarily relaxes itself at nearly every moment toward foolish and trivial things, and without any bridle of discernment thrusts or casts itself headlong into everything.

Contemplation and thought have in common that they are carried here and there in a certain free movement and according to spontaneous inclination, and are impeded in the impetus of their course by no obstacle of difficulty. Yet they differ most of all from meditation, whose task is always, by whatever labor of diligence and through whatever difficulty of soul, to grasp lofty things, break into hidden things, and penetrate secret things. It often happens, however, that in the wandering of our thoughts the mind encounters something it vehemently desires to know and pursues with earnestness. But while the mind, satisfying its desire, applies itself diligently to such an investigation, it now exceeds the manner of thought in thinking, and thought passes into meditation.

Something similar commonly occurs in meditation. For the mind is accustomed to receive with eagerness the truth long sought and at last discovered, to admire it with exultation, and to remain attached to its admiration for a longer time. And this is now to exceed meditation in meditating, and for meditation to pass into contemplation. It is therefore proper to contemplation [Col. 0068C] to remain with admiration attached to the spectacle of its delight. In this, indeed, it appears to differ from both meditation and thought. For thought, as has already been said, continually turns aside here and there in wandering course, while meditation always tends further onward by an intended advance.

## CHAPTER V. That the mode of contemplation operates in many forms

But although that penetrating ray of contemplation is always, in some respect, held in suspension by the greatness of admiration, this does not always occur in one and the same or uniform manner. For that liveliness of understanding in the contemplative soul, with marvelous agility, now goes and returns; now bends itself, as it were, in a circle; and now gathers itself, as it were, into one point and fixes itself as though immovably.

If we rightly consider the pattern of this thing, we see it every day in the birds of the air. You may see some now raising themselves to higher regions, now plunging into lower ones, and often repeating the same movements of ascent and descent. You may see others now turn to the right, now to the left, and, inclining now in this direction, now in that, advance little or almost not at all; yet they repeatedly renew with great persistence the same alternations of their courses. You may see others stretch themselves forward in great haste, but soon return backward at the same speed, often doing the same thing and, by continual repetition over a long time, continuing and prolonging the same outward and return flights. You may see others [Col. 0069A] bend themselves in a circle, and observe how suddenly or how often they repeat the same or similar circuits—now somewhat broader, now somewhat narrower—and always return to the same point. You may see others, with trembling and often-beaten wings, suspend themselves for a long time in one and the same place; by mobile movement they fix themselves as though immovable; and, clinging long and closely to the place of their suspension, depart from it not at all, as though by the performance of their work and effort they were openly crying out and saying: “It is good for us to be here” (Luke 9).

In keeping with the model of these proposed comparisons, the flight of our contemplation varies in many forms and is shaped in differing ways according to the variety of persons and matters. Now it ascends from lower things to higher, now descends from [Col. 0069B] higher things to lower; now it moves with the agility of consideration from part to whole, now from whole to part; and it draws an argument for what ought to be known now from the greater, now from the lesser. At one time it turns in one direction, at another in the opposite, deriving knowledge of contraries from knowledge of contraries; and it is accustomed to vary the course of its reasoning according to the diverse character of opposites.

At times it runs forward and suddenly returns backward, when it discovers the manner or quality of a thing from effects, or alternatively from causes and whatever antecedents or consequents there may be. At other times our speculation is led, as it were, in a circle, when it considers what things are common to each thing together with many others; when, for defining any one thing, reason is drawn and supplied now from similar things, now from things similarly constituted or commonly occurring. But the fixation of our consideration then remains, as though immovably, in one and the same place when the contemplative attention willingly lingers over discerning and admiring the being or property of some thing whatsoever.

But lest our words seem to savor of human philosophy or to depart from the plain tenor and simplicity of Catholic doctrine, perhaps we should say more fittingly that to ascend and descend, to go and return, to turn now here and now there, to proceed sometimes in a circle, or at last to remain in one place, is nothing other than for the mind, with supreme agility, now to pass from lowly to lofty things or from lofty [Col. 0069D] things to lowly, now from first things to last or from last things to first, sometimes from unlike kinds of merits or rewards to unlike kinds; sometimes, by curious examination, to survey the circumstances or connections of each thing; or finally at times, in the novelty of some contemplation and admiration at that novelty, to satisfy the soul.

You certainly see, as we have said above, how the activity of our contemplation is always suspended and prolonged with respect to something, while the contemplative soul willingly lingers over the spectacle of its delight and continually strives either to return often to it or to remain longer, immovably, in the same thing. Hear of that mode of contemplation which in some fashion is accustomed to occur forward and backward: “The living creatures went and returned [Col. 0070A] like the appearance of flashing lightning” (Ezek. 1). Receive also an example of that by which the mind is drawn in different directions and, moving now in this direction and now in that, is stirred with marvelous agility toward contrary things: “The righteous shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds” (Wis. 3). The Psalmist expressed in few words that mode which occurs, as it were, upward and downward: “They ascend,” he says, “even unto the heavens, and descend even unto the depths” (Ps. 106). You are instructed concerning that mode of contemplation which is led as if in a circle by the prophetic utterance: “Lift up your eyes round about, and see” (Isa. 59). But the ray of contemplation is fixed as though immovably in one place when each person experiences in himself what Habakkuk experienced: “The sun and moon stood in their dwelling” (Hab. [Col. 0070B] 3).

Behold, we have now taught by determination or definition what contemplation is. It remains for us to divide it by species and then to see how many kinds of contemplation there are.

## CHAPTER VI. How many kinds of contemplation there are, and what they are

There are six kinds of contemplation, wholly distinct both individually and from one another. The first is in imagination and according to imagination alone. The second is in imagination according to reason. The third is in reason according to imagination. The fourth is in reason and according to reason. The fifth is above reason, but not beyond reason. The sixth is above reason, and seems to be beyond reason. Thus there are two in imagination, two in reason, [Col. 0070C] and two in understanding.

Our contemplation is without doubt occupied in imagination when the form and image of these visible things is brought before consideration, when, in amazement, we attend—and, attending, are amazed—at how many, how great, how diverse, how beautiful or delightful are these bodily things which we take in through bodily sense; and when in them all we adore in admiration, and admire in adoration, the power, wisdom, and generosity of that creating superessentiality. Our contemplation is then occupied in imagination and shaped according to imagination alone when we seek nothing by argument and investigate nothing by reasoning, but our free mind ranges here and there wherever admiration carries it in [Col. 0070D] this kind of spectacle.

The second kind of contemplation is that which indeed abides in imagination, but is shaped and proceeds according to reason. This occurs when we seek and find a rationale for the matters considered in imagination, which we have already said belong to the first kind of contemplation—or rather, when we bring before consideration with admiration a rationale already found and known. In the former case, therefore, we investigate, contemplate, and admire the things themselves; in the latter, their rationale, order, arrangement, and the cause, manner, and usefulness of each thing. This contemplation is therefore in imagination but according to reason, because it proceeds by reasoning concerning the things occupied in imagination. And though in some respect [Col. 0071A] this contemplation, in which the rationale of visible things is sought, may seem also to abide in reason, it is rightly called to abide in imagination because whatever we seek or discover in it by reasoning we certainly apply to the things occupied in imagination, since we engage in reasoning about them and for their sake.

We said that the third kind of contemplation is formed in reason according to imagination. We truly employ this kind of contemplation when we are raised, through the likeness of visible things, to contemplation of invisible things. This contemplation abides in reason because it applies its attention and investigation solely to things which exceed imagination: it attends only to invisible things, and especially to those which it comprehends through reason. But it is said to be formed according to imagination because, in this contemplation, a likeness is drawn from the image of visible things whereby the mind is aided in investigating invisible things. And this contemplation is rightly said to be in reason but according to imagination, although it advances by reasoning, because all its reasoning and argument takes its foundation and support from imagination and draws the rationale of its inquiry and assertion from the properties of imaginable things.

The fourth kind of contemplation is formed in reason and according to reason. It occurs when, all service of imagination being set aside, the mind attends only to things which imagination does not know, but [Col. 0071C] which the mind gathers by reasoning or comprehends through reason. We engage in this kind of contemplation when we bring before consideration our own invisible realities, which we know through experience and grasp through understanding, and from considering them rise to contemplation of heavenly minds and the highest good intelligences.

This contemplation abides in reason because, sensible things being set aside, it attends only to intelligible things. It appears indeed to take both its beginning and foundation from those invisible realities of our own which the human mind is known to know through experience or comprehend by common understanding. Yet, for this reason, this contemplation is rightly said also to abide [Col. 0071D] in reason: these invisible realities of ours are comprehended by reason and in this respect do not at all transcend the manner of reasoning. It proceeds according to reason alone because, from invisible things known by experience, it gathers by reasoning other and other things which it does not know by experience.

In this contemplation the human mind first uses pure understanding; and, with every service of imagination set aside, our understanding itself seems in this activity first to understand itself through itself. For although it may seem not to be absent from those earlier kinds of contemplation, it is scarcely ever present there except when reason or even imagination is engaged in meditation. There it uses these as an instrument and beholds as through a mirror. Here it operates through itself [Col. 0072A] and contemplates as through direct sight. Here, therefore, it inclines itself, as it were, to the lowest point, since it has nowhere lower to descend through itself.

We said that the fifth kind of contemplation is above reason, though not beyond reason. We ascend, by the uplifting of the mind, to this watchtower of contemplation when by divine revelation we know things which no human reason can fully comprehend and which we cannot completely investigate by any reasoning of our own. Such are the things we believe concerning the nature of the Godhead and that simple essence, and establish by the authority of the divine Scriptures. Thus our contemplation truly rises above reason when the mind, through the uplifting of understanding, discerns that which transcends the bounds [Col. 0072B] of human capacity. But it must be judged above reason, not beyond reason, when human reason cannot contradict what is seen by the keenness of understanding, but rather readily assents to it and supports it with its testimony.

The sixth kind of contemplation is said to concern matters which are above reason and seem to be beyond, or even contrary to, reason. In this highest and most worthy watchtower of all contemplations, the mind truly exults and rejoices when, by the irradiation of divine light, it knows and considers things against which all human reason protests. Such are almost all the things which we are commanded to believe concerning the Trinity of persons. When human reason is consulted concerning them, it appears to do nothing but contradict them. [Col. 0072C]

## CHAPTER VII. What features are common to which kinds

Two of these abide in imagination, because they attend only to sensible things. Two abide in reason, because they apply themselves only to intelligible things. Two abide in understanding, because they attend only to intellectible things. By “sensible things” I mean all things visible and perceptible by bodily sense. By “intelligible things” I mean invisible things nevertheless comprehensible by reason. By “intellectible things” in this place I mean invisible things incomprehensible to human reason.

Of these six kinds of contemplation, the four lower kinds are chiefly occupied with created things; the two highest with uncreated [Col. 0072D] and divine things. Again, of these four, the two higher kinds are occupied with invisible things, while the two lowest concern visible and bodily things. For the two lowest undoubtedly concern visible and created things. The two highest, however, are chiefly concerned with invisible and uncreated things. The two middle kinds are chiefly concerned with invisible and created things.

I have said “chiefly” because among invisible and created things there are some which human reason cannot comprehend at all; in this respect they belong to the class of intellectible things and thereby show themselves rather to pertain to the two highest kinds of contemplation. Similarly, among those highest and uncreated things, some seem accessible to human reason; in this respect, when reckoned among intelligible things, [Col. 0073A] they are especially suited to those two middle kinds of contemplation.

The first two thus appear to share this: each is concerned with visible things. Yet they seem chiefly to differ in this: the first commonly ranges here and there under the impulse of admiration, without any operation of reason; but in the second, a rationale is sought and supplied for the things present in the mind through imagination, or a rationale previously familiarly known is brought forward for admiration. The second and third have this in common, uniquely above the others, that in both imagination seems mingled with reason and reason with imagination. But they differ in that, in the second, reason is sought and applied to visible things, as has been said; [Col. 0073B] whereas in the third, reason is drawn from visible things for the investigation of invisible things. In the former we are often taught from invisible things toward invisible things, proving some things from others; in the latter we are advanced from inspection of visible things to knowledge of invisible things.

The third and fourth plainly share the fact that they attend to invisible and intelligible things; yet they differ in that in the third reason is mingled with imagination, whereas in the fourth pure understanding is mingled with reason. In the fourth and fifth, reason and understanding converge into one and are especially alike in this. But in the fourth understanding advances from reason; in the fifth reason never precedes understanding, but follows it—or at most accompanies it. For what is first known by divine inspiration is afterward confirmed by reason’s testimony. [Col. 0073C] The fifth and sixth share the fact that both are occupied with intellectible things. But the fifth appears sufficiently consistent with human reason, whereas the sixth appears contrary to all human reason unless it is supported by an admixture of faith.

## CHAPTER VIII. What is proper to each kind

It is proper to the first contemplation simply to remain attached, without any reasoning, to admiration of visible things. It is proper to the second to apply itself by reasoning to the rationale of visible things. It is proper to the third to rise by reasoning from visible things to invisible things. It is proper to the fourth to gather invisible things from invisible things by reasoning, and through understanding of things experienced to advance toward knowledge of things unknown. It is proper to the fifth to admit reason into the understanding of intellectible things. It is proper to the sixth, in understanding intellectible things, to transcend all human reasoning and, as it were, to tread it beneath itself.

Although it is common to the first three kinds of contemplation that they are not without imagination, in the first imagination remains as though below reason; in the second it receives reason; in the third imagination rises to reason. Again, although it is common to the last three kinds that they are not without pure understanding, in the first of these—that is, the fourth—understanding inclines itself to reason. In the fifth it raises reason to itself. In the sixth understanding transcends reason and, as it were, leaves it beneath itself.

Again, although it is common to the four middle kinds that they are not without reasoning, in the second kind of contemplation reason descends, as it were, to the low level of imagination. In the third it draws imagination with itself, as it were, toward higher things. In the fourth it receives and leads understanding as though descending beneath it. In the fifth reason rises, as it were, above itself to understanding and accompanies it in its heights. In the first, therefore, imagination rests in itself, just as understanding [Col. 0074A] does in the sixth: it gathers itself to itself and abides in itself. In the second reason descends below itself; in the fifth the same reason rises above itself. In the third imagination rises above itself; in the fourth understanding descends beneath itself. In the first imagination holds the lowest and solitary place. In the second reason [Col. 0074B] descends to the lowest point. In the third imagination rises to the highest point. In the fourth understanding descends to the lowest point. In the fifth reason rises to the highest point. In the sixth understanding holds the solitary and highest place.

## CHAPTER IX. In what proportion the respective kinds correspond to one another, or how they are accustomed to intermingle
It should certainly be noted that, just as the last two ascend above reason, so the middle two ascend above imagination. And just as the higher of the last two scarcely admits any human reasoning, so the higher of the middle two ought to exclude from itself every imagination. And just as the lower of the two last and highest kinds stands above reason, though not beyond reason, so [Col. 0074C] the lower of the two middle kinds ascends above imagination, though it is not beyond imagination. Again, just as the two middle kinds descend beneath pure and simple understanding, so the first two and lowest kinds descend beneath discursive reasoning. By “simple understanding” I mean that which operates without the office of reason; by “pure” understanding, that which is without the intervention of imagination.

But just as the higher of the two middle kinds descends beneath simple understanding, yet does not remain beneath simple understanding [the text is corrupt or repetitive here], because among the matters with which it is occupied it comprehends some by simple understanding and gathers others by reasoning; so the higher of the two lowest kinds appears to descend beneath discursive reasoning, yet does not remain beneath it, [Col. 0074D] because it is accustomed to represent some things through imagination and to gather others by reasoning. And just as the lower of the two middle kinds is accustomed to descend beneath simple understanding and remain there, so the lower of the two lowest kinds is accustomed to relate to reason. For the latter attends only to those things which the mind gathers by reasoning from imagination, while the former attends only to those things which sense has impressed upon imagination.

Yet this first and lowest kind of contemplation is not said to remain beneath reason, or rather beneath discursive reasoning, as though it appeared irrational and altogether contrary to reason, since it is easily shown to accord with reason in its intention and even in its arrangement. Rather, [Col. 0075A] as has been said, nothing is gathered in it by reasoning, so far as its own proper character is concerned. These kinds of contemplation that we have distinguished are nevertheless sometimes accustomed to mingle with one another, and the pattern of their properties that we have set forth is confused by their mutual intermingling. Our purpose here, however, has been to teach the proper character of each one for the sake of clarity of instruction, while also showing what they have in common and what they resemble.

## CHAPTER X. That all six kinds of contemplation are scarcely attained except by the perfect.

Whoever wishes to attain the summit of knowledge must be intimately acquainted with these six kinds of contemplation. By these six wings of contemplation we are lifted from earthly things and borne up to heavenly things. Do not doubt that you are far from perfection if you still lack some of them. It goes well indeed with me and with those like me if only one pair—if even one—of these three pairs of wings is granted us. “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly and be at rest?” (Ps. XLV).

Yet I know that by those first two kinds of wings one is not enabled to fly up from earthly to heavenly things, or to seek or penetrate those lofty regions of heaven. For, as was said above, in these six kinds of contemplation the whole consideration of the first two is occupied with earthly and bodily things; nothing concerning invisible things is treated in them. Therefore, however exalted and however subtle our flights may be among these earthly things [Col. 0075C] by the first two wings of contemplation, it ought to count for little with us if we are sufficient only for those matters in which we see the philosophers of this world excel. You prove yourself to be an earthly creature and not yet a heavenly one as long as you are content with only two wings. You have something with which to cover your body and something with which you may fly.

Certainly, if you are still an earthly creature, if you still have an earthly body, and, in short, such a body as the Apostle describes and commands to be mortified, it will indeed be good to have at hand something with which, when you wish, you may cover such a body and hide it from the eyes of your recollection: “Mortify,” he says, “your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness” (Col. III). What else is it to cover such a body beneath the aforesaid wings of contemplation than to restrain—indeed, to bring into forgetfulness—the desire for worldly things through consideration of worldly mutability? You perceive, I think, how much such a covering and shadowing by wings can accomplish.

You likewise have in these wings something by which, when you wish, you may fly. It is indeed good to fly well and, as far as you can, to withdraw yourself from the love of the world. Those surely fly well by these wings who daily consider the instability of worldly change and, by continual reflection, estrange themselves from its ambition. Although, therefore, you cannot fly up to heavenly things by these paired wings, you may perhaps find, in their rowing motion, a safe and tranquil harbor of rest. Strive in them as far as you can; at least lay hold upon the furthest parts of the sea: “If I take,” he says, [Col. 0076A] “my wings at daybreak and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

The uttermost parts of the sea are the end of the world and the failing of each person’s own life. To hold the uttermost parts of the sea, therefore, is to await with longing the end of the world and the departure from worldly life. He had, I think, already seized the uttermost parts of the sea in his flight who could truly say: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). I think that you have not received these two wings of contemplation in vain if you have been able to fly thus far. Yet it should count for little with you to have received these two wings; rather, to prove that you are a heavenly creature, strive and labor to have at least two pairs, and then you will indeed have wings by which you may fly up to heavenly things.

Those four living creatures whom the prophet Ezekiel saw and described had four wings, and by this showed themselves to be heavenly, not [Col. 0076B] earthly, creatures: “Each one,” he says, “had four faces, and each one four wings” (Ezek. I). With two, as you read there, they covered their body; with the other two, without doubt, they flew. So too, when you have begun to possess four wings, when you think yourself now a heavenly creature and to bear a heavenly body, nevertheless strive to cover it beneath the aforesaid wings. For there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; and one is the glory of heavenly bodies, another that of earthly bodies. “One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and star differs from star in brightness” (I Cor. XV).

Therefore, even if your whole body is luminous and has no part of darkness within it, it will still be useful to hide it from the eyes of human arrogance and, amid the uncertainty of human mutability, to restrain the brightness of your own self-estimation. [Col. 0076C] For a human being does not know his end; but as fish are caught by a hook and birds taken in a snare, so human beings are caught in an evil time when it suddenly comes upon them (Eccles. IX). Therefore it is good for a person to conceal his good qualities, to presume nothing whatever from his merits, and always to keep himself in humility.

Thus, in the first pair of wings, let a person cover his body; in the second, let him fly toward heaven. For why should those two middle kinds of contemplation not raise a person to heavenly and invisible things, when, as has been said, they have to do with invisible things alone? Let every spiritual person therefore strive, in study and desire, always to be in heavenly things, so that he may say with the Apostle: “But our manner of life is in heaven” (Phil. III).

Yet if you prepare to penetrate, with that same Apostle, even to the third heaven (II Cor. XII), never presume that this can be done with two pairs of wings. Without doubt, whoever desires and aspires to fly as far as the secrets of the third heaven and the mysteries of the Godhead must possess all the six wings of contemplation described above. In this life, all six wings of contemplation can scarcely be possessed except by the perfect. In the life to come, all the elect, among human beings as well as angels, will possess them all, so that of either nature it may truly be said that one has six wings and the other six wings.

## CHAPTER XI. How the first four kinds of contemplation are described mystically.

[Col. 0077A]

Of these six kinds of contemplation, Moses, as it seems to me, speaks under a mystical description where, by the Lord’s command, he undertakes to make that material ark, which was indeed mystical. The first kind, then, is signified in the construction of the ark; the second in its gilding; the third in the crown of the ark; and the fourth we understand through the mercy-seat. The fifth and sixth are signified through the two cherubim.

If, however, we consider the form and material construction, then among those six objects made by hand, only the first is made of wood; all the rest consist of gold. Thus all the matters of which the first kind of contemplation consists [Col. 0077B] are taken in through bodily sense and represented by imagination whenever we wish. But all the other matters from which the remaining kinds arise we gather by reasoning or comprehend by simple understanding. Consider, then, the difference between wood and gold, and perhaps you will discover how suitably these things are signified by wood and those represented by gold: by wood, matters subject to imagination; by gold, matters subject only to understanding.

Gold shines with great brightness in itself; wood has no brightness in itself, except that it kindles fire and nourishes the flame, the servant of light. So imagination has in itself no light of prudence, nothing splendid, except that it is accustomed to stir reason toward discernment and direct it toward the pursuit of knowledge. The second kind of contemplation, in which the reason of visible things is sought, is therefore rightly represented by the gilding of the wood. For what else is the assigned reason of visible and imaginable things than, so to speak, a certain gilding of wood?

Likewise, the crown of the ark can fittingly represent by mystical signification the third kind of contemplation, in which we are accustomed to ascend from visible things to invisible ones and to rise toward their knowledge under the guidance of imagination. For the crown was affixed to the wood at the summit of the ark, yet rose beyond the highest extension of the wood. Thus that kind of contemplation which is occupied with reason according to imagination rests indeed upon imagination, while it derives reasoning from the likeness of imaginable things and raises, as it were, a ladder [Col. 0077D] by which it can ascend to the contemplation of invisible things.

But the mercy-seat is placed above the wood on every side and throughout; and it is therefore very fittingly in it that the kind of contemplation is represented which, surpassing all imagination, is occupied with reason according to reason. And just as the mercy-seat, being the lid of the ark, nowhere descends beneath the wood and does not allow itself to be fastened to the wood, so this contemplation, transcending all imagination and consenting to be mingled with none of it, looks at invisible things alone and attends to invisible things alone.

## CHAPTER XII. How the last two kinds of contemplation are mystically signified.

[Col. 0078A]

The final two kinds of contemplation are expressed by an angelic figure. And rightly so: that workmanship had not a human but an angelic form, since it had to represent by likeness those kinds of contemplation whose subject matter surpasses all human reason.

It should certainly be noted that the aforesaid four are in some fashion joined together as one. But these last two are placed separately and apart. In those first four kinds of contemplation, we grow daily by our own effort, though with divine assistance, and advance from one to another. But in these final two, everything depends on grace; they are altogether far removed and very distant from every human effort, except insofar as each person receives from heaven and has divinely bestowed upon him the disposition of angelic likeness. Perhaps not without reason this final work and angelic figure received the name cherubim: perhaps because without the addition of this highest grace no one can attain the fullness of knowledge.

But because one of the two cherubim is said to stand on one side and the other on the other side, so that one is understood to stand at the right and the other at the left, observe, I pray, how aptly they are set opposite one another and placed face to face: namely, as figures of those matters which seem to accord with reason, and of those which seem to oppose reason. But perhaps someone may continue to ask in what respect this ought particularly to be understood. Consider, then, whether perhaps in the cherub who stood at the right we should understand that kind of contemplation which is above reason, yet not beyond reason; and in the cherub at the left, that which is above reason and seems to be beyond reason.

We know that the left hand is more often held beneath garments and concealed, whereas the right hand is more often brought forth into view. Thus hidden matters are rightly understood through the left, and more manifest matters through the right. Matters that accord with reason are more manifest; matters opposed to reason are more hidden. Therefore we rightly understand the fifth kind of contemplation in the [Col. 0078D] right-hand cherub, and likewise may rightly understand the sixth in the left-hand cherub.

Perhaps these observations are sufficient for more learned minds concerning what ought to have been said about Moses’ ark or the grace of contemplation. But because we are at leisure and speak to those at leisure, we ought not, for the sake of the slower, to be slow in repeating these same matters with a useful and perhaps for some necessary supplement, and, devoting ourselves more freely to the same subject, in treating it more fully. Let us therefore speak of contemplation in the manner and course of one who contemplates; nor let us behold in passing the study of so great a delight and the spectacle of so great an admiration.

We have treated these matters briefly for the busy; for the leisurely, we explain the same matters at greater length by repeating them—taking care at once neither to detain hurried travelers contrary to their purpose [Col. 0079A] nor to press inquisitive explorers of novelties contrary to [Col. 0080A] their wish. Let us now return to each kind of contemplation and speak first of the first.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0079]

## CHAPTER I. The first kind of contemplation consists in considering and admiring visible things.

[Col. 0079A]

The first kind of contemplation, then, consists in the consideration and admiration of bodily things—in all things that enter the mind through the five bodily senses. It is indeed the lowest of all and ought to belong to beginners. For beginners, still unformed, ought to begin with this so that they may gradually ascend to higher things, as it were by certain steps of progress.

To this kind of contemplation belongs every admiration of the Creator that arises from consideration of bodily things; and it is signified in the description of this ark by the joining together of the wood. And with a sufficiently fitting distinction, matters belonging to imagination are signified by wood, just as matters that appear to belong to reason are signified by gold. Yet this ark is not permitted to be made from just any wood, but only from shittim wood, which is highly resistant to decay.

Every investigation of things that is full of integrity and uprightness pertains to incorruptible wood. Incorruptible woods are all considerations of things and all reflections upon works [Col. 0079C] that bring no corruption into the mind and preserve the integrity of sincerity and truth. Amid so great an abundance of visible things and so many kinds of spectacle, then, let each person see what he chooses, and beware lest he bring before the eyes of his mind something by which he defiles the purity of his heart. Therefore, whoever wishes to rejoice in the perpetuity of inward incorruption ought to remove provocations of pleasure from the sight of his consideration. Whatever stimulates greed, whatever excites gluttony, whatever inflames lust, let him separate from the frequent recurrence of such things in his memory.

That person usefully brings the world and the things in the world into contemplation who comes, through the sight of worldly things, to despise worldly things. That great contemplator of worldly matters sought, found, and left written this fruit of such contemplation: “Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. I). He does not take up the contemplation of vanity in vain who, from looking upon what is lowest, rises to the praise of the Creator, finding him wonderful, praiseworthy, and lovable in all his works: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is thy name in all the earth!” (Ps. VIII). Behold, wonderful. “From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is praiseworthy” (Ps. CXVIII). Behold, praiseworthy. “The Lord is righteous in all his ways and holy in all his works” (Ps. CXLIV). Behold, lovable.

Thus hard, strong, durable woods are all considerations that restore the mind’s strength, fortify it unto constancy, and establish it in perseverance. Finally, woods free from every corruption are those which contract neither the stain of ugliness nor the defect of falsehood. Therefore every true assertion and sound judgment concerning bodily things pertains equally to shittim wood, to incorruptible wood. This ark of wisdom must consequently be made of incorruptible wood, of irrefutable judgments, [Col. 0080B] so that we may judge all visible things in the world to have been made by one God and created from nothing, determining nothing in all these things that conflicts with truth.

## CHAPTER II. That the subject matter of this contemplation is abundant, and how philosophers exercised themselves in it.

This contemplation has as its subject matter, as has already been said, everything that bodily sense can touch. Its matter is indeed abundant, and its forest no small one. Let all run there; let each enter; no one is forbidden. Let each choose what he most admires. There is more than enough material for everyone to make an ark for himself. Yet let each learn to choose incorruptible wood, so that he may entertain no thought contrary to true tradition.

The philosophers of the Gentiles likewise sought to select from this same forest material for their own construction, desiring also to build for themselves an ark of wisdom. They began, then, to cut, plane, and join wood: by defining, dividing, and arguing, they discovered, retained, and handed down many things. Thus they made many arks, maintaining various opinions and establishing innumerable schools. Entering that shadowy and dense grove, they entangled themselves in infinite questions; “God gave the world over to their disputation” (Eccles. VII), but “they became vain in their thoughts” (Rom. I), and “failed in searching by searching” (Ps. LXIII), because a human being could not discover the work which God has wrought from beginning to end.

But God revealed through his Spirit to whom he wished, when he wished, [Col. 0080D] as much as it was necessary to know about these things. What wonder, then, if those instructed by the Spirit of God could accomplish a work worthy of admiration, since they were unwilling to follow their own spirit or to walk after the thoughts of their own inventions?

Even in our times certain false philosophers, makers of falsehood, have arisen. Desiring to make a name for themselves, they have labored to discover novelties. Their concern was not so much to affirm what was true as to seem to have discovered what was new. Presuming upon their own judgment, they thought that they could make themselves an ark of wisdom; following their own inventions, they handed down novel opinions, thinking that wisdom was born with them and would die with them. And behold, the lofty arks of wisdom of all these people have rotted away, because they were not made from shittim wood—that is, from incorruptible wood.

And behold, all the princes of Tanis have become fools, because God has made the wisdom of this world foolish. For that worldly philosophy, once glorious, has become so utterly foolish that countless numbers daily become mockers of it from among its professors, and adversaries of it from among its defenders. Detesting it, they profess to know nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified. And behold how many who formerly worked in Aristotle’s workshop at last, by sounder judgment, learn to forge in the Savior’s workshop; and those who formerly made vessels of dishonor are now taught to make vessels of glory, daily confessing to the Lord with the instruments of a psalm, because they repent of having made a work worthy of shame and of having long been makers of falsehood.

Where now, I ask, are the schools of the Academics, Stoics, and Peripatetics? Where are their arks? Behold, all these have now slept their sleep, “and none of these men of riches found anything in their hands” (Ps. LXXV); they “left their riches to strangers, and their tombs are their houses forever” (Ps. XLVIII). And behold, they have all rotted away with their arks, perishing together with their teachings and traditions.

But the ark of Moses remains to this present day, never firmer, never stronger than today, being confirmed by the authority of catholic truth, because it was made from shittim wood—that is, incorruptible and uncorrupted wood—and its entire narrative and teaching is woven together from true judgments and sound assertions. We have seen from what material it ought to be made; next we must learn its measure and the manner of making it, so that, following Moses’ example in all these things, we may follow not our own judgment but the instruction of divine ordinance.

Let us therefore return now to that kind of contemplation which is admittedly the lowest and first of all, and therefore proper to beginners, and which, as we have said, is figured in the description of this ark by the joining together of wood alone.

## CHAPTER III. On the threefold division of the first contemplation.

This contemplation, then, is considered in a threefold way. The first concerns things, the second works, the third morals. The contemplation concerning things belongs to the length of the ark; that concerning works belongs to its breadth; that concerning morals belongs to its height.

[Col. 0081D] For we know that length is naturally prior to breadth, just as breadth has priority in relation to height. For length without breadth, and breadth without height, can be conceived, although in the reality of things they cannot in the least be separated from each other. But height without breadth, or breadth without length, can neither exist nor be conceived. Simple length is conceived when quantity, moving from point to point and through points alone, is extended into a line at least in thought alone. We call it simple breadth when we extend in the mind quantity from line to line and through lines alone, expanding it into a surface. For just as a line is length without breadth, so a surface is breadth without height. Height, however, exists [Col. 0082A] when quantity thickens from surface to surface and produces a solid body, which receives three dimensions.

Whoever considers these things rightly will see clearly enough, I think, that length is naturally prior to breadth and breadth to height. Thus the consideration concerned with things is naturally prior to that concerned with works and to that concerned with morals.
