For who does not know that things themselves are sometimes prior to their operations even in time, and always prior by nature—things from which and in which all operations have their existence, and without which they cannot exist at all? Likewise, morals, whether good or bad, are customarily and properly considered in relation to works. Human works, indeed, insofar as they are ordered and moderate, belong for the most part to good morals; insofar as they are disordered and immoderate, they likewise belong to bad morals. It is therefore clear enough that, just as the consideration of things is prior to that of works, so the consideration of works is naturally prior to that of morals. Thus it was rightly said that the consideration of things belongs to the length of our ark, the consideration of works to its breadth, and the consideration of morals to its height.

## CHAPTER IV. That the first grade of this contemplation is concerned with matter, form, and nature.

The consideration of these three is itself divided threefold. The first consideration in this subdivision concerns matter, the second form, the third nature. Matter and form are easily apprehended by bodily sight. We distinguish a stone from wood and a triangle from a square without error. But what belongs to nature was partly exposed to sense and partly hidden more deeply, reserved for reason.

Nature is considered in the intrinsic quality of things, just as form consists in their extrinsic quality. The inner quality of things is for the most part perceived by bodily sense, as flavors by taste and odors by smell. But that power of nature which has been impressed upon things to their very marrow and lies hidden more deeply within could never have been approached by a human being through the sense of the flesh, even if he had not sinned. Yet he would easily have perceived it by the sharpness of his intellect, if the eye of reason had not been darkened by the cloud of sin and obscured beneath the mist of error.

Now, wrapped in the darkness of ignorance, whenever we inquire into it, we grope rather than see by the evidence of experience. The reason is therefore clear why the length of our ark, according to the Lord’s instruction, ought not—or rather cannot—be more than two and a half cubits. For human knowledge has a full cubit where it possesses certainty, where it can apprehend by some sense what it is necessary to know. Bodily sense, then, has one cubit in the inspection of matter; it has another cubit in the consideration of form; it has half a cubit in the apprehension of nature, which it penetrates only in part. For, as has been said, nature is partly exposed to sense and partly reserved for reason.

These three things, then—matter, form, and nature—because they coexist in bodily substance and cannot be divided from one another, stretch out as it were into a line and show themselves to belong to the length of the ark.

## CHAPTER V. That the second grade is concerned with the operation of nature and of human skill.

A mind exercised in this threefold consideration, which belongs to the contemplation of things, ought next to transfer itself to the contemplation of works. When it has learned to extend its consideration both to natural works and to artificial works, the breadth of our ark can receive the measure of its appointed size. For the operation of nature is one thing and the operation of skill another.

We can readily discern the operation of nature in grasses, trees, and animals: in grasses, how they grow and ripen; in trees, likewise, how they put forth leaves, flower, and bear fruit; in animals, how they conceive and give birth, how some are born and others die. In short, whenever we observe how all things that arise pass away and how things that increase grow old, we exercise our mind in the inspection of natural operation.

Artificial work—that is, the work of skill—is considered in carving, painting, writing, agriculture, and the other artificial works. In all these we find innumerable things for which we ought worthily to admire and venerate the condescension of the divine gift. Natural work and artificial work cooperate with one another and are thus joined to each other, as it were, side by side; they are united through their mutual contemplation. For it is certain that the work of skill takes its beginning, subsistence, and strength from natural operation; and that natural operation is improved through skill, so as to become better.

Human knowledge has a full cubit in artificial work, because if it could not comprehend it, it could not have invented it. But it cannot have a full cubit in natural work, because it comprehends it only in part. It easily judges what is usually born from what: it does not seek apples on a vine, clusters of grapes in a field of grain, or wheat on a tree. Yet when is it sufficient to explain how any of these, or any other thing, is born from another? Therefore, when the sharpness of our intellect diffuses itself on every side in this twofold consideration of nature and art, and runs in many directions here and there with marvelous liveliness of understanding, the breadth of our ark receives the measure fitting to it according to the pattern of divine institution.

## CHAPTER VI. That the third grade of this contemplation consists in both human and divine institutions.

After the first consideration, which concerns things, and the second, which concerns works, follows the third, which consists in morals and which, as we have already said, belongs to the height of our ark. The discipline of morals has proceeded partly from divine institution and partly from human institution.

Divine worship and all the sacraments of the Church belong to divine ordinances. Human laws, customs, civility, enactments of the people, civil law, and many other such things belong to human institutions. Human institution exists for the lower life; divine institution for the higher life. The former is for attaining the safety and tranquility of temporal life; the latter for obtaining salvation and the fullness of eternal blessedness.

Human knowledge can possess a full cubit in human institution, because what it can discover it can, unsurprisingly, comprehend. But in the divine sacraments we do not doubt that there are two elements. One is what we see outwardly in a thing or act; the other is that spiritual power hidden within. You can believe the reality of the sacrament which lies hidden within, but you cannot see it at all; therefore you cannot extend your knowledge in this respect to a full cubit.

This final contemplation, which concerns morals, pertains to the height of our ark, as we have already said. For truly, when human institution serves divine institution, the mind profits from both and tends upward. A mind attached to matters belonging to the first or second consideration undoubtedly still lies low. But the more perfectly it clings to matters belonging to the third, the more it continually rises to higher things.

It should certainly be noted that natural operation and divine institution have a full cubit in reality, but can possess only half a cubit in our knowledge. Conversely, artificial operation and human institution scarcely have half a cubit in reality, but can have a full cubit in our knowledge. When, then, the mind has been fully exercised in this threefold contemplation, the measure of our ark receives its fitting magnitude in every direction.

The Prophet shows himself to be engaged in this kind of contemplation when he says: “I meditated upon all thy works” (Ps. CXLII). And elsewhere: “For thou hast delighted me, O Lord, in thy making” (Ps. XCI). And elsewhere he cries out in admiration of them: “How magnified are thy works, O Lord! Thou hast made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII), and, explaining the same psalm, recounts many things concerning those same works.

We can therefore rightly divide this whole first kind of contemplation into seven grades. The first consists in that admiration of things which arises from consideration of matter. The second grade consists in that admiration of things which arises from consideration of form. The third consists in that admiration of things which the consideration of nature produces. The fourth grade of this contemplation is occupied with the consideration and admiration of works according to the operation of nature. The fifth is likewise occupied with the consideration and admiration of works, but according to the operation of skill. The sixth grade consists in considering and admiring human institutions. The seventh, finally, remains in considering and admiring divine institutions.

These seven steps of ascent first meet those who endeavor to ascend the mountain of the Lord or to enter that temple of Ezekiel. By seven steps one enters through the outer gates into the outer court: “And its ascent,” he says, “was by seven steps.” You have, therefore, the steps of beginning upon which you ought to stand, whoever you are who desire to grasp the art of contemplation. How this kind of contemplation rests in imagination or proceeds according to imagination, the preceding book has fully taught; it need not be repeated here.

## CHAPTER VII. That the second kind of contemplation consists in considering and admiring the reason of visible things.

[Col. 0085B] Now, since we have already said, as best we could, what needed to be said again concerning the first kind of contemplation, let us proceed to the second, which, as has already been said, is signified by the gilding of the ark. If, therefore, the first kind of contemplation is rightly understood to consist in considering the appearance of bodily things, it follows, I think, that the second kind of contemplation must be understood to consist in discerning the reason of those same things. Therefore, as often as we occupy ourselves in the gilding of our ark, so often do we investigate the rationale of visible things; and we are held in wonder at that rationale once found and perceived, whenever, by attending we understand and by understanding we attend to how wonderfully made, how suitably ordered, how wisely disposed are all the things that appear in this fabric of the world. [Col. 0085C] We gild our ark when we consider the cause, manner, and effect, the usefulness and rationale, of each thing.

Oh, with what gold of knowledge he abounded! How could he lack sufficient means to gild his whole ark, who truly said: “God gave me to speak according to judgment. For he gave me true knowledge of the things that are, that I might know the constitution of the world and the powers of the elements; the beginning, end, and middle of times; the changes of seasons and the divisions of times; the cycles of the year and arrangements of the stars; the natures of animals and the rage of beasts; the force of winds and the thoughts of men; [Col. 0085D] the differences of plants and the powers of roots” (Wisdom 7). Finally, hear what he adds at the end, so that you may understand more fully how great an abundance of such wealth he possessed for the work of his gilding: “And whatever things are hidden and unforeseen, I learned” (ibid.).

Therefore, the gilding of our ark consists in contemplating the rationale of divine works, judgments, mysteries, and likewise human actions or institutions. Let us, finally, be ready, according to Peter’s instruction, “to give an answer to everyone who asks” concerning the faith and hope that are in us (1 Peter 3); and we have now gilded the upper or outermost parts of our ark when we know how, by expounding them, to commend the rationale of divine mysteries and also of judgments.

## CHAPTER VIII. How abundant is the material of this contemplation

[Col. 0086A]

Whoever, then, has now advanced to this second kind of contemplation finds, amid so vast an extent of material, abundant places in which to spread the sails of his inquiry and exercise the vessels of his disputation. For who does not see how widely the sea of such consideration lies open, how variously this great and wide sea spreads itself abroad? In wonder at this immensity the Prophet cries: “Your judgments are a great deep” (Ps. 55 [56]). Truly a great deep: God’s hidden judgments are many in number, great in depth, plainly infinite, and wholly unsearchable.

Hence those wondrous sights of those “who see wonders in the deep.” For how many wonders, do you suppose, do those see in this deep who “go down to the sea in ships, doing business in great waters”? [Col. 0086B] Indeed, many gather at this great and wide sea, but some to cross it and others to fish. Those cross it who desire to pass from nation to nation and from one kingdom to another people. But those among them who are fishers of men come indeed to fish, casting out their nets for a catch. Thus, now casting the net to the left, now to the right of the vessel at the Lord’s command, they often enclose a great multitude of fish: that is, they enclose the wandering thoughts and draw the slippery affections of men out upon dry land.

Nor do they always cast the same nets, any more than they cast them for the same catch. [Col. 0086C] Now they spread nets of argument, now of exhortation: sometimes to prove some truth, sometimes to refute some falsehood, sometimes to draw out something hidden, sometimes to persuade men of what is just, sometimes to dissuade them from something unjust. These, indeed, who know how to carry on such activity in great waters—these, I say, are those who see wonders in the deep. For wisdom is drawn from hidden things by them.

Hear what that great contemplator of wisdom says: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103 [104]). “You have made all things in wisdom,” he says. Without doubt, the things he had seen were wondrous, since he cried out thus. He had indeed seen wonders in the deep [Col. 0086D] and drawn wisdom from hidden things, who discovered that all things had been made in wisdom and firmly recognized that wisdom “reaches mightily from end to end and disposes all things sweetly.” Behold how, in all divine works, this gold of wisdom appeared and shone; how the brightness of divine wisdom covered all things before his eyes.

That man truly knew well and could easily gild his ark—indeed, it is quite clear that he had already covered his ark on every side with gold—who was compelled by the greatness of his wonder to cry: “You have made all things in wisdom.” Let us also strive as much as we can and labour diligently at gilding our ark, so that all divine works may likewise appear to us as made in wisdom; so that, as far as we are permitted, we may understand, and [Col. 0087A] what we are not permitted to understand may at least be believed without hesitation to have been made in wisdom. Let us believe that not only those things which God does, but also whatever he permits to be done, never occur without a rational cause or take place without divine, though hidden, justice.

## CHAPTER IX. How philosophers exercised themselves in the material of this contemplation

But I think it should not be passed over in silence how the wise men of this world endeavoured to gild their arks, so that we may at least be ashamed not to labour at the gilding of our own ark. The philosophers of the nations likewise strove to draw wisdom from hidden things. Investigating the concealed causes of things and penetrating, by the sharpness of their intellect, into nature’s hidden recesses, they brought forth [Col. 0087B] gold from the deep. Thus they began to investigate, discover, and bring to light the hidden causes of things, and to establish every doubtful matter by undoubted assertions. Through profound investigation they discovered many things worthy of wonder: whence comes the trembling of the earth, by what force the deep seas swell, and many other things of this kind; and, committing these discoveries to writing, they took care to transmit them to posterity.

Thus they were able to gild their ark in large part—but only outwardly. For they had little concern, and no ability, to gild it inwardly. Their money soon failed them; they did not possess such abundance of gold as would have enabled them to gild it inwardly, since their resources failed even for gilding it wholly [Col. 0087C] outwardly. For it was not within the same capacity to discover the physical explanations of things and to discern the hidden causes of justice in events that occur. It is one thing, far different, to investigate and establish the hidden causes of things according to natural reasoning; it is another not to be ignorant of the rationale of divine judgments.

The investigation of nature pertains to the outward gilding of our ark; the affirmation of divine justice pertains to its inward gilding. In this respect they entirely failed, thinking that all things happened by chance rather than by divine direction. Consecrating an altar to Fortune, they believed that the goddess had no concern for human affairs, because they saw good and evil befall alike the good and the evil, the just and the unjust, one who offers sacrifices and one who despises them—although he whose “eyelids examine the children of men” [Col. 0087D] causes his sun to rise upon the good and the evil and rains equally upon the just and the unjust.

But we, for whom gold now abounds, both from the profit of our labours and from the spoils of the Egyptians, should take care to clothe our ark in gold not only outwardly but inwardly as well. Let us attend to how, in his wisdom, he made all these things; how by his wisdom he founded the earth and established the heavens by prudence; how by his wisdom the deeps burst forth and the clouds grow thick with dew—and we shall have gilded our ark outwardly. Let us likewise consider that all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, how the Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works—and we shall have gilded it inwardly.

How, do you think, [Col. 0088A] had he overlaid all the beauty of the woods in his ark with gold, who had clearly perceived and steadfastly affirmed of the Lord that “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144 [145])? Let us also endeavour, following the Prophet’s example, to cover all things with gold of this kind and to hide them beneath such splendour, even though, in comparison with the divine rationale and disposition by which all outward beauty has been made and ordered, that beauty may seem little or nothing in our eyes.

## CHAPTER X. On the division of the second contemplation

Above, when we spoke of the first kind of contemplation, we divided it into seven steps. It would be lengthy now to run through each one and show how the ark must be gilded throughout all its cubits, in length, breadth, and height. But lest we make this too long, we have judged it better to set those matters aside for the moment.

If anyone, however, is eager to undertake this work and wishes to overlay his ark with gold, there is no harm in borrowing the gold of knowledge from external sciences and secular disciplines, provided that he knows how to cleanse it of every dross of falsehood or vanity, and thoroughly refine it to the full and perfect purity required by the dignity of this work. We said that the gilding of our ark consists in assigning the rationale of visible things. But who does not know how nearly all worldly philosophy [Col. 0088C] labours chiefly to discover, by the investigation of its acuteness, the hidden causes of visible things and bring them to light? See what great and numerous riches of learning and treasures of knowledge those distinguished minds of philosophers acquired, stored up, and left to you for such uses.

Nevertheless, as has been said, all these things cannot suffice for the inward gilding of the ark. But if you wish to gild it inwardly too, you will seek material for such use more suitably from Christian theologians than from the philosophers of the world. Yet just as the treasures of the latter cannot suffice for the ark’s inward gilding, so neither can those of the former suffice for its inward gilding. For neither were the former able fully to perceive the hidden nature of things, nor could the latter perfectly penetrate [Col. 0088D] the hidden justice of God.

But behold, we show you yet one treasure, which we know to be superabundant and inexhaustible for this task. Certainly, where the gold of understanding fails, the refined gold of faith cannot be lacking. Even if you could read through and commit to memory every saying of philosophers and every treatise of the Catholic religion, you would nevertheless find innumerable matters in nature’s more secret regions and in the mysteries of divine judgments whose rationale you could not penetrate. But what you cannot understand, you can believe. Therefore, do not doubt that those things whose rationale you cannot discern are nonetheless just and ordered according to the rule of faith. Hence, concerning such matters, it is said to you: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7). Therefore believe with blessed [Col. 0089A] Job that nothing happens on earth without a cause (Job 5); believe that “the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves” (Ps. 18 [19]); and you have gilded your ark both outside and within.

## CHAPTER XI. On the characteristic of the second contemplation

It has been said that this kind of contemplation has this in common with the preceding kind: namely, that it is exercised in imagination and occupied with the consideration of visible and imaginable things. Yet they differ most of all in this: in the former nothing is sought by reasoning, but everything proceeds according to imagination; this latter is woven by reasoning and shaped according to reason. The former, therefore, is in imagination according to imagination; the latter is in imagination according to reason.

[Col. 0089B] It should be noted that even in that part in which it rests upon faith rather than is woven by understanding, it does not entirely exceed the bounds of its own characteristic. For when, by the keenness of its understanding, it perceives innumerable works of God as distinct and ordered, and his innumerable judgments as just and true, it concludes from those things which it understands to be right that those things also are right whose rationale it cannot penetrate. You see, then, that this inquiry is not wholly drawn away from the path of its reasoning even where it follows the traces of faith.

Indeed, the inquiry of which we are now speaking is conducted so much according to reason that even imagination itself seems in it to be arranged and ordered according to reason. In the first kind, thought follows imagination alone wherever wonder leads it; but in this kind imagination itself is formed, arranged, and regulated by reason. For when someone silently investigates the rationale of visible things, he not only sets them before himself in an order other than that in which he encounters them through the senses, but often depicts them under another form. For he discovers more quickly why they ought to have been made or ordered thus when he sees the evils that would follow if they were otherwise. Therefore, just as in the former kind imagination draws thought after itself, so in this one reason leads imagination about and arranges it. Both are said to consist in imagination because each is occupied with it through attention or investigation: whatever we wish, we represent by imagination. For wherever the mind is carried in this twofold [Col. 0089D] inquiry through different mirrors, the gaze of the contemplator is always fixed in imagination through the purpose or effort of his attention.

## CHAPTER XII. On the third kind of contemplation

Now let us consider the third kind of contemplation. This kind is involved whenever, through the likeness of visible things, we apprehend the character of invisible things; whenever, through the visible things of the world, we know the invisible things of God. Thus it is established what is found written: “The invisible things of God are perceived through the things made, being understood from the creation of the world.”

This contemplation, which, in order to ascend to invisible things, supports itself upon the staff of bodily likeness and raises itself to things on high by a kind of ladder of bodily properties, is rightly signified by the crown of the ark. For the crown is fastened to the wood at its lower part, but at its upper part rises beyond the measure of the wood. [Col. 0090A] The crown thus surrounds the upper portions of the ark and descends beneath the wood in part, yet for the greater part exceeds the measure of the wood.

So too this inquiry willingly inclines itself to investigate the properties of bodily things, so that it may have from them a basis upon which to draw a likeness to those invisible things. Yet, spreading itself more widely, it contains within itself the narrowness of lower things; and, not content with what it has gathered from likeness, it proves one thing from another by argument and inference, and by pursuing consequences leaves every bodily likeness far behind and rises above the upper parts of our ark in lofty consideration. Thus the crown rests upon the ark while it is raised on high, because the contemplator’s mind is greatly aided in apprehending invisible things by the likeness of visible things.

But then the crown both spreads itself wider and rises higher than the ark when the subtle contemplator clearly perceives that invisible goods surpass visible goods both in abundance and in dignity. For the greatness of invisible goods is far too abundant to be represented by even so great a multitude of bodily resemblances. Yet all bodily things have some likeness to invisible goods: some a very low, distant, and almost alien likeness; [Col. 0090C] others a nearer and clearer one, and the nearer it is, the more evident it is; and beyond these, some have a very close, kindred, as I might say, and wholly expressed likeness, so that they seem no longer merely to approach visible things, but rather to adhere to and be grafted into them than to draw near. Therefore, we ought to draw a likeness from those things which approach invisible realities more closely and bear a clearer image of them, so that our understanding may ascend from what we know to what we do not know by experience. Hence the crown of the ark does not descend all the way to its lower parts, though it joins itself to the ark in its upper portions.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, in this kind of contemplation, a person begins to become spiritual

[Col. 0090D]

At this first stage a person is led away from being animal-like and learns to become spiritual, because he then begins to acquire spiritual things and to be formed in the renewal of his mind, striving each day more and more to relish the things above, not the things upon earth. It is surely a great labour to abandon accustomed things, leave at the very bottom the low concerns of ingrained thoughts, and by lofty investigation fly up from earthly to heavenly things.

Here the wisdom of God—that light which teaches a person knowledge and enlightens every person coming into this world—first begins to enter in, now pouring the rays of its light into the eyes of the mind, now withdrawing and again concealing them. Thus it visits the mind frequently, [Col. 0091A] now raising it to the heights and again depressing it to the depths and leaving it to itself. But it returns unexpectedly, meets it where it was not hoped for, and shows itself gracious. Here at last it begins to form before the beholder’s sight a kind of prelude to a wondrous vision; and, like an eagle provoking its young to fly by the continual flight and return of its revelations, it carries itself in different directions, first inflaming the contemplator’s mind with desire to fly, and at times fully training it for complete flight.

Here the mind first recovers its ancient dignity and claims for itself the innate honour of its proper freedom. For what is so alien to a rational spirit, what so unworthily subject to servitude, as that the creature which is truly spiritual should be ignorant of spiritual things, and that one made for invisible and supreme goods should not even be able to rise to the contemplation of invisible things, much less stand there? Hence, I think, it sufficiently appears why the familiar constancy and constant familiarity of this inquiry, which holds the third place, are rightly signified by a crown and fittingly called a crown: by it the victorious mind is crowned.

Whoever has been able through contemplation of the mind to pass from the miseries of this exile into the freedom of invisible joys receives this crown of spiritual knowledge. There, at last, the rational spirit—which for a long time had sat in darkness and the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron—having finally cast off the darkness of ignorance and broken the chains of desire, through the strength of him who “brings forth those who are bound in might,” shattering the bronze gates and breaking the iron bars, overcomes the constrictions of ingrained habit and hardness. [Col. 0091C] Through the midst of the innumerable host of base desires and carnal thoughts, rushing against it on every side and resisting everywhere, it violently breaks through, and at last scarcely receives itself into the palace of its own dominion, gathering its whole self upon the throne of the heavenly dwelling. Thereafter, with its fellow-soldiers and like triumphant ones, it may confidently sing: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the division of those things that belong to this inquiry

[Col. 0091D] It should be noted that no measurement is prescribed for our crown; yet by the very fact that it is called a crown, its measurement is for the most part determined. For it would not be called a crown unless it encircled and crowned the upper portions of the ark on every side. Therefore the crown had to be extended or stretched according to the ark’s length and breadth, so that it might encircle and crown it. Accordingly, it has, in conformity with the ark’s dimensions, two and a half cubits in length and one and a half cubits in breadth.

But we cannot estimate its height by the same reasoning, nor should we make it equal to the ark’s height. For it would by no means be called a crown if it covered the whole ark, rather than adorning only its upper part. Now, as we have already said above, the characteristic of this inquiry is to draw a likeness from visible things to invisible things and, from the consideration of the former, to ascend to knowledge of the latter by establishing the intended likeness. If, then, the measurement is the same in both—if the ark on the one hand and the crown on the other have precisely the same length and breadth—what else should be understood by this except that we are taught to draw grounds of likeness for the investigation of invisible things from all those things which we have said belong to the length or breadth of our ark?

As has been said, the consideration of matter, form, and nature belongs to the ark’s length in the inquiry into things. The operation both of nature and of human skill belongs to its breadth. From all these, therefore, we can and ought to draw suitable grounds of likeness for the investigation of invisible things; and when we have skillfully employed such a practice as was fitting or proper, we have surrounded our ark with its crown.

It has also been said that, in the consideration of morals, both human and divine institution belong to the ark’s height, so that the ark of our understanding appears to have a full cubit from human institution but half a cubit from divine institution. But why does the crown mentioned seem to touch only the upper portions of the ark, unless because human institutions plainly possess a very remote and wholly foreign likeness to invisible and spiritual things? Who does not know that they were devised for the use of temporal things, not as figures of eternal things?

But all visible works of the Creator are created and arranged in such a way that they both serve the uses of the present life and bear a shadow of future goods. Hence it also follows that the operation of human skill, insofar as it imitates nature, bears within itself a shadow of invisible or future things. But human institutions are otherwise as foreign to the likeness of invisible things as their inventors thought of nothing of that sort in establishing them. Whenever, however, we find in these institutions some likeness to those realities, let us see whether perhaps it falls under one of those considerations which we assigned above to the ark’s length or breadth.

Concerning divine institutions, it should be noted that we ought to understand some simply and seek nothing mystical in them; while others ought to be practised according to the literal sense and yet signify something mystical. Therefore, because mystical understanding is required in precepts that are more exalted and deeper to understand, that half-cubit assigned to the height of our ark in divine institutions is, as it were, adorned in its upper portion by a golden crown. Yet even in this respect the fitting application of likeness does not wholly depart from the character of those five considerations mentioned above. Thus the crown extends itself according to the ark’s length and breadth, so that it may surround it on every side.

## CHAPTER XV. Why this kind of contemplation is rightly divided into five steps

[Col. 0093A]

This third kind of contemplation is therefore rightly divided into five steps, according to those five aforesaid modes of consideration from which grounds of likeness are sought or established for the investigation of invisible things. For when likeness is drawn from one thing to another, it is formed in various orders according to the same modes.

The first mode is when a likeness is taken from that from which the thing itself exists, or rather from that which the thing itself is. The second and third draw a likeness from that which is in it. The fourth and fifth draw it from that which is through it. The second is from that which is in it externally; [Col. 0093B] the third, from that which is in it internally. The fourth is from that which occurs through it under some compulsion of necessity; the fifth, from that which occurs through it by the purpose of the will.

Thus, in this inquiry, the first mode of reasoning is drawn from the property of matter. The second and third arise from the quality of the thing itself: the second from an external quality, which we called form; the third from an internal quality, which we above called nature. The fourth mode is inferred from what happens in a thing itself or through it according to natural motion. Finally, the fifth arises from what is done according to artificial motion.

A likeness is drawn from the property of matter when it is said: “His legs are columns of marble, founded upon bases of gold” (Song 5). External quality consists in colour and figure. A likeness is established from colour in the passage: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (ibid.). A likeness is drawn from the quality of figure where Scripture, in a mystical description, commends a quality: “The appearance of the wheels and their work was as though a wheel were in the midst of a wheel” (Ezek. 1).

Note that external quality belongs to sight alone, just as internal quality belongs to any of the other senses. The following establishment of a likeness belongs to hearing, where you hear: “The voice which I heard was like the voice of harpists playing upon their harps” (Rev. 14). But the following seems to refer to smell, where Wisdom speaks of herself: “Like cinnamon and fragrant balsam [Col. 0093D] I gave forth fragrance; like choice myrrh I gave sweetness of odour” (Ecclus. 24). A likeness is drawn from the delights of taste where that same Wisdom says of herself: “My spirit is sweet above honey, and my inheritance above honey and the honeycomb” (ibid.). This other passage recalls the delights of touch: “Like ointment upon the head, which ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. 132 [133]).

Let these things have been said concerning internal quality, namely insofar as bodily senses can attain it. Natural operation is brought into consideration for the sake of likeness when, in the Lord’s voice, the prophet is promised: “As rain and snow come down from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth and soak it and cause it to germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, [Col. 0094A] so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth” (Isa. 55). From artificial operation comes that application of likeness which you hear from the Apostle: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. 2).

In the construction of our crown, we have sought to scatter for you these seeds of teaching concerning the rationale of likenesses, as above concerning the gilding of the ark, so that you may have the means, whenever you wish, to gather an abundant harvest of knowledge. For this subject requires a separate treatise if it is to be explained fully and adequately. It needs more extensive and diligent investigation because the whole rationale of this inquiry rests upon this mode of reasoning.

It is clear, moreover, that in this and the following inquiry the greatest, indeed almost the chief, consolation of spiritual persons lies in our times. For exceedingly few can rise to those last two kinds of contemplation. But whoever wishes to investigate these matters more fully should remember that, in conformity with the form of the ark, its crown had four sides.

## CHAPTER XVI. Why the matters belonging to this inquiry may also be divided in another way

There is another point that we may rightly observe in this crown, if we are to understand by it the fullness of invisible goods. For the crown surrounded the mercy-seat on every side [Col. 0094C] and enclosed it wholly within itself. As regards the construction of the ark, the mercy-seat must be understood as nothing other than the ark’s lid: namely, a certain golden plate, made entirely of the purest gold, which was supported underneath by the top of the ark and, as has already been said, surrounded on every side by a golden crown.

By these two things—the crown and the mercy-seat—we understand two kinds of contemplation: one concerning invisible goods, the other concerning invisible substances, as in angelic or human spirits. What, then, does it mean that the crown encloses the whole mercy-seat within itself, except that the blessedness of the righteous comprehends all their desire within itself? So long as we live under the impoverished elements of this world, our desires extend beyond our joys, because there are infinitely more things which we desire than we can attain in this life. But that blessed multitude of heavenly spirits does not extend its desires beyond the fullness of its joys. It is wholly unable to comprehend the infinity or immensity of its happiness, which the crown of its blessedness surrounds on every side and encloses everywhere within the bosom of its magnitude.

Their joy lies not only in the contemplation of the Creator but also in contemplating his creatures. For, while they find God wonderful in all his works, what wonder if everywhere they reverence him in wonder and, reverencing him, marvel at the great deeds [Col. 0095A] of him whom they love? Thus they find in incorporeal creatures, and also in bodily creatures, grounds for wonder and for worthily reverencing their Creator.

Some things, then, are what they see above themselves; others, what they see in themselves; and others, what they see below themselves. They contemplate all these continually; contemplating, they marvel; marvelling, they rejoice. They rejoice in divine contemplation, rejoice together in mutual vision, and take delight in the inquiry into bodily things. The lowest part of the crown, which descends beneath the mercy-seat and is fastened to the wood, signifies that delightful spectacle which they have in lower creatures. The middle part of the crown, which is joined to the mercy-seat, figures that most ardent desire of love which they derive from the delight of mutual vision. The highest part of the crown, raised above the mercy-seat, expresses that ineffable joy which they drink in from unceasing contemplation of their Creator.

Let us also learn, in contemplating, to marvel, and, in marvelling, to contemplate: how the citizens of heavenly blessedness behold without limit all that is beneath them and comprehend the rationale and order of all that they see from on high; how they rejoice without end in mutual fellowship and indissoluble love; how they burn insatiably for the vision of divine brightness—and we shall have crowned our ark. Let us consider how they go out and come in and find pasture, and we shall have completed the crown of our ark in the manner appropriate to it.

You see, certainly, that spiritual pastures are found not only in inward things but also in outward, bodily things. Without doubt, bodily goods can provide spiritual spirits with spiritual pasture, insofar as they resemble invisible and incorporeal goods—and this is no wonder. For if no visible goods at all had a likeness to invisible things, they could in no way help us in investigating invisible things; nor would it stand written of them that “the invisible things of God are perceived through the things made, being understood” (Rom. 1). But if these things did not differ from those by much unlikeness, they would undoubtedly not be passing, transitory, and insufficient. Yet their unlikeness to those things is incomparably greater than their likeness. For the surpassing greatness of the future fullness is infinite in comparison with these things. Hence [Col. 0095D] the uppermost parts of the ark scarcely touch the crown and are joined to its lower portions, because the highest things here speak of the lowest things there, amid so many signs of their likeness, only in part.

## CHAPTER XVII. That in this inquiry we employ the guidance of bodily likeness
But the difference between the second kind of contemplation and this third kind, of which we are now speaking, appears to be this: the former, as we have already said above, moves within imagination and is regulated according to reason; the latter consists in reason, but follows imagination. In this speculation the mind, through all the various things it investigates, directs itself toward invisible realities and strives to apprehend them. Thus this speculation consists in reason in that it persists in investigating only those things which bodily sense is wholly unable to grasp. But because the investigation belonging to this speculation does not arrive at knowledge of invisible things without the aid of bodily likenesses, reason seems in this respect to follow the guidance of imagination, and in the course of its inquiry is shown to have imagination, as it were, for a guide upon its way.

For when imagination presents to reason the forms of visible things and, from the likeness of those same things, instructs it for the investigation of invisible things, it in some manner leads reason where it did not know how to go by itself. Reason would never rise to contemplation of invisible things unless imagination, by presenting forms of visible things, supplied it with material from which it might draw a likeness to those things and shape the method of its investigation. Hence our inner man calls the outer man his guide when he says: “But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance” (Ps. 54).

For it is certain that the mind cannot attain external knowledge except through bodily sense. Rightly, therefore, the inner man calls the outer man his guide, without whose service—or rather, instruction—he cannot reach knowledge of visible things. Nor indeed can he reach knowledge of invisible things, since he cannot rise to know them without knowledge of these visible things. Therefore, as often as he is compelled to gain experience of things to be known through bodily sense, so often, surely, our inner man appears to follow his guide.

Without doubt the sense of the flesh precedes the sense of the heart in knowing things; for unless the mind first received sensible things through bodily sense, it could not at all discover even what it might think about them. Yet perhaps it is not surprising if bodily sense leads the sense of the heart where bodily sense itself can go. But this is very wonderful: how it leads the heart where it itself cannot ascend. Bodily sense does not grasp incorporeal things; yet reason does not rise to them without its guidance, as the argument set forth above has taught.

Certainly, even if man had not sinned at all, the outward sense would assist the inward in the knowledge of things. For who would deny that Adam received his Eve as a helper? Yet it is one thing to have a companion in one’s course and another to seek a guide for one’s journey. For because Eve once drew her husband after herself, contrary to God’s counsel or command, and bent him to assent to her counsel, Adam, weakened by the punishment of his transgression, now must follow her and even now needs her daily instruction. Nevertheless, he is not merely unashamed but even glories in the guidance of his helper when, through her service, he is led by the path of bodily likenesses to contemplation of invisible things: “A man,” he says, “of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance” (Ps. 54).

How the outer man is of one mind with, or well known to, the inner man is, I think, sufficiently clear and needs no extended exposition. Consider now how the movement of the body readily answers the movement of the heart, and you will more quickly discover how harmonious with it he is. As soon as the mind wills, the foot or hand moves. At its command the eye turns about. At its discretion the tongue moves, and the lips, or any other members of the body, move. What, I ask, in the nature of things is more unlike than spirit and body? Yet where, I beg you, do we find such great unanimity of such perfect concord that almost—indeed altogether—at the same time there are willing to act and acting, willing to move and moving? There is only one bodily member, namely that in the part where lust reigns, which does not obey the command of the inner man.

But when, by divine help, he is able to restrain this member’s resistance through measured affliction, he then dares henceforth to call it harmonious with himself and names it the man of his peace: “The man,” he says, “of my peace.” See how it is harmonious. But how is it known to him? It is sufficiently clear that whatever is done in any part of the body, wherever it is injured, wherever it is soothed by any pleasure, immediately comes to the mind’s awareness. Thus no affliction or delight which affects bodily sensation can wholly escape its notice. And just as the movement of the heart, without resistance, immediately goes outward in bodily motion, so every bodily sensation enters the mind without delay; and just as bodily movement obeys the heart’s decision in all its action, so every bodily passion enters the mind without repulse. The very swift suddenness of its sympathy or rejoicing proves how truly no bodily injury or pleasure escapes the mind.

For just as willing to move and moving occur at one and the same time, so in one and the same instant the body suffers and the heart suffers with it; the body is delighted outwardly and the heart rejoices inwardly. Choose which you should wonder at more: the body’s so prompt obedience to the mind, or the mind’s so intimate acquaintance with the body. Wonderful is that obedience in which bodily movement almost anticipates every desire of the mind. Wonderful is that intimacy of knowledge in which the mind almost forefeels whatever the body feels.

Our inner man indeed has, from this intimate knowledge of his household companion, something at which to marvel; but he has nothing in which to glory. It is no great glory for the mind to know what ordinarily delights or harms its body. But this will unquestionably be great when, having begun through many proofs of experience to know with what discernment it ought both to comply with the appetite of the flesh in necessary matters and to oppose it in superfluous ones, it neither awakens an enemy by giving it too little indulgence nor nourishes a rebel; nor, by afflicting it too severely, destroys a citizen and overwhelms a helper.

Truly, the mind scarcely reaches the perfection of such knowledge except through many arguments and after many experiences; but once it has acquired it, it profits from it greatly. Without it Adam can never use his helper well. Through it our outer man is taught gradually to loathe, and finally to forget, the delights of Egypt; and nevertheless he becomes accustomed to delight in spiritual food. This may seem wonderful, or rather incredible, to someone. But if he does not believe me on this point, let him believe one who has experienced it. Let us hear him whom this experience had taught and observe what he says: “The man of my peace, in whom I hoped, who ate my breads” (Ps. 48). And again in this place: “He who together with me received sweet foods; in the house of God we walked with one accord” (ibid.).

Scripture makes plain what breads the inner man sets before the outer man, or with what foods he refreshes him, when it says: “My tears were my bread day and night, while it was said to me daily: Where is your God?” (Ps. 41). And elsewhere it again says concerning such bread: “Rise up after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126). The inner man sometimes eats such bread alone, and sometimes compels his household companion, only with much effort, to eat it with him.

The spirit eats its bread alone when the mind grieves for its sins, yet cannot by any means draw forth tears. They eat the bread of sorrow together and, as though with one mind, take the same food when the inner man groans deeply and, at his groaning, the outer man pours forth tears abundantly. Every person is first pierced by fear, but afterward pierced by love. Compunction born of fear has bitterness; compunction born of love has sweetness. Therefore, one who is still pierced by fear alone is fed indeed on spiritual food, but not on sweet food. But one who pours forth tears from desire for eternal joys certainly refreshes himself with sweet and spiritual foods.

When, therefore, that inner man begins to refresh his household companion with such foods, he can truly sing of him: “He who together with me received sweet foods.” By such pursuits, the more each man—inner and outer alike—advances in purity, the more eagerly they run. That, after the perfection of so great a harmony, the peace of their flesh and spirit is disturbed by the attack of evil spirits is plainly evident to one who rightly understands from what follows.

For why does that inner man, who was created according to God, lament over the man of his peace, the man harmonious with himself, and immediately hurl the dart of curse not at him but at others, unless it is because he rages in rebuke against those through whose violence he has lost the rest of his peace? “But you,” he says, “a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me received sweet foods; in the house of God we walked with one accord.” And immediately he adds: “Let death come upon them” (Ps. 54). He does not say, “upon you,” but “upon them.” Therefore he takes vengeance on those through whose deceit he had lost the companion of his peace.

For evil spirits, envying the peace of the spirit, often weary the flesh with sudden and violent temptation, disturb the spirit’s peace, and make of one harmonious with it an enemy, of a guide a deceiver, of one known an unknown person, and of a household companion an adversary. But see: while we have wished to examine one passage of Scripture more fully, we have been compelled to survey the surrounding material. For when the order of argument required us to say something about the guidance of the outer man, the obscurity of the surrounding words compelled us to extend our exposition somewhat more broadly.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That this kind of contemplation consists in reason according to imagination.

Let us now return to the point from which we digressed: namely, how we are assisted through the imagination of visible things in the investigation of invisible things. For the outer man assists the inner man in the course of his inquiry by presenting to him the image of invisible things through the imagination of visible things. And while fulfilling the office of his guidance, he leads the inner man by the path of likenesses where the latter does not dare to enter.

Thus servants often go before their masters on the road as far as the royal doors; yet when the masters hasten within toward the innermost parts of the palace, the servants remain outside. It is clear, therefore, I think, what we said above: how we should understand this kind of contemplation to be in reason and according to imagination. The things we behold with the mind are invisible; yet we form them for ourselves from the likeness of visible things.

For what should I call the form of visible things except a kind of picture of invisible things? Suppose that someone says that he has never seen a lion, yet desires to see one. If an image of a lion suitably depicted in some painting is shown to him, he is immediately instructed by what he sees what sort of creature he ought to imagine it to be. Finally, from the outlines which he considers expressed only on the surface, he forms in his mind solid limbs and a living animal. Consider now how great is the difference between what he sees outwardly and what he inwardly imagines in his thought.

So indeed, in this kind of contemplation, the invisible things which we turn over in the mind are far removed from those which we see through imagination; yet from the latter we draw a likeness for expressing the former. We have given, as best we could, the reason why this kind of contemplation appears to be in reason and according to imagination.

## CHAPTER XIX. How whatever the ray of contemplation surveys pertains to God’s permission or operation.

The order of argument requires us at this point to say at least a little about the rings and poles, so that the same order may be maintained in exposition which the author wished to maintain in description. First, therefore, we must consider what the sides of the ark are, so that afterward we may recognize which rings should be placed on which side. By the ark we understand the grace of contemplation, as we have already said above.

Since, therefore, the ray of contemplation now shines from on high and extends itself in every direction according to the mind’s enlarged capacity, all things that can fall under contemplation clearly show themselves to belong to this ark. One kind of consideration is that by which we observe that among things done daily some are just and others unjust; a quite different consideration is that by which we perceive that some things are advantageous for human use and others disadvantageous.

Thus two walls, opposite one another from contrary directions, rise in our ark: on this side justice, on that injustice. Two further walls facing one another are likewise formed: on this side prosperity, on that adversity. But it is greatly to be wondered at and worthy of much admiration how either a good will or an evil will, while God governs and justly orders all things, is now checked by adversity from this side, now restrained by prosperity from that, lest either one grow without limit and exceed the measure of divine ordering.

Consider now how, in our ark, the walls running lengthwise and measuring the ark’s length are intersected transversely from either side by two other walls, which confine them to a fixed measure. In accordance with this likeness, divine dispensation sometimes serves diverse wills according to their wish, so that they may find how to extend themselves, and sometimes opposes them, lest they exceed the predetermined measure of their destination. For lest we flow away, as we have already said, we are restrained on one side by the bond of desire and blocked on the other by the barrier of necessity. For we often leave many things lest we lose what we love; and likewise do many things lest we incur what we hate.

Where adversity and perversity collide, they form, as it were, one corner in our ark. Where prosperity and perversity meet, they compose another corner. The meeting of justice and prosperity constitutes a third corner. The collision of justice and adversity completes a fourth. At the first corner evil people are rebuked; at the fourth good people are corrected. Likewise, at the second evil people are abandoned; at the third good people are protected.

For by adversity the reprobate are rebuked, but not corrected. If they corrected themselves, they would certainly not be reprobate. But through adversity good people are corrected from their evils, or even advanced to better things. Likewise, through prosperity evil people are dissolved within themselves and abandoned by God. But through prosperity good people are both encouraged toward good things and protected from evil things. Therefore the first corner is for correction, the second for abandonment, the third for protection, and the fourth for correction.

It is clear, moreover, that those walls which measure the ark’s length are called by Moses the sides of the ark. Just as, in the construction of the ark, these two have a greater extent than the remaining walls, so in the signification of things and the contemplation of truth their dignity is more exalted. For who does not know how incomparably greater is the distinction between just and unjust than that between advantageous and disadvantageous? The former belongs to the walls which measure the ark’s length; the distinction between advantageous and disadvantageous belongs to those walls which measure its width.

Therefore the consideration of any things according as they are done justly or unjustly pertains to the two sides of the ark. And who does not know that things done justly are done by God’s operation, while things done unjustly are done by his permission alone?

## CHAPTER XX. That God’s wisdom, though simple and one, is brought into contemplation under diverse considerations and is called now knowledge, now foreknowledge, now disposition or predestination.

Since, therefore, we now have the sides of the ark, and have already grasped through exposition its four corners, let us further inquire what are those four golden rings which are commanded to be placed, one in each corner. It is plain enough that gold surpasses all other metals in the greatness of its brightness. But what is clearer or more luminous than divine wisdom? Nothing comparable to it can be found.

We take material from this gold, as it were, for diverse operations when we consider in different ways that which in itself is simple and one. For the wisdom of God, though, as has been said, simple and one, is called at one time foreknowledge, at another knowledge; now we call it predestination, now disposition. Thus one thing is distinguished by us in different ways, so that it may be apprehended somehow, or in part, by our smallness.

Knowledge is that by which God knows all things. Foreknowledge is that by which from eternity he foresaw all things. Predestination is that by which from eternity he preordained all, either to life or to death. Disposition is that by which, continually ordering all things everywhere, he leaves nothing disordered.

We bend these modes of our consideration, as it were, into a circle when we see beginning agree with end in every ordering of divine wisdom. For divine foreknowledge is never deceived in its providence; divine predestination is never frustrated in its purpose; God’s knowledge nowhere errs in its judgment; his disposition nowhere wavers in its counsel. Since a circle is turned back upon itself in every direction, there is unquestionably found in it neither beginning nor end.

The following consideration likewise pertains to these circles: that in contemplating every divine comprehension, our mind is unable to investigate its beginning, end, or measure. The circumference of these circles is carried equally on every side around one central point, because no divine examination wanders farther from the definition of the one and simple truth in one matter than in another. These circles embrace all things within themselves and enclose the universe in their bosom. These, I think, are the four rings which Moses commands to be arranged at the four corners of the ark.

## CHAPTER XXI. That divine wisdom, according to diverse modes of contemplation, appears more wonderful in some respects and more pleasant in others.

Two of these rings have their place on one side, and the remaining two on the other. Each is assigned to a definite location, although all cooperate together in carrying the whole ark. For each such ring ought to have its place where, in comparison with the others, it appears more wonderful or more pleasant to our consideration. For it is, as it were, farther removed from that place where it stirs less admiration in the contemplator or produces less delight in the mind of the one who admires.

Thus two take their place on one side and likewise two on the other. It was said above how those things which occur by God’s permission belong to one side, while those which occur by God’s operation appear equally to belong to the other. Therefore let the ring of foreknowledge and the ring of knowledge be arranged on the side of permission. Likewise, on the side of divine operation, let there be the ring of predestination and the ring of disposition.

Would you know how rightly and orderly the rings called knowledge and foreknowledge preside especially over those things which occur by God’s permission? Consider, then, if you can, how worthy of admiration it is that God was able from eternity to foresee all these things, whose multitude is so innumerable and variation so manifold. Yet although his foreknowledge is wonderful in both kinds of things, it appears more wonderful in evil things than in good ones. For evil things, because they are done unjustly, we know to occur by his permission alone, never by his operation.

Consider also, if you can, how worthy of admiration it is that he could foresee even those things which he left to another’s will—a will that did not yet exist and that he would never create. For he never makes an evil will, although he permits it to exist. Certainly we marvel less that he could from eternity foresee what he himself was to do, although such things are so many and almost infinite, than that he could foresee what he placed under another’s power and contrary will.

But what shall we say of his knowledge, which we know to comprehend under one ray of simple vision the quality, measure, order, place, and number of all things that exist? O truly marvelous! O truly astounding! But if you ask where it appears more wonderful to our consideration—though it is truly wonderful everywhere—who does not see it to be more wonderful in God’s hidden matters than in manifest ones?

What is it, I ask, continually to behold human secrets—the secrets, namely, of thoughts, affections, wills, and intentions—and for no movement of the heart to be able to remain hidden from the sight of divine knowledge? Whenever God observes good human thoughts and wills, what else does he behold for all these in the secret chamber of hearts except what he himself has placed there? For without contradiction he works and cooperates in every good movement of the heart.

But above all, it is marvelous that he can be ignorant of none of those things which he does not himself inspire in human hearts. This is that truly supreme and singular wonder in the penetration of divine knowledge: that nothing at all can escape him in the depths so profound and dark of evil hearts. See why the rings of providence and knowledge take their place on the side of permission, where, as clear reasoning has taught, they present themselves to our consideration as more wonderful.

The other rings—those, namely, of divine predestination and disposition—ought to occupy the other side; and why this is so, I think, needs no lengthy exposition. For, to say nothing of their appearing more wonderful in this respect, who would deny that they appear more pleasant in those things which serve the salvation of the elect, and which alone belong to this side? We embrace more dearly, venerate more delightfully, love more ardently, and magnify more honorably the rationale of divine predestination and disposition in the restoration, advancement, and glorification of those to be saved than in the just rejection, casting down, and condemnation of the wicked.

Indeed, predestination appears to belong specially and properly to this side, so much so that it is almost customarily said only of preordination to life and is applied to the other side only improperly and by extension. But although divine disposition pertains to both sides, because it leaves nothing disordered anywhere, nevertheless all its ordering serves the salvation of the elect alone. We have now stated which rings we should arrange on which side.

## CHAPTER XXII. In what contemplation divine foreknowledge or knowledge appears more wonderful.

Perhaps the mind is still troubled over the question in which corner each should be placed. Consider whether, by a certain singular superiority, the ring of foreknowledge belongs more particularly to the first corner, the ring of knowledge to the second, the ring of predestination to the third, and the ring of disposition to the fourth.

We said above that the collision of adversity and iniquity makes the first corner, and taught that it pertains to the rebuke, but not the correction, of evil people. If, therefore, you look to God’s foreknowledge, what can you find in it more worthy of wonder? Why, I ask, does he rebuke the reprobate through the scourges of hostile evils if he foreknows that they will never wish to repent of their evils? Why does he address to them words as of fatherhood, restrain them with commandments, and terrify them with threats, when he foresees them to be given over to eternal evils? Therefore, if you find nothing in divine foreknowledge at which to wonder more greatly, there is no reason to wonder that it clings more closely to this corner.

Likewise, it was shown above that the meeting of prosperity and perversity makes the second corner and that it does not at all pertain to the abandonment and delight of evil people. Now, I ask you, turn the eyes of your understanding toward consideration of divine knowledge; look more closely, I beg you; marvel, be astonished. It is exceedingly astounding how God continually beholds the evils of human beings which he so greatly detests and hates.

Can divine omnipotence not restrain so many and such great evils, which omnipotent wisdom can nowhere fail to know and omnipotent goodness can never love? To complete this wonder, there is the fact that he gives even temporal goods to evil people, through which he seems in some way to multiply in them the evils which he detests before and above all things. For through temporal goods, as was said above, evil people are dissolved within themselves and abandoned by God.

Does the penetration of divine knowledge not observe how the wicked abuse its gifts? Or perhaps does it not know what they do, or with what disposition? But who would dare to say this? Consider, then, how difficult it is to venerate with fitting admiration the tangled knot of this perplexity, and you will discover how justly the ring of such divine knowledge should be joined more closely and fitted more firmly to this corner.

## CHAPTER XXIII. In what contemplation divine predestination appears more pleasant.

The third corner likewise, as was stated above, is joined from the meeting of uprightness and prosperity and is proved to pertain to the consolation and protection of good people. Now, I ask, look from this corner to the corner opposite it, and attend carefully now to this one and now to that, so that you may more quickly discover and more penetratingly understand the rationale of the position which you seek.

At this corner the good are encouraged by the prosperities of this world; at that corner the wicked are scourged by worldly adversity. Consider more carefully and examine more often God’s mercy on this side and his severity on that: mercy toward the good, severity toward the wicked. How severe we judge it to be that he does not spare the latter even in the present life, that he does not permit those whom he assigns to eternal punishments to pass through temporal life without punishment.

But how merciful it is that he does not cease to encourage good people, so far as benefits them, with temporal goods, though he has preordained them to true and eternal goods. Examine, if you can, what a thing, how great and how merciful it can be freely to predestine these, rejecting those, to eternal goods and yet not deny them temporal goods for their use—indeed, for their benefit. What could be found sweeter than this consideration, or more pleasant in God’s predestination?

Rightly, therefore, divine predestination is described as preeminent in that corner where temporal prosperity serves the elect for their benefit. Rightly that golden ring has its fixed seat there, where the more brightly it appears, the more pleasant it consequently is.

## CHAPTER XXIV. In what contemplation of things divine disposition is accustomed to appear more pleasant.

And, that we may at last come to the fourth corner, we explained far above that it is where adversity, meeting from the opposite side, exercises uprightness. For it belongs, as was said there, to the correction of good people. Since even good people do not pass through this life without stain, and, however perfect they may be, always find room in which to progress by growing, they have from this corner a means by which to be cleansed and likewise a field in which to be exercised.

The last of our rings presides more intimately over this corner, because it has no other place in which to receive a distinctive seat. Here again, if we compare this corner with the corner opposite it, we shall more quickly find the rationale we seek. There evil people prosper; here good people are scourged. There evil people, because of the goods they receive, grow more lukewarm toward God—though by those goods they ought to love him more ardently. Here, conversely, by God’s ordering, this is accomplished in good people: that the fervor of love, which seemed likely to be extinguished in them, is kindled more intensely precisely through that from which it seemed likely to be extinguished.

For the more bitterly they are pressed by the evils of the world, the more heavily they are worn down by scourges, the more vehemently they are inflamed toward love of God. Marvel, I beg you; marvel and be greatly astonished, both at how love of God fails in evil people through a benefit and at how divine love grows in good people through a scourge. Without doubt, love of God was strengthened more in Lawrence by the fire than in Nero by imperial power; indeed, in Lawrence it glowed through the burning, while in Nero it wholly failed through the dominion of power granted to him.

And what is still greater and much more wonderful: perhaps the flame of love grew stronger in the martyr through so bitter a punishment than it could have grown through any temporal glory, however great. Whence, I ask, comes such counsel, such marvelous artistry? You see how that supreme craftsman displays the skill of his art, he who in his elect brings forth, cherishes, and nourishes opposites from opposites.

It is useful also to compare this corner with the others and, from their comparison, commend the order of divine disposition. In the first corner, as has been said, evil people are punished but not cleansed. In this one good people are scourged and corrected. Why, I ask, do the same scourges correct the same faults in these people, while they cannot correct them at all in those? Indeed, why does a small temporal flame almost wholly burn away in the elect the rust of corruption, which the vast bitterness of so many torments, and the cruel fire of Gehenna, cannot suffice to burn away eternally in the reprobate?

Why, I ask, does a cause not unlike produce an unlike effect, unless because the rationale of divine disposition, though wonderful in both cases, appears in the reprobate more just than merciful, but in the elect more merciful than severe? We have now compared this fourth corner, of which we are speaking, first with the second, and second with the first; let it now be compared in the third place with the third.

In the third corner, then, good people receive a benefit for consolation; in the fourth corner, of which we are now speaking, they feel themselves wearied by scourges. There they are cherished; here they are exercised. There they rest sweetly; here they fight bravely. There they receive from their king, as though about to serve as soldiers, military gifts; here, by fighting, they win victory, and by conquering acquire the palm of eternal recompense.

Thus, in that corner, through the divine benefit received, this is accomplished in them: that they become debtors to God in faith. But in this corner, through the merit of their patience and fortitude, it is accomplished in them that they become, if it is permitted to say so, God’s just claimants: “For the rest,” says the Apostle, “there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day” (2 Tim. 4). He says “will render,” not “will give”; and “a just judge,” not a merciful one.

But in order that afterward God might become a just debtor of so great a reward, he first freely became the giver of such merit. Consider, therefore, what it means for God, with a certain great eagerness as it were, to devise, with much exertion as it were to strive, and with marvelous artistry at times to accomplish in his elect that the guilty become just, slaves free, wretched debtors rich in merits, and heirs of the heavenly kingdom.

This, I think, is a sufficient reason why that golden ring of divine disposition singularly presides over this corner, where through contests of small labors it raises man to eternal rewards. This is that in which such a golden ring shines more fully and gleams more brightly. This, I say, is that in which divine disposition appears more glorious, and therefore more pleasant, to those who rejoice in tribulation and take pleasure in reproaches.

From what we have now said about the corners and sides of the ark, we have, I think, sufficiently and clearly shown how, on one side, the rings of foreknowledge and knowledge appear more wonderful, and how, on the other side, the rings of predestination and disposition appear more pleasant.

## CHAPTER XXV. That great admiration and immense exultation ought always to accompany the spectacle of contemplation.

[Col. 0106B]

I think it will now not be difficult to discover what kind of bars such rings ought to have, or which bar we ought to place on which side. For in those things that are more wonderful there is need—unsurprisingly—of great admiration; while in those that seem more delightful, great exultation will be useful. Let our admiration, then, be great; let our exultation be vehement, such as contemplation of the divine works demands. Let each be great, each strong; let both be sturdy in the manner of a bar, able to suffice for bearing so great a burden. Let us therefore make of each a wooden bar, not a reed staff. [Col. 0106C]

Yet it ought not to be made from just any wood, but from shittim wood—namely, strong and incorruptible wood—so that they may be unbending through strength and incorruptible through long-suffering. Both such bars are good: great and enduring admiration, immense and persevering exultation. But, in order that they may have the shape of a bar and fulfill the office of bars, let both be sturdy and let both be overlaid with gold. Let them be made from the oak of steadfastness, directed according to the rule of justice, and both covered with the gold of wisdom, so that both may be strong through fortitude, straight through equity, and resplendent through discernment.

Such gilding is altogether highly fitting upon these bars, because prudent and provident discernment is of great value in all things. Let our admiration, therefore, be discerning, so that we may admire nothing in God’s foreknowledge or in his knowledge that is false. Let our rejoicing likewise be discerning, so that we may venerate nothing in divine predestination or providential ordering that is vain. For it knows that each of the former is wonderful without the support of falsehood; it knows also that each of the latter is sweet without the seasoning of vanity. Therefore, if we admire nothing false in God’s foreknowledge or knowledge, and venerate nothing vain in God’s predestination or ordering, then we have covered our bars with the gold of wisdom, as we ought.

Let bars of this sort, then, be inserted into the golden rings, and, according to the Lord’s teaching or command, let them never be removed outside. [Col. 0107A] Let your admiration always remain within the spectacle of divine foreknowledge and divine knowledge. Let your delight always remain in the consideration of divine predestination and ordering. In the former you will always find something to admire; in the latter you will always find a cause for delight. Why, then, need you seek one thing in place of another, and run this way and that through the vain wandering of your thoughts? Nowhere is there richer material for admiration; nowhere a more useful reason for rejoicing.

Indeed, in both the one and the other you will find something to admire and something in which to delight. For although each bar clings more closely to one side, neither is far removed from the other. Therefore let your admiration always be in these things, and your delight always in those. Let bars of this kind thus remain inserted in the golden rings, and you will rejoice that you have fulfilled the Lord’s command. [Col. 0107B]

## CHAPTER XXVI. How the mode of contemplation varies according to the degree of admiration and exultation

By these bars our ark is carried about here and there; by these bars it is lifted up on high; by them again it is lowered to the depths. Certainly, in the understanding and contemplation of the divine works, the more abundantly you delight in admiring and admire in delighting, the more willingly you linger, the more diligently you investigate, and the more deeply you are illumined.

As often as your mind is carried in various directions by your admiration and is delightfully affected by individual things, so often your ark is carried about, because your contemplation is expanded.
