If your admiration draws you toward higher and deeper things and delightfully holds you suspended in investigating them, then without doubt your ark rises on high, because your understanding apprehends subtler matters. When the admiration belonging to contemplation, and the delight belonging to admiration, decline or even fail, the ark is lowered to the depths, because divine revelation ceases.

Thus, according to the quality and quantity of our admiration and exultation, the ark is now turned in a circle, now lifted to the heights, now lowered to the depths; because revelation is shaped according to the desire of the ardent mind, and understanding is illuminated in manifold ways. [Col. 0107C]

## CHAPTER XXVII. That, in every contemplation of mutable things, one must cling to consideration of divine wisdom

[Col. 0107D] Now this seems worthy of consideration: how aptly Moses immediately adds the matter of the rings and the bars, after he has set forth by mystical description the threefold kind of contemplation which, as was shown above, arises from visible things. [Col. 0108A] For who does not know to what confusion the manifold multiplicity and multiform variety of this visible structure are subject, when all things happen alike to the just and the wicked, the good and the evil, the clean and the unclean, the one offering victims and the one despising sacrifice? As is the good person, so is the sinner; as the perjurer, so also the one who spoke the truth.

What, I ask, is this order of things—or rather, how great a confusion—that all things happen equally to all; that good and evil alike befall the good, and evil and good alike befall the wicked? The darkness of this confusion so clouds the sight of the uninstructed that they doubt, or wholly despair, that God cares for human affairs. Who can deny that it was for this reason that antiquity erected a shrine to Fortune and consecrated an altar?

Certainly, if they saw only good things happen to the good and only evil things to the wicked, even the uninstructed would not deny that this occurred rightly and justly. But if only evils had happened to the good and only goods to the wicked, perhaps they would have had less difficulty in assigning a rationale for such an ordering. It might seem appropriate to divine justice to advance to eternal rewards only those proved by many labors. [Col. 0108B] But now, when a common fate enfolds all alike, how greatly, do you suppose, does human reflection toss about in so profound an abyss of divine judgments?

For if divine justice is not ignorant of so great a diversity of characters, why, I ask, does it not dispense differing things to such disparate characters? If God foresaw the end of all evil persons, and preordained certain persons to life, why, I ask, does he lavishly grant even to some reprobate persons gifts of wisdom and of the other spiritual charisms, while allowing many of the elect, bereft of these riches of virtues, to lie long in vices?

But if, amid every fluctuation of this kind, we firmly grasp with the hand of faith the aforesaid rings of divine wisdom, we more quickly raise ourselves to a firm state of certainty. If we cling firmly to these rings—if we firmly believe not only that God knows all things and orders all things, but indeed that from eternity he has foreknown and preordained all things—we shall readily be able to see how, in all these matters, he displays the mastery of his wisdom: how, in the thick darkness of so great a confusion, nothing can lie hidden from the gaze of his foreknowledge and knowledge; how, in so dense a forest of disturbances, no obstacle of any offense, however slight, can ever impede the course of his predestination and ordering; and how, amid so many windings of mutability, he runs by the paths of equity and mercy, without any wandering detour, to the appointed destination. [Col. 0108D]

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0107]

## CHAPTER I. On the subject matter and character of the fourth contemplation

[Col. 0107D] Having completed what seemed necessary to say concerning the rings and bars, the order of exposition requires that we say something about the fourth kind of contemplation. This kind of contemplation, as we have already said above, consists in incorporeal and invisible essences: namely, angelic spirits and human spirits. [Col. 0109A] A worthy subject indeed—plainly worthy of being known. For this is that noble, indeed most noble, creature, created in the image of God, set above all creatures, made for the highest good, to be blessed by the very Creator of all good things and from him.

The knowledge of all other creatures, certainly, looks upward toward the knowledge of these as though from below; and however much it grows, however greatly it raises itself, it does not attain the summit of this height. Consider how fittingly this is signified by the mercy seat, which was not merely gilded throughout but wholly golden, made entirely from purest and cleanest gold. It is commanded that this be made from pure and clean gold; you are taught thereby that, in this consideration, you must employ a subtle and pure intellect. [Col. 0109B]

What place has here imagination, the maker, regulator, and restorer of bodily phantasms? Let imagination, the fashioner of so many phantasms—daily creating new bodily forms, restoring old ones, and skillfully arranging and ordering manifold and varied forms at will—withdraw far from this undertaking. Here the copious multitude of its images is of no use; indeed, it does much harm.

Why, shameless thing, do you thrust yourself into this work? Why do you intrude yourself with such importunity into the workshop of this contemplation? What are you doing in this workshop? What have you to do with pure understanding? You do not know how to work in gold; you have no part in such craftsmanship. You do not know how to refine gold, you who always trouble pure understanding with crowds. Your gold is mixed with dross—or rather, you have no supply of gold at all. Our mercy seat must be made from the purest gold. You have nothing to offer and nothing whatever to do in such an undertaking.

In this work we have no need of your poor and undisciplined productions. You neither possess gold nor understand goldsmith’s work. Whatever you propose to offer that is not gold, we have no present use for it: take what is yours and go. In this work we have no need of goat hair, nor of ram skins, nor of any woods whatever. [Col. 0109C] However rich you may be, even if you have these things or something more besides, you still cannot have gold; nor do you have anything by which to assist goldsmiths.

Goat hair—the foul impurities of desires arising from fleshly pleasure—when carefully examined and repeatedly reconsidered, can often help the contrite in prayer. Examples of sufferings, and any ram skins reddened with their own blood, can help those afflicted by any tribulation. Works of piety, and any trees of this sort, fruitful through works of mercy, cut from the forest of the world and hewn to the rule of justice, can benefit those diligent in administration. But the remembrance of all these and of anything like them can disturb rather than assist minds held in suspense upon the watchtower of this contemplation. For the more perfectly we forget bodily phantasms, the more deeply and freely we investigate the hidden things of supramundane essences.

Let the person who longs to make himself a mercy seat therefore cleanse his gold and strive to purify his understanding from every incursion of phantasms. [Col. 0110A] Who will grant me to find a wealthy man, a man fully instructed—indeed, a man who lacks neither a supply of gold nor the industry of skill needed to make the mercy seat with which the ark must be covered? Who is the person who knows how to cleanse his gold from all dross, who knows how to purify his heart from every phantasm as thoroughly as the dignity of the work requires or the authority of the command presses?

Who is the person who knows both how to extend such a work to the limit prescribed by divine teaching and how to restrain it to a definite measure; who knows how, leaving at the bottom thoughts of the lowest things, to fix his heart solely upon the sight of supramundane spectacles, and how to diffuse the rays of his understanding in every direction as the breadth of this contemplation requires? [Col. 0110B] Who, I say, is the one who finds within himself so great a store of gold, who flourishes with such keenness of intelligence that he has sufficiently and readily available both the means and the method to extend his mercy seat to such a length and spread it to such a width as can cover the whole ark; who directs himself so far toward the harmony of heavenly minds and the concord of spiritual joys that he tramples beneath him, by contempt, all worldly glory and all human prudence, and meanwhile hides them even from himself through forgetfulness?

The best refiner of gold and skilled maker of the mercy seat is the person who knows how to adhere to heavenly things with such intentness, seeking to relish only what is above, that he regards none of the lowest things either with desire or with thought. How greatly this kind of contemplation surpasses the aforementioned three by the wonderful eminence of its dignity, clear reasoning does not allow one who looks carefully and understands rightly to overlook.

## CHAPTER II. How this kind of contemplation differs from, or surpasses, the first and second

Do you wish to know how great a difference there is between the first kind and this fourth one of which we speak? Consider, if you can, how far gold and wood differ from one another. For the first work is made of wood, the fourth of gold; and the first and second kinds of consideration are represented by the first and second works. How greatly, we may suppose, do spirit and body differ from one another? If body and body are so far apart, how great will be the difference between body and spirit? Compare, if you please, the sun with a flint, and you can easily observe the difference between the highest and lowest bodies. Yet the difference between any body whatever and any spirit whatever is believed to be far greater than any difference possible between bodies, however unlike one another. [Col. 0110D]

I think that the difference of the kinds of knowledge corresponds to the distance between their essences. At least let the respective instrument of each remind you of the difference between these contemplations which we compare with one another. The former rests upon imagination; the latter upon reason. But what difference do we think there is between imagination and reason, if not that between mistress and servant, illustrious and dishonored, learned and foolish?

You have seen how greatly this kind of contemplation surpasses the first. Now consider also how it differs from the second. Compare their two figures with one another. Consider the difference between the gilding of the ark and the golden mercy seat—that is, between the second and fourth works. [Col. 0111A] Observe the position and place of each. The former clings to the wood; the latter is laid upon it. The former rises from below; the latter lies above. And yet each work is made of gold, for in each of these contemplations the rationale of existing things is sought.

But in the former we investigate, by assigning reasons, the rationale of visible things; in the latter we investigate or marvel at the dignity or hidden mystery of invisible essences. Thus we adorn certain woods, as it were, with the gleam of gold when we examine the cause, mode, and ordering of things by giving a rational account. But the artistic work of our mercy seat is rightly carried above all the wood, because, with every encounter of bodily phantasms trampled underfoot, the mind is raised by the balance of this sublime investigation to the heights and held suspended in admiration of them.

There, indeed, the gilding of our ark gradually rises from below and, as it slowly advances to higher things, at some point reaches the summit of our ark. In this way, assuredly, from knowledge of visible things and reflection upon vanity and mutability, the mind is compelled to flee those very things at which it marvels least, and to escape from a kind of deluge of immense fluctuation into the air of true freedom; it is endangered until it has fully escaped all lower things by trampling them underfoot in contempt and resting through desire in the highest and true goods. [Col. 0111B]

Nothing is truer, nothing more certain and beyond all doubt: the more carefully the mutability of worldly things is observed, the better and more clearly it is known to be something to flee through fear and to trample underfoot through contempt. For although there are in those things countless wonders by divine ordering, those same things are nevertheless to be despised because of their mutability and fled for our advantage.

What does it mean that the mercy seat is not joined directly to the wood, but is separated by the interposition of gilding, except that we are driven away from mutable things through knowledge of them and contemplation of their mutability? Let each one of us, therefore, look upon this mercy seat and then return to himself. [Col. 0111D] Behold: our mercy seat rises above the low things and lies in the highest. It rises above in order to preside; it lies in order to rest. You too, then, ascend to the lofty heart; fix your desire upon the highest things, and you have found a resting-place as delightful as it is tranquil.

## CHAPTER III. Again, how it differs from or surpasses the second

We can, however, still show the proper and distinctive difference of these contemplations if we wish to attend more carefully to their figure. The mercy seat, as the covering of the ark, had to have some thickness; but gilding seems many times over—indeed altogether—to have no thickness, or even solidity. What could I more properly call gilding than a kind of illusion imposed upon the outward sense? For the thing upon which gilding is laid falsely presents itself to outward sight as wholly golden.

Thus, indeed, that knowledge which puffs up the eyes of certain persons who profess lofty wisdom but are foolish in a carnal manner, deceives rather than enlightens them. [Col. 0112A] What use is knowledge of outward things to you, unless perhaps it assists you toward knowledge of inward things? Otherwise your wisdom is foolishness before God. What advantage is it to you to know all other things and not know yourself, and to be ignorant of your Creator?

Why do you, philosopher, glory so greatly in the world? If one must glory, glory not in yourself but in the Lord (1 Cor. 1). Certainly, if this tasteless wisdom and unlearned learning of yours advanced you to knowledge of yourself or knowledge of God, it would make you not so much swollen with pride as fearful. If you are wise rightly, if you are wise truly, “do not be high-minded, but fear.” What have you that you did not receive? (1 Cor. 4). You ought to glory in him from whom you received it, and glorify him from whom you received it. Why, then, do you glory as though you had not received it? (Ibid.)

“If I wish to glory,” you say, “I shall not be foolish, for I shall speak the truth” (2 Cor. 12). You see, surely, that I have my name from the thing itself: I am called a philosopher, a lover of wisdom, because I have said, “You are my sister, Wisdom,” and I have called prudence my friend. You are deceived, philosopher, deceived: appearance has misled you, and desire has overturned your heart. What you think to be wisdom, what you call wisdom, is foolishness before God.

“What place, then,” you ask, “does it have in the ark of wisdom? Or why does such a work require such gilding?” If it shines only on the surface and has nothing solid, why does it hold any place in such a work? Hear then, if you please, what pleases us in our work, and what displeases us in yours. [Col. 0112C] Your ark has no covering: you do not know how to make a mercy seat. But, content with gilding alone, you boast of the completion of the work; you perform the work but do not know how to bring it to completion. You are surely worthy of everyone’s mockery, because you began to build and could not finish.

Fool and senseless man, do you not know—or do you pretend not to know—that, according to the divine command, a vessel that has no covering must easily be broken on occasion? It is indeed a vessel worthy to be broken, because it always and everywhere lies open to every defilement. You cleanse, unclean philosopher, what is outside your vessel, but within it is full of every impurity; content with reputation alone, you expend no care in cleansing your conscience.

Your ark shines outside; within, it is foul, because it has no covering. Seeker of reputation, neglecter of conscience, do you not observe that these things ought to be done without omitting those? Let your ark shine outwardly, but let it shine inwardly as well. Let it shine outwardly because of the saying, “Let your light so shine before men,” and so forth (Matt. 5). But let it shine inwardly, no less, because of the saying, “Blind Pharisee, first cleanse the inside of the cup and dish, so that what is outside may become clean” (Matt. 23). [Col. 0112D]

Our ark, therefore, needs gilding, but it ought not to be content with gilding alone. For without a covering it cannot preserve inner cleanliness. Strive, then, according to divine teaching, to make a mercy seat; receive the covering that befits the ark of wisdom. Unclean philosopher, if you wish to have an ark of wisdom clean within, if you desire to preserve purity of heart, ascend to this fourth degree of contemplation, which is signified by the mercy seat of the ark.

We have already said above that this is the contemplation concerning invisible substances, namely human and angelic spirits. The first thing in this consideration, therefore, is that you return to yourself, enter into your heart, and learn to assess your own spirit. Examine what you are, what you were, what you ought to be, and what you can be. What you were by nature; what you now are through fault; what you ought to be through effort; and what you may still be through grace. [Col. 0113A]

Learn, then, from your own spirit to know what judgment you ought to make concerning other spirits. This is the gate, this the ladder, this the entrance, this the ascent. By this one enters into the inner things; by this one is raised to the highest. This is the way to the summit of this contemplation; this is the craft of making the mercy seat; this, without doubt, is the art by which purity of heart is recovered and, once recovered, preserved.

You see, surely, how rightly we call this work the covering of the ark, by which we fortify the purity of the inward things. Certainly, if your ark, with its gilding, were subject to such a covering, to such a mercy seat—if your philosophy served such philosophy—then it too would indeed please us. But our theologians know better how to use these things than do the philosophers of the world.

Finally, hear what pleases us in our work, and what ought rightly to please you in the gilding of our ark. First, it is placed upon the wood; second, it is placed beneath the mercy seat; third, it is placed between the two. [Col. 0113C] It is laid upon the wood that it may rise above it, hide from you the lust of the eyes, and be a veil for your eyes, lest perhaps your eyes be opened and see vanity. It is placed beneath the mercy seat that it may lift you on high: that lower knowledge may serve higher knowledge, and that through much exercise it may sharpen the eye of the mind for apprehending higher things. It is interposed between the mercy seat and the wood to divide them from one another and to hold the human mind back from love of lower things, lest it be cast down from sublime things, drawn away and enticed by its own desire from the place of delight, follow after its desires, and become “a fugitive and wanderer upon the earth.”

## CHAPTER IV. How it differs from, or how greatly it surpasses, the third

We have already compared the fourth degree of contemplation with the first and second; let it also, if you please, be compared with the third. Perhaps we shall do this better by attending to the figure of each. As I attend, then, to the figure of both—the golden mercy seat and the golden crown—I find a manifold difference between them.

I pass over the fact that the crown is fastened to the wood; for the third degree of contemplation, as was shown above, rests upon imagination. The fourth, however—the one of which we are now speaking—strives, by the loftiness of its investigation, to trample down every imagination. Therefore, in order to express the likeness, our mercy seat ought neither to adhere to the wood nor to be fastened to it. [Col. 0114A]

I also pass over the fact that the crown stands and rises upward, whereas the mercy seat lies down and spreads itself in great breadth on every side. This is because, in the sweet pleasantness and pleasant sweetness of this contemplation, the mind first finds for itself a place of great security and a hidden retreat of wonderful tranquility; and this unfamiliar, untried delight gathers the desire of the heart into rest and disposes it toward peace.

But I consider the magnitude of each and do not pass over without careful reflection their difference in this respect. For behold, what I cannot deny: they differ not at all in the quality of their material, but they differ greatly in the quantity of the material. Both are formed from gold, because both are occupied with reasoning. Yet that very small quantity of gold from which the crown is produced is exceedingly slight when compared with the size of the mercy seat. Indeed, the measure of the latter is fixed with great care by divine instruction, both in length and in breadth. But regarding the former’s size there is complete silence, and no measure is described for it, as though the divine word silently suggests, concerning the making of the crown, “Whoever can receive it, let him receive it,” and “let each make as much as he can.”

I think that, if its height could have extended even to half a cubit, the divine word would by no means have passed this over in silence. But the Lord knows his creature, and he who teaches human beings knowledge could not be wholly unaware how great a poverty of gold human indigence still endures in this work, and how the narrowness of its own faculty constricts it on the watchtower of this contemplation. [Col. 0114C]

For where is there now such an abundance of the gold of wisdom, when the mind lacks every instrument for grasping what must be understood—or, if it possesses one, it is dull? What instrument, I ask, can a human being find for comprehending “the peace which surpasses all understanding”? By what faculty, I ask, can one comprehend what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and what has not ascended into the human heart? (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2).

For when Paul, or one like Paul, is raised above himself and caught up to the third heaven, he surely does not investigate those mysteries, which it is not permitted for a human being to speak, by his own spirit; rather, God reveals them to him by his Spirit. But whatever human intelligence attains in this manner through a certain ecstasy of mind, the watchtower of this third consideration does not comprehend, because it is too narrowly confined by its excessive smallness. Indeed, whatever a person glimpses swiftly through ecstasy of mind belongs to another kind of contemplation, not to this one. [Col. 0114D]

Why, then, is it surprising if the narrowness of its knowledge confines the human mind especially in that consideration in which it suffers from great poverty of faculty for investigating the matters before it? For whatever it gathers about the knowledge of invisible things by reasoning, or finds through the likeness of visible things, it discovers to be almost nothing in comparison with the truth. This is why no measure is prescribed for the crown, whereas the measure is expressed so carefully in the description of the mercy seat. I think that these considerations plainly make it understood why there is still such a scarcity of gold in this work. [Col. 0115A]

## CHAPTER V. How much it avails to persevere vigorously in this contemplation, and how the mind advances toward it through much consideration and knowledge of itself

The person who seeks to abound in the gold of wisdom ought, according to his powers, to persevere in this fourth contemplation and labor strenuously at making the mercy seat. Such a work is altogether exceedingly pleasing, and everyone freely and willingly offers for this work—not merely as much as suffices, but almost always more than is needed. A supply of gold can never fail the person who perseveres vigorously in this work.

If you seek a reason, receive the reason. When you begin to apply yourself to spiritual contemplations, to rise through consideration of your own spirit to contemplation of spirits, and in this manner to compare spiritual things with spiritual things, you yourself simultaneously begin to become spiritual; indeed, without doubt, in this contemplation you are perfected in what you begin to be in the preceding contemplation—namely, spiritual. And you know well that “the spiritual person judges all things.” What sort of knowledge will this be, and how great a supply of this gold, to be able to judge all things?

Do you wish to be shown still more plainly where you can procure this abundance of gold? Has it escaped your mind that the kingdom of God is within us? “Behold,” you say, “the kingdom of heaven is within us; but is gold likewise within us?” Why not? Have you so forgotten that the kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field? [Col. 0115C] Behold, you have readily at hand a source from which an abundant supply of gold may abound for you: dig, if you please.

Only go, sell what you have, buy this field, and seek the hidden treasure. Whatever you desire in the world, whatever you fear to lose in the world, willingly expend for freedom of heart. Once the field has been bought, dig deeply, rejoicing, surely, as those who dig for treasure and rejoice greatly when they find a tomb. This treasure must be sought in the deep, because wisdom is drawn from what is hidden.

“But alas for me: whence shall I get gold for gilding, crown, and mercy seat? I have neither silver nor gold: whence or how can these things be made? By what art, I ask, shall I procure gold for myself? I am unable to dig; I am ashamed to beg.” I know what I shall do: I shall go to my Father, the Father of mercies, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift; for he is rich toward all, gives abundantly to all, and does not reproach them.

Therefore I pour out my prayer before him, declare my poverty before him and my lack of gold, and say to him: “Lord, you know my foolishness, and my substance is as nothing before you. Give me understanding, Lord, and I possess gold and am rich. Guard my soul, for I am weak, and I have the mercy seat that I desire.” [Col. 0115D]

O how great was the supply of gold possessed by the person who could truly sing: “I have understood more than all my teachers. I have understood more than the elders, because I have sought your commandments” (Ps. 118 [119]). [Col. 0116A] O what a mercy seat he possessed who could confidently sing before the Lord: “You have protected me from the assembly of evildoers, from the multitude of those who work iniquity” (Ps. 63 [64]).

Late indeed, but nevertheless at last, Paul had made himself a mercy seat when he openly professed: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4). For without great care for his conscience he would not have known how to cleanse the ark of his conscience, and without a golden mercy seat he could not have kept the inner recesses of his heart clean. But at the time when he persecuted the Church of God, I think he lacked a mercy seat. Yet it was reckoned to him for pardon because he did this unknowingly and had no gold with which to make himself a mercy seat. How indeed could he make a mercy seat when, though his eyes were open, he saw nothing?

But after he received the light of his eyes (Acts 9), he became a man who saw his poverty; henceforth, taking more careful care of himself, he returned into himself and learned by experience that the kingdom of heaven is without doubt within us. Having found the hidden treasure in the field, he became very rich; made illustrious, he began to possess an exceedingly great substance, beyond thousands of gold and silver. Finally, hear him glorying not so much in gold as in treasure: “But,” he says, “we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4). [Col. 0116B]

O man of riches! O man truly made illustrious! Was not that man most rich among all the Orientals, who spoke wisdom among the perfect? But what shall we say of him who, not late, indeed, like Paul, but from early youth had made himself a mercy seat, by which he had preserved purity of heart, and therefore said: “For my heart has not reproached me throughout my whole life” (Job 27)?

Finally, if you too desire to fulfill the Lord’s command, “Keep your heart with all vigilance,” you have begun to make the mercy seat such as the Lord requires of you. Learn, moreover, by example what it is expedient to do. Hear how David sets himself before you as an example: “I meditated in the night with my heart; I exercised myself, and I searched my spirit” (Ps. 76 [77]). [Col. 0116C]

He meditated with his heart: meditate also with your heart. He searched his spirit: search your spirit also. Work this field; attend to yourself. Without doubt, if you persist in this exercise, you will find this treasure hidden in the field. [Col. 0116D]

## CHAPTER VI. How understanding of spiritual things is acquired, or even restored when lost, from contemplation of oneself
From this exercise the store of gold increases, knowledge is multiplied, wisdom is enlarged. By this exercise the eye of the heart is cleansed, natural ability is sharpened, understanding is broadened. No one judges rightly who does not know himself. He does not know how all worldly glory lies beneath his feet who does not weigh the dignity of his condition. He altogether does not know—does not know what he ought to think concerning the angelic spirit or concerning the divine Spirit—who has not first reflected on his own spirit. If you are not yet fit to enter into yourself, how will you be fit to investigate those things that are within or above yourself? [Col. 0117A] If you are not yet worthy to enter the first tabernacle, with what face do you presume to enter the second tabernacle, that is, the Holy of Holies? If you cannot yet undertake lofty steps, so as to ascend the high mountain with the Lord Jesus, or at least with Moses, with what presumption do you prepare to fly into heaven? Return first to yourself before you presume to investigate what is above you. The sun first illuminates the bounds of its rising before it ascends to higher regions. Hence Solomon also says: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place, being born anew everywhere,” etc. (Eccles. 1).

Therefore the sun returns to its place in order to be born anew there; and, being born anew from there, it gradually raises itself to higher things, so that afterwards it may touch the summit of heaven: “The sun,” he says, [Col. 0117B] “rises and sets, and returns to its place.” The sun rises when understanding of truth is breathed into the heart; and that same sun sets when the ray of understanding is withdrawn. But after setting, the sun returns to its place in order to be born anew. The place of this sort of sun is the mind itself. For understanding is born from the mind when it is visited by divine grace. What, then, is the sun’s return to its place, except the bending back of the mind’s gaze upon consideration of itself? Thus after its setting the sun returns to its place, because, through the withdrawal of grace, the eye of the mind is turned back upon consideration of its own deficiency. For when divine grace withdraws itself for a time, a person is compelled to recognize how insignificant he is and how powerless he is of himself. But [Col. 0117C] after returning to its place it is born anew, because lost understanding is restored through consideration of one’s own weakness.

## CHAPTER VII. How, from self-contemplation, received understanding is extended to all things.

When the sun is born anew in its own place, it gradually ascends to higher things, because through knowledge of itself it rises to contemplation of heavenly things. But when it is brought all the way to the summit, it gladly remains there, because there it is refreshed by the marvelous delight of supercelestial spectacles. It therefore zealously prolongs its stay in that region where it bends its course into a circle. For this reason it certainly makes its circuit through the south, and is not borne by desire toward—rather, it turns toward—the north.

The southern quarter is indeed exceedingly pleasant because of the abundance of light and the day’s warmth, since it is very sweet and delightful to behold the ranks of blessed spirits rejoicing in the brightness and charity of God. [Col. 0117D] Beyond doubt the northern quarter, devoted to perpetual darkness and condemned to everlasting cold, possesses nothing of the kind, since in such regions the hearts of the reprobate are fittingly tormented—cold through malice and blind through ignorance. Therefore it does not run all the way thither, but merely turns: for, I think, it is drawn by no desire toward so unlovely a region. Yet it turns in order to look from afar upon the things that are there, and to know by what precaution it ought to avoid those evils.

In the east we receive knowledge of our character and discernment of virtues and vices. In the south we contemplate the rewards [Col. 0118A] of good merits, the joys of the citizens above, and the mysteries of divine secrets. In the north we know the recompenses of evil merits and the end of malignant spirits and reprobate human beings. You see how much a person’s full self-knowledge can accomplish. By it, indeed, he advances to knowledge of all heavenly, earthly, and infernal things.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the threefold sense through which self-consideration must range.

If, then, you desire to fly upward as far as the second, or even the third, heaven, let your passage be through the first. For “the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God” (1 Cor. 2). Therefore, if you too prepare to search the deep things of God, first search the depths [Col. 0118B] of your own spirit. For the heart of man is deep—indeed, perverse—and inscrutable (Jer. 17). It is certainly inscrutable, except perhaps to one who is spiritual. For “the spiritual person judges all things, yet is himself judged by no one,” since only spiritual persons have been found worthy to see the works of God and his wonders in the deep.

In this depth you will find many astonishing and wonderful things. There you may find another kind of world, broad and spacious indeed, and another kind of fullness of the earth. There it has its own earth and its own heaven—not only one, but a second after the first, and a third after the first and second. And, in order that we may distinguish this threefold heaven by an appropriate division, let the first be called the imaginative; the second is the rational; the third, the intellectual. [Col. 0118C] Imagination, therefore, occupies the role of the first heaven; reason, of the second; and understanding, the role of the third.

Of these, the first, in comparison with the others, is gross and bodily, and in a manner palpable and corporeal, because it is imaginary and phantastic, drawing after itself and retaining within itself the forms and likenesses of bodily things. The other two, however, are in this comparison exceedingly subtle, wholly incorporeal, and far removed from its grossness. Thus this outward heaven, which we call the firmament, is undoubtedly visible and corporeal, and is itself the first and lowest of all. What the earth is to this visible heaven, bodily sense [Col. 0118D] is to that inward, phantastic, and imaginative heaven. For just as this visible heaven encompasses in the greatness of its bosom the multitude of all things that the earth produces and nourishes, so imagination encloses within its bosom the likenesses of all things which sense apprehends or desire presents. In the first heaven are contained the images and likenesses of all visible things. To the second belong the reasons and definitions of all visible things, and investigations of invisible things. To the third belong apprehensions and contemplations of spiritual things themselves, even of divine things.

## CHAPTER IX. On the intellectual sense, by which alone invisible things can be seen.

The eye of understanding is that sense by which [Col. 0119A] we see invisible things—not as with the eye of reason, by which we seek out and discover hidden and absent things through investigation, as we often comprehend causes through effects, or effects through causes, and one thing and another by every manner of reasoning. Rather, just as we are accustomed to see bodily things by bodily sense immediately, presently, and corporeally, so that intellectual sense apprehends invisible things invisibly indeed, but presently and essentially.

Yet this intellectual eye has before it a great veil, spread out and darkened by delight in sin, interwoven with the varied multiplicity of so many carnal desires. This veil bars the contemplator’s gaze from the hidden mysteries of divine secrets, except insofar as divine condescension admits any person for his own benefit or that of others. The Prophet testifies to this when he cries to the Lord: “Unveil my eyes” (Ps. 118 [119]). Surely one who asks the Lord to unveil his eyes shows that he has veiled eyes. Yet by this eye the soul sees what is on this side of the veil—that is, its own invisible things, namely, the things that are in itself—though not all of them, because not all are around the veil. And although by the eye with which it sees certain things belonging to itself, it is unable to see itself, that is, the essence of the soul itself.

But it may be doubted whether we shall see, with this same eye of understanding, those things which we have indicated to be beyond the veil, or whether there is another sense which we shall use for seeing divine invisible things, as we use another for seeing our own invisible things. But let those who maintain that the perception of higher things and the perception of lower things are different senses see how they can prove this. [Col. 0119C] I think this is why they so often confuse the meaning of this term, “understanding” (*intelligentia*): at one time they restrict its meaning to higher contemplation alone; at another, to lower contemplation alone; and at another they include both senses under the meaning of this one term.

Nevertheless, whether we call this twofold perception of higher and lower things a twofold sense as though in one head, or a double sense; whether we call it the instrument of the same sense, or a twofold effect of the same instrument—whichever of these we choose—nothing prevents us from saying that both belong to the intellectual heaven. For why should this heaven too not be said to have two great lights, as we must believe of the others: in this highest heaven, let the loftier and more subtle contemplation be the greater light, and the lower and somewhat obscurer contemplation the lesser light.

## CHAPTER X. On the intellectual mirror and its surpassing excellence.

This last and highest heaven has its day; indeed it also has its night. And if we consider this heaven, so long as we are in this life, what else do we have, or can we have, but night, until night has completed its course and the radiant dawn of light has wiped away the darkness of night? Yet this night shall be illuminated like day, because the day of each of the lower heavens is surpassed by the brightness [Col. 0120A] of this night. For God made the moon and stars to rule the night; and therefore “this night is my illumination in my delights.” For it has its moon, that lesser light which we assigned above, and it has stars: the manifold modes, indeed, of divine revelations, spreading out their light.

But those who sleep sleep at night, and cannot see the lights of this heaven or sing before the Lord with the Prophet: “For I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and stars which you have founded” (Ps. 8). Nor can they say: “At midnight I arose to give thanks to you” (Ps. 118 [119]). What shall I say of such a person, since he waits for day in vain and does not see it, nor the light of the dawn as it rises? Surely those who are such “shall be carried away like melting wax; fire has fallen upon them, and they have not seen the sun.” [Col. 0120B]

Blessed are those who confidently dare to sing of the morning of this day: “In the morning I shall stand before you and shall see, for you are not a God who wills iniquity” (Ps. 5). I think he indicated this day’s noon who said to his beloved: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you rest at noon” (Cant. 5 [Song 1:7]). I think that he wished to signify this day’s morning, and had long burned with desire for it, who said: “I hoped until morning” (Isa. 38). Which of you all rejoiced to see this day, saw it, and was glad? Surely whoever he is, he is great. Yet I do not think that anyone can reach this day’s noon while still in this corruptible flesh, although I do not dare deny this concerning the morning.

Surely whoever among you can attain the brightness [Col. 0120C] of this day, when the sun has risen from heaven, will see the truth of that saying which declares that light is undoubtedly sweet and pleasant for the eyes to see. The sun of this day has a rising, but knows no setting; likewise, the day itself lacks evening, although it begins with dawn. That heaven of heavens knows only one day. But one day in its courts is better than thousands of days of the lower heavens. For the second heaven certainly has many days and even innumerable nights, according as its sun rises and sets and returns to its place. So too the first heaven received the moon for seasons, and its sun knew its setting. But the sun and moon of the highest heaven “stood still in their dwelling.” For when the lights of this heaven have reached their summit, they fix their course and thereafter never incline toward setting.

If, indeed and beyond doubt, the kingdom of heaven is within us; if it can be found by us within ourselves, where, I ask, more rightly is it sought, more quickly found, and more safely possessed than in this summit of the heavens? I think that all the regions of that kingdom abound in gold, because “the kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field.” For if you seek and love the gold of knowledge and the treasure of wisdom, where, I ask, can you find a more abundant supply than in this summit of the heavens? Where, I beg, can the brightness of highest wisdom shine forth for you better than in its express image, than in its most excellent work—namely, the creation, restoration, and glorification of the soul? [Col. 0121A]

From this watchtower, as though from nearby, one may and usually does see what is the sublimity of the angelic spirit and what the surpassing greatness of the divine Spirit. Nowhere does the highest and everlasting blessedness of the citizens above appear nearer or shine more clearly than from the lofty summit of this throne. Nowhere more than from this most excellent heaven does that Spirit which “searches all things, even the deep things of God,” serenely contemplate those invisible things of God which are seen by being understood through the things that have been made. Nowhere in all his work, more than in the creation, restoration, and glorification of the soul, do his power appear more sublime, his wisdom more wondrous, or his mercy more delightful.

You surely see, I think, whence comes that abundance of gold which I promised you above: namely, how from much consideration and knowledge of your own spirit you may be raised to knowledge and contemplation of the angelic spirit and the divine Spirit. [Col. 0121B]

## CHAPTER XI. On the threefold division of the fourth contemplation.

But since by this exposition we now understand how we may abound in gold for such a great work, let us see what the Lord commands concerning the length and breadth of our mercy-seat, and why he says absolutely nothing concerning its height. If we consult the nature of things, we shall surely be able to learn even from bodies themselves how we ought to set the foot of inquiry upon spiritual theories. We see, indeed, in outward things that every bodily mass begins in length, increases in breadth, and ends in height.

The length [Col. 0121C] of the mercy-seat, then, if I am not mistaken, signifies those things which in spiritual nature belong to a beginning. The breadth signifies those which belong to advancement; the height, those which appear to belong to consummation. According to these three matters, therefore, we make a threefold division of divine gifts in spiritual beings. First, spiritual nature is created, that it may exist. Second, it is justified, that it may be good. Third, it is glorified, that it may be blessed.

By creation, therefore, it is initiated into the good; by justification, it is enlarged in the good; by glorification, it is consummated in the good. The goods of creation belong to beginning; the goods of justification, to advancement; the goods of glorification, to consummation. The first goods are gifts of the Creator; the second goods are [Col. 0121D] gifts of the Creator and merits of the creature; the third goods are gifts of the Creator and rewards of the creature—the consummation of gifts and recompense of merits. Thus the first goods pertain to length; the second to breadth; the last to height. For in the first, as has been said, the rational creature is initiated toward the perfection of future fullness. By the second it progresses, grows, and is enlarged. In the last it is raised to glory and consummated in glory.

## CHAPTER XII. On the subdivision of the first stage of this contemplation.

Let us first consider the length of our mercy-seat, which we are commanded to extend to two and a half cubits. As often, therefore, as we turn over in our heart, carefully investigate, suitably distinguish, and sufficiently examine those spiritual goods of our creation which we assigned above, [Col. 0122A] so often we draw out the work of our mercy-seat in length and extend it to its appointed measure. In this extension involved in constructing the mercy-seat, a threefold division of divine gifts presents itself, concerning which the frequent and careful reflection of our consideration ought alone—or especially—to be occupied.

From the condition of its creation, it is natural to every rational creature to exist, to know, and to will. Consider, then, how necessary, how just, and how fitting to divine goodness it was to give to so worthy a creature and so excellent a nature discernment of good and evil, together with freedom of choice, so that its good might be both acceptable and voluntary, both pleasing and freely given. As often as you toil in an examination of this kind, you labor at extending your mercy-seat. Search out, contemplate, and marvel at freedom of choice, discernment of judgment, and sublimity of essence; and when you do this, you extend your mercy-seat in length according to the fittingness of order and the measure of quantity. I am surprised if you do not yourself perceive how useful and necessary the continual consideration of all these things is. For by it the mind is enlightened, kindled, and strengthened in the good. [Col. 0122B]

## CHAPTER XIII. How the mind ought to exercise itself in the first stage of this contemplation, and how much such exercise accomplishes.

[Col. 0122C]

Think often, consider intensely, investigate carefully the will—not only your own, but also that of another, whether good or evil. Know your own, so that you may know what you ought to correct or for what you ought to give thanks. Consider also the minds of the perfect and of the perverse, the minds of good spirits and of malignant spirits, so that from consideration of opposites it may become clear what should be imitated and what avoided. Attend to what you know; attend to how much you do not know. Recognize how far you surpass brute spirits in natural capacity; recognize how far you lie below angelic spirits in understanding.

If you attend to how far you surpass a brute spirit in sense, you will sing from the depths of your heart: “I shall bless the Lord, who has given [Col. 0122D] me understanding” (Ps. 15 [16]). If you reflect on angelic understanding, you will surely cry: “O God, you know my foolishness” (Ps. 68 [69]). To examine my ignorance is exceedingly useful and altogether necessary for me, so that I may know what I lack and may be able to say with blessed Job: “If I have been ignorant of anything, my ignorance remains with me” (Job 6; wording uncertain in the cited form).

But whenever I reflect within myself in what manner, or how often, he has revealed to me things uncertain and hidden of his wisdom, surely my soul magnifies the Lord, who teaches us beyond the knowledge of birds and beasts, because he is the one who enlightens every person coming into this world. You surely see how great is the usefulness of this twofold consideration: namely, to attend to the disposition of the rational will and also to the sense of reason. But what shall I say concerning the third of the assigned considerations, in which we contemplate in wonder, and wonder in contemplation, at the essence of the soul, the nature of its essence, and the excellence of its nature?

I think that each person’s own experience can readily teach how much this contemplation can raise the mind against vice or encourage it toward good. Know, I beg you, O human being, your dignity. Consider that excellent nature of your soul: how God made it in his image and likeness, how he exalted it above every bodily creature; and you will immediately begin to wonder how the glorious virgin, daughter Zion, has been cast down from heaven to earth, and you will likewise begin to cry to the Lord: “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. 78 [73]). [Col. 0123A]

What wonder is it, I ask, if, when I remember my condition, if at the sight of my soul, shame of face suddenly and without delay covers me? For who would not be ashamed that the mistress of the world, a citizen of heaven, beloved of God, should have been consigned to slavery of the body, prostituted to unclean spirits, and long kept beneath the yoke of servitude, “to make provision for the flesh in its desires”? Anyone will surely be astonished when he has reflected upon his soul, when he has carefully attended to what it is or what it ought to have been, from where and to where it has been cast down. He will wonder, I say, how she has become “as a widow, the mistress of nations, the princess of provinces,” and has become subject to tribute.

I think that he wished to recall us to this consideration who said: “What is the matter with you, Israel, that you are in the land of enemies, have grown old [Col. 0123B] in a foreign land, are defiled with the dead, and are counted among those who are in hell?” (Baruch 3). Therefore, in this threefold consideration we must, as we have already said, complete the length of our mercy-seat.

## CHAPTER XIV. Indication of those things which cannot be comprehended at this stage of contemplation.

But in the first and second considerations you can extend your knowledge as far as a cubit; in the third you cannot at all. Wherever you possess an instrument adequate for knowing what ought to be known, there, without doubt, you hold, as it were, a cubit of firm certainty, because you can acquire knowledge of the thing to be known through experience. Your knowledge grows, as it were, to a full cubit when it reaches the firmness of certainty through experience.

But whom, I ask, does personal experience not teach what willing is or what knowing is? Does not everyone read this in his own heart whenever he wills? Do you not know how countless are the things you will, how countless the things you do not will, how innumerable the things you know, and how innumerable the things you do not know? But, just as you see your will and know your thought, can you equally see or know the substance of your soul? Who, I say, while still placed in this flesh, has seen his own soul, or any spiritual substance, in its purity—or could even see it? Beyond doubt, in this respect human understanding is blind from birth, and must daily cry to the Lord: “Enlighten my eyes” (Ps. 12 [13]). [Col. 0123C]

Certainly, if anyone in this corruptible flesh could see things of this sort, he was carried above himself in an ecstasy of mind; and, in what he saw, he transcended the limits of human understanding not by his own effort but through divine revelation. But whatever human experience could attain in this manner clearly belongs not to this, but to another kind of contemplation. Therefore, however much you exercise your natural ability in this consideration, however continuously you pursue your study, however much you broaden your faculty in this matter, you cannot extend your knowledge to a full cubit.

## CHAPTER XV. That we must not neglect even those things which we comprehend only in part.

Yet there are many things, far from contemptible, which we can gather concerning the property of spiritual essence either from the authority of the divine Scriptures or prove by the testimony of reason. Let us therefore strive to know as and how much as we can, although we cannot extend ourselves as far as the cubit of experience. What can be known in this consideration is little indeed, yet much: little in relation to fullness, but in every way much for usefulness. Therefore do not neglect what you can have of this cubit, although you cannot fill it at all. [Col. 0124B]

For, to pass over the other matters that seem to belong to this contemplation, how great a loss do you think you incur if you do not know and do not at all believe the immortality of the soul? If the soul’s immortality is not certain, who, I ask, will prepare himself for future recompense? Who, I beg, will restrain his life so as not to follow his own desires? Who will make satisfaction for evils committed? Who will gird himself for arduous works? Who will endure amid so many divine scourges, so bitterly, if he wholly despairs of the life to come?

Everything asserted concerning the redemption of the human race, everything believed concerning the divine sacraments, whatever is commanded concerning divine ordinances, whatever is expected concerning divine promises—all is utterly destroyed if one despairs of the soul’s perpetuity. “If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are more pitiable than all human beings.” Behold, “we have left everything and followed him”: what then shall become of us if the dead do not rise at all? Why are we put to death all day long for his sake if no crown of righteousness is to be hoped for from him, if the destruction of human beings and beasts is altogether one and the condition of both equal? [Col. 0124C]

What will it profit me if I devote greater effort to wisdom and righteousness? Do not those who eat, drink, and spend their days in prosperity, who feast splendidly every day, act much better than those who are mortified all day long? Would it not be much better to go to a house of feasting than to a house of mourning, if after this life a human being has nothing more than a beast? Why should I not go, abound in pleasures, and enjoy the good things that exist, if the dead do not rise at all? Why should we not gladly listen to the saying: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Cor. 15)?

You surely see how great are the evils that follow if the soul’s immortality is doubted. Therefore we must by no means despise what we can accomplish concerning this cubit, although we are by no means adequate to its completion. Thus from this threefold consideration of spiritual essence, its discernment, and its will, the work of our mercy-seat is begun and brought out to its fixed measure. Whoever, therefore, has fully exercised his mind in contemplation of these matters has completed the length of his mercy-seat. We have now spoken of the length of the mercy-seat; let us turn the hand of inquiry to its breadth. [Col. 0125A]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the subdivision of the second stage of contemplation.

As we have said, breadth concerns those things which belong [Col. 0125B] to a beginning. Our good, which begins from the work of creation, is enlarged by justification; and from this it shows itself to pertain to breadth. But this work is not completed without two parties. For it is never accomplished if the Creator does not cooperate with his creature. The Creator could indeed, if he willed, accomplish the whole thing by himself without the creature’s work, just as he could, when he willed, create so many and such great things from nothing. But if we, relying upon our own strength without his help, presume to act, we labor in vain.

He who speaks in his Gospel testifies to this: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), since he is the one “who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to [his] good will” (Phil. 2). “It is not of one who wills, nor of one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9). For what can I do by myself without him, when I cannot even say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit? (1 Cor. 12). He is certainly the one “who works all things in all, distributing to each as he wills” (ibid.).

Yet for the work of our justification he requires voluntary consent, he who says: “If you are willing and obey me, you shall eat the good things of the earth” (Isa. 1). Free choice is held responsible when this work is hindered, where it is said: “If my people had listened to me, if Israel had walked in my ways, perhaps I should have humbled their enemies for nothing and laid my hand upon those who afflicted them” (Ps. 80 [81]). [Col. 0125C] For if we do absolutely nothing in such a work, we invoke his help in vain and falsely call him a helper. For to act is one thing, and to help another. What is it to assist except to cooperate with one who is acting? He understood that he had God as a helper and co-worker in the good who said: “You are my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; do not delay” (Ps. 69 [70]). We seek his help daily when we cry to him in our daily prayers: “Help us, O God of our salvation” (Ps. 78 [79]).

It is clear, therefore, that this work is accomplished by two, in which the Creator cooperates with his creature. Thus this work involves personal effort and divine grace. For one relies on free choice in vain unless he is supported by divine help. Our justification, moreover, is accomplished by our own deliberation and divine inspiration. For to will rightly alone is already to be righteous. Indeed, it is from will alone that we are rightly called just or unjust, though we are assisted in either direction by our actions. [Col. 0126A]

God cooperates with us in two ways: inwardly, by a hidden breathing-in; outwardly, by the manifest ordering of his works. But that cooperation which occurs outwardly has nothing to do with this kind of contemplation, because our mercy-seat must be made of pure gold and this contemplation must subsist in pure understanding. Therefore these are the two things by which the breadth of our mercy-seat is completed: our own deliberation and divine inspiration.

## CHAPTER XVII. That in the second stage of this contemplation there are likewise certain things which cannot be comprehended.

What deliberation is, we have learned through daily use; after so many experiences we cannot hesitate concerning its certainty. Therefore in this respect we can extend our knowledge to a full cubit. But who, I ask, can suffice in this life alone to comprehend how divine grace is accustomed to visit the heart and, by its inspiration, incline it to conform wholly to its will? However much we labor in this consideration, in this respect we do not extend our work to a full cubit.

For how can human understanding comprehend the manner of divine inspiration, when the Lord in his Gospel warns us of the incomprehensibility of this very matter? “The Spirit,” he says, “breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but do not know from where he comes or where he goes” (John 3). [Col. 0126B]

We are taught concerning the help of divine grace by the authority of Scripture; and we ourselves prove it by the daily failure of our weakness and by the manifest effect of that grace’s cooperation. For this reason its grace is so often withdrawn from us: that human weakness may learn from its own failure how incapable it is of any good by itself. And for this reason the grace which was withdrawn is again restored: that through its effect we may experience what we are by God’s gift. Why is it that at one time we can do one and the same thing, and at another time cannot, unless at one time we have assisting grace and at another do not have it?

It is clear, therefore, that we may by no means doubt the help of divine grace, although we cannot comprehend the ways of its cooperation. Thus we cannot complete a cubit in the work of this consideration, because in the breadth of this inquiry our capacity does not extend to the limit of comprehension. The reason is clear, therefore, why the breadth of our mercy-seat cannot extend to two cubits, and why, in accordance with the divine instruction, it must measure a cubit and a half. [Col. 0126C] If, then, you have fully exercised your mind in this twofold consideration, you have completed the breadth of your mercy-seat according to the appropriate measure.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the first and second divisions of this contemplation, and their difference.

No one should suppose that the consideration of the will which we set forth above is the same as this consideration of deliberation which we have now assigned to breadth [Col. 0127A]. For the former concerns what takes place in the mind through the operation of nature alone; the latter, what is effected within it through the work of diligent effort. To the former belongs every power naturally implanted in the soul itself; to the latter, every virtue acquired by the soul through effort. Finally, to the former belongs every movement of the mind produced by a certain natural impulse; to the latter, every inclination of the mind guided by the rational moderation of deliberate ordering.

We are accustomed to call “will” that power of the soul which is able and accustomed to fashion itself into so many affections and to vary them in manifold ways. Likewise, we call its movement, and the act of such an instrument, “will”; and we call willing itself “will” [Col. 0127B]. Nor is only that willing which is borne along by natural motion called will; every consent of the mind accompanied by deliberation is also so called. Yet the poverty of language compels us now to extend, now to restrict, the signification of words, and suitably to vary it as necessity presses.

But, in order adequately to distinguish what we ought to assign to this consideration, every consent of the soul, and whatever is done in the mind from consent, seems to belong to this consideration; just as sensation, or any movement of the soul occurring against consent or apart from consent, is rightly assigned to the consideration of length. For, as has already been said above, the goods of creation are to be assigned to [Col. 0127C] the length of our mercy-seat; but the goods of justification to its breadth. And we know that whatever is in the soul apart from consent cannot justify a person.

Thus it belongs to the first consideration carefully to observe what goods the mind naturally possesses or lacks. The second, however, concerns knowing what goods the mind already has through virtue, or what goods it is not yet able to possess. It is easy, I think, to see or know how necessary or useful it is to make both these considerations familiar to us and frequently bring them into contemplation. From the first consideration a person learns toward which goods he is naturally readier, or toward which evils more inclined; upon which pursuits he ought to insist more vigorously; against which [Col. 0127D] evils he ought to keep a more watchful guard; by what exercises he may be better advanced; and by what vices he may be more easily corrupted. From the second consideration, however, he understands to what faults he is subject, or in what merits he excels; what punishment or reward he ought to expect for these; how much he advances or declines each day; with what diligence of mind he labours to erase past evils, avoid present ones, and forestall future ones; and with what steadfastness of mind he strives to recover lost goods and preserve or multiply those possessed.

How pleasing, how advantageous, how delightful a spectacle it is, according to the first consideration, to bring before one’s view so many qualities of the soul, so many of its thoughts, so many of its affections, and to hold the mind suspended in admiration of them! O how marvellous [Col. 0128A] a contemplation, how astonishing a delight, according to the second consideration, to have before one’s eyes so many virtues of the mind, so many of its exercises, pursuits, and merits, and to remain long absorbed in such contemplation!

## CHAPTER XIX. That the things belonging to the third definition cannot be comprehended by any of our senses.

But it now seems truly worthy of consideration why he who expressed so carefully both the length and breadth of our mercy-seat said nothing at all concerning its height. Yet it has been shown above that the things pertaining to glorification undoubtedly belong to this consideration, just as those pertaining to justification belong to its breadth [Col. 0128B]. But what human sense can grasp, what reason can comprehend, the manner of our glorification? Who has seen an experience of this thing, or a proof of such evident certainty in another, or has been deemed worthy to experience it in himself?

Certainly, in this life a person can have neither a sufficient argument for this matter nor any experience of it. Therefore no measure is prescribed for the height of the work in question, because the manner of our glorification, as has been said, is comprehended by none of our senses. And indeed the mercy-seat is believed to have some thickness, but this is not reckoned in comparison with its other dimensions. So too we possess, by the testimony of faith, certainty concerning our glorification, though we cannot yet comprehend by understanding the manner of its quality or quantity [Col. 0128C].

But human desire counts as little, and almost as nothing, whatever it does not establish by experience. We know, however, that after the full cleansing of conscience and after many exercises of righteousness, the human mind at last begins at times to hope for what before it could scarcely believe; and thus the measure of our mercy-seat rises upward and grows in solidity. I believe, indeed, that such solidity belongs to the mercy-seat when the mind begins to glory in the Lord and to rejoice greatly in the good testimony of conscience, so that it may truly dare to profess: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1).

But if you wish your mercy-seat to grow upward and receive such solidity as can fittingly be attained [Col. 0128D] in this life, never desist, never rest, until you obtain, so to speak, some earnest payments of that future fullness; until you receive however small first-fruits of eternal blessedness; until you begin to taste beforehand the sweetness of divine delight. He who said, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33), wished indeed to stir us up to desire this. Therefore we now believe your mercy-seat has some thickness if you have already tasted that the Lord is sweet.

Yet however much you may have grown in this grace, however much you may have advanced in it, you must always reckon it small and, in comparison with the greatness of future blessedness, regard it as almost nothing. This is indeed what Holy Scripture silently intimates: it says absolutely nothing concerning the height [Col. 0129A] of our mercy-seat, as though by that very silence it cried out more loudly and indicated far better that whatever the human mind can receive in this life alone from the abundance of inward sweetness ought to be regarded as almost nothing. By its silence it proclaims that it judges us altogether unworthy to be instructed about the measure of that work, to whose very beginning human weakness can scarcely rise in this life.

## CHAPTER XX. How this kind of contemplation may be divided into five degrees, and what belongs to the first degree.

Since we divided that first consideration pertaining to length into three, and the second, which concerns breadth, into two [Col. 0129B], we may divide this whole kind of contemplation into five parts and into the same number of degrees.

In the first degree of this contemplation, we consider those things which belong to the quality of the soul or the property of its essence: that it is a kind of perpetual life which can never be extinguished by any punishments or torments; that it can not only live forever itself, but can also animate the body to life and sensation; that it needs no support; that it subsists eternally without assistance; how it is diffused through all the members of the body while itself simple, indivisible, and without parts; how it exists in its whole body as in a certain world of its own, wholly present everywhere, just as [Col. 0129C] God is found wholly present everywhere in every creature of his; and how in that world of its own it moves and orders all things by will alone, just as God rules all things in this world by the mere inclination of his will, he who created all things by that same inclination of will.

In this spectacle you will find many other things worthy of consideration, which you can neither contemplate without admiration nor admire without delight. Yet what wonder if we find many marvellous and astonishing things in the rational spirit, since it is God’s chief creature and was made in his image and likeness? For since God is wonderful in his works, great and exceedingly praiseworthy in all his mighty deeds, where, I ask, will the remarkable wonders of his powers appear if not in his image, if not in his likeness? Beyond [Col. 0129D] doubt, the skill of the almighty craftsman, which appears wonderful everywhere, stands out uniquely in such a work.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the consideration of those things belonging to the second degree.

In the second degree of this contemplation, the things considered are those which serve knowledge or the pursuit of truth, and whatever contributes and is conducive to the increase of learning. In this consideration we rightly marvel at the mobility of thought, the agility of imagination, the keenness of intellect, the test of discernment, the capacity of memory, the quickness of understanding, and whatever else concerning these matters is astonishing and worthy of admiration.

For who can weigh worthily [Col. 0130A], who can estimate sufficiently, who would not be awestruck in admiration at such a consideration, if he carefully attends to the manifold mobility of human thought, its restless and indefatigable swiftness, ranging through so many, so varied, and so innumerable things; resting at no hour and at no moment of time; passing in such haste through so many stretches of place and so many expanses of time; everywhere finding so easy a passage and so agile a course from heights to depths, from depths to heights, from first things to last, and from last things to first?

But what shall we say, or what can we say worthily, about the agility of imagination and the facility of its power, which with such swiftness paints an image of all the things the mind presents? Whatever the mind receives from outside through hearing, whatever it conceives within by thought alone, imagination, without delay and setting aside every difficulty, forms by representation and represents the forms of any things whatsoever with wondrous speed [Col. 0130B]. What a thing, I ask, to make in a moment, in the blink of an eye, pictures of so many and such great things, and again to erase the same with equal ease, or to vary them in one way and another in manifold forms!

Does not the mind daily create, through imagination, a new heaven and a new earth whenever it wishes? And in that phantasmal world, like another creator, it continually produces creatures of such kinds in whatever number it pleases and fashions them at will.

Likewise, if we consider the keenness of intellect, we more quickly find what we ought to marvel at in it. See how many—indeed, almost innumerable—things are accessible to human intellect which can never be reached by any bodily sense. See how this keenness of human intellect is accustomed to investigate profundities, penetrate the innermost things, unfold, untangle, illuminate, and bring into light what is involved, perplexed, obscure, and set in darkness [Col. 0130C]. By the subtlety of its quickness, it daily approaches, breaks into, and passes through, so to speak, the hidden recesses and secret retreats of concealed nature, always hastening and striving to penetrate farther and climb to higher things. Consider how many disciplines of learning it has discovered, how it has forged so many arts, and then you will begin to be astonished and fail from excessive admiration.

Thus, if you consider the capacity and breadth of memory, you will doubtless find something that you ought worthily to admire. How great, I ask, is that recess of such immeasurable breadth which, within the compass of its extent, comprehends, conceals, and preserves so many substances of things, so many forms of substances, so many genera of things, so many species of genera, so many individuals of species, and then so many properties, qualities, quantities, actions and passions, dispositions, positions, places, and times of individuals; and after long preservation brings them forth again? Think, if you can, what those treasuries are, how many, how wide, how spacious, how deep or high, which can gather from every quarter and preserve without confusion so many treasures of learning and gems of wisdom [Col. 0130D].

The capacity of memory is undoubtedly marvellous, but no less marvellous is the quickness of understanding. How great or admirable it is may easily be discerned and gathered from what has been said. For whatever sense touches, thought produces; whatever imagination forms, intellect investigates, memory preserves. Understanding grasps knowledge of all these and, whenever it pleases, admits it into consideration or brings it into contemplation [Col. 0131A].

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the consideration of those things belonging to the third degree.

In the third degree of this contemplation, we consider the will of the rational mind and its manifold affection. For who can worthily explain how many modes of alternation it assumes in momentary changes, or how variously it is accustomed to vary itself through the movements of alternating vicissitudes? Let each person consider by what disturbances his own mind is affected every day, and from this infer how manifoldly it is changed. At one time it raises itself into confidence; at another it falls into distrust. Now it is fixed by steadfastness; now it is shaken by sudden fear. At one time anger troubles it; at another, great wrath torments it.

Nor is it so remarkable that it is affected at every moment by various qualities and different disturbances; rather, what is supremely astonishing is that at almost the same moment it is often touched by contrary affections. Now it is led by hatred, now by love; at one time it is torn by joy, at another by grief. How often, amid [Col. 0131C] the wondrous exultations of our rejoicing, a cause of sadness suddenly coming upon us and arising violently shakes and casts down the mind, and abruptly turns all that festival of the exulting soul into grief!

Yet it is not so remarkable that the mind often and suddenly assumes contrary qualities because of different things. Far more wonderful is the fact that because of one and the same thing it brings contrary affections upon contrary affections. For what we have long and greatly loved, we often afterwards pursue with excessive hatred; and what we have vehemently approved and desired, we suddenly detest.

But, that you may marvel still more, if you wish carefully to observe one and the same human affection, you will see it vary in many ways concerning one and the same thing. For now from great it becomes [Col. 0131D] small, now from small it becomes great. At times from great it becomes greater; at times from moderate it becomes still smaller. Thus the same affection of the mind grows and diminishes in relation to the same thing: now it swells mightily; now it almost, indeed altogether, fails; and after complete failure it often wholly revives.

Consider also how great human affection is in great matters and exalted in exalted matters; how small it is in small matters and base in base matters: how, I say, great and exalted it is when it raises itself on high; how small and base when it casts itself down to low things. When it raises itself to boldness, you will often see it even despise death and have no trembling amid the greatest dangers. But you will afterwards see that same affection, amid the silences of night, suddenly tremble at a faint breath, the movement of a single little branch, or even the fall of leaves, and lose its firmness of mind [Col. 0132A].

But who can enumerate all the qualities of human affection? Who can sufficiently explain all the modes of its variation? There are almost as many varieties of affections as there are diversities of things. For just as we judge different things differently in approving them, so in our affection for things we are affected in different ways concerning different things. The desire of affection is accustomed to vary according to the judgment of approval.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the consideration of those things belonging to the fourth degree.

In the fourth degree of this contemplation, we contemplate and at the same time admire the power of deliberation [Col. 0132B]: how every day it turns so many affections of the mind into virtues, orders them by discernment, and fixes them in a good intention. For virtue is nothing other than affection ordered and moderated by a good intention. It is brought about that affection is ordered; and through discernment it is brought about that it becomes moderate.
