We ought always to devote all the zeal of our deliberation vigorously to this task and to persevere in this exercise as firmly as frequently, so that every affection of ours, passing away from unlawful things, may range through lawful things; and so that even amid lawful desires it may everywhere preserve the moderation of equity. Is it not through the power of deliberation that evil affections are daily restrained, diminished, and destroyed? Is it not through the power of deliberation [Col. 0132C] that good affections are continually nourished, advanced, and strengthened?

See how it condemns some affections forever, but exalts others eternally, according to its office: “to put down the mighty from their seat, and to exalt the humble.” Thus it humbles this one and exalts that one, “raising the needy from the dust, and lifting the poor from the dung-hill.” Is it not its office to order at will that whole throng of the inner household—so many thoughts, so many affections—and, after the manner of a ruler, to subject them to its laws; daily to execute judgment and justice; “to have dominion from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth”?

Is it not its task to strike carnal desires with stern correction, violently repress the tumult of wavering thoughts [Col. 0132D], and daily gird itself for spiritual battle, “to execute vengeance upon the nations, and rebukes among the peoples”? Is it not its task vigorously to crush all rebellious movements of the mind and the pride of self-exaltation, manfully to overthrow that hostile army of vices, “to bind their kings with fetters, and their nobles with iron manacles”?

Yet it ought not merely to repress vices, but also to cultivate virtues: to strike the household of Nebuchadnezzar with stern punishment, but wisely order and diligently nourish the house of David. “He shall judge among the nations, he shall fill up the ruins, he shall crush heads over the wide earth.” Yet he shall also sit “upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom, to establish and uphold it in judgment and justice.”

But who can worthily describe [Col. 0133A] what or how great is that host of virtues, “terrible as an army set in array,” to be trained by its discipline and ordered by its governance? What, I ask, or how great should we believe those ranks of virtues to be which overthrow Pharaoh’s chariots and his army, and which surround and defend the chariot of our Solomon on every side? “The chariots of God are ten thousands, many thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is among them, in Sinai, in the sanctuary.”

But if every perfect soul possesses such great virtues even in this life, how great, I ask, will be the consummation of virtues that it shall possess in the glory of that supreme fullness to come? Consider, if you can, how great is that abundance of future goods, both bodily and spiritual, and what and how manifold is their diversity. Surely, according to [Col. 0133B] the diversity of goods there will also be a diversity of affections. For we shall not be affected in the same manner concerning lesser and greater goods, where all our affection, as it will be ordered in all things, will also undoubtedly be moderated equally in all things. What number of virtues, I ask you, will there be in so many ordered and moderated affections of the soul? If you can raise yourself to the watchtower of this consideration, I wonder whether you will not believe that “thousands of thousands minister to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stand before him.”

Consider therefore what a spectacle it is, and how delightful, to bring into contemplation the virtues which so many holy souls now possess, or are to possess in the future, and to hold the mind suspended in such admiration.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the consideration of those things belonging to the fifth degree.

[Col. 0133C]

In the fifth degree of this contemplation, as we have already said above, we marvel attentively at the quality and modes of inspiring grace, and consider them with admiration. Without doubt, whatever good is done in the hearts of the good is wrought by that sevenfold Spirit through inspiring grace. Behold, one and the same Spirit presides always and everywhere over so many minds and bestows the gifts of his grace in manifold ways. Behold, he forms the minds of so many persons in so many ways and inclines the wills of all, without any compulsion, to the purpose of his own will. With him revealing, truth [Col. 0133D] is known; with him inspiring, goodness is loved. For without cooperating grace we are wholly unable either to know truth or to love virtue.

Yet how great, how wonderful, is the fact that whatever virtue he works in us is reckoned to us as merit. In a marvellous and incomprehensible way, he so inspires in us the good pleasure of his will that whatever of his goodness grace impresses or reforms in us ought justly to be reckoned to us as merit. For, while preserving the freedom of human will and altogether without any compulsion, every good will is formed through inspiring grace into delight in divine goodness; and therefore whatever is divinely done within it from the free consent of the mind is increased for a person unto the glory of recompense [Col. 0134A].

That cooperating grace of good pursuits, however, works in us certain things that increase obligation, certain things that increase merit, and certain things which seem to be the beginning of reward. For divine kindness increases the debt of our service and makes us more beholden to itself as often as it increases in us gifts of knowledge and wisdom. Therefore these and all such things increase obligation rather than merit. But whatever virtue divine goodness inspires in us accumulates merits for recompense. Whatever inward sweetness, whatever divine delight, is divinely poured into our minds seems in some measure to belong to the beginning of reward.

The one and same Spirit works all these things. For “his anointing teaches us concerning all things”; “the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us”; and likewise it is established that every joy in the Holy Spirit comes from him. But do you wish to know more plainly for what fruit this Spirit is accustomed to make our spirit fruitful? “The fruit of the Spirit,” says the Apostle, “is love, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness” (Gal. 5) [Col. 0134B].

O how many and how great are the things which this Spirit works in us, distributing to each as he wills! “There are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit.” To one indeed is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge; to another, faith; to another, gifts of healing; to another, working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits (1 Cor. 12) [Col. 0134C]; and countless other things in this manner.

Consider, I ask, how splendid and salutary it is to bring these and similar operations of the divine Spirit into reflection, and in contemplating them to strengthen one’s mind in humility and love. For in every way the mind advances greatly both toward love of God and toward contempt of itself when it often considers and fully recognizes how it can do nothing by itself. How admirable, how worthy to be embraced, is that grace through which he so works all our works in us that they are both his and ours—his gifts and our merits!

We have already set forth above how manifold and multiform are the affections of the human heart. The Spirit of the Lord gradually tempers these every day in his elect [Col. 0134D] and forms them into one harmony. Like a most skilled lyre-player, with the plectrum of his grace, he stretches some and relaxes others, fitting them into a harmonious concord, until there resounds from them in the ears of the Lord of Hosts a melody sweet as honey and exceedingly sweet, like that of many harpists playing upon their harps.

But if so wondrous a harmony and so manifold a concord rises from one heart amid such a plurality of such manifold affections, what, I ask, or how great will be that harmonious agreement and concordant harmony of heavenly minds amid such a multitude of so many thousands of angels and so many holy souls rejoicing and praising him who lives for ages of ages? That multiform grace of the divine Spirit performs and orders all these things, he who, as has already been said above, “works all things in all” [Col. 0135A]. If, then, our faculties are trained in these five degrees of contemplation, and if we are ready and inclined toward such reflections, we have surely fulfilled our mercy-seat according to the measure proposed by the divine instruction.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0135]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the fifth and sixth kinds of contemplation.

[Col. 0135A]

It remains to discuss the fifth and sixth kinds of contemplation, which Moses seems to designate in mystical description by these words: “You shall also make two cherubim [Col. 0135B] of gold, wrought in relief, at either side of the oracle. Let one cherub be on one side and the other on the other. Let them cover both sides of the mercy-seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle. Let them look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat” (Exod. 25).

It is indeed pleasing to attend closely to this description, derive from the proposed likeness a rule for our teaching, and, in accordance with the pattern of this description, fashion the form or method of our work. For I think that something great, something excellent, is proposed to us in this work: it is expressed to us under such a form, designated by such a name, and imitates the form of angels: “You shall make,” he says, “two cherubim of gold, wrought in relief.” Truly, something great, truly something excellent—something indeed above the world and altogether more than human—ought to be represented to us under an angelic form [Col. 0135C].

Certainly, *cherubim* is said to mean “fullness of knowledge,” and under the portent of such a name it seems to set before us or promise some great thing of more secret knowledge. We should also note that we are accustomed to call not just any angels, but the highest angels, immediately joined to God, cherubim. Thus the form of such a work summons us to things above the world—indeed, above heaven—and under this presentation invites our understanding to the contemplation of the highest and divine things.

It is evident, therefore, that the matters which seem to belong to these final two kinds of contemplation are above humanity and exceed the measure or capacity of human reason [Col. 0135D]. Hence, in expressing the likeness, they had to be represented not so much under a human as under an angelic figure. For unless the subject matter of these reflections exceeded the narrow limits of human reasoning, the model for forming the work ought rather to have had the form of a human than of an angelic likeness.

Therefore we must raise ourselves above ourselves and ascend in contemplation to the things above reason, if we desire to fashion the flight of our understanding after the likeness of angels. Let us therefore inquire what those things above reason are which transcend the power of human reason and the limits of our reasoning.

## CHAPTER II. That the matters belonging to these final reflections exceed human reason.

[Col. 0136A]

Just as there are certainly certain things below reason, so there are without doubt certain things above reason [Col. 0136B]. Between these are certain middle things, which are accessible to reason. Below reason are the things perceived by bodily sense. According to reason alone are the things investigated by reason. Above reason are the things learned through revelation or established by authority alone.

We learn what is white and black, hot and cold, sweet and bitter by bodily sense; we do not establish it by reasoning. We distinguish true and false, just and unjust, useful and useless by reasoning, not by any bodily sense. But that God is personally three in one substance and substantially one in three persons, no bodily sense teaches and no human reason fully persuades. Some learn this through revelation; others are convinced and believe it by authority alone.

Therefore bodily things are below reason, but divine things above reason. Above reason is what no bodily sense can reach and no human reason can penetrate. We call that above reason which we truly believe to exist, though we can neither establish it by experience nor comprehend it by intellect. Indeed, concerning divine things there are many such matters to which human reason readily assents; it is unwilling to contradict them, but receives them as true and agrees that they are established, although it cannot establish them by experience or fully comprehend them by intellect [Col. 0136C]. Rightly, therefore, all such things are said to be above reason, since by the greatness of their incomprehensibility they transcend the smallness of our capacity.

[Col. 0136D]

Yet in those things which our smallness cannot comprehend, angelic sublimity exercises free flights of contemplation. Therefore, that we may in some manner fashion within ourselves a likeness of angels, we must keep our minds suspended with unceasing swiftness in admiration of such things and accustom the wings of our contemplation to lofty and truly angelic flights.

## CHAPTER III. That things above reason may be distinguished by a twofold division, and what belongs to each class.

We are divinely commanded to make two cherubim; therefore we are admonished to seek two kinds of contemplation among things above reason. Let us attend to the things above reason, and we shall find [Col. 0137A] that they can be distinguished by a twofold division. For among them, some are above reason but not beyond reason; others are both above reason and beyond reason.

First we wish to warn that when, concerning the highest and divine things, we assert that something is beyond reason or contrary to reason, we mean human reason, not divine reason. For whatever is found to exist in that highest and divine essence subsists in supreme and unchangeable reason. Yet we unquestionably believe many things concerning the divine nature about which, if we consult reason, all our reasoning resists and all human reason protests. For what human reason can accept that the Son is coeternal with the Father and in all things equal to him from whom he has being, life, and understanding?

Thus among things above reason many matters may be found of this kind which, if weighed by human judgment, appear altogether contrary to reason. We call above reason those things which we are unable sufficiently to establish by any experience or fully investigate by any reasoning. But those matters appear to be beyond reason [Col. 0137B] to which both examples and arguments are accustomed to be opposed. In the former, experiences are lacking and arguments fail; in the latter, both examples and arguments contradict.

The former we often establish by authorities, confirm by arguments, and commend by analogies; yet, although established and commended, we do not fully comprehend them by any understanding of ours, because, as has been said, we cannot sufficiently prove them by any experience or any evident example drawn from things known to us through experience. [Col. 0137C]

The latter, however, are now commended by miracles, now by authorities, and now learned by revelations. They have often been commended to unbelievers by a multitude of miracles; to believers they are daily commended by the authorities of Scripture; and to prophetic persons they have often been shown through the manifold variety of divine revelations.

Yet they are such that they cannot be proved at all to others, except through the mediation of faith, even by those who have learned them through revelation. Therefore their attestation requires miracles rather than examples, authorities rather than arguments, and revelation rather than reasoning. The former higher matters are such that no human reason can suffice for their investigation unless aided by divine revelations or authoritative attestations [Col. 0137D]. But when the faithful mind has been supported by such assistance, many reasons meet it from all sides, many arguments arise which help it in its investigation, confirm it in its discovery, and defend the opinion it has expressed in its assertion. Such matters are therefore rightly said, I think, to be above reason, but not beyond reason.

The latter matters, however, are such that, once they have been established and believed by miracles or authorities, if we consult human reason concerning them and resolve to submit to its counsels, everything that faith’s reasoning had previously held settled in these matters immediately begins to be shaken. And in their investigation, examination, and assertion [Col. 0138A], human reason accomplishes nothing unless supported by an admixture of faith. Therefore such matters, to speak in human terms, are rightly said to be not only above reason but also beyond reason. The former are rightly assigned to the fifth kind of contemplation; the latter appear to belong to the sixth kind of contemplation.

## CHAPTER IV. That the matters belonging to these kinds of contemplation are foreign to every imagination.

I think, however, that the person for whom the angelic workmanship of this work ought to be golden no longer needs our exposition. If those things which are occupied with reason and comprehended by reason are set forth as golden, how much more those which surpass reason? If golden are those things [Col. 0138B] which exceed imagination, how much more those which exceed reason? In this twofold speculation nothing imaginary, nothing fantastic, ought to present itself; for whatever spectacle these two mirrors of the final work set before you far surpasses every property of bodily likeness. For if any bodily phantasms are accustomed always to obscure rather than assist that fourth kind of contemplation, how much more ought they to be far removed from these worthier and far more exalted things, and not appear at all? Let imagination therefore yield for the present; let it yield and wholly withdraw: there is certainly nothing in which it can assist this work. For what can imagination do where reason succumbs? What can imagination do there where there is no change and no shadow of alternation? [Col. 0138C] Where the part is not less than its whole, nor the whole more universal than its individual; indeed, where the part is not diminished by the whole, and the whole is not constituted out of parts, because that which is universally proposed is simple, and that which is put forward as though particular is universal; where each thing is the whole, where all things are one and one is all things. In such matters human reason certainly and without doubt succumbs; and what can imagination do there? In such a spectacle it can undoubtedly hinder; it cannot assist at all.

## CHAPTER V. The pre-eminence of these final contemplations.

How great the pre-eminence of these final speculations is may easily be gathered from this: all their consideration and discernment are wholly concerned with the highest and divine things. Let him who can, therefore, consider how far human knowledge has ascended when it has deserved to be raised to these degrees of contemplation. For what is begun toward perfection in the first degrees of contemplation is brought to fullness and completion in these last two. In the first two, indeed, we are instructed in knowledge of external and bodily things. In the two middle ones we advance to knowledge of invisible and spiritual creatures. In the final two we are raised to understanding of heavenly and divine things. Therefore we ought to begin with the last and best-known things, and gradually elevate the progress of our knowledge, [Col. 0139A] ascending through knowledge of outward things to knowledge of invisible things. For when you have acquired knowledge of external things and have senses trained in their discipline, you ought to ascend to higher things and acquire knowledge of spiritual creatures. But when you have again been fully exercised in such matters to the extent of your ability, there yet remains a point to which you may ascend still higher. Far above these there yet remain the highest and divine things; strive for them and exert yourself toward them as much as you can. Certainly, if you have been raised to the speculation of these things, you will be unable to find anything beyond them to which you may ascend further. Certainly there is nothing beyond God, and therefore knowledge cannot ascend higher or further. If, then, cherubim is called “fullness of knowledge,” see how rightly that final workmanship [Col. 0139B] of our work is called cherubim, in which the supreme degrees of all knowledge are expressed figuratively. Certainly you can grow daily in the knowledge of God, and in this flight of exaltation you can be raised higher and higher each day. Yet above this watchtower of contemplation you can find no higher one at all. For it is one thing to range here and there within this kind of spectacle and enlarge one’s knowledge in the knowledge of God; it is another to wish to seek things beyond these, things higher, when you can by no means find them. Beyond God there is nothing; nor can anything be, be able to be, or be conceived beyond him. There is nowhere for knowledge to ascend higher, nor can it ascend higher. Therefore the fullness of knowledge is to know God; but the fullness of this knowledge [Col. 0139C] is the fullness of glory, the consummation of grace, the perpetuity of life: “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know thee, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John 17). Therefore to know him who is the true God is the end of every consummation. These final speculations gradually advance us toward the fullness of this knowledge and are in due course to bring us there. The perfection of this fullness is begun in this life but consummated in the life to come. Rightly, therefore, the figure of this work is called cherubim, in which we are initiated into the fullness of all knowledge.

## CHAPTER VI. That it is arduous or difficult to acquire grace for oneself in these final kinds of contemplation.

[Col. 0139D]

But now let us consider what is meant by the command that we make these final works “beaten work.” Beaten work is indeed produced by striking, and by repeated blows and much hammering it is gradually brought into its intended form. I think, therefore, that this work requires inward compunction rather than deep investigation, sighs rather than arguments, frequent groans rather than abundant disputations. We know that nothing so purges the inmost parts of the heart and restores purity of mind; nothing so wipes away the mists of uncertainty, nor brings serenity to the heart better or more swiftly, than true contrition of spirit, than deep and inward compunction of the soul. But what does Scripture say? “Blessed,” it says, [Col. 0140A] “are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Let him strive after purity of heart who longs to see God, who hastens to rise into contemplation of divine things. O how much diligence, how much carefulness, is required in such an artful pursuit and studious art, before the mind fully cleanses away the dross of earthly love and consumes it in the fire of true love; before it refines the gold of its understanding to that purity which will render it worthy and fit for the dignity of this work! Without doubt and without any contradiction, it is neither slight nor easy for the human mind to put on an angelic form and, further, to pass beyond a certain worldly and truly more-than-human condition; to receive spiritual wings and lift itself to the heights. O how often [Col. 0140B] it is necessary to put one’s gold into the fire and draw it out again, turning it now to this side, now to that, and striking it everywhere with repeated blows, before it fashions an angelic form and produces a cherub! O how much prudence, how much foresight, is needed in forming the material of our work! It must be moderated on this side by consideration of divine love, and on that by consideration of divine fear, lest, through excessive consideration of divine mercy, the mind become relaxed and melt into excessive confidence in itself; or, hardened by an immoderate view of divine severity, gradually grow cold even unto despair and utterly lose confidence in the completion of the work it has undertaken. O with what prudent watchfulness, with what frequent rebuke, must one be vigilant and persistent, lest any excess of mind or wandering of thought escape the penetrating eye of discernment [Col. 0140C] and pass without reproof and strong correction! But who can worthily describe with what skill and care it is necessary to continue until the human mind transforms itself into the figure of the heavenly winged creatures and is transfigured into their image? Certainly it must first become accustomed to walk in heavenly places with the citizens of heaven, and never descend to earthly business and care for outward things—except for the sole obligation of obedience or the office of charity—before it dares to attempt those angelic flights into the lofty mysteries of divine incomprehensibility.

## CHAPTER VII. That a person strives in vain for these theoretical flights unless assisted by divine revelations.

[Col. 0140D] Hence, I think, one may easily perceive how greatly the dignity of this final work surpasses the preceding ones in its privilege of supereminence: it imitates, by a certain emulation of its own effort, the archangelic sublimity of that supreme hierarchy among the angels. Consider, I ask, how excellent it is to draw into oneself by imitation a likeness of that order which cleaves immediately to the highest brightness, which sees face to face, without mirror and without riddle. How great a thing is it, I ask, that human understanding daily strives toward those theoretical flights of heavenly spirits and sometimes, according to the good pleasure of divine condescension, is raised to contemplate those mighty works of the supreme Majesty? Who, then, is sufficient for these things? What artisan worthy of these [Col. 0141A] works can be found unless divine grace goes before him and follows after him? For it is one thing to make an ark and another to form a cherub. We can know what it is to join an ark together, overlay it with gold, surround it with a crown, and place a covering over it; daily experience proves this, and such things are not foreign to our senses. But who has seen a cherub, or who can see one? And how can I express that form which I cannot see? I think that not even Moses would have sufficed to express it unless he himself had first learned it by revelation. Hence comes the saying addressed to him: “See that you make all things according to what was shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 27). Moses is therefore first led up the mountain; it is first shown to him by revelation, before he can know [Col. 0141B] what he ought to undertake in such a work. It is necessary, then, to ascend to the exalted heart and, by a flight of mind, learn from the Lord’s revelation what that thing is toward which one ought to sigh and strive, and to what condition of sublimity one ought to shape and accustom one’s mind. For if one has once been admitted to that light-bearing glory of angelic exaltation and has deserved to enter that spectacle of divine rays, with how deep desires, how profound sighs, how inexpressible groans do we suppose that such a person persists! With what continual remembrance, with what delightful wonder, do we believe that he revisits and turns over in his mind the brightness he has seen—desiring it, [Col. 0141C] sighing for it, contemplating it—until at last he is transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3). “By the Spirit of the Lord,” he says, not by his own spirit. Therefore the best method of craftsmanship in this undertaking, as we have already said above, is to persist in sighs and groans, if one wishes to make beaten work and form a cherub. For what else is it to produce one’s work by striking than, through much contrition of heart, to obtain from the Lord’s mercy that for which no one can suffice by himself? Yet let no one for this reason regard the matters of which we are now speaking and the works previously described as of equal weight, or suppose that they differ little from one another because they have a common material and both are made from gold. Certainly, if any metal more precious than gold could have been found, [Col. 0141D] this angelic form should undoubtedly have been made from it. The supereminence of its dignity, therefore, which could be commended less fully by its material, is commended more fully by its form. We are commanded, then, to produce cherubim, and to portray images not merely of human beings, nor even of any angels whatsoever, but of the most excellent spirits, so that the dignity of these final speculations may shine forth more clearly through such figurative representation.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the fifth kind of contemplation admits the principle of likeness, whereas the sixth surpasses every property of likeness.

I think that this should not be neglected or passed over without careful consideration: concerning [Col. 0142A] these two cherubim, the Lord commands, saying: “Let one cherub be on one side, and the other on the other side” (Exod. 25). They are therefore to be placed on both sides of the oracle, covering each side of the mercy-seat. By “oracle” we understand the same thing as by “mercy-seat.”

Let us therefore ask what these two sides of our mercy-seat are, so that we may consequently discover where one cherub ought to stand on one side and the other on the other. As we have already sufficiently shown above, by that mercy-seat we understand the kind of contemplation concerned with rational spirits. We believe that rational creatures, both angelic and human, were created in the image and likeness of God; and indeed it is written concerning man: “God created man in his image and likeness; in the image of God he created him” (Gen. 1). And concerning the angelic nature we think the following was said, which we read elsewhere: “Thou wast the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and beauty; thou wast in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28). Behold, angelic nature is called the seal of likeness even in respect of that part which did not stand in the truth. Yet the prophet David plainly proclaims and says: “There is none like thee among the gods, O Lord” (Ps. 85 [86]); and Isaiah openly declares: “All nations are before him as though they were not; they are reckoned before him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40). How, then, are they as nothing and emptiness if they possess something like the divine? Does one perhaps say what another contradicts? Far from it! For behold, in David I read: “O God, who shall be like thee?” (Ps. 82 [83]). Yet again in the same writer I find: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4). What else, then, do we gather from such differing statements except that, truly and without doubt, we are in some respect like our Creator and in some respect unlike him? Indeed, how is man not unlike him in many things, of whom it is truly written: “Every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38 [39])? Behold how he is unlike. “Nevertheless, man passes in an image” (ibid.); behold how he is like. For what man is there who can follow his king and maker? Nor, indeed, does an angel in heaven perfectly imitate that likeness of his Creator. “Who is like thee [Col. 0142D] among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like thee, magnificent in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, working wonders?” (Exod. 15). Consider, therefore, whether perhaps those things in which we are like belong to one side, and those in which we are unlike belong equally to the other. Let one side of our mercy-seat, if you please, be called the divine likeness in rational substances; and let the other be called the manifold unlikeness to the supreme Divinity in those same essences. Let us see, then, how one of the cherubim stands on one side and the other on the other side, or which ought to stand where. We have already said above that contemplation of those things which are above reason, but not beyond reason, belongs to one cherub; while contemplation of those things which are above reason [Col. 0143A] and seem to be beyond reason belongs to the other. It is evident that the first-mentioned kind is much easier than the other and, for that reason, ought to be and usually is first in our practice. The other, the more difficult it is, ought certainly to be later. Let the prior cherub therefore be called the first cherub; let the second of these contemplations be called the second cherub. Thus one cherub ought to stand on one side and the other on the other. A cherub appears to stand on one side when the ray of contemplation is fixed upon those matters for investigating or confirming which an adaptation of some kind of likeness can readily be applied. A cherub stands, as it were, on the other side when human understanding raises itself to contemplate those things to which no figurative representation of likeness can fully accommodate itself. To one side, then, [Col. 0143B] as has been said, belongs consideration of likeness, just as to the other belongs consideration of unlikeness. It is evident that those things can more easily be comprehended, and are nearer, more closely related, and more agreeable to reason, which allow themselves to be applied to some likeness. The rest, indeed, withdraw farther from human reason in proportion as they transcend the rationale of any likeness that may be applied to them. Therefore the first cherub stands on the side of likeness, and the second on the side of unlikeness, so that those things which are not beyond reason and admit some likeness may touch, as it were from nearby, the side of likeness and cleave to it through consideration. Similarly, those things which seem to be beyond or contrary to reason and surpass every property of any likeness employed [Col. 0143C] may have the side of unlikeness as it were beside them and look closely upon it. But if anyone wishes to refer what is called the one side and the other to right and left, the likeness of this consideration leads us to the same conclusion. For our right hand is more often put forward for the sake of action, and therefore is evidently seen more frequently. The left, however, is more often covered by clothing than the right and thus is seen more rarely. Rightly, then, more hidden things are denoted by the left, just as more manifest things are suitably denoted by the right. Thus the first cherub stands, as it were, at the right, because it fixes the eye of contemplation upon those things which are not wholly alien to reason. The second cherub, however, is fixed, as it were, at the left, because it chiefly contemplates those things to which all human reason seems opposed.

## CHAPTER IX. How, through these two kinds of contemplation, each person’s self-love and self-approval are moderated.

It is of great importance in every respect that these two kinds of contemplation either strengthen us against evils or assist us toward virtue. Hence the addition concerning them: “Let them cover both sides of the mercy-seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle” (Exod. 25). When we cover something, however, we are chiefly accustomed to do so in two ways: sometimes to conceal it, sometimes to protect it; and often, when we place some shade over ourselves against the sun, we moderate both its heat and its brightness for ourselves. If, therefore, we receive grace from God for these two kinds of contemplation and diligently persist in them according to the grace received, I believe they themselves will be to us “a shade by day from the heat, and a refuge and a shelter from the whirlwind and rain.” Would that we might be seized with such zeal and desire for their vision, and, in wonder at them, be carried above ourselves with such alienation of mind that our mind might for the time not know itself, while, suspended in astonishment at the vision of such cherubim, it might dare to say with the Apostle: “Whether in the body [Col. 0144B] or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Cor. 12). See how deeply one who for a time does not know himself lies hidden beneath the wings of the said cherubim. But if this shadowing of the wings cannot carry the mind’s attention into such flights of alienation, it ought nevertheless—as it always does—to cloud that golden brightness of the mercy-seat and temper it for our sight. The brightness of our mercy-seat is undoubtedly clouded by the shadow laid over it when whatever appears to shine in us is despised in comparison with a greater and more surpassing brightness. The dignity of the brightness of our mercy-seat signifies the spiritual nature, while the spreading of the wings laid over it signifies the height of divine pre-eminence. What wonder, then, if both sides [Col. 0144C] of our mercy-seat are covered by such shadowing? For whatever is seen in us as like the divine, or unlike divine things, is darkened by comparison with divine things, as has already been said. Such clouding, as we have said, is accustomed to moderate not only brightness but also heat, making each more tolerable. And it often happens—as we all know—that in our own estimation or affection for ourselves we do not know how to keep measure. But through continual contemplation and deep admiration of divine things, it is brought about within us that every excess or superfluity in each is restrained. I believe that absolutely no rational spirit can bring that private love or opinion of its own excellence within the true and lawful measure of equity except one who truly knows how to despise himself in comparison with the things of which we have spoken. Therefore the said cherubim are rightly said to cover both sides of our mercy-seat, because in us nothing whatever is found that is not, in comparison with the highest and divine things, either foreign in quality or incomparable in magnitude.

And note that just as the ark is covered by the mercy-seat, so the mercy-seat itself is commanded to be covered by the spreading of the said wings. Without doubt, just as love and approval of the world are covered by contemplation of the spiritual creature and its excellence, so love and approval of oneself are moderated in each person by contemplation of the creative essence and its supereminence.

## CHAPTER X. With what eagerness of mind spiritual persons ought, or are accustomed, to long for these final kinds of contemplation.

[Col. 0145A]

But then, without doubt, the designated cherubim sufficiently cover the sides of the mercy-seat if they sufficiently and unceasingly spread their wings. What is it to stretch out one’s wings in continual expansion except to long for divine contemplation in every place and at every time, and everywhere to persist in such study or desire? Certainly birds spread their wings when they wish to fly. So too we ought to extend the wings of our heart through desire and await the hour of divine revelation at every hour—indeed, at every moment—so that, at whatever time the breath [Col. 0145B] of divine inspiration cleanses the clouds of our mind and unveils the rays of the true sun after every cloud of darkness has been removed, the mind may immediately shake out the wings of its contemplation, rise to the heights and fly away, and, with its gaze fixed upon that light of eternity which shines from above, fly over and transcend every cloud of worldly changeableness with the swiftness of a flying eagle. I would say that the person fulfills this command or teaching of the Lord and stands upright as if with wings spread, who, after receiving grace, always endeavors, so far as lies in him, to make himself ready and prepared for such flights into these final kinds of contemplation, so that when the time of divine good pleasure comes and the breath of inspiring grace blows, he may be found fit to be admitted to that spectacle of divine secrets. [Col. 0145C] We ought, moreover, to direct our minds not only to that which we can possess in this life, but also to that spectacle of divine contemplation which we hope for in the life to come, breathing after it with vehement desire in such expectation. For grace of this kind is given to us for this purpose; for this, I say, understanding of eternal things is infused, that we may know what we ought tirelessly to seek through study or sigh for through desire. Otherwise, the abundance of divine knowledge grows in us in vain unless it increases the flame of divine love within us. Therefore both love ought always to grow in us from knowledge, and no less knowledge from love; and by mutual increase they ought to supply mutual increase, and by alternating growth their respective increases ought to grow. Therefore the perfect soul, devoted continually to contemplation of the highest things, ought every hour to await with the greatest desire the end of its pilgrimage and departure from this prison, so that it may deserve to see face to face what it now sees through a mirror and in a riddle. Hence Abraham sat at the entrance of his tent (Gen. 18). Hence Elijah stood at the entrance of his cave (3 Kings 19); each ready to depart, each waiting attentively for the Lord’s coming. Both awaited one thing: one in a cave, the other in a tent; both nevertheless at the entrance, though one standing and the other sitting. You observe, I think, that one regards the burden of this life [Col. 0146A] as misery, the other as military service, and that one judges this same pilgrimage of time to be a prison, the other a campaign. There are those who see themselves as though in a cave and regard their flesh as a prison, because they endure with distress the troubles of this life. Others make a tent, as it were, of their body, gird themselves for service in the army of their Lord, and patiently endure life so that they may serve the Lord’s gains. Thus one lives impatiently, another patiently: one fears for himself, the other attends to the Lord’s gains. Therefore one standing and laboring greatly, the other sitting and scarcely feeling or reckoning the labor at all, waits for the Lord’s coming; and both are found at the entrance and as it were at the very point of departure. To pass over for the moment those [Col. 0146B] who gladly live and lie pleasantly at rest in the inner parts of their tent—or rather, palace—both of these fear the Lord’s coming: both the one who sat at the entrance and, patiently enduring the burden of his service, breathed in expectation of meeting the Lord, and the one who stood at the entrance and, awaiting the hour of his visitation, labored almost impatiently beneath the desire of expectation. Do you wish to hear how unwillingly the one who stood at the entrance of his cave lived? “Take my soul from me, O Lord,” he says, “for I am no better than my fathers” (3 Kings 19). But why, I ask, did the man who stood thus in expectation cover his face when the Lord passed by? Perhaps in the Lord’s presence he recognized his imperfection more perfectly and was ashamed that his imperfection should be seen? Yet you wished to see, though you feared to be seen. O how many there are who already believe themselves ready, yet at the very moment of their visitation tremble in fear where previously there was no fear, and now dread the departure which they had formerly sought anxiously!

## CHAPTER XI. How, after much weariness in their longing, some are accustomed, and some are not accustomed, to be raised above themselves by visiting grace.

Behold, the one who waits standing is not recorded either to have left the entrance or to have gone to meet the Lord. Yet he looked out from the cave, though with veiled face, and heard the voice of the one passing by in his passage; and he who had already sighed for rest learned from the Lord’s revelation what he still ought to do. But the other sprang from his tent at the Lord’s coming and met him with unveiled face; he brings him in, feeds him, and receives the Lord’s promise according to the wish of his desire. He presses upon Sabaoth with questions and, receiving foreknowledge of future things, enters the inner chamber of divine judgments. But what is it to attend from one’s dwelling to the Lord’s passing by, except subtly to understand from those things which are divinely done around one the governance of the divine dispensation and the grace of its cooperation? When a mighty wind is followed by an earthquake, the earthquake by fire, and the fire by the whisper of a gentle breeze, the presence of the passing Lord is perceived; because, when the mind often suddenly feels itself wholly shaken by great and strange disturbances, now cast down by excessive trembling, now burned by excessive grief or confounded by shame, and then, contrary to hope and expectation, restored to great tranquillity or even security of mind, whether it wishes or not it perceives the working of visiting grace and recognizes more clearly than light that these things are divinely brought about. We have God present but, as it were, passing by when we are not yet able to cleave longer to contemplation of that light. To hear the voice of the Lord who admonishes, or even of his instrument, is to learn by his inspiration what is his good, pleasing, and perfect will. But he goes out, as it were, from the tent to meet the coming Lord, and having gone out gazes as if face to face, who, carried outside himself by a flight of mind, contemplates the light of supreme wisdom without any covering or shadow of figures; in short, not through a mirror and in a riddle, but in simple truth, so to speak. He draws the outwardly seen vision inward when, through much revisiting and vehement examination, he makes intelligible or even comprehensible to himself what he saw in ecstasy, and then brings it down to common understanding both by the testimony of reasons and by the adaptation of likenesses. Then the calf is killed, upon which the Lord may feed, when the human mind, strengthened by these stages of advancement, cuts away something from the pleasure of its own will that it formerly cherished and guarded gladly; when it cuts off from its own pursuits [Col. 0147C] or practices that by which it hopes to cleave more perfectly to divine contemplation or please divine mercy more highly. We feed the Lord when, through sacrifices of our virtues and the enlargement of our purpose for a stricter life, we nourish and increase his benevolence toward us in charity: “Behold,” he says, “I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter to him and dine with him” (Rev. 3). Certainly we eat with the Lord in ourselves when we gladly devote something to his service and serve his good pleasure in it, thereby increasing both his benevolence toward us and our confidence in him. By this accumulation of confidence it is brought about that the mind is suddenly encouraged, beyond hope and above expectation, toward grace long desired and greatly longed for. [Col. 0147D] We follow the Lord as he goes out when, diligently attending to understanding divinely commanded, we are raised above ourselves to contemplate higher things through that by which we marvel at the known light of divinity; and, cleaving to the footsteps of revealing grace, we accompany the passing Lord. But to stand with the Lord after he has come out is to cleave longer in contemplation to the revealed light in that state of exaltation. He stands beside the standing Lord who, by a lofty raising of mind, transcends all the slippery instability and uncertain ambiguity of human changeableness and, fixed in that light of eternity, draws into himself a likeness of the image he has seen: “We all,” says the Apostle, “beholding with unveiled face the glory of the Lord, are transformed into [Col. 0148A] the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (1 Cor. 3 [probably 2 Cor. 3]). In this elevation of mind human understanding often enters that abyss of divine judgments and is also instructed, as has already been said, in foreknowledge of future things.

## CHAPTER XII. That some things usually seen through a flight of mind can be brought down to common understanding, while others cannot at all.

It should therefore be noted that sometimes, when we are outside ourselves, we draw the Lord seen inward; sometimes, when we are within ourselves, we go out with him as he goes out. For what is known of the Lord’s brightness through a flight of mind is sometimes afterward comprehended by the sober mind; and often, from what we soberly investigate within ourselves, we are led away into alienation of mind by the greatness of our wonder. It should likewise be noted that sometimes, when outside ourselves, we bring the Lord we have seen inside, and sometimes we do not bring him inside. For we do not read that Abraham brought the Lord back after the second going out. Some matters of this kind exceed human understanding and cannot be investigated by human reason; yet, as was already said above, they are not beyond reason. When, therefore, we learn any such things through a flight of mind, we bring back with us, as it were, the vision known outwardly if afterward we discover by fitting reason those same things which we had first perceived by revelation. But those things which seem both above reason and beyond reason, when learned by revelation and as if in ecstasy, cannot, after we return to ourselves, have their rationale comprehended or assigned by any human judgment; we therefore leave the vision known, as it were, outside, retaining only a sort of memory of it. For what does Scripture say? “The Lord,” it says, “departed after he had ceased speaking to Abraham, and Abraham returned to his place” (Gen. 18). The Lord departs and Abraham returns when, revelation’s grace having been withdrawn, intellectual perception is called back to its ordinary state. Thus at his first going out Abraham compelled the one whom he saw to enter into himself through much labor. But at the second going out, after a prolonged vision and long conversation, he did not bring him back at all. We bring inside with us the one seen outwardly when, through reasoning, we afterward incline somewhat toward common understanding a theophany perceived swiftly. The one seen outwardly is by no means brought inside when theoretical revelation, the more closely it is examined according to human reason, appears the more to oppose every human opinion. For in such speculation, before the mind returns to what is customary, the Lord departs and withdraws farther away, showing by the remoteness of the vision the greatness of his incomprehensibility. These two kinds of things, then, which are known in this twofold vision through the Lord’s revelation appear to belong to the two cherubim previously mentioned. [Col. 0149A] This indeed is the fitting material from which the angelic form and winged creatures must be fashioned. From this material we form cherubim when we accustom ourselves to bring into contemplation the mysteries of our faith which either we ourselves have learned by revelation or received from theological men; when we suspend and nourish our mind in wonder at them, humble it, and kindle it keenly toward desire for divine things. Therefore, following the examples of Abraham and Elijah, we ought to await the Lord’s coming at the very exit of our dwelling and, as it were, at its entrance. Following the divine teaching, we ought to spread the wings of our cherubim and hasten with swift steps of desire to meet revealing grace.

## CHAPTER XIII. That at every hour the holy and contemplative soul ought to be ready to receive grace.

[Col. 0149B]

A holy soul, the friend of the true Bridegroom, ought always to long with the utmost desire for the coming of her beloved, always ready both to meet him when he calls and to open when he knocks. She ought, I say, always to be anxious about this and be found prepared, lest, arriving suddenly and unexpectedly, he find her insufficiently adorned, insufficiently arrayed, or, having long been kept outside by prolonged waiting, endure any vexation. “Command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little here” (Isa. 28)—words surely troublesome enough and very burdensome to ardent desire. They are the words of a sluggish soul, a lukewarm soul, a soul insufficiently watchful and exceedingly ungrateful. [Col. 0149C]

For what does such a soul say, when found amid her own filth, grieving that she has been forestalled by the unexpected coming of her lover, and blushing to be found insufficiently composed and adorned? “Certainly,” she says, “I ought to have known beforehand of your coming, so that I might receive you solemnly and meet you with the eagerness I ought. Therefore, henceforth announce your coming to me, and, with a messenger preceding you, send word beforehand of the hour of your arrival. Let a messenger pass between us, to teach me what you wish me to do. Let a messenger, I say, run as a mediator between us, instructing me about every matter; let him teach me not only about my own condition, but also about yours. Let him teach me how things are with you, or what has pleased you concerning me. Command, therefore, and command again; announce and announce again.” [Col. 0149D]

“It does not become lovers to be ignorant of one another’s mutual concerns and mutual desires; nor is it enough for a mind boiling over with ardent longing to hear once. I beg you, therefore: command, command again; command, command again.” Perhaps she loves greatly and burns greatly, she who presses so insistently and seeks intermediaries so importunately. Let us see, then, what she does. Behold, in accordance with his word, after messengers have often been sent and sent again, he at last follows his own messengers, that he may enjoy the desired embraces and be cherished by mutual love. Behold, he now stands before the doors; behold, he now knocks at the door. Behold the voice of your beloved as he knocks: “Open to me, my sister, my friend, my dove, my spotless one; for my head is full of dew, my locks with the drops of the night” (Song 5).

What, I ask, what advantage was there in sending his messengers beforehand, when he found the door shut? At the voice of your beloved, why do you not at least leap up immediately, open, bring him in, and rush into his embraces? “I have taken off my tunic,” she says, “how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (ibid.). “Let him wait a little, if he wishes, until I receive him.” He knocks and asks for entrance, and you say, “Wait”; behold, he knocks again, and you say, “Wait again.” “And what great matter,” you say, “is it if he waits a little?” Oh, how I fear that you will draw out that little into a long delay, until he departs and turns aside, leaving after long and great weariness. Your own words reveal this, as does your all-too-late complaint: “I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved; but he had turned aside and passed on” (ibid.). [Col. 0150A]

But behold, returning again and not reckoning the injury of the former contempt, he stands behind the wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattice. Hear him calling, you who wished to receive him knocking. Behold, your beloved says to you: “Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come” (Song 2). Why do you not immediately leap forth, run to meet him, seize him, and join your kisses? Why do you still say, “Wait”? Behold, he still waits; behold, he calls again: “Arise, my friend, my bride, and come into the clefts of the rock and the hollows of the wall” (ibid.). What do you say? “Wait again a little longer.” O ungrateful soul, O hard heart, how long will you afflict your friend? How long weary your beloved? He knocks, and you will not open; he calls, and you will not go out. He knocks once and again, and you bid him wait—bid him wait again—a little and a little. [Col. 0150B]

He calls once, he calls again; nonetheless, you compel him to wait and wait again, a little and a little. “A little in one place, and a little in another: a little here.” Thus your beloved is compelled to do often and for long what you call “a little and a little.” For you draw out “a little and a little” into “long and long,” and in this way you deceive your friend and weary your beloved. O how much better, how much more fitting it would be for you to keep watch at the door, to await the coming of your lover with Abraham or Elijah, to meet him when he comes, and to receive him with exultation. You ought indeed, like the dove of your beloved in the clefts of the rock and the hollows of the wall, with wings held aloft and neck stretched out, to look forth and seek and await the coming of your only one with a kind of dovelike song and moan. But perhaps our cherubim do not yet have wings; or, if they have them, they do not yet have them spread out. Perhaps we have not yet fully fashioned our work, nor wholly completed that angelic form in accordance with the Lord’s teaching. [Col. 0150C–D]

## Chapter XIV. How few always keep their minds ready to receive grace

I pass over those who are outside, who have not yet been able to know spiritual love, who daily hear the Lord’s commandments from the spoken or written words of teachers and nevertheless do not obey, sinning every day and every day asking that time for repentance be granted them. Some of these gladly hear words of life; yet what do they say through their study but, “Command, command again”? And while daily heaping sins upon sins, what do they cry in desire but, “Wait, wait again”? They daily ask for time to repent, daily propose a time for amendment, and daily put it off. Certainly, to satisfy its desire, the entire span of this life seems exceedingly short to the carnal mind. And while such a soul spends much time now on one thing, now on another, and nevertheless judges it all as but a moment, what else, I ask, resounds in the ear of divine patience but “a little here, a little here”? [Col. 0151A]

But leaving these aside for now, what, I ask, shall we say of ourselves, who have assumed the religious habit, who are devoted to spiritual exercises, who continually receive, as it were, certain pledges of divine love? And especially what shall we say of ourselves, whose only prescribed duty is to read, sing psalms, pray, meditate, reflect, contemplate, be at leisure, and see how sweet the Lord is? Shall we not be ashamed to say the same things and weary our beloved with such words? “Command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little here” (Isa. 28).

Every day, unless I am mistaken, you who devote yourselves to reading or meditation receive his messengers and learn his commands. Whenever we draw new meanings from the hidden recesses of the Scriptures, what else do we do but receive certain messengers of our beloved? All sacred reading and discerning meditation serve this purpose. Thus some intermediaries of divine mysteries meet readers, others meet those meditating, carrying to us the commands of our beloved and instructing us concerning each matter. And it often happens that one and the same Scripture, when expounded in many ways, speaks many things to us at once: morally teaching us what our beloved wishes us to do; allegorically reminding us what he himself has done for us; anagogically setting forth what he intends yet to do concerning us. [Col. 0151B–C]

In this way, then, he often commands and commands again; and, as though through one messenger, announces many things to us. Often one and the same command is set forth under various riddles and figures, so that it may be impressed more deeply upon our minds. And while the same thing is told us in many ways and many times, what else does it seem but that the same command is often given and given again? Yet many receive such messengers daily and nevertheless wish to correct little or nothing at all of their former lukewarmness or negligence. They thirst for material for boasting, not for edification. They seek knowledge, not holiness, and desire to be not so much holy as mere smatterers. Therefore, while with daily efforts they seek new senses and new interpretations, what else do they cry through inclination or study but, “Command, command again; command, command again”?

We receive such messengers every day; and while ever new ones often arrive, we importunately demand still others, crying loudly in the ears of the Lord of hosts: “Command, command again; command, command again.” Yet the more abundant the multitude of these messengers becomes, the more bitterly and painfully does our own conscience accuse and torment us. Hence it often happens that we resolve to amend our lives, yet always defer it. While we propose to do this in the future, that future always remains future—indeed, perhaps it will never come. [Col. 0151D–0152A]

Often some definite future time is fixed for correcting our life, and meanwhile we say to our beloved, “Wait”; and when that future is turned into the present, it is transferred once more into another future, and we say, “Wait again.” How many frequently propose and firmly determine within themselves that, if they are once allowed to free themselves from the foreign attachments in which they are presently entangled, they will never again fall back into the same things. Meanwhile they ask to be waited for during that little while; and when they perhaps lose those same attachments rather than cut them off, they strive vigorously to restore what they have lost, and again they wish and ask to be waited for a little longer.

Truly they say this: “a little and a little.” Whatever does not satisfy desire, however great it may be, seems small to the inclination. Such persons therefore ask to be waited for and waited for again, a little and a little. “A little here, and a little there”: a little and a little often under one attachment but at one time and another; here and there under one attachment and another, but at one and the same time. And in all these things we sing our beloved a hateful song: “Wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little here.” [Col. 0152B–C]

When, do you suppose, will such a sluggish and lukewarm soul be able to form that malleable work and fashion the angelic form, especially since this work requires an expansion of wings, compelled to this indeed by the Lord’s command, so that in such a pursuit it is never lawful to let the wings of our desires fall from the elevation of intention?

## Chapter XV. How arduous or difficult it is for any perfected soul wholly to gather itself into itself and rest in the desire for Divinity alone

I shall not speak of a year, a month, or a day: even a very brief delay is exceedingly troublesome to impatient desire. “Hope deferred afflicts the soul.” Therefore, the beloved of the true friend and the friend of the true beloved, as has already been said above, ought always to be prompt and ready, receiving the friend who knocks without any injury of delay and running to meet him who calls with all eagerness. But we know that exclusive love receives no companion and admits no associate. See, then, that you do not first begin wishing to drive out the clamorous crowd when he has already begun to knock at the door. Otherwise what will you say when such a crowd is found with you at that time? What, I say, will you say except, “Wait, wait again”? You must surely wait, and wait again, in order to drive out the crowd of strangers and the household of your own people. [Col. 0152D–0153A]

All thoughts, both vain and harmful, which serve no benefit of ours must be judged strangers. But we regard as household members or servants those which we employ for our uses or advantages. Since exclusive love loves solitude and seeks a solitary place, this entire crowd must be driven out—not only that of thoughts, but also that of affections—so that we may cling to the embraces of our beloved with greater freedom and, therefore, greater delight.

How great, I ask, is the delay in such waiting; how often must “Wait, wait again; a little here, a little here” be repeated? A little in one place, a little in another: a little in the garden, a little in the vestibule, a little in the bridal chamber, until at last, after much waiting and much weariness, he enters the inner room and occupies the innermost and most secret place. A little in the garden, while the tumultuous crowd is dispersed; a little in the vestibule, while the bridal chamber is arranged; a little in the chamber, while the bed is spread. And the beloved is compelled to wait in all these places, a little and a little, a little here and a little there. [Col. 0153B]

He is heard from the garden, seen in the vestibule, kissed in the bridal chamber, embraced in the inner room. He is heard through memory, seen through understanding, kissed through affection, embraced through rejoicing. He is heard through recollection, seen through wonder, kissed through love, embraced through delight. Or, if this pleases better: he is heard through revelation, seen through contemplation, kissed through devotion, and held fast through the infusion of his sweetness.

He is heard through revelation until, as his voice gradually grows stronger, every clamorous tumult is stilled and his voice alone is heard; until at last all that tumultuous crowd disappears and he alone remains with her alone, and she alone beholds him alone through contemplation. He is seen through contemplation until, at the sight of an unfamiliar vision and the wonder of beauty, the soul gradually grows warm, burns more and more ardently, and at length becomes wholly incandescent, until it is wholly reformed to true purity and inward beauty; until that bridal chamber of the inward dwelling is everywhere adorned with purple, fine linen, hyacinth-blue, and twice-dyed scarlet. [Col. 0153C–D]

Then, at last, when the bridal chamber is adorned and the beloved has been brought in, as confidence now grows strong and desire presses urgently, unable any longer to restrain herself, she suddenly rushes into kisses and, with lips impressed upon his, gives kisses of deepest devotion. Through devotion she often and in many ways kisses him, while meanwhile the inner room is prepared, until the innermost recess of the soul is composed in perfect peace and tranquility; until at last, with the beloved placed between her breasts, she wholly melts into desire for him through an ineffable infusion of divine sweetness, and the spirit that clings to the Lord becomes one spirit.

I think that, having experienced such sweetness and so inward a delight, that soul can thereafter no longer contrive delays when the beloved knocks, or weary him by any waiting; nor, in this respect, will she any longer say, “Wait, wait again,” especially since every delay will seem excessively long and every waiting burdensome to herself. Henceforth, I suppose, she will gladly keep watch at the entrance of her dwelling with the patriarch Abraham or even the prophet Elijah, that she may always be ready to receive her beloved. At this stage, I think, our malleable work begins to make no small progress and to approach completion, because our cherubim begin to spread their wings more broadly and, as it were, to poise themselves for flight at every hour. [Col. 0154A]

## Chapter XVI. Since it is almost impossible for any soul wholly to pour itself out beyond itself and go above itself

[Col. 0154B] Yet although at that time such a soul is ready to receive him when he comes, I do not know whether it is equally ready and unencumbered to run to meet him when he calls. I fear that in this respect it will still say entirely to its beloved: “Wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little here and a little there.” For I think it is not equally easy to receive one who comes and to follow one who calls. It is one thing to enter with him, and another to go out to him. There the soul returns to itself and enters with its beloved even to the innermost recesses of its heart. Here it is led beyond itself and raised up to contemplate sublime things.

For what is its entering except to gather itself wholly into itself? And what is its going out except to pour itself wholly out beyond itself? Therefore, for the soul to enter the inner room with its beloved, to remain alone with the one who is alone, and to enjoy sweetness, is nothing other than to forget all external things and delight supremely and inwardly in his love. It sees itself alone with its beloved when, having forgotten all outward things, it presses its desire onward from consideration of itself into love of its beloved; and from what it considers in its inward depths it kindles its mind into this affection; and, from consideration of both its good and its evil, rises to thanksgiving, offering sacrifices of inward devotion—now for grace bestowed, now for pardon granted. [Col. 0154C]

The beloved is led into the inmost place and placed in the best place when he is loved from the depths of affection and above all things. Consider what you have loved more ardently in your life, desired anxiously, what affected you more pleasantly and delighted you more deeply than all else. Consider, then, whether you feel the same intensity of affection and abundance of delight when you burn with desire for the supreme lover and rest in his love. Who can doubt that he has not yet occupied that innermost recess of your affection, if the sting of deepest love penetrates and stirs your soul less warmly in divine affections than it once used to penetrate or stir it in other affections?

But if you find within yourself an intensity of love or delight concerning divine things altogether as great, or perhaps stronger, than you have ever experienced otherwise, see whether there is still anything else in which you can take delight or consolation. Certainly, as long as we can conceive delight or consolation from any other thing, I do not yet dare say that our beloved possesses the inmost recess of most ardent love. Whatever sort of soul you may still be, strive and hasten to draw him farther into the more inward and secret recesses of your heart. [Col. 0154D–0155A]

For who would deny that the inmost chamber of the human heart has, or can possess, such recesses that, when the intensity of supreme and exclusive love has fixed something there through affection, it cannot be torn away by any foreign delight? Certainly, if you seek or receive any other consolation, then, although perhaps you love your God supremely, you do not yet love him exclusively. Therefore he is not yet led into the inmost place, not yet placed in the best place. If, then, you do not strive to bring him into your depths, how can I believe that you wish, or are able, to follow him to his heights?

Let this therefore be a sure sign for you, whatever soul you may be, that you love your beloved too little, or are loved too little by him, if you have not yet deserved to be called to those contemplative ecstasies or to follow when called. For how do you love perfectly, or how are you perfectly loved, if in desire for the highest things you are not caught up to things above and do not pass into those anagogical efforts through alienation of mind? Do you wish to know that the sublimity of divine revelations is a manifest indication of divine love? “I no longer call you servants,” he says, “but friends, because I have made known to you all things that I heard from my Father” (John 15). [Col. 0155B]

Observe also that the measure of divine revelation depends upon the greatness of divine love: “Eat, friends,” he says, “and drink, and be intoxicated, dearly beloved ones” (Song 5). Behold: those who are friends and dear eat; but those who are most dear drink—indeed, not only drink, but are also intoxicated. Certainly those who eat, while chewing the food they take, do not swallow that in which they delight without delay or some labor. But those who drink convey with the greatest speed and ease what they thirst for. Do not those, then, seem to you to eat who, with much effort and prolonged meditation, can scarcely attain to the delights of truth? But those in some sense drink who draw from divine revelations with the greatest ease and delight what they ardently desire from the inward sweetness of truth. [Col. 0155C]

The dear, then, eat, but the most dear drink, because the mode of manifestation is apportioned according to the measure of love. Intoxication produces alienation of mind, and the infusion of heavenly revelation carries only those who are most dear into ecstasy of mind. The Prophet intended to denote such intoxication when he said: “They shall be intoxicated from the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35). If, therefore, we desire to be drenched with this intoxication and frequently to experience these contemplative ecstasies of mind, let us strive to love our God inwardly and supremely, and at every hour to pant with the utmost desire for the joy of divine contemplation. This will be for our cherubim to have their wings spread out.

Behold how much labor we have expended, behold how much circumlocution we have used for this purpose: that our cherubim might spread their wings sufficiently and extend over our mercy-seat the shadowing cover that is required. [Col. 0155D–0156A]

## Chapter XVII. On matters especially pertaining to the fifth kind of contemplation

It remains now to ask why the aforesaid cherubim should look at one another, and, in looking, turn their faces toward the mercy-seat: “Let them look at one another,” he says, “with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat” (Exod. 25). We said above that matters above reason but not contrary to reason belong to the first cherub; while matters above reason which seem contrary to reason belong to the second cherub. According to this distinction, see whether perhaps matters considered concerning the unity of that supreme and simple divine essence belong especially to the first cherub, while those considered concerning the Trinity of persons belong to the second. For how many things are believed, asserted, and proved by Scriptural authority concerning the Trinity of persons which seem wholly to conflict with nature and oppose all human reason. All such things are therefore rightly said to belong to the second cherub, in which matters repugnant to human reason are brought into contemplation. [Col. 0156B]

But concerning the unity of the Godhead in one simple nature, let us see how far the matters considered exceed the measure of human intelligence, while nevertheless remaining consistent with reason; and thus they belong above all to the first cherub—that is, to the first kind of contemplation. Certainly we believe that the principal and supreme of all things is truly simple and supremely one, and that every good is in that one simple good. With respect to essence, nothing is simpler than it; with respect to efficacy, nothing is more manifold. In essence, what is simpler than that which is truly and supremely one? In efficacy, what is more manifold than that which truly and beyond all doubt can do all things? Consider how difficult it is for human reason to comprehend all that exists, and then you will understand how incomprehensible is that good in which every good is present.

It is above reason to comprehend how that good, truly simple and supremely one, is every good. Yet human reason readily assents to this assertion and gives its testimony, considering, affirming, and truly declaring that it would not be full, perfect, and altogether sufficient if any good were lacking in that supreme and eternal good. How, then, can that which is immeasurable and infinite be comprehended? “Great,” he says, “is the Lord, and exceedingly praiseworthy, and there is no end to his greatness” (Ps. 144). [Col. 0156C–D]

But what sense can grasp, what reason comprehend, how it can be both truly simple if it is immeasurable, and supremely one if it is infinite? Yet reason, by reasoning, testifies that that is truly simple which is not truly composite, because everything composite can by nature be divided, and what is by nature divisible is in some respect changeable. Reason therefore agrees that it is truly simple, because that which is acknowledged to be best and supreme of all things must be immutable: “With whom,” he says, “there is no change nor shadow of turning” (Jas. 5). If, then, it is good to be immutable, it is equally good to be simple. It follows, therefore, that what is supremely good is supremely simple. If, then, nothing is simpler than it, nothing is subtler than it; and that than which nothing is subtler, nothing is deeper; and than the deepest nothing is more unsearchable, and consequently nothing more incomprehensible.

Let us further consider what follows from the mutual comparison of simplicity and immensity, unity and universality. If every good is there, and whatever is there is supremely good, then there is supreme power, supreme wisdom, supreme goodness, and supreme blessedness. But where there is supreme simplicity, all that is is one and the very same thing. Therefore for it, being, living, understanding, being able, being good, and being blessed are one and the same; and see how incomprehensible this is. Thus it is not powerful from one source, wise from another, good from another, and blessed from another. [Col. 0157A–B]

Consider, then, what that power is for which to act is the same as to will to act. Attend to what that wisdom is for which being able is the same as knowing. Consider what that goodness is for which whatever pleases is, by the very fact that it pleases, fitting; and whatever displeases is, by the very fact that it displeases, unfitting. Consider what that life is for which to be is the same as to be blessed.

Consider also this: if he is truly omnipotent, he can act everywhere. Therefore he is everywhere potentially, both where there is place and where there is no place. And indeed both potentially and essentially, because his power is not one thing and his essence another. Therefore he is essentially within all things and outside all things; beneath all things and above all things. If within all things, nothing is more hidden; if outside all things, nothing is more remote; if beneath all things, nothing is more concealed; if above all things, nothing is more exalted. What, then, is more incomprehensible than that than which nothing is more hidden, remote, concealed, or exalted? [Col. 0157C]

Again, if he is in every place, nothing is more present; if he is outside every place, nothing is more absent. But is he not, precisely because he is most present to all things, more absent than all things; and precisely because he is more absent than all things, more present than all things—he for whom all that is does not derive its being from one source and another? But if nothing is more present than the most absent, and nothing more absent than the most present, what is more wondrous, what more incomprehensible than he?
