Again, if his power is not one thing and his blessedness another, wherever supreme power is, there also is supreme blessedness. Therefore supreme blessedness is everywhere. How, then, can there be a place of supreme misery even in hell, or how can anyone be miserable when supreme blessedness can nowhere be absent from, or ever fail, him? All these things are wondrous and truly incomprehensible. Reason approves many—indeed almost infinitely many—things concerning the unity of the Godhead and the consideration of true unity, although it does not comprehend them. All such things are above reason but not contrary to reason; and for this very reason, according to the distinction given above, they show themselves to belong to the first cherub. [Col. 0157D–0158A]

## Chapter XVIII. On matters especially pertaining to the sixth kind of contemplation

But concerning the Trinity of persons and contemplation of the Trinity, how many things are firmly believed and truly asserted which seem to be not only above reason but even contrary to reason. We believe in one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the Father from no one; the Son from the Father alone; the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son; the Son by being begotten, the Holy Spirit by proceeding. Thus we believe that one and the same God is three in persons and one in substance. Hence the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; yet the Father is not something other than the Son, nor is the Father or Son something other than the Spirit of both. For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another, although all have one substance, the same essence, and one nature alone. [Col. 0158B]

We believe all these things, profess all these things, and they are certainly true; yet in all of them, if weighed by human judgment, human reason seems vehemently to object. If the Father is unbegotten and the Son only-begotten, will the Father’s substance be unbegotten and the Son’s begotten? And since the substance of both is one and the same, will that same substance be begotten and unbegotten—that is, begotten and not begotten? Does that same substance beget itself and is it begotten from itself? Is it, then, both begotten and not begotten, born and not born?

If we say that the Son is born, what shall we say of his birth? Will his birth not be eternal, in him with whom “there is no change nor shadow of turning” (Jas. 5)? If his birth was at some time not present, how is he coeternal or coequal with the Father? And if it will at some time not be present, how will that nature be immutable in which something passes away? If it has always existed, how did he receive being from another, he who never began to be, without whom the Father could never have been? And how is his birth complete if it is still to come? Or perhaps is it repeated continuously, in order that it may always be? Then will it no longer be one but manifold and infinite, since it must be repeated without end? [Col. 0158C–D]

Whatever is said about the Son’s birth, see whether we may perhaps ask the same questions, by the same reasoning, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. Behold, these matters too, if weighed by human judgment, seem to oppose human reason. If the Holy Spirit possesses the same power as the Father, can he also do whatever the Father can do? Can he, then, beget a Son such as the Father begets? Or perhaps to beget a Son is not a power—and to beget such a Son as is omnipotent? Or perhaps he does not will it, though he can? How, then, will he possess the same likeness of will, and the same fullness of likeness, with the Father?

You will find many things of this kind, indeed almost innumerable things, concerning the Trinity of persons, which you will find not only incomprehensible to human reason but also discordant with it. You will find many such matters concerning the Trinity of persons, and many such matters concerning the union of substances in the incarnation of the Word. [Col. 0159A]

What, I ask, is that in which humanity and divinity are united, so that they can be one person? Is it something belonging to man, something belonging to God, or something belonging to both? But if it does not belong to both, how can they be united in that which is alien to either? If it is something belonging to man, then it is a creature. If it is something belonging to God, it is above creaturehood, and is no longer a creature. If it is something belonging to God and man, will it itself be both, and not be both—that is, creature and non-creature? But this question is exceedingly deep and, so far as I judge, has not hitherto been raised; and perhaps it is therefore better suppressed.

But what shall we say concerning Christ’s soul, which we do not dare deny received all fullness of grace? For whatever the Father has by nature, it received by grace. For “in it dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2). If it received all fullness of grace, then it received fullness of wisdom and fullness of power. If, therefore, it has wisdom equal to the Father’s and power equal to the Father’s—which cannot be denied—will it be equal to the Father, and can a creature be made equal to the Creator? This certainly must not be admitted. But if it unquestionably possesses equal power and equal wisdom, how can it be wholly incapable of being equal to him?

But why do we say this concerning Christ’s soul, when, concerning his body, according to the confession of faith, we believe and maintain many things which human reason attacks and judges impossible? When Christ distributed his body to his disciples, did he carry himself in his own hands? Was he himself both the one who carried and the one carried, the one who gave and the one given? When he was received by the disciples and crushed by their teeth, was he injured? Or perhaps, in that in which he was given, was he impassible, as he was invisible, although according to that which he gave he was visible and passible? Was, then, one and the same body at one and the same time visible and invisible, passible and impassible? See how incomprehensible this is, and how impossible it appears.

See in how many places Christ’s same body is daily consecrated and possessed. Is it therefore divided into parts, so that it may be possessed in so many places? How, then, can it itself truly be impassible and truly incorruptible? Or, though dispersed through so many places, does it everywhere remain whole, incorruptible, and altogether undivided? If, therefore, you consider in how many places it is, and in how many places it can be through the same power of consecration, where, I ask, will your thought lead you, unless to conclude that one and the same body can be in innumerable places, and this at one time? But see how this is not merely contrary to the nature of bodies, but even beyond every property of spirits. If, therefore, the things truly believed concerning Christ’s body are so incomprehensible and appear so incredible, how much more do those considered concerning Christ’s soul transcend all human reason by a far greater degree?

Yet incomparably more sublime are the matters that arise for consideration concerning the Trinity of persons. Accordingly, all such matters as seem not only to exceed but to confound the narrow limits of human reasoning are rightly said to belong to the second cherub. It was therefore rightly said that the matters especially considered concerning the unity of the divine substance belong to the first cherub, while those considered concerning the Trinity of persons belong especially to the second cherub. The former consideration thus belongs to the fifth kind of contemplation; the latter, to the sixth and final kind.

## Chapter XIX. On the mutual comparison of the last two contemplations

Concerning this twofold consideration—that is, the fifth and sixth kinds of contemplation—this must be carefully observed and guarded with diligent attention: we must affirm what pertains to one without destroying what pertains to the other. Thus we must establish, in those highest and divine matters, the unity of substance without emptying the Trinity of persons; and we must confirm the Trinity of persons without dissipating the unity of substance.

Those said cherubim ought therefore to look mutually upon one another, and by no consideration of their understanding turn the eyes of their contemplation away from their mutual agreement into opposition. Many, in what they think concerning the unity of supreme divinity, strive to empty the true faith of the Trinity; and likewise many, in what they assert concerning the Trinity, wish to dissolve the unity of the divine essence.

Arius says: “The Father is one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.” He would speak rightly if he said “one other,” not “another thing.” In what he says, he dissolves the unity of divinity. Sabellius says: “The same God, when he wills, is Father; when he wills, is Son; when he wills, is Holy Spirit; yet he himself is one.” In what he says, this man attempts to empty the true faith of the Trinity.

In such claims our cherubim turn their faces away from one another’s gaze, because they attend to and accept contrary assertions, very different judgments, and positions opposed to one another. According to the first cherub, we say that there is one God alone who created all things from nothing. According to the second cherub, we affirm that one is he who begot, and another he who proceeds from both. But let these two cherubim look upon one another, and let us say that one and the same God is one substantially and threefold personally.

According to the first cherub, we say that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one in one substance, one essence, one nature. According to the second cherub, we say that the Father is one person, the Son another person, and the Holy Spirit another person. Let the cherubim look mutually upon one another, and we profess without doubt that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not different things, although they are truly distinct persons. The Father, then, is one person, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, according to the second cherub; yet the Father is not one thing, the Son another thing, and the Holy Spirit another thing, according to the first cherub, since, in their mutual regard, we truly affirm that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods but one God.

According to the second cherub, we confess that the Son’s substance has been united with our substance in one person. According to the first cherub, we affirm without hesitation that the substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one and indivisible. Yet, in their mutual regard, we profess that the Son alone was truly incarnate.

A cherub looks upon a cherub when what one says is not contradicted by the other. A cherub looks upon a cherub when the fifth kind of contemplation so asserts matters belonging to its own consideration that it does not wish utterly to empty those belonging to the other. The cherubim look mutually upon one another when the final two kinds of contemplation meet one another and play together in mutual harmony and concord of truth. Again, one cherub looks upon the other when—as commonly happens—our contemplation begins with the penultimate kind and ends in the last; or, conversely, begins with the last and descends to the penultimate.

## Chapter XX. On the mutual comparison of the last three contemplations

The two cherubim ought not only to look at one another, but also, in that mutual gaze, to turn their faces toward the mercy seat. The designated cherubim turn their faces toward the mercy seat when the final two kinds of contemplation, in what they agree upon concerning sublime and divine things, draw from those matters subject to the fourth kind of contemplation an analogy of reason as testimony for their assertion.

For we understand the fourth kind of contemplation by the mercy seat, just as we understand the fifth and sixth by the two cherubim. As was said above, the fourth kind of contemplation is concerned especially with matters usually considered concerning the rational but created spirit; the fifth and sixth are concerned chiefly with matters that ought to be considered concerning the divine and uncreated Spirit. Since, then, we know that the rational creature was made in the Creator’s image, we rightly seek more familiarly from that nature an account of resemblance, and shape the method of our inquiry from it: from that nature, I say, in whose constitution we do not doubt that the traces of the divine image have been more deeply impressed and more clearly expressed.

What else, then, is it for the cherubim to turn their faces toward the mercy seat than, in contemplating and investigating divine things, to attend to the rational creature and, from the likeness examined, to advance more deeply toward understanding divinity? If you wonder how God, the maker of all things, produced from nothing into actuality, at the very beginning of the world, so many and such varied kinds of things as he wished, consider how easily the human soul can at every hour fashion by imagination any forms of things whatever, and, as often as it wills, create certain creatures, as it were, of its own kind without pre-existing matter, forming them as if from nothing. Then what perhaps previously appeared unbelievable will begin to seem less wonderful.

In this, too, you will find something very noteworthy: he reserved to himself the truth of things, which is supreme truth, but granted to his image the forming at any hour of images of things. If you wonder how one and the same God can be in every place, not divided into parts but wholly present everywhere, observe that one and the same soul is diffused through all the members of the body, yet is itself not divided into parts, but is whole and undivided in each member. The relation of the soul, in its own measure, to its body—that is, to the world under its governance, which it has received to rule—is analogous.

If you wonder how God, by a mere motion of will and without any resistance, bends all that occurs in the world to every good pleasure of his own, consider that the soul also moves, governs, and orders each member of its body by the mere decision of its will. Thus in both cases there is one manner of acting with respect to likeness, although different when measured by equality. In all these things the first cherub looks toward the mercy seat, drawing an analogy of reason from the rational creature to contemplation of the Creator.

In that same rational creature, if we attend carefully, we find, as we believe, some trace of the supreme Trinity. There is something from the mind itself—namely, its wisdom—and there is something from both the mind itself and its wisdom—namely, its love. For every mind loves its own wisdom, and therefore love of its wisdom proceeds from both. Wisdom is from the mind alone; love, however, is from mind and wisdom alike. So the Son—that is, the Father’s wisdom—is from the Father alone, while the Holy Spirit—that is, the love of both—is from Father and Son. In this way the second cherub discovers how it may profitably turn the face of its consideration toward the mercy seat, if in contemplating divine things it seeks the testimony of likeness.

It should certainly be noted that those three things which occur for consideration in the rational soul do not make a Trinity of persons, as the three things in God, according to the difference of their properties, divide into three persons. See, therefore, that in those things introduced in the rational mind as a likeness of that supreme Trinity, the dissimilarity is greater than the likeness. Yet it is no wonder that the second cherub touches the side of dissimilarity more closely in our mercy seat, while it looks, as it were, from afar upon the side of likeness.

If you wonder how the Son alone—that is, the Father’s wisdom—was incarnate, how he came to us in flesh and yet did not depart from the Father, consider that in the imaginary trinity the mind’s wisdom alone is embodied in the human voice; through the bodily voice it goes forth, having gone forth it is recognized, and having been recognized it is retained; yet it is in no way separated from the mind from which it was born. There are many such things in the rational mind for which the second cherub ought to look toward the mercy seat.

Thus we now understand from the exposition how, according to the Lord’s teaching, the two cherubim ought to look upon one another; and likewise on what grounds and for what benefit they ought to turn their faces toward the mercy seat.

## Chapter XXI. That frequent exercise of the last three contemplations is always accompanied by frequent divine revelations

Nor should we neglect or pass without careful consideration what is promised by the Lord’s word when he says to Moses: “From there I will speak to you, from above the mercy seat, that is, and from between the two cherubim” (Exod. 25). Consider how great a thing it is, and what it is like, to contemplate God whenever necessary and, in every need, to seek and receive divine counsel whenever required; then you will perceive how necessary and useful it is to have these final three kinds of contemplation as familiar companions. “From there,” he says, “I will speak to you” (ibid.). From what place, I ask, or whence? “From above the mercy seat,” he says, “and from between the two cherubim.”

Therefore, if one wishes to have the divine oracle familiarly, let one ascend to the lofty heart and, transcending in mind, hold that aforementioned mercy seat between those two cherubim, so as to ascend through the third kind of contemplation to the fifth and sixth. The mind, as though lifted above the mercy seat, moves between the two cherubim when the contemplative soul, transcending by sublime consideration not only bodily but also spiritual creature, is suspended in wonder at the supreme unity and Trinity. We are raised as though above the mercy seat into the mirror of this wonder when, from examination of the rational creature and consideration of the divine image, we are advanced more deeply toward knowledge of divinity. We move as intermediaries between the mercy seat and the two cherubim when, from the mutual comparison of the final three contemplations, we advance more fully to the perfection of each.

We ought, therefore, willingly to move among these three kinds of spectacles, and through the mirror and image of the supreme Trinity and unity penetrate more deeply to contemplate the glory of that same Trinity and unity. If we willingly reconsider, and frequently bring to consideration and wonder, both what we have learned concerning the dignity of the rational creature and what we have learned concerning the Creator’s condescension or splendor, we shall deserve to learn by divine revelation, concerning these same kinds of spectacles, matters which previously we could not understand at all. This is what is promised to you when it is said: “From there I will speak to you.”

Consider, therefore, how useful it is to our faith frequently to reconsider and retain in constant remembrance its mysteries, since through such study we may obtain frequent divine revelations. If, then, we cannot see in an ecstasy of mind, or grasp with pure and clear understanding, those things that we believe concerning the Trinity of persons and unity of substance in God, nevertheless let us hold by faith what we have received from Catholic tradition concerning them and, as far as possible, bring them frequently into consideration, so that by such study we may deserve an abundance of divine revelations.

For I think that the consolation of divine revelations will not be altogether foreign to those who look upon the secrets of divine mysteries with the eye of faith as frequently as willingly; how much more familiar will it be especially to those who, continually contemplating them with the eye of understanding and often seeing them in ecstasy of mind, cannot satisfy their desire?

Therefore, whoever performs Moses’ office, has undertaken pastoral care, and is charged by the Lord’s command to lead the Lord’s people out of the house of bondage, conduct them through desert places, and bring them into the land of promise, ought surely to range freely among those three aforementioned kinds of contemplation. Thus he may always be found worthier to be instructed worthily, whenever necessary, from the Lord’s oracle concerning both his own ignorance and that of his people, and to be made certain concerning every uncertainty. If, then, you desire to know by divine inspiration what is the good-pleasing and perfect will of God, always be ready and inclined toward these final three kinds of spectacles. By the merit of this exercise you may perhaps deserve to prove the truth of that promise: “From there I will speak to you.”

## Chapter XXII. That in every kind of contemplation it may happen that the contemplator transcends the mind

Although it is familiar and seems almost proper to the final two kinds of contemplation to see through ecstasy of mind, whereas it is domestic and almost distinctive to the first four to rise into contemplation without any alienation of mind, yet all may and commonly do occur in both ways. For some matters belonging to the first kinds of contemplation can be known through divine revelation and be seen by the eye of contemplation in ecstasy of mind. Likewise, the matters belonging to the final two kinds of contemplation we are accustomed, insofar as we know and are able, to bring under consideration and see through contemplation in the ordinary state of mind.

But because the matters belonging to the final two always exceed the penetration of the human mind, when the mind brings them under consideration according to the state ordinarily common to all—or, conversely, so that it may see something in them more penetratingly and clearly—the human mind itself exceeds itself and passes into alienation. It was therefore fitting that this very mind should be mystically represented not so much by a human image as by an angelic form.

That all these kinds of contemplation can be seen through ecstasy we learn from the mystical example of Moses. That they can be brought under contemplation without any ecstasy of mind we learn from the symbolic work of Bezalel. For Moses ascended the mountain and entered the cloud in order to see, through divine revelation, the ark and both cherubim. But Bezalel, in order to make and contemplate that mystical work, is not recorded to have sought out or entered either mountain or cloud.

What is it to ascend the mountain except, according to the prophetic saying, to ascend to a lofty heart? Such a mountain is covered by cloud when the memory of all outward things falls away from the mind. Moses remains six days on this mountain, and on the seventh he is called from the midst of the cloud to converse with the Lord. As is known, we perform our works for six days and rest on the seventh. Thus we pass, as it were, six days on this mountain when, with much labor and great effort of mind, we become accustomed to remain for a long time in such a state of sublimity.

But we come, as it were, to the seventh day when such elevation of mind becomes a delight to the mind and is attained without any labor. We reach, as it were, the seventh day when, in that state of sublimity, the soul is at last composed into supreme tranquility, so that it lays aside not merely every care and anxiety but even exceeds almost all the limits of human passibility. It is admitted to converse with the Lord when, through divine inspiration and revelation, it is brought into that abyss of divine judgments.

Moses enters the midst of the cloud when the human mind, absorbed by the immensity of that divine light, is lulled into utter forgetfulness of itself. You may then wonder—and rightly ought to wonder—how cloud agrees there with fire and fire with cloud: the cloud of ignorance with the cloud of enlightened understanding; ignorance and forgetfulness of what is known and experienced, together with revelation and understanding of what was previously unknown and hitherto unexperienced. For at one and the same time human understanding is illuminated concerning divine things and darkened concerning human things.

The psalmist comprehends in a few words this peace, darkening, and illumination of the elevated mind when he says: “In peace, in the selfsame, I will sleep and rest” (Ps. 4). The soul truly finds peace when, led above itself, it no longer feels at all the troubles of human passibility. It falls asleep in this peace when, lulled into supreme tranquility, whatever it was accustomed to think in sobriety comes into forgetfulness. For one who sleeps knows nothing at all of the things around him, indeed not even himself. Sleep therefore rightly expresses alienation of mind, by which it is removed from familiar things and, as though overcome by sleep, departs from human affairs into contemplation of divine things.

And then it sleeps “in the selfsame” when it rests through contemplation and wonder in him who is one and the same, the being of all that is, and who alone can truly say: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). What Moses denotes by the seventh day, David names more plainly as peace. What for Moses is entering the midst of the cloud is for David falling asleep. And what it is for one to rest “in the selfsame” is for another to approach when called and abide with the Lord.

Thus, one who, in likeness to Moses, ascends the summit of the mountain, enters the midst of the cloud, and, with the Lord revealing it, sees and contemplates the aforementioned ark and designated cherubim, is one who is carried upward through elevation and alienation of mind and is advanced through divine inspiration to those six kinds of contemplation which we have described. Moses was indeed told: “See that you make everything according to what was shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25). If everything was shown him by the Lord on the mountain, then not only the cherubim but also the ark. This is what I said above: matters belonging to any kind of contemplation can, when the Lord reveals them, be seen in ecstasy of mind.

Yet Bezalel’s work also makes clear that any of these matters can and commonly do come under contemplation without any ecstasy of mind. For what, I ask, is it to make the ark, clothe it with gold, surround it with a crown, cover it with the mercy seat, and add the cherubim, except gradually to acquire skill in the said kinds of contemplation; through much study and labor to learn and put into practice one thing after another; and finally to complete the work and at last be perfect in all things?

But leaving the ark aside, what shall I say of the cherubim themselves? Is Bezalel recorded, in order to make them or see them when made, to have ascended the mountain or entered the cloud? Hence it is clearly understood that even the final two kinds of contemplation, to which exercise through ecstasy of mind seems almost proper, can nevertheless sometimes be held within the bounds of human comprehension. Every kind of contemplation can occur in both ways: it is commonly exercised sometimes through ecstasy of mind and sometimes without any ecstasy of mind.

## Chapter XXIII. That some possess the gift of exceeding themselves as something fortuitous, while others possess it almost as a virtue

Among those who in their contemplations are led above themselves and carried away into ecstasy of mind, some still await and receive this solely through the calling grace; others acquire it for themselves, insofar as they can, through great diligence of mind—though with grace cooperating. The former possess this gift as though by chance; the latter already possess it almost as a virtue.

That is, as though by chance, which a person cannot in any way do whenever or however he wills. Those, therefore, have this gift as though fortuitous who can accomplish nothing in this through their own diligence but await only the hour of calling grace. Those should be said already to possess the efficacy of such grace almost as a virtue who are now able, for the most part, to do it when they will.

We have a figure of one thing in Moses and of the other in Aaron the priest. What Moses deserved—to see the ark through the cloud on the mountain—was solely the grace of the Lord who revealed it; for he did not at all have it in his own power to see it at will. Aaron, however, had already for the most part in his power, as often as order or reason required, to enter the Holy of Holies and see the ark of the Lord within the veil. It is quite evident that the Holy of Holies occupied the innermost and most secret place in the tabernacle of the covenant. Therefore, just as by the summit of the mountain we understand the highest point of the mind, so by the Holy of Holies we understand the innermost point of the human mind. But in the human soul, without doubt, the highest is the same as the innermost, and the innermost the same as the highest. Therefore, we understand the same thing by the summit of the mountain and by the sanctuary of the tabernacle of the covenant.

What, then, is it to ascend the mountain’s summit or the inner tabernacle, except to ascend, lay hold of, and maintain the highest and innermost recess of the mind? By the first tabernacle, known to all, we understand the ordinary state of mind; by the second, the state known to very few, which comes through ecstasy of mind. To the former belongs especially rational perception; to the latter intellectual perception. In the former we discern our invisible things; in the latter we contemplate divine invisible things.

But a thick veil of forgetfulness divides and separates these two states—the one known to all, the other experienced by few. For when in ecstasy of mind we are carried above or within ourselves into contemplation of divine things, we immediately forget all external matters—indeed, not only all that is outside us, but also all that is within us. And again, when we return to ourselves from that state of sublimity, we are altogether unable to recall to memory, in the truth or clarity in which we first perceived them, the things we had previously seen above ourselves. Even though we retain something of them in memory and see them as though through the middle of a veil and in the midst of a cloud, we cannot adequately comprehend or remember either the manner of seeing or the quality of the vision.

In a wonderful way, we remember without remembering and do not remember while remembering: seeing, we do not see through; looking, we do not perceive clearly; attending, we do not penetrate. You see clearly that, whether the human mind enters that innermost treasury of mysteries or comes forth from it into external things, on either side the veil of forgetfulness receives it. Thus entering the cloud and entering within the veil are the same thing.

But although Moses’ action and Aaron’s action concern one and the same thing, they differ chiefly in this: the former awaited only the hour of another’s good pleasure in this matter, while the latter had undertaken it almost as an office and performed it, for the most part, at will. Yet, in order that Aaron might be fit and ready to enter within the veil whenever he wished and whenever it was necessary, he had acquired and possessed for himself the high-priestly adornment and attire suitable for that office.

What is it to possess attire suitable for that office except to acquire those merits of virtue through which one can have the exercise of such grace in habitual use? One who wishes to penetrate to the inner side of the veil must proceed not only in high-priestly attire but also amid the obscuring smoke of spices, according to the Lord’s command. Thus, at the hour of entry, he may burn with such an exhalation of heavenly desires and such a swelling, as it were, of fragrant smoke that everything which could please in the adornment of the inward person may become contemptible to him and be reckoned altogether as nothing.

Perhaps it is the same thing for Moses to leave the crowd at the foot of the mountain and for Aaron to lay aside his common clothing before entering the tabernacle; likewise, perhaps it is the same thing for Moses to ascend the mountain with the elders of Israel and for Aaron to enter the inner part of the tabernacle in high-priestly adornment. Nor perhaps is it different for Moses, having left the elders behind during the ascent of the mountain, to attain the summit with Joshua alone, and for Aaron to hasten into the Holy of Holies with aromatic incense. And perhaps it is likewise the same for Moses to enter the cloud and for Aaron to enter within the veil—so that the sole difference between their actions, as regards mystical teaching, is that one entered into that secret colloquy of divine revelation solely at the Lord’s call, and the other by his own deliberate choice.

# Book Five

## Chapter I. That we advance toward the grace of contemplation in three ways

We advance toward the grace of contemplation in three ways: sometimes by grace alone, sometimes by diligence joined to grace, and sometimes by another’s teaching. We have a type and example of these three in three persons—Moses, Bezalel, and Aaron—if we consult their deeds. Moses first saw the ark on the mountain and in the cloud, without any labor of diligence, through the Lord’s revelation alone. Bezalel made by his own labor what he could have seen. Aaron, however, was accustomed to see the ark already fashioned by another’s work.

After the manner of Moses, we see the ark of the Lord without any human diligence when we receive the ray of contemplation solely from the Lord’s revelation. But then, as it were according to Bezalel’s example, we advance toward the same end by our own work, when through our study and labor we acquire skill in that same grace. We receive, as it were, from another’s work the power to see the Lord’s ark when we become accustomed to the exercise of such grace through another’s instruction.

But when we speak of the work of diligence, we do not mean that we can accomplish anything whatsoever without grace cooperating, since every diligence of ours is itself only from grace. It is one thing to receive divinely the grace of contemplation; it is another, with God cooperating, to acquire by one’s own exercise such a dwelling-place of grace. Thus we obtain this grace in three ways: by divine inspiration, by our own exercise, or by another’s instruction.

It should be noted, however, that some advance toward this grace through their own diligence and without a teacher’s instruction, yet are in no way carried in their contemplations as far as ecstasy of mind. Others advance toward the same grace more through another’s instruction than through the sharpness of their own mind, yet in their contemplations often rise as far as ecstasy of mind. Hence Bezalel is recorded to have made the ark but not to have entered into it. Aaron, however, is unquestionably understood to have customarily entered to the ark, already made by another’s work and placed within the veil.

Behold, in this work we have undertaken, as it were, Bezalel’s office: we have taken care to give you instruction for the study of contemplation and, as it were, to labor intensely in making the ark. Yet you far surpass me in this grace if, aided by what you hear, you can enter as far as the inner side of the veil; if you can perceive in ecstasy of mind, and as though see within the veil, what we labor over openly, comprehend, and set forth according to common experience.

It should also be noted that some, upon returning to themselves, cannot in any way grasp or recover in the ordinary state of mind what they behold in alienation of mind. Hence King Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream, but, shaken from sleep, could not recall the dream he had seen to memory (Dan. 8). Others easily reconsider afterward what they perceive in ecstasy. Others toil with great effort in order to be able to do this. Hence King Pharaoh saw a dream and retained what he had seen (Gen. 43). By contrast, King Nebuchadnezzar recovered his lost dream through much persistence; and the ark of the Lord was shown to Moses on the mountain by the Lord’s revelation, but afterward became familiar to him in the valley and was frequently seen.

Likewise, some begin at last to have as familiar what they possess rarely and as though by chance—namely, exceeding the mind in their contemplations. Hence Moses eventually entered familiarly to the Lord’s ark within the veil, though he had first been granted to see it through the cloud only at the Lord’s call and revelation. There are many mysteries in all these matters which cannot and ought not now be treated individually.

## Chapter II. In what ways every contemplation commonly occurs: namely, through enlargement of mind, elevation of mind, and alienation of mind
By three modes, as it seems to me, the character of contemplation is varied. For at one time it is brought about by the expansion of the mind, at another by the elevation of the mind, and sometimes [Col. 0170A] by the alienation of the mind. The expansion of the mind occurs when the mind’s sharpness is extended more widely and sharpened more intensely, yet in no way surpasses the measure of human effort. The elevation of the mind occurs when the liveliness of understanding, illumined by God, transcends the limits of human effort, yet does not pass into alienation of mind: so that what it sees is above itself, and yet it does not wholly depart from what is customary. Alienation of mind occurs when the memory of present things falls away from the mind, and, through a transformation wrought by divine operation, it passes into a certain unfamiliar state of soul inaccessible to human effort. Those who deserve to be raised to the highest summit of such grace experience these three modes of contemplation. The first arises from human effort, the third from divine grace alone, while the middle one [Col. 0170B] arises from the mingling of both—that is, of human effort and divine grace.

On the first level we fashion, as it were, the ark by our own labour, when by our study and effort we acquire the art of contemplation. On the second level the ark is raised upon the shoulders of those who bear it, and follows, as it were, the tracks of the cloud going before it, when effort is busy and the grace of revelation cooperates and, as it were, goes ahead, and the ray of contemplation is extended. On the third level the ark is brought into the Holy of Holies and placed, as it were, within the veil, when the acuity of the contemplative is drawn together into the innermost recess of the mind and shut off from the memory of outward things by the veil of forgetfulness and alienation.

The first level, then, pertains to the construction of the ark; the second [Col. 0170C] to the carrying forth of the ark; the third to its introduction and the drawing of the veil over it. Of the first, the words spoken by the Lord to Abraham are rightly understood: “Lift up your eyes and see from the place where you now are, northward and southward, eastward and westward. All the land that you see I will give to you” (Gen. XIII). Of the second, the words written of Moses are rightly understood: “Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the summit of Pisgah opposite Jericho. And the Lord showed him all the land of Gilead as far as Dan” (Deut. XXXIV). The third is indicated by the fact that the Lord overshadowed with a bright cloud the witnesses of His transfiguration who had been taken up the high mountain; and, as was already said above, by the fact that Moses approached the Lord through the midst of the mist (Matt. XVII).

[Col. 0170D] In the first case, indeed, Abraham is neither commanded to climb a mountain, nor do we read there that the Lord showed him anything; rather, from the place where he was, he is commanded to raise his eyes and survey the land he was to receive. No mention is made there of ascent or showing, by which either the exaltation of a mind raised up or the disclosure of divine revelation might be signified. We raise our eyes from the place where we are, or are accustomed to be, when in the spectacles of our contemplation we do not abandon the ordinary and customary state of mind. The measure of our capacity for comprehension is the place in which, for the time being, we exist by understanding. We consider the breadth of the inheritance to be received when, with the eyes of contemplation, we foresee far in advance how great a breadth of perfection we may at last someday attain through the progress of our devotion. [Col. 0171A] Nothing in these words of Scripture suggests anything that appears to exceed human effort; consequently they are rightly applied to that first level of contemplation.

But observe how expressly the second level of contemplation seems to be designated when Moses is commanded to ascend the mountain and when the Lord is said to have shown him the land of promise. What is that mountain ascent of Moses but a certain elevation of the human mind above the plain of human possibility toward things on high? And what is that showing by the Lord but an infused illumination of inward inspiration? To behold the land of promise through divine disclosure is to know, through the revelation of divine illumination, the fullness of future recompense, and to devote oneself to contemplation of this kind. That Moses ascends the mountain seems to belong to human effort; that the Lord shows him the land of promise belongs to divine grace. Thus this testimony of Scripture itself indicates that it refers to the second level of which we have spoken.

[Col. 0171B] But from what was said above we can sufficiently gather how the statement that Moses, ascending the mountain, approached the Lord through the midst of the mist refers to the third mode or level of contemplation. For what is it to enter the cloud when approaching at the divine call, except to go beyond oneself, and through the cloud of forgetfulness to have the mind darkened, as it were, to the memory of things lying near at hand? The same point is indicated by the bright cloud that overshadowed Christ’s disciples. Thus one and the same cloud both overshadowed by shining [Col. 0171C] and illumined by overshadowing, because it both illumined them toward divine things and clouded them toward human things.

By these three modes, therefore, all contemplation is accustomed to occur: through expansion of mind, elevation of mind, and alienation of mind. “Lift up your eyes round about, and see” (Gen. XIII): behold the kind of contemplation produced by expansion of mind. “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. LX): behold elevation of mind. “I said in my ecstasy, Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV): behold alienation of mind.

## CHAPTER III. On the Expansion of the Mind: by What Modes It Is Accustomed to Increase

That mode of contemplation which takes place through expansion of mind is accustomed to grow through three levels: art, practice, and attention. We truly acquire an art for some purpose [Col. 0171D] when we learn, by reliable instruction or even by shrewd investigation, how something ought to be done. Practice occurs when we put into use what we have learned by art and make ourselves prompt and skilled in the performance of such a task. Attention occurs when we apply ourselves with the utmost diligence to the pursuit we carry out. The first thing in any discipline, therefore, is to acquire its art; the second, to put it into use; the third, to apply oneself with the greatest keenness to that for which we have been taught and trained.

By these three levels, as has been said, the capacity of the mind is enlarged and made more capable of every kind of learning or discipline. Certainly, the more extensively and firmly you have learned something, the more abundantly you are enlarged for grasping broader and deeper matters. [Col. 0172A] Yet this too appears no less certain: every discipline acquired by instruction is strengthened, enlarged, and perfected by use and practice. Again, what is the reason that in one and the same pursuit in which we have been taught and trained, we sometimes see more dimly and sometimes more clearly, except that the mind’s enlargement and clarity increase in proportion to its attention? The first level, then, is the acquisition of the art itself; the second, its frequent practice; the third, diligent and studious concentration upon that practice.

The human mind is exhorted to its first level of enlargement when it is told through the prophet: “Set up for yourself a watchtower; set before yourself bitter things; direct your heart to the straight way in which you have walked” (Jer. XXXI). Of the second you hear when you read: [Col. 0172B] “I will stand upon my watch, and set my foot upon the fortress, and I will look to see what may be said to me” (Hab. II). Of the third there is this: “Cross over to the islands of Kittim and see; send to Kedar and consider most earnestly” (Jer. II).

What is it to set up a watchtower except to acquire the knowledge of contemplation? We raise a watchtower in order that from it we may see far off and extend our sight in every direction. Therefore the enlargement of mind is rightly signified in these words, in which the watchtower of contemplation is raised and knowledge of such a pursuit is acquired. What is it to stand upon the watch and set one’s foot firmly, except to strengthen by use the knowledge of contemplation? For what one calls a watchtower, another calls a watch. [Col. 0172C] We are accustomed to raise watchtowers for public or private watchfulness, so that from them, looking out, we may foresee dangers threatening from afar. Thus we too raise the grace of contemplation as a spiritual watchtower, so that we may anticipate the snares of the tempter.

But it is one thing to establish or ascend a watchtower, and another to stand upon it or set one’s foot firmly there. The former belongs to acquiring a discipline; the latter, to practising it. And when we are commanded to consider most earnestly, who, I ask, does not see how this pertains to that third mode of our enlargement? “Send to Kedar,” he says, “and consider most earnestly.” This is rightly said and commanded, because the mind’s capacity grows and is enlarged through the intensity of consideration and attention. [Col. 0172D] If, therefore, you diligently apply yourself to these three levels of progress, you will be enlarged more and more toward a great perfection of clarity. Great is the enlargement of mind in these things, but no less is the delight.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Elevation of the Mind: through What Levels It Is Accustomed to Rise

Likewise, that mode of contemplation which occurs through elevation of mind grows through three levels. Human understanding, divinely inspired and illumined by that heavenly light, is sometimes raised above knowledge, sometimes even above effort, and sometimes even above nature.

Elevation of mind rises above knowledge when one of us knows by divine revelation something that exceeds the measure of one’s own knowledge or understanding. Elevation of mind is raised above effort when human understanding is divinely illumined toward something for which no knowledge of its own suffices—neither that which it presently possesses nor any that it can acquire by its own effort. The capacity of the mind is enlarged above nature when human understanding, breathed upon by divine inspiration, goes beyond the measure and limits of effort not merely of some individual’s abilities, but generally of the whole of human nature.

The soul of the contemplative is raised above knowledge when it experiences what is said: “Let a human being approach a deep heart, and God will be exalted” (Ps. LXIII). [Col. 0173A] Then indeed God is exalted before the raised mind, when, through God’s revealing, something is shown to it concerning the loftiness of divine majesty that [Col. 0173B] appears to surpass the measure of the knowledge it has hitherto possessed. For that loftiness of the Godhead, which in itself has no way of growing or being exalted, can nevertheless daily grow in our knowledge and appear more sublime to the gaze of our contemplation.

But the raised mind is lifted above its own effort when the following is fulfilled in it: “He spread out His wings and took them up, and bore them upon His shoulders” (Deut. XXXI). Certainly it does not belong to human effort to make a journey through the air. Yet what we cannot do by walking, we can be carried by the wings of those who bear us. Therefore to travel through the air appears to be above effort, but not above nature. Thus the contemplative soul rises above the limits of its own effort when [Col. 0173C] divine condescension, by manifesting its mysteries and, as it were, spreading out or raising its wings, lifts it to that summit of surpassing knowledge to which it could never go by any effort of its own.

But that elevation of mind seems altogether to transcend the measure of human nature, for which the Prophet sighed when he said: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s, that I may fly and find rest?” (Ps. LIV). The same is indicated by what the Lord promises through Isaiah: “Those who trust in the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall take up wings like eagles” (Isa. XL). It is beyond human nature, beyond doubt, to have wings and to fly on high at the discretion of one’s will. What is it to receive wings, as though contrary to nature, except to possess, through virtue, a certain wonderful power of contemplation, by which, whenever you will, you may penetrate with the wing of your insight into the lofty regions of more secret knowledge, inaccessible to all human effort? [Col. 0173D] Thus we truly begin to be winged creatures when, by the gift of grace divinely bestowed for this very purpose, we transcend the bounds of the human condition in the flight of our contemplation.

Every kind of prophecy, however, provided it occurs without alienation of mind, appears to pertain to this third level of elevation. For is it not beyond human nature to see concerning past things what no longer exists; to see concerning future things what does not yet exist; to see concerning present things what is absent from the senses; to see the secrets of another’s heart, which are subject to no sense; and to see concerning divine things what is above sense? It remains to inquire [Col. 0174A] by what causes, that is, the ecstasy of the human mind is accustomed to occur, and through what levels it is accustomed to increase.

## CHAPTER V. That Ecstasy of the Human Mind Is Accustomed to Occur from a Threefold Cause

For three causes, as it seems to me, draw us into alienation of mind. At times, through the greatness of devotion; at times, through the greatness of wonder; and at times through the greatness of exultation, the mind comes wholly not to comprehend itself, and, lifted above itself, passes into alienation.

Through the greatness of devotion the human mind is raised above itself when it is so kindled by the fire of heavenly desire that the flame of inward love grows beyond human measure. This flame melts the human soul like wax, wholly dissolves it from its former condition, makes it thin as smoke, and lifts and sends it upward to the heights. [Col. 0174B] Through the greatness of wonder the human soul is led above itself when, irradiated by divine light and held suspended in admiration of supreme beauty, it is shaken by so vehement an astonishment that it is entirely cast out of its own state; and, like flashing lightning, the more profoundly it is cast down to the depths through contempt of itself in the sight of unseen beauty, the more sublimely and swiftly, struck back by desire for the highest things and carried above itself, it is raised to the heights.

Through the greatness of delight and exultation the human mind is alienated from itself when, having drunk—or rather, been fully intoxicated by—that inward abundance [Col. 0174C] of interior sweetness, it wholly forgets what it is and what it has been. Through the excess of its joy it is carried over into ecstasy of alienation, and is swiftly transformed into a certain supramundane disposition under a state of wonderful blessedness.

So long, therefore, as we do not perceive such ecstasies in ourselves, what else ought we to think of ourselves, as we said above, except that we are loved too little, or that we love too little? For whoever you are, if you were loved fully and perfectly, perhaps the excess of your love and the anguish of burning desire would carry you into ecstasies such as those we have described above in part. Again, if you had proved wholly worthy of divine love, if you had rendered yourself fit for such great condescension, perhaps He would irradiate the eyes of your understanding with so great a brightness of His light [Col. 0174D] and intoxicate your heart’s desire with such sweetness of His inward delight, that He would carry you above yourself and raise you to things on high through ecstasy of mind.

These three anagogical modes of ecstasy, in the same order in which we have set them out here, are, I think, mystically described in the Song of Songs. Of the first, the following is rightly understood: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke, from fragrances of myrrh and incense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Song III). Of the second, we rightly understand what we read much later in the same Song: “Who is she who comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song VI). The third is rightly applied to what [Col. 0175A] is read at the end: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song VIII).

## CHAPTER VI. That the First Mode of Ecstasy Arises from the Greatness of Devotion

Do you wish to know more clearly how fittingly we may apply that first passage to the first mode of ecstasy? The first ecstasy of mind, as you heard above, arises from the anguish of desire and the greatness of devotion. Smoke, moreover, always rises from fire. And who would deny that spiritual love is fire? Therefore the elevation of mind to things above, which arises from the fervour of love, is rightly compared, if I am not mistaken, to smoke. What do we understand by smoke of this kind [Col. 0175B] except the desire of the devout mind? The soul therefore ascends like smoke to things above when its desire, burning with love and driving it to this very end, carries it above itself.

Now a slender rod, as we all know, is both thin and straight. Therefore, if your ascent is to take upon itself the likeness of a slender rod, let your desire be anxious and single, and let it arise from a right intention. But if by myrrh we understand contrition of the flesh; by incense, devotion of heart; and by every powder of the perfumer, the perfection of all virtues: observe how all these things converge upon one meaning, though each can readily be understood in itself. For this is sufficiently evident: whoever is full of charity cannot lack the other distinctions of virtue. For, if the Apostle is to be believed, charity is the perfection of virtues.

[Col. 0175C] This must indeed be noted: a holy soul truly ascends like smoke and through the wilderness when, from the good or evil things it finds in itself, it kindles its affection into desire for the heavenly Bridegroom. Yet, as regards merit, that elevation of mind seems to me greater which, with grace indeed assisting, arises from intention—one’s own intention—than that which arises from revelation alone or some divine inspiration. Therefore, in order that it may be found worthy of the rest, the soul must begin with an ascent of this kind and first ascend, as it were, through the wilderness. Yet for it to become a slender column of smoke [Col. 0175D] (though it begins to be formed through the wilderness), it must rise above the wilderness itself. Otherwise the mind is not carried into ecstasy unless it is raised above itself, unless it leaves itself below and, by leaving itself, makes itself a wilderness; and from that wilderness it rises more and more to the heights in the manner of smoke.

## CHAPTER VII. That the First Mode of Ecstasy Sometimes Occurs through the Mere Fervent Boiling of Desire

Yet such ecstasy of mind is sometimes brought about merely through the boiling fervour of desire, and sometimes both through such fervour and through divine revelation joined to it. For why should that spiritual and incorporeal fire of divine love not possess among spiritual things the same power that this bodily fire is accustomed to have in bodily things?

We know well what this bodily fire is accustomed to do in vessels, even when they are filled with but a little liquid. First it begins to overturn the liquid from the bottom; then it throws it now to this side, now to that, now upward, now downward; and gradually raises it toward the top and fills the whole vessel, from however little there was, right up to the brim. Finally it lifts the liquid above the vessel itself, violently empties what is within, pours it out, and forcefully casts it forth.

[Col. 0176A] So too the human mind, kindled by divine fire, often seethes and rages within itself against itself, boils and foams, is angry with itself, despises itself, is vehemently indignant with itself, [Col. 0176B] vehemently tramples itself down, longs for the highest things, and yearns for things beyond the world. And while it is burned for a long time by such heat and violently tossed about, while through contempt for lower things it is driven away from the lowest and drawn upward by desires for higher things, it often happens that, by the force of the spirit and under the impulse of desire, it is thrust outside itself and above itself, wholly forgetful of itself, raised in ecstasy, and carried altogether into higher things.

In this manner, when the ardour of heavenly desire makes the human soul boil vehemently in divine love, it raises the fervent soul above itself. And, as we may prove by the preceding example, every aromatic powder of the perfumer, when cast into fire, so far as it is not consumed by the devouring flame, is driven upward by the violence of the heat in a thin, smoking exhalation. [Col. 0176C] You see, I pray, how nature, when questioned, and Scripture, when consulted, speak one and the same meaning in equal harmony. Thus the ecstasy of a mind divinely inflamed can and is accustomed to arise merely from the heat of fervent desire, as we said above.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the First Mode of Ecstasy Sometimes Occurs Both through Boiling Devotion and through Divine Revelation Joined to It

Such alienation of mind also occurs sometimes when, on one side, the desire of a fervent soul and, on the other, some wondrous mirror of divine revelation [Col. 0176D] meet one another. This may be gathered from Abraham’s first departure, of which we have spoken somewhat above. For what does Scripture say of him? “The Lord appeared to him as he sat in the valley of Mamre, sitting at the entrance of his tent in the very heat of the day. And when he had lifted up his eyes, men appeared standing near him. When he saw them, he ran to meet them from the entrance of his tent” (Gen. XVIII).

If by the tent we understand the dwelling-place of the human mind, what is such a going forth except ecstasy of the human mind? For we are led outside ourselves in two ways. At one time we go outside ourselves but descend beneath ourselves; at another, we go outside ourselves but are raised above ourselves. In the former, we are enslaved to worldly things; in the latter, we are led back to things beyond the world.

[Col. 0177A] But just as there is a twofold departure, so there is surely a twofold return. From either departure we return, as it were, to the dwelling of our manner of life when, after worldly affairs—or, rather, after the spectacles of heavenly contemplations—we bring the eyes of our mind back to examination of our conduct and, scrutinizing our inmost selves, diligently reconsider what sort of persons we ourselves are. Of the first return, the statement rightly applies which is read in the Gospel concerning the prodigal son: “Coming to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here from hunger!’” (Luke XV). Of the second return we likewise rightly understand what we read elsewhere concerning the apostle Peter: “Peter, coming to himself, said, ‘Now I know truly that [Col. 0177B] the Lord has sent His angel,’” etc. (Acts XII).

Behold: each is said to have come to himself. But why, unless they seemed first to have gone out from themselves? One is led far from himself into a distant country; the other, under angelic guidance, is raised through alienation of mind above the ordinary state of human possibility. In the first departure one descends to the depths; in the second one is raised to the heights. In the first we are made distant from the Lord; in the second we draw near to the Lord.

What, then, is that departure through which one runs to meet the Lord, except ecstasy of the human mind, by which it is carried above itself and lifted into the mysteries of divine contemplation? If, therefore, we seek the cause of his departure, we find it readily. For the vision that appeared outwardly undoubtedly drew him toward outward things. Yet the cause of the divine appearance is secretly suggested where the Lord is said to have appeared to him as he sat at the entrance of his tent in the very heat of the day.

[Col. 0177C] You see certainly that the heat of the day was burning when the Lord appeared to him. What, I ask, is this heat of the day except the ardour of burning desire? That love which loves darkness, that love, I say, which hates the light, must not be called the heat of day. For we know that “one who does evil hates the light; but one who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God” (John III).

What else, therefore, is the heat of day except fervent love of the true, desire for the true and supreme good? Under this heat the patriarch was then burning—such heat, finally, as drove him away from his household and compelled him to sit at the entrance, in leisure, occupied only in attending and seeing, doubtless longing and hoping to receive the breeze of divine inspiration and to temper the heat of his desire by that breath.

[Col. 0177D] You perceive, I think, how the fervour under which he then burned drew him to the place from which he could behold those three persons whom he would not hesitate rightly to adore. Perhaps, had he then been attending to his household and remained within the interior of his tent, he would not have seen those persons worthy of adoration; and had he not seen them, perhaps at that time he would not have gone out. Thus two things came together to furnish the occasion for that departure: the excess of fervour and the novelty of the vision.

In a similar manner it often occurs in the human mind that, while it burns with an excessive fire of heavenly desire, [Col. 0178A] it deserves to see something by divine revelation through which it is aided toward those contemplative ecstasies.

## CHAPTER IX. That the Second Mode of Ecstasy Is Accustomed to Occur through the Greatness of Wonder

Thus far we have spoken of that ecstasy of mind which arises from the greatness of devotion. We must now speak of that which is accustomed to arise from the greatness of wonder. Who does not know that wonder arises when we perceive something beyond hope and above expectation? Thus novelty of vision and a thing scarcely credible are accustomed to produce wonder in the mind when something begins to be seen that can scarcely [Col. 0178B] be believed.

Consider, then, how fittingly the ecstasy of mind arising from wonder is described in the words: “Who is she who comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song VI). What is dawn except new light mingled with darkness? And whence comes wonder, I ask, except from an unexpected and incredible sight? Wonder, therefore, itself possesses sudden light mingled with the darkness of certain remnants of unbelief and uncertainty: so that, in a wondrous manner, the mind undoubtedly sees what it can scarcely bring itself to believe.

But the more we wonder at the novelty of a thing, the more carefully we attend to it; and the more attentively we perceive, the more fully we know. Attention therefore grows from wonder, and knowledge from attention. [Col. 0178C] Thus the mind rises like dawn, advancing gradually through wonder at the vision toward increases of knowledge. Dawn indeed rises gradually; by rising it spreads; by spreading it becomes bright. Yet, in a wondrous way, when it finally passes into day, it comes through the increments of its advance to its own cessation; and from the very source from which it receives its increase, there comes to it, and finally occurs, its complete disappearance.

So likewise human understanding, illumined by divine light, while it is held suspended in contemplation of intelligible things and extended in wonder at them, is led ever toward higher and more wondrous things, and thereby is enlarged ever more abundantly. By being farther removed from the lowest things, it is found purer in itself and more sublime toward things on high. But in such elevation, while the human mind continually grows toward higher things, and by long growth at last transcends the limits of human capacity, it finally comes wholly to fail from itself and, transformed into a certain supramundane disposition, goes altogether above itself.

[Col. 0178D] And just as the morning light ceases by increasing—not to be light, but to be morning light, so that dawn itself is no longer dawn—so human understanding sometimes receives from the greatness of its enlargement that it is no longer itself: not that it ceases to be understanding, but that it is no longer human, since by a wondrous and incomprehensible transformation it becomes more than human, while, beholding the glory of the Lord, it is transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by [Col. 0179A] the Spirit of the Lord (II Cor. III).

From these things, therefore, you perceive, I think, how properly the ecstasy of mind which arises from the greatness of wonder is designated by a mystical description in the words: “Who is she who comes forth like the rising dawn?” (Song VI).

## CHAPTER X. That the Second Mode of Ecstasy Sometimes Begins from Wonder Alone and Ends in the Most Fervent Desire of Devotion

It should certainly be noted that, just as the former mode of ecstasy, of which we spoke above, arises from devotion, so conversely this second mode, of which we now speak, does not so much begin from devotion as end in it. There, one rises from an excessive desire for truth to [Col. 0179B] contemplation of truth; here, through the revelation and contemplation of truth, the mind is inflamed toward devotion.

Perhaps Scripture mystically indicates this to us when it immediately adds the following words to those we have set down above. Having said, “Who is she who comes forth like the rising dawn?” it at once adds: “Beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun” (Song VI). Let no one expect or demand from me here a full exposition either of these words or of the other words we have set down, or shall set down, except insofar as the subject at hand requires for testimony to the truth.

Dawn and the moon have light but not heat; the sun excels in both. For what is brighter than the sun, what more fervent? [Col. 0179C] You see, therefore, that the ascent of mind signified here, whose final stages are compared to the sun, does not merely end in some ordinary devotion, but at some point ends in the highest devotion, even though it begins from brightness alone and illumination of truth.

For just as in the former mode, through the excessive fervour of its devotion, the mind often deserves to be raised to contemplation of the supreme truth, so in this mode it is gradually advanced, and at last inflamed toward the highest devotion, through a certain marvellous and astounding contemplation of truth. Let us therefore consider the greatness of brightness and heat in the orb of the sun, and from this gather the advance of ascent, and the consummation of that advance, in this elevation of mind—which begins, as it were, from the dawn and [Col. 0179D] eventually takes upon itself the likeness of the sun.

## CHAPTER XI. That the Second Mode of Ecstasy Sometimes Begins from Wonder Alone and Continues in the Same Character

Yet we do not say that in this second ecstasy of mind the course of human advancement always and everywhere has the same outcome of consummation. We see in outward things what we ought to judge concerning inward things. For if you place a vessel of water beneath a ray of the sun, you will immediately see the water itself cast back from itself upward the brightness of light, and indeed raise brightness to the heights without heat. Thus many receive the rays of divine revelation, [Col. 0180A] but not all alike advance from them to the same power of love.

For, in order that the author of all good things may commend within us the gifts of His grace, He produces different effects from the same thing in different times and persons. Consider, I pray, from the example proposed, whoever reads or hears these things, what that ray of divine revelation and eternal light accomplishes within us. Observe how, by the illumination of its infusion, it raises human understanding above itself; observe how the pattern of the example set before you presents through similarity of quality this ecstasy of the human mind of which we are now speaking.

What is water except human thought, which always flows downward unless restrained under the governance of great discipline? Water collected in a vessel is thought intent upon meditation and fixed by concentration. The gathering of water is meditation of the heart. A ray of the sun is poured into such water when divine revelation meets meditation. But when the water receives into itself the ray of heavenly light, it too, as has been said, emits the splendour of light upward; and in a wondrous manner it raises from itself toward that place a ray of light to which it can in no way ascend by itself.

[Col. 0180B] And though water and light differ so greatly, water nevertheless impresses something of its own likeness upon the ray of light which it emits from itself: so that trembling water makes it tremble, still water makes it still, purer water makes it purer, more diffused water makes it more diffused.

In accordance with this likeness, when revelation of that inaccessible and eternal [Col. 0180C] light irradiates the human heart, it raises human understanding above itself—indeed, above every human measure. And, by the infusion of divine light and the rebound of wonder, the ray of understanding springs from the depths to the heights where no acuity of natural ability, no effort of art, no human reasoning is sufficient to ascend. The more deeply the splendour of divine brightness penetrates the human mind, the higher, shaken by the greatness of its astonishment and raised in ecstasy, it rebounds into the sublimity of the divine mysteries.

[Col. 0180D] Yet this must be held altogether certain: the more fully and perfectly the mind has been able to compose itself to inward peace and tranquillity, the more firmly and tenaciously it will cling, in this elevation, to the supreme light through contemplation; and beyond doubt, the purer it is toward wholeness, the more expansive toward charity, and the clearer-sighted it is, the more capable it is found for contemplation of things beyond the world and beyond the heavens.

## CHAPTER XII. That in the Second Mode of Ecstasy Divine Revelation Sometimes Meets Our Meditation
It should indeed be noted that the splendor of divine revelation sometimes meets meditation already in progress, and sometimes anticipates human meditation itself: at one time it assists one who is seeking, at another it rouses one who is sluggish or awakens one who is asleep. Thus the queen of the south presses King Solomon with questions and, having proposed riddles, learns from him everything that she set before him (3 Kings 10). Thus an angel, visiting Peter in chains with light, shakes him from the sleep of his torpor (Acts 12).

For what does Scripture say of the queen of the south, who came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, except that Solomon taught her all the words which she had proposed? Who is this queen of the south, inhabitant and mistress of that hot region, kindled with a desire to see Solomon? Who, I say, is this queen but every holy soul, ruling firmly over the senses and appetites of the flesh and over the thoughts and affections of the mind, burning with love for the supreme King and true Solomon, and ardently desiring to behold him? Such a queen assails the king of highest wisdom with proposed riddles and repeated questions when any devout soul, trusting in divine help, presses eagerly on in its zeal to investigate the truth. It hears what it seeks when it often learns by divine revelation, amid the sighs of prayer, those things which it cannot attain by its own effort.

Let us see further what the divine discourse says of this same queen when it continues: “Now when the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon’s wisdom, and the house which he had built, and the food of his table, and the dwellings of his servants, and the order of his attendants, their garments also, and the burnt offerings which he offered in the house of the Lord, she had no spirit left in her” (3 Kings 10). “When the queen of Sheba had seen,” it says. Behold: she is now described as seeing, whereas before she was presented as proposing and seeking. Yet consider what she saw, and understand how much she understood. “When the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon’s wisdom,” etc. Behold how great and what kind of things a devout, studious soul is granted to know through divine revelation. Reflect how great, observe how marvelous, were the things she learned by divine sight: after seeing long and marveling much, she finally came, through the greatness of her astonishment, to the failing of her spirit.

Behold the order in which she advanced, and the end at which she finally arrived. First she seeks and hears; afterward she sees and understands; finally she is astonished and fails. She asks in order to learn; she contemplates in order to marvel; she is stupefied so as to pass out of her mind and transcend her mind. The first belongs to meditation, the second to contemplation, the third to ecstasy. Behold by what stages of advancement the human mind is raised. By meditation one indeed rises to contemplation, by contemplation to astonishment, and by astonishment to alienation of mind.

By this manifest example, I think, you now understand that through the greatness of astonishment a person falls into an ecstasy of mind. For what else was it for her to “have no spirit,” except to pass beyond her mind? Or whence did this happen to her, except from great astonishment? For how, I ask, was this queen without spirit unless her spirit had been alienated from itself? Yet here one recalls what another says of himself: “I, John, was in the Spirit” (Apoc. 1). Behold, John testifies that he was in the Spirit; behold, the queen of the south is said to have no spirit. What then? Was he in the Spirit, while she was without spirit? And who is sufficient for these things?

If John was in the Spirit, who will explain to me whether he was there according to the flesh or according to the spirit? But how could he be in the Spirit according to the flesh, since a body cannot exist at all except in a bodily place? If, therefore, he is believed to have been there according to the spirit, who can expound how spirit is said to be in spirit? And what shall we say of the queen of the south? Did her body perhaps remain lifeless when she began to have no spirit? Who would say this? Who but a madman would dare to assert it? The queen’s flesh, therefore, was not at that time without spirit, since it could not live at all without spirit. What then? Was spirit without spirit?

Let him who can explain, and explain as he can, in what manner spirit is in spirit, or spirit without spirit, if one thing is rightly believed concerning John and the other thought concerning the queen. Or perhaps to be spirit in spirit is to gather oneself wholly within oneself, and meanwhile to be entirely unaware of what is done about the flesh or even in the flesh? And to be spirit without spirit—is it to pour oneself wholly outside oneself and above oneself, meanwhile to be entirely unaware of what occurs beneath oneself or within oneself, and to enter wholly into that mystery of Divinity?

Is not spirit rightly said to be in spirit when it forgets all outward things, is equally unaware of all that is bodily done in the body, and attends, by memory or understanding, only to those things which are enacted in the spirit or about the spirit? Why should spirit not likewise rightly be said not to possess itself when it begins to fail from itself, to pass from its own state into a certain supermundane and truly more-than-human condition, and when, by a marvelous transformation, that spirit seems to fail from the human into the divine—so that it is no longer itself during that very time in which it begins to cleave more deeply to the Lord? “For he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6). And one who is such may sing: “My soul has failed in longing for thy salvation” (Ps. 118). Thus one is in spirit who ascends to the summit of the mind; and one, as it were, fails from spirit who transcends the summit of the mind. But let us leave these matters to be examined more fully by minds better instructed.

## CHAPTER XIII. That in the second mode of passing beyond oneself, divine revelation sometimes also anticipates our meditation.

[Col. 0182D]

Let us now consider how divine revelation is accustomed sometimes to anticipate even the endeavors of our meditation, and to raise the human mind—cast down below even the ordinary condition of human freedom by the sudden violence of temptations—not only to its customary state of firmness, but even beyond the limits of human possibility.

For the human mind, after many distinguished achievements in its exercises, is often assailed by the importunate onset of temptations and, violently shaken, is cast down from that lofty citadel of its security and tranquility, lest it vainly and miserably glory as though in its own strength amid uninterrupted successes in virtue. Thus blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, after innumerable heights of merits and miracles, is seized, bound, and imprisoned. Yet when the angel visits him, he is delivered no less marvelously than he had previously been cruelly tormented by the ministers of cruelty (Acts 12).

Do you wish to know what bonds these are which can sometimes grievously entangle minds lofty even in merits? Who does not know that the incitements of pleasures arise now from without, now from within: from without through delight, from within through suggestion; through delight in the flesh, through suggestion in the mind?
