For at one time the flesh is inflamed by a filthy stimulation; at another the mind is defiled by a foul thought. Therefore we seem to enter prison darkness when, entangled in these bonds of desire, we wish but cannot escape the gloom of our confusion.

But that mind merits the revelation of divine consolation which suffers these darknesses of its confusion not so much through the slothfulness of its own torpor as through the insolence of another’s malice. Such a holy soul is delivered at the coming of the divine embassy when, by the grace of divine inspiration and the light of revelation, it is relieved of the weight of its oppression.

An angel is indeed called a messenger. And without doubt an angel is a messenger: not merely any messenger, but a divine messenger, through whom we know the good pleasure of the divine will; a messenger through whom we are enlightened to know eternal things and inflamed to desire them. But does this messenger know heavenly things only? Does he not know earthly things as well? Yet how could one who knows greater things be ignorant of lesser? This is a good embassy, sufficient not only to teach all things but also to persuade concerning all things, insofar, however, as he who sends it wills.

Do you wish to hear what embassy the apostle John promises us when he says: “His anointing will teach you concerning all things” (1 John 2)? But what is this anointing except divine inspiration? This is the messenger for whom we had long been seeking; this is an embassy truly powerful, truly sufficient to lead the human mind into every truth and incline it to every good pleasure of the divine will.

What wonder, then, if such a messenger frees an oppressed soul from the bonds of its desire and unfolds it from the darknesses of its ignorance, since he immediately infuses, whenever and as much as he pleases, both knowledge and love of heavenly and eternal things? He who said, “He sent from heaven and delivered me” (Ps. 46), had experienced such messengers in his own deliverance. But perhaps you still wish to know the nature of that embassy by which he escaped from the captivity of his soul: “God sent,” he says, “his mercy and his truth, and delivered my soul” (ibid.).

The angel coming with light is the operation of divine compassion, infusing truth. Mercy brings truth; anointing teaches. And what is it for God to send mercy and truth and to deliver a person from captivity, except by the working of his mercy to inspire truth, and by the inspiration of truth to establish one firmly in the strength of virtue? And who has ever completely escaped the perils of the soul if he has not merited to experience the benefits of this embassy?

Blessed Peter, who not only merited to be delivered by an angel, but, once delivered, also to follow the angel. I think that not all who are delivered by an angel also follow angelic footsteps. I read that apostles shut up in prison were led out by an angel, but did not follow him. Peter is commanded by the angel himself, his deliverer, to follow him. What do we say this means? How great do we suppose it is to trace angelic footsteps, to go after those heavenly, winged creatures?

Consider, if you can, what was the advance or ascent of the angel who went before and of the one who followed, whose passage neither prison guard nor iron gate could hold back or delay. What in this is not new? What is not wonderful? It is truly angelic, truly more than human, to leave the dark and dreadful realm of human passibility and pass through the steep and narrow passage of common impossibility.

Consider the exit which the first human being possessed before sinning, or which humanity would still possess had it not sinned at all. By that exit, whenever necessary, it could readily pass from worldly to supermundane things, from visible to invisible, from transient to eternal; for it would have ready access each day, through contemplation, to the citizens of heaven, could freely enter upon those divine secrets, and could worthily enter into that inward joy of its Lord. Consider next how, after sin, divine severity shut and barred this previously open passage with the doors of dire necessity and the bolts of impossibility. Consider this, I say, and perhaps by considering it you will discover what you ought to think or dare to affirm about that iron gate.

But if you are unequal to these matters, seek an answer—not indeed from us, but rather from those to whom perhaps this iron gate is familiarly known through frequent passage, and to whom, perhaps in likeness of Peter, it has often opened of itself while the angel goes before and supplies guidance. Yet, I think, I may say without presumption that Peter was far above the human level; that he departed far from himself and above himself; and that he learned all these things through experience. Otherwise, there would have been no point from which he could afterward return to himself, nor could it rightly have been written of him: “And Peter, returning to himself, said: Now I know truly,” etc. (Acts 12).

Many things might have been said concerning the present chapter, if they had needed to be said here. But it is enough for us to have sufficiently proved from his testimony our proposition: that divine revelation is sometimes accustomed to anticipate the endeavors of our meditation, awaken the sluggish mind, and raise, sometimes even above itself, the mind cast down beneath itself.

## CHAPTER XIV. That the third mode of passing beyond oneself is usually produced by the greatness of joy.

It remains, thirdly, to show how the human mind is accustomed to fall into ecstasy and exceed itself through the greatness of delight and exultation. This mode of passing beyond oneself seems to me quite fittingly expressed in the words from the Song of Songs which we placed third: “Who is this,” says Scripture, “who comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8).

If the desert is rightly understood as the human heart, what is this ascent from the desert but the passing beyond of the human mind? The human mind comes up, as it were, from the desert when it passes above itself in alienation of mind; when, leaving itself below and passing onward even to heaven, it wholly immerses itself, through contemplation and devotion, in divine things alone.

But the cause of this ascent is immediately added when she who ascends is described as overflowing with delights. What is it to overflow with delights except to abound in the fullness of spiritual joys? What, I say, is this abundance of delights except an abundance of true sweetness and a joy given from heaven and poured in lavishly? False riches can never provide this abundance of delights, any more than they can provide true joy. Otherwise they would not be false if they truly supplied real delights—indeed, an abundance of them.

Can those truly be said even to possess delights, much less to overflow with them, who, in blessed Job’s words, “count it a delight to be under thorns” (Job 30)? The impious can indeed possess these outward and false riches, but they cannot possess joy at all—unless we make a liar of him whom we hear giving true testimony in the prophet: “There is no joy for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isa. 48). Therefore, whenever you lack inward and true delights, even though you abound in outward riches, you may truly sing with the Prophet: “For I am needy and poor” (Ps. 85).

Was not he who said these words a powerful king, rich and a prince of peoples? What kind of riches, then, will those be, or what delights can they confer, amid their abundance one must still be poor and seek true joy elsewhere? “But I am a beggar and poor; the Lord is mindful of me” (Ps. 39).

Therefore you have no ground to hope for or obtain this abundance of delights and plentitude of true joys except from that intimate joy of the mind and sweetness divinely infused: “Who is this,” he says, “who comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights?” (Song 8). He does not say “having delights,” but “overflowing with delights,” because not every experience of such delights, but their abundance, produces and accomplishes this kind of ascent from the desert.

It is certain, however much progress we make, that we cannot possess these delights uninterruptedly in this life alone. Therefore, when the soul lacks such abundance, it cannot rise to the ascent of which we are now speaking, since in its ascent it must overflow with delights. But I think that it is one thing to ascend while overflowing, and another to overflow while ascending, just as it is one thing for abundance to be the cause of overflowing.

The abundance of delights is the cause of ascent when, from that infusion of divine sweetness which it feels in its inmost being, the holy soul cannot contain itself for joy and exultation—so much so that the greatness of its exultation and delight pours it outside itself and snatches it above itself. Thus vehement and immeasurable joy, when it grows beyond the human measure, raises a person above the human and suspends one raised above human things in the heights.

We can perceive an image of this even daily among animals. In their play they are accustomed to make certain leaps and suspend their bodies, however slightly, in the air. So too fish often, while playing in the waters, leap above the waters and exceed the boundaries of their native dwelling, suspending themselves briefly in the void. So, without doubt, the holy soul, when shaken from itself by some inward applause of its own rejoicing, when compelled by alienation of mind to go above itself, when wholly suspended in heavenly things and wholly immersed in angelic spectacles, seems to have passed beyond the limits of its native capacity.

Hence the saying through the Prophet: “The mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep” (Ps. 113). Who does not see that it is beyond—or rather contrary to—nature for mountains or hills, after the likeness of leaping rams or lambs, to make certain bounds upward, rebound from the earth, and balance themselves in the void? Is not earth, as it were, suspended above earth when a human being is drawn above the human, he to whom the Lord’s voice says reproachfully: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3)?

However greatly one may increase in virtue, though one rises high to the likeness of hills, or even, to the greatest degree, of mountains, one is nevertheless earth and may rightly be called earth so long as one inhabits houses of clay and has an earthly foundation. Hence the saying of the Wise Man: “Why are earth and ashes proud?” (Ecclus. 10).

If, therefore, we are content with a simple exposition, it may perhaps suffice to say that for mountains and hills to rejoice after the likeness of rams and lambs means that, in the highest and holiest persons, human nature rises beyond human nature and, through the excessive abundance of delight and exultation, passes above itself in alienation of mind. Behold, I think, we have now taught by an open example that the human mind’s passing beyond itself sometimes occurs because of the greatness of exultation.

But if this explanation of the accompanying likeness of sheep perhaps does not suffice someone, and he insists more curiously on the meaning of each detail, let him recall the ninety-nine sheep which the supreme Shepherd leaves in the heights when he seeks on earth the one which was lost. Let him therefore consider, if he can, how great a thing it is, or of what kind, for the mountains of this our earth to leap high in the force of their joy after the likeness of those sheep, and for this our nature to shape the applause of its exultation after angelic dances.

But if by the rams we understand those highest orders of angels, and by the lambs also the lower orders, we likewise recognize that such rams—that is, the highest orders of angels—go above themselves in those marvelous plays of their joy and excesses of contemplation, when they suspend themselves in the beings above them. They behold nothing other than the creative substance of all things above themselves, nor do they find any being other than himself in whom they can contemplate or marvel at his power or wisdom.

But the lesser orders of angels, who seem to be signified by the lambs, when they are carried above themselves, find in this elevation a kind of mirror still: namely, those spirits which they see, by a marvelous prerogative of dignity, to excel them. In this mirror they are able to behold the supreme Majesty marvelously and still to see, as it were, through a mirror.

Therefore, if contemplative persons are rightly understood by mountains, and speculative persons by hills, see how rightly mountains are said to rejoice like rams and hills like lambs. Although contemplation and speculation are customarily used interchangeably, and thereby often obscure and entangle the precise force of Scriptural expressions, we speak more aptly and distinctly of speculation when we see through a mirror, but of contemplation when we see truth itself in its purity, without any covering or veil of shadows.

Thus the hills rejoice like lambs when those immense rejoicings of inward solemnity lift them so far above themselves that they can at least see the mysteries of heavenly secrets “through a mirror, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13). But the mountains rejoice like rams when the greater persons, in their excesses of joy, see in pure and simple truth what the lesser, as has been said, can scarcely see through a mirror and in an enigma.

## CHAPTER XV. That every passing beyond of the mind exceeds the measure of human effort or merit.

Let no one presume upon such exultation or elevation of heart as arising from personal strength, or attribute it to personal merits. It is certain that this belongs not to human merit but to the divine gift. Hence that soul, whoever she is, who is described as having ascended from the desert, is said to lean upon her beloved. What is it for her to lean upon her beloved except to be advanced by his power and not by her own strength? What, I say, is it for her to rest upon her beloved except to presume nothing whatever, in this respect, upon her own power?

As it seems to me, one rightly presumes nothing from personal endeavor or personal prudence, especially at the point where one ascends from the desert; indeed, not even in the desert itself while travelling through it. Her beloved knows this, and therefore leads her in a cloud by day and in the illumination of fire throughout the night. For how could she endure the burden and heat of day except in the shadow of him whom her soul loves? Or what place would be safe for her from night terrors, especially in a place of horror and vast solitude, unless he himself sent forth his light and truth?

Finally, she would have no means of moderating the heat of desire unless the power of the Most High overshadowed her. Likewise, she would lack the means to illuminate the darknesses of her ignorance unless in his light she saw light. Hence she says to him: “For you light my lamp, O Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. 17).

The beloved, therefore, receives from the gift of her beloved and the benefit of her bridegroom two remedies against two principal evils: a cloud of refreshment against the desire of the flesh, and the light of revelation against ignorance of mind. How often someone recognizes the way of truth and yet does not follow it, being drawn and enticed away by personal desire. Such a person has, for the time being, the day of knowledge, but does not have the cloud of refreshing grace. And how many often have zeal, yet not zeal according to knowledge; perhaps they feel no heats of desire for the time being, but rest and recover their breath as under the coolness of night. Such people seem indeed to have night, but not the fire of enlightening grace.

It is good, therefore, to hope in the Lord and not to presume upon oneself. How blessed were those for whom he was “a covering by day and a light of stars at night,” spreading out a cloud for their protection and fire to give them light through the night. “For it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” The beloved knows this, and therefore leans upon her beloved. Hence it is written of her in veiled words: “Who is this who comes up from the desert, overflowing with delights and leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8).

## CHAPTER XVI. That in the third mode of passing beyond oneself everything depends especially upon divine benefit.

Although this beloved of her bridegroom always and everywhere needs the help of her beloved, so that without him she can do nothing, nowhere does she lean more intensely—or need more intensely to lean—upon the soul who works with her than in the place where she ascends from the desert, and especially at the time when she overflows with delights.

For if the desert is rightly understood as the human heart, what is it to ascend from the desert except to go above oneself? What, then, can a human being accomplish there, where a human rises above the human? Where human nature transcends the limits of human possibility? Yet at no time does the holy soul lean more intensely upon her beloved than when she seems to overflow with spiritual delights.

Let us imagine a young girl, tender and delicate, reared amid great abundance of delights, and now soaked with much wine because she has been brought into the wine-cellar and made to drink from the torrent of pleasure. Let us imagine that through excessive delicacy she can scarcely walk, and through excessive drunkenness cannot in any way discern the path which she ought to follow. Is not she who is described as overflowing with delights and leaning upon her beloved presented to your consideration under such a figure?

And what wonder if abundance of delights makes her delicate? Do you wish to hear how delicate it customarily makes one? Almost beyond what can be believed: so much so, indeed, that no outward pleasure can have any savor for her, nor can any glory of this world bring her any consolation. Thus she may truly dare to profess and say: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 67), because she truly feels and firmly concludes that “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isa. 40).

Finally, her soul grows weary of life whenever she is not granted her customary delights as she wishes. Life itself, therefore, turns to weariness—indeed, to hatred—for her whenever the joys of her inward solemnity are withdrawn from her for a while. Consider, then, what it is for one accustomed to such delights to have nothing of what delights her in her own power; to be unable to receive any consolation at all without them; and to be unable to acquire them by any effort or prudence of her own. Everything that avails for her consolation, everything that avails for her delight, depends upon another’s decision and another’s gift.

She rightly leans, therefore, upon his strength, from whose generosity all that she hopes for, desires, and loves is rightly expected. Oh, how often in this condition the prophet’s threat is spoken to her and becomes the Lord’s word for her: “Command upon command, command upon command; expect, expect again; expect, expect again; a little here, a little there” (Isa. 28). She is compelled, therefore, to wait and wait again, while what she desires is often, long, and greatly delayed; while she can neither possess her delights as she wishes nor moderate her mind from desires of this kind. From these things, I think, it is evident how far beyond humanity, and beyond the human measure, is everything done or felt in this ecstasy of mind.

## CHAPTER XVII. How one who has advanced to this third degree of such grace may be assisted in recovering it.

Nevertheless, one who has advanced to this grace, when already feeling it withdrawn beyond what is customary, has something that ought to be done, by which one may be greatly assisted in every way to restore it and, as far as lies within one’s power, make one’s mind fit for this undertaking.

The mind of such a person ought, therefore, to restore exultation within itself through its own meditations of heart; to recall before the eyes of memory the gifts of divine benefits lavished upon it; from such recollection to spur itself to profound and devout thanksgiving; and finally, from an inward affection, to give free play to that inward instrument of spiritual harmony in divine praises.

When, therefore, by studies of this kind the inward affection of the heart is dissolved in full devotion into the magnificence of divine confession, what else is opened but a kind of vent, so to speak, through which an outflow of heavenly sweetness and an abundance of divine pleasantness may be poured into that vessel of our heart?

Thus the prophet Elisha, when asked for the word of the Lord and finding that at that time he did not have the spirit of prophecy, had a minstrel brought to him. When the minstrel was present and playing, he immediately received the prophetic spirit and promptly opened his mouth in prophetic utterance (4 Kings 3).

Perhaps someone, following the historical narrative, may ask what it means that the prophet of the Lord sought a minstrel, or that he received the prophetic spirit while the minstrel played. But we know generally that sweet harmony is accustomed to cheer the heart and recall its joys to memory. And without doubt, the more strongly one’s own love affects one’s mind, the more deeply heard harmony touches its affection; and the more deeply it is touched in affection, the more effectively it is renewed toward its desires.

What else, therefore, ought we to think concerning the prophetic man except that outward harmony recalled to him that inward and spiritual harmony, and that the melody he heard recalled and raised the hearer’s mind to its customary joys? Why should we not judge of spiritual and true delight what daily experience proves regarding bodily and vain delight? For who does not know how memory alone of carnal pleasure sweeps a carnal mind into delight? Why should spiritual delight not possess the same—indeed, greater—power in the highest persons?

Thus, for the holy prophet, the melody he heard was nothing but a kind of ladder which raised him to customary joys; and what is often a cause of ruin to carnal persons became for him an occasion of ascent. Let one who can consider how deeply and inwardly the memory of that superheavenly sweetness, awakened by the voice of the minstrel, often touched him—touching him so as to snatch him above himself and restore prophetic spirit or perception in the prophet’s mind.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What is especially accustomed to avail for the renewal of such grace.

But you too, whatever soul you are, who are accustomed to abound in spiritual delights of this kind, to ascend often from the desert leaning upon your Beloved, to be lifted into certain theoretic ecstasies by a sudden and unexpected—indeed, unimaginable—dance of joys, and to be divinely exalted as though by certain prophetic understandings or revelations [Col. 0190C], learn from the prophetic example what you ought to do, so that in an hour of necessity you may have, as it were, at hand the means of restoring your mind to its accustomed delights. Perhaps it will not be useless, when you are under a like necessity, to bring in a psalmist also and listen to one singing psalms.

But, to state briefly what we think on this matter, what else do we call this psalmist than the heart’s exultation in God? He who said, “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. XXXI), wished us to have such a psalmist present. What is it to bring in such a psalmist, except to restore exultation by the provident meditation of the heart and, from the remembrance of divine benefits or promises, to awaken the heart’s devotion?

Without doubt, we make this psalmist sing at that time when, in a great transport of the heart, we cry aloud in jubilation over divine praises, and, rising to give thanks, resound from our inmost depths in divine praises with a great cry of the heart [Col. 0190D]. When we do these things, what else do we do but make ready the way by which we may receive the Lord as He comes and visits us? “The sacrifice of praise,” He says, “shall glorify me; and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. XLIX). Thus, by singing psalms and praising, a way is prepared for the Lord, by which He may deign to come to us and reveal Himself through certain wonderful disclosures of His mysteries. Hence it is said elsewhere: “Sing to God; sing a psalm to his name; make a way for him who ascends above the setting” (Ps. LXVII).

Perhaps you ask what it is to ascend above the setting. Usage customarily calls that region of the world in which the sun sets and daylight fails “the setting.” What, then, do we understand more fittingly by the setting than the failure of human understanding? For there the sun of understanding, as it were, encounters its setting, hides the rays of its knowledge, changes the light of day, as it were, into the dark obscurity of earth’s night, and removes all things from human sight, when the human spirit falls into alienation of mind and, failing from ordinary awareness and carried outside itself, utterly does not know what is occurring within it or around it [Col. 0191A].

What is it for the Lord to ascend in the eyes of our contemplation, except by the revelation of His greatness to multiply the increases of our knowledge? For the more sublime the things He reveals to us from the height of His greatness, the more He raises Himself to higher things in the gaze of our understanding. He truly ascends above the setting when He carries a person above himself; when He removes from him the remembrance of all that he knows according to ordinary awareness; and when, through ecstasy of mind, He shows him something of the loftiness of His majesty which, according to the ordinary condition of this life and the measure of human capacity, he could never comprehend in any way.

Let us therefore strive with great eagerness of mind to rejoice in the Lord; let us labor to sing psalms before Him with inward devotion, so that there may be persons above whose setting He may deign to ascend. In doing this, we bring in such a psalmist as is required, and listen to the singer in the fitting way. At the voice of such a psalmist the spiritual mind is touched to its marrow; as the Spirit rushes upon it, it is spiritually affected; and, while intellectual perception is opened by divine inspiration, prophetic grace is in some manner restored within it [Col. 0191C].

At such psalmody and spiritual harmony, the contemplative soul accustomed to spiritual contemplations begins to dance [Col. 0192A], to leap in a manner peculiar to itself through the excess of joy, to make certain spiritual leaps appropriate to its nature, to suspend itself from the earth and all earthly things, and, in total alienation of mind, to pass over into contemplation of heavenly things. This, then, as we have said, is what avails for the renewal of the mind; this is what is especially wont to avail for the restoration of lost grace.

## CHAPTER XIX. By what stages the ecstasy of the human mind increases

It has been said for what causes alienation of mind is wont to occur; now it seems necessary to add by what stages it also ascends. It rises sometimes above bodily sense, sometimes also above imagination, and sometimes above reason. Who would dare deny either the state above bodily sense or that above imagination, when apostolic authority proves even that which is above reason? “I know,” he says, “a man—whether in the body or outside the body, God knows—caught up in such a manner as far as the third heaven” (II Cor. XII) [Col. 0192B]. Behold: by alienation of mind he had gone beyond human reason, since he was utterly unable fully to discern what was taking place around him.

But it is better to leave a fuller explanation of this passage to minds more learned than ours than rashly to presume something beyond our powers concerning so great a subject. In this matter we are better instructed by the skill of those whom not so much another’s teaching as their own experience has advanced to the fullness of this knowledge. To the sum of our subject, therefore, which we sketched with concise brevity in the first book, we have added this fuller treatment in the following work, where, as we stated above, we have spoken as idle persons to idle persons.

## SOME ALLEGORIES OF THE TABERNACLE OF THE COVENANT, with a very brief recapitulation of the contents of the aforesaid work on the grace of contemplation

[Col. 0191]

By the tabernacle of the covenant understand the state of perfection. Where there is perfection of mind, there also is God’s dwelling. The nearer one approaches perfection, the more closely the mind is joined in covenant with God. The tabernacle itself ought to have a surrounding court. By the court understand the discipline of the body [Col. 0191C–D]; by the tabernacle, the discipline of the mind. Where outward discipline is lacking, inward discipline certainly cannot be maintained. Yet discipline of the body is certainly useless without discipline of the mind.

The court lies under the open sky, and bodily discipline is evident to all. The things that were in the tabernacle were not outwardly visible. “No one knows what belongs to the inner person except the human spirit that is in him.” The disposition of the inner person is divided into the rational and the intellectual. The rational disposition is understood through the outer tabernacle; the intellectual disposition through the inner tabernacle. By rational perception we mean that by which we discern our own affairs; here by intellectual perception we mean that by which we are raised to the contemplation of divine things [Col. 0192C].

A person goes out of the tabernacle into the court through the exercise of works. He enters the first tabernacle when he returns to himself. He enters the second when he transcends himself. In transcending himself, indeed, he is raised into God [Col. 0192D]. In the first, a person remains through consideration of himself; in the second, through contemplation of God. Thus much concerning the court, the first tabernacle, and the second.

The aforesaid three had five sanctuaries. The court had only one, as did the second tabernacle. The first tabernacle had the remaining three. In the court of the tabernacle was the altar of burnt offering. In the first tabernacle were the lampstand, table, and altar of incense. In the inner tabernacle was the ark of the testimony. The outer altar signifies affliction of the body; the inner altar, contrition of the mind. The lampstand signifies the grace of discernment; the table, the teaching of sacred reading. By the ark of the covenant understand the grace of contemplation.

On the outer altar the flesh of animals was burned, and through affliction of the body carnal desires are brought to nothing [Col. 0193A]. On the inner altar the smoke of spices was burned for the Lord, and through contrition of heart the ardor of heavenly desires is kindled. A lampstand is a bearer of light, and discernment is the lamp of the inner person. Food is set upon a table in order that the hungry may be refreshed; sacred reading, indeed, is certainly the refreshment of souls. An ark is a repository of gold and silver, and the grace of contemplation grasps the treasure of heavenly wisdom.

Thus good action belongs to the outer altar; diligent meditation to the lampstand; sacred reading to the table; devout prayer to the inner altar; contemplation of divine works to the ark. These are the five exercises in which our justification is carried out and completed. The ark is rightly called the sanctuary, in which the completion of our justification is figured. You have, then, the fivefold occupation in which all religion is practiced.

The exercise of good work belongs to the discipline of the outward person. It is plain that the others belong to the discipline of the inward person. The altar of burnt offering represents bodily exercise. It therefore rightly stands in the court and is visible in the open. The other things are in the tabernacle and lie hidden in secret. By the ark of the covenant is understood the grace of contemplation, which the Lord grants to those who love Him as a kind of pledge of love.

Contemplation is the free perspicacity of the mind, held in wonder before the spectacles of wisdom. There are six kinds of contemplation, each distinguished by its own particular property [Col. 0193B–C]. Two concern visible creatures, two invisible creatures, and the final two divine things. Those who are granted progress in only two seem to have received wings like eagles. Of those who attain four, you may suppose it said, “four wings to the one, and four wings to the other.” Those who have progressed to every kind of contemplation have received, as it were, six wings. Therefore you may suppose it said of them: “six wings to the one, and six wings to the other.”

The first four concern created visible or invisible things; the remaining two concern divine things. The first four are represented in the ark; the remaining two in the angelic form. Observe how fittingly the first are represented in a human construction, the final two in an angelic figure.

The first kind of contemplation seems to concern bringing visible things before consideration and wonder. The second kind brings hidden causes of things to light and holds the mind suspended in wonder at them. In the former, we marvel with exultation at the multitude, greatness, and usefulness of visible things; in the latter, we investigate with wonder the rationale of visible things. The first is indicated by the construction of the wood; the second by the gilding of the wood. For what is assigning a rationale in visible things except a kind of gilding of wood? Consider how great is the difference between wood and gold—that is, between things subject to reason. We contemplate the appearance of visible things by imagining; we investigate the causes of visible things by reasoning. The ark is to be made of *setim* wood, which is very resistant to decay; a true proposition concerning bodily things belongs to incorruptible wood [Col. 0193D–0194A].

The first kind of contemplation is distinguished by three stages: the first concerns things, the second works, and the third morals. Consideration of things belongs to the ark’s length; consideration of works, to its breadth; consideration of morals, to its height. By nature length precedes breadth, while height naturally follows them both. Thus things themselves naturally precede any of their operations. If things and their operations did not exist, morals would have no place. Therefore the first consideration plainly belongs to the ark’s length, the second to its breadth [Col. 0194A–B], and the third to its height.

The consideration concerning the contemplation of things, said to belong to the ark’s length, is divided threefold. It consists in considering the matter, form, and nature of things. In considering matter and form, our knowledge extends to a full cubit and is accustomed to do so. But in considering nature, it cannot at all extend to a full cubit. There our knowledge has, as it were, a whole cubit, where it is fully certain. We readily apprehend the matter and form of things, and in both we possess the cubit of certainty. But knowledge of nature is open to no one except in part. Therefore it can have only half a cubit in this respect. It is clear why the length of our ark is rightly said to measure two and a half cubits [Col. 0194C].

The consideration of operations, which we have said belongs to the ark’s breadth, is divided in two. There is one operation of art and another operation of nature. The work seen in paintings, carvings, writings, and similar things belongs to art; the operations of nature are the growth of herbs and trees and the production of flowers, leaves, and fruits. In the operation of art, human knowledge can and usually does possess a full cubit of comprehension; otherwise, how could it discover what it was unable to comprehend? Thus the manifest effect of hidden causes is evident, but we are in no way sufficient fully to comprehend the hidden causes of effects. It is therefore clear why the ark’s breadth is said to measure one and a half cubits [Col. 0194C–D].

The consideration of morals, which we have said concerns the ark’s height, is likewise divided in two. One concerns human institutions; the other divine institutions. Certainly, where human institution serves divine institution, both the mind and the structure of our ark rise upward from each. Human institutions, which a person was able to discover, he can certainly also comprehend. But in divine mysteries, one thing is the outward form apparent outside, another the inward power concealed within. In divine institutions, therefore, we do not rise to a full cubit of knowledge in all respects. The height of our ark therefore consists of one and a half cubits.

We ought to gild our ark and, insofar as it is granted, apply ourselves to the rationale of imaginable things [Col. 0195A]. We must gild it not only outwardly but inwardly also.

It is one thing to perceive the physical causes of things, and another to weigh the rationale of justice in their ordering. The former belongs to the outward gilding; the latter, to the inward gilding. Our gilding must be of the purest gold. Let there be nothing false or trivial in the assertion of your judgment, and you have the purest gold.

Once the gilding has been done, the crown of the ark must be made. By the crown, as we have said, the third kind of contemplation is understood, as the fourth is also understood through the mercy-seat. The former concerns invisible goods, the latter invisible substances. Therefore it belongs to the crown of the ark to ask what the crown of righteousness is, and what those goods are that have been laid up for the saints [Col. 0195A–B].

It should be noted that the ark’s crown was fixed to the wood itself. Thus one rises from the likeness of visible things to the contemplation of invisible things. In the fourth kind of contemplation one inquires into the highest creatures. Yet in all creation there is nothing more worthy than invisible and rational substance. This kind of contemplation is rightly understood through the mercy-seat, which was placed upon the ark.

But before we pursue more fully what is said concerning the mercy-seat, it seems fitting here to insert what must be said concerning the rings. The ark of our contemplation ought to have four golden rings, two on either side [Col. 0195B–C]. By the ark, as we have said, we understand the grace of contemplation. We can bring into contemplation, whenever we wish, absolutely everything that we know can in any way occur. Of the things that happen, some happen well and others badly: those by God’s action, these by God’s permission. Things done by God’s action belong to one side of the ark; likewise, things done by God’s permission belong to the other.

Thus much concerning the sides of the ark; now let us consider the golden rings. Among all metals, nothing is brighter or more precious than gold; and the wisdom of God shines above all things. God’s wisdom, indeed, is certainly simple and one. Yet it is distinguished by different names, so that it may be more easily grasped by us. At one time it is called foreknowledge, at another knowledge; at one time predestination, at another disposition. These, unless I am mistaken, are the rings which ought to be placed on the sides of the ark [Col. 0195C–D].

A circle turns back into itself; hence neither beginning nor end is found in it. In every ordering of eternal wisdom, the beginning agrees with the end. Therefore in this fourfold distinction of wisdom we may quite suitably understand the aforesaid golden rings. In these rings the ark of our knowledge is directed toward truth and advanced to further and higher things.

Let two of these rings be arranged on one side and the others on the other. Each has, as it were, its seat and adheres more closely where it appears more wonderful or more delightful. It has been said that things done by God’s permission belong to one side. The rings of knowledge and foreknowledge adhere more closely to that side, where they certainly appear more wonderful. It is not so wonderful that He foresaw from eternity what He Himself would at some time do. But what kind of thing is it that from eternity He foresaw what He left to another’s will? That at every hour He beholds what is done in the hidden recesses of hearts? [Col. 0196A]

It has already been said that things done by God’s action belong to the other side. The rings of predestination and disposition occupy this side, where they certainly appear more delightful. What tastes sweeter to a good heart than that every divine disposition serves the salvation of the predestined? It still remains to inquire which ring ought to be placed at which corner.

It has been said that things done by God’s permission belong to one side of the ark; likewise, things done by God’s action belong to the other. Things of equity belong to the latter; things of iniquity to the former. Both these and those vary through prosperity and adversity. Where iniquity and adversity meet, they make, as it were, a corner. In this corner the reprobate are scourged by God, yet are not corrected. But why, I ask, does He apply the blows of fatherhood to them if He foresees them to be incorrigible? Therefore the ring of foreknowledge presides at this corner, where it appears more wonderful.

Where iniquity and prosperity coincide, they form another corner [Col. 0196B]. In this corner the reprobate receive God’s gifts and are always ungrateful. Yet this certainly cannot escape God’s knowledge; nevertheless, He does not cease to summon them by prosperity to the good of gratitude. The ring of knowledge adheres more closely to this corner, where it displays itself as so wonderful.

Understand a third corner in the circumstance of equity and prosperity. Here those to be saved prosper in transient things, in order that they may be kindled toward the desire for eternal things [Col. 0196C]. What, I ask, is more gracious or more delightful than this contemplation? What kind of thing is it that He even cherishes and advances with temporal goods those whom He has predestined for eternal things? Therefore the ring of predestination has its seat here, where it appears more delightful than the rest.

The ring of divine disposition occupies the fourth corner, where there is a meeting of equity and adversity. Here good people do good things and are pressed by adversities. Yet, by God’s disposition, this is accomplished in them: they are more keenly inflamed toward the love of God. And what kind of thing is it, I ask, that one is inflamed more keenly toward His love by that through which one seemed destined to be extinguished? The ring of divine disposition therefore rightly has its seat where it appears more magnificent.

[Col. 0196D] The third kind of contemplation is to ascend through visible things to the contemplation of invisible things. This is indeed the task of attending to the rings of divine wisdom if we do not wish to err. If the ark of understanding is suspended by these rings, it is borne about in every direction without deviating into error.

The said rings should have inserted poles, which may not be removed from them. In the rings of knowledge and foreknowledge let there be abundance of wonder; in the two remaining rings let there be greatness of exultation. In divine knowledge and foreknowledge you will always find many things worthy of wonder; in predestination and God’s dispensation a righteous heart always finds what is worthy of great exultation. Let your wonder always be in the former, your exultation in the latter. Nowhere else will you find anything more worthy of wonder; nowhere else anything in which you may rightly delight more.

Let there be nothing trivial or false in either. Let each pole be gilded, that they may shine everywhere with the brilliance of truth. By these poles the ark of understanding is at one time carried forward, at another raised to higher things [Col. 0197A]. For the more familiarly the human heart delights in wonder at God’s wisdom, the more it is enlarged to receive more and greater things.

By the mercy-seat, as we have said, is understood the fourth kind of contemplation. This kind first employs pure understanding and concerns the highest intelligible creatures. The mercy-seat is made of the purest gold and placed at the summit. In these things we note the purity of understanding and the dignity of eminence. For here the instrument of reason must be used without the office of imagination. The mercy-seat is placed at the summit, and the dignity of rational creature is preferred before all others [Col. 0197A–B].

It should be observed that this work is called the mercy-seat because, through much knowledge and consideration of itself, the Lord is rendered propitious to the rational creature. Let us now see what is said about its length and breadth; no less worthy of consideration is why nothing is said of its height. We know that length naturally precedes breadth, and likewise that both precede height. Therefore, by length we understand what concerns the beginning of the rational creature; by breadth, what concerns its advancement; and by height, what concerns its completion.

The goods of its creation concern its beginning; the goods of justification, its advancement; the goods of glorification, its completion [Col. 0197B–C]. Let the contemplative mind carefully exercise itself in these matters, that its mercy-seat may receive a fitting measure.

The rational creature received three highly wonderful things from creation: subtlety of being, discernment of good and evil, and freedom of choice. What freedom of choice is is well known to a human being. We read this daily in our own hearts, and in both respects possess the cubit of certainty. But who, I ask, can see the substance of the soul itself, and by what sense? I do not see yours, nor do you see mine. Yet neither of us can here see even his own soul as it is. In this respect, while we live, we do not extend our knowledge to a full cubit. The length of the mercy-seat is therefore rightly said to be two and a half cubits [Col. 0197D].

We have already said that the justification of the rational creature belongs to the mercy-seat’s breadth. Our justification is completed through divine inspiration and personal deliberation. Every person knows by experience what deliberation is. But who, I ask, can comprehend how divine inspiration occurs in us? “For the Spirit breathes where He wills, and you do not know whence He comes or where He goes.” Thus in one case we have a cubit of comprehension; in the other we cannot have it. See, then, how rightly the breadth of the mercy-seat is said to measure one and a half cubits.

Thus much concerning the length and breadth of the mercy-seat. What concerns our glorification belongs to its height. But who can comprehend what our glorification consists in, concerning which it is said: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (I Cor. II)? [Col. 0198A] From this it is readily understood why no measure is prescribed for the height of the mercy-seat.

The final two kinds of contemplation, as was said, concern divine things. One concerns matters above reason but not contrary to reason. Above reason are those which exceed the measure of its capacity, yet agree with reason, although reason cannot comprehend them. The matters with which the final kind is concerned seem wholly contrary to reason, and are such that reason would never assent to them unless faith directed it to this very point.

These final kinds of contemplation are expressed by the angelic form. Certainly, we must put on an angelic form if we wish to fly to the contemplation of eternal and divine things [Col. 0198A–B]. This angelic form is commanded to be of beaten gold. Thus, in order that it may be golden, the contemplator’s mind must be cleansed of every phantasy. A malleable thing is extended by being beaten, and our cherubim are commanded to be malleable. Hence we clearly conclude that we advance toward such grace better by compunction than by investigation.

The excellence of these contemplations is commended by the name *cherubim*. For in this twofold contemplation we advance to fullness of knowledge. Beyond these, nothing is to be sought or found for an increase of knowledge. It was said above that we ascend through visible things to the contemplation of invisible things. Thus, through knowledge of the invisible creature, we are raised to the contemplation of the creating nature [Col. 0198B–C].

For this reason the cherubim are commanded to turn their faces toward the mercy-seat; for this reason one is commanded to stand on one side and the other on the other side. In the contemplation understood through the mercy-seat, much likeness and much unlikeness to divine things are found. For the spiritual creature is made in the image and likeness of God. Therefore one of the aforementioned cherubim should occupy the side of likeness and the other the side of unlikeness. Let the contemplation more consonant with reason stand on one side, and that less consonant with reason on the other.

The cherubim ought to spread their wings and cover the mercy-seat. What is the spreading of wings except a kind of preparation for flight? This preparation of the mind becomes both a flight toward eternal things and a shelter: a shelter, I say, from the heat of day, and a hiding-place and protection from whirlwind and rain [Col. 0198D].

The cherubim ought to turn their faces toward the mercy-seat, and, by gazing upon God’s image, be more surely instructed unto the higher things of knowledge. The said cherubim ought also to look toward one another and preserve in every respect the harmony of their respective affirmations. Let each take care that, in what he affirms, he does not contradict the other. Let an affirmation of unity be made from the one, so that confession of the Trinity may not be nullified thereby. Let confession of the Trinity be made in the other, so that the affirmation of unity may not thereby be nullified.

Let every prelate hear how useful it is to have brought together the final three contemplations. “From there,” He says, “I shall speak to you.”

[Col. 0199A] Let one who longs for divine revelations devote himself to acquiring these. The mercy-seat is rightly called an oracle, for divine answers were given from it. The Lord speaks above the mercy-seat when He inspires the spirit with that which surpasses the measure of its knowledge. It is heard, as it were, from the midst of the cherubim, what seems equally consonant with each.

The mercy-seat is covered by the wings of the cherubim, and the ark by the mercy-seat, because the knowledge of lower things is overshadowed by the prerogative of higher knowledge. According to the Lord’s command, the testimony is to be placed in the ark. For what we are taught must be done in the highest things must be firmly retained in our inmost parts while we walk in the ways. The principal commandments of God are called the testimony because they render testimony to each person’s conscience. According to the manner of observance, they testify to each person how greatly he loves his God [Col. 0199B].

I have sketched these matters concerning the grace of contemplation with the utmost brevity; elsewhere I have discussed the same subject more fully.

By the table of the Presence understand the teaching of sacred instruction. Food is placed on a table in order that it may be taken for refreshment. One refreshment is bodily, another spiritual: the former belongs to bodies, the latter to spirits. Secular learning supplies the former; divine Scripture supplies the latter. In divine Scripture, indeed, the refreshment of souls is set forth; hence it is rightly called the table of the Presence.

The state of human life under the hope of redemption yet to come was one thing; it necessarily had to be another under faith in Redemption already accomplished. The Old Testament treats of the one; the New Testament of the other. Sacred Scripture therefore treats sufficiently of both, whence it is said to have two cubits in length [Col. 0199B–C].

Certainly, both Testaments are directed solely to the care of souls. They are silent concerning the care of bodies and leave it to secular learning. Thus Scripture deals with one, not a twofold, care; hence it is said to have one cubit of breadth. As regards the manner of our restoration, it treats sufficiently of the condition of the present life, but teaches little concerning future things. Therefore its height is one and a half cubits: a full cubit with respect to the present condition, half with respect to the future.

The table of the Presence is constructed of wood, overlaid with gold, encircled with a rim, and adorned with a double crown. By the wooden work we understand the historical sense [Col. 0199C–D]; by the rim, the tropological sense; by the double crown, the allegorical and anagogical senses. The table was made of *setim* wood, said to be highly resistant to decay. Sacred history, free from every falsehood and absurdity, belongs to incorruptible wood. The gilding of the table is a subtle and wise exposition of the letter itself. A beautiful gilding is the commendation of the wise judgments of God.

It should be observed that the first work is wooden but gilded; the other three are not gilded but golden. The difference between wood and gold is the difference between the historical and mystical senses. History holds the first place in sacred Scripture. Mystical understanding is certainly threefold. The tropological holds the first place, the allegorical the middle, the anagogical the highest [Col. 0199D–0200A].

Why does not that which treats of the highest and heavenly things hold the highest place? Allegory is chiefly concerned with the mysteries of our faith—things believed rather than understood. Tropology deals with matters which everyone readily grasps and therefore occupies the lower place. By the golden rim, then, I understand mystical and moral understanding. Something important is intimated by the fact that this part of the structure is called a rim or lip. We know that all our speech is formed by the lips. Perhaps, therefore, it is suggested that common speech too ought to be shaped by tropology.

A chased crown is placed upon the rim, because allegory concerns subtler and more exalted matters. Chased work is accustomed to have certain artful engravings, as it were; and who can wonder sufficiently that allegory is interwoven with history in a wondrous way? For there are inserted allegorically things which can scarcely be believed and cannot be comprehended [Col. 0200A–B].

The chased crown has a surface now flat, now concave, elsewhere perforated: flat in matters according to reason; concave in matters beyond reason; perforated in matters that seem contrary to reason. The condition of tropology is one thing, and that of allegory very different. For what is tropology except moral knowledge, and what is allegory except the mystical doctrine of mysteries? Honorable moral principles are naturally inscribed upon the human heart. But no one certainly presumes upon the profundities of mysteries from private judgment except rashly. Hence the height of the crown is said to measure only four fingers. For what, I ask, are the holy Evangelists except the fingers of the right hand of the Most High? [Col. 0200B–C] Allegorical doctrine conforms itself to their measure when it agrees in every respect with their sayings.

It should be noted that the crown is commanded to be made upon the rim itself, because through the power of the sacraments moral discipline is made useful and capable of observance. By the crown, as was said, we understand the little crown, or aureole, of anagogical doctrine. This doctrine concerns the highest things; therefore its figure, though small, occupies the highest place. For what do we call anagoge except mystical and upward-leading understanding of supercelestial things? In the two foregoing senses, doctrine concerning morals and mysteries is sought. To anagoge belongs foresight of the rewards to be hoped for.

That the crown is called an aureole amounts to saying that it is little and golden. Yet whatever human power grasps of that “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” is a small thing [Col. 0200D].

It should be noted that Holy Scripture alone, among all writings, employs the allegorical and anagogical sense mystically; alone it is crowned with this twofold pre-eminence. Holy teachers must take the greatest care always to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks concerning the faith and hope that are in us. They should have at hand the means to prove what is true, disprove what is false, commend what is just, and dissuade from what is unjust. Whoever knows these things has fitted such circles as were appropriate into the doctrinal table. O what circles: the proof of truth, the disproof of falsehood, the persuasion toward justice, the dissuasion from injustice. Does not reasoning return to the same point and make a circle, when it concludes at the end what it set forth at the beginning? [Col. 0201A] From what has been said about one of these circles, it is easy to understand what should be thought concerning the others.

Let us now see what those corners are in which circles of this kind ought to be placed. Wherever someone doubts concerning what Holy Scripture sets forth, he in some manner encounters, as it were, a corner. Doubt and hesitation make a corner, where it does not readily occur what ought to be chosen. Often there is doubt whether what is true is true; likewise, whether what is false is false. Often there is hesitation concerning what just thing ought to be done; often concerning an unjust thing, whether it ought to be done or not done. But it is very easy to see which circle we ought to place in which corner, and this needs no assignment from us.

It remains now to ask what should be understood by the feet of the table. Upon its feet the whole body rests and is raised upright. The more firmly we rely upon the divine commandments, [Col. 0201B] the more perfectly we are raised into a state of uprightness. According to the number of the feet, observe the fourfold commandment. The first foot is a precept; the second, a prohibition; the third, an admonition; the fourth, a permission. A precept concerns those things whose performance leads to merit and whose avoidance leads to guilt. A prohibition concerns those things whose performance leads to guilt and whose avoidance leads to merit. An admonition concerns those things whose performance leads to merit in such a way that avoidance does not lead to guilt. A permission [Col. 0202A] concerns those things whose avoidance leads to merit in such a way that performance does not lead to guilt.

In precepts there is especially need of demonstration; in prohibitions, of refutation; in admonitions, of persuasion; in permissions, of dissuasion. Why this is so will readily become clear to one who inquires carefully. The office of the true preacher consists in two things: instruction in truth and exhortation to virtue. Through this twofold efficacy the doctrinal table is carried about, and by its certain, as it were, poles is conveyed from one heart to another. Let one pole, therefore, be called the discernment of instruction; the other, the discernment of exhortation. Poles of this sort must be made from the plain testimonies of the letter—like poles of shittim wood—and gilded with the meanings of mystical interpretation. All sacred instruction ought to tend toward the proof of truth and [Col. 0202B] the refutation of falsehood; all sacred exhortation, toward the commending of good and the dissuasion from evil. From this it is very easy to discern which circles ought to belong to which pole.

It should be noted that the attestation of the Scriptures belongs to the poles, while human reasoning belongs to the circles. And because the depths of mysteries exceed human reason, the circles rightly receive their place beneath the crown.

[Col. 0201]

# TREATISE ON MEDITATING UPON THE PLAGUES THAT WILL COME ABOUT THE END OF THE WORLD

[Col. 0201C] “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the time of affliction comes and the years draw near of which you will say, ‘They do not please me’” (Eccles. 12).

So far as the surface meaning of the letter is concerned, it seems to me that the great and final tribulation is described in these last words of this book, and that nearly everything which we read scattered throughout many places in Scripture is here comprehended in concise brevity. Therefore Solomon, wisest of men, foreseeing in the spirit what would come upon the whole world in the last times, addresses the entire human race as though it were one man. While the opportunity for doing good remains, he exhorts it, with provident watchfulness, to perform whatever good it can.

He says, therefore: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth.” We know [Col. 0201D] that youth is stronger than the other ages and readier and better prepared for vigorous action. Thus, in its own manner, the human race has, as it were, a youth while it still flourishes with the flowers of virtues and remains vigorous, by God’s gift, for the doing of brave deeds. Let him therefore say—let him say: “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth,” before the old age of the world comes upon you, before the time and opportunity for doing good utterly fail. For the time will come when no one will any longer be able to work. Those days of tribulation will be such as have not been from the beginning of the creation which God made [Col. 0202C] until now, nor shall be.

He wished to signify this as the tribulation of tribulations and the affliction of afflictions by an emphatic expression when he says: “Before the time of affliction comes.” For that affliction is not merely one affliction, but the supreme affliction. “Before the time of affliction comes, and the years draw near of which you will say, ‘They do not please me.’” So long as we would rather have years such as we presently endure than have no years at all, it is beyond doubt that they please us in some respect, although they displease us in comparison with better years. But it is evident that those years will truly and entirely displease humankind, because in those days people will choose to die rather than live. As it is written: “In those days people will seek death and will not find it; and they will desire [Col. 0202D] to die, and death will flee from them” (Rev. 9).

“Before the sun, and the light, and the moon, and the stars are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain.” The final tribulation which he had first outlined summarily, he now explains more fully in the matters that he subsequently enumerates in stages. He shows, therefore, by how many and how wondrous means the human race will be struck by God in that final tribulation. First, by signs and prodigies from heaven, through manifold terror. And because not even thus will they be moved to compunction and repentance, they must be overwhelmed by many kinds of crushing: by pestilence and famine, by intolerable [Col. 0203A] persecution, not only by barrenness of crops but also by the astonishing devastation of trees and vegetables, and by mutual sedition. We shall be able to find all these things in the sequence in which we have set them forth, one by one, in Solomon’s following words.

Since, therefore, all these things will at some time come upon humanity because of negligence and contempt for God, it is rightly said to it: “Remember your Creator before the sun, and the light, and the moon, and the stars are darkened.” Does this not convey the same meaning as what you read in the Gospel: “There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars” (Luke 21)? And from Joel’s utterance you hear that “the sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Joel 12 [probably 2]). See how justly those suffer outward darkness who inwardly closed their eyes to the true light. [Col. 0203B] O how justly the removal of outward light torments those whom the darkness of unbelief blinds within!

But something further is suggested in these words of Solomon. For one thing is expressly stated in them, and another is inferred from them by clear reasoning. We know that the corruption of the heavenly bodies necessarily entails the corruption of the elements. But grave pestilence always accompanies corruption of water and air. Therefore we understand that those who will live in those days are first to be struck by terrible fear, and immediately afterward to be smitten by an exceedingly grievous pestilence. And because not even thus can they be restrained from their iniquities, scourges will follow—or rather, will continually be added to—scourges.

He says, therefore: “Before the [Col. 0203C] sun, and the light, and the moon, and the stars are darkened”; and he adds: “And the clouds return after the rain.” Rain ordinarily clears away clouds and brings serenity. What else, then, is indicated by the return of the clouds except an excessive and disorderly outpouring of waters? We do not deny, however, that rain after rain often falls without delay and one rain immediately succeeds another. But this is done by clouds that remain, not by clouds that return. If, however, clouds hanging ready for rain are completely dissolved, and, once the clouds are dissolved, clouds immediately return, and in this manner clouds are often dissolved and often return, know that this cannot happen without a great disturbance of nature and a deviation from the ordinary course of things. Thus a great [Col. 0203D] inundation of waters is implied in the words: “Before the clouds return after the rain.” And certainly, since this is added, after great evils have been mentioned, as an increase of evils, it indicates that something very grave is proposed under threat.

It is certain that, just as pestilence ordinarily follows the corruption of the elements, so a severe famine must follow an excessive inundation of waters. Thus, in both cases the cause is discerned from the effect: from one, a future pestilence is inferred; from the other, a future famine. Is this not what you find in the Gospel: “There will be pestilences and famines” (Matt. 14 [probably 24])?

It should be noted, however, that although famine commonly follows sometimes an excessive inundation of waters, as has been said, and sometimes excessive drought, yet [Col. 0204A] the famine accompanying an immoderate outpouring of waters is usually much worse and much more severe. Let him say, therefore—let him say: “Remember your Creator before the clouds return after the rain.” You have heard of terror; you have heard of pestilence; you have heard of famine; hear of persecution: “When the keepers of the house are shaken, and the strongest men tremble.” For, as the Gospel says: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom” (Mark 13).

In those days the terror caused by enemies will be so great that those dwelling in less secure places will begin to migrate from their homes. At first, indeed, they will send their property, with wives and little children, to safer places; finally, as evils grow more frequent, those themselves will follow who had seemed to remain to guard the houses. Does this not seem to be what Scripture suggests when it says: “When the keepers of the house are shaken”? “When the keepers,” it says—not of riches but of houses—“are shaken”: when even those persons who seemed both able and obliged to guard deserted houses will not dare to remain there.

For not even those who appear physically robust, armed, and protected by support will be secure: “The strongest men will tremble.” What, pray, will the weak do where the strongest men tremble? “And the women grinding will be idle because their number is diminished, and those looking through the openings will grow dark.” This seems to be said according to the custom of the land of Palestine, where women commonly sit at the mill and grind grain. He says, therefore, that the women grinding will be idle, although their number is diminished. Thus he indicates two things: both the small number of grinders and [Col. 0204C] the idleness of that small number. Here we now have plainly what we said above concerning famine and barrenness of crops. For why, pray, would that small number of grinders be idle unless they could scarcely—or not at all—find anything to grind?

How great, pray, do you think will be the multitude of those perishing—here from pestilence, there from famine, elsewhere from slaughter—whose lives are endangered at every moment of every day? What consolation could there be for anyone? Who could restrain himself from tears and weeping when he sees, every hour, a husband his wife, a wife her husband, a parent a child, a child a parent, a kinsman a kinsman, a friend a friend, either miserably ending life or prolonging it still more miserably? How, pray, will fear of persecutors torment them on one side, and grief from compassion for those in peril on the other? [Col. 0204D]

So great will be the grief, so great the sorrow of mourners occasioned by pity for those in danger, that from constant weeping the eyes of those weeping will begin to grow dim. So great will be the fear of persecution, so great the stupefaction of the frightened, that at the sound of anyone passing by, terrified and stunned, they will not dare to open the door or to look to see what it is except through openings or cracks. Does this not seem to you to be suggested by these words: “And those looking through the openings will grow dark”? Why, pray, will they look out not through open doors but through openings, except because of excessive terror? Why will the eyes of those looking grow dim, except because of excessive grief? For people will wither from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world (Luke [Col. 0205A] 21). Amid so many dangers of life, what limit can there be to grief and mourning when the keepers of the house are shaken, when the strongest men tremble, when the women grinding are idle because their number is diminished?

See, then, how ingeniously this preacher sometimes indicates an effect from a cause, and sometimes, conversely, displays a cause from an effect. Above we have already said how in certain passages we ought to discern an effect from a cause. Here, conversely, the cause is inferred from an effect, where the greatness of grief is measured from the dimness of the eyes: “And those looking through the openings,” he says, “will grow dark.” To this is added: “And they will shut the doors in the street, in the low sound of the women grinding.” That at that time they will shut the doors in the street while grinding—consider whether this is perhaps said here more on account of fear of fellow citizens and neighbours than of enemies. Consider whether perhaps each person shuts the doors while grinding chiefly so that a neighbour may not run up at the sound of the mill and, driven by hunger, violently take for himself that small quantity which was being ground.

Those who grieve and mourn commonly find it natural to sing something mournful, and to do so in a subdued voice. Thus it seems fittingly suited to those perilous times when it is said: “And they will shut the doors in the street, in the low sound of the women grinding.” We have already heard under what fear they waste away above; let us hear further how evil always grows into something greater: “And they will rise at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of song will become deaf.” That they are said here to rise [Col. 0205C] at the voice of a bird—does this not seem to you like what you read in Leviticus under a threat: “The sound of a flying leaf will terrify them, and they will flee as though before a sword” (Lev. 26)?

At that time they will be possessed by such fear and such faintheartedness that the sound of a flying bird or falling leaf will be able to terrify them and startle them from their rest. Therefore they will rise at the voice of a bird, so that it may be a judgment upon them—and a mockery—as upon senseless children; and deservedly so, since at last they will begin to tremble at a bird’s voice, when before this they had, in their great arrogance, despised the voice of the supreme Majesty in His commandments.

But because Holy Scripture often causes many things to be understood [Col. 0205D] in the one thing it says, we may also consider other things here from what is said and, judging like things from like, expect to happen to these people what we read happened to the Egyptians. For we read of the Egyptians in the Book of Wisdom: “For a whistling wind, or the pleasant sound of birds among thick branches of trees, or the excessively rushing force of water, or the loud sound of falling rocks, or the unseen running of gambolling animals, or the powerful roar of bellowing beasts, or an echo resounding from the highest mountains, caused them to faint with fear” (Wis. 17). If, therefore, trembling and fearful, they rise and leap from their seats or beds at the voice of a bird, why should they not also do so at the voice of an animal, or even at any sound suddenly falling upon them with a crash? “And they will rise at the voice of a bird.”

You perceive, I think, [Col. 0206A] how the magnitude of fear is expressed in these words. Attend further to how the magnitude of grief is expressed in what follows: “And all the daughters of song,” he says, “will become deaf.” By “daughters of song,” according to the idiom of that language, he means those who are accustomed to love and frequent songs and sweet melodies, as people nurtured in such pleasures. He therefore says hyperbolically that the daughters of song become deaf, because through the excessive bitterness of grief sweet song, or anything of that kind, ceases to be pleasing to them, and every delight of the ears departs far from even the most refined soul, as though it had truly become deaf. If the daughters of song become deaf to songs, how much more to other things? If the daughters of song become deaf at the voice of song, how much more will any others?

It should be noted, moreover, how in all these matters evil continually advances into something greater. Above, the women grinding are said to act in a low voice; here, the daughters of song are said to become deaf. There it is implied that the women grinding sing something mournful in a mournful manner; here it is implied that the daughters of song neither wish nor are able to hear or take pleasure in any song, however sweet. See how evil always increases into something greater and turns toward something worse.

Above Scripture indicated that people would migrate from their homes and flee to safer places; and in this is fulfilled what is read in the Gospel: “Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains; let those who are in the midst of it depart; and let those who are in the regions not enter into it” (Matt. 24). But when they have fled [Col. 0206C] to safer places, will they be secure in more protected places? Hear what follows: “They will also fear high places, and inaccessible places will terrify them.” You see, certainly, that there is no security anywhere: neither in elevated places nor in inaccessible places, because they will fear high places and inaccessible places will terrify them.

Note here also, as above, how everything continually turns for the worse: “The almond tree will blossom, the locust will grow fat, and the caper-plant will be scattered.” He does not say of the almond tree that it will bear fruit, but that it will blossom. “It will blossom,” he says, so that under such great scarcity people may see something for which to hope, may desire it more intensely, and, when afterward they lose what they had hoped for, may groan more deeply. It will not, therefore, bear fruit [Col. 0206D] to sustain the hunger of the starving; it will merely blossom. “The locust will grow fat, and the caper-plant will be scattered.” The caper is a kind of vegetable.

Locusts, grubs, and caterpillars commonly pierce everywhere through the leaves of trees and vegetables: at one time eating part and leaving part; at another consuming everything down to the ribs, and in this way scattering and destroying all green growth. Thus, as caterpillars and tiny creatures of that kind gnaw, the caper-plant will be scattered. Does not that saying of the prophet Joel also seem fitting to those times: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the grub ate; and what the grub left, the mildew ate” (Joel 1)? Above we heard of the barrenness of crops; now devastation of fruits and vegetables is added. [Col. 0207A] For from what he said concerning one kind of tree or vegetable, according to his custom, he has given us to understand many others as well.

See how divine severity, after withdrawing the greater supports of life, finally withdraws even the lesser. At last even that is taken from humanity by which life seemed capable of being sustained somehow. See how, in vengeance for the Creator, humanity is struck on every side by every creature, scourged all around in many and wondrous ways: first from heaven, as though by the powers above; afterward on earth by mutual slaughter, human beings at the hands of human beings; and finally by locusts, caterpillars, and certain very tiny creatures. Thus, thus is human pride terrified, crushed, and trampled down. It is terrified from above by angelic powers; crushed by mutual persecutions; trampled down by dumb [Col. 0207B] and minute creatures. For signs and prodigies serve to instill fear; persecutions and slaughter, to arouse frenzy; and infestation by contemptible animals, to bring shame and indignation.

But why is humanity then struck by so many means, crushed by so many scourges, afflicted by so many miseries? The reason is added when it is said: “For man will go to the house of his eternity.” It is as if he plainly concluded and said: Therefore, in the end, humanity must labour and fail beneath such a weight of tribulations, because the time is at hand when man is removed from the face of the earth and goes to the house of his eternity. Therefore the light of sun and moon is withdrawn; therefore the other evils that are subsequently enumerated will occur; therefore evils will begin [Col. 0207C] to increase day by day and grow more and more frequent: so that, compelled to depart from here, man may at last leave the place of his pilgrimage and go to the house of his eternity.

“To the house of his eternity”: to the place of his perpetual dwelling, where he will abide forever, where he will not fail with any ending—to the house of his eternity. In eternity all things are immovable; none are transitory.
