He will go, therefore, where he may remain forever and find all things immovable. “To the house,” he says, “of his eternity.” He does not say “to the house of eternity,” but, with the addition, “to the house of his eternity.” Therefore each person will go to that dwelling-place of his own perpetuity which he has acquired for himself by his own merits, where, according to the justice of recompense, he may find either immovable goods or immovable [Col. 0207D] evils.

It is clear, therefore, that in the end man loses this world with pitiable suffering; at last, with astonishing and miserable grief, he is compelled to leave what he had long possessed with perverse delight. For this reason the end of the world is afflicted in so many ways, crushed by so many scourges, and pressed by so many and such great evils: that from its end humanity may recognize, even late, what it was that it loved against God, what it was for which it despised God, what it was for which it lost eternal goods, and what it was for which it consigned itself to eternal evils.

Those final evils of this world will therefore be so many, so great, so bitter, so intolerable, that even people of the dullest minds will understand that the world’s [Col. 0208A] end has arrived and that the human race, pressed by so many kinds of calamity, cannot endure long; so that they will begin utterly to despair of every remedy of salvation. Hence grief, hence stupefaction and horror, hence groaning, mourning, and lamentation. Does not he perceive this who immediately adds: “And mourners will go about in the street”? So great will be the common grief of all, so great the stupefaction of mourners, that shaken by excessive anguish of mind, they will be unable to remain in one place even briefly. Instead, as though made mad, they will begin to rush here and there.

And even if the common calamity perhaps puts an end to persecutions, they will nonetheless, mindful of the former evils, not dare to go out into fields or farms. Yet because they cannot contain themselves in their houses or mourn in an orderly way under the excessive agitation of their frenzy, [Col. 0208B] they will begin, as has been said, to run through the lanes and streets of the city and, whirled about in wretched dizziness like a whirlwind, groaning, lamenting, and howling, will not cease to roam everywhere or ever rest. “Mourners will therefore go about in the street.” See how at last they are more miserably tormented by their own frenzy than they had previously been by any persecution of enemies. See with what a miserable end those fail who turn their entire life into an insult to their Creator.

But as these people are afflicted and scourged, and not even thus corrected, the increase of evils does not cease to thunder forth when he adds: “Before the silver cord is broken and the golden band twists back.” We must take this up again from what was said above: “Remember your Creator”—at least, he says, after such evils, after [Col. 0208C] such great scourges, remember your Creator, lest still other things begin to follow one upon another. “For in all these things His wrath is not turned away, but His hand is still stretched out.” Remember, therefore, your Creator before the silver cord is broken and the golden band twists back.

By “a silver cord,” he does not mean one particular thing alone, but anything of that kind generally and everywhere. Such also are the statements, “the almond tree will blossom,” and “man will go to the house of his eternity.” For the former is not said of any one particular tree, nor the latter of any one particular person. So here a general statement is introduced when it says: “Before the silver cord is broken.” We know that precious ornaments, commonly made of gold and ivory or precious stones, are customarily hung or fastened in their places by silver cords—such as the idols of the gentiles, the phylacteries of Christians, and the ornaments of very wealthy and royal persons. These are the things which noble persons commonly covet with insatiable desire, expending estates and inheritances upon things of this kind. These are what captivate the eyes of fools and hold them suspended in admiration of themselves.

Let anyone who can consider what will then be in human minds, when they begin to abominate and detest all such precious objects and cannot even bear to look upon things which they formerly loved so ardently; when, in every place, as if in frenzy and indignation, they violently tear them from the places to which they had been fastened, break the silver cords, cast them to the ground, and throw them upon a dungheap. [Col. 0209A] That their dearest possessions will be thrown onto a dungheap is inferred more certainly from the words, “before the golden band twists back.” He does not say, “before it is worn away,” lest it seem to be worn away through use; rather, “before the golden band twists back.” This happens when, cast out into sun and rain, it is now loosened by dampness and now contracted by heat, until at last that alternation of changes wholly dissolves it and causes it to twist back of itself.

It should be noted that we properly speak of “twisting back” in the case of things which we see made by twisting. See to what end the pomp of the age and this glory of the world are brought; see by what outcome they are concluded. But at what value will all worldly glory be reckoned then, when life itself becomes a weariness—indeed, an object of hatred—to all? For in those [Col. 0209B] days people will seek death and not find it; they will desire to die, and death will flee from them (Rev. 9). Is this not what we have in the Gospel, where we hear it from the Lord Himself? “Then,” He says, “they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us’” (Luke 23).

People will therefore then wish for what they formerly did not wish for, ardently desire what they formerly greatly feared; and those who once mourned and wept over the desolation and failure of the world will now ardently desire that it might quickly come to its end. You perceive, I think, how the things that are set later always seem to express something worse. For the fact that they go about in the street mourning because they see man compelled to go to the house of his eternity indicates that some—indeed, a great—love of the world still remains in human minds, on account of which they seem to mourn so inconsolably. But the fact that at last each person throws away all his most precious possessions like dung—what else does it show but a certain astonishing contempt for the world? Thus loss continually grows upon loss, and worse things always follow evils that have gone before.

But when we say that they have advanced to contempt for the world, do we suppose that they have thereby been moved to compunction or corrected into repentance? Rather, let us hear what follows: “And before the pitcher is shattered over the spring, and the wheel broken over the cistern.” Do these not seem rather signs of impatience or malice than evidences of repentance? For what, pray, is meant by the fact that at last, after everything else, a pitcher is shattered everywhere over a spring, [Col. 0209D] or a wheel broken anywhere over a cistern? Will people, exasperated by so many scourges and embittered by so many miseries, be so impatient that they cannot endure one another—so much so that, when they come to draw water, one breaks another’s pitcher because the newcomer cannot bear to wait while the one who first came to draw water draws it first? Or will their malice at that time be so great that one person will begin to begrudge another even a draught of cold water?

We know that persons of lower rank come together to draw water. What will persons of higher rank do if even the humblest break out into such impatience or malice? But why do those who break another’s pitcher not at least spare the wheel [Col. 0210A]? For a pitcher serves each person’s private uses, whereas a wheel commonly serves common uses. Therefore, one who does not spare another’s loss—why does he not spare even his own? Or perhaps, as charity grows cold and iniquity abounds, their malice will at last be so great that they will prefer altogether to incur their own loss rather than fail to obstruct another’s advantage?

Let him say, therefore—let him say: “Remember your Creator before the pitcher is shattered over the spring, and the wheel broken over the cistern.” Before human malice breaks out into such madness that one person begrudges another even the smallest goods; before one person, shattering another’s pitcher, harms his neighbour even gratuitously; before, raging against the common good, people everywhere break the wheel over the cistern, so that one may purchase another’s loss even at one’s own [Col. 0210B] cost.

We have heard how many, how great, and how fearful are the evils that accompany the end of the world. Let us hear further with what dreadful outcome all these things are concluded: “Until,” he says, “the dust returns to the earth from which it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.” Certainly, if man expected no other evil in this world, if he had to experience no other, if he had everything else that he desired while he lived here, yet expected such an end with complete certainty at an uncertain hour, he ought, with the Apostle, to reckon all the things that delight and pass away here as dung.

Therefore at every hour a person ought to remember his last things. For, willing or unwilling, whatever he does, however much he abounds in pleasures, it is necessary that the dust return to the earth from which it was, and that the spirit [Col. 0210C] return to God who gave it. What he said above—“man will go to the house of his eternity”—he seems here to repeat in other words. But there he dealt simply with human death; here he sets forth distinctly an account of each of the two substances of man. For man is joined together from a twofold substance, corporeal and incorporeal: namely, flesh and soul. “Until the dust returns whence it was”: behold, this concerns the corporeal substance of man. “And the spirit returns to God who gave it”: behold, this concerns the incorporeal substance of man.

Consider, therefore, from what man was made according to the body, and you will at the same time understand to what he will return: “The Lord God formed man from the clay of the earth” (Gen. 2). Hear also whence he comes, or whither he must return: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go.” Certainly, as soon as the soul departs, the body simultaneously loses voluntary [Col. 0210D] movement and every sensation. Once the soul has departed, what is the body but earth?

You see that not even those who are found alive at the very end of the world escape this sentence of severity, although after sudden death they rise again however swiftly. Therefore the dust will return to the earth from which it was, and the spirit to God who gave it. And whom else do we say gave it but Him who breathed the breath of life into the face of the first man, who is believed daily to create new souls and to infuse those He has created into human bodies, according to the Psalmist’s words: “He who formed each one of their hearts” (Ps. 32 [33]). Behold who gave it. Hear also what kind of being He made: “And the Lord God created man in His image and likeness” (Gen. 1).

[Col. 0211A] Behold what man was made by God. Consider also what he made himself: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48 [49]). Behold what he made himself; behold whence and to what he fell: from the likeness of God into the likeness of a beast. “And the spirit,” he says, “returns to God who gave it.” O with how great a shame will he return to God who has superimposed the likeness of a beast upon the likeness of God! O with how great a shame will he appear before his Creator, who, while living here, performed deeds worthy of shame—who trampled, defiled, and effaced God’s likeness in himself!

Certainly, if the transgressor expected only this shame, if he feared no other recompense whatsoever for all his error, it ought to have been sufficient to make him guard against every evil. A person must always remember how dreadful it is to be put to shame in the presence of such majesty, before the sight of the whole universe; how terrible it is to fall into the hands of the living God. Beyond doubt, the human spirit must return and stand before its Creator in order to receive according to what it has done in its body. But who could ever explain in any speech what kind, how many, and how great are those evils which those must receive from the sentence of the Judge and endure as their deserved recompense—those, I say, whom so many adversities of the perishing world and so many scourges of divine severity cannot restrain from their perversity?

[Col. 0211]

# EXPLANATION OF DIFFICULTIES ARISING IN THE EXPOSITION OF THE TABERNACLE OF THE COVENANT

## FIRST TREATISE

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0211B]

Asked by friends to write something in explanation of the tabernacle, I confess that I was afraid to comply with their request, lest I seem, in that very matter, to detract from the authority of the Fathers. Yet he himself who published the customary exposition gives me courage to attempt it, when, in the course of his exposition, he adds: “On this most difficult subject we have endeavoured briefly to explain what we seemed to ourselves to have understood, ready to learn truer things in these matters if anyone should wish to teach us. Yet in all these matters the allegorical sense is plainly evident.” See how confidently he pronounces upon the allegorical sense, though he has prefaced the literal exposition with uncertainty. He, therefore, who so confidently bears witness to his own certainty in allegorical exposition, while withholding it from historical exposition, plainly implies that in that exposition of his he did not even satisfy himself. Why do you accuse me, or compel me to believe one who does not himself believe in himself?

But, to tell the truth, I fear more to offend those whom it is now certain stand in contemplation of the highest truth than to render them propitious, if, as though out of reverence for them, I should hesitate to put forth publicly a truth I have recognized. Let us consider how many things, how great and how profound, they treated with every diligence; how many things they expounded historically, how many allegorically, how many tropologically, with wonderful reasoning; and then it will cease to be surprising if in some place they left an exposition less than sufficient. It is therefore neither great nor surprising if in some single matter we can add something that may contribute to greater clarity or plainer understanding. [Col. 0211C–0212B] These things have been said because of those who accept nothing except what they have received from the most ancient Fathers. But is he who constantly brings forth new fruits for the refreshment of the outward person ever to be believed henceforth to bestow no advances in knowledge for renewing the faculties of the inward person? Where, then, I ask, is that saying: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall abound”? Therefore, I beg that no one be offended with me if I gather the ears remaining from the Lord’s harvest, which the hands of the reapers may have missed, and willingly distribute them to the hungry and those who ask.

## CHAPTER I. On the construction of the ark

When the Lord was about to instruct Moses concerning the construction of the tabernacle, he first of all instructed him concerning the making of the ark, thereby indicating that a certain prerogative of dignity far surpassed all the other things that were to be made in the tabernacle. What is said concerning its material, measurement, and manner of construction is sufficiently clear and needs no exposition. He commands four rings to be made at the four corners; but he subsequently shows how this is to be understood: “Let two,” he says, “be on one side, and two on the other” (Exod. 25). Thus they were not exactly at the corners, but beside the corners: two on one side and two beside the corners on the opposite side.

One may doubt what ought to be thought concerning the mercy-seat, since the author describes it separately. But I understand the mercy-seat to be nothing other than the lid of the ark itself—namely, a certain slab made wholly of the purest gold. Hence it had in every respect the same measurement as the ark, both in length and in breadth. But lest any uncertainty remain for you on this point, hear what Scripture itself says concerning the ark and concerning the mercy-seat. For it is written of the ark: “In it you shall place the testimony which I shall give you” (ibid.); and much later, of the mercy-seat: “Before the mercy-seat,” he says, “by which the testimony is covered, where I shall speak with you” (Exod. 30). How, I ask, is the testimony placed in the ark covered by the mercy-seat unless its lid and the mercy-seat are one and the same thing? Yet its exceptional dignity is indicated by the very fact that it is described separately.

From that mercy-seat responses of the Godhead were sometimes given and sometimes not given, according to the manner of divine propitiation. Rightly, therefore, it received the name mercy-seat, since there the Lord was accustomed to display or manifest the prerogative of his propitiation. It must further be understood that the golden moulding which ran around the upper part of the ark, where it was also fastened, enclosed within itself the whole mercy-seat and, rising higher, stood above its thickness. [Col. 0212C–0213A]

## CHAPTER II. On the making of the two cherubim

[Col. 0213B] Of the cherubim it is said that they looked toward one another. In body they faced toward the outer tabernacle; but with their faces turned, they directed their gaze toward the side where the ark stood between them beneath their wings. The two cherubim in Solomon’s temple were undoubtedly made in likeness of these. Therefore, what we read of those we understand equally of these: one cherub touched one wall with its wing, and the other touched the other wall with its wing (2 Chron. 3); but with their other wings they touched one another in the middle.

Thus, just as those in the temple, so neither could these stand upon the ark and mercy-seat, for the ark was only two and a half cubits long. But the spread of the joined wings of those cherubim was ten cubits; of these, five cubits. Therefore, when it is said of these that they were above the ark of the testimony, this must not be understood as though they stood upon the ark itself, but rather that they rose above the ark with their whole bodies.

## CHAPTER III. On the formation of the table

To state briefly what I think concerning the form of the table: it seems to me to have been like an ark without a bottom, though with the upper surface understood to be entirely flat and immovably fastened to the lower parts. It had a certain golden projection surrounding the top of the table, which the author himself calls a rim because of its resemblance; and to this there adhered a crown four fingers high. It was ornamented with various carvings and, where the variety of the carving required it, pierced by frequent openwork cuttings; hence it was called *interrasile*—openwork.

Above this was another piece, like a certain round and flat rod, or as though woven from several little rods, joined to the first for strength and beauty—indeed, so wholly united with it that both appeared to be one. This is sufficient concerning the table, for the rest is well known in itself. [Col. 0213C–D]

## CHAPTER IV. On the making of the lampstand

We must now consider the lampstand, especially the point concerning which there can be doubt. Its cups are described as fashioned like a nut. A cup, however, seems to have half the form of a sphere: it has a hollow and empty roundness, cut off at the top. A nut, by contrast, widening from below, swells into a belly, but above gradually sharpens and gathers into a single point at the summit. Thus the cup has a spherical but truncated roundness and an empty hollowness; the nut has an oblong roundness, but is neither hollow nor cut off.

Therefore, because it had two things in common with the cup—namely, the empty hollow and the truncation of its roundness—he calls it a cup rather than a nut; and because it had only one thing in common with the nut—namely, oblong roundness—he does not call it a nut, but declares that it has the likeness of a nut. Thus both the shaft and all six branches had this sort of ornament: first, an oblong, nut-like roundness, but cut off; then a spherical roundness, which he calls a little globe; and after these two adjoining features, a flower shaped like a lily. Accordingly, the shaft first seemed to terminate in the first cup, and then to emerge, as it were, from the middle of the flower together with two branches, one on either side. The same is to be understood at the second and third places. At the top it had a similar ornament, except for the joining of branches. From the likeness of the shaft you may understand what is meant concerning the branches.

It should further be noted that the little globe is said to be beneath the two branches at three places on the shaft. For the roots of the branches had the lily flower not so much beneath them as around them, whereas they had the little globe wholly beneath them. This is enough concerning the lampstand; we must now consider the tabernacle. [Col. 0214A–B]

## CHAPTER V. On the manner and measurements of the curtains

[Col. 0214C] First it should be noted that some accept as though authoritative everything they find written by Josephus concerning these matters. They suppose that he, being a Jew, had seen the tabernacle, and therefore wrote things both true and well known. Yet from the testimony of Scripture it is clearer to me than daylight that he never saw the tabernacle. For what Scripture, I ask, even pretends that it was brought back from the place where Jeremiah hid it by divine revelation? Let Josephus gladly be accepted in matters which he knew by experience or gathered from authentic Scriptures. But where he thinks otherwise, I confidently prefer Exodus to him, or any books that I find in the canon.

Let us therefore set forth the author’s words and draw from them, insofar as the Lord grants, what should be understood concerning the construction or erection of the tabernacle. He commands ten curtains to be made, twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits broad. He says of these curtains: “Five curtains shall be joined to one another, and the other five shall likewise be joined by a similar fastening” (Exod. 26). Thus one curtain was to be made out of five curtains, and another out of the other five. The following is understood of these large curtains: “You shall make blue loops on the sides and edges of the curtains, so that they may be joined to one another.” Here it is said that they have loops on every side; yet it is not said that they are at the ends, but only that they are on both sides. By being silent about one thing, the author gives us to understand from what he determines about the other that the end-loops are to be made in the manner of the side-loops.

“Each curtain,” he says, “shall have fifty loops on either side, so placed that loop may meet loop and one may be fitted to the other.” The statement that loop is to be joined to loop must be understood of the joined sides. What is to be thought concerning the loops of the remaining sides will be seen better below. He continues: “You shall also make fifty golden rings, by which the curtains are to be joined, so that one tabernacle may be made.” The following is read concerning the same matter: “Hence he also cast fifty golden rings, which might grip the loops of the curtains.” From this we are given to understand that the rings had certain attached teeth which seized, with a biting grip, the loops passed through the rings, and thus bound the two coverings into one. [Col. 0214D–0215B] This is enough concerning the curtains.

## CHAPTER VI. On the making of the goats’-hair coverings

“You shall make eleven goats’-hair coverings to cover the roof of the tabernacle. The length of one covering shall be thirty cubits, and its breadth four. The measurement of all the coverings shall be equal; five of them you shall join separately, and six you shall join together, so that you double the sixth covering at the front of the roof” (Exod. 26).

Here two things are said to be indicated: that it must be doubled, and that, once doubled, it must be at the front of the tabernacle. Therefore not merely a part of the covering, but the covering itself from end to end, is to be doubled, so that, folded and doubled, it measures thirty cubits in length and only two in breadth. It continues: “You shall make fifty loops on the edge of one covering, so that it may be joined to the other; fifty loops on the edge of the other covering, so that it may be coupled to the other. You shall make fifty bronze clasps by which the loops may be joined, and one covering shall be made from all.” What is said concerning the clasps of the coverings, or the loops of the joined sides, must in every respect be understood by analogy with the curtains. He says nothing about the loops at the ends, because he foresees that they can be understood from the previously stated analogy.

Thus the curtain-covering measures twenty-eight cubits, and the goats’-hair covering thirty, in one dimension. Again, the curtains measure forty cubits and the coverings forty-two in the other dimension. This is enough concerning the construction of the two coverings; and immediately he adds the point from which it may be understood how one is to be laid over the other: “What remains of the coverings prepared for the roof—that is, the one covering which is additional—shall cover the rear of the tabernacle by half of it; and one cubit shall hang down on one side and another on the other, the excess in the length of the coverings protecting each side of the tabernacle.”

For the moment, let us consider these matters as though, for the purpose of trying or showing it, one were laid on top of the other upon a flat surface, so that afterwards it may be understood more fully how they should be fitted together in the erection of the tabernacle. Let the joined curtains therefore first be spread so that the outer side of the first curtain is toward the East and that of the tenth toward the West; their ends, on either side, being directed, one toward the South and the other toward the North. Let the covering of goats’-hair be laid over this curtain-covering so that the one corresponds uniformly to the other on every side; and you will see that the upper covering exceeds the curtains all round by one cubit. This over-covering must have its doubled covering toward the East, for the tabernacle had its front on that side.

If, therefore, you compare the coverings with the curtains, matching each one with each one, you will see that one covering remains over in number. But if you consider how far either covering can extend, you will see that in the joined goats’-hair covering only half a covering is superfluous. If you attend to their position, you will see that this half covers the rear of the tabernacle—not because the whole half passes beyond the end of the tabernacle, but because that end lies opposite the middle of this half, and, in the manner of a covering, has an equal part of it on either side.

He therefore says: “What remains of the coverings,” and so forth. The text should be read thus: “But from half of that which remains of the coverings prepared for the roof—that is, one covering.” For the eleventh covering is there beyond the number of the curtains; from half, I say, of that eleventh covering you shall cover the rear of the tabernacle. The rest is sufficiently clear. [Col. 0215B–0216B]

Observe in what fitting order he treats every part of the tabernacle: first its front, where he commands the covering to be doubled; then its rear extremity, which he commands to be covered by half of the eleventh covering; third, each of its sides, where he says that one cubit of the surplus covering is to hang down on either side. But if anyone says that the said half covers the rear only insofar as it extends beyond the ends of the curtains, and insists that it must be understood in this way, even so, and according to this interpretation, one need not concede that the whole half is used for such a purpose, although it is said that this must be done from that half. For one who says that Eve was made from a rib speaks truly; and one who says that Eve was made from man speaks no less truly; yet not the whole substance of the man, as the rib did, went into such a making.

But if what has been said cannot satisfy anyone, and he insists that the whole of that half must pass beyond the ends of the curtains, and therefore that both coverings and curtains begin from one line at the front of the tabernacle, I judge it better to yield to another’s interpretation than to serve disputes. [Col. 0216B–C]

## CHAPTER VII. On the double covering of rams’ skins

[Col. 0216D] It continues: “You shall make another covering for the roof from red-dyed rams’ skins, and over this again another covering from blue skins” (Exod. 26). I find that the blue covering is above the red covering; but I do not find in the author that these two are above the goats’-hair roof-covering. Some, however, think that the same order must be maintained in erection as is maintained in description. But let them consider whether that argument may perhaps be entirely worthless. For the curtains are described first and the boards later, and yet in erecting the structure the boards are raised before the curtains are spread.

I myself rather believe that the author joins the description of the goats’-hair coverings to that of the curtains because of their similarity of construction. It is common in Holy Scripture to leave something undetermined when reason makes it easy to infer what is to be chosen. But goats’-hair is of a rougher nature, while rams’ skins are softer. Thus the softness of the skins intervenes between the roughness of the goats’-hair and the curtains, lest the curtains’ delicacy be worn away through continual rubbing against its roughness. The rams’-skin covering is doubled so that, if the first layer were wetted through the middle of the goats’-hair coverings, the second might remain dry, and the delicacy of the curtains might suffer, or be able to suffer, no harm.

Some think that the rams’-skin coverings do not descend from the top, and I should like to hear from what evidence this is proved. For if it is true, the curtains could not retain their beauty even after one heavy rainstorm. It is also clear that the top of the tabernacle had a flat, not a ridged, surface; and how, according to what some write, did it inspire astonishment in its beholders by its beauty if it had such beauty only in the part that could not be seen? I should also like to hear how a covering of this kind was secured there at the top. [Col. 0216D–0217B]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the manner and measurement of the boards

It continues: “You shall make upright boards for the tabernacle from shittim wood, each having ten cubits in length and one and a half in breadth” (Exod. 26). This is about the boards’ measurement; and immediately there is added a statement concerning their joinery. There are two kinds of joinery. The first is where one side of a board is hollowed out and the other sharpened, and one board is thus fitted into another. But joinery of this kind does not produce a flat surface on either side.

There is another kind of joinery that is made on both sides. On one side, a certain cutting is made in the edge down to half the thickness of the board from the inner side; on the other, likewise, but from the outer side. The cut of one board is fitted into the cut of another, so that the entire wall appears to be one board and the surface becomes completely even on both sides. The following is understood of this kind of joinery: “On the sides of the board two joints shall be made, by which one board may be connected with another.”

There were twenty boards with forty bases on the south side; as many, and of the same dimensions, on the north side. On the west side there were eight boards with sixteen bases, for each board had two silver bases set beneath it. Some maintain that the corner boards on either side were only half a cubit wide; but they cannot show from what this is proved. Yet, as it seems to me, they pay too little attention to the general statement which they read at the beginning of the description: “You shall make upright boards for the tabernacle from shittim wood, each of which shall have ten cubits in length and one and a half in breadth.” If each has a cubit and a half in breadth, then so do the corner boards. Or perhaps, because they are treated separately, are they rightly said to have a special measurement? On the contrary, this must be denied all the more, because when he treats them separately he nowhere excepts their measurement from the general rule.

If what we have said concerning the boards is not sufficient for anyone, let him hear what the author says much later about the bases: “There were moreover one hundred talents of silver from which were cast the bases of the sanctuary and of the entrance where the veil hangs. One hundred bases were made from one hundred talents, one talent being counted for each base.” If the corner boards had only a third of the breadth, how did they receive bases equal to the others?

But they say that the tabernacle was only ten cubits wide, and from this they infer what has just been said concerning the breadth of the corner boards. I find the evidence for the tabernacle’s being thirty cubits long; but I do not find the evidence for its being only ten cubits wide. Yet I shall state what is accustomed to trouble the mind on this point, from which we may conjecture rather than prove it. We believe that Solomon’s temple was made, according to its own scale, in likeness of this tabernacle. Accordingly, by the principle of resemblance, the tabernacle’s length will be threefold its breadth. By the principle of resemblance, the length of the inner house will equal its breadth and will be half the length of the outer house.

Yet we can maintain both what we conjecture concerning the breadth of the tabernacle and what we read generally concerning the measurement of the boards, if we say that the corner boards make up, by half a cubit on either side, the tenth cubit left over by the six boards, and extend one cubit beyond on each side. For in this way the tabernacle undoubtedly stood more firmly and withstood the force of winds more powerfully. I believe that he intended to indicate such an arrangement when he said: “For the western side of the tabernacle you shall make six boards; and again, two others which shall be raised at the corners behind the tabernacle”; and again: “He made six boards from these same materials, and two others for each corner of the tabernacle at the rear.”

For they are said to be behind, or at the back of, the tabernacle in relation to the side walls. If they are joined only at the side of the walls, there is nothing in relation to which they can be called behind or at the back. Therefore, according to what has been said, the western face of the tabernacle is ten cubits broad inside and twelve cubits broad outside. Perhaps this is what Ezekiel intended to be understood when, among other things, he adds in the description of the temple: “And he measured the fronts, six cubits broad on this side and six cubits broad on that side—the breadth of the tabernacle” (Ezek. 4). We have expounded this more fully in its place. But here one need only observe that the tabernacle’s breadth is called a doubled six.

It should further be noted that the eastern part of the temple, around the gate on the inside, had as much width as the entire external breadth of the western part of the tabernacle. It must unquestionably be maintained, according to the reading of Exodus, that there were five bars along all three walls of the tabernacle: one near the top of the boards, another near the bottom, a third near the middle, a fourth between the middle and the top, and a fifth between the middle and the bottom. For the opinion of some about bars five cubits long seems so frivolous and so contrary to authority that it scarcely appears worthy of refutation. [Col. 0217B–0218D]

## CHAPTER IX. On erecting the tabernacle

[Col. 0219A] It remains to say those things concerning the tabernacle which must be added about its erection. First the boards were raised upon their bases; then the wall-bars were inserted through the rings. Next was inserted that bar which, according to the book, passed through the middle of the boards from corner to corner to hold the walls together, at the place where the veil hung at the entrance of the tabernacle. After this, cords were stretched tightly across the tabernacle and fastened securely to pegs fixed at a distance from the tabernacle. Thus they both held the tabernacle itself firm and unmoved against the violence of winds, and supported its covering, lest it sag above and collect the water of overflowing rains—lest, in turn, both the hollow itself increase through the accumulation of water and the collection of water increase through the deepening hollow, until at last the excessive weight either tore the covering completely apart or, tearing it away, dragged it inward and downward.

On the western side, cords hooked from the inner side descended obliquely over the top of the walls to the ground below and, firmly fastened to pegs, held the tabernacle on that side. Likewise, on the eastern side, we must understand that cords descended from the aforesaid bar and from the ends of the walls, and, stretched to pegs, held the tabernacle on that side. Those who wrap the tabernacle as though in an infant’s swaddling-clothes cannot discover the use of the pegs, though they read, if they wish, the following concerning them: “You shall make of bronze all the vessels of the tabernacle for every use and ceremony, both its pegs and those of the court” (Exod. 27). [Col. 0219A–C]

## CHAPTER X. On laying on the coverings

Once the tabernacle has been erected and stretched with cords in the aforesaid manner, the covering of ten curtains must first be laid over it, so that the first has its outer side toward the East and the last has its outer side toward the West. In the dimension in which the whole covering was said above to be forty cubits, only one cubit descends at the front, thirty are spread over the length of the tabernacle, and the remaining nine cubits descend obliquely along the cords at the rear. In the dimension in which it measured twenty-eight cubits, the middle ten cubits are spread across the breadth of the tabernacle, while nine descend on this side and nine on the other side.

Then, with cords fastened to the first pegs opposite the fronts on either side, passed through the first loops of the sides, then hooked again to another peg, and so in turn attached and tightened—now to loops, now to pegs—the covering is stretched over the cords previously drawn tight, so that it appears to form a kind of hanging addition around three sides of the tabernacle. In the loops which its eastern side bore at the front, it must have a cord inserted by which the covering is to be stretched on that side, lest it be damaged by any force of wind or deflected from its proper position by any slackening.

Over this covering the red-dyed covering is to be spread, and over that the covering of blue skins. Uppermost we must lay the goats’-hair covering, so that it appears on every side to exceed the curtain-covering by one cubit, and so that it has the doubled covering entirely at the front. As we have taught concerning the curtain-covering, so we must also fasten and stretch this covering to the pegs according to the same analogy.

Now it is plainly understood how the covering is doubled at the front; how the rear of the tabernacle is covered by half of the eleventh covering; and how one cubit hangs down on each side. Now it is understood how the stated stretching of the curtains forms, as it were, a hanging addition around three sides of the tabernacle. This might serve the priests for putting on or taking off sacred garments, or for other such uses; and there those who did not dare to enter the tabernacle could behold its beauty.

For what purpose was the beauty of the hanging curtains, the gold of the rings, the gilding of the bars, or the external gilding of the boards, if everything was wrapped so that no one could see it, if everything was wrapped so that it was available for no use or benefit? Why was another veil, in likeness of the curtains, to be made at the entrance of the tabernacle if the folding back of the curtains closed the entire entrance? When Moses commands only the sixth covering to be doubled at the front, why, according to some, is another likewise doubled at the rear? But if their folding back occurs there where the sixth covering hangs at the front, that sixth covering is not merely doubled there but at least tripled. But if, conversely, the folding is laid over the three lowest cubits left beneath the hanging goats’-hair covering, so that the sixth covering may be doubled, and if this overlay is bound with cords so that it may conform to the command, there will undoubtedly no longer be any place by which the priests may enter. What follows concerning the two veils is sufficiently clear in itself and requires no exposition. [Col. 0219C–0220C]

## CHAPTER XI. Description of the altar of burnt offering

The account next concerns the altar of burnt offering, described in this manner: “You shall make an altar of shittim wood, five cubits in length and as many in breadth—that is, square—and three cubits in height. Its horns shall rise from it at the four corners” (Exod. 27). [Col. 0220D] This altar had only four walls. For it was open above; and, as is read later, it was not solid but empty and hollow within. All this is sufficiently clear. But what follows concerning the grate is very intricate and must be examined all the more carefully.

I shall first state what seems to me to be the case; afterwards I shall attempt to prove it from the authority of the text itself. First, then, let two bronze rods, thick enough to support the burnt offerings and wood placed upon them, run from one side of the altar to the other, so that their ends appear outside near the corners and have four bronze rings fitted into them. They should be fitted so that one half of the altar is above them and the other below them. From these there should rise inwardly four bronze uprights, like the four feet of the grate: two on this side near one side wall, and two on the other side near the opposite wall. At their tops a bronze grate, like a net according to the book, must be made. It should be made at such a height that it and the altar correspond in a single level.

Thus the rods first mentioned were, as it were, the bases of the grate, and the four uprights were its feet. All these things ought to be fitted and joined together so as to form, as it were, one body, and so that they cannot be torn away either from one another or from the altar. There were two little doors in the rear wall, namely in the upper half of the altar. One hung from one side and the other from the other side, and when closed they met in the middle.

The altar’s *arula*—little platform—was nothing other than a somewhat thick bronze slab. Nor was it brought in through the doorway formed by the little doors, nor laid upon the bases of the grate and upon the threshold of the doorway; nevertheless, first the entire lower half of the altar, up to the level of the grate, was filled with earth. Through this doorway wood was brought in to feed the fire, and through the same doorway ashes were removed. The altar itself was filled halfway with earth so that it might stand firm while sacrifice was being offered, and so that it might satisfy the Lord’s command: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. 20). The grate itself served as the upper surface of the altar, on which the burnt offering was customarily placed and burned with fire beneath.

Those, therefore, labour under an empty supposition who think that sacrifice could not be offered on the altar without steps or some elevation. For it was only three cubits high. We must now consider whether Scripture itself agrees with what we have said concerning the grate. The text concerning the grate reads: “And you shall make a bronze grate in the manner of a net”—where “you shall make” is understood—“at whose four corners shall be four bronze rings, which you shall place beneath the altar’s *arula*.”

Observe that the rings were at the corners of the grate and beneath the altar’s *arula*. And it adds: “The grate shall extend to the middle of the altar.” If it reaches to the middle of the altar, then it extends to its middle either from the bottom upward or from the top downward. Let us compare this passage with what is read much later concerning the same grate: “And he made its bronze grate in the manner of a net; and beneath it, in the middle of the altar, the *arula*, casting four rings at the four extremities of the net” (Exod. 38). If the *arula* was beneath the grate and in the middle of the altar, then the grate occupied the upper half of the altar; otherwise it itself would have been beneath the *arula*. [Col. 0221A–0221D]

It should be noted that the bases were connected with the grate in one respect and not connected with it in another. In one respect they seem not to belong to the grate, because grates do not normally have bases. Yet in another respect they did belong to it, because it rested upon them. Therefore it is rightly said of the hearth [Col. 0222A] that it was beneath the grate, although it lay above the bases: “He cast four rings at the four extremities of the network.” Sometimes *summitas* (“upper end”) means the same as “extremity.” Therefore they were either at the upper or at the lower extremities. But this is determined by what is said in the first description: “At its four corners there shall be four bronze rings, which you shall place beneath the hearth of the altar.” If the hearth was beneath the grate, and the rings beneath the hearth, then they were at the lower extremities. For if they were at the upper extremities, so that the hearth had the rings beneath it, it would necessarily also have the top, and thus the entire grate, beneath it.

And note that, if the rings were beneath the grate and at its corners, then [Col. 0222B] some portion of the grate was beneath the hearth, where corners could be present and from which the rings could hang, so as to be below the hearth itself. They were therefore where the bases, lying beneath the grate and rising upward as uprights, formed corners, because they hung from the extremities of the bases. Thus the rings were beneath the hearth, not because it rested upon them, but because the hearth occupied a higher position.

It remains only to ask whether the rings of the altar and of the grate were the same rings. Let us therefore hear what is added to the foregoing in the first description: “You shall make two poles for the altar of acacia wood, cover them with bronze plates, and pass them through the rings. They shall be on both sides of the altar for carrying it.” If the poles were on both sides of the altar, then so also were the rings through which the poles were to be passed. Thus [Col. 0222C] the grate has rings, and the altar has circles. But are the altar’s circles and the grate’s rings different?

Let us compare, if you please, with what is said in this description what is explained about the same matter in the recapitulation: “He cast four rings at the four extremities of the network for inserting the poles to carry it; he made the poles themselves of acacia wood, covered them with bronze plates, and inserted them into the circles projecting from the sides of the altar” (ibid.). Certainly, as you hear, he made the poles to be inserted into the rings of the grate, and “inserted them,” he says, “into the rings of the altar.” Certainly the grate was within the altar, with the hearth beneath it in the middle of the altar. But were the rings that hung from the extremities of the grate likewise within [Col. 0222D] the altar? How, then, could the very same poles be inserted into rings hidden inside and passed through rings projecting outwardly from the sides of the altar? But who could say this? It follows, therefore, that the rings of the grate and the circles of the altar are precisely the same, and that the poles inserted in them are the same poles, not different ones. It follows, therefore, that the extremities of the grate itself must also appear outwardly through the middle of the walls; from them hung the rings that projected from the sides of the altar.

Thus, what we said above concerning the altar or its grate we have established by the authority of the text itself. But what was said concerning the entrance of the little doors can be inferred not so much from manifest textual authority as from manifest reasoning, as has already partly been shown above.

## SECOND TREATISE: On Solomon’s Temple According to the Literal Sense

[Col. 0223]

[Col. 0223A] The description of Solomon’s temple according to the Book of Kings is for the most part sufficiently clear, but in certain places very perplexing and exceedingly obscure. At the urging of certain persons, whom I gladly serve, I am compelled, where explanation is needed in these matters, to state what I think.

The time of construction is first specified when it is said: “In the four hundred and eightieth year after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign over Israel, in the month Ziv—that is, the second month—he began to build the house for the Lord” (3 Kings 6). In construing the words “in the fourth year,” one should attend to “of King Solomon over Israel.” For the phrase “in the month Ziv, that is, the second month” is parenthetical. This is expressed more plainly in Chronicles, [Col. 0223B] where it is read: “He began to build in the second month, in the fourth year of his reign” (2 Chronicles 3).

The dimensions of the temple are specified in what follows: “The house which King Solomon was building for the Lord was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.” The statement that it was thirty cubits high must be understood of the first storey beneath the first upper chamber. For the whole height of the house was certainly one hundred and twenty cubits, as the Book of Chronicles declares in these words: “Its height was one hundred and twenty cubits.” The same book shows later that it had upper chambers: “He also covered the upper chambers with gold.”

It should be noted that the stated measurement of the temple’s length [Col. 0223C] and breadth is measured within the walls, as compelling reasoning makes evident from what is later said concerning the cherubim.

He describes the dimensions of the porch when he adds: “The porch before the temple was twenty cubits long, corresponding to the measure of the temple’s breadth, and it was ten cubits wide before the face of the temple.” It follows: “He made in the temple slanting windows.” That is, they were broader inside and narrower outside.

There were three exterior galleries adjoining the walls: one on one side opposite the lower part of the temple; a second above the first, opposite the first upper chamber; and a third above the second, opposite the second upper chamber. The author subsequently describes the floors that covered these galleries when he adds these words: “He built storeys against the wall of the temple round about, along the walls of the house surrounding the temple and the oracle.” These side-buildings adjoining the temple lay alongside it; indeed, they were as though its sides: “And he made,” he says, “the side-chambers.” The lower storey was five cubits wide; the middle storey was six cubits wide; and [Col. 0224A] the third storey was seven cubits wide. Thus far the measurement. He further adds the method: “He placed beams round about on the outside of the house, so that they should not be fastened into the walls of the temple.”

The phrase “so that they should not be fastened into the walls of the temple” should be understood of the storeys, not of the beams. For beams were placed against the walls opposite the floor of the first upper chamber, and columns received their ends on the other side. Upon these beams was a wooden floor covering the first gallery, five cubits wide; yet this wooden flooring or storey did not extend all the way to the wall. From what I have said concerning the first, one may understand what should be thought concerning the second and third, except that the measurement of each differed from the others, as the book specifies. The upper storey, which covered the gallery seven cubits wide, corresponded with the roof of the temple. Therefore, because the wall of the temple bore the beams with the storeys placed upon them, he says that he built storeys upon the wall of the temple.

It should further be noted how suitably each storey of the temple had galleries around it, where those who did not dare enter the temple could gather, even in rainy weather, for walking—or rather for prayer. How, or from where, one ascended from the lower to the middle level, or from the middle side to the upper, is determined sufficiently clearly after a few intervening words.

It follows: “When the house was being built, it was built of stones hewn and finished.” When something is hewn finely enough according to customary practice, and then is hewn still more finely beyond the customary degree, it is made, as it were, *dedolatum*—“re-hewn”—from what had already been hewn. Or *dedolatum* means hewn, as it were, on every side. For all the stones of that temple were hewn on all six surfaces.

Observe how orderly he proceeds in his description. Beginning with the exterior, after describing the sides he treats of the wall of the temple, which next comes first into view. But it is very remarkable what he says when he later adds: “Hammer, axe, and every iron tool were not heard in the house while it was being built.” This we can sufficiently understand concerning the stonework. For all the stones together, and all the wood, were hewn elsewhere and polished with the utmost care. Yet there are those who think that such a structure could by no means be raised and joined into one from such varied material without instruments of this kind. For, to say nothing of the rest, how could those nails, of which Scripture speaks later, be firmly driven in without some kind of hammer—golden, silver, wooden, or some other? Or perhaps the kind of hammers excluded is specified in the words, “and no iron tool was heard [Col. 0225A] in the house while it was being built”? But, to say what I think, it is not surprising if in Solomon’s works we find things which we can more rightly wonder at than investigate.

It follows: “The entrance of the middle side-chamber was in the right-hand wall of the house; and by a spiral stair they ascended to the middle upper chamber, and from the middle to the third.” Here we have what we have already maintained above. For these words describe how, and by what route, one ascended and entered from the lowest side-chamber into the middle side-chamber. “The entrance,” he says, “of the middle side-chamber”—that side-chamber which was six cubits wide and held the middle position between the lowest and the highest—“was in the right-hand wall of the house.” “Right-hand” should be read substantively; with respect to the added word “house,” transitively. Here, then, is where and at what point one entered; but how did one ascend there? “And by [Col. 0225B] a spiral stair they ascended to the middle upper chamber.”

Observe how artfully he states one thing openly and indicates another silently. He specifies the entrance of the middle side-chamber but says nothing of the entrance of the middle upper chamber. Conversely, he speaks of the route of ascent to the middle upper chamber, but seems silently to pass over the route of ascent to the middle side-chamber. Yet in each case, what he leaves unsaid about one is made understood from what he says of the other. One route of ascent served both, and an entrance thirty cubits up was open to both. This route was in the wall—that is, in the wall itself—on the right-hand, that is, southern, side; it rose gradually in a circuit toward the upper levels. Hence Scripture calls it a *coclea*, such as common usage also calls a vine.

From what has been said concerning the route and entrance of the middle side-chamber, we may understand what we ought to think concerning the third. The phrase “the middle upper chamber, and the third” must not be understood as though there were three upper chambers there; rather, the one previously discussed was the middle of the three storeys, while that discussed second held the uppermost, third position. In the two upper chambers there were three floors: namely, the floor of each, and the roof of the entire house. Some think these are here called the threefold upper chamber. But if the author had meant this, he certainly would not have said: “By the spiral stair they ascended to the middle upper chamber and from the middle to the third.” Rather, he would have said: “By the spiral stair they ascended to the first upper chamber, and from the first to the middle, and from the middle to [Col. 0225D] the third.” Nor is it correct to say that one ascends “into” a floor, but rather “to” a floor.

It follows: “He built the house and completed it.” Although, he says, the structure was great and its method of construction marvellous, where neither hammer nor axe was heard, nevertheless he built and completed it. Beginning with the exterior, after treating of the lateral extremities, he immediately adds concerning the upper extremities: “He also covered the house with cedar ceilings.” That this is said of the highest ceilings is shown by the word “covered.” He adds further concerning what was at the upper extremities: “He built a storey over the whole house, five cubits high.” The roof of the house, following Palestinian custom, is believed to have been flat. So far as appears, these storeys, five cubits high, were constructed round about at the upper extremities in order to protect from accidental falls those walking above. But the following statement must be understood of the roof of the house itself: “And he covered the house with cedar wood.”

Having described the exterior of the temple, before treating of its interior the author wonderfully commends and magnifies the work itself by a divine response. In this he makes his readers in every way attentive and well disposed, lest anyone perhaps think it idle that he describes every detail so carefully.

The author therefore adds and says: “And the word of the Lord came to Solomon, saying: ‘This house which you are building—if you walk in my precepts, perform my judgments, and keep all my commandments by walking in them—I will establish for you my word which I spoke to David your father; I will dwell among the children of Israel, and I will not abandon my people Israel.’” All this is sufficiently clear in itself and needs no exposition from us. Yet I add this also: perhaps Solomon received this divine response while at work, and divine favour graciously attended his good beginning; and the matters were written in the same order in which they were fulfilled.

It follows: “Therefore Solomon built the house and completed it.” He had already said this above; but now he repeats it after showing by the divine response how great was the dignity and authority of the house which the Lord foretold that he wished to inhabit—as if he had said more explicitly: “He built and completed the work which possessed so great a dignity.” Perhaps this commendation of the temple may also serve to prevent any reader from daring to rebuke me because he sees me examining and explaining obscure matters with such care.

Above he described the exterior of the temple; now he begins to describe its interior: “He built the walls of the house within with cedar boards.” One and the same wall was marble on the outside and covered with boards within; not merely in part, but throughout. This is explicitly determined by what follows: “From the floor of the house to the top of the walls, and up to [Col. 0226D] the ceilings, he covered the interior with wood.” He thus covered the walls everywhere with wood up to the tops of the ceilings. “And he covered the floor of the house with fir boards.” Here is the difference between floor and wall: the former is covered with fir boards, the latter with cedar boards.

After this he describes the partition that divided the outer temple from the Holy of Holies: “At the rear of the temple he built cedar boards for twenty cubits, from the floor to the upper parts, and made the inner house of the oracle into the Holy of Holies.”

It should be noted that these boards are said to have been raised from the floor to the upper parts, but not to the ceilings. For to the ceilings there were more than twenty cubits in height: the lowest storey of the temple, as stated above, was thirty cubits high. “And he made,” he says, “the inner house of the oracle into the Holy of Holies.” Properly speaking, an oracle is a divine answer given to a person by God, whether directly, through an angel, or through a human being; hence we speak of the oracles of the prophets. “Oracle” also denotes the mercy-seat, or that place in the temple where answers were given and from which they were heard, as is read in Exodus: “You shall make two golden cherubim, hammered out at each end of the oracle” (Exod. 25). Concerning this place the Lord says to Moses: “From there I shall give commands and speak to you: namely, from above the mercy-seat and between the two cherubim” (ibid.). Sometimes “oracle” means the entire inner house in which that place was contained. But here the word “oracle” must be understood in its first sense. For because it was especially dedicated to that kind of function, it is rightly called the house of the oracle.

What follows determines the length of both houses: “The temple itself before the doors of the oracle was forty cubits.” If the outer temple was forty cubits long, twenty cubits in length remained for the inner house, since the temple was sixty cubits long. Here “oracle” must mean the inner house. “Before the doors” means the same as “in front of the doors.”

He repeats the statement given above in order to add: “And the whole house inside was lined with cedar, having carved mouldings, its joints wrought by craftsmanship, and projecting carvings.” Everything was lined with cedar boards; no stone at all could appear in the wall. Concerning what is set forth here, I shall state what seems to me. I understand the cedar boards in the same way as the gold plates mentioned later: they were equal-sided, square work made with a rule, and, according to the book, had circular mouldings traced with a lathe; within the circles cherubim and palms were carved.

These boards were joined in the following manner. Between posts attached to the inner wall and evenly spaced from one another, certain small beams were fixed to the posts on both sides, arranged from floor to ceiling. They received the described boards above and below; for the boards were inserted into their grooves and secured with nails. Therefore these small beams are called “joints,” because the wall-panelling was joined into one framework by means of them. According to the same design, and with similar timbers by which the boards were joined above and below, understand joints also on both sides. In these joints there was carved an artistic interlacing, a knotty intertwining of braided bands, as the Book of Chronicles, if I recall correctly, mentions in these words: “He carved upon it”—that is, upon the house—“palms, and little chains as though embracing one another” (2 Chron. 3).

It follows: “He had made the oracle in the middle of the house, in the inner part, in order that the ark of the covenant of the Lord might be placed there.” Here “oracle” must mean the place in which [Col. 0228A] the ark stood in the middle between the cherubim. For the inner house was not in the middle of the outer house, nor could it be in the middle of itself. In saying “in the middle of the house,” “house” must here mean the entire temple; and in adding “in the inner part,” we must take “inner part” to mean the inner house.

But immediately afterward “oracle” is used for the whole inner house when he adds: “The oracle was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high; and he covered it and lined it with the purest gold.” His statement that it was twenty cubits high is meant of that wall especially made for the oracle, which he also mentioned above. [Col. 0228B] Perhaps someone will suppose that the first upper chamber was lower at that location. But if we bring forward what we read in Chronicles, perhaps what we seek will become clear more quickly. For after speaking of the inner house and the two cherubim, it immediately adds: “He also made a veil of hyacinth, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, and wove cherubim into it.” Who could doubt that this is to be understood of the veil mentioned in the Gospel: “And the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom” (Mark 5)? All teachers and interpreters of Scripture agree that the veil was torn in order that what lay within the Holy of Holies might be opened to view.

Where then, I ask, did this veil hang, separating the holy place from the Holy of Holies? If we say that it was suspended before the wall, what benefit did its tearing confer, if, once it was torn, the wall itself remained intact? We must therefore hold without ambiguity that the said veil hung opposite those ten cubits in the upper part that exceeded the wall’s height of twenty cubits, and at that point divided the holy place from the Holy of Holies.

In order better to understand what we wish to say concerning the position of the ark and the two cherubim, let us bring forward what we read in Chronicles about them in these words: “The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the Lord into its place—that is, into the oracle of the temple, into the Holy of Holies—beneath the wings of the cherubim, so that the cherubim spread their wings over the place where the ark was set, and covered the ark itself with their coverings. But because the poles by which the ark was carried were somewhat longer, their ends were visible before the oracle. Yet if anyone stood a little farther outside, he could not see them.”

It should therefore be noted what you read here concerning the poles of the ark, which, according to the wording of Exodus, always remained in the rings of the ark and were never withdrawn from them. It is said of these poles inserted in the ark’s rings that their ends appeared to those standing nearer, outside the oracle; but they could not be seen by persons slightly farther away. From this it is understood that the poles carrying the ark lay, on one side, across the top of the wall twenty cubits high, so that their ends appeared outside. These ends were covered on their outer side by the said veil descending at that point. Those who stood near the wall could see the portions showing between the top of the wall and the lower edge of the veil; but those farther away could not see them because of the intervening veil.

The following, read later in this same book concerning these same poles, seems to concur with this interpretation: “When the poles projected and their ends appeared outside the sanctuary before the oracle, they did not appear farther outside.” Here likewise we have that the ends of the poles appeared outside the sanctuary and before the oracle, from their elevated position. Observe the phrase added: “They did not appear farther outside.” First it is shown that they appeared outside; afterward it is said that they did not appear farther outside [Col. 0229B]—a new and unusual manner of speaking, “farther outside.” The place before the oracle, adjoining the wall, was indeed outside; any more distant place could be called “farther outside” by comparison. Therefore, insofar as the ends of the poles could be seen from the place immediately adjoining, it is said that they did not appear farther outside.

From this it is easy to perceive that there had to be something on the inner side to receive the poles. But precisely how this could have been done is easily perceived and is left to the conjecture of readers.

In saying that he covered the altar with cedar, it is noted that its original construction was of stone. What follows concerning the two cherubim is so clear that it needs no exposition: “At the entrance of the oracle he made little doors of olive wood, doorposts with five angles, and two doors of olive wood.” Contrary to the usage familiar to us, both at the entrance of the oracle and at the entrance of the temple there were two doors: one hung on the inner side and the other on the outer side, respectively; and each was made of two little doors—that is, two joined leaves. One leaf did not hang on one side and the other on the other side, as is customary with folding doors. Rather, two little doors were joined by a kind of golden chain into one door, so that, folded together, they occupied half the entrance, but unfolded they closed the entire doorway.

It should be noted that doorposts are sometimes cut to have four angles, sometimes five, and sometimes six, seven, or even eight. The workmanship is therefore indicated by the words: “doorposts with five angles.” These doorposts must be understood as erected before the entrance to the oracle, as far from the wall as the folded door could extend, and with as much space between one post and the other as the unfolded door could close. The space between the posts and the walls was covered with boarding above and on both sides. One of the doors hung from the post on one side, while the other hung from the wall on the other side. It is appropriate that he first says he made “little doors” and afterward says he made “doors,” since two doors were made from four little doors. The specification of the material seems superfluous.

We have now dealt with the entrance of the oracle; let us see what is said of the entrance of the temple: “At the entrance of the temple he made four-angled doorposts of olive wood, and two doors of fir wood, respectively.” Above we had five-angled posts; here we have four-angled posts. There the doors are described as of olive wood; here, of fir wood. The word “respectively” must be understood of these as of the former. For in both places there were two doors, and in both places one hung on the southern side and the other on the northern, so that one was fixed on the inner side and the other on the outer side. What is then added of these applies equally to the former: “Each door was double and opened by folding back upon itself.” In both places each door was double, because each was made, as I have already taught regarding the inner doors, from two little doors—that is, two leaves. The leaves did not hang separately on either side, but opened while holding one another; in opening and closing they were alternately folded together and unfolded.

Note that, at an entrance, projections are commonly made in the wall on both sides, against which the door strikes on either side when the entrance is closed. But since in this temple everything was covered with wood within, in place of such projections there were two posts on the inner side and two others on the outer side. Each, as is said, was four-angled, as the plan of the construction at that point, or indeed the symbolic rationale, required.

What we read here concerning the doors resembles what we find in Ezekiel’s description of the temple: “There were two doors,” he says, “in the temple and in the sanctuary; and in each of the two doors there were two little doors on either side, folding into one another. For there were two little doors on either side of the doors.”

What he says later concerning the inner wall of the court must also be understood of the temple wall; but it is said of that which would seem less likely: “He built,” he says, “the inner court with three courses of polished stones and one course of cedar wood.” In the principal buildings of our own time, only the facing stones, both inner and outer, are normally polished; the space between them is normally filled with smaller and wholly unpolished stones. But in Solomon’s works, both the stones occupying the middle and those appearing inwardly and outwardly were thoroughly polished, so that there were three courses of polished stone—the two facing courses and the third intervening course—while the fourth course was of wood, because everything inside was lined with cedar.

Having completed what he intended to say concerning the building of the temple, he repeats what he had set forth at the beginning of the description. He repeats the time when construction began, in order to add when it was completed and state how long it took: “In the fourth year the house of the Lord was founded, in the month Ziv; and in the eleventh year, in the month Bul—that is, the eighth month—the house was completed in all its work and in all [Col. 0231A] its furnishings. And he built it in seven years.”

Having completed the description of the temple, he adds concerning the house Solomon made for himself, adding also a reference to the House of the Forest of Lebanon. He treats the royal house more fully; he only mentions the House of the Forest of Lebanon: “Solomon built his own house in thirteen years and brought it entirely to completion.” Thus far the time. Then, with the House of the Forest of Lebanon inserted parenthetically, he adds concerning the form and size of the royal house. For the phrase added to what had been said of the royal house, “he also built the House of the Forest of Lebanon,” was parenthetical. What is added concerning the dimensions—“one hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, thirty cubits high, [Col. 0231B] and four galleries between cedar columns”—must not be understood of the House of the Forest of Lebanon.

Weapons were stored in the House of the Forest of Lebanon, as is read later: “King Solomon also made two hundred shields of gold and three hundred bucklers of tested gold; and the king placed them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon” (3 Kings 10). Hence that same place was called the armoury. Thus it is written in Chronicles concerning the aforesaid arms: “And the king placed them in the armoury, which was planted with trees” (2 Chronicles 9).

Note that this place is said to have been planted with trees; hence, owing to a certain resemblance, it was called the Forest of Lebanon. Thus far concerning the armoury. Let us now consider what is said of the royal house. Its dimensions are clear; let us see what is said of its construction.

As is gathered from what follows, there were three rows of columns there, each row having fifteen columns. One row divided the entire house from front to back into two halves. Another row divided one half into two; the third divided the other half into the same number. Thus there were four galleries distinguished by three rows of columns. Hence he further adds: “For he had cut cedar timbers into columns and covered the whole vaulted roof with cedar boarding.” By saying “vaulted roof” (*camera*), he expresses very concisely the construction of the upper part. For *kameron* in Greek means “curved” or “convex” in Latin. Thus the whole overlying curved structure was covered with cedar boards and supported by forty-five columns. One row had fifteen columns set opposite one another. From this passage we have what we said above concerning the rows of columns and the galleries.

Observe how ingeniously the construction of the portico is conveyed by its being called the portico of columns: namely, because on the outer side, being without a wall, it was distinguished by columns. What is subsequently added concerning the other two porticoes after the greater portico seems to mean that one of them was in front of the greater portico on one side and the other similarly on the other side; in the latter was the tribunal, that is, the judicial seat.

He briefly mentions the house of Pharaoh’s daughter, where he also adds a general statement about the preceding buildings, both of queen and king: “All were of precious stones, cut according to a certain rule and measure, both within and without, from the foundation to the top of the walls” (3 Kings 7). Stones are said to be “sawn” in buildings both inwardly and outwardly when the facing stones on both the inner and outer sides are so arranged that the joints of the upper stones do not coincide with the joints of those beneath.

But note the phrase: “according to a certain rule and measure.” They are laid in alternating courses according to one measure when the joint of the upper stones always falls opposite the middle of the lower stones. But he who first said that they were alternately laid both within and without [Col. 0232B]—why does he further add, “and from within to the great court”? What is first said, “within,” must be understood of the inner surface; what is repeated a second time, “within,” must be understood of the interior of the wall itself. For the stones hidden within were alternately laid with the stones which appeared outwardly on either side: “The foundations were of precious stones, of great stones, ten or eight cubits; and above them were precious stones cut to equal measure.”

As in the foundation, so also in the upper portions, not all could have been of precisely the same measure throughout; otherwise the writer would be found contradictory to himself. Rather, those of the same workmanship and shape were also of the same measure; and those having a similar position also had [Col. 0232C] an equal measure.

It follows: Likewise with cedar. “Likewise,” he says, “it was with cedar: for, in the manner of the stones, a corresponding workmanship was also made of cedar.” In what he had said above, “and as far as the larger court,” it is not sufficiently clear whether that court itself is excluded from, or included in, the preceding general statement; but this is settled by what is added here: “And the great court, round about, was made with three courses of hewn stones and one course of dressed cedar.” He had said the same thing much earlier concerning the inner court of the house of the Lord; what is said here is said of these buildings, but is repeated in this place because of the similarity of the work. Hence follows: “And likewise in the court of the house of the Lord.” Not in just any court, but in the inner court, [Col. 0232D] and in the porch of the house of the Lord.
