The matters said concerning the bronze columns seem very obscure and, unless carefully distinguished, are rendered greatly confused by the equivocal use of the terms themselves. Thus it is said of these columns: “And he set up two columns of bronze, eighteen cubits in height; and a line of twelve cubits encompassed each column.” Here, behold, the columns are said to be eighteen cubits high, whereas in Chronicles they are read as having thirty-five cubits (II Chron. III). But what is said here concerning the height of the column must be understood of the shaft alone, which rises between base and capital.

The word “column,” however, is sometimes taken more narrowly and sometimes more broadly. Taken broadly, it seems to have four parts: first, the base; [Col. 0233A] second, the shaft, which rises upward above the base; third, the epistyle, which is placed above the shaft; fourth, the capital, which is set at the top above the epistyle. Thus by the name “column” we sometimes understand this entire structure, and sometimes the shaft alone, as here, as we have already said.

The name “capital” also customarily has several meanings. For sometimes it denotes the epistyle; sometimes that which is placed upon the epistyle itself; sometimes both taken together. But “epistyle” is not usually said of anything except what adheres to the shaft, from which it receives its name; for *epistylium* signifies “above.” Hence it is called an epistyle because it is set above the shaft. In this description, when we read “head of the column,” it must be taken differently in different places: sometimes for the capital, sometimes for [Col. 0233B] the epistyle, sometimes for the uppermost part of the shaft itself.

Equivocations of this kind commonly confuse the understanding of readers, namely those who do not know—or neglect—to investigate carefully what they read. Since the matters said about the capitals appear very perplexing, I shall first state what seems to me, insofar as I have been able to gather it from this book and from the book of Chronicles; then I shall return to the exposition of the text.

The epistyle was four cubits wide at its base, but three cubits high, and it was fashioned in the form of a lily. A lily flower begins from a rounded form and gradually broadens upward; at its summit it seems to have as many sides as it has petals. Thus much concerning its dimensions and construction.

The second capital is described as being five cubits high [Col. 0233C] and as seeming to have as many sides as the epistyle, so that it might fit more suitably upon that epistyle itself and that conformity might adorn the composition. The second capital customarily begins from the same dimensions at which the first ends; and, ascending obliquely along every side, it often broadens as far as its middle, while its upper half customarily rises straight upward and perpendicularly.

From other considerations, therefore, we may judge what we ought to think concerning these things. In the middle of this second capital, where the workmanship changed, there was a projecting molding carved in the form of a circle, which encircled the whole capital on every side, such as is customarily made on an epistyle at the point where it adheres to the shaft. It had one such circle in the middle, as has been said, and [Col. 0233D] another of the same form at the bottom, where it adhered to the epistyle itself. But because Scripture calls these circles “cords,” we understand that they were carved so as to appear twisted like a triple cord.

There was also, opposite the upper half of this same capital, a feature of the work: a net-like chainwork of bronze. It surrounded that half on every side and hung down from its summit as far as the first cord; there were hung one hundred pomegranates, arranged in a circle around that same cord. Another hundred were set into this netting and arranged in a circle in its middle, so that their circumference divided the whole netting into seven rows [Col. 0234A] and, as it were, divided it equally.

By one “row of netting” here we mean nothing other than a single order of links or chains separating the openings of one row. Understand that the capital had, opposite its lower half, netting like that which we have arranged opposite its upper half, with just as many pomegranates arranged in the same fashion. Thus much I have said concerning these matters, insofar as I was able to gather from Scripture itself; now let us return to the exposition of the text:

“He also made two cast-bronze capitals, to be placed upon the heads of the columns.” Note that he begins his description with the capital that held the highest position in this structure: “One capital five cubits high, and the other capital five cubits high.” Thus much concerning the measurement.

It follows: “And as it were in the form of a net, and of chains woven together in marvellous workmanship.” These capitals, which had little chains, were placed upon the epistyles according to Chronicles. For there we read: “He made two columns, and epistyles, and heads, and certain nettings, as it were, which might cover the heads above the epistyles” (II Chron. III). Thus it says concerning the nets that they covered the heads which were above the epistyles. Note that what are there called “heads” are here called “capitals.”

But this author uses “heads” for epistyles when he says: “He also made two capitals, to be placed upon the heads,” that is, upon the epistyles of the columns. Yet it must not be understood of these capitals that he carved them in the form of a net. The book of Chronicles [Col. 0234C] writes that the aforementioned little chains were placed upon the capitals, not carved into them: “And he made,” it says, “little chains as it were in the oracle, and placed them upon the heads of the columns.” A little later in this description it is said that these capitals were opposite the nets. But whereas there the little chains or nets are said to have been placed upon them, here they are expressed more explicitly and more properly as set opposite them.

Still more is added concerning these capitals or nets: “Each capital of the columns was cast in bronze: nettings of seven rows on one capital, and nettings of seven rows on the other capital.” From these words, according to what we have already said above, it is plainly gathered that the nets on each capital were divided into seven rows. It would perhaps have been clearer had he said “nets of seven rows” rather than “seven nets of rows.” But note that he intends one order of chains running around a capital alone to be called a “net,” just as we call even the smallest cutting of cloth a cloth. Yet one should not be overly concerned with the words used, provided that the author’s meaning is truly understood.

It follows: “And he completed the columns, and two rows around each net, to cover the capitals which were above the summit of the pomegranates.” As we have already said above, on each capital were two nets, and twice seven rows in each net, such that one order of seven rows was above the hundred inserted pomegranates, while another order, likewise of seven rows, was above [Col. 0235A] the hundred pomegranates hanging at the bottom. Therefore it is rightly said: “He completed two rows around each of the nets,” because each had two orders of seven rows.

These nets of seven rows were arranged so as to cover the capitals: for they hung before the capitals themselves and surrounded them about. What is added, “which were above the summit of the pomegranates,” should be referred not so much to the capitals as to the nets: “Each net,” he says, “was above the summit of the pomegranates,” because the upper half of each net was above the summit of the inserted pomegranates, while its lower half was above the summit of the hanging pomegranates.

[Col. 0235B] It follows: “He made the second capital in the same manner.” In the way, he says, in which he made the capital worked first, he also made the capital worked second. For with respect to the workmanship or description, he wishes the former to be called first and the latter second.

Thus much concerning the capitals; now he adds concerning the epistyles: “But the capitals which were above the heads of the columns were fashioned, in the porch, like the work of a lily, four cubits [in size]” (III Kings VI). He describes their construction and measurement quite concisely. “The capitals,” he says—that is, the epistyles—which were above the heads of the columns, that is, above the summit of each shaft, were fashioned like the work of a lily: thus much concerning the construction; “in the porch,” thus much concerning the place; “four cubits,” thus much concerning the measurement. Note that here he calls the epistyles “capitals.”

Also note that above by “heads of the columns” he intended epistyles; but here by “heads of the columns” he intends the upper parts of the shafts. At the end of this book this capital—or, rather, epistyle—is described as three cubits high; accordingly, what is read here concerning its measurement is rightly understood of its width. It was therefore four cubits wide at the lower part, that is, slightly broader than the column, but it widened toward the top in the form of a lily.

It follows: “And again other capitals above, at the summit of the columns, according to the measure of the column, opposite the nets.” In what he now says, he returns to the capitals which he described earlier. For “and again [Col. 0235D] other” means other not than the four previously mentioned, but than the two most recently described. But, lest some uncertainty arise, this is settled by the words “opposite the nets.” For if anyone should understand “at the summit of the columns above” as referring to a third pair of capitals, their placement opposite the stated nets would certainly not hold.

What he says—that the heads were made according to the measure of the column—must not be understood as though both had the same thickness. This statement indicates not equality but proportion. For to assign the measurement of the capitals in relation to the measurement of the columns is the same as saying: the capitals had such dimensions as the size of the columns required.

Thus he briefly repeats concerning capitals and nets [Col. 0236A] in order to add more suitably concerning the pomegranates, of which he had said nothing up to this point: “There were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital” (III Kings VII). If you attend to the order of placement, the epistyle was first placed above the shaft; second came that capital which had two hundred rows of pomegranates in two nets. By this reckoning the epistyle is rightly called the first capital, while that of which he now speaks is the second: “There were,” he says, “two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital.”

Where there is no plurality, there can be no order. Wherever there is an order, therefore, there cannot be fewer than two. Thus where there were two hundred rows of pomegranates, there could not have been fewer than four hundred. Much further below we again read concerning these pomegranates: “Two rows of pomegranates in each net.” Here they are said to have been around the capital; but their arrangement is determined there, because they were in the nets that surrounded the capital. Yet I do not see how they could have been in the nets unless they were inserted or hung. But from Chronicles we have that one hundred were inserted; hence it is established that the rest were hung: “He made,” it says, “one hundred pomegranates which he inserted among the little chains” (II Chron. III).

If, therefore, one hundred pomegranates inserted in one net were arranged around the capital in such a way that each one had another hanging directly beneath it, then surely one net contained one hundred rows. But one capital had, as we have said, two nets; [Col. 0236C] and in the stated manner there were one hundred rows in one and one hundred in the other, and thus is fulfilled what is said: “There were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital.”

What he adds after a few intervening words—“and he placed above the heads of the columns work in the form of a lily”—is a repetition of the statement he had set forth above in these words: “But the capitals which were above the heads of the columns were fashioned like the work of a lily.”

And it should be noted how customary it is for this author to repeat the same statement. After these things he describes a vessel, which he also calls the Sea, in which the priests washed their hands and feet when they were about to minister in the Temple: “He also made a cast Sea, ten cubits from lip to lip, round about; its height was five cubits.” All this is sufficiently clear. But what is immediately attached seems altogether impossible: “And a cord of thirty cubits encircled it round about.” For if a round vessel measures ten cubits from one side to the opposite, it is impossible for a cord of thirty cubits to encircle it. But this question is more suitably resolved in what follows, as will be said in its place.

At the upper part, as is said, a cord of thirty cubits encircled it; but lower down, where a cord of ten cubits could surround it, it had certain pleasing and decorative carvings. This is what immediately follows when it says: “And a sculptured work beneath the lip went round it, encompassing the Sea by ten cubits. Two rows [Col. 0237A] of ribbed sculptured works were cast.” What is said is sufficiently plain and needs no exposition: “The thickness of the laver was three inches.” By “thickness” we must understand its substantial depth; by “laver” here, the same thing as the Sea.

It follows: “Its lip was like the lip of a cup, and like the leaf of an expanded lily.” From this description it is understood that its lip turned outward; and hence that measurement taken beneath the lip is understood which is described above in these words: “And a cord of thirty cubits encircled it round about.” Nor is the measurement of ten cubits taken beneath the lip, but where it reads, “from lip to lip.”

“It held two thousand baths and three thousand measures.” It seems better to pass over these measures rather than say anything, because under the same names different measures are understood among different peoples.

In what follows certain vessels are described in which the burnt offerings were washed, which this book calls *laveres* (“lavers”), while Chronicles calls them *conchae* (“basins”). There we read concerning these basins as follows: “He also made ten basins and placed five on the right and five on the left, that they might wash in them everything which they were to offer in the burnt offering” (II Chron. IV).

In this book he describes the bases of the lavers before the lavers themselves, when he says: “And he made ten bronze bases, each base four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.” Because what is said concerning the dimensions of the bases is obscure, I shall first state what seems to me concerning it; afterward the text will be explained. [Col. 0237C] But, so that our view may be understood better, let us consider the parts severally, as though limb by limb.

First, let two bronze plates, largely perforated, be set out, each four cubits in length and width. One shall have a square opening with equal sides, the other a round opening, so that the side of the square does not exceed the diameter of the other. Let the plate with the square opening lie at the bottom. Above it, around its opening, let four plates be raised, firmly joined both to the first plate and to one another at the four corners of the opening; and let them be three cubits high. At the four corners of the plate lying below, next to the joints of the upright plates, let bronze columns be raised, three cubits high.

The plate with the round opening must rest upon both the upright plates and the columns in such a way as to join everything at the top, just as the first plate joins everything below into one. Above the opening of the uppermost plate there must be placed a kind of hollow hemisphere, having in every respect the form of an inverted basin. The summit of this hemisphere ended in a flat circular surface measuring a cubit and a half in every direction, upon which the laver rested. Around the upper part of the bases, on four sides, extended certain supports, which Scripture calls “shoulders”; these received and supported the bellies of the lavers on every side. What is said concerning the wheels and their axle seems sufficiently plain; but now let us return to the exposition of the text.

[Col. 0238A] Thus it is said concerning these bases: “And the work of the bases was openwork.” This is said of that part where the carvings were. One kind of carving is that in which the outlines of a body are traced merely upon the surface; another is that in which the whole image of the body is formed limb by limb, and the ground between the carvings is hollowed out and removed partly or entirely. Thus, to distinguish it from the other kind of carving, the work of the bases was called “carved away.”

It follows: “And carvings between the joints, and between the borders and interlacings: lions and oxen and cherubim; and likewise above upon the joints.” He calls the four sides of the plate laid beneath “joints”: each of them joined together two columns, one on either side, and the adjoining upright plate. The “joints above,” however, are called the sides of the upper plate, by which the upper parts were likewise joined into one; and carvings are described as present on each of them.

On the bases, around the sides between the columns, on those plates standing upright in a square, borders were carved, and likewise interlacings, like certain twigs artfully intertwined with one another. Between these interlacings, where they folded back into themselves in a circular form, and likewise between the borders and the interlacings, lions, oxen, and cherubim are said to have been carved: “And beneath the lions and oxen, as it were, straps of bronze hanging down; and four wheels for each base, and bronze axles.” All these things are sufficiently clear. What is added concerning the shoulders is likewise clear from what has already been said: “And on the four [Col. 0238C] sides were, as it were, cast shoulders beneath the laver, facing one another.”

These things are plain, but what is added concerning the construction of the lavers seems somewhat obscure: “Moreover, the mouth of the laver was inside, at the summit of its head; and what appeared outside was wholly round, one cubit [wide], and likewise it measured a cubit and a half.” Conceive the construction of the laver itself as the round form of a box without a lid. Its “head” is its upper part; the “summit of the head” is the circumference of its opening. The summit of the head, that is, the rim of the opening itself, encircled and joined to itself a certain round hollow fashioned in the manner of a pipe, which he calls the laver’s “lip,” because what was poured into it passed through it. Its height was half a cubit; half a cubit descended into the vessel’s body, while one cubit appeared outside.

Thus it is said that the mouth of the laver was inside at the summit of its head, because the uppermost rim enclosed within itself the sort of pipe which we have described. After these remarks on the construction of the lavers, he returns to the description of the bases when he adds: “But on the corners of the columns were various carvings; and the spaces between the columns were square, not round.” Thus carvings were present not only on the borders of the bases but also on their corners, which lay outside the circle. By “spaces between the columns” he means the plates described above, raised in a square between the four columns. But if the underlying plate had had a round opening, and a round hollow had risen around it, then the spaces between the columns [Col. 0239A] would not have been square but round.

It follows: “The four wheels also, which were at the four corners of the base, were joined beneath the base.” For the axles on which the bases rested passed from one side of the bases, projected on both sides, and, being inserted into the wheels, joined the wheels to one another. What is added afterward concerning the bases or lavers seems clear from what has already been said.

At the end of the description he again mentions the columns described above, and inserts something he had not said earlier: “And he completed all the work of King Solomon in the temple of the Lord: the two columns and the two cords of the capitals above the heads of the columns, and the two nets, to cover the two cords which were above the heads of the columns.” Until now he had made no mention of the cords of the capitals; now he specifies that there were two above the heads of the columns. He calls them the cords of the capitals because they belonged to the capitals.

But when it is said that he made two cords above the heads of the columns, doubt may arise whether he made one on each, or two on each. This is settled by what is added concerning the nets: “And two nets, to cover the two cords which were above the heads of the columns.” From what has been set forth and explained above, we have that there were two nets on each capital. Therefore, when he says “two nets,” [Col. 0239C] it must be referred to the individual capitals. But the nets of each capital could not cover two cords if there were not two on each.

What else he made is added when he says: “And four hundred pomegranates upon the two nets.” It must certainly be known that here one should read “four hundred,” not “forty,” as many manuscripts, corrupted through scribal error, have. This is easily proved from what is read above: “There were two hundred rows of pomegranates around the second capital.” Whoever does not find this testimony sufficient should consult the Hebrews concerning the Hebrew truth, and will find that what we say is true.

Still more is added concerning these pomegranates, concerning how they were arranged in each net: “Two rows of pomegranates in each net, to cover the cords of the capitals which were above the heads of the columns.” This reading agrees with what is read in Chronicles, where it is written concerning the pomegranates and nets: “Four hundred pomegranates also, and two nets, such that two rows of pomegranates were joined to each net, which protected the epistyles and the heads of the columns.”

Note that one says “rows,” another calls them “orders.” According to what we read and explained above, there were two hundred rows of pomegranates in the two nets: one hundred in one net and one hundred in the other. Thus according to that reading there were one hundred orders in each; according to this reading, two in each. Without doubt there were one hundred under one reckoning and two under another. If you consider one dimension, you will find two hundreds there; if you consider another, you will find one hundred pairs there.

What he had said above about the nets, he repeats concerning the pomegranates. For of both he says that they covered the cords; hence it is understood how far the nets descended, for they had pomegranates hanging from their outer edges opposite the cords. From what has been said above, as we have already shown, it is understood that on one capital there were two nets and only two cords. One row of pomegranates of one net could therefore cover one cord, and one row of the other net likewise cover the other. Why then is it said that [Col. 0240B] in each net were two rows or orders of pomegranates to cover the cords of the capitals?

But this indicates that the beauty of the work, or the logic of its symbolism, did not allow the first row to have a cord opposite it; and therefore a second row was added to each net, so that it could be placed in front at the point where reason required the cord to be placed. Thus the first row of pomegranates in each net divided nets of seven rows, as we said above; but the second row, placed before the cords, obscured them from the sight of those looking on.

Thus I have discussed the more obscure matters as best I could. If anyone should accuse me not so much of falsehood as of prolixity, let him know that I prefer to seem overly lengthy to the learned rather than overly obscure to the simple. But what I have perhaps said too diffusely, any more skilled person is free to reduce to a concise form.

It should be noted that nothing is said concerning the measure of the bases; but how great it was is easily discovered from what is read in this book or in Chronicles. For according to this book the shaft itself was eighteen cubits, while the two capitals measured eight cubits. According to Chronicles, however, the entire column was thirty-five cubits; whence it is established that its base was nine cubits. At the beginning of this description it is read that the Temple was thirty cubits high. If, therefore, the height of the porch corresponded to the height of the Temple, how could it contain columns thirty-five cubits high? From the mutual comparison of these statements it is clearly gathered that one ascended by steps into the porch, and that at the place where the columns stood, the ground of the porch lay five cubits below its pavement.

Now let the matters said at the end of Jeremiah concerning the nets and pomegranates be brought forward, lest perhaps they appear inconsistent with what has been said above: “And the nets,” he says, “and the pomegranates, one hundred, surrounded the nets. And the nets and the pomegranates, ninety-six hanging; and all the pomegranates, one hundred, surrounded the nets” (Jer. LII).

As has been said above, in one net there were one hundred pomegranates inserted in its middle and one hundred hanging from it. From what circumstance it came about that there were no more than ninety-six hanging there in Jeremiah’s time, I confess I do not know. [Col. 0241A] According to the sense given here, one net was composed of one hundred smaller nets: one order of chains interwoven around one order of openings is intended to be understood as one net. If you count from top to bottom, you will find fourteen openings in one row. If you count around the circumference, you will find one hundred openings in a row. Thus there were fourteen nets according to one reckoning, and one hundred according to another.

[Col. 0242A] There were nets of seven rows down to the pomegranates inserted in the middle. Hence he says: “And the nets and the pomegranates, one hundred, surrounded the nets.” And there were another nets of seven rows down to the pomegranates hanging at the bottom. Hence he adds: “And the nets and the pomegranates, ninety-six hanging.” Whether the lower pomegranates hung from the outermost openings or beneath them might be uncertain; but this is determined when he adds the general statement: “And all the pomegranates, one hundred, surrounded the nets.”

## THIRD TREATISE: On the Concordance of the Times of the Kings Co-reigning over Judah and Israel. To the blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

[Col. 0241]

[Col. 0241B] In the matters stated in the book of Kings concerning the duration and varied succession of the reigns, there seems, as you say, to be much contradiction; and for that reason the computation of the numbers is thought to have been corrupted by scribal error. Therefore, before writing anything on these matters in accordance with your request, I consulted Jewish writings through Jews, and learned that both their writings and ours concur in one understanding.

It is therefore established for me that there is no contradiction in these things, although the truth itself has hitherto remained hidden even from them. Far be it from me to believe that truth has anywhere gone so far astray in the divine Scriptures that it cannot altogether be recovered! First, then, it must be known that when we read that some king reigned so many years, it must not always be understood as though each had completed the final year of his reign with no fraction remaining toward its completion. But if the year divided between successor and predecessor were attributed to neither, a large part would be subtracted from the total sum. Therefore, quite suitably and concisely, in order to avoid fractions, Scripture attributes a year shared by two to the person who held the larger part of that year.

Again, if we attend carefully, we shall certainly find that what we often see done in our own times was frequent in those times. We often see kings crown their sons while they themselves are still alive, in order to forestall the contradiction and rebellion of their subjects. This was frequent among the kings of Israel, who feared that their kingdom might return to the house of David through some rebellion. Although this is not openly stated everywhere in Scripture, the Scripture nevertheless contains material from which it can readily be demonstrated in the proper places.

And it should be noted that the periods of co-reigning are sometimes attributed to the father alone, sometimes to the son alone, sometimes both to son and father. For there are those who, although they have already crowned their sons, nevertheless in no way wish them to exercise royal authority while they are living. Such a period of reigning is rightly attributed to the father alone. There are others who, after their sons’ coronation, whether because of bodily or mental weakness, give themselves over to leisure and luxury and entrust all the affairs of the kingdom to their sons. Are not these periods of reigning more rightly ascribed to the son than to the father? But when they administered the business of the kingdom jointly and defended the kingdom against rebels sometimes together and sometimes separately—as Roman emperors are read to have done in their times—are not these periods of reigning rightly ascribed to both?

Behold, Jeroboam king of Israel is said to have reigned twenty-two years, and his son Nadab two years. But if these two are said to have completed twenty-six years in reigning, what is said concerning the comparison of the two kingdoms cannot stand at all. For if Asa king of Judah began to reign in the twentieth year of King Jeroboam, how could Nadab, as is read, begin to reign in the second year of Asa’s reign, and Baasha in the third? But if we understand that Asa began his reign at the end of Jeroboam’s twentieth year, so that the year which was Jeroboam’s twenty-first was Asa’s first, and that which was Jeroboam’s twenty-second was Asa’s second, then this same year was Nadab’s beginning and first year of reign, so that he reigned one year with his father and the greater part of the following year without his father. If, I say, you are willing to take it thus, you will see that there is no contradiction in anything.

Likewise it is said that Baasha, who killed Nadab, began to reign in the third year of Asa’s reign and reigned for twenty-four years. It is therefore understood that Baasha lasted until the twenty-seventh year of King Asa, [Col. 0242D] although he completed it only for the greater part. How then is Elah, Baasha’s son, said to have begun to reign in the twenty-sixth year of King Asa’s reign and to have reigned two years, unless he reigned with his father during Asa’s twenty-sixth year and the first part of the twenty-seventh, and without his father during the latter part of that same year? For at the end of that twenty-seventh year Zimri killed him and reigned in his place for seven days.

It is further read that, when the army [Col. 0243A] heard that Zimri had rebelled and killed the king, all Israel made Omri king for themselves. It is thus clear that the same year which was Zimri’s first year of reigning was Asa’s twenty-eighth. What then is meant by what is read concerning Omri, that he reigned in the thirty-first year of Asa’s reign? We know, however, that when Tibni rebelled, half the people followed one man and half another. Therefore, the statement that he reigned in Asa’s thirty-first year is to be understood of the time when Tibni had already died and Omri began to reign over the whole people. Scripture says that he reigned twelve years. If, then, Asa’s twenty-eighth year was Omri’s first year of reign, it is clear that Asa’s thirty-ninth year was Omri’s twelfth year in the kingdom. How then can it stand that Ahab, [Col. 0243B] Omri’s son, reigned, as is read, in Asa’s thirty-eighth year, unless Ahab undoubtedly reigned with his father for two years?

This view agrees with the statement that Jehoshaphat, son of King Asa, is said to have reigned in the fourth year of Ahab’s reign. For the same year which was Asa’s forty-first was Ahab’s fourth year in the kingdom. Scripture reports that King Asa died in the forty-first year of his reign and that his son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place. Ahab reigned twenty-two years; consequently the same year which was Jehoshaphat’s eighteenth year in the kingdom was Ahab’s twenty-second and final year. But Ahaziah, Ahab’s son, reigned, as is read, in Jehoshaphat’s seventeenth [Col. 0243C] year, and Joram, Ahaziah’s brother, in the eighteenth year: the former, namely, in the next-to-last year of his father, and the latter in that father’s final year. How, then, was it true that Ahaziah reigned two years, or how did he reign for his father, if his brother began to reign in the final year of their father?

This makes it possible to understand that he spent one year in the kingdom with his father and another with his brother. Ahaziah received the kingdom from his father at the end of his father’s penultimate year, and passed the greater part of the following year with his father. That same year, as we have said, which was Ahab’s last, was Jehoshaphat king of Judah’s eighteenth. It follows, therefore, that at the end of that eighteenth year, after his father’s death, Ahaziah was injured by a fall and, despaired of as to life while Elijah prophesied, [Col. 0243D] associated his brother with himself in the kingdom and spent another year ill together with him.

But if Joram, Ahab’s son and Ahaziah’s brother, as is read of him, reigned in the nineteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, what does it mean that shortly afterward he is said to have reigned in the second year of Joram, son of that same Jehoshaphat king of Judah? Perhaps the year which was the son’s second was the father’s eighteenth. It may indeed have happened that, because of illness or some other compelling reason, the father at that time crowned his son, although for some period he did not at all permit him to exercise royal authority.

It should be noted that, when Joram son of Ahab is said to have reigned in the second year of the other Joram, Scripture does not say “of King Joram,” nor does it say “in the second year of [Col. 0244A] his reign,” as it customarily does above with the others. Rather, after mentioning Ahaziah’s death, it adds: “And Joram his brother reigned in his place in the second year of Joram, son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah.” If Ahab’s son reigned in the second year of Jehoshaphat’s son, how is it true that, conversely, Jehoshaphat’s son is said to have reigned in the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab, unless we are meant to understand that from that time, with his father’s consent and direction, he exercised royal authority in part and administered the affairs of the kingdom together with his father?

Thus the years of their joint reign, beginning with that fifth year, are assigned both to son and father; the preceding years are assigned to the father alone. The year which was the fifth for Ahab’s son was the twenty-third for Jehoshaphat, who reigned twenty-five years. [Col. 0244B] Do you wish to know more clearly from Scripture itself that that year was common to all three? “In the fifth year,” it says, “of Joram son of Ahab king of Israel, and of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Joram son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah reigned.” Behold: the same year is said to belong to King Jehoshaphat, to be his son’s first, and to be Ahab’s son’s fifth—not because it was Jehoshaphat’s fifth year, but because it was common to him with the others. Father and son therefore reigned together for three years.

The statement that Jehoshaphat’s son is said to have reigned eight years seems to point to the same conclusion. For after his father’s death he could not have reigned so many years: in the fifth year after Jehoshaphat’s death, Jehu killed both Ahaziah, son of Jehoshaphat’s son, and Joram, [Col. 0244C] son of Ahab. In the kingdom of Judah, this son of Jehoshaphat is found to have been the first to reign jointly with his father.

It should be noted that the same year which was the eighth for Joram king of Judah was the twelfth for Joram king of Israel. How then is it said that Ahaziah, son of Joram king of Judah, reigned for his father and reigned one year, if that same year was the last for his father, for his son, and for the king of Israel? For at the same time, as has already been said, Ahaziah and the king of Israel were killed by Jehu. Yet the son may have reigned with his father for the greater part of the year, and without his father for the remainder. Since he survived his father in the kingdom, he is said to have reigned in his place.

From what has been said it will, I think, be clear how false is the opinion—if I may not say assertion—of certain persons who, in order to solve a spurious question, say that Jehoshaphat’s son reigned twenty years. For the father could not have reigned for twenty [Col. 0244D] years if his son, who reigned in his place in the eighth year of his father—or shortly thereafter—was killed by Jehu. It is clear, as has been said, that Jehu killed Joram son of Ahab, who reigned twelve years; and afterward, concerning that same Jehu, it is said that in the eleventh year of Joram son of Ahab, and of King Ahaziah over Judah, he came to Jezreel and killed Jezebel. What then is meant by the fact that what Jehu did first is said to have been done in the twelfth year of Joram king of Israel, while what he did afterward is said to have been done in the eleventh year of that same king? In a remarkable way, it indicates that, from different points of reference, one and the same year was his eleventh and twelfth. For he reigned eleven years by himself alone, [Col. 0245A] but spent one year in the kingdom with his brother.

It should further be noted that here we find a similar formulation to the one noted above. There it is read: “In the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab king of Israel, and of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Joram son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah reigned.” Here it is said: “In the eleventh year of Joram son of Ahab, and of King Ahaziah over Judah, Jehu came to Jezreel.” There the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab is said to belong both to Jehoshaphat and to Joram himself, although it was the fifth year of Joram alone in the kingdom. Here the eleventh year of that same Joram is said to belong both to Ahaziah and to Joram himself, although it was the eleventh year of Joram alone in the kingdom.

Jehu reigned over Israel eighteen years. In his seventh year Joash, son of Ahaziah, began to reign over Judah and reigned forty years. [Col. 0245B] The same year was Joash’s twenty-second and Jehu’s final year. Joash, Jehu’s son, began to reign in the twenty-third year of Joash and reigned seventeen years. The same year, therefore, was Joash’s last and the thirty-ninth of Joash king of Judah. How then is it written that Joash son of Jehoahaz reigned in the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, unless Jehoahaz appointed his son king three years before his own death?

When Jehoahaz died, his son Joash reigned alone in the fortieth and final year of Joash king of Judah. Accordingly, the first year of Amaziah, son of that king of Judah, is found to be the second year of Joash’s son. Scripture says: “In the second year of Joash, son of Jehoahaz king of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah reigned.”

[Col. 0245C] It should be noted that the time of the joint reign is assigned to the father alone; from this it is inferred that the son exercised no royal power before his father’s death. Joash king of Israel is said to have reigned sixteen years; in his second year Amaziah king of Judah reigned. Therefore, the year which was Joash’s sixteenth and final year was Amaziah’s fifteenth. How then did Jeroboam, son of Joash king of Israel, reign in Amaziah’s fifteenth year, as Scripture says, unless he reigned jointly with his father in his father’s final year? The same year, as we have said, was Joash’s sixteenth and final year, and Amaziah king of Judah’s fifteenth.

Amaziah reigned fourteen years after Joash’s death, yet it is read that he reigned twenty-nine years. [Col. 0245D] What then is meant by the statement that Amaziah lived twenty-five years after Joash’s death, although after that death Scripture finds him reigning for only fourteen years? This indicates that, after the twenty-ninth year of his reign, either because of illness or for some other reason, he withdrew from affairs and, having crowned his son, entrusted the affairs of the kingdom to him. Hence Azariah, called also Uzziah, son of Amaziah, is said to have reigned in the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, as is read later: “In the twentieth year,” it says, “of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah king of Judah reigned.”

As we have already said above, the same year was Jeroboam’s first year in the kingdom and his father’s last year both in kingdom and life. Between the first and the twenty-seventh year there are twenty-five years, during which Amaziah is said to have outlived King Joash. From that time, therefore, Azariah son of Amaziah began to exercise royal authority not merely by his father’s permission but by hereditary right. As was said above, Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the fifteenth year of Amaziah king of Judah. The same year which was Jeroboam’s fifteenth in the kingdom was Amaziah’s twenty-ninth. If Azariah son of Amaziah received the kingdom from his father immediately after his father’s twenty-ninth year, that same year was certainly Azariah’s twenty-sixth and Jeroboam’s forty-first and final year in the kingdom. For Jeroboam reigned forty-one years and Azariah fifty-two years. [Col. 0246B]

What then is meant by the statement that Zechariah, son of Jeroboam, began to reign in Azariah’s thirty-eighth year? Did the kingdom of Israel remain without a king from Azariah’s twenty-seventh year until his thirty-eighth? It may indeed be doubted whether, because of his age, rebellion, or some other cause, he was unable up to then to prevail in his father’s kingdom. The statement that Zechariah son of Jeroboam reigned in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah must be understood thus: he began to reign in the thirty-eighth year and reigned for six months, not so much of that year as of the following; and after him Shallum, who killed him, reigned for one month. After them Menahem, beginning to reign in that same thirty-ninth year, spent the smaller [Col. 0246C] part of it in the kingdom. For if he had spent the larger part of that year in it, Scripture, in accordance with its custom, would assign him not merely ten but eleven years.

What is said of Pekahiah or Pekah seems sufficiently clear. Jotham son of Uzziah is recorded to have reigned sixteen (sic) years, yet Hoshea king of Israel is reported to have reigned in Jotham’s twentieth year. This indicates that Jotham lived twenty years in the kingdom, but from the sixteenth year made his son king; and that, for whatever reason, he deserved to be so far elevated in the kingdom that the periods of joint reign were assigned to the son rather than to the father.

In the second year of Pekah, who reigned twenty years, Jotham king of Judah began to reign. Therefore the same year was Jotham’s sixteenth [Col. 0246D] and Pekah’s seventeenth. In Pekah’s seventeenth year Ahaz son of Jotham began to reign, but, as may be understood, at the end of that same year. For if he had reigned throughout that year, or for the larger part of it, I do not see why that year would not have been assigned to Ahaz, as are all those which follow. The same year was Ahaz’s third and Pekah’s twentieth, Pekah being the one whom Hoshea killed. Likewise, the same year was Ahaz’s fourth and is said to have been his father’s twentieth. Hoshea therefore reigned in Ahaz’s fourth year. What then is meant by what is said later, that he reigned in Ahaz’s twelfth year? Perhaps, as happened to Zimri, from the time when, after Pekah was killed, he seized the kingdom for himself until the twelfth [Col. 0247A] year of King Ahaz, he was unable to prevail because many rebelled. Hence it seems to have happened that the subsequent, but not the earlier, years were assigned to him in the kingdom; otherwise he would be said to have reigned eighteen (sic) years rather than nine.

[Col. 0247]

Summary explanation of the following two tables, for recognizing the apparent contradiction and the harmony of the times of the kings who reigned jointly over Judah and Israel.

[Col. 0247A] In what follows I have added two tables containing the matters discussed above. The first contains what seems capable of raising a question or suggesting a contradiction. In the second table these same matters are arranged in such an order that each point which had raised a question may appear capable of being understood from it without exposition.

In the first table, in its first row, you have arranged from top to bottom the names of the kings reigning in Judah. In the second row, [Col. 0247B] the number of years each of them reigned. In the third row are the kings of the Israelite kingdom, and in the fourth their periods of reign. The numbers written beneath certain kings indicate in which year of the reign of the king written above them those kings who are written opposite began to reign.

In the second table, its first row sets out the succession of years from the beginning of the schism to the time of the first captivity. The second row contains the succession of the kings of Judah, following one another in order. In the third row one may plainly see when sons happened to reign jointly with their fathers. What the second and third rows teach about the kings of Judah and their sons, the [Col. 0248A] fourth and fifth rows teach about the kings of Israel. In them one may also observe that certain periods of joint reign are assigned to the sons alone, certain ones to the fathers alone, and others to both sons and fathers.

[Col. 0255]

EXPLANATIONS OF CERTAIN DIFFICULTIES IN SCRIPTURE, ADDRESSED TO BLESSED BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX.

Which animals are called clean and unclean.

[Col. 0255A]

You ask: since all things in the first creation are called good, why are some animals described as clean and others as unclean when they are to be brought into the ark, since those which are unclean do not seem to be good precisely because they are unclean. But in considering things, judgment is one thing according to their original condition, another according to human custom, and another according to divine law.

According to their original condition, all things are judged good or clean; according to human custom, some appear clean and others unclean. Among the things customarily regarded as clean, however, divine ordinance has made exceptions and declared them unclean. The first judgment accords with the definition of reason; the second, with the experience of sense-perception; the third, with the decree of divine ordinance. [Col. 0255B] Reason judges according to the nature and property [Col. 0256A] implanted in things. Sense-perception judges according to its own disposition and its differing pleasure or aversion. Divine ordinance judges according to some likeness, for the sake of signification.

According to the judgment of reason, nothing is unclean except sin. Sense-perception regards as unclean what the bodily senses loathe or find nauseating. When divine ordinance declares unclean something which is naturally clean, it does this for the sake of signification and intends thereby to remove something truly unclean from human conduct. Thus many things which are accounted unclean according to custom or some institution are judged clean and good according to the rationale of their own nature.

Who is called unleavened, and what it means to be cleansed from the old leaven.

[Col. 0256B] You ask how those whom the Apostle calls “unleavened” (*azyma*) are nevertheless commanded by him [Col. 0257A] to cleanse out the old leaven. For what *azyma* means among the Greeks, *fermentum*—“leaven”—means among us; and *azyma* means “without leaven.” If, then, they are not without leaven, how can they be called unleavened? Or, if they lack all leaven, how can they cleanse out what they do not have at all? “Cleanse out,” he says, “the old leaven, that you may be a new batch, just as you are unleavened” (1 Cor. 5).

If you carefully consider these words of the Apostle, you will find, as it seems to me, not merely one question but several. But in proposing only one, you imply by that very fact that you have no doubt about the others. I shall therefore gladly try to resolve your doubt, provided that afterward you also resolve my doubt—not only one, but a double one—so that I may receive the talent entrusted to me with interest.

We grant that the same persons, in the same respect, cannot both be unleavened and have leaven; nevertheless, the same persons may, in different respects, be unleavened and yet not lack leaven. There are people who think nothing wickedly concerning God and have been cleansed of every leaven of such wickedness, but who, through living badly, have not yet deserved to be cleansed from the leaven of malice. By the rule of goodness they think truly concerning God, but by the rule of goodness they refuse to live rightly. Such people lack the leaven of wickedness, but do not yet lack the leaven of malice: “Think of the Lord in goodness,” says Scripture (Wis. 1).

See how wickedly the Jews think concerning Christ. See how the Gentiles are unable to think truly concerning God: both, therefore, are full of the leaven of wickedness. Consider any heretic: in one respect he thinks rightly concerning God; in another, he can no longer think rightly concerning God. Thus he has not yet deserved to be wholly cleansed from the leaven of wickedness. Wickedness is when someone is no longer able to think what he ought. Wickedness is when malice so intoxicates the mind and blinds it to such an extent that it can no longer think concerning God or neighbor in accordance with what the rule of truth dictates.

Now observe Christians, and you will see how many believe truthfully in every respect but do not live sincerely in every respect. They possess the unleavened bread of truth, but not the unleavened bread of sincerity. They are unleavened according to faith, but not unleavened according to conduct. Accordingly, those who are such are rightly told: “Cleanse out the old leaven, that [Col. 0257D] you may be a new batch, just as you are unleavened”: those who are already unleavened by faith should, with all diligence, cleanse out whatever impurity they have in conduct.

You have now heard what you asked. Now hear what I myself wish to have explained. Certainly a new batch cannot be eaten unless it is first baked; but bread without leaven can be eaten. Why, then, does the Apostle not invite them to that which is shown to be better and more perfect? Why are they not invited to become unleavened bread rather than a new batch? Here is my first doubt; hear also another. What is unleavened bread but food? If, then, they were unleavened, were they also to be taken as food? Yet they are commanded to feast on unleavened bread. Are the same persons both those who feast and those upon whom they feast? Are they at once banquet [Col. 0258A] and diners, eaters and food? If they themselves are unleavened bread, and are to feast upon unleavened bread, must they devour themselves?

As payment of the interest, I ask these two little questions; I ask a third free of charge. For, in accordance with the abundance of your generosity, you ought to answer at least one without charge. Since true faith always is, or should be, prior to sincere works, why are they first commanded to feast upon the unleavened bread of sincerity rather than upon the unleavened bread of truth?

“Cleanse out the old leaven,” that a person may become a new batch.

I confess that I can no longer bear the importunity of your demand with composure: you compel me to solve not only the questions you proposed to me, but also those which I proposed to you. Yet, if we are to explain them fully, we must expound the entire apostolic reading concerning the Paschal celebration. “Cleanse out the old leaven, that you may be a new batch, just as you are unleavened.”

To understand this passage of the Apostle more fully, we need, as it seems to me, a many-sided investigation: first, what leaven is; what a small quantity of leaven is; what old leaven is; what the method of cleansing is; what “unleavened” means; what a new batch is; and what is the difference between bread and dough. Finally, as I said above, why we are exhorted by the Apostle to become a new batch rather than bread without leaven.

We know what bodily leaven is and what its effect is; and from this we discern what we ought to think about spiritual leaven. Spiritual leaven, then, seems to be that which corrupts [Col. 0258C] the integrity of a spiritual and rational substance. We therefore call every sin spiritual leaven when it corrupts that substance either in understanding or in affection. It is corrupted in understanding by falsehood, but in affection by impurity. So long, then, as we can truly say, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us,” we are properly told—and it rightly seems that we ought to be told—“Cleanse out the old leaven.”

If every sin is rightly called leaven, it follows that a small quantity of leaven means venial sin, which is easily committed and easily forgiven. I call it small not because it should be lightly esteemed, [Col. 0258D] but because it is small in comparison with grave sins. But perhaps you say: “If, according to the Apostle, a small quantity of leaven can corrupt the whole mass of merits, then by ‘small leaven’ we cannot understand anything but grave sin. Moreover, the matter against which the Apostle argued above, though a great sin, was nevertheless, according to him, a small quantity of leaven; otherwise why does he then add: ‘Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass?’ (1 Cor. 5).”

Perhaps this is how it seems to you. But what then? Did the man who had his father’s wife incur only a small quantity of leaven? If a small quantity of leaven produces small corruption and a great quantity produces great corruption, shall we say that one who committed such an outrage was corrupted a little and not greatly? I rather understand the Apostle’s saying that a small quantity of leaven corrupts the whole mass to mean that his hearers might understand how great a corruption such a foul and abominable offense would inflict, and with how much diligence and urgency it ought to be cleansed out, since even a small quantity of leaven commonly corrupts the whole mass.

If, according to the Apostle John, “every sin is iniquity” (1 John 3), what will grave sin be except great iniquity? Shall we then say that great iniquity is a small corruption? That seems to follow if a small quantity of leaven is called grave sin. But how, you ask, can venial sin corrupt the whole [Col. 0259B] mass according to the Apostle? Hear what another Scripture says, and from it consider how this ought to be understood: “Whoever neglects small things gradually falls away” (Sir. 19). And we know that a fire blazes up from a small spark.

We often see, while the householder sleeps, how a fire flares up from a small beginning and, in one night or even one hour, consumes the whole substance of its owner—sometimes the inhabitant himself together with his dwelling. So too, if it is disregarded at the beginning of temptation, desire, though small, begins gradually to grow, little by little weakens the strength of the mind, and, once virtue is exhausted, drives it to crime; and in this manner corrupts the mass of our merits. Thus, indeed, if it is neglected, no small mass is often corrupted by a small quantity of leaven. But if we do not neglect it, and however shamefully we may have fallen, we persist vigorously in cleansing out the leaven of any sin, we shall be able to preserve the mass of our good works from its corruption. Hence, after a particular admonition, the Apostle rises, taking occasion from it, to general instruction when he says: “Cleanse out the old leaven.”

Do you think he teaches us to persist in cleansing out only small leaven or only great leaven, rather than both great and small? “Cleanse out,” he says, “the old leaven.” That leaven from which the mind has been infected and in its infection corrupted is rightly called old. By contrast, leaven seems fresh when it still strikes at the mind by thought alone. What is in thought alone knocks, as it were, outside at the door; what has already seized the affection occupies and defiles the inner parts. The former must therefore be repelled; the latter cleansed out.

The manner of cleansing is carried out in many ways: through self-reproach, prayer, confession, and works of repentance. Of the first you have in the Psalm: “What you say in your hearts, be contrite upon your beds” (Ps. 4). Of the second and third you have in the Apostle James: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another” (Jas. 5). Of the fourth there is the saying of John the Baptist: “Produce worthy fruits of repentance” (Luke 3). In cleansing grave sins, confession and satisfaction are certainly necessary. Contrition and prayer, however, are sometimes sufficient for cleansing venial sins. Grave sins must be cleansed out completely, both with respect to guilt and with respect to the act: with respect to guilt, so that you make satisfaction for the past [Col. 0260A] and presume nothing of the kind thereafter.

But because, so long as we live in this corruptible flesh, we can never wholly root venial sins out of our life, we must always persist in cleansing them out and renew our efforts toward daily increases in purity. “That you may be,” he says, “a new batch, just as you are unleavened.” “Unleavened” may seemingly be said both of bread without leaven and of dough not yet leavened, for *azyma* means “without leaven.” Which of these, then, should we understand when he says that they are unleavened?

But if they were already a new batch, he should not have exhorted them to become what they already were. Therefore, when he calls them unleavened, he seems to have meant bread without leaven. What then? Did he mean to urge them to cease being bread without leaven and to become a new batch? Who could say that? Dough is not normally made from bread; rather, bread is made from dough. Thus it is understood that in one respect they were unleavened and in another respect were not unleavened. In the respect in which they were not without leaven, he wished them to become a new batch.

For many are unleavened according to faith who are not unleavened according to conduct; and many seem unleavened according to conduct who are nevertheless not unleavened in intention, as hypocrites are. And some have the unleavened bread of sincerity in intention, though they do not altogether lack leaven in affection. Therefore, so long as, while consenting in mind to the law of God, we see another law in our members resisting the law of our mind and holding us captive [Col. 0260C] under the law of sin—so long, I say, as we see this in ourselves—we undoubtedly need the cleansing out of leaven. We are rightly told: “Cleanse out the old leaven, that you may be a new batch, just as you are unleavened.”

By calling it a batch—not just any batch, but a new one—he seems to mean the same as if he had said “unleavened.” For dough, even when leaven has been added to it, does not become leavened without delay. Once it has been leavened, it is no longer fresh and loses its newness. Therefore, just as in one respect they had already become, as it were, bread without leaven, so in another respect he wished them to become dough without leaven. In both respects he did not wish them to possess unleavened bread: in both he wished them to be without corruption, both in what they already were and in what they could still become.

Let us now see the difference between bread and dough. Bread, as has already been said, is made from dough; dough is not made from bread. Dough is material that is tender and soft and receptive of various forms. Bread is a thing already formed, firm, and hardened by fire. Unleavened bread, therefore, is made by an affection steadfast and strong in what is good. A new batch is made by a recent purpose of mind, still unformed and insufficiently practiced. Dough is shaped between the hands, then baked and hardened by fire, and so becomes bread. In the same way, the advancement of our merits and the renewal of progress begins from deliberation, is moderated by discernment, and is perfected in love.

When, therefore, in order to increase the purity of the mind, we resolve upon something new [Col. 0261A] and pursue that intention with much deliberation, what else are we doing but, by cleansing out leaven, making a new batch? But because not everyone can do everything, nor are all things equally advantageous for everyone, when in carrying out any resolution we learn our measure and the right way of doing good, and through our own experience are trained in discernment, so that we accomplish all things with moderation, what else are we doing but forming loaves to be baked? For bread is, as it were, baked by fire when a good resolution, through use, is turned into delight and made firm through love.

Thus the advancement of good is one thing and the confirmation of good another; likewise, the beginning of good is one thing and its completion another. The latter belongs to bread, the former to a new batch. Since no one becomes excellent all at once, nor is at once established in every beginning of good, the Apostle, speaking humanly to people because of their weakness, exhorts them to become a new batch, not bread without leaven. Yet he undoubtedly aimed at this end: that, having become a new batch, they might someday also become unleavened loaves from that new batch. No one makes dough for any other reason than that bread may be made from it.

The Apostle therefore rightly exhorts them to become what, for the time being, they were able to become, and thereby indicates the end toward which they ought to strive: namely, that at last they may become wholly unleavened and advance to the completion and confirmation of true good. You now have why they are exhorted to become a new batch rather than bread without leaven. But it remains surprising, and no less demanding of inquiry, why those who are called unleavened are invited to eat the lamb. For eating does not belong to unleavened bread, while dough neither eats nor is eaten. Once it has been said that they were unleavened, and commanded that they become a new batch, what connection, I ask, is there in adding next: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed; therefore let us feast” (1 Cor. 5)?

We know indeed that it was commanded in the Law that, when they sacrificed the lamb and celebrated Passover, they were to eat no bread at all other than unleavened bread. If, therefore, the Apostle had said that they were not themselves unleavened, but had unleavened bread, and had invited them to have it still more abundantly, it would seem quite fitting for him to add: [Col. 0261D] “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed; therefore let us feast.” What we understand there historically, we ought to understand here spiritually. For whatever is said of that Passover seems to have been said on account of this one. What is said there of bodily leaven is understood here of spiritual leaven. Therefore, those who are said not to have unleavened bread but to be unleavened bread themselves—by what reasoning, one may wonder, are they invited to eat unleavened bread or the lamb?

But anyone who wishes to understand more fully the force of the Apostle’s statement must examine these matters more deeply. We must certainly celebrate a twofold Passover; beyond doubt, we must make a twofold passage. For *Pascha*, as we have often heard, is interpreted as “passage.” First we must pass from injustice to righteousness; secondly [Col. 0262A] from misery to glory. It is a good passage to pass from wickedness to goodness; it is likewise good to pass from misery to blessedness. We ought to celebrate both joyfully and rejoice deeply in both: but in the first as a present reality, in the second in hope.

We ourselves, with his help, must accomplish the first celebration; we must await the second from his gift alone. In the first we must receive the Lamb as food; in the second we must present ourselves as fit to become his food. Thus in the first we must have unleavened bread and eat unleavened bread; in the second we must ourselves be unleavened, and yield ourselves as food for the Lamb. Nor should you wonder to hear that we must be fed by the Lamb and become the Lamb’s food, when you likewise read, if you recall, that we have put on Christ, though we are nevertheless Christ’s garment [Col. 0262B] (Rom. XIII).

We have testimonies of Scripture for both. Therefore, meanwhile we must become unleavened and be cleansed of every leaven of oldness, if we wish to be found worthy and acceptable in that future celebration. But if we wish to be unleavened, we must eat unleavened bread. “But,” you ask, “if we eat unleavened bread, shall we therefore be bread?” Certainly we know bread that is normally incorporated into the eater, not bread that incorporates the eater into itself. We know bread that usually nourishes flesh, makes flesh fat, and renders it stronger. What is this bread which causes what belongs to the flesh to fall away from itself, and makes the eater pass into its own likeness?

But, lest you wonder any further about this, hear what sort of bread, what sort of unleavened bread, we set before you to eat: [Col. 0262C] “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John VI). Without doubt, if you eat this bread, it will not be changed into you, but you will be changed into it (St. Augustine, *Confessions*, book VII, ch. 10). If you are unwilling to believe me, hear him whom you do not dare contradict: “I am food for the mature; grow, and you shall eat me. Nor will you change me into yourself, as you do the food of your flesh; but you shall be changed into me.”

But perhaps you still ask to be shown more plainly how this can happen. If you delight in truth and take pleasure in such food, do you suppose that, by hungering for and enjoying truth, you can change truth into falsehood? If you receive Christ as your food, it is better for you that he should make you truthful from a liar than that you should make him a liar from one who is truthful. Without doubt Christ is highest truth; without doubt Christ is highest purity. [Col. 0262D] The unleavened bread of truth makes the liar truthful; the unleavened bread of sincerity makes the impure pure in heart. When you have been established in truth and sincerity, without doubt you will be unleavened, and worthy to be received as food for the Lamb.

But when he yields himself as your food and receives you as his food, in each case it is not he who is changed into you, but you who are changed into him. In the first change he makes you like himself in righteousness; in the second he makes you like himself in glory. In the first, as has been said, he makes the liar truthful and the impure pure in heart; in the second, the mortal immortal and the corruptible incorruptible, when he “will transform the body of our humiliation to conform to the body of his glory.” For, as the Apostle testifies, “this corruptible [Col. 0263A] must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (II Cor. XV). Therefore, if we wish to be like him in glory, we must be unleavened; and if we wish to become unleavened, we must eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Nor is it enough to possess such unleavened bread, to grasp by understanding and retain in memory what sincerity is or what truth is, unless we add that we also eat it: that is, by acting, as though by chewing, we should strive to transform it into our affection and fill our inward parts with such sweetness and fullness. You surely see that it is one thing to have unleavened bread, another to eat unleavened bread, and yet another to be unleavened bread. If, then, we cannot be unleavened unless we eat the unleavened bread indicated, what wonder is it if he [Col. 0263B] invited them to eat unleavened bread—those who were already in part unleavened and in part were not, and whom he wished, through the new dough, to become wholly unleavened?

But above all he invites them to the eating of the Lamb, without whose grace they could not persevere either in what they already were—unleavened—or in what they were not yet, namely unleavened bread; nor could they become new dough or, from it, unleavened bread. Now, I beg you, consider how fitting and appropriate it is that, since he has made himself your food, you should make yourself his food. “You have sat at a rich man’s table: consider carefully what has been set before you, and know that you must prepare such things” [Prov. XXIII].

The Apostle desires “that we become new dough” (I Cor. V), and from the dough, bread without leaven—and rightly so. “For Christ [Col. 0263C] our Passover has been sacrificed.” Therefore let us become new dough, so that Christ may find in us what can become a feast for him. For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, so that we may find in him what we can feast upon. Moreover, from the fact that Christ has been sacrificed, both are brought about: that we ought rightly to do what the Apostle urges, and that we may also be able to accomplish it. For from the sacrifice and eating of the Lamb—provided that we eat him with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth—we receive grace so that we may fulfill the Apostle’s admonitions.

Therefore let the one who desires to be new dough, pure from every leaven, and who prepares himself fit and worthy for Christ’s food, eat the Lamb with unleavened bread. You have now received the reason why those called unleavened bread, and those urged to become new dough, are commanded [Col. 0263D] to feast upon the Lamb with unleavened bread. But there remains the matter that we placed last, and must still investigate. Since Solomon says, “Let your eyelids go before your steps” (Prov. IV), and since it is prior to look ahead rather than to proceed, to know rather than to do, why does the Apostle place the unleavened bread of truth second in his admonition, if it must come first in eating?

But that we may approach this point of inquiry more suitably, let us first examine carefully what precedes it. The Apostle teaches how it is permissible to eat the Lamb and how it is altogether impermissible to eat him. It is not permissible to eat him with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but, as you hear immediately afterwards, with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

From this one may observe the difference between the Passover [Col. 0264A] of the Jews and the Passover of Christians. There bodily leaven is forbidden; here spiritual leaven. There unleavened bread is prescribed; here the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. And rightly so: for there the legal lamb is sacrificed, but it is an animal; here the Lamb is spiritual and supercelestial. There is a brute animal; here, the man who is God, the Word of God. The sacrifice of each gives passage from slavery to freedom, but that sacrifice from bodily slavery to bodily freedom, and this one from spiritual slavery to spiritual freedom. That sacrifice gives passage from Egypt into the wilderness; this gives return from the world into Paradise. Finally, that gives passage from Pharaoh’s slavery into an earthly kingdom; this conveys us from the devil’s slavery into the kingdom of heaven.

From these things it can be understood how incomparably greater, how [Col. 0264B] inestimably worthier this solemnity is than that one—our Passover, in short, than the Passover of the Jews: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore,” he says, “let us feast” (I Cor. V). You have heard the fruit of the sacrifice. Do you wish also to hear the fruit of the feast? “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI). But lest this be thought to have been said of just any kind of life, let us hear further what is said concerning the same matter: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (ibid.). See what fruit the one who eats him finds—not everyone, certainly, but the one who approaches worthily. “Otherwise, whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (ibid.).

Therefore let us feast, but not unworthily. This is what [Col. 0264C] the Apostle wished to teach you when he adds: “Not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” To eat with the leaven of malice and wickedness is undoubtedly to eat unworthily. But, that you may become worthy, eat with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

See: two things are forbidden and two commanded. You have two set against two: the unleavened bread of sincerity against the leaven of malice; the unleavened bread of truth against the leaven of wickedness. Every spiritual corruption in human beings seems to arise either from the concupiscence of the flesh or from ignorance of the mind, and every kind of spiritual leaven is comprehended under these two. Yet the Apostle is not said, under the names “malice” and “wickedness,” to have comprehended every kind of leaven. For not every concupiscence pertains to [Col. 0264D] malice, just as not every ignorance is reckoned as wickedness.

It is one thing to feel concupiscence and another to consent to concupiscence. It is reckoned to weakness that we feel concupiscence against our will; it is reckoned to malice that we deliberately consent to concupiscence. For malice is to consent with a mind inclined toward a known evil, deliberately and by intention. What, then, is malice but unbridled concupiscence? For one kind of concupiscence is bridled and another unbridled. The former is venial; the latter condemnable. Yet both defile, both corrupt, and both show by that very fact that they belong to leaven.

Likewise, one kind of ignorance is venial and another condemnable: venial [Col. 0265A] ignorance descends from weakness, condemnable ignorance arises from malice. The former clouds the mind, but the latter blinds it. For malice often blinds a person so thoroughly that it does not allow him to judge simply and rightly concerning his neighbor, and sometimes not even concerning God. Thus malice produces and nourishes the vice which the Apostle here calls *nequitia*, “wickedness,” because in its judgment it can no longer preserve the rule of truth and goodness.

Do not be disturbed if you find this word used in another sense. Poverty of words compels us sometimes to extend, sometimes to restrict, or in some other way to vary the meaning of terms. But in such cases we must always weigh and determine the author’s meaning from the context of the text. Therefore, if we wish to follow the Apostle’s meaning, we ought, I think, to interpret it so that, just as malice is opposed to sincerity, so wickedness corresponds to truth. [Col. 0265B] It is characteristic of wickedness always to suspect the worse, to interpret everything adversely, to serve slander and detraction, to censure divine judgments, to waver in faith, and to murmur under God’s chastisements.

Therefore, just as under the name “malice” not every sort of concupiscence is understood, but unbridled concupiscence, so under the name “wickedness” not every sort of ignorance is understood, but malicious ignorance. Thus, if it were said, “not with the leaven of concupiscence and ignorance,” where it is written, “not with the leaven of malice and wickedness,” the Apostle would seem to have commanded something more perfect, and to correspond more fully, as by an opposite, to what follows: [Col. 0265C] “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.”

But the Apostle, as we have said, wished to teach how one may approach the eating of the Lamb and how one may not approach it. It is venial to approach with venial concupiscence and venial ignorance; but it is condemnable to approach with condemnable concupiscence or condemnable ignorance. Only condemnable concupiscence belongs to malice, and only condemnable ignorance to wickedness. Rightly, therefore, the Apostle did not wish to say [Col. 0266A] “not with the leaven of concupiscence and ignorance,” but something more measured: “not with the leaven of malice and wickedness,” lest he should seem to exclude every human being from eating the Lamb. For who could sufficiently cleanse away, in this life, the leaven of concupiscence and ignorance altogether, while “the flesh lusts against the spirit,” and while we do not know, as long as we are here, what we ought to pray for or how we ought to pray?

Observe, then, how discerningly and wisely the Apostle refused to command what lay above human power: he enjoins upon man only what he knew to be possible for man. He says therefore: “Not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.” Let us now ask what this reversal of order means: why he puts the unleavened bread of sincerity before that of truth, when right faith always comes before good action. [Col. 0266B] For “without faith it is impossible to please God.”

Yet it is clear that faith is a kind of certainty situated above opinion and below knowledge. Thus, the knowledge of truth that comes through faith alone is one thing, and that which comes through the understanding of truth is another. Both are indicated by the prophet when he says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII). But the knowledge that is in faith alone is accustomed always to precede good works. The knowledge that comes through understanding, however, follows good works, because by acting well we are enlightened unto truth. Hence comes that saying of the Wise Man: “My son, if you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and God will give it to you” (Ecclus. VII). The man who said, “From your commandments [Col. 0266C] I have gained understanding” (Ps. CXVIII), says this very thing of himself by experience.

Therefore the Apostle calls us to that knowledge of truth which comes through understanding when he invites us to the feast of sincerity and truth. It ought not, then, to suffice us to believe the mysteries of our faith truly and firmly, unless we also strive, so far as we can, to grasp them by understanding.
