Let us satisfy our affection from the unleavened bread of sincerity; let us refresh our intellect from the unleavened bread of truth.

[Col. 0265]

# MYSTICAL NOTES ON THE PSALMS

## NOTE ON PSALM II

[Col. 0265D] “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things?” (Ps. II.)

What do we understand by the nations, who do not know God and worship idols, except depraved and perverse thoughts? And what do we understand by peoples meditating vain things except vain and foolish thoughts? Of the former it is said: “For perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wis. I). Of the latter it is written: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (ibid.). “From thoughts,” he says, “that are without understanding.”

What, then, will become of those thoughts which we cannot entertain [Col. 0266D] without shameful and seductive desire, or of those which we willingly accept, not without some perverse consent, if the Holy Spirit withdraws from thoughts which are without understanding? Therefore, what the one openly calls perverse thoughts, the other figuratively calls nations, as though they were perverse people turned away from the true God. What the one intended to call thoughts without understanding, the other, I think, called peoples meditating vain things. Thoughts that are not without wickedness are certainly worse than those which wander about without understanding. Thus he calls the former nations and the latter [Col. 0267A] peoples. For “nations” condemns them for their stubborn conviction, while “peoples,” though faithful, humbles them for their lowliness. So every vain or idle thought is lowly, but a depraved and perverse thought is detestable. These are precisely the kinds of thoughts which the Prophet rebukes—or rather mocks—when he says: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things?”

It should certainly be noted that raging is the sound of beasts, not of human beings. For nations to rage is for depraved desires to rise up against reason. As often as we censure God’s just judgments, as often as we murmur against his chastisements, so often we exchange the human voice, as it were, for raging. Whenever we follow appetite rather than reason, as though it grieved us to be human, we imitate beasts. Let him therefore first rebuke the raging [Col. 0267B] of wickedness, and afterwards also condemn the pursuit of vanity. For in the words, “And the peoples meditated vain things,” the pursuit of vanity is reproved. Perhaps it is venial to think vain things, but to meditate upon them is altogether blameworthy. For it is one thing that we suffer through negligence or against our will, and another when we voluntarily occupy ourselves with a useless pursuit.

“The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes assembled together.” Let us first inquire who these kings are, and who those persons are whom he calls princes. He speaks of kings, but asserts that they are kings of the earth. Yet to the sinner it is said: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. III). In earth of this kind, demons—whom the Apostle calls “the princes of this world and rulers of darkness” (Eph. VI)—hold sovereignty and exercise dominion, while they impel people toward unclean [Col. 0267C] desires and distract them through worldly covetousness.

A king is so called from ruling; and by earth we rightly understand the heart that longs after earthly desires. Therefore, those demons are called kings in Holy Scripture who strive to overthrow and subjugate people by cunning rather than strength. For some possess greater craftiness, while others possess more vehement boldness. The former tempt more secretly; the latter press their attack more violently. The temptation of these is deceitful, that of those violent. These deceive as though by giving counsel; those, by pressing more fiercely, in a manner oppress. Therefore let us understand the former by kings and the latter by princes. For the former preside over people, as though by ruling; the latter, as though by taking the lead, draw them into wickedness—either deceived by craftiness or cast down by [Col. 0267D] pressure.

Let us see, then, what he says: “The kings of the earth stood up.” In the Holy Scriptures I find one spirit called a spirit of fornication, another called a spirit of pride. The same may be understood concerning other vices. Thus one holds dominion over the lustful, another over the gluttonous; one presides over the avaricious, another over the angry; this one rules the envious, that one dominates the proud. What else is it for kings of this kind to stand by one another except for each to assist another in attacking human beings? For when someone is cast down into some vice by any one of them, by that very fact he is often found weaker in resisting the others. It commonly happens that the person weighed down by drunken excess is much sooner and much more easily inflamed by lust. Thus kings stand by one another when [Col. 0268A] they mutually bring each other help in overcoming us.

The princes assemble into one because, whatever they do in our overthrow, though it be diverse, they nevertheless agree together. Therefore we rightly understand not only that these kings and princes stand by one another, but also that they stand by nations and peoples: because, while we wander with a restless mind through depraved and foolish thoughts, we open an entrance for deceptive spirits to tempt us. Thus, when nations rage and peoples meditate vain things, kings stand up and princes assemble, because malignant spirits find an opening to tempt, and receive, by God’s just judgment, permission to tempt, while perverse and vain thoughts—signified by nations and peoples—are clamoring.

Yet we may understand demons not only by kings and princes, but also [Col. 0268B] by nations and peoples, and subtly distinguish their differences by these names.

Consider now, therefore, a certain numerous multitude of demons—or rather, a manifold innumerability. Of these, some are naturally more subtle than others; so do not doubt that they are also more daring in presumption and more skillful in deception. Hence it happens that they rule over other, weaker demons, though these are greater in number, and freely exercise dominion over them. Thus among the lower subjects the multitude is more abundant, but among the higher there is greater boldness and greater prudence. Hence, on account of their greater boldness, they freely exercise dominion over the weaker; and on account of their greater prudence, they dispose at their will the endeavors and services of the foolish. [Col. 0268C]

Perhaps this is what Scripture intended to teach us when it named some kings or princes and designated others by nations and peoples. But if we seek the difference between nations and peoples, we can readily distinguish them from one another. Diversity of custom or language distinguishes nation from nation, and any nation is often accustomed to contain many peoples. Thus in the one term it indicates diversity of dispositions; in the other, their manifold multitude. For some of them prevail more in certain vices, while others more vehemently favor or pursue other vices. Therefore, because the Prophet perceived diversity of dispositions and pursuits, together with an innumerable multitude in every distinction, [Col. 0268D] he perhaps called them nations and then named peoples in succession.

If, then, we possess discernment of spirits and carefully observe their differences, we shall be able to understand differences among demons not only by kings and princes, but also by nations and peoples. Let anyone who can consider what sort of man and how great this man was; with what discernment and how great a strength he was endowed, against whom nations and peoples raged, against whom kings and princes assembled. If we knew that we had resisted, or could resist, the violence or cunning of any single demon, we should think ourselves to have made great progress; indeed, we should believe ourselves not human but above humanity. Yet this man does not merely perceive himself to be attacked by one nation or one king. Rather, he knew, wrote, and left for posterity to read that he could not be overcome by nations, peoples, kings, and princes; thus he might at least put to shame our pride—we who are nothing and yet are not ashamed to be proud. [Col. 0269A]

But if anyone wishes to refer nations and peoples to thoughts, and kings and princes to affections, I readily agree, because I do not doubt that the affections of the soul preside over thoughts.

Yet let us receive this interpretation in such a way as not to destroy the former one, since we do not doubt that Holy Scripture admits manifold exposition. Whether, therefore, we refer the whole passage to the vices of the soul, or the whole to demons, or, better, refer it partly to vicious habits and partly to the instigators of vices, it is indeed a great thing to overcome either the one or the other; but it is greater still [Col. 0269B] to be able to resist both. If, however, the Prophet could not overcome both, he would not mock them with such confidence when he says: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes assembled together.”

But if we carefully consider the words that follow, we shall sooner discover from whom he expects victory over so many enemies. For he says: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes assembled together.” But against whom? “Against the Lord,” he says, “and against his Christ.” He expects victory, therefore, from the one who was fighting tirelessly in him against so many enemies. For what else was David’s soul than a kind of tower of God, which the Lord defended for himself against so many enemies, like an almighty warrior whose name is his own? It was surely one of those towers for which David himself cries elsewhere: “Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers” (Ps. CXXI). [Col. 0269C]

Nations first attack this tower, strong beyond the rest and singular among the strong; peoples surround it with siege. But because they cannot prevail, kings at length stand up and princes assemble. Yet it remained impregnable, because the Lord continually defended it for himself. Thus David stood among so many enemies, secure in God’s protection and at last destined to triumph over so many enemies by God’s victory. Therefore he did not fear to mock those whom he saw could not prevail against him, and he says: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things? The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes assembled together against [Col. 0269D] the Lord and against his Christ.”

“Against the Lord,” he says, “and against his Christ.” There are in us gifts of nature, and there are gifts of grace. Let us likewise distinguish the Lord and his Christ. By “Lord,” understand the Creator; by “Christ,” understand the Savior. He is called Creator for one reason and Savior for another. He is Creator because he made what did not exist; he is called Savior because he restored what had perished. Therefore gifts of nature belong to the Creator, while gifts of grace seem especially to belong to the Savior.

By gifts of nature I mean when, according to their natural constitution, we see some people more inclined to mercy, others more rigorous in justice; some naturally more prudent, [Col. 0270A] others more simple; and the other such things which each person possesses naturally, not by acquired practice. Gifts of grace, however, are so called when someone strives through grace to possess what he could in no way possess by nature. Therefore, we receive the former from our first creation through the gift of the Creator; the latter we receive at a fitting time through the favor of the Savior.

Therefore, when we corrupt gifts of nature, we sin against the Creator, because we do not fear to destroy his work. But when anyone destroys gifts of grace, he acts especially against his Savior, who labored even unto death for our restoration. Since, therefore, vicious habits—or demons, the instigators of vices—strive to overthrow in us both the gifts of nature and the gifts of grace, nations and peoples, kings and princes are rightly said to stand not only against the Lord but also [Col. 0270B] against his Christ. For, to the Creator’s injury, they hasten to corrupt in us the Creator’s work; and, to the Savior’s dishonor, they endeavor to empty the work of redemption of its effect. Therefore it is rightly said: “The kings of the earth stood up, and the princes assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ.”

“Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us.” By bonds we are restrained from going where we wish to go. Under a yoke we are forced unwillingly to do what we do not wish. There are two great evils: to be hindered from good and occupied in evil. The bonds of desire call us back from good; the yoke of fear drives us into evil. According to the Prophet’s counsel, it is certainly good to break bonds of this kind, and likewise good to cast off such a yoke. [Col. 0270C] But perhaps you seek the manner and desire to hear how this can be done. Listen, but do not neglect it. “Do not love the world or the things in the world” (I John II), and you have broken the bonds. “Do not fear those who kill the body but have nothing they can do to the soul” (Matt. X), and you have cast off the yoke.

“Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast away their yoke from us. He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them.” It is very strange: if the Lord is everywhere, why is he said to be in heaven rather than everywhere? Or, if he is only in heaven, why is he believed to be everywhere? Yet our ordinary way of speaking is that a thing is seen where it is, while where it is not, it cannot be seen. Scripture, although it knows him to be everywhere, nevertheless [Col. 0270D] wished especially to assign him to heaven; and he is said to be present most especially there where he is ceaselessly seen by all its inhabitants. Thus, whoever desires to see him where he can be seen should ascend there by merit. He is indeed on earth, but we who are on earth do not see him. Nor is he absent from hell, although we do not believe that he can be seen by the inhabitants of hell. Yet we do not doubt that he is in the heavens and is seen in the heavens.

It must nevertheless be known that he is seen in one way by faith, in another by contemplation, and in another beheld by direct sight. The difference between heaven and earth is the difference between a believer and an unbeliever; and, on account of faith, we may call any perfect person a heaven. Yet above this heaven rises another heaven, namely the dignity of spiritual persons; and above that is raised a third sublimity, namely that of angels. In the first, therefore, he is seen by faith alone; in the second he is also seen by contemplation; in the third he is beheld face to face. [Col. 0271A]

We see him by faith when we firmly believe what has been written concerning him. He beholds him by contemplation who, through divine inspiration, fixes the eyes of understanding upon what he first believed concerning him. But he is seen by direct sight when he is beheld face to face, as he is, in his own substance. Nevertheless, in whatever manner he is seen, he is not seen except in heaven: in the first heaven, as we have said, by faith; in the second, by contemplation; and in the third, by direct sight.

[Col. 0271B] He dwells by grace only in heavens of this kind, though he is nowhere absent by the presence of his power or essence. Therefore, since the Lord dwells in the saints in a singular manner, Scripture rightly indicates that he has a place especially in the heavens. But if by earth we understand the flesh and by heaven the soul, there is something else that we must observe in these words. For it must be known that the sense of the flesh never enters into that hidden mystery of the Godhead; bodily sense is never admitted to those inward secrets. The soul alone, which has been made in his likeness, can see the substance of the divine nature. Nor will anyone desire to see it there bodily, just as no one here seeks to see wisdom bodily.

Therefore, because the soul alone is capable of divine brightness, to which bodily sense can never penetrate, God is rightly said to dwell in heaven—that is, in the soul—which eternally enjoys both his presence and the delight of his vision. [Col. 0271C] What wonder, then, if God defends against enemies the soul in which he has chosen to dwell eternally, as it is written: “This is my rest for ever and ever; here I shall dwell, because I have chosen her” (Ps. CXXXI)?

Therefore let me act confidently, and let me not fear, if I have such an inhabitant and find such a protector. Then at last, secure among enemies, I shall not tremble to mock them, saying: “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them.” May he who dwells in heaven, who loves to inhabit souls, [Col. 0271D] himself defend his own; may he himself repel, convict, and mock the enemies. “He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them.”

It is one thing to laugh at someone and another to mock him. Mockery by laughter is when we praise someone ironically, attributing to him and amplifying something greater than he is, or something that does not exist at all. Derision is when, in marking someone out, we transform our face with feigned ugliness and portray, by a false deformity, what he is like—or rather, what he believes us to be like. Though *subsannatio*, “derision,” seems to derive particularly from a wrinkling or drawing of the nose, any mocking distortion of lips, nose, eyes, or face is rightly called derision. Thus by laughing at someone we feign another’s beauty; by deriding someone we in some sense disguise our own—or rather, by laughing at someone we disguise his ugliness, while by deriding him we feign our own ugliness, though there is none. [Col. 0272A]

By such feigning or disguising, another’s deformity appears more deformed, and our beauty stands out more beautiful. What else, then, is it for the Lord to laugh at his enemies but to allow them to undertake certain strong or even great deeds, by which for a time they may appear glorious to themselves or others? And then he speaks, as it were, certain praises of them in their ears when he permits them to do what gives their proud mind occasion for empty glory. Such people the Prophet strikes when he says: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips, and the tongue that speaks great things; those who have said, ‘Our lips are our own; who is lord over us?’” (Ps. XI).

Thus laughter is when he feigns the strength of his enemies. [Col. 0272B] Derision, however, is when he disguises his own power or justice. For he often permits the unjust to prosper in this life and the just to be afflicted, as though he were unable to resist wickedness or unwilling to show compassion to innocence. Therefore, while he appears to perverse minds either less powerful or less just, what does he do but, so to speak, distort the straightness of his own countenance in their sight? For because he who is just is not believed to be just, the beauty of his countenance in its loveliness is, as it were, not seen by them.

For it often happens that, while the ungodly commit evil with impunity, they believe that God takes no care at all for human affairs. Such are those described who said: “The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand” (Ps. 93). [Col. 0272C] Some of them said in their heart: “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face so that he will never see” (Ps. 20). Thus the perverse are mocked when they presume things about themselves that are as false as they are great. But they are derided when, in their mad minds, they conceive thoughts about the Lord that are as profane as they are empty. They hear, as it were, their own praises—but false ones—insofar as they believe great things of themselves which are not at all true. They look upon the Lord as though deformed, so long as they entertain unworthy thoughts concerning him.

This statement seems especially applicable to malignant spirits, against whom it appears to have been uttered particularly. For they wearied David with their temptations and hastened to overthrow him by their snares; but David, secure in the Lord’s protection, sang confidently, saying: “He who dwells in heaven shall laugh them to scorn, and the Lord shall deride them.” For evil spirits are often permitted for a time to prevail against certain elect persons; hence they attempt, contrary to God’s ordering, to destroy those whom the Lord reserves for himself eternally. But since, after a fall, each of the elect often rises again so much the stronger as he rises more humble, what else do evil spirits do by their assaults than, unwillingly, serve the advancement of the good?

See, if you can, how they are mocked; recognize how they are ridiculed. There is nothing that pains them more, nothing over which they groan more deeply, than our good, than our progress. They almost hate our goods more than their own torments; indeed, they would rather have their torments increased daily than fail to diminish our goods, our [Col. 0273A] merits. Yet through so many efforts and such great hazards they accomplish nothing except that all the good become better each day. They are therefore mocked when they boast that they can do something against the elect; they are derided when they think that they can do anything against God’s ordering. For whatever hostile malignity does against the salvation of the elect serves that salvation, [Col. 0274A] and from the very act by which it vainly strives to impede God’s ordering, it is compelled to fulfill it. Rightly, therefore, it is said of them that “he shall laugh” and “the Lord shall deride them.”

Let no one wonder, let no one take offense, if those things which are said and understood literally concerning Christ we apply, for edification, to his members according to a mystical understanding.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 30

[Col. 0273]

[Col. 0273A] “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the same.” That peace through which and in which the soul falls asleep; through which it temporarily loses all recollection of external things; through [Col. 0273B] which it itself comes into forgetfulness of itself, and, surpassing itself, passes wholly into God—that peace, I say, what else does it seem to be than that inward, true, and full joy; a certain, so to speak, overflowing abundance of spiritual delights; namely, a wondrous and ineffable satisfaction of heavenly desires?

It seems truly to possess peace, truly full peace, only when every desire is utterly absorbed by the overflowing abundance of that inner sweetness. For as long as the mind pants with burning desire after things which it does not yet possess, how can it have peace? What peace has one whom the vexation of his own desires wearies? Therefore, unless our joy is full, it does not bring our desires into true peace. Certainly, in this corruptible life the human mind cannot possess perfect joy, because in the narrowness of its frailty it cannot contain perfect joy. Yet it can possess full joy, because it can possess as much as it can contain.

Thus the human mind truly enjoys its peace when it is wholly dissolved into that which it inwardly senses of divine sweetness. For this peace, if it is to be full, consists in two things: the contemplation of truth, namely, and the satisfaction of inward sweetness. It begins with the one and is perfected by the other. First, indeed, the friend of the heavenly Bridegroom and bride of the true Friend, kindled by longing for her beloved and held in suspense for his coming—first, I say, it is necessary that she see him whom her soul loves; second, that she rush into his embraces and join kisses with him; second, that she, who continually asks, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth,” may, by kissing him, draw sweetness from what is sweet and draw forth sweetness from what is delightful.

For his lips are a dripping honeycomb, and his breath is sweeter than honey. He himself is supreme beauty; he himself is supreme sweetness: beauty for sight, sweetness for taste. What is seen is, as it were, still external; what is tasted begins to be inward. To taste is more than to see. For what we taste we incorporate into ourselves, and with it we become, as it were, one. So, without doubt, when we receive an infusion of the divine Spirit, we are in some manner united to him: “He who is joined to the Lord,” says the Apostle, “is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6). This, surely, is that true and full sweetness of divine infusion, this supreme and singular delight, [Col. 0274A] which alone can satisfy the heart’s desire and prevail to sate its hunger. This alone restrains the weariness of our desires; this [Col. 0274B] alone brings the mind into true peace, because it finds nothing further to seek. For what more can it seek than that very thing which it cannot contain?

Let us now see by what stages this peace grows. First comes the long waiting of desire; waiting is followed by circumspection; circumspection by contemplation; contemplation by wonder; wonder by exultation; exultation by sweetness. Waiting begins when the bride of Christ, after the long weariness of her desire, at last begins to be assured by an inward inspiration of the coming of him whom her soul loves, while she is told daily: “Wait, wait again; a little here, a little there. For he who is to come will come and will not [Col. 0274C] delay.”

In this waiting the soul begins often to look about here and there, and with the greatest care to observe from what direction he whom she awaits may come: whether from the East, or from the West, or from the desert mountains. And behold, suddenly coming from the south—for “God shall come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran”—he rejoices like a giant to run his course. Thus he comes suddenly and swiftly, leaping upon the mountains and bounding over the hills. He hastens to meet his bride, crying aloud and saying: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly” (Song 6).

See how circumspection follows waiting, and contemplation follows circumspection. For contemplation is when at last the soul begins to see what it endured in long waiting and sought through frequent circumspection. But without doubt, when the soul begins to contemplate, it begins at the same time to wonder. For what wonder is it if it marvels at the countenance of the Beautiful One, “beautiful beyond the sons of men”? Without doubt, the more clearly it contemplates, the more vehemently it marvels; and the more it marvels, the more eagerly and attentively it contemplates. Thus the measure of wonder grows from the quality of contemplation, and from the intensity of wonder grows the diligence of contemplation.

But what, and how delightful, a spectacle do we think it is to see supreme beauty in however small a measure, to contemplate more clearly that luminous countenance of divine brightness, and to hang continually in wonder at it? From such a wondrous and delightful [Col. 0275A] spectacle arises that great and vehement rejoicing of which we have spoken. For, as was said, wonder follows contemplation, and exultation follows wonder.

In this exultation the mind is suffused with a wondrous and immense sweetness which no sense can measure and no speech can explain. For when that heavenly Bridegroom is united to his bride in the embraces of love and inclines to kiss her, at his touch the mind is suddenly suffused with a certain heavenly sweetness. It can indeed feel it, but, as was said above, cannot explain it in any fullness of speech. For that dripping honeycomb of divine lips, pressed firmly upon the bride’s fixed lips, begins to distill sweetness and pour forth delight.

That sweetness of heavenly delight, flowing in, begins first to fill the bride’s interior; afterwards it flows as far as her mouth; and at last it streams forth through her lips, so that she immediately deserves to hear from her Bridegroom: “Honey and milk are under your tongue; your lips are a dripping honeycomb” (Song 4), because “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” Yet, as in the preceding matters, so also in this increase of inward sweetness we may observe certain stages of advancement. First that inward delight begins to be felt; from it there arises a certain wondrous eagerness of enjoyment; eagerness is followed by satiety, satiety by intoxication, intoxication by security, security by tranquility.

Who does not know that sweetness once tasted sharpens eagerness? For the sweeter anything tastes to someone, the more keenly it kindles in the taster’s mind the appetite for it. But without doubt, the more eagerly we eat, the sooner we attain the desired satiety. Thus sweetness is followed by eagerness, and eagerness by satiety. We know, moreover, that those who arrive at satiety by eating become disgusted with whatever is set before or offered to them. What, then, shall we say this satiety is, of which we have spoken, except a certain distaste for every bodily pleasure and, from an inmost affection, a certain spontaneous contempt for all external things?

For it is one thing to resist an enticing pleasure and, by violently repelling it, refuse to consent to it; it is another, by a certain spontaneous movement of inward affection, to find it distasteful and to be wholly unable meanwhile to find any fleshly allurements palatable. Therefore the soul reaches the true fullness of inward satiety when, because of the abundance of that sweetness which it feels inwardly, it acquires a certain necessary rather than voluntary distaste for everything that may be presented externally. But those who abound in external pleasures cannot feel this satiety of true sweetness. For such sweetness is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly, nor can such a savor be tasted amid so many pleasant delights and such varied seasonings of food. “The poor,” he says, “shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. 21): the poor, he says, not the rich.

This satiety, as has already been said, is usually followed by intoxication. We all know that those who are wholly drunk often do not even turn aside from insults, and do not know how either to avoid surrounding dangers or even to notice them. [Col. 0276A]

When, therefore, we see many daily becoming cheerful amid abuse and reproaches, rejoicing amid dangers and losses of possessions, what ought we to judge such people to be except drunk? What shall I call so great an alienation of mind except a kind of spiritual intoxication? First, then, we must find distasteful the various but empty pleasures of the world; second, we must despise all its adversities. The first is wrought by spiritual satiety; the second by spiritual intoxication. Thus intoxication follows satiety, as is proved by their effects.

From this intoxication the mind grows into such constancy and assumes such confidence in the Lord’s protection that it hears and says with the Apostle: “I am certain that neither death,” and so forth, “which is in Christ Jesus,” and so forth (Rom. 8). This is the settled and firm security followed by that true, full tranquility of mind which we named last. For what can disturb the tranquility of that mind which no spur of desire disquiets and no sting of fear agitates? This tranquility is that peace which we have sought through prolonged speech and to which we have scarcely at last ascended by so many steps. This is the peace in which the soul falls asleep: peace which carries the mind away to inward things; peace which cuts off all recollection of external things; which surpasses the sharpness of intellect; which overwhelms the light of reason; [Col. 0276C] which fills the heart’s desire; which absorbs all understanding.

John calls this rest “silence”; the Psalmist calls it “sleep” (Ps. 126). The Apostle calls it “the peace of God which surpasses all understanding” (Phil. 4). How rightly it is called silence! How truly we may call it sleep, if it surpasses all understanding! For what can worthily be said of that which surpasses all understanding? “There was silence in heaven,” he says, “for about half an hour” (Rev. 8). We have heard why it is rightly called silence; but how will it also be sleep?

Consider what outward sleep does to the outward person; this kind of sleep does that to the inward person. Bodily sleep surpasses bodily sensation, for it removes the function of the eyes, the function of the ears, and of the other [Col. 0276D] senses and members. And just as all bodily senses are lulled to sleep by outward sleep, so by this sleep of the inward person of which we speak all the senses of the mind are surpassed. For it simultaneously absorbs thought, imagination, reason, memory, and understanding, thus confirming what the Apostle writes: that it surpasses all understanding.

The soul receives this kind of sleep amid the embraces of the true Bridegroom, when it rests in his bosom. Hence she says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 8). He had already conceived a firm hope of this rest in such a reclining-place who sang with such confidence: “In peace I shall sleep and rest in the same” (Ps. 4).

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 25

[Col. 0277]

[Col. 0277A] “Judge me, O Lord.” I would like to know what I myself am like, but I can scarcely discern the truth about myself. For the private love which I have for myself takes away my true judgment concerning myself. Judge me, therefore, O Lord, who truly know me. You say to me concerning yourself, “I am the truth”; and I know that every human being is a liar. Therefore I place little trust in myself, as in a lying human being, fearing that, if I judge myself, iniquity may lie to itself. You do this more rightly, because you are truthful; you can do it better, because you are Truth. Let Truth therefore enter my heart, bear true witness against me, and pronounce true judgment concerning me.

Judge me, therefore, O Lord; show me, I beg you, what I am like, O Lord. You pronounce the true sentence concerning me; I myself exact punishment from myself. Or, if perhaps guilt has been wiped away in me through repentance, show me what I still lack of perfect righteousness. For you judge me usefully before myself if you plainly show me what I am in your sight.

“Judge me, therefore, O Lord, for I have entered in my innocence.” You were within; I was without, and therefore I could not hear your voice. I was outside while I sought external things, while I thought upon external things. But now, having become one of those who return to the heart, I hastened to fulfill that command which says: “Return to the heart, you transgressors” (Isa. 46). And behold, Lord, I am now within: see, you who are within; for “I have entered in my innocence,” in order that I might hear you, in order that I might speak with you. For this reason I entered to you, and behold, I am now within with you.

Speak, therefore, Lord, for your servant hears. I am ready to hear what the Lord God now speaks within me. For those who are outside, who still love external things and think only of external things, cannot hear your voice. Some are outside through both thought and love; others through thought alone. Likewise, some are within through thought alone; others through both thought and love. For the person who thinks vanity and loves vanity is certainly outside, not only in thought but also in love. But those who unwillingly administer external affairs from the duty of their office, yet do not so much love the care of external things as endure it—although they are within in love, they are compelled to go outside, at least in thought. [Col. 0277D]

There are some who seek truth both curiously and diligently, yet do not love truth. Such persons are, as it were, within through their pursuit of truth, yet they are not within through love of virtue. But those who seek truth and love truth are within through both thought and love. Therefore, Lord, if I think only of inward things and love only inward things, it is surely established that I am no longer outside; it is clear that I am within with you. Judge me, therefore, O Lord, for I have entered [Col. 0278A] in my innocence.

Without doubt, if I were not innocent, I would not presume to enter to you, nor would I dare to appear in your sight. If I were not innocent, I could not—or rather, would not dare to—hear the voice of your inspiration. Therefore I shall guard myself from my iniquity, so that I may hear your words, so that I may not tremble to appear in your sight, so that I may merit the enjoyment of your conversation. Knowing indeed that you “will not withhold good things from those who walk in innocence,” I have confidently entered to you in my innocence.

I know that the corruption of the mind is greater, I know that it is worse, than that of the body. Indeed, we are often healed inwardly when we are struck outwardly; and therefore, in order to be truly innocent, I avoided harming souls. I could harm another’s soul by a bad example; I could also kill my own soul by consent to wickedness alone. But I strove to be innocent so that I might dare to come to your judgment; and now judge me, O Lord, for I have entered in my innocence. Whatever evil I could discover in myself by my own judgment, I hastened to correct; now, however, judge me, O Lord. So far as my own judgment goes, I appear already innocent; but I do not dare to trust myself sufficiently concerning myself, and therefore, I beg, judge me, O Lord. Make known to me what I am secretly in your sight. Meanwhile, to the extent that I could, I preserved innocence—perhaps my own innocence, but not yours. For it was innocence according to my own judgment, but perhaps it was not true according to your judgment. And behold: judge me, O Lord, for I have entered in my innocence.

“And hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened.” Adam was within, and he was whole; yet he could not preserve his wholeness. Having become weak, he could not remain within, because he hoped in himself, not in the Lord. But I, hoping in the Lord, shall not be weakened. The devil stood established not only in inward goods but even in the highest goods; yet he could not long preserve the stability of the wholeness which he had received in creation, because he hoped in his own strength, not in the Lord’s mercy. But I, hoping in the Lord, shall not be weakened.

Both were within; both were whole. Afterwards both became weak; afterwards both were cast out: one from heaven, the other from paradise. For each presumed upon himself. But I have entered in my innocence, and, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened. I was outside; I was weak. But now I have entered, and, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened. They were whole, they were within; I was outside, I was weak. Yet now I shall enter “into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession”; and, having entered, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened.

It is not hidden from me, Lord, how great a labor it is to remain within, to persevere in inward things; nevertheless, I believe that, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened. Certainly it was difficult to recall the mind from external to inward things, exceedingly hard to penetrate from visible things to [Col. 0279A] invisible. But perhaps it will be much more difficult to remain in them longer; nevertheless, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened.

The children of Israel could scarcely enter the land of promise except after much time and many dangers, and yet afterwards they could not defend it for themselves without great labor and great strength. I have scarcely at last touched the land flowing with milk and honey; late have I merited to taste the sweetness of contemplation; and already I see the envy of enemies inflamed more fiercely against me. Yet I am certain that, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened. “Those who trust in the Lord shall renew their strength”; how much more will they not fear weakness? Therefore, hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened.

“Test me, O Lord, and try me.” There are two things: doing good and avoiding evil. Test me, therefore, O Lord, whether I am ready to do good; try me, whether I am cautious to avoid evils. Test me, O Lord, and try me. Test me through adversities; try me through prosperities. Test me, O Lord, and try me.

There are likewise two things which make a person perfect: virtue and wisdom. I desire both, because I long for perfection. Test me, therefore, O Lord, and try me. By testing we advance toward virtue; by trial we are instructed toward truth. Our virtue is exercised by tests; our prudence is taught by trials. Test me, O Lord, and try me.

“Burn my reins and my heart.” You know that desire sometimes arises from the vice of the flesh, sometimes descends from the vice of the mind. Burn, therefore, my reins and my heart. To extinguish the itch of the flesh, burn my reins; to extinguish the desires of the heart, burn my heart. Burn my reins to consume the craving of the flesh; burn my heart to dry up the overflow of the mind. Burn my reins and my heart; burn my flesh and my mind. Burn my flesh with the fire of tribulation; burn my mind with the blaze of compunction. Let the flesh be crushed; let the heart be pierced. Let the flesh be afflicted by labor; let the heart be affected by sorrow. Let both be burned; let both be purified.

“Burn my reins and my heart, for your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleasing in your truth.” Yet I presume nothing upon my own strength, but upon your mercy; [Col. 0279D] I do not trust in my own wisdom, but in your mercy, because your mercy is before my eyes. I know that my enemy is stronger than I; I know that he is more cunning than I. Yet he need not be feared by me, because your mercy is before my eyes. I know indeed that he is more powerful and more prudent. But “my eye has looked down upon my enemies,” insofar as your mercy is before my eyes. Test, try, burn my reins and heart. In all these things I do not tremble, I do not fear, insofar as your mercy is before my eyes.

I know that “all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to his purpose.” I know, no less, that the Lord is faithful, who does not permit us to be tried beyond what we can bear, but will, together with the trial, also make a way out, so that [Col. 0280A] we may endure. Therefore I do not refuse to fight, because I hope to conquer, since your mercy is before my eyes. It is before my eyes because I acknowledge it; it is before my eyes because I look to it. The eye of foresight, the eye of understanding: both are directed, both are fixed upon you, because your mercy is before my eyes. Because I think upon it, because I know it, your mercy is before my eyes. Because I hope in it, because I look up to it, it is before my eyes.

“Because your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleasing in your truth”—not in my own virtue, but in your truth; not in my own holiness, but in your truth. For I do not trust in my merits, but presume upon your promises, because I have been pleasing in your truth. You promised me; [Col. 0280B] you predestined me from eternity. You cannot lie because you are truth; you can fulfill what you have promised; you must accomplish what you have predestined, because you are truthful. If I am such as I was ordained from eternity to be, I ought to please you; indeed, I know that I please you. And even if I am not yet such, nevertheless I please you in your sight, because I shall be such: for I have been pleasing in your truth.

In your truth I please you; in your truth I please myself, because I have been pleasing in your truth—both to you and to myself. I have pleased, I say, not in another’s flattery, not in self-exaltation, but in your truth; not according to the mouth of those who speak iniquity, not according to the heart of those who devise falsehoods, but I have been pleasing in your truth. If I am clean in body and pure in mind, then I know that I have been pleasing in your truth. If my works are righteous [Col. 0280C] and my desires chaste, then I have truly been pleasing in your truth. If I am pleasing inwardly, if I am pleasing outwardly, I am pleasing in both; I am pleasing on every side.

The philosophers of the nations cultivate virtue, but do not believe the truth. Even if their work is pleasing, their faith is displeasing; and therefore they cannot themselves be pleasing, since they despise true faith. False Christians have faith but do not have works of faith. In one respect they please, in the other they displease; therefore they too cannot be pleasing. If I possess both, I know that I truly please you. Yet I attain neither through myself; I cannot possess either from myself. But who taught me this except your truth? And for this reason I have been pleasing in your truth.

Your truth taught me that my goods are your goods, [Col. 0280D] and that my evils are my sins; and I have been pleasing in your truth. Your truth instructed me to ascribe my evils to myself and attribute my goods to you; and therefore I have been pleasing in your truth. I have learned that I cannot rise through myself; I have known that I cannot stand without you. I believe and confess that you are the one who works in me both to will and to accomplish according to your good pleasure; and for this reason I have been pleasing in your truth.

“I have not sat with the council of vanity, nor have I entered in with those who practice iniquity; I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I shall not sit with the ungodly.” There are three things which my soul has hated; it detests a fourth: vanity, iniquity, and malignity—these three are very hateful. But impiety, which is directed against God, my soul utterly execrates. Vanity is useless; iniquity evil; malignity worse; [Col. 0281A] impiety worst. Vanity is contemptible; iniquity hateful; malignity abominable; impiety detestable.

To take excessive care of the body; to cherish the flesh in fleshly desires; to indulge too much in food or sleep; to seek adornment in clothing—all this is vanity, because all this is vain. To retain one’s own possessions greedily; to seek another’s eagerly; to reduce to private ownership things which the Author of all willed to be common to all; to refuse others what we wish them to do for us—this is not at all just, because all this is contrary to equity, because all this is iniquity.

To retain hatred in the heart; to seek vengeance upon enemies; to rejoice at an enemy’s ruin; to waste away with envy at another’s prosperity—all this is malicious, all this is malign, and therefore cannot please me, because it is wholly full of malignity. To murmur, blaspheme, criticize God’s just judgments, raise the heart in pride against God, and seek one’s own glory in God’s gifts—all this is impious; a devout heart cannot receive all this, because it is wholly impiety. Nor is it good to think otherwise than piously. Therefore vanity is to be despised, iniquity hated, malignity condemned, impiety execrated.

Excessive self-love persuades toward vanity; disordered love of the world introduces iniquity; hatred of one’s neighbor produces malignity. Contempt of God nourishes impiety. For to be engrossed in the cares of the flesh is vain; to wish to surpass others in worldly glory is iniquitous; to exercise hostilities against one’s neighbors is malign; proudly to insolently defy one’s Creator is impious. Gluttony and lust suggest vanity, because what they seek is vain and what they love is vain: the former demands superfluous provision for the uses of nature, while the latter dissolves the foolish mind into extravagance, laughter, and jesting.

Avarice kindles iniquity when it reduces to individual ownership things which the one Author made common to all. For when it wickedly denies others what it wishes them to do for itself, it sins against equity. Anger and envy produce malice and inflame malignity: the former rages at its own injury, while the latter burns at another’s good fortune. Both act maliciously, in that the former rejoices in its neighbor’s misfortune, while the latter wastes away at his good.

From sorrow or pride impiety is kindled, [Col. 0281D] since both are shown, by an unholy presumption, to detract from divine goodness. For sloth often murmurs against God’s chastisements. Pride, however, appropriates to its own glory whatever it receives from God’s gift. For sorrow, when it is corrected by God, strives to accuse not its own conscience but God’s justice; and what God prepares for its correction as a kind of medicine for particular maladies, it does not hesitate to turn into an insult against him. What, I ask, is so impious, what so alien from true devotion? Pride, meanwhile, when it arrogates gifts to its own merits or powers, so far as it can, empties the glory of the one who glorifies; and who can worthily describe how impious this very thing is?

Therefore, wishing to avoid vanity, “I have not sat with the council of vanity”; and because I strive to avoid iniquity, “I shall not enter in with those who practice iniquity.” But I cannot love malignity, and therefore “I have hated the assembly of evildoers.” Yet I must confess what is true: countless thoughts often come into my mind, many affections arise, and they solicit me concerning care of the body and suggest many things about necessary needs. They meet there as if to deliberate, but in truth to deceive; many counsellors and vain advisers gather together—or rather, genuine deceivers.

They gather, as it were, into one council and as if to seek good counsel; many counsels are offered in common, but useless and vain ones, because it is a council of vanity and all their counsel concerns vanity. They advise taking [Col. 0282B] wine for the stomach, prolonging sleep for the brain, cherishing the flesh lest it waste away, refreshing the body lest it fail, relaxing abstinence somewhat, and indulging rest for a little while. Thus there is discussion of bodily care—superfluous care!—and a vain question is debated about vanity; often a whole day is consumed upon such a useless concern.

But by much experience I have already learned not to trust the counsel of vanity; and, especially so that I might not set my heart upon vain counsels, “I have not sat with the council of vanity.” For whenever I see such vain counsellors assembling, I do not sit down or rest, but shake my mind free; now I flee to work, now to prayer, saying: “Turn away my eyes, lest they behold vanity” (Ps. 118). [Col. 0282C] “Send forth your light and your truth” (Ps. 42). Nor do I cease until vanity vanishes and truth shines forth.

It is good, therefore, Lord, not to sit with the council of vanity. It is likewise good not to enter, but rather to avoid, the company of iniquity. But unless vanity is first avoided, iniquity is not avoided at all. For one who serves gluttony must necessarily serve avarice, because one who loves luxuries soon desires to have money. But if I once set my mind upon the love of money, I soon consent to wicked counsellors and those who practice iniquity, and willingly receive their counsels.

[Col. 0282D] Suddenly evil thoughts are at hand; perverse affections arise; they counsel the increase of wealth, the seeking of revenues; they teach one to extend estates, raise palaces, urge one to solicit royal taxes, not to despise the little gifts of the poor, to join field to field, house to house, to keep hands outstretched for plundering and clenched tight for giving anything, to receive everything and distribute nothing, not to love hospitality, to defraud almsgiving. They urge one to widen one’s fringes, enlarge one’s phylacteries, make one’s face pale, prolong prayer, so as to be seen by all, heard by passers-by, to deliver a discourse to the people, to shed tears in public—deceptively, as though in order to win souls, but in truth to gather money. In this way, after the council of those seeking vain things, there is often held the hateful assembly of those doing wicked things and speaking perversely.

[Col. 0283A] And so, often, when I abandon the more secret places of inner quiet, when I go out from within to think about external things, a great multitude of such thoughts suddenly surrounds me. Nor can I avoid the conversations of such wicked beings until I enter into the sanctuary of God and understand their latter end. For these reasons, and others like them, I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not enter in with those who do wicked things. Far be it from me to enter the courts of the Lord with such an assembly; far be it, I say, that I should go with them into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God. I will by no means enter, with such workers of wickedness, unto the altar of God, unto God who gladdens my youth. But after they have first been examined and excluded, I now enter confidently into the Holy of Holies—[Col. 0283B] at one time only within the first veil, into the secret place of prayer; at another, even within the second, into the mystery of contemplation.

Let such fantasies therefore first be excluded, lest, admitted within, they disturb prayer and hinder contemplation. For they commonly agitate the one and cloud the other. Within the first veil we ask heavenly goods from God. But how shall we receive them if we deny earthly things to our neighbour? It is altogether fitting that, if we wish to reap spiritual things, we should not hesitate to sow our carnal goods: “Give,” he says, “and it shall be given unto you” (Luke 6). If we give gladly, let us confidently enter within the first veil, asking that it may be given to us. Let us enter within the second, and it shall be given to us.

For within the first veil, like beggars at the door of the divine feast, we ask for alms; [Col. 0283C] but within the second, admitted as it were through the rich man’s gate, receiving certain remnants, as though of food, we taste a little of the Lord’s sweetness. And there are many even to this day who desire to receive a taste of divine sweetness, yet do not wish to show to their neighbours the humanity which they owe them. They wish that it be given to them, but themselves refuse to give; and what, I ask, is more unjust? Therefore I will not enter in with those who do wicked things, knowing that if I do not give to one who asks, I myself, when asking, do not receive.

Therefore, whatever thought or whatever affection urges me greedily to desire what belongs to another, and avariciously to retain what is my own, I do not listen to it at all; and unless it has been shaken off and removed, I do not enter the tabernacle of the Lord, because the things which it counsels are wicked, and [Col. 0283D] I will not enter in with those who do wicked things.

But what shall I say, Lord, concerning the malicious? You know, Lord, that I have hated the assembly of the malicious, and to sit with them; how much less can I enter in to you with them? Since I cannot love them, what wonder if I avoid their conversations? Those are malicious who seek or desire evil for their neighbour. I would truly call every will malicious, truly judge it malign, which incites me to injure my neighbour or inflames me to hatred of him. Yet you know, Lord, that, often assailed by injuries, I do not think of revenge; often provoked by reproaches, I do not answer harshly. For I have hated the assembly of the malicious, and I judge it malicious to acquiesce in them. I have not sat with the council of vanity; I have hated the assembly of the malicious.

O vanity, O malice! [Col. 0284A] Vanity suggests a superfluous love of the world. Malice seeks to take away love of one’s neighbour. Vanity nevertheless has some pleasure, though vain and foolish. Malice knows nothing but pain and bitterness. How, do you think, does anger tear the mind? How greatly, I ask, does envy torment the soul? And what is more malicious than either, what more bitter? Malice, then, is both punishment and guilt. These two very great evils easily persuaded me not to love malice; indeed, they compelled me to hate it. And now I have truly hated the assembly of the malicious, and I can no longer love it. For how can I love that in which I offend God, injure my neighbour, and torment myself? Certainly, if concern for my neighbour does not move me, in this matter at least I will spare myself: for malice [Col. 0284B] always torments the mind of its possessor, even though it may often be unable to harm the neighbour against whom it rages.

For such reasons I have hated the assembly of the malicious. But although all malice is evil, the worst kind of this evil is that which commits its injuries under the appearance of holiness. For often, when it rages against a neighbour through the vice of anger or the poison of envy, the thought pretends to itself that it does this from zeal for righteousness. Anyone injured by his neighbour can no longer easily look upon him with a simple eye. Whatever he observes that man doing displeases him; at nearly every hour he silently accuses him in his own thoughts. Countless grounds arise every day which show that man guilty; many arguments occur [Col. 0284C] which prove that he is culpable, that he ought to be punished.

And the evil often grows so great that he believes himself guilty before God unless he rebukes that man more severely and reproves him for his perversity. For such a malicious thought speaks within him: “How long am I to endure such a man? If I do not rebuke him, I am proved to consent to him; and by consenting, I offend God. Therefore I shall rebuke him, lest I offend God. I shall do everything not to avenge my own injury, but God’s injury; indeed, I shall thus restore him to himself.” For what is it? To rebuke one’s neighbour and chastise him—is that not to harm one’s neighbour, but to wish to benefit him?

Thus the malicious thought often speaks within itself. For its own malice has blinded it; it thinks its hatred to be love, and [Col. 0284D] imagines that it is exercising justice in its own injury. Thus such malicious thoughts gather from every side into the mind, and suppose that they are making a Church, not assembling an army. For they pretend that they meet in God’s service, not that they wish to exercise their own hatred. For one who prepares himself for his own revenge is, as it were, assembling an army. But in some sense a multitude of thoughts makes a church when it pretends to gather for God’s service. Yet I now easily mock such an assembly, because I have hated the assembly of the malicious, and I will not sit with the ungodly.

I confess that I have not yet advanced so far as to hate them, as I testified concerning the assembly of the malicious. Nevertheless, I do what I can: I avoid their company, and henceforth I will not sit with the ungodly. [Col. 0285A] I do not know how it happens that nothing so delights the mind as the possibility of glorying, although it is written: “My glory I will not give to another” (Isa. 48). The human mind therefore especially appropriates to itself that very thing which God, unwilling to give it to anyone else, reserves for himself alone. Nor are so many goods of nature and so many gifts of grace enough for a human being, unless he also adds robbery and, in order that he may clothe himself, strips his own Lord of his glory.

Hence he is always ready to excuse his sins and lay them upon his God, saying with Adam, “The woman whom thou gavest me deceived me” (Gen. 3), thinking that all his sin proceeds from the defect of the flesh, and therefore attributing blame to its author, who made it such. Conversely, he ascribes God’s gifts to his own merits and seeks from them not the glory of him whose gifts they are, but [Col. 0285B] his own glory. And what, I ask, is so impious? To wish one’s evils to be imputed to God, and God’s gifts to be ascribed to oneself—who does not see how impious and how criminal this is?

Therefore henceforth I will not sit with the ungodly, but will avoid their counsels. Would that I hated every ungodly thought as much as I have hated the assembly of the malicious! Would that I never desired to appropriate God’s glory to myself as little as I delight in my neighbour’s evil! Yet even if I have not yet been able to uproot from my affections the love of vain praise, as I believe I have advanced to hatred of the malicious, I will do what I can: I will not sit with the ungodly. But when they gather in my mind, I immediately rise up to attack them and drive them from my mind with whatever bitterness I can. [Col. 0285C] Therefore, just as I have not sat with the council of vanity, so likewise I will not sit with the ungodly.

But [Col. 0286A] because it is not enough to avoid evil unless we also add the doing of good: “I will wash my hands among the innocent.” It is therefore not enough for me, Lord, that I have not sat with the council of vanity, that I have hated the assembly of the malicious, that I will not enter in with those doing wicked things, that I will not sit with the ungodly; for all this is merely avoiding evil. But in order to please you perfectly in your sight, I shall strive to serve you in good work. Therefore I will wash my hands among the innocent.

The hand is twofold; the work is twofold: the work of justice and the work of mercy. I shall therefore exercise myself in this twofold work, that I may have hands which I can raise to you through good intention. And if, perhaps, while these hands are at work, some stain—as commonly happens—clings to them, and either the mud of pride or the dust [Col. 0286B] of vain glory defiles them, I shall indeed wash my hands among the innocent, and shall strive, as far as I can, to cleanse them. For whenever I weep before you over the stains of my deeds, I endeavour to wash the spots on my hands with the flood of tears. Whatever is defiled through guilt is cleansed through the washing of compunction. Whoever therefore wishes to have clean hands should strive to cleanse them by continual tears.

But because this is better done among the good, by whose examples we are instructed, by whose teaching we are educated, and by whose prayers we are helped, I too shall wash my hands not among just anyone, but among the innocent. I know that those are innocent, and preserve true innocence, who neither injure their own soul through consent to a perverse will nor harm another’s by the example [Col. 0286C] of perverse conduct. I strive to have such companions because I desire to have clean works.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM XXVIII

[Col. 0285]

[Col. 0285C] “Bring unto the Lord, ye sons of God; bring unto the Lord the sons of rams.”

It is to you, novices, that this is said: Take heed, if you desire to be sons of God. The choice is given to you; it is left to your own election whether you pass into the freedom of sons, remain in the subjection of hirelings, or rather serve under the condition of slaves. What each chooses to be is declared by his sacrifice. In the Law it is prescribed—or taught—that the sacrifice of princes ought to be one thing, [Col. 0285D] that of priests another, and that of the poor another. So, unless I am mistaken, one sacrifice befits a son, another a hireling, and yet another a slave. As their condition differs, so their offering ought to differ.

“Bring unto the Lord, ye sons of God; bring unto the Lord the sons of rams.” If you are sons, you act willingly; if you wish to be sons, you must act willingly. Do not appear empty in the Lord’s sight: you who are sons of God, bring to the Lord—not just anything, but sons of rams. If anyone is led as a sheep to slaughter, and, like a lamb before its shearer, is silent and does not open his mouth, he will certainly be counted among those sons who offer to the Lord sons of rams. For one who is still a slave does not suffice for such a sacrifice; it is a great thing for him if he can offer a turtledove or a dove.

[Col. 0286C] For one who still serves in fear, and does not so much love God as fear him, thinks it sufficient if only he can weep and groan and make satisfaction for former sins by lamentation and groaning, as by a kind of dove-like song. But although the hireling slaughters on the Lord’s altar the kid of former wantonness and perverse pleasure, lest he lose his reward, it does not easily happen that his hands find an immaculate lamb, a little lamb, to offer as a whole burnt offering to the Lord.

[Col. 0286D] For he who has been able to put off the fleeces of earthly riches without any resistance, willingly to endure every tribulation without hatred of his persecutors, and amid every torture to retain inner peace and tranquillity of heart—such a man has indeed offered a lamb in God’s sacrifice, and by that offering alone has shown himself to be a son. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the sons of God” (Matt. 5). It is therefore permissible, unless I am mistaken, to assess the dignity of persons by their sacrifices. For it suffices for a slave to repent of evils out of fear of hell; for a hireling, to abstain from evils for the sake of reward; for a son, it is little enough to lay down his life for the Lord in death.

Thus repentance pertains to slaves, abstinence befits hirelings, [Col. 0287A] and patience belongs to sons. Therefore bring with you lambs of patience and meekness, you who hope or sigh for adoption as sons. “Bring unto the Lord, ye sons of God; bring unto the Lord the sons of rams.”

But why did he prefer to say “sons of rams,” when “lambs” could have been said more briefly? For rams cannot beget any other sons. Perhaps he wished us, whenever we desire perfect works, to look to the leaders and princes of the Lord’s flock—namely, the prophets and apostles and those like them—and to learn from their deeds and words what we ought to do and what we ought to desire. Let us strive to produce and nurture in ourselves the same desires that they produced from themselves, and to possess the same works that they strove to possess; then without doubt we offer to the Lord sons of rams.

[Col. 0287B] “Bring unto the Lord, ye sons of God; bring unto the Lord the sons of rams.” “Bring,” “bring unto the Lord,” “unto the Lord”: each is set down twice; each is repeated. If you wish to have a double robe, double your sacrifice here. Whoever disdains to double his sacrifice here will be crushed with double crushing. For a double sacrifice a double robe will be given. For the robe of the body, offer the sacrifice of good action; for the robe of the mind, give the sacrifice of devout dedication.

“Do not fear those who kill the body, but have nothing they can do to the soul.” These can indeed rule the body, but have nothing they can do to the spirit; therefore they are lords only, not Lord of lords. Fear him, then; offer gifts to him who, after taking life away, can also cast the soul [Col. 0287C] into hell. Therefore bring to the Lord, the Lord—the Lord of bodies, the Lord of spirits. “Lord” once, because he rules in time; “Lord” a second time, because he is sovereign in eternity. “Lord,” because he gives temporal goods or evils to whom he wills; “Lord” again, because he will give eternal rewards or torments to whom he pleases.

“Bring unto the Lord, ye sons of God; bring unto the Lord the sons of rams.” The distinction of the words is fitting: “sons of God, bring unto the Lord.” If “God” denotes goodness, “Lord” signifies power. This distinction sufficiently indicates that our being sons is grace, not merit; that our rendering service is a debt, not a favour.

“Bring unto the Lord glory and honour; bring unto the Lord glory to his name.” In the preceding verse “bring” [Col. 0287D] is set down twice; in the second it is likewise found twice. First it is said, “Bring, bring,” on our own account; second, “Bring, bring,” on account of our neighbours. First, bring sons of rams for merit; second, bring glory and honour for example. “Bring unto the Lord glory and honour; bring unto the Lord glory to his name.”

Some neighbours are good, others evil. Bring glory and honour to the Lord on account of the good; bring glory to the Lord’s name on account of the evil. “So let your light shine before men,” and so forth. If you offer sons of rams, if you have works of meekness and desires of devotion, it is easy for your heart to be lifted up by such a sacrifice. Therefore it is said to you: “Bring unto the Lord glory and honour.” As though he said openly: In the sacrifices of your virtues seek not your own glory but the Lord’s [Col. 0288A] glory. In all that you do well, desire his praise, not your own. Do this; devote yourselves to this: that God may be glorified, that God may be honoured. “Bring unto the Lord glory and honour.”

God is glorified by praises; he is honoured by works. If, seeing your works, people praise God and strive to perform the same works, you have offered glory and honour to the Lord. If, seeing them, they marvel, and, marveling, imitate them, you have without doubt offered glory and honour to the Lord. For the good, bring glory and honour; but for the evil, bring glory to the Lord’s name. Since evil persons refuse to imitate your good works, let them at least find nothing in them that they can justly blame, lest perhaps through you, contrary to the Lord’s command, the name of God be blasphemed among the nations. Let them therefore see in [Col. 0288B] you what they can rightly praise, even if they are unwilling to imitate your good deeds. If the Lord’s discipline is praised through you even by those in whom he himself is not received through a good will, you have offered glory to the Lord’s name.

Therefore in good persons you have offered to the Lord not only glory but also honour, because by praising they glorify and by acting they honour. But in evil persons, at least glory to his name, because they praise his discipline, though they do not strive to keep it. “Worship the Lord in his holy court.” Above, we are commanded to offer sacrifice; here, we are commanded to worship within. First, lest we enter empty; secondly, lest we stand idle: lest you enter empty, “bring unto the Lord glory to his name”; lest you be idle within, “worship the Lord [Col. 0288C] in his holy court.”

What is worship except to cast down our whole body at his feet and incline what is highest in us to what is lowest in him? The Prophet therefore desires you to submit yourselves not only to the Lord’s higher members—that is, to the prelates—but voluntarily to humble yourselves even to his lowest members. “Be subject therefore to every human creature for God’s sake,” and without doubt you have worshipped the Lord.

Thus enter with sacrifices; having entered, worship. Take up the narrow way; enter through the strait gate—in the habit of religion, in the vow of profession. Remain in the house of discipline; hold to the ordinances of the rule. For if you have confined yourselves within cloistered discipline, you have without doubt entered the Lord’s court. But if you make the vow of profession, if you keep the ordinances of the rule, you have offered sacrifices very pleasing [Col. 0288D] to the Lord. For if, living in the cloister, you humbly obey everyone in all things, you have truly worshipped the Lord in his holy court.

But someone says: “Behold, choosing one congregation from among the rest, I propose to promise the stability of my body, but I greatly fear the excessive fickleness of my heart. Behold, I promise amendment of my conduct, but the ordinances of the canons are hard. Yet I propose to amend my conduct, especially in chastity, common life, and obedience, provided grace does not fail. But when I promise chastity, how shall I extinguish lust? I nevertheless fear common life because of weakness, and obedience because of pride.”

You do well indeed to despair of yourself, provided [Col. 0289A] that you do not cease to hope in the Lord. Reveal your way therefore to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act; and he, I know, will repel both the fluctuations of the human mind and wandering thoughts.

“But the voice of the Lord is upon the waters.” If you tremble because of your weakness or faint-heartedness, consider that “the voice of the Lord is in power; the voice of the Lord is in magnificence.” You fear pride of mind and swelling arrogance, but it is “the voice of the Lord breaking the cedars.” If, however, you fear the fires of lust, and especially the spirit of fornication, know that it is “the voice of the Lord cutting apart the flame of fire.” Think on these things; ponder them. But now let us return to each point.

Behold, you say that your mind is very fickle, exceedingly unstable, wandering and fugitive, changing itself everywhere and fluctuating from every side; that, sluggishly, it wills and does not will, changes its counsels, and alternates its desires, like a wave of the sea moved and driven about by the wind. [Col. 0289B] But he who turned the sea into dry land can easily command that the waters under heaven be gathered into one place and dry land appear. For often, at the voice of the commanding Lord, the waters of such carnal desires have returned, going and returning until the whole surface of the earth was dry. For the voice of the Lord is upon the waters, however many or however great they may be. At the nod of his will he gathers them into one place and confines them within the bounds of necessity, so that dry land may appear and the purpose of good will be made firm, because the voice of the Lord is upon the waters.

But if you have little faith in words, believe at least the examples. See how many you observe to have preceded you into religion and to hold strictly to the strictness of the order: formerly unstable and frivolous, very like you, but now steadfast in purpose and constant in good; formerly wandering in mind and vain in endeavour, but now strict in discipline and established in religion. How, I ask, could this have happened, unless the God of majesty thundered upon many waters? What does “he thundered upon many waters” mean except that he terrified minds wandering in many ways and flowing away greatly? Therefore the Lord dried up in them their excessive water and turned the sea into dry land.

He who dried up many waters in others—can he not dry up yours? Will not he who, when he willed, thundered over them be able to terrify you by thunder? For in them the God of majesty thundered: he sounded terribly, terrified their hearts, and changed their will. [Col. 0289D] Such a great and sudden change of mind was wrought by the thunder of the divine voice that, immediately abandoning the world and following Christ, they did not hesitate to cross the lake of Gennesaret with him, although wondrous surges of the sea rose and raged against them. For the wind was contrary to them, that is, the blast of diabolical suggestion. But Jesus arose, commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm.

See then how you can observe that they no longer waver or tremble at all; rather, fervent in spirit and rejoicing in hope, each one of them has “rejoiced as a giant to run the way” of the Lord’s commandments. The God of majesty thundered; the Lord was upon many waters. For sometimes he thunders as God, and sometimes he thunders as Lord: when he threatens eternal evils, he thunders as God; [Col. 0290A] when he inflicts temporal evils, he thunders as Lord. God alone can grant eternal goods or evils. A temporal lord, too, can afflict bodies.

Therefore, when you see people sound in body but compunct in heart, leaving the world and taking up the religious habit, know that the Lord of majesty has thundered, that the God of majesty has terrified their hearts. When someone, compelled by bodily illness or loss of possessions, is forced to abandon his wicked ways, recognize that the Lord has thundered upon many waters. If, therefore, you have often seen some leave a slippery life through compunction of heart, others through bodily affliction, hasten to an order, live religiously, and not look back to the luxuries of their former life, why should you any longer fear for yourself, when you see many like yourself preceding you in the Lord’s way? He who thundered over them, terrified them, and established them in good can make the fluctuations of your mind firm and likewise restrain your wandering thoughts, just as, when he willed, the God of majesty thundered upon many waters in their hearts.

[Col. 0290B] Behold, you say—at last scarcely encouraged by words or examples—“I do what you urge. But if I promise stability of body, I must also keep common life; yet I fear bodily weakness and dread faint-heartedness of mind. For I am a weak and little human being, tender and delicate, brought up, as it were, in the land of those who live pleasantly, who wear soft things and feast splendidly every day. The weak person is disgusted by everything; the childish person always longs for what is new. How then can I keep common life, when I am always disgusted by what others have, and greedily desire what others cannot possess? I count the roots of plants and every most worthless thing among the highest delicacies, provided only that others do not have them; I loathe any royal feast if everyone shares it with me in common. And, that I may explain to you more fully everything which troubles my mind, my heart fails more than my body: my soul wastes away through feeble strength and scant understanding.”

[Col. 0290C] I grant that your strength is feeble—or nonexistent—and your prudence slight. But “the voice of the Lord is in power; the voice of the Lord is in magnificence.” He who is weak rightly despairs of his own strength; nevertheless, let him hope in the Lord, because the voice of the Lord is in power. Let one whose understanding is confined not presume upon his own prudence; but let him ask that his understanding may be enlarged by the Lord, because the voice of the Lord is in magnificence. Let him who lacks wisdom ask in faith of him who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach.

“Do not fear, little flock!” The Lord will give strength to his people, because the voice of the Lord is in power. “Those who trust in the Lord shall renew their strength,” because the voice of the Lord is in power. And if perhaps you have already received strength, and perhaps the Lord has girded you with strength for battle and clothed your comeliness with strength, but you are still scant in understanding and inferior in discerning judgment and laws, know that, in answer to your request, my Lord will make you increase like the sand of the sea and will give you abundance from the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, so that you may grasp some things by understanding [Col. 0291A] and be taught others by experience—drawing here from the dew of contemplation, and there instructed by the constancy of perfect action. Then, growing amid such abundance of things, you shall become great, as one made fat, grown rich, and enlarged among a wealth of delights.

You shall be enlarged toward east and west, north and south, so that you may fully recognize and perfectly know what is to be hoped for, feared, hated, and loved.
