And the Lord will give you breadth of heart like the sand upon the seashore, so that the abundance of good thoughts may be as great as formerly was the multitude of useless and vain thoughts, when your heart still rested by desire beside this great sea of the world and clung to it with an all too excessive love. But when your heart has been enlarged, good thoughts and holy desires of heart will multiply upon the sand of the sea. Good thoughts will arise of themselves, just as formerly evil thoughts sprang up by themselves without our effort; and then not a hair from your head will perish, because not even one good thought is forgotten before God, provided it is from the head and descends from reason or proceeds from right intention.

[Col. 0291B] I believe that, marveling at and amazed by this wonderful change wrought by the right hand of the Most High in you and people like you, they will then say among the nations: “The Lord has done great things with them.” And truly the Lord has done great things with us: we have become joyful, because “the voice of the Lord is in power; the voice of the Lord is in magnificence.”

But you still say: “In an order, not only are hard things observed; unworthy things are also commanded.”

[Col. 0291C] To this is added the fact that persons who are lowly and altogether contemptible, foolish and ignoble men, of no account at all in the world, often obtain positions of authority. It would be bad enough if unworthy persons at least did not command unworthy things, or if those who command lowly things were at least not themselves lowly. But now, to crown the evil, lowly persons command lowly things with authority, and in commanding they attend not to reason but to their own pleasure. When, do you think, shall I be able to endure this—I, a freeborn and learned man, vigorous in skill and distinguished in intellect? When shall I bend my heart to such persons and such things, or when shall I be able to bend it?

[Col. 0291D] For I bear a heart hard as wood, erect as a cedar; an ungodly mind raised and exalted like the cedars of Lebanon. To this I reply briefly: “The voice of the Lord breaks the cedars,” and easily restrains exalted spirits, and can quickly bend your pride. I confess that it is very difficult—indeed impossible—for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, or for a heart swollen with arrogance voluntarily to enter the narrowness of obedience. But what is impossible with human beings is possible with God—indeed, easy. “For he has done whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.”

Where he found a heart bright in understanding like heaven, where he discovered a mind firm like earth, if he saw a heart bitter and unstable like the sea, if he perceived [Col. 0292A] a mind dark like the abyss—always and everywhere he has done whatsoever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses. And not only at the thunder of his voice, but often at his very look, often at his entrance, he has crushed mountains of arrogance, bent hills of pride, and whenever he willed, cast down the mighty from their seat.

At his look, I say, because “he looked and dissolved the nations, and the everlasting mountains were broken.” Also at his entrance, because “at the goings of my God, my King, who is in the holy place,” the hills of the world were bent by his paths of eternity. And at the Lord’s voice the cedars of exaltation have often been broken, because “the voice of the Lord breaks the cedars, and the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon.”

It is one thing to break cedars and another to break the cedars of Lebanon. For not all cedars grow, or can grow, on Mount Lebanon. Thus some cedars grow in Lebanon and others on any other mountain. Lebanon is interpreted “whitening.” Do you wish to know what this whitening is? It is the justification of the saints themselves, their being made white. This is the Apostle John’s statement, not mine: “Fine linen,” he says, “is the justifications [righteous deeds] of the saints” (Rev. 19). Therefore, “Teach me thy justifications, O Lord, and I shall be made whiter than snow.”

[Col. 0292B] The garments of my Lord Jesus, garments white as snow (Mark 9), such as no fuller upon earth can make, were overlaid with such colour or whiteness. But the heavenly fuller can do this, he whose going forth is from the highest heaven. I speak falsely if he himself does not promise this, where, admonishing sinners, he says: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and though they be red as the crimson worm, they shall be white as wool” (Isa. 1). Most beneficial is the work of such a fuller; pleasing is his whitening, because good is justification.

When such whitening has grown into a mountain and begun to rise above the height of other mountains; when someone already thinks himself uniquely great and believes himself holier than all others, he easily produces from himself great cedars of great exaltations, when he imagines that he surpasses others by a certain prerogative of virtues. But the Lord is powerful not only to crush the everlasting mountains, but, whenever he wills, easily also to break the cedars of Lebanon.

[Col. 0292C] One kind of pride arises from worldly vanity; another seems to be born, as it were, from holiness attained. The cedars signify the former; the cedars of Lebanon, the latter. You have recently come from the world. Perhaps you still pride yourself on your learning, or perhaps on your wealth; perhaps you boast of nobility of birth; perhaps you exalt yourself because of the dignity of the honour you have held. Such exaltations are indeed cedars, but they are not cedars of Lebanon, because they arise from the blackness of vanity, not from the whitening of holiness.

But at the very beginning of your good way of life, the Lord will break the cedars of worldly pomp, because “the voice of the Lord breaks the cedars.” And if later, as commonly happens, after works of virtue certain cedars of great exaltations arise, as though from perfect justification, the Lord will add the breaking of these too, because “the Lord shall break [Col. 0293A] the cedars of Lebanon.” Therefore concerning the former he uses the present tense, not the future; but speaking of the cedars of Lebanon he uses the future, not the past: “The voice,” he says, “of the Lord breaks the cedars, and the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon.”

Do you still wish to know more clearly what the cedars of Lebanon are, which the Lord’s voice alone is sufficient to break? Behold, someone has perhaps fasted a little, kept vigil somewhat more than the rest, shed a tear in prayer; at once he begins to think himself holy, to despise others in comparison with himself, and to prefer his own inventions to the institutions of the fathers who went before him. He often wonders to himself why he does not work miracles; he is indignant that he receives no precedence over others, that he is not held in greater reverence; he attributes this to others’ envy, not to his own [Col. 0293B] lack of merit. He considers that he has a pale face, not that he has a polished mind. Indeed, when he has felt himself disturbed by shameful promptings and defiled by unclean pleasure, he pretends that he suffers these things not through his own negligence, but, as it were, for the preservation of humility. Thus it happens that he does not keep watch against lust, as though it were the guardian of humility; and he considers it humility that he is not afraid to be shamefully defiled. He does not know how detestable a pride it is to regard himself, amid such great rottenness, not as a sinner but as another Paul—as though an angel of Satan, a thorn in his flesh, had been given to buffet him, lest the multitude of virtues or the greatness of revelations should exalt him.

And so it comes about in a strange—indeed, pitiable—way that he is so proud, yet does not cease to indulge lust; and so indulges lust, yet does not cease to be proud. Who, do you suppose, is sufficient to crush cedars of this kind, except him at whose voice the cedars are broken, who, when he wills, will also break the cedars of Lebanon? And, that you may marvel still more: “He will crush them like a calf of Lebanon.” Truly this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High: to crush the rigidity of a cedar into the likeness of a calf of Lebanon, and to bend every swollen heart into the image of Christ’s humility. How, do you suppose, was he “bruised for our crimes,” not for his own sins? That unique calf came from Lebanon, “from a shadowy and thickly wooded mountain”; for “his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his course unto its utmost height,” where shines the brightness of eternal light. Going forth from there, he drew with him the splendour of righteousness; [Col. 0293D] returning there, having laid aside mortality, he put on the radiance of glory. How, I say, do you suppose that calf was crushed, except in the manner written: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2)? He gave himself for us, becoming obedient to the Father unto death—indeed, death on a cross.

Consider, I beg you, the greatness of the humiliation, the immensity of the crushing. Nothing is more bitter than the torment of the cross; nothing more disgraceful than death on the cross. To this add that he suffered willingly; add further that he died without guilt of his own. Let one who desires to be crushed like a calf of Lebanon hear, I beg you, how he ought to be bent low. Let him endure what is most harsh and most vile, willingly, even [Col. 0294A] without personal fault. Yet let no one presume that he can do this by his own strength. Let him rather hope for it from the Lord’s mercy, for whom it is possible, when he wills, to crush any cedars of Lebanon.

Therefore, whenever you see people who were formerly enraged at being corrected, but afterward rejoice in tribulation; who formerly delighted in fulfilling their own desires, but afterward glory in their infirmities; who formerly swelled with their own praises, but afterward gladly suffer reproach for Jesus’ name—you may know that the Lord has crushed them like a calf of Lebanon. You too must show yourself such, if you wish to bend the rigidity of the cedar and to be humbled after the pattern of Christ’s humility. But he himself teaches you this better than I. Hear what he says, and remember to imitate it: “I came down from heaven,” he says, “not to do [Col. 0294B] my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6). He chose to do his Father’s will, and you strive to fulfil your own. Your superior is your father; Christ, who came, sought to fulfil the will of his Father, and you should endeavour to do the will of your superior. Behold, at last we have found the calf that we must slaughter in the Lord’s burnt offering. Nothing, therefore, gives forth to the Lord an odour of sweetness as does the slaughtering for the Lord of the calf of one’s own will.

Yet it matters whether it is from Lebanon or from Carmel. There are calves that feed on Lebanon’s summit, and others that are nourished in Carmel’s pastures. Those nourish the calf of Carmel who do not abandon their own will in matters that are still carnal; those feed the calves of Lebanon who follow their own will in [Col. 0294C] spiritual pursuits. One seeks richer food than the rest; he fattens his calf on Carmel’s hay. Another, wishing to abstain, disdains to eat what the others eat; he nourishes his calf in Lebanon’s pastures. One perhaps desires softer clothing; another perhaps claims for himself, beyond the others, a rougher habit. Each seeks pasture for his own calf: this one from Carmel, that one from Mount Lebanon.

Finally, whatever is done because of softness of mind and tenderness of flesh seems to belong to Carmel, since *Carmel* is interpreted “soft” or “tender.” But whatever is presumptuously undertaken, as if for holiness, above the rule’s institution or contrary to a superior’s counsel, is rightly reckoned among the herds of Lebanon. “Woe to you who trust [Col. 0294D] in the calf of Samaria,” who serve your own will with such zeal. You came into Judaea: why have you gone down to Samaria, preserving and excusing your own will? Do you not know that Jews do not associate with Samaritans? When you first came from the world, you condemned your self-willed choices in which you had placed confidence; now, falling away from that first fervour, you seek, preserve, and defend your own wills. Thus—yes, thus—you have become Samaritans from Jews. In Judaea the calf of self-will is slain for the Lord; in Samaria it is worshipped as God. If you are in Judaea, you kill the calf in the Lord’s sacrifice; if you are in Samaria, you serve your calf with all your strength. If you make provision for the flesh in its desires, you feed your calf on hay; for “all flesh is hay, and all its glory like the flower of hay.” In [Col. 0295A] this you glory: that you accomplish your desires. Your glory is not good. Is it not much better, is it not much more fitting, that “he who glories should glory in the Lord”? Do you not know that “this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience”? But they “changed their glory into the likeness of a calf that eats hay.”

But what, I ask, will become of the flesh of this calf, when not even the calf of Lebanon can be pleasing unless it is carefully crushed, as befits the victim of a burnt offering? “But in what manner,” you ask, “must it be crushed?” Moses teaches you this better than I: first he commands that it be divided into pieces, then, placed beneath the flames, reduced to ashes (Exod. 29). How, I ask, do we ever crush it more finely than when, first divided [Col. 0295B] into pieces, we afterward reduce it by fire to a fine powder?

Our calf feeds in Lebanon if we follow our own will only in honourable matters. We slaughter our calf when, out of love for obedience, we renounce every singularity; but to cut up our calf is to rebuke the mind for its presumed liberty. He divides it even into pieces who carefully distinguishes every work of his own singularity and reproves himself in each for the boldness of presumption. Then nothing further remains except that it be burned by the fire of compunction or the flame of divine love until every impulse of this arrogance is put to sleep.

From such a burnt offering there remains, as it were, a certain ash of thoughts, which ought by no means to perish from our memory; for each person usefully remembers his presumptions when, at the remembrance of them, his humbled conscience is ashamed. But behold, while we have wished to deal carefully with our calf and crush it according to the command of the law, we have digressed somewhat too far.

It remains for us to learn, at the end of our discourse, what the difference is between the cedars of Lebanon and the calves of Lebanon. By the calves of Lebanon we understand presumptions of arrogance; by the cedars we understand the haughtiness of pride. Arrogance is presuming something beyond oneself. Pride is swelling even over one’s own presumption. Therefore, as often as we presume beyond the measure of our powers—even with a good [Col. 0295D] intention—so often we nourish calves in Lebanon. Cedars, as it were, rise from Lebanon when the haughty swellings of self-exaltation lift themselves high from our good works. Beneath the shade of such cedars the calves feed pleasantly, while people do not grow weary amid such labours for the attainment of a name for holiness.

“And he will crush them like a calf of Lebanon, and the Beloved as the son of unicorns.” Therefore not only does the Lord crush the cedars like a calf of Lebanon, but this Beloved also does so, as the son of unicorns. But who is this Beloved, or whose Beloved? He does not say, “of these” or “of those”; perhaps so that we may understand him to be the Beloved of all, just as, when “the Lord” is spoken of, we understand him who is King of kings and Lord of lords. Who, then, is this uniquely Beloved, the Beloved of each individual? Who else can he be but the one “fairer than the children of men,” who, through his incomparable beauty, shows himself wonderful to all and makes himself lovable?

Would you see how he is the Beloved of all? Hear what his Father says concerning him; consider what his bride cries out for him. The Father’s voice concerning the Beloved: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). The bride’s voice concerning the Beloved: “I charge you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love” (Song 5). And of the angels it is written: “into which angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1); and likewise we read of human beings: “the Desired of all nations will come” (Hag. 2). Therefore this Beloved is beloved of his Father, beloved of his bride, beloved of human beings, [Col. 0296B] beloved of angels, beloved of all, beloved of each. It is plain, therefore, that one does not possess true love who does not burn with love for this Beloved.

We have heard whose Beloved he is; let us also hear how, or how greatly, he is beloved: “and the Beloved,” it says, “as the son of unicorns.” But what is “as the son of unicorns”? Is it perhaps that this kind of animal loves its offspring more than all others, so that a unicorn is readier to perish for its young than to lose its young, preferring to incur death for it rather than lose it even alive? But who does not see this in Christ’s lovers: how they delight to die for Christ’s name? Let the great outpoured blood of the martyrs bear witness to how Christ is beloved as the son of unicorns. For they themselves, his lovers, are indeed unicorns; and he, their Beloved, is truly their son, and therefore beloved, because he is truly a son and is loved by them as the son of unicorns, because they love him as they ought to love their own son.

Why Holy Scripture calls them unicorns has an evident explanation. Before sin, man received a twofold strength, as it were a double horn, because he was furnished with a twofold power to repel sin and remove suffering: one was integrity of body, the other integrity of mind. He received integrity of flesh against misery, integrity of mind against malice; the former against mortality, the latter against iniquity. When, through negligence, he fell in his contest with the devil, in that very fall the devil knocked one horn away from him and bent the other. Since no reasoning can enable a human being to escape death, he was, as it were, utterly stripped of one horn. But since he could not be wholly deprived of free choice, he did not lose, in a sense, his right horn; yet he bears it bent in proportion as it has been weakened. Thus, if after the first fall there were any who wished to resist sin, their adversary easily triumphed over them.

But at last, taking pity on humankind, “the Dayspring from on high visited us.” He visited us, therefore, and made redemption for his people; “and raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant.” Since, therefore, they henceforth bear only one horn, but an erect one, they patiently endure death’s punishments but stoutly attack sins as enemies of the soul, so that sin may not reign in their mortal body. Hence they sing confidently to him from whom they received the horn: “Through you we shall scatter our enemies with the horn, and in your name we shall trample down those who rise against us” (Ps. 43 [44]). For the present they receive a horn of salvation, and will one day receive a horn of security, so that they may then possess the strength of a double horn: they who now fight bravely with one and triumph gloriously over the enemy, that they may then have whereby they are free from sin and secure from every punishment, when he who has now raised for them the horn of salvation has fulfilled his promise in them: “I will break all the horns of sinners, and the horns of the righteous shall be exalted.”

You see, then, how, as regards the present, everywhere only one horn is spoken of; hence every righteous person is called a unicorn, [Col. 0297B] though his horns will one day not merely be raised but also exalted. They will not merely be raised to that height which man received while he was still to be tested, but exalted to that sublimity which glorified man ought to possess. For man’s first strength or capacity was to be able not to die and to be able not to sin; his final state, however, will be to be unable to die and unable to sin, when death has already been swallowed up in victory and man himself has been raised into glory. Thereafter he will be established in goodness and established in joy.

See how they are unicorns; but whence could they have such a son? Whence, I say, do they have such a son that he can truly be called the son of unicorns? Let us ask their Son himself: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12). What is the Father’s Son but the Father’s power and wisdom? The Father’s Word is the Father’s Son, the Father’s will. Likewise, what else is a human being’s will but a certain offspring of the mind? If, therefore, your will and the Father’s will are the same, your son and the Father’s Son are the same. Truth, wisdom, and will are conceived in the heart and generated from the heart. If, therefore, you will and understand the same thing as the Father, you have the same Son as the Father.

Do you marvel? There is more for you to marvel at. It lies within you whether you are father or mother—or rather, whether you are both father and mother. You can generate him in your own heart and in another’s heart; and you can conceive him from your own heart and from another’s mouth. He is generated by understanding, conceived by consent, born through affection, and nourished by action. When you understand the truth, or cause another to understand it, you generate Christ. When truth is commended to you by yourself or by another, Christ is truly conceived. Therefore, when you generate, you are father; when you conceive, you are mother. You know God’s will; you have consented to it, and have conceived. By loving, you will give birth; by acting, you will nourish.

See that it is left in each person’s power whether to become the mother of so great an offspring. Rightly, then, is cursed “the barren woman and she who does not bear,” although she could by her desire have had such a son. Why, do you suppose, is the person who does not generate not likewise cursed, as the barren woman and she who does not bear are cursed, unless because it is not equally within our power [Col. 0298A] to understand truth and to consent to truth? For I do not always understand truth when I wish; but, once understood, I always consent to it if I wish. Happy is the person for whom it is at hand, whenever he wishes, to have a son—and not just any son, but God.

O how great is the dignity of man: to have as a son the God of majesty! Hear, O man; listen, O man! At last raise your hope; brighten your countenance. If you are ashamed of your father, nevertheless have confidence in your son. If you blush because of your parent, rejoice in your offspring. If you are grieved in the first Adam, rejoice in the second Adam. This one is greater to raise you up than that one was to cast you down. Through the former you were expelled from paradise; through the latter you shall be glorified in heaven. Consider how glorious this one is: “He is a man, and who shall know him?” A man, I say, and a son of man—yet who shall know [Col. 0298B] him? “Who do men say that the Son of Man is?” Let Peter alone answer for all: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). Christ calls himself the Son of Man; Peter calls him the Son of God the Father. It is a wondrous thing, worthy of admiration, that one and the same person is the Son of the living God and the son of dying—or shall I say dead?—man. For if we deny that man died, how will what we read stand: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2)? But perhaps he then begins to live when he begins to have such a son.

O what humility of the Almighty, and what sublimity of man! For God to have a human being as father: incomparable humility! For a human being to have God as Son: inestimable sublimity! O how rightly is this one loved, so humble and so exalted, truly worthy of a singular love—this Beloved of ours! Beloved of human beings, beloved of angels, beloved of all, beloved as the son of unicorns.

Now it remains to ask why, after saying, “The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon,” he afterward adds, “and the Beloved as the son of unicorns.” For the Lord and the Beloved as the son of unicorns are the same—as though he had said, “the Lord and his Christ.” But after saying, “The Lord will break,” why need he add “and his Christ,” since the Lord is one and the same: not only Father and Son, but also the Holy Spirit? Does not whatever the Father does, the Son likewise do? Yet in many passages of Scripture you may find such a distinction, as in this: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2).

What, then, shall we say? We know that Christ, in that wherein he is one and the same as the Father, does the same thing as the Father and in the same manner. But why should it be surprising if, in that wherein he is other than the Father, he has another manner of working than the Father? If he acts in the same way as the Father in his divinity, wherein he is like the Father, why should it be surprising if he works differently from the Father in that wherein he is unlike the Father? That he works differently in some respect is, I think, plainly indicated by this distinction: “The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and he will crush them like a calf of Lebanon, and the Beloved [Col. 0299A] as the son of unicorns.”

As we have said, not only the Lord but also this his—or our—Beloved breaks and crushes the cedars. What is it to break or crush cedars except to shatter the rigidity or bow down the loftiness of a proud mind? Without doubt, the Lord and likewise the Beloved humble every arrogance when he wills and bend it as much as he wills. But the Lord does this through the terror of his majesty; the Beloved does it by the example of his humility. The Lord, as Lord, does it in severity; the Beloved, as sweet and gracious, does it in sweetness. Yet both are one and the same Lord, sweet and upright, gracious and gentle to all who call upon him.

Therefore, when someone, considering the Lord’s power, is ashamed to think highly of himself in the sight of so great a majesty and fears to presume anything against his will, then without doubt the Lord breaks the cedars of self-exaltation in that person’s heart. Another, seeing the wondrous humility of our Beloved, is ashamed to appear proud when he sees the Lord of majesty take the form of a servant, fulfil the law, obey human beings, and patiently endure human reproaches and the shame of the cross. Therefore, when someone, seeing the example of the Lord’s humility, is ashamed of his presumption and cast down from every height of his former swelling, it is plainly beyond doubt that this Beloved has broken the cedars of his wrongly rigid mind and crushed him like a calf of Lebanon—that is, into likeness with himself. Therefore it is rightly said: “The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon, and he will crush them like a calf of Lebanon, and the Beloved as the son of unicorns.”

[Col. 0299C] “The voice of the Lord cutting apart the flame of fire.” One fire is that which Jesus came to cast upon the earth; another is that which he came to extinguish on the earth. Coming from heaven, he brought down the heavenly fire; coming to earth, he found the earthly fire. Every love is fire, but not every love is good. There is lawful love and unlawful love; lawful love is good, and love that is not lawful is not good. Thus good love is good fire; evil love is evil fire. Good fire is the fire of charity; evil fire is the fire of lust.

The good fire is that of which Jesus said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). Therefore he came to kindle good fire, but to extinguish evil fire. For this reason, through Moses, he forbids them to offer “strange fire” upon his altar (Lev. 10); but concerning his own fire he commands that it always burn upon his altar. Therefore he loves his own fire but hates strange fire. They burned with his fire who said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?” (Luke 24). They burned with such fire who received the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire, because the Holy Spirit himself is fire—not burning up, but enlightening. Hence that bush at which Moses looked burned and was not consumed.

But evil and strange fire, on the contrary, consumes and does not enlighten: “It is,” as Job says, “a fire devouring unto destruction, uprooting all offspring, burning unto the lowest depths of hell, and consuming the foundations of the mountains” (Job 31). Yet when the Lord wills, he cuts apart the flame [Col. 0300A] of this fire; when it pleases him, he utterly extinguishes it. That he sometimes cuts it apart, so that it burns in one part and fails in another, Scripture plainly shows when it says: “The voice of the Lord cuts apart the flame of fire” (Ps. 28 [29]). That he sometimes extinguishes this fire’s flame, another Scripture clearly declares, where we read: “The angel of the Lord descended into the furnace, shook out the flame of fire, and made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing dew” (Dan. 3).

Do you see how there it is said that he shook out the flame, while here he is promised to cut it apart? But why is it not extinguished here, as there? Perhaps because those for whom that pyre was prepared were children; but perhaps those to whom David spoke were not children. They had not yet been fully converted or become as little children. They were still great in their own eyes and still ashamed to appear humble. But in order that what swells in them through self-exaltation may be dried up, the flame of fire is retained in some part; and again, lest the flame of burning should carry them as far as consent to perversity and reduce them, as it were, to ashes, that flame is cut away and extinguished for the greater part. Thus this flame usefully burns in one part for the preservation of humility and is nevertheless beneficially extinguished in a great part as a safeguard against disgrace. So Paul was given a thorn in his flesh to buffet him, lest the greatness of revelations should exalt him.

Do you see how this very thing is done for our benefit: that this flame is temporarily retained in part? But when someone has been fully converted, become as a little child, and attained perfect purity, perhaps then it will be time for it to be extinguished—as it is read and believed to have been extinguished in those three children, because they were children, because they had become children. For *puer* (“child”) is said to derive from purity, and one who is pure is rightly called a child.

There is one purity of mind, another purity of speech, and another purity of action. In the heart, simplicity; in the mouth, truthfulness; in work, sincerity. Therefore we are believed to possess these three children when what we meditate is holy, what we say is true, and what we do is just. O exceedingly blessed fellowship of these three children, pleasing to our God because of their single concord of purity in will, speech, and action alike! [Col. 0300D] The king of Babylon sees this and envies it. First he compels them to worship his golden statue; but when they refuse to worship, he commands that a furnace fire be prepared for them. For he readily mocks and despises their holiness if he can raise them from their holiness into pride.

For what is it to worship the golden statue except to serve pride and vainglory in such pursuits? He gladly permits them to remain in his kingdom when he sees their endeavours serving self-exaltation. But when he sees them despise both the height and gold of his statue, and scorn every glory of self-exaltation amid the wonders they perform, he commands the furnace to be kindled and the pyre of burning prepared for them. Those whom he cannot overcome through the glory of pride, he hopes to overcome through the flame of lust.

The king of Babylon is he who is [Col. 0301A] “king over all the children of pride.” The ministers whom he sends to such a task are those deceitful spirits which Holy Scripture customarily calls spirits of fornication. The furnace is kindled by them when our flesh is inflamed by the burning of lust. When the furnace has been kindled, they bind the children and throw them into the furnace. The children are found outside the furnace because, intent upon spiritual pursuits and contemplation of heavenly things, they almost forget that they are in the flesh. For these children are, in a certain sense, outside the flesh when they handle nothing carnal in heart, speech, or hand. But they are bound, as it were, when, oppressed by temptations, they are hindered in their pursuits; and they are as though within the furnace when, worn out by the goads of the flesh, they can think, lament, and weep about nothing else.

The angel of God comes to their aid, because divine protection never abandons its faithful in the struggle. The flame of fire is shaken out from them when the burning of lust is extinguished by divine power. The angel makes the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing dew, and releases the children’s tongue for praise of the Creator. The middle of the furnace is the inmost heart; therefore, when the Holy Spirit blows, it is drenched with heavenly dew, and through divine inspiration the whole conscience is refreshed. When the children are freed, the flame kindles the Chaldeans, because, when they cannot prevail against the good, the flame of envy consumes the malicious persons who lie in wait.

See how the testimonies of the prophets agree with one another. First, in Daniel, self-exaltation is trampled down through despising the golden statue; afterward, in the cooling of the furnace, the flame of lust is extinguished. So here too: first the cedars are broken; afterward [Col. 0301C] the flame of fire is cut apart. For unless the rigidity of self-exaltation is first bent, the flame of lust is undoubtedly not extinguished.

This, however, seems to be the difference between this passage and that one: there the whole flame is shaken out and removed; here, through David, it is promised that it will be cut apart. But because this psalm instructs beginners and the imperfect, the promise it gives ought chiefly to suit those to whom it speaks. Yet we may expound this text in such a way that it applies alike to beginners, those making progress, and the perfect. For in either case the flame is cut apart when either some part of it is divided from the flame itself, or the whole is separated from its fuel. And we know that a flame separated from its fuel cannot last even for an hour. Let us first, therefore, see how this flame increases; then it will be easy to recognize how it is cut off in parts.

It should be noted, however, that he promises not to extinguish the fire but to cut apart its flame. For as long as we live, we have this fire—that is, the fuel of sin—within ourselves; but we do not always endure its flame to the same extent. This fire bursts into flame when the heats of fleshly burning scorch us. First it tickles the flesh; second, it defiles the mind with shameful delight; finally, by consent to wickedness, it subjects reason to itself. By these stages the sulphurous flame of lust grows; and by the same stages, though in reverse order, it diminishes at the voice of the Lord who commands.

First, [Col. 0302A] in beginners and the newly converted, that voice of the Lord cutting apart the flame of fire cuts away whatever could bend reason’s consent. In those making progress, it often takes away the mind’s unlawful delight. In rare persons, and those very perfect, it removes even the flesh’s tickling. Yet many, although they have advanced to the height of perfection, have been unable to extinguish the thorn in their flesh. This has been done in them by divine dispensation, though what is more beneficial for each cannot be unknown to it. In some this occurred as a demonstration of their singular strength, because they were such as could always fight continually and triumph. In others it occurred for the preservation of humility, when they had received some singular good beyond all others.

Therefore, because in penitents it destroys the act of disgrace, in the converted the consent to pleasure, in those making progress the contagion of shameful delight, and in certain perfect persons the movement of fleshly prompting, it is rightly said here: “The voice of the Lord cuts apart the flame of fire.” Yet it must be known that, just as no one in this life is wholly without this fire, so no one continually feels its flame. For who has been able fully to destroy the fuel of sin here, or who has ever endured without interruption the heat of lust? It is a great thing, therefore, to lull this fire to sleep and extinguish its flame. Certainly this is not in human power; it is accomplished only by the voice of the Lord cutting apart the flame of fire.

“The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness, and the Lord will move the wilderness of Kadesh.” Up to this point he has strengthened us against kinds of temptation. From here onward, by promises, he enumerates gifts of grace—as it were, a crown after victory, a reward after merit, a triumph after the trophy. He says, therefore: “The voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness, and the Lord will move the wilderness of Kadesh.” He seems to bestow one thing and promise another in expectation. The phrase “shaking the wilderness” is that of one who bestows; the added phrase “he will move the wilderness of Kadesh” is, indeed, that of one who promises. Therefore the first is given immediately; the second is awaited. Such was the earlier statement: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars, and the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon.”

Moreover, this too should be noted: just as there the cedars are first broken, and afterwards the cedars of Lebanon, so [Col. 0302D] here first the wilderness is shaken, and afterwards the wilderness of Kadesh. Behold how everywhere that which belongs to the beginning is placed first, while another thing which completes perfection is promised. But let us now consider what must be said concerning the wilderness. For there is one wilderness that is good, another bad. A bad wilderness is one where the shoots of virtues are lacking; a good wilderness is one where the tumults of vices are far away. There is also a bad wilderness where there is no cultivation by human beings, no pursuit of holiness or religion. Likewise there is a good wilderness where no uproar of disturbance occurs, but in silence the voice of the turtle-dove is heard, and groaning from the desire of divine love does not cease. Thus a bad wilderness is one where heavenly and spiritual desires are absent; a good wilderness is one where [Col. 0303A] secular and carnal desires are far removed. Finally, the wilderness of Idumea is a bad wilderness, whereas the wilderness of Kadesh is a good wilderness. Yet both are shaken; both are pierced into weeping by the divine voice. But the wilderness of Idumea is pierced by fear, while the wilderness of Kadesh is pierced by love. Idumea is interpreted “earthly,” Kadesh “changed,” or “holy.” Therefore Idumea, because it knows nothing except what is earthly and passing, constitutes a bad wilderness. But Kadesh, because it loves nothing except what is just and desires nothing except what is holy, constitutes a good wilderness. In Idumea there is a desolation of holiness; in Kadesh, a desolation of earthly desire. Thus Idumea, that is, “earthly,” is rightly called a bad wilderness; Kadesh, that is, “holy,” is rightly called a good wilderness: for in the former holiness is absent and earthly [Col. 0303B] desire reigns; in the latter lust is absent and sanctity remains.

Holy Scripture designates the latter by its proper name, since it recognizes, commends, and approves it. Speaking of the bad wilderness, it does not name it, but simply says “wilderness,” so that you may understand any other thing whatever that is not holy and wholly unworthy of the name Kadesh. Yet, as we have maintained, both are shaken; both are moved, that both may be changed. For the bad wilderness is shaken in order that it may be changed into good; the good wilderness is moved in order that it may advance into what is best. To be changed from bad into good is a good change; to be transformed from good into best is a holy transformation. Therefore the wilderness which is transformed from good into best is rightly called Kadesh. For Kadesh, as has been said, is interpreted “changed” or [Col. 0303C] “holy.” Thus the wilderness which is still bad, and for that reason cannot be called Kadesh, is shaken—and, not surprisingly, pierced by consideration and horror of its own iniquity. But the wilderness of Kadesh, already good but burning for better things, is likewise shaken and pierced by desire for a fuller holiness. The former therefore is terrified at the evil it has done; the latter groans for the good it has not yet received. The former trembles at the recollection of divine majesty; the latter melts in contemplation of heavenly mercy. The former consequently is alarmed by great fear; the latter sighs from excessive love. The former fears being carried off to punishments; the latter grieves because it has not yet been lifted up to joys. To beginners, then, belongs being shaken by fear; to the perfect belongs being pierced by love. Accordingly, one is granted immediately [Col. 0303D] for a beginning, while the other is promised for perfection. Thus it is rightly said of them, “shaking” and “will move”: “The voice,” he says, “of the Lord shaking the wilderness; and the Lord will move the wilderness of Kadesh,” because the piercing compunction of fear is given to some at their very beginning. But the compunction of love is deferred until perfect charity casts fear out.

This twofold kind of compunction is the upper watering and the lower watering. Hence elsewhere the same Psalmist says: “Who divided the Red Sea into divisions” (Ps. 135). The waters of the sea are indeed very bitter. What then is the Red Sea but the bitterness of repentance? The Red Sea therefore remains, as it were, undivided for one who knows how to groan only from fear [Col. 0304A] of condemnation; but the sea is divided when compunction becomes twofold. For one doubles the bitterness of the heart when one alternates tears of compunction: now weeping for the evil one fears, now sighing for the good one desires. Sorrow arising from consideration and fear of evils is the sea on the left; sorrow arising from contemplation and expectation of goods is the sea on the right: “The waters,” he says, “were to them as a wall on the right hand and on the left” (Exod. 14). But by one we exclude concupiscence, and by the other we avoid negligence; for one who awaits a reward stretches oneself toward merit, and one who fears punishment carefully turns aside from fault. Yet it must be known that compunction of fear is earlier in time, but lower in dignity. For after many [Col. 0304B] tears of repentance we are at last brought back to hope of pardon; and only with difficulty, through many sighs and tears and unutterable groanings, are we at some point restored to assurance of blessedness. But once confidence in eternal things has been received, we groan far more anxiously and weep far more abundantly from impatient desire for good things than we previously did under fear of evils, when we desire “to be dissolved and to be with Christ,” certain that the crown of righteousness has been laid up for us. For tears of love both affect more keenly and flow more abundantly.

Hence one says: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. 38). Great indeed is the bitterness when someone renounces the world and turns to religious life. Greater still when, denying oneself, one is wearied by countless temptations of the enemy. [Col. 0304C] But greatest is the bitterness when one has tasted in part that peace which surpasses all understanding, yet is not fully admitted into it. Thus it is bitter in conversion, more bitter in temptation, most bitter in expectation of inward and eternal sweetness and in the postponement of impatient desire, because hope deferred afflicts the soul. Hence elsewhere David himself cries, saying: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. 119); and: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76). What kind and how great, do you suppose, was the magnitude of bitterness that had pierced the soul, which would accept not even consolation as relief for its pain? It torments a person greatly when love of the world is abandoned; it tortures far more when self-love is trampled down. Yet above all [Col. 0304D] the love of God pierces and penetrates the human heart, and burns it with the heats of desire. Hence comes that mournful cry: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord? My tears were my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily: Where is your God?” (Ps. 41); and that saying in the Song of Songs: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2); and the passage mentioned above: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. 38).

Thus, after weeping and groaning from fear, one sometimes arrives at the longing and sighs of love. Therefore, because the human heart is first shaken by fear and afterwards pierced by love, David rightly says: “The voice [Col. 0305A] of the Lord breaking the wilderness, and the Lord will break the wilderness of Kadesh.” “The voice of the Lord preparing the stags, and he will reveal the thickets.” Just as in the shaking of the wilderness there is the grace of compunction, so in the preparation of the stag there is the grace of ministry. For it is not enough to weep for our evils unless we subsequently gird ourselves for good works as well. Therefore the wilderness of our body is shaken so that we may be devoted to prayer. We are given the swiftness of a stag so that we may be ready for action. For the stag is a swift and timid animal, but hostile to serpents. Accordingly, in the agility of its feet we rightly understand an unimpeded and ready swiftness in action. Would you hear a stag running eagerly? “I ran,” he says, “the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118). Would you hear the voice [Col. 0305B] preparing for the swiftness of the stag? “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9). Would you hear the voice preparing for the stag’s fearfulness? “Blessed,” he says, “is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. 28), and who in his understanding reflects upon God’s watchfulness. Would you hear the voice preparing the stag against the assault of serpents? “Mortify,” he says, “your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness” (Col. 3, etc.). These three things, then, seem to belong to the stag: to run swiftly through the way of the commandments, always to regard the ambushes of demons with suspicion, and boldly to destroy the poisons of vices. Thus prompt, prudent, and righteous action makes stags: inasmuch as it is prompt, it gives swiftness; inasmuch as it is [Col. 0305C] prudent, it makes one usefully timid because it makes one cautious; inasmuch as it is righteous, it extinguishes the poisons of vices.

Many, in running swiftly, do not kill serpents but nourish them, because through their vigorous activity serpents such as pride, vainglory, and the like grow stronger. Others have a good intention in good works and strive, as far as they are able, to put to death the serpentine poisons of vices; but because they do not know how to keep measure and time in their efforts, they fall into the snares of demonic ambushes, like traps of hunters, just when they imprudently considered themselves safe.

And although these have the swiftness of a stag, they are ashamed to have the stag’s fearfulness; for, as headlong as they are swift, [Col. 0305D] they do not know—or rather, do not wish—to exercise caution. Hence the voice preparing the stags cries to them: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2); and elsewhere: “Serve the Lord in fear” (Ps. 2). Therefore, if those who desire to be numbered among such stags are to belong to the number of stags, they must run swiftly and fear cautiously. To such stags, prepared in this manner, the Lord will reveal the thickets and open the depths of the Scriptures, the obscurities of allegories, the mysteries of sacraments, and the secrets of mysteries.

For stags of this kind love to run here and there among the thick groves of Lebanon’s forest, to traverse every hidden place and penetrate what is concealed, to frequent shadowy places, and to rest in dense and shady places. [Col. 0306A] There they find hiding places against the ambushes of hunters, and refreshment against the heat of the sun. For the more deeply they receive understanding of the Scriptures and the more perfectly they penetrate their depths, the more securely and peacefully—as though hiding in thickets and resting in shade—they on the one hand mock the snares of demons and on the other despise the heats of concupiscence and carnal enticements. For by the very reading of the Scriptures we are more fully instructed against the deceits of demons, and amid so many delights of wisdom we do not even remember carnal allurements.

What wonder, then, after such great and abundant grace, that “in his temple all will speak glory”? What wonder, I say, if they seek his glory for the edification of their neighbors, from whom they have freely received so many gifts of grace? God’s temple is the congregation of the faithful. Therefore those speak praise to God in this temple and seek his glory who strive by the word of preaching to edify their neighbors and to extend God’s glory in them. They rightly first receive an understanding of the Scriptures for their own instruction, and afterwards the gift of preaching for the profit and edification of their neighbor. Understanding is first given so that they may believe what is true and understand what is right; eloquence is then added so that they may teach what is useful and persuade people of what is salutary.

Nevertheless, by “the temple” we may fittingly understand not the present Church, but the assembly of heavenly citizens. For Sacred Scripture often represents the former by the tabernacle and the latter by the temple, in order to distinguish the two. The former, still in motion and stationed for the onset of battles, is rightly represented by the tabernacle; the latter, already founded in eternal stability, is better represented by the temple. Those who have not been raised up by contemplation cannot approach it. But once admitted within, they cannot cease praising the Creator because of the greatness of their wonder; and what is said is fulfilled: “And in his temple all will speak glory.” For whoever raises themselves to it in contemplation, while they are within are not free from divine praise. Hence, returning from there, they cry: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30). Again he says: “And the remnant of thought shall keep a feast-day” [Col. 0306D] (Ps. 75). Let whoever can consider what manner of celebration, and how great, is that solemn feast which those within perform, when even the remnants of thoughts, which on returning to themselves they draw along with them from the memory or recollection of sweetness tasted, keep a festival day for the Lord God.

But if we understand God’s temple as the heart of the person himself, we shall more readily discover who they are that give thanks to God in this temple. For who else are the inhabitants of this temple than the thoughts of the mind and the affections of the heart? “For,” he says, “the thought of man shall confess to you” (ibid.). Yet it rarely happens that all the inhabitants of this temple come together as one, so that, gathered as one in his temple, all simultaneously speak glory, with no alien thought insinuating itself to disturb or diminish the joys of that divine [Col. 0307A] solemnity. Nevertheless, the person whom experience rather than reading has taught knows better that this can sometimes happen. It sometimes occurs that the mind, faithful over a few things, entering into the joy of its Lord, is made drunk from the torrent of delight and, wholly transformed into jubilation, forgets not only every outward thing but even itself. Gathered wholly into itself—indeed, raised above itself—it is completely absorbed by that sea of spiritual joy, and by happy experience now proves how true is the saying: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88). Then is fulfilled what is said: “And in his temple all will speak glory.”

According to the first exposition, therefore, this means the gift of preaching; according to the second, the grace of contemplation; according to the last, the jubilation of the mind is expressed. But which of these is the more correct interpretation, I confess I do not know, where everything that is said is true. For many receive through the understanding of the Scriptures the word of preaching; and often, while reading, the mind is suffused with the light of contemplation, or, transformed into jubilation, dances in a voice of exultation and confession. For after the voice of the Lord preparing the stags has revealed the thickets, immediately in his temple all will speak glory.

Behold how great and how worthy of wonder are the things accomplished by this voice of the Lord: the voice of the Lord breaking the cedars; the voice of the Lord cutting off the flame of fire; the voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness; the voice of the Lord preparing the stags! [Col. 0307C] It accomplishes many other things of this kind which this writer could not enumerate, or which it was not fitting to set forth here. Yet there is often a great difference between a voice and speech. Animals too, of course, have a voice; yet speech is not formed without voice, although a voice may sound without speech. Therefore he sometimes utters speech with voice, sometimes voice without speech, and at times even sound without voice. For now, as the Lord himself says of himself, he creaks like a cart laden with hay; now he hisses like the bee which is at the far end of Egypt; at another time he roars like a lion. And when he wills, “he sends his utterance to the earth; his word runs swiftly.” Thus by sound he creaks; by hissing he allures; by roaring he terrifies; by speech he teaches. When and to whom he speaks, he openly demonstrates [Col. 0307D] his good pleasure. But in voice alone he does not so much articulate as signify his will. By creaking, indeed, he conceals it more deeply and hides it more profoundly. For at the sound of creaking the hearer is not so much instructed as dismayed—or rather, made indignant. What he hears displeases him, and he often rebukes it boldly.

Hence God’s ordering of temporal things is openly criticized by some. To them the Lord seems in a certain sense to creak in governing his work, when he gives good and bad things indiscriminately to good and evil alike, he “who makes his sun rise upon the good and evil, and rains upon the just and unjust.” Others, however, return inwardly amid all these things and consult reason concerning them all. When from reason they infer that rewards are laid up for the good and punishments for the wicked, they receive, as it were, the Lord’s voice. Those who prepare themselves for the promise of recompense awaken as though to the persuasive hiss; those who fear threats of terror tremble as though at a lion’s roar. A person is stirred, as though by a hiss, when temporal advantage or eternal reward incites that person to do something. And one is confounded, as though by a roar, when consideration of some future loss or condemnation casts one down from presumption. Yet the Lord discloses himself far more excellently, and as it were through speech, to those in whom he inspires his will; for it is one thing to discern what is right, and another perfectly to understand the Lord’s good pleasure and cleave to him in love. Thus the Lord has, as it were, sound in the ordering of his work, voice in the revelation of truth, and speech in the inspiration of will.

“The Lord causes the flood to be inhabited, and the Lord will sit as king for ever.” Although the water of saving wisdom is one and the same, it does not irrigate the land of the living equally everywhere; rather, through its abundance it distributes itself in many different ways and by many modes. It makes one place a well or cistern; another a torrent, as a fountain springing up into eternal life. Here it is led into a brook; there it is gathered into a river. At one time it increases into a lake or pond; at another it overflows into an abyss or flood. Through these ten differences, I think, we can readily prove, if we attend carefully, that the distinct gifts of divine Wisdom are distinguished in Sacred Scripture. It would be much too long to examine each one carefully here—indeed, beyond our powers to say anything worthy upon so great a subject. Let us therefore say something about what presently occurs to us, which may perhaps suffice for this passage, in view of the statement: “The Lord makes the flood his dwelling.”

This water of saving wisdom, if we believe Sacred Scripture—indeed, because, laying aside every ambiguity, we ought to believe it—this water of wisdom, I say, sometimes bursts forth in such abundance and spreads itself so lavishly that it not only fills valleys and covers plains, but even rises far above all mountains and hills. Thus it completely swallows every incursion of carnal thoughts and every earthly affection; indeed, even whatever is lofty among human beings, the very summits of virtues, and, greater than all these, the contemplating soul itself falls into forgetfulness. For the soul of one contemplating, raised above itself and held entirely by heavenly things, forgets itself and what lies below it; and in so great a flood of wisdom nothing is seen except heaven and the water of wisdom itself by which it is illumined and by which it is raised on high.

But who, do you suppose, is fit for this work, and who will be found worthy to dwell in such a flood? Let no one hope for this from one’s own strength; let no one presume it through one’s own industry. It is not a matter of human merit, but of divine gift. The Lord alone can give this. For the Lord alone causes the flood to be inhabited. For such dwelling in a flood, I think, at the Lord’s prompting and instruction, that ark of a good conscience is constructed, provided that the man Noah lives and flourishes in us: he alone, solely through divine help, can suffice for so great a work. Noah is interpreted “rest,” and it is sufficiently clear that without love of rest the construction of the ark can in no way be completed. Therefore let love of rest burn within us; let us delight in that inward leisured work—or busy leisure—of searching out truth; and let us diligently fulfill what is read in the psalm: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. 45), if we intend to raise within ourselves the building of this ark, so as to be worthy or fit for the Lord to deign to make us dwellers in the appointed flood. For the Lord alone, as we have already said above, causes the flood to be inhabited.

In this one phrase, I think, we are warned of two things: not to despair that so wonderful a work can be accomplished, and not to presume that so singular an undertaking can be completed by any human skill. But now let us see what follows such an inundation of the flood, or rather what usually follows dwelling in this flood. “And,” he says, “the Lord will sit as king for ever.” Taught by Sacred Scripture, we have learned that the soul of the righteous is the seat of Wisdom. What, then, is meant by saying that the King of kings and Lord of lords, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, sits in this his own seat only after the flood? Why was the King not sitting for ever even before the flood? Perhaps because, while giants were upon the earth before the flood, Wisdom was not permitted to possess its kingdom in peace; and therefore there was no time or place for it to sit, but rather to fight. Hence, like a warrior—the Almighty is his name—he was compelled each day to take up arms and shield and rise to the aid of his own; and, as the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle, to vanquish those attacking his army, while those who were his cried to him daily: “Rise up, O Lord, help us, and deliver us for your name’s sake” (Ps. 43).

Undoubtedly, as long as giants live upon the earth, as long as that monstrous and dreadful enormity of vices still flourishes in the flesh or in the carnal heart, the Lord of hosts, the Lord of powers, is not allowed to possess his kingdom in peace. But because wisdom conquers malice, when it begins to pour itself out more broadly—indeed, to occupy the whole earth—it quickly and without delay swallows up whatever formerly lived wickedly upon it. At the Lord’s first command, when the fountains of the deep are broken up and the floodgates of heaven opened, there comes a sudden and so violent inundation of the flood that, without any delay, all the enemies of wisdom are overthrown: “All the fountains of the great deep,” he says, “were broken up, and the floodgates of heaven were opened” (Gen. 7). If, however, you wish to know what this great deep is, recall what the Prophet says of it: “Your judgments,” he says, “are a great deep” (Ps. 35). And that you may likewise know what kind of rain that voluntary rain may be which God has set apart for his inheritance, recall what you read elsewhere in the words of the same Prophet: “And your truth,” he says, “reaches unto the clouds” (ibid.). You see, surely, what kind of water such clouds bearing truth can rain down. Thus the fountains of the deep are broken up and the floodgates of heaven opened when the time comes to make a flood, so that the water of saving wisdom may partly pour itself out from the hidden vein of divine inspiration, and partly flow forth through angelic revelation. The fountains of the deep had been broken up when the Prophet said: “The fountains of waters appeared, and the foundations of the world were revealed” (Ps. 17). The floodgates of heaven had been opened when the Apostle said: “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness” (Rom. 1). Perhaps the flood had then overflowed when, elsewhere, he cried out in wonder at Wisdom: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11).

[Col. 0310B] How then, do you suppose, do carnal desires languish—indeed, with what speed do they fail—when that whole abyss of divine judgments pours itself out into manifestation, and that ocean of divine Wisdom occupies the entire earth of the human heart and utterly swallows its inhabitants, the multitude of thoughts and affections? Only those things survive this flood which live enclosed in the bosom of the ark, which do not exceed the measure of a good conscience, which do not abandon the bounds of moderation. Some things, then, outside the ark are exposed to destruction; others within the ark are reserved for life. And not only rational creatures are reserved, but irrational ones also; and among those irrational creatures, not only clean but also unclean ones, insofar, that is, as the care of necessity or caution for preserving humility requires.

Those desires which arise from reason’s deliberation seem to belong to human beings, that is, rational animals; whereas those which emerge without the judgment of discernment belong to irrational animals. In each kind there are some that are good and some that are evil, because there are righteous and unrighteous human beings, and some animals are clean and some unclean. Do you wish to know more clearly the distinction between clean and unclean animals, righteous and unrighteous human beings? Perhaps we may show it better by an example than by a definition. Behold, someone passing by sees a person afflicted by hunger or cold, or crushed by some other want, and suddenly, without any deliberation of mind, is touched to the marrow by an affection of compassion and sympathetically pities the suffering person with a sudden mercy of heart. Their thought urges them to relieve that person’s need from their own abundance, but perhaps, through excessive tenacity of avarice, they shut the ear of compassion. They determine, then, to spend none of their own goods on the person, lest they seem to suffer the loss of any diminution in their possessions. Behold a clean animal and an unrighteous human being. That affection of compassion which precedes the mind’s judgment is like a clean animal; but that impious deliberation of subsequent hardening is like an unrighteous human being.

Behold another: at the sight of a woman, the movement of lust is felt before that person can consult reason’s judgment. But after consulting reason, they rise up and courageously repel the evil. Behold an unclean animal, but a righteous human being. For what do we call the movement of lust except an unclean animal? And what ought we to judge the righteous decree of the subsequent deliberation to be except a righteous human being? Thus unclean desires which arise from appetite and precede reason’s judgment are brute and unclean animals. Clean animals, however, are those desires which suggest nothing shameful.

But it is highly remarkable and very noteworthy that clean animals often hinder good and drive one toward evil, just as unclean animals, conversely, often assist toward good and strengthen against evil. Who would deny that an ordered affection of piety toward parents is good? Yet how many has it harmed and drawn away from the love of God because they loved to retain their own relatives, whom they were unwilling to leave even for God’s sake. Who but a perverse person ever felt no shame at the stimulus of the flesh? Yet how many it has aided against pride and preserved in humility! Thus, yes, we are often drawn back from better things by certain good things, and compelled toward the best things by certain evil things. Hence countless clean animals are swallowed by the flood, while not a few unclean ones are preserved after it. For those affections, whether shameful or chaste, rightly perish in the flood of wisdom if they impede the pursuit of perfection. Only those, whether counted among chaste or unchaste affections, are rightly reserved after the flood which cooperate for good.

But if it is useless or impossible to expose all unclean animals to death, let us at least beware of admitting any perverse human being into the ark of conscience. It is one thing not yet to be able perfectly to mortify every appetite of the flesh, and quite another to admit into oneself, by deliberation, consent to perversity. What shall we now say of the giants? Do we believe that even one can survive the appointed flood? Far be it from us to believe this. For after such a flood it will not be easy for the mind to commit any criminal sins, even if it does not suffice perfectly to erase all venial ones: “Let no temptation,” says the Apostle, “take hold of you, except what is human” (1 Cor. 10). Behold how the Apostle labored to have the giants utterly destroyed from the earth.

For what can we more rightly understand by giants having monstrous, excessive form than temptation beyond what is human? How perfectly, do you suppose, had he erased giants of this kind from his own heart, when he strove with ardent zeal to uproot them even from others’ hearts! But let us see whether, after the Lord made this Paul of whom we speak dwell in the flood, any unclean animal perhaps survived in the flood that had grown in his heart from divine revelations beyond the measure of human understanding: “But lest,” he says, “the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a stimulus of my flesh” (1 Cor. 12). That the flood had then overflowed cannot be denied when he heard secret words which it was not lawful for a human being to utter; yet after such a flood he felt the stimulus of the flesh, which no one doubts must be counted among unclean animals.

Nevertheless, because the giants had utterly perished in the flood, and everything that could throw Wisdom’s kingdom into disorder had been removed, nothing now prevented it from raising its throne and sitting as king for ever. For what else do his words seem to mean, where he openly testifies: “For I am certain that neither death, nor life,” and so forth, “in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8)? Behold how secure Paul was after such a flood that Christ, who dwelt in his heart through faith, would sit as king for ever. You surely see how rightly, after it was said, “The Lord causes the flood to be inhabited,” this was immediately added: “And the Lord will sit as king for ever.” For this purpose, I think, he pours this flood over the earth: that this King may cleanse his kingdom and that the Lord may sit as king [Col. 0312B] for ever.

But what has been said about the flood, we believe, is to be understood only when the word is taken in a good sense. For it is sometimes taken in an evil sense, but there the reading is altogether different. If there is a good fire and a bad fire, a good wilderness and a bad wilderness, as we showed above, and if there is good water and bad water, why should we not likewise believe in a good flood and a bad flood? Certainly we must believe, without any hesitation, that the flood which the Lord causes to be inhabited is good, so that he may sit as king for ever. But once such a flood has occurred and the kingdom has been cleansed, then and thereafter, with his seat prepared, he begins—then, I say—to sit upon his throne and reign among his people, advancing and increasing day by day, until he reaches “from end to end mightily” and “orders all things sweetly,” and rules “from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth.”

For Wisdom has chosen to confine its kingdom within these boundaries and has decreed not to extend it beyond them. On one side, expelling the eastern sea, the bitterness of manifest malice; on the other, excluding the western sea, namely the abyss of dark ignorance. From another side, however, beginning from the river, Wisdom’s kingdom extends to the ends of the earth—beginning from the river, yet leaving the whole river outside. For Wisdom detests every flow of pleasure; extending itself through the almost boundless spaces of manifold obedience, it reaches unto the bounds of impossibility. [Col. 0312D] You see plainly, then, how rightly it establishes the limits of its kingdom between these boundaries, and why it judges it unworthy to extend it farther: namely, lest it should include within its realm the sea of bitterness, the abyss of ignorance, or the excess of concupiscence. Excluding all these altogether, it thereafter reaches to the ends of the earth, extending the borders of its people to the furthest limits of impossibilities.

These, then, are the four things that set bounds to the kingdom of this King: wickedness, ignorance, pleasure, and impossibility. Within these limits that blessed people spreads itself abroad, of whom we find it written: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88); “blessed is the people whose Lord is its God” (Ps. 143). Of this people it is said here: “The Lord will give strength to his people. The Lord [Col. 0313A] will bless his people with peace” (Ps. 28). What kind of people, however, do you think is possessed by this King, who “sits as king for ever,” and “of whose kingdom there shall be no end”? Recall now that utterance, and you will understand what kind of people it befits the Power of God and the Wisdom of God to possess: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel, and am present amid learned thoughts” (Prov. 8).

Therefore this King inhabits, possesses, governs, and directs counsels and instructed thoughts. Such a people is governed by Wisdom, instructed by Wisdom, protected by Wisdom. Every good will, every pure thought, every holy desire, every right counsel, every true understanding, every ordered affection belongs to this King’s people. The King takes very great delight in such a people and is well pleased in it, because “the Lord is well pleased [Col. 0313B] with his people.” Praiseworthy is the people whom the Lord of hosts blessed, saying: “Israel is my inheritance” (Isa. 19). In admiration of this praiseworthy people, the Prophet cried aloud, saying: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose for his own inheritance” (Ps. 32).

O how foreign a people, how unlike this people, was that people of the nations which walked in darkness until it saw a great light and began to know its King and possess wisdom! O people of the nations—perversity of wills, vanity of thoughts—how long will you fail to know your King? How long will you sit in the region of the shadow of death? How long will you remain in the region of unlikeness? At last, come out from the midst of Babylon; come out [Col. 0313C] from the darkness; hasten to the homeland of light, to the region of light. At last come out into the light; attend to the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world. “A merciful, compassionate, and righteous light has risen in darkness for the upright in heart.” “A light for the revelation of the Gentiles.” O people of the nations, who walked in darkness, run while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. “They shall walk, Lord, in the light of your countenance; and in your name they shall rejoice all the day, and in your righteousness they shall be exalted.” They shall go from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion.

But since it is vain for them to rise before the light, how much more vain is it to run. “Send forth your light and your truth,” the light [Col. 0313D] for the revelation of the nations, that in your light they may see the light by which they may run in the light of the living. Send forth, Lord, send forth your light and your truth, until this people of yours, whom you possessed, shall pass over—pass, indeed, from nation to nation, and from kingdom to another people, from the region of the shadow of death to the homeland of light. To such a people, running in this way, the God of Israel himself shall give strength and might to his people—blessed be God—so that that prophetic promise may be fulfilled in them: “The Lord will give strength to his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace.”

See and attend to the order of the divine gift. The Lord, intending to give his people strength and peace, gives strength first and peace afterward. For this people of God has innumerable adversaries—and, what is still more serious, their enemies are exceedingly strong. They therefore need strength and great might against adversaries whose utterly wicked persistence keeps continual watch against them. Do you wish to hear what kind, or how great, a strength their leader promises them—provided, however, that they keep his precepts and commands? “You shall pursue,” he says, “your enemies, and they shall fall before you. Five of you shall pursue a hundred foreigners, and a hundred of you ten thousand. Your enemies shall fall before you by the sword” (Lev. 26).

This is little; hear something greater still concerning the soldiers of this King. For there can be no doubt that those belong to this King’s army of whom one pursued a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight. A marvellous and wholly astounding strength: that one should prevail against [Col. 0314B] a thousand, and two against ten thousand.

Yet who is ignorant how great a slaughter of enemies is wrought when that outstanding soldier of this King—namely, the fear of the Lord—fights under the protection of his commander against the army of vices? What then when the chief soldier of God and prince of the army, namely the love of God, is joined to him? What multitude of enemies, I ask, can withstand their assault? “He who fears God,” Scripture says, “neglects nothing” (Eccles. 7). Behold what a warrior the fear of God is: it is accustomed to put to flight before itself not only wicked deeds, but even all negligences. Yet far more does that chosen soldier of God, distinguished among thousands by the prerogative of singular strength, take the lead: he “believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.” If, therefore, one or two prevail so greatly that ten thousand cannot [Col. 0314C] resist them, how great, I ask, is that which the whole army of this King, gathered into one, can accomplish? A wonderful King, who could thus magnify his own; altogether lovable, who was willing thus to magnify his own.

I think that he served this King who said: “I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me” (Ps. 3). Would that he might deem me worthy to enrol among his own—he who raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung-hill, that he may sit with princes; he himself who gives strength and might to his people, blessed be God. May he be my strength, my support, my refuge, and my deliverer; and then I shall sing confidently: “I shall not fear what man may do to me.” May he teach my hands for battle and [Col. 0314D] my fingers for war; and then undoubtedly, though armies stand against me, my heart shall not fear; and though battle rise against me, in this I shall hope.

You too, if you wish to serve as a soldier of that King, will not fear thousands of people. Indeed, a thousand shall fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand; and then you will be able to prove in yourself how truly it is written: “The Lord will give strength to his people” (Ps. 28). But, that you may more fully recognize what kind of strength they receive from the gift of their Lord, consider what adversaries they have and how manfully they act against them. Are not these the soldiers of this King against whom the world rages and the devil goes mad? Yet their King strengthens them, saying: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. 30). “In the world you shall indeed have tribulation; but take courage: I have overcome the world” (John 16).

Are these not those against whom the world, which is set in wickedness, brings forth that fearsome battle-line of its threefold host: the lust of the eyes, the lust of the flesh, and the pride of life?
