These are they who nevertheless destroy the kingdom of sin, “that sin may not reign in their mortal body.” This second war is much more dangerous than the first: it is civil war, indeed more than civil war, in which the kingdom of the spirit is divided against itself; in which the spirit lusts against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit; in which the appetites of the flesh rebel against the decrees of reason.

But when the first and second battles have been subdued, there still remains a third, most savage and severe, [Col. 0315B] against the powers of the air, the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places. These enemies of the soul, the most cruel of all, rage so much the more fiercely against Christ’s recruits as they see them triumph more gloriously in their double victory. But far be it from anyone to believe that even these can prevail against Christ’s soldiers, to whom their King, once his battle-line has been drawn up and battle joined, sends through James, one of his great commanders, an unambiguous sentence concerning the uncertain outcome of the war: “Resist the devil,” he says, “and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4). Hence that great athlete of this King gloried, saying: “You gave my enemies their backs to me, and you destroyed those who hated me” (Ps. 17). Hence too that other one, a chosen prince among the princes of the peoples gathered with the God of Abraham, and a foremost combatant, confidently declares: “I am certain that neither angel,” etc. (Rom. 8).

Behold what conquerors: acting manfully, they despise the kingdom of the world, destroy the kingdom of sin, and scatter the kingdom of the devil. Yet even this does not suffice them unless they invade the kingdom of heaven. For the kingdom of heaven suffers violence from such violent warriors and glorious conquerors, and the violent seize it. I think they need great strength and marvellous power before they break into that most strongly fortified dwelling: “your sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have established.” For it is established upon the highest mountains, and mountains surround [Col. 0315D] it. Nor can it be approached except by only two ways, one from this side and another from that. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.

Each way, however, is exceedingly narrow. For narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are they who enter by it. Yet there is a great difference between this way and the other. The way of truth is not only narrow but also very steep. The other is more level, but much longer, and can scarcely be completed in the whole course of a lifetime. In some persons, indeed, it is not completed before the end of the world. The former, finally, is the way of the strong; the latter, of the weak. Only men most thoroughly trained for war ascend the former; none ascend the latter except the poor, the weak, and beggars. These go to use force; those, to ask alms. This way admits only those who [Col. 0316A] have already advanced to mature manhood, to the measure of the fullness of Christ. That receives the poor and feeble, the blind and lame, and the indiscriminate crowd of those alone who make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may be received into eternal dwellings; and, following the way of mercy, are “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

But that terrible, ordered battle-line of camps—of mighty men, of those able to go forth to war—choosing the way of truth, as those who intend to use force seize eagerly upon that narrow and steep way which leads to life. With utmost haste they ascend from the valley of tears by the path of the commandments, from strength to strength; forgetting what lies behind and stretching forth toward what is within, they strive ever more and more to relish the things above, not those upon the earth, until, scarcely and with much labour, at last they grasp the summit of the mountain and reach the fortified city.

Having therefore gathered all their multitude upon the highest mountains and arranged their line in accordance with military discipline, they marvellously surround the city amid the eternal mountains and begin the siege. In the first encounter, indeed, they strive to soften the steadfastness of the citizens with a shower of missiles. On one side stand archers; on the other, slingers. Thus from some are cast arrows of sighs plucked from the depths of the heart; from others, blazing torches of kindled prayer. Everywhere fly the sharp arrows of the Mighty One, with desolating coals. On this side some strike with sling and stone; on that, others with the brightness of their flashing spear [Col. 0316C] deliver frequent blows in unutterable groanings, all roaring from the groaning of their heart.

Nor is there any doubt that in so fierce a contest, in so great a rain of such missiles, those heavenly phalanxes of angelic powers receive frequent wounds of compassion, so that the throng of wounded, under the pressure of necessity, is compelled to cry: “I am wounded by love”—as though pierced to the marrow and everywhere perforated by emotions of pity. Moreover, engines of meditation, speculation, and contemplation are raised. The city’s interior is now laid open; for from that lofty engine of contemplation the things that are within, or are done within, are easily seen.

Finally, the engines having been brought against the wall and chosen warriors from every order of strong fighters stationed within, they attack at close quarters the defenders of the city. But lest they receive wounds of error from missiles coming from the opposite side, clothed in the breastplate of faith they are protected by the helmet of hope, holding in their hands the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Thus, while these fight bravely from the engines and those from the battlements, they strike and are struck in turn; on both sides they wound and are wounded—the former receiving wounds of compunction, the latter wounds of pity.

As they contend in this manner, others erect ballistae for hurling stones and draw forth from the canon of Scriptures established propositions of irrefutable authority. Huge masses of rock are carried against the walls; stones clash with stones, so that through the frequent comparison of Scriptures the secrets [Col. 0317A] of more hidden knowledge may be disclosed. Yet these things do not suffice. Moreover, a battering ram is brought to the wall; and through the intervening straight reasoning, by the blows of powerful argument, the strength of the walls is at last broken down. As breaches of revelations multiply on every side, the city’s inner places are laid open.

At last, the city’s ramparts are overthrown by the varied assault of siege-engines; that lofty depth and deep height of the divine mysteries are penetrated; and that thick and high wall, constructed in figures and enigmas, is shattered. The wall having been broken, the strong rush in from all sides and, searching by scrutiny, penetrate even to the interior regions of the south. Some—and only those among them who are bolder—break into the inner chambers of the divine palace, where they hear those secret [Col. 0317B] words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter. The rest spread out through the streets and squares of the city, examining everything, penetrating every hidden place and the more secret rooms of the buildings, passing over nothing untouched and leaving nothing unexamined.

At last, with nothing barring their way, they enter the eternal treasuries of heavenly riches, in which lies hidden the depth of the riches of God’s wisdom and knowledge. Each seizes what he can. From one is claimed a word of wisdom; from another, a word of knowledge. To this one falls discernment of spirits; to that, kinds of tongues. In this way those treasuries of spiritual gifts are perhaps variously plundered by different persons, so that the testimony of Truth may stand: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11).

The heavenly treasure having been plundered by these robbers of virtues, all return joyfully, burdened with spoils and laden with booty, and “return by another way into their own country.” For those who had ascended by the path of truth descend by the track of mercy, so that all their ways may be mercy and truth. Their ascent belonged to strength; their descent is the work of compassion. For “whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you.” They condescend to us who are weak. Love of God snatches them upward; love of neighbour draws them downward again. It is for God, therefore, that they ascend unto the heavens; and for their neighbour that they descend unto the abyss, to visit those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, to bring forth [Col. 0317D] by a mighty hand and uplifted arm those bound in poverty and iron.

Thus, when they come, they come with exultation, bearing their booty upon their shoulders. They rejoice exceedingly, as those who rejoice in harvest, as victors exult when the prey has been taken, and as one who finds abundant spoils. Everywhere is heard the voice of exultation and confession in the tents of the righteous. These spoils of victory, unless I am mistaken, are those spoils which Benjamin, a ravening wolf, seizes in the morning but divides in the evening. So too these violent robbers, plunderers of the kingdom of heaven, descend precisely in order that, following Benjamin’s example, they may divide the spoils of their wars among those unable to go forth to battle; and so that, according to the ordinance of our David, there may be an equal portion for those going out to war and those remaining [Col. 0318A] with the baggage—those only who are occupied with the concerns of worldly things through brotherly care, not personal covetousness.

See how much those do; see how strong those become who receive from God’s gift the gift of strength, who can sing with the Prophet: “God is my strength and my praise” (Ps. 117). From these things, I think, we can readily perceive what, or how great, is that strength which the Lord is accustomed to give to his people.

“The Lord will give strength to his people; the Lord will bless his people with peace.” “He will bless,” he says, “his people with peace.” Therefore, after strength, he also grants peace. Let those who have not yet received peace hope for it, if they have already deserved to receive strength as God’s gift. For God gives strength to his own in order that, acting bravely, they may reach peace. The Lord could indeed grant them complete peace without their own exertion, but he considers it more glorious to lead his own through manifold victory to the security of peace. Hence he commanded his people, saying: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Ps. 33).

Those who serve Solomon—that is, who have resolved to serve as soldiers under him and obey his command in all things—sometimes receive peace round about. Otherwise, unless he were the prince of peace, he would vainly claim for himself the name Solomon, that is, “peaceful.” Yet each person whom his leader commands to seek and pursue peace ought carefully to consider that peace is to be sought differently from God, sought differently [Col. 0318C] from the world, and differently from the flesh or even from the devil.

The peace which is from the spirit toward God, the spirit must humbly entreat; the peace which is from the spirit toward the world, it must bravely offer; the peace which is from the spirit against the flesh, it must violently exact; the peace which is from the spirit against the devil, it must obtain from God by prayers. The first must be made by both parties—namely, by the spirit and by God. The fourth, which is the spirit’s peace against the devil, if it is to be good, must be made by neither of the two, but by God alone. The second, which is the spirit’s peace toward the world, ought to be made by the spirit alone, and not exacted from the world. The third, which is the spirit’s peace against the flesh, the spirit ought to exact violently from the flesh alone, but not itself offer to its flesh.

Certainly, the first must be made by both, because neither can the spirit obtain it by force, nor will God make it without the spirit’s voluntary consent. Therefore, that this peace may be established by both parties, the spirit must humbly submit itself to God in respect of all his will; and God likewise must mercifully condescend to the spirit’s weakness and provide for its good. For the spirit can never render God in full what it owes him; it is enough if it humbly offers what it can. But the peace which the spirit ought to desire against the devil’s assault cannot at all be made by either party, for the spirit must never consent to such a peace as the devil would wish to make; and the devil beyond doubt will never, unto eternity, consent to such a peace as it befits the spirit to approve.

But, as has been said, the spirit ought to offer peace to the world, not demand it from the world—indeed, it should even despise peace freely offered. It ought never to seek or desire that the world serve it with its delights or caress it with its service. Therefore, by despising all that belongs to the world, the spirit should cast it back upon the world; and then willingly expose itself to every injury from the world. In this respect it possesses complete peace: desiring none of the world’s prosperities and fearing none of its adversities. Conversely, the spirit must never subject itself to the reproaches of its own flesh, never serve its flesh’s will. Rather, the flesh must be wearied by continual labour and subdued by unceasing abstinence, until it humbly asks for peace, promises peace, and keeps peace. At last let it cease to lust against the spirit, begin at length to recognize its Lord, and persevere [Col. 0319B] in obedience to his every command.

After this twofold peace—which cannot be disturbed by the world or corrupted by its own body—the devil is no longer permitted to inflict any violence upon the spirit. He turns therefore to cunning arguments and tries to entrap it through deceits and snares. But against temptation of this kind the spirit must both keep watch through discernment and fight through prayer.

The first peace, then, which is toward God, is to be attained through obedience. The second, which is toward the world, is to be preserved through patience. The third, which is against the flesh, is to be acquired through abstinence. The fourth, which is against the devil, is to be obtained through prudence, and especially through persistence in prayer. Prayer, indeed, is found necessary for every peace: without it no peace is acquired and none possessed.

Of the first peace it is sung: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). Of the second it is promised: “I leave peace to you” (John 14). What sort of peace this should be is subsequently explained when it is said: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid” (ibid.). Of the third and fourth Job says: “The beasts of the earth shall be at peace with you, and you shall know that your tent has peace” (Job 5). Here, by the tent is understood the dwelling of our body; by the beasts of the earth, evil spirits.

Having thus acquired this manifold peace, “the Lord will bless his people with peace.” But what, do we think, is this blessing which the Lord will give his people, unless perhaps it is that which, as we know, the Lord is accustomed to give his people? “Increase,” he says, “and multiply” (Gen. 1). Truly a good and greatly desirable blessing, by which every good will becomes daily greater than itself, and the number of virtues becomes more abundant from day to day.

He had perceived that the Lord’s people increased by his blessing when, confidently singing what we read above in this same psalm, he said: “The voice of the Lord is in strength; the voice of the Lord is in magnificence” (Ps. 28). He desired—or rather hoped—that this people, so pleasing to the Lord, might be multiplied within him, when he said: “You will multiply strength in my soul” (Ps. 137). We certainly read that six hundred thousand and more ascended from Egypt, whom the Lord brought forth from the prison-house of the Egyptians [Col. 0320A] with a mighty hand and uplifted arm (Exod. 12). If, therefore, such could be the multitude of God’s people at Israel’s departure from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, how greatly, we think, can they be multiplied when they come into the land of promise and begin to possess the promised inheritance, free from every servitude to alien dominion?

If the Lord raises so many holy desires, inspires so many good wills, and multiplies even at the beginning of conversion the number of pure and useful thoughts in certain persons, how innumerable and almost infinite must the multitude of the divine people be believed to be which the Lord of hosts possesses in the perfect—namely, in those already established in the manner of life of perfection? “The chariot of God is multiplied by ten thousands” (Ps. [Col. 0320B] 67). It is an abundant multitude when the number extends not merely to a thousand but even to ten thousand. But how great will it be when it is multiplied by ten thousands? “The chariot of God is multiplied by ten thousands.” How many, then, will there be in the whole army of this King, if so many thousands of warriors attend his chariot alone?

O how numerous they will then be, when they have begun to multiply in their own land, if, as has already been said, they could be so numerous while they still lived in a foreign land or laboured on the way! I think they will be multiplied beyond the sand of the sea, so that they will then be either scarcely countable or not countable at all. Yet they will multiply most when that Jerusalem begins to be built “as a city whose fellowship is in the same”—they fall asleep [Col. 0320C] and rest—worthy indeed to receive blessing from him who is accustomed to give blessing to his people in peace.

You know well that Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” In such a city the King and Lord of this people gladly dwells, because “his place has been made in peace.” Those who receive blessing from the hand of their Lord undoubtedly ascend to this city. For “the tribes, the tribes of the Lord, ascended there: the testimony of Israel, to give praise to the name of the Lord.” Therefore they ascend to give confession and receive blessing. For “the Lord will bless his people with peace,” that is, in Jerusalem.

This is that Jerusalem whose form we described above through the square [Col. 0320D] in that fourfold peace concerning which we have said something beforehand. Yet the heavenly Jerusalem which is built in heaven is one thing, and this Jerusalem, which is built as a city but on earth, another. The Lord alone does not build the former; this latter, however—though not without his help—is built by his people. For I do not know in what way that peace of God which surpasses all understanding can be founded through human understanding. Surely such peace surpasses all understanding. This city excludes every human understanding; none of all human thoughts enters its gates. Surely this Jerusalem is not built except above heaven.

Nevertheless, it descends from heaven to earth for those found worthy to enter into it, even if only a little; nor can those yet unfit to ascend to the heavens and descend to the abysses ascend to it: “I saw,” he says, “the new Jerusalem descending from heaven” (Rev. 21). Those entering this Jerusalem experience how great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord. For, entering into the joy of their Lord, they are made drunk with the abundance of your house; and, having drunk from the torrent of your delight, they fall asleep and rest together in peace.

But behold, now I lay my hand upon my mouth and restrain my lip with my finger, lest I seem to defile the most holy matters of this secret with unclean lips. These things are better learned by experiencing than by expounding. Let those experienced in such a secret speak of it instead. Yet it is not even safe to bring publicly forward matters which they ought to keep stored within themselves, under the enclosure of silence, with great reverence [Col. 0321B] [Col. 0322A]. Let such persons therefore cry with the prophet and say: “My secret is for myself, my secret is for myself” (Isa. 24), lest Truth perhaps convict them either of scattering pearls before swine or of giving what is holy to dogs (Matt. 7).

But I dare say one thing: whoever has been able, in however small a measure, to attain the excellence of the final peace shall be filled beyond measure with whatever that blessing may be which the Lord will give his people in peace. But at last let this lengthy discourse set its bounds in peace. For it is good for us to be here, and it is not expedient for us to exceed the bounds of peace. Therefore let our discourse end in the contemplation of this peace, and of that peace which shall have no end; may he who is our peace [Col. 0322B] deign to give it to us through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 40

[Col. 0321]

[Col. 0321B] “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my breads, has greatly increased his supplanting of me.” “The man of my peace.” There is an outward person and there is an inward person, as the Apostle says: “Though our outward person is corrupted, yet the inward is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4). Thus the inward person complains of the outward person and says: “The man of my peace.” So long as the body is still being chastised and has not yet been fully [Col. 0321C] subjected to the spirit, conflict is certainly waged on both sides. But when the body has been chastised and reduced to servitude, peace returns, because the flesh yields to the spirit. This is the peace of the spirit, not of the body, just as that peace in which the spirit obeys the flesh belongs properly to the flesh.

Therefore the spirit finds its own peace in its own flesh when the flesh does not oppose it in good pursuits. Hence it says here: “The man of my peace.” But let no one ever put confidence in the peace of his flesh, even though its stimulus is quiet, even though it promises him complete security. Let him often remember what the prophetic saying declares: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my breads, has greatly increased his supplanting of me.”

“In whom I trusted,” he says. It is written: “Let us make for him a helper like himself” (Gen. 2). What wonder if Adam trusts in his own helper? What wonder if our inward person hopes in the man of his peace? Let him therefore say: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted,” and add: “Who ate my breads.” Elsewhere it is said: “My tears were my bread day and night” (Ps. 41), and elsewhere: “Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126). The spirit has deserved to have such breads in the valley of tears, in the place that he has appointed, when someone grieves for his sins, wishes to weep, yet cannot weep; then the spirit alone eats the bread of sorrow, while the flesh still rejects such bread.

But when the outward person weeps for what the inward person grieves, each certainly eats one bread of sorrow, and the spirit feeds the man of its peace with its own bread. Let him therefore say: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my breads, has greatly increased his supplanting of me.” He grieves—indeed, he complains—that after the man of his peace had offered him peace, after he had given him good hope, after he had made him share in the breads of his sorrow, the man of his peace rises unexpectedly against him again. Indeed, concerning the state of his tranquility he now says: “He has greatly increased his supplanting of me.”

We know that it is a graver guilt to sin after the vow of profession. Therefore, as often as one’s own flesh casts one into sin before the vow, so often it supplants him. But when it overcomes one after the vow has been made, it undoubtedly greatly increases its supplanting of him. [Col. 0322D] Thus it first supplanted him, and afterward increased its supplanting.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 44

[Col. 0321D] “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold.” The Lord of hosts, as the Psalmist says, is himself the King of glory (Ps. 23). Hence the Prophet says: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold.” Charity is rightly called the queen of virtues, because any virtue that does not serve charity loses the name of virtue. Temporal goods are at God’s left hand, eternal goods at his right. Charity, therefore, is said to stand at the right hand because it rests upon eternal, not temporal, goods.

For charity reigns only in those whom love for eternal things inflames. Those who pursue temporal things too eagerly often persecute one another even to death. Conversely, those who love one another in God lay down their lives for one another when the occasion requires. Therefore Charity the queen stands at the right hand, but in a garment of gold. It is evident, then, that she who seeks to have garments so precious wishes to please the eyes of the supreme King.

Here, I think, the error of certain people is reproved, who assert that works are nothing. “Have charity,” they say, “and do whatever you wish”—rightly enough. For, just as one full of charity commits no evil deliberately, so one readily omits no good which lies within one’s power to do. And this is surely what Augustine says, not what your negligence imagines. For the proof of charity is the performance of a work. Good works are its garments: “In a garment,” he says, “of gold.” By the garment understand works of righteousness; by the gold, the brightness of wisdom. Golden garments, therefore, are discerning works.

Perhaps you do all things vigorously, but by no means gently, because by no means wisely. You indeed have garments, but you do not have golden garments, because [Col. 0323B] “Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and [Col. 0324A] orders all things sweetly”: from the end of beginning to the end of completion. You begin vigorously but finish tepidly. Why is this, except because you do not order all things sweetly and do not know how to work wisely? You begin, run, hasten, pant, grow weary, fail, and reach not, I do not say the end, but not even the middle.

Therefore charity proceeds—or rather, stands alongside—never departing from God’s right hand: “in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety.” It is fitting, surely, that she should have a manifold and varied garment, since she is a queen. You, whoever you are, always wish to remain in contemplation; you do not know, as I hear, how to be clothed in variety. Another seeks continually to be in prayer and does not notice that charity wishes to be adorned with variety. Whoever delights in any single work, however precious, does not have the adornment of charity, which is clothed [Col. 0324B] with variety.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 74

[Col. 0323]

[Col. 0323B] “For a cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of pure wine mixed; and he has tilted it from this to that. Yet its dregs have not been emptied out.” If we attend carefully, we find three things in this cup of the Lord: pure wine, dregs, and mixture. For if there were no dregs in the cup, it would not have said, “its dregs,” that is, the cup’s dregs. Indeed, these words seem to involve a certain contradiction—rather, they seem to propose something wholly impossible. For if this cup contains pure wine, how, pray, does it [Col. 0323C] contain dregs and mixture? For if someone perhaps says that it has pure wine at the top, dregs at the bottom, and mixture in the middle, he is contradicted by the statement that it is “full of mixture.” But what is said of this cup of the Lord may be referred to different times.

Thus this cup had pure wine, whence it was called a cup of pure wine, just as Scripture is accustomed to call a basket containing dung a cophinus stercoris and a basket containing unleavened bread a canistrum azymorum, from what each is customarily capable of containing. Yet, because it does not call it full of pure wine as it later calls it full of mixture, we may rightly say that it previously contained pure wine and dregs together—pure wine at the top, but dregs at the bottom. For we see this daily in wine-vessels. Therefore it is called a cup of pure wine in order that [Col. 0323D] what it formerly contained may be clearly shown; but when Scripture subsequently calls it full of mixture, it plainly indicates what it now contains. It is sufficiently clear in itself how fittingly it says, “its dregs,” rather than “a cup of dregs,” although it had earlier called it a cup of pure wine. We have said these things beforehand according to the literal exposition. Let us now seek what mystical meaning lies hidden in these words.

The cup of the Lord is justice; pure wine is unmixed joy; dregs are utter bitterness; mixture is good and evil joined and blended together. Pure wine is eternal happiness; dregs, everlasting unhappiness. Mixture is temporal changeability, made up of prosperous and adverse circumstances. All these are poured out from the Lord’s cup, because nothing is done except justly by the just Creator, and all things are governed justly by the [Col. 0324B] just Ruler.

The Lord therefore holds the cup in his hand, because, though he is the Lord to whom no one dares say, “Why do you act thus?” he exceeds the bounds of equity in none of his works. This is the cup in which my Lord drinks—not that Joseph who was set over Egypt alone, but he to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given. He drinks from it, therefore, because it tastes sweet to him. For that especially delights which justice commends. This is [Col. 0324C] the cup in which he is accustomed to divine, because by the examination of his justice he weighs even our hidden things. He holds this cup in his hand because he exercises his justice in action. Others, indeed, carry it not in their hand but, like that Benjamin, in a sack: they grasp by knowledge what is just, but do not show in action what they retain in memory.

From this cup of the Lord, of which we have spoken, angelic nature was first made drunk; human nature was later given drink and will at some time be made drunk. For, as was said above, this cup had dregs and pure wine together, yet not mingled: pure wine at the top, but dregs at the bottom. Angelic nature was therefore made and was given drink from this cup. [Col. 0324D] Some fell through fault and were confirmed in evil; others stood through grace and were confirmed in good. Both drank from the one cup of divine justice. But the former were sufficiently made drunk from the dregs, the latter from the pure wine.

Human nature was subsequently made and was likewise to drink from the Lord’s cup. But because it fell through fault, it was not worthy to drink pure wine. What then will the just and gracious Lord do? He himself knows what to do, he whose wisdom is without number. Because it sinned, he did not give it pure wine; but because it fell through negligence under another’s prompting, he mercifully refused to make it drunk with dregs. Therefore, setting the cup in motion, he mixed the dregs with the wine; and from that time it has remained full of mixture. From this mixture, therefore, man drinks, for from the beginning to the end [Col. 0325A] of the age his lot is continually varied through prosperity and adversity.

“For the cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of mixture.” However greatly anyone flourishes here, he must feel some bitterness, because the cup is in the Lord’s hand, full of mixture. Likewise, however deeply anyone is cast down in this life, he is at some time lifted by some consolation, because the cup is in the Lord’s hand, full of mixture. Therefore, if this alternation of changing circumstances is maintained in all things and until the end of the age, it is evident how rightly the Lord’s cup is said to be full of mixture.

If, then, you are troubled, do not lose heart; if you are consoled, do not become secure. “For he has tilted it from this to that.” On the day of evils remember good things, and on the day of good things remember evils, because he has tilted it from this to that. Behold, I see a vessel of wrath drenched from [Col. 0325B] the Lord’s cup and filled with bitterness. Again the vessel of wrath is emptied of that with which it was full, and the vessel of mercy is filled from it. Why is this, I ask, unless he who holds the cup has tilted it from this to that?

Again I observe a vessel of wrath filled with the oil of temporal gladness: it spends its days in prosperity and meanwhile possesses the things that make for its peace. Then suddenly it is tilted, and that with which it was filled is poured out; and the vessel of mercy is drenched with that same oil of gladness. He who formerly grieved rejoices, and he who formerly rejoiced grieves. This variety of alternating circumstances endures as long as he who holds the cup does not cease to tilt it from this to that. Even to this day no one is found in this life who is made drunk from the Lord’s cup with pure wine, because the cup [Col. 0325C] is in the hand of the Lord, full of mixture.

Here there is never joy alone, never sorrow alone, because these are mingled, whether at the top or at the bottom of the cup. Look at fish in water disturbed by rain-waves: whether they rise or sink, up or down, they find nothing but turbid water and drink nothing but turbid water. Thus human beings rise up to heaven and descend [Col. 0326A] to the depths, and everywhere they drink from what is turbid, because the cup in the Lord’s hand is full of mixture.

For the Lord’s cup is still in motion and therefore cannot make things pure. As long as the cup is moved, the dregs do not settle but are mingled, and thus a mixture results. Do you wish to know how this cup is in motion, so that it cannot offer pure wine? Since some angels were confirmed in good and others in evil, the former drank unmixed pure wine and the latter dregs; and just as the evil expect nothing better, so the good do not fear losing what they once received. But because justice in human beings is not yet fixed, and neither side is confirmed in its state, the cup is continually moved; for in no one has justice yet been fixed immovably. For one who is unjust can be converted, and one who is just [Col. 0326B] can be perverted. Likewise, one who is good can become better, and one who is evil can become worse. For one who is filthy can become still filthier—which is to descend toward the bottom of the cup. Similarly, one who is just can still be justified—which is to be raised toward the upper part of the cup. And while this occurs, they drink only from what is turbid, because the cup in the Lord’s hand is full of mixture.

“Yet its dregs have not been emptied out.” Although they are now mingled with the pure wine and the cup is full of mixture, nevertheless its dregs have not been emptied out. For after all things are consummated, and human beings, like the angels now, are finally confirmed—these in good, those in evil—the cup will cease to move; the dregs will settle at the bottom of the cup; pure wine will be at [Col. 0326C] the top; and dregs alone will remain at the bottom. For its dregs have not been emptied out: all sinners of the earth who do not fear to persist in their sins will drink them. But the good will then drink pure wine; the evil alone will drink dregs alone, so that henceforth no good person may fare ill and no evil person may fare well.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 80

[Col. 0325]

[Col. 0325C] “When he went out from the land of Egypt, he heard a language that he did not know.” If Egypt is interpreted as “darkness,” what else is it to leave Egypt than, after dispelling the darkness of ignorance, to fix the eyes of understanding in the light of truth? As often as, forgetting temporal things, we fix the rays of contemplation upon eternity, so often do we leave Egypt. But one who leaves Egypt quickly hears a language that he did not know. For when, scorning all external things, we devote ourselves to divine contemplation, we receive the hidden things of heavenly wisdom now through angelic revelation, now through divine inspiration.

An unknown language is angelic revelation; an unfamiliar language is divine inspiration: “If I speak,” says the Apostle, [Col. 0326C] “with the tongues of human beings and of angels” (1 Cor. 13). Therefore, just as there is a language of human beings, so also there is a language of angels. Those burdened with worldly cares, seeing nothing but darkness, cannot hear this language. [Col. 0326D] Therefore let one who desires knowledge of heavenly wisdom abandon the darkness of the world. For if through love and thought we withdraw from external works, we quickly hear the voice of inward inspiration, as is written of Israel: “For when he went out from the land of Egypt, he heard a language that he did not know” (Ps. 80). The more often anyone hears this language, the more he advances in knowledge of heavenly wisdom.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 80

[Col. 0325]

[Col. 0325D] “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it.” This is not said to everyone, but only to the one whom the Lord his God [Col. 0326D] has brought out of the land of Egypt; to him, I say, it is rightly said: “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it.” For if you still [Col. 0327A] dwell in Egypt and love the darkness of this age, it is better for you to close your mouth than to open it wide, because in Egypt you can scarcely find that with which it may be filled.

Indeed, we see many who do not have enough to satisfy their belly. But it seems very strange if there is any soul, however poor, that does not have something with which it can fill its mouth. What then, I ask, is meant by this saying, which is promised as though it were something great: “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it”? But if we consider that mouth of our inner human being, we quickly find what we seek.

Let us see what the Egyptians hunger or thirst for, and we shall see how poor or needy they are, who cannot find enough to fill even one mouth. Those who are in Egypt gape only after carnal things and desire [Col. 0327B] nothing except temporal things. Conversely, those who have gone out of Egypt desire nothing except spiritual things and sigh for nothing except heavenly things. Of these it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5). Truly blessed, because the Lord fed them with the bread of life and understanding, and gave them the health-giving water of wisdom to drink. The person to whom the Lord says, “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it,” seems to belong to their number.

But what is this mouth of the inner human being but the heart’s desire? Yet all Egypt’s delights cannot fill this mouth, because all the world’s riches cannot satisfy carnal desires. See how small a part of the human body, and how narrow an opening, the mouth of flesh is. Who does not [Col. 0327C] see how small it is, since one morsel of bread can fill it? What one morsel is to the mouth of flesh, the whole world is—indeed, much less—to the mouth of the heart. One morsel easily fills the bodily mouth, but the whole world cannot fill the heart’s desire.

Consider, if you can, how vast is the heart whose mouth the whole world cannot fill. Consider how divine speech despises the abundance of the world, preferring to it by comparison one morsel of heavenly bread. If, then, you have left Egypt and learned to hunger for spiritual things, you are told: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it”; and again: “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it.” Therefore, if it is shut, you are commanded [Col. 0328A] to open it; if it is open, you are commanded to widen it.

Open your mouth, therefore, and stretch out your desire as far as you can. Stretch it greatly, that you may be able to receive greatly. The more capable you are of receiving those things, the more blessed you will be. Stretch it out, then; do not spare yourself. And if you wish to be sparing, fear for yourself, not for those things. They do not know how to fail, but you can be less fitted for them. Open wide your mouth, therefore, as much as you can, because you can never receive too much. Open and widen your mouth, and it will be filled. He who made it can easily fill it.

For this purpose he sends forth his crystal like morsels, so that he may fill what the whole world could not fill even once, not once or twice, but frequently. He sends forth, I say, his crystal like morsels—not as one morsel, but [Col. 0328B] as morsels—so that you may have something with which to fill your mouth repeatedly. But who is this crystalline bread, so hard and so pure? It is beautiful to behold, but strong to chew.

This is why almost everyone desires the heavenly bread of wisdom, but very few grasp it: “The little children asked for bread,” he says, “and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4). This bread is marvelous: little children desire it, yet not even the great can break it. Yet what wonder that little children desire it because of its crystalline beauty, or that the great cannot break it because of its crystalline hardness? Therefore, whenever the Lord wishes to refresh anyone with the bread of life and understanding, he first divides his bread into morsels; and then, at last, when and to whom he wills, through ministering angels, [Col. 0328C] he sends his crystal like morsels.

But do you suppose that even then they suffice for eating the crystalline bread, divided as it is into morsels? By no means, I think. But he who sends forth his crystal like morsels will send forth his Word and melt them; and Christ himself, coming to fulfill his promise, will pass by and minister to them. And lest drink seem lacking, his Spirit will blow and waters will flow. You see how Christ ministers in food and the Holy Spirit in drink. Oh, what a banquet, where Christ is steward and the Holy Spirit cupbearer!

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 84

[Col. 0327]

[Col. 0327D] “Justice and peace have kissed.” One peace exists before repentance, when the spirit obeys the flesh. Another peace exists after repentance has been accomplished, when the flesh is subjected to the spirit. For there is peace when the flesh desires and the spirit acquiesces. There is likewise peace when the spirit commands and the flesh obeys.

Of peace from the spirit toward the flesh it is said: “But now the things that make for your peace; but days will come, and they will hem you in on every side and cast you down to the ground” (Luke 19). And again: “Peace, peace, and there is no peace,” because a peace that is not true ought not to be called peace. Of peace from the flesh toward the spirit it is said: “And may the peace that surpasses all understanding guard your hearts and your minds” (Phil. [Col. 0328D] 4).

Between the first and the final peace discord arises, war is waged, and hatred is practiced; for the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, when the body is chastised and reduced to servitude. But after the battle has been fought and victory won, peace is established, discord is calmed, and there is a passage from peace to peace: from carnal to spiritual, from false to true, from evil to good. In the first peace the flesh rules and the spirit serves. In the second peace the spirit reigns and the flesh obeys.

The first peace is carried on in the region of unlikeness, where desire rules. The second is found in the land of promise, where [Col. 0329A] justice holds dominion. The passage is indeed difficult. For no one is granted passage from nation to nation and from kingdom to another people except by a mighty hand and an uplifted arm. What is passage from nation to nation except from the desires of the flesh to the desires of the spirit? What is passage from kingdom to kingdom except from the kingdom of iniquity to the kingdom of charity?

Distinguish, then, these three times. First, when desire is fulfilled; second, when repentance is practiced; third, when justice is loved. Therefore, as long as the flesh desires and the spirit acquiesces, there is indeed peace, but it is not good because it is not just; and for that reason justice is angered. It detests such peace and departs, and peace remains indeed, but alone. It sometimes happens that, after desire has been fulfilled, the heart is pierced with compunction, is converted to justice, [Col. 0329B] and then [Col. 0330A] the desires of the spirit rise suddenly and burn fiercely on one side, while the desires of the flesh rise on the other. The spirit desires, but the flesh resists. Peace is driven away, justice returns, and a fierce struggle begins.

Nor does the spirit rest until it recovers by right its kingdom in its flesh and binds that flesh to perpetual service. Thus the flesh serves—at first unwillingly, then willingly. Peace is again established: the conscience is made clean. Peace thus returns without justice departing. No longer do they merely tolerate one another; rather, they embrace one another more dearly and are united with one another in the kiss of charity, as it is written: “Justice and peace have kissed.” First, therefore, there is peace, but alone, during the time when desire is being tested. Second, justice alone, during the time when repentance is being practiced. Finally, peace and justice are together during the time of a cleansed conscience.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 98

[Col. 0329]

[Col. 0329B] “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.” What new thing, I ask, has occurred? What did he wish to teach us? For who will be counted among God’s priests if Moses and Aaron, from whom all priesthood took its beginning, are not numbered among them? Moreover, when Samuel was still a boy he remained in the temple day and night; how much more did he do so in David’s time, when he had already grown old? What else ought he to have done in the temple than serve the Lord and call upon the Lord? Nothing new, [Col. 0329C] I think, occurred such as would require the Prophet to say or write of him: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.”

But if we attend carefully, we find Moses and Aaron dead long before his time; and perhaps Samuel too had departed from life when the Prophet wrote such things. What then is this, I ask, that he says? What did he wish to teach us when he said, “Moses and Aaron among his priests,” and so forth? We know of a certain living temple of God, if we believe the Apostle of God writing of it: “The temple of God,” he says, “is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). Therefore we must by no means believe that God’s temple is without priests, or that it ought to be without those who call upon the Lord’s name. But [Col. 0329D] would that Moses and Aaron were among its priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.

Let us ask who these Moses, Aaron, and Samuel are. Through Moses the law was given. In Aaron the priesthood was initiated. To Samuel the gift of prophecy was granted. Moses’ office, therefore, is to command what must be done and forbid what must be omitted. Aaron’s office is to implore the Lord’s help for carrying out what Moses commands, and by prayer and offering to render God propitious again toward transgressors. Samuel’s office is to foretell what reward those who fulfill the law may hope for, and what punishment those who violate the law ought to expect.

If, therefore, you see someone newly come from the world, intent upon this all day, occupied with it every hour [Col. 0330B]—how to make satisfaction for past sins; how to keep himself guarded against future ones; what must be done, in what order, how much, or when he must apply himself to each matter—know that Moses has arisen in the heart of such a person and is, as it were, in some fashion establishing a new law. For once Moses has been born and has grown up, he begins to order conduct and arrange life. He considers how the countenance ought to be controlled, how dress and bearing should be ordered with discipline; he dictates what must be eaten, how much one must keep vigil, [Col. 0330C] how to resist anger, how to oppose gluttony, how to trample down pride, by what means to extinguish lust, how ready one ought to be for obedience, how patient in endurance, and many other things besides, which we learn better by doing than by reading and retain more firmly.

Recognize Moses, therefore, by this double sign: when you see him commanding harshly and punishing strictly. Once the law has been given and received, a person begins to wish to advance but is not granted the power to fulfill it, so that he can cry out with the Apostle: “To will is present with me, but I do not find how to accomplish it” (Rom. 7). For the mind, still proud because it presumes everything upon its own effort rather than God’s grace, is frequently left to itself when God withdraws, [Col. 0330D] so that it may learn its weakness by experience. It begins, strives, grows weary, and fails. Yet even so it is not immediately restrained from its presumption, nor recalled from self-confidence except after many experiences.

It takes up strength again and is renewed; it is angry with itself, indignant with itself, reproves and chastises itself; now for negligence, now for imprudence, it accuses itself; it punishes itself for itself and inveighs against itself. Vigils are therefore prolonged, fasts continued; the body is afflicted by cold and nakedness, and the flesh worn down by labour and lashes. Many sacrifices are therefore slain, yet upon the outer altar; there is not yet even mention of the inner altar. In so great affliction, when the body is given no rest and neither measure nor moderation is maintained, the body at last fails, [Col. 0331A] the mind grows weary; and scarcely, at last, when it sees itself failing in body and wasting away in heart, it returns to itself and recalls that apostolic saying: “It is not of one who wills or of one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9).

All hope in self-confidence being cast aside, it turns wholly to God; and having first drawn fire from the outer altar, it runs into the Holy of Holies, yet not without the blood of the calf. For once the calf of pride has been slain and all the presumptuousness of former arrogance discarded, then, despairing of itself, it begins to hope in the Lord’s help. After the many sacrifices, as we have said, offered upon the outer altar, it begins to bring to the Lord upon the inner altar groans, sighs, prayers, and tears.

The outer altar is the sensation of the flesh; the inner altar, the affection of the heart. Upon the inner altar, therefore, groans, [Col. 0331B] sighs, tears, and the other things that move the heart’s affection are offered; upon the outer altar, vigils, fasts, labour, abstinence from food, and the other things pertaining to bodily sensation. Yet fire is drawn from this outer altar when one hastens to the inner altar. For from bodily affliction the force of pain is drawn into the heart, whence afterward the incense of compunction may be kindled.

When, then, you see these things frequently practiced, do not doubt that a new priesthood is being initiated in Aaron. For, as we said above, it belongs to Aaron to seek the protection of divine propitiation and to render God propitious through offerings and prayers. To understand the priestly office more fully, there are two things that seem especially to belong to it: namely, to instruct the people and to reconcile the Lord to oneself and to the people. Moses fully performs one of these; the other is magnificently fulfilled through Aaron. Hence it is rightly said of them: “Moses and Aaron among his priests.” And there is added: “And Samuel among those who call upon his name.”

Above we said that, just as legislation and priesthood shone forth in Moses and Aaron, so the gift of prophecy was preeminent in Samuel. Why then is it now said of him, “And Samuel among those who call upon his name,” when it seems that it should instead have said, “And Samuel among his prophets”? Why, then, among those who call upon him rather than among those who prophesy? Perhaps Samuel gladly prophesies among those who call upon God; or perhaps those among whom he prophesies gladly call upon God. [Col. 0331D] It is certainly so, and there can be no doubt on this point. Samuel’s prophecy knows how to make people truly call upon God and pray in truth.

For the more fully, more frequently, and more attentively someone considers what rewards are laid up in heaven for the just and what torments in hell for the wicked, the more truly, I think, he calls upon God and the more attentively he prays. But if Samuel ceases to prophesy, priests quickly cease to call upon God; and the rarer contemplation of future things becomes, the more lukewarm prayer becomes and the more sluggish invocation arises. Therefore, for Moses to be strict in commanding and Aaron to remain devout in prayer, Samuel must persevere with subtle discernment in contemplation.

There is more to say with precision about Samuel’s office. [Col. 0332A] As we often see, at the beginning of conversion everyone is as ready for work as he is devout in prayer, since Moses and Aaron are still living and appear chiefly to preside over these affairs. But once he believes that he has made satisfaction for past sins, once he considers himself already holy and someone great, he begins again to grow negligent and to decline from his former fervour.

For when Moses and Aaron have died, the mind quickly grows lukewarm and falls into a kind of negligence, or even contempt, in accordance with Moses’ statement: “I know that after my death you will act wickedly; for while I was still living, you always behaved contentiously” (Deut. 32). The death of Moses is the failure of diligent care. Aaron’s destruction is the interruption of devout prayer. With Moses and Aaron dead, therefore, [Col. 0332B] the mind begins to fall into negligence, indeed often even to descend into contempt.

Temptations arise from every side; impure thoughts meet it everywhere; shameful pleasures suddenly arise in the heart. The flesh is sharply inflamed, the mind burns, and the entire conscience is disturbed and confounded. One has recourse to prayer, hastens to action, again becomes devout in prayer, ready in obedience, diligent in reading, fervent in compunction, swift in work. Nor does one cease this exertion until one rescues oneself from the pressing danger and restores and orders oneself once more into former tranquility.

Once all things are calmed, former tranquility returns; security follows tranquility, and idleness accompanies security. Idleness produces curiosity; curiosity introduces covetousness. And once desire—the mother of all vices—holds the citadel of the mind and violently penetrates even to the heart’s inner chambers, it readily admits a multitude of vices and, in all haste, introduces them like its army. The treasure of wisdom is seized as plunder; the populace of virtues is reduced to slavery; that person’s latter state becomes worse than the former. Again recourse is had to the help of divine propitiation; prayers are poured forth from the heart; zeal for one’s former way of life is renewed; divine kindness is again appeased and at last bent; the person’s former freedom is restored. Thus this alternation [Col. 0332D] of changes occurs, and occurs frequently: now the oppression of vices, now the succession of virtues. Often through their negligence they are handed over to enemies; often through God’s mercy they are again delivered from enemies.

This happens by a wonderful dispensation of divine kindness: through frequent falling, a person’s own weakness is made known to him; through the many attacks and snares of enemies, the enemy’s cunning is revealed to him; through continual deliverance, divine kindness is manifested to him. Whoever wishes to understand these things more fully should read the book of Judges a little more carefully. There he will undoubtedly find how the children of Israel, after their transgressions, are attacked and conquered by enemies and reduced to slavery. Afflicted by enemies, they again have recourse to divine help; they ask and seek mercy, [Col. 0333A] find it, and return to their former freedom.

What, I ask, do these attacks of enemies signify except, so to speak, certain encounters of spiritual warfare between vices and virtues? When God abandons them, or when he protects them, now these conquer, now those; now these are conquered, now those. Just as there, when Israel sins, an enemy is raised up to plunder them; and again, when Israel pleads, a saviour is raised up to deliver them.

In this matter one must carefully observe and firmly retain that they are not always oppressed by the same enemies, but are plundered now by these, now by those; they are afflicted by some for a shorter period and by others for a longer. We quickly perceive this, under God’s dispensation, to be enacted within us if we are not ignorant of that spiritual warfare and of the inward conflict [Col. 0333B] waged within us. It happens that we are attacked longer by a particular vice, until we are fully instructed in all its force and nature and its manner of attack. Once one vice has been subdued, another rises against us; once that one is conquered, another succeeds it in attacking us. The greater the violence of each, the more severe its attack upon us, or the longer the struggle, becomes.

Divine mercy wishes us to be attacked by all vices and permits us to be exercised longer by each one, so that we may carry off, as it were, a triumph of victory over them all and at length know fully and perfectly, as has been said, the force, nature, and manner of attack of each one. Hence, in the book [Col. 0333C] of Judges, the deliverers of the Hebrews are called not kings but judges. For it belongs to kings to command by the arbitrary decision of their will whatever pleases them. But the office of judges is to know laws and examine cases.

Thus a judge, or legal expert, rises within us when the mind has been fully instructed concerning a particular vice by many arguments and countless experiences: it does not command with authority whatever it wishes to be done, as kings do, but with a certain prudence strives to carry out what experience has taught it. As often as a mind instructed by many experiences is rescued from danger wisely rather than violently, so often it experiences, as a gift from God, the prudence of its judges.

Judge rises after judge, because the mind advances from knowledge of one vice to knowledge of another, until at length, after all the judges, the last judge, Samuel, may come, fully instructed concerning individual vices and every snare of the tempter. [Col. 0334A] At that time he begins not only to know all the deceits of the plotter and the natures of all vices himself, but also to disclose them openly and explain them prudently to others. Often, while silently observing another’s facial expression, bodily bearing, and manner, he recognizes almost better than the tempted person himself by which vice that person is attacked. Often at the very moment of temptation he detects the enemy’s frauds, and long beforehand foreknows what danger, or what kind of danger, may arise from any matter.

This is that Samuel to whom, as was said above, gifts of prophecy were given. Of him it is written: “All knew from Dan to Beersheba that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord” (1 Sam. 3). Does it not seem like a gift of prophecy to uncover the hidden passions of the mind and the enemy’s concealed snares, and to foresee and foretell future dangers long before they come?

Therefore, to bring into brief compass what we have said more diffusely: it belongs to Moses prudently to discern what ought to be done; to Aaron, to implore divine help for those things which we cannot accomplish by ourselves; to Samuel, cautiously to foresee what benefit or danger may arise from any matter. Thus discretion is understood through Moses, devotion through Aaron, and circumspection through Samuel. For it belongs to discretion to order conduct, to devotion to supplicate God, and to circumspection to provide against events that are coming.

If, therefore, you find your mind discerning in work, devout in prayer, and [Col. 0334C] provident in circumspection, you too may sing with the Prophet: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.” For since, as the reasoning demonstrated above proves, it belongs to priests to instruct the people by precepts and appease God by prayers, it is evident that without discretion and devotion—as though Moses and Aaron were dead—they cannot fulfill the office of their priesthood. And insofar as circumspection, like a certain Samuel, makes them fearful concerning future things, it likewise makes them devout in prayer and persistent in calling upon God.

When, therefore, you see priesthood worthily administered and God invoked as frequently as devoutly, know that these things are in no way done without the presence of Moses and Aaron, and also Samuel. The Prophet rejoices that these things are done within himself, and confesses it as humbly as truthfully, saying: “Moses and Aaron among his priests,” and so forth.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 104

[Col. 0333]

[Col. 0333D] “When they were very few in number, exceedingly few, and its sojourners.” We have, as it were, few—indeed very few—citizens when we possess only those virtues without which we cannot possibly be saved. Faith, hope, and charity are few in number and can easily be counted. It is quite clear that without them there is no true salvation, and certain that with them no one can perish. Yet it seems remarkable how, with so [Col. 0334D] small a number, passage may be open or granted, especially from nation to nation and from kingdom to another people, particularly when they travel through a foreign land to a distant region. For they are not only exceedingly few, but also sojourners and pilgrims. For faith has not yet grasped by understanding what it believes; what is hoped for is not yet possessed; and charity still enjoys its desire as long as it wanders far from the Lord in a land of pilgrimage.

We may also say that novices in virtue are still few, so long as they cannot utterly destroy the hostile cohort of vices; fewer when they cannot yet subdue them and make them at least tributary to themselves; and exceedingly few when they cannot resist them or defend their life against them without great labor and grave danger. Yet, with God leading the way, such exceedingly few often pass from nation to nation and from kingdom to another people. What is passage from nation to nation, except passage from carnal desires to the delights of the spirit? What is passage from kingdom to kingdom, except from the kingdom of desire to the kingdom of righteousness? One who thus passes is rightly called a Hebrew, for “Hebrew” means “one passing over.” Trampling [Col. 0335B] desire and grasping righteousness, the Hebrews pass from kingdom to kingdom—or rather, as the Prophet puts it, from a kingdom to another people. For which human being lives here without sin? Who here never feels carnal pleasure? Therefore righteousness has its kingdom elsewhere, not here, although even here it has another people, very far removed from vices.

Thus, for the present, the Hebrews are kept back from the kingdom of righteousness; yet they pass from a kingdom to another people, and passage is granted only through the swords of enemies in their midst. Yet, under God’s protection, they penetrate and pass through the midst of their enemies: “He did not allow anyone to harm them, and he rebuked kings on their behalf.”

Among all living creatures, human beings alone use reason; and among human beings, kings rule over others. Since the Prophet knew that some of our adversaries are more cunning and others more audacious, he rightly indicates the former by the name “man,” the latter by “kings.” The former strive to deceive by tricks and ambushes; the latter are driven by a kind of impetuosity. These are more crafty; those stronger. These tempt more subtly; those press more fiercely. By the cunning of the former our prudence is trained; by the pressure of the latter [Col. 0336A] our fortitude is exercised. Perhaps, however, if we consider more carefully, we should understand those to be indicated more aptly by “kings” in whom there is cunning boldness and bold cunning, so that their temptation is violent and at the same time deceitful. The more difficult their assault, the more dangerous it is.

Nevertheless, those whom God’s eternal providence has determined to preserve, he did not allow man to harm; but he rebuked kings on their behalf—indeed, rebuking their enemies for their sake: “Do not touch my Christs, and do not deal maliciously with my prophets.” Christs are those who have received an anointing; prophets, those who foretell things to come by foreseeing them. But we know that God’s anointing is his love. Therefore those who receive such anointing, who ardently love the things of God, are Christs of God [Col. 0336B] and may be called Christs. Rightly, therefore, by “Christs” we understand heavenly desires and vows of holiness, which we know blaze in the hearts of the saints through the anointing of divine inspiration.

As has been said, usage calls those “prophets” who can foresee the future. Thus they are rightly called prophets who search out the hidden things of the Godhead, contemplate heavenly things, penetrate inner realities, and unveil the depths of mysteries. Spiritual perceptions, then, are like certain prophets: they often attend upon heavenly secrets and fix the eye of contemplation upon invisible things. Desire for eternal things makes them Christs; knowledge of secrets makes them prophets. The fervor of love kindles the former; the subtlety of contemplation enlightens the latter. [Col. 0336C] These love deeply; those know great things. Rightly, therefore, the Lord rebukes kings, or any enemies of such persons: “Do not touch my Christs, and do not deal maliciously with my prophets.” Lukewarmness lies in wait for the former, error for the latter. The fervor of devotion readily fails and falls away in time; and understanding often grows dim and, wandering too far, casts itself headlong into error.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 113

[Col. 0335]

[Col. 0335C] “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.” It is a great spectacle to see mountains leap [Col. 0335D] like rams and hills like lambs of the flock. Such leaping, and such leapers, are not to be found on earth among those who live pleasantly. “The wicked have no joy,” says the Lord. If they have no joy, how much less can they leap in such a fashion? Such leaping, I suppose, is accustomed to occur in Israel’s departure from Egypt—not just anywhere, but in the wilderness. Therefore those who especially desire to obtain so great a miracle must depart from Egypt and flee the world.

But, that we may wonder more and desire more ardently, let us examine more deeply what kind of leaping is described, and to whom it is attributed. “The mountains,” he says, “leaped like rams.” Who are the leapers? Mountains and hills. And what is their joy like? Like that of rams, like that of lambs. I confidently affirm one thing: the leaping of rams and lambs is not found in laughter and loud guffaws. What movements, then, do they usually make in their play, or by what means do we think they express their joy? As we commonly know, in their leaping they make certain jumps, lift their bodies on high, and poise them in the air. But should we expect anything of this sort from hills or mountains? It would truly be a great and astonishing miracle to see mountains and hills leap in the manner of rams or lambs. For who would not be amazed, and who ought not rightly to be amazed, if it happened that he saw the mountain mass divided from the plain and separated from its accustomed place, earth split from earth, and so great a mass suspended, even briefly, in the air?

Certainly it was said to sinful man: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). Hence elsewhere he is reproached: “Why are you proud, earth [Col. 0337A] and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10). This earth, namely human nature, in some rises above the level of its condition and makes a mountain or hill. In others it inclines downward to the depths and becomes a valley. Mountains therefore ascend; valleys descend. Plains remain level and occupy the middle place. In mountains human effort rises above nature; in valleys it descends beneath nature; in plains it nourishes and preserves the goods which it could possess naturally: “The mountains rise, and the plains descend to the place which you established for them” (Ps. 103). Why does he say nothing about valleys? Because they do indeed descend, but not to the place the Lord appointed for them; rather, to the place that a perverse mind chose for itself. But the plains descend not below nature, but below the excellence of mountains.

The plains, then, are those who do not abandon earthly things, yet live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this world. Mountains and hills are those who seek only the things above. Such mountains, therefore, the more ardently they desire heavenly things, the more vehemently they long for eternal things, and the higher they grow, the more closely, without doubt, they touch heaven’s heights. But it is one thing to extend the summit of one’s height upward and touch heaven’s summit as if from nearby; another to make certain leaps and frisk in the manner of rams or lambs. “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.”

But, in order to distinguish mountains, hills, and plains by their proper differences, we understand mountains to mean contemplatives, hills speculatives, [Col. 0337C] and plains actives. For those in the active life do not abandon the plains of this life, while they serve in earthly activities and, in the manner of plains, bear in earthly gains certain fruits of the earth for this life’s use. Speculatives are those who attend to heavenly things, who see the invisible things of God through a mirror in an enigma. They are called *speculatives* precisely because they can see only through a mirror and in an enigma. By contemplatives we should understand those to whom it is given to see face to face, who, contemplating the Lord’s glory with unveiled face, see truth without covering, in its simplicity, without a mirror and without an enigma.

Mountains and hills, then, are those who attend to heavenly things. But speculatives [Col. 0337D] in no way transcend the cloudy veil of bodily likenesses, because they cannot see highest truth in its purity. Contemplatives, however, after the manner of mountains, by transcending in understanding the clouded heights of allegories and enigmas, touch that tranquil brightness of the higher region—the mountain summit. Concerning such hills and mountains we understand the Prophet’s saying: “On that day the mountains shall distill sweetness, and the hills shall flow with milk and honey” (Joel 3). He says of the mountains that they “shall distill sweetness,” yet does not say what kind, nor express it through any likeness. Why, I ask, except because it is so great that no likeness can worthily express it? Why, I ask, except because they draw and pour forth pure sweetness? But the sweetness of the hills is expressed by likeness, when milk or honey is named figuratively. Consider, then, what kind and how great that sweetness is which those above experience, when even that which those below perceive is called milk and honey.

The mountains, therefore, ought by dripping to sprinkle forth that ineffable sweetness which they draw in such abundance—not pour it out in its abundance—and to temper the measure of their outpouring according to the capacity of those below: “The mountains,” he says, “shall distill sweetness, and the hills shall flow with milk and honey.” Such sweetness causes mountains and hills of this kind to sing before the Lord and to make the voice of exultation and confession resound in his praises: “Mountains and hills shall sing praise before the Lord.” Such sweetness, I say, makes mountains and hills wonderfully leap in the Lord: “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills [Col. 0338B] like lambs of the flock.” But if we understand such mountains and hills, surely it ceases to be great or strange that which we have already said in wonder about them. For it will not be great for human beings to leap in the manner of rams and lambs, and to make certain jumps according to their likeness.

Let us therefore seek spiritual, not bodily, leaps in this prophetic saying—such as it befitted the Holy Spirit to teach and the prophet to describe. A bodily leap is to lift the whole body from the earth. A spiritual leap is to estrange the spirit, and all that belongs to the spirit, from earthly things. A bodily leap is wholly to abandon contact with the earth and poise all the body’s limbs in the air. A spiritual leap is to go beyond oneself in mind and, leaving lower things in the depths, pass wholly [Col. 0338C] into the contemplation of invisible things.

Consider, then, the powers of the soul, and perhaps you will more easily discover how great and what it is to lift all such things from contact with earthly matters and make spiritual leaps. First bodily sensation is put to sleep; brutish appetite is blocked; memory of external things is cut off; affection is intoxicated; reason is transformed; understanding is renewed; the whole mind is estranged from itself—so that the spiritual leap of which we speak may be made. Consider, therefore, if you can, what that rejoicing of heart is like, what vehement exultation it is, which compels the mind to abandon its accustomed things and go beyond itself, to be unaware for a time of temporal things, and in the heart’s festivities to make and repeatedly renew certain, as it were, leaps into the things above and eternal, in wonderful ways and many unfamiliar modes.

Perhaps you answer this in the voice of Nicodemus: “How can these things be?” Grant that it is great, wonderful, and altogether astonishing that this can happen; but it is far more unworthy that it should be altogether impossible. See how unworthy it is that the outward man can make certain leaps according to his own mode, while the inward man cannot at all make leaps of its own kind in the mode suitable to it. Observe how altogether astonishing—and astonishing in every respect—it is that the body, taken from earth, can leave earth temporarily in a leap and rise above itself; while spirit, a spiritual and incorporeal nature, cannot be separated even briefly from bodily and earthly things. [Col. 0339A] Do you wonder that a spiritual creature can suspend itself among spiritual things, and do you not rather wonder that spirit cannot be separated from non-spiritual things?

Has it thus ceased to seem marvelous to you that, upon due consideration, it seems almost contrary to nature for spirit to be bound so strongly and almost inseparably to bodily things that it cannot be torn away from them even for a short time? And does it seem to you less—or scarcely at all—marvelous that incorporeal nature cannot do what is judged to be according to nature: namely, return from bodily things to itself and stand fixed in its own things, that is, in incorporeal things? But, I think, you do not wonder at this because you experience it least of all in yourself. Yet if your spirit cannot yet return to itself, when will it be able to go beyond [Col. 0339B] itself and, making such leaps as befit spiritual nature, pass into divine things?

What is it for spirit, which is incorporeal, to return to itself or to its own things, except to have before its eyes only incorporeal creation and what belongs to it? And what is it for spirit, as though by making a leap, to go beyond itself and fix the eye of contemplation upon that nature which creates all things and upon what belongs to it? Therefore, when spiritual persons fall into such transports through the greatness of spiritual exultation, that is fulfilled in them which is said through the Psalmist: “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.” Certainly rational spirit was created to contemplate divine things. Why, then, do we wonder if it can do that for which it was made, when the only thing that seems wonderful is if it cannot do it?

Yet both are marvelous: both its being able, and its not being able, to do this. But one is marvelous to carnal persons, the other to spiritual persons. Its being able is marvelous because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things.” Its not being able is marvelous because “the Spirit helps our weakness.” Wonder, then, at what you wonder at, as one carnal, sold under sin. But that you may understand still more deeply how greatly you ought to wonder, and how rightly to be amazed, consider those ninety-nine sheep which the highest shepherd left upon those lofty mountains of eternal inheritance, when he sought, found, and carried back upon his own shoulders the one that had perished on earth.

[Col. 0339D] Consider, then, how great is the dignity and excellence of our mortal earth: that on the mountains of its exultation it has something in common, by a likeness of kindred nature, with that flock of heavenly hosts. Consider, I say, how full of honor and grace it is for the weakness of human nature, at least in that part in which it excels more greatly, to be able, according to the property of its likeness to angels, to make the leaps of its joy. If you consider this, where, I ask, will the greatness of your wonder lead you, except to understand that in these matters you cannot wonder enough? “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.”

If by earth we must understand human nature, and by the designated flock angelic nature, who can fail to see among the angelic powers how pleasant and sweet it is for them to run here and there through earth of this kind, to recline there, and to satisfy with the fruits of our virtues that avidity of their desires—the righteousness for which they hunger and thirst? “Are they not all ministering spirits,” says the Apostle, “sent [Col. 0340A] for service on behalf of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 1). “The mountains leaped,” and so forth.

Now we have heard what he says concerning mountains and hills. But why, I ask, does he say nothing about plains and valleys? As was said above, valleys are those who descend to the depths and below nature, corrupting nature’s goods by depraved habits. Therefore understand the plains and mountains to be the devout, but valleys to be the ungodly. The Prophet rightly says nothing here about valleys, because he knew without doubt that the ungodly cannot possess true [Col. 0340B] joy: “The wicked have no joy,” says the Lord.

But if plains belong among the number of the righteous, why, I ask, is nothing said here of their joy and exultation, when it is written: “The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” (Ps. 117)?
