Yet it is one thing to rejoice moderately, or even greatly; quite another to surpass, in the joys of one’s exultation, the bounds of human capacity; and, sporting in the manner of rams or lambs, to make particular leaps of the kind I have described, and, going beyond the mind, transcend human things. But because plains do not surpass the level of the active life in their manner of living, so they do not deserve to surpass the ordinary measure of human life in their manner of exulting. Rightly, therefore, such exultation as is mystically described here is attributed to mountains and hills alone, when it is said: “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills [Col. 0340C] like lambs of the flock.”

Here, as you hear, he mentions three things: rams, sheep, and lambs. Among animals of this sort rams undoubtedly hold the highest place, sheep the middle, and lambs the lowest. Let us therefore consider rams, sheep, and lambs on one side, and mountains, hills, and plains on the other; and we shall see that three correspond to three by a certain relation of likeness. In comparison with those above, plains hold the lowest place, hills the middle, and mountains the highest. Therefore, when it was said that mountains leap like rams, it would seem to follow that hills should be said to leap like sheep: for both hold the middle place in their own kind, just as lambs and plains hold the lowest. Why, then, are hills said to leap not like sheep, but like lambs of the flock?

But if we wish to understand more fully the sense of these words, we must attend more carefully to the particular character of the proposed comparison. By the animals mentioned above, it seems to me, is signified that threefold hierarchy of angels described by that great theologian, blessed Dionysius the Areopagite. For, as we know, he divides the whole multitude of heavenly spirits, distinguished into nine orders, into three hierarchies, assigning three orders to each: seraphim, cherubim, and thrones to the first; dominions, virtues, and principalities to the second; powers, archangels, and angels to the third.

[Col. 0341A] By rams, therefore, which, as was said above, hold the highest place among animals of their kind, is understood the chief and highest hierarchy of the heavenly orders; by sheep, the middle hierarchy; and by lambs, the lowest of all. We call highest of all that which is immediately united to God, enlightens the others, and is itself enlightened by none other than the sole hierarchy which creates all things. The middle hierarchy both enlightens and is enlightened. The lowest of all, having none beneath it to enlighten, is illuminated only by those above. We have now heard what we should understand concerning this flock and this distinction of ranks. Let us therefore seek spiritual and super-heavenly leaps in spiritual and super-heavenly flocks.

[Col. 0341B] What, then, is it for them to make leaps proper to their kind, except for them to go beyond themselves and ascend in contemplation to what is above them? When the orders of the highest hierarchy ascend above themselves in contemplation, they find nothing but that substance which creates all substances. For them, then, to make certain leaps is to see, without any mirror, the magnitude of that supreme essence in itself. For among them there is found a twofold mode of contemplating that magnitude. At one time it is seen through a mirror; at another without a mirror; and they perceive how wonderful and utterly incomprehensible it is, now in itself, now in created things placed beneath it. To behold divine power or wisdom as wonderful in themselves [Col. 0341C] is, for them, to go upon level ground. But to contemplate and marvel at the great works of that same power or wisdom in lower orders is to descend, not to make leaps.

From this it is plainly evident that for rams to make certain leaps in their exultation is nothing other than, as we have said, to see without a mirror and rise to a pure and simple manifestation of God (*theophany*). But when the orders of the middle hierarchy, like those of the last, ascend above themselves, they can indeed use a mirror, because above themselves they find orders of higher dignity, from which they rise fittingly enough into admiration of divine wisdom and power. Yet they too are accustomed to use simple contemplation, but for them this is flying rather than making leaps. For one who makes a leap does not go far from the place where he stands; whereas we know that flight ordinarily occurs in quite another way.

Since, therefore, those orders of spirits signified by rams use only simple contemplation in their, so to speak, leaps; and since the remaining orders, signified by lambs and sheep, never use anything but speculation in their leaps, the Psalmist rightly says: “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.” By mountains, as was said above, we understand contemplative persons, and by hills speculative persons. Thus, for mountains to leap in the manner of rams is nothing other than for contemplative persons, through ecstasy of mind, to attain the highest truth [Col. 0342A] by naked and open vision and see, as it were, face to face. And for hills to leap in the manner of sheep or lambs is nothing other than for speculative persons, through ecstasy of mind, to rise by speculation into admiration of that same truth.

It should certainly be noted that there are two kinds of speculation: one arising from wonder at bodily things, the other from wonder at spiritual things. This latter kind alone imitates the leaps and joyful dances of supermundane rams or sheep. If, therefore, in the hills mentioned above we understand spiritual persons, for them to make spiritual leaps and dance in the manner of intellectual lambs or sheep is nothing other than to attend to the heavenly spirits which they truly behold above themselves, [Col. 0342B] and from this spectacle rise into admiration of the Godhead by wonderful and unfamiliar movements of joy.

But since it is common to intellectual sheep and lambs to play with, so to speak, speculative leaps, why, I ask, does he say that hills leap like lambs, not like sheep, when he could have said this truly as well? Observe the wonderful reasoning: in comparing mountains with rams he said what he could say truthfully; but in comparing hills with sheep he passed over what was likewise true, lest someone should attempt to interpret such a comparison not merely as likeness but as equality—thinking that the first rank of human beings corresponds equally to the first rank of angels, and the second to the second. Therefore the Prophet passed over what was not said in order to remove the suspicion of equality, so that what he did say may be understood as said on account of likeness.

Let us briefly recapitulate, if you please, what we have said more fully. We have said that by mountains we understand contemplative persons, and by hills speculative persons. We have said that by rams we understand seraphim, cherubim, and thrones; by lambs, powers, archangels, and angels. Therefore we sing concerning mountains and hills of this kind: “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.” Let us consider, then, if we can, what a privilege and grace, what excellence and glory it is for the effort of human frailty to rise, by a kindred likeness, to that height of angelic joy [Col. 0342D] and to attain it—though seldom, swiftly, and as if through ecstasy of mind—by certain wonderful and momentary leaps of contemplation or speculation.

O blessed soul, truly happy and greatly to be glorified, to which it is granted from above, even briefly during this time of pilgrimage, to share in those wondrous joys of cherubim and seraphim; to taste those blessed delights of inward and eternal sweetness; and, amid the weariness of this wretched flesh, to receive certain firstfruits from that fullness of immensity. The memory of such tasting ought to touch our heart, penetrate the innermost places of the mind, transform affection, and pierce desire through and through, when daily we sing or ponder: “The mountains leaped like [Col. 0343A] rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.” May our heart grow warm with desire for this expectation; may the spirit glow and the soul burn in prayer and psalmody. “The mountains leaped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.” Would that we might sing wisely as often as we sing: “The mountains leaped,” and so forth.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 117

[Col. 0343]

[Col. 0344A] “The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.” Having said, “the voice of exultation,” the Prophet fittingly added at once, “and salvation.” For those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things also have their own joy, though perverse. You may see people living perversely: some rejoicing, others grieving. But whether their voice is one of joy or grief, it is not a voice of salvation but of perdition.

Likewise, among people of good conduct, one may see some rejoice while others sorrow and weep. But why do they still suffer desolation and sorrow here, mourn and grieve, when it is written: “The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous”? Perhaps those still doing penance have not yet cleansed their conscience and have not yet attained righteousness. For the present, then, they have a voice of sorrow and salvation; at some time they will have a voice of exultation and salvation. Therefore sorrow and weep for the present, you who are such persons, for “your sorrow shall be turned into joy.”

These four voices should be noted and distinguished from one another: the voice of exultation and perdition in those who rejoice perversely; the voice of sorrow and perdition in those who grieve ruinously; the voice of sorrow and salvation in [Col. 0343C] penitents; and the voice of exultation and salvation in those who live perfectly. Rightly, therefore, it is said: “The voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.” Woe to those who begin to weep here and never cease weeping in the future. Likewise, woe to those who exult for a time, only to mourn forever. Woe, I say, to those who know neither the joys of the present life nor those of the life to come. But a double woe belongs to those who always mourn both the goods they lost here and the evils they find there after departing from here. Happy too are those who mourn in time so that they may rejoice in eternity. Happy too—and indeed far happier than these—are those who in time taste beforehand that in which they will rejoice eternally. Thus, “the voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.”

“In tents,” he says. Therefore the righteous dwell in tents, not in [Col. 0343D] houses, because they who seek the city to come have no abiding city here, and set their minds on the things above, not on things upon the earth. We know that the tents of soldiers are fortifications; we too, whose life is warfare upon earth, ought to be soldiers and not lie numb in idleness. But we must carefully consider how cautiously [Col. 0344A] and how vigorously we must fight, since our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against the spiritual powers of wickedness in the heavenly places.

Righteousness is a very precious thing, and one that quickly arouses the envy of adversaries and fiercely inflames their hatred against us. For this is the issue of the battle; this is the cause of victory. We fight against evil spirits in order to keep righteousness inviolate; they fight against us, not in order to acquire it for themselves, but forcibly to take it away from us. They readily presume victory over our weakness because we carry this treasure in earthen vessels. But perhaps they give too little attention to the fact that we are not confident in ourselves but in the help of him to whom we say: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113).

But perhaps you wonder—and not without reason—how battle and joy, the voice of gladness and the cry of combat, agree or can agree with one another. Whence, then, comes so great a gladness, except from frequent victory? Thus, “the voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous.” If you wonder, if you want something at which to wonder, marvel rather how one pursued a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight. Will you not also sing a new song to the Lord, and will not the voice of exultation and salvation be heard in your tent, when that promise of your God begins to be fulfilled in you: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand”? [Col. 0344C] Rightly, therefore, the voice of exultation and salvation is heard in the tents of the righteous.

How greatly, then, do you think they will rejoice in their homeland who are so glad in a foreign land? How great will be their joy in the house, who are so cheered in exile? What will they do in that tranquility of eternal life, whose joy so overflows on campaign? It overflows to such an extent that so great a joy can no longer be confined in silence, but comes forth into the open and bursts into voice—after the manner of vessels which, when they cannot receive more of the poured liquid, spill in every direction what is poured in above. So, indeed, when that oil of gladness has filled the little vessels of hearts, it pours itself out through the voice, and at once “the voice of exultation and salvation resounds in the tents of the righteous.”

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 118

[Col. 0343]

[Col. 0343D] “Take away from me reproach and contempt.” Reproach is guilt; contempt, punishment. Guilt is iniquity; punishment, mortality. Because of iniquity I have become reproachable; because of mortality I have become contemptible. [Col. 0344D] Desire makes me abominable; misery makes me vile. Therefore take away from me reproach and contempt. If you make me righteous, you take away reproach; if you make me blessed, you take away contempt: “Concerning the judgments of your righteousness.”

Some judgments of God condemn the reprobate; others justify the elect; others make blessed those who have been justified. The first are judgments of reprobation, the second of justification, the last of glorification. The condemning judgments are exercised in hell; the justifying in the world; the beatifying are in heaven. “Your judgments will help me”: judgments of vengeance, judgments of correction, judgments of reward. By a judgment of vengeance Judas was rejected; by a judgment of correction [Col. 0346A] Saul was blinded; by a judgment of reward humble David was raised to the kingdom. The judgment of vengeance gives those who stand fear of falling; the judgment of correction gives those who have fallen hope of rising again; the judgment of reward grants the perfect love for perseverance. Therefore, if that first judgment of God produces fear, the second nourishes hope, and the third kindles charity, it is rightly said of them: “Your judgments will help me.”

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 118

[Col. 0345]

[Col. 0345A] “Make your face shine upon your servant.” What, for those who love, could ever be sweeter or more delightful [Col. 0345B] than to be cherished by mutual affection and delighted by one another’s sight? Let them see everything, provided they do not see each other: all things horrify them, all things seem foul. Thus, in the manner of lovers, the holy soul, kindled by love of the heavenly King and held in suspense by longing for the celestial Bridegroom, cries out and says: “Make your face shine upon your servant”; and elsewhere: “Lord, God of hosts, restore us; show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79); and again: “My face has sought you; your face, Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26). You will find elsewhere too—though in different words—that nothing else is sought.

With how great a love, do you suppose, did he burn who, longing, so often sought the face of him against whom he had sinned, and, seeking, longed for it? “Make your face shine,” he says, “upon your servant.” As we have said, mutual [Col. 0345C] presence and a pleasing sight are welcome to lovers. It is delightful to love and to be loved. They desire to see and to be seen. But perhaps this bride of God, this beloved of God, desired to see but shrank from being seen? Then what is the meaning of her cry elsewhere: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41).

O what love, what confidence! Love, I say, for divine beauty; confidence in a beauty not alien but her own. Her love was so great that she says: “My soul fails for your salvation, and I have hoped beyond measure in your word” (Ps. 118); and elsewhere she declares: “My spirit has failed” (Ps. 142). Moreover, her confidence in her inner loveliness was so great that she believed it altogether impossible that she could be seen and not loved. Perhaps she had heard from her Bridegroom those sweet, loving words: [Col. 0345D] “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved; you are wholly beautiful, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4). Rightly, therefore, she desires to come and appear before the face of God, to whose beauty the Author of beauty himself bore witness.

For that holy and chaste soul knew that every kind turns toward its like. Like seeks like, and God certainly loves his own likeness. Do you too wish to be loved by your God, your Savior? Restore his image in yourself, and he will love you; renew his likeness, and he will desire you. For if you restore your native beauty, which he himself made according to his image and likeness, surely the King will desire your beauty, for he is the Lord your God; he is your friend; he is your beloved.

Yet what do we think this means: that she asks only that his [Col. 0346A] face be shown her, and no longer his back, but desires to see face to face? Has she then [Col. 0346B] forgotten what the Lord long before told Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 31)? It is evident, then, that if she were still living for this world, she would never have presumed to pray such things. I am mistaken if she herself does not testify to this elsewhere, saying: “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Ps. 43).

Why, then, is she not believed to be dead, though she is put to death all day long? Perhaps because she did not say, “We die,” but, “We are put to death all day long.” Yet we know that in God’s eyes it is often of greater merit to be repeatedly put to death than actually to die. Was not the death of the martyrs more precious in proportion as the punishment preceding death was more prolonged, when those wishing to die were not permitted to be killed? Does it not contribute to the increase of glory for those predestined to life that their bodily life does not fail in them without fierce struggle and bitter suffering?

David, then, is put to death so that he may at last die, and thus may somehow be found worthy to see God’s face in jubilation. For he knows that blessed is the people who knows jubilation. Therefore strive, according to the Apostle’s counsel, to “put to death your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3), so that you too may confidently say to God with the Prophet: “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Ps. 43). Put them to death, then—put them to death, I say—but in the daylight, so that all may be done in the light of discernment, lest the wheel of your deeds run beyond or short of the boundary of measure. Thus perhaps one who has died will be granted to see God’s face in jubilation.

O good Lord, gracious Jesus, let my soul too die the death of the righteous! For it is better for me [Col. 0346D] to die than to live. “For whoever loves his soul will lose it.” Let my soul therefore die, so that I may no longer be a merely natural person. For the natural person does not receive the things of God—how much less God himself? But let us return to the Prophet’s preceding words and examine them more closely: “Make your face shine,” he says, “upon your servant.”

Light illuminates the eye so that it may behold its own brightness; and without the benefit of light the eye does not perceive other things that are not lights. The Prophet therefore asks for divine light, that he may be able to know God himself in his light and rightly assess all else. For how greatly all temporal things, whether good or evil, are to be despised, and how much future things are to be loved or feared, is more quickly understood if these matters are weighed in [Col. 0347A] his light. Therefore let him say: “Make your face shine upon your servant, that I may see you and what is yours; seeing, may understand; understanding, may love. Make your face shine upon me. Show me your light; reveal, I beseech you, your wisdom.”

“Make your face shine,” then. Your face is light, and your light is face. Make your face shine, therefore. It is face because it beholds all things; it is light because it illumines all persons for the consideration of all things. Make your face shine, then, because this bodily eye of ours can see but cannot illuminate; while this bodily light, which can illuminate, cannot see. But your eye sees for itself and shines for others, because it is “the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world.” The eye, therefore, is light; but is it [Col. 0347B] only eye? Indeed, your ear also is light, because your whole face is light.

“Make your face shine,” therefore. In the face are sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch; and in you all this is your light, and all this is one light. You see in light, hear in light, taste, smell, and feel in light, because there are no shadows there, but all things shine clearly in light. “Make your face shine,” therefore, I pray.

You observe, I think, how greatly he presumes upon God’s goodness who asks that God’s face be shown to him. For, as we have said, every bodily sense is found in the face. What else, then, is it for God to show him his face than to pour full knowledge of himself into that person’s mind? “What?” you ask me. “Do we believe that God has these senses, though we know that he is incorporeal and invisible?” Why ask me? Attend to the Scriptures: “In every place,” it says, [Col. 0347C] “the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil” (Prov. 15): here is sight. “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Ps. 10): here is hearing.

What shall we say of the others—smell, taste, and touch? Do we not find examples for them? Is it not written concerning Noah’s sacrifice: “The Lord smelled an odor of sweetness” (Gen. 8)? Abraham boldly invites him to enter and taste a little; and the prophet declares: “The Lord put forth his hand and touched my mouth” (Jer. 1). Why should we still doubt things demonstrated by the authority of Scripture? Or perhaps we suppose that he lacks sensation because we do not comprehend how it belongs incorporeally to an incorporeal nature? “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” “He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, shall he not see?”

He sees, therefore, but invisibly, since nothing escapes his wisdom. He likewise hears, because the ear of his mercy is open to the prayers of those who entreat him. By our nostrils we distinguish the quality of odors; he, by justice, distinguishes the quality of merits. He tastes when, by his goodness, he delights in the glory of the blessed; to be touched is to have compassion on the misery of the afflicted. This is the Lord’s sensation: not fivefold, but one. And who is sufficient for this? Far be it from us to assert that he sees by one thing and hears by another; yet by wisdom he sees, by mercy he hears. But the things that are different among us are not at all different in him.

We must therefore believe that the things we have enumerated are not distinct in God, though, for our instruction, we distinguish them subtly: let five be set against five—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, all of which are in one face; wisdom, mercy, justice, goodness, and compassion, all of which are one face in God. To understand all this is to advance in the knowledge of him.

Therefore let the Prophet say, let him say: “Show me your wisdom, lest I go astray; reveal your mercy, lest I despair; teach me your justice, that I may not presume; make your goodness known to me, that I may love you in your gifts, which are my goods; make your compassion known to me, lest I fail under my evils, your chastisements.” [Col. 0348B] If you show all this, you show me your face, because all this pertains to the knowledge of you. And now, I beseech you, Lord, make your face shine upon your servant.

Why, however, did he not rather say, “Let your face shine upon me,” but instead desires that your face be illumined for him? It is indeed light, as we have argued above; yet it does not shine for all, because “this light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” Why, then, does he not ask this inaccessible, inextinguishable light rather to shine upon him, since it did not need to be illumined? Perhaps that which burned in itself did not shine for the Prophet, and he seeks that it be kindled for him by grace—a light which he grieved to have extinguished in himself through fault. Or perhaps, because he knows this suits his weakness, he asks that the divine light grow gradually for him.

[Col. 0348C] When we kindle a fire, we see it gradually grow into flames. So indeed, so it ought to be: the brightness of divine light must dawn upon us little by little, so that our strengthened weakness may become accustomed to it gradually through intervals of time. Otherwise, if it should suddenly appear all at once to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, it would extinguish rather than illuminate the eye of reason.

Therefore let him say, let him say: “Make your face shine upon your servant.” Yet I wonder whether it was not night or winter when he sought the divine fire to be kindled for him. Perhaps a night of ignorance surrounded him and the torpor of negligence held him fast. These are two great evils: error and torpor. In fire are found two things, brightness and heat: brightness against error, heat against torpor. [Col. 0348D] He rightly seeks divine fire who is ashamed to be overcome by them.

It is indeed a good fire to burn and shine in desire for God: to believe and to desire. It is a very good fire to understand and love, to see and rejoice. It is a good fire, I say, to shine through knowledge, burn through love, glow through affection, and gleam through understanding. Therefore, that he may love much and understand much, let him pray and say: “Make your face shine upon your servant.”

O who will grant to me—wretched, cold, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death—who, I say, will grant that I may be warmed by this fire and illumined by it, so that I may somehow at last please God in this light of the living and see the will of the Lord all the days of my life? Truly the light is sweet, and it is delightful for the eyes to see [Col. 0349A] the sun: that sun, I say, into which angels long to gaze. O good and gracious Jesus, what joy can there be for me, who sit in darkness and do not see the light of heaven? Truly I confess that my heart has been troubled, my strength has abandoned me, and the light of my eyes—even that—is not with me. My eyes have grown weak from want of this light.

O apostles of Christ, O disciples of Christ, blessed are the eyes worthy to see what you see! For to you light has risen in darkness for the upright in heart—the Lord, merciful and compassionate. “Walk while you have the light.” I know, I know, Lord, that “in the light of your countenance they shall walk; and in your name they shall rejoice all day, and in your righteousness they shall be exalted.” I believe, indeed, that some “wandered in the wilderness” [Col. 0349B] and “found no way to a city of habitation” because the Dayspring from on high had not yet visited them, to guide their feet into the way of peace.

Where do you hasten, miserable people? Do you not know that it is vain for you to rise before the light? Yet meanwhile let us pray that he may make his face shine upon us and have mercy on us. For as we flee with Elijah from the face of Jezebel—that is, from the pursuit of carnal enticement—a great road still remains until we come to Mount Horeb, namely, the height of contemplation. Therefore, to guide our feet into the way of peace, make your face shine, I beseech you, Lord, upon your servant.

What is this, David? Do you call yourself, name yourself, a servant? Is what even friends scarcely deserve to receive granted here to servants? “Truly,” he says, [Col. 0349C] “I know that I love, because I love my Lord; nevertheless I remember that the Lord said to me: ‘You are my son.’ Yet I do not wish to call myself your friend; I do not wish to call myself his son. For one who wishes to ask great things without merits should at least remember to humble himself greatly. And now I truly confess myself his servant—not, however, merely by the right of my created condition, nor only from the obligation of necessity, but also by the intention of my will.

“For some are made servants by their very birth; others are consigned to servitude by the necessity of war; others charity, mistress of humility, subjects to service. I shall serve my Creator by the right of my condition; I shall obey my King out of reverence for his majesty; I shall submit to my Savior out of the obligation of love.” I understand how much voluntary [Col. 0349D] service can avail with him; and therefore, asking great things, I humbly recall the service of my humility and say: “Make your face shine upon your servant.”

I think no one now doubts that one vigorously frees himself from the slavery of sin who does not hesitate to call himself God’s servant. “No one can serve two masters.” But “whoever commits sin is the servant of sin.” It follows, then, that we should believe such a person not to be enslaved to sin but to resist it, so that he may truthfully assert himself to be God’s servant. Let him therefore say: “Make your face shine upon your servant.”

“Upon your servant”: you observe, I think, that he judges it unworthy to place this light under a bushel; rather, after the likeness of this bodily light, he places it on high, or like the sun, which shines better from above. Woe to those who set before this light—not, I say, themselves, but their possessions—[Col. 0350A] and who will one day lose both themselves and their possessions, and perish without end. For if this bodily light is rightly placed in an elevated position, what wonder if not only our possessions but even our soul itself is despised in admiration of the inner light? Let him therefore say: “Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your ordinances of righteousness.”

It must be known that to exist is one thing, to be righteous another, and to be blessed something far different. Existence we receive from creation; righteousness is granted through sanctification; blessedness we hope for in recompense. Therefore one who knows that he exists, but perhaps knows himself to be insufficiently righteous, rightly seeks the manner of righteousness, on which, he does not doubt, the measure of glorification depends.

Consider three works: the works of creation, the works of redemption, and the works of glorification. [Col. 0350B] Concerning those first works, namely creation, the philosophers of the nations inquire and dispute, but they have failed while searching with scrutiny. “How long, vain children of men, lying children of men, how long will you love vanity and seek falsehood?” “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” says our Ecclesiastes to you (Eccl. 1): learned and puffed up—but are you blessed? Rather, “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanities and false madness.” Perhaps this is the portion of their paternal inheritance that falls to them; but “my portion, O Lord, I have said, is to keep your law. Teach me, therefore, your ordinances of righteousness.”

Distinguish, then, creations, justifications, and glorifications. The investigation of the first may be shared even by those to be condemned; instruction in the second is granted [Col. 0350C] to those being justified; knowledge of the last will be given, but to those made blessed. Let the wise of this world therefore go—vain as the things they seek are vain. Let them seek and find things whose attainment will never make them blessed. Yet let them hear that God will destroy all the wise of Babylon, making foolish the wisdom of this world.

The Prophet, then, desiring to be justified, seeks ordinances of righteousness, because he knows that this is the way to true blessedness. Perhaps it is sufficient for angels, because they are holy, to know God’s righteous ordinances; but one who is a sinner needs to learn those ordinances in order that he may be justified. Recall the things which Jesus, the good teacher, taught when he went up the mountain and sat before his disciples, opening his mouth as they sat around him: [Col. 0350D] “Blessed are the poor in spirit; blessed are those who mourn; blessed are those who hunger; blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5).

Certainly, we know well that angels have not learned these things through experience even to this day, though we do not doubt that these same things belong to God’s righteous ordinances. We confess that what angels, we believe, grasp by understanding, they wholly lack by experience. For David did not desire merely verbal instruction in the ordinances of righteousness, but instruction in the very manner in which Jesus—who could never be ignorant of anything—“learned obedience from the things which he suffered,” obedience which he had not previously known through experience at all.

Let him therefore say: “Teach me your ordinances of righteousness: me,” he says, “not the devil, not an angel.” For the former, once rejected, ought not to be formed by these things; [Col. 0351A] the latter, perfected in good, has no need to be exercised in them. Let him seek these ordinances who needs and can be justified, not those of whom one can never become righteous and the other can never become unrighteous.

I do not pass over without wonder the fact that he asks to be instructed not by a human being, not even by an angel, but by God. Do we suppose that he understood above all his teachers and disdained further instruction from them? But let him himself be questioned about this; let him himself, by his answer, satisfy us who doubt about him: “How sweet are your words to my palate,” he says, “more than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 119). Surely they are “more desirable than much gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.” Therefore he who calls the Lord’s words sweeter plainly indicates that those things to which he prefers them by comparison are sweet. Let us now see what these are, to which he rightly gives the Lord’s words precedence. First, however, let us consider what that utterance is to which he subordinates those four things.

“I shall hear,” the same Prophet says elsewhere, “what the Lord God speaks in me, for he will speak peace to his people” (Ps. 84). Perhaps this is the utterance for which we were seeking: his speech, his inspiration, or the anointing that teaches us concerning all things. Now let us consider gold, stone, and the other things he has named.

The one who shines through eloquence glitters like gold; and the one who suffers persecution is like a very precious stone, provided it is for righteousness’ sake. The honeycomb, containing honey beneath wax, is truth hidden beneath allegory; in honey pure sweetness is found, and the mind is refreshed with wonderful sweetness by angelic consolation. He sets God’s utterances above all these when he says that they are more desirable than much gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and honeycomb.

[Col. 0351C] It is as though he said openly: “In Holy Scripture I discover what I ought to do; in human beings I see what I ought to imitate; from angelic revelation I understand what I ought to practice. Yet I know all this much better, much more clearly, and far more sweetly through divine inspiration. Therefore I confidently declare concerning my God’s utterances that they are more desirable than much gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and honeycomb.”

Yet one may observe what I think of those things which I do not hesitate to compare with gold and stone, honeycomb and honey. Let gold or stone, by comparison, teach how brightly their instruction shines for me; let honey or honeycomb, if questioned, answer how sweetly it tastes to me. Nevertheless, however brightly they may shine and however sweetly they may taste, I despise them in comparison with a greater brightness and more abundant sweetness.

That grace, then—that grace of my God’s inward inspiration, which unspeakably surpasses all the foregoing things—I seek with groans and sighs; I seek it by sighing, because its speech is certainly sweeter, its teaching easier, its meaning more subtle, and its instruction more pleasing. To it I rightly say: “Teach me your ordinances of righteousness.”

Yet by the aforesaid four—gold, stone, honeycomb, and honey—we may not inappropriately understand the fourfold sense of the divine Scriptures: namely, the moral and anagogical, the historical and allegorical. Yet the Prophet did not hesitate to prefer the Lord’s utterances—that is, the teachings of divine inspiration—to all these. [Col. 0352A] For one who works in gold is like one who, by exhortation, builds up morals; one who commends the shining brilliance of gems is like one who, by discourse, displays the splendor of heavenly rewards; one who is satisfied with honeycomb is like one who probes the depths of mysteries; and one who distributes pure honey to guests is like one who expounds truth without covering to eager hearers.

In these four, unless I am mistaken, the whole sequence of the divine Scriptures is woven together; in these consists every teaching of human beings and angels. Yet the infusion of divine inspiration rises above them all, as does his spiritual and invisible anointing, which teaches us concerning all things. Therefore David, breaking forth in a cry of praise for that which he tasted in his heart, says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb! O to whom it has been granted sincerely to declare, from the heart to sing: ‘How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth; more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and honeycomb!’”

“Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue.” O to whom it has been granted ever to experience what that Spirit of the Lord is who is sweeter than honey, even to “taste and see how sweet the Lord is”! O who will grant me such a teacher, one who does not so much wound as anoint his disciples, nor so much prick as oil them, because “his anointing teaches us concerning all things”?

Why should I still have teachers who do not instruct the mind unless they first tear [Col. 0352C] the flesh? Enough, Lord, enough are the wounds inflicted by the robbers who stripped me and, after inflicting wounds, went away leaving me half dead. But behold, our teachers still add iniquity to their iniquity, adding blows to wounds and selling words in exchange for blows. Let them go, let them go; let our teachers depart, let them depart—indeed, our collectors, but truly our vain and mad torturers, teaching and despising.

I seek him; I desire him who may anoint me by teaching and teach me by anointing. Look, Lord, consider, and touch my body, and you will know that from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no health in it. Then you will plainly recognize that there is need, not of a sore, but of an anointing. And now, Lord, I beseech you, in your mercy pour [Col. 0352D] your anointing into our senses.

For, to confess the truth, my skin has dried and shriveled; and not only this, but my bones have dried like ashes. “I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up.” You see, Lord, how everything is dry and parched—heart, skin, and bones. What remains except that your anointing be poured into them? Dry skin, dried-out skin, cracks when it is stretched and crackles when it is touched. Behold, Lord, you see that “I have become like a wineskin in frost.” It is easier, then, for it to burst than to be stretched unless this exceedingly dry wineskin is first anointed.

For, as you yourself said, people do not put new wine into old wineskins, otherwise the wineskins burst and the wine is spilled. And now I pray, Lord: anoint this wineskin with the anointing [Col. 0353A] of your mercy; anoint it, I say, and renew it, and then you will put new wine into a new wineskin. What else does your servant now await from you, this wretched little man, except that oil may make his face cheerful and wine gladden his heart? First, then, anoint with the oil of mercy; afterward fill with the wine of wisdom.

O how greatly he abounded in ointment who received it on the head, whence it descended to the hem of his garment! But I, for lack of this ointment, am dry and wasting away. How much, brother, do you suppose you have received from the oil of your God; how much do you owe my Lord? Perhaps you will say: “A hundred jars of oil.” Why do you have such an abundance of oil? Go, sell it and pay your creditors; distribute it to the poor; let you and your brothers live on the remainder; indeed, give us also of your oil. Truly, I confess, I have only a little oil in the flask with which I may be anointed. Send me some of your oil. Hear more plainly what I mean: weep and pray for me, and then I shall truly confess that you have anointed me.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 118

[Col. 0353]

[Col. 0353A] “Streams of waters have flowed from my eyes, because they [Col. 0353B] have not kept your law.” In time of drought farmers commonly lead out the channels of springs to water the land, lest, dried out by excessive aridity, it be unable to multiply the seeds entrusted to it. In imitation of them, while the rain of graces delays in descending, David does not neglect to pour the flood of tears upon the fruits of his works.

I think that, because some fault of his required it, God had at that time commanded his clouds not to rain; and consequently all things had dried up through drought, so much so that elsewhere he declares: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21). Was he not awaiting the rain of inward infusion when he cried with groaning: “My soul is as land without water before you” (Ps. 152)? Since, therefore, he did not deserve to have at will the rain of heavenly infusion, he strives to water his land, now dry and now refusing fruit, with the spring of tears.

Already the vein of compunction is led out; already the abundance of weeping is divided into many streams. One for whom it is enough to cultivate some single virtue, for whom it is enough to acquire a particular gift, needs not so much to lead out streams of tears as simply to bring them forth. For one who has chosen only one thing in particular directs the whole force of grief toward it. But one who expands the land of his heart with a manifold harvest of virtues now strives to water this seed of grace, now that; and then he will be able to sing: “Streams of waters shall flow from my eyes.”

Without doubt, water is then led out when, in alternating turns, now this fault and now that is washed away by weeping; when tears are shed in turn now for this grace, now for that. [Col. 0353D] One leads out water who weeps now for his own sins, now for those of others; water is led out when each is compuncted now by his own misery, now by another’s. One divides water who sometimes mourns evils he has committed and sometimes good things that he foolishly neglected. Water is divided when one mourns alternately out of fear of hellish torments and out of longing for heavenly joys.

Yet it must be understood that water rising in elevated places is readily directed, according to the intention of the one leading it, down to irrigate whatever low-lying places are desired. But water flowing in the depths does not rise to irrigate higher places. So likewise the stream of desires which runs in low things is not raised to seek lofty things; and [Col. 0354A] one who desires only earthly things does not know how to sigh for heavenly things.

[Col. 0354B] I say still more: for whom is it enough merely not to perish, when he groans and weeps over an idle word or a superfluous thought? Do you too wish, after the Prophet’s likeness, to lead out this health-giving water? Remember to desire lofty things; remember nevertheless to think humbly of yourself. Then you will make streams of compunction run down from the hills of your desires into the valley of your lowliness.

When, therefore, the water of compunction drips from the highest mountains, the earth will rejoice as it sprouts amid its drops; your fields will be filled with abundance; the lovely places of the wilderness will grow rich, and the valleys too will abound with grain. Then indeed you shall eat the labor of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you. You will sing with a joyful heart: “Let the peoples give thanks to you, O God; let all the peoples give thanks to you. The earth [Col. 0354C] has yielded its fruit.”

“But what kind of fruit?” you ask. “The fruits of the Spirit,” says the Apostle, “are peace, patience, long-suffering,” and the rest (Gal. 5). What kind of fruit, brother, are truth, charity, justice, and mercy believed to be? How greatly, do you suppose, does the mind abound in joy when it sees that, after the cultivation of discipline, truth has sprung up from the earth? And that joy will be increased when it begins to hope that “righteousness and abundance of peace” will arise in its days. What do you think of a land from which such fruit springs? Rightly, “its fruit shall rise above Lebanon.”

O what a fruit, how precious: truth, righteousness, and abundance of peace! It is evident, I think, that one must lead out one’s water and weep separately over each thing, if one desires to abound not in one of these fruits but in all of them. But if you are unable to water all these with tears, ask him “who brings forth winds from his storehouses, who brings clouds from the end of the earth, who makes lightnings for the rain.” For “the Lord will give goodness, and our land will yield its fruit.”

And if the rains of his goodness delay, do not cease, insofar as you are able, to lead out the waters of remembrance, that you may be able to sing and make melody from the heart: “Streams of waters have flowed from my eyes.” How many, do we suppose, are there today who have not yet received the grace of tears, who daily commit deeds to be wept over and are themselves much to be wept over, yet cannot weep at all? There are others who on the one hand magnify their sins and future punishments, while on the other hand they consider their few good deeds and then eternal rewards, so that at last they scarcely manage to break into tears. [Col. 0355A] These may indeed sing: “Waters have come forth from my eyes, because they have not kept your law.” Yet they cannot as yet truly chant: “Streams of waters have flowed from my eyes.”

But behold, there is someone so ashamed even of his slight negligence, so inflamed with longing for divine love, that he cannot hold back tears even when he wishes. For such a person, tears are not produced by effort; they themselves come forth abundantly. He does not need to bring forth water that seems ready to come out; rather, he must divide and direct that which flows out in abundance. If they come forth spontaneously, they are streams of waters and can be directed. But one who has not yet been able to bring them forth—when will he be able to direct them?

I would call that person a skillful director of waters [Col. 0355B] who has learned, at the discretion of his will, to weep whenever he wishes for whatever he wishes—now his own sins, now those of others. Yet he must see to it that only his eyes lead them out, so that he weeps only for what reason and discernment declare ought to be mourned. Water is then truly directed at the discretion of the eyes when the judgment of reason is followed by the affection of weeping.

Therefore, if tears come forth spontaneously, if they run freely according to the intention of their director, he may confidently sing: “Streams of waters have flowed from my eyes.” The same Prophet immediately adds the cause of such great weeping, saying: “Because they have not kept your law.”

O that it might someday happen to me that I should no longer need to weep for present sins but only for past ones; that no present fault may wound my conscience any longer, but only one already committed! But woe to me, wretched man, who must grieve and weep not only, Lord, because my eyes did not keep your law, but chiefly because they do not yet keep your law. Yet I think, brother, that nothing more restrains the mind from adding iniquity to iniquity, from daily heaping new sins upon old, than constantly remembering and frequently weeping for past sins.

I believe that one of this kind can sing: “Streams of waters have flowed from my eyes, because they have not kept your law.” In these words of the Prophet, it is evident, I think, what was the cause of the barrenness of which we spoke: when his soul became like land without water, so that he needed to pour out the water of tears abundantly and direct what had been poured out here and there, to irrigate all that land of his. This happened, surely, because the divine law was kept too unworthily.

I believe that, if he were still grieving over temporal things, if he were still weeping over carnal matters, he could not direct the waters of sorrow according to his purpose. For this is usually the difference between spiritual and carnal tears: spiritual tears are often directed, in accordance with the intention of the one who directs them, toward those things over which it is fitting to weep. Carnal tears, however, sweep people along with them like a torrent rather than following them. For when is a river which runs in low places said to reach the heights? And when is weeping which rises from base desires poured out for heavenly things? Will not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, and waters of similar streams pass through valleys amid mountains [Col. 0356A], and therefore be unable to be directed to irrigate higher ground? For those who are still carnal, loving carnal things, are unable indeed to be pierced with compunction for their sins; and when cause for grief over earthly matters arises, they cannot command themselves not to weep. Therefore, when weeping is shed against one’s will, what else can I call it but being carried away by a torrent? Yet my soul has very often passed through such a torrent. O Lord, let not the tempest of this water engulf me! What streams, I ask, flow past the land of the heart? Has the Lord yet magnified his dealings with you, drying up within you all the rivers of Ethan, turning rivers into desert, and the outlets of waters into thirst? Has he made his mercy wondrous to you, changing the hardness of your heart into pools of water [Col. 0356B], making within you the desert into pools of water and waterless land into outlets of waters? Drying up those former waters, as being carnal, and pouring out these latter waters, as being spiritual? Do you suppose that there has yet arisen within you a fountain of living water leaping up into eternal life, watering the mountains from its heights?

This one thing I know: if the vein of your springs rises in the heights of the mountains, and if the mind is perfectly pierced with compunction solely by desire for lofty rewards, it is easy to direct waters of this kind down the slopes of your humility, and to flood abundantly the valley of your lowliness with their irrigation on every side. If this is so, brother, you surely have reason to bless God from the fountains of Israel, who waters all things with waters. But enough has been said concerning the words, “My eyes have led forth streams of waters” [Col. 0356C]; let us now consider the cause of the weeping.

And let us learn from the example what we ought to do. “Because,” he says, “they have not kept your law.” For this law, unless I am mistaken, he prays elsewhere, saying: “Set before me, O Lord, the law, the way of your justifications, and I shall seek it always.” What, David—does the law of Moses not suffice for you, that you still seek for a law to be set before you? “No,” he says: not the law of Moses, which kills souls, but “the spotless law of the Lord, converting souls.” When Moses gave commandments to the peoples, he veiled his face; and therefore the commandment of Moses is obscure and darkens the eyes, whereas the commandment of the Lord is bright and enlightens the eyes. Certainly, if the law given through Moses had been sufficient, there would have been no need still to pray to the Lord that a law be set before me [Col. 0356D].

David therefore sought a law from the Lord; he received it and practised it, yet kept it with insufficient discernment. Therefore he says: “Streams of waters,” etc. One law is that of the flesh, another that of the mind; one is God’s, another the devil’s. And lest you suppose that I am establishing these distinctions from my own opinion, hear the Apostle carefully distinguishing the laws which we have mentioned: “I delight,” he says, “in the law of God according to the inward man. But I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and bringing me captive into the law of sin” (Rom. 7). Do you see how, in the first verse, he sets down the law of God by itself, while in the second he distinguishes three other laws, not only from that law but also from one another? For when he says, “I see another law in my members”—that is, the law of the flesh—he distinguishes the law which is in his members from that which he had called the law of God [Col. 0357A]; and when he adds, “resisting the law of my mind,” he shows it to be distinct from that as well. And when he further says, “bringing me captive into the law of sin,” he distinguishes the law of sin from both of these. The law of sin, moreover, is nothing other than the law of the devil.

Let us therefore distinguish these four laws: those of God, the devil, the mind, and the flesh. God’s law is to return good for evil. The devil’s law is to return evil for good. The law of the flesh is to repay evil with evil. The law of the mind is to return good for good. God’s law is to desire to benefit others freely; the devil’s law is to desire freely to harm them. The law of the mind is to do what is permitted; the law of the flesh is to do what one pleases. God’s law is charity; the devil’s law, iniquity; the law of the mind, equity; the law of the flesh, pleasure.

God’s law says: “Love your enemies; pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5). The devil’s law says: “Let us unjustly oppress the righteous man, because he is contrary to our works” (Wis. 2). The law of the mind says: “Tooth for tooth, eye for eye, life for life” (Exod. 21). The law of the flesh says: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. 22). The devil’s law is abominable; the law of the flesh contemptible; the law of the mind praiseworthy; God’s law desirable. The devil’s law is shameful; the law of the flesh dangerous; the law of the mind serviceable; God’s law glorious. I call God’s law glorious because it is especially, indeed solely, for this law that each person is crowned; and the devil’s law is rightly called shameful, because for it each person is punished with eternal disgrace. I call the law of the flesh dangerous because, gradually weakening the mind [Col. 0357C], it precipitates it into the devil’s law. I have rightly called the law of the mind serviceable because, gradually strengthening the soul, it raises it toward the law of God.

The Prophet had therefore overcome the devil’s law, because he hated every iniquity; he had likewise trampled underfoot the law of the flesh insofar as he despised bodily pleasure. Moreover, he had made great progress in the law of equity; but he grieved deeply that he was still far from perfect in the law of charity.

But perhaps I shall scarcely be believed in these matters unless they are confirmed by his own testimony. “I have hated and abhorred iniquity”: behold his victory over the law of iniquity. “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76): behold his contempt for pleasure. For the law of equity he confidently cries: “Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness [Col. 0357D], and according to my innocence which is upon me” (Ps. 7). Yet he lamented that he had not yet attained the summit of perfection in the law of charity, so that he says: “My eyes led forth streams of waters, because,” etc.

It is remarkable if you do not wonder why he did not prefer to say: “Because I have not kept your law.” But if he had said, “I have not kept it,” he would surely have blamed the will; and then how could that statement stand: “I have loved your law”? The fault is therefore interpreted as a fault of the eyes; the fault of the eyes alone is lamented. For concerning the service of his feet, he confidently sings to the Lord: “I have run in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart.” And concerning his hands he testifies, saying: “All day long I stretched out my hands to you” (Ps. 87). The same may easily be found concerning the ear and tongue [Col. 0358A], and the other members of the body. Here the eyes alone are reproved; for the eyes alone tears are shed. I do not maintain that he never sinned in the other members as well; rather, I carefully attend to what it is, and how, that he laments.

What then is it to lament the fault of the eyes, except to grieve with groaning because he had erred in discernment? The eye sins when the judgment of discernment errs. Many prefer private observances to common institutions, and abstinence to obedience, though it is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (1 Sam. 15). We had thought many things ought to be added concerning these eyes; but perhaps we reserve them to be said under another heading. For now, let us pursue what seems appropriate to say in the meantime.

“My eyes led forth streams of waters [Col. 0358B], because they have not kept your law.” He rebukes none of the other members here, but reproves the fault of the eyes with no small and grievous sorrow. The hand is not reproved, perhaps because it worked willingly; the tongue is not reproved, I suppose, because it spoke truth. He blamed only the eye, perhaps because it was dim in the discernment of judgment. For what else is it for the eye to stumble except to fall into some evil through a good but insufficiently discerning intention?

There are those who say that a work proceeding from a good intention cannot be evil. Then those who brought death upon the apostles acted rightly; for we read that it was written of them: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he offers service to God” (John 16). Do we therefore excuse the ignorance of the Jews, who, according to the Apostle, “have zeal, but not according to knowledge”? You glory in an evil deed because of a good intention. The Prophet weeps because he had erred in discerning; where the Prophet grieves, you rejoice; where the Prophet weeps, you laugh.

“How then,” they ask, “are we to understand what we heard from the mouth of Truth in the Gospel: ‘If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light’” (Matt. 6; Luke 11)? I hear here that the members of the body are commended by the purity of the eye—not its defects. I believe that blindness, deafness, dryness, insensibility, and the other bodily defects do not preserve the body; for neither the body nor a part of the body is what corrupts the body. Thus indeed [Col. 0358D] the good things of the virtues compose the body; evil works, being defects, corrupt or destroy it. Truth therefore does not commend evil works—which are neither the body nor part of the body—even if they are done, supposing they can be done, with a good intention. Rather, he intended to show that those things which truly constitute the body of virtues—that is, good works—are not good at all if they proceed from an evil intention. “For if your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark.”

“What then,” they ask, “does the angel mean when he says: ‘Have charity, and do what you will’?” Do we therefore suppose charity to be blind? But let us hear what the Apostle thinks of it: “Charity,” he says, “is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13 [printed: XVIII]). What, then—does charity fail to know what must be known, though the Apostle does not hesitate to call it the fulfilment of the law? Perfect charity gives full illumination; for one cannot perfectly love that of whose knowledge the mind remains in darkness. But there is no need to dwell longer on these matters, because just as charity in what is good can have only a good intention, so it is highly incredible that it can err in discernment. This, however, appears altogether credible: one who still errs in discernment is not yet perfect in charity; and one who does evil, whatever the intention, is by no means without fault. Nor should you suppose that only the eyes deserve blame when you judge good to be evil or evil to be good.

But in order that we may examine the fault of the eyes more carefully, let us first see what these eyes themselves are. There are certainly two eyes of the inner person, which everyone should strive to possess who hastens to run the way of God’s commandments with unoffending foot [Col. 0359B]. One is the eye of discernment; the other, the eye of circumspection. But let us first dispose of the left eye, namely circumspection—as the less worthy—so that we may have greater leisure to dwell on what must be said concerning the right eye, namely discernment.

There are some who call their past life to mind and judge themselves in those things which they have done badly or less well. They neglect the present and do not know how to foresee the future. Such persons do indeed look back, but they do not look around. Another carefully considers lest adversity break him or prosperity exalt him: prosperity, as it were, on the right; adversity, as it were, on the left. But one who attends only to the good and evil things immediately at hand often laments the past less than former guilt demands. Such a person, who looks at things placed beside him, is more rightly said to look than to look around; for *saepe* is sometimes used in the sense of *iuxta* (“beside”). But one who does not yet know how to look back is much less skilled in looking around.

Another is adorned with the eye of foresight, because he knows how to provide for the future; yet he makes little progress if he either despises the past or neglects the present. But if you turn your eye before and behind, to the right and to the left, by doing so you make a circle, not a sphere [Col. 0359C]. Add further that you must now raise your eyes upward and now cast them down to the depths; for it is good now to remember heavenly things, now those which are in hell, and now, sighing, to contemplate these and now those. For if you neglect to consider what is prepared for the wicked in hell, or, conversely, what is laid up for the good in heaven, you will undoubtedly be insufficiently fearful regarding the past, too little anxious about the present, and not at all provident about the future. Therefore, let it not suffice you to turn your eye around; but spread it everywhere in the likeness of a sphere.

If you look upon the form of heaven, you are certainly admonished to enclose the earth of your works within the circuit of your consideration. “But how,” you ask, “can I look simultaneously at the things around me—before and behind, right and left, above and below—and besides not neglect my own inward things, of which you have so far said nothing?” Indeed, only that Lamb whom Sacred Scripture describes as having seven eyes and seven horns is sufficient to consider all the things surrounding him at once [Col. 0360A]. But I was silent about the eye of inward inspection which you raise as an objection because I judged it superfluous to mention anything about it. For who could believe that the sun which illumines all other things has darkness within itself? So likewise, if the eye of circumspection diligently considers the things around it, reason much more does not permit it to be ignorant of the things within.

The ray of the eye, therefore, must first illuminate the place in which it stands, after the likeness of the sun; then, because it cannot attend to all surrounding things at once, it must attentively consider now these and now those. For if you could look at once upon what is before and behind, right and left, above and below, together with your own inward things, you would not employ one eye of circumspection: you would have seven. He alone can do this who sees all things in a single glance. He sees all things and can do all things who has seven eyes and seven horns. The eyes pertain to knowledge, the horns to power. Of the former it is said: “All things are naked and laid open before the eyes of God” (Heb. 4). Of the latter: “He has done whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 1). He is therefore rightly said to have seven horns, since there is no doubt that he can do all things.

But can you do likewise? Would that you had even one horn—would that you had one, so that you might rightly be called a son of unicorns! I think that for those for whom he has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant, it is for the present enough to have something by which they may resist and be able to fight against the devil. Can you renew the past, order the present [Col. 0360C], bring about the future, tread down hell, break into heaven—and do all this by your own strength? Surely not, I think, because you do not have seven horns, as does that Lamb to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given.

For the present, Lord, it is enough for me inwardly to have one horn, by which I may scatter my enemies to every wind. “For in you we shall scatter our enemies with a horn, and in your name we shall trample those who rise up against us.” Yet what a horn of freedom we should consider this to be: that we never, except willingly, bend the neck of the heart beneath sin! Though the whole host of demons clamour around us, though the whole world rage against us, it never strips our mind, fixed in God, of its own will. With God’s help, if you will, you too can have this horn [Col. 0360D]; but you cannot have the rest merely by willing, because you cannot do everything which you wish to do.

Since, therefore, we cannot exercise power in all that we wish, we must surely employ discernment. Each person must first discern what he can do, and then, among the things available to him, what is expedient. This is that eye of discernment which we called the right eye a little above. For what does it profit to recollect the past, look back upon the present, or foresee the future, unless you can discern in all these things what is good and what is evil? What, I ask, does it profit us that we look around upon our life, if we do not judge what it ought to be? Therefore, in order that the eye of circumspection may be useful, it must be assisted by the eye of discernment.

If the eye of circumspection tells you [Col. 0361A] that you have done this and that, the eye of discernment must declare what you have done well or badly in these matters. If circumspection reports the good and evil things which are imminent, discernment must provide counsel for both. If circumspection foresees what things, or how many, are available to you to do, discernment must add which things are expedient and how they should be done. Whenever the eye of circumspection looks back by contemplating heaven or hell, the eye of discernment must add by what merits each person attains the one or the other. When circumspection searches its inward things, discernment must judge what evil is deservedly ascribed to itself and what good to God.

Do you see how reason does not permit these eyes to be divided from one another among us in the discernment of matters, just as the sight of our bodily eyes, nature so ordaining, is in no way divided? Yet it must be known that negligence often steals upon the eye of circumspection, while ignorance lies in ambush for the eye of discernment. Sleep of sluggishness often closes the former; the mist of error frequently clouds the latter. For as often as someone neglects to look around upon his life, the eye of circumspection, as it were, falls asleep; and then the eye of discernment, as it were, grows dim when, through imprudence, one errs in discerning the things one sees [Col. 0361B].

There are two respects in which discernment is often deceived. It is often deceived in quality and frequently misled in quantity. One is deceived in quality who judges that what is good is evil, or believes that what is evil is good. Of such persons Isaiah says: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. 5). One is misled in quantity who, deceived, declares a thing to be greater or smaller than it is. The Prophet rebukes such persons when he says: “The sons of men are deceitful in the balances” (Ps. 61). For why is anything weighed in a balance except that its quantity or measure may be known?

One is deceived in quality who thinks brass to be gold, who takes glass for gems. One is deceived in quantity who, deceived, sells two weights of gold for one, or buys one from a seller for two. Since, therefore, we are almost always deceived in these two defects of unjust weighing, because we cannot manage this by ourselves, the Lord promises that he himself will order our life according to the balance of equity and the measure of the rule, saying: “I will rejoice and divide Shechem, and measure out the valley of the tents” (Ps. 59) [Col. 0361D]. “I will divide,” he says, “and I will measure”: division ensures that each person receives what he ought to have; measurement ensures that each receives only as much as he ought to possess.

Hence the Lord commands through Moses that every one of the children of Israel receive an inheritance by lot in the land of promise (Num. 33). Accordingly the Psalmist recalls it, saying: “He divided the land among them by lot, with the measuring-line of distribution” (Ps. 77). Then the people of God receive an inheritance according to measure, when every virtue extends itself according to the measure of equity. For virtue is nothing other than an ordered and moderated affection of the soul. It is ordered when it is directed to that which it ought to be; it is moderated when it is as great as it ought to be. When it is directed to something other than what is expedient, it sins in quality; when it is greater than it ought to be, it errs in quantity.

Therefore, in order that we may order and moderate the affections of our soul, we must first restrain disordered habits. Hence the same Prophet prefaces the sentence cited above, saying: “He cast out nations from before them,” and immediately adds: “and he divided the land among them by lot, with the measuring-line of distribution” (ibid.) [Col. 0362A]. First we cast out the nations—that is, undisciplined habits; afterward we bring the movements of the soul into order and incline them toward moderation. To divide the land with the measuring-line of distribution is nothing other than, in that which belongs properly to each virtue, to attend also to its measure.

Do you wish to see how great a caution must be employed, and how great discernment shown, in measuring the virtues? If frugality restrains itself below the proper measure, it casts itself into avarice; if generosity extends itself beyond measure, it pours itself out into prodigality. Some, under the pretext of necessity, by indulging excessively in food and drink, rashly stir up against themselves the wars of the flesh. Others, by afflicting the flesh with immoderate mortification, heedlessly destroy the support by which they might have been helped toward good. Countless things of this kind exist, in which people often cheat and are cheated, deceive and are deceived.

But you say to me: “Behold, I have now learned by experience that this eye of discernment which you called the right eye frequently affirms false things to be true for me; it often errs in judgment, and, discerning too little, causes me no small stumbling” [Col. 0362C]. And I answer you: if your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you. For it is better for you to enter into life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into Gehenna.

“What then,” you ask, “by what means, I pray, shall I, one-eyed, run the way of God’s commandments with unoffending foot—a way which even now, aided by the benefit of two eyes, I cannot complete without error?” Hear, then, what you ought to do, you who perhaps see with insufficient sharpness. He who gave you an eye has also provided you with an ear and a tongue. Therefore you have means to ask and to hear, if you do not deny that you have an ear and a tongue. Seek, then, the house of a seer, you who see little; from him you will hear what you ought to do and which way you ought to run. It is better for you to be led by the hand than to follow error of your own accord. It is therefore better for you to enter into life with one eye than, having two eyes, to be cast into Gehenna.

If, therefore, your right eye misleads you—if it utterly causes you to stumble—pluck it out and cast it away. With the left eye, as has been said, we look around upon our life; with the right, we judge what it is like or what it ought to be. But if it errs in discerning, it surely causes us to stumble. Therefore, if your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you. I do not remember having read anywhere that I ought to pluck out the left eye. This command is imposed regarding the right eye if you find in it the stumbling-block of error. Why is this? Because, I think, no one can know my own life better than I can, but another can order it with discernment far better than I can [Col. 0363A]. We must therefore entrust our life to the discernment of spiritual men, and especially of prelates, such as those to whom we know the Lord himself entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

## ANNOTATION ON PSALM 121

[Col. 0363]

[Col. 0363A] “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’” Adam addresses Eve; here Adam comforts Eve, saying: “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’” Adam no longer regards it as a great thing to return to his own house. For he does not say, “I rejoiced because we shall go into our house,” but after the miseries of a long exile he now trusts that he will arrive at the house of the Lord.

Do you wish to know who this Adam is, or who we say this Eve of his is? Understand reason by Adam; take affection by Eve. They are two: understanding and affection. They are also called soul and spirit—two, indeed, not in essence but in operation. The soul lives; the spirit discerns. Love belongs to the soul; knowledge, to the spirit. Therefore you have Adam, and you also have Eve. Adam was formed first; afterward Eve was made from Adam. For we must first prudently choose by reason what ought to be loved; then, according to the judgment of that choice, ardently love what ought to be loved. Let knowledge of the true therefore come first, and love of the just follow. First comes discerning, afterward loving.

The first discernment must be between good and evil. A second must follow between good and better; and then, from among the best things, let us choose what we ought rather to embrace in love [Col. 0363C]. For not all of us can do all things. Do you see how a certain portion, as it were, is selected from the whole Adam, from which Eve may be formed? For to discern good and evil is good; but to love evil and good is evil—or rather, to love both is impossible, though to know both is praiseworthy. And even among good things, because not everyone can do everything, a certain part is selected, from which Eve may be formed as Adam’s help.

For if Eve does not oppose Adam in the judgment of choice, she certainly makes him stronger in the knowledge of truth. Knowledge advances from love, just as love gains strength from knowledge. But if love does not support reason in the search for truth, the eye of discernment more swiftly grows dim; and then its help is turned to the opposite, when through it reason is cast down into the darkness of error. As often as Eve sends Adam from paradise into exile, she does so whenever affection entangles reason, cast down from the search for truth, in vain thoughts. O how often is Adam cast down from his house through Eve! O how often through Eve is he compelled to serve in a foreign house!

Adam’s house is truth; the devil’s house is vanity; God’s house is eternity—of whom it is said that he “inhabits eternity.” Of this house, assuredly, the text speaks here when Adam addresses his Eve: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.” Adam returns to his house when he returns from devotion to vanity to the search for truth; but he enters God’s house when, after truth has long been sought and scarcely found, he is carried beyond himself into the contemplation of eternity.

[Col. 0364A] Adam, where are you? Where do you find yourself? In paradise or in exile? Adam, I say, where are you? Consider what you are thinking, and you will discover where you are. If you think vanity, you are in vanity; if you love vanity, you are vanity. And now I no longer say to you, “Adam, where are you?” but I say, “Adam, who are you?” I believe that you are ashamed and blush to confess it.

Let the Prophet speak, who does not flatter you. “Every living man,” he says, “is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38). Not merely vanity, but utter vanity: the vanity of mutability, the vanity of mortality [Col. 0364B], the vanity of iniquity—because every living man is utter vanity. In this threefold vanity man serves as in exile; in it the devil reigns as in his own house. For, cast out from the house of eternity, the devil erects for himself a structure out of the multiplicity of vanity. From the vanity of mutability he extends for himself a portico; from the vanity of mortality he raises a house; from the vanity of iniquity he establishes for himself a bedchamber.

See, man, whose servant you are, if you still love vanity. Why do you make a homeland out of exile? Why do you enjoy a prison as though it were a house? “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name.” Or else, I beseech you, Lord, take my soul from me. For my soul is weary of my life, because every living man is utter vanity. Therefore, Lord, as Tobit says, it is better to die than to live, because every living man is utter vanity.
