Is it not for your sake, Lord, that “we are put to death all day long,” that at last we may someday die, because every living man is utter vanity? Therefore let my soul die, I beseech you, Lord, with the death of the righteous, so that I may no longer be a living man belonging to another, because every living man is utter vanity.

Bring me back, Lord, meanwhile into my own house, that you may at last bring me into your house. First establish me in love of truth; afterward raise me to the joy of eternity. “Turn away my eyes lest they see vanity,” and deliver me from the foreign house. “Send forth your light and your truth,” and I shall be in my own house. “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” [Col. 0364D], and I shall be in your house. If you call me back meanwhile to my own house, I shall hope one day to enter your house, so that I too may sing: “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’”

“I rejoiced,” he says, “at the things that were said to me.” As I hear it, he still rejoiced in hope, not yet in the thing itself. For he does not say, “at the things that were given to me,” but rather, “at the things that were said to me.” May I too hear what the Lord my God speaks within me—if perhaps he may say something also to me, if perhaps he may promise something like this to me. Speak, therefore, Lord, for your servant hears. What do you say to me, Lord? Your speech is your inspiration. Inspire in me, therefore, I beseech you, through your Holy Spirit, confidence concerning this matter; and let not my spirit arrogate this to itself through pride. Let this be said to me by you [Col. 0365A], not fashioned by me; and then I too shall sing: “I rejoiced at the things that were said: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’”

“We shall go,” he says, speaking as Adam; he did not wish to say, “I shall go.” Addressing his Eve, he did not wish to say, “You shall go”; rather, he said, “We shall go.” It was said above that we understand reason by Adam, affection by Eve, and eternity by the house of God. Knowledge belongs to Adam; love, to Eve. If you think of eternal things but do not love eternal things, Adam indeed goes, but alone. If you know eternal things and desire eternal things, Adam goes indeed, but not alone. To know the things above and to love the things above is for Adam and Eve to go together. Adam ought to contemplate; Eve ought to rejoice with him. If you see and rejoice, Adam and Eve are together. “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’”

[Col. 0365B] The Apostle boasts that he was caught up as far as the third heaven (2 Cor. 12); this man, as you hear, hopes that he will go there. The first heaven is subtlety of understanding; the second heaven, brightness of justice; the third heaven, sublimity of glory. In the first heaven is contemplation of truth; in the second, love of equity; in the third, the fullness of eternal delight. Of the first and second heavens the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in the heavens” (Phil. 3); he does not say “in heaven,” but “in the heavens,” lest you understand only one. Of the third he says: “I know such a man caught up as far as the third heaven” (2 Cor. 12).

To be caught up and to dwell are very different. One dwells in the first and second heavens, but is caught up into the third. If he were not in the first heaven—that is, in certainty of truth—he would not be Catholic; if he did not abide in the second heaven—that is, in steadfastness of justice—he certainly would not be righteous. In the first he receives the gift of being faithful; in the second he works to become good; in the third it will someday be given him to remain blessed. In the first ignorance is enlightened; in the second concupiscence is extinguished; in the third misery is swallowed up.

For the present, then, he can dwell in the first and second heavens; he can be caught up to the third, but cannot go there. We are admitted to the third as often as, through ecstasy of mind, we enjoy in some measure that inner and eternal sweetness. Then the mind of anyone who is perfect is caught up to the secrets of the third heaven, when it is absorbed in the sea of that eternal happiness and made drunk by the torrent of superheavenly delight to such an extent [Col. 0365D] that it not only loses all outward things from memory, but even comes into forgetfulness of itself. Returning afterward to itself, it cries out with the Apostle and says: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (ibid.).

What the Apostle, therefore, calls the third heaven, this writer, unless I am mistaken, intends to understand as the house of the Lord [Col. 0366A], when he says: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.” Yet the Apostle testifies that he was caught up, while this man, as we said above, hopes and declares that he will go. It is far more excellent and far more worthy to be able to go by oneself than to be caught up and carried by another. For the entrance of one who is caught up by another, so long as he is not permitted to be able to enter by himself—his entrance, I say—does not depend upon the desire of the one wishing to enter, but upon the grace and favour of the one wishing to carry him. For if I can enter by myself, I shall indeed enter whenever I wish. But one whom another must still carry cannot enter, even when he wishes, unless the carrier is pleased to do so.

What, then, shall we say to this? Was this man able to obtain something which the Apostle did not deserve to obtain? But the Apostle rejoices over the past, whereas this man speaks of the future. The Apostle glories in the reality; this man rejoices in hope. Hence he says: “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord.’”

Brother, if the light of truth shines about you, you possess the first heaven; if the flame of charity sets you ablaze, you dwell in the second; if you have sampled some taste of inward sweetness, you have been admitted to the third—provided, however, that you have tasted that the Lord is sweet, so that you may proclaim with the Prophet: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you.” Observe what he says: “If you have tasted,” he says. I believe that only a taste is given to those who are still being carried away. For after they are able to go by themselves, they will be made drunk: “They shall be made drunk, O Lord, with the abundance of your house” [Col. 0366C], “when you give them drink from the torrent of your delight.” Brother, tasting is one thing, drinking another. We receive a taste in order to experience sweetness; drink will be given for the abundance of intoxication. If you have received the taste, you will confidently await the drink. Therefore you will sing with joy; you may chant with confidence: “I rejoiced at the things said to me,” etc.

But this, brother, must be carefully considered and especially committed to memory: for Adam to wish to enter without Eve is not greatly praiseworthy; for Eve to be able to enter without Adam is altogether impossible. For what profit is there in knowing eternal things and not wishing to love eternal things? Yet if you do not first know eternal things, you do not love them at all. Thus to have eternal things alone before one’s eyes, to cling to eternal things alone [Col. 0366D], is, in a certain manner, for Adam and Eve together to be within the house of God. Meanwhile they are carried away so as to taste, but one day they will enter not to taste but to be made drunk, so that they may dare to hope and chant confidently: “We shall go into the house of the Lord.”

## Note on Psalm 134

[Col. 0365]

[Col. 0365D] “Whatever the Lord willed, he did, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses.” If he finds a heart bright with understanding, like heaven, or conversely dark with ignorance, like an abyss; likewise, if he finds a mind firm in constancy, like earth, or conversely slippery with desire, like water: everywhere indeed and always he has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses. “Bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth.” The extremities of our earth are the lowest sins and abject deeds. From such an extremity [Col. 0367A] a cloud is produced, because from the remembrance of our ugliness there arises the darkness of shame. Yet a cloud of this kind, while it overshadows the mind, provides refreshment against the heat of desire, as against the sun’s burning. For one who remembers that he has sinned and is ashamed that he has sinned, the more he grieves over the past, the more cautious he shows himself concerning the future.

“He made lightning for the rain.” Before the lightning, a cloud is produced, and likewise rain follows lightning. The cloud is the darkness of shame; lightning, the terror of majesty; rain, the tears of compunction. Thus, by the dispensation of divine mercy, first the remembrance of our ugliness is brought before the eyes of the mind; afterward, in recalling these things, it is shaken by dread of the divine terror; at last, caught between shame and fear, and long wearied [Col. 0367B], it is pierced with compunction in tears. I have seen a cloud over myself whenever shame of face covered me. I receive lightning when the terrors of the Lord wage war against me. Rain falls whenever I have been able to water my bed with my tears.

“He brings forth winds from his treasuries.” As the spirit blows where it wills, so likewise it blows when it wills. And, as you may hear here, after rain winds are brought forth: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” The spirit of fear blows in one way, the spirit of piety in another, and the spirit of fortitude in another. Such winds the Lord brings forth from his treasuries. When we search out the secrets of divine Scripture, we marvel at certain treasures of heavenly knowledge and wisdom. But while we dwell intensely upon [Col. 0367C] such wonder and attend more carefully, the astonished mind is touched now by the spirit of wisdom, now by the spirit of understanding, now by the spirit of counsel, now by the spirit of knowledge.

“He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man even unto cattle.” Pride is the beginning of every sin. The darkness of error produces such firstborn, [Col. 0368A] because by the Spirit of God the spirit of the devil is cast down, and by the spirit of meekness the spirit of pride is confounded. Rightly, after the winds are brought forth, the firstborn of Egypt die. The winds are divine inspirations; the firstborn of Egypt are diabolical exaltations; the firstborn of Egypt are human presumptions. Some are proud of bodily things; others swell with pride in spiritual things. Truly brutish and animal-like is the mind when a soul made in the image of God swells with pride in things it has in common with cattle. Thus some are proud through vanity, others through holiness. Pride in vanity is the firstborn of cattle; arrogance in holiness is the firstborn of man. Therefore, as the breath of the divine Spirit blows, the firstborn of Egypt are struck, from man even unto cattle; for when [Col. 0368B] the spirit of fear blows, every spirit of self-exaltation is easily cast down—how much more when other and other spirits are blowing, now these, now those, succeeding one another in turn?

“And he sent signs and wonders in the midst of Egypt, upon Pharaoh and upon all his servants.” We are in Egypt—that is, in darkness—as long as we live in this world, where we do not see one another’s consciences; indeed, what is more serious, we do not fully know even ourselves. It should therefore be known that all the plagues by which the Egyptian is struck by the Lord are recognized by those who understand rightly as certain portents of future evils. For they signify not only the evils that follow after death in the soul alone, but also prefigure those which, after the last day of judgment, the rejected will suffer in soul [Col. 0368C] and body together. They are signs, therefore, because they display what is to come shortly after the death of each individual. But they are rightly called wonders, as it were foretelling from afar, because they speak beforehand of what will remain for the rejected after judgment.

## Note on Psalm 134

[Col. 0367]

[Col. 0367C] “He brings forth winds from his treasuries.” We receive the breath of divine inspiration when, in the divine Scriptures, we search out with wonder, and wonder at while searching out, the treasures of heavenly wisdom. On account of these treasures of wisdom the Apostle cries out and says: “O the depth of the riches [Col. 0367D] of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. XVIII.) Do you wish to know what are the winds which he customarily brings forth from treasuries of this kind? They are the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord. Four of these belong to understanding, but three to affection. For to understanding belong wisdom, understanding, discernment, and knowledge; to affection belong trust, love, and fear. Thus the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and knowledge, correspond to understanding; but the spirit of fortitude and piety, and the spirit of fear, correspond to affection.

But we know that every affection arises from thought. For the mind is never moved with affection toward anything unless the thing itself has first been seen through thought. Thus those three spirits which we said belong to [Col. 0368C] affection customarily arise from the others which belong to understanding. For it is clear that from the spirit of wisdom, sometimes from the spirit of understanding, often from the spirit of counsel, and at times from the spirit of knowledge, the human mind is raised to fortitude [Col. 0368D] and strengthened in steadfastness.

The spirit of wisdom blows from the South; the spirit of understanding blows from the East; the spirit of counsel sounds from the North; the spirit of knowledge thunders from the West. These are the four cardinal winds. Yet when they blow fortitude, each of them has two auxiliaries, one on this side and one on that, because now they inspire piety and now they breathe in fear. For from whatever region of heaven it blows, the spirit of fortitude occupies the middle place and is cardinal, having auxiliaries on either side: at its right, the spirit of piety; at its left, the spirit of fear. These winds, therefore, he whose treasure it is brings forth from his treasuries.

Now the treasure, to say something briefly of it, since it is exceedingly great, abundant, and rich [Col. 0369A], is distinguished by four storehouses. The first is constructed in the western region, from the historical sense; the second is raised in the northern quarter, from the moral sense; the third, built from allegory, stands in the East; the fourth, from anagogy, is in the South. In the western storehouse is laid up the silver of eloquence; in the northern storehouse are stored the various and innumerable gems of virtues. In the eastern storehouse are contained purple, fine linen, and the other royal ornaments in the various sacraments of the Church. In the southern storehouse is guarded the gold of heavenly wisdom. In the first faith is instructed; in the second conduct is trained; in the third devotion is exercised; in the fourth contemplation of heavenly things begins.

[Col. 0369B] It should be noted, moreover, that the western storehouse faces an eastern doorway and stands opposite it, because whatever allegory establishes, history shows to have preceded in figure; and thus, while they look upon each other, they mutually bear witness to one another concerning the solidity of truth. Likewise, the northern storehouse stands opposite the southern doorway and looks upon it, because, when the reward of labours is seen opposite, one gladly toils in the exercises of virtues; and it is sufficiently clear [Col. 0370A] that the measure of labour and the quality of recompense correspond to one another in an equal balance.

The western and northern storehouses are joined together; likewise the southern is joined to the eastern. For after history has been known, we ought to seek morality. Likewise after this, through knowledge of allegory we advance to anagogy. Through history we learn what has been done; through morality we know what must be done; through allegory we understand how the sacraments of the Church were foretold in the figures of preceding events; through anagogy we behold the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made. Therefore from the hidden inner chambers of such storehouses come forth the breaths of divine inspiration, at the command, however, of him who brings forth winds from his treasuries. And three winds appear to proceed from each storehouse. Since which proceed from which is clear from what has gone before, it is superfluous to specify it. These are the twelve winds which range abroad and blow through the whole land of the living, your whole land, O Emmanuel. But now these, now those blow, as [Col. 0370B] and when the king and Lord of the winds wills: not the fabulous Aeolus, but he who “ascended above the cherubim and flew upon the wings of the winds.”

## Note on Psalm 138

[Col. 0369]

[Col. 0369B] “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and in your book [Col. 0369C] all shall be written; days shall be formed, and no one among them.”

One imperfection is an imperfection of form; another, an imperfection of stature. The latter concerns quantity, the former quality. One concerns the condition in which each person is such as he ought to be by nature; the other, the extent to which each person is as great as he ought naturally to grow. The former is seen in children; the latter is found in adults. When a child has all his limbs, he is perfect in form, yet he is not perfect in stature. However much monstrous births may grow, they do not recover that perfection which is according to form. Faith without good action; a good work accompanied by unbelief; chastity with pride; humility with lust—all this makes something monstrous, and none of these attains Christian perfection.

One who is such is not Christ’s, nor can it be said of him: “Your eyes saw my imperfection.” But one who has righteousness, though he does not possess it perfectly, surely belongs to Christ, although he is not yet perfect [Col. 0370B]. Rightly Christ speaks concerning him to the Father: [Col. 0370C] “Your eyes saw,” he says, “my imperfection”—not merely any imperfection, but *my* imperfection. Although such persons depart from the body, they are regarded by the gaze of divine grace, by the regard of divine mercy. “For your eyes saw my imperfection, and in your book all shall be written.” Who are “all”? Clearly, all who are his, all who belong to Christ. “If,” he says, “my imperfection, how much more my perfection?” Therefore all who are mine are seen by you, and all who are mine shall be written in your book.

But let us ask what this book is in which all his own shall be written. If we say that this is the book of the living, surely not only his own but also strangers are written there, concerning whom it is elsewhere said: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living” (Ps. LXVIII). If we say that this is the book of life, perhaps they are already written there, and how then are they still to be written there? For it is said: “And in your book all shall be written,” unless perhaps the future tense is used in place of the past.

## Note on Psalm 136

[Col. 0369]

[Col. 0369D] “Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments.” Willows are barren trees and bear no fruit at all. What, then, can more fittingly be understood in trees of this kind than barrenness of good? But this unfruitfulness and barrenness of good sometimes rules in action, sometimes in speech, sometimes in thought, sometimes in affection, [Col. 0370D] sometimes in two or three of these, and sometimes even in all of them. Behold four willows: barrenness of action, barrenness of speech, barrenness of thought, barrenness of affection. The barrenness of actions is when the grace to act well is withdrawn; barrenness of speech, when the grace to speak well is withdrawn; barrenness of thought, when the grace to understand rightly [Col. 0371A] is withdrawn; barrenness of affections, when the grace to direct one’s affections rightly is withdrawn.

In all these matters divine grace is now granted and now withdrawn, but now one grace and now another, and this not only from the wicked but also from the good: from the good for their good, from the wicked for their evil. “For all things work together for good to those who are called saints according to his purpose.” Divine grace is sometimes withdrawn from the elect so that each may understand what he is in himself. It is given or restored so that he may understand what he is by the divine gift. By the one he is taught self-contempt; by the other, love of God. By the one he advances toward humility; by the other, he is advanced toward charity. In these two lie both the foundation of goodness and the consummation of virtue.

There is also another kind of barrenness: namely, the unfitness of a vain intention. It is more detestable than all the others precisely because it corrupts everything else. Whatever springs from this root is undoubtedly rendered barren and unfruitful, even if it seems good. For whatever good we do or say, we can corrupt and bring to nothing through a perverse intention. We therefore have five willows, and all are Babylonian. The first is considered in barrenness of action; the second, in barrenness of speech; the third, in barrenness of thought; the fourth, in barrenness of affection; the fifth, in barrenness of intention. In all these we are ashamed; in all these, indeed, we ought to be ashamed; in all these we are deservedly confounded. And what else do we deserve for [Col. 0371C] all these things but confusion? Rightly, therefore, willows of this sort are called Babylonian, since they always bring confusion: for Babylon is interpreted as “confusion,” and therefore those things which work confusion rightly appear to belong to it.

Thus there are five willows, because the barrenness of human weakness is fivefold. Barrenness of action is understood in what is said through the Prophet: “Their days failed in vanity” (Ps. LXXVII). Concerning the second barrenness, the vanity of speech, there is this saying of the same Prophet: “Each spoke vain things to his neighbour” (Ps. XI). Barrenness of thoughts is condemned where it is said: “Woe to you who devise useless things” (Mic. II). He rebukes barrenness of affection who says: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. IV). Of the fifth kind of barrenness we may rightly understand also this: “Their heart is vain” (Ps. V). What is it to have a vain and empty heart except to fix one’s counsel in a vain and useless intention?

It should further be noted that in the suburb of Babylon itself the first willow-grove grows; around its gate, the second; within the walls, the third; near the middle of the city, the fourth; and in the very middle and innermost part of the same city, the fifth and last. We have already said that the first willow-grove is outside the city and, as it were, in its suburbs, because we see one another’s actions; for we cannot see at all the thoughts or pleasures of others, just as those who are outside the city [Col. 0372A] can see only exterior things. By the service of the mouth we customarily disclose our inward things and bring them into public view, and for this reason we have it as a kind of gate of our city. Thus the second willow-grove is rightly said to be, as it were, at the city gate, if barrenness of speech is rightly understood in it.

We have defined the other three willow-groves as being within the city because only we ourselves see within ourselves the quality of thought, affection, and intention. For no one knows what belongs to a person except the spirit which is in him. And affection penetrates the soul more deeply than thought alone; therefore barrenness of affection occupies, as it were, a more inward place. Intention holds the innermost and highest place, because it presides over thought and affection. Thus the fifth willow-grove is rightly said to be in the midst of Babylon, in which barrenness of intentions is represented.

These are those barren trees; these are those willows lacking every fruit and growing in the midst of Babylon: namely, vain intentions. They hang their instruments upon them who carefully attend to the barrenness of their hearts and are truly ashamed of their weakness. What is it to hang an instrument except to withhold the word of preaching and keep silent the proclamations of truth? And what is it to hang instruments of this kind upon willows except to attend to and be ashamed of one’s own weakness and the barrenness of one’s heart, and by no means presume to preach to others things that one has not done or cannot do? Therefore, as often as we are ashamed, through remembering and considering our weakness [Col. 0372C], to preach to others the good things which we ourselves cannot or will not do, so often we hang our instruments upon the willows.

Yet we see many doing shameful and detestable things, while nevertheless presuming to exercise the office of preaching. Such are those rebuked by the divine reproof: “Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. XLIX). Conversely, there are those who act badly and therefore are ashamed of, and shrink back from, the office of preaching. These hang their instruments not so much upon willows as upon thorns. There are others who perform neither great good nor great evil, but nevertheless, because of the barrenness of their works, withhold the word of edification from their neighbours. What else do they do [Col. 0372D] than hang their instruments upon willows, but around Babylon? Others customarily, or are even compelled, to refrain from the office of preaching because of a lack of eloquence; others because of a lack of understanding. These indeed seem to hang their instruments upon willows, but in different places, and not in the midst of Babylon. But one who flees the office of preaching because he perceives that with sincere and simple affection or intention he cannot fulfill it, undoubtedly hangs his instruments, as it were, in the midst of Babylon.

Moreover, we hang our instruments not only when we withhold from our neighbours a word of edification, but whenever, because our merits require it, we are poor and empty in proclaiming the truth to the praise of the Creator. For by instruments we understand any modulation of mind or mouth in the proclamation of truth. Instruments, indeed, while they emit outwardly the breath which they draw to themselves from below, produce a sweet, pleasant, and manifold melody. So too, at hidden inspiration, at the prompting and infusion of the Holy Spirit, the human mind customarily bursts forth from a good conscience into proclamations of the highest goodness, and now in heart alone, now in heart and mouth together, resounds in the praises of God.

What else, then, are instruments of the kind of which we speak except any modulation of heart or mouth ready for the proclamations of the highest truth? There are five instruments in which we ought to resound before God. The first is instruction [Col. 0373B] in truth, when what is unknown is taught. The second is the inflaming of the will, when the mind is inflamed toward what it knows. The third is the obtaining of grace, when we implore divine help for that which we know and wish to do but cannot. The fourth is the gladness of conscience, when, because of a good which is known, long desired, and at last sometime fulfilled by divine aid, we rejoice before the Lord in that very good. The fifth is the tasting and wonder of inward sweetness, when, already as the reward of recompense, we taste and see how sweet the Lord is, and rejoice before him with wonder.

Thus the first instrument of the spiritual instruments is that of instruction; the second, exhortation; the third, devotion; the fourth, exultation; the fifth [Col. 0373C], jubilation. Instruction concerns teaching the unlearned; exhortation, rebuking the negligent; devotion, making supplication to the Lord; exultation, rejoicing in the Lord for divine benefits; jubilation, rising through the experience of inward sweetness to the greatness of wonder and almost, or wholly, passing beyond oneself in mind.

Thus we chant on the first instrument when we teach the ignorant what they ought to know; on the second we sing when we inflame sluggish minds to love the good things which they have previously received through instruction; on the instrument of devotion we sound forth when we devote ourselves intensely to prayer and thanksgiving; on the fourth instrument we make melody when, through the testimony of a good conscience, we glory in the Lord [Col. 0373D]; we enjoy the fifth melody of the instrument when, because of intoxication with sweetness and the greatness of wonder, we are carried away into the mind’s astonishment.

He shows himself skilled and ready in the instrument of instruction who proposes and confidently promises of himself: “My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditation of my heart prudence” (Ps. XLVIII). But he sang as sweetly as he did beneficially on the second instrument, that of exhortation, who sounded forth with the purpose of admonishing: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he shall receive the crown of life, which,” etc. (Jas. I). He wished his son to be trained in the instrument of devotion who admonished by commanding and commanded by admonishing: “At every time [Col. 0374A] bless God, and ask him to direct your ways” (Tob. IV). We are daily admonished and daily invited to the instruments of exultation and jubilation, and to the songs of instruments of this kind: “Come, let us exult in the Lord; let us rejoice in God our saviour” (Ps. XCIV).

But just as there are different kinds of instruments, so undoubtedly there are different kinds of songs according to the different instruments; and even within one and the same kind of instrument we must often chant in different ways. Who, indeed, does not know that instruction concerns training people both in right faith and in good morals? It belongs to the doctrine of faith to know what things are true and what false. But moral instruction concerns knowing what things may not be committed at all; likewise [Col. 0374B] what things ought to be done and may not be omitted at all; and also what things, when fulfilled, so increase or accumulate merit that, if omitted, they incur no guilt whatsoever.

Thus it belongs to instruction now to establish truths, now to refute falsehoods, now to demand duties, now to restrain unlawful acts, now to set forth and commend the best things. The first is confirmation; the second, refutation; the third, prohibition; the fourth, command; the fifth, counsel. Behold five kinds of songs, and all these belong to the instrument of instruction. He who said, “Always ready to answer everyone who asks you a reason for the faith and hope which are in us” (1 Pet. III), wished us to be ready and equipped in the first kind of songs of this sort. In the second [Col. 0374C] kind we likewise ought to be instructed, so that we may always be ready to repel every falsehood, “destroying the arguments of unbelievers and the counsels of the carnal, and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ” (2 Cor. I).

In the third kind of song he sounded forth in many ways who said: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill” (Exod. XX; Deut. V), and much in this manner. The fourth kind of song includes what you hear from the mouth of the Lord: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. IV). Understand the fifth when you hear from the Apostle: “It is good for a woman not to touch” (1 Cor. VII). The Lord sings in the same key when he says: “If you wish to be perfect [Col. 0374D], go and sell all that you have, and give to the poor” (Matt. XIX).

Likewise, on the instrument of exhortation, we do not always chant in one and the same manner. At one time we exhort to love virtues; at another, to hate vices; at another, to desire rewards; at another, to fear or beware punishments. Behold again four kinds of songs. The first is commendation of merit; the second, condemnation of vice; the third, promise of reward; the fourth, threat of punishment. The commendation of virtue is what you hear from the Apostle: “God is charity, and he who abides in charity abides in God, and God in him” (1 John IV). The condemnation of vice, belonging to the second kind of song, is what you hear there: “Envy is rottenness of the bones” [Col. 0375A] (Prov. XIV). A very sweet song, delightful and pleasing to hear, is the promise of eternal inheritance: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (Isa. LXIV; 1 Cor. II). The fourth kind of song is called the threat of punishment, such as the Apostle’s: “A certain fearful expectation, and a fire of zeal which shall consume the adversaries” (Heb. X).

As we have already said of the two preceding instruments, so also on the instrument of devotion we do not always chant uniformly. For devotion consists now in accusing one’s own evils, now in imploring mercy, now in magnifying him who shows mercy, both for forgiveness granted and for any grace bestowed. Behold a threefold song according to the instrument of devotion. The first is confession of guilt [Col. 0375B]; the second, supplication for mercy; the third, glorification of him who shows mercy. A song of confession is: “I have sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea, and my sins have multiplied; and I am not worthy to see the height of heaven because of the multitude of my iniquity.” A song of supplication is: “Spare, O Lord; spare, O Lord; attend and act” (Dan. IX). A song of glorification is: “The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient, of great mercy, and true” (Ps. XV).

On the instrument of exultation there is a twofold manner of chanting. For now we exult in the Lord for our own merits, now for the good things of others. Every true and ordered exultation is either over the good of one’s neighbour or over the testimony of a good conscience. Behold a twofold song [Col. 0375C], both according to the instrument of devotion: the song of glorying and the song of congratulation—glorying in one’s own merit, congratulation for another’s success. Do you wish to hear from what source the song of glorying usually comes, or rather from what source it ought to come? “This,” says the Apostle, “is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. I).

But on this instrument, and especially in this kind of song, one must have great skill in chanting and chant with much caution. For it is very difficult not to incur at all some note of discord in this kind of song. If you touch the pipe of your glorying in such a pitch that you ascribe to your own merits or powers that in which you glory, then at the touch of such a pipe your inflated pipe will give forth a sound both false and broken [Col. 0375D], and will break out into ugly discord. If, therefore, one must glory, let the one who glories glory in the Lord, and thus rejoice in one’s merits as in gifts of God.

We undoubtedly advance to the second kind of song on this instrument when we truly know not only how to weep with those who weep, but also how to rejoice with those who rejoice.

There remains only the instrument of jubilation. It certainly knows no kind of song except one uniform and single kind. For the song of jubilation is nothing other than the greatness and multiplicity of wonder, amid the inexpressible rejoicings of the heart, because of spiritual and unexperienced sweetness and the greatness of that sweetness. But let no one deem this last kind of instrument and means of modulation of little value in comparison with the others [Col. 0376A], because it does not know, and wholly rejects, the manifold variety of singing. What it loses in variety of modulation, it recovers entirely—indeed, accumulates beyond measure—in the sweetness of its modulation and the greatness of that sweetness. For the melody of jubilation, the more barren it is than the others in multiplicity, the more fruitful it is than all the others in delightfulness. Although any one of the other instruments may greatly gladden a person, the instrument of jubilation customarily makes one blessed: “Blessed,” he says, “is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

Moreover, on the other instruments we commonly chant before anyone at all. But with the instrument of jubilation it is necessary and fitting to honour the presence of royal dignity alone: “Rejoice,” he says, “in the presence of the Lord the King” (Ps. XCVII). The song of jubilation fills the earth and gladdens heaven: “Rejoice in God, all the earth” (Ps. LXV). Do you wish also to know whether a song of this kind perhaps resounds even in heaven? “When,” he says, “the morning stars praised me, and all the sons of God rejoiced” (Job XXXI).

Thus from the five instruments you have fifteen kinds of songs: five in the first, four in the second, three in the third, two in the fourth, and only one in the last. These are the songs of Zion; these are the hymns of songs concerning which it is said or sung: “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.” Behold, you have the songs of degrees. Behold, you have fifteen kinds of songs. The first of the songs of Zion is refutation of falsehood; the second, confirmation of truth; the third, prohibition of transgression [Col. 0376C]; the fourth, command of righteousness; the fifth, setting forth of perfection; the sixth, condemnation of guilt; the seventh, commendation of virtue; the eighth, threat of damnation; the ninth, promise of blessedness; the tenth, confession of guilt; the eleventh, supplication for mercy; the twelfth, glorification of him who shows mercy; the thirteenth, glorification of humility; the fourteenth, congratulation of charity; the fifteenth, itself the last of all and the most delightful of all, the rejoicing of wonder.

Thus you have five instruments and fifteen songs: the instrument of instruction, the instrument of exhortation, the instrument of devotion, the instrument of exultation, and the instrument of jubilation. It is good, therefore, to make instruments of this kind resound; it is good [Col. 0376D] also to chant songs of this kind: “It is good,” he says, “to confess to the Lord and to chant to your name, O Most High” (Ps. XCI). Let us therefore sing not to just anyone, but to the Lord our God. Far be it from us to sing or chant to those who customarily lead us into captivity, carry us off to Babylon, and cast us down into confusion. “For there those who led us captive asked us for words of song.”

But who are those who lead us into captivity and bring us to Babylon, or confusion, except pride and vainglory? “Before ruin the heart shall be exalted”; without doubt, before ruin the heart is exalted, and before confusion it glories vainly. Pride and vainglory are always the cause of ruin and confusion, and they are indeed what truly bring the captivity of the mind. “Sing us a hymn,” they say, [Col. 0377A] “from the songs of Zion.” Pride and vainglory do not wish song to be offered to the Lord our God, but to themselves. What is it to chant to our God except, in the things we say, to seek not our own glory but divine glory? What is it to sing to pride or vainglory except, from what we say or think, to seek one’s own glory and distinction? Far be it from us to serve such tyrants and wish to satisfy them! Otherwise [Col. 0378A] it would be better to attend to the vanity and barrenness of our intention and hang our instruments upon the willows in the midst of Babylon than to chant to such taskmasters.

Hear to whom it is fitting to sing, to whom, in short, one ought to chant: “Sing to our God, sing; sing to our King, sing; sing wisely, and exult greatly in him.” He lives and reigns through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## Note on Psalm 139

[Col. 0377]

[Col. 0377A] Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; deliver me from the unjust man. Diabolical temptation is sometimes sudden, sometimes violent, sometimes fraudulent. It is sudden [Col. 0377B] when it forestalls reason’s judgment; violent when it exceeds the capacity of our strength; fraudulent whenever it deceives the test of discernment. Thus, according to the manner of temptation, the tempter himself often receives a corresponding designation. Hence Holy Scripture calls the demons who incite vices now birds, now beasts, and sometimes men, by a certain resemblance.

For he flies suddenly, as a bird, when he occupies the mind before deliberation. Often indeed my mind falls so hastily into a shameful thought that, before it can deliberate at all about it, it is carried away into delight. The tempter, then, is like a flying bird when he comes suddenly or unexpectedly. But he rages like a lion when he is felt to be violent. For it often happens, from [Col. 0377C] a preceding fault, that a vehement and altogether intolerable temptation subsequently arises. But when the malignant enemy is not granted permission to employ force, he often turns to fraud. Therefore, when he strives to prevail by cunning, he is rightly denoted by the name of man. For man alone among animals uses reason; hence, even over those animals to which he is inferior in strength, he rules through the singular excellence of his intelligence. Thus he is like a man when he employs not so much strength as cunning, when he acts not so much forcefully as shrewdly.

The same Prophet complains of birds when elsewhere he testifies, saying: “They have given the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven” (Ps. 78 [79]). Then he adds concerning beasts: “The flesh [Col. 0377D] of your saints to the beasts of the earth” (ibid.). He also feared beasts when elsewhere he cried aloud to the Lord in prayer: “Do not deliver to the beasts the souls that confess you” (Ps. 73 [74]). Here, because he is contending against a cunning tempter, he calls his plotter a man, saying: “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man; deliver me from the unjust man.”

But lest you think that I have devised this from my own interpretation, read the Gospel and you will undoubtedly find demons designated now by birds and now by a man. There you read of seed which fell by the wayside, “because the birds of heaven devoured it” (Luke 8); and concerning the tares it is said, “because an enemy, a man, did this” (Matt. 13). Moreover, that Truth intended to signify only demons by birds or by a man, he plainly declared in the explanation which follows. What could be clearer, [Col. 0378A] what more manifest, than the statement there: “the enemy, the man, is the devil”? From such an enemy-man, an unjust man, and an evil man, the Prophet sought to be [Col. 0378B] delivered when he said, “Deliver me, O Lord, from the evil man,” as though he openly confessed: “See that I endure an enemy so subtle that, in comparison with him, I appear like a brute animal. As man surpasses an animal by the privilege of reason, so the smallness of our intelligence is surpassed by the greatness of his cunning. I scarcely perceive his snares; I scarcely detect his tricks. Deliver me, therefore, O Lord, from the evil man.”

Spiritual men are indeed like men, for they readily detect his deceits. But carnal people, such as myself, in comparison with him are like animals: they notice his snares little, or not at all. Nevertheless, “you will save men and beasts, O Lord, according to the abundance of your mercy, O God.” Deliver me, therefore, from [Col. 0378C] the evil man. If it moves you little that I fight like an animal against a man, that I, being in a sense brute, contend against a cunning plotter—if, therefore, it does not move you that my enemy is a man, let it at least move you that he is evil. Deliver me, therefore, O Lord, from the man, etc.

It follows: “Deliver me from the unjust man.” Perhaps the same thing is repeated in other words, and perhaps “the evil man” and “the unjust man” mean the same. Yet let us see whether something else may perhaps lie hidden in these words which may profitably become known for our edification. To be a man (*vir*) is greater than merely to be a human being (*homo*). For women and boys too are called human beings by the general term. But we know that men surpass women in manly strength, and boys both in prudence and in powers. First, therefore, because he perceived his enemy to be cunning, he called him a man on account of the marvelous subtlety of his intelligence. But because afterwards he discovered that he acted not only shrewdly but also powerfully, he took care to call him by the fitting name, a man (*vir*).

For the force of the struggle and the weight of temptation often grow to such an extent that what was at first only fraudulent afterwards becomes violent as well: because the tempter could not prevail by cunning alone, he at least conquers by added vehemence. It is pleasing to consider, in one and the same kind of temptation, both the mercy of divine dispensation and the deceit of diabolical perversity. For the fraudulent enemy first assails a person with a lighter temptation, so that, if perhaps he falls under a light impulse, [Col. 0379A] his excuse may be the smaller in proportion as the temptation was lighter. But when, through lesser contests, he does not cast anyone’s mind down from its purpose, he suddenly prepares himself for greater ones.

Divine dispensation, however, permits the same thing for an altogether different reason, since in all it does it always provides for human salvation. It first trains a person through a lighter struggle, so that, having been trained, he may finally learn to carry off triumph from graver perils. For the Lord does nothing in our regard, nor permits anything to be done, except what he judges to be merciful or just. Hence the saying: “The Lord is just in all his ways, and holy in all his works” (Ps. 144 [145]).

On the other hand, he calls the devil evil and unjust: evil, because he always desires to harm; unjust, because he often extends the measure of his assault beyond the bounds of equity. He is rightly called evil on account of the intention of his evil will, even when, in our affliction, he does not exceed the limit of equity. At first he persecutes us as much as our fault demands; but when he sees that this cannot suffice for our overthrow, he often exceeds the measure. Yet it should be known that divine goodness then loosens the reins of his permission, when it sees that this can serve human good. Therefore, because the Prophet sees that our tempter intends evil in all that he does around us, he calls him evil; and because it is clear that he often exceeds the bounds of equity in persecuting us, he calls him unjust and says: “Deliver me, O Lord,” etc.

He wished this to happen quickly, because he said not “set me free” but “deliver me.” Perhaps he also thought it necessary for this to be done by force, [Col. 0379C] since he asked to be freed by a rescue, not by a command. Not, however, because the Lord could not accomplish this by commanding, but so that, speaking in a human fashion, he might show the greatness of the danger: “They who devised injustices in their heart, all day long prepared battles.” To devise injustice is one thing; to speak [Col. 0380A] injustice is another. What we still only think is hidden from others; what we speak begins also to be manifest to others.

Thus before perfect men evil spirits devise injustice, because, insofar as they can, they conceal the deceits of fraudulent persuasion. They wish to persuade good men to evil under the appearance of good, because they cannot draw them at all to openly evil things. What else, then, is it for them not to speak their injustice but to devise it, except fraudulently to conceal the evil that they intend? See by what stages evil grows: first it is thought, then spoken, and finally shouted aloud, as it is written: “They devised and spoke wickedness; they spoke injustice on high” (Ps. 72 [73]). First they devised, then they spoke, and finally [Col. 0380B] they spoke on high. “They devised” pertains to speech; “they spoke on high” pertains to shouting.

They seemingly think evil and do not speak it when they conceal that what they urge is evil. They speak evil, as though in secret, when they do not conceal evil but excuse it. They speak evil on high when they freely command some people to do what is manifestly evil. Thus, before those perfectly good they devise; before those imperfectly good or evil they whisper; before those perfectly evil they shout. They also preserve this order in one and the same person when they hasten to drag him into perdition. First they urge hidden evil under the appearance of good; afterwards, manifest evil under an excuse; finally, they openly command public evil. Perhaps at that time they had found David to be such a person, one to whom they could not openly urge evil. Therefore they dared to devise injustice, but not to speak it—those of whom it is said: “They who devised injustices in their heart.”

## Commentary on Psalm 143

[Col. 0379]

“Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war.” In the hands, action is understood; in the fingers, discernment. This is a worn-out observation, and almost unknown to no one. There are two hands, moreover, and each has five fingers. One hand is right and the other left. Sometimes good action is understood by the right hand and evil action by the left, as in: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does.” At other times only good is expressed in both hands, when the Prophet says: “In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands” (Ps. 73 [77]). For the Prophet would not have said that he sought God by an evil work, nor would he have believed that he could find him so.

As we all know, the right hand is stronger, but the left is gentler. To the right hand therefore belong works of strength; to the left, offices of gentleness. To the right, the rigor of severity; to the left, the mildness of mercy. To the right, finally, exercises of justice; to the left, acts [Col. 0380C] of mercy. The right hand sometimes acts by itself and sometimes is assisted by the left. Action by the left hand alone, however, is extremely rare and wholly weak—unless perhaps in matters which overturn the order of nature and make the left hand into the right.

Justice is of one kind constraining and of another permitting. Constraining justice is that which cannot at all be adapted except to one side. For certain things are so required by the equity of justice that they cannot be omitted except unjustly; and certain things are so forbidden that they can never be undertaken except unlawfully. When we carry out such things justly, we work as it were with the right hand alone. But there are other things which can be done justly and remitted mercifully; and, conversely, others which can be passed over justly and performed mercifully. In these, the action of mercy has a place and can exercise itself as far as permitting justice allows. Yet in what it graciously bestows or forgives pardonably, it must above all beware [Col. 0381A] of exceeding the bounds of just equity.

Therefore, when we perform works of mercy in such a way as not to depart from justice, we work as it were with both hands. When justice itself is established or tempered by mercy, the right hand is in a manner assisted by the left, as is written: “For mercy exults over judgment.” We have spoken of the hands; now let us look at the fingers.

Each hand is distinguished or adorned by fingers; and the activity of both justice and mercy is regulated by discernment, so that it may be useful and ordered. There are five fingers, and we may distinguish discernment into five stages. The first stage of discernment is judgment (*dijudicatio*); the second, deliberation; the third, arrangement; the fourth, dispensation; the fifth, moderation.

[Col. 0381B] First, indeed, one must judge and, by the examination of discernment, inquire what is lawful and what unlawful. But since not everything that is lawful is immediately expedient, it remains in the second place to have recourse to counsel and, through much deliberation, investigate among all lawful things what is expedient or what is altogether not expedient. Having sought and found what we may do lawfully and profitably, we must still recognize, among useful matters, what we ought to do, how, and in what order. Once the order of things to be done has been arranged and fixed, we must often, as circumstances vary, have recourse to the grace of dispensation, and according to the appropriateness of occasions remove or alter something of the rigor of our purpose and of the order of our arrangement; for human arrangement and divine [Col. 0381C] arrangement do not always converge upon the same end or everywhere lead to the same outcome.

Finally, in all that we do in an orderly and circumspect way, it is necessary not to be ignorant of the appropriate measure and, once known, to preserve it with every diligence and patience. Thus the first is judgment, the second deliberation, the third arrangement, the fourth dispensation, the fifth moderation. By judgment we separate lawful from unlawful things; by deliberation we choose useful things from useless among so many lawful things; by arrangement we bring everything into order according to the manner of our choice; by dispensation we yield, as circumstances require, to the fitness of times; by moderation we preserve in all things the restraint proper to works.

Judgment, then, distinguishes lawful from unlawful; deliberation, advantageous from disadvantageous; arrangement, ordered from disordered; dispensation, timely from untimely; moderation, moderate from immoderate. Judgment brings all things to trial and, separating good from evil, does not allow us to run out through unlawful things. Deliberation does nothing without counsel and always restrains us from superfluous things. Arrangement does all things without confusion and leaves nothing at all disordered. Dispensation yields to an occasion that arises and, providing for human weakness, does not allow human arrangement to resist divine arrangement in vain. Moderation preserves measure and does not permit us [Col. 0382A] to overstep the bounds of restraint in anything we do.

It should be noted, however, that *discretio* (“discernment”) is sometimes taken strictly, and then it means nothing other than what above we called judgment, so that there are five stages of prudence: discernment, deliberation, arrangement, dispensation, moderation. Conversely, deliberation is often taken more broadly, so that it seems to include within itself the subsequent parts. For who would say that seeking and finding order, adjustment, and measure in things to be done, altered, and completed has nothing at all to do with deliberation? According to this usage, prudence seems to contain only two parts: discernment and deliberation. Thus indeed poverty of words makes us sometimes extend, sometimes restrict, or otherwise alter their meaning.

But let us now see how, or how fittingly, the five stages of discernment assigned above correspond to the five fingers—not only in number and order, but also by a certain property of their character. The first finger is the thumb, the second the index finger, the third the middle finger, the fourth the healing finger [ring finger], and the last and smallest the little finger. Consider, then, how the thumb alone surpasses all the others in power and position, how it precedes and excels them all—whence it also gets its name. So the examination of judgment ought, and is accustomed, to hold the first place and to grant or administer to all the others their exercise and place. For unless the judgment of discernment comes first [Col. 0382C] and separates lawful from unlawful things, none of the others has anything to do. For lawful things alone lawfully admit choice, require order, permit adjustment, and demand measure. Choice belongs to deliberation; order to arrangement; adjustment to dispensation; measure to moderation. You see clearly how the determination of judgment precedes and excels the offices of all the others.

When we wish to point something out, we are accustomed to do this with the index finger. Consider, then, whether deliberation perhaps holds the office or place of the index finger, since by its choice it always points out what we ought to do. For although we discern that something is lawful, we do not therefore immediately judge that it ought to be done. Not everything lawful is equally beneficial. But whatever deliberation proves truly useful, no one fails to know should also be done. Thus, since daily deliberation points out what work needs to be done, our deliberation itself appears to fulfill the office of the index finger. Like the index finger, deliberation ought to hold the second place and precede arrangement, dispensation, and moderation together. For things which are useless and therefore to be avoided require no offices of arrangement, dispensation, or moderation.

The middle finger holds the next place after the index finger; so arrangement must always follow deliberation. For the things which we choose through deliberation we must immediately order through arrangement. The middle [Col. 0383A] finger is customarily called that which holds the middle and highest place among the others. It is customary, moreover, for a ruler to hold the middle and highest place. Those who stand or sit at his right and left are among those, that is, whose offices he is accustomed to arrange and whose mysteries he is accustomed to order. In the same way arrangement fulfills, as it were, the office or place of a ruler, since through its ministry the whole plan of our actions is ordered. It bears the office of one governing and presiding, since it arranges and disposes everything successively about itself; without its direction nothing ought to emerge in action, nothing to proceed into effect.

The healing finger follows the index and the middle finger, and dispensation often accompanies both deliberation and arrangement. When an occasion arises and urgently demands it, by dispensation we often do things greatly different from what we had first deliberated, sometimes even in an order other than that which we arranged. Therefore, by the office of dispensation it often comes about that both our deliberation and our arrangement reach a better outcome. It ought, then, to follow both, since by it both must, when necessary, be corrected. The healing finger is especially used to feel diseased limbs requiring treatment, and without doubt it takes its name, as it were, from this office of healing. And what, I ask, is dispensation but something that feels our diseased condition, while it weighs the measure of our weakness by a strong examination, so that it may know how to answer the losses of our merits with fitting adjustment and may fulfill the office of a physician?

[Col. 0383C] Our hand ends in the little finger, and moderation imposes an appropriate measure upon every fitting work. This is the finger called the ear-finger, because it is more conveniently inserted than all the others for cleaning the ears. And undoubtedly, the person who observes worthy bounds of moderation in everything he does thereby keeps the ear of hearing cleansed and prepared for hearing, and obeys the divine commands better.

Both hands ought to possess these five fingers of discernment, distinguished as we have distinguished them; and the operation of both justice and mercy ought to be ordered by these stages of prudence. “If we judged ourselves,” says the Apostle, “we certainly would not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31). Consider, I beg you, how useful the office of judgment is, since it acquits us before the judgment-seat of the Judge. He sends us to the counsels of deliberation who says: “Do everything with counsel, and you will never repent” (Ecclus. 32 [Sirach 32]). He knew well that, although all things may be lawful for some, not all things are equally expedient.

Consider how necessary the order of arrangement appears in our works, since it is proposed for observance even in our speech: “A gracious man who has compassion and lends will order his words in judgment” (Ps. 111 [112]). He expressed the character or office of stewards, and thereby of dispensations, when he said: “Here now it is required among stewards that one be found faithful” (1 Cor. 4). You are admonished to the restraint of moderation when you hear and read: “Let your moderation be known to all people” (Phil. 4).

[Col. 0384B] I think that nothing is firmly or faithfully maintained unto the recompense of merits which is not restrained within these five fingers—namely judgment, deliberation, arrangement, dispensation, and moderation—whether it is carried out by the hands of justice, mercy, or perhaps both. Behold the fingers; behold the hands. We understand one singing of such things when we hear: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war.” Let us too strive to act strongly and prudently with these hands and fingers, so that we may not be ashamed to sing with the Prophet in the same voice. Let us act steadfastly with our hands, prudently with our fingers: hands for steadfastness, fingers for prudence.

Let us carefully beware lest the rigor of justice drive us as far as cruelty, or the gentleness of mercy soften us as far as laxity. Every disordering of justice or mercy—indeed every transgression of whatever kind—arises either from desire or is produced by ignorance. From the former vices arise; from the latter errors take their origin. Vices often weaken the hands of our action, and errors likewise defile the fingers of our discernment. Thus vices assail hands with vices of the hands; errors oppose fingers with errors of the fingers. But from the strength of him to whom we sing in the Prophet we hope for victory in both conflicts: “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war.” Hands, I say, for battle against the conflict of vices; fingers for war against the assaults of errors.

## Commentary on Psalm 71

[Col. 0383]

[Col. 0383D] “He shall descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth.” The singular glory of Mary. O glory of the Virgin! O grace of the Savior! O marvelous grace! O singular glory! Wondrous the condescension of the Son; wondrous the dignity of the mother! What, and how great, was the Son’s condescension: that the Son of God the Father should become the Son of Man, that the Lord of glory should become the son of Mary! What, and how great, was the mother’s dignity: to possess the fruit of fruitfulness together with the flower of virginity; to have a son while a virgin—and not merely any son, but God!

[Col. 0384D] Truly singular is the glory of Mary: “He shall descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth.” “He shall descend”—who, I ask, and where? From where, and how? “He shall descend like rain upon fleece.” Without doubt, Christ Jesus. But from where, I ask, and how? From the bosom of the highest Father into the womb of his virgin mother. But what was the manner of his coming? “Like rain upon fleece.” You descended like rain upon fleece, that you might save the human race; we praise you, our God. Behold who comes; behold whence he comes; behold where he rests; [Col. 0385A] behold how he descends.

Who comes? “He shall be great,” he says, “and shall be called the Son of the Most High” (Luke 1). Whence does he come? “His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18 [19]); “his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” Where does he descend? “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which means, “God with us” (Isa. 7). How does he descend? “Like rain upon fleece.” Hear it more plainly: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” Behold the manner. “How,” she says, “will this be, since I do not know a man?” (Matt. 5 [citation uncertain; cf. Luke 1:34]). “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you; the power of the Most High shall overshadow you”: this is “like rain upon fleece.”

How, I ask, does rain descend upon wool, and drops upon earth? How, I ask, except gently and quietly, beneficially and fruitfully? Hail, certainly, descends upon the earth differently from drops: hail with noise, drops without noise; hail for barrenness, drops for fertility. Therefore he descends like rain upon fleece and like drops falling upon the earth: gently upon the gentle, quietly upon the quiet, sweetly upon the sweet, graciously upon the gracious, joyfully upon the joyful. Mary’s singular glory: “He shall descend like rain upon fleece.”

What, I ask, does rain do on fleece, and what do drops usually do in soil? What, I say, does water work in wool, a stream in earth? Certainly and without ambiguity, it washes the wool and irrigates the earth: it washes for cleansing and irrigates for fruitfulness. Thus, certainly, the one and same water of saving wisdom, the one and same grace of the Savior, makes the virgin mother fruitful and cleanses her: [Col. 0385C] it cleanses her mind and makes her womb fruitful; it cleanses the mind for supreme purity and makes the womb fruitful for the most excellent offspring. O purity of mind, O fruitfulness of womb! O highest purity, O singular fruitfulness! As blessed is the fruit of the womb, so glorious is the purity of mind. “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1). O blessed parent, O glorious offspring! The singular glory of Mary!

“He shall descend like rain upon fleece”: he descends like rain upon the fleece of the virgin mind; he descends like drops upon the earth of virgin flesh. He cleansed the former and made the latter fruitful. But did he cleanse the mind alone? Did he make the flesh alone fruitful? On the contrary, without ambiguity and without any contradiction, he cleansed mind and flesh and made mind and flesh fruitful. The one and same stream of the Savior’s grace wiped away the ignorance of the mind and extinguished every desire of the flesh. The one and same water of saving wisdom made the virgin’s flesh fruitful for offspring and the mother’s mind fruitful for every virtue. Thus it rendered one and the same mind free from vices and full of virtues. To one and the same flesh it granted the fruit of fruitfulness and preserved the flower of virginity.

But did the stream of grace, in accordance with Gideon’s petition, first fill only the mind, as though soaking the fleece, and afterwards fill only the flesh, as though irrigating the earth? Did it first leave the flesh in order to fill the mind? Did it afterwards withdraw from the mind in order to make the flesh fruitful? Far be it! Yet consider whether in one respect it first poured itself into the mind alone, and in another respect into the flesh alone. Certainly the stream of grace first made the mind alone fruitful for faith; afterwards the same grace made the flesh alone fruitful for offspring. Faith is in the mind alone; offspring in the flesh alone. Faith came first, offspring afterwards; unless faith in the conception had preceded, the fruitfulness of the offspring could not at all have followed. Faith preceded, and offspring followed, and faith departed. For it was no longer necessary to believe, but now to know what she had proved by the experience of the event. Rightly, then, is it said that, according to Gideon’s petition, in one respect he first filled only the fleece of the virgin mind, and afterwards, in another respect, only the earth of the virgin flesh.

[Col. 0386B] Truly singular is the glory of the Virgin Mary: “He shall descend like rain upon fleece.” What is fleece but wool shorn from flesh and taken away from flesh? O what a fleece was that virgin breast, far removed and utterly alien from carnal desires and the foul passions of bodies! O what fleece was the virgin mind: pure thoughts! O what fleece was the virgin breast: chaste affections! O what fleece was the adornment of every virtue! Who would not rejoice to be able to be clothed from the fleece of the Blessed Virgin Mary’s virtues? O how great, how noble, and how glorious an adornment for the Catholic Church—and this from the fleece of the Virgin Mary! “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed about with varieties in golden fringes.” Thus she is clothed about with variety, but this is from the fleece of the Virgin Mary. You are covered by hairs of flesh, foul hairs, goat-hairs unto shame, if you are not clothed with fleece.

Compare, if you please, hair with wool, and from the comparison infer how special is the glory in the virgin and from the Virgin Mary. Consider wool in comparison with hairs, and from its character infer both the subtlety and the sublimity of the virgin mind. O subtle thoughts, O exalted perceptions, which arise from the virgin mind, which extend themselves more subtly and more far-reachingly, not in the manner of hairs but in the likeness of wool! O exalted, O subtle understanding of the Virgin! O exalted, O subtle affections of the Virgin! O beautiful, O glorious fleece of the virgin breast! From this breast comes the adornment of every virtue; from this breast, the fullness of all glory. And behold what sort of fleece belonged to the Virgin Mary! O special glory in the virgin and from the Virgin Mary!

[Col. 0386D] “He shall descend like rain upon fleece, and like drops falling upon the earth.” What is that earth but the virginal flesh of the Lord’s mother? “Drop down dew, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth open and bring forth the Savior.” From this earth Truth sprang forth. “Truth,” he says, “has sprung from the earth.” From this earth sprang that fruit-bearing tree which is planted beside streams of water and shall yield its fruit in its season. From this earth, I say, sprang the tree of life—not life of any ordinary kind, but eternal and eternally blessed life. Truly sublime is the fruit of that earth, the fruit of eternal blessedness. Taste, I beg you, taste and see how sweet and health-giving is the fruit of this earth and the fruit of this tree.

O fruit-bearing tree, O life-giving tree! It has flowers; it has fruit: flowers of inward beauty, fruit of eternal blessedness; flowers of perfect goodness together with fruits of eternal blessedness. O marvelous and most astonishing thing! In one and the same tree fruit comes forth in such a way that the flowers do not depart; fruit ripens in such a way that the flowers do not wither. Behold what fruit that blessed earth brought forth—the glorious Virgin Mary, who bore the Savior: “Like drops,” he says, “falling upon the earth.”

In this earth was found that stone cut out without hands, which grew into a great mountain and filled the whole surface of the earth. I think that in this earth, according to the saying of Moses, gold is produced, “and the gold of that land is excellent” (Gen. 2). There also are found bdellium and the onyx stone. What kind of earth, I ask, do we call this, in which, if we wish, we easily find the finest gold and a precious stone? But what shall we say of the gold of that earth—gold so excellent and so precious? I think it is according to what is read in blessed Job: “For even this gold has a place in which it is melted” (Job 28).

[Col. 0387B] But what, I ask, is the place of this melting? Is it perhaps the virginal womb itself? Who is the melter in this work and purifier of the gold, except the Holy Spirit? By his operation the gold was melted in the virginal womb and refined to purity: human nature cleansed and purified from every stain, united to the Word, and joined into one person. In this furnace, and from such gold, was formed a ring, a precious stone; and upon it was set the likeness of the supreme King, and his image impressed and fully expressed. The finest gold is Christ’s flesh; the precious stone, Christ’s soul; the likeness and image of the Father, Christ’s divinity.

Although he is “the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance,” he was nevertheless united to our humanity, so that, from two natures and three substances, the mediator between God and human beings—the man Christ Jesus—might be, as it were, joined into one ring and become the adornment of the right hand of the Most High. With the seal of this ring was sealed that edict or written bond by which the captivity of the Jews was released. This is the ring taken from the prince Haman and entrusted by royal clemency to Mordecai; and what heretical perversity lost, the order of Catholic teachers acquired.

[Col. 0388B] O if any one among us has become the prodigal son, who was once dead and now lives again, was lost and has been found: “Put this ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet.” O with how great an honor is each of us endowed in this ring, since in such an adornment the Father himself also glories! Behold what and how great are the benefits that the virgin mother of our Savior bestowed upon us. We are clothed and adorned from her fleece. From the fruit of that earth we are fed and healed, beautified, crowned, and glorified. O truly spiritual, truly singular glory in the Virgin and from the Virgin, the Lord’s mother!

## Commentary on Psalm 90

[Col. 0387]

[Col. 0387C] “His truth will surround you as a shield; you will not fear the terror of the night; the arrow flying by day; the business that walks about in darkness; the assault and the noonday demon. A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.”

There are seven kinds of temptation. The first is importunate; the second doubtful; the third sudden; the fourth hidden; the fifth violent; the sixth deceitful; the seventh perplexing. We call an importunate temptation one which we can scarcely remove from the eyes of our memory: though often removed, it always returns to the mind and never ceases to trouble it at almost every hour. A doubtful temptation is one which so envelops the mind in a cloud of uncertainty that it cannot at all fully discern what definite judgment it ought to maintain concerning a matter; now it draws the mind toward an undecided opinion, [Col. 0387D] now it drives it toward differing or even contrary opinions, and, according to the varying outcome of circumstances and manifold considerations, it varies and multiplies its judgments. A sudden temptation is one which outruns the judgment of reason, so that the mind, forestalled by the onrush of the tempting evil, cannot anticipate its snares, and often feels itself pierced by the dart of wicked pleasure before it can arm itself with the shield of its own vigilance. We call hidden temptation that through which it often happens that we are negligent precisely where we ought to be watchful. For it causes a harmful and utterly ruinous matter not to be brought under consideration, and prevents any examination at all whether it is good or evil. And how many things, we may suppose, do we often commit through carelessness or negligence which perhaps we never bring to judgment throughout the whole course of our life. Thus we are secure concerning that for which we ought to fear judgment.

Violent temptation is that which can scarcely, or in no way, be overcome by human effort; by the vehemence of its assault it so weakens the powers of the human mind that it cannot at all resist the tempting evil unless divinely inspired. Deceitful temptation is that which seduces the mind and often fixes it immovably in a false judgment, so that it calls good what is truly evil, and likewise evil what is truly good. Through this temptation, as we all see, it frequently happens that the wicked mind quite imprudently glories in that for which it ought to be ashamed, [Col. 0388D] and often expects a reward from it as though secure, where it ought tremblingly to fear punishment. Perplexing temptation occurs when, at one and the same time, the mind is assailed by various vices, so that it may stumble in at least one. And crafty malice often arranges these encounters of vices with such art that the unwary mind, while preparing to resist one vice more vigorously, thereby runs into another and succumbs.

Importunate temptation, then, is that which presses shamelessly; doubtful temptation, that which envelops the mind in a cloud of uncertainty; sudden temptation, that which outruns the judgment of reason; hidden temptation, that which escapes the consideration of deliberation; violent temptation, that which exceeds the mind’s powers; deceitful temptation, that which seduces the mind; and perplexing temptation, that which attacks it with diverse vices.

It should further be noted that these seven modes of temptation may sometimes be simple and unmixed, and sometimes composite and mixed. Yet the last mode of temptation is always manifold in one respect, though in another it can be simple. It is manifold precisely in that it is composed of several vices; but it is simple in one respect when it operates uniformly. To be tempted by diverse vices is one thing; to be tempted, without doubt, in diverse ways is another. For just as we may be tempted by diverse vices in one and the same way, so we may be tempted in diverse ways by one and the same vice. Thus the modes of temptation, [Col. 0389B] as has already been said, are sometimes unmixed, when each operates uniformly, and sometimes composite, when they are intermingled with one another and one temptation is formed from several modes of temptation. For one and the same temptation may be sudden and violent, or sudden and deceitful. We may judge the others in the same way; but for the moment we intend here to discuss the simple forms.

Concerning the first, called importunate, it is said in Job: “Waters hollow out stones, and the earth is gradually consumed by flood” (Job 14). Consider, I beg you, by what fitting comparison importunate temptation is described when it is simple and operates uniformly:

> What is harder than rock, what softer than water?

[Col. 0389C]

> Yet hard rocks are hollowed by soft water.

What is harder than stone, what softer than water? Nevertheless:

> A drop hollows a stone, not by force, but by falling often.

Thus it often happens that importunate temptation, though it has in itself no violence and no deceit, nevertheless conquers by persistence and at times softens even the strength of a great-hearted mind into consent to wrongdoing.

The second temptation, rightly called doubtful, occurs when this takes place in a person’s heart, as is likewise read in blessed Job: “Therefore my thoughts,” he says, “succeed one another in their variety, and my mind is drawn in different directions” (Job 20).
