For the human mind is drawn in different directions when, not knowing what certainty it ought to hold regarding any matter, it is altered by a multiplicity of judgments. Of the third temptation, that is, the sudden one, we rightly understand what is said through the prophet Jeremiah: “Our pursuers were swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Jer. 4). What do we understand by “the eagles of heaven” except the subtle and lofty contemplations of the mind? Yet our pursuers are often swifter than such eagles of heaven, because sudden temptations, as has been said, sometimes forestall the deliberations of our vigilance.

For the fourth, called hidden, blessed Job supplicated the Lord when he said: “How many iniquities and sins have I? Show me my crimes and offences” (Job 13). For unless he feared that he possessed some hidden matters for which he ought to pray—matters which nevertheless he might not know—why, I ask, would he request that the Lord show him his iniquities and sins, his crimes and [Col. 0390A] offences? What then shall we do? What shall we say of ourselves, if a man so great and such as he feared that he had hidden matters—not merely venial sins, but even crimes—which he feared he might not know? For concerning manifest sins he speaks confidently when he says: “Indeed, my heart does not reproach me throughout my whole life” (Job 17). This is like the Apostle’s saying: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4).

Concerning the violent temptation, which we placed fifth, we understand what blessed Job says: “As though a wall had been breached and a gate thrown open, they rushed upon me and rolled into my miseries” (Job 30). Once a wall is broken and a gate open, enemies easily burst without obstacle into the interior and plunder the city’s spoil from every side at will. So indeed, so, when the mind’s strength has been exhausted by violent temptation, the human spirit is cast down from the state of its uprightness and stripped of the glory of its virtues.

Concerning the deceitful temptation, placed sixth, Solomon says: “There are ways which seem good to a man, but their end leads down to death” (Prov. 16). What, I ask, is more deceitful or more dreadful than that everlasting death is reaped from the very place where the fruit of eternal life had been hoped for?

Concerning perplexing temptation, which is last of all and most destructive, we rightly understand what the Lord says of blessed Job when he describes His own athlete and, using a comparison, plainly displays the greatness of his strength: “From afar,” he says, “he scents the battle, the exhortation of the commanders, and the shouting [Col. 0390C] of the army” (Job 39). What could be more glorious than that man who, from the lofty tower of his vigilance and stronghold of his courage, can discern from afar through discernment so many plots of enemies, and can calmly endure and repel so many attacks of enemies rushing upon him in a single onslaught?

Of these seven temptations, we not inappropriately take what we find in blessed Job: “In six tribulations he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not seize you” (Job 5). To these seven temptations may likewise rightly be applied what is elsewhere written: “The righteous falls seven times a day and rises again” (Prov. 24). Because of these seven temptations, every righteous person also has reason to offer praise seven times a day, so that he may truly sing before the Lord his God: “Seven times a day I have uttered praise to you, because of the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. 118). For as often as he rises after falling, and as often as he resists the tempting evil, he ought indeed to give thanks to his fellow-worker, by whose aid it has come about that, tempted, he could resist and, fallen, could rise again.

It should certainly be noted of these seven temptations, when they are simple, that the second is more dangerous than the first, and the third than the second. The same relation holds for the third and the fourth; and, in what follows, we must accordingly understand that each later temptation is always more dangerous than the preceding. For the first is more easily overcome than all the rest, since it seems to contain no trouble in itself except that the mind is wearied for a longer time by the persistence of its importunity.

The second, however—that is, the doubtful—is more dangerous than the importunate precisely because the mind often becomes slower toward good when that which is truly good is doubted to be good; likewise, it becomes more prone toward evil when it does not know to be evil that which is truly evil. Yet sudden temptation is more dangerous still than doubtful temptation. In doubtful temptation we have time to deliberate longer and investigate more deeply what we do not fully discern; or at least we may ask others about what we ourselves cannot settle. But sudden temptation, because it unexpectedly seizes the mind, does not wait for the remedy of counsel. It often wounds the mind with the dart of wicked pleasure before it rises to the guard of its own vigilance.

Yet the evil which we cannot forestall in such a temptation because it is sudden, we can and ought to erase by the swift remedy of satisfaction, since it is not violent. But hidden temptation does not readily admit such a remedy, because the blinded mind, where it fears no danger, seeks no remedy. For hidden evil, as it does not guard against itself through vigilance, so it does not ordinarily erase itself by subsequent satisfaction. In this respect hidden temptation is much more dangerous than sudden temptation. Nevertheless, hidden evil can admit some excuse, since the mind sins through ignorance, not malice. And it often happens that, when it recognizes its evil through the occasion of some reading or even exhortation, it immediately abandons it and strives to expiate it by fitting satisfaction.

But what shall we say of violent temptation, through which we often knowingly commit sin and yet cannot wholly abandon it by our own power even when we wish to do so? That weakness which descends from corruption of the will can contribute little—or rather nothing—to a true excuse. Does its weakness excuse the mind, or rather accuse the person whom an inveterate habit of sinning so enervates that he cannot at all resist a temptation when it comes upon him? Consider, therefore, how dangerous it is to fall into a danger from which you cannot retreat even when you wish.

Yet if weighed rightly, deceitful temptation is found more dangerous than all those mentioned above. In importunate, sudden, and violent temptation, we are ashamed of, and condemn, the evil which we knowingly commit. But deceitful temptation causes the wicked mind to glory in that which deserves its shame. Doubtful temptation, moreover, makes the mind timid, not swollen with pride; deceitful temptation removes fear and introduces pride. From hidden temptation the mind becomes neither timid nor proud; from deceitful temptation it becomes both proud and self-assured. Let us therefore consider how dangerous it is not to fear one’s danger while in danger, and to walk securely amid the peril of death.

Perplexing temptation, as it is the last of all, is also the most destructive of all. For if it is often difficult to conquer one vice, how laborious will it be to endure the assaults of several in one attack? I would call that man strong indeed, and no less prudent, who is neither broken by the strength nor ensnared by the deceits of so hostile a host.

It should be known that among these seven temptations there are three which exercise our endurance, and three others which exercise our prudence. For our courage is exercised through the importunate, the sudden, and the violent—that is, the first, third, and fifth—whereas our discernment is trained through the doubtful, the hidden, and the deceitful—that is, the second, fourth, and sixth. In the perplexing temptation, both our strength is exercised toward fortitude and our prudence trained toward discernment. For just as it belongs to great strength courageously to withstand the onslaught of a multitude, so it belongs no less to remarkable prudence wisely to anticipate the snares that flow round about us.

But when we say that this temptation exercises our prudence, we do not mean that through it the mind is deceived concerning the nature of a thing, so as to glory in a false good—something attributed as especially proper to deceitful temptation. Rather, it is a matter of great caution and remarkable prudence when one keeps so watchfully against the snares of a multitude that nothing can be stolen away through one’s negligence from any quarter.

The Psalmist sets forth these seven modes of temptation successively in the same order and describes them very concisely when he says: “His truth will surround you as a shield; you will not fear the terror of the night, the arrow flying [Col. 0392C] by day, the business that walks about in darkness, the assault and the noonday demon. A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.” He touches the first more obscurely than the rest, for he describes all the others quite plainly.

The first temptation, namely the importunate, as has been said, causes no trouble other than becoming burdensome to the human mind by the persistence of its shamelessness and rarely allowing the memory of that matter about which one is tempted to depart from one’s sight. By its suggestion it precedes the object’s presence; when the object itself is present, it sharpens desire; when the object is absent, it recalls it to memory. Thus it attacks from every side, since it never ceases to present itself on all sides. Therefore the saying is rightly understood of it: “His truth will surround you as a shield.” Since, as has been said, this temptation attacks us from every side, we are rightly encircled and protected on every side against it by the shield of truth.

Certainly, in violent temptation it is not enough for us to be enlightened unto truth unless we are also strengthened unto courage by cooperating grace. But in this temptation, which brings no violence upon minds made firm in a good purpose, inspiration of truth alone suffices. Thus it is rightly said of it: “His truth will surround you as a shield.”

Let us now see how he describes the next when he says: “You will not fear the terror of the night.” It often happens that when something is seen in the light of moon and stars, the mind is deceived in its judgment. Often, seeing some animal, it supposes it a human being. Likewise, when a bush or a rock is seen, one fears that an attack of wild beasts is imminent. Hence terror seizes the limbs of those looking on, and they tremble with fear where there is no fear. In this manner, through the terror of the night the mind is vainly shaken, since amid the darkness of night people often fear where they might be safe, just as, conversely, they are very often wrongly secure where they ought to fear.

In accordance with this comparison, ambiguous temptation frequently agitates the human mind with varied and vain disturbances and disquiets it with foolish suspicions. Therefore assured security from the Lord’s help is rightly promised to the devout mind concerning this temptation: “You will not fear the terror of the night.”

He intended to signify sudden temptation by “the arrow flying” when he subsequently added: “The arrow flying by day.” I do not know whether it could be described more fittingly or more concisely. Does not that temptation rush upon us with the force of a flying arrow which often shakes or drives the mind from its settled state before it can fully awaken to guard itself? For an arrow, once shot, is usually carried with such force that the blow as it comes can scarcely or not at all be avoided. And it often happens that, once you see it coming, you feel yourself wounded before you can set the shield of defense against its onrush. Thus the Psalmist rightly compares to a flying arrow a temptation which forestalls the human mind by the excess of its swiftness.

But arrows of this kind sometimes fly at night and sometimes by day. Do you wish to know arrows flying at night? “They have prepared,” he says, “their arrows in the quiver, that they may shoot the upright in heart in darkness.” And in this place you have the arrow flying by day. The arrow flies at night when sudden temptation strikes the mind and conceals that the evil it urges is evil. But it flies by day when it casts the mind headlong into an evil which nevertheless cannot be unknown to be evil. Thus sudden and hidden temptation, composed of a twofold kind of temptation, is described in the words: “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver, that they may shoot the upright in heart in darkness.” But in this place “the arrow flying by day” is spoken of, so that it should be understood as said of sudden temptation that is simple and unmixed.

Therefore let it be said concerning the doubtful temptation, and likewise concerning sudden temptation: “You will not fear the terror of the night; you will not fear the arrow flying by day.” Then concerning the hidden temptation there is added: “The business that walks about in darkness.”

We all know well what that business is which hates the light, loves darkness, and always fears being caught at night—or rather, as Scripture says, is accustomed to walk about in darkness. Thieves wishing to carry out the business of theft, because they fear detection, choose a suitable time for that work; and they seek not merely night, but a dark night, so that they may carry out their crimes all the more safely the more secretly they perform them. Thus this hateful business is conducted not so much at night as in darkness, because it is conducted on dark nights. Therefore it walks in darkness—indeed, it walks about in darkness—for those who undertake it always observe that the undertaking they have begun must be carried out and completed before the return of light.

You see, then, by what fitting comparison hidden temptation is described: it is always covered by the darkness of ignorance, and through it the unwary mind is despoiled while knowing and understanding nothing. Oh, how often it happens that, while the master of the house sleeps securely and rests in deep slumber, he does not know that robbers are robbing him; and he first recognizes his loss when he awakes to the morning light! So indeed, so often through hidden temptation we lose the spoils of virtues without knowing it, while we endure the deep darkness of ignorance and are overcome by the sleep of false security. And it often happens that the mind first recognizes the losses of its merits when, made worse amid the darkness of this life, it awakens to the light of the life to come, when God begins to reveal the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts.

Should not that malicious and abominable business be believed to have walked and walked about in darkness when hidden temptation causes the plundering of our virtues to remain largely concealed from us and not to be fully detected throughout all the shadowy time of this life?

In describing violent temptation, the Prophet calls it “an assault”; I do not know whether it could be comprehended or described more briefly and expressively. Who, seeing an enemy at a distance, would not strive rather to flee than to run toward him, unless he knew himself able to prevail by confidence in the greatness of his strength, the number of his allies, or his equipment [Col. 0394C] of weapons? But an enemy charges upon an enemy with force when he has learned that he can gain the upper hand. Therefore that temptation is rightly understood through “assault,” by which the human mind is, as it were, violently cast down from the state of its uprightness.

It should be noted that in such an assault, although we may discern a certain haste, it is nevertheless nothing like the swiftness described above in sudden temptation, through which we taught that even the judgment of reason is often forestalled. Such preoccupation cannot be understood through an assault, where, to say nothing else, from the mere noise of the onrushing arrival one can foresee its imminence and thus either take flight or arm oneself. Therefore, as has been said, violent temptation can rightly be understood through an assault.

Let us now see how the Prophet describes deceitful temptation, or how he secures constancy against it through divine help. “He who dwells in the aid of the Most High and trusts in the protection of the God of heaven: you will not fear,” he says, “the noonday demon.” Certainly, the person who trusts not in his own ability but in God’s help alone need not fear the noonday demon.

Let us see, then, what is meant by his saying not simply “demon,” but “noonday demon,” with that addition or specification. We all commonly know that the constant business of all demons is to harass God’s servants, persist in attacking them, and continually watch for their overthrow. And indeed, when they cannot prevail against us by force, they turn to deceit, that they may cast down by trickery those whom they could not overthrow by violence.

Who does not know that at the noonday hour there are normally both greater brightness and more intense heat? Demons thus come to us with supreme brightness and heat when, concealing the wickedness of their deceit, they strive and labor to lead us into perversity under a show of holiness. Light pertains to discernment and heat to devotion. Therefore demons come to us with light and brightness when, in what they deceitfully suggest, they promise—and endeavor to persuade us—that we shall act not only discerningly but devoutly. It often happens that the mind, made foolish by such deceitful temptation, becomes so senseless that in the very thing it does at demonic persuasion it believes itself both wiser than all others and holier in its conduct.

In this way Satan’s angel transforms himself into an angel of light; under the appearance of virtue and form of holiness he offers counsels of error and carries out the business of iniquity. In this way, I say, the noonday demon deceitfully trips up some persons and makes them so foolish that, in their singular practices, which they presume to undertake concerning the counsels of their brethren and the commands of the Fathers—indeed, in their rebellions, which they continually commit against their superiors, they think themselves wiser than all others and holier than all others. You now see, I think, how rightly the Prophet designates such deceitful temptation by the noonday demon: it trips up the human mind under a show of holiness.

There remains one only: the manifold and perplexing temptation, indeed fiercer than the rest and, as we have said, the most destructive of all. For this too is readily perceived from its description, if it is rightly understood and carefully weighed. Consider, then, what is said concerning it, and you will recognize how far beyond human capacity is what is promised concerning it—except perhaps to the one who abides in the protection of the God of heaven: “A thousand,” he says, “shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.”

Here one must first observe how aptly this expresses the figure of one fighting bravely and acting manfully, when it says that some fall at his side and others at his right hand. For in battle a soldier carries in his left hand the shield by which the blows of assailants are ordinarily received, and consequently presents his left side to those standing against him. When a strong warrior acts with strength, it often happens that, as he charges forcefully against enemies, he knocks down some with the thrust of his side and lays others low with the striking of his right hand. Consider, therefore, what great power and remarkable strength it is, with the side pushing, to bring down a thousand, and with the right hand striking, to overthrow ten thousand.

From this we can readily perceive what we ought to think about that spiritual conflict. In this spiritual battle a twofold host of vices is at war. Some vices are carnal, others spiritual; some are exercised in outward acts, while others are accomplished spiritually by the will alone and the heart’s delight. Therefore, if the stronger are rightly understood through the right hand and the weaker through the left, why should not carnal vices be referred to the left and spiritual ones to the right? For spiritual vices attack the spirit far more closely, far more powerfully, and indeed far more frequently than carnal vices: the former do so immediately, the latter only through the mediation of the flesh.

We triumph over carnal vices through discipline of the body, but over spiritual vices through discipline of the heart. Thus bodily discipline appropriately belongs to the left hand, just as discipline of the heart belongs to the right. Who does not know that the movement of the heart is far more changeable than that of the body, and the excess of the will more abundant than that of action? Beyond doubt, the aberration of thoughts and affections is far more numerous than the misuse of limbs or senses. Spiritual corruption is therefore more abundant than bodily corruption, and the encounter of spiritual vices much denser than the encounter of bodily vices.

Against both sorts of enemies of the soul we must surely fight bravely. Some must be crushed by affliction of the body; others, afflicted by contrition of the heart, so that the former may be cast down by the left hand and the latter by the right. Therefore the number of enemies falling at the right hand is much greater than that of those collapsing at the side, so that Scripture promises and says: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.”

Such battle and victory are not, and cannot be, for anyone except strong men, and indeed those most skilled in warfare: such as Abishai, who “lifted his spear against three hundred, whom he killed, renowned among the three and more distinguished among the three” (1 Chron. 10); or such as David, seated in the seat of wisdom, the wisest leader among the three, who killed eight hundred in one charge; or finally such as that strongest of men, who struck down a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass. Therefore, I think, someone must be long exercised and greatly tested in other matters before being able to prevail in this final temptation.

I think it was not without reason that he treated this last temptation separately. The same is found in blessed Job: concerning six he speaks together beforehand, and concerning the seventh he adds separately: “In six tribulations,” he says, “he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil shall not seize you” (Job 5). The Prophet, however, sets the first separately as though it were lighter than all the rest, and the last separately as though it were heavier than all the rest; he joins the other five under one clause, saying: “His truth will surround you as a shield”—this is understood of the first—but then, concerning the following five together, he adds: “You will not fear the terror of the night, the arrow flying by day, the business that walks about in darkness, the assault, and the noonday demon.” Finally, concerning the last, he adds what is placed last: “A thousand shall fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand.”

These seven temptations, which he here sets out in one continuous sequence, the Prophet elsewhere touches upon in various places, now one, now several. Of the importunate temptation he says elsewhere: “All day long they prepared battles” (Ps. 139). Since ignorance is signified by night and understanding by day, the mind is rightly said to be attacked by day [Col. 0397A] when it feels itself tempted by things that it manifestly recognizes as evil. Thus temptation attacks us all day, and battle presses upon us, when open evil shamelessly thrusts itself forward, in order at last to overcome by persistence what it cannot prevail over by deceit or violence.

Concerning doubtful temptation, the same Prophet says elsewhere: “Contempt was poured out upon princes, and he caused them to wander in a trackless place and not on a way” (Ps. 106). We know well who are the princes or rulers of that inner household: namely, the mind’s deliberations and discernments, which ought carefully to equip, firmly fortify, wisely order, and faithfully lead through the path of equity and the track of the commandments—that terrible cohort of virtues—amid so many enemy snares, into that land of promise flowing with milk and honey; and to lead it through bravely and introduce it faithfully.

But harsh contention is poured out upon such princes, and people truly wander from the way of truth, when, as their merits require, the light of revealing grace is withdrawn and the blinded mind is divided among various judgments, because one who investigates more carefully and deliberates longer cannot discover what it ought more rightly choose or what certainty it ought hold.

Notably, when the light of truth has been withdrawn, one first goes astray on the road, and afterwards goes astray where there is no road. They go astray on the road who, in the good things they do, do not know—or refuse—to keep measure or proportion, while they venture upon many things not merely contrary to counsel but even contrary to command. They go astray where there is no road when, in the evils which they now openly commit, they begin to doubt whether these are good or evil. The following is to be understood of sudden temptation, which elsewhere the same Prophet says: “The snares of death came before me” (Ps. XVII). Consent to wickedness is the true death of the soul, while the snare of death is attachment to wrongful pleasure. By the binding force of wrongful pleasure the mind is drawn into consenting to wickedness. Thus the affections of perverse pleasure become snares of death. Therefore an unwary mind is overtaken by the snares of death whenever, before it can flee to the stronghold of its watchfulness, it is laid low by wrongful pleasure. But concerning hidden temptation the Prophet beseeches the Lord when, in his prayers, he cries to him: “For thou lightest my lamp, O Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. XVII). The lamp of the heart is the judgment of discernment; this lamp of our heart is illuminated by the Lord whenever our understanding is enlightened by illuminating grace and directed toward the judgment of truth. Human discernment is wholly and beyond doubt powerless for the judgment of truth unless it is enlightened by that light which enlightens every person coming into this world. From him, therefore, by whose action he understands that he understood rightly the things which he did understand, he asks and awaits the power to understand his hidden things, which he feared he had not yet been able to understand. For he calls his hidden things “darkness,” which he asks the Lord to enlighten, when he says: “For thou lightest my lamp, [Col. 0398A] O Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness.” He laments violent temptation when elsewhere the same Prophet says: “Behold, they have seized my soul; the mighty have rushed upon me” (Ps. LVIII). The mighty undoubtedly rush upon one when violent temptations oppress the soul and violently drive it toward the ruin of its corruption, so that it may truthfully say: “Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me.” And perhaps they already hold the soul captive, but do not yet hold the spirit, when they possess the human mind through wrongful pleasure, though not yet through consent to wickedness. But those who feel that they are already held by violent pleasure and know that they cannot endure themselves thus for long should swiftly flee to the aid of prayer and seek the help of divine protection, lest, weighed down by the force of [Col. 0398B] vehement temptation, they fall headlong into the precipice of wrongful consent.

He prayed to the Lord against deceitful temptation when the same Prophet said: “Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. CXIX). A deceitful tongue is deceitful temptation; a deceitful tongue is false opinion; a deceitful tongue is empty self-glorification. Whenever you glory in your merits, whether in open speech or silent thought, you hear a deceitful tongue and do not know it. Such vain glorification sometimes arises from human opinion, sometimes from diabolical suggestion; in either case it comes from an unjust tongue, from a deceitful tongue. Certainly, if you willingly listen to such a tongue, you act not only foolishly but unjustly. “What have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” Consider, then, how unjust it is to be ungrateful besides toward one who gives freely, and to commit robbery against him. You attempt to take from him what he wishes to reserve for himself alone: “My glory,” he says, “I will not give to another” (Isa. XLII). If, then, the person who glories in himself over his good things is so foolish and acts so unjustly, how greatly, I ask, is the one made foolish who is brought even to glory in his evils? Therefore, whenever such vain thoughts clamour within you, crying to you, “Well done, well done,” do not cease to cry out to the Lord your God: “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ immediately bear their confusion.” And say also: “Lord, deliver my soul from unjust lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

Elsewhere the Prophet laments manifold and perplexing temptation when he says: “Those who hate me without cause are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head” (Ps. LVIII). The hairs of the head are the counsels of the heart. Such a head has such hairs. This kind of growth of hair both protects and adorns that head of the inward person, and makes the whole form of the inward person more becoming. For from whatever quarter the wind of malignant suggestion bursts forth, this mane of our hairs is accustomed—and ought—to protect that inward head against the whirlwind of temptation. But when the storm of temptations grows beyond measure, it often happens that, without the covering of divine protection, the mane of our counsels cannot at all suffice to ward off the assault of such storms.

Therefore, when the snares of enemies are multiplied on every side, [Col. 0399A] human prudence wholly fails against so many arguments of seduction, and human counsels cannot suffice against so many frauds of diabolical malice. One may indeed sing concerning his enemies who is in such a condition: “Those who hate me without cause are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” Again, concerning importunate temptation, the same Prophet says elsewhere: “Assailing me all day, he troubled me” (Ps. LV). And concerning doubtful temptation, elsewhere the same says: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a waterless place; they found no way to a city of habitation” (Ps. CVI). Concerning sudden temptation: “They came before me on the day of my affliction” (Ps. XVII). Again, concerning hidden temptation: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Ps. XVIII). And again concerning the same: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. XXIV). Elsewhere he says concerning violent temptation: “And they used violence, who sought my soul” (Ps. XXXVII). This too is understood of deceitful temptation: “They devised to trip up my steps” (Ps. CXXXIX). And concerning manifold and perplexing temptation it was said: “I will not fear thousands of people surrounding me” (Ps. III).

Thus, as may be gathered from what has been said, it belongs to importunate temptation always to disturb the mind and never permit it to be at rest. Doubtful temptation, however, is accustomed to agitate the mind and make it always wandering and fugitive. For what else do we think nocturnal fear accomplishes except to make the mind timid and trembling, and to shake it with utmost horror where there ought to be nothing to fear? Such a soul flees when no one pursues it; and even in peace it always suspects [Col. 0399C] war. Sudden temptation wounds the soul and pierces the affections with the dart of pleasure. And what else ought one to expect from the flying arrow? Hidden temptation, in the respect in which it prevails, is accustomed always to blind the mind, walking ever in darkness and transacting all its business in darkness. Violent temptation always oppresses the mind by force and utterly enfeebles it. Deceitful temptation is accustomed to make the mind foolish. For what else would the noonday demon do but make the mind foolish or drive it into madness? Manifold temptation always rends, scatters, and distracts the mind. For amid the multitude of assailants, in this temptation it is as though torn into pieces bit by bit and perhaps variously mangled by many kinds of disturbances. Thus the first temptation disturbs, the second agitates, the third wounds, the fourth blinds, the fifth enfeebles, the sixth makes foolish, the seventh rends.

When importunate temptation begins to dominate and wholly prevail in the mind, it certainly bears the form of an acute fever, which makes the sufferer pant every hour under continual heat and allows no interruption at all.

There are some who, according to this type, suffer continual weariness in certain of their desires, so much so that they can scarcely—or not at all—remove the heat of their desire from the eyes of their mind. Yet that supreme physician of our salvation heals such a soul when he wills, commanding the fever, and it leaves her. Doubtful temptation, which is accustomed to make the mind fearful and wavering in the determination of its judgment, seems to me to exhibit the form of a lame person. For it now approves, now condemns, one and the same thing. Now it raises the mind into confidence; now it again casts it down into distrust. Where the mind has confidence, there it plants the foot of its action as though more firmly; but where it distrusts, there it in some manner holds its foot suspended, and thus displays the type of one who limps. How many do we see who labour under such a condition for much, or even all, of their lives: what pleases them today displeases them tomorrow; what they long for deeply and long, they again disdain with the same ease; they always desire what they do not have, always disdain what they do have, always pass from work to work, leave one thing after another—and everything—unfinished, beginning everything and completing nothing. Yet we should not despair even of such lame persons. For we have heard in the Gospel that many lame persons were healed by our physician, and we see many healed daily by him.

Sudden temptation undoubtedly bears the form of the disease of the lunatic, who, wherever it seizes a person, dashes him down and throws him to the ground, often casting him into fire or water. I do not know whether any other disease so suddenly seizes a person, since it leaves him not even the slightest interval of time in which, if he is found near fire or water, he might draw himself back even a little from fire or water. So indeed it often happens under sudden temptation that, at a single glance or thought of the mind, the soul is burned with the heat of lust or the frost of envy, and is suddenly hurled now into unlawful love, now into unjust hatred. Hidden temptation clouds the eye of the mind and represents the condition of that blind man in the Gospel: although he sits beside the way of devotion amid temptation, he nevertheless does not see it by the illumination of discernment. Therefore one who endures such blindness must cry out strongly: “Make thy face to shine upon thy servant, and teach me thy ordinances.” The person whom violent temptation enfeebles bears the form of the paralytic, because this affliction leaves a person with no strength and no power. For a person oppressed by this affliction can never raise himself to a standing position; nor, even when raised by others, can he remain by himself in his position for even a short time. But one besieged and oppressed by deceitful temptation certainly bears the form of a demoniac: for what else would the noonday demon make him but a demoniac? Often one driven by such an affliction becomes at once deaf and mute, so that he never wishes to acknowledge his error and refuses in every way to heed one who admonishes or commands him; rather, whatever he foolishly or wickedly raves, he claims as evidence of the greatness of his own prudence and skill.

But one who allows himself to be overcome by manifold temptation bears the form of one already dead—not merely any dead person, but a corpse already decaying and putrid, which is subject to decay on every side and swarms everywhere with worms. One who is such may now say: “By night my bone is pierced with pains, and those who devour me do not sleep. My garment is consumed by their multitude” (Job 30). In some persons this enormity of foulness rules only in thought; in others it rules also in action. The former prostitute their minds to every filthy thought and shameful pleasure; the latter are not ashamed to apply themselves to every foul action. The former swarm with the worms of their decay in thought; the latter display the same corruption of their stench in deed. What, then, should I call the former but a putrid corpse that is buried, whose corruption lies hidden as it were in secret? And what should I call the latter but a putrid corpse cast out, whose corruption is manifest far and wide to all? But in all these things our physician Jesus displays his mastery of his art and gladly meets the prayers of all who seek him devoutly and ask in faith. For he heals lunatics and enlightens the blind, cures paralytics and cleanses demoniacs, and raises the dead. At the voice of Jesus calling, the man four days dead came forth from the tomb (John XI); and at the touch of the true Elisha, a cast-out corpse came back to life (IV Kings XIII). Thus the first temptation, when it begins to dominate, in some manner, as was said, makes one sick; the second makes one lame; the third a lunatic; the fourth blind; the fifth a paralytic; the sixth a demoniac; the seventh a dead person already putrid.

## EXPOSITION OF THE CANTICLE OF HABAKKUK

[Col. 0401]

[Col. 0401B] “In the midst of the years thou shalt make known” (Hab. III). What the Apostle calls “the fullness of time” (Gal. IV), the prophet Habakkuk calls “the midst of the years.” By an analogy from the human body, a statement is made concerning Christ’s body, when the prophet foresees what is to come or proclaims at what time it will come. For we pass through half our years by growing, both in stature and strength; but we spend the half that remains by gradually declining. Up to the age of thirty or forty-five, each person becomes daily greater than himself; but from forty years onward, declining from his strength, he becomes day by day less than himself. This, if I am not mistaken, occurs in Christ’s body; anyone who considers Christ’s body more subtly can readily see it—I mean the head with its members.

For at the beginning of the world, as though it were still a child, it was enough for the faithful merely to believe in God and please him through offerings or sacrifices. But it reached adolescence when it received the command of circumcision and the observances of the Law. It did not yet know—or rather, was not yet able—to leave its own things for the Lord or to lay down its life for Christ in death. But after the fullness of time had come, after it had reached full age, after it had passed through half its years—when, as we have said, the body’s stature is greater and its strength more robust—it received higher commands and splendidly fulfilled those received. For now it is told: “Love your enemies” (Matt. V); “If thou wilt be perfect, go, sell all that thou hast and give to the poor” (Luke VI); “He who loves his life more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X). But we know that no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. It is clear, therefore, that the body of Christ, which is the Church, reached full age and passed through the midst of its years when it was able even to love its enemies for the Lord’s sake, when it was fit to love its Lord even unto death.

At that time, therefore, the time foretold through Habakkuk was at hand: “In the midst of the years thou shalt make known.” Yet what was then to be made known, which perhaps the Lord has now made known? What, I ask, but that mystery previously hidden, which none of the rulers of this world knew? What, I say, but that height of the divine counsel concerning the salvation of humankind? I confidently assert that until that time no one fully knew how much God loved human salvation: he “did not spare even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” It was altogether fitting that it should then become known to humankind that God loved humanity even to the straits of human weakness, even to the reproaches of the cross and death, when humanity too was fit to despise all things in this world for the Lord and moreover to lay down its own life for him in death. But just as it ought not previously to have been revealed to humanity while it was still, as it were, weaker, so beyond doubt it ought not thereafter to have remained hidden.

Consider now where are the constancy of the martyrs and the abstinence of the confessors: almost all of this has now failed in these times. Why is this, unless the world is already declining into old age, because it has now passed the middle of its years? Therefore, because before the middle of the years that secret of the divine counsel could not be revealed to the world, still as it were weak, and because it ought not to remain hidden beyond the middle of its years, when it was necessarily to decline from its strength, it is rightly said: “In the midst of the years thou shalt make known.”

But perhaps it is more pleasing if we speak here in a moral sense: “In the midst of the years thou shalt make known.” A certain time seems to be described when God wishes to reveal some great thing, I know not what, to those who have pleased him. We find a wondrous and ineffable sweetness often described in the holy Scriptures and frequently promised to us; the more attentively it is commended, the more ardently it is desired. In Moses it is understood through the land flowing with milk and honey. In the Wisdom of Solomon it is described through food having every delight in itself and every flavour. The Apostle describes it more plainly; the Lord openly promises it in the Gospel: “What eye has not seen,” says the Apostle, “nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II). But the Lord promises a hundredfold in this age, for all that a person leaves for his love, and eternal life in the age to come (Matt. XIX).

Do you see how God, speaking in many portions and many ways to the fathers through prophets or apostles, but in these last days also speaking to us through his Son, promises something new, something great, which no one will be able to know what it is except those who have deserved to experience it? For it is hidden manna, as blessed John declares in the Apocalypse (Apoc. II), and the apostle Paul testifies that it has not entered into the heart of man. Yet he shows that it has been revealed to himself and to those like him when he says: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (I Cor. II); for the Lord expressly promises a hundredfold in the present age, lest this be expected in the future. Yet according to the letter this cannot stand. For one who has left one wife will not have a hundred in this age; nor in the age to come, where they neither marry nor are given in marriage, will he have even one.

But because sacred Scripture is accustomed to signify something heavenly through the number one hundred, when a hundredfold is promised, sweetness is promised in return for sweetness: heavenly for carnal, spiritual for animal, angelic for earthly, divine for human. But you say: “Behold, we have left all things; what then shall we have?” Or rather: when shall that which is promised be given to us? We no longer doubt the promise, but we are still uncertain about the time. Nor do we now ask what it is which cannot be known except by one who has received it. No doubt is left us that it will be given, since it is promised by the testimony of so many great men. Only tell us when these things will be, and what sign there will be when they begin to happen. It is certainly not mine to know times or seasons; and what I myself have not merited to know, I cannot disclose to others. But let the prophet Habakkuk himself answer for me; let him himself satisfy you on my behalf by his answer: “In the midst,” he says, “of the years thou shalt make known.”

Wondrous is the Prophet’s prudence: he wished you to know, but did not wish to tell you. If he were speaking to us, who could doubt that he speaks of this, as one who would not dare lie? He did not wish, therefore, to say, “In the midst of the years he will make known”; but he says, “In the midst of the years thou shalt make known.” See, then, whether you who desire these things to be made known to you, who long for them to be revealed to you, have now come to the middle of your years, whether you have now reached perfect age. For in middle age, as we all know, bodily stature is greater and strength more robust. I believe that the person has come to the middle of years who can truthfully say: “But he has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (I Cor. II).

“But,” you say, “how many have left all their possessions for the Lord and yet never tasted these spiritual delights in this present age; and they were still such that the Lord gave them milk to drink, not solid food.” Perhaps they were still like newborn infants and utterly incapable of receiving solid food. Moreover, some die in childhood; some are taken away in adolescence. Certainly none of these could reach that time of life of which the prophet Habakkuk says: “In the midst of the years thou shalt make known.” Yet I think that the kingdom of heaven belongs even to such persons, because it is written: “Thine eyes saw my imperfection, and in thy book all shall be written” (Ps. CXXXVII). For one who begins here to live well will at some time, even in the future age, come to the middle of his years. For divine grace then accomplishes in him what he could not here fulfill by himself, provided that he passes from this life to that one without a mortal wound.

[Col. 0404B] A mortal wound is a grave sin. For one who dies in grave sin is brought to the middle of his years neither here nor in the future. “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days.” For when do those arrive at the middle of their years—that is, at the robust age of virtues—who never begin to grow in good? If, therefore, you wish to attain these promises of the Lord, hasten to arrive at robust age, as it were at the middle of your years. I mean years of merits, not of time. As much as you make progress, so much you grow. Whoever attains the summit of virtue has completed half his years, because he has reached, as it were, the robust years of merits.

It must be known that negligence lies in wait for those still growing, while pride creeps upon those grown and advanced to full age. But as much as you neglect, so much you decrease, as though you were going backward. For whoever is found in negligence is without doubt recalled backward. Pray, therefore, to the Lord and say: “Do not call me back in the midst of my days.” Beware negligence; detest pride. For the mind quickly raises itself in pride when it sees that it has grown to the summit of virtue. But the higher anyone raises himself above himself through pride, the lower, God abandoning him, he is cast beneath himself through fault, as it is written: “They rise up to the heavens, and descend to the depths” (Ps. CVI). Hence it is said through Hezekiah: “I said, in the midst of my days I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. XXXVIII). For he marvels that, after completing half his years and growing in merits to the summit of virtue, he falls back to the gates of hell, though a little before he rejoiced that he had touched the heavens.

There are two gates of hell, which lead those entering through them into every evil. One is ignorance of good; the other, desire for evil. He foresaw that he would descend to these gates of death because he found that, on account of the mind’s self-exaltation, he had been abandoned by God. But he immediately fled to prayer and obtained that he should not die. What does it mean that King Hezekiah falls sick but by praying is delivered from death? It means that the mind of an elect person is often drawn after self-exaltation into pleasure, but through prayer is raised up before the death of wrongful consent.

[Col. 0405]

# EXPLANATION OF THE SONG OF SONGS

## PROLOGUE

> [Note: [Col. 0405D] This prologue is considered by some to be by St. Gregory, because it follows word for word his prologue to the Song of Songs. I, however, think it should be attributed to Richard, first because it has his style; also because it draws not a little from Richard’s rather than Gregory’s teaching—though such material is omitted by Gregory; and finally because it is attached in the manuscript to the following explanation. Let the discerning reader judge.]

[Col. 0405A]

After the human race was expelled from the joys of paradise and came into this pilgrimage of the present life, it has a heart blind to spiritual understanding. If one were to say to this blind heart in a human voice, “Follow God,” or “Love God,” as was said to it in the Law, once cast outside and made cold by the torpor of unbelief, it would not grasp what it heard. Therefore divine speech speaks to the torpid and cold soul through certain riddles, and through things it knows secretly suggests to it the love it does not know. Allegory creates for the soul set far from God a kind of engine by which it may be raised to God; for, with riddles interposed, while it recognizes in the words something that belongs to itself, it understands in the meaning of the words something that does not belong to itself, and through earthly words it is separated from the earth. For by means of what it recognizes without aversion, it understands something unknown. From things known to us, through which allegories are fashioned, divine meanings are fashioned; and while we recognize the outward words, we arrive at inward understanding.

Thus, in this book written as the Song of Songs, words of what is apparently bodily love are set forth, so that the soul, stirred by words familiar to its bodily experience, may grow warm again, and by the words of love which is below may be awakened to the love which is above. For kisses are named in this book, breasts are named, cheeks are named, thighs are named. Sacred Scripture is not to be mocked in these words; rather, the greater mercy of God is to be considered, because, while it names the members of the body, it thereby calls us to love.

It must be noted that he is wondrously with us and works mercifully. In order to kindle our heart at the prompting of sacred love, he descended even to the words of our shameful love. But from the very source in which he humbles himself in speech, he exalts us in understanding, because from the discourse of this love we learn by what power of this love we should burn in love of the Divinity. We must, however, carefully observe this: when we hear words of outward love, we must not remain in outward perceptions, lest the engine placed to lift us should itself weigh us down more heavily, so that we are not lifted. Therefore, in these bodily and outward words we must seek whatever is inward and, while they speak of the body, become as though outside the body.

We ought to come to these nuptials of bridegroom and bride with the understanding of inward charity—that is, with the wedding garment, namely a worthy understanding of charity. If we are not clothed with it, we shall be driven from this wedding feast into outer darkness, that is, into the blindness of ignorance. Through these words of passion we must pass to the virtue of impassibility. For sacred Scripture is in its words and meanings as a painting is in its colours and subjects. One is exceedingly foolish who clings to the colours of a painting in such a way as to ignore the things painted. If we embrace only the words spoken outwardly and ignore their meanings, we are like persons who, ignorant of the painted objects, hold only the colours. “The letter kills,” as it is written, “but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III). For the letter covers the spirit as chaff covers grain; but to eat chaff belongs to beasts, grain to human beings. Therefore one who uses human reason should cast away the chaff of beasts and hasten to eat the grain of the Spirit.

For this purpose it is useful that the mysteries should be hidden beneath the covering of the letter. Hence it is written: “The wise shall hide understanding” (Prov. X), because spiritual understanding is indeed covered beneath the veil of the letter. Hence again Scripture says in the same book: “It is the glory of God to conceal a word” (Prov. XXV). For to the mind seeking God, God appears more gloriously the more subtly and inwardly he is investigated in order that he may appear. But ought we not to inquire into the things which God hides in mysteries? Certainly we ought.

For it follows: “And it is the glory of kings to search out a matter.” Those who have already learned to govern and examine their bodies or the movements of the flesh are kings. Therefore it is the glory of kings to search out a matter, because it is the praise of those who live well to investigate the secrets of God’s commandments. When, therefore, we hear words concerning human life, we ought to be as though human beings from the earth, lest, if we hear what is said merely in a human way, we be unable to perceive anything divine in what we ought to hear. Paul desired his disciples no longer to be human beings, as it were, when he said: “For while there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not human?” (I Cor. III). The Lord, as it were, no longer regarded his disciples as human beings when he said: “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. XVI). When they answered with the words of men, he immediately added: “But whom do you say that I am?” Since he first says “men” and then adds, “but you,” he makes a certain distinction between men and his disciples, because, while imparting divine things to them, he made them rise above humanity, as the Apostle says: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away” (II Cor. V).

And we know that in our resurrection the body is so joined to the spirit that everything which had been subject to passion is assumed into the strength of the spirit. Therefore one who follows God ought daily to imitate this in his reason, so that even now he may have nothing passible in his heart, according to the inward person becoming already a new creation. Let him trample down whatever is old, and in ancient words seek only the power of newness. For sacred Scripture is a certain mountain from which the Lord comes into our hearts for understanding, of which mountain it is said through the prophet: “God shall come from Lebanon, and the Holy One from a shadowy and thickly wooded mountain” (Hab. III). This mountain is thick with judgments and shadowy with allegories.

But it must be known that when the voice of the Lord sounds on the mountain, we are commanded to wash our garments and cleanse ourselves of every defilement of the flesh, if we hasten to approach the mountain. For it is written: “If even a beast touch the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Heb. XII). A beast touches the mountain when persons given over to irrational impulses approach the height of sacred Scripture and understand it not as they ought, but irrationally twist it to an interpretation serving their own pleasure. Every absurd or mentally sluggish person, if seen around this mountain, should be slain by most severe judgments, like stones. For this mountain burns, because sacred Scripture, spiritually filled with the fire of love, kindles. Hence it is written: “Thy word is exceedingly fiery” (Ps. CXVIII). Thus, when certain persons walking on the way heard the words of God, they said: “Was not our heart burning within us when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke XXIV). Thus it is said through Moses: “A fiery law in his right hand” (Deut. XXXIII). By God’s left hand are understood the wicked, who do not pass to the right side. God’s right hand consists of the elect, who are separated from those on the left. Therefore there is a fiery law in God’s right hand, because divine commandments are fragrant in the hearts of the elect, who are to be set at the right hand, and are kindled by the ardour of charity. May this fire burn away whatever rust and oldness is outward in us, and offer our mind as a holocaust in the contemplation of God.

[Col. 0407D] It is not without significance that this book is called not simply “a song,” but “the Song of Songs.” For as in the Old Testament some things are holy, others the Holy of Holies; some are sabbaths, others Sabbaths of Sabbaths; so in sacred Scripture some are songs and others Songs of Songs. Holy things were those performed outwardly in the tabernacle; sabbaths were those celebrated in individual weeks; but the Holy of Holies was approached with a more secret reverence, and Sabbaths of Sabbaths were observed only at the highest festivals. This Song of Songs is a secret and a certain inward solemnity, a secret penetrated in the hidden places of one who understands. For if attention is given merely to the outward words, it is not a secret.

It must also be known that in sacred Scripture some songs are songs of victory; others are songs of exhortation and solemn witness; others are songs of exultation; others songs of help; others songs of union with God. The song of victory is that which Moses sang after crossing the Red Sea: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honoured; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. XV). The song of exhortation and solemn witness is that which Moses spoke when the Israelites were approaching the land of promise: “Give heed, O heaven, to what I speak; let the earth hear the words from my mouth” (Deut. XXXII). The song of exultation is that which Hannah sang, beholding in herself the fruitfulness of the Church: “My heart has exulted in the Lord” (I Kings II). There she expressed, through the fruitfulness represented in herself, the fruitfulness of the Church’s offspring, when she said: “The barren woman has borne many, and she who had many has become weak” (ibid.). David sang the song of help after battle: “I will love thee, O Lord, my strength” (Ps. XVII). But the song of union with God is that sung at the nuptials of bridegroom and bride, namely the Song of Songs. It surpasses all songs as much as it is offered in nuptials of a more exalted solemnity. By those songs vices are avoided; by this one each person is enriched with virtues. By those, the enemy is guarded against; by this one, the Lord is embraced with familiar love.

And it should be noted that in Sacred Scripture the Lord sometimes calls himself Lord, sometimes Father, sometimes Bridegroom. For when he wishes to be feared, he names himself Lord; when he wishes to be honored, Father; [Col. 0408C] when he wishes to be loved, Bridegroom. For he himself says through the prophet: “If I am Lord, where is my fear? If I am Father, where is my honor?” (Mal. 1). And again he says: “I have betrothed you to myself in righteousness and faith” (Hos. 2). Or indeed: “I remembered the day of your betrothal in the wilderness.” But because he first wishes to be feared, so that he may be honored, and first to be honored, so that one may come to him—he calls himself Lord on account of fear, Father on account of honor, and Bridegroom on account of love. Through fear one comes to honor, and through his honor one comes to love. For as honor is worthier than fear, so God rejoices more to be called Father than Lord. And as love is dearer than honor, so God rejoices more to be called Bridegroom than Father. Therefore in this book the Lord [Col. 0408D] and the Church are named not Lord and handmaid, but Bridegroom and bride, so that service may be rendered not only to fear, not only to reverence, but also to love, and that inward affection may be stirred by these outward words. When he calls himself Lord, he indicates that we were created; when he calls himself Father, that we were adopted; when he calls himself Bridegroom, that we have been joined to him. But to be joined to God is greater than to be created and adopted. Therefore, in this book, where he is called Bridegroom, something more sublime is suggested, since in it the covenant of union is displayed. These names are frequently recalled in the New Testament, because the union of Word and flesh, of Christ and the Church, has now been accomplished and celebrated. Thus John [Col. 0409A] says, while the Lord was living: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). Thus the Lord himself says: “The sons of the bridegroom will not fast while the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. 9). Thus it is said also to the Church: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (1 Cor. 11). And again: “That he might present to himself a glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle” (Eph. 5). And again, in the Apocalypse of John: “Blessed are those who are called to the wedding-supper of the Lamb” (Rev. 19). And again there: “And I saw the bride, as though a new bride, descending from heaven” (Rev. 21).

Nor is it remote from a great mystery that this book of Solomon is placed third among his little works. For the ancients said that there are three orders of life: the moral, the natural, and the contemplative. The Greeks called these lives ethical, physical, and theoretical. [Col. 0409B] In Proverbs the moral life is expressed, where it says: “Hear, my son, my wisdom, and incline your ear to my prudence” (Prov. 2). In Ecclesiastes, however, the natural life is expressed. There indeed it is considered that all things tend toward an end, when it says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1). In the Song of Songs the contemplative life is expressed, since in it the coming and vision of the Lord himself is desired, when it is said in the bride’s voice: “Come from Lebanon, come” (Song 4). Or it also signified the orders of the three patriarchs and their lives: namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Abraham held moral life through obedience; Isaac figured the natural life by digging wells. To dig wells in the depths is, through natural inquiry, to examine by investigation all things below. [Col. 0409C] But Jacob held the contemplative life, he who saw angels ascending and descending. Yet since natural inquiry does not lead to perfection unless moral life has first been maintained, Ecclesiastes is rightly placed after Proverbs; and since heavenly contemplation is not beheld unless these falling things below have first been despised, the Song of Songs is rightly placed after Ecclesiastes. One must first order one’s conduct; afterwards one must regard all present things as though they were not present. In the third place, with the purified keenness of the heart, one beholds inward and heavenly things. Thus, by these stages of the books, he made, as it were, a ladder toward contemplation: so that, while one first lives rightly in the world, then despises even the honorable things [Col. 0409D] of the world, finally one may behold even the inner things of God. Thus, generally, the Church awaits the Lord’s coming in this present time; but, more particularly, each soul may behold God’s entrance into its heart as the bridegroom’s entry into the bridal chamber.

And one should know that four speaking persons are introduced in this book: the Bridegroom and the bride; the young women with the bride; and the companies of companions with the Bridegroom. The bride, indeed, is the Church itself; the Bridegroom is the Lord; the young women with the bride are souls just beginning and coming to maturity through new zeal; and the Bridegroom’s companions are either angels, who have often appeared alive to human beings from him, or indeed all the perfected men in the Church [Col. 0410A] who know how to proclaim the truth to humankind. Yet those who separately are young women or companions are together wholly the bride, because together they are wholly the Church; although, with respect to each individual, all these three names may be understood. For whoever loves God perfectly is a bride; whoever preaches the Bridegroom is a companion; whoever, still inexperienced, follows the way of the good is a young woman. Let us therefore strive to be the bride. If we cannot yet achieve this, let us be companions; if we have attained neither of these, let us at least come as young women to this bridal chamber. Since, therefore, we have spoken of the Bridegroom and bride, the Lord and the Church, let us, like young women or companions, hear the Bridegroom’s words, hear the bride’s words, and learn from their speech the ardor of love. Therefore let the holy Church, [Col. 0410B] long awaiting the Lord’s coming and long thirsting for the fountain of life, say how she ought to behold the presence of her Bridegroom, how she desires it.

## CHAPTER I. How God is sought in quiet, and concerning the desire for fuller grace

“On my little bed, by night, I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3).

The soul that seeks God and desires more fully to attain to the love and knowledge of God ought to seek him on its little bed—that is, in the quiet of the mind. For it must be free and rest from the business and disturbance of earthly affairs. Unless it has rested from the care, occupation, and [Col. 0410C] love of external things, it cannot seek God or deserve to find him. God, therefore, is to be sought on the little bed, that is, in quiet of mind; and by night, that is, amid the adversities of temptations and labors, and in the struggle of virtues and vices. For the soul must labor amid many adversities, be delayed by many obstacles, and be wearied by a hard contest before it perfectly corrects its conduct, obtains purity of heart, and deserves to see God. Hence it is rightly said to seek God by night—that is, through adversities and labors. And it is not “on a bed” but “on a little bed,” because the rest enjoyed amid such things is slight and narrow: for vices, former habit, and the memory and pleasure of past sins attack the soul. For this reason she also calls it her little bed, [Col. 0410D] rather than ours, because she cannot possess it in common with the Bridegroom or enjoy him perfectly in such scant repose: for “his place was made in peace,” not in the warfare and turmoil of vices.

In this manner God is sought on the little bed by night by beginners and those not yet perfect. Afterwards he is sought in another way on the little bed and by night, when the soul, with its vices more fully mortified, temptations lulled, and conscience cleansed, has obtained fuller quiet through the grace of the Holy Spirit coming into the mind and calming vices and temptations. According to what is written: “He will break and shatter the bow; he will burn weapons and shields with fire” (Ps. 45). Then the soul will be able to be at leisure and see that the Lord is sweet. Thus [Col. 0411A] peace and tranquillity of mind are the little bed on which the bride rests. On this little bed she seeks the Beloved by night, when desires of the flesh have been lulled, victory has followed struggle and labor, and rest has been given. For by day one labors, and by night one ceases from labor and rests. Therefore, when after the burden of the day and the heat—namely, temptation—the soul comes from labor to the little bed of quiet, and to the night of respite from weariness and disturbance, then, free and at leisure, it will be able to seek the Beloved more effectively. On this little bed and in this night she sleeps, but her heart watches. She sleeps outwardly, but inwardly she watches. And to the degree that she is outwardly quiet and free, she is inwardly occupied and restless in seeking the Beloved. But she seeks him on a little bed and not on a bed, because [Col. 0411B] she does not possess full repose but narrow repose, as long as she does not enjoy the Beloved as she wishes and does not have him with her. Thus she calls the little bed itself her own, as though she alone possessed it and did not yet rest there with the Bridegroom. And therefore she is rightly said to seek by night—that is, in the darkness in which she is held—because she does not enjoy him fully or feel his presence. For he is present in essence and present in desire, and he whom she desires is already possessed, since one could not desire what was in no way possessed; yet he is not present through the revelation of his presence. For he has not yet driven away her darkness or illumined her so that she may feel his presence. Therefore she laments this night, and says that through it she seeks the Beloved yet does not find him. She desires, then, to be illumined and to have the eyes of her heart opened, so that she may find him; and, through grace drawing near, understand his presence, and feel herself seen by him and herself seeing him. For she seeks the illumination of fuller grace, understanding of his presence, and the experience of spiritual sweetness: “I sought,” she says, “him whom my soul loves.”

In the soul’s love we may note spiritual as well as affective love. When we love someone affectionately, we say that we love that person as our own soul—as though she said: “Him whom I love affectionately and spiritually, that is, for the soul’s salvation, not for temporal advantage or fleshly desire.” But the Bridegroom does not always immediately offer himself to one seeking him or present himself to one desiring him. He often delays fulfilling desires in order to increase them, and afterwards reward them when increased and fulfill them more perfectly. At times he also delays these things in order to test the seeker’s constancy, and to grant what is desired more profitably the more slowly he grants it. What is gained with labor is held more closely and guarded more carefully. And sometimes desires fulfilled quickly fail, while delayed desires increase the more. Hence the bride, feeling the delay, ignorant of its dispensation, and impatient in love, complains, saying: “I sought and did not find him” (Song 5). For she does not yet receive the grace she sought and has not yet felt the Bridegroom’s presence.

## CHAPTER II. How the soul considers the examples both of the perfect and of the imperfect

The bride, then, having endured difficulty and been, as it were, repulsed, by no means ceases from seeking but girds herself all the more for the search. [Col. 0412A] For she displays her persistence and constancy, saying: “I will arise and go about the city” (Song 3). She turns herself to humility, that she may seek through others him whom she did not find through herself, if perhaps she may find him through them. With much labor she had prepared a bed for herself: first ceasing from sins, then contending more vigorously against vices, after this withdrawing from occupations and cares, and finally becoming free from harmful activities and even from most good works, so that, diminishing her deeds, she might apprehend wisdom, which is God. But now she turns to going around and investigating the good works of others, that by this labor she may find the Bridegroom whom, in quiet, she had found less fully. She rises from quiet, going about the city. In thought she goes around [Col. 0412B] the assembly of the good, that from them she may receive examples of a better life and lessons in virtue. For in humility she judges herself to lack the adornment of virtues and purity of heart through which she might deserve to find the Bridegroom; she indicates that the house of her mind is free from vices but insufficiently adorned with virtues. To adorn it more fittingly, she goes around and surveys the virtues of the saints, investigates the special grace of each, and plucks flowers of humility from one, patience from another, obedience from another, abstinence from another, charity from another, and purity from another. She strives to transfer these into her conduct by imitation and adorn the house of her mind with them. For she measures the structure—that is, weighs the lives of the saints and considers the construction of virtues in them—so that she may be ashamed of her own imperfection. [Col. 0412C] And, as is read in Job, “he looks upon people,” that is, he attends to the saints (Job 33), so that by comparison with them she may judge herself sinful. Thus, humbled by their examples and fired for progress, she again devotes herself to cleansing her heart and cultivating virtues, so that, with her house more fully cleansed and adorned, she may become worthy to find the Bridegroom.

The bride herself goes about the city—that is, the good—in order to examine their virtues and holiness. And she seeks the Beloved through lanes and streets. Lanes are narrower and streets broader. Thus by lanes are indicated those who, leaving all things and nakedly following the naked Christ, chose for themselves the narrow way of life. By the broader streets, however, we understand the perfect of secular life, who, [Col. 0412D] walking a broader way and not abandoning all their possessions but using what they possessed well, pleased God through hospitality, almsgiving, and other good works. Avoiding the broad way that leads to death, they held to the narrow way of commandments and life. Therefore she seeks the Beloved first through lanes and afterwards through streets.

For because she is borne along by a desire for perfection, she first seeks examples from the perfect. She considers how strict a rule of life they imposed upon themselves; how scant their food was; how poor their clothing; how brief their sleep; how severe their bodily labor; how strict their discipline of heart; and how in all things they cut off bodily pleasures and drew out the heart’s self-will. Afterwards she considers how great was their loftiness and freedom of mind, and how, though dwelling in flesh, [Col. 0413A] they lived in heaven; how they transcended and trampled upon all earthly things. Some of these were sustained by a little bread and water; some lived not on bread but on herbs or roots; some received food from heaven; some passed life with almost no food at all; and some lived beneath the naked sky entirely without clothing. Rejecting not only worldly actions but every material thing, they were as though outside the flesh; and to the degree that they surpassed the world and transcended fleshly vices, they were filled with grace and absorbed by the Spirit, and searched out and knew the hidden things of the Godhead. The soul, therefore, being made fervent, ranges among these so heavenly and grace-filled persons, considers them, and loves in them what it possesses less fully in itself. Through them it seeks God, so that, [Col. 0413B] nourished by their examples, its love may at last rise to God. For since the image of God and, to a great degree, his likeness shine in them, the more it can imitate and become like them, the more it deserves to be united with God; and it receives God into itself in proportion as it has assumed his likeness. For nothing is so near to God as his stamp and likeness. When the soul becomes just, true, merciful, and wise through grace—qualities which God possesses by nature—it reforms in itself the likeness of God in proportion as it forms these virtues in itself. Therefore, when the bride attends to the perfect, strives to become like them, and walks through their examples in order to find the Beloved, she seeks through the lanes him whom her soul loves.

[Col. 0413C] She also seeks him through streets, namely among certain secular people, even married people. For she judges that examples and incentives to salvation are nowhere to be despised. Many such persons, although they followed an easier and broader manner of life, nevertheless spread abroad the fragrance of a good reputation and offered examples for imitation. What examples of holiness are not found in Abraham and Job, by which a soul seeking God might be inflamed and built up? They were so filled with grace and endowed with such love of God that one, at the Lord’s command, offered his only son to death, while the other bore with equanimity the death of all his children and gave thanks to God. One deserved to be blessed by the Lord for his outstanding merit; the other blessed the Lord in the loss of everything that he possessed. [Col. 0413D] The former deserved the fellowship of angels, whom he also welcomed and fed; the latter heard the Lord himself speaking and saw him with the illumined eyes of his heart. How great was the light of divine grace that illumined this man, whose mind was not darkened by the night of so many adversities and temptations of the enemy, and whom the whole disturbed bed of his repose did not overturn! Therefore the bride not undeservedly runs from the night and bed of her own repose, in which she did not find the Bridegroom, to this man, whom she knows to have found fuller grace in his night and troubled bed.

Moses and Samuel, among the other virtues by which they shone outstandingly, set forth that eminent example of charity: they devoutly interceded for their enemies—the former for the people stoning him, the latter [Col. 0414A] for the people removing him from leadership. The former had such charity that he asked the Lord either to forgive them their sin or to blot him out from the book of life. The latter declares that he prayed no less devoutly for those who cast him down. Who would not marvel at the humility of David, the man whom God found after his own heart? After deeds so numerous and glorious, he did not lift himself up in pride; rather, he called himself a dead dog or a single flea. That he possessed outward and inward humility he shows in these words: “I will play and become more lowly than I have become, and I shall be humble in my own eyes” (2 Sam. 6). He did not reject outward lowliness, and inwardly he was abject in his own judgment. How many such persons were there under the Law, or even in the time of grace, who gave salutary examples of virtue in themselves? Through these, therefore, the bride also seeks the Beloved and through them kindles herself to love of him.

[Col. 0414B]

## CHAPTER III. How the examples of the good, once considered, humble and inflame the soul

“I sought and did not find him” (Song 3).

The bride sought the Beloved through lanes and streets, and did not find him as she wished. For she had not yet felt his presence or received the grace she desired. Yet I do not doubt that by her circuit she gained much and increased grace within herself greatly. For through recognition of the good and their virtues, her desire for righteousness was greatly inflamed. [Col. 0414C] She came to those burning with the fire which the Lord Jesus sent upon the earth and wished vehemently to be kindled.
