When one who is lukewarm approaches them, one grows warm; and one already fervent burns more intensely. Yet because she acquired grace, she does not cease from seeking fuller grace. Her desires have been inflamed, not fulfilled; aroused, not quieted; and the more they grow, the less sufficient to her becomes what she has received. The increase of grace has awakened hunger, so that the more she receives, the more she desires. The evil or lukewarm person, because he does not love or desire the good, does not know his own deficiency or the extent of his obligation. Thus, though poor, he judges himself rich because he does not know spiritual riches. For he says, “I am rich and need nothing,” although he is wretched, miserable, poor, blind, and naked. But the good person who is making progress does not attend to what he has, but always stretches himself toward the things before him. And because he never judges himself to have grasped them, he is always humbled by desire. [Col. 0414D] Thus in the person making progress, humility grows with growing grace; and the richer that person is, the poorer that person believes himself to be, because grace once tasted inflames him more. The bride, therefore, makes progress: for in proportion as she is inflamed toward love, she is humbled. She believes she has not yet found grace when she attends to the virtues of the perfect; hence she says: “I sought and did not find him.” She says that she did not find him whom she found so perfectly in others.

Thus Antony, the greatest of monks, after finding Paul whom he had sought, judged himself nothing in comparison with him, saying: “Woe is me, a sinner, who bear the false name of monk.” [Col. 0415A] The finding of Paul brought him to this: he who had formerly been the greatest of monks now said that he was not even worthy of the name monk. How admirable in imitation: though supreme by the merit of holiness, he became lowest in his own judgment; and, though so exalted before God, he became so contemptible to himself. But how greatly, do we suppose, did this lowly view of himself make him exalted? I do not know whether any virtue in Antony, however exalted, raised him so much before God as this abasement of himself and nullification of all the merits he had previously possessed. He therefore believed that he had not yet found Christ, whom he perceived to dwell so excellently in Paul. See how much the finding of Paul and knowledge of his holiness bestowed upon Antony. Thus the bride believed that she had not found the Beloved when, by investigating, she came to know the virtues of the perfect.

[Col. 0415B] She also seeks him not only among the more perfect, but among equals and even inferiors. For these likewise may be called lanes and streets: namely, the good and the mediocre. In them she investigates, considers, reveres, and strives to imitate the gift of some grace that they have received in a special manner. Whoever fears God neglects nothing; he judges nothing to be despised where he may receive progress toward salvation. Therefore, however great she may be, she humbles herself in all things and does not refuse correction even through the lowliest. For in these she sometimes finds examples for imitation and progress that she can usefully set before herself. The good commonly kindle one another’s virtues and receive from one another incentives alike to progress and humility. [Col. 0415C] Thus it happens that, while one considers another’s patience and the other the first’s obedience; one another’s charity and the other the first’s purity, each always receives from the other something by which to grow in goodness. For they are greatly stirred to the zeal of amendment when they see in others a good which they themselves possess less fully. And while they judge one another superior to themselves, and each reveres and loves the other’s good, by loving it each makes it his own and preserves himself in humility.

[Col. 0415D] Thus Paul does not consider that he labored more than all the apostles in preaching, but looks to the innocence of the others; and because he had persecuted the Church of God, he calls himself the least of the apostles (1 Cor. 15). Peter, on the other hand, does not consider that he is the first of the apostles, but marvels at Paul’s wisdom and commends it in one place concerning him (2 Pet. 3). Peter was not inferior to Paul, though he extolled him with praise; nor was Paul inferior to the apostles, though he judged himself least. But those who were great before God necessarily seemed small to themselves. And those adorned with every virtue ought also to be adorned with the virtue of humility. For the greatest adornment of the soul is to possess humility after the perfection of all virtues, and, though of great merit, not to know itself to be great. Blessed Job did not know himself to be great when he said: “If I should be simple, my soul itself would not know it” (Job 9). He counted his own goods small because he always burned toward greater ones. [Col. 0416A] The perfect—that is, the truly humble—know and judge their own blameworthy acts; overlooking others’ evils, they instead weigh their good deeds: strict judges of themselves, but merciful toward others. Thus, when they see some small good in others, they hope for greater things in them. But when they themselves have done many things, they judge themselves useless servants. And so it happens that they think well of others while becoming contemptible to themselves, and believe themselves inferior to lesser people. Thus the bride, considering neither her own merits nor setting them before her eyes, fixes her attention upon grace bestowed upon others. She rejoices with those receiving gifts of grace and with God who bestows them; she remembers the Beloved through his members, and through those members is more inflamed toward the Beloved. And as she considers the gifts of his generosity which he grants to different persons, she rekindles her desires within herself. Hence she repeats her devout complaint, saying: “I sought and did not find.”

## CHAPTER IV. How the soul recognizes the angels’ presence and discloses its desires to them

[Col. 0416B]

“The watchmen who guard the city found me” (Song 3).

The holy angels find the soul thus desiring and thus seeking: they guard the city—that is, the Church or the faithful—whose own are fortified by the guardianship of Christ’s mercy. They are rightly called watchmen because they are wakeful and solicitous concerning the elect: that they may be defended from temptation, make progress in goodness, and be saved. For they are ministering spirits sent into service for those who receive the inheritance of salvation. Through their ministry and vigilance God protects his faithful: “He who guards Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps.” But our adversary [Col. 0416C] circles like a lion, seeking whom he may devour. Some he devours as a lion, overthrowing them in open battle; others he deceives by hidden fraud, for whom, as is read in Job, “he hides a snare in the earth and sets a trap upon the path” (Job 1), because he deceives them through earthly desires and places the snares of deception where he sees the path of their heart and sees them inclined toward sin. Thus the enemy goes about in order to deceive, but the holy angels range about in order to defend. This conflict is waged between angels of peace and angels of discord. Thus they contend for the human being, while that person does not watch for himself but grows dull. For one must see, watch, and pray: see and consider one’s danger, watch over one’s salvation, pray, and implore aid against temptation.

[Col. 0416D] For how many does this lion devour! How many does the destroying angel kill among those who do not have the sign of the living God upon their foreheads, who do not have both doorposts and the lintel of their house smeared with the blood of the Lamb of God; who do not have faith working through love and do not deserve to be fortified and defended by the banner of Christ’s cross or by the power of his Passion. Nor does Leviathan wonder if he swallows such persons: “He will swallow the river and not marvel”—namely, the wicked and carnal, who flow away like water, run from sin to sin, and descend through the slippery course of vices to the depths of torments. Alas, he even has confidence that Jordan may flow into his mouth: that is, he trusts that he can prevail against the elect. [Col. 0417A] O how great the multitude of those swallowed, and how few those delivered! But the merciful Lord hides his own in his tabernacle—that is, in the Church—on the day of evils, and protects them in the hidden place of his tabernacle—that is, in Christ—who is called the Church’s hidden place because he secretly and invisibly dwells in his elect through charity. For they are joined to him through faith and are protected from the devil’s temptation through the power of his Passion. Since Christ conquered the enemy by his Passion, he fortifies his own by the power of that same Passion, so that they may not fear the enemy, because they are made members of him who triumphed over that enemy. For God is faithful, and does not permit his own to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation also provides an outcome. [Col. 0417B] Thus he orders and tempers temptations so that the very means by which the enemy seeks to cast them down may prove them, and, once proved, crown them more abundantly. Furthermore, it happens that the enemy, attacking them in order to separate them from God, joins them more closely to God; for, when tempted, they submit themselves to God more humbly in order to be freed from temptation. Thus blessed Job says that the beasts of the earth—that is, demons—are “made peace-bringing” to the good (Job 5). He does not say “at peace,” because they do not possess peace, but “made peace-bringing,” because by attacking and afflicting the good they bring peace to them. God therefore turns to his servants’ crown what the enemy does for their ruin. But the enemy does not judge it so; his heart is set upon crushing and upon the destruction of no few nations.

Thus God hides the elect in the Church, protects them in himself on the day of evils, and fortifies them by the guardianship of angels. He provides these servants and messengers for his own, that they may minister to them for salvation, report their needs, and carry their prayers. Although he himself sees and knows every person’s causes, he nevertheless wishes these matters to be reported to him by his angels, so that he may commend his charity and condescension toward humankind, and grant more fully on account of messengers so worthy and beloved.

[Col. 0417C]

Nor is it strange that he provides his angels as servants to the elect, and also provides himself. For he too is the Angel of Great Counsel, namely of our redemption and salvation, which he was sent to work in the midst of the earth. He ministers to us by his manner of life and humility, offering in himself an example for living and placing himself as a little one in the midst of the disciples—that is, as humble—so that we may become little ones like him. [Col. 0417D] He also ministered to us by his death, in which he labored for us so that we might not labor, and suffered temporal death so that we might not suffer eternal death. Therefore the Lord ministered to us in this life; and, passing from this life, he will minister to us also in that refreshment of twofold sweetness, because he will feed us with the milk of his humanity and the honey of his divinity.

The angels’ ministry too is not merely temporal for us but everlasting, because through their present assistance we shall receive our inheritance and eternal salvation, and with them shall receive their joy without end. How, then, do we think they love our salvation, and how greatly they desire to have us as sharers with them? Who can estimate with what love and care they keep watch over those entrusted to them? How they rouse the sluggish and inflame still more the vigilant [Col. 0418A] and fervent? How they excuse evils on one side and present good things to the divine sight on the other? How they defend them or obtain grace for them? And when they have perceived a soul burning with great desire and sighing toward God with pure intention, how, do we suppose, do they love it, rejoice with it, and turn aside to it? How do they run to and fro between it and God? For they are the Bridegroom’s friends; they listen to her voice and make the Bridegroom hear it. Her voices are her desires: these cry loudly in the Bridegroom’s ear; these his friends, namely the angels, hear; in these they delight; these they report; and they invite the one soul to come, console the other, and admonish it to seek and knock, because the seeker finds and it is opened to the one who knocks.

[Col. 0418B] Therefore they frequently attend and visit the soul burning in this way until the Bridegroom comes; by the increase of fuller grace they prepare it more fully for the Bridegroom’s coming. They draw its thought to understand their presence and learn familiarity with them, so that from this knowledge it may grow and advance to divine knowledge. Thus the soul seeking God is found by them, and after going about the city, after investigation, it deserves the coming of the blessed angels, perceives their encounter, and is received by them. For they precede the Bridegroom, manifest their presence, and reveal themselves. Angels are angels of light: they come with light, and, suffused by it, the soul is at once illumined and touched, so that it understands their arrival and feels their presence. [Col. 0418C] When it receives this grace, it confesses that it has been found by the watchmen, although it says that it has not found the Beloved. Therefore, for the soul to have been found by the watchmen is for it to have found grace to feel their presence; formerly, suffering the darkness of its blindness, it perceived nothing but itself.

Then it directs its desire and thought toward them, forms familiar speech as with acquaintances, makes its petitions known, reports its love, and asks concerning the Bridegroom: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” It asks them as witnesses both of its love and of the Bridegroom’s desired presence. Certainly it knows that the angels enjoy the vision of God and do not fail to know his love and its desires; it marvels and considers it almost unjust that they should see God and leave it deprived of that vision, as though it said: “Have you not long seen my desires in him whom you desire to enjoy? [Col. 0418D] The Beloved declares that he stands at the door of the soul and knocks, and that, if anyone opens to him, he will enter and dine with that person. I have already opened my door openly through desire for him, yet he does not enter. Moreover, I have gone in to him and knock at his door, which he promises to open to the one who knocks. Yet, forgetful of both promises, he neither enters mine nor opens his own to me. I stand, and he does not look upon me; I knock, and he does not open; I cry, and he does not answer; I seek him, and do not find him. Where, then, has he gone? Have you not seen him—you who are angels always seeing him, because you always see the face, and he and the Father are one, and whoever sees one sees the other? [Col. 0419A] Therefore, since I find him neither entering my door nor opening his own, and consequently neither with me nor with himself, I shall seek him among you, inquire of you, and come over to you, that among you I may find him whom my soul loves, the Bridegroom of the Church,” etc.

## CHAPTER V. How the soul, after contemplating the angels, passes to the contemplation and discernment of God
Paululum cum pertransissem eos, inveni quem diligit anima mea (Cant. III). God can be sought out and known in His threefold creation: in the world and the things created for its adornment, in man, and in the angel. The soul thirsting for God goes round and passes beyond each of these, that it may find Him whom it seeks. From the visible appearance of the world, once inspected, it considers the invisible Creator. For this sight, once examined, makes known that the Lord Himself is God [Col. 0419B], and that He made it, and it did not make itself. But this vision is common to all, to the evil as well as to the good. For in this way all people see God, as is read in Job: each one beholds from afar (Job XXXVI), because God is seen outside, not within oneself. In this way the philosophers saw Him, yet did not find Him through love.

Therefore from this vision it passes to man, who also is passed beyond in the image, although he has lost the likeness. In him God is seen more familiarly, namely in the image of his soul, which represents Him in itself through reason and understanding. Yet it does not pass to all people, but only to the good and spiritual. For it does not turn toward those walking the broad way that leads to death, but toward those who constrain themselves for the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0419C], whom above it calls streets or lanes, and by whom it designates the less perfect and the more perfect. In these it finds not only the image of God, but a likeness in part, insofar as they have advanced in virtues or ascended toward perfection.

But because in these it does not find the full likeness—though it finds some likeness—so that it may comprehend more fully and contemplate more nearly, it passes to one contemplating more nearly: namely, the angelic creature. In this creature it considers the likeness in its fullness, as the seal of likeness, and in it the likeness marked from the beginning endures. Human beings, however good and holy, nevertheless see in the night—that is, in obscurity—but the angel at midday, that is, in full knowledge. For, as blessed Job says, the stars are darkened by the gloom of this night (Job III), because even those who shine with virtues and holiness of life are obscured by the darkness of human blindness. The angel is suffused with the light of perfect contemplation.

For he is the brightness of eternal light and the spotless mirror of the divine majesty; and as he is in no respect distant from God, so he sees God perfectly and as He is, and represents Him in himself. For he is a clean and transparent mirror to one who directs toward him the eyes of the heart—provided they have been more fully cleansed of sins and vices, and even of their images. For vices darken; their images also cast reflections, hinder contemplation, and conceal knowledge. Whoever therefore looks into this mirror in order to consider their purity sends forth clean eyes of heart [Col. 0420A]. In this mirror the likeness of God shines back upon him. For they are clean as that One is clean; they are holy as the Lord their God is holy.

Finally, from that clean one the soul passes to the Author of cleanness; from the holy ones, to the Holy of holies; from those contemplating, to Him who is contemplated; and immediately it finds the Beloved. For those ones are so near to Him that there is scarcely anything between them and Him, and after them nothing remains to be found but Him. Therefore, having found the Beloved, rejoicing with the angels and recalling the benefit obtained through them, it says: “When I had passed a little beyond them, I found him whom my soul loves.” For as soon as I passed beyond these, I found the Beloved; I passed beyond them in order to come, and I went through them in order to find. For by their meeting and assistance I obtained what I desired [Col. 0420B]: they both stirred and kindled my desire, and secured for me the meeting with the Beloved. The finding of the Bridegroom, therefore, is the experience and revelation of His presence.

To the soul that seeks and does not cease from attention, He at last shows Himself and meets its prayers. When He is present, the soul is renewed and, as though cleaving to Him, feels the sweetness of inward taste, spiritual understanding, illumination of faith, increase of hope, incentive of charity, the affection of compassion, zeal for righteousness, and delight in virtues. In prayer it has familiar conversation with God, feeling itself heard and very often answered; it speaks with God face to face, and hears what the Lord God speaks within it. In prayer it constrains God and sometimes prevails upon Him.

Illuminated by this grace [Col. 0420C], it begins to see the darkness of its own heart, to know itself, and to discern how vices hide themselves under the appearance of virtues, or secretly associate themselves with those virtues. For a new day rises in the mind after the night of ignorance, and dawn comes, at which it rises to offer the burnt offering of contrition for every virtue, lest perhaps these have been imperfect or insufficiently pure; and to burn up whatever carnal element has been mixed into them.

For the human spirit is sometimes carried toward some other good to which something carnal is joined, something which delights human nature and secretly draws it, though the person does not know it. Likewise, how often someone believes himself moved by the Spirit to do something, when he is moved by carnality, natural impulses, frivolity, some motive [Col. 0420D], or an occasion. Finally, a person sometimes does something before its time, or too late, or without discernment. He detects and judges these darknesses and hidden evils; and the dawn of compunction shows a person to himself: namely, that he is less advanced in good than he believed, that he has received only the beginning of grace, that he lay in night, that he has come to dawn and not to full day.

Thus, just as through the grace received and its illumination he knows himself, so through that same grace he understands how slight is what he has found. After Elijah heard the whisper of a gentle breeze, in which he learned that the Lord was present, he covered his face with his cloak and stood at the entrance of the cave (III Kings XIX). So a person, having received grace and through it become known to himself in his imperfection, covers his face with a cloak, because he recognizes how great an ignorance covers him; and he stands at the entrance of the cave [Col. 0421A], because, after the night of blindness has become known, he desires to leave the fault of corruption and come to the day of grace dawning upon him.

The careless and blind person neither sees himself nor loves grace, because he is wrapped in his darkness and does not know the light of grace. But the devout soul, illuminated by grace, is humbled as it sees itself and thinks little of itself; and, as it understands grace, it is kindled to desire it more. Therefore, humbled and desiring, and reasoning with itself concerning its want, it says that it has found the Beloved only a little—not perfectly, nor according to its wish.

## CHAPTER VI. How the soul receives Christ into itself, and concerning the true love of God

“I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me” [Col. 0421B] (Cant. III).

Although it has received this grace, the soul is nevertheless not forgetful of its imperfection, nor excessively confident in the gift of God. It recalls that it is often carnally affected by its own will and carried away from the Spirit; that it has not yet perfectly corrected its habits, nor laid hold of Christ’s virtues. It therefore desires that its disposition may be purified, its will mortified, its own spirit fail, and Christ be put on, as the Apostle says: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. XIII).

For although it has found the Beloved, it has not yet brought Him into lodging; and what it has received was, as it were, outside rather than within—in desire, not in effect. It understands that it has been visited and consoled, but not yet made such that the Beloved may remain with it and have a dwelling until it wholly ceases from itself. Therefore it asks for help toward this end, and to advance so far that Christ may be formed in it and it may no longer live, but Christ may live in it [Col. 0421C]. Until it reaches this condition, it declares that it will not rest or cease from the urgency of prayers, saying: “I held him, and I will not let him go,” etc.

God is held by the devotion of prayer, desire, persistence, remembrance, petition, faith, and expectation of being heard. He is not let go if attention does not cease and the face is no longer turned aside in different directions. Thus it holds the Beloved, although it is dawn, and does not let Him go until He has blessed it. It wrestled with Him throughout the whole night in which it slept, but its heart watched: that is, it ceased from outward occupation and laboured in seeking the Beloved. Even though it has come through the night to dawn [Col. 0421D], it does not cease from wrestling—that is, from urgent prayer—nor let go of the Beloved unless He gives the blessing: that it may go from virtue to virtue and see the God of gods in Zion, that is, in beholding through a mirror and in an enigma, Him whom it cannot see as He is while it lives in the body.

It seeks this blessing and the change of name, that it may no longer be called Jacob but Israel, and need no longer overthrow vices. For Jacob is said to mean “supplanter”; but, when vices have been conquered and expelled, it may enjoy the purity of virtues and contemplate God, because Israel is said to mean “seeing God.” For the vision of God is promised to purity of heart, as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V).

Having received this blessing [Col. 0422A], it will limp on one foot: for whereas it once walked with twofold desires, sensing carnal things indeed but consenting to spiritual things, now, with vices more perfectly mortified and carnality withering away, it will be borne only by spiritual desires. Longing, therefore, for this purity and perfection, it says: “I held him, and I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house.”

Our mother is the grace of the Spirit, which spiritually regenerates us. Its house is the human mind, in which that same grace is received. The soul desires to bring the Beloved into this house, so that, as it has found Him, it may remain and dwell with Him. For it desires to retain the grace received within itself, pour it into its habits, and be transformed by it in its conduct.

Christ remains in that soul which possesses His virtues: humility, meekness, patience, obedience, and charity [Col. 0422B]. Likewise, He remains in one who keeps His commandments and walks as He walked: “If anyone loves me,” He says, “he will keep my commandments; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). Such a person, therefore, truly loves and brings Christ into the house of the mind.

The affective love by which, as we said above, the soul’s love is signified sometimes moves one who loves less and is less perfect more strongly. For one does not love as much as he feels this affection, or as much as he seems to himself to love in that state; rather, he loves as much as he has been grounded in virtues and charity, and is found faithful in keeping the commandments. A sweet affection toward God is in some manner carnal [Col. 0422C] and deceptive, sometimes belonging more to human nature than to grace, to the heart than to the spirit, to sense than to reason; so that it sometimes approaches more closely to a lesser good and less closely to a greater, and to something that is more pleasing than useful.

The disciples erred through this affection and loved God carnally, unwilling to be without His bodily presence. Hence they were reproved even for not loving, because they embraced what delighted them more rather than what profited them more. So too, a carnal and imperfect person is sometimes affectively moved toward God, not because he loves greatly, but because he tastes the sweetness of grace. As long as that sweetness lasts, it helps; and as long as sweetness lasts, love also lasts. But a friend is not recognized in prosperity.

For in this day [Col. 0422D] the Lord indeed commands His mercy, but in the night of temptations and labours He makes known through commandments how much each person loves. By a visitation of grace God consoles our faint-heartedness, assists weakness, and awakens the will. And what wonder if the weak person is anointed with grace, when even an evil person gives thanks to the Lord when He has done him good? Thus it happens that the faint-hearted and eager for love is more moved by this affection, especially where sensuality and carnal appetite rule rather than reason.

Sometimes the light-minded and grace-poor person feels it more strongly: for the lighter person is more easily moved, and one without consolation receives with greater delight what is offered. Therefore the cause of this sweet affection is sometimes not an abundance of grace but a poverty of mind. Small things indeed make a poor person glad [Col. 0423A]. “Not everyone who says, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven.” Not everyone who says repeatedly, “Lord,” sweetly—that is, affectionately—shall enter, but the one who does the Father’s will and keeps His commandments.

“Call me, and I will answer thee,” says blessed Job (Job XIV). God calls through visiting grace, and the human being answers through fulfilment of the commandments. The call does not make one perfect, but lays one under obligation; the answer through commandments justifies. This sweet affection is sometimes produced by an evil spirit, so that, when it is trusted too much and, because it delights greatly, is clung to, a person may be brought to weakness of heart. Likewise, so that by its occupation a person may be called back from a more useful work. Likewise, so that someone, trusting in its abundance, may believe himself perfect and exercise himself less toward perfection [Col. 0423B].

A person may also misuse grace himself, receiving it in vain, omitting some more useful work, or setting in it the end of his progress. For just as the spirit of the prophets is remembered to be subject to the prophets, so this grace is subject to a person, so that he may use it well or badly. Thus one who does not know its use sins through it, just as even virtue turns into vice if exercised excessively or out of season.

The Bride, then, sought the Beloved affectively and at the same time desirously; but once found, she was no less solicitous to bring Him within herself. More abundant grace must be diligently sought, and one must not cease, but advance through it until perfection is reached. “Before I eat, I sigh,” says blessed Job (Job III) [Col. 0423C]. No one eats before he sighs, because unless he desires and seeks this grace, he does not receive its refreshment. Nor, unless he advances through it, does he attain perfection.

This grace is food, because it refreshes; it is light, because it illumines. For it reveals a person’s evils and strengthens him so that he may correct them. He receives it while aware of his danger who neglects, through it, to correct himself and advance inwardly. But the fervent soul, lest it receive it in vain, always labours to advance, and diligently cultivates its field by improving its habits and tending its virtues, so that it may build the house of the mind into which it brings the Beloved.

## CHAPTER VII. How in secret the mind enjoys God and is instructed by Him concerning hidden matters

[Col. 0423D]

But it is not enough for the Bride to have brought the Beloved into the house of the mind, unless she also brings Him into her chamber, where she may enjoy Him more familiarly and secretly, be alone with the Alone, converse with Him, take part in counsels with every other counsel removed, know secrets, learn hidden causes, and have God reveal to her the uncertain and hidden things of His wisdom.

There she desires to hear the hidden word—that is, the inward and secret inspiration—which in Job is called a hidden word (Job IV), because it is granted to few, or because it is silently enjoined upon the ear of the heart. This word too is said to be heard in the night, when sleep ordinarily takes hold of people: that is, when desires of the flesh have been trampled down [Col. 0424A] and repose of mind is possessed.

Therefore, in the silence of night, when God is secretly with the soul in its chamber; when all is peaceful and quiet; when peace is possessed within from the disturbance of vices and without from every restlessness and occupation; when vices are silent, as is the memory of all sins; when the outward senses and remembrance of worldly things are also asleep—when, therefore, there is such great rest and all things are already silent, then the voice of God may be heard. It does not merely speak but whispers: that is, it subtly and secretly reveals something to the human mind.

Nor does the soul then receive only God’s whisper, but furtively receives the veins of His whisper, because it understands the subtlety of divine inspiration and the sources of the causes by which grace comes to the mind. For God visits in diverse ways: now He pierces the mind with longing for divine love; now with hope and joy of future recompense; now with delight in some virtue; now with knowledge of one’s own imperfection; now with fear of punishment and remembrance of sins, or by revealing some danger or negligence; now with remembrance of some good thing; now through the example and grace of some perfect person [Col. 0424B].

By these and other means grace visits the mind—not always in the same way, but now in this way and now in that. For just as among different persons there are different gifts and distributions of the Spirit, so that one receives this grace and another that grace, so in one and the same person there are different visitations of the Spirit. Therefore the soul with whom God whispers in silence knows and distinguishes these things, and conforms and directs itself according to the manner in which it is visited. It knows the discernment and use of grace; it understands its presence and absence, its coming and departure, the causes of its coming, its movements and thoughts, and the heralds and forerunners of grace.

Frequent experience has taught it that humility above all else merits this grace; it also understands the many hidden modes and movements of humility. Nor can it be doubted that it offers a sacrifice pleasing to God and accumulates grace for itself as often as it lowers and humbles itself for God’s sake. Therefore, that it may obtain grace more abundantly, it follows the traces of humility in thought as well as in deed. In its own judgment it lowers itself inwardly; and outwardly, for God’s sake, it submits and sets itself after others [Col. 0424D]. It chooses lowliness and makes itself contemptible, that it may be precious before God; it humbles itself that it may be exalted; it rejoices in reproaches, for it knows that from God it will receive grace for insult and blessing for abuse.

David understood this, when Shimei cursed him: he preferred to endure him rather than have him punished through his soldier, foreseeing that the Lord would render him good for that curse. Thus God gives grace to the humble but resists the proud. But who can know inveterate and ingrained pride, its hidden roots, and the subtle thoughts by which it very often secretly creeps in and steals in even upon those unaware of it, unless God whispers—that is, reveals it secretly? The more it spreads in the mind, the less it is known, because the mind is more blinded by it [Col. 0425A].

Likewise it lies hidden in words and action in many ways, and is not known unless a person is taught by grace to recognize it. Pride, therefore, lies hidden in the soul, and the soul itself does not know this; but God sees it because He beholds hidden things, and on that account withdraws or does not grant His grace. The mind is thus dried up of grace not only because of manifest but also because of hidden pride, and not only because of greater but also because of lesser pride: “I will make desolate,” says the Lord, “the mountains and hills, and I will dry up all their growth” (Ps. XLII), designating through mountains the greater proud persons and through hills the lesser ones. These mountains are dried up and wither; but the valleys—that is, the humble—are watered with the water of grace and abound in spiritual grain.

To understand secretly these mountains and the sources of visiting grace, together with the causes of merit or demerit, is to receive furtively the veins of the divine whisper [Col. 0425B]. These veins creep silently and with a gentle murmur; they are not heard by a restless mind in which vices or disturbances make noise and cry out. The understanding of these things is therefore received and learned in the chamber—that is, in the secret place of the mind—where everything except God is excluded, where the soul alone whispers with the Alone. This is the solitude into which God leads the soul, that He may speak to its heart. There it can hear what the Lord God speaks within it.

There He opens only its inward ears. For the ears of the heart are opened: the tumult of worldly business closes them, and the repose of secret reflection opens them. The mind penetrates God’s words more vividly when it refuses to admit the tumult of worldly cares. This chamber is a school, where it may learn in silence; where the mysteries of the commandments are taught; where it is instructed in the knowledge of the divine will, knowledge of dispositions, discernment of virtues, and contemplation of spiritual things.

The soul ought to withdraw to this chamber, as Moses withdrew to the tabernacle of the covenant to consult the Lord concerning doubts: concerning the ordering of the house of its mind, the things to be done in it, its own condition, others’ spiritual and bodily needs, the love of God, love or defence of righteousness, discernment in exercising zeal, the time for overlooking faults, compassion for sinners, and strictness [Col. 0425D]. Here it daily examines and investigates its inward and outward matters: what its meditation is like, or what chiefly occupies it or ought to occupy it; what its speech is like—moderate or uncontrolled, humble or proud; likewise, what its work is like—vigorous or slack; and finally, how the entire house is arranged, what in it should be corrected, and what should be tolerated.

But insofar as it reaches purity of conscience, and insofar as it has joined its own will to the divine will by mortifying it and made itself one with God, it knows spiritual things and understands God’s will. Therefore, in order to receive this grace, it rightly desires to bring the Beloved into the chamber: that is, into the secret place of repose, meditation, and prayer, where, resting from outward matters, it may learn through inward and mystical meditation and obtain through prayer.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the merits and usefulness of the contemplative life, and when one ought to come to rest

[Col. 0426A]

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the field, that you do not awaken or rouse the Beloved until she herself wills it” (Cant. III).

With much labour, persistence, and prayer, the Bride found the Beloved and at last brought Him into her chamber. It is therefore fitting that after weariness she should finally rest and enjoy the Beloved, apprehended through so many sweats and wanderings, and not easily be torn from His love. Therefore God pleads for her and warns that she should not be awakened from sweet sleep—that is, from the repose of divine love—or drawn from the secrecy of the chamber into the care of governing.

For in this chamber she not only enjoys the embraces of the Beloved and attends to her own concerns, but also gives attention to others’ necessities. Here she enjoys God in different ways: now as Bridegroom, now as Teacher, now as Father; now she prays to Him for herself, now bends and placates Him by prayers for others; now she sleeps in His love, now contemplates; now arranges and orders certain things with Him, now hears and is taught by Him; now enjoys His embraces [Col. 0426B].

For she has embraces and kisses with Him; she has offspring and breasts; but all these things are not material or carnal but chaste and wholesome. In these embraces God embraces and is embraced, because He first instils and gently impresses His will upon the soul. The soul, stirred by this charity, joins itself to Him who calls and draws it, and thus, as it were, embraces Him who embraces it. For in these embraces God embraces first, and then in return the soul embraces, because it belongs to the worthier or greater lover to embrace first. Thus He loved us first, that we might be able to love Him, and also displayed that charity than which no one can display a greater or equal charity.

God embraces the soul when He draws it to Himself through grace and joins it to Himself. He kisses it when He refreshes it with the sweetness of His grace; He makes it fruitful when He increases charity. Its breasts grow rich with milk when it is filled with the sweetness of compassion. There is there a spiritual marriage: namely, harmony and union of wills. There not carnal intercourse makes the womb fruitful, but the Holy Spirit makes the mind pregnant with twin offspring—that is, with a twofold charity: love of God and love of neighbour [Col. 0426D].

Thus the soul becomes a wife and receives breasts of loving-kindness which it did not previously have when it was still little. Yet it now knows how to have compassion on sinners, but also to be indignant with youthful vigour. Here it sleeps with Christ when it closes its eyes to outward things and knows inward things through contemplation. In this sleep it sees, with Jacob, angels ascending and descending (Gen. XXVIII): ascending to contemplation of God and descending to human visitation. It contemplates in the angel this alternation of vision of God and human visitation: how they both cleave to God and condescend to us, and conduct our cause before God.

It also contemplates and considers souls already reigning with Christ: what affection they have toward us, how they desire to have us as their fellow-partakers, how they extend their help and intercession to us, and how they bear concern for us. By these, then, the daughters of Jerusalem are adjured not to awaken the Beloved, because, just as they cleave to love of the Creator and yet take up and carry out concern for human salvation, so the perfect soul rests in God’s love and attends to the salvation of neighbours [Col. 0427A].

It is also adjured by them because it too, with and among them, labours for the salvation of others; it prays not only to God but also to them and implores their aid. It reports human need to them and labours with them in this work. Therefore it is fittingly adjured by them, as those aware of and witnessing to its charity, diligence, and necessary occupation concerning neighbours.

For these are the roes and harts of the fields: namely, the angelic creature and human beings whose souls have already passed into the kingdom of heaven. These roes seek high places and see from afar, because, raised by lofty contemplation, while they behold God, they know in Him whatever is done below in His creation. The harts also pass through thorn-brakes and overcome poison. Thus the souls of the saints, leaping over the thorns of sins and overcoming the poison of the enemy’s suggestions and the malice of the world, have now passed into the kingdom.

The field of the roes is the blessedness of that life; the field of the harts is the spaciousness of this age [Col. 0427B]. Yet the roes pass into this field by the condescension of charity, while the harts have passed into that one by desire and faith. These harts, while still dwelling in the body, passed over there because their feet—that is, their affections—stood in the courts of Jerusalem. Now indeed they have passed there in soul; afterward they too will come there in body. The Bride also passes over to them in contemplation, transfers with herself to them the care of neighbours, and pleads their cause inwardly before God with them. Therefore the Bridegroom rightly warns that she is not to be awakened, because she is well occupied concerning the salvation of neighbours.

Good indeed is bodily solicitude and disturbance; but better and more exalted is spiritual occupation and care concerning many, because it is familiar both to God and to the citizens of heaven, enduring, and more secure. Outward occupation is service, because it is performed also by bodily labour. Inward solicitude and prayer are a higher and worthier office. The former serves by rendering ministry; the latter obtains before God through merits and familiarity. The Lord says that the harvest is great and commands that He be asked to send labourers into it [Col. 0427D].

This is especially accomplished by the perfect soul that cleaves to God through the familiarity of devotion. Now it supplicates God to send labourers into the harvest; now it prays that He may grant her to labour usefully in this grace of harvest. The active person occupies a part of this harvest by outward ministry, but the contemplative person occupies the entire harvest by the aid of prayer.

For there are two lives: the active and the contemplative, signified by Martha and Mary. Martha labours outside; Mary prays within. “Tell her,” Martha says, “to help me” (Luke X). Mary properly helps Martha when she implores divine assistance for her, because Martha would vainly spend labour, plant, and water unless God gave the increase [Col. 0428A]. Magdalene therefore chose the best part, exercising the grace of contemplation; and yet she is occupied in her sister’s part also, so that she may be crowned with the reward of the active life as well, in which equal charity merits equal reward.

Martha bodily labours in one place over certain matters; Mary, through charity, labours in many places over many matters. For in contemplation and love of God she sees all things, is expanded toward all things, grasps and embraces all things, so that in comparison with her Martha may be called anxious about few things. This one thing is therefore very necessary and rightly to be preferred: in it the soul cleaves to God through love and shows charity and concern for all.

Thus the Bride rightly watches over her neighbours in mind, though she sleeps—that is, rests—from outward things in body. Nor ought she to be awakened so as to keep watch outwardly, since she so keeps watch inwardly in charity and prayer. The Bride is thus rightly occupied, though she does not work outwardly, because she strives to obtain at least something for many—indeed, for all [Col. 0428B]. Therefore the Bridegroom forbids the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, souls desiring to attain the vision of eternal peace—to awaken her and draw her into outward occupation.

She is called beloved by Him for this reason also: because she rests in His love and furthers the salvation of many. But they are forbidden to awaken her until she herself wills it, because she is so joined to God and so instructed in the knowledge of His will that, when a just and necessary cause presses, she is ready, prudent, and ordered in charity to go out and return according to the divine decision. Thus she obeys the divine will so that, according to the saying of the wise man, she may have mercy on herself while pleasing God; indeed, according to wisdom itself, she may first weep over herself.

Not only does she avoid entangling herself in worldly affairs, that she may please Him to whom she has proved herself; she also withdraws herself from neighbours’ needs by which she knows that she will be weakened or impeded from attaining perfection. Yet she does this not from cruelty but from prudence. The imperfect person, while he has only a little oil of charity with which he himself alone may be anointed, and has not yet deserved to be strengthened through the inward gifts of grace, does not wish to become entangled outwardly or to be exposed to the wind of human intercourse and changeability, the heat of worldly cares, and thereby dried up from the little he has received [Col. 0428C].

For outward occupation quickly changes and casts down the imperfect, because dying flies—that is, worldly thoughts—spoil the sweet ointment of grace that has not yet been firmly poured into the soul (Eccl. X). He therefore desires first to abound for himself, so that he may then pour into others. He wishes rather to be anointed by this oil than to anoint, to pour from fullness rather than pour himself out, to flow rather than flow away.

For whoever indiscreetly desires to benefit others and pours himself out before the time always remains poor and empty of grace, hinders his own progress, and profits others less. Therefore the prudent soul does not wish to be summoned from repose and silence, in which it cultivates itself in righteousness; for the cultivation of righteousness requires silence until this cultivation has come to fruit and maturity—that is, until it has advanced perfectly. Until it is clothed with power from on high, it strives to remain in the city [Col. 0429A], that is, within the enclosure of conscience.

For some desire governance before its time, while they are still imperfect and are drawn more by carnal appetite than by an impulse of usefulness. Yet for the soul to feel this appetite and will is not for it to will it, because this will belongs to the flesh, not the spirit; and it is not its own but another’s, if the soul itself neither loves nor follows it but hates and detests it. Thus the soul itself does not will this when carnality wills it.

But when, with carnality mortified, it wishes only to benefit neighbours spiritually, then it is judged truly to will this; for this will is its own because it consents to it. The carnal will, however, is not its own, because, while it resists it, not the soul but sin dwelling in it works it. Therefore, until it reaches this condition, so that it wills this spiritually and not carnally [Col. 0429B], it ought not to be awakened or assumed for the governance of others. Yet although the Beloved has reached this spiritual will, Christ nevertheless warns that she is not to be awakened until she wills it, because He knows such a one will will it when the time is fitting.

## CHAPTER IX. On the soul’s spiritual assent, and on discernment and fervour
“What is this that comes up through the wilderness like a little rod of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and from every powder of the perfumer?” (Song of Songs 3).

The bride comes up through the wilderness—that is, through the lovers of this world, who are a wilderness: they are forsaken by God, and they forsake him, [Col. 0429C] when by their deeds they say to him: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job 21). Therefore they are forsaken by him, and their house is left desolate, so that they may not have God dwelling within them. The bride comes up through them because, while dwelling among them bodily, she surpasses them in mind: she longs for things above and rejects their base pleasures; she lives among the carnal, yet does not imitate their perverse conduct and life. She observes the good, whether far away or near at hand; in mind she approaches them and joins herself to them in thought, considers their examples, and conforms herself to their manner of life. Thus she is saved from this perverse generation when she separates herself from it and passes over and rises above it to the generation of those who seek the Lord. For it is difficult to be saved among the perverse unless they are in this way surpassed [Col. 0429D] and left behind, because their corrupt way of life draws and attracts, and their conversation and familiar talk corrupt. For the mind is easily shaped by what it frequently sees and hears; as the common saying has it, a person learns from the one beside whom he sits.

Therefore, to separate oneself from the company of the wicked, to pass in love to the good, and to imitate them—this is to ascend, because it is to be spiritually exalted. For as much as one loves the good, so much does one become good, and so much does one ascend to God. The wicked descend daily, because they fall from sin into sin; and, being in filth, they become filthier still. Again, the storm of water—that is, sin—submerges them; and the deep—that is, their iniquity—swallows them up, and the pit presses its mouth over them—that is, the depth of iniquity—[Col. 0430A] when they are not only submerged in sins but also lose access to confession. The good, however, ascend because they go from virtue to virtue and daily make progress in charity; for charity increases in them through inward good things, through will and works. Therefore, while the bride advances among those abandoned by grace, failing and descending, she comes up through the wilderness.

This world is also called a wilderness, either because it is abandoned and despised, or because it abandons itself and fails within itself. For day by day, together with time, temporal joys pass away; and as many days as pass, so many daily joys pass and fail. As many days as a person receives in which to live, so many are cut off from his living and rejoicing. Thus for a human being to live and rejoice is to fail away from life and joy. And one who enjoys transitory joy [Col. 0430B] ought not so much to be called one who rejoices as one who learns joy, because his joy passes and perishes together with time. The world, therefore, is a wilderness because it abandons and loses its joys. Hence, when the soul perfectly despises these joys and strives toward the heavenly and true joy, it comes up through the wilderness.

This wilderness not only abandons its own delights, but is also barren and withers, and bears no fruit. For it cannot bear fruit for Christ, because it cannot receive the Spirit who is from God: it neither knows him nor recognizes him. But the devout soul, while laboring for true joy, bears fruit in the barren and arid wilderness; and amid things parched and passing away, it brings forth fruit that remains. Therefore, to bear and bring forth abiding fruit in this wilderness, in this desolate land without path or water, [Col. 0430C] is to come up through the wilderness. The bride, however, comes up like a little rod of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and from every powder of the perfumer.

By myrrh we may understand the mortification and contempt of earthly affection or consolation; by frankincense, longing for heavenly things and prayer. Everyone is bound to mortify his members that are upon the earth—fornication and impurity, evil desire and greed, and the other mortal sins—and likewise to keep the commandments. For these pertain to eternal life, and this is the righteousness in which the person who performs it shall live. But the soul that wishes to rise to a higher degree [Col. 0430D] must also avoid the multitude of venial sins and lesser desires, so that it may be perfected and deserve to receive more abundant grace. It must avoid carnal and vain thoughts, and likewise thoughts of suspicion, anger, bitterness, and the like. It must also avoid earthly consolations: in food and drink, in conversation, in seeing and hearing, in curiosity, in clothing, in sleep, and in every kind of liberty. For to the extent that it mortifies and rejects these pleasures, and refuses carnal consolation, it will deserve to be consoled spiritually and quickened in grace. Grace fills the heart to the extent that it finds it empty of these things. To the extent that a person despises and rises above these perishable things, so much does he ascend, because so much does he proceed from lower things to things above. Therefore, after mortifying the greater [Col. 0431A] sins, the advancing soul, which wishes to rise to spiritual life, must mortify and trample down the lesser ones also.

Thus blessed Job, after he had girded the loins of the flesh, was commanded by the Lord also to gird the loins of the mind—that is, evil thoughts—when he was about to have converse with him and make his command known to him (Job 38). Thus the devout mind must gird these loins together with blessed Job. For this is the myrrh, that is, the mortification, of the advancing or perfect soul. With this it must also burn frankincense, because it ought not only to mortify earthly pleasures, but also to desire heavenly things and seek them through devout prayers. The smoke of mortification, desire, and prayer certainly rises together; [Col. 0431B] for each is supported by the other, so that neither can rise or please God by itself. For we cannot desire heavenly things unless we despise earthly ones, nor do we despise earthly things unless we are drawn by longing for heavenly things. The heart cannot be without delight; it must therefore be drawn by some delight, because each person is drawn by his own pleasure. Hence, when one delight is withdrawn, it more readily inclines to another; and because it is empty, it is more disposed to receive something else. Therefore, the more free it is from earthly consolation and unwilling to take delight in anything, the more it admits spiritual delight.

Again, to the extent that we know eternal things, we despise and condemn transitory things. For this is that precious pearl which, when a person finds it, he gladly leaves behind all that he previously [Col. 0431C] loved. Therefore the soul burns myrrh when it despises earthly pleasures, but frankincense when it desires and seeks heavenly things. Yet smoke is said to rise from myrrh and frankincense together with every powder of the perfumer. It does not say, “from every spice,” but “from every powder of the perfumer.” A spice is every virtue, or every work of virtue; it is ground into powder when it is examined and discerned with subtle care, lest any evil be hidden in it or anything be done indiscreetly. The perfumer is the person who grinds this powder—that is, who examines each of his works. For care must be taken that good deeds are done without an admixture of evils: greater evils destroy good deeds; lesser ones stain the person.

Manifest evils, therefore, [Col. 0431D] must be avoided. But because we cannot know all things, a general and hidden contrition must be maintained for them. At times there is a sin in a person that is concealed from him, or which he does not know to be mortal. Contrition, therefore, should be the first spice that we make and offer to God, because general contrition destroys all mortal sins, hidden and manifest, and restores charity if it has been lost. Whatever we do outside charity will by no means please God; nor, however much we grind or reduce it to powder, will it give fragrance before him. Therefore, in order that all our works may be done in charity and that we may grind a powder pleasing to God, let us first be contrite.

Then individual works must be examined: almsgiving, vigils, prayers, and other bodily labors—whether they are done purely for God; whether something else is their principal [Col. 0432A] or secondary cause; whether they are done discreetly and with due moderation; whether their end is progress and perseverance; whether there is ability to carry them out; whether it is the right time for their performance; their manner—how, how much, and how frequently they are done; and so forth. Likewise, when something ought to be interrupted, and when it ought to be pursued more vigorously. Likewise, whether it is done to the scandal or harm of others; whether frivolity, instability, or curiosity impels a person to it; whether praise is sought or secretly steals in; whether human pleasure or earthly advantage is involved. Finally, one must examine whether the virtues are pure and perfect; whether God is loved above all things; whether anything is made equal or preferred to his love; whether love of neighbor is present and offered sincerely for God’s sake; whether a friend is loved in God; whether this love is bestowed spiritually [Col. 0432B] rather than carnally; whether persons are treated with partiality; and whether the cause is considered.

For sometimes a person is moved by love, but by carnal love, or is led by private inclination, so that love is not offered purely in God; or one loves more what ought to be loved less, or the reverse. Likewise, one must see whether humility is true, rather than feigned or imperfect: whether a person so despises himself inwardly that he does not bear an outwardly inflicted injury or contempt proudly or impatiently; whether he so lowers and humbles himself outwardly that he does not inwardly become proud on that account, but maintains a humble judgment of himself and truly feels inwardly that he is what he outwardly shows himself to be. Likewise, whether he is humble where humility is honored, yet shuns humility where it is held in contempt. Likewise, whether he practices humility when he ought freely to oppose injustice, and maintains patience when he ought rather to burn [Col. 0432C] with the fire of divine zeal and be unable to endure evil—unable to bear justice being despised and perversity prevailing.

For we ought not to endure it if someone devours us, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes us in the face. If someone exalts himself and behaves arrogantly against justice, or strikes us in the face with insult, it is so when we are the cause through our own fault or vice. If, while sinning, we endure being struck, we have no reward. But if we endure these things while not sinning, this is patience pleasing to God. Likewise, one must consider whether a person displays patience outwardly in such a way that inwardly he does not grieve or plan retaliation; and likewise whether, at the very hour when an injury is received, he answers with words of impatience or insult, [Col. 0432D] or afterward retains a heart of envy or rancor.

Likewise, a person must judge whether he keeps obedience for some personal advantage or gain, or purely for God and for the commandment; whether he obeys in adversity, promptly, and devoutly. Likewise, he must consider whether he reproves modestly, corrects with restraint, and, in preserving discipline, preserves gentleness and avoids harshness, anger, bitterness, and indiscretion. And whether perhaps he is readier for rigor than compassion; and whether he grants relaxation where rigor ought to be exercised. In these matters the mind is often deceived, and believes that what it does carnally and viciously is a work of virtue. Zeal too is false if we avenge our own injury rather than God’s, and if we burn more fiercely against those who are ungrateful to us or less dear to us.

Likewise, the giving of alms is less acceptable if someone gives slowly or stingily; it is stained if it is done with pride or insult. [Col. 0433A] Likewise, someone is deceived if, under the pretext of sustaining the body, he serves pleasure, or if he deprives himself of necessary sustenance. Likewise, continence is impaired if a person is chaste in body and mind, yet, under the appearance of usefulness or of offering counsel, is urged to maintain familiar association with certain women. For nature is ready and easily assents even to that toward which one is led by a pious intention. In this matter vice secretly attaches itself, and by habit brings a person to the point that he does not understand himself and does more what delights him than what is expedient. Thus it happens that at times a person is carried toward this more by carnal than spiritual desire. Each person will be free from the danger of this temptation only insofar as he can withdraw from such familiarity with a free and untroubled mind.

Vigils and prayers are useless to you if you practice them so that, at the time when you ought to pray and keep watch, you sleep and grow sluggish; or if you maintain in them a certain singularity through which you neglect common duties and those to which you are more bound: admonishing your neighbor, consoling the sorrowful, and the other works of charity pleasing to God. Yet it happens that even these are not always done purely in God. For sometimes a person is eager for them because he suffers from sloth and is afflicted by weariness, and finds it pleasant to be occupied outwardly; or because the persons to whom he speaks please him; or because he pleases himself in these things and glories in such [Col. 0433C] favor. For even upon those who lead a quiet life, sluggishness or error sometimes steals in, so that they either become useless through torpor or fall into error through excessive examination of spiritual matters.

And likewise one sins in this life if, for the sake of quiet, all outward care for one’s neighbor is entirely abandoned. To examine all these works of virtue with subtle care, and to reconsider whether they are truly good, is to grind all spices into powder. When the perfumer mixes this powder with myrrh and frankincense—that is, with mortification and devotion—he makes a precious perfume. When it is burned with the fire of charity in the censer of the heart, it will send upward from itself smoke of sweet fragrance. But this smoke must rise like a little rod, which is straight and grows upward. [Col. 0433D] Thus grace must tend upward directly and not crookedly, seeking nothing sideways, nothing carnal or earthly. To the extent that it desires something earthly or takes pleasure in anything, this smoke rises less, because it is drawn crookedly and sideways.

For this reason it is fittingly compared to a little rod, to signify swiftness of ascent. Rods that grow thick as they grow do not rise very high; but rods that grow more swiftly and upward are finer and smaller. Therefore this smoke of mortification, devotion, and discernment must ascend swiftly like a little rod, so that we may not be sluggish in doing good or in the pursuit of progress, but eager; lest through slowness and idleness we become gross, but rather grow fine and exalted. And through fervor of mind [Col. 0434A] let us hasten upward. For we must ascend swiftly and persevere manfully, because if a person tries to ascend upward weakly, he is weighed down by the burden of the body and human frailty. For the corruptible body weighs down the soul; and unless it advances, it must necessarily fail, because nature drags downward and always seeks lower things.

We see this in heavy people: if they wish to climb a tree and creep upward, whenever they relax somewhat in climbing, they are immediately weighed down and fail. But speed and persistence in climbing overcome heaviness and bring them upward. In this manner, those who strive eagerly and diligently toward perfection and fulfill the commandments attain the summit of perfection; but the lax fail and daily become more prone to falling. Therefore the bride is compared to a little rod because of the purity of her intention and the swiftness of her progress; and because of all that has been said, it is fittingly said of her: “What is this?”—that is, how admirable, how worthy of praise, and so forth.

## CHAPTER X. On heavenly rest and how the perfect desire it

“Behold, sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s little bed, from among the mightiest of Israel” (Song of Songs 3).

Solomon is interpreted “peaceful.” He signifies Christ, who made peace between things in heaven and things on earth, reconciled sinners to the Father, restored harmony between angels and human beings, and joined converted sinners to the righteous. Those whom he joins here in concord, he also joins to himself in the kingdom [Col. 0434C] by perpetual charity and peace, and leads them to everlasting rest. This rest is called a little bed because in it there is repose from every disturbance and labor of this life. In that rest, those who have labored here for God find repose. For there, as is read in Job, “those wearied in strength rest, and those once bound are without all trouble” (Job 3).

There eternal rest refreshes and rewards those whom the labor of the commandments and progress in virtues exhausted here; and those who here were bound by the chains of human weakness there, with their chains broken, offer God a sacrifice of praise. These chains are hunger, thirst, sleep, weariness, and other such things. All these will cease there, because they shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; there will be neither labor nor pain, nor will this material sun fall upon them to burn them, [Col. 0434D] nor the heat of temptation. For then the Spirit tells them to rest from their labors and temptations. The Spirit who strengthened them to obey the commandments then tells them to rest from labor.

For those who have entered that rest have rested from their works and labors, as God rested from his own—the works by which he labored for humankind and redeemed it. He rested in himself from these labors; for these labors his members rest in him. No one ever labored as he did, because there was no sorrow like his sorrow. And according to the multitude of his sorrows, eternal consolations made his members glad: his great sorrows bestowed great joys upon his members; great labor, perpetual rest; and bitter death, the sweetness of everlasting life. Therefore [Col. 0435A] they love him incomparably and rejoice in his love. For they have the one whom they love; they know and see him—and this wholly constitutes eternal life. For resting with him, rejoicing with him, and possessing him are the same thing. Likewise, to love is to know, because love is knowledge; and to know is to see. And this is eternal life: to know the Father, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom he sent. This is blessedness, and these are the endowments of the soul: knowledge of God, love, and enjoyment.

Who can adequately conceive that mutual love of the Savior and the saved—how he loves those whom he redeemed at so precious a price; how he rejoices with them in their salvation; how they love him, rest in his love, and rejoice in him, through whom they know and always see themselves redeemed and brought to rest? And though they love him with eternal charity for their redemption, they are loved by him incomparably more. He so loved his own in the Passion, and such was the fervor of his charity in redeeming them, that he could wholly have removed the bitterness of his Passion; but he did not will it. Rather, he assumed a more bitter pain of martyrdom and willed to suffer more than any human being had ever suffered or could suffer, in order to show incomparable charity. This charity for their salvation was so great that, although he redeemed them at the price of his death, he recalls them not so much as redeemed by himself as given to him by the Father. In one place he says: “Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they too may be with me” (John 17). So greatly does he rejoice in their redemption that he does not regard as great what he endured for them, but seems to regard those whom he received as given to him more as a gift than bought at a price or acquired in recompense.

Therefore, he who so loved them in exile will love them incomparably in the kingdom as well. He had greater charity for them than for his own body, in dying for them; there also he will have greater charity for them than they can have toward him, and will rejoice more in their salvation than they can rejoice in it. Therefore he will rejoice in their salvation, and he himself will be their joy. They will taste him, keep him in memory, and hold him in desire. In these three things the soul consists, and the Son of God, who is the wisdom of God, will perfectly fulfill these three things.

For these are the streets of Jerusalem—that is, the broad ways [Col. 0435D] of the citizens of Jerusalem, who see God’s peace. These streets are reason, memory, and will; they are broad because many things flow into, enter, and leave these streets. For how much does reason comprehend, how much does memory retain, how much does the will desire? But these streets will be paved—that is, made level—and perfectly filled with pure gold, that is, divine wisdom and the enjoyment of God. For God will occupy, gladden, bless, and perfectly satisfy every part of them. Whatever reason can know, whatever memory can recall, whatever will can desire—God will be all this and will fill each of these faculties, because he will be all in all. And a song of joy will be sung to him because of the happiness of eternal blessedness.

There, while the righteous without end behold the torments of the condemned, they increase in God’s praises; and because they see in themselves the good with which they have been rewarded, and in the others the punishment they have escaped, [Col. 0436A] there will be thanksgiving and a voice of praise. They will give thanks to God their deliverer and love him with perpetual charity, while also ceaselessly looking upon the signs of their deliverance in him—namely, the scars of his wounds. And the more they recall the dangers and misery they have escaped, the more joyfully they will say: “Our soul has passed through the torrent; perhaps our soul would have passed through unbearable water.” Then, praising God, they will add: “Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth”—that is, to the teeth of demons—from whose hunters’ snare their souls were rescued. The snare was broken because temptation ceased; they themselves were delivered, while their enemies are bound by the chains of eternal damnation.

[Col. 0436B] They will also always see those enemies in hell, so that, beholding their torments, they may always rejoice, love their deliverer, and give him thanks. Hence the Lord says to Job that the elect receive the devil as an everlasting reward (Job 40): here he afflicted them by tempting them, and there they will rejoice at the sight of his punishment, which they escaped. For all these things there will be thanksgiving and a voice of praise, because they will praise forever the one whom they love. For Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace, that is, all those who behold that peace—will praise the Lord, who is their peace, exultation, and eternal blessedness. In his peace, concord, and charity he so unites and joins his own in the kingdom that whatever happiness and joy one person possesses becomes, through charity, the joy of another: one wishes for the other what he himself has, and the other loves that person’s good in him as his own good in himself. Therefore, as many as the elect who will reign with Christ, so many rewards will be there; and there will be joys from each and every person who is saved. If anyone could number the citizens of heaven, he could also number the joys of each, for there are as many joys as there are elect.

We must now see how abundant and how enduring these joys are. Let us compare the joy of this life with the joy of the heavenly homeland. Even if we double it, triple it, and multiply number by number as much as possible, we shall not attain equality with the joy of the blessed. For here is a little spark, but there, as the authority says, a furnace: “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace [Col. 0436D] is in Jerusalem.” Nor can we reach its limit, because it is infinite both in immensity and in eternity, so far as the comprehension of the present life is concerned. Thus by no comparison or calculation can we attain either the greatness or the duration of this joy.

It has been said how manifold this joy is, how great, and how enduring. We must now see what it is, or in what it consists. We must know that it is in God and is God. For it could not be called true and perfect if it were not God or were outside God. And because nothing is true or perfect outside God, nor could any creature made in God’s likeness suffice for, or perfectly fill, that likeness apart from God, this is that full joy which in the Gospel the Lord commands us to ask and seek, [Col. 0437A] and which he declares that those who ask will receive (John 16). This is that which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for his own.

“The small and the great are there, and the servant is free from his master.” Those who served God here have passed from labor to rest, from servitude to freedom; now free from fear of any punishment or separation, they possess the fear of reverence and love. For they enjoy the liberty of the children of God, the liberty by which the Son of God made them free, so that they might be truly free. Christ served so that servants might be granted freedom; he took the form of a servant so that those deformed by sin and deprived of God’s likeness might be re-formed. He took flesh from us and gave us his Spirit; thus, when he assumed the servitude [Col. 0437B] of our weakness and bestowed the freedom of his Spirit, he restored us to freedom. For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. In this Spirit we call and receive his Father as our Father also. He re-formed us in the soul according to his likeness; in the body he will re-form us according to the glory of his body.

This is the liberty of the elect; this is their joy. They glory in this liberty and rejoice in this glory: namely, that they enjoy the glory of the children of God; that they are children of God and therefore heirs; that they have God as Father and Christ as brother; that they are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ; and that they possess with Christ their brother the inheritance of their heavenly Father, in which they have the firstborn himself as their partner and companion. He is also the firstborn among many brothers. Christ has these brothers and co-heirs in his liberty and glory; he has them as companions with himself at table. For they will eat and drink at his table in his kingdom. The rest of this table, as is read in Job, is full of richness (Job 56).

The rest of this table is the refreshment of that glory, which is full of richness because it perfectly satisfies, as the Prophet says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16). We shall be satisfied by that glory and at the same time desire it; desire will have no lack, nor satiety weariness, because satiety will accompany desire and desire satiety. Its immensity will provide satiety, and the taste of its sweetness desire. Therefore it will always satisfy and always delight. This is that refreshment; this is [Col. 0437D] the rest of that table, full of richness.

For we shall be satisfied from the fat of the grain that fell into the earth—that is, from the divinity of our Savior, who assumed the weakness of our mortality in order to refresh us with his divinity. He drank from the torrent—that is, from the transitory and turbulent Passion—on the way of this world, in order that in the homeland he might give us to drink from the torrent of his delight. He drank the cup of the Passion and prepared for us the fountain of the water of eternal life. These are the delights, that refreshment, that abundance of Jerusalem, that rest and richness of that table. This is the torrent of delight by which the elect are made drunk, so that they forget and are free from every misery and rejoice without end. This is blessedness, rest, and the bed of our Peaceful One, where he feeds his own with these delights and where he reclines at noon.
