Here the bride has her bed with the bridegroom [Col. 0438A] in the night—that is, in the darkness of this life; but there she has it at noon—that is, in full charity and knowledge. Here she knows only in part; there she will know as she is known, and perfectly. There she sleeps and rests in peace without any disturbance, and rests “in the selfsame”—that is, in the peace of him who is peace and joy, who is “the selfsame.” And because he is always the same, exists in the same manner, is never changed, and never ends—for he has neither change nor shadow of variation—devout and mighty persons, who labor manfully in fulfilling the commandments, circumscribe that fullness and those delights by thought and encompass them by contemplation.

These are signified by the number sixty, which is made up of ten and six. By ten is signified the Decalogue, that is, the commandments; by six, the labor [Col. 0438B] expended in fulfilling those commandments. Therefore these mighty men surround Solomon’s little bed with desire; they do not ascend it or sleep in it. For they can only think and investigate something about it, but cannot comprehend it perfectly and as it is. However much they circumscribe it in thought or conjecture about its equality and happiness, they go around it rather than enter into perfect knowledge. Hence, because what they can know of that rest is very little, it is expressed by a diminutive: it is called not so much a bed as a little bed.

Those who still groan over past sins and need to wash their bed of sorrow and ailing conscience with tears of repentance cannot similarly surround this bed. For they do not have a quiet but a troubled bed, since conscience and the sorrowful memory of sins disturb them within. Nor can they so much surround and desire heavenly rewards as still fear punishments. But when they have been cleansed from the filth of sins by true repentance, freed after a long struggle from the passions of vices, strengthened by grace, and passed from fear and hope to perfect charity, then, with enlightened eyes, they can ascend and contemplate heavenly things.

Accordingly, mighty persons—or rather those who are among the mightiest of Israel, that is, the more devout and spiritual—surround Solomon’s bed and can fulfill in deed whatever they understand in Scripture. But those who fulfill the commandments sluggishly and live softly and dissolutely cannot [Col. 0438D] rise to contemplate this rest. For carnal and worldly desires are still strong in them: the appetite of gluttony, the fury of anger, the heat of greed, the burning of lust, the venom of impatience or envy. They are as much weaker in God as these things have less perfectly failed within them. But when these have been weakened in them by long discipline and labor, and when they have been strengthened by spiritual desires, then the more they have pressed these things beneath themselves, the stronger and more powerful they are above, and the more they can surround this little bed.

Therefore the mightiest from Israel—that is, from those who contemplate and seek God in mind, and whose spiritual desires are more fervent—surround this little bed. Inflamed by vehement desires, they go around it on every side and seek an entrance, [Col. 0439A] so that they may taste this rest and in some measure enter into it. This, therefore, is their encompassing, and this course of desire around the bed.

## CHAPTER XI. On caution in fighting against the enemy, and on the remedy for the blindness of the heart
All holding swords, and most skilled in war (Song of Songs 3). The strong men surrounding Solomon’s bed now contemplate heavenly things and attend to them; now, at a lower level, they wage war against the enemy of the human race. So that they may fight against him, they first take up, according to the Apostle, the armor of God—that is, the virtues. Armed with these, and possessing them all, they take care not to neglect any one of them. For they know that, if they offend in one point, they become guilty of all; [Col. 0439B] and then they will have none of them, and will appear before the enemy not armed but naked. Whoever lacks some virtue possesses the contrary vice, and is therefore outside charity, since virtue and vice cannot coexist. And one who is outside charity cannot have strength against the adversary.

Then they fortify and arm themselves with justice as with a breastplate; covered round about with it, they remain impenetrable to the enemy’s missiles. For whoever renders to God and neighbor what is due is protected on every side, and the enemy finds nothing in him to strike. They also have faith in things unseen as a shield, which is first set against their enemies. Although the enemies attack it first, they strike and assail this shield all the more fiercely the more spiritually they seek to overcome them. For when perfect men believe in and love future and eternal things, [Col. 0439C] they judge earthly and passing things to be of no account and despise them. Hence, when they are tempted by things they do not love, they easily conquer the tempting adversary; “for the net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures.” They are indeed winged, raised by two wings: meditation and contemplation—so that their citizenship may be in heaven, that they may desire heavenly things and rise above earthly ones.

They also take up the hope of salvation as a helmet. By this they rejoice so greatly that they not only willingly bear labors, but delight in them and count themselves blessed through them, as it is written: “Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed” (Ps. 127). Truly blessed is the one who both believes in and loves future things, and expends works for which he may await [Col. 0439D] and hope for them; who delights and rejoices in the labors he performs for their sake. Armed with these weapons, Christ’s soldiers can fight securely and manfully. For, enlightened by grace, they believe in future things and perform works for which they may hope for them; they have faith and hope, and they also have virtues and justice.

Thus armed, they take up the word of God as a sword, by which they may both defend themselves and strike their enemies. For the word of God is living and effective, like a penetrating sword, discerning the thoughts of the evil one. Therefore all the strong men of our Solomon hold swords, because they embrace Holy Scripture, retain it in memory, and cling to it in mind. In it they have diverse teachings by which they recognize and overcome the snares of the crafty enemy. For the reading and meditation of Scripture, [Col. 0440A] and the devout chanting of psalms, strengthen the mind, weaken the enemy, and nullify his powers. Therefore, while they retain this in memory and fulfill it in deed, they become most skillful in conflict with the enemy: through understanding of Scripture they are instructed, and through practice they are enlightened, as the Psalmist says: “By the understandings of their hands,” that is, through practice, “he led them back” (Ps. 77).

Their first precaution is this: when they are about to fight the enemy, they must take on humility and not trust that they can contend by their own powers. Rather, regarding themselves as weak, they must entrust themselves wholly to divine protection. They become strong in this conflict only to the degree that they trust for battle against the enemy not in themselves but in God. For no one could contend [Col. 0440B] on equal terms with the enemy of the human race if their respective powers were compared. His strength is so great that no human power can be compared with it, because of the many arts of harming that he possesses, which no one is sufficient to know.

Therefore one must engage them by divine power, which is properly merited by knowledge of one’s weakness and by humility. Humility alone, as is read in the Lives of the Fathers, can escape these snares. Thus Jonathan, surrounded by a multitude of enemies, recognized that he could not resist them and fled to divine help; and he emerged victorious (1 Sam. 14). Thus Jehoshaphat, placed in a similar danger, confessed himself weak before God, turned himself wholly to invoking God, and prevailed against his enemies (2 Chron. 17). Both triumphed more by humility and prayer than by strength. [Col. 0440C] By humility and prayer, moreover, the Lord’s Passion must be remembered and proclaimed in faith. There Christ’s soldiers receive strength against their enemies: for there the strength of God was made weak, that we might be strengthened. There the enemy proved strong, that he might be weakened; there he prevailed, that he might be cast down. Therefore Christ’s members are strong in this battle only insofar as they can place their faith in this.

Moses stood in this firmness of faith, on this stone of help, when his people fought with the Amalekites and he prayed to the Lord (Exod. 17). Although his hands had first been heavy, such strength afterwards appeared in them that they did not grow slack until the enemies were defeated. Aaron, whose name is interpreted “mountain of strength,” and Hur, who is called “fire,” supported his hands in prayer. For one must persist manfully in prayer and with fervor; this fervor is understood through that fire. Prayer, upheld by these two things—steadfastness and devotion—will triumph over enemies and obtain what it asks.

At times these peaceful soldiers of ours fight with Moses: the host of good thoughts clashes with the host of evil or vain thoughts. At times, when consolation has been withdrawn, they are as though abandoned and, with Jonathan, recover and regain help through prayer and conquer their enemies. But he, abandoned by his companions, tore his garments, put earth upon his head, and prayed; he recovered his companions and slew his enemies. So Christ’s soldiers, when in the anguish of temptation good thoughts withdraw and are thrown into confusion, tear their garments and put earth [Col. 0441A] upon their heads, considering the virtues within themselves to be torn and imperfect. They reflect that they are earth and ashes; by praying and humbling themselves, they recover the spiritual thoughts they formerly possessed and overcome their enemies.

We likewise read of Judas Maccabaeus that, when he once encountered his enemies, he was of such steadfastness and confidence that he crossed over to them before allowing them to cross over to him (1 Macc. 3). As this was a sign of victory in him, so it is in Christ’s servants. His enemies took this as a sign: if Judas first crossed the torrent lying between them, he would be victorious and they could not withstand him. This happened, and he was victorious. Thus Christ marks his soldiers as future victors if they pursue obstacles fearlessly, or are ready to bear adversities [Col. 0441B] and pass through them steadfastly.

This Judas was energetic when war was at hand, but prudent in time of peace. In war he acted manfully; when it ceased—or rather, was interrupted—he did not grow sluggish in idleness, but made arrangements for the things that had to be done. When opportunity was given, he himself cleansed polluted places, renewed holy things, and rebuilt what had been destroyed. Thus Christ’s soldiers are taught now to fight bravely with their enemies, and now to cleanse what is defiled in their own mind—which is the house of God—to build up virtues, and to renew holy pursuits and pious works. They hold these swords—that is, these teachings and examples of Scripture—and through them become most skilled in spiritual warfare:

“Each one has his sword upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night” (Song of Songs 3). In the thigh is signified carnal propagation, [Col. 0441C] since carnal impulses and the heart’s inclinations can be understood by the thigh. From each comes great propagation: as diverse thoughts are generated from the flesh, so many inclinations proceed from the heart.

To the extent that anyone follows these pleasures or inclinations, to that extent he is blinded in mind. For what is sweet to the flesh is harmful to the spirit, and what delights carnally makes the soul bitter. Earthly pleasure is that sour grape: whoever eats it has his teeth set on edge—that is, spiritual understanding is dulled. And, according to Jeremiah, this person’s teeth are broken in proportion to their number, because spiritual knowledge is broken and scattered in proportion to the number of carnal pleasures. And insofar as a person delights in these, [Col. 0441D] he is inwardly blinded, and a night of blindness arises in the mind.

This night is to be feared all the more because we unknowingly sin and take pleasure in many things. Human nature is inclined to evil and commits many faults of which it is unaware. For, as is read in Job, “we inhabit houses of clay,” have an earthly foundation, and “are consumed as by a moth,” which consumes a garment secretly and without sound (Job 4). Hence we are often stained and made abhorrent by the filth of sins: that is, such garments—our bodies—make us abominable. Again, we often sin and take pleasure in what we know too little; we sin unknowingly, in pleasures and sins which the Lord knows even though we do not. Therefore he allows us to be blinded. Again, [Col. 0442A] he knows every person’s works and therefore brings on night, as is read in Job—that is, he permits blindness to occur (Job 34).

For through sin we are blinded, and, once blinded, sin more, because we do not see how greatly we offend. Therefore these nights are to be feared. Against these terrors of the night, the sword of God’s word must be kept upon the thigh of pleasures and delights, not laid aside or placed far off, so that by it sins may be recognized and cut away. For the word of God enlightens and gives understanding concerning them. If they are guarded against less, they are recognized less. Once the mind has gradually been blinded, these things are strengthened against a person by habit, so that he cannot easily avoid them.

[Col. 0442B]

There is another effective and necessary means for recognizing and restraining these pleasures: namely, the sword of God’s love. Let the soul of one wounded by these pleasures be wounded by charity, and let it grieve with him who endured pains for it. For he himself was wounded for our transgressions, and he himself bore our pains. For these things, O human being, let the sword of love wound you, and let the sword of sorrow pass through your soul. This sword is two-edged: it wounds by love, and so opens understanding and enlightens the mind. For love produces knowledge and cuts away sins, so that you take care not to offend the one whom you love.

Therefore Christ’s soldiers have the sword of love upon the thigh of pleasures or carnal delights, because of the terrors of the night—that is, because of hidden falls into sin. For if they do not love, they offend in many things through blindness and ignorance. And again, [Col. 0442C] while they burn with love, they avoid the danger of lukewarmness; for as love enlightens, so lukewarmness blinds. In a lax mind earthly pleasures grow, and one’s own inclinations run wild. For, according to Solomon, briars and thorns fill the field of the sluggard (Prov. 24); and insofar as it has borne fruit, so much does a dark woodland of these growths arise and darken the mind, so that the lax person understands less how greatly he offends, attends to himself less, and takes hold of himself less.

This is a night to be feared, in which a person daily becomes worse and yet more secure about himself. But those who possess the sword of divine love will shake off this fear, and that fear of thorns and briars will not come upon them. For acquiring it, the remembrance of God’s benefits is especially effective: recall and consider what he has made you and remade you, what good he has done you. Consider his goodness, generosity, and liberality: how good he is in himself; how generous toward you; how lavish toward you in spending himself for you and heaping his gifts upon you. As you think on these things, you will love him whom you perceive to be such toward you. And this sword of love will cut off evils as they sprout and make you secure against this terror of the night.

## CHAPTER XII. On the virtues and perfection of the soul: purity, desire, and discernment

“King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon” (Song of Songs 3). The litter is the holy soul, which feeds and refreshes. For it refreshes Christ and also his members. It refreshes Christ when he delights in its good works, pursuits, and desires, as it is written: “My people has satisfied me with voices; it has filled me with fragrances.” It refreshes his members by example, when they are built up and corrected by its holy life and conduct. [Col. 0443A] It refreshes them by prayer, when it obtains from God for them the grace by which they are consoled and built up. It feeds them unto salvation by teaching, when it strengthens them through preaching and instructs them to savor eternal and saving things. It feeds by counsel, when it exhorts them to good, raises and restores the sorrowful through gentle admonition, and further kindles and strengthens the good. It feeds by conversation, when it speaks of what is good and, as far as it can, removes occasions for useless speech. It brings forth words of edification and supplies matter for good discourse; it devotes itself to charity and peace, does not lend an ear to a slanderous tongue, but disperses it with a sad expression. Thus the holy soul refreshes both Christ and his members.

[Col. 0443B]

Therefore Christ is said to have made this litter for himself. The holy soul is also called a *ferculum*, a litter, from *ferre*, “to carry,” because it is carried from place to place wherever the will of its Governor—God, who orders all things—directs it, so that it may refresh more people and instruct them unto salvation. Christ made this litter from the woods of Lebanon. These are the cedars that grow on Mount Lebanon, and they signify the elect, who grow and bear fruit through Christ and in Christ. For Lebanon, which is called “whitening,” signifies Christ, who proceeded from a pure Virgin without every stain [Col. 0443C] of sin.

These woods are beautiful, tall, incorruptible, fragrant, and untouched by worms. They signify the saints: beautiful through holy conduct and upright character; tall because in desire they stretch upward and seek heavenly things; incorruptible because their charity and holiness begin here in such a way that they will never end, but will be perfected in the life to come; fragrant because they give off the scent of good repute and draw others to good by their holy reputation; untouched by worms because they do not allow worms—that is, demons—to consume their inward parts, nor, while they are unaware, to eat away the strength of their minds through alien influence. Taught by many experiences, they recognize the demons’ hidden suggestions.

From these woods Christ made a litter—that is, a soul filled with every abundance of grace, [Col. 0443D] so abundantly filled within itself that it can refresh and benefit others. He makes such a soul from the woods of Lebanon—that is, from the example of the saints—when in their life and conduct he shows it the pattern it should imitate; when, in the same Spirit by which he has illuminated them, he restores it and brings it to the degree of perfection; when he builds in it the virtues with which they were adorned; and finally, when he forms and fashions it after their pattern and likeness.

The four columns of this soul are the principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. The soul is well supported when it is upheld by these: prudent, to know what pertains to salvation; strong, to accomplish what it has known; temperate, to avoid evils and do good with discernment, in its proper place and time. Once it is such, it will be just, and justice will occupy the fourth place. These columns are silver, because they make the soul supported by these virtues splendid both inwardly before God and outwardly before human beings, and display a beautiful appearance from it.

[Col. 0444A]

“He made its couch of gold.” The couch is a pure conscience, in which Christ, the wisdom of God, reclines and rests. It is golden because it has been refined in the fire of tribulation, cleansed like gold, and tested. For what is pleasing through innocence of life is made more pleasing and purer through enduring adversity, and becomes worthy to be God’s golden couch. The Jews put wood into his bread—he who is the bread of angels and human beings; they put wood upon him to torment him, not wood beneath him for reclining. [Col. 0444B] This bread was baked and made firm through suffering.

Holy soul, suffer with him, so that you may be cleansed and made firm by the fire of tribulation. Do not be consumed like lead; rather, become purer like gold. If, scorched by tribulation, you do not fail but advance through patience, you will be gold and God’s couch. He who had no couch on the cross will recline in you, and he who had not even a wooden one will make you golden. Therefore he endured the Passion and had no couch, so that through his example and love we may suffer, and so that, by endurance of adversities, we may be cleansed in such a way that he himself reclines and rests in us in this age, and we rest with him in the age to come.

Consider his charity, O soul, and incline your whole self toward his love and good pleasure, that you may expend yourself wholly for him and bear with steadfast and devoted mind whatever is brought upon you for his sake; thus may you in some measure respond to his benefits and become his couch. Therefore, that you may be a golden couch, strive also to possess the gold of spiritual wisdom. Let your wisdom not be muddy but golden; not earthly, animal, and demonic, but spiritual and divine. Of this spiritual wisdom the abyss of human wisdom says, “It is not in me”; and the sea—that is, the bitterness of vices—says, “It is not with me.” Therefore this carnal wisdom must be cast away and exchanged for spiritual wisdom. Thus pure, fiery, tested gold must be bought, so that we may become rich and possess this gold.

After spiritual wisdom and amendment of character, one must come [Col. 0444D] to this virtue of patience: willingly—indeed, cheerfully—to bear every adversity and rejoice in it for Christ’s sake. Thus, step by step and gradually, Christ advances and cleanses the soul, both by his grace and by the example of his gifts, so that it becomes gold—indeed, his golden couch.

He also makes in it an ascent of purple. He makes an ascent in the soul when, by his grace, he makes it desire heavenly things. But this ascent is purple and reddish. For such a soul sometimes suffers insults and detractions from the wicked, who envy its devotion because they neither love the good nor wish to do it. When it hears the insults of the wicked, it receives from them a certain disturbance of mind and the red blush of shame. Purple, however, is so red [Col. 0445A] that its redness appears scattered and varied. So, in the holy and devout soul, there is a varied redness: it blushes from the assault of insults, and at the same time it blushes with charity, by which it burns even toward those who insult it. It also blushes with the desire by which it is kindled toward heavenly and eternal things. These blushes are diverse, and all are precious; deservedly they adorn the devout soul and may be compared to purple.

“The midst thereof he paved with charity.” This “midst” consists of works belonging to the class of good works—namely, works that may be done with either good or bad intention, such as vigils, fasts, prayers, almsgiving, and the rest. These must be paved with charity: that is, performed in charity and with good intention. Likewise, they must be performed with fraternal charity in such a way that the weak are neither [Col. 0445B] scandalized nor weakened by them. Rather, these things should be paved—that is, done with such evenness and discernment—that the soul may walk in all of them without reproach, knowing when fittingly to practice them and when in turn to omit them. This midst will be well paved with charity if it is so ordered.

Thus Solomon now makes himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon, silver columns, a golden couch, a purple ascent, and paves the midst with charity, when he enriches the soul with fullness of grace and spiritual food, and forms it by the examples and teaching of the perfect so that it can build up others; when he adorns it with the beauty of virtues and strengthens it by perfection; when he makes it so pure that he rests in it and has it as a couch; so exalted and precious that, through desire for heavenly things, [Col. 0445C] charity toward neighbors, and endurance of evils, it may be compared to purple; and so discerning and sociable in outward conduct that it pleases the divine gaze and does not offend the sight of neighbors.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the manner of advancing, Christ’s example, and the reward

“Go forth, and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him, on the day of solemnity and gladness” (Song of Songs 3). This is an exhortation to faithful and devout souls to consider and contemplate in mind the beauty and glory Jesus Christ possesses in heaven through the suffering of his martyrdom. [Col. 0445D] These souls are daughters of Zion—that is, of that heavenly city which beholds God and which is our mother. They have been spiritually born anew and regenerated in Christ, in order that they may be daughters and heirs of that vision and blessedness.

They are told to go forth by faith and desire from earthly things to consider heavenly things, and to contemplate the diadem of our Solomon—that is, Christ—who redeemed and made peace for us. O daughters of Zion, go forth from carnal desire, sinful habit, and blindness of heart; and see—that is, spiritually contemplate—the glory of our King, the happiness of that heavenly gladness. Thus may you be drawn by that sweetness and delight and enter eagerly, so that you walk in such a way as to go forth from yourselves.

For some walk, [Col. 0446A] but do not go forth, because now they advance, now retreat; now walk slackly, now crookedly. At times some persist in good works and yet also commit evils. Through a kind of sloth and blindness of mind, while striving to do good they guard against evil too little, not attending to the fact that goods mingled with evils do not please God. Again, some are too weak for any arduous undertaking and endure the burden of faintheartedness in both spirit and body. Others think nothing more difficult to bear than resisting their own pleasures; they delight in temptations or desires and resist their passions and impulses too little. To the degree that they allow themselves to be conquered in small matters, to that degree they become weak against sins, vices, and temptations, and insufficient for walking and advancing.

[Col. 0446B]

Others advance less because they do not walk rightly and discerningly. Some devote themselves more intensely to certain good works of lesser usefulness and neglect others more suited to their progress. They persist in bodily labors and neglect virtues of the soul and piety, although bodily exercise profits little, while piety is more necessary because it is profitable for all things. Again, because they do not keep watch over the heart and lack vigilance, through this negligence they offend in many matters. And still others are very anxious about certain small and trivial things, while neither guarding against nor recognizing greater ones: they strain out a gnat while swallowing a camel.

All these, though they walk, nevertheless remain within themselves, because they do not leave behind their former habits, [Col. 0446C] ingrained imperfection, and sluggishness. Thus, with every fault corrected and the eyes of the heart cleansed, they ought to go forth to see God and Solomon crowned with a diadem. First, therefore, it is necessary that we do good in such a way that we turn away from evil; for one does not advance well who now walks, now falls. We must also strengthen weak knees and guard against excessive faintheartedness and weakness; otherwise we shall not go forth from ourselves to attain this vision. We must also make straight paths for our feet, so that we may recognize the means by which we can make the greatest progress and direct the steps of the mind there: that is, we must devote ourselves to correcting every fault, cleansing the heart, and increasing charity.

If [Col. 0446D] we walk thus, we shall indeed go forth from ourselves and, with the eyes of the heart cleansed from former affections and blindness, be able to see King Solomon. Then we shall be able to see him—that is, contemplate him—in the loftiness of mind, shining in the diadem, that is, the aureole with which his mother, Judea, crowned him in this life by inflicting martyrdom on him; through it she fashioned for him such a crown and glory. Because she crowned him with martyrdom in the time of his Passion, he was crowned with such a diadem on the day of the solemnity and gladness of his glorious Ascension.

For it was a great solemnity when the citizens of heaven came to meet their King and the Lord, Redeemer of humankind, as he arrived in triumph; great too was the joy, both of the Redeemer himself and of those same citizens, over the redeemed. [Col. 0447A] Hence it is said of him that he caused his citizens to be summoned, that they might congratulate and rejoice with him over the human being whom he had found and redeemed after having lost him. This is the day of solemnity and gladness, or of his betrothal and the gladness of his heart. For then he betrothed to himself his bride alone—namely, the heavenly Church of angels; then he entered upon those nuptials and joined himself to her. From those nuptials he will return to the nuptials of humankind at the end of the age, when he will join this bride to that bride: “On the day of his betrothal,” it says, “and of the gladness of his heart.”

How great a gladness of heart—that is, joy in his humanity, insofar as he is human—the Son of God received in that betrothal, with respect to the glory of the Redeemer, speech cannot express and understanding cannot comprehend. For as many as will be redeemed by him, over so many [Col. 0447B] will be his joy. As much as each person rejoices in his own salvation, so much—and greater—will be his joy over each of them.

O daughters of Zion, consider this glory and gladness of our King; set this example before yourselves. When you suffer adversities, go forth from your imperfection and impatience so as to bear lightly the evils inflicted on you. Look upon your King, who suffered for you and was crowned through suffering with glory and honor. And when you suffer anything for piety’s sake, reflect what persecution and opposition he endured from the ungodly for you. For if God suffered for humanity, how much more ought a human being to suffer for himself? What you can suffer is slight and brief; what you await through it is immense. “The momentary and light burden of our tribulation works in us an eternal weight of glory.” Think of the eternal, and you will bear the momentary lightly; think of the weight—that is, the greatness—of glory, and the tribulation accompanied by such a reward becomes light.

While you suffer, look upon the crown. Then a diadem is made for you, by which you will be crowned on the day of solemnity that will be yours when you depart from the body; or on the day of that betrothal, when you pass from the wedding feast of the Church Militant to the wedding feast of the Church Triumphant. Therefore, O daughters of Zion, prudent virgins, prepare your lamps; prepare for yourselves the oil of good works and the light of charity; and so go out to meet the bridegroom and bride. Then you will be “a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.”

## CHAPTER XIV. On interior and exterior humility, and its threefold distinction

[Col. 0447D]

“Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful” (Song of Songs 4). Christ commends in the perfect soul a twofold beauty: that it is beautiful outwardly through holy conduct, and inwardly through a simple intention and humility of mind. The soul’s outward beauty, therefore, consists in living moderately in all things, using simple food and clothing, avoiding every superfluous or blameworthy thing, and practicing everything that is just and honorable.

It is also adorned when it is well ordered alike in deed and speech; when it presents itself as sociable and loving to everyone, harming no one, deceiving no one, [Col. 0448A] sympathizing with all, and helping all according to its ability. And when it is prudent, chaste, gentle, meek, and adorned with every other good quality, the soul rightly possesses outward beauty: it has propriety in dress, dignity in bearing, cheerfulness in expression, ears not itching for gossip, eyes neither haughty nor inquisitive, a tongue instructed and restrained from frivolous or useless words, speaking what is good and salutary.

It is further made attractive when it is not disturbed by anger, impatience, or rancor; when it does not quarrel, slander, or judge, nor lend an ear to those who discuss such matters; when it associates with everyone not merely without reproach but with grace. It is also beautiful when it is fervent in good work, in God’s service, in the labor of fraternal charity; energetic, fervent, and discerning in all its [Col. 0448B] undertakings.

There is another, inward beauty: when in everything it does praiseworthily it possesses a single eye—that is, a pure intention—neither desiring nor caring to be praised by people, but seeking the praise that comes from God alone and desiring only heavenly things. Thus, when it is outwardly beautiful through works, it is more greatly adorned and pleasing to the divine gaze within through purity of intention, humility, and a disposition of mind by which it does great things yet always regards itself as worthless. This lowliness of mind is all the more precious because it proceeds from the fountain of love and the root of fervor. For to one who loves and is devout, what one has is never enough, nor does one count what one has done great, because anyone who continually longs for greater things judges oneself poor.

[Col. 0448C] There is, then, a humility that is devout, a humility that is voluntary, and a humility that is compelled. Humility is compelled when a person, recalling sins, weakness, and imperfection before his own eyes, as it were forces an unwilling mind—one more disposed to keep its good qualities before its eyes—to grow silent and to regard itself as worthless. Though compelled in these persons, humility is nevertheless achieved, so that the mind attains it to some extent. Yet if the discipline of compelling itself ceases through negligence, the mind immediately slips away from it and is led without delay back to its former pride.

In some people, however, the mind cannot even be compelled, always tending upward to lofty and accustomed things; nor is there anything able to press it down and subject it to the lowliness of humility. For humility is lofty to the proud; even if they sometimes attempt to climb up to it, they immediately fall back. They do not climb to it because they tend toward it with a weak desire. They both will and do not will, as Solomon says of the sluggard: “The sluggard wills and does not will” (Prov. 13).

Humility is voluntary when, guided by reason, a person sees how weak and sinful he is; sees, according to Job, that he has no help in himself; and the will consents to this reasoning, loves this judgment, and chooses to be despised, because it knows that to recognize oneself thus is expedient. Therefore one willingly humbles oneself because, enlightened by grace, one now loves humility as one loves other good things. This humility is not compelled, because, after the time of weakness has been shaken off and the passions of vices have been weakened, the soul comes to such freedom of spirit that the good delights and is pleasing to it.

[Col. 0449A] There is also another, higher humility, not compelled, not drawn by rational guidance, and not merely voluntary, but fervent and devout. The perfect soul possesses it; it is as humble as it is devout, and as it grows in spirit or knowledge, so it advances in humility. For true grace does not exalt but humbles, because it shows a person more fully to oneself; and, understanding its own loftiness, the person sees how little of it one could grasp. The more anyone eats spiritual food, the more one hungers. Because such food can never be comprehended in fullness, it never satisfies the one who desires it. Therefore it always humbles, because its delights always abound less than they are desired.

The grace it has tasted humbles such a soul, as do contemplation of good [Col. 0449B] examples, reflection on the soul’s pilgrimage and the manifold misery of human existence, love of heavenly happiness, and desire for freedom—namely, the freedom by which it will be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of God’s children. A soul purified of earthly pleasures knows how to desire only spiritual things and passes wholly into love for them and affection for the virtues. It is humbled by love for Christ, who humbled himself for it; it is humbled by love for humility itself, which it embraces because Christ especially loved and possessed it. Hence humility was also called in a singular way Christ’s virtue. Everything lowly pleases this soul because it understands that these things are lofty.

For it knows that, as soon as it is humbled inwardly, it is exalted, because it is made like Christ, who was least—that is, most humble—[Col. 0449C] in the kingdom of heaven, that is, in the present Church, though he was great and Son of the Most High. The Spirit of Christ, who kindles this soul to Christ’s love, also instructs it in Christ’s humility. The fuller it is, the more it chooses to be abased; and the more blessed it is, the poorer it is in spirit. For one who has Christ’s Spirit cannot fail to love what Christ loves and possesses. Love of Christ and humility have such a close correspondence that whoever is shown to possess one necessarily possesses the other; and as much as one has of the one, so much one has of the other. Thus, if you truly love, you are truly humble; and if you are less humble, you are proved to love less.

Therefore the perfect soul, because it loves, is humbled; and because of this humility, which proceeds from the root of love, it is deservedly called beloved and [Col. 0449D] beautiful. Its twofold beauty is commended: outward work and inward humility. One is deservedly praised who both does great things and thinks humbly of oneself; who is not high-minded but agrees with the lowly, and bears a humble disposition in all things.

## CHAPTER XV. How the soul should despise earthly things and know inward things
“Your eyes are doves’ eyes, apart from that which lies hidden within” (Song 4). Such a soul has doves’ eyes, because it looks simply upon these earthly things and is not carried away toward them by covetous desire. Indeed, it is content with little; it does not seek what belongs to others; it is not borne along by a desire for advancement or riches or any fleshly pleasure [Col. 0450A]. The inward sufficiency of the mind gives the outward gaze a pleasing quality, so that it has doves’ eyes with regard to earthly things, just as appetite gives the covetous of earthly things the eyes of kites. No anxiety over possessions afflicts it; no love torments it; no occupation wearies it. It enjoys great repose and security, because it neither seeks, cares for, nor covets these things.

For, as we read in Job: “Man is born for labour, but the bird for flying” (Job 5). Those who are men—that is, human, fleshly, occupied with desire for worldly things—have labour; but the good, because they do not love or desire these things, escape their affliction and fly away. For the evil, this labour is born from covetousness, which is the root of all evils; but the good are born, through the renewal and uplifting of the Holy Spirit, to this [Col. 0450B] flight and freedom. These are those who “fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows” (Isa. 60), because they are raised toward eternal desires and are borne toward low things by no covetousness.

The Holy Spirit, signified by the dove, works this flight and dove-like gaze in the soul. This Spirit makes the outward eyes simple and opens the inward ones, because he enlightens the human understanding and advances it to understand and grasp spiritual and heavenly things. Therefore the eyes of the devout soul are doves’ eyes, because its faculties have been enlightened through the Holy Spirit and taught to savour spiritual things: seeking those things, attending to them, trampling and despising earthly things. For they savour, according to the Spirit, those things in which wisdom, life, and peace consist. This wisdom is life because it gives life to the soul [Col. 0450C]; it is peace because it calms, orders, regulates, nourishes, delights, advances, and makes the soul blessed.

It is neither singular nor set apart, but common; it seeks not its own interests but those of others; it is not crafty or malicious, but pure, gentle, lovable, and gracious; it is not obstinate but open to persuasion; it agrees with the good and is at harmony with the benevolent. It lacks the gall of disturbances and bitterness which love of earthly things contains within itself. It savours God, while it knows God, is from God, and is in God. Hence its eyes—that is, its faculties—are called doves’ eyes, that is, [the eyes] of the Holy Spirit, because through him it sees and understands.

These dove’s eyes—that is, these spiritual faculties—this sublimity and this tranquillity of mind are in you, O soul, apart from those things [Col. 0450D] which are hidden within. For who can set forth outwardly the things which you secretly engage in with Christ in the chamber of your heart? Who can understand or express in words that mutual converse, boldness of speech with him, consolation received from him or revelation, unity of minds, harmony of delights, mutual love, zeal for righteousness and souls, longing for the vision and enjoyment of God, weariness of pilgrimage, and desire to depart?

Now the soul’s understanding is opened so that it understands the Scriptures; now it is instructed concerning hidden or doubtful matters; now it is so united to God that it is made one spirit with him; now it is so absorbed by the Spirit that it does not remember itself to be abiding in the flesh; now it recognizes certain secrets of divine inspiration which it did not previously know. But now [Col. 0451A] it is so joined to God, and feels God joined to itself, and so transfers its whole will into God, that it either understands God’s will or bends that will toward its own. For from that purity of heart by which it agrees with God’s will in all things, it also understands that will and is worthy to bend it toward what it desires.

Now by love it so binds and draws God to itself that it believes it possesses him alone; now it is so enlarged and passes into him that through charity it embraces every human being in him, sees all people by the light by which it is illumined, and has compassion upon and accommodates itself to all, because it has one and the same charity toward them. It directs its attention toward him in such a way that through him it sees and comprehends many no less than few.

Such a soul obtains certain requests because of the greatness of its faith, some [Col. 0451B] because of profound humility, and some through importunity. At times it compels God by devotion and the fervour of boundless desire; at times it bends him by the composition of its words and by gentle or careful speech; at times, having shown a just cause for mercy and reason concerning certain requests, it receives consolation regarding some things and revelation concerning others. Now it understands that it has been heard with certainty, now doubtfully; sometimes it knows that it has been heard but does not know the manner.

Thus Tobias knew that he had been heard, but the manner was not revealed to him. For he believed the manner would be that he should die, whereas rather it was that he should receive sight. In some matters it hopes that God will be favourable, because it feels itself anticipated and aided in prayer by consolation. In obtaining some things [Col. 0451C] it perceives that God must be bent and knocked upon with long-continued prayers. In certain matters it learns that it must seek and desire a man who will set the hope of his prayer against God’s vengeance. In others, however, it recognizes that God’s wrath cannot be resisted, even if Moses and Samuel should stand before him.

These and similar familiar and secret matters of prayer, meditation, and knowledge lie hidden within the perfect soul in the present life. But what lies hidden concerning future things is concealed from the eyes of all living people. For what shall then be has not yet appeared; because, when God appears in that life, it shall be like him, since it shall see him as he is. Then it shall be perfectly assimilated to God, to whom it is now assimilated in part; because when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away; and [Col. 0451D] then it shall know as it is known. Then it shall see how the Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both; then, finally, it shall see the Holy Trinity in its glory.

## CHAPTER XVI. How holy meditations are obtained from Christ through prayer

“Your hair is like flocks of goats, which have come up from Mount Gilead” (Song 3). The bride’s hair is holy meditations. As hair grows upon the head, so these arise in the mind. This hair is compared to goats because of certain likenesses. In seeking pasture, goats are accustomed to make for mountain heights and trees, and they also chew the cud. Thus holy meditations [Col. 0452A] always tend upward, labouring to investigate and know spiritual and heavenly things. So far as they are able to grasp them, they endeavour to ruminate—that is, to reconsider and reflect upon them—to call them up from the belly of the mind to memory, and to grind and break them down for savour and edification.

These trees are the good, growing and lofty in grace. Therefore, when the devout soul attends to them, meditates upon their holiness, and strives to raise itself to their imitation, it climbs these trees by meditation. When it loves and considers the vigour of their minds, the vigour of their daily progress and spiritual renewal, and carries these over alike into memory and imitation, it plucks from them, as it were, food by which it may be nourished. For one who observes those who act well and delights in their virtues, devotion, and way of life [Col. 0452B] is stirred and nourished through them toward what is good and perfect.

These she-goats also climb mountains when the soul’s meditations contemplate the exalted life and conduct of the perfect and desire to ascend to these things, join themselves to the good, and seek their fellowship, consolation, conversation, and prayer. Thus these goats climb trees or mountains; thus they always seek the heights, and, despising low things, seek and pursue heavenly things. They delight in their sight, are refreshed by their pasture, renewed by desire, make progress, and tend upward by example. They always make progress because they always attend to the good; they are always fresh and eager. For a person becomes such as are those whom he beholds, attends to, and joins himself to most intimately.

These goats, namely holy meditations, come up from Mount Gilead. Mount Gilead signifies Christ; for *Gilead* is interpreted “heap of testimony.” The saints are heaped together and gathered in Christ, and they have the testimony of Jesus and of his faith and works: living stones, indeed, belonging to the heavenly building. Mount Gilead is said to have had most abundant pastures, and Christ feeds most abundantly. He not only refreshes by example but also pours in grace. No saint builds up by example as Christ does, because no one else possessed such humility, patience, obedience, gentleness, charity, and perfection in every virtue. In him also was all fullness of grace, so that [Col. 0452D] all who have grace receive from this fullness. He is the mountain of God, a rich mountain: rich not only in himself but enriching others from himself, nourishing some with the milk of grace and refreshing others through the fuller sweetness of wisdom. Therefore there are richer pastures on this mountain.

But we must see how these goats—that is, devout meditations—come up from God. The soul lies low and is in the depths when it thinks earthly and fleshly thoughts. But it rises and ascends on high when it meditates and turns over spiritual things in its mind. Therefore in fleshly thoughts we are depressed and cast down by ourselves; toward spiritual things we are raised by God, because good meditations are from God and arise in the soul, whereas fleshly and evil meditations come from ourselves. For there is no good in us—that is, in our flesh [Col. 0453A]—because the flesh is barren and does not bear meditations of this sort, but produces thorns and thistles for us. Evil thoughts also proceed from the heart, and evil angels likewise make suggestions.

When, therefore, the soul is compuncted over past sins; when it resolves to correct and guard itself in the present; when it is inflamed with delight in some virtue or zeal for progress; when it is moved to compassion for its neighbour, to zeal for righteousness, or to love or desire of eternal life with some devotion or spiritual sweetness; when it is illumined, instructed, or stirred toward some good—such meditations and affections are from Christ, who speaks thoughts of peace in the soul and whose Spirit suggests all these things in secret. When [Col. 0453B] such things are felt in the mind, then indeed the goats come up from Mount Gilead: that is, holy meditations arise and rise up from Christ.

For one who abides in Christ and in whom Christ abides bears much fruit of these thoughts. And the one in whom these meditations are gathered and heaped up has testimony that Christ abides in him and receives from him assent to these meditations. They are therefore from Christ and ascend from him, who nourishes them in our heart and makes them rise and ascend. Now he suggests them of himself; now he must be prayed to that he may grant them. For Christ sometimes sleeps, so that, when his Spirit does not speak, the little boat of the mind is covered by waves of temptations or evil thoughts, driven by a contrary wind [Col. 0453C]. Therefore he must be awakened, that he may command these winds and the sea of these disturbances and make tranquillity in the mind.

Thus, when the soul prays and awakens Christ by the persistence of its prayers, spiritual and desired thoughts are received. For they ascend from Christ when he has been awakened and made propitious through prayer. You may see how, as the soul persists in prayers, one meditation after another rises and ascends; and as many impulses to pray arise, so many meditations rise and ascend. As the soul persists and multiplies its prayers, these thoughts are multiplied; and at length they grow so dense in the soul that it is now walled round by their vast host, though formerly it seemed alone and almost abandoned.

Since these meditations are from Christ and ascend in the mind, let the soul ascend this mountain [Col. 0453D], abide in Christ, and call upon Christ. Let it undertake the exalted office of prayer. Let it go up alone onto the mountain to pray, excluding and setting aside all occupations. Let Christ’s words abide in it; let it hear his law with the ear of the heart and keep his commands, so that whatever it wishes to ask may be done for it. For whoever hears the law, that person’s prayer will be acceptable; whoever fulfils the commandments will be heard; and from commandments fulfilled in deed one will be instructed, because God will give wisdom and knowledge of spiritual things to the person who keeps righteousness. And, as Solomon says (Prov. 6), and according to the Psalmist, one gains understanding from God’s commandments (Ps. 118).

Thus, from this rich and fertile mountain, while the devout soul prays, these goats—that is, holy meditations—ascend. But from the malignant spirit are suggested and arise useless thoughts, which dry up the richness of devotion and extinguish good meditations [Col. 0454A].

These are that people of the Amalekites. *Amalek* is interpreted “a licking people”: for they lick away and destroy the sweetness of the ointment; they consume the anointing of the Holy Spirit. Against them one must fight in prayer with Moses, lifting up one’s hands together with one’s heart, so that we may pray and at the same time keep the commandments in deed. If we thus raise both to God and do not grow weary, we shall prevail (Exod. 17). If we cease or act more sluggishly, Amalek will prevail, as we read happened there.

At times we possess holy meditations in peace and without Amalek’s attack; at times, while he fights with us and now prevails, now is overcome, prayer advances. If hands have been raised more slackly in prayer [Col. 0454B], the soul experiences these alternations: now it sees itself superior, now it is affected by spiritual delight, now it is occupied and oppressed by evil thoughts. Yet, if it does not cease or grow weary in prayer, there is no doubt that Amalek will be overcome and put to flight.

When, through our negligence and laxity of heart, we slip away from good thoughts into vain and harmful ones—at times through the adversary’s tempting and suggesting—it sometimes happens that, dried up from grace and deprived of spiritual thoughts for a long time, the soul does not experience that sweet delight. For this one must pray all the more humbly and persistently, the more we do not know whether we are in any way responsible for this deprivation. For a person is deprived of grace because of some hidden sin [Col. 0454C], or because of ingratitude—namely, by acting unworthily through it, or by failing to give thanks to its giver—or because one does not seek it as one should, or because one admits fleshly thoughts.

When this dryness has therefore come, and the soul has become like a land without water, hands must be stretched out to God in prayer. And, as Elijah sought rain after a drought of three years (3 Kings 18), one must sit in prayer and ask for the rain of grace. He sent his servant again and again to discover whether his prayers had been heard, and it did not happen before the seventh occasion. Thus, when the mind has long been dried up from the grace of devotion, one must pray and persist many times, and not cease from prayer until repose of mind—which is signified by the number seven—and grace, which is sevenfold, accomplish their work [Col. 0454D].

For without great persistence and laborious prayer, a mind dried up from grace does not deserve to receive it. Yet it cannot attain that repose with devotion by a devout prayer, since it is deprived of devotion and those sweet affections; rather, it must compensate for devotion by labour and importunity. Thus, if not because of friendship, nevertheless because of importunity it will receive what it asks.

But if its prayers are to be heard, it must cut off and circumcise superfluous speech, thought, and even action, lest it be unrestrained in thought or speak vain, superfluous, or harmful things. Nor should it be without custody of the heart, indiscriminately admitting every sort of thought, neither discerning them nor guarding itself against them. Nor should it be soft and lax [Col. 0455A] in action, occupying and doing itself not with what is fitting but with what pleases. For that mountain Carmel, where Elijah poured out this prayer and received what he asked, signifies this guarding and circumcision. *Carmel* is interpreted “knowledge of circumcision.” Those who do not know how to circumcise and cut off such things in themselves are not worthy to be heard.

For there are mountains of Gilboa, upon which neither dew nor the rain of grace descends, because upon them the shield of the mighty has been cast away—that is, manly guarding and circumcision. For without vigilance no virtue is granted, nor is fuller grace acquired. Thus let the watchful soul see and cut off superfluous and harmful things; let it persist in prayer again and again and not cease. When first a small cloud of grace rises, at length may the abundance of saving rain burst forth and follow, fully watering and soaking the mind that had long been parched by harmful dryness and lack of grace.

Therefore let it ask and await grace from this source; from this source let it prepare itself for grace and consider with what caution it may return to holy meditations. This will happen especially by returning first to meditations most recently possessed. For these are recovered more easily in proportion as they have been held more recently; return to more remote and earlier meditations is harder. In this way the end of prayer is better than its beginning. Thus the loving and diligent soul will obtain all things from Christ, who is beginning and end, and through Christ; and he will bring about within it assent to good meditations.

## CHAPTER XVII. On discernment of thoughts, and how it is attained

[Col. 0455C]

“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing” (Song 4). The teeth are the examinations of discernment, by which spiritual meditations and thoughts of the heart are examined, crushed, and distinguished: whether they are pure and truly good; whether they are from God, an evil spirit, or the human heart. For the evil spirit knows how to suggest certain thoughts that appear spiritual, and the human spirit sometimes pretends and falsely claims to be the Holy Spirit, as is read in Job: “Behold, my belly is like new wine” (Job 32).

This also happened to Elijah, who uttered words from the swelling of his own spirit, believing that he spoke them from the Holy Spirit and zeal for God. For by “belly” is understood the inner chamber of the heart, and by “new wine,” the fervour of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0455D], by which Elihu in Job thought himself stirred, though he was moved only by the impulse of his own heart. In many such matters, a person follows a movement of the heart, or even an impulse of vice, while believing himself moved by the Holy Spirit.

Demons also sometimes conceal evils under the appearance of good. They incite people to certain good things; and, in order to lead them to evil, they even foretell future events. For they can foretell some future things because they sometimes know them; some they discover through subtlety of nature; some they learn through holy angels revealing them; some they infer from the sequence of causes, some from human natural dispositions, and some from the condition of the air. For a long time they indicate some matters as they are, in order eventually to deceive [Col. 0456A] a credulous mind.

They also deceive by false devotion, because they produce in the soul certain prayers and meditations, a sweet affection, and even tears, in order to lead either the mind into error or pride, or the body into weakness. At times they suggest something from Scripture to be understood through a false interpretation in a sense other than the proper one, or to be acted upon otherwise than truth allows. They improperly make some people concerned about the salvation of others; they encourage and inflame them toward the conversion or edification of persons far away, in order to throw them down from tranquillity of mind and from their own benefit. Portraying this business in the soul as though it were some bright day, they present it as healthier and more useful than its former occupation.

When, therefore, something is suggested to us as a thing to be done, we must consider whether any element of indiscretion is mixed into it [Col. 0456B], or whether the enemy’s deceit is insinuating itself; and we must examine it fully: whether it is done with due fear and caution; whether not merely our own but also others’ benefit lies in it; whether human praise or display creeps in; whether some vanity or frivolity impels it; whether it differs in no respect from Scripture or the examples of the saints.

Whatever comes from the evil spirit can be discovered to be false in some respect, or its peril rests upon the future and will soon be uncovered. For, by revealing his fraud, the enemy will suggest more openly what he had hidden, and by this he will be recognized. The Holy Spirit likewise works in diverse ways in the soul; hence his operations must be known and distinguished. At times he converts the mind through fear of punishment; at times he raises it to love of God, yet does not bestow much knowledge [Col. 0456C]. He moves and stimulates the mind toward good and toward God, yet does not immediately make the person perfect. For in such things there is not full knowledge, but a beginning and inducement toward good, or consolation; since an infirm and imperfect person, one who attains less to spiritual knowledge and understanding, sometimes receives these things.

But when someone has advanced in knowledge and then ascends to the degree of contemplation, if that person perceives something of God and seems to himself to comprehend it perfectly, he does not understand it as it is in God. Hence Elijah, who saw the Lord pass by, because he understood the Spirit to be incomprehensible, says that the Lord is not in the commotion or fire but in the whisper of a gentle breeze. For whatever can be perfectly comprehended is not there; rather, there is felt something subtle concerning God, which cannot be fully comprehended [Col. 0456D].

Grace is given to one still a weak beginner, so that, illumined by it, he may know himself and, strengthened by it, correct himself; and thus he may arrive more fully at knowledge. Such knowledge is not attained unless greater purity of heart is gained through improved conduct. The more perfectly each person has cleansed the eyes of the heart, the more fully that person can see God; and the more fully one sees him, the more one understands that the one seen is incomprehensible.

Thus one who has advanced in knowledge has a sound understanding of God and recognizes that whatever can be grasped of him is slight. For the nearer a person approaches wisdom and knowledge, the less he thinks there is that he can grasp, because, according to Solomon, the wiser one becomes, the more wisdom itself recedes from him (Eccl. 7): that is, one understands ever more how incomprehensible it is [Col. 0457A]. Such knowledge does not puff up the soul but kindles and humbles it, showing it more fully its own blindness. Each person may know from this that his understanding is sound, and that his eye then sees God: if he rebukes himself out of humility, hungers yet more for the wisdom he has received, and recognizes as minimal what he has grasped or can grasp of it.

Therefore one must carefully distinguish between the Holy Spirit and one’s own spirit, examine oneself, and determine, when moved toward some good work, whether human delight, vice, or temptation is impelling one toward its performance. For there are certain impulses in the soul arising from a person’s disposition, from some cause or occasion, from curiosity, ambition, frivolity, vice, or temptation. Those arising from vice or temptation must be entirely avoided. Those arising from humanity and the other causes named may be tolerated and used well—namely, if we never follow them, but suffer them at our side, for service and not for harm—so that from them we may have greater eagerness to perform the work which we intend to do. For where natural qualities cooperate with us without another cause, our spirit is readier in those matters and more eagerly accomplishes what it intends [Col. 0457B].

We must therefore see to it and take every precaution that some fleshly or human pleasure does not principally impel us, and that we do not follow such an impulse, even if we endure it. But where we recognize the impulse of the Holy Spirit, there let us proceed and do what he suggests.

We must likewise consider that in a soul still weak and imperfect, fleshly movements are more prone than spiritual ones. Hence, when someone is readily moved toward some good with a certain lightness of heart, there is reason to fear that such lightness arises from carnality, especially if something is joined to it which can please human nature. Similarly, cheerfulness of heart is suspect when a person is driven to something with a certain vehemence and impatience of delay, because the Holy Spirit is modest and tranquil, and his movements are measured.

Sometimes natural lightness of heart, natural kindness, prosperity, or some arising cause of joy cooperates with devotion and lifts it more fully [Col. 0457C]. Likewise a sadder disposition, adversity, or a cause of sorrow depresses and even hinders it. Hence in prayer an uncomplicated person is sometimes falsely consoled or loses confidence, inferring signs of being heard according to the cheerfulness of spirit that he feels, prophesying from his own heart and imagining that what his heart says is the Lord speaking. The enemy also knows how to deceive someone whom he finds credulous in such matters by false consolations or false revelations.

Therefore this discernment of spirits must be known. When the devout soul judges and examines all these matters, it crushes and breaks them up, as it were, with certain teeth of discernment. These are the bride’s teeth, which are likened to flocks of shorn sheep. The shearings are harmless thoughts cutting away outward things—namely, love of earthly things and desire to possess worldly wisdom [Col. 0458A]. For love of earthly things blinds the eyes of the heart, weighs down and depresses the mind, so that it cannot rise to knowledge and discernment of spiritual things.

Worldly wisdom does not comprehend God, nor does the natural person receive the things which are of the Spirit of God. For God has made foolish the wisdom of this world: thus, the more a person savours earthly things, the less that person savours God; and the more widely the heart is stretched, the more narrowly it is confined in love of divine things. For the light of outward things and carnality so darkens a person that he less attains purity for discerning spiritual things; and in proportion as he is scattered among many things, he gathers himself less toward the one thing, the thing most necessary.

At times something inward also clings to the soul, severely hindering discernment of spiritual things: namely, one’s own will [Col. 0458B]. In proportion as it seeks its own things, it is joined less to God; and the more it remains in itself rather than ascending to God, the less it apprehends the things of God. Likewise one who loves his own will cannot attain discernment. For while he follows what pleases rather than what truth judges, as he departs from truth, so he is separated from true knowledge and thus from discernment.

This is the fleece which must be cut off at the end—that is, pleasure—the weight by which, while the soul is warmed and burdened, it is hindered from spiritual things. Thus shorn sheep—that is, these harmless thoughts—more freely grasp and discern spiritual things, and write wisdom in their freedom from such things. These thoughts come up from the washing [Col. 0458C], that is, from compunction and the tears of repentance. In this washing they are cleansed from the filth alike of sins and vices and are relieved of their weight, so that they may ascend and climb to knowledge of spiritual things.

For compunction wholly consumes sins and vices, cleanses the soul from all their filth together with the dregs of carnality, opens the pores of the heart, and pours down rains of virtues by which the soul may fly and be raised to these things. The soul thus drenched rises as though at dawn to discern every thought and see whether any has strayed, been impure, or worked without profit. Thus discernment, when after innocence, rejection of worldly things, and mortification of one’s own will it has been cleansed by the grace of compunction and trained in understanding and examining spiritual things, is rightly said to come up from the washing [Col. 0458D].

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the discernment of natural and gratuitous gifts, and the various movements of the soul

“All are bearing twins, and none among them is barren” (Song 4). Great is the virtue of discernment, by which a person investigates in what respect he is inclined to evil or disposed toward good; discerns how far the goods of nature and gifts of grace can assist him; distinguishes virtues and vices, movements of the heart, causes arising externally or inwardly, works more perfect or imperfect, consolation of grace and knowledge of these things; and finally strives to know the inward and outward [Col. 0459A] condition.

For discernment, applied to the word of God, is sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. It shows a person how there is in him a twofold affection, namely fleshly and spiritual; and that, so long as the fleshly affection has not yet been subdued, the soul cannot delight perfectly in spiritual things. Even if it rejoices in the Lord, the flesh cannot yet rejoice, as the Prophet says: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” (Ps. 83).

As long as a person is so diverse and divided, he does not rise fully to spiritual joy or to the accomplishment of any laborious work. For one still imperfect and fleshly is weak for a laborious work, when he has nothing of his own for doing it—that is, when no inclination of the heart, pleasure of the flesh, human cause, or occasion draws him toward it. With such aids he is much more able to perform spiritual things, to which he would be less ready from grace alone [Col. 0459B].

All works and desires of such a soul are imperfect, because it is carried partly by an impulse of the flesh and partly moved spiritually. With regard to such a person, we must suspect that, in every work in which he is found frequent or ready, or in which he perseveres for a long time, grace alone does not assist him, but some human pleasure assists at the same time. But if movements toward venial sins impelled such a person more frequently than reason or charity did, unless he removed those movements by repentance, there would be cause to fear that he would soon fall into mortal sin and be overwhelmed by the sand of such things.

Yet, so long as a person is not so blinded as to depart from charity, what he does will not be fruitless, because he does not lose the merit of whatever is done from charity. Finally, if the enemy incites one established in charity to some good work in order to turn him away from something more useful or deceive him in some way, even this will be meritorious for the person who does not know it and intends good, because it is done from charity. To the extent that the devil’s camps incite a person toward some good with evil intent, they serve God. For the enemy does not always attack openly; sometimes he joins himself to a person under the appearance of good in order to deceive.

Human nature itself and a person’s disposition are opposed and weak in one good work, but so ready in another that its eagerness can seem to be devotion. For natural qualities have great power in a human being, so that in the imperfect person movements of thought, speech, and action frequently proceed from them; and likewise joy or sadness, cheerfulness of heart or weariness, and the other affections of the soul [Col. 0459D]. Even in one most devout, who governs all inward and outward movements more perfectly, what that person does is nevertheless shaped by his particular disposition, and these natural qualities assist or hinder.

Just as people commonly say, whatever is in a vessel tastes of the vessel. Thus it happens that in an irascible person, even when moved by good zeal, natural bitterness becomes mingled with it. If one person is frivolous, or another more relaxed than is right, the former will exercise strictness severely, the latter [Col. 0460A] clemency loosely. Likewise, one who is sad or rigid by natural disposition shows too little kindness; one who is kindly and cheerful, too little rigor of discipline. In these and similar matters, one must guard against that human frailty which sleeps in our bosom, so that even the most devout person may beware of those impulses in which he feels nature disposed and inclined toward evil. Discretion recognizes and judges all these things, and determines how they must be dealt with so that they may become meritorious. It also understands how the works of virtues—namely humility, patience, obedience, gentleness, charity, and all the rest—may be aided or hindered by human nature or by some other cause. And it understands that a person merits not according as he is ready or slow in some one of these things, but according as he is [Col. 0460B] rooted in the virtues and possesses intense charity.

For, owing to a person’s natural qualities or some other cause, someone sometimes has greater charity while showing less eagerness in a work of virtue; while another, having less charity, shows greater eagerness. For although all virtues are equal, they cannot all be exercised equally, since one person is, by natural disposition, more inclined to exercise one than another. Yet they are all equal, because they proceed from the same root. If, therefore, someone is more inclined and better disposed to compassion than to patience, patience is nevertheless as perfect in him as compassion, because both virtues proceed from the same charity. For with as much charity as he has compassion, with [Col. 0460C] so much is he patient; and by each virtue alike he merits equally, because equal charity receives an equal reward. And although someone exercises this virtue more laboriously than that, if as much effort is directed to carrying out the one as the other, he merits as much; indeed, the one who strives and labors here may merit more, because the conflict is greater here, and charity is increased more in him.

The same judgment applies to devotion. If two persons have equal charity, and one has the grace of exercising himself in devotion, while the other labors under temptation, or wages war against some infirmity or imperfection, the latter merits as much by the impulses and effort of his struggle as the former by devotion and eagerness of mind; indeed, he may merit more if he has contended lawfully. Paul bears witness that someone can merit greatly in the labor of temptation, and that charity is increased thereby, in these words: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (II Cor. XVIII). For vehement weariness and bitterness of heart exercise the virtues; they do not overthrow them. Therefore, whether someone suffers from acedia, dryness of heart, or some temptation, or enjoys devotion, he can merit as much in that adverse condition as in this prosperous one, if his effort and striving in resistance are equally intense.

It happens, however, that a person is more strongly moved in the virtue toward which he is better disposed, and thus merits more. Hence a state of devotion is often more fruitful for the weak, whereas the robust and steadfast [Col. 0461A] merit more in an adverse state. Yet it happens that the weak person in spiritual combat is equal to the strong, because the weaker he is, the more he labors in resisting. Thus what the latter gains by strength, the former gains by greater weariness. But indeed, because both weak and strong more often fall into venial sins, and because they labor alike in resisting, it more often happens that the punishment due to venial sins is answered by the suffering of resistance, and one punishment wipes out the other. Nevertheless, in one who commits fewer venial sins charity often grows more.

Discretion understands all these things and knows how to use both adverse and prosperous conditions well. In this way, therefore, it produces a double fruit: it moderates each state and profits from it; and likewise it avoids the evil of indiscretion and prudently performs the good. For if someone has a good intention but acts with insufficient prudence, he offends; for authority says, “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” It likewise produces a double fruit by governing thoughts inwardly and prudently ordering outward work. Nor does it produce this double fruit only in itself; it also produces it in others, whom it corrects both by prudent admonition and by the example of right action. Rightly, therefore, these does are said to bear double fruit—that is, discreet examinations—which bear fruit both in themselves and in others, generating spiritual offspring; and none among them is barren. For no labor of examining these matters, no movement of pious intention—indeed, nothing done from charity—can be barren, but is fruitful and meritorious.

## Chapter XIX. On Guarding Speech and Its Sweetness

[Col. 0461C]

“Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet” (Song of Songs IV). The bride’s lips are compared to a ribbon because, just as a ribbon binds the hair lest it flow down loosely, so the devout soul binds and restrains her lips lest they speak evil or useless things and, to her own ruin or that of others, flow and run loose. This ribbon is called scarlet because charity is signified by scarlet, and by it these lips are bound. For words are held back and restrained through love of God and neighbor, lest anything be uttered that either offends God or harms one’s neighbor.

This love may be called the reading of God (*Dei lectio*) or the choosing of God (*Dei electio*). For she reads God in the school of the heart; there she learns to know God and to relish God. She also chooses God in love; and God has chosen and forechosen her. Therefore, above all else she reads and learns in Him what she thinks, says, and does. Whoever is one spirit with God no more speaks what is alien to Him than he perceives it. Whoever is joined to goodness is not separated from it by harmful things. Whoever clings to truth turns away from vanity, because truth and vanity do not dwell in one house; and whoever is devout does not run loose through useless words. Therefore the bride’s lips are compared to ribbons because they restrain words from flowing loosely; but because they are dyed through love of God, they are likened to scarlet.

Ribbons, while binding hair, also adorn the head and display that adornment to the mind. [Col. 0462A] Thus the guarding and discipline of speech adorn the mind, which is the head and principal part of the human being, and outwardly display a beautiful soul.
