Loose and foolishly uttered words deform outwardly and dissipate inwardly the mind’s rectitude. For by as many superfluous words as one uses, in so many ways is one led outside oneself and scattered from one’s guard. But when words are composed and uttered with discipline, they bear witness to firmness of mind, prudence, and discretion.

Thus the bride’s lips are compared not to just any ribbon but to a scarlet one, which is more precious, because this discipline of speech is more exalted and worthy in her insofar as it is possessed not merely through human wisdom or natural disposition, but through divine love. Someone may naturally be of good disposition [Col. 0462B] and modest speech; another may moderate his words through natural prudence, as Solomon says: “He who moderates his lips is most prudent” (Prov. X). Yet what comes from grace and charity is more pleasing and edifying. Therefore it is added that such a soul’s speech is sweet.

Speech is rightly sweet when it proceeds from grace and divine love; because it springs from such a root, it delights outwardly and edifies. What is uttered from a dry and empty heart does not edify or refresh, because it pours forth nothing from fullness. One who is poor within cannot enrich others, nor can one pour out what has not been poured into him. But he who speaks words from a full heart and fulfills by action what he says—his words have effect; they have savor and are sweet. Thus the devout soul’s speech is rightly sweet [Col. 0462C] and delights; it is welcome and edifying, because it proceeds from charity and flows from the fountain of grace.

For she tastes that the Lord is sweet; hence she pours back the sweetness which she experiences and gives utterance to the fullness she enjoys. A heart filled with spiritual delights gives utterance outwardly to the good word of sweetness, consolation, instruction, and admonition. The storehouses of the heart are full of these riches, pouring forth from this gift of grace into that one, from this spiritual meditation into that one, from one fullness into another. Thus from the heart’s abundance comes refreshment, and from tasting comes sweetness. Her words are sweet also because her conscience has been cleansed from the bitterness of vices and the dregs of carnality. Hence they do not savor of rancor, [Col. 0462D] indignation, anger, envy, detraction, or anything whatever harmful, dishonorable, or expressive of a hidden vice or imperfection of the soul.

The words of such a soul possess kindness or charity, gentleness, patience, and humility. Amid the bitterness of an injury received, they preserve sweetness because the soul retains charity. Nor is it merely patient, but also kind, so that it grieves more for the person hurting it than for its own injury, in order to have compassion on him. It is more ready to forgive than to become angry, more inclined to compassion than indignation.

For as it is read in Ecclesiasticus: “In the commandments of God are wasting-away and death” (Ecclus. XXVIII), that is, compassion by which one wastes away through compassion for the sins of neighbors, [Col. 0463A] and death, that is, the mortification of vices. Since such a person has mortified these in himself, when provoked he knows not merely how to forgive but even how to have compassion. For because he recognizes his own misery and seeks mercy from God so that he may be forgiven, he shows mercy so that God may show mercy to him. Ecclesiasticus says: “Remember the covenant of the Most High, and overlook your neighbor’s ignorance” (*ibid.*). The covenant of the Most High is the pact that, if we forgive, we shall be forgiven. Whoever wishes to be forgiven remembers this covenant and forgives so that he may be forgiven. He also overlooks—that is, despises and does not heed—the ignorance of the person who reviles or injures him. For one who harms another is foolish and does not know what he does, because he harms himself and renders service to the one whom he injures. The fool serves the wise person—namely, toward his salvation—when he afflicts him. The one who inflicts injury also occupies the place of a sick person, since he cannot restrain his impulses. But the patient and enduring person bears himself as strong and sound, since he is not conquered by evil but conquers evil by good. He would be conquered if he fell through impatience, but he conquers by enduring bravely. He neither envies nor answers abuse with abuse, nor harms the reviler in any way. Therefore he is not conquered by evil, lest he be evil together with the other; nor does he answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become like him. Rather, by a gentle answer he breaks the anger of the agitated person and tames the viper.

Such a soul knows how to excuse before herself one who is angry, and to attribute what he has said rather to infirmity or imperfection than to malice. She considers that, shortly afterward, he will repent of having so exceeded in words. [Col. 0463C] For she does not attend to his present condition and what he did while agitated, but rather to his former calmness, or even friendship, and to the fact that shortly he will return to himself. Therefore she not only sets a guard upon her mouth when the sinner stands against her, but at every time guards the paths of her words lest she sin with her tongue. For if the vessel of the mouth lacks a lid—of silence and guard—it will be unclean. And by as many superfluous words as it has contracted stains, by so much will it dry up the sweetness of grace. Therefore by guarding the mouth it preserves purity of heart, and from purity of heart it forms words outwardly.

Christ therefore commends this guard in the bride and compares it to scarlet, because it is formed by charity and knows how to speak for God’s sake, not for human praise [Col. 0463D] or respectability. He therefore praises its sweetness, because it does not proceed from flattery or a feigned kindness of words, but from grace and purity of heart.

## Chapter XX. On the Beauty of the Penitent Soul, Humility, and Its Hidden Merits

“Your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate, apart from that which lies hidden within” (Song of Songs IV). In the cheeks, which He says are like a fragment of pomegranate, modest shame is signified, because when we blush in the cheeks, we grow red. A pomegranate is red outside, white within, and full of seeds; hence it is also called the many-seeded apple. The cheeks of the devout soul are likened to it: it is red outwardly—that is, it blushes from the memory [Col. 0464A] and recollection of past sins; from the daily thought of shameful things or temptations and a shame-filled consideration of them; and also from infirmity and imperfection. It continually sees these things itself, so that God may not see them—God, to whom every heart lies open and who judges all things—so that God may not judge them.

What one has set before oneself will not be before God; and what one judges, God will not judge, for He does not judge the same thing twice. This is so, provided one has sufficiently judged one’s sins and all one’s blameworthy acts, has set before oneself what displeases God and what could be charged against one by Him, has painted their image for oneself, and blushes at them—that is, feels shame; is displeased with oneself in order to please Him; becomes contemptible to oneself and ugly in one’s own eyes. Yet by as much as one blushes for oneself and seems ugly to oneself, by so much does one become beautiful before God.

For she separates useless things [Col. 0464B] from useful ones, winnows the chaff and separates it from the grain, burns the chaff in the fire of confession and repentance, and hides the grain within by this humility, this blush of confession and shame. Thus she is cleansed from sins and made lovely before God. This blush, then, both consumes sins and beautifies the face. This bark of humility guards and preserves good things; for humility is the guardian of virtues. This blush of the cheeks adorns the soul, kindles God to love it, and invites His gaze. For the heavenly Bridegroom looks upon the modesty and humility of the devout soul. A lowered face pleases Him, not an uplifted one; eyes that are not haughty but cast down. He loves and beholds this blush so greatly that He does not see the blush of sin, by which she was reddened like a worm, but commits it wholly to oblivion.

[Col. 0464C] Wisely, therefore, the bride covers and wipes away this blush with another blush; and, judging her own deeds for God’s sake, she exchanges one blush for another, offering to the divine sight what is pleasing and hiding what is harmful. For the Lover of humankind gladly accepts this exchange, since He wills not the death of sinners but their conversion.

The soul therefore divides rightly with God, leaving its good things to divine judgment while itself reproving and judging its evil things; it changes harmful blush into saving blush, blushing through repentance after having blushed through guilt, so that what was stained may also be beautiful, beauty may replace ugliness, and a sweet fragrance replace foul odor. Thus these cheeks—that is, this blush—are compared to a pomegranate, because it has redness outside and the whiteness of seeds within. Yet they are not said to be like a whole pomegranate, but like a fragment, which partly hides and partly reveals the seeds. For even if good people conceal their virtues so that they are known to the Lord alone, nevertheless they are sometimes revealed in part and become known to people. No one can be so devout as not sometimes to be discovered, from some work of virtue, for what he is.

Likewise, where the pomegranate is broken, the seeds become visible; they are not seen while it remains whole. If the rind is opened, there too the whiteness and strength of the other hidden seeds is found. So virtues lie hidden in the perfect soul, but are disclosed when it is struck by adversities. Its patience is known when it bears injury and neither envies nor is overcome by anger; its humility, when it bears contempt with equanimity [Col. 0465A] and is not discovered to seek exaltation; its obedience, by fulfilling it amid adversities; its charity, by love for enemies; its love for God, by observing the commandments; and its compassion for its neighbor, by relief of need. Thus perfection is proved by works. And according to Job, “the bones that had been covered are laid bare” (Job XXXIII): that is, virtues that had been hidden are made manifest.

The soul also has the pomegranate’s blush in its cheeks when, for Christ’s sake, it does not flee the shame of reproach, poverty, insults, afflictions, and labors. In these things it delights for Christ’s sake, and it willingly lets itself be suffused with this blush out of love for Him, who in His passion was reddened by His precious blood poured out for it. Thus, in likeness to the pomegranate, the good blush outwardly but shine inwardly with diverse gifts of grace. Their affliction is compared not to a whole pomegranate, because they have not endured sufferings equal to Christ’s passion, nor were they, as He was, full of grace; rather, all received from His fullness.

For Christ may be likened in suffering to the pomegranate that is full and whole, because He was full of grace, which was given to Him without measure. He was reddened wholly in punishment, because He did not sustain for us merely a little or a part of pains and labors, but such great and grievous sufferings that no pain has ever been like His. His suffering was more bitter and exceeded the pains of all human beings who were to suffer from the beginning of the age until its end. His pain had to be more bitter in order that He might bear all pains, [Col. 0465C] because He was a sufficient sacrifice for all, though not efficacious for all. For He did not save all; yet this rests with those who are not saved.

From the hour of His birth He labored under poverty, flight, persecutions, hunger, thirst, many labors, and adversities. He also suffered in heart, because He was incomparably afflicted by knowing, before He endured it, the bitterness of His passion, and by knowing with certainty that He would suffer it. In the passion, moreover, He was not tortured in one part of the body but throughout His whole body. For not only were His limbs pierced with nails, but His very body endured stretching, punishment, and scourges; and His head, besides slaps and the covering of His eyes, also endured the pricking and wounds of thorns.

Therefore, because Christ suffered so grievously and in so many ways, every affliction of the elect which they endured for Christ or in Christ’s example can be compared only to a fragment, since in comparison with what He endured, what they could suffer is small and only a very slight part of it. Hence, when they consider and recognize these things, they esteem as little all that they can suffer. When they reflect on His exaltation, on the greatness of what He endured, and on the fact that, as blessed Job says, He suffered this “without iniquity in His hand” (Job XVI), and that “He was crushed for our crimes, and by His bruise we were healed” (Isa. LIII), they always humble whatever they themselves can do. They delight to endure adversities for Him; love for Him kindles them to greater things; and they always remain humble within themselves. Outwardly they blush with labors and afflictions; [Col. 0466A] inwardly they shine with virtues. They suffer evils, do good, and regard themselves as lowly. The cheeks of the devout soul are compared to a fragment of pomegranate.

Moreover, it has within it diverse merits and gifts of the Spirit: perfection in love for God and the desire to die for Him. If this is not granted in the body, it makes martyrdom for itself in the mind. It mortifies carnal desires, its own will, the vices of the heart, and depraved habits; it wrestles with its own flesh and with the enemy who ceaselessly attacks it. It also invisibly possesses in the mind the martyrdom of abstinence, when it restrains the earthly delights of the heart and the motions of sensuality, when it rejects all consolations that delight carnally. It suffers spiritually when it is scorched in the frying-pan of the mind by zeal for souls, when it is tortured by [Col. 0466B] contempt for justice and by the prevailing iniquity of the wicked. It also attains the martyrdom of suffering when it is afflicted for sinners, has compassion on the weak, and condescends to those oppressed by whatever need.

Likewise, it remains hidden and does not appear outwardly how all its glory is within; that it is a daughter of the heavenly King; how it serves Him not with servile fear but filial love; that it performs God’s ordinances not merely for reward, but willingly sacrifices to God and confesses—that is, praises—Him because He is good, loving the good for the sake of the good, delighting in goodness itself and in God’s good pleasure. Finally, it glories in God alone, not in the world or in anything else, without regard for outward or earthly gain.

Likewise, it has the testimony of a good conscience: nothing that gnaws at its conscience, nothing that it believes it does against God, nothing that it intends otherwise than according to God. It also merits in many ways secretly in the heart, because, with God alone as witness, it inwardly intends or performs many things. For it merits by impulses of desire, contemplation of heavenly things, compunction of heart, delight in the love of God, compassion for its neighbor, prayer, and the will to accomplish something which it is unable to do. Yet before God it does as much as it intends; therefore it rightly merits as much as the charity with which it intends, because it is judged to have done as much.

It also possesses hidden merits in the heart which, though concealed, are known to God, because with Him alone as witness and knower, many meritorious things are done in secret. [Col. 0466D] How many ways are there in which it secretly humbles itself for God’s sake in heart or action, or willingly bears being humbled by others? How often, when injured, does it remain silent although it could answer reasonably, lest it abandon the virtue of patience? Sometimes, even when the injury is greater and the ground for excuse is better, it does not defend or excuse itself, knowing that then virtue prospers more within it and merit increases.

“When friends are wordy, its eye drips toward God.” Those who inflict injuries are friends, because from them it gains profit: they do not harm it but serve it. For when they make a noisy disturbance with words, its eye of intention drips toward God, whom it knows to be witness of conscience and rewarder of hidden things. It knows, according to place and time, now to be silent, now to speak; now to oppose certain matters, now to endure; now to do something, now to omit it. In this it is guided not by negligence but by discretion and pure intention. These are the things hidden within, which commend the bride in the eyes of the inward Judge, who sees hidden things.

## Chapter XXI. On the Progress and Strength of the Good, and the Teachings of Scripture

“Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements” (Song of Songs IV). The neck connects the head and the limbs. Thus by the neck are signified those who, by preaching or admonition, convert others and join them to Christ the Head. These are like the tower of David: strong in grace and exalted before God. For nothing so pleases God as zeal and the gaining of souls. [Col. 0467B]

This tower is a spiritual building: namely, the construction and accumulation of good works, growth in grace, and perfect love of God and neighbor. In these things, through Christ’s grace, both preachers and other devout and perfect persons, according to their measure and ability, are made firm as they diligently devote themselves to the conversion of others. This is the tower of David, whose name is interpreted “strong of hand,” and who signifies Christ, who strengthens us so that in Christ we can do all things, and in whom every constructed building grows and advances. This tower is called not so much theirs as Christ’s, because it is completed by Christ’s strength rather than their own. “Not I,” says Paul, “but the grace of God with me” (I Cor. XV). And Job says: “Behold, I have no help in myself” (Job VI). [Col. 0467C] Thus elsewhere he shows that he had no confidence in himself, saying: “I despaired” (Job VII). By despairing of himself, he grew stronger in divine hope.

Insofar as the faithful distrust themselves, they trust in the aid of divine hope; and insofar as they become weak in themselves, they are strong and powerful in God. Just as what is sown does not grow unless it first dies, so one who wishes to make progress is not strengthened unless first he becomes weak in himself and is thereby humbled. Nor does he advance in God unless he first fails in himself and recognizes his failure. It is impossible, therefore, for anyone to triumph over himself until experience has taught him that he cannot win the victory by his own strength. Accordingly, Christ gives strength to those who recognize their weakness, humble themselves through it, and put no confidence in themselves, so that they cease to be strong carnally and grow strong spiritually. Thus, despairing of themselves and hoping in Christ, they renew their strength, take up wings like eagles, and fly.

Those who were strong in seeking earthly things should become strong in desiring heavenly and celestial things. Blessed Job says, “My soul chose hanging, and my bones death” (Job VII), because, while he hangs his intention upon heavenly things, he has mortified within himself carnal strength. But this carnal mortification is not attained at once or without labor. No one suddenly becomes supreme, nor is the top of a ladder climbed by flying, but by ascending step by step. Therefore everyone who makes progress must strive to conquer himself and break his own wills, avoiding not only greater sins but also lesser delights. [Col. 0468A] For insofar as one is conquered by one’s own will, or by delight, or by carnal consolation even in the least things, one fails in strength and becomes weak in mind. For whoever is overcome by something becomes its servant; and by as much as he is overcome, by so much is he brought into this servitude.

Likewise, by as much as he yields to the enemy’s small suggestions, by so much does he make that enemy strong against himself, as Job says in the person of such a person: “He rushed upon me like a giant” (Job XVI). Thus he can no longer resist the one to whom, by frequently yielding, he was giving strength against himself. Therefore, one who by soft and undisciplined living has supplied strength to the enemy against himself must, in turn, begin with the smallest things in order to be strengthened against him and resist him. He should often strive to prevail in such things, so that by the practice of conquering he may be strengthened, and from the victory over lesser things may gradually grow able to conquer greater ones.

He must also accustom himself to reject bodily pleasures and comforts and to break the heart’s desires. By as much as he prevails and breaks himself in these matters, by so much will he be unbroken and spiritually strong. Therefore as often as he resists either carnal impulses of the heart or the enemy’s suggestions, so often is strength added to him against vices or temptations. He must also avoid faintheartedness and feminine softness, and accustom himself to suitable bodily labors and afflictions. For if he is conquered by faintheartedness, he will gradually fail and be weakened from the strength of spirit.

By the aforementioned means, the soul which desires to construct within itself the tower [Col. 0468C] of the spiritual building must recover from weakness and pass into manly strength. Although this tower is called Christ’s “strong hand,” because it is completed through His assistance and power, nevertheless every person’s industry and labor must also be applied. The perfect have conquered all these things, because they compelled the body to serve the spirit and subjected illicit motions of the heart to reason.

Therefore preachers, or other devout persons who strive to devote themselves to the conversion of others, are compared to a tower, because those who seek to raise others to heavenly and celestial things ought to be firm and lofty through merit. This tower has battlements—namely, the diverse teachings of Scripture—by which it may defend itself against enemies, and from which it may attack and strike them. For in sacred Scripture it sees the snares and cunning devices by which enemies deceive people: now through manifest evils, now [Col. 0468D] through hidden ones, now in various other ways. Hence, in Job, the Lord declares that the enemy fights against Christ’s soldier now from the quiver through ambushes, now brandishes a spear before his face (Job XXX), because he conceals some vices under the appearance of virtues and sets others, as they are, openly before his eyes. If open battle does not deceive someone, he sets a shield against him, so that, if he does not pierce the breast of the resistor by striking it, he may at least block the path of the one making progress with certain obstacles and hinder him with alien thoughts or occupations. For he suggests something that delights a person or seems useful, in order to turn him away from the more useful thing which he intended to do.

But the Lord has composed sacred discourse, in which He exposes the devil’s arguments and sets forth remedies by which he may be opposed. For as many arguments as there can be in his temptations, so many teachings are found in Scripture against them. The Lord Himself also answered the enemy from Scripture when tempted. For when the enemy urged Him to change stones into bread, He confounded him from Scripture (Matt. IV). Therefore, when he suggests to us the eating of bread—that is, earthly delight—let us rather consider ourselves blessed if we eat the labors of our hands: that is, if we are refreshed from the tribulation of our labors by consolation of hope and joys. For one who understands from Scripture what reward he should expect for his labor, and that for individual labors there corresponds in eternal blessedness the reckoning of a thousand years and more, is rightly refreshed better by his labors than by earthly delight, and eats this more gladly.

[Col. 0469B] Let us therefore recall that saying of blessed Job: “His bread shall be turned in his belly into the gall of asps” (Job XX). For earthly delight is known at the end of recompense to have been bitter and a persuasion of demons, when those who fed upon it are brought to the bitterness of eternal torment. These two testimonies of Scripture are like two battlements by which we are defended from the enemy and conquer him.

Likewise, Scripture teaches us that the enemy advises us to cast ourselves down when he suggests aspiring to miracles. For we read that weakness of conscience is better than the vanity of signs. Paul also teaches us to leave behind what is past and stretch forth toward what lies ahead (Phil. III): namely, toward progress in virtue, not toward the glory of miracles. [Col. 0469C] For signs are given on account of unbelievers, that through them they may be converted to faith; but virtues of soul are required of believers (I Cor. XIV), for without these there is no salvation. Signs, however, have sometimes been performed by unbelievers and even by reprobates, such as Alexander of Macedon, Judas the traitor, and many others, who performed them unto damnation. By some they were performed for the faith or benefit of those standing by. Sometimes signs were also performed through demons, as it is written that certain spirits are demons working signs.

Among believers, therefore—and especially among the spiritual persons of this time—signs are rightly suspect, especially those which involve display but no usefulness, namely those which are said to occur to these women. It is shown that they are performed by demons rather than by God. For in these days there are some, according to the Apostle, who, giving heed to certain spirits of error, turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to tales and reports of novelties. For they marvel at and attend more to certain miracles—whether performed by demons or fabricated by some persons to whom they seem to occur—than to perfection of character and virtues.

For blessed Gregory says that perfection consists not in performing miracles, but in each person loving another as himself, knowing true things about God, and thinking better things of others than of oneself.

Moreover, he says that each person is perfect only to the extent that he perfectly feels the sufferings of others. And likewise, that he is truly perfect who is not impatient with the imperfection of his neighbor. Therefore charity, humility, patience, and the other virtues, together with perfect morals, make a human being perfect—not miracles. Salvation, then, lies in the virtues; upon them the soul is strengthened and stands firm. It is not made solid or founded upon miracles, but is lifted up and vainly, emptily exalted by them. Therefore those who seek miracles without a useful purpose cast themselves down and hang suspended in emptiness; they do not stand upon firm and safe ground, so as to go forward from virtue to virtue, but rather to fall back. Scripture, on the contrary, teaches us not to put God to the test by the display of miracles, but rather to strive for the perfection of the virtues and to devote effort to fulfilling the commandments. The Lord also teaches us, by his answer, to resist the third temptation when he says: “You shall worship the Lord your God” (Matt. 4). When he declares that God is to be worshipped and despises the kingdoms of the world, he calls us to God’s service and teaches us to seek true riches and despise false ones. For if we worship God and serve him, we shall possess inexhaustible riches, since for every good work a reward greater than the kingdom of the world will be given to us. Finally, we shall have a unique joy in each individual who is saved, and shall be enriched more by the abundance of each one than if we ruled the whole world. These testimonies and examples of Scripture are strongholds by which we may defend ourselves against the enemy, instruct and kindle others, and hurl darts against the foe. For that enemy tries to hinder us in the understanding of Scripture, so that we may not advance in its instruction, while defiling and darkening the purity of spiritual understanding with earthly thoughts or carnal knowledge. But when our Redeemer defends us from their temptations, the mind grasps this knowledge, as is read in Job: “The Almighty will be against your enemies, and silver will be heaped up for you” (Job 22), that is, charity and the purity of the divine word. Therefore, while God instructs his own through the understanding of Holy Scripture and refreshes them with its food, he makes them at once cautious and strong against temptations, as is rightly read in Job: “In famine he will deliver you from death, and in war from the hand of the sword” (Job 5), so that, being refreshed by God’s word, they may not be overcome in the warfare of temptation. Therefore, as often as we resist and refute the temptations of the enemy, being taught by the Scriptures and aided by God, so often we strike and wound him; and the punishment which would be inflicted upon us if we were conquered by him is turned back upon him. These teachings and testimonies of Scripture are strongholds with which the soldier of Christ arms and protects himself.

## Chapter XXII. On true perfection and the examples of the perfect

“A thousand shields hang from it” (Song 4). The shields are the virtues by which we are defended against vices and temptations. Their perfection is signified by the number one thousand. For if virtues are established in the soul, it despises itself perfectly and is truly humble; it is less wounded or burdened, and vices or temptations have no strength against it. One who perfectly despises himself and is truly humble is less harmed or burdened if he is treated with contempt. He is not pierced by the dart of pride who is founded in humility, understands humility as exaltation, and glories in contempt or rejection, as it is written: “Let the humble person glory in his exaltation” (James 1). Whoever loves his enemies has blocked the entrance to envy, for envy cannot penetrate the breast that it finds fortified by the perfection of charity. Nor can injury move one who is founded in the virtue of patience and even rejoices in reproaches. Likewise, one who through charity desires that what is his be shared with others cannot seek his own things. In the remaining virtues the soldier of Christ is fortified, so that he may oppose contrary vices; and on whatever side they attack him, they are driven back by virtues from that side, and, repulsed, recoil.

Therefore a thousand shields hang upon this tower when a person has obtained and perfectly attained all the virtues, so that no opening on any side is left for vices or the tempter. For to the extent that vices—such as carnal appetites—remain untamed in someone, they are correspondingly more powerful against him and have strength to attack him. But when they have been conquered and put to death, and illuminated by their contrary virtues, then, if they attempt or attack, they immediately recoil and cannot prevail. But one who is weak in virtues and has not yet subdued vices bears within himself the source of his temptation and weakness. Hence the Apostle says that each person is tempted by his own desire (James 1), namely, a desire still present within him and not fully conquered. So long as virtue and vice contend in a person and virtue does not occupy a peaceful place, that person must necessarily be shaken and wearied by many temptations, now superior and now inferior. But when he has perfectly possessed the virtues, he perfectly subdues carnality, overcomes and repels its assaults.

These, therefore, are signs of perfection: that he has so subjected the vices that, when tempted by the lust of the flesh, gluttony, his own will, affection for relatives, or some carnal impulse, he finds himself strong against them and easily holds them beneath himself. Again, the perfect man is governed by reason; the imperfect man is often led and weighed down by sensuality. For the perfect man ought to be head over his members—that is, over sensuality—and keep it beneath himself and restrain it by reason. But in order to govern and restrain it, he must be enlightened and strengthened by Christ, so that he may recognize carnal impulses and, having recognized them, curb them. For if Christ is the head of the man and governs reason, then the man—that is, reason—will in turn be able to govern what is beneath it, namely sensuality; and in proportion as he has received the Spirit of Christ, he will have strength to restrain it. Therefore he is perfect who, by the power of the Spirit, strongly restrains both the desires of the flesh and the will of the heart.

Again, these signs of perfection—provided that they proceed from a good conscience, not from false righteousness or presumptuous faith—produce a desire for death and patience in life for God’s sake and for the usefulness of one’s brethren. Since, therefore, such is the soldier of Christ who has attained the virtues and perfection mentioned above, he is compared to a tower fortified with a thousand shields. To this tower is added every armor of the strong. The armor of the strong consists in the lofty deeds of the good and in the examples of their virtues. The soldier of Christ strives to arm himself with this armor when he strives to reform his own life after their example. In them each person sees what labors of heart and afflictions they bore, what temptations they endured, how manfully they fought, broke their wills, and labored in fulfilling the commandments; how great in them was purity of life, purity of heart, and every perfection of virtue.

How many there were in deserts or monasteries who were never satisfied with bread, never fully refreshed by sleep, never warmed by clothing, never delighted by the comfort of a bed; yet, though needy and afflicted in these respects, they were rich in perfection of virtues and fullness of grace, commanding demons, healing the sick, and dwelling in mind in heaven. The examples of all these, and others besides, are the weapons of the strong which the soldier of Christ keeps at hand. By them he acts, arms himself, and is fortified against the enemies of the soul, against the world, and against himself. Whoever keeps these examples at hand and continually considers such persons cannot grow lukewarm in idleness, nor perish before enemies unarmed and undisciplined.

The wicked too have their weapons, namely the members which they present as weapons of iniquity to sin. With their eyes they look in order to desire evil; they use their tongue to slander, revile, or speak vain or useless words; their ears itch to hear novelty or harm; their feet run to evil; and their hands work iniquity—those whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity. In short, they fight for sin, and therefore for the devil, with heart and body alike. Their weapons do not fortify but kill; and a person is wounded by these weapons more severely in proportion as he associates more intimately with such people. For whoever joins himself to the wicked and attends to them is separated from the good.

They harm in two ways: they corrupt by example and deceive by false praise. Because they do not know what is good, they praise as excellent one who is not so, and as good one who is very wicked. When someone is affected by their praises, he gradually loses knowledge of himself and believes himself to be what he hears himself called. For he judges himself not according to the testimony of his own heart, but according to the opinion of those who think this or that about him. Thus very many are influenced by a false opinion of themselves. For things before the eyes easily incline the mind to attend to them or judge according to them. Therefore one must strive rather to look with the eyes of the heart upon the strong and perfect, and set their virtues and deeds before oneself for consideration. If one attends to the wicked and trusts their judgment, one will fall, be deceived, and descend to worse things. If one considers the good, one will be humbled and advance toward the good.

Therefore we must withdraw our minds from the wicked or dissolute, and ignore them even when they are nearby; we must turn our gaze away from contemplating them, but look upon the good with the eyes of the heart, consider their manner of life, and cultivate their virtues. We must dwell in mind among those whose citizenship is in heaven, and thus, as Scripture says, walk with the good. If we are constantly with such good people, know them as though they were familiar to us, and join ourselves to them in longing and love, we shall certainly become like them: holy with the saints, perfect with the strong. In this way we ought to compare ourselves with them, transfer their examples to ourselves, and keep near us, as weapons with which we may fight spiritually, their examples.

Thus the soldier of Christ keeps company with them; and, as is read in Job, “he dwells among the stones” (Job 8)—that is, living stones belonging to the heavenly structure, firm and squared, their vices and carnality cut away and removed. He walks with them in heart and dwells among them, not among earthly stones—namely carnal people who are of the earth, speak of the earth, and act and think in an earthly way. Whoever delights in their favor or manners dwells among them. But the good person dwells among the stones with whom he has a covenant, as Job is told: “Your covenant shall be with the stones of the fields” (Job 5). Whoever belongs to the building of the heavenly city has a covenant with the stones of the fields, in that he imitates and resembles those who are firm and strong throughout the regions of the world, whether they are now living or have lived before.

Therefore in this tower—that is, in the perfect man—is every armor of the strong: the examples and deeds of those who strive manfully in God. He stores in his memory their steadfastness in labors, patience in adversity, temperance in prosperity, charity toward enemies, obedience in hard things, endurance of injuries, devotion of mind, and loftiness of contemplation. He thinks upon these things, exercises himself in them, strives to imitate them, and by their example shows himself devoted and vigorous in spiritual warfare. For the examples of the good build up, instruct, and kindle. He therefore keeps this strong armor at hand and uses it, so that he may be made equal to them in merits and be granted rewards.

## Chapter XXIII. On the compassion of the good, and especially of the Blessed Virgin

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows incline” (Song 4). These breasts are those whom he had earlier called the neck: teachers, and also perfect persons who turn others toward the good by admonition. These breasts are filled with the milk of charity, by which they refresh the younger and weaker, nursing and nourishing them like mothers. The soul still carnal does not possess these breasts until it grows in grace and changes the blood of carnality into the milk of devotion. But when it has grown in grace and conceived compassion, it becomes a mother: it nurses the weak, consoles the desolate, and, when struck by insults or affected by injuries, pours out the milk of patience and compassion, not the blood of carnal agitation.

For, being filled with the milk of compassion, it displays the sweetness it has received; it has greater pity for the miseries of the person harming it than it is stirred by injury. In the person doing injury there is wickedness of heart and misery of soul. The person enduring it likewise has within himself that from which he may be moved either to anger or to mercy. If he is indignant rather than compassionate, he is carnal and himself subject to the misery of sin; for as the former sins through wickedness, so the latter sins through anger and impatience. “Blood touches blood,” that is, sinner touches sinner. The touch proves what each person is. If he had breasts, when touched—that is, struck by injury—he would pour out milk. But when he suffers injury and does not feel compassion, he grieves but does not grieve with another, because he does not pour out the milk of compassion. He thereby proves that he has no breasts and is not a mother, but is still a little sister without breasts.

Since, therefore, the perfect soul receives from above the grace which it pours back upon others, and is thus itself nursed, it is rightly compared to fawns, which run to milk and seek the heights. It rises in order that it may itself grow and refresh others. The two fawns are the active and contemplative persons, who do not cease to run to the milk of grace. They desire this, always tend toward perfection, and seek things above. They always reckon themselves new, always beginners and insufficient, because they stretch themselves toward what lies ahead until they meet the perfect man, until they indeed reach perfection. They never suppose that they have attained it, but say to themselves that they have only begun; in their own estimation they are always little ones—that is, humble—and therefore seek the milk of grace, strive for it, and drink it. Since they run unceasingly to this milk, they receive it and are refreshed by it; and thus they are so filled with its sweetness that its abundance suffices to supply the need of others.

These are the fawns of the gazelle—that is, of the Church, which is accustomed to seek the heights—and they are twins because both are refreshed by the same teaching, as twins are nourished by the same milk. Holy Scripture thus instructs contemplatives just as it does active persons, and both find in it nourishment for the spirit. These feed among lilies. By lilies, which shine and have fragrance, we understand the purity of those who live well and the fragrance of virtues. These twins feed among them because they delight in the purity of the good and the sweet fragrance of upright conduct. They rejoice alike in the salvation of such people and in the fragrance of their good example; they rejoice in what those people offer to others, and are pleasantly refreshed by these things. For they are distressed at the destruction of the wicked, but rejoice at the progress and prosperity of the good, so long as they dwell in the exile and blindness of this world. This is what follows: “until the day breathes and the shadows incline”—until the ignorance and misery of the present life fail away, and the day of eternity and of divine knowledge shines.

These breasts may also be applied to the Blessed Virgin. She has two breasts which pour forth the milk of twofold love, because she obtains pardon for the guilty and grace for the righteous. These breasts are like two fawns of a gazelle. We may understand these fawns as angels and human souls already transferred to the kingdom. They are rightly called fawns because they have climbed the mountain of the heavenly dwelling and are refreshed by the sweetness of divine contemplation, just as fawns are accustomed both to seek the heights and to be nourished with milk. These fawns are twins of the gazelle—that is, of Christ—from whom they alike receive and drink the milk of twofold sweetness, namely divinity and humanity. For Christ is a gazelle because he leapt upon the mountains and skipped over the hills. Thus he made a leap into the womb of the Blessed Virgin, and from it into the world, and from the world into heaven, where he feeds these fawns with heavenly milk.

Therefore, since both angels and holy souls are concerned for sinners and assist them by merits and intercession, it must be believed that the Blessed Virgin can do as much in this regard as both these creatures; indeed, she is judged greater than both, since both are restored through her: the fall of the angels was repaired through her, and human nature reconciled. What wonder, then, if the Blessed Virgin pours forth the milk of reconciliation for sinners and of grace for the devout, she who reconciled the world and bore grace itself—indeed, the very fountain of grace, which flows through the world and extends to its furthest boundary? For the Blessed Virgin is the paradise from which that fountain goes forth; it is then divided into four heads, because from the body of Christ, which proceeded from her, flowed the fountain of blood. Sacramentally it flowed thence into the four regions of the world, both to wash his own from sins and to pour grace into them.

Her mercy is therefore rightly compared to the running of fawns: it runs through the world, waters it, and pours itself into it. It is compared to the speed of fawns because her compassion comes more swiftly than she is invoked, and anticipates the cases of the wretched. She is compared to fawns because she herself drinks from above the sweetness of goodness which she bestows. These, O Blessed One, are your breasts—that is, the compassion with which you nurse the wretched while obtaining mercy for them. You nurse the wretched and are nursed by mercy itself; from it you receive what you pour back. You deserved the prerogative of singular grace, because you are privileged above women, so that you might nourish not with a woman’s milk but with virginal milk, and nourish not a mere human being but God. Hence how singular this is: she seemed to have neither a predecessor like herself nor a successor. Therefore you are rightly judged able to do as much as the holy angels and souls of the saints, and are compared with both.

To you, then, Mother of Mercy, Mother of the wretched, the exiled children of Eve cry out; miseries themselves cry out. Misery has a cry, and this valley has tears: it is indeed a valley of tears, so much so that, even if the wretched themselves do not cry out, these miseries cannot fail to sound in your ears. They cannot be silent before you or escape your hearing, because you have ears for hearing miseries, and for you to know them is to hear them. For just as, wherever the body is, the eagles gather, so wherever misery is, your mercy both runs and brings help. Your breasts are filled with compassion by God, so that, touched by knowledge of any misery, they pour forth the milk of mercy; you cannot know miseries without helping them. And what wonder if mercy abounds in you, who bore Mercy itself? Christ sucked carnal breasts from you, so that spiritual things might flow to us through you. When you nursed Mercy, you received breasts from that same Mercy. And as he took our flesh in you, so he gave us his Holy Spirit. When God sucked material milk from you, spiritual milk also began through you to flow to the children of God. From that time you became the mother of the wretched and began to nourish them with the milk of mercy.

Although God’s mercy is from eternity, it began to be more abundant in time. And when its beginning came from you, its liberality likewise received increase through you. Therefore the milk of divine mercy grew together in you and flowed from you to us. You yourself were first filled, and from you this abundance descended to us. Thus, because you are intoxicated with this milk and pour it out to us, and because your compassion runs through the world, meets the wretched, and helps them, you are rightly compared to fawns and likened to suckling kids that run at the same time. For they drink this milk in divine enjoyment and come to meet us: being filled with the contemplation of God, they meet us in charity and help us by merits and intercession. But although both angels and holy souls range about us with concern and help us, you are compared with both because you alone can do and accomplish as much as each, and more than either.

These fawns likewise feed among lilies because they desire the salvation of those still living in exile, and are refreshed by purity of life, upright conduct, and good repute; this is to feed among lilies. They certainly do this until the day of eternal blessedness dawns and the shadows—that is, the miseries of the present life—come to an end.

## Chapter XXIV. On mortification, prayer, and the perfect beauty of the soul

“I will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense” (Song 4). The mountain of myrrh is the soul that puts to death its members which are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and avarice, and so forth. This soul is lofty and rightly comparable to a mountain because it treads down and rises above earthly and low things, and lifts itself to seek and know things above, seeking those things that are above, where Christ is, and setting its mind upon them, not upon things on earth. It judges and condemns everything in this mortal life upon earth, knowing that nothing among earthly dying things is permanent or enduring. It has myrrh when it mortifies within itself carnal affections, its own will, and whatever can delight the lower part of man.

Mountains are usually high and dry, while lower places are moist. Therefore the devout are mountains because they are lofty through love of things above and dry because they extinguish and dry up within themselves the moisture of carnal desires. The Lord visits these mountains and does not come to moist places, because God does not remain in damp places, but the devil does. Therefore every devout person strives by every means to dry up this moisture and to have spiritual water poured down from above. For this purpose he stretches out his hands to God and thirsts for this grace with his soul like a land without water—that is, without carnal moisture—as land lacking moisture is accustomed to desire water. Thus he deserves to be heard swiftly, because his spirit—that is, his will and appetite for earthly and carnal things—fails.

The land of the good, therefore, is dry and has no moisture of earthly love. It is not like the land of Egypt—that is, of the world—where, when seed is scattered, channels of water are led in garden fashion for irrigation. The land of Egypt is the dark human heart, where the person who sows in the flesh casts seed and plants his root in worldly things, where he easily brings the waters of carnal pleasure through the garden of the mind. This irrigation is readily available; but as quickly as it is at hand, so quickly it fails and dries up. The mountain, however, is the devout mind dry of lower pleasures—indeed, that mountainous land which the Lord God gives to his own, because he lifts the good from earthly things to seek things above whenever he ascends to the lofty heart. This land awaits from above the rain of grace, which God is accustomed to send from the beginning of the year to its end—that is, from the time of birth to the end of life—and to pour down in heavenly irrigation.

The hearts of the good pant for these waters because, as is read in Job, “their root is open beside the waters” (Job 29): that is, their hidden thought and the intention of their mind are directed toward receiving the streams of grace and gifts of the Spirit. They thirst for these waters, and in order to become worthy to receive them, they dry up from the water of carnal pleasure and become empty. In order to obtain them, all heavenly spirits also ascend by prayer and contemplation to the waters above the heavens—those spirits who praise God and are intoxicated by the torrent of his delight. How can the soul fail to draw from this fountain and receive waters of grace when it is open to all the heavenly spirits, expands itself in longing, and knocks upon all of them with prayers?

And if it so widens and expands itself that, as it asks grace from all for itself, so it also desires and asks it for every human being—will it not deserve to be filled with it all the more abundantly, the more widely its charity expands toward many? Again, when it reaches out toward all those spirits, does it not embrace each one to whom the care of human beings has been entrusted? Therefore, when it opens the bosom of its heart to all spirits in order to receive spiritual gifts and draw grace, and in return extends itself toward each one in longing, desiring that whatever it may obtain or desire may be granted and poured back to them for the salvation of those entrusted to them, it is rightly heard: for it aids its intercessors and advocates just as it seeks their help and protection. For they desire mercy for those entrusted to them and rejoice in those who work with them for their salvation. Such a soul rightly has its advocates favorable in prayer, since it wishes to give as much as to receive.

Blessed and pleasing to God is the soul that thus sows beside all waters and casts the seed of prayer, so that it does not withhold this seed even from the land of its enemies but intercedes for them also out of charity. Its root is greatly opened when it expands toward all these spirits and at the same time is widened toward all human beings; when it ascends to the higher waters of the spirits and takes in below the necessities of all humankind. It is greatly opened when an equal intention toward all spirits is directed on behalf of all people and it strives equally to obtain grace for all people as for itself. Therefore, when the root of the soul is thus opened, multiplied, and expanded toward the waters of the Holy Spirit, the waters of holy spirits, and the waters of peoples—for “waters” are peoples—it is greatly pleasing to God, receives abundant water of grace, and is greatly enlarged in charity.

It is a lofty mountain through its desire for things above, possessing both myrrh and frankincense as it mortifies in itself every worldly and vicious affection and devoutly prays for all. Therefore Christ rightly turns aside to it and comes to it, as beautiful in his eyes, pleasing, and worthy of his visitation. Hence he praises it, saying: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.” A woman is less beautiful when the form of her body is lovely but her face is pale. But when she possesses bodily elegance as well as the blush of her cheeks, then she is judged more perfectly beautiful. So the soul, when cleansed from sins by worthy repentance and when it has destroyed the body of sin, is beautiful, as it were, in body. And when it is also cleansed from daily sins by daily confession, and suffers shame for them, it is at the same time adorned, as it were, by the blush of its cheeks, so that it may rightly be called wholly beautiful. “There is no blemish in you”: no mortal sin remains, nor even venial sin, because it never ceases daily to wash and cleanse itself through repentance and contrition. Indeed, it is cleansed from venial sins more fully in proportion as it is moved by great charity toward its neighbors and strives by prayer to obtain salvation for them.

Again, she is wholly beautiful who is adorned by good works and virtues, and made beautiful by humility and confession of the sins by which she had been stained. For by judging her sins and humbling herself on their account, she is not only cleansed from sins but acquires the adornment of humility, by which she is also beautified. And there is no blemish in her—namely, no pride. She is free from it because through desire she is always kindled toward doing greater things and considers small whatever she has done, recognizing, as she weighs the Savior’s benefits and labors, that she cannot worthily respond to them. Therefore she is wholly beautiful and without blemish, since even remembrance of evils makes her beautiful and no pride over the good she has done stains her.

## Chapter XXV. On the crown of the blessed, and how pollution and certain other things are mortal sins

“Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come” (Song 4). Lebanon is a mountain upon which myrrh and frankincense grow. Lebanon means “whitening” or “being made white.” Therefore Christ calls his bride from Lebanon when he invites her, cleansed and made white through the mortification of sins and carnality and through the devotion of prayer, to heavenly reward. His exhortation that she come is not merely doubled but tripled, indicating the immensity of his desire and love for her; and the threefold repetition testifies to immensity and firmness, for “a threefold cord is not easily broken.” Again, the repeated call indicates the joy with which he rejoices at her deliverance from present misery. It also suggests how eagerly he desires this to happen more swiftly. For a call repeated again and again expresses the affection both of one urging haste and of one rejoicing. He calls her so often also in order to indicate, by the repeated call, the greatness of the happiness to which she is called. The threefold call also signifies the enjoyment of the Trinity which she will receive after her labor: that enjoyment is eternal blessedness.

When he calls her, he also declares the grounds upon which she will be rewarded, saying: “You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the peak of Sanir and Hermon.” Amana means “restless” or “turbulent,” and signifies lovers of the world, who are both restless and turbulent. Their restlessness consists in the labor and weariness of seeking worldly pleasures; and when one obtains them, one finds no full satisfaction in them. When they are not possessed, they trouble; when possessed, they do not satisfy. For when someone wishes to satisfy desire in these things, he kindles it still more. Hence it is said that the remedies of sins are diseases: for by what a person temporarily treats desire through sinning, he afterward becomes sick with a greater desire to sin. Since it has no satisfaction, it affords no rest; nor does the Spirit of God remain in the mind that seeks earthly things, for he rests only upon the humble and quiet person. He is not grasped by a mind made restless through earthly desires, nor does he illumine with spiritual light a mind filled with carnal pleasure. For where the vessels of the heart have not been emptied of carnal things, the oil of the Spirit has nowhere to remain. The Holy Spirit neither comes nor remains in a person when he is flesh—that is, carnal.

When the soul is disturbed by these desires, it also becomes turbulent—that is, dark, confused, and alienated from the knowledge of truth. Earthly desires confuse and darken the eyes of the heart, so that a person recognizes neither himself nor his blindness and misery. But the mind of the good refuses to be comforted by these pleasures and therefore deserves to be delighted and illuminated by grace. Blessed Job condemns and curses the day of carnal pleasure (Job 3), turning it by his judgment into darkness or night, as he considers into what blindness and misery it will lead. By considering the night which he sees will follow this day, he destroys the day itself and causes it to perish within himself; and thus he comes to the day of grace. In this way he turns night into day, and after the darkness of night which he condemns, he rightly hopes for light and receives the illumination of grace.

Those, therefore, whom earthly pleasure overcomes are Amana—that is, restless and turbulent—and their head is the devil, who rules in them through these things. When the devout soul resists his persuasions and does not look upon these things, it triumphs over this head. But Christ promises to crown her not only from the summit of Amana but also from the peak of Sanir and Hermon. Sanir and Hermon are mountains of Judea inhabited by lions and leopards. These mountains signify those who stink through impurity and are separated from God and the fellowship of the good through guilt. For Sanir means “stench,” and Hermon “anathematization” or “being accursed.”

Of those who are Sanir, some are defiled by deed, others by thought, while others, consenting to some temptation or weakness or resisting impurity less than lawfully, do not escape the guilt of impurity. The impurity of actions is sufficiently evident, and there is no need to say much about it. But in thought one sins mortally either by willing to sin, or by consenting to the pleasure of the thought and lingering in that pleasure. For if you consent to pleasure in a mortal matter, even though you do not wish to commit the act, you sin mortally, especially if you remain for a long time in such pleasure after reason has detected it and it pleases you. But if the pleasure itself persists while reason does not consent or does not notice it, it is not called mortal. Thus a longer delay is sometimes venial, and a shorter one mortal, when it is noticed and not resisted but consented to.

But if some pollution and emission of seed happens to a person while awake, it is mortal unless it occurs from a certain natural infirmity. Therefore, if it occurs through pleasure, it is mortal, even though it is involuntary at the moment when it happens, if a mortal fault preceded—of familiarity, thought, looking, or the like—from which the lingering pleasure that caused it had occasion. Because these things were voluntary and lingering pleasure was entertained through them, the sin itself is not excused even if it occurs against the will. But if someone has been contrite after lingering pleasure, and pollution later happens to him and the pleasure returns, it is mortal because, at the very moment it happens, he in some degree consents to the pleasure that it should happen to him. For if he does not consent, it is a venial sin, since no sin is mortal unless voluntary. Either it happens through infirmity, in which case it is venial, or there is no sin at all if there was no pleasure in it. For it may happen through infirmity and yet there may be some pleasure in it, though venial. Likewise, if it happens to someone asleep because of some fault that is mortal, it will be mortal. But if contrition intervenes, it is venial, even though it has occasion from that fault, because that fault has been abolished through contrition.

Likewise with the madman, the ignorant person, and the one who omits a duty. For when a madman, while in his madness, kills, commits fornication, or does some other mortal act, although at that time he lacks the judgment to discern what he is doing, he nevertheless sins mortally if he fell into that very madness through his own fault and was mortally disposed to sin in his will; thus he becomes guilty through the preceding fault. So too, in the case of one asleep, pollution arising from antecedent causes is mortal. The same holds for the ignorant person: although, at the moment when he ought to know, he may not wish to be ignorant, he is nevertheless guilty because he previously neglected to learn when he could have learned. And similarly with one who omits a duty when he omits what he ought to do, because he could have shown himself diligent in doing it and thus, at the time for acting, not have omitted it.

Sanir, therefore, denotes those who are foul, whom the devil defiles either in deed or in thought—he who is read to creep upon breast and belly. Hermon, however, which is interpreted “anathema” or “accursedness,” signifies those who are anathematized: that is, those separated from God by their own iniquity, and others excluded from the communion of the Church by a sentence of excommunication on account of manifest sins. Let us speak first of those who are separated from God through mortal sins. Every mortal sin is committed by acting against the commandments or against conscience. For whatever conscience declares to be mortal—even if it were venial—the person who acted against such a conscience would sin mortally. As the Apostle says: “Everything that is not from faith,” that is, contrary to conscience, “is sin” (Rom. XIV); and what is done against conscience builds toward Gehenna. Other things that become mortal are done against the commandments.

Now some sins are always mortal, such as hatred, idolatry, poisoning, sorcery, fornication, and the like. But anger, impatience, sorrow, avarice, gluttony, pride, vainglory, detraction, and many such things are not always mortal, unless, that is, someone sins in them through grave contempt or acts against the commandment—that is, against love of God and neighbor. For anger is not mortal when a person is moved against a neighbor without will or consent to harm him in person, possessions, or reputation, provided that he incurs only the first motions of anger. And therefore “the sun does not set upon his anger” (Eph. IV), that is, Christ. The same is true of all other motions short of the will and consent to act against love of God and neighbor.

One sins mortally through impatience when one is so carried away by it that the virtue of patience is altogether abandoned. Through sorrow, when someone is so overcome that he in no way consoles himself in God, but consents completely. Through avarice, when one’s grasping is so great that one does not assist a neighbor in pressing necessity and withholds what ought to be given. Through gluttony, when through habit or frequent recurrence someone falls into excess or drunkenness and, having experienced his weakness in this matter, does not guard against it or restrain himself; or when, through burning desire for food or drink, he is overcome like Esau. And again, sometimes in these ways: too hastily, too luxuriously, too eagerly, or too studiously. Through pride or vainglory, when one prefers oneself to others and places human favor before love of God. Likewise, by detracting from another or publishing another’s sin through envy, one then sins mortally; or when one says other things by which one intends to injure another’s person or reputation, or when one strives to disparage another’s good standing.

A venial sin also becomes mortal through contempt, as Augustine says: no sin is so venial that it does not become mortal when it gives pleasure—namely, if it pleases so much that a person would commit it even if he knew it to be mortal. Or a venial sin becomes mortal by occasion, because through a multitude of venial sins one comes to commit a mortal sin. Therefore, whenever one sins mortally, this occurs either against conscience, through contempt, against something commanded, or against something forbidden. Until the first motions advance so far that something is done against one of these, there is no mortal sin. But when someone so consents to them that he offends in one of these respects, then he first sins mortally.

But however the perverse sin in the aforesaid ways, they are anathematized and separated from God by mortal sin. Those, however, who have been excommunicated by name are subject to the greater excommunication and must be avoided in prayer, at table, and in greeting. For no one can pray in church, secretly or publicly, when such persons are present. Innocent, however, says the contrary. Yet one may pray outside the church while they are present or listening. One may also pray for such persons secretly, but not publicly or in the hearing of anyone. Nevertheless, we may share with them in those things which pertain to their absolution and salvation. And if they owe something to anyone, it may be demanded from them and proceedings may be brought against them, though they may not themselves bring proceedings.

[Col. 0482B] Thus the perverse are Amana, that is, restless through love of earthly things; or Sanir, that is, foul through an unclean life; or Hermon, that is, anathematized through sin or through a sentence of excommunication. Their head or summit is the devil, who induces them to this by temptation and thereby exercises dominion in them. When every devout person resists his persuasion lest he become entangled in sins, he is crowned because he triumphs over this head. Lions and leopards, moreover, are demons: for now they deceive some by raging in open wickedness, now they seduce the upright by flattering counsels and varied frauds, just as lions are fierce and leopards are mottled with varied coloring. The dwelling-place of these lions or leopards is the wicked. When the good do not imitate their perverse habits and sins but flee them, and sometimes convert such people to good by example and teaching, they are crowned from these mountains and dens of lions and leopards and are granted eternal rewards.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the complete and perfect beauty of the blessed Virgin Mary

“You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV).

The blessed Virgin Mary was wholly beautiful because she was sanctified in the womb. Having also come forth from the womb, she never committed either mortal or venial sin. Before the conception of the Son of God, she was first preserved from sins by grace; afterward, having been overshadowed [Col. 0482D] and strengthened by the power of the Most High, she was so confirmed that she could not commit sin at all. From the time she became the temple of God, she was so privileged that she could by no means be disfigured by any stain.

Again, she was wholly beautiful because she was full of grace, so that not even the least venial sin was in her to prevent grace from having a place in her. For whenever anyone commits some venial sin, at that time he does not merit and grace is not increased in him. She was therefore wholly beautiful because grace possessed her wholly, since sin had no place in her. She also possessed virtues without the disturbances or passions of vices, and possessed them with delight in loving them and with the aid of grace. Therefore the virtues in her were perfect and continually put into practice, so that she relished, willed, and perceived nothing but good.

[Col. 0483A] Such was she in virtues; and so great was her charity that it extended not only to her own people, namely the Jews, but to strangers and acquaintances alike—to all human beings, indeed. Her charity was extended to them all; she was concerned for them, prayed for them unceasingly, and was heard when praying for them. Thus the angel Gabriel said to her: “You have found grace with God” (Luke I), namely, the grace you sought. She desired, sought, and obtained the salvation of all; indeed, the salvation of all came about through her, and therefore she is called the salvation of the world.

She was therefore wholly beautiful: cleansed in the womb and afterward confirmed in holiness and purity; first with the tinder of sin put to sleep in her so that she did not sin, and finally extinguished so that thereafter she could not sin. At last she attained angelic purity on earth, and likeness to God in virtues, holiness, and perfection of character: just, devout, prudent, modest, merciful, holy in mind and body. Rightly, then, she is proclaimed beautiful, since she attained both divine and angelic likeness on earth.

And because humility is the dwelling-place of God’s grace, so that a person is capable of grace only to the extent that he is humble, just as she possessed this virtue perfectly and wholly, so grace filled and adorned her wholly. This, then, is the inward beauty of the mind. Outwardly too there was the adornment of chastity, the radiance of virginity. She was wholly radiant in deed, having nothing dark or sinister, but everything bright and perfect, so that she was visible to others’ gaze and shone as an example, clothed in the gilded garment of virtues and surrounded by the variety of merits.

[Col. 0483C] The heavenly King desired one so beautiful; thus adorned, the Sun of righteousness poured himself into her and clothed himself in flesh within her. Nor is it surprising that she was radiant whom the splendor of glory filled, or that she was beautiful who received into herself the brightness of light. Nor should one doubt that the fire of love and inward radiance shone outwardly in her as well, so that she who had angelic purity also had an angelic countenance. She is therefore rightly called wholly beautiful, because she was beautiful in face, mind, and body. She was even terrible to the princes of darkness themselves, so that they did not dare approach or tempt her. For the flame of charity drove them away; her prayers and the fervor of devotion burned them; they were astonished at one immune from sins.

For apart from her there is no one so holy as not to have some stain and defect. The moon that shines at night and the stars are not clean in comparison with her: that is, those who shine in holiness of life like moon or stars are darkened in comparison with her amid the night of this life. For the stars—that is, the saints—are darkened by the gloom of human fault; but the Blessed Virgin was wholly beautiful, for the Sun of righteousness illumined and flooded her wholly, so that she had neither stain nor the darkness of fault.

Moreover, she was adorned with martyrdom. A sword passed through her soul—not a material sword, but one of sorrow. By this martyrdom she suffered more grievously than by iron. The more incomparably she loved, the more vehemently she grieved. Thus, just as no love was like hers, neither was there sorrow like her sorrow. In martyrs [Col. 0484A] the greatness of love softened the pain of suffering; but the more the blessed Virgin loved, the more she grieved, and the more grievous was her martyrdom. Since she loved more than all others, and the force of pain corresponded to the greatness of love, she suffered more grievously in mind than martyrs did in body.

Therefore the blessed Virgin was beautiful in the adornment of virginity, beautiful in the praise of confession, more beautiful than all others who lived holily, beautiful in the palm of martyrdom, and without every blemish. Since she was so beautiful and adorned in so many ways, she is rightly called from Lebanon, that is, from “whiteness.” She is also said to be crowned from the summit of Amana, Sanir, and Hermon—that is, from the prince of this world, ruling over lovers of the world, and over those made foul by uncleanness or separated from God by other sins. The blessed Virgin overcame, trampled down, and crushed the power of this prince of the world and head of the wicked by preserving perfect purity in body and humility in heart, so that he could have no place at all to creep either into her breast or into her mind.

She is that strong woman whose worth is far off and from the uttermost ends, bearing him who would overthrow the strong armed man peacefully possessing his court, that is, the world. And because by her merits and intercession she delivered from their hearts those whom he had either openly cast down by violence or secretly deceived while concealed under manifold fraud, she is said to be crowned from the dens or mountains of lions and leopards.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On spiritual sight, and how care for one’s own salvation and that of others pleases God

[Col. 0484C]

“You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes, and with one lock of your neck” (Song IV).

There are two kinds of sight or two eyes: one by which we contemplate things above, the other by which we behold transitory and earthly things. The Savior came to open the eye by which heavenly things are seen, as he himself says: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX). He came to us to illuminate this eye; he endured the opening of wounds and death, in order to open this light to us and make us alive unto the knowledge of salvation.

Thus he expresses by these words how greatly he loves this eye—that is, the contemplation and desire of our salvation—when he says, “You have wounded my heart.” It is as though he said: “O soul, who have deserved to be called my sister, since by taking flesh I made myself your brother; and whom I chose as my bride when I joined you to myself in love and unity of will: in seeing and seeking with the eyes of your heart eternal things rather than earthly, you delight me and become so pleasing that your love wounds my heart and penetrates it by its excess. My love for you was strong as death. Therefore I willed to die for you and to receive the harsh wounds of the body for you, that I might receive sweet love from you.”

That thought, therefore, fixing the eye of the heart upon the opening of those wounds, opens this eye alike to love and knowledge. For love opens knowledge, so that, while you love your Savior, you may understand also the immense salvation which he purchased at so great a cost of charity and of himself, and which is rightly to be desired. Loving me, then, because I endured these things for you, you also begin to love the joy which I purchased and prepared for you. Thus through the visible things of my humanity and toil you come to see and comprehend the invisible things of eternity; by contemplation you pass from seeing things concerning me to seeing me myself—from seeing me, who had no form or beauty, to my glory and majesty in heaven, where I am such that even angels delight to behold me.

Your spiritual sight, therefore, and your salvation consist in the contemplation of my love and in the enjoyment of me. For I am your Savior and salvation; I who was your price shall be your reward; and the twofold vision of me is eternal blessedness. I love this spiritual sight and this desire for your salvation in you exceedingly. With this one eye alone—that is, with the single and unique contemplation of your salvation and of my love and enjoyment—you wound my heart, and with one lock of your neck.

[Col. 0485B] The neck joins head and members. You are therefore a neck to me when you strive to convert souls and join them to me. The one lock of the neck is the single thought and chief intention with which you labor concerning this. In this twofold concern and care for both your own salvation and that of others, you claim my love for yourself in a special way and penetrate to the inner depths of my heart. The simple eye of intention, by which you seek nothing contrary to me and nothing apart from me, also pleases and touches me uniquely. For through this you are bright in your whole body—that is, in good and sincere action—so that you are deservedly praised and have learned to wound my heart by your love.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the praise of twofold compassion and sweet teaching

[Col. 0485C]

“How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride; your breasts are more beautiful than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments above all spices” (Song IV).

The two breasts are twofold compassion, bodily and spiritual. The soul possesses these when it has compassion upon those suffering bodily need or some adversity, or offers consolation and prayer to those caught in some sin or temptation. It has these breasts when it knows how to rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep, be weak with the weak, and burn with those who are scandalized.

Beautiful are the breasts of that soul which compassionately shares, from heartfelt affection, in the sufferings of all and cannot pass by anyone’s pain without pain of heart.
