It rightly sees spiritually with one of its eyes what also moves it spiritually toward its neighbors. For one who loves God embraces neighbors also in charity. Having approached goodness, it has received bowels of compassion, so that it is moved toward others in charity just as it has learned to love God. Again, just as it has one regard for its own salvation and for God, so it has one movement toward its neighbors: namely, one of compassion, not agitation or resentment.

The soul possessing such breasts is rightly beautiful and pleasing to Christ’s gaze, possessing the charity that covers its own sins and extending mercy toward the sins of others, so that it may itself obtain mercy. Of this it is written in Job: “By visiting your appearance, you shall not sin.” Our appearance is our neighbor, in whom we see what we ourselves are. [Col. 0486A] When we visit him in this way through compassion, we do not sin—that is, we are free from sin—because through this pity we are cleansed from sins. The soul is also made completely clean from sins when it not only does not draw sin from its neighbor through resentment, rash judgment, or suspicion, but moreover receives pardon for what it has committed by sharing compassionately in the other’s suffering.

She is therefore rightly commended who through compassion is both cleansed from sin and adorned with merits. Her breasts are called more beautiful than wine. In wine we may understand the rigor of justice, which greatly pleases God and adorns the soul; yet the bowels of mercy commend and adorn it more. For just as oil floats above other liquids and surpasses them in brightness, so mercy exalts itself above judgment, is preferred to it, and is stronger. Thus justice ought not to exercise any right or judgment until mercy has more fully fulfilled its own work; nor can justice accomplish anything except in what remains after mercy’s work. Mercy rightly excels and is more worthy to such an extent that, if discretion is present, it may exercise its office without fault; justice, however, cannot exercise its own office except through the mediation of mercy.

Therefore the bride’s breasts are rightly proclaimed beautiful and commended, because through this she advances so far toward the likeness of God—whose special property is to have mercy and spare—as she knows perfectly how to share suffering and bring aid. “And the fragrance of your ointments above all spices”: the fragrance of this sweetness and spiritual anointing, by which she is so kindly disposed toward all—grieving with them, lamenting, praying, and desiring that they be helped—breathes forth through its works, in the nostrils of the heavenly Bridegroom, the sweet fragrance of all virtues, and is known to please. For charity is the mother of all virtues; therefore this virtue which proceeds from its root not undeservedly merits to excel judgment and bear a preeminent reputation for good fragrance. Such is the bride in heart as she is also in speech and deed.

It continues: “Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.” The lips of a devout soul are a dripping honeycomb because they flow with the liquid of spiritual sweetness and pour it out for the edification of others. The soul gathers this honeycomb from the diverse flowers of Scripture: it seeks them out, settles upon them, and draws forth and extracts from them the sweetness of spiritual delight. It separates and despises knowledge that puffs up; it seeks edification instead, choosing sweet-smelling meanings rather than pompous eloquence.

[Col. 0486D] It also investigates and carefully considers the examples of the saints and their spiritual sayings. They indeed were flowers and “flourished like a palm tree.” As their lives were holy, so were the things they uttered or taught sweet and delightful. The soul flies about such flowers and gathers from them spiritual honey, but especially from that singular flower: the flower that sprang from the rod of Jesse, the flower of the field and not of the garden. The fragrance of this flower is “like the fragrance of a field which the Lord has blessed.” This is the full field in which the fullness of divinity dwells, in which are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, in which the righteous flourish and bear fruit both in good life and sacred learning.

[Col. 0487A] This is a flowering field—indeed, a field full of flowers—in which there are as many flowers as there are righteous persons bearing good fruit, and outside of which there is no flourishing but only withering. Like a prudent bee, the bride flies to this flowering and full field; she runs in the scent of this flower, goes to it in desire, clings to it in love and faith, sucks from it the honey of grace by the importunity of prayer, receives grace from its fullness, has charity poured into her heart through its Spirit, receives breasts of compassion, and has this grace poured into her lips, so that she may breathe forth the taste of heavenly sweetness and offer it to others.

She also has honey and milk under her tongue: refreshment for the strong and consolation for little ones, solid food for the perfect and the milk of tender teaching for the weak. For she has tasted beforehand the sweetness of the life to come, where souls will be refreshed by enjoyment of Christ’s divinity and by the milk of his humanity. She has tasted in advance that blessedness, because she is refreshed by streams from a river of honey and butter, of which it is said in Job that the hypocrite and pretender will not see them (Job XX)—that is, will not understand or taste them. This twofold sweetness, like the rush of a river, gladdens the heavenly city of God; but its streams visit those who are still good pilgrims and exiles, gently pouring themselves in and refreshing them.

From this abundance the soul has breasts by which it may bring forth the sweetness it has received; and these are the more savory and edifying insofar as it has been given to learn them through experience and teach them from conviction. “And the fragrance of her garments is like the fragrance of frankincense.” The garments of the soul are works that are in, or done in, charity; clothed with these, the elect are found before God not naked. These garments are like the fragrance of frankincense because good activity emits a good fragrance from itself just as devout prayer does. For if someone interrupts prayer because of a useful occupation, that occupation itself will be counted in place of prayer, so that, according to the Apostle, one who always works well prays without ceasing.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the soul’s twofold enclosure and hidden martyrdom

“A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain; your streams are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard” (Song IV).

The garden is the soul, in which are cultivated the plantings of virtues and the twofold plantings of spiritual studies. This garden is dug when vices are rooted out from it and habits are changed. It is dug still more deeply when a person seeks to know the nature and origins of vices. For one who works lukewarmly and is ignorant of the nature of vices will never be able to mortify vices well.

The memory of the divine Passion must therefore be dug into it, and those nails with which the impious pierced the Lord’s hands and feet pierce it when we retain their memory, share that sorrow, and consequently grieve for our sins, recalling that we are ungrateful for such great benefits. Such sorrow expels and restrains vices, so that they cannot prevail or harm us, while we grieve intensely upon considering these things. When love of God accompanies this sorrow, compunction is produced from this twofold stirring; and while it softens the heart, it also causes the virtues to advance.

This garden is enclosed by the bar of silence. For through silence it is cultivated in progress and righteousness, because the cultivation of righteousness requires silence. By it one restrains oneself not only from harmful speech but also from idle and superfluous words, because through small things one comes to greater things, and the mind is deceived and led outside itself through idle words. As Gregory says: “As many streams as there are of superfluous words by which the mind is dispersed from the discipline of its silence, so many streams lead it outside itself.” Therefore, that it may remain within itself, see itself, know itself, and correct itself, it restrains and moderates itself from idle and superfluous words.

[Col. 0488B] It also closes hearing and sight, lest they draw inward something that may disturb or stain the mind. It sets bars upon these windows because death is accustomed to enter through them. For it guards against being overcome by curiosity in seeing or hearing, since through delight in these things the strength of the spirit is weakened, and a person becomes the slave of sin to the extent that he is overcome by sin. Death does not always rush violently or suddenly through these windows; rather, it also creeps in gradually through a small negligence of mind. For a neglected bilge sinks a ship just as an invading wave does. By habitual use these things heap dust upon the mind, by which it is defiled and darkened; gradually it is overcome by them, loses its vigor, and finally willingly tolerates what it had negligently tolerated. Thus, “he who neglects small things falls little by little” (Ecclus. XIX).

Care for outward things also burns the heart and chokes the shoots of virtues so that they do not come forth; and a multitude of earthly thoughts, if it bursts into this garden, tramples it down like a beast.

[Col. 0488C] The devout soul therefore excludes these things and closes its garden against such intrusions. But because this garden is said to be enclosed a second time, we must also consider another kind of enclosure. It not only fortifies and shuts it against external dangers, but hides its good things within itself and conceals them from people, knowing that when good works become known and praised, they loosen and weaken the mind. It is difficult for anyone to be praised and honored and not take some delight in praise, or even inwardly glory in it. It is difficult for anyone to consider himself an unprofitable servant when, by the testimony of good people, he is proclaimed good. Indeed, it often happens that, deceived by praise, he believes reputation more than conscience.

Deprived of self-knowledge, a person is sometimes brought, blinded, to such pride that he believes himself to possess what he does not possess. Thus, when a man is pronounced blessed, he is led astray and the path of his steps is scattered, so that he no longer strives toward perfection but thinks that he has already attained it. The devout soul, however, conceals its good works and shuts itself against praises so as not to hear them, deaf to them like the asp that stops its ears lest it hear the voice of enchanters. For the soul is enchanted by praises, so that it does not see its evils and deceitfully exalts itself over its righteousness.

Thus the strong person closes and fortifies himself; inwardly, however, he prepares for grace and opens his heart to it, as is said in Job: “My root is open beside the waters” (Job XXIX), that is, the intention of the heart is opened through desire to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit. The more quickly and fully it draws this grace to itself, the less it is open to anything else. For its love is directed toward God more freely in proportion as it is less impeded by the delight or hindrance of praise. It asks for one thing and seeks it: that it may dwell in the house of the Lord, not made with hands but eternal; that it may behold the will of the Lord, by fulfilling which it may reach that house; and that it may visit this temple, in which all its citizens speak glory.

[Col. 0489A] It visits this temple in meditation and desire. It contemplates that temple’s happiness and joy; through contemplating them it easily rejects the joy of praise and excludes it from the entrance of the heart. A sealed fountain waters this garden so enclosed. Understand, then, by the sealed fountain spiritual understanding impressed with the seal of the Holy Spirit and fortified with the teachings of Sacred Scripture and the examples of the Fathers. What such a soul tastes and perceives is neither corrupted by the evil spirit, nor discordant in any respect with sound teaching, nor found contrary to the examples of the saints, nor spoiled by harmful novelty or presumption.

The plantings of this garden are watered by this fountain because virtues and good pursuits are formed by this knowledge; they advance and are practiced with discernment. By sober drinking from this fountain a person is made alive in the soul and obtains peace of heart. For “to be minded according to the Spirit is life and peace.” Its streams are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard.

Red pomegranates signify martyrdom in the peace of the Church: namely, that martyrdom by which vices and sins, bloody and red like scarlet, are mortified. It is martyrdom when we mortify our members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, evil desire, avarice, and other evils. Yet the pomegranate contains many white seeds within it. So too the soul has within itself many works of martyrdom which make it clean and white. For these are works of martyrdom: when someone afflicts himself through compassion for his neighbor; forgives one who harms him; loves his enemy; chastises the flesh by abstinence, vigils, or other labors; struggles against various temptations; resists his own will; and fights against the pleasures of the flesh.

[Col. 0489D] In this affliction and labor one drinks the cup of the Passion and takes up one’s cross daily. These are the seeds of the pomegranate; they have whiteness because they not only adorn the soul with merits, but cleanse it from the punishment due for sins of which it repents. Because they are laborious and penal, they are therefore said rather to erase punishment than other works which are not penal. They also adorn the soul in another way, because through them charity is believed to burn more ardently and merit thus increases.

The fruits of the orchard which this garden brings forth together are other fruitful works meriting eternal life, along with the fragrance of a good example and reputation. For it sends forth cyprus, with nard and saffron. The seed of cyprus is said to be white, like coriander seed, as is said of manna. Therefore, through the whiteness which it shares with manna, it fittingly signifies the refreshment of heavenly grace. Nard, with which the Lord’s body was anointed, signifies the anointing of love for God in the heart, because we are so anointed that we are not overcome by the fire of tribulation. When grace refreshes and fills us, it makes us strong against adversities.

Saffron, which brings relief to the burning limbs of the sick, signifies this power of charity, which moderates the mind against the heat of fleshly pleasures and kindles it toward the heavenly joys to be desired. Its streams are also cassia and cinnamon with every tree of Lebanon, myrrh and aloes with all the finest ointments. Cassia, also called *fistula*, has a strong bark and purple coloring, and is said to be effective in healing internal pains. Because of its shortness it fittingly signifies humility.

[Col. 0490B] For the humble, as though clothed in purple, are always mindful of the Lord’s Passion and always prepared to suffer for the Lord. This virtue especially restrains the inward impulses of sin and wantonness, as though they were pains of the bowels, when, reflecting that the Lord suffered for us, we recognize that we suffer less than we deserve. Cinnamon represents the same virtue. Thus, because it joins cinnamon with cassia, we may understand that we must pursue again and again the progress of humility and investigate the paths of this virtue and the ways of humbling ourselves. And because grace is chiefly obtained through humility, so through it one chiefly attains perfection.

This tree is blackish or ash-gray in color, signifying that the humble know themselves to be sinners, dust, and ashes, and judge that they ought to do penance in ashes and cinders. “Cassia,” it says, “and cinnamon with every tree of Lebanon.” Just as cassia and cinnamon signify humble assemblies of the righteous, so the trees of Lebanon indicate their lofty activity. These grow in the garden of the good when they perform great deeds yet remain always humble and small in their own estimation.

[Col. 0490C] Myrrh and aloes express continence of the flesh; the nature of these spices is such that bodies of the dead anointed with them do not readily decay. The finest ointments, however, are those of which Paul says: “Be zealous for the better gifts” (I Cor. XII). Myrrh and aloes are also fittingly joined with all the finest ointments, because when we restrain the flesh from wantonness, it follows that we receive greater gifts of the Spirit.

This paradise of trees is produced and sent forth from the root of the heart of the devout soul: namely, the well-cultivated garden, the virtues and shoots of spiritual pursuits. This is the paradise in which the soul lives and whose delights and pleasantness it enjoys. It possesses this paradise on earth and will pass from it to the heavenly paradise. The first parents had an earthly paradise and would afterward have possessed the heavenly one if they had kept the commandment. But in place of the food of the trees of paradise they deserved thorns and thistles through disobedience.

This soul, having uprooted the thorns of vices, receives the fruits of the Spirit and the paradise of virtues. This paradise is righteousness, peace, and joy; delight in the Holy Spirit; the taste and experience of virtues and of divine goodness; a foretaste of future blessedness; and hope of eternal life. [Col. 0491A] The garden of the devout soul sends forth this paradise, and from this garden it is sent forth to the enclosed garden of the heavenly city, Jerusalem, whose gate-bars have been strengthened, all misery excluded, and all happiness and everlasting blessedness enclosed within.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the fountain of the soul and the living waters of grace that flow from Christ
A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon (Song of Songs 4). The fountain is the devout soul, which streams and flows, ever rising anew because it is ever renewed in God. For it meditates, or performs what is good, or is carried forward by desire toward what lies before it. This fountain does not cease to bubble up and break forth into the love of God, [Col. 0491B] to grow in respect to itself, and to expand into love of neighbor. For it does not grow old through sluggishness, but always grows most perfectly and fully; and from the abundance in which it overflows, it visits and waters those below it and those who are weaker.

These are gardens, and they are enclosed while they guard themselves from sins and cultivate and exercise themselves in virtues and good works. Toward those who are, as it were, set nearby and joined by spiritual kinship, it flows forth; and those who wander it waters, corrects, enriches, and consoles. And those who often tremble in faintheartedness because they perceive too little progress in grace, or are too little raised up by the help of preaching or consolation—such persons the devout and perfect soul visits, for it raises them up now by consolation, now by the help of prayer, now by teaching or admonition. [Col. 0491C]

For it is a well of living waters, having attained, that is, the deep grace and knowledge of the Holy Spirit, because it abounds within itself so as to be able to pour forth again to others. It is not like that well from which the Samaritan woman drew water, from which whoever drinks thirsts again. The water of that well is the pleasure of sin: while a person drinks it, he does not so much satisfy himself as provoke within himself a thirst for sinning. Finally, while he wishes to quench his thirst, another thirst grows.

But this well contains living water, which extinguishes thirst for sin and springs up into eternal life, because it satisfies spiritually here and leads to eternal satiety. That well is deep because the things desired are obtained with difficulty; but the depth of this one does not make drawing difficult, but easy. For the more deeply and fully one receives grace, the more readily one has it at hand. For depth is a foundation and a perfection by which a person possesses the good even in affection: he loves it for the sake of the good itself, delights in that good itself, and does good not merely for reward, but confesses God because He is good. [Col. 0491D]

This is Isaac’s third well, which he called “Breadth,” because the Lord had enlarged him upon the earth. A person is enlarged upon the earth when he has reached the perfection of grace and, having passed beyond servile and initial fear, has ascended to filial love. A person digs the first well when he casts earthly soil—that is, earthly sins—away from himself through fear of punishment. The second, when he avoids sins not only through fear but also through love of the good. The third, [Col. 0492A] when out of love alone he both leaves evil and does good.

And in digging the two wells he endures accusations and enmities from the shepherds of Gerar—that is, demons who see our sojourn. For *Gerar* is interpreted “the vision of sojourn.” These shepherds feed and nourish carnal impulses in us, seeing us as sojourners and strangers upon the earth and attempting to deprive us of our homeland. But when we have come to perfect charity and spiritual fervor, and are led to every good by love, contention within us and the assault of demons cease, because they have no strength to contend with us; rather, they are weakened and unnerved in battle by spiritual fervor and love of the good.

Then the soul is so enlarged in charity and grace, and enriched by its fullness, that it pours out [Col. 0492B] even upon others from itself. And, as it is written: “From his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7). This grace of the Holy Spirit is compared to living waters, because, while it fills, it gives life to the soul here and leads it to the life to come.

These waters flow with force from Lebanon. Lebanon, which is interpreted “whiteness,” signifies Christ, who is white because He is without all sin and who shines in heaven with such brightness and beauty that His contemplation is the joy of angels and saints alike. For He is “the brightness of eternal light and the spotless mirror of God’s majesty.” He is also bright, and is “the light which enlightens every person coming into this world.” This light is diffused so abundantly that it rises even upon the ungrateful and shines in darkness, which does not at all comprehend it. [Col. 0492C]

It surrounds the wicked but does not enter them, because it does not reach their hearts. For they have shut themselves in and condemned their own entrance with the bolts of sins, lest the light of divine gifts penetrate to them. But it illuminates and enters the good, because, by fortifying the lodging-place of their hearts against the defilements of sins and striving after purity, they prepare themselves to receive grace. In them it dwells; them it fills, refreshes, and inebriates; the rush of this river makes these holy ones—the dwelling-place and city of God—glad.

Again, the waters that flow with force from Lebanon, that is, from Christ, flow into the devout and humble. Lebanon is the mountain from which the waters of Jordan flow; Jordan is interpreted “their descent.” This mountain is Christ, from whom grace descends into the hearts of those who are valleys—that is, the humble—who love lowliness and receive and seek grace with a single and simple desire. Such persons are in no way open to carnal or worldly desires, nor do they pursue human favor. Therefore they receive these streams of grace as abundantly as they diligently shut themselves against every external pleasure. [Col. 0492D]

Thus the waters of grace flow with force from Christ toward purity of heart, ardent desire, and the valley of humility. Living waters flowed down from Lebanon—that is, Christ—when the Holy Spirit poured into the disciples like a torrent and made them drunk with the sweet abundance of gifts. Likewise, when that same Spirit filled the world. These waters are therefore rightly said to flow from Christ, because from Him the time of grace began.

From Lebanon these waters flowed with force when Christ, blessing bread at the Supper, began the celebration of the sacrament of the Eucharist; and when His one passible bodily presence was taken away, He remained with us in many places until the consummation of the age. Having been offered once upon the cross, He is offered for us many times upon the altar. And He who now dies no more, and over whom death shall have no further dominion—the mystery and effect of His death are daily repeated for our salvation; for there the death of the Lord is proclaimed. [Col. 0493A]

These living waters flow with great force. For this grace runs through the boundaries of Christendom, waters and enters the faithful. The faithful receive it not only when present, but also in remote places, if they approach in desire and touch in faith. By faith the woman touched Him who came from behind and did not [Col. 0493B] press Him bodily. To those who touch the outward form of the sacrament in faith, this fruit comes: power goes out from Him—namely, fuller grace, forgiveness of sins, strength against sins, and a defense against temptations. Thus, wherever the faithful may be, in proportion as they approach in faith, they are cleansed and receive this grace.

These are the living waters drawn from the fountain of the Savior; they are rightly said to flow with force, since they fill so many people in so many ways and are known to flow so far and so broadly. Therefore, my soul, expand yourself toward this fountain which flows so widely; go round all its places, that you may draw much water of grace from this fountain. You never approach this fountain idly; you never return from it without fruit. You will draw from this fountain as much as your desire and faith shall be.

He required a spiritual touch from Mary and forbade a bodily one. For to touch and see spiritually is more salutary and more meritorious, the Lord saying: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20). Grant me, therefore, Lord Jesus, fountain of goodness, who flow with such force and spread yourself in so many places, that I may run to You so broadly in faith and touch You, so that I may draw You fully and possess You deeply; and thus may become a well of living waters, able to pour out again to others You who flow into me with force. [Col. 0493C]

## CHAPTER XXXI. On consolation in temptation, and on the greater grace which follows it

“Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and its spices shall flow” (Song of Songs 4). Although virtues are present in a person, they are sometimes pressed down by a temptation or adversity, so that they do not appear outwardly though possessed inwardly. Therefore, when someone suffers the adversity of temptation, the north wind blows in his garden: that is, a cold and dry wind. This wind constricts the waters of grace and binds the exercise of virtues; hence the north wind is called the binder of waters. Yet in such a state, if one conducts oneself well, one merits no less, though one is less able to exercise oneself freely or pleasantly in grace or virtues. For the waters of grace are hindered by the cold of this wind from flowing freely.

Lest a person be exalted if he continually enjoyed this consolation, the Lord providentially permits him now to be troubled and now kindly consoles him; and He works all these things for good. He turns this captivity as a torrent is turned in the south wind, and melts the ice of the mind by the serenity of His grace. He commands the north wind to arise—that is, to depart—and the south wind to blow—that is, for adversity to cease and the consolation of His Spirit to come. He commands this wind and the sea: that is, He causes disturbance to cease and makes tranquility not moderate but great. [Col. 0494A]

For He causes the south wind—that is, the Holy Spirit—not merely to blow in the garden of the soul devoted to Him, but to blow through this garden, that is, to occupy it wholly. Then, when the north wind has withdrawn, the ice of the body has been scattered, and the Holy Spirit blows, the waters of grace flow through the garden of the soul.

[Col. 0494B]

The south wind was indeed blowing in this garden, because the soul had charity, which is poured in only through the Holy Spirit; and when these spices flowed less freely, they were nevertheless possessed no less. For a person is not lesser in virtues when held by temptation. Even if virtues are pressed down, they are not extinguished, and as often as anyone resists, so often is he crowned. It may happen that a soul which has labored more harshly in temptation is rewarded more fully in perfection, and that the adversity of battle becomes an occasion of greater grace.

Christ permitted the enemy to rage against Himself for a time in order to destroy him; and He similarly permits His own to be tempted, that they may overcome him and therefore be rewarded with greater grace. Once the enemy is conquered, his powers are enfeebled, while the victors are spiritually strengthened and endowed with grace. [Col. 0494C]

Then the south wind—that is, the Holy Spirit—blows through the garden of the soul, because He blows perfectly within it and endows the soul with perfection. Then the spices of the virtues flow in such abundance that a person reckons every adversity prosperous and turns external losses into gain for the soul. Then patience becomes joyful, charity kind, humility devout, obedience ready. One loves an enemy not so much under the guidance of reason as from the affection of the mind. The carnal impulses of the heart are weakened because spiritual impulses are strengthened. The soul tastes and moves according to the Spirit; it is affected by spiritual sweetness and kindled by zeal and love for every good and by charity for the salvation of the brethren. Finally, it possesses virtues not so much in desire as in effect.

Then the spices of virtues flow so that the person embraces all people with bowels of compassion, correcting others as much by example as by spreading from himself the fragrance of a good reputation. The south wind so blew through the garden of a certain monk that these spices flowed from him; I have thought his conduct and manner worth recording here. [Col. 0494D]

For he was truly meek and humble in heart, inwardly judging himself and accounting himself worthless and nothing in precisely the way that outwardly he humbled himself for God’s sake. He judged himself a person of no usefulness, fed in God’s house. Although he flourished with the other virtues, he possessed in a special way the grace of gentleness. Therefore he showed himself lovable and approachable to everyone. His mouth was so restrained that scarcely ever was heard from it a sound of detraction, a jesting word, speech of vain glory, or a voice of envy. He was never found judging others or consenting with those who judged them.

He took care not merely to speak idle things; rather, whoever spoke such things feared him. Placed among those who laughed, he showed himself cheerful so as not to be burdensome, but did not admit unrestrained laughter. If he were summoned to give counsel concerning some matter, he remained sad and downcast until he was restored to the company of the brethren. Very rarely was he found absent from the solemn vigils or from the hours when the psalm-singers were in choir. In the refectory he used only the common foods; if anything beyond the usual happened to be set before him, he would not take it. Scarcely ever did he enter the infirmary unless obedience compelled him; scarcely could he be kept there once he had entered. [Col. 0495A]

If anyone had been struck by the multitude or severity of temptations, he heard from this monk’s mouth both the root of the temptation and the remedy for its cure. For he went through every corner of the sick person’s conscience so thoroughly that one might believe, from what one confessed, that he had seen everything and been present at everything. He was of such charity and had so clothed himself with bowels of compassion that he excused everyone and interceded for everyone, without the knowledge of those for whom he spoke; he was not a respecter of persons, but of needs. Finally, once he had set his foot upon the paths of the Lord Jesus, he did not draw it back until he had completed the course of the journey.

Thus the south wind—that is, the Holy Spirit—had blown through and wholly occupied such a garden, so that no place in it lay open to vice or carnality, but its spices flowed and ran onward even to others. [Col. 0495B]

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Christ’s coming into the soul, and on attaining perfection through mortification

[Col. 0495C]

“Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his trees” (Song of Songs 5). The Bride, making progress in virtues and more fully calmed in conscience, yet glorying thereby not in herself but in the Lord, prays that the Bridegroom may come, although she rejoices in the fruit of virtues acquired by her. For she knows that He rejoices in our progress and is delightfully refreshed by the fruit of salvation.

Yet He remains in the devout soul; for without Him it could not be devout, nor bear fruit unless He remained in it. But He is said to come into the soul when He increases grace and rejoices in its progress. For He comes daily into the devout, because He renews them and heaps grace upon them. She therefore says, “Let my beloved come,” etc. It is as if she said: “Not through the boldness of presumption, but trusting in a good conscience and unfeigned faith, I have persisted in cleansing my heart and preparing it for Your fuller coming. Gladden me by Your visitation; refresh me after toil; delight and feed me with the fruit of my labor.” [Col. 0495D]

She calls Him her Beloved in a singular sense, and with so much the greater confidence as, adorned more perfectly with virtues, she has prepared for Him a more pleasing dwelling. She asks Him also to come into His garden and receive His fruit. For the fruit is His and the garden is His; He is the gardener, enclosing it by His protection and giving it growth, because neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth. She therefore attributes her progress not to herself but to God, not to her own powers or effort but to divine mercy. For she knows that without Him she can do nothing, and that unless He guarded this garden, watching would be in vain in guarding it.

For if divine protection ceased, the hedge would be destroyed and it would be given over to plundering, nor would the plantings prosper. Therefore she invites Him to eat the fruit of His trees. The fruits are works of virtue, which have nourishment and fragrance. For they refresh the mind and send out to others the fragrance of good example. The Beloved eats these fruits when He is fed by these works and delights both in their progress and in ours. [Col. 0496A]

Drawn, therefore, by the Bride’s desire and delighted by the beauty of her virtues and the purity of her heart, the Bridegroom makes His presence known, saying: “I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride.” And He enumerates the same purity [Col. 0496B] and perfection which He finds in her—indeed, which He Himself has wrought in her—saying: “I have gathered my myrrh with my spices; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk” (Song of Songs 5).

“O my sister, because you are a bride and joined to me in love, I have found in you my enclosed and well-cultivated garden, that I may eat in you and refresh you after labor. You have endured the affliction of penance, battle, temptation, and the toil of reforming your conduct; and you have come to the harvest of perfection in virtues, from a laborious life to the calmer state of contemplation. Therefore I have gathered in you myrrh with spices, because together with the bitterness of the completed labors the spices of virtues have been accomplished and perfected in you, and wisdom has advanced together with the keeping of the commandments. [Col. 0496C]

“For when carnality and self-will have been mortified, then the spices of virtues flow; and through the completion and triumph of this labor one comes to the cultivation of perfection. Christ gathers myrrh when He brings to completion in the soul the preceding labors through which it reaches virtues and perfection, and sweetly strengthens it so that it gladly does what it formerly recoiled from, as is read in Job: ‘The things which my soul formerly would not touch are now, in my distress, my food’ (Job 6). Thus the apostles grew strong from weakness; thus Paul could do all things in Him who strengthened him” (Philippians 4).

It follows: “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.” The honeycomb is the sweetness of good merits which the devout soul has within; the honey is the work which it displays outwardly, fittingly compared to honey because what is rendered for it in the future is sweet. Christ eats the honeycomb when He is fed by the sweetness of good conduct, when, through reformed and peaceful conduct, a place is prepared for Him whose place “is made in peace.” He is refreshed by honey when someone performs good works; when He whose delights are to be with the children of humankind, who stands at the door and knocks, is opened to. [Col. 0496D]

For He is opened to when charity advances through works, grace increases, and is preserved. Therefore, by working more, we open more widely to Him, so that He may enter us and dine with us. Happy is the feast, and blessed the soul with which and in which Christ feasts.

Christ also drinks wine and milk in the soul when He rejoices and delights in its twofold contemplation: namely, of divinity and of glorified humanity, signified by wine and milk. Here we may also assign food and drink to the soul and explain these words in its own person. For the soul eats the honeycomb when, adorned with good conduct, it is delightfully refreshed by that sweetness. Those who are gentle in conduct indeed have great sweetness and tranquility of mind; conversely, there is no peace for the wicked and insolent.

Likewise, while they keep themselves from sins so that conscience reproves them in nothing, they always feast and always enjoy security, as it is written: “A secure mind is like a continual feast” (Proverbs 15). [Col. 0497A]

The soul then eats honey when it delights in good action, when it eats the labors of its hands: when it is inwardly fed, in the hope of reward, by what it performs outwardly; when what it does for heavenly delight becomes sweet to it, and the days of labor seem few to it in comparison with the greatness of that happiness. For it sighs to see God, whose sweetness it would not desire unless it had tasted it at least in part. Whence follows:

“I have drunk my wine with my milk.” The soul drinks wine when it perceives the savor of His divinity and is so intoxicated by this cup that it commits all earthly things to oblivion and clings to heavenly things in love. It receives milk when it thinks upon the glorified humanity of Christ in heaven. It is refreshed by this contemplation, and becomes glad and comforted in this hope and remembrance. This is the twofold blessedness of both angels and human beings in that life: the enjoyment of divinity and the contemplation of humanity. The devout soul experiences this blessedness partly in this life, but will comprehend it perfectly in the life to come, when it sees God as He is and beholds Him face to face. [Col. 0497C]

But first the honeycomb and honey are eaten, and afterward wine and milk are drunk, because reformed conduct and worthy action must come first before the grace of contemplation is granted. Leah is first set in place before one comes to Rachel’s embraces. Therefore one must labor and cleanse the eyes of the heart so that God may be seen. For God promises that He will be seen by those pure in heart, as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

Therefore, if you would see God, cleanse the eye of the heart; otherwise, you may see the world in place of God or an angel of light, receive the angel of darkness, and drink not the wine of God and sweet honey, but have the gall of dragons for your wine and the incurable venom of asps. For the sight of one who sees dimly is often deceived: the worse it sees, the more it seems to itself to see; and when one thing appears to its eyes, it believes rather that it sees two. So certain people, when they see vain things and utter false prophecies, see deceitful visions, because they believe every spirit and have too little cleansed the eyes of their hearts for seeing spiritual things and for discernment. [Col. 0497D]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On spiritual refreshment and the use of grace

“Eat, friends, and be inebriated, dearly beloved” (Song of Songs 5). The good eat when they receive spiritual consolation, [Col. 0498A] when they are fed by Christ’s love, enlightened in faith, consoled in hope, kindled in charity, and delighted in justice, truth, chastity, and the other virtues. For every virtue feeds the mind when it refreshes it with its own delight.

Scripture too is the food of the good, when it is ground and chewed, because spiritual meanings lie hidden in it which instruct and feed the mind. But the wicked receive from this Scripture not food but sickness; they take from it not edification but puffing-up. For they “spend their money not on bread, and their labor not on satiety” (Isaiah 55). The good, however, find in it as many dishes and refreshings as there are spiritual senses. They hunger for it; through it they escape dangers, as it is written: “In famine He will deliver you from death, and in war from the hand of the sword” (Job 5). [Col. 0498B]

For while they hunger for the word of God and refresh themselves with it, they are delivered from the death of sin and fortified in the battle of temptation, so that, strengthened and instructed by its food, they may neither be cast down nor deceived. Yet the good are accustomed now to be cherished by consolations, now to be filled with bitterness; now to abound in grace, now to suffer from *acedia*—spiritual listlessness. But, taught by Scripture that temptation is a testing, they are accustomed to attribute even the burden of *acedia* to temptation: namely, when the flesh struggles against the spirit and wishes to be equal to the heart or even preferred to it.

They know also that sorrow itself sometimes benefits them more than its absence: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart,” says the Psalmist, “and He will save the humble in spirit” (Psalm 33). The tribulation which the good suffer, and the very failing through which they are more humbled, make the Lord near to them. Thus the Lord sometimes abandons His own as though He were killing them, and they grieve that everything which they formerly seemed to possess has been extinguished; yet, while they are thus killed, they hope, as is read in Job: “Even if He kills me, I will hope in Him” (Job 13). [Col. 0498C]

While they are thus killed, they hope and live, because the little spark of charity preserves them. Though thus destroyed and cast down, they retain the intention of living rightly before God and in no way committing mortal sin. Therefore, while the good are afflicted, the Lord is near them; while they are killed, they hope.

But if He should smile upon them, they do not trust Him—just as Job likewise speaks of God: “If ever I laughed at them, they did not believe me” (Job 20). Therefore the good do not quickly or rashly trust a smiling God, because God knows how to grant the consolation of grace and yet is accustomed to condemn those proud of their good, ungrateful, and neglectful of the commandments.

The good know how to be consoled amid adversities, how to be humbled amid prosperity, how to be satisfied and to hunger, how to abound and to suffer want. A righteous person, filled with affliction and misery, will sometimes not lift up his head. The impious, for whom there will be woe in the future, are sometimes refreshed here even with inward gifts: “The enemies of the Lord,” he says, “lied to Him; and He fed them with the fat of wheat and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Psalm 50). [Col. 0498D]

They are therefore called enemies, and yet they are satisfied not so much with wheat as with the fat of wheat, receiving even mystical and inward things. Indeed, God does for the unworthy what belongs to love and friendship. But whoever receives grace from Him and does not in return show himself a friend—by responding to grace and acting worthily because of it—makes himself an enemy and turns that grace to an increase of his condemnation.

Grace, therefore, refreshes the good and also refreshes the reprobate. A person also has food from nature itself, because he is more pleasantly nourished by the food of sweetness. He has food also from accidental causes, for prosperity refreshes when it comes. This is not the spiritual food by which Christ refreshes. Nevertheless, it is often food for the imperfect and greens for the weak. And this vegetable food often usefully nourishes the weak, as Paul says: “The one who is weak, let him eat vegetables” (Romans 14). For it alleviates and partly cures the sickness of *acedia* which the mind suffers from lack of grace. [Col. 0499A]

[Col. 0499B]

Oh, how often the imperfect and those ignorant of grace are stirred by carnal joy or natural cheerfulness and suppose that they are moved by spiritual consolation! A person often feels something from the enemy or from his own heart and believes it to be from the Holy Spirit. And what wonder if the enemy mingles himself with devotion and speaks falsely, when he spoke even in the prophets themselves? They too sometimes spoke from their own spirit what they believed they spoke from the Holy Spirit.

Therefore a person ought not follow the suggestion or experience of his own heart, since he knows that certain prophets were sometimes deceived in such matters. Nor must these dangers be avoided only in a state of sin; rather, even in grace itself one must prudently attend to what ought to be done. “Drink wine with wisdom,” says Solomon, signifying grace by wine (Ecclesiasticus 9). And again: “The Holy Spirit will withdraw Himself from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom 1). [Col. 0499C]

God therefore grants grace, but its use is subject to the person, because one person acts through it more usefully and salutarily than another. One must therefore consider the manner of grace by which one is affected.

For the Holy Spirit is called one and manifold, because, though He is one, He nevertheless visits and affects minds in diverse ways. The soul must therefore hear what and how the Lord God speaks within it. And while He speaks, one must ask, while listening, that He may guide the listener and teach how meditations ought to be directed.

For spiritual meditations then present themselves, so that the mind sits like a king with their army standing around it. It ought therefore to govern and discern them: which meditation it should chiefly admit, in which it should exercise itself more, how long it should cling to each, and when it should pass from one to another. Every meditation is a dish because it feeds the mind. But in order that devotion itself may be kindled and that, refreshed by this dish, you may feast longer, when its flavor begins to fade, you usefully take another. [Col. 0499D]

Turn, therefore, to another meditation which presents itself more immediately and which you recognize as similar to, rather than different from, the preceding one. For although all spiritual meditations are useful, their character is such that they edify in differing, indeed sometimes contrary, ways; now these, now those, are more suitable and more pleasing to the mind. These meditations edify a mind affected in one way, and others a mind affected in another way.

But consolation of heart and spiritual refreshment are God’s gift; nevertheless, you must cooperate with this gift and exercise yourself prudently in it. For God is the author and giver of this refreshment; the person is its servant and cook, able to prepare either well or badly for himself. But when someone has fixed contemplation upon God Himself, he will have less need of this alternation of thoughts, and will cling, for as long as it is granted, to the highest good. For then Wisdom itself is the servant and cook, and makes a rich feast when it offers itself as food. There is no need of human labor or preparation when divinity provides the dishes and itself serves the refreshment. [Col. 0500A]

Thus God feeds His friends with food, as has been said. But He refreshes and gives drink more fully to His dearly beloved; indeed, He inebriates them with more abundant grace. Something has been said concerning that food; [Col. 0500B] but I fear to speak concerning this inebriation, because I have not been granted the ability to speak of it fittingly.

For the soul that is wife at the wedding of the Lamb, or daughter, knows how to be inebriated by spiritual wine—the soul that sits in this banquet at Christ’s side, or about the table, as it is written: “Your wife shall be like an abundant vine at the sides of your house; your children like young olive shoots around your table” (Psalm 127). But I, in the manner of a poor person, am not only shut off from the table but even from the banquet. Yet would that I might receive, before the doors, some of that pleasant wine in my little cup.

For I know that I have not been fully cleansed from the filth of sin; therefore I am not admitted or allowed to approach the table and drink of the children. I leave discussion of this wine and inebriation to those who have experienced it. [Col. 0500C]

But, knowing my foolishness and weakness, and also considering the sores of many, I desire to lie—that is, humble myself—before the door of the rich Christ and beg not only drink but also food from the table of my lords or ladies: that is, devout souls. For although wife and sons or daughters feast splendidly, those lower and poorer also eat and are refreshed from the remains of the table.

Therefore I do not wish to be ashamed to beg from such persons the nourishment of life, lest after this life I beg in vain with the foolish virgins. There beggars suffer rejection, but here whoever asks receives. And because more willingly and abundantly is given to acquaintances and friends, I wish to show myself a friend of the good and to love their good. Scripture says that one who loves in another a good which he does not himself possess is accounted as though he possessed it.

Therefore I wish to love whatever good may be in anyone, and to pray for the good, that they may advance in good, be guarded from evil, and attain eternal life. Thus I wish to join and associate myself with the good, so that I may make myself a companion and sharer even in their merits. [Col. 0500D]

I also contemplate that banquet of rich marrow and clarified vintage: namely, of souls transferred to heavenly things, purified from every dreg of sin, and feasting upon Christ’s table in His kingdom. There the elect are satisfied with the fat of wheat—that is, Christ’s divinity. From this table I desire crumbs to be sent to me by which I may merit to be refreshed. And I find a reason why I may receive mercy from that table. For I rejoice with the happiness of the blessed and give thanks that they have passed from the miseries of the world to the enjoyment of God.

Therefore, when I intercede for those who are still fighting and exult for those who are triumphant, I trust that I am helped by the prayers of both and enriched by their merits. Finally, I consider and gather together into one all the goods of my Lord: namely, the merits of Christ and of His members, whether those reigning with Him or those still journeying on earth; likewise the sacrament of the Eucharist, the other sacraments of the Church, various indulgences and many remissions, and, finally, the Lord’s mercies bestowed in many ways and places. [Col. 0501A]

When I turn over all these things in thought and love, and implore them both for myself and for many others, I trust that in so comprehensive a grasp and desire I am relieved in large measure from my poverty, indeed even [Col. 0501B] enriched. Therefore, from the goods already acquired I desire to share with others who are in need.

Accordingly, I consider many people sinning and dying in sin, some passing from the death of the flesh to eternal death. And since the mass of their misery is great, I consider, on the other hand, the great mass of the aforesaid goods. Then, by desire and prayer, I strive toward this end: to set these goods against those miseries and to implore them for those miseries. I try to pray and meditate in this manner, and I rest sweetly when I attain it. Therefore, while friends eat and the dearly beloved are inebriated, I wish to be their friend and their daily beggar.

I sleep, and my heart is awake. The natural movements of the heart are various and innumerable. Therefore a person is in many ways saddened or [Col. 0501C] gladdened by his own nature, disturbed or at peace. He ought not, then, to trust or yield to these movements, because, according to the changeability of human nature or of external causes, the heart varies, becoming sorrowful or cheerful and affected in one way or another. Therefore, when a faint-hearted person is greatly alarmed, almost to the point of despair, he should believe that this dejection arises from faint-heartedness and a troubled heart, not from despair. For he should be confident concerning his state, provided that he is contrite, intends to turn away from evil and do good (Ps. 37), and in no way commits a mortal sin. According to this resolution, anyone may hope to be called holy—that is, to possess charity—however heavily he may be burdened by distress or temptation.

Therefore, in an adverse condition a person ought [Col. 0501D] to trust in the prayers which he is accustomed then to offer, and thereby establish confidence in hope within himself. For confidence prevents the sorrow of adversity; indeed, he is then in a better state than before, provided that he has not fallen from charity through mortal sin, since charity advances through adversities as well as prosperities. Let him therefore learn to be confident in an adverse state and in dejection of spirit; and in prosperity let him not be deceived by false hope, but rejoice in the Lord with trembling. For, even if consolation is present, a person nevertheless does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred. Nor should he attend to the movements or experience of his heart in order to measure his condition by them, lest he be deceived.

Let reason rule over sensuality, pardon its movements, govern thoughts, keep watch—indeed, anticipate the watches—for by forestalling useless thoughts [Col. 0502A] it will more easily restrain them. Reason must therefore keep watch and maintain the night watches over the flock of its thoughts. If this is neglected, the mind incurs blindness, so that a person knows himself less, sees less clearly what he is or ought to be, how greatly he is deceived, and how greatly he sins. If, therefore, he diligently watches over the flock of good thoughts, nourishing these and repressing bad ones, divine grace will shine more abundantly upon him. As it shines and sheds its light around him, he will receive strength against evil thoughts, so as to lull them and put them to sleep.

When reason thus rules, keeps watch, and puts to sleep the movements and thoughts of sensuality, a person may say: “I sleep, and my heart is awake.” For in that part in which sensuality rules, the person is awake and is merely human, because what he then does belongs to human nature. [Col. 0502B] But when he exercises spiritual things, he is awake in heart unto salvation, because he returns to the heart and directs the heart’s care toward inward and invisible things. Then sensuality sleeps, but reason watches; evil thoughts sleep and good ones keep watch; carnal desires and temptations are lulled. Spiritual joy affects the mind, its understanding is opened, and greater knowledge is granted to it. With the eyes of the heart it contemplates that heavenly joy—the praises and song of blessed spirits. This is the harmony of heaven which God reveals to his own, but causes the reprobate to sleep through—that is, hides from them.

Thus the bride does not sleep with respect to the harmony of heaven; for, once every disturbance has been lulled, she perceives it before the eyes of her heart, keeps watch over it, desires to share in it, and entreats for it. Therefore she prays to the citizens of heaven. The citizens [Col. 0502C] of heaven pray for her; she prays to God and is awakened by him to prayer; she speaks to God and hears God speaking. For he speaks peace within her to his people, because he moves and admonishes her toward salvation and care for her neighbors. And this is what follows:

“The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister,” etc. This is the voice of the beloved—that is, the inspiration which he insinuates into her heart: because he is beloved, she should, for love of him, love her neighbors also, care for them, and strive to assist them toward salvation. He therefore wishes her, through preaching, accepting governance, admonishing, consoling, or praying, to prepare a way for him in others. Hence, to kindle her more fully for this task, he calls her sister, that is, co-heir; friend, that is, one conscious of his secrets; dove, that is, enlightened by the Holy Spirit; immaculate, that is, cleansed by him from the defilements of sins. As though he said: “Since I have bestowed such great things upon you, you too answer my benefits, and exercise toward my members the grace with which you have been specially endowed.”

“For my head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night.” As though he said: “Because I am God, I abound in mercy and in the dew of grace; and those who cling to me by faith are filled with drops of sin and blindness.” For the head of Christ is God, and Christ himself, insofar as he is man, is the head of the Church and received grace without measure. He therefore laments our misery, so that, since we are stained in many ways by sins, he may show that he mercifully wishes to have mercy on us. For he is Hermon, that is, “exalted light,” from whom [Col. 0503A] the dew of grace descends upon Mount Zion—that is, the holy Church—so that where sin abounds, his grace may abound still more. Therefore he admonishes his beloved to open to him, at the same time showing that he wishes to show mercy and to enlighten her very blindness.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How grace consoles and kindles, and concerning perfection and mortification

The bride, having heard the voice of her beloved knocking and admonishing her toward salvation and care for her neighbors, although she loves him and is ready to obey the bridegroom’s will, nevertheless fears to abandon the consolation of contemplation and again become entangled in worldly actions. Hence she adds: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5).

The tunic is an earthly garment; accordingly, earthly activity may be signified by the tunic. She therefore fears to be involved in earthly affairs which she remembers having cast aside, to be torn away from heavenly contemplation, to descend from lofty and spiritual things, and to be occupied with lowly things. Remembering also that she has washed her feet—that is, her affections—she fears to soil them again. She had placed these feet in the courts of Jerusalem and made them stand there. She washes them in living waters, that is, in contrition of heart, and afterward makes them stand in contemplation amid the things above and heavenly things. Not without reason does she fear to defile them if she draws them away from these things and commits them to outward care. Nor is it surprising that one who had fixed her feet in heavenly things should fear to engage in earthly affairs.

While, therefore, she trembles and wavers, the beloved consoles her and visits her heart with fuller [Col. 0503C] grace, penetrating it and illuminating it with a greater light of grace. And this is what follows:

“My beloved put his hand through the opening, and my inward parts swelled at his touch.” He calls this visitation of grace the sending of a hand through an opening. For grace is poured in, as it were, through a crack, when he does not bathe the whole soul but visits it with a certain measure of grace; and the one whom he thus visits in part he does not fully illuminate. The hand of the beloved may be understood as this operation and gift of grace. The belly, however, is the mind itself, in which thoughts are digested, as foods are in the belly.

The beloved also sends his hand through the opening when he recalls to the soul the benefits he has bestowed upon it through the Holy Spirit: that he redeemed it by his death, conferred upon it the gifts of his grace, and preserved those same gifts by guarding them. “For you granted it life and mercy, and your visitation preserved its spirit.” He granted it life by dying for it, mercy by pouring his own mercy into it, and his visitation preserves it by guarding it against a fall into sin. By recalling these things to the memory of his beloved, God makes an opening and entrance into her heart, so that she may be touched, kindled to love, tremble, and fear lest she fail, according to her ability, to respond to such great benefits. Thus touched and made to tremble, she is more greatly kindled for love of God and neighbor. And this is what follows:

“I rose up to open to my beloved; my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with the finest myrrh.” One rises to open to the beloved when, having received grace, one is more greatly kindled to receive it, [Col. 0504A] to love more fervently, and to devote oneself more diligently to the care and salvation of one’s neighbors. She who had previously opened to the beloved is more greatly inflamed toward him and applies herself to works of charity. Then she exercises herself in the love of God or contemplation, and offers works of mercy for her neighbors’ benefit, as their need and the occasion require. She prays for some, consoles others, gives others counsel for salvation, and prepares to accept governance or exercise the office of preaching, should the time require it, while she is thus visited by grace and strives to respond to grace and conform herself to it.

She is also kindled to mortify whatever carnal element she discovers in herself. Although she has mortified sins and vices, nevertheless, from the more abundant grace received, she is more greatly kindled for this work and finds more to correct. More enlightened, she knows her defects more fully; made better, she becomes more contemptible in her own sight. Then she condemns small defects which she had previously tolerated, and understands that she has committed many sins both in words and thoughts which she had formerly considered less evil. While she persists in the labor and work of this mortification, her hands drip with myrrh, because this operation is understood through the hands and this mortification is signified by myrrh. Her fingers are full of the finest myrrh because she does everything both discerningly and with a pure intention. For the fingers signify this discernment, by which she rightly apportions what she rightly offers—that is, makes discriminating what she intends well.

But by the finest myrrh is understood pure intention in mortification, [Col. 0504C] by which she seeks God in such a way as to mortify empty glory, despise outward praise, and keep her eye—that is, her intention—always directed toward God and toward future and true love. She is also said to be full of this mortification because she practices it both in mind and body. She chastises the body through abstinence, vigils, and other labors, cuts off luxuries and earthly pleasures, knowing that wisdom, or the grace of God, is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly. But the more one delights in such pleasure, the less one is raised up in God.

She also restrains sight and hearing from curiosity—those two things which Solomon declares insatiable—and thereby represses the other senses and keeps them from pleasure. She does not feed upon sweet odors and avoids unlawful touch. For she avoids familiarity with women, even freedom in conversation, because from such freedom one comes to the slavery of sin. For sometimes the common saying proves true: “Through bad keeping, the wolf has carried off the wool” [i.e., negligence leaves what is guarded prey to the wolf]. She therefore checks the vice of gluttony, withdrawing from herself what pleasure desires and allowing what necessity requires. In want she preserves patience; in abundance, temperance, knowing with the Apostle how to abound and how to suffer want. Thus she gains merit where evil people heap sin upon themselves—those said in Job to be “wasted with calamity and misery” (Job 30)—because pride is served in clothing, and gluttony and desire in eating.

Therefore, when the devout soul takes food temperately, deprives herself of something which appetite demands, and offers something to God even in eating, she gains merit and offers myrrh [Col. 0505A] pleasing to God. Thus she practices mortification in the body, and fulfills it also in the mind. She resists carnal pleasure, so that, if she feels it, she never consents to it. She likewise struggles against movements of anger and envy and other vices. When she endures insults, she does not answer back; she is not overcome by evil, but overcomes evil with good, loving her enemies and interceding for them. She burns with such love for Christ that she longs to die for Christ or for the salvation of her neighbors. Even if this is not granted, she nevertheless fulfills a kind of substitute for martyrdom: namely, when something delights her more according to human nature, she cuts it off and removes it from herself the more, and kills its desire.

This myrrh is rightly judged most excellent, because with such perfection she sacrifices herself to God. The bridegroom’s fingers are full of the finest myrrh when, guarding her heart with every care, she examines countless thoughts and movements of the heart, repels harmful things, and receives useful ones. Therefore, because she approves what is pure, rejects what is impure, cuts off and mortifies sins with the sword of contrition, and distinguishes and performs these things with perfect discernment, she is said to have fingers full of the finest myrrh.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How God is desired and withdraws himself, and how he is present for salvation and hears

“I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved. But he had turned aside and passed on” (Song 5). The bride recounts how, in order to enjoy her beloved, she has guarded against the smallest negligences that might provoke his displeasure: useless or superfluous speech or thought, bodily comfort, or unrestrained freedom—things which may be understood by the bolt, that is, the bar. For although the bar is small and narrow, it closes the breadth of the door, so that the door cannot stand open unless it is unfastened. Thus, unless these least things are cut off, the beloved does not deign to come to the soul in such a way as to enter it perfectly and fill it with perfect grace. Small negligences darken the soul and obstruct fuller grace.

Knowing this, the bride guards the eyes of her heart from the dust of these things, so that she may see the beloved through contemplation and receive him more fully. Thus she gives herself more fully to cleansing the heart, so that the beloved may enter her more perfectly, [Col. 0505D] as though through the door—from which she had previously known herself to be visited less fully and, as though through an opening, to be touched. But he turns aside and passes from her, not by departing but by withdrawing to one side. For he stands at her right hand so that she may not be moved from the good she has begun, though he does not appear to her face to face. For “he is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144).

She desires to contemplate him and speak with him face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend. But he hides his face when, remaining with and in her, he is felt to be less present. In this way, although he turns in toward her, he turns aside from her and passes on, lest she be exalted and attribute it to her own merits if she enjoys him as she wishes. Therefore, when she has shown herself more worthy to receive him, he does not give himself to her as she desires, but turns aside from her so as to preserve her in humility, arouse her desire more fully, and fulfill it more perfectly. For when his turning aside has humbled her and made her more fervent, both her merit thereby increases and she becomes worthy to receive him more fully.

He is said to turn aside when he does not grant her to feel his presence, though he is nevertheless present with her. The soul then does laboriously what it previously did delightfully. In that labor it is spiritually strengthened, and, acting manfully, its heart is fortified so that it may endure bravely and wait patiently for the Lord, whether he afflicts it through adversities or withdraws consolation. For the exercise of labor strengthens the mind by practice, so that it gains strength from it; and the good which it does through the strength of labor shows more than what it does through the sweetness of consolation.

Thus at the time of contemplation fervor toward God is kindled; when this has passed, the work is tested and virtue exercised. Or she complains that the beloved has turned aside, because, though partly apprehended, he is understood to be more incomprehensible, as the Psalmist says: “Man shall ascend to the lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 60). And Solomon says: “I sought wisdom, and it withdrew farther from me” (Eccl. 7). For as much as a person ascends to God, so much does he find him exalted and incomprehensible. Hence Job: “He shall not be investigated when his voice has been heard” (Job 37).

She also says that he has turned aside because the mind hungers for and desires what it has tasted; and the more it perceives his sweetness, the less sufficient is what it has grasped of him. Knowledge of his goodness shows how little it has received, awakens complaint, kindles it to greater love, and humbles it more after it has been kindled. Since she does not possess him as she wishes, she complains that he has turned aside and passed on. For she wholly melts in the love of him whose inspiration she has received. And this is what follows:

“My soul melted when the beloved spoke.” When the beloved speaks in the mind, what is strong grows soft; and things formerly thought hard because of earthly pleasures, when the soul melts and is thus warmed, soften and become delightful. As it is written: “The things which my soul formerly refused to touch have now become, because of my distress, my food” (Job 6). Then bitter things become sweet, because the soul is so melted by love that it scarcely feels whatever afflicts the body. It dissolves into tears [Col. 0506D] because of the greatness of love, and its tears become its bread by day and night, as long as it is not granted to contemplate its God.

Hence she again complains, saying: “I sought him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me.” She does not find the one sought according to her wish, nor does he answer everything she asks or desires—so as to hear her exactly as she requests or reveal to her that he has heard her. Yet, although he does not hear according to her will, he sometimes hears better for her benefit. And when he is thought not to have heard, he hears better, because he grants what he knows to be more advantageous. God heard Paul better when he did not remove the thorn of his flesh which Paul asked might be taken away (1 Cor. 12), because, if he had removed it, Paul would not have been saved.

Therefore, when he is thought not to answer, he answers better; indeed, he himself forms within the soul the words and desires to which he answers. For he himself asks—that is, he makes her ask—and he answers by granting what is expedient. At times she desires that an answer be given her concerning how many iniquities and sins she has, and that her crimes and offenses be shown to her. In this he answers her well when he forgives everything to one who is contrite—things which she neither remembers nor has ever set forth individually. Likewise, because of hidden dangers or needs, she passes into him through faith and love, and asks the one who sees all things to see these things on her behalf and assist her. For she knows that she has many needs which she does not see or know, and that many dangers lie hidden from her, which she fears less because she knows them less. Therefore she especially commits herself to him, so that he may answer by helping her where he knows [Col. 0507B] the needs. She merits such an answer in abundance according to the measure of her faith and love.

He also answers her in this: no voice of her prayer or desire is without merit, because it is made from charity. If she asks for something that is not expedient, he answers her in this, that he does not grant it; and the devout intention of her petition will not lack reward. Therefore, when she finds that the beloved does not answer her according to her desire, she seeks consolation and instruction in Scripture, and finds it. Hence follows:

“The watchmen who went about the city found me.” While the bride is thus troubled by love of the beloved and the intention of seeking him, the guards who went about the city find her—that is, the preachers who travel about in preaching in order to fortify and defend the Church against false doctrine and sins. When she seeks their teaching and asks them concerning her salvation and progress, they encounter and find her, instructing and kindling her toward greater love of God. And this is what follows:

“They struck me and wounded me.” For they strike one who loves with the sharp arrows of God’s word and wound her with greater love. These are the Lord’s arrows, which he has made burning—that is, effective for those who love. For they penetrate lovers but rebound from the sluggish. These preachers are also called guardians of the walls, because they strive to instruct those who govern the Church as well. They also take away the bride’s cloak, because whatever they discover still remaining in her from her former way of life, they remove through the office of preaching; and by their instruction they uncover the danger or sin which had been hidden from her. Scripture says: “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32). Because some neglect to do this, they wander in danger of mortal sin, and clothed in its cloak they will not have the wedding garment of charity.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the love of the beloved and its quality

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I am sick with love” (Song 5). The bride has sought the beloved by herself and has also received the instruction of preachers; now she seeks the prayers of devout souls. For these are daughters [Col. 0508A] of Jerusalem, born of God and belonging to the vision of future peace. She adjures them that, when they have found the beloved—that is, when through the grace of devotion they have him present—they may tell him of her love and desire and offer prayers for her.

She had often invoked the heavenly spirits and the souls of saints reigning with Christ, and through the angels in whose presence she was accustomed to pray and sing psalms, she conveyed her prayers to them. For these too are daughters of Jerusalem, who unceasingly contemplate that peace. But now she asks these daughters of Jerusalem—that is, devout souls dwelling on earth. For this is the way of good persons and those making progress: first, they seek God for themselves and persist in cleansing their hearts; next, they consult experienced persons about their own state and hidden dangers; and then they seek the prayers and love the companionship of the good.

For when they entrust themselves to the prayers of the good and join themselves to them intimately in charity and humility, it commonly happens that they too are kindled by the desire which they discern in them. Those whom they understand to seek God so ardently, they trust already to know him in great measure. Hence, seeking with affection, they say: “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us?” The beloved from the beloved is the Son of God from the Father; and whoever loves the Son loves the Father also, just as whoever sees the Son sees the Father.

Moreover, from admiration and desire for him, the devout souls thus kindled repeat and name the beloved, desiring also to be taught by her and refreshed by the sweetness of the beloved which she has received. They call her most beautiful because they are fully persuaded that she possesses beauty of mind and is adorned with virtues. This humility is also commonly found among good people: they think better of others than of themselves, and hear more delightfully things spoken from knowledge—that is, uttered from inward experience. Those who love also gladly speak of the one whom they desire. For devout persons, when they meet to speak of God, are accustomed to be kindled more greatly toward God by mutual conversation and, through the confidence they share, to express to one another what they feel or understand concerning God. God too is accustomed to be in their midst and to heap grace upon those gathered for his sake [Col. 0508D] and speaking of him.

Hence, more greatly kindled by the question concerning the beloved, the bride begins to describe his appearance and recount the benefits bestowed upon her by him, saying: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands.” He is white because he is the brightness of eternal light and Light from Light. He is white because he is free from every sin: “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” And he is ruddy because, in the Passion, he was drenched in his own blood—then he had neither form nor beauty—in order to make me beautiful, adorn the cheeks of my soul with his blood, and reform me who had been deformed.
