Therefore he is my beloved, because he suffered these things for me and also did these things for me.

He is also chosen from among thousands, because in the entire human race no one is without sin except him. For none is like him among lawmakers, nor among thousands of thousands and ten hundred thousand, who minister to or stand before the Lord of majesty. For gold or crystal shall not be compared with him—that is, the fellowship of heavenly citizens, whose hearts shine toward one another with brightness and are transparent with purity. And this is because he is not only man but God. Hence follows:

“His head is the finest gold.” His head is his divinity, for the head of Christ is God. That head is finest gold because the goodness of divinity surpasses all things made by it; this is the gold of the land of the living, and the gold of that land is finest. For it shines in such a way that it cannot be seen by human eyes or by those living in the flesh. “For no human being shall see God [Col. 0509B] and live.” Therefore he is my beloved, because this is his head, this his preeminent and sublime principle, which cannot be seen. I shall see it when that life appears, because then I shall be like him and shall see him as he is. He will grant me this twofold blessedness, because he will conform the body of my humility to the body of his glory and conform my soul to the likeness of his divinity.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the character of the beloved’s members

“His locks are like the branches of palm trees, black as a raven” (Song 5). The “branches of palms” are the *spatulae*, that is, the longer branches always stretching upward toward high places. The bride has described what the beloved is in himself; now she begins to explain what he is in his members. She calls his locks those who cling to him in faithful service, and says that they are like both palms and ravens.

The palm is rough below and wrapped in tighter bark, but above it is broad and beautiful in both appearance and fruit. So Christ’s members act harshly below and suffer adversities, while above, in God’s eyes, they are beautiful and fruitful. Through bodily hardships they are cleansed and advance toward beauty of soul and spiritual exaltation. Because they contemplate heavenly beauty, they willingly labor below. For their eyes are in their head—that is, in Christ—and in his golden head—that is, in his divinity. They long to attain there, tend there, be refreshed by his beauty, and be illumined by his splendor. They sigh for that vision, for that visible first principle; and, because of the greatness of love, days seem few to them and tribulation light in comparison with the weight of glory. For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory of that future vision.

Contemplation of glory and the desire for recompense kindle desire within them; desire makes labors light and carries them upward. Thus, because they contemplate and desire things above, they are strengthened below; and because they are strengthened below, they triumph over labors and grow tall in the virtues. For the palm grows greatly by ascending high and signifies victory. The beloved’s locks are like branches of palms because the elect, always raising themselves to the heights of virtue, are at times brought by God’s grace to victory. In low places their life is, as it were, wrapped in many barks while it is constrained by countless tribulations. But in the heights it is, as it were, spread out in the broadness of beautiful greenery through the greatness of recompense.

They are also said to be black as a raven. The blackness of the good consists in regarding themselves as sinners and bearing the shame of their sins upon their faces. They choose to be despised, bear contempt with equanimity, and not only do not shrink from lowly work and rough clothing but even desire them, knowing that a precious treasure lies hidden in this humility. This is the blackness of the good, in which they make themselves like ravens so that they may be made like Christ as well. For humility is Christ’s virtue; whoever possesses it will possess Christ’s likeness also. And the blacker one is through this humility, the more like Christ one will be [Col. 0510B] and the humbler in one’s own eyes. Thus the good are black and despised in their own judgment, but beautiful and precious before God.

Having described the beloved’s locks, she begins to describe his eyes, saying:

“His eyes are like doves by streams of waters, washed with milk, and sitting beside very full channels.” The beloved’s eyes are contemplatives, who contemplate heavenly and spiritual things with the eyes of the heart. They are like doves because they live simply and have a simple eye—that is, intention—so that their whole body may be full of light: whatever they do or intend, they do for God’s sake. They are also doves at the windows of their eyes, because they are not carried toward earthly things either by greed or love, having dull sight in such matters but keen and clear sight in spiritual and salutary things.

This is the right eye which, lest it cause us to stumble or lead us into error through subtle deceit, continually clings to the teachings of Scripture. This is what is meant when they are said to be “by streams of waters.” Doves are accustomed to sit by streams of water so that they may see the shadow of a hawk in the water and, casting themselves over the water, escape its talons. So the good see the shadows of demons in Scripture, because there they discover every manner of deception by which demons habitually deceive not only through manifest evils but also through hidden ones. There too they see how demons mock, now under the appearance of good and now through false interpretation, things believed sound and perfect by the simple and those less trained in spiritual matters.

Therefore, against every error or impurity suggested by the enemy, or asserted by someone erring and deceived, one must examine the divine utterances and compare with them what is suggested or heard, so that it may be received or refuted. For these are chaste utterances, silver tested by fire, proved apart from earthly things, and purified by the sevenfold Spirit. Whatever agrees and accords with Holy Scripture, which the Holy Spirit composed, must be believed sound and whole; whatever disagrees with it must be judged harmful. For nothing can be sound which differs in any respect from the Holy Spirit.

Streams also tend to make the eyes of those who look into them clearer. So Scripture, when examined, makes the eyes of the heart more discerning, because “the unfolding of the words of God gives light and gives understanding [Col. 0511A] to the little ones.” Whoever elucidates the words of God is illumined and disposed toward understanding God’s words. For mystical meanings, when they are investigated, instruct the mind and open its faculty for understanding.

These doves are also washed with milk—that is, cleansed from sins and preserved by the sweetness of mother grace. For through spiritual consolation delight, and earthly and carnal impurity, become bitter and cheap; through it one is moved to compunction, repents of sins committed, and does not commit others. Again, these washed doves sit beside very full channels. These very full channels are the perfect joys of that life, beside which they sit, because they remove themselves from earthly delight or consolation and strive to conform and draw near to knowledge and contemplation of heavenly things. For they lie down between the boundaries so that they may see that rest is good and that the land is best.

They choose the extremities of this world because they take the supports of life for sustenance, not pleasure, so that, dwelling thus at its boundaries, they may in some degree touch the boundaries of that life also and grasp something of those joys. They lie down at the boundaries because, although they are here in body, in mind they dwell there, as the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Because they use this world as though not using it, desire and contemplate the future rest, they are said to sit beside these channels. They would by no means see that rest in contemplation if they did not possess rest of mind. Hence this sitting by the channels signifies their repose, for sitting belongs to one at rest.

Thus, placed by streams of waters, washed with milk, and sitting beside very full channels, they have been illumined through Scripture and cleansed from sins and vicious affections by the operation and sweetness of grace; they have attained rest of mind and purity of heart. Through these two things they draw a sweet drink from that living fountain and thirst for the fountain itself, saying: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41).

But those who are still imperfect and weak have not been washed in this milk, because, though they have received from God some sweetness of consolation, they have not thereby received a cleansing equally complete from sins and vices. Therefore they do not sit beside these channels, because they do not yet possess this rest of mind. Their sweet affection or joy is neither perfect nor pure, because it proceeds from a heart less thoroughly cleansed. For natural frivolity, some prosperity, or a hidden temptation to sin still cooperates in them. Such persons sometimes descend, through sweet affection, into the accustomed joy of carnality. For the fire of carnal desire is still strong in them through temptation, and, when cheerfulness comes, it is easily kindled as though fuel had been added.

When their affection is directed to God, it sometimes happens that, owing to circumstances or place, a state made more unstable is changed into a carnal one, so that, having begun in the spirit, they may be consummated in the flesh. Hence some in such a state suffer movements of the flesh or even greater frailty. In them sweet affection [Col. 0512A] turns into sin. Therefore, when they sense a movement of the flesh, they ought immediately to withdraw from this sweetness and turn to some good thing. For such persons bitter things are more beneficial than sweet, hard things than soft: namely, the bitterness and pain of repentance, and the labor of struggle against the pleasures of the flesh or of their own will. Harmful pleasure is better cured by its opposite; and sweet things, just as they delight sensuality, also strengthen its powers. Thus through hard things and labors false pleasure is extinguished and rest of mind is gained, so that one may sit beside these channels and in some measure contemplate heavenly things.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the beloved’s members
His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by perfumers [Col. 0512B] (Song of Songs 5). The cheeks are the martyrs, who, shedding their blood for faith in Christ, redden like cheeks upon the bridegroom’s face. They are rightly beautiful, because they adorned the whole body of the Church, of which they were members. A great fire of love burned in them, inflaming them thus for torments. Great sweetness was within them, sweetening their most bitter death. This is charity—namely, love of God, love of the highest good—strong as death, indeed stronger than death. It had mortified bodily desires in the martyrs; therefore they were able to expose the body itself to death. Such persons lived spiritually, not carnally. They lived no longer themselves, but Christ lived in them. Thus they could die for Christ, who lived in them and whose Spirit they possessed. These are the beloved’s cheeks, which reddened on the face of the militant Church [Col. 0512C] through the suffering of martyrdom, and in the triumphant Church redden with a special beauty through the flower-bed. They are like beds of spices, filled with virtues; and virtues, after the manner of spices, possess both a sweet refreshment and a fragrance. For they delightfully refresh the mind which they fill, and send forth to others the fragrance of good repute and example. These beds are planted by perfumers. The perfumers are preachers, spiritual physicians who heal the sicknesses of souls through their instruction. They have prepared for the faithful a precious perfume, a sweet draught—that is, spiritual teachings by which they have imbued us. These beds are planted by these perfumers: the virtues have been described by them and recorded in books, concerning which it follows:

[Col. 0512D] His lips are lilies, dripping the finest myrrh. The beloved’s lips are preachers, because they speak his words and proclaim his will. These lips are like lilies because they possess the whiteness of innocence and the fragrance of good repute. Their teaching is beautiful and fragrant, because a pure life adorns and commends it. The example of good works strengthens their preaching; and those readily persuade who carry out in deed what they teach in word. Since, therefore, they do what they teach, they are white and fragrant. These are skilled physicians, first healing themselves and, instructed by the remedy for their own illness, proceeding to recognize and heal the illnesses of others. They drip the finest myrrh when they first mortify themselves and thus [Col. 0513A] preach mortification to others, beginning by doing and then teaching.

The finest myrrh is also the punishment of martyrdom, which they drip upon the faithful when they preach that the body ought to be exposed to death rather than that one should depart from God or commit a mortal sin. Christ’s death too is the finest myrrh, which they especially preach. For he is the head of martyrdom, from whom martyrdom chiefly began and through whom the faithful were strengthened to endure martyrdom. The finest myrrh is the best; therefore it signifies Christ’s death, which was best because it was the redemption of the whole world. These lips—that is, the preachers—drip this myrrh, set it before the faithful for imitation, and urge that it always be held in remembrance. When this is considered, it weakens the stings of the flesh, extinguishes the enemy’s temptations, consoles in despair, wipes away [Col. 0513B] sins, mortifies vices, strengthens the mind, and bestows grace.

Christ’s death, his sufferings, labours, and merits are ours, not his. For everything that he did or endured he merited not for himself but for us. When we come before Christ’s tribunal in death, we must place our trust especially in his merits and oppose them to the enemy who accuses us of evils committed or goods omitted. Therefore Christ’s death is the finest myrrh, the best myrrh, because it mortifies all our evils—so powerful that there is nothing tending toward death and eternal death which it does not destroy and bring to life. It follows:

His hands are golden, fashioned on a lathe, full of hyacinths. The beloved’s hands are good works, which are lathe-turned because they are straight and perfect. Just as a turning [Col. 0513C] moves correctly and smoothly, admitting in itself no unevenness or obstruction, so the good perform nothing blameworthy, doing nothing by which a neighbour may be offended, scandalized, or made weak. Therefore the good have a straight and polished activity, because they seek heavenly things alone, turning neither to the right nor to the left but walking on the royal road. For they govern and direct themselves toward what is wholesome and expedient, not toward what human desire seeks. They devote themselves more where progress is greater, and less where benefit is smaller. For many are very careful about trifles and neglect greater matters, performing works belonging to the class of good deeds but not doing them in charity. They fortify the fortress of their soul with many works [Col. 0513D], yet leave one opening through which the enemy may enter.

This will be the firm fortification of that fortress: that a person always intend not to commit a mortal sin and, if he has committed one, immediately repent; likewise, that he be diligent to recognize mortal sins and secretly grieve for those which he cannot recognize. Thus the activity of the good is enlightened by divine wisdom. Hence these hands are called golden, because they shine through divine wisdom and are not darkened through sin or ignorance. They also shine before human beings to the glory of the heavenly Father, because they are not made dusky by sins or lack of discernment, and everything they do is done for God and with a single intention. Therefore it is added that they are full of hyacinths, because they are done solely in hope and desire for heavenly things. For the hyacinth [Col. 0514A] is a stone of sky-blue and green colour. These hands are full of hyacinths because every activity and every intention of the good seeks the heavenly reward and God’s good pleasure. For this reason it gleams after the fashion of sapphire and is fresh in goodness, so as to please God and enjoy God.

Therefore they are full of hyacinths, so that no place in them may lie open to vain praise: they neither seek it nor ever accept it when offered, but always look to this stone, to the heavenly appearance, to that precious pearl, and for its sake count all things cheap and despise them. This stone also changes with the air; so the good change according to circumstances. At one time they exercise severity, at another mercy; at one time they correct excesses, at another they pass them over. They do this not through negligence but through discernment. For everything [Col. 0514B] has its time, and those who do not observe the opportunity of the time deprive themselves of the fruit of usefulness. Sometimes evil is better tolerated than reproved. Thus they change according to the time and people’s dispositions; yet this changeability does not make them unstable, but firm and steadfast. For, while they change in order to bring matters more effectively to their result, they always prosper in what they intend to do and do not suffer change as an impediment. They change their method, but not their purpose: the intention remains the same, even if the action is not the same. It follows:

His belly is ivory, studded with sapphires. The beloved’s belly is chaste married people, who comport themselves properly and use this world as though they did not use it. The elephant is a chaste animal and of a cold nature. Hence [Col. 0514C] it signifies those who marry or know one another carnally not in order to satisfy lust, but either for the begetting of children or to avoid incontinence. The intention of offspring has merit; avoidance of incontinence has pardon, for marriage excuses it; the motive of lust has condemnation, because it is a mortal sin. Married people, therefore, who serve their own pleasure are not truly the beloved’s, but the devil’s possession. Christ has no dwelling in them, but the devil has power—as the angel taught Tobias, saying that the demon has power over those who enter marriage in such a way as to indulge their lust, like horse and mule (Tobit 6).

The bridegroom’s belly, however, is studded with sapphires. Sapphire is a stone having the appearance of the clear sky [Col. 0514D]. Thus it signifies good married people, who, imbued with heavenly disciplines, meditate upon and savour heavenly things. They are studded with sapphires because, amid worldly activities, they also perform heavenly works. Although they are divided, so as to think of worldly things and how to please a spouse, they nevertheless think of heavenly things and how to please their Creator. This is the distinction of sapphire: while walking in the flesh, they do not serve as soldiers according to the flesh, but their citizenship is in heaven.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Description of certain members of the beloved, and praises of the Virgin Mary

His legs are pillars of marble, founded upon bases of gold (Song of Songs 5). These are those who support religious persons from their own resources, sharing temporal goods with them in order to receive spiritual goods from them. For whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward. Whoever supports a righteous person in serving God will not only share in that person’s reward, but will have that reward with him. These are the bridegroom’s legs, because these are those who go about visiting the sick and coming to those joined to them by flesh. Not only is their door open to the traveller, as Job’s was, but with Tobias they go to the needy and distribute from their means to each according to their ability. Like marble pillars, they are upright in knowledge and conduct [Col. 0515A], and unbreakable by vices and sins. They think rightly and soundly, not overthrown by any false teaching or religious practice. For some teach falsehood under the appearance of religion.

Demons also suggest false righteousness and a false understanding in the heart in place of the light of truth. Some indeed bend the bow of Scripture and prepare their arrows in their quiver in order to shoot their arrows in the dark at the upright in heart; and they destroy what the Lord has established—that is, made perfect and expounded through teachers—and bend it toward their own error [Col. 0515B]. Demons also work certain subtleties and revelations in some persons, and likewise certain novel and unusual things which the curious and simple admire and venerate. The good, therefore, possess a right and sound understanding; their actions are shaped in accordance with the life that proceeds from the heart. They make straight steps with their feet because they do everything with counsel, and disclose in confession not only their sins but also the hidden suggestions of the heart. For one who lives with counsel cannot err, nor can one who reveals the enemy’s suggestions be deceived by him.

Likewise, the good are upright and unbroken: they do not bend so that demons may pass over them, as it is written of the evil one, “Bend down, that we may pass over” (Isaiah 51). Nor are they broken by injustice so as to consent to the demons’ temptations and fall into sin. They are therefore upright and erect because they preserve righteousness in themselves, raise themselves up in desiring righteousness, and oppose injustice. Their firmness and constancy are compared not to any stones whatever but to marble, because they are not cheap and common, but precious and rare. Their strength is not the strength of stones, because they have not grown hard through insensibility, but through the uprightness of zeal [Col. 0515D].

These pillars are founded upon golden bases—that is, upon the faith of the prophets and apostles. For the prophets and apostles had the same faith: what the former believed was to come, the latter believed had come; what the former hoped and awaited, the latter saw and possessed. Hence one of them says: “My days were swifter than a runner; they fled and did not see good” (Job 9). These bases were golden because they shone through works. Faith without works is idle, but through works it is precious and comparable to gold, because it is formed by charity. These legs and pillars are founded upon these bases because the merciful and upright are built upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles, with Christ Jesus himself as the chief cornerstone [Col. 0516A], who joined in himself two walls—the Jews and Gentiles, righteous persons and converted sinners—and united human beings in heaven with angels. It follows:

His appearance is like Lebanon. These are virgins, possessing Christ’s beauty and likeness. For the soul which possesses charity has Christ’s likeness; and as it makes fuller progress in the correction of its conduct, it receives that likeness more fully. When someone has repented, at once in that contrition of heart the person receives, on God’s part, a likeness which he will gradually possess more fully and perfectly in the future. All the good are conformed to Christ by this likeness, but especially virgins, who along with it have the whiteness and purity of life. Hence they are compared to Lebanon, which signifies Christ and is interpreted “white”; therefore purity is close to the author of purity [Col. 0516B]. Since virgins obtain this special beauty, they are rightly called an appearance. And because they are without the stain of defilement, they are joined more intimately to the spotless Lamb. They also follow the Lamb wherever he goes. They especially follow him to whom they have made themselves especially similar.

To live in the flesh beyond the flesh is a heavenly, not an earthly, life. Therefore, when virgins subdue the sin of the flesh, which most prevails over the human race and clings to nature, they are in some sense outside the flesh and become like God, who is Spirit. Thus virgins are Christ’s appearance, like the appearance of Lebanon. For Lebanon is Christ, and he is not merely white but whitening: he makes the elect white and beautiful. Lebanon is also fruitful in noble trees; so Christ produces noble persons, namely those whom he has regenerated through his Spirit into freedom, so that they may be children of God and truly free, neither committing sin nor being slaves of sin. Among these trees the blessed Virgin was loftier and nobler: she was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon—that is, in Christ—because she is not lofty through herself, but through Christ, and was exalted and chosen by him so that she might grow thus and herself give increase to her Creator [Col. 0516C].

She is a lofty and noble tree, which produced this lofty fruit: namely, the Son of God. Finally, she herself is the cedar which grew in Lebanon—that is, Christ—and, while she bore Christ, the cedar in a manner produced Lebanon: the mountain proceeded from the tree when God came forth from a human being. This is the new and unheard-of thing which God did upon earth: that the cedar should bring forth Lebanon, the tree a mountain, the woman encompass the man—that is, God—and that the Virgin should enclose in her womb him whom the world could not contain. Virgins, then, are Christ’s appearance; but the blessed Virgin is his special appearance, who never stained her beauty by any mortal or venial sin. Therefore the heavenly King desired her beauty; taking flesh in her, he adorned this beauty more abundantly because he filled her with more abundant grace. Thus, when the world was wrapped in darkness and disfigured, she brought forth the Sun of righteousness, beautiful in form beyond the children of men, and restored the light of blindness and the beautiful form of deformity [Col. 0516D].

She, therefore, is uniquely Christ’s appearance, more beautiful than all and most like Christ: not only possessing Christ’s appearance herself but also restoring it in others. Mary is above human beings because she never committed sin, as human beings have, among whom no one has been found who does good and does not sin. She is also above angels because she surpasses them in purity, while contemplating divinity more clearly than they do. Not only did she commit no sin, but she also wiped away the sins of others; she was not only radiant in herself, but also sent forth rays of light from herself, because through her the world received the light of grace. Mary is therefore between the divine and the human, and mediatrix, so that she surpasses human things while accomplishing such lofty works through her Son. O wondrous dignity: from a woman comes forth the sun illuminating the world; from earth light shines out; through a woman the world’s darkness becomes bright with light [Col. 0517A]!

Through her this sun shone forth into the world and shone more brightly, because it more fully illuminated hearts. Thus eternal light newly arose from the temporal and spread its rays more widely. Nor was the light of grace given upon earth through her alone, but also the vision of God was given to souls in heaven. This blessed woman is that great sign in heaven, the woman clothed with the sun, because the sun of divinity shines upon her, shines around her, wholly possesses her, and, after illuminating her above all, illuminates the citizens of heaven. She first and before all received the splendour of this sun. She is clothed with this sun and is perfectly and especially suffused with the enjoyment of divinity, as though she put it on when she received such fullness of it.

She is clothed with this sun in heaven because on earth she had perfectly put on Christ, as the apostle says: “And she was full of grace” (Luke 1). The moon is beneath her feet—that is, the triumphant Church—because it is inferior and, being illumined by this sun after her, suffers diminution. And since every human being other than her has had some deficiency, that person may be illuminated by this sun, but not equally clothed with it. This blessed woman was exalted like a cedar; she was raised up like Christ. She was raised up like Christ, even as much as Christ: Christ was the least in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the present Church—while Mary was the humblest of all who were on earth. Therefore she was raised up for this purpose: that she might conceive the highest of all, and after him become the highest of all. She had rightly humbled herself with Christ, since she was to be exalted with Christ [Col. 0517C].

As Christ is at the Father’s right hand, so she is at the Son’s right hand. Christ is above all the works of his hands; Mary is above those same works after Christ, because she is exalted not only above the souls of the saints but also above the choirs of angels. Therefore Christ humbled himself in the most humble Mary in order to assume flesh, and raised up with himself her whom he had humbled. Mary is lofty, then, but Christ loftier. Hence it follows concerning him:

Chosen like the cedars. Before the beauty, strength, loftiness, and fragrance of cedars, all the glory of forests gives way; so neither the greatest persons on earth nor angels in heaven can be compared with Christ. I therefore wish to consider how lofty and pre-eminent he is in himself, and how greatly he humbled himself for me. Accordingly, when I fear the judge, I wish to consider my brother and one who shares my nature. For he will judge in the humanity which he mercifully assumed for us. May he pronounce the sentence of humanity and mercy, of a brother and not of a judge or justice. If I wish to justify myself, let him be judge and condemn me; if I confess that I am wretched, let him bestow mercy. I wish him to be judge in place of the judge, so that he may not be judge but brother in place of judge; and I wish to judge myself so that he may not judge me. If I come to judgment in this manner, and have the Mother of Mercy with me in my cause, who will deny that the judge is propitious? Mary was made Mother of God for the sake of mercy; and I believe that she exercises this without ceasing for the human race before the Father and the Son, and will exercise this office of judgment especially for those to be examined at the judgment [Col. 0518B].

She is the gate through which Christ, the noble man of the Church, will be honoured when he sits in judgment with the elders of the earth. Then the loftiness of this cedar will appear, how far he rises above human beings, and how exalted was he held to be whose spirit was in his nostrils—that is, breathed in the mouths of human beings. Let us therefore seek Mary, the Mother of Mercy and gate of heaven, and hope for mercy at the gate of judgment, so that through the gate of judgment we may enter eternal life.

## CHAPTER XL. On Christ and his merits

His throat is most sweet, and he is wholly desirable (Song of Songs 5). The bridegroom’s throat is his inward savour and spiritual consolation, which sweetly affect those who taste them through experience [Col. 0518C]. For if in thought you comprehend God’s goodness and attain its savour, you will proclaim with the bride the sweetness of this throat. The taste of his love is so sweet that it not only refreshes the mind, but also causes one to forget bodily food. If you contemplate spiritual and mystical things, whatever you can comprehend concerning him you will find sweet and delightful, so that you count everything apart from him scarcely sweet, indeed as nothing; while you judge him alone to be good, alone to be embraced and loved.

If you pass in mind to contemplating heavenly things, it will be sweet to meditate upon what it is to see God and be satisfied by his vision; that he be in us and we in him; that we be one with him; that we lack every misery; and that we rejoice with him without end. The inward savour of these things is the bridegroom’s throat. But the heart which will perceive this sweetness must be cleansed from vicious affections; for unless the vessel of the heart is pure, it receives or retains less of this sweetness of the Spirit, because it still has an admixture of the dregs of carnality. Let it therefore refuse consolation except in God; let it remember God and delight in him; and let it practise itself in this delight, until its spirit—that is, its own will—fails, and it despises what delights apart from God. To the degree that it despises outward pleasures, it will be able to delight in God [Col. 0518D].

Let it cast away worldly delights; let it leave the world, that is, worldly things; let it approach solitude of mind, sit alone, and raise itself above itself; let it raise body above body, so as to transcend bodily things and comprehend heavenly and spiritual things. Everything that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, or concupiscence of the eyes, or pride of life. Whoever has despised these things—overcoming carnal desire, recalling the self from outward things to inward and invisible things, and humbling the self after trampling down pride—truly leaves the world and comes to solitude in order to apprehend the knowledge and savour of spiritual things. This is the Egypt from which the people of God go out, and this is the solitude toward which they ought to proceed.

From this solitude messengers are sent forth and bring back the fruits of the promised land. These messengers are spiritual meditations and holy desires. They are sent by the devout soul to consider this land. Entering it through investigation, they report its abundance and sweetness and carry away its fruit. This fruit is the taste [Col. 0519A] of that sweetness, a foretaste of that delight: a fruit sweet to the throat of the devout soul tasting this fruit and experiencing its sweetness. Whoever tastes it sees—that is, knows—how sweet is this most sweet throat of the bridegroom, which not only surpasses but also drives out every sweetness.

The more its sweetness is felt, the more it is desired. In this life it produces hunger, not satiety; refreshment, not fullness. For it is so sweet that it is always desired, and so immense that it is never fully comprehended. Whoever is affected in such a way as to say that he is satisfied and wholly filled, I do not know whether he is refreshed by the bridegroom’s throat or by adultery and a false messenger. The Wisdom of God says: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Sirach 24). Here there is a slight taste of God’s goodness; in the future there is satiety, when we shall be satisfied as his glory is revealed and filled with the good things of the Lord’s house [Col. 0519B].

The true savour is distinguished from the false because it is not violent or impetuous; it does not tickle the flesh, but checks and moderates movements of the flesh. It is modest, tranquil, gentle, sweet, peaceful; it strengthens the spirit, weakens the flesh, kindles and enlightens the mind; it does not exalt but humbles. For its sweetness arouses desire and, while it kindles greater desires for progress, always makes one humble. Since what one possesses is little, one always regards oneself as needy and thus always thinks humbly of oneself. Imperfect or false savour represents a person to himself as rich, because it does not penetrate to the knowledge of the riches of God’s goodness.

The imperfect savour is that received by those still new and carnal, who have not yet attained perfect purity of heart, but have bleary eyes of the heart and cannot see clearly or comprehend spiritual things. They therefore think themselves rich because they see little and lack true knowledge. If such persons, being more enlightened, knew more and apprehended the immensity of this sweetness, they would humble themselves rather than exalt themselves, because they would understand how little they had been able to perceive of it [Col. 0519C].

False savour is what the enemy produces, which sweetly affects and cheers the mind; but it exalts rather than humbles, simulates fullness but does not possess it. How empty of true grace its recipients are will become clear if they are tested by adversities. They may therefore be compared with a bedchamber which is bright outside but empty within. Such persons gleam and shine outside because they have a certain appearance of devotion, but inwardly they are empty of virtues and lack fervour. In the secret place of this bedchamber the enemy sleeps and rests, because holy desires and burning prayers do not awaken or drive him away; rather, the lukewarmness of the mind and a false religious brilliance tolerate and foster him. Their glory is not from within, nor is it found so much in conscience as in outward reputation; and because they are poured outward, they do not know or perceive inward things. Although their savour is sweet, it is not most sweet, because it is not from the bridegroom but from the adversary.

Most sweet is that which the good perceive, those who through purity of heart have attained the true knowledge of his goodness. They can proclaim his most sweet throat because experience has taught them and they have tasted his sweetness [Col. 0520A]. If we also consider his humanity, his throat was most sweet, through which the words of divinity proceeded, because they were spirit and life, as he himself says. Sweet, therefore, was his preaching and those words by which he spoke about the kingdom of God. His throat was most sweet, then, and he was wholly desirable: the sight of his humanity was desirable on earth, but his glorified humanity in heaven is far more desirable, and is desirable even to the angels, who long to look into it. His face is desirable, for all the citizens of heaven desire his face; but the contemplation of his divinity is supremely desirable, and nothing that is desired can be compared with it.

He is wholly desirable also in his members, both those still journeying on earth and those reigning in heaven, because both their grace and their contemplated glory delight us. Here they have the splendour of holiness and there the splendour of glorification [Col. 0520B]. Their beloved holiness calls us to imitation, and their joy calls us to rejoice and enjoy it with them. Sweet is the contemplation of their joy, which we also hope for and await. This hope brings gladness, so that we may rejoice in this hope and be patient in tribulations or labours which we endure for its sake. Christ is therefore desirable also in his own, because he has made them beautiful and desirable from his glory and beauty, so that he may be desired not only for his own sake but also for the elect, whom we shall have with him as companions and partners in glory and in whose glory we shall rejoice. He is wholly desirable, therefore, in himself and in his members.

“And this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem”: this is he by whom I am loved and whom I love, not in word or human speech, but in deed and truth, because I hear his commandments and keep them. Consider his beauty; desire his love, daughters of Jerusalem—that is, souls desiring to come to the vision of heavenly peace. For through his love and fulfilment of his commandments one comes to the vision of his beauty, to heavenly blessedness and peace. May Jesus Christ, bridegroom of the Church, who lives and reigns for ages of ages, deign to bring us there. Amen.

## CHAPTER XLI. The bridegroom invites the bride to receive her inheritance

[Col. 0521A]

“Come into my garden, my sister, my bride” (Song of Songs 5). Soul, you have become a garden to me, producing within yourself for me the various fragrant growths of virtues and good works. Now also it is time for you to come into my garden, to receive the delights of my garden; for you are my sister, you are an heir. Come to the inheritance, because you are my bride; come to the embraces; come to sleep, that you may receive the inheritance. For when I have given sleep to my beloved, this is their inheritance. You slept outwardly, but watched in heart and contemplated the inheritance. Come to the joy for which you laboured; rest after labour; contemplate by sight what you contemplated by faith [Col. 0521B]. Hope refreshed you; now let vision refresh you. You rested in the left arm; let the right embrace you. Let earthly things neither bind nor surround you. Come into my garden.

My garden is a garden of delights. In my garden the roses of martyrs glow with wondrous beauty; with wondrous whiteness shine and give fragrance the lilies of confessors and virgins. In my garden are kinds of diverse fruits and as many delights as there are merits of the blessed reigning in the kingdom. In my garden is every planting of the ancient Fathers and of the new grace. Whatever was ever planted, whatever good was done from the beginning of the age, the fruit of all ascends here. Here it finally arrives; all these things have benefited you, await you, and will receive you. This is the fruit of my elect, which always remains; it belongs not only to those who do it but also to those who love it in others. By loving it, you have made it yours. For in loving me, you loved all that is mine; in loving, you made mine yours; and the merits of my elect are shared among my elect. For individual things do not belong merely to individual persons, but all things to all.

Come, therefore, here to receive all things together, because all things are prepared for you. I have kept new things together with old for you—that is, the ancient and recent merits of my own—that you may delight in all things, possess all things, and be satisfied by all things. “I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.” I gathered myrrh in the martyrs, spices in confessors and those who live well. The martyrs’ myrrh has come to harvest: their bitterness passes away and they have arrived at the fruit, for they have received rewards for their labour [Col. 0521C]. The confessors have passed from confessing their sins and my praise to confessing my name in praise without labour, the praise of peace and of my vision. The confessors were spices, for by the example of a good life they refreshed others and gave forth a good fragrance.

I have also gathered my own myrrh: I have brought the bitterness and punishment of my death to completion, but through it I have procured sweet joys of salvation for my members. The taste of that Passion is sweet to me through love; but the sweet spice of human redemption compounded from it refreshes me. Neither the martyrs’ myrrh nor the confessors’ spices would have received these joys had the myrrh of my death not received them. My blood extinguished the flaming sword set before Paradise; once it was extinguished, the cherub, which had likewise barred humanity, does not deny entry to one whom it knows has been redeemed by its Creator’s blood [Col. 0522A]. Nor does it receive that person only into its fellowship, but also into a likeness of knowledge. For “cherub” is said to mean “fullness of knowledge,” and humanity receives a likeness of knowledge, so as to know perfectly and as it is known—humanity which here knew through experience.

“I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.” In my Passion I endured bitter things, but now I receive the sweetness of resurrection. Then I was roasted like a fish; now I eat the honey of glorified humanity. I, who was as one despised and the lowest of men, am now crowned with glory and honour and set above all the Father’s works—and not only above all human beings, but also angels. I eat the honeycomb with honey, because in glorified humanity I enjoy in myself the glory of divinity and perceive the same in my members. This is my sweetness; these are my delights with the children of men; this is my feast, this my banquet. This is my food and drink: I eat it more sweetly than honey and drink it more pleasantly and delightfully than wine and milk. I enjoy these delights and nourish my members with the same food and drink. For they were honeycomb and honey, sweet to me in conduct and works; they were wine and milk, the wise and the simple. Sister and bride, come to this banquet after your labours.

## CHAPTER XLII. On Mary’s Assumption and her praises
Who is this woman who comes up, passing through the wilderness? (Song of Songs 3). Whither does she hasten, or what does she portend, covered with flowers? Marvel! Laden with riches, she does not encounter a thief: she is a singular virgin. O robber, you are now despoiled, made the virgin’s prey! [Col. 0522C] She is the enemy of Holofernes, the Hebrew woman; why, Haman, do you despise the Jews? She is the Jewish Esther; you spread out the cross for Mordecai, and by her you shall be punished. A singular fierce king is Ahasuerus; Esther is of great name. She is that rod of Jesse, which Isaiah declares to have sprung from the root, whose flower is the Messiah. The harvest of his passion has strewn the world’s ways with its hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit. She is that Shunammite woman who served David. She is Jael, so small, who crushed Sisera. She is the queen of Sheba, who came to the kingdom of King Solomon and heard his wisdom in the sanctuary. She saves her male child from Pharaoh’s hand. She is Gideon’s fleece, enriching the little vessel with dew. She is the singular dish of the true Solomon and the ivory tower, [Col. 0522D] gleaming wholly with gold, wholly beautiful. She is that upon whom the king reclines; the resting-place of travellers when he turns aside; she is the lodging-place upon which the King of eternal glory inclines his head, having no shelter. O how sweet to remember so praiseworthy a mother! She is the tree that burns yet knows not how to be consumed; the star brought forth by Jacob, herald of the true sun; the gate ever shut, passable only to the King; and also the ark of the covenant, borne upon David’s shoulders, brought in with great rejoicing. She holds the moon beneath her foot and stands clothed with the sun. Such she appears, so holy, possessing so many gifts of grace, so many figures, such great signs, bearing so many mysteries as there are stars in heaven. Consider how great she is, whoever you are that rejoice. Supported by these little flowers, surrounded by these apples, rescued from dangers, she stands crowned in harbour; [Col. 0523A] now blessed, she enjoys the longed-for kisses, joined to the Trinity! O let those now reborn applaud! O what rejoicing she rejoices in, the mother united with her Son! O how gloriously she shines, clothed in twofold splendour! Her bearer does not toss her about thus; faith thus maintains that she now reigns with God!

Hail, Mary, full of grace; may God be with you. Our corruption, which the Jew imagines. Let the deceiving Sadducee waste away in his falsehood: [Col. 0524A] for you have truly risen. O sweet mother of Christ, have mercy upon the guilty! Hail, Mary, mother of grace, queen of the world, mother of mercy, save us from ruin; fountain of life, vein of pardon, hasten to come when we draw near to death, that with you we may be able to rejoice for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0523]

## HOW CHRIST IS SET AS A SIGN FOR THE PEOPLES

[Col. 0523B] “The root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples” (Isa. 11). None of you is ignorant who this is who stands as a sign for the peoples, whom the nations will entreat, whose tomb indeed is now glorious. For who else has a glorious tomb except him who had to suffer, rise from the dead, and thus enter into his glory (Luke 24), so that his tomb should in this manner become glorious? Because, dying, he despoiled the author of death; because his death overcame death; because, having risen from the dead, he now dies no more and death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6), he made his tomb glorious. For the surpassing glory of the buried one made his tomb glorious. Or who else is he whom the nations entreat, except he of whom it is written: “All kings shall adore him; [Col. 0523C] all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71)? He has written upon his garment and upon his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 16). And rightly indeed all nations serve or entreat him, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given (Matt. 28), so that every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth rightly bends to him (Phil. 2). And whom else do we say stands as a sign for the peoples, except him who has been set for the fall and rising again of many, and as a sign that shall be contradicted? (Luke 2). Of this sign it is again written:

“He shall lift up a sign among the nations, and shall gather the fugitives of Israel and assemble the scattered of Judah from the four quarters of the earth” (Isa. 11). You hear the manner of its lifting when you read: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, [Col. 0523D] so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3). You hear the manner; consider also the fruit. The serpent is lifted on high to give a remedy to those who look upon it. The bronze serpent is lifted up: it has no venom, but destroys it; it does not inflict venom, but removes it. Certainly our first parents, and certainly all their descendants, needed such a sign, something upon which they might look in devotion and escape the sentence of death which they had contracted long ago from the venom of the serpent’s hissing, and which they do not cease to contract daily. Would that the Jews, would that our Judaizers, would attend, understand, reconsider, and reflect what kind of sign this must be—how lofty and how conspicuous—if it has been established to gather Israel’s fugitives and Judah’s scattered people [Col. 0524B] from the four quarters of the earth. Truly it must be lofty, that it may lie open to every gaze; otherwise they cannot know where they ought to run. Truly it must be conspicuous and altogether wonderful, so that by the novelty of a kind of miracle it may turn everyone’s eyes toward itself and draw universal concourse from every side into admiration of itself. Might this sign perhaps be raised upon some great and high mountain, so that it may thus be open to the sight of all? But where, I ask, can a mountain of such magnitude be found, one that can be seen by everyone and from every region of the earth? Or perhaps the mountain of the Lord’s house will for this very purpose be raised above the summit of the mountains? But if so, this mountain, whoever or whatever it is, must touch—indeed, surpass—the height of the clouds. [Col. 0524C] If it is indeed so, the Prophet rightly asks and says: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Ps. 23). But if the sign of which we speak is lifted even to heaven, can it then be visible to everyone unless it is clearly seen by some outstanding and wondrous new brightness? I venture to say: unless this sign is more splendid, loftier, and more radiant than the light of this sun, it could by no means summon the concourse of all, as has been said, into admiration of itself. Will the Lord then make something new upon the earth? Will he make a new sun, able to enlighten every person coming into this world, so that he who stands as a sign for the peoples may truly say: [Col. 0524D] “I am the light of the world” (John 8)? See whether this light may perhaps be that light which he meant to designate when he said: “For those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. 9). It is a good light, and truly to be desired, if it truly drives out—not merely the darkness of night, not merely the shadow of gloom, but the shadow of death. Certainly the visible brightness of this sun is not accustomed to do anything of the kind, nor can it do anything similar. Those who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death truly needed to receive such a sign. It was truly fitting that the Father of mercies should give such a sign as would gradually banish even the shadow of death from our borders, so that ultimately no trace whatever of death should remain among us, and he who stands as a sign for the peoples might truly say: [Col. 0525A] “O death, I shall be your death!” (Hos. 13). But what, I ask, will this light be which can drive out the darkness of death, unless it is that which the Prophet describes when he says: “Light has arisen in darkness for the upright: merciful, compassionate, and righteous” (Ps. 111)? Elsewhere you read concerning the rising of this light: “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 84). From the earth, indeed, of our humanity—from the stock of him to whom it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3)—there is born for the upright a light: the Word and Wisdom of the Father. Truth is born from the earth, I say: Christ, the power of God; Christ, the wisdom of God; and so forth—wisdom from human flesh; God the Son of God from the Virgin Mary, that he might become Emmanuel for us and God might be with us: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7), that is, [Col. 0525B] this is the sign which the Lord promised and displayed. O singular sign, O desirable sign, the sign toward which all ought fittingly to hasten with one accord! Truly a wondrous sign, such as befitted the Lord of majesty to give! “Therefore,” he says, “the Lord himself shall give you a sign” (ibid.). This indeed is the sign; this, beyond all contradiction, can truly gather the true Israelites from the four quarters of the earth and gather together into one the true children of God who were scattered abroad. For this sign it is given, and for this sign it is raised: first upon the scaffold, afterward into heaven; first upon the gibbet of the cross, afterward to the Father’s right hand. A faithful witness to this is: “Behold,” he says, “I see the heavens opened, and Jesus standing [Col. 0525C] at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts 7). Behold where, even to this day, our Emmanuel, the root of Jesse, has been raised as a sign and stands as a sign for the peoples.

“But what kind of sign,” they ask, “or a sign of what?” Listen, Jew: does it not seem to you a sufficiently great and wondrous sign that a virgin shall conceive, a virgin shall give birth, and to such a Son as is God with us? And what could be more wonderful than this sign? “But a sign of what?” you ask. Certainly, of that great promise which the prophet had a little earlier mystically signified when, prophesying of that which was left in the midst of the earth, he said: “The holy seed shall be that which remains in her” (Isa. 6). The seed conceived by the virgin and brought forth by the virgin ought truly to have been, and could be, a sign of a great and wonderful thing. The seed was fittingly a sign of holiness [Col. 0525D] because it did not take away the virgin’s holiness but increased it; did not diminish the mother’s integrity but consecrated it: “The holy seed shall be that which remains in her.” He who stands as a sign for the peoples expresses to us the nature of this future holiness: “In the resurrection,” he says, “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God” (Matt. 22). If, therefore, they are to possess angelic holiness, why not angelic blessedness also? But how can they be like the angels in heaven if similar in one respect and dissimilar in another? The principle of equity does not permit those alike in holiness to be unlike in glory. If they are to be such, they shall fittingly be displayed openly. “And they shall be displayed like the terebinth, and like the oak which spreads out its branches.” We know that trees of this sort commonly regain, at the coming of summer, the grace of foliage and verdure which they lose [Col. 0526A] in winter. Thus we are given hope of complete restoration in all that we lost during the time of this winter. Whatever the north wind took away, we shall recover in full in the summer of the future regeneration. Whatever the serpent’s hissing corrupted, the woman’s seed shall wholly restore. Of this the Lord says to the serpent: “I shall place enmities between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed” (Gen. 3). Finally, whatever we lost through the devil’s suggestion, the grace of our Mediator shall wholly restore to us, so that it will be wonderful to all how a human being could rise from such misery to such glory: “He shall be displayed like the terebinth, and like the oak which spreads out its branches” (Isa. 6). Thus a human being shall be an object of display for the angels, and an object of display for the Lord of angels. [Col. 0526B] For in the presence of his Father, before his angels, he shall glory over our merits and the fruit of his labour. Do you wish to hear the manner of this displaying? “Everyone who confesses me before human beings, I too shall confess him before my Father” (Matt. 10). A great honour. “And he shall be displayed like the oak which spreads out its branches.” Behold whence the displaying comes: from the spreading of branches. The spreading of branches is the enlargement of merits. Be enlarged, brothers, in charity, so that what is to be displayed may be worthy. Great is the enlargement of charity that extends itself even to enemies and includes all within the bosom of its breadth. Great is the enlargement of charity: to reckon all things as dung, [Col. 0526C] that you may gain Christ. Great is the enlargement of charity: for any one of us to deny himself, take up his cross, and follow Christ. These indeed, these certainly, are the things which shall not without reason be displayed openly. Therefore let us be greatly enlarged in action, that we may deserve to be greatly enlarged in recompense. Certainly, corresponding to the enlargement of merits will be the enlargement of rewards. What ought a human being not to do in order to recover what he had already lost in paradise? But consider this also: when summer arrives, oaks commonly extend their branches farther, spread them more abundantly, and strengthen them more firmly, so that they are more numerous, taller in stature, and stronger in vigour. Must we also expect something of this kind from the Lord’s promise? [Col. 0526D] Without doubt. For what we shall recover in heaven will be far more abundant and more perfect than what we lost in paradise. In paradise there was the ability to sin and the ability not to sin; in heaven there will altogether be no ability to sin. In paradise there was the ability to die and the ability not to die; in heaven there will be no ability ever to die. In paradise there was the ability to be attacked and the ability not to be conquered; in heaven there will not even be the ability to be attacked. See how at last the human being extends the branches of all honour and grace beyond the measure of his original possibility; how, by the greatness of his dignity, he grows beyond the rights of his ancient condition. Who would ever have believed this? Who could have believed that corruption and the worm would someday rise from such disgrace to such glory, unless he had received a sign—and indeed one [Col. 0527A] adequate to so great a mystery of condescension? Therefore, to assure so great a promise, the prophet sets forth a sign, one truly sufficient [Col. 0528A] to establish the security of our faith.

[Col. 0527]

## ON THE VISION OF EZEKIEL

### PROLOGUE. A Literal Explanation of the Living Creatures and the Wheels

[Col. 0527A]

Many find the divine Scriptures much sweeter when they can perceive in them some fitting literal sense. Then, as it seems to them, the structure of spiritual understanding is established more firmly [Col. 0527B] when it is suitably founded upon the solid ground of historical meaning. For who can build anything solid or establish anything firmly upon what is superfluous and empty? Since mystical meanings are drawn out and formed from the fitting resemblance of those things set forth in the letter, how can the letter itself instruct us toward spiritual understanding in places where it refutes itself or conveys nothing but triviality? Such people are therefore more often scandalized than edified when they encounter passages of this kind in Scripture.

By contrast, the ancient Fathers gladly accepted passages of this kind in Scripture when they could not stand according to the letter. For they compelled certain persons who accepted Holy Scripture but mocked its allegorical senses to flee to spiritual understanding through these absurdities of the letter, since they dared not deny that the Holy Spirit had written anything in vain, even in however great a foolishness of the letter. [Col. 0527C] I think this is why the ancient Fathers silently passed over the exposition of the letter in certain more obscure passages, or treated it somewhat more negligently. Had they applied themselves more fully, they would doubtless have been able to do this much more perfectly than any modern writer.

Nor do I pass over in silence the fact that certain people, as if from reverence for the Fathers, refuse to attempt what the Fathers omitted, lest they seem presumptuously to go beyond their elders. But, using such a covering for their own sloth, they grow numb in idleness and deride, mock, and scoff at others’ industry in investigating and discovering truth. But he who dwells in the heavens shall laugh them to scorn, and the Lord shall mock them.

Let us, however, receive with every eagerness what has been treated by the Fathers; let us seek out with every zeal what they omitted; and let us generously bring forward for common use what we have found by careful inquiry, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12). [Col. 0527D]

Behold: blessed Gregory expounds, according to mystical understanding, that wondrous vision of the heavenly living creatures which the prophet Ezekiel saw. But he does not say how it can stand according to the letter. Of the second vision he says that it cannot stand according to the letter. This is indeed true, but according to the interpretation that he himself assigned there; for if we examine [Col. 0528A] according to another interpretation the same letter of which he says this, perhaps we may draw from it a fitting understanding even according to the historical sense.

Certainly he himself says in the same exposition of Ezekiel that often something in sacred discourse is said obscurely so that, by God’s wondrous dispensation, it may be expounded in many ways. [Col. 0528B] Therefore a manifold exposition of Holy Scripture should never be rejected insofar as it appears to agree with reason or serve usefulness. Accordingly, insofar as each has received grace in this matter, let no one hesitate to seek with every diligence those things which the acumen of preceding Fathers either passed over deliberately, or was unable to explain because occupied with more necessary concerns.

I therefore gladly state what seems to me concerning that prophetic vision. For perhaps this exposition of ours, such as it is—even if it cannot satisfy another’s ingenuity—may nevertheless somewhat assist others’ diligence and zeal for inquiry in this same matter.

Behold, it is said of the living creatures (Ezek. 1): “The likeness of a human being was in them.” This likeness of a human being, so far as the letter is concerned, was partly present and partly absent, as the following statements make clear. It was partly present, because they had a human face and hands; and it was partly absent, because they had wings, calves’ feet, and several faces. Hence it is added concerning them: “Each had four faces, and each had four wings.”

If the heavenly living creatures have four faces and possess them on four sides, then, contrary to the nature of earthly creatures, they can see in every direction at the same moment. “And their feet were straight feet.” They had to have straight feet in order that, as may be inferred from what follows, they might move in every direction without any turning of the body. “And the sole of their foot was like the sole of a calf’s foot.” The said living creatures are described as having a calf-like sole, so that they may be understood to be naturally protected, not protected by artifice as human beings are. [Col. 0528D] Yet, in order that they might move equally in every direction, the form of their feet had to surpass the likeness of a calf’s foot to some extent.

In what is said—that sparks were in them, or rather came from them like glowing bronze—it is shown that they had fiery faces which scattered burning sparks. They had faces and wings on four sides. Certainly, if, as was said above, they had four faces; if, as is said here, they had them on four sides; then, so far as the letter is concerned, they must have had only one on each side. They had four wings so that, equally in whatever direction they turned, they could fly in every direction.

It should be noted that they had four faces, four wings, [Col. 0529A] four hands, and the same number of feet. Yet the number of feet does not seem to be expressed, because having four feet is neither rare nor unusual.

“And their wings were joined, one to another.” Thus the distance between the moving living creatures was as great as the joining of their outstretched wings could permit. “They did not turn when they moved, but each went straight before its face.”

Since he is later going to say, “They went and returned,” how is it said here that, while moving, they did not return? But perhaps “they returned” is used here in one sense and there in another, if we are not to make the prophet a liar. For here “they returned” seems to mean the same as “they turned”; but in what follows it appears to mean “they went back.”

Thus, while returning they did not turn back: wishing to return—that is, to go back—they did not turn back—that is, they did not turn themselves to the rear—because they did not turn around. [Col. 0529B] Hence, much later, speaking of the wheels, he says: “When they moved, they proceeded in four directions and did not turn when moving.”

Certainly, if they went in four directions, it was necessary for them both to go and to return. How, then, did they not return while moving, except in the manner determined by the words that follow? For immediately it is added: “But to the place to which the first inclined to go, the others followed, and they did not turn.”

Behold: in place of “they returned,” which he had previously used, he repeats the same thought with “they turned,” thereby clarifying what he had first stated obscurely. [Col. 0529C] But what are we to say here except that we return to the opinion of blessed Gregory: that, by God’s dispensation, this is stated obscurely in order that it may be expounded in many ways? And without doubt this obscurity of Scripture has the result that, though perhaps there is one exposition according to the letter, there may be many according to mystical understanding.

Let it therefore be said of the living creatures: “They did not turn when they moved.” Why they could go and return without any turning of the body is shown in what follows: “But each went before its face.” It is as though he plainly said: It was not necessary for them to turn their bodies when they wished to return, because they also had a face on the side toward which they wished to go. When we wish to go back, we must turn our bodies, since [Col. 0529D] we have only one face. But they returned and yet did not turn to the rear; instead, they went before their face—namely, the face they had on the side toward which they wished to go.

It follows:

“The likeness of their countenance was the face of a human being, and the face of a lion on the right side of all four of them. But the face of an ox was on the left side of all four of them, and the face of an eagle above all four of them.”

Observe how he advances by stages in his description. First he said that they had four faces; afterward he said that they had them on four sides; now, finally, he says what kind of face they had on each side.

If the said creatures had, in our usual manner, a right side, a left side, and a rear side, it would have been easy for the prophet to state each side and distinguish the faces severally according to them. But he could not do this because every side in them was a front side. He therefore did what he could: he first places one face, and distinguishes the others in relation to it.

He says, therefore: “The likeness of their countenance was the face of a human being.” Who does not know that in us the countenance is usually the preeminent and principal part? Thus it is said that their countenance—that is, their first and principal face—was the face of a human being. On the right side of that human face, in all four, was the face of a lion; and on its left side was the face of an ox.

It should be noted that he does not say on what side the eagle’s face was, because this was evident from what preceded. He said only what might have been doubtful if it had not been said: that this face was more eminent [Col. 0530B] than the others. “And,” he says, “the face of an eagle was above all four of them.” That is, it was above the others.

Birds, as we all know, commonly have longer necks than other animals. “And their faces and their wings were extended upward.” The phrase “and their faces” is an incomplete construction, as if he said: Their faces were arranged in this manner, and their wings were extended above those faces. For he introduces “and their faces” in order to introduce more suitably what he wished to say concerning the wings: “Two wings of each were joined.”

He had already said the same thing above in other words, but repeats it in order to add: “And two covered their bodies.” This is not to be understood as though they always covered their bodies with the same two wings and flew only with the other two, since they did both things with either pair, but alternately. [Col. 0530C]

When they determined to fly before the human face, they did so with the two wings on its right and left; and with those same wings they flew in the opposite direction, that is, before the eagle’s face, while they covered their bodies with the other two wings. But when they wished to fly before the lion’s or ox’s face, they did the opposite.

“And each went before its face.” He seems to repeat the thought stated above, but I believe that he here indicates something else. Above he taught that they did not turn their bodies because on the side toward which they wished to go they had a face to follow, and went before it. Here, I think, he wishes to say that they went in as many [Col. 0530D] directions as they had faces. For it is the same as if he said: Each of them went before each one of its faces.

What follows supports this interpretation:

“Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went, and they did not turn when they moved.” They truly went before each of their faces, because wherever there was an impulse of the spirit—whether to go, return, or turn aside in any direction—they went there in such a way that they did not turn, making no turn of the body in going or returning.

“And the likeness of the living creatures: their appearance was like burning coals of fire, and like the appearance of lamps.” Behold what we said above: that they had fiery faces, which emitted heat [Col. 0531A] like burning coals and light like lamps.

It follows:

“This was a vision moving to and fro in the midst of the living creatures: the splendour of fire, and lightning going forth from the fire.” These things are sufficiently clear.

“And the living creatures went and returned like flashing lightning.” Behold what we said above: that the living creatures went and returned. But how, do you suppose? Like flashing lightning—an astonishing swiftness, attributable only to heavenly living creatures.

“And as I looked at the living creatures, one wheel appeared upon the earth beside the living creatures.” Not merely one wheel beside all of them, but one beside each, as what follows makes clear. Thus one wheel appeared beside each living creature. But what kind? “Having,” he says, “four faces.” [Col. 0531B] How it had four faces will be clearer from what follows:

“And the appearance of the wheels and their work was like the appearance of the sea.” They are said to have a likeness to the sea because of their incredible magnitude.

“And the likeness of all four was one, and their appearance and work were as though there were a wheel within a wheel.” Let us imagine, as it were, two wheels inserted one into the other and joined crosswise in one construction; then we can understand how each is said to have four faces.

“Going in four directions, they went; and they did not turn when they moved.” We say the same of the wheels as we determined above concerning the living creatures.

“There was also stature in the wheels, and height, and a terrible appearance.” So far as it seems to me, whenever they stood, they did so in uniform fashion: they did not raise themselves here and there in every direction for standing, as we see in our wheels; rather, they did so where that construction, described above as of two wheels, was inserted crosswise on either side and joined together. [Col. 0531C]

When they wished to stand, they always fixed one of those sides on the ground and raised the other aloft. It is therefore easy to see how ready they were, after standing, to roll in every direction equally and without any turning of the body, since, as has been said, they had four faces.

We may also refer “terrible” both to their stature and their height, understanding them to be of such magnitude that it was terrifying to behold them. Hence it was also said above of the wheels that their appearance was like the appearance of the sea.

“And the whole body was full of eyes round about all four of them.”

“And when the living creatures moved, the wheels moved beside them; and when the living creatures were raised from the earth, the wheels were raised together.” All these things are clear and need no exposition from us.

“Wherever the spirit went, the wheels too were raised together, following it; for the spirit of life was in the wheels.” The spirit which the wheels followed appears to be one thing, and the spirit said to be within them another.

“And the likeness above the heads of the living creatures was a firmament, like the appearance of terrible crystal, stretched out above their heads.” The phrase “like terrible crystal,” I think, is said because of its enormous size.

“But beneath the firmament their wings were straight, one toward another.” Each [Col. 0532A] covered its body with two wings, and the others were similarly covered. Whenever one of them covered its body with those two wings which were on the right and left of the human face, every one of the others did likewise. Whenever one was covered by the other two wings, the others at the same time maintained the same arrangement for covering their bodies. Thus, as each covered its own body, so every other one was likewise covered.

He calls the sound “like the sound of the most high God” because it was of such magnitude that it could rightly be called divine, just as a royal song—or one worthy of a king—should be called such because it befits royal hearing.

Again, elsewhere we read concerning these wheels or living creatures: “One wheel beside one cherub, and another wheel beside one cherub. The appearance of the wheels was like the appearance [Col. 0532B] of a chrysolite stone, and the appearance of all four was one, as though there were a wheel within a wheel. And when they moved, they proceeded in four directions. They did not turn when moving; but to the place to which the first inclined to go, the others followed, and they did not turn” (Ezek. 10). All these matters are now clear from what has already been said above.

It follows:

“And their whole body, their necks, hands, wings, and rims were full of eyes round about the four wheels, and their whole body.” The word “their” must be understood as referring not only to the wheels but also to the living creatures, for both had been mentioned. Although he says “their,” he joins certain things applicable both to living creatures and to wheels; certain things applicable only to wheels; and certain things [Col. 0532C] applicable only to living creatures—unless someone thinks that wheels have necks, feet, and hands.

He would, however, have spoken more conventionally if he had used the masculine “their” rather than the feminine. But because he had spoken last of the wheels, he made the reference agree in gender with the word he had most recently used.

Such is the passage in the Psalm: “They poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan” (Ps. 105). He says “whom” in the feminine rather than the masculine, although the reference is not to the daughters alone—unless someone wishes to say that only daughters were sacrificed to the carved images. But who would say this?

Here, when it says “their whole body,” we understand this both of the wheels and the living creatures. What is added—“their necks [Col. 0532D] hands, and wings”—belongs only to the living creatures. What is afterward said—“and the rims”—must be understood only of the wheels; and the final phrase—“round about the four wheels”—must refer only to the rims.

He says, therefore, that their whole body, necks, hands, wings, and the rims round about the four wheels were full of eyes. He adds still further matters concerning the wheels, and matters applicable only to the living creatures:

“And he called these wheels ‘the rolling ones,’ in my hearing.” This concerns the wheels. Then he adds what applies only to the living creatures: “But each one had four faces.” If he were speaking only of the wheels, what does “each one” mean, and whence comes it? I think it is manifest even from this that he was not speaking only of the wheels.

It follows:

[Col. 0533A] “One face was the face of a cherub; the second face, the face of a human being; the third, the face of a lion; and the fourth, the face of an eagle.”

But where “face of a cherub” is read, some manuscripts have “face of a calf.” Yet although the wording differs, the meaning is the same in both. From the preceding discussion we have learned that the body of the said living creatures ended in a calf; and therefore, if we weigh the matter rightly, the calf’s face was more fitting to the body, so much so that by a certain right of distinctive property this face can, or ought to, be called especially the face of the creature described.

But perhaps someone will answer this and say: As it approached more closely to the nature of a calf in having calf-like soles, so, in having hands or wings, it displayed the distinctive character partly of a human being and partly of a bird.
