But we know that it is proper to a human being [Col. 0533B] to have hands. Therefore it could not have calf-like hands in the way that it had calf-like soles. The same must be understood concerning wings.

Having feet, however, is common alike to human being and ox, eagle and lion. Why, then, did the creature that had four faces receive calf-like feet, unless because the calf-like property claimed more of its own right in its body than did the others—since in those members which are common equally to the others it impressed the likeness of its own distinctive quality?

Therefore, on account of this prerogative of distinctive property, we rightly understand “face of a calf” where we read [Col. 0534A] “face of a cherub.” Nor is it a difference that above we find “face of an ox,” whereas here we find “face of a calf.” For every calf is an ox, but the converse does not hold under the name “ox,” by which the species of the animal is designated.

It should be noted that the same order of position is found here as was set forth above. But there the face of a man is numbered first, because it is more principal in dignity. Here, however, the face of a calf is first, because it is more principal in distinctive character. Yet, since the calf’s face is not more worthy than the others, he did not say, “the face of the cherub,” or “the face of the calf,” “the first face,” but “one face”: “One face,” he says, “was the face of a cherub, and the second face the face of a man.” Thus the face of a man was the second face—that is, [Col. 0534B] second in place after that which was placed first; the face of a lion was in the third place, and that of an eagle in the fourth.

## CHAPTER I. A brief overview of those buildings belonging to one half.

Before speaking of Ezekiel’s building, I wish first to survey the whole in summary, so that afterwards I may have freer and fuller scope in describing its individual parts. This building, then, had three walls: the first of six hundred cubits, the second of five hundred cubits, and the third, between these two and the smallest of all, arranged as follows.

[Col. 0533]

[Col. 0533C] Within the innermost wall was the inner court; between the innermost and the middle wall was the outer court; and between the middle and the outermost wall was the place of the common people. Of the inner court it is written: “And he measured the court, one hundred cubits in length and one hundred cubits in breadth, square” (Ezek. 40). Of the second wall it is written: “By the four winds he measured it, its wall round about on every side, five hundred cubits in length and five hundred cubits in breadth, dividing between the sanctuary and the place of the common people” (Ezek. 42). Of this sanctuary it is elsewhere written: “And it shall be sanctified on every side, five hundred by five hundred, square on all four sides round about; and its suburbs shall be fifty cubits round about” (Ezek. 45). [Col. 0534C] Quite suitably, he denotes the same place by “suburbs” and by “the place of the common people,” preserving the metaphor, since at the beginning of his description he had compared the building he saw to a city. Therefore it is clear that there were fifty cubits between the middle wall and the outermost wall, if “the suburbs” and “the place of the common people” must be understood as one and the same place. Of this outermost wall it is said at the very beginning of the description: “And behold, there was a wall outside, round about the house on every side” (Ezek. 40).

It should also be noted that this sanctified area, described as having five hundred cubits on every side, is now called a building, now a sanctuary, now a house [Col. 0535A], and now is compared to a city. Moreover, if you consult both reason and Scripture, you will find that each of these three walls had three gates: one on the east, another on the north, and a third on the south. Scripture gives a lengthy account of the three gates of the inner court and likewise of the other three gates of the outer court. It briefly mentions one of the remaining three and leaves the others to be inferred. For the inner walls would have had gates on the north and south to no purpose unless access to them lay opposite through the outer wall. The six inner gates each had its own portico. All were constructed according to the same pattern and to one measure, except that the gates of the inner court had their porticoes on the outside, [Col. 0535B] while those of the outer court lay on the inside; and except that one ascended into the outer court by seven steps and into the inner court by eight. Thus, those entering the outer court first encountered the gates and then their porticoes. Conversely, on entering the inner court, the porticoes presented themselves before the gates, so that all six porticoes lay together in the outer court. Scripture calls these porticoes now *porticus* (“porticoes”), now *vestibula* (“vestibules”); and it calls one and the same portico now a vestibule in the singular and now vestibules in the plural.

On the eastern route, between the paired porticoes of the outer and inner courts, lay a stone-paved floor, one hundred cubits [Col. 0535C] long and one hundred cubits broad, with thirty chambers (*gazophylacia*) on its two sides—fifteen on the south and fifteen on the north. Between the other porticoes there were also two further paved floors, one on the north and the other on the southern route. These two evidently had, after the model of the first, one hundred cubits in length and fifteen chambers on the eastern side. Their breadth, however, and the chambers they had on the other side, will become clearer in the description of the following parts. We represent the arrangement of the matters already described as follows.

[Col. 0535D]

## CHAPTER II. A brief preliminary survey of those buildings belonging to the other half.

[Col. 0536A]

Now, if the whole of this building is divided into two equal parts by drawing a line from the southern gate to the northern, we seem to have passed over those things belonging to one half of it, namely its eastern part. Let us now briefly survey something of its western part; for we shall discuss all these matters more fully in the work that follows.

The temple with its vestibule projected on the western side and was situated in the outer court; its vestibule on the eastern side was joined to the inner court. On three sides of it stood three buildings: one on the west, and the other two, one on the north and one on the south. [Col. 0536B] All were of the same length; for each, like the temple itself, extended one hundred cubits. Scripture calls the building on the west “the separate building,” I think because it adjoined no other building. The length of this building extended toward north and south nearly to the middle wall, whereas the other buildings extended from east to west.

The northern building had a portico extending fifty cubits and joined to the portico of the inner court. Scripture refers to this when it says: “Where there was a portico joined to a threefold portico” (Ezek. 42). From the portico of the northern gate of the inner court, this building with its portico extended westward one hundred and forty-five [Col. 0536C] cubits. For one wall of five cubits was common both to the building and to its portico. We understand that the southern building was made in every respect after the same model, because we find written: “All their entrances, forms, and doorways were according to the doorways of the chambers which were on the way facing south: a door at the head of the way, which way was before the separate vestibule for those entering by the eastern way.”

That the separate building had two vestibules, one on the north and the other on the south, can be demonstrated from this same Scripture. For if on the northern side there was a vestibule before the separate building, a way before the vestibule, [Col. 0536D] and a doorway at the head of the way—so that the entrance and the design were alike in both places—then the southern side must also have a vestibule before it, a way before the vestibule, and a doorway at the head of the way.

The temple, therefore, had the inner court on the east, the separate building on the west, one building on the north, and another on the south. Between those three buildings and the temple lay a court all round about. In these three buildings there was a threefold dwelling arrangement: chambers on the lower levels, upper rooms above, and, besides these, certain walkways before the upper chambers themselves, projecting from the very walls of the upper rooms. Some Greeks call these *exedrae* (“recesses” or “galleries”), while Scripture calls them *ethecae*. “And he measured,” says Scripture, “the *ethecae* round about on three sides [Col. 0537A] opposite the threshold of each” (Ezek. 41). We deliberately pass over here certain chambers, of which nevertheless we shall speak in their proper place, just as we shall speak of the kitchens. These few matters, then, we have briefly set forth beforehand to make what is to be said clearer; [Col. 0538A] now we shall give fuller attention to the discussion of each. We represent the arrangement of the matters already described as follows.

[Col. 0537]

## CHAPTER III. In what way, and by how many circumstances, this mystical description is commended.

[Col. 0537B]

First, it should be noted who was led, by whom, how, from where, and to where—the man who saw and wrote these things and left them for us to read: “The hand of the Lord,” he says, “came upon me, and brought me there. In visions of God he brought me into the land of Israel” (Ezek. 40). It was the Lord’s prophet who saw these things. But by whom was he led, unless by the hand of the Lord? Or how, pray, unless as it is written, “in visions of God”? He was brought into the land of promise, undoubtedly from the land of Babylon—from one land to another land, with so vast a distance between them. Whom, I ask, would it not move—or whom ought it not rightly to move—that such a man, by such an agent, in such a manner, and from so far away, was brought in order to see and hear what he would later write and leave for posterity to read? Who but a senseless person could hear carelessly, or dare to neglect, what Holy Scripture commends by so many circumstances?

Nor did it wish to pass silently over even the very time at which the prophet saw these things. For perhaps it foresaw that this also belonged to the commendation of the vision itself: “In the twenty-fifth year of our captivity, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth [Col. 0538B] day of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was struck down, on this very day the hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me there in visions of God.” Many years of the Jewish captivity had already passed; for a long time the children of Israel had laboured under great affliction. It was both merciful and necessary that, amid so many harsh and prolonged evils, they should receive some great consolation and perceive proofs of God’s mercy toward them, lest amid so many calamities they should utterly fail and completely despair of divine help.

But who could doubt that it is something great—indeed, beyond human capacity—that the prophet of the Lord, led by the hand of the Lord in visions of God, sees these things? “He brought me,” he says, “into the land of Israel and set me upon a mountain exceedingly high, upon which there was something like [Col. 0538C] the building of a city, sloping toward the south; and he brought me there” (Ezek. 43). It must not be carelessly passed over that the building shown is said to have been established upon a mountain exceedingly high. We shut ourselves off from understanding many things if we consider these matters negligently, as we can easily see from what follows.

In this building the inner court occupied the innermost place, but the temple undoubtedly occupied the highest. Hence it is read near the end of this description, where it says: “This is the law of the house: on the summit [Col. 0539A] of the mountain all its boundaries round about are the holy of holies” (Ezek. 43). Here, in his customary manner, he calls the temple “the house.” Thus the mountain gradually rose to higher ground as far as the place where the temple was built; it sloped toward that place from every side, and there spread out into a certain level and even expanse, which received the temple structure with equal elevation all around. For if the temple rose higher on any one side, its entire boundary would not, without doubt, occupy the summit of the mountain.

Let us consider first, if you please, this building as established upon a plain, so that the shape of the mountain and the position of the buildings may afterwards be understood more correctly. From what has been said above, it is established that the middle wall by which the outer court is enclosed [Col. 0539B] contains five hundred cubits from every side to the opposite side.

Accordingly, beginning from the east: of these five hundred cubits the outer court occupied two hundred; the inner court lay in the third hundred; the temple was situated in the fourth hundred; and it left the fifth hundred and more behind it. This is said only according to the consideration of the surface as a flat plane; for the swelling of the mountain added something to this measurement, a matter to be considered more carefully in its place. Yet from this consideration it is easy to perceive opposite what place the mountain rose more steeply, what shape it had, and on which side it sloped more sharply.

The building is rightly said to resemble a city because it was enclosed with walls on every side, secured by gates, [Col. 0539C] and surrounded by many buildings. “And behold, a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze, and a linen cord in his hand, and a measuring reed in his hand. He stood in the gate.” This man, described as having the appearance of bronze, seems to bear the image not of an earthly but of a heavenly being. We ought therefore to expect heavenly things from the heavenly one, sublime things from the sublime one, and carefully examine what he says or does.

But the fact that this heavenly man carries in his hand a cord and a measuring reed to measure the building may at least avail with disdainful hearers to prevent anyone from daring to rebuke us when they see us carefully inquire into and investigate the position, character, and dimensions of the individual buildings, set them forth with such diligence, and establish each point as far as we can [Col. 0539D] either by Scriptural authority or by rational demonstration. But lest what has been said so far seem insufficient to commend these matters, let us hear further what this same man says and what the Lord commands the prophet concerning them. “And the same man,” he says, “spoke to me: ‘Son of man, see with your eyes, hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you; for you have been brought here so that these things may be shown to you. Declare to the house of Israel all that you see.’”

He is commanded to perceive by sight the position and dimensions of the buildings, by hearing the rites and manner of the ceremonies, and to apply his heart to every detail: to understand them carefully, retain them in memory, and not greedily keep to himself the talents of so great a knowledge—not merely to announce them to this man or that man, but indeed to declare everything to the house of Israel. [Col. 0540A] I ask: whom could so solemn an attestation of a heavenly oracle fail to make attentive or astonished, and to kindle with desire for the understanding of these things?

But let us now return to the point that we heard this same man standing in a gate. To which of the three aforementioned walls that gate seems to belong can be perceived from what is added later.

“And he came,” it says, “to the gate which faced the eastern way, and went up by its steps.” Without doubt, the gate to which he came is different from the gate from which he came, in which he had previously stood. But it is clearer than light that the gate to which he came was that of the outer court, not of the inner court. The following words indicate this so plainly that they need no proof from us. For if he had come to this [Col. 0540B] eastern gate, which he measures first, from some gate of the inner court, he would have had to descend by its steps, not ascend. But it says: “He went up by its steps.” Yet lest we understand this of some other gate of the outer court, a manifest reason seems to oppose this. For he first takes the measurement of the eastern gate in the outer court and then proceeds in order to measure the others. Why, I ask, would he not first take the measurements of the gate in which he had first stood, if this were to be understood of some other gate of the outer court? It is therefore evident that this was the gate of the outermost wall in which he first stood—the wall of which it is said: “Behold, a wall outside round about the house on every side” (Ezek. 40).

But because I believe that I have said enough above concerning this wall and its measurement, with the accompanying testimony of Scripture, I avoid repeating the same matters here: [Col. 0540C] “And in the man’s hand was a measuring reed of six cubits and a handbreadth” (ibid.). Here it defines the measure of the reed, which earlier, when speaking of it, it did not specify. Why, I ask, is a handbreadth added to the six cubits on this reed, unless because it is grasped and held at that point while measuring? Therefore, whenever we hear that the prophet took a measurement with the measuring reed, we must understand nothing other, although some think otherwise, than six cubits. Hence a chamber is first described as having the measurement of one reed, and then, by recapitulation, the same thing is written of it: “The chambers were six cubits on this side and on that.” This can indeed be proved in many ways, [Col. 0540D] as the attentive reader will readily discover for himself: “And he measured,” it says, “the breadth of the building, one reed; its height also, one reed.” If what is said here concerning some unspecified building is referred to the whole, the truth and authority of the entire description are nullified. Is it not, I ask, much more correct and fitting to refer it to a part than, by referring it to the whole, to nullify the whole? Is it not more suitable and consistent with reason to believe that Scripture here describes the dimensions of a particular building which was beside or above the gate where it records that the man was standing and had not yet departed?

But because Scripture once named the whole a “building,” was it thereafter unable, or forbidden, to denote a part by that term? [Col. 0541A] Did it not likewise call the whole a “house,” yet did not hesitate in the following passage to apply the name to a part when it says: “And there was an inner house at the sides of the house”? What if we find this very term “building” used where it cannot possibly refer to the whole? “And before the building were chambers, and a way before them, according to the form of the chambers that were on the northern way.”

But even this alone ought to make us trust our interpretation: if here we wish to refer the term “building” to the whole, we are compelled, as was said, to destroy the credibility of everything stated here. Still, I think no one is so shameless, no one can be found so obstinate, as not to be ashamed to oppose us on this point with reasoning so [Col. 0541B] evident, or to blush at reproving us for this view, when he sees that all the other matters can stand literally according to our exposition—unless he mocks sound understanding in a truth so plain.

But enough of this. Let us return to the exposition of the text: “And he measured the breadth of the building, one reed; its height also, one reed.” If it had said, “He measured the breadth of a certain building in the place where he had previously stood,” if, I say, it had said this, it would have removed all ambiguity. Yet because it did not say this, it did not remove the truth but, in its customary manner, veiled it. One fact it compels us to understand from what follows; [Col. 0541C] another it indicates from what precedes. For it records that the man measuring these things had not yet departed from the gate where he had previously stood, and it plainly implies that this building was joined to that place.

What then are we to say of the fact that, while it speaks of breadth and height, it says nothing at all about length, although by nature length always comes before breadth or height?

But observe how skilfully, in saying “breadth,” it did not omit “length.” For where length and breadth are equal in every direction, it may rightly be called breadth.

Thus, by omitting what it ought first to have said, it shows rather cleverly [Col. 0541D] that length and breadth were equal. What we say of this one gate, we rightly understand also of the two remaining gates of the outermost wall, although Scripture does not expressly say so but leaves it to be inferred. For it was not necessary for it to dwell longer on matters that could sufficiently be inferred of themselves. Whether these buildings are to be assigned to the service of gatekeepers or of sentries is uncertain. Yet we place them above the gates as if for the duties of guards, according to what we find written: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set watchmen; all day and all night they shall not cease to praise the name of the Lord” (Isa. 62).

We make the following plan of the matters we have described: [Col. 0542A]

[Col. 0542B] It should be noted that another translation has not “building” but “wall.” Anyone wishing to apply our text to that sense frees himself from every difficulty, since he may refer the breadth to the thickness of the wall.

“And he came to the gate which faces the eastern way, and went up by its steps.” Because the gate to which he came is eastern, the gate from which he came is rightly believed also to be eastern. For if he had come from some other gate, he would with still greater propriety, because more directly, have hastened to [Col. 0542C] another—that is, to the one set before him.

After this eastern gate, he speaks in the same way of the northern and southern gates of the outer court; and only then are the other three gates of the inner court expressly named. Hence it is certainly inferred that this gate is one of the outer court, even though Scripture does not say so.

Scripture records that this gate had steps, but nowhere explicitly determines how many it had. Yet because all three gates of the inner court are each said to have eight steps, and the other two gates of the outer court each seven, we are instructed to judge like things by like; and therefore we believe that this gate likewise had seven steps, after the pattern of the outer gates.

“And he went up,” it says, “by its steps, and measured [Col. 0542D] the threshold of the gate, one reed in breadth—that is, one threshold, one reed broad—and a chamber one reed in length and one reed in breadth, and five cubits between the chambers.”

## CHAPTER IV. By gathering Scriptural testimonies from here and there, it is established here concerning one portico what must rightly be understood concerning all the others.

Since we have now come in order to the description of the gates and porticoes, and find much concerning them expressed so obscurely and said so ambiguously, it is desirable to establish here, both from this and from other passages of Scripture, concerning one portico what must without doubt be understood concerning all the rest. For all six [Col. 0543A] were alike in every aspect of their construction and of the same dimensions. So far as I recall, they had no dissimilarity except that the porticoes of the inner gates lay outside, whereas those of the outer gates lay inside; and that the ascent to the former was by eight steps and to the latter by seven.

That all these six porticoes were of the same dimensions we prove not by our own authority but by the witness of Scripture. Immediately after the dimensions of this gate, of which it has just spoken, it adds concerning the northern gate:

“He also measured the gate facing the northern way of the outer court, both in length and breadth, and its three chambers on this side and three on that, and its front and its vestibule according to [Col. 0543B] the measure of the former gate.” Likewise of the southern gate it is written: “And behold, a gate facing south; and he measured its front and its vestibule according to the preceding measures, and its windows and its vestibules round about, like the other windows.” This statement is repeatedly made in the description of all six porticoes; hence they are shown to have one and the same measure.

Each of these vestibules or porticoes was divided in several ways. Therefore Scripture frequently calls one and the same portico, now “vestibule” in the singular for the whole, now “vestibules” in the plural for its parts. Yet each portico was principally divided into three, and so one of them is later called threefold—a statement which, according to the aforementioned reasoning, is rightly applied to all of them: “Where,” it says, “there was a portico joined to a threefold portico.”

Let us therefore first consider the whole and afterwards the parts. The fronts of the outer porticoes faced toward the inner court, just as, conversely, the fronts of the inner porticoes faced toward the outer court. The measurement of these fronts is described where it says: “And he made fronts of sixty cubits.” This was the measurement of the length of all the porticoes or vestibules, though by these names we understand not a part but the whole. Thus the portico of this eastern gate had its front toward the west, while its length extended north and south. [Col. 0543D] It extended sixty cubits, according to the measurement of the front. Its breadth from east to west was fifty cubits. Hence comes the statement: “And before the face of the gate, extending to the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits.” Like the others, this portico had a gate in its front—that is, at the entrance into the court opposite the gate in the wall. Otherwise, an entrance would be opened in the wall to no purpose if it were blocked on the opposite side by the front of the vestibule. The vestibule therefore had a gate opposite a gate: one gate in the wall, the other in the front. To distinguish the two, let one be called the gate of the wall and the other the gate of the vestibule.

Here he calls the gate of the vestibule the “inner gate,” not the gate of the inner court. For between the outer gate [Col. 0544A] and that gate—apart from the space occupied by the walls—there were two hundred cubits. By “the face of the gate” he means the place before the outer gate but behind the inner gate. By “the face of the vestibule of the inner gate” he means the side of the vestibule which faced the inner gate. It is therefore manifestly inferred that the aforementioned measurement was taken within the walls.

Thus it is rightly said: “And before the face of the gate, extending to the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits.” If anyone wishes to take what we have said concerning the front or length of this vestibule in another sense, and to make its length extend not from north to south but from east to west, it cannot stand at all; [Col. 0544B] and I consider it frivolous to labour in vain in so plain a matter.

This portico, like every other, was principally divided into three. Hence, as has been said, it is rightly called a threefold portico. Of these parts or porticoes, the middle one was nothing other than the space or way lying between gate and gate: namely, from the gate of the wall to the gate of the vestibule. Its breadth was equal to the breadth of the gate, ten cubits; its length was equal to the breadth of the whole portico, fifty cubits. This middle and smallest portion was flanked by two others of equal dimensions, one on one side and the other on the other, each fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits broad. Scripture mentions these vestibules [Col. 0544C] in its description of all the other gates, and, designating them now in the singular and now in the plural, describes their measurements. Hence we read concerning the northern gate, which is described immediately after this:

“He also measured the gate facing the northern way of the outer court, both in length and breadth, and its three chambers on this side and three on that, and its front and its vestibule according to the measure of the former gate: its length fifty cubits and its breadth twenty-five cubits.” Thus, in the phrase “according to the measure of the former gate,” it is clear that the eastern gate which we are now discussing had a vestibule of such—that is, of so great—a size. But lest it be thought to have had only one such vestibule, hear what is afterwards written concerning the southern gate: “And he brought me out to the southern gate, and measured its front and its vestibule according to the preceding measures, and its windows and its vestibules round about, like the other windows: fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in breadth.” What it first calls “vestibule” refers to the whole; what it repeats as “vestibules” refers to the parts. Hence “round about” is added there, because they lay beside the middle vestibule, or the gate itself, along its two sides. These three vestibules—one middle and two lateral—were thus joined to one another and occupied sixty cubits.

[Col. 0545A]

## CHAPTER V. Concerning those matters which seem to belong to one half of each portico.

[Col. 0545B]

But it is further shown that there were other subdivisions in those two lateral vestibules, which Scripture itself also calls vestibules. There I find a vestibule of eight cubits and another of five cubits. I find the vestibule of eight cubits at the eastern gate of the outer court, where it is read: “And he measured the vestibule of the gate, eight cubits.” I find the vestibule five cubits broad at the southern gate of the inner court. Of it it is written: “And he measured the vestibule round about, twenty-five cubits in length [Col. 0545C] and five cubits in breadth.” But above we proved by the authority of Scripture that whatever we grant concerning one of these porticoes in matters of measurement, we must grant equally, on the same reasoning, concerning all together. Therefore every portico had vestibules of eight cubits, and likewise every one must have had vestibules of five cubits.

But first let us consider the position of the chambers; perhaps then we shall more readily discover the explanation of these features. Each portico had six chambers, three on this side and three on that, on either side of the way; and, as Scripture teaches, we know that they were situated within the porticoes themselves. “The chambers,” it says, “of the gate toward the eastern way, [Col. 0545D] three on this side and three on that.” This concerns the number of the chambers; and the following concerns their position: “And,” it says, “there were slanting windows in the chambers and in their fronts, which were within the gate round about on every side.” If the windows which were in the chambers were within the gate itself, then the chambers themselves were within the gate. For here, in its customary manner, it calls the gate itself together with its whole portico “the gate.” Otherwise what it says could not stand at all. Such is the statement: “And he measured the gate from the roof of one chamber to the roof of the other.” Likewise here it denotes the portico under the name “gate.”

It is evident that each chamber, together with its border, occupied eight cubits. Each was six cubits, and had a border of one cubit not only before it but also on each side, as Scripture attests when it says: “And he measured the border before the chambers, one cubit; and one cubit was the border on each side. The chambers were six cubits on this side and on that.” [Col. 0546A] Now three times eight makes twenty-four; adding ten makes thirty-four. We add these further ten cubits to the aforementioned twenty-four derived from the three chambers because we find five cubits between the first chamber and the second, and another five between the second and third, according to what we read: “And five cubits between the chambers.” Thus there were unquestionably thirty-four cubits from the beginning of the first chamber to the far end of the third.

There must be three on one side and three on the other beside the sides of the gate. Yet the vestibules which lay at the sides of the gate and were attached on each side to the central vestibule of ten cubits [Col. 0546B] were no more than twenty-five cubits broad. Therefore the breadth of the vestibules could not accommodate the arrangement of three chambers, which, as we have shown above, occupied thirty-four cubits. But since the vestibules were fifty cubits long, they could easily contain them, and more besides.

Let the three chambers therefore be placed along one side of the vestibule—namely, at the place where the roof seems to rest upon the wall—so that they appear to adjoin the wall itself; indeed, so that they have that wall as one of their own walls, and as it were one of their fronts. There, we understand, were those windows of which Scripture speaks when it says: “Slanting windows in the chambers and in their fronts, which were within the gate round about on every side.” For, apart from the other absurdities that seem to follow otherwise, which I think can easily be understood on their own, [Col. 0546C] there would have been no place from which they could receive clear light unless they adjoined the walls of the vestibule on either side, where they had windows to receive light.

Accordingly, we place here one of the lateral vestibules of the eastern portico, which adhered on either side of the gate to the central vestibule, in order to set before the eyes how the chambers adjoined the walls and how the vestibule itself was divided into seven sections.

[Col. 0546D]

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the remaining matters of the portico, for the completion of the whole description.

[Col. 0547A]

Having done this, it is beyond doubt that there are thirty-four cubits between the two outer ends of the chambers, and that eight cubits still remain on either side; for thirty-four plus twice eight plainly makes fifty. When this is established, if, opposite the side edges of the chambers, we first set back a small wall and then erect columns—as we see done in cloisters—and raise, as it were, so many walls as far as the middle vestibule, one vestibule is undoubtedly divided into seven. Thus the arrangement of the chambers divides one vestibule into seven, though it leaves them not all of the same size, but some larger and some smaller. [Col. 0547B]

Once this division has been made, we can here find what we sought above: namely, vestibules, some eight cubits wide and others five cubits wide, both, however, twenty-five cubits long. For the two spaces between the three chambers were five cubits wide but twenty-five long. The two spaces beyond the chambers on either side were eight cubits wide and twenty-five long. And the three spaces at whose ends the three chambers were situated extended six cubits in breadth within their walls. Whatever we have now said about one vestibule on one side of the way, we must understand in its entirety of the other on the other side of the way. [Col. 0547C] For it had the same number of chambers arranged in the same fashion, and was divided throughout into the same number of equal parts. Thus the two vestibules on either side are subdivided into fourteen parts; when the middle of one portico is added, fifteen subdivisions are counted beside each gate.

After what we have said about the division of the porticoes, there remains the question of what we should think concerning the thresholds mentioned by Scripture. Scripture plainly identifies three thresholds, and declares each one to be a threshold of the gate. Yet one gate could not—and ought not—have more than one threshold. Even if we assign one of these to the walls of the gate and another to the gate’s vestibule, there still remains a question about the third.

Let us therefore first ask which of these is said to belong properly to the gate, and why that which is not properly the gate’s should nevertheless be called the gate’s. None of the fourteen subdivisions shown above was more than eight cubits wide; therefore none of them could contain a threshold ten cubits wide, since their entrances were only at their fronts beside the middle vestibule. It is consequently beyond doubt that the threshold which Scripture says was ten cubits wide is properly called the gate’s threshold. Scripture sufficiently indicates this when, after describing the threshold of ten cubits, it immediately adds the length of the gate: “And he measured the width of the threshold of the gate, ten cubits, and the length of the gate, thirteen cubits.” For after indicating the gate’s width from the threshold’s width, there remained only to describe its length, which had not yet been stated. [Col. 0547D]

But since a gate on one side of the vestibule is erected opposite another on the other side, so that they appear to be one gate—and are often called one even though they are several—what reason, I ask, is there to suppose one larger and the other smaller? The other two thresholds, certainly, were only six cubits wide. If we wish to assign one of them to the other gate, we are forced to maintain that it was smaller than the first. But if Scripture understood this, or wished us to understand it, why, I ask, did it not immediately add the length after describing the threshold, as it did for the other? Why is the width of each gate expressed by the description of its thresholds, while the length of only one is carefully stated and that of the other altogether omitted? But by its silence concerning the one, after stating so carefully what it says of the other, it plainly indicates that all it says of one is meant to be understood of the other. Each gate, therefore—or, if this sounds better, one gate on each side—had a threshold ten cubits wide; it was ten cubits wide and thirteen cubits long. [Col. 0548A]

It remains to inquire whose the other thresholds are, and why those which are not properly the gate’s are called its thresholds. But since Scripture often calls the whole portico a “gate,” what is surprising if it calls something within it the gate’s? Indeed, if we wish to understand the writer’s meaning, we must undoubtedly observe and know his modes of expression rather than dispute over the strict propriety of expressions. These thresholds described as six cubits wide are called thresholds of the gate because they were within the gate; nevertheless, they are believed to belong properly to certain vestibules assigned in our final subdivision.

It is clear, however, that they cannot be said to belong to those [vestibules] that were six cubits wide if these lay open across their whole front; but if not, then they could not possibly contain a threshold six cubits wide. Nor could they belong to those lying between the chambers, for these were only five cubits wide and plainly could not contain thresholds six cubits wide. It follows, then, that the two thresholds mentioned above belonged to those vestibules which we proved above to have been eight cubits wide. For from what has been said above, the two vestibules situated beyond the chambers on either side are shown to occupy sixteen cubits. [Col. 0548C] If anyone wishes to divide these into two unequal parts, assigning less to one and more to the other, enough for one of them even to contain a threshold ten cubits wide, and thus attempts to overthrow our earlier assertion, then neither vestibule will be eight cubits wide; nor will it be possible to find one to which Scripture can rightly be applied: “And he measured the vestibule of the gate, eight cubits.” If, therefore, one of them is eight cubits wide, the other also must be eight cubits wide. For whatever is taken from one out of the total of sixteen is plainly left to the other.

But since, as I think, we have now said enough concerning the description of the portico, and have in due order pursued what seemed necessary to say here about the chambers and thresholds, the book now gathers into a single diagram the form of everything set out above in parts, so that the reader’s mind may readily learn from contemplating it the position, location, number, character, quantity, and proportion of all these things, for greater clarity regarding what has been said and what remains to be said. [Col. 0549A]

[Col. 0549]

[Col. 0549B] But because it is difficult, indeed impossible, to represent the length, breadth, and height of buildings in a plane by the same diagram, I think it sufficient to have set forth the arrangement and location of all these things and, by drawing proportional lines, to have laid down, as it were, a foundation for them all. For when we look at lines measured out proportionally, understanding by them nothing other than foundations of walls laid out or marked, it is easy to infer that walls rise upward from this tracing of lines and that a roof rests upon those walls.

If perhaps anyone charges our exposition with prolixity, let him see, I beg, how justly he does so. But, to confess the truth, I would rather be tiresome to the more subtle than obscure to the slower, especially in so obscure a matter, where almost everything said requires proof rather than exposition. But let us now return to the exposition of the text, which, so far as concerns what is said about the porticoes, we trust has already become clear for the most part.

## CHAPTER VII. Exposition of the text concerning the description of the eastern gate.

“And he measured,” it says, “the threshold of the gate, one reed in breadth—that is, one threshold, one reed in breadth.” As we showed above, although this threshold was not properly the threshold of the gate, it is nevertheless called the gate’s because it was within its portico, which Scripture is accustomed also often to designate by the name of “gate.” That the man entering the gate measures this threshold first, before the chambers, Scripture plainly indicates, I think, by showing it to be in the first of the aforesaid seven vestibules. [Col. 0551A]

But since it was first said, “He measured the threshold, one reed in breadth,” why does the text, explaining—or, as it were, correcting—what it had said somewhat improperly, immediately add: “that is, one threshold in breadth”? Yet to one who considers carefully, what else does this explanation or correction of the statement seem to be but a kind of declaration of the prophetic meaning, lest we fail to perceive what the prophet meant to say? It is as though he plainly said that he had indeed improperly called the threshold a gate-threshold, but ought to have called it a certain threshold, or one threshold. Thus, by the first explanation, he indicates in what sense this threshold can be called the gate’s; by the appended explanation, he teaches that it is not properly called the gate’s.

By calling it “one,” he further indicates that there are other thresholds there and that this one is not properly called the gate’s. By giving “breadth” twice, he wished through repetition to impress this more carefully, lest anyone should refer to the same threshold both what is said of this threshold and what is subsequently said of the threshold of ten cubits, merely because “breadth” occurs in both places. Yet if “length,” rather than “breadth,” had been used, it might perhaps seem more properly expressed. Indeed, where we have “breadth,” the Septuagint, according to Jerome’s testimony, has “length.” But “breadth” is often used, apparently not to denote a kind of dimension, but simply quantity.

It follows:

“And the chamber, one reed in length and one reed in breadth, and between the chambers five cubits”—in these words “he measured” must be repeated. Observe now in what fitting order he proceeds, and how gradually and in parts he scatters the seeds of understanding. First he speaks of the threshold in the first vestibule; afterward, of the measurement of the chamber in the second; then he adds the measurement of the space between the chambers, thereby showing that there were several. Finally, he comes to the last vestibule, situated beyond all the chambers, first describing its threshold and afterward the measurement of the vestibule itself, when he says: “And the threshold of the gate beside the inner vestibule of the gate, one reed. And he measured the vestibule of the gate, eight cubits, and its front, two cubits.” [Col. 0551C]

That this threshold too is called the gate’s is understood here in the same manner as above. He plainly specifies where this threshold was: namely, beside the vestibule that was inward and lay in the middle between the two adjoining vestibules. From this passage, I think, it is plainly shown that the fronts of the smaller vestibules were joined to the middle vestibule.

It should certainly be noted that, after calling this threshold, as above, a threshold of the gate, he immediately shows by the appended qualification that it is not properly called a threshold of the gate. For if this threshold had properly been the gate’s threshold, there would surely have been no need to add a qualification indicating where it was. But now its location is specified in the words, “beside the inner vestibule of the gate.” [Col. 0552A] Thus the threshold whose measurement he was taking lay beside that vestibule of the gate which was inward and occupied the middle position in the threefold portico.

After measuring the threshold, he adds the measurement of the vestibule itself, saying: “And he measured the vestibule of the gate, eight cubits, and its front, two cubits.” This measurement could not belong to the middle vestibule. For the middle vestibule was nothing other than the passage or way extending through the middle of the portico from gate to gate. Its length, therefore, had to be fifty cubits, according to the breadth of the whole portico. Its breadth could not be less than the breadth of the gates, which, as will later be clear, was undoubtedly ten cubits. It is therefore clear that the aforesaid measurement belonged to the vestibule whose threshold he had first described.

But when the vestibule’s measurement is given, why, I ask, is it not specified whether it is its length or its breadth? He often leaves unspecified what he foresees that an intelligent reader can understand from other circumstances. Once it is established that the two side vestibules of the threefold portico were fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide on either side, it may plainly be inferred that the smaller vestibules were twenty-five cubits long. For the smaller vestibules must be understood as transverse sections of the larger vestibules. Thus the breadth of the final vestibule is described in the words: “And he measured the vestibule of the gate, eight cubits.” [Col. 0552C]

It should also be noted that almost everything argued hitherto concerning the measurement seems to determine the breadth of the smaller vestibules. Where we have “and its front, two cubits,” Jerome again gives another reading: “and in its front,” or “at its margins, two cubits.” From these words it is plainly inferred that the two cubits indicated here are those which appeared to remain at the margins, one on either side, of the doorway six cubits wide. For if the vestibule was eight cubits wide, two cubits must remain at its front beside its doorway six cubits wide.

But the “two cubits of front,” according to our text, may perhaps better suggest the space above the gate itself up to the floor of the upper room rising above it; accordingly, the pronoun “its” should be referred not to the vestibule but to the gate. For how this statement may serve to complete the entire height will become clear below. What follows, “The vestibule of the gate was inward,” must be referred to the whole portico. Thus this portico was inward because it was situated inside the wall to which it adjoined. It follows:

“Moreover, the chambers of the gate toward the eastern way were three on this side and three on that. The measure of the three was one, and the measure of the fronts was one on either side.” [Col. 0553A] See how gradually he advances. He determines the number of chambers, which had not yet been known; and to the measurement of one chamber previously described he adds that the measurement of all three was the same.

Since the number of chambers is now known, the number of vestibules is equally known, though the measurement of all of them is not yet known. For the arrangement of the chambers, as was clear above, divides one side of the portico into seven sections, which Scripture is accustomed to call vestibules; it has already named the last of these a vestibule. The three chambers enclosed between themselves two spaces of five cubits, left two other spaces beyond themselves, and themselves occupied three spaces; all of which makes seven.

After this the threshold of the gate itself is described: “And he measured the breadth of the threshold of the gate, ten cubits, and the length of the gate, thirteen cubits.” This threshold, like those above, is called a threshold of the gate; yet here, as in the previous instances, no qualifying clause is added, and from this very fact it is indicated that it is truly and properly called the gate’s. That it is truly and properly so called can readily be established once the dimensions of all the vestibules have been determined. [Col. 0553B]

The dimensions of all of them are indeed readily established from what is immediately added: “And the border before the chambers was one cubit, and one cubit was the boundary on either side; and the chambers were six cubits on this side and that.” When it says that the border before the chambers was one cubit, and that the boundary was one cubit on either side, we should understand this in the same sense: namely, that a border of one cubit lay not only at the front of the chambers, but also on each side. We understand this border around the chamber to be nothing other than a projecting ledge of wall, such as is commonly made either for sitting or to strengthen the wall. For a wall is often founded broader below and, after it has been raised a little, is narrowed again.

If, therefore, the chambers were six cubits [wide], and still had one cubit on either side, as at the front, in the border up to the boundary, then from boundary to boundary the chambers measured eight cubits. Three chambers therefore occupied three times eight—that is, twenty-four—cubits; and there were five cubits between the first and second chamber, and likewise another five between the second and third, which, added to the preceding, make thirty-four. The final vestibule is also said to have been eight cubits, which number, when added to the preceding, extends the total to forty-two. The remaining eight out of fifty therefore belong to the first vestibule. For the whole portico from the gate to the front of the vestibule, as is later said, was fifty cubits. [Col. 0553D] Therefore no threshold of any such vestibule could have contained ten cubits. It is clear, then, that it belonged properly to the gate.

Moreover, as stated above, this is also implied by the fact that after measuring the threshold, in which the breadth of the gate is included, he immediately adds its length: “And he measured,” he says, “the breadth of the threshold of the gate, ten cubits, and the length of the gate, thirteen cubits.”

Observe how, after measuring the chambers, vestibules, and their thresholds, he describes the dimensions of this gate; from which it is understood that the gate he measures was an inner gate. See, then, how skillfully the measurement of the first gate, about which nothing is stated, is taught from the description of this gate. Reason does not permit us to believe that the outer gate was smaller than the inner, nor does the authority of Scripture allow it to be wider. For from the sides of the gates and from the sides of the middle vestibule—where the fronts of the smaller vestibules adjoined the middle vestibule—to the paired walls of the entire portico on either side were twenty-five cubits. [Col. 0554A] For the vestibules which adjoined the sides of the gates and the middle vestibule on either side, as is more fully apparent from the description of the other porticoes, were only twenty-five cubits wide. If, therefore, taking twenty-five cubits twice on either side, we add ten cubits—the breadth of the gates—we plainly complete the measurement of the fronts of the entire portico: sixty cubits. If, then, the fronts on either side were only sixty cubits, the gates cannot possibly have been more than ten cubits wide.

Above we showed how methodically he proceeded while describing one side in parts, until in due order he came to the inner gate. Having described one side, he briefly adds that the chambers had one and the same measurement on both sides, in order to teach concisely that whatever is said of one side should be understood of the other. Hence, in descriptions of the other porticoes, where he aims at brevity, he carefully describes one of the side vestibules as fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide, and passes silently over the other, leaving the same things to be understood.

## CHAPTER VIII. Matters pertaining to the description of the whole.

[Col. 0554C]

After the description of the parts, three statements are added in one continuous sequence, in which the dimensions of the whole are briefly contained and completed. The first concerns height, the second embraces the length of the whole portico, and the third its total breadth. Height is concerned in the words: “And he measured from the roof of the chamber to its roof, a breadth of twenty-five cubits, doorway opposite doorway.” Length is concerned in what follows: “And he made the fronts sixty cubits.” Breadth is concerned in the final statement: “And before the face of the gate, which reached as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits.” [Col. 0554D]

How the total height can be discerned from the first statement will be clearer from the final details of this description. We believe that there were upper chambers or stories throughout, as we find almost everywhere in the other porticoes of houses and other buildings. We therefore understand the roof of a chamber to be nothing other than the floor of the upper story, so that the same floor was both the chamber’s roof and the upper room’s pavement. And perhaps, according to the custom of Palestine, we should understand the gate’s roof to have been flat, not pitched.

Thus the upper room was twenty-five cubits high, according to the height from roof to roof. But note that he used “breadth” where he ought to have used “height”; for he often uses the word “breadth” imprecisely. Since there are three kinds of dimension—length, breadth, and height—“breadth” is often used merely to indicate the quantity of a space, not a particular kind of dimension. Thus in this place he uses “breadth” improperly, just as above when he described the thresholds. [Col. 0555A]

The words “doorway opposite doorway” are an elliptical expression; “having,” or something of that kind, may be supplied. Thus he measured the gate as having in the chambers themselves doorway opposite doorway, because the doors of the three chambers on one side stood opposite the doors of the three on the other. The “fronts” mentioned in the following words, “And he made the fronts sixty cubits,” refer to the two faces of the portico: one facing inward, the other outward. The inward face is meant in the following addition: “and to the front of the court of the gate all around.” This pavement surrounded the three sides of the portico, as the way lying on the other side plainly shows, around which the arrangement of the store-rooms was laid out. [Col. 0555B]

It should be noted that the measurement of the fronts, sixty cubits, is taken within the walls, as can easily be gathered from other passages, for example from the place where a vestibule is described as twenty-five cubits long and five cubits wide, as will be shown there. We should likewise understand the measurement of the breadth to have been taken within the walls. In the words, “And he made the fronts sixty cubits,” the whole portico’s length is determined; in what follows, its breadth is determined: “and before the face of the gate, which reached as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits.”

By “face of the gate” he means the inner surface of the wall—that which faced the person inside who was taking the measurement. He therefore measured from the inner side, not from the outer; for had he taken the measure from without, he would have found more than fifty cubits by as much as the wall’s thickness. By “the face of the vestibule of the inner gate,” he means that side of the vestibule which faced the temple and adjoined the inner gate. [Col. 0555C] The gate reached to the face of the vestibule because its portico extended to that point. The phrase “as far as the face of the vestibule” seems to answer two questions: how far the gate extended, and how far the space of fifty cubits extended. Thus he made, or measured, fifty cubits before the face of the gate, which reached as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate.

It follows:

“And he made recessed windows in the chambers and in their fronts, which were within the gate all around, above.” In these words, “he made” is repeated: he therefore made recessed windows, that is, wider inside and narrower outside. He made them in the chambers and in their fronts, especially in their fronts. These windows were within the gate—that is, within the portico—because the chambers in which the windows were were situated within the portico itself. For concerning the windows belonging to the vestibules themselves, rather than the chambers, he took care to add immediately: “Likewise,” he says, “there were windows in the vestibules all around, inward”; and he adds there, “and before the fronts was a representation of palm trees,” which needs no explanation. [Col. 0556A]

Observe that he says, in the plural, “in the vestibules” and “inward”; I think this passage readily makes known that he sometimes includes the whole portico under the designation “gate.” For although a gate ten cubits wide could readily contain one chamber, it could by no means contain several, so that it could be said of it: “recessed windows in the chambers which were within the gate.”

It follows:

“He led me out to the outer court.” He is said to be led outward, although he leaves the portico in which he had previously been. He is led out to the outer court because there was another court within. “And behold, store-rooms and pavement paved with stone all around the court. Thirty store-rooms around the pavement.” For the present we wish to say nothing else about these store-rooms except that there were fifteen on one side and fifteen on the other. This pavement had fifteen store-rooms on the north and fifteen on the south. It had the portico of the outer court on the east and the portico of the inner court on the west. Hence comes the subsequent statement: “And the pavement in front of the gates, according to the length of the gates, was lower.” [Col. 0556B]

It was lower because the gates, or the great portico itself, rose high above it, while the pavement lay below between them. This passage likewise makes clear in which direction the length of the porticoes should be understood. For if the pavement was before the gates along their length, it follows that the length of the porticoes extended alongside the pavement. He next specifies the measurement of the pavement, which he had not previously stated: “And he measured the breadth from the face of the lower gate to the front of the inner court, outward, one hundred cubits toward the east and toward the north.”

By “lower gate” he means the gate of the outer court, for the gate of the inner court was in a higher place. The building was, indeed, situated upon a very high mountain, as Scripture mentions at the beginning of the description. Thus the outer gates were also lower, and the inner ones higher. By “the face of the lower gate” we should understand the front of the outer vestibule; by “the front of the inner court outward,” the outer face of the upper portico. For the inner portico turned its face outward, while the outer likewise turned its own inward. [Col. 0556D]

It should certainly be observed from this passage that he attributes the place in which the inner porticoes stood now to the inner court and now to the outer court. Hence below he will say of the same portico or vestibule: “and its vestibule,” that is, of the outer court. The lower gate was on the east, while the inner gate was on the west.

How then did he measure from the face of the lower gate to the front of the inner court one hundred cubits “toward the east,” when this is from east to west, not from west toward east? A division of the text must therefore be made there: “And he measured the breadth from the face of the lower gate to the outward front of the inner [court].” A new sentence must be begun there, and the words “he measured” must be repeated from the preceding text, thus: “But he measured one hundred cubits toward the east and toward the north”—that is, one hundred cubits from west toward east, and likewise one hundred cubits from south toward north. Or the words “toward the east and toward the north” may be understood thus: toward the east—that is, toward the eastern quarter—he measured one hundred cubits between gate and gate; and toward the north—that is, toward the northern quarter—he likewise measured one hundred cubits between gate and gate; so that this final statement is made by anticipation. [Col. 0557A]

So far, I think, enough has been said concerning the description of one portico; what follows concerning the others can in nearly every respect be readily understood from what has been said, without exposition. Let the reader know, however, that almost everything we have discussed concerning the porticoes can be established from the authority of Scripture, and that much could have been proved by us with fuller argument, which we voluntarily pass over in order to avoid weariness.

## CHAPTER IX. The northern and southern porticoes of the outer court.

[Col. 0557C]

After the description of the eastern gate, the measurements of the northern gate are described in these words: “He also measured the gate facing the northern way of the outer court, both in length and in breadth, and its chambers, three on this side and three on that, and its front and its vestibule according to the measurement of the former gate: its length fifty cubits and its breadth twenty-five cubits.”

Here “gate” is used properly of what he measured: as with the preceding gate, thirteen cubits in length and ten cubits in breadth; its chambers, three on this side and three on that, all six cubits [wide]; its front, sixty cubits; and its vestibule according to the measure of the former gate, fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide. Such a vestibule was nowhere explicitly described there, yet, as this passage proves, it existed there; and not merely one, but two, because one lay on one side and another on the other, apart from that which lay in the middle. Nor was the one great vestibule described here any less present there because its parts were present: parts do not remove but constitute the whole. [Col. 0557D]

Hence, after first describing the parts, he subsequently adds concerning the whole: “Its windows, moreover, and its vestibule, and its carvings were according to the measure of the gate facing east.” Here “vestibule” is repeated, but what was first said of the parts is afterward referred to the whole. Thus when he first says “vestibule,” not “vestibules,” he uses the singular for the plural, just as later he uses “chamber,” not “chambers.” Yet we may also repeat “on this side and on that” from above and refer it to “vestibule.”

After this something is added which is not said of the preceding gate, but which is rightly understood of that also, according to whose measurement this one is described: “Its ascent,” he says, “was of seven steps.” What follows is common to both: “and its vestibule was before it.” All the outer gates had porticoes before them. For the inner gates, as we have already said, had their porticoes behind them.

It follows:

“And the gate of the inner court was opposite the northern gate.” For this inner northern gate had its front opposite the outer northern gate and its right side opposite the eastern gate described before. [Col. 0558A] Or, when it says that the gate of the inner court was opposite the gates of east and north, we may understand it of different gates: the gate of the inner court was opposite the northern gate, just as a gate of the inner court was opposite the eastern gate. In that case, what it says of the eastern gate is a repetition of the statement previously made concerning it.

Although he does not wish here to describe its measurement, he nevertheless briefly mentions it, so that he may more suitably add the measurement of the pavement lying between it and the outer gate: “And he measured,” he says, “from gate to gate, one hundred cubits.”

Note that he describes only the length of one hundred cubits. How broad the pavement was, or what ought to be thought concerning it, will be clearer from what follows. After describing the northern gate, he proceeds to the southern gate: “And he led me toward the southern way, and behold a gate facing south; and he measured its front and its vestibule according to the preceding measurements, and its windows and its vestibules all around, like the other windows: fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in breadth.” [Col. 0558C]

Note the words “according to the preceding measurements.” For if all are of the same measurement, whatever is said less fully in one seems to be supplied by what is added in the description of another. What is first said, “its vestibule,” should be referred to the whole; but “its vestibules,” which is repeated, refers to the parts, as is clearly evident from the description of their measurement. For the words “fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in breadth” are added to the second, not to the first.

Observe in this final sentence how two things are joined to the two preceding: “and its windows, and its vestibules all around.” Here are two; two others follow: “like the other windows, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in breadth.” To the first preceding phrase, “its windows,” the first response is, “like the other windows”; to the second preceding phrase, “and its vestibules,” the second response is, “fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in breadth.” [Col. 0558D]

He seems nowhere to have described such a vestibule at the first gate, and only one at the second. Yet this description shows that, as here, there were several there. But the reasoning of the first description does not permit there to have been more than two such [large] vestibules at each, because of what is said there concerning the measurements of length and breadth: concerning length, “and he made the fronts forty cubits”; concerning breadth, “and before the face of the gate as far as the face of the vestibule of the inner gate, fifty cubits.” If, however, it is established that there were two vestibules of such size at every gate, a third must remain at each, fifty cubits long and ten cubits wide, so that the whole may rightly be called a threefold portico and may fill the aforesaid measurement. [Col. 0559A]

It follows:

[Col. 0559B] And it was ascended to by seven steps; this indeed is also read concerning the second gate: “And the vestibule,” he says, “was before its doors,” not behind the doors as in the inner gates. It follows:

And there were carved palm trees, one on this side and another on that side, upon its front. The palms of the fronts are said sometimes to be carved, sometimes painted. But perhaps in both cases both things are to be understood: that they were carved and overlaid with colours. He had also spoken above of the carving of the palms at the upper gates. But he had not specified that one was on this side and the other on that. As above, after the description of the outer gate, he mentions the inner gate in order more suitably to introduce the measurement of the intervening pavement: “And the gate,” he says, “of the inner court [Col. 0559C] was on the south way; and he measured from gate to gate on the south way, one hundred cubits.” Observe that he understands a portico by “gate,” and that he describes only the length of the pavement; for its width will be clearer from elsewhere.

## CHAPTER X. On the three porticoes of the inner court

After the outer gates, behold, he describes the inner gates. After the last one which he described, he passes to the one nearest it, when he says: “And he brought me into the inner court by the south gate, and he measured the gate according to the former measurements: its chamber, [Col. 0559D] and its front, and its vestibule, by the same measurements; and its windows, and its vestibule round about, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width.”

What is read above concerning the outer gates is repeated concerning the inner gates: “and he measured,” he says, “the gate according to the former measurements.” In saying “its chamber” rather than “its chambers,” he puts the singular for the plural. The words appended, “and its front and its vestibule, by the same measurements,” may refer to the whole; and then in what follows one must supply “having,” or something of that kind: “And he measured its windows, and its vestibule round about, having fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width.” By “its windows,” that is, the windows of the vestibule, he means the windows of the walls [Col. 0560A] enclosing the whole exterior. But by “the windows of its vestibules,” that is, of the vestibule, he means the windows of the walls intersecting the smaller vestibules. Nor should this be passed over: he calls the parts of the whole “the vestibules of the vestibule.” But if “of the vestibule,” rather than “of the vestibules,” is read—for both readings are found—it is referred to the same sense; and what is said of the vestibule of one side is to be understood of both. Yet it should be known that Jerome has not *vestibuli* (“of the vestibule”), but *vestibulorum* (“of the vestibules”). It follows:

“And the vestibule round about, twenty-five cubits in length and five cubits in width.” See how, throughout the description, something new is still added which he had not stated in the preceding passages. He had nowhere above [Col. 0560B] described a vestibule five cubits wide; yet if it was at this gate, then it was at all the others, since it is perfectly clear that all had one and the same measurement. But where, I ask, was this vestibule unless it was between the chambers? For Scripture describes a space of five cubits between the chambers; and not only one such space, but, among three chambers, two on one side and two on the other. How then is it that, in the first description, we read of a vestibule eight cubits wide, while in this description we read of one five cubits wide? Both statements must throughout be understood of the individual vestibules. By means of this vestibule twenty-five cubits long, it may readily be proved that the measurement of forty cubits for the fronts was taken within the walls. There follows that in which the inner porticoes [Col. 0560C] differ from the upper ones: “And its vestibule,” he says, “was toward the outer court.” For the upper ones faced inward, but this one outward. “And its palms,” he says, “were on its front.” Here “it had” is to be supplied; but this too it shared with the others. It follows:

“And there were eight steps by which one ascended through it.” In this again the inner gates differ from the upper ones, which had only seven. After the south gate he passes to the east gate: “And he brought me into the inner court by the east way, and measured the gate according to the former measurements: its chamber, and its front, and its vestibules, as above; and its windows, and its vestibules round about, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width.” In this description alone “vestibules” is twice put in the plural, [Col. 0560D] and rightly so, because the description of the smaller vestibules too is completed from the preceding description. Thus, in placing “vestibules” twice, he seems in this description to mention a twofold division. One portico is first divided into three vestibules; then two of these, the larger ones, are subdivided into fourteen others. Therefore, after the measurement of the smallest, he who measures seems to proceed to the measurement of the larger. The first occurrence, then, should be referred to the smaller; the second, to the larger, whose measurement is there appended in the words, “fifty cubits in length and twenty-five cubits in width.” It follows: “and its vestibule,” that is, of the outer court—“its vestibule,” he says, “is of the outer court”—as though he openly said: that very vestibule which belongs to it, that is, to the inner court, is rightly called, in one respect, [Col. 0561A] the vestibule of the outer court. Certainly it should by no means have been called this, if, after the pattern of the outer porticoes, it had lain within its own gate; but now it is rightly called the vestibule of that to which it is joined. Then is added what is read in the preceding account: “And carved palms were on its front, on this side and on that, and its ascent was by eight steps.” Then follows the description of the last of the gates:

“And he brought me to the gate facing north, and he measured, according to the former measurements, its chamber, and its front, and its vestibule, and its windows round about, fifty cubits in length and twenty-five [Col. 0561B] cubits in width. Its vestibule faced the outer court, and carved palms were on its front, on this side and on that, and its ascent was by eight steps.” Since nothing new is added here, explanation seems superfluous. It follows: “And at each chamber was a door in the fronts of the gates. There they washed the burnt offering.” When it says that the chambers, or the doors of the chambers, were in the fronts of the gates, we must understand this of the inner porticoes. For since the doors were in the fronts of the chambers and all faced the pavements lying before the inner porticoes, it is rightly said now that the doors of the chambers were in the fronts of the gates. The location of the chambers is therefore determined by the statement: “And at each chamber was a door in the fronts of the gates.” Thus let the line by which the fronts of the gates are bounded be extended, and from it to the outer wall let the chambers be arranged; for whatever lay beyond that line would not be in the fronts of the gates. In the first description of all he spoke of the chambers, but in all the others he makes no mention of them. Why then is what is here said concerning the chambers attached to this final description, unless in order that, by this very fact, it might be understood of them all? Likewise, I think he intended what he appends concerning the eight tables to be understood of all three inner gates. All three inner gates had eight tables along the sides of their vestibules, although Scripture does not seem expressly to determine this. But see how subtly [Col. 0561D] Scripture has chosen in some places silently to pass over certain things which careful inquiry does not permit reason to leave hidden.

To be sure, concerning the chambers it is said: “There they washed the burnt offering.” But of the tables it is written: “Upon the tables, moreover, was the flesh of the offering.” Therefore, if anyone thinks that only the east gate had chambers, or that tables existed only at the north gate, let him consider, I beg, whether reason permits the east gate to lack a place where what is washed there may be laid away; or the north gate to lack a place where what is laid away there may be washed. Are things sacrificed at the north gate washed at the east gate, and things washed at the east gate sacrificed at the north gate? Or does neither happen at the south gate because its description [Col. 0562A] made no mention of chambers? I know indeed that the Fathers sometimes passed carelessly over certain passages of Scripture which they could readily have penetrated, because they desired to find—and rejoiced to find—things that could not stand according to the letter, so that at least by this means men might be compelled to accept allegory, which in those times very few would scarcely have been willing to accept. Therefore let no one be scandalized if we say something different, or differently, from what he finds in the glosses. Let no one disdain our wish to gather the remaining ears of grain; let no one wonder that some might have escaped them—or rather, that they voluntarily left them for the poor, to whom this was divinely commanded, to whom it was divinely granted to fill so many granaries of volumes from the harvest of the Scriptures. But you wish to honour and [Col. 0562B] defend the authority of the ancients; yet never do we honour lovers of truth more truly than by seeking, finding, teaching, defending, and loving the truth. Attend, then, not to whether I say something new, but whether it is true. I have little fear of saying something different, provided that I say nothing perverse. But behold, I return again to the exposition of the letter, attending more to what Scripture itself means to say than to what others may say of me.

## CHAPTER XI. On the tables where the burnt offering was sacrificed, and on the chambers of the singers

“And in the vestibule of the gate were two tables on this side and two [Col. 0562C] tables on that side, that upon them the burnt offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering might be sacrificed.” What the burnt offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering are, and many other such matters belonging to the exposition of the letter, I deliberately pass over; for at present I am wholly intent only upon something which I find nowhere else: how this exceedingly subtle description of the prophet can stand according to the letter, or how it ought to be understood. But if, as is said here, this was the office of the tables—that the burnt offering should be sacrificed upon them—let each choose what he thinks more fitting: whether victims ought to be sacrificed at this gate alone, or whether the other gates also had similar tables for this purpose. If sacrifices were offered only at this gate, what is to become of the prince’s victim, when he entered and departed by the east gate alone?
