If victims are washed only at the east gate on non-festival days, what is to become of the people’s victim when the east gate was shut and open to the prince alone? By arguments of this sort we may infer that divine Scripture silently indicates many things with a certain deliberation.

He has already said that there were four tables, two on this side and two on that, within the vestibule. He now says that there were four others outside the vestibule, likewise two at one side and two at the other: “And at the outer side,” he says, “which ascends to the entrance of the gate that goes northward, were two tables; and at the other side before the vestibule of the gate were two tables. Four tables on this side and four tables on that side: eight tables were along the sides of the gate, upon which they sacrificed.” Since, [Col. 0563A] as was said above, the temple occupied the summit of the mountain, and on every side the mountain itself gradually rose to higher ground as far as that place, this gate—unsurprisingly—had one side higher and the other lower. Thus one ascended to the gate from one side and descended to it from the other. For since this was the north gate, as Scripture itself determines, the temple undoubtedly lay on its west side; and that side rose higher than the east side. The east side is determined by the words: “And at the outer side which ascends to the entrance of the gate that goes northward were two tables.” For what follows is said of the other side: “And at the other side before the vestibule of the gate were two tables.” Thus, as is then added, there were four tables on this side and four tables on that side. For there were four [Col. 0563B] on one side, two within the vestibule and two outside it; likewise, two inside and two outside on the other side. Therefore eight tables stood along the sides of the gate, upon which they sacrificed.

What follows is sufficiently plain in itself and needs no explanation: “And four tables for the burnt offering were built of squared stones, one and a half cubits in length, one and a half cubits in width, and one cubit in height, upon which they placed the vessels with which the burnt offering and the victim were sacrificed; and their rims were one handbreadth, turned inward round about. And upon the tables was the flesh of the offering.” Thus far concerning the tables. There follows, however, something concerning certain chambers of which nothing was said in the preceding passages.

[Col. 0563C] “And outside the inner gate were chambers of the singers in the inner court, which was at the side of the gate facing north; and their fronts were toward the south way—one at the side of the east gate, facing the north way.” It is strange that it says: “in the inner court, which was at the side of the gate facing north.” For the inner court was not at the side of this gate, but rather lay before it, because it lay in the middle between the three inner gates. But when “inner court” or “outer court” is said, we ought not always understand this uniformly. The space of one hundred cubits in every direction, located in the middle, is called the inner court; and the outer court is that by which the inner court was surrounded on every side. But in the inner [Col. 0563D] court there was nothing other than one altar; all the rest—the porticoes, chambers, temple, and buildings—were in the outer court.

Yet according to another consideration, the place where the temple and those buildings stood which adjoined the temple on its three sides is called the inner court, as is read in what follows. For there were the sacred chambers in which the priests stored and ate the flesh of the offerings; and they were not permitted to carry these out into the outer court, Scripture forbidding it in the words: “This is the place where the priests shall boil the sin offering and the guilt offering, where they shall boil the sacrifice, so that they do not carry it out into the outer court and the people be sanctified” (Ezek. 46). Yet this flesh, which was forbidden to be carried into the outer court, was stored [Col. 0564A] and eaten in the aforesaid chambers, as is read concerning them: “These are the holy chambers in which the priests who draw near to the Lord in the Holy of Holies eat. There they shall place the Holy of Holies, and the offerings for sin and guilt” (Ezek. 41).

Thus for one reason the court before the temple is called the inner court, because, as has been said, it lay in the middle; but for another reason that space by which the temple was enclosed on three sides is so called, because entry into it was made through that which is properly called the inner court. Thus an inner chamber is customarily called the hall, not because it is inside the hall itself, but because it occupies a more secluded place and because access to it lies open through the hall. So certainly no place was more secluded or more remote from the entrance of the gates than that in which the temple was built. [Col. 0564B] According to this consideration, therefore, in comparison with this place even that which Scripture customarily calls the inner court may be called the outer court. Thus the place in which the temple stood is called the inner court in one respect, and the place which occupied the middle and contained the altar of burnt offering in another.

Nothing therefore prevents us from understanding the place in which the temple or the adjoining buildings stood in the words, “And opposite the inner gate were chambers of the singers in the inner court, which was at the side of the gate facing north.” In this court, adjoining the aforesaid gate on its west side, was the singers’ chamber now described; it adhered laterally to the same gate or portico. This chamber is discussed more fully in what follows, and, unless I am mistaken, is described in these words: “And he brought me into the chamber which was opposite the separate building and opposite the edifice facing north,” and the rest, of which we shall speak more fully in its place. But for now, this seems to be said concerning this chamber: its width began at this gate and extended toward the west; its length extended from north to south. Hence the statement subsequently added concerning these same chambers: “And their fronts were toward the south way.” Thus, as stated, the gate had chambers of this sort for singers on its west side. It also had others on its east side, which were certainly situated opposite both the east and north [Col. 0564D] gates. Therefore, if those opposite the east gate had their front toward the north gate, why is it added concerning them, “one at the side of the east gate, facing the north way”? He therefore says that one front of such chambers was at the side of the east gate, which front faced the north way. The wording would, however, be plainer if it had said “the fronts of certain ones,” rather than “a certain front,” or “one front of them was at the side of the east gate.” But now not only is “one” used there in place of “of certain ones,” but “their fronts” must also be supplied from the preceding words.

These chambers, which were east of the north gate, had their front toward the way, not opposite the north way, because it ran transversely before them and not toward them, just as those west of the gate faced the south way which ran toward them. [Col. 0565A] We must understand the same thing of both sides of the east gate, and likewise of one side of the south gate. But Scripture customarily, deliberately, passes over what it knows can readily be understood in itself. It follows:

“And he said to me: This is the chamber which faces the south way, belonging to the priests who keep watch over the guard of the temple. But the chamber which faces the north way shall belong to the priests who keep watch over the service of the altar.” The chamber facing the south way was nearer the temple, and therefore rightly belonged to those priests who kept watch over the temple guard; for they excelled in rank those serving the altar. But what follows is common to both groups of priests: “These are the sons of Zadok, who, from among the sons of Levi, draw near to the Lord to minister to him.”

## CHAPTER XII. On the kitchens built beneath the porticoes and on the inner court

At this point it should be observed that on the east way, on both sides around the porticoes of both the outer and inner court, a certain empty space still remains between the porticoes themselves and the chambers, as is visibly apparent from the diagrams set out above. In these places could have been those kitchens of which Scripture makes mention later, saying: “And kitchens were built beneath the porticoes round about” (Ezek. 46). But the outer north portico had only one space of the same size, adjoining it on its east side; for on its west side it had adjoining chambers. It is also clear that the south portico of the outer court had a similar space on its east side for the same purpose, while chambers adjoined it on the other side. Therefore we judge like things from like things, and accordingly leave on either side of the two porticoes of the inner court a similar space for the purpose of kitchens. After these we arrange the singers’ chambers, fifty cubits in both length and width, so that their width corresponds to their length, as we read concerning certain chambers. For the length of all the chambers of the outer court is given in one statement, when much later it says: “For the length of the chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits.” After these singers’ chambers, with a way ten cubits wide placed between them, fifteen chambers are arranged on each side on the east way, so that there may be, as is written, thirty around the pavement. There were likewise fifteen on one side only—that is, on the east side—both on the north way and on the south way. From the fronts of the inner gates to the common place, as will later be shown, there are one hundred and forty cubits. If from these we assign five cubits to the wall, and divide the remainder equally among the fifteen, we find that each chamber occupied nine cubits in width. It follows:

[Col. 0566A] “And he measured the court, one hundred cubits in length and one hundred cubits in width, square; and the altar was before the face of the temple.” From this passage it is sufficiently clear that the inner court, in respect of width, occupied all that space of one hundred cubits which lay in the middle of the five hundred cubits enclosed from north to south by that wall of five hundred cubits. But since the east porticoes had in every respect measurements like those of the other porticoes, enclosed a court of the same length, and rose by the same number of steps, it is beyond doubt that their measurement extended to the middle hundred, and that the inner court began at its beginning. But how many of those hundred cubits toward the west it occupied within itself, according to the consideration of a level plane, I do not think can yet be proved from what has been stated. For although it too had one hundred cubits in surface extent toward that direction, it is not yet apparent what, or how much, the rise of the mountain, which mounted there toward that side, took away from that middle hundred on the west side according to the level plane. For a line of one hundred cubits lying horizontally and another rising obliquely, proceeding from the same point, do not meet at the same perpendicular, nor do they enclose an equal space on the level plane; but how these matters stand will appear from what follows. [Col. 0566C] “And the altar,” he says, “was before the face of the temple.” He adds this here because the altar stood in this court which lay before the temple. Nothing concerning its measurement is said here, but it is set out carefully much further below.

In this court we make the water which came out from the temple flow down, descending at the right side of the altar. Around the lower parts of the court we divide it into four channels and lead it through the middle of the kitchens, so that it passes before the chambers, in order that there may be a place where the burnt offering can be washed, as is written: “And at each chamber was a door in the fronts of the gates, and there they washed the burnt offering.” In the final and large diagram, as may be seen there, we have set out more fully the form and pattern of all these things which we have described.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the size of the buildings adjoining the temple

[Col. 0566D]

Since, therefore, we have for the present completed what seemed necessary to say concerning the front part of this structure, we now turn our pen to describing its western part; and in their proper place we shall supply what from the foregoing is needed to complete the foregoing. Here, as above in the description of the porticoes, I should like to gather together the testimonies of Scripture from both directions and, by comparing them, establish the location, form, and arrangement of the buildings to be described; and show, with authority on the one hand and reason on the other, what ought to be understood from them.

As we taught above, the temple with its portico rose beyond the inner court on its western side; and on the other three sides the same temple had three buildings with their porticoes, though a certain court intervened, each of which occupied one hundred cubits in length. For concerning that building at the back of the temple on the west, which Scripture customarily calls “the separate [building]” because it was joined to none of the others, we read: “And he measured the length of the house, one hundred cubits; and the separate building and its walls, one hundred cubits in length.” But concerning the other buildings on the two sides, it is added: “And he measured the length of the building opposite the face of that which was separate at the back, and its side-chambers on either side, one hundred cubits.” Since a building one hundred cubits long is said to be measured on either side, it is proved that there was a building of the same length on each side. Thus we have the three buildings; let us now consider their porticoes.

That there was a portico at the north building, Scripture makes clear when it says: “Where the chambers above were lower, because the porticoes which rose from them were supported by the lower and middle stories of the building.” That this is said of the north building and its portico is plainly shown by the context of the passage, as will become evident later in the exposition of the letter. We may soundly prove that this portico, of which we have spoken beforehand, was fifty cubits [Col. 0567C] long from the fact that its enclosing wall—that is, the wall surrounding its supporting chambers—is said to have been fifty cubits long: “And the outer enclosing wall alongside the chambers, which were on the way of the outer court before the chambers, was fifty cubits in length; for the length of the chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits.” The width of this portico is expressed later in another passage: “As their length, so also their width.”

Indeed, the description of this portico and its chambers entails—and can likewise be proved more extensively from other passages—that the north building had chambers on its lower level and upper rooms on its upper level. For its portico would rise fifty cubits from the ground to no purpose unless it had behind it an upper room corresponding to it in suitable height. For what does Scripture say concerning the porticoes of this building? “Therefore,” it says, “they rose above the lower and middle stories of the building by fifty cubits from the ground.” Finally, in comparison with these chambers situated on the lower level of the building, the wall enclosing the chambers of the portico is called the outer enclosing wall because it was nearer to—indeed immediately joined to—the outer court. This portico was joined to the north portico of the inner court, whence it is written: “Where a portico was joined to the threefold portico.” But if, to the measurement which that inner-court portico had within its walls—the only measurement of which we spoke above—we add five cubits, as it were, for the thickness [Col. 0568A] of the wall, we find without doubt two hundred and fifteen cubits as far as the common place. From that place the aforesaid building with its portico extended westward one hundred and forty-five cubits, beyond which another seventy cubits remained as far as the same common place. For in that part, as will later be shown, where they were joined, they had a common wall, and therefore occupied not one hundred and fifty but only one hundred and forty-five cubits.

Between this building and the temple was a space one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide. Its measurement is determined by the statement: “Opposite the length of one hundred cubits was the north entrance, and the width was fifty cubits.” But whatever we have said concerning the configuration and measurements of the north building, we must understand in the same way of the south building, according to the same likeness; this, we think, is sufficiently clear from what has already been said above.

We now have the extent to which these buildings extended with their porticoes, but it is not yet known how much space they enclosed between them. This, however, I think will become clear when it is established how the building called “separate” was arranged between the other two. It was one hundred cubits long and eighty cubits wide. For within the walls it was ninety cubits long and seventy wide, and the wall itself was five cubits thick round about, as Scripture shows: “And the separate building, facing the way toward the sea, was seventy cubits wide. But the wall of the building was five cubits wide round about, and its length was ninety cubits.” Hence it is also added: “And he measured the length of the house, one hundred cubits; and the separate building and its walls, one hundred cubits.”

Thus it lay at the back of the temple, near the wall that divided the common place, and its length undoubtedly extended north and south; but its width extended west to east. Since only a space of seventy cubits lay beyond the aforesaid buildings situated on either side, it necessarily follows that the width of the building, which was eighty cubits [Col. 0568D], occupied a great part of the interval between those buildings. The length of the separate building, therefore, extends between the aforesaid buildings, and to it are added in each case a space of twenty cubits, because of what is read concerning their chambers: “And between the chambers, a width of twenty cubits round about the house on every side.”

It is therefore clear that between the two buildings adjoining the temple on either side there was enclosed a space of one hundred and forty cubits, according to the level plane, to be sure. But the north building, like the south, had its portico not opposite its middle but opposite its outer, or lower, part; and both began from one and the same line on the north. For where the chambers supporting this building’s portico [Col. 0569A] are described, the account immediately adds concerning their entrance: “And beneath these chambers was an entrance for those entering them from the east, from the outer court, in the width of the court’s enclosing wall which was opposite the east way, in front of the separate building.” This court, which he mentions here, was certainly north of the north building; from that building to the common place it extended its width northward. Therefore the said chambers could not have had an entrance opposite the width of this court, but rather opposite the building, unless the portico and its building began from one point on the north side.

From the north side of the same portico to the inner court were one hundred cubits, of which fifty were occupied by its width. Then, with a walkway ten cubits wide interposed, the aforesaid singers’ chamber began and extended as far as the twentieth cubit of the inner court. Hence it is clear that its length was fifty cubits. This chamber is described in what follows, when it says: “And he brought me into the chamber which was opposite the separate building and opposite the edifice facing north, opposite the length of one hundred cubits at the north entrance, and fifty cubits in width; opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court, and opposite the stone pavement where a portico was joined to the threefold portico.” I think it is plain how this chamber stood opposite the separate building, and how it lay before the intervening space one hundred cubits long and [Col. 0569C] fifty cubits wide which lay between the temple and the north building, if this chamber extended to the twentieth cubit of the inner court. It is equally plain how it stood opposite the edifice facing north, if it began at the tenth cubit beyond the portico of that building.

But we must now consider that it is said to stand opposite the pavement of the outer court; and lest we should understand anything other than the north pavement of the outer court, we are constrained by the addition in the text: “where a portico was joined to the threefold portico.” For in the eastern region we nowhere find a portico joined to a portico. But the north portico of the inner court, as is clear from the foregoing, had singers’ chambers to the east, the inner court to the south, and to the north this pavement of which we are now speaking. It is therefore clear that the portico joined to this portico adhered to it undoubtedly on the west; touching it in part, leaving the greater part of its own extent, and stretching northward, it bounded this pavement on the west. Therefore, in order that the aforesaid chamber may have some part of itself opposite this pavement, it must be joined to the threefold portico—indeed, rather, it must have a common wall with it at the very point where they join. If the portico of the north building began beyond that wall and had a wall behind its wall, certainly the chamber stood opposite the said pavement [Col. 0570A] to the extent of the thickness of its wall.

That the walkway which we have mentioned lay before this chamber is subsequently shown by Scripture when it adds: “And before the chambers was a walkway ten cubits wide.” Nor should we be troubled that the same structure is called sometimes “chambers” and sometimes “chamber,” just as the same portico is called sometimes “vestibules” and sometimes “vestibule.” For the one designation is referred to its divisions, the other to the whole.

It should indeed be noted that at the point where the northern building and its portico formed an angle before the aforesaid chamber and this place of walkway, there was a space thirty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, concerning which what seems appropriate will be said in its place [Col. 0570B]. For, as is clear from the foregoing, since there were only fifty cubits from the eastern side of that chamber to the northern building, the chamber itself could not have been more than thirty cubits wide, since twenty cubits had necessarily to remain, in order to establish the truth of Scripture’s statement concerning these chambers which lay around the temple: “And between the chambers, a width of twenty cubits around the house on every side.”

It is also clear that from the same eastern side of the same chamber to the boundary of the consecrated five hundred cubits there were two hundred and twenty cubits. Of these, thirty, as has been said, were occupied by the width of the aforesaid chamber. Then the space, or court, which stretched between it and the separate building along the length of the temple, occupied one hundred cubits according to the aforesaid authority of Scripture [Col. 0570C]. The width of the separate building was eighty cubits, leaving a width of ten cubits. Of these, five, as will later be shown, were occupied by the thickness of the wall; for the remaining five were occupied by a certain way lying between that wall and the building. But if these figures are brought together, they undoubtedly amount to two hundred and twenty.

It is now easy to see how far the temple extended: with its vestibule, as will be shown later, it was one hundred cubits long. But because the temple vestibule undoubtedly adjoined the inner court, both it and the aforesaid chamber began from the same line [Col. 0570D]. Yet because the chamber, as has been said, together with the court placed before it, extended one hundred and thirty cubits as far as the separate building, whereas the temple with its vestibule occupied only one hundred cubits, it is clear that there was an interval of thirty cubits between the temple and the separate building.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the position or arrangement of the remaining buildings situated on the western side

But, that we may pass on to the remaining matters still to be described, beyond the portico of the now often-mentioned northern building, on the north side there were ten chambers [Col. 0571A], arranged opposite that portico toward the north, as far as the outer wall, alongside the pavement; their length, corresponding to the length of the portico, was fifty cubits. These are the chambers of the outer court from which Scripture draws its comparison when it describes the length of that portico, or of the chambers beneath it, saying: “And the outer enclosure, according to the chambers which were in the way of the outer court before the chambers—its length fifty cubits, because the length of the chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits.”

“According to the chambers,” it says, “which were before the chambers.” Before which chambers, I ask, except those of which it was then speaking, and had already said much—those which were beneath the porticoes and, as was there said, supported the porticoes of the northern building itself? They are therefore described as being before the aforesaid portico, and these same chambers are called chambers of the outer court, so that their location may be explicitly determined. Yet between these chambers and the adjoining portico there was an intervening way, I think five cubits wide, where there was an entrance to the chambers before the separate building. For after describing the chambers that supported the porticoes, Scripture immediately adds concerning this entrance: “And beneath these chambers was an entrance from the east for those entering them from the outer court, in the width of the enclosure of the court which was opposite the eastern way, in front of the separate building” [Col. 0571B].

This is indeed the entrance of which we have already spoken above. From this way to the wall of the outer court there were ninety cubits. If these are divided among ten chambers, each is found to be nine cubits wide [Col. 0571C]. What has been said about the northern side must in every respect be understood, by the same analogy, of the southern side. Thus there were ten chambers on one side and ten on the other. These are, we believe, the twenty chambers of which we read later. Behold, in these chambers we find the same measurement as in those above, which we assigned a width of nine cubits, so that all are of one width, as they are also of one length.

It remains now to speak of that portico, or vestibule, of the separate building which adjoined it on the north, between the northern building and the outer wall [Col. 0571D]. Scripture determines what dimensions this vestibule had: “There was a way before the separate vestibule.” This vestibule, or portico, was therefore fifty cubits both in length and breadth; it had chambers beneath it; it rose above these from the lower and middle structures; and on its upper side, that is, on the east, it had a walkway, or way, ten cubits wide.

Scripture seems to set out all this in few words where we read: “And there were chambers before the building, and a way before them, according to the likeness of the chambers which were in the northern way.” If these chambers and the way set before them resembled in every respect those in the northern way [Col. 0572A], then these, like those, adjoined the building connected with them beneath the portico, and in the same manner; and whatever we read concerning the position, character, and size of those must, according to the proposed rule of resemblance, be applied to these.

And note that although there were other chambers along the northern way, the context of the passage compels us to understand those of which it had treated immediately before, not those concerning which it had said nothing. It calls the way which led from the north, from gate through gate toward the inner parts, the northern way, as it pleased; this way passed in front of the aforesaid chambers. But above we showed that ten cubits remained beyond the separate building [Col. 0572B], which we assigned above partly to the wall and partly to the intervening way. Therefore its portico will likewise have ten cubits beyond it on the west, if it was situated opposite the outer parts of the house in the likeness of the northern building.

And because there were seventy cubits to the west beyond the northern building, there will certainly be ten cubits between it and the separate vestibule, so that, in likeness to the upper portico, this portico too may occupy a space of fifty cubits and have, on its upper or inner side, a walkway ten cubits wide. But on its lower or outer side we must understand there to be a way five cubits wide, according to the arrangement above, so that this vestibule may have the entrance to its chambers beneath it—that is, on its lower and outer side [Col. 0572C]—in likeness to the aforesaid portico.

And, so that in this respect also the same resemblance may occur on both sides, observe where the separate building forms an angle with this its vestibule; and you will find here, just as there, a space thirty cubits long and twenty cubits wide. This is the place of which much later we read: “And there was there a place sloping toward the west; and he said to me: This is the place where the priests shall boil the offering for trespass and for sin, where they shall boil the sacrifice, so that they do not bring it out into the outer court and the people be sanctified.”

Scripture, diligently examined, does not allow it to remain hidden that this cooking-place was in that court which had the chambers of the sanctuary. For observe what is prefaced where this place is described: “And he brought me through the entrance which was at the side of the gate into the sanctuary chambers for the priests which faced north.” And it is added: “And there was there a place sloping toward the west” [Col. 0572D]. Of these chambers we read elsewhere: “The chambers of the north and the chambers of the south which are before the separate building—these are the holy chambers in which the priests who draw near to the Lord in the Holy of Holies put on their vestments. There they shall place the Holy of Holies, and the offering for sin and for trespass.” Certainly, if we carefully examine these or other passages of Scripture, we shall be able to find no other place for the aforesaid kitchen than the one we designated before.

[Col. 0573A] It should indeed be noted that this place is said to slope toward the west. From these words it is manifestly inferred that the mountain behind the temple sloped downward, where it bore the separate building. We have already said that the designated place was thirty cubits long and twenty cubits wide. One half of it—thirty cubits long and ten cubits wide—adjoining the separate building, contained the kitchens; the remaining half, namely the ten cubits of width, was occupied by the walkway, so that this way passed in front of the kitchens and at that point turned into the court of the sanctuary.

By the same analogy in every respect, we believe that the space above designated, of the same dimensions, also contained kitchens, and that the ten-cubit walkway passed before them, turned into the court of the sanctuary, and faced toward the temple [Col. 0573B].

But everything that we have said about the northern side must be understood, in the location and arrangement of the buildings, of the southern side as well, according to the same suitability of resemblance, as we read concerning it: “And all their entrances, and their forms, and their doors were according to the doors of the chambers which were in the way facing south. A door at the head of the way—the way which was before the separate vestibule—for those entering by the eastern way.”

Thus the southern side had a similar vestibule before the separate building, a similar building, a similar portico, and a similar chamber by the inner court [Col. 0573C]. One end of the aforesaid chamber therefore lay opposite the last twenty cubits of the inner court on one side, as was said above; in the same way another lay opposite the last twenty cubits of the inner court on the other side; and between those two was an interval of sixty cubits. In this interval stood the vestibule of the temple, adjoining the inner court on the east and, as has been said, having the temple adjoining it on the west.

## CHAPTER XV. How, or from what, the steepness of the mountain is inferred

[Col. 0573D] But since we have completed what seemed for the present necessary to say about the situation of the buildings, the subject requires us now to discuss, at least in part, those matters which we promised to add for the completion of the foregoing, and then to return to exposition of the text.

Let us first consider how many cubits the inner court has from east to west according to the measurement of the level plane. Its surface measurement in every direction was, beyond all doubt, one hundred cubits, as stated: “And he measured the court: one hundred cubits in length and one hundred cubits in breadth, square.” But, as has been shown above, from north toward south this court also contained one hundred cubits when measured along the level. Two porticoes, with the intervening court, occupied two hundred cubits on this side and two hundred on that [Col. 0574A], and thus there were five hundred cubits from one extremity to the other.

Because of the same similarity and dimensions of the porticoes, we observe that the eastern porticoes, with their intervening court, likewise occupied two hundred cubits according to the measurement of the level plane and extended to the middle hundred. Therefore all the inner porticoes, according to one and the same pattern, adjoined that middle hundred and faced its middle; and because they contained a measurement of sixty cubits within their walls, twenty cubits of that middle hundred remained on either side of this measurement.

But above we showed that the chambers of the sanctuary immediately adjoined the two porticoes of the inner court—the northern and southern—and bounded the western side of the inner court. Hence it is clear that the inner court from east to west occupied no more than eighty cubits according to the measurement of the level plane [Col. 0574B]. But if the eastern way rises uniformly from the outer gate to the site of the temple, then the pavement that lay between the two porticoes of one hundred cubits occupies no more than eighty cubits according to the measurement of the level plane, although its surface undoubtedly measured one hundred.

From this, then, we are given to understand that the walls of the porticoes, like those of the three aforementioned buildings, were five cubits thick. For it is clear that each had only fifty cubits within its walls [Col. 0574C]. This was why we judged above that five cubits should be assigned to the wall, and the other five to the way, out of the ten cubits which we found remaining beyond the separate building.

At this point we wish to remark that everywhere we must hold as certain and almost as a rule that whether a building stands on level ground or on a slope, this adds nothing to or takes nothing from its measurement. For whatever Scripture teaches concerning the dimensions of buildings must also be understood according to measurement along the level. Therefore, since the northern and southern porticoes were in every respect like the eastern porticoes in measurement and quality, we must judge the intervening pavements to be similar and to have occupied only eighty cubits according to the measurement of the level plane.

Yet there was this difference between these pavements and the eastern pavement: the latter had, as stated, eighty cubits in one dimension, but possessed one hundred cubits in the other even according to the measurement of the level plane. These, however, measured eighty cubits in one dimension and eighty-five in the other, according to the measurement of the level plane. For these two pavements seem to begin on the east from one and the same line as the inner court; nevertheless, they seem to extend five cubits beyond its boundary on the west, as is most evident from the foregoing [Col. 0575A]. Yet in that direction they too may have one hundred cubits at the surface, in likeness to the inner court.

Thus the northern and southern pavements are raised on two sides, while the eastern pavement and the inner court are raised on only one side. But if one asks by how much the inner court was raised on one side, anyone skilled in geometry can discover this easily and without difficulty. Beyond doubt, a court measuring eighty cubits at its base and one hundred cubits at its surface was sixty cubits higher at its elevated side. We could set forth the most certain rules for this matter, but we fear to burden less learned readers. Meanwhile we shall give some demonstration by which anyone, however unlearned, may test our assertion [Col. 0575B].

[Col. 0575C] Draw a line of any length, divided into five equal sections and marked at the individual sections with individual letters. Let the horizontal line be A B C D E F. Above it, at the fourth section—that is, above E—raise another line, so that it slopes neither way but forms right angles on both sides, equal to each other, and contains three measures, each equal to one of the aforesaid sections. Let the line raised above E be E G H K. Draw also a third line rising obliquely from A to K.

When this has been done, take a pair of compasses. If you find the first and third lines, that is, A F and A K, equal, you will have, by your own experiment, proof of our assertion [Col. 0575D]. Let each section be twenty cubits. Then A F—that is, the first line—will be one hundred cubits, and A K, equal to it—that is, the third line—will likewise be one hundred cubits. But the upright line, E K, will have sixty cubits. Therefore, as has been said, a court measuring eighty cubits at its base and one hundred cubits at its surface was undoubtedly sixty cubits higher at its raised side. You have a clear representation of this fact in the triangle A K E.

If, however far you extend the base of this triangle—that is, the horizontal line—and its hypotenuse—that is, the sloping line—and apply to them a cathetus—that is, a line raised perpendicularly—you make triangles of whatever size, you will see that its three lines always correspond in the same ratio. For the hypotenuse will always be in the ratio of six to four to the base, and the base in the ratio of six to three to the cathetus [Col. 0576A].

Therefore, from the outer side of the eastern gate to the front of the temple vestibule, the height of the mountain rose by two hundred and ten cubits, if the steepness of that mountain rose uniformly in that direction. Since each portico measured sixty cubits from its outer side to its inner side, the ground on the inner side was forty-five cubits higher according to the aforesaid rate of ascent. We believe that the seven or eight ascending steps of which we read above occupied only the wall’s thickness, which was five cubits, or seven and a half feet, so that there was one step for each foot, and the eighth step might either be counted with the other seven or not counted.

Hence we read concerning the outer southern portico: “It was ascended by seven steps”; and again concerning the inner southern portico: “There were eight steps by which one ascended through it” [Col. 0576B]. Were there steps outside it by which one ascended to it and steps inside it by which one ascended through it, so that the fifty cubits of width within the walls had only eight steps? Who could think so? Rather, one ascended both to it and through it by those very steps which occupied the wall’s thickness. One ascended through it upon them because the wall belonged to it; and one ascended to it upon them because by them access was given to its inner parts.

We can now infer from the foregoing how great was the height of one portico. The inner gate, as we read, was thirteen cubits high. If we add the two cubits which, as stated above, the gate had in front up to the upper chamber, the total rises to fifteen. From the roof of the chamber—that is, from the floor of the upper chamber—to the roof of the gate there were, as we read, twenty-five cubits [Col. 0576C]. Add these twenty-five to the preceding measurement, and we have forty. To all these we add five cubits above the roof of the gate itself, as though for making battlements, and thus we make up a height of forty-five cubits on the inner side.

But, as stated above, it was forty-five cubits lower on the outer side; and accordingly its total height from the outer side appears to rise to ninety cubits. It appears, however, to have two upper chambers on the outer side but one on the inner side; and it is said to have a third and innermost chamber:

> “And he measured the gate from the roof of the chamber to its roof.”

[Col. 0577] [Col. 0579]

## CHAPTER XVI. Description of the temple itself and of its vestibule

“And he brought me into the vestibule of the temple, and measured the vestibule: five cubits on this side and five cubits on that side.” By “on this side and on that side” we must understand not the temple gate but the vestibule gate. The width of the gate, as is read later, was ten cubits. Hence it is clear that the entire length of the vestibule, as is determined later, was twenty cubits [Col. 0580]. It follows:

> “And the width of the gate: three cubits on this side and three cubits on that side.”

If we consider ordinary speech, we are accustomed to use the name “gate” in a threefold sense. By “gate” we sometimes mean the door itself which is opened and shut; sometimes the opening or passage through which one goes; sometimes the surround by which the opening itself is enclosed—that portion of the wall which embraces the doorway and is seen to differ from the rest of the wall in material or form, for the sake of ornament, and to project above it [Col. 0581A]. For we understand differently when we hear or read: “He carried off the gates of the city,” “He stood in the gate of the city,” or “He adorned the gates of the city with variegated marble and various carvings.” Unless this ambiguity is carefully distinguished, the sense in this passage too is confused.

But it is clear from what follows that the width of the gate was ten cubits and that the sides of the gate—that is, each of the two leaves—were five cubits wide. Therefore what is read here, “he measured the width of the gate: three cubits on this side and three cubits on that side,” must be understood in the third sense. He measured the width of the gate—that is, the wall itself, ornamented with various carvings—to that extent [Col. 0581B]. Scripture itself seems to determine this meaning by saying “on this side and on that side.”

“The length of the vestibule was twenty cubits, and its breadth eleven cubits.” The length of the vestibule extended along the width of the temple, and therefore the same measurement is found for both. “And it was ascended by eight steps,” that is, to the gate; “and there were pillars at the fronts, one on this side and one on that side.” We believe that these pillars stood on either side opposite the aforesaid three cubits of the gate, where he measured “the width: three cubits on this side and three cubits on that side.”

“And he brought me into the temple, and measured the fronts: six cubits in breadth on this side and six cubits in height on that side, the breadth of the tabernacle” (Ezek. 41) [Col. 0581C]. Let those who dispute about the construction of the tabernacle consider how they understand this passage regarding the tabernacle’s width. For I do not think it belongs to the present undertaking to determine that here.

But what is said—that he measured the fronts six cubits wide on this side and six cubits high on that side—we may understand as follows. First he measured how much width there was at the side of the gate up to the wooden wall which supported the side-structures described later, on the inner side of the gate. Secondly, he measures not how much width existed on the other side, for he judges that from the measurement already taken, but what height there was from the upper part of the gate to the first upper chamber. But if the spread of the doors was ten cubits and the width of the temple within the walls was only twenty cubits, it follows that those recesses on either side, against which the doors struck when the gate was shut, must be understood as one cubit wide; and the opening between those recesses was eight cubits wide [Col. 0581D]. Otherwise we cannot find six cubits on either side.

It follows: “And the width of the gate was ten cubits, and the sides of the gate five cubits on this side and five cubits on that side.” Here is what we said above concerning the width of the gate, or doors. After this, the length and breadth of the temple itself are determined: “And he measured the length: forty cubits; and the breadth: twenty cubits.” Having described the outer house, he passes to the inner house and describes in these words what is called the Holy of Holies: “And entering within, he measured at the front two cubits, and the gate six cubits” [Col. 0582A]. Just as in the preceding description he first measured the width of the gate, three cubits on this side and three on that, so here first of all he measured two cubits at the front: namely, that portion of the wall which appeared to belong to the gate’s ornament.

It should be noted, however, that the surround of such ornament on both this and the upper gate appears to enclose them on three sides: above and on either side. But for the upper gate the measurement is taken on both sides, and what must be thought concerning the part above the gate is silently suggested. Here, however, the measurer appears to take the measurement above the gate and, by way of suggestion, to show what is to be understood on either side. This seems to be the reason why there he is said to measure “on this side and on that side,” whereas here, “at the front” [Col. 0582B]. It follows:

> “And the gate: six cubits; and the width of the gate: seven cubits.”

If the recesses on either side of the opening, against which the doors struck, are understood to be not one cubit, as above, but half a cubit, what is said will be clear. Therefore, when it says “the gate: six cubits,” it means the opening itself between the recesses. But when it adds, “and the width of the gate: seven cubits,” this must be referred to the width of the doors. For if the opening between these recesses was six cubits and it had a half-cubit recess on each side, it is evident that the joined doors occupied seven cubits in width [Col. 0582C].

Above it said how much width was at the side of the gate, but did not explicitly state how wide the opening was, though it left this to be understood. Here, conversely, it determines the measurement of the opening and leaves to be understood how much width was on either side. For if the opening itself extends only six cubits, beyond doubt seven cubits of width are found on each side. But above it showed that the same width existed above the gate and at its side. Yet it says nothing at all about how it was different in this place. What else, then, does it seem to suggest by silence, except that we should judge similar things similarly? We are therefore given to understand that there were seven cubits of width above this gate, just as on either side [Col. 0582D].

It should indeed be noted how it states some things openly and suggests others by silence; how it alternates this very manner of expression and displays, so to speak, its mastery of art. For what it expressly declares at first, when it comes later to a similar matter it tacitly suggests; and conversely, what it had suggested above by silence, it expressly determines later. This is what we admire in carved work, where interlaced knots are woven: what is laid over in one joining of the interlacements, so as to be visible, is placed beneath in the next, so as to disappear. It follows:

> “And he measured the length: twenty cubits, and the breadth: twenty cubits, before the face of the temple.”

[Col. 0583A] That the length and breadth of the inner house are described in these words is shown by the following determination, when it says: “And he said to me: This is the Holy of Holies.”

It should be noted that this measurement of length and breadth, both of the outer and of the inner house, is equal to the measurement which we read concerning Solomon’s temple, but double that which we find concerning the tabernacle. Yet since Scripture here says absolutely nothing about the height, there may be doubt concerning the outer house: to which it ought to correspond, whether to Solomon’s temple according to equality, or to the tabernacle of the covenant according to the stated proportion. For it will have twenty cubits if it is double the measure of the tabernacle, but thirty cubits if it is equal to the measure of the aforesaid temple [Col. 0583B].

But if we say it was thirty cubits high up to the first upper chamber, we must concede that a gate ten cubits wide was excessively tall and very disproportionate to its width—that is, it would be twenty-four cubits high. For from what has been said we have only six cubits of height above the gate. But if it is said that the height to the first upper chamber was twenty cubits, then the gate of both the outer and the inner house will consequently have an appropriate height proportionate to its width: the outer one fourteen cubits, the inner one thirteen. See how, from the six cubits of height above the gate which he had taken above, the height both of the two gates and of the upper chamber is inferred, though he had not stated it expressly.

He determines how thick the temple wall was when he adds: “And he measured the wall of the house: six cubits” [Col. 0583C]. It follows: “And the width of the side-structure: four cubits, all around the house.” By these side-structures which he now describes I understand nothing other than certain walkways, within and without, arranged against the wall on the two sides of the temple; they extended from the lower parts to the upper, one above another, immediately joined to each other. Hence follows this statement:

> “And side-structures beside side-structure, thirty-three twice over.”

Perhaps they are called “side-structures” because they were only along the sides of the temple, not at its fronts. But because there were only twenty cubits of height beneath the first upper chamber of the temple, it could contain no more than three side-structures. For, as is read later, from the foundation of one to the foundation of another there was only a space of six cubits. Thus there were three inside from the bottom to the upper chamber, and thirty outside from the bottom to the top. The inner parts of the temple, however, did not have side-structures of this sort in their upper portions, as what follows makes clear. Therefore it is rightly said, “thirty-three twice over,” because there were thirty-three on one side and thirty-three on the other [Col. 0583D].

He further adds to the description of these side-structures: “And there were projections which entered through the wall of the house into the side-structures all around, that they might be supported and not touch the wall of the temple.” [Col. 0584A] The beams therefore projected from the walls and supported the side-structures; but for that reason the floors built upon them did not extend entirely to the wall, namely so that they might admit sight, and the gaze of observers might range freely from the lowest to the highest levels and, taking the whole in at one view, might be able to judge the whole. It follows:

> “And there was a broad passage rising upward in a circuit by a spiral, and it led around to the upper chamber of the temple.”

For this reason the temple was broader in its upper parts, and thus one ascended from the lower parts to the upper by the middle. We see such a way, ascending by steps and bending in a circle, every day in the stairways of towers and similar lofty buildings. What it says, “For this reason the temple was broader in the upper parts,” clearly determines that the described side-structures did not extend all the way to the tops of the upper chambers, or were altogether absent in the upper parts of the temple; and therefore the temple’s breadth was greater there, where it had no such obstructions between the walls [Col. 0584B].

And the statement, “and thus one ascended from the lower parts to the upper by the middle,” seems to show that this temple had two upper chambers and was itself divided into three stories. By “the middle” we understand the first upper chamber, because that first upper chamber was the middle of the three stories. Above he had described the width of the side-structures when he said: “And the width of the side-structure: four cubits all around the house.” Now he describes their height in adding here: “And I saw in the house the height: the foundations of the side-structures were a measure of a reed, six cubits in extent” [Col. 0584C].

He does not say “six cubits and a handbreadth,” although he had previously specified the measure of the reed. From this passage too we may note what we have already said above concerning the measure of the reed. “And I saw,” he says. But where did he see them? “In the house.” Therefore, just as he saw the foundations of the side-structures in height all around, they were in the house, and according to the height of the house they were founded one above another. It follows:

And the width along the outer wall of the side-chamber: five cubits. It seems to me that the same place is denoted by these words as is later called the place of prayer. It was therefore five cubits wide, as though a kind of annex [Col. 0584D] had been made beside the wall of the first and lowest side-chamber, so that those who either could not or dared not enter the temple might gather there for prayer. He therefore measured the width of five cubits for the first side-chamber, from end to end, along its entire adjoining outer wall. It follows: “And the inner house was among the side-chambers.” This is said lest anyone suppose that side-chambers were lacking around the inner house; and between the store-chambers there was a width of twenty cubits all around the house on every side. Nothing has yet been said of these store-chambers; but, after inserting certain remarks about the place of prayer, he immediately adds their description. “And the door,” he says, “of the side-chamber opened toward the place of prayer: one door toward the northern way and one door toward the southern way; and the width of the place of prayer [Col. 0585A] was five cubits all around.” Behold, he returns to the place of prayer in order to add something. For above he had called it neither the place itself nor the place of prayer, nor had he said that it went around—that is, that it encircled the temple on three sides.

Let us now gather together what we have heard about the temple’s measurements, and first consider its width. In the first place, the temple itself, within its walls—indeed, within its side-chambers—occupied twenty cubits in width. The inner side-chambers on either side were four cubits wide, and the walls were six cubits wide. Their total comes to forty. The outer side-chambers likewise had four cubits of width on each side, while the place of prayer had five cubits on both sides. If you collect all these together, you undoubtedly find fifty-eight. There therefore remained [Col. 0586A] on either side a passage one cubit wide between the temple and the store-chambers, corresponding to the twenty cubits of the inner court which, as we read above, lay opposite it. This passage may have been under the projection of the roof which covered the place of prayer; and thus the façade of the temple extended to sixty cubits.

The temple’s length is read to have been one hundred cubits, as is stated in what follows and gathered from what precedes. For the temple itself had forty cubits of length within its walls, while the Holy of Holies had twenty; the temple vestibule, moreover, had eleven cubits of width. The four walls occupied twenty-four cubits, and the place of prayer five cubits. If you combine all these, you will make up a total of one hundred.

[Col. 0585]

## CHAPTER XVII. Description of the buildings adjoining the temple

[Col. 0587A]

Now it seems necessary to speak of those store-chambers, concerning which it is said:

“And between the store-chambers, a width of twenty cubits around the house on every side” (Ezek. XLI).

Far above we explained these store-chambers lying around the temple, and how they were twenty cubits apart from one another. But because the separate building, as was shown above, extended for one hundred cubits between the northern and southern building, while a space of twenty cubits still intervened on either side, it is clear that there were one hundred and forty [Col. 0587B] cubits on the level ground between the northern and southern building. Hence it follows that between the temple and each of the two buildings there were forty cubits on either side; for the remaining sixty were shown to be occupied by the temple’s width.

But how could that space of forty cubits contain the court said above to have been fifty cubits wide? Plainly, what the place did not have on level ground was added by the rising slope of the mountain. If, then, we understand that court as forty cubits on the level ground and fifty upon the surface, we shall see that the slope of the mountain in this place corresponds in the same proportion to that in the courts mentioned above. For one hundred bears the same proportion to eighty as fifty [Col. 0587C] does to forty.

After the description of the temple, the description of the separate building is added: “And the building which was separate, facing the way that looked toward the sea, was seventy cubits wide. And the wall of the building was five cubits wide all around, and its length was ninety cubits.” All this, I think, is sufficiently clear from what has already been said and therefore needs no further explanation.

By “sea” here he means what much later he calls the great sea, situated to the west; for there was another sea to the east, which he calls the eastern one.

After saying that this building faced the sea, he immediately adds its width, thereby indicating by that very fact according to which dimension it faced the sea [Col. 0587D].

It should further be noted that, because the temple, the separate building, the adjoining court, and both the northern and southern buildings were of one length, he records the length of them all in a single continuous statement:

“And he measured,” he says, “the length of the house”—that is, of the temple—“one hundred cubits; and the separate building and its walls were one hundred cubits long.

“The width before the face of the house, and of that which was separate toward the east, was one hundred cubits.

“And he measured the length of the building opposite the face of that which was separate at its rear, and the *ethecae* on both sides, one hundred cubits.”

[Col. 0588A] It should certainly be noted that the width of one hundred cubits which he measures before the face of the house—that is, of the temple—may be called both width and length, but in different respects. For if you consider the whole court in which the temple was situated between the northern and southern buildings, it will be one hundred and forty cubits long from south to north, and one hundred cubits wide toward the east, as he says here. But if you consider not the whole, but any one section on any side of the temple, it will, as is read below, be one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide.

In the following statement he determines the placement of the buildings. For the building described above was separate at the rear of the temple; and opposite its front, on both sides of the temple, it had a certain building.

“And he measured,” he says, “the length of the building opposite the face of that which was separate at the rear, and the *ethecae* on both sides, one hundred cubits.”

You see clearly that there was a building on both sides, that each had *ethecae*, and that, by measuring the *ethecae*, he also obtained the dimensions of the buildings.

By these *ethecae* we understand structures in front of the upper rooms, which, as Jerome testifies in these words, are called at Rome *solaria*: projections from the walls of upper chambers. Some Greeks call them *exedrae* (“recesses” or “halls”).

What follows appears to be a recapitulation with an addition:

[Col. 0588C] “And the inner temple, and the vestibules of the court, the thresholds and the slanting windows, and the *ethecae* around the three sides opposite each threshold, and the wood panelling around about.”

It is clear why he calls the temple “inner”: it occupied the middle position among the buildings mentioned above. He calls them the vestibules of the court because they adjoined the court.

Above he had indicated *ethecae* on both sides; here, however, he says that they stood on three sides. From this it follows that the separate building also had *ethecae*. From this fact we establish that the three buildings were alike both in quality and in quantity. The *ethecae*, as is said, stood opposite the threshold of each one, because they projected externally from the upper rooms themselves. [Col. 0588D] Lest they be thought higher or lower than the upper rooms themselves, the positions of the before-balconies are defined by the thresholds of the *solaria*.

By “wood panelling around about” he means the boarding with which the lower parts of the *ethecae* were covered; these, as stated, appeared to gird the three sides of the temple:

“And the ground,” he says, “was up to the windows.”

From this one may infer how great the slope of the mountain was, since the walls of the buildings on the temple side had earth reaching up to the windows.

When he says “cherubim and palms as far as the inner house,” he seems to determine that this was the Holy of Holies, while intending to say that the inner sanctuary did not have carvings of this kind. They were therefore, as is said, [Col. 0589A] as far as the inner house—that is, in the outer temple—and “outside,” namely in the vestibule, which by the same reasoning may be called outside as the inner house is called inside. The cherubim and palms, I say, were crafted to measure upon every wall around the temple and the vestibule, not only inside but also outside.

It follows:

“And between cherub and cherub was a palm; and each cherub had two faces:

“the face of a man beside the palm on this side, and the face of a lion beside the palm on the other side, depicted throughout the entire house all around.

“From the ground up to the upper part of the gateway, cherubim and [Col. 0589B] palms were carved upon the temple wall.

“The threshold was square; and the appearance of the sanctuary faced the appearance of the wooden altar.”

All these things, I think, are plain in themselves and need no explanation from us.

The final statement, however, defines the location of the inner altar, because it stood in the middle of the temple opposite the sanctuary gate. This was the altar of incense. For the altar which he touched upon briefly above, and discusses more fully below, was the altar of burnt offering.

In the following words he seems to set forth not only the dimensions but also the construction [Col. 0589C] of the work.

He says, therefore:

“Its height was three cubits, and its length two cubits.”

These refer to quantity; what follows refers to quality:

“Its corners, its length, and its walls were of wood.”

Perhaps he is silent about its width because its length and width were the same, and because “length” might be said in either direction, just as “width” might be said in either direction. It seems to have had four pieces of timber erected upright at its four corners according to its height. Four others were joined to them above and below, [Col. 0589D] running lengthwise and crosswise; boards were fastened to these and joined into a single framework. He calls the upright timbers “corners,” because they occupied the corners. He calls the timbers that measured the altar’s length its “length.”

By “walls,” however, he means the joining of the boards by which their gaps were covered.

It follows:

“And he said to me: ‘This is the table before the Lord.’”

After this is added a description of the doors both of the temple and of the sanctuary:

[Col. 0590A] “And there were two doors in the temple and in the sanctuary.

“And on the two doors, on either side, there were two small leaves which folded back upon one another. For there were two leaves on each side of the doors.”

I think this passage clearly shows that the same name is used in different senses. Otherwise, how can the statement stand: “There were two doors on each side of the doors”? What he first calls “doors,” then, must refer to the wooden construction; what he afterward calls “doors” must refer to the opening which stood open in the wall. The wall was six cubits thick, and that thickness itself contained two doors, both in the temple and in the sanctuary: one was set in the wall on the inner side and the other on the [Col. 0590B] outer side. Each of these two doors had one leaf hanging on the right and another on the left, just as in every respect was the case in Solomon’s temple.

This is what is said there: “And two doors of fir wood, each door divided into two folding leaves” (III Kings VI.34). This is what he had said above: “Side-panels of five cubits.” What there he calls *latera* (“sides” or panels), here he calls *ostiola* (“small door-leaves”). These panels were joined by iron hinges, and when the doors were opened they folded back upon one another. As is said here, and was said there, they opened by holding to one another. A door was divided into two and folded back so that, when opened, it would not exceed the width of the wall.

[Col. 0590C] “And cherubim and carvings of palms were engraved upon the doors of the temple, as they were also represented upon the walls.”

All this is sufficiently clear in itself.

The following is fittingly added:

“Therefore there were thicker timbers on the outer front of the vestibule, above which were slanting windows.”

For thicker timbers were required where, for the sake of ornament, more distinguished and outstanding carvings had to be made. These words also indicate that the walls were covered with wood, as in Solomon’s temple.

It follows:

“And a representation of palms, on this side and on that, upon the side-posts [Col. 0590D] of the vestibule, according to the sides of the house and the width of the walls.”

These things are clear:

“And he led me out into the outer court by the way leading north, and brought me into the store-chamber which was opposite the separate building.”

It is clear that he dealt last with the front of the temple vestibule. From that point he now seems to pass through the northern gate of the inner court into the store-chamber described. And rightly so. For this store-chamber faced the aforesaid ten-cubit-wide walkway, which began where the portico was joined to the portico of the northern building, [Col. 0591A] and where, as is gathered from this passage, an entrance into that store-chamber opened in the side of the threefold portico:

“And he brought me,” he says, “into the store-chamber which was opposite the separate building and opposite the structure facing north.

“Along the front, the northern doorway was one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide.

“Opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court and opposite the stone-paved floor of the outer court, where portico was joined to threefold portico.

“And before the store-chambers was a walkway ten cubits wide, facing inward, with a way one cubit wide; and their doors were toward the north.”

[Col. 0591B] We have explained all these matters above with such care that we do not know whether anything should be added to what has already been said, except perhaps for expounding the wording. By “the northern door” he means that temple door of which he had said above: “The door of the side-chamber toward the place of prayer: one door toward the north.” It should certainly be noted that what he first set forth, as it were, in the singular, he afterward denotes in the plural: “And he brought me into the store-chamber”; and later, “Before the store-chambers was a walkway ten cubits wide, facing inward, with a way one cubit wide.” As for the following words, “and their doors were toward the north”: if the reading is *earum* (“their,” feminine), it must refer to the porticoes; but if *eorum* (“their,” masculine/neuter), to the store-chambers. Either sense may be true.

[Col. 0591C] It follows:

“Where the store-chambers in the upper levels were lower,

because the porticoes which projected from the lower and middle parts of the building were supported by them.”

After the description of the walkway, “where the store-chambers were” is fittingly added; for they stood beside the walkway and adjoined it on the north.

This too should be noted: he says “porticoes” in the plural where previously he had said “portico” in the singular. Indeed, as these words readily show, both the building and its portico were divided into three storeys. For if the building had lower and middle levels, it necessarily had upper ones as well. “Middle” is not said except in relation to two extremes. Thus the building, like [Col. 0591D] its portico, had store-chambers at the bottom, one upper room in the middle, and another upper room at the top. The portico also had store-chambers in its lower parts opposite the store-chambers of the building, which supported the porticoes. For the porticoes stood above these: one opposite the first upper room, and another opposite the second upper room; they were supported by the store-chambers. The lower portico projected from the lower parts of the building because it stood above the store-chambers corresponding to the building’s lower levels. The upper portico projected from the middle parts of the building because it stood above the first portico, which corresponded to the building’s middle level.

Let us now consider what it means that the store-chambers are said to be lower in the upper levels. Certainly, if we calculate the steepness of the mountain around this place according to the earlier method, we shall find the ground on one side of the building, on the temple side, sixty cubits higher than on the other side. But who does not know that practical necessity requires the floors of buildings to be laid upon a level surface? Therefore, lest we suppose that the ground had been excavated sixty cubits on one side, Scripture says that the store-chambers were lower at the upper levels, so that we may understand one store-chamber to have been divided into several, each having floors level in themselves but some higher than others, raised one above another, like steps, according to the ascent of the mountain. Thus, where the floors were higher, the store-chambers were lower—that is, they had less height. We understand the same concerning the store-chambers beneath the porticoes. [Col. 0592B] We understand the same of that division of the six porticoes which we divided into seven sections according to their width and the mountain’s rise. We think the same of the store-chambers that lay around the floors.

These divisions were therefore necessarily long but narrow. For the store-chambers are read to have been fifty cubits long, though they seem not to have had more than nine cubits of width. Yet these divisions of the store-chambers appear to have been distinguished less by partition walls than by columns, provided that the columns were supported—as is commonly done in cloisters—by a wall of some height, which received the different elevations of the floors and made the descents between the elevations distinct. In this respect, then, the store-chambers of the outer court differed from these store-chambers: those had columns, whereas these had none.

“For they were three-storeyed,” he says, “and had no columns, such as were the columns of the courts.”

It is well added concerning these porticoes that “they projected.” Since they were supported by the store-chambers, they projected; and it is then stated how, or by how much, they projected from the ground:

“They projected,” he says, “from the lower and middle parts of the building, fifty cubits above the ground.”

If this projecting elevation of the porticoes above the ground is divided into fifty cubits and fifty cubits, the total height of the building appears to have been one hundred and fifty cubits [Col. 0592D]. Yet the lower portico did not everywhere project fifty cubits above ground, but only on the side where the ground was lower. But because, according to the reasoning already given, the ground on one side of the building, on the temple side, was sixty cubits higher, and the building’s first upper room projected according to the description of the portico, on the other side the ground appears only to rise ten cubits externally, on the temple side, above the floor of the first upper room. Therefore, what we read above—that “the ground was up to the windows”—must be understood of the windows of the first upper room, so that its doors were reached by descending several steps, as we see in cellars. The *ethecae*, however, we understand to have been opposite the upper room.

[Col. 0593]

[Col. 0593B] But because the store-chambers beneath the porticoes adjoined the building itself along with the porticoes, they had on their inner side one wall in common with the building. This wall was longer by as much as the building’s width exceeded the length of those store-chambers. Thus, by the outer wall adjoining the outer court, the length of the store-chambers is specified when it is added: “And the outer enclosure along the store-chambers which were beside the way of the outer court, before the store-chambers: its length was fifty cubits.”

It should certainly be noted that he does not say that the portico itself was [Col. 0594B] fifty cubits long, but its outer enclosure—that is, the wall which it had on the outside—was fifty cubits long, lest anyone suppose that this measurement was taken within the walls, as in the upper porticoes. It is therefore clear, as we have already said above, that it had one wall in common with the building, so that it must be counted in the measurement of each. Thus it is established concerning the store-chambers of this portico what is read concerning those store-chambers which are described after the pattern of these: “According to their length, so also was their width.” The following statement appears general: “For the length of the store-chambers of the outer court was fifty cubits.” For since it says not “their” but “of the store-chambers,” the reference seems not to be made to the foregoing alone, but a general statement is made: the length of all the store-chambers of the outer court is to be understood as one and the same.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the remaining matters through the end of the description

After the description of the store-chamber which was opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court and opposite the pavement of the outer court, and after the description of the portico adjoining both the pavement and the threefold portico, observe how remarkably he repeats what he said much earlier: “And the length,” he says, “before the face of the temple was [Col. 0595B] one hundred cubits.” Did he not express this same thing when he defined both the length and width of the inner court? But the prophet understood, from the description already given, that it followed that the length before the temple could not be one hundred cubits on the level ground. By repeating the point, therefore, he emphatically reminded us that it undoubtedly had, in some fashion, what according to the consideration of level ground it could not have had at all.

It follows:

“And beneath these store-chambers was an entrance from the east for those entering them from the outer court, in the width of the court enclosure which was opposite the eastern way, in front of the separate building.”

What store-chambers were before these store-chambers, and what entrance lay beneath these and above those—that is, between the two sets of store-chambers—we have already stated above, and we avoid repeating it. The court mentioned here, however, lay not only before the separate building, but also before the northern building, and over the greater part of the area. But because the separate building stood farther from it, it is mentioned especially in connection with that building, where it appeared least likely. Having described the store-chambers beneath the porticoes of the northern building on the northern way—store-chambers to which those beneath the porticoes of the separate building were alike in every respect—he adds a sufficiently concise description of the latter by associating them through their likeness, saying: “And store-chambers were before the building, and a way before them, according to the likeness of the store-chambers which were on the northern way.” If these [Col. 0595D] store-chambers were alike in every respect to those on the northern way before the northern building, then they supported porticoes which projected from their lower and middle parts. We likewise understand in all other respects that the two sets were alike, as we have taught above, and we need not repeat the same points. One matter which seemed to have been omitted above—their width—he appears to define in this place; and he embraces in one statement the measurement of both these and those when he says: “According to their length, so also was their width.”

Having completed the description of all the buildings to the north, he summarizes in a brief statement those standing to the south, saying: [Col. 0596A] “And all their entrances, their likenesses, and their doors were according to the doors of the store-chambers which were on the way facing south. There was a door at the head of the way; that way was before the separate vestibule, for those entering by the eastern way.” Whatever we have said of the store-chamber opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court, of the building facing north and its porticoes, or of the walkway and entrance, we must understand of those on the south according to the character of their position.
