Thus these and those have entrance corresponding to entrance, likenesses corresponding to likenesses, and doors corresponding to doors, so that in every respect there is complete likeness on either side.

Observe, however, how shrewdly he expressly mentions one point [Col. 0596B] about which there could especially be doubt. Someone might perhaps have found it difficult to believe that the separate building had two vestibules; for by having two, it would in this respect exceed the form of the other buildings, though in all other respects it retained the same likeness to them. He says, therefore: “There was a door at the head of the way, which way was before the separate vestibule.” If there was a way before the separate vestibule on one side, then undoubtedly there was both a way and a vestibule on the other side, so that the likeness on either side was the same. It is clear, moreover, that the head of that way faced east, and that it began from the outer court beside the portico of the northern building.

The remaining matters that follow are plain, down to the place where it says: “And when he had completed the measurements of the inner house, he brought me out by the way of the gate facing the eastern way, and measured it all around.” By “inner house” he means the temple, which occupied the middle place among the other buildings. When it says, “he measured it,” it should be understood either of that inner house, or of that way, or of that gate. But how had he completed the measurements of the inner house if it still had to be measured? Yet it is most clearly determined that at this point he measures the wall separating the sanctuary from the place of the people. He therefore measured the outer eastern-way gate all around by taking the measurements of that wall on either side.

“And he measured toward the east wind five hundred reeds with the measuring reed [Col. 0596D] all around. And he measured toward the north wind five hundred reeds with the measuring reed around about. And toward the south wind he measured five hundred reeds with the measuring reed all around; and toward the west wind he measured five hundred reeds with the measuring reed. He measured it on the four winds.”

What that “it” was, whose measurement he took, he shows by the explanatory statement that follows: “Its wall,” he says, “was five hundred cubits long and five hundred cubits wide all around, dividing between the sanctuary and the people’s place.”

Perhaps someone may be troubled that the same wall is said to have five hundred reeds and five hundred cubits, when above the reed is read to have been six cubits [Col. 0597A] long. But nothing prevents us from understanding different kinds of reeds, since the evident meaning of the prophet compels us to do so. Yet if this Scriptural passage seems insufficiently strong as evidence for the difference in reeds, let us see what is said later, when, shortly afterward, the altar’s measurement is described: “These,” he says, “are the altar’s measurements in the most exact cubit, which had a cubit and a palm.” What is this “most exact cubit,” in which there was a cubit and a palm? Either this is said of the instrument—that is, the reed—by which measurement is made, or of the measure taken by the instrument. For we call both the rod by which we measure and the measure which we obtain a *pertica* (“measuring-rod”). The same is true of a palm, a cubit, and a sextarius: each denotes both the measure by which something is measured and the measure that is measured.

If, then, we take “cubit” here not as the instrument but as the thing measured, how can there be a “most exact cubit” in which there was a cubit and a palm—that is, more than a cubit? But if by “cubit” we understand the instrument, namely the reed, we call it “most exact” because it had a cubit by which one measured and a palm by which one held it while measuring. It could also be—as I myself believe—that, on the part of the six-cubit reed where the palm was added, one cubit together with that palm was marked off and distinguished by some sign, so that one might measure therewith what remained below the full measurement of the reed. Just as a part of a loaf is called “bread,” and part of a house is called a “house,” so part of a reed could be called a reed. Eighty-three and one-third of the larger reeds make five hundred of the smaller [Col. 0597C] ones. Perhaps, therefore, to avoid difficulties—or rather, undoubtedly for the sake of a certain mystery, so that he might express a complete and mystical number—he employed here the smaller reeds and expressed in a mystical number what had to be taught mystically.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the description of the altar of burnt offering

It remains to speak of the altar and explain its description. “These,” he says, “are the measurements of the altar in the most exact cubit, which had a cubit and a palm” (Ezek. XLIII). We have already taught above concerning this cubit and need not repeat the same things.

“In its hollow was a cubit, and a cubit in width, and its border up to its rim all around was one palm.” To summarize briefly the dimensions of the whole altar: it was five cubits high, and up to the end of the fourth cubit it was twelve cubits both long and wide. From the fourth cubit upward, however, it had a projection of one cubit on every side, so that at its uppermost level, corresponding to the fifth cubit, the altar was fourteen cubits long and fourteen wide. That projection was therefore one cubit high and one cubit wide beyond the altar’s dimensions on every side, so that the phrase “in its hollow was a cubit, and a cubit in width” may be understood of it. The upper half of this top cubit was occupied by the altar’s crown, while the remaining half [Col. 0598A] lay beneath the crown. The crown itself was one palm thick. Hence the statement: “And its border up to its rim all around was one palm.” Here *definitio* means the same as “termination” or boundary. The upper extremity of the altar, or of its crown, where the altar ended or was finished, was therefore one palm thick. There was also, around that same edge of the crown, another small projection hanging all around, which he calls a rim. Hence he says: “And its border up to its rim all around was one palm.”

Or perhaps, more correctly, a certain opening extending from the top to the bottom in the middle of the altar is described by the phrase: “In its hollow was a cubit, and a cubit in width.” But the remaining matters that follow should be expounded according to the earlier interpretation. Beneath the altar itself there was also a pit two cubits deep, which received the ashes flowing down through that opening. Hence he adds: “This also was the hollow of the altar; and from the hollow of the ground to the lowest ledge were two cubits, and its width was one cubit.” He describes its depth and width, while saying nothing of its length; yet he indicates it by showing that the two cubits end at the lowest ledge, that is, at the altar’s base. It seems to me, therefore, that its length began under the base of the altar on the front side and extended to the rear of the altar, so that it could receive the blood poured at the base and might open at the rear of the altar, as though for drawing out the ashes that flowed into it. It follows:

[Col. 0598C] “And from the greater ledge to the lesser ledge were four cubits, and the width was one cubit.” A *crepido* may be called a break or cut in a level plane or surface. He therefore calls the altar’s twelve-cubit base the lesser ledge; the base of the projection mentioned above, which was fourteen cubits, he calls the greater ledge. Thus from one ledge to the other there were four cubits, according to the height of the *Ariel* mentioned above; and there was a width of one cubit, corresponding to the width of the projection. He rightly stated the one cubit separately and with qualification. For the placement of the four cubits rose upward, whereas the position of the one cubit turned aside and spread laterally in width.

But why, beginning with the greater [Col. 0598D] ledge, did he not put the one cubit first, since it occurs first in this order, unless he wished, in the Latin manner, to state the larger number first? It would have seemed more orderly had he wished to say thus: “And from the lesser ledge to the greater ledge were four cubits, and the width was one cubit.” The Septuagint followed this order, rendering it: “From the lesser propitiatory to the greater propitiatory,” indicating by “propitiatory” and “propitiatory” the same places which we understand as the ledges. These two places could quite properly be called propitiatories, because at these two places blood used to be placed or poured for expiation and propitiation.

“But the Ariel itself was four [Col. 0599A] cubits.” By *Ariel* he means the body of the altar itself, which was, as stated, four cubits high, with the projection mentioned above rising over it. Perhaps he named it *Ariel*, meaning “strong lion,” because, in the manner of a lion, it devoured and swallowed up the people’s victims through the opening already mentioned. “And above the Ariel were four horns,” namely at the altar’s four corners. “And the Ariel was twelve cubits long by twelve cubits wide, square, with equal sides.” This was said of the body of the altar, as we have already explained above. “And the ledge was fourteen [Col. 0600A] cubits long by fourteen cubits wide at its four corners.” We likewise said above that such was the measurement around the upper part of the altar. “And its crown was half a cubit all around,” namely in height; for its thickness was described above: “And its hollow was one cubit all around.” Recall the two interpretations we set out above: according to the first, what is now said will be a superfluous repetition; according to the second, it will be a necessary addition for completing the altar’s height.

## Chapter XX. Description or Division of the Land of Promise, and What Portion Is Owed to the Priests and What to the Levites

[Note: [Col. 0590] The following two divisions appear as a single interlinear text in Migne.][Col. 0599B]

He immediately adds a few words concerning this consecrated portion, namely that it belongs to the priests; and much later in what follows, as though he said: In all the aforesaid consecrated area there will be another consecrated area, in which the sanctuary and the Temple will stand, so that it may rightly be called the consecrated place of the consecrated place, just as it is customary to say the Holy of Holies.

What he says, “from this measure,” must not be referred merely to the immediately preceding clause, but to everything comprised in the preceding verses. What he now commands to be measured is that which shortly afterward is said to belong to the Levites.

[Col. 0600B] It is evident from what follows that the Temple was in the priests’ allotment. Therefore, what he says, “in it,” must be referred to that measured area of which he says beforehand, “and from this measure.” For the Temple was in the middle of that measure. But the inserted parenthesis and the neuter reference make the wording obscure.

In these two following verses he determines to whom the two aforesaid measurements are to belong, and, in the first, he deals with the first measurement. “The consecrated portion,” he says, “of the land shall be for the priests,” as though he said: That which I earlier called the consecrated portion—that, I say, shall belong to the priests.

[Col. 0600C] This is the measure which he set down second, where he says: “You shall measure a length of twenty-five thousand and a breadth of ten thousand.”

“The consecrated portion of the land: twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth. The consecrated portion shall be throughout all its boundary round about. And from every side it shall be consecrated, five hundred by five hundred, square on all four sides round about; and its open land shall be fifty cubits round about.” [Col. 0599C]

“And from this measure you shall measure a length of twenty-five thousand and a breadth of ten thousand.”

[Col. 0600B] “And in it shall be the Temple, even the Holy of Holies.”

“The consecrated portion of the land shall belong to the priests, the ministers of the sanctuary, who draw near for ministry.”

[Col. 0600C] “It shall be for them a place for houses and a holy place for the sanctuary; but twenty-five thousand in length and ten thousand in breadth shall belong to the Levites, who minister to the House.”

[Col. 0601]

# Two Books on Emmanuel

## Prologue

I came upon a certain treatise by Master Andrew, which he had written and published as an exposition of Isaiah, and found in it several things stated with insufficient caution and argued less than Catholicly. For in many passages of that work the Jewish interpretation is presented as though it were not so much the Jews’ view as his own, and as though it were true. On the passage, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son,” he sets forth the Jews’ objections or questions without answering them, and seems to have awarded them the victory by leaving them, as it were, insoluble.

In such statements the more learned are scandalized and the less learned are brought into disrepute, to such an extent that even today some among his disciples maintain that the prophecy set forth above was spoken not of the Blessed Mary, but rather of the prophetess. Therefore, to remove the error either of those already deceived or of those who may still be deceived, I have resolved to write something and to answer the objections which have been put forward.

At the beginning of this work I wish to set down the objections themselves, as they are found in the exposition just mentioned. Secondly, by way of testimony, I shall append certain words of Blessed Jerome, as he himself published them in his exposition of the same passage. Finally, I wish to add from my own resources whatever I think sufficient for refuting the objections.

## Objections of Master Andrew, According to What the Jews Customarily Object to Us Concerning Our Emmanuel

[Col. 0601]

[Col. 0601A] “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7). We expound this most explicit prophecy concerning the conception and Nativity of our Savior, and concerning the intactness and perpetual virginity of His ever-virgin mother, as is right. The Jews, enemies of truth, rising up against us, endeavor to shake the most solid wall of our faith with the battering ram of their sophistry.

First, they say that the Hebrew does not contain *becula*, a word meaning “virgin,” but *alma*, which sometimes means a young woman and sometimes a hidden woman. When we object and ask them how it can be a sign of future deliverance that a woman of younger age, or one concealed and secluded, should conceive and bear a child—since we see this happen very frequently—they reply:

[Col. 0601B] “The sign consisted in this: she who had not yet conceived would conceive at the first approach of a man to her, would bear a male child, and that child would be called Emmanuel by the people themselves or by his mother.” It is as if the prophet said: “O house of David, if you see this young woman, who has not yet conceived, shortly conceive and bear a son, know that this is the sign given you by the Lord of your future deliverance from the hand of the aforesaid kings.”

“But you,” they say, “who expound this of the conception and childbirth of the mother of your Virgin Jesus, answer how something which took place six hundred years or more later could be a sign to the house of David and to Ahaz that they would be delivered from the hand of Rezin, then king of Syria, and Pekah, son of Remaliah. How could that be a sign to people who had never seen it and never would see it?

“You travel by precipitous paths; we travel by a level road, with the whole content of the chapter agreeing with us. You cling to a single verse while the whole context of the text protests. To make this clearer, we shall follow the entire chapter from beginning to end.

“The Lord commanded Ahaz through the prophet to ask for a sign by which he could be assured that he need not fear the two tails of smoking firebrands. When he would not ask for a sign, the prophet turned to the people and told them that the Lord Himself would give a sign; and he immediately sets forth the sign, saying: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive,’ and so forth.

“He also adds the food of the child conceived and born of the virgin, and the reason why he would use such food. After this comes an interpolation concerning the coming of the Assyrians [Col. 0602B] into the land of Judah and what they would do there. Finally, after enumerating the things that follow desolation, the Lord commands the prophet to write plainly and legibly in a large book these two names of the child to be born of the young woman, or concealed woman: ‘Swiftly take away the spoil; hasten to plunder.’

“And so that no fraud or deception might be thought to lie beneath this, or lest what is said about the virgin—or rather, the young woman—who would bear a child should be twisted to refer to anyone other than the prophetess, namely Isaiah’s wife and the son born from her, he brought in two witnesses deserving of credence. Under their witness he approached the prophetess in marital intercourse; she conceived and bore a child, whose name, as follows, he gave by the Lord’s command. He also sets forth the reason why he ought to be so named.

“Behold,” they say, “everything proceeds rationally; everything promised is fulfilled. A young woman who had not yet conceived is promised as a sign, to bear a son. Two faithful witnesses are brought in, who by sight and hearing could recognize that the prophetess whom Isaiah approached was a young woman, and could know with complete certainty, when the time of delivery came, that she had conceived through the man’s approach to her. If you doubt the young woman, faithful witnesses will establish the fact.

“She is foretold as about to conceive; she conceived; she was to bear a son; and she bore a male child. He ate the foods which the foretold child was to eat. Behold, the sign which the Lord promised to give has been given. For did not the event follow the sign? During the infancy of the son of the virgin, or young woman, the two kings before whom Judah trembled fell: one, slain by the Assyrians; the other, murdered by Hoshea, son of Elah.

[Col. 0603B] “Behold, the sign came first and the event followed. Judah was delivered from the fear for the removal of which the sign had been given. But the birth of your virgin was neither a sign for those whose fear was to be removed, nor could it have been; nor did the event for which the sign was given follow it. Rather, the sign which you propose preceded the event by five hundred years and more.

“Explain, if you can, how Isaiah the prophet, under known and named witnesses, approached the prophetess; how through that union she conceived and bore a son whom the Lord for this reason commanded to be called ‘Hasten, take away the spoil; be swift to plunder’: namely, because during his infancy the strength of Damascus, where Rezin reigned, and the spoils of Samaria, where Pekah son of Remaliah wielded the scepter, were to be taken away by the Assyrians.

[Col. 0603C] “Holy Scripture speaks most plainly: the Lord, who cannot lie, says that before the child whom the prophetess bore to Isaiah knows how to call his father and mother, Damascus and Samaria will be destroyed by the Assyrians. If you call your virgin the mother of this child, you must consequently also say that Isaiah was his father.”

If, immediately after Isaiah’s son was born to the prophetess, and after the two kings had died, Judah was delivered from the fear they inspired—the matter for which the sign was given—it shines forth clearer than light that both the conception and the childbirth of that child’s mother were the sign of the foretold deliverance.

These are the missiles which the Jews hurl against us, calling us corruptors and violent distorters of the sacred Scriptures. To answer them is unnecessary, since others have done so before us. But whether they have been answered sufficiently, let those who answered judge for themselves. Nor is it useful, lest perhaps, entering an uncertain contest with unequal strength, we should be overcome, and they should exult as victors not only over us but also over those whose keen sharpness of intellect would readily prevail over them if they engaged with them.

Therefore, having measured our strength and left greater matters to the stronger, [Col. 0604A] let us carry through the explanation of the literal sense which we have begun.

“He will give a sign by His gratuitous will, not by your merits as perverse and unbelieving persons. The Lord will do something and give you a sign, which, when you see it, will signify to you that you are being delivered from fear of the aforesaid kings. ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear.’ The conception and birth of a young woman, or concealed woman, when you see it, will signify to you that you shall be delivered from the aforesaid fear. And you, house of Judah—or you who have conceived—shall call him Emmanuel.

“For this reason the child will be named by that name, whether by the house of Judah or by his mother: because, when they see the child whom He promised to give them as a sign now born, they will understand that God will be propitious to them and will be their helper; or because in the days of his birth the Lord had already begun to do them good.

“‘He shall eat butter and honey.’ If we take the conjunction causally, so that the knowledge of rejecting evil and choosing good is the reason why he eats butter and honey, can such eating confer such knowledge? Do not fools also eat butter and honey? But if we take it consecutively and say: ‘He shall eat butter and honey, and shall know how to reject evil and choose good,’ how will what follows be explained—‘for before the child knows,’ and so forth—unless perhaps the conjunction there, as in many places, is understood copulatively, and it is read thus: ‘He shall eat butter and honey, and shall know how to reject evil and choose good; and before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good, the land which you abhor shall be forsaken by the face of its two kings.’

[Col. 0604C] “Some read it thus: ‘He shall eat butter and honey, as one who knows how to reject evil and choose good; and before he has knowledge of this kind, it shall be forsaken,’ and so forth. They also regard it as part of the sign that, while in infancy—an age which is not ordinarily accustomed to reject any food offered—it will reject unclean foods as though they were filth, and consume only clean foods, understood synecdochically under butter and honey.

“In the words ‘he shall eat butter and honey,’ the Hebrews say there is a promise of future fertility. Where we have ‘that he may know how to reject evil,’ they have, as they say, ‘until he knows to abominate evil and choose good.’ That is to say: the prophetess’s son will eat butter and honey when he reaches the knowledge by which he can abominate evil and choose good.

“He next states why, when he reaches the years of discernment, there will be such abundance in the land devastated by enemies that it will flow with milk—understood by butter—and honey: ‘for before he knows,’ and so forth. The child will then indeed be able to eat butter and honey, because in his infancy Syria and the land of the ten tribes will be abandoned by the two kings whom you, house of Judah, fear.”

## Words of Jerome

[Col. 0603]

[Col. 0603D] [Note: [Col. 0603D] Book III of the Commentary on Isaiah, chapter 7.] When it is said, “The Lord Himself will give you a sign,” it ought to be something new and wonderful. [Col. 0604D] But if a young woman, or a girl—as the Jews wish—and not a virgin gives birth, what kind of sign can it be called, [Col. 0605A] when this is a designation of age, not of intactness?

Indeed, that we may meet the Jews on equal footing and not, by a contemptuous conclusion, give them occasion to laugh at our ignorance: in Hebrew a virgin is called by a word which is not written in the present passage. But another word is put in its place, which, apart from the Septuagint, who rendered it ἡ παρθένος, “the virgin,” all translators rendered “young woman.” Among them, however, the word is ambiguous; for it means both “young woman” and “hidden woman,” that is, ἀποκρυφή, “concealed.”

Hence also in the title of Psalm 9, where the Hebrew has *alma*, the word which the other translators rendered “for the young woman,” but which the Septuagint rendered “for the hidden things”; and in Genesis we read that Rebecca is called *alma*, which Aquila translated not “young woman” or “girl,” but “concealed woman” (Gen. 24).

Likewise, when the Shunammite woman had lost her son and had fallen at Elisha’s feet, and Gehazi was preventing her, she heard from the prophet: “Let her alone, for she is in grief, and the Lord has hidden it from me” (4 Kings 4). In the Hebrew it is written: .

Therefore, *alma* means not merely “girl” but also “virgin”; yet, with emphasis, it means a hidden and secluded virgin, who has never been exposed to the sight of men, but has been guarded with great diligence by her parents.

The Punic language also, said to flow from Hebrew sources, properly calls a virgin *alma*; and, to give the Jews occasion for laughter, in our own language too *alma* means “holy.” The Hebrews use words from almost all languages, as in that passage of the Song of Songs concerning φορεῖον, that is, a “litter” or “carriage”: “Solomon made himself a litter,” which we read thus also in Hebrew. Likewise, the Hebrews use the words *nugas* and *mensuram* in the same manner and with the same senses. And, so far as I can contend with my memory, I do not think that I have ever read *alma* of a married woman, but of one who is a virgin: not only a virgin, but a virgin of younger age, in the years of adolescence. For a virgin can be an old woman. But this virgin was in the years of girlhood; or at least she was a virgin, not merely a girl—one who could not yet know a man, but was already marriageable.

[Col. 0606B] Finally, in Deuteronomy virginity is understood under the name “girl” and “young woman.” “If,” he says, “a man finds in a field a betrothed girl and, overpowering her by force, lies with her, you shall kill only the man who lay with her, and you shall do nothing to the girl. The young woman has committed no sin deserving death; for as if someone should rise against his neighbor and take his life, so has it happened in this matter” (Deut. 22), and so forth.

# Book One

[Col. 0605]

## Chapter I. The Jewish View Is Refuted and the Christian View Confirmed

[Col. 0605C]

“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7).

Oh, how deservedly were those called “seers” who could see so far into the distance! For one who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer. Certainly, if chronographers do not deceive us, these things were foreseen and foretold more than six hundred years before they occurred. See, then, how far into the future he looked who foretold these things.

You marvel, I think, at the keenness of his foresight; marvel no less at the depth of understanding in the prophet’s words. Great indeed was that power of foreseeing, [Col. 0605D] but no less wonderful was the very manner of speaking. Behold: in those very words of the prophet by which the Christian is enlightened, the Jew is blinded and the devil is made foolish. Behold where the lamb walks, the elephant swims, but does not swim through. Behold where Christian simplicity finds a level path, runs, and does not stumble, Jewish faithlessness is submerged and the devil is suffocated.

The Christian is enlightened to such an extent that he would rather die than deny the truth; the Jew is blinded to such an extent that he is readier to die than confess the truth; the devil is so confounded that he presumes it possible to make a sinner of Him whom he knows to be the Redeemer of all. “All these things,” he says, “I will give you if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4). He invites to worship himself [Col. 0606C] Him before whom every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth is bent (Phil. 2). Behold how foolish the princes of Tanis have become.

And indeed it was necessary that the mysteries of our redemption should be veiled by ambiguity of words, lest malignant spirits or men should understand and hinder them. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

I am not of such ready eloquence or profound intelligence as to imagine that I can explain in speech or comprehend in thought the depth of the prophetic saying. It is enough for me here, if I am granted to satisfy the devotion of the faithful by expounding the plain sense of the text, and to show how this prophecy of Isaiah should be referred to the incarnation of the Word: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.”

And even if you should never be able, according to the stated interpretation, to fit this prophecy to the surrounding text, nevertheless you must believe that it was foretold of Christ and fulfilled in Christ. Whoever cannot understand the voice of the prophesying prophet, let him at least hear the meaning of the evangelist who explains it. Whoever does not understand the meaning of the prophet’s prediction, let him at least believe the judgment of the evangelist who expounds it.

Hear the one who sets it forth: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive.” Attend to the interpreter: “All this took place in order that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,’ which means, ‘God with us.’”

What is “all this”? “Do not fear, Joseph, to take Mary your wife; for what has been born of her is from the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 0607A] Behold, the evangelist says that the stated prophecy was fulfilled in the Blessed Mary. Who would dare contradict him? There a virgin is foretold as about to conceive; here she is said to have conceived by the Holy Spirit. Therefore, she conceived by the Holy Spirit, not by a man.

The Holy Spirit does not know how to corrupt a virgin, but how to sanctify her. The Holy Spirit does not know how to diminish a virgin’s purity, but how to increase it; He does not know how to defile, but how to glorify. Therefore, whoever does not yet have a heart enlightened to understand the sense of the prophesying prophet should at least bring ears not heavy in hearing to obey the expounding evangelist, lest he incur that saying of the same Isaiah: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy” (Isa. 6).

Whoever does not yet understand what he reads should at least believe from the heart, in order thus to merit understanding: “Unless you believe,” he says, “you shall not understand” (Isa. 7). This is the strongest argument for our faith: prophets and evangelists proclaim the same thing in such complete accord.

What the prophet announces beforehand—“Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel”—is what the Evangelist declares in other words: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). “He dwelt,” he says, “among us.” He dwelt indeed in order to become our Emmanuel, and to be God with us.

What the prophet expresses in one word when he calls Him Emmanuel, the angel explains more fully to Mary when he announces to her from God: “The holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

## Chapter II. What the Jews, or Those Who Judaize, Customarily Object to What We Believe Concerning Our Emmanuel

[Col. 0607C]

But the Jews object to this assertion of ours; those among us who Judaize murmur—indeed, they cry out—with them. They raise many objections by which they think to refute our assertion. They bring forward arguments from every side by which they labor to establish their own assertion.

The first task, therefore, is to expose the blindness of the Jews. The second is to break through the deafness of those who Judaize. The third, if it is granted us, is to satisfy the devotion of the faithful and of those who inquire devoutly. Let us now see what sort of things, and how much weight should be assigned to them, which these cavillers object to us.

They say that what we believe concerning our mother and child [Col. 0607D] can in no way be a sign of the matter for which it was said: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God.” Isaiah certainly relates that Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah were preparing to attack the city of Jerusalem and, after overthrowing King Ahaz, to install another in his place. The heart of the people, however, was shaken by fear of this danger as the trees of a forest are shaken by the wind.

Therefore, in order to remove this fear, Isaiah was sent by the Lord to meet Ahaz and say: “See that you are quiet, and let not your heart be afraid of these two tails of smoking firebrands,” because he would without doubt be delivered from the power of those two kings.

As evidence of the future deliverance, a sign was therefore offered according to the petitioner’s choice: “Ask for yourself,” He says, “a sign from the Lord your God, in the depths of hell or in the heights above.” Although he would not ask for a sign, a sign is nevertheless promised when it is said: “Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son,” and so forth.

“If,” they say, “this is rightly understood of your Christ, show how His conception or birth, which was to occur so much later, could be a sign of something which was soon to occur. For the sign ought to precede the event itself, and the event itself should follow the sign. But even if it is said to be a sign of another matter, the question is not removed. For this sign was proposed and was to be given in order to remove the imminent fear. How could the outcome of a thing to occur after so many ages remove an imminent fear? Finally, how could something that they had never seen and never would see be a sign to them of anything whatsoever?”

[Col. 0608B] Behold the objections they make in order to refute the truth of our assertion. Let us also see the arguments by which they labor to whitewash the opinion of their own assertion.

## Chapter III. How the Jews Think That Everything Said of Emmanuel Should Be Understood of the Prophetess’s Son

“Remove from the midst what you introduce of your own accord,” they say, “and you will see that everything said agrees with the prophetess’s son. *Becula* in Hebrew has the same meaning as our word ‘virgin.’ But in this passage the Hebrew does not read *becula*, but *alma*, which is interpreted ‘young woman’ or ‘hidden woman.’

“Observe, therefore, that the things foretold concerning the son of the young woman are repeated and seem fulfilled in the son of the prophetess. It is foretold of the young woman that she will conceive and bear a son; concerning the prophetess, it is read later that she conceived and bore a male child. It is foretold concerning the young woman’s child that, before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good, the land which you abhor will be forsaken by the face of its two kings. A promise not unlike this is repeated in other words concerning the prophetess’s child, when it is said that, before the child knows how to call his father or mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria will be taken away before the king of Assyria.

[Col. 0608C] “Behold,” they say, “the whole content of the chapter agrees with us. You walk by precipices; we walk on a level road. For while the whole context of the text protests, you cling to one verse.”

But when they are asked how it can be a sign of future deliverance that a woman of younger age, or one hidden and secluded, should conceive and bear a child, since we see this very frequently, they reply: “The sign consisted in this: she who had never conceived would conceive at the first approach of a man to her, would bear a male child, and she would be called Emmanuel by the people themselves or by the mother.”

For this purpose two faithful witnesses were also brought in, so that their testimony would make it publicly known that she had conceived from the first approach of a man to her, as they could afterward infer with complete certainty when the time of birth arrived.

## Chapter IV. How Utterly Shameless the Jewish Assertion Appears at This Point

[Col. 0609A]

But I ask: even if they saw the prophet have intercourse with the prophetess, could they, I say, equally see whether she had conceived? Does nature never allow a birth either to pass beyond or to come before the proper time for giving birth, so that any expert can infer, from the time of birth, not merely the day or the hour but even the moment of conception?

But perhaps they will say that the witnesses’ attentiveness to this matter was so great that repeated intercourse could not escape them, and that from signs of her virginity they could discover that the very intercourse of which they were witnesses was the man’s first approach to her. This is what those imply who say that she conceived at the first approach of a man to her.

[Col. 0609B] I marvel at the shamelessness of this profession. So far as it serves their cause, they wish the designated woman in childbirth to be a virgin; but so far as it serves ours, they refuse to allow her to be a virgin. But let the Jews, and our own Judaizers, see whether their interpretation is true. It is surely plain enough that it is full of much indecency.

It is very foul and exceedingly shameful to stand by people having intercourse and to seek signs of virginity with prying eyes. Behold, according to their account, so great a prophet and prophetess have intercourse under the gaze of respectable persons—something which pimps and publicly prostituted women can scarcely, or not at all, do.

How much more honorable, how much more correct it would be to say that the witnesses were introduced not for what follows, but for what precedes! Now what precedes is: “Take for yourself a large book and write in it with a man’s stylus, ‘Swiftly take away the spoil; hasten to plunder’” (Isa. 8).

But why, I ask, should what a very small sheet of parchment can contain be written in a large book? Unless perhaps because a brief subject is often more fully expounded, and one and the same thing repeated in many ways and by many modes? Or perhaps a discourse capable of being interpreted at length makes a book large even though it is brief, according to the phrase, “The matter is great to me and capable of extended exposition.” Certainly, what is profound in mystery is deservedly said to be as great as it is deep.

Yet the point will be clearer and more evident if we say that it was commanded to be written in a large book, as is customary, in order that it might be retained in memory and transmitted to the knowledge of posterity. For large books are not so easily lost or carried from place to place.

[Col. 0609D] But what was first written in the book was afterward imposed as a name upon the prophetess’s child; and the reason for both the writing and the name is added when it says: “Call his name, ‘Hasten, take away the spoil; be swift to plunder,’ because before the child knows how to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria will be taken away before the king of Assyria” (ibid.).

Behold, the prophet foretold future events, committed them to writing, and brought in witnesses, so that after they had begun to be fulfilled they might be proved to have been foretold—partly by the writing, partly by the testimony. Thus, from the things which he had foretold as about to occur shortly and which could be proved, it might also be proved true that those things were foretold which were to occur far in the future and could not be proved.

[Col. 0610A] Does it not therefore seem, as has been said, more correct to state that the witnesses had been brought in for testimony of this kind than that they were to be witnesses of indecency?

## Chapter V. How the Jewish Assertion Is Refuted by the Arguments of Its Own Objection
Now, therefore, that we may engage on equal terms with Jews or Judaizers: just as they insist that we add nothing of our own, so by the same right of fairness we require of them that they add nothing of their own to the words of the prophecy. The prophet says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” or, for the present, as they wish, “Behold, a young woman shall conceive [Col. 0610B] and bear a son.” He does not say, “Behold, the prophetess shall conceive”; he does not say, “Behold, this woman or that woman shall conceive”; nor, finally, does he say that his young woman would conceive at her husband’s first approach to her. He says simply: “Behold, she shall conceive and bear a son”; and he adds: “And his name shall be called Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey,” etc.

Have only the sons of old women, and not those of young women, customarily eaten butter and honey? In our own times they do so indiscriminately. And who cannot see how easy it is for any young woman to give her son whatever name she chooses? For a son to be conceived by a young woman, born of a young woman, receive a name as one pleases, and eat butter and honey—what is great in this, what is wonderful, what is new or unusual? What in it ought to be taken as a sign, so that it may fittingly be said: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign”? “The Lord himself,” he says, as though it were something so extraordinary and so great that it would rightly be given not through a human being, not through an angel, but by the Lord himself.

But it is surely clear enough to the wise that in all this there is nothing beyond ordinary daily experience, nor anything which should rightly be called the sign—not merely of some great matter, but even of some moderately important matter—unless perhaps they mean to say that this child, beyond customary practice and contrary to the laws of nature, acquired knowledge of good and evil prematurely, before the age of discernment, by eating butter and honey, because it is written: “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to reject [Col. 0610D] evil and choose good.” “He shall eat,” it says, “that he may know.” But if it is indeed certain that the child anticipated the age of discernment through such eating, I too admit that this was a sign of no insignificant thing.

But let us see what follows. For it is immediately added there: “Before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good, the land which you detest shall be deserted before its two kings.” Observe and consider, then, that the land was to be delivered from the presence of those two kings before the child acquired knowledge for distinguishing good and evil. Such deliverance therefore preceded that knowledge. Thus the premature knowledge could not have been a sign of a deliverance already past. For, as they themselves maintain, the sign must precede the thing itself, while the thing signified follows the sign.

By this reasoning, therefore, just as what we say concerning our Emmanuel could not be a sign of that deliverance, so neither could what they assert concerning their Emmanuel be its sign. For the stated knowledge of the child, which alone has been found capable of being a sign, is proved from the prophetic text to follow the deliverance. You gladly receive, I suppose, brothers, the sight of Goliath’s head cut off by his own sword, and the presumption of the Jewish assertion refuted by its own argument.

But they say further that the sign was to be given in order to remove the fear then imminent. Yet something to occur after so many years could not remove a fear then pressing upon them. To this I answer: just as an event to occur after many years could not remove the dread of immediate danger, so neither could an event to occur after a few months remove it. If, as they say, God wished to remove that fear by giving a sign, was his hand so weak that he could not give, on that very day, or within a week, or at least within that same month, a sign sufficient to satisfy all as to the removal of fear? What benefit did it bring them, or could it bring, amid such alarm, to wait long for a sign which, when it came, would be too late—or altogether useless?

Certainly, in Hezekiah’s sixth year, as we learn from the Book of Kings, Samaria was taken. What, then, will they say? That their child remained mute for six years, because Samaria had to be taken before he knew how to call his father or mother? Or rather, what they cannot prove: that in Hezekiah’s fifth year a prophecy was made concerning the prophetess’s child, or that in that same sixth year it was both made and fulfilled? Let the Jews therefore see how the same sign can be promised to Ahaz without being shown, and then set forth and fulfilled under Hezekiah.

Finally, they say that a thing which they had never seen and would never see could not be a sign to them of anything at all, and consequently could not remove the fear under which they then suffered. To this I again answer that the prophecy in question—whether understood of their child, or of ours, or of any other—could not possibly remove the fear for whose removal they contend that the sign was given, unless perhaps they will say that their young woman conceived [Col. 0611D] and gave birth with such haste that the novelty of the miracle itself and the suddenness of the unexpected event could readily raise their discouraged spirits to confidence and establish them firmly in the certainty of hope.

But the Jews prudently decline to say this, since they cannot prove it by the authority of Scripture. Nor indeed do they dare affirm that the designated child anticipated the knowledge of discernment through eating butter and honey, or even acquired it thereby, although Scripture seems to mean precisely this: “He shall eat butter and honey,” it says, “that he may know how to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7). Yet in this passage they interpret *ut* (“that”) consecutively, not causally; that is, as they say, it is put here as though one said: “He shall eat butter and honey, and he shall know how to reject evil and choose good.”

And what great thing, I ask, would it be that he should possess knowledge of rejecting evil and choosing good? Is this all they mean to say—that their Emmanuel will not be insane? Again I say: for a young woman to conceive and bear a child; for a young woman’s son to eat butter and honey and not be insane—what is great in this, what wonderful, what ought to be believed the sign of some great matter? Surely nothing. Otherwise, in saying that I am, as it were, a prophet, behold, I predict and promise what will happen: that a young woman will conceive and bear a son who will eat butter and honey and know how to reject evil and choose good. Believe, then, in this sign; believe, I say, what I tell you: that your opinion about your Emmanuel is false, and ours about our Emmanuel [Col. 0612B] is true. For if you are prepared to believe the sign I promise, then, that every evasion may disappear, we shall arrange also that the promised child does not lack the name Emmanuel.

## CHAPTER VI. How the objection concerning the virgin is sufficiently refuted by the reply of blessed Jerome

But what answer shall be made to that which they object to us concerning the virgin? For *alma*, as they say, which is found in their text in this place, does not seem to mean “virgin.” But surely the answer of blessed Jerome ought to have satisfied them on this point. For *alma* does not mean simply “virgin,” but “virgin” with a qualification, with an explicit indication: that is, such a virgin as he has made us understand—a young woman, or one who has been hidden away and guarded with such great parental care that there can be no doubt that she is a virgin and untouched.

Certainly, one who calls Aaron “the high priest” does not merely call him a priest, yet he does call him a priest: he calls him the supreme priest, the priest of priests. So in this passage we must understand that *alma*, this term, signifies “virgin” not simply, nor except with an explicit qualification. Finally, blessed Jerome says: “As far as I can contend from my memory, I do not think I have ever read *alma* of a married woman.”

Let us gladly accept, brothers, that by the name *alma* we are to understand not simply a virgin, but a secluded virgin. Behold, brothers, what the Jew has achieved by his objection; behold how, through that objection, he has made us understand that the Holy Spirit designated a virgin—not merely any virgin, but one secluded and wholly withdrawn from the sight of men, guarded with such care by her family that it is indisputably clear that she is truly an untouched virgin.

The Gospel narrative surely intended to designate such a virgin when it said: “Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to expose her publicly, resolved to dismiss her secretly” (Matt. 1). Had it said, “being a compassionate man,” we might suppose that his unwillingness to expose the woman whom he thought an adulteress proceeded from a certain compassion. But it says, “being a just man.” Therefore his wish to spare her arose not so much from compassion as from equity. Surely he would not have been just if, contrary to the judgment of equity and the command of the law, he had spared one whom he believed to be an adulteress.

See, then, what he thought concerning her integrity, how greatly he presumed concerning her holiness: he did not believe her to be an adulteress even when he truly knew that she was pregnant, and not by his seed. How rightly the Holy Spirit called her *alma*, concerning whom so certain and holy an opinion was to exist! But if the Jews think that our Jerome erred when he says that he had nowhere read *alma* of a married woman, they ought to convict his error by producing the testimony of Scripture. Yet even if they could do this, they would still not refute our position. For, according to the testimony of the same Jerome, in the Punic language, which derives from Hebrew sources, a virgin is properly called *alma*.

At least this much the Jews must concede: that the name *alma* is equivocal in different languages. What, then, will the Jews say if we maintain that, by using an equivocal term, the Holy Spirit wished the mystery of his counsel to be concealed under the ambiguity of a word, so that there might be grounds for blinding the Jew, according to the saying: “Blind the heart of this people and make their ears heavy” (Isa. 6)? And what will contentious Christians say if we maintain that the depth of the divine mystery is hidden beneath verbal ambiguity, so that there might be grounds for confounding the devil, according to the saying: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2)? Yet this point alone will compel the Jews to admit the ambiguity of the word in the sense which we accept, because otherwise the sign proposed by the prophet would be no sign at all.

## CHAPTER VII. How Christians who doubt the truth of our interpretation of Isaiah’s words are to be refuted

[Col. 0613C]

So far against the Jews. Let us also say something briefly against contentious Christians. Will they say that the prophet of the Lord did not possess God’s Spirit and did not speak in the Holy Spirit? Far be it from them to say or believe this! But what will they say about the Lord’s evangelist? Surely the same as about the Lord’s prophet: without doubt each possessed the same Spirit of truth; each spoke in one Spirit. If, therefore, one Spirit was present in both places, he could not think contrary things about himself.

If then, when he says through the prophet, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear [Col. 0613D] a son,” he intended someone other than blessed Mary, why is it that afterwards, through the evangelist, he expounds the same prophecy by saying: “All this took place to fulfill what had been spoken by the prophet: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son,’” etc. (Matt. 1)? Therefore, as we said above, let one who cannot understand the speaker listen to the interpreter. Whoever lacks eyes to see should at least have ears to hear. Are you also so blind that you are deaf as well? What you cannot understand, can you not at least believe? But if you believe it, why do you attack your faith with empty cavils? What benefit is there in bringing arguments of unbelief against faith, and offering no testimony of faith on behalf of your own faith? What use is it to raise a question which you are unwilling or unable to solve?

Is this not to open a cistern [Col. 0614A] and leave it uncovered? What is it to expose by argument the darkness of ambiguity and the depth of perplexity but to dig a well or open a cistern? To offer no answer to a question first proposed, but to leave it as though insoluble—what else is this but leaving a cistern open and without a cover? But if an ox or a donkey falls into it, according to the commandment of the law, the owner of the cistern shall pay the price of the animals (Exod. 21). And what is an ox or donkey falling into such a cistern except simple persons becoming entangled in the snares of doubt and entering into the danger of unbelief? But if, through our learning, a soul for whom Christ died perishes, what compensation, I ask, shall we give for that penalty? Therefore, what we cannot or will not explain, is it not better to pass over in silence than to expound the truth and scatter snares of unbelief?

## CHAPTER VIII. How the context of the text appears not to oppose, but to support, what is said concerning our Emmanuel

It remains now to meet the earnest inquiry of the devout and, so far as we can, to satisfy their desire. First, then, it must be shown how the context of the text appears not so much to oppose as to support the interpretation of our cavillers rather than our own; afterwards, we must carefully consider the circumstances by which the sign itself is commended. Finally, we must examine the sign itself; and I think this may suffice.

First, however, it must be admitted—and cannot at all be denied—that the more sacred mysteries of our faith were expressed obscurely in the sayings of the prophets. “Dark water was in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17). For there were certain things that had to be known, and likewise certain things which reason required should for a time remain unknown, for the reason already indicated above: lest the work of our redemption should be hindered by malicious spirits or people. For, as has already been said: “If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2).

Those things, therefore, in the mysteries of Christ which needed for a time to remain concealed were partly clouded beneath the veil of figures, partly by the ambiguity and obscurity of the text itself. Of the things obscured by the complexity of the surrounding text, some are such that they would never be understood to refer to Christ unless the Holy Spirit interpreted them—for example: “Out of Egypt I called my son.” Others are such that, when viewed only superficially, they seem to refer to something other than Christ; but when examined more carefully and understood more fully, they are found incapable of receiving any alien meaning.

Such, indeed, is this passage of Scripture now before us. For where it is said, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” certain things precede and certain things follow, by which the truth of the interpretation is obscured, not removed. To obscure the truth, a sign is proposed according to the king’s choice. But when he refuses to ask for it, a sign is nevertheless promised; and to a careless reader it appears to be said of the same matter. But to one who understands more fully, it will plainly appear that what is said concerning Emmanuel is not a sign of that matter; nor indeed ought it to be a sign of that matter for which it was said: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God” (Isa. 7).

The reasoning set forth above has shown that it cannot be a sign of that matter. Clear reasoning proves that it ought not to be a sign of the same matter. For the king’s refusal to ask for a sign arose not from piety but from impiety. The crafty and idolatrous king understood how it would condemn idolatry, how greatly it would shame all idolaters, and to what measure of the Lord’s glory it would rise, if, having asked a sign from the Lord, he received it. Therefore, out of great malice he refused to ask for a sign; but with no less craftiness he concealed the business of his impiety beneath a pretence of feigned religion: “I will not ask,” he said, “and I will not test the Lord.”

It was therefore no longer fitting for such a king to receive a sign in order to remove his fear—a king who preferred to suffer longer under the terror of imminent danger rather than allow that to occur whereby the Lord’s glory might increase. Another apparent obscuring of the truth is that, after a child has been promised, a child subsequently born is introduced, so that he may be thought to be the same one. But whenever something is set down in order to obscure the truth, something is added by which the truth may be established. Thus certain things are found similar, certain things dissimilar, and certain things wholly contrary.

Behold, it is said of Emmanuel that, before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good, the land shall be deserted before its two kings. Similar is what is read concerning the prophetess’s son: that before the child knows how to call his father or mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria will be taken away before the king of Assyria. Of the former it is said that his name shall be called Emmanuel. Different, however, is the command concerning the latter: “Call his name, Hurry, take away the spoils; hasten to plunder.” It does not say, “Call his name Emmanuel.” If they contend that he also bore this name, let them prove what they say by producing the testimony of Scripture.

There we read that a virgin shall conceive and bear. Wholly contrary is what we find here: that the woman who bore the child conceived through a man’s approach to her. I do not say “a virgin,” but even “a young woman” or “a secluded woman”—how could she be such, when she already had young sons, namely the one left to Isaiah and the one who, according to the Jews, fled to the enemy and abandoned his father? Unless, perhaps, they can prove from Scripture that he begot them by another wife, that she died and he married this woman, or that, while the former was still living, he committed adultery with this one. Behold with what shameless boldness in lying they wish every thing to be true which they brazenly invent. Behold how the whole context of the text is found to oppose not us, as they wish, but them.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the points which seem relevant to commending the sign: by whom, why, and to whom it is given

But before the sign itself is examined, let us first consider the circumstances by which it is commended. Let us see, then, to whom and why it was given, who gave the sign, and what kind of sign he gave. Certainly a sign is promised to the house of David when it is said: “Hear therefore, house of David” (Isa. 7). Was not David the one who received this promise from the Lord: “From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131)? How great, I ask, was the glory of David’s house: that the Messiah, mediator between God and human beings, was to be born from David’s line! Indeed, this very fact would tend to their singular glory or disgrace: to the glory of those who would be grateful, and to the shame of those who would be ungrateful.

The sign, therefore, was given to the house of David—not indeed so that it might be understood then, but so that what would be a sign of some great mystery might confer upon them a certain singular prerogative. We have heard to whom it was given; now let us hear why it was given: “Is it too little for you to weary men, that you also weary my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign.” Why? Because they were troublesome. In what respect were they troublesome? In that those from David’s house who were idolaters begrudged him his glory and therefore were unwilling, as though it were to his glory, to ask for a sign.

Thus the sign will be given chiefly for that purpose for which they most of all did not want it given. It will be given for the greatest divine glory; it will be given to them for their great confusion. Without doubt it will be given for the destruction of idolatry and the shame of every idolater. Some, however, will be put to shame as punishment; others, unto repentance. Because you are troublesome to him, because you disparage his glory, [Col. 0616C] “the Lord himself will give you a sign”—a sign, I say, in which there is a certain wonder of divine power, a commendation of wisdom, a manifestation and proof of mercy, an increase and consummation of glory.

Indeed, the Lord’s glory is increased more by this sign than by his creation of heaven and earth from nothing. Behold to whom it is given; behold why it is given. Now let us consider by whom it is given: “The Lord himself,” he says, “will give.” It could not suffice him to say “the Lord” unless he added “the Lord himself.” What does “the Lord himself” mean except the Lord through himself? Therefore the Lord will give it not through a human being, not through an angel, but through himself. The Lord himself will give it—the one to whom the Lord said: “Sit at my right hand”; “The Lord,” he says, “said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109).

Thus the Lord himself will give it, not through a subordinate creature, but through his own presence; the Lord himself in his own substance, in his own person. “The Lord himself will give you” a sign. Why, I ask, does he say “you” collectively, when it benefits only the good? But “you” is rightly said collectively, because the sign that is given is, as far as it is concerned, useful to all and can benefit all alike.

We now have who gave it, why he gave it, and to whom. But the sign which is so highly extolled, which is commended by so many circumstances, and by whose commendation or comparison the first sign is disparaged, must be a presage of a deliverance more worthy than that of which it has been proved both that it cannot be, and that it ought not be, a sign. Will it perhaps be a sign of deliverance from the hands of the king of Babylon? But hear what is said in what follows: “The Lord will bring upon you, upon your people, and upon your father’s house days which have not come since the day when Ephraim was separated from Judah—the king of Assyria.” Thus he says that they are not to be delivered but oppressed by the hands of the king of Babylon, lest perhaps the sign be thought to concern that matter; indeed, the prophet appears rather to thunder forth such threats in punishment for the trouble brought upon God, in vengeance for the divine injury.

“The Lord will shave with a hired razor, with those beyond the river, with the king of Assyria, the head and the hair of the feet, and will remove the whole beard.” Of what, then, will that which is read concerning our Emmanuel be called a sign?

## CHAPTER X. How the nature of the sign indicates that it appears to have been given to remove the cause of the first transgression

[Col. 0617B]

But when we begin to examine the nature of the sign itself, perhaps what we seek may be discerned from the manner of that nature. Let us, then, look at the sign itself and dwell more carefully on such a consideration: “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel; he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7).

Behold, everything said concerning our Emmanuel seems, as it were indirectly, to look back to original sin and to answer it from the opposite side. There, concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, the serpent says: “On whatever day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). Here, correspondingly, something similar is set forth—except that here what is promised there deceitfully is true. Certainly, eating here was for merit, there for guilt; there it belonged to transgression, here to virtue. Our Emmanuel obtained knowledge of good and evil by eating; that other could not obtain the knowledge promised to him by eating.

There it is read that man was cast out of paradise, as though from the Lord’s household and fellowship; here it is said of this child of ours that he was called Emmanuel, which is interpreted “God with us.” Here it should be noted that it is not said of God that we are with him. Rather, conversely, it is said of us that he is with us, so that we may understand not that humanity, as it were, returned to God, but that God followed humanity at once even into exile, as it is written: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1).

Therefore, what humanity lost in the first human being—namely, being with God—it appears to have recovered in the new human being. There it is said to the woman: “In pain you shall bear children” (Gen. 3); here it is said of this woman who bears the child: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” But why did that woman give birth not without pain, except because she did not conceive without lust? Lust, indeed, is the cause of pain, and pain the effect of lust. Therefore the cause is indicated from the effect when it is said: “In pain you shall bear children.”

Conversely, here the removal of the effect itself is inferred from the removal of the cause. For she who conceived while retaining virginity conceived without lust; consequently, she is understood to have given birth without pain. There, neither conception without guilt nor birth without punishment; here, because conception was without concupiscence, childbirth was without pressure. Thus, what human nature lost in the first woman bearing a child—namely, to conceive and give birth without corruption—it seems to have received in this woman who bears our child as certain firstfruits of its restoration.

You see how man is set against man and woman against woman; and how now by opposition, now in reverse order, they seem to answer one another through a certain similarity-in-dissimilarity. There, woman from man alone; here, man from woman alone. There, from the stronger sex, the stronger is brought forth for the weaker, who would restore both. Do you see how so great a dissimilarity of likeness, and likeness of dissimilarity, warns us that in these there was a beginning of newness, just as in those there was a beginning of oldness?

In the first human being there was a beginning of oldness, for the condemnation of his posterity; in the second human being, a beginning of newness, for the restoration of his race. That first Adam, therefore, is the head and source of all who perish; this one, as it were another Adam, is the head and beginning of all who rise again in him. For we have him as our head; all of us who rise again in him are his members. Behold: the very nature of this sign shows that it was given to remove the cause of the first transgression. Behold: what is said concerning Emmanuel was given as a remedy. But how as a sign? Perhaps what occurred in the head is a sign of what will occur in the body? Perhaps what first occurred in his head accomplishes one thing in his body, foretells another, and is one thing which it presently effects but another which it prefigures for the future? It presently works what belongs to justification; it prefigures for the future what belongs to glorification.

## CHAPTER XI. How the first transgression brought a threefold loss; corresponding to that loss, a threefold promise; and, corresponding to the threefold promise, a threefold sign

But since, as has been said, those things which are said concerning our Emmanuel seem to answer from the opposite side to the first human being’s transgression, let us see what humanity lost through that original guilt; and then perhaps we shall see for the strengthening of what hope, and as what most certain proof, the sign of which we speak was promised or granted.

Through the guilt of his transgression, he lost the glory of incorruption, the prerogative of dignity, and the abundance of fullness: the glory of incorruption, by which he was made immortal; the prerogative of dignity, by which he was made in God’s likeness; and the abundance of fullness, by which he was placed in a place of delight. Hear of the stripping away of immortality where you read concerning the forbidden tree: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2). The degradation of honor and the loss of dignity occurred when he fell from that height of God’s likeness into the likeness of a beast: “Man,” it says, “when he was in honor did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48).

He was emptied of the abundance of fullness when, cast out from the place of delight, he incurred that sentence of curse: “Cursed is the earth in your work; in labors you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the earth. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3). Behold a threefold loss: the loss of incorruption, dignity, and blessedness.

But the merciful and compassionate Lord, according to the riches of his goodness, did not wish to restrain his mercies in his wrath. He was found as mercifully ready to help as the devil was prone to destroy, because “with the Lord is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.” But redemption would not be abundant unless our restorer restored the fallen human being completely. Corresponding, then, to the threefold loss, humanity receives from the gift of its compassionate Lord a threefold promise: the promise of recovered immortality, the promise of recovered dignity, and the promise of recovered blessedness.

“Your dead shall live; my slain shall rise again” (Isa. 26): behold the promise of hoped-for immortality. “I will give them, in my house and within my walls, a place and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isa. 56): behold the promise of restored dignity. “Eye has not seen, apart from you, O God, the things which you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2): behold the promise of restored happiness.

Behold, as has been said, a threefold promise corresponding to a threefold loss; and now, corresponding likewise to the threefold promise, receive and observe a threefold sign in these words: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son”—behold the first. “And his name shall be called Emmanuel”—behold the second. “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to reject evil and choose good”—behold the third. You therefore have one sign in the mother and two in the offspring: a sign of incorruption in the mother; signs of recovered dignity and fullness in the offspring.

## CHAPTER XII. On the sign of recovered incorruption
Listen concerning the mother: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7). How great do you think this is? What a great, wonderful, unprecedented, astonishing sign—of what thing, or of how great a thing! Since the beginning of time [Col. 0619D], it has not been heard that a virgin conceived, that a virgin gave birth, and that after giving birth she remained inviolate. Therefore, in the Blessed Virgin Mary human nature receives certain pledges, as it were, or first-fruits of its future incorruptibility: the integrity of virginal incorruption.

Why, I ask, is one not able to live in this life without corruption, except because human nature is not conceived without corruption? For the root of our corruptibility begins to sprout from the very hour of conception. But behold, in blessed Mary that source from which it seemed to have sprouted is cut off. And we know indeed that, when the root is cut off, all subsequent fruit-bearing from it withers away. “Behold,” he says, “a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” Certainly, in saying that a virgin will conceive and a virgin will give birth, it is plainly shown that [Col. 0620A] both were to be pure: both the flesh that generated and the flesh generated.

Thus the son of this woman in childbirth alone could, in this respect, sing a new song to the Lord: “I was conceived without iniquities, and my mother conceived me without sins.” It is therefore evident that he came for the destruction of sin who, at his very entrance into the world, did not contract the stain of sin from maternal flesh but erased it. If his conception alone had such power as to remove the tinder of concupiscence and the root of all corruption, what, I ask, could his birth, humility, circumcision, manner of life, patience, obedience, passion, crucifixion accomplish toward the expiation of his body? If what occurred in one hour—or rather in a small portion of one hour—availed so much, what could the periods of so many years [Col. 0620B] devoted to the mystery of our redemption accomplish?

He who was able, at the time of his conception, by the infusion of his grace, to cleanse his mother’s womb—why should he not be believed able to cleanse, whenever and however he wills, those who have wished to share in that same grace? Why should he not be believed able to cleanse in any one of us that nature which in the Blessed Virgin he was able not merely to purify, but also to honor and glorify? For he glorified her in giving her something above nature. Indeed, in her he did something contrary to nature, something according to nature, and something above nature.

It was contrary to the nature of our infirmity that a virgin conceived. It was according to nature that, conceived and formed in the womb, he was finally born at the lawful [Col. 0620C] time of birth. It was above the nature not only of this infirmity of ours, but also of the condition of the first-created nature, that a virgin conceived without male seed. It belonged to purity that she was able to conceive without concupiscence; to honor, that she brought forth offspring clean from every contagion of sin; to glory, that she conceived not by a man but by the Holy Spirit.

Certainly, if our Emmanuel had wished to be born from both sexes, and reason required this, he could have purified both for begetting clean offspring. But if he had assumed flesh from both, he would surely have receded further from the likeness of his own proper nature and drawn less near to ours. For it would have been unlike his proper nature if he had a father and mother in his humanity, when in his divinity he had a Father alone. In this respect also he would have been less like us, if he had two fathers—which we cannot have. Sound reason likewise required that, just as there was one beginning in the propagation of our race, so there should be one beginning in its restoration.

Therefore the restorer of our race had to be born either from a man alone or from a woman alone. But if he assumed the female sex from a man, he who raised the female sex above the male would confuse the order of nature; and he would be called both Son in respect of divinity and Daughter in respect of humanity. But if both the sex he assumed and that from which he assumed it were male, then man would indeed have a twofold consolation of honor in this regard, while woman would have none.

Certainly, if he had wished to be formed from a man, he would have drawn his material from the substance of our flesh; but nature’s operation would have had no part in his incarnation, and thus he would have departed further [Col. 0621A] from the proper character of our nature. O how much honor and dignity he conferred upon women, and upon those born from women, in that the Creator of all and Savior of humankind chose to be born from a woman according to the manner of human birth! Thus he ought to be born from a woman, since, so far as reason allowed, he had to be made like his brothers in all things. But the reason stated above shows why he ought not to assume a female from the female sex. For, as was said, he would confuse the order of nature; and, with women’s consolation thereby doubled, the male sex would possess no corresponding singular privilege.

It should also be noted that God, foreknowing future things, [Col. 0621B] ordered the two sexes on either side in accordance with the fitness of two successive conditions. There, the weaker is produced from the stronger sex, when Eve is formed from Adam. So one condition follows another, and when the better is removed, the worse is introduced. The first was before sin, when man could stand manfully and act courageously. The second was after sin, when he had to live womanishly and serve in many ways the enticement of the flesh.

Here, conversely, the stronger is begotten from the weaker sex, when the second Adam is generated from another, as it were, Eve, who truly is the mother of all who truly live. Thus here one condition rises after another, and the better succeeds the worse. The first, indeed, is before the resurrection, [Col. 0621C] in which one must often fall, often rise again, and waver womanishly. The second is after the resurrection, when a human being will be able to remain immovably in the integrity of his or her perfection.

And just as it is believed of the lower sex in the Virgin that there was a time when she could sin and a time when she did not fear sinning, so in the first condition every elect person fears falling before death, but after death does not fear a fall into sin at all. And just as the stronger sex in Christ could not sin at all, so in the second condition humanity will never fear sinning.

It should also be noted concerning the mother and her offspring that in the mother the flesh was cleansed, while in the offspring it was not cleansed but clean; in her it was purified, in him pure. Thus in the first condition our nature is purified; in the second it is found wholly [Col. 0621D] pure. In the former it is sanctified; in the latter it is glorified. The first, therefore, is of purification and sanctification; the second, of purity and glorification. Thus in the mother we have a sign of our purification and sanctification; in the offspring, a sign of our future purity and glorification.

Yet we can observe a sign of both conditions in the Virgin Mother alone: a sign of our purification when she still had something that needed cleansing; a sign of our purity when, after the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit and the extinction of the tinder of sin, she remained in her purity.

## Chapter XIII. On the Sign of Recovered Dignity

Behold, we already have one sign in the mother; we have [Col. 0622A] another in what is said of her offspring: “And his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7). Certainly, according to the Evangelist, this prophecy is fulfilled in Christ. Therefore he is called Emmanuel. But I ask: is he so called nominally or substantially?
