Who, however, calls him Emmanuel merely as a name, rather than Jesus, as the angel taught? Therefore this is not said nominally but substantially. Now Emmanuel means “God with us.” If this has been said substantially and truly, then it is truly and substantially so. Therefore this child of ours is substantially God and is substantially with us. But if he is substantially with us, it follows that he is both God and man.

But what will the Jews say here, or what can they say? [Col. 0622B] Can they prove from the testimony of any Scripture either that their child was nominally called Emmanuel, or that, by the profession of any sect, he was substantially called Emmanuel? Or what sense could that name have, so that God might be said to be with them because of that child? How, then, is God with them? By the presence of his majesty, or by participation in grace?

But what great matter is it for God to be with human beings in the way in which he is with demons? For he is essentially everywhere, and nothing can escape his presence. Or perhaps he was not with the holy Fathers through participation in grace until their child began to exist under his presence? Who but a madman would say, or presume to say, this? Yet, unless I am mistaken, neither will they dare say [Col. 0622C] that he himself received a more abundant grace than all those before him, or that others received it because of him.

What, then, will be said? On what ground will God be believed truly and substantially to be with us through the presence of this child, as was said, unless it is as all Christians confess: through the union of his nature and ours into the unity of one and the same person? Rightly, therefore, is he called Emmanuel, rightly “God with us,” since in the unity of our nature he is demonstrated to be true God.

Listen also to how the Evangelist agrees with the same judgment: “Therefore the holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). Behold how he is God. But how is he God with us, unless as another Evangelist explains when he says that “the Word was made and dwelt in us”? (John 1.) If the Word was made flesh, if the Son of God was truly incarnate, you perceive, I think, how truly God is with us—unless perhaps you suppose that God’s Word, God’s Son, is something other than God. But hear the teacher: “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (ibid.).

Behold again a great and wonderful sign, one that can truly be the sign of a great and marvelous thing: that the Son of God should become the Son of Man; that the Lord of majesty should become a participant in our infirmity. Who, then, would despair—or rather, who would not rightly presume—that through God a human being can and ought to become a participant in divinity, if God, for human beings’ sake, became a participant in our humanity? Otherwise Christ emptied himself in vain, taking the form of a servant and being found [Col. 0623A] in appearance as a man.

Now therefore, if God for humanity’s sake became the Son of Man through birth, why should not humanity, through God, far more become the child of God by adoption? Behold how that condescension of divine humiliation was given as a sign of our future exaltation. Nor should this be passed over carelessly: our Emmanuel became God with us not only by assuming our nature, but also by sharing the dwelling-place of our pilgrimage.

But why, I ask, did God accompany humanity even into exile, except in order to call humanity back after himself to the kingdom? Therefore we have a most certain sign of our return to our homeland: that familiar companionship of divine cohabitation in this our pilgrimage. Certainly, all who preceded Christ’s time descended after death to the barriers of hell. Behold exile after exile, captivity after captivity: “What man,” he says, “shall live and not see death? Shall he deliver his soul from the hand of hell?” [Col. 0623B] (Isa. 88.)

Therefore, to remove fear of so great a captivity and dread of future condemnation, our Emmanuel was given to us as a sign, displaying for us, as was said, familiar companionship. For behold: after Christ’s passion and resurrection, no one among those predestined to life is believed to descend into hell. Behold for what liberation to be hoped for, behold for what fear to be removed, the sign of which we speak was given.

O how much more beneficial! O how much more salutary was the sign given for redemption from diabolical captivity [Col. 0623C] than for deliverance from the hand of the king of Syria and the son of Romeliah! This is the sacrament which demons had to remain ignorant of; this is the mystery which it was not expedient for faithless Jews to know.

## Chapter XIV. On the Sign of Recovered Blessedness

Behold, we already have sign upon sign. Yet a third still remains: “He shall eat butter and honey” (Isa. 7). If you understand what you read, if you recall what you hear, you quickly perceive how great and profound a mystery it is, and the sign of how marvelous a thing: that the child who is truly God with us, he who is truly God’s only-begotten Son, should eat and drink and voluntarily subject himself [Col. 0623D] to human necessities.

He whose glory we saw, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father—he is said to eat butter and honey. Behold, that awe-inspiring power shared with human beings and beasts in eating and drinking, though he is above the angelic powers. If, therefore, the Lord of angels for human beings’ sake became a participant in beasts, why should not humanity conversely, through him, far more become a participant in angels?

“He shall eat butter and honey.” Why does he not rather say bread and flesh? For he could have said that truly as well. Perhaps the one who expressed these particular things wished to intimate something through them. What, then, are honey and butter but the delicacies of flies? And, indeed, the one belongs to unclean flies, the other to venomous ones; for bees bear a sting and have venom. See how they labor or fight for honey, so [Col. 0624A] that they often even lay down their lives in the wound. Butter, as you know, is the fat of milk; and we certainly know how flies, through excessive gluttony, throw themselves into and immerse themselves in milk, sometimes even losing their lives.

Our Emmanuel, therefore, ate butter and honey, and for our sake descended even to participation with flies. Was it really too little for God, for humanity’s sake, to share with beasts, unless he also shared with flies for their sake? Let Jews hear it; let Christians hear it; let all hear it. Behold, one person of the Trinity became a participant in flies for human beings’ sake. Who, then, will henceforth despair that a human being can become a participant in eternal delights, if the Lord of majesty, as was said, descended for humanity’s sake even to the delights of flies?

Behold how greatly he emptied himself for [Col. 0624B] our sake, he who voluntarily subjected himself to such need. But this self-emptying of our Redeemer, as was said, was given as a sign and a most certain proof of our future fullness. Behold, alongside the threefold promise you have also a threefold sign: one in the mother, two in the offspring. Here, the integrity of the virgin; there, the humiliation and self-emptying of the divine offspring. You now see also, I think, how this threefold sign corresponds directly to the threefold promise.

It was promised to the Jew: “O death, I shall be your death; O hell, your bite” (Hos. 13). It was promised to the Christian: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15). As a sign of this promise—and as a kind of pledge of the gift—each receives the integrity [Col. 0624C] of virginal incorruption.

It was promised to the Jew: “In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ it shall be said to them, ‘Children of the living God’” (Hos. 1). It was promised to the Christian: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. 5). As a sign of this promise, each receives the humiliation of his Redeemer, namely, the assumption of our infirmity.

It was said to the Jew: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35). It was said to the Christian: “I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, that you may eat and drink at my table in my Father’s kingdom” (Luke 22). Each receives the sign of this gift in the self-emptying of supreme majesty. Behold how that threefold promise is confirmed [Col. 0624D] in this threefold sign: incorruption is the sign of incorruption, humiliation of exaltation, self-emptying of future fullness.

## Chapter XV. To What Lowly Knowledge God Descended for Humanity’s Sake, Who Assumed Experience of Both Our Goods and Our Evils

To what has been said—“He shall eat butter and honey”—there is immediately added: “That he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7). Is it then to be believed that by eating he acquired any knowledge of that kind? Certainly it is not I, but the prophet, who says this. It is not ours to distort the prophetic meaning, but to investigate it; and, if explanation is granted, to explain it; and what we cannot penetrate, at least to venerate.

[Col. 0625A] But a contentious Christian says to me: If Christ, God’s Word, was God’s wisdom, how could he acquire in time some knowledge which he did not have before? A Christian asks this; I too ask the Christian how Christ “learned obedience through the things which he suffered” (Heb. 5). For the Apostle says this too; who can contradict it? Let him tell me how Christ learned obedience from the things he suffered, and I shall tell him how, in a certain respect, he acquired some knowledge which, in that same respect, he did not previously have.

A Jew says to me: You say that your Emmanuel was God. Since it is written, “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has been with him always” (Ecclus. 1), how did he receive any knowledge in time? But let the Jew tell us how the forbidden tree was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and then perhaps together we shall discover what he seeks.

Certainly, the tree of life received its name because, by the nature implanted in it, it had the capacity to preserve the life of those eating from it. But nothing similar should be believed concerning the tree of knowledge. Otherwise, through eating it, human knowledge would increase rather than decrease. Thus it furnished not the effect of that thing, but the occasion. For before the forbidden eating, humanity knew good things through both understanding and experience; but it knew evils not at all through experience. Yet through eating the tree it came to that knowledge of evils which is by experience.

Likewise, there were certain needy and lowly goods, to the use of which humanity descended by sinning, [Col. 0625C] and the experience of which it had previously, more happily, not known. So too Christ, after emptying himself and taking the form of a servant, became obedient to God the Father; and through experience he learned what previously he did not know by experience. In this sense, through the use of eating, he learned what difference there is between the evil of hunger and the good of refreshment. By eating butter and honey, he likewise began to learn what it is for one created in the likeness of God to be likened to flies. By experience he learned how unworthy are the things which that noble creature of God commonly suffers, and thereby how one ought to sympathize with it or have mercy on it. For, as the Apostle says, he had to be made like his brothers in all things, “that he might become merciful” (Heb. 2).

Therefore, by eating, in a certain respect he could know what in that same respect he had previously not known. Certainly, after his resurrection our Emmanuel is recorded to have eaten honey: “They offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb.” What he ate before his passion and resurrection was for refreshment; what he ate after the resurrection was for dispensation alone. Thus what he ate before the resurrection could contribute to the rejection of evil; for evil is known not only from its own quality but more fully and perfectly by comparison and contrast with good. Eating for refreshment, therefore, could serve for the rejection of evil and also for the approval of good.

But it was not said there, “that he may know to reject evil and approve good,” but “to choose good.” To choose is properly to distinguish the best among good things. Therefore that eating after the resurrection was for choosing the good, in which he proved what was best. There, by experience, he proved the difference between the condition in which infirmity compels eating for bodily refreshment and that in which charity consents to eat solely for dispensation.

But because evil, as was said, is more fully known by comparison with good, and good for the same reason by comparison with the best, that eating of the risen one availed not only for rejecting evil, but also for approving good and choosing it. Thus Christ attained the fullness of that knowledge which is by experience when, after the glory of the resurrection, he ate with the disciples.

Certainly, as was said above, the first Adam is known to have fallen into this experience of evils or needy goods by eating; behold, the second Adam is known to have descended into the same experience by eating.

## Chapter XVI. That through the Lowly Knowledge He Assumed He Acquired for Our Nature the Fullness of Surpassing Knowledge

Behold to what lowly knowledge, and how lowly, God descended for human beings’ sake, when he assumed experience of both our evils and our goods. Yet in that very act he acquired for our nature not only that knowledge which the first human being lost, but also that which humanity could have acquired, not by eating what was forbidden, but by abstaining.

Certainly, before the guilt of transgression, humanity knew by experience [Col. 0626C] what the joys of paradise were like. But humanity did not yet know by experience what the joys of heaven were like. Humanity knew what it was to be in a place of delight; it did not know what it would be to exist in the glory of eternity. Did humanity not recover the former when humanity heard from the God-Man: “Today you shall be with me in paradise”? (Luke 23). Did humanity not also deserve to receive the latter, sublime knowledge, through the God-Man, when the God-Man, lifting up his hands, was borne into heaven; and, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings? (Ps. 67.)

Humanity received the former after Christ’s resurrection; it received the latter after Christ’s ascension. Our Emmanuel, therefore, as was said, through that first, lowly knowledge acquired for our nature this final, sublime one. But if by eating he attained the former, did he not also attain the latter? Certainly, because he attained the latter through the mediation of the former.

Therefore, of the same thing we should understand what is said there: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 2); and what we read here: “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7). Does not Scripture seem silently to intimate this, when it says here that something came through eating which there was falsely promised could come through eating?

Christ received this sublime and surpassing knowledge in his ascension, when he entered for ever into his glory. Attend to what is said, how we read there: “And while eating with them,” he says, [Col. 0627A] “he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem”; and, a few words later, it is added: “While they were watching, he was lifted up” (Acts 1). Behold, he ate and ascended.

By eating, Adam fell from that sublimity which he could have possessed into this lowly and abject knowledge. By eating and ascending, our Emmanuel laid aside this lowly knowledge and seized that sublime one. You say that Christ had to suffer, rise from the dead, and so enter into his glory. What if we say that Christ had to eat, ascend, and thus lay hold of that sublime knowledge of which we have spoken? You say that Christ’s passion was of such merit that, by the power of his patience, he deserved to enter into all fullness of glory, or to bring others into it. What if we say that it was of such weight before God that our Emmanuel ate butter and honey, that he even shared with flies, that by the merit of his humility he should now rightly enter into all fullness of knowledge himself, or bring others into it? [Col. 0627B]

But what was said—that our child learned by eating to reject evil and choose good—should not be understood as though he had acquired knowledge that comes by experience from eating alone. For the Apostle also says that Christ learned obedience in the things which he suffered (Heb. 5). But did he learn it only from what he suffered, and not also from what he did himself? Indeed, certainly from both these and those, because in both he carried out not his own will but the will of the Father.

So he learned what he had not previously known by experience not only by eating and drinking, but also by hungering and thirsting, without excluding any other mode of experience. And by eating, indeed, he learned not only from consuming butter and honey, but from the consumption of every food. Thus this could have been said of other foods as well as of butter and honey. But divine Scripture intentionally left some things unsaid which it could nevertheless have said truly; and from the many things that could have been said, it chose those which it recognized should be expressed uniquely for the sake of a definite mystery.

Why, then, does it say that through eating there came to this man what was falsely promised to the first man could come through eating, except that we may understand that here there was ground for merit—or even remedy—where there was unquestionably guilt? [Col. 0627D] You see, certainly, how our deceiver lost again through the seed of the woman the gains of his deceit which he had acquired through the woman.

Would that the Jews might at last awaken! Would that they might at last become wise and understand that this is the woman, and this her offspring, concerning whom the Lord said to the serpent: “I will put enmities between you and the woman, between your seed and her seed!” (Gen. 3). Why do they not understand that this seed of the woman exercised the foretold enmities and gained victory, when they hear that through eating he advanced to that from which it is clear that the first human being fell away at the serpent’s persuasion? Behold how the judgment of our assailant has been wholly reversed by this man. Whatever the former fraudulently took from humanity, the latter restored more abundantly. Therefore, from the character of the sign, one may readily discern that through it we are to be delivered from the captivity and oppression of the devil.

## Chapter XVII. That in the Passion of Our Emmanuel Many Were Taken Captive from among Malignant Spirits

But how is one to understand what is immediately added to these things: “For before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land which you detest shall be abandoned before the face of its two kings” (Isa. 7)? What it says, “before he knows to reject evil and choose good,” has the same force as if it said: “Before our Emmanuel rises and ascends into heaven.” For, as has already been said, before he rose from the dead [Col. 0628B] he did not receive the fullness of that knowledge which is by experience, nor that knowledge which through it he acquired for our nature.

Why, then, does it say that before our Emmanuel’s resurrection or ascension their land had to be liberated from the presence of two kings, when it is clear that it had been liberated not only before the resurrection but even six hundred years or more before his birth? But what is known to have preceded his birth is consequently known to have preceded his resurrection. If we say that what the prophet says is true in this sense, the Jew will nevertheless maintain that what is said is frivolous. But in the words of so great a prophet, just as nothing false is believed to have been present, so neither is anything frivolous.

But what if we say in response that the Holy Spirit intentionally veiled the depth of so great a mystery beneath a kind of foolishness of the letter? Thus, even if it appears frivolous in the sense in which it is called frivolous, it will nevertheless not be frivolous in that for whose sake it is so said.

Yet if we wish to understand kings here such as those of whom we read in Daniel, there will indeed be something in the prophet’s words which neither Jew can refute nor Christian dare deny: “And now,” he says, “I shall return to fight against the prince of the Persians. And when I departed, behold, the prince of the Greeks came” (Dan. 10). Who, however, does not see that malignant spirits must here be understood in these princes? Therefore we can—indeed, I think, absolutely must—understand kings of this kind here, unless perhaps one is troubled because here they are called kings and there princes.

But it should be observed that the same one who is called prince of the Persians is named above king of the Persians: “Behold,” he says, “Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I remained there beside the king of the Persians” (ibid.). Likewise, he who in the Gospel is called the prince of the world (John 12) is elsewhere in Scripture called king over all the children of pride (Job 41).

Kings of this kind presided over those who, whether in Syria or Samaria, served idolatry. Nor do I say that such kings are mystically designated here by the king of Syria and the son of Romeliah; rather, they themselves are properly and historically expressed in these words: “The land,” he says, [Col. 0629A] “shall be abandoned before the face of its two kings” (Isa. 7). Nothing is said here that seems to compel you toward another meaning. It does not say, “before the face of these two kings,” but “before the face of its two kings,” lest the reference oblige you to look back to what precedes and understand the kings already mentioned.

It does not say that these kings will be killed in their own land; it does not say that they will be taken captive; it does not say that anything will be done to them by the hand of the king of the Assyrians, as you read in what follows: that the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria will be taken away before the king of Assyria. It says none of these things, nor anything of the kind that could not be understood concerning the kings of spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

Scripture is indeed so understood to speak of certain kings that what is said can be applied both to spiritual and carnal kings, so that in one and the same thing there is both something by which unbelief is made foolish and something by which faith is enlightened. The ambiguity of the letter itself veils the truth. Conversely, the depth of the sacrament, the authority of prophecy, and the gravity of the sentence lead faith along the path to truth and compel it to enter.

For who does not see, given the dignity of the mystery in what has been said, that the things added contain something great and ought to correspond to the promises? Let us therefore see what Scripture declares concerning kings of the kind of which we have spoken, and we shall see how fittingly what is said corresponds to the foregoing.

It says, then: “Before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land shall be abandoned before the face of its two kings” (ibid.). Certainly, in the Book of Judges, when Jephthah speaks to Sihon, king of the Amorites, that land in which a demon was worshiped as a god is called the demon’s possession: “Are not those things which Chemosh your god possesses rightfully due to you? But those which the Lord our victorious God obtained shall pass into our possession” (Judg. 11). Why, then, should the spirits of error not be called the kings of that land, when through the teaching of unbelief and perversity they ruled there until Christ’s time?

For kings of this kind, evil and malignant spirits, some are called spirits of error, others spirits of fornication. Many kings of this kind were taken captive in Christ’s passion and finally cast down from their tyranny—those, namely, who among malignant spirits possessed greater cunning and bolder audacity than the rest; [Col. 0629D] those through whom the salvation of the people from whom the primitive Church was to be gathered and the harvest of faith propagated could be impeded, so that that divinely designated harvest of propagation might be gathered into the divine granaries, of which we read in the Gospel: “Look upon the fields, for they are already white for harvest” (John 4).

## Chapter XVIII. That, as a Sign of General Condemnation, a Certain Captivity of Demons Began in Christ’s Passion, Just as a Glorification of Those Who Rose Again Began in Christ’s Ascension
Something of this sort we have in the Gospel, where the Lord said: “Now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John 12). Behold, from where was he cast out—but, I ask, to where was he hurled? But to where more fittingly is he believed to have been hurled [Col. 0630A] than to the place designated through John in the Apocalypse? “And he seized,” he says, “the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, and shut him up, and set a seal over him, so that he should deceive the nations no more until the thousand years are ended; and after these things he must be loosed for a short time” (Rev. 20). What he here calls “the abyss,” he later calls “the lake”: “and the devil,” he says, “was cast into the lake of fire and sulphur” (ibid.). It is concerning this abyss that the demons beseech the Lord in the Gospel not to command them to go into the abyss (Luke 8).

Behold how, in the head of all the wicked, the captivity of demons was begun when, in Christ’s Passion, the ruler of the world was cast out of the world and sent into the abyss. And just as [Col. 0630B] Christ is believed not to have risen alone from the dead—for, as it is written, “many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose and appeared to many”—so, I say, as Christ is believed not to have risen alone, neither is he believed to have ascended into heaven alone. For “ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men.” Therefore, as Christ, the head of all the good, did not rise alone or ascend alone, so the devil, head of all the wicked, is believed not to have been cast out of the world and hurled into the abyss alone.

Concerning the number of those who were taken captive with the ruler of the world in Christ’s Passion, those are rightly believed to be meant of whom it is now said: “The land shall be forsaken before its two kings” (Isa. 7). How will the land in which they had long [Col. 0630C] ruled be forsaken by them, unless because they will be cast out of it and sent into the abyss? That this was accomplished in Christ’s Passion is fulfilled between his birth and his ascension, because it is said: “Before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land shall be forsaken.” Before the child, through experience, knows not only to reject evil or approve good, but also to choose good and, setting lesser goods aside, to lay hold on the best—before he ascends to heaven and by experience learns what it is, and how greatly it surpasses earthly pleasures, even by bodily presence to preside over heavenly joys and take part in the choirs of angels—before, indeed, this choice of goods, the land which King Ahaz abhorred shall be forsaken before its two kings [Col. 0630D].

For this, as has been said, occurred in the Passion; that occurred in the Ascension. And note what is said: “Because,” he says, “before the child knows.” It is as if he said: I said that the Lord will give you a sign, and that it will truly be a sign of your future deliverance. But before it is wholly completed, that which will be a sign of eternal captivity in the devil and his angels shall occur. For, just as in Christ’s ascension, and in the ascension with him of others, the liberation and exaltation of captives was begun, so likewise in the casting out and hurling down of the devil and those falling with him, the captivity of captors was begun. And just as the glory that went before in the head of all the good, or in a part of his members, is a sign of the general glorification, so the overthrow that went before [Col. 0631A] in the head of the reprobate and in a part of his members is a sign of the general damnation.

And it should certainly be noted that, just as in the general resurrection the rejection of the wicked will occur first and afterward the glorification of the righteous, according to the saying, “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26), so around the time of the first resurrection certain firstfruits of demons were first taken captive, and afterward the firstfruits of the elect were glorified.

## CHAPTER XIX. How, through the incarnation of our Emmanuel, God became as one of us.

Behold, brothers, what the Virgin’s childbirth bestowed; behold what the incarnation of our Emmanuel accomplished. This is the child who alone did not take away his mother’s integrity [Col. 0631B], but consecrated it. In this child God was made with us; through this child the human race recovered what it had lost in the first parent of all. By this child he who had previously cast down was cast down; by this child he who had previously been cast down was raised up. In this child humanity recovered its honor: he is the one who removed our reproach.

“But what reproach?” he says. “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48). Now man was made in the image and likeness of God: a great honor. But man did not understand and therefore despised it. Having despised and rejected the likeness of God, he transformed himself into the likeness of a beast. Behold what disgrace: [Col. 0631C] the greatness of the dishonor corresponds to the greatness of the honor. Hence reproach; hence insult. And justly, indeed, “the reproaches of those who reproached” fell upon him. Therefore he rightly cries: “Remove from me reproach and contempt.”

Let man weigh God’s mercy, if he can. Despised by us, he could not endure our contempt. Rejected by man, he could not bear the reproach of the one rejecting him. Man rejected the divine likeness according to which he had been formed; immediately God conformed himself to that human likeness into which man had transformed himself. O what a restoration of honor! O what a wiping away of reproach: that one transformed into the likeness of a beast should now have God like himself! Behold, to erase our reproach, God the Son of God became for us Emmanuel [Col. 0631D], eating butter and honey, so that according to the likeness of men he might know how to reject evil and choose good.

Let the old reproach therefore now cease; let that ancient insult cease. For behold, I hear one of the three persons in the Trinity uttering a voice of reproach: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us.” You reproached him rightly, certainly; but will you still reproach him? Certainly, if you say ironically that man became as one of us, henceforth we shall say as confidently as truthfully that God became as one of us. That was said deservedly as a reproach; let us now say this with thanksgiving. That was spoken in the voice of one reproaching and reviling; let us now speak this in the voice of exultation and confession.

[Col. 0632A] Behold what the offspring of our woman in childbirth—the only-begotten son of Mary, Mother of God—bestowed upon us. Rightly it was said, and rightly it is to be said: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.” Blessed was the conception, and blessed also the birth, of our Emmanuel born from her, in whom God undoubtedly became like us.

## CHAPTER XX. How man became as God, and how true man became true God.

For this purpose God became as a man, knowing how to reject evil and choose good: that man might become as God, knowing good and evil. But how does God know good, or how does he know evil? He knows evil by complete understanding without any experience; but good by complete understanding and everlasting [Col. 0632B] experience. In evil, experience is inaccessible to him; in good, his experience is undisturbed.

But man will come to know good and evil in this manner when, confirmed in good and perfected in joy forever, he will no more be able to sin than he will fear death or suffering. For “death shall be no more, neither mourning nor crying; nor shall there be pain any more, because the former things have passed away”; but everlasting joy shall be upon their heads (Rev. 21; Isa. 25).

But what wonder is it if man has become as God, when man has become true God? Certainly, if the man Christ is God—or rather, because he truly is God—he has the same divinity that the Father and the Holy Spirit have, and therefore the same power and therefore the same wisdom. [Col. 0632C] Thus the man Christ knows in the same manner as the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, what was said ironically of the first Adam, the Father and the Holy Spirit may now say declaratively of the second Adam: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil.”

That voice of reproach has now been turned into material for praise. Behold, we now dare to say that man has become as one of us by reason of his divinity; God has become as one of us by reason of his humanity. Behold what the fruit of the Virgin, the fruitfulness of virginity, bestowed upon us; behold what it accomplished for us. Rightly it was said, rightly it is to be said: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb.”

## CHAPTER XXI. How that reproach of the reproacher—“Behold, Adam has become as one of us”—has been turned into material for praise.

[Col. 0632D]

Behold, it has been shown by truth that what was first said of the first Adam as a reproach can now be said of the second Adam. But what shall we say of that same first man, conformed to Christ’s glory and glorified in Christ, according to what is written: “Who shall refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory?” (Phil. 3). Adam, therefore, thus glorified and transformed into a divine likeness, will he not truly be as one of those from whom he heard in reproach: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us”? If Christ is one of the three [Col. 0633A] persons in the Trinity, will not he who is conformed to Christ’s glory be as one of them?

Let irony now cease; let it now be said declaratively. It was said in reproach; let us now say it in glorying and glorifying the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: from whom, through whom, and in whom was accomplished all that was accomplished for our sake. Say, impious Zebulun, what use is your fraud now? Greater is what Christ’s mercy has bestowed upon us than what your deceitful malice took from us. Behold, man has become as God, knowing good and evil—which you deceitfully promised. Behold, man has become true God—which indeed you could not even have conceived.

Say then, say, impious Zebulun, what use to you now is that former bloody victory of yours? Behold, once victor, you now lie defeated by Christ’s victory. You deceived the woman and through the woman cast [man] down; and behold, deceived in a woman and cast down through a woman, you have fallen. Behold what enmities the seed [Col. 0633B] of the woman, the fruit of the Virgin Mother, exercised; how it fought, conquered, and triumphed. Let us all say to her, each one of us: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (Luke 1).

Let no one wonder; let no one be indignant that we have expanded so brief a subject with a lengthy exposition, prolonged the discourse, multiplied words, refuted objections with such sustained care and careful vigilance, established the things that ought to be held, and strengthened the judgment of truth on every side. Let no one, I say, be indignant or wonder when he sees that the prophet laid the foundations of our faith in very few words. Whenever the mystery of the incarnation is considered, examined, and commended by holy teachers, writers, and preachers, this authority is always adduced as an argument. And certainly, if the structure of our faith is not founded upon the firm ground of truth, that which is built upon it cannot be stable [Col. 0634B].

If what we have said does not suffice for our defense, I shall add something further that may suffice. The subject is certainly sweet; we have leisure; and it delights us to speak at length upon a sweet subject.

# BOOK TWO  
## In which Hugh and Richard are introduced disputing

[Col. 0633]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0633B]

After that treatise which I had composed and published concerning the Virgin’s childbirth, or the infancy of our Emmanuel, against the error of certain persons [Col. 0633C], I encountered one of Master Andrew’s disciples, whom I found still entangled in the same error. My mind therefore burned to add something further to what I had already said, so that I might satisfy even the weakness of those who seemed, under this contagion of error, to have labored almost to despair.

I believe that devout minds will greatly approve my applying my small powers with such diligence to so excellent a subject, and gladly laboring to remove error from so immeasurable a depth of so great a mystery. I have arranged the whole sequence of the following work in the form of a dialogue, because this mode of speaking or teaching is, above all others, either more pleasant to hear or more effective in persuading. I have therefore introduced one of Master Andrew’s disciples disputing with me, so that in the form of reasoning, with the alternation of questioning and answering preserved, whatever might come into doubt would be better clarified.

Let no one be disturbed if he sees me explain one and the same passage of Scripture in different ways, since he knows that this is frequent and well established among interpreters of Holy Scripture. For I wished first to set forth the interpretation above concerning the two kings because it appears to approach more closely the exposition of certain great men. But finally I chose to set forth that interpretation to which my own mind inclines more strongly. The reader’s judgment is left free to choose what he considers more correct.

## CHAPTER I. A preliminary survey of the subject treated in this work.

[Col. 0634B]

**HUGH.** Having examined that treatise which you wrote concerning Emmanuel’s conception [Col. 0634C] or birth, I found very much in it pleasing. Nevertheless, to speak the truth, it could not entirely satisfy me. For the subtle reasoning of our controversy has indeed brought me from a fixed position to an uncertain view, but it could not establish me in the assertion of the contrary side.

**RICHARD.** I think, my Hugh, that the effort of our intention has achieved something if it has now brought you from obstinacy to an uncertain position. For it is far more tolerable to doubt an assertion of truth than confidently to uphold falsehood. Yet I was both exceedingly amazed and indignant that you—that intellect of yours—could be entangled and almost inextricably ensnared by so thin a spider’s web. This entanglement of yours was undoubtedly the chief cause that compelled me to write in refutation of this nursery of error. I feared, certainly, that the error which could ensnare you would involve others; and behold, what I feared has occurred. For afterward I encountered another of your master Andrew’s disciples, whom I found ensnared by the same noose of error that had formerly ensnared you.

**HUGH.** I do not know with what face you call a spider’s web that which you cannot sufficiently tear apart with all the efforts of your contrivance. But lest anyone judge that I seek contentious verbal battles to a quarrelsome end, I am prepared to explain the matters that move me, to accept clear reasoning in all things, and to yield to reason. And, to state my mind more fully, out of reverence for so great a sacrament, I am more ready—I say, more ready—to be conquered by truth than to conquer sophistically and act contentiously.

**RICHARD.** It greatly pleases me, brother, it pleases me that, even if late, reverence for so great a sacrament touches you. But I now await hearing from you yourself what those matters are that should or can justly move your mind.

**HUGH.** First, the arguments by which you attempt to convict what you call an error still trouble my mind, since they appear weak and insufficiently necessary. The arguments which you bring forward to commend the giving of the sign, however, are pleasing enough when considered by themselves. But if we consider the context of the text, they appear to have no bearing whatever on the matter. For the interpretation which you put forward concerning the choice of good seems forced to me, and that which you offer concerning the two kings rather far-fetched.

**RICHARD.** I do not know what it is that you say pleased you in our treatise, when you criticize almost everything we said. But you must explain more fully each of the things that move you, if you seek from us a sufficient answer to each.

**HUGH.** I am grateful for your proposal.

## CHAPTER II. How the stated prophecy cannot truly be understood except of the blessed Virgin Mary alone.

**HUGH.** First, then, this still presses upon my mind: that a sign was to be given in order to remove fear, as the Lord proposed through the prophet. Behold, we grant what you say: that the king’s refusal to ask for a sign arose from great malice; and consequently such a king thereafter became unworthy to receive a sign intended to remove fear, because, as you have taught above, he preferred to remain longer in trembling anxiety under the danger then threatening than to let occur that by which the glory of the Lord might be increased. Behold, I say, let us grant these things to be true; nevertheless, it does not follow that God repented of his promise.

For often where wickedness abounds, grace abounds more exceedingly. Therefore, out of superabundant grace, he could give the promised sign even contrary to the king’s merit—he who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. But a virginal birth, as you yourselves admit, could not have been a sign of the deliverance then sought. Therefore, what is proposed to King Ahaz for the removal of fear, and promised and given to the house of David, so that it may be a sign of the matter for which it was to be given, is rightly understood as said concerning the prophetess and nonetheless fulfilled in the blessed Virgin Mary, lest anyone think us Judaizers and in error.

For what is written, “You shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. 12; John 19), was indeed spoken concerning the paschal lamb; nevertheless, according to the Evangelist, it was fulfilled in Christ.

**RICHARD.** I ask you this: do you believe that any woman other than the blessed Virgin Mary alone conceived as a virgin and gave birth as a virgin?

**HUGH.** Of another woman I certainly neither believe that it has happened nor hope that it will happen.

**RICHARD.** Then the saying, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son,” is not rightly understood as spoken of the prophetess.

**HUGH.** You would say this correctly if you read “virgin” in the Hebrew at this place. But you have surely already heard that what is read in Hebrew here does not have the same meaning as “virgin” [Col. 0636A].

**RICHARD.** So far as we can see, whatever we cried out in the preceding treatise, we spoke to deaf ears. Therefore we shall indeed cry out with a yet louder voice, if necessary, in case your deafness may thus be broken. Tell me, I beg you, from what do you perceive that the prophecy of which we speak was fulfilled in the blessed Virgin Mary?

**HUGH.** Since the Evangelist states this plainly, who but an unbeliever would dare deny it? “All this,” says the Evangelist, “happened in order that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled, saying: ‘Behold, a virgin shall have in her womb and bear a son’” (Matt. 1).

**RICHARD.** What you said was spoken by the Lord through the prophet and fulfilled in the blessed Virgin, I would have you repeat in a louder voice.

**HUGH.** O by how just a judgment of God you have incurred the mark of deafness which you so unjustly tried to fasten upon us! Raise your ears, then, and hear one shouting if you cannot hear one speaking: “Behold, a virgin shall have in her womb.”

**RICHARD.** I certainly demanded repetition and shouting from you, not in order to break our deafness, but yours. Have you not yet perceived with the ear of understanding what you yourself repeated? Why are you now silent? Why do you not, as usual, answer immediately?

**HUGH.** I swell with anger and indignation against myself, because I remember reading and hearing these things so often and now perceive that I had not perceived them at all. For, just as I understood and believed that the prophecy was fulfilled in the blessed Mother of God because the Evangelist declares this, so I ought to have understood and believed that the woman in childbirth of whom we speak was called a virgin by the Lord through the prophet. For the Evangelist affirms this also.

**RICHARD.** Since in place of what the prophet says—“shall conceive”—the Evangelist puts “shall have in her womb,” why, I ask, does no one accuse the Evangelist of lying and contend that it is not so written in Hebrew?

**HUGH.** Because in both places there is one and the same substance, although the words differ.

**RICHARD.** The same must certainly be held where *alma* is used in Hebrew and *virgo* in Latin. The Latin language has no single word that expresses the full force of the word *alma*; nevertheless, it is never customarily said of a married woman, never except of one who is a virgin. Therefore the one who said, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” or “Behold, a virgin shall have in her womb,” considered only the force of the meaning and wished to express it as he could or ought.

**HUGH.** Behold, I willingly accept that *alma* is said only of one who is a virgin; I willingly defer in this matter to the Evangelist or to blessed Jerome, especially since this answers the Jew. For the only thing that, according to his view, could have been found able to serve as a sign—namely, that his woman in childbirth should conceive at the first approach of a man to her—has no support unless he grants that the prophet designated a virgin by his words.

**RICHARD.** You do well chiefly to grant this because it answers the Jew.

**HUGH.** As it seems to me, you think you have accomplished something; but do not glory too soon.

**RICHARD.** Listen, then. Above you said that the prophecy of which we speak was spoken concerning the prophetess and nonetheless fulfilled in [Col. 0637A] blessed Mary. If, therefore, you say that to conceive as a virgin means becoming pregnant at the first approach of a man to her, and that this is what the prophet meant, then either the prophecy will not have been fulfilled in the blessed Virgin in this sense, or she conceived through the first approach of a man to her and not through the Holy Spirit. In either case you make the Evangelist a liar, since he affirmed both.

But if you confess what you cannot deny except falsely—that to conceive and give birth as a virgin is to conceive without male seed and to remain a virgin in conception and childbirth—then either the stated prophecy cannot be understood of the prophetess, or you make the prophet a liar, since he describes her as having conceived from his seed.

**HUGH.** These arguments should undoubtedly suffice for a Christian; but they do not satisfy a Jew, who neither receives the Evangelist’s testimony as authoritative nor agrees that blessed Mary conceived without male seed.

**RICHARD.** You do well, my brother, in seeking hiding places for your evasion now under the shelter of Christians, now under that of Jews.

## CHAPTER III. After an argument that satisfies a Christian, another is given which ought to satisfy a Jew.

**RICHARD.** But listen further to what, even if it does not satisfy the Jew, ought nevertheless to suffice to satisfy him. Does not the Jew, I ask, agree with you that this conception and birth were given by the Lord as a sign?

**HUGH.** In this he certainly agrees with me, and I with him; and if you dare deny it, we produce the prophetic testimony.

[Col. 0637C]

**RICHARD.** You who say that conceiving as a virgin means this occurring in the first intercourse: can you, I ask, prove that this is contrary to the law of nature or outside the range of repeated experience?

**HUGH.** Not at all.

**RICHARD.** By what reasoning, then, I ask, can it be said that it ought to be a sign of anything, if it promises that a woman will conceive at first intercourse—any more than if it foretells that at sunrise a hare will run or a dog will bark, when these things can occur indifferently every day, every hour, in different regions?

**HUGH.** Here I give the Jew room to answer for himself.

**RICHARD.** I ask you again, and the Jew together with you, whether you believe that any woman can conceive by a man and remain a virgin.

**HUGH.** Certainly not.

**RICHARD.** How then can it be said that some virgin conceives by a man, when, even though she conceives in her first intercourse, she loses at that very moment what she was before conception, namely, her virginity?

**HUGH.** According to the Jew, it is said that she conceives as a virgin because he finds her a virgin at the hour of conception.

**RICHARD.** But if he finds her a virgin at the hour of conception when having intercourse, does he likewise find her a virgin at the hour of giving birth?

**HUGH.** Far be it from us to say or in any way believe this!

**RICHARD.** Certainly both things were said of the Virgin: “She shall conceive” and “she shall bear.” It was not said, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and a non-virgin shall bear”; rather, it says, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” See how carefully, see how providently, the Holy Spirit forestalled malicious hearts and stopped the mouths of those speaking iniquity. What answer do you have here, I ask, on the Jew’s behalf?

**HUGH.** I reply that I am not a Jew and have no necessity to answer for him; here again I give him room to answer for himself. But if you wish your assertion to be capable of gaining the victory, you must prove either that the sign in the Virgin’s conception and birth was not given to remove fear, or how an event to occur after so many ages could remove the fear then pressing.

**RICHARD.** You do well to ask what you do not know, although you ought to have known this very matter from what has already been said and written.

## CHAPTER IV. How the authority of the Book of Kings proves that the Virgin’s birth was not given in order to remove fear.

**RICHARD.** But if you will not yield to reason, will you at least yield to authority?

**HUGH.** I have already said in part why I have not accepted your arguments. I am ready again to hear whether what you propose can be proved by authority.

**RICHARD.** Let it meanwhile be granted that God gave such a sign as he judged sufficient to remove fear. Should God be thought capable of being deceived in his judgment?

**HUGH.** Far be it!

**RICHARD.** Therefore, if he gave the sign in order to remove fear, he removed the fear. If he did not remove it, he did not give it in order to remove fear.

**HUGH.** Nothing is truer than this argument, nothing at all clearer.

**RICHARD.** Let us therefore consult the Book of Kings on this point, so that we may understand what judgment is to be made from it. The Book of Kings relates in these words: “Then Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel went up to Jerusalem to wage war” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 16). And again, after a few intervening words: “But Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, saying: ‘I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who have risen against me.’ And when he had gathered the silver and gold that could be found in the house of the Lord and in the king’s treasuries, he sent gifts to the king of the Assyrians” (ibid.).

Certainly, if he had not been afraid, he would not have so humbly asked for help to secure his safety. Certainly, if he had not been afraid, he would not have exhausted his own treasures and those of the Lord’s house on such gifts. Say, then, if you can, when that promised sign was given. If before the gift, the gift itself proves that it did not remove fear; if after the deliverance, how could it remove a fear that no longer existed? Or perhaps between the giving of the gift and the deliverance? But who would say that it was given by the Lord at a time when both the giver would give in vain and the recipient receive in vain?

**HUGH.** I do not wish you to labor further over this argument. I see that it conflicts both with reason and with authority to interpret what is written concerning Emmanuel as referring to Isaiah’s son, or to suppose that he himself was given as such a sign and, as it were, in order to remove fear.

**RICHARD.** Behold, you have now understood how your master’s reasoning conflicts with both reason and authority. Do you wish also to hear how it conflicts with itself?

**HUGH.** Do not call it my master’s, but the Jews’. For he sets it forth not as his own but as theirs.

**RICHARD.** Let this very point be asked of the interpretation itself: whether it is his own or another’s.

**HUGH.** Behold, I am ready to hear what you wish to say.

**RICHARD.** Let your master’s words, then, be brought forward. He sets them out in this manner.

## CHAPTER V. How the cavillers’ controversy is contrary to itself.

**RICHARD.** “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” And then, speaking in his own person, he adds: “This most manifest prophecy concerning the conception and birth of our Savior, and the integrity and perpetual virginity of his Mother—the ever-Virgin—when we expound it concerning these matters as is right, the Jews, enemies of truth, rising against us, endeavor to shake the most firm wall of our faith with the battering ram of their cavilling.”

But from other words of his it can be understood more fully with what simplicity he says this. At the end of his argument he gives the reason why it is not useful for him to answer the Jews: “Lest perhaps,” he says, “we enter upon an uncertain contest with unequal strength and succumb.” Why does he call it an uncertain contest when the prophecy is not merely plain but, as he himself declares, most plain? Perhaps, however, these are words of humility. Let us see what follows.

“We,” he says, “having measured our own strength, and leaving stronger matters to the stronger, shall pursue the explanation of the literal sense already begun.” Behold, he now promises us an explanation of the literal sense. He now sets forth not the Jews’ judgment but his own, as you hear. Thus he says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son. When you see the conception and childbirth of the young woman, or hidden maiden, it will signify to you that you are delivered from the fear predicted.”

Behold how he expounds that most manifest prophecy, which he had said concerns the conception and birth of the Savior, and the integrity and virginity of his Mother. Let us hear more plainly still. After much intervening matter, he says much later in what follows that the prophetess’s son will eat butter and honey when he comes to the knowledge by which he can abhor evil and choose good. Yet what we read concerning the eating of butter or honey is undoubtedly written of Emmanuel. What then? Will this be the most firm wall of our faith if Emmanuel is called the prophetess’s son?

Certainly blessed Mary alone among women is both virgin and mother. If, therefore, the stated prophecy, as he pleases, is most plainly about the integrity and virginity of her who is mother, it is most plainly true in the blessed Virgin Mary and most plainly false in the prophetess. Why then, in expounding it, does he apply it where it is most plainly false rather than where it is most plainly true? If those who expound it concerning the Savior and his mother do what is right, why does he expound it concerning the prophetess, as is not right? You surely see how his exposition is contrary to itself. Would he not have philosophized more correctly had he kept silent about these things?

**HUGH.** I confess, I wish he had not said it! But, as he himself admits to us, he expounded many things not according to his own judgment but according to that of the Jews.

**RICHARD.** He certainly ought to have determined this explicitly: when he was presenting his own and true view, and when the Jews’ and false one.

**HUGH.** I now await hearing from you what you already proposed: how those arguments which he put forward under the Jews’ name appear contrary to themselves and to destroy one another by reciprocal blows.

**RICHARD.** It would be far too long to treat every point; but I should like to select some of them and clearly demonstrate from them what you ask.

## CHAPTER VI. How the arguments set forth under the Jews’ name appear contrary to themselves.

RICHARD. After many preliminary remarks, he adds and says: “In the days of the infancy of the son of the virgin, or young woman, the two kings at whose presence Judah trembled died: one slain by the Assyrians, the other slaughtered by Hoshea son of Elah.” Behold, the sign came first, and the event followed. Again, elsewhere: “Most plainly,” he says, “Holy Scripture speaks of the Lord, who cannot lie, as saying that before the child whom the prophetess bore to Isaiah knows how to call his father and mother, Damascus and Samaria are to be destroyed by the Assyrians.” Attend here: according to the former view, Emmanuel was born before the death of Pekah. For, as has been said, the event followed and the sign came first. According to the latter view, in the ninth year after Pekah’s death, Isaiah’s son did not yet know how to call father and mother. For King Hoshea succeeded King Pekah, and in the ninth year of his reign Samaria was destroyed by the Assyrians. Therefore the son of Isaiah who, at the time of Samaria’s destruction, did not know how to call father and mother will be one person; and Emmanuel, who according to the former view was then plainly nine years old or more, will be another. [Col. 0640C]

Again, in a much later passage your master says: “They also consider this part of the sign: that, being in infancy—which ordinarily rejects none of the things set before it—after impure things have been refused as filth, he will take as food only clean foods, understood synecdochically under butter and honey.” If, then, this was part of the sign, and the sign preceded the event, let us grant that he was at least one year old when he received this ability to distinguish foods as a sign of the future deliverance. Accordingly, Samaria was overthrown in the tenth year of his age. If, then, they say that Emmanuel is the same person as Isaiah’s son, how can one and the same person be so knowing that, in the first year of his life, he knows how to distinguish clean from unclean things, yet so foolish that, in the tenth year of his life, he does not know how to call father and mother? Hear this also. Certainly Hezekiah succeeded King Ahaz in the kingdom; in the sixth year of his reign Samaria was destroyed. How, then, will they show that he saw as a child one who, in the sixth year after his death, did not know how to call father and mother? How, therefore, according to the logic of their argument, could a child whom the king had never seen and never would see be a sign to the king of any event? From these things, I think, you perceive how troubled and precarious is the contest which your master did not dare to undertake.

HUGO. Take care lest you err by supposing that he said these things otherwise than ironically.

RICHARD. You defend your master cleverly enough; but, without realizing it, you act against yourself in doing so. For where is that little intellect of yours—not to be rated even above the strength of a fly—if it could become so entangled in what he wove, as it were, ironically?

HUGO. Now, as it seems to me, you believe that you have achieved something great because you have been able, only at times and with the greatest labour, to untangle the things which my master, under irony, or I, for the sake of argument, proposed.

RICHARD. Good: what you formerly defended stubbornly, you now call irony. “With what knot shall I hold Proteus as he changes his forms?” But since you see yourself hard pressed, it is not very surprising if, by whatever evasions you can, you seek a way of escape.

HUGO. We must not detain the day with speech, for there are still many matters here which impel my mind to inquiry.

RICHARD. Before we move on to examine other matters, we want you to admit [Col. 0641B] whether it still truly remains established in your judgment that the one called Emmanuel is not Isaiah’s son, nor was he himself given as a sign in order to remove fear.

HUGO. Whether he be Jew or Christian, anyone who hesitates further on these points shows himself to be out of his mind.

RICHARD. Then inquire in due order whatever you wish. For in examining each matter which you propose, you shall find me ready, insofar as the Lord grants it. For the prophet seems, in the matters now before us, to have laid certain foundations of our faith; and therefore it will be laborious to treat with the utmost care each individual point worthy of inquiry.

HUGO. What you say is very satisfactory.

## CHAPTER VII. Of what matter the birth proposed by the Lord may fittingly be called a sign

[Col. 0641C] HUGO. As I said above, the things we have said about the character or commendation of the sign are quite satisfactory when considered in themselves; but they seem in no way to cohere with the surrounding text and therefore to have no bearing on the matter.

RICHARD. Do you think, pray, that this must or can everywhere be observed in the prophets: that whatever is said in them, wherever it may be said, must be fitted to what precedes and follows?

HUGO. I know that both things are common in the prophets: subsequent material sometimes coheres with what precedes, and sometimes does not. But although this coherence of statements cannot be observed everywhere, it does not follow that it ought not to be observed here. For when a sign has been proposed for a definite matter, see how absurd it is suddenly to say that a sign is displayed for another matter—indeed, for a matter of which no mention is made.

RICHARD. We have already said, and you heard, that this was done for the sake of concealing the mystery; and that ought to suffice you.

HUGO. No one can persuade me that it was difficult for the Holy Spirit, who spoke in Isaiah, to touch secretly upon the matter of which the promised child could be a sign, while nevertheless concealing the inner meaning of his mystery beneath some covering of words. Nor, if what I say is granted, will it nullify what you said about the multiplicity of the sign; rather, it will establish it. For one and the same sign can be manifold and can signify many things. Indeed, thus what I demand of you will be, so to speak, for the foundation, while what you said above will be for the superstructure.

RICHARD. At last we must comply with your insistence—if I may not say obstinacy—and satisfy your wish as one would a delicate child. Recall, then, what those kings who had come to attack Jerusalem proposed, and what the Lord consequently promised through the prophet: “Let us go up against Judah,” they say, “and stir it up, and tear it away to ourselves, and set a king in its midst, the son of Tabeel.” And the Lord replies to this: “It shall not stand, nor shall this be” (Isa. 7). For what purpose, pray, do you think they joined together to attack Judah?

HUGO. I would certainly have said: to enlarge their kingdom, had they not at once proposed to substitute another king there. Therefore they seem to me to aim and labour more at overthrowing divine worship than at enlarging their kingdom. “Let us tear Judah away to ourselves,” they say. From where, pray, and to where? From where, I say, unless from that in which Judah differed from them? Or to where, unless to that in which they themselves were one? They certainly accepted a plurality of gods; in this they unanimously agreed, and in this very matter were of one confession. But Judah differed from them precisely in this: that according to its confession it ought to worship one true God. Therefore they seem principally to strive to overthrow among them the worship of the one God, and to do so in such a way that nothing might remain from which it could again spring up. “Let us tear away,” they say: it is one thing to tear away and another to cut off. Certainly, when a tree is cut in its branches or trunk, its root remains, from which it may be restored. But when it has been uprooted, nothing remains by which it can be restored. Therefore, those who attempted to tear Judah away from the place of its fidelity, so to speak, into participation in their infidelity—what else did they intend but irreparably to overthrow among them the worship of the true Divinity?

RICHARD. You have seen all this very shrewdly, and nothing now occurs to me for which you ought justly to be reproved. Those who wished to tear Judah to themselves and ensnare it in their error desired, therefore, that the worship of the one true God should be erased from humankind—Judah being then the only people among humankind holding this confession. The Lord promises concerning the abolition of this worship when he says: “It shall not stand, nor shall this be.” Henceforth, he says, and for ever, it shall not be that Judah is torn away and the worship of the true Deity erased from humankind. What is here promised concerning Judah is elsewhere promised in other words concerning the Church: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16). As no one can prevail against Judah in uprooting God’s worship, so no one can prevail against the Church in overthrowing the catholic faith.

HUGO. I perceive what you mean. But I think that the words “this shall not be” can be understood in two ways. When the response, “this shall not be,” is made to the foregoing words, “let us tear away,” it can be understood particularly, that Judah will not be torn away by them; or generally, that it will not be torn away in any manner or at any time.

RICHARD. Which of these two, then, seems greater to you?

HUGO. Since that promise is particular—or rather singular—and this one general; since that is for a short time and this perpetual: this is incomparably greater than that.

RICHARD. Beyond doubt, the Lord promises what is greater, and, to confirm this promise, he proposes a sign when he says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear” (Isa. 7). [Col. 0643A]

## CHAPTER VIII. How it may be discerned for what matter a sign was not given, or how it was given to persons by whom it was never seen

HUGO. I certainly see that the general promise, as we have said, is incomparably worthier than the remainder; and the worthier it is, the more fitting it is to divine condescension. But I would like, if possible, to have from Scripture itself a basis on which I might infer that the sense which you prefer ought to be preferred.

RICHARD. This request of yours seems quite reasonable to us; for it is the custom of Holy Scripture frequently to intimate in one place what it leaves unsaid in another. Therefore, from the sign proposed to confirm the promise, the point you seek is easily determined. For the birth of a virgin, which was to occur after so many centuries, could not have been a sign of the matter then imminent. But that same virgin’s birth was so suitable and certain a sign of the other promise, which endures until the end of the age, from the time it began to exist and be known, that for more than a thousand years it has satisfied the desires of believers, and can satisfy them until the end.

Note also this feature in the prophet’s words, which, as you have now indicated, you wished to be present: how beneath a wrapping of words he concealed the depth of the divine mystery. For he framed his oracle in such a manner that the person to whom the promise was made could understand one thing, and he who made the promise another. For although King Ahaz was enabled to understand from the prophet’s words that the said kings could by no means overthrow his kingdom or substitute another king for him, the Lord nevertheless undoubtedly promises that his faithful people can be torn away from their fidelity by no persecution and at no time. The king, indeed, desired and hoped for deliverance from the imminent persecution by the two kings; but the Lord promised deliverance, both from the imminent and from the future persecutions of infidelity, whether of human beings or demons. And see by what a wonderful design: since the Lord proposed to do both, and would give a sign for both what he himself intended and what the king intended, if the king had wished to ask for a sign. [Col. 0643D] But because through great wickedness he refused to ask for a sign, the Lord displayed, as and when he wished, only that sign which he chiefly intended.

HUGO. How, pray, do we say that a sign was given by the Lord to those to whom it was promised—a sign, I mean, which was to occur after so many centuries and would never be seen by those to whom it was promised?

RICHARD. Certainly, the Lord promised Abraham the land of the Canaanites as an inheritance, yet Abraham received it only in his heirs. Nevertheless, no one contends that he did not receive the promised inheritance, or that the Lord failed in his promise. Abraham therefore received the promised land after nearly four hundred years in his heirs. The house of David received the promised sign after six hundred years in its successors. If that promise was worthy of so great an expectation, how much more was this worthy of a far greater one, through which man became God and God became man? Through that promise human beings became heirs of the land of the Canaanites; through this they became co-heirs of the angels. Through that the sons of Abraham became heirs of an earthly and transitory kingdom; through this the adopted children became heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.

HUGO. I see that you have answered all my questions so completely that, concerning the chapter proposed, nothing further occurs which I ought to ask.

RICHARD. Let us compare what we have just said concerning the sign given by the Lord with the things said in the preceding discussion. According to this interpretation, we hold that the faithful people can in no way and at no time be torn away from the good of fidelity. According to that interpretation, we maintain that it will again be planted in the place of delight and rooted immovably in the good of blessedness. From this we have that it cannot altogether lose the good which it recovered through the Saviour’s grace after the first sin. From that we maintain that it will fully recover everything which it lost through the wickedness of the deceiver. According to what has now been said here of the stated sign, we are secure regarding the stability of grace received. According to what was said there of the same sign, we are secure regarding the fullness and perpetuity of glory to be received.

## CHAPTER IX. That “the choosing of good” is customarily understood in different ways

HUGO. I confess that I now begin to hear you not only willingly [Col. 0644C] but eagerly; and, since what has been said on these points is sufficient, I should like you to proceed to examine the other matters which trouble me.

RICHARD. Propose what you wish, and you shall find me ready according as my powers suffice.

HUGO. As I said above, the interpretation which you offer concerning the choosing of good seems to me far too forcibly extracted; and likewise the one you offer concerning the kings seems somewhat strange. You maintain that the choosing of good means selecting the best among good things. From this you consequently endeavour to show that our Emmanuel, according to that knowledge which comes through experience, did not have a choosing of good until his resurrection, since through experience he did not until then know the good of immortality, impassibility, incorruptibility, and the good of heavenly and supramundane delight—the best goods of the outward person.

RICHARD. What, according to your view, ought “the choosing of good” to mean?

HUGO. Certainly, not merely selecting the best among good things, but also separating and accepting good things from evil ones.

RICHARD. Nor do we deny that it is customarily spoken of in this sense. For, according to common usage, we often extend, restrict, or otherwise vary the meaning of words. But amid these possibilities, the diligent reader must examine cautiously and gather from the accompanying circumstances what, how, and according to what sense ought to be expounded in each place. There must indeed be some difference between approving good and choosing good. The former belongs to discernment; the latter to deliberation. It belongs to discernment to separate good things from evil and to approve the former while rejecting the latter. It belongs to deliberation to select from good things those which are better, or which are more advantageous to each person. Therefore we cannot justly be reproved because we have used the proper sense of the word rather than the latitude of ordinary speech.

## CHAPTER X. How it may be discerned that the words, “The land shall be forsaken before its two kings,” were not said of King Rezin and Pekah

RICHARD. Yet we proved the interpretation which we gave concerning the kings by producing the example of Daniel. And an interpretation confirmed by the authority of the Scriptures is surely never deservedly reproved.

HUGO. Certainly, if there you understood the kings, according to the ordinary custom, historically; and if you extended allegorically that interpretation of yours concerning spiritual kings, it would indeed please me, and, I believe, ought deservedly to please everyone.

RICHARD. Behold, in this matter too we shall endeavour to satisfy your desire. For that text, as we believe, admits another exposition, one to which, to tell the truth, our own opinion comes closer.

HUGO. Then you ought rather to have given that interpretation than the other.

RICHARD. Rather, in order that those who stand opposed and attack us with their quibbles may be confounded, it is necessary both to have given that interpretation and not to omit this one, so that they may see and blush to find that we discover several reasonable ways out where they think to enclose us with their arguments, where they think that no way of escape lies open either to themselves or to us.

HUGO. Do not, I beg you, keep my mind in suspense through prolonged expectation. I should like to hear more quickly what I ought to think about these kings.

RICHARD. We first wish to hear from you what you think about them.

HUGO. I understand without doubt none other than Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah.

RICHARD. Add also this: what is the land which King Ahaz hated, of which those two designated kings are said to be kings, and which is foretold as to be forsaken before them?

HUGO. I marvel how easily you have led me from a settled to an uncertain opinion by a single, simple question, and made me notice what I ought to have noticed before but had not. For whether this is said of the land of Syria or of the land of Israel, he hated either of them, since he was wickedly attacked by both; yet neither of them had two kings, so that it could properly be said of it: “Before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land which you hate shall be forsaken before its two kings” (Isa. 7). [Col. 0645D]

## CHAPTER XI. That by these two kings we should not understand the two who still remained in the kingdom of Israel

HUGO. But now it occurs to me what those may say who think Emmanuel is the same as Isaiah’s son.

RICHARD. And I should like to hear what that is.

HUGO. Certainly, those of Israel and those of Judah descended from the same stock and ought to have been of the same confession. Therefore those who were of Israel and served under Pekah ought, both by the obligation of kinship and by the obligation of their confession, not to attack but to defend their brothers, the sons of Judah; and whenever necessary they ought to have set themselves as a wall against the king of Syria or against any attackers whatever. Thus King Ahaz, if I am not mistaken, principally hated the land over which Pekah ruled; and the more abominable he felt its wickedness to be toward himself, the more detestable he considered it. Now we know that only two kings of the Israelite kingdom still remained until its destruction: Pekah, who then bore the sceptre, and Hoshea, under whom it was to be destroyed. Therefore, I think, the Jews can not inappropriately refer what is said about the two kings to these kings, who shortly thereafter would no longer be able, either in themselves or in their heirs, to rule or defend that land detested by King Ahaz, because it was to be laid waste before the promised child—whom they think Isaiah’s son—knew how to call father and mother.

RICHARD. If what the preceding discussion established had not slipped your mind, this interpretation which you propose would have no place.

HUGO. What was that?

RICHARD. Certainly, if their child had been born in Pekah’s time, at the overthrow of the kingdom he was, if not older, nearly ten years old; and how shall we say that the child did not know how to call father and mother? But if he was born under Hoshea, then only one king remained in the Israelite kingdom; and it could not be said of him that “before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land which you hate shall be forsaken before its two kings.” [Col. 0646C]

HUGO. I am ashamed to have said it, and now I do not see what I ought to think concerning these kings, unless we say that the prophet puts one number for another, and that by “land” we must understand both the land of Israel and the land of Syria.

RICHARD. Unless we give what the prophet has set down here concerning these lands, or their spiritual kings, according to some manner of expression, there will be no interpretation at all.

HUGO. It is now time, if you please, to explain that interpretation of yours to which your mind, as you say, inclines more closely.
