For it does not seem plausible to me that the prophet here used one number in place of another, confusing the number on one side in one and the same statement while carefully expressing it on the other. For in speaking of the kings he even expressed the number when he said: “Before its two kings.”

RICHARD. Let it be done as you request.

## CHAPTER XII. That in the two kings are understood not merely two persons, but a double succession of kings according to a twofold mode of reigning

RICHARD. But first, if you please, I should like to hear from you how you understand what you hear in the prophet: “If these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, should be in its midst, they in their righteousness shall deliver their own souls” (Ezek. 14). Do you understand only three persons in these three men?

HUGO. Not at all; rather, a threefold class of people living according to those men’s manners.

RICHARD. What do you say of what you read in the Gospel: “Two shall be in one bed” (Luke 17)?

HUGO. Here too I understand in the same way two classes of people.

RICHARD. What if we understand what is said about the two kings in the same sense?

HUGO. Certainly we need not reject that sense here either, if we see the surrounding matters agree with it.

RICHARD. We certainly know that the land of Israel had a king in a twofold manner: at one time, so to speak, lawfully; at another time, adulterously. Lawfully, from the tribe of Judah and Davidic stock; adulterously, from any other tribe. The former was according to God’s institution; the latter according to usurpation. For in kindness he instituted the first manner; in anger he permitted the second. When those of Israel had a king according to the first institution, they reigned over them and over Judah together; but when they held the kingdom according to usurpation, they reigned only over them, not over Judah. Therefore, concerning such kings it is foretold to King Ahaz about the land which, as you taught above, he principally hated: “Before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land which you hate shall be forsaken before its two kings” (Isa. 7). This is more plainly stated thus: Before the child, insofar as he is a child, begins to gain experience of our evils and goods and to possess knowledge gained from such experience, the carnal kingdom in Israel will begin to fail; and henceforth it will never come to pass that they have a king either from the tribe of Judah or from any other tribe of their own people. For around the time of the birth of our Emmanuel, the kingdom of Israel passed to a foreigner. For Herod had already assumed imperial authority among the Jewish people. [Col. 0647C]

## CHAPTER XIII. How the failure of the Israelite kingdom is foretold, and why it is transferred to a foreigner

RICHARD. It should indeed be noted what the prophetic utterance foretells for the future and on what occasion it threatens such things. At the very time when both kings—namely, the one of Israel and the one of Judah—had broken forth into such great and manifest hatred of divine religion, there is foretold, I say, what displeased both and what each judged hateful. For true religion was so hateful to the king of Israel that, as we taught above, he contended against his own brothers more for the overthrow of divine worship than for the enlargement or enrichment of his kingdom. But to the king of Judah, as is proved in the preceding discussion, it is found to have been so hateful that he preferred to tremble in fear of imminent danger rather than receive the sign of his deliverance, prudently indeed but wickedly guarding against the Lord’s doing what would redound to His glory and advance the confirmation of His worship. Therefore, since both kings acted wickedly toward God, what is plainly hateful to both is rightly foretold as future. For it was hateful to the king of Israel and those of Israel that the succession of kings among them would fail according to the latter manner; and [Col. 0648A] it was abominable to the king of Judah and those of Judah that they could not have a king according to the former manner. Therefore, while the king of Israel wickedly raged against King Ahaz, and King Ahaz wickedly rejected the sign of his deliverance, while both acted perversely toward God, the failure of the Israelite kingdom is foretold both according to the lawful and according to the adulterous order, so that it may thereby be understood through what fault royal power was transferred to a foreigner.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the failure of the Israelite kingdom and the advent of our Emmanuel may be discerned from one another

RICHARD. We must observe how these two things correspond mutually, so that each may be discerned from the other: the failure of the Israelite kingdom and the advent of our Emmanuel. For once a foreigner begins to reign in Israel, it is certain that the time of the promised child and of virginal childbirth is at hand. Conversely, once the childbirth of a virgin womb begins to be proclaimed, it is certain that the Israelite kingdom has come to failure and can never thereafter be restored to its former condition. More than a thousand years have certainly now passed since the virginal birth began to be proclaimed, and that desolation of the Israelite kingdom, which had already preceded it, continues to this day.

Note also how in this place the prophet leaves unsaid what the patriarch foretold, and conversely, how the patriarch left unsaid what this prophet foretells as future. For what this prophet entirely left unsaid concerning the failure of the kingdom in Judah, he foretells as future in the land of Israel: “The land,” he says, “shall be forsaken before its two kings” (Isa. 7). Conversely, what this prophet leaves unspoken concerning Judah is foretold by the patriarch: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49). It is one thing for a pre-eminence to be vacant for a time, and another to fail altogether. It is one thing for the succession of kings to be interrupted, and another for royal power to be transferred from one people to another. The sceptre is, of course, taken away when it is given to outsiders. Certainly, from the time that those of Judah were granted the bearing of the sceptre and the exercise of rule, no foreigner was anointed king over Judah until Herod, under whom our Emmanuel came into the world through virginal childbirth. Therefore, the sceptre was taken away from those of Judah when it was given to Herod and transferred to his heirs. Then Judah lost, with the thing itself, even the right of reclaiming it, when Herod possessed royal power without opposition and transmitted it to his heirs. You see, certainly, how at one and the same time there is fulfilled both what the patriarch foretold concerning Judah and what the prophet foretold concerning Israel.

HUGO. Although something still troubles me in this interpretation of ours, I am very pleased that it seems to agree with that prophecy which is now read throughout the world in Christ’s Church: “When the Holy of Holies comes, anointing shall cease” (Dan. 9).

RICHARD. Now attend also to how this final interpretation concerning the promised child answers, and how fittingly, to the preceding matters. [Col. 0649A]

## CHAPTER XV. How the choice of time agrees with the character of the person who comes

RICHARD. Therefore, after he has stated that the promised child will receive the name Emmanuel, and that he will undergo experience of our evils and goods and learn such knowledge through experience, he immediately adds that before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land which Ahaz hates shall be forsaken before its two kings. It is as though the prophet declared more plainly and said: See how great and what kind of person the promised one is, and then you will understand at how fitting and necessary a time he comes. Attend diligently and consider carefully how exalted, how humble, of what power, and of how great compassion the person to be given is. Of what exaltation, pray, of what power is the person in whom God is with us; the person whose dominion is upon his shoulder—the person, I say, whose dominion lies not in many thousands of subjects or an innumerable multitude of armies, but entirely upon his own shoulder. Likewise, of what humility and how great compassion is he who, forgetful of his exaltation and concealing the majesty of his power, by eating butter and honey descended for our sake to share the condition of flies, and willingly undertook experience of both our evils and our goods? What can the person in whom God is—indeed, the person who is God with us—not be able to do for us? What will he not be willing to do for us that pertains to our salvation, when out of compassion alone he descended to our sufferings? Behold, in these things you have how great and what kind of a person he is: endowed with power and inclined to compassion, he both can effectively benefit his faithful people and unquestionably wills to do so. Let us now see how the choice of time accords and agrees with the character of the person who comes. Let us see, then, when he came. Certainly, he came at the time when he was most necessary. He came when royal protection had failed among the faithful people. He came when both successions of kings had failed among God’s people, according to the twofold manner we have described: when, because of the wickedness of those reigning, the sceptre was taken from them and given to foreigners and unbelievers. Therefore, when human consolation and protection began wholly to fail among the faithful people, divine help overflowed, so that where wickedness abounded, grace might abound still more. Thus the reason for the promised person’s coming is given in the words: “Because before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land shall be forsaken before its two kings.” It is as though it were said openly: Therefore it will come about that a child will be given us who, according to his name, is God with us, because at his coming the land will be deprived of every royal protection, being forsaken before its two kings. [Col. 0650A]

## CHAPTER XVI. That from the hour of his conception he began to undergo and possess experience of our goods and evils
HUGO. I certainly waited a long time while you were speaking, so as not to interrupt your discourse before you had finished your sentence, although in this statement of yours concerning the kings there was something that prompted my mind to a question.

RICHARD. Here we are ready to listen, if you bring forward anything that ought rightly to move you.

HUGO. Certainly, if those two kings whom you designate—that is, the twofold succession of kings, one of which you call legitimate and the other adulterous—if, I say, this twofold succession of kings [Col. 0650B] had come to its final failure during Emmanuel’s childhood, before he had reached the years of discernment appropriate to his age, there would be nothing in the interpretation you propose which, as it seems to me, could rightly be criticized. But it is sufficiently clear that before the birth of our Emmanuel—indeed, even before his conception—royal authority in Judaea had already passed to a foreigner; for Herod had already reigned for some years before his coming. If, therefore, the prophet wished to designate the time at which the Israelite kingdom failed, why does he say: “Before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land shall be forsaken before the face of its two kings”? Or why does he not rather say: “Before he is born—indeed, before he is conceived in the womb—the land shall be forsaken before the face of its two [Col. 0650C] kings”?

RICHARD. Is this, brother, the matter that moves you, or ought rightly to move you? When, then, do you think that this child, concerning whom you have already heard much—when, I say, do you think that he first became a participant in that meagre knowledge of ours which comes through experience?

HUGO. I now see that my question is resolved; I now see what I ought to have foreseen earlier. But I considered this child too carelessly, as though he were merely one among the rest. Nevertheless, say what you proposed. I gladly hear what I do not at all fail to know, if perhaps, together with what I know, I may also happen to hear something that I do not know.

RICHARD. Tell me, then: when do you think our Emmanuel first became a participant in this meagre knowledge of ours?

HUGO. I know that Christ’s soul received, from [Col. 0650D] the moment of its conception, fullness both of wisdom and of knowledge; nevertheless, it came to perfection in that knowledge which is gained through experience by intervals of time.

RICHARD. Certainly, he advanced both in knowledge and in wisdom with the passage of time; but our question concerned the beginnings of his knowledge, not his progress.

HUGO. In this matter I am more ready to hear your judgment than to state my own.

RICHARD. Certainly, if Christ’s soul had fullness of knowledge and wisdom from the moment of its conception, it could not be ignorant of what was being done concerning his flesh or concerning himself.

HUGO. Nothing is truer.

RICHARD. Therefore, he who took the form of a servant, who came in the likeness of sinful flesh, undoubtedly learned by experience from the very moment of his conception, and knew what was the good [Col. 0651A] of sensibility and the evil of passibility, since he took flesh capable of sensation and suffering. Nor was he a participant only according to the flesh, but also according to the mind, in both our goods and our evils, without sin. For he had ordered affections, yet affections capable of suffering. This is attested by the fact that, when he saw the city, he began to weep over it; and that at the time of his Passion he began to fear and to be distressed. Thus, from the very beginning of the Incarnation he learned by experiencing, and by experience knew in one respect the evil of corruptibility and in another respect the good of incorruptibility: the evil of corruptibility with respect to punishment, the good of incorruptibility with respect to guilt. Therefore, as regards the expression of time and the truth of the statement, to say nothing other than, “Before the child knows to reject [Col. 0651B] evil and choose good,” is the same as saying, “Before the child’s conception, the land shall be forsaken before the face of its two kings.”

And note that, although he first said, “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good,” he does not repeat, “before he eats butter and honey”; nor does he say, “Before, by eating butter and honey, he knows to reject evil and choose good.” He says nothing that compels us to understand the times of his infancy, or that we cannot fittingly refer to the time of his conception.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the prophet chose a manner of speaking more suitable for concealing the mystery.

[Col. 0651C]

HUGO. According to the interpretation that I gave concerning the choice of good, your solution is sufficient. But according to the interpretation set out by you in the preceding discussion, it will not be sufficient.

RICHARD. Receive, then, another explanation which may suffice for both.

HUGO. I do not reject this one which accords with my own view, and I await hearing the one you propose.

RICHARD. As we have already said elsewhere, the prophet had to frame his oracle about this child in such a way that, for a time, both who this child was, and why or when he was coming, might remain concealed; and nevertheless all this might, in its proper time, be known and proved from the same Scripture. Thus, in one and the same passage of Scripture, there would be found in a wonderful way both that by which unbelief might be blinded and that by which faith might be enlightened. Seek carefully from [Col. 0651D] this Scripture for what purpose this child is given as a sign, and you have why he came. Attend to the name imposed on him by the prophecy, and consider also that he was never actually called by that name, and you will understand who he was. Inquire more attentively when the land which Ahaz hated was deserted before the face of its two kings, and you will discover how the time of Emmanuel’s coming may be discerned.

For the purpose that what had been promised might remain hidden from those to be blinded, yet might become known in its proper time to those to be enlightened—namely, that the promised child was to be given as a confirmation of divine worship and promised as a sign of such a matter—after the preceding words, “Let us cut off Judah for ourselves,” there is not added, “It shall not be cut off,” as neither is there added, “It shall not be cut off from you”; rather, there is added that in which either may be understood, namely: “It [Col. 0652A] shall not stand, nor shall this be.”

Likewise, so that it might remain hidden from those to be blinded and become known to those to be enlightened that he who was promised would be both man and God, it was not said that he, conceived and born of a Virgin, was “God with us,” but that he would be called “God with us.” By a similar reasoning, so that the time of the divine coming might be foretold for the godly and yet hidden from impious human beings and demons alike, it was not said that before his coming the land of Israel would be forsaken by its two kinds of kings; rather, it was said: “The land which you hate shall be forsaken before the face of its two kings.”

From this ambiguity of expression it has come about that the Jews, even to this day, think that Emmanuel was promised as a sign of deliverance from the hands of Rezin and Pekah. Hence it has come about that some people think, [Col. 0652B] even to this day, that Emmanuel is the same person as Isaiah’s son. Therefore, for the sake of concealing the mystery, it was also done that it was not said, “Before Emmanuel’s birth” or “conception”; instead it was said: “Before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land which you hate shall be forsaken before the face of its two kings.” For if it had been said in that manner rather than this, it would beyond doubt have been evident that he could not be a sign of that deliverance which preceded not only his birth but also his conception. Therefore, by divine prompting the prophet chose to say what was more fitting to say for the purpose of concealing the mystery, and what was itself equally true. For what preceded [Col. 0652C] the time of conception undoubtedly also preceded the time of discernment.

HUGO. I see that you have fully satisfied me concerning the points that troubled me, so that for the present, according to the historical sense, I have nothing further to ask.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Jesus is understood to have advanced not only in age but also in wisdom.

HUGO. Yet I should like to hear from you, as something incidental, how the progress in wisdom which you touched upon above should be understood. For it seems to me altogether otherwise.

RICHARD. Since the Evangelist says this, who would dare deny it? “Jesus,” he says, “advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men” (Luke 2).

HUGO. But they say that he advanced only according to [Col. 0652D] appearance.

RICHARD. I ask you: was that appearance false or true?

HUGO. As it seems to me, false.

RICHARD. Did he also advance in age merely according to appearance?

HUGO. No, but in truth.

RICHARD. Good. So it pleases you that he should be said to advance in wisdom according to falsehood, but in age according to truth?

HUGO. I should not wish to dispute about this matter, but simply to listen and, by clear reasoning, to grasp what ought to be thought.

RICHARD. Say first whether it pleases you to adapt one and the same expression, in one and the same construction, to different meanings according to the historical sense.

HUGO. I know what I should answer if I could find another way of explaining it. But I do not wish to reject the view I presently hold until I find a better and more certain one.

[Col. 0653A]

RICHARD. Do you think, I ask, that knowledge of the virtues and skill in practicing them belong to wisdom itself?

HUGO. Certainly I do; indeed, I hold it as certain. Nevertheless, I know that Christ’s soul had, from the moment of its conception, both knowledge and efficacy of all the virtues, and received the fullness of both at once and in a single act. Hence I do not believe that he advanced, or could have advanced, in wisdom through intervals of time.

RICHARD. Certainly, from the beginning he had the efficacy of all virtues; but he did not display the effect of all of them at once, but dispensed each at its fitting time. He had skill in their exercise from the beginning, but he grew in experiential knowledge as time passed. From the very Incarnation he learned by experience what humility it was for the Lord of majesty [Col. 0653B] to bow himself down to assume the form of a servant. At the time of his circumcision and baptism, he learned by experience what condescension it was for one wholly free from sin to receive from the hands of sinners the sacraments of our salvation, without any benefit to himself. At the time of temptation, he learned by experience what discernment it was not to yield to diabolical suggestions, nor, while hungry, to serve appetite. At the time of his Passion, he learned by experience what perfection it was not to lose inward peace and tranquility of mind amid insults and terrors, and, while being crucified, to pray for his killers.

And, to state briefly what seems to us to follow from this: just as, according to the Apostle, “from the things which he suffered he learned obedience” (Hebrews 5), so in the same [Col. 0653C] manner he advanced in knowledge and advanced in wisdom.

HUGO. These points should suffice for the question I raised.

## CHAPTER XIX. What we ought to understand allegorically in the two kings mentioned.

HUGO. But since it has now been said what ought to be thought concerning the two kings according to history, it remains for you to say what ought to be thought concerning them also according to allegory.

RICHARD. As we see among men, so we may discern among malignant spirits: some preside over others; those who are craftier or bolder arrange the offices of their inferiors and exercise among them, as it were, certain rights of dominion. Such [Col. 0653D] kings acquire the right of lordship and rule over human beings as well, when people freely consent to them in crimes and shameful deeds. Thus, according to Daniel, one is called the prince of the Persians and another the prince of the Greeks (Daniel 10).

It should be observed concerning kings of this kind that, when people consent lightly and willingly to sin at their prompting, they acquire rule over them and the power of domination as if by a certain right of justice. But when, through excessive importunity of temptations and as if by force, they drive people toward a fall, then they seize rule over them as by invasion. This twofold distinction among such kings is rightly understood in those two kings of whom it is said to Ahaz: “The land which you hate shall be forsaken before the face of its two [Col. 0654A] kings” (Isaiah 7). For whether you conceive carnal or spiritual kings in that land which King Ahaz hated, some seemed to hold their kingdom justly and others unjustly.

We believe, moreover, that in the earlier treatise we spoke of this and taught there, on the same chapter, that many demons were captured in Christ’s Passion and banished from persecuting human beings; yet not demons of whatever kind, nor all demons, but those who were more effective in malice among them, and such as Scripture intended to designate by “kings”—namely, those through whom the salvation of many could be hindered, those from whom the primitive Church was to be built. Since, therefore, before the statement, “The land shall be forsaken before the face of its two kings,” there is placed, “Before the child knows to reject evil and choose good,” [Col. 0654B] if you wish to understand the choice of good according to the explanation which we have established, you will see all things converge upon the interpretation we set out there.

HUGO. Certainly I see it, and you need not labor further over this point. For if, as seems right to you, the choice of good is said to be the separating and grasping of the best goods from inferior goods, it will plainly appear that our Emmanuel, insofar as he was a child, advanced to the fullness of this knowledge, according to the measure of experience, through the resurrection and ascension. Before the resurrection, he knew by experience what a good the life of mortal flesh and passibility were. But he did not know by experience what the immortality and impassibility of the flesh were. Before the ascension he learned by experience what [Col. 0654C] life in the world was; but he did not know by experience what life in heaven was. He had first learned by experience what fellowship with human beings was; afterward he knew by experience what fellowship with angels was.

Therefore, because the child of whom Scripture speaks did not know by experience the best goods of the outward man before his resurrection, if, as seems likely, that captivity of demons took place during his Passion, Scripture rightly says of him: “Because before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land which you hate shall be forsaken before the face of its two kings.” But these matters have been discussed more fully in the earlier treatise; let anyone for whom this is insufficient seek them there.

RICHARD. You now see, we believe, under how deep an abyss of ambiguity truth is concealed, and [Col. 0654D] how difficult it is to draw forth unless it is sought by those who seek with faith and simplicity. Certainly, the height of the divine counsel ought thus to have been hidden from unbelievers and reserved for believers, so that there might be both something by which faith could be exercised and something by which unbelief could be blinded.

## CHAPTER XX. That, if possible, we ought always to keep this subject before our eyes and keep our minds intent upon its wonder by continual contemplation.

RICHARD. But now it is time to put an end to our overly prolonged discourse, unless perhaps something occurs to you that you wish to ask further concerning these matters.

HUGO. I confess that nothing occurs to me which I ought now further to ask, unless perhaps you have at hand something which can rightly be understood according to mystical interpretation concerning the food of our Emmanuel.

[Col. 0655A]

RICHARD. We would endeavor in this also to satisfy your wish, if we did not fear being accused of excessive length by those who cultivate brevity.

HUGO. Oh, how vainly we fear to spend time in study on that subject which, if possible, we ought always to keep before our eyes and keep our minds intent upon in continual contemplation!

RICHARD. What you say is unquestionably very true. We shall do as you wish, and first let us consider the eating of butter and honey.

## CHAPTER XXI. What is to be understood mystically by butter, and what such eating signifies.

RICHARD. Honey, as is said, comes down from heaven; butter, as we know, comes from flesh. Honey comes from heaven through dew; butter from flesh through milk. For what is butter but a kind of richness of milk, and what is honey but, so to speak, a kind of sweet-flowing thickness of dew? In milk, because of its sweetness, sweetness of heart is rightly understood; in butter, because of its origin, joy of heart is rightly understood. Butter is gathered from milk, and true joy of heart is generated from true sweetness of heart. The more we abound in milk, the more we can abound in butter. Thus, according to the abundance of kindness there will also be abundance of gladness.

If we consider Christ’s heart, nothing is sweeter than it, nothing kinder. Nothing among creatures could be sweeter than that heart, and nothing will ever be sweeter; no heart [Col. 0655C] rejoiced more abundantly than that heart. The true joy of our hearts is usually grounded in the testimony of conscience. “This,” he says, “is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1). The testimony of a good conscience in our heart is not to consent to desire. The testimony of conscience in that heart was to feel no desire at all. What was purer than that conscience, which felt no desire? What was sweeter than that heart, which no malice touched, which had and could have neither gall nor bitterness? According to the greatness of its sweetness, there was also in him a greatness of joy. Consider, if you can, how great was that heart’s sweetness, which such bitterness of Passion could neither disturb nor diminish. While suffering, he sympathized with his enemies more than he had pity on his own members. Above all others Emmanuel had a heart of flesh for compassion, because nothing was ever more tender toward every affection of mercy. Emmanuel alone could rejoice in the fullness and permanence of true sweetness; and this was for him, through milk, to draw butter from flesh and abound in it. For what other eating of butter was there in him than to enjoy, in continual celebration, the joy of inward sweetness?

## CHAPTER XXII. How supreme and inward delight may be understood in butter, and whence this food abounded to our Emmanuel.

This also should be observed concerning butter: no food is more pleasant than it for eating. Bread, fish, and other foods of this sort are first chewed and then swallowed. Butter, however, has neither hardness nor tenacity; thus it need not be chewed. And as nothing is sweeter than honey, so nothing is more pleasant than butter to eat. Ask taste, and you will find that nothing is sweeter for tasting; ask touch, and you will recognize that nothing is more pleasant for swallowing. Therefore understand in honey supreme sweetness, and in butter inward delight.

Do you wish, then, to know how our Emmanuel, from the moment he began to be human and in that wherein he was human, possessed butter—an abundance of inward delight—or how this itself abounded to him from the fullness of milk? Consider, then, these two qualities in milk. For milk is ordinarily of exceptional [Col. 0656B] whiteness and exquisite sweetness. Thus, indeed, milk of true goodness, if it preserves the quality proper to its nature, is accustomed and ought to possess these two things: namely, the whiteness of inward purity and the sweetness of complete goodwill—whiteness of purity in relation to oneself, sweetness of goodwill toward one’s neighbor.

That breast of the Lord, our Emmanuel, had milky whiteness in the integrity of supreme and inward purity, and milky sweetness in the fullness of supreme and inward mercy. In us, the foulness of desire sometimes lessens and sometimes removes this milky whiteness; the bitterness of malice lessens or removes the milky sweetness. But our Emmanuel experienced neither, nor could he experience either; and therefore he preserved the constancy of both in all fullness.

But we cannot, without great effort and much force, resist desire or repel malice and preserve uncorrupted the integrity of the milky liquid. For Emmanuel, however, whatever supreme purity or supreme mercy required was sweet and delightful. Therefore, in the rule of goodness, what is often hard and difficult for us was altogether sweet and delightful for him; and this was for him to gather and possess abundantly butter of supreme delight from the milk of true goodness.

But when this corruptible thing in us has put on incorruption, and this mortal thing immortality, then whatever is healthful and solely delightful because supremely praiseworthy will certainly also be sweet to us; and then there will be granted to us the full and eternal refreshment of that food, whose reception and enjoyment will be without all labor and any kind of weariness. What we shall receive in the life to come, he received in this life; what will be given to us at consummation was given to him from the moment of his conception. Thus he received, at the very entrance of this mortal life, the butter of supreme delight, the sharing of which we await in our glorification—not, as with us, in part, but in all fullness. We have now heard about butter; let us now consider honey.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On spiritual honey of supreme sweetness, and that Emmanuel was satisfied with such food from the moment of his conception.

RICHARD. Honey, as has been said, comes from heaven and descends from the heights to the depths; its sweetness incomparably surpasses every sweetness. But from what heaven do we think that honey descended, by which our Emmanuel was fed and nourished? We believe that “his going forth is from the highest heaven.” From the storehouse of the supreme Father that honeyed sweetness descended by which Emmanuel’s childhood was nourished. Undoubtedly, whatever sweetness, delight, and gladness the Father possessed, he instilled all of it into that Emmanuel. Behold from what heaven the dew descended by which that heart was watered. The Father rained dew, and he did not rain it alone: the Holy Spirit also rained it. The Father rained dew by begetting; the Holy Spirit rained dew by uniting. “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isaiah 45). The Father rained dew by sending him whom he begot; the Holy Spirit rained dew by inspiring him whom he united. For one and the same Emmanuel is begotten of the Father and conceived of the Holy Spirit: begotten of the Father according to divinity, and conceived of the Holy Spirit according to humanity; sent by the Father and anointed by the Holy Spirit. “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44).

Consider, if you can, what kind or how great this gladness was, and what shall we say—or what can we worthily say—of it? If you wish, it is oil; if you wish, it is honey. It is oil because it anoints; honey because it nourishes. Add also this, if you please: this honeyed sweetness was for him both food and drink. By it he was satisfied; by it he was inebriated. That whole torrent of delight was devoted to his use, and it is wondrous how one man—indeed, a little child—could absorb the whole of it. Others also drink and are satisfied from this torrent, but in their homeland; he drank from it even in his pilgrimage. “He drank from the torrent in the way; therefore he lifted up his head.” But, that you may wonder still more: this little child of whom we speak, who was given to us, was fed with honeyed and supercelestial sweetness before he was born. For when do you think our Emmanuel first began to eat butter and honey? Certainly from the time he began to be human; certainly from the very moment of his conception he was filled with the fullness of all sweetness and all delight.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How Emmanuel, strengthened by received blessedness, was confirmed in every good.

[Col. 0657D]

RICHARD. We have now heard how pleasant and sweet Emmanuel’s food is; let us hear also how useful it is. We have heard how much flavor it has; let us hear also what it confers and what power it possesses. “He shall eat butter and honey” (Isaiah 7). But for what purpose? “That he may know to reject evil and choose good” (ibid.). What shall we say to this? What sort of food is this, and what is its use, if such is the fruit of eating it? “That he may know,” he says, “to reject evil and choose good.” Certainly, it is the part of wisdom to know these things and the part of justice to practice them. Consider how great and what sort of this glorious one is, and what you ought to think concerning his food. What sort of child is he who advanced by eating at once in wisdom and justice? What sort of food is it which, by being eaten, advanced its eater in both wisdom [Col. 0658A] and justice?

Other people ordinarily advance toward these things through fasting, abstaining, groaning, sighing, and laboring; but he merited to attain the fullness of both through eating. We first learn in order that we may know; we know in order that we may act; we act in order that by our merits we may obtain eternal delights, so that at last we may be able to eat the butter of inward delight and the honey of supreme and everlasting sweetness. “I appoint for you,” he says, “as my Father appointed for me, that you may eat and drink at my table in the kingdom of my Father” (Luke 22). Thus, we first know in order that we may at last eat; he ate in order that he might know.

We are indeed first enlightened in order that we may be justified; we are justified in order that we may be confirmed; we are confirmed in order that we may deserve to be made blessed. From the moment he was human, according to that wherein he was human, he received the fullness of eternal blessedness. For according to that wherein he was God, he possessed it from eternity; indeed, from eternity he was full and perfect blessedness. Therefore, our child, who was made Emmanuel for us, received from the very moment of his conception the fullness of divinity and thereby the fullness of blessedness. Because he received full blessedness, he was confirmed in every good. Thus, what is last in us was first in him. Yet not first in such a way that one thing preceded and the other followed, but because no merit preceded the blessedness which he received.

Therefore, “he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good.” Do you wish more clearly to know how, from the blessedness he received, he was confirmed in every good? Do you wish, I say, to know how, from an abundance of delights, he was perfected in wisdom and confirmed in justice? Certainly, as we have already said, from the time he was human he merited to be satisfied with the butter of inward delight. Immediately and without doubt he experienced, approved, tasted, and loved inward peace, inward rest, inmost tranquility, security, and every delight of this kind; and the more fervently he burned in desire for such delight, the more fully and perfectly he rejected and held hateful its privation.

For what are bitterness of heart, disturbance of mind, unrest and weariness of spirit, except the deprivation of inward delight? Therefore, because he tasted and loved inward delight, he abhorred its deprivation and rejected it as a true evil. Anger, envy, sadness, every malice, and whatever removes or diminishes inward delight—the experience of that delight taught him how abominable these are and made him abhor them. Thus, by eating butter he learned to reject evil.

Likewise, by the eating of honey he learned to choose good. For he who, at the very entrance into this life, was satisfied with supreme sweetness came to know by tasting and experience how much it was to be preferred and chosen before every inferior good. From comparison with it he learned how small, how insignificant, and how contemptible every lower pleasure is. Emmanuel therefore learned in this manner to reject evil and choose good.

Thus, indeed, through the abundance of supreme delights he was instructed in wisdom, and nevertheless strengthened in every justice. For what was supremely sweet to him he found worthy of supreme love; and to what he judged supremely worthy of love he clung with supreme love. Therefore, from received blessedness he was confirmed in every good. And, that you may wonder still more: as from glory received he was made firm in every justice, so from justice made inwardly his own he was raised to every glory. For since he supremely loved supreme justice, he merited to be exalted to supreme gladness and glory: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44). And because by experience he learned the delights of everlasting blessedness to be supremely pleasant and supremely sweet, he clung inseparably both to their contemplation and to their love. Thus it is rightly understood of him what is written: “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good.”

## CHAPTER XXV. How God made wondrous the Blessed Virgin, who merited to bear such fruit.

RICHARD. From the foregoing you have understood, I think, how God made his handmaid wondrous; how he glorified the Blessed Virgin Mary through such a birth, so that she could truly glory and freely confess: “From this time all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1). You have heard how God magnified her offspring, so that he might be and be called Emmanuel—that is, God with us—and that this same one might be both the Only-Begotten of God and her own son. He truly and incomparably made the mother wondrous; he truly and incomprehensibly magnified the offspring.

Consider, if you can, what or how great this wonder is: that a virgin should conceive, a virgin give birth, and after giving birth remain a virgin. Estimate, if you are able, what or how great this magnificence is: that the offspring of a virgin should receive all fullness from the moment of his conception, and in the reality of humanity possess the fullness of divinity. Singular is the glory, special the grace, of the Blessed Virgin Mary, who bore and gave birth with the honor of virginity to a son—not merely any son, but God. Rightly it was said, and rightly it must be said: “Blessed are you among women . . . and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (ibid.).

Who would believe, who could have believed, that the prophet promised such fruit as God’s gift when he said: “The Lord will give kindness, and our land shall give its fruit” (Psalm 84)? Since it is written that “every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115), how magnificent it would be to have borne a truthful human being; what kind of thing, I ask, or how great, then, is it to have borne Truth itself? “Truth,” he says, “has sprung up from the earth” (Psalm 84). Thus, at the arising of Truth, the earth gave its fruit. O what fruit: magnificent fruit, glorious fruit, desirable fruit, exalted fruit! Unless I am mistaken, you recall what you read in the prophet: “In that day the branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth exalted” (Isaiah 4). And whence came this to our wretched earth, that it could bear such fruit?

## CHAPTER XXVI. That unless she had been completely purified, she could not have borne such fruit.

[Col. 0660A]

RICHARD. Certainly, the Blessed Virgin Mary herself was, even then according to the flesh, earth, when she heard from the angel: “Hail, full of grace; behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1). Without doubt, even then according to the flesh she was earth, and was going into earth: she was earth through mortality, and was going into earth through death. How then was it possible for such earth to produce such a fruit? Yet it is certain that, unless she had been wholly purified, she could not have produced so exalted a fruit. Let us say more plainly what we have said. Unless she had been utterly cleansed of every contagion of vices, she could not have begotten God, the Son of God. For a virgin to conceive and a virgin to give birth required the highest holiness and the highest purity.

By what order, then, or by what reasoning is the glorious Virgin advanced to the grace of so great an exaltation? It is described in mystical language when it is said through the prophet to Ahaz: “For before the child knows to reject evil and choose good, the land which you detest shall be abandoned before the face of its two kings” (Isa. 7). “Earth” indeed is so called from being trodden underfoot, and rightly the evil of our crushed condition is figured by it. This earth is said to have its kings [Note: [Col. 0659D] Something is missing here.], and would that they were as good as they are evil. In the two kings we understand the tyranny of the two principal vices, just as in the earth we understand the evil of our crushed and captive condition.

But that you may better recognize the character of this land of misery of which we speak, consider that threefold region of our dwelling—not Asia, Europe, and Africa, but the threefold affliction of the human condition. The first region of this wretched habitation of ours is human corruptibility; the second, human capacity for suffering; the third, human mortality. For from corruption, at first imperceptibly, one is often led into any painful and distressing suffering; and the various sufferings lead to death. Yet this wretched earth and grievous habitation has two malignant tax-gatherers, kings exercising cruel tyranny: in the vice of concupiscence it has a powerful king; in the vice of ignorance, a deceitful king. The one oppresses; the other deceives. Whatever in us resists reason serves this double king. Each, therefore, claims a kingdom for himself in the land already mentioned and hastens to extend it from day to day: the former by violence, the latter by deceit. The latter has subjected to himself all unbelievers—and would that he had subjected only them; the former has also subjected to himself all wicked believers—and would that he did not trouble even the good.

For whom, I ask, does the heat of concupiscence not trouble? Whom, I ask, does the error of ignorance not sometimes ensnare? Those who follow their lusts serve one of these kings. Those, however, serve the other at his command who call good evil and evil good, who make sweet bitter and bitter sweet, who make light darkness and darkness light. Thus it happens that we often serve such kings in the land of our captivity. Therefore in the two kings we have a double vice; in the land of our affliction we discern a threefold evil. The former belongs to guilt; the latter to punishment. It belongs to a devout mind patiently to endure what belongs to punishment, but to abhor and detest what belongs to guilt. It belongs to impiety, however, willingly to embrace what belongs to guilt and utterly to detest what belongs to punishment. Hence it is said through Isaiah to the impious king: “The land which you detest.” Without doubt the impious detest mortality, because they would wish to live forever in order that they might sin forever. They detest susceptibility to suffering, because they would wish to pass unpunished through what they commit with desire and pleasure. Thus it is rightly said to Ahaz, the impious king: “The land which you detest.” And it is added: “It shall be abandoned before the face of its two kings.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. That before Emmanuel’s conception she was freed from the double root of all vices.

The land of our mortality and susceptibility to suffering is abandoned before the face of its two kings when mortal and suffering nature is wholly cleansed both from the vice of concupiscence and from the vice of ignorance. This, surely, is what is promised to Blessed Mary, when the angel says to her: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). We read concerning the Savior’s disciples and witnesses of the Transfiguration that “a bright cloud overshadowed them” [Col. 0661C] (Matt. 17). If the cloud which overshadowed Christ’s disciples was bright, how bright must that be believed to have been which overshadowed Christ’s mother? But if that shadowing of hers was bright, it therefore supplied both light and shadow: light to drive away ignorance, shadow to extinguish concupiscence.

Wonderful was that overshadowing of the Holy Spirit which in a single instant wiped away and expelled from the Virgin both ignorance of good and desire for evil. How completely every concupiscence was extinguished in her is certainly proved by the fact that afterward, with virginity unimpaired, she conceived and gave birth. How profoundly she was enlightened is proved by the fact that she believed, with such truth and such promptness, a mystery of such profundity—a mystery which could scarcely at last, through so many and such great miracles, be persuaded to the wise of this world. Therefore the believing Virgin, who nevertheless asked how this was to take place, receives the fitting answer when the angel says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.” It is as though he plainly said to her: “That you may be made worthy and found fit for so great a mystery, the power of the Most High shall overshadow you, both to extinguish all concupiscence and to enlighten ignorance.”

This is what is promised and prophesied through Isaiah under another figure, when it is said: “For before the child knows to reject evil and choose good,” and the rest (Isa. 7). Certainly, as we said above, this child received from the very hour, or instant, of his conception the fullness of knowledge, which was united to the Word himself in unity of person. The time of conception, therefore, is expressed in the words: “Before he knows.” It is as though the prophet said more openly: Before Emmanuel is conceived in his mother, the earth of our condition—from which Truth springs—will be freed from the double root of all sins.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That in the Virgin only what belonged to punishment remained; what belonged to guilt departed.

“The land,” he says, “shall be abandoned before the face of its two kings.” It is especially to be noted that he says, “The land shall be abandoned”—not any land whatsoever, but that land which impiety detests. Nothing is said here concerning the renewal of this wretched earth of ours, but only of its liberation. Freedom is restored, but the glory of immortality is not renewed. You see, certainly, that in the Virgin what belonged to punishment remained, while what belonged to guilt departed. Viciousness departed; penal liability remained. Carnality was removed, but calamity was not taken away.

What justice, I ask, can there be in punishment remaining where guilt no longer exists? And indeed, if we consider carefully, we shall find that our viciousness itself is an effect of mortality and susceptibility to suffering. It therefore seems contrary to nature that it should endure while being deprived of its effect. But perhaps you ask how viciousness itself is an effect of our mortality. Certainly, through imposed mortality human perception was diminished, and from this came ignorance. Certainly, from contracted weakness the appetite of the flesh increased, and from this came concupiscence. For in proportion as, by sinning, a person lost the inward and spiritual delights, he burned more fiercely, through the appetite of the flesh, toward desires for lower things; and the weaker he was, the more things he needed, both to sustain his weakness and to restore health.

Therefore, while mortality and susceptibility to suffering remained in human nature, the departure of both the vice of concupiscence and the vice of ignorance seems contrary to nature. Yet when both the vice of concupiscence and the vice of ignorance have departed, the remaining mortality and susceptibility to suffering seem contrary to justice. How strange, how astonishing, that the very fountain of mercy, her Son, permitted his mother—wholly purified from every vice—to labor beneath the yoke of our captivity! Conversely, what miracle or wonder was it, I ask, that earth subject to curse and exposed to miseries could be entirely free from every exaction and disturbance of vices, and could possess full peace in this respect?

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the woman who bore our Emmanuel was perfect in every consummation of virtues.

Consider, I beseech you, how great and marvelous this wonder appeared in the Prophet’s eyes. He invited all alike to contemplate and admire it, saying: “Come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders which he has set upon the earth” (Ps. 45). What those wonders are which he so greatly marvels at is then added: “Removing wars to the end of the earth, he will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” [Col. 0663A] (Ps. 45).

What is this earth, I ask, from which all wars are removed utterly, unless it is that earth of which the same Prophet testifies elsewhere: “Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84)? From this earth, therefore, every conflict is taken away; in this earth full peace is restored. “He will break the bow,” he says, “and shatter the weapons.” In bow and arrow there is a blow that is not so much forceful as skilful. Conversely, in sword and spear there is a blow that is certainly not so much skilful as forceful. By bows, therefore, we understand deceitful temptations; by weapons, violent temptations. Observe, then, to what a citadel of security she raised herself, one to which neither violent nor deceitful temptation could thereafter gain any access: “He will break the bow,” he says, “and shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire.”

As seductions are understood by the bow and oppressions by the weapons, so by shields we understand excuses. Of these you have the following in the Prophet: “Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140). Excuses are indeed certain shields of vices, by which people fortify themselves against the darts of truth and defend themselves not a little against the missiles of virtues. But it must be known that where there is no ground for accusation, no excuse is doubtless left. For one whom his own conscience accuses in nothing has no reason why he should need to excuse himself.

Therefore that virginal mother who lacked nothing of the full consummation of virtues had absolutely no need of any excuse in any respect. For if even impossibility diminished in her anything belonging to some perfection of virtue, that impossibility itself would surely, in that respect, have furnished her an excuse. Therefore the fire of surpassing and immeasurably burning love, given from heaven, burned up those designated shields of every excuse, because the fullness of grace and the consummation of charity left no spiritual weakness, no imperfection, which had to be excused even on account of impossibility. From these things, therefore, one may perceive that the woman who bore our Emmanuel was perfect in every consummation of virtues.

Who has ever fulfilled, or will ever be able so to fulfill, that first and greatest commandment? “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deut. 6; Matt. 22; Luke 10). By this flame of burning love those shields already mentioned were consumed.

## CHAPTER XXX. That the aforesaid mother was evidently both consummated and confirmed in every gift she had received.

It should be observed that what is burned by fire is so consumed that no material remains from which it can be restored even in part. Hence this prophecy gives us to understand that divine love grew so strong in her, and so established her in every good, that thereafter no kind of spiritual defect whatever could possibly arise in her, nor anything that could be subject to any sort of excuse. Accordingly, from the hour when the Holy Spirit came upon her, from the hour when the power of the Most High overshadowed her, Blessed Virgin Mary appears, I say, not only perfected in every grace, but also confirmed in every good and gift which she had received.

But lest anyone suppose that the prophecy in question should be understood rather of Emmanuel himself than of his mother, such a person should carefully consider that shields which never existed and never will exist cannot be burned. What, then, did our Emmanuel ever have in himself, I ask, which needed or could be burned, seeing that from the hour of his conception, by receiving all fullness, he was perfected and confirmed in every good? The prophecy in question, therefore, seems to be understood of the Virgin Mary alone. Indeed, in her the earth of our miserable condition attained full peace from every assault of vices; insofar as concerned her, the earth which Ahaz held detestable was abandoned before the face of its two kings.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That beyond the other saints she had this singular distinction: that she could not even be assailed by vices.

Among the other saints it is considered a great thing that they cannot be conquered by vices; in her it seems wonderful that she herself cannot be assailed by vices even in the slightest degree. The other saints are commanded generally that sin should not reign in their mortal body; to her alone is singularly granted that sin should not dwell in her mortal body: “Let sin no longer reign in your mortal body” [Col. 0664C] (Rom. 6). See: he commands that it not reign—but does he command that it not dwell? Observe what he says elsewhere: “For if I do the evil that I do not wish, it is no longer I who do it, but the sin which dwells in me” (Rom. 7).

But what is believed to have been accomplished in the Blessed Virgin Mary—the extermination of sin—is hoped for in the future for all saints. It will be future, I say, not in their body while still mortal, but in their body once made immortal: for this corruptible must first put on incorruption, and this mortal, immortality. Yet this was extraordinarily wonderful in Blessed Virgin Mary, and singular beyond all other saints: in her so great a corruptibility could coexist with so great an incorruptibility, and so great an incorruptibility with so great a corruptibility. There was corruptibility in what pertains to punishment, incorruptibility in what pertains to guilt.

But it contributed to her increase of future glory, and to us as an instruction in patience, that she bore the yoke of our susceptibility to suffering with such purity. But since, my Hugh, in accordance with your request, we have completed what seemed to us to concern the mystical understanding, let us, if you please, bring our speaking to an end here. If anyone accuses us of prolixity on account of the brevity of the subject undertaken, I confess that I do not regret having been wordy in praise of the Word and in praise of the Virgin Mother.

HUGH. Confounded, I confess, by the depth of mysteries in the words of prophecy, and held for a long while in great wonder by contemplating them, I willingly endured your lengthy discourse. I judged it unworthy to interrupt the course of your speech, and I finally chose to venerate these matters in silent admiration precisely because they seem to me incapable of being fully explained by any discourse.

[Col. 0665]

# EXPLANATION OF CERTAIN DIFFICULT PASSAGES OF THE APOSTLE.

If the things which the Apostle says about the law in different places are compared with one another, much inconsistency seems to be found in them. For he seems contrary to himself, contrary to reason, contrary to truth, and—what is more than all these—contrary to the judgment of the Lord himself. Hear him crying out and declaring: “For by works of the law no human being shall be justified” (Rom. 3). How is he not contrary to himself in this, when elsewhere he declares: “Not hearers of the law, but doers of the law shall be justified” (Rom. 2)?

Again, in another place he says: “The law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good” (Rom. 7). Yet elsewhere the same man says: “The law works wrath” (Rom. 4). What seems more contrary to reason than that a commandment called holy, righteous, and good should, in the case of a righteous and devout Lord, produce wrath rather than grace? Elsewhere he says: “The law brings no one to perfection” [Col. 0665C] (Heb. 7). How, I ask, could this truly be said, or how was he not contrary to truth in this, when the time of the law possessed so many righteous persons and persons so perfect? Was Elijah not perfect, in whose spirit and power came the one of whom, according to the Lord’s testimony, “among those born of women none greater has arisen”? (Matt. 11.) What shall we say of the other prophets, of the righteous, and of the kings, who desired to see what the apostles saw and could not? If they were transgressors of the law, could they be righteous? If they were observers, were they not therefore righteous?

He also seems to think contrary to the Lord’s judgment when elsewhere he says: “For if a law had been given which could justify, righteousness would truly be from the law” (Gal. 3). But when a lawyer asked what he should do to possess eternal life, and, in answer to his question, set forth before the Lord the first and greatest commandments of the law, the Lord replied: “Do this, and you shall live” (Luke 10). What then? Can righteousness not be obtained by that through which eternal life is obtained? Or can eternal life be had without righteousness? Who would say, or dare to say, either of these things? “Do this,” he says, “and you shall live.” You shall live, beyond doubt, by loving your God with all your heart, all your soul, and all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.

There are those who say that works of the law are those done from fear, while works of the Gospel are those done from love. To serve without love, however, cannot justify a person. Hence, according to them, it is rightly said that no human being shall be justified by works of the law. To support their assertion, they cite what they read elsewhere in the Apostle: “For you have not received again the spirit of slavery in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry: Abba, Father” (Rom. 8). It is clear, therefore, they say, that those who received the spirit of fear rather than love served under fear. Hence they further add that the law is commandment without grace, whereas the Gospel is commandment with grace.

I confess that I do not remember reading where the law commands service from fear alone or forbids the fulfillment of commandments from true love. Are not the works of the law those which it itself enjoins? And are its works those which it does not hand down? But they say that those who were under the law received the spirit of slavery. I say boldly and affirm without doubt that among those who have existed hitherto in the time of the law and among those in the time of the Gospel, some have received the spirit of fear and others the spirit of love. Did those alone not keep the law who, with charity abounding and casting fear out, observed it from love alone? It belongs, certainly, both to the Law and to the Gospel to provide instruction; but it belongs to the Lord to give or withhold grace and to pour forth the Spirit according to his good pleasure. What, then, do those mean who say that the law is commandment without grace and the Gospel commandment with grace? How often we see in our own times unlearned hearers possess greater grace in carrying out commandments than certain most learned preachers of the Gospel. Is what those teach who most skillfully preach apostolic doctrine not the Gospel, merely because they themselves lack—and cannot give to others—the grace to fulfill it? Did those ancient people live without law who received both the law’s teaching and grace?

There are likewise those who say that only those things are rightly called works of the law which began with the law and ended with the law. But I shall state for the moment what I think and reply to these points in concise fashion. Those works of the law which began with the law and ended with the law either justified when fulfilled, or did not. If, therefore, their fulfillment could justify, how will it be true that no one is justified by works of the law?

There may be some who say—and, even if they do not, might not inappropriately say—that a distinction should properly be made between natural, legal, and evangelical works. For those works should properly be assigned especially to the Gospel which received their institution from the Gospel, such as regeneration, confirmation, communion in the Lord’s body and blood, and the establishment of any new practices. Legal works, however, should in a special sense be called only those which, as has now been said, began with the law and ended with the law. Natural works should properly be called those which human beings could have understood through natural law even if the law and the Gospel had never been instituted.

According to this distinction, someone perhaps will say that by works of the law we ought to understand only those legal institutions of which we know for certain that no flesh is justified by their fulfillment alone. By “law,” however, as someone may perhaps think, we ought to understand both natural ordinances and legal institutions, insofar as both are written in the law. For the Apostle says that doers of the law, not doers of legal works, are justified. But what he affirms of the law, he denies of the works of the law: “By works of the law,” he says, “no human being shall be justified.” He does not say, “By the law,” but, “By works of the law no flesh shall be justified.” And again elsewhere: “We reckon that a human being is justified by faith without works of the law” (Rom. 3).

There he says that a human being cannot be justified by works of the law; here he says that one can be justified without works of the law. If anyone thinks that the Apostle meant this, I ask that he answer me whether the Apostle says it of the present state or rather of the former state. If he said it of the time of the former state, he will seem to oppose the testimony of the law and the prophets in the text of that discourse. Did not the law daily cry out that the sinner who repents should offer this or that, according to the manner and measure of the sin, now for sin and now for transgression, and “it shall be forgiven him,” it says, “and the Lord shall be propitious to him” (Num. 30)? How, I ask, is a person not justified by that through which sin is forgiven and the Lord becomes propitious?

But if he intended what he said about works of the law to be understood of the condition of the present time, what important thing did he say? For if we still sacrifice animals, undoubtedly we either Judaize or, after the fashion of the Gentiles, adopt rites of idolatry. Therefore I say concerning such persons what the Apostle says concerning the sacrament of circumcision: if we still persist in sacrifices and the other ceremonies of the law, Christ will profit us nothing. Do you wish to know more plainly what I mean? Certainly, the things sacrificed under the law for the expiation of sin were sacrificed as figures of things to come. For they prefigured Christ’s passion and death, yet to come, for the redemption of sins; and precisely on that account they had the power of expiation and sanctification.

If, therefore, we still sacrifice as a figure of things to come, we serve falsehood rather than truth. For “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (1 Cor. 15). But if we sacrifice without the figure of our redemption, we adopt, as was said, the form of idolatry; and thereby we compare animal sacrifices to Christ and—even more wickedly—prefer them to him. For if we offer those sacrifices alone, despising the divine sacrifice, we undoubtedly prefer them to Christ. If we offer them together with the divine victim, as though seeking salvation from both, we undoubtedly compare them with Christ and judge Christ’s victim insufficient. What great thing, then, is it for the Apostle to say that no one is justified by legal works, when anyone who practices them will be condemned rather than justified?

But perhaps you reply to these things and say: “Because of certain zealots for the law, whom he wished rather to win than to scandalize, he spoke somewhat sparingly, yet he spoke truly. For with regard to the present state, legal institutions defile rather than sanctify. With regard to the former state, however, legal institutions alone, without natural ordinances, could not suffice for human salvation. Hence he does not say, ‘By the law,’ but ‘By works of the law no flesh shall be justified.’ And again: ‘For we reckon that a human being is justified by faith without works of the law.’ ‘Without works of the law,’ he says, not ‘without law’: by the name works he intends legal observances alone, but by the name law both legal and natural observances, since it contained both. Hence he says that doers of the law shall be justified. For what could be holier, more righteous, or finally more perfect than to love God with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, all one’s mind, and one’s neighbor as oneself? The law, therefore, could confer righteousness—not merely any righteousness, but full and perfect righteousness.”

To these things I myself reply briefly and say: If the Apostle meant that the law could confer perfect righteousness, why does he elsewhere say that the law brought no one to perfection? If righteousness is conferred by the law, how does it work wrath? Does it work wrath by conferring righteousness, and can it confer righteousness by working wrath? In my judgment, one who wishes to understand the apostolic meaning must seek an explanation other than those already stated. In my judgment, in all these matters the questions have not yet disappeared in which, as Augustine writes, the text of the Apostle’s discourse once seemed to him to oppose the testimonies of the law and the prophets. For one who says that a human being cannot be justified by legal works surely seems to oppose Moses writing—or rather the Lord commanding—“Let the person who has recognized his sin offer this or that, and it shall be forgiven him, and the Lord shall be propitious to him.”

Your insistent request compels me to say what I think concerning the matters proposed; and I confidently hope that where John asks, grace will not be lacking, both for true judgment and for profitable expression. It is not our custom, especially in great and very profound matters, to presume anything on the basis of our own opinion or to establish or affirm anything, as though by our own authority. Let us therefore draw from the testimonies of Sacred Scripture itself, insofar as the Lord grants, what may enable us to untie the knots of our doubt.

This, however, is most certain and cannot be doubted by anyone: either the law was such that, when fulfilled, it could justify, or it was such that it could not justify even when fulfilled. But if it could not justify when fulfilled, the Apostle would by no means say that doers of the law are justified. The Lord’s statement to the lawyer concerning the two greatest commandments of the law runs to the same conclusion: “Do this and you shall live.” See how certain authority proves that the law, when fulfilled, justifies.

Again, I say that either the law was such that it could be fulfilled by those to whom it was given, or such that it could not be fulfilled by them. But let us prove this very question again by apostolic testimony: “What was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Rom. 8). You perceive, I think, from these words how impossible it was for the law to justify, and how necessary for us was such a remedy: that God should send his Son; that God’s Son should empty himself and come in the likeness of sinful flesh; and that God, concerning sin, should condemn sin in the flesh, so that in this way at least the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us.

But was everything belonging to the law impossible? Not at all, but only in that part in which the law was weakened through the flesh. Do you wish also to hear how it was weakened through the flesh? “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit” (Gal. 5); and elsewhere: “I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. For willing is present to me, but I do not find the accomplishing of good” (Rom. 7).

If, therefore, we carefully examine the testimonies adduced, we shall undoubtedly find that certain commandments of the law were such that, when fulfilled, they justified; but others did not justify at all, even when fulfilled. Likewise, some were such as could be fulfilled, while others undoubtedly could not be fulfilled. But those which could be fulfilled could not justify; and conversely, those which could justify could not be fulfilled. The Apostle therefore rightly cries: “By works of the law no flesh shall be justified.” No flesh—that is, no human being, insofar as every human being is flesh, since he is carnal, sold under sin. How, I ask, can one made flesh and rendered carnal be justified either by what he can do but which cannot justify, or by what can justify but which he cannot do?

For the law teaches what a person ought to do, but it does not equally teach how he can fulfill what is commanded. From the law alone, therefore, comes knowledge alone, not also fulfillment. Hence, after the Apostle has said that no flesh shall be justified by works of the law, he immediately adds: “For through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. 3). See: you have both what is not from the law and what is from the law. Through the law comes knowledge of sin—would that abolition of sin did as well. For if abolition did come through it, undoubtedly justification would also come through it.

Therefore I say: if no one is justified by the law, then justification comes from elsewhere. For who would dare to say that no one is or has been righteous? Hear what the Lord says to the apostles: “Many righteous persons and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it” (Luke 10). If they were righteous, they were surely justified. “For all have sinned and need the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3). For he is the one who justifies “the circumcision by faith and the uncircumcision through faith” (ibid.). From these words, then, it is plainly known by what a person is justified: undoubtedly by faith, not by law. “For the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ” (ibid.). Here you have plainly that righteousness is from faith.

But it remains to ask whether justification is always from faith alone, or whether sometimes it is from faith alone without works, and sometimes from faith together with works. Let us, if you please, seek the Apostle’s own testimony on this matter: “We reckon,” he says, “that a human being is justified by faith without works of the law.” Again you have plainly that a human being can sometimes be justified by faith alone without a work of the law. But is it always by faith alone and without every work of the law? Not at all. For if one has time for acting, “faith without works is dead” [Col. 0670B] (James 2). “Not hearers of the law, but doers shall be justified.” Without doubt, so long as a person is granted time for action, God rightly requires from him faith working through love.

From the testimonies adduced, therefore, it is clearly gathered that a person is sometimes justified by faith alone, sometimes by faith together with a work of the law, but never by the law alone. From this, I think, it may be perceived that the Apostle is not contrary to himself in his statements. For when he says in one place that “by works of the law no flesh shall be justified,” he plainly gives us to understand that the teaching of the law alone, without faith in Christ and grace, is wholly insufficient for human effort: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15).

But again, lest the law should be thought such that, when fulfilled, it cannot justify, he says elsewhere of that same law: “Not hearers, but doers of the law shall be justified.” For whether it be granted or not granted that so great a grace has been, or will be, given to some person that he can fulfill it, it is nevertheless true that its fulfillment is the justification of human beings. The Apostle therefore teaches that the law by itself never confers righteousness upon a person; indeed, what is more serious, it also works wrath. But the Apostle himself adds and reveals why this happens: “For where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4). It works wrath because, through the teaching of the law alone without accompanying grace, hearers of the law are made not so much doers as transgressors.

But lest the commandments of the law should be regarded as foolish rather than impossible, the Apostle says elsewhere: “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good.” Perhaps you think this was said only of moral commandments. I boldly say it of every ordinance of the law which was holy, righteous, and good in its own time, as instituted by God and divinely imposed upon humankind.

What, I ask, were the sacrifices but a figure of Christ’s passion and death, and by that very fact sacraments of the same? Thus, in one and the same act there was both a figure of our redemption and the obedience that was due. Certainly, if Abraham had wished to slay his son without a divine command, it would have been the height of impiety and a dreadful crime. If, therefore, it was holy, just, and pious [Col. 0671A] to sacrifice his son at the Lord’s command, why should it not likewise be called holy, just, and good to offer and immolate to the Lord, at the Lord’s command, an animal that may be killed without sin? Therefore, the fact that the law produced wrath arose not from any imperfection or disorder in the law, but from human weakness and imperfection. Do you wish to hear even this, not from me, but from the Apostle himself? “We know,” he says, “that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do. For I do not do the thing that I will, but I do the thing that I hate” (Rom. VII). Here you now have the source of transgression; here you now grasp that it arises not from a defect in the law, but from a defect in man. Therefore there is nothing contrary to reason in the assertion that a commandment which is holy and just produces wrath.

According to the Lord’s testimony, it is true—and we cannot deny—that before Christ’s coming there were many righteous persons and prophets; yet it was not contrary to truth that the Apostle said that the law brought no one to perfection. For their righteousness, and whatever perfection they could have, was conferred upon them not by the bare teaching of the law, but by divine grace joined to it. “For it is not of him that wills, nor of him that runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX). For they were by no means justified without faith in and grace from Christ. Unless they believed and hoped that Christ would come, they could by no means have longed for his coming through so great a span of time. For what else is meant by the Lord’s words to the apostles: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what [Col. 0671C] you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke X)? Their justification, therefore, is attributed not so much to the law as to faith and the grace of Christ.

Let us now consider how what the Apostle thinks of the law is not contrary to the Lord’s judgment when he says: “For if a law had been given which could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the law.” You see that, according to the Apostle, the law can neither give life nor justify. But why is this so, except because it cannot be fulfilled?
