For a human being cannot fail to desire, any more than he can love with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind—though nothing is holier and certainly nothing is more just than this. Certainly, if such a law had been given to persons who were ignorant but sound, and strong enough to fulfill it, then without doubt it could, for those willing to obey, both justify and thereby sanctify [Col. 0671D] them. But it was indeed given to the weak, very ignorant, and less fit to fulfill it. Likewise, if it taught the ignorant what they ought to do, and also taught the weak how they could accomplish what was commanded, then, undoubtedly, it could—as must be admitted—both justify and give life. But the law teaches only what ought to be done; it does not teach how it can be fulfilled by the weak. The Apostle denies that a human being can be given life by knowledge or teaching alone of what must be done; and rightly so. But what the Apostle denies concerning mere knowledge of the command, the Lord affirms concerning its fulfillment: “Do this,” he says, “and you shall live.” He does not say, “If you know this, you shall live,” but, “Do this, and you shall live.” Therefore the Apostle does not deny what the Lord affirms, nor does the Lord affirm what the Apostle [Col. 0672A] denies. For, as has been said, the Apostle speaks of knowledge of the command alone, but the Lord of its actual fulfillment.

Here it is reasonably asked on what grounds failure to fulfill the law is imputed to them, or how the law produces wrath in those who could not fulfill it; or what benefit they derived from receiving a law which they could in no way fulfill. They certainly ought, and not without reason, to receive such a law, since they presumed upon their own powers rather than upon divine assistance, as when they confidently said to Moses: “All that the Lord has spoken we will do” (Exod. XXIV). What do you think of those who, after so great and steadfast a promise, neglected it altogether? Can such negligence excuse them? Or can such pride excuse those who, though striving vigorously, nevertheless failed, yet could not be humbled by their own failure and repeated experience? Or, I ask, can such sloth excuse those who, through much experience, recognized their own weakness but were sluggish in seeking the grace that helps? Who would say this, or dare to say it? From these things, therefore, you can easily judge how inexcusable are transgressors of the law they received.

Those, however, who strove according to their strength, failed, and then recognized, both through their own defect and through the defect of others, their weakness and inability, and thereafter placed their whole hope in divine aid—having obtained and received grace from God—deserved to be justified [Col. 0672C]. Thus, the law benefited some and did not benefit others at all. It benefited those who used it well; it harmed those who used it badly. Where it harmed, the fault lay not in the law but in the one abusing it. For the law was given for this purpose: although it ought to be fulfilled and could not be fulfilled, those who strove and failed might understand how vainly they presumed upon their own powers, since they could not fulfill it without divine grace.

Perhaps you still persist and say that whatever has been said of the law can also be said of the Gospel. For just as the teaching of the law without divine grace does not suffice for righteousness, so unquestionably neither does evangelical teaching without divine grace: neither can be fulfilled, neither can justify. Why, then, is what is said of the law not said of the Gospel—that by works [Col. 0672D] of the Gospel no flesh shall be justified? Does not the Gospel also bring no one to perfection, since it is agreed that it cannot be fulfilled without grace? On the same reasoning, we may judge that it cannot give life to anyone at all, just as it cannot justify.

To this I answer and say that the teaching of the law is simple, whereas the teaching of the Gospel is threefold. The Gospel teaches what ought to be done, how it can be fulfilled, and how that which has not been fulfilled can be made good. But the law, as has been said, teaches only what a person ought to do, and does not add how he can fulfill it; therefore it can justify no one. Evangelical teaching, however, in order to be wholly perfect, teaches those three things already mentioned. You are taught what you ought to do when you hear the Lord say: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XVIII). But lest anyone presume to do this by his own powers, he is taught by the same master when elsewhere he says: “Without me you can do nothing. As the branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you do anything without me” (John XV). In acquiring the grace by which we may fulfill what we will, what, I ask, will be the means of obtaining it? “If you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John XIV). If you need grace, ask as you ought, and you shall receive. But how do we ask in his name? By believing in him. This is what he wished to teach you when he says: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (ibid.). Therefore, whoever cannot fulfill what he ought to fulfill should believe in Christ, [Col. 0673B] and in Christ ask the Father, who can do all things. Let him ask for that Spirit who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to good will: that Spirit, I say, who works all things in all persons, distributing to each as he wills. If you ask him with fitting faith, you shall undoubtedly receive him. “For if you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke XI). Here, I think, you clearly have what must be done by you and how, or by what means, it can be fulfilled.

But you still ask to be shown how that which has not been fulfilled through negligence or in any other manner may be made good. First tell me how much you owe your Lord. Perhaps a hundred measures of oil? A great debt, and difficult to pay. It is a great debt to love God with the whole heart, whole mind, and whole soul. Behold the debt of ten thousand talents. It is no wonder if you are greatly afraid and tremble; but hear briefly what you must do. Forgive the hundred denarii owed to you, and your whole debt will be forgiven you; and with confidence you will be able to pray for yourself and those like you: “Forgive us our debts, as we also …” What, you ask, if nothing is owed to me? How will that which I myself owe be forgiven me? Draw, in the same order and from the same fountain from which you drew grace for fulfilling, also the pardon of mercy for showing mercy. From these things you may surely see that nothing is lacking to the perfection of Gospel teaching. In it you have the means by which you may be justified; from it you have the means by which you may be given life. “He who eats,” he says, “my flesh [Col. 0673D] and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John VI).

What more do you seek? Could that legal lamb accomplish anything of the kind? Behold, the Gospel supplies that by which a human being may be justified, whereas legal teaching cannot do so at all. Certainly, under the law many were perfect, and under the time of the Gospel many are imperfect. Yet their perfection is not attributed to the law, nor is the imperfection of these persons attributed to the Gospel. For divine grace conferred it on the former, not the teaching of the law.

“By works of the law no flesh shall be justified” (Gal. II). To be righteous is one thing; to be justified is another. God, indeed, is righteous, but he is not justified [Col. 0674A]. It is evident that sin makes a human being unrighteous. What, then, is it for a sinner to be justified except to be freed from sin? Through sin a human being becomes liable both to fault and to punishment: in one respect he is bound to guilt; in the other, to penalty. In one respect he incurs the debt of slavery; in the other, the debt of eternal condemnation: “He who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John III). But one who is a slave needs redemption in order to go free. The law neither teaches the source from which a person ought to be redeemed nor supplies the means by which he can be set free. Therefore the teaching of the law does not free from sin, and consequently no flesh shall be justified by it.

What, then, does the law do? It teaches what a person ought to do and what he ought to avoid, but does not teach how he can fulfill it. It forbids desire; it commands love for God with the whole heart. It commands ordered love and forbids disordered love. You have heard what it does; hear what it effects. What it forbids is done continually by all flesh; what it commands is never fulfilled by flesh. Hence no one is justified by its works. For whatever it teaches is either of such a kind that one cannot do it, or of such a kind that it cannot justify. From this, I think, you have understood the frequency of sinning. Now consider the force of sin. The law commands that for certain sins one transgressor be stoned, another burned, another put to death by some other mode of death. Yet many crimes of this kind were committed by hearers of the law. Thus it may easily be seen how great is the force of sin, [Col. 0674C] since in some persons it could not be restrained even by the danger of death. Therefore, once the law had been given and frequent, manifold transgression followed, it became plain how frequent sinning is and how great the force of sin.

Hence, when it has first been said, “By works of the law no flesh shall be justified,” the Apostle immediately adds: “For through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. III). It is therefore plainly given to understand—or rather, it makes us understand—that through the law there is knowledge of sin only, not also its abolition. For if there were abolition, there would surely be justification. Someone may perhaps wonder why it says “knowledge of sin” rather than “knowledge of the command”; for the latter could equally truly have been said. For just as through the law there is knowledge of sin alone and not abolition, so through the law there is knowledge of the command alone and not its fulfillment. But, as it seems to me, if he had first said that by works of the law no one was righteous or possessed righteousness, it would have been more fitting to add, “For through the law comes knowledge of the command,” than to say, “For through the law comes knowledge of sin.” For what may more rightly be called righteousness than the keeping of the divine command? A person’s justification is the same as liberation from sin. Since, then, he had spoken first of human justification, it is easy to see how fittingly he adds: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin,” rather than knowledge of the command.

“For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. VII). It is rightly asked in whose person the Apostle says these words, [Col. 0675A] especially because of what he subsequently adds.

It is therefore asked whether he speaks in the person of the weak or imperfect, or rather in the person both of these and of the perfect. For, as it seems to me, it is clearer than light that these words ought neither to be expounded of the criminally wicked nor can rightly be understood in such a sense. For who thereafter could reasonably rebuke any criminal for his crime, if he could cite the apostolic testimony in his own defense and boldly answer his accuser: “It is not I who do it, but the sin that dwelt in me”? What is it to expound these apostolic words so that they may suit even the ungodly? What else, I say, is it but to teach workers of iniquity to incline their hearts to words of malice, “to make excuses for excuses in sins” [Col. 0675B]?

But the question to be asked concerning these words of the Apostle seems to be whether they are spoken in the character of the perfect or of the imperfect. Yet how can “but I am carnal, sold under sin” suit the Apostle or any perfect man? Who could rightly be called spiritual if Paul, or persons like Paul, are believed to be carnal? If what the Apostle discusses here applies only to the weaker, it certainly does not establish what he endeavors to prove from these words. For he had said of the law that it could not confer righteousness, indeed that it produced wrath. But lest this be believed to arise from a fault in the law rather than in humanity, he subsequently adds and says that “the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good.” Here the Apostle plainly shows that the inability to be justified by the law arises from a defect in man, because he is wholly insufficient for its fulfillment.

It must first be understood that, according to different points of reference, we take the same verbal expressions in different ways. We judge a person differently according to his present state and according to the state in which he was before sin. In the present state, some are called spiritual and others carnal. But in relation to the first condition, even the most religious person is not improperly called carnal. In regard to the present state, however, those are called carnal who pursue their own desires and serve fleshly desires. Those are spiritual who vigorously resist the desires of the flesh [Col. 0675D] and earnestly devote themselves to spiritual pursuits. It belongs to the carnal both to feel and consent to the flesh’s desires; it belongs to the spiritual to feel them but not consent—to resist, oppose, and mortify them. But if we look to the state of the first condition, we are carnal precisely in this: that we feel the flesh’s desires and foul, disordered pleasures. For if man had not sinned, he would neither have loved carnal things more than was allowed nor spiritual things less than was fitting; but in loving both he could at once have known and observed the bounds of moderation and the measure of equity. But once man voluntarily abandoned the rectitude of his state, now, having once been sold under sin and made carnal, he is sufficient for neither: for he both errs in judgment in many ways and is unrestrained in desire [Col. 0676A].

How true, therefore, is that prophetic sentence: “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII); and how true likewise is that apostolic saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I). “But I am carnal, sold under sin” can thus be understood quite truly of any religious person. He also shows wherein and in what respects he is carnal when he adds: “For I do not understand what I do. I do not do what I will, but I do the thing that I hate.” Behold three evils in which our carnality consists: we do not understand what we do; we do not do what we will; we do what we do not will. But the Apostle joins the latter two, since both arise from one defect. For from the defect of concupiscence arise both our lukewarmness toward good and our ardor for evil. “For I do not understand what I do,” he says (Rom. VII), and this surely arises from the defect of ignorance. “I do not do what I will, but I do the thing that I hate.” From this twofold defect it follows that we are carnal as long as we live in the flesh.

It should be noted, however, that to the one thing which the Apostle first stated he subsequently adds two things. He first stated that he was carnal, and through the two following statements showed whence this belonged to him. The first proposition should therefore be repeated and joined to each following clause in this manner: “I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do.” “I am carnal,” I say, [Col. 0676C] “sold under sin, for I do not do what I will, but I do the thing that I hate.” Anyone can experience in himself how truly it is said: “I do not understand what I do.” Did the one who said in prayer to the Lord, “I thank you, Lord, that I am not like other people,” understand what he was doing? (Luke XVIII). Did those who said, “All that the Lord has spoken we will do,” understand well what they were saying? (Exod. XLII [probably XXIV]). The words seem to be words of great devotion, but are truly words of great presumption. Often, where a person thinks he is stirring up devotion, he nourishes self-exaltation and feeds presumption. But why is this, I ask, except because he does not understand what he does? A person often grows proud without knowing it. Often he presumes and meanwhile does not understand. For each ignorance divine grace is commonly withdrawn. For while one acts presumptuously and does not know it, grace is withdrawn lest he accomplish what he desires. While one is proud and does not know it, he is often allowed to fall into what he is ashamed of and hates; and one who is such may say: “I do not do what I will, but I do the thing that I hate.”

Even the most spiritual person errs not only in discerning but also in deliberating, when what he thinks cooperates with him for good cooperates with him for evil, and what he believes cooperates with him for evil cooperates for good. But why does this good come about except because he does not understand what he does? And what wonder is it if we do not understand what we do, when we do not know what we ought to pray for? For who cannot be deceived in prayer if the Apostle Paul himself could be deceived in this very matter? He asked three times that what had been imposed upon him, both mercifully and profitably, as a safeguard of humility might be removed.

“As a wise architect I laid a foundation. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work shall become manifest” (1 Cor. III). Some determine that the foundation here is faith working through love. I confidently say that no human being can lay such a foundation in a human heart. A person can teach another person what ought to be believed. But a person cannot pour love into another person. For the love of God is poured out in our hearts, not through a human being, but through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0677B] who has been given to us.

“As a wise architect,” he says, “I laid a foundation.” What, I ask, is that foundation which Paul laid and was able to lay? Certainly Paul could teach, and without doubt did teach, how one ought to believe in Christ. It is beyond doubt that this instruction of our faith is the foundation of the spiritual building. Before all else, one must know what one ought to believe or do, and one person can learn this from another. Therefore a preacher of truth ought diligently to teach what one ought to believe, to what works a person ought to devote himself, and how by true repentance he may blot out the evils he has committed; and this will be laying a foundation for him. How many have and retain by heart this foundation of Catholic teaching, yet build very different things upon it! Some perform good works; others sin in hope of repenting. Both, therefore, have the foundation of true faith, yet they build different things upon it. Some build gold, silver, and precious stones; others, wood, hay, and straw.

Gold, silver, and precious stones cannot be consumed by fire. These, indeed, can pass through fire and remain after the burning: “If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains,” he says, “he shall receive a reward.” If, therefore, we gain a reward through such things, what else should we understand by gold, silver, and precious stones but good works? But by wood, hay, and straw, I ask, ought good works or evil works to be understood? Fire ordinarily consumes wood, hay, and straw [Col. 0677D] and reduces them, as it were, to nothing. But far be it that that future fire should be able to consume and annihilate good works. Therefore wood, hay, and straw cannot rightly be understood except as works deserving burning and suited to be consumed rather than to remain. What, then, are these things that will burn and be consumed by fire, but evil works?

“If anyone’s work is burned, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire.” Who, I ask, are these workers who are saved, not as though by good work, but indeed as through fire? We certainly hold that no evil worker can be purified by purgatorial fire unless he has truly repented of the evils he has committed. For true repentance alone makes it possible for the commission of evils to be consumed and blotted out by purgatorial fire. No crimes are so detestable that true repentance does not make them remissible. Thus there seem to be two kinds of irreversible works and one kind of remissible works: enduring good works; the enduring evils of those who do not repent, never to be removed at any time; and the evils of those who truly repent, which are without doubt remissible and can without doubt be blotted out by purgatorial fire. Therefore, by wood, hay, and straw we understand every remissible evil. But since not only enduring good works but also irreversible evils cannot be consumed by fire and instead remain forever, why does he say, “If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he shall receive a reward”?

But what follows—“If anyone’s work remains”—must be referred only to those workers of whom he has already spoken. Thus, among those workers who build not iron, lead, and tin, but gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, and straw: of such workers, I say, if anyone’s work remains, he shall receive a reward; if anyone’s work burns, he shall suffer loss, but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire. Therefore by gold, silver, and precious stones we understand, as we have said, enduring goods; by wood, hay, and straw, remissible evils. By gold one may quite properly understand contemplation of truth; by silver, the word of preaching; by precious stones, exercises of virtue; and by wood, hay, and straw, works [Col. 0678C] of perversity, superfluity, and vanity, made remissible through true repentance.

Some may perhaps find it surprising how the Apostle judges that the disgraceful man who had his father’s wife should be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. Yet there can be no doubt that by the same power by which he could free one possessed by a demon from the demon, he could also, where reason required it, hand someone over to demonic affliction. But if a disgraceful person is handed over to Satan and becomes demon-possessed, this seems not to open but to close for him the way of salvation. For committed crimes cannot be blotted out without true repentance. But how can a person possessed by a demon, who lacks reason, have true repentance? How, then, does the Apostle judge that that disgraceful man should be handed over to Satan [Col. 0678D] so that his spirit may be saved?

It must therefore be understood that one kind of demonic affliction is continuous and another intermittent. He suffers continuous affliction who is never allowed to rest, but is driven by unceasing frenzies. He incurs intermittent affliction who, at different times, sometimes loses his reason and sometimes recovers it, and whose mind, amid many exhausting attacks, occasionally returns to itself. Therefore one handed over to intermittent affliction certainly has an opportunity to repent, and thereby an opportunity to be saved. For who could be so hardened and obstinate in mind that, during an interval in his affliction, when his mind has returned to itself, he does not grieve and deeply repent for committing that through which it came about that he incurred demonic affliction [Col. 0679A] and lay exposed to every mockery? See, then, how from an interruption of affliction it often results that the affliction itself brings him to repentance, and through repentance the affliction itself becomes his purification. The Apostle therefore clearly lets us understand what sort of affliction he wished that criminal man to undergo when he says, “that the spirit may be saved.” For just as continuous demonic affliction could rather close than open the way of salvation, so, conversely, intermittent affliction seems bound rather to open than to close it.

It should also be noted that when a person dies, his own spirit no longer uses the services of the flesh as it wishes. Thus the flesh of a demoniac in a certain way dies to its own spirit [Col. 0679B] when an evil spirit violently abuses its services and the person’s own spirit is deprived of the bodily service due to it.

Do you find it surprising that the Apostle says: “All things are lawful to me” (1 Cor. VI)? For many things are lawful, but not all things. Many things are entirely unlawful to every person. Yet we commonly understand “lawful” in two ways. We take the same expression sometimes more strictly and sometimes more broadly. We say that what can be done in an ordered manner is lawful. At other times we say that what we are free to do is lawful, whether or not it can be done in an ordered manner. Thus people commonly say of a criminal: “He would gladly have committed this or that crime if he had been allowed to do it”—that is, if he had had the capacity or opportunity to do it.

Thus Blessed Gregory says in his *Dialogues* of certain brethren who were not very religious. They had elected blessed Benedict as abbot, but already regretted having chosen him because of his stricter discipline of life; and they were preparing to destroy him by poison because they saw that, under him, things unlawful to them were not lawful. What does he mean in saying that unlawful things were not lawful to them, except that under Benedict they had no permission or freedom to do unlawful things? We know that God has placed in human freedom the choice whether to choose good or evil. Hence the saying of the Wise Man concerning the Lord: “He has set fire and water before you; stretch out your hand to whichever you will. Before man are life and death, good and evil; what pleases him shall be given to him” [Col. 0679D] (Ecclus. XV).

Accordingly, after enumerating so many evils, the Apostle adds: “All things are lawful to me”—lawful, certainly, not according to concession but according to permission alone. According to concession, ordered things alone are lawful; according to permission alone, even disordered things are lawful. For the Lord permits many things to be done which he grants to no one to do. “All things are lawful to me,” he says, undoubtedly so far as permission is concerned; “but not all things are beneficial,” not even all things done by concession. “All things are lawful to me, but I will not be brought under the power of any”—under the power, namely, of any of those things done by permission alone. For many things that are granted impede greater goods, and for that reason are not beneficial, yet they do not enslave the person using them. But “he who commits sin is the slave of sin.” Therefore, if we wish to avoid this slavery and not be brought under anyone’s power, we must carefully avoid things lawful by permission alone.

That not all things lawful by concession are beneficial he clearly shows when he adds: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. VI). Foods are indeed made for refreshing the belly and therefore are lawful by concession; yet it is not beneficial to indulge them excessively and neglect more necessary pursuits. For what good is their excessive indulgence, when it is certainly true that God will destroy both it and them? That not all things lawful by permission are lawful by concession he next shows when he immediately adds: “But the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body” (ibid.). Food is indeed for eating, and the belly for use; but the body is not for fornication, but to serve its Lord. The fact that we can often fornicate whenever we wish is not an indulgence granted by one conceding it, but a testing or abandonment by one permitting it.

Above he had said that fornicators will not possess the kingdom of God; but because he foresaw that many would find this difficult to believe and would not judge the evil of fornication so damnable, he consequently shows in two ways what we ought to think of this evil. He shows how profound such evil is and how, above all other sins, it is inward. For through the act of fornication the members of Christ are taken away and made members of a prostitute. From this it may be seen how profound this evil is: it casts down from such a height into this lowest and foul state. Hear also how it is more inward than all others: “Every sin,” he says, “whatever a person commits, is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. VI).

But if we wish more fully to understand the force of the apostolic statement, we must raise our consideration higher. As we commonly know, a human being consists of two substances: one bodily [Col. 0680D], the other incorporeal. The bodily can die; the incorporeal cannot. The incorporeal can subsist without nourishment; the bodily absolutely cannot. Yet the bodily substance, which cannot preserve its own nature from itself, can restore and even multiply itself from itself, something the spiritual substance cannot do at all. You see, then, that the prerogative of bodily substance is one thing and that of incorporeal substance another. The prerogative of incorporeal substance is that it can subsist eternally and without aid. The prerogative of bodily substance is that it can produce from its own substance a substance conformed to itself and multiply the nature of its kind by generating offspring.

But we cannot produce this conformity of substance from ourselves without, so to speak, a diminution of our own substance [Col. 0681A]. For the generation of offspring does not occur without a certain cutting-off from the begetter. In this connection it must be noted that this emission on the parent’s part for this act does not occur, nor can occur, from just any bodily member; rather, it is drawn out from the most inward part, as though from a treasury of its own kind placed in the inward parts and reserved for that function. Yet although no gift of nature appears to have been given to bodily substance more excellent than this, it is nevertheless more glorious to abstain from this function than to exercise it, because after nature’s corruption it cannot be carried out without lust and foul pleasure. For although it is lawful to exercise it with one’s own wife and solely for the begetting of offspring, this, if you consider it carefully, belongs rather to indulgence than to chastity.

There is no small pleasure in drink and food, yet it is not sinful unless it is excessive and passes into gluttony or drunkenness. But in gluttony and drunkenness there is a kind of dissipation of another’s substance. In the work of lust, however, there is a kind of dissipation and cutting-off of one’s own substance. There the demand of sinfulness is made upon another body; here it is made upon one’s own body—indeed, from the body’s own inmost part. Thus it was rightly said of the other sins that every sin is outside the body. But one who fornicates sins not merely in his own inmost part but also in his own body, because he seems to drain his body for shameful use and to abuse the prerogative of a divine gift for both his own and others’ filth.

“If anyone thinks that he knows anything, he does not yet know how he ought to know” [Col. 0681C] (1 Cor. 8). What, I ask, are we to say to these things? To pass over the rest, what shall we say of the Apostle himself? If the Apostle did not judge himself to know anything, with what face did he strive to teach others by preaching and writing? And if he does not judge true what he declares in the preceding words, why, I ask, does he affirm this very thing so firmly? If he did not judge himself to know anything, why did he state above, when he says: “Now concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all have knowledge”? Yet what he seems to say in this place appears to be contradicted in what follows: “But knowledge is not in all.” How, I ask, do all have knowledge if knowledge is not in all? And how can it be lacking to those who have it? [Col. 0681D]

It must therefore be understood that one kind of knowledge is that which all possess; another is that which some do not possess but are able to possess; and a third is that which no one possesses in this life, nor is able to possess. “We all have knowledge”: behold, the first kind. “Knowledge is not in all”: behold, the second. The Apostle refers to the third when he says: “If anyone thinks that he knows anything, he does not yet know how he ought to know” (Rom. 2). We all possess in common—Jews, Greeks, Barbarians, and Latins—the knowledge by which we distinguish true from false, good from evil, just from unjust, though some possess it more perfectly and others less perfectly. For if this knowledge were not common to believers and unbelievers, the Apostle would by no means have said: [Col. 0682A] “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature those things which belong to the law, these, though not having the law, are a law unto themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts” (ibid.). Behold the knowledge which all possess.

But many do not possess that knowledge which, together with received grace, suffices each person for salvation; yet they are still able to acquire it. It is of such knowledge that the Apostle rightly says: “But knowledge is not in all” (1 Cor. 8). That he intended such knowledge there is shown by what he had first stated: “For though there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him.” We receive the knowledge common to all so that we may seek and find that knowledge which suffices for salvation. Yet some possess this true knowledge of salvation more abundantly, some less; and it often happens that those with less are saved, while those with more perish. For greatness of knowledge is to some an incentive to pride and thereby a cause of ruin. This is what he indicates who says: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me an angel of Satan, a thorn for my flesh, to buffet me” (2 Cor. 12).

No one living in this life can know fully whether the knowledge he possesses, together with received grace, can now suffice for his salvation. This is the knowledge which no one possesses in this life, and no one can attain: “Even if I am simple,” says [Col. 0682C] Job, “my soul itself will not know this” (Job 9). Solomon speaks to the same effect: “Man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccl. 9). From his saying we have that a person does not know what is advantageous to him in his life. We have also, according to the same author: “For man does not know his end; but as fish are caught by the hook, and as birds are caught in the snare, so,” etc. (ibid.). From these words, therefore, we certainly understand that we cannot possess in this life the knowledge of assured security.

If, then, according to Solomon, all things are reserved as uncertain in the future, consider what you ought to think of your knowledge. Certainly, even if it seems a great thing in quantity, you do not know whether it is even a small thing, or whether it is of any use to you at all. What kind of estimation, I ask, is that of a thing concerning which you do not know, as regards yourself, whether it is of some value or of none? [Col. 0682D] We ought therefore, as far as we can, to advance in knowledge; nevertheless, however much we have advanced, we should account it as nothing so long as we cannot make a certain judgment concerning its outcome. According to this consideration, therefore, what is said through the Apostle is rightly understood: “If anyone thinks that he knows anything, he does not yet know how he ought to know.”

Every love is either solely gratuitous, solely due, or at once due and gratuitous. Gratuitous love may be understood in two ways. We rightly call that affection gratuitous which rests on grace alone. The fullness of true and highest love is [Col. 0683A] when it is so great and such that it cannot be greater or better. Where supreme perfection is absent, supreme love cannot—and ought not—exist. That is according to grace alone which, at the good pleasure of the giver, may justly be bestowed or not bestowed. But anything that can be described as according to grace alone is utterly foreign to the divine excellence. Again, love is not inappropriately called gratuitous where the giver, who gives everything, receives in return nothing but love.

[Col. 0683]

# Seven Books on the Apocalypse of John

## First Prologue to the Seven Books

[Col. 0683B] Receive, dearest brother, this gift of interpretations which you requested be made for you from the words of the Apocalypse of the blessed John, apostle and evangelist. For we gladly expend the labours of our study upon this work, so that from this book also, as from many other books of the New and Old Testament, you may have that which instructs your understanding, kindles your affection, advances and leads your zeal toward greater things. And, as we have said elsewhere, from all these things we attribute no credit to ourselves, but to God, from whose gift—and to the holy doctors, from whose fullness—we draw what we offer.

This book, composed through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, directed to the seven bishops and seven Churches of Asia, and rather given through divine providence for the instruction and consolation of the universal holy Church spread throughout the whole world and enriched with seven spiritual gifts, is divided into seven sections. For, after the title of the book is set down, where it is added, “John to the seven Churches,” the first vision begins where it says: “I John, your brother and companion in tribulation and kingdom and patience in Jesus.” The second vision begins where it is written: “After these things I saw, and behold, a door opened in heaven, and the first voice which I heard, as of a trumpet speaking with me.” The third begins thus: “And I saw seven angels standing in the presence [Col. 0684B] of God, and seven trumpets were given to them.” The fourth vision begins where he says: “And the temple of God was opened in heaven, and the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple.” The fifth vision begins where he says: “And I saw another sign in heaven, great and wonderful: seven angels having the last plagues, because in them the wrath of God is completed.” The sixth vision begins with these words: “And after these things I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority.” The seventh vision begins where it is written: “And I saw a new heaven and a new earth.”

According to this division of the seven visions, therefore, whatever we say in exposition we divide into seven books. The first book treats of the first vision; the second, of the second; the third, of the third; [Col. 0684C] the fourth, of the fourth; the fifth, of the fifth; the sixth, of the sixth; and the seventh, of the seventh. Receive, therefore, dearest brother, this little writing, in which, although I may not be able to reach so great a marrow of wondrous mysteries, I nevertheless endeavour to gather some things about the surface. In them you will find very many things useful to your discernment, if you take care to read what is written and commit it to memory.

## Another Prologue, Briefly Relating the Life of John the Evangelist and Also the Occasion of the Work Undertaken

[Col. 0683D] Blessed John, theologian of heavenly mysteries, whom Christ called away from a wedding and made an apostle and evangelist, reclined familiarly upon the Lord’s breast at supper by the privilege of beloved love; to him Christ entrusted his mother on the cross. After the apostles were dispersed throughout the whole world, by divine providence he preached the word of the sacred faith in Asia Minor after blessed Paul, as is recorded. Asia has seven cities: [Col. 0684D] Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea, among which Ephesus is the metropolis of the others.

After bishops had been appointed in the aforesaid cities, together with an archbishop, Saint John himself devoted himself to preaching. When the emperor Domitian heard of the blessed apostle’s steadfastness in evangelizing, he sent him into a vessel of boiling oil; and when John emerged unharmed, Domitian banished him to the island of Patmos, which lies in the Syrian sea. [Col. 0685A] While he was detained there, certain vices sprang up in the Churches of Asia through the negligence of their pastors. Concerning their correction, and concerning the present and future condition of the universal Church, he wrote down a vision revealed to him by the Lord and sent it to be read in sequence in his Churches.

But when Domitian had been killed by the senate and the Romans had ordered all his decrees to be nullified, [Col. 0686A] John was released from exile and returned to Ephesus with great joy. After some time, however, heresies concerning faith in the Trinity arose in that province. At the brothers’ request, in order to confirm the faith which he had taught, he wrote the Gospel. Afterwards he shone through many miracles and then rested in peace.

# Book One: On the First Vision

## Prologue

[Col. 0685B] God, immeasurable and eternal, who is not contained by place nor changed by time, who by his immeasurable and eternal deity powerfully created all things, that same God by his goodness mercifully redeemed his bride, namely the holy Church, from guilt and punishment. He enriches her, preserved from exile and prepared under the course and mutability of time for heavenly blessedness, with spiritual goods; he extends her throughout the world in some of her elect, and in others he blesses and exalts her in heaven.

This same Father of lights—that is, the author of spiritual gifts, from whom every good gift and every perfect donation descends daily—establishes and governs her through fitting ministers of the New Testament, and leads her by the narrow and difficult way which leads to life toward heavenly goods. On this way, for the feet of the holy Church climbing from the valley of tears to joys above, the prophetic word is a lamp, lest she stray through the ignorance of this life; it burns like a lamp shining in a dark place. [Col. 0685C]

Among such prophetic utterances, the prophecy of blessed John contained in this book, which Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator of God and men, revealed to him for the enlightenment of the holy Church, shines forth all the more gloriously and brightly because it sets forth loftier and clearer oracles concerning Christ and the Church. In this it surpasses other prophecies: it proclaims, for the most part, fulfilled mysteries concerning Christ and the Church. And as the Gospel surpasses the observances of the Law, so this prophecy surpasses the prophecies that looked from afar, since it has almost as many mysteries as words. Yet even this says too little, because every praise is inferior to the worth of the volume. In each of its words, indeed, manifold meanings lie hidden.

By exhorting the holy Church to patience, this Apocalypse—that is, Revelation—describes the many tribulations, afflictions, and persecutions which she suffers in the world, and the heavenly rewards which she will receive in heaven after time has run its course. First it presents the title to explain the work which follows. Then it adds a salutation to the seven Churches of Asia to which it sends this book, and so proceeds to the account of the seven visions by which the book itself is divided.

## Chapter One: On the Title and the Four Kinds of Visions

[Col. 0686B] “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ.” There are four kinds of visions, two inward and two outward. Two are bodily and two spiritual. The first vision is bodily when we open our eyes to outward and visible things and see heaven, earth, the forms and colours of visible objects. But this vision is the lowest and weakest. Because it is narrow, it does not comprehend the greatest things; because it is dull, it does not distinguish the smallest; because it is sluggish, it does not reach what is distant; and because it is not penetrating, it does not pierce hidden things. Finally, it contains no mystical meaning, but has only the movement and action of bodily sense.

There is another bodily vision, when a form or action is shown outwardly to the sense of sight, while inwardly it contains the great power [Col. 0686C] of mystical signification. Such was the vision which appeared visibly and outwardly to Moses in the bush, yet was full of typological significance. For what do we understand by the flame except the grace of the Holy Spirit? What by the bush—a small, rough, green, flowering tree—except the blessed Virgin Mary: humble through her self-abasement, rough against softness through the practice of virtues, green through faith, flowering through chastity? Therefore, when the Lord appeared in the bush, the flame did not harm the bush; and when the Son of God took flesh in the Virgin, under the overshadowing grace of the Holy Spirit, virginal modesty remained unharmed.

This second kind of vision, therefore, is far loftier and more excellent than the first, because the first is wholly devoid of mystery, whereas the second abounds in the power of a heavenly sacrament. Hence Moses said of the same vision: “I will go and see this great vision.” For it truly was a great vision: it both displayed a present miracle at that time and signified the incarnation of the Word and the perpetual integrity of the Virgin Mother. [Col. 0686D]

The third kind of vision does not occur through the eyes of the flesh but through the eyes of the heart: namely, when the mind, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, is led to the knowledge of invisible things through presented formal likenesses and images of visible things, as through certain figures and signs. The fourth kind of vision is when the human spirit, subtly and sweetly touched by an inward inspiration, is spiritually raised to the contemplation of heavenly things without any intervening forms or qualities of visible objects.

Of these two kinds of visions which occur not bodily but spiritually, blessed Dionysius the Areopagite writes thus in the book *On the Hierarchy*: “Besides the radiant illuminations of the most sacred sayings, when possible we shall contemplate symbolically and anagogically the hierarchies of heavenly minds—that is, of spirits—made manifest to us; that is, insofar as concerns their meaning, we shall consider heavenly priestly orders as far as we can.” A symbol is an assemblage of visible forms for the manifestation of invisible things. Anagoge is the ascent or elevation of the mind to contemplate things above. [Col. 0687A]

Here he notes a twofold manner of divine revelation, infused into the minds of theologians and prophets through visions and manifestations, which the Greeks call *theophanies*, that is, divine appearances. At times invisible things were displayed through signs resembling sensible things; at other times they were contemplated purely through anagoge alone, that is, the ascent of the mind to things above.

From these two kinds of visions arose likewise two kinds of description in sacred discourse. In one, the truth of hidden things is veiled by forms, figures, and likenesses; in the other, it is expressed nakedly and purely as it is, without a covering. Therefore, when what is hidden is made known through forms, signs, and likenesses, or when what is manifest is described in such ways, there is symbolic manifestation; but when it is shown by pure and naked revelation, or taught by plain and open reasoning, it is anagogical. [Col. 0687B]

Since, therefore, as has been said, there are four kinds of vision—two outward and two inward, two bodily and two spiritual—we must ask by which manner Saint John saw this Apocalypse, that is, Revelation. It is clear that he did not see it by the first two ways of seeing, which occur bodily and outwardly, since he testifies that he saw it in the spirit, saying: “I John, your brother and companion in tribulation and kingdom and patience in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ; I was in the spirit on the Lord’s day.” He who saw in the spirit did not see with the eyes of flesh but with the eyes of the heart.

Nor is it proved that he saw this in the fourth manner, since that fourth kind of vision is believed to occur without the mediation of forms of bodily substances—lest he be unable in this manner to conceal from evil persons what he had seen, and lest we be unable suitably to understand, without familiar words and customary visible forms, what he had seen without any forms capable of being represented. It is clear, therefore, that he contemplated it by the third manner of seeing, especially because this book is full of formal likenesses of temporal things: heaven, sun, moon, clouds, rain, hail, lightning, thunder, winds, birds, fish, beasts, living creatures, serpents, creeping things, trees, mountains, hills, air, sea, earth, and other things which are not presently before the senses. [Col. 0688A]

For our weakness, which can grasp high things only through low, spiritual things only through bodily, needed to know unknown things not by things more unknown but by things known. Hence blessed Dionysius says in the aforesaid book: “It is not possible for our mind to ascend to that immaterial imitation and contemplation of the heavenly hierarchies unless it uses the material guidance appropriate to itself.” He calls “material guidance” the images of bodily things, by which incorporeal and invisible things are figured in sacred Scripture.

Saint Dionysius himself expounds some of these with wonderful subtlety, explaining what are the formative images of angelic powers: what fingers are; what human form; what eyes, nostrils, ears, mouths, touch, eyelids, eyebrows, hearing, teeth, shoulders, arms and hands, heart, breasts, backs, feet, wings, nakedness, bright clothing, priestly attire, belts, rods, weapons, axes, geometric boundaries, winds, clouds, bronze, electrum, the colours of various stones, the form of a lion, the appearance of an eagle, horses, the distinctions of equine colours, rivers, chariots, wheels, and what is meant by the joy of angels. [Col. 0688B]

Our mind, therefore, knows visible things but does not know invisible things. Unless it used material guidance, that is, a likeness of bodily objects suited to it—namely, one which it knows—it could not ascend to immaterial contemplation. Therefore, very varied images of visible things are represented in sacred revelations, so that through familiar things our mind may learn to penetrate hidden goods, after the things it is accustomed to see.

Invisible things are figured not only by the splendid and bright likenesses of the most excellent visible things, but are very often most suitably signified by the qualities of middling and weak things. For none of the things that exist is wholly deprived of participation in goodness, since, as Scripture testifies, “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). Thus even the lowest and smallest things, and things which appear ugly in comparison with others, can fittingly figure invisible things. Of these, the aforementioned theologian says: [Col. 0688D] “Sometimes those theologians—that is, those who speak concerning the divine Scriptures—praise invisible wisdom itself by precious lights: as the sun of righteousness, as the morning star, as a mind rising in holiness, as light shining without circular motion and invisibly. At other times they praise it by middling things: as fire shining harmlessly, as water giving the fullness of life; and, to speak symbolically—that is, figuratively—as entering into the belly and as rivers overflowing with immeasurable abundance. But at other times by the lowest things: as sweet ointment, as a cornerstone. They even place a bestial form around it, adapting to it the character of a lion and panther; they say that it is leopard-like and like a raging bear. I shall add,” he says, “what is most contemptible of all and seemed to signify more: that the wise in divine matters—that is, the theologians themselves—have handed down the form of a worm as enveloping that very [divine] reality [syntax uncertain].”

Note what is said: that what is most contemptible of all seemed to signify more, namely the worm which signifies Christ, where Christ himself says of himself according to the flesh assumed: “I am a worm” (Ps. 21). For as a worm is born from the earth without intercourse, so Christ was born from Mary without male seed. Therefore the worm, said to be more contemptible than all, appears to signify more—that is, more fittingly. For every figure demonstrates the truth more clearly insofar as it figures itself through a dissimilar likeness and proves that it is not the truth. [Col. 0689A]

More dissimilar likenesses lead our mind back to truth precisely because they do not permit it to remain in the likeness alone. Hence sacred Scripture, with wonderful providence, descends to the ugly qualities of ugly things; and, by its signification of immaterial and invisible things, it employs things which do not allow our mind to rest in them, but by their ugliness compel it to pass beyond them toward immaterial things, far removed from every likeness to material things. Rightly it does not allow us to approve such ugly and temporal qualities, nor to suppose that divine and spiritual things are like them, or that anything of these things can be in them.

For if symbolic likenesses in sacred discourse were always drawn from bright, clear, and precious things, the human mind would be easily led astray—especially the minds of those who understand nothing higher than visible goods. According to the same theologian Dionysius, we might perhaps suppose that in heavenly things there are certain golden essences and certain shining men clothed in beautiful garments, and other such things by which sacred theology veils mystical meanings. [Col. 0689B]

But sometimes in the Scriptures they praise the blessedness of the superessential divinity as reason, intellect, and divine essence, thus declaring its rationality, intellect, and wisdom; they show that it is truly self-subsisting being and the true cause of the subsistence of the things that are; and they call it, as it were, light, form, and life. Although these representations are shown in some way to surpass material representations and seem to bear a purer signification toward that ineffable, incomprehensible, and boundless divinity, they nevertheless fail to express the truth as it is. For it is above every essence and life, without any light characterizing it; and all reason and intellect are left incomparably behind and far removed from likeness to it. [Col. 0689D]

For although the rational creature has been made in the image and likeness of its Creator, there is a great difference between creature and Creator, and its comparison with him fails. Blessed John, therefore, relegated to exile, removed from the noise and restlessness of the world and devoted to quiet, received and wrote this Apocalypse from the Lord, by the third manner of seeing, as has been proved above, for the benefit of the holy Church.

In receiving revelation while situated in quiet, he signifies to us that those who love inward quiet gain wondrous knowledge of invisible goods; and the farther they withdraw from temporal things, the more closely they approach eternal things. Those who involve themselves in secular business estrange themselves from inward and eternal things. They cannot consider great things concerning invisible realities, since they do not know how to call their minds back from visible things. If, therefore, we wish to draw near to God, let us lead our minds back from outward things to inward, so that, placed in the secret of quiet, we may contemplate heavenly things. [Col. 0690A]

Divine speech warns us of this, saying: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. 45), as though it said: Unless you are free from the disturbances of the world, you will not be able to contemplate me. Therefore gather yourselves from outward things, and in inward quiet see who I am. For the human mind makes itself nearer to spiritual things in proportion as it leaves temporal and bodily things farther behind; and it fixes its attention more clearly and penetratingly upon the highest things in proportion as it turns the rays of its own light away from the lowest.

Although the sea of secular disturbances may surge outwardly all around it, yet if the mind is gathered within itself through inward inspiration, it cleaves to divine things in contemplation, as though placed in the stability of an island: “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ.” Jesus and Christ are the two principal names of the Saviour most frequently repeated in the divine page. But although *Jesus* has great significance in itself, it is recognized as a name of personal designation. *Christ*, however, is solely the name of a sacrament. Jesus is interpreted “Saviour.” Many before him were called Jesus by this name, but none of them saved anyone from his sin. This one, however, saved his people from their sins. [Col. 0690C]

One sin is original, another actual. Original sin is what we contract from our parents by being born; actual sin is what we ourselves subsequently commit. But Jesus, our Saviour, saves us from both, since through the grace of baptism he frees us from both.

Again, two vices appear to be principal: malice and lust. From them, as from two springs, the remaining evils flow forth as rivers. For although gluttony too is a vice of the flesh, lust seems more properly to belong to gluttony, because lust does not cease to pour out whatever gluttony can swallow. Thus gluttony is shown to belong to lust as lust’s handmaid and servant. Gluttony gathers into the belly what lust may scatter in pleasures; and as lust strives to dissipate what has been gathered, so gluttony labours all the more through food to restore what has been dissipated.

Malice is the corruption of the whole soul, a spiritual vice and the spring and origin of spiritual vices. Therefore two greatest vices are the cause of all evils: malice and lust. Malice is within; lust is without. Malice is in the heart; lust in the flesh. Malice is the defilement of the spirit; lust, the defilement of the flesh. Malice produces the wrinkle; lust, the stain. Malice is the fuel of [Col. 0691A] spiritual vices; lust, of fleshly ones.

Sacred Scripture fittingly distinguishes and denotes these two vices where it says: “Wisdom will not enter into an ill-disposed soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1). Where it says, “into an ill-disposed soul,” it denotes malice; where it says, “in a body subject to sins,” it denotes lust. The Psalmist likewise says of these: “Burned with fire and dug down, they shall perish at the rebuke of thy countenance” (Ps. 79). For those burned in the flesh through lust and dug down in the heart through malice will perish at the rebuke of the Lord’s countenance, because when the Lord is manifested for judgment, the lustful and malicious will go, rebuked by him, into eternal fire.

These two vices are also rightly signified in Ishmael, who bears the figure of the reprobate. For it is written there: “He shall be a wild man. His hand shall be against all, and the hand of all against him; and he shall pitch his tents opposite his brothers” (Gen. 16): here malice is denoted. But where it is written that his mother would take a wife for him from the land of Egypt, lust is expressed. For what is Egypt, which is interpreted “darkness,” except a blind person who does not see himself to be blind? What is an Egyptian wife except blind lust? Therefore all the reprobate are blind; their hands are against all, and their hands provoke all against themselves; they pitch their tents opposite their brothers through the malice of pride of heart, and they obtain a wife from Egypt through the blind lust of the flesh. [Col. 0691B]

Nehemiah likewise sets forth these two evils where he describes himself as going out by the dragon’s fountain and the dung gate, to inspect the ruined wall of Jerusalem (2 Esdras 2). What is signified by the dragon’s fountain except the spring of malice? What by the dung gate except the stench of lust? What is figured by the wall of Jerusalem except those thought stronger in the holy Church? Thus, at the dragon’s fountain and the dung gate, Jerusalem’s wall is shown to have been ruined when those who seemed stronger and more exalted in the holy Church fall to lower things through malice or lust.

These, therefore, are the two greatest vices: malice, which may be so called because it denotes evils by which the spirit is corrupted; and lust, which seems to be the material of fleshly vices. But our God, our Saviour, saves us from all these, because through his grace he powerfully cleanses us from every defilement of flesh and spirit. He was therefore deservedly called by such a name, since he is so wondrous and so mighty in power.

But *Christ* is not a name of personal designation; it is solely the name of a sacrament. For in the Old Testament, those who were anointed with material anointing as kings or priests were called “christs,” that is, anointed ones. But our Redeemer was anointed not with material anointing but with the fullness of the Holy Spirit. Hence it is written: “Thou hast loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, thy God, has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy companions” (Ps. 44). [Col. 0691D]

Nor is he alone anointed in himself through the fullness of the Spirit: he also anoints his elect through participation in that same Spirit. “For from his fullness we have all received” (John 1). “Christ, ascending on high, gave gifts to men” (Ps. 67). And the Apostle says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness. To one indeed is given the word of wisdom” (1 Cor. 12), etc.

This is the anointing upon the head, which descends upon the beard and the hem of the garment (Ps. 132). The head signifies Christ, who is the head of all believers. The beard, which clings to the head and is a sign of manliness, signifies the apostles, who clung to Christ while he lived in the world. By clinging to him, they ate and drank with him; they heard his saving teaching and saw his miracles. After his ascension, having received the Holy Spirit more fully, they acted with manly strength, [Col. 0692B] because they confidently preached his faith through the kingdoms of the world. For his name they were delivered up in councils, scourged in synagogues, and led before kings and governors. In all these things they conquered manfully, departing from the council rejoicing when they were counted worthy to suffer disgrace for his name.

The hem of the garment signifies the last righteous persons who will exist at the end of the age. Therefore the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which is in the head—that is, in Christ—in fullness, descends upon the beard—that is, upon the apostles—by participation, when he said to them: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20), and when after his ascension he sent them that same Spirit and distributed the grace of tongues. It also descends upon the hem of the garment, because the same Holy Spirit will be given even to those who are to live [Col. 0692C] at the end of the world.

We may also understand the beard as the higher and more perfect persons, and the hem of the garment as the lower. But the anointing descends upon both, because the Lord through his grace blessed the little ones together with the greater. These two names, therefore, of the Redeemer of humankind—Jesus Christ—are repeated in the New Testament more frequently than any others: Jesus, because he saves us from our sins; Christ, because he is anointed with the Holy Spirit above all his companions. It follows:

“Which God gave him to make known openly to his servants.” The order of giving should be noted. God gave to Christ; Christ to the angel; the angel to John; John to the seven Churches of Asia; the Churches of Asia to the universal mother Church. [Col. 0692D] The universal mother Church daily administers and distributes it, through the voices of teachers, to the minds of individual believers. Thus every good thing given and every perfect gift that is from above descends from the Father into those predestined for life, proceeds in them variously, beautifully, and manifoldly, gathers them to the bosom of the mother who calls them, and unites them to her simplicity. But the heavenly good which we see now through a mirror and in an enigma, angelic spirits contemplate face to face. What we know in part, they know as they themselves are known. For just as sound eyes behold the brilliance of the sun clearly, whereas weak eyes cannot see it except with an intervening obstacle, so the invisible spirits of the heavenly essences—[Col. 0693A] whom no malice could corrupt when the reprobate angels fell—receive immediately the splendor of divine brightness; but human beings, darkened by the gloom of sins, are for the most part unable to behold it except through intervening figures. But when this mortal has put on immortality and this corruptible incorruption, then human beings, transferred to the lot of the angelic dwelling, will share in that same contemplation; and the divine good which they now receive in time, often through ministering angels and intervening figures, they will possess in eternity, when the ministers cease and the figures are removed.

Meanwhile, until we attain to the unity of faith and knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, the good thing given and perfect gift [Col. 0693B] flowing from God, the fountain of goodness, is generally ministered through angels and through things resembling what is perceptible to people higher in rank or merit, and is dispensed through superiors to inferiors. The purpose of the divine revelation is likewise declared in the book’s title when it says, “to make known openly.” For God gave him the Apocalypse itself for this purpose: that he might make it openly known. God wishes the talent to be put to use; he wishes a profit to be returned. He wishes us to make openly known the good that we know, and to teach others what we have learned from others. He wishes us to proclaim from the rooftops what we have heard by ear and in chambers, and that the lamp of divine knowledge lit in the mind should not be hidden beneath the measure of silence, but placed upon the lampstand of preaching, as is written at the end of the Apocalypse itself: “Let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22). [Col. 0693C] For hidden knowledge and an unseen treasure are of no use.

Therefore, just as it is sin for one who knows how to do good not to do it, so it is sin for one who knows how to speak what is good not to speak it. To whom sacred revelation ought to be made known is shown when it is added: “to his servants.” Not to proud philosophers, not to unbelieving Jews, not to unclean Christians. For holy things ought not to be given to dogs, nor pearls thrown before swine. Dogs are unbelievers, persecutors of the sacred faith, who bark against it itself. Swine are false Christians: they indeed possess faith as regards belief, but defile themselves with vices after the manner of swine. Therefore sacred mysteries must be concealed from both: from the former because of blind wickedness, from the latter because of a polluted life. [Col. 0693D] But to the servants of the Lord they must be diligently revealed, because they patiently hear what is said and devoutly do what they have heard. Thus, just as the divine good must not be disclosed to the wicked, so it must by no means be concealed from the good. And just as it is a grave fault to reveal sacred mysteries to the reprobate, so it is a grave fault to hide them from the elect. Therefore let not the useless servant, who now idles away from the office of teaching, feel secure, since on the day of judgment he must render an account of the profit on the talent entrusted to him. It follows:

“What must take place soon.” Whatever occurs in the present takes place soon, because both times and the things done within time quickly pass away. For this life is brief, the path slippery, and death uncertain. “What must take place [Col. 0694A] soon”: that is, matters—whether prosperous or adverse—that are to come upon the Church in this age, or matters to be recompensed at the end of the age. Thus all things take place soon, because present things quickly depart and future things quickly follow. And the more urgently, under the compulsion of time, the things contained in this book must be fulfilled, the more swiftly and diligently they must be announced, lest, when the moment of death comes, one who ought to have been justified through hearing perish by not hearing, and the Lord require the lost sinner from the preacher’s hand. For sacred teaching is completed for each person with the end of that person’s life; it remains to be fulfilled by the living as long as they live. It follows:

“And he signified it, sending through his angel to his servant John.” He shows the manner of sacred revelation when he says, [Col. 0694B] “He signified it.” He signified it because through certain signs, figures, and seals resembling perceptible things he revealed sacred mysteries. For he wished his mysteries to be shown through figures, so that they could not be understood without exertion, because what is acquired with labor is held more seriously and firmly. He also wished figures to be explained in some places, so that by this he might indicate that an explanation must be sought in other senses; and thus faithful seekers might find, while unbelievers who strive to distort and trample down sacred mysteries might not understand them.

“Through his angel to his servant John.” For the vision itself was shown to St John through an angel appearing in the likeness of the Son of Man, as John himself declares in what follows, where he says: “And when I turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like the Son of Man.” Therefore Christ, according to his humanity, received the mystery itself from the Father; and through an angel bearing the appearance of Christ, he transmitted it to holy John—and through him to the seven Churches, indeed to the universal holy Church—as a certain spiritual gift covered with diverse veils of figures, so as to exercise the minds of the elect and not lie open to the reprobate. [Col. 0694C]

What and how great was the authority of this most blessed John is made clear when it is added: “Who bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, to whatever he saw.” He was truly great, for he bore witness concerning Christ according to both natures, divine and human. The present wording shows that he bore witness to both natures of the Redeemer, [Col. 0694D] declaring that he bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ. He bore witness to the divinity when, contemplating heavenly secrets, he said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). He bore witness also to the humanity when he describes Christ preaching to crowds, performing miracles, dying and being buried, rising again, and appearing to the disciples. In the present wording, where “the word of God” is said, the divinity is indicated; but where “Jesus Christ” is then added, the humanity is signified. And John bore witness to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, to whatever he saw, because what he understood by contemplation with spiritual eyes concerning the mysteries of the everlasting Godhead, and what he could concerning the works of the humanity with bodily eyes, [Col. 0695A] he both proclaimed in speech and committed to writing. It follows:

“Blessed is he who reads, and he who hears the words of this prophecy, and keeps what is written in it.” At the end of the title, in order to win the goodwill and stir the diligence of those who read, hear, and keep this prophecy, he sets forth the reward: namely, eternal blessedness. In saying, “he who reads,” he indicates the educated or the teachers. In saying, “he who hears,” he denotes the laity or hearers. In saying, “he who keeps,” he means the elect from both groups. Thus nothing that is read or heard benefits salvation unless it is diligently kept in action. Therefore, if we desire to attain blessedness, let us strive not only to know by reading or hearing what is written, but more diligently to fulfill by living well what we know. Indeed, it would be better not to know the truth than, after knowing it, to turn away from the holy commandment. For the servant who knows his lord’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows. Good understanding—that is, useful understanding—belongs to those who put it into practice. [Col. 0695B] And the one who keeps what is written preserves the faith of Christ and the Church inviolate, fears the commandments, and seeks the promises. It follows:

“For the time is near”: namely, the time for labors to end and rewards to be received. Since, therefore, [Col. 0695C] the time is near for evils to end and good things to follow, let adversities on the path of this present life not break us, nor prosperity soften us, so that through the brevity of time we may arrive at the lastingness of eternity. Thus we have briefly tasted of matters concerning the book’s entrance and title, like one opening a door so as to see plainly what is within the house, in order that henceforth we may more clearly examine the mysteries contained inside.

## CHAPTER II. On the Greeting

“John, to the seven Churches that are in Asia: grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits that are before his throne.” Having set forth the title, he adds the greeting for the elucidation [Col. 0695D] and clarity of what follows; it shows to whom this prophecy is especially addressed. At the beginning of the greeting he chiefly determines three matters: to whom he sends greeting, what greeting he wishes them, and from where he desires that greeting to come to them. Where he says, “John, to the seven Churches that are in Asia,” he declares to whom he sends greeting. Where he adds, “grace to you and peace,” he indicates what greeting he wishes them. Where he then says, “from him who is, and who was, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits that are before his throne,” he makes known from where he desires it to come to them.

“John, to the seven Churches that are in Asia,” churches principally entrusted to him and particularly beloved by him, named individually in this prophecy: “Grace to you and peace”—grace to you through the forgiveness of sins, peace through divine reconciliation. Grace, so that guilt may be removed from you; peace, so that righteousness may be bestowed on you. Grace, so that you may be freed from the slavery of the devil; peace, so that you may remain in the Lord’s service. Grace having been stated, peace is immediately added, because when one, aided by grace, passes beyond the wall of one’s perversity by returning to God from the misery of sins, a most firm peace is at once restored between that person and God. Of this wall the Psalmist says: “In my God I shall pass beyond the wall” (Ps. 17). [Col. 0696A]

“From him who is, and who was, and who is to come, and from the seven spirits that are before his throne.” The phrase, “from him who is, and who was, and who is to come,” pertains to the person of the Son; and what follows, “and from the seven spirits that are before his throne,” pertains to the person of the Holy Spirit. He is silent about the Father because no one had held a wrong opinion concerning the Creator, nor had any error arisen concerning him. But he makes mention of the person of the Son and the Holy Spirit in order to dispel any harmful doubt that may have arisen concerning the faith of his readers. He speaks of the person of the Son and the Holy Spirit because almost all heresies arise in the Churches concerning them.

“He who is, and who was, and who is to come”: he who is essentially coeternal with the Father; who was with the Father in the creation of the world; who is to come in the Father’s glory on the day of judgment. He who is through the immeasurability of eternity; who was through the power of creation; who is to come through the justice of recompense. [Col. 0696C] He who is, because he subsists unchanged, God blessed above all things for ever; who was, because he created all things from nothing; who is to come, because at the end of the world he will judge the living and the dead.

“And from the seven spirits”: that is, from the sevenfold Spirit, who is simple by nature but sevenfold by grace. He distributes gifts to each as he wills. The throne of God consists of the holy angels and holy human beings, in whom God dwells and through whom he wonderfully exercises his judgments. But the seven spirits are before his throne, because the sevenfold Spirit invisibly illumines by his grace the invisible eyes of invisible minds, invisibly shows them what must be done, they always keep him before the gaze of their contemplation, and put into action what, under his teaching, they have learned should be done. [Col. 0696D] It follows:

“And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth.” Again he returns to the person of the Son, because the following discourse chiefly concerns him. He especially sets forth those matters that concern the nature of his humanity and the dispensation of human redemption, so that, hearing how great were the things he endured for us in taking on the nature of our flesh, we may consider how greatly we ought to love him.

Although, in the preceding passage, we excluded the person of the Father according to the explanation already given, we may nevertheless refer the phrase, “who is, and who was, and who is to come,” to the person of the Father, and understand the three tenses—present, past, and future, which encompass all time—as representing the immeasurable eternity of his Godhead. For what is added, “and from the seven spirits that are before his throne,” pertains to the person of the Holy Spirit; and what follows, “and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness,” pertains to the person of the Son. If we arrange the sentence in this way, we understand and say that the person of the Son is placed not second, after what has been said about the Father, but third, after what has been said about the Holy Spirit, and last for the reason that the following discourse of this chapter is principally to concern him. [Col. 0697A]

“He is the faithful witness” by preaching truth; “the firstborn from the dead” by rising again; “the ruler of the kings of the earth” by reigning in heaven.
