He is the faithful witness because he gave faithful testimony in the world concerning all things that were to be testified through him. [Col. 0697B] He is the faithful witness because he faithfully made known to his disciples whatever he heard from the Father. He is the faithful witness because he taught the way of God in truth, cared for no one’s favor, and regarded no human persons. He is the faithful witness because he announced condemnation to the reprobate and salvation to the elect. He is the faithful witness because he confirmed by miracles the truth that he taught in words. He is the faithful witness because he did not refuse, even in death, the testimony entrusted to him by the Father. He is the faithful witness because on the day of judgment he will give true testimony regarding the deeds of evil and good people.

“The firstborn from the dead.” Some are read to have been raised in the Old Testament by the prayers of prophets. But when death returned, they returned to dust. Christ, however, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer have dominion over him. For the life that he lives, he lives to God. In his flesh raised again and placed in heavenly glory, he has given us a certain hope of rising again and of attaining the heavenly and blessed dwelling. [Col. 0697C]

“And the ruler of the kings of the earth”: that is, of kings who are on the earth. Some are kings by governing those subject to them through divine disposition; some are kings by governing believers entrusted to them by God; others are kings by governing only themselves, with God’s help. The first are secular rulers; the second, pastors of Churches; the third, every individual believer. But Christ is ruler of all, because whatever is done in the world receives its right ordering from him and will receive its just recompense from him in the future. [Col. 0697D] He is ruler of all because from him come secular authority, pastoral care, and the individual diligence of every believer. Just as all these derive their origin from him, so they ought to order their action in accordance with him: rulers, through secular authority, should maintain justice among people subject to them; pastors, through pastoral care, should provide teaching to the faithful entrusted to them; and individual believers, through individual diligence, should cultivate fervent holiness in themselves. Rulers owe those subject to them protection against rapacious people; pastors owe those entrusted to them instruction against attacking demons. And individuals owe themselves resistance against vices.

Therefore these kings, if they adhere to their ruler, ought not to fear enemies in battle, [Col. 0698A] since they have such a ruler, who can defeat them by the mere nod of his will. Yet there are some among the first two kinds of kings just mentioned who disdain to adhere to the supreme ruler, who refuse to exercise in accordance with him the authority received from him, who rage against and devour those under them, and do not at all consider that they have above them a ruler who rescues the needy from the hand of those stronger than him, the destitute and poor from those who plunder them. This ruler of kings permits them to rage for a time for the testing and purification of the elect. But at the time of recompense he will judge them severely for this cruelty. Therefore let such kings—if indeed they are kings—return to conscience and recognize that they have above them a ruler to whom they must give an account of their deeds. [Col. 0698B] Just as he can confer authority, so he can also take it away. “The Lord loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord.” It follows:

“He who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood, and made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father.” He loved us through charity; he washed us through his passion. He loved us by suffering with us; he washed us by suffering. Because he loved us, he therefore washed us; for he would not have washed us had he not loved us. He washed us from our sins—original and actual, spiritual and carnal, grave and venial. He washed us in his own blood, not in the blood of animals as under the old law or covenant. That blood of the old covenant, of course, would have had no power to cleanse unless it had received it from that of which it was a sacrament: this blood. [Col. 0698C]

“And made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father”: that is, to the divine fatherhood or the paternal divinity. He made us a kingdom, so that we who were first the kingdom of the devil might now be the kingdom of God, and that God might now reign in those in whom the devil formerly reigned. He made us a kingdom so that we may destroy evil in ourselves, build up good, suppress vices, and raise up virtues. He made us priests, so that we who previously sacrificed to demons may henceforth sacrifice to God, and we who formerly offered the devil sacrifices of sins may now offer God sacrifices of good works.

“To him be glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.” Glory belongs to him with respect to the elect; dominion with respect to the reprobate. Glory, that the elect may glorify him; dominion, that the reprobate may fear him. Glory, that he may be praised by the good for benefits bestowed; dominion, that he may be feared by the wicked for evils committed. Glory, by which he glorifies the elect for righteousness; dominion, by which he condemns the reprobate for guilt. Or: glory in his own nature; dominion in creation subject to him. Glory, because he is above all things; dominion, because all things are under him. But although we distinguish these matters reasonably for the elegance and clarity of the sentence, we must nevertheless truly believe that in their highest sense and in the divine Godhead they are one and the same. [Col. 0698D] “For ages of ages”: that is, forever, truly or faithfully. Therefore glory and dominion may truly and forever belong to him who has done such and so great things for us. It follows:

[Col. 0699A] “Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him; and all tribes of the earth shall mourn themselves over him. Yes, amen.” After the greeting he adds certain matters concerning Christ’s coming and the terror of the future judgment, so that if we neglect to love God because of the benefits contained in the greeting, we may at least fear him because of the threats that follow. If because of the pleasant things that precede we disdain to do good, let us fear to commit evil because of the bitter things that follow. If what soothes us does not draw us toward God, at least let what terrifies us drive us away from the opposite course.

The phrase “he comes with the clouds” may be expounded in three ways. It may mean: he comes to the place to which clouds rise, so that, revealing himself in a lofty place, he may be plainly seen by all who rise again. Or: he comes with clouds, that is, with saints who were clouds—raining through preaching, flashing through the working of miracles, soaring through contemplation, and sheltering through intercession. Or again: he comes with clouds because it may be believed that, just as he ascended into heaven through a cloud, so he will come to perform judgment, as it is written: “This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1). [Col. 0699B] It follows:

“And every eye shall see him.” Every eye shall see him, because both good and evil, bodily and spiritual eyes, shall see him: the good to their glory, the evil to their shame. The bodily eye [Col. 0699C] shall see him as true man; the spiritual eye as true God. The good eye shall see him as worthy to be glorified; the evil eye as worthy to be blinded. The bodily eye shall see him, marveling at his brightness; the spiritual eye shall see him, carefully judging itself according to its deserts.

That the wicked too will see him he declares when he adds, “even those who pierced him,” as though saying: Not only the elect who are to receive from him the reward of blessedness will see him, but also the most wicked, who pierced him by crucifying him. Yet although the reprobate will see him, they will not contemplate his glory as the elect do. For it is written: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26). He describes a general calamity when he adds: “And all tribes [Col. 0699D] of the earth shall mourn themselves over him. Yes, amen.” By “tribes of the earth” he means all who love earthly things and prefer earthly things to Christ, as though saying: Not only those who pierced him will see him with sorrow, but all the wicked as well. “Yes, amen”: that is, truly—they will see him with sorrow and mourn themselves over him, because, when he judges, they will lose joy and go to punishment. They will mourn themselves over him because, whether through the ignorance of unbelief or through transgression of the law, they will recognize that they have deserved from him the sentence of condemnation. It follows:

“I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty.” So that we may not doubt what has been said above, but may most certainly believe his coming and the future judgment at the end, he introduces Christ himself speaking and confirms the preceding statement in Greek and Latin, so that it may be believed more firmly by hearers. For alpha, the first letter in Greek, is used for “beginning,” and omega, the last, for “end.” “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end,” as though Christ himself plainly confirms and says: Do not doubt what you hear; for as I am the beginning by creating you through power, so I am the end by judging through justice; and I who gave you the beginning of your existence will myself give the recompense for your merit. [Col. 0700A]

It should be noted that he places the Greek before the Latin because of its prerogative, namely the authority of antiquity, or so that the Latin which follows may be for us an explanation of the preceding Greek. “The Lord God says.” What he says, “Lord,” may refer to the creature subject to him; what he says, “God,” to the essence of the Godhead itself. “Who is, and who was, and who is to come” has been explained above.

“The Almighty” is almighty because he has done all that he willed in heaven and on earth: among angels, among human beings, in the creation of things made and the redemption of the elect; and because he will do whatever he wills in the glorification of the saved and the destruction of the condemned, providing all things with the governance of creation, the glorification of righteousness, and the condemnation of wickedness. He who is Creator of all is alone almighty, because everything created is partial, and is powerful only in part, just as it is wise only in part and free only in part. For not every effect is subject to a creature’s power, just as not every hidden thing is disclosed to its wisdom, nor does every elect person follow election. [Col. 0700C]

It should also be noted that in the greeting, where he used the words “who is, and who was, and who is to come,” he did not add “the Almighty.” But here he added “the Almighty” after the same words. There, in the greeting, where he wished to speak of divine benefits, he was silent concerning “the Almighty,” lest our love for the giver be diminished through fear of his omnipotence. Here, where he spoke of his coming and of the severity of the final judgment, he cried out “the Almighty” with terrible force at the end in order to strike terror into the contemptuous and negligent, as though saying: He who is now gracious through mercy in bestowing grace will at the end appear terrible through omnipotence in taking vengeance upon the contemptuous. Therefore let one who does not love him because of goodness already shown fear him because of the power he will exercise. Let one who will not love him because of the benefits set forth in the greeting fear him because of the terrors that follow that greeting. But, beloved, it is much easier and more useful to love one who is gentle than to fear one who threatens. Let us therefore love him while gentle, so that we may not come to fear him when angry. Let us wash away the filth of sins through weeping and confession, so that when he comes to judgment we may receive him not fearfully but confidently. [Col. 0700D]

## CHAPTER III. General Statement on the Seven Sacred Visions

The holy and universal mother Church, regenerated by the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, justified under [Col. 0701A] time that revolves through the number of seven days, and figured through the seven Churches of Asia, is perfectly instructed by the seven visions of this prophetic book, so that she may patiently endure present adversities as things soon to pass, and may ardently desire future goods as things that will remain forever. Although the prophecy itself is especially addressed to the seven Churches, the holy catholic Church is nevertheless taught in it generally concerning both her present state and her future. And it is rightly divided into seven parts in order to signify the perfection of doctrine contained in this prophecy, because universality is signified by seven, and the number seven is completed from four, the form of visible things, and three, the form of invisible things.

Since we are entering the deepest obscurities of heavenly mysteries, we shall briefly explain, for the elucidation of what follows, what each vision concerns, like one who enters a dense and shadowy forest and first carefully considers the path to be taken, so as better to complete it when considered. So too, as we traverse the obscure places of this book, we touch upon a few little branches of its meanings, lest we seem to have read the whole in vain. [Col. 0701B]

The first vision concerns the likeness of the Son of Man, which appeared through an angel to holy John, revealed heavenly mysteries to him, and commanded him to write. It also concerns the seven Churches and the bishops of the seven Churches; the rebuke of those bishops, and in some cases their praise and commendation; and the rewards to be given to those who conquer.

The second vision concerns the one seated on the throne and his adornment; [Col. 0701C] the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders. It also concerns the book written within, sealed with seven seals; the opening of the book and its seven seals; and the mysteries contained under the opening of the seals.

The third vision concerns the seven angels and the seven trumpets given them to sound, and the sounding of the individual angels in order. It also concerns other mysteries contained under the order of their sounding.

The fourth vision concerns the adorned woman who bore a male child; the dragon prepared to devour her son; and Michael and his angels, who conquered the dragon. It concerns the beast to which the dragon gave his power, its battle against the saints, the other beast that helped the first beast, and the condemnation of the wicked. [Col. 0701D]

The fifth vision concerns the seven angels who had the final plagues, the pouring out of the seven bowls of God’s wrath, the woman clothed in purple, the scarlet beast upon which that woman sat, and the mystery of the woman and the beast.

The sixth vision concerns the final punishments that the impious will suffer in hell. It first shows this concerning Babylon, describing its ruin, and the grief and mourning that those who loved it will have over its fall, as well as the exultation and thanksgiving the saints will offer at its destruction. It also concerns Christ, who will rule the wicked with an iron rod, and will tread them in the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty; the summoning of birds to the great supper of God, that they may [Col. 0702A] eat the flesh of the proud and wicked; and the condemnation of the beast, its false prophet, and all who worshiped the image of the beast. Then it again gives an account and describes how Satan is to be bound, so that he may deceive the nations no longer until the thousand years are completed; how, when released again, he will rage against the saints at the end; and how finally he, together with those not written in the book of life, will be thrown into the lake of fire. Describing this condemnation of the devil and all the wicked, it says that it was foretold by Christ, so that faith in it may be more certain.

The seventh vision concerns the end of the age and the renewal of the elements, when God will make all things new; the glorification of all saints and the merits by which they are to be glorified. It also concerns the heavenly city Jerusalem according to the state it will have after the day of judgment, when all its citizens have been gathered to it; it describes its brightness, foundation, wall, gates, length and height, and the other wonderful mysteries contained at the end of the book. Thus, near the beginning, we have briefly set forth each of the seven visions separately, so that we may afterward pass through their obscurities more easily. [Col. 0702B]

## CHAPTER IV. On the First Vision

“I, John, your brother and partner in tribulation and kingdom and patience in Christ Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ; I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s [Col. 0702C] day” (Rev. 1). Having set forth above what needed to be stated concerning the entrance to this book—namely, the title and greeting, the title so that we might immediately know at the beginning what he was sending, and the greeting so that we might know to whom he was sending it—he begins his account of the following visions. At the beginning of the first vision, he commends everything that follows by four things: person, place, cause, and time. He commends what follows by person when he says, “I, John, your brother and partner in tribulation and kingdom and patience in Jesus”; by place when he adds, “I was on the island called Patmos”; by cause when he adds, “because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ”; and finally by time when he says, “I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day.” [Col. 0702D]

“I, John”: as if to say, You ought gladly to hear this prophecy sent to you by me and diligently fulfill what it contains. For I, John, beloved by Christ and chosen as apostle and evangelist, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper, received it from him for your benefit and correction. To commend the matter, he adds: “your brother,” as if to say: You ought all the more willingly to receive it because you hear that it has been sent to you not only by one known to you and friendly toward you, but also by a brother.

And it should be noted that, although he could have said “master” because of his preeminence, he said “brother” because of humility. He therefore kept silent about being master, lest he seem to intimidate through authority [Col. 0703A]. He said “brother,” so that he might persuade more readily through humility. He is our brother not only by nature but also by grace; not only in Adam, but in Christ; not merely through the flesh of humanity, but through the spirit of adoption—that is, not merely according to generation, but also according to regeneration. And, so as to commend more strongly to his hearers, through his own person, the things that he writes, he adds, saying: “And a participant in the kingdom, tribulation, and patience in Christ Jesus”; as though he plainly said: “If, because of those things which I have written above concerning my person, you do not deign to hear this prophecy, at least hear it because of what follows. For you ought to hear me as a teacher all the more willingly because, in the matters mentioned [Col. 0703B], you hear that I am a participant with you.”

“A participant in tribulation and in the kingdom.” He rightly placed “in tribulation” first and added “and in the kingdom” afterwards, because “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.” For one who is unwilling, for Jesus’ sake, to endure adversities on the path of the present life cannot reign with him in the heavenly homeland. Yet since the wicked also endure many tribulations in this world—tribulations which indeed bring punishment but do not lead to the kingdom, inflict penalty but do not confer a crown—it is plainly shown which tribulation leads to a share in the kingdom when he adds, “and patience in Christ Jesus.” For then we truly make our way toward the heavenly crown: if outwardly we endure tribulation in the body, and inwardly preserve in the heart, for the love of Jesus, an inviolable strength of patience. For [Col. 0703C] he who is shaken by the lot of tribulation and inwardly disturbed by rage does not at all walk by the path through which he may attain to reigning with Jesus. Therefore, whoever desires to come to the crown of the kingdom must have patience in Jesus.

But since you have heard the quality of the person who was able to know such great mysteries, and to whom you ought to give credit concerning what he says, hear also the suitability of the place in which he could fittingly see such things: “I was on the island called Patmos.” The person was authoritative and known, honorable and friendly; the place remote, quiet, secluded, and private. In these two things—namely, person and place—we are shown that whoever longs to contemplate heavenly things must keep himself in the ark of holiness, and, withdrawing himself from worldly business, devote himself to quiet [Col. 0703D]. But because it has been written above concerning the person and the place, and we have discussed them more fully, we pass over them briefly and hasten to examine the other matters. It follows:

“For the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus Christ.” Where he says “the Word of God,” he expresses the Savior’s divinity; where he says “Jesus Christ,” his humanity. As though he said: “Because of testimony rendered to Christ’s divinity and humanity, I was sent into exile; and you ought therefore to receive this revelation more gladly, believe it more firmly, and carry it out more effectually, because, for the sake of him who revealed it, I underwent banishment in exile and suffer for righteousness, not for guilt.” “I was in the Spirit,” that is, in spiritual vision, “on the Lord’s day.”

As Gregory testifies, the quality of things is customarily indicated by the time: [Col. 0704A] Abraham saw the angel at noon, because he burned with faith; Adam saw him in the person of God after noon, because he had fallen away from the warmth of inward love; Lot saw the destruction of Sodom in the evening, because it was soon to occur; Solomon received wisdom at night, because he was not going to persevere in it. “On the Lord’s day,” as though he plainly said: As person, place, and cause commend the truth of sacred love, so also does the quality of the time; for the holier the day, the more fitting it is for divine revelation, and the quieter it is through cessation from outward labors, the more it rises through repose to inward contemplation. Thus, in the cause and the time we are shown that those who have learned to endure persecution for God and to keep festival from the servile works of sins are worthy to know heavenly secrets [Col. 0704B].

There are four things by which the matters that follow are commended: person, place, cause, and time—a worthy person, a suitable place, an innocent cause, and a fitting time. It follows:

“I heard behind me a loud voice, like a trumpet, saying: ‘What you see, write in a book and send it to the seven churches which are in Asia: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Laodicea, and Philadelphia.’” Above, he said that he had been carried into spiritual vision; now there follows an account of what he learned and to whom he was especially required to reveal what he learned. Whether he saw this vision all at once and in a single glance, or at different times on that same Lord’s day, or in the manner in which the angel showed it to him, it seems more fitting [Col. 0704C] and more true that he understood it successively rather than grasped it all at once and in a single glance.

First, up to the place where he says, “Write to the angel of Ephesus,” he describes, together with the mystery of the seven bishops and the seven churches, the likeness of the Son of Man which appeared to him through angelic ministration. He first gives instruction, common to bishops and churches alike, concerning all these matters; then, in order, he adds a particular admonition for each one, to the end of this vision. Since these matters have thus been arranged to make clear what is contained in this vision, let us consider more carefully and examine more subtly what the writer says: “And I heard behind me a loud voice, like a trumpet.” It is credible [Col. 0704D] that, just as he saw spiritually, so he also heard spiritually; and as the vision was spiritual, so too was the hearing spiritual.

Nevertheless, one must by all means ask why he who had been raised in the Spirit heard the voice not before him but behind him. Yet we shall resolve this question more quickly if we consider more attentively the cause and manner of the matter. For, separated from those under his charge and banished into exile, removed from the noise of the world and devoted to quiet, he had left far behind him every pastoral concern, all visible things, and things resembling visible things. Now, stretching himself forward and, by pure understanding with every image set aside, attending only to heavenly and invisible things, he was brought back to the instruction of those subject to him. He was taught, according to likenesses of sensible things, concerning the things that were to be written [Col. 0705A]; and thus he was, as it were, recalled from what lay before him to what lay behind. And when the Holy Spirit warned him to look, according to the formal qualities of things, upon those whom, while intent upon heavenly matters by simple contemplation, he had not been regarding, he heard the voice, as it were, behind his back.

But the size or quality of the voice expresses the force of its signification. When he says “loud,” he indicates that it signifies great things. When he adds “like a trumpet,” he shows that it exhorts the timid and slothful to fight against vices. Since we have said above that these seven churches signify the holy universal Church, with the sevenfold Spirit reigning, we judge it superfluous to discuss them again. But when he says, “What you see, write in a book and send it to the seven churches,” he indicates to us that, if we receive any useful and preeminent things from knowledge of the truth, we ought to make them known to others not only by word but also by example [Col. 0705B]. It follows:

“And I turned to see the voice which was speaking with me.” I turned from the things before me, to which I was clinging in contemplation, to the instruction of those subject to me—a task which I had set aside because of exile. I turned from the contemplation of God to the need of my neighbor, “to see the voice which was speaking with me.” For to see spiritually is to understand. As we see visible things with the bodily eye, so we understand invisible things through intelligence.

What he saw, he adds, saying: “And having turned, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands [Col. 0705C] one like the Son of Man, clothed in a robe reaching to the feet, and girded at the breasts with a golden belt.” The seven lampstands are the seven churches, as is made clear below, where it says: “The seven lampstands are the seven churches.” But it seems necessary to examine more closely why the churches themselves are compared to golden lampstands. Gold is tested by fire, beaten out by hammers, shaped into the form of a lampstand, and made an instrument of fire and light. So the churches, tested by temptations and thinned by the blows of persecutions, burn with the fire of heavenly wisdom and shine with works of charity. Lampstands stand firmly upon three feet, and holy churches are founded upon faith in the Trinity. We may also say that the churches are lampstands through knowledge of truth, and golden [Col. 0705D] through love of virtue.

What he says—“in the midst of the golden lampstands,” that is, in the midst of the churches—the likeness of the Son of Man that appeared to him accords with the Lord’s words, where the Lord says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18). Christ, therefore, is in the midst of his own, so that all may look to him and receive from his fullness. He is in the midst because all the elect alike contemplate his works with right thought and imitate them together according to their powers. He is in the midst because he grants glory to the good and condemns the evil to punishment. He is in the midst because he knows all equally and weighs and distinguishes the merits of each.

But because he testifies that he saw not the Son of Man but one “like the Son of Man,” he indicates an angel, who, in Christ’s person and likeness, displayed the mystery of divine revelation. This angel had the greater authority because he appeared in the very likeness of the Savior. Of this likeness he adds mystically, saying: “Clothed in a robe reaching to the feet.” The *poderis* is a priestly garment, and signifies the form of assumed humanity in which Christ offered himself to the Father for us and expiated the guilt of the human race [Col. 0706A]. The angel, therefore, was like Christ in the *poderis*, because the *poderis* signified his humanity; “and girded at the breasts with a golden belt.”

A belt at the loins signifies the restraint of carnal vices, for preserving the virtue of chastity. A belt at the breasts signifies the restraint of invisible thoughts, for guarding the virtue of charity. In the Old Testament an angel was seen by the prophet girded at the loins, because there the works of the flesh were forbidden. In the New Testament the angel was seen by Saint John girded at the breasts, because now even unlawful thoughts are restrained. For he who came to indicate that not only the defilement of the flesh, already forbidden in the Old Testament, but also the defilement of the spirit, more strictly forbidden in the New, must be restrained, ought to appear girded not at the loins but at the breasts. Hence, having rightly said “girded,” which signifies restraint of viciousness, and having added “at the breasts,” which indicates the restraint and breaking down of wandering thought, he did not say “of linen,” which would express the brightness of bodily purity [Col. 0706B] preserved even in ancient times. Rather, he added “golden,” which would figure the splendor of inward charity to be preserved in the present age. For while the charity of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us, every overflow of unclean thought is restrained.

But since we have heard what he said concerning the attire of the one appearing, let us now hear what he adds concerning his form. It follows:

“His head and hair were white as white wool, and as snow; and his eyes like a flame of fire; and his feet like *aurichalcum* [fine bronze], as in a burning furnace; and his voice like the sound of many waters.” The head signifies divinity; the hair, rational creation; whiteness, immortality. The head signifies divinity, as it is written: “God is the head of Christ” (1 Cor. 12 [cf. 11:3]). The hair signifies rational creation, because, just as hair has its origin from the head and receives from it the power of growth, so rational creation receives from God both its substance through creation and its growth in righteousness through the reception of heavenly grace [Col. 0706D]. Hair clings to the head, and rational creation clings to the highest Divinity. Hair is also rightly said to have the color of the head, because spiritual creation, whether angelic or human, has through divine grace the whiteness of immortality; and while, through the gift of its Maker, it abides in immortality, it is, as it were, not darkened by any corruption of death.

That not only angelic nature but also human nature united to divinity shines with the beauty of immortality, he plainly makes clear below. For he says, “as white wool, and as snow.” What do we understand by wool, which comes from earthly animals, except human nature? And what do we understand more rightly by snow, which comes from above, than angelic nature? Since, therefore, each nature is adorned before its Creator by the gift of immortality, the hairs of this head are fittingly declared to be white as white wool and as snow [Col. 0707A]. And having said “as wool,” he appropriately added “white,” in distinction from the wicked, who through guilt become dark and descend to the blackness of eternal death. The saints, however, who possess the whiteness of holiness in the world, have merited the brightness of immortality in heaven.

Yet it must be known that the whiteness which the head has by nature, the hairs possess by grace. For although created spirits also subsist immortally by nature, nevertheless, because in a certain manner they could die through guilt without the confirmation of grace, while through grace they persevere in righteousness without guilt, they endure through grace in complete and perfect immortality. According to what has been said, therefore, the head rightly signifies divinity; the hair, rational creation; whiteness, immortality; wool, human nature; snow, angelic nature.

“And his eyes were like a flame of fire.” A flame of fire gives light and warmth, inspires terror, and burns up. Thus his eyes are like a flame of fire because, looking upon the elect, he illumines them with the light of wisdom and warms them with love of righteousness; looking upon the reprobate, he terrifies them by the severity of his threat and burns up the uncorrected [Col. 0707C] with the fire of condemnation.

“And his feet like *aurichalcum*.” As we understand divinity by the head, so by the feet we ought to understand the weak and imperfect faithful, who, because they cannot wholly raise themselves from earthly things, touch the ground after the manner of feet. They are by no means like gold, but like *aurichalcum*, because they do not attain to the brightness of the wise who are perfect, but imitate them from afar as far as they can. Yet since the more they still cling to earthly things, the greater the tribulation they endure, it is rightly added: “as in a burning furnace.” For the imperfect and weak are tested in the furnace of temptations, so that, proved through the tribulation of temptations, they may be found worthy of God [Col. 0707D]. The perfect are outside the furnace because they have been proved; the imperfect are in the furnace because they must be proved. Therefore his feet are like *aurichalcum*, not gold, because those who are weak, and still weak in holiness, remain in their imperfection and have not yet come to perfection. And they are “as in a burning furnace” because they are still in the testing-place and have not yet been tested.

“And his voice like the sound of many waters.” Many waters are many Scriptures. As waters wash away dirt, so the words of the Scriptures cleanse away vices. Hence the Lord says to his disciples in the Gospel: “You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15). The voice of waters is the preaching of the Scriptures. Concerning this voice it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 19) [Col. 0708A]. Therefore, his voice is like the sound of many waters. His voice resounds in the manner of waters running through the world and watering it, while Scriptures of manifold authority proclaim his faith through the mouths of believers in every land, people, tribe, and language. And as the sound of waters is pleasing to some and hateful to others, so the preaching of the Scriptures pleases the good and displeases the evil; it soothes the good and terrifies the wicked. It soothes by the promise of heavenly rewards and terrifies by the threat of infernal torments.

But since we have heard above concerning his attire and form, let us now hear concerning his power.

“And he had in his right hand seven stars, and from his mouth went forth a two-edged sharp sword.” The seven stars are the bishops of the seven churches, as the book itself will explain below; these bishops signify all the shepherds of mother Church. They are rightly compared to stars, not planets, because they ought to remain in the same state of righteousness, not change themselves through diverse vices; they ought to have their citizenship in heaven through contemplation and provide light to those subject to them through preaching heavenly wisdom and the brightness of good works [Col. 0708B]. They are also rightly said to have been in the Redeemer’s hand—that is, in his power—so that, with his help, they might worthily govern the churches entrusted to them.

That he holds them in his hand not to punish evil but to accomplish good is shown by the words “in his right hand.” For the elect are at his right hand because they are aided in good; the reprobate are at his left because they are abandoned in evil. The right hand commonly signifies good, and the left hand evil. Therefore those are not undeservedly said to be at his right who appear destined to stand at the right; while those are at the left who are believed destined to stand at the left.

But because certain vices had sprung up in the churches entrusted to them through the bishops’ negligence, after saying that he had the seven stars in his right hand—so that this might be a consolation to them—he immediately added that a two-edged sharp sword went forth from his mouth, which might serve for correction. The former bestowed confidence through grace; the latter instilled fear through negligence, so that they might draw assurance from the one and not despair, and caution from the other [Col. 0708D] and amend themselves. This may also be applied to all persons: each ought so to presume upon pardon that he nevertheless never ceases to cleanse himself from guilt. He ought so to trust that he is at God’s right hand that he guards against being struck by his left. He ought also to rejoice in God because of mercy, yet with trembling because of strict justice.

By the sword we understand the divine word, concerning which it is written: “The word of God is living,” and so forth, “to the discerning of the thoughts of the heart” (Heb. 4). It is said to be sharp on both sides because in the Old Testament it cut off carnal vices, and in the New spiritual ones also. It is sharp on both sides because it cuts away outwardly in us the lust of the flesh, and inwardly the malice of the heart. It is sharp on both sides because, in those who despise what it commands, it punishes body and soul [Col. 0709A]. It is sharp on both sides because it distinguishes the wicked from the good and repays each one what he deserves.

But since there has been discussion above of attire, form, and power, he now adds in due sequence a discussion of glory.

For he says: “And his face shone like the sun in its strength.” Note that, after saying “his face shone like the sun,” he immediately added: “in its strength.” He said what he could; had he been able to say more, he would have said more. For if among visible things he could have found a more luminous substance to signify still further Christ’s glory, he would certainly have signified it by that. Thus he used the brightest creature to express the glory of his brightness, when he said that his face shone like the sun. But knowing that this was by no means sufficient and that he could say still more, after saying “shone like the sun,” he immediately added “in its strength.”

The sun shines in its strength when, about noon, the clouds having been removed and the air made clear, it gleams with the brightest radiance through the spaces of that air [Col. 0709B]. Let him who can, therefore, consider what the immense, eternal, incomprehensible, and ineffable brightness of divinity must be, if the appearing likeness of assumed and glorified humanity was so wondrous. But who can express in words, in Christ our Redeemer, even the glory of his blessed humanity, when the holy theologian scarcely suffices, or is able, to declare the likeness he saw? Therefore, since human intelligence does not suffice to comprehend the glory of his humanity, nor can language fittingly disclose it, let us not be searchers of majesty, lest we be overwhelmed by glory. Meanwhile, with grace assisting, let us examine and heal our weakness, that we may sometime merit to attain the contemplation of his glory. Let us labor with all our powers to arrive by merits at the brightness of that light which shines in every darkness and which no darkness can ever overcome. Let us retain in the mind, according to its strength, the glory of Christ’s manifested likeness, so that we may kindle more ardently within ourselves desire for that glory figured by this likeness.

For this reason the visible splendor is set before us in sacred vision: that by its signification of brightness our weak mind may at least contemplate the good of invisible beauty, and, when it sees such an immeasurable beauty of the Creator, blush to prefer to it any beauty of a creature [Col. 0709D]. Sacred Scripture promises us a desirable likeness of this beauty when it says: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Wisdom 31; Matt. 13). There are, therefore, four principal features by which he describes to us the likeness of the Son of Man who appeared to him: attire, form, power, and glory.

Having seen such majesty, he adds what he himself did, saying: “And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead.” Let him who can estimate what this man would have done if he had seen the glory of Christ’s divinity, when, on seeing the likeness of his glorified humanity, he fell as though dead at his feet. Let him who can consider [Col. 0710A] how weakened is the eye of the human heart, created to contemplate divinity, which nevertheless could scarcely endure to contemplate the likeness of his humanity.

“And when I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead,” because the more perfectly the human mind knows invisible goods, the more vile it becomes in its own estimation; and the more sublimely it contemplates the Creator’s power, the more it humbles itself before itself. The history of Esther aptly intimates this to us, if we set aside what it narrates according to the letter and attend to what it contains spiritually (Esther 5). For we read that Esther, beholding King Ahasuerus seated on his throne opposite his royal hall, holding a scepter in his hand and showing by his burning eyes the rage of his breast, was almost deprived of life, so that even while the king and his attendants consoled her, she could scarcely be raised up [Col. 0710B].

Whom, then—to gather many lengthy matters into one brief statement—whom, I say, does King Ahasuerus signify here except God? Whom does Esther signify except the soul? What does the royal hall signify except divinity? What does the throne signify except majesty? What the scepter except peace? What the burning of the eyes except the terror of heavenly judgment? Esther looked upon the king, was terrified, and fell; likewise the soul, contemplating God and God’s strict judgments, trembles before the divine majesty. Therefore let the saint raised up to contemplate the Savior’s likeness say: “I fell at his feet as though dead.” The words “I fell at his feet” signify humiliation; the added words “as though dead” signify the correction of fear.

[Col. 0710C] And note that he does not say “utterly dead.” If he had despaired, he would have been utterly dead. But because he was only terrified and did not despair, he fell not truly dead but as though dead. The human mind ought to govern itself by such discernment in contemplating its Creator: when it sees wondrous things concerning the invisible, it should wholly humble itself through fear because of its imperfection, yet not cast itself down through despair; and thus it should grow pale through fear, without dying. It should offer the reverence of humility without at all losing confidence in salvation.

Alternatively: “as though dead,” that is, dead to the world and alive to God. While we are in the body, we must indeed live to the world as long as bodily necessity requires, and die to the world through forgetting superfluity. We are not utterly dead because of bodily necessity, but as though dead through cutting away what is superfluous. Whoever, therefore, knows how in this way or that to humble himself or mortify himself immediately merits from God the gift of heavenly help: that he may be raised to higher things because of humility, and strengthened by the grace of divine consolation because of fear. Hence it is rightly added: “And he placed his right hand upon me, saying: ‘Do not fear.’” In placing his right hand upon him, help that raises up is expressed. In saying “Do not fear,” the grace of consolation is recognized.

But that we may know that he fails in neither respect but is almighty in both, the following makes known who, what kind, and how great he is, and gives confidence concerning both [Col. 0711A]. For he says: “I am the first and the last, and the living one; I was dead, and behold, I am alive for ever and ever; and I have the key of death and of hell.” As though he said: “When you hear that I am such and so great, see that you do not distrust in either matter, but have confidence in both. I describe to you who I am so that, when you hear my sublimity and power, you may gain confidence concerning what I say.”

“I am the first and the last.” First through creation; last through recompense. First, because before me no God was formed; last, because after me no other will be. First, because all things are from me; last, because all things are directed to me. From me as their beginning; to me as their end. First, because I am the cause of origin; last, because I am judge and end.

“And the living one; and I was dead.” In these words—as often happens in expressions and passages of Scripture—the order is inverted. For if the writer had put first “dead,” which he placed afterward, and added afterward “living,” which he placed first, he would have ordered the sentence more correctly. But although this inverted order is found in many places, it need not concern us greatly, because, even though it is contrary to customary speech, it in no way diminishes the integrity of truth; and what was not preserved in the narration may be preserved in the exposition of the narration.

“And the living one; and I was dead”: dead through the Passion, living through the Resurrection; dead in suffering for the elect, living in rising from the dead. And because, as we said above in a certain place, some are read in Scripture to have been raised, who are afterwards read to have died again, he adds in order to show the unending permanence of his life: “Behold, I am alive for ever and ever,” that is, always. For Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him; for in that he lives, he lives to God [Col. 0711C].

And because he is recognized as powerful by the matters already stated, both in the creation of the saints and in the redemption of the elect, it is rightly added: “And I have the keys of death and hell,” so that he may also be recognized as powerful in the condemnation of the reprobate. What indeed do we understand by keys except the power of opening and shutting? He therefore has the keys of death and hell because by his power he will open the gates of death and hell, where he will confine the devil and his companions to be tormented without end. Therefore he who is so great in power can truly exalt those of his who humble themselves for his sake and strengthen those who tremble in his fear.

We may understand the distinction between death and hell in this way: by “death,” the torment prepared for the reprobate; by “hell,” the place assigned to that torment. Nor do only these words of the one appearing and speaking—“I am the first and the last,” and the rest which follow—commend the foregoing matters; they also confirm those which follow. For he says: “Write, therefore, the things which you have seen, and the things which are, and the things which must happen after these things.” He rightly ought to write the things commanded, because he recognized as almighty the one who commanded him to write what he had seen [Col. 0711D].

[Col. 0712A] It should therefore be noted that he defines three times: present, past, and future. He indicates past time where he said, “the things which you have seen”; present time where he says, “and the things which are”; future time where he adds, “and the things which must happen after these things.” “Write the things which you have seen,” whether with the bodily eye or with the understanding of contemplation: namely, the dispensation of the Incarnation and the mystery of divinity. “Write the things which are”: worldly tribulation and divine consolation. “Write the things which must happen after these things”: the final persecution; the testing of the truly faithful; the reprobation of those falsely faithful; the manifestation of both; the condemnation of the wicked; and the glorification of the good. Write, so that as you are instructed through heavenly vision, so others may be instructed through the description of that same vision.

What he ought first to write, he then shows: namely, the things which he had already seen above. For it follows:

“The mystery of the seven stars which you saw in my right hand, and the seven golden lampstands”—understand, “write.” A mystery is so called as a sign of a sacred thing, where one thing is seen and another understood; as in this place, where stars and lampstands were seen, but bishops and churches were understood. The one who appeared to Saint John explained this mystery, so that he might indicate that allegory is to be sought in other passages of Scripture also. He says therefore: “The seven stars are the bishops of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the churches.” But because we have discussed above why stars designate bishops and lampstands churches, we do not judge it necessary to repeat the discussion [Col. 0712C].

We have thus expounded the beginning of this first vision with as much brevity as we could, so that by the brevity of the reading we may remove weariness, and by exposition of the truth impart instruction. And because we have already examined those things that pertain to general instruction, let us now proceed to examine those which pertain to the particular admonitions of individual bishops and individual churches.

## CHAPTER V. On the bishop of Ephesus.

And write to the angel of the church at Ephesus: “Thus says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand, who walks in the midst of the golden lampstands: I know your works, and [Col. 0712D] your labor, and your patience; and that you cannot endure evil men; and that you have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and have found them liars; and that you have patience, and have endured for my name’s sake, and have not failed” (Rev. II).

Having above given general instruction concerning him who appeared like the Son of Man, he proceeds to set forth the particular admonitions addressed to individual bishops or churches. In these admonitions are contained universal exhortations for all bishops and pastors of Christ’s churches, and they are rightly signified through these persons. For many things written individually in these admonitions apply generally to all who act negligently within the holy Church. For it is written: “What I say to one, I say to all” [Col. 0713A] (Mark XIII).

He first treats of the bishop of the church at Ephesus, who was pre-eminent above the rest in precedence and dignity, so that, when he who resided in the metropolitan city is rebuked, he may be offered to all others, once corrected, as an example of correction. Bishops themselves are called angels—that is, messengers—in prophecy, because divine commands are proclaimed through them. In the following words of this vision, moreover, he sometimes praises those to whom they are addressed, and sometimes rebukes them, so that by praising he may strengthen them in good, and by rebuking may chastise them for evil.

“And write to the angel of the church at Ephesus,” as though he said: Not only carry out in writing the things commanded you above, but write carefully the things that follow, so that the good which the sacred vision discloses to you may become known to others through your writing; and so that you, who here bear the person of the speaker, may there bear the person of the teacher—here, by seeing, in the person of a disciple; there, by writing, in the person of a master. Write first, moreover, to the metropolitan bishop, because he surpasses the others in dignity, so that, once corrected, he may become a model of correction for the rest.

He then adds what he is to write, saying: “Thus says he who holds the seven stars in his right hand and walks in the midst of the golden lampstands.” The beginning of the present chapter was expounded in the middle of the preceding chapter. In these words, namely, he holds out the assurance of attaining his grace to the seven bishops and seven churches of Asia, and in them to all the prelates and faithful of the universal mother Church. For in saying, “who holds the seven stars,” he gives assurance to the seven bishops and, in them, to all prelates. But in saying, “who walks in the midst of the golden lampstands,” he gives assurance to the seven churches, to the seven bishops, and, in the bishops, to all the faithful of the holy Church.

It is as though he said: If anyone has lost a higher rank and through negligence has fallen to lower things, let him not despair; rather, let him raise himself again to higher things, do penance, and he will find his former grace. For I, who hold the seven stars even after negligence has been committed, who walk in the midst of the seven golden lampstands—for those who sin, if they repent, I neither abandon nor despise them. Rather, I hold them by the hand so that they may recover the good they have lost, and I advance them toward greater things. I gently rescue them from evil and powerfully aid them in good. [Col. 0713D] For those whom he still held in his right hand, and in whose midst he walks, had already sinned and acted negligently; nevertheless, he did not abandon them to punishment, but warned them toward repentance.

Oh, how wonderful is the condescension of divine mercy toward us! Even among the holiest, if it wished to deal with them strictly, it would find grounds on which justly to condemn them; yet it preserves sinners, recalls those who flee, gathers the scattered, frees the perishing, gives life to the dead, justifies the ungodly, rebukes the negligent, rouses the sluggish, raises the fallen, instructs the ignorant, leads back the straying, receives those who return, and guards those whom it has received. Whoever, therefore, considers divine clemency must by no means despair of pardon.

But since we have discussed above what the stars signify, what the right hand signifies, [Col. 0714A] what the golden lampstands signify, and likewise what is meant by “in the midst,” we do not now care to repeat the same things. Only this remains to be said: what does he mean by “walks”? Christ walks in the midst of his servants because he dispenses grace to all for the perfection of virtues and good works. He walks in the midst because, while he comes to some, he distributes his goods to others. In another sense, he stands through the eternity of his divinity; he walks through the course of his humanity. Therefore he walks in the midst of the golden lampstands when he sets before all the elect, for imitation in holiness, the example of his human life.

Let us hear what he says: “I know your works and your labor.” He first praises, then rebukes, so that by praise he may raise to good and by rebuke correct from evil. He praises to strengthen; he rebukes to chastise. He praises for good; he rebukes for evil. He praises where he says: “I know your works, your labor, and your patience.” [Col. 0714B] He rebukes where he says: “But I have against you that you have left your first love.”

“I know your works”: “I know,” that is, “I approve.” For in a sense we do not know what we disapprove. Hence the Lord, who through his wisdom knows all the ways of the devil, in some manner does not know them when, in the life of blessed Job, he asks him whence he has come (Job I). Your works are good works, namely, those shown to neighbors in need; your labor is the affliction of the body; your patience is endurance in the heart. And he sets forth these three. For there are some who do not distribute to their neighbors the good things received from God; who, by delicately nourishing their bodies, do not labor at all; and who, when adversity occurs, bear it impatiently. There are others who, while distributing their goods, afflict their bodies, but do not know how to preserve patience amid adversities.

But this man is praised for all these things when it is said: “I know your works, your labor, and your patience,” as though he said: I know that you willingly distribute the good things you have received to the needy, that you labor by afflicting your body, and—what is more excellent than these—that you preserve patience in adversities. But since we have heard what kind of pastor he was in good, let us now hear what he was like also with regard to evil. For it follows:

“And you cannot endure evil men.” The inability to endure evil men is not a vice, but an instrument of great virtue. For you are by no means perfectly good if you bear evil men with equanimity in their wickedness. Whoever patiently tolerates evil men in their wickedness thereby gives assent to their wickedness and thus plainly shows that he has not yet ascended to the summit of goodness. Therefore, by this example, we ought to resist the evil as far as we can, and restrain their wickedness as far as we are able, just as blessed Paul resisted the Prince of the Apostles—that is, Peter—to his face in the matter in which he was blameworthy (Gal. II).

Therefore, if we wish to be perfect in this matter, we must oppose what we know to be against God, lest we hear what is said of some: “He who is not with me is against me” (Matt. XII; Luke VIII). Thus evil persons must by no means be tolerated in this way; rather, with love for the persons and hatred for their vices, they must be rebuked; and if [Col. 0715A] they refuse correction, they must be expelled from the fellowship of the good, lest by their deadly contagion they destroy very many.

It is therefore highly credible and worthy of imitation that the aforesaid bishop was both praiseworthy in good works and unable to endure evil men. For to be unable to endure evil men in this manner—that is, without correcting them, or, if they are incorrigible, expelling them—is not the vice of impatience but zeal for justice. Let the zeal of God’s house therefore consume us in such a way that it consumes perversity in evil persons; and let us strive to exercise virtues in ourselves in such a way that we also seek to overcome vices in others.

Indeed, what is contained above is praiseworthy; but what follows is less praiseworthy. For it is added: “And you have tested those who call themselves apostles and are not, and have found them liars.” There are those within the holy Church who appear good openly but are evil in secret, who outwardly display the appearance of holiness yet inwardly lack the truth of holiness. Their malice sometimes harms more ruinously precisely because it is more hidden; and the less it can be known, the more difficult it is to avoid. Therefore, we must carefully investigate and examine the corrupt life of such persons—who feign goodness in word or deed but are evil in the intention of their heart—and reveal their hidden malice to all unless they correct themselves, so that the more openly it is recognized, the more safely it may be avoided.

Thus by his example we must be taught not only openly to oppose evil persons, but also diligently to test those who are deceptively good; and, when they have been proved such, if they are willing to be corrected, to correct them. If not, we must disclose their perversity to others as a warning. The ruler of the Ephesian church fulfilled both things praiseworthily: he could not endure evil men, and he tested those who claimed to be apostles but were not, and found them liars. Where it is said that he could not endure evil men, it is understood that he opposed those who were evil. But where it is added that he tested those who said they were apostles and were not, and found them liars, it is plainly shown that he also examined the pretence of those who were deceptively good.

“And you have found them liars,” he says. He found them liars not only in speech, but also in life; not only through the falsity of their preaching, but also through their pretence of righteousness. Therefore, if we wish to live rightly and perfectly, let us not merely exercise virtues in ourselves, nor merely support the elect according to our strength; but let us also seek openly to restrain evil persons from their begun wickedness and prudently examine the deceitfulness of hypocrites, correcting, if possible, the malice of both. If not, at least let us sharply assail their wickedness in words.

But since, when any elect person suffers persecution from the reprobate, it is fittingly added: “And you have patience, and have endured for my name’s sake, and have not failed.”

He seems here to distinguish three things: first, that he had patience; second, that he endured for Christ’s name; third, that he did not fail in that very patience. In saying, “and you have patience,” he indicates that he had himself suffered persecution from the ungodly whom he opposed. But in concluding, “and you have not failed,” he indicates endurance in perseverance. “You have patience,” as though he said: Although the reprobate have inflicted persecution upon you on account of righteousness, you have not lost the virtue of patience; you endured for my name’s sake, not from desire for earthly gain, not for the empty praise of the crowd, nor did you suffer this for guilt, but for righteousness. “And you have not failed.”

Let each person, then, consider how great and of what character was he who shone with so many and such great works and virtues: who distributed his goods to the needy; who labored by afflicting his body; who preserved patience in his heart amid every adversity; who could not openly endure evil men; who tested and exposed those deceptively good; who did not lose patience in persecution; who endured persecution for no other reason than that the Lord’s name might be glorified; who failed in nothing but conquered bravely in all things. Yet he fell short of perfect righteousness. Therefore the rebuke is added: “But I have against you that you have left your first love.”

Above he first set forth praise and then adds rebuke. In this we are plainly taught that, if we wish to correct someone by our words, we ought first to remind him of whatever good qualities he possesses, lest, if we first embitter him by rebuke, we do not raise him to recover the good he has lost, but cast him headlong into the abyss of despair. There are, indeed, faint-hearted persons who, if harshly reproved [Col. 0716C] for what they have done wrong, sink themselves, crushed by the weight of fear, into the sorrow of excessive sadness. Therefore, great discernment must be exercised toward such persons, lest what we do for their good be turned into evil for them.

“I have against you that you have left your first love,” that is, that you have diminished either in love of God or in love of neighbor. He did not say simply that you have left love, but made a distinction, saying that you have left your first love. From this we may observe that he had indeed been diminished in good, but had not been wholly emptied of good. He had lived less securely in the grace received, had acted negligently in certain matters, and thus had fallen from the summit of his perfection to a lessening of that perfection. But the Lord, whose eyes see our imperfection, warns him to recover by repentance the rank he has lost. He says therefore: “Remember, then, from where you have fallen; repent, and do the first works.” As though he said: Consider that you have fallen from the height of your perfection and descended to the depths of imperfection; repent of your negligence, and, by doing the first works, recover your first grace. It follows:

“But if not, I will come to you quickly, and will remove your lampstand from its place unless you repent.” After the admonition he adds a threat, so that, if he should despise the admonition, he might at least fear the threat.

And it should be noted that he did not merely say, “I will come to you,” [Col. 0717A] but added “quickly,” so that by the definite announcement and swiftness of his coming he might instill greater fear in the negligent person. “And I will remove your lampstand from its place.” “I will remove your lampstand from its place,” that is, I will take from your hand the church committed to you, so that you may no longer hold or guard it. For it was said above that churches are symbolized by lampstands. Thus his lampstand would rightly be removed from its place if the church were taken from his hand and entrusted to another for governance.

Alternatively: I will take from you the gifts and virtues which you still possess, and will give to another the reward promised to you. From the aforesaid rebuke and threat, then, consider how great is the fault of acting negligently after grace has been received, and of not advancing in it but rather declining. Hence Paul warns us, saying: “We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (II Cor. VI). He receives God’s grace in vain who neglects to advance in it and instead declines. But it follows:

“But this good you have: that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.” Again he returns to praise and commend him, so that if his mind were shaken by excessive fear from what preceded, it might be strengthened through the praise which follows. Nicholas was one of the seven deacons whom we read were appointed by the apostles; he made his wife common to all. Thus, together with the good things stated at the beginning, this man commendably possessed this good and agreed with the Lord in this: that he hated, along with the Lord, the deeds of the Nicolaitans—that is, the heresy of those who followed Nicholas. [Col. 0717C]

Therefore he ought greatly to have been strengthened, since after the rebuke for negligence he knew himself praised for good. “But this good you have, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate,” as though, looking back to the things already said, he were saying: Although you hear yourself rebuked, do not rush into despair, because together with the good things mentioned above you also have this good: you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate. It follows:

“He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” He truly has an ear who possesses understanding to comprehend and retain, and the affection to love and merit the things promised. For in a sense that person lacks ears who has no concern for the heavenly goods promised to him.

“What the Spirit [Col. 0717D] says to the churches.” Spirit in this passage designates not merely the person of the Holy Spirit, but the holy and undivided Trinity itself, believed to be one Godhead and worshipped as one God. For God is spirit. He says therefore, “what the Spirit says,” that is, what God promises. And fittingly, at the end of the individual admonitions made to individual bishops, where he adds the reward that shall be given, he does not say, “what the Spirit says to this church,” or “to that church,” or, individually, to Ephesus or Smyrna, and so to the rest; but “what the Spirit says to the churches,” in the plural. Since the promised reward was common to all, in the individual admonitions he had to embrace not merely one church but all churches together, so that, when all heard the common promise, [Col. 0718A] they might hasten toward the recompense.

Let us hear what the Spirit says to the churches: “To him who conquers I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” The tree of life is Christ, who by communicating himself to his elect grants them eternal life through grace. The paradise of God is the holy Church, because of the security and delight which it has from God and in God. Therefore, whoever conquers—that is, the evil one—eats of the tree which is in paradise, because he will be fed and satisfied by the abundance of Christ’s sweetness which is in the holy Church: by participating in him now through grace and, in the future, by beholding him in glory.

But no one knows how great the sweetness, savor, delight, pleasure, and loveliness of eating from this tree are except one who tastes it. Hence it is written: “Taste and see” (Ps. XXXIV), because unless it is tasted, it is not seen. He also sweetly tastes the eating of this tree in the present life who renounces visible things not only with the bodily senses but with the affections of the heart. What it is, of what kind, and how great it is cannot be declared in words, since the excellence of no good can be worthily compared to it. Those who always behold his face in heaven are perfectly satisfied by its sweetness.

And note that when he had said, “in the paradise of God,” he added “of my God,” namely, on account of the humanity by which he is less than the Father. We may distinguish the contents of the preceding chapter by six divisions. First, where he says, “I know your works,” [Col. 0718C] he gives praise to the person addressed. Where he says, “But I have against you,” he gives rebuke. Where he adds, “Remember from where you have fallen, and repent,” he gives admonition. Where he adds, “But if not, I will come to you quickly and remove your lampstand,” he gives a threat. Where he adds, “But this good you have, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans,” he returns to commendation. Finally, where he states, “To him who conquers I will give to eat of the tree of life which is in the paradise of my God,” he indicates the common recompense of the elect.

Therefore, brothers, let us carefully heed the things written; let us do good and avoid evil, that we may at last attain the proposed recompense. Let us seek in the sacred page not only learning but also edification, because that knowledge alone is useful and praiseworthy which the companion of righteousness commends.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the bishop of Smyrna

“And write to the angel of the church at Smyrna: Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and lives: I know your tribulation and your poverty—but you are rich—and that you are blasphemed by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan. Fear none of those things which you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, that you may be tested; and you shall have tribulation for ten days. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Rev. II).

Having dealt in the preceding chapter with the bishop of Ephesus, who was metropolitan among the others, he turns his discourse to the shepherd of Smyrna. But whether, in the case of this man and the bishops of the other churches, he preserves the order contained in the sacred page according to the geographical distances of the places or according to the differing merits, we do not know. Addressing to the bishop of Smyrna the matters contained in the present chapter, he praises him for good actions and by praise urges him to better things; he foretells future tribulations and promises a crown to one who fights faithfully.

“Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and lives.” At the beginning of his discourse he describes Christ as one able to help in tribulations and, if it should happen that we die for him, one through whom we may hope to return again to life. For in saying “the first and the last,” he shows that he can help the afflicted; while in adding, “who was dead and lives,” he indicates that he can raise the dead. “Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and lives,” as though he said: Do not fail if it should happen that you suffer tribulation for my name or undergo death, because I am the first and the last: I am able to help in tribulation; and I, who was dead and live, am able to raise from death. Therefore, as you hear that I am such, take confidence in both respects; and if any adversity should happen on my account, endure it bravely. But because we discussed these words more carefully above, let us proceed to what follows.

“I know your tribulation and your poverty.” He sets forth two things: tribulation of the body and poverty of material substance. But although either one alone grievously wounds, if the other is added, it doubles the pain. It is hard to be afflicted in body, but harder still, together with bodily affliction, to suffer want of material means. Therefore this man was worthy of a twofold praise, since he endured a twofold evil for Christ. For unless he had endured it for Christ, Christ himself would not have said that he knew his tribulation and poverty; because in saying “I know,” he showed that he endured both for him and so showed that he approved both.

But amid the bodily evils he mentions spiritual grace, so that by recalling goods he may make him stronger against the evils to be endured. He says therefore: “But you are rich,” as though he said: Although you are pressed in bodily matters, do not fear, because you are enlarged in spiritual goods—in the fullness of the heavenly gift, in the exercise of virtue, in the performance of good work, in the word of preaching, and in hope of reward.

And because the life of good persons is always hateful to an assembly of evil persons, and what God commends the speech of the wicked blasphemes, it is rightly added: “And you are blasphemed by those who call themselves Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan,” that is, the assembly of the adversary, namely the devil. Thus this man had false Jews as adversaries, just as the ruler of Ephesus had false apostles. If they were true Jews or apostles, they would confess and preach Christ not with a pretence of righteousness but in truth.

It is clear from these words, as from many other passages of Scripture, that the ancient enemy seeks to accomplish through human imitators of his perversity what he cannot hinder in good or effect in evil through the demons who are accomplices of his pride. And the more numerous they are, the stronger they are to accomplish both. Therefore they are not inappropriately called the synagogue of Satan, because Satan gathers them into one wickedness in order that, through them, he may fight strongly against strong saints.

And because the corruption of the ungodly, stirred up by the devil himself, sometimes breaks out not only into blasphemy of speech but into the open attack of persecution, the sacred vision appropriately adds, forewarning and strengthening him against the future persecution:

“Fear none of the things you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison, and you shall have tribulation [Col. 0720B] for ten days,” as though, looking back to what precedes, it plainly said: Since you hear that you are rich in my goods, and must patiently and confidently bear not only your present adversity, in which you now are, but also future persecution for my name’s sake, I foretell it to you so that meanwhile you may gather strength and, when adversities rush upon you, remain unconquered, and may fortify against it those committed to you. Therefore you must take strength and encourage yourself, because I who comfort you will help you.

“Fear none of the things you are about to suffer. Behold, the devil is about to cast some of you into prison.” The devil is said to do the things done by his ministers under his direction, just as some king is said to storm or burn a city, although not he himself does this or that, but rather his army does it at his command. “Into prison,” that is, into any tribulation, for prison may be understood as any kind of tribulation. “That you may be tested,” that is, that through temptation you may be proved—whether you are truly mine and possess virtues now for your own benefit, and so that they may be revealed to others for imitation. For virtues which are manifest serve not only as merit to those who possess them but as an example to those who behold them. In temptation, not only does the one who is exercised and tested by it advance, but also many others to whom the strength of his patience becomes known.

“And you shall have tribulation for ten days.” What can be understood more fittingly by the ten days than the brightness of the Decalogue? Therefore the elect have tribulation for ten days who suffer persecution in the present life for preserving the divine law contained in the Decalogue. Let him say, therefore: “You shall have tribulation for ten days,” as though he said: So long as you walk in the light of my law, you shall always suffer tribulation for me in its observance. For it is written: “All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (II Tim. II).

“Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” Having foretold persecution, he exhorts him to the long-suffering of patience and promises a crown to one who gains victory, as though he said: Whatever evil they inflict, bear it patiently. Endurance is temporary; the crown eternal. The contest is small; the reward immense. The punishment is light; the glory beyond estimation. “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you,” after death, “for death, the eternity of life.”

“He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” Since this has been explained above, it need not be explained again here. It follows:

“He who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death.” The first death is guilt; the second, punishment. Alternatively, the first death is in the world, the second in hell. The first death is when the soul is separated from the body; the second is when soul and body will be condemned together. Therefore whoever conquers the evil demon, the wicked person, the flesh, vice, and the world shall not be harmed by the second death, because he will not be punished by eternal condemnation.

We may distinguish the contents of the aforesaid chapter by five general divisions. Where [Col. 0721B] at the beginning he says, “I know your tribulation and your poverty, but you are rich,” he praises the person addressed for good. Where he says, “Fear none of the things you are about to suffer,” he foretells future persecution. Where he adds, “Be faithful unto death,” he admonishes him concerning patience.
