Where he subsequently adds, “And I will give you the crown of life,” he promises a reward. Finally, where he concludes, “He who conquers shall not be harmed by the second death,” he makes both this man and the elect secure from condemnation. Therefore, in this man, who was praiseworthy in every respect and blameworthy in none, let us admire the praise and imitate the righteousness.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the angel of Pergamum

[Col. 0721C] “And write to the angel of the church at Pergamum: Thus says he who has the two-edged sharp sword: I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; and you hold fast my name and have not denied my faith, even in those days when Antipas, my faithful witness, was killed among you, where Satan’s throne is” (Rev. II).

In third place among the bishops, the sacred vision here places the bishop of Pergamum and directs to him the discourse of the present chapter. It first praises him for good, then rebukes him for evil, acting in the manner of a prudent physician, who first gently handles and touches all around the abscess of a faint-hearted, impatient, tender, and fearful sick person, and afterward applies the blade, wisely draws out the hidden and inflamed corruption, and, once the corruption has been removed, restores the place to health. Thus the true physician of souls, when he commends him by saying, “I know where you dwell,” soothes the sick man; then, when he rebukes him by saying, “I have a few things against you,” he wounds with the blade in order to restore health.

And it should be noted that, because this man was to be reproved for evil, the vision at the beginning of its discourse describes Christ as one who, if he wished to be corrected, could cut away not only the vices of his body but also the vices of his heart; but if he refused amendment, could punish not only his body but also his soul. Similarly, at the beginning of the preceding chapter directed to the shepherd of Smyrna, because persecution was about to come upon him, it describes Christ in these terms: “Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and lives”—one who could help the afflicted and raise again those put to death for him.

Thus the appearing likeness of the Son of Man identified the Son of Man to the bishop of Pergamum at the very beginning of the discourse, so that, if he were willing to correct what needed correction, he might take confidence in help; but if unwilling, he might fear punishment for his vice. Thus: “These things says he who has the two-edged sharp sword.” He is able to help, if you are willing to be corrected in body and spirit, and to cut away the vices of both; if you are unwilling to be corrected, he is able to condemn you in both. We have said above that the two-edged sharp sword signifies the word of God. For the two-edged sharp sword is the word of God, living and effective, and more penetrating than every two-edged sword; it cuts away not only the perverse action of the body but also the perverse thought of the heart, and condemns those who persist incorrigibly in both.

But let us hear what he who has this sword says: “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; and you hold fast my name and have not denied my faith.” First he praises him for good actions, strengthens him by praise toward better things, and in both respects prepares him better to endure the rebuke which follows. “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is,” that is: I approve that you live righteously in the midst of a corrupt nation. For it is no small praise for a righteous person to keep himself undefiled among the ungodly and to walk the straight way among the perverse.

And note that he did not say, “where Satan’s way is,” but “where Satan’s throne is.” Through some persons Satan travels swiftly in passing: namely, those whom he suddenly and unexpectedly casts down into evil. But he does not establish a throne, because, when they quickly rise through repentance, he loses the dominion of ruling in them. Others he not only treads down through sin, but through evil habit establishes in them a throne for the exercise of his rule. Presiding over them, he not only restrains them from doing good, but also carries out his own will in them as they advance in evil. Thus he walks upon or flies over the former through sin; in the latter he sits and reigns longer through habit. It is therefore clear that these people were far removed from God, since Satan is said to have had in them not a way but a throne.

How good and how great this man was among evil persons is plainly declared when it is added: “And you hold fast my name and have not denied my faith.” It was indeed great and praiseworthy, among unbelievers, to hold his name and not deny his faith in their persecution. But what he first said, “you hold fast my name,” he afterward explained when he added, “and have not denied my faith.” For we understand the Lord’s name and the Lord’s faith to be the same. What is it to be baptized in the name of the holy Trinity except to be baptized in its faith? Just as a thing becomes known in its name, so God is known by us through faith.

Therefore the ruler of Pergamum was very praiseworthy in this: that he was good among evil persons, held Christ’s faith among unbelievers, and did not deny it. For it is much easier to act well among good persons than to preserve faith among unbelievers, just as it is far easier to enter a city when no one opposes than when hostile enemies resist.

And lest he should think that he alone had preserved faith among unbelievers, or alone lived well among evil persons, and for that reason more quickly fail in either respect, Antipas, Christ’s faithful witness, is set before him. Antipas endured death’s punishments for Christ and Christ’s faith, so that, by imitating Antipas, he too might endure death for Christ if necessary. For it follows: “And in those days”—namely, yours, must be understood—“Antipas, my faithful witness, was killed among you,” that is, in Pergamum, where Satan’s throne is, not by good persons but by evil persons in whom Satan reigns.

It is as though, strengthening him through Antipas, he plainly said: I praise you indeed because until now you have lived well among evil persons and have persevered in my faith. But beware lest you think yourself steadfast and fail in this or that matter. Rather, remember Antipas, my faithful witness; by his example endure unto death the persecution of the corrupt nation for my sake. Nor should you glory even in your merit if you advance in either respect, for Antipas, who endured a greater punishment than you, far surpassed you in the strength of merit. I now set his imitation before you, urging you to gather strength by his example and attain the crown of patience. It follows:

But I have a few things against you, because you have there some who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught the children of Israel to eat and to commit fornication. He first offered praise and then adds rebuke, as though saying: “In the matters mentioned before, you are praiseworthy; in those which follow, blameworthy. For the former I praise you; for the latter I find fault with you.” What he says—“You have here those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught the children of Israel to eat and to commit fornication”—he explains clearly when he says: “So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans” [Col. 0723C]. For just as, in accordance with Balaam’s teaching, the Moabites taught the children of Israel to eat food sacrificed to idols and to commit fornication, so the Nicolaitans, in accordance with Nicholas’s teaching, taught Christians to devote themselves to banqueting and to commit fornication with women.

Therefore this man, although praiseworthy in himself, was nevertheless blameworthy in that he did not vigorously rebuke those living wickedly. In this respect he “had those who held the teaching of the Nicolaitans”: he knew that they acted wickedly and did not correct them. Let the prelates of certain churches [Col. 0723D], who themselves live wickedly and do not correct others, take heed of this. Let them reform themselves and correct those subject to them. But those who watch over themselves ought not cease from chastising those who live wickedly. For God requires from the hands of prelates the souls of subjects who perish. It follows:

Likewise, repent; otherwise I shall come to you swiftly. After the severity of rebuke he adds an admonition to amendment, and, should he refuse correction, the terror of a threat. For when he says, “Repent,” he urges repentance; but when he adds, “otherwise I shall come to you swiftly,” he frightens by a threat. “Likewise” is added here, that is, just as I commanded the bishop of Ephesus to repent, who was likewise blameworthy because he had abandoned his first love. For he did not rebuke the bishop of Smyrna at all, and therefore prescribed nothing to him concerning repentance.

“Otherwise,” namely, if you do not do this—if you do not repent, if you do not correct the wicked [Col. 0724A]—I shall come to you, that is, for judgment and to your loss; and I shall do so swiftly, lest through delay of time you contrive postponements of amendment. It follows: “And I shall fight against them with the sword of my mouth,” as if he said: “If you scorn to obey me and to correct the wicked, I shall come not only to you but also to them, and by vengeance I shall punish them with the sword of my mouth, that is, by the word which says: ‘Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire’” (Matt. 25). This is the two-edged sword which he set at the beginning of this chapter, to frighten the pastor’s negligence. All rulers of churches ought to have it, to distinguish good people from bad, defend the good, and punish the bad:

“He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches: To the victor I shall give hidden manna [Col. 0724B], and I shall give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.” The hidden manna is the hidden Divinity. No one has ever seen God. Of this it is written again: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30); and again: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), etc. He will give us this manna when the glory of his Divinity satisfies us.

What, moreover, is “I shall give a white stone” but a heavenly reward? A stone because of firmness; white because of the brightness of immortality. What is the new name on the stone but divine knowledge, now unfamiliar to human minds, revealed in the eternal reward? Therefore, upon the eternal white stone he will give us a new name written [Col. 0724C], because in the eternal and immortal reward he will make known to us the knowledge of his Divinity, now very far removed from us.

In the present age, however, we can know many things which we cannot possess. But in the heavenly homeland, what we shall know of God by understanding, we shall possess by loving. Nor can anyone know it unless it happens to him to possess it. Hence he also says: “Which no one knows except the one who receives it.”

We may arrange the matters contained in this chapter under five divisions. Where he said, “I know where you dwell,” he first offered the consolation of praise; where he said, “But I have a few things against you,” he adds the severity of rebuke; where he added, “Repent,” the admonition to amendment; where he said, “Otherwise [Col. 0724D] I shall come to you swiftly,” the terror of threat; and where at last he stated, “To the victor I shall give hidden manna,” the reward of blessedness.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the bishop of Thyatira

“And write to the angel of the church in Thyatira: Thus says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire and feet like bronze: I know your works, and your faith, and your love, your ministry and your patience, and your latter works are more numerous than the former” (Rev. 2).

In his usual manner, he places the Savior’s authority first and describes such a title as the meaning of the following chapter requires. For there were at Thyatira certain false Christians who defiled themselves by committing fornication with women or demons, and [Col. 0725A] who, by example or word, deceived others by drawing them into the same crimes. Thus he rightly says that he has eyes like a flame of fire, in order to show that by his wisdom he sees through and contemplates whatever they do; and that his feet are like bronze, in order to signify that he admonishes them to depart from their wickedness and that they ought courageously to imitate even the weak elect, who are figured by feet like bronze.

He also says: “Thus says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire and feet like bronze,” as if saying: “You at Thyatira live wickedly in scorning Christ, and you shall hear this discourse. When you hear that he has eyes like a flame of fire, recognize that he knows the secret things of your wickedness; and when you hear [Col. 0725B] that he has feet like bronze, consider that he is at least calling you to imitate his weak elect.” But since we have said more above concerning his eyes and feet, let us proceed to what follows.

“I know your works, and faith, and love.” In his usual manner he first gives praise in order to strengthen him, and then adds rebuke in order to correct him. “I know your works, and faith, and love.” In this place the order of the words does not follow the order of realities, as sometimes occurs in certain passages of Sacred Scripture: that is, what is later in the true order is placed earlier in the discourse. For faith is first among all good things comprised under righteousness; love is born from faith, and good works from love.

Therefore he says [Col. 0725C], in an order reversed with respect to the arrangement of words but not to the nature of things: “I know your works, faith, and love”—that is, in the proper order of the realities: your faith by which you believe in me; your love by which you love me; and the works by which you serve me. Since the one who believes in God by faith, loves by love, and serves by works, ought also diligently to minister from his own resources to the poor, it is rightly added: “and your ministry.” But because all who wish to live devoutly in Christ—believing in him, loving him, serving him, and ministering to the poor for God’s sake—suffer persecution, it is well added: “and your patience,” namely in adversities. He knows all these things because he has approved them.

“And your latter works [Col. 0725D] are more numerous than the former.” At the beginning he praises his works, and here he commends works again. But there, the works of beginning; here, the works of progress toward perfection. For he does not praise him for the summit of perfection, but for increase: he did not say “perfect,” “many,” or simply “more,” but comparatively, “more than the former.” Thus “latter” must not be referred to the height of perfection, but to the past performance of preceding works. It follows:

“But I have against you, because you permit the woman to eat food sacrificed to idols.” After strengthening him in praise and steadfastness, he immediately adds rebuke for his negligence, saying: “But I have a few things against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and deceive my servants” [Col. 0726A], as if saying: “I praise you because you live well, but I rebuke you because you do not correct others.”

What ought we more properly to understand by Jezebel, whose name means “flow of blood,” than those enticed by pleasures of the flesh and devoted to idolatrous worship, who called themselves prophets and therefore more easily deceived others? “To commit fornication,” that is, to commit fornication with women or demons; “and to eat food sacrificed to idols,” that is, to eat, in veneration of idols, things sacrificed to idols. Otherwise: “to eat food sacrificed to idols” means to delight in the filth of sins which they offer to demons. Others say that Jezebel denotes this bishop’s wife, who was devoted to luxury or idolatry and by her persuasions drew others into imitation of her wickedness. It follows:

“And I gave her time to repent, and she is unwilling to repent of her fornication” [Col. 0726B]. Wonderful is God’s mercy, wonderful his clemency! When we commit sin, he does not immediately impose punishment, but provides a remedy and recalls us to the wholeness of righteousness, in order to bring us to the joy of glory. But since contempt for repentance produces an increase of sin and provokes the anger of vengeance, he rightly adds a threat after rebuke because of neglected amendment. For it follows:

“Behold, I cast her into a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into very great tribulation, unless they repent of their works.” Another translation has “I cast her into mourning”; but whether we say “mourning” or “bed,” what follows is expressed here: “into very great tribulation” [Col. 0726C], that is, into eternal damnation, so that those conformed to her in sin may be joined to her in damnation.

It should also be noted that he did not say, “I shall cast,” but “I cast,” in order to strike fear by the present tense. Yet we must carefully observe and gratefully embrace the fact that the compassion of divine mercy did not say absolutely and simply, “I cast.” Rather, he tempered the threat, saying: “Unless they repent of their works” (Luke 13). For he did not wish, by unrestrained terror, to cast sinners into despair, but, by tempering the threat, to recall them—if they were willing to repent—to confidence in his mercy. It follows:

“And I shall kill her children with death, and all the churches shall know that I am he who searches kidneys and hearts. And I shall give to each of you according to your works” [Col. 0726D]. Whom can we more fittingly understand by “her children” than her followers, who by their mother’s teaching and example pursue the depravity of maternal wickedness far and wide? They too will truly be killed with death when they are punished with eternal damnation.

“And all the churches,” that is, the good congregations, shall know in the future by experience what they now believe by faith: “that I am he who searches kidneys,” that is, fleshly desires, “and hearts,” that is, evil thoughts. This is what he said at the beginning of the discourse when he declared that he has eyes like a flame of fire: he is able not only to know our outward things [Col. 0727A], but also to penetrate inner things by his wisdom.

What he says—“searching kidneys and hearts” (Jer. 7)—may also be referred not only to the wicked but to the good. He indeed searches the kidneys of the good because he loves their chastity; he searches their hearts because he loves their pure thought. Hence what is contained above in this threat seems to concern the wicked alone. But what he says, “I am he who searches kidneys and hearts, and I shall give each of you according to your works,” seems also to concern the good: I shall give to each according to your works, good things to the good and evil things to the evil.

But what follows concerns the good alone: “But to you I say, to the rest who are in Thyatira: Whoever do not hold this teaching, who have not known [Col. 0727B] the depths of Satan, as they say, I shall not lay upon you another burden; only hold fast what you have until I come.” There were at Thyatira certain elect persons who did not share in the aforesaid wickedness but faithfully served Christ alone. Others, who had gone out from Judaea, said that evangelical precepts could not suffice for them and preached that the carnal observances of the Law must be kept. Therefore he instructs the elect and makes them certain what they ought to hold. He admonishes them to hold only the precepts of grace and testifies that he will impose no burden of the Law upon them.

Thus he says: “But to you I say, to the rest who are in Thyatira”—to you others who do not participate in wicked works, but live soberly, justly, and devoutly—to all who [Col. 0727C] “do not hold this teaching,” namely Jezebel’s teaching by imitating her; who “have not known,” that is, have not approved or loved, “the depth,” that is, the pride, “of Satan,” by serving him and scorning me. “As they say,” that is, as those who went out from Judaea threaten you. “I shall not lay upon you another burden,” that is, I shall not demand from you the old observances of the Law. “Only hold fast what you have until I come”: hold by good action the Gospel which you possess by faith, until I come in recompense. It follows:

“And whoever conquers and keeps my words until the end, I shall give him authority over the nations; and he shall rule them with an iron rod, and they shall be broken like a potter’s vessel, just as I also received from my Father; and I shall give him [Col. 0727D] the morning star.” Above he spoke of good and evil persons; now he adds concerning the gift and reward of the conqueror.

“Whoever conquers,” namely the evil one, as explained above, “and whoever keeps until the end,” namely the end of life, the completion of victory, or the end—that is, the consummation of righteousness—“my works,” which I command to be done, “I shall give him” (and this is also to be understood in the present age) “authority over the nations,” that is, those living as Gentiles; “and he shall rule them with an iron rod,” that is, with inflexible righteousness; “and they shall be broken like a potter’s vessel,” so that some are wholly condemned by his judgment, while others are changed for the better by his word. For the one who strives to attain the perfection of holiness is worthy to rule others: to judge the wicked worthy of condemnation and the good worthy of salvation.

[Col. 0728A] “Just as I also received from my Father”: I received from my Father, namely according to my humanity, the power of ruling. A great promise, a great gift. He promises and grants what he himself received: what he possesses by fullness, so that his elect may possess it by participation in that fullness.

What he says—“I shall give him authority over the nations, and he shall rule them with an iron rod” (Ps. 2), “and they shall be broken like a potter’s vessel”—may also be referred only to the condemnation of the wicked: so that the one perfect in victory may judge and condemn the wicked with Christ, as it is written concerning the apostles: “You who have followed me shall sit upon thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

“And I shall give him the morning star.” The morning star is the first robe: a star because of the brightness of contemplation [Col. 0728B], morning because of the beginning of blessedness. Therefore the conqueror in the world will be given the morning star, that is, a robe in heaven, so that, having received the first, he may be secure concerning the remainder. This morning star will be changed into the noonday sun at the resurrection, when the soul is glorified in the risen body. For it is written: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13).

We may distinguish the contents of this chapter under five divisions. Where he said, “I know your works, faith, and love,” he praised the one of whom he speaks. Where he said, “But I have against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and deceive my servants,” he rebuked him. Where he added, “Behold, I cast him into a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into very great tribulation” [Col. 0728C], he threatened the wicked. Where he added, “But to you I say, to the rest who are in Thyatira,” he instructed the good concerning holding only the precepts of grace. Where he then stated, “Whoever conquers and keeps my works until the end,” he promised the dignity of spiritual and heavenly authority and the first robe.

“He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches,” that is, what God promises to the churches. Dearest brothers, let us have ears not only for hearing but also for understanding: let us read the things written, avoid the things forbidden, so that we may attain the things promised.

## CHAPTER IX. On the bishop of Sardis

“And write to the angel of the church at Sardis: Thus says he who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars: I know your works; you have a name that you live, and you are dead. Be watchful, and strengthen the things remaining, which were about to die. For I have not found your works full before my God. Therefore remember how you received and heard; keep it, and repent” (Rev. 3) [Col. 0728D].

In the fifth place among the individual admonitions, the bishop of Sardis, unlike the others previously mentioned, is not praised for some virtue or good work. Rather, he is sharply and severely rebuked by the sacred vision for feigned and simulated righteousness, and is mercifully admonished to repent. Since this bishop, veiled outwardly before human sight by the simulation of certain virtues and good works [Col. 0729A], appeared externally so, but inwardly before God’s sight was supported by no true righteousness, Christ is described to him at the beginning as one able to know even all hidden things and powerful to punish him for sin if he should offend.

Thus he says: “Thus says he who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars,” as if saying: “You who make yourself appear good before people by hypocrisy, but in secret are wicked in scorning me: when you hear that I have the seven Spirits of God, recognize that through my wisdom I see spiritually, penetrating not only visible but hidden things, not only works but thoughts. And when you hear that I have the seven stars, understand that I have power to punish you and other bishops if they sin.” But since above we have explained the seven Spirits and the seven stars [Col. 0729B], let us proceed to what follows.

“I know your works.” The words “I know” must by no means be understood here as in the chapters above, where he says that he knows the works of others—that is, knows them by approving them. “I know your works” means: I recognize them. For just as no one can corrupt almighty God by a price, because he is just; surpass him, because he is eternal; escape him by place, because he is everywhere; or overcome him by power, because he is most strong: so no one can remain concealed from him by hiding, because he is most wise.

Therefore let him say: “I know your works; you have a name that you live, and you are dead.” I know through my wisdom that you have a name—that is, among the populace, through a useless reputation—that you live by righteousness; whereas you are, on the contrary, dead through sin. In this chapter [Col. 0729C], because this man was altogether blameworthy, he did not first offer praise as in the preceding instances, but immediately brought forward rebuke. For what, in the other preceding admonitions, is said after praise in a rebuke—“But I have against you”—he does here from the beginning, when, without any mention of praise, it is written: “I know your works; you have a name that you live, and you are dead.”

It follows: “Be watchful, and strengthen the things remaining, which were about to die.” After the rebuke he adds admonition. “Be watchful,” that is, be concerned for your salvation. For the one who neglects himself and gives no thought to his salvation is not watchful. “Strengthen the things remaining, which were about to die.” The chief goods in which praise consists, such as love and humility, had already died in him; but the lesser things which, although they do not contain salvation, nevertheless aid salvation—such as knowledge of the Scriptures, teaching, preaching, and the like—were about to die if he continued in evil [Col. 0729D].

By a just judgment, one who scorns to preserve the greater goods absolutely necessary to salvation wholly loses the lesser goods, which, although not necessary to salvation, are nevertheless useful. One who neglects those things by which he was truly good before God rightly loses those things by which he was praiseworthy before people. For there are some who love more the things by which they seem great before people and make light of those without which they cannot be justified in God’s sight. They seek to grow in what is least and diminish in what is greatest. But after they despise the greatest gifts of virtues [Col. 0730A], they lose the lesser ones in which they trusted and gloried, so that they may see themselves stripped by divine grace and more swiftly recover their senses from negligence.

Yet divine mercy had still granted the bishop of Sardis certain lesser goods, concerning whose strengthening it admonished him. Thus it says: “Strengthen the things remaining, which were about to die.” It follows: “For I have not found your works full before my God.” In saying, “I have not found your works full,” he openly rebukes him for lost love. For where love is, there is fullness. “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; and if there is any other commandment, it is recapitulated in this saying.” For “love is the fullness of the law.”

Therefore he says [Col. 0730B]: “I have not found your works full, because all that you do is empty of love. Whoever fails in love loses many works and becomes guilty of all.” Therefore, although your works may seem full before people through display, before my God they are empty because love is absent. Since, therefore, your works, performed for human praise, are not at all full before my God—because, love having been lost, fraternal love is absent—remember how you received from God through the infusion of spiritual grace, and heard from a human being through evangelical preaching; preserve both by good action; and repent of the good lost and the evil committed through the satisfaction of amendment. It follows:

“If therefore you do not watch, I shall come to you like a thief, and you will not know when I shall come to you” [Col. 0730C]. After the admonition to amendment, he adds the threat of damnation, unless he corrects himself. “If you do not watch,” that is, unless you are concerned about yourself in the matters stated, “I shall come to you like a thief,” who comes to take away goods and kill the owner. So I shall come to you: I shall take away grace from you and bring punishment upon you. And I shall come as secretly and unexpectedly as a thief, so that you cannot guard against my coming. This is what he says: “You will not know at what hour I shall come to you.”

Since this man had fallen into sin and was far removed from true righteousness, he does not, as in the cases of others where he said “I shall come swiftly,” set even a small interval, so that he may fear more, more swiftly recover his senses, and correct himself more diligently. It follows:

“But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments, and they shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy” [Col. 0730D]. After rebuke, admonition, and threat, the life of the good among those subject to him is set before him, either for the relief of consolation or as an example for imitation, so that he who ought to have done more and did less may hear that there are good people in his flock, may not despair of himself, but may be ashamed and, having taken up hope, rise to righteousness by their example.

“But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments,” as if saying: “Consider the few good persons subject to you; take courage even from so small a remnant of good; and by their example [Col. 0731A] live rightly with them.” “You have a few names,” that is, a few persons known to me by the virtue of righteousness.

It should be noted that he says “few,” because although many are called everywhere, few nevertheless are chosen. Yet because there are few in Sardis, perhaps this was the bishop’s fault: while the shepherd attends to earthly things, the wolf breaks into the sheepfold, carries off and scatters the sheep, and diminishes the flock by carrying off and scattering it.

“They have not defiled their garments”: they have not, by returning to former evils, polluted the gifts of innocence and immortality received in baptism. Otherwise: they have not defiled their garments because after baptism they have not polluted their bodies through luxury and lack of self-control. Otherwise: they have not defiled their garments because they have not stained their clean works with the filth of vices [Col. 0731B].

There are some who defile their garments after baptism by living wickedly, but wash them again with tears; and this defilement is not reckoned against them for punishment, because they carefully wash it away through repentance. “And they shall walk with me in white, because they are worthy.” They shall walk with me because I went before them as an example and pattern, and they follow me in imitation. Otherwise: I shall walk with them by grace, and they with me by righteousness; for unless I bestowed grace upon them in each particular, they could not advance in righteousness, because without me they can do nothing.

They shall walk with me in the world, living justly, practicing virtues, carrying out good works, preaching righteousness to others, and doing many other good things. They shall sit with me in heaven, reigning with me forever [Col. 0731C], “in white”: in hope of future innocence and immortality, in chaste bodies, in pure works. For works are signified by garments, because the saints are, as it were, surrounded, protected, and adorned by works as by garments. “Because they are worthy.” For I receive worthy companions and leave the unworthy. Yet those who are worthy would in no way be worthy unless they had received worthiness from me. It follows:

“Whoever conquers shall thus be clothed in white garments, and I shall not blot his name out of the book of life; and I shall confess his name before my Father and before his angels.” Having completed all that pertained to an example, he adds concerning the conqueror’s gift, taking the example of the promise from the praise of those righteous persons who were in Sardis [Col. 0731D]. “Whoever conquers”: it was explained above that “thus he shall be clothed in white garments,” namely, like those elect persons who are in Sardis.

“And I shall not blot his name out of the book of life.” He says less and means more: by denying one thing, he confirms another. The book of life is the wisdom of God, in which all the elect are rightly said to be written and predestined to eternal life. For predestination itself is this writing. Those destined for damnation, although they seem to be written in this book because grace and righteousness have been granted to them for a time, are later known to be blotted out when they fall through sin and are damned by punishment. Hence it is written: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous” (Ps. 68); that is, let them be known as blotted out—or rather, as never having been written [Col. 0732A].

For those destined for damnation, although they seem to be written together with those to be saved because, for a time, they are righteous and possess faith working through love, are never nevertheless written by predestination, although for some time they are written by holiness. They are in some manner blotted from this book when they are separated from the righteous through sin or damnation; and, though they were never actually written as if written at one time, it is manifested that they were never written, because they were thought to have been written.

Pagans and Jews who die without faith in Christ are not believed ever to have been written in this book. There are also many who are to be saved who, while they are for a time entangled in crimes, seem to be blotted out of this book. Yet, as they are always predestined, so they are always written in the book of life.

Therefore what he says—“I shall not blot his name out of the book of life”—amounts to this: “His name, which is always known to me in my wisdom through predestination, will never be manifested to human beings as blotted out or as never having been written; unlike the names of the ungodly, which are blotted out and not written—that is, are manifested by damnation as blotted out or, rather, as never written. Instead, his name shall always be shown to all, through salvation, as written with me and never blotted out” [Col. 0732B].

“And I shall confess his name before my Father and before his angels” (Matt. 10), when I say: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink” (Matt. XV). [Col. 0732C] “I shall confess his name” because I shall testify that the one whom I exalt in the homeland for righteousness was known to me through righteousness on the way. And I shall do this before my Father and his angels, because before my Father and before the angels I shall give him reward according to his merits and render recompense according to his labor.

“He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” For what he says to one, he says to all: teaching good things, restraining evil things, commanding what is right, threatening punishment, and promising glory. We may therefore divide all the contents of this chapter into five divisions. Where he says, “I know your works: you have a name that you live, and you are dead,” he states the severity of rebuke. Where he says, “Be watchful,” he gives the admonition to amendment; where he says [Col. 0732D], “If you do not watch, I shall come to you like a thief,” the terror of threat; where he adds, “But you have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments,” an example for imitation; and where he says, “Whoever conquers,” the conqueror’s gift as reward.

## CHAPTER X. On the bishop of Philadelphia
“And write to the angel of the church in Philadelphia: Thus says the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens: I know your works. Behold, I have set before you an open door, which no one can shut, because you have little strength, yet have kept my name and have not denied my faith” (Rev. 3).

The heavenly vision, addressing the bishop of Philadelphia in this discourse, raises him up with praises of righteousness and, [Col. 0733A] as it does not reprove the bishop of Smyrna, neither does it reprove him for any negligence or fault. It promises him the grace of wisdom for preaching; that it will subject his Jewish adversaries to him; and aid toward his perfection in the hour of trial. Finally, it exhorts him to perseverance, lest he lose his crown.

As it customarily does in the other chapters, it describes Christ at the beginning as such as the following discourse requires, so that at the beginning of the discourse the bishop himself may perceive how greatly he can trust in the subsequent promise. For since the teaching of divine grace is promised to one who does not cease in sacred preaching or, even amid difficulties, in the administration of the Word, the promiser and giver of good is rightly declared to be Holy and True, to possess the key of David, and alone to open and [Col. 0733B] shut the secrets of wisdom.

It says therefore: “Thus says the Holy and True One who has the key of David,” as though it said: Thus says the Holy and True One: holy in goodness, true in promise; holy because he does not sin, true because he never lies. And because he has the key of David, he opens and bestows the mysteries of wisdom upon whom he wills. When you hear that he is True and Holy, believe him merciful and truthful in his promises. And when you hear that he has the key of David, believe him powerful to fulfill them.

For what did the visible likeness of the Son of Man more rightly signify to us by the key of David than the grace of spiritual wisdom, which disclosed to David more clearly than to the other prophets the mystery of human redemption? This grace is specially and properly, not inappropriately, called David: both because of the promise made to him and because of the prerogative of revelation, since David disclosed the coming of the Redeemer not, as to most prophets, through enigmas and forms of visible things, but nakedly, purely, and without a veil in the secret place of his heart. Hence he himself says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84 [85]). “In me”—not in symbols and forms, but immediately and familiarly, in the chamber and bosom of my mind.

Therefore, in saying, “Who has the key of David,” he plainly signified that he is powerful to unlock the hidden things of doctrine which he was about to promise and give, and of which the bishop himself had need in his office. “Thus says the Holy and True One who has the key of David,” as though he said: Understand what is proclaimed concerning Christ at the beginning of the discourse, [Col. 0733D] and trust, on the basis of these things, in what he himself promises you later. Hear that he is Holy and True, and consider him kind and truthful in promising good things. Hear that he has the key of David, and recognize him as powerful in bestowing those same things. And lest you believe another possesses the same power, hear that he alone is powerful: “He opens and no one shuts; he shuts and no one opens.”

He opens hearts to the understanding of faith; he opens mouths to the preaching of the word. He opens affection to love; he opens the tongues of teachers for preaching and teaching. He opens the hearts of peoples to belief. And insofar as he opens these things to the elect and shuts them to the reprobate, it is rightly said: “He shuts and no one opens.” That no one can shut what he opens is attested by the apostles in Acts when they say: “We cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” And shortly afterward, concerning the Jews: “They could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit that was speaking” (Acts 4 [cf. Acts 6:10]). But when he shuts from the reprobate those things which are right, because their sins demand it, no one can open them, because no one can correct one whom he has rejected.

It follows: “I know your works”—I know, approve, love, and receive them. In this brief statement, “I know your works,” he embraces the bishop’s praise. Immediately after this praise he adds the promise of a divine gift: “Behold, I have given before you [Col. 0734B] an open door.” “I have given,” that is, “I will give”: the past tense for the future, in order to make the gift certain, lest he remain doubtful about the promise. Or he uses the past tense because God holds the future to be so certain that it is as though it had already taken place.

“I have set before you an open door.” What is an open door except free speech? For just as we enter an open house, so through a freely preached word we enter the human heart, expel the enemy and ancient guest, and establish within it as indwelling the Maker of the heart.

Alternatively: “I have set before you an open door,” that is, I shall open to you understanding for knowledge of the Scriptures, a mouth for their preaching, and the hearts of hearers for receiving faith. “Behold, I have set before you an open door, which, when I open it, no one can shut,” because no one can prevent divine wisdom from working where it wills.

He next reveals why he purposes to give so great a grace: “Because you have little strength, and have kept my word, and have not denied my name.” For, by the providence of grace from above, he deserved to receive the gift of preaching more abundantly because he possessed little strength, whether in body or in heart, yet kept the word of God both in action and in preaching, and did not deny his name—understand, in the distress of persecution. It was indeed highly praiseworthy before God that through little strength he accomplished so much. The more difficult his labor in God’s service was because of the weakness of his strength, the more highly the Savior exalted him with praise and enriched him with the gift of grace.

It follows:

“Behold, I will give you some from the synagogue of Satan, who call themselves Jews and are not, but lie.”

After the promised gift of preaching, he pledges to grant him a gracious victory over his enemies. For there were, [Col. 0734D] as may be inferred from this epistle, Jews in Philadelphia from whose synagogue some opposed the bishop’s preaching and mocked his humility, as though, if he possessed true faith in God, God would show by more evident signs that he was his servant. Perhaps they were led to do this not by malicious hatred of his person, but through ignorance and zeal for their law. He promises, then, that these persons shall be converted to the faith and subjected to his teaching.

He says: “Behold, I will give [some] from the synagogue of Satan,” as though connecting what follows with what precedes: Because you have done the things stated above and have done what pleases me, I shall give you those who belong to Satan, and among those by whom you are opposed I shall magnify you. “Behold, I will give you some from the Jews”—that is, those who belong to Satan through unbelief, who call themselves Jews by confession of the divine name, yet are not so in truth but lie in falsehood.

How he will give them to him, he adds, saying: “Behold, I will make them”—namely, such people—“come and worship before your feet.” I shall make them come to faith by believing in me, and worship before your feet by humbling themselves, honoring you, and simply asking to be baptized, instructed, and ruled by you.

It follows:

“And they shall know that I have loved you.”

Then, once converted, they shall know what now, while turned away, they do not know; friends shall know what enemies do not know; those admitted within shall know what those placed outside do not know. Then they shall know that I have loved you with true charity—a fact they do not know while I permit you to be [Col. 0735B] tested by tribulation. He gives the reason for this love, saying: “Because you have kept the word of my patience”: you have kept the word, that is, the commandment, by patiently enduring adversities for my sake.

For this same reason, after the subjection of his opponents, he promises him the aid of his protection in trial: “And I will keep you for the hour of trial which is coming upon the whole world, to test those who dwell on the earth.” “I will keep you,” not from the hour of trial, but from the injury of trial; not so that you may not see trial, but so that you may not yield to it; not so that you may not feel it, but so that you may by no means consent to it.

By trial he means persecution, in which some are rejected rather than preserved, “which is coming upon the whole world.” For after the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth, persecution immediately burst forth throughout the whole world. “To test those who dwell on the earth”: in a certain manner the perfect already dwell in heaven, for they have perfectly renounced earthly things and the world; they are the tested, whereas these others are to be tested. Persecution therefore tests those who dwell on earth—that is, possessors of earthly things or imperfect persons—and makes known to all whether they are truly righteous. For this reason, by the ordering of divine providence, they are tested: that it may be shown who they are.

Indeed, all the perfect, even if they too endure and feel persecution from wicked people, are tested and shown to be righteous. Persecution does not burden such persons but delights them; when it comes upon them, they do not grieve but rather rejoice. For it is written: “The apostles departed rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5).

Therefore, because of the patience which this bishop had patiently maintained, divine goodness promised to preserve him from the coming trial of persecution—not so that he would not endure persecution along with the other elect, but so that, in enduring it, he would not fail but rather advance. For this is to be preserved with an increase of strength: to be guarded unharmed from fault.

It follows:

“Behold, I come quickly; hold fast what you have, lest anyone take your crown.”

Near the end of the address, he exhorts him to patience, lest he lose his crown. But since he was amid tribulation—as one dwelling among unbelievers and in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation—and heard that trial was coming, he rightly announces that he will come quickly, namely to reward him, lest he fail under pressure. He says therefore: “Behold, I come quickly,” as though he said: Manfully endure every tribulation for my sake, because behold, I come quickly to reward you. “Hold fast what you have”—namely faith and good works—and persevere in them, lest, if you lack perseverance, another receive your crown.

For since God has a fixed number of his own, when one person falls through fault, another is introduced through mercy: thus human beings ascend to the place from which demons fell, and the Gentiles entered into the divine worship which Judea abandoned.

It follows: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall never go out again; and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of the new Jerusalem, which comes down from heaven from my God, and my new name.”

Having set forth everything above that pertains to the bishop’s commendation, he finally states the victor’s gift: “The one who conquers,” as explained above, “I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God,” so that, as a pillar is in a material temple, so he may be in the spiritual building: firm through faith, upright through equity, raised through intention, lofty through contemplation; supporting some by a word of consolation, others by the help of prayer, and others by the example of action.

In this building, in which all the perfect are pillars, some are stone pillars through firmness of belief, some bronze pillars through the sound of preaching, some silver ones through eloquence, and some golden ones through wisdom. And, lest the same expression need repeatedly to be explained: wherever he says “of God” and adds “my,” or something similar, he says this on account of the humanity by which he is less than the Father.

“And he shall never go out again”: that is, if he wishes to stand in righteousness, he shall no longer sin mortally, nor depart from the fellowship of the righteous. “And I will write upon him the name of my God.” What is spoken quickly passes away; what is written endures long. Therefore, in saying “I will write,” he means the same as if he said: I shall grant it forever.

And it should be noted that he says “upon him,” not “in him,” because we can apprehend the divine good above us, but cannot comprehend it within ourselves. Thus the name of God is written upon the elect when that good which is called and is God by nature—apprehensible indeed, but incomprehensible—is granted to them by grace both to be and to be called gods, as it is written: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81 [82]).

“And the name of the city of the new Jerusalem”—namely, I will write it upon him, as said above—so that its name too may be Jerusalem: not the Jerusalem on earth, in which there is no true vision of peace and which still has much oldness, which is not wholly God’s because many within it belong to the devil; but that Jerusalem which, though still partly on earth, is nevertheless above and is our heavenly mother. In it there is no vision of strife but of peace alone; it possesses nothing of oldness but everything of newness; in it God possesses everything and the devil nothing.

“Which comes down from heaven from my God,” because “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above,” whereby our holy mother Jerusalem is prepared in her elect for eternity, coming down in time from the Father of lights, the author of gifts.

“And my new name”—understand, I will write it upon him—namely the name of Christianity, which is wholly newness and contains nothing of oldness. Moreover, everything contained in this promise and promised to the victor may be possessed by the victor not only in heaven but also in the world, and not only in the future state but in the present as well.

“He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.” This is repeated frequently so that it may be more firmly commended to hearers.

We may therefore arrange all that is contained in this discourse under six general divisions. Where he said, “I know your works,” he praised the bishop himself; where he added, “Behold, I have set before you an open door,” he promised him the grace of preaching; where he said, “Behold, I will give you some from the synagogue of Satan,” he pledged the conversion and subjection of unbelieving and hostile Jews; where he added, “I will keep you for the hour of trial,” he promised protection in persecution; where he added, “Behold, I come quickly; hold fast what you have,” he gave an admonition concerning perseverance; and where finally he said, “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God,” he promised the victor’s reward.

## Chapter XI. On the Bishop of Laodicea

“And write to the angel of the church in Laodicea: Thus says the Amen, the faithful and true witness, who is the beginning of God’s creation: I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth. Because you say, ‘I am rich, have become wealthy, and need nothing,’ and do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Rev. 3).

The sacred vision places the bishop of Laodicea seventh among its individual admonitions and the first vision. It severely reproves him for lukewarmness, arrogance, boastfulness, poverty of virtues, and lack of works of righteousness, admonishing him to repentance and promising forgiveness for his sin if he repents.

And because, on account of certain gifts and works arising from gifts which are more outwardly evident but contain less true righteousness, he believed both that he himself possessed the righteousness of which he was empty and that he was esteemed by others for riches and abundance of holiness, Christ—by whom he is reproved in all these matters—is rightly described at the beginning of the discourse as faithful and true, incapable of lying; and he is fittingly declared to be the beginning of God’s creation, without whom righteousness cannot be possessed. Thus, hearing the faithful, true, and source of good rebuking him, he might sooner return to himself; through consideration of the speaker himself give credence to the speaker’s words; reflect upon what he was and what he ought to be; recognize that he was empty of righteousness and could not possess it from himself but only from him who is the beginning of God’s creation—not only of created things through creation, but also of re-created things through redemption—and so repent, obtain mercy, receive grace, practice righteousness, and deserve glory.

He says therefore: “Thus says the Amen,” that is, “truly,” “the faithful and true One, who is the beginning of God’s creation,” as though he plainly said: Carefully attend, from the very beginning of the discourse, to who, what kind of person, and how great is the one speaking to you; rebuked by the mouth of truth, recognize yourself to be destitute of true goodness; and at the beginning of the address observe that you cannot be made rich without him.

“Thus says the Amen, the faithful and true One”: because, being truly faithful, he conceals none of the things that must not be concealed; and because he is true, he never declares what is false or ought not to be said. “Thus says he who is the beginning of God’s creation.” Without him, just as you cannot possess the origin of existence, so you cannot possess even the beginning of righteousness. He is the beginning of creation: for from him comes existence, and from him comes being good. Therefore, because he is faithful and true, believe truthfully that you are evil—as he testifies. And because he is the beginning of good, simply ask that you may be made good by him, which you are not.

But he shows that the bishop is evil when he says: “I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot.” In this man he finds no praise of righteousness, but immediately assails him with rebuke. “I know your works”: that is, I know them, not by approving, as in the case of certain others, but by rejecting. “Because you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth.”

He would be cold through unbelief, hot through charity. But, being neither, he was lukewarm between the two through faith alone. For he believed that faith alone was sufficient for him, failing to observe that charity and the action of charity were necessary; he trusted in knowledge of faith alone and reception of the sacraments. It would have been better for him to remain in unbelief than, having received faith, to live lukewarmly and not practice the works of faith—not because this would have been good, but because it would have been a lesser evil. Perhaps, if he were at some time converted to the faith, he would rise more quickly and easily to true righteousness than if, never converted, he long remained dissolved through lukewarmness in faith alone, deceived into useless security, vainly confident and proud.

Therefore he says: “Would that you were cold or hot,” as though he said: Would that you were in faith as you ought to be, for then you would be truly righteous; or at least that you still stood in unbelief, because through ignorance you would have less sin, and, if you later received the grace of conversion, you could more quickly attain true righteousness. But he adds what evil follows this lukewarmness: “But because you are lukewarm, neither cold nor hot, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth.”

It should be noted that he did not say, “I shall vomit you out,” but “I shall begin to vomit you out,” because one weakened through lukewarmness is not suddenly or entirely abandoned by grace, so as to relapse abruptly into evil. Rather, as grace departs and he first despises small things and then greater ones, he is gradually cut down and descends step by step from the heights to the depths, and at last plunges headlong to the bottom. He aptly said to you by analogy, “I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth,” because all the elect, as food digested in the stomach by natural heat, become members of Christ through love by true justification; while the lukewarm, raw because without love, are vomited out through rejection.

“Because you say, ‘I am rich, have become wealthy, and need nothing,’ and do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked.” It is as though he said: Because, although you are wretched through the sloth of your lukewarmness and your lack of spiritual goods, you consider and proclaim yourself rich through pride and vainglory, I shall deservedly begin to vomit you out of my mouth. For if you recognized your poverty and humbled yourself because of your sin, I would wait longer for your repentance and would not entirely vomit you out of my mouth.

“Rich” and “made wealthy” mean the same thing, but they are uttered twice in order to raise the abundance of possessions more highly. You say that you are rich and wealthy: whether through knowledge, preaching Scripture, the brilliance of secular eloquence, administration of the sacraments, the dignity of the pontifical summit, or empty popular praise. For from goods of this sort, among which perfect maturity does not at all consist, he exalted himself inwardly and gloried before men. The abundance of these goods is declared when he adds: “And I need nothing.” For the one who needs nothing is very rich.

But let anyone who can consider how far this bishop had departed from perfect good: he placed perfect confidence in imperfect good; he considered only what he possessed that was insufficient for salvation and declared that he needed nothing else. Truly, he was not merely lukewarm in the heat of affection but dull also in rational understanding, believing that this sufficed for him and that nothing else was necessary. Therefore it is rightly added: “And you do not know that you are wretched and pitiable”: wretched in yourself, pitiable to others. For those who examine your life closely and see that you are wretched regard you as pitiable and feel compassion for your misery.

The weight of this misery is distinguished by the three following terms: “poor, blind, and naked.” Poor through the loss of charity, because anyone without charity is poor even if possessing other goods. Blind through the loss of knowledge, because one without knowledge of truth sees neither himself nor what is useful to him. Naked through the loss of good works, because one whom the devil strips of good works has nothing with which to adorn or cover himself before his neighbor. This man, therefore, was wretched and appeared pitiable because, having lost the virtue of charity, knowledge of truth, and the garment of good work, he remained poor, blind, and naked.

It follows:

“I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire, that you may become rich; and to clothe yourself in white garments, so that the shame of your nakedness may not appear; and anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see.”

After rebuke he adds admonition, and he distinguishes these three matters in a changed order against the three he stated above. There he said that this man was poor, blind, and naked; here he counsels him to buy gold from himself, be clothed in white garments, and anoint his eyes with eye-salve. It is as though he said: Because you are poor, I counsel you to buy gold from me, that you may be enriched; because you are naked, I counsel you to be clothed in white garments, that you may be covered and adorned; and because you are blind, at my counsel anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may be able to see rightly.

“I counsel you to buy from me gold refined by fire.” What is more rightly signified by gold refined by fire than charity? Like gold, it gleams through brightness; like fire, it burns through love; and in the elect it undergoes the judgment of testing in the furnace of tribulation. He says therefore: “I counsel you to buy from me gold,” that is, charity shining with the light of inward splendor, burning with the heat of love, and tested in my elect through the furnace of tribulation. Buy it through the expenditure of prayer from me, from whom come the sure goods of spiritual grace, “that you may become rich.” For as long as you are without charity, you cannot be enriched by other goods; without it you will always be poor.

Whoever is outwardly surrounded and adorned with clean works is clothed in white garments. He appropriately adds garments after gold, because charity comes first and every good action proceeds from charity. “So that the shame of your nakedness may not appear.” One whom good action does not cover is shamed before others by his nakedness, because he is ashamed before others precisely in having lost good action. Therefore, this man, who had no good works, is rightly admonished to put on white garments—that is, clean works—so that his nakedness may thus be covered, and so that he may no longer be ashamed before observers on account of his nakedness, that is, the loss of good works.

“And anoint your eyes with eye-salve.” What more rightly do we understand by eye-salve than the divine word? And what more fittingly by eyes than our spiritual faculties? Just as we heal our eyes with eye-salve, so we enlighten our faculties with sacred speech. “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see”: that is, search the Scripture that you may know truth. For “the commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes”—that is, our faculties. Eye-salve cleanses the eyes, that is, our faculties, through its bitterness; the Lord’s commandment makes the faculties clear through its terror. Eyes are clarified by eye-salve to see the sun; faculties are clarified by the Lord’s commandment for divine contemplation.

Alternatively, eye-salve is a spiritual gift by which, when our faculties previously shut through ignorance are anointed, they are opened to behold the brightness of heavenly splendor. Alternatively, eye-salve is the bitterness of repentance, which through compunction clarifies the faculties of the heart, as eye-salve clarifies the bodily eyes through a flow of tears. Therefore, just as one who anoints his eyes with eye-salve receives sight, so one who applies any of these to the faculties of the heart receives understanding.

It follows: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise. Be zealous therefore and repent.” In order to lead him to what he counsels, he proposes along with the admonition his elect whom he loves, rebukes, and chastises, so that the bishop may observe their endurance under the divine scourge and not grow sluggish in repentance.

He says therefore: “Behold, those whom I love I rebuke and chastise; be zealous therefore and repent,” as though he said: If the preceding counsel cannot rouse you from your sloth and lukewarmness, carefully observe that I rebuke with words and chastise with scourges those whom I love, and that they endure both words and scourges. Take your example from them; emulate them in good—that is, imitate them in emulation—and do not fear the tribulation endured in performing repentance. Thus, if the word of admonition does not suffice, let an example of imitation be added to the word.

It follows:

“Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I shall enter to him, and dine with him, and he with me.”

After the admonition to repentance, he sets before him confidence in forgiveness in order to strengthen him. “Behold, I stand at the door and knock,” as though he said: Do not despair, because I am ready in mercy to enter to you, that we both may be as we ought to be in one love. For I do not withhold what I promise without distinction.

“Behold, I stand,” ready as though to enter, “at the door,” that is, at the entrance of the heart, “and knock” through the word of preaching. “If anyone hears my voice and opens”—that is, receives my preaching and opens the door to me through true faith—“I shall enter to him” through the infusion of spiritual grace, “and dine with him” through his justification, “and he with me” through the joy of a good conscience, through increase of grace, and through hope of future glory.

It should be noted that he says “if anyone,” because few obediently hear his voice and open to him the door of their heart. Nor does he say, “I shall lunch,” but “I shall dine,” so that the good which begins in the world through charity may be perfected in heaven through blessedness, and may be shown to endure always through eternity, with nothing else succeeding it through any change of time.

It follows:

“The one who conquers, I shall grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sit with my Father on his throne.”

Having set in order all that concerned the bishop, he adds, as in the other chapters, the victor’s gift: a share in the spiritual and heavenly kingdom. He sets before those who fight his own victory and session on the Father’s throne as an example, that they may hasten to the reward.

“He who has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches”: what God promises to the holy congregations.

We may also distinguish generally under four divisions all that is contained in this chapter. Where he says, “I know your works, that you are neither cold,” he rebukes the bishop’s lukewarmness; where he says, “I counsel you to buy gold from me,” he admonishes him to amendment; where he adds, “I stand at the door and knock; if anyone hears my voice and opens to me, I shall enter to him and dine with him,” he sets before the repentant person confidence in his mercy; and where finally he says, “The one who conquers, I shall make him sit upon my throne,” he promises the victor a share in the spiritual and heavenly kingdom.

And, in order that we may recall in summary, for clarity, everything contained in this first vision: first the author set forth the title of the book and the greeting to the churches. Then he described the likeness of the Son of Man appearing to him. Thirdly, he came down to holy admonitions addressed separately to individual bishops: the bishop of Ephesus, the bishop of Pergamum, and the bishop of Thyatira.

He first praised the bishop of Ephesus for good and then rebuked him for evil. He praised the bishop of Smyrna and the bishop of Philadelphia only for righteousness. But he rebuked the bishops of Sardis and Laodicea only for evil. Whoever wishes to investigate the interpretations of the names of the seven cities included in this vision will see that the deeds and the interpretations of the names agree rationally and wonderfully.

Ephesus is interpreted “fall” or “counsel.” Both interpretations correspond most rightly to the bishop of the city and his deeds: by abandoning first charity, he had fallen into a diminution of virtue; and the divine admonition offers him counsel, that by doing his first works he may again rise to his first rank.

Smyrna is interpreted “song.” This interpretation suits well the bishop whom divine revelation, judging him blameless of negligence, also exalts with praise.

Pergamum is interpreted “division of horns.” This agrees excellently with its bishop, whom the divine discourse admonishes to scatter and divide with the rigor of righteousness the proud horns of the Nicolaitans.

Thyatira is interpreted “illuminated” or “living sacrifice.” Neither meaning is foreign to its bishop: he is illuminated through spiritual teaching, and by rebuke is subtly admonished to teach fornicators to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God.

Sardis is interpreted “beginning of beauty.” This is not at all inconsistent with the life of its bishop, who possessed only rudimentary goods and merely the name, not the reality, of holiness.

Philadelphia is interpreted “love of a brother” or “saving an inheritance.” Both meanings suit its bishop and his conduct, for through brotherly love he labored manfully in preaching to convert the elect, who are the Lord’s inheritance.

Laodicea is interpreted “vomiting.” This agrees most aptly with its bishop, because, on account of his lukewarmness, the Redeemer himself was purposing to begin to vomit him from his mouth unless he repented.

Thus a diligent investigator of the sacred page can discover, not only from the deeds themselves but also from the interpretations of the names, how he may attain the light of knowledge. Up to this point, having spoken of the first vision of this book not as we ought, but as we were able, we lay aside the pen, so that, refreshed by rest, we may take it up again more eagerly to enter upon the second vision.

# Book Two. On the Second Vision

[Col. 0743]

## Prologue

[Col. 0743A]

God supremely good, from whom all good things proceed and descend variously and manifoldly into the subject creation, from whom all things have not only that they exist, but also that they are good according to nature, and from whom the rational creature possesses in a singular manner that it is upright through justice, himself distributes the grace of spiritual wisdom in many ways to his own amid the diversity and course of time, so as to gather them into the one condition of eternity. For the human mind, blinded by its manifold desire for visible things, is restored only with difficulty to the simple contemplation of spiritual goods unless it is instructed by the diversity of heavenly teaching and the variety of reading. [Col. 0743B]

Therefore not only is the whole of sacred Scripture most beautifully divided among different books, but one and the same book is distinguished by a division of diverse meanings, so that a mind distracted by diverse and false goods may, enlightened by the various readings of the sacred page, be brought back to the vision and love of that true good. Thus this sacred Apocalypse too is divided into diverse visions, so that its diligent reader may be strengthened by greater exercise and raised to the knowledge and desire of that same good.

Yet it must be understood that the visions do not all instruct equally, nor do they contain the mysteries of heavenly sacraments in the same manner. For the first vision, which precedes the others, contains teachings greater and clearer than the rest—although these too are great—since it was sent especially for the correction of one region, namely Asia. But the visions that follow contain mysteries far greater, more obscure, and more sublime, since they concern the instruction of the whole Church in general. Hence, at the entrance to this holy vision, the holy theologian is rightly told: “Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after these things” (Rev. IV). For when we are placed below, we clearly perceive lesser things; but we ascend on high in order to see greater things. It is therefore evident from the words “Come up” that the things he was about to see were more excellent than those he had seen.

This vision, as was touched upon above, deals with the one seated upon the throne; with the book sealed with seven seals; and with the Lamb opening the book. It also describes the manifold tribulations of the holy Church from the beginning of grace to the end, and the rewards of blessedness that follow, so that the elect may be forearmed against tribulations by hearing of them and made stronger by the promise of recompense.

## CHAPTER I. On the One Seated upon the Throne and His Adornment, with Regard to the Text of Chapter IV

[Col. 0744A]

“After these things I saw: and behold, a door opened in heaven, and the first voice which I heard, as it were of a trumpet speaking with me, saying: Come up here, and I will show you what must take place after these things” (Rev. IV).

Having described the mysteries of the first vision, he proceeds to the mysteries of the second vision. “After these things”: after them in the order of seeing, not through a change in what is being said. These things, namely those contained in the first vision, I “saw,” that is, understood; “and behold, a door opened in heaven.”

Heaven is the holy Church. Like heaven, it is exalted through its heavenly manner of life; strengthened through the firmness and constancy of faith; extended by bodily dwelling to the ends of the earth and by spiritual love on every side toward friends and enemies; shining with the brightness of the sun of righteousness which illumines it, with the splendor of righteousness divinely bestowed upon it, and with the distinguished conduct of holy teachers and perfect men, as though with the light of sun and moon and innumerable stars. It also prudently conceals divine mysteries from the reprobate while clearly revealing them to the righteous.

Again, it is heaven because it has now left earthly things far beneath it and has cleaved on high to heavenly things through faith, hope, and charity. The door is sacred Scripture, by whose teaching and preaching every elect person is instructed; taught through it what must be believed, he enters the holy Church. This door—that is, sacred utterance—is always closed to the reprobate, but is seen and entered by the elect because it is open. Hence the holy theologian is now rightly said to have seen in heaven not a closed door but an open one. For whoever understands sacred Scripture in accordance with the rightness of faith perceives an open door in heaven, since he recognizes in it an entrance into the holy Church.

“And the first voice which I heard, as it were of a trumpet speaking with me, saying.” The voices are divine admonitions, among which prophetic teaching is first in order. For the Law was mute in this respect: it promised temporal, not heavenly, goods. Hence it is written: “While all things kept the middle—that is, the highest and most perfect—silence” (Wisdom XVIII), namely Law and nature, because they were silent in that they neither promised nor bestowed true goods. “Your almighty word, O Lord, came from the royal thrones”: first inspiring the prophets to preach spiritual and heavenly things, then manifesting himself in the flesh to bestow them.

Thus the prophetic voice first sounded concerning inward and eternal goods, because through its preaching it first made these known to us and first invited us to seek them. It was the first to teach that the Law must be understood and observed spiritually; and it showed more clearly than light that the good which the letter promised and bestowed was temporal and passing, whereas that which it signified mystically would be spiritual and eternal. Therefore it is first in order, but not in dignity, since the evangelical and apostolic voice surpasses it in dignity as much as it shows more plainly the good of heavenly fullness. These voices too sound as often in heaven—that is, in the Church—as they invite us to the sweetness of heavenly blessedness.

The first voice, that is, prophetic teaching, is described as being like a trumpet speaking, because by its sound it strongly exhorts the spiritual army to battle against its enemies. It sounds like a trumpet because it cries aloud in admonition on account of the joys toward which it summons us. What it says to the holy theologian is made clear when it adds: “Come up here”—as if it said: “In the preceding vision, though you were situated lower down, you saw great things; but now ascend here in understanding and devotion, because you will see greater things. There you saw the state of the seven Churches of Asia; here you will see the state of the universal Church. And I will show you briefly,” namely in the disclosure of revelation, “what must take place,” whether things to be done in time or in eternity.

It should be understood, moreover, that when it says, “I will show you what must take place,” it does not deny that these things already existed, but declares that they would remain henceforth. For the dignity of the holy Church had already been exalted when Saint John beheld these things. He therefore says that some things “must take place” which were already past, because they were to remain in the same state in which they had begun.

It follows:

“And immediately I was in the Spirit; and behold, a throne was set in heaven, and one sitting upon the throne; and he that sat was like in appearance to a jasper stone and a sardius; and there was a rainbow round about the throne, like in appearance to an emerald.”

In the first vision he says that he was in the Spirit and saw the things contained in that vision. One may perhaps ask whether, after contemplating the first vision, he departed from the Spirit, remained for some interval of time in himself, and then rose again to contemplate the second; or whether, as is more likely and more rightly to be believed, he remained in the Spirit.
