To me it seems most true that he continually remained in spiritual vision and never descended from the beginning of the revelation to the end of all the visions. But whether this was so or not is uncertain. At all events, it seems wholly probable, as was shown above, that by the gift of the Spirit he was lifted more highly to contemplate what follows than he had been to see what precedes.

He therefore says again at the beginning of this vision: “Immediately I was in the Spirit,” so that we may understand: much more excellently than I was before. By saying “immediately,” he indicated both the swiftness that accompanies the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit and his own obedience, which ought to be imitated. How many wonders and how heavenly mysteries of Christ and the Church he thereafter saw, he declares in what follows. [Col. 0746A]

“And behold, a throne was set in heaven.” The throne of the supreme, incomprehensible, and divine majesty, set in heaven, consists of the holy angels and the perfect teachers and prelates set and ordained by divine providence in the holy Church. In them God chiefly dwells and reigns, and through them justly and piously governs lesser persons. They are more exalted in merit before God and more worthy of honor before human beings because he makes them his throne, deigns especially to rest in them, and judges others through their teaching.

“And one sitting upon the throne,” that is, was there. God fittingly sits above the throne because through the power of his divinity he surpasses all creatures. He is rightly said to be above the throne because he rules over all in the dignity of majesty and holds all things beneath himself by his power. He therefore sits above it by right. The greatness and character of his glory—not that glory in which he naturally and eternally subsists, incomprehensible and ineffable, but that in which he appeared figuratively for a time to Saint John—is clearly declared when it is added: “And he that sat was like in appearance to a jasper stone and a sardius.”

He was like in appearance to a stone because he remains firm in himself through the immutability of his nature. He was like in appearance to a stone because he rules all things inseparably and firmly through the power of his own strength. He was like in appearance to a stone because he possesses in himself the solidity of immortality and grants it to his own by the gift of spiritual grace.

In another sense, he was like in appearance to a stone because he breaks the hardness of the human heart. Again, he was like in appearance to a stone because he is for his elect a firm and stable foundation of justification. Again, he was like in appearance to a stone because toward both good and evil persons he steadfastly preserves the truth of his utterance.

Jasper and sardius, these two precious stones, have two distinct colors: the first is green, the second red. Green signifies the unfading quality of eternity; red, the fire of condemnation. Thus the glory of divine majesty appears through likenesses drawn from visible things. He is said to be like in appearance to stone and sardius because he firmly and unshakenly both promises eternity to the elect and threatens condemnation to the reprobate. By the promised green that never withers, he delights the elect with eternity; by the red of his threats, he terrifies the reprobate with ever-burning fire.

Therefore the statement, “He was like in appearance to a stone,” applies equally to good and evil persons. “Of jasper” applies only to the good; “of sardius,” only to the evil. For our Redeemer is like in appearance to a stone, preserving the steadfastness and love of his word toward both good and evil persons: of jasper, by promising eternity to the good; of sardius, by threatening condemnation to the evil.

And so that we may believe him to be in judgment such as we have heard him described in sacred utterance, it fittingly adds: “And there was a rainbow round about the throne, like in appearance to an emerald.” For the rainbow signifies judgment because it contains the sign of judgment. The emerald, moreover, is green and red. Thus the rainbow appearing about the throne is described as the judgment of majesty, because on both sides, at the right and the left—that is, among good and evil persons—when the just Judge judges, the due recompense is bestowed. But the rainbow is said to be like the appearance of an emerald because, when good and evil persons have been examined by divine judgment, the just are introduced into the pastures of green eternity, while the wicked are delivered over to the fire of red conflagration. Such, then, as he is proclaimed in sacred utterance, such he is in judgment.

It should be noted that the rainbow is said to be around not so much the one sitting as the throne, because it belongs to the perfect, in whom God dwells and reigns and through whom he governs lesser persons, now to preach that judgment on every side, so that they may deserve in the end to sit and judge the world. That they will sit with him and judge those to be judged is openly shown when it adds:

“And round about the throne were twenty-four seats; and upon”—that is, upon the seats—“twenty-four elders sitting, clothed in white garments, and on their heads golden crowns.” Seats are merits. For every perfect person has a seat in judgment according to what he deserves in the world. The twenty-four elders are all the holy and perfect teachers of the Old and New Testament. They are rightly comprehended together under this number because of the preeminence of the twelve patriarchs and the authority and dignity of the apostles. These perfect persons are said to sit upon individual seats because both in the present Church, while the present life continues, and at the last judgment, by the Judge’s own appointment, they receive according to their merits a seat from which to judge. [Col. 0747C]

Accordingly, above, where he said, “There was a rainbow around the throne,” he mentioned judgment; here, where he said that the twenty-four elders sit upon thrones, he added what concerns perfect persons exercising divine judgments with the Lord.

But lest difficulty arise because above we said that all perfect persons sit with the elect angels, while here we explain these same perfect human beings as sitting around the throne, we may, for convenience in the present passage and without a distorted interpretation, alter the understanding somewhat. We may say that here the throne of God should be understood chiefly as the angels—for in them God dwells far more excellently than in human beings, and through them he exercises his judgments more sublimely, and perhaps more frequently, than through human beings. In those blessed angels, more singularly, closely, and familiarly subject inwardly to the divinity and set as it were in the middle by dignity, perfect human beings—although they too, according to the former and higher exposition, are thrones of God—are described as lesser and more remote from the angels in divine ministry, joined outwardly around the throne.

As was proved above, those in whom God dwells, governing not only themselves but lesser persons through them, are thrones of God. Thus here, by their being said to sit upon individual seats, it is shown that he makes them judges with himself over others. Holy and perfect teachers and prelates, therefore, are thrones of God because they are subject to the highest divinity; yet they are around the throne because they are believed to be joined in ministry to the angels, who are inwardly and invisibly subject to God and are chiefly thrones of God, so that by the authority and dignity of teaching they may sit upon seats beside the Judge. [Col. 0748A]

They are elders because of the seriousness of maturity; clothed in white garments because of purity of chastity and good works and the hope of immortality. They have crowns upon their heads: in the world, by hope; in heaven, by possession—the glory, splendor, and endlessness of the heavenly kingdom. Their crowns are golden because of the radiance of divine contemplation.

That the rainbow and the elders are described as forming the circuit around the aforesaid throne signifies that divine judgment must be exercised continually and that those who are to exercise it must consider without omission how it ought to be carried out. That the rainbow is first described as being around the throne of God and then the elders are mentioned as being around that same throne expresses that the elders must always fear the heavenly judgment which they hear between themselves and God; by continually attending to it, they must judge themselves strictly and take from it the pattern by which to judge others.

It follows:

“And from the throne proceed lightnings, voices, and thunders.” From the throne—that is, from the seat of God, namely from the perfectly righteous, in whom God dwells and through whom he governs others—proceed lightnings, voices, and thunders. Lightnings signify the brightness of miracles flashing far and wide. Voices express measured admonitions sounding to those who hear moderately; thunders, harsh and terrible threats of punishments for the reprobate.

Thus lightnings, voices, and thunders are said to proceed from the throne of God because all perfect persons shine with miracles, preach with their voices, and sound terrifyingly with threats. Lightnings proceed when through them the blind are enlightened, lepers cleansed, and the dead raised. Voices proceed which say: “We beseech you to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your reasonable service” (Rom. XII). Thunders proceed when they threaten the reprobate terribly that they will perish without any mercy.

It follows:

“And seven burning lamps before the throne,” that is, are there. “These are the seven Spirits of God,” that is, the illuminations of the sevenfold Holy Spirit. The seven burning lamps are before the throne of God because perfect persons always attend to the illuminations of the sevenfold Spirit, and through his illumination recognize with greater clarity than light what is profitable. This Holy Spirit is figured by burning lamps, because he enlightens all whom he illumines for knowledge and inflames them for love. He also shines sevenfold in that he supplies his own with seven spiritual gifts; he shines before them when he teaches the way of righteousness.

It follows:

“And in the sight of the throne, as it were, a sea of glass like crystal.” By the sea of glass we understand baptism. Baptism is like a sea because in it the bitterness of iniquity is remitted; it is glass because in it purity and the clarity of divine knowledge are bestowed. It is rightly called like crystal because through it every elect person is strengthened unto the splendor and firmness of righteousness. It is also rightly said to be in the sight of the throne, because perfect persons, as has often been said, are thrones of God; they perfectly understand his power and through it admit only those who are worthy and fit.

But, to gather briefly all that has been said: the open door is sacred Scripture; heaven, the holy Church; the first voice, prophetic teaching; the throne of God, angels and holy perfect persons. God is like a stone because of the firmness of truth; like jasper because of the promise of eternity; like sardius because of the threat of condemnation; and the rainbow, which contains the sign of judgment, is divine judgment. The twenty-four elders are the preachers of the Old and New Testament. The seats signify offices of teaching, or merits; the crowns, rewards; the lightnings, miracles; the voices, admonitions; the thunders, threats. The seven burning lamps are the illuminations of sevenfold grace; the sea of glass—that is, baptism—because of the remission of bitter iniquity; glass, through the pure knowledge of divinity; like crystal, through the splendid firmness of righteousness; before the throne of God, that is, before the perfect persons who through spiritual consideration and understanding separate worthy persons from the unworthy.

For perfect persons have the sea of glass before them while they carefully and spiritually attend to and understand the sacrament of baptism, cautiously excluding the unworthy from entering it and mercifully admitting the worthy.

## CHAPTER II. On the Four Living Creatures

[Col. 0749C]

“And in the midst of the throne, and around the throne, four living creatures full of eyes before and behind” (Rev. IV).

Sacred prophecy variously describes the wonderful mystery of the divine vision and shows us in manifold ways the beauty of the heavenly good. In the preceding chapter, by wonderfully and beautifully arranged qualities of visible and bodily things concerning the one seated upon the throne and his adornment, it disclosed its depth to those who read mystically. In this chapter, however, through a typological description of the four evangelists, it opens his excellence yet more sublimely and subtly.

For by the four living creatures described in this vision, as the frequent tradition of the Fathers and holy teachers teaches, the four evangelists are signified. They are fittingly compared with living creatures because by their word and example all righteous persons are encouraged to attain heavenly life. They also ought to have been prefigured by the number four because their four Gospels were to be preached through the four regions of the world.

“In the midst of the throne, and around the throne, four living creatures.” In the midst of the throne—that is, of the perfect preachers—the four living creatures, namely the holy evangelists, are as supporters; around it, as defenders. Or they are in the midst of the throne because all perfect persons attend to them as placed in the midst while they devote themselves unanimously to readings in evangelical wisdom. They are around it because what they have learned inwardly by reading or meditation they preach outwardly on every side. For they are, as it were, in the midst when their writings are learned by all; they are around it when they are proclaimed everywhere.

“Full of eyes before and behind.” The holy living creatures are full of eyes through the full contemplation of the heavenly good: before, through knowledge of future things; behind, through knowledge of past things.

“And the first living creature was like a lion; and the second living creature like a calf; and the third living creature having a face as it were of a man; and the fourth living creature like a flying eagle.” The first living creature is Mark, the second Luke, the third Matthew, the fourth John.

The first living creature, that is Mark, is like a lion because at the beginning of his Gospel he says: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Luke I [as printed]), by which the lion is signified. Its nature is said to be that it is born dead, but is raised by its father’s roar on the third day. Thus Christ, after tasting death for the human race, rose on the third day by the command of the Father. Mark is therefore rightly described as like a lion because he began his Gospel in such a way as to be understood to express the mystery of Christ’s resurrection.

It should be noted that the prophet Ezekiel, who described the four evangelists through these same living creatures, placed first the face of a man, which figures the incarnation, because the things he saw were still far in the future. But John, who after the contemplation of these mysteries beheld them figuratively, is said to have seen first the likeness of the lion, through which the resurrection is signified, for the greater confirmation of the Christian faith now already fulfilled; for the whole foundation of our faith and hope rests especially upon the power of the resurrection. [Col. 0750B]

“And the second living creature like a calf.” After the face of a man Ezekiel placed the face of a lion, and for this reason he sees both on the right. They were seen on the right because the incarnation and resurrection gladdened the elect. Then he places the face of a calf, or ox, which he also describes as being on the left; this face was fittingly on the left because Christ’s passion, which it figures, made the disciples sorrowful. But blessed John did not preserve this order, because in this passage he suggested nothing concerning this joy or sorrow.

The second living creature, then, that is Luke, is like a calf because Luke at the beginning of his Gospel mentioned Zachariah the priest, whose office it was to offer a calf; by this he designated Christ’s passion. Luke is placed before Matthew in the sacred vision by a certain preeminence, because the price of our redemption is contained in the Passion. For Christ’s being born would have profited us nothing unless his redeeming us had profited us.

“And the third living creature having a face as it were of a man.” The third living creature, that is Matthew, had as it were the face of a man because at the beginning of his Gospel he said: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” (Matt. I). By this he did not signify figuratively but openly recount the incarnation of the Word.

But it must be carefully observed that it does not say, “having the face of a man,” but “a face as it were of a man.” In sacred Scripture, “man” is understood in various ways. Sometimes it is said according to the etymology of the name; sometimes according to the dignity of the created condition; sometimes according to the disposition or effect of iniquity; sometimes according to typological signification; sometimes according to the defect of frailty; sometimes according to the rectitude of equity.

“Man” is said according to the etymology of the name when it is explained as being so called because he is from the soil (*humus*). It is said according to the dignity of the created condition where he is read to have been made in the image and likeness of God. It is said according to the disposition or effect of iniquity when the Apostle says to those who sin: “Since there is among you jealousy and contention, are you not men?” (I Cor. XIII [as printed]). “You are men,” that is, you are wicked and unrighteous.

It is said according to typological signification in the Gospel, where an evil man is said to have sown tares over the good seed (Matt. XIII). Whom can we more rightly say this man is, according to typological signification, than the devil? In the likeness of a man he sowed tares over the good seed after he knew that the word had been sown upon human hearts, injecting into some diverse heresy and seeds of vices.

It is said according to the defect of frailty, as Jeremiah says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. XVII)—in man, that is, in one frail and so easily and swiftly failing. It is said according to the rectitude of equity, as Solomon says: “Fear God and keep his commandments; this is every man” (Eccles. XII). For whoever fears God and keeps his commandments is a man because he is upright through the equity of righteousness. Whoever does not do this is, as it were, not a man at all; for if he sins knowingly through contempt, he must be called a devil. [Col. 0751C]

Therefore Saint Matthew the evangelist, who described Christ’s humanity at the beginning of his Gospel, rightly had in the sacred vision, according to the sense in which “man” is sometimes taken negatively, not the face of a man but a face as it were of a man. For our Redeemer, of whom he writes, came not in sinful flesh but in the likeness of sinful flesh. With respect to evil, he had nothing of man, because he committed no sin.

“And the fourth living creature like a flying eagle.” The fourth living creature, namely Saint John himself, to whom this vision appeared, was like a flying eagle, for he flew higher than all others in contemplating the mysteries of the holy and supreme divinity. The prophet Ezekiel also describes his face as above all four. And because blessed John, by saying at the beginning of his Gospel that the Word was in the beginning, transcended not only others but himself as well. Therefore, because at the beginning of their Gospels one of the holy evangelists treated of the Savior’s resurrection, another of his passion, another of his incarnation, and another of his divinity, it is rightly said of the holy living creatures by which these evangelists are figured that one was like a lion, another like a calf, another having a face as it were of a man, and another like a flying eagle.

Having described their figurative likeness, he adds their perfect fullness: “And the four living creatures, each of them, had six wings.” What do we more fittingly understand through the figure of wings than knowledge of the Scriptures, through which, as by wings, we leave earthly things and ascend to heavenly things? This sacred knowledge is fittingly designated by the number six in order to show the power of its perfection. Six signifies perfection, either because God completed his work in six days or because it is a perfect number.

In another sense: the first wing is in the law of nature; the second, in the reading of the written Law; the third, in the reading of prophecy; the fourth, in the reading of the evangelical Law; the fifth, in the reading of apostolic instruction; the sixth, in the knowledge of teachers who followed the apostles in time and expounded obscure passages of Scripture. Although the holy evangelists came before these teachers, they must by no means be believed to have possessed less understanding than they did; for sacred authority testifies concerning them that Jesus himself opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. They are most truly to be believed not only to have been among those whose minds he opened to understand the Scriptures, but also among—and with—those to whom he gave the firstfruits of the Spirit. [Col. 0752B]

Thus the holy living creatures are rightly said each to have six wings because of the perfection and fullness of knowledge. By these wings they flew through the world; by these they ascended into heaven.

It follows:

“And around and within they are full of eyes.” This sense is joined to and refers back to the earlier statement, “full of eyes before and behind.” The holy living creatures are full of eyes through the fullness of clarity of knowledge: before, through knowledge of future things; behind, through knowledge of past things; around, through circumspection in morals; within, through clean and right discernment of thoughts.

“And they had no rest day and night, saying: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty, who is, and who was, and who is to come.” The holy living creatures have no rest in the praise of God because they never cease to praise the divine majesty. They praised him in their lifetime by word; they still praise him in writing; they praise him through the mouths of the faithful by the testimony of their authority and holiness; and in heaven they praise him by contemplation and love.

That it says, “they had no rest,” by no means indicates labor. For it is, indeed, supreme and perfect rest never to cease from the devout praise of the Creator. “They had no rest day and night,” that is, never, “saying: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty.” O how blessed are the companies of good angels and all the elect, singing without end before God the proclamations of this praise! Blessed too are those who know how to sigh in the path of present misery for that sweet harmony. For the more often they sigh for it, the more closely they approach its sweetness. And already on the way—though faintly—they taste beforehand the delight of the heavenly harmony with which they will be fully satisfied in their homeland.

The holy living creatures cry “Holy” three times because there is Trinity in persons; “Lord God Almighty” once because there is unity in the simplicity of the Godhead: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.” Holy in righteousness; Lord in glory; almighty in power; who was, and who is, and who is to come, in eternity. For in the words “who was,” observe that he is without beginning; in “is,” observe that he remains unchangeably; in “who is to come,” observe that he endures as the end of all things without end. Through past, present, and future, by which all time is comprehended, eternity is not unfittingly signified, by which all mutability also is enclosed.

Nevertheless, the phrase “who is to come” is properly shown in another sense to pertain to his humanity. Everything said of the holy living creatures is understood of perfect preachers. For they are in the midst of the throne, supporting others; around it, defending them. They are holy living creatures because they encourage us toward virtues; full of eyes on every side because they carefully consider themselves within and without. Or again: within, with regard to the Old Testament, where knowledge of the mystery of redemption lies hidden; without, with regard to the New, where it lies openly manifest.

They have a leonine face, preaching the Savior’s saving resurrection; a calf-like face, preaching his passion; a human face, preaching his humanity; an eagle’s face, preaching his divinity. They have six wings through the perfect knowledge of sacred Scripture. They have no rest day or night—that is, never, whether in prosperity or adversity—saying, “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty,” through the preaching of sacred faith and the singing of divine praise.

It follows:

And when those four living creatures gave glory and [Col. 0753C] honour and blessing to him who sits upon the throne, who lives for ever and ever, the twenty-four elders fell down before him who sits upon the throne, and worshipped him who lives for ever and ever, casting their crowns before the throne and saying: “You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory and honour and power, because you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.”

Above he described the praise of the holy and undivided Trinity, established by the ministry or writings of the four Evangelists. Now he adds what their preaching or Scripture has contributed to all preachers and to the judges of the universal Church: namely, that the twenty-four elders—that is, as was shown above, [Col. 0753D] all the preachers, judges, and rulers of the Old and New Testaments—received knowledge of the faith through the mystery of human redemption, whether by the spirit of prophecy, like the ancients, or by reading evangelical Scripture, like the moderns; they attributed their righteousnesses and victories to God, sang praises, and gave thanks.

The holy Evangelists therefore rightly precede the preachers, because they alone deserved to write the mystery of our salvation. For although the ancients preceded them in time, they are nevertheless far behind them in dignity. These latter are also rightly said to sing the praise of the Godhead after them, because they by no means precede them in authority, but follow them.

Thus it is fittingly said: “And when those four living creatures gave glory and honour and blessing to him who sits upon the throne, who lives for ever and ever, [Col. 0754A] the twenty-four elders fell down before him who sits upon the throne,” because human salvation is contained in sacred discourse and distributed to all through its preaching. The holy living creatures give glory, honour, and blessing to him who sits upon the throne and lives for ever and ever, because they preach that he alone is uniquely to be glorified, honoured, and blessed; and they proclaim that glory, honour, and blessing exist uniquely and supremely in him and descend from him upon the creature subject to him. The twenty-four elders likewise fall down before him who sits upon the throne, because all the perfect, having recognized the mystery of the Godhead, submit themselves to the supreme Majesty and worship, through right faith, him who lives for ever and ever in eternity. [Col. 0754B] They cast their crowns before the throne, attributing their victories to God; and, in giving thanks, they give glory and honour to him alone and bless him alone: “You are worthy, O Lord God, to receive glory and honour and power.”

You are worthy to receive, through thanksgiving, praise and glory and honour and power from the creature subject to you—you who always and immortally possess all things by your Godhead in your proper nature. For we give glory, power, and honour to God when we preach that he alone is glorious, worthy of honour, and unconquerable. He receives from us what we give when he graciously accepts our praises.

Finally, he plainly adds the reason why he is worthy of praise: “Because you created all things.” For he is worthy to receive praise from all, who gave to all an origin of subsistence. [Col. 0754C] But because all things were first in the divine will before they were created, it is openly added: “And by your will they existed and were created.” The number, weight, and measure of all things, and whatever may be said of created things, existed always, incomprehensibly and ineffably, in the divine will before they received their origin and appeared as created things. “By your will,” that is, according to your will, or in your will. He is therefore truly worthy of every praise, because he always possessed all things in his will through goodness, and at some time created them through power.

But since, above, where we assigned the things said concerning the holy living creatures to perfect preachers, we recapitulated the principal matters [Col. 0754D] contained in this chapter, we have not taken care here at the end, according to our usual practice, to gather together again what has been said.

## CHAPTER III. On the book sealed with seven seals, and the Lamb opening the book

“And I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals; and I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice: ‘Who is worthy to take the book and break its seals?’ And no one in heaven or on earth or beneath the earth was able to open the book or to look upon it; and I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to see it. And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of [Col. 0755A] David, has conquered, to open the book and break its seals’” (Rev. 5).

After describing him who sits upon the throne, his adornment, and the likenesses of the four living creatures, he adds an account of the book which he saw in the right hand of him who sits upon the throne, and of the Lamb who opened the book.

“And I saw in the right hand of him who sits upon the throne a book.” The book held in God’s right hand is sacred Scripture, in which is contained the universal knowledge profitable for salvation. He rightly holds it, because God is the Lord of knowledge and gives it to whom he wills. He holds it not in the left hand but in the right, because the spiritual good hidden within it is concealed from the wicked and opened to the good. Of this right hand and this book it is written: “At God’s right hand is a fiery law” (Deut. 33). Sacred Scripture is indeed a fiery law: [Col. 0755B] a law because it binds us by restraining us; fiery because it ardently kindles us to love of the Creator.

“Written within and without”: this book is written within by allegory, without by history; within by spiritual understanding, without by the letter. Within, for the exercise of the spiritually perfect; without, for the instruction of the simple and lesser. Within, so that the secret of wisdom may be hidden from the impure; without, so that truth may be revealed to the pure. Alternatively: within, with regard to the Old Testament, where knowledge of the mystery of the Redeemer lies hidden; without, with regard to the New, where it lies openly manifest.

“Sealed with seven seals.” Since all time revolves through seven days, universality is fittingly represented by the number seven. Thus the book was sealed with seven seals until the completion of [Col. 0755C] human redemption, which it announced by signs and promises; for until the coming of the Redeemer, except for a few elect persons, the whole world did not know the person through whom, or the manner by which, the human race would be redeemed. The book, therefore, was sealed with seven seals—that is, with all obscurities—because the manner of our redemption was known to very few and unknown to all others.

It is fittingly added under the figure of the ancient Fathers: “And I saw a mighty angel proclaiming with a loud voice: ‘Who is worthy to open the book and break its seals?’” For who is this mighty angel but the assembly of the ancient Fathers? An angel, because he announces good things to others; mighty, because he conquers flesh, the world, and the devil. By loudly demanding who was worthy [Col. 0755D] to take the book and break its seals, he proclaimed his desire, with great sighing, to behold the person of the coming Redeemer. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the eyes which see what you see. For I tell you that many kings and prophets wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10).

“And no one in heaven or on earth or beneath the earth was able to open the book or to look upon it.” When the ancients sought the person of the Redeemer, secretly foretold by the prophets, no one in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth was able to open the book. For neither an angel, nor a human being, nor a human spirit already stripped of the body, could fulfil sacred Scripture’s promise concerning the coming Redeemer—namely, by redeeming the human race—or show to the world the Redeemer promised in the sacred page. [Col. 0756A] Nor could anyone look upon it, because no one could either perfectly comprehend in understanding or narrate in words the generation of the Redeemer. Thus Isaiah says: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. 53). And blessed John says: “I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal” (John 1); that is, I cannot worthily or perfectly understand his generation in my mind or expound it in words.

He alone could open the book who alone could redeem the human race, and who alone could show as fulfilled the redemption promised in the veiled sacred Scripture or page. He alone perfectly understood the wondrous working of his generation who alone knows all things.

[Col. 0756B] “And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book or to see it.” This is said in the person of the ancients, because they either did not understand or grieved at the delay of that restoration itself.

It follows: “And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep.’” This elder signifies the choir of prophets, the ancient Fathers consoling and assuring others concerning the future Redeemer. For there was not consolation alone, but also great assurance concerning redemption: not only that they heard that our Redeemer would come, but that they heard specifically from what tribe he would be born.

“Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered to open the book and break its seals.” Christ is the lion. A lion sleeps with its eyes open; Christ expired while his Godhead lived. He was of Judah according to the flesh, as ancient prophecy foretold: “You, Bethlehem, land of [Col. 0756C] Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a ruler who shall govern my people Israel” (Matt. 2). He conquered in order to open the book and break its seals because, surrendering his flesh, free from all sin, for sinners, he fulfilled Scripture’s promise. He was the root of David because David firmly believed in his coming.

It follows:

“And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth. And he came and took the book from the hand of him who sat upon the throne.”

Above he set forth the promise; here he adds [Col. 0756D] the fulfilment of the promise. Yet there seems to be a great difference between promise and fulfilment. For in the promise he heard a lion; in the fulfilment he sees a lamb. There is indeed a great difference between a lion and a lamb: a lion is great; a lamb is small. But if we consider both, we recognize in both our Redeemer. For he is the great lion in his Godhead and the small lamb in his humanity; lion in the power of majesty, lamb in meekness; lion in punishing the wicked, lamb in redeeming the good; lion in strength, lamb in mercy. He is a lion in promise, so that weak hope may be strengthened; a lamb in fulfilment, so that a fearful conscience might not be afraid.

He sees this Lamb in the midst of the throne, the four [Col. 0757A] living creatures, and the elders, because Christ is the support and foundation of all his elect. All look toward him as placed in the midst, and all alike—though not equally—receive from him the gifts of spiritual grace. He fittingly sees him standing, as if ready to accomplish that for which he came; “as though slain,” because, though he died from weakness, he nevertheless lives by the power of God.

“Having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth.” Horns signify the exaltation of spiritual kingship; eyes, contemplation of truth. The Lamb—that is, Christ—therefore has seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth, because through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit he grants, to whom he wills, the sublimity of spiritual kingship and the knowledge of his truth. [Col. 0757B] He raises up those whom he wills to reign; those whom he wills he illumines for contemplation of the source of spiritual goods by the rays of that good. They are sent into all the earth so that from every land they may raise some to the height of the spiritual kingdom and illumine them for contemplation of spiritual goods.

“And he came and took the book from the right hand of him who sat upon the throne.” By assuming flesh, he came to human knowledge. According to his humanity he received from the right hand of him who sits upon the throne—that is, from the Word united to him—the book to be opened, that is, the promise to be fulfilled.

“And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb.” When he had opened the book—that is, when, by redeeming the human race, he showed in himself the fulfilment of what had been promised to the Fathers and signified in sacred Scripture—the four living creatures, that is, the four Evangelists or all preachers, and the twenty-four [Col. 0757C] elders, namely all the judges of the universal Church and whatever faithful persons are included under them, relying upon the teachings and examples of the seven prophets and apostles, fell before the Lamb. The former did so by fulfilling the mystery of human redemption through him; the latter because it had been fulfilled. They fell by humbling themselves and exalting him, humbly asking to be justified through him, and confessing by this sign that he alone is the one through whom heavenly good is bestowed.

And because all the perfect ought to attribute their good works to the Redeemer and commend to him the prayers [Col. 0757D] of others, it is fittingly added: “Each holding harps and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.” Harps, which sound sweetly under the touch of hands, fittingly signify good works, which by their effects, like certain sounds, rouse and invite neighbours toward the heavenly homeland. Bowls, which are broad and shining, signify the hearts of the saints: shining through wisdom and enlarged through charity. They are appropriately called golden because of the splendour of contemplation, and full of incense because of the abundance of devout prayers. For incense signifies prayers, because, as incense rises upward, so prayers reach the presence of the Godhead. Thus the perfect have harps because they ascribe their works to God, [Col. 0758A] and bowls because they offer prayers.

“And they sang a new song, saying: ‘You are worthy, O Lord God, to take the book and open its seals.’” As the saints have harps by ascribing their works to the Godhead and bowls by offering the prayers of others, so they also sing a new song, praising him for benefits received. It is rightly called new because it is sung concerning things always new and never growing old—namely, the restoration and glorification of the human race.

“You are worthy, O Lord God, to take the book and open its seals. Worthy, because you alone, free from sin, were slain, and redeemed us—not yourself, who were without sin—for God, so that we may belong to God, whereas formerly we belonged to the devil; by your blood, because you allowed it to be shed for us. You redeemed us not from one [Col. 0758B] race, but from every tribe and language and people and nation.”

A tribe is so called from the three orders of peoples descending from Noah’s sons, among whom are seventy languages. In each language, moreover, there are many peoples, and in each people many nations. He begins, therefore, with the general categories when he says, “From every tribe and language and people and nation,” and descends to particulars when he says: “And you made us a kingdom and priests for our God.” A kingdom, so that God may reign over us by grace, over whom the devil had reigned through sin; priests, so that we who formerly offered ourselves to the devil may henceforth offer ourselves to God; “and we shall reign over the earth,” that is, upon the earth; or, “we shall reign over the earth,” that is, we shall subject whatever is earthly and evil in us.

You are therefore worthy, O Lord, to open the book, because you have fulfilled the benefit promised in the book. [Col. 0758C] And because not human beings alone rejoice in the restoration of the human race, but angels too proclaim him worthy, through power, Godhead, wisdom, strength, honour, glory, blessing, and authority over every creature, it fittingly follows:

“And I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne, [Col. 0758D] the living creatures, and the elders.” “And I saw and heard”: as he saw spiritually, so he heard spiritually, because the vision was spiritual and the hearing also spiritual—the voice of many angels. A bodily voice is produced in one way, a spiritual voice in another: spiritual voice arises through the affection of devotion, bodily voice through the striking of air. Therefore angels, who are spirits alone, sing the Creator’s praise more sublimely insofar as they stretch themselves more sublimely in his love. Among them, those praise him uniquely who love him above all others. They sing his praise together for the restoration of the human race because they love him in gratitude for the generosity of their origin, and in the ardour of this affection raise their voice.

They are around the throne, the living creatures, and the elders, because the angelic powers protect the saints who are still placed amid the danger of this passing age and defend them against the attacks of reprobate spirits. “And their number was thousands of thousands.” By saying that their number was thousands of thousands, he does not suggest that he comprehended the number of heavenly spirits; rather, by stating immense numbers, he indicates that they are innumerable. And concerning such angelic numbers as are given in sacred discourse, [Col. 0759A] blessed Dionysius says:

> “I judge it fitting for intellectual reflection that the tradition of the sayings—understand, the divine sayings—concerning angels should speak of thousands upon thousands, and ten thousand times ten thousand, turning back upon itself and multiplying in accordance with these highest numbers, and thereby plainly signifying the innumerable orders of heavenly essences.”

For there are many blessed hosts of supramundane intellects, that is, angels, surpassing the weak and restricted measure of material numbers as understood by us—that is, of the number subject to our measure. Therefore, when he calls the number of angels “thousands of thousands,” he shows angels to be countable not by human beings but by God.

[Col. 0759B] “With a loud voice saying.” The voice of the praising angels is called great, in order to signify the greatness of their exultation and rejoicing over the salvation of the human race, and of the praise they offer to the Saviour. For if there is joy among God’s angels over one sinner who repents, let whoever can consider how great their joy is over the salvation of all the elect:

“Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and Godhead and wisdom and strength and honour and glory and blessing.” It is as though the angelic powers, praising above themselves the mediator of God and humankind, were not ashamed to proclaim his worthiness. The Redeemer of the world, who is a Lamb through innocence, who was slain through an undeserved punishment, and who redeemed the captive company, is worthy through singular excellence to receive from the [Col. 0759C] creature subject to him various proclamations of thanksgiving. He is worthy to receive from the creature, through praise offered, what he possesses according to his Godhead by nature and according to his humanity by grace. He is worthy to receive power, so that he may be proclaimed God in power; Godhead, wisdom, strength, honour, glory, and blessing, so that he may be believed and praised as God, wise, strong, worthy of honour, glorious, and blessed.

It follows:

“And every creature which is in heaven and upon the earth and beneath the earth, and which is in the sea, and the things which are in them.” As though all were briefly comprehended and distinguished, they say: The Saviour is worthy not only to receive power and the things stated above through praise and thanksgiving, but also every creature through authority.

“I heard them all saying to him who sits upon [Col. 0759D] the throne and to the Lamb.” The preceding words of praise seem to pertain more to the Godhead, although they are offered to the humanity because of the Godhead united to it. But here, where he says, “I heard them all saying,” he gathers together the hearers themselves and sets forth praise offered jointly to the Godhead and humanity. “I heard them all saying”: to him who sits upon the throne, the reigning Trinity, and to the Lamb—that is, to the humanity united to the Godhead—be blessing, honour, and glory, because he is uniquely blessed, worthy of honour, glorious, and to be glorified; and power, because he is supremely powerful for ever and ever, that is, always.

It follows:

“And the four living creatures said: ‘Amen’; and the twenty-four elders fell upon their faces and worshipped,” having heard the praise worthily offered by the heavenly spirits to him who sits upon the throne [Col. 0760A] and to the Lamb. The four living creatures said “Amen,” because it belongs especially to the office of preachers to confirm the testimony of sacred confession and divine praise. And the twenty-four elders fell upon their faces and worshipped, because all the judges of the Church, when they hear that the divine Majesty surpasses all creatures and is to be proclaimed and praised by the highest spirits, ought by no means to be proud of their pre-eminence, but should humble themselves and render to God, Creator and Redeemer, the worthy worship of veneration.

Dearest brother, we have touched, however inadequately, upon a few very small matters concerning the heavenly mysteries, because we cannot comprehend many and great things. We swim across great rivers of spiritual mysteries, but scarcely carry a few drops of hidden sweetness to the shores. Yet although we are not sufficient to draw up many waters, we do not come to the shore with dry mouths. For there is some benefit in expounding sacred discourse and labouring diligently in speaking of it.

For where he says, “I saw in the right hand of him who sits upon the throne a book,” the author dealt with sacred Scripture containing the promise of human redemption. Where he says, “I saw in the midst of the throne, the four living creatures, and the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain,” he dealt with the Lamb opening the book—that is, with the Redeemer fulfilling the promise. Where he said that the four living creatures and the elders sang a new song, he set forth testimony to that redemption and the thanksgiving of holy human beings. Where he adds, “And [Col. 0760C] I heard the voice of many angels,” he gives the testimony and praise of the heavenly spirits. Finally, where he introduces, “And the four living creatures said: ‘Amen’; and the twenty-four elders fell upon their faces,” he gives the confirmation of all preachers and the humiliation of ecclesiastical judges.

## CHAPTER IV. On the first seal and its opening

“And I saw that the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals, and I heard one of the four living creatures saying, like the voice of thunder: ‘Come and see.’ And I saw, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he went forth conquering in order to conquer” (Rev. 6).

All that is contained in the three preceding chapters of this second vision appears to pertain principally [Col. 0760D] to the mystery of human redemption. But what follows in the succeeding seven chapters, distinguished by the opening of the seven seals, concerns and sets forth the redemption and order of the subsequent time. In these following chapters the virtues of the elect, the persecutions inflicted by the reprobate upon the elect, and the tribulations of those who endure are described from the beginning of the nascent Church to the end of the world. They show in many ways that these foretold matters are fulfilled and hidden things disclosed gradually and successively—not all together and at once, but according to the ordering and opening of the seals and the progress of times.

Having fittingly described the mystery of human redemption, he adds the merits of the righteous, the persecutions of the reprobate, and the rewards of recompense, in order thereby to provide for the elect [Col. 0761A] and carefully instruct them concerning the future. For if, after announcing restoration, he had said nothing about the future tribulation of persecution and the reward of those who endure it, he would not have fortified the elect against adversities or encouraged them to endurance through promised rewards.

In this chapter he treats of the beginning and first condition of the Church being reborn: rising through baptism in Christ from oldness to newness of life, through the reception of spiritual gifts, and tending toward heavenly goods.

“And I saw that the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals.” Christ opened the first seal of sacred Scripture when, by redeeming the world and pouring out the gifts of the Spirit upon the primitive Church, he manifested in himself and through himself the beginnings of the Father’s promise, hitherto hidden until that time, as fulfilled and brought to completion.

“And I heard one”—that is, the first—“of the four living creatures saying like the voice of thunder: ‘Come and see.’” In this vision the first living creature, like a lion, was Mark, [Col. 0761B] who at the beginning of his Gospel made mention of Christ’s resurrection and represented the preachers of that resurrection. Therefore, at the opening of the first seal, it is rightly said that the first living creature spoke to him, because the first order in the New Testament—the preachers—proclaimed everywhere the bodily resurrection of Christ and the spiritual resurrection of the nascent Church. Since the first order bore testimony to the resurrection, it is fittingly said that one—that is, the first—of the four [Col. 0761C] living creatures spoke at the opening of the first seal, which concerns the resurrection of the Church being reborn.

Its voice sounded like the voice of thunder because it suddenly proclaimed new, wondrous, and great things, with miracles flashing forth: “Come and see.” Come through greater attentiveness, and see through spiritual understanding, that the mystical promise of God is now being opened through the regeneration of the human race.

But what is here spiritually shown to Saint John is spiritually referred to persons who are to be chosen and converted. To them indeed these words are spoken: that through conversion they may come, and through faith see the grace of regeneration bestowed upon the primitive Church, which they do not know; and that, by receiving grace through baptism and imitating the Church, they may proceed toward life. Since what follows is understood of the primitive Church made white through baptism, it fittingly [Col. 0761D] follows: “And behold, a white horse.”

The white horse is the number of the first elect, alike purified from all sins in the water of baptism and whitened beyond snow by spiritual gifts. It had Christ as rider in the preachers newly reborn among the first believers, and carried him throughout the world for the sending forth of the arrows of preaching. Thus it fittingly follows: “And he who sat upon it had a bow.” The bow signifies the power of preaching. For as a bow shoots arrows, so the preacher sends forth the words of preaching. Arrows kill the enemy; the words of preaching kill the devil.

“And a crown was given to him.” For as the bow signifies the office of preaching, so the crown represents the reward of eternal recompense, in which there is no end. A crown was given to him [Col. 0762A] according to his humanity, because according to his Godhead he possesses all things. According to his humanity he receives all things, who according to his Godhead grants all things. Yet a crown is given to him daily when he is crowned in his elect.

Alternatively: he has a bow in order to wound the wicked in battle, and a crown in order to crown the good in glory. He has a bow because he will say: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire”; a crown because he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25).

Alternatively: he had the bow through the power of his Godhead; a crown was given to him through the glorification of his humanity. There seems to be a great difference between saying of the bow that he had it [Col. 0762B] and saying of the crown that it was given to him. To say that he had the bow appears to concern the power of the Godhead, according to which he possesses all things by nature. But to say that the crown was given to him concerns the condition of humanity, according to which he received all things by grace.

“And he went forth conquering in order to conquer”: he went forth upon the aforesaid white horse—that is, in the newly regenerated number of the first elect. He went forth from the Jews, leaving the Jews; he went forth conquering among them by converting those whom he had predestined, in order to conquer among the Gentiles by converting those whom he wished to choose.

The opening of the seal, therefore, is the revelation of the mystery together with the fulfilment of what was promised. The first living creature is the order of preachers proclaiming the resurrection. The white horse is the number of the first elect; the rider, Christ; the bow, preaching; the crown, recompense. Or: the bow is the condemnation of the wicked; the crown, the salvation of the good. Or: the bow is the power of the Godhead; the crown, the glorification of humanity. The rider—that is, Christ—went forth from the Jews, leaving the Jews, conquering because he chose from among them whom he wished, in order to conquer among the Gentiles by choosing among them those whom he foreknew. And he rightly said, “He went forth conquering in order to conquer,” because through those whom he chose in Judaea, he converted the [Col. 0762C] Gentiles.

## CHAPTER V. On the second seal and its opening
“And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying: Come and see. And behold, another horse, red; and to him who sat upon it it was given to take peace from the earth, so that men might kill one another; and a great sword was given to him” (Rev. VI).

After the devil, through his envy, had deceived the human race in its first parents and cast it from the delight of paradise into this misery, he saw that, now that the promise of redemption had already been set forth and the mysteries of sacred Scripture had begun to be opened, humanity was rising again through the Redeemer’s grace to that highest and invisible good from which he himself had fallen [Col. 0762D]. Again inflamed by envy, he burned fiercely against humankind. Gathering his forces from every side, he openly strove to incite, for the persecution of the elect, the impious rulers of the world devoted to his worship, and he attempted to prevent them from entering the heavenly homeland.

Therefore it is said: “And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying: Come and see; and behold, another horse, red.” The red horse is the cruel rulers of the world, reddened with the blood of the martyrs.

“And when he had opened the second seal” means: when, as grace increased, the divine promise began more fully to be displayed and fulfilled, and that which had been set forth and promised in the Scriptures began to be opened and made manifest [Col. 0763A]. “I heard the second living creature saying: Come and see.” The second living creature in this vision, resembling a calf, was Luke. At the beginning of his Gospel he intimated Christ’s Passion; and, according to the sequence of the periods of preachers in this vision, he figured the Passion of the martyrs—preachers proclaiming Christ’s own Passion as an example and exhorting the martyrs to imitate him.

Thus, fittingly, just as the first living creature resembling a lion—that is, Mark, who set forth Christ’s Resurrection at the beginning of his Gospel and designated the first order of preachers in the primitive Church—is said to have spoken at the opening of the first seal, in which the spiritual resurrection is described [Col. 0763B], so the second living creature resembling a calf, by which Luke is designated, who treated figurally of the Passion at the beginning of his discourse and figured the preachers of that same Passion of Christ, is recalled as speaking at the opening of the second seal, in which the Passion of the martyrs is treated. For just as the first order of preachers, designated through Mark, proclaimed the Resurrection in the primitive Church in order to lay the foundation of Christian faith, so the second order, in the age of the martyrs, set Christ’s Passion before them by preaching it, in order to strengthen them for endurance.

There the Resurrection is chiefly believed to have been preached, so that the hearers might rise to faith; here, the Passion, so that the elect might persevere in patience [Col. 0763C]. Therefore, just as the first living creature spoke there, so the second speaks here: for what is contained there concerns the Resurrection, and what is contained here concerns the Passion. There is designated the spiritual resurrection of believers; here, the bodily Passion of the martyrs.

“Come and see.” In its being said to him once more, “Come and see,” an increase and advancement of spiritual vision are designated.

“And behold, another horse, red.” Truly another, and very different from the other. That horse was white; this one red. In the former the bright company of those newly reborn was represented; in this one, the army of cruel rulers. The former shone with the newness of regeneration; the latter was red with the shedding of blood. Christ was the rider of that horse; the devil of this one. The former bore Christ everywhere for the instruction of humankind; this one bore the devil everywhere for their destruction [Col. 0763D].

Hence it is said of this devil: “And to him who sat upon it it was given to take peace from the earth.” To the devil himself, who sat upon that army of cruel rulers, it was given—that is, permitted—to take peace from the earth by bringing persecution. The cruelty of this persecution began in Nero’s time and did not cease until the age of Constantine the Great. Thus many thousands of martyrs were slain and crowned by God for their glorious victory.

It follows: “So that they might kill one another”—that is, people. Some people killed others, whether by the material sword through slaughter or by the spiritual sword through evil persuasion. Nor did the persecutors themselves kill only strangers, unknown and far away, but also parents, acquaintances, and neighbors [Col. 0764A]. All this was given—that is, permitted—to the devil: namely, that he might inflict so great a persecution upon the faithful as to take peace from the earth.

The scale of this persecution is expressed when it is added: “And a great sword was given to him.” It was indeed great, because this persecution blazed so fiercely that it even passed beyond the rim of Ocean. It was great because, at one time, within the city of Rome alone, seventeen thousand martyrs are recorded to have been slain for Christ by the utterly impious Diocletian in not many days. It was great because it killed not merely lesser persons, of less use to the universal Church, but also the greater ones—the supports and governors of the whole community of believers—such as the apostles and the most eminent teachers.

Fittingly, therefore, it is said that the horse of the devil-rider appeared red, when the army of impious rulers stained itself crimson with the blood of so many saints [Col. 0764B]. Fittingly it is said that a great sword was given to its rider, the devil, for taking peace from the earth, when he wrought such a slaughter of saints.

The opening of the second seal is the evident manifestation of sacred discourse concerning the devil’s persecution in the shedding of the blood of Christ’s martyrs. The second living creature is the second order of preachers in the age of the martyrs, exhorting martyrs to imitate Christ’s Passion. The red horse is the cruel army of rulers, red with the shedding of the saints’ blood. The rider is the devil; the removal of peace, the bringing of persecution; the greatness of the sword, the extent of torment.

## Chapter VI. On the Third Seal and Its Opening

[Col. 0764C]

“And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: Come and see. And behold, a black horse; and he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand. And I heard, as it were, a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying: A *bilibris* of wheat for a denarius, and three *bilibres* of barley for a denarius; and do not harm the wine and the oil” (Rev. VI).

Holy Mother Church, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, suffered no loss at all through the persecution brought upon her and the slaughter of her faithful. Rather, like mustard seed, the more she was crushed, the more she increased. For when the martyrs had been killed, and miracles shone forth through them after their death, many peoples were converted to the faith; afterward they faithfully served God within the holy Church [Col. 0764D].

But when the devil saw that he had made no progress through open persecution, he sought devices for doing harm. The number of God’s servants, which he could not diminish through the manifest persecution of impious rulers, he attempted to weaken through the hidden malice of heretics. Therefore, fittingly, at the opening of this third seal it is said: “Behold, a black horse.” Black signifies what is hidden. The black horse, then, designates the concealed cunning of heretics, veiled with certain words of sacred Scripture and with certain false virtues and works, and darkened so that it may not be plainly seen.

He says, therefore: “And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: Come and see. And behold, a black horse.” “And when he had opened the seal” means: when, in the further course of time, the effect of the divine promise and the progress of human salvation began increasingly to be opened and known in sacred Scripture [Col. 0765A]. “I heard the third living creature saying: Come and see.”

The third living creature in this vision, having a face like a man, was Matthew. He began his narrative with Christ’s humanity and figured the third order of preachers, who in the time of heretics attested through their preaching the true humanity of Christ. Thus it is fittingly said that at the opening of the third seal the third living creature was heard. For just as the first living creature—that is, Mark, who treats Christ’s Resurrection at the beginning of his discourse—is recalled as speaking at the opening of the first seal, where the spiritual resurrection is treated; and the second living creature—that is, Luke, who makes figurative mention of the Passion—is said to speak at the opening of the second seal, where the sufferings of the martyrs are treated [Col. 0765B]; so the third living creature—that is, Matthew, who begins with Christ’s humanity—is described as speaking or being heard at the opening of the third seal, where heretics are treated, barking against the Savior’s humanity itself with their lies, while the third order of preachers attests it.

Therefore, because “Come and see” is repeated at each opening, an increase of spiritual vision is figured. “And behold, a black horse.” The black horse is the band of heretics, dark to those who behold them because they hide their vices by counterfeit virtues and works. The first horse was white through the brightness of regeneration; the second red through the persecution of rulers; the third black through the concealment of its vices [Col. 0765C].

“And he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand.” The rider is the devil. The balance signifies correct and equitable discernment in understanding and preaching the Scriptures. The hand signifies the heretics themselves through whom the devil works. Thus the rider is said to have held a balance in his hand because the discernment and understanding which heretics claim to possess are ascribed to the devil. Having been unable to accomplish, while riding the red horse, the malice conceived against the faithful, he attempted to bring it about by deception while riding the black horse. What he could not achieve through the fury of rulers, he wished to accomplish through the perversity of heretics.

First he inflamed rulers who were outside and alien to the Church against her. Then he corrupted those of her household by his various heresies, so that, after warfare had ceased outwardly, warfare might boil up inwardly [Col. 0765D]. The impiety of this heretical perversity especially sprang up from the days of Constantine the Great and in the reigns of the emperors who followed him. Yet, crushed by the authority of holy Church and by the disputation of ecclesiastical teachers, it at last ceased.

But because divine mercy commonly applies greater consolation in the face of greater perils, it is rightly said: “And I heard as it were a voice in the midst of the four living creatures saying: A *bilibris* of wheat for a denarius, and three *bilibres* of barley for a denarius.” “In the midst of the four living creatures” means in the common testimony of the four evangelists and of all preachers. “A *bilibris* of wheat for a denarius, and three *bilibres* of barley for a denarius”: as though it said [Col. 0766A], “Do not fear, O faithful, although you see diverse heresies succeeding persecution; for they will not be able to harm you or diminish the provisions of sacred Scripture, if you choose to stand firm in perfect faith.”

For what is more suitably understood by the denarius, in which the calculation of reckoning comes to its end, than the perfection of faith? What by wheat, except the sacred Gospel? What by barley, except the Old Testament? What by the *bilibris*, or by the significance of this two-sextarius measure, except the twofold understanding of the New or Old Testament: namely, the historical and the spiritual?

Therefore, while heretics and heresies are springing up, “a *bilibris* of wheat for a denarius, and three *bilibres* of barley for a denarius” are proclaimed to be found in the midst of the four living creatures: because, by the common testimony of the evangelists and all preachers, a perfect and twofold understanding in both Testaments is granted to the faithful who persevere in perfect faith and dispute against the perversities of heretics, for the soundness and perfection of faith [Col. 0766B].

A *bilibris* is said to be a vessel holding two *sextarii*; in it is figured the perfection of the twofold understanding, historical and spiritual. But he set one single *bilibris* of wheat at one denarius—that is, on account of the denarius, namely, on account of the unity of the evangelical mystery—and three *bilibres* of barley because the Old Testament contains the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.

“And do not harm the wine and the oil.” The wine is the perfect teachers who sharply and sternly rebuke those who live badly. The oil is likewise the perfect teachers who sweetly and gently console the fainthearted. Thus the rider of the black horse—the devil, ruler of the heretics—is forbidden to harm the wine and the oil: that is, he must not presume to corrupt through heretical perversity the perfect teachers who rebuke evil people and console the devout [Col. 0766C].

Therefore the faithful ought not to fear either the horse or its rider, since fullness and perfection of divine wisdom are promised to them, and since the devil is forbidden to harm the more perfect persons, the supports of the whole Church.

The opening of the third seal, then, is a fuller knowledge, in the course of time, of mystical discourse. The third living creature is Matthew, or the third order of preachers in the age of heretics, preaching Christ’s humanity. The black horse is the band of heretics; the rider, the devil. The balance is discerning and equitable understanding and preaching; the voice in the midst of the four living creatures, the common testimony of evangelists and preachers [Col. 0766D]. The denarius is faith; the *bilibris* of wheat, the perfect understanding of the Gospel; the three *bilibres* of barley, the perfect knowledge of the Old Testament; the wine and oil, perfect rebukers and consolers. The prohibition against harm is the restraint of temptation.

## Chapter VII. On the Fourth Seal and Its Opening

“And when he had opened the fourth seal, I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying: Come and see. And behold, a pale horse; and he who sat upon it, his name was Death, and Hell followed him; and power was given to him over the four parts of the world, to kill by sword and famine and death and the beasts of the earth” (Rev. VI).

After the ancient enemy understood that neither the persecution of rulers [Col. 0767A] nor the perversity of heretics could advance his exercise of malice, but instead did him greater harm, because Holy Mother Church is strengthened in virtues the more she is crushed by adversities, he immediately introduced false brethren walking in hypocrisy and attempted through them to disturb her household more secretly and intimately.

This is well designated in the words mentioned above: first the red horse, then the black, and afterward the pale horse are shown in the sacred vision. For what is the pale horse but the people of hypocrites? In order to be praised for religious devotion, they grievously afflict themselves before human eyes by fasts and various hardships; their strength exhausted and their blood diminished, they grow pale as though dying. They are all the more destructive to the faithful because, veiling their malice beneath counterfeit religion, they show themselves outwardly to be good [Col. 0767B].

“And when he had opened the fourth seal” means: when, in the progress of time, as the causes foretold in sacred Scripture emerged, that which had been hidden began to be increasingly manifested. “I heard the voice of the fourth living creature saying: Come and see.” The fourth living creature was Saint John himself. Like an eagle, he understood the immortality of the highest divinity more deeply than all the others, and he prefigured the order of preachers who proclaim the eternity and immortality of the divinity.

Thus, just as Mark showed the white horse, Luke the red, and Matthew the black, for the reasons indicated above, John showed the pale horse. For that evangelist, or the order of preachers designated by him, was most fittingly heard to reveal through the pale horse the band of hypocrites and its rider, whose name is Death—that is, the devil. Through him and from him the immortal divinity was especially to be described and preached, so that their concealed malice might appear more manifest because it was revealed by an evangelist, or an order, more worthy and more opposed to them in office [Col. 0767C].

“And behold, a pale horse.” The pale horse, as has already been said, is the number of hypocrites, pale and dying from excessive affliction of the flesh. The devil sits upon it because, ruling through hypocrisy by a petty intention, he exercises his malice through them. “And he who sat upon it, his name was Death.” This name, Death, fittingly belongs to the devil, because death began through him and he never ceases to draw others to death. Hence it follows: “And Hell followed him.” Hell follows the devil because all who are to be condemned imitate him.

It follows: “And power was given to him over the four parts of the earth, to kill by sword and famine and death and the beasts of the earth.” Power is given to the devil by divine permission over the four parts of the earth—that is, over those who cling to earthly things through greed—to kill them by the sword of sin, by famine of the word of God, by death—that is, bodily weakness—and by beasts, that is, beast-like deaths. For all who serve the devil through love of earthly things receive such wages from him [Col. 0767D].

Alternatively: power is given to the devil over the four parts of the earth when he is allowed to afflict by the material sword, famine, death, and beasts the good people scattered throughout the four parts of the earth [Col. 0768A]. Yet this power works evil for the devil but good for the righteous.

The opening of the fourth seal is a fuller manifestation of the mystery. The fourth living creature is John, or the preachers of Christ’s immortal divinity. The pale horse is the band of hypocrites. The rider is the devil. Hell is those to be condemned. Power is permission to harm.

## Chapter VIII. On the Fifth Seal and Its Opening

“And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held; and they cried with a loud voice, saying: How long, Lord, holy and true, do you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth? And white robes were given to each of them, and it was said to them that they should rest yet for a little time, until their fellow servants and their brethren, who are to be killed as they also were, should be fulfilled” (Rev. VI).

By the persecutions described above, lest the minds of hearers should fail under so many foretold tribulations, divine mercy comforts the sorrowful complaint of the holy martyrs in the present chapter with the gift of the first robe and the promised greeting of their fellow servants and brethren.

“And when he had opened the fifth seal.” The opening of the fifth seal is, in the succession of time, the clearer declaration of sacred discourse: the foretold failing and the presentation of what had been promised. “I saw upon the altar of God the souls [Col. 0768C] of those slain.” The altar of God is Christ. Upon him we offer to the Father, through faith, the good things that we think, speak, or do. Thus the souls of the holy slain are rightly seen beneath God’s altar, because they submit themselves to Christ through humility and seek from the Father, through him, judgment and vengeance upon persecutors out of love for justice.

He adds the reason why they were killed, saying: “For the word of God and for the testimony which they held”—that is, because of God’s command, which they fulfilled in themselves, and the witness of faith which they preached to others. “And they cried with a loud voice,” that is, with great longing and desire, saying: “How long, Lord, holy and true?” Holy in yourself; true in your promise; holy in hating iniquity; true in fulfilling your promise [Col. 0768D].

“Do you not judge and avenge?” You judge by separating the wicked from the good; you avenge by punishing the wicked. “Our blood,” that is, our death, “upon those who dwell on the earth,” not merely by habitation but also by desire.

“And white robes were given to each of them, and it was said to them that they should rest yet for a little time.” Individual robes are now given to the saints through the glorification of the soul alone; and, through the promise of the body that is to be glorified, they are told to rest in the blessedness they have received. “Yet for a little time,” until the universal resurrection; “until their fellow servants and brethren should be fulfilled,” through the completion of the foreknown number. They are fellow servants because they have the same Lord; brethren because they have the same Father, God [Col. 0769A]. “Who are to be killed as they also were,” because all the elect attain eternal glory through endurance of present labors.

It should be noted that he says “a little time,” because the course of time is brief in comparison with the condition of eternity.

The opening of the fifth seal, then, is the clearer declaration in the page of sacred discourse of the event foretold. The altar is Christ. The souls of the slain are the spirits of martyrs. The loud voice of their cry is the desire for vengeance. The gift of robes is glorification. The rest of souls is the expectation, for a little time, of the end of mutability. The fulfillment of fellow servants and brethren is the complete and perfect reward of the predestined.

## Chapter IX. On the Sixth Seal and Its Opening

[Col. 0769B]

“And I saw, when he had opened the sixth seal, and behold, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as a sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood, and the stars fell upon the earth, as a fig tree casts its unripe figs when it is shaken by a great wind” (Rev. VI).

As the end of the vision approaches, he sees and relates the things that will occur near the end of time. In this chapter he describes the tribulation to come in the days of Antichrist and the diabolic tyranny to be restrained by Christ’s rule.

“And I saw, when he had opened the sixth seal,” that is, the hidden matter of the succeeding time. “And behold, there was a great earthquake,” that is, a great stirring of those who cherish earthly things. He fittingly adds “great,” because although the reprobate are always stirred to inflict evils upon the good, in the time of Antichrist the fury of cruelty will rage more fiercely [Col. 0769C].
