“And the sun became black as a sackcloth of hair,” because Christ, the true sun of righteousness, will be darkened, inasmuch as he will shine forth neither through miracles nor through preaching. “And the whole moon became like blood,” because Holy Church everywhere will suffer the cruelty of persecution through the shedding of blood. “And the stars fell upon the earth,” because many who seemed to be stars through the brightness of faith and heavenly manner of life will fall through unbelief and the commission of impiety.

Yet these things said here about this calamity, and many things that follow, may be understood literally. For it is written: “There shall be signs in sun and moon and stars; and upon the earth distress of nations because of the confusion caused by the roaring of the sea and waves, while men wither away for fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world. For the powers of heaven shall be shaken” (Luke XXI; Matt. XXIV) [Col. 0769D].

“As a fig tree casts its unripe figs”—that is, light and empty fruit—because God permits no one to fall who serves him with true love. “When it is shaken by a great wind,” because, through the greatness of persecution, they will fall like empty things.

It follows: “And heaven departed as a scroll rolled up; and every mountain and island was moved out of its place. And the kings of the earth, and princes, and tribunes, and the rich, and the strong, and every slave and free person hid themselves in caves and rocks of the mountains.” Heaven—that is, those who live a heavenly life—departed like a scroll rolled up because they will hide themselves, concealing both themselves and the heavenly mysteries entrusted to them. “And every mountain and island was moved out of its place,” because all who are lofty through eminence in virtues, and are shaken by the waves of persecutions, will separate themselves from the wicked in faith and work [Col. 0770A].

“The kings of the earth” are those who refuse to rule either themselves or others; “princes,” those who know how to govern; “tribunes,” those who rule tribes; “the rich,” those rich in works of virtue; “the strong,” those strong against the assaults of temptations; “every slave and free person,” either with respect to social condition or with respect to marital union or freedom. “And they hid themselves in caves and rocks of the mountains,” by imitating the hidden and firm manner of life of exalted saints.

“And they shall say to the mountains and rocks”—that is, to saints lofty and firm in faith—“Fall upon us,” through loving concern, “and hide us,” through your intercession, “from the face,” that is, from the judgment, “of him who sits upon the throne,” that is, the reigning Divinity, “and from the wrath of the Lamb,” namely Christ in his humanity [Col. 0770B].

Some of the things said may, however, be understood literally: namely, that in those days people, through fear, will hide themselves in caves and rocks and will desire to be covered by them. He adds the reason why they will desire to be hidden and covered, saying: “For the great day of their wrath has come.” Indeed, the great day of their wrath will come, when the fury of so great an enemy will rage with such cruelty.

For there will be a time such as has not been from the beginning of nations until that time. “And unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh would have been saved”: that is, unless he brought that tribulation more swiftly to an end, no one could endure it. And who will be able to stand in the faith of perseverance unless aided by the prayers of the saints? Thus, in few words, he comprehends the great and miserable tribulation to come in the time of Antichrist.

But after describing the Church’s manifold warfare, he adds that in the time of this warfare the devil stands ready to do harm, yet is restrained by God lest his own people grow faint or despair. It follows:

“After these things I saw four angels standing at the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, that they should not blow upon the earth, nor upon the sea, nor upon any tree” (Rev. VII).

These four angels are all the demons, desiring in those days to possess the whole world in its four corners. They stand, considering whom they may devour throughout the breadth of the world. The four winds are the four books of the Gospels [Col. 0770D]. These winds then blow upon the earth, the sea, and the trees when perfect teachers preach the fullness of the evangelical mystery to those who love earthly things, to those who fluctuate in the brine of the age, to evil persons raised upward like trees, and to good persons who bear fruit.

Those apostate angels will think that they hold back these winds from blowing any further upon the earth, the sea, or a tree, because they will labor to prevent the word of the sacred Gospel from being preached either to the wicked or to the good. It should be noted that it says “upon the earth,” “upon the sea,” and “in a tree,” because good is offered from above to the wicked, whereas it is already possessed inwardly by the good.

It follows:

“And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God; and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees, until we have sealed the servants of our God upon their foreheads.”

Alternatively: the angel is Christ, greatly different from the angels mentioned above. He ascends from the rising of the sun because he is the preacher and giver of the Father’s brightness. Moreover, in ascending, he showed us the pattern of striving toward heavenly goods. This angel descended through the assumption of flesh and ascended through the glorification of that same flesh. He possessed God’s seal because he displayed in himself the power of immortal divinity.

He cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it was given—that is, permitted—to harm earth and sea, because he will restrain their malice by the command of his great authority [Col. 0771A]. From the fact that, when he says “to whom it was given to harm the earth and the sea,” he is silent about the trees, it may be understood that nothing harms those perfectly good persons which adverse power is permitted to oppose against them.

“Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees”: that is, do not harm the wicked who are to be converted or the good who have been converted. Do not harm them through unrestrained temptation “until we seal the servants of our God upon their foreheads,” through the public confession of faith. “Until,” that is, up to the point when, all having been sealed, we await no one else to be sealed.

“We seal”: I inwardly, through the outpouring of spiritual grace; and my ministers outwardly, through the ministry of preaching. “We seal,” by distinction; “servants,” by subjection; “of God,” by election; “our,” because of his humanity [Col. 0771B]; “upon their foreheads,” because of the manifestness of confession. The angel’s cry, then, is the restraint of the devil.

It follows:

“And I heard the number of those sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand, sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel.”

Immediately after setting forth the restraint of the reprobate angels, he adds the sealing of the elect, extending it to the breadth of those sealed. In this sealing he comprehends all the elect together: first, by naming those sealed from every tribe of Israel, namely those who preceded the Redeemer’s Passion; then by adding the innumerable multitude from every nation, those who follow him.

But he marks those who preceded redemption itself by a number in order to show that comparatively few were saved in ancient times in comparison with those whom, after the Passion, divine wisdom alone numbers as gathered by grace. Following the order of time, he first sets forth those gathered from ancient times and then those gathered from later times.

“And I heard,” that is, I understood, who were sealed: “the number of those sealed, one hundred and forty-four thousand.” This number belongs to the ancient elect predestined for blessedness. For one hundred, which in counting passes from the left to the right, figures the heavenly blessedness to which we pass from the world. Forty, composed of four tens, fittingly signifies the Decalogue of the Law and the spiritual understanding of the Gospel contained in it. Four signifies the exercise of the four principal virtues; one thousand, the perfection of all righteousness [Col. 0772A].

Thus the ancient righteous, sealed for salvation with the sign of the cross—not in reality, indeed, but in faith—are fittingly said to be one hundred and forty-four thousand: one hundred because of promised blessedness; forty because of the fulfillment of the Decalogue and the signification of the evangelical mystery; four because of the exercise of the four principal virtues.

“From every tribe of the children of Israel”: that is, not so much those who derive their flesh from Israel as those who hold his faith. He rightly saw them sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel, because divine mercy chose some from all.

“From the tribe of Judah, ten thousand sealed.” He sets Judah’s tribe, which was fourth in birth, first in significance because of its religious character and its dignity of wisdom, and because Christ took flesh from it. Dan, from whose line Antichrist will be born, is omitted from the number of the sealed, in order to show thereby that Antichrist is cast out from the company of saints [Col. 0772B]. That he does not preserve the order of birth in describing the sealing may be referred to the arrangement of spiritual dignity and merits. From each tribe he sets forth twelve thousand sealed: twelve because of the prerogative of the twelve patriarchs; thousands because of perfect righteousness; sealed because of true confession of faith.

“From the tribe of Judah, ten thousand sealed.” Judah is interpreted “confessing.” One confession is of sin; another, of praise. These are those who washed themselves from sin through confession and rendered thanksgiving in praise for benefits received.

“From the tribe of Reuben, ten thousand sealed.” Reuben is interpreted “seeing the son.” These are those who brought forth the fruit of good work and through it came to the contemplation of the Son of the highest Father.

“From the tribe of Gad, ten thousand sealed.” Gad is interpreted “girded.” These are those always prepared and ready against temptation.

“From the tribe of Asher, ten thousand sealed.” Asher is interpreted “blessed.” These are those who arrive at blessedness through the tribulation of present misery [Col. 0772C].

“From the tribe of Naphtali, ten thousand sealed.” Naphtali is interpreted “breadth.” These are those who, through the affection of charity, bestowed works of mercy upon their neighbors.

“From the tribe of Manasseh, ten thousand sealed.” Manasseh is interpreted “forgetful.” These are those who, through forgetfulness of temporal things, arrived at the reward of heavenly things.

“From the tribe of Simeon, ten thousand sealed.” Simeon is interpreted “hearing of sorrow.” These are those who through present sorrow attained true joy.

“From the tribe of Levi, ten thousand sealed.” Levi is interpreted “added.” These are those who added good things to better things and thereby received an addition of heavenly good.

“From the tribe of Issachar, ten thousand sealed.” Issachar is interpreted “reward.” These are those who rejected the reward of human praise and thereby received the reward of divine recompense.

“From the tribe of Zebulun, ten thousand sealed.” Zebulun is interpreted “dwelling of strength.” These are those who through their manner of life arrived at the heavenly dwelling.

“From the tribe of Joseph, ten thousand sealed.” Joseph is interpreted “increase.” These are those who through increase [Col. 0773A] in righteousness arrived at the fullness of glory.

“From the tribe of Benjamin, ten thousand sealed.” Benjamin is interpreted “son of the right hand.” These are those who walked in the ways on the right, which the Lord knows, and thereby deserved to be placed at the Judge’s right hand.

Dearest brother, we touch briefly upon a few things out of many, and leave many matters in all these things for your discernment to examine, passing them over for the sake of brevity. It follows:

After this I saw a great multitude, which no one could number, from every nation and tribe and people and language, standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands. Above he set forth the righteous who went before in Christ’s Passion; now he adds those who, in the time of grace, received the sign of faith. [Col. 0773B] He does not state their number in order openly to signify that human understanding cannot comprehend it. Thus he aptly says: “After this I saw a great multitude, which no one could number,” except, of course, him alone who also numbers the sands of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age.

“From every nation,” which above he designated by the name “nation,” “and tribes, and peoples, and languages”: these matters have been explained above. A tribe is so called from the three orders in which are the seventy languages; within a language are diverse peoples, and within a people are diverse nations. From every nation, even barbarian ones, tribes, and peoples: for divine mercy, like a dragnet gathering every kind of fish, chooses from every kind of human being and leads them to [Col. 0773C] life.

“Standing,” because they are ready to obey the divine commands; “before the throne,” that is, before the royal dignity of the divine majesty; “in the sight of the Lamb,” Christ the man; “clothed in white robes,” through purity of body; “and palms in their hands,” through victory over their enemies. “And they cried with a loud voice,” that is, with great devotion, saying: “Salvation to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb.” It is as though he said: Let our salvation not be attributed to ourselves, because it is not from us; rather, let it be attributed to him from whom it comes—namely, our God, who sits upon the throne, to the reigning divinity, and to Christ the Lamb as man. Alternatively: Let the salvation which divinity possesses by nature and humanity by grace be sung to divinity and humanity by rational creation. It follows:

[Col. 0773D] “And all the angels stood around the throne, and the elders, and the four living creatures; and they fell before the throne upon their faces, and worshipped him, saying: Amen.” He introduces the angels as rejoicing over the salvation of human beings and confirming the testimony of human confession. “And all the angels stood,” because they were ready to obey; “around the throne,” carrying out the ministry of the command on every side; “and [around] the elders and the four living creatures,” strengthening ecclesiastical men everywhere. “And they fell before the throne upon their faces,” humbling themselves; “and they worshipped God,” exalting him; “saying: Amen,” confirming the testimony of praise offered to God by human beings and likewise praising God with them.

Hence it is fittingly added: “Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honour, and [Col. 0774A] power, and strength be to our God for ever and ever. Amen.” It is as though they said: Everything which he has by the nature of divinity ought to be rendered to him in a song of praise. “Blessing,” because he is blessed uniquely and supremely; “glory,” because he is glorious; “wisdom,” because he is wise; “thanksgiving,” because he is to be praised for benefits bestowed; “honour,” because he is to be honoured; “power,” because he is invincible; “strength,” because he is strong, for ever and ever, without end. “Amen,” that is, truly. These seven are fittingly referred to the praise of the Creator, because the seven gifts of spiritual grace, which he distributes to those who are to be saved, are seven.

“And one of the elders answered and said to me: Who are these clothed in white robes, and from where have they come? And I said: My lord, you know.” At the sight of the multitude in the dignity of such great glory, he is instructed [Col. 0774B] to consider by what path it could have ascended to that glory, so that he in turn may teach others to look toward it and strive to attain the same glory. The one elder is the whole body of prophets, apostles, and teachers preaching the righteousness and glory of the elect. “These who are clothed in white robes”: in bodies and works made clean. “Who are they?” that is, of what dignity are they? “And from where have they come?” that is, from what furnace of tribulation?

“And I said to him: My lord, you know,” as though he said: I do not know, but teach me. And while he humbly confesses his ignorance of both things, he is taught by the angel concerning each of them, just as we too are taught by the whole body of teachers. For it follows: “And he said to me: These are those who have come out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes [Col. 0774C] and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.”

The order of the meanings is this: they “washed their robes” in baptism; they “made them white” by living well; and they did both in the blood of the Lamb, through faith in Christ’s Passion. Thus at last they came out of tribulation, out of endurance of present sufferings, because by grace bestowed they deserved to be washed in baptism, made white by good living, and to suffer adversities for Christ’s faith. “They are before the throne of God,” that is, before the reigning Divinity, “and serve him” by singing his praise, “day and night,” that is, continually, “in his temple,” in the assembly of the saints.

Their dignity is further declared when it is added: “And he who sits upon the throne,” that is, God who reigns, “shall dwell over them,” because he mercifully protects and governs them for ever, so that he may impart to them the good which he himself possesses invisibly [Col. 0774D] and in manifold ways. Their blessedness too is described more fully in what follows, showing them free from evil and filled with good: “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more,” because they will be refreshed by the bread and fountain of life. “Neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat,” because they will be protected from greater and lesser tribulation. “For the Lamb, who is in the midst of the throne,” that is, in the midst of the angels in whom God dwells and through whom he executes his judgments, “will rule them,” namely on the way, “and will lead them to springs of the waters of life,” in their homeland.

And because they will be free from every evil, so too they will be without every pain of evil. Hence it is added: “And God shall wipe every tear from their eyes.” God will wipe them away, because, as he will make them free from every evil, so he will make them immune from all pain. Thus, the opening of the sixth seal is the completion of the mystical utterance: the persecution of Antichrist, the movement and shaking of things, the persecution by wicked angels; the restraining of those who do harm, the checking of diabolical temptation; the angel, Christ; those sealed, the elect; the one hundred and forty-four thousand from every tribe of the children of Israel, the elect who precede in redemption; the great multitude, the elect who follow them; the harmony of the angels, their joy and thanksgiving for human salvation; the one elder, the whole body of teachers; the washing and whitening of robes, purity of bodies and works; the blood of the Lamb, Christ’s Passion; the removal of evil, escape from present misery; the bestowal of good, heavenly blessedness.

## CHAPTER X. On the seventh seal and its opening

[Col. 0775B]

“And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. VIII). At the end of the vision he describes those things which will occur at the end of time. “And when he had opened the seventh seal,” that is, when, by the final stage of the present age, he began to show in the sacred vision that the mystery of human redemption was now being completed, “there was silence in heaven,” that is, in the holy Church: a great [Col. 0776A] tranquillity prepared on every side. But the silence is said to take place “for about half an hour,” because judgment will come quickly.

Thus, the opening of the seventh seal is the manifestation of the sacred utterance concerning the things that will happen near the end of the age; the silence for about half an hour is the final peace and tranquillity.

To recall briefly and plainly at the end all that is contained in this vision: in the first chapter the author treated of him who sits upon the throne and his adornment; in the second, of the four living creatures; in the third, of the sealed book which he who sat upon the throne held in his right hand, and of the Lamb who opened the book; in the fourth, of the first-fruits, the reborn, and those who rise to life through grace; in the fifth, of impious persecutors; in the sixth, of heretics; in the seventh, of hypocrites; in the eighth, of the complaints of the martyrs and [Col. 0776B] the individual robes given to them; in the ninth, of the persecution of Antichrist; in the tenth, of the peace and tranquillity of a short time which will come to them after Antichrist at the end of the world; and throughout all these matters, of the testing of the righteous, their preparation for heavenly glory, and the depth of heavenly mysteries contained in the second vision of this book. We have drawn a few drops, but now we rest by laying down the pen, so that we may rise more eagerly to examine the third vision.

# BOOK III. ON THE THIRD VISION

[Col. 0775]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0775C]

God, whose power is great and whose wisdom is without number; who by his power created all things, by his wisdom ordered what he created, multiplies what he has ordered, governs what he has multiplied; who in his ineffable goodness foretells future things to his elect and plainly shows what must be done, what avoided, what endured, and what hoped for, so that he may teach them perfectly in every particular and, by teaching, forearm them for all things. Therefore, in this vision the order of narration is arranged according to the extent of time, so that everywhere the outcome of each cause may be distinguished, and the universal mother Church, instructed by sacred prophecy, may suffer no loss in those predestined to eternal life.

[Col. 0775D] This vision, under the distinction of seven angels sounding trumpets, describes the whole body of preachers, the storms of persecutions, and the recompense of rewards. It begins its narrative from the origin of the Church being reborn; describing by symbols and figures the changes of affairs according to the alternations of successive periods, it leads the Church up to the end of time. There, after many endured labours, it adds the rewards of the righteous. We shall distinguish all these matters in their places and arrange them in exposition as the order requires.

## CHAPTER I. On the seven angels sounding trumpets, and on the other angel standing before the altar

[Col. 0776C]

“And I saw seven angels standing in the presence of God, and seven trumpets were given to them” (Rev. VIII). The seven angels standing in the presence of God are all preachers throughout all time, which revolves according to the number of seven days, preaching the word of God through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit. They are called angels because they are sent by God; they stand in God’s presence because they are ready for divine service. Seven trumpets are given to them because the universal office of divine preaching is entrusted to them, so that they may sound for the strengthening of the elect and the destruction of the reprobate.

“And another [Col. 0776D] angel came and stood before the altar, having a golden censer in his hand.” The other angel is Christ, because he is the Angel of Great Counsel. He is fittingly called “other,” because he is far removed from the other angels—that is, from all preachers—in grace of holiness, excellence of dignity, and power of might. He came when he assumed the frailty of our nature. “And he stood before the altar.” Of this altar it is written typologically: “You shall make an altar of earth for me” (Exod. XVII). The altar of earth is the assumed humanity. But as coming pertains to the assumption of flesh, so standing pertains to the unchangeableness of divinity. Therefore, he who came in the flesh stood before the altar in his divinity, because in the divinity in which he remained [Col. 0777A] unchangeable, he was prior and higher than the humanity which is an altar for us.

“Having a golden censer in his hand.” The censer is the holy apostles, who were principally appointed in the holy Church to offer to the supreme Divinity the prayers of the elect. They are fittingly golden and possess the brightness of gold because they contain divine wisdom within themselves and, through it, shine upon all in the world. The angel had this censer in his hand when Christ chose the twelve apostles. It follows:

“And much incense was given to him,” that is, pleasing prayers, “that he might give,” that is, present to the Father, “from the prayers of the saints upon the golden altar,” that is, upon himself. For he himself is the altar, because upon him are offered to the Father all the vows of human [Col. 0777B] righteousness. It is golden because in him are all the hidden treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Therefore incense is given to him alone to offer, because all the prayers of the saints are commended to the Father through him. The altar is also rightly said to be golden in the sight of God, because the Father testified concerning him that he was well pleased in him. “And the smoke of the incense from the prayers of the saints ascended before God from the hand of the angel,” because that prayer alone is accepted in heaven which the Son offers to the Father. It follows:

“And the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and cast it upon the earth.” The angel took the censer which he was said above to have, and filled it with fire from the altar, when Christ, after the mystery of human redemption was completed, established the apostles in faith and gave them first-fruits of the same Spirit with which he himself was filled. He also cast the filled censer upon the earth when he sent them into the world to preach. But what followed the mission of the apostles is declared when it is added: “And there were thunders, and voices, and lightnings, and a great earthquake.”

For when the apostles preached, there were thunders, [Col. 0777C] that is, threats of severe condemnation; and voices, that is, moderate admonitions. It is fitting that after thunders he added voices, because those whom we terrify by threats we ought to soothe by promises, so that terror may break them from evil and promise may establish them in seeking the good. But because, among unbelievers, neither the terrors of threats nor persuasive words prevail without testimonies of miracles, he fittingly adds: “and lightnings.” Lightnings signify miracles flashing far and wide.

And because, after the thunders of threats and the voices of admonition had sounded over all the earth, and the lightnings of miracles had flashed over the world, many were changed from what they had been, he fittingly adds: “and an earthquake.” For after thunders, voices, and lightnings an earthquake occurred, because, as the apostles preached and worked miracles, many earthly persons—dwelling upon the earth and loving earthly things—were moved: some toward good by conversion, others toward evil by turning away. Some were moved to believe, others to persecute. It is also fitting that after he had said “earthquake” he added “great,” because, as grace bestowed, many were called by Christ [Col. 0777D] to faith, and, as guilt demanded, many, prompted by the devil, were stirred up to persecute the faith. It follows:

“And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound the trumpets.” After touching briefly above upon certain matters pertaining to the mysteries of our redemption concerning the Angel of Great Counsel, that is, Christ, and after describing typologically the apostolic mission through the censer cast upon the earth, he returns his discourse to the seven angels—that is, to the whole assembly of preachers—with whom he began and of whom he will treat in what follows. They prepare themselves to sound the trumpet because they first practise what they will afterwards preach, or because they first carefully consider what they ought to preach and to whom. Great indeed is the office of preaching; therefore those who must exercise it need both to be strengthened by the power of holiness and to employ the balance of discernment.

Thus the seven angels are all preachers; the other angel, Christ; the censer, the number twelve of the apostles; the smoke of the aromatics, the devotions of prayers; the golden altar, the assumed body; filling the censer with fire from the altar, the first-fruits of the Spirit given to the disciples; casting the censer upon the earth, sending the apostles to preach grace to earth-dwellers; thunders, threats; voices, admonitions; lightnings, the splendour of miracles; the great earthquake, the conversion and turning away of human beings; the angels’ preparation to sound, the good conduct of preachers and their prudent discernment in preaching.

## CHAPTER II. On the first angel and his trumpet

[Col. 0778C]

“And the first angel sounded the trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood came to pass, and it was cast upon the earth; and a third part of the earth was burned up, and a third part of the trees was burned up, and all green grass was burned up” (Rev. VIII). The first angel is the first order of preachers; the first trumpet, the first preaching. Therefore the first angel sounded the trumpet when, in the New Testament, the first order of preachers sounded forth the Gospel in Judaea. But what followed that preaching is declared when it is added: “And hail and fire mixed with blood came to pass.” Hail signifies the outward scourge of persecution; fire, the inward flame of burning perverse jealousy; blood, the cruelty [Col. 0778D] of slaughter.

Therefore, when the first angel sounded the trumpet, hail and fire mixed with blood came to pass, because, when the first order of preachers was preaching in Judaea at the beginning of the New Testament, the Jewish people burned fiercely in persecution, even to the shedding of blood. “And it was cast upon the earth,” that is, upon those who dwell on the earth. But because the violence of persecution harms not the good but the evil, it is fittingly added: “And a third part of the earth was burned up, and a third part of the trees was burned up, and all green grass was burned up.”

Two portions of humanity belong to God: namely, the active and the contemplative; the imperfect and the perfect; the lesser and the greater. God takes these two portions to himself, because he blessed the little ones together with the great. [Col. 0779A] The third portion, which is that of the evil, is left to the devil. When hail and fire mixed with blood came, while the two portions belonging to God remained unharmed, it was burned up, because, while the order of preachers preached and persecution raged, it was utterly deprived of the good.

The earth signifies human beings, because they too ought, after the likeness of the earth, to bear fruit through virtues and good works. Trees signify human beings because, like trees, they should raise themselves upward by desire for heavenly good. Green grass signifies human beings because, like green grass, they should always remain verdant through the virtue of perseverance. But a third part of the trees and the earth is said to be burned up so that, while the two portions which, as stated, belong to God remain unharmed by evil, that portion may be signified as cast down, withered, and barren of true good. All the grass, however, is burned up because whoever possesses only the greenness of cruelty and lacks the fruit of virtues and good works is easily consumed by the fire of evil when temptation or persecution comes.

Yet good and evil human beings are rightly comprehended under the signification of three things—earth, trees, and grass—on account of the type of three kinds of good or evil: thoughts, words, and deeds. All these are good in the good and evil in the evil. Thus human beings, whether good or evil, are not inappropriately described under the signification of three things, because they are also distinguished by a threefold quality. Many things can indeed be said concerning such interpretations; but matters which we cannot include within the present brevity [Col. 0779C] we reserve for your prudence to seek out and examine, as an exercise for your understanding. For you ought not to remain dull, resting only in what we say; rather, stretch yourself forward, moderate yourself, reach what is more remote, and comprehend what is greater.

Thus the first angel is the first order of preachers preaching in Judaea in the New Testament; the first trumpet, the first preaching; hail and fire mixed with blood, jealous persecution raging against believers; the burning of the third part of the earth and trees and of all green grass, the rejection of those to be condemned; the preservation of the two portions of earth and trees, the reception of those to be saved. These saved are said to be two portions because those to be saved are comprehended under the distinction between imperfection and [Col. 0779D] perfection.

## CHAPTER III. On the second angel and his trumpet

“And the second angel sounded the trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea; and a third part of the sea became blood, and a third part of the creatures having souls in the sea died, and a third part of the ships perished” (Rev. VIII). When believers from Judaea had been gathered to the faith through preaching, the second preaching immediately sounded among the Gentiles, who are denoted by the name of the sea, and called from them those who were to be saved. But the devil, who had grieved that some Jews had been taken away from him by the first preaching and therefore had stirred up persecution in Judaea, as soon as he saw the preaching transferred to the Gentiles, immediately stirred up persecution among the Gentiles to hinder it.

Thus it says: “And the second angel sounded the trumpet,” that is, the voice of preachers, leaving the Jews behind, sounded among the Gentiles. “And a great mountain,” that is, the devil—mountain through pride, great through the greatness of his pride, burning with fire through envy—“was cast into the sea,” that is, among the Gentiles, by divine permission. The Gentiles are aptly compared to the sea because they tossed about amid the worship of diverse idols and the bitterness of many vices. Two portions of this sea belong to God; the third to the devil, as we showed in the preceding chapter concerning the earth and trees.

When the second angel sounded the trumpet and the mountain, as it were, was cast into the sea, a third part of the sea became blood, because, after Judaea was left behind and the voice of preaching sounded among the Gentiles, a portion of the Gentiles, stirred by the devil, abandoned God and, through the torment of condemnation, turned to the cruelty of persecution. A third part also of the creatures having souls in the sea died, and a third part of the ships perished, because the portion destined for condemnation—even among those who seemed more rational and more worthy, and among those who were carriers and supporters of others—having previously died through sin, then, by rejecting the faith and remaining in unbelief, perished, assigned to eternal death.

Thus the second angel with his trumpet signifies the preachers among the Gentiles, with preaching transferred from Judaism to the Gentiles; the great mountain cast into the sea, the devil raging in stirring up the Gentile world; the two portions of the sea-dwellers having souls and of the ships, those to be saved; the third portion, those to be condemned; blood, the cruelty [Col. 0780C] of persecution; the death of those having souls and the destruction of the ships, the manifest rejection of certain persons thought more rational, and of those who were carriers and supporters of others.

## CHAPTER IV. On the third angel and his trumpet

“And the third angel sounded the trumpet, and a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven; and it fell upon a third part of the rivers and upon the springs of waters; and the name of the star is called wormwood; and a third part of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the waters because they had become bitter” (Rev. VIII).

Many matters are contained in this third vision, which are most fittingly arranged according to what was said in the second vision. For where sacred prophecy says, “Another red horse went forth,” it treats of persecutors under the opening of the second seal. Here, when it says in the preceding chapter, “A third part of the sea became blood,” it treats of persecutors under the trumpet of the second angel. There, where it said, “Behold, a black horse,” it treated of heretics under the opening of the third seal. Here, where it says, “A star fell from heaven,” it treats of heretics under the trumpet of the third angel. There, where it said, “Behold, a pale horse,” it treated of hypocrites under the opening of the fourth seal. Here, where it says, “A third part of the sun was struck,” it treats of hypocrites under the trumpet of the fourth angel. There, where it said, “There was a great earthquake,” it treated of the persecution of Antichrist under the opening of the sixth seal. Here, where it says, “Release the four angels [Col. 0781A] who are bound at the great river Euphrates,” it treats of the persecution of Antichrist under the trumpet of the sixth angel. There, where it said, “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour,” it treated of the end of the world under the opening of the seventh seal. Here, where it says, “The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ,” it treats of the end of the world under the trumpet of the seventh angel.

Thus the second seal agrees with the second angel, the third with the third, the fourth with the fourth, the fifth with the fifth, the sixth with the sixth, and the seventh with the seventh: the seal with the angel and the opening of the seal with the angel’s trumpet. Yet each treats of the same matters under different figures, in order more greatly to exercise the reader and to show that the devil wishes to hinder the office of preaching in this respect by the same means as in the fulfilment of the divine promise. We have said these things concerning the harmony of the preceding and present vision. Now let us return to the chapter before us.

“And the third angel sounded the trumpet,” that is, the third order of preachers preached; “and a star fell from heaven,” that is, a company of heretics fell from the Church. It is aptly called a great burning star: a star because of knowledge received, great because of pride, burning because of envy; “like a torch,” because while it sets others ablaze in perversity, it consumes itself. “And it fell upon a third part of the rivers and upon the springs of waters.” By rivers and springs, divine Scripture is signified, by drinking from which the human mind, thirsty for true good, is refreshed. The springs of waters are those books in which the source and sum of faith are contained, such as the books of the Law, the prophets, [Col. 0781C] the evangelists, and the apostles. The rivers are those things drawn from them, such as the expositions of teachers.

There are two portions of Scripture: namely, the historical and the spiritual understanding, which, when rightly understood, pertain to the good. The third portion is the perverse understanding of the perverse, which pertains to the evil. Therefore, the star falling from heaven fell upon a third part of the rivers and springs of waters, because heretical perversity, falling from the height of the Church, corrupted sacred Scripture in the part that supported its own assertion. “And the name of the star is called wormwood.” The name of the star—that is, of the heretical trumpet—is called wormwood because whoever is seduced by heretical perversity is led into the bitterness of perverse understanding and spiritual death. Hence it fittingly says: “And a third part of the waters became wormwood, and many people died from the waters because they became bitter.”

For when the star falls upon the waters, the waters are made bitter and those who drink die; because when heretics abandon the highest things and teach sacred Scripture on their own authority, Scripture is corrupted in their teaching, and those consenting to their perversity are killed by spiritual death. Therefore two portions remain for God, while the corrupted third is left to the devil. Since he could not altogether hinder divine preaching outwardly through persecution, he attempted to accomplish it inwardly through heretics.

Thus the third angel is the third order of preachers; the falling star, the heretic falling away from the true faith; water, Scripture; the corruption of the third portion, perversity of assertion; [Col. 0782A] the death of those who drink, the impiety of those who consent.

## CHAPTER V. On the fourth angel and his trumpet

“And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, and a third part of the sun was struck, and a third part of the moon, and a third part of the stars, so that a third part of them was darkened, and a third part of the day did not shine, and likewise of the night” (Rev. VIII). Seeing that the ancient enemy could not hinder preaching as he wished either through the persecution of unbelievers or through the perversity of heretics, he adds the pretence of hypocrites.

“And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet,” that is, the fourth order of preachers preached. “And a third part of the sun was struck,” that is, human understanding in hypocrites—who are the third portion, set on the left hand in relation to the perfect and imperfect righteous—[Col. 0782B] was darkened. “And a third part of the moon,” that is, their righteousness, which ought to increase through growth; “and a third part of the stars,” that is, their virtues, which ought to shine in many ways, “so that a third part of them might be darkened,” that is, all brightness in the conduct of hypocrites.

For two portions of spiritual good are reserved unharmed for the perfect righteous. But the third is destroyed in the reprobate, so that “a third part did not shine, and likewise of the night.” Here “day” denotes those among hypocrites who seem brighter in knowledge or life; “night,” those who appear less bright in both respects. Thus it is fittingly said that a third part of the sun, moon, and stars was darkened and that day and night did not shine, because the good of understanding, righteousness, and virtue is utterly clouded both in the higher and in the lower persons among hypocrites.

It follows:

“And I saw and heard the voice of one eagle flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a loud voice: Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell upon the earth! Because of the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet.” The eagle, which flies upward toward the sun with eyes reflecting its light, signifies the whole body of divine writers and preachers, who search the heavenly mysteries more subtly and contemplate them more loftily and clearly than other believers. They are fittingly called one eagle because their harmony is great in contemplating and preaching sacred Scripture. They fly through the midst of heaven and cry with a loud voice as often as they authoritatively [Col. 0782D] preach what is right in the common hearing of the whole Church: “Woe, woe to those who dwell upon the earth! Because of the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet.”

It is as though he said: The evils contained above are grave, but those which follow are far more grave. The threefold “woe” threatened to earth-dwellers because of the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet signifies the three most grievous tribulations that would come in the times of the three orders of preachers who were yet to preach. Thus the tribulations preceding under the trumpets of the four foregoing angels are grave, but those that follow under the trumpets of the next three are far more grievous.

By “those who dwell upon [Col. 0783A] the earth” he means those who love earthly things and prefer them to heavenly things; tribulations turn to evil for them, whereas they cooperate for good with the good. Thus the fourth angel is the fourth order of preachers; the third part of the sun, moon, stars, day, and night, the brightness of understanding, righteousness, and virtues darkened in both the higher and lower ranks of hypocrites; the eagle flying through the midst of heaven, the whole body of preachers preaching in the Church; the three following woes under the voices of the succeeding angels, tribulations to come in the times of the following preachers.

## CHAPTER VI. On the fifth angel and his trumpet
And the fifth angel sounded the trumpet. And I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth. And the key of the pit of the abyss was given to him; and he opened the pit of the abyss, and smoke rose from the pit like the smoke of a great furnace. And the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit, and locusts came out upon the earth (Rev. VIII).

After the devil saw that, through each evil separately—the cruelty of persecutors, the perversity of heretics, and the pretence of hypocrites—he could not hinder sacred preaching, he introduced every kind of evil, as will be shown below; and what he had been unable to accomplish severally, he attempted to accomplish by all together.

“And the fifth angel sounded the trumpet,” that is, the fifth order of preachers preached. “And I saw a star fallen from heaven to earth,” that is, I saw that the devil, who is called Lucifer [Col. 0783C], who fell from heaven, received dominion over earthly things and those who love earthly things. “And the key of the pit of the abyss was given to him,” that is, power over profound and hidden evil was granted to him. He opened the pit of the abyss when he brought forth and disclosed, from the hearts of all evil beings together, profound and hidden malice for doing harm.

Moreover, smoke from the pit rose like the smoke of a great furnace, because the perversity of demons and human beings, once opened, bursting forth, and released all at once, strove to reach the injury of the good who are set on high. Hence it fittingly adds: “And the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit.” The sun and the air are darkened by the smoke of the pit, because both some of those who seemed to enlighten others and some of those who are enlightened are blinded by the suggestion and teaching of demons and [Col. 0783D] perverse human beings.

And because the evil not only harm the good, so that they are darkened, but also hinder the evil from being enlightened, it rightly follows: “And locusts came out upon the earth.” For what is signified by locusts except the entire multitude of the wicked? Like locusts, they leap upward through pride and fall back to earth through covetousness. What is signified by the earth except those who love earthly things and cling to them through covetousness? Therefore locusts come out upon the earth when all the proud receive power over those who place earthly things before heavenly ones.

The character of this power is declared when it adds: “And power was given to them, as the scorpions of the earth have power.” A scorpion appears gentle in its face but harms with its tail. Thus the entire host of the perverse strives, by hidden malice, to accomplish what it cannot accomplish [Col. 0784A] through open cruelty. And because the hidden malice of the wicked in doing harm is restrained by God and is not permitted truly to injure the good in any respect, it fittingly follows: “And it was commanded them that they should not harm the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree, except only those people who do not have the sign of the living God upon their foreheads.”

Grass signifies the inexperienced, foolish, and readily bent toward deception. Green things signify persons possessing the freshness of true faith and awaiting, through hope of the eternity above, everlasting freshness. A tree signifies those who bring forth the fruit of good work through faith and hope. Thus the wicked are forbidden to harm all the truly elect—the beginners, the more advanced, and the perfect—because they are restrained, by a hidden divine ordering, from every injury. “Except only people who do not have the sign of the living God,” understood: truly, “upon their foreheads,” that is, openly. For many pretend in words that they have the sign of the living God, though by deeds they deny him. The wicked are by no means restrained from harming such people, because such persons are subjected to the voluntary power of the wicked.

But because neither heretics, who do the greatest harm, nor any crowd of other wicked people is permitted to injure at will even those who are fastened to the earth by love of earthly things and designated by the name “earth,” it rightly adds: “And it was commanded them not to kill them, but that they should torment them for five months.” Heretics and the devil’s chief ministers are commanded not only not to harm the truly good, but not even to kill those devoted to earthly things [Col. 0784C], because they are restrained from taking away their freedom to hear the word of God or to receive the true faith. They are given leave for such people to be tormented by them for five months, because those who cling to transitory things through the five bodily senses are sometimes permitted to be afflicted by the reprobate through the removal of the earthly things they love, so that, when afflicted, they may at some time come to realize that they loved these things, and, at last instructed by adversities, rise to seek true goods. It follows:

“And their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person.” This is what was said above: what the wicked cannot achieve through manifest malice and cruelty, they strive to accomplish through hidden malice. “And in those days”—that is, in the time of such great malignity, when some rise up to harm through [Col. 0784D] heresy, others through hypocrisy, others through persecution, and still others through vices of many kinds, while the devil opens the whole pit of iniquity and pours out all his strength to hinder the elect—in those days, I say, people, and especially pastors, will seek death, fearing a fall, and will not find it, because they will be preserved for the need of those subject to them.

Nor will they seek death in merely any fashion because of the impending and pressing adversity, but with great desire. Hence it fittingly adds: “And they will desire to die.” Yet though they desire to die, their desire will by no means be granted. Therefore it rightly adds: “And death will flee from them,” alone, because of the need of the flock subject to them. It follows:

[Col. 0785A] “And the likenesses of the locusts were like horses prepared for battle, and upon their heads were, as it were, crowns resembling gold.” Above he described the opening of the pit of the abyss—that is, the outpouring of all evil—the power of the wicked to harm, and the divine restraint; now he shows their manifold malice through various figures and comparisons. The likenesses of the locusts are rightly said to be like horses prepared for battle, because all wicked persons, in likeness to horses, pursue the elect in persecution swiftly, fiercely, and recklessly, and rush forward without foresight.

Upon their heads are, as it were, crowns, because they possess not true but false rewards for a perverse victory. These crowns are not gold but merely like gold, because the wisdom of this world—which belongs to fools—is foolishness [Col. 0785B] before God. He further describes their deceit and cruelty, saying: “And their faces were like the faces of men; and they had hair like women’s hair; and their teeth were like lions’ teeth.” He sets out three things: human faces, women’s hair, and lions’ teeth. These three things are said to belong, in the stated order, to the wicked, and especially to heretics: first, they pretend to do everything according to reason; then they deceitfully draw people into the softness of vices; finally, through the suggestion and commission of evil action, they cruelly tear them to pieces.

But while they attempt to attack the people of the elect, they themselves arm themselves on every side with their falsehoods, lest they be overcome by truth in any way. Hence it fittingly adds: “And they had breastplates like iron breastplates.” For the wicked have breastplates against truth through the fortification of false opinions; they are iron through the obstinacy of their hardness. The sound and tumult of these opinions are plainly declared when it adds: “And the sound of their wings was like the sound of the wheels of many chariots and horses running to battle.” Wings are opinions; the sound of the wings is the tumult of opinions. False opinions are breastplates for the wicked, and especially for heretics. For these opinions are both wings and breastplates: breastplates, because they fortify them against the good; wings, because they carry them toward worse things. Therefore the reprobate have wings whose sound is like the sound of chariots and horses running to battle, because, as different chariots are carried by different horses along different roads to the same battle, so the wicked are borne unanimously to the same battle—to attack the Church—by diverse heresies and the tumults [Col. 0785D] of disputes. It follows:

“And they had tails like scorpions, and there were stings in their tails. Their power was to harm people for five months.” All this has been expounded above, except for the statement that there were stings in their tails. The locusts have stings in their tails because at the end of the perverse persons’ suggestion comes the bite and piercing of sin.

“And they had over them a king, the angel of the abyss, whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon, in Greek Apollyon, and in Latin he has the name Exterminator.” The angel of the abyss is the devil, king and prince over the depth and darkness of all [Col. 0786A] sin. He is described in three languages so that the holy Church, spread throughout the earth, may be taught, whatever language it uses, to beware of the devil’s wiles in his deceitful satellites. The devil is called “Exterminator” because both by himself and through his own agents he strives to drive every one of the elect beyond the boundary of spiritual life.

It follows: “One woe has passed; behold, two more woes are yet coming.” One woe is the tribulation contained under the trumpet of the fifth angel. The two remaining woes follow under the trumpets of the sixth and seventh angels. Thus the fifth angel is the fifth order of preachers; the star fallen from heaven is the devil; the opening of the pit of the abyss is the outpouring of sin; the darkening of the sun and air is the injury of those above and below; the locusts are the wicked, especially heretics; the prohibition of injury is the restraint of temptation; the multiple likenesses of the locusts are the various perversities of the wicked; and the departure of one woe is the cessation of one tribulation.

## CHAPTER VII. On the sixth angel and his trumpet

“And the sixth angel sounded the trumpet, and I heard one voice from the four horns of the golden altar which is before the eyes of the Lord, saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet: Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates” (Rev. IX).

After carefully describing in the preceding chapter the opening of the pit of the abyss—that is, the universality of evil by which the holy Church is attacked—before the coming of Antichrist, he next treats in this chapter of the persecution to come under Antichrist. The immutability [Col. 0786C] of eternity is also foretold for the consolation of the elect. Finally, in this same chapter he treats of Elijah and Enoch, of their preaching and death, and of their resurrection and glorification.

“And the sixth angel sounded the trumpet,” that is, the sixth order of teachers preached concerning the time of Antichrist. “And I heard one voice,” that is, the harmony of universal teaching, “from the four horns of the golden altar,” that is, from all the preachers of Christ, who uphold and bear him by preaching the four Gospels through the four parts of the world. This altar is called golden: an altar, because upon it is offered the burnt offering of human righteousness; golden, because in Christ dwells the splendour of divine wisdom. It is also fittingly said to be before the eyes of the Lord, because the Father is well pleased in the Son, “saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet,” that is, to those [Col. 0786D] who, when the moment of that persecution is at hand, will administer ecclesiastical teaching.

For all writers and preachers of sacred learning foretell those days, and especially strive to fortify the elect preachers, who must strengthen others, against its cruelty. “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.” The four angels are all the demons raging through the four parts of the world in the days of Antichrist and stirring all the reprobate to persecute the elect. They are commanded then to be released by the elect preachers, because their release—or their having been released—will be preached by them as a warning to the good.

These are the four angels who, in the preceding vision, are read to have been forbidden to harm the earth, the sea, and [Col. 0787A] the trees. They are now bound at the great river Euphrates because they are restrained through baptism from raging against the human race at their pleasure. Then, finally, they will be released, because they will be permitted to be more unrestrained against those who bear the Christian name. Hence it follows:

“And the four angels were released, who were prepared for the hour, and day, and month, and year, to kill a third part of humankind.” The demons will then be prepared for hour, day, month, and year—that is, for every uninterrupted moment of that persecution—to kill the third part of humankind, that is, all those who are reserved for the torment of damnation.

He also fittingly states the number of the reprobate angels for the clarity of spiritual understanding, saying: “And the number of the cavalry army was twice ten thousand times ten thousand; I heard their number.” The devil is prince of all evil; his soldiers are demons, and the horses of the soldiers are perverse human beings. The number of this army is said to be twice ten thousand times ten thousand, so that it may be made clearer than light that twenty thousand fight against the saints of the New Testament, who observe certain commandments of the Law both according to the letter and according to spiritual understanding, while ten thousand fight against the ancient righteous, who simply observed the Law according to the letter, since it was then a figure of things to come. For in twenty is figured a twofold observance of the Law; in a thousand, perfect righteousness; and in ten, a simple observance of the Law. Such a number is therefore fittingly assigned to the reprobate angels, so that those against whom [Col. 0787C] they wage war may be plainly shown.

“And thus I saw the horses in the vision,” that is, according to the number of the horses. For individual demons are borne through individual people in order to attack the number of the elect. It follows:

“And those sitting upon them had breastplates of fire, sulphur, and hyacinth.” Demons have breastplates through their intricate cunning; fiery ones through burning envy; sulphurous ones through the stench of infamy; and hyacinth-coloured ones through the deceit and pretence of heavenly righteousness. For hyacinth, having the appearance of heaven, signifies heavenly life; and the angel of Satan sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light and conceals vices beneath an appearance of virtues, so that he may deceive by pretence those whom he cannot overcome [Col. 0787D] by force.

“And the heads of the horses were like the heads of lions, and fire and smoke and sulphur proceed from their mouths.” The horses are the multitude of reprobate human beings. Their heads are like lions’ heads because through their perversities they tear apart the faithful people. From their mouths proceed fire through the malignity of perverse suggestion, smoke through the darkness of blinding, and sulphur through the stench of vice and evil reputation.

And because the suggestion of the wicked harms not those who are to be saved—for to them all things work together for good—but those who are to be damned, it fittingly adds: “By these three plagues was killed a third part of humankind,” that is, the whole body of those to be damned: by the fire, namely, of perverse suggestion; the smoke of blinding; and the sulphur of corrupting vice and foul reputation, [Col. 0788A] which proceeded from their mouths, because “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV).

But because the wicked seek to harm the good not only by manifest suggestion but also by hidden deceit, it rightly follows: “For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails.” The mouth signifies manifest suggestion, the tail hidden deceit; and when the wicked cannot harm by the mouth, they harm by the tail, because they try secretly to accomplish what they cannot accomplish openly. Further describing their deceitful power, he adds: “For their tails are like serpents, which flatter with their faces and secretly infuse poison.” “Having,” he says, “heads,” namely, in their tails. For the wicked have heads in their tails because, when they cannot harm in open persecution, they take their beginnings in hidden and deceitful pretence. And in all these ways they harm, because they bite by subtly and deceitfully infusing the poison of their perversity.

But because in what precedes he spoke of those who have some degree of belief in God, he rightly turns in what follows to those who lack every faith. It follows:

“And the rest of the people”—namely pagans, or also Jews, who are not baptized and are separated from the Church—“who were not killed by these plagues,” that is, corrupted by these vices, “did not repent of the works of their hands, so as to worship demons and idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which can neither see, nor hear, nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders [Col. 0788C], nor of their sorceries, nor of their fornication, nor of their thefts”—understood: they perished.

It should be noted that where he says, “they did not repent of the works of their hands, so as not to worship demons,” there he begins to rebuke their unbelief; but where he says, “and they did not repent of their murders,” there he rebukes their evil conduct. There he shows them to be blind; here he shows them to have gone astray. Therefore all perish who act wickedly and do not come to their senses.

But because above he set forth the great, grievous, and manifold torments of that persecution, inflicted upon the faithful amid the changing instability of time, he fittingly proceeds to speak, for the consolation of the elect, of the immutability of eternity, on Christ’s testimony, so that it may be believed more certainly: “And I saw another strong angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud; and a rainbow was upon his head, and his face was like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire.” The other angel is Christ: other, because he is far different from the angels of Satan mentioned above; angel, because he is the messenger of the Father’s will; strong, because he is the power of God. He descended from heaven because he emptied himself even to the point of taking the form of a servant. He was clothed with a cloud because he appeared in assumed humanity. Upon his head was a rainbow—that is, the propitiation of divinity and reconciliation of the human race—because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.

His face was like the sun because whoever believes in him with true faith knows him to be not merely man but also God. His feet were like pillars [Col. 0789A] of fire because the preachers who bear him throughout the whole world are rightly his feet, tested by the fire of manifold tribulation.

“And he had in his hand a little open book, and he set his right foot upon the sea, but his left upon the earth, and cried as a lion roars. And when he had cried, the seven thunders uttered their voices.” From these indications and signs the person of the Redeemer is recognized. He truly has the open little book in his hand, because he both openly fulfilled in himself the promise contained concerning him in sacred Scripture and gives knowledge of himself to whom he wills.

He sets his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth because he subjects to his power the Gentile people, once tossed about in the worship of many gods and in the bitterness of many [Col. 0789B] vices, and the Jewish nation, once firmly established in faith in one God. He sets his right foot upon the Gentiles because he chose them for blessedness; his left upon the Jews because he leaves them for damnation. Again, he first set his right foot upon the sea and then his left upon the earth because he first calls the Gentiles to righteousness; and when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.

He cried as a lion roars because he terribly declared that the punishments of future damnation must be avoided. After his cry, moreover, the seven thunders uttered their voices, because after his preaching the Evangelists and Apostles, filled with the grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, preached the terror of the future judgment. It follows:

“And when the seven thunders had uttered their voices, I was about to write. And I heard a voice from heaven saying: Seal up the things which the seven thunders have spoken; do not write them.” The divine voice commands the voices of the seven thunders to be sealed and forbids them to be written, because we must disclose the sayings and writings of the saints to the elect in such a way as to conceal them from the reprobate. “Seal,” that is, place seals upon them, so that they may be open to friends and hidden from enemies.

“And the angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth raised his hand to heaven and swore by him who lives for ages of ages, who created heaven and the things in it, and earth and the things in it, and sea and the things in it, that there will be no more time; but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery [Col. 0789D] of God will be completed, as he proclaimed through his servants the prophets.”

The angel raised his hand to heaven and swore by him who created all things that time would be no more, but that the mystery of God would be completed in the days of the seventh angel, because Christ faithfully and truly affirmed, by his own and the Father’s testimony, that, in rendering honour to the Father, the instability of the changeable fluctuations of heavenly righteousness would pass away; the immobility of eternity would succeed; and it would be granted to the elect who suffer for Christ within time.

Therefore eternal immutability is foretold and promised for consolation. For the time of the reprobate will be for ages. The saints, indeed, will become immortal and incapable of suffering; the impious will return from cold to heat and from heat to cold. [Col. 0790A] Therefore the statement, “there will be no more time,” must be understood not of the impious who are to be damned but of the righteous who are to be glorified and of the elements that are to be renewed, when all things will be made new and eternal immutability will succeed the change and vanity of time. This will occur in the revelation—that is, the glorification—of the children of God.

“For the expectation of the creature awaits the revelation of the children of God,” because the creature itself is subject to vanity—that is, mutability—and will be delivered into the liberty of the children of God. By “creature” he means the material of visible, bodily, irrational things, which will be delivered from vanity—that is, mutability—into the liberty, that is, deliverance, of the children of God when they themselves are glorified at the end, because it will be changed into a state of lasting newness.

There are three kinds of vanity, or mutability. The first is in a human being; the second in things made by a human being; the third in things made for the sake of a human being. In a human being is the vanity of mortality; in things made by a human being, the vanity of curiosity; in things made for a human being, the vanity of mutability. And because the human being is the cause of all vanity, it is fittingly written: “Every living human being is altogether vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII). On account of these three vanities Solomon said: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. I). But when the human being is removed from the world, no vanity of mutability will remain in the world. Hence it is also said here: “There will be no more time,” that is, there will be no vanity of mutability.

For it may be believed that the firmament will no longer revolve, nor the planets move, nor clouds condense, nor rivers run, nor wind blow, nor earth germinate, nor animals generate. It may also be thought that all the elements—that is, bodies composed from elements—will be dissolved in the conflagration of judgment and return to the elements; that no body will thereafter be formed from the elements; and that the elements will remain eternally in their own purity.

We may also suppose that this air, now cloudy and dense through continual agitation, will be purified, made subtle, and brightened in that final conflagration; that thereafter the sun, because of its excessive subtlety, will be unable to exert heat in it, but will have a marvellous radiance; and that what is written will be fulfilled: “The brightness of the moon shall be as the brightness of the sun, and the brightness of the sun sevenfold, like the brightness of seven days” [Col. 0790D] (Isa. XXX).

For creation, now subject to the vanity of mutability, groans and labours in birth; all the elements perform their tasks with toil, but this is for our sake. When we are removed, however, they will rest; and creation will be set free into the liberty of the children of God. The children of God will be liberated from the vanity of mortality; creation will be liberated from the vanity of mutability. The children of God will be liberated through immortality; creation through immutability.

And lest the children of God themselves, afflicted by diverse persecutions in the time of Antichrist, should be broken by the prolonged and slow expectation of this deliverance, its swift and speedy bestowal is indicated where it says: “In the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet,” that is, in the days of the last preachers, after the time of Antichrist, when they begin to preach—that is, at the very beginning of their preaching—“the mystery of God will be completed”: the secret promise which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man”; which begins here in the world and is completed there in heaven. “As he proclaimed through his servants the prophets,” because from the beginning he foretold it through them to his elect.

Great, then, amid the changing adversities of the time of Antichrist, will be the consolation of the stability of eternity, promised to the elect and soon to come. The elect believe it all the more certainly because it is described as so firmly attested by the Redeemer himself: “And the voice”—understood, sounded—“which I heard from heaven again speaking with me and saying: Go, and take the open book from the hand of the angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth. And I went [Col. 0791B] to the angel, asking him to give me the book. And he said to me: Take it and devour it; and it will make your belly bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey. And I took the book from the hand of the angel and devoured it; and it was sweet as honey in my mouth. And when I had devoured it, my belly became bitter. And he said to me: You must prophesy again concerning peoples and nations and tongues and many kings” (Rev. X).

Lest Saint John, suspended from the office of preaching and banished in exile, should despair either of release from exile or of the recovery of his lost office, but should strengthen himself concerning the benefit of both, he is commanded to receive the book from the angel—that is, knowledge from Christ. It is also declared to him that he must administer sacred preaching to peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings.

By immediately fulfilling the command, he gives us an example of obedience: if we desire wisdom from him who gives generously to all and does not reproach, we should ask for it. The book’s sweetness in the mouth but bitterness in the belly signifies that holy knowledge is indeed sweet in preaching, but burdensome and bitter in its practical performance. It follows:

“And a reed like a rod was given to me, and it was said to me: Rise and measure the temple of God, and the altar, and those worshipping in it. But cast out the court which is outside the temple of God and the altar, and do not measure it, because it has been given to the Gentiles” (Rev. XI).

So that he may be made still more certain concerning the building up of the holy Church through his preaching, he is commanded to rise and measure the temple of God. What the divine voice then commanded him to do in revelation, he afterward did in preaching. For the holy Church receives increase insofar as it extends itself by the word of preaching. What he did by measuring in revelation was therefore a sign to him of future preaching.

This preaching is called a reed like a rod: a reed because it sounds; like a rod because it maintains uprightness. Whoever takes it up to measure and rises is one who raises himself through virtues and good works in order to preach the word of God. What he first calls the temple and altar, he explains by adding: “and those worshipping in it.” Those worshipping are signified by the temple and altar: the temple, the weaker persons; the altar, the holier [Col. 0792A] persons. The temple signifies those expanded outwardly in good action; the altar, those intent inwardly upon contemplation. Whoever is commanded to measure this temple or altar is admonished to administer the word of instruction to active and contemplative persons according to the capacity of each.

The court, however, consists of false Christians, who appear consecrated because they are baptized, but are full of corpses—that is, vices and evil works. Although they are joined to the faithful in name, they are far from them in conduct. These, therefore, are not included under the measure of the reed because they are not subject to the command of the Word. They have been given to the Gentiles because they have become like the Gentiles. They are cast out whenever they are proclaimed to be separated from the faithful. It follows:

“And they will trample the holy city for forty-two [Col. 0792B] months. And I will give power to my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth.”

After promising eternity above for the consolation of the elect and assuring Saint John that he would resume preaching, he returns again to his subject. Further describing the tribulation to come under Antichrist, he adds concerning Elijah and Enoch—their preaching and power, affliction, death, resurrection, and glorification. He says, therefore: “And they will trample the holy city,” that is, the Church, by persecution, “for forty-two months,” that is, for the three and a half years during which Antichrist will reign. They are “clothed in sackcloth” in order to show by example that repentance must be undertaken for evil works.

How great is their merit and power is declared below, when he adds: “These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth.” They are two olive trees because they are anointed through the grace of the Holy Spirit; two lampstands because they shine through good works; before the Lord because they attend to the divine will and command; standing because of the uprightness of righteousness.

“And if anyone wishes to harm them, fire will come out of their mouths and devour their enemies.” “If anyone wishes to harm them,” that is, to hinder them from their purpose of preaching, “fire”—that is, spiritual knowledge—will go forth from their mouths through the sound of preaching and will devour their enemies, because it will prove them worthy of damnation. “And if anyone wishes to injure them,” that is, to kill them with bodily death, “thus must he be killed,” that is, condemned by a spiritual judgment.

How great their power in bodily matters will be, even according to the literal sense, is made clear when it is added: “These have power to shut heaven, so that it may not rain in the days of their prophecy; and they have power over the waters to turn them into blood, and to strike the earth with every plague as often as they wish.” These things, and many of those that follow, seem to require a literal understanding. They will therefore have great power; yet they will strive more to preserve patience than to inflict vengeance. And the more praiseworthy their virtue of patience is in them, the more glorious will be the recompense of their crown. It follows:

And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that will ascend from the abyss will make war against them, and will conquer them [Col. 0793A] and kill them; and their bodies will lie in the streets of the great city which is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified. And men from peoples, tribes, tongues, and nations will see their bodies for three and a half days, and will not allow their bodies to be placed in tombs. And the inhabitants of the earth will rejoice over them and make merry, and will send gifts to one another, because these two prophets tormented those who dwell upon the earth. And after three and a half days the spirit of life from God entered into them. And they stood upon their feet, and great fear fell upon those who saw them. And they heard a loud voice from heaven saying to them: “Come up here.” And they ascended to heaven, clothed in a cloud, and their enemies saw them.
