Because we see that much in what has been said must be understood according to [Col. 0793B] the literal sense, we pass over it with a lighter exposition. “And when they had finished their testimony,” that is, their preaching, “the beast,” that is, Antichrist, who will rage like a beast, “which will ascend,” namely, to the summit of his kingdom, “from the abyss,” that is, from the profound and dark obscurity of universal wickedness, “will make war against them” by many and varied disputations, “and will conquer them, and kill them” bodily. “And their bodies will lie in the streets,” so that all who see them may fear to imitate and conform themselves to them, “of the great city,” namely Jerusalem. Once great through righteousness, it will then be great through wickedness; it is “spiritually,” that is, according to spiritual interpretation, “called Sodom,” that is, mute, “and Egypt,” that is, dark. It will be mute in its confession of the true [Col. 0793C] faith, and dark in ignorance and perverse conduct, “where also their Lord”—whom they themselves will serve—“was crucified” in bodily suffering.

“And men from peoples, tribes, tongues, and nations” will see, some with their eyes and some by report, “their bodies” lying upon the earth “for three and a half days”; and they “will not allow their bodies to be placed in tombs,” lest memory of them be kept. “And the inhabitants of the earth,” that is, those who love earthly things and desire to possess an abiding city here, “will rejoice over them,” namely, over those who have been killed, because “these two prophets tormented those who dwell upon the earth” by opposing their wickedness. For when the part of them that is good is humbled, then the part that is evil glories; and when the part of the good [Col. 0793D] is exalted, then the part of the evil is grieved.

But after sufficiently describing the tribulation of the righteous, he immediately adds their glorification: “And after three and a half days the spirit of life,” that is, the life-giving soul, “entered into them from God, and they stood upon their feet,” that is, they rose again. “And great fear,” at their so sudden resurrection, “fell upon those who saw them,” namely, saw them thus glorified. And Elijah and Enoch heard “a loud voice,” that is, a voice of great power, “from heaven saying to them: ‘Come up here,’” namely, from the midst of the impious to the fellowship of the righteous. “And they ascended into heaven in a cloud,” so that, having imitated the Lord in enduring tribulation for his sake, they might be like him in their ascension; “and their enemies saw them,” namely, [Col. 0794A] bodily ascending into heaven.

But it must be known that what is here said in the past tense must be understood with reference to future time. For it is the custom of prophecy sometimes thus to narrate future things as though they were already past. It follows:

“And in that hour there was a great earthquake, and a tenth part of the city fell, and in the earthquake seven thousand names of men were killed.” In that hour, namely of their glorification, there was a great earthquake, because some were moved to repentance and others to greater hardness. “And a tenth part of the city fell,” because the multitude of the wicked, despising the Decalogue, appeared manifestly hardened and destined for condemnation. “And seven thousand names of men were killed,” that is, they were manifestly left for condemnation. Seven, because all were destined for condemnation; [Col. 0794B] thousands, because they were perfect in wickedness. For by the number seven we understand universality, and by a thousand, perfection. “And the rest,” that is, all who were not hardened, “were filled with fear,” that is, they feared. “And they gave glory to the God of heaven,” confessing their own guilt and proclaiming his righteousness.

“The second woe has passed,” that is, the tribulation to be inflicted upon the elect in the time of Antichrist has passed. “And behold, the third woe will come quickly,” that is, the terror which will come at the last judgment. Thus the sixth angel is the sixth order of preachers; the four angels, all demons; the release of the angels, permission to harm; their horses, the multitude of the impious; the other angel, Christ; the testimony that time is ending, the promise of eternity; the two witnesses, Elijah and Enoch; the great city, the whole multitude of the wicked; [Col. 0794C] the killing of men, the manifest hardening of those to be condemned; the sending of the rest into fear, the conversion of those to be saved.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Seventh Angel and His Trumpet

“And the seventh angel sounded the trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying: ‘The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our God and of his Christ, and he shall reign for ages of ages. Amen’” (Rev. XI).

At the end of the vision he deals with the end of time and the reward of just recompense. “And the seventh angel sounded the trumpet,” that is, the seventh, or final, order of teachers preached; “and there were voices,” that is, praises were offered to God for the salvation of the righteous and the condemnation of the impious; “in [Col. 0794D] heaven,” that is, in the holy Church elevated by heavenly conduct, saying: “The kingdom of this world has become,” that is, the whole body of the faithful, which is still exercised by tribulations in the world and prepared for the rewards of heavenly dwellings. In a certain manner it is not yet perfectly God’s, so long as under the mutability of time and the corruptibility of mortality the craftiness of the enemy Antichrist afflicts it by tempting and persecuting it. But then it will be perfectly the kingdom of God and Christ—that is, of divinity and humanity reigning together—when, removed from the present age, it devotes itself in heaven to divine praise alone, and the faithless enemy will no longer exercise anything over it from the dominion of his power.

The tranquillity of this kingdom will also begin then in the world, when Christ kills Antichrist by the breath [Col. 0795A] of his mouth, and the holy Church, pacified thereafter in the silence of half an hour, rests until the end. Therefore, when the seventh angel sounds, and the assembly of saints gives thanks for the salvation of the righteous and the most certainly foreknown condemnation of the wicked, it is now said not “it shall become” but “it has become,” because from that point the devil’s deceit and cruelty entirely fail, and God will reign in all his faithful in perpetual peace and tranquillity, “for ages of ages,” that is, forever. “Amen”: truly and faithfully.

For God will indeed always reign, as has already been said; the saints will not, as some heretics imagined, after a fixed time return to the life of the world and to their former way of living. Finally, it must be known that “world” is understood in three ways. For, as the teachers hand down, “world” is understood one way when God is called Creator of the world; another when he is called Savior of the world; and another when the devil is called prince of the world. There is, therefore, a world of which God is Creator; there is also a world of which God is Savior; and there is likewise a world of which the devil is prince.

The world of which God is Creator means the entire structure of the world, of which it is said: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John I), and so forth. The world of which God is Savior means the universal Church of God, of which it is written: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John III). The world of which the devil is prince means the universal concupiscence of the age, of which it is said: “Do not love the world, nor the things [Col. 0795C] that are in the world” (I John II).

The first world, therefore—that is, the entire structure of the world—is always God’s, never the devil’s. But the third world—that is, the universal concupiscence of the age—is always the devil’s with respect to perverse action, and always God’s with respect to the ordering of perverse action. For although God is not the author of evil, he is nevertheless its disposer; for though evil does not derive its origin from him, he does not leave it beneath himself without order. And thus it comes about in a wonderful way that what does not have its origin from him nevertheless receives its ordering from him and according to him.

But the second world, that is, the universal Church of God, because, by the permission of divine providence, even those predestined to eternal life sometimes sin for a time, and because persecutors, stirred up by the devil, rage fiercely against those who desire to live devoutly, seems still to be craftily assailed, keenly attacked, and cruelly torn apart by him; but its foundation remains firm. For the Lord knows those who are his, and for those saints who are called according to his purpose—that is, predestination—all things work together for good.

Therefore, the kingdom of this world will then perfectly and manifestly become God’s when the holy and universal Church is wholly delivered, in all her children, from the devil’s temptation and persecution, and will devote herself to divine praise and contemplation, both in time under the trumpet of the seventh angel, or rather in eternity. That kingdom, as has been stated beforehand, will by no means be temporal [Col. 0796A] but eternal, as this sacred text also testifies when it says, “for ages of ages. Amen,” that is, forever and truly. It follows:

“And the twenty-four elders, who sit before God upon their thrones, fell upon their faces and worshipped, saying: ‘We give thanks to you, Lord God Almighty, who are and who were, because you have taken your great power and have reigned. And the nations were angry; and your wrath came, and the time to judge the dead, and to give reward to your servants the prophets and to the saints who fear your name, small and great, and to destroy those who corrupted the earth.’”

Above he set forth the general praise offered to God by all the elect for benefits bestowed; now he adds the particular thanksgiving of the perfect and greater ones. Thus it is said: “And the twenty-four elders,” that is, all preachers, teachers, ecclesiastical judges, and rulers, “who sit before God upon their thrones,” because they judge what is pleasing in God’s sight among those entrusted to them, “fell upon their faces,” humbling themselves; “and worshipped, saying,” confessing with right faith, “We give thanks to you,” to whom alone we owe such thanks for so many and such great benefits: “Lord,” whom we serve; “God,” whom we worship; “Almighty,” whom we fear; “who are” unchangeably, “who were” always.

And it should be noted that he does not add, as he is accustomed to do in other such passages, “who are to come.” This is because, in those days, all things belonging to the future judgment having now passed, they will know with complete certainty—although they do not know the day and hour—that the Judge himself is at hand and about to come, after the silence of that half-hour of past sin has elapsed. Therefore above, as has been said, he did not say, “The kingdom of our God shall become,” but “has become”; and in what follows he does not say, “Your wrath and the time to judge the dead will come,” but “has come.” And he plainly declares what kind of person he is and what time it is for which thanksgiving is to be rendered, when he adds: “Because you have taken your great power,” according to the humanity assumed, by rising from the dead, ascending into heaven, and reigning—defending your own against the devil and piously governing them in virtues and good works.

“And the nations were angry,” implicitly, because all the wicked who live in a gentile and carnal manner saw your kingdom, contrary to theirs, arise [Col. 0796D] and their own brought low. “And your wrath came,” that is, the just vengeance which is a sign of wrath, although you, Lord of Hosts, judge all things with tranquillity. “And the time”—implicitly, came—“to judge the dead,” that is, to separate the good from the wicked and the wicked from the good. And the time came “to give reward to your servants the prophets,” that is, the greater ones, “and to the saints who fear your name,” that is, the lesser ones. Changing the order, he explains this in what follows, saying, “small and great”: “small,” namely the saints who fear your name; “great,” namely your servants the prophets.

And, implicitly, the time came “to destroy,” that is, condemn, “those who corrupt the earth,” whether by living wickedly in themselves or by presenting examples of wicked living to others, and thus leading themselves or others into corruption. But where, at the end of this present chapter, he says that the time has come to destroy those who corrupt the earth, the third woe is indicated, which at the end of the preceding chapter he said would come quickly.

Thus the seventh angel is the final order of preachers, who will preach at the end of the world; the kingdom of this world, the whole body of the faithful; the voices that arose, or thanksgivings in heaven, the praises offered by the saints to God for the salvation of humankind; the time to judge the dead, the end of the age; the reward of the saints, fellowship with the angels; the destruction of the wicked, eternal condemnation. In this vision, therefore, the author first treated the angel standing before the altar and offering incense in a censer—that is, Christ commending the prayers [Col. 0797B] of the faithful to the Father. Then, from there [Col. 0798A] to the end of the vision, he treated in individual chapters the individual angels and individual trumpets.

Nor should it be passed over, but carefully observed, that the mysteries of human redemption in the second vision are to be understood, in the course of time, under the opening of the seals, as made manifest to teachers and more perfect persons, with grace assisting, through reading and meditation; but in the third vision, under the sounding of trumpets, they are declared to the lesser persons and subject peoples by teaching and preaching. And just as they are successively distinguished in two visions, so they are successively distributed, first to teachers and then to hearers. Having spoken thus far of the articles of the third vision, we relax from the labor of writing in order to proceed afresh to survey the fourth.

# BOOK FOUR. ON THE FOURTH VISION

[Col. 0797]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0797B]

God, by whose power all things were created, by whose providence created things subsist, and by whose grace corrupted things rise again to wholeness, by his wondrous and ineffable wisdom forms the holy Church in this valley of tears through manifold instructions and corrections, so that, justified, he may lead her to the joys of heavenly blessedness. For just as a wise craftsman prepares material with diverse tools, and, having prepared the material, builds a house, so almighty God in many ways and by many means instructs his elect through diverse enigmas and likenesses in the text of sacred speech, and by righteousness transfers them to glory.

Thus in this vision, as in the others, he instructs us by diverse figures; and beginning from the outset of redemption, proceeding through the course of time by teaching us, he carries the discourse onward to the end of the age, as he did in the two preceding visions. This vision treats of the woman giving birth to a male child; of the dragon prepared to devour her son; of Michael and the dragon and their battle; of the beast to which [Col. 0797D] the dragon gave his power and its battle against the saints; of the other beast that assisted the first; and of the condemnation of the wicked.

## CHAPTER I. On the Temple Opened, the Ark Seen, and the Woman Giving Birth

“And the temple of God was opened in heaven, and his ark was seen in his temple. And there were lightnings, voices, an earthquake, and great hail” (Rev. XI).

Having above described in temporal sequence everything contained in the third vision, he proceeds to narrate what is contained in the fourth vision. “And the temple of God was opened in heaven.” What more fittingly is understood here by “the temple” in heaven than the wonderful sacrament of our redemption, in which the grace of human salvation is contained as in a temple, and through whose dispensation it is daily administered faithfully and holily to the elect? And what more rightly do we understand by “heaven” than sacred Scripture, splendid with many sentences as though with many lights, exalted on high through heavenly instruction, and widened [Col. 0798B] and extended through the multiplicity of its meanings?

The temple in heaven, therefore, is the divine sacrament in sacred Scripture. The temple in heaven is opened when the mediator of God and men comes into the world and the mystery of our redemption becomes known in the text of sacred speech. But once the temple of God in heaven has been opened, his ark is seen in the temple, because, once the divine mystery has been known as fulfilled in sacred Scripture, the ark of assumed humanity by the Word—in which are contained the manna of spiritual grace, the rod of upright righteousness, and the tablets of all wisdom and knowledge—is faithfully believed and contemplated by all the elect.

Finally, when the temple is opened and the ark seen, there are lightnings, voices, an earthquake, and great hail, because after the fulfilment of the mystery and the advent of Christ miracles were displayed, words of heavenly teaching were preached, some were moved to conversion and others to turning away, and finally all the reprobate were stirred up to persecution. For the sound of hail signifies the scourge of persecution. It follows:

“And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars. And she was with child, and she cries out in travail and is in anguish to give birth” (Rev. XII).

The spiritual understanding and the effect of the manifestation are also distinguished and follow in the order of the narrative. For, once all the things mentioned above had been manifested, a woman clothed with the sun appeared, because the holy Church manifestly heard, through faith in Christ, him who enlightens every person coming [Col. 0799A] into this world. She had the moon beneath her feet because she trampled for love of him earthly things which, like the moon through its waning, decrease daily. And upon her head was a crown of twelve stars because at her beginning, or in her dignity, she deserved to possess the splendour of the twelve apostles.

And because the holy Church labours with all her strength to become Christ’s mother by doing the will of the highest Father, and to bear him, so that she may rejoice in him without end at the end, it is rightly said: “And she was with child, and cries out in travail, and is in anguish to give birth.” The holy Church, indeed, becomes the mother of Christ by accomplishing what is pleasing to the Father, because she conceives him through faith, grace making her fruitful; she labours in birth through good will; she gives birth through good action. She possesses the child who has been born and rejoices through the reward of eternity.

The term *parturitio* means, as it were, preparation for birth, so long as the embryo in the mother’s womb grows, receives life, and is formed. But *partus* means the birth when the embryo is born. Therefore the holy universal Church, which puts on Christ and despises earthly things beneath her, now having Christ in the womb through faith and labouring in birth through good will, cries out in devout prayer so that she may give birth through the fruitfulness of manifest work to that same Christ, in whom she desires to rejoice through recompense. But because as the righteousness of the holy Church increased, the envy of the ancient enemy against her also increased, it fittingly follows:

[Col. 0799C] “And another sign was seen in heaven. And behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon his heads seven diadems; and his tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them down to the earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had borne her son, he might devour him. And she bore a male son, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron. And her son was caught up to God and to his throne; and the woman fled into the wilderness, where she has a place prepared by God, so that there they may feed her for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.”

Another sign, very different from the former, was seen “in heaven,” because it was made known in sacred Scripture: “a great red dragon,” that is, the devil—dragon through cunning, great through pride, red through cruelty—“having seven heads,” through the sevenfold temptation of the seven principal vices; “and ten horns,” through the arrogant attack of the chiefs of the impious, who oppose the Decalogue of the law; “and upon his heads seven diadems,” that is, universal victory over those overthrown through sevenfold temptation.

His tail also draws a third part of the stars of heaven, because the devil deceives unto condemnation even that part of souls which, like stars of heaven, seem by their lofty way of life to remain on high and to shine for others through good works; when he cannot prevail by open cruelty, he does so by hidden deceit, which is figured in the tail. Finally, he casts them down to earth when he inflames them with the pleasures of earthly things.

This dragon also stands before the woman about to give birth because the devil unceasingly attacks the holy Church when she desires to bear Christ in the fruit of good work. And when she gives birth, he wishes to devour her son because he wishes through corruption of her work to take Christ away from her. But the devil does not attain what he desires, because the holy mother Church gives birth to Christ in good work as one strong to resist; he rules all nations, spiritual and carnal alike, rendering to the former the wages of blessedness and to the latter the wages of damnation, “with a rod of iron,” that is, with inflexible justice.

This son was caught up to God and to his throne because, according to his humanity, he ascended into heaven, sits with the Father, and rules and judges the world. And the woman fled into the wilderness where she has a place prepared by God because the holy Church, grace assisting, withdraws to a spiritual way of life, where she attends only to divine things, while the devil persecutes her. There she is fed for one thousand two hundred and sixty days because she is nourished by the most holy preaching of Christ, occurring for three and a half years, lest she die of hunger for the word of God—especially during the persecution of Antichrist, which must be endured for three and a half years.

We pass over these things briefly, lest, lingering over each point, we generate weariness for you. Thus: the temple opened in heaven is the divine mystery made manifest in sacred Scripture; the ark, assumed humanity; lightnings, miracles; voices, preachings; earthquake, the conversion of the good and turning away of the evil; hail, the tumult of persecutions; the woman, the holy Church; the sun, Christ; the moon, the world; the dragon, the devil; the male child, [Col. 0800C] Christ; the woman’s withdrawal, the hiddenness of spiritual life; the woman’s feeding, the teaching of preaching.

## CHAPTER II. On Michael, the Dragon, and Their Battle

“And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon fought, and his angels; but they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven” (Rev. XII).

In the preceding chapter he described the devil’s envy, inflamed against the holy Church; in this one he openly adds how great are the supports she has against him. But although all ministering spirits—that is, angels sent for service—are believed to exist for those who receive the inheritance of salvation, Michael is designated by name and described as the prince of the others, just as in the Old Testament he is mentioned as the prince of the people of Israel, that is, the people who see God.

“And there was a great battle in heaven,” as though it were said: Do not fear, faithful ones, if demons rage against you by bringing temptations and stirring up persecutions, because the holy Church has great aids against all their schemes—not only the teachings of holy doctors and preachers, but also the aid of angels. “And there was a great battle,” because it was fierce and long, “in heaven,” that is, in the holy Church while it remains in the world. “Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon fought, and his angels”: the former by aiding the Church, the latter by attacking it; the former by suggesting things that bring salvation, [Col. 0801A] the latter by counselling what is harmful; the dragon and his angels by assailing the army of the good; Michael and his angels by restraining their attack.

“And they did not prevail,” namely the dragon and his angels, so as to remove the aid of the holy spirits; “nor was their place found any longer in heaven,” that is, in the holy Church, so that they could either take righteousness from her or draw her into sin. For even if some member of the faithful Church—we speak of those who are called saints according to purpose—by the permission of divine providence and the devil’s wicked suggestion falls for a time into sin, the devil does not thereby conquer but is conquered. For even evil works together for good for those predestined to life; and this does not occur so much through the power of the raging adversary as through the provident ordering of the God who permits it, and is ordered toward the caution of the person who has fallen and risen again.

Therefore the devil and his angels have no place any longer, because they cannot overcome those who thirst with a true heart for heavenly goods and are predestined to attain them, either to drag them into sin at their pleasure or to keep them in it as long as they wish. Rather, since even this occurs by divine permission, their place is found on earth, that is, among those who love earthly things and disdain to merit heavenly goods. Hence it fittingly follows:

“And that great dragon was cast down, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world; he was cast down to earth, and his angels were sent with him.” Dragon through the ardour [Col. 0801C] of envy; great through the eminence of pride; serpent through the cunning of craftiness; ancient through the long-standing habit of sinning; called devil, that is, “flowing downward,” namely from the good to the evil; and Satan, that is, adversary, because he attacks the righteous; he deceives the whole world insofar as divine power permits him strength to exercise it. He and his angels are cast down from heaven to earth because, restrained by the gift of heavenly mercy from harming those who are to be saved, and by the protection of the good angels who do battle for them, they are permitted to rule over those destined for condemnation who love earthly things.

This battle is described as having occurred and been seen at the beginning of the holy Church, because then the devil’s ancient right of dominion, which he possessed over humanity through sin, was taken away by the grace of the Redeemer. But because, when the devil is cast down, joy and jubilation arise among holy angelic and human spirits, he fittingly adds: “I heard a loud voice: ‘Now salvation, power, and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ, have come, because the accuser of our brethren, who accused them before the presence of our God night and day, has been cast down. And they conquered him through the blood of the Lamb and through the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives unto death. Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them.’”

“I heard a loud voice,” because it signified great joy. “Now salvation, power, and the kingdom of our God have come,” because through him there is remission of sin, strength for good works, and dominion for trampling down vices; and authority, formerly the devil’s, has now become Christ’s—that is, of the man assumed by the Word—“because the accuser of our brethren,” that is, of those humans who are to be saved, “has been cast down,” that is, restrained. He accused them by seeking to render them blameworthy before the presence of our God, from whom nothing is hidden, especially by that whereby he terrifies them, “night and day,” that is, continually.

“And they conquered him,” not through themselves, but “through the blood of the Lamb,” that is, through faith in Christ’s passion, “and through the word of their testimony,” that is, through open confession of that same faith. “And they did not love their lives unto death,” because they willingly endure the bitterness of death for their souls. “Therefore rejoice, O heavens, and you who dwell in them.” What he had first called “heavens” he explains when he adds, “and you who dwell in them,” that is, the holy angels or the saints glorified by the first robe. For great joy must indeed be made over the casting down of the devil and the salvation of humankind. It follows:

“Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has descended to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has little time.” Earth signifies those wicked persons who persist stubbornly in some single and particular vice; the sea, those who are tossed about through the bitterness of diverse vices. To both the devil descends because he has received the power of ruling in them. Woe is rightly proclaimed to them because those who are now deceived through the devil’s deception will in the future be punished with him in the pain of eternal death.

And it is fittingly said that the devil has great wrath because he sees many taken away from him and established in the place which he lost; and because he knows that he has little time to delay the elect from entering their heavenly homeland, he labours as much as he can. Hence he advances more fiercely to battle and tries to overcome those who desire to live rightly. Thus Michael and his angels are all the heavenly orders; the dragon and his angels, all demons; salvation accomplished, human justification; the dragon’s casting down, the restraint of the ancient enemy; earth and sea, those destined for condemnation; the devil’s wrath, his malice in harming; little time, the brevity of the present life.

## CHAPTER III. On the Dragon’s Persecution and the Woman’s Flight

“And when the dragon saw that he had been cast down to earth, he persecuted the woman who had borne the male child. And two wings of the great eagle were given to the woman, so that she might fly into the wilderness, to the place where she is fed for a time, and times, and half a time, away from the face of the serpent” (Rev. XII).

Seeing that the holy Church had withdrawn into the hiding places of spiritual life; that she possessed the teaching of her preachers and the assistance of angels for her defence; that he himself had been cast from heaven in losing his right of dominion over the elect; and that he had been cast to earth in that only the portion of the damned remained to him—the devil blazed forth into a greater persecution against her, sent after her the whole river of vices, and tried to submerge her.

Thus it is said: “After the dragon saw that he had been cast down to earth, he persecuted the woman who had borne the male child.” But because the more the devil persecutes her, the more grace is increased for her, it fittingly follows: “And two wings of the great eagle were given to the woman, so that she might fly into the wilderness, to the place where she is fed for a time, and times, and half a time, away from the face of the serpent.”

The two wings are the two Testaments, or the active and contemplative life, or love of God and neighbour. With these wings the woman flies into the wilderness, where she is fed for a time and times and half a time, away from the face of the serpent, because through them the holy Church raises herself up in order to withdraw to the hiddenness of spiritual life. There she is fed by the teaching of Christ, occurring for three and a half years, lest, as was said above, she die from hunger for the word of God—especially in the persecution of Antichrist, which must be endured for three and a half years—away from the face of the serpent, that is, from the present temptation of the persecuting devil. These two wings are aptly called those of the great eagle, in order to suggest that the holy Church is powerfully lifted to heavenly things and contemplates them with unblinking eyes. It follows:

“And the serpent sent water like a river from his mouth after the woman, to make her be swept away by the river. And the earth helped the woman, and opened its mouth and swallowed the river which the dragon had sent from his mouth.”

Above he said that the dragon persecuted the woman; now he adds the manner of the persecution. The serpent sent water like a river from his mouth after the woman in order to make her be swept away by the river, because from the beginning of the holy Church the devil sought to bring in the whole mass of vice, in order to drag her children to damnation. [Col. 0803C] But the earth helps the woman by opening its mouth and swallowing the river, because, while those who love earthly things gladly receive what the devil suggests, the devil himself ceases for a time from tempting the good by harming them. And while they, namely the good, rest from temptation, they devote themselves more effectively to contemplation of heavenly things.

Alternatively: the earth helps the woman against the river because the company of those who are perfect and steadfast in faith prays unanimously against the devilish temptation persecuting the faithful of the Church, and as it were swallows up the river with its mouth when it overcomes temptation by prayer. It follows:

And the dragon was enraged against the woman, and went away to make war upon the rest of her offspring, who keep the commandments of God and hold the testimony of Jesus. The more [Col. 0803D] the devil is defeated, the more he is enraged; and the more he attempts to do harm in a worse fashion. When he is wholly unable to overcome the elect, he stirs up the unbelieving to persecution. Hence it is rightly said here: “And the dragon was enraged against the woman, and went away”—that is, ceasing from crafty temptation and stirring up open persecution through unbelievers—“to make war upon the rest of her offspring,” that is, upon the faithful who follow the primitive Church in time and imitate it in life, “who keep the commandments of God,” that is, the precepts for right living, “and hold the testimony of Jesus,” that is, the faithful confession of Christ.

Therefore, the dragon’s persecution is the temptation of the ancient enemy; the woman’s flight, the hidden character of the spiritual life; the two wings, the two lives; the river, universal temptation; the earth which helped the woman, the assembly of those who are perfect and [Col. 0804A] steadfast in faith; the dragon’s greater wrath, the increased cruelty of the enemy; war against the rest of her offspring, persecution against her imitators.

## CHAPTER IV. On the beast ascending from the sea.

“And he stood upon the sand of the sea. And I saw a beast ascending from the sea, having seven heads and ten horns; and upon its horns ten diadems, and upon its heads names of blasphemy” (Rev. XIII).

After the devil perceived that holy Church was defended by the preaching of teachers, angelic assistance, and the devout prayers of her perfect and unwaveringly faithful saints, he delayed somewhat in attacking her with the river of vices, or with the deceits of hidden temptations; and he raised open persecution against her through unbelieving [Col. 0804B] paganism. Therefore it is not unfittingly said at the beginning of the present chapter: “And he stood upon the sand of the sea.”

For what do we more fittingly understand by the sand of the sea than paganism, barren of every fruit of divine knowledge and good work, and tossed about by the worship of various idols and by the bitter waves of vices? It is rightly called sand, because sterile in what is good; of the sea, because unstable and bitter in evil. Therefore, when the devil withdrew from holy Church through a temporary cessation of temptations, he stood upon the sand of the sea: that is, he pressed more intently upon barren and vicious paganism in order to persecute the faithful through it. All pagans, and especially all rulers who remained in unbelief, stirred by the devil, cruelly persecuted [Col. 0804C] the Church. Hence it is rightly added: “And I saw a beast ascending from the sea.”

For the beast rises from the sea because the cruel rule of the nations, through diabolical inspiration, exalted itself in pride. It also had seven heads, through the totality of its rulers, and ten horns, through its arrogant assault upon the Decalogue of the sacred law. And upon its horns were seven diadems, because there is no commandment in the Decalogue which is not broken by them and concerning which they are not crowned by the devil. Upon the heads of this beast, moreover, were names of blasphemy, because the rulers of the nations blasphemed Christ, denying that he was God and saying that he had been great.

He describes the character of this beast more plainly, saying: “And the beast which I saw [Col. 0804D] was like a leopard, and its feet like those of a bear, and its mouth like the mouth of a lion.” The beast—that is, the rulers of the nations, raging beast-like against the saints—was like a leopard through the various assertions of philosophers; its feet were like those of a bear through the swiftness of its impious deeds and its trampling of the saints; and its mouth was like the mouth of a lion through their tearing apart and killing of them. It follows:

“And the dragon gave it his power and his authority.” Power: the power to perform miracles by incantation; authority: the power to bend others by compulsion. But because Antichrist will be the head and prince of the whole persecution which the impious inflict upon the faithful, since he will rage more cruelly than all the rest, the following is fittingly added concerning [Col. 0805A] him in this place: “And I saw one of its heads as if slain unto death, and its mortal wound was healed; and the whole earth marvelled after the beast. And they worshipped the dragon which gave authority to the beast, and they worshipped the beast, saying, ‘Who is like the beast, and who will be able to fight with it?’”

“And I saw one of its heads,” that is, one of its rulers, namely Antichrist, “as if slain unto death, and its mortal wound was healed,” because Antichrist, in order to deceive more effectively, will falsely pretend to be dead and risen again, in imitation of Christ. “And the whole earth marvelled,” that is, all the reprobate who love earthly things and believe in him; it marvelled after the beast, imitating it in unbelief and cruelty. “And they worshipped the dragon,” that is, the devil, “which gave [Col. 0805B] authority to the beast,” that is, to the beast-like persecutors, especially Antichrist. “And they worshipped the beast,” humbling themselves before it and saying in amazement: “Who is like the beast?”—that is, who can do such great things?—“and who will be able to fight with it?”—that is, resist its will? For the reprobate will be so astonished at Antichrist that they will suppose that no one can resist him while keeping faith. It follows:

“And a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies was given to it. And authority was given to it to act for forty-two months. And it opened its mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name and his tabernacle and those who dwell in heaven.”

It should be noted that what has been said above from the place where it is written, “And I saw one of its heads as if slain,” and the rest [Col. 0805C] which follows in this chapter, must chiefly be referred to Antichrist. His impiety is described yet more fully when it says: “And a mouth speaking great things and blasphemies was given to it, and authority was given to it to act for forty-two months.” A mouth was given to it, by divine permission, speaking great things through the magnitude of its boasting, and blasphemies through denial of divinity; and it was given forty-two months to act, that is, three years and a half, through persecution of the righteous.

“And it opened its mouth in blasphemies against God,” because it will deny Christ, “to blaspheme his name,” that is, his faith, through which he is made known to us; “and his tabernacle,” that is, the elect of the Church who serve him in the present life; “and those who [Col. 0805D] dwell in heaven,” that is, those who sing his praise in the heavenly places. It follows:

“And it was given to it to make war upon the saints and to overcome them; and authority was given to it over every tribe and people and language and nation. And all who dwell upon the earth worshipped it, whose names are written in the book of life and of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world.”

It was given to it, by divine permission, to make war upon the saints through manifold disputation; and authority was given to it over every tribe, people, language, and nation, so that from all it might break some away from the faith and draw them into unbelief, or prevent them from receiving the faith. “And they worshipped it,” humbling themselves before it—those who dwell upon the earth by loving earthly things. Their names are not written [Col. 0806A] in the book of life and of the Lamb, that is, they are not predestined to eternal life. The Lamb was slain figuratively from the foundation of the world, but truly at the end of the world. He was slain from the foundation of the world through the signification of preceding figures; at the end, through the subsequent manifestation of truth. It follows:

“If anyone has ears, let him hear. He who has led into captivity shall go into captivity. He who kills with the sword must himself be killed with the sword. Here is the patience and faith of the saints.”

At the end of the chapter, for the consolation of the elect, he adds a threat against the raging enemy. “If anyone has ears,” namely, ears of the heart, “let him hear,” that is, understand what vengeance awaits Antichrist. “He who has led into captivity,” that is, who has drawn another into unbelief, or has bodily relegated him [Col. 0806B] into exile because of faith in Christ, “shall go into exile,” or captivity, through eternal damnation. He who kills a faithful person with the sword—namely, the sword of evil persuasion or a material sword—must be killed by the sword, because, slain by the spirit of Christ’s mouth, he shall perish. Here is the patience and strength of the saints, namely, in bearing evils. For in adversities those who are truly good are tested, and those who are hidden are made manifest.

Therefore, the beast ascending from the sea is the rule of the nations; one of its heads is Antichrist; war with the saints is disputation concerning the Scriptures; his victory is bodily killing.

## CHAPTER V. On the beast ascending from the earth.

“And I saw another beast ascending from the earth, and it had two horns like a Lamb, and it spoke like [Col. 0806C] a dragon; and it exercised all the authority of the former beast in its presence. And it made the earth and those who dwell in it worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed” (Rev. XIII).

Seeing holy Church fortified with heavenly gifts and many powers and helps, firmly founded upon the rock which is Christ, the devil attacks and attempts to overthrow her not in one manner of harming, but in many. Thus he who is said in the preceding chapter to attack her through the beast ascending from the sea is declared in this chapter to assail her through the beast ascending from the earth. For he frequently disturbs her peace not only through cruel rulers of the nations, but also through false teachers and kings among false Christians; and through them [Col. 0806D] he sometimes troubles her.

For just as we understand the beast ascending from the sea as fierce rulers of the nations, tossed like the sea by the various worship of diverse idols, so fittingly we understand the beast ascending from the earth as impious rulers among false Christians, remaining fixed like the earth in one belief—although it is useless to them. The sea signifies pagans because they fluctuate amid various things; the earth, even false Christians, because they persist in belief in one God. But the rulers of both, rising above themselves in pride, are rightly compared to beasts, because they persecute the saints beastially. And since both the one and the other are shown to serve Antichrist and to have him as the head of wickedness, blasphemies and cruelties beginning with Antichrist are appropriately mentioned after the beasts in both chapters.

Therefore, because the devil persecutes the Church not only through pagans but also through false Christians, after the beast ascending from the sea the beast ascending from the earth is fittingly seen. “And I saw another beast ascending from the earth”: another, through dissimilarity; a beast, through cruelty; ascending, through pride; from the earth, that is, from the body of those who maintain the immovability of their own assertion. “And it had two horns like a Lamb, and it spoke like a dragon.” False Christians have two horns like those of the Lamb because they possess the two Testaments, one preaching Christ through signification, the other through manifestation. They possess them, I say, through intellectual knowledge, not through holiness of life. They speak [Col. 0807B] like a dragon because in impious persuasion they agree with the devil. They also exercise all the authority of the former beast in its presence, because, imitating Antichrist, who is chiefly represented through the first beast, they accomplish by their wicked deeds those things which please the devil.

It follows: “And it made the earth and those who dwell in it worship the first beast.” What it first calls “the earth,” it explains when it adds, “those who dwell in it.” For human beings are signified by the earth. Thus the second beast makes people worship the first beast because the perverse body of reprobate Christians subjects to the impiety and pride of Antichrist—as specially signified by the first beast in one of its heads, as though slain and healed—whomever it can. That the statements made here about the first beast must be referred especially to Antichrist, it makes clear when it adds: “Whose mortal wound was healed.” For, as was said in the preceding chapter, in order to deceive more effectively he will pretend that he has been slain and has been raised by the power of divinity. It follows:

“And it performed great signs, even making fire descend from heaven to earth in the sight of men; and it deceives those who dwell upon the earth through the signs which it was given to perform in the presence of the beast, telling those who dwell upon the earth to make an image of the beast which has the wound of the sword and lived. And it was given to it to give spirit to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might speak and might cause whoever would not worship the image [Col. 0807D] of the beast to be killed. And it will make all—the small and the great, the rich and the poor, the free and the enslaved—have a mark on their right hand or upon their foreheads, and that no one might be able to buy or sell unless he has the mark of the beast, or its name, or the number of its name.”

Here, in few words, he briefly embraces many great evils which he saw would be carried out through Antichrist and his ministers. Therefore, the second beast which rises from the earth performs great signs because the whole body of those who will turn from Christ to Antichrist, being craftier on account of their knowledge of the Scriptures, will shine with false miracles through the devil’s cooperation; by these it will strengthen its preaching among apostate people. It will even make fire descend from heaven to earth in [Col. 0808A] the sight of men, so that by amazement at such a great miracle it may draw any who are weak in faith away from Christ to Antichrist.

It will deceive those who dwell upon the earth—that is, those who prefer earthly things to heavenly ones—by the signs which it was given, that is, permitted, to perform in the presence of the beast, that is, Antichrist. It tells those who dwell upon the earth to make an image of the beast by conforming themselves to its impiety: of the beast which has the wound of the sword, through the pretence of its killing, and lived, through the pretence of its resurrection. And it was given to it, by divine permission, to give, through the descent of fire, a spirit—namely, an evil spirit—to the image of the beast, that is, to one conformed to Antichristian impiety; and so that the image of the beast might speak in various languages, just as it was given to the Apostles through the Holy Spirit. “And it will cause whoever does not worship the image [Col. 0808B] of the beast,” through an outward display of honour, “to be killed,” with bodily death.

Alternatively, it will make a material image of Antichrist, as we make a bodily image of the Saviour; it will cause that image to speak through incantations, thereby deceive people, and have those who refuse to worship it killed. And because they will compel people not only to maintain observance of that abominable religion but also to maintain a new commercial practice, it is fittingly added: “And it will make all—the small and the great, the rich and the poor, the free and the enslaved—have a mark,” namely, the mark of Antichrist’s name, “on their right hand or upon their foreheads,” so that it may be plainly seen and they may be known to belong more especially to Antichrist.

Why is this done? So that no one [Col. 0808C] may be able to buy or sell unless he has the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of its name; and thus many may be constrained by this necessity and compelled to worship Antichrist. Great and grievous, therefore, will be the anxiety of the faithful people, who refuse to bear the mark, the name, and the number of the name. The number of its name means that number contained in the letters with which its name is written. It follows:

“Here is wisdom.” Because the matter is obscure, he makes his hearers attentive: “Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the beast,” that is, calculate the number formed from the numerical value of the letters with which its name is written. And that it can be calculated he fittingly declares when he adds: “It is the number of a man,” namely, a number that can be counted by a human being, not of God, whose wisdom has no number—although Antichrist nevertheless wishes to be considered God by means of this number.

And in order to bring us nearer to knowledge of this number, he plainly reveals it to us, saying: “And its number is six hundred and sixty-six.” But that we may recognize the force of this number more clearly, let us examine it more closely according to the tradition of the holy doctors. For they say that, since this book was published in Greek, the number itself must be sought according to the Greeks, among whom all letters signify numbers. His name in Greek is *antemos* [ἀντέμος, perhaps an OCR-corrupted form], which is interpreted “opposed” or “contrary.” In this name, *a* signifies one, *n* fifty, *t* three hundred, *e* five, *m* forty, *o* seventy, and *s* two hundred. Their total makes six hundred and sixty-six. [Col. 0809A]

There are also other names of his whose such interpretation yields this same number. But we pass over many, since we judge that a few suffice for the present brevity. Why such a number is appropriate to Antichrist is more quickly shown if the quality of the number itself is considered more subtly. Six signifies perfection. By six we may understand the least perfection; by sixty, the intermediate; and by six hundred, the greatest and complete perfection. He is therefore rightly described by such a number, since he is found perfectly evil at every level of evils and perfectly opposed to goodness at every level of goods. In each threefold degree he will burn with all his strength, and in both directions he will fully extend the powers of his malice. Thus he will see to it that lesser evils begin and intermediate evils advance, so as to hold the greatest, as it were, in his hand; and conversely he will crush good things as they begin and impede them as they grow, so that he does not cease, insofar as possible, to diminish what is highest and perfect. He is therefore rightly comprehended under such a number: perfectly evil in the least, intermediate, and greatest evils, and perfectly opposed to the perfection of the corresponding goods.

Therefore, the second beast is the false rule of false Christians; the first beast in this chapter is Antichrist; the description of the beast is the description of Antichrist raging beastially against the faithful of the Church.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Lamb and the one hundred and forty-four thousand.

[Col. 0809C]

“And I saw, and behold, the Lamb stood upon Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written upon their foreheads” (Rev. XIV).

Above he described the most grievous persecution to be inflicted on the saints by Antichrist and his disciples, both false Christians and pagans. Now he adds Christ the helper with his household. And in order to console more fully his afflicted elect, he seems to designate those who are more exalted in merit before God: namely, those who through the incorruption of virginity and at the same time through the torment of suffering have deserved to be joined to the heavenly Lamb. For those are worthier before God who shine in these two virtues, because they draw nearer to him than all others. Such persons follow him wherever he goes, because they imitate him not only through bodily integrity but through the bitterness of suffering.

“And I saw,” namely, through spiritual understanding, “and behold, the Lamb,” through innocence, “stood,” as if ready to help, “upon Mount Zion,” because he transcends the excellence of the faithful who contemplate him. “And with him,” because, conformed to him in righteousness, they too stood—understand: because they also are helpers—“one hundred and forty-four thousand,” that is, the companies of all martyrs incorrupt in body. They are well called one hundred and forty-four thousand: one hundred, because of expectation of the heavenly homeland; forty, through fulfilment of the law and of the four Gospels; [Col. 0810A] four, through exercise of the four virtues; thousands, through the consummation of all righteousness. Since we have explained more fully above the meaning of these numbers, we do not now care to repeat it.

But it should be carefully noted that the very one hundred and forty-four thousand stand upon Mount Zion because they transcend the sublimity of other faithful persons. They have “his name,” that is, the faith by which they are called Christians, “and the name of his Father,” that is, the faith by which they are called children of God, written through unfailing perseverance “upon their foreheads,” through open confession. And it rightly places first the name of the Lamb and then the name of his Father, because no one comes to the Father except through the mediator between God and human beings. Their splendid and manifold righteousness and dignity are described in what follows after the faith which has been proclaimed. It follows:

“And I heard a voice from heaven like the sound of many waters and like the sound of great thunder. And the voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing their harps. And they were singing, as it were, a new song before the throne of God and before the four living creatures and the elders.”

“And I heard a voice from heaven”: voice signifies divine instruction; heaven, the perfect persons mentioned above who are with the Lamb through their heavenly manner of life. Thus the voice comes from heaven because divine instruction descends from the perfect to the imperfect. This voice is aptly said to be like the sound of many waters because the whole body of the saints, shining through the integrity of virginity and the merit of suffering, and singing through the ministry of preaching and the rejoicing of divine praise, is gathered from many peoples. It is rightly also said to be like the sound of great thunder because it terribly threatens the reprobate with damnation.

And because they preach what is right not merely in speech but also in action, it is fittingly added: “And the voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing their harps.” The harp, which is struck by the hands in order to give a sound, signifies good action, appropriately performed by the hands. And after saying “harps,” it rightly adds “their own,” not those of others. This is what the Apostle says: “Let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Gal. II). But because through what they say or do they do not commend themselves, but praise the author and giver of good, it is rightly added: [Col. 0810D] “And they were singing, as it were, a new song before the throne of God and before the four living creatures and the elders.”

For after the matters mentioned above, the saints sing a song before the throne of God because they praise divine goodness for benefits received. This song is called not new, but as it were new, so that its imperfection may be understood to endure until the glorification of bodies. For then it will be truly and perfectly new, when after the general resurrection it shall be consummated according to both aspects of our nature. Then there will be true newness, when all oldness has perished. “Before the throne of God,” that is, in the presence of the angels in whom God dwells and through whom he exercises his judgments. “Before the four living creatures,” [Col. 0811A] that is, in the presence of all preachers; “and before the elders,” namely, in the presence of ecclesiastical judges.

Therefore let the holy theologian, describing through a heavenly vision the dignity of the saints who help us together with Christ, say: “And I heard a voice,” namely, through divine instruction, “from heaven,” that is, from those whose manner of life is in heavenly things, “like the sound of many waters,” because they are gathered from many peoples; “like the sound of thunder,” because they threaten the reprobate with damnation; “like that of harpists,” through good works; “and they were singing, as it were, a new song,” through thanksgiving, “before the throne of God and before the four living creatures and the elders,” that is, in the presence of angels, namely holy spirits, and of human beings through whom God exercises his judgments [Col. 0811B] and fulfils his mysteries in manifold ways.

But he also plainly shows that no one can equal them in merits when he adds: “And no one could sing the song except those one hundred and forty-four thousand.” No one could sing the song because no one else can attain their merit: “who were bought from the earth,” that is, redeemed by Christ’s blood and raised from earthly desire. He distinguishes their virtue more clearly when he says: “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes.” Where he says, “for they are virgins,” he openly testifies to the integrity of their virginity. Where he adds, “these follow the Lamb wherever he goes,” he joins also the merit of suffering. Surely those follow him wherever he goes who imitate him in both respects.

But if anyone says that what is stated in this chapter concerning the one hundred and forty-four thousand is to be referred to both virtues, he will by no means depart from the rightness of the meaning. For those are believed to follow him wherever he goes who are proved to imitate him in incorruption of mind and body. He raises their praise still higher, saying: “These were bought from among human beings, firstfruits to God and to the Lamb; and in their mouth no lie was found. They are without blemish before the throne of God.” They were bought from among all people as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb because, redeemed by Christ’s blood and exalted in merit before God, they are first not in time but in dignity. “In whose mouth no lie was found,” because of their sincere confession of truth; “and they are without blemish before the throne of God,” through their inviolate observance of chastity.

Therefore the saints placed amid persecution ought not at all to be afraid, since they know that they have so great a helper, with a household of such great dignity. Thus the Lamb is Christ; Mount Zion, the sublimity of the faithful; the one hundred and forty-four thousand, the companies of virgins; the voice of thunder, the terrible threat of damnation; harps, the effects of good work; song, thanksgiving for benefits received; purchase from the earth, redemption from earthly desire.

## CHAPTER VII. On the three angels preaching successively.

[Col. 0812A]

“And I saw another angel flying through the midst of heaven, having the eternal Gospel, that he might proclaim the Gospel to those seated upon the earth, and to every nation and tribe and language and people, saying with a great voice: ‘Fear God and give him honour, because the day of judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them and springs of waters’” (Rev. XIV).

After describing above the most grievous persecution to be inflicted upon the faithful by Antichrist through the two beasts, and, for the consolation of the elect, the excellence of the Lamb with his household, he next adds an exhortation that we should come to Christ, a prophecy of Babylon’s ruin so that we may not trust in her glory, and a threat of damnation against those who worship Antichrist, so that we may fear to serve him. All these things are accomplished through the ministry of three angels, because of faith in the holy Trinity and the mystery of the three principal virtues—faith, hope, and charity.

For all preachers, signified by the angels, are rightly represented by the number three, since, although they succeed one another at different times, they unanimously preach faith in the undivided Trinity and commend to the elect the mystery of the three principal virtues. Inspired by the one and same Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills, they thunder the word of salvation to the world in various ways and administer to each person what is right. Thus the first angel in this chapter gently indicates, according to his office, that we should worship the true God. The second foretells Babylon’s ruin. The third forbids worship of the beast and frightens its worshippers by punishment.

Yet although each has his own gift from God and maintains his own manner of speaking and teaching, all preach the one power of the one mystery of human redemption, and proclaim that through righteousness one must come to one homeland. “And I saw another angel,” that is, an order of preachers; another than Christ, by as much as a servant differs from a lord; “flying,” through the swiftness and sublimity of preaching, “through the midst of heaven,” that is, the Church, lofty in virtues and bright with the splendour of divine knowledge; “having the eternal Gospel,” through its promise of eternity, “that he might proclaim the Gospel,” through the administration of his office, “to those seated upon the earth,” [Col. 0812D] that is, to the elect who rest sweetly in God through subduing earthly desire.

For eternal gifts must be announced to those who know how powerfully to subdue earthly things. “And to every nation and tribe and language and people.” Here, as often happens in many places, *and* is used in the sense of “that is.” For it explains what it first said—“to those seated upon the earth”—when it adds, “and to every nation and tribe and language and people.” For these are, even literally, those who sit upon the earth: that is, every nation, tribe, language, and people. “Every,” not merely one, because divine grace chooses from all.

[Col. 0813A] And note that it says “upon,” because every good gift and every perfect gift comes down from above, from the Father of lights. “Saying with a great voice,” that is, with great earnestness of exhortation. It follows: “Fear God,” namely, with chaste love; “and give him honour,” by singing praise and performing good works; and see that you do not fail, “because the day of his judgment has come,” so that your persecutors may be punished and you may receive the reward of merit. “And worship him who made heaven and earth and sea and all things that are in them and springs of waters.” Worship him through right faith, who made these things by his power. He made not only heaven, earth, and sea—that is, the greatest things—but also springs of waters, that is, the least. For he who deigned to create all these things for us is worthy of faith and veneration.

It follows: “And another angel followed, saying: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon, that great city, which has made all nations drink of the wine of her fornication.’” After he has above exhorted us to come to Christ in right faith, he immediately affirms the ruin of Babylon, that is, worldly confusion, so that we may not trust in her glory. “And another angel followed”: another angel, another order of preachers. “Another,” in manner or order of teaching; “angel,” in the office of preaching. Saying: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon, that great city.” He says “fallen” twice because the whole body of evildoers tossed about in the confusion of the present age falls in a twofold way. He uses the past tense because he shows what is future as certain and firm as though it were past.

Thus Babylon falls by thinking evil, falls by committing evil, falls in the world, falls in hell: in the world through wicked action; in hell through eternal damnation. It is a city because fortified by perverse teaching; great in multitude and pride. “Which has made all nations drink of the wine of the wrath of her fornication”: that is, it has corrupted all who desire to live as pagans, by the zealous wrath with which it is enraged against Christ and has committed fornication with Antichrist. Therefore no one should trust in its glory, since it is certain that it will fall. It follows:

“And the third angel followed them, saying with a great voice: ‘If anyone worships the beast and its image and receives its mark upon his forehead or upon his hand, he too shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is mixed with unmixed wine in the cup of his wrath.’”

After exhorting in the preceding passages that we join ourselves to Christ, the true helper, and that we not trust in the glory of Babylon, which is to fall, he next adds a threat of punishment against those who worship Antichrist, so that we may fear to serve him. “And the third angel followed them,” that is, the order of preachers teaching faith in the holy Trinity and the mystery of the three principal virtues; it followed in temporal order, not by imitation of belief. “Saying with a great voice,” through earnestness in preaching: “If anyone worships,” through impious faith, “the beast,” that is, Antichrist, who is a beast through cruelty, “and its image,” making himself conform to its imitators, “and receives the mark,” that is, the seal of its name, “upon his forehead,” through open confession, “or upon his hand,” through the performance of evil works, “he too shall drink”—understand: [Col. 0814A] as Babylon does—“of the wine of the wrath of God,” namely eternal damnation, which God, being angry, gives to drink, “which is mixed unmixed,” that is, pure vengeance, “in his cup,” that is, in his judgment. And it appropriately says “mixed,” because different persons suffer different torments in the one place of perdition. It follows:

“And he shall be tormented with fire and sulphur in the sight of the holy angels and before the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of his torments shall ascend for ages of ages. And those who worshipped the beast and its image, and whoever received the mark of its name, have no rest day or night.”

What it said above, “he shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God,” it explains when it adds: “And he shall be tormented with fire and sulphur.” As stated above, “he shall drink” signifies the punishment of sinners—that is, “he shall be tormented”—with fire and sulphur, a burning stench. For whoever here burns with foul lust shall there endure a foul burning; and this shall be in the sight of the holy angels and before the presence of the Lamb, so that he may be more ashamed and, through shame, suffer greater pain. “And the smoke of their torments,” that is, the darkness which will cover these evil persons and lie over them, “shall ascend for ages of ages,” because it will endure eternally. “And they have no rest day or night,” that is, continuously: those who worshipped the beast through its reprobate faith, and its image through veneration of its attendants who have conformed themselves to it. “And whoever received the mark of its name”—understand: he shall have no rest, but shall be tormented through eternal [Col. 0814C] damnation. It follows:

Here is the patience of the saints: those who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus. This patience consists, namely, in not receiving the mark of his name; for on this account the saints will suffer tribulation and attain blessedness. They keep the commandments of God by loving God and their neighbor, and the faith of Jesus by believing and confessing him to be true God. It follows:

“And I heard a voice from heaven saying: Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.” Because above he described the most grievous persecution to be inflicted by Antichrist, he now, at the end of this chapter, consoles by the rest of blessedness those who, for Christ and in Christ, taste the bitterness of death. He says therefore: “And I heard a voice from heaven,” that is, from the heavenly vision, saying to me: “Write,” not merely in your heart [Col. 0814D], but also on parchment and among the people who hear. “Write,” lest that which ought to endure for the consolation of the elect to the end should quickly pass away. “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord,” that is, in the faith and confession of the Lord: already blessed through the first robe received, and to be made blessed through the second robe yet to be received.

As though gathering up the preceding matters, he says: You have heard in the foregoing chapters of a most grievous persecution; but do not fear to suffer death for Christ, because through it you will attain blessedness. And, in order to show them more plainly to be blessed, he confirms this by the Lord’s own testimony. For he says, “From henceforth,” that is, from death itself, “the Spirit,” that is, the Holy Trinity, who is one God, “says: that they may rest,” having received [Col. 0815A] blessedness, “from their labors,” from tribulation now past.

He shows by what means they obtain this rest when he adds: “For their works,” that is, the recompenses of the works which they performed in time, “follow them” into eternity. For whoever works well in the present age is saved in the future. Let no one, therefore, if he has time to work, suppose that he can be saved without works. For faith without works is dead, if there is time for working; but if one could not have time, will alone, together with faith, is sufficient. Great and outstanding consolation, then, is here described concerning those who die in the Lord; and one who hopes through such death to attain blessedness ought not to fear it.

Thus: the three angels preaching in succession are all preachers [Col. 0815B] teaching in the holy Church the faith of the Holy Trinity and the mystery of the three chief virtues; Babylon is the world; the beast is Antichrist; the torment of the wicked is eternal damnation; the blessedness of those dying in the Lord is heavenly recompense.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the angel signifying Christ and concerning judgment

“And I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and upon the cloud one sitting like the Son of Man, having upon his head a golden crown, and in his hand a sharp sickle” (Rev. XIV).

Having shown above the recompense of the good, by which he invites men to their fellowship, he sets forth the damnation of the ungodly, so that by fear he may lead them to the same purpose. It should be noted that in the final [Col. 0815C] chapter of this vision, as also in the other visions, he treats of the end of time. For sacred theology itself so orders its sequence that it leads the Church from its birth to the end of time, describing the manifold tribulations of the righteous and the recompenses of those who endure.

“And I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and upon the cloud one sitting like the Son of Man, having upon his head a golden crown, and in his hand a sharp sickle.” “And I saw,” through spiritual understanding, “a white cloud,” that is, the assumed humanity; and upon the cloud sat Christ himself, according to his exalted and reigning divinity, “like the Son of Man,” because, having now become impassible and immortal, he transcended the bounds of human frailty. For in this respect [Col. 0815D] he appeared in the sacred vision, as it were, no longer as Son, but “like the Son of Man”: he rose from death impassible and immortal.

“Having upon his head a golden crown”: a crown because of the unendingness of eternity, golden because of the brightness of wisdom; “and in his hand a sharp sickle,” that is, judicial sentence. He has a crown in order to crown the righteous; he has a sharp sickle in order to condemn the unrighteous. Such, indeed, is the Judge of all described in the sacred vision, so that by that very description he may be known as one who will render due rewards both to good and evil. It follows:

“And another angel came out from the temple, crying with a loud voice to him who sat upon the cloud: Send forth your sickle and reap, because the hour for reaping has come, since the harvest of the earth has dried up.” This angel is the company of the perfect saints, who will devoutly pray in the last [Col. 0816A] days. He is rightly called another angel: “another” because of lesser dignity, “angel” because of sacred preaching. He also comes out of the temple because he will excel those elect who are lesser and inferior in merit of life or in the office of preaching. He will cry with a loud voice because he will long and pray with great desire for the day of judgment, for the liberation, and for the glorification of the righteous.

“Send forth your sickle,” that is, exercise judgment, “and reap,” that is, gather the human race from the earth, “because the hour for reaping has come, since the harvest of the earth has dried up”: that is, once the number of your own people has been completed, it is now brought to its end, and the wickedness of the evil has no further place. For at present the whole multitude of the wicked still has a place, flourishes, and by bringing adversity upon the good is useful for their exercise and increase [Col. 0816B] in virtues. But then it will wholly dry up and, by afflicting the saints, will no longer bear for them the fruit of eternal salvation, when, at the end, the number of those saints has been completed and this multitude has become barren in the world with respect to their benefit. This whole multitude of the wicked is aptly denoted by the name “earth,” because it always strives to cling to earthly things.

But because our Savior graciously attends to the prayers of his own and, when he is beneficially asked, strives to fulfill them without delay, it fittingly follows: “And he who sat upon the cloud cast his sickle upon the earth, and the earth was reaped.” For the angel who sat above the cloud, at the request of the other angel, cast his sickle upon the earth and reaped the earth, because the righteous Judge, at the end of time, will exercise judgment at the prayer of the saints [Col. 0816C] and cut down earthborn men from the earth.

And because the number of the holy apostles will sit with the Judge himself and judge the world with him, it is rightly added: “And another angel came out from the temple which is in heaven, having a sharp sickle.” This other angel is fittingly understood to be the assembly of the blessed apostles, who is an angel because of preaching, and “another” in dignity. He too comes out from the temple because he surpasses, at the summit of his dignity, even the height of the holy Church established in heavenly manner of life. It is further said of him that he too had a sharp sickle together with the angel sitting above the cloud, because he will exercise judicial authority with Christ. It follows:

“And another angel came out from the altar, who has power over fire; and he cried with a loud voice to him [Col. 0816D] who had the sharp sickle, saying: Send forth your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe.” By this other angel we understand the host of blessed angels. He came out not only from the temple but also from the altar because, by the immortal condition of his nature, he transcends not only the elect of the Church but even the Redeemer himself according to his assumed humanity. For it is written concerning our Redeemer, according to the humanity of flesh which he assumed from us and for us: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. VIII).

This angel has power over fire because he restrains the burning fury of demons and wicked men. He also cried with a loud voice to him who had the sickle, because the angelic dignity itself expresses in united prayers [Col. 0817A] its desire that the Judge come swiftly and that the afflicted elect be delivered in the last times; from love and longing for human beings to be glorified, it will beseech the Judge to exercise and bring forth judgment.

“Send forth your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth.” By the harvest of the earth and by the clusters of the vine of the earth we understand the same wicked persons; yet by the vine we understand more specifically those whom the devil cultivates more diligently, like a vine, for the fruitfulness of evil. These also will be gathered as a vintage along with the harvest of the earth, because they will be condemned together with other, lesser reprobates. “Send forth your sharp sickle,” that is, exercise judicial sentence, “and gather the clusters of the vine of the earth,” that is, cut down those greater in wickedness, “because its grapes are ripe,” namely through the completion [Col. 0817B] of wickedness.
