Above, then, through the prayer of perfect human beings, the damnation of lesser evildoers was indicated, where the sacred text treated of the harvest of the earth; here, through the prayer of holy angels, the damnation of the thoroughly wicked is made known, where it treats of the vintage of the vine. For when the two angels pray, both the harvest of the earth is gathered and the clusters of the vine are harvested: because, at the end, when perfect human beings and holy angels, as was said above, beseech the Judge to execute judgment, both imperfect and perfect reprobates will be condemned. Here, indeed, the damnation of the perfectly wicked is described, as follows:

“And the angel cast his sickle upon the earth, and gathered the vine of the earth, and cast it into the great winepress of the wrath of God; [Col. 0817C] and the winepress was trodden outside the city.” Christ, the Angel of Great Counsel, will cast his sickle upon the earth by exercising judgment; he will gather the vine of the earth by removing the thoroughly wicked; he will cast them into the great winepress of the wrath of God by condemning them in hell; and the winepress will be trodden through their punishment, outside the holy city, namely the heavenly Jerusalem.

For the holy city above will be free from every fault and, equally, untouched by every punishment. The winepress of God’s wrath will be trodden outside it because the assembly of the condemned will be punished in hell. Thus the container is here put for that which it contains: the winepress is trodden because the condemned are trodden in the winepress. And because that eternal damnation will torment not only condemned human beings but demons also, it fittingly follows:

“And blood came out from the winepress as high as the bridles of the horses.” [Col. 0817D] For the cruelty of eternal damnation will torment not only wicked men, who are the horses of demons, but also the demons themselves, who are the rulers of wicked men. The reason for this damnation is more plainly set out when he adds: “For one thousand six hundred stadia,” that is, four times four hundred.

For the damnation of the wicked is measured by one thousand six hundred stadia, that is, four times four hundred, in order to show that they, now spread throughout the four parts of the world, are transgressors of the commands of the fourfold Gospel during the four seasons of the year. The suffering of the damned may also be denoted as lesser, middling, and most complete in the sixfold, hundredfold, and thousandfold numbers. For these numbers signify perfection. The damnation of all the wicked is therefore well described by such a number, so that each may be shown to be perfectly condemned in his own degree.

Thus the first angel is Christ; the second, the assembly of the perfect of the last times; the third, the choir of the holy apostles; the fourth, the host of heavenly spirits; the sharp sickle, judicial sentence; harvest or vintage, the removal of the wicked; the winepress, hell; the outflow [Col. 0818A] of blood, the cruelty of damnation; the horses, human beings; the bridles, demons; the one thousand six hundred stadia, the perfect torment of the condemned.

But, in order briefly to recall to memory what this vision contains, let us say that the sacred text, in the first chapter of this vision, treats of the temple of God opened in heaven—that is, the mystery of human redemption revealed in sacred speech—and of the ark seen—that is, the humanity assumed by the Word and believed in—and of the woman giving birth—that is, the holy Church laboring in the production of the fruit of righteousness. In the second it treats of the persecution of the dragon, that is, the ancient enemy, and of the flight of the woman, that is, the withdrawal of the holy Church to the hiddenness of spiritual life. In the third, of Michael and the dragon and their battle. [Col. 0818B] In the fourth, of the beast ascending from the sea, that is, the cruel leaders of the pagans. In the fifth, of the beast ascending from the earth, that is, the fierce leaders of false Christians. In the sixth, it treats of the Lamb and the one hundred and forty-four thousand with him, that is, of Christ and the perfect saints helping the afflicted. In the seventh, of three angels preaching in succession, that is, of all preachers announcing to the faithful the mystery of the Trinity and of the three virtues—faith, hope, and charity. In the eighth, of Christ, the last judgment, and the eternal punishment of the wicked.

It should be noted that, just as the gift of human redemption in the second vision is understood to be disclosed to the holy teachers under the opening of the seals, [Col. 0818C] and in the third to be preached to the peoples under the sounding of the trumpets, so in this fourth vision it is to be understood, under the figure of the woman giving birth, as multiplied through the effect of good work into the fruit of righteousness. Here we set down the pen with which we have thus far spoken of the fourth vision, and today we rest, so that tomorrow we may rise more eagerly to enter the fifth.

# BOOK V. CONCERNING THE FIFTH VISION

[Col. 0817]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0817D]

God, whose mercies are over all his works, [Col. 0818D] who gives to all abundantly and does not reproach, who in the darkness of present ignorance illuminates his faithful with the light of wisdom and [Col. 0819A] knowledge, and shows the narrow and arduous way which leads to life—he himself, just as he dispenses to his own knowledge of truth, the word of preaching, and the effect of good work, so inflicts on the reprobate who despise his grace the fitting punishment of vengeance. For with him, just as no good goes unrewarded, so no evil is left unpunished.

Therefore, rightly after the opening of the seals described in the second vision, the sounding of the trumpets contained in the third, and the woman’s childbirth signified in the fourth—all of which are shown to concern the good—he proceeds in the fifth vision to speak in sequence of the seven plagues, which are seen to concern the wicked. For he who confers glory upon the righteous inflicts punishment upon the reprobate despisers of grace; and this punishment [Col. 0819B] may be distinguished in two ways. One punishment is that which they sometimes suffer in the world; another is that which they will suffer in hell. The former is temporary; the latter perpetual. Accordingly, the matters written in this fifth vision concerning the seven plagues are believed especially to concern the temporal affliction of the wicked; those which follow in the sixth concern their perpetual punishment.

Yet all these things—both those contained in the fifth and those in the sixth—are written so that the righteous may receive consolation from them and the reprobate may have less excuse for their wickedness. This vision, then, treats of seven angels, the seven bowls of God’s wrath, the woman clothed in purple, the scarlet beast upon which she sits, and the mystery of both.

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the seven angels and the seven last plagues

[Col. 0819C]

“And I saw another sign in heaven, great and wonderful: seven angels having the seven last plagues, because in them the wrath of God is completed” (Rev. XV).

After all the matters pertaining to the instruction and justification of the universal Church, ascending to heavenly goods amid the world’s prosperities and adversities, had been variously described in the second, third, and fourth visions, the holy theologian proceeds to describe the rejection of those to be condemned and the manifold affliction of divine vengeance upon them; and, as usual, he arranges his narrative according to the sequence of time.

“And I saw another sign in heaven”: “I saw,” through spiritual contemplation, [Col. 0819D] “another sign,” signifying what is hidden from the reprobate, “in heaven,” in the mystery of the sacred vision; or “in heaven,” that is, in the holy Church exalted on high by a heavenly way of life. “Great and wonderful”: great in itself, wonderful to us—great in its signification, wonderful because worthy of admiration. “Seven angels having seven last plagues.” The seven angels are all preachers reborn through the grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, laboring in preaching throughout all time, which revolves in the cycle of seven days. They have seven plagues because they announce to those to be condemned all divine acts of vengeance; these plagues are called “last” because no others follow them in the world.

Truly they have plagues, because they exercise the wrath of God upon the wicked; [Col. 0820A] and truly they are last, because in the present age God inflicts no others after them. Hence it is rightly added: “Because in them the wrath of God is completed.” For the wrath of God is completed in them because, after them, when the wicked have been removed from the threshing floor of the world, God will no longer exercise a sentence of judgment in the world. It follows:

“And I saw as it were a sea of glass mingled with fire, and those who conquered the beast, and his image, and the number of his name, standing upon the sea of glass, having the harps of God and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying: Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your ways, King of the ages.”

Being about to speak of the plagues of the wicked, he first sets forth a few matters concerning the righteousness of the good, so that he may clearly show that, just as the good are free from the wickedness [Col. 0820B] of the evil, so they are also exempt from their plagues. “And I saw,” through spiritual understanding, “as it were a sea of glass,” that is, baptism, which is for the righteous the beginning and gateway of salvation: a sea, through the bitter remission of sins; glass, through the sincere, pure, and bright clarity of faith; mingled with fire, through the kindling of the Holy Spirit.

For baptism is aptly compared to a sea of glass mingled with fire, because in it remission of sin, knowledge of God, and the grace of the Holy Spirit are bestowed. “And I saw,” understood, “those who conquered the beast,” that is, Antichrist, by patiently enduring his persecution, not believing his miracles, and despising his riches and blandishments; “and his image,” understood, they conquered, by not imitating the ungodly who conform to him; “and the number [Col. 0820C] of his name,” by rejecting his mark; “standing,” through firm faith and right intention, “upon the sea,” through a higher perfection; “having the harps of God,” through good action; “singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb,” through profession and preaching of both Testaments, the Old and the New, and through thanksgiving for benefits received.

They say: “Great and wonderful are your works”: great in creation, wonderful in re-creation; or great in themselves, wonderful to us. “Lord God Almighty”: Lord by excellence, God by nature, almighty by power. “Just and true are your ways, King of the ages.” The ways of God are his ordinances, through which we come to him, or he comes to us. They are just because they render to each according to merit, and true because they lead where they promise. “King of the ages”: king by governance, of the ages by eternity; or King of the ages, because you rule their order and course. It follows:

“Who will not fear you, O Lord, and magnify your name, because you alone are merciful; for all nations will come and worship before you, because your judgments are manifest?”

As though he said: And since your works are great and wonderful, and your ways just and true, who will not fear you, Lord, with filial fear, and magnify your name by work and preaching? Who, except those, understood, who will be afflicted in the world by the aforesaid plagues and are far from fellowship with you and with us? For all the rest [Col. 0821A] will truly fear—that is, love—because you alone are merciful, giving them the grace of salvation; and they will truly magnify you, because “all,” that is, some from every people, will come in faith and worship, subjecting themselves to you, choosing and doing what pleases you.

He adds a still clearer reason for this when he says: “Because your judgments are manifest.” Since the divine judgments concerning the rejection and damnation of the wicked are manifest to the elect, divine goodness should truly and perfectly be loved by them, and its justice magnified in word and deed. Thus, in brief, he comprehends the righteousness of the saints from baptism onward in the matters mentioned, and clearly indicates through it that they are immune from evil plagues.

[Col. 0821B]

Thus: the seven angels are all preachers; the seven last plagues, the tribulations of the wicked in the present time; the sea of glass, baptism; the beast, Antichrist; victory, patience; the harps, the performance of good works; the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb, the profession of both Testaments and thanksgiving for benefits received.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the seven angels and the seven bowls given to them

“And after these things I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened, and the seven angels having the seven plagues came out, clothed in pure, white stone, and girded about their breasts with golden belts” (Rev. XV).

After he had above digressed somewhat in order to show that the people of the elect, by merit of righteousness, are removed from the plagues of the ungodly, he returns again to his subject and describes in the following chapters what evils befall the wicked according to the vicissitudes [Col. 0821C] of the times.

“And after these things I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened.” The temple is the holy Church, which Christ, its inhabitant, builds from all believers as though from diverse stones, and consecrates and sanctifies by the infusion of spiritual grace. It is also fittingly called the temple of the tabernacle of testimony: “tabernacle,” because in the present age it serves God in warfare; “testimony,” because it faithfully preserves the testimony of both Testaments. It is seen in heaven because it is known to have its way of life in heaven. It is seen not closed but open, in order to show that the entrance for those called to repentance and [Col. 0821D] the exit for teachers to preach stand open.

Thus the reprobate have less excuse for their damnation, because the testimonies of the heavenly oracle declare this temple not closed but open. For the more readily they might enter it, the more severely they will be accused for remaining outside. Therefore preachers justly threaten them with plagues, and they are themselves divinely afflicted with plagues, because they hear it declared open but despise entering it. And because holy preachers not only strengthen the elect within but also go out and preach to the reprobate that divine vengeance is imminent, it is aptly said: “And the seven angels having seven plagues came out.” For the seven angels having seven plagues go out when all preachers [Col. 0822A] preach outside the whole vengeance of God, so that, if people will not love God for his promises, they may at least fear him for his threats; and if they also despise this, they may succumb to heavier punishments, not only now but without end at the last.

But because the holy action of preachers is never separated from their office, and their action always agrees with their office in all things, they are rightly described as clothed in pure, white stone and girded about their breasts with golden belts. For attire signifies action. Thus holy preachers are clothed in pure, white stone because they are adorned with firm faith, clean from vices and bright with virtues; and they are girded about their breasts with golden belts by restraining the flow of unlawful thought through the bonds of charity.

And because what holy preachers will preach until the end [Col. 0822B] of the age they receive from the institution of the earlier Fathers, it fittingly follows:

“And one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls, full of the wrath of God, who lives for ages of ages.” One of the living creatures gave the seven angels seven bowls full of the wrath of God who lives for ages of ages, because the word of preachers is strengthened and confirmed by the uniform and common testimony and authority of the four Evangelists. This word is rightly compared to golden bowls because it is brightly and clearly illuminated through divine wisdom. These bowls are also said to be full of the wrath of God who lives for ages of ages because, complete and perfect, they threaten the reprobate with the wrath of God, ever living, for the infliction of vengeance.

[Col. 0822C]

But because the divine judgment manifested to the righteous through the golden bowls is hidden from the ungodly by the smoke of ignorance, lest they understand it, it fittingly follows:

“And the temple was filled with smoke from the majesty of God and from his power.” For when the seven bowls are given to the seven angels, the temple is filled with smoke, because the heavenly judgment which is divinely revealed to the elect is wholly hidden from the reprobate, as unworthy, amid the disturbances of the present time, by the majesty of God and by his powers; for when the highest and almighty God closes, no one opens. It follows:

“And no one was able to enter into the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels should be completed.” When the temple is filled with smoke, no one can enter because no reprobate person, blinded by ignorance with God’s permission, can recognize [Col. 0822D] the rectitude of divine judgment. Hence he often blasphemes the name of God as though God acted wrongly, because he does not know the justice of his judgment.

But after the plagues are complete, they will enter in a manner of speaking: because, when the tribulations of the present time are ended and eternal torments follow, they will understand that they are justly punished and that the righteous are rightly made blessed—something they do not recognize at all now. Yet this entrance will by no means be for their joy, but for an increase of punishment. For they will suffer unspeakably in seeing that they are deservedly condemned and have justly merited the eternal wrath of God.

Therefore, when the seven plagues are completed, the wicked who are now outside through ignorance of just judgment will enter the temple, because when the evils by which they are punished in the present age [Col. 0823A]—which revolves in the cycle of seven days—have ended, they will know the divine judgment to be just. They will enter through knowledge of God’s justice over them, but they will remain outside through enduring the punishment that rages. Both will cooperate for their evil: both that they enter and that they remain outside. For by entering they will endure an evil conscience; by remaining outside, dreadful punishment.

Otherwise: “Until the seven plagues should be completed,” that is, never. For whoever neglects to enter now will by no means enter then. Otherwise: no one can enter because even the saints cannot perfectly know the hidden things of divine judgment in the present life. Then, indeed, they will enter perfectly, when time has ended and they see all things openly.

And because no one ought rashly to usurp for himself the office of preaching, but must receive the command to exercise that ministry either from God through inward inspiration or outwardly from a human superior, it fittingly follows:

[Col. 0823B]

“And I heard a voice saying to the seven angels: Go, and pour out the seven bowls of the wrath of God upon the earth” (Rev. XVI). The angels are commanded from heaven to pour out the bowls of God’s wrath in order to show that no one should undertake so great a ministry in confidence in himself alone. We read that some were chosen and appointed to preach by the teaching of the Holy Spirit alone; others, in whom no equally evident sign of so great a teaching was seen, were sent to preach by their superiors. But whoever receives this office in either manner ought to exercise it confidently, with the conscience of a good life as companion.

“Go, and pour out the bowls of the wrath of God upon the earth.” As though he said: You who are good, make progress insofar as concerns yourselves, and exercise condemnation upon the evil. “Upon the earth,” that is, upon earthly persons, who love earthly things and prefer earthly to heavenly things.

Thus the temple opened is the holy Church, ready to be entered by penitents; the seven angels, all preachers; one of the four living creatures, the unity of the four Evangelists; the filling of the temple with smoke, the people’s ignorance concerning divine judgment; the voice from heaven, divine admonition; [Col. 0823C] the pouring out of the bowls of God’s wrath, the preaching or also the stirring up of divine judgment.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the first angel and his bowl

[Col. 0823D]

“And the first went and poured out his bowl upon the earth, and there came a cruel and most grievous sore upon the people who had the mark of the beast and those who worshiped his image” (Rev. XVI).

Having completed above those matters which had to be said before beginning the narrative, he begins his account, as he is accustomed to do in the other visions, from the beginning of the Church’s birth and leads it, according to the progress of time, to the end of the world.

“And the first angel went and poured out his bowl upon the earth.” The first angel is the first order of preachers; the pouring out of the bowl is the preaching of impending divine wrath. In this place, however, “earth” denotes Judea, so long as it remained unmoved in faith in the one God. Thus the first angel poured out his bowl when the first order of preachers foretold that destruction would come upon [Col. 0824A] Judea because of the fault of unbelief.

And because, after that first preaching was made in Judea, its rejection, destruction, and scattering immediately occurred, it fittingly follows: “And there came a cruel and most grievous sore upon the people who had the mark of the beast.” When the first bowl was poured out, a cruel and most grievous sore came upon those who had the mark of the beast because, once the preaching of the earliest preachers had been proclaimed and faithless Judea left in unbelief, the cruel and most grievous wound of divine vengeance immediately came upon them: both the blow of rejection and the infliction of destruction.

For not only was the Jewish nation rejected from divine election by this wound, but it was also uprooted from the seat of its dwelling. [Col. 0824B] “Upon the people who had the mark of the beast, and upon those who worshiped his image,” that is, the Jews, who are conformed to Antichrist by opposing Christ’s faith and conform themselves to his followers by imitating them. For all evil people have the mark of Antichrist insofar as, by living wickedly, they fulfill his will. All worship his image insofar as they conform themselves to his imitators.

Thus the first angel is the first order of preachers; the pouring out of the bowl, the threat of divine vengeance; the earth, Judea; the cruel and most grievous sore, the rejection and desolation of the Jews.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the second angel and his bowl

[Col. 0824C]

“And the second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became blood like that of a dead man, and every living soul died in the sea” (Rev. XVI).

[Col. 0824D]

Just as above we understood Judea, remaining in belief in one God, by “earth,” so here we understand paganism, tossed about by a diversity of gods, by “sea.” Thus the second angel poured out his bowl into the sea when the second order of preachers announced that divine vengeance was imminent for the reprobate among the nations who remained in unbelief. “And it became blood like that of a dead man,” because divine vengeance immediately followed even in the present life, a likeness of the future torment, which turns black for the condemned in the darkness of hell.

For a dead man’s blood turns black; and therefore, because it is said not to be “blood of a dead man” but “blood like that of a dead man,” temporal vengeance is suitably understood, whereas eternal vengeance presents not the likeness but the reality of death or of a dead man. Otherwise: blood is described as becoming like that of a dead man in order to signify that that portion of paganism which remains in unbelief loses the gift of life through rejection. Hence it fittingly follows: “And every living soul died in the sea.” For every living soul dies in the sea because the reprobate portion of paganism, which chooses to live for this world, is deprived of eternal life.

Thus the second angel is the second order of preachers; the pouring out of the bowl, the preaching of divine vengeance; the blood made, the effect of vengeance; every living soul dead in the sea, that portion of paganism which lives for the world and is rejected from divine election.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the third angel and his bowl

[Col. 0825A]

“And the third angel poured out his bowl upon the rivers and upon the springs of waters, and they became blood” (Rev. XVI).

The sentence of vengeance is ordered according to the progress of impiety. First, God rejected and scattered Judea because of unbelief. Second, he cast down the nations that remained in unbelief and persecuted the sacred faith. Third, he drove out heretics and schismatics according to the deserts of their wickedness. For the matters contained in this chapter are shown to concern heretics who corrupt sacred Scripture.

“And the third angel poured out his bowl upon the rivers and upon the springs [Col. 0825B] of waters, and they became blood.” The third angel poured out his bowl upon the rivers and springs of waters when the third order of preachers announced that sacred Scripture, denoted by the name “springs,” and its expositions, denoted by the name “rivers,” would be corrupted in great measure by the perversity of heretics, and that they ought therefore to be severely punished. “And they became blood,” because the sentence of vengeance followed.

And because the overthrow of the ungodly is followed by the rejoicing and praise of the righteous, it is fittingly added:

And I heard the angel of the waters saying: “You are just, O Lord, who are and who were, the Holy One, because you have judged these things; for they have shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink, as they deserve.” The angel of the waters is the choir of teachers, which especially rejoices at the destruction of heretics and [Col. 0825C] praises the divine justice, saying: “You are just, O Lord, who are and who were, because you have judged these things.” Just, in maintaining equity; Lord, in presiding over all; who are, unchangeably; who were always holy, because free from fault; because you have judged these things, that is, you have scattered and condemned the wicked, impious, and heretical.

And it must be carefully observed that, where he says “who are and who were,” he did not add the future, because he understood that God was already, in the present, exercising vengeance in the destruction of heretics. He also openly declares that they deserved divine retribution when he says: “For they have shed the blood of saints,” that is, of the lesser elect, “and of prophets,” that is, of the greater ones—of their own will, inspired by the devil’s suggestion, and sometimes supported by the proud authority of impious princes [Col. 0825D]. “And you have given them blood to drink,” through bitter vengeance, “as they deserve,” through the perversity of their impiety. And because what the masters proclaim the disciples confirm, it fittingly follows:

“And I heard another angel saying: ‘Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are your judgments.’” And I heard another angel, that is, the body of subjects, speaking—that is, confirming the words of the masters. “Yes,” that is, what is said is true: “Lord,” by excellence; “God,” by nature; “Almighty,” by power. “True and just are your judgments”: true, because they accomplish what they promise; just, because they render recompense according to merit. For it is just that those who act cruelly should be punished cruelly.

[Col. 0826A] And it should be noted that both disciples and masters, with great devotion, direct their speech to God and declare him just. Therefore, the third angel is the third order of preachers; the pouring out of the bowl upon the rivers and fountains of waters is the condemnation of heretical opinions; the becoming blood is the effect of vengeance; the angel of the waters is the choir of teachers; the other angel is the number of subjects; the voice of both is praise of divine justice in the destruction of impious heretics.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Fourth Angel and His Bowl

“And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, [Col. 0826B] and it was given to him to afflict human beings with heat and fire. And human beings were scorched by great heat, and they blasphemed the name of God, who has power over these plagues; nor did they repent, so as to give him glory” (Rev. XVI).

All the matters contained in this fourth chapter, and in the fifth and sixth, appear to concern Antichrist and his accomplices. Yet what is described in this fourth chapter concerns Antichrist, who is the head of evils; what follows in the fifth concerns impious persons who have not been baptized; and finally, the remaining matters added in the sixth concern those baptized persons who will apostatize from Christ’s faith and serve Antichrist together with unbelievers. Since all of them choose to serve the accursed ruler Antichrist, they will not escape, together with him, the pouring out of the bowls in divine vengeance [Col. 0826C].

“And the fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun,” that is, upon Antichrist, who will be said to illumine the world by his own brightness. “And it was given to him,” namely by divine permission, “to afflict human beings”—that is, the reprobate whom he will forcibly make conform to himself—“with heat,” that is, through a lesser tribulation, “and fire,” that is, through a greater tribulation. “And human beings were scorched by great heat,” failing under the exceedingly severe tribulation brought upon them; “and they blasphemed the name of God,” through impatience, who “has power over these plagues,” because he applies them to whom he wills and removes them from whom he wills.

So bitter a divine vengeance will the reprobate deserve in the days of Antichrist that they will burst into blasphemy of the divine name. And, what is more serious, not only will they burst into blasphemy [Col. 0826D], but neither will they repent. It is serious to sin, but more serious not to repent; most serious of all is to undergo eternal torments for sin and impenitence. In the first there is guilt; in the second, obstinacy; in the third, punishment for both. Thus the fourth angel is the fourth order of preachers; the pouring out of the bowl is the preaching—or rather the infliction—of divine vengeance; the scorching of human beings is their affliction.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Fifth Angel and His Bowl

“And the fifth angel poured out his bowl upon the throne of the beast, and his kingdom became dark. And human beings gnawed their tongues because of [Col. 0827A] pain, and blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and wounds, and did not repent of their deeds” (Rev. XVI).

The matters described in this chapter seem especially to concern those unbelievers who do not receive baptism. For they are always, and without any interval of time, the beast’s throne, because they continually submit themselves to Antichrist’s condemnation. The beast particularly makes them its throne because it rests securely in them and, through them, directs others to commit impiety and persecute the good. For it does not always sit upon those who are baptized, because, so long as they preserve grace, it has no dominion over them. Therefore those are principally the beast’s throne who continuously, always, and without interruption subject themselves through unbelief to its rule [Col. 0827B].

Accordingly, the fifth angel will pour out his bowl upon the beast’s throne when the fifth succession of preachers proclaims that the unbelieving nations, which are always Antichrist’s throne, will in his days be more greatly blinded through the working of divine vengeance. Hence it fittingly follows: “And his kingdom became dark,” that is, more deeply blinded. And because, through greater blindness, they will burst forth into greater envy against the saints and greater derogation from Christ’s divinity, it fittingly follows: “And human beings gnawed their tongues because of pain,” that is, because of the envy they will have toward the saints; “and they blasphemed the God of heaven,” because they will maintain that Christ was great.

To eat one’s tongue is to waste away with envy toward another and to disparage that person’s goodness. For the person who consumes his own tongue by eating it is one who corrupts his neighbour by speech through envy and detraction [Col. 0827C], “because of their pains and wounds,” that is, because of the envy and wounds of blinding ignorance divinely inflicted upon them. Thus even the wicked themselves will endure great pain at that time. For just as the righteous groan in sorrow when they see someone lacking from Christ’s kingdom, so the reprobate in those days will grieve greatly because they cannot draw all people to Antichrist, their lord, in his novelty.

It is indeed detestable that through so great an impiety they fall into guilt; but far more detestable is that they will perform no repentance for their guilt. For concerning their impenitence it follows: “And they did not repent of [Col. 0827D] their deeds.” Great indeed is the joy not only over righteous persons persevering in righteousness, but also over sinners who repent. Therefore the fifth angel is the fifth order of preachers; the beast is Antichrist; the beast’s throne is unbelieving Gentiles; the pouring out of the bowl is the proclamation or infliction of divine vengeance; the darkness of his kingdom is the complete blinding of Gentile unbelief; the eating of tongues because of pain is wasting envy toward the saints together with reviling; the blasphemy of the God of heaven is derogation from Christ’s divinity.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Sixth Angel and His Bowl

“And the sixth angel poured out his bowl into the great river Euphrates, and dried up its waters, so that a way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun” (Rev. XVI).

Just as the matters contained in the preceding chapter are not unfittingly understood of the Gentiles, so what is written in the present chapter is aptly referred to those who have been baptized but will withdraw from Christ’s faith to the impiety of Antichrist in the final persecution. For what he writes under the fourth angel concerning the wicked generally and collectively, he distinguishes under the fifth and sixth angels particularly and separately through Gentiles and apostate Christians. Through the Euphrates, which is one of the rivers of Paradise, baptism is not unfittingly understood; and it is rightly called a great river: a river, because it washes away sins; great, because it regenerates many.

[Col. 0828A] The sixth angel poured out his bowl into this river because the sixth order of preachers will proclaim that false Christians will withdraw to Antichrist in the last days, and that through this divine vengeance will come upon them through impious blindness. The water of this river will also be dried up when, upon the approach of vengeance, the gift of spiritual grace bestowed in baptism is taken away from baptized reprobates. And a way will be prepared from the rising of the sun for the kings: that is, through apostate Christians—in whom, if they persevered in truth, the sun of righteousness ought to rise and shine—a free passage will be opened for the rulers of this darkness, the demons, to accomplish iniquity [Col. 0828B]. Hence it is fittingly said of the demons themselves:

“And I saw three unclean spirits, like frogs, come forth from the mouth of the dragon, from the mouth of the beast, and from the mouth of the false prophet.” The three unclean spirits are all the demons, attacking in the elect the sacrament of the Trinity [Col. 0828C] and the safeguard of the three chief virtues: faith, hope, and charity. They go forth from the mouth of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet because they are executors of the devil’s commands; and they will strive with all their strength, by seducing human beings, to bring to effect what will go forth from the mouth of Antichrist and his false prophets. They are also unclean like frogs because they make those whom they corrupt by suggestion loquacious through wordiness and muddy through lust. And that they are truly unclean he declares more openly when he adds:

“For they are spirits of demons, working signs. And they went forth to the kings of the whole earth, to gather them for battle on the great day of God Almighty.” Since they are spirits of demons, therefore they are unclean, “working signs,” that is, false miracles by which they deceive human beings, “going forth to the kings of the whole earth,” that is, to those who know how to govern either themselves or others in the desire for earthly things according to worldly wisdom, “to gather them for battle,” namely against the people of the faithful. But because they will do this to their own harm, it fittingly adds: “for the great day of God Almighty.” For impious demons gather reprobate human beings for battle on the great day of God Almighty because by this gathering they prepare condemnation for themselves on the day of judgment [Col. 0828D].

And so that he may more plainly declare that the Lord himself will come to judge, he introduces him affirming this same thing, saying: “Behold, I come like a thief,” that is, unexpectedly and suddenly [Col. 0829A], so that all may be uncertain of the hour of my coming and therefore better prepared. And it should be noted that he intimates his coming both by an adverb of demonstration and by a present-tense verb, in order thereby to remove the thought of a long delay and make people more attentive and watchful for his coming. He immediately adds the reward of this attentiveness or watchfulness, saying: “Blessed is the one who watches and keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame.”

For blessed is the one who watches in these matters, because the Lord will reward such a person with the reward of blessedness according to merit. “And keeps his garments,” that is, the adornments of virtues and good works, “lest he walk naked,” that is, rise at the day of judgment stripped of virtues and good works, “and they see his shame,” that is, his sins. For one who does not now watch and does not keep his garments will then walk naked and his shame will be seen, because he will rise without the adornments of virtues and good works, and his iniquity will be revealed to all [Col. 0829B]. It follows:

“And they shall gather them to the place called in Hebrew Armageddon.” He returns to the preceding sense and statement, where he said that the unclean spirits went forth to the kings of the earth and gathered them for battle. Armageddon is interpreted “mountain of thieves” or “rounded”; and it signifies Antichrist, who is a mountain through pride, of thieves through fraudulence, and rounded through cunning. The unclean spirits will gather the aforesaid kings into him—that is, into that detestable sect of impiety—because, with divine vengeance permitting, which hardened Pharaoh’s heart [Col. 0829C], they will make those kings conform to him through pride, fraudulence, and cunning.

For just as the saints are in Christ not by bodily dwelling but by spiritual faith, so the reprobate will be in Antichrist not by local dwelling but by the perpetration of iniquity. Or, as certain manuscripts have it, “he shall gather,” namely God, who will judge that they ought, deservedly and justly, because their sins demand it, to be separated from himself and joined to Antichrist. Thus the sixth angel is the sixth order of preachers; the river Euphrates is the people of the baptized; the drying of the water is the removal in the reprobate of spiritual grace; the preparing of the way for kings from the rising of the sun is free passage for demons in false Christians to accomplish iniquity; the dragon [Col. 0829D] is the devil; the beast is Antichrist; the false prophets are the company of Antichrist’s false apostles; the three unclean spirits are all the demons attacking in the elect the sacrament of the Trinity and the righteousness of the three chief virtues—faith, hope, and charity; the kings of the earth are reprobates who know how to govern either themselves or others in earthly desire; the gathering at Armageddon is their assembling to Antichrist.

For just as elect angels serve Christ in the conversion of the elect good, so demons will minister to Antichrist in the turning-away of the wicked. And just as from the beginning of the world to its end the mystery of salvation works in the elect, so in the reprobate the mystery of perdition works. And just as all righteous persons belong to Christ, so the wicked belong to Antichrist. The head of Christ [Col. 0830A] is God; the head of Antichrist is the devil. The end of those to be damned with Antichrist is Gehenna; the end of those saved with Christ is eternal life.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Seventh Angel and His Bowl

“And the seventh angel poured out his bowl into the air, and a great voice came forth from the temple, from the throne, saying: ‘It is done’” (Rev. XVI).

As he does in the other visions, so at the end of this vision he treats of the end of time. The seventh angel is the final order of preachers, which will preach after the death of Antichrist. Its bowl will fittingly be poured into the air, because the whole company of demons inhabiting this air will be grievously afflicted, through fear of the approaching judgment and eternal punishment, in the days of its preaching [Col. 0830B]. For when Antichrist has died and the seventh angel preaches, they will know with certainty that the day of judgment and Christ’s coming are at hand. Hence the imminence of both is rightly expressed: “And a great voice came forth from the temple, from the throne, saying: ‘It is done.’”

A voice will come forth from the temple, that is, from the Church; and not from any place whatever, but from the throne, that is, from those in whom the divine majesty resides and reigns, so that the more eminent the witnesses who declare the ending of the age, the more certainly it may be believed. It says: “It is done.” As though it said: “All things are completed; the end of the world is at hand.” This voice is rightly called great because what it announces is great. And because, after Antichrist’s death, some will be converted to faith through preaching, while others will be turned away through hardening to greater blindness, it fittingly follows:

“And there were lightnings, voices, thunders, and a great earthquake, such as never was since human beings began to be upon the earth—an earthquake so great.” For there will be lightnings, that is, miracles, so that those to be saved may be recalled from death; voices, that is, admonitions, so that those recalled may be strengthened in goodness; thunders, that is, threats, so that future torments may be foretold to those to be damned. And there will be a great earthquake such as has not been since human beings have been on earth, because, as has been said, some will turn to worse things. The greatness of this earthquake is stated twice in order that its magnitude may be shown more plainly. It follows:

[Col. 0830D] “And the great city became divided into three parts, and the cities of the Gentiles fell.” The things said above in this chapter concern both the good and the wicked; those that follow concern especially the wicked. In what follows he describes, under the name of the prostitute Babylon, the manifold cause of the wicked’s damnation and their consequent condemnation.

“And the great city became divided into three parts.” The great city, namely Babylon, appears destined to be divided into three parts at the end, because it is now divided according to a threefold manner of life, and then, in vengeance, will be divided according to a threefold recompense of eternal death. For it is now divided three ways in the world: according to paganism, Judaism, and false Christianity; and then, according to [Col. 0831A] this threefold sect, it will receive punishment in hell, so that those who now sin in different ways may then receive condemnation according to their merit. Pagans will be punished in one way, Jews in another, and false Christians in another.

“And the cities of the Gentiles fell,” because the assemblies of wicked persons living as Gentiles will perish. It follows:

“And great Babylon came into remembrance before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath. And every island fled, and the mountains were not found.” Babylon’s coming into divine remembrance is what he said above, more obscurely, when he spoke of the city becoming divided into three parts. Babylon—that is, the whole body of the wicked, which now lives in the confusion of vices—is a city through the gathering of many, great through pride [Col. 0831B]. It “came,” that is, will come, into remembrance before God, “to give her the cup of the wine of the indignation of his wrath,” that is, so that the measure of vengeance which God, indignant and angry, pours out may be given to her. It will come into remembrance because it will receive punishment.

For now God appears to refrain from remembering human evils while he waits for repentance; but at the end he is rightly said to bring them to remembrance when he inflicts vengeance. And because the good will by no means share the damnation of the wicked, it fittingly adds: “And every island fled, and the mountains were not found.” For every island fled, and the mountains were not found, because those who are now shaken, like islands by sea-waters, by the bitterness of persecutions yet are not moved from faith, and those who, like mountains, leave what is low and ascend to what is high, will then be wholly separated from the fellowship of those who perish [Col. 0831C]. Those who are not in guilt will not be found participants in punishment.

He openly describes the character of this punishment when he adds: “And a great hailstone, like a talent, came down from heaven upon human beings; and human beings blasphemed God because of the plague of hail, because it became exceedingly great.” The great hail is eternal punishment, like a talent, because it is weighed and measured according to the merits of those who perish. It comes down from heaven upon human beings because it will be sent by God upon those who perish. “And human beings blasphemed God because of the plague of hail.” Although the impious, placed in hell, will indeed feel that they are justly punished, nevertheless they will grieve that God has such great power [Col. 0831D], and, because of the excess of their pain, will direct blasphemy against the just judge.

Therefore, its extent is well added: the great hail became exceedingly great, because it will torment intolerably. And so that he may instruct us still more perfectly concerning matters pertaining to the wicked, in the remainder of this chapter he sets forth at length the whole body of the wicked, their empty glory, the pride of their kingdoms, and their impious cruelty toward the saints; and at its end he announces their condemnation. It follows:

“And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying: ‘Come; I shall show you the condemnation of the great prostitute, who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed fornication, and those who inhabit the earth became drunk with [Col. 0832A] the wine of her prostitution’” (Rev. XVII).

Rightly did one of the seven angels holding the bowls of God’s wrath show the holy theologian what torments await the wicked, because the unanimous unity of preachers who proclaim and execute divine wrath upon the wicked never ceases to reveal to us, in speech and writing, their everlasting damnation.

“Come, I shall show you the condemnation of the great prostitute, who sits upon many waters.” Come through spiritual understanding; I shall show you through a figurative vision the condemnation of the great prostitute, namely Babylon, which has committed fornication, abandoning God the Creator, with the devil or with this world. She sits upon many waters by reigning through her dominion over many peoples. For waters are peoples, because just as waters flow swiftly away, so peoples pass away through mortality [Col. 0832B]. Babylon sits above them because through its powerful persons it holds dominion over them.

“With whom,” that is, following whose example, “the kings of the earth committed fornication,” by abandoning God, worshipping demons, or loving the world. The kings of the earth are those who know how to govern either themselves or others in earthly desire; or “kings of the earth” may be understood literally, because the more powerful wicked persons are in authority, the worse they are in malice. They deservedly receive special mention in the description of wickedness because they are known to be more criminally defiled than others. For each person commits fornication with Babylon all the more insofar as he becomes more deeply entangled in the impurity of demons or of the present world.

When kings sin and commit fornication, sin itself becomes, in a manner of speaking, sinning beyond measure, since those who ought to govern others strive to defile themselves with crimes [Col. 0832C]. And because not only superiors but also inferiors fall into the impiety of fornication following the example of this Babylon, after speaking of the kings’ fornication he fittingly adds the drunkenness of the inhabitants of the earth. “And those who inhabit the earth became drunk with the wine of her prostitution.” Those who inhabit the earth are persons who love earthly more than heavenly things. They are rightly said to inhabit the earth because they do not swiftly pass through it but remain fixed in their love of earthly things. They are made drunk with the wine of her prostitution—that is, with the teaching of manifest fornication—because they do not soberly weigh the gravity of the evil they do. For as drunkards fear nothing, so they are blinded while they cling immoderately to earthly things, so that they neither love God nor thereafter fear punishments [Col. 0832D]. It follows:

“And he carried me away in the Spirit into the wilderness; and I saw a woman seated upon a scarlet beast, full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns. And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls, having in her hand a golden cup full of the abomination and impurity of her fornication; and upon her forehead was written a name of mystery: Great Babylon, mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth.”

He describes the manifold impiety of the reprobate in order thereby to show that they deserve damnation. “And he carried [Col. 0833A] me away in the Spirit,” namely to see higher things, “into the wilderness,” to contemplate the hearts of the reprobate, which are deserted by God. “And I saw,” through spiritual contemplation, “a woman seated,” that is, the soft and effeminate whole body of the wicked, resting “upon a scarlet beast,” that is, diabolical savagery made red by the blood of saints. She is upon the scarlet beast because wherever evil is perpetrated, there it has a diabolical foundation; “full of names of blasphemy,” because it says that the evil it does does not displease God; “having seven heads and ten horns”—we pass over this here without explanation, in order to expound it better below.

“And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls,” because the assembly of the wicked always strives to adorn itself with glory, riches, and the ornaments of this present age [Col. 0833B]. She also has a golden cup in her hand because she practises an impious doctrine, shining with the brilliance of worldly wisdom and manifest in action, so that by intoxicating others she may draw them into guilt and make them sharers in her damnation. It is “full of the abomination and impurity of fornication,” that is, of the abominable and unclean veneration of an accursed cult, or of the pleasure of unlawful desire. “And upon her forehead was written a name of mystery,” because by open profession she shows what she possesses in the hidden place of her mind, like a prostitute who displays on her forehead by adornment what she carries in her heart by impure will.

Therefore no one is excused if he commits fornication with her, since he can openly recognize the evil that he ought to avoid [Col. 0833C]. For it is written: “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. VII). “Great Babylon, mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth”: Babylon through confusion; great through pride; mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth through the invention of abominable vices, by which all are defiled who entangle themselves in earthly desire. It follows:

“And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus. And I was greatly amazed when I saw that woman.” Above he showed what Babylon is in its own viciousness; now he adds what it is in the persecution of the elect. “I saw the woman drunk with the blood of saints,” that is, of the lesser ones, “and of the martyrs of Jesus,” that is, of the greater ones. “I saw her drunk,” that is, satisfied beyond measure, because in conquering them by killing them she exulted beyond measure, like a drunkard.

But just as Saint John in the preceding passage, from the words, “Come, I shall show you the condemnation of the great prostitute,” down to this point, bore the person of one speaking, so here, where it says, “And I was greatly amazed when I saw that woman,” he bears the person of one who marvels and does not yet perfectly contemplate the ruin of the wicked [Col. 0833D]. He therefore says: “And I was greatly amazed when I saw her.” For all who are weak and imperfect greatly marvel when they see the deceptive glory and power of the reprobate, because they do not contemplate their coming damnation. If they considered more deeply the reprobates’ future ruin and the deceptive glory of present goods, they would by no means marvel at them so greatly. But because every imperfect person is instructed by perfect teachers concerning hidden matters, it fittingly follows:

“And the angel said to me: ‘Why do you marvel? I shall tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast which carries her, which has seven heads and ten horns. The beast which you saw was and is not, and will ascend from the abyss and go to destruction. And the inhabitants of the earth, whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, will marvel when they see the beast which was and is not.’”

“Why do you marvel?” Whoever marvels too greatly at the deceptive goods of the wicked is rebuked by this question. For if he examined the matter more attentively [Col. 0834A], he would understand more clearly than light that God in his just judgment permits the impious to prosper in this age, so that they may be more justly condemned in the age to come. [Col. 0834B] “Why do you marvel?” As if he said: “Do not marvel, but understand what it is. I shall tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast,” that is, I shall show you what each is. “The beast which carries her” is the devil, because the devil always carries the wicked toward the accomplishment of malice.

And it should be noted that, in revealing the mystery, he puts the beast before the woman, because the devil precedes the whole body of the wicked. “Which has seven heads and ten horns”: this we reserve for explanation below. “The beast which you saw,” that is, the devil, through whom the people of the elect are attacked bestially and cruelly, “was,” namely before Christ’s coming, because then he exercised his dominion in the world, “and is not,” because after Christ’s coming he lost that dominion [Col. 0834C]. “And will ascend from the abyss,” that is, from profound and dark evil, in the days of Antichrist; “and will go to destruction,” because he will utterly perish on the day of judgment.

“And the inhabitants of the earth, whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, will marvel when they see the beast which was and is not,” because the wicked, seeing that its power has been annihilated at the end, will grieve—not as penitents, but merely marveling and stupified by excessive pain. The wicked are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world because by living wickedly they proved that they had not been written from the beginning. It follows:

[Col. 0834D] “And this is the meaning which has wisdom.” As though he said: This is the meaning to be applied by one who has wisdom, because the matter is obscure in what follows. For he wishes to explain somewhat what he above said obscurely under the figure of the seven heads and ten horns. After revealing the beast, he intends to demonstrate the proud eminence of the woman, which is figured in the seven heads and ten horns. It follows:

“The seven heads are seven mountains upon which the woman sits, and they are seven kings. Five have already fallen; one is; and another has not yet come. And when he comes, he must remain a short time.”

The number seven expresses totality, because the whole course of this present age runs through the cycle of seven days [Col. 0835A]. Therefore, by the seven heads, mountains, or kings is understood the whole rule of the wicked, determined according to seven periods of this age. The first period was from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to Moses; the fourth from Moses to David; the fifth from David to Christ; the sixth from Christ to Antichrist; the seventh under Antichrist.

Therefore the universal rule of the wicked, determined according to these seven divisions, is rightly designated under the figure of heads, mountains, and kings: heads because of its temporal eminence; mountains because of pride; kings because the company of the wicked is governed in evil through it. The woman is said to sit upon it because the whole body of the wicked is supported by its carnal prudence [Col. 0835B]. Of these heads, mountains, or kings, five have fallen because five of the aforementioned seven periods passed before Christ’s coming and before the time of that vision. One is now present, which, because of the prerogative and abundance of grace, is very weak, and now exercises its malice against the good as much as it can. Another has not yet come because Antichrist has not yet appeared. And when he comes, he must remain a short time, that is, reign for three and a half years. He is therefore not to be feared excessively, because he will soon pass away. Although he will rage more fiercely than all others, he will nevertheless quickly fail.

It follows:

“And the beast which was and is not is itself an eighth, and is of the seven, and goes to destruction. And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings, who have not yet received a kingdom, but have authority as kings for one hour after the beast. These have one purpose, and they will hand over their strength and authority to the beast. These will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings; and those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful.”

“And the beast which you saw,” that is, the devil, through whom the people of the elect are cruelly attacked, “which was and is not,” because it had power before Christ’s coming but lost the power it possessed at his coming, “is itself an eighth and is of the seven.” It is of the seven because it sins in the same manner and will be punished in the same manner; it is eighth because it surpasses all in wickedness and punishment; and it goes to destruction because it will perish eternally [Col. 0835D].

“And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings.” Having described above the mystery of the seven heads, he adds the mystery of the ten horns. The ten horns are ten kings who, according to Daniel’s prophecy, will reign in the time of Antichrist. It is well said of them that they have not yet received a kingdom, because they have not yet come. “But they receive authority as kings for one hour,” that is, they will receive it—the words “when they come” being understood. “As kings,” because they will not be true kings but tyrants; “for one hour,” because they will endure only a short time after the beast.

Their shared wickedness is described below, where it says: “These have one purpose,” namely, to deny Christ, believe Antichrist, persecute the former [Christ], and follow the latter [Antichrist] [Col. 0836A]. “And they will hand over their strength and authority to the beast”: they will hand over to the beast the strength that they possess in themselves and the authority that they exercise over others, because they will ascribe to the devil whatever wickedness they perpetrate.

He further describes their audacious presumption and the shame resulting from it, saying: “These will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings.” They will fight with the Lamb in word and deed, attempting to take his elect away from Christ; but he will conquer them by restraining their audacity. And he declares that he can truly do this when he says, “because he is Lord of lords and King of kings,” possessing such power that he even uses the wicked for the benefit of the faithful.

But his elect, too, will keep such faith toward him that they will bravely overcome their enemies together with Christ their leader. Hence it is added: “And those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful”: with him through the profession of Christianity; called through preaching; chosen through predestination; and faithful through integrity of faith [Col. 0836B]. Therefore, in that final battle the host of enemies will be overthrown, because so great is the power of our leader and so firm the faith of his soldiers. It follows:

The waters that you saw, where the harlot sits—that is, in which she holds dominion through her kings—are peoples, nations, and tongues: namely, evil subjects gathered from every diversity of nations. The waters are peoples; for just as waters flow away in their instability, so peoples pass away in their mortality. It follows:

[Col. 0836C] “And the ten horns which you saw, and the beast, these will hate the harlot, and will make her desolate and naked. They will eat her flesh and burn her with fire.” Having sufficiently explained above the mystery of the woman and the beast, he adds how great a calamity the devil and his satellites—figured by the beast and the horns—will bring upon the wretched totality of the wicked. The horns and the beast, that is, the devil and the impious kings of the wicked, will hate the harlot, that is, the whole assembly of the wicked, separated from God the Creator by unlawful love. For that ought not to be called love by which impious teaching separates her from God, by which temporal blandishments seduce her, and by which seduction leads her to the gates of hell. These, therefore, will hate the harlot because they will bring her to punishment.

[Col. 0836D] For if they truly loved her, they would by no means prepare her for eternal fires. And they will make her desolate and naked, because by fraudulently seducing her they will now make her such in the world that afterward she may groan in hell, desolate and stripped of temporal joy and comfort. And they will eat her flesh, because they will rejoice in her bodily condemnation. For this is to eat her flesh: to exult in the torment of her flesh. For just as Christ and the holy angels will rejoice over the glory of the good, so the devil and his ministers will rejoice over the punishment of the wicked. Yet this joy will by no means turn for the devil and his princes into an increase of consolation, but into an increase of greater pain. And they will burn her with fire,

[Col. 0837A] because they themselves will administer the eternal fire. And because whatever evil comes upon the wicked is wholly brought about by God’s judgment and just permission, it fittingly follows:

“For God has given them to do what is pleasing to him, to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God are fulfilled.” God gives, by just permission, that the wicked may do by open action what is pleasing to him in view of the beauty and usefulness of the whole creation. For the Almighty would by no means permit evils to exist unless some good accrued to the whole creation from them. Indeed, because evils exist, good things seem to possess a greater beauty in comparison with them. Yet God is not unjust because he permits the wicked to act wickedly; for it is just that those to whom he has granted free choice should be allowed to use it as they please. For it would be unjust

[Col. 0837B] if he imposed upon those to whom, in their creation, he grants the freedom to choose good or evil by the gift of grace the necessity of good alone. In this, indeed, a rational creature possesses outstanding dignity: that it renders service to its Creator not under compulsion, but freely. Therefore, it is pleasing that, under him and by his gift, we use freedom of choice; but it is displeasing that, through perversity of will arising in us, we resist him. For the free power of choice implanted by God is not evil; rather, the perverse will arising under that choice is evil. Freedom is given by God; the creature abuses the gift of freedom. Therefore, in the production of evil, as regards the wicked there is nothing good; as regards God’s good pleasure there is nothing evil. For what they do is evil; what is pleasing to God is good.

“To give their kingdom to the beast”: that is, to allow themselves to be ruled by the devil and to attribute their own power to the devil, until the words of God are fulfilled—that is, until all things reach their end, and the wicked and the good receive what has been promised them. For God now permits the wicked, established in wickedness and in the kingdom of the devil, to employ great freedom, and to test, assail, and tear the good to pieces; when the age is ended, this will cease entirely. But because in this chapter he has denoted the totality of the wicked by different names, he fittingly adds, in order to show that this can appropriately be so:

“And the woman whom you saw is the great city which has dominion over the kings of the earth.” This same totality of the wicked is a woman, a great city, a harlot, Babylon. She is a woman because she softens;

[Col. 0837D] she is a city because she gathers many; she is great because she is proud; she is a harlot because she submits herself to the devil, her corrupter;

[Col. 0838A] she is Babylon because she is confused and confounds. “Which has dominion over the kings of the earth,” because all serve her and increase her commonwealth insofar as they can. Thus the seventh angel is the final order of preachers; the pouring out of the bowl into the air is divine vengeance upon the power of this air, namely, the host of demons. The voice from the temple saying, “It is done,” is the Church’s testimony that the age is now to be ended; lightnings are miracles; voices, admonitions; thunders, threats; the great earthquake, the conversion of those to be saved and the greater blinding of those to be damned; the great city, the congregation of the wicked; the great hail, eternal damnation; the beast which bears the woman, the devil who bears and sustains the wicked in evil; the seven heads, the eminent universal rule of the wicked according to the seven conditions of this age;

[Col. 0838B] the ten horns, the ten kings who are to exist in the time of Antichrist; the waters where the harlot sits, the peoples over whom she has dominion; the fulfillment of God’s words, the end of the world; the infliction of punishment, the bestowal of reward.

In this fifth vision, which under the figure of bowls treats of divine vengeance poured out upon the wicked, sacred prophecy has dealt generally first with the seven angels and seven plagues or bowls—that is, all preachers—and with the vengeance inflicted upon all contemners of divine grace in the course of the present age. The pouring out of the bowls signifies the infliction of divine wrath upon different classes of people. The first pouring is upon the earth: that is, upon Judaea, first rejected from the faith and cast out from its land. The second

[Col. 0838C] is upon the sea: that is, upon the Gentile slayers of the faithful. The third is upon rivers and springs: that is, upon heretics who corrupt the streams of the sacred page. The fourth is upon the sun: that is, Antichrist, who claims to enlighten the world. The fifth is upon the throne of the beast: that is, the rulers of the nations, among whom Antichrist himself will sit in chief authority as he reigns. The sixth is upon the river Euphrates: that is, upon baptized reprobates, whom divine vengeance will dry up from the gift of the streams of grace. The seventh is upon the air: that is, upon the demons, whom the same vengeance at the end of time will grievously torment through fear of the impending judgment. Under this bowl the sacred vision describes more fully the cause of the wicked’s damnation and plainly shows why they will be damned at the end. And having spoken thus far of the fifth vision,

[Col. 0838D] we give our tongue rest, so that, refreshed by leisure, we may proceed to examine the sixth.

# BOOK SIX. ON THE SIXTH VISION.

[Col. 0837]

## PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0837D]

God, whose wrath no one can resist, beneath whom those who bear the world are bowed down, so inflicts temporal vengeance upon evildoers that upon those who persevere in wickedness he adds eternal punishment. Therefore sacred prophecy, after describing in the preceding vision the transitory vengeance poured out upon the wicked,

[Col. 0838D] now accordingly adds their everlasting damnation, so that those who refuse to correct themselves in the world may know that they are to be punished without end in hell. For this vision concerns the final punishments which the impious will suffer in hell. It first demonstrates this in Babylon, describing

[Col. 0839A] her fall and the lament which those who loved her will make over her downfall. It also treats of the exultation and thanksgiving which the saints will offer because of her destruction. It treats also of Christ judging her; of the invitation to demons to eat the flesh of kings, tribunes, and all the wicked; and of the condemnation of Antichrist and his false apostles. Then it returns once more and describes Satan’s binding for a thousand years, how he will again be released and rage against the saints at the end, and how he will be cast with the impious into the lake of fire. It should be known that the matters contained in the preceding five visions of this book chiefly pertain to the course of the present time; those contained in the sixth and seventh pertain more to the state

[Col. 0839B] of eternity. For in this sixth vision the eternal damnation of the wicked is described, and in the seventh the eternal blessedness of the good. The damnation of the wicked described in this vision is proclaimed by Christ at the very beginning of the vision, so that it may be heard more attentively and receive greater credence.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the fall of Babylon and the lament of her lovers.

“And after these things I saw another angel descending from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was illuminated by his glory; and he cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great; and she has become a dwelling-place of demons, and a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every

[Col. 0839C] unclean bird, because all nations have drunk of the wrath of her fornication, and all the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth have become rich through the power of her wealth’” (Rev. XVIII).

Because the sacred vision above describes the temporal punishment of the wicked, it now proceeds in order to describe their eternal damnation. “And after these things I saw another angel descending from heaven, having great authority.” This other angel is rightly believed to be Christ, who differs from the other angels as a lord differs from servants. He descended from heaven because, assuming our flesh, he visited the human race. He has great authority because he presides not only over human beings but also over angels. The earth is said to be illumined by his glory because our earthliness is enlightened by the glory of his preaching.

[Col. 0839D] Finally, he cried out in a loud voice concerning the fall of the wicked because what he preached concerning it will by no means lack fulfillment, saying: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great.” By doubling the word, he doubles the ruin and indicates a twofold vengeance. For the damned will be punished outwardly in their bodies by burning flames and inwardly wounded in mind by pressing pains. Babylon denotes confusion; “great,” the gathering of many and her own exaltation. “And she has become a dwelling-place of demons, and a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean bird.” Demons are both spirits and birds: spirits because of the subtlety of their nature, birds because of the swiftness of their motion.

[Col. 0840A] Overthrown Babylon will be their dwelling-place and prison, because the totality of the wicked, condemned and filled with demons in damnation, will remain forever subject to the torments of demons. The cause of her damnation is also declared when it adds: “Because all nations have drunk of the wrath of her fornication, and all the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth have become rich through the power of her wealth.” “Of the wrath of her fornication,” that is, of the ardor of her fornication, or of the fornication for which God is wrathful, all nations have drunk by participating in it—that is, her subjects. And all the kings of the earth—that is, the earthly prelates—have committed fornication with her, withdrawing from God after her example and loving the world. And the merchants—that is, those who sell their souls for earthly things and acquire earthly things in exchange for them—have become rich through the power of her wealth, because they consider themselves rich through the glory of her riches and take greater delight in it than in the love of heavenly things.

[Col. 0840B] Babylon, by whose crime so great a multitude of persons is defiled, will therefore justly be damned. It follows:

“And I heard another voice from heaven saying: ‘Come out from her, my people, lest you share in her sins and receive of her plagues; for her sins have reached unto heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities. Render to her as she herself rendered to you, and repay her double according to her works; in the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double. As much as she glorified herself and lived in delights, so much give her torment and mourning, because she says in her heart:

[Col. 0840C] “I sit as a queen; I am not a widow, and I shall not see mourning.” Yet in one day her plagues will come: death, mourning, and famine; and she will be burned with fire, because God, who judged her, is strong.’”

Since the fall of the wicked has been foretold above, we are warned to depart from their fellowship, lest, if we are their companions in guilt, we should share their punishment. “And I heard another voice from heaven saying.” He rightly says that he heard another voice. For one voice sounds concerning the condemnation of the reprobate; another speaks concerning the warning of the elect. The former terrifies; the latter comforts. This voice sounds from heaven because it comes from the holy Church, which conceals Christ’s most holy mysteries from the unclean and unbelieving. “Come out from her, my people, and do not share in her sins,

[Col. 0840D] lest you receive of her plagues, for her sins have reached unto heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities.” “Come out from her, my people,” not so much by bodily separation as by upright intention; do not share in her sins by consent or deed, and do not receive of her plagues in eternal damnation. He then adds the reason why, and the ground on which, Babylon will be afflicted with plagues: “For her sins have reached unto heaven,” that is, as far as contempt of God through impenitence; “and God has remembered,” that is, God will remember, her iniquities, which he now mercifully appears not to see by withholding vengeance.

“Render to her as she herself rendered to you, and repay her double according to her works.” “Render to her as she rendered to you”: that is, just as she exercised my vengeance upon you while you were being purified for salvation, so avenge my injury upon her unto damnation. “And repay her double according to her works,” so that she who did not fear to sin doubly, inwardly and outwardly, corrupting either herself or others, may be compelled by your judgment to endure a double punishment. “And in the cup in which she mixed for you, mix for her double”: that is, she who inflicted temporal torment upon you may, as you judge, endure eternal punishment. As much as she glorified herself through proud boasting and lived in delights through excessive abundance, so much give her torment and mourning: torment in body, mourning in mind. Because in her heart she says proudly, “I sit as a queen,” that is, I do not fear being deprived of honor and dignity; “and I am not a widow,”

[Col. 0841B] because I have consolation in the world; “and I shall not see mourning,” that is, the damnation which Christ’s disciples threaten that I shall suffer in hell. For proud and wealthy wicked persons, radiant with honors and delightfully attached to worldly things, are sometimes so blinded by darkness that they do not at all fear being stripped of prosperity or worn down by adversity. And because they are exalted by the goods granted them and are shown to take no precautions against future evils, he fittingly adds: “Therefore in one day”—that is, at once—“her plagues will come,” namely the punishments due to her iniquities, “and death, mourning, and famine.” Death in punishments, mourning for what has been lost, famine for what is to be recovered. “And she will be burned with fire,” because she will be punished with eternal fires. And that she will be wholly unable to escape all these punishments is declared
