[Col. 0841C] when he adds: “Because he who judged her is strong”—understand: he judged her worthy of all these evils. Strong, that is, not to be moved by any prayers on the day of vengeance. Hence Solomon says: “The jealousy and wrath of a man,” that is, of Christ, “will not spare on the day of vengeance; nor will he yield to anyone’s prayers, nor receive very many gifts for redemption” (Prov. VI).

But having designated Babylon’s fall above, he next adds the lament of her lovers, describing how the kings of the earth, who seemed glorious through her, and the merchants of the earth, who were made rich through her abundance, will weep and mourn over her destruction, because glory and temporal abundance, now subject to damnation, will never again shine forth. For the universal prosperity of the wicked is a great joy to kings—that is, the proud—

[Col. 0841D] and to merchants who thirst after earthly greed. When it is overthrown, they will grieve deeply, because they have lost that in which alone they delighted. And because these matters, which in this chapter seem to be understood according to the literal sense alone, are not believed to require spiritual interpretation, it follows:

“And the kings of the earth will weep and lament themselves over her.” Pain is described in two ways, in order to show that they suffer pain within and without: “Those who committed fornication with her and lived in delights with her, when they see the smoke of her burning”—that is, her smoky fire—“standing afar off for fear of her torments,” far off only in will, not through release from torments, “saying: ‘Woe, woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that strong city,

[Col. 0842A] for in one hour your judgment has come!’” They will address their speech to her, grieving beyond measure at her destruction. “Woe” is repeated three times in order that sin committed in thought, word, and deed may be shown by the number three. Therefore, according to what she sinned in the world, she will suffer in hell. But if, as is found in certain manuscripts, “woe” is written not three times but twice, it should be understood as referring to the twofold pain, namely inward and outward. “In one hour your judgment has come,” you who were always secure, so that you might lose the world and enter hell.

“And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her.” Having described the pain of kings, he adds the pain of merchants. They will grieve over the loss of the glory of dignities, bodily pleasure,

[Col. 0842B] abundance of goods, and bitter gain. Each person will grieve in hell over what he chiefly loved and possessed in the world. He fittingly and clearly adds the reason why the merchants will grieve, saying: “Because no one will buy their merchandise any longer: merchandise of gold, silver, precious stone, pearl, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet, and every kind of thyine wood”—that is, a kind of wood; understand, no one will buy it any longer—“and every vessel of ivory, every vessel of precious stone, bronze, iron, marble, cinnamon, and merchandise of spices, ointment, incense, wine, oil, fine flour, beasts of burden, sheep, horses, carriages,” that is, wagons, “slaves, and human souls”—namely, no one will buy them any longer.

[Col. 0842C] A distinction may be made in what he says, “slaves and human souls.” Some are sold in order to be subjected to servitude for a time; others, in order to serve throughout their whole lives. Thus, in “slaves,” a shorter servitude may subtly be understood; in the added words “human souls,” a longer one may be denoted. For “soul” is sometimes used for life. Alternatively, sometimes not only bodies but souls too are sold and bought, namely when not only bodies are subjected to men in base servitude, but souls also are subjected to demons through impious worship.

But merchants, like kings, grieving deeply over her fall, will direct their complaint toward her, saying: “And the fruits desired by your soul”—that is, your lesser goods,

[Col. 0842D] which you loved desirably—“have departed from you; and all rich and splendid things,” that is, greater things, “have perished from you, and they will find them no more.” “Their merchants,” those who were made rich from her in the world, “will stand afar off,” in will, not in suffering in hell, “for fear of her torments, weeping and mourning”—that is, persevering in a twofold grief—“saying: ‘Woe, woe, great city!’” Here “woe” is doubled to show that she transgressed the divine commands not only by impious will but also by perverse action, and to express that she will be punished in soul and body. “She was clothed in fine linen, purple, and scarlet, and gilded with gold, precious stone, and pearls,” because the totality of the wicked, devoted to vanity, is accustomed to adorn itself with worldly ornaments. “For in one

[Col. 0843A] hour such great riches have been laid waste,” she herself having been removed from the world and transferred to the torments of Gehenna; “and every captain, and all who sail to a distant place, and sailors, and those who work on the sea”—that is, everyone who seeks to grow rich not merely by business on land but also by trade over the sea—“stood afar off,” because they will desire to be far removed from participation in her. “And they cried out,” that is, they will cry out, seeing the place of her burning, saying: “Who is like this great city?” Who is now in punishment like this city—that is, the totality of the wicked, formerly great in glory? “And they cast dust upon their heads,” because in hell they will recognize that they were made of earthly, fragile, mortal, transitory material—something which they do not at all consider in the world now. For, darkened by the cosmetic of pride and impiety,

[Col. 0843B] they do not attend to how brief this life is, how slippery the way, and how uncertain death; then they will be compelled always to have these matters before their eyes. “And they cried out,” that is, they will cry out, “weeping and mourning,” because of the twofold pain, “and saying: ‘Woe, woe,’” because of the torment of soul and body, “that great city,” that is, the condemned totality of the wicked, “in which all who had ships at sea became rich through her prices,” because they bring her riches from afar. Thus he has described both classes of merchants: that which labors on land and that which sails on the sea. The kings and merchants of the earth, then, will weep over Babylon’s fall, because all the proud and greedy will grieve inconsolably that the totality of the impious has been stripped of worldly glory and abundance. But what condemned Babylon will suffer is well declared when he adds:

“For in one hour she has been made desolate,” that is, stripped of every consolation. For the congregation of those to be damned now has some consolation amid worldly pains; but when the last hour has passed, it will suffer desolation alone. It must be carefully considered that, in the description of the sorrow of Babylon’s lovers, kings are named first because the more powerful any wicked persons are now in the world, the more miserable they will be in hell. For it is written: “The powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. VI). Kings and merchants of the earth alone are described in mourning over Babylon’s fall, other lovers of Babylon being left aside, because they seem preeminent among the rest; therefore the others are figured and included through them and under them.

[Col. 0843D] Finally, sacred prophecy, which above described in order Babylon’s fall and the sorrow of her lovers, exhorts the holy angels who follow, and glorified elect human beings, to exult over her fall, saying: “Rejoice over her, O heavens,” that is, angels who rejoice in the deliverance of humankind; “and holy apostles and prophets,” namely all the righteous who, after the Savior’s coming—or before it—were justified so as to receive eternal life, and who are now exalted through the heavens in order to possess it.

But note that all these things pertain not to the state of the present age but to that of the age to come. And just as heavenly and angelic spirits are denoted by heaven, so the righteous of both Testaments are rightly comprehended and denoted by apostles and prophets.

[Col. 0844A] He places apostles before prophets because of their prerogative, since the divine word shows them to be worthier than prophets, where it says: “Many prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it” (Luke X). He declares why they ought to rejoice, saying: “For God has judged our judgment against her”—that is, she unjustly inflicted torments upon us, and he has compelled her on that account to undergo torments. For the saints will be able to rejoice with great joy when they see themselves delivered and their adversaries, who used unjustly to torment them, justly tormented.

Thus the other angel is Christ; Babylon overthrown and made a dwelling-place and prison of demons is the totality of the impious, damned and handed over to demonic torments; the other voice from heaven is a gentle admonition offered to the righteous; departure from Babylon is victory over confusion; the mourning of kings and merchants is the sorrow of the proud and the greedy, whether greater or lesser. For all who loved her condition in the world will mourn over her fall in hell.

## CHAPTER II. On the example of her submersion.

“And one strong angel took up a stone like a great millstone and cast it into the sea, saying: ‘With this violence Babylon, that great city, will be cast down’” (Rev. XVIII).

Having spoken above of Babylon’s fall and the grief of her lovers, he next adds the example of her submersion; and he says that this was figuratively shown by the unanimous whole order of preachers. “And one strong angel took up

[Col. 0844C] a stone.” The one angel is the entire order of preachers. He is rightly said to be strong because he is strengthened by the virtue of constancy against the devil, the world, and vices. He takes up a stone like a great millstone and casts it into the sea because he rebukes the congregation of those to be damned as hardened by impenitence, occupied with worldly business, unstable and laborious, great through pride, and now exalted in the world; and he predicts that, when the course of time is ended, it will be cast into the bitterness of hell. For the reprobate, now raised up in the glory of this present age, will sink to the depths at the end of the age. For it is written: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Matt. XXIII; Luke XIV). “With this violence,” that is, with this figure, “that great city Babylon will be cast down”

[Col. 0844D] into eternal torments, understand; “and it will no longer be found,” namely in the world, because, damned, it will mourn in hell. And in order to prove plainly that, just as it will be afflicted by evils, so also it will be stripped of every good, he fittingly adds: “The sound of harpists, musicians, and flute-players will no longer be heard in her. Every craftsman and every craft will no longer be found in her. The sound of the mill,” by which bread-delicacies are customarily prepared, “will no longer be heard in her. The light of a lamp will no longer shine for you, and the voice of bridegroom and bride,” that is, wedding joy, “will no longer be heard in you.”

Note that he sometimes speaks about her, sometimes to her: about her, instructing his hearers; to her,

[Col. 0845A] announcing and reproaching her with her evils, or lamenting for her. Finally, he makes clear why she will be damned and stripped of every good when he adds: “For your merchants were the princes of the earth,” because, that is, your princes gave their souls for earthly things—which is no longer to be tolerated. Other causes are also added: “For through your sorceries,” that is, poisonous persuasions, “all nations went astray,” that is, some from every nation; “and in her,” that is, in Babylon, “was found the blood of prophets,” that is, of the greater ones, “and saints,” that is, of the lesser ones, “and of all who were slain upon the earth,” not only of the good but also of the wicked; and both will be reckoned to her as sin. For if an evil person kills an evil person, the wickedness of the slain does not excuse the killer.

[Col. 0845B] We pass briefly over all these matters, easy in meaning, because we hasten to other things and do not investigate spiritually what we judge should chiefly be understood according to the letter. Thus the one angel is the entire order of preachers; the lifting up of the great millstone is the rebuke of Babylon’s hard, proud, unstable exaltation; its casting into the sea is prophecy and preaching of eternal damnation; the removal of the sound of harpists, musicians, and the other things written is the removal and deprivation of temporal goods.

## CHAPTER III. On thanksgiving offered to God for her fall.

“After these things I heard as it were a great voice of many trumpets in heaven saying: ‘Alleluia. Praise and glory and power belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just; for he has judged the great harlot

[Col. 0845C] who corrupted the earth by her prostitution, and has avenged the blood of his servants at her hands.’ And again they said: ‘Alleluia.’ And her smoke rises for ages of ages” (Rev. XIX).

After the figure of the condemnation of the impious city described above, he adds the praise and thanksgiving which the saints will offer to the Godhead for her fall. For the saints had above been exhorted to rejoice in her fall, where it was said: “Rejoice over her, O heavens, and holy apostles and prophets”; and they obediently fulfill the exhortation by singing praise to God and offering thanksgiving. “After these things I heard a great voice,” because it signified great joy, “of many trumpets,”

[Col. 0845D] that is, of those who sounded in the world with the trumpets of preaching, “in heaven,” that is, in heavenly blessedness, “saying: ‘Alleluia,’” namely, the sweetness of divine praise, inexpressible in human words.

It should be noted that when he says “I heard,” he speaks of the future as though of the past, as prophets are accustomed to do. We do not take pains to explain this in many places, because we leave it for the discerning judgment of the prudent reader. But because “Alleluia” is unfamiliar, he adds what is known, saying: “Praise and glory and power belong to our God.” Praise, because he is uniquely and supremely praiseworthy; glory, because he is glorious; power, because he is invincible. He then adds the reason why all these things should be attributed to him, saying: “Because his judgments are true and just,” as though it were said: He is truly to be proclaimed praiseworthy,

[Col. 0846A] glorious, and victorious, because his judgments are true, giving to each what he promised; and just, repaying according to what each has deserved. Finally he declares the cause through its effect, adding: “Who has judged the great harlot,” namely by condemning her, “because she corrupted the earth,” corrupting herself and others, “by her prostitution,” that is, by manifest impiety, “and has avenged the blood of his servants at her hands,” which she shed by cruelly killing them. “And again they said: ‘Alleluia.’” By the repetition of praise, understand the eternity of that same praise. Or, by the repetition of praise he understands the exultation of both spiritual and bodily sense in praising God. “And her smoke,” that is, the dark bitterness of her torments, “rises for ages of ages,”

[Col. 0846B] that is, forever. This refers to what was said above: that God judged the great harlot and avenged the blood of his servants. And because not only the lesser saints but also the greater will praise God in heavenly glory, whether for the damnation of the impious or for their own salvation—and so that we may understand what was said above of the lesser and what is now added concerning the greater—it is fittingly said:

“And the twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fell down,” that is, all the Church’s judges and teachers fell, humbling themselves, “and worshiped him who sits upon the throne,” venerating him above all things, “saying: ‘Amen. Alleluia,’” proclaiming him ineffably praiseworthy. For the greater both bear witness in themselves and confirm the testimony of the lesser. But because above he arranged separately and distinctly the joy and thanksgiving of each group, he now adds an admonition to all the saints together concerning divine praise, and their common offering of that praise:

[Col. 0846C] “And a voice came forth from the throne, saying: ‘Give praise to our God, all his servants, and you who fear God, small and great.’” God’s throne is the angelic powers, in whom God reigns by sitting chiefly, and through whom he governs his elect. A voice is said to go forth from them commanding us to praise God, because through them and with them the example and fellowship of divine praise are given to us. “Give praise to our God”—understand, in heaven—you who have been delivered and rescued by him from evil. “All his servants, and you who fear God,”

[Col. 0846D] that is, you who are reverently subject to him and cling to him in chaste love. “Small and great.” The small are those unable to penetrate the higher things and unable to fulfill the divine counsel which says, “Go, sell all that you have, and follow me” (Matt. XIX). Yet smallness does not harm one whose heart and tongue are filled with divine praise. And how obediently they received the divine admonition is declared when he adds:

And I heard what was like the sound of a great trumpet, and like the sound of great thunders, saying: “Alleluia.” He appropriately says not “the sound,” but “as it were the sound,” plainly indicating that what happens in heaven surpasses in its sublimity everything that happens in the world. Yet he heard a likeness of a sound, so that by the quality of a thing known he might in some measure perceive and [Col. 0847A] make known to us the hidden sublimity of the mystical and supreme good.

“I heard as it were the sound of a great trumpet,” because those who are now trumpets in the world, by preaching the faith and commandments of God, will afterward rejoice magnificently in heaven. “I heard as it were the sound of many waters,” because the assembly of souls to be saved is gathered from many peoples. “I heard as it were the sound of great thunders,” because the exultation of glorified saints saying “Alleluia” will terrify the condemned ungodly.

This voice of divine praise is described four times in this chapter, on account of the mystery of the divine Trinity and unity. For three and one make four. Therefore “alleluia” is rightly mentioned four times—that is, three times and once—in thanksgiving and praise rendered to the Godhead, because the God who is praised is Three and One. The power of this [Col. 0847B] praise, wonderful as it is now inexplicable, will then be easy for all, when, that is, the tongue is silent and affection cries out.

Finally, the reason for the praise to be offered to the supreme and immeasurable Godhead is declared when it is added: “For the Lord our God Almighty will reign.” He will then show that he truly reigns, because now he seems by no means to reign over the reprobate, while he permits them to rage against his own. “The Lord our God Almighty”: “Lord,” by excellence; “God,” by nature; “our,” by grace; “Almighty,” by power.

But since a twofold thanksgiving will be offered to God in heaven by the saints—one for the condemnation of the wicked, the other for their own salvation—after describing above that thanksgiving for the condemnation of the ungodly, he fittingly adds in sequence that which concerns the salvation of the righteous. Yet that one is described before this one because it is shown to agree with what precedes. And the second is suitably appended after those matters to which it adheres, the first having been arranged earlier. It follows:

> “Let us rejoice and exult, and let us give glory to God, because the marriage of the Lamb has come; and his wife has prepared herself, and it has been given to her to clothe herself in shining, white linen.”

It is as though he said: Let us rejoice and exult with a twofold joy, because we possess the glorification of souls and bodies; and let us give glory to God through praise and thanksgiving—through praise because of his ineffable dignity, through thanksgiving because of our salvation. Let us rejoice [Col. 0847D] and exult, because we have been saved; let us give glory to God, because our salvation is from him.

More openly describing the reason for rejoicing, he says: “Because the marriage of the Lamb has come.” For unless the marriage of the Lamb—that is, the union of Christ and the Church—were to come, the saints could by no means rejoice in the heavenly homeland. This marriage now has its beginning in the world through grace, but will then have its consummation in heaven through glory. For it will rightly be said to have come when the universal Church, transferred in all her elect to the contemplation and embrace of the Bridegroom, is made perfect. Certainly, for the present it is coming, but it cannot yet be said in its full sense that it has come.

Therefore true and perfect joy will then exist, when the holy Church, perfectly joined in the heavenly bridal chamber to the heavenly Bridegroom, [Col. 0848A] rejoices perfectly. She will prepare herself in time for union with that Bridegroom, so as to be worthy of him in eternity. For unless she now prepared herself in the world, she could by no means be joined to him in heaven. This is the marriage from whose joy the foolish virgins will be excluded when the wise enter in.

And this preparation is now openly described: “And his wife prepared herself.” She prepares herself through righteousness, in order to attain union with the Bridegroom. She prepares herself through righteousness in order to attain glory. And because without the gift of grace she could by no means reach the brightness of righteousness, it is fittingly added: “And it was given to her to clothe herself in shining, white linen.” “Linen” denotes righteousness and merit; “shining,” the example of good works; and “white,” [Col. 0848B] the exercise of virtues.

Therefore, unless this were given her through grace, she could not prepare herself through righteousness; unless she prepared herself through righteousness, she could not at all attain the heavenly union with the Bridegroom; and unless she attained the Bridegroom’s heavenly union, the saints would not have the fulfillment of rejoicing eternally. In these words, then, he sets forth step by step, ascendingly, the order by which the fullness of heavenly joy is reached. When all these things have been fulfilled, there will be that supreme delight of joy, exultation, and divine praise of which it is now said: “Let us rejoice and exult, and let us give glory to God.”

And lest we doubt that the linen signifies righteousness, Saint John himself explains this to us, saying: “For the linen is the righteous acts of the saints.” Linen, indeed, signifies righteous acts, because just as linen or flax is brought to whiteness by much labor, so the justification of the saints is advanced through a long struggle to consummation. It follows:

> “And he said to me: Write: Blessed are those called to the marriage-supper of the Lamb. And he said to me: These words of God are true.”

Having spoken of the joy of the heavenly marriage, he invites those present to share in it, commands all who are called to its delight to be written as blessed, and says to me—namely, the angel who was speaking with me—“Write,” so that those predestined to life may read what is written and kindle themselves to seek heavenly goods, while needy and contemptuous reprobates may incur a more righteous condemnation.

“Blessed are those who are called,” not to breakfast but to supper, because they will possess everlasting joy without any succeeding change. Breakfast signifies the refreshment of present grace; but supper, after which no refreshment follows, figures the fullness of eternal blessedness. Therefore they will truly be blessed, because free from every evil they will enjoy the delight of the supreme good.

Those called are called not only by preaching but also by predestination; not only through belief but also through election. For there are many false Christians who are included in the general number of the called, of whom it is said, “Many are called” (Matt. XX); but they must by no means be called blessed, because they do not attain blessedness.

And so that we may believe more firmly and certainly what is said by the angel concerning this blessedness, [Col. 0849A] and hold it in greater authority, he declares that the words he speaks are not his own but God’s. Thus he says: “These words of God are true.” It is as though he said: You ought to believe what I say with so much greater faith as you hear more plainly both that these words are God’s and that they are true.

Indeed, it would have sufficed to say that these were words of God, even if he had not added “true.” For God is not believed capable of lying. But, speaking of divine things according to human custom, as often occurs in many places in Scripture, he says that the things he attested are both God’s and true, not so much to strengthen faith in us as a teacher, but lest he depart from our customary manner of speaking. Whoever truly believes God believes that the words God speaks are true, not false.

And because before the coming of the Savior people accustomed to worship angels appearing to them, the holy theologian wished to set forth the honor rendered by other holy angelic spirits. It follows:

> “And I fell before his feet to worship him.”

But angelic dignity, which in the Old Testament did not forbid itself to be worshipped by man, seeing God-man exalted above itself in the New Testament, did not endure being worshipped by man. Hence it is added:

> “And he said to me: See that you do not do this.”

Giving the reason, he says: “For I am your fellow-servant, and of your brethren who have the testimony of Jesus.” It is as though he said: I now fear to be worshipped by you, because I see your nature reigning above me. He alone must be worshipped by you who, exalted above all things, is the one whom I must serve together with you.

[Col. 0849C] He states this more plainly when he says: “Worship God.” And so that we may clearly know what the testimony of Jesus is, he himself explains it through himself, saying: “For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.” For all prophets, by bearing witness to Christ, serve Christ; and angels, reverently worshipping him above themselves, serve him without ceasing. Nor are they ashamed to call themselves fellow-servants of those whom they know to minister to their Lord.

Thus the voice of the many trumpets heard in heaven is the thanksgiving of holy souls who will sing in heavenly blessedness; the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders are all the preachers and judges of the holy Church; the marriage of the Lamb is the union of Christ and the Church in heavenly blessedness.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning Christ judging her, and his power

[Col. 0849D]

> “And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it was called Faithful and True, and in righteousness he judges and makes war. His eyes were like a flame of fire, and on his head were many diadems, having a name written which no one knows except himself. And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood, and his name was called the Word of God; and the armies which are in heaven followed him on white horses, clothed in white, clean linen” (Rev. XIX).

In this chapter the power and righteousness of Christ condemning the whole multitude of the ungodly are described, and it is shown from the justice of the Judge that he condemns it not unjustly but justly.

“And I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse.” The opening of heaven is the revelation of the mystery; the white horse is the man assumed by the Word, rightly called white because he is truly spotless. Therefore, heaven having been opened, a white horse was seen, because when the mystery of the sacred page is revealed, the spotless man assumed by the Word is known.

And he who sat upon it—namely, the Son of the highest Father, who according to the nature of his divinity surpasses the man he assumed—was called Faithful and True: faithful because he omitted none of the things that were to be said; true because he preached no falsehoods. “And in righteousness he judges”—understand, the human race—rendering to each one according to his work; “and makes war,” namely, against the devil and all his army.

“His eyes were like a flame of fire,” because by his gaze he burns the reprobate with the torment of condemnation, enlightens the elect with knowledge of truth, and kindles them with the love of virtue. [Col. 0850B] “And on his head were many diadems,” because by the power of his divinity he grants to his elect eternal rewards that have no end.

“Having a name written which no one knows except himself”—and understand, except one to whom he himself chooses to reveal it—because no evil person can know the name of the Godhead which he possesses eternally by nature and grants his own to possess by grace, since no evil person can possess it. “And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood,” because his flesh is red with the shedding of blood. “And his name was called the Word of God,” because he is the Word of the Father, through whom God the Father created all things and through whom he made himself known to the world.

“And the armies which are in heaven followed him,” because all the elect, fighting against the devil and living a heavenly life, imitate him, “on white horses,” that is, in clean bodies and works, “clothed in white, clean linen”: linen, that is, the brightness of righteousness; white, the exercise of virtues; clean, freedom from committing sin. His soldiers are described with him for this reason: that they may be shown to be like him. It follows:

> “And from his mouth proceeds a sharp sword, that with it he may strike the nations; and he himself will rule them with a rod of iron. And he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty. And he has written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.”

Note that he presents all that this chapter contains without regard to time, intending to show what he is like, how great he is, and how much he can do. Therefore a sharp sword proceeds from his mouth, because a subtle judgment comes forth from his mouth, in order that by it he may strike the nations—that is, distinguish the good from the evil and the evil from the good. “And he himself will rule them with a rod of iron,” that is, with unbending justice.

“And he himself treads the winepress of the wine of the fury of the wrath of God Almighty,” because he crushes the ungodly with the vengeance that God, as though enraged and angry, gives them to drink. “And he has written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords,” because even according to his humanity, and according to that origin which he had from the holy Fathers, he shows himself exalted above all. For the power which he has according to divinity by nature, he has according to humanity by grace. [Col. 0851A] By the fact that it is said to be written, it is indicated to be an indelible and everlasting good.

Thus the opening of heaven is the revelation of the mystery; the white horse, the man assumed by the Word; the eyes of the one seated, the wisdom of divinity; the many diadems, eternal rewards, which are many because they are wonderful to God alone; the written name, the good of the Godhead; the garment sprinkled with blood, suffering flesh; the army of heaven, all the elect; the sharp sword, subtle judgment; the iron rod, unbending justice; the winepress of the wine of fury and wrath, the pressure of divine vengeance; the writing on the garment and thigh—“King of kings and Lord of lords”—everlasting power according to the assumed man.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the angel inviting demons to eat the kings of Babylon and her tribunes

[Col. 0851B]

> “And I saw one angel standing in the sun; and he cried out with a loud voice, saying to all the birds which fly through the midst of heaven: Come, gather yourselves to the supper of God, that you may eat the flesh of kings, and the flesh of tribunes, and the flesh of the mighty, and the flesh of horses and of those who sit upon them, and the flesh of all, free and slave, small and great” (Rev. XIX).

Above he described the power of Christ condemning Babylon; here he adds the angel’s invitation to demons to eat the condemned. Hence it is clear that the evil which demons will inflict upon the ungodly in hell arises not so much from their free will as from divine permission. For their being invited subtly indicates [Col. 0851C] that they cannot rage unless they are permitted.

“And I saw one angel standing in the sun.” The one angel is the whole order of preachers. He stands in the sun because, raised up by good intention amid the heat of persecution, he perseveres in preaching rightly. He is also said to cry out with a loud voice, inviting demons to eat the wicked, because with great constancy he declares that malignant spirits will torment condemned people in hell. These demons fly through the midst of heaven because they dwell in the middle region of this air.

They are rightly invited not to breakfast but to supper, because reprobate spirits who delight in human torments will have no further delight after that final condemnation of humanity. For it can have no successor, because it will be everlasting, not transitory.

“That you may eat the flesh of kings and tribunes, and the flesh of the mighty.” He places the powerful first because the powerful will suffer powerful torments. “And the flesh of horses and of those who sit upon them.” The horses are bodies; the riders are spirits. Both will be eaten by demons, because demons will be pleasurably filled by the torments of both. Or the horses are subjects and the riders prelates. Both will be eaten because both will be punished.

“And the flesh of all, free and slave, small and great.” These things are to be understood literally, not interpreted spiritually. Yet it must be carefully understood that by those whom he briefly describes in this chapter he includes all who are to be condemned.

Thus the one angel is the whole order of preachers; the loud voice, the urgency of preaching; the birds, demons; the supper, the final punishment. Others say that the birds can signify the elect, because, as birds are raised to the heights in flight, so the elect are raised by contemplating heavenly things. They will also eat Babylon’s children in that they will delight, together with divine justice, in their condemnation.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the condemnation of Antichrist and his false prophet

> “And I saw the beast, and the kings of the earth, and their armies gathered to make war with him who sat on the horse and with his army. And the beast was seized, and with it the false prophet who performed great signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark of the beast and worshipped its image. These two were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with sulphur” (Rev. XIX).

After describing above the general condemnation of the wicked, he adds in this chapter the particular condemnation of Antichrist and, in the following chapter, the condemnation of the devil, so that those who rage especially in committing iniquity may be mentioned especially in the description of condemnation.

And although the sacred prophecy intends in this vision to discuss the duration of eternal condemnation, it nevertheless inserts in these two chapters certain matters that concern the course of time, by a marvelous providence: so that in each vision ungodly persecution may be described and the number of the elect fortified against its attack.

“And I saw the beast,” that is, Antichrist; “and the kings of the earth,” that is, evil prelates who know how to rule themselves or others in the desire for earthly things; “and their armies,” that is, evil subjects, gathered together in unanimity in doing evil, “to make war,” that is, persecution, “with him who sat on the horse,” that is, Christ, “and with his army,” namely, all the faithful. For the wicked always gather against the good and attempt them by their devices.

It must be carefully observed that the matters contained above in this chapter concern the present persecution which the wicked inflict upon the good, while those that follow concern their future condemnation, which they will receive for the ungodliness they have committed.

“And the beast was seized,” because Antichrist will be seized when vengeance comes, “and with it his false prophet,” that is, the entire company of his teachers and leaders, “who performed great signs before it, by which he deceived those who received the mark of the beast and worshipped its image.” Since we have sufficiently explained these matters above, we do not care to repeat them here.

“These two were cast alive into a lake of fire burning with sulphur.” These two are particularly designated by name, so that those who sin more may be recognized as liable to greater torment. They are cast “into a lake of fire burning with sulphur,” so that those who did not shudder to corrupt themselves with the stench of lust may there be tormented by the stench of burning Gehenna. Note that they are said to be cast alive into the lake because, subjected to torments while alive, they will be punished by living miserably for eternity. It follows:

> “And the rest were killed by the sword of him who sat upon the horse, which proceeds from his mouth.”

The rest will be killed by the sword of him who sits upon the horse and proceeds from his mouth, because the subjects and disciples of Antichrist and of his teachers will be struck by the divine sentence. “And all the birds were filled with their flesh.” The birds will be filled with the flesh of the condemned, because demons out of envious malice, or even the saints out of love of justice, will delight in their torments.

Thus the beast is Antichrist; the false prophet, the chorus of false teachers; the lake of fire, the depth of condemnation; the killing of the rest, the condemnation of subjects; the filling of the birds with their flesh, the delight of demons, or of saints, in the torments of the condemned.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Satan being bound and released again, and his cruelty and condemnation

[Col. 0853B]

> “And I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss, and shut and sealed it over him, so that he might no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years should be completed. And after these things he must be released for a short time” (Rev. XX).

Having declared above the condemnation of Antichrist, he next adds the condemnation of the devil. Yet before coming to the devil’s condemnation, he relates his binding and release and his cruelty, so that, by describing all these things, he may instruct the elect concerning each one and fortify them against diabolical cruelty.

“And I saw an angel descending from heaven.” The angel is Christ, who descends from heaven because, taking our nature, he humbled himself for us. He has “the key of the abyss,” because according to his own will he shuts up the opening of all evil. He has “a great chain in his hand,” because he alone, by his power, can bind the cruelty of the ancient enemy.

He also seized “the dragon, the ancient serpent,” because he rebuked him for having acted deceitfully against the human race and unjustly against himself by stirring up the ungodly at his death. That apostate spirit is a dragon by violence, a serpent by fraud, and ancient by his long-established habit of doing harm. He is also the devil—that is, one “flowing downward,” by flowing into the wicked—and Satan, that is, an adversary, by opposing the good.

The angel, having seized him, bound him for a thousand years, because Christ deprived him of his ancient power throughout this whole time in which the holy Church is perfectly restored through righteousness to glory, from Christ’s own coming until the time of Antichrist. So far as the literal sense is concerned, this thousand-year period was completed long ago; but we do not know when Antichrist will come and Satan be released. But so far as the spiritual understanding is concerned, it will by no means be fulfilled until the righteousness of holy mother Church is more fully perfected according to divine providence; for the thousand signifies perfection. Therefore Satan is bound for as long a time [Col. 0854A] as the perfection of the righteous is being completed.

Where he now resides is declared when it is added: “And he cast him into the abyss.” He cast him into the abyss because he compels him to lurk in the dark and deep hearts of unbelievers. “And he shut and sealed it,” because he does not permit him to come out from there so as to overcome his elect. Hence it is added: “So that he might no longer deceive the nations,” namely, those consenting to him in committing crimes. “Until the thousand years should be completed,” that is, until the coming of Antichrist. “And after these things he must be released for a short time,” because God has so decreed that in the days of Antichrist he should rage again, having recovered his former power. It follows:

> “And I saw thrones, and saints sat upon them, and judgment was given to them; and the souls of those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus and for the word of God, and those who did not worship the beast or its image or receive its mark upon their foreheads or hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years.”

All that this clause contains appears to belong to the time of the devil’s binding. “And I saw thrones, and saints sat upon them.” It is as though he said: The devil having been bound, I saw the faithful set free, subjects ready to obey prelates, and prelates judging their subjects rightly. For thrones signify subjects, and saints signify prelates, though the subjects themselves are also saints. Therefore saints now sit upon thrones, because prelates exercise just authority over subjects.

And understand: I saw the souls of those beheaded—namely, of holy martyrs—released from their bodies “for the testimony of Jesus,” that is, for testimony borne to his humanity; “and for the word of God,” that is, for testimony borne to his divinity. And understand: I saw those who did not worship the beast or its image, nor receive its mark upon their foreheads and hands, as explained above.

He saw these because he understood that they had suffered in the world and, released from their bodies, live and reign with Christ in heavenly places. Therefore it is fittingly added: “And they lived and reigned”: they lived through righteousness and reigned through glory, “with Christ for a thousand years,” that is, throughout this whole period in which holy Church is prepared and perfected for the eternal crown—not only in the future, when, after receiving the first robe, they will receive the second.

[Col. 0854D] Note that what is said here, “I saw thrones, and saints sat upon them,” pertains to the good who are still presently living in bodies; but what is added, “and the souls of those beheaded,” pertains to those already released from bodies. Yet his statement that he saw the souls of those beheaded concerns the greater good; while what he joins in the same sentence, “and those who did not worship the beast,” concerns the lesser.

Finally, what he at last adds, saying, “And the rest of the dead did not live until the thousand years should be completed,” pertains to the wicked, who first die spiritually and then bodily. Confined in hell, they now suffer the death of souls and do not live again until the thousand years are completed; that is, until their wickedness is consummated and the righteousness of the good perfected, so that they may return to bodies and, having taken up bodies, descend again to punishments. It follows:

> “This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is he who has a part in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power; but they will be priests of God and of Christ, and will reign with him for a thousand years.”

He returns again to the description of the righteous and describes their blessedness. “This is the first resurrection,” namely, the justification or glorification of souls, which consists in receiving the first robe, just as the second resurrection is that of bodies in receiving the second. How great a reward it is before God to have a share in the first resurrection is declared when it is said: “Blessed and holy is he who has a part in the first resurrection.” Blessed through glory; holy through righteousness.

“Over these the second death has no power,” because they do not descend into eternal condemnation, which is the second death of the wicked on account of the penal condition of their bodies. The fault or condemnation of souls which exists now is the first death; but the condemnation of bodies, which is to come, is the second death. Therefore those who are now gathered to heavenly goods through righteousness, or the first robe, are blessed because they will not taste eternal death. “But they will be priests of God and of Christ,” because they will offer praises to divinity and assumed humanity. “And they will reign with him for a thousand years,” that is, throughout this whole time, not only in the future, when it is certain that they will truly reign. It follows:

> “And when the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison, and will go out and deceive all the nations which are upon the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, and will gather them for battle; their number is like the sand of the sea.”

He returns again to what he said above: “He must be released for a short time.” “And when the thousand years are completed,” namely, at the time of Antichrist, “Satan will be released from his prison,” that is, from the depths of evil hearts; “and will go out,” having recovered power, “and deceive the nations,” that is, all who desire to live as Gentiles, by deceptive fraud, “which are upon the four corners of the earth,” because they will covet earthly desire.

“Gog and Magog”: Gog is interpreted “a covering,” Magog “from a covering.” Therefore the devil will deceive Gog and Magog because he will deceptively mislead all the wicked, especially persecutors who conceal within themselves the poison of malice and finally [Col. 0855D] proceed to open cruelty. Or, according to the literal meaning, he will deceive these two most savage and impure peoples, and through them advance to overcome others.

“And he will gather them for battle,” to attack the people, namely, of the elect. Their multitude and barrenness are likewise declared when it is added: “Their number is like the sand of the sea,” that is, they are so innumerable and so barren. Their ungodly persecution of the saints is subsequently described when it is joined: “And they went up over the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city.”

For the final persecutors will go up over the breadth of the earth because, through pride, they will exalt themselves above earthly people. They will also surround the camp [Col. 0856A] of the saints because they will attempt from every side to invade and enter their fortified unity, always ready for war; but they will not be able. And they will surround the beloved city because they will attempt to break in and scatter the holy Church. They will labor to overthrow and destroy utterly not merely one or another congregation of saints, but the universal holy Church. Therefore, after saying, “They surrounded the camp of the saints,” he rightly at once added, “and the beloved city.”

But they are by no means to be feared, because they will soon perish. For it follows: “And fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them.” Fire came down from God out of heaven and devoured them, because a sudden destruction sent upon them from heaven will condemn them. It follows:

> “And the devil who deceived them was cast into the flame of fire and sulphur, where also the beast and the false prophet will be tormented day and night for ages of ages.”

Having described all the other matters indicated in the heading of the present chapter, he finally adds the condemnation of the devil and briefly describes it. But since we have sufficiently explained these words above, we judge it superfluous to repeat the same things here.

Thus the angel is Christ; the angel’s descent, the incarnation of the Word; the great chain, divine power; the devil’s binding, restraint from doing harm; the thousand years, the period from Christ until the coming of Antichrist; the thrones, subjects; the saints seated, prelates; the rest of the dead who did not live, the reprobate already lost; the first resurrection, the present glorification of righteous souls; the second death, [Col. 0856C] the future bodily and eternal condemnation of the wicked; the devil’s release, loosening to do harm; Gog and Magog’s gathering for battle, the incitement of the wicked to persecute; the fire sent from heaven, vengeance sent by God; the flame of fire and sulphur, the burning of foul condemnation.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the day of judgment and its character

> “And I saw a great white throne, and one sitting upon it, from whose presence earth and heaven fled, and no place was found for them. And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne. And books were opened, and another book was opened, which is that of life. And the dead were judged from the things written in the book according to their works” (Rev. XX).

At the end of the vision he deals with the end of time, namely, the character of the judgment which will take place at Christ’s coming. “I saw a great white throne”: I saw the throne, that is, the dignity of Christ reigning and judging; great, through immensity; white, through immortality. “And one sitting upon it,” namely Christ, from whose presence earth and heaven fled according to their former appearance, and no place was found in them according to their former condition.

“And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne.” These matters must be understood only literally, and therefore need no exposition according to spiritual understanding. “And books were opened.” The books said to be opened then signify the consciences of the ungodly, [Col. 0857A] because they will then be revealed. “And another book was opened, which is that of life; and the dead were judged,” that is, the wicked, “from the things written in the book according to their works.”

The dead are rightly said to be judged from what was written in the book of life, because the wicked, figured by the name “dead,” will be condemned by comparison with the righteous who are written in the book of life. For in those righteous they will plainly read that they despised divine commandments, and will clearly understand that for this reason they deserved everlasting punishments.

It should be known that there are four classes of people: those judged and condemned; those to be judged and condemned; those judged and saved; and those to be judged and saved. Those judged and condemned are those whose condemnation is already certain. Those to be judged and condemned are those whose condemnation is not yet certain. Those judged and saved are those whose salvation is already certain. Those to be judged and saved are those whose salvation is not yet certain.

Therefore, the statement here about “the dead judged from the things written in the book of life according to their works” pertains especially to those to be judged and condemned. For a lesser punishment will be given to some and a greater punishment to others.

And lest anyone be thought absent from the final judgment, it is fittingly added: “And the sea gave up its dead, and hell and death likewise gave up their dead which were in them. And judgment was made concerning each one according to their works.” The sea will indeed give up the dead because it will give up the bodies of the dead; and hell, that is, the place of punishment, and death, that is, punishment itself, will give up their dead, that is, the spirits of the dead.

And it must be carefully observed that he says the sea and hell or death gave up the dead, but does not say that the earth gave up the dead. He wisely keeps silent concerning the earth, of which this is most certain, while saying of sea, hell, and death what he says, because what is more certainly believed to happen needs less to be said. “And judgment was made concerning each one according to their works,” because according to the difference of merits there will be a difference of rewards. It follows:

And hell and death were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death: and whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire. By these two, namely hell and death, we may understand the demons and the human beings to be condemned, who will be cast [Col. 0858A] into the lake of fire, that is, into the deep, enduring darkness of damnation. This is the second death. For the first death is the condemnation of souls; the second, the condemnation of souls joined to bodies. Finally, he pronounces a general sentence upon all who are to be condemned, saying: And everyone who is not found written in the book of life, that is, who is not predestined to eternal life, is cast into the lake of fire, that is, into the depths of infernal conflagration. Thus the great white throne is the immense and immortal dignity of Christ reigning and judging; the small and great dead are the whole human race; the opening of the books is the disclosure of consciences; the dead judged from the things written in the book of life according to their deeds is the condemnation [Col. 0858B] of the wicked by comparison with the righteous; the lake of fire is the depth of damnation.

In the first chapter of this sixth vision, sacred prophecy treated, under the name of Babylon, the condemnation of all the wicked and the sorrow and lamentation of each of her lovers. In the second it treated of the example of her submersion, displayed by an angel through a symbolic stone cast into the sea. In the third it treated of the praise and thanksgiving to be offered to God for her condemnation. In the fourth it treated of the power of Christ the Judge in condemning her. In the fifth, of the figurative invitation of demons to consume impious kings and all the wicked. In the sixth, of the particular condemnation of Antichrist and his false teachers. In the seventh it treated of the binding of the devil, and of his release, [Col. 0858C] cruelty, and condemnation. In the eighth it treated of the last judgment and its character. We have indeed touched briefly upon the calamity of those to be condemned and the nature of infernal torments, because we cannot set forth so immense an evil. Meanwhile, let each person carefully provide for himself and strive to live in such a way that he may not at the end descend condemned to that punishment which can neither be comprehended in thought nor explained in speech. But now we give rest to the pen, so that tomorrow, more refreshed, we may rise to contemplate and elucidate the seventh and final vision of this book.

# BOOK SEVEN. ON THE SEVENTH VISION.

[Col. 0857]

## PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0857D]

God, ruler of all and judge of the universe, who has left nothing unordered in his kingdom, dispenses to the impious the wages of damnation and likewise rewards the righteous with heavenly goods. Hence sacred theology, which in the preceding vision plainly describes, under the name of Babylon overthrown and submerged, the condemnation of the wicked, now fittingly adds in consequence, under the figure of Jerusalem, the city holy, the glorification of the good; so that, just as there the impious are described as punished without end, so here the righteous may be shown as eternally glorified. This seventh and most sacred vision deals with the future renewal of the elements, with the glorification of the righteous and their heavenly dwellings, and with the delight of the blessed; it beautifully describes these by the qualities of manifold figures and wonderfully draws the human mind toward the desire and sweetness of the highest good.

For if anyone were to attend more diligently and earnestly even to the beauty of the words alone in the sequence of this vision, he would find in it the most perfect means of stirring himself to desire so great a good, and would wish with all his desires to become an inhabitant of so beautiful and delightful a city. As for us, entering upon the task of elucidating the wondrous structure of so great a city according to its spiritual meaning, we by no means presume upon our own powers. Rather, trusting in him who gives abundantly to those who humbly ask for the gifts of his wisdom and does not reproach them, we humbly beseech that, strengthened by his aid, we may penetrate the secret depth of matters so great and so sublime. For the following vision concerns the holy heavenly Jerusalem, describing its wall, its gates, its corners, its length, [Col. 0859B] its breadth and height also, and its various foundations, signifying these by the varied figure of precious stones, together with its other wondrous mysteries contained in what follows.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the renewal of the elements.

> “And I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea is no more” (Rev. 21).

Sacred prophecy, employing wonderful providence, first sets forth the renewal of the elements and then adds the glorification of the righteous, so that we may ascend from earthly things to heavenly things and attain from visible things to the contemplation of invisible things. Thus we also read that in the beginning the world was first made, and afterward the human being, lord of the world, was created. But although there are known to be four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—here it appears to mention the renewal of only three: air, earth, and water. It indicated earth clearly and by its proper name where it said that it saw a new earth; it suggested air where it said that it saw a new heaven; and water where it said that the sea is no more.

It may be believed that it was silent about the renewal of fire because fire is known to be defiled by little or no corruption, and because by its power the other elements ought to be cleansed in that final conflagration. Yet its testimony that the first heaven and first earth passed away and that it saw new ones must by no means be understood to mean that these two elements—air and earth—will be entirely consumed and others created in their place. Rather, both will be burned according to their former form and appearance, and will arise and be renewed far and immeasurably for the better. Some say that water, because it is here said and read that “the sea is no more,” will be entirely consumed by the power of that final fire. But one must observe closely that it does not say, “water is no more,” but “the sea is no more,” so that it may be shown more clearly that water is not wholly annihilated but will then be cleansed of its grossness, every corruption, and false bitterness. The statement that the first heaven and earth passed away and that the sea is no more appears chiefly to concern the three elements—air, earth, and water—not their complete consumption, but their perfect cleansing by fire and the immeasurable renewal divinely imparted to them. Therefore the world will be renewed, not so that it may serve humanity further as though humanity were its master, but so that, while the world endures eternally, humanity may give eternal thanks to its Creator and Renewer.

But because above, in other places, we have treated at length of many matters pertaining to this, we pass over it more swiftly and hasten to examine other matters. For we do not care to burden the page with repeated arguments or words, or with many authorities brought in; rather, for firmer retention of what we write, we pass briefly and concisely through each point. Memory delights in brevity of extent and smallness of number.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the holy heavenly city Jerusalem.

[Col. 0860B]

> “And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, prepared by God, like a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev. 21).

After setting forth above the renewal of the elements, he next adds the glorification of the saints. “And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven.” I saw, through spiritual understanding, a city: namely, the immense gathering of the righteous; holy, through righteousness; Jerusalem, eternal through the vision of inward peace; new, because cleansed from oldness; descending from heaven, because it recognizes that it has perfectly from God all that it lives justly in time and lives well in eternity; prepared by God like a bride adorned for her husband. For just as a bride, after gifts have been sent by the man, is prepared for the man’s marriage-bed, so the Church, after heavenly gifts have been bestowed upon her by Christ, together with virtues and good works, is prepared for her heavenly union with Christ.

And because he says that he saw the renewal of the elements and the glorification of the righteous, lest either of these seem incredible because so unknown, he brings forward, to confirm his statement, the testimony of the holy Fathers and the testimony of God himself, so that the saying may be confirmed by both testimonies. For it follows:

> And I heard a great voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the dwelling-place of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them. They shall be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.”

What do we more rightly understand by the throne than the holy Fathers, rulers of souls, in whom God, seated and reigning, governs those beneath them piously and justly? From this throne a voice goes forth, because from the holy Fathers the promise of heavenly good reaches us. This voice is rightly called great because it promises immense and eternal goods. “Behold, the dwelling-place of God is with human beings” may be understood as the evident and manifest fellowship of the Godhead with the saved. For God’s dwelling-place will be with human beings when, in the heavenly homeland, the Godhead joins itself to us and us to itself. And because that fellowship or cohabitation will not be transitory but eternal, it rightly says: “And he will dwell with them.” By saying “he will dwell,” it signifies the eternity of this fellowship and abiding.

It further declares the bond of this fellowship when it adds: “They shall be his people, and he [Col. 0861A] will be with them as their God.” They shall indeed be his people, acclaiming his praise eternally and with one accord; and he will be their God, wonderfully and ineffably sharing his blessedness with them. Yet it must be carefully considered that it says, “God himself will be with them as their God.” For even now he is God with his own in the world, but he does not appear to be with them so long as, living in this mortality, they are not disclosed openly to his vision. But then he will truly be with them, when he reveals himself to them in their glorified state, face unveiled. Thus they shall be his people, never offending him; and he shall be with them as their God, never abandoning them.

But because it will not be in heaven as we see it to be in the world—namely, so that some evils are mingled with those highest and eternal heavenly goods—it fittingly adds:

> And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death shall be no more, neither mourning nor crying nor pain shall be any more, for the former things have passed away.

Therefore they will have every good without any evil. O how sweet these things are, and how powerfully—if only one attends to them—they draw the mind to themselves, carry it away into themselves, and sweetly intoxicate it when drawn and carried away! Let one who knows that such and so great goods are reserved for him therefore be ashamed to delight in worthless things. Let him despise what, shortly, whether he wishes or not, he must lose; let him seek what, shortly, if he wishes, he may receive and possess without end.

And it follows: “And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes,” tears which now arise when occasions present themselves through which the mind is variously distressed. That then there will be neither a greater nor a lesser cause of tears is explained below. There will be no greater cause, because there will be no death. Nor will there be a lesser cause, because there will be no mourning, crying, or pain. There will be no death because there will be no separation of soul and body. There will be no mourning because there will be no loss of loved ones: mourning is spoken of with respect to the loss of loved ones. Nor will there be crying because no injury will be inflicted. Finally, there will be no pain because no one will grieve over any loss. Of these it is said, “the former things have passed away,” because, while the present life, which is not without sin, is lived, they affect even the saints; but then, when sin from which they arise and which succeeds them has been removed, they will be entirely absent.

At present, however, the saints are purified by the evils mentioned above, being prepared for that future blessedness. But those to be condemned are also grievously afflicted by evils of this kind in this life; yet their punishment belongs not to preparation for blessedness but to the beginning of damnation. But lest the human attestation of the matters contained in the sacred vision concerning the renewal of the elements and the glorification of the righteous seem insufficient, divine authority is added. For it follows:

> And he who sat upon the throne said: “Behold, I make all things new.”

For not only does the throne—that is, the assembly of holy teachers in which God reigns by being seated—proclaim testimony to this matter, but the Godhead itself, reigning, does so. If anyone should say that the voice which went out from the throne [Col. 0862A]—where it says, “Behold, the dwelling-place of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them”—pertains rather to the glorification of the saints, whereas the testimony of the Godhead, where it adds, “Behold, I make all things new,” refers to the renewal of the elements, this would not be incongruous. Indeed, if the matter is carefully weighed, this is shown to have been done reasonably. For the glorification of the righteous appears more certain, is believed more confidently, and has more frequent authority in Sacred Scripture than the renewal of the elements. Therefore what perhaps might appear less credible ought fittingly to have been confirmed by greater testimony.

And because the things invisibly and spiritually shown to the saints are of less benefit to others unless written down, it is rightly now said:

> And he said: “Write, for these words are most trustworthy and true.”

As though he said: Entrust to writing, for the benefit of others, what has been shown to you, so that those who see may read, and those who read may advance to better things. And it is fitting that you write, because these words are most trustworthy and true. They are most trustworthy because they faithfully foretell future goods; true because everything they proclaim will truly be fulfilled. It follows:

> And he said to me: “It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.”

Lest anyone should ask what would happen after that renewal, it says that nothing remains to be done, but that all things foretold from the beginning have been completed. It declares that it is itself the consummation of all these things, saying: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end.” As though it said: Just as all things have their origin through me, so they have their consummation through me. I created the things that exist; I renewed things grown old so that they might endure eternally. I made; I remade. I made in the beginning; I remade at the end.

And because above it set forth the glorification of the righteous, it consequently invites hearers to its delight when it adds:

> “To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life. Whoever conquers shall possess these things, and I shall be his God, and he shall be my son.”

“To the thirsty I will give freely from the spring of the water of life,” because I am the source of blessedness. He thirsts for heavenly goods who thirsts and longs for them with his whole heart. For God gives from the spring of living water to one who ardently yearns for him, because he does not deprive of heavenly goods the soul that longs for him. “Freely”: for the spring of living water is given freely, because through divine grace the good of heavenly fullness is bestowed upon us. Human power does not merit it unless divine grace is first given to it, enabling it to merit it. “Whoever conquers”—namely, the ancient enemy, the world, and vice—shall possess these things because he will attain the prize. “Shall possess these things”: what things? “Things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2): things which, because of their immensity, cannot be comprehended; because of their eternity, cannot be ended; because of their goodness, cannot be assessed. O how great are these promises of heavenly goods, surpassing all understanding and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb! “And I shall be his God,” as has been explained above, “and he [Col. 0863A] shall be my son,” which above was called “my people.”

But lest the wicked, enveloped in vices and crimes, should think that by false prayers, which they often offer, or alms which they sometimes bestow upon the Church or the poor, or by any other means, they can in any degree attain a share in heavenly good unless they repent, they are in this book utterly added to damnation and separated from the fellowship of the righteous. For it follows:

> But as for the fearful, unbelieving, accursed, murderers, fornicators, poisoners, idolaters, and all liars, their portion shall be in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death.

The fearful are those who, through fear of punishments, flee from accepting the faith or abandon it once accepted. The unbelieving are those who do not at all believe in future goods. The accursed are those who are deprived by divine judgment of participation in hidden spiritual grace, or who are openly excommunicated, according to ecclesiastical custom, for their crimes. Murderers are those who kill someone either through perversity of will, persuasion in speech, or commission by deed. Fornicators are those who are not ashamed unlawfully to subject themselves either to the enticements of the flesh or to the pleasures of this world. Poisoners are those who cruelly instil the poison of malice by word or example. Idolaters are those who, abandoning the worship of true divinity, subject themselves through idolatry to demons. Liars are those who, abandoning the path of truth, deceitfully mislead their neighbours.

We read, however, in certain words of the saints that imperfect persons are not condemned for a lie when it is uttered by them for escape from danger, but that it is counted among venial sins before the merciful Judge; whereas the perfect, if need be, may indeed keep the truth silent, but ought utterly to avoid a lying word. Therefore all the persons mentioned above—that is, all the impious—shall have their portion in the lake burning with fire and sulphur, which is the second death, not with the saints in the holy heavenly Jerusalem, which is the eternal vision of peace. Indeed, to say that the wicked would have a portion in the burning lake would have sufficed to declare the truth; but he added “with fire” in order to indicate more expressly the weight of infernal conflagration. He shows the power of that conflagration more effectively, moreover, when, after saying “with fire,” he added “sulphur”; and in saying that the wicked would have a portion in the burning lake, he indicated that some would suffer more and others less.

It also seems necessary to weigh carefully that here, where the wicked to be condemned are described, eight kinds are designated: the fearful, unbelieving, accursed, murderers, fornicators, poisoners, idolaters, and liars. Thus, by such a number, they are shown to be wholly alien to and excluded from the righteous, who will be endowed with eight beatitudes. Therefore the new Jerusalem is the renewed whole body of the righteous, descending from heaven because it recognizes that it has from God the grace of justification; the dwelling-place of God with human beings and his dwelling with them is his manifest and eternal fellowship with the glorified; the wiping away of tears is the removal of evils.

## CHAPTER THREE. On the Lamb’s manifestation to the holy theologian through an angel.

[Col. 0864A]

> “And one of the seven angels having the seven bowls full of the last plagues came and spoke with me, saying: ‘Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.’ And he carried me away in the spirit onto a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, having the glory of God” (Rev. 21).

One of the seven angels signifies the entire body of preachers, united in faith and in the ministry of preaching. He is said to be one of the seven having bowls full of the last plagues because, just as holy preachers foretell divine vengeance to the wicked, so they announce to the good the recompense of righteousness and the glorification of the holy catholic Church. Hence it is rightly now said: “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.”

But it seems remarkable that the angel here promised to show the holy theologian the bride, the wife of the Lamb, whom the saint himself described as having seen a little earlier. For in the preceding chapter he said: “And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, prepared by God like a bride adorned for her husband.” What, then, did he promise to show him whom he said he had already seen, except that he had indeed already seen great things, but was still to see far greater things? This is plainly evident in what follows, where he describes in manifold and beautiful fashion the wall, gates, corners, measurement, foundations, and many other glorious mysteries [Col. 0864C] of the holy city: those things which he had already seen, though highly to be esteemed, were small in comparison with the wonders that remained to be seen.

He says, therefore: “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” As though he said: Great indeed are the things you have seen concerning the future state of the saints; but raise and enlarge your mind, because you are about to see concerning their same state wonders that you have not yet seen. The holy mother Church herself is called both bride and wife: bride, because she is united in spiritual love to Christ, her heavenly bridegroom; wife, because by his grace she is made fruitful for the begetting of many children.

“And he carried me away in the spirit,” that is, much more sublimely than I had been at first, “onto a great and high mountain,” because the things to be shown to me were great and high: great on account of the entire multitude of those to be glorified; high on account of the sublimity of the good to be possessed. “And he showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, descending from heaven”: he showed it, that is, much more excellently than I had seen it before. “From God, having the glory of God”: for no one will have from himself the glory which he will possess in heavenly blessedness. “Having the glory of God”: just as iron, when it is cast into fire, is coloured in the fire and by the fire, and takes on the appearance of fire, yet does not have from itself what it receives, so the holy mother Church will shine in blessedness, illumined by the splendour of eternal divinity.

Let whoever can estimate, then, how great and how delightful will be the harmonious and indissoluble union of human creature and Creator, where the glory which the Creator possesses by fullness will be given to the creature by participation in that fullness: what he has by nature, this one will be given to have by grace. The glory of this brightness is more expressly indicated below, in showing that she will be illuminated by that light by which the beloved Son of the Father, the bridegroom of this same glorious bride, is glorified according to his assumed humanity. For it follows:

> Its light was like a precious stone.

The precious stone is rightly said to be Christ. He is a stone because indissoluble in immortality; precious because he is fairer in form than the children of human beings. Therefore the light of the holy heavenly city is described as like a precious stone because, in the age to come, the holy assembly of the righteous, illumined by the brightness of the divinity it beholds, will be made like Christ: made heir of God and co-heir of Christ. The holy heavenly city, therefore, will have God’s brightness in likeness to Christ, though not as great as his; for just as the head surpasses the members and the bridegroom precedes the bride in dignity, so the human being assumed by the Word and united to the Word—who committed no sin, in whose mouth no deceit was found, and who became the cause of salvation to all who obey him—will surpass all others incomparably in the glory of brightness.

It follows:

> Like a jasper stone, like crystal.

Jasper is green; crystal is bright. Christ is jasper; Christ is crystal. Christ is jasper because, never failing in the execution of the Father’s will, he flourished with unfading vigour; Christ is crystal because, rising from the dead, he shone brilliantly with the glory of immortality. Therefore the light of the holy city will be like a precious stone—that is, Christ—and like a jasper stone, like crystal, because in the heavenly homeland it will flourish with Christ through the good gift of unfading eternity and shine through the gift of indissoluble immortality. Thus the seventh angel is the whole order of preachers; the Lamb’s bride is the Church of Christ; the bride’s brightness is the glorification of the Church; light like a precious stone is likeness to Christ’s brightness. “For we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

## CHAPTER FOUR. On the wall of Jerusalem, its gates, corners, and foundations.

[Col. 0865D]

> “And it had a great and high wall, having twelve gates, and at the gates twelve corners, and names written, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel” (Rev. 21).
