Having above described generally the future condition and glory of the holy city, he proceeds to describe certain of its ornaments particularly, so that, the more glorious it is shown in individual respects, the more sublimely it may be proclaimed and commended as a whole. “And it had a great and high wall.” By the great wall we fittingly understand Christ, who surrounds that holy Jerusalem on every side and now defends it on every side against attacking demons, wicked people, and vices. He is rightly called great and high: great through the incomprehensibility of his immensity and the infinity of his eternity; high through the exaltation of his humanity and the sublimity of his majesty.

“Having twelve gates.” By the gates we understand the holy apostles, through whose faith and teaching we enter the holy city. For all people who are converted to Christ enter the holy Jerusalem through their instruction. “And at the gates twelve corners.” The corners are all those who are lesser and more imperfect, and more hidden in merits. They are rightly said to be at the gates because they are gathered into the preaching and teaching of the holy apostles. For there are twelve gates in the wall and twelve corners at the gates, because the twelve apostles were gathered into Christ’s preaching, and all those lesser in life and more hidden in merits into apostolic preaching.

For an angel signifies what is hidden, and the number twelve signifies universality. It is composed of three and four multiplied together: three is the form of invisible things because of the mystery of the Trinity, and four the form of visible things because of the four elements. And, so that it may be plainly shown that the apostles commended in their preaching, teaching, and writings the faith and righteousness of the Israelite people, it fittingly adds: “And names written, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel.” For the names of the twelve tribes of Israel are rightly said to be written on the gates, because their merits are proclaimed through the apostles in Sacred Scripture to have been glorious. It follows:

> Three gates from the east, three gates from the north, [Col. 0866C] three gates from the south, three gates from the west.

By the east we may fittingly understand the righteous who lived at the beginning of the world; by the north, those converted from the gentiles, once cold toward good; by the south, the ancient righteous Jews, warm with faith in the future Saviour; and by the west, those who will be converted at the end of the age. Thus it is fittingly said that there are three gates in the city from the east, north, south, and west, because whoever is saved from the peoples mentioned above is justified through faith in the Holy Trinity, proclaimed and strengthened by apostolic preaching in the four parts of the world. No other entrance lies open, because no one has salvation from elsewhere. Even the holy people of old entered through faith in the Holy Trinity, although they did not possess its mystery as revealed as we do now.

And because our Redeemer took the origin of his flesh from the patriarchs, it fittingly follows:

> And the wall of the city had twelve foundations.

For the sacred vision revealed that the wall has twelve foundations because the Saviour, who fortifies his Church on every side, assumed flesh from the lineage of the fathers. It follows:

> And on them were the twelve names of the apostles and of the Lamb.

This is remarkable. Above, on the gates which we said signify the apostles, we read that the names of the twelve tribes of Israel were written. Here, on the foundations—in which we understand the twelve patriarchs, or the tribes themselves descended from the patriarchs—we find written the twelve names of the apostles [Col. 0867A] and of the Lamb. Wonderful, then, is the harmony of ancient and modern persons in one faith. For the names of the twelve tribes are read in the apostles, and the names of the twelve apostles written in the twelve tribes or patriarchs, because the apostles preached the faith of the Fathers in the redemption of the human race as fulfilled, while the Fathers faithfully believed that it would be preached through the apostles.

It must also be carefully noted that the name of the Lamb is read written on the foundations, not on the gates: it is believed to have been manifestly bestowed upon the latter, but to have been awaited for a long time as yet to be bestowed by the ancients. Great are these mysteries of the blessed city and deserving of examination with every effort of diligence. But we touch upon few of them and leave many for your prudence to examine. Thus the wall is Christ; the gates, the apostles; the corners, saints hidden in merit, or also those set apart from others in their manner of life; the east, the first human beings; the north, the gentiles; the south, the Jews; the west, the last righteous; the twelve foundations, the ancient Fathers.

## CHAPTER FIVE. On its measurement.

> “And he who spoke with me had a measuring rod, a golden reed, to measure the city and its gates and wall” (Rev. 21).

Measurement signifies the difference of merits among things. Above he saw the city fortified and adorned; here he is taught to observe that in the holy city some differ from others in merits. It must be carefully observed that many things set forth in the description of the holy city are shown to concern the saints’ present merits more than their future rewards. Although the intention of prophecy in this vision is to describe the heavenly condition of blessed Jerusalem, it nevertheless appropriately strives to make known certain magnificent features of its present merits, so that, while we are instructed about the saints’ magnificent virtues, we may admire their heavenly rewards more sublimely.

“And he who spoke with me had a measuring rod, a golden reed.” What do we more fittingly understand by the golden reed than Sacred Scripture? For the angel has a golden reed because the holy company of teachers, sent to instruct the Lord’s people, possesses the divine Scripture, composed and made bright by the wisdom of God, which is represented by gold. This Scripture is a reed through the sound of preaching, and golden through the brightness of divine knowledge. The angel, possessing it, measures the city because the authority of teachers administers it to the faithful according to each person’s capacity and measure, and carefully considers how much each person works and advances according to it. And, when it sees the efforts of hearers advancing according to its teaching, it rejoices wonderfully and abundantly at the enlargement of the holy city, and labours to extend the reed of discourse further forward, so that it may yet enlarge the holy building.

“To measure the city and its gates and wall.” By the city, which is designated by a particular name, we understand the lower people; by the gates, as said above, the apostles, through whose teaching others enter into the faith; [Col. 0868A] by the wall, Christ, who fortifies his own on every side and defends them against the assaults of enemies. The angel therefore measures the city when the discernment of teachers considers the capacity of the people subject to it, applies the word of preaching according to the strength of that capacity, and, after applying the word, considers the progress of the work, so that it may plainly know how far it can extend itself in building the heavenly city. It also measures the gates when it openly declares to all that apostolic teaching is the entrance to the heavenly city. Finally, it measures the wall in one respect when it preaches that our Redeemer and Defender, Jesus Christ, is true God and true human being. But the shape and immovable stability of the whole city is also described as perfect when it adds:

[Col. 0868B] “And the city is laid out as a square; its length is as great as its breadth.” The holy city has four sides: faith, hope, charity, and action. These are equal, because as much as anyone believes, so much he hopes; as much as he hopes, so much he loves; and as much as he loves, so much he acts. Therefore the city is set as a square: strong in faith, long-suffering in hope, broad in charity, effective in work.

Or, the square of the city consists of the four principal virtues in a human being—prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice—which ought to be equal in a person, and none ought to exceed another. And in order to show that the lesser members, who are not designated by a special or individual name as the wall, gates, and foundations are, but are expressed by the general designation of “city”—in order, I say, to show that these lesser persons, [Col. 0868C] whom we also call imperfect in comparison with the perfect, are not without the perfection proper to their rank and the fullness of their own perfection—he fittingly adds: “And he measured the city with the golden reed for twelve thousand stadia.” A stadium is the length of a course in which one runs to obtain a prize. Hence the Apostle says: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives the prize?” (1 Cor. VI [sic]). The number twelve signifies universality, while one thousand signifies perfection.

Thus the angel, as has been said above, measures the city whenever the diligent discernment of teachers considers the capacity of the lesser members, applies preaching to them according to that capacity, and carefully observes how far each one extends, through good conduct, toward the building of the heavenly city. But this measure is rightly said to extend through twelve thousand stadia, in order plainly to show both that they themselves are striving toward the prize of eternal blessedness and that all possess the fullness of their own perfection. For although they cannot equal the merits of the perfect, they nevertheless do not shrink from perfectly imitating them according to their own ability.

Otherwise: the angel measures the city with the golden reed through twelve thousand stadia because the authority of teachers testifies that even the lesser members, running toward the prize of eternal recompense, perfectly fulfill, according to their strength, apostolic teaching drawn from the words of sacred Scripture. For twelve signifies apostolic teaching, and a thousand [Col. 0869A] signifies perfection.

We could indeed expound such words in many senses; but, for brevity’s sake, we judge that they should be touched upon only rapidly. Yet because above, when he described the length and breadth of the blessed city by means of a square, he said nothing of its height, he now repeats its length and breadth and also describes its height, saying: “Its length, breadth, and height are equal.” Length is faith; height, hope; breadth, charity. These are equal, because as much as anyone believes, so much he hopes; and as much as he hopes, so much he loves.

Nor should you wonder that above hope is placed as one side of the city, whereas here we figure its height by it; for one and the same thing in sacred discourse often serves several meanings. Thus, through hope, which stretches out in patient expectation of future things and is raised on high in desiring heavenly things, the square arrangement of the heavenly building, joined with faith, charity, and good action, is fittingly ordered above; and here its height is appropriately represented.

Above, therefore, where it is written, “the city is laid out as a square,” we say that faith and hope, which extend toward the future, constitute its length; while charity and good action, which stretch out toward one’s neighbor to the right and left, constitute its breadth. Here, however, where it is added, “its length, height, and breadth are equal,” faith alone constitutes the length, hope the height, and charity the breadth. Here appears the wonderful power of sacred Scripture, which can vary itself in its interpretations of the same things according to different modes of signification.

It follows:

“And he measured its walls: one hundred and forty-four cubits, the measure of a man, which is that of an angel.” Above he spoke of a wall; here he speaks of walls. Our Jerusalem plainly has a wall because it has Christ as defender; it has walls because it has defenders—ecclesiastical teachers and rulers. Their measure is perfectly declared when it is said: “And he measured its walls: one hundred and forty-four cubits; the measure of a man is that of an angel.” One hundred signifies perfection; forty, which arises from four times ten, the fulfillment of the four Gospels and the Decalogue; four, the exercise of the four principal virtues; and the cubit, action.

[Col. 0869D] Therefore the walls of Jerusalem measure one hundred and forty-four cubits, because the defenders of the holy Church fulfill through perfect action the precepts of the four Gospels and the Decalogue, together with the exercise of the four principal virtues. And this is the measure of a human being, because this is the whole of righteousness. Nor is so great and such a measure insignificant or contemptible. By it a person is justified within himself; by it he is made equal in fellowship with an angel. Therefore it is called “the measure of a man, which is that of an angel.” For this measure is affirmed to be the measure of a human being and the measure of an angel, because through it a person restored in the world is joined to an angel in heaven.

Thus, the angel speaking with Saint John is the choir of holy teachers; the golden reed is Scripture; the squareness of the city is the firm and immovable constancy [Col. 0870A] of the holy Church; the twelve thousand stadia by which the city is measured are apostolic teaching perfectly fulfilled by the lesser Church as it strives toward heavenly rewards; the city’s walls are ecclesiastical defenders; and the measurement of the walls is the righteousness of ecclesiastical defenders in the perfect observance of evangelical and legal precepts and in the exercise of the four principal virtues.

## CHAPTER VI. On the character of its wall, foundations, and gates

“And the construction of its wall was of jasper stone; but the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass” (Rev. XXI).

Above he said that he had seen the city and its wall, or walls, its gates, and its foundations, and that all these differed from one another and were distinct from each other. Here he continues and shows what the wall is like, what the city is like, what the foundations are like, and what the gates are like.

“And the construction of its wall was of jasper stone.” The wall is Christ; the construction of the wall is the union of the Word and the assumed human being. This is rightly said to be of jasper stone, because they remain firmly and indissolubly united in the unity of person. Nor is this construction said to be of just any stone, but of jasper, which is green, because Christ promises us the unfading freshness of eternity.

“But the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass.” Above it was shown that the lesser Church is figured by the name “city.” Therefore the city is pure gold like clear glass, because the holy Church, even in its lesser elect members, gleams like gold with the brightness of divine knowledge and shines like glass with purity of confession. Glass conceals no stains within itself, and the holy simplicity of the elect purely reveals its sins to its superiors. Both gold and clear glass are called pure, so that the purity and perfection of each virtue may be indicated.

It follows:

“The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every precious stone. The first foundation, jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, chalcedony; the fourth, emerald; the fifth, sardonius (sardonyx); the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, topaz; the tenth, chrysoprase; the eleventh, hyacinth; the twelfth, amethyst.”

After the wall and city, he proceeds to the foundations of the wall and describes their beauty in many ways under the figure of the aforesaid stones. By the foundations of the wall we understand the twelve patriarchs, or rather other saints of the Old Testament signified through the patriarchs. They were truly adorned with every precious stone, because in their own times they shone steadfastly with every kind of virtue and left after them imitators of those virtues.

Therefore they are the foundations of the wall; they are precious stones, because Christ took flesh from their stock and because they shone with the manifold brightness of virtues. He also describes these virtues in order under the figure of precious stones and wonderfully displays their beauty.

The first foundation is jasper—that is, jasper is placed first among the foundations. Because it is green, it signifies faith, the green shoot of all good things. Sapphire, because it resembles a clear sky, signifies hope in heavenly goods. Chalcedony, because it shines like the pale flame of a lamp, signifies charity. Emerald, because it too is green, expresses the verdant beginning of good action. Sardonyx, because it is black beneath, signifies humility. Sardius, which is red, signifies suffering. Chrysolite, which emits fiery sparks, signifies the working of miracles. Beryl, which burns the hand of its holder, signifies the kindling of righteousness in one’s neighbor through a good example. Topaz, golden and ethereal in color and more precious than all gems, signifies contemplation. Green chrysoprase figures the desire for eternity that never withers. Hyacinth, which changes with the air—clear in clear weather and cloudy in cloudy weather—signifies the virtue of fraternal condescension. Purple amethyst signifies the dignity of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0871B] All these are arranged in the indicated order because the virtues of the saints are known to be not confused but ordered and beautifully disposed. If anyone wishes to consider the arrangement of the aforesaid stones more closely, he may find in it no small instruction.

For jasper, signifying faith, is placed first because faith is the beginning and origin of all virtues. Sapphire, signifying hope, is placed second because hope comes after faith in rank. Chalcedony, signifying charity, is added third because charity is ordered third among the three principal virtues. Fourth is emerald, signifying the verdant beginning of good work, because it is right that one who abounds in faith, hope, and charity should labor to bring them forth into the fruit of good work. Fifth is sardonius, or sardonyx, which by the blackness of its lower part expresses humility, because it is fitting that one who labors to bring forth good work should not grow proud but should rather strive to become humble. Sixth is sardius, which by its blood-red color signifies suffering, because one who shines in the first three virtues and performs good with humility must often endure many adversities. Seventh is chrysolite, because it emits sparks and expresses the brightness of miracles, since one who suffers evils for Christ is sometimes made glorious by the power of miracles. Eighth is beryl, which burns the hand that holds it, because such a great person not only benefits himself but also often kindles others toward righteousness.

Ninth is topaz, golden and ethereal in color, signifying contemplation of heavenly goods, because one adorned with the aforesaid goods is deservedly raised on high to contemplate heavenly things. Tenth is chrysoprase, which by its greenness signifies desire for flourishing eternity, because after a righteous person beholds eternal joys through contemplation, he burns with every desire to possess them. Eleventh is hyacinth, which changes with the air and by which the virtue of fraternal condescension is figured, because whoever burns with desire for contemplated eternity abounds in the bowels of mercy and compassion. Twelfth follows amethyst, which by its purple color signifies royal dignity, because one who shines with the aforesaid goods knows how powerfully to govern himself and others, and longs with all desires to attain the prize of heavenly dignity.

[Col. 0872A] Thus the aforesaid stones are rightly arranged in such an order, because the virtues of the saints signified through them are suitably joined in succession, as has been shown. There are also other properties or colors found in the aforesaid gems, by all of which the merits of the saints are variously figured. But we pass over these briefly, lest through excessive length we create weariness for the diligent reader.

Therefore the holy patriarchs, or any other saints of the Old Testament begotten from them and signified through them—these, I say, are the foundations of the wall; they are the precious stones. They are the foundations of the wall because Christ took the origin of his flesh from them. They are stones through the firmness of sacred faith; they are precious through the brightness of righteousness. And in order to show that the apostles and imitators of the apostles possessed that same firmness of faith and brightness of righteousness, he fittingly adds: “And the twelve gates are twelve pearls, each one”—that is, twelve pearls in each gate. “And each gate was made of a single pearl.”

The gates are the apostles, because through their teaching we have entrance into the kingdom. Twelve pearls are said to be in each of them because, from the four regions of the world, followers of the apostles in faith and righteousness are gathered to faith in the holy Trinity through the apostles’ twelvefold teaching. For there are twelve pearls in each gate because, through the saving teaching of the apostles, diverse souls of the faithful are gathered from the four quarters of the world to the one holy and undivided Trinity through the faith of belief, as imitators of those apostles. These are said to be in the gates because they enter the holy city through the teaching of the holy apostles.

And this is what is said: “The twelve gates are twelve pearls, each one.” For there are pearls through the gates, because faithful souls are saved through apostolic teaching: firm through faith and bright through righteousness. And because the holy apostles themselves could neither make nor contain other pearls unless they themselves were pearls, it is rightly added: “And each gate was made of a single pearl.” Each gate is made of a single pearl because the holy apostles were themselves firm in faith and shone far and wide with the splendor of righteousness.

Thus the foundations of the wall shine, and the gates of the city shine in themselves and through the pearls implanted in them, because patriarchs and apostles shine in themselves through their own virtue and shine in their followers through imitation of that same virtue. It is indeed great and worthy of praise for someone to gleam in himself with so great a gift of heavenly good; but it is much more praiseworthy to shine also in one’s neighbors through the transfusion of that same good.

It follows:

“And the streets of the city were pure gold, like transparent glass.” The streets of the city are the lesser saints, [Col. 0873A] who use worldly things more freely, more indulgently, and more permissively. Although they are streets through a more relaxed mode of living, they are nevertheless upright through good intention; for though the necessities of this present life somewhat humble and spread them out, the uprightness of good intention directs them. They are rightly called pure gold, because they burn inwardly like pure gold with the light of brightness, and like transparent glass because they conceal no stains of defilement within themselves. Thus they are gold through the flame of inwardly burning charity, and like transparent glass through the purity of outward and open confession. If, then, such is the beauty of the lesser and lower members, who can estimate the beauty of the greater and higher?

Finally, after the holy theologian has perfectly described in the foregoing the character of the wall, foundations, and gates of the holy city, he proceeds to indicate certain future and eternal goods of that city through the removal and absence of temporal things. Hence it follows:

“And I saw no temple in it; for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God will enlighten it, and its lamp is the Lamb.”

He saw no temple in it because a temple is here only a place of offering and prayer, which will have no place there. “For the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb,” that is, complete sanctification and the enduring bestowal of every petition. But it should be carefully noted that he almost everywhere mentions humanity under the name of the Lamb together with divinity, so that both natures may be loved in the Redeemer and common, united grace rendered to both.

“And the city has no need”—that is, it will have no need—“of sun or moon to shine upon it. For the glory of God,” namely the glory of the holy Trinity, “will enlighten it. And its lamp is the Lamb,” namely the humanity containing divinity for the illumination of others. Now, therefore, the holy city needs the light of sun and moon and many other things that are now necessary to it; if these were then present where it will be, they would be superfluous. Yet the sun and moon will exist and will shine much more brightly than now, for the praise and glory of him who could create such things and renew what he created into a better state.

It follows:

[Col. 0873D] “And the nations will walk in its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory and honor into it.” The nations are rightly understood as subjects, and kings as prelates. Therefore the nations will walk in its light, because all the elect who now submit themselves to their superiors for love of their heavenly homeland will then rejoice freely in its eternal brightness.

Otherwise: they will walk in its light because, by hoping now for its future brightness, they labor with all their powers toward it in the course of this present life. And not only the nations—that is, subjects—but also the kings of the earth—that is, prelates, who govern not only themselves but others in this earthly state—will bring, in likeness to conquerors who bear spoils into their cities, their glory and honor into it: their glory, which is a good conscience proper to themselves, [Col. 0874A] and the honor shown them by their subject household. They will bring these into it when, at the end of the world, on the day of judgment, in the universal resurrection, they enter the heavenly dwelling with those entrusted to them. For with these and innumerable other goods the holy heavenly city will be enriched and adorned, because everything which each righteous person now performs will be transferred to its beauty and adornment.

It follows:

“And its gates shall not be shut by day, for night shall not be there. And they shall bring into it the glory and honor of the nations. Nor shall anything defiled enter it, or one who practices abomination and falsehood, except those who are written in the book of life of the Lamb.”

All these things are shown to concern the future state of the blessed city, not its present state. “And its gates shall not be shut by day.” Here the gates of the city Jerusalem are shut when either preaching is justly withdrawn or someone is excluded from entrance into the Church because of his fault. This will not exist at all then, because neither the one nor the other will thereafter have a place.

Why he did not say that its gates would not be shut even by night, as he says they will not be shut by day, he himself explains, saying: “For night shall not be there.” For there will not be there this night of time, where the immeasurable splendor of divinity will shine eternally. But even if we understand night in a spiritual sense, certainly no night at all will be there, because there will be neither fault nor punishment.

O how bright, how solemn will be that day which the Lord will make—that day, the end of our sorrow! Who can now either comprehend in thought or declare in words its divine brightness, which will then be in heaven, when, the air having been purified, we read that the moon will then shine like the sun, and that the sun will shine sevenfold as on seven days in the world? If, therefore, we judge that so great a brightness of visible and bodily lights will then exist and shine in this fabric of the world, who, still placed in the blindness of this life, can comprehend the splendor of immeasurable and eternal divinity by which that heavenly city will then be illumined? Let us therefore believe by faith what we are insufficient to comprehend by understanding, so that in this way at least we may someday attain to the contemplation of that brightness.

The wonderful good of the heavenly city is further described at length when it is added: “And they shall bring into it the glory and [Col. 0874D] honor of the nations.” The aforesaid kings, namely the holy prelates, will bring into it the glory and honor of the nations—that is, the nations themselves, inwardly glorious through the witness of a good conscience and outwardly to be honored through the performance of good work—when, at the end of the world, every good ruler brings the people now entrusted to him into the eternal dwelling-place of the heavenly habitation.

But because, when the good enter blessedness, the evil are left outside for condemnation, it fittingly adds: “Nor shall anything defiled enter it,” even merely through consent in thought; nor one “who practices abomination” in action, “and falsehood” in speech. Now an unclean person enters in the world, the evil with the good, the liar with the truthful. Then no one at all who now corrupts himself by evil living will enter. For only those will then enter who now keep the divine commandments by following what is right. Hence it is said: “Except those who are written in the book of life of the Lamb.” Only those are written in the book of life who attain from grace to glory. This is called the book of life of the Lamb because the heavenly good which divinity predestined to be bestowed upon the righteous will be administered by humanity.

Thus the wall is Christ; the foundations of the wall are the patriarchs; the gates of the city are the apostles; the stones are virtues; the splendor of the stones is the example of virtues; the streets of the city are the lesser saints who use worldly things more freely; gold is the brightness of charity; glass is purity of confession.

## CHAPTER VII. On the river of living water, the tree of life, and its fruit

[Col. 0875B] “And he showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb. In the midst of its street, on either side of the river, was the tree of life, bearing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit in each month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations” (Rev. XXII).

Above he showed, by describing its walls or wall, gates, corners, foundations, length, breadth, and height, that the heavenly city is most beautiful. Now in this chapter he proceeds to show with what and how great goods it is filled, both in its present state and in the future.

“And the angel”—namely, the one speaking with me—“showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb.” The river is the grace of the Holy Spirit, whose stream makes glad the city of God. It is rightly compared to a river because, watering individual generations, it flows from one after another; and although it may at times be narrowed by being withdrawn from some, it never ceases to flow through others by being shared with them.

It is also suitably compared to living water: water because it refreshes, living because it never fails; water because it washes, living because it always flows. It is bright as crystal because in those whom it waters by enlightening them it gleams like shining crystal. It is fittingly said to proceed from the throne of God and of the Lamb because it is daily imparted, flowing from the perfect members of the Church and learned rulers, in whom God reigns seated and justly governs others.

[Col. 0875D] “In the midst of its street,” that is, the city’s street, “on either side of the river, was the tree of life.” Above we said that the street signifies the lesser members, who are permitted to use worldly things more freely. As they are lower in the world, so they will be lower in heaven; as they are lower in merit, so also in reward, for each will receive his own reward according to his labor.

So long as we are in this life, we are on this side of the river, because grace is given from above, through which the human race is justified. But those already glorified through the first robe are beyond the river, because, having been perfectly justified, they no longer need to be justified; and they have already been granted to behold the Creator himself face to face.

The tree of life is also Christ, because he preserves in perpetual immortality those to whom he gives himself as food, “bearing twelve fruits.” By the twelve fruits we understand the twelvefold teaching of the holy apostles. Thus the tree of life stands in the midst of the city’s street, bearing twelve fruits on either side of the river, because Christ gives himself as refreshment to all the elect—not only to the greater, but also to the lesser, both in the world and in heaven. Apostolic authority proclaimed that this refreshment is bestowed in the world unto righteousness and in heaven unto glory.

For Christ refreshes his own in the world through participation in his body and blood; he refreshes them in heaven through perpetual contemplation of his divinity and humanity. Therefore on either side of the river the tree of life produces fruit: on this side, the fruit of righteousness; beyond, the fruit of glory. By feeding them on this side, it makes them righteous; by feeding them beyond, it makes them blessed. Whoever is not refreshed here by the fruit of righteousness is not satisfied there by the fruit of glory.

And so that we may know that Christ feeds his own unceasingly, it fittingly adds: “Yielding its fruit in each month.” The tree of life yields fruit in every month because Christ continuously and without any interruption feeds his elect in the world and in heaven.

“And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations.” The leaves of the tree are Christ’s commandments. Leaves protect and adorn; commandments protect and adorn. These commandments are rightly said to be for the healing of the nations because, if they are fulfilled with grace’s assistance, they effect the justification of souls. For whoever is justified is healed.

But lest we doubt that the holy city—whose future state is the chief concern of the writer’s intention—is free from every evil and filled with every good, he immediately adds:

[Col. 0876C] “And there shall be no curse any more; but the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it. And his servants shall serve him, and they shall see his face, and his name shall be upon their foreheads. And night shall be no more; and they shall have no need of the light of a lamp or of the light of the sun, because the Lord God shall enlighten them, and they shall reign for ages of ages.”

The less any good is freed from present evil, the more it is diminished from its own perfection. Therefore, so that the good of the heavenly city may be shown perfect and complete in its heavenly state, it is shown in these words to be free from evil and filled with good. In the statement, “there shall be no curse any more,” it is declared free from evil; in the words that follow, filled with goods.

“There shall be no curse,” because there will be no fault and no punishment. “But the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it,” because the holy and undivided Trinity and the humanity joined to the Word will reign there without end by abiding there. “And his servants,” that is, all the elect, “shall serve him” freely—not in fear or dread, as often now, but with highest and perfect love and security, acclaiming his praise in the voices of inward love. “And they shall see his face” immediately, not in an enigma as now, but as he is. “And his name shall be”—understand, written—“upon them,” because they will be called children of God and of the Lamb; and it will be written upon their foreheads, that is, openly, just as they openly confessed.

[Col. 0877A] “And night shall be no more,” that is, there will be no ignorance; “and they shall have no need of the light of a lamp or of the light of the sun,” because they will have no need of the ministry of lesser or greater light. Or, in a spiritual sense, they will have no need of the light of lamp or sun because they will have no need of the teaching of the old or new law, or of the teaching of any ordinary or eminent teacher.

He also gives the reason why they will have no need, saying: “Because the Lord God shall enlighten them.” This wholly excludes needing another’s light, because God perfectly enlightens the blessed and leaves nothing in them to be enlightened. “And they shall reign,” because they will cling to the reigning one, “for ages of ages,” that is, eternally.

Thus the river is spiritual grace; the nearer side is the state of this present life; the farther side, the state of heavenly life; the tree of life, Christ; the offering of fruit on both sides, participation in the body and blood of Christ in the world and contemplation of his divinity and humanity in heaven; the leaves of the tree, Christ’s commandments; the healing of the nations, the justification of souls. And he appropriately adds the leaves after the fruit, because it does no good to receive Christ’s body and blood unless one strives to fulfill his commandments.

All things pertaining to the beauty and praise of the holy city—indeed, all things pertaining to the completion of the prophecy of this entire book—seem to have been sufficiently expounded in the foregoing. For what follows is shown chiefly to concern the commendation of the book and the solemn confirmation to its hearer of the words of the book itself, lest anyone presume to add anything to it or take anything away from it.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the threefold commendation of this book

[Col. 0877C] “And he said to me: These words are most faithful and true. And the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets sent his angel to show his servants the things that must soon take place” (Rev. XXII). “And behold, I come quickly.”

Having expounded above all that is thought to pertain to the description of the glorious city—or rather, having completed all that pertains to the fulfillment of the prophecy of this book in the contents from the book’s beginning to this point—he adds a commendation of the book itself, strengthening and confirming it by a threefold authority: namely, the authority of the angel speaking with him, his own authority, and Christ’s authority.

“And he said to me,” namely, the angel who showed me the other things, “These words are most faithful and true.” They are most faithful because they faithfully disclose what must be believed. They are true because all that is said will be fulfilled without falsehood. And they are indeed most faithful, true, and worthy of every faith because they have been revealed through angelic ministry.

Therefore the angel himself says of himself: “And the Lord God of the spirits of the prophets,” that is, the Lord God who gives the spirit of prophecy to prophets, “sent his angel”—namely, me—“to show his servants the things that must soon take place”: to show them to his servants, not to unbelieving Jews, cruel tyrants, or proud philosophers; the things that must soon take place because they are soon to be fulfilled and cannot remain unfulfilled.

And to prove that all things contained in this book are truly to be completed, and soon, he introduces Christ himself as speaking and affirming the swiftness of his coming, at which all things will be accomplished. For he adds: “Behold, I come quickly.” For he will by no means delay in coming; by no means will he delay in fulfilling what must be accomplished at his coming.

Just as at the beginning, so also at the end of the book, he gains the goodwill of his hearers by the promise of blessedness and invites them to the sublimity of heavenly rewards, saying: “Blessed is he who keeps the words of this book.” And the phrase “who keeps” is especially commendable. For it does no good to attain knowledge of truth by reading or hearing unless one labors with all one’s strength, by good living, to keep what one has learned. Only the person who keeps the precepts of the sacred page not only in memory but also in life attains blessedness.

Therefore the prophecy of this heavenly book must be believed in every way, because it was revealed through angelic ministry and commended by angelic authority; and it must be kept with every care and intention, because it promises eternal rewards. Yet it is commended not only by the angel’s testimony but also by the testimony of the holy theologian himself.

It follows:

“And I, John, am he who heard and saw these things.” I heard the voices; I saw the figures. “I, John”—as if he said: Not only the angel, but I, John, your teacher—not just any heretic, your friend, not just any stranger—I, together with and after that angel, endeavor to commend this prophecy to you, since I am not accustomed to announce anything false to you.

It follows:

And when I had heard and seen, I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who was showing me these things. And he said to me: “See that you do not do this. I am your fellow-servant, and that of your brothers the prophets, and of those who keep the words of this book. Worship God.”

It seems remarkable that Saint John again fell at the angel’s feet and again wished to worship him, since above he had wished to do precisely this and had immediately been forbidden by the angel. But because in this final vision he had perhaps been raised far more highly than before to contemplate heavenly goods and to consider the greater glory of the holy city in its future state, the earlier prohibition may, through astonishment and admiration at so great and supermundane a beauty, have slipped from his mind. Hence it is fittingly added here: “And when I had seen and heard,” that is, when I had seen and heard so wonderful and incomparable a beauty and joy of the holy city, stupefied after such admiration and forgetting the former prohibition, “I fell down to worship before the feet of the angel who was showing me these things.”

Or certainly, by falling again before the angel and again wishing to worship him, he indicates to us through this repetition how great a humility and veneration we ought to show to our prelates, through whose word or ministry spiritual grace is bestowed upon us; for he himself, though forbidden, wished to worship the angel who was showing him spiritual and heavenly goods. [Col. 0879A] Yet holy prelates themselves, when we bow our heads to them, wish this honor by which we venerate them to be shown them not for their own sake, but for God’s. Thus the angel who forbade the theologian to worship him rightly added after the prohibition: “Worship God.”

Therefore, following the example of blessed John, we ought with great reverence and diligence to humble ourselves before those set over us; for when we bow before them, we venerate not so much them as God in them. Yet they themselves ought not to be exalted within themselves by the honor rendered them, but rather humbled. The angel subtly indicates this when he says: “I am your fellow-servant, and that of your brothers.” Then, after saying, “I am your fellow-servant, and that of your brothers,” he adds, “the prophets, and those who keep the words of this book,” thereby including and distinguishing the chosen preachers [Col. 0879B] and those obedient to preachers. For where he says “the prophets,” he expressly denotes preachers; where he adds, “and those who keep the words of this book,” he designates those lesser persons who obey preachers. He therefore acknowledged himself fellow-servant of all, because he knew that all have the same Lord.

Why, however, the angel in the Old Testament allowed himself to be worshipped by a human being, but in the New firmly forbade this to be done, we have already given above the reason explained by the holy Fathers: namely, that he refused worship from man once he saw the nature of our humanity glorified above himself in the Redeemer of the world.

“Worship God.” As though he said: “You must now render this honor to him alone, whose humanity, reigning above me together with you, I reverence and worship. From now on I do not allow you to worship me, because I behold your nature reigning with divinity.” [Col. 0879C]

It follows:

“Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book.”

This too seems surprising, because above Saint John was commanded to seal the prophetic words of this book, where it is written: “Seal,” that is, “seal up what the seven thunders spoke; do not write them,” that is, do not disclose them in writing without the veils of figures. Yet in this place he is forbidden to seal them, where it is said: “Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book.”

But it must be understood that the words of sacred Scripture are to be sealed in one respect and not sealed in another. They are to be sealed [Col. 0879D] because they must be hidden from enemies; they are not to be sealed because they must be revealed to friends. Saint John observed and fulfilled both what was forbidden and what was commanded him. Some things he endeavored to conceal from the wicked beneath obscure veils of figures; other things he took care to reveal to the good, either by writing without figures, or by himself expounding the figures, and thus subtly intimating that mysteries lying hidden under other veils were to be sought out.

Yet although the mysteries of sacred Scripture are sealed beneath obscurities of figures in order to exercise the good and remain hidden from the wicked, the wicked themselves have no excuse for their ignorance. For they can understand the clearer words of the sacred page; and if they were willing to abandon vices and practice virtues, they could, with God’s grace assisting them, attain also to knowledge of the more hidden things. [Col. 0880A]

He then gives the reason why he forbids him to seal the words of the prophecy of this book—that is, to conceal them altogether by writing more obscurely—saying: “For the time is near”: namely, the time of Christ’s coming, when those who act rightly may be blessed and those who despise him condemned. What must necessarily be known, fulfilled in action, and will most certainly be examined and recompensed, must not be wholly concealed, but diligently proclaimed.

That the ungodly despise sacred prophecy whereas the righteous fulfill it is declared when the voice of prophecy adds:

“Let the one who does harm do harm still; and let the one who is in filth become filthy still; and let the righteous do righteousness still; and let the holy person be made holy still.”

As though he said: “Do not seal [Col. 0880B] these words, but make them manifest to others, because the time of judgment is near: by them the ungodly will be condemned and the righteous glorified. But know that, although you have made the same words known to both without distinction, the wicked, by despising them, will become worse through them, while the good, by fulfilling them, will become better.”

For it must be understood that the saying here, “Let the one who does harm do harm still,” is uttered not in the voice of one wishing this, but of one prophesying, as is similarly found in many places of sacred Scripture. He distinguishes two evils among the wicked, one belonging to malice of heart, the other to the lustfulness of the flesh. For what he says, “Let the one who does harm do harm still,” pertains to malice; but what follows, “Let the one who is in filth become filthy still,” pertains to lustfulness.

By each vice the wicked sometimes injure only themselves, and sometimes corrupt others as well. The farther they extend through the spread of both kinds of depravity, the worse they become. [Col. 0880C] Alternatively, the words “Let the one who does harm do harm still” may refer to the persecution which the wicked inflict upon the good, while “Let the one who is in filth become filthy still” refers to their own particular depravity. For doing harm seems sometimes to concern another person as well, whereas becoming filthy concerns oneself more particularly.

Likewise, among the good he sets two goods contrary to the two evils mentioned above, and arranges them in the same order. For “Let the righteous do righteousness still” is contrary to the preceding “Let the one who does harm do harm still”; and what he finally adds, “Let the holy person be made holy still,” opposes what he had set above: “Let the one who is in filth become filthy still.”

“Let the one who does harm do harm still, and let the one who is in filth become filthy still; and let the righteous do righteousness still, and let the holy person be made holy still.” As though he said: “Through sacred prophecy, the ungodly will be perverted for the worse both through malice of heart and through lustfulness of flesh; while the righteous will be changed for the better through righteousness of heart and holiness of flesh. The former, by persecuting others and defiling themselves, will become worse; the righteous, by acting justly toward others and sanctifying themselves, will become better.” [Col. 0880D]

He plainly shows that his coming is near, and that both the righteous and the ungodly will be recompensed according to their deserts, when he adds:

“Behold, I come quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to each one according to his works.”

When he says, “Behold, I come quickly,” he signifies that his coming is near. When he adds, “And my reward is with me, to render to each one according to his works,” he declares that the righteous and the ungodly are to be recompensed according to their deserts, with reward or punishment. This reward is both his and man’s: his, because he distributes it; man’s, because he receives it. It is rightly said to be with him, because both the power and the mercy by which the good person is sanctified and the wicked person condemned are in him.

And lest we suppose that someone else is judge and recompender of both, he himself confirms this, saying: “I am α and ω, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.” As though he said: “Truly I shall come and judge and recompense, and no other; because I created by power, and I shall distinguish by justice; I gave the origin of existence, and I shall give the recompense of merit.” [Col. 0881A]

This statement, “I am α and ω,” is frequently repeated in this book so that firmer faith may be placed in it. Its words differ, but its meaning is recognized as one. And because he had previously said, “Let the one who does harm do harm still, and let the one who is in filth become filthy still,” which might perhaps seem harsh and terrible—like a kind of imprecation and curse—to a sinner who does not understand the manner of sacred speech, and might easily cast that person into despair, it is fittingly added, so that the same saying may be softened and, should that person wish to repent, a most certain hope of recovered salvation may be restored:

“Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may have power over the tree of life, and may enter through the gates into the city.”

“Blessed are those who wash their robes,” that is, their bodies and works, defiled by sin after baptism, “that they may have power over the tree of life,” that is, that they may be able to possess a true participation in Christ, “and may enter through the gates,” that is, through the faith of the saints, “into the city,” namely, the heavenly Jerusalem. As though he said: “Sinners, if because of the bitter saying above you wish to repent, do not despair. For just as those who keep themselves undefiled after baptism attain blessedness, so too do those who, after sin, wash their defiled robes most cleanly. But if you scorn to be washed, you shall not enter the holy city.” For it follows:

“Outside are dogs, and the shameless, and sorcerers, and murderers, and those who serve idols, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.” [Col. 0881D]

“Dogs” are unclean and barking persons, who daily defile themselves with crimes and nevertheless presume to bark in detraction against those who do good. What follows—“the shameless, sorcerers, murderers, those who serve idols, everyone who loves and practices falsehood”—is rightly understood also literally. For nearly all such persons are described as being outside, because they do not receive a dwelling with the elect in the heavenly city.

Yet we may expound the shameless and those following them in the list also according to a spiritual sense. The shameless are those who defile not only themselves by wantonness of flesh, but others too by whatever crime. Sorcerers are those who destroy others by a perverse example or word. [Col. 0882A] Murderers are those who kill their neighbors by will, word, or an example of depravity. Those who serve idols are persons who carry out what pleases demons. Finally, the one who loves and practices falsehood is one who loves in the heart and pronounces with the mouth that by which he deceives his neighbor.

These, therefore, and all the other reprobate persons figured by them, are excluded from entrance into the blessed city, because they by no means obtain the kingdom of God. Whoever, then, wishes to enter the heavenly Jerusalem must either preserve himself undefiled after receiving grace, or, if he knows that he has been polluted by any crime, hasten diligently to cleanse his robe through repentance of heart, confession of mouth, tears, and satisfaction by good works.

It follows: “I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you of these things in the churches.”

After he has commended his prophecy by the authority of the angel and by his own authority, he endeavors to commend it by the authority of Christ, so that it may be commended by a threefold attestation and, having been commended, be more deeply confirmed among its hearers. Thus it is said: “I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify to you of these things in the churches.” For Jesus revealed the sacred mystery to the angel, the angel to John, and John to the churches. [Col. 0882B]

It should be noted that the holy theologian says not “in the Church” but “in the churches,” namely because of the churches of Asia to which he sent the book in the first instance. For at the end of the book, as at its beginning, he directs his speech to those to whom he especially addressed it.

“I, Jesus.” As though he said: “Not only the angel and John have commended to you the words of this book by the inscription of their names, but I too commend them to you by the addition of my name.” And, as though someone might ask, “Who is this Jesus?”—for many in antiquity were called Jesus—he immediately makes known plainly who this Jesus is by describing his authority. For he adds: “I am the root and offspring of David, the bright morning star.”

As though he openly said: “Since you hear how great and what kind of person I am, you ought to believe with certain faith what I say. I am the root, by creating; David’s offspring, by taking flesh from his line. I am a star, by providing light to the world; bright, by surpassing the splendor of all the saints; morning, by proclaiming the immense brightness of the future and eternal day.” [Col. 0882C]

“I therefore, so great and such as I am, commend to you the words of this prophecy, who also bestow other spiritual goods upon you and promise heavenly and eternal things. These ought to be believed by you with so much the greater faith because they are shown to be commended by my name and authority.”

Finally, how great the love and desire with which both Christ and the holy universal mother Church long for our salvation is disclosed in a gentle summons, when it is added:

“And the bridegroom and the bride say: ‘Come.’”

The bridegroom, that is Christ, speaks through inward inspiration; the bride speaks through preaching, to the person, namely, predestined for blessedness: “Come through faith and good action, through conversion and good conduct.” They are called bridegroom and bride because they promise the joys of marriage. [Col. 0883A]

And lest the one who is called and hears should remain barren as a result of others’ calling, it is fittingly added: “And let the one who hears say: ‘Come.’” The one who hears is the person who believes rightly and fulfills in action what he believes. Such a hearer is commanded to call others, lest the light of spiritual good be hidden beneath the bushel of his silence. For many grasp great things about heavenly mysteries through knowledge, but scorn to minister these things to others. Such people are shown to be blameworthy in this saying, because the good which ought to have been revealed to others through them remains hidden within them.

But lest the person who is invited should fear to come to the fullness of heavenly good, either terrified by the magnitude of sins or hindered by some faintheartedness, it is rightly added to strengthen that person so that he may gain confidence in attaining that good: “Let the one who thirsts come.” “The one who thirsts,” that is, the person who has a will for conversion, “let him come through conversion”—understand: secure concerning forgiveness—let him receive the sacraments, and his sins will be forgiven freely. [Col. 0883B]

This is indicated even more openly when it follows: “Let the one who wishes receive the water of life freely”: the water of life, that is, life-giving grace; freely, because apart from human merits. In the grace first given, the merit of the recipient gives no assistance; in grace bestowed on one already doing good so that he may act better, the merit of the one acting and receiving is not excluded. For human action, just as it is useless without grace, is always beneficial with grace. Grace is therefore first given to us; thereafter it is multiplied in us, with both grace and our merit cooperating.

Moreover, if anyone—as is believed to have happened often or to be able to happen—should aspire to conversion through grace, and receive that grace with a perfect heart, that person is saved even if prevented by death from sharing in the sacraments, namely baptism or communion in Christ’s body and blood. For one cannot perish with grace. The power of the sacraments is already contained in faith once received; and in the good will which always inwardly and inseparably accompanies true faith, the merit of good works is fulfilled. Therefore the water of life is bestowed freely, because salvation is granted to the believer, even apart from every merit of action, for good will alone.

“Let the one who wishes receive the water of life freely.” O how precious are these utterances of heavenly condescension—worthy to be preferred to every price, worthy of every acceptance, to be received with every devotion, retained in every memory, and merited by every virtue! Let each person, then, consider with how great and what kind of hearing he receives them, preserves what is received, and fulfills it. Saint John therefore commends and confirms this book among his hearers by a threefold authority, as was shown above. [Col. 0883D]

## CHAPTER IX. Saint John’s solemn warning to the hearer of the words of this prophecy.

“I solemnly testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to these things, God shall add to him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of this prophecy, God shall take away [Col. 0884A] his share from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book” (Rev. 22).

There were certain heretics in Asia who, in order to foster their errors more effectively, could readily add something to this book or take something away. To restrain their presumption, therefore, he adds a sentence of excommunication and shows what punishment is deserved by one who presumes to add or remove anything in it.

“I solemnly testify,” that is, I stand as witness to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book, so that each may beware of presuming in any way to corrupt it. “If anyone adds to these things”: the one who adds is the one who attaches falsehood; the one who takes away is the one who removes something from what is written in it or contradicts it by denial. But each is struck by the sword of excommunication, because the one is punished with evils and the other despoiled of goods.

Although, of these two evils, one is beautifully assigned by the wording of the sentence to one person and the other to the other, nevertheless each is struck by both. For the one afflicted with those evils must first necessarily be stripped of goods; and the one deprived of goods is not permitted to remain free from the infliction of evils. Thus both the adder and the subtracter are punished by both evils, both deprivation of goods and the infliction of evils, although, according to the logic and elegance of the sentence, this is referred more particularly to the former and that to the latter in the description. [Col. 0884B]

“If anyone adds to these things, God shall add to him the plagues written in this book,” whether temporal or eternal. “If anyone takes away, God shall take away his share from the book of life,” so that, namely, he may have no share in those things written in it; “and from the holy city,” so that he may not be a citizen in it; “and from the things written in this book,” so that he may not be a participant in the goods promised in it.

It follows:

“He who bears witness to these things says: ‘Yes. I come quickly.’ Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

Lest Saint John’s own testimony concerning the aforesaid excommunication seem insufficient to anyone, he adduces Christ’s testimony, by which the same thing is affirmed. Thus he says: “He who bears witness to these things,” namely Christ, who attests all things contained in this book, says: “Yes.” As though he said: “If many of you do not believe, believe the testimony of Truth.” *Yes* (*etiam*) is an adverb of affirmation, which, when added, affirms what has been promised. “I come quickly.” [Col. 0884C]

At the end of the book he mentions his coming, so that it may always be expected, lest anyone be found unprepared through some security. “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.” These are Saint John’s words, affirming and praying for the Savior’s coming. For where he joins “Amen” to the Lord’s words, “I come quickly,” he affirms that he will truly come. But where he says, “Come, Lord Jesus,” he entreats him to come.

In asking the Lord to come, he shows us how perfect he was in love. For if he loved the Lord less fully in any respect, weighed down by fear, he would by no means ask him to come. Therefore he was perfect in love, since he safely asked him to come. “For fear is not in love, but perfect love casts out fear.”

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.” In the customary manner of those writing to others, just as at the beginning of the book he wishes salvation to those to whom he writes, so at the end he prays for it for them. He prays for it also for all, so that he may openly show himself benevolent toward all and offended at no one, and thus draw them by that benevolence toward better things. [Col. 0885A]

We do not now recapitulate this vision here, because we reserve it to be recapitulated in the following chapter in the general recapitulation of all the visions.

## CHAPTER X. General recapitulation of the seven visions.

Because, dearest brother, through the disposing and helping grace of God we have at last reached the welcome harbor of our proposed discourse, it is pleasing at the end of the reading to recall to memory the sum of what has been said. Thus, after passing through all that precedes, you may have on the shore a brief recapitulation of everything, like a mirror in which you can contemplate the matter and form of the entire preceding work.

This book, placed at the end of the whole sacred page contained in the canon, seems to be like the summit and final topmost part of a tree rising from low places to high. Sacred Scripture is rightly compared to a tree, which in its teaching and exhortation is raised from the lowest things to the highest. For it fixes its root, as it were, in the earth when at its beginning it speaks of visible and transitory things, saying: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). [Col. 0885B]

Then, as time advances, the more it instructs us through the oracles of the prophets to hope for and seek heavenly things, the more it rises to greater heights. In evangelical teaching, the more sublimely and clearly it foretells the highest things, the nearer it approaches heavenly realities. Finally, in this book, divinely revealed to John the Evangelist, Christ’s friend—and especially at the end of the book—it has lifted its crown, as it were, above heaven, where it perfectly and plainly describes the future condition of the saints and the beautiful, joyful, eternal building and dwelling of the holy heavenly Jerusalem.

Although we place this book after the Gospel and say that in it sacred Scripture, in the manner of a tree, has raised its crown into heaven for the reason stated above, we in no way detract from or lower evangelical sublimity. Rather, we exalt it all the more, because we believe that this book, produced by the Evangelist, is not only Gospel, but also judge it to hold in evangelical teaching the highest place just as it holds the last place. [Col. 0885C]

Saint John, apostle and evangelist, received the prophecy of this book through divine revelation and, by divine command, committed it to writing for the benefit of believers, divided into seven visions. In the first vision, after the title, greeting, and description of the likeness appearing to him, he addresses the bishops of the seven churches especially entrusted to him. He first praises the bishop of Ephesus, the bishop of Pergamum, and the bishop of Thyatira for what is good, and then rebukes them for what is evil. He praises the bishop of Smyrna and the bishop of Philadelphia only for what is good. Finally, he rebukes the bishops of Sardis and Laodicea only for what is evil.

Having first carefully instructed those chiefly entrusted to him, he proceeds to describe the remaining visions, in which the mystery of the universal Church is contained more fully and sublimely. Thus at the beginning of the second vision he is commanded to ascend, signifying that he is about to see greater things. In the second vision, therefore, he first shows that the mystery of human redemption was fulfilled in Christ; then, under the sequence of the seven seals, he announces that the oracle of divine promise concerning human justification is fulfilled in the course of time, amid the turmoil of persecution, until the end of the world. [Col. 0886A]

Under the opening of these seals, he declares that the hidden things veiled by figures in sacred Scripture are revealed to holy teachers. For the hidden things contained in the sacred page are first opened to holy teachers by divine grace, and afterward are openly preached to the peoples, whether by them or by others. Hence, fittingly, after the opening of the seals contained in the second vision, by which the unsealing of heavenly oracles is signified, the distribution of trumpets is described in the third vision, by which the openly preached knowledge of those same oracles, now revealed, is represented.

For every good gift and every perfect gift descending from the Father of lights is first revealed to a few greater persons, that is, to prelates and teachers, because afterward it is commonly preached by them to many—to all the faithful of the Church. The opening of the seals contained in the second vision of this book thus expresses the revelation of mysteries; the bestowal of trumpets which follows in the third presents the preaching of those same mysteries. [Col. 0886B]

But because knowledge of the good, or preaching it, avails nothing unless good action follows, it is fittingly added after the seals and trumpets, in the fourth vision, that of the woman in childbirth. By her the labor of the holy Church is shown, that the good thing heard may bring forth the fruit of good action. In these three visions, moreover, together with the bestowal or reception of the three goods mentioned, the tempest of persecutions is described, because good is neither acquired nor possessed in the present life without encountering evil.

The good of spiritual grace, which the elect devote to action, is despised by the reprobate. Yet their contempt is severely avenged by almighty God, when all of them are either afflicted by temporal tribulation or punished by eternal condemnation. Thus most rightly, in the fifth vision their temporal affliction is signified under the pouring out of the bowls of God’s wrath; and in the sixth their eternal condemnation is signified under the figure of Babylon overthrown and submerged. There vengeance, transitory in the world but lasting in hell, is shown to be rendered to those who despise God. [Col. 0886C]

But just as the ungodly are condemned for guilt, so the righteous are blessed for righteousness. Accordingly, after the condemnation of the wicked has been described in the sixth vision, the glorification of the good is treated in the seventh, so that it may be plainly shown that as the reprobate receive the wages of death, so the elect receive the reward of blessedness.

We must also carefully observe in these descriptions of visions that the second and third visions, and the fourth and fifth visions, extend in narrative order from the beginning of the Church at its birth to the end of time. The sixth and seventh visions, however, deal more with the state of eternity: the sixth contains under the name Babylon the condemnation of the wicked, and the seventh under the name Jerusalem the glorification of the righteous.

These are the two cities, one of the devil, the other of God, opposed from the beginning and never at peace with one another. These are the two women, one of whom is read above as clothed with the sun, while the other sits upon a scarlet beast. For the assembly of the wicked and the whole body of the good are cities and are women: cities, because they are enriched by the numerous multitude of their citizens; women, because, joined to their husbands—Babylon to the devil, Jerusalem to Christ—they are fruitful with a manifold offspring. [Col. 0887A]

Thus, just as the sixth vision describes the condemnation of the wicked, so the seventh describes the glorification of the good, first describing the renewal of the elements and then the glorification of the saints. It treats the glorification of the saints by describing the holy heavenly Jerusalem: its brightness, its walls, its gates, its corners, its foundations, its measure, its streets, and its many other heavenly goods.

Finally, the holy theologian confirms this book by a threefold commendation and declares that anyone who presumes to take something from it or add something to it is to be struck with a most severe punishment. The sacred vision places first the renewal of the elements and then the glorification of the righteous so that we may ascend from visible things to invisible and, from the beauty of the elements, consider as far as possible what the future blessedness of the righteous will be: namely, what kind of good that is which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him.” [Col. 0888A]

We do better to be silent concerning the praise of its greatness, because we are unable to proclaim it as we ought and would wish. And we cease speaking of the sacred prophecy of the book of the Apocalypse, so that henceforth we may gather back to itself the mind dispersed by consideration of diverse matters.

What we have said less well in these writings we ascribe to ourselves. But whatever we have said worthily, we judge should faithfully be ascribed to the gift of God, who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach, who is contained by no place and changed by no time, immense and eternal, God blessed unto the ages. Amen. [Col. 0888B]

# PART TWO OF THE WORKS OF RICHARD OF SAINT VICTOR: THEOLOGICAL WORKS

[Col. 0887]

# SIX BOOKS ON THE TRINITY

## PROLOGUE
[Col. 0887C] “My righteous one lives by faith” (Rom. 1; Hab. 2): this is at once an apostolic and a prophetic statement. For the Apostle says what the prophet foretells: that the righteous person lives by faith. If this is so—indeed, because it is so—we certainly ought diligently to reflect upon, and frequently reconsider, the mysteries of our faith. For without faith it is impossible to please God. For where there is no faith, there can be no hope. For whoever approaches God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him; otherwise, what hope can there be? But where there is no hope, charity cannot exist. For who would [Col. 0888C] love one from whom he hopes for no good? Therefore, through faith we advance to hope, and through hope we make progress toward charity. Yet whatever I may possess, if I do not possess charity, it profits me nothing. But what the fruit of charity is, you hear from the mouth of Truth: “If anyone loves me, he will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14). Thus from love comes revelation, from revelation contemplation, and from contemplation knowledge.

But when Christ, our life, shall appear, then we too shall appear with him in glory; and then we shall be like him, because we shall see [Col. 0889A] him as he is. You see whence and how one arrives, or by what steps one ascends, through hope and charity from faith to divine knowledge, and through divine knowledge to eternal life: “And this,” he says, “is eternal life: to know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). Thus life comes from faith, and life comes from knowledge: from faith, the inward life; from knowledge, eternal life. From faith comes that life by which we live well for the present; from knowledge, that life by which we shall live blessedly in the future. Faith, therefore, is the beginning and foundation of every good. How earnest, then, we ought to be in faith, from which every good takes both its foundation and its support! But as in faith lies the beginning of every good, so in knowledge lies the consummation and perfection of every good.

Let us therefore be borne toward perfection; and by whatever steps we can toward progress, let us hasten from faith to knowledge. Let us strive, as far as we can, to understand what we believe. Let us consider how greatly, and how far, the philosophers of this world laboured and advanced in this knowledge, and let us be ashamed to be found inferior to them in this respect. For, as the Apostle testifies, “what may be known of God was manifest to them,” because, “although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God” (Rom. 1). Therefore they knew him. What, then, are we doing, who have received from our very cradle the tradition of the true faith? Love of truth ought to accomplish more in us than love of vanity could accomplish in them; [Col. 0889C] and we, whom faith directs, hope draws, and charity impels, ought to be able to do more in these matters.

It should therefore be too little for us merely to believe what is right and true concerning God; rather, as has been said, let us strive to understand what we believe. Let us always endeavour, insofar as it is permitted or possible, to grasp by reason what we hold by faith. But what wonder if our mind grows dim before the mysteries of divinity, when at almost every moment it is soiled by the dust of earthly thoughts? “Shake yourself from the dust, O virgin daughter of Zion.” If we are children of Zion, let us set up that lofty ladder of contemplation; let us take wings like eagles, by which we may raise ourselves above earthly things and lift ourselves to heavenly things. Let us savour what is heavenly, not what is upon earth; where Christ sits at the right hand of God, let us follow where Paul went before, who flew as far as the secret places of the third [Col. 0889D] heaven, where he heard those mysteries which it is not permitted for a human being to utter.

Let us ascend after our Head. For he ascended into heaven in order to summon and draw our desire after himself. Christ ascended, and the Spirit of Christ descended. Christ sent us his Spirit in order that he might raise our spirit after himself. Christ ascended in body; let us ascend in mind. His ascent was bodily; ours should be spiritual. For why did he offer the Spirit as the teacher and guide of our ascent, unless because he willed our ascent meanwhile to be spiritual? For that bodily ascent which is to occur in us will come about when he himself comes bodily in that flesh which he assumed for us, according to the saying: “Thus he will come, as you saw him going into heaven” [Col. 0890A] (Acts 1).

Let us therefore ascend spiritually; let us ascend intellectually, where for the present it is not permitted us to ascend bodily. Yet it should be too little for us to ascend, by the contemplation of the mind, only to the secret places of the first heaven. Let us ascend, therefore, from the first to the second, and from the second to the third. For those ascending in contemplation from visible things to invisible, from bodily things to spiritual, there first presents itself the consideration of immortality; second, the consideration of incorruptibility; third, the consideration of eternity. Behold a threefold realm: of immortality, incorruptibility, and eternity. The first is the realm of the human spirit; the second, of the angelic spirit; the third, of the divine Spirit.

The human spirit indeed possesses immortality as a kind of inheritance belonging to it by right, which it can never lose, at any time or through any duration, forever. For it must always either live in glory or endure in punishment. Thus, whenever this spirit actually devotes itself to earthly and transitory things, it as it were abandons itself and descends beneath itself. Therefore, for it to ascend to the first heaven is nothing other than to return to itself, and to ponder and do what belongs to immortality and is worthy of itself. But incorruptibility is far above it, and it cannot yet possess it. Yet what it does not now have, it is able to obtain by the merit of virtues. Thus, to ascend to the second heaven is for it to acquire by merits the glory of incorruptibility.

The angelic spirit already possesses this, as though by hereditary right; it attained it by the merit of its perseverance, on the condition that henceforth it can never lose it. But the third heaven belongs to divinity alone; for it is written of him that “he alone inhabits eternity” (Isa. 57).
