All other things that began to exist in time cannot thereby possess eternity, because they were not from eternity. But it is a singular gift, and above all others pre-eminent, to fly by the wing of contemplation as far as this heaven and fix the eyes of the intellect upon its rays.

Thus one ascends to the first heaven actually, to the second virtuously, to the third intellectually. To this last heaven the Spirit of Christ raises spiritual persons, whom, by the prerogative of revealing grace, he illumines more highly and more fully than others. For as often as, through the Spirit’s lifting, [Col. 0890D] we are raised to this heaven, so often are we advanced through the grace of contemplation to an understanding of eternal things. It should therefore be too little for us merely to believe what is true concerning eternal things, unless it is also granted us to demonstrate by the attestation of reason that which is believed. Nor should that knowledge of eternal things which comes through faith alone suffice us, unless we attain also that which comes through understanding—if we are not yet equal to that which comes through experience.

We have set these things forth beforehand in the preface to our work, in order to make our minds more attentive and ardent for such study. For we consider it to be of great merit to be very earnest in such an exercise, even if it is not granted us to accomplish according to our desire the very thing at which we aim.

# Book I

[Col. 0891]

## Chapter I. That we apprehend knowledge of things in three ways: by experience, by reasoning, and by belief

[Col. 0891A]

If we wish to ascend by the keenness of the mind to the knowledge of sublime things, it is worthwhile first to know the ways by which we are accustomed to apprehend knowledge of things. We apprehend knowledge of things, if I am not mistaken, in a threefold way. For some things we establish by experience; others we infer by reasoning; and of others we hold certainty by believing. We apprehend knowledge of temporal things through experience itself. But toward knowledge of eternal things we rise sometimes by reasoning and sometimes by believing.

For some of those things which we are commanded to believe seem to be not only above reason but even contrary to human reason, unless they are examined by profound and most subtle inquiry—or rather, made manifest by divine revelation. Therefore, in knowing or affirming these things, we are accustomed to rely more upon faith than reasoning, more upon authority than argumentation, in accordance with the prophet’s words: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7). Yet in these words this too seems deserving of careful attention: understanding of these matters is set before us as denied by this authority not universally but conditionally, when it says, “Unless you believe, you shall not understand.” Therefore those who have their senses exercised ought not to despair of attaining an understanding of such matters, provided that they know themselves to be firm in faith and of tested constancy in every respect in the confession of their faith.

## Chapter II. That nothing is held more firmly than what is apprehended by steadfast faith

[Col. 0891C]

But this is above measure remarkable in these matters: that all of us who are truly faithful hold nothing more certainly, nothing more steadfastly, than what we apprehend by faith. For these things were revealed from heaven to the Fathers and confirmed by God with so many, so great, and so marvellous miracles that it seems a kind of madness to doubt them even slightly. Countless miracles, therefore, and other things which can occur only by divine agency, establish such faith and do not permit doubt. Accordingly, in their attestation and confirmation, we use signs as arguments and wonders as experiences.

Would that the Jews would attend; would that the pagans would observe [Col. 0891D] with how great a security of conscience we shall be able to approach the divine judgment in this matter. Shall we not be able to say to God with complete confidence: “Lord, if this is an error, we have been deceived by yourself; for these things have been confirmed among us by signs and wonders so great and of such a kind as can occur only through you. Certainly they were handed down to us by men of highest holiness, and proved with the highest and most authoritative attestation, while you yourself cooperated and confirmed the word by the signs that followed.” Hence it is, indeed, that those perfectly faithful are readier to die for the faith than to deny the faith. For without doubt nothing is held more firmly than that which is apprehended by steadfast faith.

## Chapter III. That this work treats of those things concerning eternal realities which we are commanded to believe

For the knowledge of those things concerning which we are rightly told, “Unless you believe, you shall not understand,” one must indeed enter through faith; yet one must not halt at the very entrance, but always hasten toward the more inward and deeper regions of understanding. With all zeal and utmost diligence we must persist, so that by daily advances we may be able to progress toward understanding those things which we hold by faith. In their full knowledge and perfect understanding eternal life is attained. [Col. 0892B] In acquiring them lies the highest usefulness; in contemplating them, the highest delight. These are the highest riches; these are everlasting delights. In tasting them lies the final sweetness; in enjoying them, infinite pleasure.

We have therefore undertaken in this work to treat of those things which we are commanded to believe according to the rule of the Catholic faith—not of any things whatsoever, but of eternal things. For we do not intend in this work to treat at all of the mysteries of our redemption, accomplished in time, which we are commanded to believe and do believe. For the method of proceeding is different in these matters and in those.

## Chapter IV. The method of proceeding in this work: to introduce not so much authorities as to insist upon reasoning

[Col. 0892C]

Therefore it will be our purpose in this work, insofar as the Lord grants, to bring forward concerning the things we believe not merely probable but even necessary reasons, and to enrich the teachings of our faith by unfolding and explaining the truth. For I believe without doubt that, for the explanation of whatsoever necessarily is, there are not lacking not merely probable but even necessary arguments, although for the present they may lie hidden from our industry.

All things which began to exist in time by the good pleasure of the Creator can exist and can fail to exist. Consequently, their existence is not so much inferred by reasoning as established by experience. But eternal things absolutely cannot fail to exist: just as they never were not, so certainly they never will not be; indeed, they always are what they are, and cannot be anything else or exist otherwise. Yet it seems utterly impossible for anything necessary to lack a necessary reason. But it is not the office of every mind to draw forth such reasons from the deep and hidden bosom of nature and bring them, as if extracted from some innermost treasury of wisdom, into public view.

Many are less worthy of this; many less fitted for it; many less earnest in it. And concerning that which we ought always, if possible, to keep before our eyes, we scarcely or rarely think. [Col. 0893A] With what zeal, I ask, with what desire ought we sometimes to devote ourselves to that task, to yearn for that spectacle, upon which depends the supreme blessedness of all who are to be saved? Yet I believe that I shall have accomplished something if I am granted to assist earnest minds, even in a small degree, in this undertaking, and by my own zeal to stir lukewarm minds to such study.

## Chapter V. A brief preliminary survey of the matters treated in what follows

I have often read that there is but one God; that he is eternal, uncreated, and immeasurable; that he is almighty and Lord of all; that from him comes everything that exists; that he is everywhere, and wholly everywhere, not divided into parts. I have read concerning my God that he is one and three: one in substance, but three in persons. I have read all these things; but I do not remember having read how they are proved.

I have read that in true divinity there is but one substance; that in the unity of substance there are several persons, each distinguished from every other by a property of its own; that there is there a person who is from himself and not from another; that there is a person who is from one alone, but not from himself; and that there is a person who is from a twofold person, but not from one alone. Every day I hear of the three that they are not three eternal beings but one eternal being; not three uncreated beings nor three immeasurable beings, but one uncreated and one immeasurable being. I hear of the three that they are not three almighty beings but one almighty being; nevertheless, I hear that they are not three gods but one God, nor three lords but one [Col. 0893C] Lord. I find that the Father was not made and was not begotten; that the Son was not made but was begotten; and that the Holy Spirit was not made and was not begotten, but proceeds.

I often hear or read all these things, but do not recall having read how they are proved. Authorities abound for all these matters, but arguments do not equally abound. In all these matters, experiences are lacking and arguments are scarce. Therefore, as I have already said above, I believe that I shall have accomplished no small thing if I can assist earnest minds, even in a small degree, in this kind of study, even if it is not granted me to provide a full answer.

## Chapter VI. That every mode of being may universally be comprehended under a threefold division

So that the firm ground of truth may plainly and clearly stand, as it were an immovable foundation, from which the sequence of our reasoning may take its beginning—a point of which no one may doubt or presume to draw back—we may say as follows: Everything that exists or can exist either has existence from eternity, or began to exist in time. Everything that exists or can exist either has existence from itself or has existence from another than itself.

Thus every being, universally, is distinguished in a threefold manner. For the being of every existing thing is either from eternity and from itself; or, conversely, neither from eternity nor from itself; or, midway between these two, from eternity indeed but not from itself. For nature itself does not allow that fourth possibility, which seems to correspond oppositely to this third member, to exist in any way: namely, being from itself but not from eternity. For nothing whatsoever can be from itself unless it is from eternity. Whatever began to exist in time existed at a time when it was nothing; but so long as it was nothing, it possessed absolutely nothing and could do absolutely nothing. Therefore it gave neither to itself nor to another that it might exist or be able to do anything. Otherwise it gave what it did not possess and did what it could not do. From this, then, infer how impossible it is for anything whatsoever to be from itself which is not from eternity. Thus we infer by clear reasoning what we have already said above: that every being is distinguished in a threefold manner.

## Chapter VII. On that mode of being which is not from eternity and therefore not from itself

We must begin, therefore, with that class of things concerning which we cannot doubt in any way; and through those things which we know by experience, infer by reasoning what we ought to think regarding those things which are above experience. Concerning that mode of being which is not from eternity and therefore, according to the foregoing argument, not from itself, we are made certain by daily and manifold experience. We continually see some things pass away, others succeed them, and things which previously did not exist come into actuality. We see this continually in human beings and in animals. We establish daily by experience the same thing in shrubs and grasses which we see in the workings of nature; and we see the same in the works of human skill. Thus daily experience does not allow us to be unaware that countless things have not existed from eternity.

The preceding argument establishes that whatever was not from eternity cannot exist from itself; otherwise, it is plainly shown that something gave itself a beginning of existence at that instant when it possessed nothing, when it could do absolutely nothing—how wholly impossible this is cannot escape a person of sound mind. Therefore all those things which began to exist in time clearly have this in common: they are not from eternity, and consequently, as has now been said, not from themselves. Thus we have now spoken of that mode of being concerning which we cannot doubt, since we establish it by daily use and experience.

## Chapter VIII. On that mode of being which is from itself and therefore from eternity

But from that being which is neither from eternity nor from itself, reasoning infers that being which is from itself and therefore also from eternity. For if nothing existed from itself, there would be absolutely no source from which those things might exist that do not have, and cannot have, their existence from themselves. Thus it is demonstrated that something exists from itself and therefore, as has been said, from eternity. Otherwise there was a time when nothing existed; and then none of the future things would have been future, because that which could give, or could have given, either itself or others a beginning of existence did not then exist at all. The falsity of this is shown by its very obviousness and demonstrated by experience of existing things.

Thus by reasoning from the things we see, we infer that there are also things we do not see: from transitory things, eternal things; from worldly things, things beyond the world; [Col. 0895A] from human things, divine things. For “the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made, are beheld from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1).

## Chapter IX. On that mode of being which is from eternity but not from itself

Let no one think it impossible that there should have been a being from eternity which nevertheless is not from itself, as though it were necessary for a cause always to precede its effect, and for everything which derives from another its principle always to come after it. Certainly, a ray proceeds from the sun and draws its origin from it, yet it exists coeval with the sun. For from the time the sun existed, it produced a ray from itself, and at no time was it without a ray. Therefore, if this bodily light has a ray coeval with itself, why should that spiritual and inaccessible light not have a ray coeternal with itself?

In created nature we read what we ought to reflect or judge concerning uncreated nature. Every day we see how, by the operation of nature itself, existence produces existence, and existence proceeds from existence. What then? Shall there be no operation of nature in that supereminent nature, or shall it be wholly powerless? Shall that nature which bestowed this fruit of fecundity upon our nature remain altogether sterile in itself? And shall it, which granted generation to others, itself be without generation and sterile? From these considerations it seems probable that within that superessential immutability there is a being which is not from itself and yet has existed from eternity; but this will be discussed in its place by fuller and more effective reasoning.

## Chapter X. That the whole intention of this work concerns only the two modes which are from eternity

[Col. 0895C]

Therefore, in this work we intend to discuss the twofold mode of being which we have said exists from eternity, and those matters which seem to pertain to this consideration. For the present we do not intend to consider temporal things—that is, those belonging to the third mode—except insofar as we establish that their consideration is necessary or useful for the investigation of eternal things. For, as we have from the Apostle and have already said above, “the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made, are beheld” (Rom. 1).

Whenever, therefore, by the examination of visible things we rise [Col. 0895D] to contemplation of invisible things, what else do we do but erect, as it were, a ladder by which our mind may ascend to those things that are above us? Hence, in this treatise, the whole course of our reasoning takes its beginning from those things which we know by experience. Whatever, therefore, is said in this work about eternal things is said intentionally; whatever about temporal things, incidentally. For the entire purpose of this work concerns the two modes of being which are from eternity.

## Chapter XI. On the highest substance: that it is from itself and therefore from eternity, without any beginning

We must now speak more fully of that being which is from itself; hence, as has been said, it is clear that it exists from eternity. But it is most certain, and, I think, a matter concerning which no one can doubt, that amid so great a multitude of existing things and so manifold a difference of ranks, there must be something highest. By the highest of all we mean that than which nothing is greater and nothing better.

Without doubt, a rational nature is better than an irrational nature. There must therefore be a rational substance which is the highest of all, and which evidently holds the highest place in this universe of things. But it cannot receive this very status from something inferior to itself. There must therefore be some substance which possesses both: namely, to hold the highest place and to exist from itself. For, as we have already said and proved, if nothing existed from itself, nothing would exist from eternity; and then there would be neither an origin nor a succession of things.

The evident reality of experienced things therefore proves that some substance must exist from itself. For if none existed from itself, none whatever of those things which derive their origin from elsewhere and cannot exist from themselves would exist. Therefore that substance which exists only from itself belongs—indeed, belongs—to that mode of being which is from eternity and without any beginning.

## Chapter XII. Likewise, that only one substance is from itself, from which are all other things; and that it has all that it has only from itself

But what has been said of the highest substance can be proved by still fuller reasoning. It is most certain that in the whole universe of things nothing can exist unless it either has the possibility of being from itself or has received it from elsewhere. For what cannot exist does not exist at all. Therefore, for something to exist, it must receive the ability to exist from the power of being. Every thing that subsists in the universe of things receives existence, then, from the power of being.

But if all things are from that power itself, and it itself exists only from itself, it possesses nothing except from itself. If all things are from it, then every essence, every power, and every wisdom are from it. If all being is from it, it is the highest essence. If all ability is from it, it is supremely powerful. If all wisdom is from it, it is supremely wise. For it is impossible to give anything greater than one possesses. Certainly, wisdom may be given wholly at once by its possessor and wholly retained by its giver; yet one is altogether unable to impart wisdom greater than one has. Therefore that from which all wisdom draws its origin must be supremely wise.

But wisdom cannot be present at all where there is no rational substance. For wisdom can be present only in a rational substance. Therefore there is a rational substance, highest of all, in which is present the highest wisdom. It is, I say, the highest of all, from which comes every essence. Thus every rational and irrational nature—[the text appears defective]—is nothing other than the power of being, namely the highest substance. Therefore, since the power of being exists only from itself, it can be none other than the highest substance, which is nothing other than the power of being itself.

It is clear, therefore, that from the highest substance comes everything that exists; but if all things are from it, then apart from it alone none exists from itself. And if from it come all being, all ability, and all possession, beyond doubt it has from itself all that it has. Rightly, therefore, is this substance called primordial, since everything that exists derives its beginning and origin from it.

## Chapter XIII. That the highest substance is the same as power itself and the same as wisdom itself; whence each is the same as the other

Let us now consider what has already been said: that the highest substance is supremely powerful. But it is most certain that its very being powerful belongs to it from power itself, and its very being wise belongs to it from wisdom itself. Yet it has been proved that it possesses all that it has only from itself. Therefore, in order that it may have from itself alone what it has from power itself, and what it has from wisdom itself, it is necessary that these be altogether nothing other than itself. Otherwise it could not be powerful or wise without power and wisdom; and what it has from them, it would have not so much from itself as from elsewhere. It follows, moreover, that if each of these is the same as the highest substance, each is the same as the other.

## Chapter XIV. That the highest substance cannot have an equal, just as it cannot have a superior

[Col. 0897C]

At this point we must attend most carefully to the following: if the substance which is itself the highest power is one thing, another distinct substance cannot be that same highest power. Otherwise different substances would be one and the same distinct substance, which is altogether impossible. But perhaps you will say in response: What if another substance can possess the highest power? And if it cannot itself be the highest power, will they not be equal in power if both possess the highest power?

I affirm this without doubt and unhesitatingly: for if one of them can possess the highest power, and the other cannot be equal in power to it, then the latter cannot possess both capacities. For to be able in part and unable in part to do what is altogether possible to another is not to enjoy the fullness of that power, but participation in it. Yet it is much greater and much more excellent to possess the fullness of some great thing than to obtain a participation in it. From this it is plainly inferred that the primordial substance cannot have an equal, just as the foregoing makes clear that it cannot have a superior.

## Chapter XV. That it is impossible for the highest substance to have a partner in its own nature

It seems naturally inherent in the primordial substance to preside over all things and to be unable to have either an equal or a superior. For what is inherent substantially is without doubt inherent naturally. Since the primordial substance itself is altogether identical with the highest power, it is naturally inherent in it that it is supremely powerful and that it cannot have anything more powerful or equally powerful.

Let us see, then, whether it can have a companion in its own nature that is inferior to it. But how, I ask, could any substance be inferior in essence to the primordial substance if it naturally shared with it the fact that it could have neither an equal nor a superior? Accordingly, each would be the other; indeed, each would be superior and inferior, greater and lesser, than itself. Therefore it is impossible for the primordial substance to have a partner in its own nature.

## Chapter XVI. That the highest substance is identical with divinity itself, and that God is one only substantially

[Col. 0898B]

According to the foregoing argument, we now hold as certain that everything that exists is from the highest substance alone and that it has from itself all that it has. But if all things are from it, divinity itself is also from it. If, however, it gave divinity to another and did not retain it for itself, it has a superior—which, as was proved above, it cannot have. It is therefore clear that it retained divinity for itself and possesses it.

Now God is one who possesses Deity, and has his very being God from Deity. But if the highest substance has its very being God from its divinity, and possesses nothing except from itself, then Deity itself is certainly nothing other than the highest substance. Therefore it could not give to any other substance, not merely the possession of Deity, but being Deity itself; otherwise—which is impossible—it would have an equal. From this, therefore, it follows that true divinity consists in unity of substance, and true unity of substance in divinity itself. Therefore God is one only substantially.

## Chapter XVII. Likewise: that there is but one God; that everything that exists is from him; that he has all that he has only from himself; that he is identical with power itself, wisdom itself, and divinity itself

Now hear how easily we can prove that there is but one God. Since he has nothing except from himself, it is clear that divinity itself is nothing other than himself, lest he be shown to have from another than himself what he has from divinity. Divinity itself, therefore, will either be incommunicable or common to some.

If it is incommunicable, then, as follows, there is only one God. But if it is common to some, then the substance which is nothing other than divinity itself will also be common to them. But one substance cannot be common to several substances; otherwise, one and the same thing would be several, and several things one—which reason does not allow us to regard as anything but false. If it is said to be common to several persons, then, according to what has been said, that substance which is nothing other than divinity itself will likewise be common to them. In this way there will be several persons in the one divinity, but only one substance.

Therefore, whether only one person or several persons are said to exist in the one divinity, God will nevertheless be one only substantially. Thus the sole and one God exists from himself and therefore from eternity. And, according to what has been proved concerning the highest substance, which is nothing other than himself, everything that exists is from him; he has from himself all that he has; and he is identical with power itself, wisdom itself, and divinity itself.

## Chapter XVIII. That it is altogether impossible for God himself to define anything better than God

If, then, God’s wisdom and God’s power are entirely one and the same, no perfection and no completion is comprehended by the one which is not comprehended by the other in the same measure of fullness. Therefore nothing is greater or better in his knowing than in his being able, and consequently in his being; for his ability is nothing other than his being.

Therefore, whatever is found or determined to be best or most excellent by his wisdom is, in the same fullness of completeness, comprehended by his power and contained in his essence. For, with respect to the summit of perfection, if he could attain by understanding something which he could not grasp by efficacy, he would without doubt extend himself more magnificently through wisdom than through power; and one and the same substance would be greater and lesser than itself. For since God’s substance is nothing other than his power or wisdom, if it extended itself more broadly through wisdom than through power—if it could extend itself more broadly through the former than through the latter—then that one and the same substance would be greater through wisdom in comparison with power, and lesser through power in comparison with wisdom. Therefore nothing greater than God, and nothing better than God, can be defined even by God himself or attained by his understanding.

## Chapter XIX. If God himself cannot conceive anything better than God, much less can human thought

If divine knowledge cannot comprehend by understanding anything more perfect than God, how much less could human knowledge devise anything greater or better than God? For whatever human thought could grasp by understanding could not remain unknown to divine understanding. It is a kind of madness to believe that a human being can ascend in thought above that which is God, when by no investigation can he attain even that very reality which God is. Therefore, the better and more perfect that which human thought attains is, the nearer it comes to that which God is—yet it does not reach it.

## Chapter XX. What commonly serves those investigating and disputing about God as a kind of highest proposition and common conception of the mind
It seems, then, to belong almost as a natural endowment [Col. 0900A] that nearly everyone, learned and less learned alike, is accustomed to regard as familiar and to hold, as it were, as a rule: namely, that whatever they judge best they unhesitatingly attribute to God. And where clear reasoning does not teach some persons this rule by argument, devotion persuades them without any ambiguity of doubt. Hence even those who do not know how this may be proved affirm without hesitation that God is immense, eternal, unchangeable, supremely wise, and omnipotent. Thus for the learned it is, as it were, a major premise; for all alike it is a common conception of the mind: to attribute to God whatever human judgment apprehends as highest. And from this firm certainty, this foundation, as it were, of inward truth, the greatest teachers commonly take the beginning of their argument [Col. 0900B] when they intend to discuss the divine properties more deeply and closely.

## CHAPTER XXI. That God is so supremely powerful that He is also omnipotent.

That God is supremely powerful is sufficiently evident from what has preceded. Yet one may still ask whether He is called supremely powerful because no one surpasses Him in power, or whether He is supremely powerful in such a way that He can do all things and is truly omnipotent. But if we deny that He is omnipotent, we are shown already to be able to conceive something greater than God. For it is greater to possess omnipotence than to possess any sort of power which lacks something of the fullness of omnipotence. And this, which is extremely easy for a human being to understand, [Col. 0900C] cannot escape divine wisdom.

Therefore, if God understands some element of the fullness of power which He cannot possess, there will be something greater in His knowing than in His being able—though neither of these is anything other than His very being. Thus, according to the preceding argument, one and the same being will be both greater than itself and less than itself, than which nothing is more impossible. From this, then, it is undoubtedly concluded that He can do all things which it is power to be able to do.

For many things are said to be possible which it would be far better not to have been able than to be able: to be able to diminish, to be able to fail, to be able to be destroyed and reduced to nothing, and anything else of that kind. In every respect, not to be able to do these things is greater than to be able to do them. For these are marks of weakness rather than insignia of majesty. Therefore He can do all those things, and only those things, which, as we have said, [Col. 0900D] it is power to have been able to do. And we call Him omnipotent more properly and more truly insofar as we remove from His power every indication of weakness.

## CHAPTER XXII. That God’s wisdom is so supreme as to be altogether perfect.

What has now been said of divine power may similarly be asked concerning divine wisdom. Is it called supreme because none can ever be greater than it, or is it truly supreme in such a way as to be altogether perfect? But it is most certainly evident that, where omnipotence exists, fullness of wisdom cannot be lacking. For if any perfection belonging to the fullness of wisdom were lacking to Him which He could not possess, [Col. 0901A] He would without any ambiguity not be omnipotent.

It is therefore clear concerning God’s wisdom that nothing is lacking to it from the entire perfection of knowledge and prudence, the addition of which could make it greater or better. It should be noted that the fullness of His power is discerned from consideration of divine wisdom; and conversely, from consideration of omnipotence the fullness of wisdom is made manifest and established.

## CHAPTER XXIII. What is said of God’s wisdom is confirmed by another argument.

But what we have already said concerning the fullness of divine wisdom can be established by another argument. [Col. 0901B] For it is clear that whoever is wise is wise either through the fullness of wisdom itself or through participation in wisdom; but from the preceding discussion we already have that Wisdom itself is identical with the divine substance. Who, then, unless mad, would say that God’s substance possesses wisdom—that is, itself—partly, and partly does not possess it, and is unable to possess the fullness of itself? Therefore, as God’s substance cannot fail to possess itself wholly, so it cannot lack fullness.

## CHAPTER XXIV. By the same argument, what was said above concerning the fullness of divine power is confirmed.

By a similar argument, what was said above concerning omnipotence is confirmed. For just as every wise person is wise either through fullness of wisdom or through participation in it, so likewise every powerful being is powerful through fullness of power or through participation in it. But it is possible for something to participate in itself. Therefore, since God is powerful, He cannot be powerful through participation in power. For the fullness of power is nothing other than Himself. [Col. 0902A] It is therefore clear that He is powerful through the fullness of power. But where fullness of power exists, no capacity can be lacking. It follows, therefore, that He possesses omnipotence and is truly omnipotent, since every capacity is present in Him.

## CHAPTER XXV. That only one can be omnipotent, and consequently that there can be only one God.

It is impossible for there to be several omnipotent beings. [Col. 0902B] For whoever is truly omnipotent could easily bring it about that any one of the others could do nothing; otherwise he would not be truly omnipotent. Behold what sort of “omnipotent beings” these are, who can easily be made powerless. Behold how easily it is established that the very nature of things does not permit more than one omnipotent being.

But we have inferred by clear reasoning that God is omnipotent, and we can no longer doubt it. Therefore, just as only one can be omnipotent, so only one can be God. Thus what we believe, and what we have already said above, is established: true divinity remains in unity of substance, and the truth of substance in one divinity. We have now said much about the unity of divinity; it remains for us to say something about the singularity of its nature.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0901]

## CHAPTER I. That this book treats of divine properties, and first, that God is uncreated.

[Col. 0901C]

Having already said above what seemed necessary concerning the unity of divinity, it remains to say something concerning the properties of that same nature, especially those which we frequently use in everyday expressions of divine praise. Of these, some are such that the mind readily assents to them and accepts them willingly, even though it does not know by what reasoning they may be proved. To others it would adhere hardly at all, or less firmly, unless the very rule of the transmitted Catholic faith directed it to them.

For the human mind readily receives and willingly assents that God is uncreated, eternal, and immense. But it would not readily believe that several [Col. 0901D] eternal beings or several immense beings are impossible, unless the rule of faith itself persuaded it of this—especially since three are believed to exist, whose eternity and immensity every mouth confesses.

That God is uncreated is sufficiently evident from what preceded and requires no new exposition. For if He were created, He would have a creator. But He who exists only from Himself cannot have a creator. For what do we call created except what is made from nothing? He could not have come from nothing [Col. 0902C] who never was nothing, who has being from Himself and from eternity.

## CHAPTER II. That God is everlasting.

It is now clear that He who is from eternity and lacks every beginning is uncreated. We must now ask whether, as He lacks a beginning, so He also lacks an end and possesses everlasting being. For to be everlasting is to lack beginning and end.

Let us now establish from what is most certain that of which someone may doubt. It is most certain that no falsity can exist in Wisdom, which is God. Otherwise He would not be supremely wise if He could either wish to deceive or be deceived. It is therefore clear that God is truthful, and that this belongs to Him from truth itself. Truth, [Col. 0902D] then, is nothing other than Himself, since He can truly be shown to possess only from Himself that which nevertheless He possesses from truth.

But truth, just as it never was not from eternity, so will never cease to be. It was true, and will be true eternally, that this universe could exist. For if it could not exist, it would not exist at all. Therefore truth existed from eternity, by which it was true that what was from eternity existed; and truth will exist eternally, by which it will be true eternally that what will be true eternally will be true [Col. 0903A]. Therefore, if it was true through the truth which is God that what has always been true had being, and if what will always be true will indeed be so, then God, who is truth, will lack an end just as He lacks a beginning. Therefore God is everlasting, possessing everlasting being, since He lacks beginning and end.

## CHAPTER III. That He is incorruptible and altogether unchangeable.

Since it is now clear concerning God that He has everlasting being, it follows that we should ask whether He also has unchangeable being. We must know, then, that every change is either from one state to a better state, from one state to a worse state, or from one state to a state equal to the former one. Where none of these can occur, true unchangeability exists. [Col. 0903B] Let us therefore examine carefully each of the alternatives we have stated.

But how can He who is omnipotent become worse? For what is becoming worse except being corrupted? Yet no corruption can have dominion over Him who is truly omnipotent—indeed, who is Omnipotence itself. Let us now see whether He can at least increase, since it is already evident that He cannot decrease. But everything which grows receives some increase of good by which it can become better. Yet from where could that increase of good come to Him who has nothing except from Himself, and who cannot have it otherwise? For if He had it before, how did He arrive at it by growing? If He did not have it before, certainly He could give neither Himself nor another what He did not possess at all.

From these points it may be concluded that He cannot increase or diminish. But we must now see whether [Col. 0903C] He can be changed from one state to another equal state. If He passes from one state into another, even an equal one, He must in some way lose something which He formerly possessed, and, in compensation for that loss, something must accrue to Him which He did not formerly possess. Then, in one and the same alteration, He will be subject to the two changes mentioned above, both of which the preceding argument rejected.

Therefore, He who cannot become worse is incorruptible; He who cannot become better or be varied in any other manner is altogether unchangeable. Thus God truly and without any ambiguity possesses unchangeable being.

## CHAPTER IV. From which we may infer that He is eternal.

[Col. 0903D]

But if we combine into one the three points which we have set forth, we establish not only that He is everlasting, but that He is eternal. For *eternal* appears to convey something different from *everlasting*. Everlasting seems to mean that which lacks beginning and end; eternal, that which lacks both and every mutability. And although perhaps neither is found without the other, it is nevertheless right to distinguish between the meanings of the names.

What, then, is eternity except duration without beginning and end, lacking every mutability? But He who is uncreated and everlasting lacks beginning and end, and He whose state is unvarying remains without every mutability. Therefore in these three respects He is proved eternal. For these three unquestionably entail possessing eternity and being eternal.

## CHAPTER V. That He is infinite and, for that very reason, immense.

[Col. 0904A]

That which lacks beginning and end is undoubtedly infinite. One may therefore ask whether He who is infinite through eternity is also infinite through magnitude. Far above it was shown that the divine substance is identical with Power itself and Wisdom itself. By the same reasoning, it can be proved of that substance, which has nothing except from itself, that the eternity by which it is eternal and the magnitude by which it is great are nothing other than itself.

Therefore, if we establish that God’s eternity is infinite, we cannot deny that His magnitude is infinite. Otherwise, clear reasoning compels us to admit that one and the same [Col. 0904B] substance is both greater and less than itself. For if His eternity is infinite but His magnitude finite, the one and same substance will, in respect of eternity, be greater than its own magnitude—that is, greater than itself—and, in respect of magnitude, less than its own eternity—that is, less than itself.

It is therefore plainly inferred that if one is infinite, the other also will be infinite. Hence God has infinite magnitude and, for that very reason, immense magnitude. For what is infinite cannot be comprehended by any measure. God is therefore rightly called immense, whose magnitude is comprehended by no measure.

## CHAPTER VI. That not only is there not, but there cannot be, more than one immense being.

[Col. 0904C]

Let us now consider also whether it is possible for there to be several immense beings. That is rightly called immense which is comprehended by no measure. That is called immense which is found equal or comparable to no measure. If, therefore, we say that several are immense, each of them will be incomprehensible to every other, and each will be incommensurable with every other. Thus the measure of none is comprehended by the measure of any other; consequently each exceeds every other. Therefore each will be greater than every other, and each will also be less than every other.

If this is impossible—indeed, because it is impossible—it will be impossible for there to be several immense beings. But if none is greater or less than any other, then just as each is comprehensible and commensurable to itself, so each will be comprehensible and commensurable to every other. By these arguments we may undoubtedly infer that there is not, and cannot be, more than one immense being.

## CHAPTER VII. How it is proved from there being only one immense being that there can be only one eternal being.

We now know that it is impossible for several immense beings to exist. Let us see whether several eternal beings can exist. From what preceded we have learned and firmly hold that the divine substance is nothing other than its immensity and eternity itself. Hence it is clear, from immensity and eternity, [Col. 0905A] that each is identical with the other.

It is therefore clear that whoever possesses eternity cannot fail to possess immensity. But if he who is eternal cannot lack immensity, he will undoubtedly be at once eternal and immense. Therefore, just as several immense beings cannot exist, neither can several eternal beings exist.

Meanwhile, this point especially should be noted and deserves careful consideration: among the conclusions which we infer by reasoning, some we draw from considering the property of the thing under discussion; others we establish from the property of another thing and the mutual relation of the two. For we infer from the property of immensity that only one can be immense. But we establish that several eternal beings cannot exist partly from the same considered property of immensity and partly from the mutual relation of immensity and eternity [Col. 0905B].

## CHAPTER VIII. That God alone is uncreated, alone from eternity; all other things were created from nothing.

We firmly hold that the divine substance alone exists from itself, and that all other things are from it. But whatever is, or can be, from it, is either according to the operation of nature or according to the bestowal of grace. Now, as certainly as the divine nature cannot degenerate or omnipotence be corrupted, so certainly it must be that nothing could exist from the divine substance by the operation of its nature which was not God. But above we sufficiently proved [Col. 0905C] that God cannot be more than one substantially.

Therefore, from God Himself—from that one and singular substance—there can be neither another God nor anything else which is not God. It is thus clear that whatever is other than Himself is from Him according to the operation of grace. But whatever is from Him could, by the working of grace according to the choice of His good pleasure rather than by the necessity of nature, be made by Him; and it could equally not be made by Him.

Therefore, the things made by Him cannot have that divine, incorruptible, and unchangeable substance as their matter. It is clear, then, that, with the divine substance alone excepted, all other things were either made from nothing or have something mutable as matter. But, I ask, [Col. 0905D] whence came primordial matter, which absolutely could not have being from itself or have the divine substance as its matter? And if primordial matter is said to have matter, it is both asserted to be primordial and denied to be primordial.

From this it is plainly inferred that primordial matter and all material things, through the mediation of matter, and every immaterial thing, indeed all things universally, are created from nothing. Thus what we truly believe is established: God alone is uncreated. Therefore, just as He alone exists from Himself, so He alone is undoubtedly from eternity.

## CHAPTER IX. Another way of proving concerning God that He is eternal, and that only one is eternal.

Whatever receives being through creation undoubtedly was once wholly nonexistent; otherwise it could not have been created from nothing. Therefore everything created began to exist in time. But whatever is uncreated preceded all time; and that which existed when no time existed could undoubtedly not be mutable. Otherwise it would have been subject to time when time did not yet exist—which is wholly impossible. For whatever is subject to mutability is thereby subject to time. Time is always in motion and cannot stand still even for a moment; and if there were no change, there would unquestionably be no time at all.

It is therefore clear, as I said above, that what is subject to mutability is subject also to time, and that it could not be subject to mutability when no time [Col. 0906B] existed. Thus what is uncreated, since it existed before all times, could not be mutable.

Now what is unchangeable, just as it cannot change from being to non-being, so it cannot change from being to another mode of being. But what cannot change from being into non-being endures without end; what cannot change from being into another mode of being remains without every change. Therefore what is uncreated not only lacks a beginning, but also remains without end and without every mutability. But to lack beginning, end, and every mutability is to be eternal. Therefore what is uncreated is established to be eternal.

Conversely, what is eternal is clearly also uncreated. For what is eternal has existed from eternity and therefore could not be created [Col. 0906C]. Thus these arguments establish that, if only one is uncreated, only one is eternal; and conversely, if only one is eternal, only one is uncreated.

## CHAPTER X. Another way of proving concerning God that only one is immense.

What we have already said above concerning the immensity of divinity can be inferred by another argument, namely from consideration of the property of immensity itself. For anything which is subject to measure would be greater if its measure were doubled. It would be much greater if it increased tenfold, or rather a hundredfold; and if it were multiplied a thousand times—indeed, a thousand thousand times—it would increase by that amount.

From this, I think, you can perceive that to have magnitude according to measure—that is, to participate in it—is not to be magnitude itself. But God, as the preceding argument showed, is Magnitude itself; and no thing at all can participate in itself, for this is to be partly and not to be partly. Therefore God, who is Magnitude itself, is found to possess magnitude without measure, and thereby to be immense, because He is neither comprehended nor measurable by any measure [Col. 0906D].

Therefore what we believe and proclaim in daily confession stands unshaken: God is immense. This may also be proved by consideration of omnipotence. But since this is extremely easy to grasp, there is no need to dwell upon it. From what preceded, however, we have that omnipotence is nothing other than immensity and eternity themselves. It follows, therefore, that whoever possesses immensity and eternity also possesses omnipotence. Hence, just as only one can be omnipotent, so only one can be immense and only one eternal [Col. 0907A].

## CHAPTER XI. That immensity and eternity are incommunicable and cannot be common to several substances.

Far above we showed that divinity is altogether incommunicable and cannot be common to several substances. What was there said of divinity may, by similar reasoning, be said of God’s immensity and likewise of His eternity. For just as any one substance cannot be communicable to several substances, so [Col. 0907B] immensity itself and eternity itself cannot be communicable to several substances, since they are nothing other than the divine substance.

Therefore none is immense except God alone and one; none is eternal except God alone and one. But here a great question arises, which may trouble unlearned hearers unless it is resolved by a clear explanation. It was proved above that the divine substance is identical with Power itself and identical with Wisdom itself. But who would say that power is communicable while wisdom is not common to several substances? Yet if immensity and eternity themselves are called incommunicable because they are proved identical with the divine substance, [Col. 0907C] why are Power itself and Wisdom themselves not likewise called incommunicable and unable to be common to several substances? For where the same reasoning applies, why should a similar conclusion not properly follow?

But, in order to untie more easily the knot of this difficulty, let us examine by a yet deeper investigation what we said above concerning the singularity of divinity.

## CHAPTER XII. What was previously called the incommunicability of divinity is here expressed more fully and clearly.

We must know concerning every substance that it has being from its substantiality. For that in which no substantiality exists cannot properly be called a substance. By “substantiality” we mean that property of a substance from which the substance has both its name and its being. Thus the substantiality of human substance is humanity itself; for a substance which does not possess humanity cannot be called a human being except falsely.

What has been said concerning this may equally be seen in other cases. But one substantiality is general, another specific, another individual. General substantiality is that which is common to certain species, such as corporeality, which belongs to all bodies, animate and inanimate alike. Specific substantiality is that which belongs to all individuals of only one species, such as humanity, which is common to all human beings. Individual substantiality is that which belongs to one individual only and cannot at all be common to several substances [Col. 0908A].

We have no customary term for designating an individual substantiality; but for greater clarity in what we are to say, we may coin one from a proper name. Let “Danielity” be said from Daniel, just as “humanity” from human being. Let Danielity, then, be understood as the very substantiality—or, if one prefers, that substance—from which Daniel has being: that substance which he himself is and which no other humanity can participate in.

Thus, just as corporeality is common to many while Danielity is altogether incommunicable, we call it incommunicable because it belongs to him in such a way that it cannot belong to another. For whoever had this substantiality would certainly be Daniel; and whoever did not have it could not be that same Daniel. Different substantiality makes a different substance. But a singular and individual substantiality can make only one. Therefore Danielity is incommunicable, as we have said, because it belongs as the substance of one substance in such a manner that it cannot belong to another [Col. 0908B].

If, therefore, it is called incommunicable because it cannot belong to another substance, how much more so would this be the case if Daniel’s substance were in every respect identical with its own substantiality? But divinity itself is in every respect identical with the divine substance—identical, I say, with that singular substance which alone exists from itself and from which alone all other things exist.

Therefore divinity itself can no more be communicable than distinct substances can be one, or one substance be distinct. Behold how plainly we have shown that divinity itself is incommunicable, so that a reader who doubts this point appears not so much dull as blind. But immensity and eternity, according to the foregoing argument, belong to one in such a way that they cannot belong to another; and thus we judge them incommunicable. Add that they are in every respect identical with the divine substance, and it is clear that they are incommunicable [Col. 0908C].

## CHAPTER XIII. That, according to different modes of speaking, wisdom or power may be called communicable in one sense and incommunicable in another.

But let us return to the point for which we have set these matters forth: why are Power itself and [Col. 0908D] Wisdom itself not called incommunicable by the same reasoning, if they are truly proved to be identical with the divine substance? We must know that we misuse both the name *power* and the name *wisdom* when we speak sometimes of divine things and sometimes of human things, so that we seem to employ not so much a single as an equivocal predication.

We say of God that He is Wisdom; of a human being we say not that he is wisdom, but that wisdom is in him. There, by the name *wisdom*, is designated something which is substance—and more than substance; here, by the name *wisdom*, is designated something which is not any substance at all. The word is one in both cases, but the rationale of the name differs. If equivocation occurs where one name, under different meanings, designates a different substance, how much more when a single name is extended to designate what we deny to be substance and what we affirm to be substance [Col. 0909A].

Likewise, we say that a human being himself has wisdom, and we also say that God has wisdom; the statement seems equivocal, but in the case of God it is said only improperly. Nor does this impropriety seem less than if one said that Abraham was not a human being but had a human being. This impropriety of speech, or equivocation of words, confuses the meaning and prevents power and wisdom from being called incommunicable.

Finally, let us assign such a name as can belong only to divine power or divine wisdom, and we shall see that both are incommunicable. For the very name *omnipotence*, which can belong only to divine power, is plainly found to be incommunicable. For, as we have already proved, only one can be omnipotent. But we have no name comparable to *omnipotence* for expressing divine wisdom; rather, we often specify it by an addition, when we call it supreme wisdom, Wisdom itself, or fullness of wisdom.

Yet however divine and uncreated power or wisdom is expressed, so that absolutely no other power or wisdom can be understood, each will undoubtedly be incommunicable and cannot be common to several substances—not, I say, to angelic substances; not to human substances; nor even to any supposedly divine substances [Col. 0909B].

## CHAPTER XIV. The many ways of proving that there is only one God.

Apart from what we have already said above concerning the singularity of divinity, see by how many ways we can prove that there is only one God: one uncreated, one eternal, one immense—each of which proves and establishes that there is only one God.

If you attend carefully, you will also be able to prove the same thing from consideration of unity. For if someone should say that there are several gods, he may be convicted by considering that each one is [distinct] from every other, although it is proper to each of them to exist only from itself. But because we have learned that this can be perceived and proved from what was said before, we deliberately pass it over and leave its extraction to the reader’s acuteness [Col. 0909C].

## CHAPTER XV. That there can be only one Lord, just as there can be only one God.

[Col. 0909D]

Let us now ask whether, according to our daily confession, there can be only one Lord. He is truly called Lord whose freedom is constrained by no power, whose power or dominion is impeded by no impossibility. But he cannot truly be called Lord who unwillingly submits or yields to another’s will.

It therefore seems impossible for several lords to exist. For if several are said to exist, consider what absurdity follows. If any one of them wishes to subject any other to his service, and the one attacked cannot repel the oppressor’s violence, how will he be a lord rather than a servant? But if the aggressor in oppression is violently repelled and yields when defeated, how will he be a true lord, when by yielding he serves the will of the one resisting, although unwillingly?

Thus, if we maintain that several equally powerful beings are several lords, we undoubtedly make none of them truly lord. But what is established by considering the property of lordship itself is confirmed by considering omnipotence. For just as only one can be omnipotent, so only one can be Lord. What could resist the force of one who is truly established to be able to do all things? We must therefore firmly hold that there is not, and cannot be, a Lord except one—just as there is only one God, and He alone [Col. 0910A].

## CHAPTER XVI. That God Himself is the highest good, and that the highest good is universally perfect.

[Col. 0910B]

Nothing desirable can be lacking to Him who is truly omnipotent. For where omnipotence is, no fullness and no perfection can be lacking. Otherwise, if something of any perfection were lacking to the supremely powerful being which He could not possess, He would not truly be omnipotent at all.

That is universally perfect to which no perfection is lacking in any respect, nor can be lacking. But nothing can be better or greater than what is full and perfect in all things. It is therefore clear concerning the Omnipotent that He is the highest good and, consequently, that He is His own good. For just as one who holds the highest place cannot have a superior, so He who is highest of all cannot become good or blessed from something inferior to Himself [Col. 0910C].

But how could He become good or blessed from another source, He who has from Himself all that He has? Therefore He is good from Himself; He is blessed from Himself. Thus He Himself is His own highest goodness; He Himself is His own highest happiness. What was said is therefore clear: He is the highest good, and He is universally perfect. For what is blessedness except the fullness and perfection of every good? It is therefore clear that nothing whatever is lacking to that highest and universally perfect good, by the addition of which it could become better.

## CHAPTER XVII. That in that highest and universally perfect good there are true unity and supreme simplicity.

[Col. 0910D]

But if in that true and highest, universally perfect good there is a fullness of all goods, is that altogether perfect good composed of many goods? Yet what is composed of several things is naturally divisible; and what is naturally divisible is naturally mutable; and where mutability exists, eternity cannot exist, and thus neither can true blessedness.

But in the universally perfect good none of these things can be lacking. For, to pass over the rest, consideration of omnipotence alone establishes that no perfection—and consequently none of these things—could be absent there. Therefore it is clear that in that eternal blessedness and truly blessed eternity there are true unchangeability and, consequently, true and supreme simplicity [Col. 0911A].

But where there is supreme simplicity, there is true and supreme unity. Therefore whatever is in the highest good is truly and supremely one; there cannot there be one thing and another, but all that it is is one and the same thing.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How what has been said concerning the simplicity or unity of the highest good may be confirmed by another argument.

What we say here about the simplicity or unity of that highest and true good can still be demonstrated by another line of reasoning, as may be gathered from what we have already set forth above. For in the preceding discussion reason discovered that the divine substance is identical with power itself and identical with wisdom itself; hence each of these is proved to be identical with the other. Of that same substance it was said above—indeed, proved by a similar argument—that it is true immensity and is identical with eternity itself. Consider, therefore, that all these things are one and the same, and that they may indeed be predicated reciprocally of one another. What we say of these things, we can prove by the same reasoning concerning his goodness and his blessedness. For these, like the preceding attributes, admit reciprocal predication both among themselves and with those already stated; and, in short, everything said to inhere in the divine substance, or which that substance is said to possess, follows the same course. Since, therefore, whatever is in the highest substance—or rather, whatever the highest substance is—is truly and supremely one, for it being is not other than living, nor living other than understanding, nor is being powerful or wise something other and different from these. Nor, any more than these differ from themselves, is being good or blessed something different from them. From consideration of such reasoning, therefore, it may be inferred that whatever is in the highest good and true divinity truly and substantially is also supremely one.

## CHAPTER XIX. That the universally perfect good is supremely one and uniquely highest.

There must therefore be a supremely good being, a highest one, and not only supremely one but uniquely highest. For there cannot be two highest goods, any more than there can be two universally perfect beings. For if we grant that two are equally perfect, we must consequently grant that whatever fullness and whatever perfection is in the one will be in the other in precisely the same manner and measure. Thus the same fullness will be in both, and the same undifferentiated perfection in both. But where there is no difference, plurality cannot rightly be spoken of or found at all. Therefore, just as several universally perfect beings altogether are not, so they altogether cannot be.

And indeed, as has been said before us, if one universally perfect being exists, it is sufficient for all things. Otherwise it will not be perfect in every respect; and if one is wholly sufficient, another will be superfluous. But if it is wholly superfluous, how can it be useful? Or, if useless, how can it be good? Therefore that universally perfect good, as stated, is not only supremely one, but uniquely highest. Behold, as you see, what we say of the highest good follows the same consequence as the preceding reasoning discovered by reasoning about the unity of the divine substance. For if God is truly the highest good, and the highest good cannot be other than one, then it is equally true that, as we believe, there can be only one God. Thus in that true and highest blessedness, and in the divinity that is truly and supremely blessed, there is, I say, highest and substantial unity; and in unity itself true and highest simplicity—where, as was proved above, the whole of what it is is one and the same.

## CHAPTER XX. That the simplicity of this true and highest unity is incomprehensible.

But if in this unity there is true and highest simplicity, it bears no resemblance to that unity which arises from the composition of parts into one substance. If the whole of what is in it is one and the same, it bears no resemblance to that which arises from the conformity of many substances into one nature. If it is truly and supremely simple, what has it in common with the unity that consists in the union of substances of differing forms into one person? If there is simple identity in it, what has it in common with the unity that consists in the concretion of a subsisting thing and its subsistence into one? It is likewise far above that unity which arises from gathering many properties into one form. But it is incomparably and incomprehensibly above all unities of this kind, since it possesses in the identity of infinity a supremely simple and immutable being.

In that highest and universally perfect good, therefore, unity is true; in it unity is highest; in it simplicity is true; and identity is supremely simple. There, what is still more wonderful, is true unity together with the universality of fullness; there is highest simplicity together with the immensity of perfection; there is supremely simple identity together with the infinity of complete consummation. Consider, then, how incomprehensible and altogether beyond estimation is the simplicity of that true and highest unity.

## CHAPTER XXI. How anyone may, by comparison with his own knowledge, infer what he ought to think concerning that supereminent incomprehensibility.

But lest any of the simpler-minded should suppose that I am asserting things contrary to and mutually inconsistent with one another, as though what has been said could not stand together, I show such a person how he may, as it were through a mirror, see and infer from comparison within himself what he ought to think of that supereminent incomprehensibility.

If someone held a grain in his hand, would he not truly perceive and unhesitatingly affirm that no other of all things was numerically identical with it? If, then, he were questioned one by one about every grain of any vegetable or crop, would he not firmly answer that it differed from every single one? He would think the same of every hair; he would affirm the same of every strand of hair. What of each drop of the sea? What of every leaf on any tree? If the whole earth were reduced to dust, and he could be questioned about every one of its tiny particles, he would give the same answer to each question, as firmly as truly. If the size of the earth increased to infinity, he would hold the same judgment regarding its smallest parts.

I have taken pains to state this more carefully, so that anyone, however simple, may read in his own knowledge and understand how infinitely many things are comprehended under one simple truth. What wonder, then, if in that wisdom which is God, and in which all truth exists—for otherwise it would not be perfect if any truth were hidden from it—what wonder, I say, if there are in it, in one respect, highest simplicity and, in another respect, highest multiplicity? What wonder if there identity concurs and converges into one with the infinity of multiplicity, simplicity with the immensity of greatness, and true unity with the universality of all fullness? Behold, everyone has here a way to read in his own knowledge what he ought to judge concerning that supereminent incomprehensibility.

## CHAPTER XXII. What may more properly be said concerning God’s substance, and that he is great without quantity and good without quality.

From the foregoing we have learned that in that nature which is God there is true unity and highest simplicity: there is no composition there, no concretion; it itself is in nothing, and nothing is in it as in a subject. It is called, and is, as it were, highest power; it is called, and is, highest wisdom; and, lest it be thought to exist in a subject, it is called substance. But because, contrary to the nature of substances, nothing is found to adhere to it as in a subject, it is proved to be not so much substance as supersubstantial essence.

The preceding argument found, if I have not forgotten, that his goodness is not one thing and his immensity another. What then, if his immensity is the same as his goodness: will he be good by his immensity? If his goodness is the same as his immensity: will he be great by his goodness? But goodness appears to belong to quality, immensity to quantity. What then? Will he be great by quality and good by quantity? And who is sufficient for these questions? Or because his immensity and goodness are not other than his substance, will he be good without quality and great without quantity? And who is sufficient for these matters? From this, I think, it is very easy to understand how ineffable—indeed, incomprehensible—is what reason, by reasoning, compels us to think concerning our God.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That he is incomprehensibly in every place and unchangeably in every time; and how he is uniform and how multiform.

We hold from the foregoing that God is omnipotent and without doubt can do all things. If, therefore, he is truly omnipotent, he can consequently be everywhere. If he can be everywhere, he is potentially everywhere. If he is potentially everywhere, he is also essentially everywhere; for his power is not other than his essence. But if he is essentially everywhere, he is both where place exists and where place does not exist. He will therefore be within every place and outside every place; above all things, below all things; within all things, outside all things.

But because God is of a simple nature, he will not be divided into parts here and there, but will be wholly everywhere. Therefore he will be wholly in every, however small, part of any whole; wholly in the whole; and wholly outside the whole. If, therefore, he is wholly outside every place, he is confined in no place. If he is wholly in every place, he is excluded from no place. Thus he is nowhere locally, since he can be confined by no place and excluded by no place. And just as he is present in every place but locally in none, so he is eternal in every time but temporal in none.

For just as he who is supremely simple and uncompounded is not extended through places, so he who is eternal and immutable is not changed through times. Thus, just as none of the things that do not yet exist is future to him, so none of the things that no longer exist is past to him, and none of the things now present is passing for him. Therefore he is incomprehensibly in every place and unchangeably in every time; and, in a wonderful manner, he who in relation to himself is always uniform is found multiform in different beings. For if you ask about the position of him who lacks position, with respect to himself he exists uniformly everywhere according to the simplicity of his nature. Yet according to participation in grace he manifests himself as multiform in different beings. In some he is present according to participation in power, yet not according to participation in life. In others he is present according to participation in life, but not according to participation in wisdom. In some he is present according to participation in goodness, but not according to participation in blessedness. In others it is evident that he is present according to participation in both. And he who is uniform in himself and knows no change contracts the hand of his generosity in some, extends it generously in others, and more generously still in others.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That his acting is his willing a thing to come about through himself; his permitting is his not willing it to come about; and that he equally possesses what actually is and what actually is not.

And since he is truly omnipotent, whatever exists subsists either by his operation or by his permission. For unless whatever comes to be came to be at his command, he would beyond doubt not be omnipotent. Therefore, his acting is his willing a thing to come about through himself; his permitting is his not willing it to come about. And just as all his permitting is without any passion, and his suffering-with is without prior suffering, so all his acting is without motion in himself, and his unfailing making is without weariness.

But if his acting is the same as willing a thing to come about through himself, then when he made something that previously did not exist, did he, I ask, will something that he had previously not willed? But he who is truly immutable cannot change his will. Whatever, therefore, he once willed, he always willed. Did he therefore make from eternity the things which he made by willing them, because from eternity he willed that they should come to be? And if he made the things that are future, does he still make, and will he make, things that are already past and will not in future be? Does he persist in making as he does in willing? And when something ceases to exist, does he cease to possess what he formerly possessed? Or does he begin to possess something when it begins to exist, though previously it did not exist? For what ceases to exist, or has not yet begun to exist, is nothing; and what is nothing cannot be possessed. But the omnipotent possessor can neither grow rich nor diminish in his dominion.

What then? Consider whether perhaps that which actually exists is more excellently where it does not actually exist than where it actually exists. For here it is transitory; there it is eternal. And what was made, in him was life; and this was so even when it did not yet actually exist. Therefore he who can lose or acquire nothing possesses equally what actually is and what actually is not.

## CHAPTER XXV. That everything thus far said of divine properties appears to belong to that being which exists from eternity and of itself.

We wish at this point to defer discussion of those things said of God relatively, for their meaning extends more widely than can be embraced in concise brevity. For, in my view, their meaning ranges across all the categories. For together with the relation which they signify, what they co-signify is accustomed now to belong to one category, now to another. One is said to be consubstantial with another substantively; equal or unequal quantitatively; similar or dissimilar qualitatively; superior or inferior in relation to place; earlier or later in relation to time; co-sitter and co-sitting in relation to position; possessor and possession in relation to having; generator and begotten in relation to acting and being acted upon; lover and beloved. It is therefore better for the present to defer these matters than to attempt what we cannot set forth with due brevity.

It should, however, be noted here that everything said thus far concerning divine properties appears to belong to that being which exists of itself and, precisely for that reason, from eternity. For nothing less of what has been said would hold even if there had existed from eternity nothing deriving its origin from any source other than itself.

# BOOK THREE

## CHAPTER I. That thus far the discussion has concerned the unity of the divine substance, and that inquiry must now be made, in some fashion, into what should be thought concerning the plurality of divine persons.

In what has thus far been said concerning the unity or properties of the divine substance, we have proceeded as seemed fitting to us. For the rest, we have resolved to investigate what we ought to think concerning the plurality or properties of the divine persons. First, therefore, it seems necessary to ask whether in that true and simple divinity there is a true plurality, and whether the number of persons, as we believe, rises to three. Next, how unity of substance can be consistent with plurality of persons. Thirdly, it will be necessary to inquire whether, according to the teachings of our faith, there is there one person alone who exists of himself, while each of the others proceeds from another; and whether there are other matters concerning the same consideration to be examined.

If it should be granted us to establish these matters also by reason, finally we must further inquire whether in those two persons who proceed from another rather than from themselves there is a different mode of proceeding, what mode belongs properly to each, and, consequently, what names follow from the respective proper characteristics of each. Yet we must devote so much greater diligence and persist so much more ardently in the inquiries that remain as there is less to be found in the writings of the Fathers from which we can establish these things—not, I say, from testimonies of Scripture, but from the attestation of reason.

In this undertaking of my inquiry, let whoever wishes laugh, and let whoever wishes mock—and with good reason indeed. For, to confess the truth, it is not so much learning that raises me to the boldness of attempting this as the ardor of an agitated mind that urges me on. What if I am not allowed to reach the goal at which I aim? What if I fail while running? Yet I shall rejoice that, inquiring after the face of my Lord, I have always run, labored, and toiled to the utmost of my strength. And if, through the excessive length, roughness, and steepness of the way, I should fail, I shall have accomplished something if I can truthfully say: “I did what I could; I sought him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me.” And behold, that ass of Balaam which delayed its rider on his journey somehow urges and impels me to run the course I have begun. I hear it still speaking and saying to me: “He who could give me power to speak can beyond doubt give it to you also.” But now let us turn with all diligence to what we have proposed.
