## CHAPTER II. How, from the property of charity, the fullness of goodness proves that plurality of persons cannot be lacking in true divinity.

We learned above that in that highest and universally perfect good there is the fullness and perfection of all goodness. But where there is fullness of all goodness, true and highest charity cannot be lacking. For nothing is better than charity; nothing is more perfect than charity. Yet no one is properly said to possess charity because of a private and self-regarding love of himself. Love must therefore tend toward another if it is to be charity. Where plurality of persons is lacking, then, charity cannot exist at all.

But perhaps you will say that, even if there were only one person in that true divinity, he could nevertheless have charity toward his creature—indeed, he would have it—but he could certainly not have the highest charity toward a created person. For such charity would be disordered. Yet it is impossible for charity to be disordered within the goodness of highest wisdom. Therefore a divine person could not have the highest charity toward a person who was not worthy of highest love. But for charity to be highest and most perfectly complete, it must be so great that it cannot be greater, and of such a kind that it cannot be better.

So long as someone loves no other than himself, the private love which he has toward himself proves that he has not yet attained the highest degree of charity. But a divine person would certainly have no one whom he could worthily love as himself unless he had a person entirely worthy of him. And a person worthy of a divine person would not be one who was not God. Therefore, for fullness of charity to have a place in that true divinity, it was necessary that some divine person should not lack a person worthy of him and, for that very reason, should not lack divine fellowship. See, then, how easily reason proves that plurality of persons cannot be lacking in true divinity.

Certainly God alone is supremely good. Therefore God alone is supremely lovable. Hence a divine person could not bestow highest love upon a person lacking divinity. But fullness of divinity could not exist without fullness of goodness; fullness of goodness could not exist without fullness of charity; nor fullness of charity without plurality of divine persons.

## CHAPTER III. That the fullness of divine blessedness gives the same testimony as the fullness of goodness concerning plurality of divine persons.

What the fullness of goodness proves concerning plurality of persons, the fullness of blessedness approves by similar reasoning. What the one declares, the other attests. In one and the same testimony of truth, one cries out and the other responds in affirmation. Let everyone question his own conscience, and he will without doubt and without contradiction discover that, just as nothing is better than charity, so nothing is more delightful than charity. Nature itself teaches us this, and manifold experience teaches the same.

Therefore, just as the fullness of true goodness cannot lack that than which nothing is better, so the fullness of highest blessedness cannot lack that than which nothing is more delightful. Charity must therefore not be lacking in highest blessedness. But for charity to exist in the highest good, it is impossible that there should be lacking both one who may bestow it and one upon whom it may be bestowed. It is the property of love—and something without which it cannot exist at all—to desire that one whom you love greatly should love you greatly. Love cannot, therefore, be delightful unless it is mutual.

Accordingly, in that true and highest blessedness, just as delightful love cannot be lacking, so mutual love cannot be lacking. But in mutual love there must necessarily be one who expends love and one who returns love. Therefore one will be the giver of love, and another the returner of love. But where one and another are shown to exist, true plurality is found. Thus in that true fullness of blessedness plurality of persons cannot be lacking. And it is evident that highest blessedness is nothing other than divinity itself. Therefore the bestowal of gratuitous love and the due return of love undoubtedly prove that plurality of persons cannot be lacking in true divinity.

## CHAPTER IV. That what is established concerning plurality of persons by the two preceding witnesses is confirmed by considering the fullness of divine glory.

Certainly, if we say that in that true divinity there is one person only, just as there is one substance only, then plainly he will have no one with whom he can share that infinite abundance of his fullness. But, I ask, why should this be? Is it because he cannot have a participant although he wishes to? Or because he does not wish to have one although he can? But he who is without doubt omnipotent cannot be excused on grounds of impossibility. If, then, it is evidently not due to a defect of power, will it not be due solely to a defect of goodwill?

But if, although he could truly have one if he wished, he utterly refused to have a participant, consider, I ask, how great and what kind of a defect of goodwill this would be in a divine person. Certainly, as has been said, nothing is sweeter than charity, nothing more delightful than charity; rational life experiences nothing sweeter than the delights of charity. It enjoys no pleasure more delightfully. He would lack these delights for eternity if, lacking companionship, he remained solitary upon the throne of majesty.

From this we may perceive how great and what kind of a defect of goodwill it would be if he preferred to keep the abundance of his fullness greedily for himself alone rather than communicate it to another—something he could do, if he wished, with so great an increase of joys and such an augmentation of delights. If this were so, he would deservedly shun the sight of angels and of all beings; deservedly he would blush to be seen and to be known, if such a great defect of goodwill were in him. But far be it—far be it—that anything should be in that supreme majesty from which it cannot glory, or for which it ought not to be glorified. Otherwise, where would fullness of glory be? For there, as was proved above, no fullness can be lacking. And what is more glorious, what more magnificent, than to possess nothing which one is unwilling to communicate?

It is certainly evident that in that unfailing good and most wise counsel, a miserly withholding can no more exist than a disordered outpouring can exist. Behold, as you can see plainly, the very fullness of glory in that highest and supreme exaltation compels there not to be lacking a companion in glory.

## CHAPTER V. That the assertion already made of divine plurality is confirmed by threefold testimony.

Behold, we have taught the plurality of divine persons by reasoning so clear that anyone wishing to oppose such evident testimony appears to suffer from the disease of madness. For who, unless afflicted by madness, would say that the highest goodness lacks that than which nothing is more perfect, nothing better? Who, I ask, unless bereft of understanding, would deny that the highest blessedness contains that than which nothing is more delightful or sweeter? Who, I say, unless devoid of reason, would think that the fullness of glory can lack that than which nothing is more glorious, nothing more magnificent?

Certainly nothing is better, nothing more delightful, and absolutely nothing more magnificent than true, sincere, and highest charity, which cannot exist at all without plurality of persons. The assertion of this plurality is therefore confirmed by threefold testimony. For what highest goodness and highest blessedness jointly proclaim concerning this matter, the fullness of glory confirms by responding in affirmation, and responds in affirmation by confirming. Behold, concerning this article of our faith we have threefold testimony: from the highest, most exalted; from divine things, divine; from the depths, most high; from hidden things, most manifest. And we know that “every word is established by the mouth of two or three.” Behold, a threefold cord that is not easily broken, by which every frenzied assailant of our faith may, through the gift of God’s wisdom, be firmly bound.

## CHAPTER VI. That the divine persons must altogether be coeternal.

Behold, as we may plainly gather from the foregoing, the perfection of one person requires fellowship with another. We have found that nothing is more glorious, nothing more magnificent, than to will to have nothing which one is unwilling to communicate. Therefore he who was supremely good was unwilling for his majesty to lack the fellowship of another person. And, without doubt, what he willed to exist had to exist, since his will was omnipotent. What he once willed, moreover, he always willed, since his will was immutable.

Therefore an eternal person had to have a coeternal person; neither could one precede the other, nor one succeed the other. For in that eternal and immutable divinity nothing can pass away as obsolete, and nothing new can come upon it. Thus it is altogether impossible that the divine persons should not be coeternal. For where true divinity is, there is highest goodness and full blessedness. But highest goodness, as has been said, cannot exist without perfect charity; nor perfect charity without plurality of persons. Full blessedness, however, cannot exist without true immutability; nor true immutability without eternity. True charity requires plurality of persons; true immutability requires the eternity of persons.

## CHAPTER VII. That in that plurality of persons there must be both highest equality and highest likeness.

It should certainly be observed that just as true charity requires plurality of persons, so highest charity requires equality of persons. But highest charity is not yet proved to exist where one who is truly loved is not loved supremely. Yet love is not discriminating where one is loved supremely who is not supremely lovable. In the goodness of highest wisdom, however, the flame of love burns neither otherwise nor more intensely than highest wisdom directs.

Therefore, the one whom it is necessary to love supremely according to that abundance of highest charity must without doubt, according to that highest rule of [lacuna]cretionis (“discernment”), be supremely lovable. But the very property of love proves that for one who loves supremely it is not enough if the beloved does not return highest love. In mutual love, therefore, fullness of charity requires that each be supremely loved by the other and, consequently, according to the rule of discrimination mentioned above, that each be supremely lovable.

But where each is equally lovable, each must be equally perfect. Each must therefore be equally powerful, equally wise, equally good, equally blessed. Thus the highest fullness of love among mutual lovers requires highest equality of perfection. Therefore, just as in true divinity the property of charity requires plurality of persons, so the integrity of that charity requires, in true plurality, highest equality of persons. But for them to be equal in all respects, they must be alike in all respects. For likeness may exist without equality, but equality never without mutual likeness. For those who have no likeness in wisdom, how can they be equal in it? And what I say of wisdom, I say also of power; you will find the same in all other things if you examine them one by one.

## CHAPTER VIII. By what wonderful reasoning there is substantial unity in that plurality and personal plurality in true unity of substance.

We have sought and found that, in those mutual lovers and those mutually to be loved of whom we have spoken, if highest love is rightly to exist, there must be highest perfection and fullness of all perfection in each. Therefore in both there will be fullness of power, in both fullness of wisdom, fullness of goodness, fullness of divinity. Here is the point of which we made mention far above, though without determining anything: divinity, which we there found unable to be common to several substances, here plainly appears to be common to several persons.

But if, as has been said, every perfection is common to mutual lovers, it is plainly evident that if one is omnipotent, the other will be omnipotent; if one is immense, the other will be immense; if one is God, the other will be God. Yet, as we showed quite clearly above, only one can be omnipotent, only one can be immense, and only one can be God. What then? Certainly, without any doubt, each will be omnipotent in such a way that both together are only one omnipotent being. Each will be immense in such a way that both together are only one immense being. Without doubt each of them will be God in such a way that both together are only one God. And who is sufficient for this?

But if divinity itself, as we have said, is certainly the divine substance—which, as was proved above, is nothing other than divinity itself—then it follows that both have one and the same substance in common; or, if this sounds better, that both together are one and the same substance. What wonder, then, if together they are only one omnipotent, one eternal, one immense being, only one God and Lord, when together they are only one substantially? See, therefore, by what wonderful reasoning substantial unity exists in that plurality of persons, and personal plurality in the true unity of substance: so that there is distinction in the persons, unity in the substance, and equality in majesty.

## CHAPTER IX. That in the divine nature there is plurality of persons in unity of substance, and in human nature plurality of substances in unity of person.

Perhaps you marvel, hearing or reading this, how there can be more than one person where there is only one sole substance. But what wonder? He is wonderful in so many of his works; what wonder, I say, if he is above all things wonderful in himself? You marvel how in the divine nature there can be more than one person where there is not more than one substance; yet you do not equally marvel how in human nature there are more than one substance where there is not more than one person.

For a human being consists of body and soul, and these two together are only one person. Thus a human being has within himself how to read and learn what he ought, by contraries, to think concerning his God. Let us bring together, if you please, what reason has discovered by reasoning in the divine nature and what experience finds in human nature. In each there is unity; in each there is plurality. There, unity of substance; here, unity of person. There, plurality of persons; here, plurality of substances. There, indeed, plurality of persons in unity of substance; here, plurality of substances in unity of person.

See how human and divine nature seem mutually to regard each other, as if from opposite sides, each responding to the other by contraries. Created and uncreated nature, temporal and eternal, corruptible and incorruptible, mutable and immutable, so small and immense, circumscribed and infinite, ought to regard and respond to each other in this manner.

## CHAPTER X. How, from the plurality and unity he finds in himself, a human being is taught what he ought, as it were by opposition, to judge concerning the things proposed to him for belief concerning his God.

Let us add that in that plurality of persons there is complete likeness and highest equality, whereas in this plurality there is much unlikeness and great inequality. In that plurality of persons, one is incorruptible and the other incorruptible; one immutable and the other immutable; one uncircumscribed and the other uncircumscribed; this one and that one equally wise, equally good, equally blessed. But in this plurality of substances of which the human person consists, one is bodily, another incorporeal; one visible, another invisible; one mortal, another immortal; one dissoluble, the other indissoluble; one destructible, the other indestructible.

Nevertheless, they are so united into one by personal identity that in suffering or in experiencing delight together, they cannot—not merely be separated—but not even distinguished apart. Behold, you have seen how great is the dissimilarity or diversity of substances in human nature; nevertheless, you have heard how great is the likeness or equality of persons in the divine nature. Explain to me, I beg you, how personal unity exists amid such dissimilarity and diversity of substances, and I shall explain to you how substantial unity exists amid such likeness and equality of persons.

“You say, I do not grasp it; I do not comprehend it. Yet although understanding does not grasp it, experience itself persuades me.” Very well and rightly so. But if experience teaches you that something in human nature is beyond your understanding, should it not thereby teach you that something in divine nature is beyond your understanding? A human being can therefore learn from himself what he ought, as it were by contraries, to judge concerning the things proposed to him for belief concerning his God. These things have been said for those who endeavor to define or delimit the height of divine mysteries according to the measure of their own capacity, rather than according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, whom it is evident learned and taught through the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XI. How, from the perfection of charity, it is proved what kind of Trinity exists in true unity, and what true unity in a true Trinity.

But now let us continue, in the order in which we began, the course of our reasoning. We have now established the plurality of the divine persons, though not yet the Trinity. For plurality can exist even where there is no Trinity; duality itself is plurality. Let us therefore question concerning the affirmation of the Trinity the same witnesses whom we earlier brought forward to attest plurality; and first, if you please, let supreme charity be asked what it testifies in this matter. [Col. 0922C]

Supreme charity must universally be perfect. But in order to be supremely perfect, just as it must be so great that none can be greater, so it must necessarily be such that none can be better. For, as what is greatest cannot be absent from supreme charity, so neither can that which is manifestly most excellent be absent from it. Now in true charity this seems most excellent: to will that another be loved as oneself. For in mutual and intensely ardent love, nothing is rarer, nothing more splendid, than that you should wish another to be loved equally by him whom you love supremely and by whom you are loved supremely. Therefore, the proof of consummate charity is the desired sharing of the love shown to oneself. [Col. 0922D]

Certainly, for one who loves supremely and desires to be loved supremely, the chief joy is ordinarily the fulfilment of his desire—that is, the attainment of the love he seeks. He therefore proves himself not to be perfect in charity who cannot yet delight in sharing his chief joy. Thus, inability to endure partnership in love is a sign of great deficiency; to be able to endure it is a sign of great perfection; if it is great to be able to endure it, greater still is willingly to receive it. But greatest of all is to seek it out of desire: the first is a great good, the second better, the third best. Let us therefore attribute to the Supreme Being what is most excellent, and to the Best Being what is best.

Accordingly, in those mutually beloved persons whom the foregoing argument discovered, the perfection of each, if it is to be consummate, requires on equal grounds a sharer in the love shown to him. [Col. 0923A] For if he does not will what perfect goodness demands, where will fullness of goodness be? But if he wills what cannot be done, where will fullness of power be? Hence it follows by manifest reasoning that the highest degree of charity—and thereby fullness of goodness—cannot exist where a defect either of will or of capacity excludes a sharer in love and a participant in the chief joy. Therefore each of those who supremely love and are supremely lovable must, with equal desire, seek a co-beloved (*condilectus*) and, with equal harmony, possess the fulfilment of that desire.

You see, therefore, how the consummation of charity requires a Trinity of persons, without which it cannot subsist in the integrity of its fullness. Wherever, then, there is everything that is universally perfect, neither perfect charity nor true Trinity can be absent. There is therefore not merely plurality, but also a true Trinity in true unity and a true unity in true Trinity. [Col. 0923B]

## CHAPTER XII. How supreme goodness and supreme happiness jointly proclaim the affirmation of the Trinity and confirm it by mutual testimony.

But if anyone should contend that only those two mutually beloved persons found by the preceding argument exist in true divinity, what account, I ask, could he give for this assertion? Will a participant in the chief joy be lacking to each of them? Is this because neither wished to have one, or because one wished it and the other did not? But if one wished it and the other did not, where will be that quality which is customarily found, and must always be found, in true and perfect friends? [Col. 0923C] Where, I say, will be that indivisible prerogative of intimate love: unanimity of mind and inward harmony?

And certainly, if anyone says that one wills it and the other does not, he will deny that whichever of them he grants unable to prevail in his own will is supremely powerful. But if he says that neither can assent to sharing the love shown to him, how, I ask, can he excuse them from the deficiency of love described above? We know that nothing can be hidden from the supremely wise. Therefore, if they truly and supremely love one another, how can either see the deficiency of the other and not grieve? For if either sees the other's deficiency [Col. 0923D] and does not grieve, where will fullness of happiness be? It is clear that where a cause for grief can never be absent, fullness of happiness cannot exist.

Hence it follows, and is discovered by indubitable reasoning, that fullness of happiness excludes every deficiency of charity; and, as has been said, charity's consummation requires and proves that a Trinity of persons cannot be absent. Behold how supreme goodness and supreme happiness jointly proclaim the affirmation of the Trinity and confirm it by mutual testimony.

## CHAPTER XIII. That the fullness of divine glory seems to add its acclaim to the testimony of supreme goodness and happiness.

Who does not know, or who can pretend not to know, that it is a grave defect of charity to be unable to endure partnership in love? [Col. 0924A] If this defect were present in those often-mentioned mutually beloved persons, each would have not only something in the other over which to grieve, but also something in himself of which to be ashamed. For as a true and intimate friend cannot see the defect of one intimately loved without grieving, so indeed he could not fail to blush for his own deficiency before his friend's gaze.

But if that plurality of persons has something for which it ought rightly to blush, where, I ask, will be the fullness of glory which it is altogether impossible for true divinity to lack? But just as no cause for grief can exist in supreme happiness, so no ground for blushing can exist in the fullness of supreme glory. For who does not see how utterly mad it would be even faintly to suspect that anything could have existed in that supremely happy majesty [Col. 0924B] capable of dimming, even slightly, the splendor of so great a glory?

Behold how the fullness of divine goodness, the fullness of happiness, and of glory converge in one testimony to truth, and clearly show what must be held concerning the fullness of divine charity in that plurality of persons. Together they condemn every suspicion of defect in that supreme charity; together they proclaim every fullness of consummation there. But charity, in order to be true, requires a plurality of persons; in order to be consummate, it requires a Trinity of persons.

## CHAPTER XIV. That the sharing of love cannot be in fewer than three persons.

[Col. 0924C]

If, then, we grant what, after so many arguments already set forth, we cannot doubt—if, I say, we grant that some one person in true divinity possesses such benevolence that he wishes to have no riches and no delights which he does not wish to share; such power that nothing is impossible to him; such happiness that nothing is difficult to him—it follows that we must acknowledge that a Trinity of divine persons cannot be lacking.

But that this may be clearer, let us gather into one point what we have said more diffusely. Certainly, if there were only one person in divinity, he would have no one with whom to share the riches of his greatness. Conversely, he would eternally lack that abundance of delight and sweetness which could accrue to him from the offering of intimate love. [Col. 0924D] Yet the supremely good being, the fullness of goodness, does not permit him to retain the former miserly; nor does the supremely blessed being, the fullness of blessedness, permit him not to possess the latter. For he rejoices in the generosity of the former and glories in the enjoyment of the latter, to the magnificence of his honor.

From this you perceive how impossible it is for any one person in divinity to lack a companion in fellowship. Yet if he had only one companion, he would indeed not lack someone with whom to share the riches of his greatness, but he would have absolutely no one to whom to impart the delights of charity. Nothing is found more pleasant than the sweetness of love; nothing in which the mind takes greater delight. He alone does not possess the delights of such sweetness who has no companion and co-beloved in the love shown to him. [Col. 0925A] Therefore the sharing of love cannot be in fewer than three persons.

But, as has been said, nothing is more glorious, nothing more magnificent, than to bring into common possession whatever useful and sweet things one has. This cannot be hidden from supreme wisdom, nor fail to please supreme benevolence; and just as the happiness of the supremely powerful or the power of the supremely happy cannot lack what it approves, so a third person cannot fail to be joined to the two persons in divinity.

## CHAPTER XV. That the two persons in divinity must, with equal desire and on like grounds, require a third person.

[Col. 0925B]

It should certainly be noted that in those divine persons the perfection of one requires the addition of another, and consequently, in two persons, the perfection of both requires the joining of a third. For in two persons, as we have already said elsewhere, if each is rightly to be supremely loved by the other, each must be supremely perfect. Therefore, just as wisdom is one in both and power one, so likewise benevolence must be one in both, and supreme.

It is characteristic of supreme and wholly perfect benevolence to bring into common possession the whole abundance of its fullness. But where equal benevolence exists in either person, each must, with equal desire and on like grounds, seek a participant in the chief joy. For [Col. 0925C] when two mutually loving persons embrace one another with the highest desire and take supreme delight in the love of each, the chief joy of this one lies in the intimate love of that one. Conversely, the chief joy of that one lies in the love of this one. So long as this one is loved by the other alone, he seems to possess alone the delights of his own special sweetness; likewise, so long as the other has no co-beloved, he lacks a share in the chief joy. Therefore, for each to be able to share such delights, they must have a co-beloved. Thus, where mutually loving persons possess such benevolence as we have described—namely, that they wish everything that belongs to perfection to be held in common—each must, as stated, with equal desire and on equal grounds seek a co-beloved and, according to the fullness of his power, possess the object of that desire.

## CHAPTER XVI. That fullness of power and wisdom seems able to subsist in a singularity of person.

[Col. 0925D]

Among the delights of charity and of wisdom, there is ordinarily this chief difference: the delights of wisdom can and customarily are drawn from one's own heart, whereas the delights of intimate charity are drawn from another's heart. For one who loves intimately and desires to be loved intimately is not so much delighted as distressed if he does not draw from the heart of his beloved the sweetness of love for which he thirsts. But the delights of wisdom give greater pleasure when they are drawn from one's own heart.

Therefore, nothing is judged contrary to nature if fullness of wisdom is said able to subsist in a singularity of person. For, so far as appears, even if there were only one person in [Col. 0926A] divinity, he could nevertheless possess fullness of wisdom. But fullness of wisdom cannot exist without fullness of power, just as fullness of power cannot exist without fullness of wisdom. For he would undoubtedly not possess fullness of wisdom if he did not know how he might obtain what was lacking to him in omnipotence. Conversely, he unquestionably lacks fullness of power if he could unwillingly endure any deficiency of wisdom. Thus the fullness of one cannot be had without the fullness of the other. What, therefore, we have said of wisdom must consequently be understood also of power. For if omnipotence cannot be lacking where fullness of wisdom exists, it appears that the fullness both of power and of wisdom can be possessed in a singularity of person. [Col. 0926B]

## CHAPTER XVII. That the completion of true and supreme happiness seems unable to subsist without a duality of persons.

But the completion of true and supreme happiness seems in no way able to subsist without a duality of persons. This is now clearer than light from what we have said above. For if there were only one person in that true dignity, he would have no one upon whom to bestow supreme love, nor anyone to bestow supreme love upon him. Whence, then, would those supremely sweet delights abound for him—delights which, as was said, are customarily drawn not so much from one's own heart as from another's? For, as we have already stated, nothing is sweeter than these delights, nothing more delightful, nothing more wholesome than this sweetness, [Col. 0926C] nothing more splendid or more pleasant. How, then, could divine happiness possess the abundance of all fullness if supreme sweetness and supreme delight were always lacking to it? Therefore happiness, as stated, requires a duality of persons in order that it may subsist in the full integrity of all its fullness.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the consummation of true and supreme goodness seems unable to subsist without the completion of the Trinity.

Let no one be troubled or offended if, for a clearer understanding of truth, we speak of divine and supermundane things in human fashion. We adopt this manner of speech for the use of our weakness with all the more confidence [Col. 0926D] because we find it very frequently in the sacred Scriptures.

The highest degree of goodness seems to occur when supreme love is bestowed there from which nothing is desired for the fullness of one's happiness. But, as is most evident from what has already been said, this degree of supreme perfection cannot be found between only two mutually beloved persons. For there each lover bestows love, from which he undoubtedly draws those honey-sweet delights of love—delights which he would have absolutely no source from which to draw if he were alone and lived in solitude. Thus a great accumulation of joys and delights accrues to each from companionship in love both given and received.

Hence it manifestly follows that that highest degree of beneficence would have no place in divinity [Col. 0927A] if a third person were lacking in that plurality of persons. Certainly, in a mere duality of persons, neither of the two would have anyone with whom to share the chief delights of his joy. From this it is understood that the consummation of true and supreme goodness cannot subsist without the completion of the Trinity.

## CHAPTER XIX. How, from consideration of the property of co-love alone, a trace of the Trinity may be discovered.

What has been proved concerning the affirmation of the Trinity by the testimony of manifold reasoning can be confirmed by a brief and very clear consideration. Let us therefore weigh with careful consideration the force and property of co-love (*condilectio*), and we shall quickly find what we seek. When one bestows love upon another and one alone loves one alone, there is love indeed, but not co-love. When two love one another and mutually bestow the affection of highest desire, and the affection of this one runs toward that one and of that one toward this one, and thus, as it were, tends in different directions, there is love on both sides indeed, but not co-love. [Col. 0927B]

Co-love is properly so called where a third is harmoniously loved by two, loved in fellowship, and the affection of the two is fused into one by the fire of love for the third. From this it is clear that co-love would have no place in divinity if, with only two persons existing, a third person were absent. For we are not speaking here of any sort of co-love, but of supreme co-love, such as no creature ever deserves from the Creator and is never found worthy to receive. [Col. 0927C]

Who, I ask, can worthily explain how great is the power of benevolence that is supreme and wholly perfect? Who, I ask, can adequately assess what, or how great, is the dignity of intimate and supreme harmony? If, then, such dignity belongs to each of these two virtues in itself, what power, I ask, what dignity will belong where each is constituted by the other, where one is magnified by the other, and this one is perfected by that one? What else is intimate and supreme co-love but the mutual convergence of intimate and supreme harmony? Thus, just as a virtue of such dignity and surpassing excellence cannot be absent from the supreme and universally perfect good, so it cannot subsist without a Trinity of persons.

## CHAPTER XX. How the union with the third person in that Trinity ensures that harmonious and communal love is found everywhere and nowhere solitary.

[Col. 0927D]

Consider now how the union with the third person produces harmonious affection everywhere and binds communal love together through all and in all. If you consider any one of the three persons, you will see that the others love him harmoniously. If you look at another, you will find there likewise that the remaining persons agree with equal desire in love for him. If you bring the third of them under consideration, you will undoubtedly see the affection of the others flow toward him in equal harmony.

If harmony is considered, there the cord of love is made threefold, so that where suspicion of a defect of love might more readily arise, certainty may be strengthened by fuller consideration. [Col. 0928A] Behold how, through the union with the third person in that Trinity, harmonious charity and communal love are found everywhere and nowhere in isolation. Behold: in affirming the Trinity, such great and rare testimony to truth meets us on every side that anyone whom so great a confirmation cannot satisfy appears bereft of reason.

## CHAPTER XXI. That supreme equality exists in that Trinity, where all must be equally perfect.

What was proved above concerning two can be inferred on equal grounds concerning three: namely, that they must be supremely beloved and supremely lovable by each individual because they are supremely perfect. The fullness of supreme happiness requires the fullness of supreme delight. The fullness of supreme charity demands the fullness of supreme perfection. Where all must be equally perfect, they must necessarily agree in supreme equality.

Therefore all will have equal wisdom, equal power, undifferentiated glory, uniform goodness, and eternal happiness, so that it may truly stand as the daily profession of Christian doctrine teaches: that the divinity of the three is one, their glory equal, their majesty coeternal. [Col. 0928B] None there is greater than another; none is lesser than another; none is earlier; none is later. It is therefore established that in that Trinity all the persons are at once coequal and coeternal. For if they were not coeternal, they would thereby not be coequal.

## CHAPTER XXII. That in each person there is supreme simplicity, and in all together true and supreme unity, and in both respects a wondrous identity.

[Col. 0928C]

In that supreme and wholly perfect equality of persons, that supreme and supremely simple being is common to all. Therefore, for each, to be is the same as to live; to live, the same as to understand; to understand, the same as to be able. Thus wisdom there is not other than power, power other than essence; and the same conclusion applies likewise to similar things.

You see, therefore, that all that is in any person is one and the same thing; but if supreme perfection is in that equality and supreme equality in that perfection, there will be in each individually and in all together the supreme fullness of wisdom, and in each individually and in all together the supreme fullness of power. [Col. 0928D] But what is supreme and complete power except omnipotence? We know that omnipotence is so called because it can do all things. If it is truly established that omnipotence can do all things, it can easily bring it about that any other power can do nothing. Hence it is manifest that omnipotence can be only one.

But it was proved above that omnipotence is itself the same as the divine essence. Therefore, if it is common to all the persons at once to have omnipotence—indeed, to be omnipotence, since there to be is not other than to have—it will also be common to all to be one and the same essence. For the divine essence, like omnipotence, can be only one. Thus not only is all that any person is one and the same thing, but each one is itself the same thing as any other. [Col. 0929A] In each, therefore, there is supreme simplicity; in all together, true and supreme unity; and in both respects, if you consider carefully, a wondrous identity.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the stated equality is to be understood in these persons, where there is such unity and such identity.

What has been said concerning the equality of the persons can be understood both well and badly. For amid such simplicity and unity of persons, there seems to be identity rather than equality. If three golden statues are of the same purity and weight and in every respect the same appearance, we can and customarily do call them equal; but such equality is very foreign to that which exists in the Trinity of divine persons. [Col. 0929B] For in the equality of those statues, the mass of gold of one statue is one thing and the mass of gold of another statue another; accordingly, one is one thing and the other another thing.

But we must think nothing of this kind concerning that supreme Trinity, as though one thing and another existed there, though equal to one another. For, as has already been shown, what is in any one person is itself, wholly and entirely, in every other. We rightly call three rational spirits equal if they have the same power, wisdom, purity, and goodness; but in this trinity of spirits, just as there are three persons, so it is clear that there are also three substances. The supreme Trinity, however, consists in unity of substance. [Col. 0929C]

Thus, in that trinity there are one thing and another—even though equal—but such equality is far removed from the divine Trinity. Rather, in that supreme Trinity we call the persons equal for this reason: the supreme and supremely simple being which is present in the fullness and perfection in which it exists in one person is present in the fullness and perfection in which it exists in every other person.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How incomprehensible is that omniform coequality.

Certainly, one and the same substance is not something greater or lesser, better or worse, than itself. Therefore no person in the Trinity will be anything greater or better than any other, since one and the same substance truly belongs to each. And it is that same substance for each separately and for all together. Hence any two will not be anything greater or better than any one; nor will all three taken together be anything greater or better than any two, or than any one taken by itself. [Col. 0929D]

But in a trinity of persons where there are several substances, one alone is something less than two, and all three taken together are something greater than any two. Now consider, then, how incomprehensible is that all-formed and manifold coequality of greatness in the supreme Trinity, [Col. 0930A] where unity does not yield to plurality, nor plurality exceed unity.

## CHAPTER XXV. That in that Trinity no one is unlike himself or unequal in anything to another.

But in order that you may admire still more the equality of the divine persons, consider also this fact in all other persons: in any one and the same person, neither is singularity without plurality nor unity without inequality—to say nothing of the fact that he can increase or diminish and become unequal to himself. I pass over the fact that his power is one thing, his wisdom another, his justice another; and that he can be greater in one respect, lesser in another, better or worse. [Col. 0930B] Certainly his power alone and his wisdom alone are unlike and unequal to one another.

The same is true of the rest. Consider his power, and you will find that one thing is easy for him, another difficult, another impossible; and thus he is found to be unlike and unequal even to himself. Likewise, for wisdom itself one thing is comprehensible and another incomprehensible. For human or angelic intelligence can never, to say nothing of other things, comprehend the very immensity of divinity.

Therefore, while one and the same nature is more effective in some respects and weaker in others, lesser in part and greater in part, it is found unlike and unequal to itself. [Col. 0930C] From this it may be inferred that where true simplicity is absent, true equality cannot exist. But in that Trinity no one is unlike himself, nor unequal in anything to another.

Indeed, where true eternity exists, there can be no earlier or later; so where immutable immensity exists, there can be no greater or lesser. Those, therefore, in whom the same nature of eternity and immensity exists cannot have any alternation or variation of inequality. Since there is no change there, nor even the shadow of variation—nothing earlier, nothing later, nothing greater, nothing lesser—all three persons are coeternal with one another [Col. 0930D] and coequal. Behold, we have now proved by clear and manifold reasoning how true is what we are commanded to believe: namely, that we worship one God in Trinity and Trinity in unity.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0929]

## CHAPTER I. That it seems incomprehensible to human understanding that a plurality of persons exists in unity of substance.

[Col. 0929D]

Behold, at the beginning of this work we have shown by such evident and lucid reasoning what we believe concerning the unity of the divine substance that, for those who examine it attentively, no doubt ought to remain that could require them to hesitate even slightly. Likewise, in its proper place, such rare reasoning has persuaded and such manifold reasoning confirmed the assertion of our faith concerning plurality of persons that anyone unable to be satisfied by so great a testimony to truth appears deficient in mind. [Col. 0930D]

Indeed, each of these considerations and assertions, when regarded alone and separately in itself, seems to contain nothing more credible, nothing truer. But when we compare one with another and consider how they can stand together harmoniously, then—unless firmness of faith intervenes—everything which manifold reasoning has persuaded immediately becomes doubtful. For human understanding does not easily grasp how there can be more than one person where there is not more than one substance. [Col. 0931A]

Hence come those countless errors of unbelievers; hence those manifold heresies of schismatics. Hence some divide the unity of the divine substance, while others confuse the plurality of persons. Hence Arians and Sabellians are divided against one another by opposing sects. Hence, too, some of the more recent writers take the term *person* in a variety of senses and entangle with greater ambiguity the understanding of so profound a truth which they ought to have explained. For if anyone wishes to understand the term *person* in its common and proper sense, he should by no means suppose that several persons, understood in that sense, can subsist in unity of substance. [Col. 0931B]

## CHAPTER II. That there are many things which human understanding does not comprehend, though personal experience itself does not allow them to remain hidden.

But, I ask, is the stated unity of Trinity and Trinity of unity incapable of existing because it cannot be comprehended? Who but one deficient in mind could think so? Who would dare to say how many things human understanding does not comprehend, though manifold experience does not allow the human mind to remain ignorant of how true they are?

Explain to me, if you can, concerning something of which you cannot doubt at all, why the bodily eye does not perceive by seeing what is where it is, yet does perceive by seeing what is not where it is at all. In heaven, where it surely is not, it sees a star set in place; yet, when covered by the eyelid, it does not see the eyelid beneath which it lies concealed. [Col. 0931C] The other bodily senses perceive and distinguish only by contact; the sense of sight alone is dulled by contact and is active toward distant and most remote objects. Will you contend that this is not true because you do not comprehend how it is so?

Explain to me, if you can, what you do not dare deny: how body and soul, natures so utterly different, are in yourself one and the same person; then ask me how, in a supremely simple and common nature, a Trinity of persons can be one and the same substance. But if it is incomprehensible how something is which the human mind nevertheless knows through experience, how much more so is that which no human experience reaches! [Col. 0931D]

## CHAPTER III. That there are many incomprehensible things beyond the reach of experience which manifest reason nevertheless does not allow to remain hidden.

But if you say that you can in no way doubt what has been experienced, even if it seems to exceed the capacity of human understanding, I add that you do not doubt the existence of certain incomprehensible things which you do not prove by experience. For manifest reason does not allow many things to remain hidden, though the human mind is insufficient to comprehend them.

Do you comprehend God's eternity, and yet do you distrust his eternity? Do you doubt God's immensity, though you cannot comprehend it? Is God's omnipotence comprehended by all those by whom it is proclaimed and believed? If you question individual theologians, you will receive from all the answer that God's power is the same as his wisdom, and that his goodness is nothing other than the one or the other. If you ask what these three are, you will find nothing other than the divine substance. [Col. 0932A] Manifest reason establishes all these things and does not allow them to remain hidden. In this, certainly, all theologians agree; this they all defend in common.

Which of these, I ask, is more conceivable, which more comprehensible: that one substance should be called three, or that three persons should be one substance? Both are incomprehensible, yet neither is unbelievable. From this incomprehensibility, however, it seems to me that some derive the varying meaning of *person* through many usages. For there are those who say that the name *person* sometimes signifies substance, sometimes subsistences, sometimes the properties of persons. They hold that, according to their view, it signifies substance sometimes in the singular, but never in the plural, lest those who confess three persons appear also to confess three substances. [Col. 0932B]

To prove that the properties of persons are persons, they cite Jerome's authority in these words:

> “Avoiding the Sabellian heresy, we distinguish three persons expressed by their properties. For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, hypostases, that is, substances.”

But, as it seems to me, Jerome does not in these words say that persons are properties of persons, but properties of names; that is, what the names of the persons properly signify. [Col. 0932C]

## CHAPTER IV. That, for clarity of doctrine, the meaning of person must be defined, and, according to that definition, the unity of the Trinity must be set forth.

But, to say nothing of the term *hypostasis*, in which, according to Jerome, there is a suspicion of poison—to say nothing, I say, of a Greek term when we are not Greeks—we must not pass over in silence the term *subsistence*. Some explain persons as subsistences, and speak of three substances and one substance in one divinity more by assertion than by demonstration. For they pass over these things without explanation, as though it were plain to all readers that three subsistences could exist even where it is established that there is only one substance.

I do not accuse this opinion of theirs, condemn it, or maintain it to be false. But I am compelled to confess what is true: their teaching does not satisfy my simplicity. If you wish to satisfy people like myself, you must first define carefully the meaning both of *substance* and of *subsistence*, and then, according to the definition given, [Col. 0933A] show how there can be more than one subsistence where there is only one substance. Otherwise, I ask, what use is it to me to have an unknown thing explained by something more unknown? The term *person* is on everyone's lips, even the unlearned; the term *subsistence*, however, is not recognized even by all educated people. How, then, from a property of which simpler people are ignorant, can they infer that three subsistences, and thereby three persons, can exist in unity of substance? How can teaching satisfy which resolves one difficulty by another?

Since, therefore, my purpose in this work is to serve the simpler sort and, so to speak, not to teach Minerva, I shall endeavor, as the Lord grants, to define not so much the meaning of *subsistence* as that of *person*, and according to the proposed definition show how a plurality of persons can accord with unity of substance. [Col. 0933B]

## CHAPTER V. That the question before us has been asked on what necessity, and that what remains to be asked is on what ground of truth those three in the Trinity are called persons.

Certainly I will state what I think, and what I firmly and without doubt believe: that in that so sublime and pre-eminent mystery of the Trinity, the name *person* was by no means assigned without divine prompting and the teaching of the Holy Spirit. Let us consider how that same Spirit foretold through the mouths of the prophets so many mysteries of our faith, our redemption, our sanctification, and our glorification; described them through the mouths of the evangelists; [Col. 0933C] and expounded them through the mouths of teachers. Whoever considers this could never believe that He exposed to human judgment the supreme article of our faith, the most sacred and hidden mystery of the Trinity, that name which He willed to be believed by every heart and confessed by every mouth, rather than ordering it by His own inspiration.

Suppose we say that those who first transferred this name *person* to divine matters did so from necessity, so that they might have an answer for those asking what those three in the Trinity were, since they could not answer that they were three Gods. Yet the Holy Spirit, who presided over their hearts, knew for what reason and in what truth He willed what they did from necessity to be done. If, then, we faithfully believe this, [Col. 0933D] let us inquire with every care—not now under what meaning the word was first imposed on human beings, nor from what necessity it was afterward transferred to divine things, but in what truth it was inspired by the Spirit of truth into those who made the transfer, and universally employed by the Latin Church. No opinion is rendered more certain than one formed from the common conception of the mind. Therefore, following the simple and common understanding which everyone forms upon hearing the name *person*, I shall endeavor to formulate the manner of our assertion.

## CHAPTER VI. That the meaning of “substance” differs greatly from that of “person”

Let us first say what others have said: that *person* is predicated according to substance and seems to signify substance. Nevertheless, there is a great difference between the signification of the one and that of the other. But that what we say may shine forth more clearly, let us explain this more openly.

Who would deny or doubt that *animal* signifies substance? Yet there is a great difference between the signification of the one and that of the other. For by the name *animal* an animate, sentient substance is understood. *Animal*, therefore, signifies substance, but it also co-signifies something else. The name *animal* signifies substance together with an attached specific difference. Likewise, the name *man* appears to be an animal, and thereby to signify substance. For what is man except a rational, mortal animal? Thus, in what it principally signifies, it also co-signifies something. [Col. 0934A]

*Animal*, therefore, signifies substance—not just any substance, but a sentient one. But *man* signifies not every sentient being, but a rational one. Yet *person* is never said except of a rational substance. And when we name a person, we understand only one substance, some individual substance. Thus, with the understanding of substance, under the name *animal* there is implied a property common to every animal; under the name *man*, a certain property common to every human being; and under the name *person*, similarly, there is implied a property which belongs to one alone—though not determinately, as in a proper name. Thus, in one case a general property is implied, in another a specific property. [Col. 0934B] But with the name *person* there is implied an individual, singular, incommunicable property. From these points, I think, you can easily observe how greatly the meaning of *substance* differs from that of *person*.

## CHAPTER VII. That “substance” signifies not so much someone as something, and “person” not so much something as someone

If you weigh the matter well and attend carefully, by the name *substance* not so much “who?” as “what?” is signified. Conversely, by the name *person* not so much “what?” as “who?” is designated.

When something is so far from us that it cannot be distinguished, we ask what it is. And we are accustomed to receive the answer that it is an animal, a human being, a horse, or something of that sort. [Col. 0934C] But when it has come close enough that it can be discerned to be a human being, we ask no longer what it is, but who it is. We are answered that it is Matthew, Bartholomew, that man’s father, or son. You see that to the question “what?” a general or specific name, a definition, or something of that kind is given in response; but to the question “who?” a proper name, or something equivalent, is customarily given. Therefore, by “what?” one asks about a common property; by “who?” about a singular property.

It should be noted, however, that if, at the sight of an angelic apparition, one asks another who it is, and receives the answer that it is such-and-such an angel of the Lord, the answer is not according to the strict property of speech, but according to the questioner’s intention—as if he said more plainly to the inquirer: “He is not a human being, as you suppose, but an angel of the Lord.” For if he knew that it was an angel, he would neither ask such a question nor, except foolishly, accept such an answer. [Col. 0934D] Therefore, as was said, by “what?” one asks about a common property; by “who?” about a singular property. By “what?” we ask in order to be made certain of the quality of a substance; by “who?” in order to be made certain of the property of a person.

And it should be noted that to the question, “What person is this?” or “Who is this?” we customarily give the same answer, supplying a proper name or its equivalent. From these points, I think, it is sufficiently clear that under the name *substance* not so much someone as something is implied. Conversely, under the name *person* not so much something as someone is designated. Under the name *person*, moreover, no one is ever understood except one individual, distinguished from all others by a singular property. [Col. 0935A]

## CHAPTER VIII. That, wherever there are several persons, it is not necessary also to believe there are several substances

When, therefore, we speak of three persons, what else do we signify than three someones? In the same understanding in which we take *person* in the singular, we take it in the plural as well, except that here several, there one individual, is understood. When *person* is said, certainly one person is understood who is nevertheless a rational substance. When three persons are named, without doubt three persons are understood, [Col. 0935B] each of whom is a substance of rational nature. But whether they are several substances, or all one and the same substance, makes no difference to the property and truth of personhood.

Yet people judge more according to what experience proves than according to what reasoning dictates. We see human persons, but cannot see divine persons. In human nature, as many persons as there are, so many substances there are. Daily experience compels them to make similar judgments about divine things. For the carnal mind rests so much in things it has learned through experience that it can scarcely believe anything which does not approach, through some likeness, what it has known by experience. But one who slumbers with regard to faith should at least awaken to manifest reason. [Col. 0935C] We have already shown by plain reasoning that, wherever there are several persons, it is not necessary also to believe there are several substances.

## CHAPTER IX. That we define nothing contrary to itself when we say that our God is one in substance and three in persons

Certainly, wherever there are three persons, it is altogether necessary that this one be one someone, that one another someone, and that there be a third someone distinct from both; and that each be, in himself, separated from the other two by a proper distinction and a distinct property. Likewise, wherever there are three substances, it is altogether necessary that one be one thing, another another thing, and that the third be a thing other than both of them. [Col. 0935D] For if they differed from one another in nothing, they could certainly not be several. For where there is no difference, there can be no plurality.

But above we found that in that supreme Trinity there is, common to all, a supreme and supremely simple being; nor is any one something other than any other. Therefore we deny that there are three substances in that Trinity. For in rational nature, being one thing and another thing results from diversity of substances, whereas being one person and another person results from otherness of persons. But in that divine and supremely wise nature, we find this latter otherness, though not the diversity just mentioned. Therefore we believe that there are several persons there, but deny that there are several substances. Behold, then, by reasoning sufficiently clear and concise, as we think, [Col. 0936A] we have shown that we define nothing contrary to itself when we say that our God is one in substance and three in persons.

## CHAPTER X. That plurality of substances does not dissolve unity of person in human nature, nor does plurality of persons divide unity of substance in divine nature

It must be carefully noted and mutually compared that, just as being substantially one thing and another does not everywhere remove unity of person, so being personally one person and another does not everywhere split unity of substance. For in human nature body is one substance and soul another, although there is only one person. But in divine nature one person is one someone and another person another someone, [Col. 0936B] although they are only one and the same substance.

Indeed, we know, and have already shown above, that in that plurality of divine persons there is supreme likeness and supreme equality; while in the plurality of substances of human nature there is much dissimilarity and great inequality. What wonder, then, if in that great equality of persons the true unity of substance remains, since even amid such diversity of contrary quality there is found unity and identity of person? For in human nature one and the same person is bodily in one respect and incorporeal in another; visible in one respect and invisible in another; mortal in one respect and immortal in another. Nevertheless, unity of person subsists [Col. 0936C] amid such diverse substances. Therefore plurality of substances does not make one person and another person in human nature; nor does plurality of persons make one thing and another thing in divine nature. Let us add what follows: neither does plurality of substances there divide unity of person, nor does plurality of persons here dissolve unity of substance.

## CHAPTER XI. That a twofold consideration is needed in distinguishing persons: namely, that we know what kind of thing a being is and whence it has being

We have found that it is not impossible for several persons to exist in unity of substance. It follows that we must ask how otherness of persons can exist without otherness of substances. In distinguishing persons, therefore, a twofold consideration is needed, I think: namely, that we know both what kind of thing a being is and whence it has being. [Col. 0936D] One of these considerations concerns discerning the quality of a thing; the other concerns investigating its origin.

The former requires us carefully to ask what it is in itself; what it has in common with others; what is general, what specific, and finally what is proper to its assigned nature. The latter consideration requires us subtly to investigate this very point—whence it has being: whether from itself or from elsewhere; and, if from elsewhere than itself, whether in this manner, that manner, or any other mode of existing. There, the definition of the thing itself, or whatever description may be given, and an assignment of its property, are sought. Here, the order of nature, the origin of the thing itself, and every distinction of this kind are considered. [Col. 0937A]

The former consideration concerns the mode of being; the latter concerns the mode of having. The former concerns the account of essence; the latter, if I may say so, the account of *having* (*obtentia*). To pass over other matters: I know that *obtentia* is used less worthily of divine things. Yet let no one be offended if I explain, in the words available to me, what I think concerning divine matters. But I gladly accept it, and regard it as a great gift, if anything true which I have expressed less properly or suitably is explained by anyone else in suitable and more proper words.

By *obtentia* I mean here the manner in which someone possesses what he is substantially, or naturally has. For modes of possessing differ greatly from one another, whether in receiving, in not receiving, or in the manner of giving or receiving. [Col. 0937B]

## CHAPTER XII. That under the name “existence” we may understand both considerations: that concerning the account of essence and that concerning the account of having

Under the name *existence* we can understand both considerations: both that which concerns the account of essence and that which concerns the account of having. I mean both that in which one asks what kind of thing each being is, before that in which one asks whence it has being.

The name *existence* is derived from the verb *existere* (“to exist”). In the verb *sistere* (“to stand,” “to subsist”) may be noted what belongs to one consideration; likewise, through the attached preposition *ex* (“from”), may be noted what belongs to the other. By saying that something *stands* or *subsists* (*sistere*), we first exclude things which do not so much have being in themselves as exist in something else—not so much, so to speak, subsist as inhere (*insistere*), that is, adhere to a subject. [Col. 0937C]

But *sistere*, as it is said, appears applicable both to what has subsistence in some manner and to what has it in no manner; both to what ought to be a subject and to what ought not at all to be a subject. The former belongs to created nature, the latter to uncreated nature. For what is uncreated so subsists in itself that nothing inheres in it as in a subject. Therefore, *sistere* applies both to the account of created essence and to that of uncreated essence.

But when *existere* is said, it is understood not only that something has being, but that it has being from elsewhere—that is, from something. For this is conveyed by the compound verb with its attached preposition. What indeed is *existere* except to subsist from something—that is, substantially to be from something? Therefore, in this single verb *existere*, or under the single name *existentia* (“existence”), it is conveyed that one may understand both the consideration concerning the quality of a thing and that concerning its origin. [Col. 0937D]

## CHAPTER XIII. That the general variation of existences is distinguished in three ways

Existence, as may be inferred from what has been said, [Col. 0938A] can generally vary in three ways. It can vary either according to the quality of the thing alone, according to the origin of the thing alone, or according to the concurrence of both.

Existence varies according to the quality of the thing alone when several persons have one and the same origin in every respect, but each has a singular and proper substance. For several substances cannot exist at all without differing in quality. This, then, is a variation of existence according to quality alone, containing no variation according to origin.

Variation of existence according to the origin of the thing alone occurs when several persons have one and the same undifferentiated being, but are found to have mutual difference according to origin. They differ according to origin if one has an origin and another lacks one, or if, among those which have an origin, the origin of one differs from that of another. Such existence therefore varies according to origin alone, not according to any difference of quality. [Col. 0938B] Existence varies both according to the quality of the thing and according to its origin where each person has a singular and proper substance and a different origin.

Thus we have said that the general variation of existences is distinguished in three ways: either according to the quality of the existent alone, according to its origin alone, or according to alteration in both.

## CHAPTER XIV. In what respect the existence of persons varies in human nature, and in what respect it varies in angelic nature

[Col. 0938C]

In human nature, which we know by experience, we see the existence of persons vary both according to the quality of the persons and according to their origin. Certainly every human person has a singular and proper quality through which he differs, without any ambiguity, from every other. Likewise, each person has a proper origin, different from all others and distinguished by a singular property. For one principal source belongs to this person and another to that, because this person has one father and that person another. And where one father belongs to several, the division of paternal substance is nevertheless different, from which one person has been propagated rather than another.

We see, therefore, as was said, that in human persons the property of existences varies both according to the quality of each and according to the origin of each. But in angelic nature there is no propagation, but only simple creation. There is therefore one sole and undifferentiated principle for each and for all alike. [Col. 0938D] For all have as their sole principle one Creator, and each no less than all together exists according to creation alone.

But in angelic nature there are as many substances as persons, and thus they must differ in quality. For if they differed in no quality, without doubt they would not be several substances. The difference of existences in angelic nature varies according to quality alone; but in human nature, as has already been said, both according to quality and according to origin. [Col. 0939A]

## CHAPTER XV. That the difference of divine existences must be sought in origin alone

But in divine persons, as has been proved, there is absolutely nothing dissimilar and nothing unequal. As one person is, so is another, and so likewise is the third. Where all are thus alike and equal to one another, they cannot differ in quality. For those to whom there belongs in every respect one and the same—and, as plain reasoning has proved, supremely simple—being, cannot in any way be separated from one another by any difference of quality.

Therefore, since they cannot differ from one another in any property of quality, it remains that they must be believed to have some difference in the mode of origin. For where there is no difference, there can be no plurality at all. The plurality of persons therefore proves that, in that Trinity, a distinguishing property and difference of properties cannot be lacking. But because identity of substance wholly excludes every difference of quality, the differing properties of persons must be sought in origin alone. [Col. 0939B]

Thus, to state briefly what we have said at greater length: it is clear that in divine nature plurality of existences varies according to origin alone; in angelic nature according to quality alone; and in human nature according both to quality and to origin. We have now found what we proposed above to seek: namely, how otherness of persons can exist without any otherness of substances. For we have found that those several persons in the Godhead, although they have one and the same being, undifferentiated in every respect—which belongs to identity of substance—can nevertheless have mutual difference according to original cause: if one exists from himself, another derives origin from another; and if those having origin differ in their mode of having it. But wherever the property of persons is altered, there without doubt the property of existences is likewise varied. In divine nature, therefore, difference both of persons and of existences must be sought in origin alone. [Col. 0939C]

## CHAPTER XVI. That in divine nature there is an existence common to several and an existence wholly incommunicable

[Col. 0939D]

By the name *existence*, as is clear from what precedes, is understood that which has substantial being from some property. It is proper to mixed beings to have substantial being through propagation alone; it is proper to human beings to have substantial being both through propagation and through procreation. For flesh is propagated; soul is procreated. It is proper to angels to have substantial being through creation alone. It is proper to divine nature to have super-substantial being, but without creation and without beginning.

Now one existence is common to several, while another is wholly incommunicable. [Col. 0940A] For, to pass over those things which do not share the name *person*: to have rational being is common to divine, angelic, and human nature alike; but it is proper both to angelic and to human nature not to be from themselves, but from elsewhere, whereas it is proper to divine nature alone to be not from elsewhere but from itself. An incommunicable existence, however, is one which can belong only to some one person.

But, to pass over other matters, in divine nature there is without doubt an existence common to several, and there is an existence wholly incommunicable. It has been shown above that existence signifies substance, though not simply, but with the indication of some property pertaining to the consideration of original cause. To the consideration of original cause belongs not only asking and finding that origin exists where it does exist, but also asking and finding that it does not exist where it does not exist. [Col. 0940B]

It belongs to divine existence to have substantial—indeed, super-substantial—being without creation and without beginning. For it belongs properly to every substance that truly has its name from the thing itself to have composite being and to be subject to accidents. But the divine substance alone—which lies above the nature of substance—has simple, uncompounded being, and is subject to nothing inhering in it. It is therefore rightly said to have not so much substantial as super-substantial being.

It must, however, be known that *existence* designates substantial being, but sometimes as being from a common property, sometimes as being from an incommunicable property. We call an existence common when being is understood as possessed from a common property; incommunicable when being is understood as possessed from an incommunicable property. [Col. 0940C] It is as proper to divine substance not to be from any other substance but only from itself, as it is properly characteristic of a person without origin not to be from any other person. In the one case a common property is understood; in the other, an incommunicable property.

It is common to all divine persons to be that substance which is not from any other substance but from itself. Therefore, when divine substance is said or understood to be from itself, this is the same as common existence. Thus much concerning common existence; let us now consider incommunicable existence. [Col. 0940D]

## CHAPTER XVII. On what ground incommunicable existences can be in the Godhead, and that there are as many as there are persons

That is truly incommunicable which is not common and cannot be common. We must therefore consider whether, or how, incommunicable existence can be in the Godhead. But in that Trinity, without doubt, there must be as many personal properties as there are persons. A personal property, moreover, is certainly incommunicable. A personal property is that from which each has being as the person he himself is. We call personal that property by which each is one person, [Col. 0941A] distinct from all others.

For we never call anyone a person except someone individually distinguished from all the rest by a singular property. If, therefore, you maintain that a personal property is communicable, it is the same as saying that one person can be two. But if one is said to be double and double one, it is easily proved that neither is any person, since neither is distinguished from the other by a singular property. Hence we plainly infer what we said above: personal property is altogether incommunicable.

In that Trinity of persons, personal—that is, incommunicable—properties must without doubt exist. But, as has been proved, the difference of persons is the same as the difference of existences. Therefore, if persons differ by incommunicable properties, their existences also differ by incommunicable properties. There must be an incommunicable existence wherever there is an incommunicable difference. Therefore, as many persons as there are in the Godhead, so many incommunicable existences there are. [Col. 0941B]

## CHAPTER XVIII. That, in divine matters, person is nothing other than incommunicable existence

If we consider more carefully in respect to divine things, a person there is nothing other than an incommunicable existence. As has been proved above, every personal property is altogether incommunicable, and in divine things the difference of persons is precisely the same as the difference of existences.

What, then, will incommunicable existence be there except something having super-substantial being through a personal property? And what is a divine person except something having divine being through an incommunicable property? But what is divine being except super-substantial being? For whether you say divine being, super-substantial being, supremely simple being, omnipotent being, or anything else of this kind, it appears to refer to the same thing. [Col. 0941C]

Both a divine person and divine existence have divine being; both have super-substantial being; both have a personal property; both an incommunicable property. You see that everything said of one can be said of the other. Therefore, as has been said, in divine matters a divine person is nothing other than an incommunicable existence.

## CHAPTER XIX. That several existences, and consequently several persons, can exist where there is only unity of substance

[Col. 0941D]

Since from what has been said we hold that several existences can be in the Godhead, we must now consider whether they can be there while unity of substance is preserved. If usage permitted it, one could surely say—as *essentia* (“essence”) comes from *esse* (“to be”)—that *sistentia* comes from *sistere* (“to subsist”). Perhaps you laugh when you hear or read this; but I prefer that you laugh rather than that you understand too little what I mean to say and rashly deride it.

If usage allowed the word *sistentia*, it would signify simply the being of a thing, as *essentia* does. But under the name *existence* we must now understand something additional. For as *subsistence* is rightly said from subsisting beneath something, so *existence* can rightly be said because it has being from something. [Col. 0942A] Existence, therefore, signifies the being of a thing, and this being from some property.

Who does not see that it is a different existence for one to be omnipotent through this property, and for another to be omnipotent through another property? Although both have one mode of being, they do not both have one mode of existing. Who, I ask, would call it impossible, or even incredible, that two or three should be said to be equally powerful and equally wise? Or what would be called impossible, or even incredible, if that which they are in common were said to be possessed by one through one property and by another through another?

It therefore does not appear impossible or incredible that several existences, and consequently several persons, should exist in the Godhead. If we call them equal in power—as manifest reasoning proves we must—then we must admit that if one has omnipotence, the other also has omnipotence.
