[Col. 0942B] But it is certain among all theologians by indubitable reasoning that in true divinity there is supremely simple being. It must therefore follow that there, being omnipotent is identical with having omnipotence, and omnipotence is not something other than divine substance. But omnipotence, as we have shown elsewhere, can only be one.

Thus, from what is probable to everyone, and even from what according to theologians is necessary, the point we seek is inferred: several existences can exist where there is only unity of substance. But, to speak something yet more subtle for the more subtle-minded: in natural and created things, being and that which is differ; but in uncreated things, being and that which is are identical. It is therefore clear that divine substance is nothing other than substantial—indeed super-substantial—being: substantial insofar as it is the kind of thing which subsists in itself; super-substantial insofar as nothing inheres in it as in a subject. [Col. 0942C]

Those who fear where there is no fear would rightly fear confessing that persons are said according to substance if person signified substantial being simply and did not also co-signify something. But it signifies one having substantial being through some singular property. Therefore we confidently confess that persons in the Godhead are said according to substance and signify substance, and that there are several persons there but not several substances. For there are several having one and undifferentiated being through differing property. Thus unity there is according to the mode of being, plurality according to the mode of existing: unity of essence because being is one and undifferentiated; several persons because there are several existences. [Col. 0942D] For those who inquire devoutly, these things ought, I think, to suffice. For no one should seek or expect in this life fully to satisfy himself in so profound a matter.

It should also be noted how person and existence relate to one another. What is doubted on the basis of either is, in turn, proved by the other. For that there must be several in the Godhead is more easily proved from the notion of person; but that several can be in unity of substance is more readily established from the consideration of existence. [Col. 0943A]

## CHAPTER XX. How it is to be understood, or how it can agree, that some say three substances and one essence, some three subsistences and one substance, while others say three persons and one substance or essence

Perhaps someone expects me to explain how it ought to be understood, or how it can agree, that some say three substances and one essence; some, three subsistences and one substance; and others, three persons and one substance or essence. It seems greatly discordant and wholly contrary that the Latins confess one substance in the Godhead while the Greeks confess three. But far be it from them to hold different beliefs, or for either side to err in faith.

Therefore, amid this diversity of words, one truth must be understood, although the senses of the names differ among different peoples. That persons are called substances by some and subsistences by others appears to refer to the same thing. It is certain that they are called substances in relation to things which are customarily said to inhere in them, or substances to which these things appear to be subject. [Col. 0943B] And we know that throughout the world the Church of Christ sings: “In the persons is property; in the essence, unity.”

Because of such properties, which appear to inhere in the divine persons and by which they are distinguished from one another, they may, by a certain likeness to those things which truly underlie things inhering in them, be called—though less properly—substances or subsistences. For by those three in the Trinity, whether they are called persons, substances, or subsistences, we should understand nothing other than beings having substantial existence under a distinguishing and differing property.

For this reason, playing on the words, I said “under a distinguishing property,” not “from a distinguishing property,” so that you may understand why those in the Trinity are called substances or subsistences, although improperly. We indeed say that properties inhere in persons; but if we consider carefully, their inhering does not grant subsistence but existence. Therefore persons are more correctly called existences than substances or subsistences. [Col. 0943C]

But those who attend to divine things alone find no property by which the divine essence differs from another divine essence, because there is only one in the Godhead, as one person there differs from another by properties. Therefore, under this consideration, they do not find how they may call that unity substance; and for this reason they call it simply and quite properly essence. But they call that plurality in which properties inhere—though less properly—substances.

Indeed, in that uncreated essence no property is found by which it differs from another uncreated essence, where, as has been said, there is only one. Yet a property is found in it by which it differs from every created essence. Taking this into account, they call it not only essence but also substance. They transfer the name *subsistence* from its proper meaning to the designation of persons. [Col. 0943D]

To distinguish briefly between *substance* and *subsistence* according to this usage: understand by *substance* what I above called common existence; by *subsistence*, what I called incommunicable existence. Therefore, whoever knows from what I have set forth above how several existences can be in unity of substance knows likewise how several subsistences can be there. I am not unaware that these matters can be examined by more subtle reasoning; but I think this should suffice for simpler people, such as those whom I serve.

But this must be noted and firmly maintained: when you hear those three in the Trinity called substances, subsistences, or persons, understand the statement to be made according to substance. For, with regard to the truth of the matter, in all these terms [Col. 0944C] nothing else ought to be understood than three possessing rational being by a distinct and personal property. For it is clear that where there is no rational substance, rational being cannot be possessed. Yet it belongs to every person to possess rational being by an incommunicable property. I shall not speak of the Greeks, who, as Augustine writes (*On the Trinity*, book VII, ch. 4), understand “substance” differently from us; but among the Latins I think no name can be found which can be better applied to the plurality in God than the name “person.” Indeed, to a faithful mind nothing ought to be more authoritative than what resounds on everyone’s lips and is confirmed by Catholic authority.

## CHAPTER XXI. A definition of person, not of every person, but of the created person alone.

[Col. 0944D]

Behold, we have carried out, as far as we could, what we proposed above: namely, how the signification of substance differs from that of person, and how several persons can subsist in unity of substance. Let us now consider, if you please, whether Boethius’s given definition of person can apply to every person and to person alone. For if it is found to have been given generally and sufficiently, another is undoubtedly sought in vain. A definition, however, in order to be perfect, must comprehend the whole being, and only the being, of the thing to be defined. For, in order that it may receive its name from the thing, it must extend all the way to the limits of what is defined and not exceed them, so that it applies to every instance and to that alone, and can be converted [Col. 0945A] upon itself. Boethius’s definition of person is this: “an individual substance of rational nature.” Therefore, in order that it may be general and perfect, every individual substance of rational nature must be a person, and conversely every person must be an individual substance of rational nature. I ask, therefore, concerning that divine substance, since it is one and only one: I ask whether it is individual. For it is believed without doubt, and, as was proved above, manifestly demonstrated, that this substance is a certain Trinity of persons. If, then, the divine substance is to be called individual, some individual substance of rational nature will be something that is not a person. For the Trinity, which is the divine substance, is neither a person nor can rightly be called a person. Accordingly, [Col. 0945B] this definition of person does not seem capable of applying to person alone. But if that substance is not to be called individual, it is certainly the case that some person—namely, a divine one—is not an individual substance. Therefore this definition of person cannot apply to every person. Thus, whether divine substance is said to be, or not to be, an individual substance, that definition is shown not to be general.

## CHAPTER XXII. A description of person, not of every person, but of the uncreated person alone.

Without doubt, what is infinite cannot be worthily defined. Yet perhaps we may make some progress toward divine knowledge if we endeavor [Col. 0945C] to give such a description of the divine person as the Lord has granted. According to that signification of “existence” which we explained above, we may perhaps not improperly say that a divine person is an incommunicable existence of divine nature. By the name “existence,” as is clear from what precedes, is signified that something is substantial and is from some source; this is common to every substance. Now there is a general existence common to all substances; another general existence common to rational beings alone and to all of them; and a special existence common to angelic substances alone or to human substances alone. But all such cases are excluded when the meaning of “existence” is restricted and determined by the addition “of divine nature.” Likewise, if we consider carefully, we shall find in the divine nature [Col. 0945D] both an existence common to several persons and an existence belonging to one person alone, and thereby incommunicable. But what is common to several is excluded when it is called incommunicable. Therefore we may not improperly say, as we believe, that the divine person is an incommunicable existence of divine nature.

## CHAPTER XXIII. A description of person which seems capable of applying to person alone and to every person.

If we call divisible both that which can be distributed among several persons and that which can be distributed among several substances, and which can be possessed jointly by several and wholly by each; and if, on the other hand, we call individual [Col. 0946A] that which can be fitted to one alone—if, I say, we wish to take “divisible” and “individual” in this way—we may perhaps not improperly say that, just as it is true that every created person is an individual substance of rational nature, so it is true that every uncreated person is an individual existence of rational nature. But, in order that what we say may become clearer, let us examine the same point more carefully.

We said above that substantial being is signified by the name “existence.” According to the determination given above, this undoubtedly signifies not that by which a substance is called substance, but that which is principal in it and belongs to every substance. What is principal in it is not that which is subject to something else and has something adhering to it as to a subject, but that [Col. 0946B] it is such a thing as subsists in itself and adheres to nothing as to a subject. This, then, is common to every human, angelic, and divine substance. Certainly, in created substance that is more worthily and more principally called so which approaches more closely to the divine likeness. For in the very fact that it is subject to accidents, it seems to fall away from the divine likeness. Therefore, from that which is principal in every substance, it may more rightly be called essence than substance.

Furthermore, as has been said, the name “existence” indicates both that it has being in itself and that it has being from something else. This itself is evidently common to every substance. For everything that exists either is from itself or from something else. The remaining elements included in the same description [Col. 0946C] are sufficiently clear from what precedes and require no new exposition: namely, why not every existence, but an individual or incommunicable existence alone, is called a person.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Another description of person which seems capable of applying to person alone and to every person.

Perhaps it will be plainer and easier to understand if we say that a person is one existing through itself alone according to a certain singular mode of rational existence. How the word “existing” is to be understood has been sufficiently made known above. We add “through itself alone” because a person is never rightly called such unless it is one individual, distinguished from all others by a singular property. But to exist [Col. 0946D] through itself alone is common to all individuals, animate and inanimate alike. A person, however, is never spoken of except in reference to some rational substance. Therefore, to what was stated before—“one existing through itself alone”—there is added “according to a certain singular mode of rational existence.”

Now one mode of rational existence is common to several natures; another is common to several substances of the same nature; another to several persons of the same substance. But personal property requires a singular mode of rational existence, without which a person never subsists. Therefore, for one existing through itself alone to be a person, it must possess some singular mode of rational existence. How each expression is to be understood is sufficiently evident from what precedes [Col. 0947A]; hence there is no need to linger in explaining them. These are the points which we have set forth, to the extent of our ability, concerning the meaning, variation, and description of person. But if anyone understands the name “individual,” “person,” or “existence” otherwise than we have assigned, and proceeds in argument according not to our usage but to his own, and carries the conclusion of his reasoning to an absurdity, let him know that he does nothing against me. And if he thinks that he does, he deceives himself and does not know it.

## CHAPTER XXV. That it is proper to the divine nature to have a plurality of persons in unity of substance, and that by this very fact it differs from others.

It is proper to the divine nature to have a plurality of persons [Col. 0947B] [Col. 0947C] in unity of substance. Conversely, it is proper to human nature to have a plurality of substances in unity of person. For the fact that a human person is sometimes found in simplicity of substance is recognized to result not from the condition of human nature itself, but from the corruption of its condition. From this it is easy to discern how the property of the divine and the human seem opposed to one another.

Between these two, as though looking in contrary directions and answering one another by opposition, angelic property is placed as a middle term. By a likeness on both sides it is joined to each: it shares with the divine the fact that it never has a plurality of substances in unity of person, and it shares with the human the fact that it never has a plurality of persons in unity of substance. Behold how angelic property, by a certain proportional relation, connects the discord of contraries through its intermediate position and composes the dissonance of alternating terms into one harmony.

Yet in saying this I know that some think otherwise concerning angels. For there are, even today, those who think that they have bodies. But if they inquired more urgently and investigated more subtly, they would, as we believe, more quickly find the truth of this inquiry. What wise person, indeed, would dare deny that the property of a rational nature is so much higher and worthier as it approaches more nearly to the likeness of an uncompounded and supremely simple nature? And who would deny that an incorporeal creature [Col. 0947D], free from every adhesion of bodily concretion, approaches more closely to divine simplicity through the likeness of its own property—more closely [Col. 0948A] than does a nature composed of corporeal and incorporeal substance, united from two essences in the singularity of one person? Without doubt, the best kind of creature is that which consists in the sole and simple purity of spiritual nature.

Therefore, what an image of a human body without a head would be in a human work, that the fabric of the universe without the best kind of creature seems to be in the divine work. To this is added what the preceding argument set forth concerning angelic property. Tell me, I ask: what order seems more fitting to you, what more suitable to the disposition of the supremely wise? In that trinity of natures—divine, angelic, and human—is it that the properties of two are said to be wholly opposed to the third by contraries, with no middle term intervening; or [Col. 0948B] that the third intervenes between the two extremes and, joined alternately to both by likeness on either side, composes the said contrariety into one harmony?

But if this proof of our argument perhaps still appears suspect to someone, let him consider what the testimony of the Gospel ought to persuade him. Has it not become known from the Gospel that the Lord cast a legion of demons out of one man? One legion contains six thousand six hundred and sixty-six. If so many were cast out of one man, so many were in him before they were cast out. If demons have bodies, where, I ask, were they in him—in his spirit or in his body? It is clear that every body has length, breadth, and height—that is, local dimensions [Col. 0948C]—and therefore cannot subsist without spatial capacity; yet the spirit has no such capacity whatsoever. Therefore they were not in the spirit but in the body. But how, or in what part of the man, could so many bodies have been present?

Perhaps you say that angelic spirits, good as well as evil, have subtle bodies. But however subtle they may be, two bodies—especially bodies of the same size—cannot occupy one and the same place. How small, then, I ask, do you suppose an angelic body to be, if you believe that even the skin of a single man, stripped from his body, could contain so many angelic bodies? But behold, while saying this by way of excess, we have wandered too far from our purpose. I think, however, that what has been said [Col. 0948D] concerning the proposed question ought to suffice, and can suffice, for a devout and simple mind: namely, how it is in no way contrary to reason that we are commanded to worship one God in Trinity and Trinity in unity.

# BOOK V

[Col. 0947]

## CHAPTER I. Since the unity of the divine substance and the plurality of persons are now established, and likewise the harmonious mutual relation of unity and plurality, it remains to inquire into the properties of the persons.

[Col. 0947D]

As we have already said elsewhere, it belongs to every person to possess rational being by an incommunicable [Col. 0948D] property. But the divine person requires something further beyond this, in order that it may deservedly be called divine. The property of a divine person requires divine being; divine being is the same as supersubstantial being, the same as supremely simple being, for which being itself is the same as being wise. But only the divine substance possesses such being, and therefore it is deservedly called supersubstantial [Col. 0949A] essence.

And because in the divine nature there is only supremely simple and undifferentiated being, we confess there a unity of substance. But as surely as the unity of substance is established, so truly is the plurality of persons established. Yet where there is no otherness, there can be no plurality; nor can there be otherness where there is no difference. How, then, can plurality agree with undifferentiated being? But where there is not diverse being, there can nevertheless be distinct and differentiated existence. For where several possess undifferentiated being from distinct origin, they preserve unity of substance, yet several existences are not lacking. And, as we showed above, a divine person is nothing other than an incommunicable existence.

It must therefore be noted that every divine existence [Col. 0949B], if it is found to have even one thing incommunicable, is by that fact alone shown and demonstrated to be a person. For even if it has several incommunicable things, one alone suffices to prove that it is a person. For it is thereby clear that it is one individual, distinguished from all others by that property. We have briefly recapitulated these points from what was said above, so that we may approach what remains to be investigated with greater exercise and greater readiness.

But since the unity of the divine substance is established, the plurality of persons is established, and the harmonious mutual relation of unity and plurality is established, the subject now requires us to inquire into the properties of the individual persons and to assign to each its own proper attributes. For [Col. 0949C] we already know that those three in the Trinity—whether they are called persons, existences, or by any other name—are distinguished by certain properties; and we have recognized that these properties must be sought solely in the difference of their originating cause. But we have not yet grasped by reasoning which properties belong severally to which persons. Let us therefore now endeavor in these matters, as in the others already discussed, that what we hold by faith may be granted us to grasp by reason and establish by the testimony of demonstrative certainty.

## CHAPTER II. That the most delightful kinship of persons cannot be lacking in supreme blessedness, nor the most orderly disposition of properties in supreme fullness.

[Col. 0949D]

Let us first say what all of us have recognized in common by a certain natural instinct and prove by continual use in daily experience. It is plainly evident that the more intimate the plurality of persons, the more closely united it is; and the more closely united, the more delightful. Who, then, would dare attest or presume to judge that, in that fullness of supreme blessedness, what is known to be more delightful is lacking, while what is unquestionably less delightful is present?

If, therefore, each person is said to exist from itself, such a plurality is united by no affinity and bound together by no mutual kinship. But who could believe or dare affirm that the plurality of supreme unity is so united in one respect and so remote in another, and so wholly [Col. 0950A] alien to itself, that in the respect in which they are one there is supreme indifference, while in the respect in which they are separated into several they are free from every union? What plurality, I ask you, appears more beautiful or more fitting: that which is distinguished by a most orderly variety of properties and woven together in wondrous fashion by a most becoming proportion of relations; or that which is mutually connected by no harmony of differences or differing harmony, and adorned by no ordering of othernesses? I think no one judges that what is more beautiful can be absent from supreme beauty, or that what is less beautiful can be present in it.

We must therefore believe that neither the most delightful kinship of persons can be absent from supreme blessedness, nor the most orderly variety of properties [Col. 0950B] from supreme beauty. But lest the argument we have proposed appear to someone merely probable rather than necessary, let the point itself be investigated by a still higher argument.

## CHAPTER III. That the nature of things requires there to be some person who is from itself and not from some other.

What was said at the beginning of this work concerning substance can be said here without any hesitation concerning person. For in both cases the same reasoning applies, and like judgment is formed concerning like things. What was said there concerning substance, let it be said here concerning person: that there must exist some person who is from itself and not from some other; otherwise, in one Godhead there would undoubtedly be infinitely many persons [Col. 0950C]. For if this person were from that one, and that one from another, and according to this mode of progression every one were from some other, the production of such a chain would undoubtedly proceed to infinity and no end of such production would occur. Thus the series and order of things—which cannot exist without a beginning—would have no beginning: a beginning, I mean, not so much of time as of origin, or of whatever kind of origin.

But in these and similar matters the truth itself is so manifest and the reasoning so clear that they need no proof at all. For that no one does what he cannot do; that no one can give what he himself does not possess; [Col. 0950D] that whatever began to be at some time previously was not; that whatever now is, but at some time was not, began to exist in time; that no composition exists without a composer, no division without a distributor; that there is something than which nothing is greater; that there is something than which nothing is better—all this is clear to everyone who has understanding and uses reason. Whoever hears these and similar statements, if he understands the meaning of the words, immediately assents and has no ground for doubt.

Therefore, lest we extend the number of divine persons to infinity against our conscience, we must undoubtedly grant that some person exists from itself and draws its origin wholly from no other source. But since it is established that this person exists not from another person but from itself, it follows that we must inquire whether [Col. 0951A] this existence is communicable or incommunicable—whether being a person from itself belongs to one person alone, or whether this can be common to several.

## CHAPTER IV. That there can be only one person who is from itself.

Because this place calls for more diligent consideration and invites us to a more sublime understanding, we must, after the manner of builders, as it were dig more deeply there and lay the foundation of our reasoning upon the solid depth of certainty, so that the structure of our work may necessarily rise from there to the heights of a more hidden understanding. We must therefore begin from what no one can doubt.

It is clear that everything which exists is either composite or simple. It is likewise clear [Col. 0951B] that everything possessed is possessed either by participation or by fullness. It is one thing to compose one thing out of many and diverse elements, and another to divide what is one into many and distribute it among many at will. But, as we have already said, there is neither composition without a composer nor division without a distributor.

Let us therefore see whether that which is truly found to exist from itself can possess composite being. It is clear that every composition requires a composer, and that it cannot exist without the benefit of a composer. Therefore, without doubt, that which exists from itself does not possess composite being. It is evident, then, that what lacks every origin and author [Col. 0951C] must possess supremely simple being. But for that which possesses supremely simple being, being must be identical with power, and being wise identical with being powerful.

Behold, concerning its being we have what we sought; now let us consider its power. Let us inquire whether its power is possessed by fullness or by participation. But where there is participation, there is also distribution. For there is neither participation without distribution nor distribution without a distributor. Therefore, whoever can possess power only by participation undoubtedly requires the office of a distributor. It is thus clear concerning one who is from itself that, if it received power by participation, its very power would be possessed by the benefit of another. But if its power is by the benefit of another, so too is its being; for, as has now [Col. 0951D] been proved, its being and its power are not different things. Therefore, it has either both from itself or neither from itself.

Hence it follows that one who is from itself cannot possess power through participation in power. What it cannot possess by participation, therefore, it possesses by fullness. But where there is fullness of power, there is every power. Accordingly, for the person whose being is the same as its power, if its being is from itself, its power is also from itself. But its power is every power; therefore every power is from it. If every power is from it, every being is from it, and every existence is from it. From it, therefore, is everything that exists: every essence, every existence, every person—every human, angelic, and divine person. [Col. 0952A]

Therefore, if every other person has being from it, it is certain that it alone lacks a principle. It is likewise certain that no other can exist except from it, from which comes every power. You plainly see that such existence is wholly incommunicable and cannot be common to several.

## CHAPTER V. That two persons in the Godhead have being from another rather than from themselves, according to another mode of existing which is eternal, yet not from itself.

We now have it for certain that being a person from itself is a wholly incommunicable existence. We can therefore plainly infer from this that being a person from another rather than from oneself is not an incommunicable existence. Otherwise there would not [Col. 0952B] be, nor could there be, more than two persons in the Godhead. It is therefore the uniquely proper property of one person to be from itself; but it is common to the others not to be from themselves.

You see, then, that an incommunicable existence produces a communicable—indeed, common—existence, and that the latter proceeds and draws its origin from the former. Behold, we have now established by an indubitable demonstration that mode of existing of which we spoke at the beginning of this work, where we used reasoning that was more probable than necessary. For, as we said there in advance, there is a threefold mode of existing: one which is eternal and from itself; another which is neither from itself nor eternal; and a middle mode between these, which is eternal yet not from itself.

For, as was proved above, all three persons are equal [Col. 0952C] and coeternal. Therefore, just as that existence which exists from itself is eternal, so too that which proceeds from it possesses eternal being. That mode of existing which is common to two persons is eternal, yet not from itself. See, then, how diverse—indeed wholly contrary—the properties of the others are. The third mode of existing connects the contrariety of these properties by a certain proportional relation and, by its mediating position, brings the two extremes into mutual harmony: it has in common with one the fact of being eternal, and in common with the other the fact of not being from itself.

We now have what is uniquely proper to one person; we have what is common to two. But we have not yet grasped by reasoning what belongs properly to each individual one [Col. 0952D].

## CHAPTER VI. That the procession of one person from another is sometimes only immediate, sometimes only mediate, and sometimes both mediate and immediate.

From things known to us by experience we are instructed what we ought to inquire concerning things unknown and divine. For “the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made” (Rom. 1). When we desire to ascend to lofty things, we human beings, unable to fly, are accustomed to use a ladder. Let us therefore use the likeness of visible things as a ladder, so that what we cannot see in themselves by direct vision, we may deserve to see in such a mirror, as it were through a mirror.

In human affairs we see that a person [Col. 0953A] proceeds from a person, and such procession undoubtedly occurs in three ways. A person proceeds from a person sometimes only immediately, sometimes only mediately, and sometimes both mediately and immediately. Both Jacob and Isaac proceeded from Abraham’s substance, but the procession of one was only mediate and that of the other only immediate. For Jacob came forth from Abraham’s loins through Isaac as intermediary. Eve, Seth, and Enoch proceeded from Adam’s substance; but the first procession among these was only immediate, whereas the middle one was both mediate and immediate. For Seth proceeded from Adam’s substance immediately, insofar as he was from Adam’s own seed; but mediately insofar as he was from Eve’s seed.

Behold how, in human nature, personal procession is distinguished in a threefold way. And although this may appear very foreign to that singular and supereminent nature, there is nevertheless some likeness, since human nature [Col. 0953B] was made in the likeness of that nature. We must therefore raise ourselves from this nature to the mirror of contemplation of that other, and, according to the consideration just stated, investigate with utmost diligence, by the proportion of likeness and unlikeness, what is there and what is not there.

But if we say that there are three such existences there as we have distinguished above, apart from the one found to be from itself, we seem undoubtedly to introduce into that nature a number of four persons [Col. 0953C]. Therefore we must diligently inquire which of these properties are truly there, if they cannot all exist together.

## CHAPTER VII. On procession only immediate, and that there must be in the Godhead a person who is from one alone.

This, however, is most certain and altogether beyond doubt: from that most principal existence one person must proceed immediately; otherwise it would have to remain alone. For it is clear that none of the others can exist at all unless it proceeds from that one either immediately or mediately. But where there is no immediate procession, there cannot be mediate procession, nor procession that is at once mediate and immediate. Yet nothing prevents immediate procession from existing even where mediate procession happens to be absent [Col. 0953D].

Immediate procession consists in a duality of persons; mediate procession, however, never exists without a trinity of persons. Immediate procession is one in which there must be both that which produces it and that which proceeds from it. Mediate procession—apart from the persons in whom it begins and ends—also has a third person in whom the mediation consists. Now duality is naturally prior to trinity, for the former can exist without the latter, whereas the latter can never exist without the former. Therefore that procession which can subsist in a duality of persons is naturally prior to that which cannot exist without a trinity of persons.

But in that plurality of persons and true eternity, nothing precedes there and nothing follows another; thus there is nothing earlier in time and nothing later in time [Col. 0954A]. Yet what cannot be prior temporally can be prior causally and thereby naturally. For, as we said much earlier, the perfection of one person requires the fellowship of another. Thus one becomes the cause of the other.

For where there is fullness of divinity, there is also fullness of goodness, and consequently fullness of charity. But fullness of charity requires that one love another as oneself; otherwise that person’s love still has room to grow. And one must have a worthy equal, someone whom one can and deservedly ought to love as oneself. Therefore, if it is certainly true that the primordial person is supremely good, it cannot possibly fail to will what supreme charity requires. And if it is certainly true that it is omnipotent, whatever it wills [Col. 0954B] to exist cannot fail to exist. Therefore, charity requiring it to have a worthy equal, it will have the one whom it is pleased to have, power supplying that person.

Behold what we said: the perfection of one person is the cause of another’s existence. But that from which the cause of its existence comes is also the source of its existence. For it could not fail to be from that from which, as we have said, comes every power. Behold how reason bears witness to reason, and what is demonstrated from one argument is confirmed by another.

Here, then, you have person from person, existence from existence, one from one alone, the processible from the unprocessible, the begotten from the unbegotten; finally, one immediately joined to one, because one proceeds immediately from one. We have recognized beyond doubt that such an existence is present in the divine nature; but whether [Col. 0954C] it is communicable or incommunicable, we have not yet established by demonstrative reasoning.

## CHAPTER VIII. On procession which is at once immediate and mediate, and that there must be in the Godhead a person who is from two.

Since it is established that the third person in the Trinity derives its origin from somewhere other than itself, it must have its being from one of the persons mentioned, or from both together. Which of these is demonstrable by reason remains to be investigated. The clear demonstration of reason set forth above found that a supremely worthy person must have one worthy of itself. But in order to be worthy of an omnipotent person, it had to receive omnipotence from the omnipotent one, so as to possess equal—indeed, the same—power. For, as has often been said, omnipotence can be only one. But if it received the same power, it undoubtedly received that power from the one from whom comes all power, all being, all existence; from whom, as was said above, every essence and every existence has being. [Col. 0954D]

Therefore, if the same power is without doubt common to both, it follows that the third person in the Trinity has received both its being and its existence from both.

But perhaps someone will say in reply: if the begotten person has received and possesses the same power as the unbegotten person, then it has received and possesses from itself the power to exist from itself—which is the proper and distinctive attribute of the unbegotten person. But whoever says this, as it seems to me, does not rightly understand what he says. [Col. 0955A] Let us examine this matter more carefully, so that our point may become clearer.

He says that, if the unbegotten person gave the fullness of his power immediately to the one proceeding from himself alone, he consequently gave also the power to exist from itself, since that person is omnipotent and can do all things. To this I answer and confidently affirm that it exists from itself if it can exist from itself. For the divine nature is altogether unchangeable. Therefore, if it is from itself, it is clear that it is—that is, it exists—without another’s gift. But if the unbegotten person gave it this power, then it had it by another’s gift. What then? Does it have from itself, and therefore without another’s gift, that which it has by another’s gift? You see already, I think, how this assertion contradicts itself. For it is utterly contradictory for one and the same thing to be possessed by another’s gift and to be possessed without another’s gift. And what is more impossible than for one thing to be and not to be at the same time? [Col. 0955B]

Therefore, as we said above, in order that the supremely worthy person might have one worthy of itself, as the fullness of goodness required, it gave to the one proceeding immediately from itself all that an omnipotent being could truly give concerning existence. Thus that power from which all other things have both being and power is common to them. From this twofold existence, therefore, come every essence, every person, every existence—and hence also that person who is third in the Trinity.

This assertion is undoubtedly confirmed by the reasoning which we set forth above in investigating the Trinity. For there it is proved by manifest reason—indeed established by multiple demonstrations—that, just as the perfection of one is the cause of another, so the perfection of the two is the cause of the third person in the Trinity. Just as the perfection of one requires one worthy of it, so certainly the perfection of both requires a co-beloved (*condilectus*). [Col. 0955C] But since we treated these matters carefully above, there is no need to repeat them here; anyone may return to that place whenever desired.

But this must be held most certainly concerning the third person: those from whom it has the cause of existing are also those from whom it has existence. Thus we now hold by reason that the third person in the Trinity has being from the other two. We have established, therefore, that it derives its origin from two; but we have not yet established by reasoning whether such an existence is communicable or incommunicable. [Col. 0955D]

## CHAPTER IX. That a procession which is only mediate toward some person cannot exist in the divine nature

We have now discovered the greater part of what we proposed above to investigate. We have found that there must be one existence joined immediately to the unbegotten person alone. We have also found another existence united to that same existence by kinship both immediate and mediate. It remains now to ask whether there is, or can be, any existence joined to it only mediately. [Col. 0956A]

There is one thing which, I believe, no sound mind can think: namely, that there is any person in the Godhead who is not permitted, or unwilling, immediately—as one might say face to face—to behold the unbegotten person. For what else is seeing there except knowing by seeing, and seeing by knowing? And what is it to know the unbegotten person except to possess the fullness of wisdom? For there to be wise is nothing other than to be. Therefore, from where one receives the ability to be wise, from there one receives existence. From where, therefore, it has wisdom, from there also it has existence. Hence, if it receives immediately from that person the ability to be wise, it likewise receives immediately from that person the ability to exist.

But if anyone says that it does not see immediately, it follows that he must grant that it does not possess contemplation of truth in every form. Accordingly, in that respect it does not possess every fullness; and, consequently, it does not possess true divinity either. [Col. 0956B]

Perhaps someone objects: “Just as every person sees the one proceeding from itself, so every proceeding person sees the one producing it. Why, then, is it not proved by the same reasoning that the former is from the latter, as the latter is proved and established to be from the former?” To this I answer briefly: every divine person receives full wisdom in beholding another divine person; and thereby it must receive divine being from that person unless it has it elsewhere. For it necessarily has it from there if it has it nowhere else. But if it has it elsewhere, it need not have it from there also.

To make this clearer by an example: consider written truth known to one person from elsewhere, but wholly unknown to another from elsewhere. Both read and understand it; yet only the one who did not possess it from elsewhere receives knowledge of the written truth by examining the text. [Col. 0956C] Since, then, all divine persons behold one another immediately, they pour out or receive mutually the ray of the highest light. And because they see immediately, they are joined immediately. It is therefore impossible for there to be in the divine nature any person united to another only by mediate kinship.

By this same reasoning, what was said above concerning the procession of the third person is confirmed. For who would deny that it both knows the other persons by seeing and sees them by knowing? Yet the wisdom of the two persons is one and the same. Since it is established that it has nothing from itself, it follows that it receives wisdom from beholding wisdom, and thereby receives being, where being is nothing other than being wise. [Col. 0956D]

Thus what had been proposed for inquiry has now been sought and found. We have found that in the divine nature there is a procession that is only immediate; that there is one both mediate and immediate; and that one only mediate is not there at all, nor can be.

## CHAPTER X. That in the Godhead there cannot be more than one person who is from only one person, nor more than one who has being only from two

From what we have now said, we can truly and unquestionably infer that, if a fourth person could exist in the Godhead, it would undoubtedly have to derive its origin immediately from the other three. Otherwise it would be united to one of them only by mediate kinship, and would see it only mediately. And if a fifth person could exist there, it would similarly proceed immediately from the other four. According to this mode of reasoning, a similar consequence will appear in what follows, however far this series of progression may be extended in thought. [Col. 0957A]

What we say here is confirmed by matters already touched upon above. For just as the power from which the third person is known to derive its origin is common to two persons, so without doubt the power from which a fourth person would have to exist would be common to three, if a fourth had a place in the Godhead. Otherwise two would avariciously reserve for themselves what they could give to a third without impairing either person’s distinctive property. What we say of these cases, you will undoubtedly find in those that follow. [Col. 0957B] For however far you extend the line of such a sequence, you will see the same fitting correspondence everywhere arise.

It should be noted how this distinction of properties consists solely in the number of persons producing. The first has being from none; the second from one alone; the third from two. And if their number increased further, the same pattern of progression would have to be found in all. See how this order of differences arises and proceeds according to the manner and order of numbers.

It should also be noted that, according to each such distinction, it is impossible for there to be more than one person. For there can be only one from one person alone; similarly, there can be only one which is from two alone. For if two proceeded from one alone, neither of those proceeding would adhere immediately to the other. How impossible this is has been demonstrated above by manifest reasoning. [Col. 0957C] What has been said of one distinction is to be understood of every other.

Here we have the solution of the twofold question which we left above unresolved. Since only one existence can be from one person alone, and only one from two, it is clear, I say, that each is an incommunicable existence. Therefore, just as there can be in the Godhead only one person who is from itself, so there cannot be more than one who is from only one person; nor more than one who has being only from two. [Col. 0957D]

## CHAPTER XI. That there must be in the Godhead a person from whom no other proceeds, although that person is not from itself

Above we found the distinctions of personal properties, and how they are related or proceed according to the pattern and consequence of numbers. But if there were as many divine persons as there can be such distinctions, they would indeed be infinite. Therefore the properties of the persons must be examined more carefully, lest any mistaken suspicion arise concerning their number. [Col. 0958A]

Above we proved that, in that plurality of divine persons, there must be some person who derives its origin from nowhere other than itself. But just as there must be one there who is not from another, so there must also be another from whom no other proceeds. Both are established by similar reasoning; both are confirmed by equal demonstration. For if in true divinity there were no person from whom another did not proceed, but every person proceeding from another had one proceeding from itself, the extension of such a derivation would proceed to infinity, and the series of persons, extended to infinity, would receive no end to its number. But no opinion accepts this, nor does any reason admit it at all.

Therefore there must exist in the plurality of divine persons some person from whom no other derives its origin. Nevertheless, that very person must have the principle of its existence from another, just as the one which is not from any other must furnish another with the cause of existing. The same reason supports both propositions, and each is established by a similar argument. [Col. 0958B]

For since manifest reason proves that only one person can be from itself, if the person not from another had none proceeding from itself, it would remain alone forever. By a similar reasoning, the person which has none proceeding from itself, if it proceeded from no other, would be deprived forever of divine fellowship. But, as we showed above quite plainly, manifold reasoning excludes solitude from true divinity and establishes a plurality of persons. Therefore there must be one there who does not receive the principle of existing from elsewhere, but furnishes it; and equally there must be one who, conversely, receives from another what it is and bestows it upon no other. [Col. 0958C]

## CHAPTER XII. That there can be only one person in the Godhead from whom no other proceeds

Certainly there must be in the Godhead such a person as we have just described, from whom no other proceeds. But someone may still doubt whether this is the property of one person alone or can be common to several. But if two persons shared this property, neither would proceed from the other. If neither proceeded from the other, neither would adhere immediately to the other. But if neither adhered immediately to the other, they would be joined to one another only by mediate kinship. The preceding demonstration has established by the clearest reasoning how impossible that is. [Col. 0958D]

Therefore it is the proper and distinctive attribute of one person alone to have no one proceeding from itself. Hence, just as there can be in the Godhead only one person who does not proceed from another, so without ambiguity there can be only one from whom no other proceeds. Therefore this existence, like the former, will be incommunicable and cannot in any way be common to several persons. For one person alone in that plurality of persons so receives and has being from another that no other at all receives or has being from that person. [Col. 0959A]

Thus we have inferred the properties of two persons in the Trinity by reasoning so clear that we cannot doubt them at all, even slightly.

## CHAPTER XIII. That there must be in the Godhead a person who proceeds from another and has one proceeding from itself

From this twofold property of the persons mentioned, we can without any hesitation infer what we ought to think of the property of the one who stands between them. For since there can be only one there who is not from another, it follows that the person now under discussion is not from itself. Again, since there can be only one there who has none proceeding from itself, the person of whom we now speak must have one proceeding from itself. Thus it proceeds from another, while nevertheless another proceeds from it. [Col. 0959B]

Thus, as we said, we know without ambiguity what we ought to think of its property. This testimony undoubtedly accords with the conclusion found by the foregoing discussion. For that person who proceeds from the unbegotten one immediately alone appears—indeed is proved—to have both attributes. For it bestows upon another, without any loss of its integrity, the fullness of being that it receives from the unbegotten person. For the third person in the Trinity proceeds from the begotten and the unbegotten together.

See how reason meets reason, and testimony corresponds to testimony. We find, clearer now than light, three distinctions among three properties: one is not to proceed from another, yet to have one proceeding from itself; another both proceeds from another and has one proceeding from itself; the third proceeds from another, yet has none proceeding from itself. [Col. 0959C] We already know that two of these properties are incommunicable, but we have not yet established by reasoning what must be thought of the third.

## CHAPTER XIV. That in the divine nature there can be only one person who both proceeds from another and has one proceeding from itself

Since we already know by the testimony of reason that two of the stated properties are incommunicable, we are thereby prompted to judge the same concerning the third. But lest this reasoning seem probable rather than necessary, let us investigate the point more deeply. [Col. 0959D]

First, therefore, it must be noted and carefully considered how the twofold property of the two persons stands, as it were, opposite one another, and how one corresponds to the other as by contrast. For one person’s property is not to receive fullness but to give it; the other’s, conversely, is not to give but to receive. But where there is supreme beauty, where no perfection can be lacking, it is clear—and no sound mind can doubt the consequence—that the plurality of divine persons is joined by a wholly fitting beauty and distinguished by a most orderly diversity.

Therefore, in that divine plurality of persons, supremely beautiful and altogether most orderly, there must be a harmony differing mutually in either direction, and a differing harmony. It therefore seems necessary that between the one whose property is to give fullness and not receive it, and the one whose property is to receive and not give it, there should be only one intermediary whose proper and distinctive attribute is both to give and to receive; so that, placed in the middle, it should be joined to one of the outer persons in one respect and connected to the other in another. [Col. 0960A] Thus in giving it will agree with the giver, and in receiving it will agree with the receiver. Conversely, in giving it will differ from the non-giver, and in receiving from the non-receiver; so that, as we said above, there is mutual differing harmony and harmonious difference.

But if two intermediaries are said to exist between the two outer persons, let us see what incongruity follows from this assertion. Certainly the first of them will be from none, the second from one alone, the third from two, and the fourth from three, as we explained above with sufficient care. This arrangement, under this consideration, seems to have something in common with an arithmetic mean. But let us now see how, under another consideration, this fourfold arrangement confounds the form of geometric mean which, as is clear above, the Trinity of persons displays. [Col. 0960B]

Certainly the first person will have as its proper and distinctive causal property only to give fullness; the two intermediate persons will both give and receive; and the fourth will only receive, not also give. Thus the first agrees with the second in only one respect. But the second agrees with the third not in one respect only, but in two. The third, in turn, agrees with the fourth in two respects, but in one alone. You surely see how the duplication and sharing of one property does not so much exhibit as confound the principle of proportionality; it does not increase but diminishes the beauty of order.

But who would say that in that supreme beauty there is, or could have been, anything which diminishes beauty and confounds order? In the earlier arrangement of properties, however, under one consideration an arithmetic mean, under another a geometric mean, and in relation to the conjunction of Trinity and unity a harmonic mean, meet in appearance and correspond to one another by a wonderful principle. [Col. 0960C–D] It is therefore clear from this that it is the proper and distinctive property of one person both to give and to receive fullness, and that this property, like the other two, is incommunicable.

## CHAPTER XV. That there cannot be a fourth person in the divine nature

It is undoubtedly common to all divine persons to possess every fullness. But the distinction of properties turns upon two things: giving and receiving. For, as is clear from what has preceded, one person’s property consists in giving alone, another’s in receiving alone. The intermediate person between them both gives and receives. [Col. 0961A]

But perhaps someone will say: if one property consists in giving alone, another in receiving alone, and the middle property in both giving and receiving, why should there not be a fourth, without giving or receiving, consisting in possessing alone? If we admit this, we seem to confess a quaternity of divine persons. But the reasoning above has untied the knot of this question so clearly that a careful reader, however unlearned, can scarcely remain doubtful about it.

For, as was shown above, manifest reason establishes that only one person in the Godhead can be from itself. Therefore one who does not receive from elsewhere either existence or any power, if it bestowed upon no one what it has, would undoubtedly, as was said elsewhere, remain alone forever. [Col. 0961B] Thus the fourth property is found to have no place in the Godhead, and every suspicion of a quaternity is excluded. It is clear, therefore, that a fourth person cannot exist at all in the divine nature.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the fullness of true love and the distinction of properties considered in relation to it

What was said above in order to remove the suspicion of a quaternity from the divine nature can be confirmed by a still deeper and clearer reasoning. For if we bring into consideration the fullness of true love and carefully attend to the distinction of properties pertaining to that consideration, we may perhaps find more quickly what we seek. [Col. 0961C]

The fullness of true love consists only in love that is supreme and universally perfect. Supreme love is rightly called that love which is so great that no greater can be, and at the same time so good that no better can be. From this one may observe that the fullness of true love cannot be possessed by any person who is not God. Otherwise, if someone besides God could possess the fullness of true love, a person who was not God could be equal to God in charity and therefore in goodness. But who would say this, or presume even faintly to imagine it?

It is clear, moreover, that true love may be either gratuitous alone, or owed alone, or mixed from both: owed in one respect and gratuitous in another. Love is gratuitous when someone willingly gives love to one from whom he receives no gift. Love is owed when someone returns nothing but love to one from whom he receives freely. Love mixed from both is that by which a person, loving in turn, both receives freely and gives freely. [Col. 0961D]

But neither the fullness of gratuitous love nor the fullness of owed love—just as neither the fullness that is perfect in both respects—can in any way be possessed by a person who is not God. Since this is sufficiently clear from what precedes, it requires no added explanation.

## CHAPTER XVII. To which person in the Trinity it belongs to possess the fullness of gratuitous love alone

It is now most evident that one person in the Trinity has nothing except from itself. [Col. 0962A] It receives absolutely nothing from another and possesses nothing at all by another’s gift. Therefore the person who is found to have received nothing from any other, by which it might become obligated or indebted in any respect, evidently cannot possess owed love of the kind described above.

But it shows itself to possess gratuitous love when it freely, willingly, and lavishly bestows upon those proceeding from it the abundance of its fullness. For what can persons proceeding from it claim from it as owed, when they receive from its gift even the owed love which they return to their gratuitous lover? Otherwise they would possess something which they had not received from it. The preceding arguments teach how false that is.

Therefore it has gratuitous love, and gratuitous love alone. [Col. 0962B] It has gratuitous love, I say; and, what is still more, the person who reserves nothing of the fullness it possesses for itself alone but communicates all of it shows that it possesses the fullness of gratuitous love. If it possessed all fullness but, though able, did not wish to communicate it, it would not possess the fullness of gratuitous love. It is therefore proved to have the fullness of love, since it lacks neither will nor power for every effect of benevolence.

## CHAPTER XVIII. To which person in the Trinity it belongs to possess the fullness of owed love

That person whose property is to proceed, yet not to have one proceeding from itself—because it receives from elsewhere all that it has—must possess the fullness of owed love. Otherwise, if it did not return supreme love to those who love it supremely, it would not be worthy of supreme love. It is indeed loved with supreme love by those from whom it is known to have received all fullness. [Col. 0962C]

What love not owed can it return to those from whom it is established to have received all fullness freely? And since, as we have said, it is proper to it not to have one proceeding from itself, there is no one in the Godhead to whom it can display the fullness of gratuitous love. It may indeed have gratuitous love toward a created person, but it cannot possess the fullness of gratuitous love toward a creature, since it cannot have disordered love. For it would be disordered love if it loved with supreme love one who was not supremely worthy of being loved. For one who is not supremely good is in no way worthy of supreme love. But a person who is not God cannot be supremely good, because it cannot be equal to God. [Col. 0962D]

Therefore the person mentioned both can have and does have the fullness of owed love, according to the reasoning given above. But it does not have, nor can it have, the fullness of gratuitous love. Accordingly, the person which, as stated, has none proceeding from itself must possess the fullness of owed love alone.

## CHAPTER XIX. To which person in the Trinity it is proper and distinctive to possess the fullness of both gratuitous and owed love

From what we have said concerning the two persons in the present consideration, it becomes sufficiently clear what we ought to think of the remaining one. Since it is its proper and distinctive attribute both to proceed from another and to have one proceeding from itself, it must abound in both gratuitous and owed love, and display the fullness of each whole and entire: of one love to one person, of the other to the other. [Col. 0963A]

For its love is owed because it loves supremely the one from whom it receives everything and bestows nothing; but it is gratuitous because it loves supremely the one from whom it receives nothing but upon whom it bestows everything. Thus we now hold by clear reasoning how we ought to distinguish the proper characteristics of each under this consideration. For in one of the three there is supreme love and gratuitous love alone; in another, love is supreme in such a manner as to be owed love alone; and in the third, it is supreme in such a manner as to be owed in one respect and wholly gratuitous in another. [Col. 0963B]

Thus there is a threefold distinction of properties in supreme love, although in all there is one and the same love, namely supreme and truly eternal love. From this consideration of true and supreme love, then, we can infer whether a fourth person can have a place in that plurality of divine persons.

## CHAPTER XX. How reason manifestly establishes that a fourth person cannot have a place in the Godhead

The foregoing sufficiently proves and establishes that in the Godhead there can be only one person who is from itself. From this the diligent investigator of truth can also infer by unquestionable reasoning that, in the mutual charity of the persons, there can be no love which is not either gratuitous alone, owed alone, or both owed and gratuitous together. [Col. 0963C]

Likewise, it is clear concerning the three persons mentioned that the fullness of gratuitous love is in one alone; the fullness of owed love is in another alone; and the fullness of both owed and gratuitous love is in the third alone. But what shall we say to this? Is there in any of these three something other than its love? Is being other than loving, or loving other than being, for any of them? Where, then, is that true and supreme simplicity which we sought and found above, and proved by the testimony of many arguments?

Therefore, in supreme simplicity, being and loving must without doubt be one and the same. [Col. 0963D] Hence each of the three is the same as its own love. Thus, there is nothing else in there being several persons in one Godhead than that several possess—or rather are—the one and same supreme love according to differing properties. This person is nothing other than supreme love distinguished by this property; the other person is nothing other than supreme love distinguished by another property; nor is the third person anything other than supreme love distinguished by a third property.

Therefore the number of persons will correspond to the number of properties. Since, then, as we have said, every person is the same as its love, and the distinction assigned to each consists in the three just mentioned, we can no more find a fourth property there than a fourth person. [Col. 0964A]

But lest anyone understand us insufficiently and therefore criticize us rashly because we have used the terms “gratuitous” and “owed,” we are not unaware that they are not always understood in the same sense. We say that one ought to love another because the latter is worthy. We also say that one ought to love another because some gift or benefit has made one indebted. Likewise, “gratuitous” may be taken in different senses in different contexts. But we have specified, by an added definition, the sense in which we wish each term to be understood here, so that no opening may remain for objection.

Let no one be surprised or indignant if we express, as we can, what we think concerning so great a depth by means of such words as we can use. Like the Virgin Mother, bringing forth the truth conceived, I wrap it in the little swaddling-clothes of words, since I am unable to clothe in the silks of polished discourse what I know I do not possess. But where the truth of the judgment is established, nothing remains for the prudent reader except to supply fitting words to true assertions—which I receive with every act of thanksgiving. [Col. 0964B]

Thus we have now explained how reason manifestly establishes, in confirmation of the foregoing argument, that a fourth person cannot have a place in the Godhead.

## CHAPTER XXI. How much may be inferred from the last consideration

If anyone with a mind trained in such matters wishes to dwell carefully on this final consideration, he may perhaps infer and establish by probable argument from this one consideration alone many things discussed above and proved by various demonstrations.

Whoever understands more deeply that God is one recognizes by manifest reason that he is supremely good and supremely blessed. But if such a person doubts the plurality of persons, he may rise from what he already believes to what he has not yet grasped through this contemplation. [Col. 0964C] From this single consideration, I think, he can derive and support by probable proofs the plurality of persons—indeed, the whole Trinity.

This contemplation, as the preceding reasoning teaches, excludes the suspicion of a quaternity. It commends the plurality of persons to those who believe and truly confess true divinity in such a way that it also establishes unity of substance. From this consideration the property of each person becomes clear and comes to manifestation. For when carefully examined, it declares with transparent reasoning that in the Godhead there is a person whose being is not from any other, one which derives its origin from one alone, and another from two. [Col. 0964D]

Let the reader consider how great and useful it is to have ready and familiar the ability to give, from one contemplation, a reason to everyone asking concerning all these matters. But since from what we have already said we have constructed an accessible path toward investigating them, we leave them to more diligent inquirers for fuller examination.

## CHAPTER XXII. That saying the fullness of gratuitous love lies in giving alone and the fullness of owed love in receiving alone must not be understood as though it were a work of grace rather than an operation of nature

What we have said—that one person has, or is, the fullness of gratuitous love, and another the fullness of owed love—must not be taken to mean that one person surpasses another in any respect, or has or is something better or more perfect. There is no difference of rank there, no diversity of dignity. [Col. 0965A]

It is clear that one person’s property is to give fullness without having received it, while another’s is to have received it without giving it. Must we therefore believe one better or worthier than the other? Far be every such suspicion. Such a suspicion has overthrown many and scattered them through various errors.

The one who has received none of what it has from another possesses nothing greater or at all better than the one who has nothing which it did not receive. Whatever perfection, goodness, or blessedness belongs to the one whose property is giving alone, the one whose property is receiving all possesses in the same fullness.

But when it is said that the fullness of gratuitous love is in giving alone and the fullness of owed love in receiving alone, no one should understand this as though, in that undifferentiated equality, it were a work of grace rather than an operation of nature. [Col. 0965B] Yet the depth of so great a mystery is exceedingly profound and can scarcely, or perhaps never, be explained by any human being in suitable words.

Therefore let no one be surprised or indignant if, after the manner of the Virgin Mother, I bring forth the truth conceived and wrap it in the swaddling-clothes of words, since I cannot clothe what I know I do not possess in the silks of cultivated speech. But where the truth of the proposition is established, nothing remains for the prudent reader except to apply fitting words to true assertions—and this I receive with all thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That, as regards the substance of love, love is supreme and one in all, although it is distinguished in each by the differentiation of properties

[Col. 0965C]

True and intimate love has the property of bringing it about, even in persons whose being is different, that they have the same will and the same refusal. How much more will identity of will belong to those persons for whom being is the same as willing, and consequently, as their being is one, so too their willing is one? Therefore, in that Trinity there is for all one will, one charity, one undifferentiated goodness. Accordingly, with respect to the substance of love, there will be one and the same love in all the persons. And since it is one and supreme in all, it cannot be greater in one than in another; it cannot be in one in any way [Col. 0965D] better than in another. Certainly, if the same willing in every respect is present in all, each loves the other as himself, and as much as himself. If each of them loves the other as himself, he wills for every other, as for himself, all that is communicable. If he loves as much as himself, whatever is communicable there he neither desires more ardently for himself than for another, nor more tepidly for another than for himself. Such love, therefore, in one will be of such a kind that none can be better; in another, so great that none can be greater. Thus, as was said, with respect to the substance of love, love will be one and the same in all, though in a wonderful manner distinguished in each according to the differentiation of properties. For, according to the sense which we assigned above, in relation to the one it will be wholly gratuitous, and in the other, [Col. 0966A] in relation to the former, wholly due. In the third it is due in relation to one, and gratuitous in relation to the other. For according to the human manner of speaking, we rightly call that love gratuitous which, receiving nothing, expends everything; but that love due which expends nothing upon the one from whom it has received everything. Let that flood of Divinity and overflowing of highest love, then, be called in one only flowing out and not infused; in another both flowing out and infused; in the third not flowing out but only infused—though it is nevertheless one and the same in all, and in all these statements there is one truth, even if there is a diversity of ways of speaking about it.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That with respect to the wholeness of perfection there is no difference of love or dignity in the Trinity.

Meanwhile, perhaps someone, thinking something human [Col. 0966B] about the divine persons, regards as of greater dignity and judges superior to the rest that person which has from itself all that it is known to possess. But far be it that any disparity of dignities should be believed to exist there where truly and without doubt there is supreme equality. Yet one who does not yet grasp this by understanding has a means of restraining his thought by another consideration. It must therefore be known, as I have already said above, that whatever is communicable to all, there each person loves it for another as much as for itself; conversely, whatever belongs to a property and is incommunicable, each loves it more for itself than for another. For every person, from that which is common to all, has being as the same substance as the others; from that which is its own property and incommunicable [Col. 0966C], it has being as a singular person distinct from the others.

If, then, each person loved what belongs to its own property more for another than for itself, and what belongs to another’s property more for itself than for the other, what else would this be, or what else could it appear to be, than not to wish to be the person which it is and to wish to be the person which it is not? But I think that no one is so mad as to dare to suppose this or to be able patiently to hear it. That person, indeed, whose property is what you regard as a prerogative of dignity, without any ambiguity wills it more for itself than for the others; and the others, without any contradiction, will it more for that person than for themselves. What then? Are those to be judged greater in kindness who prefer to another person rather than to their own that which you think an excellence of pre-eminence [Col. 0966D], than the one who prefers it to its own person rather than to any other? But if they are rightly judged kinder, why are they not, for that very reason, also more worthy?

Perhaps you still say that it is much more glorious to possess fullness and give it than merely to possess it and give it to no one. Behold again: as it seems to you, if we judge according to human standards, we find in two persons a certain prerogative of glory. Yet again, because the third person in the Trinity, according to the reasoning already given, prefers this supposed prerogative to the others rather than to itself, whereas the others prefer it to themselves rather than to that person, will that person therefore be called kinder than the rest, and consequently more glorious? Behold, while we proceed according to human judgments, every divine [Col. 0967A] person is found to be more and less kind, more and less worthy, than another. Behold a false opinion found contrary to itself. We must therefore cast these phantasies out of our hearts and believe firmly, without reservation, what we are not yet able to grasp by understanding. Certainly and without any ambiguity, with respect to the wholeness of perfection, there is no difference of love or dignity in the Trinity.

## CHAPTER XXV. What things are common to which persons, what belongs properly to each, and what still remains to be sought concerning them.

Now, then, if you please, let us briefly gather together what we have set forth by reasoning in this book. It is common to all the divine persons to possess all fullness [Col. 0967B]. It is common to two alone to give all fullness. It is common to two alone to have received all fullness. It is common to two alone not to have both of these. For it is the property of one to be only in giving; the property of another to be only in receiving; and the property of the third to be both in receiving and in giving. It is common to two alone to have a person proceeding from themselves. It is common to two alone [Col. 0968A] to proceed from another. It is common to two alone not to have both. It is the property of one not merely to have a person proceeding from itself; it is the property of another merely to proceed; while the property of the third is both to proceed from another and to have one proceeding from itself. It is proper to one person alone to proceed from none; proper to another alone to proceed from one alone; proper to the third alone to proceed from two. For there is one alone from whom none proceeds; one alone from whom one alone proceeds; and likewise one alone from whom two proceed.

Since, therefore, it is common to two persons not to be from themselves but to proceed from another, it remains to inquire with the utmost diligence wherein the procession of the one differs from the procession of the other. Once the difference in their mutual relation has been found, it is finally necessary, by reason of the similarity, to assign a proper name. I had indeed proposed to state publicly what I thought concerning these matters; but because in them there is a lofty profundity, it will be better to leave them for loftier minds to examine more deeply, and to learn from the judgment of others what gratitude or ingratitude I deserve for what has already been said.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0967]

## CHAPTER I. That in true divinity nothing exists by the gift of bestowing grace, but everything by the endowment and property of nature.

[Col. 0967C]

As was said, it is established that it is common to two persons alone not to be from themselves but to proceed from another. In this there still seems to remain for inquiry whether the mode of proceeding is the same in the one as in the other, or rather one in this person and another in that. The subject is quite small, but very profound and most worthy of careful investigation. Yet I think that from what has already been said there shines forth, not faintly, something that can greatly avail for resolving this difficulty.
