But since, according to the Apostle, “the invisible things of God are understood and perceived through the things that have been made” [Col. 0967D] (Rom. VIII), where some profound matter concerning divine things is sought, one rightly has recourse to that nature in which, God working, the image of God appears to be depicted. It is most well known that man was made in the image and likeness of God. And although the ground of dissimilarity is incomparably more abundant than that of similarity, there is nevertheless some—indeed much—likeness of human nature to the divine. We may therefore, I believe, behold in this mirror of the divine image, and even discern by the judgment of a reasoning mind, what there is there to approve on the ground of likeness or disapprove on the ground of unlikeness.

We find, then, that in human persons the production of person from person is not everywhere uniform. For if we return to the origin of our propagation [Col. 0968C], we see in the first-formed man himself that the production of his wife was one thing, while the production of his offspring was another, far different indeed. The former was above nature; the latter according to nature. The former was according only to the operation of creative grace; the latter according to the operation of nature. But in the divine nature nothing is, or can be, from grace as operative cause. For what is from the operation of grace alone can, according to the good pleasure of its author, be or not be. But nothing of that kind can exist in Divinity itself. Otherwise mutability would belong to it, and it would not possess true eternity. Therefore nothing exists there by the gift of bestowing grace, but everything by the property required by nature. For just as it is natural to the unbegotten not to proceed from another, so it is certainly natural to it to have one proceeding from itself [Col. 0968D].

## CHAPTER II. That the kinship between parent and offspring appears to exist altogether between the unbegotten and the person principally proceeding from it.

We must therefore examine carefully the natural order of proceeding among human beings, and inquire with every acuteness what it has in itself similar to the divine. Once this is found and known, we must, according to the custom of theological teaching, transfer from human matters to divine matters the names of properties on the ground of similarity. In human nature, then, we see, as we have already said above, that the production or procession of person from person is in one case only immediate, in another only mediate, and in another both mediate and immediate [Col. 0969A]. Immediate procession is that of offspring from either parent, which occurs with no other person intervening. Mediate procession is what we see only in the grandson of some man, which occurs only through the intervention of his offspring. There is both mediate and immediate procession where it happens that one and the same man is someone’s son and grandson.

In human nature mediate procession is multiple and manifold; in the divine nature it cannot exist at all. According to the varying order of proceeding and mode of relationship, the degrees and names of kinship vary and multiply in human nature. For the kinship which a man has to his son is one thing, and that which he has to his grandson another. What I say concerning these may be understood also of the others. Yet amid so great a multitude of kinships, the first and principal place belongs to that kinship which is between parent and offspring. For unless it had come first in human nature, none of all the rest could have existed at all; and even if none of all the rest existed, this one nevertheless could undoubtedly exist. Where it happens that one and the same person has many children, they are all indeed called the same thing on one and the same ground. And if it happens that one and the same man is both grandson and son of the same person, he is called both, though not on the same but on very different grounds [Col. 0969B].

It should be noted, however, that Eve was immediately produced from Adam’s substance, but not, as we have already said above, according to the operation of nature [Col. 0969C]. Hence she is not called his offspring, nor is he called her parent. But where one person is produced from the substance of another in the principal order of proceeding and according to the operation of nature, we customarily and without doubt call one of those persons parent and the other offspring. Since, therefore, according to the custom of the divine Scriptures, we transfer names of human kinship to divine things on the ground of similarity, we may not inappropriately say that the kinship between the unbegotten and the person principally proceeding from it is that which exists between parent and offspring. For that procession of person from person is wholly immediate, and follows the principal order of proceeding and the operation of nature. Since this is sufficiently clear from what precedes, it needs no fuller exposition [Col. 0969D].

## CHAPTER III. That the mode of producing offspring differs according to the diversity of nature.

That the mode of producing offspring differs according to the diversity of nature, I think no one can doubt. But if we wish to know what that singular mode of production is in that pre-eminent and surpassingly excellent nature of Deity, let us consider the goodness, wisdom, and power of the unbegotten, and perhaps we shall quickly find what we seek. Certainly, one in whom supremely wise goodness exists can will nothing at all, especially concerning divine things, except for an inward and supreme reason, so to speak [Col. 0970A]. And if it is certainly true that he is omnipotent, whatever he wills to exist there will exist according to his will. For if by willing alone he cannot obtain what he wills, how, I ask, can he truthfully be called omnipotent? Therefore, reason requiring it, he will immovably will to produce from himself one consubstantial and conformed to himself. This will undoubtedly be, for him, to produce offspring: in this very thing to be wholly pleased with himself.

## CHAPTER IV. That usage appropriately prevailed that, in that Trinity, one of the two should be called Father and the other Son.

It should be observed that in human nature sex is twofold, and therefore the names of kinship vary according to the different sex: in one sex we call a parent father; in the other, mother [Col. 0970B]. In one sex we call offspring son; in the other, daughter. But in the divine nature, as we commonly know, there is no sex at all. It was therefore fitting that names should be transferred from the sex recognized as more worthy to that which is most worthy of all. You see, then, how appropriately usage has prevailed that one of the two in the Trinity is called Father and the other Son.

But lest anything should remain undiscussed by us which might justly trouble a weak hearer, let us examine more carefully this very point which we have made about the transfer of names. Someone may perhaps wonder why names are transferred to divine things from the case in which the ground of similarity is present, rather than from that in which the comparison of relations agrees in some respect. For human nature does not admit that a Son proceeds from the Father alone according to the operation of nature. Only one man in the human race proceeded from a mother alone without a carnal father, but not without the operation of nature [Col. 0970C]. If, therefore, it is unfitting to transfer terms of kinship to divine things solely in the respect in which some ground of similarity is suggested, how will it be fitting to transfer them from a case in which no correspondence of proportion occurs?

First, then, we should note that, if it is rightly said in that Deity that the Son proceeds from one alone, and that he from whom the Son alone and uniquely derives his origin is rightly called Father, we are admonished by these terms that the principal kinship there is undoubtedly such as can in no way exist here in our nature. By these terms, I say, the carnal mind is compelled to entertain nothing carnal concerning the divine generation, but to rise in heart to a higher understanding and to judge nothing rashly according to human standards concerning a mystery of such depth [Col. 0970D].

## CHAPTER V. How we hold by certain and manifest reasoning why we call one Father and the other his Son.

But if we return to that which we have already established by indubitable reasoning, we can draw from it what suffices to resolve this difficulty. We sought and found that it belongs to the unbegotten to produce offspring from itself, reason requiring it to will this very thing [Col. 0971A]. Doubtless, if that first-formed Adam had it naturally that, according to his will, he could produce from himself alone one consubstantial with and in every respect conformed to himself, they would nevertheless be joined by the principal kinship, and he would rightly be called father and the other son by the same names of kinship. For if they were wholly conformed, they would not differ even in sex. You see, then, how from this consideration a manifest reason arises and clearly shows how fittingly, in that Trinity of persons, one of the two is called Father in relation to the other, and the other is called Son in relation to that same one.

Behold how, in the depth of so great a mystery, in the likeness-image of divinity and the consideration of our weakness, there shines forth neither unlikeness without likeness nor likeness without unlikeness [Col. 0971B]. The unlikeness is undoubtedly that, in our nature, a son cannot proceed from the father alone. The likeness is that, if this could have been and had occurred, the same names of kinship would belong to each in a similar kinship. Thus, I think, we now hold by certain and manifest reasoning why we call one Father and the other his Son: Father, indeed, him who is from none; but Son, his who is from him alone.

## CHAPTER VI. Since it is common to the other two to proceed from the Father, what is the difference between the procession of the one and that of the other?

[Col. 0971C]

We now have the kinship of one person to another; it remains to ask what ought to be thought concerning the kinship of both to the third. Someone may perhaps suppose that the one who proceeds immediately from both may rightly be called their son. But if he is the son of the Son, will not the unbegotten be both his father and grandfather, and will that unbegotten be both his grandson and son? These matters must be investigated with so much the greater diligence because they are more hidden and have not yet been examined by a resolution of reasoning. Yet it is now entirely certain that it is common to the other two persons to proceed from the unbegotten person. We must therefore first inquire, according to the intention of the producer, what is the difference between the procession of the one and that of the other.

For although each proceeds from the paternal will [Col. 0971D], the cause in this twofold procession may nevertheless be different. But if we retain in mind what we discovered above by reasoning, perhaps we need not labor long or much over this argument. For manifest reason there clearly apprehended that the unbegotten willed to have one worthy in equal measure with himself, and had to have such according to his will, so that there might be one upon whom he could bestow supreme love and who might return supreme love to him. Nor did he will merely to have one worthy in equal measure, but also one beloved together with him; and he had to have such according to his will, so that he might have a companion in love and reserve nothing for himself alone which could be brought into common possession. Therefore he willed to have one worthy in equal measure, so that there might be one to whom he might communicate the riches of his greatness; but one beloved together with him, so that he might have one to whom he might communicate the delights of charity [Col. 0972A]. Communion of majesty was, so to speak, the original cause of the one; communion of love appears to have been a kind of original cause of the other. Therefore, although the production of each person proceeds, as we have said, from the paternal will, there is nevertheless in this twofold production or procession a different rationale, a different and distinct cause.

## CHAPTER VII. That the kinship which the unbegotten has to one is different from that which it has to the other.

There is in every way a great difference between willing to have one worthy in equal measure and willing to have one beloved together with oneself. Let us now see which of these is prior and which subsequent. By “prior” and “subsequent” here we mean not a succession of times but an order of nature [Col. 0972B]. What is it to will to have one worthy in equal measure, except to will to have one whom he loves intimately and whom, by reason of coequality, he ought worthily to love? But what is it to will to have one beloved together with him, except to will to have one who is loved together with him by his beloved and who enjoys with him the delights of the love bestowed upon him?

But the former can exist in a duality of persons alone. The latter cannot subsist at all without a Trinity of persons. Yet with respect to the order of nature, duality is prior to Trinity. For where there is Trinity, duality cannot be absent; but duality can exist even where Trinity happens to be absent. It is therefore established that, by nature, having a beloved is prior to having one beloved together with oneself. Accordingly, in the order of nature that procession is more principal in which there is a more principal cause of proceeding. But we know that according to the order of procession, without doubt, will also be the order of kinship.

Certainly, in human nature the kinship of a man to his son holds the first place; that of a man to his grandson the second; that which any man has to his great-grandson holds the third place; and so one may observe the same in those following [Col. 0972C]. What produces these differing degrees of kinship in our nature except a different mode of proceeding in different cases? For where there is no manifoldness of proceeding among several, there is no diversity in kinship. It may happen that one and the same man has several children, but because the mode of proceeding is the same, the kinship which he has to all of them is one. Thus, certainly, according to a similar or dissimilar mode of procession, the character of kinship also undoubtedly varies. But it is now clearer than light that each of the two proceeds from the Father. Yet the mode of proceeding is one in the one and another in the other. Therefore the kinship which the unbegotten has to the one must be different from that which it has to the other [Col. 0972D].

## CHAPTER VIII. That he who proceeds from the Father and the Son cannot rightly be called their son.

The procession of that one who is known to proceed from the unbegotten alone is principal according to the mode of nature [Col. 0973A]. But where there is principal procession, there is also principal kinship. The kinship between father and son occupies the principal place. Therefore, as we have already said above, he is rightly called his son who is shown to proceed principally from the unbegotten. But if the kinship which the unbegotten has to one is different from that which, as we have proved, it has to the other, and if one of them is truly called his son, the other cannot truly be called his son. For what does it mean to say that one is another’s son except that he is joined to him by principal kinship? But he who is the third person in the Trinity is not joined to the unbegotten by principal kinship, as we have proved; hence he cannot rightly be called his son.

But we know, as we have sufficiently proved above, that the third in the Trinity proceeds from the other two [Col. 0973B]. Therefore, if he is not the son of the one, neither will he be the son of the other. For he proceeds in altogether one and the same way from Father and Son alike; indeed, in both cases the rationale is one and the same in every respect. But since this is sufficiently evident from what precedes, it is unnecessary to explain the same things again. But if he is not the Son’s son, neither will the Father of the Son be his grandfather, nor will he be that Father’s grandson. Yet between the kinship of father to son and that of the same person to his grandson, no intermediate kinship occurs in human nature. What kinship, then, I ask, will that be which Father and Son have to the person who is third in the Trinity?

Certainly, in human nature every principal procession of person from person is immediate; but, as is now most evident, it happens otherwise in the divine nature [Col. 0973C]. For there you find one procession which is immediate and principal, and another which is immediate yet not principal. Since, therefore, that which is immediate but not principal does not exist at all in human nature, a term for such kinship cannot be transferred from human to divine things. You see plainly that ordinary language is wholly inadequate to express the kinship of Father and Son to the person who proceeds from both.

## CHAPTER IX. On what ground the Spirit of God is so called, who proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Since, therefore, a term of kinship could not be fitted according to our customary usage, it was not altogether without a ground of similarity that he is called in the divine Scriptures the Spirit of God or the Holy Spirit [Col. 0973D]. That which proceeds from a human being and without which a human being does not live at all is called spirit. But if the one of whom we speak is asserted to be called the Spirit of God on account of this likeness, such a designation may seem altogether strange in relation to him to some learned person. For the spirit which proceeds from a human being is certainly not consubstantial with the human being himself; but the Spirit of God is certainly consubstantial with him from whom he proceeds and altogether equal in every respect.

What wonder, however, if he is called the breath of Father and Son by reason of similarity, when he is called the finger of God in the divine Scriptures? In being called God’s finger, no inequality is indicated; rather, the expression refers to a certain likeness of his property [Col. 0974A]. We point with a finger when we wish to show something to someone’s eyes. Therefore, when God reveals to someone inner and hidden matters of his wisdom through the illumination of his Spirit, what else does he do than show with his finger what he wishes to be seen? For Father and Son, one and the same God in every respect, teach us concerning all things by the inspiration of their Spirit. Did not the teacher of truth teach, as by a likeness, that the Holy Spirit is a divine breath, when, appearing to the disciples, he breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20)?

As we said above, spirit proceeds from a human being, and without it a human being does not live at all. Therefore, in the fact that the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of God, an eternal procession from him who is eternal is denoted [Col. 0974B]. Indeed, in the very fact that he has an eternal procession from God, it is thereby given to understand that he is consubstantial with God: for that which proceeds from God and possesses eternity cannot fail to be God. How, however, a certain singular property of his is expressed in his being called God’s breath, or exhalation, or Spirit of God, will be explained more suitably in what follows.

## CHAPTER X. On what ground he who proceeds from two is called the Holy Spirit.

It calls us to a deeper understanding, and is not devoid of great mystery, that he who proceeds from two, as we have said, is called the Holy Spirit. For the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, as we have learned from the Gospel: “God is spirit.” Likewise, the Father is holy and the Son is undoubtedly holy; and either term can truthfully be said of either [Col. 0974C]. How, then, does he alone receive as though a proper name what belongs to both on an equal ground? Yet the appropriation of such a designation seems altogether without any rationale for expressing any property.

But if the spirit which proceeds from a human body and is corporeal has something similar to a divine property, why much more does not the spirit which proceeds from a human spirit and is spiritual? What is that spirit which breathes more gently from some human hearts, more vehemently from others; which burns more lukewarmly in these, more ardently in those, except the inward affection of the soul and the impulse of fervent love [Col. 0974D]? Hence those are said to have one spirit and to walk in one spirit who have one counsel and the same purpose, who love the same things, seek the same things, and desire with an equal wish.

But this spiritual spirit is truly holy, and can truly be called holy, when it is impelled by piety and moved according to truth. Without this spirit no spirit is holy, neither human spirit nor angelic spirit. For a human spirit undoubtedly begins to be holy when it loves what belongs to piety and detests and hates what belongs to impiety: this, indeed, is the affection of piety. When this spirit breathes, it makes one heart and one soul out of many hearts in many persons. Therefore, in likeness to this spirit which proceeds and breathes from the hearts of many, that Spirit who proceeds from two in the Trinity of persons is called the Holy Spirit [Col. 0975A]. For who, unless led by utter madness, would doubt that in Father and Son there is the same affection of piety, and love truly the same and one? This love, then, common to both, is called the Holy Spirit. This is he whom Father and Son inspire into holy hearts, and through whom they are sanctified so that they may deserve to be holy. As the human spirit is the life of bodies, so this divine Spirit is the life of spirits. The former is life that gives sensation; the latter, life that sanctifies. Therefore he is rightly called the Holy Spirit, without whom no spirit becomes holy. Thus he has a name from the thing itself; he has a name by reason of similarity.

## CHAPTER XI. On what ground the Son of God alone is called the image of the Father.

[Col. 0975B]

This name, then—Holy Spirit—is attributed to one alone as though proper to him, although by reason of substance it appears common to all. It should be noted that there are certain names of properties which can, on no ground, belong except to one person alone. Hence one alone is called Father, and one alone is called Son, as we have already sufficiently shown above. Hence the Son of God alone is called the image of the Father; hence likewise he alone is termed the Word.

Catholic faith confesses, and manifold reasoning attests, that as the Father is, so are the Son and the Holy Spirit. Undoubtedly each is like the Father, each is in every respect coequal with the Father. If you consider wisdom, power, goodness, or blessedness, you will find, with every ambiguity removed, nothing greater in one or less in the other [Col. 0975C]. If, therefore, the Son of God is rightly called the image of the Father because of the likeness expressed in him, why should not the Holy Spirit likewise rightly be called the image of the Father, since each is found alike and coequal? But, I think, we shall quickly untie the knot of this question if we return to consideration of the properties.

It is common to all, as we have already said above, to possess all fullness. It is common to Father and Son both to possess and to give; but it is proper to the Holy Spirit to possess and to give to no one. Therefore the Son alone has in himself an expressed likeness of the Father and bears his image, because, as the fullness of Divinity flows from the one, so the same bestowal of fullness flows from the other [Col. 0975D]. Nor does the Holy Spirit receive anything less, or in any different manner, from the one than from the other. But no person at all receives fullness of divinity from the Holy Spirit; and therefore he does not express in himself the image of the Father. Thus you have why the Son alone, and not also the Holy Spirit, is called the image of the Father.

But let us state what we have said more plainly still, or, if I may say so, more crudely, for the simpler-minded. According to human usage, an image is more commonly so called because of external than because of internal likeness. Thus we call a statue an image of a human being, and this is certainly only because of external likeness [Col. 0976A]. For if you consider the interior of the statue, you will find not so much likeness as unlikeness. Therefore, that we may say something concerning that Trinity of persons according to the human mode: what each person has in itself is, as it were, inward; but the relation it has to another is, as it were, outward.

But the relation which the Father has to the Holy Spirit, the Son is known to have as well. Therefore, because the Son appears to display the Father’s relation in the bestowal of his fullness, the Son alone is rightly called the image of the Father. For the Holy Spirit is called the image neither of the Father nor of the Son, because in the relation mentioned he resembles neither. Behold, in so deep a mystery, where we cannot see clearly, we grope by touching upon likenesses [Col. 0976B]. Nor should this be passed over: perhaps the Holy Spirit is not without reason so called in order thereby to oppose a false opinion, lest anyone, because of his aforementioned property, seem to think too poorly of his kindness.

## CHAPTER XII. On what ground the Son of God alone is called the Word.

Likewise, if it is asked why the Son of God alone is called the Word, this too seems to be derived from a consideration of the properties. Let us say, then, that the word of one who utters it is ordinarily an indication of the understanding and wisdom of the one from whom it is uttered. Thus he through whom knowledge of the Father—who is the fountain of wisdom—is made manifest is rightly called the Word. But perhaps in reply you say: the name of the Father is made manifest not only through the Son but also through the Holy Spirit, since the Holy Spirit himself is that anointing which teaches us concerning all things; he himself teaches and suggests all things to us and leads us into all truth. If the Son is called the Word on this account, why should the Holy Spirit not likewise also be called the word?

Let us add, therefore, that a word is born from the heart alone, and by it the intention of the speaker is disclosed. Hence the sole offspring of the Father alone is rightly called the Word, through whom the Father himself, who is wisdom in the primary sense, is made manifest. Accordingly, the designation Word seems, on the ground of similarity, to belong to the Son alone. But perhaps you still say again that the word of the heart seems to be one thing, and the word of the mouth another: the former arises from the heart, whereas the latter is uttered by the mouth. The former lies hidden within; through the latter knowledge of the heart is ordinarily made plain. Neither of them possesses both of the properties mentioned, but one appears to possess one and the other the other. But I say that, if you consider more subtly, you will find that the word conceived in the heart and that uttered by the voice are the same word. For what is the voice except the vehicle of the word—or, if you prefer, the word’s garment? Is a man clothed one person, and another person when he has been unclothed? I ask: could you have uttered by your mouth the word which you utter, unless you had first had that very word in your heart through thought? And when the uttered word has been understood by the hearer, does not that same word begin to be in his heart which was previously in yours? If he had an ear for the speech of the heart as he has for the speech of the mouth, he would have no need at all for an external utterance to be made to him. From these things, I think, you plainly understand that the word of the mouth is the same as the word of the heart; but in the heart it is without voice, whereas in the mouth it is with voice.

Without doubt, one and the same truth is conceived in the heart, uttered in a word, and learned by hearing. The word has its being from the heart alone; hearing, however, from both. Since, then, the word proceeds from the heart alone, and through it the discernment of the heart becomes known, the Son of God is rightly, by analogy, called the Word of the Father, through whom the Father’s brightness is made manifest. In the Father is every conception of truth; in his Word, every utterance of truth; in the Holy Spirit, every hearing of truth—according to what is read in the Gospel concerning him: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever things he hears, he will speak” (John 16). [Col. 0977B] Therefore the Father cannot be called the Word, for he is not from anyone; nor can the Holy Spirit, for he is not from one alone. But the Son alone can be so called, for he is from one alone, from whom every manifestation of truth flows forth.

Of this Word you have in the Psalm: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Psalm 44 [Vulgate; Psalm 45]). In this Word the Father speaks to the Holy Spirit. In this Word he speaks to created spirit, angelic and human. Speech, however, according to what was said above, is one kind inward and another outward. The inward is that which the Holy Spirit alone receives; the outward is that which a created spirit receives. And just as inward speech takes place in us without the cooperation of human breath, whereas outward speech does not take place at all unless breath cooperates, so too, certainly, in that supremely exalted nature the inward speech is effected with the Father alone as its author. For the Father alone speaks; the Holy Spirit alone hears. [Col. 0977C] But the outward speech is carried out with the cooperation also of the divine breath, that is, the Holy Spirit. Hence this same Spirit is called now *flamen* (“breath”), now *spiramen* (“breathing” or “breath”), now the Spirit of God, through whom the Word of God is breathed into angelic spirits and human spirits. Thus you have what we set forth above: why only one in the Trinity is called the Spirit of God; and likewise why the Son alone is called the Word of God.

## CHAPTER XIII. According to a certain mode of glorifying, the Son is not alone in glorifying his Father; and for this reason he is not without cause called his Word.

Behold, while we labor to solve one question, we incidentally encounter another. [Col. 0977D] We have said that the Son of God is called the Word because he speaks the Father’s brightness, and manifests through himself what and how great the Father is. But as the Son glorifies his Father (John 17), does not the Father too glorify his Son by his revelation, according to what the Son himself says to Peter: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16)? But consider whether perhaps the Son glorifies his Father according to a certain mode of glorifying according to which, nevertheless, the Father does not glorify his Son. For the Son is from his Father, whereas the Father is not from the Son. Thus there appears in the Son how great is the glory of the Father’s property, since he both willed and was able to have a Son such as this, equal to himself in all things.

[Col. 0978A] How great was the kindness, sweetness, and benevolence in that, from the riches of his greatness, he reserved nothing for himself alone and willed to have nothing that he did not communicate to him. Here you have a certain unique mode of glorifying, according to which the Son glorifies his Father. But perhaps you object to this and say that the Father is glorified in the same way also by the Holy Spirit. For just as he willed the Son to coexist with him, so that he might have someone to whom to communicate the riches of his greatness, so he also willed the Holy Spirit to adhere to him, so that he might have someone to whom to communicate the delights of his love. Both declare the Father’s glory; in both the Father’s property is made clear.

But observe that the aforesaid glorification of the Father’s property, which the Father has in the Son, is not shared by him [Col. 0978B] with anyone, since the Son is from the Father alone. But the glorification which shines forth in the Holy Spirit is not a declaration of fatherhood, nor does it belong to the Father alone; rather, he shares it with his Son. For the Holy Spirit is not from the Father alone, but in precisely equal fashion from both Father and Son. Therefore the Son is rightly called the Father’s Word or tongue, since in him alone, according to the mode described above, the glory of fatherhood is made manifest.

## CHAPTER XIV. Why the Holy Spirit is called the gift of God, and whence, or how, he can be sent or given.

It seems worthy of careful consideration on what ground the Holy Spirit is called the gift of God. As we showed above in a clear explanation, in the Father is the fullness of gratuitous love; in the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0978C] the fullness of owed love; in the Son, the fullness of love both owed and gratuitous. I have there explained carefully enough how all these things ought to be understood. But in that supremely simple nature, where no composition can exist, the Holy Spirit himself is certainly not one thing and his love another. What, then, is the giving or sending of the Holy Spirit except the infusion of owed love? The Holy Spirit, therefore, is given to a human being by God when love owed to the Godhead is breathed into the human mind. For when this Spirit enters a rational spirit, he kindles its affection with divine ardor and transforms it into the likeness of his own property, so that it may render to its author the love which it owes.

For what is the Holy Spirit [Col. 0978D] except divine fire? Every love is fire, but spiritual fire. What bodily fire does to iron, this fire of which we speak does to the foul, cold, and hard heart. For when this fire is imparted, the human soul gradually puts off every blackness, coldness, and hardness, and passes wholly into the likeness of him by whom it is kindled. For through the kindling of divine fire it glows, burns wholly, and likewise melts away into love of God, according to that saying of the Apostle: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Romans 5).

But why, I ask, is it said “through the Holy Spirit” rather than through the Father and the Son? We know that the Father has no author or giver, and therefore can possess only gratuitous love. [Col. 0979A] The Son, however, as was said above, possesses both gratuitous and owed love. Thus in divine love we cannot be conformed to the property of the Son or to that of the Father, since we cannot have toward God both kinds of love at once, or even gratuitous love alone. For in what respect, I ask, can a creature love its Creator gratuitously, from whom it has everything that it has? Therefore, insofar as we render owed love to our author, we are certainly conformed to the property of the Holy Spirit. For this purpose he is given to a human being; for this purpose he is breathed into that person: that the person may be conformed to him as far as possible.

This gift is sent—or this sending is given—at once and equally by both the Father and the Son. For the Holy Spirit has from both everything that he has. Therefore, if he has from both his being, power, and will, they are rightly said to send or give him, from whom he has received the ability and the will to come and to dwell in us. [Col. 0979B]

## CHAPTER XV. Why, in a particular manner of speaking, power is attributed to the Unbegotten, wisdom to the Begotten, and goodness to the Holy Spirit.

I am pleased here to repeat what I recall having written elsewhere: why, in a particular manner of speaking, power is attributed to the Unbegotten, wisdom to the Begotten, and goodness to the Holy Spirit. What power, wisdom, goodness, or love is, we all know in a general way and have tested by daily experience. Thus, through things that are manifest and known to us, we are instructed, unless I am mistaken, toward knowledge of those things that exceed the measure of human capacity. For in these three a certain form and image of the supreme Trinity is expressed. A kind of mirror is set before us, so that “the invisible things of God may be discerned, being understood through the things that have been made” (Romans 1).

The things, then, which are in this trinity correspond to those which are in that Trinity: three to three, like to like, properties to properties, each to each. We see that manifold power can exist even where there is no wisdom, and where wisdom cannot exist. I pass over the elements and any inanimate things. Even among animate and brute beings there is the power of hearing, seeing, walking, eating, drinking, and other such powers. Yet in these there is no wisdom, nor can any naturally inhere in them. It is therefore established, as was said above, [Col. 0979D] that manifold power can exist where no wisdom can exist.

Conversely, where there is no power, no wisdom can inhere. For being able to be wise is unquestionably a kind of ability. Therefore it is not wisdom that gives ability to power, but power that gives ability to wisdom. Again, it is evident that Lucifer, who rose in the morning, possesses much power and much wisdom, but absolutely no good will. Goodness, however, is willing well; for what is goodness except good will? Thus that Lucifer, hardened in his perversity, testifies that manifold power and multifarious wisdom can exist where no traces of goodness remain. Conversely, no goodness can exist where wisdom or power is wholly lacking. For to be able [Col. 0980A] to will well is a kind of ability. And it belongs to wisdom to discern between good and evil; without such discernment the will does not know what it ought to choose.

Therefore, in order to possess goodness, you must know and be able to choose the good: power gives the capacity; wisdom gives the knowledge; without these goodness does not come into being. True goodness therefore derives its being both from wisdom and from power. In this trinity of things, power alone is not from either of the others; wisdom, however, is from power alone; goodness is from power together with wisdom. You plainly see how, in this trinity of things, the properties of that supreme and eternal Trinity are expressed. There is there the person of the Unbegotten, who is not from another; there is the person of the Begotten, who is from the Unbegotten alone; there is the person of the Holy Spirit, who is from both the Unbegotten and the Begotten.

Since, therefore, the property of the Unbegotten is expressed in power, power is deservedly ascribed to him in a particular mode of consideration. But since the property of the Begotten is expressed in wisdom, wisdom too is deservedly ascribed to him in the same manner. Again, because the property of the Holy Spirit is found in goodness, goodness is deservedly assigned to him as a special attribute. Thus from this trinity of things arises the reflection by which it is shown through an example how what is read concerning the divine properties can be understood. [Col. 0980B]

## CHAPTER XVI. Why the Father is called unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither unbegotten nor begotten.

Why the Father is called unbegotten and the Son [Col. 0980C] begotten is very easy to see and requires no laborious explanation. The Father alone is from no other, and for that reason can in no way be called begotten. For if he were begotten, he would have received from another that which he is. He therefore rightly received the name Unbegotten, since he did not have his origin from any other. But if he had not begotten a Son, he could not at all have been called Father. That he had the Son from eternity has already become clear from what was said above. The Son, therefore, whom he had from eternity, was begotten from eternity and rightly is said to have received being from eternity. Thus he is called begotten—not merely begotten, but also only-begotten. For in the Trinity there is but one Son.

For the kinship which the Father has to the Son is not possessed by either the Father or the Son [Col. 0980D] with respect to the Holy Spirit. In human nature, where one person is begotten from another person, the one is called father and the other son. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is rightly not called begotten, lest one who is not the Son be thought to be a Son. Yet he is not called unbegotten either, lest it thereby be denied that he who is not from himself has his origin from elsewhere.

For we take the term “begotten” sometimes more strictly and sometimes more broadly. We do not, in ordinary speech, give the same kinship names to all things which we call generators or generated. When a human being begets a human being, customary speech calls the one parent and the other offspring; the one father and the other son; the one begetter and the other begotten. A tree is said to produce a branch, yet the tree is not called the branch’s parent, nor the branch its offspring. A branch produces a flower, yet the former is not customarily called father and the latter son. A worm is produced from a fruit, yet the former is not called its begetter nor the latter its begotten. [Col. 0981A] Thus we call the worm “begotten” in one sense and deny that it is begotten in another sense.

When generation is taken broadly, it seems to be nothing other than the production of an existing thing from an existing thing through the operation of nature. But production not effected through nature’s operation cannot, in ordinary usage, be called generation. Eve was not produced from Adam through nature’s operation, and therefore is not called generated. Some natural production admits the aforesaid names of kinship; some, as we have said, does not admit them at all. Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit is unquestionably not such as ought to be called Son, he is rightly not called begotten. But because his procession is a production according to nature, he ought not to be called unbegotten. Thus, as we have said, he is reasonably not called begotten, lest one who is not the Son should be believed to be a Son; nevertheless, he is reasonably not called unbegotten, lest it be denied that he has a natural origin. [Col. 0981B]

## CHAPTER XVII. What it is for the Father to beget; for the Son to be born from the Father; to proceed by generation; and to proceed without generation.

So far as human nature is concerned, to produce from oneself one consubstantial with oneself seems to be the same as begetting offspring or generating a son. But in the divine nature, if it is rightly weighed, the matter is found to be very different. For the Father produces from himself both the Son and the Holy Spirit, and each exists as consubstantial with him. Yet both cannot be called his Son, because the production of each is not uniform. For if both were uniform, one would not be prior to the other according to the order of nature. That one is prior to the other has been established by the foregoing argument.

We know that in the propagation of human persons there are diverse modes according to the different degrees of kinship, as we said above. For there is one mode by which a son proceeds from his father, another by which a grandson proceeds from a grandfather, and another by which a great-grandson proceeds from a great-grandfather. What I say of these can be seen also in the remaining cases: among all modes of proceeding, it is clear that first place belongs, and greater priority than the rest, to the mode by which the Son proceeds from the Father. For unless this has preceded, none of the other modes can have any place at all in being. [Col. 0981D]

But when terms are transferred from human things to divine things, it is evident that this is done for the sake of similarity, according to what is read in the Apostle: “The invisible things of God are discerned, being understood through the things that have been made” (Romans 1). Therefore, according to the rationale of the proposed similarity, what else is understood when God is said to beget God, when God the Father is said to generate God the Son? What else, I say, must be understood except that the one who produces another proceeding from himself produces him according to the principal mode of proceeding?

[Col. 0982A] We believe, and have inferred from the testimony of reason, that the Father begets, and consequently that the Son is born from the Father. The procession of the Son is held to be by generation; the procession of the Holy Spirit, without generation. If you ask what it is for God to beget a divine person, it is to produce from himself one conformed and consubstantial to himself according to the principal mode of proceeding. If you ask what it is for the Son to be born from the Father, it is for one to proceed from another according to the principal mode of proceeding. To proceed by generation appears to mean to possess, in proceeding, the principal mode of proceeding. To proceed without generation appears to mean not to possess that principal mode of proceeding at all.

Generation, birth, and procession must in every respect be understood in a manner proportioned to the mode and dignity of such excellence and to the property of that surpassing nature. If, then, you ask what the mode of producing is, it is certainly the one already stated above. For the one who produces, who is omnipotence itself, to produce another from himself is the same as to will that very thing from a most orderly cause. But to will it from a more primary cause is the same as to generate. For although both modes of proceeding are grounded in will, they differ according to the difference of their cause; and thus in the more primary cause there is clearly the more primary mode of proceeding.

Do you wish to hear a brief statement concerning these matters which we have already set forth at greater length? For the Unbegotten to will to have from himself one conformed and equal in dignity to himself seems to me to be the same as begetting the Son. [Col. 0982C] For both the Begotten and the Unbegotten to will to have a co-beloved seems to be the same as producing the Holy Spirit. In the former observe a communion of honor; in the latter, a communion of love. As to our saying “conformed,” the careful reader should inquire more attentively lest perhaps this can or ought to be referred to that respect in which, according to a certain conformity of properties, the Son alone bears the image of the Father.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Again, another account is given of what it is for the Father to generate the Son.

As we have already noted above, the poverty of human speech compels us often to vary the signification of words. Hence, as we have said, we sometimes extend and sometimes restrict the meaning of “generation”; and what has been said about generation we say also about procession. For when we say “to proceed,” we certainly do not ordinarily understand it uniformly. In its general sense, to be generated seems to be the same as an existing thing’s being produced from an existing thing through a natural operation. According to this sense, the Father alone in the Trinity is called unbegotten, and the Holy Spirit is denied to be unbegotten.

The production of an existing thing from an existing thing, however, is undoubtedly manifold according to differing natures. Yet above all other modes, by reason of the dignity of nature, that mode of production seems preeminent which is effected according to a natural appetite—an appetite which cannot belong to inanimate things—and according to which alone the one who generates is called begetter and father, and the one generated is called begotten and son. [Col. 0983A] According to this consideration, we may say that the natural production of an animate being from an animate being into conformity of substance seems to be the same as a parent’s generating offspring.

But not every production of an animate being from an animate being through nature’s operation can fall within this definition. For when a worm is born from a human being, who would admit that it is human offspring or that the human is its parent? It should further be known that, if humanity had not sinned and had preserved the integrity of its nature, it would indeed be led in producing offspring not so much by animal appetite as by rational consent. Therefore, in the propagation of its kind, human beings would have a production of offspring not so much appetitive as voluntary, in conformity with their own image. If humanity had preserved the integrity of its original purity, it would have come closer in this respect to the pattern of divine likeness.

But to return to that for the sake of which we introduced these points: for God the Father to beget the Son seems to be the same as naturally and willingly producing a person from his own substance according to a certain unique configuration of his property. To possess the fullness of divinity is common to all in that Trinity. But it is specially proper to the Holy Spirit to possess it and not give it to any person. It is common to the Father and the Son both to possess and to give it. Therefore the one to whom the Father inwardly impressed and fully expressed this figure of his property and form of his image ought rightly to be called his Son. [Col. 0983C] Because of this expression of conformity, the Son alone is called the image of the Father; for this reason the Son alone is rightly called the figure of that substance.

Since, therefore, in producing the Holy Spirit the Father did not impress upon him, so to speak, the form of the image, he ought not to be called his Son, even though he proceeded naturally from him. So too, not in every procession of an existing thing from an existing thing through the operation of nature does ordinary usage assign to one the name offspring and to the other that of parent.

## CHAPTER XIX. That the Holy Spirit is not the image of the Only-Begotten, nor ought he to be called his Son.

But just as it is common to the Father and the Son naturally to give the fullness of divinity, so it is common [Col. 0983D] to the Son and the Holy Spirit not to have the fullness of divinity from themselves. If, therefore, the Son is rightly called the Father’s image on account of the likeness of property which he has with his Father, why is the Holy Spirit not, on the same ground, called the image of the Son on account of the likeness of property which he has with him? It thus seems common both to the Son and to the Father to produce from their own person a person in the image of their likeness; in each case the one proceeding from the other seems to be the image of the producer. If, then, the Son of the Unbegotten is rightly called his Son whom he produces from himself in the image of his likeness, why is the Holy Spirit not, on the same ground, rightly called the Son of the Begotten, whom the Begotten produces from himself under the image of his likeness?

But one thing is not customarily called the image of another because both lack something alike, but because both possess something alike. How, then, can one be called the other’s image on the ground that each is said not to have? For neither has being from himself, nor anything from himself. Otherwise, a stone would rightly be called the image of a human being, and a human being the image of a stone, because neither has, nor can have, what it has from itself. No one fails to understand how frivolous that would be.

But perhaps you say in reply: just as it is common to the Father and Son to give the fullness of divinity, so it is common to the Son and Holy Spirit to have received that same fullness. Why, then, is the same affinity of kinship not reciprocally ascribed in both cases because of the conformity of their mutual likeness? But it must be noted that the Holy Spirit’s reception is from both the Father and the Son. [Col. 0984B] Yet, with respect to receiving, he cannot be called the image of the Father, who receives absolutely nothing from anyone else; for in this respect there is dissimilarity rather than similarity between the one and the other. Therefore he cannot rightly be called the image or Son of one in the respect in which he is unlike him.

But if he is not the Son of the one, neither ought he to be called the Son of the other, because the kinship which he has to the one he unquestionably has to the other: he proceeds wholly uniformly from both the Unbegotten and the Only-Begotten, and everything he receives from one he receives from the other, and in the same way. Finally, from the statement that the Holy Spirit has received all fullness, it is shown that he does not possess it from himself. And because, as we said, he is said not to have it from himself, he is not rightly called another’s image on that account.

But when one proceeding in the image and likeness of the producer is not generated, then, according to ordinary speech, neither is the one who generates called Father nor the one generated called Son. It is written of Adam that he “begot [a son] in his image and likeness” (Genesis 5). [Col. 0984C] Ordinary usage applies those chief names of kinship only in generation of this kind. From what I have said it follows, therefore, that the Holy Spirit is not the image of the Only-Begotten, nor ought he to be called his Son.

## CHAPTER XX. That the paternal image must be sought where there is mutual congruity not without some difference, and difference not without the greatest mutual agreement.

Perhaps someone will suppose that the Son was called the image of the Father because he is altogether similar and wholly equal to him in power, wisdom, and goodness. But if the Son were called the image of his Father on this ground, why would the Holy Spirit not on the same ground be called the image of both Father and Son? For where it has been said, “Such as the Father is, such is the Son,” it is immediately added, “such is the Holy Spirit.” Where it is first stated, “The Father is almighty, the Son almighty,” there is immediately added, “the Holy Spirit almighty.” It is said, “God the Father, God the Son,” and likewise added that the Holy Spirit is God. If, therefore, the Son is called the Father’s image because of such similarity or equality, why should we not think corresponding things of the Holy Spirit for like reasons?

But it must be carefully noted and considered with the greatest diligence what is said less properly concerning divine things because of the smallness of our capacity, and what is said more explicitly. [Col. 0985A] In Sacred Scripture many things are indeed said, as if intentionally, less properly, so that they may more easily be grasped by our limited capacity. Yet it often corrects what it says less properly by a clearer expression. Hence, where it first says, “the Father eternal, the Son eternal, the Holy Spirit eternal,” it immediately adds, as if to state the truth more exactly: “and yet they are not three eternals, but one eternal.” So also, where it says, “the Father almighty, the Son almighty, the Holy Spirit almighty,” it subsequently adds, as if correcting itself: “and yet they are not three almighties, but one almighty.” Likewise, after saying, “God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit,” it immediately adds: “and yet not three gods, but one God.”

Where, then, there is simple unity and supreme simplicity, what place is there for “such as” and “so”? Nothing is rightly said to be equal to itself. Where true unity exists, identity can more fittingly be spoken of than equality. The Father is power; the Son is power; the Holy Spirit is power; yet Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are nothing but one and the same power. What we say about divine power, we say also about divine wisdom, and in every respect about divine substance. Nor is God’s power or wisdom anything other than his substance.

In human nature the substance of a son can fittingly be called the image of his father’s substance, because the substance of the father is one thing and that of the son another. But in the divine [Col. 0985C] nature, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one and the same substance. What comparison, then, can there be where true unity exists? For in supreme simple unity neither similarity nor dissimilarity can exist. The paternal image must be sought where there is mutual congruity, not without some difference, and difference not without the greatest agreement.

Therefore one must have recourse to consideration of the properties, if one wishes more fully to understand the matters of which we speak. As we have often said, it is common to all to possess the fullness of divinity. But it is proper to the Father not to have received, but to give; proper to the Son both to have received and to give. Thus there is agreement in giving, but difference in receiving. How the Son bears the Father’s image in this mutual agreement, as we taught above, is shown by manifest reasoning. [Col. 0985D]

## CHAPTER XXI. Why God’s Only-Begotten is called the figure of his substance.

Deep reflection is necessary if we wish more certainly to know why God the Son is called the figure of his substance. Where the figure of a substance is mentioned, we can, unless I am mistaken, understand this in two ways. For if we turn to human things in order to see through a mirror, one kind of figure is that of a human being, which gives form to his substance; another is the figure of an image, which represents him. Both are nevertheless figures, and each may be called his figure. Where, therefore, there is a twofold substance, there can be on one side a forming figure and on the other a representing figure. But the Father and Son have one and the same substance. Accordingly, in this sense the Son cannot be called the figure of the Father’s substance.

But if he cannot be called a representing figure in this sense, can he be called a forming figure? Yet if the Son gave form to the Father, he would thereby make him beautiful, and then the Son would receive beauty not so much from the Father as the Father from the Son. But neither reason consents to this nor catholic faith admits it, since, on the testimony of Truth, we have learned: “God is spirit” (John 4). Therefore let us ask spiritual nature about the questions we are considering.

Your soul is a spiritual nature; and your soul is either beautiful or deformed according to its will. A good will makes it beautiful; an evil will makes it deformed. Its goodness makes it beautiful; its wickedness makes it deformed. From these things one may discern what the figure of a spiritual substance is. Without doubt, by the Lord’s gift, the same form of perfection can give form to your soul and to mine. Therefore, if we seek the conformity or configuration of Father and Son according to similarity of will, we shall without doubt and without any contradiction find that, as the Father wills to have a person proceeding from himself to whom he can communicate the delights of the love bestowed upon him, so the Son in every respect similarly both wills and has this according to his will.

Thus, as we said above about the image, configuration too must be inferred from a consideration of the properties—[Col. 0986C] where, as we have said, mutual congruity is found, yet not without some difference, and difference not without the greatest agreement.

## CHAPTER XXII. That we ought to believe what we have received from the holy Fathers, according to the catholic faith, concerning unbegotten and begotten substance, although for the present we may be unable to grasp by understanding how true it is.

But perhaps you say in reply to this: “Where there is no plurality, there can be no conformity.” Yet in the true Godhead there is no plurality of substances, although there truly is plurality of persons. Why, then, is the Son called the figure of the Father’s substance, rather than of the Father’s person? For, as has been said, he cannot be called the figure of the Father’s substance as though forming it; nor, if both possess one and the same substance, does he seem able to be called a figure representing the figure of the Father’s substance. But it should be noted that when the Apostle calls the Son “the figure of the Father’s substance” (Heb. 1), this has the same force as if he said “the figure of the unbegotten substance.” Likewise, if he were called the figure of the unbegotten substance, it would mean the same as “the figure of the unbegotten person.” If you say Father, if you say unbegotten substance, if you name unbegotten person, you undoubtedly designate the same person. Beyond doubt, the person of the Father is nothing other than unbegotten substance, and the person of the Son nothing other than begotten substance.

But in our times many have arisen who do not dare to say this; indeed, what is far more dangerous, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers and to so many attestations of the traditions of the Fathers, they dare to deny it and strive by every means to refute it. They by no means concede that substance begets substance, or wisdom wisdom. They stubbornly deny what all the saints affirm, while they cannot find authority for what they themselves say. Let them produce, if they can, not several authorities, but at least one which denies that substance begets substance. For the position we maintain is supported even by many authorities which they themselves bring forward; and, like Goliath, carrying the sword by which they are to be slain, they advance to battle.

“But,” they say, “the Fathers’ words must be understood thus: the Fathers rightly say that substance begets substance; our interpretation maintains that we must believe substance does not beget substance.” A faithful interpretation indeed, and worthy of every acceptance: it maintains that what the holy Fathers all alike proclaim is false, and that what no saint asserts is true. But they say: “If the Son’s substance is begotten, while the Father’s is unbegotten, how can both have one and the same substance?” Beyond doubt, the Son’s substance is begotten and the Father’s substance unbegotten; the unbegotten substance is not begotten, nor is the begotten unbegotten. Yet it does not follow that there is one substance and another substance there, but one person and another person.

Certainly, the case is different in the divine nature from what it is in human nature. In human nature, if one person’s substance is begotten and another’s unbegotten, it follows without any contradiction that one has one substance and the other an altogether different substance. But in the divine nature, without doubt, one person’s substance is unbegotten and another’s begotten; yet it does not follow that one has one substance and the other another, but that this one has one personhood and that one another. “I do not grasp it,” he says; “I do not understand.” But what you cannot grasp by understanding, you can believe through the devotion of faith. Otherwise it is said to you and to those like you: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7).

Why do you not believe what you know the universal Church daily confesses concerning Christ: “God, begotten from the substance of the Father before all ages”? But perhaps you refuse to believe this because you cannot prove it by an example or grasp it by understanding. Can you grasp by understanding, or prove by example, that unity of substance can exist in a plurality of persons, and plurality of persons in unity of substance? Does that which you stubbornly deny exceed human understanding more than that which you truly affirm together with us? If you know the explanation of the proposition you assert, why do you not bring it into the light? Why do you begrudge it to your brothers? And if the explanation of both escapes you, why do you believe the holy Fathers in the one case but not equally believe them in the other? If they are rightly believed, the Father’s person is nothing other than unbegotten substance, nor is the Son’s person anything other than begotten substance.

To state briefly what we think concerning the question proposed: begotten substance bears the figure of unbegotten substance in this, that it produces the same person that the latter produces from itself, and in the same manner; and it is the cause and source, author and principle, of the same gift. Indeed, the same bestowal of the whole fullness flows in every respect both from the one and from the other, from begotten as from unbegotten substance.

## Chapter XXIII. By what reasoning it may be demonstrated that the Catholic faith teaches concerning unbegotten and begotten substance

When we strive to investigate and demonstrate sublime and invisible matters, we gladly use the ladder of likenesses, so that those who have not yet received the wings of contemplation may have something by which to ascend. Therefore, in that nature which we have recognized as made in the image and likeness of God, we gladly seek a divine likeness, and draw out something from which we may be raised to an understanding of divine things.

Behold two persons: one, by his own reflection, discovers knowledge of some subject or acquaintance with some art; he transmits to the other everything that could be imparted from it, and instructs him fully and completely. What then? Is not the same knowledge, the same truth, unquestionably present in the heart of one as in the heart of the other? Otherwise he did not teach the same knowledge which the other discovered. Behold: one of them imparted knowledge and the other received it. You plainly see that one person’s knowledge was received from another, while the other’s was, so to speak, wholly unreceived. Yet is this knowledge something other than that? If everything of truth which is in the one is wholly and identically in the other, undoubtedly the knowledge of both is essentially one.

Nevertheless, it is equally evident that received knowledge is not unreceived, nor can unreceived knowledge be called received, although the unreceived and the received knowledge, as has been said, are essentially one. From this consideration of things, I think, we may discern what we ought to think concerning divine things. Relying upon this watchtower, therefore, let us see whether those who have not yet believed concerning unbegotten substance may be refuted from matters which they believe together with us.

They believe with us that whatever the Father has, he has from himself. They believe with us that the Son received from the Father whatever he possessed from eternity. Therefore it is evident that the Son received from the Father the fullness of wisdom. They grant with us that the Father’s wisdom is not one thing and the Son’s another, but one and the same in every respect, both Father’s and Son’s. Yet it is nonetheless clear that the Son’s wisdom is received and the Father’s wisdom unreceived. It is equally clear that unreceived wisdom is not received, nor received wisdom unreceived, although both the received and the unreceived are undoubtedly essentially one.

Who is so simple or dull as to deny concerning divine wisdom what he sees to be possible in human knowledge? But, that we may pursue this consideration yet more carefully, we all know this in common: the Son has being from the Father by the Father’s generation. If he has being by generation, then he also has wisdom by generation; for for him to be is not one thing and to be wise another. Therefore he has wisdom from the same source from which he has essence. And because he received being through generation, he himself is plainly begotten. It is clear that the Son’s wisdom—or rather, the Son, who is Wisdom—is begotten from the Father. Nor is it anything other for the Father to have given wisdom to the Son, or for the Son to have received it, than for the Father to have begotten him who is Wisdom. For the Father both gives to the Son by begetting and begets by giving.

Thus the Son is rightly called begotten Wisdom, just as the Father is called unbegotten Wisdom. Yet neither knows anything at all which the other does not equally know. In both, then, there is one and the same wisdom, although the unbegotten is not begotten and the begotten is not unbegotten. But if the Son is begotten Wisdom, he is consequently begotten Substance; for his wisdom is nothing other than his substance. What has therefore been said of begotten and unbegotten wisdom must, by the same consequence, be granted concerning begotten and unbegotten substance.

In vain, then, do some fear to say that substance begets substance, wisdom wisdom, and that the Father is unbegotten substance and the Son begotten substance, as though this could establish that the unbegotten has one substance and the begotten another. For, as we have already said above, from the fact that the Father is unbegotten substance and the Son begotten substance, it does not follow that there is one substance and another; rather, there is altogether one person and another person.

## Chapter XXIV. From what consideration it may be inferred that a duplication of person can exist without a duplication of substance

But so that what we have said concerning duplication of person without duplication of substance may appear more fully, let us examine the preceding example still more carefully.

Above we showed that one and the same knowledge can be in two persons, if one who has grasped acquaintance with some art teaches another fully. If, therefore, the term *teaching* (*doctrina*) is understood both passively and actively—so that it is said alike of the one who teaches and of the one who is taught—then, if we understand teaching in this twofold way, one person’s teaching will be one thing and another person’s teaching another.

As knowledge is named from knowing, so teaching is named from teaching. In both there is the same knowing, but in both there is not the same teaching: one teaches and the other is taught; one instructs and the other is instructed. Thus in one there is teaching that teaches, and in the other teaching that learns. Therefore one person’s teaching differs from another’s. In this sense your teaching can be one thing and mine another, although in both, both in learning and in teaching, there is one and the same knowledge.

And if, for each of us, our substance were the same thing as our knowledge, then our substance could be one, just as our knowledge is one. And if, for each of us, our person were the same thing as our teaching, then one person would be one, like one person’s teaching, and the other another, like the other’s teaching. If my knowledge derives its origin from yours, is not one in some manner begotten from the other? If in human nature knowledge is begotten from knowledge, why should it not be said far more fittingly in the divine nature that Wisdom begets Wisdom, where Wisdom is shown to be altogether identical with substance?

As, in human nature, teaching knowledge and taught knowledge are one and the same knowledge, though the teaching is one thing and another; so in the divine nature, begetting Wisdom and begotten Wisdom are one and the same Wisdom—and consequently one and the same substance—though the person is one and another. Therefore, just as in human nature it by no means follows, from the fact that one person’s knowledge is received and another’s unreceived, and that the received is not unreceived, that there is one knowledge and another in them, but rather one teaching and another; so in the divine nature it in no way follows, from the fact that one person’s substance is begotten and another’s unbegotten, and that the begotten is not unbegotten, that there is one substance and another there, but rather one person and another person.

## Chapter XXV. From what consideration, and as it were by an example, what Catholics believe concerning Trinity and unity is confirmed

It has been said of the Father that he is unbegotten substance. It has been said of the Son that he is begotten substance. It must be said of the Holy Spirit that he is substance neither begotten nor unbegotten. How this should be understood is clear from what has gone before. But although the Father alone is called unbegotten substance, the Son alone begotten substance, and the Holy Spirit alone substance neither begotten nor unbegotten, nevertheless the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possess one and the same substance, just as they possess one and the same wisdom. For, as has often already been said, divine substance is not one thing and divine wisdom another.

For the example set out above, when somewhat more fully developed, also instructs us concerning the matter now under discussion. Behold three persons: one discovers and teaches some knowledge; another learns it from that discoverer and writes it down; a third reads and understands it. The first has it from himself; the second from the first alone; the third from both the first and the second. For because the first discovered it and the other wrote it down, it came to the third’s knowledge. If, then, the same truth of understanding is complete and whole in all, is one person’s knowledge different from another’s with respect to the truth of its essence?

Finally, if he who learned by hearing had learned by reading, or he who learned by reading had learned by hearing, would the knowledge acquired by either be different? If, then, one and the same knowledge can exist in three persons, why should it not much more readily be believed that one and the same Wisdom exists in those three persons of the divine Trinity? Yet wisdom received from one alone is not wisdom received from no one, nor is wisdom received from two the wisdom received from one alone. Nevertheless, beyond doubt there is in all of them only one and the same wisdom and, consequently, only one and the same substance.

Yet the Father’s substance, like his wisdom, is not from any other; the Son’s substance is from the Father alone; and the Holy Spirit’s substance is from both Father and Son. Everything said of wisdom can likewise be said of substance, because wisdom and substance in divine matters do not posit two different things. And if the knowledge of one who has been instructed is called *disciplina* because it has been fully learned—so that *disciplina* means, as it were, complete learning—and if we refer what we call *disciplina* to the manner of learning, then in this sense the learning of one who learns by reflection is one thing, that of one who learns by hearing another, and that of one who learns by reading yet another.

Behold, as you see, in human nature there can be a threefold *disciplina* where there is only one and the same knowledge. What wonder, then, if in that nature where substance is identical with wisdom, there is a threefold person where there is only one substance? See how plainly and openly this example confirms what the Catholic faith confesses concerning divine unity and Trinity.

Let us also consider this: if I, you, and a third person possessed the same and altogether equal knowledge, would mine together with his be something greater than yours alone; or mine together with yours something greater than his alone; or his together with yours something greater than mine alone? Finally, would mine, yours, and his be something greater than mine alone, yours alone, or his alone? Who could say this without showing that he understands nothing whatever? So in that Trinity, any two persons together, or all three persons together, are not something greater than the person of the Unbegotten alone, or the person of the Only-begotten alone, or the person of the Holy Spirit alone.

At the end of this work we wish to repeat and commit to memory what we have shown sufficiently clearly above: from consideration of omnipotence it is easily demonstrated that God is not, and cannot be, other than one; from the fullness of goodness, that he is personally threefold; and from the fullness of wisdom it is clearly inferred how unity of substance accords with plurality of persons.

[Col. 0991]

# On the Three Persons Appropriated in the Trinity

To the holy Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

You ask me, my Bernard, what I think of Augustine’s statement in which unity is attributed to the Father, equality to the Son, and the concord of both to the Holy Spirit. I gladly reveal to another what I think, wishing to share whatever I understand rightly, even in however small a degree, and also desiring correction if I think otherwise. Let us, if you please, consider what is proper to each; perhaps what we seek will become clear.

The subsistence of the Unbegotten, which is not from another, introduces no plurality and implies no plurality in that which it is substantially or personally. For in begetting it confers nothing upon itself, but only upon the Son. But the subsistence of the Begotten, which has received from another what it has, can no more exist through itself than be understood through itself. If, therefore, the subsistence of the Son introduces plurality, how much more does the subsistence of the Holy Spirit, which is from two?

Unity is therefore rightly attributed to the Father, since in considering his subsistence no plurality seems to enter. Let us add this as well: whatever can be said substantially is truly one. But you say that this too is common to him and the others. Yet undoubtedly the Father alone has this, so to speak, priority of principle; for the others have it by reception and in likeness to another. Thus it is inferred why unity, under this consideration, is attributed to him as though especially his own.

See how unity is in the Father; let us ask how equality is in the Son. Certainly, where there is no plurality, equality can neither properly be spoken nor understood. For just as nothing is properly said to be like itself, neither is it said to be equal to itself. Therefore, where plurality first occurs, there equality must first be sought. It is evident, however, that the Son is the image of his Father, but the Father is not the image of the Son. Hence Augustine says: “The Father and Son together are not both the image; the Son alone is the image of the Father.” Hear also this from the same author: “If an image perfectly fulfills that of which it is the image, it is made coequal to it; that original is not made coequal to its image.”

Now it is certain that the Son comprehends and expresses the fullness of him whose image he is. Therefore, according to Augustine’s judgment, the Son is coequal to the Father, not the Father to his image. Equality is thus rightly attributed not to the Father but to the Son. “But why,” you ask, “not also to the Holy Spirit?” If you give the reason why the Son alone in the Trinity is called the image of another, you will consequently understand why equality is attributed to the Son alone and not also to the Holy Spirit.
