In matters spoken according to substance, equality is attributed not only to the Son but also to the Holy Spirit; but with respect to priority of principle, the Son alone has this, not the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, if precision were preserved in this manner of speaking, identity rather than equality would be said. You now have why unity is attributed to the Father and equality to the Son. It remains to inquire why the concord of both is attributed to the Holy Spirit.

Just as there is no equality without plurality among things subsisting, so there is no concord of two without a Trinity among things subsisting. In the Father is the origin of unity; in the Son, the beginning of plurality; in the Holy Spirit, the completion of Trinity. Hence it should become clear to you how fittingly he who is the third person in the Trinity is called the concord of the others.

Let us now consider what is proper to each, and we shall see that the Father’s relation to the Son differs from his relation to the Holy Spirit. Likewise, the Son relates differently to the same Spirit and to his Father. But both Father and Son have the same relation to the Spirit of both; conversely, that same Spirit has the same relation both to the Father and to the Son. He is therefore rightly called the concord of the others, in whom uniformity of relation is found in every respect.

Let us add this also: fullness of concord is produced by willing the same things and refusing the same things. Therefore he who is the love of both is rightly called the concord of two. Why he is called love rather than the wisdom of both is another question. Let us now see how Augustine’s addition to the points stated and explained above is to be understood: “And these three are all one on account of the Father, all equal on account of the Son, all connected on account of the Holy Spirit.”

If the person of the Unbegotten alone existed, there would nevertheless be unity in the Godhead. Thus unity is, so to speak, primordially in the Unbegotten alone, but by likeness to him or by emanation from him it is also in both the Only-begotten and the Holy Spirit. Again, if the person of the Unbegotten alone existed, there would be no equality in the Godhead; and if the person of the Holy Spirit alone were absent, there would nevertheless be equality in the Godhead. From this one may see that equality is primordially in the Only-begotten alone, although it is also in the Holy Spirit by likeness to him.

Remove the Holy Spirit, and there will be no one in the Godhead who is the connection of several. But perhaps you still ask why, when the Trinity exists, the connection of all is attributed to the Holy Spirit alone. We know that the other two relate differently to the Only-begotten; but the Holy Spirit alone relates without distinction to both the Unbegotten and the Begotten, and both of those relate uniformly to the Holy Spirit. Therefore the connection of all is attributed singularly to the Holy Spirit: singularly, I say, with respect to the other persons in the Godhead, and primordially also with respect to creatures. For whatever connection is ordinarily found in creatures is by imitation or likeness of the Holy Spirit.

Do not be surprised that we have stated the foregoing by way of exclusion, in order that we may understand more plainly and fully what ought to be thought. Unity, therefore, belongs primordially to the Unbegotten, and for that reason in the Trinity all are one on account of him. Equality belongs primordially to the Only-begotten, and for that reason in the Trinity all are equal on account of him. Connection belongs singularly to the Holy Spirit, and therefore in the Trinity all are connected on account of him.

## Why power is attributed to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit

You further ask what reason I think there is why, in Holy Scripture, power is attributed more especially to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and charity or goodness to the Holy Spirit. If I say nothing except what is found in your books, perhaps it will be judged superfluous; if I say anything else, perhaps it will be scorned. I should rightly fear this sort of thing if I did not know in whose ear I was speaking and pouring forth my words or thoughts. To you, certainly—to you, I say—I gladly state what I think.

What power is, what wisdom is, what charity or goodness is, we all know in common and prove by daily experience. By things which are manifest and known to us, we are instructed, unless I am mistaken, toward knowledge of those things which exceed the measure of human capacity. For in these three a certain form and image of the supreme Trinity is expressed, and a kind of mirror is set before us, so that “the invisible things of God may be perceived through the things that have been made.” The things in this trinity, then, correspond to those things which are in that Trinity: three to three, like to like, proper characteristics to proper characteristics, each to each.

We see that there can be manifold power even where there is no wisdom, nor can there be any. I pass over the elements and any inanimate things. Among animate irrational creatures there is power to hear, see, walk, eat, drink, and so forth; but in these there is no wisdom, nor can wisdom naturally inhere in them. It is evident, then, as was said above, that there can be manifold power where wisdom cannot exist. Conversely, where there is no power, wisdom cannot exist. For to be able to be wise is undoubtedly to be able to do something. Thus wisdom does not give power the capacity to be; rather, power gives wisdom its capacity to be.

Likewise, it is evident that Lucifer, that one who rose in the morning, has much power and much wisdom, but no good will at all. For goodness consists in willing well. What indeed is goodness except good will? Thus that Lucifer, hardened in his perversity, bears witness that manifold power and multifarious wisdom can coexist where no trace of goodness remains. Conversely, no goodness can exist where wisdom or power is altogether lacking. For to be able to will well is to be able to do something. And it belongs to wisdom to discern between good and evil; without such discernment the will does not know what it ought to choose.

Therefore, if you are to possess goodness, you must know and be able to choose the good. Power gives ability; wisdom gives knowledge; without these, goodness cannot exist. Thus goodness derives its being not so much from wisdom as from power. In this trinity of things, power alone is not from either of the others; wisdom is from power alone; goodness is from power together with wisdom. You see, then, how the properties of that supreme and eternal Trinity are expressed in this trinity of things. There is the person of the Unbegotten, who is not from any other; there is the person of the Begotten, who is from the Unbegotten alone; there is the person of the Holy Spirit, who is from both Begotten and Unbegotten.

Since, therefore, the property of the Unbegotten is expressed in power, power is rightly ascribed to him by a special mode of consideration. Since the property of the Begotten is expressed in wisdom, wisdom is rightly ascribed to him in the same manner. Likewise, because the property of the Holy Spirit is found in goodness, goodness is rightly assigned more especially to him. See how, from this trinity of things, arises a consideration by which it is shown through an example how what is read concerning divine properties can be understood. But from the same consideration of things arises a much loftier consideration, from which reasoning establishes that one must confess exactly this. Yet here we set a limit, because we believe that we have now satisfied your question.

[Col. 0995]

# Book on the Incarnate Word

In which he most acutely shows, so far as the human mind can grasp, that it was necessary for God to become incarnate, and that no person was more fitting than the Son.

To the holy Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

## Chapter I

[Col. 0995A]

> “One cries to me from Seir: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’ The watchman said: ‘Morning comes, and also night. If you seek, seek; return, and come’” (Isa. 21).

These are the words you propose for me to expound, and you are not ashamed to weary my foolishness. To confess the truth, these words seem to me very profound and, because of their subtlety, no less delightful if rightly understood. I know—I know, and am not ashamed to confess—that their depths are beyond my powers to penetrate; and I do not know whether I shall be able suitably to express, in fitting words, even what I dream concerning them.

“One cries to me from Seir.” Seir is the same one who is called Edom or Esau, from whom the land of Idumaea is also named Seir. Now Esau and Jacob, who is also Israel, were brothers; from the former came the Idumaeans, from the latter the Israelites. Of these two brothers we read that the Lord said through the prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1). Thus Jacob was chosen, Esau rejected; the Israelites were children of election, the Idumaeans children of rejection.

But, O wondrous change and pitiable reversal! The children of strangers cry to the Lord, while those whom he chose as his inheritance do not cry to him. Therefore, to rebuke those who are in Judaea, it is said what those in Idumaea are doing. The Idumaean cries out; the Jew is silent. The former entreats; the latter is mute. “They cry to me from Seir.” From Mount Seir there is crying; on Mount Zion there is silence. From there they cry in confession; here they are silent in contempt. Thus, while the Idumaeans cry, the Jews are silent—not all, however, but many. Yet many of those crying do not cry to their own God but to a foreign god. Therefore what is now said to them by way of reproach is cast up against the shame of such people: “To me—to me, I say—one cries from Seir.”

Unhappy and foolish Jew: strangers cry to your God, while you cry to a foreign god; they to the true God, you to a false god. “One cries to me from Seir.”

Observe what he says: he does not say, “They cry,” but “One cries.” He does not say “this man” or “that man,” nor does he specify anyone; rather, the expression is indefinite, so that no single person, or only one person, may be understood. Understand it, therefore, as said indefinitely both with regard to the number and to the kind of persons; and in this is commended the unity of those who pray. One intention and one devotion make many into one; they make them one heart and one soul. Just as the unity of one who is personally one is broken apart when, through distraction of mind, he is divided among many gods, so many are one—and rightly called one—when they are made one in one Spirit.

He therefore says: “One cries to me from Seir.” The unity of those who repent, the unanimity of those who trust, cries to me from Seir. “To me,” he says, “one cries.” He does not say, “He prays”; he does not say, “He entreats”; rather, “He cries.” What is this cry except intense prayer, except greatness of devotion? If you pray with great desire, you cry out. The more fervently you pray, the more vehemently you cry in God’s ears. As vehement desire increases, the cry of supplication rises more highly. The cry of the inward person, then, is the fervent desire of the mind.

Hence the Lord says to Moses: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14). He is not recorded as having said anything, and yet is reported to have cried out. Such a cry penetrates heaven, appeases wrath, obtains pardon, prepares grace, and reconciles the Lord, in accordance with what we read in the Psalmist: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor” (Ps. 10). Consider, if you can, what and how much one advances who cries in this way.

## Chapter II

“One cries to me from Seir.” Yet not only many of those who were in Seir appealed to the Lord with cries of this kind; innumerable persons from other nations also sighed, desired, and awaited with all longing the coming of Christ. Hence comes Jacob the patriarch’s prophecy concerning Christ: “He himself,” he says, “shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49). Those who cried to the Lord from Seir with sighs of devotion bore, in mystery, the figure of all these. For those from Seir were one with the other nations in this: all alike had been strangers to God’s covenant. Therefore it is said concerning those who are strangers in respect of the devotion of their minds: “One cries to me from Seir.”

## Chapter III
But let us now, if you please, seek to apply to our own times, for our own benefit, these things which we have heard concerning the ancients from the Lord’s utterance. “He cries to me from Seir.” What is Seir? Seir is interpreted “rough” or “hairy.” Esau, indeed, was called Seir because he was exceedingly hairy and rough like a skin. Hair arises from the flesh, yet by its growth it far exceeds the flesh’s measure. [Col. 0996D] So too, the desires of the flesh arise indeed from the necessity of the flesh; but unless they are restrained by temperance and frugality, they exceed the bounds of necessity and moderation. Thus carnal pleasure, worldly vanity, and every sort of excess in such desires belong to hairs. Hair is cut without injury; it cannot be plucked out without injury. So, without doubt, the motions of the flesh can and ought to be cut away without danger where they are excessive, and tolerated where they are necessary. Hence they are commanded gently to shave, not pluck out, the hairs of their flesh: for the desires of the flesh must be moderated, though we cannot eradicate them.

Those, then, are as though in Seir who seek superfluities, love superfluities, and live amid every excess. Whether you are in religious life or outside it, if you pursue what is superfluous, if you delight in excess, you are reckoned among the inhabitants of Seir. But woe to you, whoever you are there, if you are silent in the confidence of a ruinous security. Woe to you if you inhabit Seir and do not cry to the Lord. He cries who is pierced with compunction; he cries who confesses; he cries who supplicates. He cries from Seir who accuses himself for pleasure or vanity. He cries from Judaea who praises the Lord for forgiveness granted or grace bestowed.

And it often happens that those who are in religious life and live, as it were, in the promised land grow sluggish through excessive security; they presume beyond measure upon their own holiness, and fall silent both from self-accusation and from the praise of God. Conversely, those who still live in secular dress often, after fulfilling their desires, return to repentance; they are pierced in heart, confess with their mouths, accuse themselves, condemn themselves, and, while rigorously judging themselves for their perversity, strike the ears of the Lord of Hosts with loud cries. See how it often happens [Col. 0997C] that religious persons are silent through sloth, while secular persons cry out through devotion. Therefore, to shame those who languish in religious life and keep silence in foolish security, what secular persons do is said to them reproachfully: “He cries to me from Seir.”

Already rough and hairy, foul with the deformity of vices, he cries to me with a contrite heart; already he appeals to me with repeated sighs. Yet you are silent because you think yourself holy, saying in your heart, “I am rich, and need nothing,” and you do not know that you are wretched and miserable (Rev. 3): “He cries to me from Seir.” Let the monk blush; let the negligent and slothful canon, idle in all things and mute in the praise of God, blush—often singing with his mouth while silent in his heart. Let him blush, I say, and groan when he hears and reads from the Lord’s utterance: [Col. 0997D] “He cries to me from Seir.”

Let the anchorite blush; let the hermit blush, if, wandering in heart, he neglects God’s praises. Blush also, wretched man, you yourself who dictate and write these words: you who, though mute in God’s praises, condemn men like yourself and accuse them of silence. Blush also, you who read and hear these things, if before the angels you recognize yourself as mute and like me. What will any contemplative say if he neglects that praise for which he was taken up? Are you silent too, you who have no other office? Why are you not stirred by the prophetic, or even the angelic, example? Hear the Prophet’s voice: “I will bless the Lord at all times” (Ps. 33). And the angels do not cease to cry night and day: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who is, [Col. 0998A] and who was, and who is to come” (Rev. 4). Behold, the angels cry continually; why then do you not always cry with the Prophet?

But what if you cry and do not cry to the Lord? Perhaps you boast before your neighbour; perhaps you magnify yourself before yourself. You cry, but not to the Lord. Perhaps you say to yourself: “I am not like the rest of the brethren; indeed, I am not like this carnal man, who every day serves his belly and gluttony, because he himself, having abandoned Zion, has become an inhabitant of Seir and has received among the Edomites both fellowship and inheritance.” This is to make a tumult within yourself, not to cry to the Lord. But perhaps he whom you judge already condemns himself, already accuses himself, and perhaps already cries to the Lord and goes down justified rather than you; so that you rightly deserve to hear from the Lord as a reproach: [Col. 0998B] “He cries to me from Seir.”

## CHAPTER IV

Above we heard concerning the inhabitant of Seir how, on occasion, and how fervently he prays; let us still hear concerning the same man how humbly he prays and how wisely. We heard how devoutly he prays; let us hear how discerningly he prays. “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” Behold, this man who cries to the Lord from Seir considers where he lives and what he is; and the more deeply he considers that he has sinned, the more grievously he has acted, the more modestly and humbly he prays. “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

He considers how unjustly he has lived and does not dare to say, “Hear, O Lord, my righteousness.” He considers how many he has injured, and does not dare to say, “Judge me, O Lord, according to my innocence” (Ps. 7). He remembers that he has never possessed bowels of mercy; and therefore he does not even presume to pray thus: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50). For “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). He sees that, if judged strictly, he is unworthy of every mercy. Therefore he does not presume to ask anything; he merely shows in his prayer the disposition of a suppliant, without inserting a petition, and by suggestion alone indicates what he wishes: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

He names as Watchman the one whom he invokes, and from the designation of his office indicates what, by the law of his condition, he owes to his sheep. You are he who ought to guard the rational creature [Col. 0998D] made in your image: you alone who can guard it, you yourself who are accustomed to guard it. You ought to do so because it is your creature; you can do so because you are almighty; you are accustomed to do so because you are most merciful. “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” It belongs to a watchman to guard those placed under his care, seek the lost, call back the straying, gather the scattered, and apply healing to the sick. I am a sick sheep, a feeble sheep. You know better than I what you ought to do; you see more clearly what ought to be done concerning me. “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

Perhaps such a suppliant was enduring the deep night of excessive adversity when he supplicated the Lord in this manner: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” Surely he himself is the one who guards us by day; he himself is the one who [Col. 0999A] guards us by night. By day he guards his own, lest any adversity strike them; by night he guards them, lest the scourge of adversity exceed the measure of justice. To some it seems that the Lord has abandoned his own when he exposes them to the nightly terrors of tribulations; he seems to guard them when the day of prosperity smiles upon them. Behold, here the suppliant is silent concerning that of which all are certain—the day—but confesses that about which doubt might arise—the night: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

Certainly, in interpreting day as prosperity and night as adversity, we do not depart from the historical sense. For it is customary often to adorn a historical meaning with figurative speech, as one may very easily observe in secular writings. Thus, as has been said, the suppliant was already in the night and desired the same thing; but because of excessive shame and humility he did not dare to ask. For why is he answered by the Lord, “Morning comes,” unless the true searcher of hearts knew that he desired the day? Thus, by implication, what he says in his repeated supplication to the Lord is understood: [Col. 0999B] “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

## CHAPTER V

Certainly, whenever anything is undertaken against the divine command, contumacy acts against majesty. But when we wish to propitiate offended majesty, we flee to its mercy. Therefore, in order to propitiate majesty, we have recourse to its goodness—and not only to that, but also to its truth. For pardon has undoubtedly been promised to those who truly repent by him—by him, I say—who cannot lie at all. Thus we possess God’s mercy and God’s truth as a double anchor of hope amid the storms of temptations and the shipwrecks of transgressions, lest, falling into the Charybdis of despair, we be wholly swept away. These are what bring us, after many shipwrecks, to the harbour of salvation. These are what lead us from the utmost dangers into the citadel of true security: “God,” says the Prophet, “sent forth his mercy and his truth, and delivered my soul” (Ps. 56).

Therefore, after committing many crimes, when we return again and again to the laments of repentance, we set God’s truth and God’s mercy before God, that we may appease divine wrath. You know, then, that this name, God, is common to the three [persons]. You know likewise that it is the custom of Holy Scripture to attribute power, as it were specially, to the Father; wisdom to the Son; and goodness to the Holy Spirit. Why these particular attributes are assigned to each, we wrote to you elsewhere, my Bernard, and need not repeat here. By consideration of certain properties, then, majesty belongs especially to the Father, truth to the Son, and kindness to the Holy Spirit.

When, therefore, we seek to appease offended majesty, what else do we strive to do but soften the Father’s offence? But when we claim the mercy promised to penitents and the truth of that promise, what else do we attempt but, through the Holy Spirit together with the Son, to soften the Father’s wrath? When we appeal to supreme truth and supreme wisdom, we invoke the Son. To implore supreme clemency and supreme goodness is nothing other than to supplicate the Holy Spirit. Wisdom expels the darkness of error; goodness expels the coldness of iniquity. Wisdom guards us amid nightly terrors; goodness guards us amid nightly chills. Thus the Son of God is Watchman, and the Holy Spirit is Watchman. For the former frees us from error, the latter from iniquity. Since, therefore, through these two we have access to the principal light, the phrase is rightly repeated: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” And it is added, “and the Watchman said.” Behold, the Watchman’s name is repeated a third time, because the Trinity of persons is found in one Godhead. Rightly, indeed, the Father himself can also be called our Watchman. For as it belongs to truth to protect from error, and to goodness to protect from iniquity, so it belongs to majesty to protect from every adversity.

## CHAPTER VI

But let us still examine the letter itself more subtly, and diligently investigate from what is said what should be assigned to each person: “He cries to me from Seir: Watchman, what of the night?” Unless he recognized himself as Watchman, he certainly would not rightly say, “He cries to me,” in the words, “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” What, then, is it that he adds afterward: “And the Watchman said”? He does not say, “I said,” but “the Watchman said,” as though he himself were not the Watchman.

Or perhaps the Watchman is both the one invoked and also the one from whom the answer is given—yet not one person and another, but one and the same Lord and God? But the “me” placed first and the “said” placed afterward show a plurality of persons in one Godhead. Again, since he does not say, “He cries to us,” but “He cries to me,” we understand that only one person is invoked in the repeated words, “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” But perhaps one may also ask which person it is who is specially invoked here.

Certainly we know that whatever the Son has, he has from the Father; therefore he has both the power to guard and the habitual exercise of guarding. What I say of the Son, I say also of the Holy Spirit. The Father, therefore, guards through the Son, guards through the Holy Spirit, and guards through himself. If then, in that invocation, “Watchman, [Col. 1000D] what of the night?” were repeated a third time, it could fittingly be understood only of the Father. For the Son guards through himself and guards through the Holy Spirit, but not through his Father. The Holy Spirit alone in the Trinity does not guard through himself: for no person in the Trinity receives from him the ability to do, or to be able to do, anything.

Since, therefore, the doubling of “Watchman” occurs in the invocation, we cannot rightly understand this of the Holy Spirit. For the repetition in the invocation compels us to understand the saying as concerning the Son. Thus the Son is invoked when it says: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” But behold, when one person is invoked, another is won over. He is won over, I say, not only to reconciliation but also to the promise of what is desired. For what the suppliant desires is promised when it says: “Morning comes.” We have seen which person is invoked; let us see also which is appeased. But, to speak briefly, the principal person is understood as the one to be appeased, while another is interposed.

The Father is the source of the Only-Begotten; the Only-Begotten, however, is the source also of the Holy Spirit. Thus, as the begotten one is understood in the mediator and propitiator, so the unbegotten one is understood in the one propitiated, not the Holy Spirit. For it is not fitting that the Holy Spirit should demand satisfaction for what the Son forgives, since the same Spirit has from the Son all that he has. You now see, I think, more clearly what we said above: how, in the fact that “Watchman” occurs a third time, the Trinity of persons is understood. For the Son is first called Watchman because he guards through himself; second, he is named again because he guards through the Holy Spirit. In the first occurrence the Son alone is understood; in the second the Holy Spirit is understood together with him; in the third the unbegotten one alone.

The unbegotten one alone is understood in what is written: “The Watchman said: Morning comes, and night.” What is speaking but bringing forth the Word? The Father’s speaking is the utterance of truth; the Father’s speaking is the begetting of wisdom. But he speaks to us when, by the revelation of his wisdom, he makes his good pleasure known to us. Then something in accordance with our desire is promised to us by the inward speech of the Father, when a firm certainty of our hope and expectation is poured into our heart. Now, I believe, it is clear to whom the words belong: [Col. 1001C] “The Watchman said: Morning comes, and night.” We have seen what God’s speaking or promising is.

## CHAPTER VII

Let us now see the nature of what he promises: “Morning comes, and night.” As was said above, they groaned under the night of great tribulation and longed for the day of long-desired prosperity. What, then, is it that in the promise there is proposed to them not only the morning which they wanted, but also the night which they did not want? One is promised for consolation, the other foretold for instruction; both for benefit: “Morning comes, and night.” What is morning except the end of night, and what is night except the end of light? In one morning we have the end of night and the beginning of day. Morning therefore comes, because the night which you dread will now end, and the day for which you so greatly long will immediately begin.

But when the long-hoped-for day has arrived, it will not remain; for “morning comes, and night.” As though he said more plainly: So will night pass that it will return again; so will day return that it will depart again. “Morning comes, and night.” If you are in night, do not despair, for morning will come; if you are in day, do not be confident, for night will come. Morning, then, is promised lest those who labour should fail; the coming night is foretold that they may become watchful. The former is for healing, the latter for caution. “Morning comes, and night.”

But what else is it to say this to someone except to show the mutability of this time and the variety of alternating changes, to form the mind toward contempt both of worldly prosperity and of worldly adversity, and to stir it toward the desire for eternal things? Thus he says: “Morning comes, and night.”

## CHAPTER VIII

Behold, we have now heard what these words mean according to the historical sense. Let us hear further what they signify according to the mystical understanding: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night? The Watchman said: Morning comes, and night.” As was already said above, many, not only among the Jews but also among the Gentiles, had foreknown Christ’s coming and awaited it with great desire, according to the saying: “Behold, the Desired One of all nations shall come” (Hag. 2). He does not say “the one to be desired,” but “the Desired One,” so that you may understand that in every nation some persons at some time burned with desire for him.

His coming, then, was foreknown by many Gentiles and ardently desired. Yet they rose gradually to this knowledge, and step by step through intervals of time. At first, some of them, divinely enlightened and instructed by natural reason, understood in what great darkness almost the whole human race was enveloped: it served idolatry in such ugly multiplicity and such manifold ugliness that it said to wood and stone, “You are my God.” Yet they were not able fully to understand under what burden of captivity even those laboured who believed in and worshipped the one true God.

Later, others, more deeply enlightened, understood more fully the misery of our captivity and the sentence of condemnation: how human nature, after sin and the wound of mortality inflicted upon it, was cast from paradise into the world, as from a homeland into exile, and afterward was to be cast by death from the world into hell, as from exile into a prison-house. They therefore understood the magnitude of the danger, but were not equally able to understand the means of escape. Neither the former nor the latter had escaped the darkness of the land of night, since they were benighted beneath the covering of such great ignorance.

Others, searching yet more deeply and discerning more subtly under the guidance of grace, discovered and perceived with clear vision not only the magnitude of condemnation but also the means of restoration. Those of this kind understood the means of restoration, but did not know God’s good pleasure concerning this very matter. Finally, to certain persons not only among the Jews but also among the Gentiles, the divine purpose was revealed, so that they might foreknow the mystery of our restoration in great measure; some even proclaimed it, and some at last committed it to writing. The proclamations of the prophets and the oracles of the nations bear witness to these things.

But setting the rest aside, let us for the present attend only to those who, as we said, understood the means of restoration but did not know the divine disposition concerning it. Led by reason, though preceded by the light of divine revelation, they understood that, if man had not sinned, he could have ascended to heavenly blessedness through justice. But if, after his fall, he recovered—or even was promised—what he had lost by mercy alone, with no justice intervening, he would bear forever the reproach of his fall. For the devil could always reproach him that he had no right to what he possessed, and it would thus be clear that he had not recovered his former dignity. But where there was not a complete restoration of the first dignity, there was not complete restoration.

Therefore, if man was to rise again according to the requirement of justice, satisfaction was necessary. And this further point is added: if man rendered no satisfaction, even if he had no external creditor exacting payment for guilt, he would never completely erase the exaction of his biting conscience and the mark of shame. Did not Eve believe the serpent more than her own and so beneficent Creator? Did not Adam choose rather to offend the Almighty than [Col. 1003B] his wife? How, then, after the boldness of so great a presumption, could they gain a tranquil conscience or erase from their hearts the mark of shame if they made satisfaction in nothing?

But now the devotion of the faithful glories more in the satisfaction of its redemption than it was formerly ashamed of the reproach of so great a fall; so much so that everywhere on earth the Church of the faithful sings with complete confidence: “O certainly necessary sin of Adam—and ours—blotted out by Christ’s death! O happy fault, which deserved to have such and so great a Redeemer!” Clear reason, therefore, teaches that without satisfaction man could not be completely restored.

For satisfaction to be complete, the humiliation in expiation had to be as great as the presumption in transgression had been. God occupies the highest place among rational beings, while man occupies the lowest. Therefore, when man presumed against God, there was an exaltation from the lowest to the highest. Thus, for the remedy of expiation, there had to be a humiliation from the highest to the lowest; but this could occur only in some person of the Trinity. Again, if man could recover, and did recover, justice through a creature rather than through the Creator, and through justice the glory of future blessedness, would he not thereafter, contrary to the excellence of his first dignity, be more indebted to the creature than to the Creator, to the thing made than to its maker? For surely to be justified and made blessed is greater than to be created.

Therefore, for man’s complete restoration, a person who was not God would by no means suffice. Nevertheless, it is clear that, as far as the requirement of justice is concerned, nothing done by any person who was not man would pertain to man. For who does not see that it is equitable, fully lawful, and altogether reasonable that a son should make satisfaction for his father, a brother for his brother, if the former cannot and the latter is not fit for these things? Human redemption therefore required a man, who by the merit of his own nature might assist according to the debt of his condition.

Again, through disobedience man incurred the debt of death; and, to expiate that debt, he had to pay by obedience an undeserved death in place of the death he owed. But this could occur only through a mortal and righteous man, in no respect subject to the sentence of death. Thus, for the person of the human Redeemer to be fit for satisfaction of the debt, he had to be true God, able to suffice for this purpose, and true man, able by the right of kinship to render payment by merit. And how, I ask, could he be a true and perfect mediator between God and man if he had nothing in common with either? Conversely, no mediation could be stronger or firmer than that accomplished through one who shared in both natures. Behold how reason concludes that the mediator between God and human beings had to be true God and true man.

## CHAPTER IX

Moreover, investigation by the same reason discovers to which person of the supreme Trinity this dispensation of mercy most properly belongs. As was shown above, for man to recover his first dignity completely, satisfaction was necessary. But for satisfaction to occur, there had to be one who required it and another who rendered it. To punish guilt, however, or exact any satisfaction for it, which the Father might forgive, could not at all be fitting either to the Son or to the Holy Spirit, since each has from the Father all that he has. Therefore, in this respect, either the Father or no one had to make the exaction; and, likewise, either the Son or the Holy Spirit had to make satisfaction for humanity.

But if the Holy Spirit assumed the office of mediator, perhaps man would regard this mediation with suspicion. What wonder, I ask, if in this matter man thought as man and feared as man? Perhaps he would fear that the Son would favour the Father, from whom he has all that he has, more than the Holy Spirit, from whom he has none of the things he possesses. And if a man had two against him and one for him, perhaps he would not wholly trust such a mediation. Yet it was necessary that the nature which fell by believing should rise by believing: it fell by believing the serpent and should rise by believing the Redeemer, so that what it lost through faith it might recover through faith, and that humanity might be compelled to return by the same gate through which it had chosen to depart from God’s good pleasure.

But if the Son of God undertook humanity’s cause, he would introduce no suspicion into humanity. For the Holy Spirit, by the argument set forth above, could not refuse to forgive a fault which the Son wished to remit—much less one which he wished to blot out by his own satisfaction. Indeed, without doubt, if the Son undertook humanity’s cause, the Holy Spirit ought rather to exercise the office of fellow-worker than that of exactor. Behold how plain reason demonstrates that, for humanity’s expiation, the human cause specially required the person of the Son.

## CHAPTER X

Hear this also. Certainly, through presumption concerning what was forbidden, and as if by robbery, man desired to rise to the likeness of God. Therefore, for the manner of satisfaction to correspond to the manner of transgression, reason required that the repairer of our ruin should, through self-emptying, descend from the likeness of God to the likeness of the fallen one. But the Son is the image and figure of the Father. Therefore it was fitting that he—he himself—should descend in accordance with the required manner of due expiation and assume the likeness of man, so that one and the same person might possess the likeness of God by divine generation and the likeness of man by human generation.

We know, moreover, that the natural manner of human propagation does not permit a human being to proceed from a human being without a begetter. But it belongs to the property of the Holy Spirit that he proceeds as God from God without generation. Therefore, just as the Holy Spirit could not descend from the highest to the lowest in accordance with the reciprocal fitness of these likenesses, so it was not fitting that he should undertake humanity’s cause in order to erase the fault of a likeness wrongfully sought.

## CHAPTER XI

Observe furthermore what man specially desired in that robbery, and you will find—unsurprisingly—that this desire was a special injury to the Son: “You shall be,” he says, “like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 2). What is the Son of God but the wisdom of God? Thus he who wished to obtain knowledge by robbery sinned especially against wisdom. Consider, if you can, how just it was in the one respect and how merciful in the other that the Father should avenge the injury done to his Son, while the Son should forgive it. Learn, O man, what you do and what you ought to do. Learn, I say, to forgive an injury done to yourself and avenge an injury done to another.

It was too little for the Son of God merely to forgive his own injury, unless he also expiated that very injury before the Father. O astonishing mercy, immeasurable love! And, that contraries may be cured by contraries, observe how fitting and how artful it appears that he who had fallen through folly should rise through wisdom. It was fitting that, as falsehood had been the cause of destruction, truth should become the way of salvation. It was fitting that he who incurred death through the devil’s word should return to life through God’s Word.

From the foregoing it is sufficiently clear, I think, that no other person in the Trinity was more suited to be propitiated by another than the Father, and none was more fitting than the Son to expiate humanity’s cause before the Father. Therefore that supreme Trinity of persons, one God, divided among itself the work of human salvation: the Father punished the one and same fault of humanity, the Son expiated it, and the Holy Spirit forgave it. Thus, for the greater glory of fallen humanity, that it might rise through justice, the Father exacts satisfaction, [Col. 1005D] the Son renders it, and the Holy Spirit places himself between them as mediator. This is the way; this is the gate of salvation. This is the highest and unique means of human restoration.

Many of the ancient Fathers, not only among the Jews but also among the Gentiles, understood this; for, as was said, they had been instructed in this matter both by innate reason and by divine revelation. But though they understood it, they did not know the divine good pleasure concerning it and in no way presumed to ask for it. For who would ever presume to ask that the Son of God should visit the human race in his own person and redeem it in his own person—visit it by the incarnation, redeem it by the passion? Who, I say, would presume to ask this unless he had first learned God’s purpose concerning it through divine revelation?

Yet they desired what they did not dare to ask. They longed for it, sighed for it, appealed to the Lord for it with groans and tears, and cried aloud to him with the cries of burning desire. Their type is expressed in the Lord’s words: “He cries to me from Seir: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’” “Watchman,” they say, “what of the night?” As though by implication they expressed what they sought with such burning heat of desire. “We know,” they say, “Son of God, Word of the Most High, we know that your coming is necessary for us, but we do not presume to ask for it. We know that our satisfaction depends upon your incarnation and your passion; but you do this if you will. For who would dare to ask or presume to request this unless he had first recognized your good pleasure concerning it? ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’”

## CHAPTER XII

To whom, I ask, does he speak? Surely a creature speaks to its Creator. Why then, in invoking the Creator, does he not say, “Creator, Creator”? Who, I say, hears these words, and from whom are they heard? Surely the Lord, and from a servant? Why then is he not addressed, “Lord, Lord”? Certainly, that they had him as Creator, God, and Lord was common to them with all others; but that they did not, together with the rest, walk in the broad way of destruction was theirs beyond others through his guardianship. Therefore they set before him the prerogative of grace which they had received from his gift: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

“You are he who guarded us from the night, lest the darkness of unbelief should envelop us with the rest. You are he who guarded us from the night, lest the coldness of malice should extinguish our love. Beneficence once begun gives us confidence to presume upon greater things. We hope that salvation begun will be completed. But in order to complete the salvation begun, you must come. You must come in your own person, and not only this, but you must also come through your Spirit. ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’”

The ancients therefore foresaw through the Spirit that the Son of God had to come and, likewise, that he had to send the Holy Spirit. They foresaw this, I say, and therefore repeated their cry: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” See how necessary the advent of each is. Through the advent of the Son, the faith of believers is founded; through the advent of the Holy Spirit, the faith of the faithful is confirmed. The Son works the one and same salvation of humanity; the Holy Spirit works together with him. Why then should man still doubt concerning the appeasement of the Father, when he sees that in this work he has two co-operating helpers of equal power? Let him therefore say to the one who guards, and will guard, now through himself, now through the Holy Spirit: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

## CHAPTER XIII
And the watchman said: “Morning comes, and also night.” From the very hour of the first transgression until Christ, all were under night, and could not find the way of returning to their homeland, the gate of entering into life; therefore they desired it truly to be said: “Morning comes,” since they knew what darkness they endured. And behold, in accordance with their desire, the answer is given them when the Lord says: “Morning comes.” What is morning but a certain beginning of daylight? You know who says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8). Christ is the light of the world and the sun of righteousness, who enlightens every person coming into this world. Therefore the coming of our Savior is the beginning of the true light. For when the sun of righteousness rises, true morning begins. Concerning this morning we have in the Prophet: “A light has arisen in darkness for the upright, the Lord merciful and compassionate” (Ps. 3). He therefore says: “Morning comes.” You desire morning; you shall have morning. You sigh for the coming of my Son. He whom you seek will come soon. The watchman said: “Morning comes.” As has already been said above, he does not say, “I said,” but “he said.” Thus, the person invoked is one, and the person from whom the answer is given another. The Son is entreated, and the Father is propitiated. The Son is appealed to; the Father has mercy. The Son is implored; the Father bestows. The watchman said: “Morning comes.”

As has been said, the Father’s “saying” is his revealing. The Father’s promising is his pouring, through the assurance of hope, the good pleasure of his purpose into the human mind. Behold what we said far above: certain persons understood the manner in which human restoration had to take place; but, because they did not know the divine good pleasure concerning this very matter, they by no means dared to ask for it. Such understanding was given them so that they might understand what they ought to desire, for what they ought to sigh. And by desiring, groaning, and sighing long and earnestly, they might become worthy to be made certain concerning it. And behold: to those anxiously desiring and humbly supplicating, the coming of the Redeemer is revealed—though formerly thirsted for, it had not been foreknown. For now they deserve to hear: “Morning comes.” Thus the coming of the Son of God is revealed to the Gentiles in the words addressed to the mystical Idumaeans: “Morning comes.” The oracles of the prophet Balaam testify to what we say (Num. 24); the prophecies of the Sibyl likewise testify to it. And, unless I am mistaken, that altar at Athens consecrated to the unknown God bears witness to this testimony (Acts 17). When the Apostle Paul inquired whether the one to come would be a man or a spirit of the gods, blessed Dionysius answered: “True God and true man; and he himself will renew the world.” From these things, therefore, it is plain that the Gentiles knew beforehand of Christ’s coming through revelation.

Having received this divine revelation, prophetic men, whether from the Gentiles or from the Jews, sought with every earnestness—or confidence—what they had previously not dared to ask. What else did that voice of the prophet seek from the Father? “Send forth the lamb, ruler of the earth” (Isa. 16). What else did that voice of the Psalmist breathe forth toward him? “Send forth your hand from on high” (Ps. 143). Is not his coming sought from the Son himself both devoutly and no less openly, when it is said to him through the prophet: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and come!” (Isa. 64). Did not the Psalmist quite plainly request his coming when he cried out to him: “Stir up your power and come, that you may save us” (Ps. 79)?

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 1008A]

Thus the coming of Christ is foretold, and not Christ’s alone, but also that of Antichrist: “Morning comes, and night.” Christ’s coming makes day; Antichrist’s coming brings on night. O dark night, full of every horror, which the presence of Antichrist produces! For at that time such a darkness of deception will come upon the whole world that even the elect, if possible, will be led into error. Therefore he says: “Morning comes, and night.”

But if we return in these foregoing words to the tropological sense, perhaps we shall find something by which we may be built up. “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” Certainly, all of us who have been reborn in Christ, being children of light, ought to walk as children of light. Beyond doubt, the Idumaean’s night is one thing, and the Christian’s another; likewise, this one’s day is one thing, and that one’s another. The Idumaean’s day, as we have said, is the prosperity of this world, and his night its adversity. But what is said to the faithful man? “He will bring forth your righteousness like light, and your judgment as the noonday” (Ps. 36). “For the path of the righteous is like a shining light, and grows unto the perfect day” (Ps. 4). Therefore our day is righteousness, not unrighteousness. Diabolical temptation brings night; divine inspiration makes day. We encounter the darkness of night as often as we sin through ignorance or malice, and we need to cry out to our Samaritan: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

Who is this watchman to whom the cry is made in the night, if not that Samaritan who had mercy on the man who fell among robbers and cared for him (Luke 10)? For *Samaritan* is interpreted “watchman.” This Samaritan indeed watches over us in the day; he watches over us in the night. He watches over us in the day, I say, so long as he grants us perseverance in good. He watches over us in the night, lest, after a fall into sin, we be given over to a reprobate mind and, proceeding from evil to evil, finally fall into despair or perversity of mind. Therefore he is our watchman; he is likewise our comforter. He who watches over us in temptation is he who comforts us in tribulation. We have him as watchman and comforter; at his request and by his bestowal we receive another: “I will ask the Father,” he says, “and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14). *Paraclete* means the same as “comforter.” Concerning that same Paraclete, whom we receive through the Son, the Son himself says elsewhere: “When the Spirit, the Paraclete, comes, whom I shall send to you from my Father” (John 15).

Since, therefore, the only-begotten Son of God both watches over us by comforting us and comforts us by watching over us—and does so now through himself and now through his Spirit—it is rightly said to him twice over: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” Yet although, as has been said, he watches over us both by day and by night, the person who cries thus indicates that he is in the night, since he mentions not the daytime watch, but only the nighttime one. But the prayer of one walking in the day ought to be different from that of one walking in the night; different, finally, for one who performs works of light and for one who performs works of darkness.

We know that “he who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be made manifest” (John 3). Do you wish to hear how confidently such a worker prays, because he himself was walking in the light? “In whatever day,” he says, “I call upon you, quickly hear me” (Ps. 55). Hear, on the contrary, how timidly and bashfully one supplicates who recognizes that he has fallen into the darkness of wickedness: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” He does not say, “Spare me, spare me”; he does not say, “Have mercy.” O how tremblingly he supplicates who does not dare to say, “Have mercy upon me, O God, have mercy upon me”; who does not presume to say, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” We often hear those begging alms cry nothing else to a wealthy passerby but simply: “Sir, sir!” Thus this man cries with a suppliant’s voice to the ever-watchful and untiring guardian of our weakness: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

But what wonder if the Christian cries so humbly, when, as was said above, the Idumaean cries in this way? For the higher the rank, the worse the fall. Hence any Christian who has fallen into one sin is restored to life much more difficultly than any unbeliever whatsoever who is liable to however many crimes. Hear concerning this not my judgment, but the Apostle’s: “It is impossible,” he says, “for those who have once been enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift and been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have nevertheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and who have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance” (Heb. 6).

For unbelievers of whatever kind who flock to baptism are sufficiently aided by repentance alone, without any satisfaction. But for believing sinners who repent, repentance alone without fitting satisfaction is not sufficient. For Christians’ expiation after a fall is not customarily accomplished without the mortification of their own flesh; Christ’s passion customarily supplies to repentant unbelievers only the mortification of another’s flesh. For “if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins.” What wonder, then, if those who know the magnitude of their guilt groan humbly? Let those who are such therefore say, let them say: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?” By implication they show what they wish to ask but do not presume to do so. As though they said more openly: “We desire to ask forgiveness and to recover grace. But, recognizing how shamelessly we have behaved, we do not presume to ask. Of our own will we abandoned the ways of truth; deliberately we fell into works of darkness. We now wish to return, but among nocturnal terrors, among nocturnal horrors, we neither can nor know how. You indeed are he who can recall such persons, who is accustomed to recall such persons. Therefore, if you will, you do it. What you grant to others, you can grant also to us. Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”

But if every Christian rightly prays so humbly and so suppliantly after a fall, how much more one who has professed an order and religious life? For the reproach and shame of those who grow lukewarm and fall away in religious life is cast upon them and reproached to them by the Lord through what even secular persons often do: “From Seir one cries to me: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’” If an inhabitant of Seir cries so humbly, what more ought one to do whom the name of religious life honors, especially if he sees that he has fallen shamefully? Or do such people not know that “a little leaven corrupts the whole mass”? What good is it to gather wages and put them into a pierced vessel, and to lose from a small thing and in a moment whatever has been accumulated here and there over much time and through many labors? O how many years’ merits, how many rewards of merits, can be lost through the fall of one sin—and a single sin! Do you not know that “he who offends in one thing is guilty of all” (James 2)?

For one who by even one grievous sin has made God offended with him makes himself guilty also in all the other matters which he has observed: guilty, I say, though not to the extent that he should be punished in hell as though for transgressing those things, but to the extent that he is deprived of that reward of incorruption which he would have had in heaven for preserving the rest. Therefore, the person who, for momentary pleasure, despises God and Lord of the universe, abandons the fellowship of angels, and loses the kingdom of heaven—what, I ask, will he say when he stands to beseech God? Let him at least learn from the example what he ought to do. Let him learn, I say, how humbly he ought to pray and how bashfully he ought to supplicate, if the inhabitant of Seir prays so reverently and cries with such humble devotion—one who never held any place of holiness, who never deserved to taste how sweet the Lord is, how good the God of Israel is to those who are upright of heart. “From Seir,” he says, “one cries to me: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’”

## CHAPTER XV

But whoever you are who hear these things, if you consider the greatness of your downfall, you nevertheless have no reason to despair. For hear next what should rightly revive you to hope: “And the watchman said: ‘Morning comes.’” Behold, to one laboring in the night, to one supplicating for the attainment of morning, what he seeks with such humility is suddenly and unexpectedly promised. Therefore, in no enormity of vices should one despair of his mercy, for he is so abundant in forgiving.

But ought we therefore to implore him shamelessly and irreverently, because we have learned that he is so ready to pardon? On the contrary, the more kind and gracious we have found him whom we have stubbornly offended, the more we ought to blush in his presence and humbly ask forgiveness: “The watchman said: ‘Morning comes.’” For this watchman, to speak by promising—or to promise by speaking—is to pour into the supplicating soul, through the inspiration of his grace, the certainty of hope, and to remove every distrust or doubt from its expectation of what it desires. Therefore, by this promise, it is understood to be said in mystical speech what is answered through the watchman: “Morning comes, and night.”

[Col. 1011]

## HOW THE HOLY SPIRIT IS THE LOVE OF THE FATHER AND THE SON

[Col. 1011A] You ask to know how what Augustine says is true. For he says that the Father loves the Son through the Holy Spirit, and the Son loves his Father through the same Spirit. Yet he wholly denies that the Father is wise through that wisdom by which the Son is wise, and proves this by the following reasoning. For if he were wise through the wisdom which is the Son, he would be not so much Son from the Father as Father from the Son—among those for whom to be is the same as to be wise.

Hence some object in this way and say: since loving there is the same as being, how is it said that the Father or the Son does not exist by that love by which each loves the other? Therefore, since the Father is denied to be wise by the wisdom which he begot, lest he be understood to be through it, there is, as it seems to me, a great difference between doing and being made, between instructing and being instructed, between making wise and being made wise. Certainly, if the Father were wise and made wise by that wisdom which is the Son, he would without doubt be from him for whom to be is the same as to be wise and to be wise.

But when the Father instructs someone through the Son, he does something through that wisdom which is the Son, yet it does not follow that he is from the Son. Therefore, just as the Father instructs through the Son and yet it does not follow that he is from the Son, so he loves through the Holy Spirit, and yet it does not follow that he is from the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, when it is said that the Father or the Son loves through the Holy Spirit, this can be understood rightly or wrongly, and interpreted in a true or false sense. But perhaps you ask me to make this very distinction: how it can be understood now in the true, now in the false sense.

Without doubt, what the Son does, the Father does, from whom the Son receives the ability both to act and to be able to act. Hence comes that saying of blessed Hilary: “Understand the Son as acting. In the same manner, I say, understand the Holy Spirit as acting, and through him not only the Father but also the Son as acting. The Son instructs; the Holy Spirit loves; and in both cases the Father acts, because each receives from him the ability to do what he does. But when the Father is said to work through the Son, this is not understood as though the Son were the author and source of the power by which the Father is and does what he wills; rather, the Father is the author and source of the power by which the Son is, and the Son does what he does according to his good pleasure. Likewise, when the Father is said to love through the Holy Spirit, this is not understood as though the Holy Spirit were the author and source of the love by which the Father is and loves what he loves according to his will; rather, the Father breathes forth that love by which the Son is loved and which is the Holy Spirit, and he is its author and source. Therefore the Father is said to love through the Holy Spirit, not because he has love through him, but because he displays it through him; not because he receives love from him, but because he bestows it through him.”

Augustine says concerning the Son: “The Son spoke and the Father taught; and the Son said of himself: ‘My teaching is not mine.’ Why should not the Holy Spirit say, on equal grounds: ‘My love is not mine, but the Father’s, from whom I proceed, and the Son’s, who breathed it forth’? If the Holy Spirit is the love of both, why should the Father not rightly be said to love through the Holy Spirit—that is, through his own love? Why should the Son not likewise rightly be said to love through the Holy Spirit—that is, through his own love?”

The human mind is not love, but love proceeds from it; and therefore it does not love through itself, but through the love which proceeds from itself. But the Father is love, and the Holy Spirit is his love; and therefore the Father loves through himself, he loves through the Holy Spirit. He loves through himself as love; he loves through his own love. Who does not know that Jesus, the son of blessed Mary, and Jesus, the son of Nave [Joshua], are called *Jesus* equivocally? Likewise, “your love” and “divine love” would be called equivocally if the Holy Spirit were called the love of your heart, just as the Holy Spirit is called the love of the Father and the Son. Who, I ask, could deny that you love through the Holy Spirit—that is, through your own love? If you are rightly said to love through the love which proceeds from you, why should the Father and Son not rightly be said to love through the love which proceeds from them? Is this, brother, the question which they regard, call, and write of as insoluble?

[Col. 1011]

## ON THE EXCEEDING BAPTISM OF CHRIST

[Col. 1011D] To his kinsman by blood, his lord in holiness, his beloved N., his own unworthy R.: may they be of one mind in one will.

Moved by repentance concerning my promise, I almost preferred to have promised falsely rather than to write vainly, because, concerning the matters which you asked me to explain to you, I had no thought whatever that I judged worthy of utterance, much less of writing—especially because, in those things which I do understand slightly, I suffer from a lack of words. But because the child Jesus was not ashamed to lie hidden in swaddling-clothes (Luke 2), neither was I ashamed to send my poor understanding, slight though it is, clothed in the swaddling-clothes of words. Mary wraps her little child in swaddling-clothes as often as a chaste mind sets forth in simple words the truth which it perceives, however slightly. And perhaps, unless I am mistaken, it is preferable to incur empty speech rather than false speech.

Therefore, I beg you, attend more to who speaks, and to whom, than to what is said or how it is said. In return for this discourse, I ask not so much for an eloquent prayer as for a devout one; not one distinguished by a variety of words, but one filled with a rain of tears. Yet if you yourselves judge more rightly concerning the matters you ask of me, I claim that from you by right of recompense. But now I turn my pen to the prophet’s words, full of novelty and worthy of wonder, which you desire to have disclosed to you: “Illuminate your face,” etc. (Ps. 118).

But God gives increase by inwardly enlightening and sanctifying. Behold how great John was, how great Paul was. Yet they did not think great things of themselves, but humble things, because they had been enlightened so as to know themselves. We are nothing, and yet think great things of ourselves, because we are blind, having a film over our eyes. “He who sent me to baptize in water, he said to me: ‘Upon whom you see,’” etc. (John 1).

Some simpler people understand the descent of the Holy Spirit, as also the mission of the Son himself, insufficiently soundly. For when they hear Truth itself say: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16), they understand it as though he had previously been in the Father and not in the world; as though, when he went forth from the Father, he left the Father and departed from him; and as though, when he came into the world, he came to a place where he had not previously been. This understanding is wrong and must be cast out from every faithful heart.

For such people do not consider God’s immensity. Since God is immeasurable, he is in every place, filling every place. Consequently, he cannot pass from place to place as though leaving one place and occupying another. Moreover, he is not only in every place because he is immeasurable, but is wholly everywhere because he is simple. For this is the nature of simplicity: wherever it is, there it is wholly. Therefore, since God is immeasurable and simple, it follows that he is wholly everywhere. Nor, when he is said to be wholly everywhere, is he proclaimed to have parts; rather, precisely in this he is denied to have parts, because, if he had parts, he would not be wholly everywhere. Nor, when he is said to be wholly everywhere, should this be understood as though he poured himself into every creature according to fullness. Rather, he is wholly everywhere in himself: that is, wherever he is, he possesses his whole self. This must be understood concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

What, then, is the mission of the Son but the assumption of the form of a servant? And what is the descent of the Holy Spirit but a symbolic manifestation and mystical signification of him? For in descending in the form of a dove, he was not moved in himself, he who always remains unmoved in himself. Nor did he in any way begin to be in the Lord in whom he had not previously been. He is given to us who do not have him, and to those who have him, so that he may be possessed more fully. He was not given to the Lord as though the Lord did not have him, nor to one who had him so that he might possess him more fully; for he was given to him in the fullness at his conception. For just as the Father was with the Son in majesty and by the infusion of grace in the assumed man, so also was the Holy Spirit. But the Son alone was in him by personal union. Hence he alone—not the Father, not the Holy Spirit—is called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.”

Therefore, the descent of the Holy Spirit is nothing but a certain mystical signification of him. For in visibly manifesting himself in such a form above the baptized Lord, he indicated what is invisibly done in us when we are reborn in Christ; just as the Son was baptized, not for his own sake, as though needing any remedy, but in order to provide us with an example of humility and bestow the remedy of salvation. And the Father himself thundered thus: “This is my beloved Son,” etc. (Matt. 3), thereby showing that through the power of so great a sacrament we are made his sons.

Consider how great is the dignity of this sacrament: the Son himself commended it by receiving it; the Holy Spirit, by presenting himself; and the Father, by thundering thus. Through its efficacy we are made members of Christ, a temple of the Holy Spirit, and sons of God. Moreover, the heavens, formerly closed through guilt, are opened to us. Not without great mystery did the Holy Spirit descend—not in a raven, a kite, or another form, but only in the form of a dove. Of the dove it is written in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, one to her mother” (Song 6). By the dove the Church is understood. The Church is the body of Christ; the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Christ. Thus the Holy Spirit fittingly appeared in a dove, and not in another form, because the Spirit of Christ is nowhere but in the body of Christ. And only the body of Christ lives by the Spirit of Christ, just as my body alone lives by my spirit, and your body by your spirit. In Christ’s body nothing dead is found; outside it, nothing living.

The Apostle calls us to the unity of this body, saying: “Be diligent to preserve the truth of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4). He calls this unity “Spirit,” that unity which the Spirit produces in Christ’s body, which is the Church; and the bond of this unity is peace. To this unity he calls us, saying: “One body and one Spirit” (ibid.), as though to say: We ought therefore to preserve the unity of the Spirit, because we are one body and one Spirit: one body with our neighbor, and one Spirit with God; one body by mutually supplying one another’s needs, one Spirit by willing the same thing. We are one body by the union of many members, and one Spirit dwells in us. Therefore we ought also to preserve the unity of the Spirit, because we have one Lord, one faith, and one baptism.

We ought not to disagree because of a diversity of lords, because we have one Lord: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Those who have different lords sometimes disagree because their lords disagree. There are also those who have the same lord, but he does not remain one for long; rather, he changes almost every moment, now joyful, now sad, now just, now unjust. But our Lord, as he is one, so he always remains one and the same. There is also one faith: we are all commanded to believe the same thing, just as we are commanded to say the same thing. It does not become us who are faithful to disagree in confession of the faith. Let the integrity of faith therefore be pure and sincere in the heart, and let confession of faith be pure and sincere in the mouth; for with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

If we cannot fully understand everything that must be believed, let us at least retain the usage and manner of speaking which the holy Fathers have handed down to us in the Scriptures, especially when the subject is the incarnation of the Word or his eternal generation. Just as children are first taught to form sound words, and afterwards must be taught to understand what they say, so it is here. Behold, every day I hear in the Church that Christ is perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh; and likewise that he was begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages.

Many speak against this manner of speech, saying that Christ is not something insofar as he is man, nor begotten from the substance of the Father, since the saints say in many places that the divine essence begot divine essence, nature nature, substance substance, just as God begot God and person person. It is no wonder that those whose hands are leprous have leprous tongues. For there is a kind of wandering leprosy which passes from limb to limb. What wonder, then, that those who live badly understand wrongly? Blind men and leaders of the blind prefer arguments—indeed, fragments—of human reasoning to the most solid authorities of the holy Fathers; all such arguments are shattered against the rock of faith like a reed staff.

True is the judgment of Truth which he uttered concerning the firmness of faith: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16). And: “My sheep hear my voice, and do not follow a stranger” (John 10). And the Apostle says: “The firm foundation of faith stands, having this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’” (2 Tim. 2). But you, brothers, are the Lord’s sheep, children of the dove, children of Mother Church, members of Christ, whom that anointing itself teaches concerning all things: remain in unity, because we have one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.

“One baptism,” that is, of the same power and efficacy, by whomever it may be administered, because he who works inwardly is within and works without distinction through different ministers. Many boast that they have the Holy Spirit, although they do not have him. The nature of the dove teaches us to recognize those in whom the Holy Spirit is. For the dove is simple, without any gall; it does not live by plunder; it groans from love. Therefore the Holy Spirit dwells in those who are simple, free from the gall of all malice, groaning from love and from longing for the future life; and in those who are harmonious and preserve true peace and love among themselves, signified by the kisses of doves.

Scripture commends this innocence of simplicity to us through the lamb, and also through the child. Hence the Lord himself was called “the Lamb of God” (John 1) because of his complete innocence. And he says to Peter concerning those like him: “Feed my lambs” (John 21). He is called the shepherd of the sheep, and the faithful are the sheep of his pasture (John 10). The law also commanded that the priests should offer two lambs daily, one in the morning and the other in the evening (Exod. 29). In the morning people begin to work. Therefore the morning signifies the beginning of action, just as evening signifies its end. What, then, is it to offer two lambs but to begin works of innocence and carry them through to the end? This is the continual sacrifice, because God always requires from us the virtue of innocence, which is also signified by the child.

Thus: “Behold, I and my children” (Isa. 8); and in the Gospel: “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10); and elsewhere: “Unless you are converted and become like this little child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18). Therefore, if we wish to belong to the Lord’s flock, let us be lambs. If we wish to enter the kingdom of heaven, let us be children—but in malice, not in wisdom. If we wish the Holy Spirit to descend upon us and remain in us, let us be simple as doves; and moreover prudent as serpents. This is the serpent’s chief prudence: to guard its head. Therefore let us guard with every vigilance our head, in which is our life—namely Christ, who is the wisdom of God. Let us always fix our eyes upon this head, according to the saying: “The eyes of the wise are in his head” (Eccl. 2). If anyone plucks his eyes away from this head, he must become blind.

But someone may say: This head is now in heaven; it does not need me to guard it. Let him hear here what the Apostle says: that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts (Eph. 3). For faith in Christ in your heart is Christ in your heart. Therefore let us guard this head unharmed and whole, because our life is in this head, since “the righteous lives by faith.” Let us guard this head, as did he who said: “I have kept the faith,” like a prudent serpent.

But lest our simplicity be cold, we ought to be fervent in spirit. Hence the Holy Spirit appeared over the apostles in fire. And because this fervor of spirit is said to be not only in the heart but also in the mouth, so that we may rebuke sinners and kindle the cold, the gracious Spirit showed himself in tongues of fire. There are some who carry a foreign fire in their mouth, who bite in secret like a serpent. That fire is not heavenly but Gehenna’s; it is not bright but dark, because “he who does evil hates the light.”

“He who sent me to baptize,” etc. John baptized in water only, as man. Jesus baptizes in water and the Holy Spirit, as man and God. To baptize in the Spirit is to cleanse from every defilement of sin and, further, to infuse graces. For the Lord Jesus, when baptizing in the Spirit, first pours out bitterness and afterwards infuses sweetness; first he cleanses the vessels of hearts, then fills them when cleansed. Hence the Apostle says: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, that he might present her glorious, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5).

Consider the order and force of the words: “He loved, and gave himself up.” A great proof of great love. What did that self-giving confer upon her? Hear: first, that he might cleanse her from every contagion of sin; then, that he might sanctify her by the bestowal of gifts; and finally, that in the future he might present her to himself glorious—that is, radiant in soul and body, adorned with a double robe, having neither stain in the flesh nor wrinkle in the mind. And he did all this not because of works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his great mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly [Col. 1017A]; that is, through the washing of baptism, through which we are reborn as children of adoption, though formerly we were children of perdition. And through the Holy Spirit given to us in this sacrament, having put off the old nature, we are daily renewed in the knowledge and love of God.

“He poured him out upon us abundantly,” that is, for the remission of all sins and an abundance of virtues. Through remission of sins we are rescued from the power of darkness; through an abundance of virtues we are transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God. Through remission of sins we begin not to be what we were; through an abundance of virtues we begin to be what we were not. Contemplate with me the love of Christ surpassing knowledge: because of it he willed not only to become man, but also, having become man, to die for us. First he gave himself to us; then he gave himself [Col. 1017B] for us: to us through the incarnation, for us through the Passion. He sent his Spirit into our hearts, promised the vision of the Father, and granted the power by which we might become children of God.
