And he bestowed such dignity that we should have himself as our head, be his members, and be heirs of eternal life. Since, therefore, he is omnipotent, what more could he have given us? For this dignity was not granted to angelic nature, that it should be assumed by the Word of God into unity of person.

Let us therefore return such thanks as we can for so great a grace, since we cannot render thanks worthy of it. Let us not be ungrateful. Let no one call the blood of Christ—the blood of the New Testament, the blood by which he was sanctified—unclean. Let no one commit an outrage against the Holy Spirit. I tell you that he deserves far [Col. 1017C] worse punishments who despises the Son of God now glorified, now exalted above every dignity of the supracelestial essences, and seated on the throne of paternal majesty, than the Jews deserved who crucified him while he was still mortal, through ignorance. We have now known the truth, and therefore we shall be without excuse if we despise so great a salvation.

Both ways have been announced to us: the one leading to the left and the one leading to the right; the broad and spacious way leading to destruction [Col. 1018A], and the narrow way leading to life. The way of salvation is indeed narrow at the beginning—that is, for beginners, as though at its entrance—because it begins with fear of Gehenna and the mortification of vices, which is not accomplished without bitterness. But once a person has passed through the entrance and has taken his place in the courts of the Lord, he will encounter the breadth of charity and the sweetness of inward delight; through these, what had formerly seemed bitter will become pleasant.

Then at last the dove will utter its groan. What is the dove’s groan? “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. CXIX); and, “When shall I come, when shall I appear before the face of the Lord?” (Ps. XL); and, “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I); and, “Come, Lord Jesus, come, show your face” (Ps. LXXIX). “My soul refused to be comforted; I remembered God and was delighted” [Col. 1018B] (Ps. LXXVI). For every soul devoted to God, wounded by charity, and faint with love finds nothing under the sun in which it may take comfort. The remembrance of God alone delights it; its entire desire is to be before the Lord.

But the raven has a far different groan. The raven groans when it lacks carcasses in whose stench it may plunge its beak; the raven groans when it is told to depart from the body. Then it cries and says, “Not today, but tomorrow; not today, but tomorrow.” The dove does not say “tomorrow,” but “today,” when it is urged to leave prison. Let each person therefore see what he loves, and thus understand whence he is and what he is: a raven or a dove.

Brothers, let our every effort and our whole inward attention be directed to mortifying the diseased affection of the flesh [Col. 1018C], tearing the mind away from worldly desires, and kindling our hearts in the love of eternal life. This is accomplished by persistence in prayer, reading, and meditation. May he deign to bring us to that life in which no one dies, no one is born, no one hungers, no one thirsts, no one fears an enemy, no one betrays a friend; in which there is eternal satisfaction and supreme blessedness: he who is God above all, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1017]

## SERMON ON THE SENDING OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

[Col. 1017D] “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of voice” (Wis. I). Behold, brothers, what a Paraclete we receive by the Lord’s promise; behold what a comforter we have. Perhaps you desire to know more plainly how great he is, or of what kind. He is everywhere, can do all things, and absolutely nothing can be hidden from him. Surely such a one had to be he who could come to meet all people everywhere: he who had to bring back so many exiles, gather together those so scattered, strengthen so many mourners, and restore so many despairing persons to pardon.

Likewise, he had to be such that he could fill whatever he willed: he who had to heal so many sick persons [Col. 1018D], protect so many oppressed persons, preserve them amid so many dangers, and fortify them against so many temptations. Finally, he had to be such that he knew everything: he who nevertheless had to convert so many unbelievers, teach so many who did not believe, instruct so many untaught persons, and educate so many ignorant persons. We have received, then, the comforter, protector, and teacher that was required: a comforter present everywhere, an omnipotent protector, and a teacher knowing all things. And certainly those burdened by so many miseries required a comforter present everywhere; those corrupted by so many vices, an omnipotent protector; those led astray by so many errors, a teacher knowing all things.

O sweet comforter! [Col. 1019A] O mighty protector! O effective teacher, who is everywhere, who can do all things, who knows all things! And what else do the words set above appear to declare, if they are duly weighed, than that our promised and sent Paraclete is everywhere, can do all things, and knows all things? “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of voice.”

If this Spirit of the Lord fills the whole world, how much more must he fill the kingdom of heaven? For who could doubt that he is in heaven? Scripture therefore affirms this concerning that part about which perhaps someone could doubt. Thus we have an argument from the lesser: this Spirit must be believed to be present everywhere. For if he is everywhere on earth, how much more, as has been said, everywhere in heaven? He will therefore be everywhere in all places.

Do you also wish to know that this Spirit, whom it is already established is everywhere, can do all things? But how can he not have power over all things who contains all things? Certainly, if anything could subsist without him, this Spirit could by no means be said to contain all things. If, therefore, nothing can subsist without him, then everything that exists has its being from him. Since from him comes the being of all things, it is clearly established that he can do all things. It is thus an argument from the whole that he can do all things: nothing subsists, or can subsist, without him.

You have heard concerning his presence; you have heard concerning his power. Do you still wish to know what should be thought of his knowledge? Attend, then, to what is asserted of him in the words: “And that which contains all things has knowledge of voice.” This is the same as if it said [Col. 1019C], “knowledge of all speeches,” except that the former expression is more appropriately understood than the latter, because it applies not merely to particulars, as the latter does, but also to universals, to which the latter cannot aptly be applied. This Spirit therefore has knowledge not only of speech in general, but also specifically of every kind of speech, and even singularly of each individual utterance.

But because he has knowledge of utterances, does he also have knowledge of things? Certainly, without doubt. For complete knowledge of utterances is always accompanied by knowledge of things, though knowledge of things is not always accompanied by knowledge of utterances. We often think that we know many things whose names we nevertheless do not know or have forgotten. But who has full knowledge of the word *bos* (“ox”) if he wholly ignores the thing itself? Yet I think that angels would have complete knowledge of things even if there were no words. Knowledge of things can therefore exist naturally even where there is no knowledge of words. Certainly Adam, who gave names to things before their names existed, had knowledge of the things. Otherwise, how could he have assigned suitable names to things of which he had no knowledge? “Whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name” (Gen. II). It therefore seems to be more to have knowledge of utterances than of things, since, as was said, knowledge of things always accompanies knowledge of utterances.

It should certainly be noted that he does not say “knowledge of discourse” (*sermo*) [Col. 1020A], but “of voice” (*vox*). Every discourse is a voice, but the proposition cannot be reversed: not every voice is discourse. Some voices have a natural capacity to signify, such as the lowing of oxen and the bleating of sheep; but discourse is a meaningful voice according to convention. Thus every voice has the capacity to signify something either naturally or accidentally. I do not think that there is anything which cannot be expressed in discourse or signified by a voice. Therefore, because the signification of *voice* extends more widely than that of *discourse*, it is rightly said of this Spirit that he has knowledge of voice.

But, as was already said above, knowledge of utterances always entails knowledge of things. It is therefore an argument that this Spirit knows all things, because he is said to have knowledge of voice. If he knows that which is greater, then much more does he know that which is less. But it has been shown that knowledge of utterances is more than knowledge of things. It is therefore an argument from the greater that all things must be known by this Spirit. The first argument, then, is drawn from the lesser; the third, as has been said, is drawn from the greater; while the middle argument is an argument from the whole.

Let it therefore be said of this Spirit, let it be said: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of voice” (Gen. II). Let it be said that he fills the whole world, that he may be believed to be everywhere; let it be said that he contains all things, that he may be understood to be able to do all things; let it be said that he has knowledge of voice, that he may be understood to know all things.

It should further be noted in these words how fittingly and distinctly both the plurality of persons and unity of substance are commended. For after the statement, “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world,” it immediately adds, “and that which contains all things,” not “he who contains all things,” although this too could rightly have been said. But sacred Scripture, by a wonderful design, wished, as has been said, to show in so few words both the plurality of persons and the unity of substance. The plurality of persons is shown in that this Spirit is called the Spirit of the Lord. For he is one, and the one whose Spirit he is said to be is another. Yet identity of substance is shown when this same Spirit is said to be that through which all things are contained.

This Spirit, therefore, is the very same thing as he from whom are all things; the very same thing as he through whom [Col. 1020D] are all things; the very same thing as he who in the beginning created heaven and earth; that which is he through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made. This Spirit, then, is the same as the Father and the same as the Son, because Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, one substance, one nature, one divinity, one majesty. Thus it is rightly written of this Spirit: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of voice.”

But if this Spirit both contains and fills all things alike, what, I ask, did the disciples of the Lord receive on this day, if they had already before this day been filled with the Spirit who fills all things? Why, at this celebration of Pentecost, do we recollect or worship the coming of the Holy Spirit, whom we know to be everywhere [Col. 1021A] and to fill all things? From where could he come, if he is everywhere and can be absent nowhere? Or what more could they receive of him if they had already been filled with this Spirit?

But it must be understood that this Spirit, like the whole Trinity, is present in one manner through the everywhere-present power of his majesty, and in another through grace that breathes within. The presence of his majesty is with every bodily and incorporeal creature, both inanimate and animate. For the Spirit of wisdom reaches everywhere because of his purity. Through enlightening wisdom, this same Spirit is present only to rational creatures, yet to all of them, whether good or evil, blessed or miserable. For he enlightens every human being coming into this world; and if every human being, then the just and unjust, those to be blessed [Col. 1021B] and those to be condemned. Through inspiring grace he is present to all the good, both perfect and imperfect, blessed and to be blessed. For he is the one who works all things in all, distributing to each as he wills.

Thus he is in all creatures by the diffusion of his substance; he is present to all rational beings by participation in his wisdom; and he is present to all good persons by the co-operation of his grace. The presence of his majesty is therefore at hand to every creature, always and everywhere present, so that it can no more ever be absent than it can ever not be present. According to this mode, therefore, he cannot depart from anywhere or return to anywhere, but remains immovably everywhere at every time.

But by participation in his wisdom, just as he is immovably absent from certain of his creatures, so he is always present to others. To the former he can never be present in this respect; from the latter he can never wholly be absent in the same respect. For he cannot be wholly absent from rational creatures, to whom participation in his wisdom is always communicable. Otherwise, how, I ask, could those creatures be rational which could not at all be capable of reason or participants in wisdom? But an irrational creature, because it is not capable of reason, cannot receive this Spirit according to participation in wisdom. Otherwise it would not be irrational if it were capable of reason and wisdom.

According to the infusion of grace, however, he can be present to these same creatures after a long absence and, after a long presence, again be absent [Col. 1021D] and remain absent longer. According to this mode, therefore, this Spirit goes and comes, departs and returns. “For the Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John III). As was said, this Spirit now withdraws and now imparts the infusion of his grace, and in this manner often goes and comes.

But, to make you wonder still more, it often happens that at one and the same time this Spirit remains in one respect and departs in another. For when the Spirit of manifold grace withdraws from a person some one grace previously possessed, while permitting him at the same time to retain another, does he not, with respect to the same person and at the same time, as has been distinguished, go away in one respect and come in another? You see, therefore, how differently the Spirit is ordinarily related to these persons according to the threefold mode of infusion: namely, of his substance, wisdom, or grace.

Certainly, according to the diffusion of his substance he is believed to be everywhere; but according to the infusion of grace, it is established that on this day he descended upon that land and filled it with the illumination of his grace—the land of which it is written: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will, except that it burn?” (Luke XII). What is this land but the primitive Church? What, I say, is that land into which the heavenly fire descended but the Church of Christ, into which today the Holy Spirit descended in fire and tongues? This is the land that stands for ever, because it has been founded upon a firm rock, and therefore the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

Whoever remains steadfast in the faith and charity of Christ belongs to this land [Col. 1022B]. But whoever wavers in faith or still fluctuates through various desires is like a wave of the sea, moved and driven about by the wind. Such a person cannot belong to that land, or world, of which it is written: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. XXIV). Rather, he appears to belong to those seas above which that world was established by the working of its founder, the Lord, of whom it also says: “For he founded it upon the seas and prepared it upon the rivers” (ibid.).

But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to this world: “For whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ, this one is not his.” If therefore, truly and without doubt, “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it,” then whoever desires to belong to this world must have the Spirit of the Lord. It is therefore rightly understood of this world that today it is sung so festively: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world.” Was not the Lord’s land saturated—indeed, filled—with this Spirit when the primitive Church, as has been said, received in fiery tongues that Paraclete who proceeds from the Father? Does it not seem to you that at that time what is sung in the Psalm was fulfilled: “You visited the earth and made it drunk” (Ps. LXIV)? For the inhabitants of this land were so intoxicated by that spiritual new wine that anyone who could hear them then might rightly have wondered how they could be drunk when it was already the third hour of the day [Col. 1022D]. For they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various tongues as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance (Acts II). This, indeed, is what we ought to recollect each year; this is what we recollect annually when we sing: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world.”

Do you also wish to know how he contained all things in that land which he had filled entirely? Consider, then, how steadfastly he acted after this filling by the Spirit—the man who had formerly been frightened by the voice of a maidservant and had denied Christ. Likewise the others, who had formerly hidden themselves for fear of the Jews, now openly confess Christ before the rulers of the priests. Whence came this to them, except that they were clothed with power from on high in receiving the Spirit of the Lord? “For the Spirit of his mouth is all their strength” [Col. 1023A] (Ps. XXXII). Whatever steadfastness, whatever endurance they possessed, came from that Spirit who had filled their hearts. In short, whatever power and whatever strength they had, they received from the same Spirit who contains all things.

Let no one, therefore, attribute to himself that he stands firm in faith or perseveres in goodness. For no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit. If one cannot say anything good without this Spirit, when can one do anything good without him? For he is the one who works all things in all, distributing to each as he wills. Thus everyone who perseveres in goodness stands in him; and “let him who stands take heed lest he fall.”

“But,” you ask, “how can anyone fall—indeed, how can anything good fail anyone—if this Spirit contains all things?” Perhaps the things which this Spirit deigns to contain are said to be. For who would deny that whoever is abandoned by this Spirit loses true being? In no way can things not sustained by this Spirit belong to true being, since he is known to contain all things. For how can things be said to exist if they have lost true being? Yet those same persons return, as it were, to being when they receive this Spirit of the Lord, through the action of him who “calls those things which are not as though they were” (Rom. IV). “He will send forth his Spirit, and they shall be created, and he shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. CIII). Every state of rectitude, therefore, is both attained through him and likewise sustained by him. And because what is abandoned by him in some measure ceases to be [Col. 1023C], this Spirit is rightly said to contain all things.

But I ask again how this same Spirit had knowledge of voice. Was it perhaps in that he caused it to be possessed? Thus it was also said to Abraham (Gen. XXII): “Now I know that you fear God,” meaning, “I have caused it to be known.” The Jews—devout men from every nation under heaven—testify how wondrous and astonishing was that knowledge of voice which the Spirit gave when he filled the hearts of the disciples: “Behold,” they say, “are not all these who speak Galileans? And how have we each heard our own language in which we were born?” (Acts II).

But lest it seem little to you that they spoke in the languages of all nations, ask those same Jews further what they spoke in those languages. “We have heard them,” they say, “speaking in our tongues the mighty works of God” [Col. 1023D] (ibid.). O how great a thing it is to speak the mighty works of God even in one language! Yet although it was great that they sounded these things outwardly in speech, far greater, nevertheless, is believed to be what they themselves heard inwardly. It was indeed great to hear that voice through which the disciples of Christ taught the mighty works of God; but far greater was it to understand that voice of inward inspiration through which they themselves learned. Yet they possessed knowledge of both voices: both the voice through which they learned and that through which they taught. Otherwise they would neither have known the mighty works of God themselves nor made them known to others.

The voice which they outwardly formed was bodily; the voice which they inwardly heard was spiritual. The former sounded outwardly with noise and expressed one thing after another to the hearers, in whatever way and to whatever extent it could; the latter breathed inwardly without any noise, and in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, impressed upon their minds whatever it willed and as much as it pleased. O how great is the difference between voice and voice, between bodily voice and that spiritual voice! Yet that Spirit who contains all things both has knowledge of each and causes knowledge of each to be possessed.

For since, as you read, “that which contains all things has knowledge of voice,” let it not be enough for you who hear or read these things to have heard or known only that voice which usually resounds outwardly, and to possess knowledge of it. Strive and labor to hear and understand that voice which alone suffices to lead one into all truth, and which alone teaches a person knowledge without the noise of words. The prophet sought this voice of inward inspiration when he said: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” [Col. 1024B] (Ps. CXVIII).

What wonder, however, that he longed and sighed for that voice, whose power and sweetness he had learned so thoroughly and experienced so often? You have heard above concerning its power; do you also wish to hear concerning its sweetness? You have heard how effective those inward utterances are for teaching; now attend to how sweet they are to hear. Yet let the one say this whom experience had taught: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” (Ps. XCIII). If it is so great and pleasant—so far as I speak from experience—to hear spiritual persons and to have teachers of truth who are so learned, how much greater and more pleasant is it to learn daily from God himself, and daily to have learned from him! “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law.”

The prophet feared losing this blessedness and losing the teaching of his Lord when he said in prayer: “O Lord, who shall be like you? Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God” (Ps. LXXXII). It is indeed little to me if I speak with the tongues of human beings and angels, unless I may one day deserve to hear and understand what the Lord God speaks in me. For what does it avail to have knowledge of human or angelic speech, yet not to know the voice of him who has knowledge of every voice and, when he wills, causes it to be possessed? O truly blessed apostles, who had such a teacher, who received the Spirit of truth [Col. 1024D], who had knowledge of all things and could give knowledge of all things! O truly blessed those whose hearts this Spirit filled with his grace, whose souls he strengthened for every virtue, whose minds he enlightened for every knowledge! Rightly, in recollection of his deed, we sing what we have already repeated so often and do not cease to repeat: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of voice.”

We have now said in what respect Christ’s disciples could receive the Spirit of the Lord, who nevertheless, in a certain respect, could never be absent from them, since he is known to be everywhere and to fill all things. For he who is everywhere according to the presence of his majesty can, according to the bestowal of his grace, as we have already said, be present and absent. Thus this Spirit granted them an abundance of his presence in pouring into them an abundance of his grace [Col. 1025A]. Truly, therefore, and without doubt, on this day those who awaited the coming of the Holy Spirit with faith and longing according to Christ’s promise received the Holy Spirit.

But again I ask: before that coming of the Holy Spirit, were they without the Holy Spirit? Before that day of Pentecost, did they not have the grace of the Holy Spirit? If no one can say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit, was Peter then without him when he so confidently and truly dared to confess concerning Christ before Christ: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI)? Were Christ’s disciples without the Holy Spirit when they cast the unclean spirit out of possessed bodies and performed many other signs of this sort? (Luke X). Certainly, before that day we know it happened—and must not doubt it—because we read in the Gospel that Jesus breathed on them, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John XX).

But, to pass over the rest, they could not even believe in Christ without the grace of the Holy Spirit. What then did they receive on this day, if even before this day they had been saturated with the grace of the Holy Spirit? It is certainly established that drops of grace of this kind are given sometimes merely as an infusion, sometimes to the point of diffusion, and at times even to the point of effusion [Col. 1025C]. Infusion exists even when less flows in than the vessel can receive. Diffusion is when it is poured in until no part of it is left empty. Infusion passes into effusion when what has been poured in overflows.

In accordance with this analogy, many receive the grace of the Holy Spirit: some only to the point of infusion, others to the point of diffusion, and still others to the point of effusion. The person who receives only to the point of infusion receives grace indeed, but less than could suffice for him. The person who receives to the point of diffusion receives as much grace as can suffice for him. The person who receives to the point of effusion has such an abundance that it can suffice both for himself and for others. Infusion is for sustenance, diffusion for satisfaction, effusion for distribution. Infusion is for refreshment, diffusion for filling [Col. 1025D], effusion for dispensing. Infusion is for the beginning of good; diffusion and effusion are for the completion of good. Infusion is for the building up of oneself; effusion, for the building up of one’s neighbor. Through the latter a person receives so as to benefit others; through the former, so as to make progress himself.

Thus we can have grace and yet lack its fullness. For it is one thing to have grace present, and another to have sufficient grace. Certainly the disciples of the Lord were not without grace before this day, but on this day they received fullness of grace. Indeed, one among them was he whom Scripture declares to be full of grace when it says: “Stephen, full of grace and strength, performed many signs and wonders among the people” (Acts VI).

At that time, therefore, the apostles received the infusion of the Holy Spirit to the point of diffusion, because “they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” [Col. 1026A]; and not merely to the point of diffusion, but also to the point of effusion, because “they began to speak in various tongues the mighty works of God.” Those who were filled with the Holy Spirit therefore received the fullness of grace. And those who had previously possessed grace present began now to possess sufficient grace. Peter’s fall testifies to the character of the first grace; Stephen’s steadfastness declares the character of the second. Certainly Peter would not have fallen if he had possessed the fullness of grace; nor would Stephen have stood at so lofty a height of virtues if he had lacked fullness.

But when we say that they received fullness of grace, we mean, certainly, that they received sufficient grace, not that after that infusion they possessed every grace. For to possess or be able to receive every grace belongs only to him “from whose fullness we all have received.” We therefore mean nothing else by saying that someone receives fullness of grace than that, according to the condition of the present life and the capacity of each person, he has sufficient grace. For the fullness of grace which a human being could have—or rather did have—before sin was one thing; that which he now has or can have in the condition of present misery is another.

Before sin, indeed, a human being had sufficient grace both to avoid every evil and to discharge every obligation; otherwise he could not have avoided sin. But no one has this fullness of grace in this life, nor can anyone have it without doubt. To which human being was it ever given either to fulfill every obligation or to avoid every unlawful act? This is rightly believed only of him of whom it is truly written: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Col. 1026C] (I Pet. II).

Thus, with regard to the condition of the present life, we mean nothing else by saying that someone is full of the Holy Spirit or has fullness of grace than that he has received from the Lord sufficient grace for all those things which God wills strictly to require of him, although not for all those things which he mercifully intends to forgive him. Yet many things are great—indeed, more arduous and difficult than all the rest—which God requires from a human being after he has sinned, though he would never require them if humanity had never sinned. “For through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God.”

Recall, I ask, how much those endured for Christ who heard from him: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XXI; Luke IX). You know well enough by what way Christ entered eternal life. “For it was necessary that Christ suffer and rise from the dead, and thus enter into his glory” (Luke XXIV). Likewise the saints, having experienced mockery and scourges, and furthermore chains and prisons, “were stoned, were sawn asunder, were tempted, were put to death by the sword” [Col. 1026D] (Heb. XI), so that they might run after Christ and, keeping Christ’s way, enter into life with Christ.

But would God have required from man endurance of tribulations and labours, injuries and insults, suffering and [Col. 1027A] death, if man had not sinned? He certainly would not have required it. But behold, he now requires all such things from man, and for all such things he mercifully grants and lavishly bestows his grace upon many. Thus, in some respect, a person seems able in this state of our mortality to receive a greater grace, although he cannot fully recover the integrity of that first perfection. And in a wonderful way, one who is unequal to that first path of perfect purity now girds himself for greater contests of virtues.

Therefore, just as we call a vessel full when it holds as much as it can hold, so we declare a person full of grace when he receives grace such and so great as he is fitted to receive according to the capacity of his condition. Thus one receives more, another less; and according to the distributions of graces, “to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness.” To one indeed, through the Spirit, is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in one Spirit. And in this manner the one and same Spirit works many other things, distributing to each as he wills.

Behold, brothers, what a Paraclete—what a Comforter—those received who deserved to hear from the Lord: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John XIV). Oh, what it will be to have that Comforter himself, who is powerful to work all things in all people and to distribute to each [Col. 1027C] as he wills! If, therefore, we wish to have such a Comforter, let us strive to be such persons as he may deign to descend upon with his grace: “Upon whom,” he says, “does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who fears my words?” (Isa. LXVI). Behold what one must be who awaits the coming of this Spirit. Oh, how gladly and joyfully ought we to cast ourselves down into every submission and incline ourselves to every humility, that we may deserve to receive this Spirit and have such a Comforter!

Consider, I beg you, how sweet and delightful it is to be cherished by his consolation and filled with his sweetness—whose pleasantness surpasses every pleasantness, whose sweetness exceeds every sweetness. Hear what he thinks of the one from whom this sweetness flows: “My Spirit,” he says, [Col. 1027D] “is sweeter than honey” (Ecclus. XXIV). O happy heart, filled with this honey! O blessed soul, refreshed by this pleasantness! “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient.” Taste and see, I beseech you who are such; taste, I say, and see how pleasant is that Spirit, sweeter than honey. I am astonished if you do not cry out with a voice of exultation and thanksgiving: “O Lord, how sweet is your Spirit within us!” Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for this inward sweetness, for they shall be filled when they taste it.

I boldly affirm that a single drop of this honey can do what the whole world cannot do. A heart which all the abundance of the world does not satisfy is completely intoxicated by one drop of this sweetness. Certainly that great Alexander, who was able to subdue the whole world, [Col. 1028A] was unable to satisfy his desire. For after the world had been subdued to him, if there were yet another world which he believed he could bring under his rule, he would strive to subdue it with no less eagerness. And if, after that too had been subdued, still others and others remained, they could rather provoke than satisfy the voracity of his heart.

Consider, therefore, how great is the breadth of that world which is within, since this outer world, however much enlarged or however often multiplied, cannot satisfy it. Do not philosophers seem to have erred in calling man a *microcosm*, that is, a lesser world? Is not the human mind rightly to be called a greater world, since it is certainly greater than the world—a mind which the whole world, by no enlargement or multiplication of itself, can satisfy? For if this globe of earth is compared with the breadth of one heart, what else does it appear, in comparison with that heart’s capacity or appetite, than some small morsel which, cast into the mouth of the inner person, cannot fill it at all—indeed, scarcely appears there?

But if you thirst for that inward and heavenly sweetness, if you long for true and eternal pleasantness, hear what is divinely commanded to you and attend also to what is promised you: “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX). Certainly, if you hunger for earthly delights and thirst for carnal pleasures, it is better for you to contract rather than enlarge your mouth, to restrain rather than extend your desire, since nowhere [Col. 1028C] can you find what will satisfy it and fulfil it. What is the mouth of the inner person except the desire of the heart? For it is neither a great promise for God nor a great gain for man to fill the mouth of the outer person, since one mouthful of bread can and usually does fill it. But that mouth of the inner person—that is, the desire of the heart—is never satisfied or filled except inwardly with spiritual delights; and blessed is the person who has filled his desire from them.

Certainly, whoever you are who have spiritual delights at hand, or can have them, you have wherewith to fill your mouth; you have wherewith to fill your belly; you also have wherewith to fill your tent. “Enlarge the place of your tent, make your cords long, stretch them out; do not spare.” The delights of the Spirit are sufficient [Col. 1028D] and superabundant to fill your mouth, your belly, your tent—in short, to fill that entire world whose breadth we have said much about already, though we have not been able worthily to express it.

Therefore, when the Spirit of the Lord has in this manner filled that world with inward sweetness, and has “filled your desire with good things,” you will begin to wonder how that land which is not satisfied with water can be satisfied with such sweetness. Or can that which cannot be filled with water perhaps be filled with honey? Or can that which cannot be satisfied with water be intoxicated with spiritual wine? “You visited the earth and made it drunk” (Ps. LXIV). Those whom the Jews wondered were drunk, though it was scarcely the third hour of the day, were surely made drunk with such wine.

You have heard of those intoxicated with wine; hear also of those satisfied with honey: “He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. LXXX). He entirely fails to know what true and full refreshment is, who is not satisfied by that superheavenly sweetness, sweeter than honey; and such a person can sing to the Lord: “For my soul is to you like land without water” (Ps. CXLII). Conversely, whenever that spiritual sweetness has satisfied the empty soul and filled the hungry soul with good things, it ought to sing and say: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. I), because he himself has fulfilled every desire with good things.

Yet, as we have already indicated, not all receive this infusion of inward sweetness in equal measure: some receive it only as an infusion, [Col. 1029B] others up to a diffusion, while others receive it even up to an outpouring. If you are still content with infusion alone, it will rightly be said to you: “Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song IV). But when you have been filled with a more abundant supply of such infusion, not only in the bosom of your mind but also in your mouth, and have received this instillation of spiritual sweetness up to diffusion, you will think these words addressed to you: “Grace has been poured out upon your lips” (Ps. XLIV). But when this flood of spiritual grace begins to rise higher, to flow abundantly through the mouth, and the infusion of sweetness passes into outpouring, then, I think, after such an outpouring has come about, it will rightly be said to you—whoever you are, whose soul has been drenched by such an outpouring: “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb” (Song IV).

Certainly, he had experienced this abundance of inward sweetness who said: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. XXX). Without doubt he had experienced it who rejected every other consolation whenever he grieved at its withdrawal, and therefore said: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. LXXVI). For this sweetness alone gives form to the mind in its depths, and does not permit it to run after and wander among alien desires. Thus, the wandering and fugitive human mind upon the earth—which flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state—has reason to wonder, if it is permitted to experience these things, how it clings wholly to one desire for inward pleasantness; how that entire host of so many desires binds itself to a single longing; and [Col. 1029D] how so great a household of innumerable thoughts remains fixed upon one and the same object of its desire.

But whence, I ask, comes this, except because the Spirit of the Lord, who fills all things, also at the same time holds all things together? In filling, he also contains. For by the very means through which he touches our inward parts with his sweetness, he turns every movement of the heart toward himself and fixes it in the longing for that sweetness which it has experienced. The restless course of fluctuating desires and turbulent thoughts is never checked unless it is satisfied by inward refreshment. For as long as the mind cannot attain true and full refreshment, it always has something toward which it hastens in desire. Thus one and the same spiritual sweetness alone suffices to satisfy our inward parts and bring them into one peace; so that the same Spirit is rightly said both to fill all things and to contain all things.

Yet poverty of spirit more effectively secures and more easily acquires this spiritual satisfaction than abundance of wealth. Truly, “blessed are the poor in spirit,” according to the saying of the Lord Jesus (Matt. V). “For the poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord.” Conversely, “the rich have lacked and hungered.” Therefore the poor rightly praise, since they have deserved to be satisfied. Oh, how delightful is the praise that follows this satisfaction! Oh, how inward is the exultation that accompanies this sweetness! “They shall utter the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and shall exult in your righteousness” (Ps. CXLIV).

The Prophet was inviting the guests of that inward sweetness to this praise and such exultation when he said: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name” (Ps. CII). And the reason follows when it is said: “Who fills your desire with good things” (*ibid.*). How great, I ask, is the acclamation; how great, I beseech you, is the cry that ascends on high and reaches the ears of the Lord of Hosts, when that whole inner household cries out together in divine praise and resounds in harmonious accord with a voice of exultation and thanksgiving; when the whole substance of the inner person is dissolved into dancing, and the mind of the person, dissolved to its marrow, is wholly turned into jubilation! This is that voice of salvation heard in the tents of the righteous. Truly it is a voice of salvation, a voice of jubilation: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. CXVII).

Who, then, can worthily explain the dignity of this voice, or even worthily estimate it? Therefore the Spirit of the Lord alone knows it and is sufficient to weigh it worthily—the Spirit who by his sweetness dissolves hardness of heart into such dancing. What other voice, I ask, is more rightly understood in the words: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice” (Wis. I)? What, I say, is this voice which the Spirit of the Lord is said to know, whose knowledge he deigns especially to possess? You see how “voice” is here used without qualification, so that whatever voice is more worthy and excellent than all others by the loftiness of its greatness and prerogative of dignity is rightly understood. Thus, when “the Prophet” or “the Apostle” is mentioned without qualification, no other is consequently understood than the foremost of prophets and the preeminent of apostles: David [Col. 1030D] and Paul.

What then is this voice of voices, except that which alone can and customarily does make a people blessed? “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation.” Blessed is the one who finds within himself, who feels in his inmost parts, wherewith he may sing for himself and, as it were, from conviction: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice.” Blessed is the person whose desire has been so satisfied and filled with a certain spiritual sweetness that, concerning the breadth or appetite of his heart, he may dare truthfully to confess: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world.” Blessed is the soul whose every inmost affection has been so fixed in a desire for divine sweetness alone and is so free from every fall into concupiscence [Col. 1031A] that, upon the testimony of conscience and concerning its inmost parts, it may dare to profess: “The Spirit of the Lord is that which contains all things.” Blessed is the soul which attends within itself to such a cry of joy and thanksgiving, and rightly ascribes knowledge of it to him alone who in it fills all things and contains all things, so that it says with confidence and sings from experience: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world; and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice.”

Truly and without doubt, that person seems to me to experience the power of this solemnity whose tongue, upon the testimony of conscience, is released into this confession, when from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, so that he truthfully professes concerning himself: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world; and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice.”

[Col. 1031]

## ON THE COMPARISON OF CHRIST TO A FLOWER AND MARY TO A ROD

[Col. 1031A] The Virgin Mother of God is the rod; her Son is the flower. For blessed Virgin Mary is rightly called a rod: a straight rod, [Col. 1031B] an upright rod reaching even to heaven, a slender rod, a flexible rod, a flowering rod, a fruitful rod. Straight through faith; upright through sight; tall through long-suffering; slender through humility; flexible through compassion; flowering through virginal conception; fruitful through the birth of salvation. The Virgin Mother of God is the rod; her Son is the flower.

Oh, how fittingly and rightly is he called a flower who is produced from the virginal rod! What is more delicate than a flower? What more tender? What softer to the touch? What lighter to carry? What more beautiful than a flower, what more fragrant, what more fruitful, if we consider its effect? For in the flower is honey-making; from the flower comes fruit-bearing. Thus from the flower come honeycomb and fruit. In the honeycomb are honey and wax; in the fruit, drink and food. If these things are small, I add that in the flower there is also [Col. 1031C] medicine. For what is more delicate than a flower when it is gathered? What more tender when crushed? What softer when handled? What lighter when carried? What more beautiful when viewed? What more fragrant when smelled? What more useful, if its effects are considered?

There are therefore seven things which we admire in a flower: delicacy, [Col. 1032A] tenderness, softness, lightness, beauty, fragrance, usefulness. From these, then, infer what kind of Son of the Virgin is found by those for whom he is changed into a flower. For he who is to unbelievers and transgressors “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence” is a flower to those who cling to him in hope and love: a flower indeed wonderful, singular in hope and usefulness. The Son of the Virgin, I say, is a flower: delicate in indignation, tender in compassion, gentle in meekness, light in condemnation, beautiful in conduct, fragrant in promise, useful in recompense. Thus he is delicate in scourges, tender in mercies, gentle in gifts, light in commandments, beautiful in examples, fragrant in promises, fruitful in rewards.

This flower has become medicine for us: from him come honey and wax; in him are drink and food. Medicine in redemption; drink and food in justification; honey and wax in glorification. [Col. 1032C] From this medicine comes the health of everlasting incorruptibility; from his food, the refreshment of inward satisfaction; from such drink, the intoxication of eternal security; from his wax, the splendour of highest brightness; in his honey, the sweetness of unfailing blessedness.

[Col. 1031]

## ON THE SACRIFICE OF THE PROPHET DAVID, AND HOW IT DIFFERS FROM THE SACRIFICE OF THE PATRIARCH ABRAHAM

[Col. 1031C] “I will offer you marrow-rich burnt offerings with the incense [Col. 1031D] of rams; I will offer you oxen with goats” (Ps. LXX). Let us consider, if you please, what sacrifices of this sort signify: ram’s flesh, ox’s flesh, goat’s flesh. For I think all these things are spoken figuratively. Otherwise, if you understand them all carnally, if you attend only to the letter, attend to what is said to you: “Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. XLIX). Therefore, in the carnal sacrifices of the Jews let us understand nothing carnally, but examine spiritually those things which according to the letter savour of flesh.

For the Prophet would never promise ram’s, ox’s, or goat’s flesh to the Lord as though it were some great thing, unless he perceived that something great and very pleasing to the Lord was foreshadowed in these things. The ram is a very gentle animal, which is silent before its shearer and does not open its mouth. In this it bears the form of gentleness which preserves patience amid oppressions and insults. Do you wish to hear how great is the power of gentleness, or what is the reward for this gift? “But the gentle,” he says, “shall inherit the earth, and shall delight in an abundance of peace” (Ps. XXXVI). How great, I ask, it is to receive an eternal inheritance and possess it in peace! But what kind of peace? “They shall delight,” he says, “in an abundance of peace.” It was too little for him to say, “They shall delight in peace”; rather, he said, “They shall delight in an abundance of peace,” because that peace shall have no end.

Moreover, the ram is leader of the flock. Therefore, through the virtue of gentleness one must offer oneself as a pattern to the whole congregation, so that whoever wishes to be an exemplar of this gift may be an example to all others. To possess proven gentleness, then, and gentleness imitable by all, is to offer a ram; but proven virtue rebukes [Col. 1033A] the foolish. Behold, concerning the ram. Let us now see concerning the ox.

The ox, as we know, willingly bends its neck to bear the yoke. This is the image of obedience, which customarily and ought always to submit itself to another’s will. Therefore, as proven gentleness is understood in the ram, so voluntary submission is understood in the ox. Oh, what a great sacrifice it is entirely to put aside one’s own will, to expose one’s whole self to another’s judgment, and to reserve nothing for oneself! Oh, how confidently will one stand beside the Crucified who submits himself for his sake to every obedience! With what security of conscience will the truly obedient person approach the throne of grace of him who became obedient to the Father even unto death—indeed, death on a cross! With how many trophies will that person leave the arena of this life who utterly rejects himself for Christ’s sake and dedicates himself to another’s service, according to Solomon’s saying: “An obedient person speaks victories” (Prov. XI).

Indeed, he speaks in action what he speaks in words. What a victory it is to conquer sin! What a victory to conquer oneself, conquer the world, conquer the devil! Thus he conquers all things who conquers his own will, who willingly puts his neck beneath the yoke of obedience. Therefore, to offer an ox is willingly to display voluntary submission. Behold concerning ox flesh. Let us now consider what should be understood concerning goat flesh.

We know well that virtue which makes a person become contemptible in his own eyes and, as it were, stink in his own nostrils. The goat indeed has a foul smell; and we offer a goat to the Lord, as it were, through voluntary self-contempt. [Col. 1033C] Therefore, as voluntary submission is figured fittingly in the ox, so voluntary self-abasement is figured in the goat. To expose oneself to every lowliness and abasement for the Lord’s sake, and humbly to acknowledge one’s own weakness, is to offer goat’s flesh to the Lord. The less such flesh pleases the human palate, the more it pleases the divine palate. “For the Lord is high, and he regards the lowly; and he knows the lofty from afar.”

We have now said what sacrifices of this sort mean: ram’s flesh, ox’s flesh, goat’s flesh. Ram’s flesh: proven gentleness; ox’s flesh: voluntary submission; goat’s flesh: voluntary self-abasement. These are marrow-rich sacrifices, sacrifices exceedingly pleasing to the Lord. Marrow lies hidden within bones and makes them fat. The marrow of virtues is good intention; the marrow of virtues is inward devotion. For virtues are watered from good intention and inward devotion of the soul, and are strengthened unto the firmness of perseverance. Thus marrow-rich sacrifices are devout services. Let our gentleness, our obedience, and our humility be devout, so that each of our offerings may be fattened.

Behold, we have what victims we ought to offer to the Lord. Behold, we have what dishes we ought to set before him when we desire it. I think that if we place before him three dishes from the animals designated, we can provide him with a very pleasing supper: “Behold,” he says, “I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will enter to him and sup with him” (Rev. IV). Let us meanwhile bring him into our supper, so that at some time we may deserve to be brought into his supper.

[Col. 1034A] But if among you there are persons rich in virtues for whom it is too little to set before him only three dishes after David’s likeness, let them strive, after Abraham’s example, to add a fourth and fifth. For Abraham offered the Lord a fivefold sacrifice, as he received it from the Lord’s own command. For when Abraham had received the promise concerning the land of the Canaanites, which he was to possess in his heirs, he humbly sought from the Lord a sign concerning this very matter, with the great boldness of familiarity which he enjoyed with the Lord: “Lord God,” he said, “how can I know that I shall possess it?” And the Lord said to Abraham: “Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram; also a turtledove and a dove” (Gen. XV).

Abraham did what he had received from the divine command; and, when heavenly fire had come upon his victims, he obtained the sign he had desired. Because he received fire from heaven, it was certainly a sign of great love and rightly afforded him great confidence in hoping for greater things. For lesser benefits freely bestowed undoubtedly give boldness to expect greater ones. Thus we receive earnest-money, so that we may hold the certainty of the agreement unshaken. Therefore that fire sent from heaven, which consumed Abraham’s victims, was for Abraham a kind of earnest of the divine promise.

I think that we too, if we receive heavenly fire, fire divinely sent, will thereafter be wholly unable to doubt the divine promises: “I came,” he says, “to send fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it should burn?” (Luke [Col. 1034C] XII). But when Jesus brought this fire down from on high, was there then no fire on earth, or perhaps no good fire? Without doubt he found earthly fire, but brought heavenly fire. The former he came to extinguish; the latter he came vigorously to kindle. Every love is fire, but not every love is good. Bad fire is worldly love, love of the flesh, love of shameful things. Good fire is spiritual love, love of truth, love of virtue. Therefore it is good to extinguish the former, and likewise good to kindle and carefully nourish the latter.

Good fire is the fire of charity: a good fire, and one to be nourished most diligently. This is the fire that comes from heaven, that descended upon the disciples in tongues of fire: “The charity of God,” says the Apostle, “has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” [Col. 1034D] (Rom. V). Behold the fire sent from heaven; behold the fire that is given only by God. Without doubt, whoever has received this fire can no longer doubt the promise of the eternal inheritance. Certainly, where abundance of charity is, there can be no place for distrust. “For perfect charity casts out fear.”

But do you wish to know more clearly that those who receive this fire cannot hesitate concerning the promise of the eternal inheritance? “Charity,” he says, “bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things” (I Cor. XIII). For how can that which believes all things and hopes all things distrust divine promises? I think that the Prophet had received this heavenly fire when he said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI). To Abraham, indeed, the land of the Canaanites is promised; and, having received the pledge, as it were, in the fire sent down from above, he is strengthened in the certainty of his hope.

Since promises were therefore made to Abraham, if we desire to be co-heirs of promises of this kind, let us endeavour to obtain from the Lord by prayer the fire that has been indicated. Let us consider what it is to receive as an inheritance a land flowing with milk and honey, and forcibly to wrest it from the hands of the Canaanites. It is surely a great and very difficult matter. The patriarch knew this—and knew it well—and therefore sought to have his confidence in so great a promise confirmed by a sign.

But what, we suppose, is this land flowing with milk and honey, overflowing everywhere with so great a sweetness? Where, I ask, is this land? Where is it to be sought, or how is it to be found? The catholic faith has most certainly recognized concerning the kingdom of heaven that it is within us. But why should that heaven which is not within not have a land of its own kind, just as the visible heaven has its own earth? If the kingdom of heaven is within us, why should the land of the living not also be within us? Certainly, the inheritance promised to spiritual persons is proved to be spiritual. If you wish, it is earth; if you wish, it is heaven: earth because of stability, heaven because of loftiness. If we are spiritual, if we understand spiritually, let us seek this land flowing with milk and honey inwardly, not outwardly.

Let us therefore seek what this land is, which refreshes, gives drink to, and feeds its cultivators with wonderful sweetness. We know that, while the other elements are always in motion and can never rest, the earth alone remains in one place and settles itself in profound repose. We know likewise that fear is accustomed continually to shake the mind, whereas security establishes it and settles it into rest. Thus security of conscience bears the likeness of earth precisely in that it is accustomed always to gather the human heart into rest. This land flows with much sweetness, because security of conscience produces joy of heart. The land of promise is a secure conscience; the honey-flowing land is a joyful conscience.

Such a land is rightly taken from the Canaanites and rightly given to the Jews. The worst race of all people then upon the earth was the race of the Canaanites; the best race of all people then upon the earth was the race of the Hebrews. [Col. 1035D] You see that this land belongs either to very bad people or to very good people. Indeed, none but the very bad or the very good can or usually do possess security of conscience. Do you wish to know more clearly how very bad people customarily possess such a land? “There are wicked persons who are so secure as though they had the works of the righteous” (Eccles. VIII). “For when the wicked person has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII).

We know likewise that perfect charity casts out fear and immediately admits security. “For if our heart does not reproach us, let us have confidence before him.” You certainly see that either great perversity or great perfection produces security of conscience. A bad but secure conscience belongs to the very bad; a good and secure conscience [Col. 1036A] to the very good; a bad but insecure conscience to those not very bad; a good but insecure conscience to those not very good. Therefore, as long as the conscience is secure and bad, the Canaanites still remain in the land. But when the conscience begins to be secure and good, know that the Jews are now dwelling in the land. For nothing at all customarily produces security of conscience except either extreme enormity of vices or great perfection of virtues.

This is the inheritance which must at all costs be wrested from the hands of the Canaanites and cleansed with the utmost care from every stain of vices. This is the inheritance that flows with milk and honey, because security of conscience is accustomed to fill the human mind with joy and exultation. He wished us to be refreshed with the sweetness of milk and honey when he said: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, righteous ones” (Ps. [Col. 1036B] XXXII). False security produces false joy; true security, true joy. Oh, what great joy is found in the testimony of a good conscience! “This,” he says, “is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I).

Understand in milk and honey a twofold joy: that of a secure conscience and that of a good conscience. An unblemished conscience indeed produces a double joy: joy in the blessedness of the body and joy in the blessedness of the mind. From this twofold reward we rejoice meanwhile in hope, but in the future we shall rejoice in reality. Milk flows from flesh; honey descends from heaven with the dew. Milky sweetness is drawn from flesh when joy and exultation arise from bodily blessedness. Honeyed sweetness flows down as if from heaven when an inestimable rejoicing arises from the incorruptibility of the mind.

Milk is also that sweetness which we shall draw from contemplating creatures; honey, however, is that which intoxicates the mind through contemplation of the Creator. Is it not also to suck milk, to rejoice in beholding Christ’s humanity? Is it not to be refreshed by the honey of supreme sweetness, to glory beyond measure in beholding Christ’s divinity? In milk there is sweetness alone, but not the highest sweetness; in honey there is both sweetness alone and the highest sweetness. For what is sweeter than honey? In contemplating Christ’s humanity there is indeed great joy, but not the highest; in contemplating his divinity there is joy both unique and highest.

It belongs to the blessedness of the outer person to see with bodily eyes, in God, human nature. But it belongs [Col. 1036D] to the blessedness of the inner person to see with inward eyes, in the human being, divine nature. Therefore, understand by milk whatever beatifying sweetness bodily substance supplies to bodily senses; by honey receive whatever glorifying joy incorporeal substance distils into bodily senses.

What else, then, will it be to receive as an inheritance a land flowing with milk and honey, if not to possess for ever the eternal security of a twofold blessedness? If, therefore, we desire with faithful Abraham to inherit promises of this kind, for the certainty of our hope let us seek that heavenly fire, previously indicated, as a sign. For, as we have taught above, a heart wholly kindled by the fire of charity can be enveloped neither by any cloud of ignorance nor by any numbness of distrust [Col. 1037A]. But whoever desires, after Abraham’s likeness, to receive fire sent from heaven should strive likewise to offer a similar sacrifice. Abraham is accordingly commanded, as has already been said, to take a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, together with a turtledove and a pigeon (Gen. 15). Let us now see what this sacrifice of Abraham signifies, and in what respect it seems to differ from the sacrifice of David already mentioned.

Why, I ask, does the Lord require from the supreme patriarch not an ox but a cow? Does he perhaps love the female more than the male in this kind of victim? Perhaps so. For he would not demand from so great a friend that which he loved less himself. If things spoken mystically are examined by mystical interpretation, I think the truth of what is said becomes plainly evident [Col. 1037B]: we know that an ox can bear the yoke, but cannot give milk. A cow, however, can do both: give milk and bear her master’s yoke. What a sacrifice it is both humbly to bear the yoke of obedience, and amid whatever hardships obedience entails to preserve sweetness of heart, and to distil through one’s words nothing but milky sweetness! Many, when hard commands are given them, find them burdensome and endure them not so sweetly as stoutly. We know, moreover, that the male sex is stronger than the female; yet it cannot give milk. Strong obedience therefore makes an ox; sweet obedience, a cow. To offer an ox is to obey manfully; to offer a cow is to obey gladly. We offer an ox by obeying steadfastly; we offer a cow by obeying joyfully [Col. 1037C]. Ox-flesh is robust obedience; cow-flesh, pleasant obedience. Let him who can offer cow-flesh; let him who cannot offer ox-flesh. Whoever can do neither of these, let him at least offer a calf from the herd.

A calf, indeed, is being raised to bear the yoke, though for the present it is not placed beneath it. Its present failure to bear it arises not from the fault of kicking against it, but from lack of ability. Therefore, if you do not profess obedience, not because you are unwilling but because you are unable, you vow and pay a calf. For what do we understand by the calf, except a purpose of obeying, just as in the ox and cow we understand the practice of obedience? If, then, you cannot offer a cow or an ox, offer at least a calf [Col. 1037D], which, whenever you truly will it, you can have at hand. Certainly, if you cannot have the office or practice of obedience, you can have the purpose of obedience; you can have the desire for obedience; and whenever you will, you can offer such a calf. Those joined in marriage cannot immediately profess obedience whenever they wish. For persons joined in marriage cannot separate from one another without the other’s permission, and therefore cannot profess obedience. Let such persons offer a calf—those who cannot take upon themselves the yoke of obedience at their own mental discretion.

Hence under the Law, for the sin of ignorance, an anointed priest is commanded to offer a calf. The anointed priest is a prelate endowed with charity. The anointed priest is a prelate compassionate toward his neighbour and devoted toward God [Col. 1038A]. The more truly such a priest loves his subjects, the more vehemently he pursues and hates their errors. Yet often, while he punishes their faults with insufficient discernment, while he does not know or neglects to weigh the strength of those whom he strikes, he incautiously strikes out charity in them and extinguishes it. Thus he sins through ignorance when he increases the evil which he ought to have cut away. Therefore, let the priest who, acting without discernment, errs while intending good, offer a calf for his sin, and henceforth have the desire to obey rather than command, since experience has now shown him that he cannot fully administer as he ought the office of government entrusted to him. For what else is his offering a calf than, having already acted badly, desiring to be subject rather than set over others, and to render obedience to others rather than exact it from them [Col. 1038B]? He therefore offers a calf from the herd who now desires to become, as it were, one of the subjects.

It should indeed be noted that the priest sinning through ignorance is commanded to offer, for sin, not an ox but a calf, lest he dare rashly and inconsiderately cast off the pastoral care once received. Therefore one who is such ought not so much to assume as to seek a place of subjection, not so much to seize as to desire it; and this will be to offer not so much an ox as a calf. Let him then cut off from his affections the love of pre-eminence, but retain the office of pre-eminence for the fear of God and the neighbour’s benefit, until he finds a fitting and reasonable departure; and meanwhile let him offer a calf for his sin through the desire for subjection [Col. 1038C].

But what, we ask, is the meaning of this: David promises not an ox but oxen, whereas the Lord chose to require from Abraham’s hand not cows but a cow? If it is more to promise and pay oxen than an ox, why should it not likewise be greater to present cows rather than a cow in sacrifice to God? Yet in Abraham’s sacrifice must we suppose that something less than perfect could have been possible? To whom, then, is perfection rightly ascribed if it is denied to the supreme patriarch? Who would say either that the Lord had not trained so great a friend for the highest things, or that so great a man lacked a mind ready for the practices of perfection?

To say briefly what I understand by an ox or oxen: to offer an ox, as it seems to me, is to stretch out one’s hand vigorously to render fully the obedience owed [Col. 1038D]. This victim is doubled when the hand of our action is manfully stretched out to both owed and unowed obedience. Almost all of us, when we enter religious life, promise obedience with a qualification, for we profess obedience according to an order. Therefore it is not in a superior’s power forcibly to compel a subject to things beyond the rule of his profession. What is commanded according to the order is owed; what is beyond the profession is unowed. We therefore offer oxen with the Prophet, because we exact from our own mind and steadfastly render both owed and unowed obedience. But we truly offer cows when we render both kinds of obedience not merely with equanimity but also with delight [Col. 1039A].

How then is a cow alone required from Abraham, or only one rendered by so great a man, as has been said? For neither unowed obedience alone suffices for the performance of what is owed, nor owed obedience alone for perfection. I will say it—certainly I will say what my mind suggests to me on this matter; let each judge as he pleases. If you wish, you can make no obedience unowed for yourself; and then I do not see how God can require more than one cow from you. If you promise before your God, or profess before your superior, obedience in all things, then henceforth no obedience will be unowed for you; and for the debt of obedience it is enough for you to offer one cow. In my view, one cow is offered better in this manner [Col. 1039B] than when your victim is doubled in the manner stated above. No obedience will seem burdensome or unbearable to you if you perfectly imitate the example of him who became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2). We therefore offer a cow in the Lord’s sacrifice after Abraham’s example if we promise complete obedience in all things and render it with joy. And let us, so far as lies in us, be prompt and prepared to give such obedience not only to better or equal persons, but even to worse; and without doubt it will be established that we have offered a three-year-old cow according to the Lord’s command or teaching. He who said, “Be subject for God’s sake to every human creature” (1 Pet. 2), wished us to offer such a victim—a three-year-old cow indeed [Col. 1039C].

Behold, concerning the cow; now let us consider the goat. It is easy, I think, to gather from what has gone before why the Lord preferred to require from Abraham a she-goat rather than a he-goat. In the he-goat or she-goat voluntary contempt is understood. But the she-goat is accustomed to provide milk; the he-goat is not. To offer a she-goat, therefore, is to endure one’s own contempt with great sweetness of heart. As has been said above, the male sex is stronger than the female. Thus a he-goat, not a she-goat, is offered when a person’s own contempt is received not so gladly as it is endured stoutly. Whoever cannot offer a she-goat, let him offer at least a he-goat; whoever can offer neither, let him offer at least a kid. A kid is a tender creature and can scarcely, or perhaps not at all, live without its mother’s milk [Col. 1039D]. Thus one offers a kid who endures his own contempt painfully and with great distress, yet, refreshed by the milk of another’s consolation, forces himself to patience.

Accordingly, while one bears his own contempt patiently, another stoutly, and another gladly, one seems to offer a kid, another a he-goat, another a she-goat. If, therefore, you embrace patience under contempt, you offer a kid from the goats. You offer a he-goat by treating your contempt with contempt. You offer a she-goat by becoming cheerful at an injury inflicted upon you. A she-goat, I think, was the offering of those concerning whom you read in the Acts of the Apostles: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been accounted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). But if you are poor and cannot manage the offering of a she-goat or he-goat, offer at least a kid from the goats [Col. 1040A]. Surely Jacob satisfied his father with kid-flesh and received the blessing due to his brother. You hear the blessing; consider also its character: “May God give you,” he says, “of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of grain and wine and oil; may peoples serve you and tribes worship you. Be lord over your brothers, and may the sons of your mother bow before you. Whoever curses you, let him be cursed; and whoever blesses you, let him be filled with blessings” (Gen. 27). Whoever, therefore, desires to inherit such a blessing should heed Rebekah’s counsel: “Bring me,” she says, “two choice kids, that I may make from them food for your father, which he gladly eats” (ibid.). You see surely that he who longs for so great a blessing must prepare two kids [Col. 1040B].

Certainly, when you act wrongly, you are justly despised. What else do you offer but kid-flesh if you embrace patience? But whoever is despised even amid good works and yet embraces patience seems to double his victim. Thus to offer twin kids is to bear patiently both just and unjust contempt. Anyone seems to offer a double he-goat when he is found ready to endure stoutly both just and unjust contempt. But to offer she-goats is to rejoice in mind under either form of contempt, and amid whatever injuries, however unjust, to retain sweetness of heart within the heart. Yet he who can truly say with blessed Job, “Indeed, my heart does not reproach me in all my life” (Job 27), I do not know how his victim can be doubled in this kind of sacrifice [Col. 1040C].

For how, I ask, can one incur just contempt whose own conscience reproves him in nothing? Rightly, therefore, the Lord required from Abraham only one she-goat, since his life was irreproachable and he could be despised by others only undeservedly. Rightly David doubled his victim in this respect, since amid the many good things he did he also committed certain very grievous evils. He therefore had in his life grounds upon which he might have been reproved or despised both justly and only unjustly; hence it was necessary for him to double his victim in the Lord’s sacrifice. Happy is he who so lives that there is no ground on which he can rightly be reproved by others [Col. 1040D]. For one who is such, it is enough to offer a single he-goat and to bear unjust contempt with equanimity. But a she-goat is the offering of a perfect man when, though unjustly spurned, he receives it with joy.

We are despised now by superiors, now by equals, now by inferiors. Yet we ought gladly—indeed, joyfully—to receive the unjust mockery and reproaches of any persons whatsoever; and this, I think, will be to offer a three-year-old she-goat. Behold concerning the cow; behold concerning the goat. It remains to consider the offering of the ram. A sheep is a gentle animal, and therefore, as we have already taught, such an animal can signify gentleness. You therefore offer a sheep when you exhibit gentleness. But it is within your power whether you wish to offer a lamb, a ewe, or a ram, and set it in the Lord’s sacrifice. A lamb, as we know, does not pour forth milk so much as suck it [Col. 1041A]. Conversely, a ewe does not suck so much as pour forth milk. A ram, however, is accustomed to do neither, but rather to strike with its horns.

Thus he is made a lamb who advances to the grace of gentleness from the sweetness of another’s consolation. He presents a ewe in the Lord’s sacrifice who, through the pursuit of kindly consolation and devout concern, advances others to the grace of gentleness. But we truly offer a ram if we rebuke those who sin in a spirit of gentleness and, zealous for the Lord, assail transgressors with the horns of devout severity. In the lamb, therefore, we understand timid gentleness; in the ewe, soothing gentleness; in the ram, zealous gentleness. In the lamb, fearful gentleness; in the ewe, pious gentleness; in the ram [Col. 1041B], severe gentleness. You offer a lamb by yielding humbly, a ewe by encouraging devoutly, a ram by rebuking piously.

“Receive with gentleness the implanted word, which can save your souls,” and you have offered a lamb. “Strengthen the weary hands and make firm the feeble knees,” and you sacrifice a ewe. But, in accordance with the Apostle, “reprove, entreat, rebuke” (2 Tim. 4), while preserving everywhere the power of gentleness, and, I think, a ram will be your offering. I think you no longer wonder why the Lord required from Abraham the male sex in this kind of victim, though in the other kinds of victims he preferred the female. It is neither strange nor unusual for a mind founded in gentleness to preserve the sweetness of heart within the heart and, after the likeness of a ewe [Col. 1041C], to pour out the sweetness conceived as though it were milk and distil it through words. But this is truly great, truly wonderful: when a gentle and pious heart, compelled by zeal for the Lord, strikes sinners with the horns of rebuke.

For my own part, I marvel more at—and prefer—one ram, according to Daniel’s vision, butting toward the west, north, and south, than many ewes abundant in milk. What a sacrifice, and how great, not even to spare oneself for the testimony of truth, but voluntarily to provoke against oneself the rage of persecutors for zeal of righteousness! What a sacrifice: to endure one’s own wrongs with gentleness and gladly forget them, to be vehemently indignant at the Lord’s wrongs, and vigorously exact vengeance by fiercely using the horns of rebuke [Col. 1041D]! This, I think, is to offer a ram and set it in the Lord’s sacrifice.

Yet rightly, in this place too, in accordance with the foregoing manner, it is asked why only one ram is required from Abraham, whereas the prophet David seems to propose or promise something greater in saying, “I will offer you fat burnt-offerings with the incense of rams” (Ps. 65). He does not say “with the incense of a ram,” but “with the incense of rams.” But as we taught concerning the immolation of the she-goat that we are sometimes despised justly and sometimes unjustly, so also we are sometimes afflicted justly and sometimes unjustly, and in turn suffer just or unjust persecution.
