Whoever, therefore, whenever he incurs just persecution bears it with gentleness, offers, as it were, one ram of this sort in sacrifice to the Lord [Col. 1042A]. But he who, while being zealous for the Lord, is afflicted now justly, now unjustly, and bears either persecution without injury to his gentleness, plainly seems to double his victim. Those who are without complaint and live irreproachably have no ground on which they either ought or can double their victim. I think the offering of one ram alone was sufficient for the perfection of those of whom we have this testimony in the Gospel: “They were both,” says the Evangelist, “righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame” (Luke 1). You observe, I think, that to offer one ram in this manner is greater than to double one’s victim in the manner previously stated.

He offers the Lord a three-year-old ram who, whenever zeal for righteousness requires it or the rule of truth dictates it, attacks not only those less powerful or equally powerful, but even those more powerful, with the horns of free rebuke [Col. 1042B]. Behold, we have now said what we should understand concerning the cow, the she-goat, and finally the ram. From these things, therefore, you perceive, I think, what dishes you ought to prepare for the Lord’s table. But if we wish to present the Lord with a rich table, we ought, after Abraham’s likeness, to add from the turtledove and pigeon a fourth or fifth dish still further. Therefore, to the pursuits of perfect action let us add also the pursuits of contemplation. The former belong to quadrupeds; the latter to birds. Quadrupeds live on the ground; birds raise themselves aloft on wings [Col. 1042C]. Through action we dwell, as it were, upon earth; through thought and desire we hang suspended in the heights. We therefore offer the Lord winged animals whenever, through the duty of devotion, we fly on the wing of contemplation to the consideration of future things.

By the turtledove and pigeon understand a twofold contemplation: in the turtledove, contemplation of eternal evils; in the pigeon, contemplation of eternal goods. These birds are accustomed not so much to sing as to moan, and they have moaning in place of song. As in the wing understand the grace of contemplation, so in their song or moaning understand the power of compunction. We ought therefore to meditate and contemplate eternal evils and eternal goods alike, and be pierced with compunction in considering them; and this will be to offer a turtledove and a pigeon and, in one respect, to double our victim [Col. 1042D].

The turtledove loves solitude and goes about alone; in this it bears the form of fear, which always seeks a retreat. The pigeon flies in flocks, and thereby displays the form of love, which always gathers hearts and binds them together in the one concord of peace. In the turtledove, therefore, is the compunction of fear; in the pigeon is perceived the compunction of love. If you meditate upon eternal evils and are not pierced with compunction in considering them, you have the wings of a turtledove but not its song. If you fix yourself upon the contemplation of eternal goods, burn with desire for them, and shed tears, you show plainly that you possess both the flight and the song of the pigeon.

[Col. 1043]

## ON THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN ABRAHAM’S SACRIFICE AND THE SACRIFICE OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 1043A] We have heard that the great patriarch Abraham offered a turtledove and a pigeon in sacrifice to the Lord, whereas the sacrifice of the Blessed Virgin Mary was a pair of turtledoves and two young pigeons. The sacrifice of the patriarch Abraham seems altogether very different from the sacrifice of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Which is greater? Which is better? But who would dare to prefer or compare any of the saints, save the Holy of Holies alone, to the Blessed Virgin Mary? Without hesitation, then, we attribute what is best to so great a Lady; yet again it is very hard to detract anything from the perfection of so great a patriarch. Still, so great a difference among the victims does not appear to be without cause. But if it is pleasing to understand these matters more fully, a deeper consideration is necessary.

It seems to belong to the flight and song of the turtledove to pour forth groaning and lamentation in considering eternal evils. But to groan and sigh in contemplating eternal goods is to possess the song of the pigeon [Col. 1043B]. Let a person, therefore, recall what good he has lost by sinning, or what evil he has in the same way incurred, so that he may understand better and more fully toward what state he ought to strive, groan, sigh, and long. For by sinning he incurred a twofold captivity and lost a twofold dignity. Voluntarily subjected to guilt, he was unwillingly handed over to punishment; and thereafter he lost the stability of grace and the perpetuity of glory. Stripped of such grace and glory, whether willing or unwilling man serves sin and is subject to the scourge; living but a short time, he is filled with many miseries—he who comes forth like a flower and is crushed, flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same state [Col. 1043C].

Therefore, by being born we contract a twofold captivity—the exaction of guilt and punishment; and so long as we live here we cannot recover the fixed stability of grace and the perpetuity of glory. Hence with every diligence and with all the earnestness we can exert, we ought indeed to labour and attain moderation in all things, so that we may lay aside in dying the evils contracted in being born, and obtain at the very entrance into the life that follows those goods which we cannot recover during the course of this life. For perfect persons, at the very departure of the soul, at the very beginning of the life then commencing, are freed from guilt and released from punishment, confirmed in grace, and exalted in glory [Col. 1043D].

What else shall I call this twofold freedom from guilt and punishment, and this twofold dignity in grace and glory, which perfect persons alone receive at the soul’s departure, except certain first-fruits of the fullness to come? The perfect, therefore, receive these first-fruits in the soul alone, later to receive fullness in both natures. To groan and sigh for the first-fruits of this twofold freedom, and to hold firm hope that they will be obtained through death: this, I think, will be to offer a pair of turtledoves. But to pour out groans and sighs for the first-fruits of this twofold dignity, and to trust in the Lord’s mercy that they will be obtained at the soul’s departure: this, I think, will be to devote two pigeons in sacrifice to the Lord [Col. 1044A].

Perfect persons alone receive this twofold freedom and this twofold dignity, as we have said, in death; but all the elect receive one freedom and one dignity only. For immediately after the soul’s departure, in the same instant of time, they are freed from sin and confirmed in good. Indeed, the souls of the elect who are less perfect, like the rest, receive the sentence of their lot immediately upon laying aside their bodies. Because they have escaped eternal condemnation, because they foreknow their future glorification, because they recognize that, after so many offences, they have never been abandoned by the grace of Christ their Saviour, they grow strong in such love of their Creator that thereafter none of them would wish to do anything whatever by which God might be offended, even if it were permitted without punishment [Col. 1044B].

On the contrary, all the reprobate, after receiving the sentence of their condemnation, never rise to even the smallest spark of divine love. Since they wholly despair of eternal goods, they desire to return to the things they knew and perversely loved in this life, and would wish to live in them always if they could do so without punishment. It is therefore evident that they remain servants of sin for ever, not so much in action as in will. Thus the souls of the evil are confirmed in evil at their departure; those of the good are confirmed in good.

And although certain elect persons, though less perfect, are still held by a debt of satisfaction and are perhaps cleansed of vice over a long time, God forbid that they should thereafter in any way serve sin. They are freed from guilt, yet not released from punishment; confirmed in grace, yet not exalted in glory. But what is done after the Saviour’s death for those less perfect was done, before the price of our redemption was paid, even for those very perfect persons [Col. 1044C]. For they were emancipated from the slavery of sinning, yet not released from every obligation to suffer. To say nothing of other things, they surely suffered exile and confinement. But what confinement? Certainly, hell. I pass over the fact that they were not caught up to the joys of heaven; they did not even return to the delights of Paradise. Although, therefore, they were confirmed in good, they were not yet consummated in joy.

I say boldly that not even Abraham himself received, at the laying aside of the body, that twofold freedom which is from guilt and punishment; for he neither dared to seek nor presume to hope for freedom from the captivity of a distant pilgrimage [Col. 1044D]. Rightly, therefore, he offered not turtledoves but a turtledove, and in this respect ought not to have doubled his victim. What I say concerning the attainment of twofold freedom, I say likewise concerning the attainment of twofold dignity. For he received at death the stability of the former grace which he hoped and sought, but before the Saviour’s coming he could not pass into the glory of eternity. Rightly, therefore, his offering in this kind of birds was only one pigeon. But the Blessed Virgin Mary, because she was assured of obtaining at the laying aside of the flesh both kinds of freedom and dignity, could rightly double her victim in both respects. By now, I think, you understand why such a difference rightly had to exist between Abraham’s sacrifice and that of the Blessed Virgin Mary [Col. 1045A].

Yet one matter still seems worthy of inquiry here: why she chose rather to offer a pair of turtledoves than a pair of pigeons, and, conversely, two young pigeons rather than two young turtledoves. One thing I know: the more certainly and confidently we hope for heavenly and eternal goods, the more willingly and earnestly we labour for them. The more abundantly we toil for them, the greater or more excellent are the things for which we hope. The better the things for which we hope, the more ardently we love. The more ardently we love, the more vehemently and anxiously we desire. Thus, indeed, anxiety of desire is born from the security of hope. You have, then, the bird in the security of hope; you have its young in the anxiety of desire [Col. 1045B].

Hope which longs for heavenly and eternal things flies, after the manner of birds, to heights and distances. A young bird is born from a bird, and the anxiety of desire is generated, in the order described, from the certainty of hope. Young birds are accustomed to cry constantly and rarely cease crying. He knew this who said, “Like a young swallow, so shall I cry” (Isa. 38). A young bird is thus accustomed to cry very anxiously, and anxious desire has, in the Creator’s ear, the voice of a great cry. Hence the Lord says to Moses, silent but burning with anxious desire: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14). Hence also the Psalmist’s saying: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor” (Ps. 10).

Such desire is sometimes accustomed to increase so greatly in some persons that they grow weary of living, so that their voice may truly seem to be: “My soul is weary of my life” (Job 10) [Col. 1045C]. For who, I ask, can await with the certainty of hope that good which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, and not burn with immense desire, and live almost, if not altogether, impatiently? As has been said, confidence of hope belongs to the bird; impatience of desire to its young. Hear the voice of a bird sweetly singing in a place of solitude: “We know,” he says, “that if the earthly house of this our dwelling is dissolved, we have from God a building, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5). Behold the greatness of the confidence of hope. Consider, in another place, the intensity of desire; and at the same time understand the cry of the loudly calling young bird: “When,” he says, “shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41) [Col. 1045D].

But when someone burns with weariness of this life and desire for the life to come, it matters greatly with what intention this is done. One person is driven to this by fear; another is drawn by the intensity of love. The former is troubled by fear of a twofold danger and impending evil; the latter by love and the burning desire of enjoyment. Hear the voice of one made anxious amid dangers: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7). Receive also the voice of one burning with excess of love: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). In both places you hear desire for death and weariness of the present life. The former voice belongs to the young of turtledoves; the latter, to the young of pigeons.

For he who now desires to die from hatred of the twofold captivity distinguished above and desire for twofold freedom, and longs for this through many groans and sighs—what else does he cry in God’s ears but, as young turtledoves cry from their nest [Col. 1046A]? But one who, desiring death, prays and weeps for the abundance of grace and glory which he expects in the future—what else does he cry out, after the manner of young birds, with a pigeon’s voice? Firmly to hope for twofold freedom at the laying aside of the flesh and to live patiently in this expectation is, as we have said, to offer a pair of turtledoves. But to burn more ardently with the desire for these freedoms, to wish to die sooner in order to obtain them, and to bear impatiently the very fact of being alive—this seems to be to immolate a victim from the young of turtledoves.

Likewise, whoever patiently awaits in the hope of certainty the exaltation of twofold dignity immolates a pair of pigeons in sacrifice to the Lord [Col. 1046B]. But whoever, impatient of delay, longs and burns for this same end prepares for the Lord a sacrifice from the young of pigeons.

For who, however perfect in this life, can attain that fullness of grace and glory which, immediately after the soul’s departure, he does not doubt he will attain—so as to be able to cling unceasingly to divine contemplation, to be drawn away from it by no thought, to delight in it alone, and to glory in it every hour or moment? It does not belong to this life that one, however perfect, should interrupt by sleep, to say nothing of other things, the sweetness of so great a delight. Who can in this life fully fulfil that first and greatest commandment: namely, to love God with all one’s heart, [Col. 1046D] all one’s soul, and all one’s strength? Therefore, whoever loathes this life because he desires to obtain such fullness, and, to hasten the fulfilment of his desire, sighs, groans, and sheds tears, offers young doves in sacrifice to the Lord.

Many are amid great tribulations and temptations, and behave bravely, secure regarding the twofold freedom, provided perseverance is granted them. Yet often, not a few of those who are in such a condition, fearing a fall and weary of suffering, desire to die quickly, so that henceforth they may be secure from every suspicion of danger. But take heed lest perhaps fleeing the contests of suffering seem to be a sign of some impatience, or trembling excessively through fear of falling likewise a sign of some distrust. For all who are perfect ought to be certain that God is faithful, who will not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but will also provide with the temptation a way out, so that we may endure it (1 Cor. 10). Hence some conduct themselves amid the greatest dangers with such constancy, and stand so secure in the Lord’s protection, that they dare confidently and say: neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8).

Thus, so far as consideration of escape from danger is concerned, firm security of hope in the Lord’s protection seems greater than an excessive vehemence of desire. But the former belongs to the pair of turtledoves; the latter to their young. [Col. 1047B] Therefore it seems greater to offer a pair of turtledoves than to offer their young. Yet without doubt the law of fear seems one thing, and, unless I am mistaken, the law of love another. To wish to rest and be secure is not so much the part of one loving his friend as of one loving himself. But to wish to see him whom one’s soul loves, to burn with desire for him, and to be unable in any way to rest until one sees, embraces, and clings to him, seems a sign of the highest devotion and wondrous charity.

Accordingly, in this respect the impatience of burning desire seems a much greater thing than security of hope alone without ardent desire. But the latter belongs to a pair of doves, the former to their young. Therefore it seems a greater sacrifice [Col. 1047C] to offer two young doves than the doves themselves. Behold, at last we have found what we long sought: that it is a greater thing to offer a pair of turtledoves than their young; whereas, conversely, it seems less to offer a pair of doves than their young.

You no longer wonder, I suppose, that Mary, the holiest of holy women, the perpetual Virgin, in both kinds of offering presented what she knew, according to the dignity of the mystery, to be best in each case. Far be it from us to say or believe that the blessed Virgin Mary was driven by desire for death through fear of suffering or fear of falling. For of no saint is it more rightly believed than of her that, so far as lay in her, she was always prepared to endure every kind of torment for Christ’s name. And how could she have been oppressed by fear of falling, [Col. 1047D] she who, in the flesh in which she conceived, nourished, and bore Christ’s flesh, bore no contradiction?

At the momentary touch of the saving right hand, the leper is cleansed (Matt. 8); at the touch of the hem of his garment, the woman suffering from an issue of blood was cleansed (Luke 8). How much more was it necessary that she should be cleansed from every contagion of mind and body, who for so long enclosed him wholly in her womb, so often held him wholly in her bosom, and sufficiently possessed the fullness of his remedy—now poured within, now applied outwardly—of that remedy, I say, which can more than suffice to remove every disease of all who are sick? How, I ask, could she have been oppressed unto weariness of life by fear of falling or suffering, she who, according to the angelic proclamation, was full of grace [Col. 1048A]?

Yet what fear could not drive her toward, love could draw her toward. Who among all Christ’s lovers ever wished more gladly to die in order to see his divinity and cleave, in perpetual contemplation, to his majesty and immensity? Who ever burned more ardently with the fervour of such desire? Certainly, the more she loved above all others, the more ardently she desired above all others the sweetness of the divine vision and the eternity of that sweetness. I say boldly that not even she, who loved above all others, could cling inseparably to this sweetness or drink of it alone and without interruption while she remained in this life and bore a corruptible body. For the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things [Col. 1048B] (Wisdom 8).

Since, then, she could not attain in this life that fullness of grace and glory which she received at her Assumption, what wonder if she ardently desired the hour of that reception, when no fear of falling or suffering could have driven her to desire death? She offered a pair of turtledoves in that she awaited, as confidently as patiently, the twofold freedom in the laying aside of her flesh. But she offered young doves rather than a pair of doves in that she longed, even with desire for death, for that twofold fullness of grace and glory already mentioned above.

Abraham, however, as has been said, was secure with regard to the laying aside of the flesh, not concerning the attainment of glory, but concerning the reception of stable grace alone; and not even in the fullness which the blessed Virgin Mary, or any of the perfect under this dispensation, received. What wonder, then, if he desired the hour of reception more coolly, since he hoped for less? Rightly, therefore, he offered not young doves, or a young dove, but a dove alone. Thus Abraham offered a turtledove in the certain hope of obtaining freedom from guilt, and a dove in the certain hope of receiving perpetual stability in grace.

If we wish to emulate the pursuits of perfection and become spiritual, we must, in the Lord’s sacrifice, following Abraham’s example, join birds to the animals. Birds suspend themselves in the air, which animals certainly cannot do. Therefore understand spiritual pursuits in the birds, [Col. 1048D] bodily exercises in the animals. External pursuits belong to animals; internal pursuits to birds. To the former belong exercises of the body; to the latter, exercises of the mind. God alone sees our inner things; our neighbour also can see our outer things. What we do inwardly is done for God alone; what we perform outwardly is done partly for God alone and partly also for our neighbour. For many things are done solely for the divine good pleasure, and many for human benefit or good pleasure.

Therefore Scripture rightly says of Abraham that he divided the animals but did not divide the birds (Gen. 15). For in those exercises which lie open solely to the divine sight, and are such as we have said belong to birds, we ought to intend nothing except that they may deservedly please [Col. 1049A] the divine will. But in bodily exercises, which we undertake both for God and for our neighbour, we have a twofold intention, and in this respect divide our offering. We ought, however, not merely to divide our offering in this manner, but also to set the divisions opposite one another and weigh each part by reciprocal consideration. For in what we do for our neighbour, we must with every caution avoid offending God; and in what we perform for God, we must, as far as possible, avoid scandalising our neighbour.

We ought to divide only that offering which consists of animals; but both this offering and that consisting of birds must, following Abraham’s example, be defended from the rapacity of birds of prey (ibid.). [Col. 1049B] For, as it is written, birds came down upon his offering, and Abraham drove them away. What are we to understand by birds of this kind except vain and foolish thoughts? Often, because of good works which we perform inwardly or outwardly, we are touched now by pride, now by vainglory, and glory immeasurably within ourselves. But unless we resist such foolish thoughts manfully, we render void for ourselves in God’s sight the fruit of a good work.

The aforesaid birds descend, as it were, to plunder our sacrifices when wicked thoughts, sent by evil spirits to corrupt our merits, come upon our heart. For evil spirits are, as it were, above us precisely because they are of a more exalted rank and an angelic nature; and in the Gospel they are called birds of heaven (Matt. 13; Mark 4; Luke 8). We must therefore strike down foolish thoughts and every suggestion introduced through evil angels by rebuke; and this will be to drive away birds of this kind. Whoever therefore hears or reads this should learn from apostolic teaching how the rapacity of self-exaltation or foolish boasting ought to be driven away. “What,” he says, “do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4). You can possess evil from yourself alone, but no good except by divine gift. Consider, therefore, how shameless it is to boast of your own evil, or of a good that is not your own. If we ponder these things diligently and frequently, we more readily rescue the offering of our devotion from that rapacity of birds [Col. 1049D] of which we have spoken.

Behold, we have what offerings we ought to make to the Lord our God; behold, we have how they should be defended from the onset of rapacity. Would that each of us might persist in pursuits of this sort until the sun sets, vanity’s love gradually fails, and, when the ray of carnal prudence is withdrawn, the heat of concupiscence cools. For by the fiery and bodily globe which never ceases to circle the mass of the earth and, travelling its circuit, never rests, what can we understand here better or more fittingly than love of earthly, transitory things, which encompasses what is lowest and permits no rest to the mind it inflames? This sun shines through prudence of the flesh and burns through the flesh’s concupiscence. This sun [Col. 1050A] undoubtedly sets when carnal prudence grows dull and carnal concupiscence gradually becomes cold.

But that we may know what sometimes follows the setting of such a sun, let us hear what Scripture says: “And when the sun had set, sleep fell upon Abraham, and a great and dark horror seized him” (Gen. 15). Sleep follows the setting of the sun, and horror follows sleep. Through bodily sleep, as we all know, bodily sense is lulled, and the human mind is withdrawn from surrounding things. Thus, quite fittingly, a withdrawal of the mind is understood by sleep. In sleep of this kind the mind often knows by divine revelation and sees, as if in a dream through a fitting vision, what it could previously scarcely know even faintly, as though awake, or could not know at all.

Hence Elihu says in Job: “In a dream, in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon men and they sleep in their beds, then he opens the ears of men and, instructing them, teaches them discipline” (Job 33). Such sleep does not come at human discretion, but according to the good pleasure of him who is accustomed to send it. It is rightly said of this sleep that it “fell,” because it comes suddenly and unexpectedly. Sleep therefore falls when a spiritual person passes by a sudden impulse into withdrawal of mind. But when a person is thus put to sleep and carried outside himself, the things often seen in ecstasy are marvellous and astounding.

Perhaps you who hear this wonder because [Col. 1050C] you have not yet experienced anything of the kind in yourself. Do you not know that everything has its time? Certainly wakefulness and sleep have their times: wakefulness in the day, sleep in the night. Perhaps the sun has not yet set for you; love of vanity has not yet failed. While the sun is hot, the sleep of which we have spoken does not know how to fall. As we have said, sleep follows the setting of the sun; and horror in turn sometimes follows sleep. For during such sleep the human mind often sees many things which it cannot behold without fear and trembling, or even horror.

Hence Eliphaz the Temanite says: “In the terror of a vision by night, when sleep is wont to seize men, fear took hold of me, and trembling, and all my bones were terrified” (Job 4). Hear another, and observe what he understood as if in a dream: “I said in the ecstasy of my mind: I am cast away from before your eyes” [Col. 1050D] (Ps. 30). What wonder if his mind was horrified when he saw himself cast away from the Lord’s presence? Job himself speaks of such terror or horror: “If I say, ‘My bed will comfort me, and I shall be relieved by speaking with myself on my couch,’ you will terrify me through dreams and shake me with horror through visions” (Job 17). One is, as it were, frightened through dreams and shaken with horror through visions when the human mind is raised above itself and caught up into contemplation of divine judgments, and by divine revelation sees how great are the dangers to which it is subject at every moment of every day. It sees how infinite are the eternal goods it has lost, how dreadful are the eternal evils it has deserved; it sees how easy it is to fall at any hour, and how impossible it is, once fallen, to rise by itself. [Col. 1051A] It sees how some fall from the highest pursuits of virtue to the depths of vice, while conversely others rise from the depths of vice to the highest summits of virtue. And amid all these things, a person does not know his end; but as fish are caught with a hook, and as birds are taken in a snare, so people are caught in an evil time when it suddenly comes upon them.

What wonder, then, if those whom God instructs how precariously human weakness struggles amid so great an uncertainty of dangers are shaken with a certain horror? Finally, observe what Abraham learned, as if through sleep, and you will see how rightly he was horrified. For it was said to him: “Know beforehand that your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own; and they will subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years” (Gen. 15). [Col. 1051B] By Abraham’s seed, if you wish, understand the virtues themselves. By Abraham’s seed, if you wish, understand those who emulate the virtues, live according to Abraham’s example, and imitate his life. Do not the virtues themselves serve King Pharaoh when they are performed with a perverse intention and, corrupted through hypocrisy, seek nothing except the profits of death?

And it often happens that pursuits of virtue begun with a good intention are eventually practised with an evil intention. Does not Abraham’s seed serve King Pharaoh in mud and brick when any strong emulator of the virtues—one who, leaving his land and kindred, has long followed Abraham’s example—nevertheless at last, after the manner of David, falls into some disgraceful sin? For anyone of this kind, if he returns again to righteousness, is counted [Col. 1051C] among Abraham’s children. Consider, then, how full of both fear and horror it is that no place of security is granted to a person in this life, even upon some lofty height or summit of virtue.

It is very rare, and truly the privilege of few, to do great things without thinking oneself great, to surpass many without despising anyone. For whenever any one of us does marvellous things and outstrips others in the vigour of good pursuits, it is easy to say inwardly what the Pharisee said: “I am not like other people” (Luke 11). Hence it often happens that divine grace is withdrawn from such persons, they are permitted to fall, and are sometimes gradually brought so far that at last they are as stubborn in evil as they were formerly steadfast [Col. 1051D] in good.

Is this not what the Lord threatens when Abraham is told: “Know beforehand that your seed will be a stranger in a land not its own”? Although the other elements are always liable to change, earth alone stands forever; consequently it quite fittingly signifies stability of heart. But as good as it is to be steadfast in a good purpose, so evil is it to be steadfast in an evil purpose. The former is constancy; the latter stubbornness. Thus constancy in good is the land of the good; stubbornness in evil is the land of the evil. Therefore, when any who are predestined for the eternal way are gradually brought into such stubbornness, they truly sojourn in an alien land, a land not their own. Behold what pride does; behold what arrogance does.

Thus vessels of mercy, [Col. 1052A] when they begin to swell with their own merits, are by God’s merciful dispensation allowed to fall, so that they may learn humble wisdom and form a true judgment of their own weakness. Full knowledge of human weakness consists in four degrees: two in the consideration of evil and two in the consideration of good. In the consideration of evil: first, that we know we can avoid no evil by our own power; second, that we know we can rise from no evil after falling by our own power. In the consideration of good: first, that we recognize that we can attain no good by our own effort; second, that we recognize that we cannot persevere by our own effort even in what we have received from God.

But what is manifold advancement in progress toward self-knowledge except a succession, as it were, of alternating days? Every alternation of waxing and waning days is enclosed within a year and completed by the sun’s course. Therefore a year rightly signifies fullness and completion of knowledge in any matter. For this reason, as stated above, a person is permitted to fall repeatedly and in many ways into some one vice, so that through many experiences he may learn fully and completely that he can be freed from such slavery by no power of his own. When this variety of experience is brought to fullness of knowledge, a year, as it were, is completed.

But when someone learns the same failure of his own weakness through daily experience in one vice after another, and infers by reason in other cases the same judgment of truth which experience has proved in many cases, and at last judges the same thing universally in all matters, then the number of years rises, in the multiplication of knowledge, to a hundred. For, since all the fingers and joints, named from the same source and composed from both hands, are contained within a hundred, the hundred rightly figures universality. Therefore understand fullness in the year and universality in the hundred. When, then, we possess an abundance of necessary knowledge both sufficiently in individual matters and generally in all, we extend the yearly course of our instruction into a hundredfold number.

We have above distinguished knowledge of our weakness by four degrees. Therefore we must, as it were, complete the number of four hundred years if we wish [Col. 1052D] to attain the fullness of that fourfold knowledge of which we have spoken. Hold it for certain, and do not hesitate: you must remain subject to Pharaoh and the Egyptians—to vices and to the instigators of vices—until the teaching of experience has taught you to judge rightly concerning your weakness; until you fully learn to presume absolutely nothing upon your own strength in avoiding or correcting evils, or in attaining or preserving goods.

Behold, we have now heard why the patriarch was horrified, and indeed why he rightly ought to have been horrified. We have heard what was fitted to inspire terror; let us hear also what could provide consolation: “Nevertheless,” he says, “I will judge the nation whom they shall serve; and afterward they shall come out with great substance. But you shall go to your fathers in peace, [Col. 1053A] buried in a good old age. In the fourth generation they shall return here; for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete until the present time” (Gen. 15).

Behold, as we can perceive from these things, by divine revelation, and as if in a dream, we learn now sorrowful things, now joyful things, and now things mingled from both. “I will judge the nation whom they shall serve.” Whether by the nations you choose to understand vices or the instigators of vices, God certainly has the power by his judgment to crush them and expel them from good hearts: the former by crushing them so that they are utterly nowhere; the latter by condemning them so that henceforth they are always miserable and can never prevail eternally against the good in any respect.

“And afterward,” he says, [Col. 1053B] “they shall come out with great substance.” We know indeed that the children of reconciliation are taught by their fall to discernment, circumspection, humility and compassion, constancy, patience, and perseverance together. Thus they go out with great substance when they carry away with them gains in virtues of this kind and talents of knowledge. You have, then, the wealth of souls in fruits of repentance and gains in virtues; you have the wealth of virtues in treasures of knowledge and wisdom. The Psalm refers to the treasure of such wealth when it says: “And he brought them forth with gold and silver” (Ps. 104).

See, therefore, how marvellous, joyful, and astounding it is that even moral ruin works together for good to those who are good, and that what is read in the Apostle is fulfilled: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those saints who are called according to his purpose” (Rom. 6). Thus it works for good that those who at one time serve in a land not their own eventually come out of it with great substance. It works for good that those who for a little while are overcome by vices later rise again: the more experienced, the more cautious; the more humble, the more steadfast or vigorous.

Yet those are to be judged exceedingly happy who advance to the grace of humility by the gift of foresight, and who learn the measure of human weakness not so much from their own ruin as from another’s. Their person is represented in Abraham, [Col. 1053D] to whom the Lord says: “But you shall go to your fathers in peace, buried in a good old age.” Neither does the Lord foretell, nor does any Scripture suggest, that Abraham was ever subjected anywhere to anyone’s service. Therefore he did not advance to the grace of humility by falling often, rising often, and serving vices. Rather, while, through God’s revelation, he reads in the book of providence, he proves by the examples of others what he ought to think concerning his own weakness.

Let us see, then, whether we can find in the words of this man taught by God that revealed humility which we have distinguished above in four degrees. Let us hear him speaking to the Lord: “I will speak with my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). Dust is scattered from its place by every breath, and, wherever thrown down, is never raised except by another’s impulse. Behold the image of human defect, so far as concerns the consideration of evil. [Col. 1054A]

For once divine grace and protection are withdrawn, a person is cast down by the enemy’s suggestion into whatever evil, and, once cast down, is not strengthened by his own power to return to uprightness of condition. Ash produces absolutely no seed from itself; nor can it sufficiently nourish by any richness of its own what it receives from elsewhere—not merely unto growth, but even unto maintenance. Here again you have the image of human defect, so far as concerns the consideration of good. A person can produce no seed of good work from himself without grace at work; and, when through grace at work he has already begun to possess it, he cannot preserve it at all through himself [Col. 1054B] without grace’s cooperation.

Behold, Abraham, as is understood from these sayings of his, is found to have been divinely instructed unto that fullness of humility which many attain, after many experiences, by a fourfold hundred years. What others scarcely attain through many experiences, others learn easily by divine revelation. “But you shall go”: you whom I have anticipated with more abundant grace than others; you whom I have enlightened more deeply than others. “You shall go to your fathers in peace,” free from every oppression of unworthy and harsh slavery.

What is it to go to one’s fathers but, by the same path of virtues through which others have preceded upon life’s way, to hasten through the activity of good works toward the tranquillity of inward rest? Therefore, he who was to go in peace was hastening toward peace. He went through peace and toward peace: through inward peace, toward eternal peace; through that peace which reconciles every sense to itself, toward that peace which surpasses every sense. Therefore the discord between flesh and spirit must be put to sleep, so that one may pass to that peace which is above every sense.

And what is it for the Lord to make promises of this kind to someone, except by inward inspiration to animate him toward such hope and certainty? “But you shall go to your fathers in peace, buried in a good old age.” In old age both the sense and the appetite of the outward person ordinarily languish and, through daily losses, draw near to failure. Old age is good when, at the same time as the appetite for outward and passing things [Col. 1054D] diminishes, that for inward and eternal things is renewed. Old age is good when outward sense decreases and inward sense grows. Old age is good when the inward person is strengthened precisely as the outward person is weakened: “For when I am weak,” he says, “then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Cor. 12).

Better is old age of character than of years, of merits than of time. It is more glorious for desire for external goods to languish through the exertion of disciplined effort than through nature’s infirmity. “Buried,” he says, “in a good old age.” A person first dies in order afterward to be buried. The dead person indeed ceases to see, but does not immediately cease to be seen. The buried person ceases both to see and to be seen. Therefore whoever wishes to be dead to this world must close those eyes which we read were opened in the first parents, and neither attend to nor turn toward the pleasures of the senses.

But such a person then finds burial, as it were, after death, when through the pursuit of wisdom and desire for eternity, passing beyond worldly things even from worldly things, he advances to a state such as no carnal person can, I do not say know, but even suspect. Through the active life we are mortified; through the speculative and contemplative life we are, with Abraham, as it were buried in a double cave. It belongs to the speculative life to behold God’s invisible things, understood through the things that have been made, and to see as if through a mirror and in an enigma. It belongs to the contemplative life to see truth without a covering and as if face to face. Thus through the speculative and contemplative life we withdraw from human things and, as was said, are as it were buried in a double cave. [Col. 1055B]

It is good for the desire’s appetite and the endeavour of study to languish, fail, and withdraw from human things; and, immersed in heavenly contemplations, to remain hidden from the gaze of those who think carnally. Thus the man who emulates virtues grows old, dies, and is buried. We have heard concerning Abraham, or those whom he represents. Now let us hear what consolation is added concerning the children of the sojourn: “And in the fourth generation,” he says, “they shall return here.”

When that inward household of thoughts or wills is carried off into a foreign land and, under the pressure of temptations, consigned to the slavery of vices, conscience at first does not cease every hour to murmur and act restlessly. But as evil habit gradually gains strength, it is brought to such a point that it ceases to kick against its taskmasters and, like a trained heifer that loves threshing, serves without murmur or contradiction. Yet when the time of favour and the time of mercy have come before the Lord, and after many evils it has been visited by the Lord’s mercy, as if through Moses’ office, and pierced with compunction unto repentance, it begins to kick back and to wish to shake off the yoke of captivity; but it cannot yet prevail.

Then, as divine consolations become more frequent and many things flash forth like miracles, it begins gradually to recover strength, acquire vigour, take courage, and at last prevail over its enemies—but not without great labour and the utmost difficulty. [Col. 1055D]

At last, when the tyranny of vices has been subdued and that whole army of Pharaoh, as it were, has been drowned by the cleansing of inward compunction, as zeal for good habit gains strength and fear of the enemies is removed, one begins now to rejoice in the tranquillity of a good conscience and to draw near to the promised land of delightful security. Thus the first generation consists of those who serve and do not protest; the second, of those who protest but do not prevail; the third, of those who prevail and labour; the fourth, of those who prevail and rest.

For those dwelling in the wilderness and living on heavenly food, what other kind of occupation ought there to be than to be at leisure and [Col. 1056A] see that the Lord is sweet? In the first stage conscience is tranquil and evil; in the second, disturbed and evil; in the third, disturbed but good; in the fourth, tranquil and good. Through tranquillity of conscience, moreover, one approaches security of conscience. The delight [security] of a secure conscience is that land flowing with milk and honey which, as was said above, is promised and given by the Lord to Abraham’s heirs. Rightly, therefore, it is said: “But in the fourth generation they shall return here.” And it is added: “For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete, even unto the present time.”

The merits of individuals are apportioned according to differences in character. Some are more ashamed or pierced with compunction by a shameful thought than others are by a most shameful deed. Hence some, [Col. 1056B] after a shameful thought, are carried away into wicked delight. Others slip from wicked delight into mere consent to wickedness; others, even after consent, plunge into action. Some also turn a perverse action into a habit. Thus the fall of each is moderated according to the judgment of Him by whose dispensation all things work together for good to those who are good.

There are indeed some of such great shamelessness, hardness, and pride that after many evils they can scarcely be instructed into a full knowledge of their weakness, scarcely be truly humbled, scarcely be inwardly pierced with compunction for their perversity. Therefore the iniquities of the Amorites seem to be complete when, by the dispensation of Him who governs all things, [Col. 1056C] they are permitted to grow to such enormity as will in due time abundantly suffice to confound, crush, and trample down the heart’s shamelessness, hardness, and pride.

We have now heard how much Abraham learned through divine revelation after the sun had set for him, sleep had fallen upon him, and horror had seized him. Scripture repeats what it had already said above, in order to show more fully what things are accustomed to follow the setting of the sun: “When the sun had set,” it says, “a dark gloom came to be, and there appeared a smoking furnace and a lamp of fire passing between those divisions” (Gen. 15). It stated what he heard; it says again what he saw after this sun had set for him and carnal love had failed. We have heard what he heard; let us also attend to what he saw. First fire smoking, afterwards [Col. 1056D] fire blazing; first fire kindling, afterwards fire illuminating.

He therefore saw a smoking furnace and a lamp. No one, certainly, lights a lamp for warmth, but only for illumination. Conversely, no one kindles a furnace for the benefit of illumination, but for warming. In the smoking furnace, therefore, understand the burning of love; in the lamp, the light of revealing grace. Notice also this: we put fire into a furnace in order to warm its interior, not its exterior. In the burning of the furnace, therefore, understand love of spiritual things, inward love, love of virtues.

Fire is kindled as though in a furnace and held enclosed as though in its interior, when love is nourished in the inward places of the heart; and then it is truly held, as though [Col. 1057A] enclosed within, where it arises, when the mind is more ardently inflamed to love and desire the mind’s own goods. We kindle a furnace, as it were, when we more vehemently inflame the heart’s desire for those things which should be desired more inwardly. By the true and inward goods of the mind, truly and inwardly to be desired, we mean virtue itself and goodness itself. Therefore, when virtue is loved for virtue’s own sake, without regard to reward, and when goodness itself is loved for its own sake, even without an intention of recompense, then truly and beyond doubt the fire of love seems to be kindled in the depths and restrained there, lest it burst forth toward external things.

But it is rightly asked why a smoking furnace, rather than a blazing one, is shown to Abraham. Yet we know that, when a furnace is kindled, smoke always rises at the beginning [Col. 1057B]; but as the fire gradually increases, the smoke itself gradually diminishes and at length seems wholly to fail. What else, then, is expressed by the fact that a smoking furnace is shown to Abraham in the vision, except a certain beginning of inward love? For however much a person may seem to have advanced in the increase of charity in this life, if you consider the fullness of the life to come, it will appear, by comparison with it, to have been only a certain beginning of perfection.

Smoke indeed stings the eyes and brings forth tears; and charity, however much it has progressed in the condition of the present life, when carefully tested and closely examined, pierces the mind with the reproach of conscience, because, so long as one lives here, one does not love Him with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s mind, as is divinely commanded. [Col. 1057C] Thus in the smoking furnace is expressed the beginning of inward and supreme love. For in charity nothing is found more exalted, nothing more splendid, than when goodness itself is loved for its own sake.

But as in the smoking furnace there is rightly understood a certain beginning of inward and supreme love, so in the lamp there is suitably expressed a certain beginning of inward and supreme light. For no one lights a lamp in order to see the region all around, or the things situated all around within it. Rather, we light a lamp in order to see nearby things, and those which are in the inner recesses of our dwelling. But what is nearer to the spirit than the spirit itself—unless perhaps, by pursuing vain things, it abandons itself, and, casting away its inward things, withdraws from itself? What can be nearer or more inward to it than that Spirit who is everywhere and can be absent nowhere?

Certainly the human heart is perverse and unsearchable; it cannot be known, just as it cannot be seen, except by the light of a lamp sent from above and divinely kindled. For such a lamp is sent from above to Abraham, and the Psalmist is divinely illumined: “For thou dost light my lamp, O Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. 17). If, therefore, without the benefit of the divine lamp you cannot see your own inward things, how much less can you see divine mysteries? A lamp is divinely lit for a person when the surpassing excellence of inward goods is made manifest to that person in divine light.

But [Col. 1058A] if the form of divine revelation had to be shown to Abraham, why is it expressed to him in a lamp rather than in the sun? However greatly human understanding may advance in this life in the manifestation of inward light, it does not grow unto the perfect day; it receives only a certain beginning, as it were, of that future fullness. Therefore, just as in the smoking furnace there is rightly understood a certain beginning of the future fullness in the love of supreme goodness, so in the burning lamp we rightly understand a certain beginning of the future fullness in contemplation of supreme wisdom.

These two, moreover, are accustomed to confer mutual growth upon one another: love grows from knowledge, and knowledge from love. Yet it happens that, at the very time when a person burns greatly with desire, [Col. 1058B] that person sees little; and conversely, at the time when one sees much, one burns little. In these matters, beyond doubt, that supreme craftsman displays the skill of his own art. And He makes known how powerless a human being is without the cooperation of the divine gift, while effects in their causes occur to that person beyond hope and expectation. This is what is expressed when a smoking furnace and a lamp are shown to Abraham, and the forms both of divine inspiration and of revelation are set forth separately and distinctly.

It must further be observed how it is seen here: “Passing,” it says, “between the divisions themselves” (Gen. 15). What we discern figuratively, we prove by experience in actual things. For the revelation of goodness and truth always tends toward the source of all goods, and draws after itself into that same reality the mind which it affects.

But [Col. 1058C] what is meant by the fact that the spiritual pattern which the patriarch saw appeared to him amid the divisions? As we have already said above, those divide their sacrifices who strive, in the good deeds they do, to please both God and neighbour, and who resolve with all diligence to avoid both the wrath of God and scandal to their neighbour. Without doubt, nothing is more laborious or more difficult. See, then, that double grace described above, which is rightly bestowed or increased from the very source from which the human mind is more earnestly pressed on account of God: for this is why a furnace and a lamp are described as appearing to Abraham amid the divisions.

But it should be noted that, before Abraham saw these things, he encountered dark gloom. Certainly, [Col. 1058D] whoever has not yet recognized the obscurity of human error and the hidden dangers amid which one moves cannot attain that fire of true love which does not know how to cling to low things. Whoever does not yet understand that human life upon earth is temptation, ignorant of the exile one suffers, does not know how to sigh for the homeland, does not know inward light, does not know the ardour of true and inward love.

This is the fire sent from heaven, given after the setting of the sun. This is the fire that begets trust, prepares confidence, nourishes hope, and removes fear. “Charity believes all things, hopes all things.” Finally, perfect charity casts out fear. For after Abraham deserved to receive that fire sent from heaven, nowhere thereafter is he read to have doubted the Lord’s promises. And certainly, if we desire to inherit that land flowing with milk and honey, [Col. 1059A] we ought, so far as we can, to pant after receiving such fire. Let us prepare for the Patriarch such a sacrifice, and in the very order in which he himself offered it; and without doubt, as a sign of the inheritance we are to receive, we shall receive the fire for which we long.

[Col. 1059]

## TREATISE ON THE TWOFOLD PASSOVER

### SERMON FOR PALM SUNDAY

[Col. 1059A]

We observe a twofold Passover; indeed, we ought to celebrate a twofold Passover. The first is that which is commonly called the flowering Passover, and concerning which we are now obliged to say something appropriate to the occasion. But who, I ask, [Col. 1059B] would not delight to speak of such a season? Whom would its loveliness not stir to praise it or inflame to love it? O lovely season, welcome season, flowering season! A lovely season, distinguished by the manifold variety of flowers; a welcome season, sprinkled all around with pleasing fragrance. To whom, I ask, would it not be pleasing and welcome, when it may now truly be said: “For now the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared; the flowering vines have given their fragrance” (Song 2)?

Who would not wish, in its praise, to cry out that apostolic saying: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6)? An acceptable season indeed, adorned with flowers; and no less health-giving, since fruit is also hoped for from it. Without any doubt, unless [Col. 1059C] the flowering season comes first, we await fruit in vain and with empty hope. Let the flower-bearing Passover therefore precede, so that the fruit-bearing Passover may follow.

We ought indeed to keep this twofold Passover as a feast and receive it with every solemn celebration. Do you wish to know more plainly what we mean? You know, I think, that *pascha* means “passing over,” and is called Passover from the passing over of the Lord. What, then, do we call the flowering Passover except a worthy and pleasing passage? And what the fruit-bearing Passover except a joyful passage full of every gladness? Receive, then, the twofold passage: both pleasing, both worthy. The first is that we pass from wickedness to righteousness; the second, that we pass from misery to glory.

Brothers, what shall we say of these things, or what sort of [Col. 1059D] passages do we think they are? What, I ask, will it be like to pass from iniquity to goodness, from calamity to blessedness? The first passage belongs to the first Passover; the second to the second Passover. You see, I beg you, how gladly and gratefully we ought to keep such a festive season and celebrate it solemnly. Certainly, we all love and desire alike that second Passover. But is the first received with equal devotion or celebrated with equal zeal? Would that all were as zealous to be good as they desire to be blessed; then indeed they would be as blessed as they are good in the life to come! Would that all desired the beginnings of the righteous as much as they desire their end! Balaam says: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last things be like theirs” (Num. [Col. 1060A] 23). But those who wish their end to be like that of the righteous should strive to have the same beginning. Let them meanwhile flower through righteousness, and they shall receive from it the fruit, eternal life.

From a righteous life comes eternal life; from a good life, a blessed life; from such a flower, such fruit; from a perfect life, [Col. 1060B] everlasting life. “Every tree is known by its fruit.” There is no bad tree which bears good fruit. If the tree is good, its fruit is good, and its flowers are pleasing. But flowers must always come first for fruit to follow; otherwise fruit is hoped for in vain without preceding flowers. Let the flowering Passover therefore precede, that the fruit-bearing Passover may follow. Meanwhile let us pass from dishonour to honour, so that afterwards we may pass from unhappiness to happiness. If we are still evil, let us pass from evil to good; if good, let us pass from good to better, and through better to best—and so we have kept the flowering Passover.

Why, I ask, do people gather on this flowering Passover, except to make the customary procession? Is not proceeding itself a passing over and a keeping of Passover? [Col. 1060C] We make this Passover flowering when we pass in due order toward worthier things; and we make a beautiful procession when we advance in goodness. How beautiful, how splendid, we think, is the procession of going from virtue to virtue, forgetting the things behind and stretching forth toward those before! O what flowers true virtues are! Let us therefore strew our way with such flowers and pass through the flowering places of the virtues; let us proceed purely and honourably, so that we may make our procession beautiful and pleasing and accomplish the flowering Passover with worthy celebration.

O how pure and delightful it will be to go amid flowers and pass through the pleasant places of the virtues: through the crocus of charity, the lily of chastity, the rose of suffering, and the violet of humility! O how praiseworthy, how lovely it is to scatter a pleasing fragrance everywhere, diffuse on every side the sweetness of one’s reputation, draw the minds of those running together from every direction to the delightful spectacle of one’s procession, and move the minds of beholders by the example of one’s integrity!

This, then, is the first procession, and it belongs to the first Passover; for there is another, and it belongs to the second Passover. The first procession is an advance toward the perfection of goodness; the second procession is an advance toward the fullness of blessedness. Christ made a twofold procession; indeed, he willed us also to make one: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16). His departure from the highest heaven is the first procession; his return to its summit is the [Col. 1061A] second. First he descended; afterwards he ascended. The first procession is one of humiliation; the second, one of exaltation.

If we are truly Christians, we must imitate Christ. For “he who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as Christ walked.” Let us first be humbled with Christ, so that afterwards we may be exalted with Christ. “Humble yourselves meanwhile under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you on the day of judgment,” at the time of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let us therefore follow Christ meanwhile where he went on earth, so that we may at last deserve to follow where he went in heaven. “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccles. 2). If you are wise and have Christ as your head, you ought to look to him. Observe the footprints of his journey and strive to follow by whatever virtue you can.

See, therefore, how he proceeded, or by what way he went before you. Certainly this Paschal procession of today’s festival proceeds generally from the remembrance or imitation of his deeds. Observe, then, what procession the evangelist describes to you and sets before you for imitation. Let us see from where he began, whither he went, through what place he passed, and how he proceeded. This is what I mean, what I urge you to attend to: from where, whither, through what place, and how Christ made his procession.

From where did he begin? From Bethany (John 12; Matt. 21; Mark 11; Luke 19). Whither does he go? To Jerusalem. Through what place did he pass? Through the Mount of Olives. How did he come? On a donkey. Thus he began his journey from Bethany and went to Jerusalem, sitting on a donkey and passing through Olivet. This is Christ’s procession, which Christians ought to imitate.

Behold the order and the kind of journey by which we ought to go to Jerusalem; behold the end toward which we ought to tend in all that we do. Keep, brothers, the unity of faith in the bond of peace, and you are in Jerusalem, and you have completed the procession taught by Christ. For Jerusalem, as you know, is interpreted “vision of peace.” Behold, brothers, what we wish to exhort you toward: that we seek peace, grasp peace, and preserve peace. “Turn away from evil and do good,” and you have begun the procession fitting for a Christian; “seek peace and pursue it,” and you have arrived at Jerusalem and completed the procession.

Finally, let there be in us peace with all, and we are in Jerusalem. We have some who are our superiors, others our inferiors, and others our equals. Let us therefore have peace with superiors, peace with inferiors, peace with equals; then we have peace with all and have reached Jerusalem. First, indeed, and most necessary in every way, is that we not disturb the peace of our prelates, to whom the Lord said: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me” (Luke 10). Let us be ready at every hour for every act of obedience, and without doubt we shall have full peace with our prelates. In what respect, I ask, can they be troubled concerning us if we refuse all that they refuse and will all that they will? If, therefore, we wish to journey toward Jerusalem and attain true peace, we must begin with obedience and [Col. 1062A] begin the way of peace from Bethany. For Bethany is interpreted “house of obedience.”

But I think we should not pass over this point here, though I wish to mention it briefly: some are our superiors in power, others in dignity; the former by office, the latter by merit. The former preside by certain ranks of honour and power; the latter excel by certain attainments of wisdom and holiness. Human election has made the former complete; divine ordering has exalted the latter. Consider, then, what it is to revere those whom human institution has put before you, yet to refuse veneration to those whom divine providence has singularly magnified. If those who temporarily preside over us are to be venerated with due honour, how worthy of honour are those who, by the merit of holiness, surpass us eternally in everlasting exaltation?

Hence [Col. 1062B] good prelates venerate such subjects with great honour, though they rule them, as stated, by certain ranks of prelation. First, therefore, and especially, we must strive to have peace with all who are above us; but this must not suffice unless we also endeavour to preserve the bond of peace with inferiors and the weaker. We ought to soothe superiors by service and obedience, and aid inferiors by compassion for their weakness. Obedience must be shown to superiors; mercy must be extended to inferiors. Therefore the journey must begin from Bethany, but pass through Olivet.

For *elaion* (ἔλαιον) among the Greeks signifies “mercy,” and oil itself denotes works of piety. We pass through the Mount of Olives when we perform works of piety for any who are weaker, when we sympathize with their weakness rather than becoming angry or indignant. Certainly you see how greatly this contributes to obtaining peace with the weak and possessing tranquillity of your own mind. For one who is disturbed and indignant at every offence one sees—when, I ask, will such a person find peace? When, I beg you, will that person obtain, or even hope to obtain, true tranquillity of mind? One will always find in weaker persons something rightly to rebuke and mercifully to endure. Otherwise they would not be weak if they had nothing of weakness.

Let the advancement or procession of our progress, then, take place through the Mount of Olives, and let our piety grow immeasurably, so that by reason of its greatness it may rightly be called a mountain. Let us learn to endure with tranquillity of mind not merely the least but even the greatest failings of the weak, and patiently and piously bear our neighbours’ weakness, not only bodily but also spiritual. Certainly, if we do these things, we are now drawing near to Jerusalem and touch the fullness of peace the more closely as we attain more deeply to the perfection of obedience and mercy.

I think that it is now necessary to seek a donkey and, among such marks of virtue, claim for oneself the support of humility. Thus Christ Jesus, when they were drawing near to Jerusalem, caused a donkey to be brought to him and sat upon it. We all know that the donkey is an unclean and lowly animal, certainly very gentle, but almost more contemptible than all others. It therefore bears, I think, the image of humility, through which the mind becomes lowly in its own eyes and comes into contempt.

Indeed, without such an animal our procession may perhaps be splendid, but without it it certainly will not, and cannot, be so admirable. Who, I ask, would not rightly marvel to see a donkey among choirs going before and singing psalms on either side, and such a lowly animal appearing among such glorious and solemn displays? As for me, it seems more remarkable to my eyes for a man clothed in pontifical vestments to sit on a donkey and not blush at such a seat amid such insignia, than for him to carry in his hands that wood which is pleasing to nearly all, or to wear a mitre upon his head [Col. 1063B] or a pallium upon his shoulders.

It is neither new nor remarkable to glory in virtues. But this is great and marvellous: not to disdain a donkey amid the highest ornaments of virtues; to cling firmly to the good of humility; for one and the same person to appear admirable to all others but contemptible to oneself alone. In this order we make our procession admirable: if, amid the heights of obedience and mercy, we do not abandon humility’s modesty. By this art we shall be able to win over our equals, if with utmost diligence we strive always to occupy the last place, sincerely preferring them to ourselves in the duty of reverence and the place of honour—indeed, truly believing that they ought to be preferred, persuading ourselves of this, and desiring that others too be persuaded of it.

You see, certainly, that in this matter we need something which has almost slipped from us: a she-donkey and her colt. There are two things: humility and humiliation. Humility is signified in the she-donkey; humiliation in the colt. The colt is born from the she-donkey, and true humiliation arises from humility. Humility is inward; humiliation outward. Humility is in the heart; humiliation in action. Humility belongs to disposition; humiliation, to deed. But only that humiliation is necessarily true which proceeds from humility.

Whoever truly recognizes one’s own weakness and becomes lowly in one’s own eyes has already brought the she-donkey, as it were, into one’s presence. But if one blushes to humble oneself in the sight of people or to appear contemptible, one has the mother present but still lacks the colt’s presence. If you humble yourself outwardly but think something great of yourself, you have the colt but not the mother. Let us therefore bring the she-donkey and the colt with her, so that, being truly humble in mind, we may display true humiliation in action. Otherwise, if you humble yourself falsely and walk deceitfully, then, according to the Prophet’s saying, “you shall be compelled to cross rivers, uncover your legs”; without doubt your shame will be revealed (Isa. 47), because nothing is covered that shall not be revealed.

Let us therefore strive to be truly humble and to appear truly humble; and in this way, I think, we shall be able to win over our equals. For it is plain that envy is especially accustomed to arise among equals, and discord from envy. But if we sit on the donkey, as was said, and hold among them the lowest, a lowly, and abject place, we cut off the fuel of envy. Without doubt, true humiliation not only restores peace among equals but also confirms it with superiors and inferiors.

See, then, what it means to seek such a seat, and, if necessary, even to bring it from far away. For some take it easily from nearby, but for others it must be brought from far away. Those who still live outrageously and commit shameful deeds find ready at hand sufficient cause for shame and self-humiliation. Such was that publican who was ashamed even to lift his eyes to heaven. But those who find nothing shameful in their life—such, I think, as come from Bethany and pass through [Col. 1064B] Olivet, who keep the flowering Passover and strew their way with the flowers of virtues—must, I think, bring the donkey from afar and draw matter for their humiliation either from the fall of their former life or from the condition of the future life.

Thus Paul, because he had no nearby ground from which to obtain for himself a donkey—for he was conscious of nothing against himself—sent the scouts of his reflection along the path of his former manner of life and from there sought material by which to humble himself. Hear from where he brings himself a donkey, or what low place of abasement he chooses for himself, when he says: “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15).

But what [Col. 1064C] shall one do who can say with blessed Job: “My heart does not reproach me throughout my whole life” (Job 27)? Certainly one who is such has no source from which to bring a donkey from things already left behind, because one finds nothing in one’s former conduct by which to become lowly in one’s own eyes. But see what one may do: let one send before oneself the measure of supreme perfection not yet attained, in order to consider it. Let one consider what is that perfection of angelic purity, what consummation of angelic integrity; and without doubt one can gather, by comparison, the measure of one’s imperfection in the village set over against oneself.

Let one consider what purity belongs to the future life, and what its integrity is like: how pure it is from every evil and how whole in every good; pure from every corruption, [Col. 1064D] whole from every imperfection. I think that by this twofold ministry one can bring oneself a donkey and find grounds for truly humbling oneself. Certainly it will not be safe, without such a humble seat, to meet the children of the Hebrews while they cry from every side, “Well done, well done!” For they are children and therefore cannot discern whom, when, or how they ought to praise.

I think that the Apostle wished us to seek such a seat when he warned us not to think highly of ourselves: “Not thinking high things,” he says, “but consenting to lowly things” (Rom. 12). This is the manner of procession which Christ followed and which he certainly willed us also to follow. Do you wish to know more plainly that he came from Bethany and that in all he did he maintained obedience? “I came,” he says, “not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6). And the Apostle declares that he “became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2).

Certainly he also passed through the Mount of Olives, and by the death which he underwent for us he showed how greatly he loved us. “For no one has greater charity than this: that one lay down one’s life for one’s friends.” Do you wish to know how he sat upon a donkey, or how humble was his coming? Though he was in the form of God, “he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man.” But who does not know that throughout all such a way he tends toward Jerusalem—unless perhaps one can be ignorant that he himself is [Col. 1065B] our peace, who made both one, breaking down the dividing wall of hostility in his flesh and abolishing the law of commandments in decrees?

Behold how Christ passed; behold with what flowers he strews his way, in order to keep the flowering Passover and pass through the pleasant places of virtues. Behold what Christ’s procession was. Behold from where and whither; behold through what place and how: the points which I remember having set forth above. From obedience through piety, with humility, toward peace. I do not know whether that which a more extended discourse expounded more copiously could have been recapitulated more briefly.

Remember also to strew your own way with such flowers, if you desire to celebrate the flowering Passover. Good flowers are obedience and mercy; good flowers are humility and peace. “But,” you say, [Col. 1065D] “you have spoken of flowers: where are the fruits?” Do you wish to know in Christ what fruits arose from the obedience he maintained and the mercy he bestowed, in that he became obedient to the Father for us unto death? Recall that saying of the Apostle: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6).

Receive also what is the fruit of the peace sought and humility embraced: “Therefore,” he says, “God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). Behold what a passage; behold how fruitful! From death to life; from tribulation to glory. Behold the second Passover; behold the fruit-bearing Passover. O what fruits: life and glory! O sweet fruit, O exalted fruit: everlasting life with supreme glory, and supreme glory with everlasting life.

But Christ did not wish to eat these fruits alone; rather, he scattered them and gave them to the poor. And now: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits; afterwards, those who are his” (1 Cor. 15). And in the place where it was said, “You are not my people,” it is now said to them, “sons of the living God” (Hos. 1). For as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many are made righteous. “For if, through the offence of one, death reigned through one, much more shall those receiving the abundance of grace, gift, and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ” (Rom. [Col. 1066A] 5).

Knowing, therefore, that the fruit of obedience is true immortality and the incorruption of eternal life, let us all run with great haste to Bethany, submitting ourselves to every obedience. Let us not doubt at all concerning its fruit, but hold without any hesitation that “this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.”

But because, according to the Apostle, bodily exercise is useful for a little, whereas godliness is of value in every respect, holding promise for the life that now is and for that which is to come, let us cross the Mount of Olives, training ourselves in godliness, knowing without doubt that we shall receive oil for oil: the oil of gladness for the oil of mercy. For blessed are the merciful, because they shall obtain mercy. Nor should you be ashamed to sit upon an ass [Col. 1066B], or to recline in the lowest place, knowing that God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Let nothing therefore be done through rivalry or vain glory, but in humility, each counting the others superior to himself; not each considering his own interests, but those of others. We willingly humble ourselves, I think, if we have regard for the fruit of true humiliation. Without doubt, just as everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, so everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted. Consider, however, what that exaltation is, so that you may recognize what fruit true humiliation bears. What, or how great, do you suppose it is to possess the kingdom of heaven? For I judge that this itself is the fruit of true humiliation. For blessed are the poor in spirit, because theirs [Col. 1066C] is the kingdom of heaven. See then in what order, toward what fruit or end, we ought to proceed and make our way to Jerusalem. Certainly, if we advance in this order, if we hasten with this intention, we draw near to Jerusalem; if we keep obedience together with charity and humility, we more swiftly find the true peace which we seek. O foolish, O blind person, who does not eagerly hasten where he may find peace—and true peace! Yet do you wish to know its fruit, that from this you may gather how urgently one ought to hasten in order to obtain it? “Blessed,” I say, “are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. V). O wonderful fruit, O singular fruit—what great glory for a servant, and such an unworthy servant, to become a child of God! What, I ask, can now taste sweet or give satisfaction to one whom desire for this fruit does not draw? If we hunger for this fruit, if we desire to enjoy it, let us strive for true peace. Meanwhile let us hold fast the peace which Christ left us, and securely await that which he promised: “Peace,” he says, “I leave you; my peace I give you” (John XIV). Therefore let not your heart be troubled or afraid: you possess the peace which Christ left you and wished you to preserve. But perhaps you also seek to know what that peace is which Christ promised, or called his own. Yet by what words, I ask, can I explain what is that peace of God which surpasses all understanding?
