Let us therefore run through peace toward peace: through inward peace toward eternal peace. For there is a peace that is only outward, a peace that is only inward, and a peace that is at once inward and outward. The first belongs [Col. 1067A] to the flesh alone, the second to the mind alone, the third to both mind and flesh together. We can possess the first and the second in this life, but never at the same time; we always observe them separately, each in contrary conditions. The third we hope for only in the life to come, and for this reason we have called it eternal. Christ came to destroy the first, establish the second, and give the third—though reserving it for the future. Of the first he says: “I came not to bring peace upon earth, but a sword” (Matt. XI). Of the second and third we understand what we have already set forth above: “Peace I leave you; my peace I give you” (John XII). Let us therefore detest that peace which Christ condemned, love that which Christ taught, and hope for that which Christ has laid up for us, because he who promised is faithful [Col. 1067B]. Let us love the inward peace and hope for the eternal. The former belongs to the flower; the latter to the fruit. The former belongs to the first Passover; the latter belongs to the second Passover. Whoever still loves the first must leave it and pass to the second, certain that through it he will pass to the third. Whoever has passed to the second has already celebrated the first Passover, the flowering Passover. Whoever has made the second passage from the second to the third, and tasted of its fruits, has already passed to the second Passover, whose celebration shall be everlasting. Behold, we have spoken of flowers; behold, of fruits. Let us desire these, and may we merit those—[the text is corrupt: “ut in aeternum fuit”]—and rejoice without end in the eternal celebration.

## SERMON FOR EASTER DAY

[Col. 1067C] “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” brethren. You know the Scriptures and their power. Therefore our discourse to you will not be instruction, but admonition and a recalling to memory of things already known. For you drink from the fountain from which I drink. Where I draw water, you also draw. If I draw with joy waters from the springs of the Saviour, you also draw from them. Judge therefore, as spiritual persons, whether the water which I shall offer you flows from the midst of the springs, or has been drawn from the springs of the Saviour.

“Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.” The Lord’s fruitful passion and his glorious resurrection are not merely events and signs, but also remedies. They are not merely truth and figure, but medicine as well. They are truth, because he who truly died [Col. 1067D] through weakness rose through power. They are signs and figure, because he died and rose again so that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness. They are medicine, because he died for our offences and rose again for our justification. Let us therefore, according to our measure, speak of the example and remedy of the Passion, and of the remedy and example of the Resurrection.

Christ became obedient unto death and gave us an example of perfect humility and consummate charity. What true, unfeigned humility is, he expressed in his very words when he spoke to the Father, saying: “Not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Matt. XXVI). This is the voice of true humility, which always prefers the divine will to the human and is thereby directed away from human things toward divine things. Nor does it do this only: it also prefers another person’s will to its own—not only that of one greater, or of an equal, but even that of one inferior. The contrary is the voice of pride: “Not as thou wilt, but as I will.” Its characteristic is to prefer its own will, not only to another human will but even to the divine will; and thereby it is plunged down from divine things into the lowest depths. The humble person, therefore, does not his own will but God’s; the proud person does not God’s will but his own. The humble person seeks not his own glory but God’s; the proud person seeks not God’s glory but his own. The humble builds upon rock; the proud upon sand. Therefore all proud persons are disciples of the devil, who is king and master over the children of pride. But all humble persons are disciples of Christ, who, in order to teach humility and become the master of humility, became humble [Col. 1068B]. Hence he glories in his disciples, he who is humble in the humble, saying: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me” (Isa. VIII). For he gives such persons to the Son, drawing them to the Son, according to the saying: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John VI). Those who come to the Son drawn by the Father do not come unwillingly, but without compulsion, without necessity: by will, love, and the bond of the heart. For in this the Father draws the humble to the Son: that he reveals the Son to them. Hence: “Thou hast hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI). The Son, however, does not cast out those who come to him, but receives them kindly. And, to test whether they love him, he lays upon them a bundle of myrrh, of which he himself also ate, just as he drank from the torrent while passing [Col. 1068C] through the eye of a needle—that is, through the straits of the Passion. But they, because of the greatness of their love, do not feel the bitterness of the myrrh, glorying in tribulation. Hence one of them says: “We know that neither death nor life can separate us from the charity of Christ” (Rom. VIII).

He also gave us an example of consummate charity in his very sacrifice, praying for his enemies. He described this charity when he said: “No one has greater charity than to lay down his life for his friends” (John XV). But the Lord Jesus laid down his life while we were enemies, and thereby commended his charity. The Apostle says that it surpasses knowledge. Indeed, we cannot comprehend it unless we are rooted and grounded in charity: rooted after the likeness of a tree, grounded [Col. 1068D] after the likeness of a house; grounded through love of God, through which we are God’s house and temple, and God dwells in us; rooted through love of neighbour, through which we are fruit-bearing trees, bringing forth leaves of protection and fruit of support. Those who are thus rooted and grounded in charity can comprehend, with all the saints, what are the breadth and length and height and depth of charity. The breadth of charity is seen in loving one’s enemy; its length, in persevering to the end; its height, in doing all things for God’s sake. The depth of charity is considered in this: that a person attributes no good to himself, but everything to the grace of God, whose reasons it is too deep to investigate, surpassing human understanding—namely, why he hardens one person [Col. 1069A] and calls another. Hence the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments!” (Rom. XI).

The disease of all self-exaltation is healed by the medicine of humility. The infirmity of covetousness is cured by the gift of charity. For through these two, namely pride and concupiscence, the prince of this world dwelt in us: through pride in the mind, through concupiscence in the flesh. But now the prince of this world has been cast out by the grace of Christ. Hence he himself says: “Behold, I cast out demons and accomplish healings” (Luke XXIII). In the forgiveness of sins demons are cast out; in the infusion of virtues into minds healings are accomplished.

Concerning the remedy of the Passion, it remains to be said that it is understood in justice and mercy. For our Saviour [Col. 1069B], though omnipotent, could by the mere word of his power have freed humankind from the power of darkness. But in our liberation he chose rather to employ justice than power, because the devil is a lover of power and a deserter of justice. In this human beings chiefly imitate him when they seek power and hold justice in hatred. What is that justice? Hear.

Christ is innocent and free from every sin, alone among the dead free, having no liability to sin under the author of sin. As he himself says: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John XIV). For the entire possession of the ancient enemy is sin: it was given to him as an inheritance—a land barren of hope, full of thorns and briars, a land cursed by the Lord, whose boundary-lines fell in dark and shadowy places [Col. 1069C]. Of all his substance nothing is found in Christ; nevertheless, he killed the innocent one, and therefore was commanded to withdraw from the guilty who flee to Christ. He killed him who owed nothing to death, and was commanded to withdraw from those indebted to death who believe in him who died for them.

The mercy of our redemption is indicated in this: Christ, out of charity alone, obedient to the Father out of compassion for our misery, endured death; and thereby he merited greatly before God the Father and granted all his merit to his own members. In his Passion he destroyed him who held the power of death, expiated humanity’s guilt, reconciled the sinner to God the Father, and, as David killed Goliath with Goliath’s own sword [Col. 1069D], so Christ slew the devil with his own weapons. What were the devil’s weapons by which he conquered the world and by which Christ conquered him? Death. For the author of sin, by divine sentence, was able to inflict bodily death upon whomever he wished; and therefore human beings were subject, through fear, to the slavery of sin or the devil, and endured anything lest they die. Hence Job says: “Skin for skin, and a man will give everything for his life” (Job II). But the Saviour voluntarily accepted death and, by dying, destroyed death, and thus rescued human beings from the fear of death. Hence the saints now fear death, but desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. Of this remedy the Saviour says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not [Col. 1070A] perish but have eternal life” (John III).

You know the history: how the children of Israel, murmuring in the desert, were struck by fiery serpents. Then Moses, by the Lord’s command, raised a bronze serpent upon a pole; and the children of Israel, looking upon it, were healed from the serpents’ bites. By this bronze serpent raised upon a pole we understand Christ crucified; for death entered the world through the serpent, and therefore death is figured by it. That bronze serpent had the likeness of a serpent but had no venom. So too Christ had the likeness of sinful flesh, but did not have the venom of sin. For if he had possessed sin’s venom, he would not free us from the venom of sin. Therefore, whenever we are struck by serpents—that is, wounded by demons—let us look to this serpent with the eye of the flesh and the eye of the mind: with the eye of the flesh, by imitation of the example, that we may crucify the flesh with its vices and desires; with the eye of the mind, by faith in the remedy, saying with Peter: “For there is no other name in which we must be saved” (Acts IV). And without doubt we shall be perfectly healed from every wound: through imitation of the example we shall be healed from every sinful act; through faith in the remedy we shall be cleansed from every guilt. This is the weakness of God, which is stronger than human beings. For what human being could accomplish what Christ effected through his death? None—indeed, not even the whole world. This is the foolishness of God, which is wiser than human beings.

Now we must speak of the remedy of the Resurrection [Col. 1070C]: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.” *Pascha* means “passage,” and this belongs to the Resurrection; indeed, the Lord’s passage is his very Resurrection. Thus the present day is called both the day of Passover and the day of Resurrection. For Christ, rising from the dead, passed from death to life, from corruptibility to incorruption; and in this he became our Passover, because in him and through him we pass from darkness to light, from vices to virtues, from the enemy to the Father, from death to life.

And see how it is established that the just person lives by faith. Where faith is absent, justice and life are absent. But at Christ’s death, faith in him was dead even in the apostles, because, when [Col. 1070D] the shepherd was struck, the sheep were scattered. When he rose and appeared to his disciples, faith was restored in the apostles. Moreover, their hearts were kindled and inflamed with love and desire for immortality and future blessedness; and thus, inwardly made alive and justified, they passed over from unbelief to faith, from sin to righteousness, and so passed from the death of the soul to life. For today, as the Apostle says, Christ was given the name which is above every name (Phil. XXI). From eternity indeed he possessed, according to his divinity, the name above every name; and in his incarnation this name was given to his humanity by grace; but what had hitherto lain hidden came publicly to light through the Resurrection. Therefore the Lord proved this Resurrection by so many evidences. For once it stands, the rest stand; it is like the base beneath a column, like the foundation of foundations, upon which all the articles of faith rest. Hence the Apostle placed the entire sum of our salvation in it, saying: “If you believe in your heart and confess with your mouth that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved” (Rom. X). Therefore we must not only believe this, but also keep it in continual remembrance. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “Remember the Lord Jesus, risen from the dead” (II Tim. II). For just as evil desires and harmful passions arise from covetousness, which is the root of all evils and plunges a person into destruction and ruin, so holy desires and devout affections, contempt of the world, and love of eternal things arise from the continual remembrance of the Resurrection; and the person is changed [Col. 1071B] into another man and becomes spiritual.

The one Resurrection of the Lord according to the flesh produces our twofold resurrection: that of souls in the present, of which John says in the Apocalypse: “Blessed is he who has a share in the first resurrection, because he shall not be harmed by the second death” (Apoc. XX); and the resurrection of bodies in the future. Of this the Apostle says: “And he shall refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. III). It remains to speak of the example of the Resurrection, of which the Apostle says: “As Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so let us also walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI). Therefore, now renewed and placed in newness of life, let us walk from newness to newness, from glory to glory [Col. 1071C], from strength to strength; for in that same strength we advance from degree to degree.

These outward processions, which during these days we have observed more solemnly, signify these inward processions, spiritual advances, and increases of virtues. We ought to celebrate them with great devotion, rejoicing both in the resurrection of our Head, in the present resurrection of our minds, and in the resurrection of our bodies which shall be in the future—but above all in the resurrection of Jesus Christ, which is the cause of our twofold resurrection. Thus our greatest joy arises from that for which we sing: “Christ, rising from the dead,” etc. The inward processions, however, are to be made at every time, but especially in this solemnity, in which they are not merely performed but represented.

For them to be carried out profitably [Col. 1071D], two things are necessary: the harp and the psaltery—not material instruments, but the things signified by them. The harp sounds from below and therefore signifies the mortification of vices; the psaltery sounds from above and therefore signifies the performance of good works. Whoever plays the harp but does not play the psaltery, or plays the psaltery but does not play the harp, does not advance or make progress, because neither instrument produces a pleasing sound without the other, because the psaltery is pleasant with the harp. For, as it is written: “The honour of the king loves judgment” (Ps. XCV). We give honour to the highest King when we render thanks for his benefits. But this honour loves judgment, by which evils are punished and vices mortified, because praise is not fitting in the mouth of sinners. For praise befits the upright alone. Hence [Col. 1072A] the Apostle too, teaching us to celebrate this Paschal solemnity, says: “Purge out the old leaven” (I Cor. V). He calls every mortal sin “old leaven,” because it corrupts us and makes us old and sour. Hence Paul previously said: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (*ibid.*). For one deadly sin makes all good merits useless and insufficient for salvation, according to the saying: “Whoever offends in one thing is guilty of all” (Jas. II).

This should not be understood as though one who has one sin has every sin and must be punished for all; nor do we concede the corresponding claim about virtues, that one who has one possesses all. For Jerome says that “whoever has one virtue has all virtues” is a philosophical proposition [Col. 1072B], not a divine one. “Nor,” he says, “does it concern us what Aristotle says, but what Paul says.” How, then, should “whoever offends in one thing is guilty of all” be understood? Is one who commits theft guilty of murder, adultery, sacrilege, and other offences? To be guilty of something is said in more than one way. One is called guilty of sin in one way, guilty of a capital offence in another. Someone is guilty of sin—that is, worthy to be punished for sin. Someone is guilty of a capital offence—that is, worthy to lose his head. Thus when it is said, “Whoever offends in one thing is guilty of all,” it is not understood as meaning guilty of all sins, as though he must be punished for all of them; rather, he is understood to be guilty in respect of all the good works he has done, so as to lose them. For if someone performs nine commandments and transgresses only one, by offending in one thing he has become [Col. 1072C] guilty of all—that is, worthy to lose the merit of the nine commandments—because one transgression is more efficacious for condemnation than nine fulfilled commandments are for salvation. Solomon confirms this interpretation, saying: “Whoever offends in one thing shall lose many good things” (Eccles. IX). Therefore these three authorities—“a little leaven corrupts the whole lump,” “whoever offends in one thing is guilty of all,” and “whoever offends in one thing shall lose many good things”—must be understood in the same sense.

You therefore, brethren, who have lived commendably for a long time, must take care lest a little leaven corrupt the whole mass of your good merits; lest, offending in one thing, you become guilty of all and lose many good things. Therefore, lest this happen, celebrate the Paschal solemnity in your souls according to the Apostle [Col. 1072D]. Unleavened bread is without leaven if it produces sincerity—that is, purity from vices. But in being solid it signifies truth—that is, the performance of good works. Sincerity belongs in part to the harp, truth to the psaltery. But behold, there is someone who mortifies vices and does good deeds, yet directs everything to his own glory. Such a person advances, but does not make progress, because he does not seek God’s glory. Hence the Lord says through the Prophet: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. XXXVI). For it profits nothing to carry harp and psaltery unless everything is done for God. We must turn away from evils and persist in good things, for God’s praise and glory. Hence the Apostle: “Man is the image and glory of God” (I Cor. XXI): man in the mortification of vices, image in doing good deeds. For whoever says that he abides in Christ ought to walk as Christ himself walked—that is, to imitate him; and thus *image* (*imago*) derives from imitation (*imitando*), and “glory of God” means that God, not the man himself, may be glorified in all things.

The Lord signifies this same procession when he says: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (Mark II). Rise from vices; take up your bed—that is, carry the one by whom you were carried: as your brother bore your infirmities, so you bear your brother’s infirmities. By doing these things, walk with a right intention to your house—that is, to paradise—doing everything for the hope of future life. Let no one look back with Lot’s wife, return like a dog to its vomit, or go in mind with the children of Israel back to Egypt and its cooking pots [Col. 1073B], because, according to Truth: “No one putting his hand to the plough” (Luke IX), etc.

Let us now briefly consider whence this procession ought to begin and how far it ought to reach or advance. Let the mind therefore rejoice, the spirit exult, and mouth and tongue bring forth a new song. Let the left hand beat the timbrel or play the harp. Let the right hand play the psaltery—indeed, let us use both hands as the right hand, so that everything inward and outward may resound with praise [Col. 1074A] and glory to God, so that the whole person may tend toward God, according to the saying: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to heaven,” so that he who made the whole may possess the whole (Lam. III). Let us proceed thus until we all meet, as a perfect man, in the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ, to meet Christ in the air.

May God, the good shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep, bring us into the true land of promise, into the land of the living, which flows with milk and honey. This land of the living was promised to us by Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God. He will give it to us as an inheritance when he reveals himself to us, leading us to the vision of the Father, to enjoyment of the highest good, to an abundance of all delights. And, going out and entering in, we shall find pastures [Col. 1074B]. We shall go out through the sense of the flesh and find pasture in the milk of Christ’s humanity. We shall enter through the faculty of reason and find pasture in the honey of his divinity. There shall be eternal fullness, complete joy which no one shall take from us, because it shall be eternal: at the end, without end. May he himself, the author of godliness, bring us to it. Amen.

[Col. 1073]

# ON THE EXTERMINATION OF EVIL AND THE ADVANCEMENT OF GOOD

## FIRST TREATISE

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1073C]

“What is the matter with you, O sea, that you fled; and with you, O Jordan, that you turned backward?” (Ps. CXIII). This utterance of the Prophet is an exclamation joined with wonder; the wonder is joined with exultation. For he saw a certain divine miracle: not merely one, but twofold—each great, each marvellous, each exceedingly astonishing. He saw the sea flee before Israel’s presence; he saw the Jordan turn the force of its current back toward its source; he saw both yield to the Hebrew people and leave a free path for their journey. What of these things was not new? What was not marvellous? He contemplated both; he wondered at both; he rejoiced in both. Therefore he cries out in a voice of exultation and confession: “What is the matter with you, O sea, that you fled; and with you, O Jordan, that you turned backward?” [Col. 1073D]

The first miracle occurred at Israel’s departure from Egypt; the second occurred at Israel’s departure from the desert. Who will at last grant me perfectly to leave the region of dissimilarity? Who can grant me to enter the land of promise, so that I may equally behold the flight of the sea and the turning of the Jordan? It is a beautiful and very pleasant sight: to see the sea-water flee, to see the water of the Jordan return, bitterness retreat and sweetness flow back, bitterness fail [Col. 1074C] and sweetness overflow. Whoever sees these things, I wonder if he too will not cry out: “What is the matter with you, O sea, that you fled; and with you, O Jordan, that you turned backward?” Such miracles are never wont to occur except before true Jews, except before good Hebrews.

## CHAPTER II. On the twofold confession and the twofold advancement

Confession makes a Jew; passage makes a Hebrew. For *Judaeus* means “one confessing,” and *Hebraeus*, “one passing over.” There is true confession and feigned confession; likewise there is a good passage and a bad passage. True confession makes a true Jew, and good passage makes a good Hebrew. To ascribe your evils to yourself, to ascribe your goods to your God: this is true and right confession. The former is confession of guilt, the latter confession of praise; both are certainly useful, both praiseworthy. Likewise there is a twofold passage; each is good, each necessary. One who passes from evil to good passes well; and one who passes from good to what is better likewise makes a good passage. Recognize and confess your evils, and do not remain in them; but pass beyond them, and the first passage and first confession have been made. Likewise, confess to God concerning your goods, praise him for his goods, and do not grow sluggish in them; but strive as far as you can toward better things, and pass to the best, and the second passage and second confession have been made. [Col. 1075A] At the first confession the first miracle is ordinarily performed; at the second confession the second miracle is ordinarily performed. For through confession of guilt the sea’s flight is accomplished, and at confession of praise the Jordan immediately turns.

## CHAPTER III. How confession of guilt avails for the extermination of evil

For everything is washed in confession: the conscience is cleansed, bitterness is removed, the sea flees, tranquillity returns, hope revives, and the soul becomes cheerful. For blessed are those who mourn, because they shall be comforted. What is mourning or sorrowing but being tossed by the storms of the sea? And what is the joy of consolation but the sea’s flight and the departure of sorrow? Hear the Jew confessing his offences, and observe the water of the sea fleeing before him: “I said,” he says, “I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord, and thou hast forgiven the ungodliness of my sin” (Ps. XXXI). He confessed his iniquity and the sea fled, because ungodliness was forgiven. For ungodliness is a sea: it cannot make sweet water; rather, its water is very salty and very bitter, and its bitterness is most bitter. What sweetness, I ask, does envy possess? What sweetness, I beg you, does anger possess? What pleasantness does impatience possess? Such waters, I think, are all bitter and make a sea, because they can delight absolutely no one and please no one. Do you see, then, what sort of great sea, broad in extent [Col. 1075C], this is, which may be called the sea of malice? For there is another that may be called the sea of misery; it too has water by no means sweet, yet less bitter. But blessed is he who rules from sea to sea, so that he is subject to no fault and succumbs to no punishment: so that no iniquity rules him and no adversity oppresses him. Blessed is he before whose presence the sea flees: malice withdraws, misery gives way, conscience becomes cheerful. Can a person of this kind not sing confidently: “What is the matter with you, O sea, that you fled?” If, therefore, you too wish to make yourself a Jew of good profession, confess your sin from the heart, so that you may also see such a spectacle, so great a miracle, and may not hesitate to sing such a hymn: [Col. 1075D] “What is the matter with you, O sea, that you fled?”

## CHAPTER IV. How confession of praise avails for the advancement of good

But let us now consider how the turning of the Jordan is ordinarily brought about by confession of praise. Yet we learn this, I think, better by doing than by disputing; we prove it more quickly by experiencing than by speaking. Therefore you too should earnestly endeavour to confess, wonder at, and reverence God’s power, God’s wisdom, and God’s mercy; and be certain that the more you praise, the more ardently you will love. Therefore do not be reluctant to praise divine grace greatly, that you may love greatly; to love greatly, that you may desire greatly. For the more fervently you desire, the more quickly you will obtain [Col. 1076A] what you greatly long for. Love what you formerly despised; despise what you formerly loved; and be assured that the Jordan has turned. Love God, despise the world, and I shall truly confess that the Jordan has turned backward. What a turning of Jordan this is, I ask: how wonderful, how praiseworthy, how lovely—to make the entire force of love, the entire flood of affection, the entire abundance of delight run with great haste not downward but upward; to seek the things above, not those upon the earth—so that you can truthfully profess that the Jordan has turned backward!

This was, I think, the reason why the Prophet neither regretted nor was ashamed to become a Jew: because he truly recognized that “it is good to confess to the Lord and to sing to thy name, O Most High” (Ps. XCI). Hence comes that firm profession and devout promise: “I will confess to the Lord exceedingly with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him” (Ps. CVIII). Did he not wish to declare himself a Jew when he said: “Praise the Lord, O my soul” (Ps. CXLV)? Did he not forbid the water of the Jordan to flow downward when he admonished his soul with gentle address: “Hope in God, for I shall still confess to him, the salvation of my countenance and my God” (Ps. XLII)? Did he not desire the Jordan’s streams to turn when he said: “Return, O my soul, to thy rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with thee” (Ps. CXIV)? I wonder whether, upon hearing this, you too do not desire to become a Jew and confess to the Lord that he is good, that his mercy endures for ever, and to be found worthy that the Lord may deign [Col. 1076C] to show you so great a miracle, so that with the Prophet you may sing: “for the Jordan turned backward.”

## CHAPTER V. That the first advancement in virtue lies in contempt of the world

Yet this is not sufficient for you, I ask, when you have become a Jew, unless you become at the same time a Hebrew. Indeed, the Hebrews themselves are also Jews, though Jews from one thing and Hebrews from another. For confession, as has been said, makes a Jew, and passage makes a Hebrew. Thus you too, if you are in Egypt, pass over and leave Egypt, and you will make yourself a Hebrew of good hope; and in the sea’s flight you shall see that great and astounding miracle. But if you also strive to cross the desert itself, you shall see miracles still greater than these [Col. 1076D] in the turning of the Jordan. The first passage, therefore, is from Egypt; the second, from the desert. First pass from the world to yourself; secondly, from yourself into God. You loved the world: despise the world and pass over. Leave the cares of this age and take care of yourself, and you begin to be a cultivator of the wilderness. Returning from Egypt’s darkness, from worldly errors, to the more hidden places of the heart, you will find nothing but a place of horror and vast solitude. For this is that deserted, trackless, waterless land: namely, the conscience long neglected, wholly uncultivated, overgrown with thorns and thistles, and full of every horror. Therefore you must leave Egypt and seek such a desert if you wish to behold with your own eyes the sea’s flight, just as David fled far away and remained in solitude. Fulfil, O transgressor, what is commanded to transgressors where it says: “Return, O transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. XLVI); and the first passage has been made, and thereafter you are rightly called a Hebrew.

## CHAPTER VI. That the second advancement in virtue lies in contempt of self
Return, then, to yourself, and guard your heart with all vigilance. But woe to you if you remain there. Do not remain, but pass on, going and passing through to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God. Pass beyond yourself, then; go onward into your God; seek and lay hold of the highest good. Hear her who cries aloud in the streets; listen to the voice of Wisdom, exhorting us to this second passage: “Pass over to me, all you who desire me” (Ecclus. [Col. 1077B] XXIV). Forsake the world, and Israel’s passage out of Egypt has taken place. Despise yourself, and Israel’s passage out of the wilderness has taken place. Contempt for the world, therefore, makes the first passage; contempt for oneself accomplishes the second. At the first passage the sea flees; at the second, the Jordan turns back. The flight of the sea is the removal of bitterness; the turning back of the Jordan is the reordering of love.

## CHAPTER VII. How the destruction of evil comes about through contempt for the world.

Would you hear more plainly? Learn more fully how, at the first passage of the Hebrews—that is, at contempt for the world—the sea flees and bitterness is removed. [Col. 1077C] As soon, without doubt, as you have forsaken Egypt, as soon as you have cast the whole world behind you, the cause of fear, the cause of pain, and the root of bitterness perish—for “the root of all evils is covetousness.” For when will you be able fully to escape the world? When you begin neither to desire any of its prosperities nor to fear any of its adversities. What then will remain that can disturb your mind? What, I ask, do we understand more rightly by the flight of the sea than freedom from being harassed by disturbances of any kind? “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid”: then the sea, fleeing before our sight, has gone away and withdrawn.

I think that the sea will be no more when God wipes every tear from the eyes of the saints, when there shall no longer be mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because [Col. 1077D] the former things have passed away. For what are fear, trembling, and sorrow except exceedingly bitter waters of the sea, utterly devoid of sweetness? The Prophet, unless I am mistaken, entered into the depths of this sea when he said: “Fear and trembling came upon me” (Ps. LIV); and: “Tribulation and distress found me” (Ps. CXVIII). All who forsake Egypt, seek the wilderness, and desire the land of promise encounter such a sea. For “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God.”

## CHAPTER VIII. How contrition of spirit is now a help and now a support of good.

Some have this sea before them, others beside them, and others behind them. For those who have it before them, it is an impediment; for those who have it beside them, it is a help; for those who have it behind them, it is a support. Thus the Israelites, forsaking Egypt, wishing to enter the wilderness, and longing for the promised land, first had the sea before them as an impediment to their journey. Afterwards they had it beside them as an aid to their defence, when it was to them as a wall on the right and on the left. Finally, they had it behind them as a support of security, their enemies having been drowned in it or shut off by it.

What is before us is future; what is beside us is present; what is behind us is past. The sea before us is fear of future dangers. The sea beside us is the labour of pressing conflicts. The sea behind us is sorrow for evils committed. The sea before us is the fear of faint-heartedness; the sea beside us is the labour [Col. 1078B] of anxious vigilance; the sea behind us is the sorrow of repentance. Fear born of faint-heartedness hinders; the labour of vigilance fortifies; the sorrow of repentance protects.

One person, considering the life and striving of others, sees that many, even after the vow of religious profession, return to their vomit and return to the world; he does not even dare to begin what is good. This person has the sea before him, but as an impediment. For what is the trembling of the heart and hesitation of the mind but a kind of tossing of the sea? “He who hesitates is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.”

Another man tramples this fear manfully underfoot, drives away before him the tossing of the sea, corrects his heart’s trembling, courageously prepares his spirit to endure whatever dangers may come for the Lord’s sake, and in this respect does not hesitate to sing: “The sea saw and fled” [Col. 1078C]—because every useless trembling flees and departs before his face. Yet, because he remains solicitous as to how he should avoid negligence in good things and escape the stealthy onset of evils, he does indeed suffer the sea, though not before him, but on either side: for he must act steadfastly here for good and there against evil, labour greatly, and be watchful on both sides.

But blessed are those whom the exercises of virtue and contests of labour no longer weary so much as delight them, and who only lament that they spent some periods of their former life in wickedness or wasted them in vanity. Whoever is such a person shows that he has the sea behind his back, like the man who said: “I will recount to you all my years in the bitterness of my soul” [Col. 1078D] (Isa. XXXVIII). Who could doubt that such persons have left the sea behind their backs, as a most secure support and for the overthrow of their enemies? For the bitterness of repentance customarily not only erases evils already committed by making satisfaction, but also commonly brings about within us that what is forbidden no longer pleases us to repeat.

## CHAPTER IX. On useful and useless contrition.

Let us also consider how here the water of the sea, the wave of bitterness, is for some outside the way and for others in the way. Who doubts that this life is the way to the life to come? One grieves over matters belonging to the present life; another over matters belonging to the future life. For him who grieves over what belongs to this life, the sea is in the way. For him who grieves over what belongs outside this life, the sea is beside the way.

In this life there are both good and evil; in that life there are either goods alone or evils alone. Thus those things that are entirely dissimilar differ greatly from one another and touch one another by no proximity of likeness, because between them a great chasm has been fixed and no proportion of similar quality can be found in them. But this present life lies between the goods and evils of the future life as a kind of middle good-yet-evil, because it approaches both sides by some likeness, having good and evil mingled together. Accordingly, it is joined by an imaginal affinity to the goods of that life through its own goods—though with a shadowy likeness—and likewise to the evils of that life through its own evils. Outside, therefore, [Col. 1079B] this way are the things that meet us after this life: outside indeed, yet beside it, not only through likeness of quality but through connection in time. As soon as we leave these things, we fall into those without delay. Whoever therefore fears, grieves, and weeps on account of those things pours out the wave of sorrow, the flood of bitterness, like sea-water beside the path of his course.

## CHAPTER X. On the twofold compunction of the heart.

Sorrow for eternal goods is the sea on the right; sorrow for eternal evils is the sea on the left. Certainly, if we are of sound mind, we ought to fear and grieve for both, and to flow with the bitter tears of compunction. Let us fear losing the former; let us fear incurring the latter; [Col. 1079C] and we shall have a twofold sea, strongly guarding us on both sides.

Rightly, I think, we strike the sea which meets us in the way, impedes the course of our journey, and blocks the progress of our advance, with the rod of just severity; we frighten it by reflection upon divine rigor; we remove it by remembrance of the coming judgment. Therefore let all our fear and all our sorrow be removed from the path; and instead of fruitless concern for worldly life, let our compunction be divided into two, so that by the sorrow of fear we may wash away eternal evils, and by tears of longing may obtain eternal goods.

Blessed are those who pass beyond even this twofold sea of double sorrow, who leave far behind every uncertainty and fear concerning what is to come, and pass beyond all the grief of distrust by the security of certain hope. Would that such fear and sorrow might also be swallowed up in us by the security of confidence that comes upon us! Let even such a sea flee and depart, that we too may sing with the Prophet: “What ails you, O sea, that you fled?” Was not the sea beside him fleeing away who said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the just judge will render to me on that day” [Col. 1079D] (II Tim. IV)? I think he had left every sea far behind him, and that there was no longer any cause by which he ought to be saddened or disturbed, when he said: “I am conscious of nothing against myself.”

## CHAPTER XI. On vain or true contempt for the world.

But what, I ask, are we to say of the fact that, down to the present day, we see so many people forsake Egypt who nevertheless do not deserve to behold so great a miracle in the flight of the sea? If they truly forsake Egypt, if they are true Hebrews because they pass out of the world and make the first passage of the Hebrews, why do they not experience even the first miracle? Perhaps they leave the world in profession but not in conduct; in outward habit, but not in affection.

“If I must boast, I can boast in this respect alone: for they are Hebrews, and so am I.” But see lest perhaps it is not enough for us and you to have changed place but not mind. Those who cross the sea change the world, not their mind. What good is it to cross over and not become a Hebrew? Without doubt, in Israel’s going forth from Egypt, the flight of the sea shows how rightly each person claims for himself the dignity of this name [Col. 1080B].

## CHAPTER XII. How difficult it is to attain perfect contempt for oneself.

Let us pass out of Egypt in body and also in heart. But let us not think that even this can suffice for us. For a great road still remains if we wish to attain the vision of the second miracle. Undoubtedly, leaving Egypt and crossing the wilderness, leaving the world and conquering oneself and casting oneself behind, are not of the same power or ease. The former is comparatively small, completed in a short time; the latter, after many labours and through many temptations, is scarcely at last ever completed even by a few. The former is the work of one day; the latter we scarcely fulfil after long periods.

Hard, difficult, and great is the task of abandoning oneself: examining oneself well, despising oneself fully, [testing or approving oneself ‘perfecto’: the supplied reading is uncertain], and utterly disapproving oneself. Here is labour; here is groaning. “The heart of man is perverse and unsearchable: who shall know it?” Sons of men, how long will you be heavy-hearted, stiff-necked, and of an untamable heart? And who shall conquer it? [Col. 1080C]

## CHAPTER XIII. By what means the mind is trained toward full contempt for itself.

O how often it is necessary to change places, how often to pitch camp, how many temptations to endure: to test everything, hold fast what is good, and abstain from every appearance of evil! O how often it is necessary to go and return; to forget the things behind and stretch forward to those before; and again, by returning behind, to gain experience of oneself and through one’s own failure to be instructed in one’s own weakness! O how often it is necessary to fall among, explore, and observe so many byways of error, so many shadowy regions of uncertainty, so many monsters of vice, before one reaches the farthest bounds of the wilderness, arrives at the lowest depths of humility, and perfectly attains the highest contempt for oneself!

O how often it is necessary to flee to God’s mercy and, when caught among so many dangers, to seek divine mercy and obtain grace! O what astonishing mighty works! O what pleasant miracles! O what wonderful benefits they experience, marvel at, and revere in so many divine revelations, such great visitations, and such consolations—those whom [Col. 1081A] the vastness of the wilderness and the greatness of their own weakness have taught to place no confidence in their own strength, but to hope wholly in God’s goodness, cast their care upon the Lord, and set their hope in the Lord God!

There one may experience, in the sweetness of heavenly food, how great is the abundance of sweetness which God has hidden for those who love him; one may “taste and see how sweet the Lord is,” and how good the God of Israel is to those who are upright in heart. There those who ascend the mountain of the Lord and draw near to his feet receive from his teaching, proving and confessing that his power is great and that there is no number to his wisdom. Whoever has appeared in that desert and waterless land “as in the sanctuary,” so as to behold his power and glory, knows this, having experienced the saying: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness.”

But who could sufficiently enumerate how innumerable alternations of such desolations and consolations must be experienced, how many proofs of human weakness and how many evidences of divine goodness it happens to inhabitants of the wilderness and worshippers of God to see, before they reach the farthest limits of the wilderness and attain the bounds of perfect humility; before the wave of Jordan yields to those who come, turns its course back to its source, and the human mind, despising its own things and itself, wholly passes into God, runs in desire toward him from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift, and turns back the whole force of its love toward [Col. 1081C] God, the living fountain.

## CHAPTER XIV. How excessive self-love is more difficult to conquer amid the successes of virtues.

O happy soul, worthy for whose sake the Lord deigns to perform so great a miracle; to whom it is granted to see such a spectacle: the lower waters, and every stream of desire tending downward, running away and failing; while the waters coming from above—that is, desires for things above—stand gathered in a single mass, so that it may truly sing: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI).

O unhappy soul, who delay, who do not hasten, who do not greatly pant to run and see, marvel, and stand astonished when the streams of Jordan first stop their course and stand in one place; then adhere immovably to the one desire for eternity; afterwards fail utterly in lower things and gradually increase in higher things. What miracle, I ask you, what prodigy do you suppose it is for Jordan to be driven back and the rush of so great a river to return upward—especially if this happens at harvest-time, when it customarily fills the banks of its channel?

For when that seed which fell into good ground begins to produce fruit of itself, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, some a hundredfold, then indeed the Jordan’s wave usually swells more deeply: the human mind naturally thinks highly of itself and considers itself somebody great when it sees itself bearing much fruit and reaching the harvest of maturity. Then it is no wonder that, the more highly it judges itself, the more worthy of greater love it considers itself; and it is a very great thing if it does not overflow even to the depths of excess and exceed the boundaries of just equity and the banks of usefulness. How great, then, how mighty a miracle do you think it is to become vile in your own eyes and increasingly displeasing to yourself, especially when you begin truly to be great and to appear great to everyone? [Col. 1082A]

Certainly—and this too is no wonder—during icy cold or the dryness of summer heat, the waters of Jordan are accustomed to diminish and decrease. Likewise, however exalted the mind may be, amid the cold of wickedness and the excessive heats of desire it becomes vile in its own sight, recognizes its weakness even unwillingly, and greatly subsides from its estimation of itself. Who, I ask, is so monstrously foolish that he does not at some time displease himself amid crimes and shameful deeds? But it will be a great thing if, at harvest-time and amid the successes of virtue, the Jordan can contain its waters within the banks of its channel and restrain the force of private love within the bounds of moderation. It will be great if it does not burst out into unlawful things or overflow into useless ones. It will be great if one does not love even oneself except so far as is fitting or expedient.

“But Jordan,” says Scripture, “had filled the banks of its channel at harvest-time” (Josh. VIII). It says “had filled,” not “had exceeded.” Therefore, I think, it is not harmful to fill the banks, but to exceed them [Col. 1082B].

## CHAPTER XV. How the soul must be advanced by degrees toward contempt for itself.

[Col. 1082C]

The first task for each person, then, is to restrict self-love to a definite measure, so that afterwards he may deserve also to see that great and astonishing miracle: namely, Jordan first to stop its course, then to swell, and at last to go back and ascend to higher things. The first act—to restrain excess, though great—is not yet wonderful; but to turn the course toward the mountains is a marvellous sight and a striking miracle. Without question, it is one thing to moderate self-love, and another to suspend and redirect it. Moderate self-love is one thing; great contempt for oneself another.

I think it is not without reason that such a miracle was celebrated only in the Jordan, whose name is interpreted “their descent.” But what is this descent except the humbling of the heart? Or whose descent is it, except that of those who descend and humble themselves voluntarily? For the descent of persons whose humiliation is not voluntary is indeed in them, but in a sense is not theirs, because it does them no good. Therefore it must be voluntary if it is to profit them and may truly be called theirs. Are those of whom we read, “You cast them down while they were being lifted up” (Ps. LXXXVIII), thought to have descended voluntarily or to have profited in any respect by it?

Therefore whoever wishes to see that great miracle must descend from every exaltation of mind and humble himself by free choice—not like those who were cast down unwillingly, to the praise indeed of God but to no benefit of themselves. Thus, in the Jordan—only in “their descent,” in the descent of those descending, in the humiliation of those humbling themselves—this celebrated and heavenly miracle takes place [Col. 1083A]. The greater you are, therefore, humble yourself in all things, and you will keep within the banks of Jordan: worthy that Jordan should yield to you and that the Lord should show you miracles.

## CHAPTER XVI. How, when vain love is exhausted, the soul is enlarged in the love of God.

Would you see the waters of Jordan stop their course and stand in one place? “But for me, it is good to cling to God; to set my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. LXXXII). Would you see the lower waters run down and fail? “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. LXXXVI). Would you see the upper waters swell and run upward? “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” [Col. 1083B] (Ps. XLI).

Again: “Do not go after your own desires,” and you have stopped the waters. “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world,” and the lower waters running downward have failed. Again: “Delight in the Lord,” and you will see them standing fixed in one place. “Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind,” and you will see the waters swelling mightily and rising, unsurprisingly, into a great mass. I think you will find no wider space in which to spread them than to pour them forth with your whole heart, extend them through your whole soul, and fill your whole mind with them.

O how mightily this saving flood had swollen in the breast of him who said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ!” [Col. 1083C] (Phil. VIII). The Prophet’s sung utterance concerning himself has the same sense: “My soul has failed for your salvation” (Ps. CXVIII). But what a flood of waters, I ask, was that in which a father is compelled to cry out for his parricidal son: “Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Who would grant that I might die for you, my son Absalom?” (II Kings XXIX). I think no place could be found in which they might spread themselves more broadly. For no one has greater love than that one lay down his life for his friends.

Likewise, that flood swelled no little concerning which we have the Lord’s testimony: “Many sins have been forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke VII). What wonder, I ask, that waters which had greatly swollen appeared from afar? Do you wish to know how far away appeared [Col. 1083D] the flood of that love which burned so intensely, which bowed itself even to kissing and anointing feet? “Amen, I say to you: wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she also has done shall be spoken of in memory of her” (Matt. XXVI).

Would you know even more plainly how far they can appear, provided they have swollen like a mountain? “By this all will know that you are my disciples: if you have love for one another” (John XIII). How far away, I ask, does that appear which all must know? But, as we have already said, the streams of true love must swell like a mountain if they are to appear so far away. Perhaps, however, you still seek the mountain to whose likeness you read that the waters swell. See whether it may be that “fat mountain, a mountain of curds,” the mountain of the house of the Lord prepared on the summit of the mountains, because the Lord has exalted it and given him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal [Col. 1084A].

He who desires the waters to appear from afar and to fulfil the Lord’s command must understand that they ought to swell after the likeness of this mountain—after the likeness of that great and wonderful love by which he laid down his life for his sheep: “This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you” (ibid.). Hear the likeness and apply the imitation: “As I have loved you,” he says. The likeness of love is the likeness of a mountain. How greatly did he love us, who died for us?

Did not those who for Christ were stoned, sawn asunder, tested, and died by the sword’s slaughter preserve in their love the likeness of this mountain? Therefore, I think, “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world,” that they might appear from afar, be seen by all, and be imitated by them all. But why, I ask, do we marvel that waters appeared far off which, as Scripture says, “swelled as far as Sartan” (Josh. III)? Sartan is interpreted “their tribulation.” But what is “their tribulation,” according to what we have already said about Jordan, except the tribulation of those who undergo tribulation?

A voluntary tribulation is each person’s own. For whatever one accepts patiently or even willingly, one makes one’s own, because one compels it to serve one’s own advantage. Therefore, just as “their descent” is the descent of those who voluntarily [Col. 1084C] humble themselves, so “their tribulation” is the tribulation of those who love tribulation for the Lord’s sake. That, therefore, is the tribulation of the afflicted which is reckoned to the afflicted as merit. See, then, how much those waters which were higher had increased and swollen, since they extended even as far as Sartan.

O love strong as death, which extend even to Sartan and spread your bosom even as far as voluntary tribulation! What, I ask, is this enlargement of love, this flood of waters: to extend and enlarge one’s heart as far as voluntary tribulation, spontaneous suffering, and death freely chosen? Therefore do not doubt that the upper waters have extended to this place whenever you see people rejoicing in tribulation and loving their tribulation for the Lord’s sake, as the apostles went away rejoicing from before the council because they were deemed worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus [Col. 1084D].

## CHAPTER XVII. On the failure of vain love and the advance of true love.

Therefore the upper waters ascend as far as Sartan, and the lower waters descend as far as the sea. The former ascend and increase; the latter descend and decrease. The former increase and swell; the latter decrease and fail. It is a beautiful sight for the upper waters to swell about Sartan and the lower waters to fail in the sea. Attend here and be astonished. Attend carefully here and be greatly astonished. Among things so great and so marvellous choose what you should first, what you should more greatly, marvel at: waters in the high places not flowing downward but swelling, or waters from waters not swelling but failing.

“But the waters,” says Scripture, “which were lower, descended into the sea of the wilderness, now called the Dead Sea, until they wholly failed” (Josh. III). Therefore, those waters that are lower must descend into the sea and fail in the sea. We know that waters, however sweet they may be, cannot preserve their sweetness when they reach the sea. Thus waters which descend into the sea quickly become bitter. “Let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into sorrow” [Col. 1085B] (Jas. IV): this is sweet water descending into the sea, losing its sweetness, and changing from sweet to bitter.

Laughter and joy certainly make sweet water, and each person drinks such water as eagerly as he thirsts for it and as gladly as he can. But mourning and sorrow cannot make sweet water, and people do not readily wish to drink such water. As often as laughter is turned into mourning, so often lower water slips into the sea and is changed into bitterness. For laughter cannot belong to the upper waters when the mouth of Truth has said of it: “Woe to you who now laugh, for you shall weep.”

What, then, is it for lower waters to run into the sea and fail, except to draw carnal and lowest pleasures into sorrow and extinguish them by repentance? For one who weeps and groans over pleasure already committed, abhors and rejects pleasure as it approaches, and fears and tries to avoid future pleasure—what else does he do but turn sweetness into bitterness for himself? This, then—this, I say—is what we marvelled at above and still marvel at: changing sweet into bitter, mourning joy, grieving over pleasure, and thus causing sweetness to fail in the sea [Col. 1085C]. So do the waters swell around Sartan, and do the waters fail in the sea? Is this how you, O human being, rejoice in tribulation? Is this how you are troubled by pleasure? O strange and astonishing thing! Joys are heaped up in voluntary tribulation; pleasures that present themselves are destroyed by voluntary grief.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How disturbances of mind fail through the failure of vain love.

But what, I ask, does it mean that the sea in which this celebrated event occurred is called the Dead Sea [Col. 1085D]? Why did it receive such a name? For Scripture sufficiently suggests that it did not bear that name previously when it says: “the sea of the wilderness, now called the Dead Sea” (Josh. III). I think that not every sea of wilderness, nor every bitterness of desolation—indeed, not even this very sea of which we are now speaking—deserves such a name; nor should it be called dead unless perhaps the miracle mentioned above takes place in it.

We know that what is dead cannot move itself at all. Perhaps this sea, after the incoming water had failed, after it no longer had an inflowing and driving torrent, lost its heat and those swelling and bubbling storms of its waves. For the incoming force and most rapid course of Jordan, by its exceedingly violent inrush, drove and agitated it, and did not permit it to be wholly tranquil and at rest. Thus at that time it went swelling, foaming, and violently boiling, as though fiercely resenting the affront of its own agitation and unrest.

But after the incoming flood began to fail and the cause of its agitation to perish, the sea itself also began to rest from its stormy agitation, to lose—as though dead—the motion of its former unrest, and to change its name. Thus indeed the torrent of carnal pleasure and the vehement impulse of the flesh, while they remain strong, are accustomed to cause swelling and indignation. They commonly disturb the whole conscience, stir up waves of bitterness, overturn from its depths that profound abyss of the human heart, and agitate that great sea with great storms [Col. 1086B].

For the mind that burns with heavenly desire, strives for purity, and tends toward perfection, so long as it is compelled to feel shameful pleasures from the impulse of the flesh, must resist the lowest desires which flow downward. Hence it is angry with itself, indignant against itself, and seems to rage against itself. I think that disturbance, tumult, and vehement tossing of this kind make the sea not dead but living, strong, and restless.

But when the lower waters begin to run down and fail, and the streams of lowest pleasures to weaken and vanish, conscience also begins gradually to compose itself toward peace and tranquillity, increasingly to lay aside the fear of future judgment, and to lose the boiling agitations of former indignation and anxiety; like something dead, it has no movement of trembling and disturbance [Col. 1086C]. Thus the torrent of carnal pleasure, drained, dried up, and entirely consumed, makes the sea feeble, weak, tranquil, and rightly called dead. You see, I think, how rightly the sea changed its name and took the name of the dead, in which the flow of the lower waters fell and failed.

## CHAPTER XIX. With what caution we ought to remove disturbances of heart.

It should be noted, however, how this sea ought in one respect to remain, and yet in another respect to be dead. We must always repent of evils committed, pursue them with hatred and detestation, and abhor them; yet we must not always weep over them and tremble. Rather, after worthy satisfaction and the taming of desire, we should receive consolation and restore the mind to the repose of hope in pardon and security.

O truly happy and greatly blessed person, to whom it is given to restrain disturbances of heart and storms of sadness, and to settle those great and wonderful swellings of the sea into tranquillity! One thing I know, and I dare not doubt it: as long as love is scattered among many things and diverted downward, it is never brought to complete peace, never made serene in the tranquillity of true security.

O unhappy and wretched soul, [Col. 1087A] how long are you anxious and troubled about many things? Yet one thing is necessary: at last fix your desire; love the One. Blessed are the citizens of that city “whose fellowship is into one.” “Let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place”: do not allow them to flow downward. Do you not know that “one who lets loose his waters is the beginning of strife”? Why do you flow downward through low desires? What have you to do with perishing goods and joys destined for mourning? Do you not know that every water which runs downward descends into the sea? For all rivers enter the sea, and every low pleasure ends in sorrow.

“For laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy,” because every sweet water descends into the sea and loses its sweetness. For the world and its desire pass away. And we know that what is possessed with love is not left behind without pain. How much better, then, to savour the things above, seek the things above, and turn Jordan’s streams back to their source, so that we too may dare to adopt for the practice of our confession that voice of rejoicing: “What ails you, O sea, that you fled; and you, O Jordan, that you turned back?”

## SECOND TREATISE. From this point the subject is the pursuit of contemplation, and how, and to what extent, it avails for the restoration of true love.

[Col. 1087]

## CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 1087B]

But I think that we must not pass over here the question by what art and effort it may be brought about that the Jordan should turn back of its own accord and, at a spontaneous prompting, return to its source. For it is one thing to know what is advantageous or what ought to be done, and another not to be ignorant how you may attain what you do not doubt will be useful, or even necessary. Who would not despair that the rush of so great a river could be turned toward the mountains? Who, I say, would presume that the most rapid natural course of human feeling, and its most violent downward drive, can be checked and diverted in the opposite direction, unless he receives the art by which he may hope to accomplish this?

In short, we have often heard, and frequently [Col. 1087C] seen, the course of flowing water impeded, and we do not judge this impossible. But it is one thing often to restrain consent in necessary appetites and natural affections; another to change the affection itself, to turn the outflow of human desire toward the mountains of virtue, and by some spontaneous movement of inward love to rise, contrary to custom, toward desires for heavenly things. Therefore I think it insufficient to offer my own judgment, or that of any man, on this point. Let us learn from Him who teaches man knowledge. Let us then hear what He sets before us in this matter, or what He promises as its outcome. “When the priests who carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord God of all the earth have set the soles of their feet in the waters of the Jordan, the lower waters will flow away and fail; [Col. 1087D] but those which come down from above will stand together in one mass.”

Therefore, as we hear, we must have the ark of the covenant of the Lord present, if we desire the lower waters to fail and the upper ones to rise together in one mass. O happy are they who can have it present, if not always, yet frequently—at whose presence such great and delightful miracles occur! But what, I ask, is this ark of the covenant, [Col. 1088B] unless perhaps it is that grace, pre-eminent among divine gifts, namely contemplation? What is that gilded ark except human intelligence made radiant by the brightness of heavenly wisdom and illuminated by the light of divine inspiration? What more fittingly do we understand by that venerable sanctuary and repository of sacred things than the spiritual understanding of spiritual persons, which both grasps by intelligence the more sacred divine secrets and hidden things of wisdom, and preserves them by memory?

But why do we say that this ark is called the ark of the covenant? Does not He who loves those who love Him, and makes them worthy of His love, usually give so great a grace as a sign of affection and a pledge of charity, so that they deserve to hear from Him: “I will no longer call you servants, but [Col. 1088C] friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John 15)? This ark, then, is not always present, because the grace of contemplation is sometimes withdrawn even from those to whom it is granted for a time. We have the ark present when, through inspiring grace, we receive a ray of contemplation. We carry this ark with us when we apply ourselves diligently to divine contemplation and attend earnestly, by investigation or reconsideration, to the study of saving wisdom.

## CHAPTER II. How investigation and reconsideration of saving matters can correct the mind

These, if I am not mistaken, are the bearers of our ark, [Col. 1088D] by whom it is usually either lifted to higher things or carried forward: namely, investigation of what is unknown and reconsideration of what is known. Without these it quickly either slips downward or is driven backward. For without reconsideration it is not kept from the fall of forgetfulness, and without investigation it is never advanced in the progress of knowledge.

Now, as we all know, it is ordinarily the office of priests to keep watch over the preservation of salvation and the care [Col. 1089A] of souls. Therefore our investigation and our reconsideration ought diligently to attend, and unceasingly apply themselves, to saving matters and to matters affecting salvation, so that by their merits they may claim for themselves the dignity of priesthood and uphold the honor of that name. O worthy priests! O fitting bearers of the ark: investigation of saving things, reconsideration of wholesome things! By the ministry of these priests we carry our ark to the Jordan’s streams when, through devoted investigation and reconsideration, we turn the eye of our contemplation toward the consideration of our desires.

At their entry, therefore, and at the ark’s approach, you will see the course of the Jordan and its force of dissolution first slacken, then halt, and finally turn back. Without doubt, the more perfectly [Col. 1089B] you inspect the outflow of human affection, and the more fully you come to know it, the more greatly you will marvel at it and the more vehemently you will detest it. Consider frequently, contemplate diligently, the extravagance of your heart and the overflow of your desires. Look, then, at your love: from where and where it runs; toward what it tends through desire; or from what it retreats through disgust. You will see how it falls from lofty things to low, and is drawn down from the highest to the lowest. Without doubt, when you begin diligently to inspect and deeply to understand these things, you will also begin to cry out with the Prophet: “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. 72).

## CHAPTER III. That it is easier to correct the mind than to penetrate its depths

[Col. 1089C]

But how worthy of wonder, and with how great a delight worthy of being embraced, is this: that God does not wish to delay His miracle longer, or prolong our expectation indefinitely; nor does He compel us to descend even to the depths of the Jordan and penetrate to that inscrutable abyss of the human heart before He begins to fulfill His promise. Since He knew our frame, He does not wish to leave us suspended by the delay of a long waiting, knowing truly that the human heart is perverse and inscrutable. For who can comprehend it worthily? Who can adequately explain how great a folly, [Col. 1089D] how infinite a misery it is voluntarily to abandon supreme goods, avidly to seek the lowest goods, to disdain eternal joys, ardently to desire transitory things, to lose infinite rewards for perishable things, and incur eternal evils?

The incomprehensibility of this consideration seems to be why we are not compelled by the Lord to penetrate to this depth of immensity, lest He should seem to demand from us not merely difficult things but impossible ones. But what does Scripture say? “When,” it says, “the priests entered the Jordan and their feet were dipped in part of the water, the descending waters stood in one place and appeared at a distance, swelling up like a mountain” (Josh. 3). Observe, I beg you, how at the very first dipping of their feet the Jordan begins to check its course and turn backward. They had scarcely touched [Col. 1090A] part of the water, as you hear, and already the streams of the Jordan were turning their rush back upon themselves.

## CHAPTER IV. How much it avails to remain longer in consideration joined with a profound wonder at our weakness

But who, I ask, are these feet of the priests, at whose dipping the Jordan turns backward? If by the priest we rightly understand investigation, what is more fittingly understood by his foot—which is the lowest part of his body—than the depth of investigation? The priest’s foot, therefore, is the profundity of investigation. To set the foot in the water is to penetrate hidden things by deep investigation. A foot of this kind is dipped in water when the mind marvels at the subtlety of its discovery and delights in its own wonder.

For what is it to be dipped except to be affected? And what is it to be affected except to contemplate, to marvel, to delight? Although we do not extend the feet of our investigation all the way to the bottom of the whirlpool, because we penetrate the errors of our desires only in part, still we dip those feet deeply, though they are placed only in part, greatly astonished at what we scarcely comprehend, or comprehend only in a small measure. We ought, therefore, in searching out the inner things of the heart, at least to descend so far into the waters that we may fully dip the feet of our investigation and turn our mind, in considering our error, toward wonder and amazement.

For this very thing which we can comprehend concerning our follies and errors, I think, can suffice so that the [Col. 1090C] Jordan of its own accord checks the rush of its course and, by spontaneous motion, runs back, condemning and detesting the wandering paths of its former habit, voluntarily restraining the fall of its ways, and directing itself toward the opposite course. I think that the Prophet had then lifted the ark of his understanding over the waters of the Jordan when he uttered a general judgment, not only concerning his own heart but concerning every human heart: “Every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38). He saw whither the streams of the Jordan ran when he cried out in rebuke: “How long will you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 14). He saw where its course ended and in what sea it failed when he said: “Man passes away in an image, yet he is troubled in vain” (Ps. 38). He had dipped his feet deeply in the water when he burst forth in this cry of wonder: “What have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?” (Ps. 78). I think that, at this dipping of the feet and this wonder of consideration, the Jordan, abandoning the depths of its desires, returns upward and seeks its source, so far as to say: “My soul refused to be comforted; I remembered God, and I was delighted” (Ps. 76).

## CHAPTER V. How, after full self-correction, the mind is introduced to contemplation of eternal things

No one, therefore, ought to neglect what can be comprehended from considering his own corruption, or regard it carelessly and as if in passing. [Col. 1091A] Rather, at the ark’s entry and the dipping of the feet, he should fix his step and prolong his stay until the upper water increases, the lower fails, and the whole people of the Hebrews passes over.

For when we begin to reconsider and examine our life, and to dip the feet of our inquiry in the water, as soon as we perceive that our mind is affected—marveling and being indignant at the consideration of itself—we ought willingly to remain in this spectacle of our wonder until the upper water swells and the lower water wholly fails; until the entire multitude of our desires passes over and, in the certainty of its hope, reaches and takes possession of the land of promise. Then at last, I judge, it will be time for the ark of our own understanding also to enter the land of promise, [Col. 1091B] once it has sent ahead the whole people of its vows and wills.

For it is first necessary to believe, hope for, love, and greatly desire the good things of the Lord in the land of the living, before we are granted to know and understand them, seeing face to face. “Unless you believe,” He says, “you shall not understand” (Isa. 7). “He who loves me,” He says, “will be loved by my Father, and I will manifest myself to him” (John 14). Love, therefore, precedes manifestation, so that manifestation may follow love. Let the multitude of affections go before the ark, so that the ark of contemplation may follow the multitude. We must first possess the land of promise through desire before possessing it through understanding.

I think that the Apostle had brought across the entire multitude of his thoughts and affections when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” [Col. 1091C] (Phil. 1). What did he retain for himself from the desires of this life, he who did not love even life itself because of his excessive desire for Christ? Therefore, I judge, he prevailed in bringing the ark of his contemplation into the land flowing with milk and honey, so that he saw the good things of Jerusalem all the days of his life, and by the Lord’s revelation learned what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man. I am false if he himself does not boast that such a man was caught up even to the third heaven and heard there secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak.

## CHAPTER VI. That in the future life, after contemplation of eternal things, the mind is released into every pleasure of its desire

[Col. 1091D] I think that we ourselves also, after the passage of so great a multitude of our inner household, when we begin to bring the ark of our contemplation in there and see no longer through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face—when we possess in actuality what we now possess in affection—will no longer need to suspend the Jordan’s streams in their channel and restrain their rush by resistance.

Far be it, far be it, when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality—far be it, I say, far be it—that it should still be necessary to chastise the body and reduce it to slavery, and even then to be put to death all day long. For the righteous, Christ Himself testifying, “will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13), and the wicked man will be taken away so that he may not see God’s glory. We shall by no means be told any longer: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world,” when the Lord has made a new heaven and a new earth, according to which creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the liberty of the children of God.

And although there will then be in creatures a beauty incomparably greater and lovelier than now, and in bodily enjoyments a sweetness more abundant and delightful, there will be nothing among all that bodily sense touches that can diminish the desires of the spirit. The desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes will not know how to extinguish the desires of the spirit, but to kindle them; not to cool them, but to inflame them more intensely. Whatever presents itself outwardly, whatever inwardly, will furnish nourishment to spiritual love and divine affection.

Then without doubt [Col. 1092B] the mind will delight inwardly and delight outwardly. It will delight in spiritual things; it will delight in bodily things; and it will “go in and go out and find pasture.” Then the waters of the Jordan will return to their channel and flow as they formerly used to flow. The Jordan’s channel is the appetite for what is advantageous.
