In such a channel the Jordanian waters are borne along with force, because the heart’s desires are carried now here, now there, according to their appetite for what is advantageous.

Where, do you suppose, does such a flowing of waters tend except toward pleasure? What, then, is it for the waters to run as they formerly did, except to follow and attain pleasure? Every appetite is naturally drawn toward what is advantageous, and no one is forbidden to follow the course of this channel in that desire of his. Many things please here which nevertheless are not fitting, and therefore ought not to be done. Thus it is often necessary in this life to check the waters’ force and bravely break the violence of desires. There, nothing will please except what is also permitted. Therefore it will do no harm for the streams of desire to flow according to one’s wish and run toward every pleasure.

The Prophet, I judge, hoped and sighed for the freedom to do this when he proclaimed in psalmody: “Make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing, O Lord” (Ps. 118). The voluntary offerings of the mouth and the pleasures of the heart are often different, and to an excessive degree. For we desire one thing in mind, while the things that we approve with our mouth are another. Often, indeed, the things which please by judgment are different from those which please by desire. The former please through judgment; [Col. 1092D] the latter through desire. The former through decision; the latter through delight. The Prophet therefore asks that those very things which are offered voluntarily may also be pleasing, so that vow and pleasure, judgment and desire, decision and delight may converge in one and always meet one another.

“Make the voluntary offerings of my mouth pleasing, O Lord”: let whatever pleases through discernment please through delight, and let only those things please through delight which are permitted through deliberation. Let the Hebrew people pass over, then; let the ark pass after it into that land flowing with milk and honey, into that heavenly and everlasting joy, so that at last it may see face to face what it had so earnestly sought beforehand with great desire.

Let that great host of so many desires pass over; [Col. 1093A] let that contemplative ark of intelligence also pass into those inward and eternal joys, so that then the Jordan may resume its free course and all human affection may freely and without restraint pour itself into every pleasure, while the human mind—firmly and immovably adhering to the highest and spiritual goods—finds nothing contrary in outward and lower things. If I am not mistaken, the wave which had risen above will return to its channel with greater force than before, spread itself more widely, and exceed the bounds of its former limitation, because the love of the Word and of creatures finds most abundant fuel for a greater fire and therefore rushes everywhere toward all things with a more fervent desire.

## CHAPTER VII. How some persons, even in this life, are raised to contemplation of eternal things

[Col. 1093B]

But what is read concerning the passage of the ark appears capable, in some measure, of being fulfilled even in this life. This is proved by the apostolic testimony which we cited above; we do not doubt that the man uttering such things was still living in this corruptible life. “I know,” he says, “a man in Christ—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know, God knows—such a one caught up to the third heaven; and I know such a one, that he was caught up into paradise and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter” (2 Cor. 12).

See where he had introduced the ark of his contemplation: he who had fixed the eye of his understanding even upon the secrets of the third heaven. But I think that not even Paul himself [Col. 1093C] would have lifted the ark to that place unless he had first sent there the whole household of his desires, so completely that he counted all things as dung in order to gain Christ. Many, I think, possess by merit the land of promise of which we speak, yet cannot bring their ark into it after Paul’s likeness, because by desire they still keep outside that land some members of the inward household of their affections.

But when this whole multitude of Hebrews has crossed the Jordan, and the ark of the covenant itself has been brought into the land of promise, what, I ask, will then prevent it from resuming its course and, according to its custom, flowing back into its channel—provided that it does not exceed the banks of fitting advantage and just necessity; provided that, following the channel of equity and moderation, it does not overflow into the open field of excessive freedom? For what is it for the multitude of Hebrews to have crossed the Jordan’s channel except for heavenly desires, tending toward future glory, to have so subdued the appetite of the flesh that it can no longer entangle or impede them?

Indeed, before the people of the Lord with the Lord’s ark cross over, it is necessary, lest the Jordan’s wave hinder their passage, to restrain its course, break the flesh’s impetus, and often turn the mind away even from necessary desire. For human affection is never perfectly inflamed toward the desire of eternity, and human understanding is never fully sharpened for contemplation of eternal things, unless care for the flesh is frequently and vigorously repelled even in lawful and highly necessary matters. [Col. 1094A] The body must therefore be chastised and reduced to slavery until it can no longer in any way hinder the progress of merits.

But after it has let the passing multitude and the ark that accompanies it cross, everyone may follow the channel of what is advantageous to him, insofar as this cannot hinder spiritual exercises. This is why we have often seen many persons first afflict their bodies with remarkable abstinence and incur grave—even incurable—illnesses, and afterward, once desire had been subdued and grace received from God, relax the reins of their former rigor and indulge their bodies, in food and drink, sleep and clothing, much more than preserved health itself would have required. For it often serves spiritual pursuits when a person full of grace preserves or restores bodily strength insofar as this can be useful.

Yet one who now indulges himself according to this permission must take care not to let the waters loose too far, lest they leave the channel of their advantage and exceed the banks of moderation. Let them at least flow as they formerly used to flow—those waters of which it is written that they had filled the banks of their channel. This, I think, only those know how to do well who already savor the things above, have already tasted the sweetness of heavenly things, disdain earthly things, and have already introduced their ark into that land of promise. One cannot, I think, attain the perfect height of outward goods who has not yet merited, by tasting, to experience the sweetness of inward goods.

I think that unless the Prophet had first tasted how sweet the Lord is, and how great is the abundance of sweetness in His house—unless he had learned this by experience—he could not at all have said with conviction: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76). Therefore, lest it always be necessary to restrain the Jordan’s course, we must carry our ark across to its farther side; but this too is not permitted unless we can first send ahead that entire multitude of our vows.

## CHAPTER VIII. That by the study of contemplation we must always foresee where we should tend by desire

This ark must certainly neither always follow nor always be sent ahead. In a place of terror and vast solitude it should precede the multitude; when the multitude enters the land of promise, it should follow it. Let it go before in relation to our own affairs; let it follow in relation to divine things. On this side of the Jordan are matters that concern us; beyond the Jordan are matters above us.

Here we are commanded to examine, approve, and then retain: “Test all things,” says the Apostle; “hold fast what is good” (1 Thess. 5). There we are commanded to believe, in order that we may someday deserve also to understand: “Unless you believe,” He says, “you shall not understand” (Isa. 7). Therefore, while we are still in the desert, while we journey through the wilderness, we must send our ark ahead of us and carefully foresee where the household of virtues ought to tend by study or desire, following it: “That you may,” says the Lord, “see and know by what way you are to go, because you have not walked by it before” [Col. 1095A] (Josh. 3). The saying of the Wise Man agrees with this: “Let your eyelids go before your steps” (Prov. 4).

But toward those things beyond the Jordan, which surpass our understanding, we strive better by desire than by study, by affection than by intellect, because we are commanded to send the multitude ahead, not the ark. In this matter it is better greatly to desire than greatly to investigate, that we may deserve to be brought where we cannot break in by our own power. “For he who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25). There, therefore, let the ark go before in order to show the way.

## CHAPTER IX. On the twofold imperfection which we must always keep before our eyes

But divine discourse also did not wish to pass over in silence the distance by which the ark ought to go before the multitude that follows it. “Let there be,” it says, “a space of two thousand cubits before the ark.” Do you wish to know what it is for the ark to be with the multitude, or for the ark to go before the multitude? When we diligently consider what kind of persons we are through our deeds or desires, we have our ark with us and, as it were, present. But when we look closely at what kind of persons we ought to be, we send the ark of our understanding before our face, so that we may not be ignorant where we must tend.

Who, I ask, can boast either that he does everything which he can usefully do, or that he can do everything which ought to be done, if it were possible to do it? For just as people do not will all that they are able to do, so neither are they able to do all that they ought. [Col. 1095C] Thus capacity extends farther than will, and necessity is much more remote than capacity. Let us therefore send our ark ahead not only as far as the consideration of our possibility, but even as far as the contemplation of necessary usefulness, so that we attend not only to what we could do better than we do, but also to what ought to be done better than we are able to do.

Thus he sends his ark about a thousand cubits ahead of his face who diligently and frequently considers where he could have been in merit if he had neglected none of the things possible to him. But he advances farther, up to two thousand cubits, who contemplates not merely frequently but almost without ceasing how innumerable are the things which he does not do, and how innumerable also are the things which he cannot do, though they ought to be done if his strength did not fail in fulfilling them. When we wish to act vigorously, we extend our cubit—that is, our forearm; and therefore exercises of virtue are rightly understood through cubits. The number one thousand usually signifies perfection, because our reckoning has no greater number. Two thousand cubits, then, seem, I think, to signify a twofold perfection: the integrity of the will and the fullness of strength. But whoever neither yet can do all that he ought, nor indeed completes all that he can, lacks both perfections.

What, then, is it to send the ark of one’s intelligence two thousand cubits ahead of oneself except prudently to foresee how much one lacks of the twofold perfection, neither part of which one can yet fulfill? Yet, to speak truly what I think, I consider that only the person who judges himself not to have attained even the beginnings of this twofold perfection has fulfilled this command of the Lord; only he, I say, do I judge to have sent his ark two thousand cubits ahead. For if by walking, approaching, and hastening he had cut off even a single cubit from so great a distance, and had claimed for himself even the beginnings of completed perfection, he would not see himself remaining two thousand cubits behind the ark.

O perfect man, founded in the deepest humility, who can always progress by hastening and hasten by progressing, yet preserve this humility always: always advancing in good, yet always believing himself not even to possess the beginnings [Col. 1096B] of perfection! It is a great spectacle to see the ark hasten onward in front, to observe the multitude accelerate as it follows, and yet always to maintain so great a distance between them. The more the ark advances, the more eagerly the multitude hastens; and the more swiftly the following multitude proceeds, the more the leading ark accelerates its course.

Certainly, the better we know the grace of perfection, the more ardently we desire it; and the more we are kindled toward love, the more perfectly we are illuminated toward knowledge. The righteous person will always find a way to place it two thousand cubits before himself, because in this life willing, being able, and being obliged can never coincide. That belongs to the time to come, not to the present life. There, indeed, just as one will will all that one can rightly do, so one will be able to do all that one ought rightly to do. Here, however, capacity for acting exceeds action, and the necessity of duty exceeds possibility of doing.

It is evident that each grows from the other: as our willing increases, so also does our ability; and with the increase of both, our obligation also grows. For the more ardently we desire the good, the more easily we accomplish it; and the greater the things we can do, the greater also the things we ought to do. In this way the ark must always advance forward and the following multitude hasten after it. But it should be too little for you, who are hastening to the land of promise, merely to send your ark ahead of your face, unless it goes two thousand cubits ahead of your way and shows you where you ought to follow. Strive, therefore, in considering and contemplating your perfection, to penetrate so far into what lies beyond that you may truly believe that you have not yet reached even its beginnings, whether in affection or in effect.

## CHAPTER X. An example or pattern of the proposed consideration

Do you wish to hear a man traveling two thousand cubits behind the ark and claiming for himself not even the beginnings of a more perfect life? “While I was still beginning,” he says, “he cut me down” (Isa. 38). He does not say, “while I was still weaving,” but “while I was still beginning.” What is beginning except planning beforehand? And what is weaving except doing? For what else is it to begin things to be woven and to weave things begun, except to arrange beforehand what is to be done and to do what has been arranged beforehand?

“While I was still beginning,” he says—while I was still planning, while I was still seeking in meditation what I ought to do and had not yet been able fully to find it—He stretched out His hand and cut me down. I had not yet woven anything, he says; I had not yet begun to do good; I was not permitted to begin the web of an ordered life, because, while I was still beginning, He cut me down. I confess indeed that I had already resolved to do good things, had already arranged how they might be done, and had already begun my web in great part; but while I was still beginning, He cut me down, and I could not—not merely finish, but not even begin—the web of my purpose.

How great, I ask, was this man, who thinks so humbly of himself, who claims for himself not even the beginnings of good when he believes that he is still only beginning? Does he not seem to you still to be beginning the web which he had woven together with many, [Col. 1097B] he who diligently sought to find and see what it was good for human beings to do under the sun during the number of the days of their life? Does not he too seem to himself still to be beginning, not weaving, who had long labored to know the reason which his soul still seeks and could not find? “Behold, this I have found,” says Ecclesiastes, “one and another, that I might find the reason which my soul still seeks and has not found” (Eccl. 7).

What good, what great thing, I ask, could this man have believed that he had done, when he confesses that he had sought but had not found what it was needful to do under the sun during the number of the days of his life? It is clear that he had sent the ark of his intelligence ahead of his face, since he sought where he ought to follow by desire or action. [Col. 1097C] But, I think, he regards the multitude of his desires as now standing idle, because he confesses that he has not yet found the reason he sought.

Do you still desire to hear more plainly a man who scarcely ascribes to himself the beginnings of goodness and who, as it were, was then traveling two thousand cubits behind the ark? Hear, then, what he says: “And I said: Now I have begun; this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76). I have scarcely ever begun, he says; I, who believed that I had begun, scarcely began late to become good from evil, righteous from unrighteous. I declared myself to be as I found myself, and was not ashamed to confess my imperfection; but I said: “Now I have begun; this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.”

He does not say “formerly” or “from then on,” but “now.” Nor does he deny that he has now begun, lest you suppose that he remained more than two thousand cubits behind the ark. He says that he has scarcely at last attained certain beginnings of good, showing, in accordance with the rule of divine instruction, that he follows his ark. But lest anyone think that he claims even this beginning of good for himself, let him hear what he adds to this statement: “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.” It was not enough for him to say, “this is the change of God,” unless he said, “this is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High.” He preferred to identify by description the One to whom he refused to attribute this work to himself. He calls Him “Most High” who did this, and names His right hand—as if to say openly: He did this mightily who is accustomed powerfully to accomplish mighty things.

It was indeed marvelous in his eyes to be changed from evil to good, being such a person as he remembered himself once to have been. What, I ask, did that other man believe himself to have accomplished in the way [Col. 1098A] of perfection, who compared all his righteousnesses to the cloth of a menstruating woman? We therefore have an example of how we ought to send the ark of our understanding before our face by a fixed measure: however much we hasten, we must never venture, through presumptuous estimation, to reduce anything from the distance of two thousand cubits, always judging that we have scarcely reached the beginnings of perfection.

Therefore, while we are in the desert, we ought in advancing our ark to gather the course of our own progress and, by another consideration, to know beforehand where we ought to follow through the study of good conduct.

## CHAPTER XI. On matters pertaining to meditation or contemplation, and how much such apprehensions avail for the advancement of virtue

[Col. 1098B]

But it is not equally easy to order the course of the present life and to assess the glory of the life to come, to examine the quality of merits and to weigh the magnitude of eternal rewards. For we shall assess with difficulty the things that are on earth, and we shall discover with labour those things that lie before our eyes; but who can investigate the things that are in heaven? Thus, to find what is on earth is difficult, but to investigate what is in heaven is impossible. Hence the Apostle’s warning: “Do not be high-minded” (Rom. 11). Rightly, therefore, the ark of the Lord is introduced only after the Hebrews have entered that land of promise, so that where our understanding is not permitted to break in by the steps of its own inquiry, it may be admitted under the guidance of divine revelation [Col. 1098C].

Yet we do not deny that concerning the nature of the future life there are some things—indeed, many great things—which we can seek by investigation, discover by reasoning, and establish by argument. “For the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made.” Therefore, the things which may be found through inquiry are by no means to be neglected; just as we must not presume, from our own ability, concerning those matters which exceed our understanding and human reason. The former are according to reason; the latter are above reason. The former we must diligently investigate by profound inquiry; the latter we must humbly await from divine revelation. The former belong to meditation; the latter to contemplation [Col. 1098D].

The mind is never fully kindled with desire for eternal goods unless it earnestly premeditates what kind they are and how great. And just as it never deserves to be raised to their contemplation without immense desire, so assuredly it is never perfectly inflamed with longing for eternal things without vehement application. Hence, before Israel enters the promised kingdom, scouts are sent ahead; yet the ark is not brought in until after the multitude has entered. For what is it to send scouts before one’s entrance, and to wish by keen inquiry to know beforehand the nature of that land into which we hasten to enter, except to direct the thoughts of one’s mind, as explorers of heavenly goods, into the investigation of invisible things, and to devote one’s meditations to this task [Col. 1099A]: namely, that by inquiry one may discover what can impel the multitude of one’s affections into love of them?

Let us therefore send our scouts before us, as those Israelites once sent theirs: not only once, but others after others, and second scouts after the first. Whenever we carefully investigate some point concerning the future goods for which we are to hope or which we are to earn, we send scouting messengers ahead of ourselves.

## CHAPTER XII. On the twofold premeditation: namely, of rewards and of merits

But it is one thing to inquire what sort, how great, or what manner of goods we ought to hope for as the recompense of merits; and another to investigate diligently by what pursuits or exercises [Col. 1099B] we may be able vigorously to obtain them. The former comes first, the latter second. First, investigate the goods to be hoped for; second, the goods to be done. For who would resolutely gird himself for contests of labour unless he knew beforehand the greatness of the reward granted by divine recompense?

But what advantage is there in believing and desiring eternal recompense, unless one seeks with equal diligence to know by what endeavours of merit one may acquire it? Therefore it is necessary to send messenger after messenger ahead, and to dispatch other scouts after the first. The first messengers are scouts of rewards; the second are scouts of merits. The former are scouts of recompenses; the latter, scouts of works.

Thus there are one set of scouts sent by Moses, and another set [Col. 1099C] sent by Joshua. There are some sent ahead by the Lord’s prophet and others sent ahead by the Lord’s athlete. The prophet’s office is one thing; the athlete’s another. It is the prophet’s office to foretell what is to come; the athlete’s office to arrange beforehand what is to be done. To the former belongs knowing beforehand what must firmly be believed; to the latter belongs premeditating what must vigorously be done. The former belongs to foreknowledge; the latter to providence. The former is to foresee; the latter to provide for. For what is foresight except an exploration of future things? And what is providence except an exploration of things to be done?

We therefore have two kinds of scouts, both active, both necessary. The first seems to pertain to Moses, the second to [Col. 1099D] Joshua. Accordingly, in keeping with this analogy of our thoughts, some must be foreseers of future things and others providers for things to be done; both are indeed explorers of hidden things and investigators of what is unknown.

Would you hear a man premeditating future things, after the likeness of Moses, sending scouts before himself? “I meditated in the night with my heart,” he says. “Will God cast off for ever, and will he no longer be favourable? Or will he cut off his mercy to the end, from generation to generation? Or will God forget to show mercy? Or will he, in his anger, restrain his mercies?” (Ps. 76).

Would you hear a man providing for things to be done, and, after the likeness of Joshua, sending scouts before himself? “What,” he says, “shall I render to the Lord for all [Col. 1100A] that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115).

Would you hear what one of the subtle scouts discovered by his exploration, or how he answered in judgment to that first question of the Prophet? “God,” he says, “will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints; and there shall no longer be either mourning or crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21). See how graciously he foresaw in the future that God of whom David asks whether he will ever again be favourable.

But, I think, what he found elsewhere concerns the second exploration; hence he says: “It is good to give thanks to the Lord and to sing praise to your name, O Most High” (Ps. 91). It belongs to the first scouts to persuade negligent minds of what is right; it belongs to the second to instruct eager minds, ready for every work to be done [Col. 1100B].

Observe, therefore, what kind of reports good scouts are accustomed to bring back from those regions, or how much the very things they bring back avail to raise the mind; and endeavour to seek and report similar things, so that you too may be able to raise the minds of hearers to longing for like things.

This is the voice of a scout: “This corruptible thing must put on incorruption, and this mortal thing must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15).

This is the voice of a scout: “The righteous shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds; they shall judge nations and reign for ever” (Wis. 3).

This is the voice of a scout: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30).

Should we suppose that this outstanding scout had not entered that land flowing with milk and honey and carefully surveyed it [Col. 1100C], when he dares to promise so boldly to those about to enter it: “They shall be inebriated by the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35)?

Does he not seem, in these words, to concur with the statement of the scouts where it is said: “We entered the land to which you sent us, and it truly flows with milk and honey, as may be known from these fruits” (Num. 13)?

## CHAPTER XIII. How one ought to apply oneself more earnestly to the consideration of rewards

This exploration, I think, ought to be pursued more earnestly than the others, and one ought to apply oneself more frequently to the first than to the second meditation, because it is easier to distinguish what is right than to persuade oneself to undertake arduous things [Col. 1100D]. Hence, I think, the children of Israel send more men in the first embassy, but fewer are sent in the second exploration. And rightly so. For, as has been said, the first inquiry explores rewards, while the second investigates merits.

But the rewards of future blessedness are incomparably greater than any merits of ours can be. “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us.” Therefore many are sent first, but few are sent second. Many are rightly sent where many things are sought; few are directed to seek few things. There we find twelve; here, two. There six is found; here one is doubled [Col. 1101A].

The unity from which six begins rightly signifies a beginning, just as six, by reason of its perfection, is acknowledged to signify perfection. Therefore what is sought there belongs to perfection, not to a beginning; but what is found here appears to belong to a beginning, not to perfection. There is the perfection of our glorification; here there is only a certain beginning of our justification.

In that glorification there will be the removal of every evil and the fullness of every good. But in this our justification there is neither complete extirpation of vices nor perfect consummation of virtues. There is full security and perfect joy. Here there is neither full purity nor perfect wholeness. There is full security, where no evil is feared; there is perfect joy, where every good is possessed [Col. 1101B]. Here there is no full purity, where vice resists; here no perfect wholeness, where weakness rules.

Therefore there one blessedness is consummated from the twofold perfection of security and joy, so that six is doubled and twelve is made complete. Here our justification begins from the twofold imperfection of purity and wholeness, so that from the doubling of unity each six takes the beginning of its perfection toward the completion of twelve.

Thus twelve scouts are rightly sent on that mission, where the blessedness of twofold perfection is sought by investigation. Two are rightly dispatched on that delegation, where scarcely certain beginnings of perfect justification are found. Finally, if I remember correctly, twelve are sent in the first exploration, and twelve things are commanded to be explored [Col. 1101C]. Likewise, two are sent in the second exploration, and two things are commanded to be investigated. Many things may be said concerning the first exploration; but to expound them worthily requires a treatise of its own.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the consideration of merits consists in two things

But, to say something more fully about the second, it is enough in this exploration to seek sufficiently those things which can suffice for that prophetic admonition: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36). It is enough, I say, diligently to provide how cautiously we may avoid evils and how discerningly we may accomplish goods.

Premeditation in avoiding evils is one thing; premeditation in fulfilling goods is another [Col. 1101D]. But although the two are distinct, neither should be without the other. Let them go together, run together, and assist one another; without the help of each, let them never fully accomplish their task.

These, I think, are the two scouts: prudent caution against evil and prudent diligence in good, whom we ought to send before us to test out the paths of our advancement. “Go,” Joshua says, “and consider the land and the city of Jericho” (Josh. 2). Consider, he says, the land and the character of its regions; carefully inquire into the suitability of places, so that we may know beforehand in what location we can more advantageously pitch camp, where it is expedient to turn aside in a crisis of need, and whence we ought to obtain necessities for daily use.

Consider, therefore, and investigate whatever is useful [Col. 1102A], whatever is suitable and necessary for use. But consider not only goods, but evils also; advantages and disadvantages; defences and dangers. Therefore consider the land and the city of Jericho. Consider the city, the strength of its fortifications and the multitude of its enemies, so that we may know how we ought to arrange the siege, how to attack, and against what enemies to wage war.

Examine, then, the land and the city. Examine the land which God made and the city which human invention established. Distinguish the good which God created for our good from the evil which man devised for his own evil. Consider land and city, nature and custom. Distinguish the good of creation from the evil of corruption; the good of condition from the evil of custom.

If we know the good of nature [Col. 1102B], we know what we ought to cultivate, nourish, and multiply. If we discern the evil of our habits, we do not doubt which enemies we must avoid, which adversaries attack, and what foes kill. See what kind of scouts we ought to send before our entry, so that we may know against what evils to be guarded and toward what goods to be watchful in acting. Whoever sends such scouts before himself will not fear the byways of error.

## CHAPTER XV. What belongs to meditation and what to contemplation

But that army of virtues proceeds securely and has no distrust of the certainty of its path when it is instructed by the shrewdness of scouts [Col. 1102C] and guided on its journey by the ordered advance of the ark. Let it not be enough for us to send scouts ahead of the Hebrew multitude; let us also make our ark precede us after the scouts’ tracks.

First, we must seek out and discover, through the exploratory work of our meditations, the rationale of things to be done; and afterwards we must bring it into contemplation, so that we may possess it as something known, ready at hand, and familiar. Contemplation belongs to the carrying forward of the ark, just as meditation belongs to exploration. Contemplation is one thing, meditation another.

It belongs to meditation to investigate hidden things; it belongs to contemplation to admire things made clear. For meditation is the diligent investigation of hidden truth. Contemplation is the delightful admiration of manifest truth. But hidden things [Col. 1102D] are accustomed to come to manifestation, sometimes through one’s own meditation, sometimes through divine revelation.

Where, therefore, we have the grace of revelation present, we do not need the office of meditation. But where divine revelation is lacking, the human mind, unsurprisingly, necessarily has recourse to the labour of meditation and, as it were, flees to the office of scouts.

But whatever the human mind can learn, through the exploration of meditations, concerning instruction in morals, it ought again to bring into contemplation and thereby strengthen the mind in certainty and desire for those things. When the discovery of meditation is brought into contemplation, what else occurs but that a path first explored is retraced for the carrying forward of the ark, so that the troop of virtues may safely follow without fear [Col. 1103A] of going astray?

By meditation, therefore, it is brought about that we do not fail to know whatever ought usefully to be done. But contemplation also customarily brings it about that discovered truth adheres more tenaciously to memory and inflames desire more keenly. By meditation [Col. 1104A], therefore, we are instructed toward the good; by contemplation we are made firm in the good. This, I think, is why we ought to test out the path of our advancement both by the exploration of meditation and by the progress of the intellectual ark.

# THIRD TREATISE. Thus far, on the advancement of the good; henceforth, on its confirmation

[Col. 1103]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1103A]

It is also pleasing to consider why the Lord commands stones to be gathered from the midst of the Jordan, from the place where the priests’ feet stood [Col. 1103B], and placed at the site of the camp, while other stones collected from elsewhere are set back in the former place. Let us therefore ask what that place is where the priests’ feet halt at the time of performing the miracle, and likewise what place it is where the camp must be pitched after the miracle has been accomplished.

Who doubts that it exceeds human power for the Jordan to turn back and for the mass of waters to rise into a single heap? Who, I ask, unless he has lost his mind, would presume such a stupendous miracle from his own strength? Where, then, amid expectation of so great a thing, ought the mind to fix its hope except in confidence in divine magnificence? A secure station and a place of great safety is trust in the aid of divine mercy.

But there is another place very unlike this: namely, the insinuation of distrust and despair [Col. 1103C]. It is indeed a dreadful place, full of fear and anxiety, and one fit to be secured with encampments, surrounded with a rampart, and guarded with sentries, because it is unsafe to proceed farther on account of the dangers threatening near at hand.

We encounter the first place in the time of divine visitation, but the second in the time of trial. For the dispensation of divine mercy is accustomed to strengthen a person by its visitation and then to test him again by diverse kinds of temptations: “You visit him in the morning,” Job says, “and suddenly test him” (Job 7). See, we have identified two places: one of confidence, the other of distrust; one where divine miracles commonly occur, the other where the camp ought to be pitched.

“Those who trust in the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall take wings as eagles; they shall run and not fail.” Is it not wholly above human power to renew strength, to fly in the likeness of an eagle, and to run without failing? Yet this can be done only by those who trust in the Lord’s mercy, not in their own strength [Col. 1103D]. Thus Peter was able to walk upon the waves so long as he kept his foot in the place of hope-filled confidence (Matt. 14). But after he began to leave this place of his security, the wave could no longer hold him afloat upon its heights.

You see how a violent wind, coming upon him, cast him down from the place of confidence to the place of distrust, because the Lord, according to his custom, had visited him in the morning and suddenly tested him. Thus the children of Israel, after the miracle had been performed and seen, came to the site of the camp.

## CHAPTER II. On the strengthening of the mind in good and the hardening of the mind in evil

[Col. 1104A]

[Col. 1104B] We have set out the difference between the places; let us also consider the two kinds of stones. I think there is one kind of good stones and another kind of evil stones. To good stones belongs every strengthening of the mind in good; to evil stones belongs every hardening of the mind in evil.

What do you think? Solidity, stability, firmness, weightiness, and many things of this kind—do they not seem to you to bear in themselves a certain likeness to stones and, by right of that likeness, rightly claim such a name? What shall we say of hardness of heart, stubbornness or obstinacy? What of harshness, austerity, and cruelty? Do not those things claim the name of stone because they bear in themselves a likeness to stones? But the former belong to good stones, as the latter belong to evil stones [Col. 1104C].

Yet I think it is not equally easy to find good and evil stones, because good stones are harder to find than an abundance of bad ones. For everything precious is rare. Good stones, therefore, are gathered from the middle of the Jordan; evil ones from any place whatever. Concerning the former, Scripture plainly indicates where they ought to be sought or found; concerning the latter, it judges the location of their discovery too obvious to specify.

## CHAPTER III. On the evil of presumption or despair

But this seems strange and highly worthy of wonder: we are commanded to place good stones, gathered from a good place, in a bad place; and to collect evil stones [Col. 1104D], gathered from anywhere, in a good place. The good place is the confidence of trust; the bad place is the despair of distrust. Yet we ought to gather evil stones in the place of confidence and good stones in the place of distrust.

“In the day of good things, do not forget evil things”: then you have gathered evil stones in a good place. “And in the day of evil things, do not forget good things”: then you have gathered good stones in a bad place.

For what is it to gather good stones from the midst of the Jordan—that is, from the place where the marvel was wrought—except carefully to review what the state of the mind was in the time of divine visitation, to investigate minutely how great its firmness was in each virtue, and, by entrusting this to memory, to raise as it were a mound of testimony? But we never possess an abundance of such stones unless we have first received the grace of divine visitation and inspiration.

He testifies to this who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Therefore good stones cannot be gathered anywhere except through his working. But we readily find an innumerable multitude of bad stones, which we gather abundantly and readily at hand from our whole life. Why then was it necessary to specify the place of those which we can collect plentifully from anywhere?

Let each person consider, therefore, how hard-hearted and obstinate he has been whenever divine grace abandoned him and left him to himself; and in doing this he raises a mound of evil stones. In this way we can raise mounds and establish diverse ones in different places: one here from good stones, another there from evil stones.

He established for himself a heap [Col. 1105B] of good stones who said: “I shall never forget your ordinances, for by them you have given me life” (Ps. 118). He had raised a mound of evil stones when he said: “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50).

## CHAPTER IV. How presumption ought to be restrained by remembering our evils

Thus, when you perceive yourself to be in the place of confidence, and see that you are presuming too highly upon your merits, immediately remember what you once were; and, turning your eyes toward the heap of evil stones, preserve yourself in humility. It is indeed good to hope confidently—not, however, in your own strength, but in the Lord’s mercy.

The gathering of evil stones in a good place is useful to each person for this purpose: that through the memory of his evils he may never presume upon his own powers. Therefore, that everyone may learn to trust not in himself but in the Lord, let the memory of his evils always meet him in the place of presumption [Col. 1105C]. That confidence of trust which humility commends appeases the Lord and obtains great things: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion.”

Conversely, that confidence of presumption which pride produces is abominable. “For a king is not saved by his great strength, nor shall a giant be saved by the multitude of his strength.” Therefore, “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm; for he shall be like tamarisk in the desert and shall not be satisfied when summer comes.” How useful, then, we think, will be in such a place the gathering of evil stones and the remembrance of vices which we have described: it can preserve us from this execrable pattern of pride and protect us from such a curse [Col. 1105D].

## CHAPTER V. How despair ought to be repelled by remembering our goods

Likewise, when danger threatens and temptation comes upon you, and you perceive your mind touched by despair, cast down into the place of distrust, and brought down to the appointed site of the camp, you ought to have ready the mound of good stones; turn your eyes toward the remembrance of past virtues, and renew the confidence of your hope from their recollection.

Thus Job, stripped of possessions, bereft of children, and struck with an ulcer, when he saw himself caught at the site of the camp and felt himself attacked by the evil of despair, had recourse to the heap of good stones. By remembrance of his good deeds he fortified his camp on every side and vigorously repelled the assaults of despair, saying: “I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame; I was a father to the poor, and I carefully investigated the cause which I did not know. I broke the jaws of the wicked and tore the prey from his teeth” (Job 29) [Col. 1106A].

Likewise Hezekiah, in a crisis of necessity, had recourse to the defences of such stones when he despaired of life. By setting his good deeds before God, he invoked the Lord’s mercy and, through the force of his prayers, drove away the dangers of distrust: “Remember, O Lord,” he says, “how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your sight” (4 Kings 20).

Therefore we too must keep ready and familiar, at every time of temptation, the present memory of former goods. When we have brought this practice into continual use, we have, as it were, placed good stones, chosen according to the divine instruction, at the site of the camp. For to gather chosen stones into one place is nothing other than diligently to review the forms of divine strengthening and support, and to commit them to memory [Col. 1106C]; and to have fixed them at the site of the camp is nothing other than firmly to have accustomed oneself to such remembrance in every crisis of temptation.

## CHAPTER VI. On the twelve principal virtues in which the mind must be made firm

We gather these stones from the bed of the Jordan, dried up through God’s power, according to the number of the twelve tribes, when we carefully examine the state of our mind as it was in the time of divine visitation and minutely inquire what we then were, in some measure, in each of the principal virtues. For this is for individual men from individual tribes to take up their stone: to have truthfully discovered how great a firmness one has at some time possessed, by the grace of inspiration, in relation to each virtue [Col. 1106D].

What we think concerning the twelve sons of Jacob, from whom these twelve tribes derive their origin, we have already stated elsewhere. By Reuben and Simeon we understand fear and compunction; by Levi, hope; by Judah, charity; by Issachar, joy; by Zebulun, severity; Gad signifies abstinence; Asher, patience; Dan and Naphtali, circumspection and speculation; Joseph and Benjamin, discernment and contemplation of invisible things.

We now wish to set out here the rationale of these, concerning which we have already said elsewhere what seemed to us more correct. But whoever trusts that his seed has been multiplied into twelve tribes from such offspring should learn what stones he ought to take from the midst of the Jordan [Col. 1107A], when he has advanced this progeny of virtues up to its crossing. Let him recall what strength, fortitude, or firmness he felt himself to have received at the breath of divine inspiration: that is to have taken chosen stones from the designated place.

But in order that this selection of stones may be made by individual men from individual tribes, let him apply the labour of his reflection to each of the virtues which we have distinguished, and extend the number of his stones to twelve. Therefore let whoever desires, after the turning back of the Jordan, to fulfil this commandment of the Lord, consider—let him consider, I say—how vigorous he was, in some measure, in each virtue during the time of divine visitation.

Let him consider how much solidity he then had in fear, how much weightiness in compunction [Col. 1107B], how much stability in hope, how much wholeness in charity, how much maturity in joy, how much sternness in severity. Let him consider how austere he was in abstinence, how strong in patience, how watchful in circumspection, how constant in speculation, how certain in discernment, how tranquil in contemplation.

When he has fully considered and committed all these things to memory, he has raised the mound which was required. It would be an infinite task, which no one could at all accomplish, if the Lord commanded every person from every tribe to take his stone, because no one could sufficiently assess himself worthily as to what he is in every respect—not in every virtue, I say, but even in any single virtue.

It is enough, therefore, to distinguish through all the virtues we have specified some one outstanding and notable desire of one’s ardour, to establish the practice of such remembrance, and, in this recollection, to fight against the evil of despair in every danger of distrust [Col. 1107C]. For one who recalls what he once was through divine working readily restores his mind, however cast down and however assaulted by temptation, to hope in divine mercy and to the state of confidence. Certainly and without doubt, the person to whom it has been granted to know how much this diligent gathering of stones can accomplish, or how useful it is, gladly applies himself to such a discipline.

## CHAPTER VII. On the solidity of fear

[Col. 1107D] How useful, I ask, do we think that stone is which we placed first: namely, the solidity of fear, through which the mind is founded upon the firm ground of humility? How much it avails is shown by that saying of the Lord: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 56).

This is “the stone of stumbling and the rock of offence”—unless perhaps you doubt that this is the stone which the builders rejected and which was made the head of the corner. For proud minds, wishing to establish their own righteousness, ordinarily endure nothing more painfully and resent nothing more than to appear despised and to be thought worthless.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the weightiness of compunction

[Col. 1108A]

I think the second stone, called the weightiness of compunction, can be found in Jeremiah, who asked that his head be given waters in order that he might weep for the slain of his people (Jer. 5). And I do not doubt that this was granted him by him who “turns the rock into pools of water and cliffs into a fountain of waters.”

I think this same rock may be found in Peter, because, struck inwardly by sorrow of heart, he went outside and wept bitterly—striking the rock twice, and most abundant waters came forth, and there came to be an upper watering-place and a lower watering-place.

## CHAPTER IX. On the long-suffering of hope

[Col. 1108B] I do not doubt that the third rock, which is the long-suffering of hope, may be found in Job. From it streams of oil poured out for him, by which he soothed the pains of his body. For he hoped until morning amid all his losses and wounds of suffering, never exhausted of the oil of his hope and nowhere despairing of the anointing of divine mercy: “Even if he kills me,” he says, “I will hope in him” (Job 13).

## CHAPTER X. On the wholeness of charity

Likewise, I find the fourth rock in Peter, to whom we do not doubt that the Lord said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16), because he loved Christ the Lord [Col. 1108C] with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind, truly recognizing that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God.

Where, I ask, is the wholeness of charity found if you do not find it in Peter, who dares to profess before the Searcher of hearts and say: “Lord, you know that I love you” (John 21)?

## CHAPTER XI. On the maturity of joy

Who would dare doubt that the fifth rock is found in that people whom the Lord’s Prophet, among the other teachings of prophecy, pronounces blessed? “Blessed,” he says, “is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88). Who, indeed, would deny that those are blessed whom the Lord “fed with the fat of wheat” and “satisfied with honey from the rock”? For he has stored up joy and exultation [Col. 1108D] upon them.

You perceive, I think, how great it is to possess this stone among the others: it flows with the honey of joy and satisfies with inward sweetness the one who enters into the joy of his Lord. How great, I ask, will it be whenever it is fitting to be satisfied with honey from the rock and to drink and be inebriated, on the way, from the torrent of delight?

This is that fifth stone, as was said, which is called the maturity of joy. Therefore let one who hungers and thirsts only for that which flows from this stone have nothing frivolous, nothing transient, nothing carnal in his understanding; rather, let him compose his mind to the great gravity of maturity.

## CHAPTER XII. On the harshness of severity

But, I think, he fought with the sixth stone [Col. 1109A] to whom the Lord said: “Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads; like adamant and like flint I have made your face” (Ezek. 3). Jeremiah, therefore, crushed the provoking house of Israel with adamant and flint, because it had a brazen forehead and a hard heart; standing at the gate of the Lord’s house, he proclaimed their crimes to them, fearing neither their words nor their faces.

That strong king, mighty in battle, holds this stone in his hands; by it the strong armed man, a warrior from his youth, was cast down. For David prevailed over the Philistine with sling and stone in the name of the Lord. You see, certainly, by what weapons that young man—despised and small in stature—cast down the utterly monstrous giant Goliath: he had been taught by the Lord to have hands trained for battle and fingers trained for war.

Indeed, he had weapons not carnal but mighty through God for the destruction of fortifications; and he was thereby fighting and destroying every height that exalted itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity to the obedience of Christ. For he understood more than all who taught him, and therefore confidently proclaimed the righteousness of the Lord in the great assembly, as he himself testified concerning the past and promised concerning the future: “I have proclaimed your righteousness in the great assembly; behold, I will not restrain my lips: Lord, you know” (Ps. 39) [Col. 1109B].

You therefore have at hand the means to avenge every disobedience: he rebuked the proud, reproved the restless, and by the stone of most severe rebuke and the harshness of correction cast down the enemies of truth. And although he was the mildest and gentlest man among his people—“Remember, O Lord, David and all his gentleness” (Ps. 131)—yet, although he possessed such great gentleness, he nevertheless “slew every morning all sinners of the land, that he might destroy from the city of the Lord all workers of iniquity” [Col. 1109C].

## CHAPTER XIII. On the austerity of abstinence
The seventh stone, we said, is the austerity of abstinence. Upon this rock the father of Samson offered a holocaust to the Lord, and obtained the begetting, from a barren woman, of the mightiest of men, to the disgrace of the nations and the glory of his people Israel [Col. 1109D] (Judg. 13). He was indeed ashamed that he had for so long nourished one who was barren and did not bear; and he no longer wished, as indeed he ought not, to be a debtor to the flesh so as to live according to the flesh. Rather, chastising his body and reducing it to servitude, sacrificing the flesh of kids upon the rock of abstinence, and consuming, by fire received from heaven, the right to flesh together with the flesh itself, he refused thereafter, having restrained the unruly impulses of the body, to follow his own desires. And thus, having subdued the impulse of the flesh, he strengthened the impulse of the spirit, which becomes stronger through the weakness of the flesh.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the strength of patience.

After these stones follows the strength of patience, which stone I recall having counted in the eighth place [Col. 1110A]. Behold, a most strong and hardest stone. That standard-bearer of the heavenly host, the proto-martyr Stephen, held this stone in his hands, and it became for him a tower of strength against the enemy. Upon this stone he bravely endured the blows of stones pressing upon him; he did not fear the hands of those stoning him, nor their onslaught who gnashed their teeth at him (Acts 7).

O strong and hard stone, yet full of sweetness! O breast most robust, yet full of compassion! You marvel, whoever hears this, at how in his patience he possessed his soul; but rather you ought to have wondered how his spirit, under such bitterness of persecution, did not lose its sweetness. He was oppressed by enemies, and prayed for his enemies. He endured human cruelty and [Col. 1110B] beheld divine glory: “Behold,” he says, “I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of the power of God” (ibid.). He was oppressed on earth and consoled from heaven. He was afflicted by misery inflicted upon him, moved by mercy implanted within him, and rejoiced in the glory he beheld. Behold, at one and the same time he saw below that for which he might feel compassion, and above that in which he might delight. Behold how compassion flowed from the same breast with joy, and joy with compassion. Behold how from the same vessel oil flowed with honey: the oil of compassion with the honey of joy.

What, I ask, is this unmixed mingling and mingled non-confusion of oil and honey in this stone? I wonder if you do not wonder how the valiant fighter, in one and the same moment, drew honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone. [Col. 1110C] Wondrous is the virtue of patience; and who can worthily weigh the value of this rock, which distils oil with honey in such abundance? How great, I ask, is the abundance of oil and honey found where mercy is diminished by no malice, where sweetness is lessened by no pain? Indeed, in a wonderful fashion delight grows from pain, and compassion from suffering. For while the martyr was being stoned, he had greater pity for his enemies than for his own limbs. For, kneeling, he prayed, saying: “Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge, for they do not know what they are doing” (ibid.).

Behold: through the bending of his knees oil was poured out; and thereafter his name became like oil poured out. For there was an outpouring of oil in compassion toward his enemy, so great that [Col. 1110D] the young man sitting at a distance was sprinkled by the fragrance of the ointment. For, as Stephen’s body was bent and his head inclined, oil began to flow; it became as ointment upon the head and descended to the hem of the garment of him who guarded the garments. Therefore he who had long sat in darkness and in the shadow of death swiftly arose and began to run after the fragrance of the ointments; and, rejoicing like a giant to run his course, wherever the impulse of the Spirit was, there he walked, and thereafter he became the good fragrance of Christ in every place.

## CHAPTER XV. On the carefulness of circumspection.

I find the ninth rock in Hezekiah; I find it also in the bride of the friend and the friend of the bridegroom, to whom [Col. 1111A] it is said in the Song of Songs: “Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, and come, my dove, into the clefts of the rock, into the hollow of the wall” (Song 2). Thus Hezekiah too, choosing rest in the likeness of the bride, seeking seclusion, and sitting in the clefts of the rock, or likewise in the hollow of the wall, cried out like a swallow’s chick and meditated like a dove: “Oh that someone would give me wings like a dove’s, and I would fly and be at rest—if only I might fly away to that place where the sparrow finds itself a house, and the turtledove a nest in which to lay her young!”

Where, I ask, can anything safer be found, if it is not found in the clefts of such a rock, where diligent forethought foresees every danger before it occurs; and, anticipating what is to come, infers future events from past ones and often foreknows definite outcomes in uncertain matters? For what else is circumspection but an anxious and discerning examination of surrounding evils? It includes recollection of past evils, consideration of present ones, and forethought concerning future ones, so that it may truly be circumspection according to its name. Constant practice of this makes a person cautious and, so far as possible, safe.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the constancy of contemplation.

The tenth stone was called constancy of contemplation. Jacob, turning away from evil and giving place to wrath, as he hurried on his journey in exile—lest his flight should occur in winter or on the Sabbath—found this stone on the road [Col. 1111C] and placed it beneath his head, lest he have nowhere to lay his head while he slept on the way (Gen. 28). Upon this stone he sleeps and rests in peace, wholly at one with himself; and on his journey he finds a rest which those clothed in soft garments and dwelling in kings’ houses cannot find even in chambers furnished with purple coverings.

Thus, with his head laid upon this stone and his eyes of desire closed—eyes which we read were open in the first parent—while he is lulled into deep rest upon this headrest, and gladly forgets all external things, his mind awakens to inward things and sees what, while awake and seeing, it had not been able to see. A ladder stretching to heaven is raised before his eyes, and the Lord is seen leaning upon the ladder, so that through an invisible form and a figure of invisible things [Col. 1111D] the mind of the contemplative may be lifted to an understanding of intelligible things. Blessed is he for whom knowledge of visible things becomes a ladder for knowing invisible things.

It is a beautiful sight to see the steps of this ladder fittingly arranged, proportionately placed, and extended in a continuous sequence of ordered distinctions all the way to the summit, so that through the manifold difference of creatures and the orderly distinction and distinctly ordered gradation of ranks, the mind may gradually advance toward higher things, ascending ever to greater heights by the steps of its progress, until the invisible things of God, understood through the things that have been made from the creation of the world, are perceived, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder is seen. Who, I ask, would see this except one sleeping on this headrest? Who, while awake, could accomplish this: stretch [Col. 1112A] the ladder of his ascent to heaven and join contemplation of invisible things to contemplation of visible things?

Moreover, in this path of ascent the aid of angelic encounter freely presents itself, so that divine revelation may meet human investigation. Thus angels are seen upon this ladder, now ascending and now descending, instructing the mind now in higher things, now in lower things, so that by divine revelation it may know many things, both divine and human, which it could not know by itself. Angels could indeed, without the service of a ladder, descend to the lowest things or fly to the highest as they chose; nor would divine inspiration need, in any manifestation of its revelations, to seek the instrument of any bodily likeness—unless it wished us first to see through a mirror and in an enigma, rather than immediately face to face.

Therefore angels ascend and descend on this ladder of likenesses; some after others approach and depart, so that, while one of many revelations is imparted and another withdrawn, the contemplative mind may be illuminated in many ways, and may understand separately, successively, and through intervals of delay those things which, owing to the narrowness of its understanding, it could not grasp all at once. [Col. 1112B] Behold what those find who sleep upon this stone. Blessed are those for whom what is usually a cause of ruin to others is changed into a ladder. Blessed are those for whom knowledge of outward things becomes a ladder of ascent, not a downfall of descent. Blessed are those for whom that knowledge which puffs up serves not for puffing up but for the inflaming of that which builds up. Blessed are those for whom the beauty of temporal things becomes an incitement to eternity [Col. 1112C]. Therefore, as you see, one must lay one’s head upon the stone, harden one’s mind in the desire for this contemplation, and persevere stubbornly in this pursuit, if one wishes to find this ladder of ascent.

## CHAPTER XVII. On certainty of discernment.

We called certainty of discernment the eleventh stone; if we seek it diligently, we find it most readily in Paul. For he has such confidence in the gift of discernment, such assurance in the certainty of his judgment, that he confidently gives counsel where he has no command of the Lord: “Concerning virgins,” he says, “I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7 [Col. 1112D]). Hence it is that he sets himself before others as an example of conduct and offers his own life as a pattern of living for his followers, when he says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (I Cor. XL).

And rightly so, since he had set his feet upon a rock and directed his steps. With stones such as these, I think, the path of those travelers was paved, of whom the Prophet cries out in admiration: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Rom. 10). With these stones, unless I am mistaken, that great patriarch Joseph—whom the ruler of peoples appointed lord of his household and prince over all his possessions, that he might instruct his princes as himself and teach his elders wisdom—[Col. 1113A] is rightly believed to have paved the streets of Egypt. Thus the children of Israel had no need to serve in mud and brick all the days of their life.

The Prophet was still suffering the lack of these stones and laboring under a great want of discernment while he remained fixed in the mire of the deep, because the firm certainty of sound judgment had not yet become settled within him; so much so that he cried out to the Lord and said: “How long shall I devise counsels in my soul?” (Ps. 18). Yet he would never have fully emerged from that deep mire unless he had at last found the rock of which we speak: “He set me on a rock,” he says, “and now he has lifted up my head above my enemies” (Ps. 26). Whoever does not pave his own way with stones of this kind never walks cleanly and never plants stable steps. Therefore whoever wishes to walk firmly and honorably ought never to act rashly; he should make sure that he has paved his way with the stone required, and then may proceed securely. “Do all things,” says the Wise Man, “with counsel, and you will never repent” (Ecclus. 32 [Col. 1113B]).

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the repose of contemplation.

The twelfth and final stone of all, I think, may be found at the Lord’s tomb. As was said above, this stone is called the tranquility of contemplation. Joseph of Arimathea cut tombs for himself out of stones of this kind, but Jesus rested there in death; for the repose which prudence seeks for itself through meditation and defines by definition, wisdom finds through contemplation [Col. 1113C] and grasps through experience.

True prudence always seeks, and ought always to seek, that peace which Christ taught: that it should neither be troubled nor afraid. It always strives to find such peace and continually endeavors to secure for itself true safety; but it always finds something to grieve over from the past, something to contend against in the present, and something to guard against and fear for the future. The mind may therefore diligently seek this peace by prudence and subtly investigate it through meditation, but can never find it except through wisdom and the grace of contemplation.

But when the mind begins, through pure understanding, to transcend itself; to enter wholly into the brightness of incorporeal light [Col. 1113D]; to draw from what it sees in its inmost depths a certain taste of inward sweetness; to season its understanding thereby and transform it into wisdom—then, in this ecstasy of mind, that peace which is neither disturbed nor afraid is found and attained. There comes to be silence in heaven, as it were for half an hour, so that the contemplative mind is troubled by no tumult of disputing thoughts. You will find nothing at all which it seeks through desire, rebukes through weariness, or accuses through hatred.

Thus he is ordered toward the highest peace who is buried in this stone, who is wholly gathered and enclosed within the tranquility of contemplation. For this stone is not placed only beneath the head, like Jacob’s stone, nor laid under the feet, like the preceding one; rather, it is fitted and applied to the whole [Col. 1114A] body. This stone therefore surrounds, encloses, and encompasses the whole body on every side, because that peace which surpasses all understanding wholly absorbs every human sense and, in a blessed transformation, changes the purer part of the soul into a certain divine disposition. Here the body lies without sense or movement in this monument of the Lord. Sensuality does nothing; imagination does nothing; and every lower power of the soul is meanwhile occupied with its own function.

For this stone tomb, unlike that stony headrest of the patriarch Jacob, does not receive a living body, even though asleep; it receives only a body that has been mortified. To sleep is one thing; to die is another. To gather one’s whole spirit into oneself is one thing; to rise above oneself and leave oneself behind is another. To have restrained appetite and let concern for outward things slip from the heart is one thing; to pass into forgetfulness even of oneself is another.

Therefore, before one may enter into that secret place of inward rest and mystery of highest tranquility, there must occur, I say, that very grave and truly wondrous—not dissolution of soul and body, but another division, far more wondrous and far more glorious, of which this dissolution is a type: namely, the division of soul and spirit [Col. 1114B]. As the Apostle testifies, the living and efficacious word of God, more penetrating than any two-edged sword, customarily works this in us, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit.

What, I ask, is seen anywhere among creatures more wonderful than this division, in which that which is essentially one and indivisible is divided within itself, and that which is simple in itself and has no parts is divided and separated from itself? For in a single human being the spirit is not one essence and the soul another; rather, they are wholly one and the same substance of a simple nature. A twofold substance is not meant by this double term; but, when it is employed to distinguish them, two powers of the same essence are designated: the higher by “spirit,” the lower by “soul.”

In this division, then, the soul and what is animal remain below, but the spirit and what is spiritual fly upward. That which is bodily and dreg-like, as though a dead body, fails and falls back into itself [Col. 1114C] and beneath itself; that which is subtle and purified, like a spirit breathed forth, rises and transcends itself within and beyond itself. O deep rest, O sublime repose, where everything that is ordinarily moved in a human way loses every motion; where every motion that then exists comes from God and passes into God!

This spirit, breathed forth and commended into the Father’s hands, does not, like Jacob the dreamer, need a ladder in order to fly to the third heaven—or, indeed, I should say, to the first. Why should one need a ladder whom the Father carries between His hands, in order to snatch him up into the mysteries of the third heaven, so that he may boast and say: “Your right hand has received me. You held my right hand, led me according to your will, and received me with glory” (Ps. 17)? Therefore the Spirit [Col. 1115A], taken away from the midst, has no need here of a ladder’s service, nor does it require, in this ascent of its subtlety, the support of any shadowed bodily likeness, where it sees face to face, not through a mirror and in an enigma.

I lie if those who are such do not themselves affirm the same concerning themselves: “But we all,” they say, “with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3). You surely see what that division of soul and spirit, of which we have already spoken above, accomplishes; and, I think, you understand its power. The spirit is divided from lower things in order that it may be raised to the highest. The spirit is separated from the soul in order that it may be united to the Lord. “For he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit.”

Happy division and desirable separation, in which that which is recognized as passible and corruptible meanwhile dies to its own passions, so completely that no passibility or corruptibility is then felt; and in which that which is spiritual and subtle is raised to the contemplation of divine glory and transformed into the same image [Col. 1115B]. The lower part is thus composed into highest peace and tranquility, while the higher part is elevated to glory and joy. Thus we know that the face of Moses—the higher part, indeed, of the body—was glorified through companionship with the Lord, so that the children of Israel could not look upon his face because of its brightness.

Who, I ask, can worthily say or adequately explain what perfection the spirit gains in the glorification of its ecstasy, even if it does not prolong its sojourn to the third day, even if it does not extend the duration of silence to half an hour [Col. 1115C], even though it goes and returns in the likeness of flashing lightning? Thus Moses, returning from the fellowship of divine conversation with a glorified face, even brings back horns, showing what power and strength he has acquired through companionship with Him who gives strength and power to His people—blessed be God.

At last, therefore, that spirit which had gone far beyond itself returns and comes back to itself; and, having laid aside what was passible and corruptible, it takes it up again as though impassible and incorruptible in comparison with its former state, and rises into newness of life. What do you think it is to rejoice at an injury inflicted, not to blush at an insult cast upon one, to delight in tribulation? Is this not to walk in newness of life, to show oneself in some measure impassible, and not to lie subject to one’s passions? [Col. 1116A] Behold how far those advance who rest upon this stone.

Many things might have been said on this subject, if they ought to have been said in this place and did not exceed the measure of a moderate digression. For I think this final kind of stones is the worthiest and most precious of all. Yet we must despise none of them, but seek at least one of each kind and gather them together into one.

It should certainly be noted that this is the first work commanded to be done in the land of promise: first of all, an everlasting memorial of divine works is to be established. For without this heap of stones, that Lordly promise of eternal inheritance is never acquired strongly, never possessed securely. Whoever forgets benefits received from God [Col. 1116B] does not deserve to advance toward the attainment of greater ones.

[Col. 1115]

# ON THE CONDITION OF THE INNER MAN

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1115C]

Late indeed have I sent what I promised to the one who asked. But, most beloved man, the reason I did not earlier do what I had earlier wished to do was necessity, not will: many intervening occasions hindered my purpose [Col. 1115D], and I could not fulfill your command. One thing seemed to remain for me after so long a postponement of my promise: I resolved at least to compensate for the loss caused by the protracted delay with a more abundant interest upon the debt.

Meanwhile, my friend, let it please you to weigh the mind of a friend: it was sweet to him to remain longer attached to the services of a sweet friend and, that his labor might serve that friend’s will for longer—not, I dare say, his advantage—to prolong deliberately a brief work into a long one. Taking, therefore, both the occasion for writing and the rule for speaking from those words of Isaiah which you asked me to expound as my gift to you, I have discussed at greater length certain matters concerning the condition of the inner man.

Thus, like one strolling rather than traveling, I lengthened the short cuts of a brief journey by manifold wandering, exploring and admiring—not pleasant places [Col. 1116C], but depths of words and heights of meanings—with a curious leisure and a leisurely curiosity. For who would not rightly marvel at the condition of our old age, fully comprehended in so concise a brevity of words? Consider, I beseech you [Col. 1116D], in what fitting order and by what wondrous method vices are first, and sins afterward, mystically described; and how contempt for remedies is added, in which three things the whole sum of spiritual corruption is contained.

There is a threefold vice, a threefold sin, and a threefold remedy: weakness, ignorance, and concupiscence. These three are vices of the inner man, which, when they entice consent, become sins. Accordingly, there is a threefold kind of vice and a threefold kind of sin. Some sins we contract through weakness, some through error, and others we commit voluntarily from sheer perversity of will. We understand a threefold remedy in divine ordinances, divine threatenings, and divine promises.

These nine things, therefore, are comprehended in the same order and in the greatest brevity in a few words of Isaiah; and they are indicated by a wondrous method in the mystical description, which will be expounded more fully in their respective places [Col. 1117A]. Truly, something great, something profound—indeed, something most salutary—must have been that which sounded from the mouth of God and flowed forth from the divine oracle. If human teaching is despised, is divine teaching at least to be held in contempt?

But when you read my writings and find much to criticize, you will readily grant me pardon. For if I have become foolish, you compelled me. Grant pardon, reader: I have not presumed to teach, but wished to satisfy a friend who asked.

# FIRST TREATISE. On the condition of the inner man after the Fall.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1117B]

“Every head is sick, and every heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in it. Wound, bruise, and swollen sore: it has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor soothed with oil” (Isa. 5 [citation as printed]).

The Lord knows His creature, and neither the multiplicity nor the magnitude of diseases can be hidden from the supreme physician. Behold, He describes for you the character and magnitude of the disease, so that you may know what you ought to lament, what you ought to treat, and for what you ought to beseech Him. “Every head,” He says, “is sick, and every heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in it.” Behold innate evils; hear now of others also: wound, bruise, and swollen sore. Behold inflicted evils; behold what kind they are, behold how great. Some evils arise within us; others are inflicted. Some are suffered inwardly; others we encounter outwardly. The former are generated from one’s own corruption; the latter are often brought upon one by another’s assault. Sickness, sorrow, and weakness arise from within; wound, bruise, and swollen sore come from without.

To complete the evils comes contempt for remedies, wherein truly lies the despair of the sick. “It has not,” He says, “been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor soothed with oil.” Behold how many evils press us, behold what hardships daily oppress us.
