Learn, O human being: even if you disdain to learn from a human being, learn at least from Him who teaches humanity knowledge. Learn, I say, grieve, and lament so great an affliction [Col. 1117C] and such misery. Attend to and recognize the magnitude of the disease, so that you may desire anxiously, seek more carefully, and love more ardently the remedies of the physician.

See, then, how the condition of the inner man is described to you in accordance with the nature of the outer man, so that through outward evils—whose kind and magnitude you do not fail to know—you may learn what you ought to fear regarding inward evils. For who does not see that this cannot stand wholly in the literal sense? Has it ever been seen or heard that every head is sick, or every human heart sorrowful? “Every head,” He says, “is sick, and every heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in it.” Certain members of the outer human being are named here, so that, when we hear head, heart, and foot named, we may be compelled by them to form some analogy with inward things, concerning which we need to know what is fitting [Col. 1117D].

## CHAPTER II. On the three principal things in a human being.

We know that in the human body the head occupies the highest place, the foot the lowest, and the heart the middle and inmost place. The head is free will; the heart, counsel; the foot, carnal desire. The head rises above the whole body, and free will presides over every action. The heart occupies the middle and inmost place, and sound counsel can scarcely be drawn from concealment and found in secrecy. The foot lies at the bottom, and carnal desire clings through appetite to the lowest things.

Free will presides over every action; indeed, it presides over appetite, because even when you have acted badly, when sin is already at the door, “its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it.” What does “it shall be under you” mean except “under your will,” since no appetite comes forth into action without the spontaneous impulse and voluntary consent of the will? Counsel is sought in secrecy and drawn out from the depths, because wisdom is drawn from what is hidden. Concupiscence of the flesh lies below, so long as “my soul cleaves to the pavement,” so long as “our belly is glued to the earth” [Col. 1118B].

## CHAPTER III. On the dignity of free will.

Among all the goods of creation, nothing in a human being is higher or more worthy than free will; nothing more useful or more hidden than sound counsel; nothing is lower or weaker than carnal desire. What, I ask, can be found in a human being higher or worthier than that in which he was created in the image of God? Freedom of choice certainly bears the image not only of eternity but also of divine majesty. How closely, we may suppose, does free will in this respect approach unchangeable eternity more than all other things and bear its image within itself more expressly: no fault whatsoever, no misery whatever, can—I do not say destroy it—but cannot even diminish it.

Do you wish also to perceive the likeness of majesty in it and recognize clearly how it is stamped with that image? God has no superior and cannot have one; free will endures no mastery and cannot endure it, because it is not fitting for the Creator to do violence to it, nor is any creature able to do so [Col. 1118C]. Let all hell, all the world, indeed the entire army of the heavenly host, come together and conspire in this one thing: no consent of free will in any matter can be forced from one who is unwilling.

## CHAPTER IV. On the usefulness of counsel.

But just as nothing in a human being is more excellent than this freedom of choice, so nothing is more salutary than prudent counsel and considered prudence. “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom, and who abounds in prudence. Its acquisition is better than the trade of silver and gold. For it is more precious than all riches, and all things that are desired cannot be compared to it.”

Yet nothing is possessed more usefully, nor found with greater difficulty, than this gift of wisdom. For it is a treasure hidden in a field, because, as has been said, “Wisdom is drawn from what is hidden” (Job 28). But what is this hidden place, or what is the field that we say conceals this treasure? “Where is wisdom found, and what is the place of understanding?” Let us seek with blessed Job the place of wisdom and understanding, and we shall find it with Solomon: “I, Wisdom,” he says, “dwell in counsel, and I am present among learned thoughts” (Prov. 8).

Let us therefore seek her who dwells in counsel within our heart, which we have already said is counsel. “Guard your heart with all vigilance,” then, whoever desires this most desirable treasure, lest, if you refuse to guard it, you be compelled to lament with the Prophet and say: “My heart has abandoned me” [Col. 1119B] (Ps. 39), grieving and mourning because you then have nowhere to seek this treasure or find it. I think that their heart had abandoned those men and all counsel had failed them to whom the Lord said in rebuke: “Ephraim is a deceived dove without a heart” (Hos. 7). Therefore it is rightly said of them: “A nation without counsel and without prudence; would that they were wise, understood, and foresaw their latter end!”

How carefully, then, must the heart be guarded, in which is found that treasure than which none richer or safer is possessed! For if wisdom enters your heart, according to the testimony of the Wise Man, and knowledge pleases your soul, counsel will guard you and prudence preserve you [Col. 1119C].

## CHAPTER V. On the weakness of carnal desire.

But just as nothing is more useful than prudent counsel, so nothing is lower or weaker than carnal desire, because, in likeness to the foot, it holds the lowest place and clings to earthly things through delight of the flesh. What, I ask, is weaker or more abject than this: that we cannot even fully resist those things of which we are ashamed? How great, I ask, is the baseness and weakness of consenting in mind that the law of God is good, yet daily seeing another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin? From these things do you see further how rightly free will is understood by the head, counsel by the heart, and carnal desire by the foot?

## CHAPTER VI. On the sovereignty of free will.

[Col. 1120A]

From the head the whole body is governed, by the heart the whole body is enlivened, and by the feet it is carried about. The head governs the whole, and free will has by right of its nature received the rule and direction of all that is in a human being. Just as it acknowledges no master among all things outside the human being, so by the dignity of its freedom it rules over all things within that person.

For even if some movement arises in a human being contrary to or apart from that person’s will, yet just as the person never consents to it except by freedom of choice, so it never breaks into action except by that person’s permission. The movement of sensuality very often commands bodily movement, and the affection of the soul frequently commands not only the senses but also the appetites [Col. 1120B]. Yet none of all these brings its attempt to its intended effect except at the prompting of free will and with voluntary consent.

The voluntary consent of free will therefore rules over all things; because, according to the teaching of wisdom, “one high person has another higher than himself, and yet others are higher than they; and the king rules over the whole earth that serves him.” This king rules over the whole earth because, although every movement serves him at his command through all the other members of the body, even that which alone does not obey him as he wishes but often rebels in great opposition, he can restrain while headlong from action, strike severely when unbridled, and break and soften the boldness of its fierceness by strong chastisement. Thus even what contradicts and strongly resists him shamelessly does not wholly escape his power [Col. 1120C]. Rightly, therefore, I think, is that which rules all the rest compared to the head.

## CHAPTER VII. On the power of useful counsel.

But the heart gives life to that same body which, as has been said, the head governs. For, to speak somewhat of these matters according to the physicians: just as the animal spirit has its seat in the head, and the natural spirit in the liver, so the vital spirit has its seat in the heart. And, just as the body is endowed with sensation and ordered by the animal spirit, and nourished by the natural spirit, so it is made alive by the vital spirit. [Col. 1120D] Thus every sensation and every voluntary movement comes from the animal spirit; growth, however, from the natural spirit; and life from the vital spirit.

What a body is without life, a work is without good intention. Therefore any action, however good it may seem, is judged, as it were, dead unless, through counsel, it is animated toward a good intention. As life proceeds from the heart and diffuses itself through all the members, so good intention arises from counsel and ordinarily animates the works of virtues toward the flourishing of merit. Therefore the Wise Man rightly commands: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, because life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4). Life proceeds from it when a depraved intention is corrected through counsel. But death rather than life proceeds from it when a good intention is corrupted through counsel. [Col. 1121A]

For what benefit is there in begetting the offspring of good works and then killing it through the corruption of one’s intention? And what will it be like, I ask, if our own conscience convicts us of being the killers of our children? Some corrupt their works at their very outset through an evil intention; others, after the practice of virtues, become empty of their former intention through the offering of vain praise. What do the former do except produce miscarried offspring, while the latter kill them when they have already been born, or even when grown up? Is it not better not to beget than to cause miscarriage, and far more useful not to bear offspring than either to crush them while sleeping or to kill them deliberately? Is it not better that I should go childless than sacrifice my sons and daughters to demons? Is not the barren woman, who does not give birth, far happier than those merciless killers of their children, eaters of human entrails, devourers of blood, and parent-authors of helpless souls? [Col. 1121B] (Wis. 12).

Always remember that, although it lies within your power to kill those who are living, it is not equally within your power to raise the dead. He alone can do this who is able to raise up children of Abraham from stones. Yet at the Lord’s command, when the Son of Man prophesied over the dry bones found in the field, the spirit entered into them and they lived. What, I ask, is meant by dry bones—bones without soul and dead—except strong works without good intention, and therefore devoid of the merit of virtues and disappointed of the reward of recompense? Nevertheless, works of this kind receive the spirit at the Lord’s command, revive, and, once their intention has been corrected by the grace of his inspiration, grow green again in hope of eternal recompense. [Col. 1121C] But because intention receives from counsel the quality of being right and good, it proceeds, as it were, from the heart as spirit, since, going forth to enliven the body, it diffuses itself through all the members of the virtues. Therefore, in my judgment, counsel is rightly signified by the heart, whose likeness it imitates.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Restlessness of Carnal Desire

We have also easily shown how what we said about the feet is suited, in relation to affection or appetite, to carnal desire. For just as the body is carried about by its feet, so the mind is stirred and led about by carnal desire. When the mind, enticed and drawn away by carnal desire, now follows its affection, now its appetite, it is never permitted to be at rest or tranquil anywhere. For as long as it lives as a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth, it daily runs after its lusts; filled with many miseries, it never remains in the same condition, since it always strives either to seize what it desires or to escape what it hates.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Restlessness of Human Affection

Who, I ask, could adequately set out in how many ways human affection is accustomed to change itself? It changes itself in many ways; and with every alternation of its change it lets loose its force upon many things—indeed, almost innumerable things—always moving from one thing to another, [Col. 1122A] becoming weary of one thing after another, and often returning with greater eagerness to that which it had previously despised. Hence Solomon says: “The spirit goes round, surveying all things in a circuit, and returns to its own circuits” (Eccl. 1).

The spirit is rightly said to go round, surveying all things in a circuit, because, as has already been said, the affection of the heart is swept through diverse things and changes in many forms. Since it finds sufficient delight nowhere, it always moves from one thing to another. Now it loves this, now that; now it desires this, now that; and it despises again what it had previously loved and grows weary again of what it had long and greatly desired. Yet after weariness it often returns more eagerly to its rejected desires; and in this way it goes in a circuit and bends its course into a circle. [Col. 1122B]

Thus love, pride, hope, grief, and every other affection are led through diverse things and vary in many ways. But amid all the movements and modes of its affections, the mind always returns to its own circuits, since it is again affected in the same manner concerning the same or a similar thing. Nor is it especially surprising that a stirred spirit, driven in any one direction, is carried through diverse things and borne through varied pleasures to satisfy its desires, and that, as though surveying the whole surface of the earth, it returns again to its customary and ancient delights.

But this is very marvelous and worthy of wonder: often, suddenly driven by contrary winds, it is carried now in this direction, now in the opposite [Col. 1122C] one, so that what it had previously loved ardently it afterward pursues with insatiable hatred. Of all the elements, that which we call spirit or air is the most changeable and subject to various passions. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, it grows warm and again cools with equal ease—so much so that, from one mouth and almost at the same time, when gently exhaled or forcibly driven forth, it comes out now warm and now bursts forth cold. So that spiritual spirit and passible affection are easily affected and, by a slight change, transformed into contrary passions.

Who does not know how a man is at once wholly inclined to favor by the faint breath of one who praises him, but, if from the same mouth and at the same time a wind of detraction bursts forth, immediately turns his affection [Col. 1122D] in the other direction and changes it into hatred and fury? Truly it is marvelous—indeed, pitiable—that that noble creature made in the image of God and set above every creature should be violently shaken from the state of its uprightness by a small word, a faint breath, the sound of a tongue, and a stroke of air; and then, in a wonderful fashion, be snatched now here, now there, and whirled in giddiness like a storm.

## CHAPTER X. On the Restlessness of Carnal Appetite

Likewise, the appetite of the flesh is always in motion, always in passage, and can never remain in the same state. It advances and withdraws, increases and decreases; and it always withdraws and decreases so that it may return and increase again, and always returns and increases so that it may withdraw and decrease again. [Col. 1123A]

Yet appetite does not stir and disturb the mind with the same wandering course or equal impulse as affection. It is not varied, like the winds, by daily change through manifold courses, nor is it driven in opposite directions by contrary blasts in alternating turns. Rather, like a river, it follows the channel of its current until it attains the object of its desire. It does not change the bed of its accustomed course through momentary alternations, so as to repent successively of successive desires even before it has obtained what it desired. Nor does it check the course of its desire or turn aside in the opposite direction until it has satisfied its desire—as does affection, which clothes itself in different qualities [Col. 1123B] at every moment and often, in a single instant, turns the blast of its impulse in the opposite direction, changing its love with astonishing speed into hatred.

For it is one thing to seek varied delights, to move, as it were, from place to place, and, once satisfied, to grow weary of one thing after another, as though abandoning one place after another; it is another thing to bend one’s course in the opposite direction and, after downward courses, return to the heights—something neither water can do nor appetite is accustomed to do. Yet it always runs and passes on, and always returns to the same point; whence Solomon says: “To the place from which the rivers go out, they return, that they may flow again” (Eccl. 1).

The appetite of the flesh is that great abyss from which so many rivers flow out, from which so many and such innumerable desires arise. [Col. 1123C] Let us therefore see the place from which rivers of this kind issue, the place to which they arrive by running. Let us see by what way they run and by what way they return. The place from which the outflow of carnal appetite emerges is necessity; the place toward which it tends is satiety; the way by which it passes is pleasure; the way by which it returns is desire. The place from which it rushes forth is the loss caused by our deficiency; the place through which it flows down is delight; the place to which it runs is weariness; the place through which it returns is desire.

After great weariness from its satiety, every appetite returns again to its place in a great longing of concupiscence, so that it may flow anew; for it is compelled by the same necessity as before to seek again the pleasures which delight it, in order to repair the losses of its body. And just as every course of waters passes over the surface of the earth through visible channels and likewise returns through subterranean and invisible channels, so every appetite is gradually expelled through the unseen process of action and the fulfillment of desire, and again is recalled, by a certain hidden operation of nature and by the movements of nourishment, to the unfamiliar returns of its accustomed course. [Col. 1123D]

What a thing, I ask, and how miserable it is always to be driven under this whirling motion and always to be entangled in the agitation of so great a restlessness! How desirable—indeed, how detestable—are those delights of our desires, which are always generated from deficiency and turned into weariness. But why do we say that they end in weariness, when Scripture itself testifies that they always end their course in bitterness? [Col. 1124A] “All rivers,” Scripture says, “enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow” (ibid.). We know that rivers make water sweet, while seas make it bitter. What, then, is it for rivers to enter the sea except for every carnal delight to end in bitterness? Every river, therefore, enters the sea, because grief occupies the end of joy. Everything sweet that falls into the sea is changed into bitterness, since laughter will be mingled with sorrow.

All rivers are borne into the sea, and all sweet water is changed into bitter, because, as has been said, delight turns into weariness and every pleasure of the flesh ends in bitterness. Since human perversity does not know how to use its good things well, or despises them, heavenly justice afterward turns into a scourge for each person that by which he had first sinned through unrighteous pleasure. [Col. 1124B] But the rivers enter the sea and the sea does not overflow, because in every one of our afflictions and in every blow it inflicts, divine equity observes measure; in all that strikes us for vengeance or correction, it does not exceed the bounds of justice. Thus the sea does not overflow because the magnitude of our misery does not exceed the desert of our wickedness.

From these things, then, one may judge how the feet of concupiscence, of which we have already spoken, distract us through either affection or appetite, and to what end they bring the extremes of their courses.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Threefold Affliction of Man

But since we believe enough has now been said concerning what we understand by the head, heart, and foot, let us see what, from divine teaching, we ought to understand concerning such members of the inner man: “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him” (Isa. 1). [Col. 1124C]

The head is sick, the heart grieves, and the foot suffers with the whole body, because from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in him. As has been said, the head is free choice, the heart counsel, and the foot carnal desire. Therefore the head is sick because free choice is sluggish toward every good. The heart grieves because counsel can neither fail to know nor conceal the evil that it suffers. The foot suffers with the whole body because the evil of concupiscence burns on every side.

He wished to show us the sickness of the head when he said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). What is more sickly than that which, by itself, cannot gain strength for any good whatever, even the least? [Col. 1124D] “For it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.” The heart grieves; for counsel itself teaches that it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting. Certainly, the more a person advances in counsel, the more he also grows in mourning, because “in much wisdom is much indignation; and he who adds knowledge adds sorrow.” For the more fully anyone recognizes through counsel the evil at which he grieves, the more vehemently he is angered at his own perversities; and the more perfectly he perceives the evil he suffers, the more sharply he is pressed by the sting of pain.

The foot suffers with the whole [Col. 1125A] body because its own weakness wrings pain from each of the members. For, as has been said, from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it. Since weakness thus possesses the whole, what wonder if it suffers on every side? The Prophet says: “There is no health in my flesh; there is no peace in my bones, because of my sins” (Ps. 37). How great, I ask, is the crushing affliction where neither flesh can possess health nor bones have peace! Thus Job too was struck with a most grievous ulcer, so that from the sole of his foot to the crown there was no soundness in him.

Who, I ask, should boast of the health of his body, when even the chief of the prophets complains of his weakness, and the man like whom there was none upon earth is smitten with a most grievous ulcer? For each person is tempted, drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence. “The life of man upon earth is temptation.” Thus there is sickness in the head, grief in the heart, and pain in the whole body. For “the whole head is sick, and the whole heart sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in him.” [Col. 1125B]

Let us consider, if you please, these three things which he sets forth: sickness, grief, and the absence of health. Sickness is a continuing weakness that enervates the whole body. Grief is pain raging more sharply within and breaking forth outwardly through tears. Health is the soundness of the natural constitution and the proportionate balance of all the humors. Weakness, however, is nothing other than the deprivation of health and the corruption of soundness.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Weakness of Free Choice

[Col. 1125C]

See, then, how great and of what kind is the weakness of this head, which he compared with sickness. Since, as has been said, sickness is a continuing weakness that enervates the whole body, why does he call the head sick except because its defect oppresses the whole and cannot be fully healed until the end of life? How rightly is that called sick which of itself is never moved toward any good whatever? For what good can it do of itself, when it cannot even say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit? It is indeed often moved toward good, yet never except by the Holy Spirit.

You have heard how widely this weakness spreads: it occupies and enervates the whole. Do you also wish to hear how long one must waste away under this sickness [Col. 1125D] and endure the sentence of the curse? “Until you return,” he says, “to the earth from which you were taken” (Gen. 3). But how, you ask, can such great freedom accord with such great weakness, or such great weakness with such great freedom? Certainly, to be free is one thing, to be strong another; and you can be free and weak, just as, conversely, you can be healthy and a slave. One who is healthy and strong can do many and great things. But one who is free cannot justly be compelled to anything.

## CHAPTER XIII. What Freedom Is, and What Power Is

We do not call human choice free because it has ready at hand the ability to do good or evil, [Col. 1126A] but because it is free not to consent to good or evil. To be able to do evil belongs to weakness; to be able to do good belongs to power; but neither belongs to freedom. Freedom consists in this: its consent cannot be extorted or restrained. For it can consent or not consent to divine inspiration, and likewise to diabolical suggestion. Each is possible through freedom, but neither is necessary.

Therefore it is one thing to possess freedom and another to possess power. It belongs to freedom that one cannot be compelled to will something; the deprivation of power is the inability to perform some good sufficiently. By sinning, then, man could lose the power to merit; but freedom of choice, just as he has never lacked it, so he will never lack it, because—as has already been said above [Col. 1126B]—it can never be lost or diminished by any sin or punishment whatsoever. Therefore he lost power, not freedom.

But what power, you ask? Hear what kind he received, and you will understand what kind he lost. “You have subjected all things under his feet: all sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea” (Ps. 8). Do you wish to know how this declaration has been reversed, and how the power bestowed was taken away? Observe how he is now oppressed by those whom he had formerly ruled: “Birds shall devour them with most bitter bite; I will send upon them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of creatures that drag themselves upon the earth, and of serpents” (Deut. 32).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Power of Free Choice Before Sin

[Col. 1126C]

Seek, I ask, in the microcosm—for man too is thus called; seek, I say, in the microcosm, that is, in the lesser world; seek in the human heart what it is that is formed in the image and likeness of God, that is set above all other things by the privilege of its dignity, under whose feet all other things are subjected. You will find, I think, nothing other than the free and rational consent, of which this passage is most rightly understood.

For why should consent of this kind not rightly be called made in the image and likeness of God: inasmuch as it is free, it is in the image; inasmuch as it is rational, it is in the likeness? Before transgression it had all things subjected to itself and found no contradiction whatever among the things subjected to it. As long as it willingly subjected itself to its superior, it received from its inferiors the obedience it rendered as due to its own superior. Nothing in man opposed its command. It governed all things, ordered all things, commanded all things. Nothing moved against its will; nothing moved apart from its will. Every bodily movement, every sensation, every appetite, every affection, every thought was moved, directed, checked, and restrained at its bidding. [Col. 1126D]

O sublime power! O mighty sublimity: to command the beasts of the earth, to hold under one’s power the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea! O dignity of sublimity! O sublimity of power: to possess under the right of one’s choice, to arrange as one wills, and to bend to the bidding of one’s rule so many flights of birds, so many courses of beasts, so many movements of fish, in so many pursuits, [Col. 1127A], so many exercises, so many delights of sublime inquiries, manifold affections, and various pleasures!

## CHAPTER XV. On the Loss of the First Power

But now the transgressor has lost this service of such great obedience because he scorned to show the reverence of due servitude to his Creator. For “the zeal of the Creator, taking up armor, armed creation for vengeance against his enemies, and the world fights for him against the senseless.” Now the roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour; the lion’s cubs roar in order to seize; the dragon rages with the fury of creatures that drag themselves upon the earth, and of serpents. [Col. 1127B]

Do you wish to know how birds now devour the transgressor, in accordance with his deserving from transgression, with a most bitter bite, according to the Lord’s word? “My thoughts,” he says, “are scattered, tormenting my heart” (Job 17). The Prophet feared the teeth of beasts when he prayed to the Lord for protection from them: “Save me from the mouth of the lion, and my lowliness from the horns of unicorns” (Ps. 21). He certainly knew that “anger kills the fool, and envy slays the little one”; nor could one who had experienced it be unaware how greatly the ferocity of such beasts was to be feared. “My eye,” he says elsewhere, “has been troubled by fury” (Ps. 6).

Yet in a remarkable way, according to the practice of human skill, the same Prophet tamed beasts for hunting; and, with tamed beasts, hunted untamed ones to death: [Col. 1127C] “I roared from the groaning of my heart” (Ps. 37). See how the roar of one groaning stifled the roar that had formerly raged. See what contradiction, what rebellion, the transgressor found in the kingdom which he had formerly possessed as peaceful and tranquil. Therefore he could lose his former power and forfeit the kingdom he had received, but he can never regain or retain it except by the gift of him who “raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dungheap, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.” For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will rule the nations.

The one who said, “Power is yours; yours is the kingdom, Lord,” knew this. The Prophet also knew that the Lord himself is ruler, and that honor and dominion are in his hand, [Col. 1127D] and that he will give it to whom he wills; and therefore he humbly entreats him to restore his kingdom to him, saying: “Give rule to your servant” (Ps. 85).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Recovery of the First Power

The King daily restores this kingdom gradually and in parts among his elect, yet never in this life to that peace or security which man had in paradise before sin. For the sickness of the head cannot be fully healed, and free choice cannot perfectly recover the vigor of its first condition. Thus human free choice, which of itself can do no good, begins to be able when, and insofar as, he who can do all things wills. For “what is impossible with men is possible with God.” [Col. 1128A]

It therefore begins, by divine assistance, to be able to do what it cannot do of itself; and, what it can no longer do through nature, it receives through grace—the ability to do good. It daily grows toward good and is daily strengthened against evil. It grows toward good so that, now established in authority and having soldiers under it, it can say to one, “Go,” and he goes; to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to its servant, “Do this,” and he does it. It is likewise strengthened against evil, so that sin may no longer reign in this mortal body; and it is often granted by God to believe that the saying has already been spoken to it: “Without your command, no one shall move hand or foot in all the land of Egypt.”

And how great do we think it is to be able to repress all the rebellious movements of the soul and prevent them from acting, although it cannot yet perfectly destroy them all and restore its kingdom to complete peace? Although, therefore, it cannot extinguish all the enemies of peace or cut off everyone’s hands or feet, it will nevertheless be a great thing if no one is permitted, without its command, to move hand or foot. One who is such may truly sing: “But I have been established by him as king over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2). [Col. 1128B]

Thus that free consent of choice—the emperor and lord of the entire land of so many thoughts, affections, appetites, and sensations—cannot yet remove all scandals from its kingdom or establish full and everlasting peace. But when that which is perfect comes, and that which is partial is abolished; when death, the last enemy, is destroyed in victory—[Col. 1128C] then without doubt its dominion will be multiplied beyond measure, and there will be no end to its peace. Then at last it will rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the world. In those days Judah shall be saved and Israel shall dwell securely, because there will be no one to terrify them.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Disturbance of Inner Peace and the Conflict of Virtues with Vices

But as long as the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, that king—who ought to preside over and command both spiritual and carnal desires—cannot find complete peace and lasting security. Hence that prince of peoples, namely the free consent of the mind, finds in his kingdom so many contradictions, rebellions, conflicts, and disputes: thoughts contradict thoughts, affections resist affections, contrary movements encounter contrary movements; nation rises against nation and kingdom against kingdom; good things often rise against evil things, are divided against themselves; and the Lord causes Egyptians to clash against Egyptians. [Col. 1128D]

Indeed—and more marvelous than all this—good things rise against good things: a man fights against his brother and a man against his friend; city against city and kingdom against kingdom; and each person devours the flesh of his own arm—[Col. 1129A] Ephraim Manasseh, and Manasseh Ephraim, and together they are against Judah.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Vice Resists Vice

Who does not know how grave and how prolonged a dispute often arises between avarice and gluttony—not over a talent, but over a single coin—when the one wishes it spent and the other commands it saved? Thus pride often opposes luxury, and each is fiercely hostile to the other; luxury is many times checked so that the exalted mind may have something of which to boast. How many things does stinginess prohibit which vain glory nevertheless commands and prevails upon us to do! And in all these cases the kingdom is divided against itself.

Yet who does not know how often it happens that, when pride confronts pride, so that one yields to the other, even the very fact that pride is defeated is proved to serve pride? Thus we often cast off the trappings of pride and swell all the more over humble clothing. Thus lofty honor is despised, so that through contempt for honor we may be exalted all the higher, the more secretly so. But when you see Egyptians rushing against Egyptians in this way, [Col. 1129B] do not wonder or be afraid; know rather that its desolation is near. For every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and house shall fall upon house.

Therefore, when you hear of battles, disturbances, and reports of wars, do not be alarmed. For he who came from heaven, mighty in hand, the strong and mighty king in battle, did not come to bring peace upon earth but a sword. [Col. 1129C] For he came to separate father against son and son against his father; and this rightly, because a good father often begets an evil son, and a good son very often has an evil father. When the mind is ashamed and humbled by shameful pleasure, and humility is born from such a parent, such offspring is rightly separated from such a father. Likewise, when chastity begets pride, such a parent rightly detests and hates its own offspring, divides itself against it, and in this manner a man often fights against his brother and a man against his friend; and “a man’s enemies are those of his own household.” [Col. 1129D]

## CHAPTER XIX. How Virtue Contradicts Virtue

But to crown this great and extraordinary wonder there is the further fact—which portends, I know not what, a great marvel—that contention also arises among disciples: good things contend against good things, and great contradiction and vehement dispute arise among them. Justice often says one thing and mercy another; what is said by one is contradicted by the other. Between fellow citizens of heaven of this kind there arises harsh contention. The same fault which justice commands to be punished, mercy commands to be forgiven. Justice often does not allow itself to be relaxed from its rigor, even a little; nor does mercy permit itself to depart even in the least from its gentleness.

Justice commands the whole penalty to be exacted; mercy strives for complete pardon. Each transgresses the boundary of its own possession [Col. 1130A] and endeavors to occupy the other’s estate; contrary to the ordinances of divine sanction and contrary to the rule of discretion, they do not permit the land to be divided between them by the line of allotment. In this way, then, good things are often divided against good things; some rise against others; the kingdom of Israel is split into two parts; they often stir up battles and disturbances among themselves; and never in this life, at whatever stage or advancement, is firm peace or complete rest found.

But whence, I ask, comes this manifold altercation and endless contention in the human heart, unless from the sickness of the head, the failure of native strength, and the loss of ancient power? To this day every head remains sick; and although human choice is truly free, it nevertheless remains weak and cannot be fully healed until this mortal puts on immortality and this corruptible puts on incorruption. [Col. 1130B] For how can our inner man fail to have a sick head, when of itself it can neither rise even a little nor sustain even a little, even once it has been lifted up by the hand of divine aid? It is never raised to good except by another’s hand, and without delay falls back upon itself—or even beneath itself—when the lifting hand is withdrawn.

## CHAPTER XX. On Grace and Nature

But, you ask, could man do any good of himself even before sin, while he was still in paradise? For what did he have that he had not received? [Col. 1130C] He certainly had nothing that he had not received from another, and he could do absolutely nothing except from and according to what he had received. But some things he could do by nature and others by grace. For the goods of nature are one thing, and the gifts of grace another. Yet it is clear that both the one and the other are from grace, since nature itself is certainly from grace. The first goods, then, are from prevenient grace; the second goods are from subsequent grace. Both, therefore, may rightly be called grace, prevenient and subsequent; but the former is the first, the latter the second.

Custom, however, assigns a common name especially to one thing, narrows its meaning to the designation of that one alone, and calls “grace,” according to customary usage, subsequent grace. For we call the first grace nature rather than grace. Therefore, when we say that man before sin could do some good of himself, we mean nothing other than that he could do so through natural good. Thus, when we deny that he can do any good of himself, we understand that he can now do no good from natural good alone. [Col. 1130D]

But shall we say that he could do no good through nature—that is, through the first grace—before nature was corrupted? If he could do some good, he received it from the very nature of his created condition; this is what he lost by sinning. Therefore he lost power, not freedom. For to be able to do good is truly to be able, just as not to be able to be compelled is truly to be free. If he could be compelled by another to good or evil, he would not be free at all; and if he could do good or avoid evil, he would be not only [Col. 1131A] free but also powerful.

But even if we deny that before sin he could do any good without grace added, we nevertheless cannot deny that by sinning he lost no small capacity for doing good. For what he could do through grace he truly could do; and what great things he could do through grace, that was a great capacity.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Integrity of Grace Before Sin

Consider, then, what kind of grace he received and how much he could do through it; then you will understand what power he lost. Certainly, beyond doubt and without any contradiction, he had sufficient grace before sin—not for doing every good thing, but for paying every debt and avoiding every evil. [Col. 1131B] How great, I ask, was this power toward good and against evil which he had through cooperating grace? Who can boast that he has recovered this integrity of capacity, or presume that he can recover it in this life? Who, I ask, can boast that he has either done everything that he ought or omitted everything that he was not permitted to do?

When, I ask, can a man pay every debt, who, according to Job’s judgment, cannot answer one thing out of a thousand? We also know that “we all offend in many things”; and “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” Therefore he can recover grace—yet freely given—and can grow daily in grace once recovered. Nevertheless, he cannot recover the integrity of the first capacity. And even if he can recover greater [Col. 1131C] grace in some respect, he cannot possess it in its fullness in this life.

A child once maimed may have a larger body, but can never have an entirely whole one. He would truly possess grace whole if it sufficed him for paying every debt and avoiding every unlawful thing. But, according to Solomon’s teaching, “there is no righteous man on earth who does not sin” (Eccl. 7). Therefore he cannot recover integral grace or progress, after the evil of his corruption, to the integrity of his first capacity, because the head is sick and its weakness admits of no complete cure.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Stability of Grace Before Sin
[Col. 1131D] To this must be added that the grace which man once received before sin could not justly have been withdrawn. Although he had received it apart from merit, he nevertheless ought not to have lost it without fault. Now, however, it can justly be withdrawn at every hour, because a human being can never be found without fault. And just as he cannot of himself recover it once it has been lost, so too he cannot preserve it when gratuitously recovered except under another’s protection. See, then, how great is the difference between the first state and the second: that, namely, which existed before sin, and this which exists after humanity’s fall. At first he had grace whole and stable; now, however, neither whole nor stable. But in the life to come—after death has been swallowed up in victory—he will have it not only stable [Col. 1132A] but also immovable. For before sin he had stable grace, because he was always able to preserve it once received. But that he did not have it immovably is evident from the fact that he afterwards lost it. Yet then he will possess it immovably, when he will no longer be able to lose it. But now, as long as we live mortally in the body of sin, we can possess it not merely immovably, but not even stably. Often, while we are negligent and sluggish, it is freely offered to us; and often, despite many great efforts of ours, it is suddenly and unexpectedly withdrawn.

Therefore, so long as we cannot restore lost grace to its former wholeness or stability, we do not restore the strength of the mind to the firmness of its first vigor, do not recover in its entirety the power for good which was received in the first possibility, and necessarily bear, in whatever progress [Col. 1132B] of virtues we make, much of the sickness of the head. Thus weakness remains with freedom, and freedom with weakness, so that neither prejudices the other: neither weakness freedom nor freedom weakness. For weakness does not diminish freedom, nor does freedom remove weakness. Therefore, when you read or hear that free choice is captive, understand nothing other than that it is weak and deprived of the power of its native possibility. This is what he wished to remind us of who signified it by “a sick head.” Otherwise, those who call the human will both free and captive contradict themselves with contrary assertions and refute themselves. But perhaps those who call it captive mean this only in part: that it is free in part and captive in part. But who does not know that, if I had a thousand masters and, though freed by all the rest, were still oppressed by one alone—since I would still have a master—I certainly could not rightly be called free? It is therefore clear that the human will cannot be called free if it has lost freedom even in part.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Three Degrees of Freedom, and How Man Possesses the Highest Freedom

But if we attend carefully, I think we shall find that man is not merely not without freedom, but possesses great—indeed, the highest—freedom. The first degree of freedom is to be subject to no compulsion. The second is to be bound to submit to no one. [Col. 1132D] The third—and itself the highest—is to be unable to submit to anyone whatsoever. How, then, is man’s will not truly—indeed, supremely—free, since no force and no power can deprive it of its freedom? For no creature can do this, nor would it be fitting for the Creator to do it. But how can even the Creator do this, since He can do nothing unfitting? Therefore, if no violence can deprive the will of its freedom, it plainly possesses the highest freedom.

Nevertheless, as was shown above, will opposes will, will resists will, and one is assailed by another; now this will, now that, is taken captive. But in the contest of this conflict, just as there is a will that attacks and a will that is attacked, so there is a will that [Col. 1133A] conquers and a will that is conquered. Yet in all these things freedom remains unimpaired, because will always triumphs. This freedom of choice is neither greater in the good nor less in the wicked; it is neither diminished by sin nor increased by merit. For that which holds the highest degree in all persons can neither increase nor decrease.

But just as the freedom of the will, which cannot be compelled by another, is admirable, so its weakness in growing sluggish toward every good within itself is altogether pitiable. Therefore, because among the natural goods in that inner man nothing is found more worthy or more exalted than this freedom, it is rightly signified by the head. And because every human being lives and dies with the weakness assigned to him, it is aptly compared to sickness.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Ignorance of Good and Evil

[Col. 1133B]

“Every head,” he says, “is sick, and every heart sorrowful.” And rightly so: as long as every head is sick, every heart also grieves. For pain in the head is a sufficient cause of pain. Therefore, if we have a heart, if we are not wholly senseless, unless we are utterly deprived of counsel, we neither can nor ought to conceal so great an evil. For if, as has been said, counsel is rightly understood by “heart,” one who has such a heart cannot be without sorrow, because he cannot endure without grief the evil which he sees in himself. Indeed, the better he recognizes it and the more wisely he acts, the more abundantly he laments. For he who adds knowledge adds sorrow.

Our sorrow ought both to press us more sharply within [Col. 1133C] and to appear outwardly: inwardly for remedy, outwardly for example. For, as has already been said, grief is pain raging more sharply within and breaking out through tears without. Therefore, if we are not altogether “a deceived dove, without heart,” if we do not exist without counsel and prudence, let us demonstrate in deed how truly we grieve in heart, and let what we suffer inwardly appear outwardly.

But, to state what I think of this, I judge that in these words the cause is put for the effect. For in the saying, “every heart grieves,” the effect, as I suppose, silently indicates its cause. But when we find the cause put for the effect, we ought, in exposition or definition, to inquire rather what proceeds from it than what the thing itself is which is set forth. According to this consideration, then, what else is grief but an outpouring of tears and a dulling of sight? For continual shedding of tears damages the sharpness of the eyes and makes them grow dim more quickly. Thus it is rightly said that every heart grieves, because it has the sharpness of reason for every counsel. Hence comes that command—or instruction—of the Wise Man: “Do not lean upon your own prudence” [Col. 1133D] (Prov. 3). For a person does not know what is beneficial for him in his life, during the numbered days of his pilgrimage and the time which passes like a shadow. Unless that inner eye were dim, he would undoubtedly err far less often in judgments of truth. Whence, I ask, come counsels so often opposed and opinions so diverse—not from different hearts, I say, but from one and the same heart, and almost at the same time? Whence, I ask, except from the heart’s dimness and truth’s uncertainty?

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Twofold Error of Judgment

We sin in two ways when examining our judgment, while we still frequently make our way beneath the cloud of such great uncertainty. For we err sometimes in discerning quality and sometimes in assessing quantity. Whoever calls good evil, or evil good, errs as to the quality of things; and whoever says that what is greater is lesser, and what is lesser greater, sins as to quantity. Certainly the quality of deeds had deceived those whom the Prophet rebuked when he said: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter [Col. 1134B] sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. 5).

The error rebuked through the Prophet in the words, “The sons of men are deceitful in the scales, that they may together deceive by vanity itself” (Ps. 61), is found to concern the assessment of quantity. Something is indeed weighed on a scale so that its quantity may not be unknown. Thus we ascertain the weight of gold and silver in order to assess their price correctly. But no one would be deceitful on the scales if no one deceived another, and if no one had been deceived by another. Hence the saying of the Wise Man: “A deceitful scale and a deceitful weight, both are an abomination to God” (Prov. 20). Conversely, the Law commands: “Let the measure be just and the sextary fair” (Lev. 19).

Hence it is that when the children of Israel receive the promised inheritance among themselves, they divide it with the measuring-line [Col. 1134C] of distribution, so that each virtue in its action may maintain the measure of just equity and not overstep the limits of right discernment. Who can find me a person who never errs in estimating quality or quantity, who is never ensnared by “the thing that walks in darkness”?  The best trader is one who can never be deceived in evaluating the quality or quantity of things, and never wishes to deceive. But when can this be achieved by a person wrapped in darkness and dwelling in the region of the shadow of death? It is indeed impossible for every person while darkness lies upon the face of the abyss, until he who said that light should shine out of darkness, sending forth his light and his truth, begins to divide light from darkness, [Col. 1134D] and there comes to be evening and morning.

For when understanding of truth is given and received, a person immediately begins to distinguish light from darkness: first, goods from evils and evils from goods; afterwards, better goods from goods and worse evils from evils; and finally, the best from the better and the worst from the worse. In this manner, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “the path of the righteous is as a growing light, and increases unto the perfect day” (Prov. 4). And there is fulfilled what is said: “He shall bring forth thy justice as light, and thy judgment as the noonday” (Ps. 36). The received light gradually advances and grows unto the perfect day, when received understanding of truth gradually improves and at last reaches full discernment.

“One,” says the Apostle, “judges between day and day, and another judges every day” [Col. 1135A] (Rom. 14). What a gift of God, do you think, is it to grant judgment to him who is the Son of Man? The first stage is that a person know how to judge between day and night; the final—and this itself the highest—is that he know how to judge every day. Therefore we must ascend by certain stages of knowledge if we wish to reach from this lowest point to that highest summit of ascent.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Five Degrees of Discernment

The first, then, as we have already said, is to judge between day and night; the second, between night and night; the third, between day and day; the fourth is to judge every night; the fifth, to judge [Col. 1135B] every day. We judge between day and night when we separate goods from evils. He judges between night and night who knows how to distinguish worse evils from evil and the worst from the worse. Likewise, to judge between day and day is to choose better goods from goods and the best from the better. He judges every night who weighs every vice by due examination. Likewise, to judge every day is to assess every virtue according to its proper worth.

Whoever has deserved to receive from the Lord’s generosity these five talents of true discernment and useful knowledge should endeavor to work with them and gain five more, so that the image of truth impressed upon knowledge by inspiring grace may, through human effort and cooperating grace, also be impressed upon affection. Otherwise, it is better not to have known the rule of truth than to scorn it once known. Therefore we make worthy profit from the talents received, and acquire, as it were, five more from five, if we endeavor to shape the quality of our affection according to the rule of discernment we have learned. [Col. 1135C] Let us therefore strive to love what we have learned deserves love, and not at all love what is not worthy of our love.

Yet it ought not to suffice us to have ascended this first degree of virtue unless we also ascend the second, and from the second the third. Therefore let us pursue with greater hatred those things that are worse among evils, and embrace with closer love those things that are better among goods; and let us rejoice that by means of the second degree we have ascended to the third degree of virtue. But we can undoubtedly love less what is lesser and love more what is better, and yet fail to preserve a fitting measure in either love. Likewise, in rejecting contraries it often happens that we sin through a similar ignorance. Let us therefore endeavor to ascend through the fourth degree to the fifth, so that in every evil or good we may know how to preserve the fitting measure of hatred or love.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That the Grace of Discernment Is Sometimes Given and Sometimes Withdrawn

Perhaps you wonder how the preceding prophetic saying accords with this apostolic assertion. For how can it truly be said that every heart grieves and grows dim through grief, if one is truly found who [Col. 1136A] can judge every day? Or perhaps, because it was not said, “Every heart grieves at every time,” although it was said, “Every heart grieves,” both statements can rightly be understood. For there is a time for weeping and a time for laughing. Indeed, weeping shall linger until evening, and joy until morning. Evening is a time of sadness; morning a time of joy. The former is a time for weeping; the latter, a time for laughing. A time of dimness is a time of grief; a time of light is a time of exultation. He knew this who said: “What joy can there be for me, who sit in darkness and do not see the light of heaven?” (Tob. 5).

Why then does every heart grieve, except because no heart has an everlasting day here, since it cannot always possess the light of heaven present? For “the sun rises and sets, and returns to its place,” because understanding of truth is sometimes given and sometimes withdrawn; and after it is withdrawn, the same grace which existed before is recovered once again. What wonder, then, if every heart grieves so long as it endures the necessary darkness of these alternating changes? As long as we live on earth, as long as we are upon earth, we necessarily endure these changes of times. In heaven, day without night; in hell, night without day; on earth, neither night without day nor day without night. Thus in heaven there is joy without disturbance; in hell, pain without consolation; on earth, neither pain without hope nor joy without fear. In the highest place is perpetual laughter; in the lowest, perpetual weeping; in the middle, a time for laughing and a time for weeping. For laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and grief occupies the end of joy [Col. 1136C]. Therefore every heart must suffer and mourn until it fully escapes its darkness, until it possesses the throne of glory and its throne becomes like the days of heaven. What wonder, then, if even one who can judge every day is said to mourn, because he cannot always possess the day?

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Two Degrees of Deliberation

But if we consider more carefully what judgment is and what counsel is, we shall find that counsel often wavers even where judgment stands firm, and that where counsel grows dim, judgment often sees clearly. As we said above, we understand counsel by “heart.” Consider, then, whether counsel may grow dim even where judgment is certain, so that it may rightly be said that every heart grieves, although one is found who judges every day.

It is one thing to examine what is good or evil in itself, and another to deliberate what is or is not expedient for each person. The former belongs to judgment, the latter to counsel. For just as not all persons can do all things, so neither are all things expedient for everyone. Often what is in itself a greater good is less expedient for some; and what is in itself lesser is nevertheless more expedient for others. For it often happens that what is an accumulation of condemnation for one person is an occasion of salvation for another, and what increases one person’s crown is another’s cause of ruin. How many do we see falling grievously from a height, who were accustomed—or able—to stand firmly at a lower rank. How many [Col. 1137A] do we see setting firm steps in the ascent of virtues and the advancement of religious life, and hastening greatly, who had moved sluggishly and often fallen on the level ground of secular life.

Therefore a person does not know what is beneficial to him in his life, during the numbered days of his pilgrimage and the time that passes like a shadow. This, indeed, is why every heart grieves: why the eye of counsel grows dim even in one who judges every day. Do you wish finally to know more plainly how much judgment can do which counsel nevertheless cannot do? How many things, I ask, do we find concerning which we dare to affirm without doubt that they are good; and likewise how innumerable are the things concerning which we do not doubt at all that they are truly evil. Find me one person who can show me one thing which cannot become the cause of some evil. What, I ask, is so good that it cannot become an occasion of falling? Or what is so evil that it cannot become a warning for caution? Behold how every heart wavers in every counsel; behold how every counsel grows dim in every act of foresight, so that it is rightly said that every heart grieves, its grief indicating the dimness it endures.

You see, certainly, that it is easier to judge what is permitted and what is not permitted than to choose what is expedient. The former belongs to discernment, the latter to deliberation; the former to judgment, the latter to counsel. Thus the former knowledge is one thing, and the latter knowledge quite another. The talents of the first knowledge are one thing, those of the second another; both are rare and both precious. Yet the second is much rarer than the first. [Col. 1137C] But though rare, it is not nonexistent. For who can deny that, through divine inspiration, many people know not only how to choose useful things but, since they cannot suffice for everything, also how to distinguish the more useful from useful things and shrewdly perceive what is more expedient, less expedient, and not at all expedient?

Know, therefore, that you have received from the Lord’s entrustment two exceedingly precious talents when you begin rightly to distinguish between useful and useless things, and likewise among useful things which are more useful than others. When, then, you have received from the Lord’s bounty these talents of twofold deliberation, endeavor to work with them and gain from them, so that you may express outwardly in deed what has been impressed inwardly upon knowledge, and, gaining two from two, may carry back doubled talents as profit for the Lord [Col. 1137D].

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Rule of Discernment and Deliberation, and Which Talents Must Be Increased, and How

It must therefore be observed that those former five talents are to be enlarged and multiplied in affection, whereas these are to be enlarged in action. For what has there once been impressed upon diligent knowledge through the discernment of judgment must afterwards also be impressed upon affection; but here what has been prefigured in knowledge through the deliberation of counsel must be conformed in deed to the same rule of prudence. According to the former rule of prudence, we ought to love more greatly the things that are greater goods, though not necessarily practise them more, since they are often impossible or less useful. But, as we are taught by this second rule of prudence, the things to be practised more are those that are more expedient, although the better things are often those which cannot be practised or are least expedient [Col. 1138A]. Thus let us strive to love the better things more, while knowing, when expediency requires it, to practise better things less; and let us practise more abundantly those things which are more expedient, though less good, so that we may love more those better things which are practised less. In this manner, then, from one and the same Lord some receive five talents in discernment of judgment, while others receive two in deliberation of counsel.

## CHAPTER XXX. Why There Are Not Five Degrees of Deliberation as There Are of Discernment

But perhaps you wonder why, here in the deliberation of counsel, five talents have not been assigned as they were above in the discernment of judgment, although they could be assigned here as above. But inquire more carefully, and concerning the remaining three you will find without delay that to seek one of them would be useless, to possess another impossible, and to seek the third as useless as it would be impossible to possess it.

For among things which are certainly useless, what advantage is there in seeking and investigating which of them are more trifling, since it is clear that all must be removed from our pursuits? Yet through discernment of judgment we inquire among evils which are worse than others, so that we may know which ought to be punished less and which more, lest, if we strike them here with less than due severity, they be reserved for punishment on the last day. But I think no one can comprehend what benefit each individual expedient thing confers, or how much benefit it confers [Col. 1138C]; nor do I believe that anyone has received this talent of knowledge in this life, although many are clearly able through the Lord’s inspiration to recognize useless things and choose more useful ones. And among things which are useless and not at all expedient, to seek out and assign the particular character of each would, as is evident from the two preceding cases, be as useless as it is impossible.

Therefore, when we receive such talents from the Lord’s bounty, we must work with them all the more eagerly in order to return them with profit, because it is clear that we possess them by another’s gift. Let no one therefore attribute it to himself when he judges rightly or deliberates upon useful things.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That We Do Not Always Have Illuminating Grace Present, and Never Have It Sufficiently

[Col. 1138D]

Even one who has already deserved to receive talents of this kind should not be so secure as though he could no longer be deceived. For just as only the person whom divine grace inspires and whose inspiration it illumines discerns wisely and takes prudent counsel for himself, so he can usefully do either only when he has inspiring grace present. But who is there that always has, or can have, grace present in this life? “You visit him in the morning,” says Job, “and suddenly test him” (Job 7). But if that eminent prophet had always had present the light of divine revelation, he certainly would not have cried out to the Lord: “Enlighten my eyes” (Ps. 11); and: “Send forth your light and your truth” [Col. 1139A] (Ps. 42).

Therefore the divine ray of inward inspiration is sometimes poured in and sometimes withdrawn. “He made darkness, and night came to be; in it all the beasts of the forest shall pass through.” But again, at the Lord’s command, the sun rose, and they gathered together and were laid down in their dens. Thus, as the sun sets and rises again, evening and morning come to be, so that there is a time for weeping and a time for laughing, because weeping shall linger until evening and joy until morning. What wonder, then, if every heart grieves, since it cannot always have divine light present, without which it sees nothing clearly and discerns nothing rightly?

I venture to say something further, which, I think, no one would dare deny: even if a person had grace present, he would still not altogether escape the causes of grief. For in this life a human being never has grace sufficient even in this respect, although he sometimes has grace present. What we said above about freedom of choice, we affirm likewise about discernment of judgment. For just as in this life we never have grace sufficient for doing good, so here we can never have grace sufficient for discerning truth. Consider now, I beg you, how great is the multitude of innumerable goods, from the highest creature to the lowest. Find me one person among them all who fully comprehends even one of these goods, concerning which he dares securely to say and truthfully affirm: “This is worth precisely so much, neither more nor less; and it ought to be loved precisely so much, neither more nor less” [Col. 1139C]. Even the one said to judge every day cannot presume this. You ought therefore rightly to wonder how he can judge every day when he cannot fully comprehend even one.

See how great is the dimness of uncertainty which the human heart endures, and must endure while life is lived here, so that it is deservedly said that every heart grieves. It grieves on account of the mind’s dimness, and grows dim because of the mind’s grief. The more it grieves, the duller it becomes; and the duller it becomes, the more violently it grieves, because it is dulled by grief and renewed for grief by dullness. Above we learned, through the sickness of the head, of the weakness of free choice; here we have now learned, through the grief of the heart, of the uncertainty of counsel. It remains to hear and understand, through the weakness of the body, the restlessness of desire [Col. 1139D].

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Desire for Evil

“From the sole,” he says, “of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in him.” By the foot, as has been said, we understand carnal desire; by the head, free choice. The sole is the lowest part of the foot, and the crown the highest part of the head. But what lies lower than what is under necessity, and what rises higher than what is within one’s power? Thus the sole of the foot is the necessity of the lowest desire, and the crown of the head is the power of free choice. The sole of the foot is necessary concupiscence; [Col. 1140A] the crown of the head is voluntary power. To the foot belongs the necessity of desiring; to the crown, the ability to act. The lowest part of the foot is the necessity of desiring evil; the highest part of the head, the ability to do good. Here by “good” I mean what is advantageous, not what is meritorious. Merit belongs to health, not to weakness; and so it should not be spoken of in connection with such a crown. “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in him”—unless perhaps someone claims that “to” is exclusive here rather than inclusive, exempting the crown alone from the condition of the remaining members. But would that man possessed true good in his power as truly as he possesses true evil under necessity.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That Everything in Man Is Subject to Weakness

[Col. 1140B]

There is a certain good which pertains to merit; there is a certain good which pertains to guilt; and there is a certain good which pertains neither to merit nor to guilt. But that which pertains to guilt is more correctly called evil than good, although those who willingly commit evil call and love it as though it were good. Good which pertains neither to merit nor to guilt we call more suitably *commodum*, “advantage” or “expediency.” Man has many such things, not merely in freedom but often also in his power. Likewise, of those things which pertain to guilt, he often has many not merely in his will but under necessity. But of those things which pertain to merit, he has nothing in free choice except through divine assistance.

Of the difficulty of what pertains to merit it is said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Of the ability concerning what pertains neither to merit nor to guilt it is said: “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give a good spirit to those who ask him?” [Col. 1140C] (Matt. 7). Of the necessity of what pertains to guilt we read: “For the evil which I do not will, that I do” (Rom. 7).

Thus, among these three kinds of things which we have distinguished, you may have some in your power, some in freedom, some in your will, and some under necessity. That is in one’s power which can be done or omitted at the will’s choice. We have that in freedom to which we cannot be compelled by another’s violence. Something is in the will when you wish it to be done, even if you cannot bring it about; but you have something under necessity when you are unable to resist it even though you wish to do so.

We might further compare these four degrees of distinction with one another and combine them in turn, distinguish the body of our inner man into many members, and arrange the course of our consideration upward from the sole of the foot or downward from the crown of the head. But, lest we linger over these matters too long, let us consider what is said here of such a body and must not be passed over: “From the sole,” he says, “of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in him” (Isa. 1). If only that which avails for merit pertains to health, everything belonging to man is subject to weakness: for that which is in his power does not avail for merit; that which is under necessity is not free from fault; and both that which is in the will and that which is in freedom are subject to disadvantage [Col. 1141A]. Therefore, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in him.

For how can that pertain to sound health which does not avail for merit, which counts for nothing in the judgment of recompense, and cannot assist toward true good—indeed, rather makes one liable to true evil and renders one guilty? From the sole, therefore, to the crown there is no health in him. Weakness occupies the whole from the head to the crown, because power neither expels necessity nor fulfils the will, nor unfolds freedom, but entangles it still more. For the more things it can do, the more things there are for which it must render an account. Thus weakness has occupied the whole, and from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no health in him.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How Affection Is Disordered or Immoderate

[Col. 1141B]

At last, look to the analogy, you who wish to know spiritual weakness more fully. You hear the members of the outer man named so that from what is known you may learn what you do not know about the condition of the inner man. Consider, therefore, what the weakness of the outer man is, or whence it comes, and you will recognize what you ought to think about spiritual weakness. As we have already said above, bodily health is the wholeness of the natural constitution and the proportionate balance of all humors. Weakness is the deprivation of health and the corruption of wholeness.

There are, then, four humors from which every body is formed, enlivened, regulated, nourished, and preserved. All of these combine in every body under one fixed law, though in differing proportions among differing persons, and produce different constitutions in different persons. A fitting order and fitting measure, according to the manner of nature, must therefore exist in each, so that, as has been said, there may be a proportionate balance in them. But so long as each occupies its proper place and maintains the measure suitable to it, the body persists in health.

What the four humors are in the body, the four principal affections are in the heart; and what sense is in the flesh, intellect is in the mind. Sight, too, has the heart’s sense, as [the text appears to say] bodily sense; hence we customarily speak of a judgment (*sententia*) from the heart—or from the heart’s sense—not from bodily sense [Col. 1141D]. Love and hatred, joy and sorrow, then, are the four principal affections from which all other desires, volitions, wishes, and affections derive their origin. See, then, how many things we love or hate which we ought not to love or hate at all, or ought to love or hate more moderately; and likewise how many things there are on account of which we rejoice or grieve in a disordered or immoderate manner.

And just as humors in the body produce various illnesses according as they disturb fitting order and measure, so affections do in the heart. Above we have seen how dull the heart’s understanding is. Let us now see how weak the heart’s affection is. Show me one thing toward which you restrain your affection according to so certain and lawful a measure that you ought in no respect to extend it otherwise, more, or less. But how can the mind restrain its affection to the perfect law of equity in even one matter so long as the intellect cannot fully comprehend any thing, or assign the measure of its worth with perfect determination? For how can what cannot be known be done? If the definite measure of full and perfect love, or of any other affection, is not known, how can a measure which cannot be known be preserved?

Therefore, if the affection of the mind is disordered in many matters and in none at all moderated to the supreme measure of equity, you have no reason to wonder or doubt when you read: “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in him” [Col. 1142B]. At every hour—indeed, at almost every moment—we are deceived in our estimation; and, having broken the reins of equity, we are let loose toward our desires. Nowhere is measure, nowhere is a fixed standard preserved, while the mind is always driven hither and thither like a whirlwind by the impulse of the flesh. Therefore, from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in him.

Blessed is the time and eagerly awaited the hour when no thought any longer errs in its examination and no affection runs unrestrained in its desire. Meanwhile, we can attain no such wholeness of knowledge and perfection of virtue by any thought, nor preserve it through any effort of the mind.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How Man Is Brought to the Lawful Measure of Wholeness

[Col. 1142C]

This is that wholeness of the promised denarius, and the integrity of true and supreme perfection, which is promised to those laboring in the Lord’s vineyard, but is bestowed only at the end of the day, after the work has been completed. The Lord’s vineyard is the human conscience. This is the chosen vineyard of the Lord, in which He planted every true seed. The Lord goes out for the cultivation of this vineyard when He makes His will known through inward inspiration; the Lord’s going out, therefore, is His manifestation. A repeated going out is an increase of knowledge. A manifold going out is a manifold manifestation. [Col. 1142D] The diversity of hours signifies the various degrees of progress. Therefore the Lord goes out according to the sequence and succession of the hours, because divine knowledge increases according to one’s advance in perfection and growth in virtues. The vineyard’s cultivators are thoughts and affections. Such cultivators ought to labor in cultivating the vineyard, because both must toil in cleansing the conscience. The former must be exercised in the investigation of truth; the latter in the exercise of virtue. It belongs to the former to dig deeply and penetrate hidden things; it belongs to the latter to cut away the superfluities of the branches and prune what is useless in conduct. Their labor is the correction of errors; the labor of the latter is the chastisement of vices.

Those who labor in the vineyard and toil in such cultivation are introduced in the morning, at the third, [Col. 1143A] sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours. At first light begins to appear; by the third hour the day usually begins to grow warm; by the sixth it burns more fiercely; by the ninth the sun is known to decline toward the west and the heat to moderate; but by the eleventh both heat and light gradually begin to fail. What, then, is the rising of light but the illumination of truth? And what is the beginning of heat but the acceptance of goodness? The burning of heat is the fervor of love. The moderation of heat is abhorrence of vanity. And what else is the withdrawal of heat and light but the restraint of desire, or even the dulling of carnal prudence?
