Thus the morning produces discernment of good and evil; the third hour, an appetite for the true good; midday, desire for the [Col. 1143B] highest good; the ninth hour, disgust with the false good; and the eleventh, hatred—or even forgetfulness—of the true evil. Thus in the morning the understanding is enlightened; at the third hour consent is corrected; at the sixth the affection is enkindled; at the ninth bodily sense is restrained or even dulled; at the eleventh carnal appetite is cooled.

For unless bodily sense is restrained from its wandering, the unrest of carnal appetite is not extinguished. But when bodily sense is manfully endowed with the strength of abstinence and forcibly restrained by the rigor of discipline, it begins to take less and less pleasure in customary delights and to become more and more dulled toward its former pleasures. Slowness of appetite necessarily follows dullness of the senses. Therefore, insofar as appetite or the other [Col. 1143C] senses of a person are restrained to the measure of equity, the more quickly the denarius of recompense and the form of perfection are received, and the nearer one approaches to the wholeness of integrity. For all receiving the denarius at the end means nothing other than finally possessing the form of perfection in all our faculties.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. By what stages we are brought to the fullness of integrity

First of all, then, one must seek counsel; having found it, correct the will; and thus, through the exercise of virtues, kindle the mind toward desire for heavenly things. But after desire for eternal things, we must also restrain our senses even from lawful things, so that we may moderate—or, insofar as possible, wholly extinguish—the appetite for unlawful things. [Col. 1143D] Who can doubt that all these cooperate in cultivating the spiritual vineyard: rightness of counsels, correction of wills, the ardor of heavenly desires, restraint of the senses, and moderation of appetites?

It should further be noted concerning the cultivators of this Lord’s vineyard that the later each arrives, the less he labors. For as the day of our progress grows longer, the exercise of virtues surely becomes ever sweeter; and as the appetite of desires is further moderated, the burden and heat of the day are surely felt less and less. For in proportion as love increases, labor decreases. Through love, [Col. 1144A] indeed, the yoke becomes sweet and the burden light which before seemed intolerable. This also must be known: the longer we extend the day of our progress, and the nearer we approach its end, the purer and more perfect are our vows or desires. Hence those who arrive later receive the denarius first, because in those who are progressing, later attainments always draw nearer to perfect integrity.

The order of remuneration begins with the last, because first the tinder of sin, which chiefly rules appetite, is removed; appetite is restrained to the lawful mode and measure of equity and endowed with the denarius of integrity; and only afterward is the human being glorified in the remaining faculties. For just as the will is never amended except through good counsel, and the senses or appetite are never restrained and corrected except after the will has been corrected, so conversely it is undoubtedly necessary that the vice of appetites or senses be destroyed before [Col. 1144B] the good will is formed into true peace. And so long as the will finds something for which it ought to blush, thought always has something which it ought to accuse.

All the vineyard’s cultivators who persevere in cultivating it receive the denarius at evening. What is evening but the end of the day, the limit of labor, the hour of rest, the time of recompense? Therefore the denarius is received by all at evening, because, after labor has been completed and at the time of recompense, every human faculty is raised, as stated, to the integrity of perfection. One and the same time, then, is the end of labor and the beginning of rest, the completion of work and the hour of recompense. For the labor of cultivation never ends, and the unrest of conscience is never quieted, unless the soul’s progress is brought to the limit of perfection.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That the same form of perfection will exist in thought and affection

But what are we to say of this, that one and the same measure of recompense is bestowed on all? Nothing is added to the first; nothing is taken from the last. Who does not know that right counsels in cultivating the vineyard precede both right desires and right works? For what is desired or done without counsel contributes not to the cultivation of the vineyard but to its injury. The labor of thoughts in the vineyard is therefore prior [Col. 1144D] to that of affections. Yet as long as we are in this life, as long as we labor in the vineyard, we are surely able to attain more of the fullness of perfection in thought than we can meanwhile imprint upon full affection or accomplish in deed. For who can do all that he knows he ought, or is fitting, to do?

But when the time of recompense arrives, when the denarius—the grace of perfection—has been rendered as the wage to the Lord’s workers, there will be nothing greater in counsel than in desire, nothing less in affection than in thought. Beyond doubt, after receiving recompense, whatever each person recognizes that he ought or is fitting to do, he will wholly be able to do and wholly fulfill. Therefore the same [Col. 1145A] form of perfection which will be in knowledge will be precisely and entirely the same in love. Thus the last receive the same denarius which the first deserve to receive.

But who is that laborer who is introduced first but rewarded last, to whom it is also said in rebuke: “Take what is yours and go. Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. 20.) Who would pant with such difficulty for purity of heart? Who would expend so much labor in this cultivation, unless his conscience reproached him? The first laborer in the vineyard, then, is thought, the accuser of conscience. The eye of this laborer is the more evil and troublesome to us the more kind and generous the Lord has been toward us. For the greater [Col. 1145B] the grace we receive from the Lord, the more sharply we are pressed by the goad of a reproaching conscience whenever we sin. So long as it can find anything imperfect in us, its regard confounds, disturbs, and tortures us.

The labor of this worker, therefore, never ends until every imperfection has been removed and the human being has been refashioned unto the fullness of integrity, [Col. 1146A] and endowed with the denarius of perfection. But after recompense has been completed, it will take what is its own and go away, because, finding nothing which it may justly reproach, the goad of rebuke will rest and vanish. O what perfection of knowledge there will then be! O what completion of virtue! There no judgment is deceived, even in the least degree; no affection anywhere runs unrestrained. But what we then hope concerning every affection and in every respect, we now dare presume concerning none, or in any matter whatsoever. See, then, how great our power will be there; see how great our deficiency is here. O how great the firmness of the human being will then be; how great, meanwhile, is his weakness! For “from the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him.” Indeed, the supreme measure of equity, which then one will be able to [Col. 1146B] know and keep in every matter, no one here confidently claims to know or be able to keep in any matter, except presumptuously. You see clearly, I think, how widely this corruption of human weakness ranges, how completely it rules every affection in all things, so that it is rightly said of it: “From the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in him.”

## SECOND TREATISE. Thus far concerning the threefold vice; now concerning the threefold sin

[Col. 1145]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1145C]

Let us now consider what follows: “A wound, and a bruise, and a swelling sore: it has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil” (Isa. 1). He has already described a threefold evil above; behold, he now adds three others: a wound, namely, a bruise, and a swelling sore. The first three that he set forth are, as it were, generated from within; but the three he now adds are, as it were, inflicted from without. Weakness of the head, sorrow of the heart, and pain of the infirm body arise, as it were, from within, through a defect of nature. A wound, a bruise, and a swelling sore, as it were, come from without through a supervening occasion.

By weakness of the head, as was said, we understand the weakness of free will toward good; by infirmity of the body, the unrest of [Col. 1145D] desire toward evil; by sorrow of the heart, the darkness and uncertainty of judgment in discerning both. Thus in weakness is understood inability for good; in the distress of infirmity, desire for evil; in the cloudiness of sorrow, ignorance of good and evil. Who does not see that these three evils are so inbred that, however much one takes precautions and however cautiously one acts, a person cannot be free of these evils which arise inwardly from a defect of nature? For who is there who does not sometimes grow sluggish in doing good, even against his will? Who does not sometimes fall, unwillingly, into the darkness of ignorance? Who so entirely escapes the snares of desire that he does not sometimes fall into them, even while carefully fleeing and stoutly resisting them? But those things which we admit by consent, we endure, as it were, through our own negligence or lack of care.

These things, then, which are admitted by consent, are inflicted upon the nature of the soul as certain wounds. For those things which we endure even unwillingly, and against which no prudence or effort can resist, are, as stated, innate to nature rather than externally inflicted. Hear, then, how these three evils—which are, as it were, inflicted on a human being from without—are described: “A wound, and a bruise, and a swelling sore: it has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.” Let us first consider what distinction he intended between a sore (*plaga*) and a wound (*vulnus*). Perhaps, however, the thing we seek is indicated by the fact that when *plaga* is used, “swelling” is added, so that *plaga* is understood as a sore which swells, and *vulnus* as a wound wholly without swelling. A wound, then, is where the limb is injured inwardly only to the extent that it is opened outwardly. A bruise is where it is damaged inwardly by a blow, yet is not opened outwardly after the manner of a wound. But a swelling sore is where it is both more extensively crushed inwardly and yet, in part, opened outwardly after the manner of a wound. Each appears to have its own distinction; yet they agree in this, that they are inflicted outwardly by a supervening blow, just as the first three arise inwardly from inward corruption.

Therefore we rightly refer the three things placed first to all things generally, and these three vices now added to sins alone, just as we refer the three things placed last [Col. 1147A] to the remedies of both. By weakness of the head, sorrow of the heart, and infirmity of the body, then, let us understand threefold vice; by wound, bruise, and swelling sore, threefold sin; by bandage, medicine, and oil, threefold remedy.

## CHAPTER II. What vice is, and what sin is

Certainly, just as disease is one thing and a wound another, so beyond doubt vice is one thing and sin another. As we see in the body, so we must understand concerning the heart: inward corruption issuing from concealment is one thing, and manifest injury inflicted outwardly another. Thus it is one thing when evil is perceived in thought alone, even from its beginning, [Col. 1147B] and another when it is committed by voluntary assent following deliberation. The former is born, as it were, from within; the latter is inflicted, as it were, from without. Vice, therefore, is the very infirmity of natural corruption; sin is the wrongful assent to tempting infirmity. Vice is a kind of passion or condition of nature; sin is a voluntary action of deliberate agency. Vice is the very appetite for evil, which usually precedes or provokes consent; sin is the consent to evil itself, which often follows or accompanies appetite.

Certainly it is one thing to feel a wrongful movement in the heart, and another to consent to a wrongful movement. That we feel the wrongful movement is vice; that we consent to it is sin. Vice, therefore, exists in perception and affection; sin, however, only in consent or in effect. When what is true seems false to us and what is false seems true, this is vice in perception. When what is just seems bitter to us and what is unjust seems pleasant, this is vice in affection. But when we give credence to a false opinion, the vice of our perception already passes into sin. Likewise, when we acquiesce in wrongful delight, the vice of our affection likewise passes into guilt. In this way vices pass into sins and make the one who consents guilty.

Vice of the faculties, therefore, becomes the source of errors; vice of the affections, the root of iniquities. Here by “faculty” (*sensus*) we do not mean that of the body but of the heart, whence we do not hesitate to call it judgment (*sententia*). [Col. 1147D] Thus dull faculty and disordered affection are the source of all evils, as we have said. In this way vice rules the faculty and affection, and when it draws forth consent or even passes into effect, it becomes the cause of sin. Consent, however, is not always followed by effect; but when prevented by necessity, the guilt of sin is completed by consent alone.

We have now distinguished how vice and sin differ from one another, according to which mode of distinction we have shown a threefold vice and a threefold sin: aversion to good, desire for evil, and uncertainty in discerning the two. Behold the threefold vice of which we have already spoken above. For in weakness of the head it was shown how sluggish—indeed, how incapable—a person is toward good; in infirmity [Col. 1148A] of the body, how fervent and restless he is toward evil; in sorrow of the heart, how dull and bleary-eyed he is in discerning both. Behold three vices: incapacity, ignorance, and desire. But since we have already said above what seemed necessary to say about these, we should not repeat them here.

## CHAPTER III. That we incur sins in three ways

Corresponding to this threefold kind of vices is a threefold kind of sins. Some are those into which we fall through weakness; some those we incur through error; some those we commit through iniquity alone. We call sins of weakness those which, although we persist vigorously and prudently, we nevertheless cannot wholly avoid. When we commit evil because we think it good, we sin through error and ignorance. But one who knows what is evil, yet deliberately commits what he could avoid, sins through malice alone, because he transgresses solely from love and desire of evil.

According to this threefold way of sinning, we are said to sin against the Father, to sin against the Son, and to sin against the Holy Spirit. For although the power, wisdom, and goodness of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same, nevertheless, according to a certain manner of speaking, in some passages of Scripture power seems to be assigned, as it were especially, to the Father; wisdom to the Son; and benevolence to the Holy Spirit. Therefore one who sins through weakness is greatly opposed to Him who is supreme power. One who sins through ignorance is greatly opposed to Him who is supreme wisdom. But how can one who offends through malice alone be more opposed to Him who is supreme goodness? According to this mode of consideration, then, the one who sins through weakness seems especially to act against the Father; one who sins through ignorance acts especially against the Son; and that which is committed through malice especially opposes the Holy Spirit.

It is rightly said that the one who sins against the Holy Spirit is not forgiven in this age or the future, because one who sins through malice, if he repents in the present life, is rightly required to make full satisfaction; but one who does not repent is owed full condemnation in the future. Those who sin through weakness or ignorance, however, just as they have some excuse in their fault, ought likewise to have some remission in their punishment. It is right that more lenient treatment be given, whether in present satisfaction or future condemnation, to those whose fault is lightened by the excuse of incapacity or ignorance. Likewise, those who have no excuse in their fault rightly receive no remission in punishment.

Thus, in a remarkable way, those who repent in this life of voluntary sins receive remission without remission. For they receive full remission of the crime committed, without any remission of the satisfaction proportionate to it. Therefore, as stated, to sin against the Father is to sin through incapacity; to sin against the Son is to sin through ignorance; to sin against the Holy Spirit is to sin through malice.

## CHAPTER IV. What belongs properly to each kind of sin

[Col. 1149A]

Let us hear, then, how the same evils are described in Isaiah by the same teacher of truth when it says: “A wound,” he says, “and a bruise, and a swelling sore.” By the wound, then, we understand that sin which is committed through weakness alone; by the bruise, that which is incurred through error alone; by the swelling sore, that which is completed through iniquity. For if by a wound we understand an injury which is outwardly opened but by no means turns into swelling within, see how rightly sin of weakness is designated by it. What is an outwardly open injury but manifest fault [Col. 1149B] without any pretense or contradiction? And what is injury without swelling but fault without exaltation—fault accompanied by humiliation and shame? Such, surely, are the sins which we commit through weakness, and as it were unwillingly: we blush at them most deeply and condemn them most severely.

Sins of ignorance, however, we are more accustomed to deny than accuse; and sins of malice we are more accustomed either to boast of through shamelessness or defend through obstinacy. Such are surely those whom Wisdom describes as being reproved, of whom it says: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2). A bruise is where injury is covered by skin, and the very skin by which it is covered prevents the discharge of pus. So the sin of ignorance, lest it come forth openly, veils itself beneath the shadow of its uncertainty; and lest the rottenness of its corruption break out through the opening of confession, it cloaks itself in the covering of false opinion.

Yet a mind which yields to its own error and acquiesces in a false opinion is often not permitted even thus to rest in its darkness so as to seem secure to itself. Rather, the alternation of differing judgments and the fluctuation of manifold uncertainty drive the mind now here, now there, and do not permit it to be at rest; and thus, after the likeness of a bruise, they both torment the trembling conscience through anxiety and turn it black with fear. A sin of malice is rightly expressed by a swelling sore, because it cannot be committed without contempt of God. For a sin which we can easily avoid and which we unquestionably recognize to be sin—how, I ask, can we commit it without contempt of God? Such sins are rightly called sins of malice, since they are committed neither through ignorance nor through weakness, but by evil will alone. What, then, is swelling in the injury of a blow but obstinacy in committing fault and contempt of God in transgressing the commandment? Therefore, as we have said, by the wound which does not become a swelling is expressed sin of weakness; rightly by the bruise which is covered by skin, sin of error; and rightly by the sore inflated with swelling, sin of malice.

## CHAPTER V. On the threefold sin of action, thought, and habit

[Col. 1150A]

Or we may understand by the wound the dead person outside the house; by the bruise, the dead person inside the house; and by the swelling sore, the dead person already decaying within the tomb: by the wound, sin of action; by the bruise, sin of thought; and by the swelling sore, sin of habit.

And it should be noted that, just as a swelling sore is nothing other than a wound turned into swelling, so sin of habit is nothing other than the evil of action brought into habit. Therefore sin made manifest through action—what else is it but an open wound, a corpse carried out? And what else is sin still hidden in thought but a bruise rotting beneath the skin, or a corpse that has not yet left the hiding place of its own house? Or what else is an evil habit, already decayed through infamy, than a sore already swollen from putrefaction, or the limbs of a stinking corpse already wasting away? [Col. 1150B]

Let no one be troubled that the injury of the wound is placed before that of the bruise, although sin of action must be understood by the wound and sin of thought by the bruise. For perhaps the pattern of our corruption would seem more rightly arranged and distinguished according to suitable stages of increase if the bruise were placed first, the wound second, and the swelling sore last, so that the evil of thought, then the evil of action, and after both of these the evil of habit might be described. Yet it must be known that, although sin of action is in one respect the greater sin, sin of thought is in one respect the more dangerous. For although sin of action may perhaps be greater with respect to guilt, consider whether sin of thought may not be harder to heal.

For the more we blush at manifest sin, the more quickly we often correct it. Often also a fault made manifest through action is corrected by admonition, or, struck by punishment, is abandoned even unwillingly. Hence in Luke’s Gospel the young man who was dead and carried outside the house is read to have been raised before the girl who was dead and still found within the house. Therefore, if we rightly understand sin of action by the wound and sin of thought by the bruise, what wonder if we find the wound first and the bruise afterward in the mystical reading, since sin of thought appears more dangerous than sin of action, and since we approve the rationale of this order by the evangelical example? The swelling sore is rightly placed last, as a kind of summit, by which the evil of wrongful habit is designated, because it is found more grievous for guilt and harder to heal than all the rest.

## CHAPTER VI. That each of the foregoing may be understood in three ways

Or by the wound, which is without swelling but nevertheless without any treatment, we may understand the sin which we accuse but do not abandon; by the bruise, the sin which we cover by hypocrisy; [Col. 1151A] by the swelling sore, the sin which we defend through obstinacy. Therefore the injury of sin is opened in three ways, covered in three ways, and swells in three ways. It is opened after the manner of a wound; covered after the manner of a bruise; swollen after the manner of a swelling sore.

An open wound is manifest sin. But the wound of sin is made manifest to a person in one way in himself, in another way to his neighbor, and in another way to God: to himself through knowledge, to his neighbor through action, to God through confession. For, so far as lies within us, we hide from God what we refuse to condemn before Him by our own confession. Likewise, the injury of sin is hidden in three ways and, after the likeness of a bruise, covered over by a kind of skin of concealment. For it is hidden one way from ourselves, another from God’s eyes, and another from our neighbor. It is hidden from us through error; from God through silence; from our neighbor through pretense.

Likewise, the stain of sin swells in three ways and expands through inflation after the manner of a swelling sore. In oneself it festers through malice; before one’s neighbor, through shamelessness; against God, it swells through obstinacy. For a person first destroys himself through malice, ruins his neighbor through shamelessness, and assails God through obstinacy.

## CHAPTER VII. What is characteristic of each kind of sin

But although we seem generally to attribute these three conditions to every sin—since we are accustomed to find one and the same evil of corruption in different persons, or in the same person at different times, now open, now hidden, now swollen—nevertheless it is usual and, indeed, characteristic of certain sins to come forth openly with a certain freedom rather than swelling; of others to erupt with enormous inflated pride; and of still others never to wish to be detected but always to lie hidden. [Col. 1151C]

For who does not know how sorrow is accustomed to express its entire self in words, to pour itself out in complaint, and, in the manner of a wound, to shed in weeping and groaning a kind of flow of blood? But the evil of envy hides itself in silence, because the envious mind is ashamed to reveal its vice; it therefore cloaks itself in the skin of dissimulation, lest, if it came openly forth, it be exposed to contempt and become vile in everyone’s eyes. Yet this evil is accustomed always to reveal itself, though unwillingly, through a manifest sign: for it commonly has a grim look, a bitter answer, a pale face, and the other signs of a hidden infirmity. Thus, although it wishes to lie hidden, it cannot entirely do so. [Col. 1152A] Rather, in the likeness of a bruise it appears plainly outwardly, even though, hidden beneath the skin of dissimulation, as stated, it does not break out in speech.

Anger, however, swelling in indignation at an injury received and bursting outward after the manner of a swelling sore through threats and insults, is often largely restrained by shame or fear; yet it spreads more widely inwardly through desire than outwardly through speech into the evil of vengeance. You perceive, I think, how great is the likeness between sorrow and a wound, envy and a bruise, anger and a swelling sore. We are taught how great and fearful these evils are by divine Scripture itself. For what a great evil sorrow must be, if, as the Apostle testifies, it produces death! [Col. 1152C] (2 Cor. 7.) And what we ought to think of envy and anger, we repeatedly confirm by the testimony of sacred Scripture: “Anger kills the foolish man, and envy slays the little one” (Job 5). Attend, then, to how rightly each of these is judged to be a great evil, since all of them, according to Scripture’s testimony, produce death.

## THIRD TREATISE. Thus far concerning the threefold sin; now concerning the threefold remedy

[Col. 1151]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1151D]

To increase the evil, this too is added: these deadly things can scarcely be wholly avoided by any skill or prudence. Who, I ask, keeps himself with such caution and vigilance that he never feels a bite of sorrow, of envy, or of anger? But if we cannot wholly avoid such great evils, why do we at least despise the remedies? Contempt for remedies is certainly shown in the words: “A wound, and a bruise, and a swelling sore: it has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.” Three evils are set forth first, and three remedies are subsequently added: a wound, a bruise, and a swelling sore. Behold the threefold evil to which a threefold remedy is joined: [Col. 1152D] bandages, treatments, and fomentations.

Perhaps someone may think that each should be fitted to its corresponding term: bandages to the wound, treatments to the bruise, and fomentations to the swelling sore. But the grammar of the text itself prevents us from following this distinction of words. For since *circumligata* (“bound up,” feminine), not *circumligatum* (neuter), is used, it is shown that this does not refer to the wound alone. Similarly, since we read *curata* (“treated,” feminine), not *curatus*, I do not see how it should be referred only to the bruise. Therefore, since we read “bound up,” “treated,” and “softened” in the feminine, we are compelled to refer each of these to the sore (*plaga*). Yet nothing prevents each of them from being referred also to the two preceding terms, since neither the letter forbids this nor the sense resists it. We understand the bandages as commandments, treatments as threats, and fomentations as promises.

## CHAPTER II. On the threefold instruction

[Col. 1153A]

The likeness between bonds and commandments is quite fitting. For we are restrained by bonds, and we are surely restrained from our own wills by divine commandments. By bonds we are drawn, held back, and bound fast. Drawing bonds are precepts; restraining bonds are prohibitions; binding bonds are admonitions. A precept concerns things which ought to be done. A prohibition concerns things which it is not lawful to do. An admonition concerns things which are indeed advantageous to do, though they may be omitted without fault.

By precepts we are often urged toward a place to which we do not direct the step of good work without difficulty. By prohibitions we are often drawn back from a place toward which we hurry through desire. By admonitions we bind more tightly the gaping or loose parts of our hearts, when we often restrain our wills even from the use of lawful things. Thus the drawing bonds are: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself.” “Honor your father and your mother.” The restraining bonds are: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal.” The binding bonds are: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor”; and the Lord’s statement concerning virginity: “Let the one who is able to receive it, receive it” (Matt. 10); whence also the Apostle: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel. It is good for a person to remain thus” (1 Cor. 7); and elsewhere: “It is good for a person [Col. 1153C] not to touch a woman” (ibid.).

Therefore, with bonds of this kind we bind up and fortify from without the gaping wounds of our vices and the injuries of the soul, whenever we restrain harmful desires from action or even from consent.

## CHAPTER III. On the threefold threat
But for the restoration of perfect health it is not enough to restrain the evil of perverse assent by applying the bonds of the commandments, unless we also strive, with equal diligence, to eradicate the harmful humours of carnal affections and the corruption of pleasures by applying the remedies of suitable cures. Behold, we have shown you a threefold kind of treatment in the divine [Col. 1153D] threats, just as we previously taught concerning the bonds: the threat of correction, the threat of reprobation, and the threat of condemnation.

Of the first it is said: “For whom God loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XI). Of the second it is written: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. IX). Of the third there is this: “Then he will say to those who are at his left: Depart, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

The threat of chastisement is: “If you walk contrary to me and refuse to listen to me, I shall add your plagues sevenfold because of your sins” (Lev. XXVI); and that which is set forth a little earlier: “I shall add your corrections sevenfold because of your sins, and I shall crush the pride of your hardness” [Col. 1154A] [of heart]. The threat of hardening is: “Behold, I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. IV). The threat of condemnation is: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Mark IX).

Bitter indeed is the juice of herbs such as these, but it is most effective in drying up the harmful humours of vices. For who is so unrestrained that he would not endeavour to moderate his desires, if he carefully considers and remembers that the Lord is accustomed, even in this life, to punish evil pleasures sevenfold in some of his elect? Who would not fear to persist stubbornly in perverse habits? Or who would not hasten to correct a depraved practice, when he hears that some are given, even in this life, over to a reprobate mind, compared to irrational beasts, and—because of their obstinacy [Col. 1154B] and bondage to sin—irretrievably consigned to the punishments of Gehenna, lest perhaps, when they may wish to come to their senses while still able, they may thereafter be wholly unable to do so?

There remains a third kind, the most effective and powerful of all, and more excellent than every other for healing diseases of this sort. For this is that remedy which is accustomed most effectively to cure inveterate diseases of vice and to restore those who are almost desperate invalids to complete health. For what person of so senseless and stubborn a mind could anywhere be found who would not shudder and utterly recoil from buying transient carnal allurements at the price of eternal torments, if he carefully examined and continually considered how slight—even momentary—are all these delights of the flesh which pass away, [Col. 1154C] and how immense and terrible are those eternal torments which have no end and cannot have one?

See, therefore, that it lies very largely within our power to recover our health, if we endeavour to apply to our diseases a remedy of this sort in a fitting manner. Therefore, where there is a wound, a bruise, and a swelling sore which has not been bound up or treated with such medicine, why should we now wonder or complain if it cannot recover health? Justly indeed he fails and perishes amid his brokenness who, although such suitable medicinal remedies were abundantly available to him, refused to apply them to his diseases.

Do you not know, you who despise remedies of this kind, that according to the saying of the Wise Man, “Treatment causes even the greatest sins to cease” (Eccles. X)? But perhaps you shrink from the juice of the herbs mentioned above, since it is bitter and exceedingly biting; and perhaps for this reason you fear to apply it to your wounds. Yet if their bitterness seems to you most bitter, attend also to this: their remedy is most effective.

## CHAPTER IV. On the threefold promise.

Receive, then, also a threefold kind of oil in the divine promises, so that you may have something by which, when it is appropriate, to relieve the severity of pain, to cherish limbs which are already beginning to recover strength, and even to nourish those already healed.

The first kind of oil, therefore, is the promise of pardon; the second, the promise [Col. 1155A] of grace; the third, the promise of glory. For the merciful and compassionate Lord is surpassingly good over against evil; and the Lord will give not only forgiveness of offences, but also grace and glory.

Does not this seem to belong to that first kind of oil, which we have called the promise of pardon: “Though your sins,” he says, “be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and though they be red as crimson, they shall be white as wool” (Isa. I)? But to the second, that is, the promise of grace, seems to belong that of which the Apostle says:

> “There are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God who works all things in all. But to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit [Col. 1155B] for usefulness. To one indeed, through the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in the one Spirit; to another, the working of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of utterances. But the one and same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each severally as he wills” (I Cor. XII).

But if we understand the third kind of oil as the promise of glory, does not that seem to belong to it which we read elsewhere in the same Apostle?

> “One glory indeed belongs to heavenly things, another to earthly things. One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars. For star differs from star in brightness; so also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; [Col. 1155C] it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonour; it shall rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it shall rise in power. It is sown an animate body; it shall rise a spiritual body” (I Cor. XV).

## CHAPTER V. On the threefold power of the threefold promise.

Behold, you have three kinds of oil, each certainly of no cheap or ordinary price. All are precious and necessary for various uses: whether for preparing food, maintaining lamps, or healing wounds. Yet the first is primary and especially suited for the use of anointing; the second, for the use of light; the third, for the use of refreshment. The first cherishes more healthfully, the second burns more brightly, the third tastes more sweetly.

That kind of oil [Col. 1155D] seems to taste sweeter than the others which Scripture commonly calls “the oil of gladness” (Ps. XLVI); and what else is this but participation in glory? But that seems to burn more brightly and illuminate more effectively than all the rest, concerning which we read that its anointing teaches us concerning all things. For just as, without the illumination of grace, we cannot keep to the way of truth even for a little while, so without its guidance we cannot lose the way of life or wander anywhere from it.

Likewise, among the others that kind of oil seems better suited to the healing cure, concerning which you have: “The yoke shall decay from before the oil,” because by the compassionate forgiveness of God the practice of sin and the slavery of sin perish (John VIII). But although we have assigned these matters particularly to their respective kinds, daily experience can show us that each kind is useful and very effective for relieving pain. For what severity of any pain, I ask, can we find which that great sweetness of the divine promises cannot alleviate?

## CHAPTER VI. On the threefold relief against threefold pain.

Some suffer pain from the infliction of brokenness and a wound; others from the languor of weakness; others from exhaustion caused by tribulation and labour. The infliction of a wound is the commission of a crime. The languor of weakness is a deficiency of strength. Exhaustion from labour is weariness in waiting, arising from the multitude of tribulations and from an impatient desire for the promised recompense. From all these things pain [Col. 1156B] arises and afflicts the soul of man in many ways.

But against this threefold pain you have the threefold hope of oil. If, therefore, you suffer because of a wound and the commission of a crime, you have the oil of promised pardon, namely from the Lord’s promise. If you suffer from weakness and failure of strength has taken hold of you, you have the oil of promised grace. If you suffer, exhausted by affliction, anoint yourself with the oil of gladness in the hope of promised grace.

Therefore, if the pain of repentance afflicts your heart and the consciousness of sins presses you too bitterly, receive an anointing and receive consolation. For there is that voice of the Lord—indeed, an outpouring of divine anointing: “As I live, says the Lord God, I do not will the death of the wicked, but that the wicked should turn from his way and live. Turn from your most evil ways; and why will you die, house of Israel?” [Col. 1156C] (Ezek. XXXIII). What bitterness of brokenness and repentance, however immense, can this infusion of divine anointing not soften?

If you suffer from your languor and failure, persist in prayers and do not cease until you are clothed with power from on high, until you rest and wholly recover from all your pain and languor, as one anointed with that most precious ointment of the Gospel vessel: “For if you,” he says, “though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give a good spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke XI).

But, that you may marvel still more: it is left within our power by him who gives and does not reproach, that anyone may take as much as he wishes, since he says: “For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it shall be opened” (Matt. VIII). Therefore do not be sparing in spending, nor miserly in giving out. The more you give out, the more abundantly you possess: “Freely,” he says, “you have received; freely give” (Matt. X). The outpouring of grace and the flow of this oil does not cease in the widow’s hands, unless empty vessels fail which it can fill.

If you fail amid tribulations or are wearied by excessive labour, you have the anointing of glory, by which you may ease the pain of your weariness, when you receive from that precious perfumer what you hear: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII); for “that which is momentary and light in our tribulation works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory on high” [Col. 1157A] (II Cor. IV). Hear also that perfumer bringing forth the same kind of oil and anointing of glory: “For when Christ,” he says, “your life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with him in glory” (Col. I).

## CHAPTER VII. Assignment of the threefold promise.

The first kind of oil was surely that which the Samaritan poured into the wounds of the man who fell among robbers, who also stripped him and, having inflicted wounds, departed, leaving him half-dead (Luke X). By this kind of ointment that sinful woman healed the wounds of her sins and at last mitigated the excess of her pain, she who deserved finally to hear from the Lord: “Her many sins are forgiven” (Luke VII).

[Col. 1157B] With this ointment, by the Lord’s gift, the rich man came to the Lord’s feet and lavishly bestowed an anointing of compassion upon the Lord’s lowliest members. He recognized that he had received it from above as a sinner and penitent, so that, as a sinner and penitent, he might bestow upon sinners and penitents the benefit of compassion which he remembered having himself received freely from God’s mercy.

That ointment of compassion the wicked servant refused to pour upon his lord’s feet, although he had received it in such abundance from his lord’s gift. Therefore he is afterwards compelled to repay what he had first received freely, when he is reproached in these words: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all your debt because you begged me. Ought you not, then, also to have had mercy on your fellow-servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matt. XVIII).

The second kind of oil, I think, was that whose debtor he acknowledged himself to be, when he answered the question put to him: “How much,” he says, “do you owe my lord?” And he replied: “A hundred measures of oil” (Luke XVI). Consider, I beg you, in what abundance he had received the oil of grace, since he did not deny that he owed a hundred measures of oil.

He who urgently admonished his lord’s debtors in speaking to them compelled them to repay this debt of oil: “See,” he says, [Col. 1157C] “that you do not receive the grace of God in vain” (I Cor. VI). He recognized this debt of oil in himself and was not ashamed to confess it when he said: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV). How greatly he laboured to repay this debt of oil, he shows in what he immediately adds: “And his grace in me was not empty; but I laboured more abundantly than all of them. Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.).

The third kind of oil, unless I am mistaken, was that in which those five prudent virgins abounded; hence their lamps could not be extinguished, since they did not fear a lack of oil. Therefore they run and hasten in the abundance of this oil; and while the foolish virgins stand outside, they enter confidently into the joy of their Lord and recline in everlasting gladness at the marriage-feast of the Lamb (Matt. XXV).

He had received the fullness of this oil, and was at last fully anointed with it, concerning whom the Prophet truly declares: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV; Heb. I). Rightly indeed above his companions or sharers: not merely above human beings, but even above angels. For he was made so much better than angels as he inherited a more excellent name than they [Col. 1158A] (Heb. I). Crowned indeed with glory and honour, he received the name which is above every name, “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings” (Phil. II; Heb. I).

He was worthy indeed to receive the fullness of glory, having first received the fullness of grace: “We saw,” he says, “his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I). Nor is there any doubt that he truly received every fullness, according to each kind of oil assigned above, “in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily” (Col. II). For he is the fountain of mercy; from him flow the streams of all grace; in him is the abyss of eternal and infinite glory.

Why, I ask, do we still suffer want of oil of this kind? “For we all received from his fullness” (John I), if we willed it. Let us only ask, and we shall receive. That kind of oil called the oil of gladness, or glory, is most precious; yet he himself commands us to ask for it and promises to give it: “Ask,” he says, “and you shall receive, that your joy may be full” (John XVI). Thus we have sufficiently at hand that which, whenever we will wholeheartedly, we receive upon asking.

## CHAPTER VIII. Assignment of the manifold usefulness of the divine promises, and recapitulation of what has been said.

We have, therefore, three kinds of oil, all as necessary as they are useful. The first against the threefold brokenness of wound, bruise, and swelling sore. [Col. 1158C] The second against the threefold pain of a languid head, a sorrowful heart, and a sick body. The third against the threefold exhaustion, even of a healthy body: that of labour, poverty, and persecution.

You have the oil of divine mercy, in which to cherish the wounds of sins; you have the oil of grace, in which to relieve the diseases of vices; you have the oil of glory, in which to ease the weariness of struggles. Just as disease is one thing and wound another, as we taught above, so vice is one thing and sin another. Vice is the involuntary defect of natural good itself; sin is voluntary consent to an evil that tempts. Vice, therefore, is the corruption of nature, through which it becomes prone and desirous, often even of that evil to which it nevertheless does not wish to consent. But sin is the perversion of one’s faculty of action, through which one often voluntarily consents even to that evil which one could easily have resisted.

Therefore, first, the wounds of sins must be healed. Second, the diseases of vices must be treated. Third, the pains of exhaustion must be relieved. Thus, for the healing of sins, as has been said, we have the oil of mercy; for the treatment of vices, the oil of grace; for guarding against deficiencies, the oil of glory.

For the healing of sins, you have that prophetic preparation made from the first kind of oil: “Blessed,” he says, “are they whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. XXXI). A marvellous ointment of mercy, which not only makes the sick healthy but makes the miserable blessed: “Blessed,” he says, “is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (ibid.).

Against the diseases of vices and the corruption [Col. 1159A] of nature, receive yet another preparation of ointment from the oil of grace: “Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXLV). Receive another anointing made from the same oil of grace: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. XCIII). Receive also this: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord; the Lord shall be his confidence” (Jer. XVII).

Blessed is the man who has the Lord as helper, teacher, and protector. Blessed is he whom the Lord helps, teaches, and protects: he helps toward good, defends against evil, and teaches how to discern both. To help, teach, and defend is wholly the work of grace. The first is against deficiency of strength; the second against deficiency of truth; the third against deficiency of virtue—all against a deficiency of natural good. The first is against the weakness of a languid head, the second against the darkness of a sorrowful heart, the third against the anxiety of a sick body and the restlessness of burning desire.

We have yet a third kind of oil, and likewise a threefold preparation of ointment from it, against the threefold exhaustion of a body now recovering strength. Against weariness from labour, you have: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII). Against the affliction of poverty, you have: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). Against the tribulation of persecution, you have: [Col. 1160A] “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.).

Who, I ask, amid so many struggles of tribulations, would not merely fail to suffer pain, but indeed rejoice, when by the testimony of sacred Scripture he learns—and does not dare to doubt—that “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him” (Jas. I)? Hence the apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus (Acts V).

How rightly this third kind of oil is called the oil of gladness, since it causes even tribulation to be a cause of joy! For who would not rejoice—indeed, glory—in weaknesses and tribulations, when he hopes to receive as the prize of the contest that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II)?

We have now spoken of the different kinds of oil, so that we may know what kinds we possess and for what useful or even necessary purposes they are suited. Nor should it suffice us to have learned this concerning such kinds of oil and to have been able to distinguish their usefulness from one another, unless we endeavour, according to the use and power of each, to cherish our infirmities with them, lest that sentence of divine rebuke should seem to accuse us: “A wound, and a bruise, and a swelling sore has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor soothed with oil” (Isa. I).

[Col. 1159]

# TREATISE ON THE POWER OF BINDING AND LOOSING.

## CHAPTER I.

[Col. 1159C]

“Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI). You ask me whether this power of binding and loosing, given to the apostle Peter in these words, is the same as that elsewhere granted in common to all the apostles and, in them, to all their vicars, when it is said: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John XX).

For you say that different people hold differing opinions and explain differently the power of binding and loosing, forgiving and retaining sins, and likewise the keys of the kingdom of heaven. You ask, therefore, whether the apostles and their vicars received in those words of the Lord the power to absolve human beings from the debt of eternal damnation. For, as you say, some affirm this, and likewise others deny it.

Hence you further ask in objection—and object in asking—whether, if priests have been given the power to loose people from the debt of eternal damnation, they can also bind some persons with that same debt. Behold, two persons come to [Col. 1160C] a priest: one hardened in crime and thereby bound; the other truly righteous and thereby loosed. Can he either loose the one who is bound or bind the one who is loosed? For there is no loosing except of one who was previously bound, nor binding except of one who was previously loosed.

Again, behold, two criminals come to the priest: one truly repentant, the other wholly unrepentant. Can he, I ask, forgive the sins of the unrepentant man and, at his own pleasure, retain those of the truly repentant one?

## CHAPTER II.

First, therefore, it must be noted that the obligation arising from sins is considered in relation to two things. One is the obligation by which a person is bound to guilt; the other is that by which he is bound to punishment. In the one he is bound by the bond of captivity; in the other he is bound by the debt of damnation.

For if a person falls into some grave sin, it is no longer in his power to rise again by himself. By himself he can depart from the Lord, but by himself he cannot return to him. For, according to the Psalmist, he is “a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. LXXVII). Hence also the saying of the same Psalmist: “Blessed [Col. 1161A] is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. I).

Thus the obligation of guilt is called the death of the soul, because just as by outward death the body is restrained from works belonging to life, so by the obligation of guilt the soul is mortified to works belonging to eternal life. But would that the man once bound and made captive were held only in captivity. Yet, what is more miserable, he is also held in slavery to sin. For “he who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII). Consequently, he pays daily interest, and the debt of his guilt increases daily.

Hence is that promise which you have in the Psalm: “From usury and iniquity he shall redeem their souls” (Ps. VII). The obligation of guilt, therefore, concerns two things: in the one the bond of captivity is kindled; in the other, the debt of slavery. Behold, this is concerning the obligation of guilt. Let us now consider the obligation of punishment.

## CHAPTER III.

To complete his misery, the transgressor, by the merit of his transgression, is held not only bound to guilt but also assigned to punishment. For in committing that which, so far as it lies in him, he cannot amend eternally, and which is an injury to him who lives eternally, he thereby incurs the debt of eternal damnation. Eternal damnation, moreover, is called in sacred Scripture “the second death” (Apoc. XX); for just as, through the obligation of guilt, the soul is withdrawn from the divine good pleasure, so through the infliction of eternal damnation the soul is alienated from every [Col. 1161C] good pleasure of its own.

Only he who is truly omnipotent and can do all things can loose a man bound by bonds of this kind. “The things which are impossible with men are possible with God” (Luke XVIII). For there is no heart so stony, hard, or obstinate that the Lord cannot immediately soften to true repentance when he wills. Hence surely is that saying of blessed John the Baptist: “The Lord is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham” (Matt. III; Luke III).

When, therefore, he who can do all things pierces the transgressor with true repentance, what else does he do, I ask, but make perpetual guilt—and consequently perpetual punishment—capable of ending? Thus indeed punishment passes into punishment: from eternal into transitory; and he who had formerly been held by the debt of damnation is now held by the debt of expiation. Behold, you have that the obligation of punishment concerns two things. For the debt of damnation is one thing, and the debt of expiation quite another.

We now clearly grasp, as we have learned from what precedes, that two things are considered concerning the obligation of guilt and likewise two concerning the obligation of punishment. For in the obligation of guilt, as has been said, you find the bond of captivity and the bond of slavery. By the bond of captivity one is entangled so as not to return to doing good; by the bond of slavery one is drawn and driven to increase evil—both toward an increase of damnation.

Likewise, in the obligation of punishment, there is unquestionably a double bond: the bond of damnation and the bond of expiation. By the former a person is held [Col. 1162A] to eternal punishment; by the latter, to transitory punishment: by the one, indeed, for his harm; by the other, for his good. For by the former a person is tormented and not purified; by the latter he is so afflicted that he is purified.

And it must be noted that one and the same person is held at one and the same time by the obligation of captivity and slavery; but one and the same person is never held at one time by both the bond of damnation and the bond of expiation. For often, by the very fact that he is held by the debt of expiation, he is absolved from the debt of damnation.

## CHAPTER IV.

Just as there is a double obligation, therefore, so without doubt there is a double loosing. The Lord always accomplishes the first loosing by himself; the second, sometimes by himself alone and sometimes through his minister. The Lord alone is accustomed and able to dissolve the obligation of guilt, although he sometimes performs this with some cooperation from his ministers. Yet this cooperation is not confined to priests, but extends also to others. Nor do any possess this grace of cooperation under their own control; rather, now these persons, now those, receive it or do not receive it according to divine dispensation.

Priests alone, however, have under their control the authority which they have divinely received in binding and loosing, and can exercise it at every time as reason dictates. It must be observed that at one and the same moment, upon consenting to a crime, the consenting mind is bound by a threefold cord and, so far as it lies in itself alone, is indissolubly bound by the bonds of captivity, slavery, and damnation [Col. 1162C]. For we know that “a threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccles. IV). Truly and without doubt it is difficult to break, since it cannot be broken except by him alone who is three and one.

But this threefold cord, difficult to break, is broken by the very fact that the sinful soul is pierced with true repentance by him who can do all things. Thus the transgressor is loosed at one and the same time from the obligation of guilt and from the debt of eternal damnation. For, because his guilt came to an end, he simultaneously obtained that his punishment could come to an end and that eternal punishment could pass into transitory punishment.

Hence the prophet David, truly repentant and saying, “I have sinned,” immediately received this answer from the prophetic oracle: “The Lord also has taken away your sin” (II Kings XIII). For immediately upon true repentance punishment passes into punishment, from eternal into transitory, not from non-purgatorial into purgatorial. Hence is that prophetic saying, as true as it is well known: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII). At the time when he groaned healthfully, he truly acquired the cause by which he could be saved, if he had been taken away in that same moment.

The statement spoken through the Psalmist seems to express the same sense: “I said: I shall confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. XXXII). From this prophetic statement it is understood that, upon true contrition and confession of heart, the iniquity of the truly repentant person is forgiven.

[Col. 1163A] Carefully note that it does not say, “You forgave my sin,” but, “the impiety of my sin.” Whatever in the sin was iniquity and impiety, and undoubtedly deserved eternal punishment, is immediately forgiven upon the true contrition of the repentant soul, although whatever impurity there is in that sin is afterwards purged by transitory punishment.

For what else is understood by the name *impiety* (*impietas*) than a special injury to the Creator? For we are from him, and from him we have whatever good we have. What, then, is more impious or can be more injurious than to commit wickedly against the Lord of so great compassion, and against him who lives eternally, that which, so far as it lies in you, you cannot correct eternally? The impiety of sin, therefore, is truly forgiven when, upon the true repentance [Col. 1163B] of the transgressing soul, the injury done to the Creator is pardoned, and the person who deserved eternal punishment is punished only with purgatorial and transitory punishment.

It must also be noted here that unbelievers and criminals who receive baptism with faith are so absolved from the debt of damnation that they are not held by the debt of expiation; but faithful persons and criminals who, after a fall, truly repent are so absolved from the debt of damnation that they are nevertheless held under the debt of expiation.

## CHAPTER V.

True repentance is the abhorrence of sin together with the intention of guarding against it, confessing it, and making satisfaction for it. For true repentance ought to have these four things. Our own conscience teaches us two of them; authoritative teaching teaches the remaining two.

For whom does his own conscience not teach that, after an injury has been received, one person cannot be reconciled to another person unless he is convinced that the offender repents of the injury inflicted and does not wish to repeat it? Concerning the remedy of confession there is this saying of the blessed apostle James: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. V). Concerning the rendering of worthy satisfaction, there is that of John the Baptist: “Bring forth,” he says, “worthy fruits of repentance” (Luke III).

Thus a transgressor who repents is bound by the duty of confession and satisfaction so long as time and opportunity for this are divinely granted him. Therefore, so long as he is given the ability to do this, he needs priestly absolution. Only the person to whom the capacity for performing it is divinely denied is not held under this condition.

We have spoken in advance of these matters up to this point [Col. 1163D] so that we may understand more fully, in the liberation and absolution of sins, what the Lord does by himself alone; what he does by himself together with his minister; and what he sometimes does through his minister alone. Let us now attend more diligently to that consideration for which we undertook the whole discussion.

## CHAPTER VI.

It must be known, therefore, that the priestly power of binding and loosing is chiefly concerned with the twofold manner of expiating. For the manner of expiating consists in two things. Since no sin goes unpunished, it must be expiated either in this life, according to the judgment of a priest, by a worthy fruit of repentance, or in the future life, according to the divine judgment, by purgatorial fire.

Thus the sinful soul, released by God alone from the debt of damnation but still liable for the debt of expiation, has, I say, both a way in which it may usefully be bound through the priestly office and a matter from which it needs mercifully to be absolved. For the truly repentant person willingly submits to human judgment in order that he may deservedly escape divine judgment. Therefore he is bound by the priest to the obligation of worthy satisfaction, and loosed from that debt of future purgation which deserves fire.

For by the very fact that he devoutly accepts the human sentence, he merits to escape the divine sentence. Behold how you have it that a person is loosed and bound at one and the same time. Understand the Lord’s saying concerning this power of binding and loosing: “Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound in [Col. 1164B] heaven, and whatever you loose,” and so forth.

It should be noted, however, that just as, in divine release, punishment is transferred into punishment—from eternal to temporary—so in priestly absolution a judgment is transferred into a judgment—from divine to human. Thus in both cases the sinner is released, and in both cases bound; but there absolution is the cause of obligation, while here, conversely, obligation is the cause of absolution. Hence, when it is said to Peter, “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven,” there is first added: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.” For, as we have already said, precisely by being bound here for the time being by a human being to the debt of present satisfaction, a person is thereafter absolved from the debt of deserved punishment. To this power of loosing [Col. 1164C] seems also to belong what the Lord says to all the apostles, and in them to all their vicars: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.” For what is it to forgive sins, except to absolve by relaxing the sentence of strictness due to sins, and, in absolving, to relax it? And what is it to retain sins, except to refuse absolution to those who are not truly penitent? For many who confess seek absolution, yet are unwilling wholly to abandon their crimes. Many promise prudence for the future, but are unwilling to make satisfaction. All such persons, because they are not truly penitent, undoubtedly ought not to be absolved. For this is truly to repent: to grieve over past transgression with the firm purpose of confessing, making satisfaction, and guarding against it with every [Col. 1164D] precaution. Those who repent in this manner ought deservedly to be absolved. Otherwise, they are dismissed without absolution; and this is to retain sins.

## CHAPTER VII

From what we have now said, we may plainly understand, in the remission of sins, what the Lord does by himself, what he does through his minister, and what he does both by himself and through the office of his ministers. By himself he looses the bond of hard-heartedness; both by himself and through his minister [Col. 1165A], the debt of eternal damnation; but through his minister, the debt of future purgation. He reserved to himself alone the power of the first release; he accomplishes the second release both by himself and through his minister; but the third the Lord is accustomed to accomplish not so much by himself as through his minister. It is rightly said that the Lord absolves the truly penitent person from the bond of damnation; and it is likewise rightly said that the priest does this. The Lord does so in response to confession of the heart, and the priest in response to confession of the mouth. For confession of the heart alone truly suffices for the penitent person’s salvation of soul when a case of necessity excludes oral confession and priestly absolution; hence we rightly say that then the Lord absolves. But since oral confession and priestly absolution are required of the truly penitent person as long as God grants him the opportunity for them, absolution from deserved damnation is rightly ascribed also to the priest. We thus have the reason why we ascribe such absolution both to the Lord and to his minister.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 1165B]

Now this deserves consideration: why is that release from the debt of future purgation attributed especially to the priest? We know that a truly penitent person can escape eternal damnation without priestly absolution when he cannot obtain it. But we do not similarly say that a truly penitent person can escape the debt of future purgation without priestly absolution and imposed satisfaction whenever a case of necessity has excluded them.

It should be noted that the Lord looses the bond of damnation conditionally, whereas the Lord’s minister does so simply and, so to speak, completely. God absolves the penitent person from the debt of damnation on this [Col. 1165C] condition: that, insofar as he can, he must seek priestly absolution and make satisfaction in the due manner according to the priest’s judgment. For if he neglects to do so, he does not escape eternal danger. But once priestly absolution has been received and the condition binding him has been fulfilled, even if it should happen that he dies immediately, he has escaped eternal damnation. Yet, just as the debt of eternal damnation is conditionally loosed by the Lord, so certainly the debt of future purgation is conditionally loosed by the servant. For every criminal absolved by a priest remains bound under the condition of rendering satisfaction, so that he may escape the fire of future purgation. Therefore the priest looses the debt of eternal damnation wholly and absolutely, but the debt of future purgation conditionally. [Col. 1165D] Priestly absolution frees one who has the firm purpose of making satisfaction from the debt of damnation, whether or not he has time to carry it out; but it does not equally free him from the debt of future purgation.

## CHAPTER IX

Again, it should be noted that a twofold binding, just as a twofold loosing, belongs to the priestly office. One loosing is that by which they loose penitents from the debt of damnation; another is that by which they loose such persons from the debt of future purgation. Likewise, one binding is that by which they bind those truly penitent to the debt of imposed satisfaction; another is that by which they bind those who commit intolerable deeds and yet do not repent with the bond of anathema. They bind the former in order to absolve them from a more dangerous [Col. 1166A] bond; the latter, in order to bring them to repentance. Thus the saying of the Lord, “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained,” is to be understood of that absolution by which a transgressor is absolved from the debt of damnation. For priests can and ought to forgive the sins of those truly penitent and accepting due satisfaction, and to absolve them from the debt of damnation; but they ought to dismiss the rest without absolution. And the saying to Peter, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven,” must be understood especially of that absolution by which priests customarily—and ought—to loose by binding and bind by loosing. For precisely by binding penitents to the [Col. 1166B] debt of present satisfaction, they loose them from the debt of future purgation.

## CHAPTER X

It is therefore established, as we said above, that the Lord alone can and customarily does loose by himself that bond which concerns the obligation of guilt; but he customarily breaks the bond which concerns the obligation of punishment both by himself and through his minister. In the raising of Lazarus you will find both things symbolized. For the Lord both raises him by himself and looses him through the service of attendants. Thus through the Lord himself he is loosed from inward bonds, but through the ministry of those serving from outward bonds. Who does not know that death binds the limbs of dying persons so unlooseably that none of them [Col. 1166C] can perform any function, or even move himself in the slightest degree? The Lord loosed Lazarus from these bonds when he restored him to life. But, when Lazarus had been raised and freed from the bonds of death, the Lord said: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11). What is it for a person previously buried to come forth, except for anyone bound by mortal sin willingly to abandon that dark hiding-place of his own stony hard-heartedness? And what is it to come forth bound with bands, and to present oneself before the eyes of those attending the Lord, except by oral confession to show those who have received the power to loose by what bonds of sins one is held fast for the sentence of divine vengeance? “Loose him,” he says, “and let him [Col. 1166D] go” (ibid.). It is appropriately said of one raised and bound: “Loose him, and let him go.” For unless he had first been loosed, he would not have the free ability to go and enter his own house. We know without doubt that a sinner, even if penitent, cannot enter that house which Paul describes so long as he is held and not loosed by the debt either of damnation or of future purgation: “We know,” he says, “that if our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5). After the dissolution of this earthly dwelling, the person who has incurred in this life nothing that must be purged in the future life freely enters that house. Otherwise he must first pay the debt of purgation. But if anyone has incurred what deserved bitter [Col. 1167A] and lengthy purgation, and has merited to be absolved in this life through satisfaction imposed and fulfilled, then, when this earthly dwelling has been dissolved, he will at once joyfully enter that abode of eternal rest. From this it may be understood how the power of binding and loosing, divinely received, customarily opens through pastoral ministry the entrance of paradise and the gate of heaven which [Col. 1167B] divine severity closes to those who act criminally. Therefore the power of binding and loosing appears to be those keys of which the Lord said to Peter: “And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” We now have what we proposed to seek: we have what that power of binding and loosing given to priests is, and how, and whose, sins they can and ought to forgive or retain [Col. 1167C] sins.

## CHAPTER XI

But you persist and say: If they cannot alike bind and absolve anyone whatsoever, forgive the sins of anyone whatsoever, or retain those of anyone whatsoever, why is it said generally to Peter, “Whatever you bind, whatever you loose”? Likewise, the statement addressed jointly and generally to all the apostles is: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained.” This question would rightly trouble you if the Lord had said to Peter, “Whatever you wish to bind shall be bound, and whatever you wish to loose shall be loosed.” But he did not say this, nor did he wish it to be understood in this way. If someone wishes to bind what he cannot bind, will it [Col. 1167C] therefore be bound? Who would say so? He therefore does not say, “Whatever you wish to bind,” but “Whatever you bind shall be bound in heaven.” That person is truly bound who, in accordance with the tenor of his confession, is bound to the just debt of satisfaction. That person is truly absolved through the priestly office whose sin is justly forgiven for the purpose of fitting satisfaction. Thus a just priestly sentence binds and absolves; an unjust priestly sentence does neither.

## CHAPTER XII

Thus, certainly, the sins of those who deserve to be justly absolved are forgiven; while the sins of those to whom absolution from sins is justly—not unjustly—[Col. 1167D] denied are undoubtedly retained. Therefore what the Lord says to Peter is equivalent to saying in other words: “What shall have been bound or loosed by you shall be bound or loosed also with me. Whoever is constrained by you through the imposition of due satisfaction is held before me as a debtor of that same satisfaction; and whoever has deserved from you due absolution from his sins can, by my judgment, no longer be bound further in this respect.” In this manner we must also understand what is said to all the apostles: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose you retain are retained.” For the sins of offenders shall be forgiven or retained before the Lord which have been justly forgiven or retained through his priestly ministers. Both are truly done by them when, in carrying out either [Col. 1168A] act, they proceed according to canonical order; for they can do neither according to their own will, but only according to merit and the established order.

There is an opinion of some concerning the power of binding and loosing so frivolous that it appears deserving of ridicule rather than refutation. They think and proclaim that priests possess the power not of binding and loosing, but of showing persons to be loosed or bound. But does the Lord say, “Whatever you show to be bound shall be bound, and whatever you show to be loosed shall be loosed”? They say that apostolic men do not possess the power of forgiving or retaining sins, although the Lord says this. They say that they possess only the power of showing both, although the Lord does not say this: “Whose sins you forgive,” he says—not “whose [Col. 1168B] sins you show to have been forgiven”—“are forgiven them.” They say that evangelical priests have, in forgiving or retaining faults, the same legal right and office that priests under the Law once possessed in treating lepers. Yet those legal priests did not possess the power to cure, but to judge and show whether persons thought to be leprous were or were not leprous. We grant that the former and the latter have the same office: the former, of distinguishing leprosy from leprosy; the latter, of judging fault from fault. Would that, as truly as they possess this office, they exercised it as worthily!

## CHAPTER XIII

But I ask whether they receive, through ordination or rather through education, the ability to distinguish leprosy from leprosy and fault from fault. I say boldly [Col. 1168C] that if they come to ordination without the knowledge of discernment, they leave it without that knowledge; and if they go to it with that knowledge and return with it, they had it from elsewhere. It follows, therefore, that in ordination they receive no other power—hence no power at all. Where, then, will that power of binding and loosing be?

But to this they say: What is sin but leprosy? And what is cleansing leprosy but cutting away sin? Yet the Lord sent the leper to the priest, not so that the priest might cleanse him, but so that the priest might show him to be cleansed. But without doubt the Lord commands neither that he go for this purpose nor for that. “Go,” he says, “show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded” (Matt. 8). Just as he does not say, “Go to the priest so that he may make you clean,” neither does he say, “Go to the priest [Col. 1168D] so that he may show you clean.” The Lord did one thing and commanded three: he cleansed the leper, and at the same time commanded him to go, to show himself, and to offer. What is it to cleanse the leper, except for any sinner to abhor the filth of his sins? What is it for the cleansed leper to go, except to leave the condition of his former life and abandon sins previously committed? To show himself to the priest is to disclose by confession what he was before and what intention he now has. He offers the gift, such as Moses ordained, who submits himself to every satisfaction prescribed by canonical institution according to the priest’s judgment. In the first is considered hatred of sin; in the second, the vow of restraint; in the third, the purpose of confessing; in the fourth, [Col. 1169A] the effort to make satisfaction.
