The “vow of restraint” is here taken broadly: not only restraint from lust, but also from every crime. Certainly all these four are required in true repentance. Where any one of them is lacking, there is no true repentance, without which the leprosy of sins cannot be cleansed. When God grants the sinful soul to hate what it formerly loved and to detest what it previously desired, together with the vow of restraint, confession, and satisfaction, the leper’s cleansing is immediately made whole and complete. What else is it to command those three things to the leper in the cleansing of leprosy, except by an inward inspiration to urge upon the soul to be cleansed the vow of restraint, confession, and satisfaction?

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 1169B]

“But,” you say, “the Lord himself accomplishes all these things. What then is left for the priest?” Much in every respect: truly great, indeed very great. Just as raising a dead person is one thing and loosing one bound is another, so cleansing a leper is one thing and loosing his bonds another. “Was that leper, then,” you ask, “bound?” “Are you a teacher in Israel and do not know these things?” Truly, indeed, he was bound by the hard knot of necessity with which Moses had constrained him: “All the time,” he says, “that he is leprous and unclean, he shall dwell alone outside the camp” (Lev. 13). O harsh and utterly detestable bond, by which one who is bound is held so unlooseably that he is altogether forbidden either to enter the camp of Christ’s soldiers or to return home. Does not the priest [Col. 1169C] bind and loose the leper—not while leprous, but once cleansed? He binds him by requiring the sacrifice of due satisfaction and purification; he looses him by granting permission to return. And, if you are willing to receive it, the cleansing of the leper is not merely one but threefold. Of these the Lord accomplishes only one by himself; the other two through his minister. But what this threefold cleansing of the leper is, let it for the present be left to the reader’s judgment.

## CHAPTER XV

It should be noted in the healing of lepers that some are cleansed immediately and are then sent to the priest, while others are sent and are healed as they go. Some, at the first compunction of their repentance, have a mind prompt and ready to render every debt of true repentance. In them, therefore, there is no delay in cleansing, because in their very compunction they receive grace for the three things already mentioned above, having a mind prepared for restraint, confession, and satisfaction. Others, however, struck with compunction for repentance, do indeed have the purpose of restraint and confession, but are lukewarm toward fitting satisfaction. Hence, concerning those ten lepers, only two things are commanded, while the third is left unmentioned: “Go,” he says, “show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17), and they are not commanded to offer any gift. They could do only what they had received from God. For, in order that the Lord may show that all our good things are from him, he sometimes bestows his grace in one person and withholds it in another. You see, I think, why cleansing is deservedly delayed for those lacking the fullness of true [Col. 1170A] repentance: “As they went,” he says, “they were cleansed” (ibid.). What is going except making progress? Therefore those go who, from what they have already received, advance to being able to do what they previously could not do. Thus those who, by grieving ever more deeply over evil already committed, advance through the vow of restraint and confession to the vow of satisfaction, and add vow to vow, because they now possess the perfection of true repentance, lay aside the leprosy of sin, as it were, in going. Note that, compared with those cleansed without delay, more have their cleansing deferred, because those sluggish toward satisfaction are more numerous than those prompt toward satisfaction.

## CHAPTER XVI

From what has already been said, we know that many are healed in the priest’s absence. Likewise, some [Col. 1170B] are healed in the priest’s presence. For at the raising of Lazarus there were present also those who were to loose him. Some, therefore, are healed in the very sending, others in the journey itself, and still others upon their very arrival. Among those who come to the priest are many who have only the will to confess, yet wholly lack the vow either of restraint or of making satisfaction. For they have already been so corrupted by evil habit that they entirely despair of being able to restrain themselves or to suffice for satisfaction. Yet some such persons, after much exhortation by the priest, or even after prolonged discussion, when they are taught to place their trust in the Lord’s mercy alone and not in their own effort, are touched by visiting grace unto true [Col. 1170C] repentance and are divinely quickened into newness of life. From this, I think, you understand how beneficial it is for many such persons to hasten to confession.

## CHAPTER XVII

But there are some who have none of the three things mentioned above, but lie dead like Lazarus in a stone tomb with a stone laid over it. A dead person is held in a stone tomb when he is hardened in his transgression through great obstinacy of mind. A mass of stone is placed over one dead in sins when, through the greatness of despair, the hope which he ought to have in God is shut off. “Take away the stone,” he says (John 11). What is taking away the stone except, through the grace of exhortation given by God, wholly to remove the mass of hardened despair and open a way to the radiant [Col. 1170D] light from above? In accordance with Isaiah: “Prepare the ways of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40). Pastoral care then labors effectively, rather than in vain, at this very work when the Lord intends and commands it to be done. For what is the Lord’s commanding it, except to urge the pastor’s mind inwardly toward this work and to give grace? The Lord’s minister then beneficially performs what belongs to the pastor when the Lord himself deigns to perform what belongs to the Savior: “Lazarus,” he says, “come forth” (John 11:43). In this one summons he conveys three things. One who comes out leaves the place in which he was before. To come forth is to present oneself to the sight of those standing outside. And to come is to approach the one calling. What, then, is it for one raised from the place where he lay dead [Col. 1171A] to come out, except wholly and forever to abandon his sin? What is it for one bound to present himself to the sight of those by whom he could be loosed, except for any criminal to disclose by self-accusation the bonds of sins by which he is held? The person approaches the calling Lord who, day by day, propitiates God by worthy fruits of repentance. The first concerns the vow of restraint, the second the vow of confession, and the third the vow of satisfaction. Thus some receive, in the pastor’s presence, this threefold vow which they previously did not possess at all.

## CHAPTER XVIII

But now let us return to the point for which we have set out all the foregoing. Let us carefully distinguish what the Lord does by himself and what he does [Col. 1171B] through his minister. By himself he raises the dead; through his ministers he looses the bound. By himself he cleanses the leper; through the ministry of the priest he restores the expelled person. Raising the dead and cleansing the leper appear to refer to the same thing, for in each case the obligation of guilt is removed. Likewise, loosing the bound and restoring the expelled person appear to refer to the same thing, because in each case the obligation of punishment follows. The leper is cleansed when any perverse person is divinely stripped of the filth of his perversity; the dead person is raised when one captive to sin is divinely quickened to live well. After cleansing from leprosy, through the intervention of the priestly office, one formerly expelled is restored to his own place when he is known to have recovered, through imposed [Col. 1171C] satisfaction, the dwelling of eternal rest which he had lost by sinning. Wrapped in bands and loosed by the Lord’s ministers, he is permitted to go away and return to his own when, through the priest’s absolution and counsel, he is reformed into newness of life.

## CHAPTER XIX

To what has been said above, some object and say: Those who truly repent of their crimes certainly already possess charity. Otherwise, how can what is written concerning them be rightly understood: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 33)? No one can save one capable of charity without charity. Yet, they think, one who has charity cannot be held by the debt of eternal damnation. How, then, does the priest absolve him from such a debt if, before priestly absolution, he has already deserved to be absolved through the intervention of charity?

But beyond all doubt the patriarchs and prophets possessed charity, and yet they were held by the debt of eternal damnation. [Col. 1171D] Otherwise they would neither have descended to the lower regions nor needed Christ’s death or any redemption. Therefore, beyond all ambiguity, they were held by the debt of eternal damnation—not because it was eternal for them, but because it would have been eternal for them unless Christ’s death had absolved them from this debt. It is therefore clear that both may occur at once: that a person has charity, and that the debt of damnation still holds him.

“But,” they ask, “did not this sinner begin to be a member of Christ from the moment that he began [Col. 1172A] to possess charity? How, then, can he be a member of Christ and be held by the debt of damnation?” A person may be called a member of Christ in two respects: according to predestination or according to disposition. According to predestination, someone can be a member of Christ and not yet have charity; and conversely, someone can fail to be a member of Christ and yet have charity. For according to the Lord’s testimony, “The charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24). Thus, in this sense, it happens that a person is a member of Christ and is still held by the bond of deserved damnation. According to disposition, however, a person is called a member of Christ when he has within himself that by which he becomes such. But does that charity make a member of Christ which burns for a time [Col. 1172B] and soon grows cold? Undoubtedly, those who never receive persevering charity were never among those true members of Christ which complete the integrity of his body. Yet in a certain sense we can and customarily do call those who have transitory charity members of Christ because of the conformity to his members which they seem to possess for a time.

## CHAPTER XX

But in order to remove every scruple from devout inquirers, we say that we customarily call someone a member of Christ in three ways: by predestination, by preparation, and by incorporation. By predestination: one divinely foreordained to life. By preparation: when a pagan [Col. 1172C] or false Christian is truly touched with compunction and is imbued with truth and charity. By incorporation: when the former through the washing of the body, and the latter through priestly absolution, is joined to the Church of Christ. The first takes place by the purpose of the divine will; the second by the purpose of one’s own deliberation; the third through the office of the priest.

From a bodily building we may perceive what we should think about spiritual building. See: timber is selected from a forest to be placed in a building; afterward it is hewn, and by hewing is prepared for its suitable size and form. Finally it is joined to the building and fitted into its own place. See how one and the same timber becomes a member of the building: first through selection alone, second through preparation, third through joining together. Thus [Col. 1172D] many are already members of Christ by predestination, but not yet by preparation; while many are by preparation, but not yet by incorporation. Augustine, while still an unbeliever, was a member of Christ according to predestination. He became a member of Christ through preparation for conformity when, believing in heart and fervent in devotion, he hastened to baptism. But once baptized and joined to the Church, he was incorporated with Christ’s members. Therefore, if someone possesses charity before receiving the sacrament of our reconciliation, he may be called a member of Christ by a certain preparation of conformity, though not yet by incorporation. For through Christ’s death we are reconciled to God, and through baptism we are buried together with Christ and incorporated with his members. From this it is now clear, I think, [Col. 1173A] in what sense someone can be called a member of Christ and still be held by the debt of damnation. From what has been said concerning the pagan, one may understand what should be thought concerning the criminal yet penitent Christian.

## CHAPTER XXI

But perhaps you reply that the condition of a Christian differs from that of a gentile. Perhaps you think that every Christian, at the very moment of true compunction, is loosed from the debt of damnation, even if we should think otherwise about the unbaptized. For no one is loosed from the debt of damnation except through participation in our redemption. Through baptism and Christ’s other sacraments a person receives the means by which he can become a participant in it. But I say that what the pagan receives [Col. 1173B] in being baptized, the criminal Christian loses by sinning. For a perpetrator of crimes loses the share in Christ’s sacraments which he formerly received in baptism. I say boldly that, if before priestly absolution he approaches the communion of Christ’s body and blood, he surely eats and drinks judgment to himself, even if he now greatly repents of having sinned and grieves and groans intensely. On what grounds, then, do you contend and say that one inwardly penitent has been loosed from the debt of damnation before approaching the priest, when, before priestly absolution, he cannot participate in the sacraments of our salvation except to increase his damnation? Thus both the criminal Christian and every pagan require reconciliation; and, where necessity [Col. 1173C] does not prevent it, each must be effected through priestly ministry—the latter by washing, the former by absolution.

## CHAPTER XXII

And, if you wish to know and can hear patiently, a pagan is more easily reconciled after a hundred crimes than any Christian after a single one. Hence, no satisfaction is imposed upon any pagan, however criminal, once baptism has been received; whereas for a Christian who has sinned criminally, yet already repents and confesses, priestly absolution alone does not suffice without imposed satisfaction. But Christ’s sacrifice alone—namely, the flesh that was slain—makes satisfaction for one recently baptized. For those who sin through ignorance, the offering of the sacrifice prescribed by the Law makes satisfaction for expiation. But for those who sin willfully, according to the Apostle [Col. 1173D], “there remains no sacrifice for sin” (Heb. 10). What was mystically commanded in the Law is more truly fulfilled daily in this time, with the veil of figure removed. It is commanded in the Law that the soul which has sinned through ignorance offer this or that for sin, and what it committed through ignorance is forgiven it (Lev. 5). But concerning those who sin willfully, it is commanded: “life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot” (Lev. 24; Deut. 19).

Whatever is committed by an unbeliever is reckoned among sins of ignorance. For even if, while sinning, he knows that he has sinned, he nevertheless does not know how to assess the weight of sin; for he does not know that it cannot be expiated except through the death of the Man of God. Therefore the darkness of such ignorance greatly lightens the enormity of [Col. 1174A] guilt. But Christians, who know themselves to have been redeemed from death by Christ’s death, certainly cannot be excused by such ignorance. Therefore, for complete satisfaction for sin, a sacrifice is granted to the former, but none at all remains for the latter. Where sin is expiated through a sacrifice, reconciliation is effected by the slaying of another’s flesh rather than one’s own. Thus no satisfaction and no affliction of the flesh are imposed upon the unbeliever who converts and is baptized into Christ’s faith, because, owing to his former ignorance, a sacrifice is granted him for expiating sin; for through Christ’s passion and death he is wholly cleansed from every guilt. But the criminal Christian, because he is in no way excused from his crimes by the ignorance of unbelief, is punished in his own flesh; and, as upon one who has sinned willfully [Col. 1174B] after receiving knowledge of the truth, voluntary satisfaction is imposed. What he has now presumptuously done against God not in ignorance is purged not by the offering of the sacrifice alone, but by the affliction and mortification of his own flesh.

This is what we said above: that a criminal Christian is more difficult to expiate than a criminal pagan. But why, I ask, is he more difficult to expiate, unless because he has offended more grievously? You say that a criminal and penitent Christian is loosed from the debt of damnation before priestly absolution, yet you do not dare say that a criminal and penitent pagan is loosed from the same debt before priestly absolution. And you do not consider how contrary it is to common judgment—indeed, to all reason—to say that one who has sinned more greatly is immediately [Col. 1174C] loosed upon true repentance, while one who has sinned less greatly is not said to be immediately loosed upon true repentance.

It is commonly established that no one can absolve the impenitent. According to some, however, no one absolves the penitent, because at the very hour of compunction, as they say, the penitent has received absolution from God. But if no one absolves the impenitent, and no one the penitent, then no one absolves anyone. But whoever believes this makes a deceiver of him who says: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.” It is therefore certain that priests forgive sins and absolve penitents. At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall indeed be saved in this: that, from being a person who could not be absolved, he becomes one to whom absolution cannot be denied.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 1174D]

There are still those who wonder and ask how God, or God’s minister, is said to forgive sins, when in fact each is found both to expiate the sins of penitents by punishing them and to punish them by expiating them. “What,” they ask, “is this forgiveness, where a long-lasting and often quite painful expiation is required?” From what I said much earlier, the point at issue seems to me sufficiently clear. But, for greater clarity, I shall not hesitate, where appropriate, to add something to what has already been said.

In every sin two things must be considered: namely, the injury done to God and the corruption of the one committing it. The former belongs to injustice and impiety; the latter to dishonour and deformity. For one and the same sin is injustice in relation to God and deformity in relation to the sinner himself. [Col. 1175A] Hence that saying of the Evangelist John: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity” (1 John 3).

Beyond doubt it is injustice when someone wrongfully harms his neighbour; and in this, I think, there is no one who does not agree. It is injustice when someone reproaches, accuses, or blasphemes his God; and no one except a person deficient in understanding would dare deny it. But perhaps someone, when he satisfies his own desires in gluttony, drunkenness, lust, and other such things, does not believe it to be injustice, especially if he does so without harming his neighbour. Yet certainly, when he does this, he offends God. For how great an injury to the Creator it is to defile with the filth of vices the most noble creature, made in God’s likeness, and to overlay the divine likeness with the likeness of a beast! [Col. 1175B] “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Psalm 48).

Let a man consider how great were the things his Creator did for him, what things his Redeemer suffered for him; and from this he will be able more rightly to judge how unjust and impious it is to repay injury for benefits to so great a Lord and such a beneficent friend, and to offend him even in a small matter. He offends God who corrupts that most noble work of his; and he corrupts it who commits sin. Therefore, whoever commits sin also commits iniquity, because sin itself, as we have said, is injustice or indeed impiety insofar as it offends God, and dishonour and deformity insofar as it corrupts the sinner. [Col. 1175C]

God is therefore able, and accustomed, in one and the same crime both to forgive that which is injustice and impiety, and to cleanse by himself in purgatorial fire that which is dishonour and impurity; or to entrust to the administration of his ministers whatever ought to be forgiven of this debt of purification, or whatever ought to be healed by the remedy of satisfaction. What do you think that supreme physician has done, and does daily, in such work, except forgive what pertains to the injury done to himself and apply to his sick servant the remedy which his corruption required?

From this, I think, it is clearly apparent how true and full of mercy is that forgiveness of sins which God grants when, to one truly penitent, he forgives the injury done to himself and, by that very fact, the eternal punishment. [Col. 1175D] For the person who stubbornly presumes, so far as lies in him, that he cannot be corrected for ever, and who acts to the injury of him who lives for ever and is omnipotent, undoubtedly incurs the debt of eternal condemnation. But for a human being to be divinely absolved from such a debt—how great, I ask, and how unspeakable a mercy is this! Does it obscure God’s beneficence—or rather magnify it—that, by such remedies as are fitting for the sinful soul, he both expiates sin and cleanses vice? Who, I ask, would deny that this is true forgiveness, full of mercy, when at true repentance, setting aside the injury done to himself, he remits eternal punishment and furthermore applies medicine to the illnesses of the sick person?

From this, then, we may gather how great in power and excellence is that priestly absolution which frees one who is truly penitent and diligently making satisfaction, not only from the dreadful blaze of eternal punishment, but even from the burning of purgatorial fire. [Col. 1176A] From bodily diseases let us judge what we ought to think concerning spiritual ones. We know that some are healed by cautery, others by ointment. It is a great and merciful thing to be healed of a deadly disease, however bitter the remedy may be. How great, then, I ask, is the indulgence and beneficence of treating with the mild ointment a festering disease which shortly afterward would have had to be healed by cautery! But what is any penitential satisfaction except a mild ointment in comparison with the burning of purgatory? You now have what you ought to think of both divine and priestly forgiveness.

## Chapter XXIV

[Col. 1176B]

We may nevertheless say that forgiving sins (*remittere peccata*) is one thing, and dismissing sins (*dimittere peccata*) another, although perhaps one is found used for the other. To dismiss sins is to pardon them wholly. To forgive sins, however, is to moderate the punishment due to them and relax it for the greater part. How great, then, I ask, do you think is the forgiveness of sin, or relaxation of punishment, when by divine gift eternal punishment is transferred into purgatorial and transitory punishment, or when, through the priestly office, that purgatorial burning is changed into a penitential punishment?

You now have what you asked: namely, what or what kind of divine or priestly forgiveness [Col. 1176C] there is where a long-lasting, often quite painful expiation is required. That priests can forgive sins and extinguish future fires by penitential satisfaction, we all commonly believe and maintain. But that they can wholly dismiss sins of whatever kind, however criminal, and grant complete pardon without any satisfaction whatever and without danger—this we neither believe nor maintain.

See certainly how great is the difference between forgiving and dismissing. For to forgive is to moderate the punishment of sin according to a fitting measure of mercy; but to dismiss is to pardon the whole and leave it without punishment. Hence it is said to us: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6); and rightly so, that we may not retain anger in part, but wholly dismiss those whom we wish wholly to have dismissed for us. Hence in our daily prayer we say to the Lord: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6).

[Col. 1176D] But because it belongs to both justice and mercy to strike while sparing in part, and because it profits the healing of our purification to be punished in part, the power to forgive rather than to dismiss is conferred in the saying: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them.” Hence he who confesses to the Lord rejoices over forgiveness, not dismissal: “You forgave the impiety of my sin.” For one who had escaped the sentence of eternal condemnation still awaited, not without fear, the remedy of his purification.

## Chapter XXV

[Col. 1177A]

The purification of sins, it seems to me, is effected in three ways. It is sometimes effected according to severity alone, sometimes according to mercy alone, and sometimes according to a moderation of both, so that mercy itself is not without some severity, nor severity without mercy. For in purgatorial fire there is intolerable affliction without any remedy of consolation. In voluntary satisfaction there is affliction together with manifold consolation. In the laver of regeneration there is complete cleansing containing no affliction.

The first purification is effected by fire, the second by scourging, the third by washing. By the burning of purgatorial fire the dross of sin is burned out; by the scourge of satisfaction the chaff of sin is shaken off; by the laver of regeneration the stain of sin is washed away without punishment.

There are many who truly repent at the end of life, but, prevented by death, have no time to make satisfaction. [Col. 1177B] To these, indeed, at their true repentance, that in their sins which is injustice and impiety is forgiven; but that which is shamefulness and impurity is burned out by purgatorial fire. Understand from this the saying found in the Psalm: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven!” (Psalm 31).

[Col. 1178A] Others come to confession with great devotion, discharge their satisfaction with every zeal and care, and cover their shamefulness with works of charity and a variety of virtues. Thus is fulfilled in them what you read elsewhere: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4). In them is fulfilled that prophetic saying: “Blessed are those whose sins are covered” (Psalm 31).

Many, after many outrages and blasphemies, coming from Jews or Gentiles, are regenerated in Christ; yet no satisfaction is imposed on them for their former evils, because nothing from their past evils is imputed to those reborn in Christ. Of any such person understand it to have been said: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord did not impute sin” (ibid.).

And there are some who repent so deeply and inwardly, burn with so great an ardour of devotion in their very repentance, and presume so greatly upon the Lord’s mercy, that this alone suffices them for the expiation of their sins and renders the Lord altogether gracious toward them. This is attested by that Gospel thief who repented so late and at once deserved to hear: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). [Col. 1178B] Any such person belongs to the merit of those to whom sin is not imputed by the Lord, but many sins are dismissed to them because they love much.

Thus, in the matters we have now discussed, it appears more clearly than light that which we hear through the Psalmist: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.”

[Col. 1177]

## Treatise on Judicial Power in the Final and Universal Judgment

[Col. 1177C]

“In the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). Behold, we have heard what Truth itself promises to the apostolic men. But let us hear also what he says elsewhere: “He who does not believe,” he says, “has already been judged” (John 3).

From this double Scripture, unless I am mistaken, arises the view that there are four orders of those who come to that dreadful judgment. For from the first saying three orders are gathered: those who will judge; those who will be judged and saved; and those who will be judged and condemned. To these three, according to the other saying, a fourth order is added: those already judged and condemned.

But if persons of this sort are called already judged because their condemnation is held certain, I do not sufficiently see why we should not add a fifth order to these four which we have just named. For the salvation of infants dying immediately after baptism is as certain as the condemnation of unbelievers, [Col. 1177D] unless perhaps someone wishes to ascribe the highest degree of perfection to those who have never had any merit of their own, and to number them among the order of judges.

But I say this: if some who are still in this life are called already judged, why should those who have already received the sentence of their condemnation not much more rightly be called already judged? For it is not only those who do not believe who descend to hell immediately after death. But if anyone maintains that only they descend into hell before the general [Col. 1178C] judgment, he will at least not dare deny that all, at the departure of the soul, receive either a good or an evil sentence, and that each goes either to punishment or to refreshment.

Those who are to be punished and saved are purified precisely by being punished. Therefore the fire through which the rust of sin is consumed in them is called purgatorial. Those, however, who are punished and purified thereby recognize that they are being reserved for salvation, since they see themselves gradually cleansed of every stain. The rest, however, thereby recognize the sentence of their condemnation because they receive no remedy of purification. Therefore, although the salvation or condemnation of any of the dead is uncertain to us, it nevertheless appears certain to them. [Col. 1178D]

If, then, those who have not yet received the recompense of their merits are rightly called already judged, why should those who have already received it and, as has been said, have most certainly recognized the sentence of their salvation or condemnation, not much more so be called already judged? Who, then, are those whom the apostolic men are said to judge?

If we say that they are only those who will be found alive at the Saviour’s coming and have not yet received any sentence concerning their recompense, John’s statement contradicts us. For in his Apocalypse he writes: “And the sea,” he says, “gave up the dead that were in it; and death and hell gave up the dead that were in them; and each was judged according to his works [Col. 1179A]” (Revelation 20). Behold, you hear that death and hell gave up the dead who were in them, so that each might be judged according to his works.

Perhaps you thought that only those whose salvation or condemnation remains uncertain would be judged in that final examination. But whose condemnation, I ask, is more certain than that of evil spirits? Yet what does the Apostle say about them? “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6). Behold, those are said to be judged who, in one respect, are rightly called already judged. See, then, whether similarly those who are now called already judged may rightly also be said still to be judged.

Or do you seek a further proof of this? “The righteous shall shine and run to and fro like sparks among reeds; they shall judge nations” (Wisdom 5). What is plainer? “They shall judge nations.” Are these not those who do not believe and are therefore already judged? Thus all appear either to judge or to be judged; and among those judged, some are to be saved and others condemned. Thus, in that future judgment, there appear to be only three orders. How then are there four—or rather five?

[Col. 1179B] To pass over the rest, why are those again judged whose condemnation is not merely foreknown, but is most rightly believed already to have begun? And in what way will the apostles judge those who beyond doubt are to judge them? Shall we perhaps say that the apostles’ rendering of judgment consists in telling the condemned that they are condemned, and the saved that they are saved? But what great thing would it be to tell those that they will be condemned—those, I mean, who have recognized or even received the sentence of their condemnation?

[Col. 1179C] But perhaps you say that the apostolic men judge their inferiors by examining each person’s conscience and discerning how justly these are saved and those condemned. For how is God believed on that day to reveal the hidden things of darkness except by undoubtedly unveiling the inmost and secret things of consciences? Therefore that judgment will not take place in a contest of words, but in the manifestation of thoughts: according to the Apostle, each person’s conscience bearing witness, and their thoughts mutually accusing or even defending one another, on the day when the Lord shall judge the secrets of men (Romans 2).

But undoubtedly, at the mutual inspection of consciences, just as it will be plain to the apostles how rightly the reprobate are condemned, so it will be plain to the reprobate how rightly the apostles are glorified. Therefore, just as the apostles are said to judge the reprobate, why should the reprobate not also rightly be said to judge the apostles?

[Col. 1179D] Or shall we perhaps say that the good see the consciences of the evil, but the evil do not see the consciences of the good? Yet if all good people behold one another’s consciences, why, according to the stated notion of judging, will they not judge one another? Thus, just as inferiors are judged by superiors, so superiors will be judged by inferiors.

[Col. 1180A] Or perhaps the more perfect will see the consciences of their inferiors, whereas the inferiors will not see the consciences of the perfect? But if all superiors see the consciences of inferiors, surely all the good will see the consciences of the evil. Why then are not any of the elect said to judge the reprobate, just as the apostles are? But if, for their greater confusion, the consciences of the wicked are laid open to all, why, equally, should the consciences of the good not be laid open to all for their greater glory? How, then, will those who see each other outwardly and inwardly not judge one another? What, therefore, is promised to the apostles as though it were something great, when the Lord says to them: “You also shall sit, judging the twelve tribes of Israel”?

[Col. 1180B] From this perplexity of statements, I think it is clear how deeply truth lies concealed beneath a covering in all these matters. First, then, it must be understood that judgment is considered in one way insofar as it is exercised solely in thought, and in another way insofar as it is exercised in act. The former is of foreknowledge; the latter, so to speak, of experience. The former belongs to knowledge; the latter to execution. The former belongs to the present life; the latter to the future life.

Therefore, that judgment called foreknowledge does not prevent that in which the sentence is executed. Thus the judgment of the present life does not remove that of the future life; indeed, if the latter were not to come, the former would be nothing. If, then, you consider the judgment of the present Church according to the mode of this life, you will find four orders, or rather five. For, apart from those whom it knows will rise to the place of judges, it is certain concerning some that they are condemned, certain concerning others that they are saved; and regarding those about whom it has no certain sentence, it knows that some belong to life and others to death.

[Col. 1180C] But with respect to the final examination of the future life, only three orders are found. Some judge and are not judged; others are judged and saved; others are judged and condemned. You now see, I think, how rightly those who are already called judged are also said still to be judged. For the judgment foreknown in the present is inflicted in the future.

Yet it may still seem wonderful to some that those who after death have received recompense according to the quality of their merits are still to come to judgment and to be judged for their merits—especially those who have both recognized and received the sentence of their condemnation. [Col. 1180D] It must therefore be understood that judgment is sometimes partial and sometimes complete. It is partial when it concerns the quality of the sentence only, not its quantity. Such is the judgment of the present Church. For we know concerning some the quality of their sentence—that is, whether they are to be condemned or saved—but in this life we cannot know the quantity of punishments even for any one condemned person.

But the judgment that follows a person’s death will be dispensed not only in quality but also in quantity, according to the measure of merits. The quantity of recompense will be proportioned both according to number and according to magnitude: according to number, so that where guilt was manifold, punishment too may be manifold; according to magnitude, so that in every kind of sin, where guilt was greater, punishment may be more intense.

[Col. 1181A] The judgment of this life, therefore, appears uniform, for, as we have said, it concerns the quality of the sentence alone. But that which is given at a person’s death appears manifold, though not universal in every respect. For although it is measured according to the whole of a person’s life, it is not according to the whole of what the person is. Although each receives at death according to what he has done in the body, he receives it in the soul alone, not in soul and body together.

[Col. 1181B] See, therefore, the difference between this second and that third and final judgment: this which occurs at each person’s death, and that which will occur in the common resurrection of all. This, as was said, concerns the whole of a person’s life, yet not according to the whole of what the person is. But that final judgment will concern the whole and be according to the whole. This takes place with some persons and before some persons; that will take place simultaneously concerning all and before all.

See how rightly one who here did not fear to offend the Lord of all is confounded before all. See how rightly one who glorified the Lord of all in all things is glorified before all. See how rightly the chief of perdition receives before all the disgrace of his overthrow, who from the beginning of all laboured for their overthrow.

[Col. 1181C] Consider, moreover, how fitting—or, if I may say so, necessary—that final judgment is. We often criticize divine judgments as if they were unjust; we often murmur against his scourges. There, with the apostolic men judging, it will be made manifest before all how the Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works. That final judgment, then, will be altogether complete, so that it sufficiently answers the consciences both of each individual and of all together. It will therefore be universal in every respect, able to satisfy every question.

Let the first judgment therefore be called uniform, the second manifold, and the third universal in every respect. The first and second judgments are partial; the third alone will be complete. For although the second is much fuller than the first, the third will nevertheless be incomparably fuller than the second. Thus, as the first requires the second, so the second requires the third.

[Col. 1181D] One question alone remains: what is that manner of judging which is promised to the apostles when it is said, “You also shall sit, judging the twelve tribes of Israel,” or, “The saints shall judge nations and rule peoples” (Wisdom 3)? Let us see what John says of this judgment when he writes in his Apocalypse: “And I saw,” he says, “the dead, great and small, standing before the throne; and books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged from the things written in the books, according to their works” (Revelation 20).

What are we to understand by these books but the consciences of individuals? The opening of the books, then, is the manifestation of consciences. In these books is inscribed whatever they retain in memory. In these books, as though written, is preserved whatever they comprehend with full understanding. [Col. 1182A] In some books of this kind human merits are contained; in others, divine judgments also. In the former is the quality of actions; in the latter, the quality of recompenses as well.

For each person carries in his heart, as though written there, that by which his own conscience accuses or defends him. But those who attend divine contemplation, who read daily in the book of Wisdom, transcribe, as it were, into the volumes of their hearts whatever they already comprehend by a clear understanding of truth. What, then, are the consciences of those to be judged but, so to speak, written records of actions? And what are the hearts of the judges, divinely instructed in all truth, but certain decrees, as it were, of canons? From this double writing is drawn every sentence by which each of those to be judged is condemned or absolved.

[Col. 1182B] Thus, to judge persons is nothing other than for the books of their actions to be opened before the judges—that is, for them to be unable to conceal their consciences from the judges. And for the judges to read in such documents is nothing other than to penetrate the hidden things of consciences by manifest vision, and to recognize without doubt the merit in which each person excels or the filth in which each is stained.

Moreover, for judges to open the books of their decrees before those to be judged is to admit the sight of any inferiors to an inspection of their hearts and to reveal their understanding in matters pertaining to the rule of judgment. Those to be judged, while they read in such decrees, as it were of the canons, find the sentence of recompense and the reason for the sentence which each deserves. To read such a writing, then, will be for them to receive the sentence of judgment. And for the apostolic men to judge each of those to be judged will be to set before their eyes the reason for the sentence being given.

[Col. 1182C] Certainly, if I had an ear open to the word of the heart as I have to the word of the mouth, you could teach me by thought alone whatever you wished concerning your secrets. For to think the things to be taught would be to teach them, and to understand one thinking the things to be taught would be to have learned the things to be learned. Everything said by one who understands is thought before it is said. Therefore, when a question has been proposed, to think out the solution would be to solve the question, if we could see one another’s thoughts.

[Col. 1182D] See how easy instruction would be if we had an ear open to the thought of another’s heart—how much more if we had an eye open to that person’s understanding. Attend to what I say. It is one thing to see a thought, and quite another to see an understanding. I have many things in my knowledge which I do not at present have in thought. Countless matters are those concerning which I hold a certain and ready judgment, though at present I think nothing about them. In such matters, whenever I wish, I can see my understanding and bring it into consideration.

What takes place in my heart, I suppose, also takes place in yours. If, then, I could see your heart as it sees itself, the ignorance of my heart could often be instructed by contemplation alone of your understanding; and what is now done by the word of the mouth would then be done by the word of the heart. For what is it for the heart to speak except to have such an understanding? The word of the heart: the judgment [of] understandings. [Col. 1183A]

> [Note: [Col. 1183D] Something is missing here.]

Therefore, to have seen and understood the judge’s judgment through an inspection of his heart is to have given and received judgment. In that final examination, will not the conscience of those to be judged, even while remaining silent, declare before those who judge: “Such and such is my fault”? Will not the understanding of those who judge, even while remaining silent, affirm before those to be judged that for such and such a fault such and such a punishment is due? For what is this confession or attestation except a mutual revelation, one to another, of consciences or understandings?

[Col. 1183B] Perhaps you wonder at what you hear. Hear further matter for wonder. Certainly, if we could read one another’s understandings in each other’s hearts in turn, a hundred persons could consult you at one and the same time concerning different questions and receive an answer. Would it not be the same for each to have received the solution of the question proposed and to have read the certain truth of your judgment in your heart? Nothing, then, prevents, at the final examination, even one judge from giving different sentences to different persons simultaneously and in the same instant for different causes.

Otherwise, how will twelve people be able to judge the twelve tribes of Israel, unless perhaps you think they will spend much time on this business? Or, because many enter the number of judges, must we suppose that they will divide the office among themselves and thus, by some method or order, hasten the business? But how small, I ask, is the number of judges compared with those to be judged?

[Col. 1183C] Why, then, do we not believe concerning invisible things what we prove in visible things by the testimony of analogy? Certainly, if solutions to many questions were written in one volume, opened before many readers, and read by different persons on different questions, it could at one and the same moment, simultaneously and at the same time, satisfy different persons concerning different matters and untie the knots of doubts. Why, then, should it not be believed that an incorporeal page inscribed by the finger of God can provide to incorporeal eyes what a corporeal page written by a human finger is proved to provide to corporeal eyes?

[Col. 1183D] Perhaps you say in response: “Let us grant that one and the same judge can, in the same instant, satisfy many persons in their several cases according to the reasoning of the analogy presented. But must we likewise grant that one and the same human being can, all at once and simultaneously, both render an account for everything he has done and receive for each particular act the sentence of recompense? For we have testimony from the Gospel that we must render an account even for every idle word” (Matthew 12).

[Col. 1184A] But if we believe that we must answer individually and successively for particular words or deeds, thoughts and wills, how much time, I ask, must be spent in examining one who, as is written, lived nine hundred years and more? Yet we wonder at, or scarcely believe, things which we have not experienced. We wonder, indeed, because meanwhile we do not see other people’s consciences, and know our own only by groping and only in part.

Certainly, if it happens that someone enters any house amid the thick darkness of night, he can discover by touch many things that lie hidden there. But if another arrives and enters with a lamp, consider how many things that person can show to himself and others by one simple glance—not only things which he could scarcely have come to know by touch over a long time, but also things which he could in no way have discovered by touch.

For, to say nothing of other cases, when could we distinguish by touch between white and black, between beautiful and ugly, as we judge them at once by the light of a lamp under a single first glance? And what are the hearts of the perfect, illumined by the radiance of divine wisdom, but lighted lamps? Of these lamps the Lord threatens when he speaks through the prophet: “At that time I will search the houses of Jerusalem with lamps” (Zeph. 1). Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” The houses of Jerusalem, therefore, are secure consciences; for these are those which seem to possess inward peace. What, then, will become of the houses of Babylon, when even the houses of Jerusalem must be searched with lamps? What will become of shameful and despairing consciences, if the presumption of confidence is taken away even from those who are wrongly secure? The houses of Jerusalem, therefore, are said to be searched by the Lord, because even in those consciences which seemed secure to themselves, nothing hidden, nothing unexamined, will remain which is not exposed by the light of truth.

The Lord declares that he will carry out this searching of houses with lamps because he will judge even hidden thoughts and wills through the ministry, undoubtedly, of those whom the supreme understanding of truth has inwardly enlightened for every examination of judgment. Therefore a certain radiance of divine light will shine forth from the hearts of the perfect, and will lay bare to each person, in manifest vision, all the good and evil things hidden in that person’s heart. Consider how, when bodily light is admitted, someone immediately surveys everything in his house, and apprehends under one simple glance not only the quantity but also the quality of things. Yet it is certain that that incorporeal light is far more excellent and far more effective in its own kind than this light is, or can be, in its own kind. Therefore it is too little to say, as I said, that that incorporeal ray fully reveals each individual to himself; indeed, it reveals him both to himself and to others.

We see how, at the first beam of the rising sun, it restores to every eye those things which blind night had taken away from every eye, and how everything that was formerly concealed at once lies open. The mountaintops scarcely yet receive the beam of light, and already, from the reflection of light which they cast back into the valleys, everything there, everything done there, becomes apparent to everyone. Thus indeed the highest and most perfect men, founded in perpetual steadfastness, exalted in astounding sublimity, and truly eternal mountains, immediately receive the ray of divine wisdom; and, from the reflection they have received—which, so to speak, they diffuse in every direction—they bring to light in an instant everything which ought to be made manifest in accordance with judgment.

Hence is that saying which you hear in the Psalms: “You shine forth wondrously from the eternal mountains” (Ps. 75). By now, I think, you partly perceive how this illumination from the eternal mountains is wondrous beyond all doubt. For from the light of divine splendor which they receive immediately, as they pour it forth upon those beneath them, they disclose by unambiguous vision every quality, both of merits and of recompense, in whatever persons are to be judged. Certainly, while we are still in this life, when we wish to enlighten some persons, we cannot enlighten many at the same time toward the same end, much less different persons toward different ends. But if we cannot simultaneously and at one time instruct different persons in different things, how much less can we instruct one and the same person in many and very different things? Consider, then, how wondrous is that illumination in which, under one vision, every individual among a vast multitude is simultaneously and at once enlightened concerning innumerable matters.

But because we cannot yet prove by experience this expansion of the mind, by which the human spirit is expanded in God’s light so as to comprehend so many things under one vision, we find it difficult to believe. Here there comes to mind what the venerable Pope Gregory writes concerning blessed Benedict (*Dialogues*, book II, ch. 35). For he relates that, on one occasion, while Benedict was engaged in nocturnal prayers, a light suddenly poured down from above, and the whole world, as though gathered beneath a single ray of the sun, was brought before his eyes. But let us hear what Gregory himself adds, as though explaining this: “When it is said that the world was gathered before his eyes, heaven and earth were not contracted; rather, the mind of the beholder was expanded.”

If, then, the mind of one still placed in this world could be so greatly expanded in God’s light—though surrounded by mortal flesh and remaining thus far under the condition of this life—what ought we to believe concerning that state of the life to come, in which we shall mutually behold one another’s consciences? But if innumerable things can fall under one glance when bodily light is admitted, how much more ought we to believe that incomparably more can be comprehended under one simple vision when that incorporeal light is admitted? If, therefore, in accordance with the analogy of their respective properties, we grant to incorporeal light what experience proves concerning visible light, I do not know what prevents that final judgment from occurring with complete speed.

Or perhaps the Lord intended to express this very thing by a comparison when he said: “As lightning comes forth from the east and appears as far as the west, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24). Certainly, when lightning appears, it appears suddenly and vanishes with complete speed. Must we then believe concerning that light which uncovers the consciences of the wicked and shows what sort of things they deserve, that it will suddenly appear to them and suddenly vanish, although the memory of what they have seen will by no means perish? For perhaps it was not without reason that he compared his coming to lightning rather than to a ray of the sun. For the sun’s ray also extends from east to west, but lightning never appears except briefly; the sun’s ray usually behaves very differently.

It will therefore appear as lightning, reaching from east to west, from one end to the other, so that with wondrous speed it may bring into the light all things which are, will be, or have been anywhere on earth, and so that, so far as the reckoning of judgment is concerned, all things may simultaneously and at once come forth for manifestation. “We shall all rise,” says the Apostle, “but we shall not all be changed. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye,” etc. (1 Cor. 15). He who can restore all bodies with such haste, surely can, with the same speed, illumine all hearts in whatever ways and to whatever extent he wills.

If we do not think that a ray of such brightness as we described above shines forth from the hearts of apostolic men, what shall we say of that heart in which dwells the brightness of eternal light, in which are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, in which dwells the fullness of that light “which enlightens every human being coming into this world”? Surely no believer dares doubt that light sufficient for all things can shine forth from Christ’s heart; and consequently no one presumes to deny that apostolic men immediately receive the rays of so great an illumination and pour them forth upon others, so that the written saying may stand: “You shine forth wondrously from the eternal mountains.”

Therefore apostolic men will undoubtedly surpass other human beings—indeed, all evil spirits—not only in penetration of the understanding of truth, but also in the prerogative of power, so that no one whatsoever among all the rest will be able either to refute their sentence or resist their force. For even the demons who torment, who formerly dragged human beings to torments, will then, with the order reversed, be assigned to penal places according to the decrees of judging human beings. Behold, I think, it is now apparent what is that prerogative of judicial power granted to apostolic men by the one Lord of all. Behold, what was formerly thought of no consequence has been found to possess such sublimity that the less learned can scarcely believe it.

[Col. 1185]

## TREATISE ON THE SPIRIT OF BLASPHEMY

What is read in the Gospel concerning the spirit of blasphemy is, as you say, very obscure and perplexing. You ask and expect to hear from me what I think about it. Yet it is a dangerous presumption to rely upon one’s own ingenuity concerning a matter which most brilliant minds have left, not untouched, but undefined. It certainly belongs to the Lord alone to reveal such matters when and to whom he wills. But, to confess the truth, it seems to me very hard to fail your request altogether. Therefore, if anything seems possible concerning this obscurity, let us speak by inquiry, not by definition.

There are some who confess that they do not know what the spirit of blasphemy is. Yet they boldly maintain that this kind of fault is altogether inexpiable, so that whoever has fallen into it even once can thereafter by no means be saved. There are also men of the highest authority who believe that no sin is inexpiable except what impenitence renders incurable. Hence comes the opinion of those who think that sin against the Holy Spirit occurs through impenitence, because in this matter one acts especially against him through whom there is all forgiveness of sins.

Some think that the sin against the Holy Spirit is to despair of God’s mercy because of the enormity of one’s crimes. But if such a person returns again to truth and truly repents, who would deny that forgiveness lies open to him? Observe, therefore, that for despairing persons impenitence alone closes the way of salvation. Some think that to have an obstinate mind is the sin against the Holy Spirit. According to them, obstinacy is the utmost hardening of the mind, so hardened that it can no longer repent. But what in itself removes from them the place of pardon except persistence in impenitence? What we have therefore said of the despairing, let us say also of the obstinate: impenitence closes to them the way of salvation.

Others also, who call sin against the Spirit an incurable evil, affirm that it becomes so because people are immediately hardened in such a way that they cannot thereafter repent. But on this account itself they lack every remedy: because they cannot repent. Observe, therefore, that the opinion of all these converges on this one point: impenitence alone makes sins insoluble.

It should be noted, however, that they say the impenitent sin against the Holy Spirit, but they do not say that all the impenitent possess the spirit of blasphemy. In accordance with the fact that Holy Scripture specially attributes power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Holy Spirit, they say that to sin through weakness is to sin against the Father; to sin through ignorance is to sin against the Son; but to sin through malice alone is to sin against the Holy Spirit. Those who sin through weakness or ignorance, just as they have some excuse in their fault, so receive some remission in their punishment. But those who sin against the Holy Spirit by sinning through malice alone receive no such remission, and it is not forgiven them in this age or in the age to come. For if they repent, full satisfaction is required of them; if they do not repent, full condemnation. Yet although those who sin through malice are said to sin against the Holy Spirit, not all such persons can be said to possess the spirit of blasphemy, just as not all the impenitent possess it.

From the Lord’s own words we may gather that this kind of fault is more detestable than all others. Let us therefore inquire more carefully what sort of sin is most detestable of all. Some human sins relate especially to one’s own corruption, such as drunkenness and sexual immorality; some especially to injury of one’s neighbor, such as murder and theft; some especially to insult against God, as blasphemy does. But who does not know that insulting the Creator is more detestable than the rest?

But if someone blasphemes under compulsion of torments or through deception by ignorance, who would deny that this is more tolerable than blaspheming when led by malice alone? Therefore, in its malice, blasphemy is the worst of all. Yet within this class there is something most wicked, in which malice reaches its height: when someone delights in insults against God and glories in them. What is blasphemy but disparagement of God? Each person aspires to what his inclination pursues and strongly desires. What else, then, does the spirit of blasphemy seem to be but an inclination and desire to disparage God?

Someone may wonder, and perhaps not believe, that human corruptibility can still ascend—indeed, descend—to such a degree of malice. But let the person troubled by such a thought hear what the Lord says concerning people of this sort: “But now they have hated both me and my Father” (John 15). Certainly, whatever anyone hates, he disapproves, disparages, and desires to be hated and disparaged by others as well. Hence those who were such people said of Christ that he had an unclean spirit (Matt. 3). Certainly they did not say this because they believed it true; for they constantly saw him do things which no one could do unless God were with him. Yet they said it because they wished to stir up in others hatred and disparagement of the one whom they hated.

Observe, therefore, how contrary these spirits are: the spirit of blasphemy and the Spirit of God. The spirit of blasphemy aspires to hatred of God; the Holy Spirit inspires love of God. For “the love of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). You see, then, how the spirit of blasphemy opposes the Holy Spirit and always strives toward the contrary. Of this spirit the Lord says that it will not be forgiven human beings (Matt. 12). He refers to the same thing when elsewhere he says: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but is liable to an eternal sin” (Mark 3).

From these words of the Lord, I think, those who call the spirit of blasphemy an altogether incurable evil draw an argument for their assertion. I believe Augustine read these things, yet understood them very differently from them. What the Lord says through the Prophet, “I will turn [them] into the depths of the sea” (Ps. 67), Augustine understands concerning persons in the most desperate condition. Elsewhere he says that the Lord makes teachers of the obstinate, in that “he sends his crystal like a morsel” (Ps. 147). In his *Retractations* he accuses—or rather excuses—himself for having written somewhat incautiously in one place concerning sin against the Holy Spirit; yet he had spoken it as an opinion rather than an assertion. There he plainly says that no one, however wicked in this life, is to be despaired of; rather, one ought to pray for him, since one does not pray presumptuously for a person of whom one does not despair.

For what is it to say that there is a kind of sin for which a person cannot obtain forgiveness? What else, I ask, is it to say this than to teach such a person to despair, and, with Cain, to say: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness” (Gen. 3)? Who would dare say that the measure of human malice exceeds the measure of divine mercy? The Psalmist says of the Lord: “With him is abundant redemption” (Ps. 129). But how, I ask, will it be abundant if there is a kind of sin which it never dissolves in anyone? Behold, according to some, a limit to our misery is found from which no one turns to the Lord, contrary to the saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. 21). Would it not be better humbly to confess that one understands those words of the Lord only slightly, than by one’s exposition to drive some persons into despair? Would it not be better to follow the opinion of that great theologian of our time—I mean Master Hugh—than to cut off for some persons the bridge of mercy and cast them down into the depths of despair? Above we briefly sampled his view; now let us proceed to consider the explanation in accordance with its tenor.

According to the evangelist Matthew, you hear the Lord saying: “Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven human beings, but the spirit of blasphemy shall not be forgiven; and whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12). First he states the general proposition, then he excepts what is to be excepted. He sets forth things forgivable, and excepts things unforgivable. “The spirit of blasphemy,” he says, “is not forgiven,” because this evil contains in itself no excuse and deserves to receive no remission on the ground of excuse.

What he said concerning this evil, he adds likewise concerning every word spoken against the Holy Spirit: “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” What will those say here who consign everyone who blasphemes the Spirit even once to eternal damnation? Will they say that everyone who utters any word whatever against the Holy Spirit will perish eternally? If they recoil from saying this, let them explain to us how we ought to understand the statement concerning a word spoken against the Holy Spirit, that it shall not be forgiven in this age or in the age to come. For if they say that this evil is expiable, but nevertheless unforgivable in some respect, they should see whether the same may not be said of the spirit of blasphemy.

For it is one thing for a sin to be inexpiable, and another for it to be unforgivable in the sense in which that term is used here. The devil’s sin is inexpiable, because it cannot be purged by any remedy. But that human sin may fittingly be called unforgivable to which no relaxation of punishment is granted, as can occur in sins actually similar. Behold: one person commits the same blasphemy under compulsion; another through some deception; a third through malice alone. In these three, the fault is in every respect alike as regards the action. Yet the first two receive some remission because they have some excuse. The third receives no such remission because he has no excuse.

The first of these sins against the Father; the second against the Son; the third—the one to whom it is not forgiven—sins against the Holy Spirit. This is what the Lord says according to the evangelist Mark: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever” (Mark 3). When forgiveness is said to be given or not given, according to the reciprocal relation of those who receive or do not receive it, this must be understood of the same deed. For in the strictest judgment, for the same blasphemy something is forgiven those who blaspheme against the Father and the Son, but nothing to those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit.

It is therefore rightly said of one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit that he has no forgiveness forever. For if he repents, nothing is remitted to him from the fullness of the strictest expiation; if he does not repent, nothing is remitted to him from the fullness of the strictest condemnation. Why this rightly occurs is added next when he says: “But he is liable to an eternal sin.” This means the same as if he had said more openly: “For this reason he has no forgiveness, nor ought he to have it, because he is not liable for such a sin as should have anything remitted to it.” Rather, he is liable for the worst of all sins, because he is liable to an eternal sin; and he is such that no determinate relaxation of punishment ought to be granted him, as we have taught above. That is, to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit is to utter a word of blasphemy through malice alone.

But such blasphemy can never be a sin without detestable and execrable hatred of God; and, beyond doubt, hatred of God is an eternal sin. An eternal sin is called that which never fails, that which continues forever. Certainly, just as love of God never fails, so hatred of God never fails: “Love,” says the Apostle, “never fails” (1 Cor. 13). What the Apostle said concerning love of God may also be said concerning hatred of God. And just as love of God may properly be called eternal merit, so hatred of God is rightly called an eternal sin. The statement concerning charity, that it never fails, should not be understood to mean that once possessed it cannot be lost, but that, unlike faith and hope, it does not cease to exist eternally.

Thus some evils have a place only in this life, such as adulteries and thefts; but others have a place both in this life and the future. For one who departs this life in hatred of God wastes away forever under the same disease; and one who hates eternally sins eternally, and by sinning without cessation deserves to suffer without cessation. Whoever, therefore, is guilty of divine hatred is guilty of an eternal sin. But, as was shown above, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is never without hatred of God. It is rightly said, therefore, of such a blasphemer that he is liable to an eternal sin.

Some, however, add from themselves what the Lord does not say to what he says. The Lord says that he is liable to an eternal sin; they say that he is eternally liable to an eternal sin. For does not one who says that such a person can by no means obtain forgiveness say that he is eternally liable to an eternal sin? Perhaps they infer this from the Lord’s declaration: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever.” But was not the same thing said by the same Lord concerning a word spoken against the Holy Spirit? “Whoever speaks,” he says, “a word against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.” How many people, I ask, can be found who dare say that they have never uttered some word against the Holy Spirit? Are all the rest to be despaired of who do not presume to say this? Must those who do not dare say it despair of themselves? But if, through such teaching, an ox or an ass falls into the pit of despair, I fear that the Lord of animals may demand from the hand of the teacher—or rather, the thrower-down—the price of human animals.

Some are temporarily liable for a temporal and transitory sin; some are eternally liable for a temporal and transitory sin. Again, others are eternally liable for an eternal sin. Why should there not also be others temporarily liable for an eternal sin? Adultery is actually committed in time and passes away, and it makes the adulterer liable; but liable temporarily if he truly repents, and eternally if he refuses to repent. Whoever passes from this life in hatred of God will be eternally liable for an eternal sin. Thus too, a sin which, as we have said, can be called eternal makes one who truly repents liable only for a time. Since, according to divine justice, persons can be eternally liable for a temporal sin, why should some not be believed, according to divine mercy, to be liable for an eternal sin only for a time? “His mercies are over all his works.” Indeed, nothing is more wondrous than his mercies, and for that very reason they are above all his works.

Let us consider further what Mark adds of his own to the words the Lord had spoken: “For they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit’” (Mark 3). In these words the evangelist seems to give the reason why the Lord spoke of the worst kind of blasphemy. The evangelist shows, therefore, that the Lord taught them about blasphemy which has no forgiveness because they were saying that he had an unclean spirit. Beyond all ambiguity, this insult to Christ was detestable blasphemy. But, I ask, was that blasphemous word against the Son of Man himself, or against the Holy Spirit? If it was against the Son of Man, it will be a forgivable word; if against the Holy Spirit, it will be unforgivable. But if it is called a forgivable word, it has nothing to do with that blasphemy which has no forgiveness forever; and thus what the evangelist adds does not answer the Lord’s preceding words.

The coherence of the statements therefore compels us to believe that Christ’s slanderers blasphemed against the Holy Spirit. What, then, shall we say? Did they sin against him whom they did not disparage, and did they not blaspheme him whom they profaned with their words? Who is adequate for these things? From authority and reason together we may clearly gather that those who profaned Christ blasphemed so wickedly, not through ignorance but through malice alone. They understood beyond all ambiguity that no one could perform such signs unless God were with him. Therefore, because they blasphemed through malice alone, they sinned against him to whom goodness is customarily especially attributed; and for this very reason, so far as that kind of sin is concerned, they were unworthy of mitigation and remission of the most severe punishment.

For if they had sinned through ignorance and transgressed against him who is the wisdom of God, they would have been dealt with more leniently in punishment for their sin and would have received some remission in it. From these words of the Lord it is plainly gathered that some things common to all the Persons are appropriated to certain Persons not without great mystery. There remain many matters concerning these words of the Lord worthy of diligent investigation. But it is better and wiser to leave this to deeper minds. Concerning what you asked of me, I have said what I could. “If I have become foolish, you compelled me.”

[Col. 1191]

## ON THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN MORTAL AND VENIAL SIN

Because I could not satisfy your question orally, I shall try, if possible, to satisfy it in writing. You say that you learned from teachers that venial sin is punished by a temporal penalty, whereas mortal sin deserves everlasting punishment. From this you proceed to ask concerning those who, according to Job, “spend their days in prosperity and in a moment go down to hell” (Job 21): if they are overtaken and seized with both venial and mortal sin, whether something is added, on account of venial sin, to the punishment which they suffer for mortal sin. I have not dared deny this, because no sin is believed to go unpunished.

But you go further and ask whether that addition is eternal for them. Nor do I presume to deny even this, reading and believing that in hell there is no redemption. “What then,” you say, “is the teaching of our masters, by which a distinction is made between the two, if both are punished by eternal punishment? And how is it called venial if it deserves no pardon eternally? And if it does deserve pardon, why does the just Judge grant it no pardon eternally? Would not anyone of this kind seem condemned to eternal death even if, with the punishment for all criminal sins removed, he suffered eternally only this punishment inflicted for venial sin? And on this account would not even such a sin more properly be called mortal than venial? For it is called venial in relation to a graver sin; by the same reasoning fornication can be called a venial sin in relation to adultery, and adultery in relation to a heinous crime.”

These are your objections and the grounds of your astonishment. But, although you endeavor to prove from one consideration that both the sins mentioned are mortal, I wonder why you do not attend equally to another consideration and contend by the same reasoning that both are venial. For just as in some persons both are punished by eternal punishment, so in some persons both are purged by temporal punishment. For just as in the unrepentant who despise them both are struck by eternal punishment, so in those who confess and truly repent both are cleansed by transitory punishment. What then? Will both be venial and not venial, mortal and not mortal?

But if you wish rightly to distinguish between them, you must consider what each does in itself, without the addition of the other. Behold, some person rich in many merits departs this life with one venial sin of whatever kind; overtaken by death, he could have no opportunity to confess or repent. Will he incur eternal death on account of it, rather than receive forgiveness when temporal punishment has cleansed him? Again, suppose another person, engaged in many good works, suddenly falls into one mortal sin and is overtaken by sudden death, having no time whatever to confess or repent. Do you think that he can escape eternal death through transitory punishment? Who would say or presume to say this?

From these examples, I think, one may observe, at least in those who believe in Christ, what each sin does in itself, and with how much reason one is called venial and the other mortal. Behold, I think, my assertion differs little from the opinion of your teachers, if we weigh the meaning rather than the words. To say what I think concerning your question, and to distinguish briefly between venial and mortal sin: venial sin seems to me to be that which, in those reborn in Christ, never of itself brings eternal punishment, even if the remedy of repentance is absent. Mortal sin, however, even if it is alone, brings eternal death if the remedy of repentance is absent.

Venial sin in those reborn in Christ, insofar as it stands alone, always belongs to forgiveness; mortal sin, insofar as it stands alone, always belongs to eternal death. Mortal sin, as it seems to me, is rightly distinguished in a threefold way. Mortal is that which no one can commit without great corruption of himself. Likewise, mortal is that which cannot be committed without serious injury to one’s neighbor. Mortal, moreover, is that which cannot be committed without great contempt of God. All other sins seem to me venial. Venial sin is guilt for which, insofar as it stands alone, eternal condemnation is never due through faith. Mortal sin is guilt for which, insofar as it stands alone, eternal condemnation is always due.

“Father’s almsgiving will not be forgotten, and good will be restored to you for your mother’s sin.”

“Your father’s almsgiving will not be forgotten; for good will be restored to you for your mother’s sin” (Ecclus. 3). “The first of these statements,” you say, “can be understood. Of the other, I do not know what it means.” Let us therefore consider the first.
