If we say that almsgiving cannot come into human forgetfulness, the saying will appear false, if that saying of Solomon does not deceive us: “There is no remembrance of former things, nor will there be remembrance of things to come among those who shall be in the end” (Eccles. 1). If the saying is referred to God’s memory, it will seem not so much false as frivolous. Does it not seem frivolous, I ask, to say that almsgiving is not forgotten by one of whom it is certain that nothing whatever can come into his forgetfulness?

If, therefore, these sayings are considered only superficially, one may perhaps think one frivolous and the other false. For why should good favor rather than wrath be restored for a mother’s sin? Yet, in any saying of the divine Scriptures, we no more dare say that there is anything frivolous than that there is anything false.

We must therefore carefully note what is said. It does not say, “a person’s almsgiving,” but “a father’s almsgiving.” Thus the reference is to the son in what Scripture says concerning the father. For a father’s almsgiving then seems, as it were, consigned to forgetfulness, when no grace whatever is bestowed by God upon the son on its account. What, then, does Holy Scripture wish to teach in this place, except that it lies in the son’s power whether his father’s almsgiving is or is not forgotten as regards himself, and—what is much more marvelous—that even his mother’s sin may benefit him?

Consider something marvelous, yet not false. It lies in you that no grace be bestowed upon you for your father’s good deed. Likewise, it lies in you that good favor be restored to you for your mother’s evil deed. Scripture tells you, therefore, what can be done, but leaves the manner of fulfilling it to your discernment. Let each statement, then, serve you as an emblem; for each requires interpretation. Would you briefly hear how your father’s good may benefit you? By honoring your father and at the same time imitating him. Would you likewise know how even your mother’s evil may benefit you? By honoring your mother, yet not imitating her.

What is said concerning the father’s almsgiving could truthfully have been said concerning the mother’s almsgiving; and conversely, what is said concerning the mother’s sin could have been said concerning the father’s sin. But, according to the custom of Holy Scripture, what is left unspoken in either place is implied in either. This should nevertheless be noted: both mother and father cherish and nurture their offspring more tenderly, and for that very reason are often loved by their offspring more ardently. Hence it happens that it is almost natural and nearly unavoidable to become accustomed to a mother’s vices. Greater merit therefore seems to lie in avoiding, from hatred of iniquity, the evil of one whom you love more; and conversely, in imitating, from love of virtue, the good of one less loved.

[Col. 1195]

## TREATISE ON THE DEGREES OF CHARITY

### CHAPTER ONE. On the invincibility of charity.

To a friend beloved in the tender mercies of Jesus Christ. The bridegroom’s left hand is under her head, and his right hand embraces her.

The infancy of your charity compels me, most beloved friend, to write something to you about charity, and to presume beyond myself and beyond the measure of my smallness—or rather, as I seem to myself to perceive it, to pour forth from emptiness and to give what I do not possess. My mind finds it difficult, I tell you, to consent to say anything concerning it, feeling that neither heart nor tongue suffices to treat it worthily. For how shall a man speak of love who does not love, who does not feel love’s power? Of other matters, indeed, abundant material presents itself in books; but this matter is either wholly within, or nowhere at all. [Col. 1195B] For it does not convey the secrets of its sweetness from outward things to inward things, but transmits them from inward things to outward. Therefore he alone speaks worthily of it who frames words according to what his heart dictates.

Do not wonder, then, if I would rather hear another speak of it than speak of it myself. I would hear, I say, one who dipped the pen of his tongue in the blood of his heart; for doctrine is then true and venerable when what the tongue speaks conscience dictates, charity suggests, and the Spirit inspires. You are mistaken if you think me such a man—indeed, I am mistaken myself. For it is pious in you, in that charity which “believes all things,” to think of me above what is in me. But it is hard for me to think well of myself when I do not possess that good; and even if I did possess something, perhaps it would be better that it remained unknown.

And when what is loved is not what exists, but what is thought to exist, it is not love or the lover that is nonexistent, but the thing loved. [Col. 1195C] O great power of charity, which calls things that are not as though they were! O mighty power, which, despoiling no one, seizes everything, makes all things your own, and takes from no one what is theirs, since by loving you acquire the good which you love in another! It may indeed happen that you labour in vain at the good which you do; but that I should love in vain is altogether impossible. Behold, here is the strength of love that you seek: who can resist it? It subjects all things to itself; it compels all things to serve its progress; it overcomes enemies by loving them, and makes them its friends even against their will. For though it may have rivals, it has no enemies at all.

[Col. 1195D] It alone does not fail amid adversities, because it is patient (1 Cor. 13); it does not repay injuries, because it is kind; another’s happiness does not torment it, because it does not envy; an evil conscience does not sting it, because it does no wrong; honour does not exalt it, because it is not puffed up; it does not strive for pre-eminence, because it is not ambitious; greed does not confine it, because it does not seek its own; injury does not provoke it, because it is not irritable; sinister suspicions do not defile it, because it thinks no evil; the evils of others do not delight it, because it does not rejoice in iniquity; [Col. 1196A] errors do not blind it, because it rejoices together with truth; persecutions do not break it, because it bears all things; perfidy does not harden it, because it believes all things, though not everyone; despair does not swallow it up, because it hopes all things; impatience does not cast it down, because it endures all things—that is, it patiently awaits all things promised by God; separation by death does not interrupt it, because it never fails.

What, then, is not conquered by death, when it is strong as death—indeed stronger than death, since it compelled death itself to die in the death of the Redeemer? O unconquerable power, charity, which has overcome even Him who is unconquerable, and has in some manner subjected to all things Him to whom all things are subject: for God, conquered by love, humbled himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming not merely man, but “the reproach of men and the outcast of the people”!

[Col. 1196B] For because of the excessive charity by which he loved us, he could not, in his wrath, restrain his mercies from exposing that beloved soul to enemies on behalf of his friends, in order to remove alike the terror and the force of death from his friends. And if charity was strong against God, how much more will it prevail against men?

Hence comes that fearless steadfastness of heart in the faithful, by which, scorning punishments and trampling death underfoot, they joyfully return to their homeland through the very jaws of death. Dying, they exult and taunt death, saying: “Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15). Now you are not a sting but a shout of joy, since through your midst you open a broad and joyous passage from misery into the kingdom.

[Col. 1196C] Thus charity makes them not fear, but desire, to die for him—or in him—by whom they see themselves so loved that, lest they themselves should die, he was willing to be condemned to a most shameful death. For, wondering at and embracing in Christ that excess of love by which, for the joy set before him, he endured the cross, despising human shame, they are ashamed not to render something in return. Spurred on by the mockeries of his Passion as by certain goads, they rush without restraint into the abyss of love, into the depth of charity, seeking wholly and only this: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115). Thus, carried beyond themselves in a certain sound and holy madness, they count themselves to love too little when they are so loved.

[Col. 1196D] For the vehement force of love is not restrained by reason, because, as the Apostle testifies, it surpasses knowledge in majesty (Eph. 3). It is not terrified, because it casts fear outside. It is not repressed by miseries, because it is perfected in weakness. Truly it is an all-powerful strength, which makes miseries themselves powerful, since it turns into aid those things prepared to harm. Supported by it, Christ’s soldiers fight without fear; certain of victory, they advance through the midst of dangers in complete safety, fearing neither demon nor man.

[Col. 1197A] Hence Paul, after enumerating the many dangers over which he had gloriously triumphed, adds the cause of his triumph: “In all these things we overcome through him who loved us” (Rom. 8). Secure amid the flashing spears and whirling darts of enemies raging on every side, he sleeps with charity, which alone is able to quench the fiery darts of the evil one, and which many waters cannot extinguish. Finally, it covers and overwhelms a multitude of sins, and will not be overcome by the dead flies of temptations. It prevails, subdues, and makes that Jebusite people and the other peoples of Canaanite stock serve as tribute and material for the exercise of virtue. It is surely a greater power to cast down an enemy already raised up than to repress one who is trying to rise.

[Col. 1197B] Therefore charity’s work is not to destroy temptations so that they do not arise, but, when they have arisen, to throw them down so that they do not advance. Thus it should be called not so much a powerful virtue as the power of virtues, because from it all receive the power truly to be virtues. This is the life of faith, the strength of hope, the inward force and marrow of all virtues. It orders life, kindles affections, gives form to acts, corrects excesses, and arranges conduct. Powerful for all things and prevailing over all things, it even makes omnipotence itself in some sense powerless.

Is not this what, in Moses, stood against divine justice and power and prevailed in strength? “Let me alone,” he says, “that my wrath may burn against this people” (Exod. 32). You hear, “Let me alone,” and need not doubt that God is held fast, and by no other force than the strength of love. You ask whose love? Surely that of the faithful servant who refused to become greater and more glorious through becoming a greater people in place of the people; not because he was held by a carnal affection, as is customary, but lest God’s glory should be assailed by the poisoned darts of blasphemers. “Do not, I beg,” he says, “let the Egyptians say: ‘He brought them out craftily in order to destroy them in the mountains, and was unable to bring them into the land that he promised’” (ibid.).

[Col. 1197C] Why should not power yield, and justice yield, where charity from so pure a heart did not so much ask as press its suit? O how greatly we suffer from the scarcity of such men, who would stand before the Lord on account of our sins, appease his wrath, and turn aside vengeance! “There is none,” says the prophet, “who calls upon your name, who rises up and holds fast to you” (Isa. 64). Love alone is the power that can hold God fast; by it he not only permits himself to be held, but also laments piously through the prophet that he is not held: “I sought among them for a man who would set up a hedge and stand in opposition before me on behalf of the land, lest I destroy it, and I found none” (Ezek. 22).

[Col. 1197D] God seeks someone to oppose him when he is angry—although mercy is properly his own, while vengeance is foreign to him. “His work is foreign to him”: what work? Surely the work of vengeance and wrath. Charity, therefore, in its strength restrains God’s outstretched hand lest it strike. It crushes Satan beneath its feet and heaps coals upon the heads of enemies. It is mighty not only against flesh and blood, but also against the principalities and powers of these darknesses, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places; strong in adversity, but stronger in prosperity.

[Col. 1198A] For Christ’s love alone wholly spurns and spits upon the blandishments of smiling and mocking fortune, delighted by a sweeter savour. In comparison with it, every sweetness is bitter, every pleasure grief; everything beautiful is ugly, everything pleasant troublesome. Let this suffice concerning charity’s unconquerableness; and if it does not match the abundance of the subject—which is exceedingly great—may it at least serve your occupation. Let us now proceed to its insatiability.

## CHAPTER II. On the Insatiability of Love

Certainly, love’s strength is produced by the sweetness which it feels; those who taste it easily love God by that taste. The soul despises everything that cannot be loved except by despising this sweetness, knowing that it cannot first find the Beloved unless it has passed beyond the form of this passing world with a certain contempt. [Col. 1198B] Hence, gathering itself wholly into itself, it no longer uses ascending steps or paces, but is carried by unexpected leaps and transports, flying rather than walking into those sublime, heavenly secrets. Thus Paul is said not to have ascended into the third heaven, but to have been caught up.

To be affected in this way is, as it were, to be deified: the mind, intoxicated with divine love, forgets all things and passes wholly into God, tasting what no one knows except the one who receives it. But whenever it shares that happiness, it must be unaware of this misery, since the two cannot coexist. Yet although mortals are sometimes permitted to attain this degree of love, they are altogether forbidden to remain there long, until, having cast off their corruptible remains, they have freely escaped into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.

[Col. 1198C] Nevertheless they strive and are drawn by desire for that face, which, according to the prophet, the Father has set as an adamant, so that it may draw all things of iron by the cords of charity (Hos. 11). Although this drawing has a certain sweet violence, it nevertheless signifies more the weakness of mortality: weighed down by its burden, the wretched soul often falls from its flight and fails in its endeavour, unless it is drawn by him who, lifted up from the earth, draws all things to himself.

Thus loving spirits, held back and stretched out by the body’s corruption, have frequent joy at God’s visitation, but no abundance of it, because they are permitted to be neither full nor lingering. Hence, in a certain delightful fashion, God seems meanwhile to play with the children of men. When he is thought to be held, he slips from their hands; pursued, he allows himself to be grasped; then, disappearing, he is not seen again until, called back anew by tears and prayers, he returns. Thus, although the visitation delights, its alternation troubles.

[Col. 1198D] But with what astonishment, do you suppose, is the soul overwhelmed when that sweetness is withdrawn and it is dragged captive back to these snares of the senses? Does it not seem, as though expelled from the homeland of spirits into the valley of bodies, to have fallen into some other world unknown to itself and far unlike the former—a world in which charity grows cold and sensuality reigns, the eye of the mind is dimmed and bodily sense flourishes? Then it clings and draws deep sighs from the very source whence it is made blessed. For the more pleasingly it had experienced those things, the more painfully it endures their withdrawal. The removal of the beloved thing is an increase of desire; and what you desire more ardently, you lack more painfully.

[Col. 1199A] This is love’s languishing, which is nothing other than the weariness of impatient desire by which the mind of one who loves intensely must be affected when the beloved is absent. O present absence and absent presence of him who is at once lost and possessed! In vain, I think, does anyone seek to soften the pain or moderate the grief of a soul thus languishing, when the sweet wound of love must be healed from within. The sacred bitterness of this hidden pain is soothed by no human comfort; for when the inward taste of sweetness has been removed, nothing outward can console it. Rather, in the judgment of blessed Job, it regards “all comforters as burdensome” (Job 30).

[Col. 1199B] He felt this who said: “My soul refused to be comforted; I remembered God, and was delighted” (Ps. 76). Blessed sadness, conceived not from the creature but from the Creator, which mourns none of the hardships of this present life! It is altogether fitting that one who refuses to be comforted by any abundance of fleeting things should have as comforter the God of all consolation. Therefore one who has learned to love nothing apart from God has nowhere, except in God, from which to receive consolation. Let others have their vain and varied comforts, to whom it is said: “Woe to you rich, who have your consolation here” (Luke 6). He alone is his own comforter who is also his indweller.

Charity is God, who, although he never fails the righteous for their merit, nevertheless often withdraws from them for their consolation; the former is more useful, the latter more pleasant. Thus the sweetness once possessed, though hidden, lies concealed when it does not touch the heart’s perception. But while the one whom it desires delays, the soul no longer slumbers or sleeps with those foolish ones. Shaken by frequent sighs and groans, it can no longer disguise its sadness or hide the fire that burns its sorrowful breast.

[Col. 1199C] It no longer deliberates, consults reason, feels shame, or knows measure and order. Its whole and sole concern is how the sweetness whose presence it desires may return; and it counts any speed, however great, as delay. This, sweetest friend, is what you once asked: what blessed Augustine means when he says, “The love of God takes no consolation from impossibility.” Every desire is usually softened by reason when the desired object cannot be possessed. Yet love’s violence is restrained by no impossibility.

[Col. 1199D] For although everyone knows it wholly impossible for a soul weighed down by earthly dwelling and sunk in mud to enjoy that happiness completely, this impossibility offers no comfort to one who loves in this way, preventing him from burning and glowing with desire to enjoy it. Though reason is blinded by this desire, God is not at all offended; for he seems to have intimated something similar in his command: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with all your mind” (Deut. 6). Though it is evident that this cannot be fulfilled by anyone in this mortal life—or rather, this life-like death—nevertheless it ought to be desired by every person. Thus it is said in the description of the righteous man: “He will desire exceedingly in his commandments” (Ps. 111).

[Col. 1200A] What is it to desire exceedingly, except to desire more than one can accomplish? In this sense, I think, it is also said: “The young maidens loved you exceedingly” (Song 1). For God, toward whom their love tends, is infinite and immeasurable; therefore love ought to have neither end nor measure. Such a loving soul loves, therefore; although it loves no less than its capacity permits, it nevertheless loves less than it wills. It takes no consolation from this impossibility, but rather receives an increase of desire.

“My soul,” says one, “has longed to desire your justifications” (Ps. 118). He could not be satisfied with desire who longed to desire nothing. For the soul’s hunger is desire. Thus the soul that loves God is not sated with love, because God is love; and whoever loves him loves love. But to love love makes a circle, so that love has no end. You see, therefore, how charity, as unconquerable, overcomes all things; and how, as insatiable, it devours all things and produces poverty from abundance, since from pleasures already tasted it burns ever more ardently in desire.

[Col. 1200B] And even if these things are granted in fullness, they are never granted unto satiety: “Those who eat me,” she says, “will still hunger” (Ecclus. 24). O good God, whom to love is to eat: how do you so refresh those who love you that they hunger the more, unless you are at once food and hungry? And one who has not tasted you does not at all know how to hunger for you. Therefore you feed in order to make them hunger: “He has filled the hungry,” says that maiden, “with good things” (Luke 1); he filled them, he did not sate them. For the goods of love satisfy less as they fill more.

[Col. 1200C] “He filled them with good things.” With what goods? Do not ask me what are the goods of charity. Surely I think them to be those of which it is said: “No eye has seen apart from you what you have prepared for those who love you”; and elsewhere: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). You hear that they are prepared for those who love, so that you may not doubt that they are the goods of love. For in charity are stored up the delights of eternity and every heavenly sweetness. In it are peace, patience, long-suffering, and joy in the Holy Spirit, and whatever the mind conceives as pleasant—and beyond it. These, I say, you have prepared for those who love you; but you have hidden them from those who fear you, until charity casts out the veil of fear, so that they may see how great is the abundance of your sweetness, which, though it fills, never satisfies.

I do not dare to say this even of those, if any there be, who are clothed with the second robe.

[Col. 1200D] Perhaps you object with the words: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16), and those addressed to the Jerusalem above: “He satisfies you with the fat of wheat” (Ps. 147). But you should understand that satiety there denotes abundance to one who desires, not an end of desire. For the end of desire, as someone has said, is satiety. But those who always hunger are plainly not sated. Yet blessed indeed is the hunger which hungers only for what it possesses, and possesses only what it hungers for.

Having thus persuaded your charity that no one can be sated in the future by the sweetness of divine love, nor filled with it in the present, may you take no consolation from this impossibility as your consolation. I wish you patience; but to be patient in this matter is more expedient.

## CHAPTER III. That Love Unceasingly Sees the Beloved

[Col. 1201A] Having touched on these matters in some fashion, let the pen run on to investigate the rest, insofar as God in his sweetness deigns to open a way to such worthy matters for one who is poor. Yet entry into these matters is more readily opened to those who knock devoutly than to those who search subtly. He knocks who desires and who prays; and to one who knocks, it is opened. For we must not doubt that he gladly opens to one knocking, since he urges even one who has not yet knocked to knock.

Thus God first wishes to be asked for what he promises; and therefore he first promises what he has determined to give, so as to provide boldness for prayer and to let devout prayer obtain what he was going to give freely. In this he exacts merits from us while he goes before us by granting what he may reward; he acts freely so that he may not grant freely. He is plainly worthy to be loved in return, since he thus goes before us in loving: “In this,” says John, “is charity: not that we loved him, but that he himself first loved us” (1 John 4).

[Col. 1201B] His love therefore precedes ours, more gracious indeed than ours; but ours is blameworthy, for he still loves the ungrateful freely, whereas we undoubtedly love by his gift and as a debt. He gives that by which, and accomplishes that whereby, he is loved, so that he may be loved alike from what is his own and for what is his own. I pass over the pursuit of this gift, because it is ineffable. For although it may be felt by a small number of spiritual persons, it can be expressed by no one. Only he who gives and he who receives know it; all others are excluded. Even to the recipients and possessors themselves the very bestowal is doubtful and uncertain—and this beneficially, lest they presume.

[Col. 1201C] But now, I ask you, my Severinus, turn your eyes to these lower things and see what most people, though seeing, do not see. Observe whether all things that either serve us in prosperity or rage against us in adversity are not certain spurs of charity, in some manner urging us forward in love’s course. For all things direct their courses toward providing for human needs and pleasures, or at least relieving deficiencies. Heaven and earth, sea and air, and the circuit of seasons—which renews ancient things with returning springs, reforms what has decayed, and restores what has been consumed—do not cease to accomplish this. And just as no one can reject these continual common benefits, so no one ought not to love him who does good.

[Col. 1201D] Perhaps you agree concerning prosperity; but you wish to know how adversities teach or demand love. Since human ingratitude often arrogantly claims for itself the Creator’s gifts, the same Creator of humanity wills, by a lofty and salutary counsel, that human beings should be exercised by tribulations, so that, when a human being fails and God comes to help, God may be loved by the human being as is fitting. This is what he says: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall honour me” (Ps. 49).

From the occasion of frequent needs, therefore, God must necessarily be frequently visited by human beings in tribulations; by being frequently visited, he is tasted; by being tasted, it is proved how sweet God is. Thus the iron heart that could not be softened by benefits melts into gratitude when schooled by scourges and by the deliverer’s grace; and it learns to love God, if not for his goodness, at least for its own benefit. This is the first degree of love for those beginning to love; but for those already loving, it is the lowest, when we love God not for his own sake but for ours (1 John 2).

[Col. 1202A] It is clear, therefore, how adversities instruct and in some manner compel even one who loves carnally and earthly things toward the love of God. But even after such people have been kindled with love, prosperity is sometimes withdrawn and adversity imposed, not by an inferior counsel, lest perhaps flattering prosperity should steal for itself some portion of love—which is difficult to avoid—and succeeding adversity should take it away. Adversity alone, according to the teaching of blessed John, truly teaches us “not to love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2).

Thus the Israelites are compelled by the Egyptians to leave Egypt (Exod. 12), because, as blessed Gregory testifies, while the world strikes the mind with calamities, it cries nothing other than that it should not be loved. Therefore love alone is what God requires of us, whether he overwhelms us with benefits, corrects us with scourges, instructs us by counsels, or binds us by commandments. Charity is the fullness of the law and contains the law and the prophets, because whatever is commanded or forbidden by divine law is reduced to love alone. Pay the tribute of love, and you will know that the Lord has been satisfied.

[Col. 1202B] “What then,” you say, “does such great frugality in our food, lowliness in our clothing, and continual austerity in vigils and disciplines profit us?” Receive the answer briefly: certain works are services of charity, pleasing to God and winning him over, if they are done in charity. But without charity they profit nothing. For this is the power in which no work, however small, is rejected, and without which no work, however great, is accepted: not preaching, even if it is performed in the tongues of angels; not faith, even if it moves mountains; not almsgiving, even if it distributes all one’s goods as food for the poor; not affliction of the body, even if the body is handed over so that it may burn; not the solemnities of Masses, because an offering is forbidden before reconciliation with one’s brother.

[Col. 1202C] For God himself is the lover of humanity, to whom every creature rightly confesses and says: “You have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15). Yet he requires from humanity only that which is certainly difficult for no one. For love alone, as blessed Augustine says, does not know the name of difficulty; though it has expended much for a friend, it judges that it has expended little or nothing. Hence those many years “seemed few to Jacob because of the greatness of his love” (Gen. 29). For the mind of a true lover scarcely feels, in comparison with love, whatever it suffers for the beloved, being so wholly intent on love that it is permitted to think of no pain apart from the beloved, because it bears the seal upon its heart and upon its arm.

[Col. 1202D] Finally, by what route could forgetfulness of him steal in, when, besides those rays of unsetting light, besides those streams of incorruptible sweetness by which he ineffably pours himself into the soul, he does not cease to show himself to one who loves even in visible things? For the whole lover of God, wherever he turns, has a familiar reminder of love. He uses these things as mirrors, and in everything that he sees the remembrance of his lover resounds back to him. He beholds all things that God has created and the end for which he created them; and in them God appears to him not so much admirable as lovable. From the pledge of love which he has already bestowed, he wisely estimates how great a dowry he has reserved.

[Col. 1203A] Love is surely a chaste and dove-like eye: in things granted for human use it fixes itself on no lust, but contemplates the eternal in transitory things. This is the eye that is not closed, because it lacks the eyelid of carnality; it is disturbed by no thing cast into it, because it admits nothing from without; no darkness blinds it, because there are no shadows in it; no sleep weighs it down, according to the witness of him who says: “I sleep, and my heart is awake” (Song 5).

It is a direct eye, truly a right eye, which no leftward intention turns aside and no earthly affection bends downward. It is a single and prudent eye, shaken by no uncertain suspicion and detained by no curious anxiety, gazing unceasingly upon him into whom the angels desire to look. For, as blessed Augustine says, vehement love cannot fail to see the one it loves, because love is an eye and loving is seeing.

[Col. 1203B] He who says, “You have wounded me with one of your eyes” (Song 4), confesses that he is wounded by this eye. The soul has, indeed, two eyes: one by which it understands, and another by which it seeks him who looks down upon the children of men to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God. Of these two, love is the right eye; it wounds by seeking. For the one who leaps over mountains and springs across hills—surpassing every sense, human and angelic alike—is grasped only by the wound of love.

You ask what it is for God to be wounded. I answer: it is for that omnipotence to condescend mercifully to our weakness, and, as if by a certain opening of a wound, to disclose the secrets of inward sweetness. He, therefore, can be wounded who, though impassible, is not without compassion. This wound is inflicted without anger and felt without pain.

[Col. 1203C] The king of the Ammonites attempts, by his unhappy treaty, to tear out this wounding eye: “On this condition,” he says, “I will make a covenant with you: that I may tear out the right eyes of all of you” (1 Sam. 11). For when love, which is the right eye, has been taken away, understanding alone remains for error; and this we have called the left eye. For their error was to understand without loving: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, but became vain in their thoughts” (Rom. 1). Many who seem to pursue errors are blinded by this very error; perhaps none worse can be found.

[Col. 1203D] Thus God is seen by lovers with both eyes, but he is wounded by one, because where understanding grows dim, love penetrates; and where the former is repelled, the latter is admitted. We are forbidden to search too deeply and to be wise beyond what is fitting, but we are commanded to love even beyond what we can accomplish. Therefore the eye of love cannot be stopped from seeing the one it loves. Though he is not seen as he is—which, according to blessed John’s testimony, is reserved as a reward (1 John 4)—yet he is indeed seen, insofar as he wills and insofar as, in the present, this is granted for consolation.

[Col. 1204A] For each lover sees according to the manner in which he loves: one in this way, another in that, according to the variety of affections by which they are drawn toward him. Some more fervently thirst after the mysteries of divinity. Others more securely marvel at the mysteries of humanity, contemplating God’s most high counsel concerning the salvation of the human race. Everything which the eye of love beholds is indeed safe: it alone now sees for merit and will one day see for reward, when the cloud of corruption has been removed. Then, as it is written, it “will see that face in joy” (Job 33).

Much more might be added that would profit the hungry, though not the fastidious; but lest I burden you with too long a discourse, I restrain my pen, though, I confess, it desires much more.

## CHAPTER IV. On Love’s Inseparability

Now let us come to the middle portion of your final request—especially to that matter which you urgently ask, most devout Severinus, to be explained by my lips indeed, but certainly through your merits, in which I trust not moderately, not only in studies but in every necessity.

[Col. 1204B] But so that the discourse may proceed in its proper course concerning the matters proposed, let what has been said be recalled in a brief summary. In what precedes, you have that charity fights unconquerably, tastes insatiably, and sees unceasingly. It burns in the hands and clings inseparably. So tenacious, indeed, is love’s glue that it is said not so much to join as to unite.

[Col. 1204C] Truly, according to the prophet, “a good glue” unites the man of virtue in three ways (Isa. 41): namely, to himself, to his neighbour, and to God, so that he agrees and cleaves to him in unity. Through love, a person is made one within himself, when, gathering himself within himself and withdrawing all his affections from the places where they are held captive, he loves one thing alone immutably and is no longer altered into diverse things. For a person dispersed through love among many things is nowhere found one and the same to himself, but is always unlike himself, because he is compelled to change as often as what he loves changes. Whoever leans upon what is falling must necessarily fall with it.

By charity, a person is united to his neighbour when, not only without complaint, so far as lies in him, he strives to become the same to all, but also adapts himself to the success of all: rejoicing with those who rejoice, weeping with those who weep, becoming weak with the weak, and burning with those who are scandalized, as it is written: “A companion in tribulation and kingdom” (Rev. 1). Thus the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; the text reads quam [cujus] (“which/whose”): neither diversity of wills nor private ownership of possessions divided their minds, but charity bound them firmly and sweetly held them together in the unity of the Spirit, in the bond of peace. [Col. 1204D]

Alas, into how inferior an age we have fallen! Alas, to what ends—or rather, to what dregs—of the ages have human beings come! For, to say nothing of worldly people, whom ambition has blinded, even the choice of religious life itself is scattered by such division in our miserable time that scarcely one person agrees with another in unity, unless perhaps against the Lord and against his Christ. Everywhere the cracks of David’s city appear, and they now gape so widely as altogether to threaten an approaching ruin.

Beneath one tunic and similar clothing is kept a variegated and wholly dissimilar heart, so that scarcely any signs of the ancient religious life remain. And to those who come to the Lord’s tomb—which is the cloister—seeking Christ, only the linen cloths lie open: that is, the form of the habit [lacuna].

[Col. 1205A] I confess that I am weary of being here; let us leave this place. For it is not our purpose here to speak of vices. Charity also unites God to humanity and humanity to God, not only by that ineffable union whereby our nature is united to the eternal Word in unity of person—a union accomplished by that charity through which he loved us before the foundation of the world—but also by that union of which the Apostle says: “He who cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6).

Certainly this is the unity of love by which a man according to God’s heart, with all his desires conformed to the heavenly and eternal will, is united to God by a glue that shall not dissolve and by a bond that shall not be broken. For charity is the bond of perfection, by which the members of the faithful cleave to one another in the closest embrace and are joined through every joint to their head into one body, sharing mutually in all good things, [Col. 1205B] so that each may confidently say: “I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments” (Ps. 118 [119]). Of this, I think, it was said: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccles. 4). It is called threefold because, as I said above, it binds in three ways. Would you have the Apostle describe the threefold cord for you? “The end,” he says, “of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 5 [1:5]). Only the pure heart does not know how to run out; nothing is more readily defiled than an exposed heart, which charity alone contains, lest it lie open to no purpose. Moreover, according to the Apostle, he has a good conscience toward all who loves his neighbor’s good as much as his own; for one who seeks his own interests is thereby shown not to have it. Unfeigned faith [Col. 1205C] is that which works through love; otherwise James does not hesitate to call it not merely feigned but even dead (Jas. 2). And truly this threefold cord is not easily broken: bound by it, Paul dares to say, “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness?” (Rom. 8). Surely it is a strong bond, against which no violence prevails, holding lover and beloved inseparably together.

Let no one suppose that I think—or rather, rave—with those who maintain that charity, once possessed, can no longer be lost. For if everyone who has charity also has perseverance, the Lord would vainly have warned his disciples, saying: “Remain in my love” (John 15). Yet on this point I would judge without hesitation that charity can be abandoned voluntarily, but cannot be violently taken away. It is offered to everyone, taken from no one, so that no one lacks it except through his own fault. But in order that the affections of lovers may flow together into one through this uniting power, the lover’s heart must melt away from itself, so that it can be poured out, transformed, changed into him whom it loves, and united to the other—just as a drop of water poured into wine seems wholly to lose itself when it takes on the other’s flavor and color. Hence those frequent failings—or rather, advances—of the devoutly loving: they feel nothing of themselves in themselves except what is in Christ Jesus. You know what I mean; no one knows it better than you. Only what is liquid fits every form, and this is especially fitting for the heart of a lover. “My heart,” says he, “has become like melting wax” (Ps. 21 [22]). A thing, by melting, is softened, expanded, and cleansed. Now consider this threefold [Col. 1206A] effect in love, which is truly a divine fire, dissolving hearts, cleansing them, and fusing them into the mass of unity, just as various metals melted by fire flow together into one.

At its touch that hateful hardness—the insensibility of the heart—is softened and yields: for such a person feels neither himself nor another; he is bent neither by pity nor moved by prayers; he is not led by examples, frightened by threats, hardened by benefits, or instructed by blows. Brazen toward shameful things, prone to what is forbidden, knowing not how to submit except when he can no longer resist—such a one is Pharaoh, the man of hard heart, made an example for you. But the heart is softened, and, according to the teaching of blessed Paul, enlarged in charity (2 Cor. 6); it spreads everywhere, to right and left alike, helping enemies and friends together, and with a grateful [Col. 1206B] and spontaneous course hastens to meet all, rejoicing with neighbors in their progress and grieving with them in their failures. It therefore flows, but does not flow out: it so pours itself forth toward others that it does not altogether depart from itself.

See whether perhaps the Prophet meant this of the heart itself when, having compared his heart to melting wax, he immediately added: “in the midst of my belly” (Ps. 21 [22]). It was liquid, therefore, but did not flow out beyond itself. Only he flows out who attends to others in such a way that he does not attend to himself: “Take heed,” says the Apostle, “lest perhaps you drift away” (Heb. 2). Nor is it necessary to say that in those ecstasies in which human spirits are torn by God’s gift from muddy senses, they are outside themselves, since Paul says that in his rapture he utterly did not know whether he was in the body or outside the body. “Where then are they?” you ask. They are in that which is inward [Col. 1206C] within themselves. The heart of man is deep and unsearchable; for a man is hidden to himself, since he alone knows what is inward in himself. Thus spirits are not led out but led in to that inner upper room, so that there, with the doors of the senses shut apart, they may meet more safely and secretly in a most chaste embrace with the Beloved; there they are more fully with themselves, and when they are there together in this way, they possess themselves more safely.

Moreover, the melted heart must be cleansed and refined to purity, if it has any dross, by love itself, which is a consuming fire, cleansing the chaff of ignorance and the sins of youth and making the most purified soul worthy of divine marriage, “having neither spot nor wrinkle.” Hear the devouring flame: [Col. 1206D] “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7). Finally, “all things work together for good” to those who love God, and nothing is reckoned against them unto death; whatever he himself has not reckoned is as though it were not: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. 31 [32]). For no one is without sin, except him who is “free among the dead.”

A heart thus warmed and melted is easily pierced and boils over at every word of the Beloved, experiencing what is sung: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5), and what is read in the Gospel: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?” (Luke 24). O sweet converse of God in the soul, formed without the noise of tongue and lips, received without the ear, [Col. 1207A] but under silence heard only by him who speaks and by him to whom he speaks, from which every stranger is excluded! These words are certain streams from the heavenly fountain, watering hearts parched and wearied by love’s longing. Their sweet account of the city of God—of the city’s peace and abundance, the glory of its citizens, and the beauty of its most radiant dwelling—drives weariness from the heart and fatigue from the body, announcing to the friend that it is his possession and that he can ascend to it. Nor did he seek or suffer anything else who said: “My soul has slumbered from weariness; strengthen me in your words” (Ps. 118 [119]).

Words of truth resemble our thoughts, and no observer of inward movements is so watchful that he can easily discern what the heart brings forth or what it hears, except the one who attends to the Lord speaking: [Col. 1207B] “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9); and: “Evil thoughts proceed from the heart” (Matt. 15); and again: “He who speaks a lie speaks from his own resources” (John 8); and the Apostle’s saying: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think anything” (2 Cor. 3). Thus we speak evil things in our hearts, in accordance with: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13 [14]). But we hear good things: “Therefore I will hear what the Lord God shall speak in me” (Ps. 84 [85]). And to this hearing joy and gladness will indeed be given; nor will the word return empty, but will accomplish whatever he sent it to do, watering and making fruitful the inner chambers of the heart. Those taught by such words are teachable by God, and the anointing teaches them—the anointing that alone teaches all truth with sweet and swift instruction. It speaks certain deep mysteries of God which it is not permitted for a man to utter and which, if it were permitted to hear them, are of a kind never heard among the masters of the world. By their power and hearing hearts melt; by melting they fail, and by failing they are made perfect.

Hard things flow together into that unity for which the Savior prays and longs in the Gospel for his own: “That they may be one,” he says, “as we also are one” (John 17). Saint John recalls this in his Epistle, saying: “As he is, so are we in the world” (1 John 4), so that, just as that blessed, beatifying Trinity of persons is held together by eternal love without confusion or division—so that he who does not multiply the essence does not disturb the unity [Col. 1208B] of the divine persons, nor does the unity reduce the Trinity to the singularity of one person—so they too may be united and ordered in charity, indeed by comparison but by some sort of likeness. Nor should it be thought absurd that I have said God is held together by love, since I have said that he is held by nothing other than himself and by himself.

May your charity receive these few remarks in such a way that, once you have read them, you permit them to be copied for no one except those for whom you judge such things beneficial to the edification of the soul. For you know how prone some are to scorn simple statements, attending only to matters that generate disputes about words, of which there is no end and little fruit.

[Col. 1207]

## TREATISE ON THE FOUR DEGREES OF THE VIOLENCE OF CHARITY

[Col. 1207C] “I am wounded by charity.” Charity urges me to speak of charity; I gladly devote myself to the service of charity, and it is sweet indeed and altogether delightful to speak of love. The subject is pleasant and sufficiently abundant; it can produce neither weariness in the writer nor distaste in the reader. For what is seasoned with charity is exceedingly sweet to the palate of the heart: “If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as though it were nothing.” Great is love’s force, wondrous is charity’s power. It has many degrees, and among these there is great difference. Who could sufficiently distinguish them worthily, or even number them? There is in it indeed the affection of humanity, companionship, affinity, blood relationship, brotherhood, and many others of this kind. Yet above all these degrees of love [Col. 1207D] is that ardent and fervent love which penetrates the heart, inflames the affection, and pierces the very soul to its marrow, so that it can truly say: “I am wounded by charity.”

Let us therefore consider what that surpassing excellence of Christ’s charity is which transcends—or extinguishes—love for parents, attachment to children, and affection for a wife, and moreover turns even one’s own soul into hatred. O vehemence of love! [Col. 1208C] O violence of charity! O excellence, O surpassing greatness of Christ’s charity! This, brothers, is what we intend; this is what we wish to discuss: the vehemence of charity, the surpassing greatness of perfect zeal. You know well enough that it is one thing to speak of charity itself, another of its consummation; one thing to speak of charity itself, another of its violence.

I consider the effects of violent charity, and I find what the vehemence of perfect zeal is. Behold, I see some wounded, some bound, some languishing, some failing—yet not failing away from charity. Charity wounds; charity binds; charity makes one languish; charity brings one to failure. What of these is not marvelous? What of these is not violent? These are the degrees to which, for the present, direct your whole attention—to that charity which you greatly desire: hear of it and breathe after that which you eagerly seek. Do you wish to hear of wounding charity? “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride, with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck” (Song 4). Do you wish to hear of binding charity? “I will draw them with the cords of Adam, with the bonds of charity” (Hos. 1 [11:4]). Do you wish to hear of languishing charity? “Daughters of Jerusalem, if you find [Col. 1209A] my beloved, tell him that I languish with love” (Song 5). Do you wish to hear of charity that fails and brings one to failure? “My soul has failed for your salvation, and I have hoped exceedingly in your word” (Ps. 118 [119]). Charity, then, causes failure and brings languor. Charity has bonds; charity makes wounds.

But what are these cords of Adam, our first parent, if not God’s gifts? What, I ask, are these bonds of charity if not God’s benefits? The goods of nature, grace, and glory. By these bonds of beneficence he made us indebted, and established us as debtors of goodwill. He created nature, bestowed grace, promised glory. Behold the threefold cord: the gifts of creation, the goods of justification, the rewards of glorification. And we know that a threefold cord is not easily broken, [Col. 1209B] yet it was broken. For from of old man broke the yoke and burst the bonds. But the Lord also added this: with a mighty hand he multiplied over us the bonds of his charity, that he might bind us more closely and entangle us more deeply with himself. He gave us his good things; he endured our evils for us, in order to render us indebted to him on both grounds: for the good things he gave us and for the evils he endured for us. In cords of charity such as these he led captivity captive, lavishly giving gifts to men and willingly suffering evils for men.

O how badly strong is he whom so many bonds of charity cannot hold! O how badly free is he whom the laws of this captivity do not enfold! But behold, we return to that degree of love which we placed first and called wounding. Does he not seem struck in the heart when that fiery goad of love penetrates the mind of a man to its marrow and, meanwhile, pierces through his affection, so that he is utterly unable either to restrain or conceal the heat of his desire? He burns with longing, glows with affection, boils over, pants, groaning deeply and drawing long sighs. Let groans and sighs, a pale and wasting face, be sure signs to you of a wounded soul. Yet this degree admits interruption, and is cut short by the cares and anxieties of pressing affairs. Thus, like those fever patients afflicted with this condition, at one time they burn more fiercely, at another they are somewhat refreshed by the occasion of their occupations. But after a brief interruption the seething, more fervent ardor returns and burns the mind, now weakened, more sharply and fiercely. [Col. 1209C] Often withdrawing and always returning greater than itself, it gradually softens the mind, breaks its strength, and exhausts it, until it fully subdues and lays the mind beneath itself. The memory of its yoke occupies, entangles, and binds the whole person, so that he cannot cast it off or think of anything else; and thus it passes from the first degree to the second. For we called the first degree that which wounds, the second that which binds.

Is the mind not truly and without any contradiction bound when it cannot forget this one thing or meditate upon another? Whatever it does or says, this is always turned over in the mind and retained in everlasting memory. Sleeping, it dreams of this; waking, it recalls this at every hour. From this, I think, it is easy to see how this degree surpasses the former, since it does not permit a man’s mind to be at rest even for an hour. Thus it was rightly said that the degree which wounds comes first, while the degree which binds comes second. For it is often less to be wounded than to be bound. Who does not know how often it happens that a soldier, struck and wounded in the conflict of battle, escapes the hand of his pursuer and, though wounded, nonetheless gets away free? But once in the encounter of battle a soldier is struck down, he is seized after falling; seized, he is led away; led away, he is imprisoned; imprisoned, he is chained and bound—now he is held wholly captive.

What, I ask, is greater or more burdensome than this? [Col. 1210B] Is it not more tolerable to escape, though wounded, yet free, than to be taken and held captive in bonds? This degree, however, unlike the preceding one, admits no interruption; rather, like an acute fever, it burns the mind with continual heat and inflames it with the fever of its heavy desire, allowing the soul no rest by day or night. Thus, just as one lying in bed or restrained by a chain cannot be removed from the place to which he is confined, so he who has been swallowed up by this second degree of violent charity cannot, whatever he does or wherever he turns, be torn away from that one inner care of his concern.

Therefore, in wrongful desires, we must—and can—repel the onset of the first degree not by resisting but by turning aside, not so much by struggling as by fleeing, if we always take provident refuge, with watchful mind, in useful and honorable occupations and meditations, and fulfill what is written: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6). The violence of the first degree can be avoided; it cannot be overcome. But the vehemence of the second degree can altogether neither be overcome by resistance nor avoided by flight. Hear the captive, groaning and despairing of escape: “Flight has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul” (Ps. 141 [142]). But often, as we see, those who cannot flee can ransom themselves. Therefore, when we cannot repel temptation by strength or avoid it by prudence, we must ransom ourselves through works of mercy and obedience, and rescue ourselves from the yoke of slavery. These are the true and proper riches of which it is written: “A man’s own riches are the redemption [Col. 1210D] of his soul” (Prov. 13).

But when love has grown to this second degree of vehemence, what further scope can it have? What can be more vehement than this vehemence, if it cannot be overcome or avoided? If it is altogether unconquerable, altogether inseparable, what can be more vehement than this vehemence? If it cannot be overcome by another affection, it is supreme; and if it clings inseparably, it is everlasting. What can be more violent than its violence if it is supreme and everlasting? But to be supreme is one thing, to be alone another; just as always to be present is one thing, and never at all to admit a companion another. For we may be present and still have many companions, while holding the foremost place above them all. You see, then, how great a capacity for further growth in surpassing greatness remains to it: having already become supreme, it can also become alone. Thus love rises to the third degree of violence when it excludes every other affection, when it loves nothing except the one thing or for the sake of the one thing. In this third degree of violent charity, nothing whatever can satisfy except the one, just as nothing can have savor except for the one. It loves one, cherishes one, thirsts for one, longs for one. It pants toward it, sighs into it, burns from it, rests in it. It alone refreshes; it alone satisfies. Nothing becomes sweet, nothing has savor unless it is seasoned by this one. Whatever freely offers itself, whatever spontaneously presents itself, is swiftly [Col. 1211B] rejected and suddenly trampled down if it does not serve its affection or minister to such desire.

But who can worthily describe the tyranny of this affection—how it expels every desire, excludes every pursuit, violently suppresses every host which it does not perceive to serve its own longing? Whatever it does, whatever happens, seems useless—indeed, intolerable—unless it converges upon and contributes to the one end of its desire. When it can enjoy what it loves, it believes that it possesses everything together. Without it, all things are dreadful and all things vile. For if it cannot enjoy it, the body fails and the heart wastes away. It receives no counsel, assents to no reasoning, admits no consolation at all.

At the second degree it can still indeed be occupied in other people’s business by action, [Col. 1211C] but not by thought, because it cannot altogether forget what it loves. At this degree, however, the mind, wasting away and languishing through love’s excess, just as it cannot meditate on other things, so it cannot perform other people’s tasks. That degree entangles thoughts; this one also dissolves actions. That binds in thought; this weakens in action. At that degree we still have hands and feet free, and, like a fever patient, can stretch and toss them here and there, because according to the judgment of discretion we still can—and ought—to direct them and exercise them in good work. At this degree, however, love’s excess weakens hands and feet in the manner of illness, so that henceforth the mind does nothing at all by its own choice. In this state, therefore, the mind remains as though immovable, and moves nowhere, either in thought or action, except where desire draws or affection drives it.

But in wrongful desires, at the first degree it can flee through the care of circumspection, as was said above; at the second degree, where there is absolutely no place for flight, it can still ransom itself by good works. But what help can there be at this degree, what kind of remedy, for those who can now neither meditate on necessary things nor perform useful ones? Hear one languishing both in heart and body, wasting in body and troubled in heart: “My heart is troubled within me; my strength has left me” (Ps. 57 [38]). Under this extremity of necessity I find no other kind of remedy than to look to divine [Col. 1212A] clemency and implore its mercy. If you are wholly languishing, if you do not have hands and feet free, you surely still have a tongue and can move your lips. Therefore, if no way of escape has been left to your own effort, cry out to him who can do all things.

You see, I think, how greatly that force of love has now prevailed when, through its operation, it has risen to the vehemence of this third degree; and it is remarkable if it still has anything by which it can rise further. In the first degree it pierces the affection; in the second it binds thought; in the third it dissolves action. Thus affection is captured in the first, thought in the second, action in the third. In these consists the whole human being: what more can he have beyond these? Therefore, if everything that belongs to man is captive, what further can happen to him? If love’s force possesses everything, if love’s greatness swallows everything, in what, I ask, can it extend itself further? For if it has obtained everything, there is nothing that it can claim further. But what are we to say if it obtains everything and yet everything cannot suffice it? What, I say, shall we say if all is in its power and yet all cannot satisfy its desire? Surely what a human being cannot do is incomparably greater than whatever a human being can do. Yet both may be desired: what a human being can do and what a human being cannot do. See, then, how infinite is that into which desire can extend itself, even after it has reached the third degree.

The fourth degree of violent charity, therefore, is when absolutely nothing can now satisfy the desire of a seething mind. Since this degree has once exceeded the boundaries of human possibility, it knows no limit of growth, as the others do, because it always finds something that it can still desire. Whatever it does, whatever happens to it, does not satisfy the longing of the burning soul. It thirsts and drinks, yet by drinking it does not extinguish its thirst; rather, the more it drinks, the more it thirsts. For the thirst or hunger of the eager—indeed insatiable—soul is not assuaged but provoked while it enjoys the object of its wish according to its wish. In this state the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing, whether it speaks of the absent one or beholds the present one. But who can worthily explain the violence of this highest degree, or sufficiently weigh its surpassing greatness? What, I ask, [Col. 1212D] penetrates a human heart more deeply, torments it more bitterly, agitates it more vehemently? What is more burdensome or more bitter when one can neither moderate thirst by resistance nor extinguish it by drinking to excess? It is a marvelous—indeed pitiable—voracity, which is expelled by no treatment and assuaged by no satisfaction. It is an incurable and wholly desperate disease, in which a remedy is always sought and nowhere found; indeed, whatever is attempted as a remedy for health is turned into an increase of madness.

This is the degree, as we said, that brings failure and causes one now to despair of remedy. And just as a desperate sick man, lying as though his limbs had already died before him, has no longer anything to do or to expect from another, and all physicians’ care is now withdrawn from him, [Col. 1213A] so that he is left wholly to himself, still breathing only with his spirit and approaching his end, as it were, at every hour—he draws his final breath, and neither notices nor observes what is done around him or what is done to him—so, indeed, one who pants under the ardor of such a seething desire cannot derive any remedy or receive any consolation from whatever is done to him. Therefore, when any consolation applied does not touch the mind at all, he is in some sense like one already dead and does not feel at all what takes place around him.

But in wrongful desires, when the human mind is violently drawn into this state, nothing remains except that others should pray for him, if perhaps the Lord, looking upon their faith and restoring him to life, may give him back to his mother—he who is able even to raise children of Abraham from stones and, whenever he wills, leads down to hell [Col. 1213B] and brings back. In this state love often turns almost to madness unless its impulses are restrained by marvelous prudence and equal steadfastness. In this state anger often arises among lovers; they often enter into quarrels, and, when true grounds of enmity are lacking, they invent false ones, often not even plausible ones. In this state love often passes into hatred because nothing can satisfy their mutual desire. Hence comes what we have often seen in some: the more ardently they formerly seemed to love one another, the more violently they afterward pursued one another with hatred. Indeed—and this is more remarkable—often at one and the same time they hate in such a way that they nevertheless do not cease to burn with longing, and they love in such a way that they nevertheless do not cease to pursue one another as if from hatred. Thus in loving they hate, and in hating they love; and in a marvelous—indeed pitiable—fashion hatred grows from longing and longing from hatred. Fire and hail are borne along mingled together, since neither can the heat of desire melt the frost of hatred, nor can the hail of detestation extinguish the fire of burning concupiscence. Beyond measure—indeed beyond nature—fire gains strength in water, because the blaze of love boils more fiercely through either party’s opposition than it could grow through mutual peace.

Behold, then, we now have in ardent love the four degrees of violence which we proposed above. The first degree of violence, therefore, is when the mind cannot resist its desire; the second [Col. 1213D] degree, when it cannot forget it; the third, when it cannot take delight in anything else; the fourth and last, when even the object itself cannot satisfy it. Thus in the first degree love is unconquerable; in the second, inseparable; in the third, exclusive; in the fourth, insatiable. It is unconquerable when it yields to no other affection; inseparable when it never departs from memory; exclusive when it admits no companion; insatiable when it cannot be satisfied.

Although something particular may be observed in each degree, yet in the first degree love’s excellence is especially marked; in the second, its intensity; in the third, its violence; in the fourth, its surpassing greatness. How great is the excellence of that love which surpasses every other affection! How great, I ask, is the intensity of that love which [Col. 1214A] does not allow the mind to rest! How great, I beseech you, is the violence of charity which forcibly expels every other affection! How great is the surpassing force of that zeal for which absolutely nothing is enough! O excellence of love! O intensity of affection! O violence of charity! O surpassing force of zeal!

These four degrees of love are otherwise found in divine affections than in human affections, and altogether otherwise in spiritual desires than in carnal desires. In spiritual desires, the greater they are, the better. In carnal desires, the greater they are, the worse. In divine affections, that which is highest is also chief. In human affections, that which is highest is also worst. Indeed, among human affections the first may be good; the second is undoubtedly [Col. 1214B] bad; the third is worse; but the fourth is worst of all.

We know that in human affections conjugal love ought to hold the first place; and therefore, in the marriage-bed, that degree of love which usually rules over every other affection can be good. For a mutual affection of intimate love binds the bonds of peace between those joined in covenant, and makes that indissoluble and enduring partnership agreeable and delightful. Therefore, as was said, the first degree in human affections may be good; but the second is undoubtedly bad. For when it has bound the mind inseparably, and does not permit it to turn to another concern, it often removes both care for what must be provided and foresight in arranging what must be arranged.

But that third [Col. 1214C] degree of love which excludes every other affection is not merely bad; indeed, it begins to be bitter. For it is impossible always to enjoy the fulfillment of one’s desire according to one’s wish, and one cannot receive consolation from any other thing. The fourth degree, as we have said, is the worst of all. What can be found worse than that which makes the soul not only evil, but miserable? What is more wretched than always to be wearied by desire for a thing whose enjoyment can never satisfy you? Above we taught how, under this degree, the mind is burned by continual heat and cold, since neither hatred is extinguished by desire nor desire by hatred. And what else does this appear to be but a kind of image of future damnation, where one always passes from the heat of fires to the cold of snow, and from the cold of snow to the heat [Col. 1214D] of fires?

Thus this last degree of love is worst of all in human desires, but, as has been said, chief of all in divine affections. There, whatever happens to the human mind cannot suffice for it; here, whatever it may do for its God cannot satisfy its desire. There the mind is always concerned about what is done to itself, not about what it does. Here the mind takes greater concern over what it itself may do than over what may be done to it. Therefore, in heavenly desires, the greater the affection and the higher the degree, the better and more precious it is.

O how precious is that first degree of affection in the love of God, when it is unconquerable! Much more precious is the second, when ardent affection begins to be inseparable! Yet far better still is the state when it cannot take delight [Col. 1215A] in anything other than God. But the highest and chief degree of love is when nothing can satisfy its desire.

Already in the first degree: “Many waters could not quench love, neither shall rivers overwhelm it” (Song of Songs 8), because it is unconquerable. In the second degree: the soul places its beloved “as a seal upon her heart” (ibid.), because it cannot forget him at all. In the third degree: “If a man should give all the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as nothing” (ibid.), because one cannot delight in anything else. In the fourth degree: “Love is strong as death, and zeal is hard as hell” (ibid.), because whatever one can do or endure for one’s God is too little.

In the first degree love [Col. 1215B] is called unconquerable: “I will love thee, O Lord, my strength” (Psalm 17). In the second, love is called inseparable: “Let my tongue cleave to my jaws if I do not remember thee” (Psalm 136). In the third degree, love is called exclusive: “My soul refused to be consoled; I remembered God and was delighted” (Psalm 76). In the fourth, love is called insatiable: “What shall I render unto the Lord for all that he hath rendered unto me?” (Psalm 115).

In the first it is unconquerable, and it is said: “Who shall separate us from charity? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword?” (Romans 8). In the second, charity never fails because it is inseparable; hence it is said: “My soul hath cleaved after thee” (Psalm 62), because it cannot be torn away from him. In the third: one “counts all things as dung, that he may gain Christ” [Col. 1215C] (Philippians 3). In the fourth, for him to live is Christ and to die is gain, because he desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Philippians 1).

In the first degree God is loved with heart, soul, and mind, though none of these is done wholly. In the second, he is loved with the whole heart. In the third, he is loved with the whole soul. In the fourth, he is loved with all one’s strength. Love from the heart is love proceeding from deliberation; to love from the soul is to love from affection. Counsel belongs to the heart, but desire to the soul.

Do you wish to know that we ought to refer counsel to the heart? “Ephraim,” he says, “is a deceived dove, having no heart” (Hosea 7). What does it mean for a people to have no heart except to be without counsel? What, I say, does it mean for a people to be a deceived dove and without heart, except what is said elsewhere: “A nation without counsel and without prudence” (Deuteronomy 32)? Thus, to be without heart is nothing else than to lack counsel and prudence. But, as has already been said, just as counsel belongs to the heart, so desire belongs to the soul: “He who loses,” he says, “his soul in this world keeps it unto eternal life” [Col. 1215D] (John 12). What else is it to lose one’s soul in this world except, in this world, as has elsewhere been commanded, “not to go after one’s own lusts” (Ecclesiasticus 18)? For insofar as anyone mortifies his desires in this world for God’s sake, so much the more truly does he enlarge them toward eternal fullness.

To love from the heart, therefore, is to love through counsel and deliberation. To love from the soul is to love [Col. 1216A] through desire and affection. The former is by diligence; the latter according to desire. To love with the whole heart, the whole soul, and all one’s strength is to devote every diligence, every desire, and every activity to this one end.

We are often drawn by affection to love something, yet resist by reason. And we often love many things by deliberate resolve which nevertheless we do not desire through the appetite of longing. Therefore, in carnal desires, loving from the soul often comes before loving from the heart. In spiritual matters, however, loving from deliberation always comes before loving from affection. For we never love spiritual things through desire unless we kindle our minds toward their affection with great diligence. If, therefore, we wish to love God with our whole soul, let us first strive [Col. 1216B] to love with our whole heart. Let all our thought be directed to this, all our deliberation to this, all our meditation upon this, if we wish to love with our whole desire.

But just as we never love with the whole soul unless we first love with the whole heart, so we never love with all our strength unless we first love with the whole soul. For if we have an affection for something that we do not love for God’s sake, that adulterous affection certainly weakens the constancy and diminishes the strength of the highest charity insofar as it draws or impels the mind toward alien desires. Therefore, as has been said, in the first degree one loves from the heart; in the second, with the whole heart; in the third, with the whole soul; and in the fourth, with all one’s strength.

Perhaps David was still in the first degree, yet was already presuming upon the second, when [Col. 1216C] he sang: “I will confess to thee, O Lord, with my whole heart” (Psalm 110). He who is in the second degree can confidently sing: “With my whole heart I have sought thee” (Psalm 118). He who possesses the third degree can indeed now say: “My soul hath longed, O Lord, to desire thy ordinances at all times” (ibid.). He who has ascended to the fourth degree and loves God with all his strength can certainly say: “I will not fear what man shall do unto me” (Psalm 117), because his heart is ready to hope in the Lord; his heart is established, and he shall not be moved for ever, until he looks down upon his enemies.

In the first degree there is betrothal; in the second, marriage; in the third, union; in the fourth, childbirth. In the first degree it is said to the beloved: [Col. 1216D] “I will betroth thee unto myself for ever; and I will betroth thee unto myself in justice, and judgment, and mercy, and compassion; and I will betroth thee unto myself in faith” (Hosea 2). In the second degree, the marriage takes place at Cana of Galilee, and it is said to her: “Behold, I am thy husband, and thou shalt not cease to follow after me” (Jeremiah 3). Of the third degree it is said: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6). Of the fourth it is said: “We have conceived, and as it were have been in labour, and have brought forth spirit” (Isaiah 26).

Therefore, in the first degree the beloved is frequently visited; in the second she is led away; in the third she is joined to the Beloved; in the fourth she is made fruitful. Thus, in the first degree, always awaiting the return of her Beloved, she cries and says: “Come, my beloved; be like the roe or the young hart upon the mountains of Bethel” (Song of Songs 2). In the second, she is invited to come, and [Col. 1217A] it is said to her: “Come from Lebanon, my sister, my bride; come from Lebanon” (Song of Songs 4). In the third degree, joined to the Beloved, she lies down and says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs 8). In the fourth she glories in her fruitfulness and says: “My little children, of whom I travail again until Christ be formed in you” (Galatians 4). Hence it is said to her: “Thy two breasts are like two young roes that feed among the lilies” (Song of Songs 4).

Let us penetrate still more deeply and speak more plainly. In the first degree the soul thirsts; in the second it thirsts toward God; in the third it thirsts into God; in the fourth it thirsts according to God. The soul thirsts for God when it says: “My soul hath desired thee in the night, and with my spirit within me I will watch for thee in the morning” (Isaiah 26). The soul thirsts toward God when it says: “My soul hath thirsted [Col. 1217B] for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” (Psalm 41). The soul thirsts into God when it says: “My soul hath thirsted for thee; how greatly hath my flesh also thirsted for thee” (Psalm 62). The soul thirsts according to God when it is said: “My soul hath longed, O Lord, for thy ordinances at all times” (Psalm 118).

The soul thirsts for God when it desires to experience that inward sweetness which is accustomed to inebriate the human mind when it begins to taste and see how sweet the Lord is. The soul thirsts toward God when, by the grace of contemplation, it desires to be raised above itself and to behold the Law in its beauty, so that it may truly dare to say: “Because I have seen the Lord face to face, my soul has been saved” (Genesis 32). The soul then thirsts into God when, through ecstasy of mind, it longs to pass wholly [Col. 1217C] into God, so that, utterly forgetful of itself, it may truly say: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Corinthians 12). The soul thirsts according to God when the mind leaves nothing to its own choice from its own will—not merely in carnal matters, but even in spiritual ones—but commits everything to the Lord, never thinking of its own concerns but of those of Jesus Christ; so that it too may say: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John 5).

Therefore, in the first degree God enters the mind, and the mind returns to itself. In the second degree it rises above itself and is lifted up to God. In the third degree the mind, lifted up to God, passes wholly into him. In the [Col. 1217D] fourth the mind goes forth for God’s sake and descends beneath itself. In the first the mind enters into itself; in the second it passes beyond itself. In the first it proceeds into itself; in the third it proceeds into its God. In the first it enters for its own sake; in the fourth it goes out for its neighbour’s sake. In the first it enters by meditation; in the second it ascends by contemplation; in the third it is drawn back in exultation; in the fourth it goes out through compassion.

Therefore, in the first degree that Spirit sweeter than honey enters the soul and so inebriates it by his sweetness that it has honey and milk under its tongue and its lips become a dripping honeycomb.
