Those of this kind “shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of his sweetness,” because “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.” This is the first consolation which receives those renouncing the world [Col. 1218A] and is accustomed to establish them in their good resolve. This is that heavenly food which refreshes those leaving Egypt and feeds them through the wilderness: this is the hidden manna which no one knows except the one who receives it. This is that spiritual sweetness and inward delight which is accustomed to nurse and nourish them like newborn infants, and gradually bring them to the strength of maturity.

In this state, therefore, the soul is led by the Lord into the wilderness and there nourished, so that it may be inebriated with inward sweetness. Hear what is said of this state, where the Lord speaks through the prophet: “Therefore, behold, I will nourish her, and will lead her into the wilderness, and will speak to her heart” (Hosea 2). But Egypt must first be abandoned; the Red Sea must first [Col. 1218B] be crossed. The Egyptians must first perish in the waters, and the foods of Egypt must first fail, before we can receive this spiritual nourishment and heavenly food. Let him abandon Egypt not only in body but also in heart, and utterly lay aside love of the world, who desires those heavenly foods of the wilderness. Let him cross the Red Sea, and strive to drive every sorrow and bitterness from his heart, who desires to be filled with inward sweetness. The Egyptians must first be subdued and perverse habits made obedient, lest the angelic citizens disdain an unworthy guest. The foods of Egypt must first fail, and carnal pleasures be turned into abomination, before one may experience what those inward and eternal delights are.

Without doubt, the more fully the love of God conquers every other affection, the more often [Col. 1218C] and more abundantly it refreshes the mind with inward joy. Under this state the mind sucks honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone. Under this state the mountains shall drop sweetness, and the hills shall flow with milk and honey. Under this state the Lord often visits the hungry and thirsty soul, often fills it with inward sweetness, and inebriates it with the delight of his Spirit. Often in this state the Lord descends from heaven; often he visits one sitting in darkness and the shadow of death; often the glory of the Lord fills the tabernacle of the covenant.

Yet he manifests his presence in such a way that he does not show his face. He pours in his sweetness, but does not show his beauty. He pours in delight, but does not show brightness. His sweetness, therefore, is felt, but his form [Col. 1218D] is not seen. Clouds and darkness are still around him. His throne is still in the pillar of cloud. What is felt is indeed gentle and very pleasant, but what is seen is wholly clouded. For he does not yet appear in light. And though he appears in fire, it is more in fire that kindles than in fire that illumines. For he kindles affection, but does not yet illumine understanding. He inflames desire, but does not illumine understanding.

Therefore, in this state the soul can feel its Beloved, but, as has been said, cannot see him. And if it sees, it sees as in the night, as beneath a cloud; finally, it sees through a mirror in an enigma, not yet face to face. Hence it says: “Make thy face to shine upon thy servant” (Psalm 118). Therefore, this is accomplished by this first [Col. 1219A] degree of love: while the mind is often visited, often refreshed, often inebriated, it is at length stirred to dare greater things. It eventually begins to presume greater things and ask for higher ones, so much that it dares to say: “If I have found grace in thy sight, show me thyself” (Exodus 33).

Yet what is asked is not immediately received according to one’s desire, although it is sought with deepest longing. One must indeed ask ardently, seek diligently, knock vigorously, and persist obstinately in all these things, if one wishes to obtain what one desires. Does not he seem already to have laboured long and much, and now nearly to fail and as though to have fallen from hope, who says: “How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget me utterly? How long dost thou turn thy face away from me?” (Psalm 112)? But knowing that everyone who asks receives, that he who seeks finds, and that it shall be opened to the one who knocks, he again and again recovers confidence [Col. 1219B] and renews his strength, saying: “My face hath sought thee; thy face, O Lord, will I seek” (Psalm 26).

When, therefore, the mind advances with great diligence and ardent longing to the grace of divine contemplation, it advances, as it were, to the second degree of love, when it deserves through revelation to behold what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, so that it may truly say: “God hath revealed it to us by his Spirit” (1 Corinthians 2). Does not he seem to have received this grace who was granted to see angels ascending and descending, together with the Lord leaning upon the ladder? Hence he says: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my soul has been saved” (Genesis 32).

He had received this grace, and repeated it as though accustomed to it, who said: “Send forth thy light and thy truth; they have led me and brought me unto thy holy mountain and unto thy tabernacles” (Psalm 42). They had received this grace, and were flying on the wing of contemplation, whom the prophet beheld in amazement and marvelled at as he beheld them: “Who are these,” he says, “that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” [Col. 1219C] (Isaiah 60). In this degree some ask to be given wings like eagles: “Who,” he says, “will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly and be at rest?” (Psalm 54). And elsewhere the prophet says: “Those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall take up wings like eagles; they shall fly and not fail” (Psalm 40).

In this degree, the wings of contemplation raise souls above the height of the clouds; in this degree they fly on such wings up to heaven, not only to the first heaven but also to the second, so that thereafter they may say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3). Above this twofold heaven is still a third heaven, called the heaven of heavens. Yet even those who have advanced to the second degree of love cannot altogether ascend to this third heaven. What the earth is to the first heaven, and what the first heaven is to the second, that is the second heaven to the heaven of heavens. Therefore, if you wish, the second heaven is earth and heaven—indeed, heaven of heaven. But it is heaven of heaven in relation to the first heaven, while it is earth [Col. 1220A] in relation to the heaven of heavens.

This earth, I think, the Prophet intended to signify when he says: “My portion is in the land of the living” (Psalm 141). This earth has its own heaven and its own sun. And I think this is none other than that sun which the Lord promises through the prophet: “Thy sun shall go down no more, and thy moon shall not diminish, because the Lord shall be unto thee an everlasting light” (Isaiah 60). If, then, you are in this heaven, or in this earth, you have the power to see that sun beneath which those angelic spirits called seraphim—that is, “burning ones”—are hot and burn. They deserved to receive their name from the thing itself, because among them there is none who hides himself from its heat.

Therefore, you can see the Sun of righteousness if you are in this earth and have advanced to the second degree of love; and it is said to you: “Thou shalt no longer have the sun to shine by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon give thee light; but the Lord shall be unto thee an everlasting light, and thy God thy glory” [Col. 1220B] (ibid.). In this state one may experience the truth of that saying: “Sweet is the light, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun” (Ecclesiastes 11). In this state, taught by the instruction of experience, the soul sings with conviction: “One day in thy courts is better than thousands” (Psalm 83).

But who can worthily express how great is the joy of this vision? This joy, once experienced and once tasted, cannot be cloying while present, nor forgotten while absent. For when the mind descends from that light and falls back upon itself, it draws thence certain remnants of thoughts with it, by which it refreshes itself—or rather, keeps festival—as Scripture says: “The remnants of thoughts shall keep festival for thee” (Psalm 78). Consider, then, how great is the solemnity in the abundance of vision, if a feast is kept from the remnants of thought. What joy will there be in the vision itself, if its remembrance brings such delight?

Thus, in this state, the revelation of divine light and the wonder at that revelation bind the mind so inseparably by continual recollection and enduring memory that it cannot forget the joy it has experienced. And as, in the former degree, sweetness tasted fills the mind and transforms its affection, so in this degree brightness beheld binds thought, so that it cannot forget it or think of anything else [Col. 1220C].

Therefore, in the second degree, as was said, the heaven of heavens and that inaccessible light can be seen, but cannot be approached; otherwise it would not be inaccessible if it could be approached: “The blessed and only mighty one,” says the Apostle, “the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone hath immortality and inhabiteth inaccessible light” (1 Timothy 6). Therefore, that which is inaccessible cannot be approached.

Finally, the Apostle also boasts that he was caught up into the region of eternal light: “I know,” he says, “a man in Christ—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—such a one caught up even to the third heaven” (2 Corinthians 12). Therefore, the third degree of love is when the human mind is caught up into that abyss of divine light, so that in this state the human mind, wholly forgetful of all external things, [Col. 1221A] utterly loses awareness of itself, passes wholly into its God, and does what is written: “Even those who do not believe [shall] dwell in the Lord God” (Psalm 67; wording uncertain in the supplied text).

In this state, therefore, the crowd of carnal desires is completely restrained and profoundly put to sleep, and there is silence in heaven for about half an hour. Whatever distress is present is swallowed up by glory. In this state, while the mind is alienated from itself, while it is caught up into the inner chamber of the divine mystery, while it is surrounded on every side, inwardly penetrated, and everywhere inflamed by that fire of divine love, it wholly puts off itself, puts on a certain divine affection, and, conformed to the beauty it has beheld, passes wholly into another glory.

See what a difference there is between iron and iron: between cold iron and glowing iron—that is, between mind [Col. 1221B] and mind, between a lukewarm mind and a mind inflamed by the divine fire. When iron is thrown into fire, it first appears cold and black. But as it remains in the burning fire, it gradually grows hot, gradually lays aside its blackness, and little by little, becoming incandescent, draws into itself the likeness of fire, until at last it wholly melts, wholly fails from itself, and passes completely into another quality.

So too, so too, the soul swallowed up by the furnace of divine ardour and the fire of inward love, and surrounded on every side by the blazing spheres of eternal desires, first grows warm, then glows, and finally wholly melts and utterly ceases from its former state. Do you wish to hear those already warmed by such fire and now beginning to burn with the heat of inward desires? “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24). Do not those also glow from the surrounding flame of divinity and, as it were, from the glory they have beheld, and, conformed to the divine light, pass, as it were, into another glory—those who, “with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord”? [Col. 1221C]

Do you wish further to hear a soul kindled and melted by the fire of divine speech? “My soul melted when my Beloved spoke” (Song of Songs 5). For as soon as it is admitted to that inward chamber of the divine mystery, through the magnitude of its wonder and the abundance of its joy it is wholly dissolved in itself—or rather, in him who speaks—when it begins to hear those secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter, and to understand that the uncertain and hidden things of divine wisdom are being revealed to it.

In this state the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. In this state he who cleaves to the Lord is one Spirit. In this state, as has been said, the soul wholly melts into him whom it loves and wholly languishes within itself; hence it says: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song of Songs 2). Just as in liquids or melted things we see no hardness or firmness, but see them yield without difficulty to everything hard and rigid; and just as in those who languish we see no strength of their own, no native power, but see all that helps them depend upon another’s will; so those who have advanced to this third degree of love do nothing now by their own will. They leave nothing at all to their own choice, but commit everything to the divine disposition. Their every intention and every desire depends upon the divine beckoning and looks to the divine decision. And as the first degree wounds affection, and the second binds thought, so the third entangles action, so that one cannot occupy oneself with anything at all unless the power of the divine will draws or impels one toward it.

When, therefore, the soul has in this manner been refined by the divine fire, softened to its marrow, and utterly melted, what remains but that there be set before it what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God, as a kind of pattern by which the perfection of its virtue may be formed? [Col. 1222B] For just as founders, with molten metals and patterns set before them, cast whatever image they please according to the choice of their will, and produce vessels of every sort according to the appropriate measure and intended form, so the soul in this state readily adapts itself to every nod of the divine will; indeed, by a certain spontaneous desire it accommodates itself to every divine decision and shapes its entire will according to the measure of the divine good pleasure. And just as molten metal, wherever an outlet is opened for it, readily runs and flows down to lower places, so the soul in this state willingly humbles itself to every obedience and gladly inclines to every humility according to the order of the divine dispensation.

In this state, therefore, the pattern of Christ’s will is set before such a soul, whence it is said to it: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and being found in outward appearance as a man; moreover he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). This is the pattern of Christ’s humility, to which whoever wishes to attain the highest degree of perfected charity must conform himself. For no one has greater charity than that a person lay down his life for his friends.

Those, therefore, have advanced to the summit of charity and are now placed in the fourth degree of charity who can lay down their lives for their friends and can now fulfill that apostolic injunction: “Be imitators of God as most beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ also loved you and gave himself up for you, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor” (Eph. 5). In the third degree, then, the soul is glorified in God; in the fourth, it is humbled for God’s sake. In the third degree it is conformed to divine brightness; in the fourth it is conformed to Christian humility. And although in the third degree it was in some manner, as it were, in the form of God, nonetheless in the fourth degree it begins to empty itself, taking the form of a servant and again being found in outward appearance as a human being. In the third degree, therefore, it is in some manner mortified in God; in the fourth it is, as it were, raised again in Christ.

Whoever is in the fourth degree can truly say: “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). Such a person therefore begins to walk in newness of life, because henceforth for him Christ is life, and death is gain. He is indeed constrained by two desires, having a desire to depart and be with Christ—for that is far better—yet judging it necessary, for our sake, to remain in the flesh. For the charity of Christ presses him on. Let such a person, then, be a new creation: the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new. Mortified in the third degree and in the fourth, as it were, rising from the dead, he now dies no more; death will have no further dominion over him, for insofar as he lives, he lives to God.

Accordingly, in a certain manner the soul in this degree becomes immortal and impassible. [Col. 1223B] For how is it mortal if it cannot die? Or how can it die if he who is life cannot be separated from it? We know well whose saying this is: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). How, then, can one die who cannot be separated from these things? “I am certain,” he says, “that neither death nor life, nor angels nor archangels, nor principalities nor powers nor virtues, nor things present nor things to come, nor strength, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature, can separate us from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8).

Might not that person also be considered impassible in a certain manner who does not feel injuries inflicted upon him, who is always cheerful in the face of every wrong, and who regards everything inflicted as punishment wholly as glory, according to that saying of the Apostle: “I will gladly glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12)? For he remains, as it were, impassible, to whom sufferings and reproaches for Christ are pleasing: “Therefore,” he says, “I take pleasure in weaknesses, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ” (ibid.). Whoever is in this degree can confidently say: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4), because he knows how to be filled and to hunger, to abound and to suffer want.

In this degree charity bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. In this degree charity is patient, is kind, is not ambitious, does not seek its own things, does not know how to repay evil for evil or curse for curse. [Col. 1223D] On the contrary, it blesses. Whoever has ascended to this degree of charity is without doubt in that degree of love in which he can truly say: “I have become all things to all people, that I might save all” (1 Cor. 9). Finally, such a person desires to become anathema, separated from Christ, for his brothers.

What then shall we say? Does not this degree of love seem to turn the human mind almost into madness, since it does not allow it to observe limit or measure in its zeal? Does it not appear the height of madness to reject true life, to charge supreme wisdom with fault, and to resist omnipotence? Does not the person reject life who desires to be separated from Christ for his brothers, as does he who says: “Either forgive them this sin, or blot me out of the book which you have written” (Exod. 32)? Does not the person seem to charge wisdom with fault, or to wish to instruct it, who says to the Lord: “Far be it from you to do this thing and kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should become as the wicked. This is not yours, you who judge the whole earth; will you by no means execute judgment?” (Gen. 18). Did a human being not attempt to resist omnipotence, and presume—and prevail—to mitigate the wrath of the Almighty, when, with the sentence already issued by the Lord and the fire already raging, he threw himself before the furious flame, stood between those who feared and those who were dying, and put an end to the calamity?

See to what bold audacity of presumption the perfection of charity is accustomed to raise the human mind; see how it causes a human being to presume beyond the human. For everything is more than human that it presumes concerning the Lord, does for the Lord, does in the Lord, and lives in the Lord. [Col. 1224C] Everything is wonderful; everything astonishing. As much as it presumes concerning the Lord, so much does it abase itself for the Lord. As much as it ascends through confidence, so much does it descend through humility. As what it ascends to through trust is above humanity, so what it descends to through patience is beyond humanity.

Thus, in the first degree, as was said, the mind returns to itself; in the second it ascends into God; in the third it passes into God; in the fourth it descends beneath itself. In the first and second it is raised up; in the third and fourth it is transformed. In the first it ascends to itself; in the second it transcends itself; in the third it is conformed to the brightness of God; in the fourth it is conformed to the humility of Christ. Or, in the first it is brought back, in the second transported, in the third transformed, and in the fourth [Col. 1224D] raised again.

## PART THREE OF THE WORKS OF RICHARD OF ST VICTOR

[Col. 1225]

## LETTERS AND MISCELLANEA

### LETTER I

*(Letters of St Thomas of Canterbury, ed. Giles, vol. II, p. 200.)*  
**ERNISIUS, ABBOT, AND R., PRIOR OF ST VICTOR, PARIS, TO ROBERT OF HEREFORD**

[Col. 1225A]

To Robert, bishop of Hereford, Ernisius, abbot, and R., prior of St Victor at Paris.

Our Church conceived great joy at your promotion, and your hearers were gladdened by no slight hope; indeed, all scholars were encouraged by the example of your labour and success toward love of learning and the cultivation of virtues. We ourselves rejoiced for this reason: because we loved you above others, and because we trusted that the Church of the English—which, beyond the charity we have for all Churches, we love with a certain special affection, nature prompting us—would advance through your learning, be stirred through your religious devotion to the observance of the divine law, be strengthened against adversities through the office of your preaching and the example of your virtue.

But now we grieve beyond measure, because neither have our desires concerning you been fulfilled nor has the Lord heard our prayers for you. Would that your ears were attentive to the mouths of scholars and that you heard the sighs of religious people, so that your spirit—which, they say, is weighed down by riches, weakened by the love of holding the episcopal office, and by an abundance of pleasures—might thus be raised up. For, as they say, the riches which you used in the schools and in frequent verbal exchanges to call “dog-born” (*canigenas*) have strengthened you. At that time you portrayed in words a handsome ideal of bishops, which now, according to our desire, you ought to express by learning [Col. 1225C] and life. Were you then performing the office of a whetstone,

> [lacuna] able to render iron sharp,  
> though itself incapable of cutting?  
> *(Horace, Ars Poetica 304.)*

It is strange if your ears do not ring from the conversations of scholars, the detraction of rivals, and the complaints of friends. Recently you appealed, with others who seek the overthrow of justice and their own ruin, against your father and consecrator, who is likewise in exile for justice and the liberty of the Church. By casting your lot with the wicked, a thing for which we deeply grieve, you have greatly blackened your reputation.

Did you not see the letters of appeal [Col. 1225D] which the bishops sent to their archbishop? Certainly, if you did not see them, it was foolish—may charity, with your leave, speak the truth—to sign testimony in so grave a matter, a matter to be brought before the Roman Church, without having examined it. But if you saw them, with what conscience, with what face, did you dare to assert—and, as you write, to proclaim with every confidence—what not merely the entire neighbourhood but almost the whole Latin world knows to be false?

For you proclaim, and you sign a document with the bishop of London so that it may especially avail through your authority, that your king, although he has sometimes sinned as a man, is ready to correct all his offences, to obey justice in all things, and, should he not be believed, even offers surety. You add: “For he loves those who correct him and gladly listens to those who rebuke him.” But whoever believes this to be true, what will he believe false? For the man’s character is well known; if you are to preach such things, you must seek out a foreigner—and one outside the Latin world.

But you who uphold his justice, what innocence do you allege in the expulsion of women and the proscription of innocent little children? The Lord will judge these things and others like them, and will strike both the perpetrator and those who consent with equal punishment. Meanwhile, consider what sentence those bishops will then receive who now patronize such great wrongs.

Dearest Father, we have written this to you in sincere charity, that you may remember your learning, your office, our desire, and the divine judgment; that you may redeem your reputation and endeavour to raise up the Church, which is collapsing in your hands. We have been yours, we are yours, and, God willing, we shall always be ready for your honour and service [Col. 1226C].

### LETTER II. OF THE PRIOR OF ST VICTOR, PARIS, AND R., ABBOT OF ST AUGUSTINE, TO POPE ALEXANDER

*(Ibid.)*

To Pope Alexander, the prior of St Victor and R. . . ., formerly abbot of St Augustine.

“To holy men,” etc.—See under Alexander III.

### LETTER III. WILLIAM, PRIOR OF OURSCAMP, TO RICHARD, PRIOR OF ST VICTOR

[Note: [Col. 1225] Ourscamp, a distinguished monastery of the Cistercian order, founded in 1129.]

He asks for one of Richard’s minor works to be copied.

*(Martene, Amplissima Collectio, VI, 235.)*

To his beloved lord Richard, prior of St Victor, Brother William, called prior of Ourscamp, greeting in the Lord.

I myself brought back during Lent your little book which you had instructed to be returned to you. But because you were not then at St Victor, I entrusted it to your hospitaller brother Hugh, informing him that he should return it to you. We ask, however, that you send us some little work of yours which we have not yet had—namely, that on Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, or *“Make your face shine upon your servant.”* For we too had begun to copy this latter work, but found it incomplete in your exemplar. Farewell.

### LETTER IV. G., PRIEST OF ANILCOURT, TO RICHARD, PRIOR OF ST VICTOR

He asks him for the Passion, or nine lessons, concerning St Victor, to insert in a breviary.

*(Martene, ibid.)*

[Col. 1227B]

G., by the grace of God priest of the Church of Anilcourt, to his beloved brother R., venerable prior of the Church of St Victor at Paris, greeting.

We direct and request your affection to send us, through the bearer of this letter, either the Passion of Blessed Victor, which is not found among us, or nine lessons transcribed from that Passion. For we are writing a certain book called a Breviary, into which we have judged it fitting to insert them. Farewell.

### LETTER V. G. TO RICHARD, PRIOR OF ST VICTOR

[Note: [Col. 1227] William, I think, canon of St Geneviève.]

He wishes to learn what Richard has accomplished with the king and the abbot of St Germain in his affair.

*(Martene, ibid., col. 237.)*

[Col. 1227C]

To his dearest Richard, venerable prior of St Victor, humble brother G. sends the same greeting that he wishes for himself.

If you have had a prosperous journey home from us; if you have found favour in the king’s sight; if you have properly and successfully met with Lord Abbot—namely, the abbot of St Germain—concerning our business, may your affection not think it burdensome to inform us through the bearer of this letter. Greet for us Lord Abbot, who will find our humility ready not only to serve him but also to obey him in whatever pleases him. Greet for us our dearest Lord Roger, abbot of Augé.

### LETTER VI. G., PRIOR OF THE CHURCH OF ST ALBAN, TO R. OF ST VICTOR

*(Duchesne, Scriptores Francorum, IV, 747; the following letters issue from the same source.)*

[Col. 1227D]

To the venerable lord and friend Master R., prior of St Victor, his own G., prior of the Church of St Alban, greeting and the integrity of sincere affection.

I owe you thanks beyond expression because so abundant a benefit from your favour has fallen to my brother Matthew; and from what you have bestowed upon him I measure how greatly I ought to commend to you with confidence the bearer of this letter, my nephew. I pray, therefore, that the kindness shown to one may extend to both, and that doubled charity may make me indebted to you in many ways. And, that I may rise to still fuller joy, may your affection send me word of some wish of yours, by which you may gain proof of my love. Farewell.

### LETTER VII. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME

To his venerable friend and deservedly honourable Richard, prior of St Victor, his own G., prior of the Church of St Alban, greeting and the affection of due love.

Because you have provided for my brother M., who travels as a stranger in your parts for the love of learning, with such singular favour and such a special privilege of generosity, I give thanks to your affection. Nor could mute letters easily explain what love and service my heart promises you. [Col. 1228B] But would that it might happen that the execution of deeds should speak aloud of the affection with which I embrace you! For how could I hope for the kindness which the aforesaid Matthew proclaims was bestowed on him by you, from your eminence, from whom I have deserved absolutely nothing? I plainly see how prudence has committed to your tenacious memory that loving saying of Cato: “If you wish to be loved, love.”

It remains, therefore, that you should be willing to clothe with a robe reaching to the ankles that which you have begun with so fruitful a beginning. Though I lack the means of repaying you, I shall not lack the will. I send you this small gift, not as a gift, but as a token of love; and in return I ask that, when an opportunity is found, you make known to me by letter the titles of your writings [Col. 1228C]. I, however, will see to it that, if copies are available, our England shines with the treasure of your learning.

### LETTER VIII. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME

To the venerable brother and friend R., prior of St Victor, Brother S., humble minister of the Church of St Alban, greeting and the service due to sincere affection.

We have collected, with the greatest zeal and most exact diligence, such minor works of Master Hugh as we have been able to find anywhere in our regions, as writings deserving such great veneration; and from them we have formed several volumes. But we have learned by reliable report that several treatises of the aforesaid man are preserved among you which either are entirely absent from the lands on this side of the sea or are still scarce in our England. We have therefore supplied the bearer of this letter with concise lists of those works held by us. [Col. 1228D]

We trust, indeed, in your charity that, in the work entrusted to him, he ought through our intervention to obtain the fullness of favour in the eyes of your sincerity. We therefore earnestly request and ask your holiness kindly, if it please you, to grant the aforesaid bearer permission to inspect Master Hugh’s treatises, out of reverence for blessed Alban and in consideration of our request; and we pray that, in the present undertaking, fraternal charity may incline you to grant him both your counsel and assistance, so that he may arrange in whatever way is most convenient for the copying of those works [Col. 1229A] which he discovers are not held among us. Farewell.

### LETTER IX. M. TO RICHARD

To Lord R., by the grace of God prior of the Church of St Victor, his own M., who more eagerly desires to ascend joyfully to that Church, greeting.

Among the things which I left in your house are two sheets and two towels, whose use I now need. Therefore may your kindness arrange that each item be distinguished from the other, and that one of the sheets, the one without embroidery, together with whichever of the towels is newer, be sent to me through this friend of ours, Brother Walter. Let the remaining things, placed together, be kept in your custody as before, until I come to you.

Give thanks to your venerable friend the prior of St Evroult, and to this bearer of the letter, Brother Walter, who, out of reverence for you, are prepared to offer me more than I wish to receive from them freely. Farewell forever in Christ Jesus our Lord. Wherever in the world I may be, I am yours, desiring to comply with your will and to serve your generosity. The event itself, God permitting, will show this, if at some future time an opportunity of serving you is granted us.

### LETTER X. OF THE SAME TO THE SAME

[Col. 1229C]

To Lord R., by God’s grace prior of St Victor, his own M., greeting, to whom the way of truth leads.

Whoever relies upon the favour of those whose friendship he has earned makes known the signs of his success. For each person rightfully performs the services of those whose affection he has gained by merit, insofar as this is fitting to honour. I, however, was not led into your friendship by this path, by which the kindness inherent in you showed me the approaches; I entered freely into your favour without price. For when I recall the condition of your goodness, it becomes perfectly evident to me that your generosity lies open to all, as is fitting and expedient.

Therefore, that I may conform to your excellent custom, I appeal to the magnificence of your charity, that you grant me some place with you for peaceful affection and pious desire. I offer you many thanks concerning the friendship of Lord Walter, prior of St Evroult. If you wish, you may send a message through this my messenger to your friend, the prior of St Alban. Farewell. If any of your friends live in places through which this boy will travel, I pray that your kindness send him to them, lest they allow him to suffer wrongs on the road. [Col. 1230B] Farewell forever.

### LETTER XI. G., PRIOR OF ST ALBAN, TO RICHARD

To his venerable and deservedly honourable friend Richard, prior of St Victor, G., prior of the Church of St Alban, greeting and the affection of due love.

Because you have diligently endeavoured to carry out the requests which I entrusted to your care some time ago, I confidently add this present request to the others. Therefore, as your custom allows, be moved by my prayers, and may your affection receive with my recommendation the bearer of this letter, my brother M.; and in whatever he needs, may your counsel support him, so that I may have more abundant reasons for thanksgiving to you. May your affection graciously receive the small gift which I sent to be presented to you on my behalf, and attend rather to the affection of the sender than to the smallness of what is sent. Farewell.

[Col. 1229]

## THREE BOOKS ON THE EDUCATION OF THE INNER PERSON

Occasioned by Nebuchadnezzar’s dream in Daniel.

### BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE. On the mystical dream of King Nebuchadnezzar and the overall intention of the whole work

[Col. 1229D]

What Nebuchadnezzar’s dream signifies according to the letter is taught by that most authoritative exposition of Daniel. But it should not be displeasing if a tropological investigation draws from the same subject matter something that edifies the reader toward knowledge of truth or the discipline of morals. To state its main intention briefly, the prophet seems here, through a mystical vision, to indicate how men of virtue may gradually decline, fall through certain degrees of loss into the depths, and sometimes rise again through visiting grace to their former—or rather, a better—state of mind.

This corruption through change, or this remedy through restoration, is accustomed to occur in each kind of life: in the active as well as in the contemplative. The type of both, unless I am mistaken, is expressed in this single vision, if it is rightly weighed. For what does it mean that Nebuchadnezzar received a mystical vision, lost it, and afterward came to know it again more fully? At last he deserved to receive the vision itself together with its interpretation. What, I ask, is suggested to us by all this except that the grace of contemplation is sometimes given by God, sometimes withdrawn, and finally restored more abundantly?

The losses of the active life, however, are signified in the statue which begins in gold and ends in clay: golden at the top, silver or bronze in the middle, iron or clay at the bottom. Behold: as you see, the lower it is, the worse it is always found to be than itself. In the varied change of metals are signified the varied losses of kingdoms, and in both the manifold defects of morals or merits. [Col. 1231B] But behold, after the manifold failure of kingdoms, that kingdom is raised up which shall not be destroyed forever. So the human mind, after manifold ruin, often returns to righteousness, pierced by divine inspiration; and instructed and humbled by its very fall, it rises again all the stronger in proportion as it is more learned and more humble.

It should also be noted that the grace of the contemplative life slips away more readily than that of the active life, but is restored with much greater difficulty. Hence Nebuchadnezzar recovered with such difficulty the vision of the dream which he had so easily lost. Hence the loss of kingdoms is described at greater length and distinguished by stages, while the introduction of the indestructible kingdom is stated briefly and inserted suddenly, without any gradual decline.

Perhaps what is said of either grace of the twofold life may be understood of both. For sacred Scripture often says one thing and suggests another. Thus either event may in turn occur: a person practised in the active life may fall suddenly and unexpectedly, and likewise one cast down from the contemplative life may rise again with wondrous ease through visiting grace. Yet in this passage, where the fall or restoration of each life is under discussion, it fittingly expresses the property of each and shows in what proportion they correspond to one another. For we fall more easily from the contemplative life and rise more easily to the active life.

This vision of King Nebuchadnezzar, moreover, like his other visions, shows quite clearly how aptly he received such a name. For the dream which he saw was undoubtedly a prediction of future things. Yet what he foresaw in the future through that prediction was nevertheless a sign of other realities, for it expressed occurrences of moral life. See, then, how rightly he bears such a name. Nebuchadnezzar, indeed, is interpreted as “prophesying such a sign.” Did not Nebuchadnezzar prophesy through the mystical vision, and was not his vision therefore prophecy, foretelling the various failures of kingdoms? Who, moreover, does not know that all these things happened to them in a figure? That change of kingdoms was therefore a figure, because it signified something else through mystery; it was a sign of spiritual realities. Thus he prophesied a sign who, in the prediction of future events, foresaw figures of spiritual realities.

But what kind of sign? [Col. 1232A] A sign “of this sort”: that is, such a sign, whatever it is like or however true it may be, as can be tested by experience and, as it were, shown to the eye; or a sign “of this sort,” like the sign of a thing that can be pointed out with the finger. For if the decline of morals is said to be understood in the decline of kingdoms, in what place or time, I ask, can this not be shown and seen?

This interpretation of the name suits him sufficiently in respect of what happened to him. But there is another, no less suitable, in respect of what he did: Nebuchadnezzar is interpreted as “sitting in the knowledge of distress.” What is sitting but humbling oneself? Consider, however, how greatly this king humbled himself when he worshipped Daniel, a servant bound to him from captivity, after learning from Daniel’s explanation of the downfall of his kingdom—a downfall which he could not know without distress. Thus he sat in the knowledge of distress when, having heard of the impending danger, he humbly prostrated himself at the feet of the one prophesying to him.

What has been said concerning the interpretation of the name seems to allude to the historical narrative; nevertheless, it should also be considered how it may accord with the mystery. For what else does this great personage signify, who appears at once to be king and prophet, except a mind endowed with the twofold grace and fully exercised in both active and contemplative life? Does not the human mind seem in itself to bear, in some manner, a royal person when it has begun, both by the right of free choice and by the bestowal of grace, to preside vigorously over affections and passions, to command with authority, and to claim manfully that kingdom within us, the kingdom of heaven? Does it not seem to possess a gift akin to prophecy when, by the gift of providence, it has received the ability to foresee and foretell impending dangers—especially when it has begun through the grace of contemplation to investigate the depths of mysteries and, through ecstasy of mind and as if by a dream, to marvel at the secrets of divine judgments?

He is rightly called Nebuchadnezzar who is endowed with the gift of foresight; and such a person truly prophesies a sign when, from preceding causes, he foresees moral decline. For losses of merit always signify losses of reward. Without doubt, in proportion as merit is diminished, reward too is always diminished. Therefore he prophesies a sign—indeed, a sign of this kind—who predicts the sign of such a thing, or the sign of a thing whose nature can in some way be pointed out with the finger and tested by experience.

Often the failure of good desires foretells the failure of good works. For when the will grows sluggish, the mind must afterward become lukewarm in good endeavour. But the converse also commonly occurs. Yet to one who is given the ability to foresee impending dangers and evils still to come, if he takes care and strives to bring them before his mind with sorrow and anguish of spirit, and humbles himself in expectation of them, the same name may suit according to the other interpretation. For Nebuchadnezzar, as was said, is interpreted as “sitting in the knowledge of distress.”

No one should be surprised that by an unjust king is said to be understood a manly mind and a person of virtues. For who does not know—unless ignorant of sacred literature—how often in the Scriptures the serpent, a venomous animal, and the lion, a most savage animal, signify Christ? And if we believe blessed Gregory expounding the matter, Christ is understood mystically in David the adulterer, while that faithless Jewish people is understood in innocent Uriah. What wonder, then, if by an unjust king whom we disapprove we understand a just thing which we approve? For although the unjust king’s will was disordered, his power was nevertheless ordered. “There is no power except from God”; and, as the Apostle testifies, “those that are from God are ordered” (Rom. 13). [Col. 1233B] Thus royal power fittingly signifies the virtuous mind which claims that inner kingdom for itself by its moral qualities: that is, the free choice through which, by cooperating grace, the mind rules its affections and passions.

### CHAPTER II. How the grace of contemplation is sometimes given to certain persons, sometimes withdrawn, and meanwhile, when lost, recovered

“In the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream; his spirit was terrified, and his dream fled from him” (Dan. 2).

The first endeavour of a manly mind ought to be to rule its affections; the second, to command its thoughts; the third [the text is defective]: “the mind, all spiritual things.” Thus the spiritual mind, the soul victorious over its vices, begins thenceforth to possess its kingdom when, having subdued its excesses, it is strong enough to command not only its affections but also its thoughts, so that it may restrain the former from unlawful desire and the latter from futile wandering.

What is it to see a dream and to foresee predictions of future things or mysteries of hidden things, except to receive from God the grace of contemplation and, through ecstasy of mind, to receive from divine revelation knowledge of divine judgments? This king rightly saw a dream in the second year, because every spiritual person, after subduing desire and acquiring the discipline of knowledge, eventually becomes able and accustomed to devote himself to the pursuit of contemplation.

But it often happens that when the human mind is led to contemplate the subtlety or even the strictness of divine judgments, it is suddenly shaken to the marrow by fear from the very consideration of divine strictness which it perceives. For when a mind still unformed and insufficiently instructed in heavenly disciplines presumes everything from its own effort rather than from divine grace, it easily falls into this fear through contemplation of divine severity and consideration of that justice. A presumptuous mind, seeing with wondrous subtlety how far above human power it is to respond adequately to divine benefits, and how strictly divine severity can—or ought, by the right of justice—to deal with us, is often accustomed to cast itself into immeasurable fear, indeed almost into despair.

But when the trembling mind is confounded by such dread—leaving aside how justly this happens, beyond all doubt, and how mercifully and beneficially—then at this critical point the grace of contemplation is withdrawn, lest the mind be entirely hurled by the excess of its subtlety into the pit of despair. Thus the dream, as it were, flees from it when it loses that light of contemplation which it was accustomed to see through ecstasy of mind.

But the king commanded that the diviners, magicians, sorcerers, and Chaldeans be summoned to tell the king his dreams. A person certainly has a royal mind if he is accustomed to rule his desires and to arrange his pursuits and exercises according to the judgment of deliberation. Such a royal mind brings together all the wise men of Babylon and in some manner compels diverse schools to unite in one investigation whenever it devotes to the one and only business of heavenly doctrine all the care and inquiry which it was accustomed to disperse among various studies and exercises.

We seek, as it were, our lost dreams from wise people of this sort, gathered as it were into one, when we endeavour by the manifold and tireless application of our studies to restore the visions of our contemplation that have been withdrawn. “When they had come, they stood before the king.” Behold what is said; behold what sort of summons is described as standing before the king. Do not suppose that you yet possess a royal mind if you are not yet able to gather at will from every quarter those most subtle points of your thoughts and, according to the freedom of your choice, fix them steadfastly upon the pursuit of whatever intention you choose.

And the king said to them: “I have seen a dream, and, confused in mind, I do not know what I have seen.” We address the assembly of our wise men when inwardly we rebuke the wandering of our inquiries or inflame them toward investigation of higher things. Let us, then, in accordance with this likeness, not neglect the losses of our progress, but rather stir our studies toward their restoration.

It is indeed to be noted that above he says that he was terrified, but here that he was confused in mind. Yet we must know that, when the human mind is raised up to contemplate more clearly the lofty things of divine equity, it is, by the recoil arising from its own weakness, at one and the same time confounded by that which terrifies it. For undoubtedly, in considering divine justice and comparing it with human frailty, a person both shudders at and blushes for his own weakness.

“And the Chaldeans answered the king in Syriac: ‘O king, live for ever. Tell the dream to your servants, and we will declare its interpretation.’” First we must consider to whom and in what manner they answered. Surely, to the Chaldean king, in Syriac—which, as Jerome has explained upon this very passage, is the same as saying “in Chaldean.” What then is it to answer the king in his own language, except to convey openly and plainly what he ought to know? For when something is said to anyone in an alien and unknown language, the sound of the voice indeed reaches the ears, but its meaning does not enter the mind. Thus an answer is given, as it were, in a proper and familiar language when that which the occasion requires is suitably communicated.

But if we turn to the interpretation of the name, we are undoubtedly led back to the same meaning. For *Syria* is interpreted “lofty.” What, then, will it be to answer in Syriac, except to answer loftily? And what will it be to answer loftily, except to answer fittingly and sufficiently? Now the mind recognizes nothing better, nothing more certain, nothing more lofty, than what it has learned by experience; and perhaps this is the proper, principal, and altogether loftiest mode by which the human soul learns—when we prove something by our own experience.

Do not your thoughts or occupations answer you as properly and openly, and instruct you sufficiently loftily toward truth, when they teach you from your own failure and speak, as it were, through experience, how vainly or rashly anything beyond human measure is presumed upon through one’s own exertion? The whole of their reply seems especially to contain this: that what the king was violently demanding was altogether impossible. Thus, in wise persons of the kind we showed above, their answer will, I think, be to teach their impossibility through their own experience. Let us examine each element of their reply, and first consider the first.

## CHAPTER III. That in everything we do we ought to strive for a good intention and rely upon divine grace.

[Col. 1235C]

“‘O king,’ they say, ‘live for ever’” (Dan. 2). Therefore, that we may compare outward things with inward, bodily with spiritual, would that we possessed that inward household as well disciplined as we have recognized this outward one to be disciplined. We have heard what they first answer their king; and perhaps he himself had taught them this very thing. Let us teach our own household, in every one of our efforts, to give a like answer: “O king, live for ever.”

But what, I ask, is this: a wish or an admonition? Is it a wish that he may be able to do this, or an admonition that he should devote all effort to this very thing? What is the life of that inward prince, of that ruler of the inward household? What, I say, is the life of that ruling power in the soul—that is, the human mind—except a good intention? Whatever a person does, even if it is good, will nevertheless be useless unless it is done with a good intention. The human mind dies even amid good works when its intention is corrupted. Truth itself bears witness: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matt. 6).

What then is it to live for ever, except to have a good intention in every good work? Would that, at every effort of ours and every good undertaking, this answer might first occur to us; that all our thought might long and strive for this: that we may live eternally. This will indeed happen [Col. 1236A] if we do nothing except what is good, and do nothing without a good intention.

For, to pass over other things, how often we seek truth itself not for truth but for vanity; and love truth when found, not in truth but for vanity. And, most miserable of all, in words of life we traffic for the profits of death. Or rather, we rightly understand the life of the inward person to be divine grace. For as the body can do nothing without its life—that is, without the soul—so our inward person can do nothing good without divine grace. “By the grace of God,” says the Apostle, “I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15). And Truth himself says of himself: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

What then is it to say, “live for ever,” except to cling unceasingly to grace? Whatever you plan, presume not upon your own industry but upon divine grace; whatever you accomplish, ascribe it to that grace, not to yourself. Certainly this ought to have been said to that king, and especially at the time when he was seeking by human means what he had received from God, and was relying, for something hoped for, more upon human industry than upon divine grace.

But it is very strange—indeed, astonishing beyond human measure—that often, when we speak these things silently within ourselves and feel them inwardly, we nevertheless at the same time rely upon our own industry as though we wholly ignored cooperating grace. Often, while we speak subtly to our neighbours in praise of divine grace, we privately glory in the subtlety of our own speech. O infinite folly of humankind! You rightly say that a human being can do nothing without grace; but if you speak the truth, why do you glory?

Let us therefore teach those most subtle searchers-out of hidden things—namely, our thoughts—that in every study and every undertaking they should first and chiefly strive for this, first instilling in us this concern: that we should seek to presume that all we propose comes from grace, to ascribe to divine grace all that we accomplish. And this belongs to living for ever.

## CHAPTER IV. How, according to the varying outcomes of their pursuits, some cast themselves down feebly or vainly exalt themselves.

“Tell the dream to your servants,” they say, “and we will declare [Col. 1236D] its interpretation” (Dan. 2). Observe what they say. They demand one thing and promise another. They demand from the king the vision and promise its interpretation. Yet their demand is as vain as their promise is false. There was one thing which they could truly have said, had they wished to confess the truth: namely, that they did not know the vision and could not possibly know it by themselves.

Why then do those who profess falsehood not at least confess truth? Common modesty conceals its own inability; universal shamelessness presumes beyond ability.

“And the king answered and said to the Chaldeans: ‘The matter has departed from me. Unless you make known to me the dream and its interpretation, you shall perish and your houses shall be confiscated. But if you tell the dream and its interpretation, [Col. 1237A] you shall receive from me rewards, gifts, and great honour.’”

Who, I ask, would not freely rebuke King Nebuchadnezzar because he consigns his wise men to destruction on such a ground, when he himself perhaps does the same or worse? For what is it voluntarily to destroy one’s wise men, except wholly to abandon the pursuits of wisdom and to be unwilling any longer to exercise the most subtle powers of one’s intellect in investigating any doctrine? And what is it to confiscate the houses of the wise and turn them over to common use?

By “houses” we are accustomed to mean that place of our dwelling to which, after manifold labours and wanderings, we regularly return for the sake of rest. What then can be understood more appropriately by the house of the wise than those private and hidden leisures of repose in which all devoted students are accustomed to engage in the pursuits of learning? Thus the houses of our wise men are, in a sense, made public when the studious leisures of our repose are exposed to every wandering of dissipation, and the inner sanctuaries of learning are prostituted to every care or curiosity.

How many do we see, after the splendid distinctions of their studies and great achievements of learning, when perhaps they have been promoted to some rank of honour or assumed responsibility for some administration, immediately despise all the discipline of their learning, devote themselves wholly and continually to secular business, destroy in a single day every cultivator of wisdom, and make their hidden secrets public? [Col. 1237C] What would such persons do if they received Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom?

Likewise, how many do we see, after sustained zeal in spiritual exercises and after receiving at last the grace of contemplation, when perhaps they have been cast down from that state of exaltation by some temptation or weariness, and see that they cannot return to that summit without some labour, or perhaps without great labour, immediately lay aside or condemn all zeal for spiritual pursuits, exposing themselves at every hour to all wandering and vain distractions. You may see them not only fail to return to those leisures of contemplation, but even wholly abandon every diligence of meditation or reading.

What else do such people do but kill their wise men, when by the varied fluctuation of their desires they obscure within themselves every spiritual understanding? We have heard of threats; let us now consider the promises. “But if you tell the dream and its interpretation,” he says, “you shall receive from me rewards, gifts, and great honour.” A reward is received when we receive what we have deserved; a gift, when we receive what we have not yet deserved; honour, when we obtain even that for whose earning we are less fit. Thus a reward is rendered for merits, a gift is bestowed freely, and honour is conferred from dignity alone: “You shall receive from me rewards, gifts, and great honour.”

Nothing, brothers, is truer: how readily we pay our wise men the wages of merit, how gladly we confer upon them honour, whether due or gratuitous! To state fully what I mean, I await nothing more certainly and fear nothing more than that someone may strive to bestow excessive honour and greater reverence than is fitting upon wise men of this kind, when they have perhaps satisfied their desires and their wishes have answered as they wished.

Who does not ascribe more to his own pursuits and disciplines than Truth itself declares? Who, I ask, would not wish to extend the reputation of his learning and wisdom, not only according to the measure of equity but beyond—indeed above—the obligation of equity? Therefore whenever the mind gladly applies itself to its studies and promises itself thereby an enlargement of reputation and glory, it speaks, as it were, to its wise men: “You shall receive rewards, gifts, [Col. 1238B] and great honour.”

## CHAPTER V. In how many ways the mind deceives itself and is not unwilling to hide its own fault from itself.

Having proposed the reward, the king immediately adds and says: “Therefore make known to me the dream and its interpretation” (Dan. 2). He asks two things: the dream and its interpretation. It is one thing to know, through divine revelation, the hidden things of divine judgments; another to have been able to weigh or penetrate their rationale. The former belongs to knowing the dream, the latter to interpreting it. How many divine judgments we know whose reason we do not penetrate by any examination of our own!

“They answered a second time and said: ‘Let the king tell the dream to his servants, and we will declare its interpretation.’” What is it to answer again except to teach, through a second failure of one’s mind, more fully and perfectly one’s own inability? O how difficult it is to restrain human shamelessness from its presumption! After many trials, impossible things are still demanded; impossible things are still promised.

But let us see what follows. The king answered and said: “Certainly I know that you are buying time, since you know that the matter has departed from me. Therefore, if you do not make known the dream to me, there is one judgment concerning you: that you have also devised a false interpretation, full of deception, in order to speak to me until the time has passed. Therefore tell me the dream, that I may know that you also speak its true interpretation.”

Behold, by his persistence the king has made no small progress, since at last he has detected their duplicity. And do not suppose that you have made little progress when you can clearly detect the duplicity of your own heart. How many things we often pretend; how many we conceal! We gladly conceal our weaknesses, and we pretend that we can do, or possess, goods that we cannot do or possess at all. It is indeed very strange that the mind gladly deceives itself and is not unwilling to hide its own fault from itself.

Behold, the king detects in his subjects both faults, pretence and concealment: concealment, indeed, when he says, “Certainly I know that you are buying time”; pretence when, a little later, he adds, “There is one judgment concerning you: that you have also devised a false interpretation.” They concealed their ignorance and did not wish openly to confess it, and in this they were buying time; yet they falsely promised an interpretation of the dream.

But the king proved the evil of their concealment by experience; the evil of their pretence he knew by reasoning, inferring one fault from the other. For if they could not do the lesser thing, how could they have done the greater? From this, I think, you perceive and observe that some things in us we prove by experience, while others we infer by reason.

“Then the Chaldeans answered before the king and said: ‘There is no man upon earth who can fulfil your demand, O king.’” Behold, they answer now for a third time, and at last plainly disclose their failure. If we distinguish the three successive answers by stages, perhaps the first answer is one of doubt, the second of fear, and the third of despair. At the first attempt, when we begin something but do not complete it, we often begin to doubt the completion of what we have undertaken. At the second, we fear more greatly. At the third attempt, when we attain no result, we are accustomed to despair altogether.

Observe that doubt and fear have an ambiguous answer, but despair has a manifest answer. Thus at the first and second reply they diminish their ignorance rather than declare it. But at the third, they now openly profess it. Yet let us hear how falsely they speak what is true: “There is no man,” they say, [Col. 1239C] “upon earth who can fulfil your demand.” They do not simply say, “We cannot,” which was indeed true, but “There is no person on earth who can,” which was undoubtedly false. For Daniel was a man and was upon earth, and he was able to do this, as the outcome afterward proved.

Yet he was able to do so not by his own industry but through divine grace. Who could say that he was unable to do what he could obtain by prayer? See in how many ways and how often the human mind deceives itself; but who could sufficiently explain this? How many things we presume that we can do when we cannot do them at all; and how many things that we cannot do at all we think that no one can do!

Why, I ask, is it that the human mind does not at all proclaim to others the good which it finds proved in itself, yet adds others to itself in respect of the evil which it finds in itself? Behold, these wise men did not ascribe universally and equally to all what they presumed concerning the interpretation of the dream. Yet what they could not do concerning the recovery of the dream, they asserted that no one could do. But, if we consider all this with reference to one and the same mind, we ought neither rashly to presume nor rashly to despair concerning anything in ourselves. For often what we cannot do in one way, we accomplish easily in another. How many things that we cannot obtain by acting, we obtain by praying.

## CHAPTER VI. How rashly or vainly we presume from human industry what we ought to await solely from angelic or divine revelation.

[Col. 1240A]

Let us see, then, what else they add, carefully examining what they say wrongly and what perhaps truly. For statements uttered incautiously serve to make us cautious, while rightly uttered statements should form us toward zeal for imitation. “But no great and mighty king,” they say, “asks such a matter of every diviner, magician, and Chaldean” (Dan. 2).

He is rightly called king who is raised to a kingdom. But what says that King, truly King of kings and Lord of lords? “The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is within you” (Luke 17). We can indeed be raised to this kingdom if we will it perfectly. This kingdom existing within us has many inhabitants and countless dwellers. The more anyone enlarges such a kingdom, administers it more faithfully, governs it more strictly, and orders it more wisely, the more powerful he becomes and the greater he is judged.

Yet poverty of spirit contributes more and more profitably to this kingdom than abundance of understanding: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Whoever receives such a kingdom sings confidently when he says: “But I have been established king by him” (Ps. 2). And it is well said of kings of this kind: “But no great and mighty king asks such a matter of every diviner, magician, and Chaldean.”

These kings are great in this respect, and preserve their own power, because they presume nothing from their own strength—much less things that are above humankind. Certainly the king had received that matter from God, and it was wholly of such a kind that it could not be known except by God’s revelation. Therefore, with what rashness is that which cannot be known except from God presumed from a human diviner, magician, or Chaldean? What, then, is it neither to wish nor to be obliged to ask such a matter from any wise person of that sort, except that things above humankind must not be presumed from any human industry or art?

Hence it is added: “For the matter which you ask, O king, is difficult, and no one will be found to declare it in the king’s presence except the gods, whose dwelling is not with human beings.” Certainly the king ought not to have demanded from a human being what was above human capacity. What is heavier or more burdensome than for one person to demand impossibilities from another person, and to wish to extort from human ability things that are beyond human measure? But “what is impossible with human beings is possible with God.”

“Except the gods,” they say, “whose dwelling is not with human beings.” Here we rightly understand by “gods” the holy angels. For if human beings have been called gods because they share in the image or even likeness, how much more rightly are angels so called? “I said: You are gods, and sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81). Angels indeed are among human beings at every hour—indeed, at almost every moment—yet they do not dwell with them, because even when they are among humans, [Col. 1241A] they live not humanly but heavenly and truly divinely.

Who can deny or not know that angels have been able, and are accustomed, to reveal to humans many things above humankind? Yet, to carry the comparison further from outward things to our inward life: we often know through divine revelations and inspirations what we penetrate by none of our own investigations.

But if anyone wishes by “gods” to understand not angels but divinely inspired persons, whose dwelling is no longer with human beings—that is, with those who have human wisdom—because they can now truly say, “Our citizenship is in heaven,” nothing truer can be said. For by divine inspiration they know many things which exceed human inquiry. But if the preceding statement is fitted to this meaning, nothing but what is right seems to sound in it where it says: “There is no man upon earth who can fulfil your demand, O king”—as though it said: None of those who are upon earth, except only those who ascend to heaven by a heavenly manner of life.

## CHAPTER VII. How, after the splendid distinctions of their pursuits, the mind often abandons its concern for both secular and spiritual learning and wholly gives itself over to outward affairs.

“On hearing this, the king, in great fury and anger, commanded that all the wise men of Babylon should perish. And the decree went out, and the wise men were being killed” (Dan. 2). Behold what we have already said above. After the king despaired of recovering his dream, he decreed in fury and anger that all his wise men should perish. As we have said, this is to destroy one’s wise men: no longer to seek, according to former custom and accustomed exercise, those sharp and subtle understandings of knowledge and wisdom, nor to give any effort or attention at all to the pursuits of any learning.

A dream that has been seen is, as it were, lost when the grace of contemplation by which the mind was frequently raised to lofty things is withdrawn. We then despair, as it were, of recovering it when, after long and great labour with no progress, we lose confidence that we can again recover that delight of our spiritual visions.

Yet it often happens that, when the mind loses that contemplation of divine revelations which it had been accustomed to love, broken now by prolonged weariness, it lays aside concern not only for the thing whose restoration exhausted it, but for every kind of study whatsoever, and thus plans in some sense to destroy all its wise men. “In fury,” he says, “and great anger.” Fury is a disturbance of the mind wholly devoid of reason. Anger is a great disturbance of the mind, but not wholly alien to reason. We are agitated and driven as though in fury when, without regard for reason, we hurl ourselves headlong into what ought not to be done. When stirred by anger, we often understand what should be done, yet cannot restrain ourselves if the anger is great.

Thus, in the first onset of our disturbance, we often do not even look to reason. Afterwards we indeed see reason, but cannot follow it; at last we behold and follow it. Therefore fury is rightly placed first and anger afterwards.

It should certainly be noted that the wise men of Babylon are said to be those whom it is commanded should perish here. I think the wise men of the Babylonians are one thing, and the wise men of the Jews another. The former are occupied with earthly matters; the latter with divine. The former pursue the wisdom of the world, which is foolishness with God; the latter, being spiritual and comparing spiritual things with spiritual, search even the depths of God. What, then, do we understand by the wise men of the Babylonians except secular branches of knowledge? And what by the wise men of the Jews except spiritual teachings?

Thus we consign the wise men of Babylon to destruction when we cut secular disciplines away from our pursuits. Our conscience more easily acquiesces in their removal and consents the more readily to their rejection because it regards them as by no means necessary, however useful they may be for something relating to human well-being. Therefore the wise men of Babylon are killed first, whence it is said of them: “And the decree went out, and the wise men were being killed.” A decree goes forth when someone finally manifests in action what he has deliberated and determined in mind. What still turns about and lies hidden in the mind is, as it were, still within; and it begins, as it were, already to be exercised when it appears in action.

It follows: “Daniel and his companions were sought, that they might perish.” Behold how evil spreads. We heard above how the wise men of Babylon were being killed; behold, now the wise men [Col. 1242C] of the Jews are sought to be killed. Behold the stages by which an earnest mind is often dissolved from its vitality and gradually falls back from higher things to worse: it first abandons concern for secular learning and then for spiritual teaching; it gives itself entirely to outward business, and, as it were, kills within itself every cultivator of knowledge and wisdom, when, after despising the human arts, it wholly abandons the diligence of contemplation, meditation, reading, and prayer.

Yet observe that it is said of the wise men of the Jews that they were sought for destruction. What, I ask, is it to seek a place where wise men of this kind may be found for destruction, except to seize upon an occasion or some opportunity for excuse, by which the undisciplined mind may more safely, freely, and with a more secure conscience cast aside even the pursuits of sacred learning? For we often plead bodily weakness when we abandon spiritual exercises. We often pretend that it is charity when, abandoning the contemplative life, we give ourselves wholly to outward affairs. In this way an occasion and, as it were, a suitable place are sought where Daniel with the other wise men of the Jews may be found to be killed.

If we consult this Daniel’s deeds, what could we find more fittingly represented in him than the devotion of the heart? Observe how, in every adversity and necessity, he always has recourse to the Lord and consults him, implores and receives divine aid. [Col. 1243A] Who does not know that it belongs to true devotion, at every point of necessity, to flee to divine assistance and humbly request, and effectively obtain, counsel in uncertainties and help in adversities?

But we know that the mind never prays inwardly and devoutly unless it first arouses itself to devotion by diligent preliminary meditations. For careful, discerning, and provident thoughts are the inseparable companions of true devotion. Without companions and fellow-workers of this kind, none of our devotion knows or is able to pray as it ought.

## CHAPTER VIII. How in every purpose or undertaking we ought to consult the rule of equity and recall imprudently established determinations to a sounder judgment.

[Col. 1243B]

“Then Daniel sought information concerning the law and the decree from Arioch, the captain of the king’s guard, who had gone out to kill the wise men of Babylon; and he questioned the one who had received authority from the king, why so cruel a decree had gone forth from the presence of the king. When Arioch had made the matter known to Daniel, Daniel went in and requested the king to grant him time, that he might declare the solution to the king” (Dan. 2).

As Daniel signifies the fervour of devotion, so by the captain of the guard we rightly, I think, understand zeal for rectitude and the rigour of strict severity. Certainly, without the rigour of just severity, it is not possible even to possess in peace or security that kingdom in which people are accustomed to rule people and in which people are accustomed to disturb the peace of those who possess authority. What ruler was ever able to enjoy or rejoice in lasting peace if he refused, when he could and ought, to judge strictly and strike forcefully the adversaries of peace?

How much more, then, in that kingdom in which “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places”—how much more, I say, in such a kingdom, ought we to act bravely and strike with strict correction every tumult of clamouring thoughts or affections, and all disturbers of inward peace? This captain of the guard is good indeed—that is, the rigour and severity of justice. Whoever does not obey his laws or disciplines excludes himself from the fellowship of that heavenly army.

This captain of the guard is rightly, I think, called Arioch. For *Arioch* is interpreted “bringing into solitude.” We know that the kingdom of heaven is within us. Therefore this captain of the guard ought to overthrow by vigorous assault and bring into everlasting solitude every kingdom or region that he sees rising or rebelling against this kingdom and refusing obedience to the laws of the eternal King; and, if possible, to destroy it for ever.

If, then, by Daniel we ought to understand devotion, and by Arioch zeal for rectitude, what is it for Daniel to ask Arioch about the king’s law and decree, except for a contrite mind to consult the judgment of equity and, from great devotion, to examine intensely whether that which it remembers having first determined through an impulse of its own spirit is perhaps just or unjust? For in a time of contrition and prayer the human mind finds many things evil and unjust which it had first determined from an impulse of mind, and, as it were, precipitately; yet at that time it did not perceive them to be unjust.

A person often dictates many things against his own conscience from the same impulse of his spirit; yet afterward, during prayer and devotion, he moderates that same precipitancy of mind and reforms it to a sounder judgment. We ought therefore to examine carefully those things which we establish precipitately rather than prudently and fear to be evil; and by shrewd reconsideration to inquire whether they are just or unjust, useful or useless. In this way, as it were, through Daniel, the office of Arioch is sought concerning a law or decree issued, when, concerning any less-considered purpose of the mind, the rule of true equity and highest discernment is at last consulted in great devotion.

What it is to go out to kill the wise men can easily be gathered from what has been said above. We should know, however, that we often recognize more easily and fear more greatly the determination or character of an inconsiderate decree when we have already proved what it is like through the act itself and, as it were, by experience. Hence Arioch here is first consulted concerning the issuance of the decree when he is already on the point of going out to carry it out.

## CHAPTER IX. That whatever is accustomed to happen to us, under God’s dispensation, corresponds to the free choice of the mind according to the quality of merits.

[Col. 1244C]

But if Arioch rightly signifies the strictness of equity, it may perhaps seem strange to someone, and not without reason, how the execution of such a decree can be said to belong to Arioch’s office, since that decree is judged just neither according to the historical sense nor according to the mystical understanding. Or perhaps, in the historical sense, the king, disturbed by fury, believed just what was not truly just, because he could then truly have said: “My eye is troubled by anger.”

Thus, according to the pattern of this likeness, some people indeed generate zeal for rectitude but lack knowledge. They believe, or feign, that it is right to kill their wise men, setting before themselves or promising themselves greater gains of merit from bodily exercises than from spiritual ones, in which, meanwhile, they cannot make as much or as easy progress as they wish.
