But if we look more deeply still and have recourse to divine judgments, we immediately see that God permits nothing except justly, even though a person may plan or do many things unjustly. Why, then, should not even those things be said to belong to Arioch’s office which, under this consideration, are found to correspond to our merits according to the equity of divine strictness?

“And he questioned,” it says, “the one who had received authority from the king.” Observe, then, that this Arioch received authority from the king, because whatever happens to us, beneficially or harmfully, proceeds from the merit or fault of free choice. Arioch receives from the king authority to execute a decree, sometimes beneficial and sometimes harmful: at times from a king who knows and wills; at times from one who knows and does not will; at times from one who does not know and wills; and at times from one who neither knows nor wills.

For, as has been said, whatever is accustomed to happen to each person, under God’s dispensation, corresponds through freedom of choice to the quality of merits. Therefore whatever is done concerning us, as recompense for merits and by right of equity, is governed by God’s just judgment. But the provident gaze of the mind, even under the force of its great disturbance, often recognizes the good pleasure or judgment of the Almighty and acquiesces. At times it recognizes and does not acquiesce; at other times it is so disposed that it desires only God’s will to be done concerning it, even though it does not meanwhile understand that will fully. But at another time it is so affected that it cannot at all acquiesce in God’s will, even if it could fully know the will which meanwhile it cannot know.

But what wonder is it if the human mind cannot always acquiesce even in the divine will it knows, when it often cannot acquiesce even in what is beneficial to itself? For through impatience it often pronounces a judgment which it does not at all fail to know is contrary to its own benefit. Therefore that captain of the guard receives from his king authority to execute a decree not only when such a king orders something justly and beneficially, but also when through shamelessness or impatience he orders something which, under God’s dispensation and in consequence of his preceding merits, corresponds to the recompense of equity; indeed, even when he does something by which he incurs an odious, although just, judgment.

## CHAPTER X. By what considerations we should weigh the things that happen to us.

Let us consider further what it is that Daniel asks Arioch again. “For what reason had so cruel a decree gone forth from the king’s presence?” The proper order, and one to be carefully observed, is first to inquire into the law and the decree, and afterward into the cause of that same decree. Without doubt, in matters that are doubtful and especially perilous, one must inquire diligently and examine intensely [Col. 1245D], first concerning the character of the act and then concerning the character of the intention. For often the fault incurred by an action is somewhat mitigated by the character of the intention.

Yet his inquiry into the cause of the decree may, I think, indeed ought to be referred to two things: namely, with what intention it is done, or by what dispensation of God it happens to be done. With regard to the action, one asks whether it is advantageous or disadvantageous, just or unjust. With regard to the intention, whether perhaps it is pious or impious, prudent or imprudent. But with regard to God’s dispensation, in examining a terrible or harsh decree, each person should inquire especially whether it strikes us for our benefit or for vengeance. For certainly, when He strikes us [Col. 1246A], or permits us to be struck, He does so sometimes for our instruction, sometimes for our correction, sometimes for our rebuke, sometimes for condemnation, or in some other way still.

All these matters must be diligently investigated and subtly examined. All these instill a salutary fear and pierce the mind in prayer. All these humble the mind, awaken our devotion, and kindle us toward supplication. You see, surely, how rightly and prudently Daniel investigates all these things before he perseveres in prayers or applies himself to supplication. Hence it is said, in what follows: “When Arioch had therefore made the matter known to Daniel, Daniel entered and asked the king.” But what is that aforementioned learning by Daniel from Arioch, except that the devout mind, after much discussion, comes at last more fully to know the character of the decree and its cause, sought out by diligent and devout consultation of the strict [Col. 1246B] rule of equity?

## CHAPTER XI. How, in the time of our disturbance, we ought to have recourse to the remedies of prayer and put such aid into practice.

It remains now to inquire what it means for Daniel to enter to the king. Perhaps we rightly understand by the king—who presides and rules over all things in this place—a vehement movement of the soul and a strong impulse of free will, to which every other affection readily yields or submits. And how many people, when they are violently affected or sharply stirred, do not think at all of consulting reason or discernment—much less [Col. 1246C] of having recourse to prayer or admitting any devotion! But what else do we say this is than that none of the wise dare appear before the king?

Yet such persons often, after the soul’s impulse has been calmed and they have returned to themselves, have recourse to the judgment of discernment and the duty of devotion, striving to correct the things in which they transgressed during the time of disturbance. But if we are as zealous for the discipline of the heart as we ought to be, let us teach and train our soul, under every impulse and in every time of disturbance, to resort to the counsels of discernment; and this is to admit the wise before the king.

But because it often happens that it cannot soften the headlong force of its disturbance by any testimony of reason [Col. 1246D], the mind ought, at such a point of necessity, to resort to the helps of devotion and obtain the assistance of divine mercy to quiet the violence of its disturbance. It must put this remedy of devotion into practice; and this is for Daniel to enter to the king. For Daniel, as it were, enters to the king when devotion affords aid, even under the very onset of precipitancy, to calm the soul’s impulse.

It should be noted that above he is said to have been *introduced*, whereas here it is simply stated that he *entered*. I think that being introduced by another and entering by oneself are different things. As is clear from what precedes, to have the aid of devout prayer ready under every vehement impulse of the soul is for Daniel not to be absent in the presence of the raging king. But, as we all commonly accomplish with effort, we obtain some things by praying and by supplicating God. Therefore, when by human alertness and the exercise of devotion one becomes accustomed to have help ready to calm the soul’s impulse, our Daniel is in some manner introduced before the presence of the aforesaid king through another’s service [Col. 1247A]. But when this is accomplished not so much by meditation as by prayer, Daniel undoubtedly enters to the king by himself.

Accordingly, by diligent and intelligent premeditation we ought to stir our mind to devotion, and this will be to introduce Daniel through another’s service. Again, because we often cannot pray devoutly even when necessity demands and presses us, let us pray in the time of divine visitation and our compunction [Col. 1247B], so that we may be able to pray in the time of necessity. If, therefore, the ability to pray is obtained through prayer, Daniel certainly enters by himself.

Nor should we carelessly pass over the fact that he is said to have entered during the time of royal disturbance and fury. For at the time of his introduction we receive no indication whatever of royal disturbance. We should not believe that this king is always angry and troubled by some rage. It is one thing for the soul’s impulse to be vehement, another for it to be headlong. It is one thing, I say, for it to be strong and unconquered, another for it to be full of anger and madness. Finally, it is one thing for it to be invincible and nearly immovable, another for it to be unbearable and wholly irrational [Col. 1247C].

But who, I ask, would presume, or dare, during the time of royal fury to bring Daniel before the king? I judge that, in a time of such great and intimate disturbance, applying oneself to prayer lies beyond human industry and strength, since at that time it scarcely happens—or rather cannot happen at all—that one even remembers it. Therefore Daniel must, in the manner mentioned above, enter by himself before the troubled king if he wishes, at such a point of necessity, to resist danger.

Thus the diligent mind, solicitous for its salvation, which when disturbed still does not know how to resist its disturbance by prayer and has not yet obtained such practice or grace, should pray and obtain from God, in a time of tranquillity, the grace to pray in a time of disturbance. [Col. 1247D] In this way perhaps Daniel will at some time be granted to enter to the king by himself even while the king is raging. Then perhaps he will be able, not merely once but often and continually, to ask for and obtain a postponement of the evil decree, in order afterward to erase it altogether.

When, in the time of its inward disturbance, the devout mind humbly asks and supplicates that divine mercy not permit it, under the impetus of inflamed rage, to do something through impatience for which it will afterward have to repent, then, if it obtains what it seeks, what else does Daniel, representing our devotion, appear to do but mitigate the madness of the raging king? When, however, someone feels himself drawn by the violence of a headlong affection toward something whose rightness, amid such a cloud or tempest of disturbance, he cannot meanwhile fully recognize [Col. 1248A], and asks for patience until, in a time of tranquillity, he can more rightly discern what ought to be done, then in receiving what he asks, what else does he seem to accomplish but to ask for and receive a reprieve?

“Daniel,” it says, “entered and asked the king to give him time to make known the interpretation to the king.” You see surely that devotion piously and beneficially often presumes upon the Lord’s mercy for what it cannot accomplish by any human cleverness or industry. And how justly we greatly presume upon the Lord’s mercy, if, for love of Him and with His help, we overcome our own greatness of soul.

## CHAPTER XII. By what meditations the soul ought to be inflamed to devotion, or how we ought to restore the earnestness of our pursuits.

[Col. 1248B]

But let us see what Daniel did afterward, or what is written of him: “And having entered his own house, he made the matter known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions, that they might seek mercy from the face of the God of heaven concerning this mystery, and that Daniel and his companions might not perish with the other wise men of Babylon” (Dan. 2).

By these three, Daniel’s inseparable companions and indivisible associates, we understand circumspection, discernment, and deliberation, without which daily experience proves that the office of true devotion cannot in any way be fulfilled. For if we wish to pray inwardly and devoutly, the first thing is to survey our life [Col. 1248C]. Let us see in what pursuits or exercises we have been accustomed to engage, what still occupies us, and what purpose we hold concerning these things for the future.

But what good is it to bring these matters into consideration unless we also labor with equal care to distinguish every one of them by rigorous examination, and to separate good things from evil by watchful discernment, so that we may know for what we ought to supplicate the Lord, or also give thanks? Once our good and evil have been recognized, it remains to inquire by prudent deliberation what occupation or effort may enable us to make satisfaction for past evils, extricate ourselves from present ones, and provide more carefully against future ones. The first belongs to circumspection, the second to discernment, the third to deliberation.

It belongs to circumspection [Col. 1248D] to bring the condition of our morals under consideration; to discernment, to pass judgment on everything; but deliberation seeks and finds counsel. Circumspection says: “I shall recall to mind all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38). Discernment confesses: “I have performed judgment and justice” (Ps. 98). Deliberation says: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that He has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115).

He is called back to the pursuit of circumspection to whom it is said: “Lift up your eyes round about” (Isa. 49), and then see where you have been cast down, O harlot. He who said, “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11), wished to encourage us to the examination of discernment. The duty of deliberation is commanded, or also commended, when it is said through the wise man: “Do everything with counsel, [Col. 1249A] and you shall never repent” (Ecclus. 32).

Who does not see how necessary these functions are to true devotion? For who has ever been able to pray inwardly and devoutly if he has neglected to survey, examine, and order his life? Whenever, therefore, necessity presses us to apply ourselves more earnestly to devout prayer, we must have recourse to the offices of circumspection, discernment, and deliberation, and by such pursuits and laborious meditations inflame our soul to devotion. This is for Daniel to enlist the assistance of his companions for the use of his prayer.

Thus Daniel, as it were, withdraws to the inner rooms of his house and seeks fellow workers for the more perfect fulfillment of the business of his prayer, when, with the time of prayer already at hand or at a point of pressing necessity [Col. 1249B], the devout mind seeks again the habitual quiet suitable and necessary for this duty, and strives by certain prudent meditations fitted for such use to stir up or inflame its devotion. “He made the matter known to his companions.” The matter is, as it were, made known by Daniel to Daniel’s companions when devotion causes the impending matter to be brought to consideration, examination, and consultation. Mercy to be obtained is proposed when the contrite mind, in what it devoutly performs, relies not on its own merits but on divine mercies.

It should certainly be noted, according to the history, that the prophet Daniel calls this matter a “mystery”; who then can doubt that a mystical understanding of realities lies hidden in it? [Col. 1249C] “And Daniel and his companions,” it says, “might not perish with the other wise men of Babylon.”

Following this example, when we see that our mind, after contempt for worldly pursuits, has also grown sluggish in spiritual exercises and is gradually failing, and that danger threatens our wise men, we too must by every means ask the Lord for that by which we may restore or strengthen the accustomed earnestness of our pursuits. For, as we alike know, there is very great labor both in the practice of prayer and in meditation, and it is almost unbearable for wandering and restless minds. But in contemplation there is a wonderful and almost unique delight. Therefore, when the grace of contemplation is granted to studious minds [Col. 1249D], the labor of the other pursuits is sweetened by its sweetness insofar as it is lightened or moderated.

If, then, we have not yet received such grace, or grieve that it has been withdrawn, we ought to ask it from the Lord for the strengthening or restoration of our pursuits. When we do this, what else, I ask, do we appear to have done but seek dreams of divine revelations, so that we may have the means to preserve in their integrity those wise men of ours indicated above?

“Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision by night.” The revelation of the mystery is received, as it were, at night, when the illumination of truth is seen faintly and in part, as though by moonlight. We receive the revelation of the mystery, as it were, at night, when we ourselves understand what ought to be thought concerning some secret of the Godhead, but do not yet have readily at hand an argument by which we may prove it also to others. The light of revelation appears as it were in the night and amid darkness when someone is unable to explain in speech, and bring as it were into open light, the disclosure of the mystery which he sees by understanding [Col. 1250A].

But when afterward, through prolonged reflection, we bring it about that the understanding of truth which we ourselves could at first scarcely or faintly see may be declared to others by clear demonstration, what else do we do but bring into the light of day what we received by night? Thus there is rightly no further mention of night where Daniel at last speaks openly in the king’s presence what he had first received by night.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, whenever understanding is renewed, we ought to magnify not our own industry but the Lord’s magnificence.

[Col. 1250B]

But, having received the revelation of the mystery, let us see further what Daniel does or says: “And Daniel blessed the God of heaven, and spoke, saying: ‘Blessed be the name of the Lord from age unto age, because wisdom and strength are His; and He changes times and seasons, removes kingdoms and establishes them’” (Dan. 2).

Let us learn from this example what we ourselves ought to do when we receive the light of revealing grace. Therefore, following Daniel’s example, let us strive to render glory, honor, and thanksgiving to Him from whom we have the power to be wise [Col. 1250C] and to understand, and whatever good we are known to possess. For many, when they receive the light of truth, immediately ascribe it to their own merits or studies, magnify and exalt themselves, and despise all others in comparison with themselves. The soul of such a person says within itself, “I have understood more than all who teach me.” It endeavors, as imprudently as vainly, to apply to itself that saying of Solomon: “I surpassed in wisdom all who were before me” (Eccl. 1).

On the contrary, let us give glory to Him from whom we have received understanding. Let us strive always, at the very rising of revealing grace, at the very renewal of illuminated understanding, to offer God worthy proclamations of praise. “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your solemnity.” The new moon, the new moon, is understanding renewed and divinely inspired. We know that the moon has no light of itself but receives it from the sun so that it may shine. So indeed human understanding has received from God the power to shine with the rays of true light.

Whenever, therefore, we receive new rays of divine illumination and learn by divine revelation something surpassing human understanding [Col. 1250D], we ought immediately to rise in thanksgiving and resound the trumpet of magnificence in proclamation of divine goodness: “Magnify the Lord with me,” it says, “and let us exalt His name together” (Ps. 33). See how the trumpet sounded; see how, at the trumpet’s blast, he stirred both himself and others. He wished—or promised—to make the sound of such a trumpet at the new moon when he said: “I shall bless the Lord who has given me understanding” [Col. 1251A] (Ps. 15).

Thus, when Daniel received the light of revealing grace, he sounded the trumpet of magnificence as at the rising of a new moon, saying: “Blessed be the name of the Lord from age unto age, because wisdom and strength are His.”

## CHAPTER XIV. That the office of true devotion is threefold.

It should certainly be noted that the office of true and perfect devotion is threefold. The first is confession of sin; the second, the petition for mercy; the third, glorification of the One who shows mercy. The first is accusation of fault; the second, supplication for pardon; the third, magnification of divine generosity.

Our Daniel performs all these magnificently, as may be known from his words. There is confession and accusation of fault where, in another place, he speaks to the Lord [Col. 1251B] in prayer: “We have sinned, committed iniquity, acted wickedly, revolted, and turned aside from Your commandments and judgments” (Dan. 9). There is supplication and imploring for pardon where you read him saying likewise: “Hear, O Lord; be appeased, O Lord; attend and act” (ibid.). There is glorification and magnification of his Creator, who has shown him mercy, beyond doubt where you read in this passage: “Blessed be the name of the Lord from age unto age, because wisdom and strength are His; and He changes times and seasons, removes kingdoms, and establishes them” (Dan. 2).

Wisdom and strength are indeed goods possessed by the recipient, but beyond doubt they are the goods of the God who bestows them. For whoever have wisdom and strength, whoever have been able to act wisely and courageously, received them from His gift [Col. 1251C]. “What do you have,” says the Apostle, “that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 14).

“He changes times and seasons.” We know that everything has its time, and that all things under heaven pass through their appointed periods: “a time to plant, and a time to uproot what has been planted.” The same can be considered in other matters as well. Accordingly, from the circumstance of time we receive an opportunity to do now this, now that, more usefully or more readily. He changes times for our uses when He now provides opportunity for the exercises of these virtues, now of those.

But what good, I ask, is receiving an opportunity for exercise unless, by the gift of the same generosity, we also receive the ability to carry it out? We know, moreover [Col. 1251D], that different ages are more suited to different effects. Certainly, what we learn in childhood we retain more deeply and express more readily. In youth bodily strength is more robust and the mind more daring; therefore that age is more effective for exercise. Into more advanced age, both manifold learning and manifold experience of affairs increase knowledge through daily growth; therefore that age flourishes in counsels and possesses prudence beyond all the rest.

The first, then, of the ages mentioned prevails in learning, the second in exercising, and the third in discerning. By analogy with years and merits, so to speak, we consider ages, and according to the difference of various advances we recognize that we possess the effectiveness of different virtues. Thus different degrees of effectiveness are in some way the ages of different years [Col. 1252A]. Therefore that most excellent governor alternates the modes of times and ages of merits, who by the dispensation of His mercy administers now the capacity and opportunity for these virtues, now for those.

“He removes kingdoms and establishes them,” when, having overthrown the tyranny of vices, He causes virtues to reign. Of these peoples of vices and virtues, and of both the destruction of the former and the exaltation of the latter, it is written mystically when the Prophet says: “You transplanted a vine from Egypt; You cast out the nations and planted it” (Ps. 79). A vine is planted when a good purpose is fixed in a good intention. Nations are cast out when, by the decree of confession and the vow of profession, sins are denounced and vices renounced.

The same meaning is conveyed by what the same Prophet elsewhere says concerning the uprooting of vices or the planting of virtues: “You cast out nations and planted them; You afflicted peoples and drove them out” (ibid.) [Col. 1252B]. That hateful people of vices is driven out by the greatness of affliction when the soul, long and greatly oppressed by the dominion of carnal desires, is at last freed by both bodily contrition and compunction of heart. Thus, in this way, the author and protector of our salvation, while He destroys in us the dominion of vices and restores virtues in their place, removes kingdoms and establishes them.

And rightly so, because “the kingdom belongs to the Lord, and He shall rule over the nations.” “He gives,” it says, “wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who understand discipline. He reveals deep and hidden things, knows what is set in darkness, and light is with Him.” Therefore let no one presume upon his own talent; let no one attribute knowledge of inner or outward things to his own studies or merits. For He is the one who gives wisdom to the wise; He likewise gives knowledge to those who understand discipline.

Without doubt he proceeds to the same conclusion who says: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with Him, and is before the age” (Ecclus. 1). He agrees with both who says: “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1). “He reveals deep and hidden things, and knows what is set in darkness.” With regard to those things that are truly profound and exceed the measure of human understanding, the Apostle cries out [Col. 1252D], saying: “O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments and unsearchable His ways!” (Rom. 11).

Yet through His Spirit He reveals even these lofty and profound things, as much as ought to be known or is expedient for us. He therefore reveals the deep things and secrets of His hidden counsel; and not these only, but also the hidden counsels of another, which hostile malice conceals from us in order more easily to deceive us. You have heard what we ought to desire or hope concerning His revelation; hear now also what we ought to fear concerning His knowledge. “He knows what is set in darkness”: He knows our inmost things and every hidden thing of our heart—not only those things which we alone know about ourselves and wish to hide from others, but even things into whose recesses we ourselves cannot sufficiently penetrate in the hiding places of our conscience.

He therefore reveals His own things; He reveals another’s things; He knows ours. He reveals His own secrets; He reveals the deceptive things of another; He knows our hidden things. He reveals the deep things of His dispensation; He reveals the hidden things of diabolical fraud; He knows the dark things of human conscience [Col. 1253A]. He reveals His own deep things so that we may know what we ought to believe concerning Him and what we ought to hope from Him. He reveals another’s hidden things so that we may know what we ought to fear and avoid. He knows our dark things lest we believe that anything can be hidden from Him and deceive ourselves with vain hope.

“He reveals deep and hidden things, and knows what is set in darkness”: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of Your wisdom” (Ps. 50). See the revelation of deep things; and elsewhere he prays to the same effect: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of Your law” (Ps. 118). He feared hidden things belonging to another who said: “You will bring me out of this snare which they have hidden for me” (Ps. 30). The same point is intended by what he sings elsewhere: “They dealt deceitfully with their tongues; the poison of asps was under their lips” (Ps. 13). Did they not wish to conceal the poison which they carried beneath the tongue?

He believed that our hidden things could not be hidden from Him who said: “But all things are naked and open to the eyes of God” (Heb. 4) [Col. 1253B]. It is Solomon’s judgment that He alone knows—or knows all—the hearts of the children of men (Wis. 9). In harmony with this judgment is the saying: “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Ps. 12).

But what does he mean when he says, “and light is with Him”? Without doubt, God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all. Why then does he not say what he could truly have said, namely, that God is light, but says instead, “and light is with Him”? Did he perhaps wish to teach us that wherever God remains through indwelling grace, the light of necessary knowledge cannot be absent? For the light which He Himself is, as He is in Himself, we cannot yet see in this life; but the light which is with Him we are accustomed to receive not only for consolation but also for aid.

But what kind of light do we call this, by which we recognize what we ought to do, avoid, love, hate, believe, or hope? What kind, I ask, is this light that knows deep and hidden things—He Himself revealing and inspiring, He who gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge of discipline to those who understand?

Up to this point Daniel glorified God for the common good; now he does so for the special benefit specially bestowed upon himself and his companions [Col. 1253D]. “To You,” he says, “God of my fathers, I confess and praise You, because You have given me wisdom and strength, and have now shown me the things that we asked of You, because You have revealed to us the king’s word.”

Above he said, “He gives wisdom to the wise.” But here he says, “Because You have given me wisdom and strength,” and again, “Because You have revealed to us the king’s word.” The chief order of charity is to prefer common goods to private ones. For charity “does not seek its own things, but those of others.” Therefore, if he preferred common goods to his own by the prompting of charity, what wonder is it that he first offered a sacrifice of praise for the things which he loved more?

It should also be noted that we may discern together in this one verse those three things which we assigned above to Daniel’s office [Col. 1254A]. Observe the voice of confession and glorification in what you read: “To You, God of my fathers, I confess and praise You.” But he shows that he had offered prayers of supplication in saying: “And You have now shown us the things that we asked of You.” In these three, unless I am mistaken, the office of true devotion is contained or fulfilled.

## CHAPTER XV. How we ought to consult the rule of equity more strictly, especially at the time when we must fulfill any office of exalted rank.

After this Daniel entered to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon, and spoke to him thus: “Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon; introduce me into the king’s presence, and I shall make known the interpretation to the king” [Col. 1254B] (Dan. 2).

If by Daniel we rightly understand the fervor of devotion, and by Arioch the strictness of equity, what else will it be to wish to enter to Arioch but to seek more deeply the more secret mysteries of equity and to wish, by inward investigation, to see what strict justice requires? This action is rightly ascribed to Daniel when the human mind is urged to it by great devotion of soul. Thus Daniel enters to Arioch when devotion seeks the counsels of equity.

There is also another reason for entering to him, perhaps no less necessary: namely, when we wish to instill deeply in him that which, by divine revelation, we have recognized must be corrected in his judgments. There we enter to him so that through much investigation and examination of justice we may recognize what is right; here we enter to him so that we may more firmly impress, by zeal for rectitude, what has been divinely recognized as right [Col. 1254C]. Thus there we enter for the sake of learning, here for the sake of teaching; there for seeking, here for persuading.

But we perceive the reason for entering more readily if we attend to what he says: “Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon.” See: what the troubled king commanded to be done, Daniel, enlightened by God, forbade to be done. It often happens that what we, disturbed and carried away by the soul’s impulse, discern as if it were right, and presume can or ought to be done under Arioch’s office, we afterward, once turned to prayers and prayer and divinely enlightened amid the tears of our compunction, find to be unjust although we had previously thought it right. Thus devotion often finds to be iniquitous, and forbids to be done, what the violent impulse of the soul decreed should be done as if under royal fury: “Do not destroy,” he says, “the wise men of Babylon.”

And he adds: “Introduce me into the king’s presence, and I shall make known the interpretation to the king.” Why, I ask, does he here request to be introduced by another, when above he entered the king’s presence by himself? Above he entered to supplicate the king; here, however, to teach the king. The former was an act of humility; the latter, of great exaltation. It was, I say, a matter of great exaltation to teach the king something he could have learned from no one else [Col. 1254D]. Therefore he willingly offered himself for the services of humility, but shrank from shamelessly thrusting himself forward for the offices of high rank.

Let us learn from his example what we ought to do in such matters. When we must undertake a place of teaching, whether by command or by office, let the mind first enter to Arioch. Let it seek the counsels of justice and, so that it may perform a good work well and justly, foresee matters by careful examination. “Do the good thing well.” A thing becomes good when a good work arises from a good intention and proceeds in a fitting manner.

It is easy for ambition or vainglory to impel us toward a conspicuous and illustrious work. It is easy for the leaven of the Pharisees to corrupt the whole mass of our good work. We are by no means introduced by Arioch when we are impelled to a good work by a perverse intention. Therefore, whenever we undertake the office of teaching, let us foresee how justly and orderly we are to fulfill the office undertaken. Let us see that we say nothing false or frivolous, nothing inept or disordered [Col. 1255A].

He keeps, unless I am mistaken, this rule of learning or teaching to whom the Psalmist’s saying may apply: “Blessed is the man who shows mercy and lends; he shall order his words in judgment” (Ps. 111). And perhaps this will be to consult Arioch outwardly: to fortify ourselves by the counsels of rectitude against faults of speech or action. But Arioch is consulted inwardly when inquiry is made concerning interior things and the soul is fortified by the principles of justice against the corruption of thoughts or afflictions.

Especially at the time when we must appear in a position of eminence or fulfill an office of high rank, we ought to enter to Arioch, seek his guidance, and do nothing without premeditation or protection of justice. “Introduce me,” he says, “into the king’s presence, and I shall make known the interpretation [Col. 1255B] to the king.” Our Daniel truly makes use of the guidance of the aforesaid Arioch when the mind is pierced by remembrance of divine strictness and consideration of true justice. And then, as it were, it is introduced by such a guide before the royal presence when, under every impulse of the soul and as if in the presence of royal power, the human heart is readily inflamed to devotion by consideration of strict examination.

## CHAPTER XVI. By what stages the knowledge of mysteries advances, and to what perfection of knowledge the mind often ascends through the merit of devotion.

“And I will declare the interpretation to the king,” he says. What is this interpretation of the mystical vision, if not the ready unravelling of divine sacraments and mysteries, and their prompt explanation? [Col. 1255D] But if by the king we ought to understand the power of free choice, what else will it mean for such an interpretation to reach the king’s awareness than to hold the meaning of the divine mysteries openly and readily available? If, therefore, whenever we wish, we are free and ready, and it lies within our power, to bring the unravelling of hidden things before the public, we do not doubt that the knowledge and interpretation of divine mysteries is within our choice and has, as it were, now reached royal power.

Such a great expansion of knowledge or teaching is rightly attributed to Daniel when grace of this kind is acquired and possessed through the merit of devotion. Let us therefore see by what stages of advancement knowledge of divine things is enlarged. First of all, Daniel received knowledge of the mystical vision through divine revelation. [Col. 1256A] Afterwards the same matter became known also to his companions; finally, knowledge of that same matter reached the king’s awareness. Of the first it is said: “Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision by night.” Later Daniel declares, both for himself and for his companions: “Because,” he says, “you have disclosed the king’s word to us.” And now he himself promises to reveal knowledge of the same matter to the king: “Bring me before the king, and I will declare the interpretation to the king.”

To state briefly what I think about this: some receive divine revelation in their prayer, others in their meditation, and others frequently even in their very speaking; and through divine inspiration they know whatever things are lofty and profound. Yet we rightly attribute to Daniel not only what we penetrate while praying, but also what we penetrate subtly while meditating [Col. 1256B] or speaking, when we acquire any of these through the merit of devotion.

There are some who can never rise to contemplate or penetrate lofty things except after inward compunction and, as it were, purification of the heart. Job represented such persons in himself when he said: “Before I eat I sigh, and my groaning is like overflowing waters” (Job 3). He who must sigh before eating is one who cannot in any way attain inward refreshment of the soul and the food of truth except through the grace of compunction and after an outpouring of tears.

Others abound in divine revelations in their meditations; [Col. 1256C] and perhaps there are still such persons as cannot at all penetrate subtle matters, or discuss them subtly, without prior meditation. The former, therefore, kindle for themselves the fire of divine revelation by their prayers; the latter by their meditations: “And in my meditation fire shall blaze,” says the Psalmist (Ps. 38). Fire blazes in meditation when the mind advances, through its own investigations, to the light of divine revelation and the manifestation of hidden things. Fire blazes in meditation when, from its own inquiry, the mind is kindled toward knowledge and love of truth.

It is plain that some have advanced to such learning that they can at any hour discuss subtle matters subtly, and can almost always answer sufficiently, without any prior meditation [Col. 1256D], whatever questions are put to them—always ready, as it is written, “to give an answer to everyone who asks a reason for the faith and hope that are in us” (1 Pet. 3). Some among such people possess the light of divine revelation so familiarly that many things are revealed to them even while speaking, things which they themselves had previously not known.

So long, then, as the mind obtains divine revelation through compunction of heart alone, Daniel alone, as it were, still possesses knowledge of the mysteries. But when divine revelation meets us so fully in our meditations, recognition of the mystical vision has now reached Daniel’s companions. And when the mind has begun to possess illuminating grace so familiarly, and as though ready to hand, that [Col. 1257A] at will and whenever it pleases it can suffice at almost any hour for examining, establishing, and defending any matter, then the unravelling of hidden things begins to spread as far as the king’s awareness. Is not profound knowledge or learning held by a kind of royal right in one’s power when, at the discretion of one’s will, one discusses any mystical and profound matters easily and without any difficulty?

See to what perfection of knowledge the mind is often led through the merit of devotion; see what fruit true devotion often brings forth. Before a prudent mind obtains this fruit of its devotion, it often foresees it wisely and awaits it confidently. This is especially why it applies itself more intensely to the pursuits of devotion. “I will declare the interpretation to the king,” he says.

And it is added: “Then Arioch quickly brought Daniel before the king and said to him: ‘I have found a man among the children of the captivity of Judah who will make known the interpretation to the king.’” [Col. 1257B] Behold: as you hear, once the promise had been received of that interpretation which the king greatly desired, Arioch brought Daniel before the king. As was said above, Daniel is led to Arioch when fervour of devotion is kindled by the sight of strict equity. The human mind, however, is moved to compunction in many ways and under many considerations. But almost the best kind of compunction is that which arises from consideration of the strict judgment. Daniel, therefore, is brought in not by just anyone, but, as it were, by Arioch when [Col. 1257C] the mind is inwardly moved to compunction through consideration of true justice insufficiently observed.

He is brought before the king and, as it were, stands in the presence of royal power when true devotion is possessed as a virtue and the mind employs it at will. He is brought in quickly when, whenever necessary, the mind is readily and without delay softened to contrition of heart. Let him, then, who desires to attain that enlargement of knowledge which we described above strive to possess such capacity, or readiness, for compunction and devotion. For Daniel must first enter through Arioch and with haste before the desired word becomes known to the king.

## CHAPTER XVII. That he attains the highest summit of devotion who attributes to his own deserts whatever trouble befalls him, even beyond his deserts.

“I have found,” says Arioch, “a man among the children of the captivity [Col. 1257D] of Judah, who will announce the interpretation to the king.” Arioch finds what is discovered to be just and right by the judgment of equity. Thus Arioch finds Daniel fit and worthy to receive so great a grace: worthy to receive revelation of mysteries from God and to announce the interpretation to the king.

And perhaps the fact that he was among the children of the captivity of Judah—the captivity which Daniel endured patiently for so long—helped his merit in this respect and made him more fit to receive so great a grace. This Daniel, certainly, had been taken captive from Jerusalem to Babylon; and perhaps he had committed nothing for which he would deserve to incur such captivity, unless the common disaster had swept him away and another’s wickedness had unjustly oppressed him. Nevertheless, he attributed to his own deserts the captivity [Col. 1258A] which he endured without fault: “We have sinned, we have committed iniquity, we have acted wickedly, and we have departed and turned aside from your commandments and judgments” (Dan. 9).

He is therefore rightly called one of the children of the captivity of Judah, since even amid the scourges of undeserved oppression he humbly confesses to the Lord. For Judah is interpreted “confessing.” See, therefore, how rightly he deserved to be glorified by God who, living and confessing amid such great and such affliction, sought divine glory rather than his own.

How many incur the stain of suspicion not so much through their own fault as through another’s malice, and pass, as it were, from Jerusalem to [Col. 1258B] Babylon—from a place of peace and quiet to a place of confusion and captivity. Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace,” Babylon “confusion.” What, then, is it unjustly to pass captive from Jerusalem to Babylon except to suffer under an unfavourable yet false suspicion? It is characteristic of the wicked always to tear apart the life of the good; when they cannot assail them by true accusations, they assail them by false ones; and when they fail to defame their deeds, they try, if they can, to cloud that single eye of their intention with the stain of adverse suspicion.

Thus, after the manner of Daniel, the mind of a just person is held in unjust captivity in Babylon when, suffering under false suspicion, it is afflicted, as shamelessly as irreverently, by the reproach of unjust disgrace. Did not he groan under Babylonian affliction, so to speak, who said: “All day long my shame is before me, and confusion of my face has covered me” (Ps. 43)? Consider [Col. 1258C] , nevertheless, that captivity of disgrace which he then endured, which at that time he bore without fault, who could say with a secure conscience: “All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, nor acted unjustly in your covenant” (ibid.).

But when, amid pressing scourges, we do not discover any present fault in ourselves, we ought not even then to be secure. He taught us this by his own example, saying: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4). For we are often struck because of an earlier fault, often because of a present but hidden fault—and indeed for a fault which we thought wholly nonexistent, or perhaps erased by satisfaction. And, to confess the whole truth, we are not always struck for correction or purification. Rather, we are sometimes scourged for instruction, [Col. 1258D] sometimes for testing, or in some other way.

But it belongs to true and perfect devotion always to ascribe to one’s own deserts the punishment one suffers, and to fear secretly the fault which one does not find in oneself. That fervour of devotion, therefore, has as it were already reached the highest summit of perfection which attributes to its own deserts every unjust reproach of disgrace, and whatever happens to it even beyond its deserts; which glorifies the Lord in every affliction and accuses itself in all things without resentment. How rightly that fervour of devotion is counted among the children of the captivity of Judah, when amid every disgrace of unjust reproach it always humbly confesses to the Lord.

Often, moreover, those who are such as seek divine glory above all others, who [Col. 1259A] see themselves as inglorious and do not shrink from being seen so, receive grace from God above others. “I have found,” he says, “a man among the children of the captivity who will announce the interpretation to the king.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. That we often presume less from the power of devotion than we ought, and that the gift of mystical understanding is one thing and the gift of mystical teaching another.

The king answered and said to Daniel, whose name was Balthasar: “Do you really think that you can tell me the dream which I saw, and its interpretation?” The king’s answering Daniel and showing his distrust is nothing other than a defect of mind which cannot remain hidden from true devotion. For we often perceive easily, in the hour of compunction and amid the tears of our devotion, certain faults which at another time [Col. 1259B] we cannot perceive. Perfect devotion, indeed, examines everything and judges everything. “The spiritual person judges all things, yet is himself judged by no one.”

It should certainly be noted that when Daniel seeks profound and mystical matters, when he promises lofty and subtle things, he is called Balthasar, a name interpreted “hair of the head.” Hair of the head, as you know, is very long and very fine. What, then, is hair of the head but the mind’s subtle depth and profound subtlety? Perfect devotion undoubtedly both enlightens the mind unto depth and sharpens it unto every subtlety.

Hair of the head is also an ornament; and the human mind, through true devotion, is [Col. 1259C] without doubt adorned or beautified in proportion as it is purified from vices, enlightened unto truth, and kindled toward virtue. Observe, therefore, that he too distrusts Balthasar’s promise who gave him such a name. For he received such a name from the king. It happens, indeed, that the mind feels and understands itself to be sharpened to marvellous subtlety through much devotion, yet in time of need presumes less than it can or ought upon the power of devotion.

“Do you really think,” he says, “that you can tell me the dream which I saw, and its interpretation?” Yet Daniel had said above: “Bring me before the king, and I will declare the interpretation to the king.” See: Daniel presumes and confidently promises, while [Col. 1259D] royal anxiety distrusts. All this often occurs within one and the same mind; and it is varied by almost as many judgments as it is touched by affections. It now hopes, now despairs of one and the same thing; and according to varying effects or considerations, it alternates the judgments of its own estimate.

But this fluctuation of alternating vicissitudes is finally concluded with a useful result and an excellent end, when that of which human effort despaired is at last wholly presumed from divine grace through the instruction of devotion. For what is Daniel’s answer except the teaching of true devotion?

“And Daniel answered before the king and said: ‘The mystery which the king asks of the wise men, magicians, diviners, and soothsayers, they cannot declare to the king. But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, who has made known to you, Nebuchadnezzar, what will come to pass in the last times.’” [Col. 1260A]

But because Daniel had already recognized the mystical vision which royal anxiety still sought, someone may perhaps wish to be shown more plainly how one and the same thing can, in one respect, be known by the same mind and, in another respect, not known. Yet it is one thing to grasp the depths of mysteries through understanding alone, and another to be able, whenever one wishes, easily to explain and expound them. See how rare are those who can penetrate the mystical meanings of Scripture without another’s labour and exposition; yet far fewer can make their explanation known to others by speech or writing. You see, therefore, I think, that the gift of mystical understanding is one thing and the gift of mystical teaching another. Some excel in the one, others in the other, [Col. 1260B] while others are eminent in both.

If we consult Moses’ words on this matter, we recognize that he himself excelled in wisdom and his brother in eloquence. If we look to David, we shall find both in one person: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Ps. 50). There is one gift. And again, for the other: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter propositions from the beginning” (Ps. 77).

Some have already received the first gift and utterly distrust themselves concerning the second. Jeremiah had already recognized the mystical vision when, questioned on this very point, he said: “I see a watching rod”; and again: “I see a boiling pot, and its face is from the face of the north” (Jer. 1). You now hear him professing one gift; hear the same man still distrusting himself concerning the other: “Ah, ah, ah, [Col. 1260C] Lord, I do not know how to speak.” Such distrust is indeed expressed when one who already knows the vision is told: “Do you really think that you can tell me the dream which I saw?”

Such distrust is rebuked, and the source from which grace of this kind ought to be despaired of or hoped for is shown, when it is said: “The mystery which the king asks of the wise men, magicians, diviners, and soothsayers, they cannot declare to the king. But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries.” Thus our Daniel teaches us by these words utterly to despair of human effort in matters above humanity and exceeding human understanding, and to await them from the revelation of the Lord alone.

But when he says that what would come to pass in the last times was shown to him, he seems undoubtedly to refer [Col. 1260D] to what is added after the rest at the end of the vision: “But the stone which had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.” No one skilled in the Holy Scriptures can fail to know how great, how profound, and how worthy of reverence are the things which this vision declares according to its allegorical—indeed, almost according to its historical—sense. Yet we discuss these matters according to their moral sense for our own edification or that of others, in such a way that we do not presume, according to a more sacred understanding, to diminish or weaken anything of the authority of so great a mystery.

There arises, therefore, this astonishing and highly admirable consideration: how widely the eyes of contemplation are opened when, with the cooperation of divine revelation, they extend themselves to survey even those things which occur at the end. “Who has made known to you, King Nebuchadnezzar, what will come to pass in the last times” [Col. 1261A]: he does not say, “what will come to pass to you,” but “what will come to pass in the last times.”

We must inquire, then, whether perhaps something lies hidden in these words that can apply in some respect not merely to a single person but to many, or indeed, in some respect, to almost all the perfected. [Col. 1261B] For the kingdom of heaven is raised up nowhere except among the elect: the kingdom which, according to Daniel’s declaration, is never destroyed; the kingdom which is said to be within us: “The kingdom of heaven,” says the Lord, “is within you” (Luke 17). The Lord surely raises up this kingdom in his elect at their last things, whatever storms he may permit them to undergo through diverse temptations in their beginnings.

## CHAPTER XIX. That we recover the lost grace of contemplation better through devotion than through inquiry, and that we also obtain freely what we acquire through the merit of devotion.

But now Daniel proceeds to recount or expound the vision, adding: “Your dream and the visions of your head upon your bed were these” (Dan. 2). Because bodily sense is lulled to sleep by a dream, we rightly understand by it the mind’s ecstasy, and by the dream those things which we see in ecstasy of mind. The head is the highest and principal member of the body; and the mind is the governing part of the inward [Col. 1261C] human being. Thus the visions of the head are contemplations of the mind.

We are accustomed to rest in bed, and therefore in it we rightly understand the leisure of repose. Our inward human being is placed in this bed, as it were to rest, when the mind is disposed to the highest tranquillity. In this bed a kind of dream is then seen when, amid the repose of its inward quiet and utmost tranquillity, the mind is raised to contemplate lofty things. “Your dream,” he says, “and the visions of your head were these.”

For our Daniel to say these things, to recover the lost dream, and to teach the king, is nothing other than for a devout mind, after it has lost the grace of contemplation, often to recall what it was once like in that grace, and through much persistence in compunction [Col. 1261D] to restore it, and finally to possess it more firmly and more perfectly. For through Daniel’s ministry the king recognized his vision more firmly and perfectly than he had first received it by himself.

Often, indeed, grace of this kind is given to certain persons in its beginnings and then withdrawn, so that through experience they may recognize what they ought to seek with what eagerness. It is given again to be recovered—though not without great labour—so that it may become more clearly known how strictly it must be guarded.

But let us proceed to what follows. Before explaining the vision, Daniel endeavours to preface two points: namely, how the king had first obtained it, and how Daniel himself could afterwards recover it. Of the first: “You, O king,” he says, “began to think [Col. 1262A] upon your bed what should happen after you; and he who reveals mysteries showed you what would come to pass.” As though he said openly: Because you diligently inquired into future things, you deserved to receive revelation of the future.

Of the second he adds: “But this mystery has been revealed to me, not because there is wisdom in me more than in all living persons, but that the interpretation might be made known to the king and that you might know the thoughts of your mind.” As though he said more plainly to the king: It too has been revealed to me, not through my own understanding, not because of my merit, but for your benefit.

I think it plain to everyone, as far as the historical sense is concerned, that he does not ascribe to his own effort or merits that which he obtained by prayer. “You, O king,” he says, “began.” And you too, consider and [Col. 1262B] reflect, if you can, how greatly reflection upon future things avails before God, since it is customarily rewarded by God with revelation of future things.

Hear a man concerned with future things and intensely occupied with thoughts of this kind: “Will God cast off forever, and will he no longer be favourable? Or will he cut off his mercy forever, from generation to generation?” (Ps. 76). Hear the same man instructed concerning such matters and deeply enlightened concerning the things he had sought: “The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and greatly merciful; he will not be angry forever, nor threaten eternally” (Ps. 102).

Perhaps he had lost revelation of future things and grieved that he had lost it when he said: “There is now no prophet, [Col. 1262C] and he will no longer know us” (Ps. 73); and again: “Even the light of my eyes is not with me” (Ps. 37). He aspired, I think, to his former grace who said: “Who will grant me that I may be as in former days?” (Job 29). He sought anew the customary revelation of mysteries who asked the Lord: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118).

You likewise, who hear or read these things, if you feel that you have fallen away from grace of this kind, attend carefully to what you silently do within yourself; consider what thoughts intensely occupy you. If you meditate only upon vain things and pressing concerns, what wonder if you are deprived of revelation of profound and future things? At the beginning of your conversion, when you thought only of eternal, spiritual, and future things, when you longed only for lofty [Col. 1262D] things, what wonder if you deserved to be consoled according to your desire? “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor.”

You have ceased to sit and rest at the Lord’s feet after the likeness of Mary. You are now troubled about many things after the likeness of Martha. Remember, therefore, from where you have fallen; repent, and do the former works. If you desire to restore that former grace, if you seek to recover the visions of your head upon your bed, return to Daniel; renew devotion. For renewing the heart and restoring lost grace, you advance better and more swiftly through inward devotion than through profound inquiry—unless, perhaps, your inquiry concerns your losses and remedies for those losses.

Daniel’s statement accords with these words: [Col. 1263A] “This mystery has been revealed to me, not because there is wisdom in me more than in all living persons.” Certainly the king, who sought every word of wisdom and understanding, found in Daniel tenfold more than in all diviners and magicians. Yet a man of such wisdom obtained by prayer, rather than inquiry, what he sought. Let no one, then, seek by human wisdom those things which are above human understanding.

Perhaps a deeper understanding calls us to note that Daniel does not ascribe even to himself what he had obtained through the merit of devotion. “But that the interpretation,” he says, “might be made known to the king.” Perhaps even what is acquired through the merit of devotion is obtained freely. For we do not possess devotion itself from ourselves, but receive it from the gift of the Giver: “What do you have,” says the Apostle, “that you did not [Col. 1263B] receive?” (1 Cor. 4). Therefore both devotion and grace are gifts: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10).

If, then, we receive devotion freely, that which we obtain through its merit is also gratuitous. When grace is bestowed for grace, the second gift, like the first, is obtained freely. Therefore we do not receive God’s gifts because we have deserved them, but so that through them we may advance or benefit. We receive understanding of truth for our own advancement; but teaching of truth for the advancement of others. By both, free choice is helped toward good, and both are bestowed upon it by God for cooperation in good.

By the king, as we have said, we understand freedom of choice. Thus the interpretation of difficult [Col. 1263C] matters, the meaning of divine judgments, is given to Daniel, as it were, so that it may be made known to the king, when devotion is enlightened unto truth so that free choice may have and recognize in what it ought to exercise itself, what it ought to avoid, and what it ought to choose.

## CHAPTER XX. A concise recapitulation of the foregoing, with confirmation from a parallel.

It is pleasant here to consider how this passage and the Gospel passage seem to accord with one another in mystical meaning. Luke the Evangelist recounts how the Lord wished to show his presence to the disciples as they journeyed, under the appearance of a stranger, and [Col. 1263D] afterwards to withdraw; but, when they begged him, to remain; when they urged him, to enter; and at last, amid the meal, to show the appearance by which they recognized him (Luke 24).

What, then, is it to have Christ—that is, the Wisdom of God—present under the appearance of a stranger, except to see truth not in its own simplicity but through a mirror or riddle? This vision is shown outside the house and, as it were, on the road, when contemplation of lofty things is seen in ecstasy of mind and as though in passing. Those who go out are, as it were, two persons who behold such things as they walk, when reason and understanding, exceeding the human measure, secretly and swiftly pass through spectacles of lofty things.

The Lord then pretends to go farther, yet does not [Col. 1264A] withdraw entirely, when he withdraws for a time, no less beneficially, the grace of contemplation which he is accustomed mercifully to bestow, so that through experience he may better teach with what eagerness it ought to be sought and retained. But he is compelled to remain and to go in to them when lost grace is restored through much persistence in prayer, so that it may draw inward the vision offered outwardly and, returning to itself, the mind may retain in memory what it saw in ecstasy and thereafter possess the grace of contemplation more familiarly.

We set before him such food as the Lord loves and is accustomed to delight in when, for recovery or increase of grace, we praise, honour, and magnify him with the voice of exultation [Col. 1264B] and confession: “With the voice,” he says, “of exultation and confession—the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 41). Amid these hymns of our exultation and confession, the capacity of the mind is often enlarged, its perception sharpened, and understanding enlightened to penetrate mystical matters and often to search even into the secrets of the Godhead: “The sacrifice of praise,” he says, “will honour me; and there is the way by which I shall show the salvation of God” (Ps. 49).

Bread is undoubtedly broken before us by the Lord when the depth of mysteries is opened by mystical interpretation and known through his own revelation. From this breaking of bread and revelation of mysteries it comes about that the Lord is recognized in his own appearance, and Truth itself—once the veil of figures has been removed—is perceived in its own simplicity; and the Lord’s presence is discerned from the infusion of grace [Col. 1264C] itself.

But the Lord, who is also God’s Wisdom, vanishes from the eyes of those who look upon him when, from contemplation and admiration of divine wisdom, it becomes known to the mind that contemplates and admires how greatly his incomprehensibility exceeds all human understanding: “O the depth,” he says, “of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11). For the more subtly the human mind is enlightened to contemplate God’s wisdom, the more powerfully it is driven back into itself by the immensity of that light. This is for it to vanish from the eyes of the beholder and, as it were, to withdraw itself precisely by showing itself.

From these things one may judge with what proportion of resemblance these two passages appear [Col. 1264D] to answer one another. The Lord’s showing himself under the appearance of a stranger is the same as Nebuchadnezzar’s receiving revelation of truth under a mystical veil. The Lord’s pretending there to continue farther on his journey is the same as the vision shown to the king withdrawing itself from his memory for a short time. The one who had appeared there being compelled to remain and enter is the same as the vision here, having withdrawn, being sought with much persistence and at last perceived or retained much more deeply and perfectly through Daniel’s care. The one who appeared there at last being recognized by clear sight is the same as the truth obscured by the withdrawal of the vision here finally being made manifest through prophetic interpretation.

In these respects, and in some others, the two passages will appear [Col. 1265A] to accord with one another to anyone willing to investigate these matters more deeply. Yet that passage has certain features of its own, and so has this one, of which it is not now the place to speak separately. Having therefore examined these matters in passing and compared them to establish the parallel, let us return to the explication, or explanation, of the vision.

## CHAPTER XXI. How each person who desires someday to remain fixed in true stability ought to be brought down from the height of his own presumption.

“Thou, O king, wast looking, and behold, as it were one statue—a great statue; that great statue, of lofty stature, stood before thee, and its appearance was terrible. The head of this statue was of the finest gold; its breast and arms of silver; its belly and thighs of bronze; its legs of iron. [Col. 1265B] Part of its feet was of iron and part of clay. Thou wast looking until a stone was cut out without hands, and struck the statue upon its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them. Then iron, pottery, bronze, silver, and gold were all crushed together and reduced like the chaff of a summer threshing-floor, which the wind carried away, and no place was found for them. But the stone that struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth. This is the dream” (Dan. II).

Behold, as you can see, that image which is seen in the vision is always led, through varied change, toward worse things; and that which begins in sleep with the most precious material, passing through manifold losses, finally ends in the most worthless material. For what begins in gold is at last [Col. 1265C] completed in mud. To state briefly what I think concerning these matters, according to a certain general consideration: I believe that, in accordance with the form of the displayed vision, everyone ought within himself to diminish from his own self-estimation, to fail more and more from self-confidence, and to moderate presumption, if he desires the kingdom of heaven to be built inwardly within himself—that kingdom, indeed, which can never come to an end.

Every human being naturally loves and approves himself; and certainly, insofar as he loves himself, he also esteems himself highly. Yet the measure of one’s self-estimation always depends upon the greatness of one’s love; for when the measure of love is without measure, the greatness of one’s estimation of oneself is without measure. Oh, how rare it is to find a person [Col. 1265D] who, contrary to the Apostle’s statement, does not think himself to be something when he is nothing! But does he at least think himself something small? On the contrary: truly great—very great beyond measure—and, to speak figuratively, almost more than golden, though in truth he is worthless mud: “Why dost thou boast, O earth and ashes?” “Though thou shalt be exalted like an eagle, and though thou shalt place thy nest among the stars of heaven, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the Lord” (Obad. IV).

Therefore, one who still swells immeasurably in his own eyes must deflate from that monstrous height of self-estimation; he must descend by degrees to the depths of true humility; and at last reckon himself as nothing and emptiness—despising and trampling himself as worthless mud, and regarding himself every hour as ashes and cinders—if he desires the kingdom of eternal stability to rise within him. [Col. 1266A] He to whom none upon earth was comparable agrees with this judgment: “I have been compared to mud and made like ashes and cinders” (Job XXX).

Would you hear still more plainly how completely he who appeared great among all the peoples of the East had cast down every confidence in himself? “I have despaired,” he says, “that I shall live any longer” (Job VII). He says that he despaired; but perhaps you doubt concerning what—whether concerning the Lord or concerning himself. Hear, then, what he says elsewhere, and recognize how firmly he remained fixed in confidence in the Lord: “Even if He should kill me, I shall hope in Him” (Job XIII). Thus he hoped—but in the Lord. Nevertheless, he despaired—but of himself.

Oh, what perversity it is to presume concerning oneself and to despair of the Lord’s mercy! If you have great confidence in your own strength, then you raise yourself high and [Col. 1266B] swell as though into a mountain precisely where you ought to lower yourself and make yourself like a valley. It is good, then, to command this mountain to be lifted up and cast into the sea. “Because of mountains such as these, the earth shall be troubled, and mountains shall be transferred into the heart of the sea.” Conversely, if you distrust the Lord’s protection, you undoubtedly make a valley, most wrongly and perversely, precisely where you should have had a hill—indeed, a mountain, and a very high mountain. Therefore, so that crooked things may become straight and rough things smooth paths, “every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low”; and then “the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be raised above the summit of the mountains.”

Oh, what elevation of mind! What strength and firmness, to trust in the Lord’s mercy alone and remain fixed in such [Col. 1266C] confidence! This is the mountain which, after the overthrow of the statue and the weakening—or destruction—of self-confidence, grows from smallness into immensity, so that it cannot be moved for ever: “He who trusts in the Lord,” he says, “is as Mount Sion; he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. CXXIV). This is the mountain which ought to fill the whole surface of the earth, so that a person may dare nothing from his own skill and presume absolutely nothing except from the Lord’s power.

I think that the city set upon this mountain cannot be hidden. If you believe me, you will build for yourself upon this mountain that structure “which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same,” so that it may be “a foundation in the earth upon the summits of the mountains.” On this lofty height the kingdom of charity ought to have its capital and the seat [Col. 1266D] of its rule; and “of its kingdom there shall be no end.” For the kingdom of charity, if I am not mistaken, is that kingdom which, according to Daniel’s declaration, shall never be destroyed. Behold what the raising or overthrow of this statue sets before you; behold what things, and how great, it represents to you through the likeness.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the character of the human condition or corruptibility, and on the need to fear a collapse of conduct even at every summit of virtues.

What is a statue except a human likeness? What, then, is it to behold in a vision a statue—that is, a human likeness—except to look upon, as in a mirror and in an enigma, the manner or order of human life with the eye of contemplation? “Thou, O king,” he says, “wast looking, and behold, as it were one great statue” (Dan. II). If you wish to investigate the manner or quality of human life—if you turn your attention to the dignity of its condition, to the ease of its restoration, or to any of these things—you will find yourself deficient in every respect and unable fully to comprehend any of them. See, therefore, how great is that which cannot be wholly comprehended even by the eyes of one looking upon it: “That statue,” he says, “was great and of lofty stature; it stood before thee, and its appearance was terrible.”

He suitably adds “lofty,” perhaps, after having called it great. For it is one thing to be great, another to be high. A field, for example, is called great even though it rises to no height. Thus certain things are almost incomprehensible, yet are not worthy of much investigation or admiration. But since we have heard that this statue is great, lofty, and terrible, we may fittingly apply these terms to a threefold consideration. For the condition of human life, represented in this statue, although each of these things is found in it in some respect, is nevertheless more particularly and expressly found to be great in one respect, lofty in another, and terrible in another. Thus one consideration of the human condition is immense in the respect in which it is subject to corruption; lofty in the respect in which it is reserved for restoration; and terrible in the respect in which it lies open to perdition.

Would you hear how great is the immensity of corruption? “To whom shall I compare thee, or to whom shall I liken thee, daughter of Jerusalem? To whom shall I make thee equal and console thee, virgin daughter of Sion? Thy destruction is great as the sea. Who shall heal thee?” (Lam. II). Would you recognize how great is the loftiness of restoration? “For whom He foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, that He might be the firstborn among many brethren. And those whom He predestined, them He also called; and those whom He called, them He also justified; and those whom He justified, them He also magnified” (Rom. VIII). Would you also know how great is the terror of the divine blow? “Who,” he says, “knows the power of Thy wrath, and can number Thy wrath because of Thy fear?” (Ps. LXXXIX). “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety and injustice of those human beings who hold the truth of God in injustice.”

Consider, then, the greatness of our statue in the consideration of guilt; its height in the consideration of grace; and its terror in the consideration of punishment. Seek the greatness of guilt, both according to original guilt and according to actual guilt. Concerning original guilt, hear what is said of humankind to humankind: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. XLVIII). And concerning actual guilt, receive the voice of reproach: “Upon every high hill and beneath every leafy tree thou wast cast down as a harlot” (Jer. II). Therefore it is said to her: “Lift up thine eyes round about and see where thou now lie as a harlot.”

Oh, the height of grace—both justifying grace, confirming grace, and glorifying grace! [Col. 1268A] Measure, if you can, the height of exaltation according to justifying grace: “As far as the east is from the west, so far hath He removed our iniquities from us” (Ps. CII). Receive also the height of eminence according to confirming grace: “According to the height of heaven above the earth, He hath strengthened His mercy upon those who fear Him.” Estimate, if you can, the sublimity of dignity according to glorifying grace: “For whoever are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God. And if sons, then heirs: heirs indeed of God and co-heirs of Christ” (Rom. XIV).

Oh, the truly terrible appearance of our statue according to its assignment to punishment: terrible according to the judgment of corruption; terrible according to the judgment of reprobation; terrible according to the judgment of damnation! Oh, an appearance of terror according to the judgment of corruption! “For evils without number have surrounded me; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I could not see. They are multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” Oh, an appearance full of horror according to the judgment of reprobation! “And as they did not see fit,” says the Apostle, “to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are unfitting: filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, avarice, wickedness” (Rom. I). Oh, an appearance full of terror and full of horror according to the judgment of damnation! For, according to the same Apostle, there is “a certain terrible expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire which shall consume [Col. 1268C] the adversaries.” “For their fire shall not be extinguished, and their worm shall not die”—the fire and worm, indeed, of those “who spend their days in prosperity and in a moment go down to hell.”

From all these things, I think, you perceive how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God. What more terrible can be said, what more horrible can be imagined? “And its appearance,” he says, “was terrible.” The phrase said of the statue, “it stood before thee,” needs little exposition. Such a statue is undoubtedly set up before any individual when the foulness, weakness, and wretchedness of the contemplating soul are presented to his eyes, and by revelation he is shown what he is and what he may yet become, so that his shamelessness, pride, and hardness may be confounded, humbled, and broken: “I will rebuke thee,” He says, “and set thee before thy face” (Ps. XLIX).

A person is rebuked by God when a soul, already touched by divine inspiration, is confounded by the accusation of its own conscience. And the transgressing soul is, as it were, set before its own face when, in considering its foulness, it appears to act against itself through rebuke. Therefore, the statue is in some fashion set before the contemplating mind when, for its own confusion and humiliation, an image of its corruptibility is proposed to it by a certain divine prompting.

Learn, therefore, O human being—learn to lay aside confidence in yourself, if not suddenly and at once, then at least gradually and at intervals of time. Endeavour always to think lower and lower of yourself, so that, even if late, you may attain to true and perfect humility. These are the unshaken foundations of perfected charity; these are the firm defences of a soul ruling in eternal security. Put off arrogance, suppress pride, crush that perverse confidence in your own strength, and cast your care upon the Lord. Regard all your power, all your strength, and all your skill as ashes and cinders.

What else does cinder signify except yielding to every whirlwind—indeed, scattering at every even slight breath—and abandoning the place of its rest? Ashes and cinders are a sufficiently fitting representation of our corruption, an image appropriately expressed.
