Take care, whoever you are, lest perhaps, whether you wish it or not, you may one day become such inwardly or outwardly: inwardly in your own estimation, or outwardly also before [Col. 1269B] others in your action; inwardly, I say, by the purpose and effort of your will, or outwardly through the defect and fluctuation of human corruptibility. How many there are who by no means descend from the height of their self-estimation until they first fall shamefully outwardly in action! For some are undoubtedly permitted to fall disgracefully in action, and to change their gold into silver, their silver into bronze, their bronze into iron, and their iron into pottery, so that through their own failure, and as it were by experience, they may learn what they ought to think about their own power and strength.

Let us therefore see how some persons, according to the form of the displayed image, happen to fall through various failures of corruption from almost the highest goods to the lowest evils, ending, as it were, a golden head in feet of clay; so that we may learn to fear a collapse of conduct at every summit of virtues, and may endeavour always and everywhere to maintain the form and measure of true and perfect humility.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the human mind often falls by degrees from a great summit of virtues to the depths.

“He who stands,” says the Apostle, “let him take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X). From however lofty a summit one may easily fall to the depths or sink into the abyss; indeed, undoubtedly, the higher the degree, the worse the fall. This dream of Nebuchadnezzar ought always to make us cautious and watchful. Look, I beg you, at the statue of his vision. See from how great a height it begins and to what an end it is finally led. It indeed has a golden head and a clayey end. What is more precious than gold? What more worthless than pottery? Notice also how it bends by degrees toward worse things and at length ends in the foulest end. The first part is described as golden, the second silver, the third bronze, the fourth iron, and the fifth clay.

In gold charity is understood; in silver, truth; in bronze, pretence; in iron, cruelty; in earthenware, fragility. Pottery is easily broken, and therefore aptly represents the fragility of impatience. Iron, which crushes and subdues all other metals, suitably signifies the violence of cruelty, which presses down everything that resists in order to oppress it. Bronze imitates silver in sound, but differs greatly in value. Thus pretence has the sweet ringing of flattery in speech; it resounds pleasantly and gives a sweet echo in action. Yet as much as it soothes outwardly through word and performance, so much does it grow pale inwardly through intention and desire.

Moreover, the more silver is worn through frequent use, the brighter it becomes; so truth is commended all the better by vigorous examination, and the more certainly the counsels of truth are established through the practice of experience, the brighter they become. The brightness of gold expresses the radiance of charity, which burns with the fire of heavenly desire; and as gold is preferred to other metals, so charity surpasses all other virtues.

Oh, how great the distance between pottery and gold, between the statue’s end and its beginning! The statue begins in gold and ends in pottery. [Col. 1270B] I think that no one becomes utterly shameful all at once; but whoever neglects small things gradually slips away. As one ascends by certain stages of progress to high things, so likewise one descends by degrees to the depths. Observe how, in this statue, gold comes first, then silver; after these, bronze intervenes, and iron follows. Oh, how great the difference between gold and iron! How greatly charity and cruelty differ from one another! Yet what does Truth say concerning them? “Iniquity,” He says, “shall abound, and the charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. XXIV). See, I pray, from what point and to what point one comes: from abundance of charity to abundance of iniquity. Charity belongs to gold; iniquity to iron.

Oh, the astonishing—indeed detestable—change from charity to iniquity! “If the righteous man shall turn away from his righteousness and commit iniquity, none of the righteous deeds that he did shall be remembered” (Ezek. XVIII). It is a detestable work, worthy of shame, which begins in gold and is completed in pottery and iron. Thus part of the feet is described as iron and part as clay. Oh, shameful workers, who at the beginning of their conversion begin their work in gold and finally complete it in mud! We know that often, when an unclean spirit has gone out of a person, seeking rest and finding none, it returns with seven spirits more wicked than itself to its house; entering it, it dwells there, and that person’s last state becomes worse than the first.

How many we see who, at the beginning of their conversion, rejoice in hope, are fervent in spirit, patient in tribulation, diligent in work, devoted to reading, and earnest in prayer. What do these seem to you to be doing except working in gold and being initiated in charity? For charity, as it is written, “is patient, is kind, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (I Cor. XIII). Does he not seem to you to work in gold to whom the Lord said: “I know thy works, and charity, and faith, and ministry, and patience” (Apoc. VIII [sic])? But there are many who believe for a time and fall away in time of temptation. Yet those of this kind do not immediately plunge into the depths. Rather, first they fall from good to worse; then from less good to evil; and finally from evil to worse still. “For a falling mountain gradually wastes away, and the earth is consumed by erosion.” Such persons gradually begin to grow cold from their former desire [Col. 1271A] and to fail more and more in their former fervour.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How, or through what degrees of corruption, the human mind often falls from the heights to the depths.

Yet they do not immediately abandon what they have begun; rather, they still do such good as they can. For when charity grows cold, they indeed perform good deeds from deliberation. But what, we ask, is the difference between that former state and this second one? It is great in every respect. It is one thing to pursue the good from desire, and another from counsel alone. It is one thing, I say, to do good with great delight, and another from deliberation alone. The latter is good; the former is best. The latter belongs to silver; the former to gold. Silver is indeed a precious metal, although far less valuable than gold.

Therefore, let one who perhaps lacks an abundance of gold endeavour to work in silver. If you cannot do good from delight, at least do it from truth, and truth will set you free. But would you know how the work done from such silver shines, how greatly it pleases, and how rich or secure it makes its possessor? “Everyone,” He says, “who does the truth comes to the light, that his works may be made manifest, because they are good” (John III). It is good, then, to abound in such silver; but it is no less foolish to change one’s gold into silver. “For every man who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of God.”

Would you know how the divine word strikes in rebuke the one who has changed a golden work into silver? “I know,” He says, “thy works, and labour, and patience” (Luke IX). Behold a good work; behold the arms; behold the silver breast. But let us see what follows when He subsequently adds: “But I have against thee that thou hast left thy first charity” (Apoc. VIII [sic]). Thus one who still does good is rebuked because he has abandoned his first charity and bent his golden head down into a silver breast. Whoever recognizes himself to be such, remember whence thou hast fallen; repent; and do the first works. Otherwise fear what follows, the threat of the divine word against failure to recover one’s senses: “But if not, I come to thee and will remove thy candlestick from [Col. 1271D] its place unless thou repent” (Apoc. II).

Fear, therefore, lest, unless you return swiftly to your former goods, you fall still further into worse things. Choose which you prefer: to ascend or to descend. For a person cannot remain fixed for long in the same state. He flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition. Keep this firmly in mind, and fear it not moderately: whoever does not return to first charity will soon have his candlestick removed from its place. What is the candlestick bearing light except a good work, a work of truth? Such a candlestick stands in its place when a good work rises from a good intention. But such a candlestick is removed from its place when the good intention of a good work is changed into an evil one. Thus a silver work passes into bronze.

This evil is indeed common among the children of men. For often what a person previously did from truth, once corrupted by desire for human praise, he later does for human favour: “My people,” He says, “those who call thee blessed deceive thee and destroy the way of thy steps” (Isa. III). Therefore, whoever presents himself as flattering in speech, kind in action, but warped and perverse in thought and will, has certainly cast aside silver and now works in bronze. For like bronze he rings sweetly outwardly, but grows pale inwardly through the corruption of his will.

Does not the work of those who “speak peace with their neighbour, but have evils in their hearts” seem to you such a work? In such work, I think, the one laboured whom the Lord rebuked in saying: “I know thy works: thou hast a name that thou livest, and thou art dead” (Apoc. III). But whoever you are who are such, do not suppose that you can remain hidden long: “Though thou shalt be exalted like an eagle and place thy nest among the stars, I will bring thee down from thence, saith the Lord” (Obad. I). At some point you must hear the prophetic—indeed, the Lord’s own—voice: “Uncover thy shame, bare thy shoulder, reveal thy legs, cross the rivers. Then thy disgrace shall be uncovered, and thy reproach shall be seen” (Isa. XLVII).

When your shame has been uncovered, and your bronze belly and thighs have begun to appear, you will quickly become foul in the eyes of your admirers—indeed, now your mockers—and daily grow more and more contemptible. Then you will begin to be angry with, resent, detest, and cruelly persecute those persons whom you had previously sought greatly to please. And as flattering as you were before, so harsh and hard will you afterward be. Thus your bronze will be changed into iron, and it will be said to you: “How hast thou been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. II).

Without doubt, the bronze work has changed into iron: gentleness into severity. Their mouth “is full of cursing and bitterness”; they who formerly dealt deceitfully with their tongues have “the poison of asps under their lips.” You who formerly showed yourselves so flattering and so kind, whence are there now wars and disputes among you? You now have bitter jealousy and contention among yourselves. You kill and are jealous; you quarrel and make war. Whence comes this fierce cruelty and hardness of iron in you? What, do you suppose, is the reason that their feet are so swift [Col. 1272D] to shed blood, except that they have iron legs and soles—those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things?

But in these people this is the most astonishing—indeed, above all, the most pitiable—thing: as prompt and bold as they are in inflicting evils, so faint-hearted and beyond measure impatient are they in enduring evils inflicted upon them. Thus you may rightly wonder how iron can agree with pottery: such cruelty with such impatience. Behold the end to which our statue comes, having received clay soles after a golden head. “The renowned sons of Sion, clothed in finest gold—how have they been accounted earthen vessels, the work of a potter’s hands?” What is more precious than gold, what more worthless than pottery? How, then, has gold been darkened and its finest colour changed? [Col. 1273A] What is more malleable than gold, what more fragile than pottery? How does charity allow itself to be handled and thinned away, charity which bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things? But what is more contemptible than a will, what more degraded than a delicate mind, which in prosperity is loosened through desire and in adversity broken through impatience? “Woe to those who have lost endurance, who have abandoned right ways and turned aside into crooked ones” (Eccle. II). “For destruction and unhappiness are in their ways”: destruction because of the brittleness of pottery, and unhappiness because of the hardness of iron, since part of the feet is of pottery and part of iron.

Why is it that such people turn again to their own desires, and that after works of bronze and iron they are drawn to the potter’s work? It is because they have nowhere to take delight except in their lusts: first through pretence they lost the joy of a good conscience, and afterward through cruelty the glory of reputation. To recapitulate briefly what we have now said at greater length: in the golden head devotion is understood; in the silver members, discernment; in bronze, pretence; in iron, indignation; in pottery, dissipation.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the difference among the aforesaid degrees and the quality of each.

We should certainly observe what is said of the various members and how each is described. The head is described as golden, the breast silver, and the arms silver; the belly and thighs bronze; the legs iron; and the feet partly iron and partly clay. The whole body is ruled by the head; therefore intention is aptly signified by it, since through intention the whole body of our action is led either to a good or an evil end. Counsel pertains to the heart, and the heart lies hidden beneath the breast. With our arms we carry out our works when we wish something to be done by us. The belly, the softer part of the body and a covering for foulness, signifies the service of compassion. The thigh lies beneath the genitals, and humility, which bends down to lowly and unworthy things, wishes to seem perfect. The legs bear bones longer and stronger than those of the other members; thus they aptly signify the rigidity of severity. With our feet we touch the earth even while standing upright; and however much the mind stretches toward heavenly things, it cannot sustain its necessities without the supports of this life.

By the head, therefore, as has been said, intention is understood; by the breast, deliberation; by the arm, action; by the belly, compassion; by the thigh, humility; by the leg, severity; by the foot, necessity. By the head is understood the desire of intention; by the breast, the application of deliberation; by the arm, the exercise of action; by the belly, the service of piety; by the thigh, the service of subjection; by the leg, the scourge of severity; by the foot, the support of necessity.

If, therefore, the head is intention and gold devotion, what is a golden head except a devout intention? If the breast is deliberation, the arm action, and silver discernment, what else are a silver breast and arms except discerning counsels and works? In the belly is compassion, in the thigh subjection, and in bronze pretence. What, then, are a bronze belly and thighs except feigned piety and feigned humility? If severity is signified by the leg and cruelty by iron, what else is understood by iron legs except cruel severity? The foot signifies necessity, pottery pleasure. Thus a clay sole signifies luxurious superfluity. The foot is described as partly iron and partly clay because a delicate mind is at one time hardened into hatred of those by whom it is perhaps restrained from its desires, and at another, when the things it desires are available, dissolves into their indulgence.

What, then, is the gleam of the golden head except the fervour of heavenly desire? The brightness of the silver breast and silver arm is the certainty of right counsel and the rectitude of assured action. The resonance of the bronze belly and thigh is the flattery of false piety and feigned humility. The strength of the iron leg is the harshness of immoderate discipline; the fragility of the clay foot, unbridled superfluity. Thus holy desires make the head golden; right counsels and works make the breast and arm silver; feigned observances and services make the belly and thigh bronze; cruel scourges make the legs iron; delicate supports make the clay sole.

## CHAPTER XXVI. It has been said how a person often declines from good to evil; now it is said how one often falls from evil to evil, and from vice to vice.

But if anyone wishes to take everything said concerning the statue in an evil sense, I readily yield to his interpretation without hesitation. Yet one who holds such an interpretation should endeavour to establish his own meaning in such a way that he does not dare to condemn what has been said before, since the Holy Spirit often signifies several things in one thing that He says. For just as there is something in this writing more easily accommodated to that interpretation, so something is found in it that may more readily be applied to this one.

Gold in this statue, since it is read to be the finest, seems more suitably capable of being taken in the better sense. Yet just as this is rightly understood according to the reality of the matter in the foregoing interpretation, so in this interpretation it may quite fittingly be referred to the self-estimation of the soul that is proud of itself. Likewise, the fact that the thing seen by revelation is described as a statue rather than an animal more readily favours this second interpretation, in which it is pleasing to take everything said in an evil sense. For what else is such a statue except a human figure or human life? And what else is a human figure without a rational soul except an action that is appropriate but lacks right intention? Therefore, whenever a person governs his conduct according to the prudence of the flesh—which is hostile to God—not an animal, I would say, but a statue after a human likeness is fashioned.

Let us therefore see what members of such a statue the divine word describes when it says: “The head of this statue was of the finest gold,” and so forth. According to this interpretation, in which we refer the whole matter to an evil sense, gold may be understood as arrogance; silver as boastfulness; bronze as obstinacy; iron as cruelty; and pottery as impatience. Gold surpasses all metals in the dignity of its value, and the proud mind despises all others in comparison with itself. Silver has a pleasant and exceedingly sweet sound, and boastfulness presents itself as pleasing and agreeable in proclaiming its own praise. Bronze, since it is considered highly durable, very aptly signifies obstinacy, which can scarcely or never be turned away from its own counsel or purpose. Iron, which is accustomed to subdue other metals, very suitably signifies cruelty, which is accustomed to oppress others. Pottery, easily broken, aptly signifies impatience.

Thus one fashions a golden head for oneself who arrogates holiness to oneself. One seems to bear a silver breast and silver arms who glories in the rectitude of one’s counsel and work. One has, as it were, a bronze belly and thighs who remains obstinate even in things which, because of their baseness, one ought to despise, or, because of their dishonour, to be ashamed of. One shows oneself to have iron legs who both rises up against superiors through audacity and oppresses inferiors through cruelty. One rests upon clay soles who, leaning too immoderately into love of earthly things, runs unchecked into impatience.

It should indeed be noted by what stages of corruption the evil of our failing receives its increase, and how, declining step by step toward worse things, it descends even to the depths. See how boasting follows arrogance, obstinacy follows boasting, cruelty follows obstinacy, impatience follows cruelty. Arrogance surely precedes boasting, because unless the mind, first lifted up, thought highly of itself, it would never boast so shamelessly of its knowledge or holiness. But when it believes that others too are persuaded of what it thinks within itself concerning its own knowledge or holiness, what wonder is it if it persists obstinately in its own counsel or purpose? Unless it first persisted obstinately in its counsel or purpose, it would never rage so wickedly against others in defending them. Cruelty produces impatience, because the less anyone loves his neighbour, the more grievously he endures even slight troubles. We know, moreover, that the more the channel of love toward one’s neighbour is blocked from without, the more deeply it swells within toward oneself. And the more miserably anyone languishes in himself through private self-love, the more painfully he bears his troubles, and the more difficultly restrains his desires. Hence one who is severe toward others and lax in himself—at one moment raging against others, at another growing slack within himself—walks on feet partly of iron and partly of clay. Indeed, some who at the beginning of conversion boldly undertook certain great efforts often collapse so enormously that, in the great dissoluteness in which they eventually live so feebly, they cannot patiently hear even a slight word—not merely of reproach, but not even of correction, indeed not even of gentle admonition. Woe to the wretched! What, I ask, can now be done for such people, or what further hope can there be for those who, because of arrogance, cannot in any way be cast down from their swelling pride; because of obstinacy, cannot be convicted of their error; because of the hardness of iron, cannot be turned from their rigidity; and because of clay-like brittleness, cannot be reproved concerning their own body?

## Chapter XXVII. By what stages of restoration a mind that falls from great goods into the depths often rises again through divine operation

Yet we must not despise even their iron or stony hardness, for the Lord is able to raise up children of Abraham from these stones. For what is impossible with men is possible with God. Observe what follows: “You were looking,” he says, “until a stone was cut out without hands, and it struck the statue upon its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them” (Dan. 2). Behold: a stone is cut out without hands, by which the hardness of iron is shattered—and rightly so. What hand could cut or even hew out such a stone, capable of crushing or pulverizing iron? But what human labour or any human skill cannot accomplish is done by divine will alone. God alone can act, without any effort or movement of his own, whenever and whatever he wills; remaining unmoved, he causes all things to be moved.

But why, I ask, did he who could and willed to do this by hands not will to accomplish these things? Perhaps, in minds such as these, iron-hard and hardened, he works better by inspiration than by striking, and one whom scourges cannot correct is often corrected by inward illumination. “I struck your children,” he says, “and they did not grieve; they refused to receive discipline” (Jer. 5). But although with us speaking is far easier than doing, nevertheless even in those minds in which the work of the striking hand seems to have failed, he works in a wondrous and incomprehensible fashion through his inward word or whisper: “The word that shall go forth from my mouth shall not return to me empty; but it shall accomplish whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in those matters for which I sent it” (Isa. 55). Thus too the Holy Spirit breathes where he wills. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.” Therefore the stone cut out without hands is fear of the Lord divinely inspired: at the blow of this stone the statue is cast down and the monstrous construction is destroyed.

As by fear the mind is cast down from a good purpose, so also by fear it is shaken free from an evil purpose. For as pride is the beginning of every sin, so fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. By such a stone the statue is shaken, so that the shame-prone mind may be put to shame and humbled. What is such a blow except inward compunction? And what is the crushing of the struck statue except the contrition and humiliation of the compunct heart? But we know that God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart. It is therefore better to be crushed upon this stone than to stand erect and think proudly. “It struck,” he says, “the statue upon its feet of iron and clay, and crushed them.” The statue is surely shaken in its lower and worse parts when the proud and perverse mind is struck back, by the spirit of the fear of the Lord, to consideration of its own wickedness and weakness.

This merciful blow of the Lord is directed as compassionately as it is profitably fulfilled in us in this life, when he says: “I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (Ps. 49). The man who said, “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50), had surely been rebuked in this way, struck in his weak part, and through such a blow had set himself against himself. But after iron and clay are shaken, the other materials too are crushed. “Then,” he says, “iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold were crushed together.” Above you saw by what stages goodness failed and perversity grew. Now see how humility, the foundation of all goodness, advances by stages: first we blush for real evils; afterwards for false goods; and finally even for real goods, when they are imperfect and unfinished. Thus iron and clay are first crushed, then the bronze members, and last the silver and golden ones.

In evils we more readily blush for wickedness than for weakness. In goods, however, we blush sooner for imperfection than for omission. Hence in the lowest members iron is crushed before clay. In the higher members, silver is more quickly pulverized than gold. First, therefore, in the crushing of iron we condemn evils committed through wickedness; in the crushing of clay, those contracted through weakness. What is the crushing of bronze except the rejection of pretended good? In the silver members, what displeases us—and ought most certainly not to please us—is not that they are good, but that they are not best. In a golden work, however, this alone is truly blameworthy: that the beginning of the best work is not carried through to the heel—that is, the very end—worthy or due to it. Thus in the crushing of silver the imperfection of a good work is condemned; in the crushing of gold, the abandonment of an excellent work is reproved. This, then, is what we have said concerning the crushing of this statue, according to the first interpretation we set forth, in which we understood its parts partly as good and partly as evil.

## Chapter XXVIII. By what stages of advance a mind that slips from great evil into worse things is often restored by divine action

Now, however, let us say something according to the interpretation placed second. Just as nothing is more readily recognized as shameful than malice, so nothing is more difficult to recognize or blush for than arrogance. For arrogance clouds or blinds the eye of the mind, so that it cannot even know itself. For whatever sort of person the exalted mind imagines itself to be by its own estimation, that it undoubtedly believes itself truly to be. See, then, how difficult it is for us to reproach, accuse, and by rebuke and rejection crush in ourselves those things by which we have long believed that we ought truly to please both ourselves and others.

But boasting, while it strives to spread its glory abroad, mixes false things with true, and persuades others of its own worth not only in matters it knows to be true of itself, but even in matters it knows to be false. There it is undoubtedly more easily cast down into shame, where it is convicted of false display by the testimony of its own conscience. Hence the silver of boasting is more easily—and therefore more quickly—worn away than the gold of arrogance. Yet, just as we blush much more difficultly for arrogance than for boasting, so we blush much more laboriously for boasting than for obstinacy. For from boasting we often doubtlessly increased our reputation; but from obstinacy we have always diminished it. We call obstinacy nothing other than shameless persistence in our own opinion against the counsels of others. Who would not more readily blush for that evil in which he knows very well that he has greatly displeased others? Bronze, therefore, is rightly described as crushed before silver, because, as has been said, the mind is more readily ashamed of obstinacy than of boasting.

The crushing of clay pertains to shame arising from consideration of one’s own weakness and impatience. But when the perverse mind reaches such weakness and impatience that it is altogether unable, even when it wishes, to resist its passions, who does not see how readily it blushes when it considers its own brittleness? Yet, as was said above, we excuse more readily those things which we incur through weakness than those which we commit out of malice alone; hence we blush sooner for the latter. Therefore, as the text reads, iron is crushed before clay; and after these, bronze, silver, and gold are rightly described as crushed. This order of crushing is thus described when it says: “Then iron, clay, bronze, silver, and gold were crushed together, and were reduced as it were to the dust of a summer threshing-floor, which the wind carried away; and no place was found for them.”

## Chapter XXIX. How, and to what perfection, a person often rises again through divine operation after repeated falling

What do we understand by summer except fervour of spirit, and by a threshing-floor except prudence of spirit? What, then, is a summer threshing-floor except spiritual understanding? On this floor grains of truth are beaten out from the chaff of figures by the threshing of vigorous examination. On this floor the harvest of virtue is separated from the ears of vices by the winnowing of strict examination. We labour in the threshing of this floor, and separate, as it were, grain from chaff whenever we distinguish true and eternal goods from false and transitory ones.

Nor should it suffice us to shake off the chaff: let us strive also to turn its heap, by putting fire beneath it, into ashes; to change the brightness of passing things into blackness; and to transform our affection for them into contempt or hatred. Whoever desires to be spiritual toils upon this floor. For the spiritual person judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one. Hear a spiritual person labouring upon this floor: “I set my heart,” he says, “to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things done under the sun” (Eccl. 1). Behold the floor; behold the threshing. And where is the chaff, where the ear? “Vanity of vanities,” he says, “and all is vanity.” Behold the chaff. “And I saw,” he says, “that in all things there was vanity and affliction of spirit” (ibid.). Behold chaff together with the ear. But where are the ashes? “What fruit, then,” says the Apostle, “did you have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6). What is the blackness of ashes except the shame of embarrassment? See, then, how those who were already ashamed of things in which they had once been accustomed to delight had changed the brightness of stubble into the blackness of abhorrence.

Hear also him who had changed the chaff of vanities not only into blackness but into stench, when he said: “I have regarded all things as dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3). The sorrow of repentance, moreover, is that fire by which spiritual men are accustomed to burn the ears of vanities and change them into ashes of abhorrence. We indeed continue to endure these ashes upon the floor of our conscience as long as we are ashamed or apprehensive because of past sins. But when the wind blows, the ashes are carried away: at the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, every fear and apprehension of our guilt is swallowed up, and through hope of pardon the floor of our conscience is cleansed of every blackness of shame, so that we may truly sing to the Lord: “You have cast all my sins behind your back.”

Was not even the golden head of the statue, not to mention its other iron or bronze members, reduced to ashes when the Prophet said: “The shame of my face has covered me” (Ps. 43)? Would he not pray to the Lord for the dispersal of the ashes when he cried out to the Lord in prayer: “In you I have hoped; let me not be confounded for ever” (Ps. 30)? Were not those black ashes of his shame carried off and removed by the wind when, cleansed from the stains of his sins through confident hope of pardon, he broke forth into a confession of praise, saying: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses, who forgives all your iniquities” (Ps. 102)?

See, then, that the substance of corruption is reduced to ashes and afterwards carried off and removed by the wind. For unless the transgressing soul first recognizes and blushes for its shame, and burns it up and consumes it by the fitting sorrow of repentance, it does not cleanse the floor of its conscience from the stains of its sins and never raises itself to full assurance of pardon. But when they have been carried away by the wind, no place is found for them: for after pardon has long been sought and scarcely obtained, the mind becomes not only more cautious but stronger against similar temptations; indeed, it is made invincible against the injuries of like corruptions. No place can be found for them when neither the understanding can be deceived nor the affection corrupted by a similar corruption.

But what does it mean that the stone by which the statue is struck and, when struck, crushed—what, I ask, does it mean that the stone does not grow into a cliff but is changed into a mountain, and does not become a large stone but rather grows into a great and lofty mountain? We know that perfect charity casts out fear. For perfection of charity does not know how to increase fearfulness, but changes it and magnifies it into a mountain of confidence. “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion: he who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved for ever.” Do you see, I ask, how prophetic sayings converge, how David agrees with Daniel, truth with figure, the Prophet’s statement with the prophetic vision? “But the stone,” he says, “which struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.” How great, I ask, is the mountain that filled the whole earth, that shall not be moved for ever? Do you wish to hear how great, how firm, how vast, how immovable it is? Hear another who holds this mountain of confidence and speaks of its greatness and immovability: “I am certain,” he says, “that neither death,” [etc.,] “unto that which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8).

## Chapter XXX. What freedom we possess by nature, what power we receive by grace, and what freedom and power are

Behold, we have heard the dream. But do we still need its interpretation? As he has already said above, it is one thing to know the mysteries of divine judgments through divine revelation, and another to have been able to weigh or penetrate their rationale. It is one thing, I say, to see by clear contemplation what commonly does or ought to happen in the whole order of things; another to know what ought to happen to what person, for what reason, and with what benefit for the person to whom it happens. The one belongs, as it were, to seeing the dream; the other to interpreting the dream.

By divine revelation King Nebuchadnezzar was granted to see figuratively how a human being may fall from the summit of exaltation into the depths and again rise to the state of integrity and the height of perfection; but he was not equally granted to recognize the nature of the person to whom such a thing ought to happen. But what he could not see by himself, he learned from another, when he heard through Daniel: “You are the golden head, and after you another kingdom, inferior to you, will arise.” Therefore one grace enables us to know divine judgments, while another enables us to judge our own merits or those of others. The former is the gift of contemplation; the latter, of meditation—or rather, devotion. For that meditation by which the condition of our life and the quality of our merits are judged is rightly ascribed to devotion.

Indeed, we never know the corruption of our weakness better, nor discover it more fully anywhere, than when amid tears of compunction we pour out our whole heart before the Lord. If, then, Daniel is rightly understood as devotion, the grace by which the condition or corruption of our life is discovered is fittingly attributed to him. It often happens that one person is perfect in one of the graces I have mentioned and another in the other, and that what each cannot do by himself he learns from the other. Sometimes, however, one and the same person receives the fullness of both graces; yet in one and the same mind one person, as it were, consults another when he learns by one disposition of mind what he could not through another. For many things that we cannot attain through the grace of contemplation we obtain by the merit of devotion.

This is why Daniel is consulted by the king; this is why the king is instructed through Daniel: “This,” he says, “is the dream, and we shall tell its interpretation before you, O king.” Blessed is the person to whom this vision is still shown and its interpretation revealed while he is still king, while he can rule his passions. “You,” he says, “are king of kings.” We know that bodily sense presides over bodily motion; desire over sense; affection over desire; and rational consent over them all, according to what is written: “One who is high watches over one who is high, and there are higher ones over them; moreover, the king of the whole earth rules his servant.” The rational consent, therefore, is king of kings: it presides over all motions of heart and body and restrains them within the bounds of its dominion—yet by a power received from God.

Hear what is said, and understand from whom this power is given: “You,” he says, “are king of kings, and the Lord of heaven has given you kingdom, strength, dominion, and glory.” Human free choice has and receives kingdom in that it ought to preside over all other things within the human being. It has and receives strength as long as it can bravely resist its passions. It has and receives dominion as long as it acts, or can act, upon deeds, wills, and thoughts for good. It has and receives glory as long as it still rejoices in a good conscience: “This,” he says, “is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1).

We know who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Therefore we can do only as much as we have received the ability to do. “For what have you that you have not received?” To have such power and strength is nothing other than to have cooperating grace. Your power is cooperating grace. As much grace as you have, so much power you have; and as received grace increases, so your power advances; and as grace diminishes, so power is taken from you; and whenever grace is withdrawn, power perishes with it. It is thus clear that the power of choice is one thing and the freedom of choice another. For to be able to do great things is one thing; to be free is another.

You can be both free and weak; conversely, you can be healthy and a slave. If you are healthy and strong, you can do many and great things; nevertheless, if you are free, you cannot and ought not be compelled to do anything. And if you lose health, you lose your former power, but not your freedom. It belongs to power, then, that we can do good as long as we are able to do it; it belongs to freedom that we cannot be forced unwillingly to any good or evil. How many err in defining free choice because they do not know, or pretend not to know, how to distinguish power from freedom! Yet consider the difference: a person often loses power, but can never lose freedom. Again, no one receives power for every good, but every person receives freedom for every good or evil. For, as has already been said, no one can be compelled unwillingly to any good or evil. But though one is free in respect of all things, one does not have power in respect of all things; otherwise one would be omnipotent.

It is in every way a great thing when one receives power for those things sufficient for salvation. But what if one also has at hand those things sufficient for perfection? As it is said here: “He gave into your hand all things in which the children of men dwell, the beasts of the field, and the birds of heaven, and established all things under your dominion.” One holds in one’s hand all things in which human beings dwell when one has cooperating grace in relation to those things which ordinarily become subject, by divine help, to human counsels and efforts. One possesses the beasts of the field within the bounds of one’s power when one can firmly restrain the impulses of worldly desires within the limits of equity. One powerfully rules the birds of heaven when one occupies one’s thoughts, whenever one wills, with good meditations and spiritual contemplations. Thus one deserves to have all things placed beneath one’s dominion when one has received divine grace for each of the things we have described.

## Chapter XXXI. On the different stages of corruption and their characteristics in those descending from good to evil

But let us ask what is meant by what is added here: “You,” he says, “are therefore the golden head, and after you another kingdom, inferior to you, will arise” (Dan. 2). Attend, I ask, to what he says and what he proposes to teach us by his interpretation: “You,” he says, “are the golden head.” For, to say nothing of the rest, I think this alone is enough to require an interpreter; and would that we may understand the interpreter and know even this through him.

Does not one statue represent the person of one human being, and, as we have explained, signify the transgression of anyone falling from the heights into the depths? If such a person is one person, having a golden head, a silver breast, and other members of bronze or iron, why, I ask, if the person addressed is the golden head, is he not also the silver breast and the other parts in the same manner? Or perhaps in the part in which you are golden, you are yourself, and in the part in which you are not golden, you are not yourself? Whoever you are, then, when after the golden head you have begun to have a silver breast, look—and attend carefully—lest perhaps you are no longer yourself.

If after much charity and great devotion of mind you cease to be devout and cease to be golden, will you still be the same person you were before? “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he has been compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. 48). To be like God is a marvellous honour; to be like cattle is a miserable disgrace. Therefore the person like God and the person like cattle are different persons. The human being was made good and created for goodness: “Only this,” says Ecclesiastes, “have I found: that God made man upright, and he entangled himself in endless questions” (Ecclus. 7). If, therefore, you burn with charity and remain in the love of good, you have a golden head and you are yourself, because you are what and for what you were made, and what you ought to be. But when charity grows cold in you and you begin to fail from your former fervour, will you still be yourself, and not rather another, inferior to yourself? “You,” he says, “are the golden head, and after you another kingdom, inferior to you, will arise.”

Are you not already less than yourself when you begin to do by mere counsel what you formerly did from deep counsel and great desire? “And after you,” he says, “another kingdom, inferior to you, will arise.” Is it not another kingdom when the mind is governed by counsel alone, than when it is also moved by desire for good? Is counsel alone without desire not a lesser kingdom than fervent desire joined to prudent counsel? Is it not a lesser thing to do good from deliberation alone than also from great love or delight? Therefore it is rightly said: “After you another kingdom, inferior to you, will arise.” And then a third kingdom is added when it says: “And a third kingdom, another, of bronze, which shall rule over the whole earth.”

Just as gold belongs to what is done from love, and silver to what is done from deliberation alone, so bronze belongs to good done from pretence. In the first kingdom charity reigns; in the second, truth; in the third, pretence (*simultas*) reigns. See, then, how fitting it seems to this third kingdom that it is described as ruling over the whole earth. For the ruler of this kingdom, who exercises his body in good works but neglects to nourish his heart with a good will, has no share in the kingdom of heaven: “The kingdom of heaven,” he says, “is within you” (Luke 17). Charity truly reigns within—within the heart—and truth reigns within; yet they are not content with those confines but break forth outward through good work. Consider, then, whether those first two kingdoms perhaps belong to the kingdom of heaven, if indeed the kingdom of heaven is within us, because both may be found within us.

But the king and ruler of the third kingdom, having no share in the kingdom of heaven, has been driven down from the height and cast out; and because he cannot rule in heaven, he claims a kingdom for himself on earth. For he has cast away his inward things in his life and cannot say: “Our commonwealth is in heaven.” How much less, then, can his dominion be in heaven? Yet he rules over the whole earth, exercising the flesh in good works while leaving the mind empty of good intention. “And the fourth kingdom,” he says, “will be like iron. As iron crushes and subdues all things, so it will crush and break all these things.” What does he mean by “all these things,” except that this kingdom crushes the other kingdoms already mentioned? How does iron customarily crush the other metals—namely gold and silver? As charity is signified in gold, truth in silver, and pretence in bronze, so, as was said above, cruelty is signified in iron. Who does not know how the severity of cruelty is accustomed to scatter and destroy holy desire, which belongs to gold; true counsel, which belongs to silver; and pious but pretended service, which belongs to bronze work? Therefore it is well said: “The fourth kingdom will be like iron.”

## Chapter XXXII. On the different stages of corruption and their characteristics in those descending from evil to evil

But we must return briefly again to what has been said above and show how this interpretation also fits the other reading. According to that interpretation, the first kingdom is arrogance, the second boasting, the third obstinacy, the fourth cruelty. Arrogance belongs to the golden work, boasting to the silver work, obstinacy to the bronze, cruelty to the iron. Let us see what our interpreter says and thinks about the golden head, and how it suits this sense: “You,” he says, “are king of kings; and the God of heaven has given you kingdom, strength, dominion, and glory, and has given into your hand all things in which the children of men dwell, the beasts of the field, and the birds of heaven, and has established all things under your dominion.”

When we receive such great grace as is described here, or as we heard expounded above, it often happens that we become proud against God from the very source from which we ought to have become more devout or more indebted to God. But how pious and how worthy of wonder it is that, when our swollen mind rises proudly against God, he does not immediately strike us with strict judgment or at once withdraw his grace. Rather, he first summons us by gentle admonition, now inwardly and now outwardly: inwardly through divine revelation, outwardly through human exhortation; inwardly through inward inspiration, outwardly through human reasoning—as here, first secretly through a dream, afterwards openly through speech.

“You,” he says, “are king of kings,” because, being stronger than the strong and stronger still, you can rule even the strongest, since you still possess assisting grace. Therefore repent while you can, while you still have cooperating grace. You are still king of kings and can still rule principally over vices and govern your passions, because although you have abandoned grace, you have not yet been abandoned by it. “Do not,” he says, “be proud; do not think highly of yourself. Cast off the arrogance of your heart quickly, and do not ascribe to yourself what you can do through God’s gift. For the God of heaven has given you kingdom, strength, dominion, and glory.”

You still have kingdom over the movements of your heart and body, because you can order good things; strength, because you can resist evils; dominion, because you can press on the negligent; glory, because you can overcome the rebellious. Yet there is no reason for you to be proud, nothing to attribute to yourself. For the God of heaven gave you all these things, and gave into your hand all things in which the children of men dwell, the beasts of the field, and the birds of heaven, and placed all things under your dominion. That you preside over the beasts of the field and birds of heaven; that you can rule the appetites of the flesh and the thoughts of the mind; that you can do good deeds and meditate on profitable things—you have not from your own strength, but from divine gift. For all things in which the children of men dwell, and all things that obey reason and right counsels, occur through his gift, are brought into act by his cooperation, prosper, and succeed favourably. Whatever you can usefully do, you can do from him and through him, who is not unable to do anything because he can do all things. Every capacity you possess, therefore, comes from his gift, who has established all these things under your dominion.

“You,” therefore, he says, “are the golden head,” since, while grace still accompanies you, you can both correct evils and practise goods. Crush pride, then, lest you lose grace also; for “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.” We know that pride is the beginning of every sin. But “he who commits sin is the slave of sin.” What then? When sin has begun to rule and you have begun to render it service, will there not then be another kingdom than there was when you could suppress sin so that it did not reign in your mortal body? I think, therefore, that when through pride you begin to lose grace—and to lose yourself, without which you can do nothing—then another kingdom, inferior to you, will arise, according to what is written: “You are the golden head, and after you another kingdom, inferior to you, will arise.”

But because every arrogant person glories in himself, while boasting glories in another’s favour, something may rightly be said of the golden head—that is, the arrogant person—to the effect that he is still himself, because he has not yet abandoned himself: he has located his glory in himself. But he departs from himself when he places his glory in another. Consider, moreover, how much less it is to glory in the hissing of another’s mouth and in false praises than in one’s own goods, often true though received from another. Thus it is rightly said: “You are the golden head, and after you another kingdom, inferior to you, will arise”; and it is added: “And another third kingdom of bronze, which shall rule over the whole earth.”

Because bronze is very durable, it rightly signifies obstinacy, as we said above. Who, then, has a belly and thighs, adjacent to the shameful parts, as though of bronze? It is the person who clings obstinately even to things for which he ought to blush. See, therefore, how aptly it seems to suit this kingdom that it is said to rule over the whole earth. How does that not rule over the whole earth which extends its tyranny even to ruling shameful things? “And the fourth kingdom,” he says, “will be like iron. As iron crushes and subdues all things, so it will crush all these things and break them.” If we must understand cruelty by iron, how, I ask, can such a kingdom crush and break the other kingdoms?

Without doubt, however shameless the mind may be, cruelty nevertheless altogether disturbs and confounds—nor is this surprising—the glory which it was accustomed to have in itself through arrogance or in another through boasting. For who, amid so many openly mad acts of his cruelty, could believe himself holy or trust that another could believe him so? The violent claims of cruelty are also accustomed so to crush and confound the kingdom of obstinacy that, in the time of its frenzy, the mind can persevere in no purpose, however right or honourable. Whatever, in a time of calm, the mind determines and arranges concerning peace or patience, even by vow or oath, a fury arriving in the time of disturbance scatters and dissolves.

What we have said thus far about the exposition of this vision we have considered, according to a twofold interpretation, in keeping with the measure of our understanding. But the remaining matters agree in the same sense with both interpretations and do not require a double exposition, as did what preceded. For what is cruelty but harshness? And impatience likewise—what else is it but pitiable weakness? Thus under different names we must understand the same thing.

## Chapter XXXIII. How the mind is divided, torn, and confounded within itself when the extremes of corruption are reached
Now therefore let us consider what follows: “Moreover,” he says, “[Col. 1286B] because you saw part of the feet and toes to be potter’s clay, and part iron, the kingdom shall be divided; yet it shall arise from the planting of iron” (Dan. I). But if necessity is signified by the foot, and cruelty by iron, what does it mean that a certain part of the feet is described as iron? Is anyone found harsh, pitiless, or even inflexible toward his own necessities? We know that the covetous person will not be filled with money, and that one who loves riches will reap no fruit from them; yet he does not cease from labour, nor are the eyes satisfied by riches, nor does he reflect, saying: “For whom do I labour and deprive my soul of good things?” Does he not seem to you to walk upon an iron sole who all the days of his life eats in darkness, amid many cares, affliction, and [Col. 1286C] sorrow? Truly, as it is written, “Nothing is more wicked than a miser” (Eccles. X), who neither has compassion on his neighbour nor pity on himself. Why are we surprised that such a man has iron shins, when he already has iron soles? Why complain that he is harsh toward his neighbours, when he is already hardened toward his own needs? “He who is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good?”

Observe, however, that such a person first becomes hardened, in his iron shins, toward his neighbour; afterward he becomes hardened, even in his iron feet, toward himself. See therefore, whoever reads this, lest perhaps after love and pursuit of wisdom you return to love and gain of money—that is, turn the golden head down toward iron feet. “The entrails of the miser are cruel.” Set now before your eyes and consider any [Col. 1286D] misers. See, I ask you, how anxious they are, how laborious, how sparing, how severe toward themselves. Yet what do they often customarily do, or what would they still do, if they were freely fed, clothed, and protected at another’s expense? You would certainly see them wishing to dress softly, soaked in gluttony and drunkenness, sluggish through sleep and idleness, becoming angry and indignant whenever they see something of their usual comforts lacking. Do such people not seem to you to walk with feet partly iron and partly clay, when you see one and the same person so sparing in what is his own and so extravagant in what is another’s, now serving austerity, now luxury? “Moreover,” he says, “because you saw part of the feet and toes to be potter’s clay and part iron, the kingdom shall be divided; yet it shall arise from the planting of iron.”

[Col. 1287A] The foot is divided into five toes, and the condition of necessity is doubtless divided into five when it extends to all the bodily senses. But when we eagerly seek the pleasures of the senses or cautiously avoid them, what else do we do than exert ourselves, as it were, on two feet, now to the right and now to the left, and walk through prosperity and adversity along the path of our desires? Yet you may often see some people yielding more intensely to one sense and others to another, and willingly enduring the discomforts of the other senses for the delights of some one particular sense. How many acquire, over a long time and through great labour, what they spend in the gluttony or drunkenness of a single day or hour? How many fears, honours, and chills from enemy, night, and cold do adulterers willingly endure in order to attain [Col. 1287B] the momentary foul allurements of pleasure? Do not all such persons have one part of the feet or toes clay and another iron, since in one respect they are so patient and almost insensible, while in another they are so impatient? “Moreover, because you saw,” he says, “part of the feet and toes to be potter’s clay and part iron, the kingdom shall be divided.” Truly, whatever is of this sort will be divided. For, to offer one example among many: when one and the same person is often both miserly and gluttonous, how great, I ask, is the frequent strife or contention in his heart, when gluttony commands him to spend the very coin which avarice commands him to keep? Thus, often for a slight cause, the kingdom is divided against itself, disturbed and thrown into confusion, until it is utterly desolated. For “[Col. 1287C] every kingdom divided against itself shall be desolated, and house shall fall upon house.”

It should certainly be noted that of this kingdom it is said: “Yet, he says, it shall arise from the planting of iron.” For when the transgressing mind first returns to worldly desires, the spirit is hardened to bear the labours of the world; and then, according to Job’s saying, it counts its delights to be under thorns (Job XXII), provided that it may somehow reach the end of its desires. O how blessed they would be if they patiently endured for love of righteousness what they bear for love of money, or for attaining some worldly splendour or glory! Yet those who so often patiently [Col. 1287D] endure so many troubles, injuries, and insults for the profit of desire cannot calmly hear even one light word of correction for love of virtue. I think this is what follows, when it is immediately added: “According as you saw iron mixed with clay from mud, and the toes partly iron and partly earthenware, it shall be partly strong and partly broken.” For, as has been said, such people are strong and patient in that respect in which their labour might serve virtue. But what does he mean by “from potsherd, from mud”? What is such a potsherd but a foul habit? Mud, as it were, hardens into potsherd when a foul action is drawn into habit; but from the hardening of foul habit a person is cast down into impatience and, like a potsherd, is now easily broken through anger, now [Col. 1288A] dissolved into concupiscence.

But, as we have shown concerning misers, many seem gladly to satisfy their pleasures when they can do so without expense of money; when they cannot do so without loss of profit, however, they resist vehemently. Do these people not seem to mix iron and clay potsherd together? “But because you saw,” he says, “iron mixed with clay potsherd, they shall indeed mingle with human seed, but they shall not adhere to one another, just as iron cannot be mixed with potsherd.” What are “human seeds” but the counsels of carnal prudence? The prudence of the flesh teaches us to seek money for things necessary to use. It likewise teaches us to take much away from the necessities of life and spare money, lest it seem to fail in necessary uses. See how it adheres to human seed, when [Col. 1288B] one seems, as it were, to require the other by counsel; yet they are not intermixed, because one often seems to contradict the other. The love of riches commands one thing, the love of pleasures another; the heat of pleasure one thing, the greed of gain another. But when diverse vices thus seize a person in different directions or drive him toward opposites, they miserably torment him and allow him to rest neither day nor night. In a wondrous and pitiable fashion, those who are such anticipate the times of their own condemnation, while through inward anxiety of mind or outward affliction they rage against themselves; and unless heavenly mercy looks upon them, they pass through temporal torments to eternal ones.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How a man is sometimes divinely advanced from the depths of iniquity to the highest summit of charity.

[Col. 1288C]

But divine mercy often comes as an aid to salvation, where, so far as such persons themselves are concerned, there is an accumulation of condemnation, according to what is written: “Where iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more” (Matt. XXIV). For often, while heavenly grace visits such persons amid the straits of their calamities, it sets this very enormity of their misery before their eyes; by considering it, they are pierced into the tears of repentance; and, drawn out from the pit of misery and the mire of filth, they are advanced by certain steps of progress from the depths of iniquity to the highest summit of charity. Is not this what Scripture says, [Col. 1288D] where it subsequently adds: “In the days of those kingdoms the God of heaven shall raise up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed, and its kingdom shall not be given to another people. It shall crush and consume all these kingdoms, and it itself shall stand for ever, according as you saw that a stone was cut from the mountain without hands, and crushed the potsherd, iron, bronze, silver, and gold” (Dan. II).

Therefore, in the days of those kingdoms, in the time of such great wickedness and such great misery, an abundance of grace is given, and the kingdom of charity is raised up—a kingdom that can never perish. For he who remains in love shall remain for ever. Thus this kingdom shall never be destroyed. For “charity bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. XIII). And its kingdom shall not be given to another people, [Col. 1289A] for this is that fountain, as Augustine says, “of which a stranger does not partake.” “It shall crush,” he says, “and consume all these kingdoms.” Do you wish to know how charity crushes and consumes all these kingdoms? “Charity,” says the Apostle, “is patient, is kind; charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek what is its own, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices together with truth.” It is further said of this kingdom that “it itself shall stand for ever”; and, says the Apostle, “Charity never fails.” “According as you saw,” he says, “that a stone was cut from the mountain without hands and crushed the potsherd, iron, bronze, silver, and gold.”

[Col. 1289B] The destruction of the opposing kingdoms begins in fear and is completed in charity. By fear they are uprooted from consent; by charity they are torn away from effect. [Col. 1289C] Therefore charity, which is patient, crushes clay-like fragility; charity, which is kind, crushes iron rigidity. What, I ask, is that in which the bronze of pretence is crushed, except charity which does not envy? And what crushes brazen obstinacy, except charity which does not act perversely? If boasting is understood in silver and arrogance in gold, what is more contrary to them than charity, which is neither puffed up nor ambitious nor seeks what is its own? Or if in silver is understood that work which is done from deliberation alone rather than from love, and is done not so much from love as from truth, what is more consonant with charity, which rejoices together with truth? If, in the golden head, the defect of even an excellent work is censured because it is not brought to the completion of its due end, what better rebukes or corrects such a work than perfect charity, which never fails?

[Col. 1289D] O blessed kingdom of charity, which remains for ever! O blessed kingdom, which shall never be destroyed, when it shall be given for ever to another people! Blessed is the kingdom in which patience endures and kindness perseveres! Blessed is the kingdom in which no one envies; blessed indeed that in which no perversity is done, no one is puffed up; truly blessed that in which no ambitious person seeks what is his own; no one burns! Perhaps the author intimates something to us in this: although above, in enumerating the crushing, he placed iron first and potsherd afterward, here he clearly puts potsherd first and then iron. But we know that in some fear and in others shame has the greater sway. Some are more fearful than ashamed; [Col. 1290A] others are more ashamed than fearful. Those who are more timid are more readily pierced by consideration of their own cruelty than of their pleasure. But those who are more susceptible to shame are more readily softened into repentance by remembrance of foul pleasure than of wickedness. Therefore, if cruelty is rightly understood by iron and pleasure by potsherd, what wonder is it if iron and potsherd are read as crushed now in one order and now another, since according to the disposition of minds or character, in different persons the order or occasion of inward compunction and true contrition varies?

## CHAPTER XXXV. What prudence is excessively late, and what is useful and certain prudence.

Daniel continues and adds: “The great God,” [Col. 1290B] he says, “has shown the king what shall happen hereafter” (Dan. II). “The great God”: perhaps He had grown in the king’s thought and love, He who had revealed to him so profound a depth of mysteries, so that he ought deservedly to magnify His greatness above all else. “The great God has shown the king”—not just any person, but the king the Lord has shown these things, so that he who longs for foreknowledge of future things and grace of this kind may recognize that he ought, by royal freedom and authority, to govern and order what belongs to him. “The great God has shown the king what shall happen hereafter.” O what divine mercy is at work, when a man’s ruin is revealed to him while it is still future, while it can still be guarded against, so that with such concern he may foresee and recognize what he ought to fear, what to avoid, what danger [Col. 1290C] to resist. Indeed, prudence is late and far too late when imminent danger can no longer be avoided. “The great God has shown the king what shall happen hereafter.” Blessed is he who can foresee impending ruin while he is still king, while he can still rule his passions and avert the danger that presses upon him.

Let us see, however, what is added after all this, when it is said: “And the dream is true, and its interpretation faithful.” We often penetrate many depths of divine mysteries through the quickness of innate reason, and, with prudent concern, foresee by the eye of prudence some future things before they arrive. Yet in these matters constancy often wavers and does not fully grasp what it may hold unshaken with the security of certainty. For “the thoughts of mortals are timid, and our foresight uncertain.” On the other hand, what we see in the light of God and know by His revelation we hold with such certainty and confidence that we cannot be assailed by any two-sided uncertainty concerning it. This is what the Psalmist expresses figuratively when he says: “Before the brightness in His sight, the clouds passed away” (Ps. XVII). For the Lord to look is to illumine. Since He is the true light, He acts as the sun does: by the very fact that He looks, He makes bright, kindles, and enlightens. Therefore, at the divine gaze we are often filled with such a splendour of divine light that, in what is divinely revealed, every clouding of ambiguity or hesitation is at once removed. Thus clouds pass away when those doubts which used to cloud the mind withdraw. For clouds to pass away [Col. 1291A] is to possess the clear-sightedness of truth and the serenity of understanding without any questioning. He taught that he possessed such certainty, and such security of certainty, in affirming his judgment when he confidently declared: “And the dream is true, and its interpretation faithful.” But Scripture goes on to relate what the king did in response.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That unstable and undiscerning humiliation is indeed worthy of rebuke.

“Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell upon his face and worshipped Daniel, and commanded that sacrifices and incense be offered to him” (Dan. II). He humbled himself greatly—and no wonder—and deserved to be humbled after learning that such a great danger threatened him. [Col. 1291B] But who would not rightly rebuke him in this, that he bestowed upon a mortal man the honour due to God alone? Yet perhaps, because he had found Daniel to be a true temple, he judged him worthy of such honour. But for our edification we must carefully examine these matters, and subtly inquire what is customarily enacted within us in a manner analogous to them. “He fell,” he says, “upon his face.” A man is recognized by his face, and in man that part is considered more comely or more dignified than the others. What else, therefore, is it to fall upon one’s face than, through lofty desire, to despise even that which is chief or best in oneself, and to regard as weak and almost—[Col. 1291C] or altogether—nothing that by which one was customarily known to others and appeared, as it were, venerable? Observe how he fell upon his face, how he humbled himself—or wished us to humble ourselves—he who compared all our righteousnesses to a menstrual cloth. But it is neither especially great nor particularly surprising if we cast ourselves down at the time when we already see our danger approaching. “Then,” he says, “the king fell upon his face.” He fell when, under Daniel’s instruction, he recognized his danger. But it must be known that humiliation without perseverance cannot resist imminent danger.

It must also be observed that the more rashly and excessively a person casts himself down, the more he later breaks out into a madder and more monstrous pride. Observe in the king an unstable and undiscerning humiliation, [Col. 1291D] and afterward pride more than human. For he who first worshipped Daniel later commanded his own statue to be worshipped.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That we ought not to trust or wish to glory in any virtue of our own.

“He commanded,” he says, “that sacrifices and incense be offered to him.” To kill animals for Daniel, or burn incense, and expend such things in any way for his use or benefit, would not at all have been blameworthy. But it was blameworthy to sacrifice these things to him and bestow divine honour upon a mortal man. In the immolation of a victim, the flesh of brute and irrational creatures is slaughtered; in the burning of incense, a sweet fragrance is spread more widely. Thus living but brute flesh is, as it were, slain [Col. 1292A] when some irrational appetite or affection in us is mortified by contrition of the flesh; and then we spread abroad, as it were, the odour of incense when we extend the reputation of some virtue by worthy proclamations of praise. Therefore, to slay for our Daniel those things which still live beastially in our appetites or affections, and to exercise such mortification for the use and benefit of our devotion, will unquestionably not be useless.

But when we commend Daniel’s office with manifold praise, and by the commendation of our speech spread everywhere the sweet fame of devotion’s virtue, we indeed do a good work, if in all this we seek not so much the glory as the benefit of our Daniel. And, to state more plainly [Col. 1292B] what I think: it is indeed good, for the grace of devotion and insistence in prayer, to restrain our life; it is good to commend and extol the virtue of prayer in praises—provided this is done so that our devotion may grow better and rise more fervently, not that it may appear more glorious. How many there are who, when they believe that through persistence in prayer they have obtained some grace, already presume greatly upon their devotion or holiness and wish it to be highly esteemed by others! This is what Nebuchadnezzar did after he attained through Daniel the desire of his vow: he heaped upon him an honour as foolish as it was vain.

What we rebuke regarding this virtue of which we speak we must guard against in every virtue or grace. Hear openly, consider carefully, retain in memory: if you trust, presume, or glory in any grace, ability, or virtue of your own, you bestow upon it divine honour, and quite shamefully—indeed, quite shamefully—if not actually make a god of it for yourself. “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord.” “Cursed is the man who trusts in man”; therefore also one who trusts in himself or in any virtue of his own. “I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to a graven image” (Isa. XLII).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How many seek knowledge of the virtues and instruction in morals for display, not for usefulness.

How many glory and wish to be glorious in human eyes—not, I say, because they have virtues or holiness, but because they know how to discourse wisely and argue eloquently [Col. 1292D] about virtues. O how much better, how much more useful for you not to possess the gold of knowledge and the silver of eloquence than to make an idol for yourself from them! “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.” To depict and retain in memory by understanding and teaching merely the pattern and form of virtues, while lacking their actual effect, is what else but to carry certain idols in the heart? Knowledge of holiness without good intention—what else is it but an image without life? Knowledge alone, without the effect of holiness and the affection of goodness—what else is it but a vain image without movement or sensation? “They have a mouth and shall not speak; they have eyes and shall not see; ears they have and shall not hear; nostrils they have and shall not smell. [Col. 1293A] They have hands and shall not touch; feet they have and shall not walk; they shall not cry out with their throat” (Ps. CXIII).

The mouth, as we all know, is the instrument of speech; the eyes, the instrument of sight; the ears, the instrument of hearing; and the same manner of interpretation must be made regarding the rest. What, therefore, is it to have a mouth, eyes, ears, or any such things and exercise them for no use, except to possess the instruments of duties but lack the duties of those instruments? You read that “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X). Thus confession belongs to the mouth; watchfulness to the eyes; obedience to the ears; discernment to the nostrils; action to the hands; progress to the feet; supplication to the throat.

See: perhaps your empty knowledge knows very well what the virtue of confession is. [Col. 1293B] It knows that all things are washed in confession. Perhaps it knows how one ought to confess, yet it does not confess. It therefore has a mouth and does not speak. Perhaps it knows how it ought to watch over its life, yet neglects to watch over it as it should. You have, in a sense, the instrument of seeing, but lack the office of seeing. Perhaps you know what the virtue of obedience is and what it ought to be, yet you will not obey. This is to have ears and not hear. Through knowledge you perhaps possess the instrument for discerning spiritual fragrance; but since you devote no effort to discernment in conduct, you glory vainly in a useless instrument. You know how you ought to exercise yourself in good work, yet you do not wish to gain by experience the fruit of good work: this is to have hands [Col. 1293C] and not touch. For what is it to touch with the hands except to prove by experience the fruits of works? You have received through knowledge the feet of progress if you have learned how you ought to stretch forward. But though you have feet, you do not walk if you do not strive toward progress. You have received the teaching of supplication and do not wish to supplicate: this is to have a throat and not wish to cry out.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. That these seven things must be observed in the practice of any virtue.

But if we attend carefully, we must observe these seven things in the practice of any virtue. First, that which belongs to the mouth: condemn and accuse past evils. Second, that [Col. 1293D] which belongs to the eyes: diligently investigate and discover through investigation what should be done. Third, that which belongs to obedience: agree with the counsel found, rest in it, and wish to obey it. Fourth, which is as it were concerned with the nostrils: while doing good, cautiously detect the evils that lie in wait and prudently discern them. Fifth, which also, as it were, concerns the hands: complete by action the good that has been decided upon. Sixth, by a kind of forward movement of the feet: always press on from the good begun toward better things. But since we are not sufficient in ourselves for any of these, we must implore divine assistance for them all.

If we know these things but do not exercise them in action, what else do we make [Col. 1294A] or worship, in acquiring and cultivating idle and useless branches of knowledge, than vain and empty idols, while we are content with the bare knowledge of virtues? See how perverse and damnable it is to seek spiritual teaching solely for display and not for edification. This is surely prudence of the flesh, wholly hostile to God. What, I ask, is the benefit—or rather, how great is the harm—of seeking, investigating, and anxiously desiring to know, with great labour and the utmost zeal, things which in no way you are willing to put into practice? For it is clearer than light that the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it, but rather does things unworthy, “shall be beaten with many stripes.” O what a sort of counsel, and how useless, to seek counsels of life only so that you may possess something by which to appear wiser than others and obtain the name of teacher! What acute prudence, what shrewd foresight, [Col. 1294B] to persist vehemently in seeking those counsels which, once obtained, you in no way wish to follow!

Yet we often see that, by God’s just judgment, something happens to minds of this sort: those who were formerly endowed with spiritual prudence concerning spiritual things afterward become carnally prudent concerning carnal things.
