Such spiritual counsels as they formerly devised concerning heavenly and divine things, such carnal counsels they are soon found to devise concerning worldly and human things. For just as, in spiritual matters and gains of the soul, they first see what they could usefully do and yet refuse to do it, so afterward in bodily conveniences and temporal gains they see what ought usefully to be done, yet, conquered by desire or bound by sloth, are wholly unable to do it. This very thing often happens [Col. 1294C] to some people beneficially, so that from it they begin to detest and abhor their vices and, because they see that even amid the greatest dangers they cannot restrain themselves from their transgressions, implore divine help concerning this very matter. Hence comes that prophetic imprecation—or petition: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. CXIII).

But to return to the point from which we digressed, let us at least gather from this how foolish and empty it is to wish to glory in mere empty knowledges of the virtues and in things that are, as it were, their idols, since before God it is detestable for a person to presume upon any virtue of his own. See, we rebuke Nebuchadnezzar—and rightly ought to rebuke him—because he commanded Daniel, though [Col. 1294D] a faithful man, to be given divine honour; how much more if he had wished the same honour to be rendered to Daniel’s image.

## CHAPTER XL. That desire is often corrupted by that through which understanding is enlightened.

But amid these things let us see how truly he thought or spoke concerning God, he who wished such vain things to be done. Therefore the king, speaking to Daniel, said: “Truly your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, revealing mysteries, because you were able to disclose this secret” (Dan. II). See how soundly he thinks concerning divine things, and yet how similar to idolatry is what he did in action. Yes, indeed: at one and the same time Moses is lifted up on the mountain to contemplate the highest and divine things, while [Col. 1295A] the people entrusted to him are cast down in the valley to the crime of idolatry and worship of the calf. So it often happens in one and the same mind, in a wondrous and pitiable way, that, by the very means through which human understanding is enlightened to divine things on high, it is no less corrupted by the throng of desires.

For who does not know how the greatness of revelations raises an unwary mind into pride, when the Apostle himself says of himself: “Lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me” (1 Cor. XII)? Often, indeed, some persons, still placed amid the very spectacles of divine revelations, secretly grow proud in their own minds: already thinking highly of themselves, they judge themselves worthy of high esteem from others; [Col. 1295B] they diligently seek how they may become known to others; they pursue the breath of empty favour; and they exchange the true glory which they had been accustomed to possess before God for a vain one. Of such persons the Psalmist says: “And they changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay” (Ps. CV). For it is written: “All flesh is hay, and all its glory is like the flower of hay” (Isa. XL). What then is a calf eating hay, except an appetite for human favour, seeking carnal and temporal glory? What, therefore, is it to worship a calf, an animal indeed wanton and brutish, except to serve an irrational appetite in the ambition for temporal glory and to establish one’s glory in temporal and vain glory?

[Col. 1295C] Nebuchadnezzar, however—whom we nevertheless rightly rebuke—did something more tolerable, since he bestowed divine honour on a human being, that is, on a rational animal. For undoubtedly it is more irrational to worship an irrational animal than a rational one. Some trust and glory in their own virtue, while others do so in mere reputation for virtue. The former glory in what they possess or believe themselves to possess; the latter in what others judge them to be. The former glory in the testimony of conscience, though not as before God; the latter in the testimony of reputation, as before their neighbour alone. The former, then, is like an irrational animal; the latter like a rational one. Blessed is one who glories in the testimony of conscience, provided that he does so in the Lord. Otherwise, it is very ungrateful to glory in the gift but not in the author of the gift. How much better and more rightly would the king in question [Col. 1295D] have worshipped God rather than Daniel, and sacrificed to Him who, although through Daniel’s ministry, had taught him what he sought.

## CHAPTER XLI. That some things we know from divine revelation, others we infer through reason.

But since, as we have said, he did blameworthy things, let us see how rightly he thought concerning God when he said: “Truly your God is God of gods and Lord of kings.” Since royal power is chief and highest, what is it for a king to say this except to hold it firmly and immovably from the inmost sense of his soul? What is it for Daniel to hear this from the king except that the inward sense of the soul and true devotion of mind neither ought nor can remain hidden? Or perhaps in the fact that sacred Scripture says Daniel learned some things [Col. 1296A] from God and heard others from the king, it mystically indicates that, for the exercise of our devotion, some things are learned by divine revelation and others are weighed by the quickness of reason implanted in us.

When, speaking of God, he says “your” and “our,” he regards the relation of grace, not the condition of nature. For, in a special way, God properly belonged to those who through the gift of that grace itself and the privilege of their merits had obtained a singular place of familiarity with Him, and boldness of confidence before Him, beyond others. And without doubt it is devotion that both renders God propitious and makes Him familiar. “God of gods and Lord of kings.” For although there are those called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, according to the saying, “I said: You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI), [Col. 1296B] they can indeed be called so by name; but what God is naturally and substantially, they cannot possibly be. Therefore He is God of gods and Lord of kings, because, as the Apostle testifies, “There is no authority except from God” (Rom. XIII). For the fact that some rule over others, and that men of virtue can rule over their vices and passions, they receive from the gift of the supreme King.

He therefore says: “Truly your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, revealing mysteries”; and he immediately adds the ground from which he gathers and infers this, saying: “Because you were able to disclose this secret.” For from the fact that He revealed to him the secrets of his own heart, and likewise the hidden counsels of God—one concerning the past, the other concerning the future—at one and the same time, [Col. 1296C] he discerned with remarkable quickness of intellect a revelation of supreme divinity. From the fact that he heard about the secret of his own heart and found it true, he also inferred that the other matter was true, which he was unable at that time to test by experience—the matter of divine counsel or purpose. Wisely, therefore, he recognized that supreme wisdom was that which could disclose to Daniel the secrets of another’s conscience in so dark an abyss of the human heart. For, according to Solomon’s saying, God alone knows the heart of all the children of men. Likewise, he shrewdly perceived that supreme power was that which could reveal to Daniel, according to its good pleasure, the order and disposition of future events and actions. For who other than God could make the divine counsel known to him? In accordance with [Col. 1296D] what Isaiah said: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counsellor?” (Isa. XL). For, as the Apostle testifies, just as no one knows the things of a person except the person’s spirit which is within him, so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. Therefore it is rightly said: “Truly your God is God of gods and Lord of kings, revealing mysteries, because you were able to disclose this secret.”

## CHAPTER XLII. That it is best for our devotion to advance so far that no occupation can interrupt its exercise.

Then the king exalted Daniel on high and gave him great and many gifts. If we rightly understand devotion by Daniel, what else is it to raise Daniel on high [Col. 1297A] than to regard the office of devotion as principal and pre-eminent among all other offices, and to hold it, as it were, in the highest place? Now it commonly happens that, after the mind has learned by experience how great is the power of true devotion, it applies itself more earnestly to its pursuits and diligently persists in its advancement: by investigating it seeks, by seeking it finds, the means by which it may thereby advance to better things. What else, therefore, are the great and many gifts which Daniel, that is, our devotion, receives, when from study eagerly devoted it readily finds, as it were, certain talents of understanding and gains of prudence by which it may grow toward greater things and extend itself more widely?

“And he appointed him,” he says, “ruler over all the provinces of Babylon, and chief of the magistrates over all the wise men of Babylon” (Dan. 2). [Col. 1297B] Would that our devotion might advance so far that it should appear superior to all the rulers of Babylon, wiser than all the prudent men of Babylonia, and, in the judgment of our mind, stand forth as more precious than everything that pleases in the world or seems valuable, and by the decree of our choice obtain the higher gain! This, I think, is for Daniel to receive from the king the summit of rule and mastery. Would that at last, some day, our devotion might attain such perfection that no affection, however vehement, no occupation, no anxiety, no suggestion or persuasion could in us—not, I say, dissipate its application, but even interrupt it—and that apostolic command might be fulfilled: “Pray without ceasing” [Col. 1297C] (1 Thess. 5). Would that all other duties might be so arranged and ordered as to be found to serve, indeed to minister, to the uses and benefits of our devotion!

## CHAPTER XLIII. That even in the requirements of our necessity we ought to do nothing improvidently or without deliberation.

But Daniel asked the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the works of the province of Babylon (Dan. 2). The king undoubtedly assents to Daniel when he readily accepts and receives whatever conscience suggests to him in the time of inward devotion. But what, I ask, was this province of Babylon, or what were the works of that province? Certainly God made the land surrounding Babylon [Col. 1297D]; human industry, however, filled it with walls and buildings. If, therefore, Babylon is rightly interpreted as “confusion,” and if all things belonging to it seem subject to confusion, how, I ask, could that which God made and established belong to Babylon or be subject to confusion?

Yet we know that God subjected man to manifold necessity: for from the very law of his condition he received the need to eat, to drink, and the like. But had man remained in that first state of his creation, he would in no way blush for these things, because he could have performed them without any sin. But now we rightly blush even for these offices of necessity, because, conquered by the defect of our corruption, we cannot perform them without fault. Thus that broad and truly very extensive corruption of our infirmity is rightly assigned to Babylonian possession, since it is undoubtedly subject to confusion. In such a province, therefore, and in the office or works of our necessity, it will be altogether useful to set those three men mentioned above over them and bring everything under their ordering. As we have already said above, by these three men we must understand circumspection, discretion, and deliberation. Therefore, not only in spiritual pursuits and exercises, but also in secular affairs and the uses of necessity, we ought to do nothing without circumspection, nothing [Col. 1298B] without discernment, nothing without foresight. And this is to appoint Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over all the works of the province of Babylon.

Thus, even in those matters in which we provide for human necessity or serve our common infirmity, let us do nothing without moderation, nothing without measure, nothing without good intention, nothing contrary to order, nothing contrary to reason; and we shall possess that form of mastery which Daniel, as our teacher, wished us to have in the Babylonian province. Finally, according to the saying of the Wise Man, “Do everything with counsel”; and you have such a mastery as the prophet signifies to you mystically. For circumspection and discretion are altogether necessary if we wish to do nothing improvidently or without deliberation.

## CHAPTER XLIV. That whatever strikes the soul through thought ought to awaken the devotion of the mind.

[Col. 1298C]

Finally, at the close of the discourse, it is added: “But Daniel himself was at the king’s gates” (Dan. 2). We know that through gates an entrance to what lies within is opened. Daniel, then, keeps watch, as it were, at the king’s gates when our devotion vigilantly guards against every suggestion and resists in prayer, at the very entrance of temptation, every device of the evil one, lest any assault or violence oppress the unwary mind, or fraud deceive it. Blessed is that state of soul, and to be sought with every effort, when everything that strikes the soul through thought immediately, without any delay, awakens the devotion of the mind. The devotion [Col. 1298D] of the mind ought, therefore, diligently to anticipate every consent of the will and fortify it beforehand by prayer. And this is for Daniel to preside at the king’s gates. At every suggestion, at every thought that arises, let us ask the Lord not to lead us into temptation, and let us have Daniel presiding at the gates of our city. Hear what the Wise Man counsels in accordance with this, when he says: “At all times bless God, and ask him to direct your ways” (Tob. 4). May he direct our ways unto true life, he who lives and reigns without end. Amen.

# BOOK II

[Col. 1299]

## CHAPTER I. On the security of conscience, or the renewal of progress.

[Col. 1299A]

“I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace” (Dan. 4). What do we understand by “house” except conscience, and what by “palace” except security of conscience and confidence in that security? For a palace too is a house, though not every house can be called a palace. A palace is a house that is strong, lofty, and royal. If by house we must understand conscience, then security of conscience is rightly understood by palace. Therefore, he sits at ease in his own house whom his conscience does not reproach. Worthy satisfaction for evils past, and cautious and provident avoidance of evils present, produce a quiet conscience. He therefore remains at ease in his house whom his conscience reproaches neither for past nor for present fault.

He was at ease in his house who truthfully said: “For my heart does not reproach me in all my life” (Job 27). He was at ease in his own house who could truthfully say: “For I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4). Certainly he was then at ease in his house and flourishing in his palace when he said: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). Since fruit is hoped for in blossom, a sure expectation of future goods is rightly signified by the blossom. Since blossom is the beginning of future fruit, renewal of progress is likewise rightly understood by blossom. Thus, in the blossom is signified either a sure expectation of rewards or a new advancement in merits. Therefore, he truly flourishes in his palace who, under the testimony of a good conscience, securely awaits the crown of glory.

Hear one at rest in his house and flourishing in his palace: “But I shall appear in your presence in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). What he says, “I shall appear in righteousness,” pertains to the rest of the house. What he says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears,” pertains to flourishing. Likewise, he was flourishing in his palace who, with the consciousness of great security, said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will render to me on that day” [Col. 1299D] (2 Tim. 6). Does not he also seem to you to flourish in his palace whose understanding is renewed from day to day? He sits and flourishes in his palace who, amid his great works which he gladly performs, still proposes greater and better things in his heart.

## CHAPTER II. On the illumination of the intellectual faculty, and how the spectacles of our contemplation commonly instill a salutary fear into the mind.

“I saw a dream,” he says, “which terrified me; and my thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head troubled me” (Dan. 4). [Col. 1300A] We sleep before we see a dream. Since in sleep the bodily sense is lulled, sleep is rightly understood as an alienation of the mind through which memory of all external things is utterly cut off. To see a dream, however, is for the mind to enter into the secret place of divine contemplation. Thus he sleeps and sees a dream who ascends through ecstasy of mind into the contemplation of higher things: “I saw a dream,” he says, “which terrified me.”

Of dreams of this kind, some terrify, some soothe, some make sorrowful, some make joyful. The contemplation of eternal joys indeed gladdens—and this is no wonder—but the consideration of divine judgments terrifies. For who could worthily express how happy, how delightful, his vision or revelation makes the person to whom God has revealed through his Spirit what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man”? But, conversely, how his vision terrifies the one who, raised in mind through contemplation, sees by what wondrous and hidden judgment of God one person sometimes comes forth from prison and chains to a kingdom, while another, born in a kingdom, is consumed by poverty! Whom, I ask, would the abyss of divine judgments not terrify when, touched by divine light, the understanding of the mind perceives that “the race is not for the swift, nor the battle for the strong, nor bread for the wise, nor riches for the learned, nor favor for the skilled,” but time and chance attend them all?

The Prophet certainly saw that the judgments of the Lord are a great abyss, and the visions of his head terrified him, when he said to the Lord: “I feared because of your judgments” [Col. 1300C] (Ps. 118). Yet visions of this kind commonly terrify not so much at the time when they are seen in ecstasy of mind as afterward, when, after sleep has been shaken off, they are recalled to memory and silently reconsidered within by subtle examination. Hence follows the statement: “And my thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head troubled me.” He declares that he was troubled by two things: by his thoughts and by the visions of his head.

For when, through divine revelation, the mind considers something astonishing—indeed, something fearful—and afterward, returning to itself and reflecting within itself, judges itself by rigorous examination, lest perhaps it be worthy for such a thing to happen to it, then its own thoughts deal with it in such a way that its vision terrifies it. “My thoughts,” he says, “upon my bed.” What is understood here by bed except the repose of most inward rest, and by vision of the head except illumination of the intellectual faculty? “And the visions,” he says, “of my head troubled me.” Therefore each person’s thoughts upon his bed and visions of his head then terrify and, by terrifying, trouble him when, from what he considers within himself after the secret of divine revelation, in the busy leisure of his meditation, he awakens to salutary concern and useful fear.

For when someone learns by divine revelation how one person commonly advances from good to better, another declines from evil to worse, how some fall from the highest goods into the lowest evils, or ascend from the lowest evils to the heights of virtue—what wonder, I ask, if his own vision compels him to fear? For man does not know his end; but, just as fish are caught by the hook and birds taken in a snare, so men are caught in an evil time when it suddenly comes upon them (Eccles. 9).

## CHAPTER III. That the grace by which we know divine judgments is one thing, and that by which we discern our own merits another.

[Col. 1301B]

See, however, how astonishing and fearful it is that the mind, often illuminated by divine light, sees through contemplation what ought rightly to happen to a person such as itself, and yet at that time does not know that it is such a person as deserves that judgment under the divine sentence. Did not this same thing happen to King Nebuchadnezzar, who learned from God’s revelation the divine sentence concerning the felling of the tree, yet did not know to apply the likeness of the tree shown to himself? He saw what, by divine sentence, would befall a person who bore in himself the image or likeness of such a tree [Col. 1301C], and yet, because he could not know through himself that he was such a person, he learned it through another.

See, therefore, that the grace by which we know divine judgments is one thing, and that by which we discern our own merits is another. We discover the former by contemplation, the latter by meditation. The former ability we receive from the grace of contemplation; the latter from the practice of meditation and the grace of discretion. Often one and the same person receives both graces together, although at one and the same time he cannot exercise both together. Thus, one person, as it were, consults another when, from a different state and at another time, he learns what he could not fully achieve through one and the same state of mind, and what may meanwhile suffice for his full self-knowledge.

Hence Nebuchadnezzar is instructed through Daniel concerning matters about which he himself appears to be in doubt in his vision. And in a wonderful manner, while the king tells the prophet his vision, he unknowingly teaches another what he is to learn from him; and Daniel learns from the questioning and ignorant man what he ought to teach the learner. So indeed, so often, the mind wisely brings back from the light of contemplation, without itself knowing, what it afterward discovers and knows more fully through meditation. Meditation receives from the foreknown light of revelation the means of untying the knots of doubt.

As we have already said above, by the king we understand free will, and by Daniel devotion. Therefore, contemplation belongs to such a king when it lies subject to the mind’s choice, so that the soul already has it at hand and exercises it as though by its own power. Likewise, that meditation seems to belong to Daniel which the devout mind commonly exercises through devotion’s application in scrutinizing its own morals. Thus the king, signified in Daniel, seeks and finds, as it were, the interpretation of his dreams when the soul afterward reads in its own conduct, by meditation and circumspection, and understands more deeply what it beheld amid the free flights of its contemplation. But let us now see how urgently Nebuchadnezzar sought what he did not know.

## CHAPTER IV. How one ought to lay aside secular pursuits and turn to the investigation of spiritual things.

Meanwhile, let those whom visions of the head and the ensuing thoughts trouble learn from the example of King Nebuchadnezzar what they ought to do: “And through me,” he says, “a decree was set forth, that all the wise men of Babylon should be brought before me and should make known to me the interpretation of the dream” (Dan. 4). [Col. 1302B] See how diligently, see how urgently, he seeks what he does not know: he does not cease until he finds the interpretation of his dream which he seeks. Hence Job says of himself: “The cause which I did not know I diligently investigated” (Job 29).

To set forth a decree is to determine something firmly, something which it is altogether not lawful to violate rashly. See, therefore, how earnestly he wished the thing to be done concerning which he issued a decree. The wisdom of this world, which is foolishness with God, belongs to the wise men of Babylon. The prudence of the flesh, which is hostile to God, belongs to the wise men [Col. 1302C] of Babylon. The wise men of Babylon, therefore, are the exceedingly sharp inquiries of worldly philosophy. The wise men of Babylon are the exceedingly sharp counsels of fleshly prudence.

What, then, is it to bring in such wise men and call them back to the inward parts, except to turn toward spiritual pursuits those exceedingly sharp investigations of inquiry which we used to devote to secular affairs? For those things which can be perceived by external sense are, as it were, outside; but those which cannot be comprehended at all except by inward sense are, as it were, within. Spiritual things are within, bodily things without. Therefore, we bring in the wise men of Babylon when we turn secular and all external pursuits toward spiritual understanding and the investigation of spiritual things. To bring in the wise men of Babylon is to postpone concern for external things and to devote one’s application solely to spiritual exercises. He kept his wise men within who said: “I considered the days of old, and kept eternal years in my mind. In the night I meditated with my heart; I exercised myself and searched my spirit” [Col. 1302D] (Ps. 76).

It should be noted, however, that our wise men are now within, now without, and yet are not in our sight. That is held, as it were, in the sight of our choice which is done intentionally and from deliberation. But it often happens, through the great habit of our studies, that the mind runs incidentally back to accustomed inquiries and, before it notices what it intends, spends much time there. This is not to have one’s wise men before one’s sight. But he undoubtedly causes his wise men to stand before his sight who restrains his studies from every wandering and, according to the purpose of his deliberation, devotes them solely to useful and necessary matters. The mind holds and watches its wise men, as it were, in its sight when it keeps such careful watch over its diligent meditations that it permits the foot of its inquiry to turn nowhere except where it had directed it by deliberation, so that no wandering of its investigations can cause even for a little while the diligence of its acuteness to escape it.

## CHAPTER V. How one who longs for the resolution of divine mysteries ought to persist.

[Col. 1303B]

But let us now see why he gathers his wise men into one place or compels them inward: “That they might,” he says, “make known to me the interpretation of the dream.” As we have already said in the exposition of another vision, it is one thing to behold divine judgments with the eye of contemplation, as it were in a dream; it is another to weigh their reason and judge, by the liveliness of discernment, with what justice or usefulness they come to pass. The former belongs to the vision of the dream; the latter to the interpretation of the dream.

Therefore, we somehow see a dream when we bring the hidden judgments of God into contemplation and admiration. We seek the interpretation of our dream when, after the spectacles of our contemplation, we investigate the reason, manner, and order of those things which we saw in the elevation of the mind [Col. 1303C]. Does it not belong to the vision of a dream to bring into consideration those astonishing mighty works of divine judgments which we read in the Scriptures, and to remain attached to their wonder for a longer and more attentive time? Does it not belong to the interpretation of a dream to seek their mystical meaning and be able to explain it through exposition? Was not the man longing for dreams of this kind who said in prayer: “Enlighten my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118)?

You can judge from this statement how great he considered it to receive from God the grace of interpreting dreams of this kind. For after he had said of the Lord, “Who declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel,” he immediately adds: “He has not done thus to every nation, and he has not made his judgments known to them” [Col. 1303D] (Ps. 147). He had, as it were, already seen the dream in what he had perceived by the light of his contemplation: that all things happen equally to the righteous and the wicked, the good and the evil, the clean and the unclean, the one sacrificing victims and the one despising sacrifice. He had sought the interpretation of the dream but had not yet found it when elsewhere he said: “Behold, this have I found, says Ecclesiastes, one thing and another, that I might find the reason, which my soul still seeks and I have not found” (Eccles. 7).

Therefore, one who desires to obtain the grace of interpreting dreams of the kind we have now defined ought to gather his wise men into one and call them back inward. “Then the diviners, magicians, Chaldeans, and soothsayers entered.” “Then,” he says, [Col. 1304A] “they entered.” What does “then” mean except after the decree, after the purpose of deliberation? For many people often propose many things but do not do them at all, because as easily as they decide something, so easily they again reject what they have decided.

First, therefore, we must take care to decide upon useful things. Second, we must firmly maintain what has been usefully decided. Observe how firmly that excellent deliberator established what he judged to be best: “I have sworn,” he says, “and determined to keep the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. 128). You have heard of the making of the vow; hear also of carrying it out: “I will pay my vows in the sight of all his people” (Ps. 115). “Then the diviners, magicians, Chaldeans, and soothsayers entered.” Above, he spoke generally of the wise men of Babylon; here he named some of them specifically: “diviners,” he says, “magicians, Chaldeans, and soothsayers.” But because it is certainly true that wise men of this kind are not truly wise, sacred Scripture almost never calls them wise without qualification, but calls them now the wise men of Babylon, now the king’s wise men of his kingdom, or something similar.

If, therefore, by diviners, magicians, Chaldeans, and soothsayers we understand evil, frivolous, foolish, and vain pursuits, see how courageously and beneficially we turn such pursuits toward spiritual exercises. Thus we compel the wise men of Babylon inward when we devote solely to spiritual matters the care and concern which we used to expend upon superfluous things. We occupy the wise men of Babylon, as it were, with interpreting dreams when, having entirely set aside superfluous pursuits, we persist single-mindedly in unraveling divine mysteries or judgments.

## CHAPTER VI. How vain it is to search out the depths of mysteries without the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

But after the wise men have been brought in, the king adds and says: “And I told the dream in their sight, and they did not make known to me its interpretation” (Dan. 4). What, I ask, is it to tell our dreams in the sight of our wise men except, after contemplation, to recall the spectacles of our contemplation to memory, reconsider them in keen meditation, examine them with diligent thoughts, and from comparison with those things which we know [Col. 1304D] unravel the knots of our questions, wishing to shape the investigation of spiritual things according to the accustomed manner of our inquiries?

Do we not tell our dreams in the sight of our wise men and seek their interpretation when we compare, by mutual comparison, what we know of human things and what we desire to know of divine things; when we presume to examine and penetrate the complexities of divine mysteries or judgments according to the learned method and order of handed-down disciplines? But whatever is presumptuously attempted in divine secrets by human industry is attempted in vain; and so long as it is sought in this manner, one labors to no purpose. Accordingly, concerning this dream it is said: “And they did not make known to me its interpretation.”

Our wise men do not at all discover the interpretation of dreams divinely shown, because the disciplines of our knowledge or any human traditions cannot suffice for examining and investigating divine secrets. For who would presume to search out from his own understanding that height of the divine counsel when he hears the Lord’s prophet crying out and protesting: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Isa. 40). Who would trust in his own acuteness to penetrate that depth of mysteries and divine Scriptures when he reads how the Apostle Peter alike restrains everyone from such presumption? “Understanding this first,” he says, “that prophecy of Scripture is not produced by one’s own interpretation” [Col. 1305B] (2 Pet. 1). Without doubt, the proper interpretation of sacred Scriptures is never made without the teaching of him who inspired them.

## CHAPTER VII. That for the unraveling of mysteries we advance more by devotion than by investigation, and that it belongs to true devotion to examine all things in order to judge all things.

If, therefore, we wish to be instructed in the mystical understanding of the divine Scriptures and in the knowledge of divine judgments, we advance in this matter better by prayer than by investigation; we are more deeply enlightened by devout compunction than by profound inquiry. Hence, immediately after the matters we have set forth, it is added: “Until Daniel, my colleague, entered before me, whose name is Belteshazzar according to the name of my god, who has in himself the spirit of the holy gods” [Col. 1305C] (Dan. 4).

Behold, he is said to have the spirit of the holy gods who is found fit to interpret the dream. Certainly, in calling these gods “holy gods,” those are excluded of whom it is sung in the psalm: “All the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 113). But those signified here are undoubtedly believed to have the Holy Spirit, because, if they did not have the Holy Spirit, they would not be holy gods. He is found to belong to the number of these gods to whom the divine voice says: “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7). The Psalmist described gods of this kind when he said elsewhere: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81).

Every saint receives the spirit of gods of this kind in order that he may be holy. For all our justification and all our sanctification is, beyond any doubt, from this Spirit. Without this Spirit we do not know what we should pray for as we ought; for, as the Apostle teaches, we have learned that he himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom. 8). Therefore, in order that our devotion may be true, it must have this Spirit. If, then, true devotion is understood by Daniel, Nebuchadnezzar rightly says of him: “Who has in himself the spirit of the holy gods.”

But since above he specified certain wise men, who, as is certainly clear, are not truly wise, it is strange how Daniel is called their colleague here. For unless he has something in common with them, I do not know how he can be their colleague. Yet I know this: that the Spirit which Daniel received according to the testimony of Scripture makes men spiritual. “The spiritual person judges all things, yet is himself judged by no one.” For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. If the spiritual person judges all things, if the Spirit searches all things, then it judges and searches the very things examined by worldly philosophy, the very things examined by fleshly prudence. If all things, then even those treated by every perverse doctrine.

For one who is spiritual commonly examines all things so that he may judge all things. Hear, then, how that spiritual man tried all things in his wisdom so that he might judge all things: “I gave my heart to know prudence and doctrine, errors also and folly” [Col. 1306B] (Eccles. 1). You see how he investigates, how he searches out, not only good conduct but errors also, not only prudence but folly also. It belongs, therefore, to true devotion to bring both good and evil into consideration, to investigate all things, to examine all things, so that afterward it may be able to judge all things. True devotion therefore has something in common with the wise men of Babylon in investigation and inquiry, so that it is rightly called their colleague on that account.

Yet they differ in intention. For true devotion does not investigate vain and perverse doctrines in order to cling to them or put any confidence in them, but in order, by judging them, to convict, refute, and condemn them. Thus our Daniel and the wise men of the world run the same course in investigation, although in intention they do not reach the same end. Daniel is therefore rightly called the colleague of those with whom he seems to share, to some extent, in the courses of his studies.

## CHAPTER VIII. In what exercises of devotion one ought to persist who awaits from God a revelation of hidden things.

“Until Daniel, my colleague, entered before me.” From this, I think, you perceive how this Daniel now enters from external things into internal things, now goes out from internal things to external things. He is outside when our devotion is concerned, by meditating, judging, and praying, with external things. He is within when it is occupied and concerned with the same exercises or studies [Col. 1306D] regarding internal things. For one must provide things good before God and before men: before men in speech and deed, before God in thought and will.

Thus, to call our deeds and words to judgment and to entreat the Lord concerning them is for Daniel to be outside. To search thoughts, affections, wills, and intentions by deep inquiry, and to be contrite in prayer concerning such things, is for Daniel to remain within. Or this is for Daniel to be outside: to weigh both our inward and outward matters according to human judgment; and this is for Daniel to be within: to assess both the one and the other according to divine judgment.

When, even among the good works that we do and the useful things that we say [Col. 1307A], we carefully weigh by subtle examination what people would think of us, what they ought to think, if they saw our intentions, our sordid thoughts, our disordered affections—when, I say, we do this, we hold Daniel as it were outside. But when we seek by diligent examination how our deeds or words are judged in God’s sight, even when they seem good according to human judgment—when we persist in such study with great devotion, our Daniel is found within.

What, then, is it for Daniel to enter the inward parts except, through innermost devotion, to have recourse to divine judgment in matters concerning both outward and inward things that are to be examined or sought? And it often happens that, while our wise men fail in the interpretation of dreams—while diligent meditations and inward inquiries presume, but cannot, penetrate the deep secrets of divine judgments and mysteries—it often happens, I say, that the mind, warned by this very failure, returns to itself, attends more diligently to its own weakness, and comes more fully to recognize that without God’s help it can do nothing. Then, from consideration of its weakness, it begins to groan, to sigh, to accuse its presumptions, and, having previously presumed vainly on its own studies, to hope now solely in the Lord’s revelation and to devote itself wholly to the pursuit of devotion. And this is for Daniel to enter after the wise men.

## CHAPTER IX. How great is the power of true devotion, which makes a son of God and joins the human soul to God.

[Col. 1307C]

Until, he says, Daniel entered before me, my companion, whose name is Balthassar. Balthassar is interpreted “hair of the head.” Daniel is therefore rightly called Balthassar, because our mind is adorned by true devotion and, through true devotion, made subtle for every depth. Yet when Daniel is here called Balthassar, something further is added which conceals a meaning and, as I think, summons us to a deeper understanding: “Daniel, whose name was Balthassar, according to the name of my god.”

We wish first to point out that many passages of Scripture, according to the historical sense, seem to convey something unsuitable or perverse, though when examined mystically they speak something right according to spiritual understanding. For Daniel’s being called Balthassar by the king according to the name of his god—what does this appear to suggest according to the letter except idolatry? But, as blessed Gregory says: “Often a thing is a virtue in history and a fault in signification; just as an event which, in its occurrence, is a cause of condemnation is, in writing, a prophecy of virtue.”

For, when he was treating David’s fault and Uriah’s innocence, and wished to interpret the adulterous David as Christ and the innocent Uriah as the Jewish people, what, he says, can be called more wicked in this event than David, or more pure than Uriah? Yet again, in mystery, what is found more holy than David, or more faithless than Uriah, when the former, through the fault of his life, signifies innocence in prophecy, while the latter, through the innocence of his life, expresses guilt in prophecy? For the power of sacred discourse narrates past events in such a way as to express things to come. It approves a thing in the event in such a way as to contradict it in the mystery. It condemns deeds in such a way as mystically to commend their performance.

Thus here also, what is blameworthy according to history can express something commendable according to mystery. “Whose name,” he says, “was Balthassar, according to the name of my god.” If by the person of the king we rightly understand the royal mind, whom, I ask, does it call its God except Christ? For although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are truly one and the same God, nevertheless every religious person may rightly, in a certain manner of speaking, call Christ his own: one remembers oneself marked by his name, anticipated by his grace, and recognizes oneself as more intimately united to his person through the mystery of the Incarnation, by the communion of nature.

If Balthassar is interpreted “hair of the head,” let us now see how this name appears suitable for Christ, and how the mystical Daniel is deservedly so named according to the name of his God. We know that the head of man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God. We know without doubt that the Trinity is God and the beginning of all creatures; we know likewise that the person of the Father is the beginning of the other persons in the Trinity. And although “beginning” is said here and there in different senses, it can nevertheless be said fittingly and truly in both cases.

Therefore, since the person of the Father is the beginning of all, he can rightly be designated by the head. If, then, the finger of God is called the Holy Spirit by similitude, why should Christ not likewise be called, by similitude, the hair of this head? Hair springs from the head, and Christ is begotten from the Father: “The Lord said to me, You are my Son; this day I have begotten you” (Heb. 1). The head is adorned by hair, and the Father is glorified through Christ: “Father,” he says, “glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17).

You see, surely, how rightly Christ is called Balthassar—that is, “hair of the head”—whom Catholic faith truly confesses as the true Son of God the Father. Do we not also receive this name in the same sense, when from Christ and through Christ we obtain the right to be called sons of God? “Beloved,” says the apostle John, “we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (1 John 3). Hence in daily prayer we say to him who freely begot us by the word of his power: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6).

Therefore, if Christ can quite fittingly be called Balthassar because he is the Son of the supreme Father, why should not the true Christian likewise be called Balthassar according to the stated meaning of the name, since by the grace of adoption he is counted among the sons of that same God the Father? Yet not every Christian is worthy of this name or honor. Devotion alone distinguishes them; devotion alone makes sons of God. Therefore, if devotion is understood in Daniel, see how rightly he is called Balthassar by its effect, through which anyone is adopted into the freedom of the sons.

What else is devotion but the fervent love of the mind for God? “The charity of God is poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). Devotion is therefore rightly called the hair of the head, since it appears, as it were, to flow from the supreme head of all things, being produced by the inspiration of the supreme Father. He is rightly called Balthassar who, after the manner of hair, appears to cling to the supreme head of all things.

From these matters, I think, you perceive how great is the power of true devotion: it makes one a son of God, joins the human mind to God, and makes it, as it were, one spirit with him. “For he who cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6).

## CHAPTER X. That under the time of prayer intellectual understanding is especially wont to be opened to some.

[Col. 1309B]

When Daniel had entered, the king speaks the dream before him, as the following words show: “And I spoke the dream before him” (Dan. 4). To speak such a dream before Daniel is for the memory, during prayer, to be touched by mysteries concerning which we desire divine instruction, and while praying to be moved by the desire for divine revelation.

For, as those recognize by experience who have deserved often to be raised and gladdened by divine revelations, it is especially during prayer that they are wont to receive the light of illuminating grace and, by its inspiration, penetrate the depths of mysteries. For by inward compunction the mind is washed and cleansed; and unquestionably, the purer it is made, the more easily and more deeply it is enlightened.

Hence Balaam testifies concerning himself: “The hearer of the words of God has spoken, who has beheld the vision of almighty God, who falls, and thus his eyes shall be opened” (Num. 24). What is meant by the statement that the eyes are opened by falling, except that intellectual understanding is often opened during prayer? We commonly prostrate our whole bodies upon the ground when we wish to pray more attentively. Therefore, as far as the literal exposition seems concerned, the eyes are opened, as it were, by falling, for the one who receives the light of revealing grace while prostrating himself in prayer.

But if the same letter is investigated mystically, it appears to converge upon the same meaning. For what is falling except humbling oneself through the remembrance of one’s sins and, through true contrition of heart, laying aside hardness? Yet when the mind casts itself down in this manner, it often rises in greater grace, because by falling it recovers the light of its eyes, which, wrongly raised up, it had kept shut.

Nevertheless, we may say that to fall undoubtedly means to consent to enticing sin. We know that some are puffed up by the multitude of their revelations. Those who are such are permitted, by the just judgment of God, to fall, so that they may cease from pride. When they fall into sin, therefore, they are put to shame and are pierced with compunction; pierced with compunction, they are cleansed; cleansed, they are enlightened. But if, when enlightened, they become proud again, by pride they lose the light which they had received.

Thus, enlightened and exalted, they are cast down again and again; fallen and humbled, they are enlightened again and again. They often alternate this cycle of falling and rising, and many practice these alternating patterns long and frequently. But many at last bring this habit of alternation to a most evil end. It is evident that they received the grace of spiritual gifts not so much for their own benefit as for that of others. Balaam undoubtedly bore their type in his deeds and expressed their character in his words when he said: “The hearer of the words of God has spoken, who sees the vision of the Almighty, who falls, and thus his eyes are opened.”

## CHAPTER XI. That secular learning ought to serve spiritual pursuits and labor for the gains of true devotion.

[Col. 1310B]

But to return to the point from which we digressed, we hold as certain that many often receive the light of revealing grace during prayer, and that many advance toward such grace through the power of devotion. Hence the king demands the interpretation of his dream from Daniel with complete confidence, saying: “Balthassar, chief of the diviners, whom I know to have the spirit of the holy gods within you, and no mystery is impossible for you: tell me the visions of my dreams which I have seen and their interpretation” (Dan. 4).

In these words we must first note that he who above was called their companion—not only theirs, but also of the other wise men of Babylon—is here called “chief of the diviners.” Among secular branches of learning, we recognize some as useful and necessary for use, but others, such as the art of divination, as altogether perverse. If true devotion can turn even those which are undoubtedly perverse to some use of virtue and exercise in them a kind of leadership in spiritual warfare—as we may infer here from the art of divination—what should we then think of those which may be useful and good?

For, to pass over other examples, does not Daniel then rule? Is not every perverse science compelled to serve devotion, when by considering it human error is more fully recognized; when through reviewing it the mind is humbled, ashamed, pierced with compunction, and incited to the pursuits of devotion? Does not every perverse science serve devotion when the mind exacts from itself the time which it was accustomed to waste in such futile studies, and when by comparison it gathers how zealously it ought to attend to spiritual studies, remembering that it once labored so hard at such absurdities?

Daniel, therefore, should be understood as the companion of the wise men mentioned, in such a way that he is believed to hold among them, by the law of equity, a kind of primacy in spiritual warfare. All secular learning, then, ought to serve spiritual pursuits and undertake nothing in its exercises that does not labor for the gains of true devotion. Whenever, therefore, we persist unduly in secular learning, whenever by the importunity of our studies we interrupt the exercises of our devotion, we compel Daniel—the one who ought to rule—to serve.

But we must consider how evil it is to misuse even good branches of knowledge, and through their misuse to impede better pursuits, when every perverse science ought, and is wont, through the office of devotion, to be turned toward good uses.

## CHAPTER XII. That it is useful to devote the greatest care to the highest devotion.

Devotion is rightly preferred to good studies, rightly rules over evil ones, and Daniel is rightly granted precedence among all the wise men of Babylon, if what Nebuchadnezzar says is true: “I know that you have the spirit of the holy gods within you, and no mystery is impossible for you.”

Does not what is heard from the mouth of Truth, if rightly weighed, seem to accord with this statement? “Amen I say to you: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you receive it, and it shall be yours” (Mark VI). True and complete devotion is not present where one cannot believe the testimony of Truth. But if it can believe, it can obtain by asking and believing. Thus no mystery is impossible to the highest devotion, if it can be obtained through faith.

The will of the mind therefore rightly endeavors, through the power of devotion, to obtain what the testimony of Truth proves not to be impossible to it. “Tell,” he says, “the visions of my dreams which I have seen and their interpretations.” The best kind of study, therefore, is to devote the greatest care to the highest devotion, because, according to the reason shown, no mystery is impossible to it.

Following the example of King Nebuchadnezzar, then, let us set our Daniel above all our wise men; let us compel every study and all our exercises to serve the gains of true devotion. Then, without doubt, we shall not attempt in vain whatever, concerning divine mysteries, we usefully presume to undertake with God’s help through its office. But now let us continue the order of the vision and investigate the meaning of spiritual understanding, leaving greater matters to greater intellects, at least according to moral edification.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the manner or quality of contemplation; and that things are seen differently in their own being than in reason alone or in supreme truth.

[Col. 1311D]

“The vision,” he says, “of my head upon my bed. I looked, and behold, a tree in the midst of the earth, and its height was exceedingly great. The tree was great and strong, and its stature reached heaven; its appearance extended to the ends of the whole earth. Its leaves were exceedingly beautiful, its fruit excessive, and in it was food for all. Beneath it dwelt animals and beasts, and in its branches the birds of heaven made their home; and all flesh fed from it” (Dan. 4).

As appears from what was said above, the vision of the head is the understanding of the mind. The bed is the tranquility of the heart and the leisure of studious repose. A vision of the head is received from God upon the bed when, amid the secluded leisure of its study, the human mind is raised by divine inspiration to the contemplation of truth.

“I looked,” he says, “and behold, a tree in the midst of the earth.” It is one thing to see things themselves in their own being, and another to see them in reason alone or in supreme truth. It is one thing for someone to see them in their own essence, and quite another to see them in wisdom alone. It is one thing to see the substances of things in their genera and species, and another to see individual things in their particular instances. The latter belongs to sense or imagination; the former belongs to reason and contemplation.

When, therefore, the mind is carried away to a certain universal consideration of things and is divinely raised to contemplate the beauty of the universe; when it is delightfully fixed and wonderfully refreshed in such contemplation and in the sweetness of contemplation, it often sees in the divine light how many kinds of things, and what kinds, ought to exist. It firmly holds that none of all those things which the order of highest disposition and the beauty of the universe demand can be wholly lacking.

For example, it sees that there must be good people and evil people alike; among the good, some better than others and some best; likewise among the evil, some worse than others and some worst. It sees also that some must be evil and persevere in evil; some must be evil and abandon wickedness forever; while others abandon it for a time and return again to wickedness. Conversely, it sees that some must be good and persevere in goodness; some must fall irrecoverably; and some, after falling, return to goodness.

Nebuchadnezzar seems to contemplate in God’s light one belonging to this sixth class of things: one shown to him through a likeness, and one at whom, after returning to himself, he wondered or even felt pity. He saw that the beauty of the universe required such a one, and that such a one could not possibly be absent; yet he did not know that he himself was such, or bore within himself the image of such a person—one who would suddenly fall from so great a height, lie long in the depths, and yet finally return to his former state.

This is why the great tree is first raised on high, then cut down, while its roots are preserved in the earth so that it may be restored again. Let us therefore also see and learn from him what sort of tree it is that he sees, how it fell, or how one so great and such as this could fall.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the greatness of the grace of a mind destined later to fall; and, amid so great a fullness of grace, what is usually the cause of ruin.

[Col. 1312D]

“I looked,” he says, “and behold, a great tree in the midst of the earth, and its height exceedingly great.” What are we to understand by the greatness of the tree except the immense strength of virtue? Was not that also a great tree which received fullness of grace and strength? “Stephen,” it says, “full of grace and strength” (Acts 6).

“Behold, a great tree in the midst of the earth, and its height exceedingly great.” Thus this tree was great, it was high, and it stood in the midst of the earth. By virtue it extended itself toward many and great things; by subtlety it raised itself toward high things; by intention it stood in the depths. It stretched toward difficult things, raised itself toward the highest things, and remained fixed in the depths. It was in great things by exercise, in the highest things by study, and in the depths by desire.

Therefore, because it did mighty deeds, it was a great tree; because it desired inward goods, it stood in the midst of the earth; because it understood sublime matters subtly, its height was great. “The tree was great and strong, and its stature reached heaven.” Behold: a great tree, a sturdy tree, a lofty tree—great for doing good, strong for enduring evil, lofty for contemplating sublime things; great in actions, strong in temptations, sublime in investigations.

Observe how high the one was whose stature even touched heaven. Its stature touched heaven because the sublimity of its investigation penetrated heavenly things. Its stature, therefore, was high, and its height was lofty. Truly great was the height which immersed itself in the highest and heavenly things. Choose, then, in considering this tree, which you marvel at more: its greatness, strength, or loftiness.

“The tree was great and strong, and its stature reached heaven.” It was a great tree which could truly say: “Everywhere and in all things I have been instructed. I know how to be humbled; I know also how to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things in him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4). It was a strong tree which could confidently say: “I will not fear what man may do to me. Though an army should stand against me, my heart shall not fear” (Ps. 55). “Though battle should rise against me, in this I will hope” (Ps. 26). It was loftier than the other trees which did not hesitate to say of itself: “I surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my mind contemplated and learned many things wisely” (Eccl. 1).

Its stature touched heaven—one who could truly say: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, yet not the wisdom of this age nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed. But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, wisdom hidden, which he predestined before the ages, which none of the rulers of this age knew” (II Cor. XXIX).

But whoever hears or reads these things, see whether perhaps your height is great; see, I say, and diligently beware lest it also be excessive. Perhaps this was blameworthy in the tree described here; perhaps the cause of its cutting down was that its height was excessive. “And its height,” he says, “was exceedingly great.” Perhaps Nebuchadnezzar walked in things great and marvelous beyond himself, and this was perhaps the cause of his fall. Perhaps Nebuchadnezzar thought lofty thoughts, and therefore his height was excessive: “Do not think highly,” says the Apostle, “but fear” (Rom. 11).

For as it is not good for one to eat much honey, so one who searches into majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory. Therefore seek not things higher than yourself, lest your stature perhaps be too high. The investigator of majesty is overwhelmed by glory, and the tree whose height is excessive deserves the sentence of cutting down. Were not trees of this kind high, and did they not rightly deserve to be cut down, when, knowing God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened? (Rom. 1).

## CHAPTER XV. On the greatness of authority in a mind destined later to fall.

[Col. 1314A]

But let us hear what is further said of this tree in what follows: “Its appearance extended to the ends of the whole earth.” The appearance of such a tree reaches to the ends of the whole earth when those near to it in likeness of character and those far from it in dissimilarity of character alike revere the dignity of its name; and when its authority is loved by the good as much as it is feared by the evil.

Did not the appearance of that one extend to the ends of the whole earth, of whom the truth of that saying was evident: “We are the good odor of Christ to God among those who are saved and among those who perish: to some indeed an odor of death unto death, but to others an odor of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2)? And did not the appearance of those trees extend to the ends of the whole earth, of whom it is truly said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 81)?

In another sense, too, the appearance of our tree extends within ourselves to the ends of the whole earth when the experience of our own virtue no longer leaves any one of us unknown to himself, whether in great matters or least ones. For if we take the tree as virtue and the appearance of the tree as knowledge of virtue, then, when through much study and exercise we have learned what we can do in each matter, what else have we done but reveal the appearance of our tree to the ends of the whole earth?

Had not the one who had already begun to gain experience of his own virtue in all things revealed the appearance of his tree to the ends of the whole earth, when he truly declared concerning himself what we have already cited above: “For I have learned in whatever circumstances I am sufficient. I know how to be humbled, and I know how to abound; everywhere and in all things I have been instructed” (Philipp. VI).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the abundance of knowledge in a mind destined to fall; and, amid so great a fullness of knowledge, what is usually the cause of ruin.

Further it is said of this tree: “Its leaves were exceedingly beautiful, its fruit excessive, and in it was food for all.” In the leaves are words; in the fruit, knowledge; in the food, teaching. Fruit is clothed with leaves, and meaning is adorned with composed words: “For the mouth of the wise adorns knowledge” (Prov. 15).

Good fruit has savor and nourishes; spiritual knowledge sweetly refreshes spiritual hunger through sacred instruction. Thus beautiful leaves are eloquent words; abundant fruit is learned meaning and manifold understanding. Food for all is complete instruction for everyone, and discerning admonition for each individual.

That tree, I think, had beautiful leaves of words and abounded in fruits of good meanings and useful counsels, which could truly say: “Those who heard me waited for my judgment, and they listened attentively in silence to my counsel. They dared add nothing to my words, and my speech distilled upon them” (Job 29). That tree had abundant fruit which could truly say: “God gave me to speak according to judgment; for he himself gave me true knowledge of the things that are, that I might know the ordering of the world and the powers of the elements; the beginning, end, and middle of times; the changes of seasons and the completion of times; the changes of customs and the divisions of times; the courses of the year and the positions of the stars; the natures of animals and the rage of beasts; the force of winds and the thoughts of human beings; the differences of shrubs and the powers of roots; and whatever is hidden and unforeseen, I have learned” (Wis. 7).

Was not food for all in him who recognized himself as debtor precisely in this respect when he said: “I am debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to wise and foolish alike” (Rom. 1)? Is not food for all in the one who can edify everyone by his teaching? Does not one have food for all within himself who, through the spirit of counsel presiding over his mind and the grace of discernment in which he excels, can sufficiently instruct by wholesome counsel and raise by gentle admonition those ensnared by any temptation or oppressed by any tribulation?

Likewise, as regards himself, does not one find within himself food for all who knows, as often and as much as he wishes, how to nourish every holy desire and kindle his own mind toward every good work by his meditations and spiritual contemplations?

But, as we suggested above concerning the height of the tree, let us see whether perhaps this too is blameworthy in it: that it is said to have excessive fruit. For it is not said that its fruit was much or abundant, but that “its fruit,” he says, “was excessive.” He reproves excessive fruit who says: “In superfluous matters do not inquire too much.” It is one thing to seek impossibilities importunately, though they may perhaps be useful; it is another to investigate useless matters curiously, though they themselves may be possible. The former pertains to excess of height; the latter to superfluity of fruit.

The presumption of things incomprehensible is forbidden when it is said: “Seek not things higher than yourself, and search not things stronger than yourself; but what God has commanded you,” etc. (Eccl. 3). Curiosity about superfluous matters is reproved in the statement: “In superfluous matters do not inquire too much, and in his many works do not be curious.” Do you wish to hear concerning trees of this kind—those unwilling to restrain the boldness of presumption and curiosity—how they often incur the sentence of cutting down? “For their suspicion,” he says, “has supplanted many, and has held their understanding in vanity” (Ecclus. 3).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the rigor of discipline which a mind destined to fall often exercises toward others.

From what precedes we have heard what knowledge belonged to the person signified by this tree; let us hear from what follows what discipline belonged to him. We have heard how through teaching he could educate the unlearned and instruct the uninformed; let us hear how through discipline he was wont both to restrain the carnal and to exalt the spiritual.

“Beneath it dwelt animals and beasts, and in its branches the birds of heaven made their home; and all flesh fed from it.” By animals and beasts understand animal-like people, carnal and worldly minds; by birds understand spiritual people, flying heavenward on the wings of good pursuits and holy desires.

We are accustomed to see two kinds of carnal people: one serves concupiscence, the other yields to anger. By animals, therefore, we understand minds given over to pleasure; by beasts, angry minds. If by *bestiae* we can fittingly understand only wild animals, it remains that by the name *animalia* we must here understand tame animals alone. Thus minds devoted to pleasure are rightly designated by animals which serve the belly alone. Likewise, angry minds are rightly designated by beasts which rage with tooth and claw.

Of such persons, therefore, it is rightly said: “Beneath it dwelt animals and beasts,” because minds disordered by concupiscence or anger ought rightly to be restrained by the rigor of discipline. The birds of heaven dwelt in its branches and, as it were, in higher places, because spiritual men, kindled with heavenly desires, ought deservedly both to be raised to authority and exalted with worthy honor: “Beneath it,” he says, “dwelt animals and beasts, and in its branches the birds of heaven made their home.”

Thus it restrained the beastly in the lower places but raised the spiritual to higher things. Let our prelates learn here what they ought to do; let them learn, I say, to restrain undisciplined conduct and to raise up and honor the good. What kind of monstrosity is this: that the trees of our time bear bears and lions, or any other beastly minds of this sort, in their branches, while they press the birds of heaven and every winged creature down into the depths—against the laws of their nature and the ordinances of the Creator?

How often have I myself seen it, and seeing it groaned: the ungodly one exalted and raised above the cedars of Lebanon. What, I ask, are you doing, you who raise such brutish and beastly hearts aloft and suspend them, as it were, in the air? If you truly love them, why do you not spare them? What do you prepare for them but ruin, when you hang them on high and bear them, as it were, in the branches? What else will anyone say at the end, on the very brink of ruin, to the one who lifted him up—or rather, threw him down—except: “By lifting me up, you dashed me down”?

Let the birds of heaven dwell in the branches, and let those whom the wing of holiness raises occupy the highest place. Let beasts occupy a place beneath the branches, in the lower regions; and let those whose faces are bent downward by the appetite of the flesh feel the restraint of pious severity and just humiliation.

“Beneath it dwelt animals and beasts, and in its branches the birds of heaven made their home; and all flesh fed from it.” All flesh indeed feeds from that tree by whose examples of virtue all are edified, by whose consolations all are cherished, by whose benefits all are strengthened, and by whose teaching all are refreshed. O what a tree, O how lofty, to which so great a proclamation of praise is appropriate!

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the rigor of discipline which a mind destined to fall is wont to exercise within itself.

[Col. 1317A]

We also fulfill in ourselves this very thing said of the tree, if we restrain carnal affections under the rigor of discipline, occupy our thoughts in the examination of our conduct, and nourish all our senses in good desires through spiritual meditations. For what do we understand by flying creatures except subtle thoughts, and what by quadrupeds and earthly creatures except carnal affections?

By animals, understand those desires which arise apart from reason; by beasts, those which strive against reason—vain and frivolous desires apart from reason, perverse and harmful ones against reason. By the tree, as has been said, we understand the strength of fortitude; and by the branches of the tree we rightly understand works and exercises of virtue.

From branches of this kind we gather in due season the fruit of good merits, as we have heard through the Prophet: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127). From branches of this kind come the fruits of wholesome counsels and subtle understandings, when, through many experiences in the exercises of virtues, they train a person toward perfection in discernment and knowledge.

For many things which we cannot learn by investigation, we learn more fully and more certainly by experience. Hence the Psalmist’s statement: “From your commandments I have understood” (Ps. 118). One understands from the commandments when, from what one does, one advances toward greater understanding. Hence it is written elsewhere: “He led them in the understandings of their hands” (Ps. 67). One leads another in the understandings of his hands when one directs him by sure stages of progress toward the way of truth which one has learned through the experience of works.

Small and uncertain is that knowledge which the experience of things does not assist and confirm. Hence the Wise Man says: “He who has not experienced knows few things” (Eccl. 34). Nor are we instructed in discernment only by the good things which we do; we are also made more prudent by the evil things which we endure and by temptations themselves. The saying of the Wise Man admonishes us of this: “He who has not been tempted, what does he know?” (ibid.). “A man experienced in many things has thought much, and he who has learned much will declare understanding.”

Therefore fruit is gathered from the branches of the tree, because knowledge is multiplied from much exercise in the virtues. The more perfect and proven anyone is, the richer fruit he bears and the more delightfully he refreshes. “But solid food,” says the Apostle, “belongs to the perfect, to those who through practice have their senses trained for the discernment of good and evil” (Heb. 5).

The branches of a good and noble tree are those which bear such fruit and produce food for souls: which receive the birds of heaven and suspend lofty thoughts on high; which shelter beasts and press down the impulses of the flesh. I think that the Apostle too pressed animals downward beneath branches of this kind when he said: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude” (1 Cor. 9).

But whoever wishes to accustom the birds of heaven to the branches of such a tree, let his delight be in the law of the Lord, and let him meditate in that law day and night.

Let us therefore beware, after the manner of certain birds, of making our nest upon the earth or dwelling in watery places and abandoning the branches of the tree. Let us be ashamed to cling to worldly cares and carnal desires amid the incessant importunity of our thoughts. “Set your minds,” says the Apostle, “on things above, not on things upon the earth” (Col. III). Our birds ought therefore, in due season, to rise to heavenly things and remain poised in contemplation of eternal realities; and then, after their lofty flights, return again to the branches of their tree, remaining there—indeed, dwelling there. For what else is it for the birds of heaven always to return to the branches of their tree and live there, [Col. 1318B] except frequently to recall the thoughts of one’s heart to consideration of one’s character and deeds, to apply oneself more often to their examination, and to devote oneself to it more earnestly?

Hence it is said through Solomon: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place” (Eccl. I). For the sun of understanding, after its rising and ascent into lofty contemplation, returns again to its place; the eye of the heart is recalled to self-examination, so that it may again be raised to higher things. For a heart that falls asleep with respect to its own keeping quickly loses the grace of contemplation which it had received. Rightly, then, it is said of this tree, “and the birds of heaven dwelt in its branches,” because the watchful examinations of the mind ought especially to keep vigil over self-guardianship.

We have now heard what we ought to understand concerning such a tree. Yet let no one suppose that I believe King Nebuchadnezzar to have been such as he hears me describe him by mystical signification. He was not such in his own person; rather, in his person he prefigured such a man, and in the tree he saw he designated such a one. But let us meanwhile continue the mystical description; perhaps we shall find in it something at which we may rightly marvel—and not merely something we ought to admire, but something we ought worthily to lament and rightly to fear for ourselves.

## CHAPTER XIX. That at every summit of virtue one must always fear a collapse of character.

Let us therefore hear what he says further about this tree, and let each person learn what he ought to fear and mourn over:

[Col. 1318D] “I saw in the vision of my head upon my bed, and behold, a watcher and a holy one came down from heaven. And he cried aloud and said thus: ‘Cut down the tree and lop off its branches; shake off its leaves and scatter its fruit. Let the beasts that are beneath it flee, and the birds from its branches’” (Dan. IV).

Woe to the sons of Adam; woe to the human condition! Tell me: however much one has advanced, however high one has ascended, how can one thereafter be secure, if so great and so perfect a man could fall from such a height, as though in the moment of a single hour? Let us recall, then, what sort of man is described above through the mystical tree—the man who is here commanded to be cut down. We shall then better recognize how rightly those established upon any summit of virtue fear the ruin of their character. In the tree’s greatness we marvel at the measure of his strength; in its height, the depth of his subtle discernment; in the breadth of its appearance, the greatness of his authority. In the beauty of its leaves, eloquence of speech; in the abundance of its fruit, the multitude of his learning; in food for all, teaching that edifies; in the subjection of the beasts, rigor of severity; in the birds’ dwelling with it, prudent watchfulness.

Who, then, unless he is mad, promises himself security amid so great a peril of changeability, if one who was truly once such a man was later cut down and fell? Truly, as Scripture says: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful.” For “he does not know what the coming day will bring forth” (Prov. XXVIII).

## CHAPTER XX. That everything done concerning us is ordered by God’s disposition and administered by angels.

[Col. 1319B]

Yet let no one think that God does not care for human affairs; let no one rashly dare to criticize His judgments when he sees or hears that something has happened contrary to expectation or, as it seems to him, contrary to reason. Behold: the one from whom the sentence of cutting down is given, or administered, is said to have come down from heaven and to have been holy. “Behold,” he says, “a holy watcher came down from heaven.” Therefore, when you hear that the minister of this work comes from heaven, understand that it is done by God’s ordering; and when you read that he is holy, believe that he justly carries out what is just.

“Behold, a watcher and a holy one came down from heaven.” Both good angels and evil angels devote unceasing concern to the care of humankind, and neither by night nor by day do they withdraw themselves even briefly from this concern. The evil ones keep watch in order to attack; the good, in order to protect. Thus both may quite properly be called watchers. Yet that this is a good angel who either learned such a sentence from heaven or arranged it on earth is sufficiently shown by the statement that he was holy and came down from heaven.

O how fittingly this name belongs to good angels, to whom the sleep of error or forgetfulness never steals in concerning the affairs of our salvation! O the height of angelic compassion! Secure concerning themselves, they still bear concern for us. Concerning this vigilance and watchful guardianship of angels over our salvation, the Apostle speaks: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to minister for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. I).
