What else, then, is it for such watchers to descend from heaven, except for the ministers of our salvation to care for earthly things and, according as they learn from God in the heights, to order human affairs in the depths? Rightly, therefore, it is said: “Behold, a watcher and a holy one came down from heaven, and cried aloud, and said thus: ‘Lop off the tree.’”

There are, then, some things which good angels do by themselves; there are others which they permit to be done. Nothing whatever happens anywhere without their ordering. Good things thus occur through their cooperation; evil things through their permission. Good things, therefore, are administered through good angels; evil things through evil ones. Since a good angel knows it to be evil to overthrow one established in uprightness, he did not wish to cut down the tree; nevertheless, because he knew that the merit of one person or the good of the community required it, he permitted it to be done. When he says, “Lop off the tree,” understand permission, not command. For obedience is not here imposed upon evil spirits; permission is granted them. At last he allowed them to do what he knew they had long and greatly desired to do. Thus the Lord says to Judas the betrayer: “What you are doing, do quickly” (John XIII). He does not impose a command upon him in this matter, but grants him the opportunity to act.

It is known to all that we are accustomed to use a loud cry whenever we wish to make something known to persons far away. But what are farther apart from one another than an angelic spirit and an evil spirit—not so much through distance of place as through difference of will? Thus the prodigal son, who is read in the Gospel to have squandered all his substance by living extravagantly with harlots, is said to have gone into a far country (Luke XV), because, estranged by the corruption of his will from the good pleasure of the supreme Father, he became alienated.

Accordingly, in this sense the angel confirmed in good and the angel confirmed in evil, the angel appointed to glory and the angel consigned to Gehenna, are indeed far distant from one another, distinguished and separated by lots so various and opposed. Rightly, therefore, that watcher and holy one is said to have cried aloud, so that it might be plainly understood what manner of angels, and how far removed from a good angel, were those to whom the sentence of the watchers, dictated from heaven, is announced only with a loud cry.

Yet among certain good angels there is also a great distance—not a difference of opposed wills, but a divinely and fittingly ordered difference of surpassing dignity. Hence it does not seem incongruous if a cry is described among them, by which their difference of dignity is indicated. Rightly, therefore, the angel who is here introduced as granting evil spirits permission to tempt is said not merely to have cried, but to have cried aloud. “Behold,” he says, “a watcher and a holy one came down from heaven and cried aloud, and said thus: ‘Cut down the tree.’”

## CHAPTER XXI. That evil spirits can do nothing against us except by God’s permission.

[Col. 1320D] From the present passage we can plainly gather two things. First, evil spirits cannot tempt us beyond the extent to which they are permitted. Second, if they were unleashed with all their power for our assault, no one could endure their attack. For those who can and wish to cut down the tree, yet do not cut it down unless permitted, plainly undertake nothing in persecuting us without God’s permission. But what would they dare against human beings without God’s permission, when, as the Gospel testifies, they did not dare even to invade a herd of swine without divine leave? (Matt. VIII; Mark V; Luke VIII.)

Accordingly, only so much liberty is granted them in attacking the elect as their benefit requires or justice deserves. For what human strength could withstand their assault, if, once divine permission was granted, they could immediately overthrow a tree of such a kind and greatness? But the Apostle Paul consoles us in this matter: “The Lord,” he says, “is faithful, and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (I Cor. X).

Therefore, unless this tree had been too lofty, swollen with its own strength, and excessively presumptuous, it would not have received from God the sentence of cutting down. Consider now a great tree, excessively presuming upon the abundance of its strength: “I said,” it declares, “in my abundance, ‘I shall never be moved’” (Ps. XXIX). But immediately, when grace was withdrawn and temptation came upon it, it learned what, or how much, it could do of itself: “You turned your face away from me,” it says, “and I became troubled” (ibid.).

Thus the tree is cut down when the strength of steadfastness is gradually diminished by temptations and at last utterly removed. Was not the strength of that tree cut down which said: “My strength has forsaken me, and even the light of my eyes is not with me” (Ps. XXXVII)? Was not its strength withdrawn and its tree cut down, falling to the depths, when at the sight of a single object of desire it fell into adultery, and from adultery into murder?

## CHAPTER XXII. How, and in what order, the human mind usually falls when grace is withdrawn.

[Col. 1321C] When the tree is cut down, its branches too are lopped off, because, as the strength of the soul fails, good works are gradually removed. The tree is cut down and the branch lopped off when virtue fails in secret and the work of virtue fails openly. First the strength of the soul is withdrawn; afterward the capacity and opportunity to act well are also taken away. When the tree’s strength has been cut down and its branches lopped off, its leaves are shaken off and its fruit scattered, because, when the purpose and exercise of virtues fail, the grace of speaking well is first removed, and then the grace of understanding rightly is also withdrawn.

Rightly, after zeal for good action has failed, eloquence of speech is withdrawn; for every rebuke or exhortation from a corrupt preacher can scandalize rather than edify those who hear it, when anyone silently answers the speaker: “Why, then, do you not do these things yourself?” But God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my righteous acts and take my covenant upon your lips?” The grace of the leaves is shaken off when, because of a previously acquired disreputable suspicion, confidence or authority in speaking is lost. The fruit is scattered when his teaching is despised; even though it may perhaps seem useful in insight or counsel, because of the evil example of his life it is readily trampled underfoot.

The fruit is scattered when the effort of meditation is dissipated by the importunate onslaught of varied desires, and the subtlety of inquiry and ease of understanding are confused by the wandering of thoughts. See how easily, see in what order, a mind is cast down from on high when, as its merits require, it is abandoned by divine grace and handed over by divine permission to evil exacters. Rightly, therefore, it is said of this tree: “Shake off its leaves, and scatter its fruit.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. How, after its shameful overthrow, the mind is thereafter despised by others and dissolves within itself.

But when a person begins to lose the branches of virtues and the fruit of counsel, and possesses neither uprightness of life nor authority of teaching at all, who will any longer think him worthy either of the obedience of carnal persons or of the intimate companionship of spiritual persons? Rightly, therefore, there is added what is further said concerning this tree: “Let the beasts which are beneath it flee, and the birds from its branches.”

The beasts that were formerly beneath it flee when those subject to it reject its obedience and all carnal persons despise its instruction. For the birds of heaven to flee from its branches is for spiritual persons to recoil from the disgrace of that life and avoid its companionship. Did not the younger men abhor the shade of that great tree—of which, according to the Lord’s testimony, there was no equal upon earth, because he was truly “a great man among all the men of the East,” foremost among the eminent? Did not the beasts already disdain to be beneath it when he truthfully testified of himself: “But now those younger than I mock me, whose fathers I would not have considered worthy to set among the dogs of my flock; the strength of whose hands was as nothing to me, and they were deemed unworthy even of life itself” (Job XXX)?

Tell me, what did the elders do, if younger men, and men so contemptible, derided him—because that great tree had by the Lord’s permission been cut down and struck from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head with a grievous ulcer? How great also was that tree to which the Lord bore witness that He had found a man according to His own heart! Did not the birds of heaven dwell in its branches when he truthfully declared of himself: “For the innocent and upright have clung to me” (Ps. XXIV)? Did they not then flee from its branches when again in prayer he cried: “You have removed my acquaintances far from me; they have made me an abomination to themselves” (Ps. LXXXVII); and again: “You have removed friend and neighbor far from me, and my acquaintances because of misery” (ibid.)?

But then, in the case of any man of virtue, what is written concerning this tree is fulfilled: when the strength of the tree is cut down, the beasts dwelling beneath it flee. For when the vigor of the soul is broken and exhausted by temptations, the mind is no longer able to restrain carnal impulses or curb irrational desires under reason’s rule. We lose the dwelling company of the birds of heaven when, troubled by the intrusion of so many phantasms, we cannot cultivate the delightful sights of sublime investigations. The tree loses the birds dwelling in its branches when it can no longer exercise its meditations in the accustomed examination of its own character.

We often grieve that we have lost the company of such birds when we cannot restrain our thoughts from foolish wandering, so that each of us may rightly say within himself what blessed Job said when he sees that his birds have flown away, not without his grief: “My thoughts are scattered, tormenting my heart” (Job VII).

## CHAPTER XXIV. That divine mercy often both preserves for repentance and awaits the correction of those who have fallen shamefully and been cast down from on high.

How merciful, and how worthy of great wonder, is the fact that divine mercy often neither utterly abandons such persons nor wholly deserts them after such a fall and ruin, but still frequently waits for their correction and preserves them for repentance. Woe to you, whoever you are who discover yourself to be such a person, if you despise the riches of His goodness, patience, and long-suffering. Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance—He who has not yet cut off the roots of your hope, but has hidden them in the secret counsel of His judgments, as it were in the bosom of the earth?

Let us hear, then, how that height of divine compassion tempers the sentence of its severity, when, after the devastation of such great dissipation, it still adds something concerning this tree for our consolation: “Nevertheless,” it says, “leave the stump of its roots in the earth.” This is something which we can neither pass over nor ought to pass over without wonder at divine goodness: He commands that the stump of its roots be left in the earth, so that the tree may be restored again and reformed to its former fullness. “Nevertheless, leave the stump of its roots in the earth.”

Then a tree is, as it were, uprooted when, after committing evils, it is also hurled into despair. The tree loses, as it were, its roots when it loses all hope of correction and falls into despair. That tree had been uprooted, and had remained fallen without a shoot for restoration, which, speaking to the Lord and despairing of pardon, said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve to be forgiven for” (Gen. IV).

For what else are the shoot or root of such a tree but the purpose of correction and hope in divine propitiation? Every good work sprouts from a good purpose so that it may come forth into effect and grow strong into the stability of good habit. In vain does a tree of virtue strive toward other things if it is not rooted in hope of divine propitiation: “For it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX).

What else, then, is it for the shoot of the roots to remain to such a tree after its fall, except that, after a fall into sin, a person retain a purpose of repentance and hope from divine compassion for the fruit of repentance—so much so that, trusting in the Lord’s goodness, he may dare to say: “He will not be angry forever, nor will He threaten forever” (Ps. CII). “When He has been angry, He will remember mercy” (Hab. III).

How many do we see every day who, amid the crimes they continually commit, do not lose their hope or purpose of coming to their senses, and who purpose not merely to abandon their sins but even to leave behind everything belonging to the world and enter an order and religious life. What else do these persons retain but the roots of a good shoot? When the time for mercy arrives according to the divine good pleasure, they sprout into zeal for good.

Others, however, when they are urged toward conversion, declare—even upon oath—that they will never enter an order or religious life; and, when rebuked for their sins, they affirm with an oath that they cannot restrain themselves from their pleasures. Therefore, do not those who are such—who have lost hope and purpose of correction—also lose, with the tree of virtue, the shoot of its roots? In contrast, it is said of this tree: “Nevertheless, leave the stump of its roots in the earth.”

## CHAPTER XXV. To what perversity a mind is sometimes hardened, though it is nevertheless reserved by God for pardon.

It is indeed remarkable how many people fall into despair immediately after a single crime. Others do not lose hope or the purpose of returning to their senses even after many, great, and long-lasting evils. This is also rightly understood in what is further said here concerning this tree: “Let it be bound with a band of iron and bronze among the herbs which are outside; and let it be drenched with the dew of heaven, and let its portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth. Let its heart be changed from human, and let the heart of a beast be given to it” (Dan. IV).

From these things you may surely perceive, I think, how great the evils are; but hear further how long-lasting they are: “And let seven times,” he says, “be changed over him.” What is more rightly understood by a band of iron and bronze than an invincible habit of perversity? Iron signifies audacity; bronze, obstinacy; and the herbs of the earth, lowly, earthly goods. For what are these earthly goods but certain herbs of the earth, common to us and to beasts? Of them it is rightly said: “which are outside.” For precisely because they are bodily and carnal, not spiritual, they are outside. Spiritual goods are internal; bodily goods external. The former belong to the inward person, the latter to the outward person. The former are invisible, the latter visible; the former eternal, the latter temporal: “For,” says the Apostle, “the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. IV). The former belong to the mind, the latter to the flesh. But “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass.”

When a corrupt mind begins to incline itself toward such lowly goods, to satisfy carnal desires as though in the grass of the earth, and to make such pleasures its habitual practice, the evil habit gradually gaining strength, it often finally comes to pass that it can no longer restrain its appetite from their love or use. Thus the corrupt mind is bound, as it were, by a band of iron in the grass of the earth when it is hardened by evil habit in love of carnal pleasures.

Because iron subdues all other metals, it rightly, as has been said, signifies audacity, which fears and dreads no one. And because bronze is more durable than all others, we have rightly said that it signifies obstinacy. Thus evil habit hardens, as it were, in the hardness of iron or bronze, when the corrupt mind clings to its accustomed desires as obstinately as it does boldly. Is not one bound with an iron and bronze band who is never turned away from accustomed desires by anyone’s terror or warning? Does not one already feel iron or bronze bonds who yields neither to threats nor to counsel?

It is clear, therefore, that minds of this kind cannot be corrected at all except by the power of Him who, whenever He willed, “broke the gates of bronze and shattered the bars of iron.” We obstruct the passage of those going out by gates, while we secure and strengthen the closure itself by bars. What, then, do we understand by a gate except contradiction, and by a bar except rebellion? We know, indeed, that it is not enough for some to contradict the warnings or commands of their superiors. When they cannot refute or overturn their superiors’ ordinances by words, they endeavor also to oppose them by deeds, rebel in action, and, as it were, strengthen the gates of their contradictions with the bars of their rebellions.

Therefore, if, as has already been said, obstinacy is signified by bronze and audacity by iron, what else is a bronze gate but stubborn contradiction, and an iron bar but bold rebellion? What else is it for the Lord to break gates of bronze and bars of iron than to restrain stubborn contradiction and bold rebellion by inward inspiration and contrition of heart? It belongs to God alone, therefore, as has been said, to break this great hardness of heart and soften it toward repentance and humility. Accordingly, when anyone is bound, in the manner described, with a band of iron and bronze among the herbs which are outside, release from so great a hardening and bondage must be awaited from God’s mercy alone.

## CHAPTER XXVI. How a mind whose conduct is corrupted is afterward imbued with errors or deceits.

But, to increase the evil still further, this is added: “And let it be drenched with the dew of heaven.” What do we understand by the dew of heaven except the subtle and scarcely perceptible suggestions of the devil? For if the earth fittingly signifies the body, why should heaven not likewise rightly signify spirit? In comparison with bodies, those spiritual substances in demons may be called heavens. In the Gospel they are called birds of heaven, not because of righteousness or glory, but because of their angelic and spiritual nature.

Thus the corrupt mind is drenched with the dew of heaven when it is imbued through the devil’s suggestions with various errors. From delight in its own desires it often incurs such a darkness of error that it calls evil good and good evil, making darkness light and light darkness, bitter sweet and sweet bitter. Therefore, one bound outside in the herbs of the earth must be drenched with dew; for after the corruption of conduct, the understanding too is corrupted and easily entangled in many errors.

Thus, at the destruction of Jerusalem, the king first lost his sons and afterward his eyes (IV Kings XXV). He loses spiritual sons who loses the offspring of virtues that he had long nourished. But when the sons have been lost, the light of the eyes is put out, because the keenness of understanding is often veiled and darkened through the corruption of the will. Therefore, one who loses heavenly desires, entangles himself in love of earthly things, and is bound by the bond of cupidity as though by a diet of herbs, must at times incur the darkness of errors and, as the clouds of heaven drip down, infect himself with a certain dew of seduction.

Does not one also seem to you to be drenched with the dew of heaven who, by the suggestion of evil spirits, is instructed in every deceit, so that in likeness to them he willingly wishes, and readily can, deceive and ensnare his neighbors by frauds? For without doubt, when excessive love of earthly things begins to reign, it gradually introduces deceitfulness and in the end drives one to violence and robbery. Hence there follows: “And let its portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. How the mind is at times let loose into every cruelty, though it is nevertheless reserved by God for repentance.

[Col. 1326B]

It is indeed remarkable, but no less true, that the divine dispensation permits some persons to be let loose into the utmost cruelty while nevertheless intending to preserve them for repentance, as persons whom it has predestined for eternal life. Thus it is said of such a person: “And let its portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth.”

By beasts, which rage with tooth and claw—and are called *feroces*, “fierce,” from *feritas*, “ferocity”—we may quite properly understand all cruel persons. Of such persons the Psalmist says: “The sons of men—their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. LVI). By the grass of the earth we understand the pleasures of mortal flesh and the glory of this passing life. For “all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass.”

Accordingly, those seem to have a portion with cruel persons, as it were with beasts, in the grass of the earth who, because of avarice and ambition, are let loose into robbery, deceit, and every cruelty. For what is it to have a portion with ministers of cruelty and such beasts except, with such associates, to receive a lot alike in similarity of conduct and in the debt of recompense? Conversely, the Prophet earnestly avoided association with such people or receiving a portion with them, when he said: “I have hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the ungodly” (Ps. C). Hence also elsewhere: “A perverse heart has not clung to me” (ibid.).

“Let its heart be changed from human.” The heart of a transgressing soul falling into low things is changed from human when every affection of humanity and compassion is entirely lost; when, through love of temporal things and the vice of avarice, it becomes hardened to the core against works of mercy, according to the saying: “The entrails of the avaricious are cruel” (Prov. XII).

But after so many stages of corruption, this too is still added as an increase of evil: “And let the heart of a beast be given to it.” A beast’s heart is given and received when one neighbor pursues another, without regard to any advantage, through the impulse of malice alone, as vainly as cruelly. Hear what the Prophet thinks of such persons: “The Lord will abhor the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. V).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How evil advances in those who continually decline into worse things.

[Col. 1327A]

Observe, I beg you, how evil advances. First good things are lost; afterward evil things are committed. In the shaking off of the leaves and scattering of the fruit, understand the loss of good things. In the binding among the herbs and the hardening of the heart, understand the increase of evils.

This must be noted: by what stages the accumulation of vices increases. A person is first cast down into avarice and then, through many stages of corruption, is let loose into every cruelty. Thus the transgressing soul is first bound by an iron and bronze band when, with strenuous labor and stubborn care, it is tirelessly occupied with acquiring earthly goods. It is drenched with the dew of heaven when, through evil suggestion, it is imbued with deceit, so that, at avarice’s prompting, it may obtain through fraud what it cannot obtain through industry. At last its portion comes to be with the beasts in the herbs of the earth when it desires and endeavors to obtain through violence and robbery what it cannot acquire through industry or fraud.

See how the disease of avarice grows and introduces the evil of cruelty. The first stage of savagery is when, for some personal advantage, one presumes, or endures, to act savagely against a neighbor—though not without remorse of conscience. The heart is changed from human when one is moved by no compassion, softened by no humanity; when, while committing robberies, one is stung by no regard for divine fear, by no dread of punishment, or by no prick of conscience whatever. He receives a beast’s heart who is cruel even gratuitously, who breaks forth without any cause into manifest malice. The first stage of malice, therefore, is when one becomes entirely hardened against one’s neighbor without cause. The second is when one is touched by no compassion amid a neighbor’s miseries. The third and worst is when one is already fed and delighted by that neighbor’s evils.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That a mind may often be corrupted in every respect, though it is nevertheless known to be preserved for repentance through divine mercy.

One thing still remains, added as though in the final place, in which the sentence of severity seems to be completed: “And let seven times be changed over him.” Seven times are changed when the condition of our weakness is altered through various stages of corruption, while it is always turned toward worse things.

Do we not then enter another time, as it were contrary to the former, when we begin to be altogether unable to prevail against a vice which we had previously been able to resist? Thus the time concerning any person is altered in many ways when the manner of that person’s corruption is varied in many forms. The dominion of vices gradually softens the mind, renders it ever weaker and weaker, and drives it step by step toward worse things.

Now, as we commonly know, the whole course of time is unfolded in seven days; and therefore totality is often signified by the number seven itself. Again, seven capital vices are said to exist. Hence in the Gospel we read that an unclean spirit brings seven spirits with it and inhabits its house which it had left for a time, because any one vice, once it has begun to rule, often gradually introduces the whole detestable company of vices. Conversely, the sinful woman is described as cleansed from seven demons, because she is freed from every tyranny of vices through sevenfold grace.

The sevenfold alteration of times, therefore, is a manifold—indeed universal—corruption of character. For seven times are, as it were, changed over a person who is corrupted in every respect and eventually bends enfeebled to every servitude of vices. But now see what is remarkable: divine mercy is accustomed at times to preserve such a person for repentance.

## CHAPTER XXX. How the fall of certain persons from on high is accustomed to serve the benefit of many.

“The decree is by the sentence of the watchers, and the word of the holy ones, and the petition, until the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever He wills, and sets over it the lowliest of men” (Dan. IV).

As we have already said above, by the watchers in this place we understand holy angels. From the Apostle’s teaching, moreover, we have learned that all are ministering spirits sent for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation. Thus angels, the cooperators in our salvation and ministers of divine ordering, arrange human affairs according as, through God’s revelation, they know this to accord with the common benefit of humankind.

Now it often serves the benefit of many when some fall from a great height of eminence, so that others may learn not to think highly of themselves, but always to think humbly of themselves; to fear a collapse of character at every summit of virtue; and truly to recognize that the Lord alone works in us both willing and accomplishing according to His good will. The prophetic utterance indicates this benefit of such a fall, saying: “Until the living may know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men.”

Therefore, when the common benefit requires it, men of great authority are permitted by divine dispensation to fall precisely when they are found to be proud of their own greatness. Thus, in the same person, one and the same judgment is both just and merciful: just with respect to that person himself, merciful insofar as it profits the caution of others. For it is altogether just that one who is insolently puffed up by divine gifts should learn through his own fall how insignificant he is and how powerless he is by himself.

This decree is called the word of the holy ones because what some foresee in the light of God as future is communicated publicly. It is called the petition of the holy ones because they not only will it to occur, but also seek with desire what they foreknow to be beneficial to many and conducive to divine glory. Such a judgment, therefore, will be the decree of the holy ones because it is mercifully just; the word of the holy ones because it is truly future; and the petition because it is justly merciful.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How some learn from their own fall, and others from the fall of another, that they ought to attribute nothing to their own powers.

Until the living recognize that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men. Behold the benefit: that the living may recognize it. The affections within us live according to God when they are strong in good and grow vigorous for works of virtue, when they have cooperating grace and are able to exercise themselves in spiritual pursuits. They undoubtedly die when cooperating grace is withdrawn from them. It is withdrawn when a perverse mind grows proud of its good works and divine gifts, and attributes merits to itself. Once grace has been withdrawn, good affections fail [Col. 1329B] and languish toward every good; thus, from living they become dead. For what else is the failure of virtues but a kind of destruction of them? Those, therefore, who first heed their own weakness and divine grace only when they are already failing in good, learn and recognize, after death and as it were through death, the instruction or benefit of divine rule and governance.

What, then, is it for the living to recognize the dominion and sovereignty of the heavenly Majesty in the kingdom of men, except for each person, even while he still lives in good works, to heed his own weakness; to attribute nothing to himself, nothing to his own merits; and, amid whatever exercises of virtue, not to abandon the safeguard of humility [Col. 1329C], but truthfully and without pretence to attribute whatever evil there is to himself, and whatever good there is to divine grace? Heavenly mercy is indeed accustomed even to humble men of virtue in certain respects and to withdraw grace, until they learn amid whatever distinctions of character to think nothing lofty of themselves and presume nothing upon their own virtue. Happy are those who learn the frailties of human fragility from another's fall rather than their own, and advance in the grace of humility. Yet it also goes well with those who awake from their own ruin to the preservation of humility, when at last, after the fall occasioned by their weakness, they rise again stronger. The type of both things is expressed in the fall or restoration of King Nebuchadnezzar: for he himself is restored after his fall to greater glory, and many are instructed through his fall toward the prudent caution [Col. 1329D] of watchfulness.

“Until the living,” he says, “recognize that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men.” Thus, to have such recognition while living is for anyone leading a just and heavenly life to persevere in good zeal and attribute nothing to himself from his good works. The living surely have this recognition when they endure in a good intention and presume nothing upon their own strength, but ascribe to the Lord everything useful that they can do, because he alone rules in the kingdom of men: “For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule over the nations.” Indeed, both that outward kingdom by which men commonly preside over men, and likewise that inward kingdom by which they ought to rule over their own vices and passions, are ordered and administered by him, and each is possessed through his gift [Col. 1330A].

But the former must certainly be avoided and altogether fled, as Truth herself teaches us by her own example. The latter, however, we ought to desire, seek, ask with the greatest longing, and entreat with the Prophet: “Give dominion to thy servant” (Ps. LXXXV). Must we suppose, I ask, that the prophetic soul was possessed by such ambition that it asked the Lord for the kingdom of Israel, and that not even shame restrained it from such a request? But if it could not restrain his tongue from making this request, why did it not at least prevent his hand from writing such a thing? Far be it from us to suspect anything of the sort concerning so holy and prophetic a soul. Rather, he was asking the Lord’s mercy for such a kingdom or dominion as would give him hope for the attainment or advancement of his salvation.

“Give dominion,” he says, “to thy servant, and save the son of thy handmaid” [Col. 1330B]. You too, therefore, ask such dominion or kingdom from the Lord your God, that in this respect you may be able to sing: “But I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. II). For the saying is entirely true: “He will give it to whomever he wills.” For it is not of the one who wills, nor of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy. If you have nothing that you did not receive, how much more so a kingdom?

## CHAPTER XXXII. That the measure of greatness depends upon the degree of humility.

“And he shall set the lowliest man over it,” he says. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble”; and certainly, the humbler a person is, the more exalted he is. [Col. 1330C] Undoubtedly, if we consider that inward kingdom, in this kingdom you will be the more exalted, and without ambiguity the greater, the humbler you are, and the smaller you are in your own eyes. Who, I ask, could doubt that in the outward kingdom it often happens very differently, or even contrariwise? But in that inward kingdom the measure of greatness always depends upon the measure of humility. For he “shall set the humble, even the lowliest, over it.”

The humble person is one who truly despises himself in his own estimation; the humbler person is one who does not shrink even from being despised by others; but the lowliest is one who not only despises his own contempt, but earnestly desires it. What, then, I ask, can pride do against one to whom his own low estate has become contemptible? Since, therefore, according to the testimony of Scripture, “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X), what can sin do against one from whom, through victory over pride, the beginning of every sin is far removed? Consider, then, how strong and powerful such a person is found in that kingdom which is established against sin and is destroyed or scattered only by sin [Col. 1330D].

Behold, from the end of the vision we now clearly gather what we stated much earlier: that the common good and the advantage of the whole required such a man as is represented in the tree—such a man, I say, as would, after the likeness of a tree, fall from a lofty state and rise again, so that by his fall he might instil in those standing the fear of falling, and by his restoration might renew in those lying fallen the hope of rising again.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That it is one thing to see divine judgments through contemplation, and another to weigh their reason.

[Col. 1331A]

Behold the dream that Nebuchadnezzar saw, though he still seeks its interpretation; hence he says: “This dream I, King Nebuchadnezzar, have seen. Therefore, Belteshazzar, quickly declare its interpretation, because all the wise men of my kingdom are unable to tell me its solution. But you can, because the spirit of the holy gods is in you” (Dan. IV).

As I have already said above, it is one thing to behold divine judgments with the eye of discernment or foresight, and another to penetrate and know their reason by the judgment of discretion and the keenness of understanding. The former belongs to seeing the dream; the latter belongs to interpreting it [Col. 1331B]. To the dream’s vision belongs knowing by divine revelation what must come to pass; to the dream’s interpretation belongs understanding the character of the person to whom this must happen—that is, considering the cause that ordinarily drives a given person toward such a fall. This is what Daniel discovered by investigation and disclosed to the king in interpreting it, when he said: “You are that tree which you saw.” For what is it to say, “You are,” except, “I judge that you are such a person; I find such a cause within you, and therefore I do not doubt that something of this kind must happen to you”?

Do you wish to know still more plainly how, after a vision has been divinely shown, we are accustomed—and indeed ought—to seek its interpretation? Suppose that someone, through the light of contemplation, sees how the common good requires the fall [Col. 1331C] and restoration of certain exalted persons. He sees how this commends the grace of God, how it instructs those still standing toward caution, how it restores the fallen to hope, how through it the beauty of the whole universe appears more wonderful; and he is certain that it must occur, because almighty goodness neither wishes nor ought to hinder the common good. But he begins again to wonder how this can accord with supreme justice, or how it can be just that some should be permitted to fall, even for the benefit of the whole. For, just as he who made all things owes something to the whole, so he who established each thing owes something to each individual. And as it is merciful not to hinder the common good, so it must also be just [Col. 1331D] that there is always some cause in the person about to fall for which he ought deservedly to be exposed to impending ruin.

Therefore, one who desires to know such a cause and earnestly seeks the rationale of divine judgments seeks nothing other than the interpretation of the vision shown to him. He demands such an interpretation, as it were, from Daniel when he does not cease to wrest from the Lord, by outstanding zeal and the highest devotion, what he cannot attain by investigation. “This dream,” he says, “I, Nebuchadnezzar, have seen. Therefore, Belteshazzar, quickly declare its interpretation.” You perceive, I think, that the king sees some things by himself and wrings other things from Daniel; for some things freely and easily occur to the mind, while others cannot be known without great labor and intense concern. By the former [Col. 1332A] the mind is stirred to rise toward greater things; by the latter it is exercised and humbled, lest it presume. It is suggested that, in what the king had seen, he was not without fear, since he seeks the interpretation in haste. We too are admonished to seek with all haste the resolution of a matter where the suspicion of danger can inspire fear.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That we often acquire by the merit of devotion knowledge which no sagacity or effort of our own can penetrate.

It should indeed be noted that Daniel is called Belteshazzar, that is, “hair of the head,” when he is invited to a subtle explanation of sublime matters. For among human members what is higher than the head, or subtler than hair? [Col. 1332B] Therefore, he is fittingly called “hair of the head,” from whom is required the subtlety of sublime understanding. And true devotion of mind, by its effect, is rightly, unless I am mistaken, called “hair of the head,” because through it the mind is undoubtedly sharpened to every subtlety. Thus, by its effect, it is itself the hair of the head, itself the subtlety of mind.

Let us hear further what he adds to this: “Because all the wise men of my kingdom are unable to tell me its solution.” Who, I ask, are the wise men of that inward kingdom, except the sharpest capacities and most acute perceptions of the human heart? Consider, therefore, what the power of devotion is, and why it is rightly called hair of the head, if through it the mind can do what it cannot do through all the wise men of its kingdom. When, then, the mind persists in seeking what it seeks in many ways beyond its own understanding, it fails by persisting, and by failing loses confidence [Col. 1332C]. What else does it then say silently to itself through that loss of confidence than what King Nebuchadnezzar openly professes: “All the wise men of my kingdom are unable to tell me its solution”?

But since Truth says: “Amen I say to you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you receive it, and it shall be yours” (Mark XI), if the mind believes what it hears, turns itself to prayer, and through true and inward devotion does not despair of obtaining what it could not obtain through investigation, what else does it assert within itself, by the confidence of hope and constancy of faith, than the very thing the king says to Daniel: “But you can”? He also adds the reason: “Because the spirit of the holy gods is in you.” We know that in the Holy Scriptures holy human beings have been called gods, and on the same reasoning this may also be said of angels. Who, then, is the spirit of these gods except the Holy Spirit? [Col. 1332D] He assuredly is the one who intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings; he suggests what we should pray for; he teaches how we ought to pray. Without this Spirit our devotion cannot be true; what it undertakes with him and through him cannot come to nothing. “But you can,” he says, “because the spirit of the holy gods is in you.”

It should also be noted that King Nebuchadnezzar did not seek useless or superfluous matters through Daniel’s office, but matters which it was necessary to know in order to avoid danger. What we ask will likewise be given to us if, following his example, we seek in faith and true devotion [Col. 1333A] that which we cannot safely remain ignorant of.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That, when the mind is humbled by much consideration of its weakness, it is often divinely illumined to sublime understanding.

“Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, began silently to think within himself for about one hour, and his thoughts troubled him” (Dan. IV). I think it belongs to Daniel, and is the office of true devotion, to return to oneself, forget outward things, and consider inward things—especially when one ought to provide for one’s own salvation or that of another. One time is for investigating matters above oneself; another is for examining matters within oneself [Col. 1333B]. For everything has its season. Thus, there is a time for contemplating the great works of God, and a time for considering our own weaknesses.

This is the time for rejoicing. For “weeping shall remain until evening, and joy until morning.” Why should there not be a time for rejoicing in the morning of divine revelation and contemplation of eternal light? Why should there not be a time for weeping in the evening of a dreadful vision, when one considers the darkness of human conscience? Evening is the time when the light of revealing grace emerges before the eyes of the contemplative, turns him toward wonder at itself, and often raptures him beyond himself upon the height of the mind: “You will delight the goings forth of morning and evening,” he says (Ps. LXIV). What are these goings forth of the morning except the ecstasies of the human mind toward the radiance of the true sun?

He says, therefore, that the goings forth of morning delight; but why should not evening also delight, or the inward entries of evening? For in the morning we are accustomed to go out from inward things to outward, and in the evening to return from outward things to inward [Col. 1333C]. Who can adequately wonder how sweet and delightful it is, when charity is now aflame and, as it were, under the summer season, to shake oneself from sleep toward the morning light of radiant divinity, burst forth beyond the narrow confines of the human mind into the air of freedom, and pass, in the mind’s alienation from itself, into that broad field of divine spectacles? The goings forth of morning, therefore, delight; but the inward entries of evening sadden, undoubtedly when the mind returns to consideration of itself: “My soul was troubled within me” (Ps. XLI).

But amid the terror of a nocturnal vision, in considering a dreadful conscience, there is one sure consolation for the mind: namely, remembrance of its God. This is what is added there: “My soul was troubled within me; therefore I will remember thee.” This is what he says elsewhere: “I remembered God and was delighted” (Ps. LXXVI). And in this place: “You will delight the goings forth of morning and evening.” “You,” he says, “will delight”—not the hour itself, nor the inward entries of evening-time. For what delight, I ask, can there be in considering that dark abyss of the human heart? For the heart of man is perverse and inscrutable; who shall know it? This is why Daniel, while he thinks long, is troubled within himself by his thoughts. But one who willingly considers his weaknesses, carefully reviews them [Col. 1334A], and humbles himself in considering them, while he diligently examines what he could discover within himself by himself, is often divinely illumined even to what he could not know by himself. This is why Daniel, while he meditates long and silently within himself, is divinely taught beforehand the ruin of the royal power and the cause of that ruin.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning true devotion of mind and how it ought to examine itself.

One who wishes to be instructed in a deep and full knowledge of himself, and desires that things necessary to his own or another’s salvation be revealed to him, ought not to meditate upon his inner life moderately, as if merely in passing. Thus Daniel thought within himself for about one hour [Col. 1334B] and obtained the cause he sought. The hour of inquiry is finally brought to its proper conclusion when what is sought has been found.

Therefore, when necessity presses, let us strive to pray, seek, and knock as much as necessity compels, opportunity allows, and the continuation of our effort fills the urgent hour. But if Daniel ought to be understood as devotion, perhaps for Daniel to think within himself means for our devotion to examine itself, test itself, and ask within itself how fervent, how frequent, and how supplicatory it is. It thinks within itself when it weighs the quality, measure, and intention of its own zeal and practice. It thinks within itself when it diligently asks whether, in the very good thing toward which it directs itself, it relies not upon its own strength but upon the Lord’s mercy alone [Col. 1334C].

Thus, when our devotion often does this with itself, it discovers the vice of arrogance that was formerly hidden within it. But once the vice of arrogance begins to prevail in the mind, it is always accustomed to be a cause of ruin. Therefore, when devotion finds that this vice has grown to such enormity within it, it infers that the mind’s future ruin is impending and is greatly afraid. For it knows that “before ruin the heart shall be exalted,” and that “God resists the proud.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. How devotion sometimes discerns the whole state of the inward person, perceiving both the present and foreseeing the future.

[Col. 1334D]

The king answered: “Belteshazzar, let neither the dream nor its interpretations trouble you” (Dan. IV). What else is it that the king forbids Daniel to be troubled, except that the mind deceives itself and often removes useful fear by empty hope? But Daniel does what, when danger threatens, he wished us to do, and what belongs to true devotion: he turns himself to prayer. Belteshazzar answered and said: “My lord, let the dream be for those who hate thee, and its interpretation for thine enemies.”

The malignant spirits are those who burn against us with unquenchable hatred. Vices are the true enemies of the soul, driving it toward eternal destruction. We are taught to pray for their ruin in the words: “Let the dream be for those who hate thee, and its interpretation for thine enemies.” Therefore, when the mind is assailed by the spirit of pride and instigators of vices of this kind, when it is oppressed by arrogance and vainglory [Col. 1335A], it ought to flee to prayer and, after Daniel’s example, demand their ruin.

But when devotion of mind cannot prevail against arrogance and vainglory through prayer, it often understands more deeply and infers more surely from that very fact that the swelling of the mind cannot be healed except through its own shameful and humiliating overthrow. This is what Daniel says mysteriously when he says: “They shall cast thee out from among men, and thy dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals.” Let us now hear what he says, and gather from it how devotion often discerns the whole condition of the inward person, both describing the present and foreseeing the future. Let it say, then, now that ruin is impending, what the mind presently is through grace, what it will become through fault, and finally add the cause of its ruin or restoration. You will find this order, unless I am mistaken, in Daniel’s words to the king, if you examine them correctly:

“The tree,” he says, “which thou sawest, lofty and strong, whose height reaches to heaven and whose appearance extends over all the earth, whose branches are most beautiful and whose fruit is abundant, in which is food for all, under which the beasts of the field dwell and in whose branches the birds of heaven make their home—thou art the king, who hast been magnified and grown strong; thy greatness has increased and reached to heaven, and thy power to the ends of the whole earth” [Col. 1335B].

How in these words a state of great perfection is described, we have already said above, and ought not to repeat here.

But note the statement: “The tree which thou sawest, thou art.” If by such a tree we must understand some great strength of admirable virtue, and if by the divinely shown vision we must understand a revelation of contemplation, what, I ask, does “Thou art the tree which thou sawest” mean except: You received such grace as you had first seen through contemplation; and, by the grace of contemplation, you understood what a man of great perfection ought to be; and by divine gift you merited to become such and so great. Thus, in the tree the grace received from God is mystically described; but in the following words the approaching ruin of an arrogant soul is expressed:

“And whereas,” he says, “the king saw a watcher and a holy one [Col. 1335C] come down from heaven and say, ‘Cut down the tree and scatter it; nevertheless leave the stump of its roots in the earth, and let it be bound with iron and bronze amid the grass outdoors, sprinkled with the dew of heaven; and let its food be with the wild beasts, until seven times are changed over it’: this is the interpretation of the decree of the Most High, which has come upon my lord the king. They shall cast thee out from among men, and thy dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals; thou shalt eat grass like an ox and be drenched with the dew of heaven. Seven times also shall be changed over thee.”

How these words express the type of a soul falling from a certain lofty state to the depths has been set out above.

Note here also that, as above, the thing is first divinely shown through contemplation and afterward must be fulfilled in deed. “The king saw”—this belongs to contemplation; but what is added afterward, “They shall cast thee out from among men,” belongs to the execution of the vision. It is as though he were saying: According to what you saw in contemplation—that such a ruin can and commonly does occur from such an exalted state—I see a like danger threatening you, because I find within you the cause of ruin [Col. 1336A]. The cause of ruin is suggested in what is lastly added: “Until thou know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he wills.” In saying, “Until thou know,” he notes that he had not yet recognized this as he ought.

The words that follow express what he will at last become through grace, and why or how he is to be restored after his fall. “But whereas he commanded,” he says, “that the stump of its roots—that is, of the tree—should be left, thy kingdom shall remain for thee after thou hast recognized that the power is heavenly.” To hear all these things through Daniel is, through the practice of our devotion, to discover the enormity of our arrogance, which is always accustomed to cause ruin; and, after discovering and perceiving the cause of ruin, to incur a most violent fear of falling, yet steadfastly retain an utterly firm hope of coming to one’s senses and rising again. How all these things ought to be understood more fully can easily be recognized from the preceding exposition [Col. 1336B].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How one ought to resist imminent danger, and how much almsgiving avails if it is done with a simple intention.

[Col. 1336C]

Once the impending danger has been recognized and set forth, Daniel finally adds what ought to be done at such a moment of necessity, or how one ought to resist the imminent danger: “Therefore, O king, let my counsel please thee: redeem thy sins by alms, and thine iniquities by mercies to the poor; perhaps God will forgive thy sins” (Dan. IV).

What, I ask, is more prudent or more advantageous, when danger presses, than to flee to divine protection and seek the propitiation of him to whom nothing is impossible? It is altogether just that one who seeks aid from his superior in his own necessity should give the assistance that he can and ought to give to his inferior; that one who desires mercy for himself should willingly bestow mercy, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). Therefore it is rightly said: “Redeem thy sins by alms, and thine iniquities by mercies to the poor” [Col. 1336D].

Perhaps the sentence is repeated in this twofold clause, so that redeeming iniquities is the same as redeeming sins. Yet we may understand sins to be transgressions in deed, and iniquities to be perversities of will. For that psalm warns us that a distinction in these matters may or ought to be made: “Thou hast forgiven,” he says, “the impiety of my sin” (Ps. XXXI). Likewise, in alms we rightly understand an act of compassion, and in mercies an affection of compassion. Observe how fittingly a deed is expiated by a deed, and an act by an affection. “Redeem thy sins,” he says, “by alms, and thine iniquities by mercies to the poor.”

A person is made poor by a lack of outward goods; yet far more is one made poor by want of inward goods. Poor is the person who lacks discretion, who has no counsel, who lacks the riches of virtues. But where there is poverty, there too almsgiving can exist. And the truer the poverty, the greater the almsgiving. It is a great alms to restore with food the flesh that will someday die; but it is greater to nourish with the food proper to its kind a soul that will live forever. It is almsgiving to clothe the naked; but greater still to adorn the undisciplined with moral discipline. The best kind of almsgiving is to correct the restless, console the faint-hearted, and be patient toward all [Col. 1337A].

It is great mercy to suffer with another’s affliction; but greater to be pierced with sorrow for another’s errors. A splendid kind of mercy is to weep for sinners, grant pardon to penitents, and wipe away others’ sins with one’s own tears. We who do not possess outward riches ought to exercise ourselves in these works of mercy. “Perhaps,” he says, “he will forgive thy sins.” Why does he say “perhaps” and place it, as it were, in doubt, except because the mind, corrupted by the infection of pride and vainglory, cannot have full confidence even in these works of mercy, when it cannot perform them with a pure and simple intention?

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How patiently and mercifully God’s long-suffering awaits our amendment, and how a perverse mind is accustomed to abuse his patience.

[Col. 1337C]

“All these things came upon King Nebuchadnezzar” (Dan. IV). “All,” he says, “came upon the king”—and upon such a king. All things came; all things can come upon a royal mind and upon one such as the royal person mystically represents: “After the end of twelve months he was walking in the palace of Babylon. The king answered and said: ‘Is not this great Babylon, which I have built as the house of the kingdom, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my splendor?’”

Who, I ask, can adequately weigh the depths of divine mercy: that he does not immediately punish contempt of himself, but awaits satisfaction in our amendment and prolongs the time of his propitiation? “After the end,” he says, “of twelve months”: in the number twelve, six is doubled; and in six, because of its perfection, perfection is signified. What, then, does it mean that divine governance doubles six in the delay of its waiting, except that it dispenses the postponement of its vengeance in accordance with the fullness of its justice and mercy? For it is too little for him to await our amendment only as much as justice requires, unless he adds also what mercy requires, so that his waiting may be as just as it is merciful, as perfect in equity as it is full of compassion [Col. 1337D].

But many abuse God’s kindness and become worse through what should have corrected them. Behold, while Nebuchadnezzar receives from God time for making satisfaction, he becomes more puffed up through that by which he ought to have corrected himself. “He was walking in the palace of Babylon.” Perhaps true humility is a palace and the firmest dwelling-place, the guardian of virtues. But such a dwelling belongs to Jerusalem: “Jerusalem,” he says, “which is built as a city, whose participation is unto the same thing” (Ps. CXXI). But as true humility belongs to Jerusalem, so feigned humility belongs to Babylon. For what else does feigned humility prepare except disgrace? What else does it await except confusion?

Therefore, a Babylonian palace is feigned humility. The palace of Babylon without humility is a discipline of humiliation. He does not sit or lie down, but walks in the palace of Babylon when his conscience, reproaching him, keeps him restless. He walks in the Babylonian palace when his conscience wearies him with accusation concerning his feigned humility. To walk is not to go in one direction, but to wander here and there in every direction. Therefore, the person whose conscience’s goad drives him on from every side is walking [Col. 1338A].

## CHAPTER XL. On the type of the arrogant soul, and how it is accustomed to magnify itself.

[Col. 1338B]

“And the king answered and said.” What kind of answer, I ask, is this, where no question precedes? Or perhaps he was answering another’s thought—perhaps a thought that did not exist, though he believed it did. Perhaps he was answering the thoughts of those whom he supposed to admire his greatness and authority. An arrogant mind has this characteristic: it believes that everyone admires its eminence, which it itself magnifies within itself at every hour. Consequently, it confidently bursts forth before others into words of boasting, and expresses the same thing as Nebuchadnezzar, though in different words.

Let us consider now how greatly he was puffed up when he burst into the words set above: “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built?” Behold display. “As the house of the kingdom”: behold ambition. “By the strength of my power”: behold arrogance. “And for the glory of my splendor”: behold vainglory [Col. 1338C].

“This is great Babylon, which I have built.” We say that Babylon signifies confusion. For a soul that is proud and acts with duplicity, to build Babylon is to incline itself to every humiliation and, as though under the pretext of religion, expose itself to every indignity and abasement, and to all things at which people are commonly ashamed—such as cheap clothing, humble bearing, meagre food, and voluntary servitude. Let it therefore say: “This is great Babylon; this is profound humiliation; this is voluntary abasement; this is chosen confusion, which I have built, which I have resolved to observe.” But to what end, to what advantage? “As the house,” he says, “of the kingdom.”

Does he not seem to you to build as though for a house who acts in order to gain authority and the art of mastery, so that he may appear to everyone so great and such a person as ought worthily to be promoted, preferred to others, and exalted in dignity or even power? “By the strength,” he says, “of my power.” Behold what great arrogance he attributed to himself in something wholly dependent upon divine grace. He does not say, “By the gift of divine mercy,” but, “By the strength of my power.” How differently Truth herself both thought and taught when she said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV). But what the perverse mind thinks it achieves through its own strength, [Col. 1339A] it consequently turns toward its own glory: “By the strength,” he says, “of my power, and for the glory of my splendor” [Col. 1338D].

How differently this kind of boaster acts from the Apostle’s command, and how differently from Truth our teacher’s ordinance: “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Cor. II); and: “So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V). But this man says, “For the glory of my splendor.”

## CHAPTER XLI. How suddenly and how deeply those who abuse God’s patience often fall.

“While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: ‘To thee it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom has passed from thee’” (Dan. IV). The voice falls while the word is still in his mouth, namely, at the very time when he is still glorying. For an shameless mind, while glorying without measure, is often suddenly dismayed in the midst of its glorying, as conscience reproaches it; shaken by a sudden horror through a certain divine prompting, it is hurled from fear of falling into despair of escape.

The voice falls from heaven when what it perceives with the ear of the heart comes from the innermost senses of the soul. Like earth, it hears whatever it draws in through bodily sense. What it recognizes through the Spirit comes from heaven. It learns from heaven what it comprehends intellectually. “To thee it is said, Nebuchadnezzar”: to thee, so vainly proud; to thee, so vainly glorying. “The kingdom has passed from thee, and they shall cast thee out from among men, and thy dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals” [Col. 1339B].

[Col. 1339C]

The kingdom passes from anyone when he loses the grace divinely bestowed on him, through which he was accustomed to rule his desires and passions. “They shall cast thee out from among men.” As far as you exalted yourself above men through arrogance, so far shall you be cast down below men through fault; “and thy dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals.” He who abandons rational conduct descends from men to beasts and wild animals and lives with them; living bestially and acting savagely, he is given over to every carnality with those who live bestially, and unbridled toward every cruelty with those who act savagely.

He adds further: “Thou shalt eat grass like an ox.” When an ox receives grass, it regards it as the greatest delight and seeks nothing more sumptuous. [Col. 1339D]

Since all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass, he eats grass like an ox who places all his joy in temporal glory and carnal pleasures, and altogether seeks no spiritual delights, neither through effort nor through desire. Behold into what a depth one falls who abuses God’s patience. Behold the end to which one comes who received time for repentance in vain.

## CHAPTER XLII. That one and the same sentence is foreknown through contemplation, threatened through fear, and confirmed through despair.

“And seven times shall be changed over thee, until thou know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wills” (Dan. IV). We have already expounded these matters above and ought not to repeat them again [Col. 1340A].

One must certainly note that the same thing is repeated several times, and that one and the same sentence of divine severity is reiterated a third time. To distinguish it for you by its proper differences: first, through contemplation, as though through a vision, the mind recognizes what is wont to happen; second, through devotion, and as though by Daniel’s office, it discovers what it ought now to fear for itself; finally, when grace has been withdrawn and it is already broken by despair, it manifestly perceives what it can no longer avoid. Thus one and the same sentence is foreknown through contemplation, threatened through fear, and confirmed through despair.

## CHAPTER XLIII. That without divine protection no one can resist either his own passions or evil suggestions.

[Col. 1340B]

At that same hour the word was fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: he was cast out from among men (Dan. IV). What is “at that same hour,” except immediately, upon the withdrawal of grace, to yield to temptations and to be unable to resist the evil spirits who tempt? “At that same hour”—not because conceived wickedness at once comes forth into action, since an opportunity for sin is not always at hand; but the mind is cast down and falls as soon as it consents to sin. It is cast down and falls as soon as it seeks an opportunity.

From this passage, I think, we may plainly gather that without divine protection no one could resist, even for a little while, either his own passions or evil suggestions. Therefore at that same hour he was cast out from among men, ate grass like an ox, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven. We have already expounded all these matters above. But something is further added which we did not read above: “Until his hair grew like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws.”

## CHAPTER XLIV. How one may fall from the summit of virtues into the depths of vices.

Hairs are thin and long, and deep and very sharp counsels may rightly be understood by them. The bodies of eagles, moreover, are covered with a dense abundance of feathers. Eagles are accustomed to see more keenly and fly more loftily than all other living creatures.

[Col. 1340D] Therefore he has hair “like eagles’ feathers” who is skilled in much prudence and in the greatest cunning, who is found inferior or slower than no one in discovering deceits and weaving plots. Birds of prey, as we all know, rage with their claws; and birds generally tear and injure whatever they seize with their claws. What, then, is it to have nails like those of birds, except to injure all whom one has power to overcome?

But if the work of cruelty is rightly understood under the figure of claws, is not that same thing expressed above under another image, where it says: “And your dwelling shall be with the wild beasts”? Yet wild beasts do not hunt birds, nor do they have anything at all to do with birds. Therefore, those who gladly oppress worldly and carnal persons, as though creatures brooding upon the earth, what else do they do but rage against animals in the manner of wild beasts?

[Col. 1341A] Are not those rightly called animals who serve the belly alone, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame? But those who persecute spiritual men—what else do they do but lie in wait for birds in the manner of birds, and rage as though with claws? Do not those seem to you to be birds of heaven who can truly say, “But our commonwealth is in heaven”? Are not those to be called birds of heaven who suspend themselves aloft upon the wing of contemplation?

In the former statement, therefore, we have how such people are hostile to carnal persons; in this one we have how at last they do not spare even spiritual persons. Let it therefore be said of such a man: “Until his hair grew like eagles’ feathers, and his nails [Col. 1341B] like birds’ claws”—so that he is as ready to ensnare even the cautious as he is undoubtedly inclined to oppress men conspicuous even for virtue. Here he is effective in deceiving; here he is bold and shameless in persecuting. “Your mouth,” says the Psalmist, “overflowed with malice, and your tongue devised deceits” (Ps. XLIX [50]). See how he rebukes the deceitful. Hear also how he confounds the audacious: “They will lie in wait for the soul of the righteous, and condemn innocent blood” (Ps. XCIII [94]). Do not those lie in wait for birds of heaven and rage as with claws, who hunt the soul of the righteous and condemn the innocent?

Or demons may be understood by “birds,” as we learn from the Gospel reading (Luke VIII). What, then, is it to have nails like those birds, except to assail any good persons solely at the prompting of malice? We now see from how lofty a summit of perfection a man of virtues may fall into the depths of vices, so that a person may learn, at whatever height of holiness, always to fear a collapse of character. Recall how he was described above through the mystical tree, and at the same time consider the end to which he eventually came.

For of the tree you read that birds of heaven dwelt in its branches and that all flesh fed from it. Thus it was a protection for the good and a consolation for all, since birds of heaven dwelt in it and all flesh fed from it. See: this same man, after all these things, rages tooth and claw against everyone, because his portion was with the wild beasts and [Col. 1341D] he received nails like birds’ claws.

## CHAPTER XLV. How one who first fell from on high sometimes rises again to greater glory.

What follows brings great joy when, after these things, it is added: “Therefore, after the end of the days, I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding was restored to me; and I blessed the Most High, and praised and glorified him who lives for ever, because his power is everlasting power, and his kingdom is from generation to generation. And all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing before him” (Dan. IV).

See, he rises again; see, he returns to his former—indeed, rather to a greater—glory, he who fell from so lofty a height into so deep an abyss. Who would not marvel? Who would not be astonished? [Col. 1342A] Who can adequately weigh the depths of divine mercy? I ask: what sinner, however great, should not take confidence from divine compassion and revive in hope of pardon?

“After the end,” he says, “of the days, I lifted up my eyes to heaven.” The end of the days is the completion of the divine judgments. If justice, or human judgments, are light, why should divine judgments not be so much more? “He will bring forth,” he says, “your righteousness as the light, and your judgment as the noonday” (Ps. XXXVII [38]). If your judgment can be a day—indeed, a noonday—how much more can the divine judgment be so? God’s judgments are days because they take place in the light of truth and in the brightness of rectitude. For “the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves.”

The number of such days is completed upon anyone afflicted when the severity of divine judgments is fulfilled in his chastisement. The end of such days comes when the punishment of divine severity is changed into mercy. Nebuchadnezzar received the end of these days in his humiliation, when divine compassion had already looked upon him. For if it had not looked upon him, he himself would not have lifted his eyes to heaven.

To lift one’s eyes to heaven is to think on heavenly and eternal things, and, setting aside care and anxiety about worldly things, to keep spiritual realities alone before one’s eyes. It is to look toward heaven, keep the region of light before one’s eyes, and fix the eyes of understanding with complete intent upon that light of eternity. He had already fixed his eyes there who said: “I considered the days of old, and kept the eternal years in mind” [Col. 1342C] (Ps. LXXVIII [77]).

But see: he who lifted his eyes to heaven recovered the understanding he had lost. Consider, then, how useful it is to lift one’s eyes to heaven in this manner. “I,” says Nebuchadnezzar, “lifted my eyes to heaven, and my understanding was restored to me.” The perception of the flesh is that of an animal; the perception of the mind is that of a human being. Animal perception distinguishes white from black; human perception distinguishes good from evil, truth from falsehood.

Those who call good evil and evil good, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter, darkness light and light darkness, lost this perception together with Nebuchadnezzar—or never possessed it. Those who judge between one day and another receive it in great measure; but those who judge every day receive it more fully. “One person,” says the Apostle, “judges between day and day; another judges every day” (Rom. XIV). Therefore one recovers one’s own understanding when one at last awakens to the judgment of discernment.

It is not said, however, that his understanding was given, but restored; hence it is evident that it had formerly been possessed but was lost. Lost understanding is restored to each person when the grace of discernment which that person had been accustomed to possess is renewed within. He receives understanding while lifting up his eyes, because the mind, while thinking upon eternal and heavenly things, awakens to the judgment of discernment. For while it gives intense attention to heavenly things, it sees how nothing is all that earthly and transient things which it loved. Whoever, therefore, longs for the grace of discernment should give attention to heavenly things, that he may recover [Col. 1343A] the light of his eyes; and, having recovered it, may cry aloud to his Lord and say: “What indeed have I in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?”

N e b u c h a d n e z z a r shows by the words that follow that he did not receive his understanding in vain.

## CHAPTER XLVI. How he glorifies God alone who had so shamelessly magnified himself.

“And I blessed,” he says, “the Most High.” See: he who had above magnified himself so shamelessly now glorifies him alone who, according to the Apostle, “is over all, God blessed for ever”: “And I praised and glorified him who lives for ever” (Rom. IX). He who lives for ever is, indeed, Life itself: he for whom being is nothing other than living, nor living anything other than being.

“Because his power is everlasting power”: because he who is almighty always can do what he can do once. “And his kingdom is from generation to generation”: because nothing is added to him from time and nothing withdrawn from him, with whom there is neither change nor shadow of variation. “And all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing before him.” Understand by inhabitants of earth lovers of earthly things, who neither know how to seek the things above nor can say with the Apostle: “But our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. III).

They are truly accounted as nothing because they have lost true being; indeed, it would be better for them not to exist at all than to exist thus—unless someone thinks it better to be miserable forever than not to exist at all. “He does according to his will, both among the powers of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and there is none who can resist his hand or say to him, ‘Why have you done this?’” The Psalmist’s saying agrees with this: “Whatever the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Ps. CXXXIV [135]).

Since Nebuchadnezzar himself says later in praise of God that all his works are true and his ways are judgments, why does he here say that God does all things according to his will? Certainly, if all his works are true, all things are done in truth; certainly, if all his ways are judgments, all things are done in equity. How, then, according to his will? Perhaps to be done according to equity is to be done according to his will; and precisely because something is done in equity, it is done according to his will. But if being done according to equity is altogether the same as being done according to his will, then his will is the same as equity, and equity the same as will.

“And there is none who can resist his hand or say, ‘Why have you done this?’” Who can resist him? Who can contradict him? For he does all things as powerfully as he does wisely; no one can restrain omnipotence or accuse supreme wisdom.

## CHAPTER XLVII. What proud self-glorification does, and what devout glorification accomplishes.

“At that same time,” he says, “my understanding returned to me; and I came to the honor and splendor of my kingdom, and my appearance returned to me” (Dan. IV). “At that same time,” he says: at the very time when I blessed God, when I praised and glorified him.

Certainly, if we remember well what was said above, there he fell when he magnified himself with excessive pride. See: that same man rises when he devoutly glorifies God, his Lord. You surely see what proud self-glorification does; you surely see what devout glorification accomplishes. Proud self-glorification deserves casting down; devout glorification, exaltation.

See: now that he glories not in himself but in the Lord, his understanding returns to himself. What he previously said—that his understanding was restored to him—he now says by stating that it returned to him. Or perhaps each person’s understanding returns to that person when the eye of discernment is recalled to self-examination. Understanding returns to itself when, by divine illumination, it is brought to consider and know its own merits.

[Col. 1344B] Therefore, while the human mind glorifies its God, its understanding returns to itself; for while it opens its eyes to that light of divinity and gazes intently upon it, it more fully recognizes the darkness of its own weakness. “Come to him,” says the Psalmist, “and be enlightened” (Ps. XXXIII [34]). What wonder that, by approaching light, we are enlightened? What wonder that light is kindled from light? “And in your light,” he says, “we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV [36]).

Light is seen in light when, through the knowledge and operation of divine brightness, the mind is more fully enlightened to know human weakness. Yet these two kinds of knowledge usually provide alternating increases to one another, and each truly grows out of the other. For through knowledge of God the mind advances to reflection upon itself, and likewise through much knowledge of itself it grows in knowledge of God.

But see: when the understanding which had been lost returns, he recovers the kingdom which he had lost. Without doubt, unless the grace of discernment is restored within him, the mind is never brought to the full integrity of virtue.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. How discipline of character is usually reformed through discerning judgment and watchfulness over oneself.
