“I came,” he says, “to the honor and splendor of my kingdom.” Clearly, a human being receives and holds a kingdom by divine gift when he is now able to restrain evil movements of the heart from evil. But this kingdom becomes honorable when, by God’s gift, he is now able to exercise good movements of the heart in good. It is further endowed with fitting splendor when every good thing done within it is ordered with the highest moderation and great discernment.

Therefore he receives and possesses a kingdom who bravely tames and manfully restrains the rebellious movements of the mind. And then such a person “will judge among the nations, fill up ruins, [Col. 1344D] and shatter heads over many lands.” His kingdom is also then honorable, when he becomes the Lord of hosts amid so great a multitude of countless virtues; having soldiers under him, he says to this one, “Go,” and he goes; to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to his servant, “Do this,” and he does it.

This kingdom is especially adorned when he governs all things, conducting himself modestly, with gentleness and tranquility: “My son,” it says, “perform your works in gentleness, and you shall be loved above human glory” (Ecclus. XIII). Thus the honor of the kingdom is to act powerfully; its splendor is to act wisely—so that in this kingdom, its possessor may “reach from end to end mightily and order all things sweetly.”

“And my appearance returned to me.” Appearance is an external quality, namely the outward form of the body. Bodily discipline belongs to external quality, just as the ordering of the mind belongs to internal quality. Therefore, by appearance, which consists in bodily features, one rightly understands discipline of the body, the form of religious life, and the bearing and ordering of the outward person. Appearance returns when the form of religious life, lost for a time, is restored according to its former practice. When understanding returns, appearance returns, because through discerning judgment and watchfulness over oneself, discipline of character is either newly established or an old discipline is renewed.

## CHAPTER XLIX. How a fallen mind ought to examine itself and renew itself in its former fervor.

N e b u c h a d n e z z a r further adds and says: “And my nobles and my magistrates sought me out, and I was restored to my kingdom, and greater magnificence was added to me” (Dan. IV). See by whom he is sought and restored to his kingdom: “my nobles and my magistrates.” What is noble in a person except good intentions? And who should exercise governance, or order that inner kingdom, except discerning deliberations?

Thus, by the nobles of the mind we understand intentions, and by magistrates, deliberations. What is it for such nobles and magistrates to seek the lost head of the kingdom and restore it to its place, except with utmost intention and deliberation to investigate how, after a fall, the lost strength of the mind may be restored, even if late, to its original soundness?

The soul ought at times diligently to inquire what it was like, how steadfastly it acted, and what measure of perfection it attained. It should next deliberate how it may be restored to its former state; and this, I think, is to seek by intention that royal dignity of the mind and desire to restore it to its rank.

[Col. 1345D] They sought this royal dignity in another’s heart and desired it to be restored to its place, believing it cast down, when they said: “Where is your fear, and your strength, your patience, and the perfection of your ways?” (Job IV). Not only those who fall into evil, but also those who grow lukewarm in good, ought to examine themselves and renew within themselves that former fervor of religious life. Hence it is written to the angel of Ephesus in the Apocalypse: “I have something against you: that you have abandoned your first love. Remember from where you have fallen, repent, and do the first works” (Apoc. II).

Yet it should certainly be noted that this king is said to have been sought by his own people, not restored by them. But who, I ask, restored him except him toward whom he lifted his eyes, whom he blessed and glorified? For even if it may now be in our power, by deliberation, to inquire what the state of our mind is at present or has been in the past, it is not likewise in our power to repair the losses of our virtue at will. But if we diligently carry out what we have already received power to do by divine gift, perhaps that also will be added which we have not yet been able to do. “And I was restored,” he says, “to my kingdom, and greater magnificence was added to me.”

## CHAPTER L. How, through the virtue of humility, the mind is strengthened in good and established in perseverance in good.

Greater magnificence is added after a fall for full restoration, because a person is often instructed in true humility by that very fall. Magnificence is then truly increased when, among the great works of virtues, the virtue of humility too is steadfastly preserved. Through the virtue of humility, the mind’s progress is both strengthened in good and made firm for perseverance in good.

Thus magnificence is truly increased when, for the completion of good, the grace of perseverance is also given. The increase of magnificence is the virtue of perseverance; the increase of greatness, through the addition of humility’s virtue, is the divinely given grace of strengthening. The Prophet requested this increase of magnificence when he prayed in song: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a sovereign spirit” (Ps. L [51]). We seek such an increase every day when we say: “Strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us” (Ps. LXVII [68]).

[Col. 1346C] From these things, I think, you see that many fall by God’s dispensation in order to rise again stronger; and those who before their fall possessed only assisting grace receive, after the restoration from ruin, strengthening grace as well. Truly, as it is written: “The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to hell and brings back” (1 Sam. II). Truly, he is the one who humbles and raises up, he who strikes in order to heal (Job V).

## CHAPTER LI. How and to what end God ought to be praised.

“Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise, magnify, and glorify the King of heaven, because all his works are true, and his ways are judgments, and he can humble those who walk in pride” (Dan. IV).

Above, as we have already heard, he blessed, praised, and magnified. Here again he praises, magnifies, and glorifies. Above he praised when he received understanding; and because he was not ungrateful for divine benefits, he deserved to be advanced to greater things. For he received his lost kingdom together with an increase of magnificence. Having received the kingdom, he again praises and again magnifies. Thus it came about that he would not again disgracefully lose what he had received in humiliation and now possessed with devotion.

When you receive a benefit, praise also, that you may deserve to advance to greater things. When raised to higher things, praise nonetheless, that you may deserve to persevere in them. If, in Nebuchadnezzar’s likeness, you have recovered your understanding, if you have been able to understand what ought to be done, praise and glorify, so that you may be granted by inspiring grace to accomplish what you received power to understand by revealing grace.

If, in the likeness of that same Nebuchadnezzar, you have recovered your kingdom—if you have been able to rule your passions and have received the ability to exercise good affections in good—praise, magnify, and glorify, so that, having received the grace of progress, you may receive likewise the grace of perseverance. Therefore gladly praise him who is supremely good; glorify him who is supremely blessed; magnify him who is immeasurable in majesty and infinite in eternity.

“For all his works are true, and his ways are judgments.” His works are his ways: the ways, I say, by which he comes to us, the ways by which he makes himself known and manifests himself to our understanding. For by his works we advance to knowledge of him. Therefore all his works are true because all his ways are judgments, and all are true because they are made in truth.

[Col. 1347B] We often err in our judgments; hence we often acquit the guilty and condemn the innocent. But he from whom nothing can be hidden cannot err in his judgment. Yet since it is written, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV [25]), are even those things judgments which he himself does mercifully? But beyond all contradiction, that divine mercy does not abandon the bounds of equity in anything it mercifully bestows.

When we are moved by compassion, we often overstep the limits of equity, and in what we believe we are granting as mercy, we often act against justice. But heavenly mercy so dispenses its works of compassion that in all these things it does nothing against justice and commits no iniquity. Therefore his ways are judgments, because they do not depart from equity’s constancy and justice’s rectitude.

“And he can humble those who walk in pride.” Why, I ask, does he say that he can do this alone, of him of whom it is truly certain that he can do all things? But perhaps, because one should believe the experienced person, he wished to express especially what he had proved in himself by a third personal experience. Or perhaps he wished above all to impress upon our minds what it is most beneficial to retain in memory. We know that “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X). We know that “before ruin the heart is exalted” (Prov. XVI). Therefore, whoever fears a collapse of character must above all keep watch against pride.

It is especially effective for crushing pride and preserving true humility always to retain in one’s mind that he who is accustomed to resist the proud can, whenever he wills, humble those who walk in pride. Nebuchadnezzar taught them by word and us by example that he can humble those who walk in pride, in whatever way and whenever he wills.

# BOOK III

[Col. 1347]

## CHAPTER I. On the threefold vice of changeability and the inconstancy of the mind.

[Col. 1347C]

“I was looking in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were fighting upon the great sea. And four great beasts, different from one another, were coming up from the sea. The first was like a lioness and had eagle’s wings. I watched until its wings were plucked out, and it was lifted up from the earth. And it stood upon its feet like a human being, and a human heart was given to it” (Dan. VII).

Let us now see what this great sea is in which the prophet Daniel saw this conflict of winds, whatever it may be. Who does not know how unstable and restless the sea is, always moved by every condition and impulse of the winds? Therefore, if I am not mistaken, it fittingly figures the changeability and inconstancy of the heart, because it is truly like a wave of the sea moved and driven about by the wind.

This evil is threefold. There is changeability of purpose, changeability of promise, and likewise changeability of vow. A purpose is what a person determines within oneself; a promise is what one determines in relation to one’s neighbor; a vow is what one determines, as it were, in relation to God. Concerning changeability of purpose is the saying: “The sluggard wills and does not will” (Prov. XIII). Hear also how changeability of promise is rebuked in the statement: “Clouds and wind, and rain not following: a boastful man who does not fulfill promises” (Prov. XXIII).

He who says, “If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay to fulfill it, for the unfaithful and foolish promise displeases God” (Eccles. III), wished us to guard against the changeability of vow. A foolish promise is one made concerning something which it is not permitted to do, or which God forbids to be done. A foolish promise concerns something which it is not expedient to do: when someone either exceeds the bounds of moderation or presumes something contrary to obedience. Of such vows Scripture says that “the vows of fools must be broken.”

Yet those who have bound themselves by such a vow ought not to break such a bond at their own pleasure, but they must be released at the judgment of those who have received and possess the power of binding and loosing. An unfaithful promise is one followed by repentance or accompanied by duplicity of heart. Therefore it is good to vow good things, and to vow them well, lest the promise be foolish. It is good also to fulfill well-made promises completely, lest the promise be unfaithful: “Vow,” he says, “and render to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him” (Ps. CLXXV [76]). Otherwise, it is better not to vow than not to fulfill vows (Eccles. V).

In changeability of purpose, the vice of an inconstant mind is noted; in changeability of promise, scandal to one’s neighbor; in changeability of vow, contempt and injury to God. Thus the first evil changeability is bad, the second worse, and the third worst of all. Oh, how bitter this final evil is above the rest; how fearful and troubled it makes the human conscience!

[Col. 1349A] This is that stormy water of the sea: restless through fear and salty through bitterness. This is the great sea we seek, in comparison with which any of the others is reckoned as nothing. We have identified the sea; it remains to investigate the winds and their conflict.

What is this conflict of winds except the strong assault and violence of temptations? For human life upon earth is temptation. Hence we are rightly commanded—or admonished: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II). The different winds of heaven are the contrary affections of the mind. Desire breathes one way, anger blows another; confidence and distrust likewise blow in different ways.

Who does not recognize from experience how desire breathes and pants, how violently it shakes the mind, how forcefully it inclines it toward what it seeks? “Each person is tempted,” indeed, “being drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (Jas. I). But often, amid desire’s strong heats and violent assaults, the mind returns to itself, reproves itself, and sharply rebukes itself. It is angry with itself and indignant at itself; and anger, blowing from the opposite direction, strongly resists and struggles against the gusts of desire.

He who said, “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV), wished such gusts and rebounds of anger to take place. Thus the gusts of desire and anger often clash with one another and rise against each other. Each of us is accustomed to experience and must endure the conflict of such alternating blasts as long as “the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh.”

[Col. 1349C] For although desire sometimes appears to be quiet, even for a short time, it begins again and again to rise and attack more fiercely. “The land of Judah,” Scripture says, “was quiet for a few days” (1 Macc. VII). If land—even the land of Judah—can scarcely be quiet for a few days, how much less the sea? For what is signified by the sea except an unstable heart? And what more fittingly by the land—namely, the solid and immovable element—than a firm and stable heart? If, therefore, a stable heart rarely rests, and only for a few days, what wonder if a restless and slippery heart, such as is denoted by the great sea, rarely falls silent and scarcely does so even for a few moments?

That fiercely burning wind—namely desire, breathing and blazing—often rises more violently after momentary calm, drives more forcefully than usual, and almost overturns the mind’s stability. The mind begins to grow weary, nearly to fail, to despair of perseverance, and to fall into distrust. When the wind of distrust blows, the mind often comes into more wretched danger than could result from any assaults of desire.

For one must greatly fear lest that violent wind suddenly rush in from the region of the desert and, shaking the house of conscience, overturn the whole state of the mind. “Who can stand before its cold?” Unless perhaps, as often happens, God breathes and contrary gusts rise from the opposite direction.

[Col. 1350A] For after much trembling of distrust and excessive weariness, it often happens that the mind at last returns to conscience, has recourse to divine mercy, casts its care upon the Lord, restores constancy, and only late and with difficulty recovers confidence. From then on confidence and distrust begin to rebel and fight strongly against each other, to drive with contrary blasts, and by turns now this, now that, to gain the upper hand.

This, if I am not mistaken, is the conflict of winds which the prophet Daniel saw and described in mystical language, and which perhaps experience itself has taught some of you what it is like. And would that I knew and could describe it as usefully as I have certainly experienced what it is like. But let us see what sometimes follows this conflict of winds. Let us see what kinds of monsters that great sea of which we spoke above may bring forth.

## CHAPTER II. What kind and degree of conflict of temptation arises from inconstancy of mind.

“Four great beasts,” he says, “were coming up from the sea, different from one another.” What, I ask, is it for beasts to come up from the sea after a conflict of winds, except for beastly movements and irrational impulses to arise from the instability of the heart after the violence of temptations and burst forth openly?

For one who lives beastially, as it were puts on a beastly form. Without doubt, one who lives irrationally and beastially is beastly insofar as one is irrational. What are individual vices but certain beasts? What are perverse desires but beasts? Such beasts tear apart character, slaughter virtues, and suffocate souls.

The Psalmist feared the attacks of such beasts when, singing in prayer and praying in song, he said: “Do not deliver to beasts the souls confessing you” (Ps. LXXIII [74]). There are beasts which kill the body but cannot do anything to the soul. Yet holy persons, such as they are, need not greatly fear these—especially those who, by voluntary resolve, “are put to death all day,” lest they seem to incur that prophetic reproach: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear.”

“Do not deliver,” he says, “to the beast souls confessing you” (Ps. XIII [14]). He does not say, “the bodies of those confessing you,” nor “the flesh of those confessing you,” but “Do not deliver to beasts souls confessing you.” Those, indeed, are the beasts truly to be feared which can kill souls.

[Col. 1350D] We quickly encounter the attacks of such beasts when, as our merits require, we lose the light of divine illumination: “You have made darkness, and night has come; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through” (Ps. CIII [104]). The Lord threatens those who presume upon themselves and boast in their own merits with the attacks of such beasts when he speaks through the Prophet in the song of Deuteronomy: “I will send the teeth of beasts upon them” (Deut. XXXVIII [32]).

It remains now to ask why these beasts are said to be only four, and how they differ from one another.

## CHAPTER III. That the manner of beastly living is fourfold.

[Col. 1351A]

To state briefly what I think: every mode of living bestially seems to me to be fourfold. Some appear to practise good things, but without moderation or measure and without any discernment. And although perhaps they have a good intention, this is beastly in them: that they live without measure and rush headlong on, without the judgment of reason and without counsel. And although perhaps they have zeal for rectitude, they do not have it according to knowledge. Others, however, practise evil, but timidly, and therefore secretly; and so, according to the Psalmist’s words, “they will dwell and hide themselves” (Ps. 55), because they fear reproof or are ashamed of being caught. Others again practise good in outward action, [Col. 1351B] but indeed hypocritically and without any good intention: such as those who love the chief places at banquets, the first seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men. Others again practise evils everywhere, openly and freely, without any fear or shame, so that they appear to be without a brow, because a harlot’s brow has been made theirs and they do not know how to blush.

You see, then, how different such workers are from one another. The first and third occupy themselves with good things; the second and fourth, with evil things. The first and third do good, but not well: the first indiscreetly, the third deceptively, and thus they differ from one another. Both the second and the fourth occupy themselves with evil; but the former secretly, the latter as openly as shamelessly, and therefore they too differ among themselves. The first are those who “walk in things great and wonderful above themselves” [Col. 1351C] (Ps. 130). The second are those who “sit in ambush with the rich in secret places, that they may kill the innocent” (Ps. 10). The third are those who “do all their works in order to be seen by men” (Matt. 23). The fourth, however, are those who “neither fear God nor respect men” (Luke 18). Thus in the first is undiscerning religion; in the second, hidden transgression; in the third, feigned religion; in the fourth, manifest transgression. These are the four states of those who live irrationally and bestially—if indeed they should be called states rather than falls—which always drive a person from bad to worse.

And it should be noted that, among these four degrees of corruption, the second is worse than the first, the third than the second, and the fourth is worst of all. [Col. 1351D] Perhaps someone may doubt how the third is worse than the second. But what is the third state other than simulated righteousness? Yet, as Augustine testifies, we have learned that simulated righteousness is not righteousness but double iniquity.

## CHAPTER IV. The degrees of corruption through which the human mind often falls.

In the first state, then, there is foolish justice; in the second, unbridled malice; in the third, counterfeit justice; in the fourth, unrestrained malice. In the first reigns singularity; in the second, impiety; in the third, cunning; in the fourth, cruelty. In the first, I say, singularity reigns, and it is said of it: “Woe to one who is alone, because when he falls he has no one [Col. 1352A] to raise him up” (Eccl. 4). Woe, I say, to one who is alone: that is, to one who presumes upon himself alone and upon his own counsel, and lives in a certain solitary presumption. In the second impiety reigns, and of it it is said: “Woe to the ungodly unto evil” (Isa. 3). In the third cunning reigns. The cunning provoke God’s wrath, and it is said of them: “Woe to the double-hearted person, who enters the land by two ways” (Ecclus. 2). In the fourth cruelty reigns, and the cruel are told: “Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself also be plundered?” (Isa. 33).

Cruelty is robbery; robbery is when someone takes another’s possessions. What do you think of one who sows discord among brothers? The person who takes your money acts impiously toward you; but what of one who takes away your peace? Does one who takes away your garment act cruelly, [Col. 1352B] and does not one who takes away your charity act much more cruelly? But if it is cruel to take from a person external, perishable goods, much more cruel will it be to take from a person inward goods, goods that remain for eternity. For “charity never fails” (2 Cor. 13). Without doubt, one who takes charity from a person takes God away as well: “for God is charity” (1 John 4). “Woe to you who plunder: will you not be plundered?” As much as you take, so much you lose. You take God away and lose God. You take heaven away and forfeit heaven. What is crueller than this impiety? What is more mad than this cruelty?

See from where and to where one arrives; see likewise the path by which one descends. “From where,” you ask, “and to where?” From the highest singularity to the utmost cruelty. “But by what path,” you ask, “and how?” Through impiety and duplicity. From the first [Col. 1352C] degree one descends to the second, from the second to the third, from the third to the fourth. For undoubtedly, cast-down presumption is accustomed to produce envy; despised envy, pretence; cast-down pretence, unrestrainedness of mind. Presumption belongs to the first state; envy to the second; pretence to the third; unrestrainedness of mind to the fourth. Insolence belongs to the first; enviousness to the second; fraudulence to the third; shamelessness to the fourth. And perhaps these are the beasts which it was necessary to seek.

## CHAPTER V. On the vice of insolence.

In the description of the first beast, therefore, we understand the vice of insolence. We call something *insolitum*—as it were, “unaccustomed”—what is not customary or is contrary to custom; and from this we think *insolentia*, “insolence,” is named. Insolence is therefore rightly called that condition in which one presumes everywhere and rashly beyond what is customary. Thus the vice of insolence is headlong and rash presumption, or headlong and presumptuous rashness, beyond what is customary. This evil is manifold. For insolence sometimes raises itself above what is customary, sometimes holds itself below what is customary, and sometimes sets itself against what is customary.

But let us now see how Holy Scripture describes this first beast, and how aptly it expresses the characteristic of insolence. “The first,” it says, “was like a lioness, and had the wings of an eagle.” A lion is said to be so fierce that, when provoked, it does not fear even death—so much so that it does not restrain the onset of its rage even because of mortal danger. “The lion,” it says, “strongest of beasts, will fear no encounter” [Col. 1353A] (Prov. 30). You see in the lion how foolish is its boldness and how bold its foolishness. Does it not seem like lion-like audacity, in order to make a name for oneself, to walk in things great and wonderful above oneself, to presume everything beyond one’s strength, to scorn the counsel of teachers and despise the command of elders, to extend fasts, vigils, and observances of that kind beyond measure, and neither spare one’s bodily health nor dread the death of the soul in contempt of due obedience?

Note that it is compared not to a lion but to a lioness, because this sex is found more headstrong and stubborn in the violence of its onset. See, then, how irrational, beastly, and truly lion-like it is to yield to no counsel [Col. 1353B] and no command, but stubbornly persist in the boldness of one’s own rashness. Do you wish also briefly to hear what I think concerning the wings of such a beast? One seems to me to be precipitancy, the other presumption. Behold two wings, both eagle’s wings. Who does not know of the eagle that it is accustomed to fly more swiftly and more loftily than almost all other birds? In precipitancy observe the swiftness of flight; in presumption consider its loftiness. It has already been said above that insolence is headlong and presumptuous rashness beyond what is customary. Therefore, to draw together in concise brevity what has been said more diffusely, recognize the lion-like character in the rashness of singularity. Observe in the eagle’s wings the vice of presumption [Col. 1353C] and the vice of precipitancy.

The eagle is called king of birds and the lion king of beasts. Does not that person therefore seem to have something of the lioness and something of the eagle who presumes, in both the active and contemplative life, to precede everyone and to hold a singular and highest place in each life? On earth he is a lioness; in heaven, an eagle: he who presumes to advance more vigorously and fly more loftily than all others—to advance through action and fly through contemplation.

## CHAPTER VI. The degrees of insolence by which the human mind is gradually corrupted.

But let us now see what Solomon thinks of such a person, who does everything precipitately and presumptuously, who observes neither measure [Col. 1353D] nor moderation in his undertakings: “He who is hasty with his feet stumbles” (Prov. 19). Hence elsewhere he says: “An inheritance hastily acquired in the beginning shall lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20). The following addition concerning the aforesaid beast seems to accord with the same meaning: “I watched until its wings were plucked out; and it was lifted from the earth and stood on its feet like a man, and a heart was given to it.”

See how those who presume about themselves beyond measure gradually lose the very things from which they swell with pride and despise others. First the wings are plucked out; afterward the beast’s body itself is lifted from the earth. First the grace of the contemplative life is lost; afterwards, that of the active life also. For what is it to lose one’s wings except to lose those lofty flights of contemplation? When, after many excesses of fasting and vigils, the body begins to waste away and the head to ache, whether one wishes it or not, one must lay aside the wings, return to the earth, and attend to the body’s care. It is better that they be laid aside voluntarily than torn off unwillingly. What is it for wings to be plucked out except to lose them with great pain and without any hope of recovery? Wings are plucked out when the boldness of precipitancy and presumption is cut short by pressing illness and compelling necessity. Does not the Lord threaten such plucking out of wings when he speaks through the prophet: “Though you are exalted like an eagle and place your nest among the stars of heaven, from there I will draw you down, says the Lord” [Col. 1354A] (Obad. 1)?

After the plucking out of its wings, it is lifted from the earth. Thus through an elevation of mind, and because of mental pride, it is shaken from the earth. And rightly so, I think, because through swelling with pride, bursting, wasting away, and rotting, they may nevertheless at some time become like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth. Thus, after the loss of wings, dwelling on earth too is lost, because after the grace of contemplation has been withdrawn, as was said, the grace of doing good is also withdrawn from the proud soul. And the one who formerly presumed to go vigorously before everyone must now begin to follow behind everyone and at last remain behind. The one who formerly stretched himself beyond the customary through insolence subsequently remains short of the customary; and so he falls from the first degree of insolence into the second—eventually, I fear, to fall back from the second into the third.

But where, I ask, will the beast now be after being cast down from heaven, its wings [Col. 1354B] lost, and lifted from earth? Will it perhaps return to where it came from and descend again into the sea, though it rose from the sea? So indeed, so often, what is presumed from the lightness of the heart afterwards ends in much mental turbulence and bitterness. And this perhaps is to lose the earth: to lose every stability of one’s purpose, and, bearing one’s humiliation unworthily, to incur excessive bitterness of heart. Thus one passes from earth into the sea; thus mountains are moved into the heart of the sea. For what is it for mountains to pass into the heart of the sea, except to fall from the summit of great endeavour into the inmost malice of the heart? For according to the testimony of Truth, “because iniquity abounds, the charity of many will grow cold” (Matt. 24). Therefore no one, however lofty his virtues, ought to presume anything from his own powers, but everything from the Lord, and to sing with the Psalmist: “Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the sea” [Col. 1354C] (Ps. 25). Mountains are indeed moved then, when John’s saying is fulfilled: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2).

## CHAPTER VII. How from the vice of insolence a person falls into the vice of enviousness.

But if no place now remains for this beast except the sea—for it appears to have lost both heaven and earth—it is remarkable how it is said to have stood upon its feet. Perhaps it is thought to have stood upon some crag or rock, where it was surrounded on every side by the sea and continually battered by marine waves. O how harsh a punishment, yet one worthy of presumptuous singularity! Behold, the creature which formerly presumed to outrun everyone and wear itself out through its own presumption now has nowhere to go and finds no way to rest. “And it stood on its feet like a man.” Would that, even late, it might cease to think itself an angel and finally at some time stop presuming to be above a human being. Behold: having put off the angel, it no longer flies on high but walks in low places; indeed, it no longer walks but stands, having lost love and hope of making progress. Yet it does not lie down; it stands, so as never to rest. Therefore it continually stands, because it labours without interruption. It tires its feet without walking and labours without fruit. It stands, then—but how? Upon its feet, like a man.

It is a great spectacle but a hideous [Col. 1355A] marvel to see a four-footed beast, indeed a lion-like form, rear itself upon two feet against heaven and stand erect against nature. What is this monstrous erectness except a certain enormous and utterly detestable pride? One raises oneself against God who swells against the heavenly majesty. Does not one swell against God who censures his judgments? And who does not know how presumptuous minds tend to murmur against divine chastisements, envy the progress of others, and bear impatiently the losses of their own glory? They murmur not only against God’s justice but also against God’s goodness: against his justice in their own evils, against his goodness in the goods of others. For the insolent mind, greedy for its own excellence, when through excessive pride it falls into enviousness, almost more painfully bears another’s progress than its own failure.

O monstrous presumption, which therefore murmurs against the divine majesty because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Luke 4). “Is your eye evil,” he says, “because I am good?” (Matt. 20). Those who are of this kind are accustomed to weave certain seemingly reasonable complaints and to represent the causes of their murmuring—though they are truly irrational—as though they were just. And perhaps this is to raise the beastly form to a human likeness: in irrational murmuring against God, to wish to put forward something like reasons. The following statement concerning [Col. 1355B] this beast seems to agree with this interpretation. For after it had been said, “It stood upon its feet like a man,” it is immediately added: “and a heart was given to it.”

Whose heart? Either a human heart or a lioness’s heart. But why is the lioness said to have received its own heart, which it is not said to have lost? It received the heart of a human being who is carnally wise when, with God permitting, it falls into the prudence of the flesh; or it truly receives a human heart when, through much experience, it understands its error and more fully recognizes both its own failure and others’ progress. But what is divinely granted to a human being for good, that same human being often abuses for evil. Having recognized the unequal merits of itself or others, from which it ought to be pierced with penitence, it grows instead into greater enviousness. For behold, after the lioness described has received a human heart, it is succeeded not by a lamb but by a bear. For a heart greedy for glory and jaundiced with envy often falls into enviousness when it sees others’ glory and its own disgrace. Thus vice succeeds vice: insolence comes first and enviousness follows; and, what is worse, insolence does not depart.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the vice of enviousness.

*Invidentia* seems to convey something more than *invidia* (“envy”). Just as one is not correctly called “reading” except at the time when one is engaged in reading, so one is correctly called *invidens* (“being envious”) at the time when one is affected by envy. From *invidens* comes *invidentia*. Thus envy truly grows into enviousness when it agitates the mind to such an extent that it allows it almost no time at all to rest. Enviousness, therefore, is frequent envy which does not allow the mind to rest.

In the second beast, then, enviousness is rightly understood, unless I am mistaken. But, that this may become clearer, let us hear how prophetic speech describes it: “And behold,” it says, “another beast, like a bear; it stood on one side, and there were three rows in its mouth and in its teeth; and thus they said to it: ‘Rise, devour much flesh’” [Col. 1356A] (Dan. 7). As we all know, the bear is a misshapen animal, accustomed to live in remote and hidden places; and in this very respect it bears the form of envy. For envy itself too, as though ashamed of its ugliness, always seeks to hide. The bear is also a malicious and savage animal, and perhaps the vice of envy is such. Envy is hatred of another’s happiness; and what is more malicious? What, then, is envy other than a light-fleeing and lurking malice? Enviousness, however, is malice burning and raging in secret.

The bear is a very restless animal, so that, when tied to a post, it almost never ceases either to go round and round or, with its feet fixed, to toss its head now in this direction and now in that. In this it bears the form not merely of envy but of enviousness, which allows the mind almost no moment of rest. This beast is said to have stood on one side. Thus a person in this state does not yet abandon good things altogether; yet neither does he, as in the former state, extend himself to all of them. He stands on one side because he appears still to persist in certain good things. [Col. 1356B] For no one suddenly becomes utterly vile, just as, conversely, no one suddenly becomes perfect. Thus he still in some way stands in part, since an old habit still draws a person to do certain good things. Behold how, in this state, the mind is not yet unrestrained in open malice, insofar as it is either restricted by fear or held back by shame.

## CHAPTER IX. The stages through which the evil of enviousness tends to increase.

“And there were three rows,” it says, “in its mouth and in its teeth.” Scripture itself defines how the three rows were in its mouth, that is, in its teeth. And what can we understand more rightly by teeth than the bites of malice and enviousness? Who does not know how customary, familiar, and, as it were, especially proper to envy it is to gnaw at another’s life and tear it to pieces with the bites of hostile criticism? This evil tends to increase by certain stages. For among human beings some things are plainly evil, while others are doubtful, so that it may be uncertain whether they are good or evil. The envious mind is accustomed always to exaggerate manifest evils more extensively, to interpret every doubtful matter in the worse sense, and, since it cannot deny evident goods, to obscure them by every art it can and to diminish something in them.

The first is hostile criticism; the second, disparagement; the third, detraction. Hostile criticism is when biting and reproachful speech concerns, or is made on account of, an evil truly present in a person. One who knows what it means to ask may, from its opposite, recognize what it means to disparage, since these answer one another by contraries just as persuading and dissuading do. Does not disparagement seem to you to occur when a person who has a good opinion of another is told: “Do not believe so; do not think so; you are mistaken; you are deceived; it is far otherwise than you think; you take darkness for light and make bitter into sweet”? This certainly has no place where goods are evident, because what is manifest cannot be bent to the opposite sense. But to detract is to wish to diminish something from evident goods when one cannot entirely nullify them. For one detracts who, by snarling, takes something away from that by which he believes a person’s reputation is made more glorious. Thus hostile criticism is the dissemination of a bad opinion; disparagement, the nullification of a good opinion; detraction, the weakening of a good opinion.

The Psalmist feared a hostile tongue when he said: “All day my shame is before me, and confusion of face has covered me, because of the voice of the reproacher and hostile critic” [Col. 1357A] (Ps. 43). He touches upon disparagers when elsewhere he says: “They hunted for the soul of the righteous and condemned innocent blood” (Ps. 93). He describes detractors when he says: “Those who render evils for goods were detracting from me, because I followed goodness” (Ps. 37). Thus you have the three rows of teeth in the multiplicity of detractions, disparagements, and hostile criticisms.

## CHAPTER X. How from the vice of enviousness the mind falls into the vice of fraudulence.

It is now easy to see how fittingly the final words are applied to this beast: “Rise, devour much flesh.” For what is it to eat flesh except to tear another’s weaknesses with a malicious tooth? Those who gladly gnaw at another’s life, zealously devote themselves to disparagements, and delightfully pick at their neighbours’ weaknesses—what else do they do but eat flesh? The Prophet already knew such devourers of flesh through experience when he said: “Evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh” [Col. 1357B] (Ps. 26). But when it says, “Rise, devour,” what, I ask, is this: a command or a permission, a suggestion or an incitement? If we suppose it spoken by good angels, then consistently we should understand in their words permission alone. Such is what is said to Judas: “What you are doing, do quickly” (John 13). But if it is established that it was spoken by evil angels, we may understand in such words both suggestion and incitement. For evil spirits always suggest evil things to malicious minds and incite them to every evil.

How malicious and how destructive it is to serve detractions and to gratify one’s own vice in this respect may be learned from Solomon’s saying: “If a serpent bites in silence, he who secretly detracts is no less harmful” (Ecclus. 10). Does not what the Psalmist says of such people agree with this: “Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they dealt deceitfully; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 5)? O evil detestable and deadly alike to speaker and hearer: “Rise,” it says, “devour much flesh.” And what else does a bear, what else does this savage beast know, except either to suck its own paws or to tear another’s flesh? What other office, I ask, does the monster of enviousness perform except either to lament its own afflictions or to carp at another’s weaknesses? But would that they tore flesh only; would that they at least spared the bones! Now, however, they mangle all, tear all; and so at last they become hateful to everyone. For one who speaks, I say, cannot remain hidden. But when they begin to be recognized, they begin likewise to be despised and hated.

But how great, do you suppose, is the pain that burns the envious and proud mind; with how great an envy is it tormented when it sees others advance day by day to better things, while it sees itself daily decline in all reputation and become more and more [Col. 1357C] contemptible? Hence it often turns to cunning contrivances, as it seeks with utmost zeal and anxiety how it may either enlarge its own glory or cloud that of others. Thus from that point it begins to feign holiness and gradually, through hypocrisy, to surrender itself to every fraudulence. Thus the leopard succeeds the bear, while the slippery mind flows from vice to vice and falls through the evil of enviousness into fraudulence.

## CHAPTER XI. On the vice of fraudulence.

Then without doubt fraud grows into fraudulence when, from abundant malice, it comes about that the mind altogether wishes gladly to deceive whenever it can; and when, after much use and practice, it moreover possesses such great cunning that it can easily deceive whenever it wishes. For what else is fraudulence except cunning malice, as prone as it is ready for every fraud? The fraudulence of hypocrites is aptly represented by the leopard, whose whole body is sprinkled with certain spots. For hypocrites indeed outwardly display holiness in their conduct; but what they love is perverse, and what lives within in their affection must sometime break forth and appear in action. Those who are such therefore do good openly and evil secretly. Those who secretly break out into deeds of dissolution, or whenever possible plausibly do so, what else do they do except sprinkle the body of their action with certain spots? Let us therefore see [Col. 1358A] what this beast is said to be like, which is described third. “After these things,” it says, “I was looking, and behold another like a leopard; it had four wings of a bird upon it, and the beast had four heads, and authority was given to it” (Dan. 7).

Observe how rightly those signified in this beast are said to have wings. Certainly when birds fly, they raise themselves above themselves. Certainly when they wish to fly, they suspend themselves in empty space. Do not minds of this kind raise themselves above themselves and suspend themselves in emptiness when, for the sake of ambition and empty glory, they extend observances of harsh discipline almost beyond the measure of human possibility? For to pursue the studies of virtue and not care for or seek either the merits or rewards of virtues—what else is that except to suspend oneself on high in emptiness? And what else is it to have many heads except to do nothing simply? For just as we understand activity and exercise in the wings, so in the head we understand intention. For the head governs the whole body, and every one of our actions serves intention.

## CHAPTER XII. How multifarious the evil of fraudulence is in action.

Do you wish to know still more fully what wings fraudulence is accustomed to have? To state briefly what I think: let one be called simulation, another dissimulation, a third ostentation, a fourth excuse-making. For minds given to pretence and serving hypocrisy are accustomed, I say, not only to boast of what they possess, but even to pretend to possess [Col. 1358B] goods which they do not possess at all. Conversely, they are accustomed cunningly to excuse manifest evils, and craftily to conceal hidden evils as though they had none at all. Simulation and dissimulation concern hidden matters: simulation, hidden goods; dissimulation, hidden evils. Conversely, ostentation and excuse-making are accustomed to concern manifest matters: the former, manifest goods; the latter, manifest evils. For in goods that are manifest and cannot be denied, ostentation has a place, just as excuse-making is sought only in manifest evils.

Our left hand is brought into public less often than the right and, for that very reason, is seen less often. Thus we rightly understand more hidden things by the left hand, and more manifest things by the right. Therefore the wings of simulation and dissimulation appear to belong to the left, just as the wings of ostentation and excuse-making belong to the right. Thus in ostentation and simulation you have the first pair of wings. Likewise, in excuse-making and dissimulation you have the second pair. For ostentation and simulation concern goods alone: the former, true and manifest goods, like a wing on the right; the latter, fictitious goods, like a wing on the left. With these two wings they fly and, commending themselves to their neighbours and making their reputation known, spread their glory everywhere.

But excuse-making and dissimulation concern evils alone: the former, manifest evils, like one wing on the right; the latter, hidden evils, like the other wing on the left. Just as with the first two, as has been said, they fly, so with these latter two they cover their body. For without doubt pretenders and hypocrites are accustomed on either side to cover their rear and more dishonourable parts under a covering of excuse-making and dissimulation [Col. 1358C].

## CHAPTER XIII. How manifold the evil of fraudulence is in intention.

Behold, concerning the number of wings, let us consider also the plurality of heads. We know that the fraudulence of hypocrites, in everything it does, pants after the advancement of its own honour. For everything it does or intends in doing serves ambition. But ambition is nothing other than the pursuit of honour. The first kind of this evil is the pursuit of freedom; the second, the pursuit of rank; the third, the pursuit of authority; the fourth, the pursuit of power. See how ambition divides itself into four heads, and every action of hypocrites, as has been said, serves it.

The pursuit of freedom occurs when someone now evades being subject to others. The pursuit of rank occurs when someone, always desiring higher things, pants from grade to grade. The pursuit of authority occurs when someone now seeks to appear to everyone as a person of great counsel and holiness, and desires every matter to be established or determined according to his counsel or judgment. The pursuit of power occurs when someone now seeks to preside over others. We often see even those who have professed voluntary obedience accept troublesome and burdensome occupations willingly and eagerly, in order to obtain, through the occasion of their administration, a somewhat greater freedom to go out, speak, and act. What is this, I ask, except ambition for freedom?

[Col. 1358D] We see others always striving from rank to rank: those of lower rank aspiring to the subdiaconate, subdeacons to the diaconate, deacons to the priesthood. And although perhaps they acquire from this no greater freedom or power, nevertheless they think they hold, before others, at least a higher place. Whence comes this in them except ambition for rank? The man speaking of that Ahithophel teaches us what ambition for authority can accomplish in some; the traitor and parricide Absalom teaches us what ambition for power can do.

## CHAPTER XIV. How from the vice of fraudulence the mind falls into the vice of shamelessness.

It should be noted that concerning this beast it is said: “Authority was given to it.” And without doubt, by God’s wondrous and hidden judgment, hypocrites can do—and do do—things greater in many respects, and observe stricter disciplines of life, than those who afflict themselves for God’s sake. Although it is established that “all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass,” nevertheless pursuers of vanity often labour more for vain and transient glory than true emulators do for true and eternal glory. But it is very difficult—indeed almost impossible—for such people to remain hidden for long. Hear what Solomon thinks here when he says: “He who walks simply walks confidently, but he who perverts his ways will be made manifest” [Col. 1359A] (Prov. 10).

Those who walk doubly and fraudulently, and who pervert their ways, must therefore be exposed; and in them that prophetic word must be fulfilled: “Strip bare your shame; uncover your shoulder; reveal your legs; cross the rivers; your ignominy shall be exposed and your reproach shall be seen” (Isa. 47). Such persons, when they have been detected in this state of fraudulence, often rush into still worse things. For when they despair of being able any longer to remain hidden in their perversities, when they lose the one joy of their self-glorification without any hope of recovering it, they immediately break out into open shamelessness. See how a person is driven through fraudulence into shamelessness.

## CHAPTER XV. On the vice of shamelessness.

Consider, I beg you, how beastly—and more than beastly—is the life that, rejecting human shame, rushes headlong into everything, and does not blush even at things that ought to cause shame before the divine gaze or human faces, and finally gives itself over to every unrestrained evil. For what else is shamelessness except headlong and unbridled malice? Let us now hear what is said concerning this last beast: “After these things,” it says, “I was looking in a vision of the night; and behold, a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest under its feet. But it was unlike the other beasts which I had seen before it, and it had ten horns” [Col. 1359B] (Dan. 7).

Behold, it calls it a beast, yet does not say what beast it is or to what beast it is like, as it did with the preceding ones. See what kind of monster among vices is now described mystically—a monster to which no comparable creature is found among so many monstrous beasts. We know that a mind corrupted by enviousness and shamelessness spares no one at all thereafter, neither itself nor others. For enviousness takes from a person love and compassion for the neighbour; shamelessness, moderation and self-restraint. And people of this kind often endure many labours and many pains patiently—indeed willingly—in order to afflict others; and they prefer themselves to suffer misery rather than not inflict it upon others. See, then, how wonderful and horrible it is for a human being, forgetful of humanity, to put off the human being and put on a beastly heart—indeed, one more than beastly.

“And behold,” it says, “a fourth beast, terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong.” Is it not strong, exceedingly strong, which, in order to inflict evils on neighbours, is so patient in enduring evils? One who gives himself unrestrainedly to every cruelty is said to have iron teeth and claws. For iron, which subdues all other metals, fittingly signifies cruelty. Thus one receives iron teeth and claws who rages against neighbours in word and deed. Of another beast it was said that it devours much flesh; but of this one it is said that it crushes everything. Therefore the one which crushes everything not only seizes, condemns, and annihilates others’ weaknesses, but even their strengths. It tears everything by defamation, and what it cannot defame it tramples in contempt. But, to pass over the rest, this beast seems especially unlike the others in this: in this final state the wicked mind does not know how to blush. “It was unlike,” it says, “the other beasts which I had seen before it, and it had ten horns” [Col. 1359C].

## CHAPTER XVI. How the mind is hardened through the vice of shamelessness, first against God.

O bloodthirsty beast, which both tramples underfoot all those beneath it through contempt, and attacks those above it with the horns of rebellion! Would that concerning horns of this sort there might be fulfilled what he who speaks in the Psalm usefully threatens: “I will break all the horns of sinners, and exalt the horns of the righteous” (Ps. 74). Let us therefore examine more carefully what kinds of horns shamelessness possesses, [Col. 1362B] by which it is accustomed either to resist or to attack. We know, moreover, that horns grow out from flesh and harden above the sensitivity of the flesh. In ten ways, it seems to me, the shameless soul becomes hardened and loses that sensitivity of heart which it ought to possess. For the mind becomes hardened in three ways toward God, in three ways within itself, and in four ways against its neighbour: toward God through arrogance, self-exaltation, and obstinacy.

Arrogance is when a person ascribes to himself what he has received from God. Self-exaltation is when one raises himself above what he has received: through arrogance he glories in himself over what he has; through self-exaltation, even over what he does not have. Through arrogance and self-exaltation [Col. 1362C] it comes about that divine grace is deservedly withdrawn, and the person is hardened into obstinacy; once forsaken, he becomes a transgressor. Yet there is never a voluntary transgression of a commandment without contempt for God. Obstinacy, therefore, is when one despises God both as commanding and as threatening.

Through arrogance the goodness of God is attacked; through self-exaltation, the truth of God; through obstinacy, the power of God. We know certainly and without any hesitation that it is God who works all things according to his good will (Eph. 1). Therefore, solely from God’s goodness comes whatever good there is, or can be, in us. Whoever arrogates to himself that for which he ought to glorify God—what else does he do but strip God’s goodness of its glory for his own? Whoever exalts himself above what he is wishes what is true to be believed false, and [Col. 1362D] what is false to be believed true. But whoever rests upon falsehood is convicted of resisting God’s truth. Whatever a wicked mind presumptuously undertakes through obstinacy is especially an affront to divine power.

## CHAPTER XVII. How, through the vice of shamelessness, the mind becomes hardened within itself.

Likewise, by three downward steps the human spirit is accustomed to stiffen within itself: the binding of the mind, the hardening of the mind, and the unbridling of the mind.

The binding of the mind is when habitual pleasure entangles it so inextricably that, even when it wishes to do so, it cannot free itself from the entanglement of habitual sin; and it no longer ceases altogether from sinning, insofar as impunity permits it. See how the one whom arrogance [Col. 1363A] strips bare, self-exaltation weakens; the one whom self-exaltation weakens, obstinacy casts headlong; and the one whom obstinacy casts headlong into sin, the habit of sin gradually afterwards binds. To such a soul, and so bound, that prophetic voice cries: “Loosen the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isa. 52). Released from such bonds and made free, it can sing with the Psalmist: “You have burst my bonds apart; to you I will offer a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115).

But hardening of heart is when one who is of this kind can no longer be restrained from his excesses by fear of any punishment or by any severity of vengeance. To use plain examples: wicked people know what condemnation they suffer, or ought to suffer, when caught in their crimes; yet they cannot restrain themselves even from committing those crimes. It is one thing not to be able to restrain one’s desire [Col. 1363B] when impunity is enticing; it is another not even to be able to avoid what is not committed without the greatest danger. In the preceding degree, then, the spirit is bound inextricably to guilt; in this one it is, as it were, insensibly hardened against punishment. In the former shame is trampled down; in this, fear. Hear what is said of those who are hardened against punishment at this stage: “I struck them,” he says, “and they did not suffer pain” (Jer. 5).

The unbridling of the mind is when, without any hesitation or reconsideration, the spirit exposes itself to every transgression; having cast off the halter of shame and the bridle of fear, it rushes headlong into everything and thereafter becomes like “the horse and mule which have no understanding” (Ps. 31). In the two higher stages, the spirit is overcome by its desires even while it struggles against them. [Col. 1363C] At this stage, however, it does not struggle at all; but, whenever any wind of temptation blows, it is carried away in every direction, according to the prophet’s imprecation: “My God, make them like a wheel, and like chaff before the face of the wind” (Ps. 82). And just as in the first three horns it attacks God, so in the following three it resists God. For the mind, badly fortified by its own binding, hardening, and unbridling, resists strongly, lest any prompting of divine fear should readily humble it.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How, through the vice of shamelessness, the mind becomes hardened toward its neighbour.

There remain four of the aforesaid horns: the horn [Col. 1363D] of rejection, the horn of opposition, the horn of overthrow, and the horn of subjection. By these four degrees the wicked mind becomes hardened against its neighbour—and, what is worse, against those to whom it owes humble service. For just as it tramples those below it with iron claws, so it arms itself against those above it with these four horns of rebellion.

For the shameless soul, once it has shaken off the yoke of fear, now rises with wicked recklessness against its own authority. Thus the horn of rejection rebels when it now disdains obedience; the horn of opposition, when it strives always and everywhere to resist forcefully the efforts of its prelates; the horn of overthrow, when it endeavours to cast down its prelates; and the horn of subjection, when it now endeavours to subject them even to itself. See how evil [Col. 1364A] spreads; see by what stages the perverse soul is hardened into the utmost shamelessness; see how a person is led so far as neither to fear God nor respect man (Luke 18).

## CHAPTER XIX. How, when the mind has reached the depth of evils, it often also falls into despair.

But the corrupted soul, when it has reached the depth of evils, often loses, after all its evils, even hope of recovery and falls into despair. This is that final horn: the evil of despair; a horn, I say, small through distrust, yet harder than the rest through the obstinacy of distrust. “I considered the horns,” he says, “and behold, another little horn arose from among them, and three of [Col. 1364B] the first horns were plucked up before it. And behold, there were eyes like the eyes of a man in this horn, and a mouth speaking great things” (Dan. 7).

This horn arises from among the others, because the mind is especially cast headlong into despair by the binding of the heart, the hardening of the heart, and unbridling. For when, through these three, a person begins to lose mastery over himself, he likewise begins gradually to despair of salvation. Yet the evil of despair makes the spirit not so swollen as fearful, and in this very respect it casts down the horn of obstinacy. The evil of despair is accustomed not so much to lift the spirit up as to cast it down, and therefore the horn of self-exaltation cannot stand before it. The evil of despair makes the spirit more disparaging of its own powers, because it always makes it fear more than it ought; hence the horn of arrogance cannot stand in its presence.

A soul once despairing of its salvation and wholly deprived of divine grace, when it feels itself unable to resist inveterate habit or restrain itself from its perversity, often tries to present itself as excusable and casts its blame upon the Creator. And this is what it means for the horn of despair to have eyes like those of a man and a mouth speaking great things. Man alone among living creatures possesses reason and is skilled in prudence. When, therefore, after the evil of despair, someone begins cleverly to weave and ingeniously to advance ostensibly rational causes as arguments in his own excuse, he seems to have eyes like those of a man. [Col. 1364D] “Things must happen as they have been predestined; who can resist God’s will, who his ordinance? He made us such as he wished us to be. For ‘he has done whatsoever he wished in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the deeps’” (Ps. 134). “What, then, can we do? What are we? Can we create merits for ourselves? ‘It is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy’” (Rom. 9). “Why then does he not show mercy? Why does he not work in us what pleases him, he who works all things in all according to his will?” (Eph. 1).

A mouth speaking great things—things as mad as they are empty. To excuse yourself, do you accuse God? To justify yourself, do you blaspheme God? Does this not seem to be what is read in what follows: “and he will speak words against the Most High”? See by what stages one descends to the depths. See whence, [Col. 1365A] whither, and how one comes from excessive lightness of mind to shameless unbridling of mind, from great presumption of heart to final despair.

We have heard how the mind, always falling from evil into worse evil, is finally led down into the depth of evils. Let us hear how, or from what source, that same mind is sometimes, after many and ultimate evils, restored to the wholeness of righteousness. For if we rightly consider what precedes and follows in this vision, I think that in this mystical description we recognize what we read in the Apostle: “For where [Col. 1366A] iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more.” From this passage of Scripture it is easy to perceive that no malice of ours can overcome divine mercy. For what does it mean that, after the beasts succeeding one another, a throne having been set in place, the Ancient of Days sat down, except that after the many ravages of vices, he who is eternal before all times, through visiting grace, fixes the unstable heart in the firm stability of its resolve and makes it his dwelling-place? And what does it mean that the power of the beasts is taken away, except that, through visiting grace, the tyranny of vices having been put to sleep, the reign of sin is destroyed?

[Col. 1365]

# TREATISE OF EXCERPTS

Containing the origin and classification of the arts, the situation of lands, and a summary of histories; divided into four books.

(See among the Appendices to the Works of Hugh of Saint Victor, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXVII, cols. 193–225.)

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF RICHARD OF SAINT VICTOR

LETTERS OF GILDUIN, ACHARD, ERVISIUS, AND GUARIN, ABBOTS OF SAINT VICTOR OF PARIS, AND OF VARIOUS PERSONS TO THEM.

(Dom Edmond Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, col. 227.)

[Col. 1365]

## [NOTICE.]

### I. NOTICE CONCERNING GILDUIN.

(*Gallia Christiana*, VII, 658.)

[Col. 1365B] Gilduin, born at Paris, joined himself as a companion to Master William of Champeaux when the latter was organizing regular canons; and when William was raised to the episcopal mitre of Châlons, Gilduin was appointed in his place in the governance of the Victorine house, under the same title of prior. This is clear from the bull addressed to this prior by Pope Paschal II, dated 1 December, indiction VIII, in the year 1114 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the sixteenth of his pontificate. By it the possessions of the monastery are confirmed and the Victorine canons are freely granted the power to elect an abbot. Accordingly, they soon established him as their first abbot.

For many years he held this office. During that time, as Robert of Torigni relates, many noble and learned young men were admitted into this congregation. Among them he praises Hugh, afterwards surnamed of Saint Victor, a Saxon by nation [Col. 1366B] from the diocese of Halberstadt. Born in 1097, he gave his name to this community and subsequently flourished as one highly skilled in every branch of sacred learning. He had an uncle of the same name, Hugh, his companion in conversion, whose distinguished memory is recorded in the martyrology of this house on the third day before the Nones of May in these words:

> “The solemn anniversary of the blessed memory of Hugh, priest and archdeacon of the church of Halberstadt, who came to us from Saxony, following his nephew Master Hugh, a canon of our church. Having received the regular habit in our church, he commendably completed his life in it. He greatly enriched our house from his own resources with gold and silver, precious garments, carpets and curtains, and other various furnishings. But concerning him we especially wish to commend and commit to memory that, at his own expense and cost, the building of this our church was made and constructed.”

Meanwhile Gilduin contributed so much to the adornment of the Abbey of Saint Victor that, just as William of Champeaux was the institutor of regular discipline in that house, King Louis the Fat its founder and generous donor of temporal estates, and Girbert, bishop of Paris, the donor of its temporal site, so Gilduin was the diligent enlarger of this monastery [Note: [Col. 1367D] Malingre, *Antiquités de Paris*, p. 434.]. This resulted from the generosity of many, especially Dean Berner and the whole assembly of the Church of Paris, who in 1122, with the bishop’s consent, granted to the canons of Saint Victor one ploughland of arable land at the village of Civiliacum, from their own property in both the territory of Civiliacum and that of Orliacum. They granted them 120 jugera of arable land to cultivate, and an *olchia* [a measure or holding of uncertain extent], with all customary rights and revenues.

In 1125 King Louis, for whom Gilduin was confessor, [Col. 1367B] transferred to the church of Blessed Victor—the church distinguished by the order of regular canons—the *annualia* of the canons in churches founded by his predecessors or acquired after foundation: that is, the revenue of the first year of vacant prebends. This he did with the consent of the abbots and canons serving God there, since, after death, they receive the sacrifice of the Mediator each day for a year for the remission of sins [Note: [Col. 1368D] *History of the Church of Paris*, vol. II, p. 80.].

These are the churches: at Château-Landon, those of Saint Severinus and Saint Tudualdus, Saint Ugal—later a priory—as also at Melun, the church of Saint Saviour annexed to Saint Severinus when this became a regular abbey; at Melun, Saint Mary and Saint Saviour; at Étampes, Saint Mary; at Poissy, Saint Mary; at Pontoise, Saint Mellon; at Montlhéry, Saint Peter; at Corbeil, Saint Mary, in which eleven *annualia* and those of Saint Guenailus were designated. King Louis granted the *annualia* of all these churches to the church of Saint Victor with the joint consent of the abbots and canons, so that it should receive in full for one year the income of prebends after the death of canons, and should render no service on this account either to the church or to the deceased except the annual observance.

The king added to this gift that, should any of these canons leave a prebend, that same church of Saint Victor should possess the revenues of that prebend. So that these benefits might be possessed by lawful gift and in lawful order, they were bestowed upon and confirmed for that church through the hand of Henry, archbishop of Sens; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; and Stephen of Paris. In the preceding year Stephen had, with the king’s consent, granted to the same church of Saint Victor the *annualia* of the prebends of the mother church of Blessed Mary, Blessed Marcellus, Blessed Germanus, Blessed Clodoaldus, and Blessed Martin of Champeaux.

> “Done publicly at Paris in the year of the Incarnate Word 1125, the nineteenth of our reign, with the assent of our wife Adelaide and our son Philip. The sign of Henry, archbishop; the sign of Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; the sign of Stephen, bishop of Paris; the sign of Berner, abbot of Corbeil; the sign of Stephen, abbot of Melun; the sign of Berard, abbot of Château-Landon; the sign of Pagan, abbot of Étampes; the sign of Stephen, abbot of Montlhéry; the sign of Samson, abbot of Meudon; the sign of Henry, abbot of Poissy and Pontoise, being present, etc.”

The bishops to whom this matter belonged further confirmed these *annualia* by separate letters: namely Henry, archbishop of Sens; Hugh, archbishop of Rouen; Stephen, bishop of Paris; Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; and finally Pope Honorius II, whose letter is copied in the Victorine Annals under the year 1125.

Gilduin the abbot became so renowned [Col. 1368A] that in 1132 he acted as vicar-general for Stephen, bishop of Paris, in which capacity he placed all the goods of Stephen of Garlande, archdeacon of Paris, under interdict. In the same year Pope Innocent II confirmed all the privileges of this church, and in the following year approved, through the hand of Alberic, cardinal and chancellor, the gift of the church of Floriacum in Brie.

At the request of this same pontiff, Stephen, bishop of Paris, in that same year 1133 granted Saint Victor one prebend in the church of Blessed Mary of Paris, and in the churches of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, Saint Marcellus, Saint Clodoaldus, and Saint Martin of Champeaux in Brie. The charter of Bartholomew, dean, and of the chapter of Paris confirming this gift says as follows:

> “That is, the canons of Saint Victor shall place one vicar in each of the aforesaid churches. Further, concerning what pertains to them, it should be known that the church of Blessed Victor, which has a prebend in our church, ought to perform no other service therein itself [Col. 1368B] except this alone: in Saint Victor’s week, a canon is to sing the principal Mass; but the vicar must perform the morning Mass and all the rest of the service in its entirety.”

See the complete charter in vol. VI of Dom Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 223.

In 1134 the oft-praised King Louis the Fat, ever more warmly disposed toward the Victorines, delivered to them the church of Saint Guenailus at Corbeil, in which the king appointed the abbot, on condition that whenever the abbot then in office should leave the abbey for any reason, the church of Blessed Victor should possess it in perpetual right. Meanwhile, as the canons holding prebends in that church of Saint Guenailus died, those prebends were freely to pass into the right and authority of the church of Blessed Victor.

> “But in order,” says the king, “that this desire of ours might be brought to effect in lawful order, we surrendered into the hands of Lord Stephen, bishop of Paris, in whose diocese the same church is situated, that authority and every right which we held in the aforesaid church. And, according to our will and petition, he reinvested Abbot Gilduin of the church of Blessed Victor, and the church itself, with the same authority and right. This was also added: that the abbot of Saint Guenailus, for as long as he holds that abbey, and thereafter the other canons of that church, should answer to, render account to, and obey the abbot of Saint Victor in all things belonging to that church, just as they had hitherto done to us.”

Indeed, Bishop Stephen of Paris gave his consent to this gift in his own letters.

> “And further,” the king continues, “we have enfranchised the aforesaid church of Saint Guenailus to the canons of Saint Victor with full liberty, so that they might place in that church such and as many of the brethren as they wished, and might order the affairs of the church according as reason should dictate and the advantage of the church of Saint Victor require. Algrin the chancellor subscribed.”

In the course of time, once its canons had died out, this church became a priory dependent upon the conventual mensa of Saint Victor.

Also in 1134, at Gilduin’s request, King Louis gave the Victorines the place of Ambert, which later passed to the Célestine Fathers through the gift of King Philip IV. By way of compensation, he assigned Saint Victor an annual revenue of forty Parisian pounds to be received from the royal treasury. Gilduin also appears in 1135 in the cartulary of Cagiae. In his time the monastery of Saint Bartholomew of Noyon joined the Victorine congregation, according to the manuscript history of Saint Bartholomew by Christopher Labbe. The author of the *History of the City and University of Paris*, quarto edition, vol. I, p. 372, likewise asserts this concerning the monasteries of Blessed Mary of Augo in Normandy, Cagiae in the city of Meaux, Saint Evurtius of Orléans, [Col. 1369A] Saint Geneviève of Paris, and the cathedral church of Sées [Note: [Col. 1369D] Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 763.]. Certainly, there survives a letter of John, count of Augo, to Guarin, abbot of Saint Victor, directing that the canons whom he sent to Augo should observe the customs of Arrouaise, or otherwise depart.

At that time, as we have already said, many men distinguished for learning and piety adorned the Victorine house, especially Hugh of Saint Victor, whose works have frequently been published in three volumes. He died in the year of the Lord 1140, on the third day before the Ides of February, before he had completed his forty-fourth year. His body was buried at the entrance to the cloister, with this epitaph carved on the tombstone:

> In this tomb is buried Hugh, a most celebrated teacher,  
> Whom a small urn contains, though he was an exceptional man.  
> Eminent in doctrine, second to none in the world,  
> He shone in intellect, character, speech, and style.

Then, when Hugh was translated in 1335, this second inscription was added [Col. 1369B]; in its second verse, *quinis* should be read in place of *tribus*:

> Hugh, a man Saxon by origin, lay beneath this stone  
> For two hundred years, yet three [read: five] were added thereafter.  
> He caused himself to be placed in the lowest part of the first cloister,  
> Unwilling to be adorned by the world or trodden underfoot.  
> On the eleventh day before the light of February, his bones  
> Were raised from the earth and transferred to the left side of the choir.  
> In the year one thousand three hundred and thirty-five  
> Of Christ, the choir of brethren stood on either side.

About the time of this same Hugh flourished the excellent and celebrated teacher Master Adam, canon of Saint Victor, Breton by nation, humble and agreeable in manner of life, useful and eminent in doctrine and learning, “so much so that without his works a man could scarcely set foot in Saint Jerome’s prologues on the Bible, or find a reasonable exposition of difficult matters,” etc.

Among these distinguished men it is also fitting to mention [Col. 1369C] Ivo, whom Pope Innocent II created cardinal. Sent to Gaul as legate in 1141, he died in Gaul two years later, on 20 June 1143. The Victorine necrology thus commemorates him on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July:

> “The anniversary of Master Ivo, our canon, priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See.”

There is preserved in the monastery archives a bull of Innocent II confirming all the royal privileges of Saint Victor, conferred through the hand of Chancellor Aimeric in 1137. In the following year King Louis VII, when confirming the gift of prebends granted to Saint Victor in 1133, records “that Stephen, dean of Saint Geneviève of the Mount, and all the canons of that place, by common consent, freely granted one prebend in their church of Blessed Geneviève to the church of Blessed Victor, to be possessed as a perpetual gift.” Many settlements were subsequently made concerning this prebend between the two communities, after Saint Geneviève became a house of regular canons.

In the same manner Matthew of Montmorency, constable of France, gave one prebend to Saint Victor in his church of Saint Martin of Montmorency. John, surnamed de la Chaîne, secular abbot of Saint Peter of Montlhéry, likewise granted one from that church. When it was later given to the monks of Longpont to be converted into a priory, an agreement was made between them and the canons of Saint Victor, of which more below.
