In the aforesaid year 1138, the abbot and convent of Saint Vincent of Senlis acknowledged to Gilduin that they recognized him as head of the order; Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis, in his *Life of Louis the Fat*, celebrates him as a man approved by works of piety [Note: [Col. 1369D] Vol. VI, Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 222.]. Henry, brother of Louis VII, “by God’s permission abbot of the royal abbeys,” gave the canons of Saint Victor one prebend in the church of Saint Exuperius of Corbeil, with the consent of the canons of that church, in 1146, and granted that they should hold it in perpetuity.

> “Nor,” he says, “do we wish it to be unknown that my aforesaid brother not only gave his consent to this gift, but also both wished and requested that we should make it.”

Especially notable are these words from the charter of donation:

> “It has already come to the knowledge of many that my father, Louis, by God’s grace king of the Franks, of illustrious memory, raised the church of Blessed Victor from the dust of poverty and established it as an abbey distinguished by the order of regular canons. In accordance with royal generosity he also bestowed very many benefits upon it; and as a proof of true affection he directed that some of our sons and brothers, when they departed this life, should be buried in that house of religion,”

namely in the chapter house.

There is also a letter from King Louis VII to his brother Henry and to the archdeacons Ist. and Jal. [Note: [Col. 1369D] Ibid., col. 227.], directing them to hand over the church of Saint Martin [Col. 1370B] of Champeaux to the canons of Saint Victor, so that regular canons might be established there. Finally, Philip, brother of King Louis VII and, after his brother Henry, abbot of the royal churches—namely Blessed Mary of Étampes, Saint Mary of Corbeil, Saint Mary of Meudon, Saint Mary of Poissy, and Saint Mellon of Pontoise—confirmed to the monastery of Saint Victor the *annualia* of canons who died in those churches [Note: [Col. 1370D] Ibid., cols. 228 and 229.].

In Gilduin’s time the Victorine house also had, as we have said, one whole prebend and the *annualia* of other prebends in the secular church of Saint Peter of Montlhéry. When that church was transferred to the monks of Longpont, an agreement being made with them, G., abbot of Saint Victor, received in compensation lands, vineyards, a tithe, and whatever at all the church of Longpont possessed at Athegias; likewise, two solidi of rent in the same village, which the aforesaid church of Saint Peter received there.

Saint Bernard wrote to Gilduin Letter 410; read it with its notes in the most recent edition of the works of Saint Bernard. Certainly this saint was closely bound in friendship with the Victorines. He obtained from Abbot Odo and the convent of Saint Geneviève permission for them to bring the stream Beverim to their monastery and to build a mill there, about 1150. Saint Bernard also commended the Victorine abbey to Suger in Letter 369. Preserved in its treasury is the cowl of that saint himself, a lasting monument of his love for it, together with the charter from which Saint Bernard’s seal hangs.

Moreover, the letter of Gilduin, abbot of Fontaine-Jean, to G., abbot of Saint Victor, seems to concern either Gilduin or Gunther, his successor with one intervening abbot [Note: [Col. 1370D] Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 758.]; the latter had asked him to lend grain. Gilduin finally, after governing the community of the Victorine house excellently for almost forty-four years and months, died in old age on the Ides of April in the year [Col. 1370D] 1155. His death is recorded on that very day in an extract from the old necrology of La Sauve-Majeure. He is reported as dying on the same day, or 13 April, under the title of Blessed in Ferrari’s catalogue; but in the supplement to the Gallican martyrology he is called only an abbot of pious memory.

His body was placed in the middle of the choir at the feet of Stephen, bishop of Paris, with an inscription. When the tomb was renewed, the following heading was prefixed:

> The religious epitaph, restored from a manuscript, of the Reverend Father Gilduin, first abbot of this church and confessor to Louis the Fat, king of the Franks. [Note: Malingre, *Antiquités de Paris*, line 2, p. 48; [Col. 1370D].]

> Gilduin departs victorious from the battlefield to the court,  
> On the Ides of April, called by his King.  
> The first pillar of the house, guardian of the flock, founder of the order,  
> Here lies, worthy of the everlasting love of this place.

[Col. 1371A] Gilduin is commemorated in the Victorine necrology on the day of his death as follows:

> “The solemn anniversary of our venerable father Gilduin, first abbot of this church, a man of great authority and holiness. Zealous for God and for the order, he restored the canonical order, which had almost wholly failed. In his days our house held primacy above the other houses of our order and, through the pre-eminence of its religious life, shone far and wide like a most brilliant star. He began and completed the church and the other buildings from their foundations; and, apart from the royal endowment, he enriched it with prebends, *annualia*, and many other revenues. Therefore it has been decreed that the memory of so great a Father should be solemnly celebrated each year above that of others; that a commemoration be made before Mass; and that, in perpetuity, an entire prebend be distributed daily as alms for his soul.”

I pass over many distinguished men among Gilduin’s disciples: Guarin, the first regular prior of Saint Victor, who in 1131 served as dean in the cathedral church of Sées; [Col. 1371B] and Odo [Note: [Col. 1371C] Malingre, p. 480.], likewise first prior of Saint Victor and then first abbot of Saint Geneviève, as this distich teaches:

> But, Geneviève, your abbot Odo, jewel of modesty,  
> Sat after Thomas in the cloister, in the prior’s seat.

But I cannot pass over Blessed Thomas, who was second prior of Saint Victor and was cruelly killed in 1133, as Mabillon proves at length in the notes to Saint Bernard’s Letter 158, by the nephews of Theobald, archdeacon of Paris, whom Thomas had reproved for simony. He was killed in the hands of Stephen, bishop of Paris, whose penitentiary and chief vicar Thomas was. On this matter see Peter the Venerable, Letter 17 of Book I; Saint Bernard, the cited Letter 158; and the following four letters to Pope Innocent II, for which see Mabillon’s notes.

Thomas was first buried beneath the cloister, then transferred to the chapel of Saint Denis behind the choir, and from there, in 1667, to the side of the high altar. In place of the former inscription, [Col. 1371C] which follows, another, given immediately below, was placed in the same year:

> Here lies Thomas, an eminent prior, afterwards stained with blood,  
> A sober man, girded with the path of equity,  
> A father in piety, most upright in judgment.  
> This brother was not bent by the whirlwind of gifts;  
> Longing for martyrdom, compassionate at the losses of the poor,  
> A priest intolerant of the deceptions of pastoral cares.  
> While he serves with zeal for justice, he is struck by the sword.  
> His spirit is in heaven; his body is buried in the earth.  
> Stephen, then bishop of Paris, mourns him piously;  
> Bernard of Clairvaux honours him in writing.  
> At the command of the supreme pontiff, this place receives him.  
> O Christ, join us to Thomas among the companies of angels.

[Col. 1372A]

We add the new inscription:

> Here lie the venerable bones of Blessed Thomas of Saint Victor, who suffered martyrdom in the hands of Stephen, bishop of Paris, in defence of ecclesiastical right, in the year of the Lord 1130. His devoted fellow-canons of Saint Victor erected this bronze memorial in the year 1667, on the day before the Kalends of January.

There are extant in vol. VI of Dom Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 220, letters of Stephen, bishop of Paris, to his archpriests, directing them to publish the sentence of excommunication which he had pronounced against the killers of Thomas, prior of Saint Victor; he reserved absolution and penance for himself alone.

Burchard, bishop of Meaux, died in the Victorine house in 1134 and was buried on the day before the Nones of January in the chapel of the Holy Cross beside Blessed Thomas the prior. They once shared this epitaph:

> This man is a bishop; that one a prior; this one a confessor; that one a martyr.  
> This one is lesser in rank; that one in merits.  
> Burchard was father of Meaux, but Thomas was prior  
> Of this church; both were alike in character.  
> They were lovers of justice and teachers of morals,  
> Grave with piety, pious with gravity.  
> Those whom reason, religion, and integrity unite,  
> [Col. 1372C] the tomb also unites, and the very site of their burial.

### II. NOTICE CONCERNING ACHARD.

(Oudin, *Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 1298.)

[Col. 1371]

[Col. 1371C] Achard, bishop of Avranches, was by nationality an Englishman, from Bridlington according to Gérard Jean Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, book II, chapter 52, p. 422 of the latest edition; from Northumbria according to César Égasse du Boulay, *Fourth Century of the University of Paris*, in the *Catalogue*, p. 715. But according to the Sammarthan brothers, *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 925, under “Abbots of Saint-Victor of Paris,” he was a Norman of noble origin from the county of Domfront; Arnulf of Lisieux speaks of him in his letters. This man, wonderfully distinguished by integrity of life and manifold learning, devoted his adolescence to humane letters, his youth to philosophy, and his more mature age to theology, so that in each field he made exceptional progress, as Pits reports from the manuscript writers Leland and Boston. After a long career of teaching, wearied by earthly disturbances, he joined the Regular Canons of Saint-Victor. In the course of time, after Gilduin—whom the Lord took to Himself in 1155, on 20 March—he became their second abbot.

Pope Adrian IV sent several diplomas to him as abbot: one concerning the churches of Saint-Brice and Villiers-le-Bel; likewise another forbidding laypeople to usurp tithes belonging to Victorine parishes. John of Toulouse discusses these in his very extensive manuscript *History of the Abbey of Saint-Victor*. Having become abbot after Gilduin, as stated above, he by no means hid in idleness the talents entrusted to him, but wrote little works which alike demonstrate the seriousness and uprightness of the man.

One of these is entitled *On the Temptation of Christ*, manuscript in the celebrated library of Saint-Victor at Paris, of which he was abbot, shelfmark SS. 19, fol. 162. It begins: “Jesus was led into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil,” etc. “Thus far concerning the sequence of the Gospel reading. In the present sermon one ought not to wander abroad, but only a little …” Another little work is entitled *On the Division of Soul and Spirit*, likewise held there in manuscript, shelfmarks LL. 7 and II. 15; it begins: “The inward substance which, together with the body, constitutes the human being …” It is also held at Cambridge among the manuscript books of Cambridge University, codex 1558; in the library of St Benedict’s College, codex 291, no. 9, under the explicit title: “Master Achard’s Treatise on the Division of Soul and Spirit.” In the Victorine manuscripts it is read with the initial letter A alone [Col. 1373A]; consequently, from conjecture, the first compiler of the catalogue of this celebrated library in 1512 assigned it to Adam of Saint-Victor.

In the celebrated library of Clairvaux there are *Sermons of Master Achard*, which I still judge to belong to Achard of Saint-Victor, a most learned man who wrote several works. Flourishing because of the splendid gifts of his mind and virtue, after long exercise in every kind of discipline, Achard was raised and consecrated in 1162, through the assistance of Henry, king of the English, from Regular Canon of Saint-Victor and abbot of that church to the bishopric of Avranches in Normandy. This promotion displeased Louis, king of the Franks. He immediately dismissed the man and, lest he thereafter retain any part in the government of the same house, forbade it by the following letter:

> Louis, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to the prior and all the brethren of Saint-Victor: greeting and affection.
>
> [Col. 1373B] This church was founded both through the benefaction of our predecessors and of the Church of Paris; for this reason we love it especially. Your abbot has been called to another church. We do not wish the goods of the church, whose care especially concerns us, to be diminished in any respect, but rather to increase. Therefore, by royal authority, we command you that Abbot Achard shall henceforth have no power either to alienate or to receive the goods of this church; nor, while he is present, are you to begin any discussion concerning an election. Farewell.

Having been made bishop of Avranches, he left to posterity, according to Gérard Jean Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, book II, chapter 52, p. 422 of the latest edition, a *Life of Saint Geselin the Monk*, although Bale does not mention it. Yet the *Life of Saint Getselin the Hermit*, published at Douai in 1626, is attributed to another Achard, a monk of Clairvaux, whom Charles du Fresne du Cange states to have flourished in 1140, in the *Index of Authors* prefixed to his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, col. 79, where he mentions both Achards.

After prudently and piously governing the church of Avranches for ten years, making many donations to the surrounding abbeys, and especially to the abbey of the Holy Trinity of La Lucerne, of the Premonstratensian order—which he frequently visited and dearly loved—he died on 29 March 1172. He was buried in the said abbey of the same diocese, to which he had granted the annual revenues of vacant prebends of the Church of Avranches, after the model of the Victorine canons’ relation to the Church of Paris. His tomb is visible at the entrance to the cloister, beneath an old stone vault, bearing this inscription: “Here lies Achard, bishop, by whose charity our poverty was enriched.” Another ancient metrical inscription concerning Achard in a manuscript of Saint-Victor reads:

> [Col. 1374B] The olive-tree of this house, the glory of the English clergy,  
> Long worthy to be cherished in heavenly light,  
> Happy Achard, flourishing in old age,  
> Bishop of Avranches, is marked out from this fold.

He is mentioned by Robert of Torigni, continuator of Sigebert’s Chronicle, under the year 1162, when he was elevated to the bishopric of Avranches; by Beatus Rhenanus in his commentary on the works of Tertullian, where he comments on the book *On the Trinity*; by the Sammarthan brothers in *Gallia Christiana*, vol. II, under “Bishops of Avranches,” p. 6, and vol. IV, under “Monastery of Saint-Victor,” p. 925; and in the *Fourth Century of the University of Paris*, p. 300, and in the *Catalogue of Distinguished Academics*, p. 725.

## III. NOTICE ON ERVISIUS

(*New Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 667.)

[Col. 1373]

[Col. 1373C] Ervisius, or Erveus, and sometimes Erneis, or Ernisius and Ernestus, an Englishman by nationality, succeeded as abbot. Peter, canon of Saint-Victor—chaplain to Pope Alexander III and later made cardinal by him—congratulates him in Alexander’s name on his election [Note: [Col. 1373D] Vol. VI, Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 232.]. He is named as abbot in a charter for the purchase of the land of Villepuy, confirmed by the king in 1162 through the hand of Hugh the chancellor.

About that time Pope Alexander wrote to the abbot of Châteaunant [Note: [Col. 1373D] Ibid., col. 240, and Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 751.], directing him to allow the abbot and brethren of Saint-Victor of Paris to possess quietly and peacefully the annual revenues which they were known to have possessed canonically in the church of Saint-Sauveur for a long time, until an agreement should be reached with them concerning these matters. There survives for Ervisius a letter [Note: [Col. 1373D] Ibid., col. 245.] from Gerbert, bishop of Hereford, asking for someone from his flock to be placed over the church of Worcester, deprived of its pastor; likewise, there is one from Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, concerning the church and convent of Eu.

Several letters to him from Jonah, canon of Saint-Victor, are also read concerning the affair of the house of Ambert, according to the Sammarthan brothers. This Jonah, having on one occasion been sent to the burg of Caesar, asks Ervisius to recall him to Saint-Victor. Pope Alexander III wrote to the same abbot, the prior and subprior of Saint-Victor, the abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and Odo, former abbot of Sainte-Geneviève [Note: [Col. 1374D] Ibid., col. 233.], directing them to investigate the punishments imposed upon William, canon of Sainte-Geneviève, in 1164.

Ervisius, together with Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and Odo, formerly of Sainte-Geneviève, was godfather and sponsor at the holy baptism of Philip, son of Louis VII [Note: [Col. 1374D] Ibid., col. 235.], later king Philip Augustus. We read that this occurred on Sunday, 22 August, in the octave of the Assumption of Blessed Mary, in 1165. Asked by O., cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, to persuade the king to grant him free permission to return to his brother cardinals [Note: [Col. 1374D] Ibid., col. 240.], the same abbot replied that he had had a private and sufficiently familiar conversation with the king about it, and that the king was well disposed to allow him to go to his brother cardinals wherever they might be, etc.

Henry, archbishop of Reims and brother of King Henry, sought the support of the same H. (Hervisius) with the king. He asked that Hervisius, as a faithful interpreter of the letters he was sending the king concerning the reconciliation with the king of Hugh, bishop of Soissons and chancellor [Col. 1374D], should present them if Hugh had indeed, as was said, fallen from royal favour; but should not present them if the report were false, or if Hugh had already returned to favour and the king had restored his seal to him. This is from Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 570. The letters as presented are read there on p. 569.

This also appears to be E., abbot of Saint-Victor [Col. 1375A], to whom and to the chapter there survives, in the same volume of Duchesne, p. 765, a letter from B. of Montmorency. He begs that, since the place called Wood of Saint Peter had been given by his father to the church of Saint-Victor on condition that the divine office be celebrated there daily, and was then vacant, and since it had, as rumour said, been stripped of its chalice, vestments, horse, and certain other things, they restore its goods to the place and send there Ralph—whom he loved because of services rendered to himself and his sick brother—or some other man of good reputation.

During Ervisius’s administration, in 1167, John, bishop of the city of Palaea, came from Palestine into France. When he died at Paris, he was buried in the Victorine basilica. Ervisius was present in 1170 at the agreement concluded between Ivo, abbot of Saint-Denis, and the canons of Saint-Paul in that city. In the same year Maurice, bishop of Paris, testifies from the Victorine cartulary that he invested Lord Hugh, bishop of Soissons, and Lord Hervisius, abbot of Saint-Victor, with the tithe of the cleric William, restored from his patrimony into the bishop’s hands [Col. 1375B].

Ervisius was meanwhile accused [Note: [Col. 1375] Vol. VI, Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*, cols. 349, 250 and following.] of having relaxed regular discipline. Concerning its restoration Pope Alexander wrote to King Louis VII, grieving greatly that sacred religious life had so grown cold in the church of Saint-Victor, “that she who had stretched out her hand to many running on the path of salvation now needs outside assistance and finds none to support her … Not that there are not many there who have knowledge and love of religious life; but, while certain members languish along with their head, the fervour of religion in that church is known to have cooled.”

Accordingly, in 1169 the same pontiff ordered William, archbishop of Sens, Stephen, bishop of Meaux, and Nicholas, abbot of Vaux-de-Cernay, to apply to this evil whatever remedy they considered necessary. See the many letters of this pontiff on the subject in the second appendix to vol. X of Labbe’s *Councils*, [Col. 1375C] col. 1319 and following, and vol. IV of *Writers of French History*, p. 602 and following. But from letter 45, written to the Victorine ascetics, in which the pontiff rejoices and offers congratulations that discipline has been restored, we learn that this was accomplished by Stephen, archbishop of Bourges, formerly bishop of Meaux, and by the archbishop of Sens, whose letter to E., abbot of Saint-Victor, survives in Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 747.

Nevertheless, without any hearing being held, Ervisius is recorded merely to have been admonished and to have resigned his dignity in April, during Lent, in 1172. He was banished for a time to the priory of Saint-Paul of Alnet, near Caproisia, dependent on Saint-Victor. When he tried to retain it, Cardinals Alexander and Theodoric wrote to William, archbishop of Sens, and Stephen, archbishop of Bourges, directing them to oppose him [Note: [Col. 1375C] Ibid., col. 252.].

Ervisius is commemorated in the Victorine necrology as follows: “13 May: anniversary of Lord Hervisius, formerly abbot of this church.” Claude Malingre, in his *Parisian Antiquities*, p. 449, writes that he died three or four years after resigning the administration; certainly, however, not before 1177, if Martène’s note on Pope Alexander III’s letter to Robert, prior, and the chapter of Saint-Victor is correct. In it, the pope says that he had admonished Abbot Ervisius to administer both the internal and external affairs of the church of Saint-Victor with the counsel of the greater and sounder part of the chapter [Col. 1376B].

For Ervisius was accused of wishing to determine everything in the house of Saint-Victor at his own pleasure and without counsel of the elders and chapter. Therefore succeeding abbots were bound by solemn oath to preserve the counsel of the elders of the chamber and undertake nothing without their assent, as is clear from authentic charters preserved at Saint-Victor. To these was added a decree of the general chapter of 3 April 1538, confirmed by codicils concerning the partition of goods made between abbot and convent. “Since, therefore,” says Alexander in the letter cited, “we believe and hope that the same abbot will willingly act in accordance with our admonition and command, we direct and command your discretion by apostolic letters that, while rendering to the same abbot due obedience and reverence [Col. 1376C], you shall prudently and effectively assist him in ordering and disposing of the affairs of your church. Given at Venice, 13 May.” Yet everyone can see that this letter preceded Ervisius’s resignation itself; otherwise there would have been two abbots at the same time, which is impossible.

## IV. NOTICE ON GUARINUS

(*Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, col. 669.)

[Col. 1375]

[Col. 1375C] After Ervisius’s resignation, Guarinus was chosen abbot from Cagia, with Richard as prior presiding [Col. 1375D], and was blessed by Maurice, bishop of Paris. Since Ervisius was attempting to retain the church treasury, Maurice wrote to William, archbishop of Sens [Note: [Col. 1375D] Vol. VI, Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 253.], asking him to go to Saint-Victor and restore it to Guarinus. Conversely, W., archbishop of Sens, wrote to M., bishop of Paris, asking him to go as soon as possible to the church of Saint-Victor, and, in the presence of G., the abbot, and the brethren of the said church, to have the chests and little repositories of the aforesaid Er. searched, and to assign to the abbot and brethren the gold chalice and other things found there belonging by right to the church of Blessed Victor.

There is there also, p. 569, a letter of Pope Alexander to Simon, archdeacon of Paris, which seems to concern [Col. 1376C] this abbot. The pope rebukes the archdeacon for demanding one hundred solidi from him after he had been installed in possession of the abbey [Col. 1376D]. Cardinals Alexander and Theodoric congratulate Abbot Guarinus on his promotion [Note: [Col. 1375D] Alexius Duchesne, vol. IV, p. 604; vol. VI, Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 253.]. Brother Frederick of Saint-Victor, chaplain of Pope Alexander III, also congratulates him; the pope himself likewise congratulated him in letter 46, appendix 2 to vol. X of Labbe’s *Councils*, and confirmed both Ervisius’s resignation and Guarinus’s promotion.

Moreover, the same pope and Cardinal John Piuzutus of Naples, a canon of Saint-Victor, earnestly requested in letters that Guarinus send them two Victorine canons together with other members of the same congregation. Guarinus eventually did so [Note: [Col. 1376D] Duchesne, vol. IV, pp. 749 and 750.], after first excusing himself on account of the deaths, in the first year of his administration [Col. 1377A], of many distinguished men of his house—namely, the man called Richard of Saint-Victor, canon and prior of the Victorine church, pre-eminent in piety and learning and renowned for his learned books. He died in 1173, on Friday, 10 March. He was buried in the cloister beside the abbey gate with this epitaph:

> Distinguished in character, intellect, learning, and art,  
> Learned Richard, you lie covered here in dusty burial.  
> Scotland’s blessed soil bore you;  
> France’s land shelters you in her own bosom.  
> Cruel, sparing fate did you no harm,  
> Though with harsh hand it broke the threads drawn out  
> Over too short a span of time.  
> For very many memorials of your labour survive,  
> Which shall bring you everlasting renown.  
> As death moves more slowly toward guilty dwellings,  
> So with all too hasty a step it enters pious homes.

Guarinus’s grief over these deaths was somewhat mitigated by news that Hugh of Peter Leo, canon of Saint-Victor, had been promoted to the cardinalate in that same year, 1173 [Col. 1377B]. He soon wrote to Guarinus and the chapter of Saint-Victor, condoling with them over the conduct of Ervisius, their former abbot, and offering them his services.

Under the same Guarinus died Adam, called “of Saint-Victor” from the place of his profession, a native of Lesser Brittany, renowned for his writings, especially for a biblical vocabulary commonly called the *Summa of Brito*, on 8 July 1177 according to the Sammarthan brothers, and in 1192 according to vol. I of the *History of Paris*, p. 197.

Nothing demonstrates more clearly the fame of the Victorines in this age than the retirement among them of men also resplendent in episcopal dignity. Among these was Stephen, first canon of the Church of Paris, then bishop of Meaux, and finally archbishop of Bourges. After two years he withdrew to the Victorines in 1174, and died there on 12 January 1181 or 1182. He lies in the choir, to the left of the bishop of Paris. The 155th letter of Stephen of Tournai, then abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, to Pope Alexander III, concerning the church of Saint-Victor, should be read in this connection:

> [Col. 1377C] “Prudent and powerful men of their generation, who at that time held office in the Church of Paris, pursued the church of Saint-Victor with such affection of love and devotion that, touched and drawn alike by the fragrance of sacred religious life there, most of them not only bestowed their goods but offered themselves as well.”

Such men, as Claude du Molinet notes, were Stephen and, in the view of some, Bishop Odo, Berner the dean, Adam the precentor, and others. Nor was the wholesome way of life of the Victorines spread only nearby, but also to distant places. Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, is a witness: in 1181, having laid aside his bishopric, he fled to the Victorine house, where he became a Regular Canon, as is noted in the necrology on the date of his death, 31 August 1184, in these words:

> “The solemn anniversary of our father of pious memory, Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, who, moved by the great affection of devotion which he had borne toward our church for many years past, came to us from his bishopric and became our canon. Among all others he chose this church as the place of his rest and burial, leaving to posterity, through many great benefits, a worthy and enduring memorial of his name and love.”

He lay buried in the chapel of the old church called Holy Cross. After the new church had been built, he was transferred to the right side of the chapel of Saint Denis, where this epitaph is read: “Epitaph of Lord Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, who, after presiding powerfully in word and deed for forty years, became our brother and, dying, was at last buried in the old basilica; now transferred, he rests here”:

> [Col. 1378A] You who were rich and a great bishop, why  
> Did you exchange your lot for one of poorer estate?  
> Rather, I exchanged poverty at great interest:  
> I was rich in the world; it was greater to be rich in God.

Under the administration of the same Guarinus flourished the distinguished poet Leonius. First a canon in the church of Saint Benedict at Paris, he then withdrew to the Victorine house. Encouraged by the counsels of Abbot Guarinus, he wrote in concise language the history of the sacred Law, which Moses delivered in five books, and the books of Judges, which he composed in twelve books of verse; these survive in manuscript in the Victorine library. He died in 1187, in December, or on 28 December, according to vol. II of the *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, p. 197.

Furthermore, it brought no small honour to the Victorine house and to Abbot Guarinus that canons were summoned from that monastery to teach the canons of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes at Soissons their customs and to form them in the right pattern of canonical life [Col. 1378B]. This is the G., abbot of Saint-Victor, mentioned in 1185 [Note: [Col. 1377D] Letter 143 of Stephen of Tournai, p. 209.] in a charter of Saint-Magloire. Together with H., abbot of Saint-Denis, F., abbot of Saint-Germain, and S., abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, he rendered an account to the Supreme Pontiff of what they had decided in the affair of the Grandmontines.

Guarinus also wrote alone to Philip, king of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1378D] Vol. VI, Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 266.], asking him to put an end to this dispute; and he congratulated Celestine III upon his election as Supreme Pontiff. Finally, after Abbot Guarinus had spent twenty-one years in this office and had devoted much effort to repairing the injuries which Ervisius had inflicted upon the most holy community, he died on 19 October 1192, according to words recently added to the old inscription on his tomb, given below. Yet the year 1193 is read in vol. II of the *History of the Church of Paris*, p. 176; and 1194 in vol. I of the *History of Paris*, p. 197, and in vol. I of Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*, col. 1013, where “in the month of November” is also read instead of “14 Kalends of November.” [Col. 1378C] The more distant from these years is the year 1180 assigned by Claude du Molinet in his note on letter 42 of Stephen of Tournai, p. 58, the further it departs from the truth.

In the *Diplomatique*, p. 371, there is a text from manuscript no. 66 of Saint-Germain-des-Prés: when a certain cleric named Nicholas, dying at Saint-Victor, entrusted his possessions to the abbot of that church, namely Lord Garin, a most religious man, to distribute them prudently after his death among neighbouring churches as a wise steward, Garin—because he was bound to love our church, that of Saint-Germain, more than the others—proposed to bestow upon this church, from the goods committed to him, a Psalter for the salvation of the soul of the said cleric.

Guarinus was buried in the choir of the church beside Abbot Gilduin, with this distich. The following words were prefixed on the new tomb: “Eulogy, here placed from a manuscript, of the eloquent and religious Father Guarinus, fifth abbot of this church in succession”:

> [Col. 1378D] Abbot Guarinus, light-bearer of the Roman world,  
> While living, shines as a stone in the starry city.

The following words were also added: “He died on 19 October 1192.” On that day the necrology of Saint-Victor has: “The solemn anniversary of Lord Guarinus, of blessed memory, abbot of this church”; and the necrology of Cagia: “20 October: anniversary of the venerable Garin, abbot of Saint-Victor and our canon.” Yet I read that in 1194 he established [something] upon the rights of Ivry. Manuscript volumes of sermons composed by him are said to be preserved in the Victorine library.

## EPITAPH OF ACHARD

(*Neustria Pia*, p. 795.)

[Col. 1379]

Blessed Achard, bishop of Avranches. He not only gave counsel regarding the most recent foundation of the abbey of La Lucerne, but also, in 1164, devoutly received, blessed, and placed in the foundations the chief and corner stone offered by the founders for construction of the abbey church. He then willingly granted those religious the right of *Deportus* in the Church of Avranches; and at his death he wished to be buried in their abbey basilica, outside the choir indeed, but beside the wall of the choir itself, at the Epistle corner before the doorway leading to the cloister. There he still rests, bearing this epitaph:

> Famous teacher Achard, bishop of Avranches,  
> Lies here, that earth may be restored to earth.  
> Heavenly grace gave him the gifts of wisdom  
> And worthily set him over the Church.  
> I now pass over in silence the many good works of his piety,  
> Which have been sufficiently heard of and sufficiently seen.  
> He was himself abbot in the church of Saint-Victor;  
> And fulfilled the work in character, speech, and deed.  
> This house has been ennobled by his remains;  
> From above, so great a grace has been given to us.  
> Therefore may so great a father, patron of faith and law,  
> Whose pastoral teaching sounded from his mouth,  
> Behold the joys of the divine countenance,  
> And may the dwelling of the good bishop be granted him.  
>
> [Note: [Col. 1379] From the papers of the abbey and convent of La Lucerne.]

[Col. 1379]

## LETTERS OF ABBOT GILDUIN

### I. To the Bishop of Beauvais.—He commends to him a priest whose brother had died intestate.

[Col. 1379A]

To the lord bishop of Beauvais, G., called abbot of Blessed Victor of Paris: may you glory in the supreme Shepherd and worthily imitate His footsteps.

This priest, bearer of the present letter, had a brother who died intestate, except that, as we have been told, he left one horse to the Regular Canons of Saint-Quentin [Note: [Col. 1379B] A distinguished monastery of Regular Canons near Beauvais, founded in 1067 by Guy, bishop of that city. Its first abbot was the celebrated Ivo, later bishop of Chartres.], upon whose land he lived. For he had been waiting for this brother of his, but before the latter arrived, the former died. The aforementioned canons then came, took the dead man’s body, buried it among themselves, and at the same time carried off whatever he seemed to possess. Therefore this man asks you, through our smallness, to render him justice and cause the property of his brother to be restored to him. Farewell.

### II. Gilduin’s letter concerning the church of Saint Peter of Mont-Lethéric granted to the monks of Longpont, and concerning the compensation made to the canons of Saint-Victor, who possessed in it a prebend and annual revenues.

G., called abbot of the monastery of Saint-Victor, together with all his brethren, to all the faithful, both future and present, forever.

It belongs to all good people, and especially to religious persons, to rejoice in the propagation and advancement of all holiness and religious life. By God’s mercy, this joy was offered and granted in our time to our pious desires in the transfer of the church of Blessed Peter of Mont-Lethéric [Col. 1380A]. For, through God’s grace and the will, counsel, and assent of the most pious Louis, king of the Franks, that church was raised from a secular state to a religious state; and for this purpose it was assigned and granted in perpetuity to God’s servants, namely the monks of Longpont [Note: [Col. 1379B] Longpont is a distinguished cell of the Cluniac order [Col. 1380B] in the diocese of Paris, where there were formerly twenty-two monks together with the prior. There is another Longpont, three leagues from Soissons, where there is a celebrated abbey of the Cistercian order.].

Accordingly, since in the aforesaid church of Saint Peter we possess one complete prebend and the annual revenues of other prebends, we desire and approve this change for the better. Through the hand of our lord Theobald, bishop of Paris, we grant in perpetuity to the church of Longpont the aforesaid prebend and annual revenues. But so that our church should not be burdened with too great a loss of its revenues because of that church’s transfer and our benevolent concession, the monks of Longpont, at the counsel, mediation—or rather, through the action—of the aforesaid bishop of Paris, in whose judgment and power the whole matter rested with the assent of both parties, rendered us reciprocal compensation. With the common assent of their own church and the church of Saint Peter, they gave to our church for perpetual possession the following:

At Athegias: lands, vineyards, the tithe, and everything whatsoever that the church of Longpont possessed there. In the same village, two solidi of rent which the aforesaid church of Saint Peter possessed there [Col. 1381A]. All these things, as stated, the church of Longpont granted to our church to possess forever freely and peacefully, and confirmed the grant with the impression of its seal. That our concession concerning the transfer of the aforesaid church of Saint Peter, and the prebend and annual revenues, might remain valid forever, we wrote this charter containing the tenor of our concession [Col. 1382A], confirmed it with the impression of our seal, and delivered it to the monks of Longpont to possess and preserve. We have also subscribed the names of our brethren as testimony and for greater security. Sign of Abbot G., etc.

[Col. 1381]

## LETTERS OF ABBOT ACHARD, LATER BISHOP OF AVRANCHES

### I. To Henry II, King of the English.—That he compel Richard of Ely, his treasurer, to pay money left by a Parisian canon to the poor and to churches.

[Col. 1381B]

To HENRY, by the grace of God most glorious king of the English, A. [Note: [Col. 1381D] Achard, second abbot of Saint-Victor, succeeded Gilduin, who died in 1155, 13 April.] called, though unworthy, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Victor of Paris: greeting, and may you merit eternal reward through the administration of your temporal kingdom.

A certain canon of Paris, named F., moved by generosity alone and with no expectation of greater gain, entrusted twenty pounds in Parisian money to Master Richard of Ely, your treasurer, until a specified date. It happened, however, that before the stated term the same canon entered [Col. 1381C] upon the way of all flesh. When at the point of death, he assigned his entire property to churches and poor people, more to some and less to others, according to the counsel of religious men. Those who were present at his testament therefore sent a messenger to the aforesaid Richard in England, requiring payment of the money mentioned above. But he, forgetful of so great a benefit, contemptuously refused payment.

Therefore poor Christ, on behalf of the churches and poor, entreats Your Majesty and urgently asks your protection in this special cause of His. And lest, God forbid, blame for his transgression should through negligence redound upon you, compel, by the authority divinely granted to you, this man who dangerously resists restoring Christ’s money. Thus the zeal of joy may plainly appear in you, and the cause of the churches and poor, having been aided, may intercede for you before the supreme Judge. Moreover, know this for certain: at the moment of death, before three priests of honourable reputation, he confessed that he had entrusted the aforesaid money freely, without any increase [Col. 1382B], to the aforesaid Richard for a fixed time. Farewell.

### II. To A., Bishop of Lisieux.—He commends his church to him.

To the most illustrious lord and one in every way most worthy of reverence, A. [Note: [Col. 1382D] Arnulf, who was made bishop of Lisieux after having been archdeacon of Sées.], bishop of Lisieux: A., abbot of Saint-Victor, greeting and the service of devoted affection.

We cannot render adequate thanks to your kindness, because it has both cultivated our house with remarkable affection and bound us to itself by generous benefits. We therefore entrust the rendering of thanks to Him to whom you do whatever you do to one of His least ones. Moreover, we ask your exaltedness and entreat you with most urgent prayers [Col. 1382C] that the affection which your kindness bore toward us while our father and predecessor Abbot Gilduin, of pious memory, was alive may not grow cold; that the former breadth of your charity may not in any degree be narrowed, but may be enlarged day by day the more because we now stand in greater need.

We are wholly bound to you: all of us, your devoted servants, are most ready, as is our duty, with most willing intention to do for you whatever our lowliness can accomplish. No day passes in which forgetfulness removes your memory from us. We now send Brother Rayner to you, concerning the matter which he himself will explain. Know, moreover, that the affair for which he is sent is as he will affirm. We therefore offer many prayers to your serenity, that you may extend a pious hand to a pious cause [Col. 1382D], and provide both counsel and help so that debts due to the poor may be paid. May Christ Jesus preserve your blessedness, most illustrious lord and one in every way most worthy of reverence.

[Col. 1381]

## LETTERS OF ABBOT ERVISIUS

### I. Concerning Ervisius, abbot of Saint-Victor, godfather of King Philip.

[Col. 1381D]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1145, on the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, during the night, while the morning office was being celebrated, the most noble offspring of Louis, formerly king of France, came forth into the light—namely his son Philip. A messenger bearing the joyful news of his birth came to Saint-Germain-des-Prés and announced these happy tidings at the very hour when the monks began to sing the prophetic canticle: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people,” etc. [Luke 1:68]. That this occurred by divine oracle may be inferred from clear indications. The report of this so greatly desired child spread everywhere and filled all the French with the greatest joy; for they had long and earnestly desired a male successor descended from the king’s line, who, after the death of his glorious father, might occupy the throne of royal majesty. The Lord granted them their desire, and they were not disappointed of their wish.

Accordingly, after the royal child had been born, on the day following his birth—that is, on Sunday—his father King Louis caused his son to be confirmed by the sacrament of baptism. To perform it, Maurice, bishop of Paris, clothed himself in priestly vestments by the king’s command and solemnly regenerated the royal child in the church of Saint Michael of the Square. Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain at Paris, acted as godfather and held the boy in his arms over the baptismal font; Ervisius, abbot of Saint Victor, and Odo, formerly abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, were likewise godfathers. Constance, sister of King Louis and wife of Raymond, count of Saint-Gilles, together with two Parisian widows, were godmothers.

## II. Letter of King Louis to Ervisius, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*He requests justice against the men of Amponville.*

[Col. 1383C]

Louis, by God’s grace king of the Franks, to his friend Ervisius, illustrious abbot of Saint Victor, greetings.

It has come to our knowledge that we have our right in the case against the men of Amponville, five of whose number have rendered us satisfaction. Therefore we command you to secure for us the treasure as it is found, and to bring your men, since they were ours, to justice from Wednesday eight days hence. If you do not do this, we shall turn against the town itself. For if certain persons had broken into our house, even if they had not taken away money, they would nevertheless be bound to make restitution for the whole; and we wish our men to make satisfaction to us for the fortune that was dug up.

## III. Letter of P., Chaplain of Saint Chrysogonus and of the Pope, to Ervisius, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*For love of him, he says that he lent money to Robert of Bristol.*

[Col. 1383D]

To Ervisius, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint Victor at Paris, Brother P., chaplain of Saint Chrysogonus and of the lord pope, greetings and the affection of deepest devotion.

The requests and offerings of prayers which you deign to present to me for the relief of your friends I strive all the more willingly to carry into effect because I am bound to your person by a closer affection of charity. You may know this in the affair of Brother Robert of Bristol and others. For him, both because of your love and because of the obligation owed to his brother and uncle, I lent two marks of silver, or thereabouts. As I testify, he spent them for the business of his church. I therefore ask your affection to make this known by your letters to the aforesaid abbot, so that he may conduct himself in this matter in such a way that, if occasion requires, I may the more willingly render heartfelt assistance to someone of our order. I have as witnesses to this the lord of Albano and his clerk Roger, Hugh, chaplain of the lord pope, and our servant John, whom you know well.

## IV. Letter of G., Bishop of Hereford, to Ervisius, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*He asks for someone from his flock to be placed over the Church of Worcester, bereft of a shepherd.*

G., by God’s grace bishop of Hereford, to his beloved in the Lord E., abbot of Saint Victor, and to the brethren entrusted to his care, greetings, grace, and blessing.

Love, commanding from the hearts of your brethren, compels us at present to write to you and to offer earnest prayers to your kindness. For the Church of Worcester has long wept bitterly in the night of her sorrow, and the tears clinging to her cheeks cannot be lightly restrained or dried except through you. Therefore, desiring after the loss of its shepherd that a father be appointed to it according to custom, it returns to the pastures from which it first received a shepherd, and from which, by the Lord’s ordering, it first received the rudiments of canonical discipline. Therefore we make most humble supplication to you, joining our prayers to the petitioner’s: provide for the church planted by your right hand a suitable shepherd, such as you know to be fitting for it, and grant him from your community, so that you may have them bound by continual obedience, and us, insofar as we can, debtors in grace and service. You ought to prosper in the Lord, beloved ones.

## V. Letter of Ervisius, Abbot of Saint Victor, to O., Cardinal and Legate of the Apostolic See  
*The king grants him free permission to return to his brother cardinals.*

To the reverend father and lord O., by God’s grace cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate of the apostolic see, Brother Er., called by God’s forbearance abbot of the church of Saint Victor, due reverence and obedience with devoted greeting.

[Col. 1384D]

I have done what your dignity enjoined upon me. I went to the king and dutifully greeted him on your behalf. I had with him a private and quite familiar conversation concerning you. Anxiously, I carefully disclosed the cares and afflictions of your heart, and set forth your desire and intention to return and to obey the commands of the lord pope, if an excessively dangerous difficulty did not stand in the way. Finally, concerning all this, I sought his own will.

Displaying serenity of face and mind, he made known to me his view of each point and did not conceal his intention. I must therefore report to you, my lord, the plain truth of his answer. He freely grants that you may go to your brother cardinals wherever they may be, and consult with them about returning as soon as possible to the lord pope. For love of you, and because of the standing and honour of the court, he will also give safe-conduct for your person and goods throughout all his land, and through the lands of his barons as far as Saint-Gilles. There he will command the count and his sister to receive and keep you with honour and in complete security until you find passage from there.

But he would not in any way give his consent to your remaining in his land; indeed, he forbade me to speak further to him on this subject. Now therefore, concerning safe-conduct, send to him securely as you learn will be expedient for you. Yet he told me that certain crossings are under the authority of the king of England. Through those he will not give you safe-conduct, but only through crossings belonging to his barons. Farewell; and command whatever you wish of me, your servant.

## VI. Letter of Pope Alexander III to the Abbot of Saint Victor  
*He commends to him Alexius, a deacon residing at Saint Victor.*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and the whole chapter of the church of Saint Victor, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Since all …,” etc. See under Alexander III, for the year 1181.

## VII. Letter of Lawrence, Abbot of Westin, to Ernest [Ervisius], Abbot of Saint Victor  
*He commends to him John, kinsman of his prior, who wished to direct schools.*

[Col. 1385C]

Lawrence, abbot of Westin, to his beloved kinsman E., abbot of Saint Victor, greetings.

Let it be known to your affection that John, the bearer of this letter, is the kinsman of our prior and is familiar to us. We therefore entreat your charity that in your regions, for the love of God and of us, you may support him with the help of your counsel and consolation. And because, God willing, he desires to direct schools, provide him at our request with some castle or town suitable for carrying his purpose into effect. Whatever generosity and benefit your kindness confers upon him, we shall without doubt consider bestowed upon ourselves. May your holiness prosper.

## VIII. Letter of E. to Ervisius, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*He reports the injuries inflicted upon him by the knight Ursinus.*

[Col. 1385D]

To his venerable father E., abbot of Saint Victor, his son E. wishes blessedness in both lives.

My dearest father, I thought it necessary to tell you, and to report as quickly as possible, the evils inflicted upon us by the knight Ursinus. He has stripped your land of all its goods, forbidden your men to cultivate your land, and moreover hired certain retainers who lie in wait for our spoil night and day. Therefore, having been summoned by us in your presence on the Tuesday of the octave of Pentecost, he scarcely accepted a day [for a hearing]. I therefore ask you to indicate to us by the bearer of this letter a certain date for your arrival. Farewell.

## IX. Letter of R., Abbot of Saint Evurtius, to Ervisius, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*He excuses his failure to visit him and commends to him the affairs of his monastery.*

To the venerable father and heartfelt friend E., by God’s grace abbot of Saint Victor, Brother R.—[Note: Roger or Robert, who governed the monastery of Saint Evurtius during the time of Abbot Ervisius.]—the humble minister of the poor of Saint Evurtius at Orléans, his whole self, and whatever besides that he can offer.

Let it not surprise you, beloved father, that we have delayed in coming to you. For if we had received the desired message concerning our affair, about which we wrote to your affection and under which we are still pressed by no slight distress, we would hasten joyfully to meet you. Yet even without any hope in that matter, if you shall have acted in anything on behalf of our littleness, we serve your fatherhood no less willingly and devotedly.

As we wrote to you, so now, with the crisis of necessity at hand, we write and earnestly beg that, with all the compassion of mercy, you sympathize with this need of ours and strive by every means to bring the matter, as we instructed you, to its completion. For our house is burdened by an obligation of debt, increased daily by interest. Send back to us through our brother of Bourges what may please you in this matter.

We are deeply grieved by your illness. Therefore, as we have said, if we are needed by you in anything, we shall come quickly. Concerning the prebend of the dean of Saint-Marcel, which Aurel. holds, and of which we previously made mention to you, we ask that, when an opportunity occurs, you speak on our behalf. For he himself will derive the least advantage from it. But you, by God’s grace, hold great favour both with him and with the dean. Farewell.

## X. Letter of Richard, Abbot of Bristol, to Ervisius, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*He praises the holiness of Saint Victor’s monastery and gives thanks for benefits bestowed on Robert.*

To the venerable lord and dearest father E., by God’s grace abbot of Saint Victor, Brother Richard, unworthy priest of the monastery of Saint Augustine at Bristol, greetings and undiminished affection.

My spirit rejoices in the Lord over what we gladly learn and frequently hear of your holy religious life and wisdom in the house of God, where care for outward concerns is so conducted that the virtue of religion flourishes within. For these things we are bound to give you thanks as much as we can and know how—indeed, in every way beyond our ability—for what your excellence has deigned to write to our littleness concerning the present condition and health of your holy house. Likewise also for the benefits which you bestowed upon our brother Robert, in word, deed, and counsel, in every service and act of kindness. Since we cannot render these and other things to you, may God, the recompender of all good things, repay you.

But we and our brethren, devoted servants of your fatherhood, are in tranquillity and the good of peace, striving to make progress in the house of God according to the small measure of our strength. Farewell.

## XI. Letter of G. to Ervisius, Her Brother and Abbot  
*She commends herself to his prayers and sends him small gifts.*

To her reverend lord and most loving brother Ervisius, abbot of the church of Saint Victor, G., his sister, wishes to be there where she is near him.

[Col. 1387B]

“The persistent prayer of a righteous person avails much” [James 5:16]; how much more, then, does the prayer excel of one who, by the special prerogative of holiness, treads beneath his feet the world together with its flower, and in mind and deed attends upon the divine will. Therefore, my beloved brother, although no small gulf of distance separates us, I desire to be bound to you not only by kinship of flesh but also by devotion of prayers in Christ.

Accordingly, informing your holiness of the state of my prosperity, I openly declare that my husband and I are well and cheerful. Receive also, as gratefully as gladly, this little gift—not with less care because it is small, but embracing it with as much affection as though it were great. For through Peter, the bearer, I send you a white bearskin, a *rotalline* tooth [uncertain identification], and two knives gilt with silver.

Furthermore, many of our countrymen, claiming to come on my husband’s behalf, will take refuge at the harbour of your kindness. To what can I say that such people are more like than a hungry dog, which gets food wherever it can prevail? Therefore I say truly that I have sent no one to you except Solomon and John. To expose the evasions of those who come to you as though sent on my behalf, I ask that something be sent from you to me which can serve as a token between us in this matter. I also ask that you send me cloves and cinnamon. Solomon greets you for the whole benefit conferred upon him through your kindness, remaining your devoted debtor in gratitude. He will also consider himself greatly obliged to your will if you should wish to give him any command.

## XII. Letter of Cardinal Odo to Ervisius, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*He commends to him his servant and the business entrusted to him.*

Odo, by God’s grace called cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate of the apostolic see, to his beloved brother E., abbot of Saint Victor, greetings.

We commend to your affection the bearer of this letter, our servant, whom we have sent to you on certain affairs of ours, so that you may exercise diligence in seeking the things which we have entrusted to him. We wish him, if he finds it expedient, to acquire two staffs, a chalice, a censer, and the remaining items for a chapel, and to make an exchange; and we ask that you help him.

## XIII. Letter of the Canon Jonas to Ervisius, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*Sent to Caesaris Burgum, he asks to be recalled to Saint Victor.*

To his spiritual father Ervisius, by God’s grace abbot of Blessed Victor at Paris, Brother Jonas, his unworthy canon, a miserable exile and pilgrim, sends the greeting which he himself does not possess.

My dearest father, I have found the following saying most true:

> By I know not what sweetness one’s native soil draws all,  
> And does not suffer them to forget itself.  
> Thus beast, thus bird, thus fish seeks out  
> The familiar pastures in the places where it was first nourished.

For I rightly prefer that place above all places in which mother grace bore me, together with many brethren, to Christ her bridegroom—a place where I would wish to be, so that I might not be at Caesaris Burgum. Nor is this surprising:

> Here the people are faithless, and the king’s favour is to be feared.  
> Here the lands are barren, and no vine survives;  
> The forest lacks leaves, the meadows lack their pastures;  
> The sea is nearby, yet there are a thousand perils of death.  
> Nothing here is sweeter than being able to suffer evils.

There are besides things hidden within:

> The anxious care of a household; scant possession of goods—  
> A thing which many seek; not to give it will be a crime.

That I should suffer these things—what crime have I committed? If none, your obedience could have prescribed, and my ignorance could have found, a gentler exile. Therefore let not so merciful a shepherd be reluctant to bring back the hundredth sheep, nor so kindly a father to receive his lost son returning from the land of unlikeness. I do not ask for the first robe; I do not ask for the fatted calf. But let it be done for me as for one of your hired servants. Farewell.

# Letters of Abbot Guarin

## I. Letter of Cardinals Alexander and Theoderic to Abbot Guarin  
*They congratulate him on his promotion and exhort him not to devote himself to erecting great buildings.*

Alexander, by divine favour cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and Theoderic, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the apostolic see, to their beloved brother in Christ Guarin, abbot of Saint Victor: may you always be occupied in the ordinances of God.

We write to our brethren, the archbishops of Sens and Bourges, as we believe to be expedient for you and your Church. Certainly, concerning the honour conferred upon you, we rejoice at what has been done, because, with the Lord’s help, we hope that much good will come of it. We are glad that you recognize and fear the difficulty of the charge laid upon you. Would that your religious life always considered this, and considered with fear and trembling to whom and from what you must render an account on the day of judgment. For we believe that negligence will not readily find room if this is diligently kept in your mind.

Your predecessor, like many others, was concerned with constructing great buildings. But you, who were chosen by the Lord and, when entering religious life, left such things in the world—[Note: From this it may be inferred that Guarin was of illustrious birth.]—sit at Jesus’ feet with Mary, and hear the word from his mouth, which you must set before the sheep entrusted to you and others who come to you. Otherwise, should you perhaps determine to persist in constructing earthly buildings, you may hear that evangelical saying: “All these buildings shall be destroyed, and not one stone shall be left upon another” [cf. Matthew 24:2].

Moreover, encouraged by the good hope which we have conceived of your religious life and informed by the testimony of your pious conduct, we intend to hold your person in the bowels of charity, and we willingly wish, in the fear of God, to advance the affairs of the Church entrusted to you.

## II. Letter of Pope Alexander III to the Canons of Saint Victor  
*He confirms Ervisius’s resignation and Guarin’s promotion.*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the canons of the Church of Saint Victor at Paris, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Since your church …,” etc. See under Pope Alexander III.

## III. Letter of Pope Alexander III to Guarin, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*He congratulates him on his election and exhorts him diligently to perform a shepherd’s duties.*

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Guarin, abbot of Saint Victor at Paris, greetings and apostolic blessing.

“Having learned and ascertained …,” etc. See under Pope Alexander III.

## IV. Letter of Guarin, Abbot of Saint Victor, to John, Cardinal of Naples  
*He cannot send the brethren requested: one has died and the other is gravely ill; others too can scarcely be sent.*

To the reverend lord and dearest father in Christ J., by God’s grace cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Guarin, humble minister of the church of Blessed Victor at Paris, greetings in the Lord and prompt service with devotion.

Your sublimity instructed my predecessor concerning two brethren and, again, by a sealed letter gave the same instruction to my littleness. In both letters you specified by name those whom you wanted, namely Peter of Périgueux and Hugh of Saint-Germain. One of them, called by God, has passed away; the other is sick with an incurable illness, without hope of recovery.

Since neither could be sent, being prevented by death and the hardship of sickness, and since I did not know what to do, I consulted the lords archbishops of Sens and Bourges and other prudent and religious men about what I ought to do. Since your letter had left no discretion to choose another according to another person’s judgment, they advised that it was unsafe to send others, lest I should send not those whom you wanted but others, who might perhaps be burdensome rather than welcome. They therefore advised delay, so that, when you learned of the manifold need of the Church, your kindness might condescend in compassion and spare it.

For the religious men by whose religious life and prudence the Church was formerly governed have for the most part died, and few have arisen after them. The house is worn down by disturbances, oppressed by debts, and stripped of temporal goods. If, amid so many anxieties, I am compelled to dismiss those few who remain to me and who ought to sustain me by assisting me; and if I lose the eyes which ought to show me the path of religious observance and discipline, I shall certainly easily go astray, nor shall I be able alone to bear the burden and management of the house.

Finally—to speak humanly, covering death with the secret weakness of illness—the brethren are greatly frightened both by the unfamiliar harshness of the land and by the corrupt quality of the air. For if our laymen, who go there and have complete freedom to travel, go about, and return, can scarcely live even a little, how could these men, shut up in a cloister, live in distant parts? The brethren put forward these reasons and pretexts. Thus I consider it most grave to impose upon them what, if done, is undertaken against their will, and, if not done, is very dangerously refused. Therefore, lord, let the greatness of your clemency now spare our weaknesses and attend to the pressing necessities of the Church. For my part, I am ready to obey your commands in whatever I can.

## V. Letter of Guarin, Abbot of Saint Victor, to Pope Alexander III  
*On the same subject.*

To the most holy father and lord Alexander, by God’s grace supreme pontiff of the universal Church, Guarin, humble minister of the Church of Saint Victor at Paris, greetings in the Lord and the most devoted service of complete submission.

“To my littleness …,” etc. See under Pope Alexander III.

## VI. Letter of Gilduin, Abbot of Fontaine-Jean, to Guarin, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*Concerning grain which he had requested from him as a loan.*

To the venerable and beloved father Guarin, abbot of the monastery of Saint Victor, Brother Gilduin, abbot of Fontaine-Jean—[Note: Fontaine-Jean is a Cistercian monastery in the diocese of Sens, founded in 1124 by the lords of Courtenay. Saint William, later archbishop of Bourges, formerly made his monastic profession there.]—greetings with service.

We are willing to serve your affection and that of your brethren to the full extent of our ability. The grain which you request to be lent to you, however, has already for the most part been prepared, namely winnowed from the chaff. Therefore let your charity arrange that we find your messenger present at our grange near Moret on Thursday after the feast of Saint James. Let no boat be sent, however, until your messenger has arrived, so that he may inspect the grain with us; and whatever we can lend without burdening our house, we shall lend most willingly. Farewell.

## VII. Letter of John, Count of Eu, to Guarin, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*The canons whom he sent to Eu must observe the customs of Arrouaise; otherwise they are to depart.*

John, count of Eu, to Guarin, by God’s grace abbot of Saint Victor at Paris, greetings and affection.

By this letter I have taken care to make known to the discretion of your fatherhood how grievously, harshly, and almost hostilely my barons have risen against me, and how all my clergy and many most religious persons continually reproach and afflict me because I have rashly determined, contrary to reason, to dispose of the Church of Eu in this fashion, and because I received your canons into it contrary to the institution of my father and myself.

They allege against me what is true: namely, that after my father, moved by zeal for God, established regular canons at Eu, he immediately, with the consent of Geoffrey, archdeacon of Rouen, and afterward at the request, admonition, and exhortation of Hugh, archbishop of Rouen—[Note: This is that most famous Hugh, formerly abbot of Reading and made archbishop of Rouen, whose seven books of *Dialogues* we published in volume V of the *Anecdota*.]—gave, and I granted, the aforesaid church into the hand of the abbot of Arrouaise—[Note: Arrouaise, also called Aridagamantia, is a distinguished abbey in the diocese of Arras, head of the Order or Congregation of Arrouaise; an encomium of it is found in Jacques de Vitry’s *Western History*.]—to hold and preserve the order in perpetuity according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. It was also ordained that the abbot of Eu should once each year visit the chapter of the church of Saint Nicholas of Arrouaise, so that any deficiency might be repaired.

Therefore I command—and, commanding, most earnestly entreat, ask, and beseech your most diligent fatherhood above all things—that peace be maintained in the Church of Eu. Command Roger the abbot and his companions whom you sent to us, by obedience, and impose upon them by your command that they maintain in the Church of Eu the religious order according to the manner and custom of Arrouaise, or else depart altogether. For I do not wish to endure any longer the sentence of excommunication pronounced against me every Sunday on that account. It seems grievous to me that I have borne it for so long. If you do not do this, I tell you truly that I shall never again love them; rather, I shall destroy them in every way I can. Farewell.

## VIII. Letter of P., Cardinal, to Guarin, Abbot of Saint Victor  
*What he has done in Saint Victor’s cause, and what course he advises.*

To G., by God’s grace abbot of Saint Victor, and the whole convent, P., by the same grace cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, greetings and enduring sincere affection.

We recently received the letters of your devotion and grieved not only over the burden of the Church but also that your prudence, by the counsel or cunning of I know not whom, had declined so far that, humbled at the archbishop’s feet, you promised to pay what another had seized. While we, for the liberation of your Church, were opposing the adverse party with all our efforts and solicitude, a twofold labour lay upon us. First, to prove that a thing committed to such a person and in such a manner was by no means owed by you. Then, because you had fallen in the case, to recall your innocence and poverty and humbly and devoutly ask the lord pope to release you wholly from the archbishop’s claim, thereby relieving you from so grave a calamity.

But because of the great difficulty of the affair, while the archbishop was imperiously and categorically demanding everything as if by right, our petition was unheard. At last we obtained the best letters we could, and judges to whom we offer earnest prayers by our letters that they may strive by every means to preserve your right unimpaired.

You must now keep your eyes open and watchful. If no friendly settlement can be reached between you and the archbishop, then, since the lord pope—when he has heard the arguments of both sides—will by no means compel you to pay except what is proved to have been converted to the uses of the Church, and will command the judges not this but only that the case be concluded by due judgment, you must answer firmly if you judge yourselves injured by prejudice in any respect. If through lack of caution we promised anything not owed, we can neither pay it nor ought to pay it. Rather, like a ward, if one has fallen through a slippery counsel or the fraud of adversaries, we must be restored; otherwise we may freely proceed by appeal, since the lord pope’s letters are so worded that they do not at all forbid you to appeal.

Nor will it then be necessary for any of the brethren to exhaust himself by coming all the way to us on this account. Let merely one of your servants report to us what has occurred, and you will be able to experience our solicitude for you.

## IX. Letter of Cardinal Hugh Pierleone to Guarin and the Chapter of Saint Victor  
*He grieves at the act of Ervisius, their former abbot, and offers them his services.*

To his beloved brethren in Christ, Guarin the abbot, the prior, and the whole chapter of Saint Victor, Hugh Pierleone—[Note: In 1173 he was made cardinal-deacon by Alexander III and was legate of the apostolic see in France, England, and Scotland.]—by God’s grace cardinal-deacon of Saint Angelo, greetings and affectionate regard.

The more sincerely we embrace your affection in the arms of charity, the more deeply are we grieved and troubled when we hear that you or your monastery are subject to any adversity. We rejoice in its prosperity and cherish it before the other monasteries of the French province because of its honour and religious life, and we have learned that its name has risen to greater renown.

Having seen your letters, by which you informed us of the deed of Ervisius, once your abbot, we were troubled and struck by bitter anguish of heart. For we consider your sorrow wholly our own, and rejoice greatly in your joy. Therefore, for healing so great a sorrow and burden, we have taken care to advance your petition with such urgency and diligence as we could. That it has not been brought in every respect to the result we wished displeases us as much as we fear that your will may fail.

Accordingly, we earnestly ask and beseech your whole community that, placing fuller confidence in us as in your special friend, and regarding our power in every way as your own, you may have recourse to us with complete confidence in the affairs of yourselves and your Church. Thus, by the demonstration of action, it may shine more clearly than light how fervently we are moved by love for you and how wholly ready and prepared we are to render services pleasing to you. For we have a fixed and unshaken purpose to accomplish whatever we know will please you and will contribute to the honour and increase of your house and religious life.

## X. Letter of Cardinal Bernard to Abbot Guarin and the Chapter of Saint Victor  
*He sympathizes with the burden laid upon Saint Victor’s monastery and commends to them his nephew Bernard.*

Bernard—[Note: He had been a canon of the Lateran, was made cardinal of the title of Saint Clement by Eugenius III, and was transferred by Adrian IV to the bishopric of Porto and Saint Rufina.]—by God’s grace bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina, to his venerable brother Guarin, abbot of the church of Blessed Victor, and to the chapter, greetings and the vision of “the God of gods in Zion” [Psalm 84:7].

Having gladly received the letters of your religious community, we did not fail to consider their tenor in careful reflection, noting the ruin and no small burden of your house. But because it is ours to protect churches from repeated exactions, and especially yours, which we regard almost as our own and by whose continual prayer we believe ourselves to be protected, we intervened, urgently urging the lord pope to protect and more diligently defend your Church with pontifical favour in so great a crisis.

We believe that this has at length been so accomplished that, if your more earnest care shall strive diligently, restitution of little or no money will burden your aforesaid Church. We therefore ask and earnestly urge you not to withdraw from us the gift of your prayers, but to deign to entreat God for us without ceasing; for our protection, insofar as we can provide it, will in no way fail you.

We ask that you love our nephew Bernard in the customary manner, honestly granting him for lodging that which you promised him together with our clerk Nicholas. We shall value this more highly than if it were placed in our own chamber. Moreover, we ask that your discretion provide mercifully for the bearer of this letter, paying him a suitable benefit for the service he has rendered, so that he may sustain his needy life. For you know that he has many times faithfully exposed himself to death and dangers for your Church.

## XI. Letter of John, Cardinal of Naples, to Abbot Guarin and the Brethren of Saint Victor  
*He thanks them for granting Peter, the canon whom they sent him, and promises every care and solicitude for their affairs.*

[Col. 1394B]

John of Naples—[Note: He had been a regular canon of Saint Victor at Paris, as Ciaconius writes, and was made cardinal by Adrian IV, who himself had been a regular canon of Saint-Ruf.]—unworthy cardinal-priest, to his beloved brethren and dearest friends in the Lord, G., abbot, and the convent of Saint Victor at Paris, greetings and sincere love.

We render to you manifold thanksgivings, because, in accordance with the tenor of the lord pope’s command and our request, you have sent us Brother Peter, a man indeed commendable for the uprightness of his character and for learning. We received him with honour and keep him about us with much honour. And after we have received [Col. 1394C] other canons from churches of your order, to whom the lord pope has written in the same manner as to you, we shall install them with great and solemn honour in the church which, by God’s grace, we have magnificently built and endowed with very ample possessions. Henceforth, therefore, as though by obligation, we shall be bound throughout our life to love and assist your Church more earnestly, to the full extent of our ability and according to your wishes.

And even now, concerning that matter which the archbishop of Lund is known improperly to have raised against you, we have assisted as effectively as was fitting and necessary. You will understand this more fully after you have read the reply-letter of the lord pope, which he is sending on your behalf to the archbishop of Lund [Col. 1394D], so that the judges whom the lord pope has delegated to hear and decide the complaint which the aforesaid archbishop brings against you may be favourably disposed toward you. In order that they may strive to support your side more attentively, we send them our letters, offer them our prayers on your behalf, and show them by the clearest reasoning how they ought to proceed in the judgment of that case. Many also of our brother cardinals, out of regard [Col. 1395A] for our affection, are sending their own letters to those judges in the form of ours. All these things will become clearer to you from the disclosure of the reply-letters.

XII. Peter, papal chamberlain, to Guarin, abbot of Saint Victor.—He grieves over the troubles of his house.

To the venerable and worthily reverend Father G., by God’s grace abbot of Saint Victor of Paris, Brother PETER, chamberlain of the lord pope, greetings and devoted reverence.

We have kindly received your letter as that of a most beloved Father, since we are disposed and ready to devote ourselves to your honour and service. Having heard of the affliction of your house, we grieved; and God knows how concerned we have been about it, and we have endeavoured to show this in deed as far as [Col. 1395B] we reasonably could. We ask your goodness to commend us to your chapter and to its prayers.

XIII. Cardinals Alexander and Th. to the prior and brethren of Saint Victor.—They exhort them to observe the rule.

ALEXANDER, by divine favour cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina, and TH. [Note: [Col. 1395D] Ciaconius calls him Theodinus; above he is called Theoderic.] cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Vitalis, legates of the Apostolic See, to the brethren, beloved and ever to be beloved in Christ, the prior and chapter of Saint Victor: not to look to vanities and false madness.

What we write to you and the greeting-address by which we visit your whole community [Col. 1395C] proceed from heartfelt affection and from the goodwill which we bear toward you. For, considering how greatly your Church formerly shone in religious life, and how by its light it illuminated others’ darkness in many places, we greatly desire—and, if the opportunity is granted, willingly wish—to be helpers.
