Since your field has appeared less fruitful these past days, perhaps through the neglect of its cultivator, may it, by God’s granting, recover its former fruitfulness; and may it so flourish anew in the observance of holy religion and in the fruit of life that the canonical order, which seems somewhat weakened in many places, may through your example and teaching, with God’s help, recover its lost vigour.

For many years we know that much effort has been expended so that the condition of your Church might be changed [Col. 1395D] for the better and that what was said to hinder the fruitfulness of the divine seed might be removed from its midst. You see that this has until now been delayed and reserved for the time when it could more easily be accomplished and with a lighter burden to you. Do not believe that this work has been the work of man, but rather of Him who “set the sand as the boundary of the sea, and said to it: ‘Thus far shall you come, and here you shall break your swelling waves’” (Job 38:11).

Therefore we admonish and exhort your whole community in the Lord that, being grateful to Him for so great a sign of His kindness toward you, you may lift up your hearts together with your hands [Col. 1396A] to Him in heaven, and direct your utmost efforts to the observance of holy religion. Since God has had care for you—if He had not helped you, your soul would almost have dwelt in hell—do not yourselves become negligent regarding your salvation, nor regard as a small matter the fact that God has willed so mercifully and gently to provide for you. Obey the abbot whom you see has been granted to you by divine mercy; hold him in all reverence and honour as the father of your souls; and, all rivalries and scandals having been quieted, strive with united vows and all your strength that the good fragrance of religious life, which formerly diffused its scent everywhere from your place, may increasingly be smelled throughout the Church of God.

Assuredly, we who embrace him for his religious life in the arms of sincere [Col. 1396B] charity, and count his advancement as our own in the Lord, shall hold you so much dearer in the inward affections of Christ, and shall take so much more willing care to advance your affairs through ourselves and those who trust us, as we know you to be more obedient and devoted to him, and hear that you walk with him in a greater sincerity of love.

XIV. Pope Alexander III to Robert, prior, and the chapter of Saint Victor.—On the same subject.

ALEXANDER, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, prior, and the chapter of Saint Victor of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1396C] We have often admonished and now also by our writings command our beloved son Ervisius, your abbot, that he attend to the affairs [Note: [Col. 1395D] From this it appears that Ervisius, on relinquishing the abbatial dignity, was not stripped of every charge, but that certain matters were reserved for his administration.] of your Church, etc. See under Alexander III.

XV. Guarin, abbot of Saint Victor, to Pope Celestine III.—He congratulates him on his promotion and commends the Church of Saint Victor to him.

To the most holy lord and Father COELESTINE [Note: [Col. 1396D] He was created supreme pontiff on 12 April 1191.] by God’s grace supreme pontiff, Brother GUARIN, humble minister of the poor of the Church of Saint Victor of Paris, together with the other brethren of that place: the obedience due to so great a Father, with the fullness of reverence.

[Col. 1396D] To Almighty God, holy Father, etc. See under Celestine III, among the letters of various persons to him.

XVI. Guarin, abbot of Saint Victor, to Philip, king of the French.—That he may put an end to the dissension among the Grandmontines.

To the most illustrious PHILIP, by God’s grace king of the French, GUARIN, by divine favour humble minister of the poor of the Church of Saint Victor: may he so govern the earthly kingdom by divine mercy that he may be able to reign in heaven.

[Col. 1397A] When, through trustworthy report, we learn of deeds belonging both to the advancement of your soul before God and to your honour before men, know that they are exceedingly pleasing and welcome to us. Hence we rejoice not a little in the Lord because, concerning the poor clerics of Grandmont, the power of the Holy Spirit has touched your heart and inclined your disposition to compassion. To the shame of holy mother Church and the reproach of all religious life, they have been compelled to endure an exile grievous to all who fear God.

Your Excellency’s nobility, and that of other princes who serve God, reverently honours the ministers of the heavenly sacraments, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been entrusted by the Lord. But the converted lay brothers of Grandmont, who ought to have been brethren in religion, dishonour them shamefully by treating them [Col. 1397B] disgracefully! Yet they themselves desire with such zeal to be honoured by you and other great persons. They preach obedience and humility toward the ministers of the Church, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God; but they demand that the Church’s ministers obey them, rather than that they themselves obey the ministers—though they are the more disobedient and rebellious, [Col. 1398A] even against God Himself, which is graver, because they oppose God’s vicars.

Men of spiritual power, who without any hesitation possess God’s Spirit, marvel; so too does so vast a multitude of wise and religious persons that it can scarcely be counted: how the ministers of God could have endured such intolerable treatment for so long, unless it was because, while their condition lay buried, the light did not yet shine in the darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it. But by the ordering, as we believe, of God’s mercy, correction has been reserved for your times, so that this work of God, so great and excellent, may confidently have you, the minister of the eternal King, as its supporter and fellow-worker in good.

We therefore earnestly beseech your Highness to bring to a happy conclusion that resolution of right counsel which, as we have said, divine mercy inspired in you from the beginning, [Note: [Col. 1397B] In 1177 Philip Augustus, on the counsel of his barons, issued certain articles, published by us in vol. I of the *Anecdota*, p. 847, for reconciling [Col. 1398B] the clerics and lay brothers of Grandmont. The lay brothers do not appear to have complied with them, as may be inferred from the outstanding letter of Pope Innocent III, written in 1215 to his legate Robert de Courçon, who favoured the lay brothers beyond measure.], [Col. 1398B] carefully avoiding the tongues of malicious people, who under the appearance of good offer the poisons of devilish wickedness and, by the artifice of the malignant enemy, strive to destroy the fruitful correction of holy religion which the Holy Spirit has resolved to reserve for your days. May God preserve you unharmed for long ages for the honour of holy Church.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1166. ODO, PRIOR OF SAINT VICTOR, LATER ABBOT OF SAINTE-GENEVIÈVE OF PARIS

[Col. 1397]

NOTICE

(OUDIN, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 1255.)

Odo, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève of Paris, was first a Regular Canon of the Order of Saint Augustine in the abbey of Saint Victor outside the walls of Paris. A man of exceptional piety and learning, after the death in 1140 of the most distinguished and learned Hugh of Saint Victor, he became prior of that Church under Abbot Gilduin. Then, chosen from the priorate to govern the new abbey of Sainte-Geneviève of Paris, he was installed as its first abbot in 1147 by Suger, chief minister of the realm under Louis the Fat.

At the request of Saint Bernard, who, when coming to Paris, was accustomed to be received and lodge at Saint Victor, and at the request of his brethren of Saint Victor, Suger permitted, for the benefit of his old monastery, the water of its little river, the Beveris—commonly called the Bièvre—to be diverted from its customary channel through the gardens of Saint Victor, where it still flows today.

The learned and eloquent Odo wrote several letters to various persons, found in manuscript codex 656 of the library of Saint-Germain at Paris. Lord Luc d’Achery extracted and published them in volume II of his *Spicilegium*. William Cave wrongly attributes these letters, in his *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 677, under the year 1160, to Odo of Kent, a Benedictine monk and prior of the monastery of Canterbury. Had he deigned even to glance cursorily at them, he would by no means have supposed that they belonged to this monk Odo—especially since Luc d’Achery ascribes them to Odo, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève and Regular Canon. Cave did not even so much as look at, or wish to turn over, d’Achery’s work.

In this manuscript codex of which we have spoken, five hundred years old, there are also the following sermons, which Odo wrote while he was prior of the abbey of Saint Victor.

1. On the saying of the Lord, beginning: “He who is of God hears the words of God.” “It is a great and necessary good, dearest brethren, to be of God,” etc.

[Col. 1399] 2. By the same, on Ascension Day. “On this day, lifting our hearts on high, we render to you, good Jesus, immeasurable thanksgivings,” etc.

3. Sermon to the people. “Which do you wish me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” “You have often heard these words, dearest brethren,” etc.

4. On the Ascension of the Lord. “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth.” “O whoever you are, your mind is filled with great and inestimable joy,” etc.

5. On the Rogation Days. “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you,” etc.

6. On the Ascension of the Lord. “Humble yourselves for the blessing.” “I beseech you, dearest brethren; I beseech you, children of God,” etc.

7. Sermon in Holy Week. “They have pierced my hands and my feet; they have numbered all my bones.” “The present week, dearest brethren, deriving its name from the thing itself, is called laborious; or, to speak popularly, from the rustic word *poena* (‘punishment’), it is called *poenosa* (‘painful’),” etc.

8. On Epiphany. “To the lord and brother 6, Brother Odo.” “The sermon which the lord abbot delivered in our chapter on the holy day of Epiphany,” etc. The same sermon on Epiphany is in codex 648 of the same library, together with two other sermons by Master Peter Comestor, on the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary and on her Assumption, and two more by Maurice, canon of Saint Victor—one for the feast of Saint Victor, the other on a common subject. The Epiphany sermon begins: “And behold, the star which they had seen,” etc., through “with exceedingly great joy.” “The feast of the present day is adorned by three miracles and devoutly celebrated by the faithful throughout the world,” etc.

This Odo, with Hugh, abbot of Saint-Germain, and Herneus, abbot of Saint Victor, received Philip Augustus from the baptismal font in 1165. That rite, with the three abbots, may be seen carved on a stone vessel preserved among the canons of Vincennes. Full of days, he died in 1166 and was buried at Saint Victor, from which he had never been absent except in body. At Sainte-Geneviève he left many disciples of his virtues and piety, among whom was that Saint William whose *Acts* are found in Surius.

Odo’s epitaph in that same Victorine monastery reads as follows:

> Odo was first prior of the Martyr and afterward abbot of the Virgin;  
> Through virginity he learned to follow martyrdom.  
> From Victor he obtained [roses?] of the contest; from Geneviève  
> He earned lilies, with fullness of modesty.  
> He bore these flowers into paradise in the season of flowers,  
> An old man from childhood, a virgin youth in old age.  
> Gentle with Moses, faithful with Nathanael,  
> Holy with Samuel, reverent with Simeon.  
> Lest you perish, Paris, bereft of a father, through him prepare yourself  
> For paradise a successor who shall not perish.

Odo, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève of Paris, is treated by the Sammarthani brothers’ *Gallia Christiana*, vol. IV, p. 470; by the fourth century [volume] of the University of Paris, in its Catalogue, p. 756; and by all who have written on the antiquities of the city of Paris.

[Col. 1399]

LETTERS OF ODO. ON THE RIGHT FULFILMENT OF THE PROFESSION OF CANONS REGULAR.

(From Dom Luc d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, new edition, vol. III, p. 529.)

LETTER I. To Brother R. Brother ODO: fulfilment of the vow of canonical profession.

[Col. 1399A]

On the regular observance of Canons Regular.—Dearest brother, it was leisure more than any definite business that compelled me to write to you; confidence in brotherly affection more than any learning in letters. But because I think that my words, whatever they may be, will please you, I preferred to write something rather than to remain silent. I pray, therefore, that you do not weigh the words of an idle man idly, and that whatever I may say foolishly you will consider wisely in order to correct it.

What is promised by vows.—In our profession, then, which we made, we promised three things, as you well know: [Col. 1399B] chastity, common life, and obedience. If we attend to these words only superficially, we immediately rejoice, unspeakably but childishly, as though we had observed our profession. For someone may perhaps say: “The profession which, by God’s inspiration, I promised, I have thus far kept with His help. I preserve bodily chastity; possessing nothing as my own, I live in common; doing what is commanded me, I keep obedience.” If it is as he says, his condition is in some measure good; nevertheless, one who says this ought not to be secure. For if we attend more carefully to the words of the profession and investigate a little more subtly what lies within, we shall plainly see that we have perhaps not even begun what we vainly thought we had accomplished.

Twofold chastity. What a chaste mind is.—But since we promised chastity first, let us first see whether it has been properly kept. Sacred Scripture declares that chastity is twofold: namely, integrity of the flesh and purity of the mind. I ask, then, which corruption is worse: that of the mind or that of the body? The solution of this question is evident to the wise person, if true discernment accompanies him. The corruption of the mind is incomparably worse in proportion as its nature is incomparably better. What bodily integrity is, is known to nearly everyone; but what purity of mind is, is unknown to many—which is worse.

Yet, as it seems to me, that mind is proved most chaste which, though placed among all things, loves God above all things and, for love of Him, consents to no sin, not even in thought. For as often as we consent to any sin, however slight, and as often as we love anything apart from God, so often we corrupt the chastity of our mind. Leaving the Creator, the spouse of the soul, and joining ourselves through unlawful love to a creature, we in some sense commit spiritual fornication. I shall say something more. As often as we think idly and uselessly about transitory things, so often we violate purity of mind in the sight of the Lord. Those who said that fornication is a momentary withdrawal from the contemplation of Christ knew this to be entirely true. Perfect persons cling through contemplation to inward sweetness with such ardour of love that, when through sloth or negligence they withdraw from it even a little, they judge themselves to have committed fornication.

David, avoiding this fornication and desiring this chastity, said: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you. But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72:27). Yet it is very difficult, almost impossible, for our frailty to maintain this kind of chastity. To say nothing of the body, who shall boast that he has a pure heart? Therefore perhaps you say: no one promised this chastity; no one has kept it. For who would dare promise what he knew he could not keep? Who has ever maintained [Col. 1401C] this chastity so as to consent in no degree whatever to any sin, or to cling to God without interruption by contemplation?

Definition of chastity.—Compelled, then, by our weakness in this question, although we do not regret having said the foregoing, we describe in what follows such chastity as by God’s grace we both can and ought to possess. Let us say, therefore, that chastity is that integrity of the flesh which is never corrupted in virgins, or which, in those already corrupted, is restored through confession and penance and thereafter continually preserved out of love for religious life. Let us add also, if you please, that purity of mind concerning whose corruption the Gospel reads thus: “Whoever looks upon [Col. 1401D] a woman in order to lust after her has committed adultery with her already in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). I think that none of us will deny having professed this kind of chastity: namely, neither to carry out in the flesh the act of fornication nor to entertain in the heart consent to fornication.

If, then, we cannot maintain the higher chastity, so as to consent to no sin however slight, let us at least maintain this final kind: that neither an impure violation may corrupt the body nor an unlawful desire to fornicate may, through consent, defile the mind. So much concerning chastity.

What true religious poverty and common life are.—Let us speak of common life. As we said above, because a person sees that he possesses nothing external as his own, he therefore thinks that he keeps common life perfectly. He observes [Col. 1402A] perhaps that he has no bread of his own and no garment of his own, but does not observe that he has a will of his own. He observes that he shares a dwelling with the others, but does not observe that he does not share love with the others. Whoever attends in this way is blind; he is outside. Let him return within, open the eyes of his heart, and observe the truth of inward common life.

For that fellowship is judged true and holy of which we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Their heart was one and their soul one” (Acts 4:31). One heart among many is worth more than a common storeroom; one soul more than a common table. What, indeed, does it profit to be joined to others in food and drink yet to be separated from them by one’s own will? A common possession of resources profits little [Col. 1402B] where there is a tearing apart of wills. Further, if one person likes sobriety and another drunkenness; one silence and another excessive talk; one brotherly concord and another brotherly discord: how, I ask, can an outward common possession of things have force where there is such an impious and detestable division of manners?

Therefore no one who either keeps his own will for himself or divides brotherly unity by evil habits should imagine that he fulfils the profession of common life merely because he dwells in one house, shares one table, or—what is greater—receives the one body and blood of the Lord. So much concerning common life.

When obedience is true.—Now let us say a little concerning obedience. Obedience is certainly a great virtue [Col. 1402C] and necessary to all subjects. But what is obedience except, setting aside every earthly fear and affection, to fulfil what is commanded solely for the love of God? There are some, however, who render obedience because their superiors command nothing except what is agreeable to them. But if something harsh and burdensome is imposed upon them, it is immediately shown whether their obedience was true. Such people are rightly compared to the lily, which, when untouched, gives off a most pleasant scent, but when pressed emits the foulest stench.

It should be known, moreover, that we ought sometimes to join our will to the obedience imposed on us and at other times wholly remove it from that obedience. When my abbot [Col. 1402D] commands me to fast, keep silence, receive correction for my offenses, or perform some work, even the lowliest, I ought to receive such obedience joyfully and with a glad will. But if he commands me for some reason to eat more luxurious foods, to run frequently here and there on various business, to undertake the management of estates, or to do other things pleasing to the flesh and prosperous, I ought not arrogantly to reject such obedience as though on grounds of religious principle; yet I ought in no way to seek in it the delight of my own will.

Thus, in rendering obedience, this distinction must be kept: if a burdensome or even lowly obedience is imposed, let the discernment—or devotion—of a good will accompany it. But if an agreeable obedience, pleasing to the flesh, is imposed, let the desire of one’s own will immediately be driven away from it. For whoever has once, for love of God, left behind the blandishments and hindrances of the world undoubtedly sins if he ever returns to them from his own will.

But if anyone should contend that our profession ought to be understood simply and according to the sound of the words, I prefer humbly and peacefully to yield to his interpretation rather than proudly and contentiously to resist it. For when I consider my own frailty and imperfection, I account even the person who observes it simply and humbly to be great in my eyes. Yet it seems better to me prudently to be suspicious as though it had not been observed than imprudently to be secure as though it had [Col. 1403B] been observed.

But enough of this. See, my brother: because I was somewhat—indeed, excessively—idle, I have become verbose in speech by drawing out this letter at length. Thus vice is born from vice; thus an evil shoot springs from an evil root. For see: because I pursued idleness, I incurred excessive speech, in which, according to Solomon, I do not think I have escaped sin. But since I have now conveyed what I wished, I set a limit to verbosity. Farewell, and pray for me. Grace be with you. I greet our brethren from my whole heart and humbly entreat and beseech them to love one another, do nothing through contention, be of one mind, and receive visiting strangers with charity.

LETTER II.

[Col. 1403C]

To Brother N. Brother ODO: happiness and the perpetuity of happiness.

He consoles his brother and exhorts him to remain in the monastery.—While you were still staying, dearest brother, at Apponi-Villa, you made your wish known to me and instructed me through a messenger to ask the lord abbot for your return. If it could be done, you wished gladly to remain with us; you wished to see the brethren whom you love; you wished to share in their sweet conversation. Their companionship would be sweet to you, their conversation sweet, their consolation sweet. I do not wonder at this. For, to confess the truth, our brethren are lovable in fellowship and useful for imitation. They are, I say, [Col. 1403D] lovable in fellowship, both because of the holiness of their life and because of the gentleness of their manners.

Nevertheless, my brother, do not grieve at our absence; do not take this heavily. Certainly, if you had left us of your own will, for some worldly pleasure, and had gone out by your own permission, then you would rightly have had cause to grieve. But now, since true obedience has compelled you to leave your own will and, beyond this, the beloved company of your brethren, exult and rejoice, and embrace the virtue of obedience with your whole heart’s love.

But if you wished for our company for the sake of study, let that wise old man in the *Lives of the Fathers*, rather than I, answer you: “Your cell,” he says, “can teach you all things.” “How?” you will ask. “How can that which does not understand instruct? How can that which has no voice teach?” Hear briefly: it indeed instructs if there is one who attends, if there is one who opens the ears of the heart. For the cell is said to instruct when the person sitting in it is instructed by the illumination of the Holy Spirit; when, stationed in it, he is agitated by various temptations but is delivered through God’s grace. The teaching given by temptations is great indeed, because through it a person comes to understand both his own weakness, the malice of the tempting devil, and the kindness of God who delivers.

We see many unlearned people dwelling in cells discuss moral matters with subtlety, detect the devil’s hidden snares with remarkable swiftness, avoid them once detected, and moreover love and seek God above all things. Who, I ask, taught them? Not the eloquence of teachers, but the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1404B] and the experience of temptations. Apply yourself, then, to this teaching, and remain continually in your cell for God’s sake. For, as it is written, “He who sits in his cell for God’s sake shall be where Abbot Antony is.” You certainly have with you great consolation, namely Brother G., who can teach you by word and form you by good works. Farewell, and pray for me. Grace be with you.

LETTER III.

How eminent is the virtue of obedience.—You know, dearest brother, that “obedience is better than sacrifices.” And again: “An obedient man speaks victories” (Prov. 16:32). And: “A patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his spirit than one who captures cities” (Prov. 21:28). The Apostle says: “Obey your superiors in all things” [Col. 1404C] (Heb. 13:17). But why do I bring forward so many testimonies concerning obedience? If some outsider heard or read them, he might perhaps suspect you of disobedience. But let this be far from the case. By these words I do not intend to rebuke you for disobedience; rather, I intend to strengthen you in the virtue of obedience which you faithfully render.

Yet, since I have begun this, I shall speak to you with a certain veil left in place: both so that what I wish to say may be clear to you, and so that it may remain hidden from those who do not know, should they read it. Your conscience knows, and I likewise learned when you disclosed it, that before the lord abbot imposed on you this obedience which you now exercise, you would have preferred, if it had been permitted, to do something else. Whatever you had planned to do, you wished to do with good intention and pious usefulness. For if your plan had achieved its result, some fruit would have followed, as you hoped. But after you suddenly and unexpectedly received from the lord abbot the command of obedience to come here, you immediately left all that you had planned—though good, though useful—and, abandoning your own will, said with the Lord Jesus: “I came not to do my own will” (John 5:30).

What the obedient person must observe.—You ought nevertheless to know that the devil often makes those whom he cannot draw into disobedience murmur in their obedience, so that he may at least diminish the merit of obedience through hidden murmuring when he does not overthrow them through open disobedience. We must therefore keep careful watch against the devil’s [Col. 1405A] snares. For he is that adversary who, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour.

But because I have cited these words from the Apostle, I will briefly expound them—not from necessity, that is, but as something additional—for the capacity of my understanding. The devil is rightly called an adversary because he strives to oppose those who are on the way of God and run toward Him with the whole desire of their heart, and opposes them as far as he can lest they arrive at Him. And when he desires to devour anyone, he goes about like a roaring lion. Savagery is denoted by the roar, cunning by the circuit. Thus he roars in order to terrify; he goes about in order to deceive. By roaring he terrifies the fearful; by going about he deceives the unwary. But strengthened and enlightened through Christ, who is the power and wisdom of God, and armed against both, let us despise the roar through fortitude and guard against the circuit through prudence.

I would still like, if I could, to investigate the devil’s circuit more subtly and disclose his snares more clearly so that they may be avoided. Therefore, when the devil wishes to overthrow someone, if he can do so easily, he does not care to labour there longer. Consequently, first of all, openly—as it were, face to face—he urges a person to commit a crime or disgraceful act, so that he may overthrow him quickly and without labour. He wants the person openly to see the evil he suggests and nevertheless commit it, in order to entangle him in greater guilt. But if, defeated from the front, he withdraws, he immediately begins to go around, turning somewhat hiddenly to the left side. Understand by the left side an evil deed.

But it should be noted [Col. 1405C] that what stands at our side is viewed by our eye not directly opposite but imperfectly and obliquely. The devil therefore introduces temptation from the left when whatever he suggests is evil, but, lest it be seen clearly, hides it under the covering either of necessity or of frailty. Thus he induces in many the vice of gluttony under the pretext of necessity, and introduces the fault of harmful frivolity under the excuse of frailty. He says: “You must eat much, because your need requires it. You may laugh and talk, because such is human frailty.”

But if he sees himself detected there too, he immediately goes round to the back so that he may at least strike a person where he does not see, since he cannot deceive him by manifest evil in front or by veiled evil at the side. For he often conceals his deceptions so secretly that, as though coming from behind, he strikes suddenly and unexpectedly. But perhaps the person who is tempted has, after the manner of the holy living creatures, eyes not only in front but also behind; and therefore that devilish temptation, swiftly detected, does him no harm whatsoever.

By what means Satan corrupts good.—But when the enemy sees that the malice which he had prepared behind the back has been exposed, he proceeds, so as to make the full circuit, to the right. But what is denoted by the right except a good action? He moves to the right, therefore, not in order to advise good, but rather to corrupt good. Since, while he advises evil, he is repelled and shut out on every side, driven by his own wickedness, when he can do no more, he at least strives to taint the good. [Col. 1406A] I shall show briefly the ways in which he corrupts it: through pride, vain glory, and indiscretion.

A good work is corrupted through pride when the heart of one who acts well is puffed up in lofty arrogance by despising others and preferring itself to them. The devil had tainted the Pharisee’s good deeds with this evil of pride when, preferring himself to the tax collector standing at a distance and repenting, he said: “I am not like other people, or even like this tax collector” (Luke 18:11). Vain glory also introduces its stain when one who does good seeks his own praise from people. Of such persons Truth says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2). [Col. 1406B] These words show a great corruption of a good work, when the reward of eternal recompense is exchanged, through the worst corruption, for passing praise.

Thirdly, the good a person does is spoiled if discernment is not maintained in the performance of the good work. Thus it is said: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” For one offers rightly but does not divide rightly when one does perform a good deed, but does not subtly distinguish, by discernment, the time and manner of performing it.

There are also many other kinds of corruption by which our good works, such as they are, are frequently tainted; it would be both too long to write of them and tiresome to hear of them—and, what is truer, I am blind and dumb, able neither to see nor to utter them. But [Col. 1406C] let what has been said to you, brother, concerning the devil’s circuit suffice; may God in his mercy grant us both to understand it and to avoid it.

## LETTER IV

Brother ODO to Brother R., greetings.

Religious should conduct themselves cautiously outside the monastery.—Dearest brother, it is fitting that you and our other brothers who live outside on obediences should carefully guard your words and deeds, partly because of the vow of your profession and partly from love of the religious life. For the eyes of certain detractors often look upon you with fault-finding and malice; they watch you attentively, but not out of affection; they consider your works not to imitate them but to tear them apart; they listen to your words not for edification but rather [Col. 1406D] for detraction. If they see anything blameworthy in them, rejoicing and triumphing, they blaspheme through mockery and derision. For they say: “See what monks are like; what Regular Canons are like. See how greedy they are, how proud, how angry, how envious. Look: that Regular seized another’s property greedily; look: he answered this or that person with insulting words; look: he had a quarrel not only with a stranger but even with his own brother.”

Would that our detractors said these things of you only because of their own wickedness, and not because they were true. Would that they found absolutely none of all these things in us. But woe to us if what is said is true, if through us the name of the Lord is blasphemed among men. For this [Col. 1407A] is to cause the Lord’s name to be blasphemed through us: namely, to bring reproach upon divine worship and sacred religion because of our greed and quarrels.

Therefore we must keep careful watch over our life, and, as far as we can, for the love of God show ourselves before men irreproachable in words and deeds. Yet there are some who carefully guard themselves with respect to their actions and attain a certain perfection by fasting and watching; nevertheless, they do not reach the heights of that perfection of which the blessed Apostle James says: “If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2). He rightly calls that person a perfect man who, standing manfully like a man, does not falter by stumbling in his speech. For he is shown to be frail and, as it were, feminine [Col. 1407B] who not only utters idle or trivial things and, as it were, stumbles in the smallest matters, wavering and slipping this way and that; but who, under the driving force of anger and the headlong rush of fury, keeps no restraint upon the bridle of his tongue, and by quarrelling and hurling insults, as though stumbling violently, falling grievously, is utterly shattered.

For it is dangerous to utter idle words, but far more dangerous to heap insults upon others. An account is rendered for an idle word; punishment is paid for an insulting one. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “For every idle word that men have spoken, they shall render account for it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36). And elsewhere: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘You fool,’ shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 5:22).

[Col. 1407C] See how these words clearly show what I said before: an idle word is followed by an inquiry into one’s account, while an insult inflicted brings the punishment of certain condemnation. Great indeed is the sin through which a human being is separated from the kingdom of heaven. When the prophet David asked, “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?” (Ps. 14:3), he added: “He who walks without blemish”; and shortly afterward: “He has not done evil to his neighbour, nor accepted reproach against his neighbour” (ibid.). But what is it to accept reproach against one’s neighbour except gladly to listen to reproach brought against one’s neighbour? For the person who gladly listens accepts it. Therefore, if one who accepts reproach against a neighbour is excluded from God’s tabernacle, [Col. 1407D] how much more the person who inflicted it?

The same prophet, asking elsewhere who would desire life and love to see good days, added: “Keep your tongue from evil” (Ps. 33:14), as if saying: “If you keep your tongue from evil, you will without doubt attain life and good days.” Solomon likewise says: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21). For often, because of an evil utterance, both the speaker’s and the hearer’s soul die; and again, because of a good utterance, the speaker deserves life, while the hearer is raised from the death of the soul. Since evil speech, like a sword, kills by inflicting death upon the soul, the prophet David in one place calls the instruments of speech instruments of death, saying: “The sons of men—their teeth are weapons and arrows, and [Col. 1408A] their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5). Again, because good speech bestows life, Sacred Scripture says elsewhere: “A gentle tongue is a tree of life” (Prov. 15:4). Therefore we must restrain the tongue from evil if we wish to come to life.

But perhaps you say: “You who live within the monastery, who keep silence at fixed hours, who devote yourselves continually to reading and prayer, can very easily avoid offences of the tongue. But we, who are constantly outside, who run to and fro for countless reasons, who can speak whenever we wish, frequently stumble in our words. Silence binds your tongues so that they do not flow destructively; but the permission granted to us to speak loosens ours.”

To these words of yours I reply thus: it is true that both spiritual discipline and appointed silence greatly assist us in guarding the mouth, so that, helped by both, we have neither the desire nor often even the opportunity to utter idle words. But [Col. 1408B] to you who are outside, though permission to speak has been given because of necessity, no power to sin has been granted. You have not been granted permission to speak in order that you may either quarrel with strangers or heap insults upon one another. If you quarrel with those outside and disparage one another within, I confess to you that you stray very far from the path of the Rule.

Let us then consider your outward appearance a little more carefully. If we consider our name and habit, it does not fit well to be called a Regular Canon and to be misshapen in unlawful words and deeds. A shaven head and a proud heart [Col. 1408C] never harmonize well; a religious cloak and a quarrelsome tongue. The outward signs of humility profit little if pride rules within the mind. It profits little to wear cut-off stockings in the manner of a penitent and to feel no penitential sorrow for evils committed. It profits little that the crown of the head is enlarged if charity is growing cold and constricted in the heart. A high tonsure profits little if moderation is not maintained in speech.

Therefore let us consider our outward habit and attend to what it admonishes us. If, because of human weakness and continual speaking, we cannot wholly abandon idle words and other things that seem very small, nevertheless, by God’s grace, we both can and must [Col. 1408D] utterly root out quarrelling and detraction. But if at any time—God forbid—through the devil’s persuasion and anger’s prompting, one inflicts insult or abuse upon another, then, according to the counsel of our Rule, the one who inflicted it must make satisfaction as quickly as possible, and the one who was injured must abandon his dispute. In order that we may avoid the many offences of the tongue, let us say with the Prophet to the Lord our God: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth,” etc.

See, my brother: although I have sent this letter especially to you, I have said what is written generally concerning all the brothers. For it pleased me to admonish all together while speaking with you, and, in admonishing all, not to exempt you.

## LETTER V

[Col. 1409A]

Brother ODO to Brother R., greetings.

He supplies most useful instructions. Right action and a simple intention are plainly necessary.—I pray you, dearest brother, to conduct yourself in the obedience entrusted to you in such a way that God may be praised and honoured in your life, and that our Church may be exalted through your good reputation. See that outwardly you have a good testimony before men, and inwardly rejoice before God in a good conscience. Your conscience will be good if you do no evil deliberately and perform whatever good you do with a simple intention. Otherwise, unless your intention is simple and right, neither will your outward reputation be true nor your inward conscience good.

The simplicity [Col. 1409B] of intention is proved most certainly to be this: that in a good work human praise is entirely rejected, and only the praise of God and the neighbour’s benefit are sought. Thus these two right things—namely, right action and simple intention—produce two goods: for simple intention inwardly gladdens the worker’s mind through a good conscience, while right action, shown outwardly, invites others to praise God and forms them to do good. Let us say with the Apostle—if indeed we can say it truthfully—“This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12). For only the person whose good conscience bears inward testimony can glory with complete certainty.

Certainly, as it seems to me, a human being is very easily deceived, [Col. 1409C] but God is in no way mocked: “Man sees the face, but God sees the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7). Therefore, before God, who sees within, let our conscience appear pure and simple; and before men, who see the face, let your good work shine, so that God may be glorified.

What knowledge accomplishes in the good and in the wicked.—Therefore, if action is right, let intention be simple and pure; for our action proceeds before the eyes in vain if good intention does not go before it. Nor does the conscience have inward rest when either guilt already committed terrifies it or human praise sought for a good work stings it with remorse.

Yet if we wish to have true knowledge of our conscience, knowledge must precede conscience. For where there is no [Col. 1409D] knowledge, there can be neither a good nor an evil conscience. But where knowledge comes first, it immediately becomes evident whether the conscience is good or evil.

There are some good people who, because of the purity of their lives, do not have an evil conscience. They examine themselves carefully through knowledge; but because they are pure and clean, they are conscious of no evil in themselves. In these, knowledge comes first and a good conscience follows.

There are others who are indeed wicked, but recognize themselves through their knowledge. In recognizing themselves, they have an evil conscience; nevertheless, grieving and groaning, they sometimes turn to repentance. An evil conscience follows their knowledge, but conscience, enlightened by knowledge, is changed into good through repentance.

There are also [Col. 1410A] others, worse and much more depraved than those just mentioned, who, because of their folly, do not attend to their own wickedness. Since they either refuse or neglect to examine themselves through knowledge, lacking the light of knowledge, they sleep most dangerously in their sins as in the foulest night. Such persons scarcely ever, or never, return to repentance, because they have lost the way of repentance—that is, knowledge. For it is written: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1:28). From this it is plainly evident that one who has no knowledge cannot grieve for his sins.

We see many righteous persons weep most bitterly for very slight faults; and conversely, certain utterly wicked people feel no sorrow for horrible crimes, indeed—even more grievously—rejoice and exult, of whom it is written: [Col. 1410B] “Who rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the most wicked things” (Prov. 2:14). But why is this, unless because the righteous, enlightened by the light of knowledge, severely rebuke themselves even for the smallest things they recognize in themselves; whereas the wicked, having no light of knowledge and entirely ignorant of themselves, do not know how to lament in repentance even the dreadful crimes they commit? Therefore, if we desire to know truthfully what our consciences are like, we must apply ourselves to knowledge, and not presume to acquire it by our own industry, but solely through God’s mercy and his overflowing grace. Let us therefore ask God’s mercy and implore his grace, that he may give us knowledge and a good conscience, so that through knowledge we may truly know ourselves, and [Col. 1410C] through a good conscience may rejoice ineffably in his sight.

But woe to me, miserable as I am, who do not have a good conscience and yet presume to speak of a good conscience. How can my conscience be good, when I have committed many evils which I have not worthily erased through repentance, and, sluggish and negligent, have refused to do the good things I ought to have done? For our conscience can be good in no other way than if we both lament worthily in repentance the evils we have done and, with God’s grace going before us, do the good that we can.

O good conscience, how lovable and delightful you are! O great treasure, not comparable to any earthly riches! Certainly nothing in this life is happier, [Col. 1410D] nothing more delightful.

But perhaps you say: “How do you know that nothing is happier, nothing more delightful? Sometimes we call food good because we know this by experience; but you, as you have said, do not have a good conscience. How can you know that nothing is happier?” Perhaps you say this; but what am I to say? I cannot truthfully say what the Apostle says, “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4:4); indeed, I am conscious of much. Yet hear a comparison and understand the reasoning.

Certainly, with our eyes we see many things that we do not possess; so too by reason we recognize many things to be good which we nevertheless do not do. By that same reason we discourse at length about many virtues of which we are devoid. Thus I myself, speaking of a good [Col. 1411A] conscience and discoursing by reason about many matters, see, as it were, through a good eye what I nevertheless do not possess in myself.

Hear another comparison. Often, when we taste the bitterness of gall, we praise the sweetness of honey; and although at present we feel only gall’s bitterness, by comparison with it we approve the sweetness of honey which we do not feel. Likewise, one born in poverty and brought up entirely amid miseries, when he considers those powerful in the world and possessing riches, calls them happy and himself miserable; although feeling only his own misery, he does not know by experience what their happiness is like. So we often praise abundance; when we are ill, we say that health is good. Thus I too, from the unhappiness of the evil conscience which I feel, weigh how great is the happiness [Col. 1411B] of a good conscience; and because I know by experience that nothing is sadder than an evil conscience, from that very sadness I judge that nothing is more delightful than a good conscience.

Certainly, if the choice were granted me, I would rather endure all the miseries of the world with a good conscience than possess all the riches of the world with an evil conscience. But because those outside cannot see our consciences, at least our reputation, which can reach them, ought not to stink in their ears. For if, confident in our conscience, we neglect our reputation—as blessed Augustine says—we are cruel. Indeed, I think that we do not even have a good conscience if through our negligence [Col. 1411C] we incur disgrace. Conversely, if human reputation praises us while conscience reproves us within, we are like those who are proclaimed rich in public but privately are tormented by the distress of poverty.

Therefore, my brother, apply diligence; examine your conscience. Carefully consider what testimony it gives: attend to what it truthfully testifies to you concerning your deeds, words, and thoughts. Consider, I say, whether there is holiness in deed, truth in speech, purity in thought, and simplicity in intention. If your conscience is conscious to itself of the testimony of these things, it can most rightly say the Apostle’s statement mentioned above: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience.”

[Col. 1411D] But if by the example of an evil deed you have destroyed someone; if by your word you have inflicted abuse or insult upon someone; if you have defiled the purity of your heart with an unlawful thought—if you have done these things and have not yet made satisfaction through repentance—I think that you not only do not glory in these things in conscience, but are also tormented by inward shame. There are also other matters by which our conscience is often put to shame: namely pride, anger, and sadness. May God first take all these from us and grant us a clean conscience. Farewell, and pray for me.

## LETTER VI

He invites one expelled from the king’s court, a man of great power, to contempt for the world.—[Col. 1412A] He alone truly knows with how great desire and affection I desire your good and your salvation: he who alone knows the secrets of hearts. But now, because I cannot speak face to face with you in person, I send these little letters of exhortation to your affection. I write to you not because of any necessity of mine, but solely out of regard for charity. For the adversity that has befallen you, although it has taken from me our present conversation, has not been able to take love from my heart; although it has taken away your bodily presence, it has not taken away remembrance of you from my prayers.

For, to confess the truth, when we celebrate the solemnities of the Mass, we implore the mercy of almighty God, that he who through ignorance [forgets] no one may remember you through grace. Now, before I begin this exhortation, I first offer prayer, that [Col. 1412B] God’s grace may go before our admonition and open the ears of your heart, so that it may willingly hear, faithfully retain, and effectually fulfil those things which pertain to true salvation.

What then shall I say first? Where shall I begin the exhortation? I, as a faithful servant and true friend, wish to tear my lord and friend away from love of the present life and to raise his desire toward love of his Creator and the heavenly homeland. Therefore I ought first to set forth something concerning contempt for the world, and afterward to add those things that can stir his mind to the love of God. But because I know that you are absorbed in worldly cares, I would, if I could, explain my admonition in few words.

[Col. 1412C] Let Solomon, then, the wisest of men, come forward first and put before you his true judgment concerning contempt for the world, saying: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. 1:2). O my lord, do you understand that what you hear is true? Certainly there is no reason for you to doubt. Lend your ear and understand the truth; open your eyes and behold vanity. I ask you carefully to consider the course of your life, because, unless I am mistaken, in your very life you will fully recognize how vain all things are.

Recall how much worldly power was granted you in the time of your prosperity, how great an abundance of riches, and how great—what is more—prudence in administering temporal affairs. You used to sit first among the courtiers; you arranged the whole kingdom of the Franks according to your pleasure. Indeed, in accordance with what Solomon [Col. 1412D] records himself as having done, you magnified your works with great achievement: you built lofty towers and beautiful palaces, planted vineyards, possessed male and female servants and a large household, heaped up for yourself silver and gold, the wealth of kings and provinces, and were filled with the delights of the children of men. But pause briefly to consider how much vanity and instability there are in all these things.

Look: the very king in whose affection you placed great confidence, beside whom you used to sit because of intimacy and rank of honour, pursues you as an enemy; and everything that you had built in Paris with great labour is wholly destroyed at the queen’s command. The silver, gold, and money that you gathered in the time of peace, [Col. 1413A] you must now spend in the time of war; and lest your enemies overwhelm you unawares, you must think anxiously night and day. Therefore, my lord, you can clearly recognize in your own life that Solomon’s judgment concerning vanity is true.

Certainly, this Solomon was exalted in royal power, unequalled in the gift of wisdom, and rich in abundance of wealth. Yet, although all these things were available to him in plenty, he attributed no reality to them; rather, because he saw that they pass away, he rightly called them vanity. Therefore he is to be believed all the more because he learned by experience the things he said.

If I were not seeking brevity, I could still say some things concerning contempt for the world which would not only rationally recall your mind from its desire for it, but also powerfully frighten it away. Such as this: [Col. 1413B] “The world will pass away, and its desire” (1 John 2:17). And this: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this age shall be made an enemy of God” (James 4:4). A fearful judgment! What could be said more terrible, since whoever becomes a friend of this age is shown to be an enemy of God?

There is another reason why the rational mind ought to despise these worldly things: they are acquired with the greatest labour, guarded with anxiety, and lost with grief. It is also written: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6:7); and: “Those who possess riches attain the kingdom of God with difficulty” (Gal. 5:21). But what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his soul? (Matt. 16:26). Let what has been said concerning contempt for the world suffice.

[Col. 1413C] But if your love desires to raise its mind toward the love of God, you ought frequently to call to mind the benefits God has bestowed upon you. Consider how great his grace toward you has been, how great his mercy: grace, in that he freely bestowed his good things upon you; mercy, in that he patiently endured your evils. Certainly, if you are willing to attend carefully, this reason alone may suffice to make you love God: that by grace he gave good things in order to kindle you to love of him, and by mercy endured your evils in order to summon you to repentance.

Finally, after he had shown patience, like a loving father toward his beloved son, he applied discipline, so that [Col. 1413D] the person unwilling to return when moved by benefits might at least return to the Father under the lash. For it is written: “God scourges every one whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). This war and persecution which you are enduring are indeed God’s scourge. For although your enemies persecute you out of hatred, what they do is preceded by a hidden and just ordering of God.

Therefore do not murmur against God because of this scourge, for it would be hard for you to kick against the goad. Remember that, when King David fled the persecution of his son Absalom and a certain utterly wicked Shimei cursed him, the men who were with David grieved at the king’s injury and wished to kill Shimei. Yet David restrained them, saying: “Let him curse, for the Lord commanded him to curse David; [Col. 1414A] perhaps the Lord will repay me with blessing for this curse today” (2 Sam. 16:12).

I beg you, for God’s sake, attend carefully and do as David did. See: he endured a curse from an enemy, and yet, though he could easily have done so, he did not wish to avenge himself upon him. He attributed that curse not to Shimei but to the Lord, when he said: “The Lord commanded him to curse David.” For David was one of God’s sons; he knew that he was being scourged by a merciful Father. He would not consider the wickedness of the one cursing him, but the benefit of the curse. Therefore he said: “Perhaps the Lord will repay me with blessing for this curse today.”

I think, too, that he recalled his past sins to memory. I think that he grieved deeply [Col. 1414B] in his heart over adultery and homicide, and therefore endured most patiently the persecution of his son and the curse of his servant. I have set forth this example of David so that you also may diligently consider your sins, open and hidden, lesser and greater; and, in the persecution you are presently enduring, may consider not the utterly wicked will of your enemies, but the most merciful kindness of the Lord who admonishes you.

Hear what the Lord says: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3:19). He strikes in order to heal; he scourges the sinner in order to cleanse him. Therefore do not reject God’s calling by closing the ears of your heart; do not receive God’s scourges with a hardened heart. Do not cling so tenaciously and stubbornly in the mire of the deep, in love of the world. Allow [Col. 1414C] God to draw you out of the lake of misery and the mire of filth.

Do not become like a cart sunk in mud: oxen draw it strongly from the front, people push it with all their might from behind, and yet neither by pulling nor pushing can they draw it out of the mud. See: the merciful God first granted you prosperity in order to draw you; now he has applied the hand of adversity in order to push you. Therefore, since in your conversion you make the Lord, so to speak, labour so greatly, see that you do not provoke him to anger. For it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10:13). For if he is stirred, who can resist him? Do not, in accordance with the Psalm’s saying, place your confidence in princes or in the sons of men, [Col. 1414D] in whom there is no salvation (Ps. 145:3), but in him alone who can deliver you from every distress.

But, setting exhortation aside for the moment, I ask that you consult inwardly your reason concerning what I say. It is strange that your reason, which is so vigorous in providing for and ordering worldly affairs—it is strange, I say—that it lies as though dead when it comes to recognizing and doing good things. Yet perhaps your reason understands by discernment the things that are good, but pride resisting does not carry them out. For pride rules your reason and tyrannically opposes it. Reason says: “If you did this or that, you would be acceptable to God.” Pride says: “If you did this or that, you would be contemptible in the sight of men.”

O [Col. 1415A] wicked and detestable slavery: reason, which ought to rule as mistress, obeys pride as a maidservant. I ask that reason may return to its proper freedom; that pride, expelled from your heart, may depart, and that true humility, dear to God, may occupy its place.

## LETTER VII

Brother ODO to Brother F., greetings.

He exhorts him to religious exercises.—When you came to us during the weekdays of Pentecost, dearest brother, you called me aside and reproached me, saying: “You have no concern for me, but have cast me aside as something worthless and useless.” When I carefully asked why you said this, you replied: “You frequently send your consoling letters to the other brothers, but to me, who need them more than all the rest and endure many temptations, you offer no consolation whatever.”

On hearing this, I gratefully accepted your rebuke and promised that, if I had leisure, I would give you some consolation in the future. Nevertheless, you should know that I am often entangled in such great occupations and harassed inwardly and outwardly by so many cares, however small, that I do not have leisure according to my desire either to attend to reading, to write anything, or, better still, to devote myself to prayer. But because through your messenger you again reminded me to remember my promise, although, as I have said, I am impeded by many things, charity urging me, I shall briefly do what I promised.

[Col. 1415C] Temptations must be endured most patiently for God.—Therefore, brother, do not wonder if you suffer various temptations. For “the life of man upon earth is temptation” (Job 7:1). Hence it is also written: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your heart for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). In this saying you plainly have what you ought to do. You have now come to God’s service; you have now promised to serve God and to live religiously. You must stand in justice and fear and prepare your soul for temptation, not for rest.

For many, when they come to God’s service, return to their former sins, with God’s permission, because they shrink from labouring to acquire virtues. Therefore, if you wish to escape the snares of temptations, you must endure [Col. 1415D] many labours of both heart and body. For who can, without labour, pierce his heart with lamentation, cast away his own wills, and fulfil in every respect the good wills of others? Who, I say, can without labour and constant diligence fully recognize the devil’s many snares and, once recognized, avoid them? The labour of temptations is certainly great and not to be despised; nevertheless it must be endured most patiently for love of God. And lest temptation cause you to fall into despair, hear what the blessed Apostle James says: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you encounter various temptations” (James 1:2).

The usefulness of temptations. How a religious person ought to fight the devil.—Dearest brother, the usefulness of temptations is great, because true [Col. 1416A] humility is acquired through temptations. For, I believe, our pride would raise itself very high unless, by God’s permission, the weight of temptations pressed that same pride down to the depths. Often, while we suffer no outward temptations, we are more gravely endangered in the heart through self-exaltation. Since we neglect to consider our own iniquity, we think great and incomparable things of ourselves and despise everyone else as better than ourselves in comparison.

But the merciful God sometimes, when he compassionately sees our self-exaltation, permits the temptation of the flesh to come upon us for our correction. He wishes that the temptation of the flesh may humble the exaltation of the heart; he wishes that, conscious of our weakness, we may think lowly and contemptible things of ourselves, so that through [Col. 1416B] humility we may put before ourselves even those lesser than us.

It is also good, whenever you endure some temptation, to recall the profession you made. For you professed chastity, common life, and obedience. When you made this profession, you grievously offended the devil. He saw this profession and envied it; therefore, against each profession he applies particular temptations. Against the profession of chastity he suggests the lust of the flesh; against the profession of common life he kindles a desire for some private possession; against the virtue of obedience he opposes the vice of disobedience.

But you, my brother, hold fast to your profession and carefully avoid temptation. If the devil attacks you, beware lest he conquer you; beware lest he overcome you. [Col. 1416C] Resist firmly; fight manfully. If he has hurled the dart of concupiscence, oppose to it the shield of chastity. If he brings to your memory past actions and past pleasures, then instead consider the pains of hell and its horrible punishments. For if you carefully attend to the fire of Gehenna, you will quickly extinguish the fire of lust.

You must also preserve inwardly the disposition of your heart and restrain outwardly the gaze of your eyes. For a corrupt disposition often directs the eyes’ keenness toward unlawful things, and an unlawful gaze corrupts the inward disposition. Therefore you must purify the disposition within and restrain the gaze outside through discipline. Consider often how great is the purity of chastity, how pleasing and acceptable it is to God. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded” [Col. 1416D] (Luke 12:35). For what is it to gird the loins except to restrain the flow of lust by the girdle of chastity?

O pure chastity, how high you dwell! O impure lust, how low you lie! Certainly chastity joins a human being to God and preserves the temple of God undefiled; lust, on the other hand, separates a human being from God, joins him to the devil, and violates God’s temple. Therefore embrace the virtue of chastity; shudder at the vice of lust. Love the beauty of the former; flee the ugliness of the latter.

How chastity is preserved.—Chastity is certainly a great and most beautiful virtue, provided that humility is maintained together with chastity. Otherwise we cannot please God by chastity alone, unless we also truly possess humility with chastity. Indeed, [Col. 1417A] chastity often suffers great assaults of temptations precisely because pride is not expelled from the heart. Therefore, if you wish to be secure in chastity, be grounded in humility.

Finally, because the devil sees that we please God through the virtue of chastity, even if he cannot take it away, he nevertheless does not cease to trouble it. Hence, while we are awake, he introduces shameful thoughts if he can; while we sleep, he assumes forms of various appearances to deceive us. So great are his wickedness and envy that he does not consider what he makes of himself or what vile forms he assumes, so long as he may entice and deceive us.

But we, whether awake or asleep, belonging to the Lord and tending [Col. 1417B] toward God, should repel shameful thoughts with good thoughts set against them; and, fortified by the sign of the holy cross, should in no way fear nocturnal illusions.

It is also good for one who desires to preserve chastity to maintain sobriety in food and drink, and to persist frequently in prayer. For when the devil sees that the natural fire of desire has been made to burn a little by the addition of food, he immediately gathers within himself the spirit of wickedness and, in order to kindle the fire of desire, sends forth with all his effort the breath of temptation. [Col. 1418A] Therefore it is good that the fire of desire be extinguished by the water of moderation, and that the devil’s breath be repelled by the spirit of prayer. There are many things that greatly help to preserve chastity; but let these words, dearest brother, suffice for you.

But if I wished still to discuss the profession of common life and obedience, the letter would now exceed its proper length, and an overlong discourse would breed weariness in the reader. Yet I say this briefly; this I want you to know: whoever, after professing common life, keeps in his own possession a horse, a garment, or, less still, a penny, can have no share with God and no communion with His saints unless he repents worthily. Likewise, whoever, after promising obedience, refuses in obstinate pride to obey the command of his superior, [Col. 1418B] can by no means be a co-heir of Jesus Christ, who became obedient unto death. Therefore it is good that we have absolutely no private property, that we do not lose the beloved fellowship of the saints, and that we maintain obedience with the Lord Jesus Christ unto death, so that after death we may be able to receive from that same Lord the fruit of obedience. Farewell, and pray for me.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1175 . . . GODFREY OF ST. VICTOR**

[Col. 1417]

## NOTICE AND FRAGMENTS

[Col. 1417C] Godfrey, superior of St. Victor at Paris, a Frenchman by nation and a master of sacred letters in the University of Paris, was led by a desire for a holier life and a more secluded retreat to be admitted, before the year 1170, among the members of St. Victor under Abbot Ervisius. Not long afterward, namely in 1174, under Prior Walter, many people attached to the world—his contemporaries and equals—mocked his conversion and his renewed manner of life under the profession he had undertaken, taunting him for having passed from a life useful to many, distinguished by learning, and honorable in conduct, to an idle and inactive life.

Seeking to answer their frivolous remarks and to stop the mouths of his detractors, he wrote three excellent books *On the Microcosm*, treating of the rational human being, endowed with the powers of the soul; [Col. 1417D] in the prologue to these books he gives a full account of his way of life. This work exists in manuscript in the library of St. Victor, shelfmark II, 14, fols. 1–107. It bears in red letters the title: *Microcosm of Godfrey, canon of St. Victor at Paris*. The prologue begins: “I judged it almost expedient, both for myself and for all readers of this little book, if I should set down beforehand, at its beginning, the reason for this work,” etc. The first book begins: [Col. 1418C] “Both philosopher and theologian testify that a human being is very often called by the name of world,” etc.

The work proceeds in three parts according to the endowments of the soul: natural endowments, such as arts and sciences; harmful endowments, namely the vices that must be subdued; and spiritual endowments, namely the virtues which must daily be acquired, through the aid of charity, their chief. Its author’s labor is occupied with an examination of the work of the six days in the created world; under the first three days he lucidly expounds the mechanical and natural arts, and thus brings the first book to an end.

In the same manuscript codex, fol. 107: fourteen sermons by the same Godfrey on various subjects, the first of which, for Advent, begins: “Looking from afar, behold, I see the power of God coming, and a cloud covering the whole earth.” [Col. 1418D] “This utterance, dearest brothers, is the first responsory of the first reading in the first nocturn of this feast.” The same *Microcosm* of Godfrey in three books exists in manuscript in the same library, shelfmark NNN. 19, fol. 1; and fourteen sermons of the same author on varied subjects, there at fol. 104, the first of which begins: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us,” etc. “The noble eagle had flown aloft and settled upon the summit of the lofty mountain,” etc. [Col. 1419A] Hence either these sermons differ from those mentioned above, or they occur in another order; I have not had leisure to investigate the matter.

He also composed another work, dedicated to Stephen, then abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at Paris, entitled *The Fountain of Philosophy*. It is divided into four books and written in certain rhymed verses, arranged four at a time and ending in one and the same final syllable—a kind of verse very common in that age. In it he teaches that true philosophy is not that which gives itself to speculation or to the skirmishing of arguments and reasonings, but that which is occupied in rooting out vices and planting virtues. The work is in manuscript in the same library of St. Victor at Paris, shelfmark II, 15. Its title, in red letters, is: *The Book Called The Fountain of Philosophy, in Four Metrical Books*. The letter of Godfrey [Col. 1419B] to Stephen, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève on the Mount, which is itself the prologue to the following work:

“To Lord Stephen, abbot of Mont-Sainte-Geneviève, a man distinguished by the graces of every virtue and learning, G., a certain poor man of Christ, sends his own good wishes. Father, I have sent you a full cup of mixed learning, to be examined by your judgment,” etc., fol. 145.

Then, in red letters: *The Fountain of Philosophy*. It begins:

> It was the end of night, and of my sleep,  
> And the herald of day was driving away the darkness.  
> I awoke, unaware of what was to come,  
> Led by sacred counsels and by God’s prompting, etc.

Then he enters upon the *Trivium*, as it is called, whose parts—grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric—he presents in the form of three rivers. Of the first:

> [Col. 1419C] [lacuna] It spreads over a broader field  
> And glides across the plains by a straighter course;  
> With its dew it creates tender shrubs,  
> With its fuller stream it makes other things fruitful.

Of the second:

> [lacuna] Passing through shadowy places,  
> It breaks rugged cliffs, groves, and impassable obstacles;  
> Its path is narrower and winding,  
> Its water stronger and more impetuous.

Of the third:

> [lacuna] Sporting through the delights of a meadow,  
> Its painted bosom blooms with varied flowers;  
> Its waves wander farther than the rest,  
> Slow at first, then running swiftly.

After praising the teachers of antiquity, he laments that the liberal and mechanical arts have fallen into contempt; then he introduces the more recent [Col. 1419D] schools and schoolmasters. Thus he speaks of the Nominalists and Realists:

> Certain Nominalists add themselves as companions to these,  
> Allies of such men in name, not in divine power.  
> Others stand nearby, whom the thing itself has called  
> “Realists,” because they are such.  
>
> For if, because of the various guilt of their errors,  
> The name “Realists” could be applied to them,  
> Yet their error is excusable:  
> It is the habit of madmen to contradict the mind.  
>
> For what mind could even think that a name is a genus?  
> Only one alienated from his mind would believe this,  
> Since, if the world is full of so many genera of things,  
> Whose genus is “name,” it must always be barren.  
>
> Moreover, there are very many sects of “Realists,”  
> Whom you may rightly call “guilty ones” (*reales* / *reatus*);  
> [Col. 1420A] For they do not walk directly upon the path of truth,  
> Nor do they drink fully from the streams of grace.

On Gilbert of Poitiers and his disciples:

> Some of these season the condiments of Porry [Gilbert],  
> Whose genus is believed to be contained in two things;  
> They triple the ten categories of things—  
> By this the foundations of the ancients are overthrown.

On the disciples of Robert of Melun:

> On the summit of the rock [Note: that is, Mont-Sainte-Geneviève.] cling Robert’s crowds,  
> Of stony or adamantine hardness,  
> Whom neither rain nor the dew of learning waters:  
> The threats of the crags bar access to the stream.  
>
> They themselves falsely maintain that they truly follow nothing;  
> Yet they themselves went after those  
> Who invent almost a thousand things from the name alone:  
> Therefore one may count them as nothing.

On Master John of Petit-Pont and his disciples, [Col. 1420B] or the Petit-Pontians:

> Certain men built a bridge with their own hands  
> And made an easy crossing over the waters;  
> On it each of them established houses for himself,  
> Whence they received the name “dwellers on the bridge.”  
>
> The material is fitting, and fitting is the shape;  
> A square foundation of cubical stones lies beneath;  
> Its solid structure stands on bronze columns,  
> Never to collapse under any movement.  
>
> The work is set above pavements,  
> Adorned with golden and silver images,  
> Defended on every side by raised walls,  
> So that the unlearned crowd may not fear a fall.  
>
> But it also has chambers from which they gaze out  
> And search the hidden bed of the river;  
> Others also delight in swimming  
> And, scorched by summer suns, refresh themselves.  
>
> Here sits a venerable order of elders,  
> Pre-eminent in the grace of learning and character;  
> [Col. 1420C] They instruct the simple crowds of the people.  
> O blessed people, with rulers such as these!

At the end of the work, fol. 221: a metrical eulogy of Saint Augustine, beginning: “To heap up in rhythm, so far as may be granted, praises worthy of Augustine’s glorious merits,” etc.; together with a certain canticle to the Blessed Virgin Mary and a lament, both by the same author and furnished with musical notation. But at the beginning of this codex are nineteen sermons by the same Godfrey, beginning as above in shelfmark II, 14, and differing only in number, since there are nineteen. The first: “Looking from afar, behold, I see,” etc. “This utterance, dearest brothers,” etc.

The manuscript historian of St. Victor at Paris continues as follows on page 102 of his history:

> “There are also other little works by him, composed in the same rhymed verses: namely, a Canticle to the Virgin Mother of God, a Lament of the Blessed Virgin Mary, and a Eulogy of Saint Augustine, bishop and Doctor of the Church. Likewise: thirty-one sermons delivered among us on the various feasts of the year. All these our library preserves in manuscript. In the archives of our church, in the year 1194, Godfrey the sacristan is recorded as subscribing with Robert the abbot, Anselm the prior, and William the subprior; nor is any other man of that name found among us in that period. Hence it is clear that he relinquished the office of subprior in 1186, as we have observed in our Annals, and that he died after the aforesaid year 1194, [Col. 1421A] on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December [21 November], as is recorded in the Victorine necrology in these words: ‘Godfrey, priest and professed canon of our community, died.’”

We have taken this almost word for word from the manuscript [Col. 1422A] *History of the Royal Abbey of St. Victor at Paris*, written by John of Toulouse, canon of that church.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1173: ADAM OF ST. VICTOR**

[Col. 1421]

## NOTICE WRITTEN BY A VERY ANCIENT AUTHOR

(Marten, *Amplissima collectio*, VI, 220)

[Col. 1421B] About the time of that most excellent doctor, Master Hugh of St. Victor, there flourished an outstanding and celebrated teacher, Master Adam, professed canon of the same church of St. Victor at Paris. He was a Breton by birth, humble and agreeable in manner of life, useful and illustrious in doctrine and learning—so much so that without his works a person could scarcely set foot in the prologues of St. Jerome on the Bible, or discover a reasonable exposition of their difficulties. For he expounded them—both those on the Old Testament and those on the New—as “wheel within wheel,” though they are involved in many and great obscurities, whether from their brief and concise account of manifold mysteries or from the insertion of words that seem unusual. He explained them clearly word by word, as is evident to one who carefully examines [Col. 1421C] his book composed for this exposition of the prologues, which begins: “When the parts of the text have been expounded, a new concern arises and breaks frail shoulders with an unbearable burden.”

In this book he also very often mentions a book that he himself composed, called the *Summa on Biblical Words*, or the *Summa of Brito*, and other worthy works. He also deserves to be commended on the meritorious ground that he composed very many sequences concerning the blessed Trinity, the Holy Spirit, the glorious Virgin Mary—to whom he is known to have had a special devotion—the apostles, and many other saints. Proceeding concisely and in articulated clauses, subtly adorned by a graceful marriage of words, wonderfully painted with the little flowers of thought, they are composed in a most fitting form. Although he interweaves prophecies and figures which, in the meaning they convey, seemed most obscure, he nonetheless adapts them to his purpose so plainly that they seem rather to weave a narrative than a figure. Yet, this being so, although he adds something superfluous to them, you will find nothing diminished in them.
