Let whoever has seen this present writing therefore say what Scripture says: “Adam, my example from my youth.” [Col. 1422B] And rightly he ought to be an example to religious persons, because it was said of him and of them: “I shall draw them with the cords of Adam, with the bonds of charity.” But if you ask with Scripture, “Adam, where are you?” the answer is that beneath this vaulted tomb, in the earth from which Adam likewise was formed, is buried the man who, while he lived in this human world, spoke so excellently and outstandingly. And because it is written, “The Lord will render to human beings according to their deeds and according to the works of Adam,” we have judged that some of the works which the Holy Spirit produced through him should be written here, so that whoever reads, sees, and hears them may bless God, worthy of praise for ever, and pray that the breath of life which He breathed into the face of this Adam may, through the vision of His most blessed [Col. 1422C] essence, make him glorious with His saints and elect.

## EPITAPH OF MASTER ADAM, CANON OF ST. VICTOR

> Here lies the heir of the first father’s name and punishment;  
> He becomes earth, bearing a name from the name of earth.  
>
> Do not wonder, O man, that Adam turns to ashes beneath the soil:  
> The earth gave him both his surname and his substance.  
>
> In life he shone upon others; under his guidance  
> Let Adam declare how deceitful is the abundance of things.  
>
> He whom virtue cherished, to whom worldly glory was favorable—  
> Behold, he turns to ashes beneath the turf of a foreign land.

## ANOTHER EPITAPH, WHICH HE COMPOSED CONCERNING HIMSELF

[Note: This epitaph, engraved on bronze and formerly read in the cloister of St. Victor at Paris, was bought for a price in 1793 from the furnace of a workman, where it was about to be thrown, by M. Petit-Radel, a most zealous student of the fine arts. [Col. 1422D] It was recently publicly placed as a most precious monument in the buildings of the Mazarine Library, in the courtyard called the Colbert Court.]

> Heir of sin, by nature a child of wrath,  
> Every human being is born guilty of exile.  
>
> Why does man grow proud, whose conception is guilt,  
> [Col. 1422D] Whose birth is punishment, whose life is labor, whose death is necessity?  
>
> Vain is human welfare, vain is beauty; all things are vain:  
> Among vain things, nothing is vainer than man.  
>
> While the glory of this present life plays all the more alluringly,  
> It passes away—indeed it flees; it does not flee—indeed it perishes.  
>
> After man comes the worm; after the worm comes ash—alas, alas!  
> Thus our glory too returns together into ash.  
>
> Here I lie, wretched and pitiable Adam;  
> As my highest gift I ask one prayer.  
>
> I have sinned, I confess it; I seek forgiveness: spare one who confesses.  
> Spare me, Father; brothers, spare me; spare me, God.

[Col. 1423]

# SEQUENCES OF ADAM OF ST. VICTOR

(Clichtoveus, *Ecclesiastical Elucidarium*, Basel, 1517, folio)

## I. ON SAINT STEPHEN

[Col. 1423A] This sequence preserves rhythmic consonance according to a fixed rule. For the most part, each verse contains three rhythmic clauses. The first two have a similar ending in their final syllables, and each has eight syllables, of which the penultimate is long. The third clause of each verse consists of seven syllables, of which the penultimate is short; and it answers with a similar syllabic cadence to the third clause of the verse immediately following. Nevertheless, so that variety and diversity of rhythmic composition may bring ornament and beauty to the texture of the discourse, the aforementioned form of rhythm is sometimes varied: the first two rhythmic clauses sometimes contain seven syllables each, with a short penultimate, as in the sixth and eighth verses. At times, however, four rhythmic clauses are placed in the same verse, responding alternately, so that the first rhymes with the third and the second with the fourth, as in the last four verses. Sometimes the first three of four clauses in the same verse correspond among themselves by a similar cadence, while the fourth of one verse corresponds with the fourth of another, as in the nineteenth and twentieth verses. All this anyone may easily perceive from reading alone and from the measure of the clauses.

This form of composing sequences is very frequent and more widely used than any other in the ecclesiastical office. Its author was the distinguished man Adam of St. Victor, no less eminent in virtue than in learning, exceedingly fertile and ready in the rhythmic setting of sequences, as the very many sequences composed by him, which will be placed in their proper locations, clearly show. In the present sequence, the outstanding virtue of blessed Stephen in confessing the faith, and his invincible constancy in suffering and death, are commended; these are sufficiently clear and evident from the sixth and seventh chapters of the Acts of the Apostles. The miracles wrought through the merits of blessed Stephen in raising the dead, and the downpour of rain at the time his most sacred body was discovered, are also related, as the notes will show.

> Yesterday the world rejoiced,  
> And rejoicing celebrated  
> Christ’s birth.
>
> Yesterday the choir of angels  
> [5] Attended with joy  
> The King of heaven.
>
> The first martyr and deacon,  
> [Col. 1424B] Bright in faith, bright in life,  
> Bright also in miracles,
>
> [10] Triumphed beneath this day of light,  
> And in triumph taunted  
> Stephen’s unbelieving foes.

[Note: [Col. 1423C] **Stephen taunted the unbelievers.** That is, when, after a lengthy refutation of the charge of blasphemy brought against him, he said to them: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, of whom you have now become betrayers and murderers—you who received the law through the disposition of angels and did not keep it” (Acts 7).]

> Therefore they rage like wild beasts,  
> Because, defeated, they have failed—  
> [15] Enemies of the light.

[Note: [Col. 1423C] **They appoint false witnesses.** Luke in the Acts of the Apostles: [Col. 1423D] “Then they secretly induced men to say that they had heard him speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God. And so they stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes; they came upon him, seized him, brought him before the council, and set up false witnesses, who said: [Col. 1424C] ‘This man does not cease to speak words against this holy place and the law’” (ibid.). When the author here calls them offspring of vipers, he alludes to John the Baptist’s saying to the scribes and Pharisees: “Brood of vipers, who will enable you to flee from the wrath to come?” (Matt. 3). For the Jews persecuting Stephen were full of the venom of cruelty and unbelief, and were born from parents no less venomous.]

> They appoint false witnesses  
> And sharpen their tongues,  
> You offspring of vipers.

[Note: [Col. 1424C] **Athlete, yield to no one.** This verse and the five following—indeed also the fifteenth and sixteenth—contain the words of the faithful people exhorting Saint Stephen to constancy and courage in his suffering. This is not because Christ’s vigorous athlete, who was full of grace and strength, needed an exhortation of this kind, nor because it was actually given at that time. Rather, by this figure and manner of speech, those outstanding deeds which Stephen then performed are approved and commended by all: he is wonderfully encouraged and praised because he yielded to no one, struggled certain of his reward, and so forth. Thus when the Psalms say, “Praise the Lord, all His angels” (Ps. 148), and “Bless the Lord, all His angels” (Ps. 103), they do not by these words incite the angels to praise God, since they praise Him continually and without ceasing; rather, they approve and commend in the angels the fact that they praise God without interruption. Moreover, blessed Stephen is here called an *agonist*—a combatant, boxer, and athlete who fights and contends in an arena—because he endured a hard contest for Christ against the wickedness of the Jews.]

> Athlete, yield to no one;  
> [20] Strive, certain of your reward;  
> Persevere, Stephen.
>
> Stand against the false witnesses;  
> Refute by your words  
> Satan’s synagogue.

[Note: [Col. 1425C] **Satan’s synagogue.** The author rightly calls by this name that multitude and crowd of Jews which resisted the truth and labored to crush Stephen, the witness of evangelical grace. For *synagogue* is a Greek word signifying an assembly and congregation. But that gathering of Jews against Stephen came about through Satan’s instigation, as he urged on the minds of opponents, who were doing Satan’s work, with the torches of rivalry and zeal. The author alludes here to the saying in Revelation: “I know your tribulation and your poverty—yet you are rich—and that you are slandered by those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are a synagogue of Satan” (Rev. 2).]

> [25] Your witness is in heaven,  
> A true and faithful witness,  
> A witness to your innocence.
>
> You bear the name of one crowned;  
> It is fitting that you suffer torments  
> [30] For the crown of glory.
>
> For the crown that does not wither,  
> Endure the force of brief torment:  
> Victory awaits you.
>
> Death shall become your birthday.

[Note: [Col. 1425D] **You bear the name of one crowned.** For Stephen in Greek means “crown,” and, according to Tortelli, is derived from the Greek verb *stephanō*, meaning “to crown.” Thus the name Stephen—considering not its Latin but its Greek formation—is derived and named from a crown. It was therefore fitting, by reason of that name, that he should endure persecution and fight bravely to attain the crown of eternal glory. For Paul says: “One who strives in the contest is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2).]

[Note: [Col. 1425D] **Your death shall become your birthday.** This death of the body, which martyrs endure here, is for them a kind of birth, way, and begetting into everlasting life. Hence the Church also calls the day of the saints’ death their birthdays. This temporal punishment, which is ended in a brief moment, is for them a kind of beginning and entrance into everlasting and unending joy, which immediately follows.]

> [35] [Col. 1425B] Your finite punishment  
> Gives the beginnings of life.
>
> Full of the Holy Spirit,  
> Stephen penetrates heaven  
> With his gaze.
>
> [40] Seeing God’s glory,  
> He grows toward victory  
> And longs for his rewards.
>
> Behold Jesus standing  
> At God’s right hand, [45] Fighting for you—  
> Stephen, consider!
>
> The heavens are opened to you;  
> Christ is revealed to you:  
> Proclaim it with a free voice.
>
> He commends himself to the Savior,  
> [50] For whom he counts it sweet to die  
> Beneath the very stones.
>
> Saul keeps the garments  
> Of all who stone him,  
> Stoning in them all.

[Note: [Col. 1426C] **Stoning in them all.** Namely, by consenting to Stephen’s death and to the stoning inflicted upon him. For Saul, so to speak, stoned with all their hands when he kept the garments of the witnesses who were stoning him; since those who commit evil and those who consent to it incur a like guilt and are to be punished with an equal punishment.]

> [55] That sin may not be charged  
> To those by whom he is stoned,  
> He kneels and prays,  
> Grieving for their madness.
>
> Thus he fell asleep in Christ,  
> [60] Who thus obeyed Christ,  
> And lives always with Christ—  
> [Col. 1426B] The firstfruits of martyrs.
>
> That he raised six  
> Dead persons in Africa,  
> [65] Augustine declares;  
> Common report relates it.

[Note: [Col. 1426C] **The firstfruits of martyrs.** In the Old Testament, “firstfruits” meant the first and earliest-ripened fruits, offered to God in sacrifice and more pleasing and sacred than the rest. Thus blessed Stephen, because after Christ’s Ascension he first received a place among Christ’s martyrs and obtained among them precedence in both time and rank, is rightly called here the firstfruits of martyrs.]

[Note: [Col. 1426C] **Augustine declares.** Namely, in Book 22, chapter 8, of *The City of God*, where he recounts many miracles worthy of remembrance performed through the relics and commemoration of blessed Stephen in the provinces of Hippo and Calama and other African settlements: [Col. 1426D] not only the raising of the dead, but also the restoration to complete health of persons very near death; the return to their former sound bodily condition of some afflicted by a dreadful and continual trembling of the whole body; the illumination of the blind; and the freeing of others from various diseases, such as fistula and stone.]

> Through the grace of God,  
> When his body is revealed,  
> Rain is given to the world  
> [70] In a time of drought.

[Note: [Col. 1426D] **When his body was revealed.** The revelation of the body of blessed Stephen took place through the appearance of Gamaliel to the venerable priest Lucian, as the narrative of the discovery of the body, written by Lucian himself, records. Since there had previously been a great dryness of the earth and a scarcity of rain, when the most holy relics and ashes of blessed Stephen were raised from the earth with due honor, a great flood of rain burst forth and fell from heaven, most salutary and necessary to the world.]

> By fragrance alone he drives away  
> Diseases and demons,  
> Worthy of praise and honor  
> [Col. 1427A] And unceasing remembrance.
>
> [75] Martyr, whose name is sweet  
> In the Church,  
> Comfort the world that languishes  
> With heavenly fragrance. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1426D] **By fragrance alone he drives away.** I believe mention is made here of that most sweet fragrance which, when the tomb of Saint Stephen was opened at the time of the discovery of his body, was suddenly perceived by those standing by. By the efficacy and power of that fragrance, seventy-three persons suffering from various illnesses were healed at once: the possessed were freed, the blind enlightened, and the lame made upright, as the aforementioned Lucian, who was present at these events, testifies. Thus the author here turns to a mystical sense, praying that blessed Stephen may be pleased to warm and strengthen a world weakened by sins with the sweetness and fragrance of heavenly grace.]

## II. ON SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST

This sequence observes exactly the law of rhythmic consonance and is composed in nearly the same manner as the sequence on Saint Stephen, “Yesterday the world rejoiced,” explained shortly before. Its author is said to have been the eminent father Adam of St. Victor, no less distinguished for religious devotion than for learning, and exceedingly elegant in the composition of ecclesiastical sequences, as this one sequence affords no obscure proof. It contains many distinguished praises of blessed John [Col. 1427B] the Evangelist, on account of the singular prerogatives of virtues and graces in which he shone wonderfully beyond others. For he alone embraced every order, rank, and title of the saints: angel in office, patriarch of the new law, prophet, apostle, evangelist, martyr, confessor, and virgin—something very rarely found in other saints.

[Note: [Col. 1427C] **Let us rejoice at the festival.** *Festivum* here means what is solemn and celebrated. Hence *festivitas* is very often used in ecclesiastical prayers for a feast day. *Votivum*, however, is what is promised to be given in fulfillment of a vow. Horace: “A votive heifer is fed for your return.” Votive words are those used in making vows; votive prayers are those in which we ask for something with a vow. So too a votive praise is one rendered to someone in fulfillment of a previously made vow, or ardently desired by a great vow. Sometimes, indeed, that too is called votive which is sought with ardent desires. Jerome: “It was then the Christians’ ardent wish to be struck by the sword for the name of God.”]

> Let us rejoice at the festival;  
> Let us delight in the votive  
> Praise of John.
>
> Let praise thus be upon the lips,  
> [5] Yet let the heart not be deprived of the savor  
> By which it tastes joy.

[Note: [Col. 1427D] **Lest the heart be deprived of savor.** If the tongue alone sounds forth the praise of God or of the saints, while the mind does not attend to it, the one praising does not perceive the inward sweetness and delight in such praise, which he merely makes a noise with his lips. Therefore the author asks that not only the tongue but also our mind may offer praise to God, so that it may inwardly taste it, because the Lord is sweet and may be enjoyed in spiritual joy.]

> This is Christ’s beloved disciple,  
> Who, reclining upon His breast,  
> Drank wisdom.
>
> [10] To him on the cross  
> Christ entrusted His mother; he preserved her,  
> A virgin ignorant of man.
>
> Burning inwardly with charity,  
> Shining outwardly with integrity  
> [15] In signs and speech,
>
> As he was immune from criminal heat,  
> So, immune from penal heat,  
> He came forth from the cauldron.

[Note: [Col. 1427D] **As from criminal heat.** Just as, the author says, blessed John was free from the heat and desire of the flesh, which commonly has sin attached to it, so too he escaped unhurt from the heat of punishment—that is, from boiling oil—when, sent by the impious Domitian into a vat of boiling oil, he came out more vigorous and sounder than when he entered. Bede likewise affirms this in his homily on the Gospel for the present feast, saying: “John, sent by Emperor Domitian into a vat of boiling oil, is related in ecclesiastical history to have emerged from it, while divine grace protected him, as untouched as he had been free from the corruption of fleshly desire.”]

> He overcame the power of poison,  
> [20] He exercised power over death and diseases,  
> And likewise over demons.
>
> Yet a man of such power  
> Was no less compassionate  
> Toward the afflicted.

[Note: [Col. 1428B] **He overcame the power of poison.** When the priests of idols had stirred up a sedition against blessed John, they offered him deadly poison to drink. He fearlessly drank it, after making the sign of the cross, and suffered no injury. He also commanded death, since he recalled to life two men killed by that poison. Likewise he commanded diseases and demons, since by prayer alone he restored to health persons afflicted with various diseases and drove demons from the bodies of the possessed.]

> [25] When he had made whole the broken pieces of gems,  
> He sold them and gave the proceeds  
> To the poor.
>
> He possesses an inexhaustible treasure—  
> He who made gold from rods,  
> [30] [Col. 1429A] And gems from stones.

[Note: [Col. 1428C] **When he had made whole the broken pieces of gems.** Crathon the philosopher, having summoned the people into the public square, smashed into pieces most precious gems bought by selling the inherited property of two very noble Ephesian youths, in order publicly to display contempt for this world. Blessed John, who happened to pass that way, rightly rebuked this empty contempt of the world, which served only display and the pursuit of popular applause. He said that, as Christ taught, the value of those gems ought rather to have been distributed to the poor, so that God’s glory and the relief of one’s neighbor might thereby be promoted. At Crathon’s suggestion, he restored the broken gems by his prayer, and, after they had been sold, ensured that all the money was distributed to the poor.]

[Note: [Col. 1428D] **He who made gold from rods.** Two other highly distinguished young men, stirred by the example of the former, sold all their possessions, distributed them among the poor, and followed blessed John. But shortly afterward, when they saw their servants dressed in fine and splendid clothing while they themselves wore a cheap little cloak and thin garment, they deeply grieved over their lot and condition, longing for the pleasures and magnificence of their former life. When the Apostle noticed this, he ordered them to gather rods and stones from the seashore; those brought to him he changed into gold and precious gems. Handing them over, he said: “Go and buy back the lands you sold, for you have lost at once the estates and the rewards of heaven.”]

> Invited by a friend  
> To feast—by “friend” I mean Christ,  
> Seen with His disciples.

[Note: [Col. 1429B] **He is invited by a friend.** When blessed John had been worn down by extreme old age, the Lord appeared to him with His disciples, now perfected in glorious death, and with the greatest kindness invited him to the banquet of heavenly glory, saying: “Come, my beloved; it is time for you to feast with me in my kingdom with my brethren.” But the author, expressing this thought in this verse, first says in general terms that John is invited by a friend; he then explains whom he specifically understands by this general term “friend,” saying that by “friend” he means Christ, seen with the disciples in that sacred appearance.

[Note: [Col. 1429C] On the tomb into which he descended. Here the author seems to hold that, after Saint John had descended publicly into the tomb which he had ordered to be dug for himself, he there passed away in a peaceful death; and, after some intervening time (known to God), was raised to immortal life through the complete resurrection, in a glorified body, and was assumed, soul and body, to heavenly glory. This opinion draws strength and support from the fact that no relics or traces of that sacred body were afterwards found at the place of his burial. And indeed [Col. 1429D] this one, among the various accounts reported concerning the happy end of his life, is regarded as the most weighty and as preferable to the others.] From the tomb into which he descended,

[35] Thus restored to life he ascended,

To enjoy the highest feast.

[Note: [Col. 1429D] You have the people as witness. The testimony adduced here for that blessed glorification of Saint John, both in body and soul, is that manna is seen continually flowing from his tomb, as a certain sign and indication of that most sweet refreshment with which Saint John is satisfied in the heavenly kingdom. Yet that food of supreme glory is wholly spiritual and invisible, though signified by that perceptible manna.] You have the people as witness—

Or rather, if you wish, your eyes—

That at his tomb

[40] Manna wells up: a feast

From Christ’s banquet.

[Note: [Col. 1429D] Writing the Gospel. In the mystical vision of the four living creatures signifying the holy Evangelists—shown both to the prophet Ezekiel (ch. I) and to John himself in the Apocalypse (ch. IV)—Saint John is represented by the flying eagle. For, according to Bede in his homily on the opening of John’s Gospel, the eagle is accustomed to fly higher than all birds and to fix its gaze more clearly than all living creatures upon the sun’s rays; while the other Evangelists, as it were, walk on earth with the Lord, since, sufficiently setting forth both his temporal generation and his temporal deeds, they say little concerning his divinity. But John flies, as it were, to heaven with the Lord: discussing very little of his temporal acts, he came, soaring in mind more sublimely and contemplating more clearly, to know the eternal power of his divinity, through which all things were made, and handed it down to us to be known by writing. Thus Bede. John, however, after the manner of an eagle, mystically saw the ray of the sun, as the text here says, because he knew the Son of God proceeding from the Father by eternal generation, as a ray flows from the sun. He also saw the Word as the Beginning in the Beginning, because he contemplated the Word of God, who, when the Jews asked him who he was, answered of himself: “The Beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII). And in the Apocalypse he frequently says of himself: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Apoc. I). Moreover, that same Word was in the Beginning, namely in the Father, who is the first of all things and the primary Beginning. John saw these sacred mysteries when, filled with the divine Spirit, he uttered that opening of the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word” (John [Col. 1430D] I), and what follows.] Writing the Gospel,

He bears the eagle’s property:

Beholding the sun’s ray,

[45] Namely, the Beginning—

The Word in the Beginning.

By his signs was converted

The Gentile people, the perverse people—

[Note: [Col. 1430D] The people of all Asia. Asia is the third part of the world in number, but in extent half of it. It contains very many regions, chiefly lying toward the East, such as Phrygia, Lycia, Armenia, Lycaonia, India, and others. In it likewise is the very famous city of Ephesus, where Saint John especially governed the Church; in neighbouring cities he appointed bishops, and tirelessly preached the word of God to the people, so that through his zeal and labour a very great multitude from the regions of Asia was converted to the Lord.] The people of all Asia.

[50] [Note: [Col. 1430D] It is enlightened by his writings. Namely, by his Gospel, which, as Ecclesiastical History relates, he wrote after the other three Evangelists; further, by his three Catholic Epistles, commonly called canonical; and finally by the Apocalypse, which, at the Lord’s revelation, he composed concerning the future state of the Church on the island of Patmos, where he had been exiled.] It is enlightened by his writings;

Being enlightened, the unity

Of the Church is strengthened.

Hail, vessel of saving modesty,

Vessel full of heavenly dew,

[55] Pure within, bright without,

Noble in every respect.

Make us follow holiness.

Through purity of mind,

Make us behold the Trinity

[60] In one substance. Amen.

### III. THE SUNDAY WITHIN THE OCTAVE OF THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

This prose-poem has a varied kind of rhythm in its different verses. For each of the first six verses contains only two rhythmic clauses, though in different manners. In the first two verses those clauses correspond in alternate positions: the first of one verse answers the first of the other in a similar syllabic ending, and the second answers the second. In the remaining four verses, the first clause of each [Col. 1430B] maintains consonance and a similar vocalic sound in its middle and ending. But the second clause of one verse corresponds harmoniously to the second clause of the next verse. All the remaining verses of this prose-poem, except the fifteenth—which consists of four rhythmic clauses maintaining an alternating response in corresponding cadence, the first to the third and the second to the fourth—contain three clauses joined by rhythmic modulation. The first two in the same verse always correspond to one another, and the third of one verse answers, in like sound, the third of the next. In all these [Col. 1431A] rhythmic forms, one clause is sometimes completed by eight syllables, of which the penultimate is long; at other times a rhythmic clause is composed of only seven syllables, and then has a short penultimate. But all this is better perceived from reading the prose-poem itself than it can be conveyed by fixed rules or exact description.

Its author is the venerable Father Adam of Saint Victor, who, during his lifetime, adorned the house of Saint Victor, built in the suburbs of Paris and most observant of religious and regular discipline, by the remarkable brilliance of his learning and holiness of life. There I found this prose-poem, along with many others noted in their places above and to be noted below, ascribed to him as author. On the strength of that testimony I have assigned them to him, and have placed each in its proper location under his name, as proceeding from his workshop. It commends the mystery of the Lord’s Nativity [Col. 1431B] because of the ineffable kindness of the Son of God, who deigned to assume the form of our substance from a virgin mother in order to redeem the human race, held in the miserable captivity of the devil. Moreover, the virginal integrity of the Mother of God is shown not to have been impaired in that wondrous birth, through natural analogies from perceptible things and mystical figures of the Old Testament once set forth by God to prefigure this miracle. The figures of the leafy rod and the dewy fleece are then fittingly and correctly applied to the matter itself, and shown to be suitably adapted to Christ, as the notes explain more fully.

[Note: [Col. 1431C] Splendour and image of the Father. By this designation Christ, the Son of God, is here indicated. Saint Paul, in the Epistle to the Hebrews (ch. I), calls him the splendour of the Father’s glory and the image of his substance. He is splendour, I say, because he is “the brightness of eternal light” (Wisdom VI), and an outflow of the radiance of almighty God, proceeding from the Father just as splendour proceeds from light. The Son of God is called the image of the Father’s substance because he is the character and seal of the Father’s hypostasis and subsistence, and the image of the invisible God (Col. I). Yet the Son of God, of such sublimity and majesty, conformed himself to humankind, because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in habit as a man” (Phil. II).]

The Father’s splendour and image,

Conforming himself to humankind,

By power, not by nature,

[Col. 1432A] Gave birth through a virgin.

[5] [Note: [Col. 1431C] At last glad, old Adam. “Old Adam” means the first parent, from whom the entire human race was propagated according to the flesh. He is called old in comparison with Christ, who, though later in the order of time if one considers the flesh, is called the new Adam and the restorer and author of human salvation, as has already been said in the first book in the exposition of the hymn:

> Let every age acknowledge  
> That life’s reward has come,

where occurs the verse needing explanation:

> What old Adam defiled,  
> New Adam washed away.

For since through the former Adam the oldness of sin was brought into the world, while through the latter the newness of life was introduced by grace, the former is rightly called old and the latter new. Yet when old Adam is named here, it must be understood not only of the first parent in his own person, but also of the entire human race, plunged through him into the oldness of sin. For it had fled from God and was condemned to exile because of the ancient transgression of the first-created human; it had also been reduced to the captivity [Col. 1432C] of the prince of darkness and miserably subjected to his harsh dominion. Now, however, the human race is invited to gladness and joy in the Lord, to sing a new song to God because of the new benefit of redemption and the grace of the new law. In this place it is likewise urged to come confidently into public, as one endowed with freedom and vindicated into liberty, whereas formerly, because of the miserable lot of servitude and captivity, it lay hidden, not daring, through shame and embarrassment, to raise its face.]

At last, let old Adam be glad;

Let him bring forth a new song.

Fugitive and captive,

Let him come forth in public.

Eve’s mourning—the fruit of life

[10] The rejoicing Virgin bore.

Nor because of him did she lose

The seal of chastity.

[Note: [Col. 1432C] If crystal is moistened. Here an example from a perceptible thing guides us to understand that the most holy Virgin and Mother of God remained inviolate in giving birth. If, he says, crystal is drenched with watery moisture and exposed to the sun’s ray, it emits sparks of fire, yet without being torn apart or broken. So indeed the God-bearing Virgin—clear as crystal and compacted by the firmness of every virtue, drenched with heavenly dew and the grace of the Holy Spirit overshadowing her—brought forth the Saviour of the world, glowing with fiery love, yet without any weakening or injury to her virginal purity.]

If crystal is moistened

And exposed to the sun,

[15] It sparkles with a little fire,

Yet the crystal is not broken;

Nor in childbirth is dissolved

The seal of modesty.

[Col. 1432B] At such a birth

Custom and nature are astonished,

And reason fails.

The matter is ineffable:

So gracious, so humble

Christ’s generation.

[25] [Note: [Col. 1432D] Leaf, flower, nut, from the dry rod. As the Book of Numbers (ch. XVII) relates, “Aaron’s rod, wholly dry, by divine power put forth leaves, flowered, and produced fruit. For Moses, when he returned the next day after placing it in the tabernacle of testimony before the Lord, found that Aaron’s rod in the house of Levi had budded; swelling buds had burst into flowers, which, with leaves spread out, had developed into almonds.” In the same way, above the laws and rights of nature, the most holy Virgin, by God’s power alone, bore a Son while remaining untouched.]

From a dry rod comes leaf, flower, nut;

And the chaste Virgin, the Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 1432D] The fleece bears heavenly dew. Gideon had sought from the Lord a sign of the victory to be won through him against the Midianites (Judges VI): that dew should be upon the fleece alone when it was spread out on the threshing-floor, while all the ground was dry; and this came to pass. That fleece [Col. 1433B] was a symbol and sign of the most holy Virgin, who, watered with divine dew and the grace of the Holy Spirit, bore the Son of God—the creature, that is, her Creator, who indeed is the ransom-price of the creature. For he was offered on the cross for us as the price of our redemption, we who are God’s creatures.]

The fleece bears heavenly dew:

The creature, her Creator;

[30] The creature’s ransom-price.

The mysteries of leaf, flower, nut, dew

[Col. 1433A] Suit the Saviour’s loving-kindness.

[Note: [Col. 1433B] Christ is a leaf by protecting. The two figures drawn from the Old Testament and already explained in the eleventh and twelfth verses are here applied to the subject. This verse briefly sets out how Christ is mystically called leaf, or foliage, flower, and nut produced from the dry rod, and likewise why he is called dew, gently shed upon Gideon’s fleece. Christ, [Col. 1433C] he says, is called a leaf because he protects his own from the heat of vices, lest the sun scorch them by day or the moon by night (Ps. CXX), just as a tree’s leaf protects its fruit from injury by the sun’s burning heat. He is called a flower because of the most sweet fragrance of all virtues, which he has spread through the whole world with wondrous sweetness: “I am,” he says, “the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II). Thirdly, Christ is spiritually called a nut because he feeds faithful souls by his saving teaching—indeed, by the banquet of his most sacred body—as the material nut itself is a pleasant food for people. He attests this in the Gospel, saying: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI). Finally, fourthly, Christ is called dew because he waters dry human minds with heavenly grace, so that they may bear the fruit of good works, just as dew falling from above moistens the earth and nourishes and quickens plants wet by its dewy shower.]

Christ is a leaf by protecting,

[35] A flower by sweetness, a nut by feeding,

Dew by heavenly grace.

Why is it a scandal to the Jews

That a virgin should give birth,

When a dry rod has produced

[40] An almond?

[Note: [Col. 1433C] Let us consider the nut further. This verse proposes that the example of the nut, which had above been applied to Christ in the third place, should be considered more carefully. For when the nature of a nut is examined attentively and laid open, it signifies the sacred mysteries of the true Light, namely Christ, which the following verses unfold.]

Let us consider the nut further,

For the nut brought into the light

Is a mystery of light.

Bearing a threefold union,

[45] [Note: [Col. 1433D] Bearing a threefold union. A material nut contains three things in itself, compacted in some fashion into one whole substance: an outer husk, a shell covered by the husk, and a kernel enclosed in the shell. Again, the nut provides three benefits to humankind: anointing and light, through the oil pressed from it, and food, through its kernel, which is eaten. But in applying these things to allegory and spiritual understanding, the entire nut indicates and represents Christ, who in one person contains two natures and suffered the bitterness of death in one of them. Thus the nut’s husk, which is rough and of bitter juice, [Col. 1434B] signifies the harshness of the Passion and death which Christ endured in his flesh. The hard shell of the nut, enclosed by the husk, signifies Christ’s human nature, exposed to the bitter sufferings of the Passion—namely, his sacred soul and body, compacted with bones and sinews. Finally, the kernel hidden in the shell represents Christ’s most august divinity, concealed in the flesh and surrounded by its veil. The kernel has a very sweet taste, most pleasing to those who eat it. So indeed the Lord is sweet to those who taste him (Ps. XXXIII), filling with the torrent of his delight (Ps. XXXV) those who are satisfied with his glory. This mystical meaning is splendidly expressed in the eighteenth and nineteenth verses of this prose-poem.

Moreover, the three benefits mentioned above which the nut provides to people—anointing, light, and food—also apply mystically to Christ. For he is spiritual anointing for those sick with sin, healing the wounds of sins by grace. He is also spiritual light, enlightening the blind and driving from human minds the darkness of ignorance. Finally, he is nourishment and spiritual food for the good and upright in heart, whom he feeds by his teaching and satisfies with his most sacred body: “I,” he says, “am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John VI); and again: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI). This mystical application of the nut’s three effects to Christ is briefly explained in the twentieth verse of this prose-poem.]

It affords three things: anointing,

Light, and food.

[Col. 1433B] The nut is Christ; the nut’s husk

Is the punishment of the cross around the flesh.

[Col. 1434A] The shell is the body of bones.

[50] Divinity clothed in flesh,

And Christ’s sweetness,

Are signified by the kernel.

Christ is light to the blind, ointment

To the sick, and comfort

[55] To pious souls.

[Note: [Col. 1434C] O how sweet a sacrament. This verse makes clearer the third usefulness of the nut, already applied to Christ, showing how he is food to the faithful. Great, he says, is that sacrament [Col. 1434D] and wonderful mystery by which Christ provides his flesh as food and life-giving bread to the Christian people in the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist. Moreover, the author here calls Christ’s most sacred flesh “the hay of flesh,” because of its natural weakness and frailty, which by a dispensation of condescension he possessed before the Passion, almost alluding to Isaiah’s saying: “All flesh is hay, and all its glory is as the flower of the field. The hay has dried up and the flower has fallen, because the Spirit of the Lord has breathed upon it. Truly the people are hay” (Isa. XL). By “grain” is meant here that heavenly and life-giving bread which is presented to the faithful for communion under the appearance of grain and wheaten bread. Thus Christ changes the hay of flesh into grain for the faithful, because he gives them his most sacred body as saving food, consecrated under the appearance and form of grain.]

O how sweet a sacrament:

He changes the hay of flesh

Into grain for the faithful.

[Note: [Col. 1434D] Those whom under the shadow of the sacrament. Here the “shadow of the sacrament” does not mean a figure, appearance, or image of the sacrament of the Eucharist which merely represents it and does not truly contain it, so that shadow is distinguished from reality. In this sense, the Paschal Lamb in the Old Testament, the manna [Col. 1435B] in the wilderness, the loaves of presentation, and the other figures were called a shadow of the most sacred sacrament of the altar, because they prefigured it; in the same way the Apostle says that the Law possessed a shadow of good things to come (Heb. X). But in that sense the Christian people do not possess the shadow of this sacrament of communion, but the thing itself and the reality. Yet because it is not seen nakedly but veiled under the appearances of bread and wine, covered as though by a veil or shade, so that Christ’s sacred flesh is not visible to our eyes nor his blood in its proper and natural appearance and form, Christ is said here to feed the faithful under the shadow of the sacrament. And there is an earnest prayer that, once this shadow and veil of appearances is removed, he may feed us in the heavenly kingdom with his face now unveiled, by the presence of his divine countenance. May he himself grant this to us, the supremely good and merciful Lord, blessed for ever. Amen.]

Those whom under the sacrament’s shadow

[60] Jesus feeds in the present,

Satisfy with your countenance.

Splendour coeternal with the Father,

Transfer us hence to the joys

[Col. 1434B] Of paternal brightness. Amen.

### IV. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

[Col. 1435A]

This prose-poem too is wholly rhythmic. Each of its first four verses contains seven rhythmic clauses, each clause comprising seven syllables and always having a short penultimate. These clauses have consonance in their syllabic endings, sometimes in alternating positions, as in the first verse, and sometimes in adjacent positions, as in the following verses; and the final clause always has its response either in a clause placed in the middle of the same verse or in the final clause of the next verse. Each of the final two verses contains four rhythmic clauses: the first two correspond to one another, the third of one verse corresponds to the third of the other, and the fourth to the fourth. Its author is Adam of Saint Victor. [Col. 1435B] It describes the joy of the Lord’s resurrection as diffused not only among angels and human beings, but also through all the perceptible bodies of this world—the heavens, elements, and mixed bodies. All these, by a more joyful aspect and a more pleasing disposition than they had before, display a certain delight at the Lord’s resurrection and bear witness to their joy with cheerful countenance, as though they rejoiced in some fashion with the risen Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1435C] The renewal of the world. The Lord’s resurrection itself is here called the renewal of the world, because the whole human race, understood by the name “world,” was renewed in it, transferred from the oldness of sin to the newness of grace and from death to life. Add that in Christ’s resurrection was represented and prefigured the resurrection of all human beings, in which there will undoubtedly be a renewal of the whole world and of all people, when this corruptible shall put on incorruption and this mortal immortality (I Cor. XV). Therefore it is also called regeneration in the Gospel (Matt. XIX), because the body will be born again to immortality and unending life. Christ’s resurrection, which is the cause and pattern of our resurrection, is therefore not inappropriately called the renewal of the world.]

The world’s renewal

Brings forth new joys;

[Col. 1436A] With the rising Lord

All things rise again.

[5] The elements serve

And perceive how great

The Creator’s solemnities are:

Mobile fire flies,

And rolling air,

[10] Flowing water flows,

Stable earth remains.

Light things seek the heights;

Heavy things hold the centre.

[Note: [Col. 1435D] All things are renewed. Saint Augustine eloquently and copiously expresses this common joy of all perceptible creation and its kind of rejoicing at Christ’s resurrection, described at length in these verses, in one of his sermons for the Paschal solemnity, in these words: “Thus the whole countenance of the earth, now putting forth shoots, more joyful through the varied ornament of its fruits, raises up with its risen Lord the whole nature of things, hitherto as though dead. There the pleasing beauty of trees and grasses, though differing in the gift of its shoots, yet with an equal gesture of joy, meets this unique solemnity in festal array. And what shall I say of the sky, until now in some measure sad in aspect but now cheerful, which for some time, covered with the thick darkness of clouds, troubled all the expanse of this air? Behold, suddenly, as though righteousness were looking down from heaven upon earth (Ps. LXXXIV), a wondrous serenity smiles upon the world; and the desires of heaven and earth unite in one joy to welcome Christ, God and man, in common exultation—he who came to bring peace common to both and, breaking down the middle wall of division, made the two one. Hence the source of all stars, that solar splendour, now cleanses his brow, much wrinkled until then; and, like a king conspicuous in the diadem of his head, on the day of his marriage and the day of his heart’s joy, bestows more abundant gifts of his light upon the other stars, as though upon his companions. For the moon, from the day of its rising always subject to a certain diminution of itself, makes itself ready in full brightness for Paschal joys. And, to touch on all things briefly: just as everything that subsists among created things serves human dominion by divine dispensation, so all alike are bound to rejoice at human salvation. Therefore, since for humankind all creation displays its joys by such great signs, it follows that human beings themselves should not lack testimonies to such joy.” Thus Augustine.]

All things are renewed.

[15] Heaven grows more serene,

And sea more tranquil.

[Col. 1436B] The breeze breathes more gently.

Our valley has flowered;

Dry things grow green again;

[20] Cold things grow warm again,

[Note: [Col. 1436D] After which spring grew mild. The word *quae* here is not copulative but relative, and refers to the dry and cold bodies of winter, after which the warmth of spring itself follows, a mild warmth and the most pleasant of all the seasons of the year. Christ’s resurrection occurred in springtime.]

After which spring grew mild.

[Note: [Col. 1436D] The frost of death is dissolved. The author alludes to the season in which Christ’s resurrection occurred. Then winter frost and ice congealed by wintry cold melt in spring. [Col. 1437C] So, through the life-giving warmth of divine grace manifested in the Lord’s resurrection, the deadly cold of eternal death was dissolved, and death itself lies cast down through the renewal of life. In the same verse the prince of this world is said to have lost his own right to hold the human race any longer in captivity when he sought to hold Christ as though Christ too were subject to death and sin, though he alone was free among the dead and the prince had no claim upon him, since he was wholly free from sin. The prince of this world’s claim upon humanity is sin alone. Hence Christ said of him: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John XIV).]

The frost of death is dissolved;

The prince of this world is removed,

And his dominion

[25] In us is destroyed.

While he sought to hold

Him in whom he had nothing,

He lost his own right.

Life conquers death;

Humankind now recovers

[30] (What it had formerly lost)

The joy of Paradise.

He provides an easy way,

Removing the Cherub’s turning

(As God had promised)

[35] Sword. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1437C] Removing the sword. After our first parents had been cast out of Paradise for transgressing the divine command, the Lord placed before the Paradise of delight a cherub and a flaming, turning sword to guard the way [Col. 1437D] to the tree of life (Gen. III). This signifies that entry into the heavenly kingdom had been barred to the human race before satisfaction was made for that universal offence which overflowed to the entire posterity. But by Christ’s death and Passion satisfaction was abundantly made for that sin; the heavenly kingdom formerly closed was opened to humankind, and heaven’s gate was thrown open. Therefore Christ is said then to have removed the cherub’s turning sword and to have provided an easy way to heaven.]

### V. ANOTHER PROSE-POEM ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

This prose-poem is bound by the measures [Col. 1437B] of rhythmic modulation, like that concerning Saint Stephen, “Yesterday the world rejoiced,” and approaches that composition in form and character. It unfolds the wondrous mysteries of the Lord’s resurrection, prefigured by many figures in the Old Testament and more clearly manifested to us in the New by divine goodness. Hence many figures of the old law are enumerated here, beneath whose veil and shadow such great sacraments of human redemption were prefigured and covered, as the notes will explain one by one. Indeed this prose-poem is exceedingly divine, containing much in little and splendidly drawn throughout from sacred Scripture; its author, Adam of Saint Victor, aptly and copiously applies both the narratives and the teachings of Scripture to his subject, and thereby clearly proves himself exceptionally practised and ready in the divine Scriptures. He diligently maintains the same practice in several prose-poems of his own composition—many of which are included in this [Col. 1437C] book—as one wholly devoted to their study.

[Note: [Col. 1437D] Let the old leaven be purged out. *Zyma* means leaven and in Scripture bears the type and representation of sin (Exod. XII; Lev. II), when it commands that the Paschal lamb must be eaten without leaven and forbids leaven to be mixed into the Lord’s sacrifice. [Col. 1438C] The author therefore warns in these words that the oldness of sin must be purged from us, so that we may worthily celebrate so great a solemnity in sincerity of heart, as though he were crying aloud in our ears with the Apostle: “Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump” (I Cor. V).]

Let the old leaven be purged out,

That the new resurrection

[Col. 1438A] May be sincerely celebrated.

This is the day of our hope.

[5] The wondrous power of this day

Is attested by the Law.

[Note: [Col. 1438C] This day despoiled Egypt. Whatever occurred under the old Law as a figure prefiguring this sacred day is rightly attributed to this day as to the reality and chief exemplar toward which every type and shadow tended. Thus this day of resurrection despoiled Egypt, because it was signified by that day on which the Hebrews despoiled the Egyptians of gold, silver, and precious garments received on loan, and on which the Hebrews were freed from Egypt’s iron furnace, the house of slavery, and Pharaoh’s heavy yoke (Exod. XII). Thus also on this day Christ despoiled hell and redeemed the human race [Col. 1438D] from the intolerable slavery of the prince of darkness.]

This day despoiled Egypt

And freed the Hebrews

From the iron furnace.

[10] Confined in a narrow place,

Their work of slavery was

Mud, brick, straw.

Now let the voice of divine power,

Now of triumph, now of salvation,

[15] Break forth freely.

This is the day the Lord has made,

The day that ends our sorrow,

[Col. 1438B] The saving day.

The Law is a shadow of things to come.

[20] Christ is the end of promises,

Who brings all things to fulfilment.

Christ’s blood blunted

The flaming sword,

Its guard removed.

[25] [Note: [Col. 1438D] The boy, a figure of our laughter. Isaac, Abraham’s son by Sarah, is here called a form or figure of our laughter and joy, which we ought rightly to have because of the Lord’s resurrection and the restoration of life. His name Isaac was derived from laughter, when Sarah, now delivered by that birth, said: “God has made laughter for me, and whoever hears will laugh with me” (Gen. XXI). But a ram, or male sheep, is read to have been killed in his stead, when the angel called from heaven and forbade Abraham to sacrifice his son, as Abraham had resolved to do in obedience to the divine voice. “Then Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw behind him a ram caught by its horns among the thorns; taking it, [Col. 1439C] he offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son” (ibid.). Isaac was indeed a sign and symbol both of the Lord’s Passion and of resurrection to life, since he had been destined for death and was prepared to undergo it; yet after this intended offering—indeed, after the ram had been killed in his stead—he remained alive.]

The boy, a figure of our laughter,

For whom a ram was slain,

Signifies life’s joy.

Joseph comes out of the pit;

Christ returns to the heights

[30] After death’s punishment.

Here a dragon devours

Pharaoh’s dragons,

Himself immune from the dragon’s

[Col. 1438C] Malice.

[35] Those whom the fiery one wounds,

The presence of the bronze serpent

Frees from the serpent.

Christ is the hook and bracelet;

He pierces the serpent in the jaw.

[40] The weaned child puts his hand

Into the basilisk’s den;

Thus the ancient guest of the world

Is driven out and flees.

Elisha’s mockers,

[45] While he ascends to the house of God,

Feel the bald man’s zeal.

David, the possessed man,

The scapegoat,

And the sparrow escape.

[50] With a jawbone Samson strikes down a thousand,

And rejects marriage

From his own tribe.

Samson opens Gaza’s bars

And, carrying away its gates, climbs

[55] The summit of the mountain.

Thus the mighty lion of Judah,

Having shattered the gates of dreadful death,

Rises on the third day.

[Note: [Col. 1439D] By the Father’s roaring voice. The lion is said by its roar to awaken its cubs when they lie newly brought into the light, as if lifeless. Alluding to this natural characteristic, the author, having called Christ a lion, says that Christ was raised from the dead at the command of God the Father—expressed by the name of a roaring voice—since Scripture frequently testifies concerning Christ that God the Father raised him from the dead. After his resurrection, Christ ascended into heaven, led captivity captive, and brought back to heaven with him the spoils taken from the infernal lake, namely the holy Fathers, to the bosom of our heavenly mother, Jerusalem, and of the triumphant Church.]

By the Father’s roaring voice,

[60] He brought back so many spoils

To his heavenly mother’s bosom.

The sea-monster restores the fugitive Jonah,

A sign of the true Jonah,

Alive after three days,

[65] From the confinement of its belly.

The cluster of Cyprus blooms again,

Spreads out and grows;

The synagogue’s flower withers,

And the Church flowers.

[70] Death and life contended;

Christ truly rose,

And with Christ rose again

Many witnesses of glory.

[Note: [Col. 1439D] A new morning, a joyful morning. This statement is taken from verse of Psalm XXIX: “Weeping shall remain in the evening, and joy in the morning” (Ps. XXIX). Explaining it, Saint Jerome says: “Weeping remained in the evening because, when the Lord had suffered and was buried, the Apostles and the women remained in weeping and lamentation. [Col. 1440C] And joy in the morning, because when they came to the tomb in the morning, they received from the angels the glory of the resurrection” (Mark XV).]

A new morning, a joyful morning,

[75] Wipes away evening weeping.

Because life has conquered death,

It is a time of joy.

Jesus the conqueror, Jesus the life,

Jesus, the well-trodden way of life,

[80] By whose death death was put to sleep,

Invite us confidently

To the Paschal table.

Living bread, life-giving water,

True and fruitful vine,

[85] Feed us; cleanse us,

That from the second death.

May your grace save [us]. Amen.

## VI. FOR THE FEASTS OF EASTER: ANOTHER PROSE

[Col. 1440B] This prose likewise consists of definite measures of rhythmic consonance. For the most part, each of its verses contains only two rhythmic clauses, corresponding to one another in their syllabic endings. Each of these clauses has eight syllables, with the penultimate always short. Sometimes, however, a single verse contains four such clauses, preserving consonance in alternating positions: thus the first answers the third, and the second the fourth, in a similar syllabic ending. At other times likewise, the four clauses of the same verse end in precisely the same way; as the attentive reader will readily judge at a first glance at the text itself. Its author is Adam of Saint Victor. In it the glorious resurrection of Christ is commended with many praises because of the great benefits which it conferred upon humankind: namely, redemption from the ancient enemy, restoration of life, deliverance from death, and the hope that we shall attain immortality at the consummation of the age. And since Christ’s resurrection took place on the Lord’s Day, that day also is extolled with distinguished titles and praises.

[Note: [Col. 1440D] *The Lord’s-Day light has shone.* That “light” is often used by authors for “day” is too well known to require proof or explanation. Thus it is understood here whenever it stands in the nominative. For in the second verse, where the noun is in the genitive, it signifies brightness or radiance. The Lord’s Day is the day immediately following the Sabbath—or rather, following the Sabbath as the seventh in sequence. For it is the first day, both in chronological order and in excellence of dignity. And because in the New Testament this day has been consecrated to the Lord, so that God himself may be worshipped on it more particularly and more fully than on the other days of the week, as in the Old Testament on the Sabbath, it therefore receives the name of the Lord’s Day. And it is called the Lord’s Day, as though the day of the Lord, specially dedicated and assigned to the Lord.]

The Lord’s-Day light has shone,  
A signal light, a single light:  
The light of light and gladness,  
The light of immortal glory.

[5] [Note: [Col. 1440D] *The world’s creation.* The creation or formation of the world—here called its “founding,” because the world was founded by God—commends the Lord’s Day, since the production of the world itself began on the Lord’s Day. It was the first of the six days on which the world was formed, as was shown in the first book of this work, in the exposition of that hymn:

> First of all days,  
> On which the created world came into being.

[Col. 1441C] A second dignity is added to it: Christ’s resurrection was accomplished on that day. For Christ rose early on the first day of the Sabbath—that is, on the first day after the Sabbath (Mark 16). This is the Lord’s Day. Because of such excellences, this day is called in the first verse of this prose a distinguished and unique day—that is, chief or primary. In the second, it is also called the day of light and gladness, and likewise the day of immortal glory, because through Christ’s resurrection it brought us light, gladness, and immortal glory. For this reason the fourth verse says that Christ’s resurrection adorned the Lord’s Day itself with a remarkable privilege and singular dignity.]

The world’s creation  
Commends it from the beginning.

[Col. 1441A] Christ’s resurrection  
Enriched it with privilege,  
With hope of everlasting joy.

[10] [Note: [Col. 1441C] *Let the children of light rejoice.* “God is light,” as John says, “and there is no darkness in him” (1 John 1). Therefore those who imitate God and keep his commandments are children of God and children of light, because they perform works of light and flee works of darkness. Thus the Lord himself calls them in the Gospel when he says to the Jews: “While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may be children of light” (John 12). In the sixth verse, moreover, the members of the mystical body are the faithful, who by good works possess within themselves the life of grace and are joined to Christ himself, their head, by the bond of love, so that they may belong to the wholeness and perfection of Christ’s sacred body. This verse therefore exhorts the faithful to obtain this for themselves by good works and purity of life: that at last they may deserve to be made conformed to Christ the head and to rise into immortal glory, as he too rose.]

Let the children of light rejoice.  
Let the members, by merit, claim  
Conformity to the head.

The celebration is solemn,  
And solemn are the vows.

[15] The dignity of the first day  
Demands foremost joys.

The glory of solemn feasts  
Is the Paschal victory,  
Formerly promised to the fathers  
Under many mysteries.

[20] [Note: [Col. 1441D] *Now that the veil has been torn, it lay open.* In the Lord’s passion the veil of the Temple is read to have been torn from top to bottom (Matthew 27). This tearing mystically signified that the covering of the Old Testament, which concealed beneath various figures the mysteries of the new law, had now been removed. With the reality itself now present, the most sacred mysteries of our redemption—which until then had lain hidden and obscured under the covering of figures—were made manifest, just as, when a veil is removed, whatever was previously covered by it is seen openly.]

Now that the veil has been torn, there lay open  
What the old law had sung beforehand.

[Col. 1441B] Reality destroys the figure,  
And light illuminates the shadow.

[25] [Note: [Col. 1442B] *What the spotless lamb…* In Exodus the children of Israel were commanded to sacrifice a lamb without blemish, [Col. 1442C] and likewise to take a kid on the evening of Passover. By sprinkling its blood on the doorposts and lintels of their houses, they were delivered from the angel who struck the firstborn of Egypt. That lamb bore the type and figure of Christ, the true and immaculate Lamb, by whose precious blood shed upon the cross we have been delivered from demonic bondage, as has been very often stated and more fully explained above.]

What the spotless lamb,  
What the kid prefigured,  
The Messiah reveals to us,  
Cleansing our sins.

[Note: [Col. 1442C] *By an undeserved death.* Christ was not liable to death, because he was altogether free from sin; and death was introduced through sin. But all of us are liable to death, because we are subject to sin. Therefore Christ, through the death not owed by him which he freely endured, delivered us from the death owed by us—not only temporal but also eternal death. The verse immediately following, however, refers not so much to Christ as to the devil. Attempting, in opposition to Christ, to seize unlawful prey—namely Christ, in whom he had no right—he is justly deprived of lawful prey, namely the whole human race, over which he had claimed a right because of the contagion and stain of sin.]

By an undeserved death  
He released us from deserved death.

[Col. 1442A] Seeking unlawful prey,  
The spoiler loses lawful prey.

[Note: [Col. 1442D] *The flesh destroys reproaches.* Christ’s flesh, wholly free from every sin, destroys the reproaches and stains of our truly sinful flesh. For he, having indeed the likeness of sinful flesh but not sinful flesh itself, took sin away from us, who certainly do possess sinful flesh. Nor did he remove from our flesh only the reproaches of guilt, but also those of punishment—namely mortality, passibility, and corruptibility—through the glory of the completed resurrection. Christ’s own flesh, blooming again on the third day through its return to immortal life, strengthened the doubting hearts of the disciples, who had long been uncertain concerning the truth of his resurrection (John 20), to whom “he presented himself alive by many proofs” (Acts 1).]

The flesh that knows no sin  
Destroys the flesh’s reproaches.

[35] Blooming again on the third day,  
It strengthens doubting hearts.

O wondrous death of Christ,  
Make us alive with Christ;  
O death not subject to death,

[40] Grant us life’s rewards. Amen.

## VII. ANOTHER PROSE ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

This prose has a rhythmic composition similar to that explained shortly before, *On the first morning of the Sabbath, the Son of God rising*. Its author is [Col. 1442B] Adam of Saint Victor. It proclaims the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, through which we have been shaken free from the jaws of the roaring lion, as this had been foreshadowed by many figures of the Old Testament. Through that resurrection, and likewise through Christ’s death, grace flows into the whole Church; this grace is undoubtedly received by all who confess in word and deed that Christ is the author of life and the Savior of the world, from whom alone salvation must be hoped for.

Behold the festal day:  
Light succeeds darkness;

[Col. 1443A] Resurrection succeeds death.  
Let sorrow yield to joy.

[5] [Note: [Col. 1443B] *Since the glory is greater.* The first disgrace was introduced by the transgression of our first parents and their violation of the divine command. Because of it, the entire human race was subjected to a curse and banished from the kingdom of heaven. But now, in Christ’s resurrection, the glory of the human race is greater than that dignity which was lost through the first disgrace. Human nature has now been raised to an immortality by which it can never die; it has now been endowed with an incorruptibility and impassibility by which it will never be able to suffer corruption or the affliction of passion. Before the first disgrace, however, our nature was not simply immortal and incorruptible, but only in a qualified sense: it could avoid dissolution by death and remain untouched by corruption so long as it persisted in its uprightness. Yet the first disgrace was as evil as the condition of humankind lost by that disgrace was good. [Col. 1443C] But our condition before the fall was not so bright and excellent as is the state of human nature glorified through the resurrection, as has now been shown. Therefore the first disgrace was not as evil as the condition of our flesh made blessed through the resurrection is good. Thus the glory of humankind after the resurrection is now greater than was the first disgrace through sin; which is the point at issue.]

Since the glory is greater  
Than the first disgrace,

Truth puts shadow to flight,  
Newness oldness,  
Consolation mourning.

[10] Keep the new Passover  
Which goes before in the head;  
Let every member hope.

Our Passover is Christ,  
Who suffered for us,

[15] The Lamb without blemish.

[Col. 1444A] [Note: [Col. 1443C] *The enemy who circles about us.* When Samson went with his parents to Timnah, a city of the Philistines, to take a wife there, and had come to the vineyards of the town, a fierce roaring lion cub appeared and confronted him. But the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson, and he tore the lion to pieces as though tearing a kid, having absolutely nothing in his hand, as the book of Judges relates (chapter 14). In this action Samson was a figure of Christ, and the roaring lion of the devil himself, of whom blessed Peter says: “Your adversary the devil prowls about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5). Christ indeed rescued the entire human race—which was the prey of our enemy—from his hands; he gloriously defeated him and cast him to the ground, breaking and crushing his strength.]

The enemy who circles about us—  
Christ snatches away his prey.

What Samson sang beforehand  
When he tore the lion apart.

[20] [Note: [Col. 1443D] *David, strong in might.* Before his conflict with Goliath, David spoke to King Saul and described this very matter in these words: “Your servant was tending his father’s flock; and a lion or a bear came and took a ram from the midst of the flock. I pursued them and struck them and rescued it from their mouth. And they rose up against me; I seized their jaws and choked and killed them. For I, your servant, have killed both lion and bear” (1 Samuel 17). David, moreover—whose name is interpreted “strong in hand” and “desirable in countenance”—signifies Christ, strong in battle and fairer in form than the children of men (Psalm 44), who rescues his Father’s flock, that is, the entire human race, from the jaws and claws of the devil, [Col. 1444B] signified by the bear and the lion; and he does this through his death and passion.]

David, strong in might,  
From the lion’s claws  
And the bear’s jaws  
Rescues his Father’s flock.

[Note: [Col. 1444B] *That in death he struck down more.* When the Philistines were celebrating a solemn feast, praising Dagon their god because Samson their enemy had been captured by them, they ordered Samson to be brought out of prison during the meal so that he might entertain them. After giving them some spectacle of sport, he was led by the boy guiding his steps to the pillars upon which the whole house rested, in order to rest there awhile. Having invoked God, he grasped in his hands the two pillars and violently struck them together with such force that the whole house fell upon those reclining there, crushing about three thousand men and women. In that collapse he too was killed, and he killed far more in death than he had done while alive. Thus Christ, prefigured by Samson, more powerfully and perfectly crushed the powers of darkness by his death than [Col. 1444C] he had done while still alive. For while he lived on earth before his passion, he expelled demons bit by bit from possessed bodies and once crushed a whole legion of them, expelling it by the command of his word alone (Luke 8). But by his death he conquered not merely one demon or another, but drove out the prince of this world himself with all his dark host, and powerfully routed him, casting down that entire company of evil powers by the force of his death.]

That in death he struck down more,  
Samson prefigured Christ—  
Whose death is victory.

[Note: [Col. 1444C] *Samson is called “their sun.”* This verse shows, from the interpretation of Samson’s name, that Christ is rightly signified by him. For Samson, it says, is interpreted “their sun,” that is, the sun of the Hebrews, whom in his own time he wonderfully enlightened by judicial leadership, notable strength, and protection from enemies. Christ, however, is both the Sun of righteousness and the light of the elect; in this life he illumines them with the light of grace, and in the next with the brightness of his glory. [Col. 1444D] Thus the meaning of Samson’s name fittingly applies to Christ. Further, Samson was announced by an angel to his parents before his conception (Judges 13); so Christ’s conception was announced by Gabriel to his most holy mother. Samson was born of a barren mother; Christ of a virgin mother, the Holy Spirit overshadowing her. Likewise Samson was a Nazarite, that is, consecrated to the Lord, throughout his life; but of Christ the prophet said: “He shall be called a Nazarene” (Matthew 2). Again, Samson surpassed other people in marvelous bodily strength. But Isaiah says of Christ: “His name shall be called Mighty God” (Isaiah 6 [OCR; likely 9]). And the prophet says of him in the Psalm: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm 23). Finally, Samson delivered the Hebrew people for a time from the hands of the Philistines, but Christ permanently rescued humankind from the hands of spiritual wickedness and roaring lions.]

Samson, called their sun—  
Christ is the light of the elect,

[Col. 1445A] Whom grace illumines.

[30] [Note: [Col. 1445B] *Now from the sacred beam of the cross.* In one sense, *vectis* means a pole or staff by which something is carried and borne, as we read in Exodus (chapter 25) that the Lord commanded Moses to make poles for carrying the ark. The holy cross bore the King and Lord of heaven; therefore here it is rightly designated by the name *vectis*, “carrying-beam.” *Penetrale*, -alis, as a substantive noun, means the more inward or inner part of a house or temple; indeed, whatever is most inward to a thing is expressed by the term *penetrale*, as when we speak of the inmost recesses of our breast. When the final letter is removed by apocope, *penetral*, -alis, is used with the same meaning. Finally, *botrus* means a whole cluster of grapes. The sense of this verse, therefore, is that just as a grape pressed in the winepress sends down its wine into the vessels placed below, so Christ’s precious blood, pressed out upon the instrument of the cross, flows into the heart and inmost being of the beloved Church, Christ’s bride. For with that blood the holy Church was watered and sprinkled; from it she also received sanctification [Col. 1445C] and the chief efficacy of all her saving sacraments.]

Now from the sacred carrying-beam of the cross  
The cluster flows into the inner sanctuary  
Of the beloved Church.

[Note: [Col. 1445C] *Now that the winepress has been trodden.* After grapes have been pressed in a winepress, anyone who drinks too freely of the must flowing from it readily falls into drunkenness. But Christ, as the prophet says, trod the winepress alone, and there was no man of the nations with him (Isaiah 63), when he endured the punishment of the cross. From that winepress flowed the grace of Christ’s passion to the multitude of nations converted to the faith by apostolic preaching. Those first among the nations to receive Christ were intoxicated, as it were, by this spiritual must; for they were filled with a lavish outpouring of the charisms of the Holy Spirit, and more abundantly than others.]

Now that the winepress has been trodden,  
The firstfruits of the nations rejoice  
To be made drunk with must.

[35] [Note: [Col. 1445C] *The torn and pierced sack.* By metaphorical expression, Christ’s sacred body is here called a torn and pierced sack, on account of its condition of mortality and passibility, [Col. 1445D] since in his bitter passion it was wounded by thorns, scourged by whips, and pierced by nails and spear. But it passed into royal use when, through the resurrection, it was clothed in the garment of immortality and girded with the power of incorruptibility, as Christ says to the Father in the Psalm: “You have torn my sackcloth and surrounded me with gladness” (Psalm 29). That is: now that the mortality of the flesh has been laid aside, you have crowned me with the glory of immortality. In the same sense the *saccus* (“sack”) becomes the *soccus* (“slipper”) of grace, because Christ’s formerly mortal flesh becomes the distinguished receptacle of immortality and is endowed with the grace of incorruptibility. Finally, through the resurrection Christ’s flesh became the conqueror of passibility and corruption, which belong to the misery of the human condition.]

The torn and pierced sack  
Passes into royal use.  
The sack becomes grace’s slipper;  
The flesh conquers misery.

[40] Because they killed the King,  
The guilty lost their kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1446B] *But Cain, set as a sign, is not utterly destroyed.* Cain, inflamed by the torches of envy because he saw that his brother was preferred before him by merit in God’s sight, killed him (Genesis 4). But, so that the punishment for this murder might be longer lasting, the Lord did not will that Cain should be killed by anyone through a swift and sudden death. Rather, he placed a mark upon him as he wandered and fled over the earth, so that whoever found him should not kill him. Thus the Jews, out of envy, delivered to death Christ, their brother by kinship of flesh and the shepherd of our souls. In punishment for this dreadful crime, their kingdom having been lost, they were scattered across the whole earth and taken into captivity. Nor did God will their descendants to be utterly destroyed, so that some might always survive as a sign and memorial of so great a crime: persons in whom might be read the gravity of the vengeance inflicted by God, who might be a testimony of Christ’s death brought about by the Jews and of the severe affliction imposed upon them by God on that account, [Col. 1446C] as the Psalm says of the Jews: “Do not kill them, lest my people forget; scatter them in your power, and cast them down, O Lord, my protector” (Psalm 58). Thus Abel was a type and figure of Christ, Cain of the Jews.]

But Cain, set as a sign,  
Is not utterly destroyed.

[Col. 1446A] [Note: [Col. 1446C] *Rejected and cast aside.* This passage is taken from Psalm 117, where the prophet says concerning Christ: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.” Christ himself, in the Gospel, showed that this verse was fulfilled in himself, when in disputing with the scribes and Pharisees he intimated that he was that stone rejected by them, yet raised by God as head of the whole Church and placed as the cornerstone in the foundation of the entire ecclesiastical building (Matthew 22 [OCR; likely 21]).]

Rejected and cast aside,  
[45] This stone is now chosen;  
It stands raised as a trophy  
And as the head of the corner.

Destroying guilt, not nature,  
He creates a new creature.

[Note: [Col. 1446C] *He creates a new creature.* Christ is said here to create a new creature, not through a newness [Col. 1446D] of nature and substance, but of profession and innocence. For, casting off the oldness of sin through baptismal regeneration, he bestowed on all who receive him a newness of spiritual life and renewal of mind. Thus blessed Paul says that we are made a new creature in Christ (2 Corinthians 5). In the same verse Christ is said to hold in himself the binding, joining, and union of the two peoples—namely Jewish and Gentile. For he joined both in the confession of the true faith and the reception of the Gospel law. As blessed Paul says of Christ: “He is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2). For he joined Jews and Gentiles into the one Catholic Church, and from them there came to be one flock, over which Christ the one shepherd presides (John 10).]

[50] Holding in himself the union  
Of the two peoples.

Glory be to the head,  
And harmony to the members.  
Amen.

## VIII. ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

This prose exactly observes the rule of rhythmic consonance, [Col. 1447A] being very similar in its compositional form to the prose explained earlier, *Let the old leaven be purged out*. Its author is Adam of Saint Victor. It variously commends the mystery of the sending of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, and shows that it was foreshadowed by various figures and events of the old law. Then the prayer of the whole Church is directed to the Holy Spirit, asking that he lead us, purified from sins, into the eternal tabernacles of heaven.

Pleasant light, distinguished light,  
By which fire sent from the throne  
Fills the hearts of Christ’s disciples  
And enriches their tongues;

[5] It invites us to the harmonious  
Measures of tongue and heart.

[Note: [Col. 1447B] *The tongue [to] the heart’s melodies.* Then the heart’s melodies accord with the tongue itself when the heart devoutly meditates upon that proclamation of God which the tongue utters, so that not only the tongue may produce the melody of divine praises, but the heart also may attend to their meaning and sense; that, with the Apostle (1 Corinthians 14), we may sing psalms with the spirit and sing psalms also with the mind. Therefore it is clear that here the noun *linguae* (“to the tongue”) is in the dative case and is construed with the adjective *concordes* (“harmonious”).]
