[Note: [Col. 1447B] *Christ sent what he promised.* Our Lord had indeed promised his disciples: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” [Col. 1447C] (John 14); and again: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16), and in many other places. Thus, faithful and true, he sent this pledge of his love to the Church, his bride, on the day of Pentecost. The Holy Spirit is rightly called a pledge here. For he is designated by that name also in blessed Paul, when he writes to the Corinthians: “He who establishes us with you in Christ, and who anointed us, is God; he also sealed us and gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts” (2 Corinthians 1). Again, elsewhere to the same people: “He who brings us to this very thing is God, who gave us the pledge of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 5). Further, writing to the Ephesians, he says: “In whom, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance unto the redemption of the possession” (Ephesians 1). Finally, on the fiftieth day after his resurrection Christ revisited his bride, the Church, not indeed in his own person but [Col. 1447D] in the sending of the Holy Spirit, who is of the same substance and nature as he.]

Christ sent what he promised,  
The pledge to the bride whom he revisits

[Col. 1447B] On the fiftieth day.

[10] [Note: [Col. 1447D] *After honeyed sweetness.* By the sweetness of honey flowing from the rock is rightly understood here the Gospel teaching that flowed from Christ’s sacred mouth as he preached to the people before his passion (Matthew 16). For according to the Apostle Christ is the rock, indeed the firm rock upon which the Church is founded (1 Corinthians 10). The prophet, however, in the Psalm compares the words of the Lord with honey when he says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Psalm 118). And again: “The judgments of the Lord are right, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 18). What words of the Lord could you give that are holier and more august than those contained in the Gospel, uttered by Christ’s divine mouth? By oil, however, the Holy Spirit and the outpouring of his grace upon people are aptly understood, according to the manner of Scripture. For God the Father, speaking of the Holy Spirit to the Son, says in the Psalm: “Therefore God, your God, has blessed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44). And blessed Peter, speaking of [Col. 1448B] Christ in the Acts of the Apostles, says: “God anointed him with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 10). Anointing is done with oil. Likewise, in Scripture the Holy Spirit is often understood by the name of anointing. The sense of this verse, therefore, is that after the Gospel teaching Christ poured out upon the disciples the charisms of the Holy Spirit.]

After honeyed sweetness,  
The rock poured forth oil—  
The now most steadfast rock.

[Note: [Col. 1448B] *On tablets of stone.* The giving of the Mosaic law on Mount Sinai to the people, on the fiftieth day after the children of Israel departed from Egypt (Exodus 20), was a figure of the sending of the Holy Spirit to the disciples on the day of Pentecost. Yet there was a great difference between that event and this. Moses’ law was written on [Col. 1448C] tablets of stone, as Exodus relates (chapter 31). But the new law, promulgated through the sending of the Holy Spirit, is written upon human hearts as living tablets, as the Lord had promised through Jeremiah in these words: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I shall make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah; not according to the covenant which I made with your fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. But this shall be the covenant which I shall make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I shall put my law in their inward parts, and I shall write it in their heart; and I shall be their God, and they shall be my people.”

Again, Moses’ law was not given in fiery tongues, but with lightning, thunder, and burning lamps that inspire terror (Exodus 19). But the Holy Spirit was sent in the form of fiery tongues to signify the effect of his power: that he united in the disciples speech in different languages and joined together all languages in them. Further, Moses’ law was proclaimed to the entire Israelite people, the Lord speaking (Exodus 20). But the Holy Spirit, and through him the new law, was first bestowed upon a few—namely, the one hundred and twenty faithful assembled together (Acts 2)—but through them that newness of law was to be spread through the whole world. Finally, Moses’ law was given from the mountain and on the summit of Mount Sinai; the new law in the holy upper room, where the disciples were assembled and persevering in prayer.]

On tablets of stone,  
Not in fiery tongues,  
The law came from the mountain to the people.

[15] To a few, the heart’s newness  
And the unity of tongues  
Are given in the upper room.

O how happy, how festive  
[20] The day on which the primitive  
Church is founded!

[Note: [Col. 1448D] *The firstfruits are living.* Under the Mosaic law, on the day of Pentecost itself a sacrifice from the firstfruits of the crops was offered to the Lord, and firstfruits were commanded to be offered to the Lord on that day, as Leviticus states (chapter 23). Thus mystically, on the day of Pentecost itself, the firstfruits of believers were offered to the Lord by the apostles. Therefore the living firstfruits of the Church at its birth are those who first believed after the outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples. In the Acts of the Apostles these are said to have numbered three thousand. For after blessed Peter’s address to the people that day, blessed Luke adds: “Those therefore who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls” (Acts 2).]

The living firstfruits  
Of the Church at its birth,

[Col. 1448B] Were three thousand at first.

[25] [Note: [Col. 1449B] *The first loaves of the law.* On Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day after Passover, the children of Israel, according to the ordinances of the old law set out in Leviticus (chapter 23), were required to offer the Lord two loaves of firstfruits, made of two tenths of leavened fine flour, to be baked as firstfruits for the Lord. Thus, at the beginning of the Church at its birth, when reality succeeded the figures, on the Pentecost when the Holy Spirit was sent upon the apostles, two mystical loaves of firstfruits were offered to the Lord: the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile, called into the adoption of grace under the one faith of Christ. For then both the Jewish people and the Gentiles began, through the apostles’ preaching, to be offered to the Lord in the obedience of faith.]

The first loaves of the law,  
Under one faith, are the adopted  
Two peoples.

[Note: [Col. 1449B] *He set himself between the two.* According to the statement of the Psalm cited often above, Christ is the stone rejected by the builders, yet made by God the head of the corner (Psalm 117). In this spiritual structure [Col. 1449C] Christ set himself between those two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, because he placed himself as their mediator in order to join both in himself; and in this way he made those two peoples one people, namely the Christian people. For in the primitive Church those taken both from the Jews and from the Gentiles formed the Church and assembly of believers.]

He set himself between the two,  
And thus the stone, head of the corner,  
Made the two one.

[30] [Note: [Col. 1449C] *New wineskins, not old.* This passage is taken from the Gospel, where the Lord says to the Jewish crowds: “Neither do they put new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins burst, the wine is poured out, and the wineskins perish. But they put new wine into new wineskins, and both are preserved” (Matthew 9). Explaining this passage, Remigius says: “Christ calls his disciples old wineskins, because before his passion they had not yet been perfectly renewed. He calls the fullness of the Holy Spirit and the deep things of heavenly mysteries new wine, which the disciples then [Col. 1449D] were unable to bear. But after the resurrection they became new wineskins and received new wine, when the Holy Spirit filled their hearts (Acts 2). Hence some said: ‘All these men are full of must.’” Thus Remigius. From his words the meaning of this verse, as regards its first two clauses, is sufficiently clear. Its third clause belongs to the meaning of the following verse and should be referred to it, as will immediately appear.]

New wineskins, not old,  
Are able to hold the new must.  
The widow prepares vessels;

[Note: [Col. 1449D] *Elisha gives the liquid.* When a certain woman among the wives of the prophets complained to Elisha that, after her husband’s death, a creditor wished to take her two sons and reduce them to slavery until the debt was paid, Elisha commanded her to borrow many empty vessels and to pour into each some of the oil which she said she possessed. When she had done this, the oil poured into the vessels was so multiplied that they were all filled to the brim with oil. When she reported this to Elisha, he ordered her to sell the oil and satisfy the creditor. She and her sons were to live from what remained (2 Kings 4). Mystically, that oil signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is abundantly bestowed upon us by God, signified by Elisha, through the widow signified, provided that we have empty vessels—that is, hearts not filled with wickedness but suitably disposed for receiving this sacred liquid.]

Elisha gives the liquid.

[35] God gives us sacred dew,  
If our hearts are fit.

We are not worthy of this must,  
This liquid, this dew,  
If our conduct is discordant.

[40] In darkened or divided hearts,

[Col. 1450A] [Note: [Col. 1450B] *This paraclisis cannot dwell.* Just as *Paracletus* or *Paraclitus* in Greek means “comforter,” and is used especially for the Holy Spirit in sacred Scripture, so *paraclisis* means consolation and the grace of the Holy Spirit that comforts sorrowful hearts. Since it was said shortly before that God grants us the sacred dew of the Holy Spirit, provided that the vessels of our hearts are fit to receive it, this verse aptly shows what makes our hearts unfit for receiving the sacred charisms. It chiefly identifies two obstacles to such great goods: the darkness and obscuring of the heart through sins, and the discord of minds through disputes and hatreds. Since the Holy Spirit is spiritual light and “the God of peace and love” (2 Corinthians 13), he never chooses as the dwelling-place or seat of his majesty either hearts darkened or hearts divided from one another through dissensions and quarrels.]

This consolation cannot  
Dwell in hearts.

Kind Comforter, come;  
Rule our tongues, soothe our hearts.

[45] Let there be no gall or poison  
Under your presence.

Nothing pleasant, nothing delightful,  
Nothing healthful, nothing serene,  
Nothing sweet, nothing full,

[50] Except through your grace.

You are light and ointment;  
You are heaven’s seasoning.

[Note: [Col. 1450C] Enriching the element of water. This may be said both because at the beginning of the world's creation the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters, as was stated above (Gen. I), and also because by his power the Holy Spirit sanctifies waters, so that they produce the saving washing of baptism [Col. 1450D], by which, when sprinkled, people are washed from their sins and become new creatures in Christ, reborn of water and the Holy Spirit. Hence too the Holy Spirit appeared over Christ when he was baptized in the Jordan (John I), to signify that in baptism rightly received the Holy Spirit is given.]

Enriching the element of water  
By the power of mystery.

[55] Made a new creature,  
[Col. 1450B] We praise you with a pure mind.

[Note: [Col. 1450D] Now children of grace, but by nature. When we are born, still defiled by the stain of original sin, we are children of wrath, of curse, and of perdition, as blessed Paul says to the Ephesians: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II). But after receiving the sacrament of baptism and receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, we become children of grace and adoption, and children of the kingdom, through such spiritual regeneration in Christ. For then we are born of God and made children of God. But we must strive with all earnestness [Col. 1451C] to preserve whole and inviolate in ourselves, through sincere faith and the fruit of good works, this divine sonship received in baptism. We must not, through our own sloth, fall from the number of God’s children and become children of Satan, by imitating him and fulfilling his desires, after losing so great a dignity, by which we are called and are children of God. For our guilt will be so much the graver if, through the irrational impulses of our desires, we fall away from the lot of God’s children, as God’s condescension toward us was greater when he admitted us into the company and number of his children and poured out his Holy Spirit into our hearts as the guest and indweller of our souls. If we offer him outrage by driving him from us through sins and willingly admitting Satan’s spirit into the inner chambers of our heart, we shall not escape God’s avenging wrath. May the Spirit of all goodness preserve us from it in his kindness. Amen.]

Now children of grace, but by nature  
[Col. 1451A] Formerly children of wrath.

[Note: [Col. 1451D] You who are both giver and gift. The Holy Spirit is a giver because he bestows his gifts upon human beings. As sacred Paul shows in writing to the Corinthians: “To one through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another faith in the same Spirit” (I Cor. XII). And at last he concludes: “One and the same Spirit works all these things, apportioning to each as he wills” (ibid.). He is himself also a gift, because he is given by God to those who ask that he be given to them, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel: “If you,” he says, “though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke II). The Holy Spirit himself is also said to produce—that is, create, bring forth, and form—every good thing, because he is the Spirit present in all, through whom every good flows forth into creatures, and to whom goodness is especially attributed.]

You who are both giver and gift,

[60] You who create every good thing,  
Make the heart ready for praise,  
Fashioning the sound of our tongue  
For your proclamations.

Cleanse us from sins,

[65] You yourself, author of purity;  
And, renewed in Christ,  
Grant us the full joys  
Of perfect newness. Amen.

## IX. ANOTHER PROSE HYMN ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

This prose hymn observes the law of rhythmic composition, just as does that explained above, [Col. 1451B] *On the first morning of the Sabbath*. Yet it has this peculiarity beyond the former: in the ninth and tenth verses it has only two rhythmic clauses. The first preserves a syllabic consonance in its own middle and end; the latter clause of one of the given verses answers in a similar ending to the latter clause of the other verse. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It celebrates in splendid praises the sending of the Holy Spirit upon the disciples, through which the New Law was promulgated; and it sets forth the manifold excellence and dignity of this New Law over the Old. It also describes the great power and effectiveness in action of the apostles, who are the Fathers of the New Testament. Finally, it compares the day of Pentecost itself with the Jewish year of jubilee, through a certain correspondence in condition and properties.

[Note: [Col. 1451D] Simple in essence. Solomon says in the Book of Wisdom concerning the supremely divine wisdom itself that [Col. 1452C] “in her is a holy spirit of understanding, unique, manifold, subtle, eloquent, mobile, undefiled” (Wis. VII), and so on concerning its other properties, which he subsequently adds. But who is the Spirit of eternal Wisdom except the Holy Spirit, whom the Apostle calls the Spirit of the Son and the Spirit of Christ (Gal. IV; Rom. VIII)? Christ, moreover, is God’s power and God’s wisdom (I Cor. I). Therefore the Holy Spirit is both one and manifold: one in substance, manifold in gifts. This too is indicated here when the Spirit is called simple and indivisible in essence, yet sevenfold in grace and gift. Just as the sun is one in nature yet produces manifold operations in these lower things, which it nourishes, cherishes, illumines, warms, and gives life; and just as the soul in our body is one, yet produces many works according to its various powers.]

Simple in essence,  
Sevenfold in grace,  
[Col. 1452A] May the Spirit remake us.

May light sent from heaven  
Cleanse the darknesses of the heart  
[5] And the enticements of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 1452C] The Law went before in figure. From the third verse through the tenth, the Old Law is compared with the New [Col. 1452D] in respect of their relative excellence and manner of giving: the former is figure, the latter truth; the former harsh and burdensome, the latter sweet and light. The former is shadow, the latter light; the former contains the killing letter, the latter the life-giving Spirit; the former conceals spiritual meaning beneath the veil and bark of the letter, the latter uncovers and reveals what was hidden. The former was given on the mountain, the latter in the upper room; the former to the whole people, the latter to a few disciples. The former amid trumpet-blast, lightning, thunder, fire, and smoke; the latter amid a mighty sound, announcing the coming Holy Spirit, and fiery tongues. The former was given in terror to instil fear; the latter in the gentle descent of harmless fire, to foster love. Finally, the former was imposed in servitude upon a stiff-necked people; the latter was given in freedom to the children of the heavenly Father. In sum, the former is a law of fear and severity, but the latter of love and gentleness.]

The Law went before in figure,  
A penal law, a dark law;  
The light of the Gospel,

[10] Spiritual understanding,  
Hidden beneath the leafy covering of the letter,  
Comes forth into public view.

The Law from the mountain, to the people;  
To a few in the upper room,

[15] New grace is given.  
The locations teach us  
The pre-eminence  
Of the commandments and the gifts.

Fire, trumpet-blast, bugles,

[20] Crash with darkness,  
The darting of flames,  
Instil terror  
And do not nourish love,  
Which anointing has poured out.

[25] Thus on Sinai the divine Law  
Was imposed upon the guilty:  
A law of fear, not of love,  
Punishing unlawful deeds.

[Note: [Col. 1452D] Behold the fathers chosen beforehand. From the eleventh verse through the fourteenth is offered a manifold commendation of the holy apostles [Col. 1453C] who received the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit. First, they are called fathers chosen beforehand because they were selected above others to be not merely fathers but also patriarchs of the New Testament, prefigured by the twelve patriarchs of the Old Testament. They are also called gods by participation, because the Holy Spirit coming upon them rendered them godlike, almost divine. Of them is understood that saying of the Psalm: “The princes of the peoples are gathered with the God of Abraham, because the mighty gods of the earth have been greatly exalted” (Ps. XLVI). The apostles also rain by their word, because they instilled the saving rain of their teaching orally into the dry minds of human beings, so that they might produce the fruit of salvation. For this reason they are designated by the name of clouds in Isaiah, when he says (ch. LX): “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” They likewise thunder with threats. For their powerful voice, threatening and denouncing eternal punishments for the wicked, stirred their hearers’ minds like thunder. Hence the Psalm says of their preaching: “The voice of your thunder was in the wheel; your lightnings illumined the world; the earth was shaken and trembled” (Ps. LXXVI). Moreover, miracles harmonize with their teaching, since they confirmed their teaching by the newness and power of signs, as Mark says: “And they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed” (Mark XVI). Finally, that they have the power of binding and loosing is clear from the Lord’s words in Matthew (ch. XVIII) and John (ch. XX).]

Behold, the fathers chosen beforehand,

[30] Have newly been made gods;  
[Col. 1453A] They loose the bonds of guilt.

They rain by their word, thunder with threats;  
With new tongues and teachings  
Miracles sound in harmony.

[35] Giving care to the sick,  
They condemn the disease, not nature;  
Pursuing crimes,  
They press and chastise the guilty;  
Now they loose, now they bind,

[40] With free authority.

[Note: [Col. 1453D] It bears the type of the jubilee. From this verse to the end, this day of the Holy Spirit’s coming upon the disciples is compared with the Jewish jubilee year—which was also called the fiftieth because it came every fiftieth year—in a correspondence of properties that applied carnally to the Jews but spiritually to us. For jubilee means, [Col. 1454C] as is said here, “releasing” or “changed,” because in that year debts were remitted; those who had previously been slaves were manumitted; exiles returned to their homeland; and each person returned to the house and possession he had previously sold, as is clear from Leviticus chapter twenty-five. Thus the former state and condition of things was changed for the better. Those who were previously slaves then became free; those formerly banished from their native soil became its inhabitants; and those previously deprived of their lands or houses became their possessors, while former debtors were released from their debts. All these things, however, were fulfilled spiritually in humankind through the coming of the Holy Spirit. The debts of sins were remitted, slavery to sin was removed, possession of the virtues was restored after we had been sold under sin, and return to the homeland of heaven—whence we had been excluded—was granted. According to others, moreover, *jubilee* means “initiated” or “remissive,” because that fiftieth year, by divine ordinance, was believed to be consecrated and dedicated to God, granting remission of debt and release from bondage. This interpretation too aptly suits the time of the Holy Spirit’s sending, through whom people once devoted to the worship of idols were initiated into God’s sacred rites, bound to his service, and obtained remission of their sins.]

This day bears the type of jubilee,  
If you seek the mysteries  
Of the day.

When three thousand  
[45] Ran to the faith,  
[Col. 1453B] The Church sprang up.

It was called jubilee:  
Either “releasing” or “changed,”  
Calling back to former conditions

[50] Things freely alienated.  
May the law of charity free us,  
Alienated under sins,  
And make us worthy of the gift  
Of perfect freedom. Amen.

## X. ANOTHER PROSE HYMN ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

[Col. 1454A]

In this prose hymn a similar principle of rhythmic composition is observable, as in the penultimate hymn, *Pleasant Light, Noble Light*, except that in the thirteenth and fourteenth verses the first clause has no matching syllabic ending with the second clause of the same verse. Instead, each has an ending consonant with its own middle, so that the middle of one and the same clause answers in a similar ending to its own end. It commends the Holy Spirit in many ways: first, from his divine properties and his relation to the Father and Son, near the beginning and end of the present prose hymn; then from the various works of his goodness in creatures, especially human beings, whose souls he visits and illumines by his condescension. Finally, from the seventeenth verse to the twenty-first, it offers a humble supplication to him on behalf of the faithful people. And because [Col. 1454B] the entire texture of the prose hymn is very easy and accessible to readers, it will be treated with few annotations. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor.

You proceed in power from both,  
From begetter and begotten alike,  
O Paraclete.

Make tongues eloquent;

[5] Make hearts fervent in you

[Note: [Col. 1454D] By your rich flame. The flame of the Holy Spirit is that spiritual and heavenly fire which he sends into human hearts. It is rich because of the manifold gifts following that sacred kindling. For he bestows an abundance of graces and the riches of his gifts upon those who prepare the storehouse of their heart to receive and store those heavenly treasures. For the Holy Spirit is, to use Paul’s words (Rom. X), rich toward all who call upon him; and he is the maker of all things, knowing all things [lacuna].]

By your rich flame.

Love of Father and Son,  
Equal to both, and to each  
Comparable and like,

[10] You fill all things, cherish all things;  
[Col. 1455A] You rule the stars, move heaven,

[Note: [Col. 1455D] Remaining unmoved. What is said in the seventh chapter of the Book of Wisdom concerning eternal Wisdom is fittingly applied also to the Holy Spirit, since he is of the same nature as the Son of God and has all properties consequent upon the divine substance in common with him—such as those now under discussion: though one, he can do all things; remaining in himself, he renews all things; and passing through nations into holy souls, he makes friends of God and prophets (Wis. VII). From this it follows at once that he rules the stars and moves heaven, while nevertheless remaining unmoved:

“Remaining stable, he gives all things to be moved,” as Boethius sings (*The Consolation of Philosophy*, bk. III, met. 9).]

Remaining unmoved.

Bright light, dear light,  
You drive away the gloom  
[15] Of inward darkness.

Through you, those who are clean are cleansed;  
You destroy sin  
And sin’s rust.

You make truth known

[20] And show the way of peace,  
And the path of righteousness.  
You avoid the hearts of the perverse  
And enrich good hearts  
With the gift of knowledge.

[25] With you teaching, nothing is obscure;  
[Col. 1455B] with you present, nothing impure.  
Under your presence  
The glad mind rejoices;  
Through you cheerful, through you clean,

[30] The conscience rejoices.

[Note: [Col. 1455D] You change the elements. This is not to be understood according to their substance, but according to their use and power. For the element of water, consecrated by the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, is fitted for the washing of baptism and takes on a new power, as it were [Col. 1456D]: what formerly washed bodies only is now also suited to cleanse the stains of the soul. Nor is only the sacrament of baptism performed by the power of the Holy Spirit; all the others also are performed by it and derive their efficacy from it. For no sacrament is completed unless it is brought to fulfillment by the invocation of the Holy Spirit.]

You change the elements;  
Through you the sacraments  
Have their efficacy.

You repel harmful force;

[35] You refute and repel  
The wickedness of enemies.

When you come, you soothe hearts;  
When you enter, the darkness  
Of the black cloud flees.

[40] [Col. 1455C] [Note: [Col. 1456D] Sacred fire, you inflame the breast. In the first occurrence, *fire* is in the vocative case. For throughout the prose hymn the address is directed to the Holy Spirit. In the second occurrence, it is the second person of the present indicative of the verb *ignio, -is, -ire*, meaning “to set aflame,” and is joined with an accusative. That sacred fire, moreover, is the one of which the Church sings: “The divine fire came, not burning but illumining; not consuming but shining; and it found the hearts of the disciples clean receptacles and bestowed upon them the gifts of charisms.”]

Sacred fire, you inflame the breast;  
You do not burn, but cleanse from cares  
When you visit.

Minds previously unlearned,  
Asleep and forgetful,

[45] You teach and awaken.  
You warm tongues, shape their sound;  
Charity given by you  
Makes the heart inclined to good.

O help of the oppressed!  
O consolation of the wretched!

[50] Refuge of the poor!  
Grant contempt for earthly things;  
Draw desire  
To the love of things above.

[55] [Col. 1456A] Drive away evils, wipe off stains;  
Make those at discord concordant;  
And bring aid.

You who once visited,  
Taught, and strengthened

[60] The fearful disciples:  
Deign to visit us.  
If it please you, console us  
And the peoples who believe.

Equal is the majesty  
[65] Of the persons; equal  
Is their power and common deity.

You who proceed from two  
Are coequal with both:  
In nothing is there disparity.

[70] [Col. 1456B] For you are as great and such  
As the Father is great and such.  
May the humility of servants  
Render due praises  
To God the Father and the Son,

[75] To the Redeemer, and to you also.  
Amen.

## XI. ON THE HOLY TRINITY

This prose hymn has a uniform form of rhythmic modulation in all its verses. For each contains three rhythmic clauses. The first two have a mutual consonance in their endings, and each comprises [Col. 1456C] eight syllables, its penultimate always long, or very similar in the flow of pronunciation to a long syllable. The third clause of each verse answers the third clause of the next verse in a similar ending; it has seven syllables and a short penultimate. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It expounds with elegance, aptness, and coherence the most exalted mystery of the Holy Trinity: how in it the unity of deity does not conflict with the Trinity of persons, nor their plurality with its simplicity; how the persons themselves, though of one essence, nevertheless have singular and personal properties through which their distinction is considered and understood. Other matters of this kind pertaining to this most sacred secret and hidden sacrament of faith are here fittingly and lucidly disclosed. They may be made sufficiently plain and clear from the Athanasian Creed and its explanation set forth in the second book; therefore there is no need to linger longer upon their exposition [Col. 1457A] here.

Professing unity,  
Let us venerate the Trinity  
With reverence for the Father.

Affirming three persons,

[5] Differing from one another  
By personal distinction.

[Note: [Col. 1457B] These are said relatively. The divine persons are called relative to one another, according to the relation which explains their inward processes and emanations: thus the Father is related to the Son, and the Son to the Father, from whom he proceeds by eternal and ineffable generation. So the Holy Spirit has relation to the Father and Son, from both of whom he emanates by an inward procession. Yet this relation to one another does not prevent them from being one principle of all things substantively, or according to substance, rather than three principles; for they are one God, not three gods.]

These are said relatively,  
Though they are one substantively,  
Not three principles.

[10] [Note: [Col. 1457B] Whether you say “three” in the masculine or neuter. Personal distinction in the divine persons makes it possible for us, in Catholic usage, to state in the plural number that there are three persons, three hypostases, or three subsistences in the most holy Trinity. Approved authors use these three names—person, hypostasis, and subsistence—for the same thing. This distinction of persons likewise permits us rightly and truly to say that in the supreme Trinity there are three subjects, three singulars, three individuals, since these names are equivalent to one another and to the three preceding names in their mode of signification. Nevertheless, in the three divine persons the substance is simple, called *ousia* (οὐσία) in Greek. Hence according to the tradition of orthodox faith we must confess the Son of God to be *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιος), that is, consubstantial, with the Father. Therefore there is not in those three persons a triple essence or substance, since it is one and simple. For the simplicity of that same essence is incompatible, in the same respect, with multiplicity, and unity with plurality.]

Whether you say “three” in the masculine or neuter,  
Yet the *ousia* (οὐσία) is simple,  
Not a triple essence.

Simple being, simple power,  
[Col. 1457B] Simple willing, simple knowing:

[15] Let all things be simple.

[Note: [Col. 1457D] Not less in one than in two. Since God the Father is omnipotent, and likewise the Son and Holy Spirit, power and potency in the Father alone are no less than in the Father and Son or in all three persons together. For if you grant that the Father alone has less efficacy or power in acting than two or three persons, then the Father will not be supremely powerful or omnipotent—which is contrary to the hypothesis and proposition. For he cannot do that in which his power is less and weaker than that of two or three persons. The same argument applies to wisdom, goodness, perfection, and the other divine properties. The judgment is the same in all cases, and not without reason. For the power, wisdom, goodness, and perfection of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are altogether one and the same, as their substance and essence are one. How then can it be less in one person than in several, or greater in several than in one? It would then be [Col. 1458B] truly less than itself, whether power or wisdom, though it is the same in all.]

Not less in one than in two  
[Col. 1458A] Or three persons  
Is the efficacy.

Father, offspring, sacred breath,

[20] [Note: [Col. 1458B] Yet these have certain properties of their own. For the Father has a singular property distinguishing him from the Son and Holy Spirit: unbegottenness, or ingenerateness, because he proceeds from no one but subsists by himself alone. The Son has begottenness or birth, because he is begotten from the Father alone. The Holy Spirit has the personal property customarily called processibility or procession, because he proceeds from the Father and Son by an inward process inscrutable to us. Yet, as the verse immediately following says, one person is the same *what* as another. For this personal distinction and difference of properties produces no diversity of substance or nature. The pronoun “this” and “what,” and similar nouns or pronouns in the neuter gender, indicate substance, as is shown by the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John X).]

God is one, yet these  
[Note: [Col. 1458B] Yet these have certain properties of their own. For the Father has a singular property distinguishing him from the Son and Holy Spirit: unbegottenness, or ingenerateness, because he proceeds from no one but subsists by himself alone. The Son has begottenness or birth, because he is begotten from the Father alone. The Holy Spirit has the personal property customarily called processibility or procession, because he proceeds from the Father and Son by an inward process inscrutable to us. Yet, as the verse immediately following says, one person is the same *what* as another. For this personal distinction and difference of properties produces no diversity of substance or nature. The pronoun “this” and “what,” and similar nouns or pronouns in the neuter gender, indicate substance, as is shown by the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John X).]

Have certain properties of their own.  
One power, one divinity,  
One splendor, one light:  
One person is the same *what* as another.

[25] The offspring is equal to the Father,  
Nor does the personal distinction  
Of the two remove this.  
A spiritual union, equal to Father and Son,

[Note: [Col. 1458C] A spiritual union proceeds from both. The “spiritual union” here means the Holy Spirit, who is called the bond and love of Father and Son, by which the Father loves the Son, as the Gospel says: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John III). And the Son says of himself: “But that the world may know that I love the Father, I do as the Father commanded me” (John XIV). Indeed, it is the property of love to bind and unite several things to one another by the gentle bond of affection and to fasten them together in mutual union, just as discord scatters and separates. The Holy Spirit, moreover, is love; rightly, therefore, he is here called union [Col. 1458D].]

From both

[30] Proceeds.

These persons  
[Col. 1458B] And their distinction  
Cannot be comprehended by human reason.

[Note: [Col. 1458D] This is not an order of time. The three persons are coeternal with one another: as the Father is eternal, so the Son and Holy Spirit are coeternal with the Father. There is therefore no order of duration among them, nor can one person be called earlier or later than another in temporal order. Again, since place and position in a place, and likewise local circumscription and containment, belong only to bodies and things extended in mass and endowed with magnitude—whereas “God is spirit” (John IV), and every divine person is superspiritual, without shape or quantity—it is plain that neither local position nor circumscription is found in the divine persons. For how can God be circumscribed, who is immeasurable, who fills heaven and earth (Jer. XXIII), who is above in heaven and below in the depths?]

This is not an order of time,

[35] [Col. 1459A] Nor such position or local  
Circumscription of things.

Nothing in God is other than God,

[Note: [Col. 1459C] No cause exists besides him who causes caused things. Heaven, the sun, and the elements are causes of things, but not first causes; for they have a prior cause, God, who is the first cause of all and cause without qualification. Moreover, the causes of things that exist under God do not possess from themselves the principle and power of causality, but from God, who communicates causality to other things and grants them to be causes after himself. But God neither borrows from another nor receives by sufferance the character of cause; he has from himself, and first, that he is cause. Therefore it is rightly said here that there is no first, absolute, and perfect cause besides him who produces all caused things and all effects. The term “caused things” means the effects themselves that are produced and proceed from causes.]

No cause besides him

[Note: [Col. 1459C] No cause exists besides him who causes caused things. Heaven, the sun, and the elements are causes of things, but not first causes; for they have a prior cause, God, who is the first cause of all and cause without qualification. Moreover, the causes of things that exist under God do not possess from themselves the principle and power of causality, but from God, who communicates causality to other things and grants them to be causes after himself. But God neither borrows from another nor receives by sufferance the character of cause; he has from himself, and first, that he is cause. Therefore it is rightly said here that there is no first, absolute, and perfect cause besides him who produces all caused things and all effects. The term “caused things” means the effects themselves that are produced and proceed from causes.]

Who causes caused things.

[40] [Note: [Col. 1459C] Efficient, formal, and final. Unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity in God are disclosed by many indications in things, especially by the threefold account of cause: God is one cause, indeed supremely one, yet threefold in conception—efficient, formal, and final [Col. 1459D]. Efficient, because all things are from him as their first author; formal, because all things subsist through him, for he gives things being and preserves them in being; and final, because all things are referred to him as their highest end, and all things are done for his sake. For what is better ought always to be established as the end of other things. If someone assigns efficient causality to the Father, because all things are from him; form to the Son, because all things are through him; and finality to the Holy Spirit, because all things are brought back to him, this is not an unsuitable accommodation. Nevertheless, the three persons themselves are one cause of all things—efficient, formal, and final—and each is an efficient cause, form, and end. But the character of material cause does not apply to God, since nothing is made from him as a substrate for another’s composition, nor is anything received in him as in a subject so as to inhere in him by way of accident.]

Efficient, formal,  
And final cause is God,  
But never matter.

To speak worthily of the persons  
Transcends the power of reason,

[43] Surpasses intellects.  
What it is to be begotten, what procession is,  
I profess that I do not know,  
Yet with an undoubting faith.

Who thus believes, let him not hasten,

[50] [Col. 1459B] Nor rashly turn aside  
From the royal way.  
Let him preserve faith, shape his conduct,  
And not turn aside into errors  
Which the Church condemns.

[55] Let us glory in the faith;  
Let us sing in one  
Steadfastness of faith.

To the threefold unity be praise,  
And to the simple Trinity

[60] Coeternal glory. Amen.

## XII. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 1460A]

This prose hymn preserves a uniform rule of rhythmic measure. In each verse it has four rhythmic clauses: the first three have similar syllabic endings to one another, and each has ten syllables with a short penultimate. The fourth clause, which always ends the verse, contains only four syllables and observes neither a fixed rule of quantity in its penultimate nor a corresponding syllabic ending with another clause. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. In it he sings a sweet epithalamium, a nuptial song of the betrothal of Christ the bridegroom and his bride the Church, whom he acquired by his own blood, that she might be holy and spotless before him, having neither stain nor wrinkle (Eph. V). The Church is likewise shown to have been prefigured by many figures of the Old Testament [Col. 1460B], which foreshadowed her wonderful dignity, fruitfulness, and adornment; but all these things are recognized as having been fulfilled in her more wonderfully still, according to their mystical meaning.

[Note: [Col. 1460C] Daughters of Jerusalem and Zion. The daughter of Jerusalem is called the Church triumphant in heaven, where there is the true vision of peace. The daughter of Zion is the Church militant on earth, which still beholds God through faith and now sees through a mirror and in an enigma (I Cor. XIII). For Zion is interpreted as “mirror” or “contemplation,” while Jerusalem means “vision of peace.” Hence the Psalm says of faithful souls, who are daughters of the Church militant: “Let the daughters of Zion rejoice in their king” (Ps. CXLIX). And in the Song of Songs the Bride says to the same: “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal” (Song III). Yet either name is used interchangeably for the other; thus faithful souls of the Church militant are very often called daughters of Jerusalem in the Song of Songs, as when it says in the passage mentioned above of King Solomon, truly peaceful: “He paved the ascent of purple with charity in its midst, for the daughters of Jerusalem.” And daughters of Zion are souls of the saints in heaven contemplating God [Col. 1460D]. Hence the Psalmist joins these two names, as customarily received for the same, in one verse: “A hymn befits you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall a vow be rendered in Jerusalem” (Ps. LXIV). The sense of this verse, therefore, is: May the entire company of faithful people sing to the Church, triumphant as well as militant, the sweet song of unceasing joy, namely, Alleluia.]

Daughters of Jerusalem and Zion,  
Assembly of the whole faithful court,  
Sing a melody of perpetual joy:  
Alleluia.

[5] For Christ today betroths  
Our mother, the pattern of righteousness,

[Note: [Col. 1460D] Whom he drew from the pit of misery. Christ drew our mother, the Church militant—which gave us birth to Christ through baptism—from the pit of misery, namely guilt itself, when he redeemed her by his blood and washed her from sins. But he drew our other mother, the Jerusalem above, which reigns in heaven, from the pit of the miseries, tribulations, and temptations of this world when he raised her to the heavens and freed her from this evil age.]

Whom he drew from the pit of misery:  
The Church.

In the mercy of the Holy Spirit,

[10] The bride rejoices in the favor of the bridegroom.

[Note: [Col. 1460D] With glory, called blessed by queens of praise. This passage [Col. 1461B] is taken from the Song of Songs, where Solomon says of the Bride of the eternal King, namely the holy Church: “The daughters of Zion saw her and proclaimed her most blessed; queens and concubines praised her” (Song VI). A nearly similar sense occurs in the final chapter of Proverbs concerning the Church itself, under the figure of the valiant woman: “Her children rose up and called her most blessed; her husband also praised her” (Prov. XXXI).]

With glory, called blessed  
By queens of praise.  
As the dowry is given, joy increases.

[Note: [Col. 1461B] What dowry, and how great? In a betrothal and earnest of marriage, people customarily assign a dowry. Thus, in those spiritual nuptials of Christ and the Church, there was no lack of a lavish and mystical dowry, bestowed by the Bridegroom upon the Bride herself. For this Bridegroom, Lord of all and author of good things, endowed his Bride; the bride did not endow the bridegroom, as among human beings. But if you ask of what kind and how great was the dowry given in this marriage, this verse answers that the dowry is so abundant that in its compass it embraces heaven, earth, and the realms below. For there are those who belong to the fellowship of the holy Church not only in heaven and on earth, but also among the dead: those, namely, who are purified by purgatorial fire and are at last to be transferred to the heavenly Jerusalem. That most generous dowry therefore embraces the threefold fabric of the world—heaven, earth, and the abyss. Behold how ample is the gift received from the Bridegroom, by which the Bride herself was joined to him in the covenant of marriage.] What dowry, and how great? A threefold power,

[15] Touching heaven, earth, and the Stygian

Judgments.

I speak wonders—and wholesome things to believe:

She, joined in covenant by so great a gift,

[Note: [Col. 1461C] He brought forth from his own side. When the side of Christ, sleeping in death upon the cross, was opened by a soldier’s lance, blood and water flowed from it (John XIX), from which the Church’s sacraments received their efficacy. Then indeed Christ formed the Church from that pierced side of his, since he cleansed her from her former stains and washed her in that blood and water. This mystery, moreover—as the following verse says—was prefigured in the creation of the first woman, who, in Genesis, is said to have been formed from the side of the sleeping man and from Adam’s rib (ch. II).] He brought her forth from his own side,

[20] God made man,

That thus the Church might be formed;

It is figured in an equal glory.

Woman, formed from Adam’s ribs:

Eve the enemy.

[25] [Note: [Col. 1461D] Eve was a stepmother to her descendants. Since Eve, formed from the rib of the man, bore the type of the Church, just as Adam bore the type of Christ himself, this verse now declares how great was the difference between figure and truth. Certainly Eve was both enemy and stepmother to her offspring, because through her transgression she subjected them to curse, death, and condemnation. The Church, however, is a most loving mother, who begets children of election, not perdition; children of grace, not wrath; children of life, not death.] Eve was a stepmother to her descendants;

[Col. 1462A] This is the mother of the chosen race,

A harbor of life, a refuge for the wretched,

And protection.

[Note: [Col. 1461D] Fair, mighty, wondrous in childbirth. In this place the eminent qualities of the Church, Christ’s Bride, are set forth. First, that she is fair; for the Bridegroom says of her in the Song of Songs: “You are altogether fair, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Cant. IV). And again: “Behold, you are fair, my beloved; behold, you are fair; your eyes are those of doves” (Cant. I). Second, that she is mighty. For the Bride is distinguished and honored by the titles of her Bridegroom. Her Bridegroom, moreover, is “the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII). Therefore she too is adorned with the same title of might. Third, that she is wondrous in childbirth: ever fruitful and never exhausted, blessed with a numerous offspring and happy in a manifold progeny, yet always remaining a virgin, because she is the Bride of him who was born of a virgin mother. Fourth, that she is bright as the moon and conspicuous as the sun, because of the splendor and radiance of her virtues. Fifth, that she is more terrible than an army arrayed in battle, against hostile bands and spiritual wickedness. These final two qualities are taken from that praise of the Church set in the Song of Songs: “Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed for battle?” (Cant. VI).] Fair, mighty, wondrous in childbirth:

[30] Like the moon, she shines; like the sun, she is splendid to behold.

Far more terrible than an army

Arrayed in order.

[Note: [Col. 1462B] She is manifold, singular, one. This verse explains other properties of the Church, diverse among themselves by a kind of opposition, yet in no way contradictory. The first is that the Church herself is manifold and at the same time singular. She is manifold indeed because she consists of every nation under heaven, and of every tribe, people, and tongue. Yet she is singular because she is united in one faith and confession of the divine name in the Spirit. Hence the Bridegroom says of her in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, my perfect one; she is one to her mother, chosen by her that bore her” (ibid.). Second, she is universal yet indivisible. Universal indeed with respect to her extension and compass, by which she embraces all peoples and regions of the earth. Yet indivisible, because she admits neither schisms, heresies, and gatherings of heretics, nor departures from the integrity of the faith. For there was one ark which saved Noah and his family from the flood (Gen. VII); likewise one house in which the Passover lamb was eaten among the Hebrews (Exod. XII); and again the one house of Rahab, in which all who were found within it were saved when the city of Jericho was overthrown (Josh. VI). These three examples already adduced are a kind of symbol and sign of the Church’s unity. Third, she bears children for Christ of every age and sex. For not infants alone are received for baptism, but also adults and persons burdened with old age; and not men alone, but women as well. It is marvelous that, although from the beginning of the Church’s birth she has never ceased to bear children, nor will cease until the end of the world, she has nevertheless neither been broken by such frequent childbirth nor made weaker, but remains ever vigorous and sound, robust in strength: she who endures neither time’s course nor the inconveniences of old age, but is established in perpetual strength above time and age.] She is manifold, singular, one,

Universal and indivisible.

[35] She alone bears companies of every age

And sex.

[Note: [Col. 1462D] She is marked by the waters of Jordan. The holy Church was marked by the streams of Jordan: first, because the Hebrews’ passage through the waters of Jordan (Josh. III), as they entered the promised land, prefigured baptism, through which one reaches the land of the living, flowing with milk and honey; and second, because the Lord, baptized in Jordan, consecrated baptism, through which the Church’s children are reborn. Moreover, the queen of Sheba, who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, as the Third Book of Kings relates (ch. X), [Col. 1463C] was a figure of the Church from the Gentiles, which came from earth’s furthest regions, stirred by the apostles’ preaching, to Christ, the wisdom of God, in order to embrace his law, hear his teaching, and undertake his commandments.] She is marked by the waters of Jordan.

She who comes from the ends of the earth

To hear at close hand the wisdom

[40] [Col. 1463A] Of Solomon.

[Note: [Col. 1463C] She is portrayed in typological senses. The Church is said to be portrayed in typological, or figurative, meanings because she is represented by the manifold portrayals of the Old Testament figures, as the following prose will explain more fully. She is likewise clad in wedding garments because Christ her Bridegroom has adorned her with the varied ornament of virtues and graces, in which she gleams brightly as in splendid garments. The Prophet too bears witness to this in the Psalm, saying: “The queen stood at your right hand in golden raiment, surrounded with variety” (Ps. XLIV). And again: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; in golden fringes she is clothed about with varieties” (ibid.).] She is portrayed in typological meanings,

Clad in wedding garments;

Today, joined to Christ, she presides over the citizens of heaven.

[45] O feast of solemn joy,

[Note: [Col. 1463C] In which Christ is united to the Church. Blessed John speaks of this spiritual union in the Apocalypse, saying: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven, prepared by God as a bride adorned for her husband. And I heard a great voice from the throne saying: Behold, the dwelling of God is with men, and he shall dwell with them” (Apoc. XXI). In that place he repeatedly speaks of the nuptials of the Bride and the Lamb.] In which Christ is united to the Church,

In which the nuptials of our salvation

Are celebrated.

A blessed assembly, a sweet banquet,

[50] Where consolation is given to the fallen,

And room for breathing

Is offered to the despairing.

From it the rewards of the righteous are bestowed.

[Note: [Col. 1463D] The joys of the angels are renewed. For if there is joy among the angels over one sinner doing penance, who still stands in danger of falling back into former evils, how much greater is their joy over the rewards of the righteous (Luke XV), who are brought into heaven and joined to the fellowship of the blessed, since the angels’ own loss is thereby repaired. Such joy is prompted by the sincere charity and love which the angels have for humankind.] The joys of the angels are renewed,

[55] [Col. 1463B] By the exceedingly broad grace

Of charity.

[Note: [Col. 1463D] From eternity, the fountain of wisdom. This is confirmed by the saying of blessed Paul, who writes to the Ephesians concerning God the Father: “He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blemish before him in charity” (Eph. I). And this is indeed by grace alone. For by grace alone, and the freely bestowed gift of God, we have been called to faith and to the bosom of mother Church. Paul also attests this in writing to the Ephesians: “By grace you are saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves. For it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast” (Eph. II).] From eternity, the fountain of wisdom,

By the regard of grace alone,

Thus foresaw, in the order of things,

[60] These things to come.

Therefore may Christ make us,

Refreshed by his nuptials with true delights,

Participants with the fellowship

[Col. 1464A] Of the elect. Amen.

## XIII. PROSE FOR THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

This prose displays a varied form of rhythmic composition. For at its beginning and near its end, the individual verse-endings have consonance and a similar syllabic termination in both their middle and end. In the remaining verses, however, three rhythmic clauses are set down: two consonant with one another, and the third clause of one verse corresponding to the third clause of the next. This kind of rhythm is very common in proses. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It expounds the praises, glories, and mysteries of holy mother Church, prefigured in many ways through Old Testament figures and wonderfully proclaimed also in the Psalms and the Gospel, as the notes appended below will make clear.

[Note: [Col. 1464C] How beloved are the tabernacles. The opening of this prose is taken from Psalm eighty-three, where the Prophet says: “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts; my soul longs and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII), and what follows thereafter. For there, by the tabernacles and courts of the Lord, the Church is understood, both militant and triumphant; concerning it he adds in the same place: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise you” (ibid.).] How beloved are the tabernacles

And courts of the Lord of hosts.

[Note: [Col. 1464C] How chosen the architects. The thought of this and the immediately following verse is taken from the Gospel, where the Lord says that one who hears his words and does them is like “a man building a house, who dug deep and laid its foundation upon rock. When a flood came, the stream beat against that house, and could not move it, for it was founded upon rock” (Luke VI). Now this wise architect, chosen from among thousands, is Christ, who built his house, namely the Church, upon himself, the most steadfast rock; and “the gates of hell have not,” nor “shall ever prevail against it” (Matt. XVI). The streams of tribulations indeed came, and the winds of persecutions, stirred up by tyrants and heretics against the Church, blew; yet they could not dislodge her from her place, because she rested upon the stability of the spiritual rock.] How chosen the architect,

How secure his buildings,

[5] Which wind, flood, and rain do not move,

But rather foster.

[Note: [Col. 1464D] How fair the foundations. Of these foundations the Prophet says in the Psalm: “Her foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. LXXXVI). The shadows’ harmonious sacraments went before as foundations, because they were prefigured by the diverse figures of the Old Testament, here subsequently arranged in their order. These figures, moreover, are here called sacraments because they were signs of a sacred reality to be fulfilled in the New Testament. The Old Testament is called a shadow here because it was shadowed and veiled in figures. Finally, those sacraments of the shadow were harmonious because they were most apt and fitting to the truth signified through them.] How fair the foundations,

[Col. 1465A] Going before through the harmonious sacraments

Of the shadow.

[10] [Note: [Col. 1465B] The side of sleeping Adam. The first figure of the Church expressed here was Eve, formed from the side of her sleeping husband (Gen. II), which was more fully explained in the preceding prose. The second: Noah’s ark, constructed of wood, preserved him and his family from the flood (Gen. VII). Thus the Church, resting upon Christ’s cross, preserves safe and unharmed those contained within her amid the waves and storms of the world. The third: Sarah, long barren, bore in extreme old age her son Isaac, so named from his mother’s laughter (Gen. XXI). He signified Christ, our true joy. Thus the Church from the Gentiles, barren for a long time—throughout the whole period before Christ’s coming in the flesh—brought forth an abundant offspring in the last days after Christ’s ascension into heaven.] The side of sleeping Adam

Poured forth Eve into the beginnings

Of an abiding union.

The ark, made of wood,

Steered, saves Noah

[15] Through the flood of the world.

At last made fruitful with her late-born child,

Old Sarah laughs in joy,

Nursing our joy.

[Note: [Col. 1465C] The servant drinks, he who is sent as an envoy. The fourth figure of the Church is Rebecca, summoned by an honorable embassy to become Isaac’s wife. She gave the servant of Abraham drink from her pitcher and received from him, as a gift, earrings and bracelets with which to adorn herself (Gen. XXIV). Thus the Church was called to be Christ’s bride; she offers a generous drink of saving teaching to her servants, and is in turn adorned by him with the beauty of diverse virtues. Fifth figure: Jacob stole the blessing from his brother Esau while Esau wandered through the fields intent upon hunting (Gen. XXVII). Thus the Church obtained blessing from Christ when the Synagogue, clinging and relying too much on the letter of the law, strayed from the straight path of truth. Further, in the tenth verse explaining this fifth figure, the author of the present prose uses *fretus* with the dative case, in order to preserve the corresponding syllabic ending with the immediately following verse. This is nevertheless contrary to the usage of approved authors, who employ that word only with the ablative, as Virgil does:

> Supported by Thracian lyre and tuneful strings.]

The servant drinks, who is sent as an envoy,

[20] And the camel is watered

From Rebecca’s pitcher.

She fits to herself earrings

[Col. 1465B] And bracelets, that by them

She may become fitting for her husband.

[25] [Col. 1466A] The Synagogue is supplanted

By Jacob, while she wanders,

Relying too much on the letter.

[Note: [Col. 1465D] Many things lie hidden from bleary-eyed Leah. Sixth figure: Leah, whose eyes were weak (Gen. XXIX), signifies the Synagogue, seeing dimly and groping with veiled eyes; many mysteries of God’s dispensation toward humanity were hidden from her. But Rachel, fair of face and comely in appearance, with bright eyes, signifies Christ’s Church, which discerns in the light and brightness of the Gospel those mysteries that had been hidden from the Synagogue. Both sisters were joined to Jacob by the bond of marriage, because both the Synagogue and the Church belonged to Christ himself—the former first, the latter afterward (Gen. XXXVIII). Seventh figure: Tamar, widowed by two husbands, when she was not given as wife to Judah’s now-grown third son, sat at the crossroads like a harlot; concealing her face lest she be recognized, she conceived by Judah, son of Jacob, two twins, Zerah and Perez. Thus the Church, long deserted and adulterous through idolatrous worship, at last became fruitful when visited by Christ her Bridegroom and bore him many children in the Spirit, so that Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled in her: “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. LIV). For the offspring of the Church, which had been deserted, was more abundant than that of the Synagogue, which had God as its bridegroom. And as Hannah, Samuel’s mother, sang (I Kings II), then the barren Church bore very many children, while the Synagogue, which had many children, became weak. Eighth figure: Moses, newly born, when he could no longer be concealed by his parents, was placed in a little basket woven of rush and reed and set out on the river. There he was found by the daughter of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who happened at that time to go out to the river to wash herself (Exod. II). Thus the Church, led away by God through diverse errors and exposed to grave danger of being submerged in the abyss, was received by Christ in pity for her sad plight and tenderly brought up. Ninth figure: the Passover lamb was commanded to be eaten in one Hebrew house; the doorposts sprinkled with its blood drove away the destroyer of the firstborn (Exod. XII). Thus, in the one house of the Church, Christ the true Lamb is received by the faithful, and Christians drink his blood in the holy banquet of the sacred Eucharist.] Many things lie hidden from bleary-eyed Leah,

But seeing Rachel, supported by them,

[30] Marries under an equal covenant.

Naked, veiling herself at the crossroads,

Long-widowed Tamar bears twins

By Judah.

Here Moses is found by a maiden,

[35] While she washes herself, in a basket

Of rushes.

Here a male lamb is sacrificed,

By which Israel is fed,

Stained with his blood.

[40] [Col. 1466B] [Note: [Col. 1466C] Here the red wave is crossed. Tenth figure: the Israelite people, led by Moses, passed unharmed through the Red Sea, in which the Egyptians were drowned (Exod. I). Thus, by Christ’s institution, baptism—prefigured by the Red Sea—is received in the Church, and in it the entire army of demons and the throng of vices are submerged. Eleventh: in the ark of the covenant made by Moses was a vessel filled with heavenly manna and stone tablets containing the Ten Commandments of the Law (Heb. IX). Likewise, in the Church, prefigured by the ark, are contained the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist and the Gospel, which explains God’s commands more perfectly. Twelfth: the tabernacle of testimony built by Moses was adorned with a great variety of sacred vessels and implements pertaining to God’s worship, as Exodus relates (ch. XXVI). This represented the Church, distinguished by the great beauty of sacraments and the varied order of its ministers. Thirteenth: Aaron the high priest had diverse sacred vestments, woven with wonderful skill. The first of all, and that which is put on before the others, is the *poderis*, the ankle-length garment flowing down to the feet—from which it takes its name—also called by Josephus and in Exodus (ch. XXVIII) a linen tunic, woven of double fine linen. John also mentions it in the Apocalypse, saying: “Turning, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like the Son of Man, clothed in a *poderis* and girded at the breasts with a golden belt” (Apoc. I). Thus Christ’s Church possesses a manifold adornment of virtues, with which she is decked as with precious garments. Fourteenth: Uriah, Bathsheba’s husband, was killed in battle against the sons of Ammon; Bathsheba afterward married King David and became queen (II Kings II). Thus the Synagogue, understood through Uriah, was abolished and died; but the Church, signified by Bathsheba, was joined by the covenant of marriage to Christ the eternal King.] Here the red wave is crossed,

Overwhelming the Egyptians beneath

[Col. 1467A] A deep gulf.

Here is the vessel full of manna;

Here are the ten commandments of the Law,

But in the ark of the covenant.

Here are the ornaments of the sanctuary;

Here are Aaron’s garments,

Which the *poderis* precedes.

Here Uriah is bereaved;

[50] Bathsheba is exalted,

Companion of the royal throne.

[Note: [Col. 1467B] She stands before the King in a garment of variety. Fifteenth figure: the Church herself is signified in the Psalm by the queen who stands at the right hand of the eternal King and Son of God, in golden raiment, surrounded with variety (Ps. XLIV). For the Church is queen because she is the King’s Bride; she stands in the golden garment of charity and the other virtues, surrounded by the variety of ecclesiastical orders and of those ministering in her according to diverse ranks and offices. The phrase which the present text adds, “like daughters of kings,” also answers to that passage of the same Psalm: “Myrrh and drops and cassia from your garments, from ivory palaces, from which the daughters of kings have delighted you in your honor” (ibid.); and likewise to this passage: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; in golden fringes, clothed about with varieties” (ibid.). Sixteenth: the queen of Sheba came from the southern region, or south, to Jerusalem with a great retinue and riches, in order to hear Solomon’s wisdom, which she had previously learned of by report (III Kings X). Thus the Church comes from the distant ends of the earth in order to hear Christ, the true Solomon, speaking through the evangelical law, as has already been explained in the preceding prose. The seventeenth figure is expressed here: finally, the Church herself is signified by that Bride who says of herself in the Song of Songs: “I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon” (Cant. I); and of whom the wondering assembly of the faithful says in the same book: “Who is this who ascends through the desert like a rod of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and of every powder of the perfumer?” (Cant. III). Indeed, all the things mentioned above were shadowed forth in figures of the Old Testament, but were disclosed and brought into the open through the day of grace, that is, the light of the New Testament.] Before the King she stands in a garment

Of golden variety,

Like daughters of kings.

[55] Here comes the queen of the south,

Whom Solomon’s divine wisdom

[Col. 1467B] Establishes.

[Col. 1468A] She is black but beautiful,

A smoky rod of myrrh and frankincense,

[60] Of aromatic powder.

The day of grace has disclosed to us

These things to come which the figure

Had shadowed forth.

[Note: [Col. 1467D] Now upon the bed with the beloved. The Bridegroom’s bed, often mentioned in the Song of Songs, signifies the soul’s peaceful repose in the Lord, when, free of every care and estranged from the world, it meditates upon and continually contemplates him alone. The present verse urges us to embrace this tranquility and rest, so that, setting aside worldly business and calming our affections, we may “in peace sleep in him and rest” (Ps. IV) in the Lord, because of the celebration of Christ’s nuptials with the Church, in which one ought to keep festival.] Now upon the bed with the beloved

[65] Let us rest and sing psalms:

For the nuptials are at hand.

[Note: [Col. 1468B] Whose beginning resounds in trumpets. Trumpets indicate to us the condition of the Old Testament, because in it they were commanded by the Lord to be made for moving camp, summoning the multitude, going forth to war, and finally celebrating feasts. For concerning the fourth reason for their institution, God is read to have said to the children of Israel: “Whenever you have a feast and feast days and calends, you shall sound the trumpets over the holocausts and peace-offerings and victims, that they may be for you a remembrance of your God” (Num. X). And again elsewhere: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your solemnity” (Ps. LXXX). Again the Prophet says elsewhere in the Psalms: “The sound of one feasting, in a voice of exultation and praise” (Ps. XLI). The psaltery, however, is a musical instrument which has ten strings and gives forth a melody much sweeter and more pleasant to hear than the loud, clamorous sound of trumpets. It suggests the state of the New Testament, consisting especially in the perfect observance of God’s Ten Commandments. Although these were delivered in the old law, they have been made much clearer by the teaching of evangelical perfection, and the commandments are more perfectly observed. Therefore the meaning of this verse is that the beginning of these nuptials of Christ and the Church was in the Old Testament, indeed shortly after the creation of humankind; for, according to Gregory and the other doctors, Christ’s Church began with righteous Abel and continued and advanced throughout the entire course of the Old Testament. But the end of those nuptials belongs to the New Testament, in which those spiritual nuptials, before that time not yet perfect, were consummated and completed. For the gathering of the Gentiles into the faith through the apostles had not yet occurred, nor had the fullness of the Gentiles yet entered into Christ; rather, the Church then consisted only of Jews, apart from a few exceptions. But in the New Testament the multitude of Jews and Gentiles alike was joined together by the cornerstone into the perfect structure of the Church. Therefore the ending, completion, and perfection of those nuptials pertains to the dignity and state of the New Testament.] Whose beginning resounds

In the trumpets of those feasting,

And whose end is through the psaltery.

[70] [Note: [Col. 1468D]

The Bridegroom, thousands upon thousands. This passage is taken from the Apocalypse, where blessed John says: “I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne, the living creatures, and the elders; and their number was thousands upon thousands, saying with a great voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity, and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing” (Apoc. V). The slain Lamb is Jesus Christ, Bridegroom of the Church, who is thus praised by thousands upon thousands. “Thousands upon thousands” and “thousand thousands” form the same number, namely a thousand thousands, or a thousand times a thousand. Thus exactly the same number is signified here by “thousands upon thousands” and in the Apocalypse by “thousand thousands” [Col. 1469C]; and this passage of the prose fittingly corresponds to that one.

Moreover, the author of this prose, Adam of Saint-Victor, composed another prose on the dedication of a church, no less elegant than these last two, whose opening is: “King Solomon made the temple, whose likeness and exemplar are Christ and the Church.” In it he applies the entire construction of Solomon’s temple to the mystical sense and spiritual fabric of the Church. But since it sufficiently explains itself and reveals its hidden meaning, it has deliberately been omitted here.] 

Thousands upon thousands praise the Bridegroom

In one melody,

Saying without end: Alleluia. Amen.

## XIV. ON SAINT ANDREW

[Col. 1469A]

This prose observes the law of rhythmic measure, like that described a little above, “Praise, O Zion, the Savior.” Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It describes the illustrious praises of Saint Andrew: his calling to Christ, his preaching of the Gospel among the Gentiles, and his glorious death upon the cross.

Let us exult and rejoice,

And delight in the praises

Of Andrew the apostle.

His faith, teaching, and character,

[5] And all his labors for Christ,

Are rightly to be recalled.

He led Peter to the faith,

[Col. 1469B] On whom light first dawned

At John’s indication,

[10] Beside the Sea of Galilee.

The calling of Peter and Andrew

Follows together:

Both, formerly fishermen,

Become champions of the Word,

[15] And a pattern of righteousness.

[Note: [Col. 1469D] They cast out the net for a catch. This is a metaphorical expression, by which the brothers’ zeal and diligence in preaching for the conversion of peoples is conveyed through the casting-out of a net for a catch. For the word of their preaching was a spiritual net by which they fished up many people submerged in the waves of unbelief and vices, that they might emerge from the gulf of damnation into the light of life. This clause corresponds to the Lord’s words spoken to them about material fishing: “Cast out your nets for a catch” (Luke V). Then, after a great multitude of fish had been enclosed in the nets—which signified the immense multitude of people to be converted through them—“they left their nets and boat and followed the Lord” (ibid.).] They cast out the net for a catch,

And maintain watchful care

For the newborn Church.

He is separated from his brother,

[20] And Andrew is sent

Into the regions of Achaia.

By God’s grace, a great part of the province

[Col. 1469C] Runs into Andrew’s nets.

[25] By faith, life, word, and miracles,

A gracious and distinguished teacher,

He forms the people’s heart.

When Aegeas learns

[30] [Col. 1470A] What Andrew has done,

The goads of anger rise.

A mind untroubled, a manly mind,

To which this present life is cheap,

Flourishes in patience.

[35] Neither blandishments nor torments,

Nor the judge’s madness, enfeeble

The strength of his mind.

[Note: [Col. 1469D] Seeing the cross prepared. In one of her antiphons the Church thus sings of the holy apostle of God: When blessed Andrew reached the place where the cross had been prepared, he cried aloud and said: “O good cross, long desired and now prepared for my longing soul, I come to you confident and rejoicing, so that you may joyfully receive me, the disciple of him who hung upon you.”] Seeing the cross prepared,

The disciple longs to be conformed

[40] To his Master.

[Note: [Col. 1470C] Death is paid for death. That is, Andrew’s death is paid in return for Christ’s death. The death which Christ deigned to suffer for the salvation of all, Saint Andrew, dying upon the cross, rendered to the Savior; and for Christ’s death he repaid his own [Col. 1470D] death, rejoicing greatly precisely because in a like manner of death, namely crucifixion, he was conformed to his Master. The cross is here called a triumphal title because Christ triumphed on it over the prince of this world; and Saint Andrew triumphed over Aegeas, the impious persecutor who did not prevail upon him to permit his removal alive from the cross.] Death is paid for death,

And the triumphal title

Of the cross is sought.

Upon the cross he lived two days,

[45] [Col. 1470B] To live forever,

Nor, though the people desire it, does he wish to be taken down

From the gibbet.

For about half an hour,

Flooded with exceeding light,

[50] With light and with joy

He goes to the courts of light.

O glorious Andrew,

Whose precious prayers—

[Note: [Col. 1470D] Whose death was radiant. The author calls Saint Andrew’s death radiant because it was filled with heavenly light. For, as the preceding verse says, when the apostle beloved by God had already hung two days upon the cross, teaching the people from it as from a teacher’s chair, at last such brightness, poured out from heaven, shone around him that mortal eyes could not fix their gaze upon him. When that light had remained there for about half an hour, it gradually departed; he yielded up his blessed spirit and happily fell asleep in the Lord.] Whose radiant death

[55] Has a sweet remembrance—

From this valley of tears,

O merciful shepherd of souls,

By your grace translate us to that clear light.

[Col. 1470C] Amen.

## XV. ON SAINT NICHOLAS

This prose has rhythmic measure in its structure, but of a varied kind. At one time it contains two rhythmic clauses in a single verse, at another four; nor does it preserve a uniform consonance in the termination and ending of its syllables, as anyone may readily discern from reading it. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It praises the eminent glories of blessed Nicholas: the wondrous character of his childhood, which laid the foundations of the great virtues later displayed in him; the deeds accomplished by God through him; his call to the episcopate; and the brilliance and frequency of his miracles both during life and after death. These matters, however, are clear from his Life, which is in everyone’s hands, and do not require extensive explanation.

Let us rejoice together and exult

In vocal harmony

At the festal solemnities

Of blessed Nicholas.

[5] Even while he still lay in the cradle,

[Col. 1471B] By observing fasts,

[Note: [Col. 1471C] From the breasts he began to merit the highest joys.
