A *papilla* is the very tip and extremity of the breast from which milk is drawn, so called because, being a small papule or protuberance, the head of such a little breast resembles a papule. It is also sometimes used for the whole breast, as in Virgil’s *Aeneid*:

> Until the spear, driven beneath her bared breast,  
> Stuck fast.

And it is taken in this second sense here. Nicholas began from the breasts to merit the highest joys of heaven because from his mother’s breast and from infancy he began to apply himself to works of fasting; through these, with the addition of the practices of other virtues, he finally merited the eternal joys of heaven.] From the breasts he began to merit

The highest joys.

As a youth he embraces

[10] The pursuit of letters,

A stranger and immune

To all wantonness.

A blessed confessor,

Whose rank

[15] Was announced by a voice from heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1471D] By which, promoted, he is raised to the height of the episcopate. Here *provectus* is a participle derived from the passive verb *provehor*, meaning “promoted,” “raised,” or “lifted up.” Virgil says:

> Having advanced here, they conceal themselves on a distant shore.

This word is also sometimes found as a verbal noun meaning promotion or advancement. In this place it should not be construed with the noun *praesulatus*, which is in the genitive case, but with the preceding noun *confessor*, or Nicholas, so that the sense is this: By that voice fallen from heaven, Nicholas himself, being promoted, is raised to the highest heights, to the summit of the episcopate and pontifical dignity.] By which, promoted,

He is raised to the highest heights

Of the episcopate.

Within his soul

[20] Was exceptional compassion,

[Col. 1471C] And he bestowed many benefits

Upon the oppressed.

Through him, with gold,

The disgrace of maidens

[25] Is removed,

And the poverty of their father

[Col. 1472A] Is relieved.

> **[Note: Col. 1471D] Certain sailors sailing.** Among the many miracles which God worked through blessed Nicholas, the author here recounts only two, so that he may subsequently apply them to a mystical sense and adapt them suitably to our petition. The first concerns sailors who, when a storm arose, invoked the aid of blessed Nicholas and were delivered by his help from the imminent danger of death. Thus, in the nineteenth verse, we who make our way in this world, overwhelmed by storms of vices, ask, under blessed Nicholas’s guidance, to reach the harbour of eternal salvation. The second miracle, in the seventeenth verse, is indicated by the flowing of oil from the tomb of blessed Nicholas. Likewise, in the twenty-first verse we ask that spiritual anointing and the grace of the Holy Spirit may be obtained for us from God through the prayers of blessed Nicholas, so that, when anointed, the sores and wounds of our souls may be healed. Thus the two petitions here made by the faithful people correspond in fitting proportion to the two miracles mentioned above.
>
> Certain sailors, sailing  
> And struggling against  
> The savagery of the waves,  
> Their ship almost broken apart,  
> Despairing now of life,  
> Set amid such great  
> Danger, cry out  
> With one voice, all saying:
>
> “O blessed Nicholas,  
> Draw us to the harbour of the sea  
> From the strait of death.  
> Draw us to the harbour of the sea,  
> You who give help to so many  
> By the grace of your mercy.”
>
> **[Col. 1472B]** While they cried out—and not in vain—  
> Behold, someone says, “I am present  
> To aid you.”  
> At once a favourable breeze is given,  
> And the storm is calmed;  
> The seas grew still.
>
> From his tomb flows  
> An abundance of anointing,  
> Which heals all the sick  
> Through his intercessions.
>
> We who are in this world,  
> In the depths of vices,  
> Having now suffered shipwreck—  
> Glorious Nicholas,  
> Draw us to the harbour of salvation,  
> **[Col. 1472C]** Where peace and glory are.
>
> May you obtain from the Lord for us  
> That same anointing,  
> Through your holy prayer.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1472D] May you obtain it from the Lord.** Here one must read not *impetret* (“may he obtain”), as some books have it, but *impetres* (“may you obtain”), so that the supplicatory address to Saint Nicholas may continue and the prayer be directed to him. Just as the preceding verse is directed by a verb in the second person, so in the twenty-second verse one must read not the masculine relative *qui* (“who”), but the feminine *quae* (“which”), so that it refers to the preceding noun *unctionem* (“anointing”). For although the pronoun *qui* could be referred to the antecedent *Domino* (“the Lord”), the wording would not be so significant or so well suited to the preceding sentence as it is when the relation here is to the anointing.
>
> **[Col. 1473A]** Which healed the wound  
> Of many sins  
> In Mary.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1473D] Of many sins in Mary.** This must be understood of blessed Mary Magdalene, whose many sins the anointing of divine grace healed, when the heavenly physician said of her: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.” And again to her: “Your sins are forgiven” (Luke 7).
>
> Celebrating her feast,  
> May they rejoice for ever;  
> And may Christ crown them  
> After life’s course. Amen.
>
> ## XVI. OF SAINT AGNES
>
> This prose follows the rule of rhythmic modulation familiar and customary in ecclesiastical proses. For, in several verses, all the rhythmic clauses preceding the last correspond with one another in their very endings, and each consists of eight syllables, of which the penultimate is long. The final clause of those verses, however, has an answering consonance with the last clause of the following verse; it consists of seven syllables, with a short penultimate. But in the fifth and sixth verses, and likewise in the ninth and tenth, each rhythmic clause contains six syllables; in the first four, the penultimate syllable is always short. In the fifth clause of the ninth and tenth verses, however, the penultimate syllable is long. Further, the first four clauses of the aforementioned verses sometimes have a reciprocal correspondence in like endings at alternating positions, so that the first agrees with the third and the second with the fourth; at other times, being placed in adjacent positions, they end in similar sounds, so that the first corresponds to the second and the third to the fourth. Finally, the last clause of the ninth verse keeps its conformity with the last of the tenth.
>
> Its author is Adam of Saint Victor, who in elegant and tuneful modulation embraces the entire passion of the glorious virgin Agnes, pursuing it from beginning to end—as is his customary and distinctive practice in other proses on saints describing their lives and martyrdoms. Moreover, this author here indicates that holy apparition by which, after her blessed death, she revealed her glory to her parents as they mourned her death, and also the healing of Queen Constantia bestowed through the merits of blessed Agnes. But since blessed Ambrose has written excellently and copiously on this sacred virgin’s life and struggle for Christ, and since that work, included among his other writings, may readily be had and read by all, those matters concerning the history of her passion need not be repeated here for clearer explanation; rather, they should be drawn from that most delightful source itself. Therefore, for understanding these things, let Ambrose be read.
>
> Let us be encouraged for the contest,  
> Recalling the passion  
> **[Col. 1474A]** Of the glorious virgin.
>
> Handling the sacred flower,  
> Let us breathe in the fragrance  
> Of sweetness poured upon us.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1473D] Handling the sacred flower.** Whoever touches with the hands a beautiful flower, sweetly fragrant, is without doubt sprinkled with the flower’s pleasant scent and receives its gentle breath. Thus, he says, as we recall the character, life, and deeds of Agnes, the virgin consecrated to God—who is a spiritual flower, shining with virginal whiteness, rosy through the shedding of her blood, and breathing the sweetest fragrance of every virtue—may we be sprinkled with the sweetness of her virtues and, through diligent imitation, run in the fragrance of her ointments [Col. 1474D].
>
> Beautiful, prudent, and illustrious,  
> Agnes, now having completed two periods of five years,  
> Was adding three years.
>
> The governor’s son loves her;  
> But the virgin refuses  
> To bend to his desire.
>
> Wondrous is the power of faith;  
> Wondrous is virginity;  
> Wondrous the integrity  
> Of a virginal heart.
>
> Thus the Son of God,  
> **[Col. 1474B]** By a marvellous will,  
> Reveals himself more marvellously  
> In what is fragile.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1474D] He reveals himself more marvellously in what is fragile.** Writing to the Corinthians, blessed Paul says of Christ that he chose the weak things of this world in order to confound the strong; this is certainly demonstrated with manifest evidence in the victory of holy virgins over the tyrants of this age. For he displays his power far more widely in those tender little virgins, frail in sex and age, when in them he breaks the strength of tyrants and demons, than in men stronger in spirit and endowed with masculine vigour. Therefore holy Church, commending God’s omnipotence, ascribes to him the praise that, among the other miracles of his power, he has granted the victory of martyrdom even to the frail sex.
>
> The lover languishes, lies in bed;  
> His illness becomes known to the governor;  
> He hastens remedies.  
> He offers much, promises more—  
> Perishable things, being himself to perish—  
> But all things grow worthless.
>
> The governor exposes her naked  
> To acts of shame,  
> Whom Christ clothes  
> With the fringes of her hair  
> And with a heavenly robe.
>
> A heavenly messenger  
> Stands close by;  
> The chamber of lust  
> Becomes a place of light;  
> The unchaste are confounded.
>
> The blinded lover is enraged  
> And, rushing in, is suffocated  
> By an evil spirit.
>
> His father mourns; all mourn;  
> Rome wept at the death  
> Of the young man.
>
> He is raised by Agnes.  
> The crowd rages indiscriminately:  
> They prepare a pyre for the virgin.
>
> The burning pyre burns the guilty;  
> **[Col. 1475A]** The flame rages against the enraged,  
> Giving honour to the Godhead.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1475C] Giving honour to the Godhead.** Just as the fire of the Babylonian furnace, burning the king’s servants who kindled it while leaving the three youths wholly untouched (Daniel 3), declared God’s glory and power and showed itself obedient to him beyond nature, so also the fire into which blessed Agnes was cast by the seditious and raging crowd gave honour to God. For, as though sensing the will and command of its Maker, it burned the wicked worshippers of idols and preserved holy Agnes unharmed. Thus God’s glory was manifested and the honour of his name increased.
>
> Giving thanks to the Saviour,  
> She offers her throat to the executioner  
> And does not fear to die even for a moment,  
> Conscious of her purity.
>
> Agnes, standing at the right hand  
> Of the saving Lamb, you glory  
> And console your parents,  
> Inviting them to joys.
>
> So that they might not mourn you as dead,  
> Though now joined to your heavenly bridegroom,  
> He revealed to them, in the form of a lamb, his glory  
> And your virginal glory.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1475C] To them, in the form of a lamb, his glory.** These words—as also those preceding and following—are directed by the faithful people to the most holy virgin Agnes in a manner of praise and proclamation. “O Agnes,” it says, “your heavenly bridegroom Jesus Christ revealed his glory to these your parents under the form of a lamb, appearing to them with you, whiter than snow. He also revealed to them your virginal glory, which after the course of this life you possess unfading in heaven.” But this revelation—on account of which the feast of blessed Agnes was instituted to be celebrated a second time, namely on the eighth day after its first observance—is clearly and fully explained by blessed Ambrose in his account of her passion.
>
> **[Col. 1475B]** Do not allow us to be separated  
> From the saving Lamb  
> To whom you consecrated yourself wholly,  
> By whose aid you healed  
> Noble Constantia.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1475D] You healed noble Constantia.** This Constantia was the daughter of Constantine, emperor of the Romans. She was afflicted with a severe illness and with sores over her entire body. Having heard of the marvels worked by the Lord through blessed Agnes, she came to Agnes’s tomb to recover health. Nor was she disappointed in her desire: there, overcome by gentle sleep and visited in dreams by glorious Agnes, she was restored to perfect health, as Ambrose elegantly recounts in the place mentioned above [Col. 1476C].
>
> Chosen vessel, vessel of honour,  
> Flower of incorrupt fragrance,  
> Pleasing to the choirs of angels,  
> You offer the world  
> A model of honour and modesty.
>
> Enjoying the triumphant palm,  
> Flourishing with virginal bloom,  
> Make us, unworthy though we are of a special title,  
> At least be enrolled  
> Under the general title of saints. Amen.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1476C] Us unworthy of a special [title].** “There is not in us,” he says, “such holiness of life and excellence of sanctity that we may deserve the special title of saints, or be called and accounted holy by the particular designation, like those who are entered individually and by name in the catalogue of saints. But grant this one thing to the servants who serve you, O blessed Agnes: that we may at least be inscribed under the general title of saints and comprehended under their universal designation, having a share of inheritance in the kingdom of God. For whoever ultimately attain that inheritance are undoubtedly included under the common name of saints, even if they do not merit that particular designation among human beings, nor are entered among the order of saints on earth” [Col. 1476D].
>
> ## XVII. OF SAINT VINCENT
>
> **[Col. 1475C]**
>
> This prose maintains the measure of rhythmic composition, but a varied one in different verses. In some verses, every clause except the last has eight syllables and a long penultimate. In others it has seven syllables and a short penultimate. There also occur some verses in which each clause before the final one contains eleven syllables, while the final clause contains sometimes four syllables, as in the ninth and tenth verses, and sometimes seven, as in the thirteenth and fourteenth. Finally, there are other verses in which every clause preceding the final includes ten syllables, while the final has eight, as in the nineteenth and twentieth. Sometimes the individual clauses of the same verse before the last retain a medial consonance toward their ending, as in the twenty-fourth verse.
>
> Its author is Adam of Saint Victor. It contains the sacred struggle of blessed Vincent for Christ: chains, prison, the rack, the gridiron, and fragments of pottery. Having overcome all these, the blessed martyr entered heaven in distinguished triumph. It also recounts the victory, through the remains of this holy body, over the cruel tyrant, both on land and at sea. But these matters, sufficiently well known from the sacred history of his life, may readily be perceived and need not be repeated here.
>
> Behold the longed-for day,  
> A happy day, a welcome day,  
> A day worthy of joy.  
> Let us venerate this day  
> And marvel at Christ  
> Fighting in Vincent.
>
> Illustrious in birth, faith, holiness,  
> Understanding, speech, rank,  
> And office,  
> He held the summit of the diaconate  
> Under the authority  
> **[Col. 1476C]** Of Father Valerius.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1476D] Here [he held] the summit of the diaconate.** *Arcem* means a height, summit, dignity, or highest rank. Blessed Vincent had already been initiated into sacred orders and had received the order of deacon under Saint Valerius, his bishop and spiritual father, in whose company and service he performed ecclesiastical ministry. Hence Vincent is called a Levite, because he conformed in divine worship to the Levites of the Old Testament, descended from the tribe of Levi. Certainly he was a Levite not by flesh but by spirit, being devoted, like them, to the ministry of the tabernacle and altar.
>
> The bishop, hindered in speech, devotes himself to God;  
> And to the Levite  
> He gives the duties of the word.
>
> Sound teaching adorns his tongue,  
> And a twofold knowledge  
> His single-hearted breast.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1477B–C] A twofold knowledge also [adorns] a simple breast.** In blessed Vincent there was a twofold knowledge: knowledge of the active life and likewise of the contemplative life. For he knew and practised what belonged to the active life, teaching the people by constant preaching and instruction in sacred matters, and illuminating them also by administering the sacraments. He likewise knew and performed the offices belonging to the contemplative life, withdrawing himself from action into contemplation of divine things and, through devotion to prayer and inward recollection, raising himself to tranquil contemplation of God in the secret chambers of his soul. Hence holy Church sings of him: “Saint Vincent, devoted from childhood to the study of letters, by the providence of heavenly mercy shone most effectively in a twofold knowledge.” This twofold knowledge adorned his simple breast—that is, one neither crafty nor deceitful. So Job is called a simple and upright man, fearing God (Job 1); and the apostles are commanded by the Lord to be simple as doves (Matthew 10).
>
> While he teaches the sound faith  
> To the people of Caesaraugusta,  
> With grace accompanying him,  
> The governor’s envy, zealous for idolatry,  
> Rages against the Church.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1477D] The people of Caesaraugusta.** Caesaraugusta is a city of Tarraconensian Spain, in which Saint Valerius was bishop and Vincent deacon. From it is formed the adjective *Caesaraugustanus*, a demonym. Likewise, *Valentia* in this place is the proper name of a city; as a common noun it means strength or health, just as its opposite *invalentia* means weakness or ill health.
>
> After hearing of their constancy in faith,  
> He orders both to be dragged to Valencia  
> In chains.
>
> He spares neither the distinguished young man,  
> Nor does the impious man heed  
> The holy old man’s age.
>
> Weary from the journey,  
> Oppressed by the weight of iron,  
> He shuts them in a foul prison,  
> Denying them provisions.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1477D] Denying provisions.** *Victualia* denotes what pertains to sustenance and nourishment, including both food and drink. Ambrose, *On Bees*: “You may see all competing in their task: some keeping watch in seeking provisions, others applying vigilant protection to the camp.”
>
> Thus he harmed them to the extent of his power,  
> Yet could not do so to the extent of his desire,  
> Because Christ’s providence  
> Nourished his own.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1477D–1478C] Thus he harmed [them] to the extent of his power.** Among authors one scarcely finds the preposition *pro* joined to an infinitive verb standing in the place of an accusative or ablative; for such a phrase as *secundum posse meum* or *pro posse meo id feci* (“I did it according to my power” or “to the extent of my power”) would have been considered commonplace and inelegant. Yet the author should be excused and deemed worthy of pardon, because, in order to maintain a fixed number of syllables in that clause, he could not say *pro viribus*, *pro virili*, or something similarly more elegant.
>
> The governor banishes the elder into exile;  
> He reserves the younger for  
> A harsher punishment.
>
> Having endured the rack and the claws,  
> Vincent mounts the gridiron  
> With a spirit still stronger.
>
> **[Col. 1478A]** While being roasted, he is not terrified;  
> He confesses Christ more strongly  
> And does not fear the tyrant  
> In his presence.
>
> His face burns; the inhuman man’s  
> Tongue sticks fast; his hand trembles;  
> Dacian cannot contain himself  
> For the madness of his heart.
>
> Then the martyr is thrust back into a cave  
> And, fixed upon potsherds, is dashed down.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1478C] And, fixed upon potsherds, is dashed down.** Here one should read *illiditur*, with *i* in the second syllable (“is dashed against”), rather than *illuditur*, with *u* (“is mocked”), as some books have it, because the former meaning is more suitable and congruent with the sense intended. Vincent was not then mocked or assailed with derisive and insulting words; rather, he is reported to have been dashed upon fragments of potsherds spread across the floor of the prison.
>
> Yet here he enjoys much light,  
> Visited by angels.  
> At last, laid upon a bed,  
> He passes as a veteran to those above.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1478C–D] He passes as a veteran to those above.** A soldier is called *emeritus* when he has completed military service and, owing to advancing age, is released from its labours and granted exemption. Claudian: “The yoked teams lead the veterans to their familiar pastures.” Thus blessed Vincent, having completed the hard contest of martyrdom in which he laboured to the point of death, now discharged from that service, ascended triumphantly to heaven.
>
> Thus his spirit, triumphing in its own manner,  
> **[Col. 1478B]** Is presented to its Prince.
>
> By no common law does malice permit  
> The man to be given burial;  
> It violates at once  
> The force of law and nature.
>
> The judge rages against the dead;  
> Hence the dead man’s praise increased.  
> The beast fears what it is accustomed to eat.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1478D] For what it is accustomed to eat.** A raven is accustomed to feed upon corpses; but now, by divine decree, it became the guardian of the dead sacred body. Not only did it not touch it, but it also prevented other wild beasts from touching it, just as the raven—an animal given to gluttony—is formerly said to have brought bread and flesh to the prophet Elijah (3 Kings 17). Moreover, here *consuevit* must be read as a four-syllable word by diaeresis, so that the clause may have eight syllables.
>
> Behold, a raven guards  
> The unburied body unharmed,  
> And thus frustrates  
> The criminal’s intention.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1478D] Frustrates [his] intention.** *Frustratur*, a deponent verb, here has an active meaning. For it takes an accusative with it, and means the same as *fraudat*, *fallit*, or *eludit*: “deceives” or “thwarts.” Plautus: “I do not know what trickster is deceiving this woman.” When it has a passive meaning, it is rather joined with an ablative, as: “the wicked governor was frustrated in his intention.” But this is immediately evident.
>
> **[Col. 1479A]** But profane Dacian,  
> What he cannot have consumed on land,  
> Wishes to have hidden beneath  
> The silence of the deep gulf.
>
> Yet he can neither be held down by a millstone  
> Nor be concealed by the sea,  
> Whom the Church now strives  
> To venerate with equal devotion  
> And singular praise.
>
> Burned by fire, his body  
> Becomes renowned by land and sea.  
> Jesus, graciously grant us  
> That with the saints we may worthily  
> Praise you in our homeland. Amen.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1479C] A body burned by fire.** *Ustulare*, “to burn” or “to consume by fire,” is derived from *uro*, whose supine is *ustum*. Pacuvius: “To burn the hair with glowing iron.” Hence the participle *ustulatus*, that is, “scorched” or “burned.” Livy: “A few half-burned men came into captivity.”
>
> ## XVIII. ON THE CONVERSION OF SAINT PAUL
>
> **[Col. 1479B]**
>
> This prose has a rhythmic composition similar to the preceding one, but not so varied. For here every verse always contains three rhythmic clauses, the last of which always ends in seven syllables. The preceding clauses contain sometimes seven syllables, as in the second verse; sometimes eight, as in the first; and sometimes ten, as in the fourth. Its author is Adam of Saint Victor. It describes the wondrous conversion of blessed Paul to Christ, explained in Acts of the Apostles, chapter 9; his zeal and diligence in preaching the Gospel, clearly evident also from his epistles and the sacred history of Acts; and finally the blessed completion of his course in martyrdom.
>
> **[Col. 1479C]** With heart and voice raised to heaven,  
> Church of the Gentiles, sing  
> A triumphal melody.
>
> Paul, teacher of the Gentiles,  
> **[Col. 1480A]** Completed his race,  
> Triumphing in glory.
>
> Here is Benjamin, a young man,  
> A ravening wolf, feeding on prey,  
> The enemy of the faithful.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1479C–D] Here is Benjamin, a young man.** This sentence is drawn from the prophecy of Jacob himself, who, blessing his sons before his death, said to Benjamin: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf: in the morning he shall devour the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Genesis 49). The gloss in the same place declares that these words are to be understood of blessed Paul: “Paul is signified, who was of Benjamin, who at the beginning persecuted the faithful, but in the evening divided the spoils because, having become faithful, he dispensed the sacred writings.”
>
> A wolf in the morning, but a sheep at evening;  
> After darkness, when the star shines,  
> He teaches the Gospel.
>
> He takes up the way of death,  
> Whom the way of life seizes  
> As he journeys to Damascus.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1479D] Here he takes up the way of death.** The way of death is that broad road which leads to perdition. Whoever commits sin and, neglecting God, hastens toward destruction takes up that way. But Christ is the way of life, who says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14).
>
> He breathes threats, but now yields;  
> Being cast down, he now obeys;  
> And now he is led bound.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1479D–1480C] But now he is led bound.** This must not be understood of material chains. For his companions, who led him by the hand to Damascus because he was blinded and almost deprived of sight by the apparition made to him on the road, did not bind him with chains, since they were his intimates and household companions (Acts 9). It should rather be understood of the bonds of obedience to God, by which he was so bound that he willingly went wherever God commanded him to go.
>
> He is sent to Ananias;  
> **[Col. 1480B]** The wolf is led to the sheep;  
> His savage mind grows calm.
>
> He undergoes the sacrament of the font;  
> The life-giving water  
> Changes poison into balm.
>
> A sacred vessel, a divine vessel,  
> A vessel offering sweet wine  
> Of teaching grace.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1480C] A sacred vessel, a divine vessel.** The author alludes to those words of the Lord spoken to Ananias concerning Paul: “Go, for this man is a vessel of election to me, to bear my name before Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel” (ibid.). Indeed, he himself was a marvellous vessel and a work of the Most High, adorned with every precious stone of graces and virtues (Ecclesiasticus 43).
>
> He goes through the synagogues;  
> He establishes Christ’s faith  
> By the sequence of the prophets.
>
> He proclaims the word of the cross;  
> For the cause of the cross he is tortured;  
> In a thousand ways he dies.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1480C–D] He proclaims the word of the cross.** “The word of the cross” here means faith in Christ crucified, the Saviour of the whole world. Of him Paul says: “But we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling-block indeed to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (1 Corinthians 1). Paul also uses this mode of speech when he says: “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish” (ibid.). Thus, in the sixteenth verse, the cross is said to triumph, because through Paul’s preaching faith in Christ’s cross spread everywhere and eliminated from the world the worship of idols and the filth of superstitions. How grave were the persecutions and torments Paul suffered for the word of the cross, and how often he was among deaths and in dangers, is more fully explained in 2 Corinthians, chapters 11 and 12; there also mention is made of his rapture into heaven, of which the fourteenth verse speaks.
>
> **[Col. 1480C]** Yet he remains a living sacrifice,  
> And by unconquered constancy  
> Every punishment is overcome.
>
> Separated out, he teaches the Gentiles,  
> He conquers the world’s wise  
> By God’s wisdom.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1480D–1481C] Separated out, he teaches the Gentiles.** This corresponds to the words of blessed Paul, who, writing to the Romans, calls himself an apostle called and “separated unto the Gospel of God” (Romans 1 [the printed text has “II”]). It also corresponds to the statement in Acts: “As they ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said to them: ‘Separate for me Saul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13). He is said to teach the Gentiles because he was chosen by God for this ministry, to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles, as Paul himself testifies concerning himself to the Galatians: “But when it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles” (Galatians 1). Thus the remaining statements of this prose should likewise be referred to some passage in either Acts of the Apostles or Paul’s epistles from which they have been drawn.
>
> **[Col. 1481A]** Caught up to the third heaven,  
> He sees the Father and the Son  
> In one substance.
>
> Mighty Rome and learned Greece  
> Bow their necks and learn the mysteries;  
> Christ’s faith prospers.
>
> The cross triumphs; Nero rages;  
> The faith grew through his teaching,  
> And Nero kills Paul by the sword.
>
> Thus, stripped of the burden of flesh,  
> Paul sees the true sun,  
> The Father’s only-begotten.
>
> He sees light in light,  
> By whose divine power may we avoid  
> A hellish end. Amen.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1481C–D] He sees light in light.** That is, God the Father in the Son, who is light from light, according to the verse of the Psalm from which this passage is taken: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35 [Vulgate numbering]). Or Paul sees God, who is the true light, in the spiritual and supra-intellectual light of heavenly glory.
>
> ## XIX. ON THE PURIFICATION OF BLESSED MARY
>
> This prose has a rather uniform rhythmic composition. For in nearly every verse all the rhythmic clauses have eight syllables and a long penultimate, except in the fifteenth and sixteenth verses, where the individual clauses are restricted to seven syllables and have a short penultimate. Its author is Adam of Saint Victor. In it the most sacred Virgin Mary is commended in many ways for the outstanding endowments and gifts of grace with which she was enriched by the Lord. She is also shown to have been foreshadowed by many figures of the ancient law and distinguished by various names under which she is recognized as honoured and praised in the page of Old Testament Scripture.
>
> A venerable light has come,  
> A light to be celebrated in choirs  
> With radiant hearts.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1481D–1482C] A light to be celebrated in choirs.** *Chorus*, with aspiration, sometimes signifies an assembly and multitude of people, and, as it were, the garland of those gathered for games or of those dancing and singing, for it consists in the voices and harmony of many. Jerome: “Wherever there is a choir, diverse voices are gathered into one song. For just as different strings produce one song’s sound, so diverse voices, when gathered together, make the Lord’s choir.” Its first syllable is short. Virgil: “Feasting, and singing a joyful paean in chorus.” The same author: “Whom all the choir and rejoicing companions accompany.” Sometimes, however, as Jerome writes to Dardanus, a *chorus* is a musical instrument made of a single skin with two bronze pipes: one is breathed into and through the other the sound is emitted. This is the sense in the Psalm: “Praise the Lord with drum and chorus; praise him with strings and organ” (Psalm 150). Here it may be taken in either of the two senses given, for in both the meaning is fitting.
>
> The joyful light of this day  
> Recalls a feast  
> To be dedicated to praises of the Mother of God.
>
> Let the voice exult in melody;  
> Let the heart resound from its inmost marrow,  
> Lest praise be useless.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1482C–D] Let the heart resound from its inmost marrow.** By “marrow” the author here indicates the fatness and richness of the spirit and the heart’s affectionate motion toward God. Praise is useless where there is only vocal melody while the mind itself lies inert, languishes dry, and is moved by no affection toward God.
>
> Thus let praise be sung to God,  
> That in it may be praised  
> His noble Mother.
>
> Glorious in dignity,  
> Full of tender mercy,  
> Piercing hearts by her name,  
> She shines in heaven’s height  
> With matronly honour  
> And virginal modesty.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1482C–D] Piercing hearts by her name.** Because her name, frequently invoked, brings the compunction of devotion into human hearts, as does the name of Jesus, blessed for ever. Those who often have that venerable name upon their lips feel a certain distinctive motion of the heart toward God which otherwise they would not perceive.
>
> Once the bush was burning,  
> Yet the fire did not consume it  
> Or harm its greenness.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1482D] Once the bush was burning.** The bush seen by Moses burning (Exodus 3), yet unharmed, signified the unviolated virginity of the Mother of God, as was also said previously in the second book in the explanation of the antiphon, “The bush which Moses saw unconsumed.” Further, the verb *noceo* (“to harm”) almost always requires a dative. Yet it is sometimes found joined to an accusative in Holy Scripture, as in Judith’s song: “But the Lord Almighty harmed him and delivered him into the hands of a woman, and she pierced him” (Judith 16). And in Luke’s Gospel: “And when the demon had thrown him into the midst, it came out of him and harmed him not at all” (Luke 4). So it is used here too, though this is not to be imitated.
>
> Thus, by spiritual ardour,  
> Not by conjugal touch,  
> The Virgin bore God.
>
> This is the sealed fountain,  
> The enclosed garden, made fruitful  
> By the seeds of virtues.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1482D–1483C] This is that sealed fountain.** The sacred Virgin Mary is also indicated by that fountain and garden of which Solomon says in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song of Songs 4). A garden, I say, enclosed by divine protection and the fortifications of virtues, so that hostile snares may not find entrance into it; likewise a fountain sealed with the seal of the whole Trinity and with the special seal of the Son of God himself.
>
> **[Col. 1483A]** This is that closed gate  
> Which God, for a hidden reason,  
> Had shut to human beings.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1483C] This is that closed gate.** As has already been said in the preceding prose, Ezekiel’s closed gate (chapter 44) signifies the untouched integrity of the holy Mother of God. God closed it to all human beings, so that it might be passable for himself alone and yet always closed. The reason for this closure was then hidden from humanity; but now, as he himself reveals it and opens the mystery through the fact accomplished, it has been made plain.
>
> This is the fleece drawing down dew,  
> The full field giving fragrance  
> To all the ends of the earth.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1483C–D] This is the fleece drawing down dew.** The blessed Mother of God was also signified by Gideon’s fleece watered by heavenly dew (Judges 6): alone among all women made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, she brought forth heavenly offspring. She was signified by the field full of fruits and wonderfully fragrant, of which Isaac, about to bless his son Jacob, said: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Genesis 27).
>
> This is the rod bearing a flower,  
> The earth bringing forth  
> Its Saviour for the faithful.
>
> **[Note: Col. 1483D] This is the rod bearing a flower.** The consecrated Virgin was likewise signified by Aaron’s rod, blooming without aid from the earth and laden with fruit (Numbers 17; printed text: “XXVII”). Thus she too brought forth fruit without a man’s assistance, fruit bringing salvation to the entire world. Finally, the most holy Mother of God was signified by that earth of which Isaiah says: “Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” (Isaiah 45). Indeed, she herself is that mystical earth, blessed by the Lord, which brought forth the Saviour.

[Note: [Col. 1483D] This is said by way of example. Six illustrious names are expressed here, by which the blessed Virgin Mary is designated and named in the sacred Scriptures. First, she is called a mountain in Daniel, when, in explaining the dream of the king of Babylon, he says that a stone cut from a mountain without hands struck the statue and crushed it (Dan. II). There the stone is understood as Christ, and the mountain as [Col. 1484C] the blessed Virgin Mary, lofty in excellence of virtues and surpassing other human beings, from whom Christ’s birth without human intercourse is there also indicated. Second, she herself is called a fortress, especially in that passage of Luke’s Gospel: “Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha received him into her house” (Luke X). There, according to the mystical sense, the holy Virgin Mary is understood under the name of the village, as Anselm attests in his homily on the same Gospel. Third, she is called the hall of God, because the Son of God deigned to dwell in her as in his tabernacle, as in the allegorically understood verse of the Psalm: “Worship the Lord in his holy hall” (Ps. XXVIII); or, as another translation has it, “in his holy court.” Fourth, she is called the temple of the Lord, as in that mystically understood verse of the Psalm: “We have received, O God, your mercy in the midst of your temple” (Ps. XLVII). Fifth, she is called the bridal chamber of God, as when the prophet says of our Lord that “he is like a bridegroom coming forth [Col. 1484D] from his bridal chamber” (Ps. XVIII). Sixth, she too is called the city of God, as in that metaphorically understood Psalm saying: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI). And in a similar manner, as the following verse says, the exalted designation of other distinguished and illustrious names is assigned to this same sacred Virgin in Scripture, since by the names already mentioned other names which occur throughout the sacred writings are likewise to be understood.]

This is said, by way of example,

Mountain, fortress, hall, temple,

Bridal chamber, and city.

[40] Thus to the same one the loftiness

Of other chosen

Names is assigned.

[Col. 1483B] Whose prayers overcome vices,

Whose name overcomes sorrows,

[45] Whose fragrance surpasses lilies,

Whose lips surpass

The honeycomb in sweetness.

More savoury than wine,

Whiter than snow,

[50] Dewier than the rose,

Brighter than the moon,

By the radiance of the true sun.

Empress of those above,

Conqueress of those below,

[55] [Col. 1484A] Path to heaven to be chosen,

To be held fast in faithful hope:

Those separated far from you,

Join, once recalled by you,

To the fellowship of your own.

[60] Good Mother, whom we beseech,

Grant us what we desire.

Do not so reject sinners

That you do not behold petitioners

Guilty and despairing of themselves,

[65] Yet trusting in you:

Present them to your Son. Amen.

## XX. ON THE FINDING OF THE HOLY CROSS

[Col. 1484B] This prose follows the pattern of rhythmic modulation found in that concerning the holy sacrament of the Eucharist, *Lauda, Sion, salvatorem* (“Praise, O Zion, the Saviour”). Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It celebrates with distinguished praises the glories of the holy Cross, recounting the figures of the ancient Law by which it was prefigured, and its power displayed in the new Law through the victories of the emperors Constantine and Heraclius. Then, proclaiming its wondrous power, it sets forth the vows and supplication of the faithful people addressed to it.

Let us exalt the praises of the Cross,

We who exult in the Cross

With special glory.

[Note: [Col. 1484D] For in the Cross we triumph. This verse is absent from most books and has been omitted; yet it is not superfluous—indeed, it is necessary to the integrity of the rhythm, so that the first verse may have a line whose ending of intermediate syllables answers to it. Otherwise either no verse with a like cadential ending will correspond to the first verse, or three successive verses will be given, mutually rhyming at their ends. Both alternatives are contrary to the law of rhythm, in which always two verses, neither more [Col. 1485B] nor fewer, have a reciprocal correspondence in their final cadence.] For in the Cross we triumph,

[5] [Col. 1485A] We overcome the fierce enemy

With life-giving victory.

Let sweet melody reach the heavens;

We deem the sweet wood worthy

Of sweet song.

[10] Let life not discord with the voice.

[Note: [Col. 1485B] While the voice does not reproach life. When both our lips praise God and our deeds are performed according to the rule of his commandments, then the voice does not reproach life, nor does life discord with the voice. But if our voice sounds divine praises while we perform deeds contrary to God’s commandments, such a melody of praise is unwelcome to God; for, as Ecclesiasticus says, “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV), and the man newly given sight says in the Gospel: “We know [Col. 1485C] that God does not hear sinners” (John IX).] While the voice does not reproach life,

Sweet is the harmony.

Let servants of the Cross praise the Cross,

Who through the Cross rejoice that

[15] The gifts of life are given them.

Let all speak, and let each one speak:

Hail, salvation of the whole age,

Life-giving tree!

O how blessed, how illustrious

[20] [Col. 1485B] Was this altar of salvation,

Red with the blood of the Lamb—

The spotless Lamb,

Who cleansed the ages

From ancient sin.

[25] [Col. 1486A] [Note: [Col. 1485C] This is the ladder of sinners. The holy Cross is mystically called the ladder of sinners, because through it, and through the sacrifice of the true Lamb made upon it, sinners ascend to heaven. It is fittingly prefigured by that ladder extending from the lowest earth to the summit of heaven, which Jacob saw in a dream; upon it he also beheld the Lord standing, and the angels of the Lord ascending and descending by it (Gen. XXVIII). That Christ drew all things to himself through it is attested by his words to the Jews: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” “But this he said,” as the Evangelist adds, “signifying by what death he was to die” (John XII). Now Christ was lifted up from the earth when he was raised upon the Cross, and it is only of this kind of lifting-up that he speaks there.] This is the ladder of sinners,

Through which Christ, King of heaven,

Drew all things to himself.

Its form demonstrates this,

For it encompasses the earth’s

[30] [Note: [Col. 1485C] Four boundaries: namely, east, west, south, and north, the four regions [Col. 1485D] of the earth. Thus, if the front of the Cross, to which the Lord was affixed, faced west—as Christian devotion customarily represents the crucified Christ at the very centre of churches—the rear faced east; the left hand faced south, and the right north. Thus the four extremities of the earth are encompassed in the figure of the Cross. If anyone should say that Christ crucified faced east, or any other region of heaven, the figure of the Cross will still assign four directions corresponding to the same number of regions of the earth. But what else did this signify except that, through the mystery of the Cross, people from the four regions of the earth were to be called to salvation and to acknowledgment of the true God? “Many,” says the Lord in the Gospel, “shall come from east and west, and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VIII). And Isaiah, announcing the calling of the nations to faith, says: “Behold, these shall come from afar; behold, those from the north and the sea, and these from the southern land [Col. 1486B]” (Isa. XLIX). Another explanation of the four boundaries of the earth according to the figure of the Cross will be given a little later in the exposition of the fifteenth verse.] Four boundaries.

These are not new mysteries,

Nor has this religion

Of the Cross been recently invented.

[Note: [Col. 1486B] It made bitter waters sweet. By the wood shown by God to Moses and cast into the exceedingly bitter waters of Marah, by which the waters themselves were turned to sweetness (Exod. XV), the holy Cross is understood. Its shame and bitterness, borne by Christ, were transformed into the sweetness, delight, and grace of the redemption of the entire world. Likewise, by the rod which, in Moses’ ministry, struck the rock and brought waters forth from it (Exod. [Col. 1486C] XVII), the holy Cross is also signified: from Christ, the spiritual rock, pierced by a soldier’s spear, it poured forth water saving to the whole world.] It made bitter waters sweet.

[35] Through it the rock cast forth waters,

By Moses’ ministry.

[Note: [Col. 1486C] There is no safety in a house. Both doorposts and the lintels of the Israelites’ houses, sprinkled with the blood of the sacrificed lamb (Exod. XII), were types and figures of the life-giving Cross, sprinkled with the precious blood of the spotless Lamb. For as the Hebrews were delivered from the angel striking down the firstborn of Egypt by such staining and sprinkling with the blood of the typical lamb, so by the power of the saving Cross we are delivered from the assault and attack of demons. When they behold the Lord’s Cross, unable to endure its presence, they flee in terror and lose the power to injure.] There is no safety in a house,

Unless a person has fortified

Its lintels with the Cross.

[40] [Col. 1486B] Nor did anyone suffer the sword

Or lose a son

Who did these things.

[Note: [Col. 1486C] Gathering wood at Zarephath. The widow of Zarephath—to whom Elijah was sent by the Lord, that she might sustain him—is written to have gathered two pieces of wood (3 Kings XVII), in order to cook food for herself and her son. Obeying the prophet’s word, she first baked him a hearth-cake; and neither her oil in the flask or oil-jar nor her flour in the jar was diminished, through the continual provision of food from them for her whole household, until the Lord should give rain upon the earth, according to Elijah’s word. Moreover, those two pieces of wood gathered by the widow represent the holy Cross, consisting chiefly of two parts: one stretched lengthwise from top to bottom, the other extended crosswise from right to left. Correspondingly, the Cross of the Lord supplies four distinct positions of the world, which may likewise be understood by the four boundaries expressed in the tenth verse: namely, above and below, right and left, assigned according to the Cross’s four extremities. This signifies that Christ, by the death of the Cross which he endured, opened for us the heavenly kingdoms which are above; broke the infernal realms which are below; and drew back to himself all earthly things situated in the middle, which, as it were, constitute right and left through the stretching out and embrace of his [Col. 1487B] arms. Thus he received dominion and sovereignty over heavenly, earthly, and infernal things, and reconciled to God the Father all things above, below, and in between through the blood of the Cross. By those same two pieces of wood which constitute the holy Cross are also understood its four dimensions and positions: length, breadth, height, and depth, from which the figure of the Cross is formed. As blessed Augustine explains in expounding the Apostle’s saying to the Ephesians: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is [Col. 1487C] the breadth and length and height and depth” (Eph. III). “In these words,” he says, “the figure and mystery of the Cross are shown. For its breadth is the transverse wood on which the hands are nailed; its length is the part extending from that transverse beam to the ground, visible from it down to the ground. The height of the Cross is the wood which projects upward from the same transverse beam toward the head. Its depth is the part of the wood which does not appear, because, planted in the earth, it is hidden.” Thus Augustine.] Gathering wood at Zarephath,

The poor little woman obtained

[45] [Col. 1487A] The hope of salvation.

Without the woods of faith,

Neither the flask of oil

Nor the little store of flour avails.

[Note: [Col. 1487C] Rome saw all the ships. As *Ecclesiastical History*, book XI, chapter 9 relates, the emperor Constantine, about to fight Maxentius, who was then exercising tyranny at Rome, had implored divine help before joining battle with the enemy. He saw in the air a Cross flashing with ruddy brightness, and an angel saying to him: “In this sign, Constantine, you will conquer.” At once he ordered the sign of the Cross to be depicted and formed on all his standards. Maxentius had treacherously laid bridges of ships across the Milvian Bridge, so that, when Constantine crossed there, the ships would sink under excessive weight and—thinking the bridges sound—he and his whole army would be drowned. But hearing that Constantine was approaching Rome, Maxentius rushed hurriedly out of the Roman gates to meet him. Forgetting his own trap, he led his troops at a headlong pace over those bridges, fell into the pit he had made, and was drowned in the river with his soldiers; indeed, the ships too, pressed by the excessive weight, were submerged in the waters. In this way Constantine gained victory without the shedding of human blood, which he had especially begged of God.] Rome saw all the ships

[50] Sunk in the depths,

Together with Maxentius.

[Note: [Col. 1487D] The Thracians routed, the Persians slain. Under the Roman emperor Heraclius, Chosroes, king of the Persians, having assembled a great army, invaded the borders of the Roman Empire and harassed Syria and Palestine with a grievous incursion, devastating all things by plundering and fire. [Col. 1488B] To check his attack, Heraclius too assembled forces and halted at the Danube, where Chosroes’ son met him with a most fully equipped host of soldiers. Heraclius, aided by God, whom before the encounter he had most earnestly invoked through devout appeal to the holy Cross, attacked and defeated him in single combat upon a bridge over the Danube. Then, after Chosroes was killed, he brought back with due honour and reverence to Jerusalem a part of the holy Cross which that impious man had carried off from it. Hence the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross began to be observed in the Church, as the history of the aforesaid solemnity explains more fully.] The Thracians routed, the Persians slain;

And the leader of the opposing party too

Was conquered by Heraclius.

[55] In the Scriptures these things lie hidden under figures,

But now the benefits of the Cross

Are manifest.

Kings believe; enemies yield.

By the Cross alone, with Christ as leader,

[60] [Col. 1487B] [Note: [Col. 1488C] One puts thousands to flight. This statement is drawn from the Lord’s promise to the people of Israel in Leviticus: “Five of you shall pursue a hundred strangers, and a hundred of you ten thousand” (Lev. XXVI); and from the words of Moses’ song: “How could one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight?” (Deut. XXXII). Just as these promises are sometimes read as fulfilled among the patriarchs of the Old Testament, especially under the godly kings of Judah and the renowned Maccabees, so they were fulfilled in the New Testament under those glorious Christian kings and princes who, armed with the mighty Cross of Christ, undertook campaigns against the enemies of the faith and drove them out of their territories.] One puts thousands to flight.

It always makes its own people stronger

And victorious.

It heals illnesses and infirmities;

[Col. 1488A] It represses demons.

[65] It gives captives freedom,

Grants renewal of life,

And restores all things

To their former dignity.

O Cross, triumphant wood,

[70] True salvation of the world, hail!

[Note: [Col. 1488C] No wood among woods is like it. This praise of the Cross corresponds to that song sung in praise of it in the hymn on the Lord’s Passion:

> Faithful Cross, among all,
> The one noble tree;
> 
> [Col. 1488D] No forest brings forth another such,
> In leaf, flower, and fruit.

Since the author calls the holy Cross a tree, he continues the fitting metaphorical expression by naming its leaf, flower, and fruit. These, however, must be understood mystically and referred to Christ, who alone is the leaf, flower, and fruit of that tree: its leaf, because of the unfading verdure and vigour of his virtues; its flower, because of the most sweet fragrance and surpassing beauty of his goodness; and its fruit, because of the fruit and benefit of his Passion gathered from that tree. Whatever is said here about the Cross must be understood not absolutely, as directed to the material of the Cross, but by referring it to Christ fastened upon it, who consecrated and sanctified it by his glorious Passion.] No wood among woods is like it,

In leaf, flower, and fruit.

Christian medicine,

Keep the healthy safe; heal the sick.

[75] What human strength cannot accomplish

Is done in your name.

You who attend the Cross’s praise,

Consecrator of the Cross, hear;

[Col. 1488B] And your servants of the Cross,

[80] After this life transfer

To the palaces of true light.

[Note: [Col. 1488D] Those whom you will to serve punishment. God himself does not, by his primary will and in himself, will anyone to perish; rather, according to blessed Paul’s saying, “he wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. II). Yet consequently, and in view of human deeds, he is said to will those to serve punishment who have earned by their sins the eternal penalties of Gehenna. For the rectitude of his justice requires that persons persisting in evil until the end of life be consigned to infernal punishments. This prayer therefore asks that he grant, while time remains, to those whom he recognizes—according to their present state and the dispensation of their deeds—to be worthy of perpetual damnation, the grace to amend their lives and by repentance escape the punishments which they deserve. Finally, this author calls the day of final judgment the day [Col. 1489D] of wrath, because it is so called in the prophet Zephaniah, who says: “The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man shall be distressed there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and alarm, against fortified cities and against lofty angels” (Zeph. I).] Those whom you will to serve punishment,

[Col. 1489A] Grant not to feel punishments.

But when the day of wrath comes,

[85] Bestow and grant us

Everlasting joys. Amen.

## XXI. ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

This prose is very similar in the form of its rhythmic composition to that prose on Saint Nicholas explained earlier, *Congaudentes exsultemus, vocali concordia* (“Let us rejoice together and exult in vocal harmony”). For it too has a variety of rhythms in its different verses. Some verses have only two rhythmic clauses, the first corresponding to the first clause of the next verse in the rhyme of their final syllables, and the second to the second. Other verses contain three rhythmic clauses: the first two mutually rhyming [Col. 1489B] with each other, and the third corresponding to the third clause of the next verse. Verses also occur consisting of four clauses, of which the first corresponds to the third and the second to the fourth. Finally, other forms of rhythm will present themselves here to readers and may easily be perceived from reading alone. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. This prose celebrates the illustrious praises of blessed John the Baptist: his conception, birth, the miracles divinely displayed in them, the privileges of his graces, and his manifold dignity.

In honour of you, Christ,

Let the Church commemorate

The birthday feast

Of your Forerunner and Baptist.

[5] [Note: [Col. 1489D] The king’s praise is in his herald’s proclamation. Just as the Lord is praised in his saints because he, the source of all holiness and the only Holy One, advanced them to holiness, so, when blessed John, the lofty-speaking herald of Christ, is praised, that praise redounds to God, who endowed him with such great gifts of grace. Whoever praises a skillfully made work also praises the industrious craftsman of that work.] The king’s praise lies in the proclamation

[Col. 1489C] Of his own herald,

Whom he enriches with gifts of virtues

And exalts by his office.

When Gabriel promised

[10] A son to the old man,

He hesitated and lost

The use of speech.

A child is born:

Herald, trumpet, standard-bearer

[15] Of the new Law and the new King.

[Note: [Col. 1489D] The voice precedes the Word. Just as blessed John’s birth preceded the birth of our Saviour by the course of six months, so John preceded Christ in the ministry of baptizing, preaching, [Col. 1490C] and dying for justice and truth. This was fitting: John was the voice of one crying in the wilderness, while Christ was the Word of God the Father. John also was the bridegroom’s friend and attendant, whereas Christ was the Bridegroom of the Church. Finally, John was the rising morning star and herald of the day of the new Law; Christ, however, is the sun of justice.] The voice precedes the Word;

The bridegroom’s attendant precedes the Bridegroom;

The morning star precedes the sun’s rising.

The mother by word, the father by writing,

[20] Gives the child his name;

And the father’s mute tongue,

Released from its bond, is loosed.

John is foreshadowed by a heavenly

Oracle,

[25] And revealed from the very hiding-place

[Col. 1490B] Of the womb.

[Note: [Col. 1490C] Because at an untimely age. Abraham, already a hundred years old, had from his wife Sarah, ninety years old, the son of promise, Isaac, whom God appointed heir of his father’s goods (Gen. XXI). This was a figure of the birth of blessed John also from barren parents, by heavenly admonition. For many things in the birth of each—Isaac, that is, and John—correspond to each other, attesting divine power. John is therefore foreshadowed by a heavenly oracle, as the preceding verse says, not only by the angel who announced his birth, but also by the figures of the Old Testament and by the prophecies of Isaiah, Malachi, and the Psalms concerning him. Isaiah foretold him by the voice crying in the wilderness (Isa. XL); Malachi by the angel sent before the Lord’s face (Mal. III [printed “XXXII”]); and the Psalm by the lamp prepared for Christ the Lord (Ps. CXXXI). Likewise, from the very hiding-place of the womb John was shown beforehand to be what and how great he would become. For that leaping in his mother’s womb at Christ’s presence provided clear evidence that he would at last be great before the Lord.] What is given as an heir at an untimely age

Is a figure of what a parent,

Long barren—a profound matter—

[30] Brings forth.

Against the laws of flesh indeed,

John’s birth is of this kind.

Grace, not nature,

Forms such offspring.

[35] A virgin encloses God in her womb;

This one, enclosed, rejoices at the enclosed one,

Despite the confinement of the womb.

In the open, the voice crying in the wilderness

Shows the Lamb—

[40] [Col. 1490C] The voice that heralds the Word.

Burning with faith, shining by the Word,

And leading many thousands to the true light,

He teaches.

[Note: [Col. 1490D] This man was not the light, but a lamp. John was not that primal and true light which enlightens [Col. 1491C] every person coming into this world (John I). The Evangelist testifies this thus: “He was not the light, but was to bear witness to the light” (ibid.). John, however, was a lamp and a brightly shining light, bringing and presenting that primary light to human eyes, just as our Lord bears witness concerning him: “He was a burning and shining lamp” (John V). But because Christ is God, he is eternal and unfailing light, casting the beneficent rays of his brightness upon all: “I,” he says, “am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John VIII).] This man was not the light, but a lamp;

[45] [Col. 1491A] Christ, however, is eternal light,

Light enlightening all things.

Clothed in a garment of haircloth,

Girded with a belt of skin,

With locusts he took wild honey

[50] For food.

With Christ himself testifying of him,

No greater man has arisen than he,

Born of woman.

[Note: [Col. 1491C] Christ excepted himself in this way. In the Lord’s saying that among those born of women none greater than John the Baptist has arisen, the statement concerns males alone and those begotten in the customary course of nature. Therefore the most sacred Mother of God, undoubtedly greater than John, is excepted from this universality. Our Lord too is excepted: born indeed of a woman, but above nature’s law and without intercourse with a man. Further, in the third clause of the preceding verse the author made its penultimate syllable long, since the noun *mulier* (“woman”) lengthens the penultimate syllable in the oblique cases. Yet, under the rule of rhythmic metre, he ought there to have placed the short penultimate syllable of some word, so that in quantity as well as ending that clause would correspond to the final clause of the present verse, to which it must be compared. But compelled by a lack of vocabulary and the need to express the meaning, he did this contrary to the law of rhythm.] Christ excepted himself thus,

[55] He who took flesh from flesh

Without the work of the flesh.

Martyr of God, although we are guilty

And unworthy

Of your praise,

[60] [Col. 1491B] Hear us,

Who praise you and hope

In your mercy.

[Note: [Col. 1491D] *Natali* in “Tuo nobis in natale.” *Natalis* is masculine; *natale* is neuter; and *natalitium, -ii* is used for the day on which someone was born. Virgil:

> Send Phyllis to me: Iollas, it is my birthday.

Here too *natalis* may be masculine or feminine, *natale* neuter, and *natalitius, -a, -um*, with the same meaning; but the substantive *dies* (“day”) is added to them. Pope Leo: “Let us therefore celebrate the birthday [Col. 1492C] day of the Lord.” The substantive noun *natalis* has in the singular ablative more commonly *natali*. Ovid:

> Alas for me, torn apart on your birthday.

Yet this author, to preserve the similar final ending with the first clause of the following verse, to which it must correspond, formed the ablative *natale*, which is certainly rarer and less customary.] On your birthday feast

Give us the promised joy.

[65] Nor let your triumphant

Martyrdom delight us less.

We venerate and marvel at

So many mysteries in you.

May Christ grant us, through you,

[70] To enjoy his presence. Amen.

## XXII. ON SAINT PETER THE APOSTLE

[Col. 1491C] This prose keeps the form of rhythmic metre, like the prose on John the Forerunner and Baptist explained a little earlier. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It contains illustrious praises of blessed Peter: his ready conversion to Christ, the frequency and remarkable efficacy of his miracles, his sincere confession of faith, his conflict with Simon Magus and victory over him, and finally his death on the Cross inflicted by Nero. Much of this is evident from the sacred history of the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles and requires no fuller elucidation here.

[Note: [Col. 1492C] Rejoice, Rome, head of the world. Rome is here called the head of the world because of the dominion and monarchy which it once held throughout the whole world, as was said a little above. Hence Virgil says of it:

> Thus too Rome was made the most beautiful of all things.

And:

> He calls the Romans lords of the world, a people clad in the toga.

This verse urges Rome to rejoice because in her blessed Peter, the first of all pontiffs, governed the Apostolic See, consecrated her with his blood, and adorns her with his sacred body. Christ, however, is the first shepherd, who says of himself: “I am the good shepherd” (John X). Blessed Peter is the second shepherd, to whom the Lord likewise said a third time: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI; printed “XI”).] Rejoice, Rome, head of the world.

Let the first shepherd be praised in the victory

Of the second.

Let the whole world rejoice;

[5] And let the ardour of virtue increase

From the memory of Peter.

Peter, torch of sacred love,

[Col. 1492B] Light of doctrine, salt of sweetness;

Peter, mountain of righteousness.

[10] Peter is a fountain of the Saviour:

A tree of fruit and fragrance,

A tree lacking decay.

And what worthy thing will you say of Peter?

At Christ’s first summons, seeing no sign,

[15] He left his net, left his boat,

Not yet fully beholding

The truth in spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1492D] Lacking gold and silver. For when Peter first said to the poor man lame from his mother’s womb: “Gold and silver I do not possess; but what I have I give to you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk,” immediately his feet and ankles were strengthened, and, leaping up, he stood and walked, glorifying God (Acts III). Likewise, as the following verse says, Aeneas, afflicted for eight years with paralysis and lying on a bed, heard Peter say: “Aeneas, the Lord Jesus Christ heals you. Rise and make your bed.” Immediately he rose up sound. Because of this sign [Col. 1493B] many inhabitants of the city of Lydda were converted to the Lord (Acts IX).] Lacking gold and silver,

[20] He shines with miracles.

At the instant he releases the lame man

[Col. 1492C] From the bonds of his sinews.

Aeneas, weakened by paralysis,

[Col. 1493A] Is raised up.

[25] God’s present power attends Peter

In accordance with his desire.

[Note: [Col. 1493C] Peter gives life to Tabitha. This is taken from the Acts of the Apostles, where a certain female disciple of Christ, named Tabitha or Dorcas, in Joppa, full of good works, is said to have died of a severe illness. Peter, summoned to her by the disciples, poured out prayer to God and restored her to life. When the novelty of this sign had been spread throughout all Joppa, many believed in the Lord (ibid.). But that Peter also restored a young man to life, as this verse says, is not found in sacred Scripture, so far as I remember, but in some other history unknown to me; nevertheless, it should not be wholly disbelieved. For sacred Scripture does not encompass the whole body of the apostles’ miracles.] Peter gives life to Tabitha

And restores a young man to life

By free power.

[30] He treads the waves of the sea;

And, when he wavers, a saving

Hand directs him.

[Note: [Col. 1493C] When Christ asked the question. Christ’s question to the disciples was: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter’s answer follows: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI). In this answer Peter expresses Christ’s unity of person, as the following verse says, for he confesses him to be both Christ and Son of God, and indicates him by the same pronoun. Peter also intimates in those words the distinction of Christ’s two natures, divine and human. For in calling him Christ, he indicates his human nature, according to which he was anointed by God with the oil of gladness above his companions (Ps. XLIV). But in confessing that same one to be the Son of God, he indicates his divine nature.] When Christ asked the question,

In a brief statement he encloses

[35] The necessary faith.

He calls this one person one;

Yet he does not leave unspoken

The fitting distinction of natures.

[Col. 1493B] Though by denying three times he sinned,

[40] [Note: [Col. 1493D] A simple love atoned for it. After Christ had appeared to the disciples for the third time after rising from the dead, and after the plentiful catch of fish, he asked Peter once, twice, and three times whether he loved him. Peter always answered that Christ knew and perceived that he loved him (John XXI). This answer expresses Peter’s simple, single, and ever-unchanging love for Christ; yet that love is affirmed by a threefold confession, made three times, so that this threefold confession of love might wipe away the guilt of his threefold denial in Christ’s Passion [Col. 1494B] (Matt. XXVI).] A simple love atoned for it,

And a threefold confession.

An angel freely releases Peter

From prison,

Doomed to the sword.

[45] His shadow heals the sick;

It heals bodies, heals minds,

Makes diseases powerless

By the power of the physician.

Simon Magus hates Peter;

[50] Simon Peter exposes the magician.

[Col. 1494A] He warns and guards the people

Against the magician’s deceit.

[Note: [Col. 1494B] Here Peter is said to be from the rock. Many manuscripts arrange the first clause of this verse thus: “Here the rock is said to be from Peter”; but this is wrongly and corruptly written. For blessed Peter is nowhere read to have been called “rock” by the Lord, since that name belongs properly to Christ alone, as the Apostle testifies to the Corinthians: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X). And when, in Matthew, the Lord is read to have said to Peter, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI), by “this rock” he means not Peter but himself; for the Church was founded not upon Peter but upon Christ, as the stone laid in the foundations. Moreover, the rock is not named from Peter, but Peter from the rock, just as Christ is not named from Christian, but Christian derived from Christ. Therefore that first rhythmic clause should rather be read: “Here Peter is said to be from the rock.” The sense of the entire verse will then be appropriate: because Peter resembled a rock in the steadfastness of his faith and in unconquered courage in conflict against the wicked, [Col. 1494D] he received that name from it.] Here Peter is said to be from the rock;

In conflict he stands unconquered,

[55] Though the struggle is continual

And the contest severe.

While the magician seeks to fly,

He falls headlong and utterly perishes—

He whom divine vengeance rightly strikes

[60] And condemns.

Nero roars in fury;

Nero laments the impious man;

Nero, whose rule

The world could scarcely endure.

[65] Therefore a Cross is prepared for Peter

[Col. 1494B] By the ministers of wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 1494D] He declares that Christ is to be crucified again in this. When Peter, cast into chains by Nero, had secretly left prison free at the urging of his Christian brethren, and was about to pass out through the city gate, he saw Christ coming to meet him. Adoring him, he said: “Lord, where are you going?” The Lord answered: “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.” Peter then said to him: “Lord, will you be crucified again?” The Lord said: “Yes, I shall be crucified again.” Peter replied: “Lord, I shall return and follow you.” When these words had been spoken, Christ ascended into heaven. Peter, raising his eyes to heaven, followed him with sweetest tears; then, coming to himself, he understood that this word of the Lord referred to his own Passion. At once he returned joyfully to the city and prison, related these things to the brethren, gloriously completed his contest, and was crucified at Rome, as the Lord had indicated.] He declares that in this Christ

Is to be crucified again.

Peter was entrusted with the sheep,

[70] And given the keys of heaven.

Peter’s judgment takes precedence,

Binding and loosing all things.

By the merits and saving prayer

Of our shepherd,

[75] Eternal Shepherd, free us

From the debts of sin. Amen.

## XXIII. ON THE HOLY APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

[Col. 1495A]

This prose has a rhythmic composition closely resembling that of the preceding piece in almost all its verses. If at times some variation occurs, it can readily be noticed by anyone while reading, with little effort. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It proclaims the outstanding praises of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul: the singular gifts of grace granted them by God in announcing evangelical truth for the conversion of humankind, and in the diligent governance of the whole Church. Finally, it describes their sacred martyrdom and their death—precious in the sight of the Lord.

May Rome glory in Peter;  
may Rome venerate Paul  
with equal reverence.

[Col. 1495B] Indeed, may the whole Church rejoice,

[5] and be occupied  
with joyful praises.

[Note: [Col. 1495B] These are her foundations. Christ is first and the chief foundation of the Church, of whom the Apostle says: “No one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is [Col. 1495C] Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. III). But the Apostles, and especially Peter and Paul, are secondary foundations of the Church, after Christ. Hence the Apostle writes to the Ephesians that they are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Eph. II). Thus Christ is the first founder; these are secondary founders, under Christ the principal architect. Similarly, they are the bases and supports, or sustaining pillars, of the Church, and likewise its epistylia, “architraves.” An *epistylium* is the capital placed above a column, or the upper part of a column, just as the base is its lower part. For the Greek preposition *epi* means “above,” and *stylos* means “column.” Hence *epistylium*: that which is above the column.] These are her foundations,

her founders, supports,  
bases, architraves.

[10] [Note: [Col. 1495C] The same men are the tent-cloths and curtains. In the construction of the tabernacle of the old Law there were goat-hair tent-cloths (Exod. XXVI), curtains of hyacinth-blue skins, for covering the tabernacle itself. On the shaft and branches of the lampstand in the same tabernacle there were cups, spheres, and lilies, for ornamenting that lampstand. And [Col. 1495D] these were indeed made from different materials, differed in substance, and were applied to different uses. But Peter and Paul, in the tabernacle of the new Law and the Church of Christ, are—in a mystical and spiritual sense—tent-cloths, curtains, hyacinth-blue skins, cups, spheres, and lilies, each under a different aspect, because they contribute greatly to the Church’s adornment and splendor, and illuminate her wondrously through the manifold variety and usefulness of their graces.] These same men are tent-cloths and curtains,

the hyacinth-blue skins of the temple,  
cups, spheres, lilies.

[Note: [Col. 1495D] These are flashing clouds. Both apostles are also called spiritual clouds because they poured the rain of evangelical truth upon the parched hearts of humankind and made them fruitful in producing the fruit of good works. Again, clouds produce thunder and emit lightning. Thus, mystically, these clouds thundered the voice of their preaching to the whole world and scattered far and wide over the entire earth the radiance of doctrine and miracles.] These are flashing clouds,

watering the earth of the heart

[15] [Col. 1496A] now with dew, now with rain.

These are heralds of the new Law  
and leaders of the new flock  
to Christ’s manger.

[Note: [Col. 1495D] Fellow laborers thresh the threshing-floor. In that commandment of [Col. 1496B] the old Law: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deut. XXV), the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says that by the ox treading in the threshing-floor is meant a preacher of the divine word, who prepares the grain of doctrine [Col. 1496C] as food for the souls of the faithful (1 Cor. IX). In the parable recorded by Matthew concerning those working in the vineyard for a day’s denarius, the cultivators of the vineyard signify those laboring in God’s Church for their neighbors’ salvation (Matt. XX). Since, therefore, these two apostles are both preachers and governors of the Church, they are here said to thresh the floor and cultivate the vineyard.] Fellow laborers

[20] [Note: [Col. 1495D] Fellow laborers thresh the threshing-floor. In that commandment of [Col. 1496B] the old Law: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deut. XXV), the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, says that by the ox treading in the threshing-floor is meant a preacher of the divine word, who prepares the grain of doctrine [Col. 1496C] as food for the souls of the faithful (1 Cor. IX). In the parable recorded by Matthew concerning those working in the vineyard for a day’s denarius, the cultivators of the vineyard signify those laboring in God’s Church for their neighbors’ salvation (Matt. XX). Since, therefore, these two apostles are both preachers and governors of the Church, they are here said to thresh the floor and cultivate the vineyard.] thresh the threshing-floor;

in hope of the denarius,  
they cultivate the vineyard.

[Note: [Col. 1496C] As they winnow. Saint John the Baptist, speaking to the Pharisees about Christ, said: “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing-fan is in his hand; he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing-floor, gather his wheat into his granary, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matt. III). From these words comes the statement of this verse, in which the apostles are called winnowers because by their doctrine and writings they distinguish and separate the good from the evil. The departing chaff means the evil people who do not receive the apostles’ admonitions and are therefore separated from the fellowship of [Col. 1496D] the righteous. Finally, the new grain means the good, filled with an abundant harvest of righteousness, who are received into the granaries of the heavenly kingdom.] As they winnow,

the chaff departs;

[25] and with fresh grain  
the granaries are filled.

[Note: [Col. 1496D] They are called mountains. Visible mountains rise higher than valleys and the level ground, and are the first to receive in themselves the rays of the rising sun, which they then transmit to lower and more depressed places. So these apostles surpass other people in wisdom and virtue. They were likewise first illuminated by Christ, the true sun, with the ray of divine light; thereafter they poured it forth by communicating it to others and to the people subject to them. For the same reason, in Holy Scripture these apostles are sometimes denoted by the name of the firmament or of the heavens: because of their unbending constancy in good, the sublimity of their dignity, and their power to illuminate minds—as in the Psalm verse: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. XVIII).] They themselves are called mountains;
