they themselves are first illumined  
by the light of the true sun.

[30] [Col. 1496B] Wondrous is their power:

by the name of firmament  
or of heavens they are designated.

They command diseases to flee;  
they overcome the laws of death;

[35] they drive out demons.

They destroy idolatry;  
they grant pardon to the guilty,  
consolation to the wretched.

The praise of both is shared,

[40] though each has

[Col. 1497A] his own proper dignities.

[Note: [Col. 1497C] Peter takes precedence in primacy. For Peter was appointed by the Lord prince of the apostles, so that that sacred number might be gathered into one head and reduced to a certain unity. This occurred when he said to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI), something not said individually to any of the other apostles. He was also appointed shepherd of the Lord’s flock, when the Lord said to him: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI). The other apostles belonged to the number and fullness of that flock. But Paul [Col. 1497D] was appointed by God teacher and doctor of the Gentiles, from whom the Church was chiefly formed; therefore the instruction and teaching of the whole Church were entrusted to him by God. He also indicates this when writing to the Corinthians: “My daily burden and concern for all the churches” (2 Cor. XI).] Peter takes precedence in primacy;

Paul excels in the teaching office  
of the whole Church.

[45] Primacy is given to one,

and the unity  
of Catholic faith is commended.

[Note: [Col. 1497D] One rind encloses the grains. In legumes, pomegranates, poppies, and other fruits of that kind, one rind contains many seeds and keeps them from being scattered by enclosing them. Yet all those seeds have one and the same power, because they are of the same kind and similar nature. Thus Christ, like a rind, encompasses and protects all the apostles within the embrace of his divine power, as grains contained in the same rind; and he is their faithful guardian. “Father,” he says, “of those whom you gave me, I have lost none” (John XVII). Yet their power is equal and the same—the apostolic dignity received from Christ—although [Col. 1498C] the particular virtues of each are different.] One rind encloses the grains;

yet the many have one power

[50] beneath the same rind.

The messengers of salvation  
had assembled in Rome,

where they knew there was  
more vice,

[55] and no discipline.

[Col. 1497B] The faithful physicians  
press upon its vices.

[Note: [Col. 1498C] The frenzied resist the remedies of life. *Phrenesis* is a disease that harms the mind and leads it to madness and frenzy. Hence a *phrenetic* person is one suffering from that disorder, namely derangement of mind. It is characteristic of the frenzied, when they are held by the gravest disease, to suppose themselves healthy and to attack those who wish to bring them medical aid. Such were the Romans, who, although deceived by the vanity of countless superstitions, thought themselves [Col. 1498D] exceedingly religious and most savagely persecuted the apostles for condemning the worship of idols. Thus they proved spiritually frenzied.] The frenzied

resist the remedies of life.

[Note: [Col. 1498C] The frenzied resist the remedies of life. *Phrenesis* is a disease that harms the mind and leads it to madness and frenzy. Hence a *phrenetic* person is one suffering from that disorder, namely derangement of mind. It is characteristic of the frenzied, when they are held by the gravest disease, to suppose themselves healthy and to attack those who wish to bring them medical aid. Such were the Romans, who, although deceived by the vanity of countless superstitions, thought themselves [Col. 1498D] exceedingly religious and most savagely persecuted the apostles for condemning the worship of idols. Thus they proved spiritually frenzied.] They resist,

[60] fools, doctrine.

At mention of Christ’s deeds,  
Simon Magus and Nero  
are disturbed by this report  
and do not yield to the apostles.

[65] Sickness yields; death obeys.

The magician bursts apart; Rome believes;  
and the world returns to life,  
its idols rejected.

Criminal Nero rages,

[70] desolated by the magician’s death.

[Col. 1497C] His error, dear to him,  
is a steep downfall.

The chosen warriors  
cannot be turned from faith;

[75] but stand upright in battle  
and do not fear the sword.

[Col. 1498A] Peter, heir of the true light,

[Note: [Col. 1498D] He bears the punishment of the cross inverted. To invert is to turn something to the contrary, as when a garment or skin has its inner side placed outside and its outside turned inward. Virgil: “He turns the clods with the plough. . . .” Therefore, since blessed Peter was crucified—at his own request—with his head turned downward and his feet raised upward, he is rightly said here to have undergone the punishment of the cross inverted.] bears the punishment of the cross inverted;

Paul, the stroke of the dagger.

[80] Nor do differing sufferings  
have differing rewards.

Fathers of the highest dignity,  
reigning with the highest King,

may the effective judgment  
of your power release

[85] the bonds of our perversity. Amen.

## XXIV. OF SAINT LAWRENCE

This prose preserves the exact measure of rhythmic sonority, just as does the piece on Saint Peter set out earlier, “Rejoice, Rome, head of the world.” Its author [Col. 1498B] is Adam of Saint-Victor. It fittingly celebrates blessed Lawrence’s unconquered steadfastness in enduring torments for Christ’s name and his precious death, by which he was perfected. Whatever historical matter is here alluded to, or is needed for understanding the present text, should be sought in his widely known life, and likewise in Prudentius’s most elegant hymn composed on his passion: “Mother of ancient shrines, now Rome devoted to Christ, victorious under Lawrence’s leadership, you triumph over the barbarous rite.” This hymn is iambic dimeter and quite extensive in the same author; the diligent reader will find it among his other hymns in his works.

Let us marvel at Lawrence,  
given to the coals;  
let us venerate the laurel-crowned one  
with praises.

[Col. 1498C] Let us venerate with trembling;

[5] let us entreat with love  
this outstanding martyr.

Accused, he did not deny;  
but when beaten he resounded

[Note: [Col. 1498D] On drawn-out trumpets. I think this is said because among the musical instruments by which the Prophet bids God be praised in the Psalm, drawn-out trumpets are named: “Sing to the Lord with the harp, with harp and the voice of psalm, with drawn-out trumpets and the sound of a horn trumpet” (Ps. XCVII). And [Col. 1499B] they are fittingly named here in particular. For just as they produce sound when drawn, stretched, and drawn back in both directions, [Col. 1499C] so blessed Lawrence, tortured and harassed by the repeated infliction of torments, resounded with divine praises.] upon drawn-out trumpets.

[10] [Col. 1499A] While amid sufferings fulfilling his desire  
he exulted and sounded forth  
in divine praises,

as the string of musicians  
at last gives a resonant sound

[15] [Note: [Col. 1499C] By the service of the plectrum. A *plectrum* is the instrument of a lyre-player with which the strings of the lyre are plucked and struck. Martial: “Lest a burning blister arise for you from your worn thumb, let talkative plectra adorn the responsive lyre.” In Latin it is sometimes called a *pecten*, “comb.” Virgil: “. . . Now he strikes with an ivory plectrum.” *Chelys*, a Greek noun of the third declension, means “lyre” or “cithara”; it has the accusative *chelym* and the ablative *chely*. Thus the sense of this verse and the following one is that, just as strings stretched on a lyre and struck with a plectrum are resonant and give back sweet harmony, so blessed Lawrence, amid the harshness of torments, sang the melody of divine praise.] by the plectrum’s service.

So, upon the *chelys* of torments,  
the tension of this confessor of Christ  
gave forth melody.

Decius, behold: because in faith

[20] he stands unconquered amid blows,  
threats, and fires.

Inner hope and a heavenly voice  
comfort and exhort  
the man to steadfastness.

[25] [Col. 1499B] For the treasures you seek

you do not acquire for yourself through torments,  
but for Lawrence.

Christ heaps these up in himself;  
Christ preserves this man’s contest

[30] for the reward of the triumphant.

[Note: [Col. 1499D] The saint’s night knows no darkness. These words accord with blessed Lawrence’s response to cruel Decius, who threatened that the entire night would be spent in punishments inflicted upon him. “My night,” he said, “has no darkness, but all things shine clearly in light.” Similarly, the statement in the following verse, “nor would he give light to the blind,” is taken from the encomium sung of him: “Lawrence performed a good work, who enlightened the blind through the sign of the cross.” Finally, in the thirteenth verse the author alludes to the Lord’s Gospel words: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may shine for all who are in the house” (Matt. V).] The saint’s night knows no darkness,

so that amid sufferings  
a wavering faith may handle something impure.

Nor would he give light to the blind,

[35] unless the presence  
of light shone upon him.

[Col. 1500A] The confession of faith  
shines in Lawrence.

He does not put the light under a bushel;

[40] he sets it in the midst  
before all people.

[Note: [Col. 1499D] God’s servant delights. The word *juvat* is impersonal here, meaning “it delights,” as Virgil uses it: “Thus, thus it delights to go beneath the shades.” Here it governs an accusative followed by an infinitive, *fieri*, “to become.” Blessed Lawrence is called bearer [Col. 1500B] of his own cross because he endured the tribulations and persecutions of this world, designated by the name of the cross. [Col. 1500C] Thus the Lord also says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke IX). The author says here that he was made a spectacle to angels and people, relying upon blessed Paul’s words to the Corinthians: “We have been made a spectacle to angels, to God, and to people” (1 Cor. IV). For not people alone, but angels from heaven, watched the outstanding struggle of blessed Lawrence against the tyrants. Thus in the following verse the author alludes to blessed Paul’s words in the Epistle to the Philippians: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). In the sixteenth verse, to these Gospel words of the Lord: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matt. X).] It delights God’s servant,

the bearer of his own cross,  
to become a spectacle—

[45] roasted like a dish—  
to angels and nations.

He does not shrink from being rolled upon coals,  
who longs to be released from the flesh  
and to live with Christ.

[50] Nor does he fear those who kill  
the body but have no power

[Col. 1500B] to kill the soul.

[Note: [Col. 1500C] As the vessels of potters. This statement is taken from Ecclesiasticus: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII). And Solomon says of holy martyrs in the Book of Wisdom that, “having been afflicted in few things, they shall be greatly rewarded, for God tested them and found them worthy of himself. He tested them as gold in the furnace and received them as a sacrificial offering of holocaust” (Wis. III).] As the furnace tests potters’ vessels

and makes their substance firm,

[55] so the fire roasts this man  
and renders him firm in constancy,  
as a witness.

[Note: [Col. 1500D] For while the old man is being corrupted. The “old man” here means the outward person, consisting of the body and material limbs, which in blessed Lawrence was corrupted through affliction and temporary death. The “other man” is the inward person, concerning the soul and its inward powers, both natural and acquired. This man was made firm in blessed Lawrence through constancy in suffering and the sure hope of unfading glory. This verse corresponds to blessed Paul’s words to the Corinthians: “Although our outward person is corrupted, yet our inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. IV).] For while the old man is being corrupted,

[60] the other man is strengthened  
by the old man’s burning.

Thus the athlete’s preeminence  
was greatly strengthened

[Col. 1501A] in God’s service.

[65] The force of love  
and zeal for righteousness  
think that this heat, outwardly produced, is dew.

A burning fire that does not consume  
overcomes the coals which you heap together,

[70] O impious minister.

[Note: [Col. 1501C] You little understand the power of mustard. Saint Gregory splendidly expresses this thought in the prologue to his *Morals on Job*: “Just as perfumes, unless stirred, cannot spread their fragrance more widely, and just as spices do not diffuse their fragrance except when set on fire, so holy persons make known in tribulations all the fragrance they possess in virtues. Thus the Gospel rightly says: ‘If you have faith like a grain of mustard, you will say to this mountain, Pass from here, and it will pass; and nothing will be impossible for you’ (Matt. XVII). Unless a grain of mustard is crushed, its power is not at all known. Uncrushed, it is insignificant; but if it is crushed, it grows hot and reveals what fierce power lay hidden within it. So every holy person, when not struck, appears contemptible and insignificant. But if the threshing of persecution presses upon him, he immediately displays all that has a burning savor within him; whatever seemed contemptible and weak in him is transformed into fervor of virtue, and what he had willingly [Col. 1501D] concealed in himself in a time of tranquility is compelled, when harassed by tribulations, to become known.” Thus Gregory.] You little understand mustard’s power,

unless you touch it, unless you crush it;  
and incense cast into fire  
fragrances more richly when it burns.

[75] So, pressed and roasted  
under heat and hardship,  
the martyr gives a fuller fragrance  
of virtues.

[Col. 1501B] O Lawrence, lavishly blessed,

[80] sublime king after the king’s defeat,  
mighty soldier of the King of kings,  
who counted pains as trifling  
while striving for righteousness:

you who conquered so many evils  
for Christ’s good things to be contemplated,

[85] make us scorn evils;  
make us rejoice in good things,  
by the grace of your merits. Amen.

## XXV. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN

This prose preserves the rhythmic measure and form of the piece on Saint Lawrence set out above, “Let us marvel at Lawrence, given to the coals.” Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It commends the blessed [Col. 1502A] Virgin Mary with eminent praises, expressing her notable virtues through various comparisons from nature—fragrant spices, flowers, shrubs, and trees—taken from different passages of Holy Scripture. It likewise describes, through fitting material forms, her exceptional exaltation by which she became the throne and dwelling-place of the Son of God; and finally proclaims her lofty eminence in heavenly glory above all ranks of saints. Certainly, among the other prose pieces concerning the Blessed Virgin, this one is especially remarkable and most sweetly woven.

Hail, Mother of the Savior,  
chosen vessel, vessel of honor,  
vessel of heavenly grace.

A vessel foreseen from eternity;

[5] a distinguished vessel, a vessel cut out

[Col. 1502B] by Wisdom’s hand.

Hail, sacred mother of the Word,

[Note: [Col. 1501D] A flower from thorns, lacking the thorn. When the Lord cursed the earth because of the transgression of the first parents, he is recorded as having said to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your work. In toil you shall eat from it all the days of your life. It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth” (Gen. III). Accordingly, the name “thorns” may here reasonably be understood of human offspring subject to the curse and bound by sins. For sin wounds and lacerates the soul just as a thorn pricks and draws blood from the body. Therefore, because the Blessed Virgin sprang from ancestors subject to the sin and curse of the first parents, but was herself free from sin and the curse, [Col. 1502C] she is rightly called here a flower from thorns, lacking the thorn. Hence this saying from the Song of Songs is fittingly applied to her: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song II). The same thought is beautifully expressed in the first verse of another prose piece for the solemnity of the Assumption of the glorious Virgin, composed in prose, whose beginning is: “From the barren stock of mother Eve, the flowering rose Mary came forth.” Because this is sufficiently easy to understand and contains no intricate ideas, it has deliberately been omitted here.] a flower from thorns, lacking the thorn,

a flower, the glory of the thorn-brake.

[10] We are the thorn-brake;  
we are thorns, bloodied by sin;  
but you do not know the thorn.

A closed gate, a garden fountain,  
a storehouse guarding perfumes,

[15] [Note: [Col. 1502C] A storehouse of spices. A *pigmentum* is a sweet-smelling compound made from various aromatic species. Jerome: “Finally, those who understand plants and are skilled in spices report that there are certain compounds whose smell, when some animals begin to perceive it, causes them immediately to die; but others are revived by the same fragrance and recover life.” Hence every ointment can be denoted by the name *pigmentum*. Here, however, spices, compounds, ointments, and other such things are understood spiritually [Col. 1502D] as virtues of the soul spreading their fragrance widely, as we read in the Song of Songs: “Your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments” (Song I). And again: “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments” (ibid.).] a storehouse of spices.

You surpass in fragrance  
cinnamon, calamus,  
myrrh, incense, and balsam.

Hail, glory of virgins,

[20] mediator of humankind,  
bearer of salvation.

[Note: [Col. 1502D] Myrtle of temperance. Myrtle is a tree producing berries of distinctive flavor, from which a wine called myrtle-wine is made. Nard is likewise a shrub of most pleasing fragrance, as shown by that saying in the Song of Songs: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance” (ibid.). Yet by these names of trees the different virtues of the glorious Virgin are indicated, as also by that passage from Ecclesiasticus, applied to the same Virgin: “I was exalted as a cedar in Lebanon, and as a cypress on Mount Zion, [Col. 1503C] as a palm I was exalted in Kadesh, and as a rose plantation in Jericho” (Ecclus. XXIV). By the different names of trees and shrubs, the manifoldness of her virtues is expressed.] Myrtle of temperance,

[Col. 1503A] rose of patience,  
fragrant nard.

[25] You are the lowly valley,  
the untilled earth  
that brought forth fruit.

[Note: [Col. 1503C] Flower of the field, of the valleys. That flower of the field is Jesus Christ our Lord, who says of himself in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II). He came forth from the Virgin as from untilled earth, as the preceding verse says; for just as it surpasses nature for unsown earth, unploughed by the plough and receiving no seed, to produce fruit, so also it surpasses nature for a virgin unknown to a man to bear a son. In the following verse, when the Blessed Virgin is called the heavenly paradise, “paradise” means a garden of delight planted with every kind of tree and flower. The consecrated Virgin herself is called in the Song of Songs (ch. IV) a “garden enclosed.” When she is called here Lebanon uncut, Lebanon is not taken as a mountain—as it often is elsewhere—but [Col. 1503D] as the incense-producing tree, and in that sense may be either masculine or feminine. This designation of the Blessed Virgin is taken from Ecclesiasticus: “Like Lebanon uncut, I filled my dwelling with fragrance” (Ecclus. XXIV).] The singular lily  
of the field and valleys,

[30] Christ, came forth from you.

You are the heavenly paradise  
and Lebanon uncut,  
breathing forth sweetness.

You have fullness

[35] of brightness and beauty,  
of sweetness and fragrance.

[Note: [Col. 1503D] You are Solomon’s throne. The Third Book of Kings reports, among the other buildings splendidly constructed by Solomon, that he also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with exceedingly bright gold, having six steps: “No work like it,” it says, “was made in all the kingdoms” (3 Kings X). But the Blessed Virgin Mary is the spiritual, living, and animate throne of the true Solomon, namely Christ, on which the King of kings deigned to sit and rest. This mystical throne is composed of the white ivory of virginal purity and the bright gold of ardent charity; and it has many steps of virtues [Col. 1504C] by which it ascends toward God. In this marvelous throne there is such adornment of graces and virtues, such splendor of holiness and beauty of integrity, that no comparable throne has ever been formed among the whole company of saints.] You are Solomon’s throne,

[Col. 1503B] to which no throne is equal  
in workmanship or material.

The shining ivory of chastity  
and bright gold of charity

[40] signify mysteries.

You bear an incomparable palm;  
you have no equal on earth  
or in the court of heaven.

Praise of the human race,

[45] possessing, above others,  
the privileges of virtues.

The sun is brighter than the moon,  
and the moon than the stars:

[50] so Mary is worthier  
than all creatures.

The Virgin’s chastity  
is light that knows no eclipse;

[55] her love is unfailing fire,  
immortal charity.

Hail, mother of mercy,

[Note: [Col. 1504C] And noble triclinium of the whole Trinity. What is called in Greek a *triclinium* may in Latin be called a dining-room or supper-room. It is the place in which guests once reclined and ate; it is so named from the triple arrangement of couches on which the ancients, sitting upon them, customarily reclined at table. Quintilian says of the poet Simonides: “Scarcely had he gone out across the threshold when that triclinium collapsed upon the guests.” But the most sacred Virgin Mary is the spiritual triclinium, not of a human being but of God; the resting-place not of merely one divine person but of the whole Trinity. For the divine persons indwell one another inseparably, and the Son is never separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, both before [Col. 1504D] our flesh was assumed in the sacred Virgin and after that assumption—when the Son of God chose in her a dwelling-place—the Father and the Holy Spirit were present, dwelling in her likewise. For our Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). But who, I ask, loved God more ardently or kept his words more diligently than this Blessed Virgin? Therefore the Father and Son made their dwelling in her. Again, Paul writes to the Corinthians who believed in Christ: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. III). Why, then, before the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation was accomplished, should the Holy Spirit not also have dwelt in her, who is proclaimed to have been full of grace even then? Consequently, the whole [Col. 1505C] Trinity must have inhabited the sacred triclinium of this most holy Virgin. Yet the Son of God alone took the form of our substance in her; and in this dispensation of flesh neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit shared with him in respect to assumption. Therefore this most blessed Virgin is rightly said here to have prepared a special lodging for the majesty of the Son of God, in which, and from which, he might assume our flesh.] and noble triclinium  
of the whole Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 1504C] And noble triclinium of the whole Trinity. What is called in Greek a *triclinium* may in Latin be called a dining-room or supper-room. It is the place in which guests once reclined and ate; it is so named from the triple arrangement of couches on which the ancients, sitting upon them, customarily reclined at table. Quintilian says of the poet Simonides: “Scarcely had he gone out across the threshold when that triclinium collapsed upon the guests.” But the most sacred Virgin Mary is the spiritual triclinium, not of a human being but of God; the resting-place not of merely one divine person but of the whole Trinity. For the divine persons indwell one another inseparably, and the Son is never separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, both before [Col. 1504D] our flesh was assumed in the sacred Virgin and after that assumption—when the Son of God chose in her a dwelling-place—the Father and the Holy Spirit were present, dwelling in her likewise. For our Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John XIV). But who, I ask, loved God more ardently or kept his words more diligently than this Blessed Virgin? Therefore the Father and Son made their dwelling in her. Again, Paul writes to the Corinthians who believed in Christ: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. III). Why, then, before the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation was accomplished, should the Holy Spirit not also have dwelt in her, who is proclaimed to have been full of grace even then? Consequently, the whole [Col. 1505C] Trinity must have inhabited the sacred triclinium of this most holy Virgin. Yet the Son of God alone took the form of our substance in her; and in this dispensation of flesh neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit shared with him in respect to assumption. Therefore this most blessed Virgin is rightly said here to have prepared a special lodging for the majesty of the Son of God, in which, and from which, he might assume our flesh.]

[60] Yet you prepared a special lodging  
for the majesty  
of the incarnate Word.

O Mary, star of the sea,  
singular in dignity,

[65] set above all  
the ranks of heaven.

Set in heaven’s highest region,  
commend us to your offspring.

[Col. 1504B] May neither terrors nor deceits

[70] of enemies trip us up.

Standing ready for battle,  
may we be safe under your protection.

May the deceit of the obstinate and crafty foe

[75] yield to your provident power.

Jesus, Word of the highest Father:  
preserve the servants of your mother;  
release the guilty, save us freely,  
and conform us to the glory

[80] of your brightness.

Amen.

## XXVI. OF SAINT BARTHOLOMEW

[Col. 1505A]

This prose maintains a fairly uniform measure of rhythmic form. For in all its verses it has only clauses of eight syllables, whose penultimate syllable is short. In some verses, such as the first and last, it contains only two such clauses, rhyming with one another. In others, especially those placed about the middle, it contains four clauses, at times each maintaining its rhyming pattern with the clause next to it, so that the first rhymes with the second and the third with the fourth. At other times it has correspondence in the final ending at alternating positions, so that the first corresponds to the third and the second to the fourth.

Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It describes the holiness of blessed Bartholomew’s life; his power of restraining demons, exercised against the false divine powers of idols [Col. 1505B]; his zeal and labor in preaching the Gospel; and finally, as in the preceding piece, his glorious death.

Let all praise  
Bartholomew’s illustrious merits,

whose sacred feast  
inspires joys in us.

[5] A hundred times a day  
he prayed with bended knees.

No less in the time of night,  
prostrate with his whole body.

In his presence

[10] demons fall silent.

[Note: [Col. 1505C] At the sounding of Christ’s trumpet. This is said because of the anthem which the Church sings concerning this saint: “The voice of Saint Bartholomew is like a mighty trumpet; the angels of God walk with him.” Moreover, this saint was Christ’s trumpet, since he was a loud-sounding herald of evangelical truth, so that his sound was heard throughout all India.] At the sounding of Christ’s trumpet,  
false deities are terrified.

Astaroth cannot deceive
[He] permitted [it] to the wretched people;

[15] [Col. 1506A] Neither to deceive nor to harm,

[Note: [Col. 1505D] Nor can he spare the injured. Astaroth, he says, cannot cease from injuring those whom he had previously afflicted with diseases or bodily distress, even though he might greatly wish to deal with them more mildly and harm them no further, so that, by ceasing from injury, he might appear to heal those whom he had burdened with sickness. For by such mocking tricks that demon, lurking in the idol Astaroth, was accustomed to deceive the wretched; but because of the apostle’s presence, this derisive deception and subtle power were restrained.] Nor can she spare those she has injured.

Worthy of grievous punishment,  
He is tormented by fire;  
How great is his torture  
Berith makes manifest.

Through the apostle’s miracles  
The devil’s fraud is laid bare.  
His crafty art detected,  
The idol’s worshippers cease [to worship].

[25] [Note: [Col. 1505D] Pseustius rejoices, freed. Pseustius, formerly tormented by a demon, was freed from such an affliction through the power and aid of Saint Bartholomew. Likewise, the daughter of King Polymnius, formerly mad and possessed by an unclean spirit, was restored to full health through the apostle. On account of these signs, the people of that region, together with their king, competed in believing in Christ.] Pseustius rejoices, freed,  
The enemy’s rage restrained.  
King Polymnius too believes,  
Because of his daughter’s healing.

[Note: [Col. 1505D] Permitted by the apostle. As has been handed down in the Life of Saint Bartholomew, after the apostle’s arrival in India and his first manifestation to the people and king through the idol Astaroth, the priests of the temples were sacrificing to the idol. Then the demon began to cry out from it, saying: “Cease, wretches, from sacrificing to me, lest worse things befall me; for I am bound in fiery chains by the angels of the living God.” The apostle commanded the demon, on leaving the idol, to shatter it. Immediately departing, he himself broke all the idols of the temple. Then the angel of the Lord appeared there, flew around the temple, and inscribed the sign of the cross with his finger at its four corners. He commanded them all to mark the same sign upon their foreheads, so that they might be able, without horror or fear, to behold their god whom until then they had worshipped. When all had obeyed his word, [Col. 1506D] he showed them an Ethiopian, blacker than soot and terrible in horrible appearance, whose eyes sparkled like glowing iron and whose hands were bound behind his back in chains. He commanded him to go away into a desert place where no human habitation existed. He departed amid tremendous noise and loud howling, yet without striking anyone with terror, because they had first been fortified by the sign of the cross. Then the angel vanished from their sight. All the sick, after prayer had been poured out to God, were healed by the apostle, and King Polymnius with all his people received the life-giving washing of baptism. This narrative makes clear the meaning of this verse and of the four following. It also makes evident that in the thirty-eighth verse *sigilla* means idols, images, or carved figures—certain signs representing to idolaters the divinity of false gods. They are called *sigilla*, as it were, “little signs.”] Permitted by the apostle,

[30] [Col. 1506B] The demon bellows from the idol:

“Wretches, I ask of you  
No longer to perform sacred rites.  
I confess that I can do nothing now,  
I who, scarcely breathing, am tormented,

[35] Before the day of judgment,  
Bearing the punishment of fire.”

Having spoken thus, he disappeared  
And shattered the images.  
Yet he did not terrify those present,

[40] For the power of the cross was there.

With Christ’s sign  
An angelic hand marks the temple;  
By wondrous power  
It freely releases the afflicted.

[45] [Col. 1506C] [Note: [Col. 1506D] India swiftly changes its skin. By “skin” the author here metaphorically means the quality and condition of the mind, in respect of faith and morals. The people of India indeed changed this at the apostle’s preaching and display of miracles. For formerly devoted to the worship of idols, they then embraced the sincere faith of Christ. Thus, stripping off the old skin, they put on a new one: having put off the old man with his deeds, they assumed the new man, created according to God in righteousness and truth.] India swiftly changes its skin,  
Dyed with baptismal grace.

[Col. 1507A] Free from wrinkle and stain,  
She rejoices in heavenly union.  
Therefore the priests run

[50] As suppliants to Astyages,  
Seeking the death  
Of the athlete now a veteran.

Under Christ’s witness  
He offered his head to the sword.

[55] Thus today triumphed  
India’s teacher and conqueror.  
Bartholomew, make earnest petition  
For your servants,  
That after life’s course

[60] They may praise Christ for ever. Amen.

## XXVII. OF SAINT AUGUSTINE

[Col. 1507B]

This prose piece is, in rhythmic modulation, exceedingly similar to that on Saint Bartholomew explained above: “Let us all praise the illustrious merits of Bartholomew.” Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It describes, with very sweet melody, that heavenly glory which the saints receive in the heavenly city of Jerusalem and will possess eternally with God: where there is no longer any place for pain or sorrow, but an abundance of every good thing and unending joy. Moreover, this prose agrees almost wholly and plainly in meaning, as also in its kind of rhythm, with that most elegant rhythmic song by the same author, soon to be explained, concerning all saints: “Let the Church represent the joys of the heavenly mother.” The sole difference between this prose and that one is that the latter suits all saints of every order, while this is particular and proper to the sacred doctors of the Catholic Church, who have greatly enlightened her by their teaching and interpretation of Holy Scripture. Yet although only the name of Saint Augustine is expressed in the first clause of the nineteenth verse of this prose, so that it is here specially fitted to him, it may nevertheless be applied most fittingly to any other doctor of the Church, merely by changing [Col. 1508A] Augustine’s name in that place to Jerome, Ambrose, or Gregory. Such a change does not damage the rhythmical sound; indeed, because of the short penultimate syllable of those names, it makes it more musical. Nor does it offend against the meaning, for it is found to apply no less fully to each of the other doctors than to Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 1507C] The joys of the inward feast. By “inward feast” the author means that inward joy and exultation in the Lord which a devout soul, flooded with divine sweetness, experiences within itself when, feeling tranquillity and peace of conscience with God, separated and free from all worldly cares, it attends solely to God and is continually intent upon his praise and contemplation. A soul which has attained this inward repose through cleanness and purity of life, and thus in some measure celebrates a spiritual Sabbath, scents and faintly tastes beforehand those joys of the heavenly kingdom which the saints enjoy most happily. Longing ardently for them, it often bursts into this cry: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. XLI).] The joys of the inward feast  
Our harmony sings,

Whereby the mind, at peace within itself,  
Keeps the true Sabbaths.

[5] With the joy of a pure heart,  
Scenting true joys,  
It eagerly tastes beforehand  
What is the glory of the saints,

The glory in which, in their homeland,

[10] [Col. 1508B] The court of heaven’s dwellers rejoices,  
Beholding in his glory  
The King bestowing his rewards.

That blessed homeland  
Which knows only joys:

[15] [Note: [Col. 1507D] For the citizens of this homeland. This agrees with the saying of the divine Psalmist: “Blessed are they who dwell in thy house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise thee” (Ps. LXXXIV). That the citizens of that house are no longer shaken by any hostile tempest, as this text says, John, revealer of divine visions, testifies in the Apocalypse, saying of them: “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more; neither shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat, because the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne shall rule them and lead them to fountains of the waters of life; and God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Apoc. VII). “And death shall be no more; neither mourning, nor crying, nor pain shall be any more, because the former things have passed away” (Apoc. XXI). Finally, that one day in that most radiant land of the living is better than many thousands of days in this calamitous life is also affirmed by the psalmist: “For one day in thy courts is better than thousands” (Ps. XLVIII). Lastly, Saint John indicates the remarkable splendour of that divine house in these words: “And the city has no need of sun or moon to shine in it; for the glory of God shall illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb. And its gates shall not be shut by day, for night shall not be there” (Apoc. XXI).] For the citizens of this homeland  
Never cease to sing praises.  
That sweetness affects them  
Which no sorrow taints.

No enemy assails them,

[20] Nor does any tempest shake them.

There, one most radiant day  
Is better than thousands;  
Shining with resplendent light,

[Col. 1508C] Full of the knowledge of God.

[25] [Note: [Col. 1508D] Which the human mind cannot grasp. This agrees with the judgment of Saint Paul, writing thus to the Corinthians: “Neither eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II). Yet these things will first be perceived by those who are children of the kingdom when life itself has attained victory over this mortal condition of ours—that is, when mortality’s lot in us has been ended by the glory of immortality. This happens in part to the saints themselves when their blessed souls, released from bodily bonds, obtain immortal life in heaven. But it will be fulfilled perfectly and completely at the end of the world, when death is swallowed up in the victory of life, when this mortal shall put on immortality and this corruptible incorruption (I Cor. XV). Then victorious life will transform these mortal things of death; for it will also remove from our bodies the misery of mortality and gird them with immortal power. Likewise, in that eternal happiness God will be, as Paul says, “all things in all” (*ibid.*); and for those saintly citizens of heaven he will be the fullness, abundance, and supply of every good that can be desired. Indeed, he will be for them the fountain of life, unfailing strength, and knowledge of every kind; likewise food and perpetual refreshment; also spiritual clothing, surrounding them with the immeasurable light of his glory; and every other good that could be desired for the perfection of the soul.] Which the human mind cannot grasp,  
Nor the tongue express,

Until life’s victory  
Transforms these mortal things,  
When God is all things:

[30] [Col. 1509A] Life, strength, knowledge,  
Food, clothing, and all else  
That a devout mind can desire.

Let the sober mind meditate on this  
In this wretched vale.

[35] Let it feel this in sleep;  
Let it ponder this while awake,  
So that after the world’s exile  
It may be crowned in its homeland  
And, in the glory of beauty,

[40] Praise the King for ever.

[Note: [Col. 1509D] The proclamations of these praises. The Catholic Church on earth, he says, expresses in a certain symbolic manner the joys, happiness, and glory of the blessed in heaven when it annually celebrates the solemnities of the saints and their happy passage from this world to heaven. For these feast-days of the saints, solemnly celebrated here, are as it were an image and representation of that supreme delight and joy which they possess continually and without interruption in heaven. Yet these festivals are annual, whereas those in the heavenly Jerusalem are perpetual. These have an end and return with the cycle of time; those are endless and know no end. These often become mournful because of some intervening sad event, as was said through the prophet Amos: “Your feast-days shall be turned into lamentation and mourning” (Tob. II). But those are free from all sorrow and mourning. Finally, days of labour follow our festivals; whereas those have a continual Sabbath and peaceful rest. [Col. 1510C] “From henceforth, says the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours” (Apoc. XIV). For on that festal day of the heavenly city rewards are distributed for labours already endured to those who have lawfully striven amid the labour of this life. Thus the saints who shed their blood for Christ receive a rose-coloured crown, because its crimson colour corresponds to martyrdom. Those who preserved untainted chastity of body and soul receive a white crown, that the whiteness may be the sign of virginal purity. Finally, those who elucidated through their labour the doctrine of the sacred faith are distinguished by a golden torque: both because Scripture frequently indicates the splendour of divine utterances by gold, and because among the ancients the wise were customarily adorned with that ornament, namely a golden neck-ring, which adorns the neck and breast. Wisdom is both stored in the breast [Col. 1510D] and brought forth in speech. Hence the Wise Man says in Proverbs: “That grace may be added to thy head, and a necklace to thy neck” (Prov. I).] The Church imitates  
The proclamations of these praises  
When the saints’ birthdays  
Are annually recounted.

[45] [Col. 1509B] When, after battles completed,  
Worthy rewards are given:  
A rose-coloured crown for suffering,  
A white one for chastity.

A golden torque too is given

[50] For Catholic doctrine,  
By which Augustine shines forth  
In the court of the highest King.

Through the abundance of his books  
The one faith is formed.

[55] Hence Mother Church  
Avoids the byways of errors,  
And follows his footsteps  
And preaches his doctrines.

[Col. 1509C] By true and fervent faith,  
May our Mother grant us grace.

[60] Amen.

## XXVIII. ON THE FEAST OF THE BEHEADING OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

[Col. 1510A]

This prose observes a uniform rule of rhythmic consonance, like the one on the Nativity of this same Saint John previously explained: “Of the Forerunner and Baptist.” Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It commends blessed John for his illustrious virtues, especially for his unconquered constancy of mind, by which he fearlessly rebuked the scribes and Pharisees—and even King Herod for adultery. For this he was cast into prison and finally beheaded; he endured all things with equanimity in defence of righteousness and truth, as is clear and evident from the Gospel reading.

Let the Church celebrate  
The Forerunner of the highest King  
And herald of the new law

[Col. 1510B] In this most festive light.

[5] Rejoice, mother, and with devotion  
Bring forth proclamations of praise.  
Let us venerate his birth,  
And no less delight  
In his martyrdom.

[10] Let all the world be glad.

[Note: [Col. 1510D] This martyr is second to none. Most books give this clause as *Nullus martyr huic secundus* (“No martyr is second to this one”), but wrongly and corruptly. For “second” is said of one who follows another in place, order, virtue, or dignity, and is later than another. Thus someone who says that no martyr is second to this John is certainly saying that no other martyr yields to John in holiness or is inferior to him, but is either equal to him in virtue or superior. This proposition is not only false but wholly contrary to the meaning which the author intends to express by these words, namely to mark blessed John’s pre-eminence above the rest. One should rather read, as the text has it, *Nulli martyr hic secundus* (“This martyr is second to none”). For this phrase means that John yields to none of the martyrs or saints in virtue or reward, and is inferior to no other; this wonderfully demonstrates his surpassing excellence above the others and wholly accords with the Lord’s words: “Among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. XI). Ovid likewise, in a similar manner of speech, to signify that Aeneas surpassed all others in piety, said of him:

> A man great in war, second to none in piety.

]

This martyr is second to none  
In virtue or reward.

It is not for our littleness  
To praise in every respect  
A man of such great holiness.

[15] Let the sum of the matter be told,  
That affection may be kindled  
By his remembrance.

[Col. 1510C] [Note: [Col. 1511C] Not a reed of fickleness. This expression is drawn from the Gospel, where the Lord, in praise of John, is recorded as saying to the crowds: “What went you out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (*ibid.*). By this interrogative manner and figure Christ implies that John was not such a man: neither inconstant nor light-minded, nor readily bent in any direction by human impulse like a reed shaken by the wind. Rather, he was a pillar of truth, steadfast in spirit and unbending from truth and righteousness. Therefore he did not indulgently overlook or silently pass over any vices, but with fervent zeal and without any flattery rebuked people of every kind.] Not a reed of fickleness,

[20] But a pillar of truth,  
He flatters no sins.

[Note: [Col. 1511C] He rebukes scribes and doctors. This is evident from the Gospel, where Matthew writes of John that, seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees coming [Col. 1511D] to his baptism, he said to them: “Brood of vipers, who will show you how to flee from the wrath to come? Therefore bring forth fruit worthy of repentance” (Matt. III). Luke (ch. III), describing the same passage, says that they were called by John “offspring of vipers.” This comes back to the same sense as Matthew’s wording, but is closer to and more fitting for this verse in respect of verbal construction.] He rebukes scribes and doctors,  
Calling transgressors of the law  
A brood of vipers.

[25] He rebuked Herod  
And was not frightened by him  
When bound in prison.

The righteous man bears an unjust penalty,  
Detesting that utterly shameful deed  
Of the king and adulteress.

[30] The tyrant’s violence rages against him.  
Thereby John’s praise increases:  
A punishment to the tyrant.

[Col. 1511B] [Note: [Col. 1511D] The fool serves the wise. The meaning of this clause agrees with and is derived from Solomon’s saying in Proverbs: “He who is foolish shall serve the wise” (Prov. XI). In this mortal life, the wicked and depraved commonly afflict the good with troubles and oppress them by persecutions. When righteous men bear these with an even mind, they are cleansed through them in patience from stains of vice incurred through human frailty. Accordingly, for the expiation of sins of this kind, the evil offer the good service, material, [Col. 1512B] and occasion; they are as it were instruments of this purification. In this way the wicked serve the good whom they persecute, just as one who beats chaff from wheat with a flail, or refines gold in a furnace, serves in cleansing the wheat and the gold.] The fool serves the wise,

[35] Because the righteous in the present life  
Is purified through the wicked.

At the banquet of his birthday,  
The king commands John  
To be punished with a capital penalty.

[40] The executioner gives the head  
To the dancing girl;  
The dancing girl gives her mother  
The head she had requested.

[Col. 1512A] [Note: [Col. 1512B] The cross signifies Christ’s exaltation. This verse expounds John’s proclamation concerning Christ written in the Gospel: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John III), as though John said it to indicate the manner of Christ’s death and of his own: Christ, he supposedly said, must increase because he would be raised up from the earth upon the cross; but John himself must decrease because he would be beheaded and thereby become smaller in bodily size. Yet, although this interpretation appears ingeniously devised and, according to the event which later came about, agreeable to human preference, inclination, and judgment, it does not, in my opinion, correspond to Saint John’s intention or to the literal sense of the passage where he is written to have uttered these words. Rather, the true meaning of that saying is the one assigned by Saint Gregory in the homily on the Gospel read on the Ember Saturday in Advent. Explaining the Gospel words quoted above, he says: “In this matter we must ask in what Christ increased and John decreased, unless it is this: seeing John’s abstinence and perceiving him to be removed from human society, the people thought him to be Christ. But seeing Christ eating with publicans and walking among sinners, they believed him to be not Christ but a prophet (Luke III). Yet when, with the passage of time, Christ, whom they had thought a prophet, was acknowledged as Christ, and John, whom they had thought Christ, became known as a prophet, what his Forerunner foretold of Christ was fulfilled: ‘He must increase, but I must decrease.’ For in the people’s estimation Christ increased and was known to be what he was, while John decreased because he ceased to be called what he was not.” Thus Gregory. One should adhere to and accept this interpretation, since it can be adapted to the Gospel sense and is more appropriate to the subject, rather than the arbitrary meaning of the present verse.] The cross signifies Christ’s exaltation,  
But the cutting off of the head  
This man’s diminishing.

[45] Precious is the death of the righteous,  
Preceded by a glorious  
Conduct of life.

Christ, in praise of your  
Forerunner and Baptist,

[50] We observe these solemnities.  
Lead us from this vale of death  
By the straight way to life  
Through his footsteps. Amen.

## XXIX. ON THE EXALTATION OF THE HOLY CROSS

[Col. 1512B]

This prose keeps the norm of rhythmic sound, but in many and varied forms. Sometimes one clause contains only four syllables, as in the eleventh verse and the three following; sometimes five, as in the first verse and those following through the sixth; sometimes six syllables in the same clause, as in the seventh verse and those thereafter through the tenth. At times it includes seven and even eight syllables in the same clause, as in the final verse, whose first two clauses each have eight syllables and whose latter two have [Col. 1513A] seven. More often, however, clauses having different numbers of syllables are mixed in the same verse, as a mere reading will readily teach anyone who observes attentively. It will also plainly show how the rhythmical clauses preserve consonance with one another, and to which clause each has its corresponding answer. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It recounts the illustrious praises and eminent names of the holy cross, revealing its life-giving power and wondrous efficacy. It also recalls the twofold victory granted through its invocation and protection to two Roman emperors, Constantine and Heraclius. The history of both victories, however, has already been related in the exposition of the prose on the Finding of the Holy Cross, namely, “Let us extol the praises of the cross,” and should be sought there. Finally, at the end there is a devout invocation by the faithful people to the holy cross, to which the address throughout the prose is directed, whether in praise or prayer.

[Note: [Col. 1513B] The illustrious tree of life. The most sacred [Col. 1513C] cross is called the tree of life because through Christ, who suffered death upon it, it brought life to the whole world. Therefore it is rightly called both life-bearing and life-giving; and it is believed to have been prefigured by that tree of life which stood in the middle of Paradise at the world’s first creation, for that tree had power to preserve bodily life whole and unimpaired. The cross, however, through Christ who consecrated it, restored to the whole world the life it had lost. In a similar way, the particular reason should be assigned for the other most worthy titles bestowed here upon the holy cross.] Hail, Cross, illustrious  
Tree of life,

Christ’s standard,  
Throne and altar.

[5] O Cross,  
Terror and ruin to the profane,  
You are divine strength,  
Salvation and victory  
To Christians.

[10] You are the glory of Constantine  
Hastening against Maxentius;

[Note: [Col. 1513C] You who fight beside the Danube. How Constantine, taking arms against the tyrant Maxentius, emerged victorious through the benefit of the holy cross has already been related. But since the present text recalls how, while waging war beside the Danube, the Scythian river also called the Ister, he won victory with the holy cross’s assistance, it must now be briefly told. In the time when Constantine held the reins of the Roman Empire, an innumerable multitude of barbarians assembled beside the River Danube, intending to cross it and bring all western regions under their power. When Constantine learned of this, he gathered a vast army and pitched camp at the Danube, intending, if possible, to prevent their crossing. But as the barbarian host increased day by day and was already crossing the river against Constantine’s will, while he was unable to prevent it, he was shaken by great fear, anxiously turning over in his mind that on the next day he must join battle with stronger enemies. The next night, while oppressed by sleep, an angel woke him and instructed him to raise his eyes to heaven. Raising his gaze upward, he saw in the air the sign of the cross gleaming with radiant light, bearing this inscription in golden letters: “By this sign you will conquer.” Strengthened by the heavenly vision, he ordered the form of the cross to be represented on his standards [Col. 1514B] and carried before him in battle. He then rushed upon [Col. 1514C] the enemy, utterly routed them, slew a great multitude of them, and put the rest to flight.] You who fight

[Col. 1514A] Beside the Danube,  
You are Constantine’s glory.

[15] Favouring Heraclius,  
You destroy impious Chosroes  
With his son.

[Note: [Col. 1514C] In this saving wood. This thought answers Saint Paul’s words to the Galatians: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world” (Gal. VI). From this are taken the words sung by ecclesiastical institution at the beginning of the Mass of the Holy Cross: “But it behoves us to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom is our salvation, life, and resurrection; through whom we have been saved and delivered.” Hence is taken the meaning of this verse.] In this saving  
Wood it befits  
The Christian to glory.

[20] The cross’s length, breadth,  
Height, and depth,  
Revealed to the saints,

[Note: [Col. 1514C] The four-cornered form saves the world. The world is here called fourfold because of its four principal regions, as it were the sides of a square: east, west, south, and north, in which human beings have obtained salvation through the mystery of the cross. The cross itself is said [Col. 1514D] to contain the form of a square either because of its four extremities—one above, one below, one on the right, and a fourth on the left—or because of the four intervals of its dimensions: its length extending from top to bottom; its breadth spread from right to left; its height assigned in its upper summit from the top; and its depth taken in the lower part which was fixed in the earth. This fourfold spatial arrangement of the holy cross is said here to have been revealed to the saints because the mystical explanation of the position and figure of the cross, and of the sacred mystery embodied in that form, was inspired in the saints by God and then declared in writing by holy authors and doctors of the Church to all the faithful. A fuller discussion of the dimensions assigned to the holy cross has, however, been given in the prose on its Finding.] The four-cornered [cross] saves the world  
Under a four-cornered form.

[25] True medicine:  
Christ upon the balance  
Of the cross was stretched out  
And became the ransom;  
He paid death’s claims.

[30] The cross is the balance  
Of our righteousness;  
The king’s sceptre,  
The rod of power;

[35] The cross,  
The sign of heavenly victory,  
Strength in war,  
And palm of glory.

You are ladder; you are raft;

[40] [Note: [Col. 1514D] You Cross, the supreme plank for the despairing. [Col. 1515C] Just as penance is customarily called the second plank after shipwreck, so all rightly say of the holy cross that it is the first and chief plank after the shipwreck brought about by our first parents. Leaning upon it, the whole shipwrecked world reaches the harbour of eternal salvation and rests, received into a peaceful haven.] You Cross, the supreme plank  
For the despairing.

You have drawn beauty  
From Christ’s limbs,  
The diadem of kings.

[45] Through you, blessed Cross,  
Cross consecrated by blood,  
May heavenly grace grant us  
Everlasting joys. Amen.

## XXX. OF SAINT MATTHEW THE EVANGELIST

This prose preserves a rhythmic form like that explained shortly before concerning the Blessed Virgin: “The good and sweet Word.” Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It explains the mysteries of the four holy [Col. 1515B] Evangelists, who in the vision of the prophet Ezekiel, and likewise in the Apocalypse, are symbolized by four living creatures: a man, lion, ox, and eagle. It plainly discusses which creature corresponds to each Evangelist and for what mystical reason. This prose is common to every Evangelist and may rightly be sung on the feast of each, since it comprehensively includes all that belongs in common to the praise and commendation of the holy Evangelists.

Rejoice, faithful people,  
Whose Father is in heaven,

[Note: [Col. 1515C] Recalling the praises of the prophet Ezekiel. Ezekiel, chapter I, describing a vision shown him from heaven, says among other things that he beheld the likeness of four living creatures amid fire and brightness. Their faces had the likeness of a man; the likeness of a lion on the right side of all four; the likeness of an ox on the left side of all four; and the likeness of an eagle above all four. Saint Gregory, in a homily on Ezekiel, applies these four figures of living creatures to the mystery of the four Evangelists; and the whole Church follows Gregory’s exposition.] Recalling the praises  
Of the prophet Ezekiel.

[5] [Note: [Col. 1515D] John himself is a witness. So that the sacred number and eminent dignity of the holy Evangelists may be made known by the testimony not only of the Old but also of the New Law, John the Evangelist supports Ezekiel himself and comes forward as a witness in that sacred and figurative description of them. In the Apocalypse he sets forth the mystical vision of the four living creatures, also shown to himself, in this way: “Behold, a throne was set in heaven, and One sat upon the throne; and in the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes before and behind. And the first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third had a face like that of a man, and the fourth was like a flying eagle” (Apoc. IV).] John himself is witness,  
Saying in the Apocalypse:

“I truly saw; I truly wrote  
True testimonies.”

[Col. 1516A] Around the throne of majesty,  
With the blessed spirits,

[10] Four living creatures  
Of differing kinds stand.

The first bears an eagle’s form,  
The second a lion’s;

[15] But the other two bear  
Human and bovine forms.

The creatures’ forms portray  
The forms of the Evangelists,

Whose rain of teachings

[20] Distils into the Church.

These are Mark and Matthew—
[Note: [Col. 1515D] And he whose father was Zebedee. By this description and circumlocution the author here indicates the blessed John the Evangelist, who was the son of Zebedee and [Col. 1516C] was called by Christ to the apostleship together with his brother James, when they were with their father in a boat mending their nets, as Matthew relates in chapter IV, and as has also been cited above.] Lucas, and he whose father was Zebedee,

[Note: [Col. 1515D] And he whose father was Zebedee. By this description and circumlocution the author here indicates the blessed John the Evangelist, who was the son of Zebedee and [Col. 1516C] was called by Christ to the apostleship together with his brother James, when they were with their father in a boat mending their nets, as Matthew relates in chapter IV, and as has also been cited above.] The Father God sent to you

[Col. 1516B] While he was casting out his nets.

[25] [Note: [Col. 1516C] They assign Matthew the form of a man. Blessed Gregory, in his commentary on Ezekiel, briefly sets forth the mystical rationale for representing the Evangelists by the four animals mentioned above: because he began with the human generation, Matthew is rightly signified by a man; because he began with the cry in the wilderness, Mark rightly by a lion; because he began from sacrifice, Luke fittingly by a calf; and finally, because he began from the divinity of the Word, John is worthily signified by an eagle.]

They assign Matthew the form of a man,

Because he thus wrote of God:

How He descended from him

Whom He had fashioned—the human being.

Luke is an ox in figure,

[30] As he foreshows in Scripture,

Touching upon the rites of sacrifices

Under the covering of the Law.

[Note: [Col. 1516C] Mark, a lion in the wilderness. This statement concerns and refers to the beginning of Mark’s Gospel (chap. I), in which he describes the preaching of John the Baptist in the wilderness and adduces Isaiah the prophet’s testimony concerning him: “A voice crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make His paths straight” (Isa. XL). This prophecy is likewise expressed in the present verse. Blessed Mark was therefore said to be signified by a lion, which is accustomed to utter its roar in the woods.]

Mark, a lion in the wilderness,

Cries aloud and roars openly:

[35] “Let a sure way be made for God,

A heart cleansed of sin.”

[Note: [Col. 1516D] But John has the twofold wing of charity. The eagle is borne upward on two wings and gazes upon the disk of the sun with an undazzled sharpness of sight. So blessed John, through the force of his contemplative mind, ascended in writing his Gospel to the lofty mysteries of supreme deity, and with fearless mental vision beheld the Word who was in the beginning with God (John II). Moreover, by the two wings of charity the author here means love of God and of one’s neighbor, which are set forth in the two chief and primary commandments upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. XXII). Supported by these two wings, the faithful soul is borne in swift flight to the lofty courts of heaven.]

But John, with the twofold wing

[Note: [Col. 1516D] But John has the twofold wing of charity. The eagle is borne upward on two wings and gazes upon the disk of the sun with an undazzled sharpness of sight. So blessed John, through the force of his contemplative mind, ascended in writing his Gospel to the lofty mysteries of supreme deity, and with fearless mental vision beheld the Word who was in the beginning with God (John II). Moreover, by the two wings of charity the author here means love of God and of one’s neighbor, which are set forth in the two chief and primary commandments upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. XXII). Supported by these two wings, the faithful soul is borne in swift flight to the lofty courts of heaven.]

Of charity—an eagle’s

[Col. 1516C] Form—is borne into divine things

[10] [Col. 1517A] In purer light.

Behold the animal form

Which prophetic Scripture

Records; but this is

A material imposition.

[45] [Note: [Col. 1517C] They run on wheels and fly on wings. This is taken from the vision of Ezekiel the prophet (previously mentioned), where, after describing the four animals, the prophet says: “And when I looked upon the animals, there appeared one wheel upon the earth beside the animals, having four faces. And the appearance of the wheels and their workmanship was like the appearance of the sea; and the four had one likeness, [Col. 1517D] and their appearance and workmanship were as if a wheel were in the midst of a wheel. When the animals moved, the wheels also moved beside them; and when the animals were raised from the earth, the wheels were raised together with them” (Ezek. I). Of their wings the same prophet says a little earlier: “And the hand of a man was under their wings on their four sides; and they had faces and wings on their four sides, and their wings were joined one to another. Their faces and their wings were extended above. Two wings of each were joined, and two covered their bodies” (ibid.). Likewise, blessed John says in the Apocalypse: “And the four animals, each of them, had six wings” (Apoc. IV). What mystical meaning those wheels and wings signify, the present verse explains plainly and clearly enough.]

They run on wheels; they fly on wings:

The vision and the spiritual sense.

The wheel is an even course of walking;

The wing, contemplation.

These four describe

[50] [Note: [Col. 1517D] The fourfold acts of Christ. That is, each Evangelist signifies Christ’s nativity, passion, resurrection, and ascension by [Col. 1518C] his own form and figure. Matthew, through the figure of a man, signifies Christ’s nativity according to the flesh; Luke, by the appearance of a calf, His passion; Mark, by the image of a lion, Christ’s resurrection; and John, by the form of an eagle, His ascension into heaven. Indeed, as the following verse indicates, Christ Himself also—one in person, but fourfold in operation—is signified by these four animals, and is mystically man, calf, lion, and eagle: man through His birth into this world; calf because He was sacrificed for us on the cross; lion because, rising from the dead, He conquered death; and eagle because He ascended above all the heavens.]

The fourfold acts of Christ,

And, as you have heard, represent them,

Each by its own form.

Born, He is declared a man;

A calf, He is sacrificed.

[55] [Col. 1517B] A lion, He despoils death;

But as an eagle, He ascends.

[Note: [Col. 1518D] Paradise is watered by these. In Genesis, chapter II, we read that a river went out from the place of delight to water Paradise, and thence divided into four heads. The name of the first river is Pishon; of the second, Gihon; of the third, Tigris; and the name of the fourth is Euphrates. Thus from Christ, the eternal fountain of wisdom proceeding from the abyss of divinity, come forth the four Evangelists as spiritual streams. By their teaching the catholic Church is watered, and the human mind made fruitful for producing the fruit of righteousness and good works.]

Paradise is watered by these;

It grows green, blooms, and bears fruit.

By these it abounds; by these it rejoices,

[60] In four rivers.

Christ is the fountain; these are the streams.

The fountain is deep; these run downward,

To minister to the faithful

The savor of the living fountain.

[65] May their teaching draw us

From the bilge-water of vices,

Lest by sudden death

We be condemned with the ungodly.

[Col. 1517C] Drunk from their fountain,

[70] May our thirst for charity increase,

That we may enjoy

The joys of heavenly brightness. Amen.

## XXXI. ON SAINT MICHAEL

This prose has a rhythmical form similar to that which was explained a little earlier concerning the beheading of Saint John: *The Forerunner of the supreme King*. Yet it differs from that one in certain verses; anyone may readily perceive this while reading. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It comprises praises and proclamations of the heavenly spirits, recounting their distinctions, orders, and offices, most orderly established by God. Above all, it extols Saint Michael in fitting praise for his victory over the ancient serpent, and for the guardianship by which he protects our souls and defends them with his aid.

Let praise burst forth from affection;

Let the choir sing before

The heavenly citizens.

Let praise be pleasant, praise becoming,

[5] When in harmony with praise

[Col. 1518B] Is purity of heart.

Let all praise Michael,

And let none deprive themselves

Of this day’s joy.

[10] Happy is the day on which

The solemn victory of the holy angels

Is celebrated anew.

[Note: [Col. 1518D] The ancient dragon is driven out. The meaning of this verse and the five following depends on the passage from the Apocalypse cited in the final note to the preceding prose, and therefore need not be repeated here.]

The ancient dragon is driven out,

And the dragon’s hostile legion

[15] Is put to flight.

The disturber has been expelled,

And the accuser cast down

From heaven’s height.

Under Michael’s protection

[20] There is peace on earth, peace in heaven,

[Col. 1518C] Praise and jubilation.

Since he is mighty in strength,

Standing for the common salvation,

He triumphs in battle.

[25] The instigator of wickedness,

Driven from the heights,

Wanders through

The regions of this air.

He keeps watch with deceits;

[30] [Col. 1519A] He hisses forth poison.

But this present guardianship

Brings him to nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1519B] Three distinct hierarchies. Blessed Father Dionysius gives an illustrious and divine exposition in his book entitled *On the Celestial Hierarchy* concerning the threefold hierarchy and sacred principality of the heavenly [Col. 1519C] spirits, and the threefold order within each hierarchy. From it one may abundantly draw everything worth knowing concerning their sacred distinctions, functions, offices, and names. These heavenly spirits themselves continually devote themselves to the contemplation of God—called *theoria* in Greek, from sight and contemplation—and to psalmody and praise of the divine name, in accordance with the Prophet’s saying in the Psalm: “Blessed are they who dwell in thy house, O Lord; they shall praise thee for ever and ever” (Ps. LXXXIII). Nevertheless, the angelic spirits sent out for external offices—such as the governance of peoples and kingdoms and the guardianship of individual persons—do not, because of these ministries and duties which they perform outside, cease from the continual contemplation and vision of God. For neither does the management of outward affairs impede their contemplation, nor contemplation their administration. This is plainly evident from the words of our Lord in the Gospel concerning the angels who guard little ones: “Amen, I say to you, that their angels always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).]

Three distinct hierarchies

Devote themselves to unceasing *theoria*

[35] And to unceasing psalmody.

Neither *theoria*,

Nor continual harmony,

Hinders continual ministry.

O what marvelous charity

[40] Is the thrice-threefold distinction

Of the heavenly city,

Which loves and guards us,

That its diminution

May be restored from among us.

[45] [Col. 1519B] [Note: [Col. 1519D] As human beings have diverse graces. Just as, he says, people have received diverse gifts of grace and, according to that diversity, possess diverse good works in this life—in which some labor more, some less; some advance to the kingdom by a narrower way, others by a more level path—so too human beings will attain the rewards of diverse orders and be assumed into diverse ranks of angelic spirits. Those, indeed, who have led a more austere and holy life will be raised to the higher orders: those inflamed with zeal for divine charity to the order of the holy seraphim, those devoted to contemplation of divine things to the order of the holy cherubim, and so with the rest. But those who have lived a less harsh and difficult life, yet have not departed from the Lord’s commandments, will be promoted to the lower orders of heavenly spirits, such as that of the angels. Our Lord plainly testifies to this in the Gospel when He says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV).]

As human beings have

[Note: [Col. 1519D] As human beings have diverse graces. Just as, he says, people have received diverse gifts of grace and, according to that diversity, possess diverse good works in this life—in which some labor more, some less; some advance to the kingdom by a narrower way, others by a more level path—so too human beings will attain the rewards of diverse orders and be assumed into diverse ranks of angelic spirits. Those, indeed, who have led a more austere and holy life will be raised to the higher orders: those inflamed with zeal for divine charity to the order of the holy seraphim, those devoted to contemplation of divine things to the order of the holy cherubim, and so with the rest. But those who have lived a less harsh and difficult life, yet have not departed from the Lord’s commandments, will be promoted to the lower orders of heavenly spirits, such as that of the angels. Our Lord plainly testifies to this in the Gospel when He says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV).]

Diverse graces,

So distinct glories of orders

Will be the reward

Of the righteous.

[50] [Note: [Col. 1520C] The dignity of the sun differs from that of the moon. This statement is taken from the Apostle’s words to the Corinthians: “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but one is the glory of the heavenly, another that of the earthly. One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in brightness: so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV). Thus some will rise to a more exalted glory, because their good works are more numerous and greater. Others will rise to a lesser dignity of glory, because their good works are fewer and less; and according to these, glory is apportioned.]

The dignity of the sun differs

[Note: [Col. 1520C] The dignity of the sun differs from that of the moon. This statement is taken from the Apostle’s words to the Corinthians: “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; but one is the glory of the heavenly, another that of the earthly. One is the brightness of the sun, another the brightness of the moon, and another the brightness of the stars; for star differs from star in brightness: so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV). Thus some will rise to a more exalted glory, because their good works are more numerous and greater. Others will rise to a lesser dignity of glory, because their good works are fewer and less; and according to these, glory is apportioned.]

From that of the moon.

The varied brightness of the stars

Shines forth; so is the resurrection.

[55] [Note: [Col. 1520C] The old man to newness. The “old man” is one who walks according to the flesh and seeks the things of the flesh. The “new man” is one who walks according to the Spirit and seeks the things of God. If, therefore, we wish—and all of us ought to wish—to be raised to the glory of the angelic spirits, we ought to put off the old man with his deeds, as Paul says, and put on “the new man, who according to God is created in righteousness and truth” (Eph. IV); casting off “the oldness of sin,” we should “walk in newness of life” (Col. III). Thus the earthly person here means one who pursues worldly desires and the lusts of this world; the heavenly person, one who savors the things above, not those upon earth, and is carried away by desire for eternal goods. In this very respect such a person is made like the heavenly spirits and blessed citizens, who direct themselves most earnestly toward God alone. Therefore, if we wish at last to attain the fellowship of the holy angels, we must scrape away from our minds the contagions of earthly affection and, as far as our strength permits, make ourselves like the purity of heavenly spirits. For if we are like them in virtue and purity of soul, we shall likewise be very like them in reward and glory.]

Let the old man, being earthly, conform himself to the newness

[Col. 1520A] and purity of the heavenly ones.

Being to become their equal,

Though not yet wholly pure,

[60] Let him confidently expect the reward in hope.

That we may be aided by them,

Let us devoutly venerate them,

Constant in service.

Sincere devotion reconciles us

[65] To God, and joins us

To the angels.

For the present, keeping silence concerning

The secrets of heaven,

Let us raise pure minds

[70] To heaven with our hands,

[Col. 1520B] That the heavenly court may deign

To make us fellow-heirs,

And that divine grace may be praised

By both alike.

[75] Glory be to the Head,

And harmony to the members. Amen.

## XXXII. ON SAINT DIONYSIUS

This prose has a rhythmical measure of consonance similar to that customarily sung at the Paschal solemnity and explained above, *Early on the first day of the Sabbath*. Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It describes the origin of the blessed Father Dionysius, his arrival in Gaul, and his proclamation of Gospel truth among the Parisians, with a great increase of spiritual benefit. Then it describes his holy contest for Christ, completed, after various kinds of torments, by the severing of his head; and the carrying of his own head, now cut off, to the place of his burial, where his sacred ashes are even now kept in solemn veneration. All these matters are more plainly known from the history of his life and passion, which is commonly read, and especially from the work of the most distinguished man Baptista Mantuanus, who in recent years composed, in three books of most elegant verse, an account of the deeds of this holy Father.

[Note: [Col. 1521C] Rejoice in your offspring, Greece. That Greece bore Dionysius as her offspring but Gaul as her father may first be understood in terms of bodily age: he was born and educated in Greece, but spent his mature and almost elderly years in Gaul. It may likewise be understood in terms of the quality and condition of the soul: Dionysius was reborn in Greece from water and the Holy Spirit, and was a son of the Apostle Paul in baptism, as the Acts of the Apostles plainly testify. But in Gaul and among the Parisians he begot spiritual children to God through the Gospel, of whom he may deservedly be called father according to the Spirit.]

Rejoice in your offspring, Greece;

[Col. 1521B] Let Gaul glory

In Father Dionysius.

Let renowned Paris rejoice more abundantly

[5] In its blessed

And illustrious martyrdom.

The happy assembly rejoices

With a special joy

In the presence of martyrs.

[10] Through their patronage

The whole region rejoices;

The power of the kingdom stands firm.
