[Note: [Col. 1521C] Placed beside their father. This verse speaks of Saints Rusticus and Eleutherius, companions of blessed Dionysius. They were his faithful companions on his journey into Gaul, his associates in preaching the Gospel, and were not separated from him even in death. Since blessed Dionysius cherished them with paternal affection and guided them, as sons, in the things of God, he is rightly here called their father by dignity, care, and authority. In the sixth verse, the royal Gallican Church is meant, because it is governed by the sceptre of a single king; that Church especially venerates Dionysius as its apostle and protecting patron. But if anyone wishes “Church” to be understood of the universal Church, it is called royal just as Saint Peter calls it “a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II).]

Placed beside their Father,

The illustrious warriors

[15] Are worthy of remembrance;

But above all

The royal Church

Remembers him continually.

[Col. 1522A] Sent to Gaul

[20] By the supreme bishop,

He does not fear

The madness of an unbelieving people.

The apostle of the Gauls

[Note: [Col. 1521D] Had come to Lutetia. Lutetia is a most celebrated city in Gaul, a mart for every kind of good learning; in the fifth verse of this prose it is also called Paris. For it is called by both names in approved authors: Caesar too mentions Lutetia of the Parisians in his commentaries. Amid the many things for which it is nobly renowned—its flourishing academy of studies, the supreme senate of Gallic justice, its episcopal see, the multitude of inhabitants, and the abundance of all things conducive to life—it has nothing more ancient or of which it ought more to boast than that it was first enlightened by the preaching of the blessed Father Dionysius, received through his diligence and labor the brightness of the true faith, and was consecrated to the Lord by his holy blood.]

Had come to Lutetia,

[25] Which the crafty enemy held

As if it were his own.

Here was a mass of errors

And every uncleanness;

Here an unhappy people,

[30] Rejoicing in idolatry,

Worshipped the idol

[Note: [Col. 1522C] Of deceitful Mercury. The author aptly expresses Mercury’s characteristic when he calls him deceitful. Among poets and pagans Mercury was considered the master of fraud and theft. Though unknowingly, they said something almost true: by Mercury is meant a demon, ingenious at every theft, who suggests to human beings lies, tricks, frauds, and deceits, by which they secretly take away what belongs to others, devote themselves to thefts, and through every wickedness steal for themselves the possessions of others. A lofty mountain rising to the north of Paris was once called Mount Mercury because a shrine had been built there for him and he was worshipped there. But after those holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius were slain upon that mountain and shed their blood, deceitful Mercury was driven from it, every superstition of his worship was abolished, and, together with the new religion, the mountain’s name was changed: thereafter it was called the Mount of Martyrs, after the holy martyrs slain there.]

Of deceitful Mercury.

But the faith of Dionysius

[Col. 1522B] Conquered the devil.

There, having built God’s temple,

He teaches by word and example,

And shines with miracles.

The crowd believes; error yields;

Faith grows, and the name

[40] Of so great a bishop shines forth.

Hearing this, cruel Domitian rages

And sends Sisinnius,

That he may drag to punishment

The shepherd of souls,

[45] Renowned for faith, life, and signs.

Punishments are inflicted on the old man:

[Col. 1522C] Whips, prison, and chains.

[Note: [Col. 1522D] The catasta, an iron bed. A *catasta* is a wooden contrivance in which bound slaves were held. Pliny says: “At last, Chrysogonus of Sulla was seen on the [Col. 1523C] *catasta*.” Hence that wooden device by which prisoners’ feet are fastened in prison is aptly denoted by this name. An *ergastulum*—for the following verse uses that term—is a place where some work is performed by enslaved persons in chains; among the ancients, bound slaves and captives were compelled to labor more harshly in prison. Hence *ergastulum* is very often used for “prison,” as in this place.]

The *catasta*, the iron bed,

[50] And fiery heat he overcomes.

By prayer he tames savage beasts,

Quenches the pyre, endures crosses.

After nails and the gibbet,

He is conveyed to the *ergastulum*.

[55] While the old man celebrates Mass,

With the crowd standing round,

Christ is present, attended

By the heavenly host.

In the prison’s cavernous enclosure

[60] He consoles him, and feeds him

With the life-giving, immortal bread,

To be crowned with glory.

The martyr comes forth to contend,

[Note: [Col. 1523C] He stands untroubled beneath the axe. This is said because the heads of Saint Dionysius and his companions were cut off not with a sword—as is now generally done in the execution of criminals—but with blunt and dulled axes, in accordance with the Roman custom of striking those condemned to death by beheading with an axe.]

He stands untroubled beneath the axe.

[65] The executioner strikes, and thus the victor

[Col. 1523B] Is consummated by the sword.

His body immediately rose up;

[Note: [Col. 1523C]

The trunk bore the severed head. *Truncus* as a noun is the part of a tree remaining when its branches have been cut off. Horace:

> “Once I was a fig-tree trunk, useless timber.”

It is also used of a body whose head has been cut off. Virgil says of slain Priam:

> “A mighty trunk lies upon the shore,  
> A head torn from its shoulders, a nameless body.”

But *truncus* as an adjective means “mutilated” or “severed.” Virgil:

> “And noses maimed by a shameful wound.”

Therefore, in this clause the word is a noun in the first occurrence and an adjective in the second.]

The body bore its severed head,

Whither the legion of angels

[70] Directed him as he bore it.

May so glorious a passion

Fill us with joy. Amen.

## XXXIII. ON SAINT LUKE THE EVANGELIST

This prose is woven in a rhythmical measure similar to that concerning the Feast of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist: *The Forerunner of the supreme King*. For in each verse it uniformly comprises three rhythmical clauses: the first two, each of eight [Col. 1523C] syllables, rhyme with one another; while the third, of seven syllables, corresponds in its ending and final termination with the third clause of the following verse. [Col. 1524A] Its author is Adam of Saint-Victor. It notably commends the surpassing goodness of God, who appointed four Evangelists, writers of Christ’s words and works, for the illumination and salvation of the whole world. They are signified by Ezekiel’s four animals and by the four rivers of Paradise flowing forth over the whole earth, as all this has been explained more fully in the prose on Saint Matthew, *Rejoice, faithful people*—to which this closely corresponds in subject matter and sense. What is said there contributes very greatly to understanding this prose also. This prose, moreover, like that one, is common to all the Evangelists and may rightly and properly be sung of any one of them.

[Note: [Col. 1523D] Let the choir sing with a pure heart. Some read this clause as follows: “Let the choir rejoice with joyful applause,” and thus begin this prose; and they do so correctly, just as the others do. For whether it is said in this way or that, the meaning remains complete and the fitting sound of the rhythm. Therefore, where variation in the text of copies and books sometimes occurs in this prose or in others, neither this manuscript nor that should immediately be corrected, provided the wholeness of the sense and the rhythm’s sonority are preserved. In compositions made by human effort, exact identity or conformity is not to be maintained to the same degree as in things divinely communicated.]

Let the choir sing with a pure heart;

Let it exalt those through whom

The Gospel words sound to the world.

[Col. 1524B] From whose voice salvation flowed,

[5] Night withdrew, and there dawned

The sun that illumines all things.

Caring for His flock,

The good shepherd, author of the Law,

[Note: [Col. 1524C] He appointed four. As blessed Luke testifies in the prologue to his Gospel, many undertook to write evangelical accounts of Christ’s works and words, and most of them were moved to this more by their own judgment than by the divine Spirit. Yet these four alone whom we read were chosen by God for this office: to set forth for us the form of divine law and Gospel law, and the safeguard for rightly discerning, avoiding evil, and doing good. These alone were received by the catholic Church as Evangelists. That God appointed four Evangelists, rather than some other number, is explained by the following verse in a reason quite suited to the matter: that the world, four-part and fourfold, divided into east, west, south, and north, might be healed by the writings of these four as by spiritual antidotes from the grave sickness of ignorance and vices by which it suffered.]

Appointed four,

[10] For the healing of the fourfold world:

The form of law and its safeguard

He willed to be written through them.

[Note: [Col. 1524D] Concerning the general theme. The general theme and common subject which all the Evangelists treat is the recording of Christ’s works, words, and signs, which He spoke and performed while living on earth. There is no Evangelist who does not treat and record these. But the special privilege of style is an individual account, made by one of them and not by the others, of certain words or deeds of Christ. For each Evangelist has certain matters peculiar to himself which none of the others recount. There are likewise matters which all recount together; matters in which only three coincide; and matters in which only two do, as is plainly evident from Saint Jerome’s prologue to the Evangelists and from the canons compiled by Eusebius on this matter.]

Concerning the general theme,

Each has a special

[15] Privilege of style,

Which the form, portrayed under the distinct

Faces of animals,

Foreshadows in the prophet.

[Col. 1524C] As he ascends above the heavens,

[20] He apprehends the Son,

[Col. 1525A] Of the supreme Father, before the ages.

Dispelling the cloud of our burden,

John, in the eagle, beholds

The splendor of the sun.

[25] Mark has the face of a roaring lion,

[Note: [Col. 1525C] Whose power shines forth in the Resurrection. Through the form of the lion assigned to Saint Mark, the power of Christ’s Resurrection shines forth. For according to the Apostle, Christ was raised through power (II Cor. XIII), and the power of His divinity was made known in the Resurrection, when He raised the temple of His body in three days and again took up the life which He had laid down. “The lion, strongest of beasts, will fear no encounter” (Prov. XXX). It is likewise said that by its roar the lion rouses newly born cubs, lying as if dead and lifeless, to living motion (Ps. LXVII). Thus Christ too was recalled to life by the voice of the Father—who gave to His voice the voice of power—and by His will and power. Indeed, Christ was slain as a lamb, but rose as a lion, as John indicates in the Apocalypse when he says: “The lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Apoc. V).]

In whom the power of the risen one

[Note: [Col. 1525C] Whose power shines forth in the Resurrection. Through the form of the lion assigned to Saint Mark, the power of Christ’s Resurrection shines forth. For according to the Apostle, Christ was raised through power (II Cor. XIII), and the power of His divinity was made known in the Resurrection, when He raised the temple of His body in three days and again took up the life which He had laid down. “The lion, strongest of beasts, will fear no encounter” (Prov. XXX). It is likewise said that by its roar the lion rouses newly born cubs, lying as if dead and lifeless, to living motion (Ps. LXVII). Thus Christ too was recalled to life by the voice of the Father—who gave to His voice the voice of power—and by His will and power. Indeed, Christ was slain as a lamb, but rose as a lion, as John indicates in the Apocalypse when he says: “The lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Apoc. V).]

Shines forth.

Awakened by the Father’s voice,

Christ rises, crowned

[30] With immortal glory.

Matthew has the human face;

In human form, it gives the genealogy

Of God who dictates it.

Thus he traces His lineage,

[35] Showing that it proceeds from David’s stock

[Col. 1525B] Through fleshly descent.

The form of an ox is assigned to Luke,

In whose form is represented

[Note: [Col. 1525C] Christ, a new sacrifice. Some books have this clause written “a new resurrection,” [Col. 1525D] but wrongly and corruptly. For resurrection is not signified by the form of an ox or calf; rather, Christ’s immolation upon the cross is signified, since an ox is an animal for sacrifice. Christ is the new sacrifice offered for the salvation of the world. This passage must therefore be corrected, and the third clause of the present verse should read, “Christ, a new sacrifice.” The third clause of the verse immediately following, corresponding to this one in ending and similar cadence, should be read thus: “the old observance.” I found both clauses written in this form in a more corrected copy, and judged that wording more suited to express the meaning.]

Christ, a new sacrifice.

[40] [Note: [Col. 1525D] The gentle one at the altar of the cross. Just as in verse a syllable is sometimes divided into two by diaeresis in order to complete the metrical feet, so also in rhythmic musical composition, which requires a fixed number of syllables in every clause. This must especially be done in this place: the word *mansuetus* (“gentle”) must be pronounced as four syllables in this clause, though in ordinary usage it has three.]

At the altar of the cross, the gentle one

Is sacrificed; and thus the old observance

Passes away.

These streams of Paradise,

New sacraments, flow,

[45] Which descend from heaven.

[Col. 1526A] [Note: [Col. 1526B] By these four chariots He is carried. In Zechariah, chapter VI, the prophet says that in the spirit he saw four chariots coming forth from between two mountains, with various horses in them, which were commanded to travel through the whole earth. These chariots are figures of the four holy Evangelists, by whom the knowledge of God is carried and proclaimed throughout the world. Moreover, in Exodus, chapter XXV, four golden rings are commanded to be made on the sides of the ark, two on one side and two on the other. Poles of shittim wood overlaid with gold are likewise commanded to be made and inserted through the rings fixed on the sides of the ark, so that the ark might be carried by those poles. The poles are also commanded always to be left in the rings and never drawn out of them. By these four rings and the poles inserted in them, by which the ark was carried, are understood the holy Evangelists themselves, by whose Gospel narrative Christ—the mystical and spiritual ark—is conveyed, so far as the knowledge of Him is concerned, into every part of the world.]

By these four chariots God is carried

Through the world; by these poles

The ark is lifted up.

[Note: [Col. 1526C] The house will not fall. The Third Book of Kings (chapter V), describing the Temple of the Lord magnificently built by Solomon, reports that the king commanded his workmen to take up great stones, precious stones, for the foundation of the Temple, and to square them. By these squared stones placed in the foundation are here understood the holy Evangelists themselves, who were set in the foundation of the Lord’s house, namely, of the Church Militant. And just as, in Luke (chapter VI), the house built by the wise man upon the rock could not be destroyed when the storm of waves and the tempest of winds broke upon it, because it was founded upon the firm rock, so indeed the house of the Lord, built upon the foundation of the four Evangelists, can be shaken or overthrown by no whirlwind of persecutions. For this is the firmly built house of the Lord; it is well founded upon the firm rock, namely Christ, to whom these four squared stones are joined in solid structure in this spiritual building.] The house will not fall,

[50] Supported by this square foundation.

This is the house of the Lord.

Let us glory in this house,

In which man happily lives,

God joined to man. Amen.

### XXXIV. OF ALL SAINTS

This prose has a similar rhythmic harmony to that previously explained concerning Saint Bartholomew: “Let us praise all the illustrious merits of Bartholomew.” Its author is Adam of Saint Victor. In a charming and exceedingly sweet modulation, it describes the blessed joys of the heavenly homeland enjoyed by all the saints who dwell in the court of heaven. It first sets before our minds the misery of this life and the dangers of temptations; then it draws out the blessedness of that ethereal city, in that it is altogether free from every storm, unrest, and fear. It elegantly and sweetly expresses how great is the beauty of order there, in the most orderly placement of angelic spirits and of all the saints according to their rank and lot; and how great is the sweetness of the divine vision, with continual satisfaction without weariness and unceasing desire without the bitterness of tedium. [Col. 1527A] Indeed, the very reading of this prose, with purity of mind and attentiveness, in some fashion draws the reader’s soul by a devout affection and a burning desire to obtain that eternal blessedness.

May the Church represent

The joys of the mother above.

While she keeps her yearly feasts,

May she sigh for the everlasting ones.

[5] In this vale of misery,

[Note: [Col. 1527B] May the mother aid her daughter. The author calls “mother” that heavenly and triumphant Church in heaven, which he also calls the mother above in the first verse. That indeed is the Jerusalem which is above, our mother (Gal. IV). By “daughter,” however, he means the Church Militant here on earth, which still toils in the arena and runs in the course of this world. And in comparison with the other, it is rightly called daughter, [Col. 1527C] because it is inferior in dignity and excellence, and because it continually needs the aid and guidance of that heavenly Church, as a daughter needs her mother. This aid he seeks in the following verse, when he prays that the heavenly watch, namely the angelic guardianship which continually watches and attends over us, may stand with us in battle against spiritual enemies and bring us assistance.] May the mother aid her daughter.

Here may the heavenly watch

Stand with us in battle.

[Note: [Col. 1527C] The world, the flesh, demons. What Job says is wholly true: “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job VII); or, as another translation has it, “The life of man upon earth is temptation.” For the world flatters in order to deceive, displaying an appearance of good in these external and passing goods, which are not truly good. The flesh, moreover, lusts against the spirit and by its allurements draws one toward pleasures, whose end is occupied by grief (Prov. XIV). Finally, “our adversary the devil goes about as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V). Clearly, through the assault and attack of so many hostile temptations, the sabbath and tranquillity of the soul are disturbed; scarcely any rest at all is granted us while this present life continues, without the mind’s being assailed by the suggestions and impulses of one enemy or another.] The world, the flesh, demons,

[10] Stir up diverse battles.

[Col. 1527B] By the assault of so many phantoms

The sabbath of the heart is disturbed.

[Note: [Col. 1527D] This alliance hates feast days. This alliance is the kinship and affinity of the three enemies mentioned above, in suggesting things harmful to our salvation. For these three seem to have conspired and, by mutual consent, made a compact together in order to turn us human beings away from heaven. This alliance, however, pursues feast days with hatred, since it is hostile to virtue and good works, which are especially practised on feast days; it resents men’s being devoted to God and intent upon divine offices, as especially occurs in the celebration of solemn days. Therefore, as though by a conspiracy, this confederacy of our enemies in evil labours with all its strength to take from the land [Col. 1528B] of our souls peace and tranquillity of conscience, to throw everything into confusion by civil wars, and in our kingdom to confound the highest with the lowest and the lowest with the highest.] This alliance

Hates feast days together.

[15] And with an equal compact it strives

To take peace from the earth.

Here all things are confused:

[Note: [Col. 1528B] Hope, fear, sorrow, joy. Here, briefly and fittingly, are expressed the four principal affections of our souls, from which almost all the gravest disturbances arise within us. [Col. 1528C] Hope is the desire for a future good. Fear, opposed to it, is dread of an impending evil. Sorrow is oppressive sadness of mind because of a present evil. Joy, however, is exultant gladness because of a present good. Thus, owing to the continual tempests and tumult brought about by these passions, silence is scarcely found even for a very short time in our heaven and chamber of the heart. The Apocalypse indeed testifies (chapter VIII) that silence was made in heaven for about half an hour. But in the secret place of our soul and in those inner chambers of the heart—which God, who is in heaven and whose seat is proclaimed to be in heaven, seeks to inhabit (Ps. X)—there is scarcely even a very brief moment of silence and tranquillity from the agitation and disturbance of the aforesaid affections.] Hope, fear, sorrow, joy:

[Col. 1528A] Scarcely for an hour or half an hour

Is silence made in heaven.

How happy is that city

In which the festival is unceasing;

And how pleasant the court

Which knows no care at all.

[25] Here there is neither weakness nor old age,

Nor deceit, nor terror from enemies,

But one voice of those rejoicing

And one ardour of hearts.

There the angelic citizens,

[30] Under a threefold hierarchy,

Rejoice to be subject to a Trinity

[Note: [Col. 1528C] To a simple monarchy. “Monarchy” is a Greek name, meaning a single rule. And because God is one over all and the Lord is one, his rule and dominion over all is rightly called monarchy. Such a monarchy is both threefold and simple: threefold in the distinction of persons, but simple in unity of substance, because God is one in essence and three in persons.] And a simple monarchy.

They marvel and do not fail

[Col. 1528B] Before him whom they behold.

[35] They enjoy him and do not grow weary,

Whom they thirst all the more to enjoy.

There the Fathers, arranged

According to the quality of their merit,

[Note: [Col. 1528D] Now that the darkness has been removed. “For now,” as Paul says, “we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII). And blessed John says in his Epistle: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III). Thus, since the saints in the heavenly kingdom see God face to face and see him as he is, all the darkness of the enigma and the veil have been removed from them; and, in the light of glory surrounding and shining upon them, they see that unbounded light of supreme Deity, according to the psalmist’s words: “For with thee is the fountain of life, and in thy light we shall see light” (Ps. 35).] With darkness now removed,

[40] See light in light.

[Note: [Col. 1528D] These saints whose feast is celebrated today. In very many churches this prose is commonly sung for any holy confessor, with the plural number of these nouns, pronouns, and verbs altered to the singular in order to vary the wording, as follows: “This saint, whose solemnities / Are celebrated today, / Now with face unveiled / Beholds the King in glory.” And in the twenty-first verse: “May grace lead us / To the glory of the saints / Through his intercessions.” Yet this prose, as it is composed here, is more fittingly sung of all saints than of any one holy confessor, [Col. 1529D] because it contains no thought which ought to be applied more to one confessor than to another saint—to an apostle, martyr, or virgin—and whatever is said in it is common to saints of every order.] These saints, whose solemnities

[Col. 1529A] Are celebrated today,

Now with face unveiled

Behold the King in glory.

[45] There may the Queen of virgins,

Surpassing the summit of the orders,

Excuse before the Lord

The falls of our sins.

May Christ’s grace lead us

[50] To the glory of the saints

Through their intercessions,

After this present misery. Amen.

### XXXV. OF SAINT MARTIN

This prose maintains the same measure of rhythmic sound [Col. 1529B] as that previously explained for the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, “The Nativity of the Virgin Mary,” and that also earlier expounded for the Dedication of a Church, “Daughters of Jerusalem and Sion.” This prose has, however, the special feature that all its verses from the second through the tenth, both inclusive, have the same opening and bear at their very beginning a recurrence of the same words, elaborated with wonderful sweetness and elegance. The penultimate and final verses also agree with one another in their opening, suitably for an invocatory prayer. Its author is Adam of Saint Victor. It embraces the holy conduct of the blessed man before he received the grace of baptism, and, after he received its seal, his virtue and power in displaying miracles and working signs. It also describes his blessed falling asleep, and the revelation of his death made to Saint Severinus, bishop of Cologne, and to Ambrose of Milan. All these matters are more fully set out in the Life of the same Blessed Martin written by [Col. 1529C] Sulpicius Severus, and are widely known to all.

Rejoice, Sion, which recalls the day

On which Martin, equal to the apostles,

Conquering the world and joined to the dwellers in heaven,

Is crowned.

[5] [Col. 1530A] This Martin, poor and humble,

[Note: [Col. 1529D] A prudent servant, a faithful steward. These designations are very aptly gathered from the Gospel, where Truth itself says concerning the prudent servant: “Who, thinkest thou, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season?” (Luke XII). And elsewhere: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will set thee over many; enter into the joy of thy Lord” (Matt. XXV). Blessed Martin is called a faithful steward in contrast to that steward of iniquity who was accused before his lord of having squandered his goods (Luke XVI). Finally, he is called an angelic citizen because he was made a fellow-citizen with the angelic spirits in the kingdom of heaven, and he entered heaven, rich in virtues and in the fruit of good works, though he had lived poor, humble, and despised in this world.] A prudent servant, a faithful steward,

Rich in heaven, an angelic citizen,

Is exalted.

This Martin, now a catechumen,

[10] Clothes the naked man, and immediately, on the following night,

The Lord is clothed in that garment.

This Martin, despising military service,

Makes ready to go unarmed against enemies,

[15] Having received the grace of baptism.

This Martin, while offering the sacrifice,

Burns within through God’s grace.

[Note: [Col. 1530C] A globe of fire appears above him as he sits. This heavenly testimony to Blessed Martin’s excellence is expressed thus in the ecclesiastical office: “While Blessed Martin was offering the sacraments, a globe of fire appeared above his head.” This outwardly visible fire was a symbol and sign of the most burning charity toward God with which Martin inwardly blazed; the fire flashing forth in sensible form plainly declared how intensely he burned inwardly with the heat of divine love. Thus ecclesiastical usage also expresses the sense of the seventh verse in this way: “O ineffable man, conquered neither by toil nor to be conquered by death, who neither feared to die nor refused to live!”] Above him as he sits appears also

[20] [Col. 1530B] A globe of fire.

This Martin, who opens heaven,

Rules the sea and commands the lands,

Heals diseases and overcomes monsters,

A remarkable man.

[25] This Martin neither feared to die

Nor shrank from the labour of living,

But gave himself wholly to God’s

Will.

This Martin, who harmed no one.

This Martin, who benefited all.

This Martin, who pleased the threefold

Majesty.

This Martin, whose death

Was made known to Severinus in a vision.

[35] [Col. 1530C] While the heavenly host sings

A sweet melody.

This Martin, whose life Sulpicius writes,

While Ambrose stands by his burial, conscious of no fault,

[Note: [Col. 1530D] Conscious of no fault, he enters heaven. When Blessed Martin was about to render his spirit to God, lying upon a bed of haircloth and ashes, he saw Satan standing at the foot of his bed. Rebuking him, he said: “What are you doing here, bloody beast? You will find nothing fatal in me; Abraham’s bosom will receive me.” Then Satan, finding nothing of his own in the man of God, vanished in confusion like smoke. In the same manner, the statements of the preceding verses that recount either his miracles or his notable deeds must be explained from what is written concerning his life or drawn from ecclesiastical chant.] Conscious of no fault,

[40] [Note: [Col. 1530D] Conscious of no fault, he enters heaven. When Blessed Martin was about to render his spirit to God, lying upon a bed of haircloth and ashes, he saw Satan standing at the foot of his bed. Rebuking him, he said: “What are you doing here, bloody beast? You will find nothing fatal in me; Abraham’s bosom will receive me.” Then Satan, finding nothing of his own in the man of God, vanished in confusion like smoke. In the same manner, the statements of the preceding verses that recount either his miracles or his notable deeds must be explained from what is written concerning his life or drawn from ecclesiastical chant.] He enters heaven.

[Col. 1531A] O Martin, outstanding shepherd,

O companion of the heavenly host,

Defend us from the fury

Of the raging wolf.

[45] [Note: [Col. 1531C] O Martin, now do what you formerly did. “Now,” it says, “O Martin, accomplish for us what you once did while you still lived a mortal life.” You were then accustomed to be constant in prayer, as the Church sings of you: “With eyes and hands always directed toward heaven, Martin did not relax his spirit, unconquered in prayer.” We therefore ask that you now also show the same diligence in prayer for us. And as you once made it your endeavour continually to pour out prayers to God for human salvation, so now too be for our salvation a perpetual intercessor, patron, and advocate before God, and keep us constantly in remembrance.

> “Woman: ever a changing and fickle thing.”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.569.)] O Martin, now do what you formerly did:

Offer prayers to God for us.

Be mindful of your people, whom you must never forsake. Amen.

### XXXVI. OF SAINT CATHERINE

This prose has a form of rhythmic structure similar to that previously explained concerning Saint Luke: “Let the choir sing with a pure heart.” Nevertheless, in the penultimate and final verse the rhythmic form differs from all the preceding verses: each of its clauses [Col. 1531B] contains seven syllables, whose penultimate syllable is short, and at alternating positions they answer one another with like sound, so that the first answers the third and fifth, while the second answers the fourth and sixth. Its author is Adam of Saint Victor. It celebrates the praises and glories of the holy virgin Catherine, first recounting the nobility of her birth and the brilliance of her learning; then commemorating her passion and precious death for Christ’s name, and her honourable burial performed by angelic ministry. All this, as has already been said, is made clear from the second *Parthenice* of Mantuan and the history of her passion.

May the resonant voice of our choir

Sound to our Creator,

Who orders all things;

Through whom the unarmed one fights,

[5] [Col. 1531C] Through whom victory over men

Is given even to maidens;

Through whom the people of Alexandria,

[Note: [Col. 1531D] Marvelled at a woman’s unfeminine intellect. “Unfeminine”: not fragile, soft, unstable, and inconstant. For, as the poet says, womanly intellect, according to the proper condition of nature, is weaker and more infirm than a man’s intellect. But in this exceptional virgin grace overcame and strengthened nature, and gave her, in a female body, a manly mind—unshaken and [Col. 1532C] immovable from confession of the faith—so that, beyond a woman’s lot and measure, she was steadfast; transcending her sex, she even overcame men: the learned by superior learning, and the fierce and cruel by patience. The following verse indicates and develops this point in its final clause, calling “iron” the hard and cruel mind of Maxentius, which could in no way be softened toward the piety of faith and the embrace of true religion, but remained hardened like adamant.] Marvelled at a woman’s unfeminine intellect.

[Note: [Col. 1531D] Marvelled at a woman’s unfeminine intellect. “Unfeminine”: not fragile, soft, unstable, and inconstant. For, as the poet says, womanly intellect, according to the proper condition of nature, is weaker and more infirm than a man’s intellect. But in this exceptional virgin grace overcame and strengthened nature, and gave her, in a female body, a manly mind—unshaken and [Col. 1532C] immovable from confession of the faith—so that, beyond a woman’s lot and measure, she was steadfast; transcending her sex, she even overcame men: the learned by superior learning, and the fierce and cruel by patience. The following verse indicates and develops this point in its final clause, calling “iron” the hard and cruel mind of Maxentius, which could in no way be softened toward the piety of faith and the embrace of true religion, but remained hardened like adamant.] Marvelled at her intellect.

[10] When blessed Catherine

Conquered the learned by learning,

And iron by patience.

She gave to the glory of her parents

A fair ornament:

[15] The privileges of good character.

[Col. 1532A] Distinguished through her ancestors,

She shone through holy character

With ampler grace.

The pursuits of reading and labour

[20] Drew away the flower of her tender beauty.

For in her youth she thoroughly read

The secular and divine disciplines.

A chosen vessel, a vessel of virtues,

She reckoned as mud

[25] Transitory goods.

And she brought into contempt

Her father’s wealth and her parents’

[30] Abundant inheritances.

[Col. 1532B] [Note: [Col. 1532D] Enclosing oil in vessels. This is taken from the Gospel parable of the ten virgins (Matt. XXV), five prudent and five foolish, who, taking their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and bride. Blessed Catherine is here said to have been among the wise virgins and, having taken oil in her lamps, to have gone out with the light to meet the bridegroom; that is, adorned with charity, graced with humility, and endowed with the other virtues, she was brought after death to the heavenly Bridegroom. In the first clause of the present verse, *vasis* is the dative plural, not the genitive singular: for the participle *includens* (“enclosing”) governs a dative together with an accusative.] Enclosing oil in vessels,

A wise and prudent virgin,

She goes to meet the Bridegroom,

So that, when the hour of his coming arrives,

[35] Ready and without delay,

She may enter the banquet.

She is brought before the emperor,

Desiring to die for Christ,

In whose presence

[40] The eloquence of the virgin

Renders fifty wise men mute and silent.

The prison’s dreadful confinement,

The grim apparatus of wheels,

[45] [Col. 1532C] Hunger and fasts,

And whatever is done to her,

She endures for love of God,

The same in all things.

Tortured, she overcomes her torturer;

[50] A woman’s constancy overcomes

The emperor.

The emperor is tormented

Because the tormentor strikes,

And punishments avail nothing.

[55] At last she is punished by beheading.

[Col. 1533A] [Note: [Col. 1533A] And when death is ended by death. Since the present life is a continual course and hastening toward death, it is sometimes expressed by the name of death, as in this place. For, if it is compared with everlasting, endless, and unfailing life, which no fear of death can shake, it ought to be called death rather than [Col. 1533B] life. Just as a slight and dim light, compared with the immeasurable radiance of the sun, is considered shadow and darkness. The second occurrence of the word “death” in this clause may also rightly be understood as mortality, or the mortal condition of the present life; when this was ended in Blessed Catherine through the bodily death inflicted by the tyrant, she entered the joys of eternal life.] And when death is ended by death,

She enters the joys of life.

The angels soon took care

To give her body burial

[60] In a far-off land.

Oil flows from her,

Which, by manifest grace, heals

Many sick persons.

[65] It gives us a good ointment,

[Col. 1534A] If, through her intercession,

It heals our vices.

[Note: [Col. 1534A] May she herself behold joyfully. This passage asks that Blessed Catherine, by her favour and grace, may be present at this assembly, behold gladly and willingly—indeed, accept—the joys celebrated by us on her feast. May she also grant us the joys of the future life, which she has granted in the present on this day made glad, festive, and joyful for us because of her passion. It likewise asks that Blessed Catherine may rejoice for us in this life, because of our progress in virtues and the honour paid to her; while we may rejoice for her in heaven after this life, because of the height and greatness of her glory. For the verb *gaudere*, when used with the dative as here, means to congratulate someone upon a good possessed.] May she herself joyfully behold

The present joys concerning her.

And may she grant the future joys

Which she has given in the present.

[70] May she rejoice here for us,

And we for her in glory. Amen.

## IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1174: JOSCELIN, ARCHBISHOP OF TOURS

[Col. 1533]

### NOTICE

(*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XIII, col. 582)

Josse (Judocus, Joscius, Gocius, Josselin, Jothon, Gothon), archbishop of Tours, was born in Brittany [Note: [Col. 1533] Maan; *Ecclesia Turonensis*, Tours, 1667, folio, part I, pp. 119–123.], was bishop of Saint-Brieuc for nearly six years, and was elected archbishop of Tours in 1157. He died around 1173 or 1174. Alexander III wrote him several letters, two of which were at the same time addressed to other French prelates. Josse, together with the bishop of Autun, was charged with examining the sentence of excommunication pronounced by the archbishop of Reims against Count Henry [Note: [Col. 1533] Ibid., p. 221.]. We have from this prelate a charter and six letters addressed to King Louis the Younger [Note: [Col. 1533] Duchesne, *Script. Rer. Gall.*, vol. IV, pp. 640–642, 680.], all relating only to particular affairs, such as a rebellion by the canons of Saint-Martin, a dispute between the dean and treasurer of the church of Tours, the election of an abbot of Saint-Julien, Louis’s excessive confidence in monks, and so forth.

[Col. 1535]

## LETTERS OF JOSCELIN

(DUCHESNE, *Writers of French Affairs*, IV, 640.)

### I. To Louis VII, King of the Franks

[Col. 1535A]

To his most excellent lord LOUIS, by the grace of God the magnificent king of the Franks, Jos., humble minister of Tours, greeting, and salvation from him who gives salvation to kings.

As we have learned from the canons of the Church of Blessed Martin and from those who were then present in chapter, concerning certain complaints which the treasurer and his party had against our faithful dean: the dean offered to submit to the judgment of the chapter and to make amends according to the chapter’s judgment, since it is contrary to all right that, when any canon of the church refuses to submit to the judgment of the chapter, the church should cease divine services on his account. But the treasurer and his party rejected this. Therefore the dean appealed to [Col. 1535B] your hearing, because the matters in dispute belonged to your fief.

Although the treasurer and his party received your command in person; although also your most faithful dean came into chapter and there offered himself for every judgment, as we have learned from those present: your command, O our glorious king, has not been carried into effect. For they wish first to be invested by the dean, whether justly or unjustly, before it has been heard whether they ought to be invested. Therefore, supplicating your royal majesty, in which we place full confidence, we ask and request that, by royal authority and as abbot of the same church, you earnestly command the treasurer and the chapter to restore to their church [Col. 1535C] its service, and then to receive justice from the dean in chapter. If they refuse to carry this into effect, we do not believe that your royal excellence is unaware what ought to be done or what is fitting for your honour. May your kingdom prosper.

### II. To the Same

To the most beloved father and lord LOUIS, by the grace of God illustrious king of the Franks, Jos., unworthy minister of the Church of Tours, salvation from him who gives salvation to kings.

The grave necessity of our situation compels us repeatedly to knock, with such urgent prayers, upon the ears of your mercy; indeed, unless the unconquerable contention of affairs held us back, nothing would burn more ardently in our breast than to seek the favourable countenance of your graciousness, greatly trusting that the affection of your mercy would soothe the straits of our distress. For we are more urgently burdened [Col. 1536A] and troubled by those who, out of regard for you, ought especially to defend and protect us more zealously, as though they held these things from you.

Under pretext of a certain borough which they strive to claim for themselves by a grant of your father and of yourself, they seek to take from us our rights in the Church of Saint-Pierre-le-Puellier. Yet they can prove neither by your privilege nor by your father’s privilege, nor by oral testimony, that they ought to obtain any part of our right except by force. We therefore earnestly implore your excellence, from whose generosity and under whose sole protection all our affairs depend, again entreating that you would, if it pleased you, inform your friends, the lords cardinals, and the lord pope that you have granted them, and could have granted them, absolutely nothing from the archbishop’s right—especially in spiritual matters, which cannot belong to you.

Again we ask that you procure for us, who remain here amid great [Col. 1536B] numbers and expenses, a prompt settlement, at least out of regard for you, by judgment or agreement. How greatly we ought to trust in you is made manifest by the record of deeds rather than words. May your prosperity endure long for us and for your Church.

### III. To the Same

To his most excellent lord LOUIS, by the grace of God illustrious king of the Franks, Jos., humble minister of Tours, salvation from him who gives salvation to kings.

We have recourse to royal aid, in which our hope is never confounded, O our glorious king, whenever we perceive injury to our kingdom or our honour. The abbot of Saint-Julien of Tours has lately departed this world. His monastery was founded entirely from what is yours by royal right and what is ours; we hold that abbey specially from you, and they have no advocate except me. In their election they ought to look to us as to their prince. Yet certain of our rivals whisper otherwise into the ears of the monks, diminishing what belongs to your dignity and to our lordship. Take heed, therefore, our prince, lest what belongs to you pass under another’s rule. By royal command firmly enjoin those monks that, as from the foundation of the Church they have always looked to the archbishop of Tours in all elections of abbots, so they should do now, and dare to introduce no innovation. If [Col. 1536D] they do not obey your command, forbid them all your royal rights, as is fitting for a king, so that others who aspire to such wrongdoing may be frightened by a like penalty. We also humbly ask that you send your letters to the lord pope concerning this matter, as the bearers of the present letter have requested; and we beg you to place faith in their words as in those of your faithful servants.

### IV. To the Same

To his most excellent lord LOUIS, by the grace of God illustrious king of the Franks, Josc., humble minister of Tours, greeting and salvation from him who gives salvation to kings.

Not without great astonishment, O our glorious king, can we pass over the fact that your highness has inclined its ears to the prior of Châteaufort and certain monkish accomplices of his, men of no consequence. Far be it, we beseech you, that royal discernment should be further misled through such persons. For we wish you to know that the case which they had presumed to bring against their abbot, [Col. 1537B] a man of most proven reputation, was committed by the lord pope to us, the bishop of Angers, and the abbot of Marmoutier, for hearing and final determination according to canon law.

We therefore, to whom the case had been delegated, met at the monastery of Bourgueil. There, on the appointed day, we questioned the aforesaid prior concerning the abbot’s life and concerning the charge he made against him. But he had nothing to say; rather, falling at our feet, he begged mercy. Since all the monks of that monastery unanimously cried out for punishment of the aforesaid prior and his accomplices—especially because the wrongdoing of that prior and of the others acting with him was manifest—we expelled both the prior and the monks from their own monastery [Col. 1537C] forever, and bound them in anathema until they should receive from us the letters of their proscription which they had deserved. Should they appear again before you, turn your face away from them, for an evil spirit is in their mouth. May your kingdom prosper.

### V. To the Same

To his most excellent lord LOUIS, by the grace of God illustrious king of the Franks, Jos., humble minister of the Church of Tours, greeting from him who gives salvation to kings.

How favourable and kindly your royal excellence has always been toward us, the frequency of your benefits makes it difficult for us either to know or to remember. Yet, O our glorious king, I consider it especially necessary to recall [Col. 1537D] that, recently, when we had a case before the lord pope, you sent royal letters on our behalf, and through you our labour obtained a speedy result. Indeed, our case was settled by judgment; compelled by reason, apostolic authority acknowledged our right, and our possession was adjudged to us and confirmed by privilege.

Yet when the apostolic judgment ought to have been put into execution, as we approached the Church of Saint Peter by command of the lord pope, in accordance with what had been judged, the canons of Blessed Martin rose against us and shut against us the gates of your castle and of our parish. How great our sorrow, how great the bitterness, how great the injury inflicted upon us—disturbance of mind does not permit us [Col. 1538A] to recount it. Our messenger, a canon of the Church of Tours, will explain more fully. I ask that your ear show itself gentle toward his words and believe him as you would believe us, for we have placed our words in his mouth. May your kingdom prosper.

### VI. To the Same

To his most loving father and most worthily revered lord LOUIS, by the grace of God illustrious king of the Franks, Jos., humble minister of the Church of Tours, himself and salvation from him who gives salvation to kings.

How illustrious your forefathers and great-grandfathers, the magnificent kings of the Franks, always proved devoted and faithful to the Church of God, and how many benefits and services of devotion they bestowed upon her, we have clearly learned from the many and great advantages which came through them. The whole Gallican Church also knows this fully, as do all who cultivate justice and love truth. You, therefore, the praiseworthy imitator of your forebears and the true successor and heir of your father’s virtues, have, after the example of those ancestors, loved with particular devotion the singular and only mother, the Church of God, and have loved to govern her more devotedly since the kingdom was committed to your excellence; and, by faithfully standing beside her in her tribulations, nothing has ever been able to restrain your royal mind from devotion to her and assistance for her.

Accordingly, we should seem forgetful of all humanity unless we took care at every time worthily to respond to the honour, increase, and advancement of you and your kingdom, and, in return for so ardent a fervour of love, to attend always to your will. Since it pertains to the honour and office of royal majesty to reverence churches and ecclesiastical persons, and to bar the way to those who perversely break out into injustice, we have thought it safe to implore the merciful kindness of your benignity—which we have found fervent and devout in this respect—on behalf of our most beloved son Am., the venerable abbot of Bourgueil: that, if any author of injuries and executor of perversity should presume—God forbid!—to insinuate into the ears of your highness anything unfavourable or contrary to honour concerning him, he may be struck dumb before the sight of your majesty as an instrument of falsehood; and that, within the sanctuary of your breast, the words of detractors may find no opportunity for maligning a servant of Jesus Christ.

For concerning this we have God, who sees in secret, as witness: insofar as human frailty permits us to know, our aforesaid son the abbot is of unblemished repute before God and men, and of most upright life and conduct. When he was compelled to undertake the dignity of such a burden, and the monastery, almost breathing its last, was near its end, he recovered its goods, alienated through the neglect of certain persons, and greatly enlarged them. Like a pious father of both the inner and outer person, supplying on either side the pious nourishment of life, he reformed spiritual order according to the Rule of blessed Benedict. Moreover, in all our necessities he has at all times been fervent and devoted; and in matters known to concern your honour, his affection has never appeared idle. May your life endure long for us and for your Church.

[Col. 1539]

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1174. HENRY THE ARCHDEACON

[Col. 1539]

HISTORY OF THE CALAMITIES OF THE CHURCH OF SALZBURG, ADDRESSED TO ARCHBISHOP ADELBERT

(R. P. Bern. Pez, *Anecdota*, II, III, 197)

NOTICE.

The author of the *History of the Calamities of the Church of Salzburg*, concerning Archbishop Adilbert or Albert and Emperor Frederick I, must be investigated. At the head of his little work he indicates rather than states his name by the single letter H. Unless, however, we are greatly mistaken, this H. is none other than Henry, provost of Berchtesgaden, who in the year 1174, after Adilbert’s expulsion, administered the archbishopric of Salzburg—as may be seen both in the Salzburg Chronicle published by Canisius, vol. VI of *Antiquae Lectiones*, and in Pez, vol. I of *Scriptores rerum Austriacarum*, col. 345; and finally in Hund and Gewold, *Metropolis Salzburgensis*, vols. I and II.

Certainly H., whoever he may ultimately have been, plainly teaches us in the final chapter that, during Adilbert’s absence, he undertook a special care for ecclesiastical discipline in the archbishopric of Salzburg; indeed, he calls himself an archdeacon. This dignity is so great that, in the Roman Order, he is called the bishop’s vicar, because he performs the bishop’s functions in his diocese and undertakes in the bishop’s place the task of visiting churches, as Charles Du Fresne states in his *Glossary*, under “Archdeacon.” Everyone sees how excellently all this suits Henry, governing the archbishopric on Adilbert’s behalf. Finally, suspicion of plots and machinations against the exiled Archbishop Adilbert could more justly fall upon no one than Henry, appointed in his place to administer the archbishopric with the favour of Emperor Frederick; yet H. strives to show himself free from that stain both in the preface and throughout the whole work.

PREFACE.

[Col. 1539B]

To his lord A., Archbishop of Salzburg: from H., his devoted and faithful cleric, the spirit of consolation and salvation in all his adversities.

Having sent, through the lord dean of Salzburg, a letter of my excuses, I hope, with God’s help, that I have sufficiently cleared myself before your clemency against the empty whisperings and snares of my accusers; so that I ought not at all to be reckoned among those said to have plotted or schemed against your honour. I am so far removed from their counsel that, with the Lord Almighty, searcher of reins and heart, as witness, I have never known the persons, names, or conspiracies, nor have I been conscious of any fraud.

Therefore I have now directed my mind and turned my pen to writing you other matters, which I trust will be all the more pleasing to you because your prudence ought to know and truly believe that what is written has flowed from a heart harboring no duplicity against you. I ask you to devote a small hour to reading them.

## Chapter I. By God’s hidden counsel all evils are moderated. The occasion of evils arising in the Church of Salzburg was the dreadful schism stirred up by the emperors, from which the Church of Salzburg alone kept itself free and pure.

[Col. 1540B]

In all the tribulations and pressures which you began to suffer as soon as you were raised to the episcopal see of Salzburg, your mind ought carefully and wisely to consider that the cause of this tribulation arose not from man but from God, so that you may deservedly say, giving thanks to God: “Blessed is the man whom thou dost discipline, O Lord, and teachest out of thy law, to give him rest from evil days” (Psalm 93 [94]).

For divine providence, piously solicitous for the salvation of its elect, knows how to turn the malice of men who rage and persecute unjustly to the benefit of those who are afflicted; just as it knows how, by its power, so to moderate the blows of the hammer of the whole earth—that is, of the devil—that Christ’s faithful are not crushed beneath it but instructed.

Let your prudence therefore recognize that the emperor had one intention in your afflictions, and He in whose hand is the king’s heart another. This may beyond doubt be inferred from the fact that, although through officials and citizens in Bavaria and Carinthia he did many things in the bishopric or concerning it, against the provosts and the entire clergy, he could by neither force nor cunning attain his desired purpose. Yet no one doubts that in power and craft he surpassed nearly all kings and emperors who preceded him. Who, then, can doubt the truth of Solomon’s saying: “There is no wisdom, no prudence, no counsel against the Lord” (Prov. 21:30)?

Because of the schism, which the Church of Salzburg most vigorously opposed, a grave storm of the emperor’s indignation and rage arose against that Church, so that the whole bishopric was endangered; and by fire, plundering, and slaughter episcopal possessions were reduced to desolation. The property of canons, monks, and nuns was likewise devastated, as is still apparent today in the church of the blessed prince of the apostles, also called the church of Saint Rupert. Burned with the whole city, it still presents to all who look upon it a pitiable and lamentable spectacle, since scarcely one stone has remained upon another there. O miserable and pitiable event!

The error of schism seized the entire West. The Church of Salzburg alone remained free from this pestilence; alone it fearlessly preserved obedience to Pope Alexander; alone it acknowledged its mother, the Roman Church. For when all archbishops and bishops of the German kingdom, abbots and provosts, together with the whole flock of clerics and monks, entered upon Balaam’s way and renounced the name of the Lord and also Pope Alexander—with such persistence, indeed, that all the princes bound themselves by oath that, should the emperor die, they would never elect or receive another unless he swore never to communicate with Pope Alexander or with any successor of his—Eberhard alone, archbishop of the aforesaid Church, like an immovable pillar, together with his colleague and suffragan Hartmann of Brixen, a Catholic and most holy man, recognized the ship of Peter, of which Christ taught. These alone rejected Samaria and Jeroboam’s calves; reverencing the place chosen by the Lord, they did not hesitate to communicate with the universal and Catholic pope.

## Chapter II. By the death of Archbishop Eberhard and the election of Conrad, no remedy was brought to the evils of the Church of Salzburg; indeed, the emperor’s anger against it was more greatly inflamed and much increased by Adalbert’s appointment.

Although the aforesaid oaths, by which the bishops were terribly bound not only not to communicate personally with the Roman pontiff but also to compel all clergy and, through parish priests, the people to do the same, were made in their time, the emperor nevertheless acted more mildly against the Church of Salzburg throughout their lives. But after Archbishop Eberhard died, those who seemed the leading men in that Church feared that, once his death became known, the emperor would give them a schismatic bishop according to his own pleasure, whom they could not resist and with whom it would be dangerous to communicate. In great haste, therefore, they elected Conrad, then bishop of Passau, although with great anxiety, because he was the emperor’s uncle and they feared that he might easily be swept away by the love of flesh and blood.

Yet God mercifully delivered his Church from this anxiety. For as soon as he was elected and entered the Church of Salzburg, he who had formerly concealed himself for fear of the Jews gave his unreserved consent to communion with Pope Alexander and, under him, accepted the obedience of all the canons and prelates. As soon as this reached the prince’s ears, he roared like a lion, and, giving a roar at which the whole kingdom trembled, proscribed all Salzburgers as public enemies of the entire empire, because they had made his uncle, torn from his own bowels, take up arms against him. He saw him fortifying castles, appointing guards and defenders, and providing fortifications with pay and whatever seemed necessary for repelling adversities.

Yet while doing this most diligently, Conrad did not cease, with the utmost zeal, to promise the lord emperor—on his own behalf, for his favour, and for the peace of the bishopric—as well as the empress and the court, money, benefices, and whatever appeared suited to so great an undertaking, to be given gladly at once and annually, in whatever amounts might be requested.

Meanwhile death intervened and took from the world this resolute and most steadfast man, leaving the Church amid the greatest dangers. Ignorant what it should do amid such a confusion of evils, it began with the greatest care to seek a man by whose help and the support of whose friends the emperor’s rage and indignation might either cease or be mitigated. Your person was found, thought fit and suitable in so great a storm because, through you, once every adversity had been calmed, the most peaceful tranquillity of affairs might, with the help of divine mercy, come to the long-troubled Church.

For all had the greatest hope that the emperor would doubtless understand your election to have been made in his favour, and that he would never allow the son of his aunt to fall into the error of schism, mercifully providing for his honour in the future; lest Christ, who now seemed to sleep in his ship, perhaps aroused by the prayers of his faithful, should command the winds and sea, and a great calm should come about, and then, once the things wrought by the error of schism had been changed, the lamp of the schismatics should be extinguished.

It was also thought that the emperor would recall how greatly your father had formerly helped him in warfare, or how, by henceforth graciously advancing your honour in his presence, he would awaken the emperor’s attention and affection. It was believed that the most noble multitude of all your friends would always cherish with more devoted zeal the Church over which you presided, love it with kindness, reverence it with piety, and always stand by it in its needs. But it is evident that everything thought likely to help has been turned to the contrary. For he who does what he wills, and to whom no one dares say, “Why do you do this?”, does not regard your election as made in his favour. Rather, privately and publicly, in courts and assemblies, he complains against the Salzburgers with immense indignation that, relying on the multitude of troops and strength of arms, they had elected for themselves the son of the king of Bohemia, believing that they would have a bishop through warfare and tyranny. Thus he began to regard both you and your father, together with your electors, as enemies and foes.

## Chapter III. The siege of the city of Salzburg decreed by Emperor Frederick, and the overthrow of the whole bishopric. The Salzburgers’ incredible fear and anxiety, etc.

Therefore, burning with anger and roaring like a lion, he moved his forces against the city, intending, as was said, not only to reduce it to everlasting desolation but also to divide the whole bishopric among soldiers, destroy the monasteries, lay them waste to their foundations, and either scatter or entirely destroy all the clergy. What then could the miserable Salzburgers do, when no one could say to them, “Be comforted, be comforted; do not fear”? Desolation, destruction, everlasting solitude, and death itself stood at their doors.

Then the greatness of their fear overcame their fear of impending dangers, just as the violence of passion sometimes overcomes the force of pain. Those who had formerly been so terrified by reports of his coming that they dared not remain in the city now awaited the emperor’s presence, plainly prepared either for death or to endure every evil which he would not fear to inflict.

What shall we say, my lord, concerning all these things? In so immense a tempest of waves battering the ship—that is, the Church of Salzburg—so that the whole world raged against it and reproached it with the name of the Lord and the name of Pope Alexander, while good and evil alike, and all nations and peoples, said with one mouth: “Is this the Church which alone believed itself able to resist the emperor and dared to maintain another pope against him?”—in so great a confusion of evils, I say, was Christ asleep or awake?

Let whoever wishes maintain that he slept; the event proves that he was awake. As though asleep, he did not see outwardly the evils being done; inwardly he ordered matters lest they should harm. He openly allowed his confessors to be shaken by adversities, while secretly sustaining them lest they sink—the one who set the sand as a limit to the sea, saying: “Thus far shall you come, and no farther; here shall your waves be broken” (Job 38:11). Thus, as though asleep, he permits tribulation to reach the fear of death; but, as though awake, he moderates that tribulation to the display and wonder of his power, so that when all human counsel and consolation wholly fail, he alone may be glorified who alone is wonderful in all his works.

Indeed, who that carefully considers the Salzburgers’ actions and examines them can fail to see that God was toward us such as the reading of the same book shows him to have been toward the Maccabees? For the Maccabees, fighting bravely for the law of their God, as long as they sought help from God alone, joyfully defeated in battle enemies far superior in numbers, arms, and strength. But when, transferring their hope from God, they considered that assistance should be sought from the Romans, they were abandoned by God and oppressed by their enemies, as though the prophet said to them: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from God” (Jer. 17:5). Once the divine power which had made them glorious by repeated victories no longer seemed sufficient to them, and they began to flee to human aid, relying upon human protection they lost the glory which they had won while God fought for them and with them.

In the same way, as long as the Salzburgers preserved Catholic truth and unity under the guidance of the two archbishops, Eberhard and Conrad, like two lights of heaven, they were glorious throughout the German kingdom, and the fame of their praise had flown from West to East, even as far as the region of Jerusalem. Would that they had remained in that same strength and steadfastness, with the end agreeing with the beginning!

## Chapter IV. Salzburg was delivered into Frederick’s power through the treason and perfidy of certain persons. Adalbert was compelled to abandon the bishopric. The loss of temporal goods must be borne bravely, so long as spiritual goods remain intact.

But alas! Those who for some time under the aforesaid men, filled with the Spirit of God, had fought bravely against the error of schism, paying no attention to those who said, “Lo, here is Christ!” or “Lo, there!” (Mark 13:21), turning neither right nor left but taking only the royal road, dwelling in the help of the Most High and abiding under the protection of the God of heaven—wearied at length by the duration of the schism and frightened also by the thunderclaps and crashes of royal communion and indignation, partly lost divine assistance and had their glory changed into shame.

For, murmuring against the Lord—not all of them, for the abbots and provosts and the entire clergy still firmly maintained Catholic unity, but only those who customarily break Peter’s nets, pursuing their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ—they said that, being daily proscribed, cut off from all the world, and made strangers to every empire, they could no longer bear the emperor’s indignation.

Accordingly, by frequent secret embassies they summoned him and promised to deliver both themselves and all the castles to him, counting as nothing the oaths which they had previously sworn to their lord archbishop. When he came and awaited fulfillment of their promises, they requested, with remarkable cunning, that the same lord whom they had summoned from Carinthia, ostensibly to defend the castles, present himself to the emperor and bring aid to their necessities at the final extremity.

Then occurred that for which the entire bishopric and the whole land, wherever report of the deed has reached, groan; and which has produced for you, my lord, irreparable scandal and evil. Yet by what design it was done remains unknown, though all affirm their innocence by oath. The emperor received, as though by surrender, authority over all the castles, revenues, and indeed the entire bishopric. Since this was done without any condition being imposed, he became possessor and lord of all things belonging to you, expelled your person, and made you an outcast, an exile, and a stranger to every honour divinely bestowed upon you.

Those about the emperor marveled beyond expression at this betrayal and perfidy, and with open mockery, reproaches, and grave execration denounced the authors of so great a treason. They saw the strength of the castles, the narrowness and difficulty of the mountain passes, and the solidity of the enclosed strongholds. Fortified by all these, the Salzburgers could have powerfully repelled not merely the emperor but the entire world advancing against them; yet, compelled by no necessity, they failed, leaving no proof of courage for posterity.

Amid all this, my lord, do not lose heart as you contemplate all the afflictions by which your youth is harassed. Though your adversary may seem powerful, your protector is more powerful, defending you with heavenly arms. Let your prudence remember that what you still possess far excels what you have lost. You have lost that from which you were called “lord”; there remain to you those things from which you are bishop. Things have been taken away which, being external, could be taken away; you still possess what neither king, emperor, tyrant, nor sword can take from you in any way except with life itself.

Things have been taken from you for which, by custom, you had to swear fealty to a mortal man; you still possess those things for which, once persecution ceases, you must render account to the immortal God regarding the administration of the entire bishopric of Salzburg. Whether all kings, all emperors, all powers of this world, and all who gird themselves with the sword will it or not, there will remain to you, and cannot perish, what your canonical election conferred; what episcopal blessing bestowed when it anointed your hands to consecrate the body and blood of the Lord; what the anointing with chrism consecrated when it made you bishop; and finally what the dignity of the pallium established when it made you archbishop. These are things which no one can take from you for any reason except yourself; and through their aid, when times have changed, divine reconciliation will restore in a better condition those things which human persecution has taken away.

## Chapter V. The evils suffered in Frederick’s schism by Ulrich, patriarch of Aquileia, and by Pope Alexander; in comparison with which those afflicting Adalbert, Archbishop of Salzburg, are slight.

[Col. 1546A]

Nor should you be ashamed to endure the furnace of tribulation with the Catholic Church, which alone has conferred upon you those things that no persecution can ever prevail to take away. For the Catholic Church elected you. A Catholic patriarch, who with immense labour and peril of life restored his Church, cleansed of every dreg of schismatic error, to Catholic unity, consecrated you at once priest and bishop. Pope Alexander, a Catholic, raised you by the dignity of the pallium and exalted you with the name and honour of archbishop, so that no opportunity might remain for schismatics to mock or reproach your person or the Church of Salzburg.

It should therefore be glorious for you, through the Lord’s favour, to be tested by human trials with such men as your ordainers; and, when the Lord commands the winds and the sea and there is a great calm, to rejoice and exult with them, when those who now rejoice and exult in evil things will be clothed with their own confusion as with a double garment.

For although the things you have suffered and are suffering are great, compared with what they endured they seem small. You found the Catholic Church; Lord Patriarch Ulrich found in his whole patriarchate scarcely a Catholic person, or one able to distinguish his right hand from his left. So much was this so that, on the holy Saturday of Easter, at the blessing of the candle, no one could be found willing or daring to pronounce the name of Pope Alexander.

For while he alone struggled with vigorous courage against the entire clergy and people and insisted that Alexander must be named, they on the contrary cried out that the heretic of Viterbo must be named. What was God’s champion to do? Not knowing what to do, he entered the sanctuary, and there, shedding most bitter tears, cried to the Lord, saying with Moses: “Lord, only a little more, and the people will stone me” (Exod. 17:4). While the man of God was placed in such affliction and expectation of death, He who does not despise a contrite and humbled heart comforted him.

For when the hour had already passed and the people wished to depart each to his own house, a certain deacon among the canons entered and offered himself to him for the blessing of the candle, placing his life in his hands. Then the patriarch for the first time received consolation, put on the sacred vestments, and, looking only to death, went out with his deacon to the people. When the name of Alexander was heard, shouting and tumult rose to heaven; and, as everyone went out and fled the name of the Catholic pope as though it were profane, scarcely any remained with the patriarch.

What shall be said of the lord pope? What should be recalled of his sufferings? When he did not dare remain in the city after the emperor stirred up sedition there, he departed for Gaul, to the protection of the king of the Franks, where the refuge of all popes had always been accustomed to be. When the emperor planned evil against the king of the Franks because he had received and, to the emperor’s injury, maintained an enemy of the empire, and therefore thought of leading an army against him, the lord pope left Gaul and returned to Rome.

Thus the emperor, pursuing him, also came to Rome, bringing with him, as it were the pith of the cedar, all the strength of the empire. While Pope Alexander sat in the city, the emperor pitched camp before it. What hope of life could there then be for one who had fled from Rome to France and from France again to Rome, while his mighty persecutor sat before his eyes with all his adversaries—that is, the schismatics? What could he await but the hour when he would be captured, set before the face of his enemies for judgment, and, because Peter’s see had been invaded, crucified like Peter?

If this had happened, it would undoubtedly have happened for his own good; but with him the Catholic Church would have been condemned and extinguished, and the schism confirmed. But far be it that He who redeemed the Church with his blood, and founded it upon the Rock, saying, “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18), should thus abandon it.

Glory to you, Christ, who were most greatly magnified where you were thought to be overcome by those who powerfully hated you. For where could you have triumphed more gloriously over your enemies than where they, in mad and impious hearts, thought that they had triumphed over you? Those who sat in the chair of pestilence, having consciences seared, came either to put to death or to subject to insults the man whom you chose according to your heart and placed in the seat of your apostle Peter, so that from there he might enlighten and govern the Church which you redeemed from the enemy’s hand. But they were crushed, repelled, and compelled to return to their own land with great disgrace—though, by God’s mercy, life was granted to them.

## Chapter VI. The pestilence by which Frederick’s army was struck and compelled to abandon the siege of Rome.

Then occurred something never read or heard to have occurred from the ages, and whoever hears it to the end of the age will have his ears ring. Let the annalistic books of ancient kings be searched; let histories of nations be unrolled: where can it ever be shown that what is reported to have happened there occurred? Those who saw it, and who were able to escape death, report that the noblest, most powerful, and wealthiest men produced by Germany did not die as men die, nor fall like one of the princes; rather, they were found suffocated in heaps in the camp, like rain-worms or locusts drowned in a flood of waters.

Although we do not presume to set forth fully and in order the sequence of what happened there, lest those who know more fully or more truly charge us with saying either too much or too little, we nevertheless wish to mention some things, lest by keeping entirely silent we sin more grievously against the works of the Lord, sought out in all his purposes.

The army began the siege of Saint Peter’s church; then, immediately assaulting the church itself, they hacked down its doors with axes and swords. Some, as though they had accomplished a memorable and glorious deed, boasted wantonly that they would carry home to their wives the splinters which they had cut out with swords, as a token of victory—or rather, of Saint Peter’s disgrace. They also burned with fire the chapel of Blessed Mary before the portico, omitting nothing that in their mad minds they devised for the dishonour of God and Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.

Immediately a pestilence followed and avenged the Lord’s wrath. For vapour and mist rose from the earth and struck the army as though by contagion; such a plague fell upon the people that, before they reached the summit of the slope, where the whole road appears paved with stones, a hundred or more soldiers suddenly lay dead. Then, spreading through the entire multitude, the calamity quickly struck down more than a thousand soldiers, although the astonishment arose not so much from the number dying as from the horror of those suddenly falling.

For when, after the camp had been arranged, a company of about a hundred mail-clad knights reclined together in their tents—men who were nearest the emperor and customarily first before him in procession—and all the tents had been taken down, the king, sitting on horseback, wondered at their delay because he saw no one of that great company moving. He sent to discover what was the matter. The messenger came and found the horses tied to their posts, all the equipment lying as it had been arranged in the evening, and both knights and servants lifeless. All, stricken and terrified by fear, fled from death yet could not escape it. As they went, they suddenly fell from their horses; others, still standing sound on the ground, when they tried to mount their horses, suddenly fell dead backward to the ground.

## Chapter VII. The number and rank of those who died of the pestilence before the city. The miserable death of Rainald, Archbishop of Cologne, and of other German princes.

Against this power let any mortal man boast and exalt his own might—for the emperor too is certainly a mortal man—and say: “I will pursue and overtake; I will divide the spoil; my desire shall be satisfied; I will draw my sword; my hand shall kill them.” “Your right hand, O Lord—your right hand, I say—is glorious in strength; your right hand, O Lord, struck down the enemy; in the greatness of your glory you overthrew your adversaries. You sent forth your wrath, which consumed them like stubble. Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like you, glorious in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, working wonders?” (Exod. 15:9–11.) Hear now things not indeed greater, but more cruel and terrible.

Because the slaughter in the army was so great, and many were ashamed to leave their dead friends in an enemy land, they devised the plan of boiling their corpses, sprinkling them with salt, and thus bringing them with them to the land of their fathers. While one brother was boiling another, someone else sent urgently asking for the cauldron to be sent to him for a similar necessary use.
