The first replied that this could not be done, because when his brother had been boiled, he himself had first to be boiled; and this was done.

No one should suppose that this plague befell merely common people and only those at the rear of the army, whose memory, however great their number falling in battle or by any mishap, would be erased by easy oblivion. For valiant warriors and the strength of the army perished there—men each of whom, had he died a fitting natural death, would have been most worthy of mourning and funeral rites. Thus Rainald, Archbishop of Cologne, head and leader of the schism, perished with his brother Liutold. Frederick, son of King Conrad, who even while alive was a cause of fear to the emperor through his power and wealth, perished together with his nephew Berengar, son of Gebhard of Sulzbach.

But who could enumerate one by one all who died there? Their number was so great, their nobility of blood, their abundance of wealth, and their distinction such that, had they not raised their horns against the Lord and died in peace, they would have been worthy of the mourning of the entire empire. But because “the kings of the earth stood up, and the princes assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ,” they were fit to proclaim God’s glory by their death and, dying, to say: “You have conquered, Galilean; you have conquered!”

Yet in their death this is more pitiable, and to be lamented by every age: bearing arms against Rome to dishonour him to whom our Lord Jesus Christ, in Peter’s stead, prince of the apostles, gave the keys of heaven, saying, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 16:19), they died bound in their sins, and there is none on earth to loose them.

Let those who wish now go and raise their necks against the King of kings and Lord of lords, who knows and can so easily break the forces of his enemies and crush their power. Considering his strength, the prophet cries out: “Who will not fear you, O King of the ages?” (Jer. 10:7). It was indeed fitting that our Lord Jesus Christ should show his glory thus: that his enemies might be terrified in succeeding ages; that his Church might glorify him for so glorious a deliverance through generation after generation; and that it might give immense thanks to its triumphant deliverer and sing the praises due to him.

## Chapter VIII. Frederick’s persistence in persecuting Adalbert, whom the author exhorts to trust in God’s help alone. The corruption of morals introduced into the Salzburg clergy through the schism.

But above all that has been said, this is more terrible, this more pitiable: that Pharaoh’s heart was so hardened that, amid the grievous blow which we have described—not indeed in its entirety, but having scarcely touched upon a small part of it—neither the miserable death of his kinsmen or relations, nor that of princes and magnates, nor the destruction of a most noble army, touched his heart or shook it into recognizing God’s power, so that, humbled, he might acknowledge his contrition [Col. 1550A], withdraw from the schism, and venerate and love the holy Church, assuredly his mother. For if he were willing to do this, he would by no means pursue the Church of Salzburg with such zeal; he would by no means persecute with such impiety your person, elected by it as lord and bishop—his own blood.

Yet your persecution is undoubtedly, through the aid of divine providence, a loving discipline. For what would the son of the emperor’s aunt do? The son of the king of Bohemia? The son of the sister of the duke of Austria, still a young man, elected to so noble a Church as Salzburg—indeed, raised to govern the whole province of Bavaria—if, before ruling so many and such innumerable peoples and so many bishops, [Col. 1550B] he were not himself governed by bit and bridle?

Therefore, my lord, bear—bear with humility and patience—the bit and bridle laid upon your jaws, not by any ordinary persecutor, but by a father who corrects and instructs you; and he also knows when it is time to remove them, and to grant to you and to the Church peace and security, and rest from all adversities. Like a woman in travail, the Church daily cries with you to the Lord for her own deliverance and yours. He delays this, however, while your father and uncle labor for you as far as they are able, together with the whole multitude of your friends, so that you may not place your hope in a reed for a staff, or suppose that thanks owed to God should be rendered to men who cannot save. And what harm is there in delay to him [Col. 1550C] who, as soon as he wills, has the power at hand to do good? To him Queen Esther says: “Lord, almighty king, all things are placed under your dominion, and there is none who can resist your will” (Esther 13). For just as human will and purpose are ineffective when the Lord opposes them, so, when he gives aid, every human power and malice is powerless to resist. Hence that saying in Job: “Those who bear the world bow beneath him” (Job 9).

Therefore let the confidence of your mind be directed toward him; let all your hope be placed in him, who is most merciful in goodness and most mighty in majesty. Let your heart be wholly with him, firmly resolving within yourselves always to walk in the way of your Fathers, [Col. 1550D] diligently acting so that in your days the Church of God which you have undertaken to govern may remain in its proper state. As is known throughout the whole kingdom, this Church far surpassed other churches in piety, hospitality, chastity, and every form of both secular and spiritual propriety. Adorned with these virtues, the Church of Salzburg shone like a firmament radiant with stars, so that at royal courts the archbishops of Salzburg received exceptional honor above other princes, and all the clergy enjoyed the highest reverence, both those established under the Rule in cloisters and those ordered outside in parishes.

But truly, since the error of schism arose, and both your own care and that of your uncle have been exhausted and brought to a standstill by countless pressures—because amid arms the laws are silent—it has been so changed that, unless God in mercy grants you peace and steadfastness to uproot and cut away the shoots of vice, the splendid lamp of the Church will be extinguished when the good things mentioned above have been destroyed [Col. 1551A]. Remember your word, by which you gave hope to us all, who grieve deeply to see the beauty of God’s house, which we ourselves have seen with our eyes, perish. For immediately upon your entry you said that in your episcopate you would never allow Mass to be sung by anyone who believed it lawful for him to live with women.

## CHAPTER IX. It is shown how necessary is a remedy for so many vices and crimes breaking out during Adelbert’s absence, to which concubinary and shameless clerics are especially liable.

[Col. 1551B] O my lord, keep your word. Let it be fixed in your heart. Press the matter when opportunity offers, so that it may become clear also in action. Otherwise, unless that accursed Jezebel—who now goes about priests’ houses as insolently as she does freely, with eyes painted with stibium and a decorated head—is cast down by your exertion, animated by zeal for God, she will soon extend her strength so far that she will despise your rod and staff. Rejoicing in her impunity, she will proceed so far that there will be only a slight difference between a layman and a priest, apart from the Mass alone; and a parish priest will freely do what a layman does not even dare to presume or attempt.

For a cleric, whether he proclaims Christ from pretext or from truth, restrains a layman from fornications and adulteries by public penance. . . [Col. 1551C] Yet the cleric is checked by no fear. Even if his life is most shameful, he refuses to be rebuked by a layman; he despises the dean and the archdeacon. Unless he is accused—and there is no accuser, since all do the same thing and foster their own crimes in others—nothing is done. These are indeed the scales of Leviathan, so joined together that no weapon passes through to wound the pestilential body. Certainly this affair will advance so far that a priest with only one wife, like a layman, will be proclaimed pious and holy because he abstains from other men’s wives and does not violate the fidelity of another’s bed.

For what else can be expected, when we know that among us there are such men as lead a shameful life and also hold the profane teaching of the Nicolaitans, which the Lord declares in the Apocalypse that he hates? They read the sacred canons to their hearers and show them how they ought to defend the crimes of their fornications. Relying on this authority, a certain priest joined his nieces in marriage to priests, while himself having numerous offspring by a woman whom he is said to have abjured six times before my predecessor [Col. 1551D].

[Col. 1552A] What am I to say of the fact that, although I forbid it according to the custom of this Church, sons of priests who remain with wives whom they took away while their husbands were still living come to ordination fortified with letters from certain prelates, and are ordained; and, despite me, they sing Mass within my archdeaconry and aspire to parishes? Although the sacred canons utterly exclude such men from holy orders, and if you had known them, I know that you would never have laid hands upon them, nevertheless, if it pleases you and you command that they sing, I bear it patiently, though unwillingly, because “the disciple is not above the master” (Matthew 10).

But if not, may it please your discernment to command that they cease from the ministry of the altar until their case is examined by you, or until it is established by whom they were presented to you, or by what introducers, when the question was put to you, “Is he worthy? Is he upright?” and the answer was given: “He is worthy; he is upright.” For this commends you and accords alike with reverence for the canons and ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 1552B]. Otherwise, since I ought to be your eye, and willingly desire, in accordance with the obedience and fidelity owed to you, to see what concerns the honor of God and of yourself and to attend to the office entrusted to me—if, seeing transgressions such as these and similar ones, I must keep silence, I would rather wholly lack the archdeaconry and not share in other men’s sins, awaiting nothing but condemnation.

There are many things like these which call for your correction. But because you do not have time for rebuking and judging, I do not wish to increase the agitation of your thoughts and your anxieties. Yet it would be useful and good that matters which you cannot correct through your personal presence should be amended through us, who, as we have said, are your eyes, lest the insolence of evil men grow without measure. Your prudence certainly ought to know, and not doubt, that if he whose eyes subtly see our imperfection sees anything in your own life less than is fitting, you should nevertheless not despair of pardon and indulgence, provided that, in accordance with the stewardship entrusted to you, you eliminate and cast out the abominations and transgressions such as are customarily committed by violators of God’s commandments, sweeping them away with the broom, according to the prophet; so that you may be able, as confidently [Col. 1552D] as truthfully, to say with the Psalmist: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place where your glory dwells” (Psalm 25).

May almighty God, who is the father of orphans and judge of widows, guard, protect, defend, and deliver you, my lord, from every evil. Amen.

ANNO DOMINI 1174: HUGH OF FOLIET

[Col. 1553]

## NOTICE

(MABILLON, *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. VI, p. 457)

The place now calls upon us to speak of Hugh of Foliet, a man celebrated in those times, concerning whom it is astonishing how diverse are the opinions that circulate; nor has it hitherto been sufficiently established what judgment ought to be made of them. Gabriel Pennotus, raving in his usual manner, says that Hugh of Foliet was a regular canon of the Church of Córdoba in the province of Seville. Ciaconius ranks Hugh among the cardinals and writes that he was a Frenchman, a regular canon of the monastery of St. Peter of Corbie in Saxony. As many words, so many errors. As for the earlier writers: William of Nangis [Note: [Col. 1553] *Spicilegium*, vol. XI, under the year 1140.] calls him a monk; Vincent of Beauvais, following the opinion of others, and St. Antoninus following Vincent, say that Hugh of Foliet is asserted to have been a canon of St. Peter of Corbie. Others, coming closer to the truth, think that he was a monk of St. Peter of Corbie in the cell of St. Lawrence at Heilly. Finally, most writers, with Ciaconius, make him a cardinal. It is worthwhile to investigate what may certainly be determined concerning these claims.

Hugh of Foliet, so called from the suburb of that name near ancient Corbie, where he was born, was without doubt a regular canon of the Order of St. Augustine in the monastery of St. Lawrence at Heilly, a place more than three miles distant from Corbie. This place had first been granted to the monks of St. John of Angély, as we said above; but shortly afterward it was given to clerics who observed the Rule of St. Augustine in great poverty. This happened at the beginning of the twelfth century, in the episcopate of St. Geoffrey, bishop of Amiens, with the assent of the abbot of Corbie, whose fief included the land of Heilly and consequently the place in which this church of St. Lawrence stood.

The same rule remained there in force in the year in which Eugenius III granted the privilege of apostolic protection to his beloved sons Ulric, prior of the church of St. Lawrence near Corbie, and his brethren professing the canonical life, and indeed according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, as is stated in the text of the charter. This bull was issued at Viterbo, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the preceding year according to the old reckoning, in the fifth year of Eugenius. The same canonical order remained there until the year 1205, when the regular canons of that place, with the assent of the abbot of Corbie, submitted themselves to the monks of Lehon in Santerre, of the Cluniac Order. But in the end this place, abandoned by the monks of Lehon, returned to the Corbie monks, its lords of the soil. There, in an uncultivated, solitary, and barren place, there remains only the chapel of St. Lawrence, together with a few traces of the former monastery.

In that place Hugh of Foliet lived the canonical and indeed poor life under Prior Ulric. In 1153 he became prior after Ulric and died while holding that office, as we shall shortly see. Certainly, in 1152, when Guarinus, abbot of St. Vaast, settled with those canons concerning the tithes of Dodo’s estate in the diocese of Amiens, the witnesses named among the clerics were Ulric the superior, Hugh of Foliet, and Rorgo the subprior. But in the following year Hugh was prior. In that year Theodoric, bishop of Amiens, absolved Baldwin of Durz—commonly Dours—and his wife Beatrice from the excommunication they had incurred for injuries inflicted upon the Church of Amiens, through the hand of Lord Hugh, venerable prior of the same place of St. Lawrence, after they had first made a modest satisfaction to the Church of Amiens.

In 1174 Simon had succeeded Hugh as prior. In that year Theobald, bishop of Amiens, at the request of Simon, prior of St. Lawrence, confirmed the agreement made in the time of Bishop Theodoric between Simon’s church and Baldwin of Dours in order to obtain the aforementioned absolution. Eight years later Milo was prior of that place, as appears from letters of Hugh, abbot of Corbie, to be cited in their proper place. At the same time Theobald, bishop of Amiens, entrusted to Milo, prior of St. Lawrence, and to his brethren professing the regular life, the church of St. Nicholas at Regniac to be ordered according to the form of their institutions. After this Milo, no other prior of St. Lawrence appears in the archive of Corbie, from which we have received all these facts. In the necrology of Corbie is noted: “7 September: Hugh, prior of St. Lawrence.” I do not know whether this is the same Hugh of Foliet recorded in the necrology of St. Peter of Chartres on 2 October. Be that as it may, these facts sufficiently show that this Hugh of Foliet, prior of St. Lawrence, to whom, as we shall soon see, the books *On the Cloister of the Soul* must be assigned, was not a cardinal of the Roman Church.

What especially commends Hugh of Foliet is that, when he was requested as abbot by the regular canons of St. Denis near Reims, he refused to accept the request. This happened after the death of Abbot Ursio, whom Marlot [Note: [Col. 1553] *Metropolis Remensis*, vol. II, p. 153.] says died on 26 February in this year. Then Hugh of Foliet was elected, through the action of Guerric, abbot of Igny, as we learn from his unpublished letter, certainly worthy to be reproduced here in full in order to illustrate the modesty of this most pious and learned man. It is contained as follows in a certain parchment of Corbie:

> To Lord H., Brother HUGH of St. Lawrence: salvation from him who saves the upright in heart.
>
> The election said to have been made of me by the canons of Blessed Denis, with the assent of Samson, venerable archbishop of Reims, has, as we have heard, become public through the counsel of Lord Guerric, abbot of Igny. We are astonished at the discernment of a prudent man in such a matter, when he endeavors to join me to brethren of so different a profession. He sews sackcloth to silk and, as it were, attaches a peacock’s tail to a vulture’s hindquarters. To speak figuratively again: he fashions a goat-stag; and not only fashions it, but paints it too. He fashions a goat-stag if anyone thinks of me anything beyond what he sees in me or hears from me. He paints a goat-stag who adorns my person with the names of various virtues, as with diverse colors. Why does he desire to join an animal of such shaggy fleece to an animal clothed in delicate hairs? Nature did not produce the one; custom forbids the other.
>
> If one asks about my person, I have little of the man in me; if my character is examined, I am turbulent among the brethren; if my capacity for work is questioned, I am faint-hearted in great matters. That place is exalted; it requires an exalted person. It is close to the court, and requires a man fortified with counsel, discerning, and eloquent; but he will find none of these things in me. You know our manner of life. The brethren abound in riches; we are subjected to poverty. If I renounce poverty, I become a great reproach to my neighbors. If I draw near to riches, I fear a fall in the ascent and ruin in high station. I am exceedingly constrained. If I depart, many of our brethren declare that they too will depart. If I encounter riches, the people accuse me of having formerly professed poverty; I become a scandal to the brethren and a reproach to the people. Distresses surround me on every side, because I have heard the reproach of many dwelling round about.
>
> Some say: “He refuses to be an abbot; he desires a bishopric.” God is witness: may my soul perish from the people of God if from my youth to this day I have desired primacy in the Church. A reason is sought; God is the reason. Again, I am not equal to such a task. I scarcely suffice for myself; and, even if willingness were present, infirmity would refuse. For a long time I suffered from the frequent vomiting of a failing stomach. The flood of vomiting has ceased somewhat, but is sometimes stirred by a slight occasion. I report a known fact. I am accustomed to be afflicted by various sorts of infirmities. Yet I am pressed by the friendly compulsion of our metropolitan—friendly, unless I am mistaken—for he compels an unknown person to become familiar to him, a lowly person to be raised up, and a poor man to become rich. I indeed rejoice that I have deserved to become familiar with a person of so great a name; but I greatly fear that, if I refuse what he asks, I shall seem all the more grievous in his eyes.
>
> I ask you to excuse me. The reason for my excuse is fitting. I have an aged and infirm father: namely, Lord Ulric, our prior. Shall I abandon him in sickness and refuse to serve him in old age? For he loves me as a father, and I love him; and I shall remain with him while he lives, if I can. Therefore suggest to the lord of Igny that he should not trouble the water of a poor man, which had been accustomed to run quietly. For I fear that, if I come to Reims, I shall live more laxly.

Thus far Hugh’s letter. Where he says that he is surprised that Abbot Guerric endeavors to join him to brethren of so different a profession, this must not be understood as though he followed a rule different from theirs; rather, they were near the archbishop’s court, whereas these men were placed in a harsh solitude; they abounded in riches, whereas these lived in extreme poverty, a condition which Hugh says he could not exchange without scandal.

Now that we have come to this point, it remains to inquire concerning his writings, if any survive. In many manuscripts which we have seen, four books *On the Cloister of the Soul* are attributed to Hugh of Foliet; these were published among the works of Hugh of St. Victor. At the end, however, Thomas Garzonius, a regular canon, observes that he found these books printed under the name of Master Hugh of St. Victor; but since they differ somewhat from his style and profession, he himself rather agrees with those who judge them to be by Hugh of Foliet. The same editor further adds that Hugh, when writing these books, had passed from the canonical rule of St. Augustine to the stricter rule of St. Benedict—whom he frequently mentions, as also St. Augustine. Though I would gladly admit this for the honor of our order, because of so great a man’s merit, I shall nevertheless show from Hugh’s own words shortly, when I have established that these books are his, that this is false.

For a long time the author’s name was doubted, even among the older writers. This happened because in the prologue the author directed that his name be withheld from the anonymous brother at whose request he had undertaken to write these books. “Therefore,” he says, “brother, reveal our name to no one, lest, through the author’s foolishness and the lowliness of his person, the labor of our work be cheapened.” Hence, in a manuscript of the monastery of Cheminon in the diocese of Châlons, the following title is attached to those books: “Here begins the prologue of an unnamed author to the following work, *On the Cloister of the Soul*.” Yet they say that the author of the work was Hugh of Corbie, canon and prior of St. Lawrence.

But in a manuscript of Foucarmont in the diocese of Rouen there is a little book of Lord Hugh of Foliet addressed to a friend wishing to marry; and in the same manuscript, after two sermons of St. Bernard and a letter, follows: “Likewise, of Hugh, canon and prior of Foliet, *On the Twelve Abuses of the Cloister*,” which is the subject of the second book *On the Cloister of the Soul*. Moreover, in the manuscript formerly belonging to Thou, now to Colbert: “Here begins the prologue of Master Hugh of Foliet, prior of the canons of St. Lawrence in the district of Amiens, in the book *On the Cloister of the Body and Soul*.” Finally, in the catalogue of manuscripts of Belgium, Hugh of St. Lawrence is called the author of those books in three places. William of Nangis indeed calls Hugh of Foliet, who wrote the book *On the Cloister of Body and Soul*, a monk of St. Peter of Corbie; but he immediately adds that others say that this Hugh was a regular canon in the district of Amiens, which can easily be proved from the context of his work.

This work is excellent and especially worthy to be read by religious men, and it seemed proper to give here some sample of it. The work is divided into four books. The first explains the temptations of cloistered persons and the benefits of religious life. The second concerns the ordering and arrangement of the material cloister. The third orders the cloister of the soul. The fourth commends the dwelling-place of the unmade cloister, that is, heaven, as something to be sought.

In the first, four temptations of cloistered persons are disclosed: namely, the attractiveness of places, such as cities and towns; the abundance of a place; costly ornament; and intercourse with women. The author then explains the benefits of religious life.

In the second, speaking of the number of brethren to be received, he says that only as many should be admitted as can live in orderly fashion, lest either, under the pretext of poverty, they live irregularly, or, owing to the multitude living together, seek unlawful things for their necessities. There he disapproves of two or three, or even four or five, living in cells together; and he praises certain monks, doubtless Cistercians, whom he calls heirs of blessed Benedict, who send no fewer than twelve brethren to new monasteries, lest the work of religion be corrupted by the negligence caused by too few persons.

He lays down the following concerning food: “Let them use the fruits of trees and the produce of the earth; let their dishes be seasoned with butter, oil, or milk, but not animal fat. Let them abstain from meat, unless necessity or a dispensation should permit it somewhere outside the community. The brethren may use wine in the community; nevertheless we believe that we must by all means avoid—what we are about to say with shame—that what is mercifully granted should, as some are accustomed to do, be demanded as though it were owed. For we do not promise it, but grant it. But if place or poverty denies what we grant, let them use without murmuring what the region or their property provides. Therefore let none of our profession recoil from an abstinence which excludes only the use of meat from every kind of food, but permits and generously supplies all the rest.”

Where he treats of the number of dishes, he assigns two cooked dishes to each person, and on fast-days a third, uncooked dish from the produce of the earth, in accordance with the mind of St. Benedict; on other days, at dinner, two cooked dishes; at supper, one uncooked or cooked dish, according to the superior’s will. With regard to clothing, he says that each brother needs two tunics, one fur garment, a surplice, skins or a cloak, a hooded cape, drawers, hose, socks, and, for labor, a scapular; all of which he plainly understands of regular canons.

He then treats of the twelve abuses of the cloister. In the seventh, which concerns costly dress, he says: “According to the Rule”—namely, that of St. Benedict—“I think that what is cheaper when found should be bought, not what is dearer, so that there may be a difference between the clothing of a palace and that of a monk.” He then adds: “I, such as I am, a canon, speak about monks. But what ought to be said of certain canons of our order makes both mind and face blush deeply. Their beds are supported by feather mattresses and carefully prepared with linen and coverlets,” etc. From this it is clearer than light that Hugh was a regular canon when he wrote below: “Even among those clothed in tunics—that is, monks—pleasure has set foot: not because they wear shirts, but because they wear a certain delicate cloth called in common speech *saia*. Thus, in displaying a woolen garment they show the harshness of their way of life; but in the enjoyment of delicate cloth they seek the softness of comfort. I myself,” he says, “have seen, if I am not mistaken, a monk wearing a shirt, jesting and saying: ‘The warp is more expensive than the shirt; but wearing a tunic is a great hardship.’ Yet perhaps you will say that such a man was sick. On the contrary, he was healthy and insolent, riding a fat horse, abounding in possessions, and frequenting courts; though before putting on the habit of conversion he had been accustomed to go on foot and was not always clothed in linen.” I pass over the rest, lest I be too long—though perhaps some will already judge me to have been too long.

In the prologue of the third book Hugh says that the regulations concerning the material cloister set out in the preceding book had not merely been written, but had also been arranged according to place, time, and persons, and put into practice where he lived. No one had withdrawn, and all had consented to this ordering, except certain laymen or lay brethren, “who,” he says, “still bear the yoke and murmur; and such persons had lived more poorly in the world than they now live, and now seek in the monastery what they could not have possessed outside.” And below: “None of the clerics, dearest one, now disagrees, but each kindly bears the burden of religion; and what was formerly more burdensome to them is now more welcome. Therefore I labor in order always to live quietly with them and to die with them in peace, a fellow-servant and brother with them and under them.” Hugh certainly fulfilled this in deed when he steadfastly refused the abbacy of St. Denis near Reims.

These examples of the books *On the Cloister of the Soul* by Hugh may suffice. I do not doubt that he was educated and trained in letters at the monastery of Corbie before withdrawing to the solitude of St. Lawrence. Hence he repeatedly praises the Rule of St. Benedict in those books, and indeed follows it in many respects.

The same author also composed other writings, such as the little book addressed to a friend wishing to marry, which is inscribed under the name of Lord Hugh of Foliet in the manuscript of Foucarmont, as we observed above. Moreover, in a manuscript of the Cistercian monastery of Aulne in Belgium, we once read a book by Master Hugh of St. Lawrence, *On the Medicine of the Soul*, whose prologue begins: “You compel me, dearest brother,” etc. Finally, we read there another prologue of Master Hugh, prior of St. Lawrence, in a book *On Shepherds and Sheep*, beginning: “To you, brother, who are in the flock,” etc. These are the matters which came before us concerning this eminent man in the course of examining libraries.

[Col. 1557]

## SECOND NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Library of Medieval and Later Latin*, vol. III, p. 294)

Hugh of Foliet, a regular canon of St. Peter of Corbie in Picardy and prior of St. Lawrence in the territory of Amiens, and finally a cardinal about the year 1140. He is commended by St. Antoninus at the beginning of Title XVIII of the *Summa historialis* for the singular excellence of his life and for the distinguished nobility of his learning and eloquence. He wrote a fourfold book: *On the Twelve Abuses of the Cloister* [Note: [Col. 1557] Those twelve abuses are: a negligent superior; a disobedient disciple; an idle young man; an obstinate old man; a courtly monk; a litigious religious; costly dress; refined food; noise in the cloister; quarrelling in chapter; disorder in choir; irreverence at the altar.], and *On the Material Cloister*, *On the Spiritual Cloister*, *On the Cloister of the Soul*, and *On the Cloister of Paradise*.

See Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 374; *Illustrious Benedictines*, II, 115; and those who offer excerpts from this book of Hugh: Vincent of Beauvais, *Mirror of History*, book XXVII, ch. 18 ff.; and Antoninus, Title XVII of the *Summa historialis*, ch. 2. The book itself was published among the works of Hugh of St. Victor, to whom it was mistakenly attributed, as noted by Labbe, vol. I, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 482; G. Colvenerius, in his notes on John Nider’s *Formicarius*, p. 47 ff.; and others.

Besides this book, under *On the Cloister of the Soul*, p. 134, Sander’s *Catalogue of Belgian Manuscripts* mentions, p. 224, the treatise *On the Three Doves*; p. 93, the little book addressed to Brother Rainer, entitled *The Silvered Dove* (*Columba deargentata*); and p. 131, *On the Turtledove and the Sparrow*. These are not different from the book *On Birds*, addressed to Raynerius, which occurs in manuscript copies with illustrations of birds and owes much to Peter Damian’s tract 52. It was published among the works of Hugh of St. Victor together with three books *On the Properties of Beasts and Animals*, of which learned men attribute the first to Alan of Lille and the third and fourth to William Peraldus.

See Oudin, vol. II, p. 1107 ff., who also assigns to Hugh of Foliet two books *On Carnal and Spiritual Marriages*, or *On Marriages to Be Avoided*, addressed to a companion wishing to marry; also four little books *On the Vanity of the World* and five books *On the Ark*, in mystical and moral interpretation, which are printed among the works of Hugh of St. Victor; and the *Mirror of Sinners*, found in the appendix to volume VI of Augustine, p. 635 of the Amsterdam edition. If we follow Alberic, p. 264 of the *Chronicle*, under the year 1130, Hugh belonged to the Premonstratensian Order and wrote *On the Nature of Birds*, morally and allegorically, *On the Cloister of the Soul*, and *On the Medicine of the Soul*. I omit that G. Joseph Eggs, in *Learned Purple*, vol. I, p. 75, attributes to Hugh of Foliet a little book *On the Patriarchs and on Discipline*, addressed to religious persons, which perhaps ought more correctly to be referred to another author named Hugh.

## [THE COMPLETE WORKS OF HUGH OF FOLIET.]

[Col. 1557]

## [ON HUGH’S WRITINGS.]

For the writings of Hugh of Foliet, see our Prolegomena to Hugh of St. Victor and the Appendices to the works of the same, *Patrologia*, vols. CLXXV, CLXXVI, CLXXVII. EDITOR.

ANNO DOMINI 1175: HENRY I, BROTHER OF KING LOUIS VII, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

[Col. 1559]

## NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, new ed., IX, 88)

[Col. 1559A] Henry, brother of King Louis VII, was transferred from the bishopric of Beauvais to the see of Reims on 14 January 1162, according to the Chronicle of Reims just cited; Pope Alexander III approved the election and sent him the pallium through the abbot of La Grande-Sauve. Without delay Henry, together with his suffragans, devoted himself, when the opportunity arose, to the honor of the Church of Châlons. The matter concerned the election of a bishop, which Henry, count of Champagne, opposed, and King Louis did so at his instigation. When nothing was achieved after many disputes, the matter was referred to Alexander.

Alexander first wrote in July to the archbishop of Reims that he was prepared to comply with his wishes unless he perceived a contrary will in the king; but he had postponed determination of the matter until the feast of St. Luke, so that in the meantime the archbishop might soften the king and bring him by gentle words to his own view [Col. 1559B]. A few days later, while at Brioude, Alexander invited the same prelate and the king to a private conference concerning that business at Clermont, where Marlot, on the authority of Wassebourg, observes that Alexander held a council. What was done at that council for the Church of Châlons, and whether the king and archbishop attended it, is wholly unknown to us. One thing alone we know: the two agreed that “if the case of the election celebrated in the Church of Châlons should be lawfully examined in the pope’s presence, this would be neither in any way burdensome nor troublesome to that same king.”

[Col. 1559C] Meanwhile Emperor Frederick and Henry, count of Champagne, strongly supported the cause of the antipope Octavian and endeavored to draw King Louis to their side. For that reason Frederick had summoned a conference at Pont-laon—commonly Saint-Jean-de-Laon—having called together all the prelates of the Empire; and he had written letters, found in Duchesne, *History of France*, vol. IV, pp. 576 and 580, to the archbishops of Lyon and Reims, inviting them to the conference. But when Henry received these letters, he immediately warned his brother the king to beware of the trap prepared for him, in these words:

> “To the reverend lord and his brother Louis, by God’s grace king of the Franks: Henry, called archbishop of Reims, greeting. We are greatly astonished and still more disturbed by what has been reported to us: namely, that Count Henry, as is said, has given oaths and most binding assurances on your behalf to the emperor that you ought generally, together with the Gallican Church, to receive that Octavian as pope. From whom this has been reported to us, we neither have nor ought to disclose to you. In this crisis of such necessity, let your prudent judgment be watchful, lest through the sons of darkness your innocence suffer a miserable shipwreck, both of soul and body. Farewell.”

Alexander, no less fearful of the emperor’s schemes, firmly refused to attend the conference and wrote to Henry as follows [Col. 1560B]:

> “By these letters we urge your prudence to devote yourself in every way to disrupting that conference which the same king proposes to hold with Frederick, the so-called emperor, and to ensure by whatever means you can that this purpose of such a kind has no fulfillment.”

Alexander’s affairs at last turned out as he wished. Louis, having turned away from the emperor, frustrated all his plans, at the prompting, it is believed, of his brother Henry and, as Alberic says in his chronicle, “at the instigation of the men of Clairvaux”; thereafter he adhered with the greatest constancy to the lawful pope. The chronicler of Vézelay recounts all this at length, *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 578. Subsequently Alexander wrote very frequently [Col. 1560C] to Henry, both concerning his own pressing affairs and those of the Church. There survive letters written by him in the same year: recommending his legate at the king’s court; concerning the election of the bishop of Arras; concerning the expulsion of secular canons from each of the two monasteries of St Mary and St Wulmar at Boulogne and the restoration of regular canons; concerning Matthew, count of Boulogne, who had married a nun; concerning the bishop of Orléans; and concerning certain heretics. In 1163 Henry confirmed to the church of St Just the annual revenues of five churches which he had already bestowed upon it, while he presided over the church of Beauvais. But since in that same [Col. 1561A] year he could not attend the Council of Tours because of illness, Alexander, greatly anxious over that illness, wrote to him in these terms:

> “We know, and hold as a complete truth, how you, like a true Israelite, have fought bravely and steadfastly for the exaltation and defence of the most holy Church; and how, setting yourself against Damascus, the tower of strength, you have endeavoured faithfully to conduct and manage the cause of that Church as though it were your own. Therefore, as we and our brethren firmly impress all these things upon our memory, we sympathize with you, as with a most beloved brother and a most vigorous champion of the Church, with the earnest affection of our hearts concerning the infirmity with which the right hand of the heavenly Creator has visited you; and we grieve greatly in the Lord. Accordingly, being exceedingly anxious and concerned for your recovery, we have thought fit to visit your most beloved brotherhood by the greeting of the apostolic blessing and by our letters . . . For, if it should please and be acceptable to you, we shall send some of the more eminent persons among our brethren to visit you; and we ourselves, in person, would not hesitate to undergo the labour, if we believed it would profit and benefit you.”

In 1164, after recovering his health, Henry took action regarding the injury inflicted upon the archbishop of Lyons by the count of Roucy, who had wickedly despoiled that prelate’s messenger carrying money. He then received new letters from Alexander concerning various conferences being conducted in the king’s council and relating to ecclesiastical affairs.

[Col. 1561C] In the same year disturbances arising from the newly established communes had grown everywhere to such a degree that blood was often shed. Indeed, nothing seemed more just, nothing better suited to the public advantage, than the royal ordinance—provided that the aldermen did not exceed the limits of the authority granted them. But, relying upon the circumstances of the time and the discord among the popes, they did not fear in many places violently to lay hands on ecclesiastical liberty and subject even the priesthood to their profane dominion. These disturbances finally boiled over at Reims; arms were taken up more than once, and the city was shaken and convulsed until the commune was fully established. For when the aldermen overstepped the bounds of their privilege and indiscriminately offered protection to everyone, without distinction, including persons subject to ecclesiastical jurisdiction, Henry judged that he ought to resist their undertaking, both from the duty of his office and because of the complaints of ministers oppressed by them. But, that it may be better understood with how much zeal—indeed, with what sharpness and severity—he did this, we must cite the words of John of Salisbury, who vividly describes the wretched condition of the commonwealth at the time of these events, the satisfaction voluntarily offered by the citizens, their spirit in defending ancestral liberty, and the entire course and outcome of the affair.

> “John of Salisbury to Lord John, bishop of Poitiers. The collisions of kingdoms, great earthquakes, and the consequences of imminent dangers have long compelled me [Col. 1562A] to lay aside my pen and wait for more favourable times for writing. For the tumults of war, raging through almost the whole summer, prevented the carriers of letters from passing through; and the sedition arising in the city of Reims so disturbed the province that it was scarcely safe to enter or leave the city. For the citizens, with the counsel of the clergy and the aid of knights, had conspired against the archbishop, who wished to impose upon the city certain new, unjust, and intolerable servitudes. Having seized the towers of the churches and the more fortified houses, and driven the archbishop’s officials and friends from the city, they inflicted many injuries upon him.
>
> “At first they displayed every humility toward him, ready, as many testify, to pay two thousand pounds into his treasury [Col. 1562B] provided that he treated them according to law and allowed them to live under the laws which the city had continuously used since the time of St Remigius, apostle of the Franks. They had even approached the Most Christian king; but they could not bend the archbishop’s severity even through him. They therefore fled to Count Henry and, on his advice, yielded to the king, whom the archbishop had brought in so that he might crush the city by his arm. The king, grieved but nevertheless satisfying his brother’s will, had about fifty houses demolished and departed. On the third day the citizens returned and, in revenge for the demolished houses, utterly destroyed the houses of the knights who favoured the archbishop—namely, those of his vidame and of another who had held the prefecture in the city.
>
> “Whereupon the archbishop, moved to anger, invoked the aid [Col. 1562C] of the count of Flanders and brought him to Reims with a thousand knights, so that the citizens might perish by the sword or be cast into chains to be ransomed and tortured. But, foreseeing the count’s arrival, they again withdrew, so completely emptying the city that the Flemings, worn out by hunger, could scarcely endure a stay of one day and one night. And the archbishop, who on their departure did not doubt that the citizens would return to their homes, made peace with them through his brother Count Robert, without the Flemings’ knowledge. He received four hundred and fifty pounds as compensation for losses which, not to mention the many injuries and insults, had increased fourfold; and he conceded that henceforward they should use their ancient customs. Thus, after making a ruinous and ignominious peace [Col. 1562D] with the citizens, he still carries on hostilities with the clergy and harasses churches that offer themselves to the law.”

These are Salisbury’s words, to which Marlot appends his observations as follows:

> “This foreign scholar, recently received as a guest at Reims, briefly touches upon how fiercely the city was disturbed under Henry; but he does not sufficiently explain what those unjust servitudes were which Henry strove to impose upon the citizens, nor the laws or customs which he asserts that they had used since the time of St Remigius—indeed, before the Frankish monarchy, as some maintain. I would certainly not deny that they possessed municipal laws, although Flodoard nowhere mentions them. But whether the archbishop first attempted to abolish those laws, thereby giving rise to the dispute, is not sufficiently clear.
>
> “Indeed, he seems rather to have been especially enraged against the leaders of the commune because, emboldened by his absence, they had arrogated too much to themselves by imposing burdens upon his men—as other bishops of this period so often complained to the king. This is further proved by Philip’s rescript addressed to the chief men of the communes throughout the province of Reims. Yet Henry, not content to oppose the establishment of the new commune, as was done elsewhere, wished to abolish the former mode of life, or the customs according to which the aldermen administered justice, so that, once these were removed, he might subject the citizens entirely to the jurisdiction of his own officials. But when he perceived their resistance and the whole city aroused against him, he was at last compelled to permit them to use [Col. 1563B] their own laws, though apparently with the aldermen’s authority prohibited; for William the Cardinal, Henry’s successor, restored them in 1182.
>
> “As to the hostilities which he likewise exercised against the clergy or canons, I think this arose from the infringement of privileges which granted them power to excommunicate, or even absolve, those who had violated the chapter’s rights or invaded clerical property. It is likely that he refused to subscribe, at his joyful arrival, to privileges of this kind confirmed by Urban II, because they no less conflicted with archiepiscopal dignity than the enlarged jurisdiction of the aldermen under the commune conflicted with his temporal dominion, which he so vehemently defended. There survive many letters of Pope Alexander III [Col. 1563C] written both to settle complaints of this kind and concerning other affairs of Reims; see them in Marlot, vol. II, p. 393, and in the very extensive collection of our Martène, vol. II, p. 665 ff. Moreover, Pagi proves that these disturbances had ceased in 1167, vol. IV, p. 629.”

As for the other notable events of his life, in that same year, 1164, he translated the body of St Rictrude, with Andrew, bishop of Arras, present; and he confirmed the possessions of the monastery of St Lawrence of the Wood. About 1165 he was chosen by the king, together with Henry, count of Troyes, as arbitrator between the count of Nevers and the monks of Vézelay. In 1166, upon the death of Gerald, bishop of Tournai, the clergy and people [Col. 1563D] elected Walter, dean of that church; and when they presented the elect to Henry for confirmation and consecration, the canons of Noyon—who bitterly resented the separation of the church of Tournai from their own—opposed his ordination and appealed Walter to the Apostolic See. But Henry, knowing both the elect’s merit and the injustice of the appellants, set these disputes aside and nevertheless ordained Walter. On hearing this, Alexander was greatly astonished that such an act had escaped the archbishop; he sternly admonished him to forbid the bishop whom he had ordained from exercising his office until he and those who had elected him presented themselves for judgment.

Not long afterwards the archbishop complained that the pope’s favour and affection toward him had grown cold because Alexander had refused to grant his requests in the affair of the bishop of Arras. He received from the same pope [Col. 1564A] a letter full of kindness and praise, though he was admonished to treat his suffragans kindly and not to dispose as his own of the churches of St Peter—that is, exempt churches—situated in his province, but to permit them to enjoy their liberty. At about the same time, while visiting the dioceses of Flanders, he discovered certain adherents of the Manichaean heresy so puffed up by madness that they thought themselves wholly free from defilement, although in fact they were stained by the foulest vices. The archbishop first warned them to return to the bosom of the Church, lest iniquity strike deeper roots. When this achieved nothing, and they appealed to the Apostolic See against the censures he eventually employed against them, King Louis asked Alexander by letter not to hear them; see the letter in Marlot, vol. II, p. 396.

The supreme pontiff, delighted by the zeal with which the archbishop of Reims acted in these matters, afterwards entrusted to his prudence and wisdom certain further business: namely, to determine, together with William of Sens, the governance of the Paris schools; and publicly to denounce, with lighted candles, the murderers of the bishop-elect of Cambrai. When, because of a crime committed, Henry had placed the land of a certain man in the diocese of Beauvais under interdict, and King Louis had written to the supreme pontiff for that man’s release, Alexander decided that letters of intercession should first be sent to the archbishop, and that nothing should be done about relaxing the interdict [Col. 1564C] until the case had received its due conclusion in Henry’s court or in that of the bishop of Beauvais: “For otherwise,” he said, “it would be less honourable for us lightly to dissolve, without his knowledge, a sentence canonically pronounced by so great a man, if that is grievous to him.”

The same archbishop also expended much care and concern on behalf of Hugh, bishop of Soissons, chancellor of King Louis, against hostile persons who envied him this distinguished office. But his prayers to Alexander on behalf of a regular canon who eagerly sought the secular dignity of chancellor in the church of Noyon were fruitless, as is clear from the rescript of that pope, which Marlot arranged to have printed after Vassor.

About 1167, certain disputes having arisen between Henry and the bishop [Col. 1564D] of Beauvais, Alexander wrote to him ordering him to correct what he had done improperly, in several letters whose order appears somewhat confused. See the register of the same supreme pontiff in Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. II, letters 167, 169, 240, 336, and 357. But these matters will seem of lesser importance when account is taken of his merits, whose fame had spread to the most distant peoples. This is attested by the letters of Amalric, king of Jerusalem, and of L . . . . , bishop of Nazareth; see them there, pp. 803 and 864. In 1168 he granted a privilege to the monastery of St Theoderic; and he gave to the monastery of Élan land called Foresta. In 1169, together with Hugh, bishop of Soissons, he reconciled the estranged kings of France and England [Col. 1565A]; afterward he prevented both the marriage of King Louis’s daughter to the son of Emperor Frederick and that of the emperor’s daughter to the king’s son. About 1170 he gave the annual revenues of canonries of St Symphorian to the canons of Saint-Denis at Reims.

In the same year, to erase the charge of excessive severity by a special favour toward the citizens, he ordered fairs to be held beginning on Easter Day and ending on the following Sunday, enticing foreign merchants to attend by the hope of profit and by indulgences and ceremonial display. But these were later transferred to another day because of the dignity of the feast. Again in the same year, since observance of the regular life and common life had greatly declined among the canons of Reims, he confirmed the decree of his predecessor Samson that bread alone should be distributed to non-resident canons [Col. 1565B]; yet common life could not then be restored. Alexander III wrote him stern letters on this matter, and similarly stern letters to the canons, exhorting them to resume, for their own good, what they had wrongly abandoned—both in vain.

At that time Henry was attacked in a most violent war by the count of Troyes because of the castles and fortifications he had constructed against the Coterelli, most wicked brigands of all; and the matter was referred to the supreme pontiff. Since the thickets or little woods between St Basolus and Vidula provided a refuge for those brigands, who secretly laid ambushes for travellers going from Châlons to Reims, the archbishop had nothing more at heart, once he had provided for his own household’s [Col. 1565C] advantage, than to restrain or suppress murders, robberies, and thefts, and to establish complete peace and tranquillity around the city’s environs. To prevent their daring anything similar in future, he built, with an armed body of men whom he always kept ready, a tower at Seven Willows, to be governed by a castellan. From Ascelin, abbot of St Basolus, he granted that castellan the rights of ban, justice, mills, and fishing, for his own support and the pay of his soldiers, as appears from the charter of that monastery issued in 1171 and published by Marlot. In the same year he invested Hubert, abbot [Col. 1566A] of St Theoderic, with half the viscounty of St Theoderic.

He died in 1175 and was buried in the cathedral church before the high altar. The necrology of that church says of him:

> “On 13 November died Henry, our archbishop of pious memory, son of the great King Louis; and he rests within. He acquired for the bishopric the castle called Seven Willows; he added to the church lighting twenty-four candles, each weighing four pounds, except for four, of which two are to burn continually before the bodies of the saints and two above the altar, each costing two pounds. He also bestowed many ornaments: a cross set with gems, a silver basin, candlesticks with staffs, and one hundred pounds for purchasing [Col. 1566B] revenues.”

He is also praised for such affection and generosity toward learned men that he retained with him those whom he could support, providing them assistance for the honour and adornment of his church. Among them were Ralph, dean of Reims, and John of Salisbury, both Englishmen. He wrote letters in a rather free style to the cardinals of the Roman Church and to Pope Alexander III, found in vol. II of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*, p. 228 ff. Arnulf of Lisieux wrote to him on behalf of Philip of Chaumont, Henry’s kinsman, a man of royal blood, from whom Henry had withdrawn favour after conferring many benefits upon him.

Moreover, although most writers begin, with William his successor, the line of bishops of the church of Reims [Col. 1566C] who were called dukes and peers of France, Henry was nevertheless called peer of France, duke, and archbishop of Reims in a letter written in 1171 to Henry II, king of England, by Peter Bernardi, corrector of Vincennes of the Order of Grandmont, after he had heard of the murder of Thomas of Canterbury. Read concerning him what our Martène wrote in the preface to *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. II, p. 36 ff., from which we have transcribed a great part of this material, as well as much of what we say about him in the church of Beauvais.

[Col. 1565]

# LETTERS OF HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF REIMS

## I. To Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, on behalf of the Bishop of Alet. (1147.)

[*Bibliotheca Patrum Lugdunensis*, vol. XXI, p. 524.]

[Col. 1565D]

To his father, his son HENRY: whatever a son may owe his father.

[Col. 1566D] It is not presumption but confidence that makes me write to you, most kindly Father. I know that it is not for me to speak like wounded N. and one sleeping in tombs; but zeal, I confess, burns my soul for this poor bishop who, because he cultivated justice, desired equity. He has been struck by the wound of an enemy; with cruel punishment, because he wished to sit in his own see and to resign episcopal office to a bishop—this is the greatest and first sin. Behold, this blood is demanded from his hand. If therefore I have any influence in the eyes of the Father—or rather, because I have much influence—take up his cause as you know will best serve him. Henceforth I am joyful and safe, and await seeing the face of God. For the day of my betrothal is near, when through your hand I shall make a covenant with the Lord God, and under your guardianship I shall serve him day and night and all the days of my life, most loving Father.

## II. To Suger, Abbot of St Denis.—Having been sought as bishop of Beauvais, he asks that another be elected. (1149.)

[Col. 1567B]

[This survives among Suger’s letters, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI, col. 1374.]

## III. To Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny.—That, unwillingly, he accepted the episcopal charge entrusted to him by Peter’s counsel. (1149.)

[This survives among the letters of Peter the Venerable, book V, letter 9—see *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXIX, col. 399.]

## IV. To St Hildegard.—He commends himself to her prayers.

[See among the various letters to St Hildegard, [Col. 1567C] *Patrologia*, vol. CXCIX.]

## V. To Hugh of Compiègne.—Rebuking and persuasive.

To his own HUGH, brother HENRY: greeting and sincere love.

Although you have forgotten yourself, I nevertheless do not forget. Truly, you have forgotten yourself—indeed both yourself and me—for to forget yourself is blindness, but to forget me is cruelty, and infinite cruelty. For I loved you as my own soul and am bound to you with as much intimacy as I know and as you cannot fail to know. What wrong, then, had I done you that you could remove me altogether from your heart? That saying is all too true: those who have cultivated the rich scorn to look upon the poor.

For after I passed into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, and chose rather to be lowly in the house of my God than to dwell in the tents of sinners, I have deserved to receive from you neither messenger, nor letter, nor your face, nor anything to hear or see from you. I had resolved to be silent; silently I considered the matter and had put my hand over my mouth. I said: “He will not forget forever; he will come, and will not delay, and will seek one who loves him and is loved by him—hastening so much the more quickly as it is fitting to hasten more devoutly.” But alas, all has come to nothing. For, as the prophet says, I wait, wait again, and send messages again; but I can say what follows: [Col. 1568A] “A little here, a little there.” Therefore now, if a friend’s prayers have any power with a friend, and if you will not come in order to see me, at least come so that I may see you, for I have earnestly desired to see your face.

## V bis. To King Louis.—Against Victor the antipope. (1159.)

[DUCHESNE, *Writers of French Affairs*, IV, 576.]

To the reverend lord and his brother LOUIS, by God’s grace king of the Franks, HENRY, called archbishop of Reims: greeting and the affection of brotherly love.

We are greatly astonished, and more greatly disturbed, by what has been reported to us: namely, that Count Henry, on your behalf, as is said, has given the emperor oaths and most binding assurances that you must generally receive that Octavian as pope together with the Gallican Church. From whom this has been reported to us, we neither can nor ought to tell you. The contents of the letter sent to us on this subject are as follows:

> **[Note: Col. 1567D. This letter is from Emperor Frederick.]**
>
> “Among all the swelling storms of tempests by which the little ship of blessed Peter has long been tossed, and amid the various pressures by which the holy Church of God has frequently been afflicted and troubled, at last that true Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who marked and redeemed his Church as his only bride with the distinctive seal of his precious blood, has shown by clear and manifest signs the grace of consolation which, when ascending into heaven, he promised to his faithful, saying: ‘I will not leave you orphans; behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.’
>
> “For he himself, like the morning star rising amid the cloud, in his accustomed mercy has looked upon his Church in tribulation; and, rising, commanded the winds and the sea, and there came a great calm. For the controversy which has long been carried on between us and the king of the Franks concerning the schism of the Roman Church has at length, by the inspiration of the grace of the Holy Spirit, who makes men dwell together in unity in the house of the Lord, been settled between us, through envoys on either side, by equal will and unanimous agreement. Namely, we are together to celebrate a general council with the archbishops, bishops, orthodox Fathers, religious men, barons, and all the princes of both kingdoms, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September—that is, the day of the Beheading of St John the Baptist—upon the River Saône in the diocese of Besançon.
>
> “At this council the king of the Franks, our beloved kinsman, together with all his archbishops, bishops, all the princes of his kingdom, and the whole Gallican Church, shall receive our reverend father the lord pope, as pope and universal pontiff of the holy Church of God, according to the arrangements made by oaths and most binding assurances; and he shall render due reverence. But since this matter, so arduous, salutary, and necessary, in which the reconciliation of the holy Church and the salvation of all Christendom are jointly at issue, neither ought nor can be completed without the presence of your discernment and that of the other princes and faithful of Christ, we entreat and command you, by the faith which you owe to the Empire, to the holy Church of God, and to your own soul, to set aside every excuse and meet us at Besançon, four days before the aforesaid date, in the customary familiar manner of the court, accompanied by the wise, most suitable, and learned persons of your diocese, in order to proceed with us to the council. There, by God’s grace, the entire affair of Lord Pope Victor will be brought to an honourable conclusion, for the glory of God, the peace and unity of the holy Church, and the complete honour of the Empire [Col. 1569B]. Therefore, in this crisis of such necessity, let your prudent discretion take heed, lest through the sons of darkness your innocence suffer a wretched shipwreck, both of soul and body. Farewell.”

## VI. Eberhard, Archbishop of Salzburg, to Henry.—For Pope Alexander. (1159.)

[Works of GRETSER, vol. VI, p. 592.]

To the reverend father and lord HENRY, archbishop of Reims, EBERHARD, unworthy minister of the church of Salzburg: whatever force the prayer of a sinner may have, together with devoted service.

Because from many reports we have learned concerning your holiness [Col. 1569C] that amid the storms of the tossing Church you stand fast like an immovable pillar, and by your example strengthen the wavering minds of very many in the unity of the Catholic Church, we have judged it fitting in this uncertain situation to consult your holiness concerning the condition of the churches and kingdoms of France and England. For we are pressed by grave anxiety while we are disturbed by various rumours from those who favour Octavian’s party and strive to blow away Pope Alexander—indeed, the whole Church as represented in Pope Alexander. They say that, having rejected Pope Alexander, the Gallican Church wishes to bring in Octavian. We are not indeed scandalized by this, knowing that the enemies of truth, through the operation in them of the spirit of falsehood, deal only in deceit and fraud; nevertheless, because of the weak who are scandalized, we cannot but burn. We therefore beseech your holiness in the Lord to make us certain concerning this doubtful matter and to strengthen, by the authority of your letters, the little ones of the Church living in our kingdom. Farewell, and pray for us.

## VII. Henry’s reply to Eberhard.—On the same subject. (1159.)

[Works of GRETSER, vol. VI, p. 592.]

To EBERHARD, venerable archbishop of the church of Salzburg, HENRY, called archbishop of the church of Reims: steadfastness in faith and the eye of charity.

We pursue your holiness with abundant thanksgiving, for we do not doubt in the least that you are constant in faith, an immovable pillar of the Church, keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. We trust in the Lord that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion unto the end; and that, as he has provided you as a faithful helper of the most holy Roman Church, so he will grant effectiveness to the honourable purpose of your faith and religion.

What you have asked concerning the condition of the Gallican Church toward the lord pope accords with your holiness, which, retaining the custom of a good son, watches devoutly over holy mother Church. Let this therefore be made certain to your diligence: the Gallican Church [Col. 1570B] serves Lord Pope Alexander devotedly and will obey him unto death. Our lord and brother, the king of the Franks, likewise renders him the service of due submission and declares that he would rather have his head cut off than withdraw from what he has honourably and justly undertaken.

## VIII. To King Louis.—On the election of the bishop of Châlons. (1163.)

[DUCHESNE, *French Writers*, IV, 636.]

To his most beloved lord and brother LOUIS, by God’s grace most excellent king of the Franks, H., called archbishop of Reims: greeting and the affection of true love.

[Col. 1570C] From your letters we have learned that you gave a gracious response to those delegated to you on behalf of the church of Châlons. Moreover, you wished to advise them that the outcome of their affair should depend on our counsel. You promised that, if they should undertake anything contrary to this, you would strive in every way to render their undertaking void. For all this we give very great thanks to your Highness, for whose honour and advantage we are ready, so far as we can, to be watchful. For whatever we are and can do is yours.

## IX. To the same.—He informs him of his illness. (1164.)

[There.]

[Col. 1570D]

To the reverend lord and brother LOUIS, by God’s grace most pious king of the Franks, H., humble minister of the church of Reims by divine mercy: greeting and happiness in both lives.

After returning from Flavigny, though we still could not ride because of the excessive illness of our body, we nevertheless came to Paris carried in a litter. On arriving there, we were so exhausted and afflicted that we again fell into an acute illness. By the mercy of the heavenly physician visiting us, we have been delivered from it and are recovering. We therefore inform your royal majesty that, since the fear you had concerning us has fled from you, you should believe no one reporting anything unfavourable about this; for you may know beyond doubt [Col. 1571A] that we suffer no evil except bodily weakness. We did not wish to send you any messenger until we had been freed from the illness by which we were held.

## IX bis. To the same.—On behalf of the Count of Roucy.

[DUCHESNE, *French Writers*, IV, 636.]

To the reverend lord and brother LOUIS, by God’s grace most pious king of the Franks, HENRY, humble minister of the church of Reims by divine mercy: greeting and happiness in both lives.

Guischard, count of Roucy, your kinsman, has come into your presence. We ask your royal majesty’s clemency for him and with him, that you may mercifully hear him in his just petitions, knowing that he is ready in all things to obey your will and, as he has informed us, has satisfied the abbot of Fusniac concerning his complaint.

## X. To his suffragans.—On injuries inflicted upon him by Count Henry. (Before 1167.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 866.]

HENRY, called archbishop of Reims, to his venerable brothers and fellow bishops, his suffragans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

According to the saying of the Wise Man, “A brother helping a brother shall be strengthened, like a fortified and strong city”; and those whom eternal justice has advanced to the place of judgment ought not to be divided in the execution of justice. For more worthy is the generation which the Holy Spirit works in the children of grace than that which is revealed in the hearts of the children of men by the ink of flesh and blood. Therefore we have thought it fitting to make known to your brotherhood how great is the malice which Count H. has exercised and does not cease to exercise against our person and the churches entrusted to us.

Although he was our liege man, saving fidelity to the lord king, and had not renounced his fealty to us, he supported and received, against our will, certain knights who were our men and who were making war upon us in the land of our fief, so that they carried off with him our booty and that of the churches entrusted to us. [Col. 1571D] We caused him to be summoned to answer and admonished through our own messengers to have our property restored to us; but he neither caused ours to be restored nor expelled our wrongdoers from our fief. Rather, seeking an evasion, as afterwards became clear, he had us appealed to the hearing of the lord pope. We endured this, though by law we might have acted otherwise, because robbers have no right of appeal.

Afterwards his fury did not even thus turn aside, but his hand was still stretched out. For his knights and Coterelli—[Note: **[Col. 1571D]** The Coterelli appear to be men clad in a *cotta*, or military cloak. In the letter of Emperor Frederick, the Coterelli are the same as the Brabançons. The Brabançons, moreover, [Col. 1572D] were brigands. See Cange under “Brabantiones.”]—entered our land and that of the churches entrusted to us and ravaged our people with such cruelty, killing some and dragging others in chains to prison, that they burned thirty-six men in one church [Col. 1572A]. Sparing no sex, they plundered and devastated nearly the entire surrounding region.

We sent our messenger to him, that he should cause what belonged to us and to the churches to be restored; but the messenger could not speak with him. Therefore, in the presence of our clergy, we passed a sentence of excommunication upon him; but at that time we did not proclaim it in church. Afterwards he sent persons to arrange a truce between us, and we granted it, though the matter remained as it stood, since he had been excommunicated by us, although we had not proclaimed it in church, and on the condition that in the meantime he should have our property restored to us. The days of truce passed, and our property was not restored to us, nor that of the churches to them. Therefore we pronounced against him the sentence of excommunication with an extinguished candle [Col. 1572B].

After the sentence had been passed, he sent persons again to appeal to the hearing of the lord pope. Therefore, because he has acted so wrongfully toward us and our churches, we have instructed—and by instructing commanded—your brotherhood to cause him to be declared our excommunicate in every church in your bishoprics, and to cause him to be excommunicated every Sunday in each church, together with all who have given him assistance to the injury of us and of our churches.

## XI. To the Bishop of Laon.—He explains why he has not obeyed that bishop’s judgment and commands. (About 1167.)

[MARTÈNE, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, col. 776.]

[Col. 1572C]

HENRY, archbishop of Reims, to G., bishop of Laon.

We are greatly astonished that, in the letters directed by you to us, you arrogate to yourselves jurisdiction over an appeal made to us. Though you are our brother, you are neither judge nor lord; and when an appeal is made to a higher hearing, the lower courts have no right to proceed in the cases, but rather ought to suspend action and defer to their superiors. You showed us too little deference in this: although we ordered that the priest of Revetra be summoned once, a second, and a third time, you neither summoned him nor caused him to be summoned, and you treated as void what we so often commanded you to do. Whether you feign ignorance of it or scorn to do what we command, we do not know with what outlook; nevertheless it is incumbent upon us to discharge our office and restrain contemners by the punishment due. Therefore we have pronounced sentence against the aforesaid priest, and we hold—and shall hold—it valid. Otherwise the metropolitan see, if it did not observe the lines of justice, would be a source of trouble and a cause of loss, though by the duty of its dignity it ought to be the refuge of the oppressed and the seat of judgment. Moreover, because you did not summon the aforesaid priest when we had ordered you a third time to do so, we appoint for your fraternity a day for making satisfaction in our court before the Ascension of the Lord. If, because of illness, you cannot come to it, send a person adequate for this purpose.

XII. To King Louis.—Concerning a conference to be held at Béthisy. [Note: [Col. 1573] On this conference see below the letter of Hugh of Campo-Florido to King Louis. EDITORS.] (Year 1167.)

[DUCHESNE, *Script. Franc.*, IV, 635.]

To the reverend lord and brother LOUIS, by God’s grace most glorious king of the Franks, H., by divine mercy archbishop of Reims: greeting and happiness in both lives.

It has been reported to us that you are to hold a conference shortly at Béthisy. Since very recently, on our return from Soissons, we received envoys of the count of Flanders, seeking to speak with us concerning certain private matters, we ask Your Highness to deign to inform us as soon as possible whether you will hold a conference in the place named above, or where we may speak with you together with the aforesaid envoys.

XIII. To the bishops and cardinals of the Roman Church.—On behalf of Drogo, chancellor of Noyon. (Year 1168.)

[MARTÈNE, *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 788.]

To the reverend fathers in Christ, the bishops and cardinals, sons of the holy Roman Church, HENRY, called archbishop of Reims: greeting and reverence.

Not without great amazement and disturbance of mind do I recount that with you neither service merits favour, nor love a return, nor humility assistance. If divine mercy has placed you at the summit and hinge of affairs, it seeks from those who profess its service acts not contrary to itself but resembling its will. He who says, “I love those who love me,” receives this saying from His servant: “But Thou, Lord of Hosts, dost judge all things with tranquillity and dost order us with great reverence.” If divine condescension bends down to your lowliness, if eternal Majesty bestows the gift of love, tranquillity, and reverence upon the service of human beings, what ought one human being to render to another, who is not indeed a servant but a fellow-servant under the rule of the Creator? The angel forbids the apostle to worship him: he considers not the condition of flesh, but the will of his own Lord. Nor does the apostle swell with pride when honour is received; nor is the angel ashamed to reverence a human being, knowing that the human race had been restored by the blood of his Lord.

You hold His place; you ought to perform His offices and imitate the pattern of His likeness. If we serve you not under compulsion of necessity but at the command of the divine voice, ought we not to merit favour? Yet the Lord returns grace for grace to those who serve Him, and comforts those who love Him with manifold help. For service we receive offence; for benefits, quarrels; for peace, dissensions; for love, harassment. What we foster you oppress; what we oppose you support. Thus our devotion comes to nothing, though in time of need we have constantly shown it to you, not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth. Divine goodness gives abundantly to all and reproaches no one; nor do we rehearse our services to you in order to reproach you, but we wish to be satisfied by a just return from the fruit of our works. Enough has been said to the wise. Subsequent correction levels whatever is excessive.

Do therefore what you ought; and if we count for anything in your eyes, if we have any influence with you, if we have deserved well of you in any respect, let our beloved and intimate friend Drogo, chancellor of Noyon, experience the effective power of your affection. The lord pope appears, as it pleased him—though not, we believe, as was fitting—to have deprived him by the harsh pronouncement of his sentence; its affliction touches us undeservedly and distresses us with shame, which he is believed to endure without any preceding fault.

XIV. To Pope Alexander III.—On the same subject. (Year 1168.)

[See among the letters of various persons to Alexander, after his *Regesta*.]

XV. To the same.—In the case of St Thomas of Canterbury. (Year 1169.)

[See the place cited above.]

XVI. To King Louis.—On behalf of Hugh of Campo-Florido, bishop of Soissons and the king’s chancellor. (Year 1171.)

[DUCHESNE, *Script. Franc.*, IV, 569.]

To the most beloved lord and brother LOUIS, by God’s grace most excellent king of the Franks, HENRY, called archbishop of Reims: greeting and the affection of true love.

It has been reported to us that, since we departed from you, certain persons have intervened, declaring that the lord bishop of Soissons, your chancellor, was unfaithful to you, and thereby causing him to fall from your favour. Since we hold you most dear as lord, brother, and friend, and are bound to provide according to our ability for your honour and advantage, we beseech Your Highness in every way not to give assent to anyone whatsoever in these matters. For we both believe and know that the said chancellor is most faithful to you. Besides, he is your man; nor could you in any way tear from him what is his own without blame rebounding upon you and you being held blameworthy in this matter. I am anxious about this business, for I fear that, if you withdraw from him, you may incur the displeasure of God and the people. I ask, entreat, and advise that you withdraw from him nowhere, and that you do not place yourself and your possessions from the hands of faithful men into those of unfaithful men.

XVII. To Ervisius, abbot of St Victor at Paris.—That he should forward the preceding letter to the king. (Same year.)

[DUCHESNE, *Script. Franc.*, IV, p. 570.]

HENRY, called archbishop of Reims, to his dearest H., the venerable abbot of St Victor: greeting and love in the Lord.

It has been reported to us that, after our departure from Paris, certain intervening persons caused our most beloved lord of Soissons to fall from the favour of the lord king. We have written to the lord king on this matter, entreating and advising him not to assent to anyone concerning it. We write also to your affection, asking that you forward on our behalf to him the letter which we send, and be its faithful interpreter.
