Moreover, if the lord of Soissons has returned to the favour of the lord king and restored his seal to him, do not present our letter to the king.

XVIII. To Hugh of Campo-Florido, the king’s chancellor.—That he has written to the king on his behalf. (Same year.)

[Same work, p. 575.]

HENRY, called archbishop of Reims, to his venerable brother HUGH, by God’s grace bishop of Soissons: greeting and love in the Lord.

We have written to the lord king concerning your affair, asking and in every way advising him not to withdraw his favour from you at all, nor to assent to anyone in this matter. Take care, therefore, that you are not moved or troubled by any adversities. We are ready diligently to exert ourselves for your honour and advantage. We are sending [the letter] to the abbot of St Victor, so that he may present our letter to the lord king, because we believe he will be a faithful interpreter.

XIX. To Pope Alexander III.—Complaint concerning a certain Robert of Aria intruded into the Church of Cambrai. (Year 1174.)

[See among the letters of various persons to Alexander, after his *Regesta*.]

XX. A lamenting letter of Nicholas of Clairvaux, notary of St Bernard, to Henry, the king’s brother, a monk of Clairvaux, who had departed because of illness.

To his special brother and lord HENRY, brother NICHOLAS: health of both the inner and outer person.

After your departure, my joy departed from me, and my soul was troubled within me. Nor is this surprising, for half my soul was leaving me, and the better part of me was withdrawing from before my face. When you mounted the horse, and that blood of such great nobility was marked by rustic trappings, I began to marvel greatly and be more violently troubled. I had abundant matter for both reactions, and it was neither certain nor possible which way I ought to incline more strongly. For I marvelled at the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High: that you, who a little before had been fiery in scarlet, gleaming with gold, bright in silk, whom a horse—or rather horses—laden with shining gems preceded and followed, had withdrawn into this sanctuary of discipline so completely that you could be an example even to those whom we have held as examples.

But I was troubled because my very entrails were torn away from me, because either the distance of places or the intervals of time deprived me, if only for an hour, of the bodily sight of you. Yet my will agrees with the Lord’s will. That illness would never have occurred for which we sent you away on pilgrimage, light of our eyes and mirror of our whole community. [Note: [Col. 1575] He has imitated the passage in Tobit, chapter 10: “Alas for me, my son, why did we send you to travel abroad, light of our eyes, staff of our old age?”] Certainly the sweet remembrance of you neither leaves nor will leave me; but the sweeter the memory, the more grievous the absence. What the philosopher says is altogether true: sight and conversation possess a certain living pleasure which those who are absent cannot have.

Thus I am both affected and worn down by this journey of yours, so that I have no desire to read or pray, nor any delight in writing or dictating. Hence this present letter proceeds with a slow and thin style, adorned neither by order nor by the beauty of flourishing eloquence. Although my own foolishness is the cause, your remembrance greatly increases my foolishness. For while I consider what and how to write, your memory, made newly fresh from recentness, rides between the thought of the meditator and the pen of the writer, and strikes back the flames of feeling as it does the waves of words. When I try to resist and recollect myself, it is as though I were fighting arrows with straws. For the feeling of grief is too deep; when it affects me with all its strength, my spirit fails, and my hand is not sufficient to hold the pen.

I do not wish this to be unknown to my lord, my brother, my friend—my friend not through any presumption of mine, but through his own condescension. Returning from you, I entered your writing-room alone, and truly alone, since you alone happened not to be present. There the dormant grief broke out afresh; left to me alone, it spread through the whole depth of my mind in thoughts. I considered the freedom of your spirit toward me, and the singular intimacy with which you had embraced me, not as one among the rest, but as one above the rest. And I said to myself: Who is he, and who am I? As nothing has no comparison with something, so I cannot be worthy while he is of greater worth and I of lesser. What then is it that one so great does not disdain to love one so little with such love? What pleased your nobility in me? You surely saw something, but I cannot see that something. For I know the frailty of my sick soul; nor am I weighed down by the burden of false glory, knowing that the kingdom is not in word but in power (1 Cor. 4), and that he is blessed whose life is more beautiful than his fine speech.

I say this because, wherever you are, you apply great titles of praise to my character and thoughts, and, when you find or make an occasion, extol a man—and a man not to be extolled. Most unworthy of all mortals, I refuse to do what I have to say, and by my own words I daily pronounce a condemnatory judgment upon myself. You certainly believe, friend, what you say; but you ought to remember the philosopher’s saying: “As true praise adorns, so false praise chastens.” But if I measure your mind rightly, you too have done this artfully: you lavish upon me, a most contemptible worm, with all familiarity the worm-like splendour of friendship. Thus your lofty sublimity appears humbler when it condescends to one lowest of all, and shines forth in a more brilliant position.

You would deserve praise, unless, while you strive considerably to praise me, you were strongly to forbid praise for yourself—one whom singular nobility, special humility, generous companionship, and most sweet character bind together. And though Scripture says, “Do not praise a man in his lifetime,” [Note: [Col. 1577C] Ecclesiasticus 11:29, where the Vulgate has: “Before death praise no man”; and according to the Greek version: “Before death call no one blessed.”] nevertheless I shall preserve the text of Scripture and praise my Henry—mine, I say, and specially mine in the bowels of Jesus Christ. “Do not praise,” it says, “a man in his lifetime.” Can you be praised in your own life, you who live not for yourself but for Christ, for whom to live is Christ and to die is gain? (Phil. 1). Do you not also have cause to say, “I now live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2), and, “The life which I live in the flesh, I live in the faith of the Son of God, who gave Himself for me” (ibid.)? Therefore you do not live in your own life but in Christ’s life, you who are dead to sin yet live to God (Rom. 6).

Job is praised because he patiently lost his own possessions; shall Henry not be praised because he openly relinquished his own and distributed them generously? Of him, indeed, there follows more truly what comes next: “Who is this? And we shall praise him; for he has done wonders in his life” (Ecclus. 31). Truly wonders: for he set aside a kingdom, abandoned his brother—and a king as brother; [Note: [Col. 1578C] Adela, or, as others write, Elisa, daughter of Count Hubert.] he left his mother, and did so in the very flower of prosperity and life. If the man who did not go after gold is praised (ibid.), will he not deserve something greater, who cast it away—and cast it away in this manner? But where am I going? The letter must be closed, because I have wandered farther than I hoped while imagining that I was conversing with you. For the absences of friends would be unbearable if the remedies of letters did not intervene.

Therefore, my beloved, endure the Lord’s hand not only patiently but willingly, so that with the Apostle you may take pleasure in your infirmities (2 Cor. 12). Hold firmly to this: the loving Father will turn the scourge into a benefit. Thus was formed all that choir of saints, whose voices the boy harpist expresses thus: “For I am ready for scourges” (Ps. 36 [37]). O man according to God’s heart, who dictates judgment from the heart of God, not merely patient under scourges but ready for scourges, knowing that power is perfected in weakness (2 Cor. 12).

Meanwhile you will be sweet to me in expectation, sweeter in arrival, sweetest in sight. For though I am absent in place, you have with you in affection my soul and your soul: the lord of Reims, who loves you singularly and me specially, whom we regard, in the whole and from the whole order, not as one alone but as the unique friend above and before all others. You also have with you Gerard of Péronne, to be loved in every respect; entering into this trinity of friendship, he did not add a fourth, but completes the unity. The Lord knows that I write these final words with tears. Return, return, my beloved; return, that we may behold you. Return for my sorrow; return for your honour; return for Andrew and for our community, which awaits you as an angel of God. And when you come, bring the lord of Reims with you, so that we may have a festive day and rejoice more abundantly in Him who above all is God, blessed for ever.

HENRY I’S DIPLOMAS.

I. Charter of Henry, archbishop of Reims, for the church of St Just. (Year 1163.)

[LOUVET, *Antiquités de la ville de Beauvais*, ed. 1631, II, 267.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen.

I, HENRY, by God’s mercy archbishop of Reims, send everlasting greeting to all children of the Church, present and future.

Since the care of our government requires us continually to defend the patrimonies of churches and the alms of the faithful, for the honour of God and the benefit of the Church itself, against the calumnies continually arising from a malignant age, we have therefore taken care to confirm to our church of St Just, once our foster-child, and to our most beloved sons serving God there as novices, certain benefactions formerly granted to it by us while we presided over the church of Beauvais: namely, the house of Morangles with all its appurtenances, and the annual revenues of five churches of Beauvais—St Mary, St Michael, St Bartholomew, St Lawrence, and St Vedast—in whatever manner a change may be made. In order that this may remain valid and unshaken for ever, we have ordered it to be fortified by the authority of the present document and of our seal, and by the subscriptions of witnesses.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1163, in the eleventh indiction, in the thirty-third year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, and the second of our archiepiscopate.

II. Charter concerning a fair established at Reims for the benefit of lepers, beginning on Easter Day. (Year 1170.)

[*Actes de la province ecclésiastique de Reims*, II, 303.]

HENRY, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, to all God’s faithful, present and future, for ever.

Since, as time slips away, the memory of events also slips away, we faithfully cause to be recorded in the characters of writing those things which we wish to transmit to the memory of posterity. Let both present and future persons therefore know that, providing with fatherly care for the sick people of Reims and condescending with fatherly compassion, we have granted, for their benefit, that a fair be held every year for eight days—that is, from Easter Day until the evening of the following Sunday—beside their house outside the city of Reims. All proceeds arising from that fair shall pass freely and peacefully into the right and ownership of them and their successors, except for the *sesterlage*, [Note: [Col. 1579D] *Sesterlage*: a right of measuring.] the *ban*, [Note: [Col. 1579D] *Ban*: fines.] forfeitures, road-dues, [Note: [Col. 1579D] *Viatoria*: road or street jurisdiction.] and blood-money.

Nevertheless, lest our archiepiscopal revenues appear diminished because a market was formerly held at Reims, they shall pay us and our successors each year, during the term of the same fair, one hundred shillings in Reims currency for toll and *thoagium*, [Note: [Col. 1579D] *Thoagium*, for *taulagium*: toll; the fee for a place at the fair.] and ten [shillings] for our money-changers. This is on the condition that no market shall be held at Reims within the stated term except at the site of the fair. In order that this may remain valid and be incapable of infringement by anyone, we have caused it to be confirmed by the impression of our seal, under the witnesses designated below.

The sign of Philip and Boso, archdeacons. The sign of Drogo, provost. The sign of Fulk, dean; Gregory, cantor; Thomas and Lawrence, priests. The seal of the abbot of St Denis. The sign of Peter, abbot of St Martin of Épernay. The sign of Raynold, cantor of Compiègne and canon of Reims.

Done at Reims in the year of the Incarnate Word 1170, in the fortieth year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks, our brother, and the tenth of our archiepiscopate.

III. He confirms the statute of Sanson, his predecessor, concerning non-resident canons. (Year 1170.)

[Same work, p. 307.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, HENRY, by God’s grace archbishop of Reims, to present and future persons for ever.

Lord Sanson, our predecessor of good memory, by God’s mercy inflamed with zeal for God’s house and wishing the canons of this holy mother church to engage in divine worship and the praises of God, decreed and instituted, with the common assent of the whole chapter, that anyone promoted as a canon of Reims after Hugh, archdeacon of Orléans, should have only canonical bread if he were not a resident in the city. I, Henry, by the same grace archbishop of Reims, likewise wishing there to be a multitude united in one service, have judged it necessary, with the assent of the body of brethren, to enact, confirm, and establish for perpetual observance the same provision instituted by him, and to strengthen it with the impression of our seal. The income received from the prebends of absent brethren shall be distributed among the canons who have attended Matins.

The sign of Philip and Boso, archdeacons. The sign of Fulk, dean. The sign of Gregory, cantor. The sign of Gregory, Walter, Lawrence, and Thomas, priests. The sign of Roger, Stephen, Nicholas, Stephen, Herluin, Lethold, Rodulf, and John, deacons. The sign of Hilduin, *vicedominus*. The sign of Henry, treasurer. The sign of Rodulf, Erland, Nicholas, Zacharias, Milo, Gervase, Roger, Alberic, Gervase, Elenus, Hugh, Fulk, Leo, Guy, and Rainold, subdeacons.

Done at Reims in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1170, in the fortieth year of the reign of Louis, most glorious king of the Franks, and the ninth of our archiepiscopate.

John the chancellor examined, wrote, and subscribed [Note: [Col. 1579D] We do not believe that this document has yet been published; M. Varin has merely noted it in the administrative archives of the city of Reims. We took it from the original kept in the library of Reims, among the chapter archives, bundle 10, file 18, no. 1. It is accompanied by three bulls: the first, of Alexander III, confirms Sanson’s decree; the second, of the same pontiff, confirms Henry’s statute; the third, of Innocent IV, orders that this statute be executed and that canons opposing it be compelled to submit to it.].

IV. Charter concerning Sampigny, purchased by the archbishop of Reims. (Year 1171.)

[VARIN, *Archives de la ville de Reims*, I, I, 362.—Cartulary G of the Chapter, fol. 23.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity.

I, HENRY, called archbishop of Reims by God’s grace, to all, future as well as present, for ever.

Since, by the administration of the pastoral office, we are bound to provide for the quiet and peace of our subjects—especially because it is fitting for us, according to place and time, to wield both swords against those who hate peace and oppose justice—we must with more earnest consideration ensure that, when appropriate, the material sword is accompanied by the spiritual, lest one who escapes the one congratulate himself that he has escaped the other. Truly, the world lies in wickedness, so much so that evil sons, although they perceive one or both swords hanging over their necks, scarcely fear to restrain themselves from habitual wrongdoing.

Moreover, moved by compassion at the oppression of the poor, trusting in God’s help and the counsel of our friends, we destroyed the stronghold of Sampigny, which was as a nest and refuge of robbers who disturbed the country, committing robberies and murders, excessively burdening the villages of churches entrusted to us, and extorting unlawful dues from travellers along the public road leading from our city of Reims to Châlons—sometimes by threat of death, sometimes by inflicting wounds—so that they did not even fear to lay hands upon ecclesiastics.

In the year after we had destroyed that stronghold, Boso, knight, who was lord and possessor of Sampigny, sold us for three hundred pounds the village of Sampigny and everything he possessed in the territory of that village, whether in fiefs or in his own demesne: arable land, pastures, meadows, waters, fisheries, mills, and everything that he held in the said village or its territory. Those who held anything there in fief from him shall hold it from us and our successors and shall do homage to us for it.

This sale by Boso was approved by his mother the countess, his wife Helisendis, his son Hugh, his daughters and brothers—Guy, Ulric, Oliver, Witer—and his sisters Ada and Helvidis; likewise Ferric, Ada’s husband, and Ulric, Colin, and Hersendis, children of Helvidis. Present were our clerk Galeran, our canon of Reims; Hugh of Sillery; Peter of Avenay; Ralph of the Gate of Mars; Gerard of the Postern; Odo of Cormicy, knights and our servants; Ferric; Fulk of the Treasury; Peter of Tours-sur-Marne; Rainer; Buiron; Ralph; and Aquilon.

At Sept-Saulx, Wermund of Châtillon and Witer of Sarnay also approved this, in the presence of John the chancellor, the aforesaid Galeran, Rabo and Baldwin, knights, and Herleband and Ralph, our servants. At Mailly, Wermund of Wiron, from whom the aforesaid Boso held Sampigny, also approved it and resigned into our hand the lordship which he held there, freely granting us possession of it, in the presence of the aforesaid John and Galeran, Matthew Rufus, Peter of Avenay, and Goslin of Sept-Monts.

[Note: [Col. 1581C] The completion of all these ratifications is found in Cartulary G of the chapter, fol. 24v, in the following charter:

“In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Guy, by God’s grace bishop of Châlons, have taken care to transmit to the knowledge of posterity by the written characters of the present letters that the venerable lord Henry, archbishop of Reims, purchased from Boso, knight, possessor and lord of Sampigny, everything that he possessed there in the demesne of that village, with the assent of the knight Wermund of Orron, from whose fief the aforesaid properties descended. We also, because the aforesaid Wermund held them from us and they were of our fief, have approved, praised, and ratified that purchase; and, with the assent of the persons [of the church] and of the whole chapter of our Church, we have resigned to the same lord archbishop our fief in all that possession, just as he purchased it in its entirety. Therefore, let this remain valid for ever, etc. [lacuna] The sign of Guy; the sign of Baldwin; the sign of Master Robert; the sign of Guy of Rocey, archdeacons; the sign of Bovo, dean; the sign of James, treasurer; the sign of Rainald, cantor; the sign of Peter Seneschal; the sign of Ulric, Robert, and Renaud, priests; the sign of Roger and Master James, deacons; the sign of Roger of Roset and Hugh of Vitry, subdeacons.

Done at Châlons in the year 1173. Gerard the chancellor wrote and subscribed.”]

Afterwards, the aforesaid Boso came to us at Reims and, in our presence and that of certain of our household whose names are subscribed below, acknowledged, praised, and approved that sale. For the aforesaid village and its appurtenances he received three hundred pounds from us through the hand of a certain man of the Temple, named Danibert.

[Note: [Col. 1582C] The church which St Remigius had caused to be built in the city in honour of St Martin, and which was afterwards called that of the Trinity, was restored in the eleventh century by Constant, dean of the church of Reims. He founded there four prebends (see Marl., I, 143; *Gallia Christiana*, IX, 12 and 171), to which his nephew and successor in the deanery added six more. In 1170 the chapter of the church of Reims gave this church and these prebends to the Knights [Templar] [lacuna]. It is now (1759) the best-endowed serving commandery of Malta. (BIDET, *Mémoires*, II, p. 172.) “[Lacuna] Around the year 1170, the archbishop named Henry granted the said church and all the revenues of the said prebends to the brethren Templars, on condition that they continue the service founded by Constant. Around the year 1309 [lacuna] the house of the Temple at Reims and all its dependencies were given to the brethren Hospitallers [lacuna], and since then the said house has always been held by commanders and religious of the Order of St John of Jerusalem.” (*Bibliothèque Royale*, MS supplementary French 1515, Rogier, vol. II, fol. 332).]

These are the names of those who were present: Peter, abbot of St Remigius; Boso, archdeacon of Reims; Drogo, provost; Fulk, dean; Lawrence, priest; Roger of the Prison Gate; and Master Ralph, deacon; Milo and Rainald, subdeacons. Of the knights: Simon Peslupi, who himself also approved it because he was related to the aforesaid Boso; Peter of Avenay; Goslin of Sept-Monts; and Wilard. Of the burgesses: Richer “Biting-Flesh,” Walter of Manso, and Simon the goldsmith.

We therefore assign and grant to our successors, the archbishops of Reims, to possess for ever after our death both the village of Sampigny and all its appurtenances which, as stated above, we purchased, together with the stronghold which we caused to be built at Sept-Saulx. But if anyone, etc., etc.

Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1171, in the fortieth year of the reign of our lord and brother Louis, and the tenth of our archiepiscopate.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1175. HUGH OF CAMPO-FLORIDO, BISHOP OF SOISSONS, CHANCELLOR OF KING LOUIS VII.

NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. IX, col. 361.)

[Col. 1583B] At the Paris synod of 1147, two masters were brought forward against Gilbert of Poitiers; one of them was Hugh of Campfleury. At about that time he seems to have held an altar-benefice in the diocese of Arras, by the gift of Bishop Alvisus. Later he became chancellor of King Louis VII, archdeacon of Arras, and canon of Paris, Orléans, and Soissons. Nevertheless Pope Adrian IV wrote Letter 13 on his behalf to Theobald, bishop of Paris, asking that he be given the first vacant benefice or dignity. Likewise, by Letter 14 he asked the Paris chapter to reserve for him the first dignity to fall vacant in the chapter, and the first houses in the cloister.

These are the earliest traces of papal dispensations both for plurality of benefices [Col. 1583C] and for exemption from the law of residence. The same may be said of the reservation of benefices before they became vacant, and of the mandates by which the supreme pontiff later drew to himself the rights of ordinaries. Finally, on 5 March 1159, Pope Adrian informed Hugh, then elect, and the chapter of Soissons that he had assigned Hugh’s prebend to William the dean and to his successors as deans. It follows that Ansculf died in 1158 and that Hugh was elected in 1159.

Once made bishop, however, Hugh did not cease to be chancellor. Hence it is not surprising that he dealt with so many and such great affairs for the realm and King Louis, and very few for his own Church. This is the origin of the many letters concerning him, addressed to him, and written by him, in Duchesne, Labbe, and Martène. Thus he is found in 1159 in register 74 [Col. 1584B] of the treasury of charters. In 1160 he approved Evrard of Muret’s alms-gift to Blessed Mary of Longpont, and in 1163 the grant of land by Evrard the knight. In the same year, the fourth of his episcopate, he made an agreement with Marsilia, abbess of St Mary’s. At about that time he came to an arrangement with the chapter concerning two prebends held by the cantor. He gave one of them to the cantor’s successor, to be assigned after that successor’s death to anyone; and Alexander III ratified this agreement at Sens, 21 December 1164.

In 1166 he approved the alms-gift of Gerard of Chérisy, and in 1167 the gift of land by Nivelo of Chérisy, a canon. At about this time, delegated by Alexander III together with P., abbot of St Remigius, he adjudged the church of Bragny to the monks of Noyers against Gossed of Mâzières and his son John, who had occupied its provostship and prebend. He had a dispute with the chapter over prebends which he refused to grant to the dean and cantor, and which he was ordered by the supreme pontiff to confer upon them in 1169. In the same year he granted the chapter, according to its custom approved by the supreme pontiff, authority to impose interdict upon and absolve its offenders and their lands without consulting the bishop.

The twelfth year of his episcopate is connected with 1170 and 1171 in the charters of St Crispin. At about that time Alexander III sent letters from Tusculum on 7 March to Henry, archbishop of Reims, directing him to warn the bishop of Soissons that, having relinquished the chancellorship, he should apply himself diligently to the care and administration of the responsibility entrusted to him, and should remain watchful over the guardianship of the Church and people committed to him, since each office requires the whole, undivided person. [Col. 1585A]

Hugh does not seem to have obeyed the supreme pontiff’s admonitions: we find him subscribing various diplomas from 1131 to 1173. To this seems to pertain the letter of William, archbishop of Sens, to Alexander III, in which he commends Hugh, bishop of Soissons and chancellor of the king of the French, as a prudent, honourable, learned man, most steadfast in papal affairs; and asks the pope to act kindly in matters in which he can hear and support him. Yet what Alexander’s warnings could not do, the promptings of ill-wishers did: Hugh fell from the king’s favour, and the king took his seal from him. Henry, archbishop of Reims, did write to Louis, his brother, [Col. 1585B] to restore him to favour; but whether the king returned the seal to him we do not know. This alone may be regarded as certain: the chancellorship was vacant in 1173, from which year Hugh the chancellor no longer subscribed charters.

Yet in the following year, in letters issued at Anagni on 17 February, Alexander III, placed in the greatest difficulties, asked Bishop Hugh of Soissons for a monetary subsidy, as he had already given one, and urged him to exhort the abbots and provosts of churches in his diocese to do the same. In 1175 Hugh confirmed the property of the nuns of St John in the Wood; in that same year he is mentioned in the charters of Collinances. [Col. 1586A] Finally, before his death he returned to the king’s favour, as is clear from the letter which, lying at the point of death, he gave to the abbot of St Victor at Paris, his particular friend, for delivery to the king. For when the king visited him at this critical point of his life, Hugh, both delighted by his presence and disturbed by illness, could not reveal his feelings; but he wrote, declaring that he had never knowingly departed from loyalty to the king and that he had intended still to serve him more faithfully.

You will find this letter, as also the others mentioned above, in volume IV of Duchesne, volume X of Labbe’s *Councils*, and volume II of Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*. Hugh died on 4 September 1175. The cathedral martyrology reads:

> “On the day before the Nones of September died Lord Hugh, of blessed memory, bishop of this Church and chancellor of the illustrious king of the French, Louis. He gave us the altar-benefice of L’Aigle in its entirety and two hangings. We also received on his account sixty pounds for purchasing the final rents of Abellac. He gave us books and other goods. Likewise, from his property we bought the mayoralty of Ambleny, from whose land-rents and wine-dues we have every year sixty solidi to distribute among the brethren on the day of his anniversary.”

He also has an anniversary entry in the necrology of the house of St Victor at Paris, where the chancellor resided and perhaps was buried. [Col. 1586B]

[Col. 1585]

# LETTERS OF HUGH OF CAMPFLEURY

(Duchesne, *Script. Rer. Franc.*, IV, 635 ff.)

## I. To the bishop of Porto.—He commends the cleric Peter.

[Col. 1585C]

To his lord and friend G., by God’s grace venerable bishop of Porto, HUGH, called bishop of Soissons, greetings and fullest affection.

We commend to your kindness our kinsman Peter, your cleric, who has always had a remarkable affection for you. We ask that, for love of us, you graciously hear him in his just petitions and assist him with the lord pope. Farewell.

## II. To King Louis.—Concerning a conference held with the Normans.

[Col. 1585D]

To his dearest lord LOUIS, by God’s grace most serene king of the French, HUGH, humble minister of the Church of Soissons, and T. of Gisors, greetings and faithful service.

We held a conference with the bishop of Évreux and other Normans, and agreed with them upon the day on which we are to release the hostages: the Wednesday immediately [Col. 1586C] after the octave of St Andrew, at Pontoise. We named sureties to them. When they said that they would bring either those men or others who were suitable, we answered that we would accept none but those men. We have heard, moreover, that the king of England will not cross the sea here before after Easter, and that the counts of Auvergne are in Normandy. Farewell. There are also certain other matters which we do not wish to commit to letters and which we shall tell you orally.

## III. To the same.—Concerning the lifting of the interdict from the Church of Soissons.

To his dearest lord LOUIS, by God’s grace most illustrious king of the [Col. 1586D] French, H., by the same grace bishop of Soissons, greetings and willing service.

On leaving you, we came as far as Bistisiacum, where we heard that, through your favour, the lord archbishop had restored to the Church of Soissons the celebration of divine offices. When we sent here to Lord Cono of Pierrefonds, he had still done nothing with us; but we have hope concerning him. As we told you, we are sending [someone] here; and, if it please you, make known your will to us. [Col. 1587A] Farewell.

## IV. To the same.—He reports what he did after returning to Soissons.

To his dearest lord LOUIS, by God’s grace illustrious king of the French, H., by the same grace bishop of Soissons and his cleric, greetings and ready service.

After we came to Soissons, we had much to do. For we found our household affairs in disorder, and various matters were reported to us from different quarters. Because of these matters, having taken no rest since we left you, we became greatly exhausted; and, to the extreme grief of our hearts, we received [Col. 1587B] a report concerning the child, so that sorrow pierced our souls. But now, by God’s grace, the matter has turned for the better.

We would very much like to know how you are and what you are doing, and whether you may soon draw near our regions and come towards Compiègne. If it please you, deign to entrust these things to our concern. Farewell.

## V. To the same.—Concerning a conference held with the Normans.

To his excellent and illustrious lord LOUIS, by God’s grace king of the French, H., humble master of Soissons, greetings and prosperity.

On the appointed day, the bishop of Beauvais, the count of Beaumont, E. of Gisors, [Col. 1587C] and I met with them, together with many others on your side. On the other side were the bishop of Évreux, R. of St Valery, G., son of Haimo, R. of Lomet, and many others. We set before them your answer, as your barons had advised you: that they should direct the counts of Auvergne to come beforehand at a suitable place and time, and that we would willingly release the hostages. They answered, to the contrary, that they could not cause the counts to come, because we held them in prison and as hostages. We said that we would do this, having no further instruction from you.

They again requested that we should send the counts on your side, and that they likewise should send them on their side. After taking counsel on this, we asked [Col. 1587D] them to give us a short delay, until we had received your counsel. They answered that they would grant no delay, and that they would not have granted one to you when they were at Paris either, unless you had bound them by the faith of the king of England. We and they then carefully discussed many other matters on both sides until nightfall. On the following day they sent to us, asking that we appoint another day for settling the other matters. We sent to Gisors for a day to be named; but those whom we had sent had not yet returned when we wrote this to you.

So that your mind might be anxious about nothing, I have briefly reported these matters to your serenity; when I am present, I shall explain each one more fully. The whole affair has indeed been conducted and carried through in a manner honourable to you.

## VI. To the provost of Chialfmunt.

[Col. 1588A]

H., by God’s grace bishop of Soissons and chancellor of the king of the French, to I., provost of Chialfmunt, greetings.

The cloak which clerics from Norway, passing through your territory, left as a pledge: we direct and request that, for our sake, you release it to them freely. For nothing ought lawfully to be demanded from men who, having set out abroad for prayer, carried nothing with them for sale.

## VII. To the canons of Auxerre and William of Dampierre.

HUGH, by God’s grace bishop of Soissons, to the canons [Col. 1588B] of Auxerre and William of DAMPIERRE, greetings.

The lord pope has committed to the lord of Paris and to us your matter and that of the church of St Germanus. But because of the affairs of the lord pope as well as those of the realm, we cannot come on the appointed day. We send in our place the abbot of St Victor, and direct you to do for him as much as you would do for us if we were present. Farewell.

## VIII. To King Louis.—At the point of death he tries to clear himself before the king of the accusations made against him. He commends his clerics.

To his dearest lord LOUIS, king of the French, [Col. 1588C] HUGH, called bishop of Soissons, ever his servant, greetings, and affection even after death.

I speak truthfully, and before God. Since I entered your service, I have never knowingly departed from loyalty to you. I had intended, if the Lord permitted, still to serve you more faithfully. But now, God disposing otherwise, placed at the end of my life, I have dictated this letter to be sent to you after my death as a final farewell. For, gladdened by your presence when I last saw you, and troubled by illness, I could not at once disclose to you the feeling of my heart; nor did I think that I would so soon enter the way of all flesh.

Leaving your company and service in fear, I commend my soul to your prayers and to those of the saints whom your kindness may cause to pray for me. [Col. 1588D] I entreat your kindness for my clerics, who served me in your court. But above all, I commend and entrust to you Peter, whom I raised from childhood, loved above the rest of my kin, and always wished to offer for your service. I did not do for him what I ought; and now, overtaken by the cruelty of death, I cannot fulfil for him what I had intended. But because I wholly trust in your generosity, it gives me great consolation that I leave him in your hand. Farewell.

What I communicate by letter I also communicate to you through the abbot of St Victor, faithful to you and to me, so that what I could not do orally I might accomplish through a letter and through such a messenger. Farewell.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1175 . . . NICHOLAS, FIRST A MONK OF AUREMARS, THEN OF CLAIRVAUX, SECRETARY TO ST BERNARD

[Col. 1589]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

Nicholas was first a monk of the monastery of Auremars, of the Cluniac order, in the diocese of Troyes; afterwards he was a monk at Clairvaux under St Bernard and Bernard’s secretary. But because the holy Father found perversity in him, he removed him from that office; whereupon Nicholas left Clairvaux and became Bernard’s enemy. St Bernard complains of him to Pope Eugenius in Letters 84 and 98. Where, when, and in what manner he died is unknown.

We give his letters here, but omit his nineteen sermons, since they are found among the works of Blessed Peter Damian and St Bernard.

[Col. 1589]

# LETTERS OF NICHOLAS, EDITED BY JOHN PICARD, REGULAR CANON OF ST VICTOR AT PARIS

(*Bibliotheca Patrum Lugdunensis*, XXI, 517.)

## PREFACE To the most reverend and at the same time most religious Father and Lord Denis Argenterius, abbot of Clairvaux.

The letters which Nicholas, formerly your monk from Cluny, issued in the name of St Bernard, I restore to you—indeed, I give them to you wholeheartedly. “Of course,” you will say, “you give me what is mine, as though such things were not gifts without gifts” [Greek: *adora dōra*, “gifts without gifts”; Sophocles]; and indeed they would be, if they belonged to an enemy [Greek: *tou echthrou*], whereas in fact they belong to a man who is both yours and your most loving and devoted friend. Besides, even stewards win a little favour from their masters when they offer them the first-fruits of their own fields.

Receive, therefore, your Nicholas with kindly eyes—and, through you, let the learned receive him as well. For he will be yours all the more as he belongs to more people. I called him yours because he was once your monk and the copyist of the men of Clairvaux, and is to be claimed by far the stronger right than Homer was claimed by the Colophonians, Chians, Salaminians, Smyrnaeans, Athenians, Argives, and Cumaeans.

But, lest a suspicious reader suppose that this assertion is vain boasting, let him consider this brief portrayal of the author’s outstanding qualities, as a pledge, and devote a few hours more willingly to reading the letters. Nicholas professed the monastic life at Cluny and, after some time, received from Peter the Venerable, abbot of the monastery, the charge of the school of Cluny—a charge worthy, I say, of so great a director. For what could one desire in a man? Talent? He possessed it in the greatest degree, lively and ardent. Humanity [Greek: *philanthrōpian*]? From mathematics, philosophy, and the liberal arts he had assembled such abundance that one could scarcely perceive what he lacked, especially in that age.

“Theology,” someone will say: “unless I see it flourishing and manifold in a man, what you give me will be mere words.” I shall indeed give words, not mine but those of my Nicholas’s letters. He had the sacred books at his fingertips—for no one but an atheist [Greek: *atheos*] would deny that from them, as from a true paradise, flow perennial and most abundant fountains of every kind of theology—so that he interweaves nearly every clause and phrase with their inserted words as with heavenly little flowers, compelling you to utter that saying of Lucilius:

> How charmingly the words are arranged, all like little tesserae,
>
> By art, in a pavement, and in a vermiculate mosaic emblem.

The passages of the heavenly volumes marked in the margin, especially the fuller ones, will bear witness to this assertion. To annotate every passage, particularly the brief ones, would have been labour as fruitless as it was insane. Besides, Letters 49 and 52 provide a pledge both of the theology and of the philosophy in which Nicholas excelled; and very many more letters missing from the exemplar would undoubtedly do so as well.

Meanwhile, reader, kiss and contemplate these few letters as Protogenes contemplated the line drawn on a panel by the hand of Apelles. For here you may read that our Nicholas possessed an extraordinary power of expression, as his age permitted, and surpassed others by as much as he did in exceptional learning—not to mention, for the moment, the wit, charm, and whole world of discourse with which, as you will read, he endeavoured to adorn his letters. Indeed Peter the Venerable, replying to him in Letters 38 and 56, says among [Col. 1591] other things: “You are not only a follower of your Tully, a true Tullian, of whom you wrote that he transferred the contents of his mind into speech with the greatest ease.” But let the reliability and authority of this saying rest with Peter.

Nicholas himself recalls his mastership in Letter 2, in precisely these words: “I expected you to write to me and to pay honour to your master: my senior in rank, my superior in age, and, greater than these, your friend in care.” And again, near the end: “You were also told that, if you returned, I would teach no longer. But the authority of love deigns to refute the claim that I would abandon the school because of you.”

Among his pupils I have found only one, L. Lescelin, whom he addresses in Letter 38 with these endearments: “You clung to my side; you pleased my heart, my brother and son, and—if you think fit to remember it—my disciple; or rather, my fellow-disciple under Him whose school is on earth and whose chair is in heaven.” In accordance with the habit of scholars, he certainly devoted himself diligently to intellectual pursuits and applied himself familiarly to reading the philosopher Seneca, as Peter of Celle, archimandrite, testifies in Letter 51 of this book: “Your Seneca, the most intimate of your intimate friends, divides human minds into three kinds.”

But dignities, even though religion attends them as an inseparable companion, nevertheless make even pious men foolish, unless they guard against the deafening flatteries of courtiers. Nicholas, quite aware how far he surpassed most people in brilliance of talent, reputation for learning, and rank of office, became unconscious of himself; he began to act too freely, to seek popular favour, and at length not to know himself—he who, by a change far happier than Circe’s, transformed the ignorant into the knowing. He was not ashamed either to do these things or to recount them in Letter 45.

At this time—indeed, before this—the Cluniacs had departed by more than a finger’s breadth from their ancestral observances. Robert, St Bernard’s nephew, too, enticed by the harmful whisperings of certain persons, had defected to the Cluniacs. Bernard, deeply distressed by his nephew’s departure, by the irreligious disgrace which this otherwise most religious household had suffered from the defection, and by Robert’s turning aside onto a broad path not far from destruction, sent him letters fuller, freer, and so explicit that even short-sighted monks could see that they were scarcely distinguished from laymen except by their monastic cowl. I need not recall the mutual accusations repeatedly exchanged by Cistercians and Cluniacs in Letters 28 and 53 of Peter the Venerable.

Then, I say, Nicholas, who had lived too freely and knew almost everything except himself, returned to himself. Changing only his mind and habit, he entered Clairvaux. How deliberately he did so, he testifies in Letter 8 to Theobald:

> “We have flown from the Old Testament and the shadow of the Cluniacs to the purity of the Cistercians. For, according to Paul’s saying, if the former had been free from fault, we should certainly not seek a place for the second. Your observances really bear some resemblance to the observances of the Jews. For they made gold and purple, foods and drinks, and various washings the whole ritual of divine worship; so also among you: where there is more gold, there is believed to be more merit; where there are more hangings, more morals; where there are more feasts and garments, there is a truer observance of the commandments. We did not do this through a sudden impulse, as persons usually tossed by agitation do; but, strengthened by deliberate consideration, we gave our right hands to the community under the sacrament of Godhead.”

Thus far Nicholas, who in the preceding letter calls Clairvaux a holy place, a wooded valley, an abundant valley, a paradise of delights, a harbour of graces, the camp of God, the house of God, and the gate of heaven, around which and over which circles a multitude of heavenly legions; and says that unless he were there and lived there, he would die. How painfully he achieved this, the reader will learn from his Letter 45.

Meanwhile the year had turned to 1119, memorable for the monastic profession of Henry, son of Louis the Fat, king of the French. In the manner of religious novices, overcome by unwonted and prolonged vigils, a harsher regimen, and the burden of more severe exercises, he left Clairvaux to recover his health. Nicholas accompanied him when he departed, in Letter 39; and Nicholas himself soon became so seriously ill that St Bernard, repeatedly approached by letters of Peter the Venerable asking permission to see him, replied in Letter 245: “The man whom you order to be sent is not now with me, but with the lord of Auxerre; and he is so sick that he is said to be unable to come even as far as us without great inconvenience.”

Since life at Clairvaux was conducted with the fullest community of all things—as it still is today—and likewise with a society of monks, a man seemed highly necessary who might handle correspondence not only for the abbot but also for the monks, so that both he and they might be freer for their most serious affairs. I shall not deny that, besides Nicholas, others also customarily sent letters, but, I suppose, letters of less weight and importance. However that may be, it is most certain that Nicholas wrote for persons of both conditions far more works than those which we publish. Otherwise his own assertion in Letter 25 would be unreliable: “From the morning watch until night I do nothing else”—namely, as he had said a little earlier—“than turn over pen and tablets. Let those who imposed this burden upon me, and made me write and reply to many persons, not be blamed.”

Yet only a few of those many letters have come down to us. Without injustice I would include among them two letters long afterward brought back by me from Book VI of Peter the Venerable, their headings too restored in the same faithful manner in which you read the rest of Peter’s letters. Nor have I thought it burdensome to append notes to them as to the rest, and to add a new, though brief, supplement to French history: namely, the monastic profession of Henry, son of King Louis the Fat; the counts of Armorican Brittany invited to an expedition to Jerusalem; and the emperor of Constantinople, with many others, petitioned on behalf of the bishop of Aleth, whom they call bishop of Saint-Malo.

Above all, we must congratulate Henry, scion of the French lilies, and Gerard of Péronne, who at last persuaded Nicholas to gather together his scattered letters. We must congratulate them, I say, through whom we are refreshed by the sweetness even of a few. Nicholas of Damascus was held in such esteem by Caesar Augustus that, if he sent as a gift sweetmeats, little cakes, pastries, and such confections, they were called “Nicolases” after Nicholas; and the name Nicholas thus remained attached to many sweet foods, just as the loaves brought to the hermit Apollonius, of which Palladius speaks in the *Lausiac History*. If we likewise call the letters of our Nicholas, seasoned with Christian ambrosia, “Nicolases,” no one should accuse us of novelty; for the Aquilian law teaches that where the reason is the same, the law ought to be the same also.

But just as I recently said that those whose urging made Nicholas collect his dispersed letters should be congratulated, so too should Nicholas Camuzaeus, most distinguished canon of St Peter’s at Troyes. With praiseworthy diligence he discovered them; with remarkable devotion he rescued them from impious and savage bookworms; and he spared no expense to bring them to light—letters which perhaps had once been, or secretly would have been, sent into exile under the barbarous edict of the Licinii: not, I say, temporary exile, but perpetual.

# LETTERS OF NICHOLAS OF CLAIRVAUX

[Col. 1593]

## LETTER I. Dedicatory letter to the brothers Gerard and Henry.

[Col. 1593A]

To his most beloved brothers GERARD and HENRY F., NICHOLAS: may you please in all things Him who is above all things, God blessed for ever.

The following letters—if indeed [Note: [Col. 1593C] “Perhaps, however, more correctly.”] they ought to be reckoned under the name of letters—were not originally put together into one body by my wish. In my judgment there is nothing [Note: [Col. 1593C] “The conjunction *enim* (‘for’) or *siquidem* (‘indeed’) seems to be missing.”] in them worthy of remembrance, since neither elevation of expression nor depth of thought can be found in them in any degree. I dictated them not to be preserved, but to be sent—and surely to be discarded, if I could have foreknown it.

For when a multitude of diverse business descended upon me, I most eagerly wiped my hand free of the pen [Col. 1593B] and my mind free of such scholarly work; and I did this no less quickly than willingly. My soul slept from weariness, provoked by the multitude of tiresome work; nor could I keep watch over many things as I could over individual matters. I watched only so that I might dispatch more quickly those who petitioned or waited. Hence many similar expressions occur here; many things, from both old and new letters, are now printed covertly, now expressed conspicuously, since memory came to my aid better than talent.

I do not say this as though, had I wished, I could have levelled a work rich in thought into polished eloquence. Slowness of talent, infrequency of practice, and the variety of my pursuits have kept that far from me. I am no orator, nor the son of an orator, but a simple man dwelling at home, a rustic indeed, and one who pinches sycamore figs. [Note: [Col. 1593C] Nicholas applies to himself what the prophet Amos says of himself in chapter VII.] I wholly leave the hunting of words to those who gladly walk through forests of expressions and boast of plucking rhetorical figures like flowering branches. Such men flee from the Lord’s sayings—pure sayings, as though they were thorny things (Psalm 11)—and, recoiling from the roughness of the harvest-fields, long for the flowers of thorns: full, indeed, of vanity, not truth, if anyone can be filled with vanity.

Therefore, beloved friends, you who wished to select and collect these letters into one, suppress words that were spoken rather than composed, and do not bring into public view what is ashamed to be public. Otherwise I shall be endangered in my modesty, and you in your friendship; [Col. 1594A] and in a matter which especially hates offence, you will cause offence. I do not say this because I doubt, or ought to doubt, you, since I am permanently entwined in the inward affections of both of you in the love of God and the patience of Christ.

For you are the resplendent star of royal stock [Note: [Col. 1593C] This must necessarily be understood of Henry, to whom this letter is addressed: son of Louis the Fat, king of the French. On him see our note to Letter 355 of St Bernard’s edition. Read shortly below Letter 13, written in his name; see also Letter 352 and Letter 39 addressed to him.], who, coming from the highest summit of worldly affairs, shattered the glory of the world upon the ground. Both singular nobility and special humility have made you no less lovable than admirable. You, the other, are a mirror and example of the sweetest manner of life: cheerful severity, severe cheerfulness, and affability have made you both approachable and worthy of imitation.

May He who chose you before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1), and called you into His marvellous light, be for you the way in your conduct, truth in your words, and life in splendours when the splendour of His glory and the image of His substance appears (Hebrews 1), to judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in His truth (Psalm 35). [Col. 1594B]

## LETTER II. To a companion of his who, having left the cloister, was living in the city.

To his dearest brother, NICHOLAS, that dearest brother of his: the charity of brotherhood and the brotherhood of charity in Christ.

Drawn back by the many and manifold allurements of worldly friendship, you are asleep and have long been “redeeming the time”; I undertake to awaken you with a sweeter letter. Do not look here for the beauty [Col. 1594C] of golden discourse or the distinctions of an alluring style; instead receive the affection closely and cautiously impressed here. True affection does not earn reward, does not seek favour, employs no cosmetic of flattery, but pleads its thoughts nakedly, in their full foliage. Hear then what it is fitting for you to hear and proper for me to say. Nothing grows old among human beings so swiftly as a kindness, although all proclaim that it should be fixed in everlasting memory.

God is my witness, and the secret of your conscience does not escape you: from the very beginnings of childhood your affection made an abiding dwelling in my breast. When I recognized your natural disposition, I praised it; and I invited, as far as I could, your talent—apt for formation—by the more subtle lines of demonstration, toward the throne of starry wisdom. While others whispered and said with envious murmuring why I had leaned so much of my heart upon you, I confronted, secure in conscience, the lips of those who rose against me; and, justice being turned into judgment, I completed more firmly what I had begun firmly.

Moreover, if there was anything pleasing to you within the limits of my means, you saw me giving with readier heart and more cheerful face than you received; and it was my greatest endeavour [Col. 1595A] to anticipate, by the slightest opening of recognition, the point at which a burdensome request had to be made with downcast countenance. For I knew that your face, fashioned in the workshop of modesty, could scarcely breathe toward the door of asking if anyone showed you the face either of one who hated or one who envied you. [Uncertain text:] “either brought back common favour or common danger.” But, lest this recollection, in accordance with the comic poet, be a reproach for a benefit received, I shall spare words and leave the verbosity of my style to your conscience.

You chose to go to Troyes; I confess, it displeased me. Why it displeased me has not escaped my memory. [Note: [Col. 1595D] Terence, *Andria*, act I, scene I.] But, putting aside that principal cause which has not left the instability of your heart, [the text lacks a clear subject:] “it entered through your windows; and the eyes of the dove wholly put off the dove.” I changed my expression before you, though I had not changed my mind, in order that I might at least draw back, by a nobler regard, the course of one fleeing; but I could not. At last, hurt and seeking pardon, overcome, I confess, by the smallness of my spirit, I brought back into calm whatever was turbulent, thereby sustaining defeat and gaining the fruit of it.

I expected you to write to me and to honour your master: my senior in rank, my superior in age, and—greater than these—your friend in concern. [Col. 1595C] But it did no good. Seeing that I was making no progress and that so great a fire had vanished into thin sparks, I feared lest it should altogether perish into dead ashes; with the breath of a gentler spirit I endeavour to kindle it anew. Foolish boy, who has turned your mind away from the constancy of such a great friendship? Whom did you believe, unbelieving man, so as to separate your only one from your own inward affections?

Certain men slipped away from our side, hating all the more the more they should have loved, biting one another and consumed by one another. All of them, as though with one mouth, conceived grief, etc. But that man who lay beside you [Col. 1595D] also—whom more private speech disdains to name—mixed poison with honey. He “knew [the quantity of] the mixture of myrrh and aloes: more than a hundred pounds” (John 21): a young man dedicated to perpetual frivolity and endless chattering.

> Loving no one and loved by no one.  
> Juvenal, V.12.
>
> A teacher of loving those who hate him, and hating those who love him.

That man, or others, filled your credulous ears and alienated your mind from me by saying: “Nicholas says this,” when Nicholas did not say it. If I had believed informers accusing you, I would have woven a long parable of reproach, which the brevity of a letter rejects. But the inconstancy of frivolity has not so overthrown my mind that I can believe anything has yet issued from your mouth which would redound to my injury.

You were also told that, if you returned, I would teach no longer. How could one do this who was able to love so greatly as to make you feel the same, and to season a teachable talent with more mature judgment—one who does not believe every spirit, because “he who believes quickly is light of heart” (Ecclesiasticus 19)? [Col. 1596A] The authority of love deigns to refute the claim that I would abandon the school because of you. Since that claim is absurd and collapses without any defence of excuses, write back, therefore, and show yourself to yourself as another person.

## LETTER III. Again to the same person.

To his beloved brother N., Brother NICHOLAS: the spirit of counsel [Col. 1596B] and consolation.

At last my heart has returned to me; my heart came back to me, and I to my heart. Happy the day on which I resolved to write to you; yet far happier that on which you chose to reply. The memory of it shall not depart, nor shall it be abandoned for ever; rather, it shall be bright and solemn to me, growing ever brighter with eternal joys. “My friends and my neighbours withdrew from me as though they were strangers” (Job 19), and I was bewildered. They added still further: “Entreat me,” for they drew near against me, stood fast, and I grieved. Moreover, committing a very great offence, they tried to take from me the light of my eyes; all my bones were shaken; here “my heart was troubled, my strength forsook me” (Ps. 37). And though I had endured the two preceding trials with a stronger mind, I languished, overcome by the third.

But your noble spirit, deriving its origin from the heavenly seat, gathered itself again into its orbit and assumed the courage of a reviving spirit. Moved by the indignity of this final outrage, it cleared its innocence by sweeter letters; and, shutting the mouths of detractors, it imposed perpetual silence on whisperers and envious persons: “Iniquity has therefore lied to itself” (Ps. 26). For the majesty of friendship, set upon the throne of constancy, mocked with lofty security tongues that pass over the earth. Now therefore the pen must be polished and sprinkled with more graceful language, lest nakedness of words accuse the power of my talent.

Who will grant me never to abandon remembrance of you, and never to be abandoned by it? Yet how could it endure so long and so silent an absence? When I sit as judge of my own thoughts and enter alone into the solitude of my heart, I marvel greatly. And if it was not permitted to see you, why at least were letters absent—letters which bring the true traces and authentic marks of a friend? What am I saying: that it was not permitted to see you? What excuse was there? One cloaked in shadowy falsehoods? Did the Ocean Sea flow between us as far as Troyes? Or had the impenetrable Riphaean mountains been thrown in our way? Yet, even if all these obstacles had met together, nothing ought to have been inaccessible to love, nothing arduous to one who loves. Love is accustomed to swim above the clouds, and waters cannot extinguish it, because it alone has known beforehand how to mock the assault of difficulties by the leap of its own subtlety. It makes what is difficult and narrow light; it declares broad reproach to be glory, and insists that contempt is exaltation.

Whom shall I accuse first, or whom shall I judge more justly in our complaint? If I wish to confess the truth: “It is I who have sinned; I have acted wickedly” (2 Kings 24). For what have you done—you, most simple and gentle boy, enclosed with marvellous reserve in the very inner chambers of modesty? You scarcely dare lift your eyes to heaven or look upon those standing round you; and I have confounded your profound modesty by a still more profound forgetfulness. I became to you like a bear and a lion, and with the disdain of proud eyes I broke the tenderness of your mind. Therefore I rebuke myself: transfer this sin from me.

But henceforth, if chatterers and subverters overthrow you, let them overthrow you no more (Ps. 25). Do not sit with the council of vanity, and do not mingle with men who breathe venomous words. Remember that no one willingly tells anything to an unwilling listener. But because dead letters cannot convey what I feel:

> Write nothing back to me; nevertheless, come yourself. — Ovid, *Epistles*.

For sight and conversation possess something of living delight which the characters of letters cannot contain.

## LETTER IV. To Atto, Bishop of Troyes

[Note: [Col. 1597D] This Hatto, formerly a monk of Cluny, was made bishop of Troyes in the year 1122, as D. Canus noted.]

A strongly commendatory and laudatory letter.

To the great priest and especially his own Father, brother NICOLAS: may you exercise the priesthood in the sight of God.

[Col. 1597C] Perhaps I shall be accused of irreverence because I do not fear to write to one so worthy of reverence. For what is a servant to his lord, a disciple to his master, a monk to a bishop? There is nothing in common between him and me, since supreme dignity defines him and lowliness defines me. I shall therefore be silent, lest by speaking I incur the mark of talkativeness. Rather, I shall presume to speak to my lord: “May my speech be pleasing to him” (Ps. 104).

A shared mode of speech, an old love, and undivided intimacy give confidence to my pen. The woman of the Gospel is praised because she did what she had (Mark 12; Luke 21); thus I too do what I have: I have letters, and I send letters. Happy letters which draw not toward madness but toward moderation; happy learning which possesses purity of conscience. Perfect understanding is that which displays the serpent in such a way that it does not abandon the dove, and so tempers the dove that the serpent does not grow cold.

[Note: [Col. 1597D] In the manuscript: *composuit*, “arranged/ordered.”]

Lofty eloquence, which neither rushes headlong nor drives others headlong; which teaches order, shapes conduct, puts on patience, and speaks honourably (Prov. 26). A learned tongue which knows when it ought to utter speech, which is silent in an evil time; which does not pour out all its spirit at once, but reserves something for the future. A provident breast, full of counsel, where reverence sits, discretion reigns, and modesty rules.

[Col. 1598A] For what is understanding worth if we do not do what is sensible? What is wisdom if, on the occasion of wisdom, we behave foolishly? What are letters if we do not know their effect? What is eloquence if we do not know how to speak and be silent? Whoever is intelligent in order to dissent, wise in order to act foolishly, learned in order to move the earth, eloquent in order to seem a mere talker, has no share in the kingdom of Christ and God. The righteous man who has not known literary learning shall enter into the powers of the Lord (Ps. 70). Moses, slow and impeded of tongue (Exod. 4), is set over six hundred thousand armed men; fishermen and unlearned men are chosen, so that the wise and philosophers may be confounded. And [lacuna] claims glory for itself from the gifts of the Creator.

A perfect spirit, distinguished by the parts of a perfect composition, made honourable by riper judgment, more discerning speech, and more reverent bearing—this form, sweetest Father, the Most High has impressed upon you, and your life has risen to the height of the virtues. For who judges more rightly, speaks more gracefully, or lives more moderately? But lest you think that I again obscure the brightness of realities by flattering speech, I shall omit the rest.

Yet among all the virtues, that which has chosen for itself pre-eminence in your breast is, unless I am mistaken, patience. I have seen with eyewitness faith peoples raging, making a din, and barking all around; many clerics disturbed; the ground before your face, and flying words rising into hateful clamour. You sat quietly, fortified by a rampart through which snarling folly could not appear.

[Note: [Col. 1597D] In the manuscript, previously and incorrectly: *occulta*, “hidden.”]

[Col. 1598C] I saw wicked men acting wickedly and offenders exalting their horn—men whom episcopal authority could have overthrown with a single word, if it had pleased you to rush upon them. But you waited a little, and laughed more securely at the thundering storm of evildoers, until either they dashed against one another or were restrained by higher powers. It is a singular virtue in a man to show patience toward those whom he has the power to punish whenever he wishes.

My pen was running on and expressing my feeling in every sort of phrase, until I looked back and understood that the length of my discourse had exceeded the limit of a letter. I therefore make an end and ask that, amid your intervening cares, you write something back and relieve your boy with the consolations of that noble eloquence.

## LETTER V. To Master G., Archdeacon

[Note: [Col. 1597D] I suspect that this solitary letter refers to Gebuin, whom St Bernard mentions in Epistle 17, and Peter of Cluny in Book IV, Epistles 34 and 135, where he is called Master Gebuin the archdeacon. That he was not unskilled in preaching, as Nicolas here mentions, is attested by five books of his sermons preserved in our library.]

A strongly commendatory letter.

[Col. 1598D]

To his heart’s friend and most reverend master, G., archdeacon, brother NICOLAS: may you acquire a good rank in good ministry.

To you alone I dare write, though it is great presumption to write to you. For the poverty of my understanding and the nakedness of my style fear your wisdom and reverence your eloquence. Both have been granted to you in abundant good fortune: to think wisely and speak profitably. And because to meditate upon wisdom is consummate understanding, the authority of the starry Scriptures has found a seat in you, remains with you, and makes an armory of you.

[Col. 1599A] The well-considered discretion of your eloquence, shining in the lofty clarity of your speech, tempers itself with such variety that it benefits the learned without failing the unlearned. Learned discourse, polished speech, a more cheerful countenance, and a rhetorical spirit—pleasing to friends and not displeasing to enemies—have overcome unhappy envy with happier glory. The distributor of all talents has given you two talents, and with a more lavish spirit the subtle and discerning Spirit of understanding has poured a double spirit into you.

Let others extol philosophers and praise grammarians; let those who do not know how to speak make a clamour with garrulous derivation. You alone suffice for me, perfected in consummate perfection by more prudent judgment and more graceful speech. Thus I saw the masters of Gaul, whom the image of a famous name had brought forward, tremble before your eloquence and, with their murmuring suppressed, depart one after another, bearing glory away to you and shame to themselves. But when there was a judgment in which lay a great abyss, your eyes did not grow dim; rather, flying ahead with swifter intelligence, they discovered the hidden meaning when the obscurities had been removed.

[Col. 1599B] To this is added the more pleasing weakness of your mortality, which seasons joy with seriousness and so kindles the secret place of your mind that you seem not contrary to others, but unlike them. Your more honourable manner of life, marked by the titles of golden moderation, has repelled avarice and ambition with marvellous restraint. Your disciplined household, possessing at home what it might learn, “has not done evil to its neighbour, nor accepted reproach against its neighbours” (Ps. 14).

[Col. 1599C] Thus approved by the endowments of wisdom, eloquence, and discipline, you have become the ornament of the Church, the voice of the city, and an example to peoples. Happy would you be, city of Troyes, if you too had recognized him; if you had changed the accumulation of envy into the glory of admiration. I know what I say, nor do I seek to veil the truth of things with obscuring speech; but I yield to lords and spare friends. It is shameless impudence—

[Note: [Col. 1599D] More correctly, *frontositas*, “impudence/boldness.”]

—to flee from and drive away the man whom it is a lesson to follow, while to overtake him is the highest wisdom. Envy is a frenzied plague, exceeding the very strength of the heart, and it disturbs both substances by a more grievous weakening.

[Col. 1599D] Oh, if it were granted me from above to cling to you, hear you, and not be removed from your company! But promised stability and a professed vow of a stricter rule exclude me from your audience and establish a living burial for me. While the fluency of your tongue pours itself forth in golden speech, I confess that Cicero, Quintilian, or one of those ancient workshops is speaking in full voice. And although in much wisdom there is much indignation, such humility shapes your loftiness that what is said seems fulfilled in you: “And in your truth you have humbled me” (Ps. 118).

[Col. 1600A] I have gone too far, I confess; forgetful of my own slightness, I have presented a long and naked composition to your eyes. Therefore, sweetest master, let the integrity of my affection excuse the defect of my discourse, and let friendship cover what inexperience has laid bare. May it please your gracious dignity to send me that sermon which you were accustomed to deliver upon the saying of the Saviour: “If the Son has made you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8), so that he who alone was free among the dead may free us from the death of sin—Jesus Christ, bridegroom of the Church, Son of God.

## LETTER VI. To Peter, Dean of Troyes, on Unity and Affection

[Note: [Col. 1599D] He writes to him again in Epistle 17.]

To his dean, and truly his own, brother NICOLAS: may you be set over ten cities by the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1599D] I have restored more confidently the little word *super*, “over.” For the author looked to the parable set forth.]

[Col. 1600B] I must write to you differently, because I commit myself to you with my whole affection. You are the one whom my affection claims for itself and glories to draw wholly to itself with its whole self. For from two we make one, and we have excluded the binary, prince of alternation. Nor does duality have a place in us, whom unity of minds commends. Unity is a spiritual power, and the summit of that unity is made one—

[Note: [Col. 1600D] It appears one should read *imitatur*, “imitates.”]

—in which whatever is, is one. A multitude of causes has bound so great a unity between you and me, and manifold composition has produced this simplicity. Sweet conversation, good familiarity, constant companionship, love of the Scriptures, gracefulness of conduct, charm of character, equality of youth, sweetness of nature, modesty of discipline, and—greater than these—the same willing and the same unwilling, have fused two minds into the unity of simplicity.

[Col. 1600C] Beyond all this, your good spirit, poured forth in sweeter speech, softened my roughness and reduced to measure whatever had been excessive. It found in me neither the subtlety of a more cultivated mind nor the insignia of vaunting eloquence; but it graciously anticipated its friend, cherished him when anticipated, and does not cease to cherish him. Truly welcome is a confederation which flattery did not extort, which masked prosperity did not know, and which the success of flattering fortune did not counterfeit. For where inequality of persons stands out, it should be called favour rather than love; and rarely does the greatness of friendship make unequal fortunes produce equal minds.

[Col. 1600D] None of these things hindered us, whom neither money, nor fortune, nor the widely proclaimed renown of a famous name, but great love joined together with happier glory. Let philosophers blush, and let the tongues of the Academics be turned backward: they, confusing the simple with the composite, believed that nothing simple could shine forth from composite parts. Behold, two are reduced to one (Luke 17), and the assault of Aristotelian subtlety is enfeebled; trusting in a multiplicity of words, it does not know the mystery of indivisible unity. Nor does the separate division of outward clothing prejudice this, because not the colour of garments but the love of hearts builds the majesty of friendship.

[Col. 1601A] I rejoice over you and, while you live, laugh at either fortune: since prosperity shared with you is more joyful, and adversity, with you sympathizing, is milder. If proud fortune has cut short for me the course of clearer favour, consolation has been hidden from your eyes, and your face did not put on a more serene expression before serenity was restored to me. If caressing and joyful fortune restored me with more gracious delight, at once a happier mind, more cheerful countenance, and more composed speech overflowed within me. They turned night into day for the happy soul; but for me, unhappy man, they turned day into night, who separated us in body when they could not separate us in heart.

Although difference of distance does not diminish a lover’s affection, companionship and conversation have something of living pleasure, and exchanged conversations make sweet friendships sweeter. Behold, I have become a monk in the length of my letter, but abundant affection drove on the running pen. Let one who knows affection spare affection, and count its prolixity as charity. You are happy, but I am much happier: our associated minds had received bodily companionship also. Meanwhile, let memory stand in place of presence until the joy of both is fulfilled.

## LETTER VII. To the Prior and Elders of Clairvaux concerning His Reception

[Note: [Col. 1601D] St Bernard mentions his reception already accomplished in Epistle 35, after the edition.]

To the reverend lords and fathers, Prior R. and his council, brother NICOLAS: may you show mercy to him who fell among thieves (Luke 10).

[Col. 1601C] On this occasion bear with a little of my foolishness, and endure me as well. For your humility, our necessity, and that third thing in which you gave me hope—the reception of our littleness—all inspire me with confidence. “We have received, O God, your mercy” (Ps. 47), when we received that fellowship, made companions of the heavenly virtues which are poured out more abundantly in the place of Clairvaux for those who shall inherit salvation. Therefore this is not an occasion for vanity, but an affection for truth; for it is not that which puffs up, but that which builds up, that is at issue.

My soul is free from this excess, although it cannot deny that it is bound by weightier things. I had indeed shut myself within myself, so that there was no speech upon my tongue; but I could no longer command my affection sufficiently to prevent myself from communicating my heart to your hearts, at least by this remedy. My impatient spirit, eager to declare itself in words, both dares and fears to speak: it burns to open itself, yet fears lest it displease. Nevertheless I loosen the reins, and with freer will pour my whole self into speech. It will be familiar to wise men to tolerate one who does not know.

[Col. 1601D] I departed from you in joy; but do not believe that my joy is full. For what joy shall there be for me, who sit in darkness, who do not see the light of heaven, the light of Clairvaux?

[Note: [Col. 1601D] Hence the time when Nicolas entered Clairvaux becomes clear: that is, after the year 1145.]

O light descending from the Father of lights (James 1), where luminaries shine in the firmament of heaven, whence was taken Eugene the pope, that greater luminary to illuminate the earth! O happy land, where I saw the children of Israel proceeding in ranks and companies: all busy, none idle; all holding swords and most skilled for battle in the spirit of strength, entering the promised land! There I saw the Bride of Christ, who is almost everywhere wrinkled, without wrinkle or spot (Eph. 5); her who truly wounded the heart of her bridegroom; her who, with one lock of hair and the sparkle of one little eye, stirs the King of heaven, Lord of angels, Son of God the Father. And I said: “These are the camps of God” (Gen. 32). “This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 1602D] He digresses in praise of Clairvaux.]

[Col. 1602A] A multitude of heavenly legions flies about and surrounds it, for security and shelter from storm and rain. Seeing these things, I raised myself above myself, and, carried away in an ecstasy of mind, swore and resolved to follow poor Christ with the poor, so that I might find the reward of poverty. I could neither extinguish the kindled spirit nor wished to do so any longer. In a short time, after much had been buried beneath a manifold multitude of feelings, I came to you as from sea to harbour, from promise to reward, from labour to rest, from despair to hope.

I came to the place which the Lord chose out of all places, so that there, and nowhere else, I might sit at the feet of my Lord until I heard remission of sins in peace. That place is a holy place: a wooded valley, an abundant valley, a paradise of delights, a garden of graces, in which, if I am not there and live, I shall die. Bitterly defrauded of my desire, I speak before God: if all the kingdoms of the world and their glory were conferred upon me, it would be nothing if I did not happen to be present with you and in that place.

[Col. 1602C] Clairvaux is in my affection, Clairvaux in my thought, Clairvaux in my presence, Clairvaux in my memory, Clairvaux in my mouth, Clairvaux in my heart; and it kindles my tender soul with most tender meditation. I willingly accept and shall accept your decision; but if there is any pity, if any affection of charity, have mercy on me, have mercy, and lead the captive from the prison-house, for everywhere is a prison without you. Could it not be obtained from the brethren—indeed, from our enemies—that they let us remain in this place until the common father comes, he for whom it is reserved to divide by the breath of his mouth between day and night, or between day and day? In so great a council, could not even this little counsel of remaining among you be found?
