[Col. 1602D] Remember the prior, whom old age itself renders venerable, and the young man, whom good will and great usefulness make lovable: they have no consolation or counsel except from you and in you. I feel that I am advancing too far and going beyond the measure of my littleness; but let compassion excuse what my petition has dared, and let charity cover its prolixity. Since, after God, I have cast all my care upon you, may it please your gracious dignity to send us Lord Gaucher—

[Note: [Col. 1602D] I think this is Gaucher whom St Bernard, Epistle 267, calls Walter, recently transferred to Clairvaux from Cluny, and to whom you will later read Epistle 45.]

—for I have many things to tell you which I have not dared to write, lest perhaps the letter fall into the hands of curious persons. Announce to us your gracious decision and free us from this circuit, so that he may free you from every evil who alone was free among the dead, the Bridegroom of the Church, Son of Mary, our Lord God.

## LETTER VIII. To Prior Theobald, Who Entered and Left the Order with Him, Calling Him Back

I grieve for you, Father Theobald, and this grief is always before me. Each day it grows fresher and, inflicting wound upon wound—

[Note: [Col. 1603D] Better: *infligens*, “inflicting.”]

—it afflicts my spirit as sharply as it does persistently. My soul refuses to be comforted; I remembered you, and was saddened, and my spirit failed (Ps. 76). Nor do I remember you so as to forget, but so as to burn more and more.

[Col. 1603B] Perhaps you believed that I had forgotten you and belonged to the number of those who honour their neighbour while things go well, but do not recognize him when they go badly. I know that things go badly for you; nor have they gone worse for anyone, unless another has wandered similarly. You were a man set in honour, full of days and letters, of good will and great usefulness, and of sweetest companionship. Both the princes of the court and of the Church knew you; and you had so lived in the order against the order that you were not removed from worldly affairs. Whatever sweetness it possessed, you had possessed and had poured forth from this into that.

You were bound to me also by so great an intimacy that even our own people marvelled that Scipio and Laelius had come to life again in our times.

[Note: [Col. 1603D] Cicero, in *Laelius*, testifies that the friendship of the two was memorable.]

[Col. 1603C] Finally, with one accord we left everything, and flew from the Old Testament and the shadow of the Cluniacs to the purity of the Cistercians. For, according to the saying of Paul, if the first had been free from fault, we should certainly not seek a place for the second.

[Note: [Col. 1603D] The passage is chapter 8 of the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the Apostle places the ministry of the New Testament before the Old.]

And indeed the observances of your people have some resemblance to the observances of the Jews. For they had introduced the whole rite of divine worship in gold and purple, in foods and drinks and various washings; so too among you—

[Note: [Col. 1604D] That is, among the Cluniacs, concerning whom see similar remarks in Epistle 1 of St Bernard.]

—where there is more gold, there is believed to be more merit; where more cloaks, more morals; where more feasts and garments, there is a truer observance of the commandments. Yet we did this not in a sudden agitation, as often happens, but, strengthened by deliberate consideration, we gave the hands of fellowship under oath and witness of the Godhead. And with a strong hand indeed we withdrew from them and came to these, where I saw you a man of virtue, whom neither threats could shake nor flatteries seduce.

[Col. 1603D] Why say more? Having gone out from them, you entered among these; having entered among these, you returned to them. Your departure was praiseworthy, your entry commendable, but your return detestable. This is not a return to the father. By going out you left scandal to your own people; by returning you multiplied it. For our people saw and grieved, but were moved by compassion, not disturbed by your return or transgression.

[Col. 1604A] If woe is yours through whom any scandal comes (Matt. 18), what of the man through whom so many and such grave scandals have arisen? But perhaps you say: “The tunic pricked me, food disturbed me, heat oppressed me, vigils wearied me, silence tortured me, thought twisted me.” These indeed were the first hardships of abstinence, and the point was near at which desire would weaken and your God would come to your aid. If you had cried, “When my strength fails, do not forsake me” (Ps. 70), would he have withdrawn his hand, he who fills every living thing with blessing? (Ps. 143.) “Call upon me,” he says, “in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49).

I too was formed from the same clay, reared in such tenderness and exaltation as I knew and you did not fail to know.

[Col. 1604B] At least I ought to have held you back, both for the sake of example and because of affection. But, forgetful of uprightness and obligation, you went out from the counsel of many and the congregation at the first impulse. Prophetic and evangelical utterances fell to the ground in you. For he who, according to the prophet, had forsaken you for a moment and a little while, was returning to you in his mercy and abundant compassions (Isa. 54). Does the world have anything new to offer one who returns again? Or, according to the words of Barzillai (1 Kings 19), when you have passed seventy years, do your senses still retain their vigour to distinguish sweet from bitter? Can food or drink delight you, or the voice of male or female singers soothe your ears?

[Col. 1604C] How much better, following the example of that most glorious old man—

[Note: [Col. 1604D] His name was Eleazar. Read again the story in 2 Maccabees 6, where these words occur in another order.]

—even if you had to die, to embrace a glorious death rather than a hateful life, and say with him: “By enduring bravely, I shall appear worthy of old age. But I shall perhaps leave the young a noble example, lest I incur a stain or curse upon my old age. For though at the present time I escape bodily punishments, yet I shall not escape the hand of the Almighty, either alive or dead.” These things befitted a man first in order, a master in honour, advanced in age, venerable in grey hair.

Let no one flatter you concerning your return, because, according to your satirist:

> No guilty person is acquitted when he is his own judge.  
> — Juvenal, *Satires* 13.

You carry your conscience with you; and woe to you, miserable man, if you despise this witness.

[Col. 1604D] For this reason I have wept and shall not cease to weep when I see another self so gravely endangered—lest I say apostatizing—and death threatening extreme old age. For one whom old age leads to death has nothing to hope for, since death must follow old age. Therefore, my beloved, return to your heart and hasten to come to the man of God. Spurning every counsel, entrust your soul to his counsel, lest you lose it.

[Col. 1605A] Beware of putting your hand again to men or secular business, for that would be both the height of disgrace and the extremity of madness. But if you persist, saying, “I shall not do this, but shall follow the will of my perverse heart, and [shall regard] neither my iniquity nor my sin any longer,” this letter shall stand between me and you as a testimony before the dreadful tribunal of him who then will neither spare nor have mercy, because his right hand shall be full of justice.

But if you wish briefly to hear from me about what concerns me: your Nicolas has lost death and found life unto the fullness of his vows. Your resurrection is lacking to me; if it should happen that I see and hear of it, I shall not be defrauded of my desire. Farewell, and remember your last things.

## LETTER IX. From Brocard, Abbot of Balerna, to Nicolas Himself, Congratulating Him on His Conversion and New Affection

[Note: [Col. 1605D] In Epistle 146 of St Bernard he is called Burcard. See the notes on that same letter.]

[Col. 1605B]

To NICOLAS, much beloved and greatly cherished by him, brother BROCARD of Balerna: from salvation to happiness.

On this first occasion receive me in a simple style; and permit me, without measure, by a certain arrangement of steps, to ascend from an unfeathered little beast to the first winged animal. If it is a tortoise, how shall it speak to a winged bird? If a mole, how shall it leap with a stag? If a cicada, how shall it *citillabit* [reading uncertain] to the melody of a swan?

[Note: [Col. 1606D] Here one seems to need to read *saltitabit*, “it will hop/dance.”]

Grant, I pray, that in my simplicity I may approach, like a dull old man, a young man of steel. I have felt the edge of a cutting blade; therefore let steel, by likeness, furnish me my argument. Yet the dull and blunt man also has need of steel. Let this little preface stand here.

[Col. 1605C] I give thanks to God, who makes all things new, for the new wonder of the new transformation of Nicolas made new: he who made white from black has done a new and wondrous thing. But this is more wondrous among all new things, and newer than new, that from such blackness such whiteness has been made. He who is known to have done it could well and most excellently bring it about that the Ethiopian should change his skin (Jer. 13). “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76).

Let us bless that refiner in whom you have been so smelted and purified as to attain the brightness of whiteness, with new wonder and new joy. But what is this newness to me? Much in every way. For I glory that in this newness I have newly received new grace: a new acquaintance, new familiarity, and new affection; a new intention and new treasures from a new friend newly found.

[Col. 1605D] Of him it is written: “A faithful friend is a strong protection; whoever finds him finds a treasure” (Ecclus. 6). His memory produces incomparable delights for me; remembrance, joy; consideration, an abundance of sweetness; and enjoyment, a newness of delight. Are not these new things, flowing from a new discovery and overflowing most abundantly? These things come from you to me; but what from me to you? I say: cleanse, polish, file, scrape, carve, renew, lay aside, wash, wipe away, so that our whiteness, once cleansed, may there be cleansed still more, more than sevenfold.

## LETTER X. Reply to the Same, on United Affection

[Col. 1606A]

To the most reverend Father and dearest friend, BROCARD, Abbot of Balerna, brother NICOLAS: greetings in him who is true salvation.

I saw your letters—or rather, I encountered you yourselves in your letters—and I ran into sparks flying from the furnace of a most burning kiln. Yet I was not scorched by them, but kindled; the flaming words descended into the marrow of my heart and set it ablaze. Blessed indeed is the breast which the flame of charity has more deeply absorbed in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. Happy the soul in which true poverty has built an impregnable refuge and a singular rest. Most sweet is the spirit upon which [Col. 1606B] the spirit of humility most gently sprinkles a more abundant stream of graces. Most watchful is the mind from which the springs alike of wisdom and eloquence bubble forth perpetually and abundantly. Finally, you are a man most fully perfected, in whom the harmony of virtues and the assembly of learning have consecrated for themselves a venerable bridal chamber. Are these words of variety, rather than of truth? I speak the truth; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me. That divine gaze also knows—before whose eyes all things are naked and exposed (Heb. IV)—that, as it is in writing, so it is in the mind; and the soul feels what the page contains, and far more sublimely than lifeless letters can convey.

You are the one and only person, after that One whom [Col. 1606C] my soul loves, who has the chief dwelling-place in my breast. And I, received into the sanctuary of your love, have been incorporated into your inmost affections for ever and ever. Death alone, which knows how to make a dreadful divorce of friends, will be able to interrupt this unity; indeed, not even death itself. Perhaps it too will be made equal to this unity, when we shall meet in unity so much the more uniquely as invisibly, “in the unity of faith, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV). Then, every artifice of the crafty evader having been mocked and crushed, we shall see God in ourselves, seeing one another in the other with subtle delight and delightful subtlety; for “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI). If, therefore, when all [Col. 1606D] are joined to the Lord, we shall be one spirit with the Lord, then in that fortified and united city unity alone shall reign; and that shall be fulfilled which the boy harp-player thus sings: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city,” etc. (Ps. CXXI).

But let him consider these things who is sufficient to consider them. Though I am stirred by them, I confess that my spirit fails and does not rise even to contemplate the mystery of so great a condescension. Here there is need both of purer sight and of deeper understanding, and I do not doubt that both are far from and beyond me. Meanwhile, I call and judge myself most fortunate, since your acquaintance alone has abundantly repaid a hundredfold whatever I had left behind.

[Col. 1607A] Thus, although you are distant from me in bodily presence, you are wholly with me in the memory of my heart—in me and with me—not without much sweetness of joy. If my thought can be taken from me, then your love can be taken from me too. So long as that thought is within me, you will not be absent from me; for that saying is altogether true: the mind is to be possessed by its friend; and this is never absent. But enough of this.

Are you now willing to play in this way with this little boy—very graciously and amicably, certainly? Yet if you play in such a way as not to mock, you ask to be received by me in a simple style, while I have been utterly amazed by the light of your arrows, by the brilliance of your flashing page. The whole page is adorned with trappings, gilded with rhetorical splendors, and sparkling with the majesty of most fruitful thoughts and maxims. You alter the same words on the same page with a subtlety that is most difficult, yet most easy for you. The colours of the orators are wax in your hand. Is that creature, then, featherless which has sewn the most flourishing and manifold feathers of the arts onto its thoughts, so that the arrow of its words may fly more straight? Is he a tortoise who is raised to the summit of things by both knowledge and love of truth? How is he a mole who has the eyes of his heart enlightened, who despises earth and earthly things? Or a cicada, who cries aloud to God, and after God, by day and by night? Great humility is to be great and not to feel oneself great.

Am I a winged creature? Of the six wings of winged creatures, not yet has a feather grown, nor yet a wing. [Col. 1607C] Am I a stag, who have not yet made my feet like those of stags and been set upon high places? (Ps. XVII.) Am I thus called a swan, who have not yet given to my voice the voice of strength, and whose whiteness, if there is any, has not yet been purified into the most spotless brightness? But it is a friend who speaks, and he has deeply impressed upon his heart the one of whom he speaks. He believes what he says, and fervently believes of a friend what he would most gladly believe even of an enemy.

Moreover, I gathered and placed among my own words those two more secret words which you entrusted to me; and although they are not masked, they have nevertheless ceased to crawl. I shall take pains to polish away and remove what remains, lest there be anything in a friend that offends his friend. Your H. sends you greetings.

[Note: [Col. 1607D] Either I am mistaken, or H. signifies the hermit Henry mentioned in the letter.]

He tells you [Col. 1607D] that the day is near on which he will strike a covenant with the Lord his God; he earnestly begs and steadfastly requires that you be present. For you promised. My G. also—and yours, who received these things, the inseparable companion of my writings—has most fully placed the remembrance of your spirit within his own spirit. Farewell, and pray for both of us, for both are yours.

## LETTER XI. In the person of Father Brother Gerard of Perona, to one of his dependants, concerning ingratitude.

[Col. 1608A]

Brother GERARD to his beloved N.: may you love judgment and justice.

It is an old proverb and a maxim celebrated by the lips of the ancients: the memory of benefits is unstable, but that of injuries tenacious. For, as the philosopher says, among human things nothing grows old so quickly as a benefit, though it ought to be fixed by all in everlasting remembrance. The children of men have adopted this most wicked custom, that they may spread themselves in it: they are ungrateful for favours and unwilling to repay benefits. Ingratitude is the worst vice: the scattering of virtues, the emptying of merits, a raging and burning wind [Col. 1608B] which dries up the fountain of mercy, wipes away the dew of piety, and stops the streams of grace.

[Note: [Col. 1607D] St Bernard, *Sermon 51 on the Song of Songs*, writes almost the same: “Ingratitude is a burning wind, drying up for itself the fountain of piety, the dew of mercy, and the streams of grace; ingratitude is the enemy of the soul, the emptying of merits, the scattering of virtues, the loss of benefits.” In *Letter* 2, he employed the same saying from the comic poet in the *Andria*.]

Although I say this wholly on your account, wishing to move you to repay benefits, you know that I have done you many good turns, and I rejoice that I have done them. This is not a reminder as though reproaching you with a benefit received, but a warning: what you can no longer do for me, do for my son, because he is in me and I in him (John VI). For nature and custom require that one who loves the father should love the son, and be loved by the father (ibid.). He owes you much, but you owe me much; and this much ought to be a certain release for a debtor against much. Show him favour and kindness, for whatever you do to him is done to me. Thus you shall be acquitted before God and men; [Col. 1608C] and all who hear will say: “This man has done what he ought to have done.” But I ask you, G., as one most dear to me, to read this letter more attentively to the aforesaid R. and examine it word by word.

## LETTER XII. To the Abbot of Igniacum, in the person of the Prior, concerning reconciliation.

And to his beloved and much-beloved Father, Brother R. of Clairvaux, Abbot of Igniacum: may you be kindled with holy fire.

[Note: [Col. 1608D] He plays upon the name *Igniacensis*, “of Igniacum,” associated with *ignis*, “fire.”]

We write to you with so much the greater confidence as we love you more sincerely, and this concerns your own affair. For all that is yours is ours, and what is ours is yours, most beloved father. There is a matter between our monks of Igniacum and your monks of Clairvaux which G. M.—indeed yours as well as ours—will report to you [Col. 1608D] orally; for you will hear him as though you heard us. We therefore beg that, for the sake of your mother-house Igniacum, you go there with the aforesaid G.; and that you settle the matter in accordance with what he shall tell you on our behalf. For when our common father, the lord of Clairvaux, comes, then every case and every dispute will also be decided according to your counsel. But if you cannot go—which indeed is not expedient—let it please your gracious dignity to send Brother Henry of Vivisember to that place, [Col. 1609A] so that in your stead he may establish what must be established.

## LETTER XIII. In the person of Henry, brother of the King of France, to the lord of Clairvaux on behalf of the Bishop of Alicensis.

(See Letter 1 of Henry, Archbishop of Reims, above in this volume, col. 1573.)

## LETTER XIV. In the person of the Lord of Clairvaux, to the counts and barons of Brittany concerning the business of the cross.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII, col. 672, among the letters of St Bernard.)

## LETTER XV. To a certain companion: he commends the monks of Clairvaux and urges him to fulfil his vows.

[Col. 1609B]

May he who bore our sorrows (Isa. LIII) know how sorrowfully I sympathize with you. Far be it from me to have despised you because I did not write, when by fraternity and friendship I owe you whatever I am, and by charity whatever I can do in the Lord. But you know that I live among men in whom the rigor of discipline prevails: gravity of conduct, maturity of counsel, weight of authority, the distinction of silence. I do not wish to be accused of singularity, so that, while they are at leisure and see that He is God, I should turn over pen and tablets and fly back to the trappings and glory of words. Yet from the morning watch until night I do nothing else. Let it not be imputed to those who laid this burden upon me and set me to write much and to answer many people. I ought [Col. 1609C] to weep and pray, and, according to the prophet (Jer. III), put my mouth in the dust—if perhaps there may be hope; if perhaps the Lord may see my humility and my labour, and forgive all my sins (Ps. XXIV).

You say that I care for no one. It is otherwise. For because I am at Clairvaux, I have neither stripped off nor gone beyond human affections; rather, God is witness to me how I hold you all in my inmost affections. Though I have withdrawn from you bodily, I shall not withdraw in heart for ever and ever. But I have set you more especially as a seal upon my heart: I know your mind in part, and for you I have often spread out my hands to him who neither rejected nor despised the prayer of the poor. Yet [Col. 1609D] I do not know whether he has set my tears before his sight.

That you are worldly and joined to worldly people, your own knowledge and conscience do not fail to know how near you are to death. What you do not dare lay bare to me in writing—the secrets of your mind—you could disclose in conversation, unless you fear men more than God. What you hoped to be drawn after me and by me would already have been fulfilled, had you not trembled with fear where there was no fear. You know how faithfully and effectively I wished to draw you from the iron furnace of great Babylon; but you slipped from my hands back to the old fire. You say that you have blotted out the sin of this departure with tears and the hoe of repentance. Whether that is true—yet to remain in sin and obtain pardon for sin is not the part of one who says, “By your mouth you shall be justified, or by your mouth you shall be condemned.” If you know what you have not discharged—especially when you know how to pass either from evil to good or from good to better—see whether, while you fail to do it, you can sleep with both ears. Hear concerning this what I think: not mine alone, but also that of blessed Gregory in his *Pastoral Rule*.

[Note: [Col. 1609D] *Pastoral Rule*, Admonition 28, near the end.]

“Whoever has resolved to undertake a greater good has made unlawful to himself the lesser good which he was able to do.”

Again, he himself in the third homily on Ezekiel:

[Note: [Col. 1609D] Near the end.]

“There are some who indeed do the good things they know; and while doing these, they deliberate about better things. Yet, while awaiting (*exspectantes*) [Note: [Col. 1609D] The printed editions read *retractantes*, ‘reconsidering’.] the better things upon which they deliberate, [Col. 1610B] they change (*mutantur*).”

[Note: [Col. 1610D] The printed editions read *immutantur*, “they are changed.”]

“They certainly do the good things they had begun; but they fall away from the better things they had resolved upon. Such people seem to stand in their works before human judgments, but they have fallen in their deliberation before the eyes of almighty God.”

Behold the mirror: in it consider not the face of your birth, but the deed of your return. What is greater or lesser good, higher or lower, stricter or more relaxed, the whole church of the saints knows. As for why I did not immediately reply to your letter: I could not, because of the Passion of the Lord, during which I scarcely had either opportunity or desire to speak with your messenger. I have not yet had the verses of that Humbert—who has put off the human being—concerning the common father of whom you are doubtful, composed by my Walter, indeed by yours as well. [Col. 1610C] But even if I had seen them, I would not have read through them, because we receive nothing that is constrained by the laws of a harlot. Behold, I send him the letter—

[Note: [Col. 1610D] Namely, the following one.]

—which I entrust to your fidelity under the testimony of God: reseal it as you find it, sealed and intact; and when he has seen it, see it yourself. Our lord abbot will come presently, as he has informed us. Thereafter I am ready in all things, with the Lord’s will, to do your will. Farewell; and consider that you must die and go there where the house of all youth has been appointed. Whatever I say, Gerard also says.

## LETTER XVI. To Walter, a noble young man, asking him to return to the order.

[Col. 1610D]

Nicholas to his Walter.

At the very beginning of my conversion I had especially resolved to write to you rather than to proscribe you; and though I was unable, I nevertheless wished it. I remember that I sinned in many ways, through many things, and greatly; but upon no one did such a great tumult of my malice descend, and against no one did my indignation more often burn than against those who returned evil for good to me and hatred for my love. Yet toward you I was converted by an accursed conversion, exchanging friendship for enmity. There is no need to renew in an epistolary form those errors and horrors which are buried before the eyes of men, [Col. 1611A] but not asleep before the Lord. “For,” says the saint, “a thousand years before your eyes are like yesterday which has passed” (Ps. LXXXIX). Therefore, “against you alone have I sinned, and done evil before you” (Ps. L). Truly evil: for I was evil in will, worse in power, but worst in authority. Everything answered my wishes all too fully while the favour of flatterers surrounded and confounded me, and there was not even one person to blunt me. For who would oppose a raging and burning wind which, from the regions of the North, hissed by every art? It would have been good for that man never to have been born, to whom will and . . . are ready, if kindness is lacking. But this was the hour and power of darkness, in which the pit was already opening its mouth over me, unless that merciful gaze of compassion had watched over me with all the depths of mercy.

For this reason I had bound my tongue and sheathed my pen, lest perhaps I provoke you to anger rather than call you back to grace. But you, though injured, ask pardon and anticipate me with blessings of sweetness, begging me to write something to you as a token of our old friendship. Joyfully and boldly I meet returning grace; and, as they say, with both hands I draw and draw you back to my heart. Come then: receive my affection—but another affection, and otherwise than I formerly gave it. Do not attend here to the brilliance of more splendid eloquence, for this is one of the things I have forgotten and left behind, which often supplied me with insolence and arrogance. A style sparkling with the majesty of maxims and radiant in the arrangement of flourishing speech befits a philosopher, not a monk; an orator, not an investigator of his own sins.

[Col. 1611C] You have put off the boy; you have put off the adolescent, restoring the man in stature and age. You are noble, you are young, you are learned, you are sworn into the army of the King whose kingdom is of all ages. To offer you that Virgilian saying (*Aeneid*):

> “Now there is need of courage, Aeneas; now of a steadfast breast.”

Now indeed there is need of a more mature mind and a weightier body, so that whatever vices childhood introduced, adolescence seized, may at least be removed and polished away by manhood. Even if not for fear of hell’s punishment or hope of the kingdom’s glory, this must nevertheless be undertaken for the ordering of conduct and the eradication of vices. For a noble soul, issuing from the heavenly workshops in the image of the Trinity, ought to be ashamed to serve foul limbs, and to serve its flesh in such a way that it leads and brings it back at a nod, more swiftly than a nod itself.

Solomon declares that house disordered and exposed to destruction (Prov. XXX), in which a servant reigns, a fool is filled, and a maidservant casts out her mistress. The mistress is the mind; the maidservant, the flesh. For the maidservant to rule and the mistress to be enslaved is the height of madness. If reason demands this from every human being, what do you owe to reason and to the author of reason—you whom conscience binds, obedience calls, power touches, necessity presses? For almost from your mother’s breasts [Col. 1612A] you were placed in God’s sanctuary, to live holily and serve the living God.

If you have preserved the garment of the flesh undefiled, if the single brightness of virginity has continually clothed your boyish limbs, you must stand firm and press on until you pass into the company of those clad in white, who follow the Virgin’s Son, the Bridegroom of virgins, through flowering mansions. But if, as the prophet says (Ezek. XXXIII), your hands were broken in Egypt, and while Christ slept with you, you uncovered yourself and received an adulterer, you must go out more quickly and pass more devoutly to the place where life is; where worthy fruits of repentance may restore the first robe of innocence and recall and bring you back to paternal embraces.

If reverence for religion, fear of presumption, and love for my former dwelling did not restrain me, most beloved young man, my old talkativeness would already sprout again, and I would show you how grim and dreadful it is to live where you do not dare die. Yet, lest I wholly extinguish the spirit of freedom, attend to a few things to which I strongly wish you to attend. What will those who are “in order” do before your face, Lord Jesus, where no order but everlasting horror dwells? With what brow, what eyes, what mind, what conscience will those gaze upon the countenance of your glory who have covered the whole mountain of pride with the idol of the vilest abomination? Though covered in their iniquity and impiety, they have nevertheless been uncovered: they have become a reproach to clerics, a mockery to secular people, a fable to the world, [Col. 1612C] and ruin to the order.

Who will give me the sword of Phinehas—

[Note: [Col. 1611D] With which Zimri, the Hebrew fornicator, was killed together with the Midianite woman; Num. 25.]

—the zeal of Mattathias—

[Note: [Col. 1612D] Read chapter II of I Maccabees.]

—or the fervour of Peter—

[Note: [Col. 1612D] Namely, that with which he cut off Malchus’s ear.]

—or who will stand with me against those who work iniquity? But I am going too far and ought to restrain the course of my speech, lest perhaps it accomplish nothing and displease your eyes. What should I leave unsaid by speaking? Rather, what I wish to say by keeping silent, your knowledge and conscience know. Who will grant that I may have my brother among my brothers of Clairvaux—so I speak, that your dross may be smelted pure—so that they may fashion you into a precious stone in the crown of the eternal King?

Oh, if you too knew how sweet it is to have fled and put to flight desires; to be content with the meanest food and roughest garment; to have the world under one’s feet; and, from the highest lookout of poverty, to look back upon and despise [Col. 1612D] “vain and mad false things” (Ps. XCIII). Oh, if ever I might deserve to have you as a companion in the school of piety, in the place of holiness, under Jesus as master and with Jesus as Lord; so that those whom one friendship held may be held by one discipline. How gladly I would share with you hot loaves, freshly drawn—as they say—from the oven, baked with the fat of wheat in the heavenly Jerusalem, which God prepared in his sweetness for the poor. How often we recognize the Lord in the breaking of the bread, of which whoever has tasted once shall not see death for ever.

But you will say: “How can these things be? Do you not know that the whole [Col. 1613A] land is full of my relatives, and all those around us are connected with me by blood?” And I answer: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark IX); to one who wills, they are easy; to one who loves, light. He easily despises all things who considers that when he dies he will not take everything with him, nor will his glory descend with him. But now this letter must be ended. At its close I beseech you, through the depths of the mercy of our God, that you know how to possess your vessel in sanctification and honour. Consider how great a shame it is, on account of shameful bodily parts and corpse-like, hollow limbs, to be ashamed and to destroy [oneself?]—

[Note: [Col. 1613D] I think *perire*, “to perish,” is better; for “for ever” was also added, though why and on what ground someone deleted it escapes me.]

—without end, beyond endurance, incessantly. “In the evening,” says the saint, speaking of the human being, “let him fall, grow hard, and dry up”: let him fall in death, grow hard in the corpse, dry up in the dust. Come now, pride: [Col. 1613B] this is the glory of Adam’s children. This is that sublime honour which receives those departing from the world: they come to pallor and horror, to pus and stench, to the worm and ashes, to be punished even in the grave. The children of men see these things and laugh (Ps. LI), anxious lest they lose material for their anxieties.

Nor is this surprising, because a fruitful end, a glorious place, and a splendid companion await them: namely destruction, hell, and the devil. For “the death of sinners is most evil” (Ps. XXXIII); their glory is in hell, and they are with the devil and his angels. Turn these and such things over in your mind, and flee sweet gatherings, for nothing so feminizes a man and drives him from the way of truth. Flatteries always serve vices; pleasant things entice toward sins; strong and austere things are friends to virtues.

But although you are distant from me in presence, you are wholly with me in memory. Those who behold one another with their minds are more present than those who behold one another with their eyes; and it is greater to be united in heart than in body. You have what you asked for; and would that it may be as you asked. But let this not escape you: I am yours and shall be yours as long as I am in the inward parts of Jesus Christ, who may deign to grant to me and to you forgiveness of sins, the grace of virtues, and the glory of heaven. And let the end of this letter be that end which is unto righteousness for one who believes.

## LETTER XVII. To Peter—

[Note: [Col. 1613D] He wrote above to this man in Letter 6.]

—Dean of Troyes, an exhortation to enter the order and despise the world.

To Master PETER, Dean of Troyes and dear to my heart, [Col. 1613D] Brother NICHOLAS: may you sing to God upon the ten-stringed psaltery.

I do not wish to make a long prologue for you, or adorn the page for the sake of more shining eloquence; for speech that is florid and pursues verbal ornaments befits a philosopher, not a monk. I begin with the matter itself, that the matter itself may impress both knowledge and devotion upon your heart. It happened one day, while I was weeping and praying at the feet of my Lord that he might be merciful [Col. 1614A] to my sin—for it is great—that your memory occupied my mind and breast more deeply and closely. Raising my eyes to the decree of that surpassing majesty, I broke out into these words: “Where are your ancient mercies, Lord?” (Ps. LXXXV). Where is the multitude of your tender mercies, where their inexhaustible depth? You who look upon the sinner, lest sin become sinful beyond measure (Rom. VII).

[Note: [Col. 1613D] The adverb *hic* (“here”) had not been inserted, but was removed by me as superfluous.]

For what profit is there in his blood, that you should seek out his iniquity and investigate his sin in that judicial and terrible inquiry, when you will even search Jerusalem with lamps (Zeph. I), lest you seize him in the works of his hands? O merciful Lord, rather gather together the record of your humanity: graciously consider what you have bestowed upon him [Col. 1614B] and what you have borne for him. Consider the condescension of those infant needs of yours; remember the labours which you endured in preaching, weariness in travelling about, temptations in fasting, vigils in prayer, tears in compassion, snares in converse, insults, spittle, blows, nails, and things like these, which you performed for our salvation in the midst of the earth. He whom you despise is generous, lovable, teachable, and young; only carnality, in its customary malice, flatters him. Anticipate him with blessings of sweetness; touch his heart, and at the voice of a single command he will count all these things, with the Apostle, as dung.

Thus I contended and pleaded for you, and concerning you, with the Lord and before the Lord of hosts. I do not know whether he has set my tears before his sight. One thing I know: he has never rejected or despised the supplication of the poor—he, such a lover of poverty, who chose to rejoice in heaven so that he might be poor on earth. Now I turn my pen to you, beseeching the Father of spirits that he may, through Him who supplied you with his flesh as food, his blood as drink, and his soul as a ransom, shape and pierce your heart.

It will be yours to hear patiently your friend, who loves you sincerely and will love you perpetually, who wishes to call you to his heart, call you back to the way, and urge you toward grace. You ought not to be angry with one who exhorts and heals you, when you are not angry with those who shoot at you and toss you about amid many wounds and winding paths. “Amen, I say to you, Peter: in this night, before the cock—”

[Note: [Col. 1614D] He aptly redirects Christ’s warning to the Apostle Peter toward Peter the dean.]

—that morning cock—summons the whole world with a briefer call, you sleep too much and suffer too much from lethargy.”

[Note: [Col. 1614D] The text incorrectly read *letagam*.]

The world passes away, and you pass away with that which passes; yet before it passes, it will send you forth. When you perish, you will neither take nor consume everything; all things will remain, and you will go your way—the way which leads to the city. Those of this kind have not found the way to the city of habitation.

[Col. 1615A] Two things attack you violently and assail you unceasingly, against which you must fight and resist, if you choose to return rather than perish: pride in the mind and pleasure in the body. From these two springs the whole abyss of vices rises and overwhelms the entire surface of the earth. These marshes have reigned over the whole breadth of the world and, overflowing everywhere, threaten to pour even upon the mountain-tops. O pride: veiling of hearts, confusion of bodies, infusion of presumptions, teacher of singularity, lover of novelty, disturber of peace, destroyer of unity, dissension from community. Whoever follows it incurs envy, because the multitude pursues no one more relentlessly than the person who arrogates to himself precedence over the multitude. Nothing so batters the citadel of virtue and overthrows the foundation of all discipline as pride. To repress and cast it down, that Majesty which shakes the world with a nod gave itself wholly.

Let the glory of Alexander of Macedon be compared with you and set before you: when the former was stationed in Babylon, the crown of the western nations was offered him; when the latter was in Spain, the same favour was brought back to him by all the eastern peoples. Yet you must die and go there where the house has been appointed for every living person. Death, coming after, will cut down all things, and will bury for ever and ever in the deepest depth the much-sought branches of human and popular glory—hardly found, scarcely possessed. [Col. 1615C] These things concern glory and pride.

But concerning pleasure, hear a brief but true judgment. To eat, drink, sleep, indulge in lust, and turn the wheel of one’s birth through this most unhappy world is not the way of a human being, but of a beast. To be surrounded and confounded by delights and riches—whose whole use, according to a most biting writer, is either in the belly or beneath the belly—is the mark of brutish gluttony, not of the divine likeness. And you, with your leave, having all night gorged yourself on varied dishes, belch your indigestion toward heaven, so that in you one human being may be another’s tomb; and in the human being I see not a human being, but a corpse. A multiplicity of foods casts down the vital organs, weakens the stomach, corrupts the blood, spoils the humours, inflames bile, and finally aggravates the fever’s burning. [Col. 1615D] Thus lust creeps through the flesh, seethes in the veins, enters the bones, lodges in the marrow, burns in the blood, and bursts forth into the madness of vices.

Lust took the prodigal son from his father’s bosom, drove him from home, removed him from his homeland, stripped him of reputation, and made him naked of chastity (Luke XV). It changed a citizen into an exile, a son into a hired servant, a wealthy man into a needy one, and a free man into a slave. You move and are tormented amid these things; and do not consider that whatever vices childhood received, adolescence seized, and youth invaded, at least old age at its end should correct—so that one who lived in crime may even die innocent.

But the letter must now be folded and sealed, lest it come without honour and decorum to an honoured person. Therefore, for the sake of him who for your whole self exposed his whole self to death and torments, consider childhood’s vanities, adolescence’s falls, youth’s ruin, old age’s diseases, and come here to make an end of your end. Nowhere is there a straighter way, nor a holier life in all holiness, than that which the Holy of Holies left on earth. Great affection has forced out a great letter, because, while I imagine myself conversing with you, I have extended my pen into the distance. Write back your intention to me; and send us the letters of the lord of Le Mans—

[Note: [Col. 1615D] He appears to mean Hildebert.]

—for we wish to copy them, and, if it can be done:

> “Write nothing back to me; nevertheless, come yourself.”

## LETTER XVIII. In the person of Brother Gaucherius to a certain knight of the Temple, concerning spiritual friendship.

[Col. 1616B]

GAUCHERIUS to his own knight and Christ’s knight: O brother, may you be enrolled in the heavenly warfare.

Would that I could see you rather than write to you; then God would fulfill my desire upon earth. For I have longed with longing to see your face, but this is far from me and beyond my hope. The boundless expanses of land and the interposed abyss of the vastest sea begrudge me the sweetness of this desired and desirable sight. Moreover, the discipline of soldiers and of Christ’s warfare, to which you have put your hand, binds you; while the penitence of Christ’s poor, which I have vowed and resolved to observe, shuts me in. A great chasm has been fixed between you and me, so that you cannot descend to me nor I ascend to you. Oh, if—what is more possible—my eyes might see some weight of business draw you to us, then I should not be cheated of my desire.

But if our bodies are divided, can our hearts be divided for ever? If distances of place or intervals of time separate the bodily presence, can they cut off the unity and concord of our souls? Far from it! For we do not love one another as men who love each other merely as men, seeking, in flesh and blood, the presence of flesh and blood. Our love descends wholly from purity; it wholly breathes the Spirit, having nothing earthly mingled with it. “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John VI). For what else is flesh than flesh? A frail little body, a worthless slave: the smallest part of me is absent from you. Your good spirit is always within my spirit; it remains with me, perseveres with me, never departs from me. I shall pour forth remembrance of your sweetness as long as I live. I shall never forget you; nor can the malice of time cause you to be snatched from my breast even for an hour. Love of this kind is wholly ignorant of the inconveniences of place and time: for it is always permitted to love, even when it is not permitted to see the one whom one loves.

The charity of Christ renders you present to me though absent; and the farther you have gone away from me, the more ardently you have remained in my inmost being. Far be it that your love should be taken from me by the waves of the sea, when it is written: “Many waters could not quench love, neither shall floods overwhelm it” (Song of Songs VIII). Yet: “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet” (Psalm XLI) see Him—if not on earth, at least in heaven—when we shall see You, Lord Jesus, on the day of Your eternity, in splendour at the right hand of the Father.

Meanwhile, my beloved, I pray for you—if a sinner’s prayer has any power—to Him who “did not scorn nor despise the supplication of the poor.” Besides, “blessed are the eyes which have seen the things that you see.” Every day you walk through the workshops of our redemption and adore in the place where His feet stood. You see where He was born, where He was wearied, where He worked miracles, where He endured death; and with blessed eyes you marvel at the whole course of His journey.

[Col. 1617B] At last, you see the tomb in which the body of Jesus was buried, where the virginal flower of Mary was laid away with linen cloths and spices. From there also rose that first and greatest flower which appeared in our land. There do not let remembrance of your Walter pass you by; but pray to the King of glory that He who gave you to see these things with your eyes may plant them in my mind, and may not remove your prayer or His mercy from me. And behold, Walter my nephew comes to you, to represent me to you both in name and in blood. Do you see him? You see me. Whatever you do to him is done to me. Let him discover in you how much favour I have with you, sweetest and most loving brother.

Furthermore, noble man and beloved of God, that you may know—and not merely know, but also feel—how warmly our love burns toward you, we have sent you two hides from Clairvaux, through a fellow Knight Templar of yours, as a dowry of love. I have also taken care to send this same letter to you by other messengers, so that, if through some chance the absence of one should leave anything lacking to you in this delivery, the presence of another may supply it. Fare well.

## LETTER XIX. In the person of Brother Adam, to the Abbot of Cazé, when he entered the order.

To the lord and most beloved father S., Abbot of Cazé, Brother Adam wishes not to be grieved by whatever may befall him.

A man’s ways are not in his own power; and who has found or known especially the way of a young man? This is that fourth thing which Solomon, singular in wisdom, exalted in glory, abounding in possessions, secure in peace, wholly declares that he does not know (Proverbs XXX). For the fickleness that accompanies youth, the disorder of nature, and the infusion of vices flit through the ways of adolescence by twisting paths, so that one can scarcely recognize whence a young man comes or where he goes.

I have said this in order to prepare the way for the following letter and to open to you my heart, which I had long covered before your face. To what does such a long circuit of words aim, and where does such bold—but not false—speech tend? Hear briefly, lord Father, the affection of my heart, which has impressed your memory upon its breast for ever and unto ages of ages. It is long since I resolved in my heart to enter into my heart, to come to your men of Clairvaux, and to spend the remainder of my days among them and with them. I concealed it, I confess, and wrapped the conceived purpose within my breast, lest, once disclosed, it should quickly slip away.

In this spirit I came to the men of God, and knocked for so long until I obtained entrance; and behold, I am with them as though one of them. May this burnt offering which I have offered from my body and heart to the Lord of majesty please you, lord Father; and may it be according to your good will that you declare your will to your boy, for I am yours, and have been yours, and shall be yours for ever.

## LETTER XXIII. In the person of Prior Rualen, to the Archbishop of Tours, concerning guidance, love, and charity.

To the lord HUGH, worthy of reverence, Archbishop of Tours, Brother R. wishes success in the Lord in both lives.

[Note: [Col. 1617D] This is doubtless Hugh, whose memory occurs in letter 9, book V, of Peter the Venerable.]

Although I write little to you, nevertheless I love you not a little in the inward parts of Christ. You ask how greatly; and, to answer safely and sincerely, I answer: greatly. You add: in what manner? Certainly, as much as my ability permits, faithfully, wisely, and bravely; in charity, because “love is strong as death” (Song of Songs VIII). In these three degrees I judge that both the feeling and the effect of holy love are most fully expressed.

And because he has once begun, I shall still speak to my Lord: may my speech be pleasing to Him. The place which you hold is great and demands great charity from you. Without this, faith is nothing; martyrdom profits nothing. The distribution of possessions has no value at all. I desire this to increase in my lord and father, so that all your things may be done in charity. For united to this and made one through it, you will go securely before our high priest,

[Note: [Col. 1618D] Namely Christ, of whom St Paul says these things in Hebrews IV.]

who has penetrated the heavens.

Moreover, your fatherhood knows well what the Abbot of St Albin has done and is doing concerning the alms of the lord of Magnet, of which you had been appointed guardian. At least he ought to have returned the deposit that I had deposited with him, and then said whatever was to be said. When you have caused this wrong to be amended, you will uphold your own honour, most loving Father.

I commend the lord of Alet to your holiness,

[Note: [Col. 1619D] This is the bishop of Alet, or of St Malo, concerning whom see above, letter 13.]

because whatever you do to him is done to us. This is your glory: to protect and honour a poor bishop who is yours and such a one as he. But I was yours, am yours, and shall be yours, as long as I exist and wherever I can be; it is my will to make your will, together with the will of the Lord, my will.

(See above, letter 51.)

## LETTER XXVI. In the person of Henry, the king’s brother, to Hugh of Compiègne, reproving and drawing him onward.

(See above, col. 1567 of this volume, among the letters of Henry, Archbishop of Reims, brother of King Louis VII.)

## LETTER XXVII. To Odo, Abbot of Poultiers, thanking him for the tunic which he had sent.

To his most beloved father and friend dear to his heart, O., Abbot of Poultiers, Brother N. sends himself to his feet.

The witness both that I love you and that I am loved by you is our long-standing intimacy. For although fortune had placed me in a lowly position and you in a lofty one, love—which, once it is love, unites both king and poor man—had made the two of us one. That love still warmed within your breast when you sent me your gifts. I might indeed have put on your tunic, had it not been the only one. It is too precious and handsome for this soil; it is not good because it is too good, most beloved Father. I neither wish nor am able—indeed, ought not—to put it on among those clothed in little rags and half-girdles; nor shall I walk about purple-clad and tunic-clad.

Far, far be it that a splendid garment should again be fitted to sinful flesh, lest it be carried away into its follies. Therefore [Col. 1619D] I return it to you, since there is no one among us who either would dare or ought to wear it. You put it on, lord Father, since both your order and your dignity permit you to do so. For when you put on the tunic, you do something beyond your customary practice and rule; but you know what He said: “Whatever you spend beyond this, I will repay you when I return.”

Yet I pursue with much thanksgiving both the quality of the gift and the magnitude of the generosity. Indeed, I love the gift returned just as I would have loved it retained, because I look not at the thing given but at the mind of the giver. I certainly, who was previously the servant of your holiness, am so now and was so before. For the change of order has not changed the firmness of friendship, but increased it.

One thing at the end of the letter I beg: pray, and have your sons and our brothers pray, for me; greet them on our behalf, if you judge it fitting. Greet also your Joscelin, and ask him, in the days of his youth, to remember his death before the years come of which he will say: “They do not please me.”

## LETTER XXVIII. To Peter of Celle. An exhortation against evil men and concerning correction.

(See in Peter of Celle, *Patrologia*, vol. CII, letter 52.)

## LETTER XXIX. In the person of Brother Philip. To the Emperor’s Chancellor: an exhortation, advice concerning books, etc.

[Col. 1620B]

To his most beloved lord and friend, the provost of the Church of Cologne and chancellor of the emperor, Brother Philip wishes him to order his affairs well, as his own.

[Note: [Col. 1619D] “Philippi” in the manuscript is incorrect. For up to the year 1200 not one emperor of this name reigned. The more correct reading, therefore, is “Philip”: he, moved by St Bernard’s powerful exhortation, despised the honours of chancellor and canon of Cologne, became a monk of Clairvaux, and shortly afterwards wrote an elegant letter to the canons of Cologne whom he had left; it is found in chapter 9, book VI of the *Miracles of St Bernard*.]

That I may speak to you in the words of the prophet, my beloved: “My soul desired you in the night, and my spirit also within my inward parts” (Isaiah XXVI, 10, 4). I had resolved to be silent and, with the prophet, to set my mouth in the dust, “if perhaps there may be hope” (Lamentations III), if perhaps that merciful gaze of compassion might look upon my humility and my labour. I had proposed these things lest, by speaking too, I should incur the reproach of talkativeness. But I confess that I could no longer command my feeling, so as not at least to communicate my heart to you by the remedy of this present letter.

And if the pen should run on, let one who knows affection spare affection, and ascribe its length to charity. Would that it had been granted me from above to say these things by living voice! For the eyes of the speaker would offer, or create, belief; and living speech would be more effective than writing, the tongue than the letter. I would kiss that head, sweetest and most friendly to me, and hang wholly upon the neck of that man whose remembrance has occupied my breast more widely, penetrated it more deeply, possesses it more firmly, and lives with me. Nor is this surprising, because your good spirit has gone before me in blessings of sweetness and, to tell the truth, emptied itself in kindly gathering up a lowly person, though fortune had placed you at the summit of affairs.

Therefore this alliance is the sweeter because flattery did not extort it, feigned prosperity did not know it, nor did the eminence of fortune’s favour simulate it in another. For when inequality of persons stands out and the superior joins himself to the inferior in every respect, this is surely singular humility; because only very rarely does the greatness of friendship make friends equal amid unequal fortune. Therefore I say to you: you alone are both in the world and of the world whom I have singularly and without limit impressed upon my inmost being.

Come now: it has been heard in our land that you have taken up the banner of the cross, that you have resolved to go to the city of Jerusalem where the virginal flower of Mary was laid away with linen cloths and spices, and whence rose that first and greatest flower which appeared in our land. There is neither time nor need for you to display your wisdom; rather, order your household in a manner fitting both to the honour of your person and to your soul’s salvation for ever and unto ages of ages.

Because you belong to the Lord’s portion and are of that portion, you have no wife; your brother has no children; your sister has no husband; the whole household has lost hope of offspring. I judge that this happened so that barrenness of flesh might be changed into profit for the soul, and that you might know it is happier to be fruitful in spirit than in flesh, and more glorious to give birth for heaven than for the tomb. Therefore, since the names of all family ties have been removed, who ought to be made heir except Him who gave all things, who made you when you did not exist, who redeemed you when you were lost, who calls you into His service, and who—the Lord Jesus Christ—is able to restore you on that day?

But also your singular and noble treasure—your library, I mean—which you have gathered as wonderfully as incomparably: see that you leave it to Christ’s poor, so that they may pray and weep for you, that the God of our salvation may make your journey prosperous. When you have visited them with your blessings, lift up your eyes toward this house in which I dwell; and if not for its sake, at least for mine, your servant’s. And, to speak in your ear, there is no place more ordered, no people more lovable, no life holier in all holiness, than that which the Holy of Holies left on earth.

But though you are far from me in presence, you are wholly with me in memory, because I am yours and shall be yours as long as I exist. I shall see you continually in my heart, because those who behold each other with their souls rather than their eyes are more present; and to be bound together in heart is more than to be bound in body. But that your remembrance may be set before my bodily eyes also, send me something suitable for a monk. Greet the lord king for me as well. Though perhaps he has forgotten me because of great affairs, I nevertheless shall not forget him for ever.

## LETTER XXX. In the person of the lord of Clairvaux, to the Emperor of Constantinople, that he may make a new knight.

(It is letter 468 of St Bernard. See *Patrologia*, [Col. 1621D] vol. CLXXXII.)

## LETTER XXXI. In the person of Brother Walter, to W., his brother: an exhortation to contempt of the world.

[Note: [Col. 1621D] That this Walter is the very man mentioned in chapter 11, book I, of the *Life of St Bernard* will be quite clear to the reader.]

To his most beloved brother WALTER, his brother W. wishes him to enter the way of truth and not depart from it.

Though I am removed from you by a great distance of land and the intervening difficulty of the sea, yet in memory I am beside you, and I do not cease to pray for you to Him who did not scorn nor despise the supplication of the poor. For, though I am at Clairvaux, I have not cast off or abandoned human affections; rather I hear the Apostle of God—indeed, the Lord preaching in the Apostle: “If anyone does not provide for his own, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Timothy X). Therefore I have impressed the memorial of your name more closely upon my inmost being, knowing that all your things are mine and that you are mine, sweetest brother.

I shall neither trust nor have trusted the servant of my brother.

[Note: [Col. 1621D] That is, a boy or servant. I have again observed this word in ancient Cistercian constitutions. It appears to have been formed from the Spanish word *garzone*.]

I had long known of my brother’s death and had caused prayers to be made for him, and shall still do so. You write that our brother Achetimus has taken a wife; but would that you had written that, for my love’s sake, you had granted him his land for a third year, as you had done for two years. If I have found favour in your eyes, let it still be granted for a third year through my intercession.

But that you have resolved, under the lord king of Scotland,

[Note: [Col. 1622D] Namely Henry, whom William of Newburgh commends at length in book I of his *History of English Affairs*, entire chapter 23.]

under whom virtue does not lack reward and vice does not lack punishment, to go to Jerusalem, pleases my soul. For this is to fight the good fight: to visit and defend the workshops of our redemption against those who have raised their head against the King of glory. I know that the earth has been moved and trembled at the sound of this report, and that kings, princes, and the peoples of the earth fly forth in rivalry in order to proclaim in Zion the Lord’s name and His praise in Jerusalem. And I do not wish it to be said to you: “Are you the only stranger, and do you not know what has happened in Jerusalem in these days?”

[Note: [Col. 1622D] This is the answer of the apostles to Christ, who appeared in the guise of a traveller.]  
(Luke XXIV).

Yet it would be better and safer for you to leave the whole world, because “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity”; and this is the singular counsel of salvation: to be in the council and congregation of the righteous. But if the Spirit of God has touched you so that you resolve to go there in any case, order your household, and do so in a manner befitting your valour and pleasing to my soul.

Cause the land which the lord king gave you to be confirmed by the royal seal and by the assent of his son before witnesses. When this has been done, cause both it and the remainder to be confirmed to your brother, if I have any power in your heart, if remembrance of my name touches you. For who will preserve it for you better and more faithfully? And if you should die—which God avert—

[Note: [Col. 1622D] Here a word, “no one,” seems to be missing.]

who would succeed more justly than brother to brother? For it is better that your brother should inherit your land than that the son of a foreigner should be brought into it, he who has joined himself to our family through our sister. Behold, you have my heart; hear my counsel, and heed me, if you are my brother and wish me to be your brother for ever.

## LETTER XXXII. In the person of Brother Franco, to the companions who remained behind: an exhortation to flee the world.

To his most beloved companions, their most beloved [Col. 1623A] companion Franco wishes them swiftly to flee from the wrath to come, because the time is short.

Though I have departed from you in body, I have nevertheless remained with you in heart—or rather, you have remained with me in the inward parts of Jesus Christ. The sweet memory of you does not at all leave me. But the sweeter the memory, the more burdensome would be absence, unless He were the cause, to whom all things are fitting, and to whom we have proposed, by a blessed necessity, both to live and to die.

What are you doing, you who see and understand that “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes I), that “every man is vainly troubled” (Psalm XXXVIII)? Days and days, years and years pass away; the world hastens with unretardable course toward its end. Yet the sons of men do not cease from acquiring whatever they see that can fall away; and, according to the Prophet, “there is no end of their possessions.” What end shall there be for those who behold all things without end?

The world rages, the body presses, the soul trembles, death follows you, life flees, the enemy presses from behind; near is the Judge, who stood beneath judgment so that He might render to each according to his works. Amid all these things you doze and sleep, though it is most true and incontestable that nothing is more certain to mortals than death, nothing more uncertain than the hour of death; and, according to Solomon, “What has a man more from all his labour which he labours under the sun?” (Ecclesiastes I). Death, coming after, cuts down everything and convicts the past of vanity and error.

Therefore, for the sake of Him who chose to rejoice from heaven in order to bring you back to heaven, flee from the furnace of Egypt and come into the land of promise, where we, your friends and brothers, have already gone before you; for there is no way more direct, no way holier, most beloved brothers.

## LETTER XXXIII. To Philip, Archdeacon of Liège, recalling friendship and urging him toward religious life.

To his old and familiar lord and friend PHILIP, Archdeacon of Liège, Brother NICOLAS wishes him to serve Him whom to serve is to reign.

Perhaps you wonder who it is that writes to you. But do not wonder at this, because he is your servant; and, if you judge him worthy, your friend. This is he who crossed and passed with you mountains made slippery with ice or rough with rocks,

[Note: [Col. 1623D] Here it is necessary to read *transcendit*, “crossed over,” or something similar, in order to remove the superfluity of repetition.]

who was with you in Rome both in heart and body, and kept watch with you in the Tiburtine hills. Let this alone serve as a reminder and recollection of our former alliance: not because of the places themselves, but because of the friendship which we formed in those places, are they remembered.

For what are all these things but vanity of vanities, and all vanity? Where is the numerous army and that military youth adorned with triumphal ornaments? Where, finally, is that lofty and mighty man upon the throne of his glory, at whose nod senate and people—and clergy as well—stood more quickly than his nod? All these things have passed like a shadow, and that singular splendour has vanished like smoke. Yet your love has fixed an everlasting dwelling in my breast; and from that day your memory has penetrated my breast more deeply, occupied it more widely, possessed it more firmly, and lived with me.

Until now I had restrained my pen, considered the matter silently, and, like a deaf man, did not hear the voices of those murmuring; like a mute man, I did not open my mouth. Some said: “The time of his coming is near, and his days will not be prolonged.” Others, however: “How long does he hold our soul in suspense and not more swiftly and earnestly break everything off—he who is desired and desirable?” I was of little faith and did not believe those who brought and reported this saying, fearing the pleasures and riches amid which you had been continually preserved from the flower of youth itself.

Yet, considering the riches of the Lord’s mercies, I repeated most often: “Who knows whether God will turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind Him?” (Joel XI). While the weakness and faint-heartedness of your friend thus wavered and changed, behold, suddenly there came a messenger full of hope—which does not confound—who said that your surrender had been solemnly made and that you were now not only coming, but also faithfully and effectually gathering those who were to come with you. I confess: I cannot contain myself for joy, and I hang suspended between preparation and expectation, until I hold you and will not let you go, unless I bring you into the house of my mother and into the chamber of her who bore me, and until you rejoice at the voice of bridegroom and bride all the days of your life.

Will it truly be, Lord Jesus, that You conceal in Your tabernacle, in the day of evils, a man of such noble blood and such usefulness—and not merely in the tabernacle, but in the secret place of Your tabernacle? How gladly will that great eye of providence see so great and such a vessel stolen from the Egyptians and set apart among the Lord’s offerings! Therefore let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult; let the glory of this celebrated and yet-to-be-celebrated conversion be spread to the ends of the earth, because Philip has descended to the poverty of Christ’s poor, and their honourable name is before him.

Come therefore, lord, and do not delay. For if you trust business, business will never come to an end. “No one swims out with baggage,” says that secular orator.

[Note: [Col. 1624D] Seneca, letter 21.]

This most welcome arrival will be swift, restoring you to conscience and us to joy. And because true love trembles in fear even where there is no fear, give attention for a little while to what I say, since I say it for your sake. Do not think that I seek the flowers of rhetoric; rather receive a concentrated affection, cautiously marked.

According to the word of the wise, in the field of a repentant mind you have conceived the spirit: a truly delicate conception, easily shaken out before birth. There are a thousand poisons of demons; when these are introduced, the seed of God’s word either will not be formed or will be deformed. For the flesh breathes most tenderly, and frequently urges the spirit that has gone out from Sodom to look back; nor does it despair of victory, since we all know how easily it flies back toward the alluring pleasure of the senses, and the flesh’s effort toward sin is more effective than the spirit’s toward virtue.

But you must go forward bravely with a brave spirit, and not care if the itch of pleasures mutters behind you.

[Note: [Col. 1625D] In the exemplar, *inusitet*; we have restored *mussitet*, “mutters.” For itching flesh does not dare to address a heavenly soul in a raised voice concerning filth; rather, with frequent muttering it tries to insinuate and awaken the mind’s inclination, as I have noted. The same wording occurs in Hildebert of Le Mans, letter 41, writing to them; indeed, more plainly: “If, while you begin to flee, the itch of pleasures should mutter, as it were, behind your back,” etc.]

Rather, as Augustine recalls concerning himself, shake off your garment of flesh. Nor will there be lacking those who say to you, “Well done, well done,” who urge you to postpone your holy resolve until colder years, and remove from your eyes the truth that the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night. They will say: “What have you to do with this life, which you ought rather to avoid than invite yourself to? What are you dreaming? Can tender limbs, reared amid refined luxuries, endure a long martyrdom? Begin—but begin in a way that you will not regret beginning. No one ever regrets too late whom death finds repenting. When, at the end of life, the thief obtained paradise, he left an example.”

If you listen to these Sirens, sweet even to the end, you will be drawn farther into the whirlpool of pleasures. There will also be present that fraudulent wrestler—one from whom no one has ever extracted a truce from doing harm—under whom falling is frequent and recovery difficult, and victory rare and never secure; and he will say to you: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.”

[Note: [Col. 1625D] These are the words of that same wrestler tempting Christ: Matthew IV.]

But since you have a most watchful eye, do you not see how great is the world’s madness? The matter would go on without end if, according to the wise man, I wished to enumerate the perils of princes; the complaints of troubled marriage; a thousand grieving Menedemuses; sons given to debauchery; wealth wickedly amassed or shamefully squandered; possessions claimed by arms, expended on debauchery, seized by fraud, transferred by legal prejudice, and—than which nothing is held more contemptible in this age—acquired at the loss of a good name and of honour.

Therefore, from the Church and with him

[Note: [Col. 1625D] Namely St Philip. These are the words of the Holy Spirit exhorting St Philip to join the chariot of Candace’s Ethiopian and unbelieving servant, who was reading the prophet Isaiah; see the narrative again in Acts VIII. The passage is not ill suited to this purpose in sermon I of St Bernard, *On the Dedication of the Church*, not far from the beginning.]

whose name you bear, join yourself to this chariot. Here are thousands rejoicing, and the Lord is among them. For this place was made by God; it is the place which the Lord chose from all places of the earth, that His name might be there. And wretched sons of Adam, if they do not end their end here! Finally, an infinite multitude of weak, noble, refined, and learned persons perseveres with us—persons also formed from the same clay. I have exceeded, I confess, the measure of a letter; but abundant affection has driven my running pen. Come then, my beloved: come by beginning; come by advancing; you will come and pass through by being made perfect, unto the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even unto the house of God.

## LETTER XXXIV. To Amadeus, Bishop of Lausanne: affectionate and laudatory.

[Col. 1625D]

Brother NICOLAS sends himself to the feet of his father.

It would be great presumption, if there were not great love, for me to presume to write to your eminence. For affection draws me: it neither obeys laws nor can kings command it. I do not know how, but from the moment I saw you, your love poured itself abundantly into the inner chambers of my soul. Nor was there any delay between sight and affection, though I had speech with you later.

Therefore, if I write confidently, it is because I love faithfully: as though, if I am bold, I am not false. Love does not know a lord; it recognizes a friend. Though you wear the mitre, it is ignorant of rank; rich in condescension, powerful in affection, effective in persuasion, and clear-sighted in purity. What then if you have ascended on high, my lord—indeed, rather, my beloved? Even above the wings of the winds you will not withdraw yourself from my affection; and if you ascend to heaven, I shall follow wherever you go.

For I do not love the bishop, but the man who has bestowed zeal for the law upon the chair, not received it from the chair. “What,” they ask, “is that vigour, that quickness of spirit, which by the leap of its subtlety breaks through every obstacle, and which can philosophize concerning each of the arts even with each of its practitioners?” Therefore that liberality of your mortal nature stands out above the rest, which, according to the orator, shows itself gentle to boys, gracious to young men, serious to old men, strengthening all, adapting itself to all—common in speech, equal in companionship, outstanding in counsel, and greatly to be sought because least of all ambitious.

For I have seen you noble without pride, powerful without envy, devout without superstition, learned without boasting, serious without foolishness, witty without affectation, steadfast without harshness, and accessible without indiscriminate familiarity. I marvel at this: that in the midst of eminent learning you possess a still higher conscience. Such does my spirit believe you; such does my affection describe you, ever whispering to me the spirit of your sweetness.

I send you a well-punctuated and, unless I am mistaken, corrected book of Master Anselm concerning the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1626D] Namely St Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, whose work entitled *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* is still read by learned men today. He is, I say, the very same person mentioned in letters 21 and 22 and by Hildebert of Le Mans, in order that I may remove a scruple introduced by a scholium appended to the same. For in book III of the manuscript letters of this same St Anselm I expressly read the names both of the writers and of the person to whom he wrote.]

I, I say, who am yours and shall be yours as long as I exist, most loving Father.

## LETTER XXXV. To Walter, a noble and discerning man: an exhortation to religious life, commending Clairvaux.

[Note: [Col. 1626D] Letter 31 was written in the name of another Walter; this one, however, in his own name.]

To Brother Walter, Brother NICOLAS wishes him to tend thither where life is.

I received your letter as gladly as I had eagerly desired it. When, through a faithful messenger, it came into my hands, I freed myself at once from every occupation and distraction; scarcely trusting myself to myself, I set to it.

I have a little writing-room in my Clairvaux.

[Note: Here he begins a description of the cenobitic life of Clairvaux and continues it to the end of the letter.]

It is surrounded on every side by heavenly workshops, which conceal it. Its door opens into the cell of the novices, where a numerous company, both noble and learned, bring forth the new man in newness of life; by their groans bending heaven, by their tears inclining the angels, and not ceasing until, by the vehemence of prayer, they fly beyond cherubim and seraphim and are caught up before the merciful eyes of the most sweet Lord.

On the right rises the cloister of the monks, where that more flourishing community walks about: they have advanced and failed away into the courts of the Lord with happy security, or secure happiness, toward something better and more joyful. There, under the most rigorous discipline, they open one by one the books of the divine utterances, not to display the treasures of their learning, but to draw forth love, compunction, and devotion.

On the left stands out the house and walking-place of the sick, where bodies worn down and spent by regular discipline are restored with more generous food, until, healed or improved, they fly back to the flock of labourers and pray-ers, who do violence to the kingdom of heaven and seize it by force. Nor should you despise my little dwelling: it is desirable to affection, delightful to sight, and suited to retirement. It is full of most choice and divine books. In their pleasant inspection I recognize contempt for this worldly vanity, considering that “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” and that nothing is vainer than vanity. This place has been entrusted to me for reading, writing, dictating, meditating, praying, and worshipping the Lord of majesty.

Here, often oppressed by the burden of an unhappy conscience, I alone enter the solitude of my heart. Reason is my judge, conscience my witness.

[Note: He seems to have had in view Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria*, V.11: “Conscience [is worth] a thousand witnesses.”]

Fear is my executioner; and I set myself before my own face, lest that terrible Majesty set me before his face, into whose hands it is dreadful to fall. Here I opened your letter; with swiftly passing eyes I read it eagerly, read it again more eagerly, and now read it most eagerly. Its whole texture was manly, surpassing the powers of your talent—of that talent, I mean, which I had left behind.
