In it were, as the most eloquent man says, rhetorical divisions, oratorical jewels, and flourishing periods, working not boyishly but manfully.

I do not say this as though such things ought to occupy my heart, or do occupy it. Though they are not wholly forgotten, they have nevertheless been entirely abandoned. But because I love you, I also love in you the fact that you love letters. For it is some part of uprightness to know the better things, and he is near to goodness who loves the ornaments of learning.

When, then, I had read your letter more attentively and intently, I thought of the ancient days between us, according to the world and the things of the world, when two souls and one mind had stirred us; and I said: “Ah, ah, Lord God! You have deceived me, Lord, and I have been deceived; you were stronger than I and prevailed. You have received one part of my soul into heaven, and have left another part in the mire. I am without him without whom nevertheless I cannot be. Shall my life thus fail in sorrow, and my years in groanings? If I have found favour in your eyes, restore him to himself—indeed, to yourself—and thereby to me: you who forgive sins, grant merits, and restore rewards, Lord my God. Restore Robert, restore Lecelinus, restore Walter.”

[Note: Letters 16, 31, and 32 testify that he was held by a remarkable longing for him.]

“And if I am not heard concerning two, let me at least be heard concerning the third. Spare me, that I may be refreshed before I depart,” and see half my soul living according to your will among my men of Clairvaux—among, indeed, the young maidens with timbrels: maidens who loved God exceedingly, timbrel-players who crucified their flesh with its vices and desires. I shall not cease from prayers, O Lord of hosts, until you rise after the pattern of the Gospel giver.”

[Note: The manuscript wrongly has *Evangelii*, “of the Gospel.” He calls “evangelical giver” the one who gave three loaves to his friend asking by night, overcome by the man’s importunity.]

“If not because of friendship, then at least because of importunity.”

When I had turned over the words of your letter in summary, and again examined them one by one, I rejoiced. Yet a fuller sorrow buried that joy. For I conjectured that you were running ever more eagerly and cheerfully after false vanities and madnesses, and that you had returned not even one little word in reply to what I had proposed to you concerning Clairvaux (*reposuisse*; alternatively *respondisse*, “replied”).

I know that you are lovable, approachable, and tractable, and that you fear and somewhat reverence the eyes of the Judge who sees all things. Yet destroyers are with you—or rather, you have begun to be with destroyers: I mean those two, foxes in cunning, lions in pride, bulls for arrogance—indeed bulls for consuming. Are they not the very men whom, in Sidonius’s phrase, this province is especially destined to bring accusations, report persons, issue threats, and seize property? Following their counsels, you would become bloodier than Phalaris, greedier than Midas, more boastful than Ancus, prouder than Tarquinius, more cunning than Tiberius, more dangerous than Gaius, duller than Claudius, more impure than Nero, greedier than Galba, more extravagant than Vitellius, and more savage than Domitian.

[Note: Observe his cruelty from the brazen bull, concerning which see Valerius Maximus, IX.2; Seneca, *On Benefits*, VII.19, incidentally; *On Anger*, II.4; and *On Clemency*, XI.4.]

[Note: Re-read Erasmus, *Proverbs*: “The riches of Midas,” chiliad 1, centuria 6, proverb 8.]

[Note: Thus Virgil, *Aeneid*, VI.]

[Note: On account of his contemptuous pride; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, I.53, first decade.]

[Note: He seems especially to refer to chapter 59 of Suetonius.]

[Note: He calls him more dangerous on account of the various perils of war to which he exposed himself.]

[Note: His avarice will be seen in chapter 12.]

[Note: Suetonius, chapter 13, and Eutropius afterwards, book VII, describe it.]

[Note: His savagery is most familiar from ecclesiastical histories, martyrologies, and Suetonius, chapters 10 and 21.]

My son, do not walk with them. They will rub their own rust upon you and entangle you in many pains and labours, from which you will not be able to escape even when you wish to do so, once you feel yourself oppressed. Yet what are they to me? They stand or fall to their own master. I have said this not to press you, but to warn you, lest they perhaps turn you aside or pervert you if you imbibe their manners. For I know that it belongs to folly to see the vices of others and forget one’s own.

[Note: “It is folly to perceive others’ faults and despise one’s own.”]

Now the speech must be turned back toward you. Allow me briefly to touch your heart—indeed, my own—if it is true, as your letter says, that we are one, and that you are my soul. You are young—certainly a youth of few years, but of many sins and no merits. You have not yet completed repentance; indeed, you have not even begun it. Nor does my watchfulness deceive me. Do you ask how I know this? Because that place is assuredly a place not of repentance but of pestilence, where, when they have made one proselyte, they make him twice as much a son of Gehenna as themselves. There is no room for evasion: “I know them both inside and under the skin.” They are whitewashed tombs, inwardly full of dead men’s bones.

[Note: He turns to his own purpose the severe satirical saying of Christ against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, Anath. 24.]

I pass over what lies hidden within, because I am ashamed to say it and it does not become you to hear it. I come to what is manifest. If, in the phrase of a biting writer, you have breathed upon the noses of those two—who are rightly two because divided from unity—with the rusty air of a purse, will you not immediately see there the eyes of Argus, the hands of Briareus, the claws of sphinxes, the cunning of Ulysses, the deceits of Sinon, the perjuries of Laomedon, the faith of Polymnestor, and the piety of Pygmalion employed?

[Note: The manuscript has *aurae*, “of air”; someone, I do not know who, wrote *anima*, “soul,” in the margin. But the following word, *afflaveris*, “you have breathed upon,” sufficiently shows that *aura*, “air,” must be restored.]

[Note: Although the matter did not require it, he had necessarily to put “hands” in the plural. Briareus was hundred-handed; see Phornutus, *On the Nature of the Gods*, in the *Speculator*. St Gregory Nazianzen used it in the same sense in his funeral oration for his father: “And seeing others too, laying Briareus’ hands upon public property.”]

[Note: *Sphingarum*; more correctly *Sphingum*, after Mela, III.10, Pliny, and others.]

[Note: The cunning of Ulysses. Re-read the proverb, “a device worthy of Ulysses.”]

[Note: Simon, or Sinon, that crafty man by whose agency the Trojans destroyed their walls in order to bring the wooden horse into their city; Virgil treats this in *Aeneid* II.]

[Note: The perjuries of Laomedon are enumerated by Hyginus, fable 89.]

[Note: The faith—rather the treachery—of Polymnestor, described by Hyginus, fable 109.]

[Note: “The piety of Pygmalion” is plainly said ironically, as appears from *Aeneid* I: “Pygmalion, more savage in wickedness than all others.”]

Perhaps you answer: “I shall allot joy to youth and repentance to old age, when the blood has cooled and the very strong, very hot fire of youthful marrow has departed.” My beloved, death does not preserve this order: it compels both young and old to depart, enfolding alike the lowly and exalted head. Nothing is more certain to mortals than death; nothing more uncertain than the hour of death. Dearest young man, the sum of our happiness must not be placed in the flesh. Honour is cheap to him whose body is too dear. For he does not live whose mind has no thought except how he may live.

[Note: “He does not live whose sole concern is that he may live.”]

We see nothing new; and the man of this age grows nauseated. Spring presses upon winter, summer upon spring, autumn upon summer, and all things are carried round in a circle. We eat, drink, and sleep; and, what is more miserable than all miseries, we both choose and love our miseries, shut up within the horrible, foul prison of the body.

[Note: The manuscript wrongly reads *fetulenti*.]

Therefore, for the sake of him who made you, redeemed you, and called you into his marvellous light, come here to bring your end to its end. And if not for your own sake, then at least for mine, for I spend anxious days and troubled nights through love and fear for you. Let the death of your Iterius be for you an argument and a seasoning: bitter death cut him down and killed him in the very flower of his age and learning. Whatever others suffer, you too can suffer, for you were formed from the same clay. Nothing can be burdensome to you if you remember what he drank at the gibbet, he who invites us to heaven. If you follow his example, you will also attain the kingdom—the kingdom of all ages.

Is not that Henry too—the king’s son and the king’s brother—with us, as though one of us? He is singular in birth, exalted in glory, abundant in possessions, secure in peace, noble according to the flesh, powerful according to the world, learned beyond his age; fortune and nature alike had sworn themselves to his service. Yet all that royal splendour has swelled down into the deepest humility, so that he may be an example even to those whom we ourselves have received as examples.

[Note: He was son of Louis the Fat, king of the Franks.]

[Note: And brother of Louis VII, likewise king, as again in Letter 39.]

Write back to me, above all, your intention; and I believe you will speak truly, since from boyhood it has been natural to you not to wish to lie. Yet if you do not come, do not therefore think that I can be turned or diverted from loving you. The friendship once begun and received I shall retain, even until death and after death, in the bowels of Jesus Christ. From this source, whatever I possess, whatever I am, whatever I can do, is yours—provided only that your will agrees with the Lord’s will.

Now let this overlong page teach you that, although I have not lost the image of a dictator, I have lost the truth of discourse. Cicero, king of orators and prince of Roman eloquence, maintains that the chief excellence of speech is that which contains much in few words and aims rather to accomplish the case than fill the page. But your love greatly adds to this fault: I begin dictating to you while occupied, and reluctantly lay it down, because by this remedy at least I wish to communicate my heart to you. For the absences of friends would be intolerable if letters did not intervene as a means between them.

But now the letter must be folded and entrusted to wax, so that paper may at least set a limit to my talkativeness where modesty could not. When it is opened by your fingers and examined by your eyes, pray to the Lord who made us, that he may not impute to us what we ourselves have done; but that, when uncleanness has perished, he may truly be called pure. May the Pure One show us himself in the form of God, on the day of his power, amid the splendours of the saints; and may he be the end of this letter whom it is the end to behold.

## LETTER XXXVI. To the clerics of Périgueux, written in the person of Brother Alquerius; an exhortation toward the order of Clairvaux

Brother ALQUERIUS to his beloved clerics of Périgueux: May you live the life by which one lives in heaven.

I write to you from a far country, though you are not far from my heart. For charity, which in the sanctuary of love both loves a friend in God and gathers an enemy for God’s sake, does not permit you to be absent from me even for an hour. It is easy for charity to do this, since it makes earth and heaven one commonwealth. In it, with it, and for it, I boldly venture to approach you—for your sakes, because I am concerned for your souls.

You see that, in the words of the Wise Man, there is nothing beneath the sun but labour, pain, and affliction of spirit; and that whatever exists in this time or in this body hastens in an unretardable course to its end. “The end is coming, the end is coming,” most beloved, upon the children of men who have not known the Son of Man, who would not have him reign over them. Rather, lust has reigned in them, worldly glory, the pride of the devil, and every material of vices: children of Adam, children of Eve, children of wrath, children of Gehenna, children of the world, children of the devil, children of death, children of captivity. Why do you love vanity and neglect truth, forgetting that man is born in sorrow, lives in labour, and dies in pain?

“Concerning the rich,” Scripture says, “they spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment descend into hell” (Job 21). O harsh descent, not to be endured—indeed, a descent that must always be endured; or rather a precipice, so that one descends in such a way as never to rise there. How? “Like sheep they are placed in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Psalm 48). How aptly, “like sheep”: for, stripped severely and closely of the fleece of worldly riches, they are wrapped in everlasting fires. Death shall feed upon them—and truly feed upon them—for they will live forever in order to die forever, and die forever in order to live forever.

Happy, therefore, Lord Jesus, are those who serve you. To serve you is to reign, because here they will possess security in conscience, and there happiness in glory. You alone are accustomed both to strengthen your friends here upon the way and to comfort them there in their homeland: here consolation, there reward; here [lacuna], there glorious and making others glorious.

What, then, are you doing, most dear ones? Why do you not come to this house, where the children of Israel, in the battle-array of watchful soldiery, cross that Jordan with unharmed and tireless foot, already seeing, though from afar, the holy city Jerusalem and worshipping the riches of the heavenly palace? This religious life is not like the religious communities in your land. For they are secular and joined to secular people, and have brought the name of religion into contempt and reproach. But our people have utterly rejected and cast out the world and the things of the world from their thoughts and deeds.

For this reason this glorious fellowship is gathered and is being gathered in the name of the Trinity into a threefold order: novices, monks, and lay brothers (*conversi*). The novices are those being tested; the monks, those approved; the lay brothers (*conversi*), those who work, so that Christ’s poor—or rather Christ in the poor—may be supported. This is the house in which the Saviour is diligently received: where Martha ministers, Mary gives herself to contemplation, and Lazarus is raised again. Understand Martha as the labouring lay brothers (*conversi*), Mary as the contemplating monks, Lazarus as the weeping novices, who have recently been raised from the dead.

It is not safe for you to have care of souls and yet not care for souls; to live from Christ’s patrimony and not serve Christ. “The days of man upon earth are short” (Job 14), and nothing is more unworthy than to lose the torrent of delight for a brief pleasure. Come, therefore, most loving brothers; enter the holy tabernacle, and fly from this place to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God. Know, however, that there is no easier crossing into the city of God, nor any shorter. May the Lord of hosts give the word of power and grant you to do his will for your own benefit, with a good heart and a willing spirit.

## LETTER XXXVII. In the person of the abbot of Clairvaux, to Bishop Lucanus; an exhortation to courage and justice

[Note: He appears to be the same man whom St Bernard mentions in Letter 368 of the final edition.]

(This is Letter 469 of St Bernard. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXX.)

## LETTER XXXVIII. To his companion Lecelinus, who delayed greatly; reproving and drawing him onward

Brother NICOLAUS to Brother LECELINUS: Walk not in frivolity but in the truth of the Spirit.

“Love is strong as death; jealousy hard as hell” (Song of Songs 8)—the jealousy with which I am jealous for you. For I am jealous with God’s jealousy. I had resolved neither to see you, nor speak with you, nor even write to you. I could have sent you the title and name of “deceiver”—not to say “traitor”—and have suggested or pressed upon you with my whole voice that saying of the Wise Man: “He who reveals a friend’s secrets loses trust” (Ecclesiasticus 27).

I had indeed composed a letter in secret, yet reproaching you for secret matters, setting you before your own face, so that you might know what you lacked, what you possessed, and what would profit you. I confess that I spoke boldly, as securely with you as with myself, believing that we were one heart and one soul. My evidence was our old familiar intercourse and the greatness—or multitude—of benefits by which I had anticipated you in all your needs, throughout all the days of your life among us and with us. As a mother loves her only son, so I loved you. You clung to my side, you pleased my heart: you were both my brother and my son; and, if you think it worthy to remember, my disciple—rather, my fellow-disciple—under that master whose school is on earth and whose chair is in heaven.

Hence it came that the small amount of learning which I had poured into my own soul I poured back into yours, paying too little attention to what I was doing, in order to satisfy you. For you had led—or led back—me so far into philosophical vanities that, unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell. And, to state the whole matter once more in brief summary: while I was still with you, as one of you, I had no one so wholly of one mind with me.

What evil, then, had I deserved from you, that you should show those little letters to the abbot or to the abbot’s associates? They seek my soul in order to take it away; to them even the memory of my name is more grievous than death. Because I have been zealous for the God of Israel, they call zeal deceit, conscience arrogance, truth iniquity. If I am silent, their deeds will not be silent; rather, what one from the workshop of the satirists proclaims will come to pass:

> Let men be silent; the beasts are speaking.

And what did you write to the abbot of the German island?

[Note: That the abbot of the German island is the same as the abbot of Celles, see the note to Letter 20.]

That man too neither keeps the order nor is kept by the order; his office is not a sacrifice but a butchery. That instigator of evils, that distorter of laws—what did he extort from you? You gave him a pledge against faith: that you would remain in your treachery and not render to God the vows which your lips had uttered. Your soul has attached itself, surely, to a singular teacher and incomparable master, because he has spent and completed all his actions upon the death of the poor and the plunder of widows. In this he busies and torments himself: to do violence to the cause of the humble among God’s people.

Concerning the letters which you made public, set beside them, briefly, my own conjecture. Whether it has anything certain, I leave to your judgment. You did this either willingly or unwillingly. If willingly, why do we still need witnesses? But if unwillingly, how could that be, when those men neither wish, nor can, nor dare offend your eyes even in the slightest thing? For they fear what perhaps may someday happen: that you may depart from them and come to these men, leave the shadow and hold the truth. Will not God therefore require these things?

Although you hide this in your heart, you know nevertheless that I should collide these reasons against one another and consider what might be fixed or inflicted upon your judgment. Yet I abandon and forgive all this, treating what has been done as though it had not been done—provided only that it is not repeated. For if it were repeated, I would not say that I should withdraw friendship, but I would withdraw intimacy from friendship; and that without hope of recovery. When you remember yourself, have pity upon your youth and your brightness, by which you followed me, although you did not attain me.

But Gerard, mine—indeed yours—who took much delight in you, has not only encouraged me toward pardon but armed me for favour, so that I am ready to help and meet you, according to the prophet, “with bread for the fugitive” (Isaiah 21). For now a more joyful and burning prayer will go forth, descending from the furnace of love.

[Note: This is the Gerard to whom he writes Letter 1, and in whose person he writes Letters 11 and 21.]

Why, then, does my beloved delay in finding his way? Why does he not sooner and more anxiously break through everything in order to follow him who is above all, running not with stealthy step but with swiftest course, with the giant who rejoices to run his way? I know where you live, where the seat is of him who does not sit upon the throne. “From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no health in it” (Isaiah 1). That one good and righteous man alone did not consent to their counsel and deeds. I mean Isembard, who himself also awaits the kingdom of God.

As for the rest, run through them all, run through each one, and see whether they do not all seek their own things, not those of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 13). What have you to do with them—you who are learned and have been anticipated by the Father of spirits with blessings of sweetness, and to whom, unless I am mistaken, both the world and the things of the world have become worthless in heart and body? To be holy with the holy is a great happiness; to be good among the evil is a supreme difficulty. And, to state it briefly: whatever burns you or can burn you, hear your friend.

Do you hesitate about your profession? This alone is to be doubted: you vowed what you have not fulfilled. You must seek where you may fulfil it, because, as the lawgiver says, everywhere one God is served and one king is fought for. Do you await reform of the monastery? But the multitude of the wicked has gained strength and prevailed, and the last day is not known to you. Do your parents detain you, whose crowd flies around and besieges you? Yet you are commanded to disregard your father’s burial (Matthew 8). Do you fear scandal? Better that scandal arise than that truth be abandoned. Do you think God unwilling to forgive sins? Yet he nailed them to his cross with his hands. Are you afraid because you are tender and delicate? Yet he himself knew your frame. Are you bound by the habit of sinning? Yet “the Lord releases those in bonds” (Psalm 145). Are your sins many? Yet where sin abounded, grace is accustomed to abound beyond measure. Are you anxious about food, drink, and clothing? Yet your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things (Luke 9). Do you wait until old age and decrepitude? Yet nothing is more certain than death, nothing more uncertain than the hour of death. Do you fear that you will come among strangers? Yet we are all one in Christ. In me too you have found the names of every kind of kinship, and now you will find them much more fully. Why, then, do you doubt, you of little faith? (Matthew 14.) The excuse of evasions has been taken away; there is nowhere for you to turn.

“But,” you say, “you have forgotten still.” For some of ours, who returned to us from you, frightened me. They ought not to move you as much as I ought to move you, I whom the Spirit of truth has retained; whom you saw surrounded by delights and riches, reared in such softness as both I know and you do not ignore. I have refrained from saying anything about those whom you know to have given their tender marrow a first draught of that which endured in their bones as a habit:

> Whatever fresh vessel once has been steeped in will long retain the scent.  
> —Horace, *Epistles*, I.11

You see that inveterate man, how he has returned to his vomit, carrying the tablets of his testament upon his head so that he may seal and bruise orphans and widows, not knowing that he will be driven from the presence of the Father of orphans and Judge of widows. But the other always had a bovine understanding. Do you think he can change the skin of his redness? It is not much, for when he came to you he did not strip it off; rather, he clothed an ass in a lion’s skin. Now, the royal skin having been stripped away, he has returned to the sluggishness innate and familiar to him.

Pass over, then, my beloved. Nothing will be difficult for you except the crossing itself; for every sudden change of circumstances occurs only with a certain conflict of minds. You will come to men unknown to you, but not as an unknown person, for I have prepared the way for my friend. Come, then, and see the way of the Lord, who has set wonders upon the earth: many powerful men, many nobles, many learned men, many delicately reared men, sons of kings and princes from every nation under heaven, gathered in that place which the Lord chose from all places of the earth, that his name might be there. Then you will say: “These are the camps of God.”

[Note: These are Jacob’s words after the vision of angels ascending and descending; Genesis 18.]

There is nothing else here but the house of God and the gate of heaven, my Lecelinus. There is no straighter way, no holier life in all holiness, than that which the Holy of Holies left upon earth. But you say: “I am ready and am not troubled” (Psalm 118), yet I cannot depart. First show them their ways and their pursuits; and if they refuse to listen to you, say persistently and steadfastly—say that you are in a trackless place, not on the way, and that you will go to those men, so that Christ may become the way for you in example, truth in promise, and life in reward. Say—say—that this is not a house of prayer but a den of thieves, apart from what lies hidden within. Say: “In the house of Israel I saw horrible things, and those mourning for Adonis.” If they see your boldness and perseverance, they will not wait for you to leave; they will force you out and lay a finger upon their mouth.

Do you remember that, at my urging—indeed, my compulsion—you found the man of God favourable? On one occasion that heavenly pipe and unique instrument of the Holy Spirit answered thus, with his own mouth, concerning your order: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it fear” (Isaiah 7). For whatever I commanded in the earlier letter, fulfil all of it; and I shall still add beyond measure whatever I can gather from whatever source.

I have placed the rest in the mouth of the bearer present, who will tell you what you must do. He alone will give the letter to you alone. If any eye besides your own sees it, you have lost me for ever and ever, world without end. I say this not because I fear truth for truth’s sake, but because neither prudence nor foresight consists in causing scandal and achieving nothing, while safeguarding good things before God and men. For I know where I have read it: both are guilty, the one who conceals truth and the one who speaks falsehood, because the former does not wish to profit another and the latter desires to harm.

Therefore, for the sake of him who wholly exposed himself to death and torments for your whole self, come and refresh my soul. I am tormented in this flame when I see one part of my soul received into heaven and another part left in the mire. If not for your own sake, then at least for mine, cross over. Remove from me the sword of fear which pierces my inmost parts unto the division of spirit and soul; it cannot be removed unless you move your foot from that place which is not holy ground.

All day long, as I hear, you read philosophers, rhetoricians, and poets. Do you think that you understand what you read? Believe me: you will find more among us in the axe and adze than among yourselves in writing and on the page. For with us the mountains drip sweetness, the hills flow with milk and honey, oil flows from the hardest rock, and all the trees of the forest clap their hands.

But see: while I think I am merely telling you tales, I have extended my pen to a great length, forgetting how much distance I had left behind me. If this letter seems insufficiently brilliant and not heaped with elaborately spread-out words, recall what is written: embellished speech does not please a prudent man, but strong speech does. For I have not chosen what would be subtler in logical sequence, but what would be more useful to conscience. Yet how much, in this small piece, I may have lost of my small devotion, he knows who knows the secrets of the heart.

Farewell, and pray for me. Write your heart back to your heart; and, if possible:

> Write nothing back to me; only come yourself.  
> —Ovid, *Heroides*

The letter had already been folded when it came into my mind to send you a messenger as great and such as your eyes behold. Whatever he tells you, attend to it and do it. See that he finds in you no “yes and no”; and as he shall have arranged it in your heart, set it there. See that you pass over not one iota of the things I have told you. Beware of losing the favourable opportunity, for if you neglect it now, you will never be able to recover it.

## LETTER XXXIX. To Henry, the king’s brother, a monk of Clairvaux

(See above, column 1575 of this volume.)

## LETTER XL. To the abbot of Arremar, when he made peace with him

Brother NICOLAUS to his father: May you show a father’s bowels of compassion.

Perhaps it will be attributed either to imprudence or to impudence that I presume to write to you. Yet I resume the case of one who loves his homeland thus: human nature blames something more effectively, more quickly, and more ardently than it praises; and it is easier for the children of Adam to slip into evils than into good things. Each person will abound in his own opinion. Therefore I shall no longer conceal the fire which burns my sorrowful breast, but pour it out into the flames and sparks of words. For I remember, though not where I read it, what I read:

> The more the fire is concealed, the more fiercely it burns.

This fire is grief: grief indeed singular, and my grief is ever before me; grief supreme and consuming my spirit, not lessened by tears but increased by them, violently breaking into the very seat of the soul. You know, almighty Father, before whose eyes all things are naked and laid open, that tears accompany me as I write; may they be admitted before the Father’s eyes as they are shed from mine. I say, the Father—not mine, but that of my brethren—for “I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (Luke 15), since I turned your face away from me and became troubled.

And I, who had been his most tenderly cherished son—whom he chose, loved, and gathered into the multitude of his mercies, not as one among the rest but as one above the rest. I was young in years, weak in heart, faint-spirited, frivolous in speech, undiscerning in action, foul of tongue, stained in conscience, proud in learning—although that learning was either none or slight. Yet for all these things his hand was against everyone, and everyone’s hand against him, for my sake, while he wished to restore me to myself—indeed, to himself also. And for this, “O Lord my God” [A, a: “Ah, Lord God”] (Jer. 1), how often he grieved lest I should grieve! Going before me, cautiously and anxiously he overcame those attacking me, lest even the faint whisper of those who murmured should strike my ears.

How often, at his table, while he himself was present and presiding, did I sit down not as though I were a companion and fellow-servant, but as a master. And truly I said to this one, “Go,” and he went; and to another, “Come,” and he came (Luke 7); at a word from my mouth both guest and banquet were made ready. Since he knew that I was accustomed to more splendid fare, he prepared and set before me every delicacy, feeding himself with fasts and me with luxuries. Although I had passed beyond the bounds of vainglory—this I say without vainglory—past the poison of envy, nevertheless he was careful to ensure that no one could envy me; for he wished me to be more loved than admired. Why say more? He was wholly occupied in doing everything I wished, and he credited to himself whatever could distinguish me.

Meanwhile my thoughts passed into the affection of my heart, so that I might pass to this stronghold of poverty and summit of discipline, after my mind had long been tossed in contrary directions. For I compared both the man and the Order: I considered the softness of the former and the severity of the latter. But the fear of God grew warm and prevailed; therefore I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness according to the institutions of the Cistercians.

The report spread among the brethren. It could not be concealed from him whom it was capable of wounding with a deeper wound. Terrified, therefore, he summoned both me and my companions, and discovered that what flew from mouth to mouth among the people was true. At once his color changed; and grief, drawing deep sighs, boiled up into fountains of tears. He pleaded with prayers and pressed me with commands. But my iniquities had risen above my head and had to be broken by a harsher penance. I became like a man who does not hear; and, having broken the bonds of the most weighty affections, I did not delay my purpose, but betook myself to this house of the Lord our God. When I entered it, I allowed nothing to remain within me, but entrusted to it whatever burned me or could burn me.

To this man, upon whom the eyes of all Israel look, I spoke one thing which I wish I had not said; and [Note: The text has *a. q. u. n.*; I think this should be read: “and I heard things which I could not say everywhere”] I could say that I spoke it in order to relieve my conscience, to honor that Church, and to do honor to his native land. But I come to accuse myself, not to excuse myself.

Come then, lord Father: “I am he who sinned; I who acted wickedly” (2 Sam. 24). I returned evil for good and hatred for his love. I proved ungrateful to you; I did not answer your benefits. An enemy of nature, wicked toward you and more wicked toward myself, worthy of a thousand deaths and unworthy of pardon, on this occasion too I came into the depths of iniquity. I did not look up to the Lord; I did not look back upon my father. I despised my friend and sinned grievously against the laws of friendship; and, in Paul’s words (Rom. 8), sinning beyond measure, I made myself another Absalom—and in this respect worse than Absalom. For whereas his father did not set him above his other sons, this man set me above them all.

Would that I might hear the father’s voice: “Preserve for me the young man Absalom” (2 Sam. 18), that I might have leave to breathe after the affliction and sorrow caused by my evils. Would that it had been granted me from above to say this, not dictate it; to pray, not deliver an oration; and not entrust to lifeless letters what was owed to living voices. I would cast myself at his feet, embrace his knees, clasp his hands, hang wholly from his neck, and kiss that sweetest and most beloved head, until I heard forgiveness of my crimes and dismissal in peace. Truly, by frequent tears I would bend him, because he is kind and merciful, and skilled

> To spare the submissive and subdue the proud.

> [Note: VIRGIL, *Aeneid*, Book VI, near the end.]

Lord Father and God of my life, you are witness for me how often I seem to myself to stand naked before him, holding rods in my hands and offering my whole body to words and blows, so that, according to the saying of the holy man, this may be my consolation: that, though he afflicts me with pain, he does not spare me; and if he does not spare me now, then he will spare me. I shall reckon the greatness of the punishment as the multitude of grace, because, if he scourges me, it is a sign that he receives his son.

May I find the pardon of my Lord in your sight. “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is ever before me; against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. 50). Do not hold a sinner—judged by himself and judged by you—as condemned; but remember that the tears of the sinful woman and the Savior’s pardon are joined together without interval. For I, who was able to offend, wish to uphold whatever I offended against; and through devoted service and humble satisfaction, here I shall be yours as long as I live, and I shall make your friend, my father—indeed, from a friend, the most beloved father of all—still more beloved. And I shall bind this holy community to him in an everlasting covenant, giving it a special lord and friend.

Nor should you think such progress—or benefit—small; for these men will be a shield to you in temporal affairs and a very great aid in spiritual matters. For, by the Lord’s grace, I have found favor in their eyes, loving all and loved by all, especially by him whom my soul especially loves. Here I shall show you that I am not dead to you and yours, but have come back to life; and, if you deign to test them, you will prove that these things are true not in word or speech, but in deed and truth.

Why, then, do you hide your face and consider me your enemy? You display your power not against a leaf but against a son, and you persecute your own soul. What glory will it be to you to pursue dead flesh and a single flea?

> [Note: More correctly, “a dead dog.” These are David’s words when he entreats Saul: “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? You pursue a dead dog and a single flea” (1 Sam. 24).]

Whether you will or not, I was yours, I am yours, and I shall be yours as long as I live. And I know that, when you have gone within yourself, you will remember mercy. Who compels me to say these things? Fear? No; for I fear nothing from that quarter, since care for my body has passed to another. Perhaps hope? Far be it! For there is nothing—or, if there is something, very little—in that Order which accords with that Order and with these customs. For you chose the gentler way, we the stronger; yet each seeks God, each finds God, since God is the author of both.

It is love, therefore—love less loving than mad—which brings back to me the tears you poured out for me in my extremity, sets your benefits again before me, and moves me to do this. Most loving Father, choose whatever punishment you will, and impose it as you will: I am ready to undergo it, provided only that my purpose remains safe. For to return or depart would be death to me, not salvation to you; a burden, not an honor; destruction to many.

Therefore, for the sake of him who was so great a lover of mercy that he chose rather to die than not to show mercy, “have mercy upon me according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50): grant pardon, restore favor, and increase glory unto the glory of God. Let not that voice which descended from heaven pass you by: “To forgive faults is heavenly; to exact vengeance, earthly.”

> [Note: Heavenly utterance: “To forgive faults is heavenly; to exact vengeance, earthly.”]

For whatever you forgive me, you give to yourself when you come before the Judge who stood before a judge.

> [Note: Namely Jesus Christ, who stood before Pilate the judge.]

And may he, the Lord Jesus Christ, who has no end, be the end of this letter. The bearer of the present letter will report the rest to you more effectively in personal conversation.

## LETTER XLI. To the lord of Clairvaux, in the person of Prior Rualen, recommending the bishop of Alet.

> [Note: Bernard wrote to him in Letter 260.]

Brother Rualen to his brother.

This man is a poor bishop, a friend of the poor—and, what is greater, a lover of poverty. Coming from the city, he came to us, hoping through us to find you with us. By common counsel we detained him, both because of the familiarity by which he is bound to us and because of his need, for he had nowhere to lay his head. All friends had become enemies; all his dependents, adversaries. And the hand of the mighty man, the son of the castaways, had gathered itself against him.

Our eyes have seen how graciously he came in and went out among us, and how much fellowship he has with poverty. There is no counsel, no aid, indeed no refuge, except with you and in you. He himself comes to you; and we come with him and for him, if not in body, yet in spirit. Open to him the widest bosom of your compassion, for—unless we are greatly mistaken—the cause is God’s; and if it is God’s, it is ours and yours. He has pleased our whole community by his truth, meekness, and justice, which can make him commendable even to his enemies.

But if on this occasion you return to your people at Clairvaux, bring him back with you. Then you will see how great is our concern and tenderness for his afflictions. You may also speak of his case with Brother Gregory, whom the lord Pope sent to you on his own business.

## LETTER XLII. To Geoffrey, recommending the bishop of Alet.

Geoffrey, his own, from Nicholas, his own: that he is his.

That I call you mine is evidence not of flattery but of affection. Nor is it strange if you are mine, since I am yours and shall be yours as long as I live. By your manner of life and learning alike you have deserved to be embraced, and have earned a lasting dwelling in my heart. Thus, although you are far from me in presence, you are wholly present to me in memory. For in the sanctuary of chaste and sanctifying love, those who behold one another with their souls rather than their eyes are more present to one another; for to be joined in heart is more than to be joined in body.

Let the lord bishop of Alet experience in his affair all that secret intimacy which you preserve for me in your heart. For he is wholly the bishop, having nothing in dress or manners mingled with the haughtiness of the Pharisees. He is poor and a friend of the poor; and, what is greater, a lover of poverty. Men without mercy have risen against him: my former brethren, for whom it is an old practice to pour out gold and silver so that they may confound peoples throughout the earth. Everywhere this pestilential disease has spread, and as yet there has been no one to restrain the insolent, to stand as a wall for the house of Israel, or to expend his arrows upon them.

I had thought that he whom they set as keeper of the vineyards would consider vines of this kind unfruitful and cut away the barren branches. But the matter has turned out otherwise. For the men of the greater monastery have made themselves greater in the curia—whether by greater money, I do not know; God knows. The poor bishop has been delivered over to the will of his enemies; and those whom he regarded as suspects he has received as judges, so that he may truly say: “Our enemies are judges” (Deut. 32).

Yet one impregnable refuge remains to him: your Father—indeed, mine also.

> [Note: He means St Bernard.]

The monks will never be able to corrupt him with gold, shake him by threats, or seduce him by blandishments. For one man has been excepted from the sons of Adam: sound amid gifts and fearless amid threats, he has put on the likeness of God, with whom there is no respect of persons (Rom. 2; Deut. 10; 2 Chr. 19; Acts 10).

Work earnestly and bring it about with him that the poor bishop may be rescued from those plundering him, exalted among his neighbors, and look down upon his enemies. For the little letters which you wrote to him and on his behalf not only did no good, but did much harm, because they taught the lord Pope to resort, from the ambiguity of his words, to Roman evasiveness. But enough of this.

Pray for me; and ask my father to pray for me, to care for me, and to stand beside me in compassion. For our whole community awaits him, that it may behold his face as the countenance of an angel standing among them. Farewell, and love one who loves you. Greet Lord Philip for me; for my soul has long been knit to his soul.

## LETTER XLIII. To Rualen, abbot of Saint Anastasius: a complaint concerning his absence, and recommendation.

> [Note: This is at Rome, the monastery repaired on 25 October 1140 and inhabited by the monks of Clairvaux.]

To his Rualen, from that one who is his: that he is his.

Perhaps you ask—or complain—that, although I have placed your name at the head, I have not added beneath it “abbot”: abbot exalted by the hands of blessed Peter.

> [Note: He calls Pope Eugenius, by antonomasia, the successor of St Peter in the apostolic see. Bernard’s letter to Eugenius concerning Rualen’s promotion is relevant here.]

Let those say this who say to you, “Well done, well done”; those who chew upon titled names and do not blush to sell abundantly the oil of the sinner. Not so I, not so. For pride gives way when affection draws near, and personal reverence diminishes when familiar friendship begins to speak freely.

Although the guardian of men has placed and called you to the City—which, according to the philosopher, we know to have been the dwelling-place of laws, the school of letters, the court of dignities, the summit of the world, and the homeland of liberty—I recognize no one except my Rualen: mine, I say, mine, and particularly mine in the bowels of Jesus Christ. The eye of my mind presents to me him whom I saw loving all and loved by all, fixing the gaze of both heart and body upon the riches of poverty alone.

How true, Lord Jesus, is what you established with that holy mouth of yours: “Do not think that I came to bring peace upon earth; I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10; Luke 12). How harsh this sword would be, if it were not yours—the sword which set the better part of me upon the Roman heights and left the worse in the valley of tears, in the place which you appointed for your name to be there. You have removed friend and neighbor far from me: friend by the most similar will, neighbor by one profession.

Is it then pleasing before you, lord Father, that those whom you had joined together should be scattered from one another over the face of the earth? But where am I going? Do I too wish to dispute with God? Far be it. I do not contradict the words of the Holy One; for although I grieve, I do not murmur. “No living being shall be justified in your sight,” Lord; nor can he answer one thing for a thousand (Job 9). Rualen was yours; you made from your own possession your own work, because all things serve you.

Yet I am wounded: a sword has passed through my soul; all these evils have fallen back upon me. The man of one heart with me, according to my heart, has been taken from me: gracious in favor, pleasing in manners, regarding nothing as alien except what was unsuitable to virtue. With what most ardent love did he rush upon me and I upon him! Hardly could the splendor of Roman eloquence have adequately described him, of whom it is written:

> [Note: Peter the Venerable, Letter 37 to Book VI, attributes this to our Nicholas, saying: “You, a Ciceronian, do not merely follow your own Tully, of whom you wrote that he transferred the whole heart into the tongue with the greatest ease.”]

> What study had shaped, affection urged, and art carried out: with the greatest ease transferring his whole heart into speech.

He bound me to Rualen by the benefits of his kindnesses; and one so great anticipated one so small with such condescension that he stole me away for you in the abundance of his sweetness. Yet he was in a high place, but knew nothing of loftiness; doubting neither that nothing is dearer to God nor rarer among men. And though all found in him every name of every relationship, I nevertheless looked up to him as lord, loved him as friend, revered him as father, and embraced him as my most intimate companion.

Therefore I grieve, and shall continue to grieve. Nor will that plausible but untrue maxim console me: “Let no one flatter himself concerning absence: those who behold one another with their souls rather than their eyes are more present; and more so in heart than in body.” For although knowledge is fuller in the spirit, sight and conversation possess a certain living delight which those who love allegorically cannot supply.

Therefore, my beloved, since I cannot have your presence, I shall pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of your sweetness. That distinctive quality of your character will possess the breast of your friend as eternally as spiritually. And unless our common Father held me back—

> [Note: He means St Bernard, whose very great praise is here contained in a single word.]

—in whose merits we looked upon more exalted ages and the mouths of the prophets whom we read, he knows my desire—he into whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1).

“Why, then, are you sorrowful, O my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him” (Ps. 42). If not on earth, at least in heaven: in that city whose king is truth, whose law is love, and whose measure is eternity; where we shall always be, where we shall be well, where we shall be together—without fear, without weariness, without failure. Meanwhile, whatever I am and whatever I can do is yours:

> And you, O Rualen, whatever you may wish,  
> I strive to discover; it is right for me to carry out your commands.

> [Note: Adapted from the *Aeneid* to suit the author’s purpose.]

Only do not disdain to command me. And because no one uses greater confidence than one who loves out of affection, I now address you as a portion of my soul, bringing before you a familiar and sorrowful complaint. For although you are never silent to me—for I know that I have never been absent from your heart—nevertheless I have received no letter from you in which you might converse with your friend, in which the image of your presence might shine forth.

How will you be generous in deeds when you are so miserly and hard in words? Nor do I say this as though I sought what is yours, for I seek you alone. For I look keenly upon the world and the things which are in the world, if not as already passing away, at least as most certainly about to pass away. He judges ill of you—and no better of me—who thinks that your absence should be compensated by gifts, or that I should be redeemed by gifts.

But my pen must be restrained, lest my discourse wander beyond the limits of a letter, since I know how much you delight in concise brevity. At the end of my letter I both beseech you as a father and advise you as a friend: consider your burden imposed rather than undertaken, and make necessity into virtue. Far be it that a foreign place should alter you; for that by which a human being fares well is in the human being, not in a place.

> [Note: “That by which a human being fares well is in the human being, not in a place.”]

You have changed not your homeland but your place. For it is most true that the fool is an exile everywhere, while the wise person is a pilgrim wherever he may be. If, then, you love the bishop, feed his sheep: “Because you love me,” he says, “feed my sheep” (John 21).

> [Note: What an abbot ought to consider himself.]

Always think yourself not the lord of monks, but one of them: servant of the good, terror of the bad, teacher of the ignorant, nurse of the weak, and example to all.

I send you an ivory knife with silverwork and that Irish handle, which is no less precious by grace than by nature. For it has, beyond nature, the power to drive away poison. A certain saint planted with his own hands the tree from which it was cut, and that tree, as we have learned, is preserved as among the highest relics. I extracted it with great difficulty from the hands of the man whom you know.

> [Note: Perhaps “Irish”; indeed this must necessarily be read so. The following may refer to the staff whose virtue Gerald of Wales recounts in *Topography of Ireland*, ch. 34: “Among all the staffs in Ireland, and those of wooden nature, that powerful and famous relic of the saints, which they call the Staff of Jesus, seems deservedly to be first. By it, according to popular belief, St Patrick expelled venomous creatures from the island.” Or, if anyone prefers, let him understand this of the willow which, in compassion for St Kevin’s sick little boy who desired apples, bore apples not far from the church—health-giving both to the boy and to other sick persons, as the same Gerald says in the aforementioned book, ch. 28.]

Farewell, and pray for me, that my eyes may see you before I die. Deign to greet your Airad—indeed, mine also—with your mouth and in our spirit.

## LETTER XLIV. In the person of the prior, to Garnier of Cluny: congratulations on his conversion.

> [Note: Peter the Venerable, Book VI, Letter 35, addressed to St Bernard, mentions Garnier as sent to Clairvaux with his authorization.]

To Brother Garnier, Brother R. [sends] the spirit of fortitude.

We saw your letter; we rejoiced and were delighted—not with any ordinary joy, but with exceedingly great joy. Blessed is that unique poor man who has made you a lover of his poverty and unity, because he will make you a fellow-heir of his inheritance above your companions. We were indeed glad concerning your manner of life, but we still had concern about your conversion. Now, however, our soul rejoices in both your manner of life and your conversion, because your letters cry out: “Make perfect my steps in your paths, that my footsteps may not be moved” (Ps. 16).

Who would have thought that from such great eminence you would either wish or be able to descend to such humility? Blessed is this descent, in which one descends so as to ascend, where one hears: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14). But accursed are those who ascend to the heavens, because they descend to the abyss; those who have called lands by their own names, who by the loud applause of eloquence have made for themselves a great name, like the names of the great who are on earth. They are on the earth and have loved neither poverty nor poverty’s reward, which is the kingdom of heaven.

Suppose that, contrary to the Order, you abounded in riches and luxuries within the Order: yet can anyone be in honor without pain, in prelacy without tribulation, in eminence without vanity? What end can there be for those who desire all things without end? The mind which has not been purely and thoroughly cleansed from the defilement of this world will have neither peace nor rest.

Who will give us that you, our brother, might suck the breasts of our mother, so that we might find you within? For “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44). This is what you desire: to be with us, while we desire much more to be with you—in this place, nevertheless, which you chose above all places. This has not fallen from our heart; rather, with every effort we labor that your joy may be full, and that our joy may at last have one place for those whom one soul contains. We believe this will happen soon.

Your Nicholas and Brother Thomas, that royal young man—whom earthly nobility commends, but heavenly nobility much more—greet you. All of them love you not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth. You have found Lord William such as we wished. To him, to the abbot, and to the community of that place, we render our own thanks in our own letters; and humbly entreat them to bring to a better completion what they have well begun in you and concerning you.

Brother Hugh to his brother Garnier, greeting in the Lord. You wrote briefly, but I reply more briefly still. When I saw your letter, my spirit revived. It is enough for me if I see you with us before I die.

## LETTER XLV. To Brother Gaucher: when he had resolved to enter the Order; a recommendation of Clairvaux and the religious life.

> [Note: Peter the Venerable, Book VI, Letter 36, calls him Gaucher, cellarer of Clairvaux; and our Nicholas mentions Gaucher, as here, in his final letter to Cluny.]

To Brother Gaucher, Brother Nicholas: put on the bowels of mercy.

My soul is sorrowful as far as you, because I have hoped in you, Lord—not in you as in a human being.

> [Note: It seems it should read: “not that I have placed the foundation of my hope in myself as in a human being.”]

For it is written: “Cursed is he who puts his hope in man, so that his heart departs from God.”

> [Note: Jer. 17, where the Vulgate has *confidit*, “trusts,” in place of “puts his hope.”]

For thus we depart from the Lord, and the Lord departs from us. But not so have I hoped either concerning you or in you. Rather, to the extent that one human being can or ought to trust another, what did I desire from you upon the rock except to see you, speak with you, and live with you? For you are the first to whom I opened the first fruits of my heart under witness of the Godhead; and I found you according to my heart and according to God. I was burning, but you made me more fervent; yet you left me most fervent.

For, going in and out beneath the garments of Christ’s humility, I leapt into the whirlpool of pleasures; and from the inheritance of the Crucified One, from the price of the wounds of my Lord, I made myself a monk without rule and a priest without reverence, not merely within the sanctuary of saints but within the Holy of Holies.

> [Note: This sentence would be purer as: “within the sanctuary,” or “within the Holy of Holies.”]

For, by going to and returning from the Roman curia too inquisitively, I had made for myself a great name, like the names of the great who are on earth; and throughout my whole life I do not remember that I lived even one day. I remembered this and poured out my soul within me, because I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God.

By the tabernacle I understand Clairvaux, a house not made with hands. From this tabernacle the passage to that house is easy: whoever stands here shall sit there. Blessed is the tabernacle where I saw men who were not men—indeed, truly men; and, what is truer, men walking above the human level. I saw armed soldiers of Christ standing about Solomon’s bed, each with his sword upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night. I saw them standing upon the Lord’s watches all days and all nights, clothed with the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of salvation, holding the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

With the faith of sight I beheld men of one manner dwelling in a house: rising by night to give praise to the Lord’s name; at evening, morning, and noon recounting and declaring his praise; and gathering their whole diligence into the circle of divine service. I saw them eating the labor of their own hands—not the tears of widows, not the blood of the poor; nor, under the pretext of piety, introducing the slaughterhouse of cruelty. The benches were full of singers; they resounded on high in harmony and equal voice, so that in happy envy I could have thought them sworn to “make a joyful noise to God with the voice of exultation.” Whether I wished or did not wish it, I was drawn by their devotion, and said: “These are the camps of God” (Gen. 32)—“This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28).

I tell you truly that from that time my soul desired and failed for the courts of the Lord; and I was affected by so great a desire that I counted a day as a year. Hence I did not pass beyond the time you had fixed for me, but came before it—after suffering many things which the brevity of a letter does not allow me to include; and would that I had suffered something for righteousness’ sake.

Who can enumerate the tears of the abbot, the groaning of the monks, the lamentation of the servants, the leave sought but not obtained? Who can describe how we escaped from their hands without garments, money, servants, or horses, and scarcely reached Aripatorium? And, driven away from there too, we fled to our refuge—I mean Clairvaux—unable to contain ourselves for joy because at last we had deserved to see the tabernacle of God with humankind.

We were already in harbor and expected nothing but to behold this great vision and become as one of you. But the matter turned out otherwise: “I am humbled and troubled” (Ps. 87); I have been sent far away to the ends of the earth. My very bowels have been torn from me, and I from my bowels. Therefore the pain in my heart is not momentary but continual, because I am not with you, because I am compelled to live without you.

The distresses of my brethren who followed me have added to the pain of my wounds: they are afflicted with death all day long, and I cannot ease them even for an hour because I cannot be with you. By this alone are we desolated. There is none among all our dear ones to console us; rather, we are compelled to dwell as strangers with strangers. Besides these, there are many other matters which I judge should be entrusted not to lifeless letters but to your ears.

G., man of God, if you have any bowels of compassion, any affection of charity; if the remembrance of your friend touches you—and of that friend who entrusted himself to you and rejoices to have entrusted himself—come swiftly to us. Remember the word spoken to your servant, in which you gave me hope. If you do not come quickly, know that sorrows are added to sorrows, and God will require our blood at your hand.

Guard the boy who bears this letter, according to his age, as you would guard me; and bring him back with you to me. He alone followed me after I was made alone, and has not turned aside from your servant. Blessed shall I be if I can repay him. Farewell, and come.

## LETTER XLVI. To Fremund, hospitaller of Clairvaux: congratulations on a remarkable conversion.

To his brother, Brother Nicholas: wholly forget both the world and the things that are in the world.

> [Note: These are the words of St Peter, Acts 10.]

In truth I have learned that God shows no partiality, and you are my proof: the spirit of devotion has brought you, without me, from the iron furnace of Babylon to a place of religious life. This Spirit is manifold and subtle; he has led you into the right way, not because of your own justifications, but because of his many mercies. For what do I say to your glory? Are you not the man who troubled the earth, who traversed kingdoms, who filled the whole world with notorious disgrace? And now, the more destructive you had been, the more glorious you have appeared. [Col. 1647B] If there is joy among the angels over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15), what joy is there over you—so great and such a sinner—now not only doing penance yourself, but also urging others to penance? This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High: a change that has filled those most exalted workshops with more abundant joy.

Consider, therefore, how unmerited is the mercy, how unforeseen the condescension, how astonishing the sweetness of him who called you into his wonderful light; who transferred you into the kingdom of the Son of his brightness; who assigned you a share in the lot of the saints and enrolled you among the battle-lines of the mightiest soldiers. All [wickedness] had set itself against your whole self, and rejoiced that, with your whole being, you blasphemed him wholly—the more joyfully [Col. 1647C] the more wickedly. It was not enough for you to perish for ever and ever unless you dragged others also into everlasting destruction. But where sin abounded, grace abounded still more (Romans 5); and that great eye of providence shook off your garment of flesh and fastened you with its fear. He granted you the rags of his humility; he placed you among men who live in the manner of angels; and in a wonderful way he set you as an example, so that you might take example from the righteous and become an example to sinners.

I speak before God: you alone have consoled me, and while I yet live I am kindled because you wish to go before me into the kingdom of God. And now what will you give to your deliverer for so great a gift of his, so beautiful and precious—beautiful for its loveliness, precious for its usefulness? Keep for him your body and soul, since for you [Col. 1647D] he gave his body and soul. He asks nothing from you except yourself—nor even yourself except for your own sake. He does not need either you or what is yours; but you need both him and what is his.

What would my dry and fasting tongue dare to whisper to your spirit, which drips with such devotion of the Holy Spirit? Shall I tell you to leave the world and the things which are in the world, when I see that you have thoroughly wiped away not only worldly possessions but also the desires of your mind? Shall I tell you to deny more sumptuous provision to your raging appetite, when broth and vegetables serve it in unchangeable succession? Shall I tell you to live chastely, when I do not doubt that in you nothing remains to be crucified, but everything has already been crucified? [Col. 1648A] Shall I tell you not to sit in the council of vanity, when I behold you sitting in the council of the righteous, whom that blessed region of Clairvaux surrounds?

Yet one thing is necessary: let perseverance hold you—or rather, do not abandon perseverance—and you shall be blessed, and it shall go well with you. Perseverance is the singular daughter of the supreme King; she introduces the assembly of the remaining virtues into the chamber of their lord. This is for you.

But if you wish to hear me too, hear briefly what concerns me. Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, since I am compelled to live without you—without whom I do not live, but die? Clairvaux remains with me in my mouth, Clairvaux in my heart, Clairvaux in my whole self, Clairvaux in all my parts; it remains with me, perseveres with me, and never [Col. 1648B] departs from me. Hence come frequent groans, continual tears, repeated vigils, deep sighs, innumerable sobs, anxious thought, and things which cannot be disclosed even at the tomb.

O Lord Jesus, why do you not judge and avenge my blood upon those who delay my journey, who bar the way of one coming to you and trusting in you? Therefore, dearest friend Fromund, whom I love greatly and by whom I am greatly loved, urge our fathers and brothers to bring me out of this prison and lead me into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, lest I die in the bitterness of my soul. For if I remain here longer, death is better for me than life. Let them bring it about and labour to secure it, that I may have permission—or be received even without permission, which is no permission—to go [Col. 1648C] to the Lord.

The rest this cleric of mine—indeed, yours also—will report in person. Alone he has followed me in my solitude, and, though young, learned and faithful in what has been entrusted to him, he will by no means allow himself to depart from me. I commend him to your freedom, as my consolation in the place of my pilgrimage. Farewell, and pray for me.

## LETTER XLVII. In the persons of Gaucher and Girard. Counsel concerning a vow, to Henry, a noble knight.

To the illustrious man HENRY, GAUCHER and GIRARD: may a good resolution be brought to a good end.

Do you think that we have forgotten you, noble and faithful man, gracious in character, sweet in favour, untiring in service—and, what is greater, not embracing the world while in the world? Far from it: your friends will never forget you; nor can the malice of time make you absent from our hearts even for an hour. We have found a man after our own heart, one who seeks God in the world, who professes himself a monk beneath a soldier’s belt.

“Was not our heart burning within us” (Luke 24) concerning Jesus, while we spoke with you on the way about him who is the way, the truth, and the life? (John 14). Would that it had been granted us from above to say these things rather than dictate them, so that we might speak with you and delight in your company. Now indeed we have learned by experience that love is pleasant among those present, [Col. 1649A] burdensome among those absent. For sight and conversation possess a certain living delight which dead letters cannot express.

What then? Though we do not see you with the eyes of the body, we nevertheless see you with the eyes of the heart in the tender mercies of Jesus Christ. May he deign to grant both you and us forgiveness of sins, the grace of virtues, and the glory of heaven, when he rises to strike the earth with the rod of his mouth. Meanwhile, we shall pray for you to him who made you, that he may inspire you with his will—for your benefit, for our joy, and for the exultation of the whole earth. For we are yours and shall be yours as long as we exist: yours, I say, and especially we who together pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness.

## LETTER XLVIII. To Peter, Abbot of Celle.

[Col. 1649B]

(See Peter of Celle, Letter 62, *Patrologia*, vol. CCII.)

## LETTER XLIX. To the same, who complained that he did not write at greater length.

(See the same place, Letter 63.)

## LETTER L. To the cantor of Grandiselve, in the person of Matthew: affectionate and commendatory.

[Note: [Col. 1649D] Grandiselve Abbey, brought under the authority of the Abbot of Clairvaux in 1144, is mentioned in Book IV, chapters 1 and 4, of the *Life of St Bernard* [Col. 1650D].]

To his dearest brother B., brother NICHOLAS: sing to God with a voice of exultation.

How greatly I love you in the tender mercies of Jesus [Col. 1649C] Christ is known to him who knows the hidden things of the heart. For the memory of you has entered my breast more deeply, occupied it more widely, possessed it more firmly, and dwells with me while I live. Who will grant me never to forsake the remembrance of you, nor ever to be forsaken by it? Far be it from me to abandon it; it shall not depart from me for ever and ever. Happy am I, who have deserved to love and know you; your character and many gracious qualities sufficiently call for love and exalt you still more. But far happier is he whom you have deigned to embrace and gather to yourself with generous love and no small intimacy.

For all this I bear your absence heavily and sigh for your presence, with sighs and groans beyond utterance. Since I cannot possess your presence, I shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and say [Col. 1649D] to my soul: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Psalm 41). Hope in God, for I shall yet see him—if not on earth, at least in heaven—and shall be filled with his presence when the glory of my Lord appears. There no one will be able to hinder me, for there will be no bodies or bodily obstacles capable either of excluding or enclosing my desire.

[Note: [Col. 1650D] There is something similar in Letter 47.]

I know that sight and conversation possess a certain living delight, but this is among worldly persons. True love is ignorant of the inconveniences of place or time, because affection rules in that in which it is always its own master. For charity [Col. 1650A] embraces all that the Ocean contains, and in the sanctuary of love it permits no one not to be present to us. In this love and with this love your good spirit lives in my spirit; and when I recall your affection, my heart and my flesh exult in the living God.

This is for myself. Now I commend to you our brothers who are with you: if they remain there, cherish them and show them favour; for they themselves are in me, and I in them. And if a friend’s prayers avail anything with a friend, preserve in your heart that zeal for the Order and concerning your Order, and keep it without end, so that at the end your reward may be great in heaven.

Moreover, Samuel and I are one: I have no one so wholly of one mind with me, or to whom I could commend you more intimately. I greeted him [Col. 1650B] on your behalf and placed your letter in his hands. That religious and faithful young man received it, and rejoiced—not with any ordinary joy, but with exceedingly great joy. He read it eagerly, reread it more eagerly still, hiding it in his bosom and in his heart for ever and ever. Why say more? Your love has established a lasting dwelling in my breast. Whatever I say, he too says; and the entire sequence of this letter is no less his than mine.

Thus we two are in you, one; and you are in us, two. This Trinity in unity entreats that one Trinity—or rather, that threefold Unity—that, as we are joined by charity on earth, so we may be joined by truth in heaven. And, to disclose my heart briefly to my heart: among human things, nothing is sweeter to me than your person; [Col. 1650C] and I pray God that my eyes may see you before I die.

I have exceeded, I confess, the proper measure of a letter; but abundant affection has urged on my running pen. While my heart was happily occupied in the hidden places of friendship, forgetting how much distance it had left behind it, it was always reaching forward. For I do not know how it is that we never grow weary of speaking about what we love greatly. I therefore end this letter, though I shall by no means set an end to my love for you, sweetest and most loving brother.
