## LETTER LVI. To Henry, Count of Champagne.

(BALUZE, *Miscellanies*, folio edition, vol. III, p. 76.)

[Col. 1651A]

To the most serene prince and his dearest lord HENRY, Count of Troyes, brother NICHOLAS—by life a sinner, by habit a monk—greeting from salvation.

The philosopher says: “I judge the condition of human affairs to be happy whenever philosophers happen to rule, or rulers to philosophize.” A living saying, fashioned not only by a human mouth but by God. For what is a man without letters but the tomb of a rational soul, living and buried? Letters are the pathways to virtue, and virtue is the fruit [Col. 1651B] of letters. Although understanding discovers letters rather than letters understanding, the discovery nevertheless adorns and orders its discoverer, like a fairer son shining forth from a fair father.

For there is an old proverb, a maxim celebrated by the lips of the ancients: “As far as men differ from beasts, so far do the learned differ from the unlearned.” Letters were first devised by God, written by his finger, and given and commended to mortals as a singular gift. Through them, what was past is present. They gather within themselves whatever has been done anywhere or at any time.

Yet why do I praise them except to praise you, to whom it has been granted to retain a ruler in the philosopher and a philosopher in the ruler? I should therefore call our times happy, since they are pre-eminently distinguished by your rule: through you clerics are enriched, churches are endowed [Col. 1651C] and adorned alike. Let not the knights be jealous, for you also meet their needs. Yet you are not merely one among the princes of the earth, but as though the only one: your most generous hand, unequalled among the children of men, distributes from its possessions to poor and rich alike, so that the rich person may be more firmly bound and the poor more fittingly sustained.

You regard money as straw, scattered almost without distinction among all. You and it have nothing in common: when it comes to you, it finds you not hiding it but pouring it out. Often it has already been conferred and assigned before it arrives, so that it may think itself more gladly sent out than admitted. I wonder, nevertheless, how your right hand suffices and does not fail, unless it be true as Scripture says: “It is difficult for resources to abandon a wealthy spirit, while abundance follows a man poor in mind.”

Thus, seated between the learned and knightly orders, you magnify both, magnificent and generous toward both. No one like you has been found in this gift of nature, as those now living tell and posterity will tell—children of children, and those to be born from them. The Lord has also given you understanding and an instructed tongue for this purpose: that the blood of such great nobility might shine forth both in speech and intellect.

Nor do I say this as though I wished, by flattering speech, to heighten the splendour of your deeds, but in order to stir and invite you to a holy work worthy of blessing. For you know that nothing is truer than the word of truth, which says: “Give to everyone who asks of you”; and, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20). You also know that [Col. 1652A] I seek from you nothing except yourself and your favour, and that I have never wished to be either importunate or ungrateful.

And what of this? From my earliest youth I have pleased great and supreme princes of this world. Yet to you, in a singular manner, I owe whatever I am by the dominion of nature, and whatever I can do by the office of friendship. The wise man says:

> It is no small praise to have pleased men who are princes.

If this is so with princes, how much more with that prince who, by right of precedence, surpasses in my estimation all other princes? And because I know that your excellence devotes every effort to liberal studies, especially eloquence, I send to your highness certain letters which, within these past two years, I remember dedicating with some care to the lord pope, the chancellor, and other high-ranking persons. Thus you may know that, if I had more, I would send more—as the Son of the Virgin testifies concerning the sinful woman: “She did what she had.” Not that I think there is anything in me or from me that ought to be approved, but because I am so disposed toward your nobility that I prefer to disclose my trifles before you rather than conceal them.

Spare, too, the affection which, according to philosophy, obeys not even kings and upon which laws cannot impose commands. May the King of kings and Lord of lords grant you so to exercise lordship in earthly dominion that you are not deprived of the eternal, when the Lord rises to strike with the rod of his mouth and render to each according to his works (Romans 2).

## LETTER LVII. To William, Archbishop of Rheims.

(BALUZE, same work, p. 77.)

[Col. 1652C]

To his lord, the Archbishop of Rheims and legate of the Apostolic See, NICHOLAS, his own because he is his own.

I confess to you, Father, that I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son (Luke 15), unless your condescension restores one unworthy. For unworthy is he who does not heed a benefit, but turns his face away from his benefactor—unworthy and likewise ungrateful. Ingratitude is a scorching wind, drying up the fountain of mercy and swallowing up the rivers of graces. Such am I, and such are the things that I have prepared.

You are that Archbishop of Rheims whose oarage brings the ship of the Gallican Church safely through its most stormy places. You received me within the sanctuary of your friendship, which is rare in receiving but most constant in retaining. It does not easily yield itself except to one to whom it knows itself ought to yield, and then only after more deliberate consideration. For it is written: “Noble friendship is always dangerous, and after long deliberation shameful.” But once someone has been received, he is not deceived; he becomes acceptable to one in whom, in this respect, there is no change nor shadow of turning.

A whisperer has no place with you; no slanderer appears, knowing that he will be caught if suddenly observed. “A king who loves whispering words,” says the wise man, “has all his ministers wicked.” No one serves you in such a ministry, though distinguished and great men in these days are bewitched by the fault of credulity, not observing or not caring that it is written: “He who believes quickly is light of heart” (Sirach 19).

I, so small and so base, was received so and in such a manner by one so great and such as you, that by his blessings he took me away from myself. Yet what did I do? Many days have passed since I neither saw him nor wrote to him, although mute affection presents the appearance of one who does not love, and sight has a certain living delight which dead letters cannot experience. Shall I excuse myself by the difficulty of the journey and the distance of the region between the city of Rheims and the church of Arras? But the journey is short, the road level, and all around it full of my friends. Shall I say that I was busy, so that within a period of four days I could not steal myself away from myself? Surely a great man is occupied with great matters. But who could say this? Indeed, beside such a claim, an ant drawing a wagon is an instrument [Col. 1653A].

Shall I add that I could not obtain permission to come, when I go and come, depart and return, throughout the day? I could say these things if I were placed under such authority that I could not have command of myself. Every defence of making excuses to excuse sins has been removed. Nothing remains but for me to seek pardon and approach the feet of him who knows

> To spare the conquered and subdue the proud.  
> —Virgil

The humble man finds him a lamb; the exalted man finds him an elephant. He will add further kindness, that he may be still more gracious. He will not restrain his mercies in his anger. When he sees his servant, he will have mercy on him, for he is abundant in forgiveness, since he sees that I acknowledge my sin voluntarily and am ready to do so.

These things, lord Father, I have said so that you may understand that, even if you do not think so, I nevertheless think so of myself. Among my joys, venerable lord, nothing is more joyful to me, nor equally joyful, than your love. For I rejoice in it the more because I am the more certain that it would not fail me in times of need and tribulation. May it please you to write back to me when, at Rheims after the octave of Easter, I may find your reverence and see your long-desired face.

[Col. 1653]

# HENRY, ARCHDEACON OF SALZBURG

## HISTORY OF THE CALAMITIES OF THE CHURCH OF SALZBURG

Preface. 1539

CH. I.—By God’s hidden counsel all evils are tempered. The occasion of the evils arising in the Church of Salzburg was the dreadful schism stirred up by the emperors, from which the Church of Salzburg alone kept itself free and pure. 1540

CH. II.—The death of Archbishop Eberhard and the election of Conrad brought no remedy for the evils of the Church of Salzburg; rather, the emperor’s anger against it was more inflamed and was greatly increased by the appointment of Adalbert. 1541

CH. III.—The siege of the city of Salzburg decreed by Emperor Frederick, and the overthrow of the entire diocese. The resulting incredible fear and anxiety of the people of Salzburg, etc. 1543

CH. IV.—Salzburg was delivered into Frederick’s power through the treachery and perfidy of certain persons. Bishop Adalbert was compelled to abandon his diocese. The loss of temporal goods must be borne bravely, provided spiritual goods remain unimpaired. 1544

CH. V.—On the evils suffered by Ulrich, Patriarch of Aquileia, and Pope Alexander in Frederick’s schism, in comparison with which the afflictions endured by Adalbert, Archbishop of Salzburg, are slight. 1546

CH. VI.—On the pestilence by which Frederick’s invading army was compelled to abandon the siege of the city of Rome. 1547

CH. VII.—How great was the number and dignity of those who died of the plague before the city. The miserable death of Rainald, Archbishop of Cologne, and of other princes of Germany. 1548

CH. VIII.—Frederick’s obstinacy in persecuting Adalbert; the author exhorts Adalbert to trust in God’s help alone. The corruption of morals introduced into the clergy of Salzburg through the schism. 1549

CH. IX.—It is shown how necessary a remedy is for the many vices and crimes that, in Adalbert’s absence, burst forth; to which concubinary and shameless clerics are especially liable. 1551
